title: P versus NP
importance_reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.
focus_reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.
formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
context:
A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.
why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.
status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.
progress: 1971–1973: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation. | 1975–2009: Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions. | 2011: Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). | 2026-09-10: The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

working_summary: P versus NP asks whether every problem with efficiently checkable solutions also has an efficient deterministic decision algorithm. Boolean satisfiability is a representative test case because all NP problems reduce to it. Checking one assignment is easy, while deciding whether any assignment works requires accounting for all possibilities. The target concerns worst-case polynomial time on arbitrarily large inputs. A resolution would establish a fundamental relationship between searching and verifying, without by itself determining practical exponents or average-case difficulty.

title: P versus PSPACE
importance_reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.
focus_reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.
formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form \(Q_{1}x_{1}\cdots Q_{m}x_{m} \varphi (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m})\), where each \(Q_{i}\) is \(\exists\) or \(\forall\), quantified variables are distinct, and \(\varphi\) is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over \(\{0,1\}\). The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\). The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
context:
Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, \(\forall x\exists y (y=x)\) is true because y may depend on x, whereas \(\exists y\forall x (y=x)\) is false. Both variables range over \(\{0,1\}\). A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) because \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\). A proof of \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds \(t(n)\ge n, a\) time-t multitape computation can be simulated in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) for every \(\varepsilon >0\). The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.
why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.
status_note: Primary-source review and a search for subsequent results on 11 September 2026 found no resolution. Williams’ 2025 simulation and August 2026 MFCS survey concern time-space bounds; neither states an equality or separation of P and PSPACE.
progress: 1970s–1981: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time. | 1992: Shamir proves \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\), giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation. | 2025 conference / 2026 journal: Williams proves the \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old \(O(t/\log  t)\) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages. | 2026-08: Williams’ MFCS invited survey discusses this simulation and further space-complexity developments. It supplies no separation of the unions P and PSPACE.
working_summary: Polynomial space permits a computation to reuse its memory while exploring potentially enormous collections of possibilities. The question asks whether every problem solvable with that memory budget is also solvable in polynomial time. Truth of quantified Boolean formulas supplies a concrete complete problem. Alternating existential and universal choices describe strategies that can be much larger than one ordinary certificate. The project tests whether repeated reuse of a modest workspace gives strictly more decision power than any polynomial-time computation.

title: L versus P
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.
focus_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most \(C \log _{2}(n+2)\) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in \(O((n+2)^{c})\) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{P}\) in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
context:
A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about \(\log _{2} n\) bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

\(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\), where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{NL}\) would therefore separate L from P, but \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\) would not itself settle \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\). Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller \(O(\log  n)\) target unresolved.
why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.
status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.
progress: 1975: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question. | 2005–2008: Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems. | 2025–2026: Williams obtains the \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case. | 2026: Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.
working_summary: Logarithmic-space computation can retain only a few input indices and counters while repeatedly rereading the input. The question asks whether that memory always suffices for every polynomial-time decision problem. Evaluating a supplied Boolean circuit is a representative complete task. Shared dependencies make naive recomputation expensive, while storing all intermediate gate values exceeds the space budget. The project tests whether efficient computation fundamentally needs substantial working memory or can always reorganize its information into an extremely small state.

title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) versus \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)
importance_reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.
focus_reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family \(f=(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\})\) in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) such that for every fixed depth \(d\ge 1\), exponent \(k\ge 1\), and constant \(M\ge 1\), there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing \(f_{n}\) exactly has size greater than \(M(n+1)^{k}\)?
definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\), optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than \(m/2\) inputs equal 1. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of all families with such circuits of size \(M(n+1)^{k}\) and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size \(M(n+1)^{k}\), and depth at most \(b \log _{2}(n+1)\), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) or \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}=\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family admit such a family.
context:
The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subseteq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group \(S_{5}\), capture \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under very simple reductions. \(S_{5}\) consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\). Here \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) allows deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The target here concerns an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.
why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.
status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.
progress: 2002: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth. | 2018–2019: Chen and Tell show how improvements in the depth dependence of superlinear wire lower bounds for certain \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-complete problems would yield superpolynomial \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) lower bounds. | 2025-12-09: Dawar and Evans characterize uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open. | 2026: Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) function; the result does not supply an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) separation against every constant depth.
working_summary: TC0 circuits use a constant number of layers of powerful majority gates. NC1 circuits use logarithmically many layers of ordinary bounded-input Boolean gates. The question asks whether the former nonuniform class is strictly weaker than the latter. Many arithmetic tasks already fit in TC0, so their familiar sequential implementations do not provide separating examples. The project seeks a function whose nested logical dependencies cannot be compressed into a fixed-depth network even when each gate can aggregate many inputs at once.

title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
importance_reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.
focus_reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.
formal: For every pair of languages \(A,B\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that f and \(f^{- 1}\) are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string \(x, x\in A\) if and only if \(f(x)\in B\)?
definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(g(x)\in A\). A is NP-complete if \(A\in \mathrm{NP}\) and every \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NP}\) reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an assumption.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an added hypothesis.
context:
NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), but its negation does not automatically imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). To see the first point, suppose \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Then the nontrivial languages {0} and \(0\{0,1\}\)* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) reductions, with nonuniform depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.
why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.
status_note: The 2022 primary-author problem column states that the full conjecture is open. A later-source search on 11 September 2026 located the 2025 recovery-reduction preprint, which still uses it as a conjectural hypothesis, and found no resolution. Its truth-table recovery consequence is conditional.
progress: 1977: Berman–Hartmanis prove isomorphism for paddable complete languages and formulate the unrestricted conjecture. | 1989: Kurtz–Mahaney–Royer present random-oracle counterexamples at STOC; a journal treatment follows in 1995. | 1996: Fenner–Fortnow–Kurtz publish an oracle relative to which the conjecture holds. | 1998: Agrawal–Allender–Rudich prove the nonuniform \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) isomorphism and gap theorems. | 2009: Agrawal–Watanabe give conditional nonuniform structural results involving one-way functions and easy cylinders. | 2022: The Hartmanis open-problems column retains the full conjecture and discusses the remaining cylinder and reduction questions. | 2025: Nareddy and Mishra’s recovery-reduction preprint states the isomorphism conjecture and derives a random-corruption recovery consequence conditional on it.
working_summary: Polynomial-time reductions show that NP-complete problems can simulate each other, but may erase information. The Berman-Hartmanis conjecture asks whether every pair instead admits a polynomial-time computable bijection with a polynomial-time inverse. That bijection must preserve yes and no instances across the entire string space. Padding provides evidence for familiar complete problems without covering all possible complete languages. The project asks whether completeness forces one efficiently reversible organization of instances, reaching beyond ordinary mutual reducibility.

title: Strictness of the polynomial hierarchy
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.
formal: For every integer \(k\ge0\), is \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\)? In other words, must each additional fixed block of polynomially bounded alternating Boolean quantifiers enable a decision language that cannot be expressed with k blocks? The classes are the uniform, unrelativized classes defined below.
definitions: All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\); membership is a total yes/no decision on every finite binary string. Let \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\Pi_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\), where P consists of languages decided by a single deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^d\) transitions on every length-n string, for fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\). Machines have a finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. For fixed \(k\ge1\), a language L belongs to \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\) if there exist integers \(a\ge1,b\ge0\) and one deterministic polynomial-time Boolean predicate R such that for every x, with \(n=|x|\) and \(p(n)=a(n+1)^b\), \(x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\ R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1\). Here \(Q_i\) is existential for odd i and universal for even i. An entire string is chosen in each block; k does not count individual quantified bits. To fix the predicate input, encode a tuple by concatenating \(1^{|s|}0s\) for each of its k+1 components in order. R is computed by one machine in the model above, halting within \(C(M+1)^d\) on all length-M strings for fixed C,d and rejecting malformed tuple encodings. Runtime counts all transitions and all input bits. Restricting the common witness bound to this form of p loses no languages, because a larger polynomial bound can pad each witness and ignore unused bits. The integers, machines and time bounds may depend on L and on the fixed k, but not on x or the quantified strings. Define \(\Pi_k^{\mathrm P}=\{\{0,1\}^*\setminus L:L\in\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\}\) and \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). Thus \(\Sigma_1^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\Pi_1^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{coNP}\). No advice, random bits, quantum operations, external oracle or promise inputs are present. The inclusion between consecutive existential levels always holds; strictness means that there exists a language \(L_k\in\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\setminus\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). This language may depend on k; there is no added requirement of an effective generator for all separating languages.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of strict containment for every nonnegative integer k, or prove that \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}=\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\) for some fixed nonnegative integer k. The negative answer is exactly the logical negation, since the inclusions are unconditional. Equality at one adjacent pair collapses all higher finite levels. A separation of finitely many initial levels, an oracle separation, or a collapse conditional on an unproved hypothesis is insufficient to settle the displayed all-level assertion. No concrete finite input is required as a witness to a class equality or separation.
context:
NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because an additional unused block is harmless. Equality of neighboring levels would make all subsequent levels equal as well, a standard collapse property of bounded alternation. Thus the negative answer asserts a finite level at which the hierarchy stabilizes; it does not require separating or collapsing every level independently.

Strictness includes \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) at its first step, but \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

The quantifier count is fixed separately for each class. It does not describe an algorithm that receives an arbitrary level number and solves all those levels with one common polynomial bound. Similarly, strictness may use a different separating language at every level, and the statement does not impose a uniform procedure generating all such languages.
why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.
status_note: The strictness conjecture is explicit in the checked 2015 survey and 2019 book. The checked 2026 revision supplies conditional collapses and related containments, while the 2015 theorem is relativized. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified unconditional resolution; this review checks statement scope rather than independently certifying every proof.
progress: 1972–1976: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy, and Stockmeyer develops its structure and complete problems. The source survey traces this history and gives the quantified-predicate definition used here. | 1980–1986: Karp–Lipton relates polynomial-size circuits for NP to a collapse of PH; Yao and Håstad establish infinitude in a suitably chosen oracle world. These concern a conditional implication and a relativized separation, respectively. | 2015-04-14: Rossman, Servedio and Tan prove that a random oracle gives an infinite polynomial hierarchy with probability one. Each binary string independently belongs to that oracle with probability one half. | 2019-08-06: Wigderson’s book still states strictness of successive unrelativized levels as a conjecture and distinguishes fixed-depth quantification from unrestricted polynomial-space reasoning. | 2026-03-30: Hirsch and Volkovich’s revised paper compares classes associated with the Linear Ordering Principle and strengthens Karp–Lipton-style conditional conclusions. Its assumptions do not establish an unconditional collapse of PH.
working_summary: The polynomial hierarchy classifies decision languages by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal blocks. Each block chooses polynomially many bits, followed by a uniform polynomial-time check. The question asks whether every added block strictly increases the class of expressible languages. Equality of any neighboring levels would make the entire hierarchy stabilize at a finite level. Known oracle separations and conditional collapses reveal consequences and barriers while leaving this unrelativized conjecture unresolved.

title: NP versus P/poly
importance_reason: A foundational strengthening of P≠NP and the central target of general Boolean circuit lower bounds. Its consequences and methods reach across complexity, derandomization, learning, and cryptography.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist one language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) such that \[\forall C,k,N\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists n\geq N:\quad\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k,\] where \(n\) is an integer, \(L_n\) is the characteristic function of \(L\) on \(n\)-bit strings and \(\operatorname{CC}\) is minimum Boolean circuit size in the model below?
definitions:
A language is a subset \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), including the possible empty string. For each integer \(n\geq0\), its characteristic function \(L_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is 1 exactly on strings in \(L\). An \(n\)-input Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input nodes \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), optional constant nodes 0 and 1, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output node. Gate inputs are edges from earlier nodes in a topological order; two inputs to a gate may be the same node. A node may feed arbitrarily many later gates. There is no depth restriction. Size is the number of AND, OR and NOT gates; input and constant nodes and output designation cost no gates. In particular a constant function has size zero. Every gate is evaluated in the ordinary Boolean way, and the output must equal \(L_n\) on every input, without error. Define \(\operatorname{CC}(L_n)\) as the minimum circuit size; a finite circuit always exists, for example from the truth table.

A circuit family is one circuit \(B_n\) for each length \(n\). It is nonuniform: there need not be a computable procedure mapping \(n\) to \(B_n\). The chosen circuit may depend on the length and on \(L\), but not on the particular input string of that length. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) consists of languages for which there exist integers \(C,k\geq1\) and such a family computing \(L_n\) with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates for every \(n\geq0\). These constants may depend on \(L\), but not on \(n\).

For \(\mathrm{NP}\), require one deterministic multitape Turing-machine verifier \(V\), with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet and no advice or oracle, and integers \(a,b,D,d\geq1\), such that for every binary string \(x\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\{0,1\}^*,\ |y|\leq a(|x|+1)^b:\ V(x,y)=1.\] On every pair of binary strings \((x,y)\), the verifier halts with one output bit within \(D(|x|+|y|+1)^d\) transitions. One explicit pair encoding is \(1^{|x|}0xy\), with the remainder after the indicated \(x\) interpreted as \(y\); malformed encodings are rejected in polynomial time. Each transition costs one step, including all bit arithmetic and input processing. The same verifier and constants work for every input of this one language.

The language \(L\) is chosen before the universal quantifiers over circuit bounds. It cannot change with \(k\), \(C\) or \(N\). Exceeding each bound at arbitrarily large lengths suffices; the conjecture does not demand exceeding it at every sufficiently large length. Conversely, if a polynomial bound holds except at finitely many lengths, enlarging its constant covers those lengths too, so this formulation is exactly noncontainment in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the noncontainment proposition or of its negation \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). A separation must supply one NP language that escapes every polynomial circuit-size bound with the quantifier order stated above. Different languages for different exponents are insufficient. To establish containment, prove that every NP language has a polynomial-size nonuniform family; equivalently, polynomial-size circuits for one NP-complete language such as SAT at all input lengths suffice. No efficient or computable circuit generator is required. Lower bounds for circuits with extra depth or gate restrictions, or for a language only known to lie in a larger class than NP, do not alone settle the target.
context:
Unrolling a polynomial-time computation gives polynomial-size circuits, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). The reverse containment fails: a language whose membership depends only on length can be represented by one constant circuit per length even if the sequence of membership bits is undecidable. Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\) implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); a uniform P versus NP separation alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting shows that most Boolean truth tables need exponentially large circuits. It does not identify one language in NP: choosing a hard truth table independently at each length need not give polynomially verifiable membership. This explains the requirement that one fixed NP language escape every polynomial bound.

By the Karp–Lipton theorem, the opposite outcome \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\) would imply \(\mathrm{PH}=\Sigma_2^{\mathrm P}\), collapsing the polynomial hierarchy to its second level. That consequence is not a known contradiction: strictness of the hierarchy is itself unresolved.

SAT asks whether a finite Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment. Its NP-completeness and closure of polynomial-size circuit computation under polynomial-time reductions make polynomial-size circuits for SAT equivalent to \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). An ordinary explicit formula encoding is sufficient for this equivalence; the main statement uses languages directly and imposes no encoding-dependent exponential lower-bound target.

The natural-proofs barrier is conditional on the strong cryptographic hardness premise in Razborov and Rudich’s theorem. Roughly, a property of \(n\)-variable truth tables cannot simultaneously be recognizable in time polynomial in the \(2^n\)-bit table, hold for a sufficiently large fraction of tables and be useful against polynomial-size circuits under that premise. The running-time scale is the full truth table. This limits a specified class of properties, rather than every mathematical proof.

Williams proves \(\mathrm{NEXP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{ACC}\), where NEXP allows nondeterministic time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), and ACC families have fixed depth and a fixed modulus \(m>1\), with unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and modular-counting gates and NOT gates. A modular gate tests whether the number of 1 inputs is divisible by \(m\). Both the allowed language class and the restricted circuit class differ from this card’s target.

Chen, Tal and Wang’s March 2026 Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a function in \(\mathrm E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) without \(n^{2.5-\varepsilon}\)-size depth-two threshold circuits. Here \(\mathrm E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) means deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) with an NP oracle; a threshold gate tests whether a weighted sum of its Boolean inputs reaches a threshold. The function is not asserted to be in NP, the circuits have depth two and the bound has a fixed polynomial exponent. The paper explicitly retains NP versus P/poly as the broader open target.
why: This is the central unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound question for efficiently verifiable languages. It asks whether NP remains hard even when a separate circuit can be chosen for each input length without an effective construction rule. A separation would strengthen Boolean P versus NP and illuminate the limits of nonuniform computation, with connections to the polynomial hierarchy, pseudorandomness and learning.
status_note: Explicitly posed by Wigderson and retained as the flagship circuit problem in Chen–Tal–Wang’s March 2026 introduction. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no unconditional resolution of NP versus unrestricted polynomial-size circuits. The checked ACC, threshold and natural-proofs results have different language classes, circuit restrictions or hypotheses; this review does not independently verify every cited proof.

It constrains the specified properties, not all proofs of circuit lower bounds. | 2011–2014: Williams proves that NEXP has no polynomial-size nonuniform ACC family, first at CCC 2011 and then in JACM 2014. It explicitly names NP versus P/poly as the broader open problem.

working_summary: A nonuniform Boolean circuit family may choose a completely different circuit for each input length without any computable construction rule. The question asks whether one fixed language in NP nevertheless exceeds every polynomial bound on the number of Boolean gates. The card specifies the verifier model, exact circuit evaluation and the required arbitrarily large violating lengths. Counting arguments produce hard truth tables but do not by themselves supply the required polynomially verifiable language. Karp–Lipton, natural proofs and newer restricted-circuit lower bounds explain the surrounding landscape while leaving the full NP versus P/poly target unresolved.

title: NP versus coNP
importance_reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.
formal:
Do there exist a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and constants \(C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every explicitly encoded Boolean CNF formula \(F\),
\[F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\ |\pi|\le C(|F|+1)^k\ \text{ and }\ V(F,\pi)=1?\]
In addition, require soundness on certificates of every length: \(V(F,\pi)=0\) for every satisfiable \(F\) and every binary string \(\pi\). Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\)? All constants and the verifier are fixed independently of the formula.
question_excerpt: The sources ask whether NP differs from coNP and identify equality with the existence of a polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable propositional proof system.
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes a value in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation; a clause is a disjunction of literals; a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the variables occurring in the formula makes every clause true. The empty clause is false and the conjunction of no clauses is true. Unsatisfiability means that every assignment fails.

Use an explicit binary list of clauses and their signed, binary-encoded variable identifiers, with self-delimiting lengths. The size \(N=|F|\) counts every occurrence, identifier and delimiter. Identifiers may be large integers; assignments need specify only the distinct variables actually occurring, whose number is at most \(N\). There is no circuit, compressed formula or oracle representation of an exponentially large list of clauses. Any fixed efficiently interconvertible explicit encoding gives the same target. Malformed encodings are rejected.

A certificate \(\pi\) is an arbitrary finite binary string, not a derivation in a preselected proof calculus. The verifier is a fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine program with ordinary bit operations and finite-alphabet tapes. There are constants \(D,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), independent of both inputs, such that it halts on every pair in at most \(D(N+|\pi|+1)^d\) steps. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, interaction or uncharged primitive solving another problem. Soundness forbids every accepted certificate for a satisfiable formula, including certificates longer than the proposed short-proof bound. Completeness requires at least one short accepted certificate for each unsatisfiable formula; neither uniqueness nor an efficient algorithm to find it is required. One can reject overlong certificates without changing the existence question.

For a language \(A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\) means that \(x\in A\) exactly when some certificate of length polynomial in \(|x|\) is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class \(\mathrm{coNP}\) consists of complements, within \(\{0,1\}^{*}\), of NP languages. The language of valid unsatisfiable CNF encodings is coNP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: a reduction computes one instance whose yes/no answer is preserved. Consequently its membership in NP is equivalent to the displayed class equality. The family of all possible short certificates may be exponentially large; polynomial verification time is measured on one supplied certificate.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\) or of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), with the stated machine, encoding and resource definitions. For the certificate formulation, an affirmative answer must supply \(V,C,k,D,d\) and prove total polynomial-time verification, soundness for every formula and certificate, and short-certificate completeness for every unsatisfiable formula. A negative answer must show that for every sound polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and every \(C,k\ge1\), there is an unsatisfiable formula \(F\) for which all certificates of length at most \(C(|F|+1)^k\) are rejected. The verifier in this universal statement need not already be a complete proof system. A formulation through complexity classes must also justify the equivalence to the concrete target. Lower bounds for one proof calculus, a fixed polynomial bound, or a chosen verifier do not establish the universal negative statement. Efficient proof search is not required for an affirmative answer. This is an exact yes/no question, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.
why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.
status_note: Source-open. The Cook–Reckhow characterization and the March 2018 book’s Conjecture 3.8, Definitions 6.3–6.4 and Theorem 6.5 support the exact target; Theorems 6.9 and 6.11 support the restricted-system comparison. The August 2026 ICTS program still presents NP/coNP separation as the aim of this research program. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This review checks definitions, quantifiers, the original characterization argument and cited theorem scopes; it does not independently verify every proof in the proof-complexity literature.
progress: 1979: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\) and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target. | 1985–1987: Haken proves an exponential resolution lower bound for pigeonhole formulas; Buss gives polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system. | 2026-08: The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

working_summary: NP asks for short efficiently checkable evidence that an input is a yes instance. coNP describes the corresponding evidence for no instances of NP problems. The concrete target asks whether every unsatisfiable CNF formula has a polynomial-length certificate accepted by one fixed sound verifier. The verifier may use any proof format, and the question does not require efficiently finding a certificate. Separating the classes requires excluding all such verifiers, beyond lower bounds for individual proof systems.

title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
importance_reason: A fundamental lower-bound milestone for unrestricted computation, with connections to matrix complexity, proof techniques and the limitations of nonuniform algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist one total, length-preserving, deterministic polynomial-time function
\[F:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad |F(x)|=|x|,\]
whose unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not linear? Precisely, writing \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n}\) for its restriction to inputs of length \(n\), the requested lower bound is
\[\forall C>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{CC}(F_n)>Cn.\]
Here \(C\) is real and \(N,n\) are integers. Preserve the card's polynomial-time meaning of “explicit” and its allowance of \(n\) output bits. The lower bound need only exceed every fixed linear bound at arbitrarily large lengths.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 5.8 asks for an explicit n-input, n-output function whose Boolean circuit size is not O(n). This card retains its previously selected polynomial-time interpretation of explicitness and writes out the negation of a linear bound.
definitions:
A binary string is a finite sequence of bits; \(\{0,1\}^{*}\) contains all such strings, including the empty string. Length preservation requires exactly \(n\) output bits on an \(n\)-bit input, and the empty output on the empty input. Polynomial-time computation means that a single deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no advice or oracle, outputs \(F(x)\) and halts on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps, for fixed constants \(a\ge1\) and integer \(d\ge1\). Writing the output counts toward the running time.

For each fixed \(n\), a competing circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(n\) input wires, optional free constants 0 and 1, gates computing arbitrary Boolean functions of at most two input bits, and an ordered list of \(n\) output wires. This is the full \(B_2\) basis: all two-input truth tables are allowed, including AND, OR, XOR and functions that ignore an input; unary NOT is also allowed. Each gate contributes one unit of size. Inputs, constants and output designations contribute zero. A wire may feed arbitrarily many gates or output positions, and intermediate gates may be shared by several outputs. Depth is unrestricted. An output may be an input wire, a constant or a gate output.

The circuit computes \(F_n\) exactly if its ordered output vector equals \(F_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). The number \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)\) is the minimum gate count of any such circuit. Competing circuits are nonuniform: the choice at each length is independent, and no algorithm is required to construct their descriptions. In contrast, the polynomial-time algorithm for \(F\) must work uniformly at all lengths. This distinction is part of the target.

The statement \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)=O(n)\) means that there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(N\ge1\) such that \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)\le Cn\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The displayed target is its exact negation. It does not require \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)/n\) to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. The function, its program and its running-time polynomial are chosen before all the lower-bound quantifiers.

The source uses AND, OR and NOT gates and leaves “explicit” broad. Every full-basis gate has a constant-size AND/OR/NOT implementation, and those gates are already allowed in \(B_2\). Thus changing between these two fixed bases changes minimum size by at most a constant factor and preserves the not-\(O(n)\) target. The polynomial-time explicitness convention is the previously recorded specialization of the source; it is not claimed to be equivalent to every possible meaning of “explicit.” No linearity or other algebraic restriction is imposed on \(F\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence claim. A positive answer must specify one total length-preserving function, prove that one uniform deterministic algorithm computes it in polynomial time, and prove the displayed lower bound against every circuit in the full model. A negative answer must show that every such polynomial-time function has \(O(n)\)-size nonuniform circuits, allowing the constant and starting length to depend on the function. A fixed constant-factor lower bound does not establish the target. Nor does a lower bound only for formulas, monotone circuits, XOR-only circuits or a fixed depth bound without a proof extending it to unrestricted circuits. The claim is unconditional, and an oracle-relative or conditional separation alone does not settle it. All complexity and quantifier requirements are exact; no numerical acceptance tolerance applies.
context:
A circuit may reuse any intermediate result and share it among different outputs. Those permissions make it stronger than a formula, whose computation is organized as a tree. The question retains all this circuit power and asks for an efficiently computable function that cannot be implemented with a fixed number of gates per input bit.

Counting proves that most Boolean truth tables require exponentially many gates. It does not supply a function computable by one polynomial-time algorithm, so it does not satisfy this card’s explicitness requirement. The challenge is obtaining a size lower bound for a computationally accessible function.

Linear maps over \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\), with addition modulo two, form a significant special case. An efficiently constructible binary matrix \(A_n\) defines \(F_n(x)=A_nx\). Counting gives matrices needing \(\Omega(n^2/\log n)\) gates, but the 2026 source still identifies a superlinear lower bound for explicit matrices as open. A lower bound for circuits using only XOR gates would not automatically apply to circuits with arbitrary Boolean gates.

The desired function already has polynomial-size circuits because its uniform polynomial-time computation can be simulated by circuits. The question therefore separates linear size from polynomial size within efficient computation. Such a lower bound alone is not a proof that \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Conversely, a hard NP language need not be polynomial-time computable and so need not meet this card’s explicitness condition.

Li and Yang prove a \(3.1n-o(n)\) lower bound for suitable affine dispersers in the full two-input Boolean basis. An affine disperser is nonconstant on every affine subspace above its specified dimension threshold; suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. This is a substantial improvement of the known linear constant, while every fixed constant remains compatible with \(O(n)\) circuits.

The 2025 covering paper relates circuit lower bounds to combinatorial cover complexity and proves bounds for random graphs. Its results do not exhibit a polynomial-time function with the superlinear unrestricted circuit lower bound requested here.

The February 2026 gate-elimination preprint gives formal simplification results for selected bases and an efficiently checkable form of a classical linear parity lower bound. Its additional proof structure does not supply a superlinear unrestricted bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision proves conditional barriers for matrix natural proofs: proofs identifying a sufficiently large set of hard matrices recognizable in time polynomial in the matrix description. Under the cryptographic assumptions stated in that paper, pseudorandom matrices with small circuits obstruct this defined proof class. The near-linear and linear circuit-size barriers rely on different assumptions; neither rules out all possible proofs of this card’s target.
why: A superlinear lower bound would establish a basic limitation on unrestricted nonuniform computation for an efficiently computable function. It would surpass every fixed linear gate count, even when a circuit can reuse work freely across outputs, and expose structure that simple counting does not identify.
status_note: Source-open with bounded later-work checking through 16 September 2026. The 2018 source formulation, Li–Yang Theorem 1.1 and basis, the 2025 cover-work introduction, the February 2026 gate-simplification abstract/introduction, and the July 2026 matrix-natural-proofs revision including Corollary 1’s proof and Corollaries 3–4 were read. These later works do not supply the requested superlinear unrestricted bound. No matching unconditional resolution was located; this does not independently verify every cited theorem or exhaust the literature. The polynomial-time specialization predates this review and remains explicitly distinguished from the source’s broader wording.

working_summary: The question asks for a polynomial-time computable function with as many output bits as input bits that needs more than linear circuit size. Competing circuits may use every two-input Boolean operation and share intermediate work without depth or fan-out restrictions. The lower-bound ratio must be unbounded at arbitrarily large input lengths, not necessarily tend to infinity at every length. Known explicit full-basis lower bounds improve fixed linear constants, and recent conditional barriers apply only to specified proof classes. A complete answer must prove or refute the existence of one uniformly computable function satisfying the entire claim.

title: Exponential circuit lower bounds for 3-SAT
importance_reason: A sweeping quantitative lower-bound target for the canonical efficiently verifiable problem, directly connected to nonuniform complexity and the foundations of exponential-time algorithms.
formal:
For the explicitly encoded \(n\)-variable 3-SAT function \(\mathrm{SAT}_n\) below, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[\forall n\ge n_0,\qquad \operatorname{CC}(\mathrm{SAT}_n)\ge 2^{cn}?\]
The circuit lower bound is against arbitrary nonuniform Boolean circuits of fan-in at most two. Its exponential parameter is the number \(n\) of variables, not the number of input bits in the clause-incidence encoding. The card retains this previously recorded variable-parameter specialization of the source’s exponential-SAT conjecture.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 5.7 proposes an exponential circuit lower bound for SAT. The card’s existing editorial version fixes 3-CNF, a total clause-incidence representation and the number of variables as the exponential parameter, instead of treating the source’s informal size notation as a complete encoding specification.
definitions:
Fix an integer \(n\ge1\) and variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A clause is a disjunction of zero, one, two or three literals on distinct variables. Each literal is either \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). The empty clause is false. Clauses never contain both signs of one variable or repeated variables. The list contains
\[M(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{3}2^{j}\binom{n}{j}\]
clauses, with \(\binom{n}{j}=0\) when \(j>n\). Order them first by their length, then lexicographically by their increasing tuple of variable indices, then lexicographically by their sign bits, with 0 meaning positive and 1 negated.

An input is a bit vector \(b\in\{0,1\}^{M(n)}\). Its \(i\)-th bit specifies whether clause \(i\) is included. Let \(\Phi_b\) be the conjunction of exactly those included clauses; the empty conjunction is true. Define
\[\mathrm{SAT}_n(b)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists a\in\{0,1\}^{n}\text{ satisfying }\Phi_b.\]
Every input vector is valid. Formulas are specified in full, not by a circuit or oracle that answers clause queries. All assignments are permitted; there is no uniqueness, sparsity or satisfiability promise. This representation includes clauses of width at most three. In ordinary lists, repeated literals can be removed, tautological clauses discarded and duplicate clauses merged without changing satisfiability.

A competing circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(M(n)\) input bits and one designated output. Each gate computes any Boolean function of at most two bits, the full \(B_2\) basis. Free constant sources 0 and 1 are allowed. Gates may have arbitrary fan-out and the depth is unrestricted. The gate count charges one per gate, including a unary gate, while input nodes, constants, wires and the output designation are free. The circuit must compute \(\mathrm{SAT}_n\) exactly on every \(b\). Its minimum possible number of gates is \(\operatorname{CC}(\mathrm{SAT}_n)\). A different circuit may be chosen independently for every \(n\), with no algorithm required to generate that family.

The circuit has \(M(n)=\Theta(n^3)\) inputs, so the conjectured size is \(2^{\Omega(n)}=2^{\Omega(M(n)^{1/3})}\). A claim exponential in the raw input length would be a different target and is not asserted. Switching between \(B_2\) and the bounded-fan-in AND/OR/NOT basis changes size by at most a fixed constant factor, preserving the existence of a positive exponential lower-bound exponent after adjusting constants.

The quantifiers are almost everywhere in the variable count: one positive exponent \(c\) must work at every sufficiently large \(n\). Their exact negation is
\[\forall c>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{CC}(\mathrm{SAT}_n)<2^{cn}.\]
The integers \(n_0,N,n\) and real \(c\) have the domains just stated. A size bound \(2^{o(n)}\) at all lengths would imply the negative answer, but is stronger than this negation, which permits different favorable lengths for different exponents.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed eventual exponential circuit lower bound for the exact total function family defined here. A positive answer must establish one fixed \(c>0\) and threshold \(n_0\), and prove the lower bound against every correct circuit at every \(n\ge n_0\). A negative answer must establish the quantified negation stated above. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded depth, uniform algorithms or restricted proof systems do not meet the criterion. A uniform exponential-time upper bound with a fixed positive exponent remains compatible with a smaller positive lower-bound exponent. Neither a conditional theorem nor an oracle-relative theorem alone resolves this unconditional target. Asymptotic quantifiers are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance is not applied to exponents or big-O notation.
context:
Checking a proposed assignment is efficient. The conjecture says that determining whether an assignment exists needs exponentially many gates in the variable count, even when each input length gets its own independently designed circuit. It is a quantitative lower-bound demand beyond merely excluding polynomial-size circuits.

The fixed input representation separates two quantities that are often both called size. There are \(n\) variables, but \(\Theta(n^3)\) possible distinct clauses and therefore that many incidence bits. Polynomially equivalent encodings need not preserve claims exponential in their raw bit length; fixing both quantities is essential.

Exhaustive assignment testing gives the unconditional upper bound \(O(M(n)2^n)\) on circuit size. Thus the conjecture concerns the presence of some positive exponential lower exponent, while allowing improvements in its constant.

The sparsification lemma writes a fixed-width CNF as a disjunction of at most \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) sparse formulas for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with linear clause bounds depending on \(\varepsilon\) and the width. This supports reductions in exponential-time complexity. It does not convert a lower bound for uniform algorithms into one against arbitrary nonuniform circuits.

Li and Yang prove a \(3.1N-o(N)\) gate lower bound for suitable explicit \(N\)-input affine dispersers. It is a full-basis linear lower bound for particular functions, not an exponential bound for SAT. Counting yields much larger bounds for most truth tables but does not identify SAT among them.

Williams’s lower bound excludes polynomial-size ACC circuits for a language in nondeterministic exponential time. ACC imposes constant depth, unlike this card’s circuits, and the hard language is not asserted to be SAT. Both distinctions prevent that theorem from resolving this question.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports an \(O^{*}(1.307031578^n)\) randomized running-time bound for general 3-SAT, with a slightly smaller base for unique 3-SAT; \(O^{*}\) suppresses polynomial factors. The reported improvement remains within exponential time. It is an upper-bound claim in a preprint, not an unconditional lower bound for exact circuits.

A positive answer would imply \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm P/\mathrm{poly}\) and hence \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). A negative answer need not imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\): circuit sizes such as \(2^{\sqrt n}\) would already defeat every positive eventual exponential lower exponent while remaining superpolynomial, and nonuniform circuits need not yield an efficient uniform algorithm.
why: An exponential unrestricted circuit lower bound for 3-SAT would establish a quantitative limit on even nonuniform solutions to a canonical NP-complete problem. Fixing the variable parameter makes its relationship to exponential-time hypotheses precise without assuming that algorithmic and circuit lower bounds are interchangeable.
status_note: Source-open with a bounded literature check through 16 September 2026. The original SAT circuit conjecture and the card’s previously documented variable-parameter specialization were checked. The sparsification theorem, Li–Yang main statement, Williams’s restricted ACC theorem and the 2026 PPSZ preprint’s unique/general statements were read; none gives a resolution of the defined total 3-SAT circuit target. No matching unconditional exponential lower bound or refutation was located. The PPSZ numerical certificate was not independently rerun, and the preprint is identified as such; no exhaustive present-status certification is claimed.
