working_summary: The question asks whether n-variable 3-SAT requires Boolean circuits of size at least two to a positive constant times n at every sufficiently large n. Inputs are complete incidence vectors for all clauses of width at most three, giving Theta(n cubed) input bits. The circuit model permits every two-input Boolean gate, arbitrary sharing and independent nonuniform designs at each length. Known restricted-circuit lower bounds and randomized exponential-time improvements do not settle this unrestricted lower-bound target. A complete answer must prove the eventual exponential bound or its exact quantified negation in Lean.

title: PH versus PSPACE
importance_reason: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? Equivalently, is there a fixed integer \(k\ge 0\) such that the truth problem for fully quantified Boolean formulas belongs to \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\)?
definitions: Languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*. PSPACE contains the languages decided by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input of length n while using at most \(C(n+1)^{a}\) work-tape cells, for constants C,a depending on the machine. The read-only input tape is not charged, and there is no polynomial time limit. Set \(\Sigma ^{p}_{0}=\mathrm{P}\), the deterministic polynomial-time languages. For \(k\ge 1, a\) language L lies in \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R and a polynomial p such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when \(\exists y_{1}\forall y_{2}\exists y_{3}\cdots Q_{k} y_{k} R(x,y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k})=1\), where each \(y_{i}\) ranges over \(\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) and \(Q_{k}\) is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Set \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup _{k\ge 0}\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\). The integer k is fixed for an entire language; it cannot grow with an input. Machines and predicates are uniform and have no advice or oracle. A fully quantified Boolean formula is an explicit Boolean formula using AND, OR and NOT, preceded by quantifiers binding every variable exactly once; variable names and the entire formula are binary encoded. Its truth uses the ordinary successive quantifier semantics over \(\{0,1\}\). The language TQBF consists of its true well-formed encodings; malformed strings are rejected. The number of quantifier blocks in TQBF inputs is unrestricted.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq \mathrm{PH}\); the reverse inclusion is already known. Equivalently it places TQBF in one fixed \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\), which would put every PSPACE language in that same level by polynomial-time reductions. A negative resolution proves that some PSPACE language, equivalently TQBF, is outside every fixed level. A separation at one fixed level or an oracle-relative result alone does not answer the question.
context:
Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

The formula \(\forall x\exists y (x=y)\) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula \(\exists y\forall x (x=y)\) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\) and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation \(\mathrm{PH}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.
why: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
status_note: No established resolution found in the primary-source search through 11 September 2026. The checked 2026 results concern completeness and relativized class relationships. Historical preprint claims of equality or non-collapse are not counted as settled theorems; their proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2007: The cited textbook draft states TQBF completeness, \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) and the collapse consequence of equality. | 2026-02: New multilevel optimization completeness theorems preserve the bounded-level versus PSPACE classification without separating the classes. | 2026-02: A sparse-oracle construction separates PH from PSPACE while allowing PH to collapse; the result is explicitly relativized.
working_summary: Does every polynomial-space decision problem lie in the polynomial hierarchy? PH allows a fixed number of alternating quantifier blocks for each language. PSPACE also describes polynomial-time alternation with no fixed bound on the number of alternations. Equality would put TQBF in one finite level and hence collapse PH to that level. Completeness and oracle results illuminate the distinction without settling the ordinary class equality.

title: NEXP versus nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)
importance_reason: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
formal: Is there a language \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NEXP}\) such that, for every fixed circuit depth \(d\ge 1\), every fixed exponent \(k\ge 1\), every constant \(C\ge 1\) and every \(N\ge 1\), some \(n\ge N\) has no depth-at-most-d Boolean circuit of size at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) with AND, OR, NOT and majority gates that computes L correctly on every n-bit input? Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subset \mathrm{TC}^{0}\) for nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)?
definitions: \(\mathrm{NEXP}=\bigcup _{a\ge 1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{n^{a}}): a\) language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time \(2^{n^{a}}\), up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least \(\lceil m/2\rceil\) of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq \mathrm{TC}^{0}\). A bound ruling out only \(n^{k}\) gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.
context:
A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\), exponential time with an NP oracle. Their \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\).
why: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
status_note: No \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subset \mathrm{TC}^{0}\) resolution found through 11 September 2026. The checked March, July and September results retain different hard-language models or fixed depth and polynomial quantitative bounds. The September preprint has a source comment raising concerns and is recorded as an unverified claim.
progress: 2011: Williams separates nondeterministic exponential time from polynomial-size ACC circuits, a subclass of \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). | 2026-03: Chen–Tal–Wang prove \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) gate lower bounds for depth-two threshold circuits and a hard function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\). | 2026-07: Ren–Williams prove near-maximum unrestricted bounds for a class with a promise-MA oracle and advice. | 2026-09: Near-cubic depth-two wire bounds are claimed in a preprint with a critical source comment; this is not a \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) separation.
working_summary: Does some NEXP language escape all polynomial-size constant-depth majority circuits? Majority gates make this circuit class substantially more powerful than constant-depth \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) circuits. Williams established the corresponding separation for ACC circuits with fixed-modulus gates. Recent threshold-circuit bounds still restrict depth or polynomial size and use different hard-language classes. The target requires one ordinary NEXP language outside the entire nonuniform class \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\).

title: Minimum Circuit Size Problem
importance_reason: A central longstanding metacomplexity problem, with independent roles in circuit lower bounds, learning, proof complexity and cryptography. Standard NP-hardness remains separate from major successes for nearby minimization variants and from conditional reductions.
formal:
Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP), with a complete truth table as input, NP-complete under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time function \(g\) such that
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad x\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g(x)\in\mathrm{MCSP}?\]
Use the exact circuit model and language below. The target is unconditional and unrelativized. A reduction may not use random bits, advice, an oracle, a gap promise, a partial truth table or an implicitly represented truth table.
question_excerpt: The primary source asks whether ordinary MCSP is NP-hard and separately whether it may be in BPP. The two previously consolidated sources also explicitly ask about NP-hardness. This card takes their common NP-hardness question as its single target and fixes deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions.
definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an \(n\)-input Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), optional constant sources 0 and 1, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one designated output wire. Wires may feed arbitrarily many gates. An input, a constant or a gate may be the output. The size is the total number of AND, OR and NOT gates; input and constant sources, wires and the output designation are not charged. In particular, NOT gates count. Write \(\operatorname{CC}(f)\) for the minimum such size computing \(f\) on every input. This fixes the total-gate convention, corresponding to the source's \(R\) size measure. It is not the measure that counts only binary gates, nor the basis of all two-input Boolean functions.

The truth table \(t\in\{0,1\}^{N}\), where \(N=2^n\), lists the values of a total function \(f_t:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) in lexicographic input order. A well-formed instance is \((t,s)\), with integer \(0\le s\le N\) written in binary. It is a yes-instance exactly when \(\operatorname{CC}(f_t)\le s\). To fix a binary language, encode a pair as \(1^{|t|}0t\operatorname{bin}(s)\), with no leading zeros in \(\operatorname{bin}(s)\), except that zero is encoded as the single bit 0. Strings failing this syntax, the power-of-two length requirement, \(n\ge1\), or the threshold bound are no-instances. The input length is \(2N+1+O(\log(N+1))\), so polynomial time is measured in the full truth-table length, not merely in the number \(n\) of variables. The redundant unary length prefix is only a fixed efficiently decodable pair encoding.

Constants have been made explicit to remove a convention left implicit in the source. For a nonconstant function, constant inputs can be eliminated gate by gate without increasing size, so allowing them does not change its optimum. For the two constant functions the answer follows directly from the specified convention. No claim that all Boolean bases preserve exact optimum sizes is needed.

A deterministic polynomial-time function is computed by one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts on every input of length \(m\) within \(C(m+1)^d\) steps, for some constants \(C,d\). It has no advice or oracle. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(L\) to \(K\) is such a function \(g\) satisfying \(x\in L\) if and only if \(g(x)\in K\) for every binary string \(x\). Its output is one ordinary instance, whose entire description is written within that time bound. SAT is satisfiability of finite Boolean formulas over AND, OR and NOT in a fixed explicit binary syntax; malformed formulas are no-instances. Any two usual efficiently interconvertible formula encodings give the same reduction question.

NP consists of languages for which a yes-instance has a certificate of polynomial length that a uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine verifies, with no certificate accepted on a no-instance. A language is NP-hard here if every language in NP reduces to it by the specified many-one reductions, and NP-complete if it is also in NP. MCSP is in NP: a circuit with at most \(s\le N\) gates has an explicit topologically ordered description of \(O(N\log(N+1))\) bits, and evaluating it on all \(N\) assignments checks the entire table in polynomial time. Thus the displayed SAT reduction suffices, by SAT's NP-completeness, and its nonexistence would refute NP-completeness under this reduction convention.

For context only, P denotes uniform deterministic polynomial time and BPP uniform randomized polynomial time with worst-case polynomial running time and error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The source also asks whether MCSP might lie in BPP. That is a separate proposition, not the logical negation of NP-hardness: the two possibilities are not an unconditional exhaustive or disjoint classification.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the displayed SAT-to-MCSP reduction. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic reduction, prove its polynomial running time and output length, and prove the yes/no equivalence for every input using the exact total truth-table and gate-count conventions above. A negative answer must prove that every deterministic polynomial-time candidate reduction fails on some input. A conditional theorem, an oracle-relative theorem, hardness under randomized or quasipolynomial-time reductions, a lower bound for a restricted proof system, or hardness of a partial, implicit or gap variant does not alone meet this criterion. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this exact language-reduction statement.
context:
MCSP asks whether a fully specified Boolean function has a short circuit. Finding a short representation is an optimization task; this decision version asks whether a proposed size threshold can be met. Its input already contains every function value, which makes checking a proposed circuit efficient.

The main target is the NP-hardness question shared by the three source passages consolidated into this card with user approval on 12 September 2026. The original primary passage also raises membership in BPP. That broader classification is retained here as context rather than being silently identified with the negation of NP-hardness.

The circuit basis matters for exact minimization. The 2026 source treats both counting all gates and counting only binary gates; this card explicitly uses its total-gate convention. The source continues to identify ordinary MCSP hardness as open and distinguishes it from successful hardness results for partial specifications.

Austrin and Risse establish strong lower bounds for sum-of-squares refutations of formulas asserting that a small circuit exists. Sum-of-squares is a particular algebraic proof system. Its limitations give information about a restricted method of certifying circuit lower bounds, without proving that every efficient algorithm for ordinary MCSP fails.

Hirahara and Ilango obtain deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness, including constant-factor approximation, under three assumptions together: subexponentially secure noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs for SAT, almost-everywhere subexponential nondeterministic circuit lower bounds for coNP, and almost-everywhere near-maximum circuit lower bounds for \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here nonadaptive means that a reduction prepares all oracle questions before receiving answers. Both its assumptions and its longer running time distinguish this result from the target.

The June 2026 ECCC manuscript studies an implicit version whose function is represented by a circuit sampling labeled examples, rather than by the full table. Its randomized gap-hardness result assumes subexponential versions of indistinguishability obfuscation and the nonexistence of an optimal propositional proof system. This is further progress on a related representation, not an unconditional many-one reduction to the language defined here.
why: MCSP asks how hard it is to recognize computational simplicity from complete data. Its classification connects NP-completeness with circuit lower bounds, learning and cryptography. A proof or refutation of standard NP-hardness would settle a central question about whether circuit minimization has the same reduction-based difficulty as general NP search.

The 2023 primary formulation and gate-model passages, CCC 2023 Theorems 1 and 3/Proposition 2, FOCS 2025 Theorems I.1 and V.7, and the June 2026 ECCC abstract/introduction were checked. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no unconditional deterministic polynomial-time many-one hardness proof or refutation for ordinary MCSP. The 2025 conditional quasipolynomial theorem and 2026 implicit-input preprint do not meet this target. This is a scoped literature check, not independent verification of all cited proofs or exhaustive certification of present openness.

The card fixes AND, OR and NOT gates, counts all gates, and measures input length by the full truth table. title: NL versus UL
importance_reason: A basic class equality tying directed reachability, isolation, pseudorandomness and the structure of low-memory witnesses.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist one nondeterministic Turing machine \(M\) and constants \(C,D,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, on every explicitly encoded directed-reachability input \(x=(G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), every computation branch halts within \(D(N+2)^k\) steps and visits at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells, and
\[\#\{\text{accepting computation branches of }M(x)\}=
\begin{cases}1,&t\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }G,\\0,&\text{otherwise}?\end{cases}\]
The constants and machine are independent of the input. Unreachable and malformed inputs must have no accepting branch.
question_excerpt: The inherited paper asks whether every nondeterministic logarithmic-space language can be recognized unambiguously, with only one accepting computation on each yes input.
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Use a self-delimiting explicit binary list of all vertices and all directed edges, together with \(s,t\in[n]\). In particular, isolated vertices are represented and \(N\ge n\); a binary vertex count is not a succinct description of an exponentially large graph. Edges are ordered pairs of vertices. Self-loops are allowed, and repeated edge entries may be interpreted as the same edge. A directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) follows the listed edge directions, and the length-zero path is allowed when \(s=t\). No planarity, acyclicity, bounded-degree or unique-path promise is present. Invalid list structure or out-of-range vertices make the encoding malformed. Validity is deterministically checkable in logarithmic space, by rescanning the input if needed. Explicit adjacency lists, edge lists and adjacency matrices are interchangeable here through deterministic logarithmic-space reductions of polynomial output length.

The machine has a finite description with a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over finite alphabets. Heads use ordinary Turing-machine moves. The space bound counts all distinct work-tape cells visited on a branch, including blank cells crossed, counters and every temporary record. Input cells and finite control do not count. The output is acceptance or rejection. No advice, randomness, oracle, writable input, catalytic tape or other uncharged storage is available. Every branch, including a rejecting branch, obeys the same polynomial clock and logarithmic-space bounds.

A computation branch is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to halting. Two sequences that merge into the same configuration still count as distinct branches. The condition counts successful computations, not distinct accepting configurations, output values, graph paths or certificates after identifying equivalent strings. Rejecting branches need not be unique. The machine is not required to output the graph path or to behave deterministically.

For languages of binary strings, \(\mathrm{NL}\) is acceptance by nondeterministic machines under these time and space bounds, allowing any positive number of accepting branches on a yes input and none on a no input. The subclass \(\mathrm{UL}\) requires at most one accepting branch on every input, hence exactly one on a yes input. A polynomial all-branch clock is the usual equivalent convention for logarithmic-space acceptance. The class equality quantifies separately over languages and machines: every language in NL must have some UL machine. It does not additionally require an effective compiler mapping descriptions of arbitrary NL machines to UL machines.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such reductions preserve the answer and can be composed with a UL machine by deterministically recomputing required output bits; this does not add accepting branches. Its membership in UL therefore implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\); the reverse inclusion follows from the definitions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) for the specified uniform model. An affirmative reachability construction must supply one machine and fixed constants and establish its exact accepting-branch count, correctness on all inputs, and every-branch time and space bounds. A negative answer must prove that some NL language is outside UL, equivalently exclude every proposed reachability machine with these guarantees; the class/reachability equivalence must be justified if used. The graph itself may have arbitrarily many paths, so a promise of a unique graph path cannot replace the required algorithmic unambiguity. A larger-space simulation, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, an oracle, an unproved hardness assumption or a lower bound only for a restricted isolation procedure does not settle the exact question. No approximate branch count or resource estimate is accepted.
context:
A nondeterministic computation may have many successful branches. Unambiguity permits extensive guessing and arbitrarily many rejecting branches, but requires only one successful branch on each yes input. The restriction is on computations of the algorithm, not on the number of paths that happen to exist in the input graph.

The inclusions \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) explain the stakes. An equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) would not by itself remove nondeterminism. A separation would also imply \(\mathrm{L}\ne\mathrm{NL}\). Requiring every reachable machine configuration to have a unique path from the start is a stronger condition, called reach unambiguity, and is not imposed here.

Reinhardt and Allender’s theorem connects unambiguous reachability with min-isolation: positive integer edge weights are min-isolating when every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. With polynomially bounded weights that are available in deterministic logarithmic space, this condition supports logarithmic-space unambiguous reachability. Existence of suitable weights alone does not guarantee that a uniform small-space machine can obtain them.

Their nonuniform result is \(\mathrm{NL}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{UL}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here an advice string of polynomial length may depend on the input length and be shared by all inputs of that length, with no efficient procedure required to generate it. Ordinary UL has no such advice.

Van Melkebeek and Prakriya prove that every NL language has an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation using \(O((\log N)^{3/2})\) workspace. This is an unconditional simulation for all inputs, but the extra square-root-of-logarithm factor is unbounded and prevents this theorem from establishing membership in UL.

The 2025 hardness-based result concerns the scaled-up inclusion \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\mathrm{USPACE}[O(n)]\): these classes use linear nondeterministic and unambiguous workspace. Its hypothesis is a circuit lower bound with specified uniformity and unambiguous-space oracle access. The 2026 survey’s Theorems 3.12 and 3.13 distinguish an older conditional logspace equality from the refined conditional linear-space theorem. Neither is an unconditional resolution.

The February 2026 catalytic result permits \(O((\log N)^2)\) additional writable bits initially containing arbitrary data, whose contents must be restored, as well as a UL oracle. It keeps ordinary workspace logarithmic and time polynomial. Both the extra restorable tape and the oracle are absent from the machine model in this card.

Hoza’s July 2026 theorem concerns a single weight function chosen without inspecting which edges are present. If it must min-isolate every layered graph of width \(w\ge2\) and length \(\ell\ge2\), the maximum weight must be at least \(2^{\Omega(\log w\log\ell)}\). Layered means there are \(\ell+1\) successive layers of \(w\) vertices each, with edges only to the next layer. This excludes polynomially bounded universal weights in the general regime, but does not exclude graph-dependent weights or arbitrary unambiguous algorithms.

The August 2026 MFCS paper gives unambiguous and co-unambiguous logarithmic-space algorithms for recognizing simple path graphs and for their reachability problem. Such a graph has at most one simple path from the specified start to each vertex; directed cycles are still permitted. Recognition is part of the result, but the graph restriction remains essential.
why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.
status_note: Source-open. Checked Reinhardt–Allender §2, van Melkebeek–Prakriya Theorems 1.1–1.3, the inherited 2025 Theorem 6 and the 2026 survey’s Theorems 3.12–3.13. The catalytic v3 definitions and main bound retain additional storage/oracle resources; Hoza’s July Theorem 1.3 retains oblivious weights. The August MFCS paper’s introduction and Theorem 1 retain the simple-path-graph restriction. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of unrestricted uniform NL versus UL. These are source and theorem-scope checks, not independent verification of all cited proofs.

working_summary: NL permits many accepting computation branches while using only logarithmic workspace. UL requires exactly one accepting branch on a yes input and none on a no input. The question asks whether one uniform unambiguous small-space machine can decide reachability in every directed graph. Known general simulations need more workspace or extra resources, while recent lower bounds and algorithms concern restricted models or graph families. The uniqueness guarantee concerns the machine’s computations, not a promise that the input graph already has a unique path.

title: L versus NL
importance_reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and a constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), directed graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(s,t\in[n]\), the machine halts, correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and visits at most
\[C\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\]
work-tape cells? The graph is given explicitly by its adjacency matrix; the input is read-only. The machine and constant must work for all input sizes.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 14.8 states that nondeterministic logarithmic space differs from deterministic logarithmic space; the accompanying text identifies directed connectivity as the complete algorithmic question.
definitions:
A directed graph has a set \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) of ordered edges. Self-loops are allowed. Reachability asks whether there are vertices \(v_0=s,\ldots,v_\ell=t\), with \(\ell\ge0\), such that \((v_{i-1},v_i)\in E\) for every \(1\le i\le\ell\). In particular \(s=t\) is a yes instance. No degree, planarity, acyclicity or unique-path restriction is imposed.

The input contains a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\), all \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, and \(s,t\) in fixed-length binary vertex fields. Its bit length is \(N=\Theta(n^2)\), so logarithmic bounds in \(N+2\) and \(n+2\) agree up to constants. Malformed strings, including invalid dimensions and vertex fields, are rejected with logarithmic workspace in their actual length. A validity check does not need to store the matrix. The representation is an explicit string, not an adjacency oracle or a circuit describing a much larger graph.

The computation uses a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Heads move by ordinary Turing-machine steps. Space is the total number of distinct work-tape cells visited during the computation, including blank cells crossed by heads, all counters, stacks and auxiliary records. The finite control and read-only input cells are uncharged. There is no advice depending on input size, oracle, random tape, external storage, writable input or extra tape whose contents can temporarily be borrowed. The output is a single accept/reject decision. Input rescanning and arbitrary finite computation are permitted, but every input must eventually halt.

The class \(\mathrm{L}\) consists of languages of binary strings decided by such deterministic machines using \(O(\log(N+2))\) space. The class \(\mathrm{NL}\) uses a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation with the same space bound: an input is accepted exactly when at least one computation branch accepts. One may require a polynomial clock on every branch without changing NL. A logarithmic-space configuration has only polynomially many possibilities, including input-head positions; any accepting computation can therefore be shortened and a logarithmic-size clock suffices. A halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine automatically runs in polynomial time because a repeated complete configuration would repeat forever.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such a reduction writes one polynomial-length instance and preserves its yes/no answer while using logarithmic workspace; output bits can be recomputed when composing it with another small-space machine. Thus a positive answer for the specified matrix representation implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{L}\), and \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) already holds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\), using the stated uniform machine model. An affirmative reachability solution must specify one machine and a constant, and prove correctness, termination, malformed-input handling and the space bound on every input. A negative solution must exclude every such machine: equivalently, for every always-halting correct deterministic reachability decider and every constant \(C\), some valid instance exceeds \(C\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) visited work cells. A class-based argument must establish the equivalence to this concrete reachability target. A lower bound for one search procedure, or a successful algorithm restricted to undirected graphs, using advice, nondeterminism or a higher power of logarithmic space, is insufficient. No numerical approximation of a resource bound answers this exact class-equality question.
context:
Ordinary graph search can remember which vertices have been visited. Logarithmic space holds only a constant number of vertex names and counters, so a separate visited bit for each vertex does not fit. Repeated scans of the input are free of a space penalty, but any saved information between scans counts.

Directed reachability captures an entire complexity class because a small-space machine has only polynomially many configurations. Its legal next steps form the edges of a directed graph, and acceptance is reachability of an accepting configuration. This correspondence is computable with logarithmic workspace.

Savitch’s theorem gives deterministic reachability using \(O((\log n)^2)\) workspace, with a quasipolynomial time bound. The gap between one and two logarithmic factors is exactly relevant to membership in L: an always-halting deterministic machine using only logarithmic space has polynomially many configurations, and hence polynomial running time.

Reingold’s theorem meets the logarithmic-space target when edges are undirected. Directed graphs therefore cannot be replaced by their undirected versions: forgetting an arrow can create paths absent from the original instance.

The equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) means that nondeterministic logarithmic space can recognize both reachability and nonreachability. It is a closure theorem within the nondeterministic model, and does not establish that either task has a deterministic logarithmic-space algorithm.

The 2025 alternative links graph connectivity to random-walk estimation, but its successful procedure may differ from graph to graph. Its deterministic branch uses polylogarithmic rather than logarithmic space. Neither qualification disappears merely because both algorithms signal their own failures.

The 2026 hardness result locates the difficulty even in graphs whose edges split into two sets, each a collection of directed paths of length at most two. This remains NL-hard when the decomposition is part of the input. The pieces are simple, but paths using edges from both pieces can still express general directed reachability.
why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of unrestricted uniform L versus NL. The 2026 sparse-graph result is checked at the theorem-statement level, not by a complete independent proof audit.

Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm. | 1987–1988: Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
importance_reason: A central longstanding completeness question for all of TFNP, with consequences for the organization of total search and established links to bounded arithmetic and proof complexity.
formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.
question_excerpt: The search for a complete problem in TFNP is of primary concern to certain fields such as cryptography, but it remains open whether such a […]
definitions:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), let \(\Sigma^*\) include the empty string, and let \(|x|\) be bit length. A search relation is a subset \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\). An answer to input \(x\) is any string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); no uniqueness or ordering of valid answers is required.

The relation belongs to \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) if all three conditions hold. First, there are positive integers \(a,b\), fixed for \(R\), such that every valid pair satisfies \(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\). Second, a deterministic algorithm decides \(R(x,y)\) in time at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\), for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Third,
\[\forall x\in\Sigma^*\ \exists y\in\Sigma^*,\qquad R(x,y).\]
Thus totality applies to every binary input. A relation based on a structured encoding must also prescribe a valid answer for malformed instances; restricting the domain to inputs promised to have a solution is insufficient. The output bound is part of the relation: an overlong string is not a valid answer.

Algorithms use uniform finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machines over fixed finite alphabets, with binary input and output. Time counts bit operations, input handling and writing the output, in the worst case over all inputs. A pair can be encoded as \(\langle x,z\rangle=1^{|x|}0xz\), whose length is linear in \(|x|+|z|+1\); malformed encodings may be assigned an arbitrary fixed output. All functions used below are total and polynomial-time computable on their full encoded domains. There is no randomness, advice, nonuniform circuit family or external oracle available to these functions.

For \(R,Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\), the reduction \(R\le_m^p Q\) means that there are functions \(f:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) and \(g:\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) computed in deterministic polynomial time such that
\[\forall x,z\in\Sigma^*,\qquad Q(f(x),z)\ \Longrightarrow\ R(x,g(x,z)).\]
The bound for \(f\) is polynomial in \(|x|\), and that for \(g\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\). The decoder may use the original input \(x\). This is a single transformed instance with a single returned answer; correctness must hold for every possible valid answer, without controlling which answer is returned. The reduction does not itself compute an answer to \(Q\), and the quantification over valid answers is not an oracle supplied to \(f\) or \(g\). Multiple adaptive instance queries are not the reduction in this question.

The complete problem \(Q\), its verifier and its balance bound are fixed before \(R\) is chosen. The reduction functions and their polynomial constants may depend on \(R\) and \(Q\), but not on the particular input. No single effective procedure that recognizes TFNP membership or produces reductions from arbitrary verifier descriptions is required.

A negative answer is the exact opposite quantifier statement:
\[\forall Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \exists R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\not\le_m^p Q.\]
The target is completeness for a search class under the specified search reduction. Completeness of a decision language, completeness for a proper TFNP subclass, or an NP search problem that lacks answers on some inputs does not by itself satisfy it.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify one relation \(Q\), prove its polynomial balance, deterministic polynomial-time verifiability and totality on all binary inputs, and establish the stated reductions from every \(R\in\mathrm{TFNP}\). A negative answer must prove that every candidate \(Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\) fails to receive such a reduction from some relation in the class. No effective enumeration of all TFNP problems is additionally required. A subclass-completeness result, a separation relative to an oracle or a conditional consequence alone is insufficient.
context:
The source states nonexistence of a many-one complete TFNP problem among the central conjectures connecting computational complexity and proof systems. This card asks the equivalent yes-or-no existence question, so the commonly stated conjecture predicts a negative answer.

Polynomial verifiability and a polynomial answer bound can be given by machine descriptions, but totality asserts a condition over all inputs. This semantic requirement prevents simply treating every polynomial-time verifier as a total search problem. Pudlák relates the general completeness question to the ability of fixed arithmetical theories to capture total search, and proves a universal-problem result for suitable classes whose totality is provable in a fixed theory.

Many important subclasses have complete problems tied to particular existence principles. The December 2025 manuscript studies further oracle hierarchies and collapses within TFNP; these subclass results do not supply a complete problem for the entire class.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.
why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.

The checked sources do not resolve existence of an unrelativized many-one complete problem for all TFNP. This is a bounded source-open review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

working_summary: TFNP contains search problems with polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable answers guaranteed to exist for every binary input. The question asks whether one problem in this class is complete for all the others under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions. Each reduction makes one transformed instance and must decode every valid returned answer correctly. The complete relation is fixed universally, while the reduction and its polynomial bounds may vary with the source problem. Known subclass completeness and oracle results clarify the structure without settling this general existence question.

title: Ruling out quasilinear-time SAT without a space restriction
importance_reason: A basic unconditional time lower-bound frontier for the canonical NP-complete problem, with no small-memory qualification. It is weaker than P versus NP yet would establish a general computation obstruction beyond the known resource tradeoffs.
formal:
Is Boolean-formula satisfiability outside deterministic quasilinear time, with no independent bound on the algorithm’s working memory? In the uniform random-access model below, the exact target is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\right],\]
where \(N\) is the full bit length of the explicitly written formula and \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. Thus every fixed polynomial-logarithmic factor must be excluded. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this meaning of the source’s “near-linear time”; the stronger exclusion of all \(N^{1+o(1)}\)-time algorithms is not required.
question_excerpt: The conclusion identifies proving that Boolean-formula satisfiability cannot be solved in near-linear time as a weaker unresolved goal on the way to P versus NP.
definitions:
A Boolean formula is a finite explicitly written expression built from Boolean variables, constants 0 and 1, binary AND and OR, and unary NOT. Its parse structure is a tree; repeated subexpressions are written separately. Variable occurrences use binary identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers allowed. Fix a self-delimiting prefix encoding with gate tokens and delimited identifiers. The total bit length \(N\) includes the parse structure and every identifier occurrence. SAT consists of the well-formed encodings for which some assignment to the occurring variables makes the formula evaluate to 1. All malformed strings are rejected. This is decision, not counting assignments or outputting one. Inputs are arbitrary explicit strings, not succinct circuits describing exponentially long formulas.

Fix a uniform deterministic word-RAM with logarithmic-size words. A machine is one finite program independent of \(N\), together with a fixed integer \(b\ge1\) giving word length \(w_N=b\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). It has a fixed number of word registers and an initially zero writable memory array addressed by \(w_N\)-bit integers. The input is separately read-only, packed into words with zero padding in its final word, and its bit length is available. One step is a register copy, Boolean bitwise operation, addition or subtraction modulo \(2^{w_N}\), comparison, conditional branch, shift by a register-specified count, or indexed read/write of one word. Shifts by at least \(w_N\) return zero. Registers and memory words contain exactly \(w_N\) bits; no unbounded-integer operation has unit cost. The program has no advice, oracle, nondeterminism or random bits. It halts with a single accept/reject answer on every input. Standard additional arithmetic operations on logarithmic words can be implemented with polynomial-logarithmic overhead and do not change the union of time bounds in this question.

There is no logarithmic, sublinear or other independent workspace requirement. The algorithm may use any addressable working memory it can access during its allowed running time. Initial memory is zero, not an input-dependent precomputed table; reading and writing memory are charged. The word-size/address convention is the ordinary polynomial-address-space convention of this RAM model, not a small-space promise. In particular, maintaining an input-sized array is allowed. The purpose of random access is to charge actual computation rather than the distance a sequential input head must travel.

For a fixed \(k\), membership in the displayed time class means that some one machine and constant \(D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) correctly decide every input \(x\) within
\[D(N+2)\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\]
steps, including parsing and rejection of malformed inputs. Here \(k,D,b\) and the finite program are independent of the particular input and its length. The target’s positive statement excludes every such choice. Its negative statement requires just one correct algorithm and one fixed exponent \(k\); it does not require a linear-time algorithm.

The chosen bound is \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\), the union over all fixed logarithmic powers. It is smaller than the broader \(N^{1+o(1)}\) family: for example, \(N2^{\sqrt{\log_2 N}}\) is in the latter family but exceeds \(N(\log N)^k\) for every fixed \(k\). Excluding every \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\) algorithm does not require proving a fixed exponent lower bound \(N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The user-approved clarification retains the absence of a memory restriction and records which of these meanings is being benchmarked.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed time-only nonmembership statement for the stated uniform machine and input model. A positive answer must exclude all fixed \(k,D,b\) and all correct total programs, with no extra workspace restriction. Equivalently, for every correct total program, every \(k\), and every \(D\), some input exceeds its proposed quasilinear bound. A negative answer must provide one program and fixed constants and prove correctness and that time bound on all inputs. A lower bound only for logarithmic-memory algorithms, a restricted SAT-solver family, a particular input distribution, or a sequential-access model does not establish this RAM target. A conditional lower bound under P ≠ NP or an exponential-time hypothesis is not an unconditional solution. Exact asymptotic quantifiers apply; no finite timing experiment or numerical error tolerance settles the question.
context:
P versus NP asks whether SAT admits any polynomial-time algorithm. This card asks for a much smaller first exclusion: algorithms only a fixed logarithmic factor slower than reading the input. Such an exclusion would still be consistent with a quadratic or higher-degree polynomial-time SAT algorithm.

Checking a supplied assignment is easy relative to the size of an explicit formula, but this does not show that deciding whether an assignment exists must take longer. The target requires an unconditional separation between existence testing and this very fast deterministic computation, over all possible programs.

Known time-space bounds exclude algorithms that are simultaneously fast and use little writable memory. Williams’s theorem reaches a polynomial time exponent below 2 cos(π/7) when workspace is subpolynomial. Here memory is unrestricted, so that qualification cannot be dropped.

The 2016 column also describes an either/or theorem: SAT cannot have both a quasilinear-time algorithm and a logarithmic-space algorithm, even if these are different algorithms. An either/or conclusion does not identify the time alternative as the true one. It therefore leaves this time-only target unresolved.

Hirahara, Lu and Ren’s 2023 Remark 47 explicitly separates simultaneous time-space bounds from separate-algorithm alternatives. Their discussion still allows the unresolved possibility of quasilinear-time SAT together with polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth parallel circuits. That discussion supplies no quasilinear SAT algorithm and no time-only lower bound.

The source uses “near-linear” informally. The selected meaning excludes every fixed logarithmic power, including arbitrarily large fixed ones. This gives a definite success condition without demanding the stronger exclusion of every subpolynomial overhead or a particular positive power improvement. The selection was made explicitly by the user.
why: An unconditional time-only lower bound for SAT in a general random-access model would cross a fundamental barrier in complexity theory. Even this comparatively weak exclusion remains separate from the substantial lower bounds known when memory is restricted.
status_note: Source-open under the user-selected n·polylog(n) interpretation without an independent space restriction. The 2009 conclusion provides the target; the complete 2016 column, 2008 SAT theorem statement and 2023 §4/Remark 47 support the distinction from time-space tradeoffs. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no unconditional matching time-only resolution. The source does not define “near-linear”; this precise scope was explicitly selected by the user, not attributed verbatim to Fortnow. No complete independent proof audit or new lower-bound proof is claimed.

The target excludes every deterministic running time n times a fixed polynomial in log n in a uniform random-access model. There is no independent restriction on working memory. title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
importance_reason: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,b,d,q\), real constants \(c>0\) and \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic oracle Turing machine \(V\) satisfying the following conditions? For every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\) of bit length \(N\), set
\[
 r_N=\left\lceil a\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil,\qquad
 M_N=(N+2)^b,\qquad \Sigma_N=\{0,1,\ldots,M_N-1\}.
\]
Given \(F\), a uniformly random string \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r_N}\), and oracle access to a fixed proof \(\pi\in\Sigma_N^{M_N}\), the verifier makes at most \(q\) symbol queries, halts in at most \(K(N+2)^d\) bit operations, and accepts or rejects. It must have perfect completeness and inverse-polynomial soundness:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F\text{ satisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \exists\pi\ \forall R:\ V^\pi(F,R)=1,\\
 F\text{ unsatisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \forall\pi:\ \Pr_R[V^\pi(F,R)=1]\le (N+2)^{-c}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All constants and the verifier are independent of \(F\) and \(N\).
question_excerpt: Conjecture 1.3 asks for a constant-query PCP whose alphabet grows polynomially with inverse error while the randomness remains logarithmic. The selected endpoint asks for some inverse-polynomial error and polynomial-size alphabet and proof. Main Theorem 1.4 reaches inverse-polynomial error with a polyloglogarithmic, rather than constant, number of queries.
definitions:
A Boolean literal is a variable or its negation. A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. Satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values to all variables appearing in the formula makes every clause true. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false; repeated literals and repeated clauses are allowed.

Fix the following explicit encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) be its binary expansion, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\), and encode it by \(1^t0\operatorname{bin}(z)\), where \(t\) is the expansion length. Encode a formula by its clause count, then for each clause its length in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), then its literals. A literal is one sign bit followed by the code of its positive integer variable index. There is no additional declared variable count and no trailing data. The parameter \(N\) is the length of this entire binary representation, including indices and delimiters. Invalid encodings may simply be rejected and are not part of the completeness and soundness requirements.

The proof has \(M_N\) addressable locations, each containing one symbol from \(\Sigma_N\). A query specifies one index in \(\{1,\ldots,M_N\}\) and returns that symbol encoded in \(\lceil\log_2 M_N\rceil\) bits. The same index always gives the same answer. A query reads one whole symbol, not one arbitrary subset of the proof or an unbounded-length answer. Repeated requests count again toward the query limit. The verifier has no other access to the proof; it may not scan the proof without paying queries. Forming addresses and reading or processing the returned bits count toward its bit running time.

The proof is chosen before \(R\) and is fixed throughout the verification. On a satisfiable formula, the same witnessing proof must be accepted for every random string. On an unsatisfiable formula the error bound holds for every possible proof, including proofs produced with unlimited computation and proofs unrelated to any satisfying assignment. No proof may depend on the subsequently sampled verifier randomness. The verifier may choose later query addresses using earlier answers, as allowed by the existing card; it is otherwise deterministic once the input, random string and oracle are fixed. A standard nonadaptive verifier satisfying these guarantees would in particular meet the target, but nonadaptivity is not an additional requirement here.

Using exactly the displayed proof length, alphabet and random-tape length is a padding convention. Shorter proofs and smaller alphabets can be embedded in these bounds and unused random bits can be ignored. Positive integer exponents absorb constant polynomial factors and logarithmic ceiling effects. The common exponent \(b\) bounds both proof length and alphabet size; it need not be optimal. There is no required relation between \(a,b,c\) beyond positivity. The query bound \(q\) is a fixed integer, while each queried symbol contains \(O(\log(N+2))\) bits. Thus the target permits more than a constant number of proof bits, but not a growing number of queried symbols.

The verifier is a single finite classical program, with no advice, cryptographic assumption, trusted setup, interaction or quantum operations. All of its computation, including parsing, computing the displayed parameters, reading randomness, generating query addresses and computing the decision, must satisfy the polynomial bit-time bound for every valid formula, proof and random string. The construction of a witnessing proof need not be efficient; the assertion is its existence. There is no separate honest prover participating during verification.

Only some fixed positive exponent \(c\) is requested. The question does not demand an optimal exponent, a two-query verifier, an alphabet of constant size, or proof length linear in the formula size. The near-linear-size constant-error PCP problem is a different parameter target.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the constants and uniform verifier, including the two proof/randomness quantifier orders, the resource bounds on every execution, perfect completeness and the stated information-theoretic soundness; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A positive result must achieve polynomial length, polynomial alphabet, logarithmic randomness, constant symbol-query complexity and inverse-polynomial error simultaneously. A constant-error construction, an error exponent tending to zero, a superconstant query bound, or a superpolynomial-size proof is insufficient without an additional proved transformation establishing every required bound. A negative answer must exclude every choice of the fixed constants and every permitted verifier, including adaptive verifiers. Conditional implications under unproved assumptions do not unconditionally decide the target.
context:
The usual PCP theorem provides constant error with constant local access. The selected endpoint asks for error falling as a fixed inverse power of input size without increasing the number of queried symbols.

The modular-composition result achieves the desired inverse-polynomial error but still makes a polyloglogarithmic number of queries. This does not provide a fixed query constant.

The 2025 high-dimensional-expander construction improves proof size while permitting arbitrarily small constant error. Fixing any such constant does not produce the input-dependent error required here.

The March 2026 Macaulay-basis revision reduces the number of composition steps in a PCP construction. Its stated constant-soundness result and larger basic proof ingredient do not establish this endpoint.

The March 2026 lattice-hardness revision still states the polynomial-error constant-query PCP assertion as a conjecture and uses it conditionally for a stronger consequence.
why: Achieving very small verification error while reading only a constant number of logarithmic-size proof symbols would strengthen the quantitative reach of PCP theory and its hardness-of-approximation consequences.
status_note: The source conjecture and the explicit restatement in the 29 March 2026 lattice-hardness revision remain unresolved in the bounded primary-source check through 17 September 2026. The recent constant-error and composition results do not establish all selected parameters simultaneously. This review does not independently audit their full proofs.
progress: 2015-05-23: The source gives inverse-polynomial soundness with a polyloglogarithmic number of symbol queries. | 2025-06-15: The STOC 2025 construction obtains quasi-linear proof size and two queries with arbitrarily small constant soundness. | 2026-03-24: The revised Macaulay-basis construction gives a PCP theorem with one composition step, retaining constant soundness. | 2026-03-29: The revised lattice-hardness paper records the inverse-polynomial-error endpoint as Conjecture 7.1.
working_summary: A PCP verifier checks a fixed proof by inspecting a few selected symbols. The target asks for constant symbol queries, logarithmic randomness, and polynomial proof length and alphabet size. Satisfiable formulas must have a proof accepted on every random string. For an unsatisfiable formula, every proof must be accepted with probability at most a fixed inverse power of the input length. A complete Lean-checked resolution must achieve or rule out all of these guarantees simultaneously for one uniform verifier.

title: \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)
importance_reason: The defining complexity-class question for exact computation over the reals, connecting TCS to algebraic geometry and numerical computation.
formal:
Is
\[\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\]
in the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered real field, with arbitrary real inputs and arbitrary finitely many fixed real machine constants? Equivalently, does every set of finite real tuples with polynomial-length real witnesses checkable in polynomial BSS time have a deterministic polynomial-time BSS decider? The decider and its finite constants may depend on the set, but must be fixed for all input lengths.
question_excerpt: After defining real polynomial time and real nondeterministic polynomial time, Meer and Michaux ask whether the two classes differ and identify this as the central unresolved comparison in real structural complexity.
definitions:
The input domain is the disjoint union \(\mathbb R^{*}=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb R^{n}\). An input is a tuple \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\); its size is its dimension \(n\), independent of the magnitudes, precision or computability of its coordinates. Length is supplied as part of the input convention. Distinct tuple lengths remain distinct even when trailing coordinates are zero.

A deterministic BSS machine has a finite control graph and real registers, initially containing the input and zeros elsewhere, with a fixed finite set of real constants including 0 and 1. Constants may be transcendental or uncomputable; there is no requirement for finite binary descriptions of their values. The same program and constants serve all inputs and all dimensions. Each arithmetic instruction adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides two stored reals, or loads a fixed machine constant; a division is allowed only with nonzero denominator. A branch tests equality to zero or order relative to zero, exactly. Copies, control steps and register shifts each have unit cost, as do arithmetic operations and tests. Accepting and rejecting states output the bits 1 and 0.

For a concrete standard register convention, use a doubly infinite sequence of real registers with finite support at every finite time. Ordinary arithmetic, copy and test instructions refer to finitely many fixed register offsets in the program. A shift moves the sequence one position left or right, giving access to arbitrary input coordinates over time. Initially register 0 holds \(n\), registers 1 through \(n\) hold the input, and the others hold zero. The verifier input similarly records the two lengths and the two tuples in adjacent registers. This is the ordinary shift-register presentation of BSS computation, polynomially equivalent to the source's restricted copy-address presentation. Division by zero is treated as rejection, so a proposed decider must still meet correctness and totality on every input. There is no primitive floor, digit extraction, transcendental-function evaluation, square root, oracle or random instruction. An arithmetic step costs one even when its value would need arbitrarily many bits in a discrete representation.

For \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\) means that there exist one such deterministic machine \(M\) and constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N\), with \(C\ge1\), such that, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), it halts within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps and accepts exactly when \(x\in L\).

Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there are one deterministic BSS verifier \(V\) and fixed polynomial bounds \(p,q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(V(x,y)\) halts within \(q(n)\) steps for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and every real tuple \(y\) of length at most \(p(n)\), and
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists m\le p(n)\;\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The time bound depends on \(n\), not on the coordinate values; polynomial bounds may be written as \(C(n+1)^d\). A padded fixed witness length gives the same class. No-instance inputs must be rejected for every permitted witness. The witness contains arbitrary exact reals, not just rationals or finite strings. The verifier's constants and polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\), \(n\) or the witness. Equality of classes quantifies over every such \(L\), with no promise on input coordinates.

The notation \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}^{0}\) restricts the machine constants to 0 and 1. The Boolean part of a class restricts its input tuples to coordinates in \(\{0,1\}\); write it as \(\mathrm{BP}(\cdot)\). These are different restrictions from the full target. In particular, \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})\) concerns finitely encoded problems, while this card retains all real tuples and arbitrary fixed real constants. Neither finite-precision computation nor bit-cost arithmetic is the model being compared.

For the cited discrete comparison, PosSLP asks whether a finite arithmetic straight-line program, starting from 0 and 1 and using addition, subtraction and multiplication, outputs a positive integer. Such a program is an explicitly listed acyclic sequence of operations on earlier values. \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) is ordinary polynomial-time Turing computation with a unit-cost yes/no oracle for this language; \(/\mathrm{poly}\) permits an additional polynomial-length advice string depending only on input length. The counting hierarchy is the union of the levels \(\mathrm C_0\mathrm P=\mathrm P\) and \(\mathrm C_{k+1}\mathrm P=\mathrm{PP}^{\mathrm C_k\mathrm P}\), where PP uses a strict majority of the computation paths of a polynomial-time nondeterministic binary machine.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the stated class equality or its negation in this precise full BSS model. A positive answer must establish a uniform polynomial-time BSS decider for every language having the defined verifier, allowing a different fixed program and finite constants for each language. A negative answer must establish some \(L\in\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\setminus\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\), ruling out every polynomial-time deterministic BSS decider even with arbitrary finite real constants. A result only for constant-free machines, only for Boolean inputs, with extra oracle operations, or under an unproved complexity assumption does not alone prove the full unconditional target. All decisions are exact; numerical approximation tolerance does not apply.
context:
A real witness can specify a point satisfying a system of polynomial constraints, and the BSS verifier can check those constraints using exact field operations. The question asks whether finding the existence of such a point can always be made as efficient as checking a supplied point.

The source proves that deciding whether a real-coefficient polynomial of degree at most four has a real zero is \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)-complete when its coefficients are explicitly listed. Feasibility of a system of quadratic equations is another complete problem. Completeness here uses polynomial-time BSS reductions, rather than reductions between binary encodings.

The cost measure deliberately separates algebraic operations from the precision needed on physical hardware. This makes the question central to algebraic complexity, while preventing automatic transfer of a resolution to the ordinary P versus NP problem.

The recommended numerical-analysis paper proves \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) in Proposition 1.1, and places PosSLP in the counting hierarchy in Theorem 1.4. These are statements about Boolean inputs and restricted constants, not a deterministic simulation of all real witnesses.

For arbitrary fixed real constants, \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R})=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}/\mathrm{poly}\) is Conjecture 1.2 of that same paper. The paper proves the inclusion from the right into the left, but does not prove the displayed equality. This distinction preserves the scope of the reader-recommended reference.

The 2025 paper explicitly distinguishes the full BSS model from the constant-free Boolean-input characterization of \(\exists\mathbb R\). Its oracle separation for full BSS machines additionally gives them an exact integer-membership oracle; that is an enlarged instruction set and does not settle this card.
why: This is the central determinism-versus-verification question for exact algebraic computation. It would classify the cost of real polynomial feasibility in a model that isolates arithmetic complexity from finite-precision representation, linking complexity theory to real algebraic geometry.
