working_summary: Williams showed that a time-bounded multitape computation can be simulated using roughly the square root of its time as ordinary workspace. The question asks whether one fixed positive saving in the square-root exponent is always possible. The saving must apply to every time bound at least as large as the input length. The simulator may take more time but receives no random bits, advice or catalytic tape. An answer would clarify a basic time-versus-space boundary and its consequences for lower bounds.

title: P versus NP intersect coNP
importance_reason: Tests whether two-sided efficiently checkable evidence guarantees efficient computation, with relevance to total search and cryptographic candidates.
formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decided on every input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^k\) steps for fixed constants \(C,k\). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm P\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm P\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.
context:
A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.
why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.
status_note: Conjecture 3.9 is open in the saved August 2019 draft. The formulation was checked against that source on 13 September 2026. The bounded related-literature check supplied no verified resolution or new status theorem, so the card remains source_open rather than claiming exhaustive current verification.
progress: 2019-08-06: Conjecture 3.9 states NP ∩ coNP ≠ P. The nearby discussion distinguishes two-sided verifiability from known polynomial-time algorithms and from the larger P versus NP question.

title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits
importance_reason: Unrestricted threshold-of-threshold lower bounds test the power of a basic shallow circuit model.
formal: Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), in the source’s sense \(\mathrm{NP}\), and constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\), such that every unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit computing \(f_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) gates for every \(n\geq n_0\)?
definitions: A threshold gate on Boolean inputs \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) outputs one if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_i z_i\geq\theta\), where all weights \(w_i\) and the threshold \(\theta\) are arbitrary real numbers of either sign. An unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit on \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) consists of any finite number \(s\) of such gates applied to the original input bits, followed by one threshold output gate applied to their outputs. Arbitrary fan-in, fan-out and length-dependent weights are permitted; omitted inputs can have weight zero. Its size is \(s+1\), the number of threshold gates, not total weight magnitude or the number of bits encoding weights. Constants and direct input-to-output connections can be represented by additional threshold gates, changing size by at most \(n+1\), which does not alter exponential-size existence. Computation must agree with \(f_n\) on every input, with no approximation. The family is explicit in the definition of Section 1.5.1 of the source: there exist a polynomial \(q\) and a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \(f_n(x)=1\) precisely when some binary witness \(y\) with \(|y|\leq q(n)\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). Verifier cost is measured on a standard bit Turing machine. Neither circuit weights nor circuits are required to be uniform or polynomially bounded. The exponential target is interpreted as \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for all sufficiently large input lengths, with one fixed positive exponent coefficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof by specifying one uniform NP verifier defining the family and proving the stated exponential gate lower bound for every sufficiently large length, or prove that no such NP family and constants exist. A counting argument without an NP witness family, a bound on total weight, a restriction on signs or magnitudes, or a conditional complexity consequence does not meet the full target.
context:
Research Problem 11.40 asks for an exponential lower bound for unrestricted depth-two threshold circuits. The preceding discussion obtains strong bounds under restrictions on the weights; dropping such restrictions is the point of the question.

The source explicitly defines “explicit” in Section 1.5.1 through polynomial-time verification, corresponding to NP. Requiring the chosen function to lie in P would add a stronger condition that is not imposed here. Counting the existence of hard truth tables without this uniform verification condition would miss the intended explicit lower bound.

Chen’s 2018 paper describes even superpolynomial unrestricted depth-two threshold lower bounds for NEXP as a major frontier and develops conditional implications. Those implications do not supply the unconditional exponential lower bound for an NP family required by this card.
why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a basic model of two layers of weighted Boolean decisions. An exponential lower bound with unrestricted real weights would establish a strong limit on this expressive shallow architecture for an explicitly verifiable computational task.
status_note: The source states this challenge as open. The source-wide explicitness convention and circuit model were rechecked on 13 September 2026, together with the abstract of Chen’s subsequent work and a limited later-work search. No unconditional resolution was verified; this is not an exhaustive status review, and status remains source_open.

title: Black-Box Hypothesis
importance_reason: A broad foundational hypothesis about the computational value of program descriptions, implying a major complexity separation and supported by a continuing theory of restricted variants.
formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.
question_excerpt: The main statement, which we will call here ‘the Black-Box Hypothesis’, remains open.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge0\), a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) has the length-\(2^n\) truth table \(\operatorname{tt}(f)\), ordered lexicographically by input. A property is an arbitrary family \(F=(F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of total Boolean predicates on these tables. It need not be invariant under permutations of the input variables or table positions. Its semantic character means that two circuits computing the same \(n\)-input function have the same required property value.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. Wires may share gate outputs; unrestricted depth is allowed. Unused designated input vertices are retained. Its size \(s(C)\) is the number of vertices plus wires, and its computed function is \(f_C\). Define \(s(f)=\min\{s(C):f_C=f\}\). Counting input vertices is a harmless explicit convention because the black-box resource bound includes \(n\).

Descriptions list all vertices in topological order, their types and earlier incoming indices, followed by the output index; integers use self-delimiting binary fields. This gives a polynomial-time parsable encoding of length polynomial in \(s(C)+1\), including all \(n\) input vertices. Any fixed encoding with these properties gives the same polynomial-time target. Malformed descriptions are rejected.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{wbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,k\) such that \(A\) halts on every input and every random-bit sequence within \(c(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is description length, and
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr[A(\operatorname{desc}(C))=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f_C))]\ge2/3.\]
The same machine must work across all sizes and arities and on every representation of a function, including padded or redundant circuits. The acceptance probabilities for different representations need not be equal; each must give the correct Boolean property value with the stated error bound.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{bbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(d,\ell\) such that \(B^f(1^n,1^m)\) halts within \(d(n+m+1)^\ell\) steps on every random-bit sequence, and
\[\forall n\ge0\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\ \forall m\ge1,\quad m\ge s(f)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[B^f(1^n,1^m)=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f))]\ge2/3.\]
Here \(m\) is an integer upper bound, not necessarily the minimum circuit size. Both parameters are in unary. A query consists of an explicitly written \(n\)-bit string \(x\); the oracle returns \(f(x)\) in one step. Writing and manipulating the query counts toward time. Invalid-length queries return a fixed zero bit. Queries may be adaptive, and all computation between queries also counts. Thus the bound is on running time, not merely the number of oracle calls. The same machine and polynomial work for all valid bounds \(m\). If \(m<s(f)\), no correctness is required, but the running-time bound remains.

Both machines use independent fair random bits, and all probabilities above are over those bits for each fixed input or oracle. They have no advice or other oracle. In the black-box case, \(f\) and the unary parameters are the only supplied information about the function; no circuit, truth table, distribution on circuits or special representation is given. The circuit-size promise in this definition does not turn \(F_n\) into a partial property: \(F_n\) is defined on every Boolean function.

The quantifiers allow \(A,B\) and their polynomial constants to depend on \(F\). The conclusion is existence of a suitable \(B\) for every white-box decidable property, not an additional requirement of an effective procedure that transforms arbitrary machine descriptions into black-box algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal implication. A proof must establish a uniform black-box algorithm with the stated total running-time and pointwise error guarantees for every total semantic property in white-box BPP. A refutation must specify one such property and a correct white-box BPP algorithm and prove that no black-box BPP algorithm decides it under the supplied-size-bound model. A property defined only on a promised family of circuits, a distinction between two encodings of the same function, or a lower bound only for nonadaptive queries does not alone meet this criterion.
context:
The 2017 source identifies this as the total-property form of the scaled-down Rice’s theorem conjecture originating in work on program obfuscation. It distinguishes the still-open hypothesis from conditional counterexamples to a promise version; those counterexamples do not decide a property on every circuit.

The authors prove consequences of particular kinds of hypothetical counterexamples, including ones with highly sensitive low-complexity functions. These are conditional implications for circuit satisfiability, rather than a general proof or disproof of the hypothesis.

The 2021 paper retains the original hypothesis as open and studies other combinations of analysts and represented computations. Its positive results for restricted circuit analysts, and its equivalence involving nondeterministic circuits as boxes, change the computational models and do not settle ordinary circuits with uniform BPP analysts.

The cost of black-box computation includes the unary circuit-size bound. This avoids demanding a polynomial-in-arity algorithm for properties of functions whose smallest circuits are already exponentially large, and makes the two kinds of access comparable.
why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the 2017 conference paper Sections 2–3.1 and the 2021 paper introduction and results overview. The latter explicitly calls the original hypothesis open; its proved variants do not use the same pair of computational models. A bounded later-work search found no matching unconditional resolution. Conditional consequences quoted from these sources were checked for scope, not independently reproved.
progress: 2017-12-01: The publisher releases the MFCS formulation with explicit unary arity and size inputs, the wbBPP/bbBPP definitions and conditional consequences of particular counterexamples. | 2021-08-18: MFCS publishes a broader framework connecting several restricted black-box hypotheses to lower bounds while explicitly leaving the original hypothesis open.
working_summary: The Black-Box Hypothesis compares access to a Boolean circuit’s code with access to its input-output behavior. It concerns total semantic properties that a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm decides correctly on every circuit representation. The proposed black-box algorithm receives unary input length and circuit-size bounds and may make adaptive evaluations of the function. Its total running time, including queries, must be polynomial in those bounds with error at most one third on each input. Known restricted-model results and promise-property counterexamples do not settle this general hypothesis.

title: Does NP-hardness of MCSP imply circuit lower bounds for EXP?
importance_reason: Whether ordinary NP-hardness of circuit minimization entails exponential-time circuit lower bounds is a central connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.
formal: If the Minimum Circuit Size Problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, must \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly? The hypothesis uses unrestricted ordinary polynomial-time reductions, with no locality, uniform-\(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) or naturalness promise.
question_excerpt: We conjecture that the consequence of Theorem 1.3 can be strengthened to \(\mathrm{EXP} 6\subset  \mathrm{P}\)/poly , and that MCSP is (unconditionally) not NP-hard under uniform […]
definitions: An MCSP input is the complete truth table \(t\in \{0,1\}^{2^{n}}\) of a Boolean function on \(n\ge 1\) input bits, in lexicographic order, together with a nonnegative integer size threshold s in binary. It is accepted if some Boolean circuit of size at most s computes that function. Circuits are finite acyclic graphs over binary AND and OR, unary NOT, input variables and constants 0,1, with one designated output and unrestricted sharing. Size counts noninput gates, including constant gates. The total encoded input length counts the truth table, threshold and delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. NP-hardness means that for every language L in NP there is a deterministic polynomial-time map r such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(r(x)\in\)MCSP. NP consists of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup _{k\ge 1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{k}}); \mathrm{P}\)/poly consists of languages decided by families of Boolean circuits whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in input length, with no uniformity condition on their construction. \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly means that some language in EXP has no such polynomial-size circuit family.
answer_criterion: Prove the conditional implication or its logical negation in these exact reduction and circuit models. Deriving only \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\) or \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly is a weaker consequence. A theorem for a restricted reduction class or for partial, promise or approximate circuit minimization does not prove the stated implication.
context:
MCSP tests whether an explicit truth table has a small circuit. An NP-hardness proof would relate efficient reductions to the same lower bounds that the output instances ask us to establish.

The source derives \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly, and consequently \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\), from ordinary polynomial-time NP-hardness. These statements do not assert that EXP itself lacks polynomial-size circuits.

The original source also discusses stronger restrictions on reductions. The retained card selects the general implication to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly and does not combine it with the separate uniform-\(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) reduction conjecture.
why: Whether ordinary NP-hardness of circuit minimization entails exponential-time circuit lower bounds is a central connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.
status_note: The original conjecture and the 2017 journal consequences were checked. The stronger EXP nonuniform lower bound is not established by the weaker known consequence; no resolution was located in the bounded later-work search.
progress: 2017: The journal treatment records weaker consequences of polynomial-time NP-hardness; the stronger EXP nonuniform lower bound is the selected conjectural consequence.
working_summary: MCSP asks whether a fully listed Boolean function has a small circuit. The question concerns what proving its ordinary NP-hardness would force elsewhere in complexity theory. The proposed consequence is that some exponential-time language requires superpolynomial circuits. Existing consequences separate EXP from smaller intersections or randomized classes and do not yield that circuit lower bound. The target captures a major proposed connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.

title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
importance_reason: Connects the arithmetic nature of numbers to an elementary resource bound on computing their digits.
formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b- 1; a\) terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(\mathrm{P}(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.
context:
For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.
why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked 2024 research paper and June 2026 thesis abstract. The May 2026 automata paper uses a different input representation. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. A June 2026 listing titled “FIS Application: Hartmanis-Stearns” supplied no theorem statement or full text at https://uvsmpublications.com/publications/fis-application-hartmanis-stearns/ and is not evidence of a resolution. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1970: Linear-time and real-time sequence generation are shown to coincide for multitape machines. | 2020: The published revisiting paper proves transcendence restrictions for pushdown and exponential-growth morphic models. | 2024: ICALP work proves additional word-based transcendence results while explicitly retaining the full conjecture. | 2026: Automata compute digits from specially represented inputs; a June thesis abstract still describes the general conjecture as open.
working_summary: The question concerns a fixed machine that prints all digits of a real number with bounded delay between outputs. Every rational number permits this because its expansion is eventually periodic. The conjecture says that any irrational number generated this quickly must be transcendental. It quantifies over unrestricted deterministic multitape machines, beyond the restricted automata covered by known partial results. A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.

title: UNSAT multi-prover proofs with efficient SAT-oracle provers
importance_reason: A longstanding program-checking question for the canonical NP-complete problem, with links to interactive proofs, total search and worst-case hardness. The honest-prover resource restriction exposes a substantial structural gap beyond ordinary coNP interactive proofs.
formal:
Does UNSAT have a classical multi-prover interactive proof with a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and uniform probabilistic polynomial-time honest provers that may query SAT? The verifier has no oracle. For one fixed protocol, every unsatisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\) when all provers are honest, while every satisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\) for every collection of computationally unbounded, noncommunicating classical provers.

This restores the complement bar on SAT in the original Conjecture 6.2. The imported card lost that bar and incorrectly named SAT as the language to be proved; the oracle available to the honest provers is still SAT.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 6.2 asks for a multi-prover interactive proof of the complement of SAT whose honest provers use probabilistic polynomial time with a SAT oracle.
definitions:
Fix a binary encoding of finite Boolean formulas as explicitly written AND/OR/NOT expression trees with binary variable identifiers and delimiters. Its full bit length is \(n\). SAT consists of the well-formed formulas having a satisfying assignment. UNSAT consists of the well-formed formulas having none. The verifier rejects malformed encodings deterministically before any interaction. This convention differs from the literal language complement of SAT only on efficiently recognizable malformed strings and does not change the existence question. All participants receive the same input formula.

A protocol specifies one constant number \(k\ge2\) of provers, one uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing-machine verifier \(V\), and one honest probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(P_i^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). All are fixed finite programs, independent of input length. There is one polynomial bound \(p(n)\) on the verifier’s total computation and number of fair random bits, the number of message exchanges, and the total communication bits. Each honest prover has polynomial total running time in \(n\) throughout the protocol, on every random tape and within the communication bounds; its bound may depend on the fixed protocol. Writing SAT queries and processing their answers are charged, while the oracle returns one exact satisfiability bit per invocation. Malformed oracle queries return 0. Queries are allowed to depend on the prover’s local transcript and private randomness. There is no nonuniform advice or additional oracle.

The verifier uses private random bits and sends classical messages to individually addressed provers. Each prover’s response may depend only on the common input, its identity, its own received and sent messages, and its internal random bits and state. It cannot see messages exchanged with another prover except information that the verifier explicitly forwards. Provers cannot communicate with one another once interaction starts. Classical shared randomness independent of the verifier’s private randomness is allowed: for the honest protocol, a common uniform seed of polynomial length, together with independent private fair bits, suffices to specify it. There is no entanglement or quantum communication. No constant bound on the number of rounds is required.

The verifier must respect its polynomial clock even when provers cheat. Messages longer than its prescribed bounds, invalidly formatted messages or failure to answer a requested message cause rejection. Soundness quantifies over all classical prover strategies subject only to the communication and information restrictions. Cheating provers may have unlimited computation, arbitrary input-dependent prearranged strategies and shared classical randomness; they are not limited to SAT-oracle polynomial time. For fixed input and fixed private/shared prover randomness, a strategy gives each response as a function of that prover’s local transcript. Equivalently, randomized strategies are distributions over such deterministic strategy tuples. The provers have no access to the verifier’s private bits except through the messages they receive.

Let \(\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1,\ldots,P_k)(F)=1]\) mean the probability that the verifier accepts formula \(F\), over the verifier’s fair bits and the honest or cheating strategy’s randomness as applicable. The requirements are
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{UNSAT},\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^{\mathrm{SAT}},\ldots,P_k^{\mathrm{SAT}})(F)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \forall(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*),\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*)(F)=1]\le1/3.\]
One fixed tuple of honest algorithms must meet completeness for all yes-inputs. The soundness bound holds even for cheating strategies tailored separately to each no-input. Polynomial time is worst-case over randomness and allowed transcripts, not merely expected time. These constant error thresholds fix the ordinary bounded-error convention; no cryptographic hardness assumption or computational soundness restriction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated protocol. A positive answer must specify its verifier, finite prover count, honest SAT-oracle algorithms and polynomial bounds, and prove completeness and soundness against every permitted cheating strategy. A negative answer must exclude every such fixed protocol, rather than one round bound or construction. A proof system with unbounded honest provers, a verifier that can itself query SAT, efficient-cheater-only soundness, or quantum/entangled provers does not answer this target. A relativized counterexample or a consequence conditional on an unproved class separation does not refute the unrelativized statement. Exact probability inequalities and asymptotic bounds apply; numerical approximation tolerance is irrelevant.
context:
A satisfying assignment can be checked directly, and a SAT oracle can find such an assignment by deciding successive partial assignments. Consequently, the analogous efficient-prover statement for satisfiable formulas is straightforward. Certifying unsatisfiability is the substantive target; losing the complement bar changes the mathematical question.

Several provers can be cross-examined while being prevented from coordinating their answers during the interaction. The verifier remains computationally weak. The extra requirement here is that honest provers can prepare all their responses using only randomized polynomial time with SAT decisions, while dishonest provers receive no computational restriction.

The source relates this protocol to SAT program checking. In that setting a randomized polynomial-time checker can query a purported solver: it must flag an error with high probability if the answer on the designated input is wrong, and accept the answer with high probability if the solver is correct on all inputs. Correctness only on the designated input need not force acceptance.

Fortnow states the characterization connecting checkability to efficient-oracle-prover multi-prover proofs for a language and its complement. The SAT side is straightforward; the UNSAT side is the unresolved requirement. Ordinary interactive proofs for coNP with unrestricted honest prover computation do not establish this stronger efficiency statement.

Mahmoody and Xiao record the implication \(\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{TFNP}}\Rightarrow\mathrm{SAT}\text{ is checkable}\). Here TFNP consists of total search relations with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time-checkable solutions, and the antecedent means that a randomized polynomial-time SAT algorithm can use an oracle returning any valid solution of one such relation. The antecedent is not known, so this is a conditional connection rather than a protocol satisfying the card.

The 2025 range-avoidance paper explicitly retains SAT checkability as open in its §2.4 and recalls the same conditional implication. Its new protocols concern range avoidance and circuit image sizes; that discussion does not assert the requested UNSAT protocol.
why: This asks whether the output of a solver for an NP-complete problem can be checked using only the computational power of that solver. It connects the trustworthiness of hard computation to interactive proofs and to the limits of reductions between NP and total search.
status_note: Source-open after a verified extraction correction: Conjecture 6.2 of the 2021 PDF uses the complement of SAT as the language and ordinary SAT as the oracle. The displayed overline was checked visually; extracted plain text and the inherited summary had lost it. The 2010 author manuscript §1.3.1 and 2025 ECCC TR25-210 §2.4 were read for the conditional program-checking connection; the latter explicitly calls SAT checkability open. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The current review does not independently reprove the historical characterization or certify every later paper exhaustively.
progress: 1989–1995 / 2021: The program-checking framework and its connection to multi-prover proofs motivate the efficient-honest-prover question, explicitly restated as Conjecture 6.2 in 2021. | 2010: A randomized reduction from SAT to a total NP search oracle would imply SAT checkability; the result is conditional on the existence of that reduction. | 2025: The range-avoidance manuscript’s §2.4 still states that SAT checkability is open and recalls the TFNP implication as Theorem 2.11.
working_summary: The actual source asks for interactive proofs of unsatisfiability, with several noncommunicating classical provers. Honest provers must run in randomized polynomial time with SAT-oracle access, while the verifier is polynomial-time and has no oracle. Soundness must hold against all computationally unbounded classical cheating strategies. The target is tied to checking a purported SAT solver and remains distinct from ordinary interactive proofs with unrestricted honest provers. The imported SAT label lost a complement bar; the card restores UNSAT and records the correction explicitly.

title: Excluding one-sided randomized quasilinear-time log-space SAT
importance_reason: A sharply stated frontier for unconditional SAT lower bounds: it asks to handle fresh random bits in a resource regime already excluded deterministically, while preserving the error direction used by incomplete randomized solvers.
formal:
Is it true that no uniform randomized random-access algorithm decides Boolean satisfiability with one-sided error while using both quasilinear time and logarithmic workspace? More precisely, for every integer \(k\ge0\), is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{RTISP}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k,\ \log_2(N+2)\right]?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length. The two bounds hold simultaneously for one machine on every input and every sequence of coin flips. The error is allowed only on satisfiable inputs: each is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), whereas an unsatisfiable input is never accepted.
question_excerpt: Problem 5 asks to rule out a randomized SAT algorithm using n times a fixed polynomial in log n time and logarithmic space, with possible error on satisfiable inputs only.
definitions:
An input is an explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula: a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most three literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. An assignment gives a Boolean value to every variable occurring; the formula is satisfiable when some assignment makes it true. Variable identifiers, signs, all occurrences and clause delimiters are written in a fixed self-delimiting binary list encoding. Identifiers can be taken from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers permitted; \(N\) counts bits, not variables or clauses. Malformed encodings are no instances. There is no compressed formula or promise on the formula’s structure. The source explicitly permits 3-CNF satisfiability as its SAT target.

For definiteness, a random-access machine is a finite Turing-machine program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes and an address tape. When the address tape contains a binary index, one query step reads that indexed input bit; an out-of-range index returns a fixed endmarker. Writing, modifying and storing an address are charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only; all work tapes start blank. The total number of distinct work-tape cells visited, including the address tape and all temporary counters, is the workspace. This permits unrestricted repeated input access without charging the distance between input positions. Work-tape access uses ordinary moves. With only logarithmic work storage, the usual random-access work-memory or logarithmic-word variants can be simulated with polynomial-logarithmic time overhead and logarithmic space, so this quasilinear-time union is unchanged. There is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers, advice, oracle, external storage or extra catalytic tape.

At a random step the machine receives one fresh independent unbiased bit, at unit time cost. The random stream is available only in order and cannot be reread unless the machine stores the desired bits in its charged workspace. A random step is not a query to a random-access tape of reusable random bits. The machine eventually outputs accept or reject, without needing to output an assignment.

Write \(\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Membership in the displayed RTISP class would mean that one fixed machine and positive integer constants \(C,D\) satisfy, on every input and every random stream,
\[\text{time}\le T_N=D(N+2)\ell_N^k,\qquad \text{visited work cells}\le C\ell_N.\]
The harmless \(N+2\) makes the bound total at small lengths. Constants and \(k\) may depend on the machine, but not on the formula. In particular, this is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time or high-probability resource guarantee. At most \(T_N\) random bits can be consumed. Acceptance probability can therefore be defined as the fraction of strings in \(\{0,1\}^{T_N}\) that make the machine accept, ignoring unused trailing bits. For every valid satisfiable formula this fraction is at least \(2/3\); for every unsatisfiable or malformed input it is zero. A fixed positive success constant in place of \(2/3\) is equivalent by a constant number of repetitions, preserving the resource form and error direction.

The conjecture quantifies over every fixed \(k,C,D\) and every finite program. It concerns the simultaneous time-and-space class: a fast algorithm with large memory and a separate slow logarithmic-space algorithm would not supply the forbidden machine. The randomness is internal to the algorithm; inputs are arbitrary, not drawn from a specified distribution.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonexistence claim. A positive answer must exclude every uniform randomized machine, every fixed logarithmic-space constant, and every fixed polynomial-logarithmic time factor, with the specified one-way coins and error direction. A negative answer must give one machine and fixed \(k,C,D\), prove its time and space bounds on every random branch, and prove zero acceptance on no instances and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes instance. Bounds for deterministic machines, the opposite one-sided error, quantified formulas with extra quantifier alternations, a selected family of SAT solvers or expected resource usage do not establish this assertion. Neither an unproved separation such as P ≠ NP nor a conditional lower bound settles the unconditional target. The conclusion and probabilities have their exact stated meanings; no numerical approximation tolerance applies.
context:
Randomized search for a satisfying assignment may miss an assignment that exists, while an accepted assignment can be checked for correctness. This motivates the source’s error direction. The target nevertheless ranges over all decision algorithms with this error behavior, not just procedures that explicitly search for or output an assignment.

Logarithmic memory holds only a small number of indices and counters. The input can be read repeatedly, but the time bound permits only a polynomial-logarithmic amount of overhead beyond its length. Randomness supplies fresh choices without furnishing free reusable storage. All three features—input access, memory and access to coins—matter.

Diehl and van Melkebeek prove polynomial-strength randomized lower bounds for quantified Boolean formulas with at least two quantifier blocks. Their theorem’s restriction excludes plain existential satisfiability. Higher-level quantified formulas cannot simply be substituted for the SAT instances in this card.

Their one-sided lower bound for tautology yields a bound for SAT with the opposite permitted error: always accept a satisfiable formula, but possibly accept an unsatisfiable one. Complementing outputs switches both the language and the error side. It does not yield the requested lower bound for algorithms that never accept an unsatisfiable input.

The 2016 source explains why ordinary space-efficient derandomization does not already settle the question. Its polynomial running-time overhead is too large for the known deterministic time-space lower bounds to contradict the resulting SAT algorithm. A qualitative polynomial-time simulation does not preserve the near-linear time requirement.

The 2021 paper extends time-space lower bounds to problems with randomized or quantum verification. Its Main Theorem 3 concerns linear-time Merlin–Arthur and quantum Merlin–Arthur classes against randomized logarithmic-space machines. Such a verifier receives an additional proposed witness; lower bounds for those larger classes are not automatically lower bounds for SAT.
why: This asks whether the known obstruction to extremely fast, very low-memory SAT algorithms survives useful one-sided randomness. An unconditional answer would advance lower bounds for a central NP-complete problem in a general computation model.
status_note: Source-open for the one-sided-error direction in the original Problem 5. The full source column, Diehl–van Melkebeek’s 2006 main statements and §§2.1–2.2 model conventions, and the 2021 Main Theorem 3/Definition 1 were read. The checked randomized results concern the opposite error direction or larger quantified/verification classes. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of this exact randomized SAT target; this is not an exhaustive literature or independent proof certification.
progress: 2006: Randomized time-space lower bounds are proved for higher levels of the polynomial hierarchy and for tautology with one-sided error; the SAT error direction asked here remains distinct. | 2016: Problem 5 explicitly isolates randomized quasilinear-time logarithmic-space SAT with no error on unsatisfiable inputs. | 2021: New randomized time-space lower bounds apply to problems admitting Merlin–Arthur verification, with Main Theorem 3 retaining that larger problem class.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary explicitly written satisfiability instance. A candidate algorithm may use fresh random bits, logarithmic working memory and time n times a fixed polynomial in log n. It must never accept an unsatisfiable formula and must accept each satisfiable formula with constant probability. Both resource bounds hold for the same machine on every sequence of random choices. The target is an unconditional lower bound against every such algorithm; known opposite-error and larger-class results do not settle it.

title: Real quantifier alternation versus summation
importance_reason: The question asks whether a counting-like arithmetic extension can absorb all fixed levels of real quantifier alternation. It would organize a broad hierarchy of real-feasibility and geometric decision problems and distinguish the power of Boolean summation from the stronger succinct and product extensions.
formal: For every fixed \(t\ge1\), does the truth problem for closed real-arithmetic sentences with at most \(t\) alternating quantifier blocks admit a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\), the existential theory of the reals with Boolean summation binders? Equivalently, is every fixed level of the real polynomial hierarchy contained in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) as defined below? The polynomial-time reduction and its degree may depend on \(t\); the number of real variables in each block is unrestricted. Either existential or universal first blocks are included.
definitions:
The source input is a closed prenex sentence \(Q_1X_1\cdots Q_sX_s\,\phi\), where \(0\le s\le t\), each \(X_j\) is a finite tuple of distinct real variables, consecutive \(Q_j\in\{\exists,\forall\}\) differ, and every quantified variable ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\). There are no free variables. The matrix \(\phi\) is a finite Boolean formula using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and comparisons \(u=v\), \(u<v\), or \(u\le v\). Its arithmetic terms are finite expression trees built from integer constants, variables, binary addition, subtraction and multiplication. Integers are encoded by a sign and ordinary binary magnitude; variable indices are binary integers. Fix a parenthesized prefix encoding over a finite alphabet for all tree nodes, operators, variable indices and tuple lists. Input size is the full bit length of this encoding. There is no shared-subexpression circuit, implicit large power, summation binder or succinct indexing in these source terms. Binary integer constants and subtraction can equivalently be expressed using the source papers’ constants \(0,1\) and ring operations with polynomial overhead.

A target \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\) instance is a closed sentence \(\exists y_1\cdots\exists y_m\,\psi\), where \(m\ge0\), \(\psi\) is a Boolean formula of the same comparisons, and its arithmetic expression trees additionally allow the binder \(\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}}u\). This denotes \(u[b:=0]+u[b:=1]\). The bound symbol \(b\) is a local dummy scalar variable, distinct from the existentially quantified real variables and from other active dummy variables; usual capture-free substitution fixes its semantics. Binders may be nested, and their body is stored once, so nesting can describe exponentially many summands. All free variables in terms must be among the explicitly listed \(y_j\) or in scope of a summation binder. A dummy value may occur as a number in a term but cannot select a variable name: an expression such as \(y_b\), with a value-dependent index, is forbidden. No product binder, Boolean-formula binder, arbitrary real constant, real exponentiation, extra real quantifier alternation or succinct circuit representation is allowed. The size counts the finite syntax including each binder and its body, rather than the fully expanded sum. Thus the number of distinct existential real variables is at most the target length.

A deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction is a single finite-program multitape Turing machine that, on each valid input string of length \(L\), outputs one valid target sentence within \(C_t(L+1)^{c_t}\) bit transitions and preserves truth in both directions. It uses no random bits, advice, real-arithmetic oracle or decision oracle. Output length and all construction work count. Constants \(C_t,c_t\) and the machine may depend on the fixed block bound \(t\), but not on a particular input. The target class \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) consists of binary-string languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to truth of these target sentences. The real polynomial hierarchy here is the union of the analogous closures of the source truth problems over all fixed \(t\). Its definition does not allow the block bound to grow with the input length.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof providing a truth-preserving polynomial-time reduction for every fixed block bound \(t\), or a complete Lean proof that such a reduction fails for at least one fixed \(t\). The affirmative proof must respect the target’s explicit variable list and summation-only syntax. context:

title: Downward self-reducibility of PLS-complete problems
importance_reason: The universal structural question is now equivalent to the major algorithmic frontier PLS versus polynomial-time search. It illustrates a consequential dependence on representation and distinguishes a conditional structural obstruction from an unconditional search lower bound.
formal:
Is every PLS-complete total search problem downward self-reducible with respect to the bit length of its input? Precisely, for every binary relation \(R\) that is PLS-complete under polynomial-time search many-one reductions, must there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time oracle algorithm that finds an \(R\)-solution on every input \(x\), using an oracle for the same relation \(R\) only on strings \(z\) with \(|z|<|x|\)? It must work for every valid choice of solutions returned by that oracle.

The SODA 2026 result identifies this universal statement with \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). This is an equivalence with an unresolved complexity-class equality, rather than an unconditional affirmative or negative resolution of the card.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 3.4 asks whether every PLS-complete problem is downward self-reducible.
definitions:
A total NP search problem is a relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\{0,1\}^{*}\) with three properties. Every input \(x\) has at least one valid output \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); all such outputs have length at most one fixed polynomial \(p(|x|)\); and membership \(R(x,y)\) is decidable by a uniform deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in \(|x|+|y|\). The class of these relations is TFNP. Solving \(R\) means producing any one valid output on every input, not enumerating all outputs or selecting a preferred one. Inputs include every binary string; any malformed-instance convention must be specified as part of the relation and preserve totality.

A polynomial-time search many-one reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of uniform polynomial-time functions \(a(x)\) and \(b(x,y)\) such that
\[\forall x,y,\qquad Q(a(x),y)\Longrightarrow R(x,b(x,y)).\]
Thus every solution of the transformed instance must decode to a valid original solution. There is one oracle instance per reduction, with no promise about which solution will be returned.

PLS, polynomial local search, can be defined using the following standard circuit local-optimum problem. An instance explicitly describes positive integers \(m,r\) and Boolean circuits \(S:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(v:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{r}\). Circuit outputs of \(v\) are read as unsigned binary integers. Find a string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{m}\) such that
\[v(S(u))\le v(u).\]
Circuits are finite acyclic lists of AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with input and output wires explicitly listed; full descriptions, indices and dimensions count toward instance bit length. There is always a valid \(u\), for example any point maximizing \(v\) over the finite domain. On malformed circuit descriptions the only valid output is the empty string. This gives a total, polynomially balanced, efficiently verifiable relation. PLS consists of the TFNP relations reducible to this circuit problem by the reductions above; this is the usual polynomial-local-search class, equivalently presented by the source’s Sink-of-DAG complete problem. A relation \(R\) is PLS-complete if it is in PLS and every relation in PLS reduces to it. Completeness is not restricted to familiar combinatorial problems or any preferred encoding.

A solution oracle for \(R\) is any total selector \(O:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) satisfying \(R(z,O(z))\) for every \(z\). The selector need not be computable. Downward self-reducibility requires one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(A\) and constants \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid selector \(O\) and every input \(x\), the computation \(A^O(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) steps, outputs a valid \(R\)-solution for \(x\), and queries only strings shorter than \(x\). Query writing, answer reading and ordinary computation are charged; the oracle’s computation of an answer is not. Later queries may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries receive the selector’s same answer. The machine must handle every selector, rather than assume a canonical or favorable solution. In particular, on the empty input it can make no query. All programs and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed relation \(R\), but not on its individual input or the chosen selector.

“Smaller” means strictly fewer input bits, \(|z|<|x|\). It does not mean a smaller potential value, fewer circuit variables with a longer description, or a separately chosen well-founded measure. Queries must be to the identical encoded relation \(R\), not to an interchangeable PLS-complete problem. The total polynomial bound covers the one oracle computation; it does not presume that expanding all recursive oracle calls takes polynomial time.

In the known equivalence, \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\) is shorthand for: every relation in PLS has a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm producing a valid solution on every input. This does not identify a relation with a single-valued function. The question’s quantifier order is: for every PLS-complete relation, there exist a machine and polynomial bound that work for every input and every valid solution selector.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal statement for the stated many-one reductions and strict bit-length notion. A positive answer must establish downward self-reducibility for every PLS-complete relation. A negative answer must establish a PLS-complete relation for which no such oracle algorithm exists, with the completeness and nonexistence proofs both checked. It is equivalent to settle whether all PLS problems have polynomial-time solution algorithms, provided the equivalence is also supplied or imported as a proved Lean theorem. Merely proving the existing equivalence, assuming \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), or giving a counterexample conditional on that assumption does not answer the exact yes/no target. Nor does a result only about a broader size measure, a restricted family of encodings or one chosen complete problem. Asymptotic class and quantifier statements are exact; no numerical tolerance applies.
context:
A downward self-reduction turns a problem into calls to smaller instances of itself. For a total search problem, each call always has some valid answer, but a reduction cannot choose which answer it receives. This combines a recursive structure with a requirement of robustness to all solutions.

The original paper proves downward self-reducibility for a canonical PLS-complete problem and proves that every downward self-reducible TFNP problem belongs to PLS. These statements establish an important connection, but neither says that downward self-reducibility transfers through every completeness reduction.

Input representation matters because a polynomial-time reduction may increase bit length. A query that is smaller in one presentation need not remain smaller after translating back to another complete problem. The universal target includes all binary encodings satisfying the definitions, rather than only natural examples.

The later paper proves the exact equivalence: every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). Its §7.1 gives a PLS-complete relation whose downward self-reducibility would force a polynomial-time solver. Therefore, under \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), the answer is no. The theorem does not prove that assumption.

The equivalence changes how the original question should be understood: a universal affirmative answer would settle the algorithmic complexity of all polynomial local search, while an unconditional negative answer would prove that some such total search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. The card keeps that unconditional target.

The 2026 paper also studies self-reductions that decrease a more general size measure. Its final discussion leaves a separate universal question for that broader notion. That question is not substituted for the original strict input-length formulation.
why: The question tests whether a recursive structure characterizes every representation of hard local search. The newer equivalence shows that its unconditional resolution would also resolve whether all PLS problems can be solved in polynomial time.
status_note: Source-open as an unconditional yes/no target, with major subsequent classification: the SODA 2026 paper (published 7 January; open 2025 full manuscript Theorem 6 and §7.1) proves that every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if PLS=FP. Definitions 2.1–2.8 and the entire §7.1 conditional counterexample proof were read, along with the original ITCS definitions and Open Problem 3.4. This does not prove PLS≠FP, so no unconditional negative answer or archival resolution is claimed. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching unconditional resolution. No independent Lean formalization of the cited proof was performed.

working_summary: The target asks whether every PLS-complete total search relation can be solved using only shorter instances of itself. Shorter means fewer bits in the full input encoding, and the reduction must work for every valid solution oracle. The original paper proves the property for a canonical complete problem and places downward self-reducible total NP search in PLS. A SODA 2026 result proves that the universal statement holds exactly when every PLS problem is solvable in polynomial time. Its conditional negative result is recorded as progress; the card retains the unconditional yes/no question.

title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) perfect matching
importance_reason: A concrete major test of the logarithmic-depth and polynomial-formula frontier, with a direct implication for nonuniform class separation and a clear distinction from the broader NC matching question.
formal:
Does perfect-matching decision for general undirected graphs have nonuniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and logarithmic depth?

For each integer \(v\ge2\), let \(\mathrm{PM}_v:\{0,1\}^{\binom v2}\to\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the encoded graph has a perfect matching. The target is the existence of fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\) and circuits \((C_v)_{v\ge2}\) such that
\[\forall v\ge2,\quad |C_v|\le a(v+1)^b,\qquad\operatorname{depth}(C_v)\le d\lceil\log_2(v+2)\rceil,\]
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\binom v2},\qquad C_v(x)=\mathrm{PM}_v(x).\]
The gates have fan-in at most two, and negation is allowed. The circuits need not be generated uniformly, and the output is only the decision bit.
definitions:
A graph has vertex set \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and an arbitrary set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices as edges. It is simple, undirected and unweighted, with no promise of bipartiteness, planarity, bounded degree or a matching already known to exist. Its input bits are \(x_{ij}\) for \(1\le i<j\le v\), in lexicographic order; \(x_{ij}=1\) precisely when the edge is present. Every bit string of this length is a valid graph. The input length \(m=\binom v2\) is polynomially related to \(v\), so the polynomial-size and logarithmic-depth requirements have the same meaning with either parameter. The statement starts at \(v=2\); the fixed zero- and one-vertex cases do not affect the asymptotic question.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to exactly one selected edge. Consequently \(\mathrm{PM}_v=0\) for odd \(v\). The algorithmic target is to output one bit indicating existence, not to construct a matching, count matchings or decide a weighted exact-value variant.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with variable inputs, constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. A gate output can feed arbitrarily many later gates. The size \(|C|\) is the number of computational gates, and depth is the maximum number of such gates on a path to the output. Variable and constant inputs have depth zero and do not count toward size. Input handling here is entirely through the indicated input wires; no oracle, random bits, threshold gates or unbounded-fan-in AND/OR primitives are present. Correctness is exact on every assignment.

Nonuniform means that each \(C_v\) may be chosen independently; there is no computability, logspace generation or polynomial-time construction requirement on the sequence. The integers \(a,b,d\) must nevertheless be fixed across all graph orders. This is the usual nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) target. A circuit satisfying the logarithmic depth bound can be expanded into a tree of polynomial size, so the simultaneous size requirement causes no additional asymptotic restriction in this single-output bounded-fan-in setting.

Equivalently, \(\mathrm{PM}_v\) must have polynomial-size De Morgan formulas. Such a formula is a rooted tree of binary AND/OR gates with possibly negated variable leaves; each repeated occurrence of a variable is counted separately, and internal values cannot be shared. Formula balancing yields logarithmic depth from polynomial leaf size. A negative answer is failure of every polynomial formula bound for this fixed family, or equivalently that its minimum circuit depth is not \(O(\log v)\); a lower bound may be witnessed at arbitrarily large graph orders rather than at every order.

For source fidelity, the draft’s function \(\mathrm{Match}_v\) asks whether the maximum matching size is at least \(v/3+1\), interpreted as the integer threshold \(k_v=\lceil v/3+1\rceil\). The two decision families are equivalent for the present circuit class. To express a size-at-least-\(k\) question as perfect matching, when \(0\le k\le v/2\), add \(v-2k\) new vertices adjacent to every original vertex and to no new vertex. The enlarged graph has a perfect matching exactly when the original graph has a matching of size at least \(k\). Thresholds above \(\lfloor v/2\rfloor\) are constantly false. Conversely, for a graph on \(2q\) vertices with \(q\ge3\), adding \(q-3\) isolated vertices makes the source threshold \((3q-3)/3+1=q\), so its Match answer is exactly the original perfect-matching answer. Smaller graph orders and odd perfect-matching orders have fixed finite answers. These transformations copy input bits and add fixed adjacency bits with only linear growth in vertex count, and hence preserve the nonuniform logarithmic-depth question in both directions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonuniform circuit-family existence claim. A positive answer must establish polynomial size, logarithmic depth and exact correctness on every general graph with constants fixed across graph orders; a uniform construction is welcome but not required. A negative answer must prove that no such family exists, equivalently that perfect matching has no polynomial-size De Morgan formula family. A lower bound only for monotone circuits, a polylogarithmic-depth upper bound, a bipartite-only result or a quasipolynomial size bound is insufficient.
context:
The source places the matching question immediately after its general polynomial-size versus logarithmic-depth question. It proves a linear depth lower bound for monotone matching circuits, where negative occurrences are forbidden. That restriction is absent from the present target, so the monotone theorem does not answer it.

The source names a matching-size threshold rather than perfect matching. The explicit transformations in the definitions justify retaining the inherited perfect-matching title without silently attributing that exact wording to the draft.

The 2017 general-graph algorithm achieves polylogarithmic parallel time using quasipolynomially many processors. This is an important deterministic upper bound, but neither its depth nor its processor count meets the NC-one target.

The July 2026 revision claims deterministic NC algorithms for bipartite matching, including weighted and search variants. Even accepting the stated theorem, bipartite graphs and polylogarithmic depth do not give the general-graph logarithmic-depth decision family requested here.
why: Perfect matching is a central polynomial-time graph problem whose exact bounded-fan-in depth remains poorly understood. A negative answer would separate nonuniform NC-one from P/poly using a concrete polynomial-time task. A positive answer would put the decision problem at a much shallower level than the broad polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithms studied in most matching work.

title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
importance_reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.
formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
definitions: Encode symbols \(0,1,2\) by \(00,01,10\), respectively, using a fixed ordered pair of bits for each input position. A circuit for length \(n\) is a finite acyclic directed Boolean circuit with \(2n\) ordered input bits and \(2n\) ordered output bits. Its non-input gates are binary AND, binary OR, unary NOT and optional constant-0 or constant-1 gates. Each such gate, including a constant gate, contributes one to size. Fan-out is unrestricted. Wires and output designations have no separate cost, and the same gate or input can feed multiple gates and outputs. The circuit is deterministic. It must be correct on every concatenation of valid input encodings; behavior on any input containing a pair \(11\) is unrestricted. For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1,2\}^n\), let \(i_1<\cdots<i_m\) be exactly the indices where \(a_i\ne2\). The required output encodes \(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}\) followed by \(n-m\) copies of \(2\). This definition includes \(m=0\) and \(m=n\). In particular, it preserves the relative order of a \(0\) and a \(1\); it does not sort them against each other. All output positions must be produced by one circuit and their gates are counted jointly. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum permitted circuit size for this promise function. The quantifiers are \(\exists C\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\exists\mathcal C_n\), with \(|\mathcal C_n|\le Cn\) and exact correctness on all valid inputs. The circuit may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and no algorithm constructing \(\mathcal C_n\) is required. The circuit may compute on the individual encoding bits; it is not restricted to comparing or routing indivisible records.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(s(n)\le Cn\) for some universal \(C\) and all \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation \(\forall C\ge1\;\exists n\ge1,\ s(n)>Cn\). The negative statement rules out every nonuniform family in the defined unrestricted Boolean model; a lower bound for comparators or indivisible-record routing does not suffice. A conditional result under an additional conjecture settles only that conditional version. A positive answer must retain the original order of the \(0\)s and \(1\)s, with an exact linear size bound rather than a bound multiplied by an unbounded iterated-logarithm factor.
context:
Regan’s July 2007 problem defines precisely the order-preserving movement of all dummy symbols to the right. The present two-bit encoding and complete Boolean basis make its nonuniform linear-size target explicit.

Ordinary ternary sorting discards the order between retained zeros and ones. Stable compaction must preserve that binary sequence, so a circuit that only counts occurrences of the three symbols computes a different function.

Asharov, Lin and Shi obtain improved Boolean circuits for compaction and sorting short keys, but their construction deliberately does not preserve stability. Their discussion distinguishes unrestricted Boolean computation from the indivisible-payload model used in some stable-compaction lower bounds.

Lin and Shi’s SODA 2022 work improves the depth of short-key sorting circuits while retaining near-linear size bounds with iterated-logarithm factors in the relevant short-key regime. Its Introduction explicitly states that the sorting is not stable. This result therefore does not provide a linear-size circuit for the stable ternary function.

The checked literature also discusses conditional lower bounds based on the Li–Li network-coding conjecture. Such conditional bounds and lower bounds for restricted data-movement models are not unconditional impossibility results for this card.
why: This is an elementary deterministic rearrangement whose output preserves an arbitrary binary subsequence. Its sequential simplicity contrasts with the difficulty of arranging all output bits in a fixed circuit. Resolving linear circuit size would sharpen the boundary between data movement with input-dependent access and unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean computation.
status_note: The original author question is from 2007. The checked 2021/2022 sorting advances are non-stable and do not settle its exact linear-size target. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-16 found no unconditional resolution in the stated Boolean model; this is a limited review, not a certification of all subsequent literature.

working_summary: Stable ternary compaction moves every 2 to the end while preserving the order of all zeros and ones. The question asks whether each input length admits an exact Boolean circuit of size proportional to that length. Circuits may have arbitrary depth and fan-out and may compute freely on the fixed two-bit alphabet encoding. Non-stable compaction and ordinary ternary sorting do not retain the binary sequence required in the answer. The checked short-key sorting advances and conditional or restricted lower bounds do not resolve this nonuniform linear-size question.

title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
importance_reason: A structural conjecture about formula composition that could turn local lower bounds into stronger general formula lower bounds.
formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[L(g\circ f)\ge\alpha L(g)L(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
definitions:
For a positive integer \(r\), a total Boolean function is a map \(h:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\). Nonconstant means that it takes both values on its domain; it need not depend on every designated input coordinate. A De Morgan formula for \(h\) is a finite rooted tree whose internal operations are binary AND, binary OR, and unary NOT, and whose leaves are input variables or the constant bits zero and one. Its value is obtained by the usual Boolean operations from leaves to the root. It must compute \(h\) exactly on every input, with no randomness or promise on input values. There are no parity, threshold, arbitrary truth-table or unbounded-fan-in gates.

Formula size is the number of occurrences of input variables among its leaves. Positive and negated occurrences both count, and different occurrences of the same variable count separately. Constant leaves are free and can be eliminated from an optimum for a nonconstant function. NOT operations can be pushed onto variables without changing this measure. The minimum over all such formulas is \(L(h)\); it is a finite positive integer for nonconstant \(h\). No internal value can be shared between two parent operations: such reuse would produce a circuit rather than a formula.

The composed function has exactly \(mn\) designated coordinates \(x^{(j)}_i\), with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Block coordinates are distinct and unconstrained. The same inner function \(f\) is applied to every block, and its outputs, in block order, become the inputs of \(g\). The composition symbol here means this block operation, not ordinary composition of two maps with the same domain. Both functions and their composition may be specified by arbitrary finite truth tables, and no uniformity, polynomial-time evaluability, or monotonicity is assumed.

Since both functions are nonconstant, every Boolean vector supplied to \(g\) can be realized by some collection of blocks, and the composition is nonconstant. The usual substitution bound gives \(L(g\circ f)\le L(g)L(f)\). The question is whether the ratio to that upper bound is bounded away from zero uniformly over all functions and dimensions. Equivalently, is the infimum of these positive ratios strictly positive? This infimum need not be attained. Restricting \(0<\alpha\le1\) is equivalent.

The negation says that for every positive \(\alpha\), some pair and dimensions have ratio smaller than \(\alpha\). Thus a single saving relative to exact multiplication, or even failure of one proposed constant, is insufficient to refute the claim. Allowing constant functions with the convention \(L(h)=0\) would add only trivial inequalities; their exclusion makes the ratio formulation well-defined. Minimum depth, which counts gates along a longest path, is a different measure from the number of leaves.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the constant-loss formula-size statement. A positive answer must establish one strictly positive factor for every permitted pair and dimensions. A negative answer must establish ratios arbitrarily close to zero, not merely a finite violation of equality or an unbounded additive saving in formula depth. Bounds for almost all functions, for special inner functions, for monotone formulas, or for a stronger communication search task do not alone prove the all-function claim. A composition inequality with a loss depending on either dimension, even polylogarithmically, is a weaker result unless upgraded to the fixed constant required here.
context:
The book displays an absolute multiplicative constant in Conjecture 5.13. Its accompanying footnote also permits investigation of weaker losses and typical-function variants. The title and acceptance criterion identify which of those possibilities this record actually asks for.

The 1995 paper’s Open Question 4.1 asks about depth under composition and records examples with a growing additive loss in that measure. Those depth examples are not, by themselves, counterexamples to a constant-factor statement about minimum formula leaf count. The original paper and the later size formulation must be distinguished.

The 2023 paper explicitly distinguishes the original depth conjecture from the formula-size variant. Its Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2 prove composition bounds involving a separate inner-function complexity measure and dimension-dependent losses. Those theorems give important restricted comparisons without supplying the universal constant asserted in this card.

The 2025 STACS result concerns strong composition of communication relations: in addition to finding a differing input bit, the answer must lie in a block where the two inner-function outputs differ. That added requirement makes a different search task. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.
