title: A counting characterization of P with NP access
importance_reason: A structural comparison of two central forms of computation: NP-oracle decision and exact witness counting. Its connection to the polynomial hierarchy and the consequence of a negative answer make it substantial beyond one representation or reduction.
formal:
Does there exist one total counting function \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) such that
\[\mathrm P^f=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}?\]
The oracle for \(f\) returns its exact nonnegative integer value in binary. Both sides are classes of decision problems with deterministic, adaptive polynomial-time oracle access. This asks about the ordinary, unrelativized classes; no auxiliary oracle or complexity separation is assumed.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 6.3 asks whether a #P function can have exactly the polynomial-time oracle power of NP.
definitions:
All inputs and oracle queries are finite binary strings. Write \(|x|\) for the full bit length, and let \(\mathbb N\) include zero. A function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathbb N\) belongs to \(\#\mathrm P\) if there are one deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(V(x,y)\) and one polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable length function \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[f(x)=\bigl|\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\}\bigr|\]
for every string \(x\). Each witness string is counted once. This is an exact count, not a signed difference of counts, an approximation, a parity bit or a mere indication of nonemptiness. In particular, \(f(x)\le2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has polynomial length; zero is encoded as the one-bit string 0.

Use uniform deterministic multitape oracle Turing machines. A machine has one finite program independent of input length, a read-only input tape and ordinary work, query and answer tapes. It writes a query string \(z\), invokes the fixed oracle and receives the canonical binary expansion of \(f(z)\). The oracle's internal computation is not charged; writing queries, reading answer bits and all subsequent computation are charged. The oracle response is exact. The machine must halt on every input of length \(n\) in at most \(C(n+1)^d\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,d\). It may make polynomially many queries, and later queries may depend on earlier answers. There is no advice, randomness, nondeterminism or second oracle. The union over such machines defines the language class \(\mathrm P^f\); different languages may use different programs and polynomial bounds, but all use the same \(f\).

For the decision oracle, fix an explicit binary encoding of Boolean formulas as finite AND/OR/NOT expression trees with variable identifiers. SAT returns 1 exactly for a well-formed satisfiable formula, and returns 0 on an unsatisfiable formula or malformed string. The whole formula is written explicitly, including identifiers and delimiters. Since SAT is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) here means \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}\). An SAT-oracle machine receives one exact decision bit per query; it has the same uniformity, adaptive access and polynomial running-time convention. \(\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) denotes the analogous functions computed by machines that output a finite binary string instead of a decision bit.

The displayed equality has the equivalent concrete requirements
\[\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm P^f\qquad\text{and}\qquad f\in\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}.\]
Thus one fixed counting function must be strong enough to decide SAT, yet every value of that function must be computable using only polynomial time and SAT queries. Equality implies the second requirement because querying a particular output bit of \(f\) is a decision problem in \(\mathrm P^f\), and there are polynomially many bits. The converse follows by replacing oracle calls by the stated simulations. This equivalence fixes the decision/function distinction; it adds no single-query, nonadaptive or parsimonious-reduction requirement.

The existential quantifier is over all \(\#\mathrm P\) functions. The selected function need not be \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete or count satisfying assignments of its input formula. There is no requirement that one algorithm uniformly discover a suitable function from an arbitrary verifier. A refutation must rule out every possible fixed \(\#\mathrm P\) function, not just the familiar \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) function.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. A positive answer must define one total \(f\), prove its \(\#\mathrm P\) representation and prove both class containments, with the uniform polynomial-time oracle simulations justified. Equivalently, prove both concrete requirements in the definitions. A negative answer must prove that every \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) fails at least one containment. An oracle-relative separation, a conditional statement assuming an unproved class separation, an approximate count, or one candidate that fails does not settle this unrelativized question. The target is exact class equality; numerical approximation tolerances do not apply.
context:
A SAT oracle reports whether a witness exists. A counting oracle can disclose far more information by reporting how many witnesses exist. This question asks whether some genuine count has exactly the power of repeated SAT decisions, with neither a deficit nor a surplus of computational power.

The familiar choice \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) counts all satisfying assignments. Toda’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\mathrm P^{\#\mathrm{SAT}}\), where \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}\), \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\), and \(\Sigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}}\). Therefore equality with \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) for this particular complete counting function would collapse the whole polynomial hierarchy to \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\). This is a conditional consequence, not a proof that this candidate or every other candidate fails.

Fortnow places the question next to the checkability of SAT: whether a randomized polynomial-time checker can assess the answer of a purported SAT solver using that solver as an oracle. The source describes a possible connection between counting and checking, not a proved equivalence between the two open questions.

The 2021 source does not even know a counting function satisfying the weaker pair \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm P^f\subseteq\mathrm{PH}\). That observation is dated context; the benchmark retains the stronger equality of Conjecture 6.3.

The surrounding article studies relativization: what happens when machines receive an additional fixed oracle. Its section heading requests an oracle world with no such counting characterization. That separate construction would not refute the ordinary-world target stated here.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the constant-zero counting function already meets the equality. Consequently, a negative answer here would imply \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). This is an immediate consequence of the definitions, not an additional hypothesis in the card.
why: The question asks whether existential search has a precise counting counterpart at the level of computational power. Resolving it would clarify the boundary between deciding existence, counting witnesses and the polynomial hierarchy, while a negative answer would also separate P from NP.

Theorem 1.1 and §§2–4 of the 2009 Theory of Computing paper were read for the hierarchy comparison. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification. The equivalence of the two simulation requirements and the P=NP observation are elementary editorial consequences of the stated definitions, not new attributed theorems.

working_summary: The target asks for one #P counting function whose polynomial-time oracle power is exactly P with an NP oracle. The count is an exact nonnegative integer returned in binary, and oracle queries may be adaptive. The same function must allow SAT decisions while itself being computable using SAT queries. Complete counting can already capture the whole polynomial hierarchy, so choosing a weaker count is a substantive requirement. The question concerns ordinary complexity classes, separately from the source’s request for a relativized counterexample.

title: Improving the log-space SAT time exponent beyond 2 cos(π/7)
importance_reason: A modest-looking quantitative improvement sits beyond a proved limit of a major lower-bound method. The concrete target advances the uniform SAT frontier, though one exponent alone would not settle a standard class separation.
formal:
Let \(\alpha=2\cos(\pi/7)\), approximately \(1.8019377\). Does there exist a rational constant \(q>\alpha\) such that no uniform deterministic random-access algorithm decides SAT using both \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) workspace on every input of bit length \(N\)? In symbols, is
\[\exists q\in\mathbb Q,\quad q>2\cos(\pi/7)\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]?\]
This is the fixed positive improvement explicitly proposed in Problem 1. The two resource bounds must belong to the same machine.
question_excerpt: Problem 1 asks to improve SAT time lower bounds on logarithmic-space machines and explicitly proposes excluding time n raised to 2 cos(π/7) plus a fixed positive constant.
definitions:
SAT is satisfiability of explicitly encoded Boolean 3-CNF formulas, as permitted by the source. Each clause contains at most three literals, each a variable or its negation; the formula is a conjunction of clauses. It is satisfiable if some Boolean assignment to its occurring variables makes it true. Empty clauses are false and the conjunction of no clauses is true. The input is a fixed self-delimiting binary list of clauses, signed variable identifiers and delimiters. Identifiers can be chosen from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused names permitted. All occurrences and identifiers count in the total bit length \(N\). The encoding is explicit, and malformed strings are rejected. Size is not just the number of variables, and there is no promise of sparse occurrences or compressed access to the formula.

Fix a deterministic random-access bit-machine model: a finite Turing-machine program with a fixed number of initially blank finite-alphabet work tapes, including a tape for a binary input address. A query reads the input bit at that address in one step, returning an endmarker out of range. Constructing, changing and storing addresses uses charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only. Work heads use ordinary tape moves; every distinct work cell visited, including address bits, counters and blank cells crossed, counts toward space. There are no random bits, nondeterministic choices, advice, oracles, catalytic storage or unbounded-precision unit-cost operations. The machine halts with an accept/reject answer on every input.

For a fixed \(q\), membership in \(\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]\) means that there exist one such correct machine and constants \(C,D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with
\[\text{time on }x\le D\left\lceil(N+2)^q\right\rceil,\qquad
\text{visited work cells on }x\le C\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\]
for every binary input \(x\) of length \(N\). Bounds include parsing and malformed inputs. They are worst-case bounds with no distribution on formulas. The hidden constants may depend on the machine and on \(q\), but not on the input or its length. A different slow small-space algorithm and fast large-space algorithm do not establish this simultaneous membership.

The general-purpose random-access convention prevents a lower bound caused solely by slow movement across the input. Standard logarithmic-workspace word or work-memory random-access models can be simulated in this bit model using logarithmic space and a polynomial-logarithmic time factor. Conversely, a word machine can implement its elementary bit operations. Since the target asks for some fixed exponent strictly larger than \(\alpha\), such factors can be absorbed by choosing a slightly smaller positive improvement. This convention does not ask for a sharp model-dependent boundary at the exponent \(\alpha\) itself.

The outer quantifier chooses one \(q>\alpha\); the resulting lower bound must exclude every eligible machine and all \(C,D\). Allowing an arbitrary real exponent instead of a rational one gives the same existence question, since a rational exponent can be chosen strictly between \(\alpha\) and any proposed larger exponent. The exact trigonometric constant defines the threshold; its displayed decimal is only explanatory. A negative answer would mean that for every rational \(q>\alpha\) some eligible algorithm achieves the stated time and space bounds. These algorithms may depend on \(q\); the negation does not require a single algorithm simultaneously meeting all exponents or running in \(N^{\alpha+o(1)}\) time.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential lower-bound statement. A positive answer must specify an exponent \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\) and rule out every correct, total deterministic algorithm with simultaneous \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) visited workspace. A negative answer must establish the existence of an appropriate correct algorithm for every rational \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\), with its own fixed resource constants allowed. A result only below the threshold, for a restricted algorithm or proof paradigm, for counting satisfiable assignments, or for a larger verification class does not settle this target. Neither evidence from proof search nor an unproved hardness assumption is an unconditional solution. The exponent comparison and asymptotic quantifiers must be proved exactly; the decimal approximation and a numerical tolerance cannot replace them.
context:
A logarithmic-space algorithm may repeatedly reread the formula while retaining very little information. Repeated reading saves memory but costs time. This card asks for a larger unconditional exponent in that time cost, with logarithmic memory kept fixed.

Williams’s lower bound rules out deterministic subpolynomial-space SAT algorithms with time exponent below \(2\cos(\pi/7)\). Subpolynomial space means \(N^{o(1)}\): smaller than every fixed positive power of \(N\), and includes logarithmic space. The target here asks to move strictly above that exponent in the particular logarithmic-space regime.

Buss and Williams prove an exact limitation of a formalized family of alternation-trading arguments. Theorem 1.1 concerns their inference rules R0–R2; these rules cannot establish a contradiction beyond the threshold. This is a theorem about those proof rules, not an upper-bound algorithm for SAT or an impossibility theorem for all mathematical lower-bound arguments.

The 2021 paper obtains stronger exponents for problems admitting quantum or randomized verification with a proposed witness. It also recovers the classical SAT threshold in its general framework. The stronger results retain their different verification classes and cannot be read as an improved SAT exponent.

The 2023 discussion separates two kinds of lower bounds. A simultaneous bound excludes a single machine that is both fast and space-efficient. A separate-algorithm alternative says that SAT cannot have both a fast algorithm and another sufficiently space-efficient algorithm. The logical forms differ, and neither removes its space qualification automatically.

Proving one larger fixed exponent would be a concrete advance, but would not by itself prove P ≠ NP or L ≠ NP. A logarithmic-space SAT algorithm, if one existed, could still have a larger fixed polynomial running time. Excluding all polynomial exponents in logarithmic space would be the stronger class separation.
why: A fixed improvement would cross a precisely understood limit of the established proof framework for unconditional SAT time-space lower bounds. It would strengthen our understanding of how little memory constrains computation on an NP-complete problem.

Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 found no fixed improvement matching the stated logarithmic-space SAT target. Source/model and theorem scopes were checked; no independent proof certification of the complete lower-bound literature is claimed.

working_summary: The input is a Boolean satisfiability formula measured by its complete binary length. The proposed lower bound applies to deterministic algorithms that use only logarithmic writable memory and can query any input location. The goal is to exclude some time exponent strictly larger than 2 cos(π/7), with the same machine subject to both resource bounds. Known lower bounds approach the threshold from below, and a theorem limits a formalized proof method at that threshold. A refutation must provide algorithms for every larger exponent, possibly different algorithms for different exponents.

title: NEXP circuit lower bounds from uniform obfuscation
importance_reason: A consequential link between uniform cryptographic security and a major unrestricted circuit lower bound. The source proves the conclusion with stronger nonuniform security, making the exact missing hypothesis substantive rather than a cosmetic model choice.
formal:
Prove or refute the following implication:
\[\text{a uniform polynomial-time, perfectly correct, uniformly secure IO exists}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}.\]
IO means indistinguishability obfuscation for general Boolean circuits, with the source's security definition specified below. Security is required only against uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this particular circuit lower bound from the source's broader question. The target keeps perfect correctness and removes the stronger nonuniform-security hypothesis under which the source already proves this conclusion.
question_excerpt: Section 9 asks whether circuit lower bounds follow from obfuscation secure against uniform efficient algorithms. The user selected the particular conclusion NEXP not contained in P/poly, under perfect correctness; the source proves that conclusion under stronger security against nonuniform polynomial-size circuits.
definitions:
An input circuit is an explicitly encoded finite acyclic Boolean circuit with a listed set of input bits, AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, optional constants, and one output bit. Wires may be reused without restriction and depth is unrestricted. Gate types and wire indices are written in a topologically ordered list; the number of inputs and the output wire are included. Circuit size for the obfuscation definition means the bit length \(s\) of this explicit description. The encoding admits ignored padding, so a circuit can be represented by larger descriptions without changing its function, as in the source's Remark 6. Write \(C_0\equiv C_1\) when they have the same input arity and output the same bit on every input. The algorithm must handle all finite circuits, not merely a selected efficiently generated circuit family.

An obfuscator \(\mathcal O\) is one uniform randomized Turing-machine algorithm. For some fixed polynomial \(p\), on every valid circuit description \(C\) and every choice of its fair random bits it halts within \(p(|C|)\) steps and outputs a valid circuit of length at most \(p(|C|)\) with the same input arity. Its randomness can be taken as a uniformly random string of \(p(|C|)\) bits, with unused bits ignored. There is no oracle, advice or secret setup. No separate security parameter is supplied: input-description size, including padding, plays that role.

Perfect correctness requires
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr_r[\mathcal O(C;r)\equiv C]=1.\]
Thus every random choice of positive probability preserves the entire function exactly, not just its value at a random input. Merely negligible correctness error would be a different hypothesis.

A function \(\delta:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(k\ge1\) there exists \(s_k\) such that \(\delta(s)\le s^{-k}\) for all \(s\ge s_k\). Uniform security is the following quantifier order, matching Definition 4:
there exists a negligible \(\delta\) such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time bit-output algorithm \(D\), there exists \(s_D\) such that for all \(s\ge s_D\) and all equivalent input circuits \(C_0,C_1\) with \(|C_0|=|C_1|=s\),
\[\left|\Pr[D(\mathcal O(C_0;r_0))=1]-\Pr[D(\mathcal O(C_1;r_1))=1]\right|\le\delta(s).\]
Each probability includes fresh independent fair coins for the obfuscator and the distinguisher. The running time of \(D\) is worst-case polynomial in the length of the obfuscated description; its fixed polynomial may depend on \(D\). The only input to \(D\) is that description. In particular, the definition does not give \(D\) the pair \((C_0,C_1)\), auxiliary information or a length-dependent advice string. The source quantifies over all equal-length equivalent pairs, not just pairs that a uniform algorithm generates. These choices retain its particular uniform-security model rather than replacing it with a stronger auxiliary-input game.

NEXP is the class of languages \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decided by a uniform nondeterministic multitape Turing machine in time \(2^{a(n+1)^d}\), for some fixed constants \(a,d\ge1\): every computation path halts within that time, yes-inputs have at least one accepting path, and no-inputs have none. P/poly is the class of languages having a family of exact Boolean circuits \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) such that \(B_n\) decides membership on all \(n\)-bit inputs and uses at most \(b(n+1)^k\) AND/OR/NOT gates, for some fixed \(b,k\). Inputs, constants and output wires are free; depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The family is nonuniform: no efficient construction algorithm is required. Using description length instead of gate count defines the same polynomial-size class.

The conclusion requires one language \(L\in\mathrm{NEXP}\) with no polynomial-size family: for every \(b>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and integer \(N\ge1\), some \(n\ge N\) has no circuit with at most \(b(n+1)^k\) gates correct on all \(n\)-bit inputs. It does not assert a fixed exponential lower bound. The premise is the existence of at least one obfuscator with all the stated properties; the task is to establish the implication, not to construct that obfuscator unconditionally.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication with precisely the defined security, correctness and circuit models. A positive answer must derive \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) from only the existence premise, without adding nonuniform security or an independent hardness assumption. It need not separately prove that such an obfuscator exists. A negative answer must prove both that such a uniformly secure perfectly correct obfuscator exists and that \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\); pointing to a failed proof or giving an oracle-relative counterexample does not refute the unrelativized implication. A separation of uniform time classes or a lower bound only for restricted circuit classes is insufficient. All quantifiers and probability guarantees are exact; no numerical tolerance applies.
context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation transforms a circuit into another circuit with the same input-output behavior. For two equivalent source circuits of the same size, efficient distinguishers should not be able to tell which one was transformed. It does not promise to hide facts already revealed by evaluating the function.

Uniform and nonuniform security differ in what an adversary may possess. A uniform adversary is one algorithm for all input lengths. A nonuniform adversary may use a separately selected circuit or advice string at every length. The proposed theorem would turn the former security assumption into a lower bound against the latter computational model.

The source’s Theorem 1, restated and proved as Theorem 28, already implies \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) from perfectly correct obfuscation secure against nonuniform circuits. It also gives fixed-degree lower bounds for NP. These are conditional theorems with a stronger security premise, not solutions to the uniform-security question.

Under uniform security, Theorem 3/30 instead gives \(\mathrm{ZPEXP}\ne\mathrm{BPP}\). Here ZPEXP allows zero-error randomized computation with expected exponential time, and BPP allows two-sided error at most \(1/3\) in worst-case polynomial time. That separation concerns uniform algorithms and does not by itself establish the selected nonuniform circuit lower bound.

Williams’s unconditional NEXP lower bound concerns ACC: constant-depth circuits with unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and fixed-modulus counting gates. It is a major restricted-circuit result, while P/poly in this card permits arbitrary polynomial-depth circuits.

The June 2026 implicit-MCSP manuscript combines subexponential obfuscation security against nonuniform adversaries with an additional proof-complexity assumption. Its hypotheses and conclusion differ from the selected implication; it does not remove the uniform/nonuniform gap here.

The original question did not specify the desired circuit lower bound. The user chose the NEXP conclusion on 16 September 2026. This is an explicit specialization, not a claim that every possible answer to the broader source question would meet this criterion.
why: This implication asks whether cryptographic security against one effective algorithm at a time already forces a language in nondeterministic exponential time to resist every polynomial-size circuit family. It isolates the role of nonuniform adversaries in a known connection between obfuscation and circuit lower bounds.

The obfuscator preserves every circuit’s function exactly and hides equivalent equal-size representations from uniform randomized polynomial-time distinguishers. title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A simple natural problem in NP ∩ coNP with connections to total search, fixed points and stochastic games. The general polynomial-time question remains distinct from extensive graph-specific algorithmic progress.
formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm P\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(L\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether its terminating two-destination ARRIVAL decision problem belongs to P, while establishing verifiable certificates for both possible destinations.
definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. The class \(\mathrm P\) means one uniform deterministic program deciding this language on all input strings in a worst-case polynomial number of ordinary bit operations. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm P\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.
context:
The local rule is elementary, but a vertex remembers which of its two arcs should be used next. With n vertices there are 2ⁿ possible switch configurations in addition to the token position. Long deterministic runs therefore do not contradict the small size of the graph. Ordinary reachability ignores these switch settings and does not decide which sink the token actually reaches.

The source gives short verifiable certificates for both answers using switching flows: counts of traversals that obey conservation and alternation. This places the decision problem in NP ∩ coNP. Certificates can establish the outcome without listing an exponentially long trajectory, but their existence does not itself provide a polynomial-time way to find them.

The 2021 algorithm runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) time and becomes polynomial when deleting a fixed number of vertices makes the graph acyclic. The former is a general improvement over direct simulation; the latter keeps a structural restriction. Neither is the all-instance polynomial bound asked for here.

The 2025 work gives a bound \(2^{O(k\log^2 n)}\) for treewidth \(k\), which is quasipolynomial, not polynomial, even when \(k\) is fixed. It also relates ARRIVAL to approximate fixed points of contractions in the ℓ₁ metric. The paper explicitly distinguishes polynomially many function evaluations from a polynomial total running time.

The 2026 paper proves polynomial time for binary ladders: simple switch graphs with exactly two vertices at each occupied distance level from the two sinks. Such graphs can frustrate earlier algorithms, so solving them is meaningful progress. The restriction concerns the shortest-distance layers of the graph and is not satisfied by general instances.

A polynomial-time algorithm would settle a basic deterministic process whose YES and NO answers already have efficiently checked evidence. A lower bound excluding all such algorithms would be a major complexity separation; the difficulty of simulating the process is only one part of that question.
why: ARRIVAL isolates the complexity of a finite deterministic process with one bit of memory at each switch. Its outcome has short verifiable evidence on both sides, but a general efficient decision algorithm would need to go beyond following the potentially exponential trajectory.
status_note: Source-open. The 2021 source’s complete instance definition, termination lemmas, main runtime theorem and proof were checked. The 2025 recursive/contraction paper and the published May 2026 ladder paper explicitly retain the general polynomial-time question; their restrictions and complexity measures were checked. Bounded later-work searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. The full later proofs have not been independently audited or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2021-07-02: The source proves the general \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\)-time upper bound and a polynomial-time special case for bounded feedback vertex set. | 2025: A recursive framework yields quasipolynomial time at bounded treewidth and a reduction to ℓ₁-contraction; the general polynomial-time question remains open. | 2026-05-15: The FUN paper proves polynomial time on binary ladders and explicitly retains the general ARRIVAL-in-P question.
working_summary: ARRIVAL asks which of two destinations is reached by one token following deterministic alternating switches. The graph and both successor choices are explicit, and every vertex can reach at least one sink in the underlying graph. The target is one deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, without requiring it to list the token trajectory. General subexponential algorithms and newer bounded-treewidth or ladder results leave that all-instance target open. Short certificates for both outcomes make this a basic unresolved question at the boundary of efficient decision and total search.

title: Closure of UL under complement
importance_reason: A central closure question for a longstanding small-space complexity class, connected to the NL-versus-UL conjecture and to the foundations of unambiguous graph algorithms and function composition.
formal:
Is unambiguous logarithmic space closed under Boolean complement?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*,\qquad L\in\mathrm{UL}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{0,1\}^*\setminus L\in\mathrm{UL}.\]
Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{coUL}\)? A language is in \(\mathrm{UL}\) if one uniform nondeterministic machine decides it using logarithmic work space and has at most one accepting computation path on every input.

The complementing machine must also have at most one accepting path on every input and logarithmic space with its own fixed constants. The question concerns ordinary uniform machines with no advice or oracle and arbitrary binary input languages, not only planar graph problems.
question_excerpt: Thus it is far less clear what it should mean to say that a function is “computable in UL” since it remains an open question […]
definitions:
A language is any set of finite binary strings, and \(n=|x|\) denotes input length. Use a nondeterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite control and fixed finite tape alphabets, a two-way read-only input tape with end markers, and finitely many initially blank work tapes. Each transition has at most two choices. The input cannot be modified or used as additional writable memory. Work space is the total number of work-tape cells visited along a computation, measured in bits up to the fixed alphabet factor; the input cells and fixed finite control are not charged as work space.

A machine is logarithmic-space bounded if there is a constant \(c\) such that every computation on every input of length \(n\) visits at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. Use the standard halting convention: some fixed polynomial \(K(n+2)^d\) bounds the number of steps along every computation path, including rejecting paths. The machine and \(c,K,d\) are fixed independently of the input. A polynomial clock fits in logarithmic space; this convention does not add a nonuniform resource.

A computation path is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to an accepting or rejecting halt. Distinct choice histories count as distinct paths even when they later reach the same configuration. Acceptance means that at least one path accepts. The machine decides \(L\) when it accepts exactly the strings of \(L\); all paths on strings outside \(L\) reject.

Unambiguity means at most one accepting path for every binary input. Therefore a yes-instance has exactly one accepting path, while a no-instance has none. There may be many rejecting paths in either case. No probability distribution or bounded-error interpretation of these paths is intended. This is not the stronger requirement that every configuration, or every pair of configurations, be connected by at most one path.

The class \(\mathrm{UL}\) consists of languages decided by some machine satisfying all these conditions. Define \(\mathrm{coUL}=\{\overline L:L\in\mathrm{UL}\}\), where \(\overline L=\{0,1\}^*\setminus L\). Dropping only the unambiguity restriction gives \(\mathrm{NL}\), and restricting to deterministic transitions gives \(\mathrm L\). The usual inclusions are \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\). The known closure \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) makes \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{NL}\) sufficient for the requested closure; no equivalence to that stronger equality is asserted.

The quantifier is over languages: for each language with a qualifying machine, another qualifying machine for its complement must exist. An effective compiler that transforms every description of an unambiguous machine into a complement machine is not additionally required. Nor must the original and complement machines have the same space constant or polynomial clock. A negative answer is a language in \(\mathrm{UL}\) whose complement is not in \(\mathrm{UL}\), with nonmembership excluding all possible unambiguous logarithmic-space machines.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of closure in the declared uniform model. A proof must establish a qualifying complement machine for every language in UL, with exact acceptance, unambiguity on all inputs and logarithmic work space. A refutation must establish a language in UL and prove that its complement has no such machine. Merely complementing nondeterministic logspace while allowing multiple accepting paths, adding advice or an oracle, or settling a restricted family of graph inputs does not meet the full criterion. An oracle separation or a conditional separation alone is not an unconditional refutation.
context:
The source explicitly distinguishes UL from its intersection with coUL when defining functions computed using unambiguous subroutines. Its convenient oracle, circuit and bit-graph descriptions agree for that intersection, whereas general UL complementation is still an open premise.

Nondeterministic space at least logarithmic is known to be closed under complement. The theorem permits several accepting histories, so it does not alone give an unambiguous complement machine.

The 2026 long-path paper obtains new parameterized algorithms and states separate unambiguous and co-unambiguous guarantees for one resource bound. Such results concern a specified graph task and its parameter; they do not establish closure for every UL language. Only its abstract and stated resource scope were used in this status check.
why: Unambiguity retains existential computation while limiting each positive instance to a unique accepting history. Complement closure asks whether the same economy is available for negative instances. Its resolution would clarify a basic structural property between deterministic and nondeterministic logarithmic space and the interpretation and composition of functions computed using unambiguous subroutines.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: MFCS 2021 Section 2, the primary publisher statement of nondeterministic-space complementation, and the MFCS 2026 long-path abstract and metadata. A bounded later-work search found no general uniform UL-complementation proof or counterexample. The recent parameterized result and catalytic variants use different scopes or models. This source-open classification records those limitations and does not independently certify current openness.
progress: 2021-08-18: The planar depth-first-search paper explicitly records UL complementation as open and explains its function-class significance. | 2026-08-21: MFCS publishes parameterized long-path results with separate unambiguous and co-unambiguous resource guarantees, leaving the universal class question outside their scope.
working_summary: UL contains languages decided with logarithmic work space and at most one accepting computation path per input. The question asks whether the complement of every such language also has an unambiguous logarithmic-space decider. The original and complement machines are uniform, exact and have no oracle or nonuniform advice. Ordinary nondeterministic logspace is closed under complement, but its complementing procedures need not preserve unambiguity. A resolution would clarify both the structure of small-space complexity classes and the use of unambiguous subroutines in graph algorithms.

title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
importance_reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.
formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
question_excerpt: The survey identifies simultaneous time and space efficiency as the main general reversible-simulation question and asks in particular for almost-linear time and space. This card retains its earlier explicitly fixed target of polynomial time and O(S) total space, with one computable input-preserving compiler.
definitions:
Each machine has a finite transition table, finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet containing 0, 1, a blank and delimiters, and a fixed finite number of two-way tapes with one head per tape. A transition reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes are indexed by integers, and all heads initially sit at a designated origin. The machine description lists these finite objects explicitly in a fixed effectively decodable binary syntax. Alphabet size, tape count and states may depend on the fixed machine but not on its input. There are no oracle, advice, random or external-storage tapes.

Initially the binary input \(x\), with fixed delimiters, occupies consecutive cells of one tape; all other cells are blank. A halting run has a finite designated binary output \(M(x)\), with delimiters on an output tape. A transition is a partial deterministic function on full configurations; a configuration with no next transition is terminal. The full configuration includes the state, every tape's contents and every head position. A simulator must implement the stated terminal-output convention on its intended input runs.

A machine is reversible if its partial one-step map is injective on its entire configuration space: whenever transitions from configurations \(u\) and \(v\) produce the same configuration, \(u=v\). Thus no step may merge two different predecessor configurations. This property concerns the finite machine's full transition semantics, not just the particular run from a blank workspace. Halting states have no outgoing step; injectivity does not require every configuration to have a predecessor. Reversibility is logical reversibility of a classical machine, not a physical energy model or a quantum operation.

For a halting run, \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct tape cells initially occupied or visited during the entire run, summed over all tapes, with a minimum of 1. A cell still counts if it is later erased. Input, output, delimiter, history and work cells all count. Let
\[T_M(x)=\max\{1,|x|,\text{number of transitions before halting}\}.\]
Define \(S_R,T_R\) in exactly the same way. This is a per-input resource comparison, not a comparison of unrelated worst-case inputs of a given length. Finite control is part of the fixed machine description, while every tape cell used at run time is included. No additional initially full catalytic tape is supplied for free.

At termination, the simulator has two designated output tracks or tapes containing the original \(x\) and \(M(x)\), with the fixed delimiters, and all auxiliary tape contents are blank. Retaining \(x\) is essential: different inputs can yield the same \(M(x)\), but a reversible computation cannot merge their histories into an identical final configuration. The output pair is required exactly; leaving a computation-history string as garbage is not accepted. The simulator need only preserve the partial function in this input-preserving sense, rather than reproduce each intermediate configuration of \(M\).

The compiler is a single total deterministic computable function on valid machine descriptions; its compilation time is unrestricted. It outputs a finite reversible machine description, with no dependence on the later input \(x\). Neither the compiler nor the simulator is given the eventual halting time or space use as an extra input. The constants \(c_M,d_M\) may depend on \(M\), but are fixed before quantifying over all \(x\). No halting-time or resource bound is required on divergent runs beyond preservation of nontermination. A simulator chosen separately for every individual input would not satisfy the compiler requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this compiler. A positive answer must establish total computability of compilation, reversibility of every output machine on its full configuration space, preservation of the partial function and nontermination behavior, clean input-preserving output, and the two simultaneous per-input resource bounds. A negative answer must prove that no compiler can satisfy these requirements for all machines and inputs; failure of one known construction does not suffice. Separate simulators achieving the time and space bounds independently do not settle the conjunction. A lower bound only for reversible pebble games, an oracle-relative simulation model or circuits does not refute unrestricted reversible multitape simulation. The resource requirements are exact asymptotic claims, without additive numerical tolerance.
context:
An irreversible computation may overwrite information that is no longer needed. A reversible machine must retain enough information elsewhere to make each transition invertible on its image. The question asks whether doing so can always preserve the original storage scale while incurring only polynomial time overhead.

Input preservation and clearing auxiliary tapes specify what counts as a completed simulation. They prevent two easy ambiguities: erasing distinct inputs that have the same answer, and treating a large retained execution history as an acceptable final result.

Bennett’s simulations establish polynomial-time reversible computation with space \(O(S\log(T+2))\), among other tradeoffs. The logarithmic multiplier is not bounded by one machine-dependent constant as the input grows, so this bound does not establish the card’s \(O(S)\) requirement.

Lange, McKenzie and Tapp show that deterministic space can be preserved by reversible computation. The general construction can take exponential time, so space preservation alone does not imply the required polynomial overhead in the original running time.

Buhrman, Tromp and Vitányi give intermediate time-space tradeoffs and discuss how to remove an advance bound on the simulated running time. Their result bridges the classical extremes but does not give the required simultaneous polynomial-time and constant-factor-space guarantee for every machine.

Reversible pebble games model a particular style of simulation, with memory snapshots represented by pebbles. A lower bound for that model need not apply to all reversible machines. The space-preserving theorem itself demonstrated that general simulation can escape restrictions of that particular model.

The 2026 catalytic-computation paper studies an additional tape initialized with arbitrary contents that must be restored. Its reversible-space lemma has no general polynomial-time-overhead guarantee. Both its separate catalytic resource and the missing time bound matter: it is related progress, not a solution to the total-storage target here.

Logical reversibility is relevant to the information erased during computation, but this card does not set an energy bound for hardware. Its mathematical success criterion is entirely the classical compiler, correctness, time and space statement.
why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.
status_note: Historically source-open with bounded follow-up checking through 16 September 2026. The 2005 survey’s machine/compiler model and main open problem and the 2001 tradeoff theorem/proof sketch and unknown-time discussion were read. The classical 1989/2000 publisher statements were checked, with the latter’s time limitation corroborated in the 2001 paper. A 2026 primary catalytic-computation paper was read at Definitions 1–4, Lemma 11 and Theorem 10; it does not claim the simultaneous general bound. No matching resolution or recent primary source explicitly certifying this exact compiler target as open was located. The earlier polynomial-time/O(S)-space specialization is retained and labeled; current openness is less directly evidenced than the historical formulation.

working_summary: The question asks whether every deterministic computation can be compiled into a reversible one with polynomial time overhead and only a constant-factor space increase. The simulator preserves the input and exact output, clears auxiliary storage and retains nontermination on divergent inputs. Time and space are compared on the same input, and input, output and history storage all count. Known general simulations attain the two desired efficiencies separately or with a tradeoff, while catalytic-space results use a different resource model. A complete answer must prove or refute one computable compiler meeting all of these guarantees simultaneously.

title: Closure of SZK under truth-table reductions
importance_reason: A longstanding structural closure problem for a central proof-system class. It separates formula composition from general efficient circuit composition and bears directly on whether many private verification tasks retain zero knowledge when combined.
formal:
Is statistical zero knowledge closed under deterministic polynomial-time truth-table reductions, using the promise-problem and three-valued circuit semantics of the source? In symbols,
\[\forall A,B,\qquad B\in\mathrm{SZK}\ \land\ A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\in\mathrm{SZK}.\]
The reduction writes all queries before obtaining their answers and combines those answers with an arbitrary polynomial-size Boolean circuit. Its circuit need not have logarithmic depth or be a polynomial-size formula. Queries outside the oracle’s promise are permitted under the explicit rules below.
question_excerpt: After proving the Boolean-formula characterization of SZK, the source says that closure under general polynomial-time truth-table reductions remains open.
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(A=(A_Y,A_N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\). Correctness requires acceptance on \(A_Y\) and rejection on \(A_N\); inputs outside their union have no required answer. A polynomial-time many-one reduction \(h\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is one uniform deterministic algorithm with running time at most \(C(n+1)^d\), for fixed constants \(C,d\), such that \(h(A_Y)\subseteq B_Y\) and \(h(A_N)\subseteq B_N\). Its behavior outside the promise is unrestricted. All lengths and time bounds refer to full explicit binary encodings.

For a self-contained definition of SZK, use its standard complete promise problem Statistical Difference, SD. A well-formed SD instance is a pair of explicitly described Boolean sampling circuits \(C:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) and \(D:\{0,1\}^{r}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\). A circuit is a finite acyclic list of binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants, with its input and output wires explicitly listed. The integers \(m,r,\ell\) and all wire indices are part of the description; each listed input wire receives an independent fair bit. Let \(X=C(U_m)\) and \(Y=D(U_r)\), with \(U_s\) uniform on all \(s\)-bit strings. Their statistical distance is
\[\Delta(X,Y)=\frac12\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}}\bigl|\Pr[X=z]-\Pr[Y=z]\bigr|.\]
Set \(\mathrm{SD}_Y=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)>2/3\}\) and \(\mathrm{SD}_N=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)<1/3\}\). Intermediate-distance pairs and malformed descriptions lie outside the promise. SZK is the class of all promise problems having a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to SD. By the completeness theorem this is the usual classical statistical-zero-knowledge class; no additional choice of a protocol definition is needed for this formulation.

For any promise problem \(B\), define its partial characteristic value by \(\chi_B(z)=1\) on \(B_Y\), \(0\) on \(B_N\), and \(*\) outside the promise. The reduction \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\) means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine maps each input \(x\) to a finite list \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\) and a Boolean circuit \(F\) with those \(k\) answer variables, satisfying
\[x\in A_Y\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=1,\]
\[x\in A_N\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=0.\]
The number of queries, sum of their bit lengths and size of the explicitly written circuit are all polynomially bounded in \(|x|\). The generating machine does not query \(B\) while preparing them. \(F\) is an acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuit with constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate wires; its depth is limited only by its polynomial size. The query count may be zero. No randomized, adaptive or nonuniform reduction is allowed.

Evaluate \(F\) gate by gate over \(\{0,1,*\}\). NOT exchanges 0 and 1 and leaves \(*\) unchanged. AND returns 0 if either input is 0, returns 1 if both are 1, and returns \(*\) otherwise. OR returns 1 if either input is 1, returns 0 if both are 0, and returns \(*\) otherwise. Constants retain their values. These rules are part of the source’s definition, including on queries outside the promise. A required final value 0 or 1 is stable under replacing unknown inputs by bits, but the converse fails: \(u\lor\neg u\) evaluates to \(*\) at \(u=*\), although it is 1 on both Boolean assignments. Thus mere agreement on all Boolean completions is not silently substituted for the specified circuit semantics. Requiring every query to satisfy the promise would also change the stated reduction notion.

A Boolean formula is a circuit presented as a tree, with repeated subcomputations written out separately. Closure for polynomial-size formulas or logarithmic-depth circuits is the known restricted case. The target permits arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, whose compact descriptions may reuse intermediate results many times. The quantifiers range over arbitrary promise problems and every valid reduction of the stated kind; the polynomial bounds and programs may depend on the fixed problems and reduction, but not on individual inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal closure statement. A positive answer must show that every promise problem reducing in the specified way to any SZK promise problem itself reduces to SD, or give an equivalent fully justified SZK protocol. A negative answer must establish promise problems \(A,B\), prove \(B\in\mathrm{SZK}\) and \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\), and prove \(A\notin\mathrm{SZK}\). The reduction’s treatment of unknown answers and its uniform polynomial bounds must be included. Closure only for formulas, logarithmic-depth circuits, or a special oracle problem does not prove the full claim without an equivalence proof. An oracle-relative or conditional separation does not refute this unrelativized target. All class, promise and probability thresholds are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance is irrelevant.
context:
Statistical zero knowledge allows a verifier to be convinced of a statement without learning additional information, in the sense that the verifier’s view can be simulated with negligible statistical error. This card asks whether that property survives taking many nonadaptive questions and performing an arbitrary efficient Boolean computation on their answers.

The Statistical Difference complete problem makes the class concrete: distinguish two efficiently sampled distributions that are far apart from ones that are close. The middle range is deliberately left outside the promise. The card uses this characterization as its exact definition of SZK.

Sahai and Vadhan prove closure under polynomial-size Boolean formulas, and therefore under polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. This is stronger than closure under a constant number of AND, OR and NOT operations, but still leaves general polynomial-depth circuit composition open.

The distinction is computational rather than a choice of logical connectives. Formulas must repeat each reused subcomputation, while circuits can share it. Replacing a circuit by its expanded expression tree need not preserve polynomial size.

The 2023 paper explicitly retains the general truth-table question while using the known formula closure in a characterization based on Kolmogorov complexity. That characterization does not claim general circuit closure.

The later space-bounded work proves a corresponding Boolean-formula closure for the logarithmic-space statistical-zero-knowledge class. Its Theorem 7.8 is a result about a restricted model and formula reductions; it does not establish the general circuit target here.

Handling queries outside the promise is essential: an SD oracle need not give meaningful information for distributions in the gap. The precise three-valued rules prevent such queries from being treated as reliable facts and preserve the formulation actually used by the source.
why: A positive answer would make statistical zero knowledge robust under a broad form of efficient nonadaptive composition. A negative answer would reveal a basic limitation on combining individually private verification tasks, despite the known strong formula closure.
status_note: Source-open: the final ITCS 2023 paper explicitly poses the question after Theorem 20, under its Definition 19. The original JACM 2003 Definitions 4.6 and 4.12–4.13 and the formula-closure proof/Corollary 4.14 were read to recover the precise promise semantics. The accepted December 2024 manuscript of the 2025 TOCT paper was checked at §7/Definitions 7.1–7.2/Theorem 7.8 and the surrounding proof for the restricted later result. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general closure theorem or unconditional refutation; no exhaustive open-status certification or independent verification of every cited proof is claimed.
progress: 2003: Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.14 establish Boolean-formula and logarithmic-depth truth-table closure; the same section explicitly raises general circuit closure. | 2023: Definition 19 and Theorem 20 preserve the promise semantics and formula closure; the following paragraph states the general truth-table closure question as open. | 2024 manuscript / 2025 publication: Theorem 7.8 proves the analogous formula-reduction closure for the space-bounded class, with no claimed extension to general polynomial-size circuits.
working_summary: The question asks whether statistical zero knowledge is closed under arbitrary polynomial-time nonadaptive truth-table reductions. The reduction prepares all queries first and combines their answers with a polynomial-size Boolean circuit. Promise-violating queries are handled by the source’s explicit gate-by-gate three-valued logic. Closure is known for Boolean formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits, leaving general circuit composition unresolved in the source. The card defines SZK through Statistical Difference and requires a complete proof or counterexample to the full closure statement.

title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
importance_reason: A longstanding structural question about randomized verification and existential quantification, with an oracle barrier and direct relevance to how semantic and promise conditions interact in complexity hierarchies.
formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. One verifier with intermediate acceptance probabilities, or an oracle separation, does not by itself refute the ordinary class equality.
context:
Definition 16 applies the existential operator to ordinary languages. Remark 17 explains why fixing a witness in an MA verifier need not leave a BPP computation: a nonwinning witness on a yes-instance may lie inside the error gap. This does not itself prove that the language has no other suitable verifier.

The source encounters this distinction when bounding quantum hierarchies with classical witnesses. Its stronger-oracle simulations handle a different resource class; they do not establish the desired ordinary BPP predicate.

Fenner, Fortnow, Kurtz and Li construct an oracle relative to which MA is not contained even in nondeterministic polynomial time with access to a BPP oracle. Since existential BPP is contained in that latter class, the two target classes can differ relative to a common oracle. This is an obstruction to a proof valid under every oracle, not an unconditional separation.
why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

The former explicitly leaves equality open and the latter proves a relativized separation only. A bounded later-work search found no matching general equality or unrelativized separation. The source-open status does not certify an exhaustive literature search.
