working_summary: The question asks whether existential quantification over an ordinary BPP language has exactly the power of Merlin–Arthur verification. Both settings use a polynomial-size witness chosen before a uniform randomized polynomial-time check. Existential BPP additionally requires a bounded-error gap for every input-witness pair, even for unsuccessful witnesses on yes-instances. Equality permits changing the verifier, so one verifier with intermediate probabilities is not a counterexample. An oracle separation is known, while the ordinary class equality remains the source’s unresolved target.

title: Effective enumeration of BPP
importance_reason: A general effective-characterization problem for BPP, connecting derandomization, proof-theoretic certification and the distinction between a complexity class and all program codes representing it.
formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.
question_excerpt: The existence of an effective enumerable family of algorithms deciding all and only the problems in BPP is still an open question.
definitions:
All languages are subsets of finite binary strings. A randomized decision machine is a finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, initially blank work tapes, a one-bit output and independent fair random bits. It has no oracle, advice or arbitrary real-number operations. Time counts ordinary tape operations, generation of random bits and output writing, in the worst case over random choices.

For each enumerated machine \(M_i\), there must exist positive integers \(C_i,d_i\) such that it halts with a decision bit within \(C_i(n+2)^{d_i}\) bit steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random-bit sequence. These constants may depend on \(i\), but not on the input or random choices. No common polynomial must bound the whole family. The time bounds are existential properties of the emitted programs; no computable method of finding their constants from \(i\), or proof certificate for those constants, is additionally required. An enumeration supplying explicit clocks would be a sufficient special case.

For every finite input, the runtime bound limits the number of coin tosses, so the acceptance probability is a well-defined dyadic rational from a finite probability space. Unused coin bits do not change an output. A machine has bounded error when its acceptance probability never lies strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\). It then decides the unique language whose yes-instances have acceptance probability at least \(2/3\); every no-instance has acceptance probability at most \(1/3\). The gap must hold on every input, including the empty string.

The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of all languages decided by some randomized polynomial-time machine with this gap. Equivalently, \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) if some such machine satisfies \(\Pr[M(x)=\mathbf 1_L(x)]\ge2/3\) for every \(x\). The class \(\mathrm P\), used in the context, consists of languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time machines. Both classes use worst-case polynomial runtime.

Total computable means that one deterministic Turing machine, given the binary encoding of any nonnegative integer \(i\), halts and returns the finite transition-table code of \(M_i\). It may use arbitrarily large finite time and space as a function of \(i\). No finite or infinite advice sequence and no oracle are allowed. Codes use an ordinary effective finite encoding of machine states, tape symbols and transitions; standard such encodings can be effectively translated without changing the represented machine or its polynomial-time property.

Soundness requires every emitted machine to run in polynomial time and have the displayed gap on every input. Coverage requires that for each \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\), some index \(i\) satisfies \(L=L_i\) on all strings. Neither an index for a given language nor a decision procedure for whether an arbitrary program has the gap is requested. In particular, \(E\) may omit a bounded-error program if it lists another program deciding the same language.

The negative answer excludes every total computable enumeration with these two properties. An inability to enumerate all codes of polynomial-time bounded-error programs is a different assertion: the target only needs an effectively chosen representative family that covers all the languages. No specific logical theory or proof system is prescribed for that family.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such an enumeration. A positive answer must specify a total computable enumerator and prove the polynomial-time and all-input error guarantees for every emitted machine, as well as coverage of every BPP language. The mathematical runtime proof may establish separately quantified constants for each index without providing an algorithm computing them. A negative answer must rule out every such representative-family enumeration, including families whose time bounds are not supplied effectively. Showing that the set of all valid machine codes is undecidable or not computably enumerable does not suffice. An enumeration covering only the languages whose correctness is proved in one selected theory also does not suffice without proving that it covers all of BPP.
context:
Section 2 emphasizes the difference between listing all algorithms with a property and listing enough algorithms to cover the same languages. The former code sets can be recursion-theoretically difficult even for deterministic polynomial time, while the latter can have a simple effective enumeration.

The source gives characterizations of BPP in arithmetic and effectively enumerable subclasses based on error guarantees provable in a sound recursively enumerable theory. Its conclusion does not show that one such subclass contains every BPP language.

Proposition 20 shows that P equal to BPP would imply the desired kind of effective characterization. Thus a proof that no covering enumeration exists would in particular separate P from BPP. The reverse implication is not asserted.

The paper proves hardness of recognizing its all-input error condition and gives an enumerable sound-theory subclass containing polynomial identity testing. These results expose the certification issue and supply substantial examples, but neither code-recognition hardness nor one such subclass settles complete language coverage.
why: Polynomial running time can be guaranteed syntactically by a clock, but bounded error is a condition on every possible input. The question asks whether a computably generated family can still capture all feasible randomized decision problems while guaranteeing that condition. A resolution would clarify the relationship between semantic complexity classes, programming formalisms and what arithmetical theories can certify about randomized computation.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: CSL 2024 Sections 1–2, Definitions 12–19, Propositions 20–21 and the concluding discussion, plus the extended-preprint metadata. The published source explicitly leaves a covering enumeration open and does not infer its impossibility from recognition hardness. A bounded later-work search found no matching complete enumeration or impossibility proof; no exhaustive openness guarantee is made.
progress: 2023-11-25: The extended preprint introduces arithmetic characterizations and enumerable subclasses, while retaining the general coverage question. | 2024-02-07: CSL publishes the distinction between code recognition and language enumeration, the conditional consequence of P equal to BPP, and the identity-testing example.
working_summary: The problem asks for a computable list of randomized polynomial-time algorithms covering every language in BPP. Each listed algorithm must have the required error gap on every input, but the list may repeat languages and omit alternative implementations. The enumerator itself has no efficiency requirement, and the listed programs may have different polynomial time bounds that need not be supplied effectively. Recognizing all bounded-error program codes is a different task from finding a representative family with complete language coverage. Known arithmetical characterizations give useful enumerable subclasses, while a negative answer would separate BPP from deterministic polynomial time.

title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
importance_reason: Separates computation with reuse from formula computation, a basic structural distinction in circuit complexity.
formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[S(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad L(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(S\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(S(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N:\quad L(f_n)>n^k.\]
This is the source's absence-of-any-polynomial-upper-bound claim. It does not silently strengthen that claim to a lower bound beating each polynomial at every sufficiently large length.
definitions:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input nodes for \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and one designated output. Every computational gate is binary AND, binary OR, or unary NOT. Inputs may also supply the constant bits zero and one. Each node carries one bit, which is evaluated by applying its assigned operation to the incoming values. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and a gate value can be reused several times. The output can be an input, a constant or a computed gate. Size is the number of computational gates; input and constant nodes and wires are not charged. The circuit must output \(f_n(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). No parity or arbitrary truth-table gate is a primitive, and no random or promise-only correctness is allowed. \(S(f_n)\) is the minimum such size.

A formula is a finite rooted tree with binary AND/OR or unary NOT internal nodes and input-variable or constant leaves. Each occurrence of an input in this tree is separate; an internal computation cannot feed two parent nodes. The size of a formula is the number of variable-leaf occurrences, as in the source. Constant leaves are free; an optimum for a nonconstant function can eliminate constant subformulas. One may equivalently place all NOT operations directly on variables by De Morgan's laws, leaving the leaf count unchanged. Negated and unnegated occurrences of the same variable are each counted. \(L(f_n)\) is the minimum leaf count over formulas computing the function exactly. Constant functions have \(L=0\), and a literal has \(L=1\).

The sequence of functions, and the optimal circuits and formulas at different lengths, need not have an efficiently computable description. In particular this card does not impose an extra polynomial-time evaluator or uniform circuit-generation algorithm on the family. The source's conjecture is stated using its nonuniform size measures. A family with such extra uniformity would also qualify if it has the required sizes.

The same constant \(C\) bounds circuit size at every length. Allowing finitely many exceptions would be equivalent, since increasing \(C\) absorbs them. The formula condition is equivalent to saying that there do not exist constants \(D>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and onset \(N\) with \(L(f_n)\le Dn^k\) for all \(n\ge N\). Thus arbitrarily large violating lengths may depend on the polynomial exponent; the family itself may not. The target asserts no particular exponential or quasipolynomial lower-bound rate.

The two minima compare computations of the same single-output function. Linear circuit size does not bound circuit depth by a logarithm. A size separation using unbounded-fan-in threshold gates, only monotone formulas, or a growing number of outputs is a different statement.

The existence claim is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\subsetneq\mathrm{P/poly}\) for nonuniform Boolean circuit families. Here \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) means \(S(f_n)\le a(n+1)^b\) for some fixed positive integers \(a,b\), and \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) means a family of binary De Morgan circuits of depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for one constant \(d\); such circuits can be taken polynomial in size. No uniform generation is required in either class. Polynomial-size formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits are equivalent by formula balancing and expansion of a bounded-depth circuit into a tree.

The restriction to linear circuit size does not change this family-existence question. A separating polynomial-size family can be regarded, at lengths \(N_n=a(n+1)^b\), as a function of \(N_n\) variables that ignores the extra variables; at other lengths set the function to a constant. The circuit bound becomes linear, whereas a polynomial formula bound in \(N_n\) would give a polynomial formula bound in \(n\). This is a comparison of nonuniform families and retains the arbitrarily-large-length quantifiers. Conversely, a linear-size family is already in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). Thus an answer to the equality question has the opposite Boolean polarity from the separation question in this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed family-existence claim. A positive answer must specify or mathematically establish the existence of one family satisfying both the single linear circuit bound and failure of every polynomial formula bound. A nonconstructive family can qualify; no efficient generator is part of the target. A negative answer must show that every family with a uniform linear circuit-size constant has some polynomial formula-size bound, whose exponent and coefficient may depend on that family. Proving only one fixed polynomial separation, even with a large exponent, or refuting one candidate family does not settle the question.
context:
Theorem 5.10 records families with linear-size circuits and nearly cubic formula lower bounds. Conjecture 5.11 asks for a qualitative increase beyond every fixed polynomial, not a further fixed-power improvement.

The 2023 paper proves nearly cubic De Morgan formula bounds for a family already computable by polynomial-size constant-depth unbounded-fan-in formulas. This strengthens the class of target functions for a known lower-bound scale; its Theorem 1.1 does not state the superpolynomial separation requested here.

The source connects its conjecture to questions about formula size under block composition. The related KRW card records a particular formula-size composition statement. This connection is contextual; the present target is stated directly in terms of the two computational size measures.

The STACS 2025 paper continues to describe super-logarithmic formula-depth lower bounds as a major open challenge. Its result is for a strengthened communication relation, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a formula lower bound for ordinary composition.

Open Problem 8.3 in the Rao–Yehudayoff draft asks whether every polynomial-size circuit family has logarithmic-depth circuits. Formula balancing and polynomial padding give precisely the equivalence recorded in the definitions. The former active card TCS-6712 is consolidated here, preserving its source question rather than retaining two benchmark entries for opposite polarities of the same proposition.

Amarilli’s companion question asks more broadly whether the known nearly cubic circuit/formula gap can be improved. That broader quantitative question motivated the earlier consolidation, but a fixed-power improvement alone would not meet this card’s superpolynomial target.
why: Circuits can reuse intermediate values and formulas must duplicate the computation when it is needed again. This question asks whether reuse can turn a task requiring superpolynomial tree size into a circuit of only linear size. It isolates a fundamental limitation of formulas while allowing the circuit computation to have unrestricted depth.
status_note: Conjecture 5.11 and the source’s size definitions were checked on 2026-09-14, together with Filmus–Meir–Tal’s published Theorem 1.1 and introductory status discussion and Chukhin–Kulikov–Mihajlin’s STACS 2025 introduction. A bounded search through this date found no matching superpolynomial formula separation for a linear-size circuit family or a contrary universal simulation. The source-open status has these literature-check limits; the cited proofs have not been independently formalized.
progress: 2018-03-27: The source draft states the linear-circuit versus superpolynomial-formula conjecture and records the nearly cubic benchmark. | 2023-12-05: The Theory of Computing paper extends nearly cubic formula lower bounds to a family in constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean computation. | 2025: The STACS paper gives a strong-composition communication lower bound and retains the distinction from unrestricted formula lower bounds.
working_summary: The conjecture asks for Boolean functions with linear-size circuits but no polynomial-size formulas. Circuits may reuse intermediate results, while formulas have a tree structure and count repeated variable occurrences separately. The computational basis is binary AND and OR with unary negation, and correctness is exact on every input. The nonuniform separation is equivalent to NC-one being strictly smaller than P/poly, and arbitrarily large violating lengths are sufficient. Known nearly cubic gaps and recent composition results do not yet give the required superpolynomial separation.

title: Complete problem for Search-SZK
importance_reason: A structural completeness question for zero-knowledge search, linking simulation-based privacy with solution-preserving computational reductions. Its interest lies in the full search class beyond the known prefix subclass, not in a single protocol construction.
formal:
Does Search-SZK, the class of promise search problems with statistical zero-knowledge protocols defined below, have a complete problem under the authors' deterministic polynomial-time Levin reductions? Precisely, is there one promise search problem \(R^{\star}\) such that
\[R^{\star}\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK}\quad\text{and}\quad \forall R\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK},\ R\le_{\mathrm L}^{\mathrm P}R^{\star}?\]
The user selected the statistical version on 16 September 2026. The source also asks the separate computational-zero-knowledge version; that question is not an additional required target here.
question_excerpt: The source leaves complete problems open for both computational and statistical search zero knowledge. With user approval, this card selects statistical Search-SZK under the full version’s ordinary Levin reductions.
definitions:
A promise search problem is a pair \(R=(R_Y,L_N)\), where \(R_Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\{0,1\}^{*}\) is a binary relation and \(L_N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). Put
\[R_Y(x)=\{y:(x,y)\in R_Y\},\qquad L_Y=\{x:R_Y(x)\ne\varnothing\},\]
and require \(L_Y\cap L_N=\varnothing\). On a yes-instance \(x\in L_Y\), a valid answer is any \(y\in R_Y(x)\); on a no-instance \(x\in L_N\), it is the distinguished symbol \(\bot\), which is not a binary string. Inputs outside \(L_Y\cup L_N\) are outside the promise. No general polynomial-time test for membership in \(R_Y\) is assumed. Nor is this a total-search class: no-instances are permitted. The relation itself need not bound the length of every legal solution; a polynomial-time verifier can output only polynomially many bits on its own runs.

A protocol \((P,V)\) has a common binary input \(x\), classical messages and independent private fair random bits. The honest verifier \(V\) is one uniform probabilistic polynomial-time interactive Turing machine: its running time, communication and output length on every execution are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\). A computationally unbounded prover \(P\) interacts with it; prover computation is not charged to verifier time. Malformed or overlong messages may cause rejection. The verifier outputs a binary string or \(\bot\). Write \((P,V)(x)\) for that output distribution, over the parties' random choices. There is no setup, shared secret, oracle or advice.

The authors' Search-IP conditions, retained exactly, are:
\[\forall x\in L_Y,\qquad \Pr[(P,V)(x)\in R_Y(x)]=1;\]
\[\forall P^{*}\ \forall x\in L_N,\qquad \Pr[(P^{*},V)(x)=\bot]\ge\tfrac12;\]
\[\forall P^{*}\ \forall x\in L_Y,\qquad \Pr[(P^{*},V)(x)\in R_Y(x)\cup\{\bot\}]\ge\tfrac12.\]
The first is perfect completeness. The other two quantify over all cheating prover strategies without a computational restriction. Thus a cheating prover must not force an invalid output with probability greater than one half, even on a yes-instance with some valid solutions. The source does not give a general soundness-amplification theorem for this search definition; the threshold is not silently replaced by negligible error.

For any uniform probabilistic polynomial-time cheating verifier \(V^{*}\), its view \(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^{*}}(x)\) is the explicitly encoded tuple of \(x\), its private random tape used in the execution, and all exchanged messages. The honest prover is used in this interaction. No external auxiliary input is supplied to \(V^{*}\).

Search-SZK requires a single universal simulator \(S\). Given \(x\), a finite description \(\langle V^{*}\rangle\) and one sample \(Y_x\) from the honest-output distribution \((P,V)(x)\), it produces a simulated view. For each fixed polynomial-time verifier \(V^{*}\), this simulation has expected running time polynomial in \(|x|\) on the stated inputs; the polynomial may depend on that verifier and the fixed protocol. This is the usual simulator convention when the verifier program, whose own polynomial time bound may vary, is supplied as a parameter. The simulator is one algorithm, not a separately chosen program for each verifier.

For every such \(V^{*}\) there must be a negligible function \(\eta_{V^{*}}\) such that, on every \(x\in L_Y\),
\[\Delta\bigl(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^{*}}(x),\ S(x,\langle V^{*}\rangle,Y_x)\bigr)\le\eta_{V^{*}}(|x|).\]
For distributions on encoded finite strings, \(\Delta(U,W)=\tfrac12\sum_z|\Pr[U=z]-\Pr[W=z]|\). A nonnegative function \(\eta\) is negligible if for every integer \(k\ge1\) there exists \(n_k\) such that \(\eta(n)\le n^{-k}\) for all \(n\ge n_k\). The bound is worst-case over yes-inputs of a given length, not an average over input distributions. All sampling coins are fresh; on the simulator side the honest sample and the simulator's coins are independent. The sample is from the protocol's own honest output law, not from an arbitrary distribution on legal solutions or from the cheating verifier's output. Statistical distance protects against all distinguishing tests, even computationally unbounded ones. The verifier being simulated nevertheless remains polynomial-time. No zero-knowledge requirement is imposed on no-instances or outside the promise.

For \(R=(R_Y,L_N)\) and \(Q=(Q_Y,K_N)\), the relation \(R\le_{\mathrm L}^{\mathrm P}Q\) means that there exist two uniform deterministic polynomial-time machines \(A,B\) satisfying
\[x\in L_Y\Longrightarrow A(x)\in K_Y,\qquad x\in L_N\Longrightarrow A(x)\in K_N,\]
\[\forall x\in L_Y\ \forall z\in Q_Y(A(x)),\qquad B(x,z)\in R_Y(x),\]
where \(K_Y=\{u:Q_Y(u)\ne\varnothing\}\). The time of \(A\) is polynomial in \(|x|\); that of \(B\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\), using explicit binary encodings. Both halt on all inputs. There is one target instance and one answer transformation, with no randomness, advice or oracle. The decoder must work for every legal target answer, including answers that a particular target protocol never outputs. Outside the promise there is no correctness condition. The two programs and their polynomial bounds may depend on \(R\), but the complete problem \(R^{\star}\) is fixed before the universal quantifier over \(R\). The authors also define stronger solution-preserving reductions, requiring identical solution sets; that extra condition is not part of ordinary Levin completeness here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed completeness claim. A positive answer must define one fixed promise search problem, establish a protocol and simulator satisfying the entire statistical definition, and prove that every Search-SZK problem has a Levin reduction to it with both promise directions and correctness for every valid target solution. A negative answer must show that no member of Search-SZK can be such a complete problem: for every candidate in the class, some Search-SZK problem fails to reduce to it. Completeness of decision-SZK, a restricted search subclass, or the computational search variant is not enough. Changing the simulator's sample distribution, adding auxiliary-input requirements or changing soundness requires an equivalence proof before it can answer this card. The target is unconditional and unrelativized; all probability and quantifier requirements are exact, without numerical tolerance.
context:
A decision zero-knowledge protocol answers whether an instance has a property. A search protocol must return an actual solution while revealing no more than a sample of the solution that the honest protocol would produce. The intended disclosure therefore includes an output distribution, not only a yes/no answer.

Many legal answers may exist, and the prover’s soundness obligation is meaningful even when the input is a yes-instance: a cheating prover should not convince the verifier to output an invalid answer. The original one-half error bound is retained because repeated search executions can return different answers, and the paper does not infer the ordinary decision-protocol amplification rule.

The simulator is given one honest-protocol output sample. It is not guaranteed simulation from every individual valid answer, and it receives no external auxiliary information. The paper explicitly distinguishes these choices from other possible zero-knowledge definitions.

The paper defines a subclass called Prefix-SZK, where the prover first supplies a solution and then proves a suitable decision statement about it in statistical zero knowledge. Section 4.1 gives a complete problem for this subclass, even under the stronger solution-preserving reductions. It does not establish a complete problem for the entire Search-SZK class.

Ordinary Levin reductions preserve both sides of the promise and recover a valid source answer from every valid target answer. A complete problem would therefore provide one universal representative for the class’s search tasks, with precise control over solutions rather than just over accept/reject decisions.

The original draft combined statistical and computational completeness questions. The user selected the statistical question on 16 September 2026. The computational variant remains part of the source history, not a second success condition for this card.
why: A complete problem would provide a single representative of statistical zero-knowledge search, as complete decision problems do for familiar complexity classes. The issue tests whether privacy of a revealed solution admits a common reduction-based structure even when protocols can produce many different legal outputs.
status_note: Source-open: the 2018 announcement and full-version future-directions paragraph explicitly ask the statistical completeness question. The full promise/reduction/protocol definitions and §4.1 prefix completeness argument were read. Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general Search-SZK complete problem or nonexistence theorem; no recent primary source independently certifying this precise target was located. This is a historically source-open question with that present-status limit, not an exhaustive current-openness certification. The statistical specialization follows the user’s explicit choice.
progress: 2018: The ICALP announcement introduces search zero knowledge and states completeness as open for its statistical and computational variants. | 2018 full version: Definitions 10–11 specify perfect completeness, two soundness requirements and simulation from an honest-output sample. Remarks 8 and 12 distinguish auxiliary-input and output-distribution variants. | 2018 full version: Section 4.1 proves completeness for Prefix-SZK under solution-preserving Levin reductions, retaining the broader Search-SZK completeness question.
working_summary: The question asks whether the authors’ statistical zero-knowledge search class has one complete promise search problem. Protocols output a legal solution with perfect completeness and retain the source’s two soundness conditions. A universal simulator receives one sample of the honest protocol’s output distribution and must reproduce any efficient verifier’s view up to negligible statistical distance. Reductions must preserve yes and no promises and decode every legal target answer into a valid source answer. Completeness is known for the Prefix-SZK subclass, while this card retains the full Search-SZK question selected by the user.

title: Subexponential derandomization with two-way random-tape access
importance_reason: A substantive general derandomization frontier isolating the power of rereadable randomness under a stringent memory bound, with a much weaker time target than full polynomial-time derandomization.
formal:
Can every bounded-error randomized logspace decision algorithm with two-way access to polynomially many random bits be simulated by a deterministic algorithm in time \(2^{o(n)}\)?

Precisely, does every language \(L\in\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) admit one deterministic decider \(D\) whose worst-case running time \(T_D(n)\) satisfies
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(T_D(n)+2)}{n}=0?\]
There is no additional space restriction on \(D\). This card uses the single-decider \(2^{o(n)}\) meaning of subexponential time, matching the explicit time scale discussed in the source. The source question is about arbitrary two-way random-tape access, even though the paper’s main advice theorem concerns a bounded number of one-way passes.
question_excerpt: For example, while we know that BPL is in P, we do not know whether 2-wayBPL is even in deterministic sub-exponential time (note that it […]
definitions:
Inputs are finite binary strings \(x\), with length \(n\). A randomized machine is a uniform finite-program multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, a read-only random tape and a fixed number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input and random heads may each move one cell left or right, or stay in place, at a step; their boundaries are marked and cannot be crossed. The input may be reread without restriction.

For fixed positive integers \(a,b,c,d\) depending only on the machine, the random tape holds
\[r(n)=a(n+1)^b\]
bits sampled uniformly and independently at the start of the run, and the total work-tape storage is at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits on every input and every random string. Padding the random tape by unused random bits is allowed. A reread of a random cell returns its original sampled bit; it does not toss a new coin. The read-only input and random tapes do not count as writable work space. Any work-tape storage used for counters, remembered bits or bookkeeping does count. There is no additional stream of fresh randomness, writable uncharged auxiliary tape, advice or external oracle.

The machine halts with a one-bit accept/reject answer within \(d(n+1)^d\) steps for every random tape. This is a worst-case polynomial clock, not an expected-time convention. Polynomial time also bounds the number of changes of direction or complete passes. Head movements, tape operations and reading a random bit each cost a machine step. The algorithm may inspect random positions adaptively; no bound by a fixed number of sweeps is imposed.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) if some such machine \(M\) satisfies
\[\forall x\in L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall x\notin L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\le1/3.\]
The random-string variable in these displays is a full tape content. Correctness is required for every input separately, and all binary strings are either yes- or no-instances; there is no promise gap in the input domain. The newer notation \(\mathrm{BP}\!\cdot\!\mathrm L\) in the cited 2024 paper refers to this persistent, rereadable randomness model for decision languages. Ordinary BPL instead restricts the random tape to one-way access.

The deterministic simulator is a uniform multitape Turing decider with no random tape, advice or oracle. It must output \(1\) exactly on \(L\) and halt on every binary input. Set
\[T_D(n)=\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\operatorname{time}_D(x).\]
The required limit is equivalently: for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N_\varepsilon\) such that \(T_D(n)\le2^{\varepsilon n}\) for all \(n\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same \(D\) must satisfy all these bounds. It may depend on \(L\), as may the thresholds; the assertion does not require an effective compiler from descriptions of randomized machines.

The criterion is not merely a running time \(2^{n^k}\) for some fixed \(k\), nor a fixed exponential saving \(2^{0.99n}\). It also does not demand the stronger family of bounds \(2^{n^\varepsilon}\) for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The selected convention is explicitly the limit above. A refutation is a language in the stated randomized class for which every correct deterministic decider fails that limit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the containment under the specified tape and runtime conventions. A proof must establish one exact deterministic decider of sublinear-exponent worst-case time for every language in the class. It need not preserve the logarithmic space bound or effectively transform arbitrary randomized machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some language in the class has no deterministic decider meeting the displayed limit. A simulation with advice, a bound only for restricted random-tape movements, correctness on most inputs or a conditional hardness-to-randomness implication alone is insufficient.
context:
The 2016 introduction contrasts the known polynomial-time deterministic simulation of ordinary BPL with the unresolved simulation of its two-way-randomness counterpart. The whole random tape is fixed for the run, so repeated access cannot be treated as independent fresh coin tosses.

The paper proves that certain machines making fewer than linearly many passes admit a deterministic logspace simulation with linear advice. Advice is a separate string chosen for each input length; that result does not construct the uniform deterministic decider requested here.

The 2024 paper explicitly works with two-way randomness and obtains an equivalence between a leakage-resilient hardness condition and a form of deterministic promise-search simulation. Its theorem is conditional on the hardness property and does not establish the unconditional time containment in this card.

The inherited title conflated the paper’s multipass theorem with the separate question in its introduction. This review restores the latter model and states the \(2^{o(n)}\) convention explicitly; the requested simulator has no separate space bound.
why: Rereading random bits costs no additional writable memory in this model, but it creates dependencies that ordinary one-way randomized-space simulations do not directly handle. Even a subexponential deterministic simulation would clarify how much computational power persistent randomness supplies under a logarithmic memory bound. The problem is a concrete derandomization question between ordinary randomized logspace and unrestricted polynomial-time randomness.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: MFCS 2016 introduction and preliminaries, and MFCS 2024 Sections 1 and 3.1 and Theorem 3.1. The later theorem concerns a hardness equivalence, and the original multipass theorem allows advice. Neither gives the unconditional uniform 2^{o(n)}-time simulation specified here. Bounded searches under two-way randomness, multipass logspace and BP·L found no matching resolution; this does not establish exhaustive current openness.
progress: 2016-08-19: MFCS publishes the two-way-randomness question alongside the distinct multipass simulation with advice. | 2024-08-23: MFCS publishes a hardness equivalence for a stronger promise-search form of two-way-randomness derandomization; it is not an unconditional simulation.
working_summary: This question concerns randomized logspace algorithms that can reread a fixed polynomial-length random tape in either direction. It asks whether every language they decide has a uniform exact deterministic algorithm whose worst-case runtime has an exponent sublinear in input length. The deterministic algorithm has no separate space restriction and receives no advice. The source’s simulation for restricted passes with advice and later conditional promise-search results do not provide this algorithm. The formulation explicitly separates persistent randomness from the one-way coin access used in ordinary BPL.

title: Doubly efficient \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
importance_reason: Tests the efficiency limits of the IP = PSPACE phenomenon when both verifier and prover costs matter, across the full time range.
formal: For every uniform deterministic polynomial-space decider \(M\) and every time-constructible bound \(T(n)\ge n+2\) on its running time, does the language \(L(M)\) have a uniform classical single-prover interactive proof with a verifier running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time and an honest prover running in \(\operatorname{poly}(T(n))\) total time, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) against every cheating prover? The quantifier covers the full time range, rather than only \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\).
definitions:
Fix the standard bit-cost model of deterministic multitape Turing machines with a read-only binary input tape. A decider halts and accepts or rejects on every binary input. For each fixed \(M\), there is a polynomial \(q\) such that on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), \(M\) uses at most \(q(n+2)\) work-tape cells and takes at most \(T(n)\) steps. The same machine must satisfy both bounds. Here \(T:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) is time-constructible in the following convention: some fixed deterministic machine, on unary input \(1^n\), outputs the binary representation of \(T(n)\) within \(K T(n)\) steps for a constant \(K\). The requirement \(T(n)\ge n+2\) merely absorbs bounded lengths. Define \(L(M)=\{x:M\text{ accepts }x\}\).

An interactive proof consists of two fixed finite programs, an honest prover \(P\) and a verifier \(V\), which both receive only the common input \(x\) and exchange finite binary messages. They may use independent private fair random bits. A protocol may expose verifier randomness through its messages, but public coins and perfect completeness are not extra requirements. The machines know their fixed protocol and may incorporate the fixed descriptions of \(M\) and a constructor for \(T\). They receive no advice depending on input length, trusted preprocessing, shared secret, additional witness, oracle, or separately supplied value of \(T(n)\).

For each fixed \(M,T\), there must be constants \(C,a,b\ge1\) and one such pair \(P,V\), all independent of \(n,x\), satisfying these bounds for every input. The verifier's total number of bit operations is at most \(C(n+2)^a\), on every random tape and against every possible sequence of prover messages. It accepts or rejects within that bound. The total number of messages, all transmitted or read message bits and verifier random bits are charged to this bound; malformed or oversized messages may be rejected. The honest prover's total number of bit operations during an interaction with \(V\) is at most \(C(T(n)+2)^b\), on every choice of both random tapes, including inputs outside the language. All input-dependent preprocessing, message generation and communication are included. No separate restriction to polynomial prover space is imposed.

Completeness requires
\[
\Pr[\langle P,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3
\quad\text{for every }x\in L(M),
\]
where the probability is over both machines' independent random bits. Soundness requires, for every \(x\notin L(M)\) and every cheating strategy \(P^*\),
\[
\Pr[\langle P^*,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\le1/3.
\]
A cheating strategy can depend arbitrarily on \(x\) and its visible transcript and can perform unlimited computation; it has no access to unexposed verifier randomness. It may be randomized, with its private randomness independent of the verifier's. There is only one prover, and no computational assumption restricts soundness.

The quantifier order is: for every fixed pair \(M,T\) satisfying the time and polynomial-space premises, there exist \(P,V,C,a,b\) that work for all inputs and lengths. No algorithm transforming descriptions of \(M,T\) into protocols is additionally demanded. The prover bound refers to the specified \(T(n)\), not to an unrestricted exponential in the space bound. The verifier bound remains polynomial in the original input length even when \(T\) is superquasipolynomial.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal protocol-existence assertion with all stated uniformity, total worst-case running-time, completeness and soundness requirements, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. A result covering only a restricted time range, an efficient verifier with no honest-prover bound, or computational soundness under a cryptographic assumption does not settle the assertion. The time bounds are asymptotic resource requirements, not numerical quantities with \(1/100\) additive tolerance.
context:
The card retains its earlier time-constructible, uniform single-prover formulation and constant error gap. The June 2026 source constructs public-coin protocols with perfect completeness, which meet a stronger interface within the time range it covers. The source’s particular round format is not imposed on a solution of this card.

Polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed computation and time bound, but the programs and exponents must remain fixed over all input lengths. Time constructibility does not give the verifier a free time-bound oracle; any work it performs is included in its own bound.

The checked June paper covers polynomial-space computations with \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\). Its more general theorem has verifier time \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log_2 T})}S^2\operatorname{poly}(\sigma,\log S)\), where \(S\) is the space bound and \(2^{-\sigma}\) is the soundness error. This factor is not polynomial in \(n\) throughout the full time range.

The two running-time requirements concern the honest participants. Restricting honest proof generation does not restrict cheating strategies. This distinguishes the question from argument systems whose soundness relies on an adversary’s computational limitations.

The July 2026 one-way-function result gives efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computation, with a stated bound on the size of cheating provers. It does not give the information-theoretic soundness required here.
why: The class equality IP = PSPACE says that polynomial space can be verified efficiently, but does not by itself control the cost of generating the proof relative to the original computation. The target asks whether that prover overhead can always be polynomial while retaining soundness against an unlimited adversary.
status_note: The checked June 2026 source proves the quasipolynomial range and discusses extending it. The July argument-system and oracle-computation abstracts do not state a resolution of this full-time-range unconditional target. Later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.
progress: 2025: Berger, Goyal, Hong and Kalai extend doubly efficient protocols to \(T(n)=n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}\), as recorded in the June 2026 paper’s comparison. | 2026-06-21: ECCC revision 1 gives the \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time range; Section 4, Theorem 5 and Corollary 1 specify the prover and verifier bounds. The revision notice says the change from the original report fixes title encoding. | 2026-07-02: A separate report constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions. Its abstract explicitly limits soundness to cheating provers of bounded circuit size.
working_summary: An interactive proof lets a verifier check a computation through a conversation with one prover. The question asks for a verifier polynomial in input length and an honest prover polynomial in the specified computation time for every polynomial-space decider. The protocol must be uniform across input lengths and must remain sound against arbitrarily powerful cheating strategies. The checked June 2026 theorem covers quasipolynomial computation times, while the card asks for the full time range. A resolution would strengthen IP = PSPACE by controlling proof-generation overhead without replacing information-theoretic soundness with a cryptographic assumption.

title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
importance_reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.
formal: Put \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). For \(0\le p<1/2\), let \(\mathcal C_p(n)\) be the finite noisy circuits defined below. Define reliable computation at noise \(p\) by \[\operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff \exists\delta\in(0,1/2]\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\ \exists C\in\mathcal C_p(n)\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\Pr[C(x)=f(x)]\ge1/2+\delta.\] Is the following proposition true? \[\forall p\in[0,1/2):\quad \operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff p<\beta.\] In particular, the proposition includes impossibility at \(p=\beta\).
definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with labeled input sources \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), noiseless constant sources \(0,1\), and one designated output wire. A computational gate has one or two ordered input wires and an arbitrary fixed Boolean truth table on those bits. Wires may connect a source or an earlier gate to any number of later gates; both inputs of a gate may come from the same predecessor. There are no other gates, external coins, auxiliary inputs, or oracle operations. A gate-free output is allowed to read one source directly.

For every computational gate \(v\), independently sample \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Z_v=1]=p\). Evaluate the DAG in topological order. If the gate truth table applied to its received bits gives \(b\), its actual value is \(b\mathbin{\oplus}Z_v\), where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Every outgoing wire carries this same actual value. All gate failures are mutually independent and independent of the input; wire values sharing a predecessor need not be independent. Input sources and wires are perfect. All computational gates, including NOT and any output gate, have exactly the same flip probability \(p\); no noiseless output decoder is supplied.

The probability in the target is only over this finite product of gate-failure distributions, for a fixed input \(x\). The circuit and its wiring and truth tables may depend on the real parameter \(p\), the integer \(n\), and the entire function \(f\), but not on the actual input \(x\) or realized failures. The advantage \(\delta\) may depend on \(p\), but is chosen before \(n\) and \(f\). Circuit size, depth and construction time are unrestricted, and no uniform algorithm constructing the circuits is required. A formula is the special case where every computational gate has at most one outgoing wire; an input variable can still occur on multiple leaves.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal equivalence or its logical negation, in the specified independent gate-flip model. The same positive advantage must work for every input length and every Boolean function at each fixed noise level. The boundary \(p=\beta\) is part of the claim. A theorem only for formulas, only for a restricted gate basis, or with a separate noiseless decoder does not decide this circuit proposition. A negative resolution of reliable computation must rule out all finite circuit sizes; failure of one construction is insufficient.
context:
The task concerns whether arbitrary computation remains possible at all under local errors, even when unlimited redundancy is permitted. The target keeps a positive correctness margin independent of the function and its number of inputs. It is not a circuit-size overhead problem or an average over randomly chosen inputs.

Unger’s theorem gives the sharp formula boundary \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\), including failure of universal reliable computation at equality, and explicitly conjectures the extension to circuits. Formulas cannot reuse an intermediate noisy gate value; circuits can, so independent gate failures do not make the received signals independent. The positive formula result below \(\beta\) also provides circuits.

The later formulation of reliable computation in Definition 2.1 of Shutty, Wootters and Hayden uses one advantage for all Boolean functions, as here. Their survey distinguishes the symmetric two-input formula threshold from the known general-circuit upper bound \(1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})\). Their main asymmetric model permits gate-dependent errors, including noiseless XOR, and its proposed circuit extension is conditional. Those statements do not settle the identical-noise circuit claim.

The July 2025 essay revisits established circuit-noise bounds and discusses majority gates of higher arity. Its stated scope does not supply the missing exact threshold for arbitrary two-input circuits.
why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.
status_note: The circuit extension is explicitly conjectured in Unger’s 2008 paper. The 2023 revision of Shutty–Wootters–Hayden was checked in full text at the cited definitions, survey and conditional statements; its arXiv history still ends at version 5. The 2025 essay was checked for its stated scope. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching resolution; this is historical source openness with a limited later-work review, not an exhaustive or Lean-verified status certification.
progress: 2008: The two-input formula threshold, including its boundary, is established; the unrestricted circuit counterpart is stated as a conjecture. | 2023-05-01: The revised asymmetric-noise paper retains distinct formula and circuit bounds and makes its circuit strengthening conditional. | 2025-07-20: A later expository manuscript revisits noise bounds and higher-arity majority gates; its abstract and opening model were checked for scope.
working_summary: Each gate of a Boolean circuit independently flips its computed output with the same probability. The circuit may reuse noisy intermediate values and may be arbitrarily large. The question asks whether universal reliable computation is possible exactly below the known two-input formula threshold. Reliability requires one positive correctness advantage that works for every Boolean function and input length at the chosen noise level. A resolution would determine whether sharing intermediate computations changes the fundamental tolerance to gate errors.

title: Polynomial-size closure of d-DNNF under negation
importance_reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.
formal:
Do constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set \(X\) and every d-DNNF circuit \(C\) over \(X\), there is a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over \(X\) with
\[s(D)\le c\bigl(s(C)+1\bigr)^k\quad\text{and}\quad\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\ f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The constants are universal: they cannot depend on \(X\), \(C\) or its Boolean function. No algorithm, uniformity or bound on the time needed to find \(D\) is required. Its internal decompositions may differ from those of \(C\), with no global variable-tree restriction on either circuit.
definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

The output uses only variables of \(X\), interpreted on the same coordinates, with no auxiliary variables or existential projection. It need not mention every variable. The size counts the complete circuit rather than an implicit description or an oracle for evaluating it. The target is nonconstructive representational closure with polynomial overhead, not closure as a set of Boolean functions alone.

The exact negation of the claim is that for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some finite \(X\) and some d-DNNF \(C\) have the property that every d-DNNF \(D\) computing its complement satisfies \(s(D)>c(s(C)+1)^k\). This need not be witnessed by one fixed input circuit defeating all polynomials, or by an efficiently constructible family. A uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm would imply the size bound; the converse is not part of this statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal polynomial-size closure statement. A proof must supply universal constants and establish a complement representation satisfying the bound for every input circuit. A refutation must establish the quantified superpolynomial obstruction for general output d-DNNFs. A lower bound that only excludes structured outputs, a particular decomposition or a particular algorithm is insufficient. Computational difficulty in finding a complement alone also does not refute existence of a small complement.
context:
The source question explicitly separates efficient complementation from existence of a small complement. Every Boolean complement has some d-DNNF representation; the issue is a polynomial bound, and for the computational version a uniform algorithm achieving one.

The knowledge-compilation map treats negation as a transformation with an output representation, separately from queries such as counting satisfying assignments or comparing functions. Its d-DNNF negation entry is unresolved.

Vinall-Smeeth proves a superpolynomial complement-size lower bound when the output must remain structured, even without output determinism. The source leaves unstructured d-DNNF complementation open: removing the global variable-tree restriction changes the target of the lower bound.

The 2026 probabilistic-word paper connects complement gates in tractable circuit representations to the unresolved succinctness question for d-DNNFs. This is evidence of an additional counting-language connection, not a general complement construction or lower bound.
why: This question isolates whether Boolean negation inherently destroys the succinctness of a central tractable representation. It separates a representational obstruction from the algorithmic difficulty of discovering a representation. A negative answer would exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between compact descriptions of a set of assignments and its complement; a positive answer would establish polynomial-size robustness under negation.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: Amarilli’s explicit polynomial-size companion question, the knowledge-compilation definitions, IJCAI 2024 Theorem 2 and Section 6, and STACS 2026 Section 7. The known complement-size separation restricts the output to structured circuits. A bounded later-work check found no matching theorem for all unstructured d-DNNF outputs. This individual audit does not independently verify every cited proof.
progress: 2024-02-07: The structured-class separation is first posted as arXiv:2402.04832 and later published at IJCAI 2024; its output restriction leaves the general question open. | 2026-02-25: The STACS paper explicitly retains d-DNNF complementation as an open question in its conclusion.
working_summary: The question asks whether every d-DNNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representing its Boolean complement. One polynomial must bound the size increase for every circuit and every finite variable set. The complement may use entirely different decompositions, provided that decomposability and determinism are retained. No efficient procedure for finding the complement is required in this representational question. The published failure of closure for structured circuits does not settle closure for general d-DNNFs.

title: Supercubic uniform formula lower bounds for SAT
importance_reason: Improving explicit formula or depth-three circuit lower bounds would go beyond established lower-bound techniques.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon >0\) such that no LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family computing \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}\) for every n has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves?
definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for \(x_{i}\), 1 for \(\neg x_{i}\)), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: \(\lfloor \log _{2}i\rfloor\) zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with AND and OR gates of fan-in two. Each leaf is an input bit, its negation, or a Boolean constant. Equivalently, unary NOT gates can be used anywhere and then pushed to the leaves without changing the leaf count. Internal computations cannot be shared between two parents. Its size is the number of leaf occurrences, so repeated uses of the same variable are charged separately. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in \(O(\log  n)\) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves if some constant C bounds its size by \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and \(\varepsilon\), but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family has, for every \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\), some \(n\ge N_{0}\) with more than \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) leaves. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.
context:
The object computing SAT receives the bits of a formula and outputs whether some assignment satisfies it. This card asks whether even a uniformly described De Morgan formula must exceed the \(n^{3}\) scale by a fixed positive exponent. The circuit or formula that decides SAT is distinct from the 3-CNF formula encoded in its input.

The formula \((a\land b)\lor (a\land c)\) has four leaf occurrences, although it mentions only three variables. This illustrates why a formula-size bound counts uses of inputs, not distinct variable names. The benchmark size is for the formula computing SAT on n encoding bits.

A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. The input to that description algorithm is the input length and a position in the description, not a particular SAT instance.

The question is whether SAT lies outside the uniform size-\(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) class for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Thus every correct uniform family must exceed any constant multiple of that bound at arbitrarily large lengths. This uses the standard class-nonmembership interpretation of the source’s lower-bound question; it does not add an almost-everywhere requirement.

The 2016 column records nearly cubic De Morgan formula lower bounds for SAT. Bathie and Williams’s ITCS 2024 paper obtains a depth lower bound of \(3.603 \log _{2} n\) for polylogtime-uniform NAND circuits solving SAT. NAND depth uses a restricted gate basis and a different cost measure; this statement alone does not settle the requested De Morgan leaf-size bound.
why: Would cross the cubic exponent for uniform De Morgan formula lower bounds on SAT. This quantifies a limitation of tree-shaped Boolean computation on an NP-complete problem without demanding a full separation from every polynomial-size family.
status_note: Source statement, model and the cited subsequent or baseline result checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact uniform SAT size question. No exhaustive literature or independent proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2016: Williams states the supercubic uniform SAT formula question and records the nearly cubic lower-bound baseline. | 2024: Bathie and Williams prove a larger-than-\(3 \log _{2} n\) depth lower bound for uniform NAND circuits solving SAT. Their paper explicitly distinguishes circuit depth, gate basis and formula-size lower bounds.
working_summary: A De Morgan formula computes with binary AND and OR gates and input negations, without sharing internal computations. Its size counts leaf occurrences, and the target function is SAT on n bits encoding a 3-CNF formula. The source asks whether a fixed positive exponent can raise the required size beyond the cubic scale when the formula family is LOGTIME-uniform. Later NAND depth lower bounds use a different gate basis and cost measure, so they do not directly settle this question. The problem seeks a concrete improvement in uniform formula lower bounds for a central NP-complete language.

title: Depth-three lower bounds beyond the log-depth simulation threshold
importance_reason: Improving explicit formula or depth-three circuit lower bounds would go beyond established lower-bound techniques.
formal:
Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) such that
\[S_3(f_n)=2^{\omega(n/\log\log n)}?\]
Here explicit means membership in NP, as in the source, and \(S_3\) counts gates in the smallest unrestricted-fan-in AND/OR circuit of depth three with negations available on inputs. Both top-gate orientations are covered. To avoid undefined small-length logarithms, the precise scale in the quantifiers is \(h(n)=n/\log_2\log_2(n+4)\), which has the stated asymptotics. This is Research Problem 11.2's quantitative target; the inherited description in terms of a switching-lemma barrier did not specify its much stronger exponent.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), the target \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is a total Boolean function. A literal is an input \(x_i\) or its complement \(1-x_i\). The two constant bits are also permitted as leaves. A \(\Sigma_3\) circuit has a single top OR gate, middle AND gates and bottom OR gates; edges go between successive layers, and bottom gates receive literals or constants. A \(\Pi_3\) circuit interchanges AND and OR. Every gate has finite but unrestricted fan-in, fan-out is unrestricted, and sharing of bottom gates is allowed. Fan-in-one gates permit padding to three layers. Empty AND and OR evaluate to one and zero respectively. There are no other operations, internal negations, parity gates, thresholds, modular gates, or auxiliary witness inputs.

Size is the total number of AND and OR gates, including the output gate and any padding gates. Input literals, constants and edges are not charged. Let \(S_{\Sigma_3}(f_n)\) and \(S_{\Pi_3}(f_n)\) be the respective minimum sizes of circuits computing \(f_n(x)\) exactly on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\); define \(S_3(f_n)\) as their minimum. The circuit at each length may be arbitrary and nonuniform. There is no bounded-bottom-fan-in, monotonicity, canonical form beyond the stated layers, or formula/no-sharing promise. Circuit minimization measures size rather than the time to find the circuit. Gates with repeated inputs can be simplified, so forbidding parallel copies of the same edge does not change the measure.

“Explicit” follows the source's Section 1.5.1: the language \(\{x:f_{|x|}(x)=1\}\) belongs to NP. Concretely, there must be one deterministic finite-program multitape Turing verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,b\), such that
\[f_n(x)=1\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{(n+1)^a}:V(x,y)=1,\]
and \(V\) halts within \((n+|y|+1)^b+b\) steps on every pair. Padding gives this exact witness length without changing NP. All reading and bit operations are charged, and no advice or oracles are available to \(V\). Polynomial-time computable functions are allowed, but polynomial-time evaluation is not additionally required. This uniform requirement belongs to the target family, not to the circuits ruled out. A counting existence proof of hard arbitrary truth tables without such a verifier does not establish explicitness.

All logarithms are base two. For a positive scale \(h(n)\), the notation \(S(f_n)=2^{\omega(h(n))}\) in the target means that for every positive integer \(r\) there is an integer \(N_r\) such that \(S(f_n)\ge2^{r h(n)}\) for every \(n\ge N_r\). One target family and one verifier must serve all these bounds; the family cannot change with \(r\). The onset may depend on \(r\). This all-sufficiently-large-length convention is part of the displayed asymptotic target, not a mere increase of a fixed constant in an exponent.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this NP family with the stated lower bound against both orientations. A positive answer must specify the family and its verifier, prove exact-function hardness for every sufficiently large length at every exponent multiplier, and use the stated gate-count model. A negative answer must rule out every qualifying family; it need not give one finite counterexample. A \(2^{c n/\log\log n}\) lower bound for one fixed \(c\), a \(2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}\) lower bound alone, or a theorem for only monotone, bounded-bottom-fan-in or canonical circuits does not establish this claim. A conditional lower bound qualifies only if its assumption is also proved.
context:
Lemma 11.1 gives a simulation of linear-size logarithmic-depth binary circuits by depth-three circuits of size \(2^{O(n/\log\log n)}\). Research Problem 11.2 asks to exceed every constant at that exponent scale. The conclusion concerns the combined linear-size and logarithmic-depth resource bound, and does not by itself rule out arbitrary-depth linear-size circuits.

The same chapter separately asks to exceed the \(2^{O(\sqrt n)}\) scale in Research Problem 11.15. That weaker quantitative frontier has its own active card. A solution to the present problem would exceed it by a much larger margin.

The February 2026 paper still describes the square-root exponent barrier for general depth-three circuits. Its new optimum for Majority restricts circuits to positive literals and bottom fan-in at most three, so it does not meet the unrestricted target here.

The March 2026 report discusses the same general frontier. Its stronger exponents in Corollary 4 apply under a complexity hypothesis to a specially defined canonical circuit class; they are not unconditional bounds for all circuits allowed by this card.
why: This is the depth-three threshold that would exclude linear-size circuits of logarithmic depth for an explicit problem. It asks for a quantitative jump beyond the square-root exponent frontier, while retaining arbitrary sharing and unrestricted bottom fan-in in the shallow circuit. It therefore connects a very restricted depth model to a longstanding lower-bound goal for more general computation.

title: FBPP versus negligible-error FBPP
importance_reason: A foundational distinction between error conventions for general relational randomized computation, with consequences for interpreting randomized search and separations from deterministic computation.
formal:
Under the following relational error conventions, is
\[\mathrm{FBPP}\subseteq\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}?\]
In \(\mathrm{FBPP}\), a uniform randomized algorithm receives a precision parameter \(m\ge1\) in unary, must produce a valid answer with probability at least \(1-1/m\), and may take time polynomial in \(|x|+m\). In \(\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}\), one uniform randomized algorithm receives only \(x\), runs in time polynomial in \(|x|\), and has error smaller than every inverse polynomial for all sufficiently long inputs.

Both classes range over the same polynomially bounded binary relations. Relations may be partial and need not have decidable membership. The inclusion quantifies over every such relation; a negligible-error algorithm may depend on the relation but must be one fixed algorithm for all input lengths and all inverse-polynomial comparisons.
definitions:
A relation is any set \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*\). Its domain is \(\operatorname{dom}(R)=\{x:\exists y\ (x,y)\in R\}\). On a domain input \(x\), any \(y\) with \((x,y)\in R\) is a valid output. On inputs outside the domain, no correctness condition is imposed. Polynomially bounded means that fixed positive integers \(a,b\) exist with
\[|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in R.\]
This bound is independent of a requested precision. There is no promise that membership in \(R\), its domain, or validity of a proposed answer can be computed or efficiently verified. All these relations, not merely NP search relations or total relations, are included in the quantifier.

Use finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines with binary input, a binary output string and independent unbiased random bits. Reading and writing bits and generating each random bit count as steps. There is no oracle, nonuniform advice or arbitrary real-arithmetic primitive. Runtime bounds are worst-case bounds over every input and every random-bit sequence. Each machine must halt on every run. Success probabilities refer only to its internal random bits for a fixed input, never to an average input distribution.

Formally, \(R\in\mathrm{FBPP}\) when there are a machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that \(A\), given the self-delimited pair \((x,1^m)\), halts within \(C(|x|+m+1)^d\) steps for every binary \(x\) and integer \(m\ge1\), and
\[\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(R)\ \forall m\ge1,\quad\Pr[(x,A(x,1^m))\in R]\ge1-\frac1m.\]
Here \(1^m\) is a unary string of length \(m\), not the binary encoding of \(m\). This discrete convention gives the source's arbitrary positive-error definition by taking \(m=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\). For \(\varepsilon\ge1\) the success requirement is vacuous. The fixed polynomial output bound is a property of valid pairs; outputs on unsuccessful runs may be any strings allowed by the machine's runtime.

Formally, \(R\in\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}\) when there are a single machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(D,e\) such that \(B(x)\) halts within \(D(|x|+1)^e\) steps on every run, and
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists N_k\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(R),\quad |x|\ge N_k\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[(x,B(x))\notin R]\le(|x|+2)^{-k}.\]
The exponent \(k\) ranges over positive integers and is not an input to \(B\). The threshold \(N_k\) may depend on \(B,R,k\), but not on the particular input. The same \(B,D,e\) must satisfy all these bounds. The shift by two only avoids small-length singularities and does not alter negligibility. Equivalently, the worst error over domain inputs of each length is bounded by some negligible function of that length; no computability requirement is imposed on that bounding function. At lengths with no domain inputs the guarantee is vacuous.

The first class therefore permits increasingly costly precision requests; the second requires one polynomial running-time bound with negligible error as the input length grows. No distribution on the valid answers is prescribed in either class. Different outputs on independent runs may all be valid, so this is not the unique-answer decision setting.

An affirmative answer says that every relation meeting the first definition admits some machine meeting the second. It does not require an effective transformation from descriptions of \(A\) to descriptions of \(B\). A negative answer is a polynomially bounded relation admitting such an \(A\) but no qualifying \(B\). The reverse noninclusion is a separate, already established result in the source.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated inclusion for the full class of polynomially bounded relations. A proof must establish one negligible-error, fixed-polynomial-time algorithm for each relation in FBPP, with the displayed order of quantifiers. A refutation must exhibit a relation in FBPP and exclude every algorithm meeting the negligible-error definition. Separate algorithms or polynomial exponents for separate values of the error exponent do not establish membership in the latter class. Restricting to efficiently checkable, decidable or total relations does not prove the universal inclusion. Reproving the reverse noninclusion does not refute it.
context:
Definition 1 deliberately permits relations without an efficient validity test. It also imposes a precision-independent polynomial bound on valid output lengths, preventing improved accuracy from being obtained by changing to longer and longer answer domains.

Section 5 proves that negligible-error FBPP is not contained in the precision-parameter version. Proposition 23 uses the broader relation convention, including noncomputable validity sets. The unresolved direction here is therefore whether the precision-parameter class is properly contained in the negligible-error class or the two are incomparable.

For comparison, the source also defines a class allowing time polynomial in input length and the logarithm of reciprocal error. That stronger runtime guarantee implies negligible-error membership. Its inclusion does not answer the question for algorithms allowed polynomial dependence on reciprocal error itself.

The source’s class separations and advice results emphasize that relational randomized computation can behave differently from BPP decision languages. This card isolates the error-convention question and includes no advice, quantum computation or prescribed sampling distribution.
why: For a decision problem, repeated trials concern one correct bit. A relation may instead allow many different valid answers without any procedure for recognizing them. This question tests whether adjustable inverse-error running time can always be replaced by negligible failure at one fixed polynomial cost, clarifying which error-reduction properties survive in general randomized search.

A bounded later-work search found no matching resolution using the same polynomially bounded, possibly undecidable relation convention. It does not establish exhaustive present openness.
