working_summary: The question compares two error requirements for randomized algorithms that may return any valid answer to a relation. FBPP here allows a unary precision parameter and running time polynomial in reciprocal error. The negligible-error class instead requires one algorithm with a fixed polynomial time bound and error eventually below every inverse polynomial. Relations may be partial and need not have an effective test for valid answers. The source proves noninclusion in the reverse direction, leaving this inclusion versus incomparability unresolved.

title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
importance_reason: Stronger time-space or uniform circuit lower bounds would constrain natural satisfiability and graph problems in standard resource regimes.
formal: For every space-constructible function \(s:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) with \(s(n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\), is every language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) decidable deterministically in \(o(s(n)^{2})\) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an \(O(s(n))\)-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace \(g_{D}(n)\) on n-bit inputs satisfies \(\lim (n\to \infty ) g_{D}(n)/s(n)^{2}=0\)?
definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) denotes languages with such a machine using at most \(C s(n)\) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on \(1^{n}\) can output \(1^{s}(n)\) using \(O(s(n))\) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving \(s^{2- \varepsilon}\) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of \(s(n)^{2}\). Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in \(s(n)^{2}, a\) simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.
context:
A nondeterministic machine can choose among several next moves and accepts if some sequence of choices succeeds. A deterministic simulation must decide the same question without those choices. Savitch’s theorem shows that squaring the workspace is enough, even though the simulation may take much longer.

If a nondeterministic computation uses about s cells, the target is a deterministic simulation whose memory divided by \(s^{2}\) tends to zero. A bound such as \(s^{2}/\log (s+2)\) would qualify, while \(0.01s^{2}\) would not. These expressions illustrate the meaning of little-o; the question imposes no particular rate of improvement.

For \(s(n)\) of order log n, the target becomes deterministic \(o(\log ^{2} n)\) space for every language in nondeterministic logarithmic space. This includes directed reachability: given a directed graph and two vertices, decide whether there is a directed path between them. The full card quantifies over all admitted s and does not restrict inputs to a special graph family.

The source was posed after Cook and Mertz’s STOC 2024 improvement for tree evaluation. That problem evaluates a tree of explicitly supplied functions and leaf values, and its stated space bound is \(O(\log  N\cdot \log  \log  N)\) in the tree-evaluation input size N. The general nondeterministic-space simulation remains the target of the 2025 question.

The 2025 connectivity paper states alternatives linking improvements in reachability and derandomization. Its abstract does not give an unconditional simulation of every nondeterministic-space computation in \(o(s^{2})\) space.

A 2026 directed-reachability preprint trades ordinary workspace against catalytic memory, which begins with arbitrary contents and must be restored. Its abstract does not state the requested improvement in total ordinary workspace.
why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.

Subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no unconditional resolution of the displayed general containment. Related 2025 conditional results and 2026 catalytic-memory results were checked at abstract level; full proofs were not audited.

This card asks whether every at-least-logarithmic space-constructible bound admits an improvement to \(o(s^{2})\). The machine is deterministic and all ordinary working memory is charged, with no restriction on running time. A constant-factor improvement does not suffice, while no fixed polynomial saving is required. A resolution would sharpen the general memory cost of eliminating nondeterminism, including for logarithmic-space computation.

title: Deterministic query complexity of tournament kings
importance_reason: A well-established query-complexity gap for a canonical total graph search problem, with a pronounced deterministic–randomized distinction and sustained independent work since 2003.
formal: Determine the asymptotic order of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\), the minimum worst-case number of edge-orientation queries needed by a deterministic decision tree to output one king of every tournament on \([n]\). The domain is the integers \(n\ge 2\). The required precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to absolute constant factors: supply a positive function \(f\) and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge 2\) such that \(c f(n)\le D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\le C f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\).
definitions: A tournament on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a loopless directed graph having exactly one of the arcs \(i\to j\) and \(j\to i\) for each distinct pair. Represent it by a bit \(x_{ij}\) for each \(1\le i<j\le n\): value 1 means \(i\to j\), and value 0 means \(j\to i\). Every assignment of these \(\binom n2\) bits is a valid input; there are no transitivity, degree or distribution promises. A vertex \(v\) is a king if for every \(u\ne v\), either \(v\to u\), or there exists \(w\in[n]\setminus\{u,v\}\) with \(v\to w\) and \(w\to u\). Thus the path must follow the arrows and have at most two edges. The task is to output any one such vertex, rather than to decide whether one exists, to verify a given candidate, or to output every king. A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node names a pair \(i<j\), its two outgoing edges are labeled 0 and 1, and each leaf names one vertex. Starting at the root, the input follows the edge matching the named input bit. The tree is correct if the leaf reached is a king for every complete bit assignment. Its cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited over all inputs. Define \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) as the minimum cost of a correct tree for that n. The tree may choose later queries from previous answers. Only single-edge queries are charged; internal computation, storage, knowledge of n and production of the vertex label are free. Separate trees may be chosen for each n; no polynomial-time construction or uniform generation of their descriptions is required. There are no random coins, quantum queries or additional graph oracles. Every nonempty tournament has a king, so this minimum is finite; the omitted one-vertex case has cost zero. Constants in the asymptotic answer are independent of n and of the tournament, and logarithmic factors are not absorbed into those constants.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked characterization of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) to the stated constant-factor precision. An acceptable positive function \(f\) must be specified by an unambiguous mathematical description and accompanied by proofs of both bounds for every sufficiently large integer n in the stated decision-tree model. The upper bound must establish correct trees at all such sizes; the lower bound must apply to every correct tree. Merely renaming the defining minimum, bounding only its exponent while leaving nonconstant factors unspecified, or improving just one side of the gap does not meet this criterion. This is an asymptotic target, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not an additive tolerance on its growth rate.
context:
Pairwise outcomes can cycle: one player defeats a second, the second defeats a third, and the third defeats the first. A king need not defeat everyone directly; it must defeat each other player either directly or through one intermediary. In that three-cycle all three vertices qualify. The task therefore allows multiple correct outputs and does not impose an ordering or tie-breaking rule.

The graph is hidden behind edge queries. Reading its entire adjacency table always supplies enough information, but a search algorithm may stop once the answers force one output vertex to be a king in every tournament consistent with them. The central question is the optimal amount of information for this search relation, with unrestricted computation on what has been learned.

The source asks to determine the deterministic complexity without proposing a particular exponent as the answer. This card makes the requested asymptotic precision explicit as \(\Theta\), preserving the full gap question. An upper bound of \(O(n^{4/3})\) or a lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) would match a known opposite bound, but neither exponent is imposed as the conjectured answer.

A zero-error randomized algorithm can have a small expected number of queries while some random outcomes use more. A bounded-error randomized algorithm instead permits a small failure probability on each fixed tournament. Both differ from the deterministic worst-case target. Similarly, reaching a fixed fraction of vertices is a weaker output requirement than being a king.

The 2025 paper resolves two nearby questions: deciding king existence in arbitrary directed graphs, and finding a strong king in a tournament. A strong king satisfies an additional comparison between numbers of two-edge paths in opposite directions. Neither result gives the optimum for finding an ordinary king in a tournament, and the paper explicitly keeps this latter question open.
why: This is a longstanding total search problem in which existence is elementary but the information needed for deterministic discovery is unresolved. It isolates a substantial gap between deterministic and randomized access to a graph, without the computational cost of processing already known edges. A tight bound would explain how much pairwise information is inherently required to identify a vertex with global two-step reachability, a tournament solution motivated by pairwise competition and social choice.
status_note: The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves this deterministic gap open. The original bounds and the 2022–2024 related results were checked against primary papers. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified improvement settling the target; this is a bounded search, not an independent verification of all proofs or an exhaustive current-status certification.
progress: 2003-08-06: Shen, Sheng and Wu prove an \(O(n^{3/2})\) upper bound and an \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) lower bound for finding one king. Their matching \(\Theta(n^{3/2})\) result concerns a sorted sequence of kings and does not close the single-output gap. | 2022: Lachish, Reidl and Trehan obtain \(O(n^{4/3}\operatorname{polylog} n)\) queries for a vertex that reaches at least a \(1/2+2/17\) fraction of all vertices within two steps. The fraction is strictly below one. | 2023: Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh prove randomized bounds between \(\Omega(n)\) and \(O(n\log\log n)\), and quantum bounds matching up to polylogarithmic factors around \(\sqrt n\), with bounded error. These do not alter the deterministic bounds. | 2024: Abboud, Grossman, Naor and Solomon give a zero-error randomized algorithm using at most \(2n\) queries in expectation. Their Question 7 separately restates the unresolved deterministic gap. | 2025: Ismaili Alaoui and Mande prove \(\Theta(n^2)\) randomized query complexity for king existence in general digraphs and for strong-king search in tournaments. Their concluding Section 5 again identifies ordinary deterministic king search as open with the 2003 bounds.
working_summary: A king in a tournament reaches every other vertex along a directed path of at most two edges. A deterministic algorithm learns the orientation of one chosen edge per query and must output a king for every tournament. The target is its optimal worst-case query count up to constant factors as the number of vertices grows. The checked deterministic bounds remain \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) and \(O(n^{3/2})\), whereas randomization permits linear expected query cost. Closing the deterministic gap would quantify how much pairwise information this total search task inherently requires.

title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
importance_reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that decides weighted falsifiability for every unambiguous DNF? Given
\[F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j,\qquad w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,\]
it must decide whether
\[\exists a\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\qquad F(a)=0\quad\land\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t.\]
Each term \(T_j\) is explicitly listed, and the weights and threshold are binary integers. Unambiguity means that no assignment satisfies two distinct term occurrences. The threshold is “at least,” not exact equality.
question_excerpt: The maintained problem list asks whether one can decide in polynomial time if an unambiguous DNF has a falsifying assignment with total binary-encoded weight at least a given threshold. Monet’s original post gives the equivalent optimization and strict-threshold versions.
definitions:
An instance lists integers \(n,m\ge0\), a DNF formula on \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), one nonnegative weight for each of the \(n\) variables, and a signed integer threshold. A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). Each term \(T_j\) is a finite list of literals interpreted as their conjunction, and \(F\) is the disjunction of the terms. The empty term is true; a DNF with no terms is false. Repeating a literal within a term has no effect, and a term containing both signs of a variable is always false. Such contradictory terms may be deleted without changing the function or its unambiguity.

A Boolean assignment \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) gives each variable a bit; a positive literal is true when the bit is 1 and a negative literal when it is 0. Formally, unambiguity is
\[\forall a\in\{0,1\}^{n},\qquad |\{j:T_j(a)=1\}|\le1.\]
For consistent terms, this is equivalent to every pair containing opposite signs of some common variable. Thus unambiguity can be checked in polynomial time from the explicit lists. Duplicate consistent term occurrences violate the condition. Unused variables remain part of the assignment and contribute their weights.

Use a fixed explicitly delimited binary encoding of the lists: variable indices, list lengths and nonnegative integers are binary, literal signs and the threshold sign are explicit, and every list entry is written in full. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits, including the formula, all weights and the threshold. The question concerns a deterministic multitape Turing machine with running time at most \(C(L+1)^d\) for fixed constants \(C,d\), on all inputs. It has no randomness, oracle, advice or unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers. The cost of exact integer arithmetic is included. Syntactically invalid inputs, invalid variable indices, negative weights and formulas failing unambiguity are rejected. Because validity and unambiguity are polynomial-time checkable, this total-language convention preserves the intended promised-input question.

An accepted input must have at least one falsifying assignment meeting the threshold. If \(F\) is a tautology there is no such assignment, whatever \(t\) is. With \(W=\sum_iw_i\), a threshold larger than \(W\) always gives no, and a threshold at most zero asks ordinary falsifiability. The definitions also cover \(n=0\), where there is one empty assignment and its score is zero. Weights and comparisons are exact, without rounding or error probability.

The original author phrases the optimization version as the maximum score of a falsifying assignment, with value \(-\infty\) for a tautology. Its strict comparison \(\text{score}>t\) is equivalent to \(\text{score}\ge t+1\) for integer scores. The maintained problem list uses the latter non-strict convention. The card retains its existing decision target, equivalent to polynomial-time exact optimization because finite attainable scores lie between 0 and \(W\), whose binary length is polynomial in the input size.

A pseudopolynomial algorithm has running time polynomial in \(L\) and the numerical weight sum \(W\). This can be exponential in the bit length of a binary weight and therefore is not the requested polynomial bound. Membership in P means the existence of the single uniform machine defined above. Membership in NP means that a polynomial-length binary witness can be checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier; this problem lies in NP because an \(n\)-bit assignment is such a witness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation that the defined language is in P. A positive answer must provide one deterministic algorithm and prove exact correctness and a running time polynomial in the full binary input length, including arbitrarily large binary weights. A negative answer must prove that no such polynomial-time decider exists. NP-hardness alone supplies a negative conclusion only under the additional assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); an assumption-dependent conclusion is not an unconditional refutation of this card. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, an unweighted algorithm, hardness without the unambiguity condition or hardness for exact-score equality does not settle this target. The decision and time guarantees are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance does not apply.
context:
Unambiguity makes the satisfying sets of the individual terms disjoint. This makes the total number of satisfying assignments easy to count, and ordinary falsifiability can be decided from that count. The unresolved weighted task asks whether the complement contains a sufficiently high-scoring assignment, which is information the total count alone does not supply.

For example, \(F=(x\land y)\lor(\neg x\land z)\) is unambiguous. With weights 8, 3 and 5, the assignment \((1,0,1)\) falsifies it and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has score 16 but satisfies the formula. Thus a maximum unconstrained score need not occur outside the satisfying region.

Weighted satisfaction is polynomial-time solvable even for general DNFs, whereas weighted falsification requires all terms to fail at once. The author also notes that dropping unambiguity makes the decision problem NP-complete. These nearby easy and hard cases isolate the significance of the disjointness restriction.

For unary weights, the authors’ observations give a polynomial-time algorithm; for binary weights the same bound is only pseudopolynomial. Replacing the inequality by exact equality gives a different, NP-hard problem, so that modification cannot be used as a resolution of the stated threshold question.

The seminar report places this question among problems about compact Boolean representations used in database provenance and explanations. The issue illustrates that efficient counting and efficient optimization of falsifying assignments need not follow from the same representation properties.

The maintained list also discusses larger compiled-circuit representations. Those connections motivate the problem, while this card asks only about explicitly listed unambiguous DNFs and one additive score threshold.
why: The problem isolates whether a representation with easy exact counting also supports optimization over its complement. Binary weights create a sharp distinction from the unweighted and unary cases, with consequences for the operations supported by compact Boolean representations.
status_note: Source-open in the maintained primary problem list checked on 16 September 2026. The original 4 January 2024 post was read through the public page and Stack Exchange API, which returned zero answers; §6.1 of the 2024 seminar report was checked as a pointer to that same formulation. The maintained list still records the polynomial-time threshold question and partial results. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no matching algorithm or hardness resolution. An unanswered post and a maintained list do not exhaustively certify current openness; this review records those limits.
progress: January 2024: Monet posts the binary-weight problem, NP-membership observation and the distinction between weighted satisfaction and falsification. | July 2024: The Dagstuhl seminar report publishes the question in §6.1 by linking to the original post. | 16 September 2026 check: The maintained list still explicitly asks for a polynomial-time threshold algorithm and distinguishes unary weights and exact equality. The original post still has no posted answer; this is not by itself an exhaustive literature-status check.
working_summary: The question asks whether an unambiguous DNF has a falsifying assignment whose additive integer score meets a threshold. Every weight is encoded in binary, and the requested deterministic running time is polynomial in the entire bit representation. Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint and ordinary falsifiability easy. Unary-weight algorithms and hardness for exact-score equality leave the binary threshold question unsettled in the checked sources. A complete answer must establish or refute polynomial-time decidability with the stated representation and guarantee.

title: Cost of restricting linear circuits to depth two
importance_reason: The question tests structural limits of linear computation, including depth, inversion, and the possible usefulness of nonlinear operations.
formal:
Determine the asymptotic order, up to constant factors, of each of the three depth-restriction penalties
\[D_L(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{L,2}(A)}{C_L(A)},\qquad L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}.\]
The numerator restricts a circuit to two leveled addition layers and the denominator allows arbitrary depth, with the same operation and matrix in each ratio. Size counts wires, fan-in is unrestricted, and matrices are square of dimension \(n\). This quantifies Problem 7.6 for the three linear-computation systems in the book; it does not ask only whether a gap can grow.
definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M_n=\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}\) for integers \(n\ge1\). Rows index outputs and columns index inputs. For \(A=(a_{ij})\), the output coordinate is \(y_i=\mathop{\circ}_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\), where the operation is Boolean OR, nonnegative-integer addition (SUM), or addition modulo two (XOR). An empty sum is zero. OR and XOR inputs range over \(\{0,1\}^n\); SUM inputs range over \(\mathbb N^n\), with \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). The matrix entries only select terms; multiplication gates are not part of the model.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(n\) distinct designated input vertices of indegree zero and \(n\) distinct designated output vertices of outdegree zero, disjoint from the input vertices. Every noninput vertex sums the values of its incoming neighbors using the one chosen operation. An indegree-zero noninput vertex, in particular a zero output, computes zero. Fan-in and fan-out have no finite uniform bound, and a value may be reused at several later vertices. Graph edges carry one value and there are no parallel edges. Unary gates copy a value. Circuits compute all output coordinates exactly and simultaneously, for every input in the relevant domain. There are no negative coefficients, NOT gates, mixed operations, advice inputs, or random errors in these three addition models.

Size is the number of edges, also called wires. Every edge counts, including input edges and edges into outputs; gate count and the bit complexity of evaluating an integer sum are not the size measure. Let \(C_L(A)\) be the minimum size for \(L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}\), with depth unrestricted. This is a nonuniform minimum: the circuit can depend arbitrarily on the full matrix, and no efficient construction from its encoding is required. Matrices with nonzero entries have positive complexity. The all-zero matrix is excluded from ratios to avoid \(0/0\).

For the depth-two version \(C_{L,2}(A)\), follow the source's leveled convention: inputs, one intermediate layer, and outputs are three disjoint levels, with edges only from inputs to the intermediate layer or from that layer to outputs. Direct input-to-output edges are not allowed in this version. The intermediate layer may have any finite size; zero outputs and unary gates are allowed. Equivalently, \(C_{L,2}(A)\) minimizes \(|P|+|Q|\) over Boolean matrices \(P\in\{0,1\}^{n\times r}\), \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{r\times n}\), for any integer \(r\ge0\), satisfying \(A=PQ\) over the specified semiring, where \(|P|,|Q|\) count their one-entries. Thus in the SUM case the integer product must have exactly the prescribed zero-one entries, without duplicate contributions.

All these minima exist, and maxima over \(\mathcal M_n\) exist because the matrix set is finite. The extremizing matrices in two different ratios need not be the same. A dimensional asymptotic bound concerns \(n\to\infty\) through all positive integers, with base-two logarithms.
answer_criterion: Give positive comparison functions \(d_{\mathrm{OR}},d_{\mathrm{SUM}},d_{\mathrm{XOR}}\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(D_L(n)=\Theta(d_L(n))\) for each specified operation. The constants and onset may depend on the selected operation but not on the matrix or dimension. Bounds must hold at every sufficiently large dimension, with a universal upper bound on all matrices and a matching extremal lower bound. No common extremizing matrix across the three operations is required. A proven nonconstructive existence theorem can establish an extremal lower bound. Merely improving a known lower bound, showing an unbounded or polynomial gap, or restating the circuit-minimization definition does not determine the requested orders.
context:
The 2013 discussion gives a roughly square-root depth penalty for OR circuits and weaker explicit examples for XOR. It distinguishes the broad quantitative Problem 7.6 from Problem 7.7, which merely asks whether the XOR penalty can exceed all polylogarithmic bounds.

The author-hosted June 2017 note resolves that narrower Problem 7.7 affirmatively: it states a family of \(N\times N\) matrices with \(C_{\mathrm{XOR},2}(A)/C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)=\Omega(N^{0.3}/\log N)\). This is a polynomial separation, so the earlier polylogarithmic frontier must not be reported as current. The note does not claim to determine the maximum penalty up to constants.

Both unrestricted and depth-two complexity are nonuniform optima in this question. Efficiently finding a shallow circuit from a given deep circuit is a different algorithmic problem. Likewise, comparing OR with SUM at the same depth changes the allowed operation and belongs to the related separation card.

The source uses a leveled depth convention. The factorization definition in this card makes explicit that a direct input-to-output wire must be represented through the intermediate level, so numerical circuit-size conventions do not remain implicit.
why: Sharing through many intermediate stages can make a linear transformation substantially cheaper than a single layer of shared sums followed by outputs. These three functions quantify that saving for merging, exact addition, and parity cancellation. They isolate the role of depth without changing the operation or the target matrix.
status_note: The book’s conventions and Problem 7.6 were read on 2026-09-14. The author’s update index and the full June 2017 solution note were checked; the latter explicitly establishes a polynomial XOR depth gap. Bounded subsequent searches did not locate constant-factor determinations of all three maximal penalties. The card remains source-open for this quantitative target and does not retain the obsolete claim that only polylogarithmic XOR gaps are known. The author note is identified by its publication format and date, rather than represented as a separate peer-reviewed paper.
progress: 2013: Problem 7.6 asks how large the depth-two penalty can be for linear circuits. | 2017-06-04: An author note establishes a polynomial XOR depth penalty, resolving the narrower Problem 7.7 but not the maximal-order question.
working_summary: The problem asks how much more expensive a matrix transformation can become when its circuit is restricted to two addition layers. It compares the minimum wire count at depth two with the unrestricted minimum for the same matrix and operation. Boolean OR, ordinary addition and addition modulo two have separate extremal penalty functions. A 2017 result already gives a polynomial penalty for XOR, resolving a narrower earlier question. The remaining target is the optimal asymptotic order of each penalty, with upper and lower bounds matching within constants.

title: Nonlinear-gate advantages for binary linear operators
importance_reason: The question tests structural limits of linear computation, including depth, inversion, and the possible usefulness of nonlinear operations.
formal:
Can arbitrary Boolean gates give an unbounded wire saving over XOR gates for computing a binary linear operator? Determine whether
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A).\]
Both models allow unrestricted fan-in, fan-out and depth and must compute the entire same map \(x\mapsto Ax\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) on every input. GEN permits an arbitrary Boolean function at each gate and charges its incoming wires, not the gate's internal implementation. This adopts the unbounded-factor meaning of “help” made explicit by the constant-factor comparison following Problem 7.18.
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo two. For an integer \(n\ge1\), a matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) defines the total map \(x\mapsto Ax\) from \(\mathbb F_2^n\) to itself, with \((Ax)_i=\bigoplus_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\). An empty XOR is zero.

Both types of circuit are finite directed acyclic graphs with distinct input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and distinct output vertices \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), with the input and output sets disjoint. Inputs have indegree zero and outputs have outdegree zero. Intermediate nodes and output nodes compute functions of their incoming values. Fan-in and fan-out are unrestricted; every edge counts as one wire, including edges into output nodes. Unary gates are permitted. The graph has no parallel edges and there is no depth bound. Size counts wires, not gates, truth-table bits, or the time to evaluate the gates.

In the XOR model every noninput node computes the XOR of all its incoming bits, with a zero-input node computing zero. In the GEN model a noninput node of indegree \(k\) may compute any fixed Boolean function \(\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\); this includes unary negation, constants and nonlinear functions. Its input wires are ordered when specifying this function. Gate functions and wiring may depend arbitrarily on \(A\), but not on the input vector beyond the values carried by their specified wires. The gate's truth table is not charged; each value transmitted along a wire is one bit. There are no external oracles, advice inputs, random choices, or correctness promises on the input vector.

Write \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) for the respective minimum wire counts of circuits computing every coordinate of \(Ax\) exactly for every \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\). These finite minima are nonuniform circuit quantities; no efficient algorithm producing an optimum from \(A\) is required. For a nonzero matrix both minima are positive, and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\le C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) because parity is an allowed general gate. Restricting to nonzero matrices avoids undefined ratios. Arbitrary gates of unbounded fan-in are essential to the source's GEN model; replacing them with a fixed binary Boolean basis would change the question.

The positive constant \(K\) is chosen before the dimension and matrix. They may depend on \(K\), and may be obtained by a nonconstructive argument. A negative answer is exactly a finite constant \(K\) for which \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) holds for all dimensions and matrices. Computation only on the unit basis vectors is insufficient: nonlinear circuits need not be determined on other inputs by their behavior on that basis.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated unbounded-ratio assertion. A positive answer must establish arbitrarily large wire savings for some matrices, with no prescribed rate or efficient-generation requirement. A negative answer must establish a universal finite simulation factor for every square matrix. A result only for most matrices, for bounded depth, for gates with a bounded arity or fixed basis, or for correctness solely on a selected set of inputs does not settle the claim. A static data-structure lower bound must be shown to imply the exact unrestricted circuit comparison before it can serve as a resolution. No complexity conjecture is assumed.
context:
Chapter 6 defines GEN using arbitrary Boolean gate functions and wire count. The paragraph following Problem 7.18 identifies a constant-factor XOR/GEN bound as a negative answer. Accordingly the target is an unbounded asymptotic advantage, not any finite example with a smaller constant-size circuit.

The source distinguishes full computation of a linear operator from correct behavior only on the unit basis vectors. In the latter relaxed problem, nonlinear gates can offer large savings; for full computation, those values alone do not constrain arbitrary gates on other inputs.

The source relates a universal negative answer to a separate min-rank conjecture about partially specified matrices. That conjectural implication supplies context, not an additional assumption in this card.

Ko’s September 2025 preprint studies nonlinear preprocessing for a fixed linear query family and obtains new bounds for random operators, together with consequences for circuits at fixed depth. Its introduction continues to describe the general nonlinear advantage issue as a longstanding question. Such restricted or typical-matrix lower bounds do not establish a constant-factor comparison for every matrix at unrestricted depth.
why: The final map is linear, but a general circuit may pass through nonlinear intermediate values. The question asks whether such intermediate computation can ever save an unbounded number of wires relative to staying linear throughout. It tests a basic structural limitation of circuit computation over the two-element field, where familiar linearization statements from infinite-field settings cannot simply be imported.
status_note: Problem 7.18, Chapter 6 and the following comparison discussion were read on 2026-09-14. Ko’s arXiv:2509.02730v1 introduction, main-result discussion and Section 4.1 were checked for later-work scope. Its preprocessing and fixed-depth results do not settle the every-matrix unrestricted-depth ratio. A bounded search through this date did not locate a matching separation or constant-factor theorem. The preprint is identified as such, and cited proof correctness is not independently certified by this editorial review.
progress: 2013: Problem 7.18 isolates unrestricted nonlinear-gate advantages for full binary linear computation. | 2025-09-02: A preprint obtains new static-data-structure and fixed-depth arbitrary-gate lower bounds for linear operators, while distinguishing the general question.
working_summary: The problem asks whether nonlinear intermediate computation can save an unbounded number of wires when the final output map is linear over the two-element field. The comparison is between XOR-only circuits and circuits with arbitrary Boolean gate functions. Both have unrestricted depth and fan-in and must compute the same map exactly on every input. Correctness only on basis vectors and results restricted to shallow circuits do not answer this question. A positive answer establishes arbitrarily large savings, while a negative answer gives one simulation factor for every matrix.

title: Largest separation between SUM and OR circuits
importance_reason: A separation between closely related circuit models would clarify which operations account for their computational power.

The first ratio allows both circuits arbitrary depth; the second restricts both to the source's two-layer addition model. This retains the two comparisons explicitly motivating Problem 7.1. context:
The source records an unrestricted gap at least of order \(\sqrt n/\log^2 n\), and its separate depth-two example gives a gap of order at least \(\log n\). The same matrices that give the former separation need not give a growing gap when both models are restricted to depth two; Theorem 5.2 spells out that distinction.

The JCSS paper proves the \(\Omega(\sqrt n/\log^2 n)\) unrestricted separation and reviews an \(O(n/\log n)\) universal upper bound for model ratios. It describes closing the separation gap as open. Its earlier preprint preceded the book, so the 2016 publication is not a new post-book improvement to that lower bound.

The largest complexity of a matrix considered in either model separately has the same quadratic-over-logarithmic order. That worst-case agreement does not determine the ratio on a single matrix. Both quantities in this card keep the coefficient matrix fixed within each ratio.

The circuit-rewriting result in Theorem 2 of the JCSS paper concerns the time to transform a supplied representation under a complexity assumption. A lower bound for performing that transformation is distinct from an unconditional separation between the sizes of the best two representations.
why: OR can merge repeated contributions while ordinary addition must count each contribution exactly once. The largest possible size difference quantifies how much this idempotence helps when many outputs share partial computations. Separating the unrestricted and depth-two gaps tests how this advantage interacts with the number of computational layers.

title: Unbounded XOR-over-OR complexity separations
importance_reason: A separation between closely related circuit models would clarify which operations account for their computational power.
formal:
Can XOR wire complexity exceed OR wire complexity by an unbounded factor on the same zero-one matrix? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\mathcal M_n:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A).\]
Both circuit depths are unrestricted. Their outputs use the same coefficient matrix, but OR outputs are Boolean unions and XOR outputs are sums modulo two. No explicitness or efficient matrix-generation condition is imposed. This is the unrestricted ratio question in Problem 7.11, not its depth-two analogue.
definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M_n=\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}\) for integers \(n\ge1\). Rows index outputs and columns index inputs. For \(A=(a_{ij})\), the output coordinate is \(y_i=\mathop{\circ}_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\), where the operation is Boolean OR, nonnegative-integer addition (SUM), or addition modulo two (XOR). An empty sum is zero. OR and XOR inputs range over \(\{0,1\}^n\); SUM inputs range over \(\mathbb N^n\), with \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). The matrix entries only select terms; multiplication gates are not part of the model.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(n\) distinct designated input vertices of indegree zero and \(n\) distinct designated output vertices of outdegree zero, disjoint from the input vertices. Every noninput vertex sums the values of its incoming neighbors using the one chosen operation. An indegree-zero noninput vertex, in particular a zero output, computes zero. Fan-in and fan-out have no finite uniform bound, and a value may be reused at several later vertices. Graph edges carry one value and there are no parallel edges. Unary gates copy a value. Circuits compute all output coordinates exactly and simultaneously, for every input in the relevant domain. There are no negative coefficients, NOT gates, mixed operations, advice inputs, or random errors in these three addition models.

Size is the number of edges, also called wires. Every edge counts, including input edges and edges into outputs; gate count and the bit complexity of evaluating an integer sum are not the size measure. Let \(C_L(A)\) be the minimum size for \(L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}\), with depth unrestricted. This is a nonuniform minimum: the circuit can depend arbitrarily on the full matrix, and no efficient construction from its encoding is required. Matrices with nonzero entries have positive complexity. The all-zero matrix is excluded from ratios to avoid \(0/0\).

For the depth-two version \(C_{L,2}(A)\), follow the source's leveled convention: inputs, one intermediate layer, and outputs are three disjoint levels, with edges only from inputs to the intermediate layer or from that layer to outputs. Direct input-to-output edges are not allowed in this version. The intermediate layer may have any finite size; zero outputs and unary gates are allowed. Equivalently, \(C_{L,2}(A)\) minimizes \(|P|+|Q|\) over Boolean matrices \(P\in\{0,1\}^{n\times r}\), \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{r\times n}\), for any integer \(r\ge0\), satisfying \(A=PQ\) over the specified semiring, where \(|P|,|Q|\) count their one-entries. Thus in the SUM case the integer product must have exactly the prescribed zero-one entries, without duplicate contributions.

All these minima exist, and maxima over \(\mathcal M_n\) exist because the matrix set is finite. The extremizing matrices in two different ratios need not be the same. A dimensional asymptotic bound concerns \(n\to\infty\) through all positive integers, with base-two logarithms.

Here \(K\) is any positive real constant and may be replaced by a positive integer without changing the claim. The matrix and its dimension may depend on \(K\). Its negation is the existence of one finite universal \(K\) bounding \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A)\) at every dimension and every nonzero matrix. Defining \(R(n)\) as the maximum of this ratio makes the question equivalent to unboundedness of \(R\). Appending zero rows and columns preserves both unrestricted minima, so these maxima are nondecreasing; unboundedness is consequently equivalent to \(R(n)\to\infty\). No one finite matrix can by itself show the unbounded assertion.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed quantifiers. A positive answer needs arbitrarily large ratios and may be nonconstructive; it need not attain a specified polynomial rate. A negative answer must supply or establish a uniform finite bound for every matrix. A ratio in the reverse direction, a separation requiring shallow XOR circuits, or a lower bound on the time to rewrite an OR circuit as an XOR circuit does not prove the required unrestricted size separation. Conditional evidence alone does not resolve this unconditional question.
context:
The source gives a growing XOR-over-OR gap when both models are restricted to depth two. That lower bound applies to the restricted XOR minimum and need not survive when arbitrary-depth XOR circuits are allowed.

The JCSS paper explicitly reports that it cannot prove a superconstant unrestricted XOR-over-OR gap. Its discussion distinguishes this from the reverse OR-over-XOR direction, where large separations are known. Those reverse-direction matrices do not answer the present quantifiers.

The same paper proves that a truly subquadratic-time general rewriting procedure from OR circuits to XOR circuits would contradict its version of the strong exponential time hypothesis. This concerns computing a new representation, and cannot be substituted for an unconditional size comparison of two optimal representations.

The matrix itself is fixed before either circuit is chosen; treating the two output maps as the same Boolean function would be incorrect. Their common object is the zero-one coefficient pattern, interpreted in two different semirings.
why: XOR can cancel duplicate contributions, while OR can merge them. There is no immediate pointwise ordering between the most efficient circuits for these different output semantics. An unbounded gap in this direction would show a systematic limitation of parity computation relative to idempotent merging, even when both can use arbitrary depth.

working_summary: The question asks whether some zero-one matrices are arbitrarily more costly to evaluate with XOR gates than with OR gates. Cost is the minimum number of wires, and both circuits may have unrestricted depth. The same coefficient matrix specifies parity outputs in one model and union outputs in the other. Known shallow-circuit gaps and hardness of rewriting representations do not establish this unrestricted size separation. A proof needs arbitrarily large ratios, while a refutation needs one universal constant bound.

title: UEOPL versus EOPL
importance_reason: A structural boundary within total search, distinguishing uniqueness-based problems from the full local-search/directed-path intersection. Existing score retained.
formal: Does EndOfPotentialLine reduce to UniqueEOPL by a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction for total search problems? Equivalently, is UEOPL=EOPL? Instances contain explicit Boolean circuits, and the reduction may inspect their descriptions. The question concerns the ordinary classes without an oracle.
definitions:
A total NP search problem is a polynomial-time decidable relation \(R(a,z)\) with polynomially bounded witnesses z and at least one witness for every input a. A reduction \(R\le S\) consists of deterministic polynomial-time maps F and G such that every S-witness w for \(F(a)\) gives an R-witness \(G(a,w)\); running times are polynomial in the explicit input lengths. For EndOfPotentialLine, an instance consists of circuits \(\mathrm{P},S:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,\ldots ,2^{m}- 1\}\), for \(n,m\ge 1\), with \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}, S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\) and \(V(0^{n})=0\). Potentials are m-bit nonnegative integers. A valid answer is a vertex x satisfying at least one of: \((a) \mathrm{P}(S(x))
e x; (b) x
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(x))
e x; (c) x
e S(x), \mathrm{P}(S(x))=x\) and \(V(S(x))\le V(x)\). UniqueEOPL has the same instances and accepts all these answers, and additionally accepts two vertices \(x
e y\) with \(x
e S(x), y
e S(y)\), and either \(V(x)=V(y)\) or \(V(x)<V(y)<V(S(x))\). Thus uniqueness is enforced by additional verifiable witnesses, not assumed as an unverifiable promise. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with their complete gate lists as input; size includes all gates, wires, input and output labels. The displayed restrictions at \(0^{n}\) are directly checkable; malformed encodings or failed restrictions may be assigned a distinguished trivial answer. EOPL and UEOPL consist of all total NP search problems reducible to their respective canonical problems by the reductions just defined. In particular UEOPL\(\subseteq\)EOPL, since an EndOfPotentialLine answer is always also a UniqueEOPL answer.
answer_criterion: Prove equality by a polynomial-time reduction from EndOfPotentialLine to UniqueEOPL, valid for every output that the target relation permits, or prove that no such reduction exists. A separation limited to oracle queries or decision trees does not establish inequality of the ordinary circuit-defined classes.
context:
The circuits describe a graph too large to list: each vertex has at most one predecessor and successor, and a potential labels progress. An answer may be an endpoint or a locally checkable failure of the proposed path structure.

UniqueEOPL also accepts a pair whose potentials witness incompatible lines. This extra set of acceptable outputs can make the search easier. It is essential to the definition; merely promising one line would give a different problem.

The 2022 theorem identifies EOPL with \(\mathrm{PLS}\cap\)PPAD, combining local-search and directed-path existence principles. The equality here asks whether the additional structure captured by UEOPL loses any of that computational power.

The JACM 2024 theorem separates EOPL from UEOPL in the decision-tree model and consequently relative to an oracle. Reductions receiving full circuit descriptions are more general, so this theorem leaves the displayed question open.
why: Would determine whether uniqueness with efficiently detectable violations defines a strictly easier form of total search inside \(\mathrm{PLS}\cap\)PPAD, affecting the classification of fixed-point, orientation and game problems captured by UEOPL.

Searches through 12 September 2026, including the abstracts of Super Unique Tarski is in UEOPL and On Cutting Cakes and Crossing Curves, found no resolution of the ordinary class equality. Those later applications are not equality or separation results.

The question asks whether both ordinary circuit-defined classes nevertheless have the same power. A published theorem separates them in the black-box model, which does not decide this equality. Resolving it would clarify the computational role of uniqueness in total search.

title: Unconditional exclusion of linear-time CNF satisfiability
importance_reason: A fundamental lower-bound challenge for satisfiability and general computation. A precise modest time separation would already be consequential, but importance does not determine the omitted model and endpoint. Existing score retained.
formal: Is CNF satisfiability outside deterministic linear time on multitape Turing machines: does no deterministic machine decide every explicitly encoded CNF formula in \(O(L)\) time, where \(L\) is its full input bit length and no additional workspace restriction is imposed?
definitions: A CNF formula is an AND of a finite list of clauses, each clause an OR of a finite list of signed variable occurrences. A variable takes a Boolean value; a positive occurrence is true at value 1 and a negative occurrence at value 0. Empty clauses are false and an empty conjunction is true. Clause width and the number of occurrences are unrestricted; repeated occurrences or clauses are allowed. The input alphabet is a fixed finite alphabet encoded by a fixed-length binary code. Each variable identifier is a nonempty canonical binary representation of a positive integer, preceded by a sign symbol; clause separators and an end marker delimit the full list. The complete explicit string, including every identifier bit, sign and separator, has length \(L\). Unused or nonconsecutive identifiers are allowed and denote no extra work beyond their written bits. There are no circuit or compressed-formula encodings. A deterministic multitape Turing machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite tape alphabets and a fixed finite number of tapes with one head per tape. In one step it reads and writes a constant number of symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; it has no random access, word arithmetic instruction, advice, randomness or oracle. The input tape initially holds the encoding and other tapes are blank. Deciding SAT means halting with YES exactly when some assignment satisfies the formula. On malformed inputs it may reject. Linear time means that there are a correct machine and constants \(C,L_0\) such that every valid formula of length \(L\ge L_0\) is decided within \(CL\) steps. The claim negates the existence of such a machine and constants; it does not demand a fixed superlinear power or exponential variable dependence. Memory is unrestricted except for what can be visited within the elapsed time. An unconditional proof may not assume a complexity separation or a fine-grained hardness hypothesis.
answer_criterion: Provide an unconditional Lean proof that no machine has the stated linear worst-case bound, or a Lean-certified deterministic linear-time SAT algorithm in the stated encoding and machine model. A lower bound requiring an additional workspace bound, a conditional lower bound, or hardness of a different language does not meet this criterion.
context:
The source contrasts a broad ambition of exponential SAT lower bounds with the more modest unresolved milestone of excluding linear time without a workspace restriction.

The user-authorized variant selects that modest milestone for explicitly encoded CNF formulas on deterministic multitape Turing machines. It does not assert a random-access lower bound or an exponential lower bound in the variable count.

The recent square-root-space simulation theorem concerns general multitape computation and yields hard languages, but the checked corollary does not identify SAT as such a language.
why: An unconditional lower bound for satisfiability would establish a limitation of general computation for a central natural problem, beyond limitations of a solver family or consequences of a conjecture. Even a modest bound is significant when it applies without an extra memory restriction. Its precise computational model is part of the mathematical achievement.
