working_summary: An additive spanner keeps original graph edges while limiting the increase in every pairwise distance. This card fixes the increase to at most four and asks for the optimal worst-case number of edges. The target is the complete asymptotic function up to universal constant factors. The familiar candidate is \(n^{4/3}\), while recent constructions still have exponent \(7/5\) up to logarithmic factors. This gap is a fundamental unresolved regime of distance compression, and the variable-error linear-size tradeoff has its own card.

title: Quasipolynomial dependence on vertices for hypergraph isomorphism
importance_reason: A central isomorphism parameter-dependence question for general set systems, with consequences for symmetry algorithms using structural decompositions.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that decides isomorphism of two explicitly represented hypergraphs in time \[2^{C(\log_2(n+2))^{a}}\,N^{b},\] for fixed constants \(C,a,b\geq1\), where \(n\) is the maximum number of underlying vertices and \(N\) is the combined input bit length?
definitions: A hypergraph is a finite pair \((V,\mathcal E)\) with \(V=[n]\) and \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\). Empty hyperedges and isolated vertices are allowed; edges have no colors, order, weights or repeated copies. The input lists the vertices and every hyperedge explicitly by its incidence bit vector; vertex counts and list lengths are included in the binary encoding. Input length \(N\) therefore includes all incidences and at least \(n\) symbols. An isomorphism from \((V_1,\mathcal E_1)\) to \((V_2,\mathcal E_2)\) is a bijection \(\pi:V_1\to V_2\) with \(\{\pi(e):e\in\mathcal E_1\}=\mathcal E_2\). The algorithm must decide whether one exists and must be correct on every well-formed input; unequal vertex counts imply rejection. Time is worst-case bit time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice or oracle. Neither the hyperedge size nor the number of hyperedges is bounded polynomially in \(n\). All constants and exponents are uniform over both parameters. Replacing incidence vectors by explicit incidence lists changes length by at most a polynomial and preserves the requested two-parameter bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with fixed constants satisfying the displayed two-parameter bound, or prove that no such deterministic uniform algorithm exists. A quasipolynomial bound in the full incidence-graph size, or a polynomial exponent depending on the number of vertices or maximum hyperedge size, does not meet the target.
context:
The source distinguishes a quasipolynomial dependence on the number of vertices from a polynomial dependence on the possibly much larger collection of hyperedges. Encoding a hypergraph as a bipartite incidence graph does not automatically give that separation of dependencies.

Wiebking discusses a bound whose exponent on total hypergraph size depends polylogarithmically on the vertex count, and explicitly asks for the stronger bound in which the hyperedge-size exponent is constant. The same open question reappears in the outlook section.
why: This asks whether symmetry testing can depend quasipolynomially only on the underlying universe, while remaining polynomial in the amount of set-system data. It matters for hypergraphs with many large edges and for algorithms that encode structural graph information as set systems.
status_note: The stronger separated-parameter bound is explicitly open in the 2020 source. The source passages were checked on 13 September 2026; a bounded subsequent-work search supplied no verified resolution. Status is source_open.
progress: 2020: The paper explicitly separates a vertex-dependent exponent on total hypergraph size from the desired fixed polynomial dependence on the number of hyperedges, and leaves the stronger bound open.
working_summary: Hypergraph isomorphism asks whether a relabeling of vertices makes two explicitly listed set systems identical. The target running time is quasipolynomial in the number of vertices and polynomial in the full input size. The exponent on input size must be a fixed constant even when many hyperedges are listed. The source explains why a quasipolynomial bound in the larger incidence representation does not automatically provide this guarantee. A resolution would extend efficient symmetry testing to rich set systems over comparatively small universes.

title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
importance_reason: A fundamental unresolved planar edge-coloring decision problem at maximum degree three, closely tied to the boundary of Four-Color-Theorem consequences.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?
question_excerpt: The computational complexity of the 3-Edge Colorability-problem for planar graphs remains open, while it is known to be NP-complete already for 3-regular, but not necessarily […]
definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.
context:
The source poses this as Question 1 and explains why the Four-Color Theorem settles the cubic bridgeless case without settling all subcubic planar graphs. A graph with degree-two vertices need not lie in a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph.

The 2022 paper gives a polynomial-time test for augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph. Its concluding discussion keeps general planar three-edge-colorability open and states a stronger proposed structural characterization.

The expanded journal article, published online in November 2025 and appearing in Algorithmica’s 2026 volume, again poses planar three-edge-colorability as an open question. Its recognition results concern specified cubic supergraphs and do not identify that augmentation task with the full coloring decision problem.
why: This is a basic unresolved coloring decision problem on planar graphs with very small maximum degree. A resolution would clarify exactly how far the algorithmic consequences of the Four-Color Theorem extend beyond regular planar graphs.
status_note: The question is open in the 2022 source and explicitly retained in the journal version published online on 25 November 2025. These source statements were checked on 13 September 2026; no subsequent resolution was verified. Status is source_open.
progress: 2022: The source gives polynomial-time recognition of graphs admitting a cubic bridgeless planar augmentation while explicitly leaving general planar three-edge-colorability open. | 2025-11-25: The expanded journal version retains the general coloring question and distinguishes it from its polynomial and hardness results for specified supergraph recognition tasks.
working_summary: Three-edge-colorability asks whether the edges of a graph can receive three colors with different colors on every pair meeting at a vertex. The selected question asks for the computational complexity of this decision problem on planar graphs. The source studies a sufficient route through augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph, where three-edge-colorability follows from the Four-Color Theorem. It also discusses a conjectured characterization for two-connected planar graphs of maximum degree three. A full classification would determine whether the remaining planar cases admit an efficient coloring test or conceal an NP-hard obstruction.

title: Planarity dichotomy for induced subdivision detection
importance_reason: A broad fixed-pattern complexity classification linking planarity to induced-subdivision detection, beyond the known isolated hardness example.
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), is it true that for every fixed finite subcubic graph \(H\), detecting an induced subdivision of \(H\) in an arbitrary input graph belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if and only if \(H\) is planar?
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Subcubic means maximum degree at most three; \(H\) need not be connected. A subdivision of \(H\) is obtained by replacing each edge by a path of positive length, with pairwise disjoint internal vertex sets, none of which contains a vertex of \(H\). An induced subdivision in \(G\) is a set \(W\subseteq V(G)\) such that the induced graph \(G[W]\) is isomorphic to a subdivision of \(H\). Equivalently, choose distinct branch vertices for all vertices of \(H\), including its isolated vertices, and replacement paths with exactly the prescribed edges and no additional edges anywhere among the selected vertices. For each fixed \(H\), the decision problem takes only \(G\), encoded by its binary adjacency matrix, and answers whether such \(W\) exists; no degree, planarity or connectivity promise is made on \(G\). Polynomial time means a deterministic Turing machine with running time \(C_H(|V(G)|+1)^{k_H}\) for constants depending on \(H\), but not on \(G\). An algorithm need not be uniform in the pattern \(H\), which is not part of the input. Planarity means admitting a crossing-free drawing in the plane. The complexity assumption uses the ordinary uniform deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial-time language classes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal equivalence under the stated P ≠ NP hypothesis, or a proof of its negation under that hypothesis. A counterexample must identify a fixed subcubic pattern and establish the failure of the corresponding direction. Proving hardness for one nonplanar pattern, or algorithms for only some planar patterns, does not settle the whole conjecture. NP-completeness of every nonplanar case would suffice for that direction but is not silently added as a stronger required conclusion.
context:
The source proposes planarity of a fixed subcubic pattern as the complete boundary for tractable induced-subdivision detection. Its assumption P ≠ NP is essential to the stated if-and-only-if claim.

The paper exhibits a fixed subcubic pattern whose induced-subdivision containment problem is NP-complete. This establishes an obstruction within low-degree patterns but does not classify every such pattern. Induced containment additionally forbids unwanted edges between the selected paths, unlike ordinary subdivision containment.
why: A resolution would give one structural explanation for the complexity of an entire family of induced pattern-detection problems. It asks whether the geometry of the fixed pattern, rather than just its bounded degree, controls tractability.
status_note: The published 2025 paper explicitly states Conjecture 5 under P ≠ NP. The statement and model were checked on 13 September 2026; the bounded subsequent-work search supplied no verified resolution. Status is source_open.
progress: 2025: The paper proves hardness for a particular fixed subcubic induced-subdivision pattern and states the general planarity characterization as Conjecture 5.
working_summary: For a fixed graph H, induced-subdivision detection asks whether an input graph contains a subdivided copy of H as an induced subgraph. Extra edges between selected vertices are forbidden. The conjecture concerns patterns H of maximum degree three and predicts tractability exactly for planar patterns, assuming P differs from NP. Existing algorithms and hardness constructions motivate the proposed boundary. This would classify a natural family of pattern-detection problems by a geometric property of the fixed pattern itself.

title: Isomorphism dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes
importance_reason: A general finite-description dichotomy for hereditary isomorphism, asking whether finite induced obstructions eliminate intermediate complexity.
formal: For every finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite graphs, is graph isomorphism restricted to graphs containing no induced copy of a member of \(\mathcal F\) either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or complete for general graph isomorphism under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
question_excerpt: However, this statement does not carry over to forbidden induced subgraphs and the question of the existence of intermediate graph classes characterized by finitely many […]
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple, with binary adjacency-matrix encodings. The finite forbidden family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed, not part of the input. Let \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\) contain every graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal F\). Its isomorphism task receives two members \(G_1,G_2\) and asks whether there is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. Polynomial time means worst-case deterministic bit time bounded by a polynomial in their combined encoding length; the machine and polynomial may depend on \(\mathcal F\). Graph-isomorphism completeness means that there is a deterministic polynomial-time map from any pair of arbitrary simple graphs to a pair in \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\), preserving the YES/NO isomorphism answer. The reverse reduction is the identity. Outputs of the hardness reduction must satisfy the class promise on both YES and NO inputs. Class membership can be checked in polynomial time for fixed finite \(\mathcal F\), so a total-language formulation may reject encodings outside the class. No algorithm deciding which side applies from an input description of \(\mathcal F\) is required. The alternatives need not be disjoint if general graph isomorphism is in P; the conjecture asserts their union covers every finite forbidden family.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal dichotomy, or exhibit a fixed finite forbidden family and prove that its restricted isomorphism problem has neither property. A complete proof may use a mathematically specified classification without an effective classifier for forbidden families. A two-pattern theorem alone, a result for ordinary subgraph exclusion, or NP-hardness terminology without the required graph-isomorphism reductions does not settle the target.
context:
Schweitzer’s Conjecture 1 asks for a polynomial-time versus general-isomorphism-complete dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes. Finiteness of the forbidden induced family is essential: the discussion distinguishes conditional intermediate examples requiring infinite descriptions.

The source obtains the dichotomy for all but finitely many two-forbidden-graph cases. A classification by forbidden ordinary subgraphs also does not settle the conjecture, because induced exclusions allow a broader range of structural behavior.
why: A finite list of forbidden induced patterns is a simple and widely used graph-class description. The conjecture asks whether such finite structural restrictions always make symmetry testing tractable or retain the full difficulty of unrestricted graph isomorphism.
status_note: Conjecture 1 is explicit in the 2015 source. Its quantifiers and partial theorem were checked on 13 September 2026; the limited later-work check supplied no verified resolution for arbitrary finite forbidden families. Status is source_open.
progress: 2015: The paper states the finite-family dichotomy as Conjecture 1 and establishes the polynomial-time versus isomorphism-complete alternatives for all but finitely many two-forbidden-pattern cases.
working_summary: Hereditary graph classes can be specified by finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs. The question asks whether graph isomorphism on such a class can have complexity intermediate between polynomial time and general graph-isomorphism completeness. The source establishes broad classifications and resolves most two-forbidden-pattern cases. Results for forbidden ordinary subgraphs do not immediately extend to induced exclusions. The project seeks a dichotomy explaining whether a finite structural prohibition always makes isomorphism substantially easier or leaves its full general difficulty intact.

title: Quadratic-size submodular hypergraph sparsifiers
importance_reason: A general quadratic compression conjecture for arbitrary submodular cut objectives, including asymmetric and unbounded-range splitting functions.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that every submodular hypergraph on \(n\geq1\) vertices and every \(0<\varepsilon<1\) admit a reweighted sub-hypergraph with at most \(C n^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}\) hyperedges that simultaneously approximates every cut value within factors \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(1+\varepsilon\)?
definitions: A submodular hypergraph \(H=(V,E,(g_e)_{e\in E})\) has a finite vertex set \(V\), \(|V|=n\), a finite set \(E\subseteq2^V\) of hyperedges, and, for each \(e\), a function \(g_e:2^e\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with \(g_e(\varnothing)=0\). Submodularity means \(g_e(A\cup B)+g_e(A\cap B)\leq g_e(A)+g_e(B)\) for every \(A,B\subseteq e\). Neither symmetry under complementation nor monotonicity, bounded positive-value ratios, integral values or bounded hyperedge rank is assumed; in particular \(g_e(e)\) need not vanish. A cut is any \(S\subseteq V\) and its value is \(F_H(S)=\sum_{e\in E}g_e(S\cap e)\). A reweighted sub-hypergraph chooses \(E'\subseteq E\) and one real scalar \(w_e>0\) for each retained edge, giving \(F_{H'}(S)=\sum_{e\in E'}w_e g_e(S\cap e)\). It must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)F_H(S)\leq F_{H'}(S)\leq(1+\varepsilon)F_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\), including exact preservation of zero-valued cuts. Size counts retained hyperedges, not total incidences, splitting-function descriptions or bits. This is an existence theorem: no input-oracle representation, construction time, coefficient bit bound or random failure probability is imposed. The constant \(C\) must be independent of every hypergraph parameter and of \(\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a universal constant and the stated simultaneous reweighted sparsifier bound, or prove its negation. A refutation must rule out every possible universal constant, not just one proposed bound. Bounds with additional logarithmic losses, a worse power of inverse accuracy, restricted splitting functions, or newly invented splitting functions do not establish the conjecture.
context:
Theorem 1.4 of Kenneth and Krauthgamer gives an \(O(n^3/\varepsilon^2)\) reweighted sparsifier for arbitrary nonnegative submodular splitting functions. Their Conjecture 1.14 asks whether the vertex dependence can be reduced to quadratic, while retaining the stated accuracy dependence and the original splitting functions.

A July 2026 preprint proves a \(\widetilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^4)\) bound when all functions take values in a fixed finite integer range. Its Theorem 1.5 and following discussion explicitly leave arbitrary nonnegative submodular functions outside that result.

An August 2026 preprint reports \(O(n/\varepsilon^2)\) sparsifiers for sums of symmetric submodular functions. Symmetry is an additional promise absent here; it does not cover arbitrary directed or asymmetric splitting costs.
why: The question asks whether rich higher-order cut objectives always have representations using quadratically many original terms, independent of their complexity and value ranges. Such a theorem would provide a general compression guarantee across submodular optimization models.
status_note: Conjecture 1.14 is explicit in the 2024 paper. On 13 September 2026 the later-work check verified the statement, but not the proof, of a July theorem restricted to bounded integral functions and the abstract of an August symmetric-function result. Neither states the full conjectured bound for arbitrary splitting functions; status remains source_open.
progress: 2024: The source proves a general cubic bound in \(n\) and poses Conjecture 1.14 for the quadratic bound. | 2026-07-17: Theorem 1.5 of the new preprint gives a nearly quadratic bound with inverse-fourth accuracy dependence for bounded integral submodular functions. The general nonnegative case remains outside its stated theorem. | 2026-08-04: A separate preprint reports linear-size sparsifiers for symmetric submodular sums. Its abstract was checked, but the proof was not independently verified.
working_summary: A submodular hypergraph assigns each hyperedge a flexible submodular cost for being split by a cut. A sparsifier retains and reweights hyperedges so that every cut value remains approximately correct. The conjecture proposes a quadratic-in-vertices size bound with inverse-squared accuracy dependence in the source's size measure. Preserving exponentially many cuts simultaneously is the main obstacle identified there. The project seeks a compression theorem extending beyond ordinary all-or-nothing hyperedge cuts to richer models used in optimization and learning.

title: Three disjoint directed shortest paths
importance_reason: The first unresolved fixed number of directed disjoint shortest-path pairs, isolating a basic barrier in exact multi-pair routing.
formal: Does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decide whether a directed graph with positive rational arc lengths and three prescribed source-target pairs contains three mutually vertex-disjoint paths, each individually shortest between its own endpoints?
question_excerpt: This is because while k-DSP is polynomial-time solvable for constant k in undirected graphs, it remains open whether even 3-DSP over directed graphs can be […]
definitions: The input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), with \(V=[n]\), no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair, together with a length \(\ell(a)\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) for each arc and three pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in V^2\), \(i=1,2,3\). Graph incidences and all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicitly encoded in binary. A directed path follows the arcs and has no repeated vertex; a zero-arc path is permitted when its endpoints coincide. Its length is the sum of its arc lengths. The distance \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum path length, or infinity when no path exists. A valid answer YES means there are paths \(P_i\) from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\), each of length \(d_G(s_i,t_i)\), with \(V(P_i)\cap V(P_j)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Disjointness includes all terminals. Repeated terminals across different pairs therefore force NO. Distances are measured in the original graph, not after deleting other paths; minimizing the total length of three disjoint paths is a different condition. Time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine bit time polynomial in the total encoding length, including lengths. No acyclicity or planarity promise, uniqueness of shortest paths, randomness, advice or oracle is allowed. Strict positivity follows the source preliminaries; allowing zero-length directed cycles is not part of this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the deterministic polynomial-time decision statement or its negation for the specified positive-rational-length model. An NP-hardness reduction is a conditional negative result under P ≠ NP and must be stated with that hypothesis. A randomized algorithm alone, an algorithm for two pairs or acyclic inputs, or a solution minimizing only total path length does not settle the exact statement.
context:
The source’s congested shortest-path task includes mutually vertex-disjoint shortest paths as the congestion-one case. It states that the directed three-pair problem remains open even though fixed numbers of pairs are tractable on undirected graphs and directed acyclic graphs.

A January 2026 paper improves randomized algorithms for two disjoint shortest paths in general directed graphs. Its Open Problem 6.3 again asks for polynomial-time solvability or hardness of the three-pair case. The two-pair theorem and the three-pair question must remain separate.
why: Three pairs form a small and sharply defined test of whether directed shortest-path constraints can be coordinated efficiently. A resolution would distinguish the difficulty of selecting individually optimal routes from ordinary shortest-path computation and from undirected routing.
status_note: The 2023 source and January 2026 follow-up both state the directed three-pair question as open. Those statements and the positive-weight model were checked on 13 September 2026. No later resolution was verified; status is source_open.
progress: 2023: The paper states the directed three-disjoint-shortest-paths problem as open and uses strictly positive edge weights throughout. | 2026-01-23: The later paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms and repeats the directed three-pair question as Open Problem 6.3.
working_summary: The input specifies three source-target pairs in a directed graph with positive arc lengths. Each selected path must be shortest for its own pair in the original graph, and no vertex may belong to two paths. The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the full binary input length. A 2026 paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms but explicitly leaves three pairs unresolved. A resolution would explain whether several individually optimal directed routes can be selected efficiently while avoiding all conflicts.

title: Optimal additive error of linear-size spanners
importance_reason: The general additive-distance loss forced by a linear edge budget is a central sparsity-versus-accuracy question for graph metrics.
formal: Determine the optimal worst-case additive error \(A_c(n)\) of a spanner with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges, up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), for every fixed real constant \(c\geq1\). The graph is arbitrary, undirected and unweighted; the edge budget is genuinely linear, without hidden factors depending on \(n\).
definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. A result up to constant factors supplies a nonnegative function \(a(n,c)\) and, for each fixed \(c\), constants \(0<L_c\leq U_c<\infty\) and \(n_c\) with \(L_c a(n,c)\leq A_c(n)\leq U_c a(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_c\). Constants may depend on \(c\), never on \(n\). This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target.

The upper bound must cover every input graph and the lower bound must establish matching worst cases under the same edge budget. Determining only an exponent with an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic gap does not meet this precision; a numerical tolerance of 1/100 is not an additive error on asymptotic notation.

title: Polynomial-time detection of fixed pivot- and vertex-minors
importance_reason: A general algorithmic counterpart to structural graph containment, connecting width theory with transformations used in quantum graph states.
formal: For each relation \(\rho\in\{\text{pivot-minor},\text{vertex-minor}\}\) and each fixed finite simple graph \(H\), does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple graph \(G\), decides whether some \(\rho\) of \(G\) is isomorphic to \(H\)?
definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and have no parallel edges. Local complementation at a vertex \(v\) toggles adjacency between each pair of distinct neighbors of \(v\), leaving all other adjacencies unchanged. If \(uv\) is an edge in the current graph, pivoting on \(uv\) means local complementation at \(u\), then \(v\), then \(u\). A vertex-minor is obtained by a finite sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions; a pivot-minor instead permits edge pivots and vertex deletions. A deletion removes the chosen vertex and all its incident edges. Isomorphism is a bijection preserving adjacency in both directions; target vertices have no prescribed locations in the host. The empty target is allowed. For each fixed pair \((\rho,H)\), the algorithm receives only \(G\), encoded by its vertex count and adjacency matrix in binary. There must be constants \(C_{\rho,H},a_{\rho,H}>0\) such that it always returns the correct bit in at most \(C_{\rho,H}(n+1)^{a_{\rho,H}}\) Turing steps on every \(n\)-vertex host. Its program and these constants may depend on the fixed target and relation. No uniform construction from an input \(H\), fixed-parameter bound, containment witness or host-width promise is required. There is no advice depending on the growing host.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified polynomial-time decision algorithms for both relations and every fixed target, or a Lean refutation for some fixed target and relation. A result only for hosts of bounded width or a bound exponential in host size does not meet the assertion. A uniform fixed-parameter algorithm would be sufficient but is not required.
context:
Local complementation and edge pivoting define graph containment relations that differ from ordinary edge-contraction minors. The source asks whether fixed targets can be recognized efficiently in arbitrary hosts.

The 2024 survey repeats fixed-target vertex-minor detection as Conjecture 14.1. Its following conjecture concerns specified target vertices, a different formulation.
why: Efficient fixed-pattern detection would make local-transformation graph structure algorithmically accessible, with consequences for graph classes and graph-state transformations.

title: Complexity of general vertex-connectivity augmentation
importance_reason: Exact unweighted augmentation with all links available isolates the unresolved complexity of general target vertex connectivity.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a simple undirected graph \(G\) and a target \(1\leq\lambda<|V(G)|\), computes the minimum number of new edges needed to make \(G\) \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected, when every missing edge is available at unit cost?
definitions: The graph is finite, undirected and simple, with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\geq2\), and an explicit binary adjacency matrix. The integer \(\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is part of the input, encoded in binary, and need not be fixed. The available links are exactly \(\binom{V(G)}{2}\setminus E(G)\). An augmentation is any subset \(F\) of these links; its cost is \(|F|\), and no new vertices are permitted. The graph \(G+F\) is \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected if deleting any set of fewer than \(\lambda\) vertices leaves a connected graph. The condition \(\lambda<n\) excludes ambiguous conventions on graphs with too few vertices. The optimum is finite because adding every missing edge produces a complete graph. The algorithm must output the exact minimum integer; equivalently it may decide, for a binary budget \(k\geq0\), whether some augmentation has \(|F|\leq k\). The two tasks are polynomial-time equivalent using the finite \(\binom n2\) budget range. Running time is worst-case bit time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the whole input length, with no exponent or multiplicative nonpolynomial dependence on \(\lambda\). The input graph may have arbitrary initial connectivity; there is no promise that the target increases connectivity by only one.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm for all target values, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An algorithm polynomial only for fixed target connectivity, a parameterized algorithm exponential in the target or budget, an approximation, or a one-increment result does not meet the guarantee. NP-hardness implies a negative answer only under an explicitly stated P ≠ NP hypothesis.
context:

This is progress for a more general input model, but its exponential parameter dependence does not provide a polynomial algorithm when the target is unrestricted.
why: The question asks whether optimal resilience to vertex failures can be added efficiently when all new links have the same cost and are freely available. These simple input conditions isolate the difficulty of vertex connectivity itself from costly or forbidden links.

title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
importance_reason: A broad structural classification across finite-forbidden hereditary graph modification problems, with a uniform conceptual reach beyond individual classes or parameterized bounds.
formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm P\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.
context:
The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.
why: Edge deletion is a basic graph-repair operation whose tractability changes with the desired hereditary property. A dichotomy for every finite forbidden list would explain this variation across many graph classes and locate a general boundary between efficient repair and NP-completeness.

title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
importance_reason: A simple central offline counting task exposes a basic gap in the power of word-RAM algorithms, despite having only one output value and already rank-compressed input.
formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required. The array has one entry per word; no compressed representation, streaming restriction or comparison-only restriction is imposed. The algorithm may use auxiliary random-access memory, but allocating, initializing and accessing that memory consumes the counted steps. The output is one word containing the exact nonnegative integer. Neither a list of all inverted pairs nor individual per-position counts are required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must specify one fixed program and prove its exact count and linear worst-case running time for every legal permutation in the specified model. A negative answer must exclude all such programs and all fixed constants. A relative-error estimate, an algorithm that is linear only on nearly sorted inputs, an expected-time randomized algorithm, or an improvement still superlinear in the worst case does not meet this target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication.
context:
An inversion is a pair of positions whose values occur in decreasing order. Its total is the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps required to sort the permutation.

Chan and Pătraşcu give a deterministic exact \(O(n\sqrt{\log_2 n})\)-time word-RAM algorithm. They also give a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation, which does not supply the exact output requested here.

Elmasry’s adaptive algorithm improves the time on inputs with fewer inversions, but retains a superlinear worst-case bound over all permutations.

Kempa and Kociumaka’s STOC 2025 paper again identifies inversion counting among the central problems whose fastest known algorithms have the square-root-logarithmic overhead. Theorem 1.3 transfers any improved inversion-counting time to a packed Dictionary Matching problem. Its bounded-integer array formulation and the permutation formulation have the same linear-time endpoint.

In that Dictionary Matching problem, the input consists of a packed binary text occupying a linear number of logarithmic-size words and a linear number of patterns, each of logarithmic bit length; the output says whether any pattern occurs. The connection is a conditional consequence for another task, not an unconditional superlinear lower bound. The linear exact endpoint remains the card’s explicit editorial formulation of the gap.
why: Exact inversion counting compresses a permutation’s pairwise disorder into one integer and is a fundamental offline aggregation task. Its complexity remains separated from the cost of sorting already rank-bounded integers. The 2025 hardness connections show that a linear-time solution would also change the algorithmic frontier for packed-string processing.
status_note: The checked STOC 2025 primary paper explicitly includes inversion counting among problems retaining an O(n sqrt(log n)) best-known word-RAM bound and proves a conditional connection to Dictionary Matching. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no exact deterministic linear-time algorithm or unconditional refutation. The linear endpoint is an editorial formulation of this documented gap, not an attributed named conjecture; the review is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.
progress: 2010: Chan–Pătraşcu publish exact \(O(n\sqrt{\log_2 n})\) counting and a linear-time relative approximation. | 2015-03-04: Elmasry posts an adaptive inversion-counting algorithm, with improved performance on low-inversion inputs. | 2025: Kempa–Kociumaka publish the Dictionary Matching hardness connection at STOC; their Theorem 1.3 transfers the inversion-counting running time to that task.
working_summary: An inversion is a pair of permutation positions whose values appear in decreasing order. The task is to return the exact total number of such pairs as one integer. The question asks whether one deterministic program can do this in linear worst-case time on a word RAM with logarithmic words. Known approximation and adaptive algorithms do not provide that exact guarantee for every permutation. A STOC 2025 result links faster exact inversion counting to faster packed Dictionary Matching, giving the question broader algorithmic significance.

title: Near-linear constant-factor minimum-degree spanning trees
importance_reason: Maintaining low-degree spanning trees is a focused dynamic optimization frontier.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), absolute constants \(K,C\ge1\), and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq G\) satisfying \(\Delta(T)\le K\Delta^\star(G)\) in at most \(C(m+n)(\log_2(n+2))^b\) word-RAM operations? Here \(\Delta(T)=\max_{v\in[n]}\deg_T(v)\) and \(\Delta^\star(G)=\min\{\Delta(T):T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). All constants and the program must be independent of the graph. This is a static construction problem; the graph is supplied once, and no update sequence is part of the input.
definitions: The vertices are labelled \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), all edges are unweighted unordered pairs of distinct vertices, and the input has no repeated edges. A spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph with vertex set \([n]\) and edge set contained in \(E\); it has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Its degree counts incident tree edges. The minimum defining \(\Delta^\star(G)\) exists because the graph is finite and connected; for \(n\ge2\), it is at least one. Input is an explicit adjacency-list array with vertex offsets, an entry for each endpoint of each edge, and the integers \(n,m\); each identifier or offset occupies one word. Output is an explicit list of the tree’s \(n-1\) endpoint pairs. The algorithm is a single finite program independent of \(n,m\), with words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed integer \(d\ge4\). Each operation reads or writes constantly many addressed words, compares, branches, performs Boolean operations or shifts, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), or divides unsigned words by a nonzero divisor with quotient and remainder. Shifts by at least \(W\) return zero. Work memory initially contains zero. All input access, initialization performed by the program, preprocessing, addressing and output writes are charged; no oracle for the optimum, graph-dependent advice, real arithmetic or random coins is available. The time bound is worst-case for every valid input. Near-linear means the displayed bound with one fixed logarithmic exponent; the approximation factor is one universal constant, not a function of \(n\), \(m\) or the optimum. The deterministic convention makes explicit the type of algorithm in the currently reported resolution.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean establishing the algorithmic existence statement with explicit finite program, approximation constant and time-bound constants, or proving its negation. An affirmative proof must cover every connected input graph and produce the tree itself, without being given \(\Delta^\star(G)\). An estimate of the optimum, a guarantee restricted to dense graphs or large optimal degree, or an additive error growing with \(n\) does not by itself establish a universal constant ratio. This yes/no question does not ask to optimize \(K\) or approximate the integer optimum within \(1/100\). A cited theorem or an unformalized implementation is not a Lean-verified submission.
context:
Saranurak’s question in Seminar 24471 concerns one input graph. It asks for a near-linear-time algorithm achieving a constant multiplicative approximation to the minimum possible maximum tree degree. Its occurrence in a seminar about distributed and dynamic algorithms does not add update operations to this particular question.

The classical Fürer–Raghavachari result has additive error at most one, but its \(O(mn)\)-scale running time is much larger than near-linear. Later near-linear constructions allowed additive terms logarithmic in the number of vertices; such terms do not yield a uniform constant ratio when the optimal degree is small.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad and Wang’s STOC 2026 result gives an additive-one approximation in \(\widetilde O(mn^{3/4})\) time. It improves the earlier construction time without itself meeting the near-linear target.

The July 2026 preprint by Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad, Saranurak and Wang states a deterministic construction with degree at most \(\lceil(1+\varepsilon)\Delta^\star\rceil+1\) in \(\widetilde O(m/\varepsilon^2)\) time. Its Theorem 1.1 explicitly identifies this as resolving the constant-factor question. For any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\le1\), this degree guarantee implies a universal constant factor because \(\Delta^\star\ge1\).

The preprint’s theorem, concluding proof and treatment of unknown optimum were inspected. Its full collection of technical lemmas and data-structure proofs has not been independently verified in this review, and the checked author record presents it as an arXiv manuscript. The card therefore records a reported resolution with uncertain verification status, rather than asserting that a new open gap remains or certifying a completed proof.
why: A low-degree spanning tree supplies a connected backbone while limiting the largest number of connections handled by one vertex. A constant approximation in near-linear time would make a strong structural guarantee available at a cost close to reading the graph. The target is substantially weaker than exact degree minimization, but stronger than bounds whose approximation grows with the graph size. This is a static construction frontier, despite the dynamic setting of the seminar collection.

The target correspondence, concluding proof and handling of unknown optimum were checked on 14 September 2026, but the full technical proof was not independently verified and no accepted publication of this particular result was confirmed. Status remains uncertain to express that verification limit; it should not be read as a newly certified open problem.

The source asks whether a universal constant approximation can be constructed in near-linear time. This is a static algorithmic question, despite its inherited placement among dynamic graph problems.
