importance_reason: Two central recognition gaps for automata used in synthesis and probabilistic verification. The first separates fixed-index tractability from unrestricted parity acceptance; the second certifies preservation of optimal probabilities for every finite MDP.
formal: Determine the exact worst-case computational complexity of each of the following two recognition languages: \[\mathrm{GFG}_{\mathrm{par}}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-games parity automaton}\},\qquad \mathrm{GFM}_{\mathrm B}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-MDP Büchi automaton}\}.\] The input is an explicit finite nondeterministic automaton, and the number of parity priorities is unbounded and part of the first input. The requested classification is for each language separately, with matching complexity-class upper and hardness bounds under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The source's two recognition tasks are retained; no particular class membership conjecture is substituted for either classification.
question_excerpt: Finally, the exact complexity of deciding whether a parity automaton is GFG, or whether a Büchi automaton is GFM, remains open.
definitions:
An automaton has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), an initial state \(q_0\), and a complete transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\). Completeness means that every state and letter admit a transition; a rejecting sink handles missing transitions. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\) follows transitions \((q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\) from \(q_0\). A parity automaton has a map \(p:\Delta\to\mathbb N\) and accepts a run when the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A Büchi automaton has a marked set \(F\subseteq\Delta\) and accepts a run when transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often. Its language \(L(\mathcal A)\) contains the words with some accepting run. A good-for-games (GFG) automaton admits a single deterministic rule that selects each next transition using only the finite input prefix read so far, so that its induced run accepts every \(w\in L(\mathcal A)\). The rule may remember the entire past; it cannot inspect future letters. One rule must work on all words.

A finite Markov decision process (MDP) over \(\Sigma\) has finite state and action sets \(S,U\), an initial state \(s_0\), a nonempty set \(U(s)\) of enabled actions at each state, a label \(\ell(s,u)\in\Sigma\), and a distribution \(P(s,u,\cdot)\) on \(S\) for each enabled pair. Distribution entries are real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. A policy maps the observed finite history of states and actions to a distribution on the enabled actions. It generates a path by choosing \(u_i\), emitting \(\ell(s_i,u_i)\), and sampling \(s_{i+1}\) using \(P\); products of these conditional probabilities give the path measure. Define \[V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)=\sup_\pi\Pr_M^\pi[\ell(s_0,u_0)\ell(s_1,u_1)\cdots\in L(\mathcal A)].\] In the product with \(\mathcal A\), a policy observes the joint state \((s_i,q_i)\), chooses an enabled pair consisting of \(u_i\) and a transition \((q_i,\ell(s_i,u_i),q_{i+1})\), then samples \(s_{i+1}\) from \(P(s_i,u_i,\cdot)\). Thus the automaton choice precedes that next random state and sees no future. Let \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)\) be the supremum, over all such history-dependent randomized product policies, of the probability that the selected automaton run satisfies its Büchi condition. The automaton is good-for-MDP (GFM) if \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)=V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)\) for every finite MDP over its alphabet and every initial MDP state. The product policy may depend on the MDP. This is exact equality of probabilities, without approximation or a probability-one promise.

Only the automaton is input to recognition; MDPs, policies and GFG rules are quantified objects. States, letters and transitions are explicitly enumerated; indices and priorities use binary integers with delimiters. Input size \(n\) is the total bit length, and invalid descriptions are rejected. The alphabet size, graph size and number of priorities are not fixed parameters. Computational bounds use uniform Turing machines and worst-case resource use over inputs of length at most \(n\), with exact acceptance and no randomized error. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(X\) to \(Y\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) with \(x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y\). A language is \(\mathcal C\)-complete if it belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and every language in \(\mathcal C\) reduces to it in this sense. Here \(\mathrm P\) is deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{NP}\) is nondeterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) is deterministic polynomial space, and \(\mathrm{EXPTIME}\) is deterministic time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\).
answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked matching complexity classifications for both recognition languages with the specified explicit input encoding and reduction convention. For each claimed complete class \(\mathcal C\), prove the resource upper bound and \(\mathcal C\)-hardness. Any other class used in the answer must have an independent machine/resource or logical definition, not a definition that merely renames this recognition problem or the collection of problems reducible to it. The precision requested is complexity-class completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions, not an exact leading constant in running time. An isolated improvement of one bound, an algorithm requiring a fixed priority count, or a result only for one recognition language is partial progress. Numerical approximation of the MDP values is not the acceptance criterion.
context:
Existence of an accepting run is a hindsight property: a nondeterministic automaton can have a successful branch for each word without any single online method selecting those branches. GFG demands such a uniform method. The input automaton is not promised to have the property; recognizing whether it does is the task.

GFM asks a different compositional question. An MDP describes both choices controlled by a policy and transitions sampled from fixed distributions. Its semantic objective only asks that the generated word have some accepting run. Its product objective also requires choosing that run as the word is produced. The second probability cannot exceed the first, and GFM requires equality for every finite MDP.

The policy in the product may be designed for the particular MDP, observing its current state and its past behavior. GFG instead requires one prefix-based resolution valid for every input word. This distinction makes GFM more permissive; it does not turn the two recognition languages into the same problem.

The 2-token theorem settles a major structural characterization of GFG parity automata and yields polynomial-time recognition at each fixed priority count. It does not yield one polynomial-time bound uniform in the number of priorities. The unrestricted input family remains NP-hard and in PSPACE in the checked 2026 survey.

GFM Büchi recognition is already decidable, with a PSPACE hardness lower bound and an EXPTIME algorithm. Consequently the missing result is a matching complexity classification, not an existence proof for some terminating algorithm. The source proves that a qualitative version based on probability-one preservation agrees with its quantitative GFM property, but the card states the original full-probability definition.

The interpretation of “exact complexity” here is the complexity-class classification used by the source when presenting these gaps. Both problems and the unrestricted priority parameter are preserved. Recognition does not ask for a smallest equivalent automaton, and recent minimization or state-reduction results do not automatically classify it.
why: These recognition problems measure the cost of checking whether a compact nondeterministic specification supports composition with an adversarial system or with a probabilistic controller. Their semantic definitions quantify over infinitely many behaviors, although their inputs are finite graphs. Matching classifications would explain the computational price of certifying these useful restrictions on nondeterminism and the difference between their game and probabilistic settings.
status_note: Both classifications are explicitly source-open in the CONCUR survey published 24 August 2026. The checked bounds are NP-hardness and PSPACE membership for unrestricted GFG parity recognition, and PSPACE-hardness and EXPTIME membership for GFM Büchi recognition. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The 2-token theorem settles fixed-index recognition, not the unrestricted target; cited proofs were not independently formalized.
progress: 2023: The CONCUR paper establishes PSPACE-hardness and an EXPTIME upper bound for GFM Büchi recognition; its finite-MDP definition quantifies over all initial states and arbitrary history-dependent policies. | 2025: The 2-token theorem yields polynomial-time GFG parity recognition for every fixed number of priorities. Prakash’s thesis records PSPACE membership and NP-hardness when the priority count is part of the input. | 2026-08-24: The CONCUR survey explicitly retains both exact complexity questions: NP-hard versus PSPACE for unrestricted GFG parity recognition, and PSPACE-hard versus EXPTIME for GFM Büchi recognition. | 2026-09-16: The survey statements, source semantics and original bounds were checked. A bounded later-work search located no matching classification closing either gap; the literature check does not independently certify the cited proofs.
working_summary: Good-for-games automata admit one online deterministic resolution that accepts every word in their language. Good-for-MDP automata preserve optimal acceptance probabilities when composed with every finite Markov decision process. The project asks matching complexity classifications for GFG parity recognition with unbounded priority count and GFM Büchi recognition. The checked gaps are NP-hardness versus PSPACE and PSPACE-hardness versus EXPTIME, respectively. Closing these gaps would identify the cost of certifying that compact specifications support adversarial or probabilistic composition.

title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
importance_reason: Equivalence is a foundational comparison problem for quantitative languages and a prerequisite for certified model replacement. The open general rational-discount case persists despite decidable deterministic, integral-base and other structured fragments, exposing a substantial arithmetic and nondeterministic boundary.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.
question_excerpt: Determine whether exact equivalence of nondeterministic discounted-sum automata over infinite words is decidable.
definitions: Such an automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,q_0,\Sigma,E,\gamma)\), where \(Q\) is a finite nonempty state set, \(q_0\in Q\), \(E\) is a finite set of transitions with source, target and label in \(Q,Q,\Sigma\), and \(\gamma:E\to\mathbb Q\) gives their weights. Parallel transitions, including differently weighted transitions with the same endpoints and label, are allowed. Totality means that every pair \((q,a)\in Q\times\Sigma\) has at least one outgoing transition. There are no empty-label transitions, final-state tests, fairness requirements or restrictions on which infinite runs count. For an infinite word \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run \(\rho=e_0e_1\cdots\) starts at \(q_0\), consecutive transitions have matching endpoints, and \(e_i\) has label \(a_i\). Set \[\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i\gamma(e_i),\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\sup_{\rho\text{ a run of }\mathcal A\text{ on }w}\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho).\] If \(W=\max_{e\in E}|\gamma(e)|\), every series converges absolutely and has absolute value at most \(W/(1-\lambda)\); totality ensures a nonempty run set, so the supremum is a finite real number. Nondeterministic choices are optimized separately for each complete word. No single online strategy is required to select them. All finite sets and transition tables are explicit, and rational weights and the common multiplier \(\lambda\) are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. The deciding machine takes these finite descriptions, not an infinite word as an oracle input. It must answer correctly on every well-formed pair and every allowed factor, without a resource bound. Equality is exact equality of real-valued functions on all infinite words; this yes-or-no decidability question has no approximation tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one total computable algorithm decides the stated equality for every encoded input, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A positive result must handle arbitrary rational \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), unrestricted finite nondeterminism, signed rational weights and all infinite words under supremum semantics. A result for deterministic or functional automata, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words, or comparison up to a positive tolerance does not settle the full target. A negative result obtained by permitting different discount factors on different transitions does not settle this single-factor problem.
context:
A transition weight represents a local reward or cost. Multiplication by successive powers of the discount factor gives later weights less influence. The automaton chooses the best run separately on each input word, producing a quantitative language rather than a set of accepted words. Equivalence compares those whole functions.

The source considers total automata, rational weights and supremum semantics on infinite words. Its shared value-function convention is made explicit by supplying one multiplier for both automata. Some papers instead divide the weight at position \(i\) by \(\beta^i\), with \(\beta>1\), and take infima; their discount corresponds to \(\lambda=1/\beta\), and negating all weights interchanges the two extremum conventions.

Convergence does not turn exact function equality into a test of finitely many sampled behaviors or fixed-precision values. The 2023 paper can decide whether one discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function while explicitly leaving arbitrary equivalence open. Constancy is a special case and does not give the required pairwise comparison procedure.

Later results depend sharply on the model. Reciprocal-integer multipliers belong to a decidable family, and more general real-valued Pisot-base results extend that family outside the rational domain. Conversely, undecidability with transition-dependent discount factors concerns a richer interface. Neither result settles all rational multipliers shared throughout a pair of nondeterministic automata.
why: Exact equivalence is a basic correctness test for quantitative specifications: it asks whether replacing one finite-state description by another preserves the value of every possible infinite behavior. Discounting makes each value convergent but leaves a difficult interaction between exact arithmetic and nondeterministic choices. Resolving equivalence for the basic rational single-factor model would establish a central algorithmic boundary for quantitative automata.
status_note: Source-open for general total nondeterministic automata over infinite words with one shared rational factor. Checked the CONCUR 2023 open statement and LICS 2024 comparison scope, followed by the 2025 LMCS multiple-factor results, the November 2025 revised target-sum paper, and a September 2026 probabilistic preprint. No matching general resolution was found in this bounded review on 15 September 2026. New preprints and cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2023: The CONCUR paper defines the supremum semantics in §2 and explicitly leaves discounted-sum equivalence open in §3. Its Theorem 3.3 proves PSPACE-completeness of deciding whether a discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function. | 2024-07: Boker’s LICS 2024 Theorems 5.4–5.5 give decidability for Pisot divisor discount factors and suitable algebraic weights. In particular this includes integer divisors, hence reciprocal-integer multipliers here; it does not cover arbitrary rational multipliers. | 2025-06-05: The LMCS paper proves equivalence undecidable for a model allowing different integral divisor factors on different transitions. A single common rational multiplier is not that model. | 2025-11-28: The revised target discounted-sum manuscript gives positive results for functional automata over finite words in §6. Its word domain and restricted run values differ from the present general infinite-word problem. | 2026-09-03: A preprint on target discounted sums computes probabilities for finite Markov chains and studies related strategy objectives. These probabilistic questions do not provide a pointwise equivalence algorithm for the automata here.
working_summary: A discounted-sum automaton assigns a convergent weighted value to each infinite run, with later weights geometrically discounted. Its value on an infinite word is the supremum over all runs carrying that word. The question asks for exact decidability of equality of two such functions for every input rational discount factor shared by the automata. Known results for constant functions, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words and transition-dependent discounting have different scopes. A resolution would determine whether arbitrary nondeterministic quantitative specifications in this basic model can be compared algorithmically.

title: Primitive words and context-freeness
importance_reason: A canonical elementary language whose grammar expressibility remains a fundamental question in combinatorics on words and automata theory.
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.
context:
Primitivity excludes every nontrivial repetition of a shorter word. The question asks whether a context-free grammar can express that condition over all lengths.

The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains context-freeness of primitive words as open while proving a result about probabilistic membership.
why: The primitive-word language is a basic boundary case linking periodicity of words with the expressive power of context-free grammars.
status_note: Explicitly open in the STACS 2026 introduction and retained on the checked author problem list. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the probabilistic-membership result is a different target and no general context-freeness resolution was identified.
progress: 2026-02-25: The STACS paper treats context-freeness of primitive words as a longstanding open question; its probabilistic-membership theorem does not resolve it.
working_summary: A primitive word is nonempty and is not a power of any shorter nonempty word. The language contains all such words over a fixed finite alphabet with at least two symbols. The conjecture says that no context-free grammar generates exactly this language. Grammars may be ambiguous, so unique-parse limitations would not settle the question. A 2026 paper still states this grammar-expressibility question as open.

title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
importance_reason: Determine the intrinsic sequential cost of a canonical finite-state operation, beyond the limitations of its classical algorithmic framework.
formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
question_excerpt: Can the classical O(n log n) worst-case bound for minimization over a fixed finite alphabet be improved to linear time by an unrestricted sequential algorithm?
definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an input DFA is \(A=([n],[a],\delta,s,F)\), where \(\delta:[n]\times[a]\to[n]\) is total, \(s\in[n]\), and \(F\subseteq[n]\). Its explicit input consists of \(n\), \(s\), the \(an\) transition targets, and \(n\) accepting-state bits, one target or bit per input word. Extend \(\delta\) to finite words by \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ub)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),b)\). The recognized language is \(\{u:\delta^*(s,u)\in F\}\). The output is an explicit complete DFA \(B=([k],[a],\delta',s',F')\), \(1\le k\le n\), recognizing exactly that language, with \(k\) minimal among all complete DFAs over the same alphabet. Unreachable input states may be discarded; no equivalence partition for them is required. Both input and output transitions are explicitly represented.

Use one sequential deterministic word-RAM with word length \(w=\lceil2\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), addressed word memory and finitely many registers. Reading or writing one addressed word, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by an amount less than \(w\), comparisons and conditional branches each cost one step. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle instruction or externally supplied lookup table is available. The finite program may depend on the fixed alphabet size but not on the input size. All algorithmic preprocessing, auxiliary-table construction, initialization and output writing are charged to the running time; memory beyond the input has a fixed blank initial value. The asymptotic target is considered for \(n\ge n_a\ge a\), so the explicit \(an\)-word transition table fits the chosen word address space. Finitely many smaller sizes for each fixed alphabet are finite exceptions to the asymptotic claim. This spells out the input-addressing convention without changing the saved logarithmic word formula. The cost is in word operations, not bit operations: the input uses \(\Theta(n)\) words for fixed \(a\). There is no randomization, expected-time qualification, distribution on inputs, language approximation or promise on the transition graph.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation, including correctness, minimality, explicit output and the stated RAM cost. A positive proof must cover every fixed \(a\ge2\) by a uniform-in-\(n\) finite program and fixed constants. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(a\ge2\), every correct program in this full RAM model fails an \(O(n)\) worst-case bound: no constants \(C,n_0\) work for all sufficiently large inputs. A lower bound restricted to partition refinement, a comparison model or one particular minimization algorithm does not prove this negation. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional version.
context:
Two reachable states are equivalent exactly when every continuation word is either accepted from both or rejected from both. A smallest recognizer retains one representative of each such behavior. The task asks for the resulting explicit automaton, not merely a test of whether the input is already minimal.

Hopcroft’s algorithm minimizes a complete DFA in \(O(an\log n)\) time. For a fixed alphabet this is \(O(n\log n)\), while the input and a largest possible minimal output each occupy only linearly many words. The target is therefore removal of one logarithmic factor in worst-case sequential time.

Partition refinement begins with blocks distinguished by acceptance and repeatedly separates states whose transitions lead to different blocks. The 2023 lower-bound paper formalizes costs of such refinements and proves a logarithmic-factor obstruction even on deterministic systems with two actions. Its theorem quantifies over that method class, not over all multiplication-capable word-RAM programs.

Unary automata have a functional-graph structure that admits linear-time methods outside ordinary partition refinement. The saved target deliberately starts at alphabet size two, where two successor functions can interact. The successful unary case cannot be substituted for the multi-letter statement.

There are also linear-time results for special transition graphs, such as those whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles. These are meaningful positive cases but do not impose the arbitrary transition-graph guarantee requested here.

The source concerns symbolic automata, where transitions can carry predicates describing large or infinite alphabets. This card uses only its ordinary finite-alphabet minimization baseline. The precise word operations, input layout and uniformity convention are editorial choices already present in the saved target; they are not attributed as a conjecture made verbatim by the source authors.
why: DFA minimization is a basic preprocessing step for recognizers, regular-language operations and finite-state verification. Its classical algorithm is almost linear, and the logarithmic factor has resisted removal for general transition graphs. Resolving the target would distinguish an inherent cost of the problem from the cost of the partition-refinement paradigm.
status_note: The source supports the classical O(an log n) baseline, not the exact editorial word-RAM statement as a verbatim open question. The 2023 primary lower-bound paper explicitly restricts its result to partition-refinement algorithms. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted deterministic linear-time algorithm or lower bound in the saved RAM model. This is a source-supported editorial target with a dated status check, not a proof of present openness.
progress: 1971: The classical Hopcroft bound, recorded in the source, gives O(an log n) worst-case minimization time. | 2008: Almeida and Zeitoun establish linear minimization for automata whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles. | 2014: The cited symbolic-automata paper identifies Hopcroft’s algorithm as the ordinary-DFA baseline and distinguishes its cost from symbolic-alphabet costs. | 2023: The checked lower-bound paper proves barriers for sequential partition-refinement algorithms, including deterministic two-action instances, without an unrestricted RAM lower bound. | 2026-09-16: The fixed alphabet, explicit word-RAM model and stronger unrestricted target were checked; bounded later-primary searches found no matching linear algorithm or full-model impossibility result.
working_summary: A deterministic finite automaton can be minimized by merging reachable states that accept exactly the same continuation words. The question asks whether every complete automaton over any fixed alphabet of at least two letters can be minimized in deterministic linear worst-case word-RAM time. The output must be an explicit smallest automaton recognizing exactly the original language, and all preprocessing and output work count. Classical algorithms take O(n log n) time, while known logarithmic-factor lower bounds concern partition refinement rather than every algorithm in the stated model. A resolution would determine whether the extra logarithmic cost reflects the general problem or the structure of its classical algorithms.

title: Decidability of stochastic resolvability for \(\omega\)-automata
importance_reason: A foundational recognition question for online randomized automata, separating finite-memory synthesis from verification of a supplied resolver. Its relation to history determinism, probabilistic automata and good-for-MDP composition gives it significance beyond one representation.
formal: For each of the two acceptance conditions \(c\in\{\mathrm{B\ddot uchi},\mathrm{coB\ddot uchi}\}\), is stochastic resolvability decidable for finite nondeterministic word automata with condition \(c\)? More precisely, does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on every encoded automaton \(\mathcal A\) of that type, halts and decides whether there exists a finite-memory stochastic resolver \(\mathcal R\) such that \[\forall w\in L(\mathcal A),\qquad \Pr_{\mathcal R,w}[\text{the constructed run of }\mathcal A\text{ is accepting}]=1?\] The resolver is chosen before the word and must work for every accepted word; the word is fixed independently of its random choices. The source asks both the Büchi and coBüchi questions, and their decidability statuses are to be determined separately.
question_excerpt: Is it decidable to check if a given (co)Büchi automaton is SR?
definitions: An input automaton consists of finite nonempty sets \(Q\) of states and \(\Sigma\) of letters, an initial state \(q_0\), a transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and a marked transition set \(F\subseteq\Delta\). For each state and letter at least one transition is present. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\) is a sequence \(q_0\xrightarrow{a_0}q_1\xrightarrow{a_1}\cdots\) using \(\Delta\). Büchi acceptance means that transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often; coBüchi acceptance means that they occur only finitely often. Thus \(F\) is accepting in the first convention and rejecting in the second. The language \(L(\mathcal A)\) consists of words with at least one accepting run. A resolver is a tuple \((M,m_0,\mu,p)\): a finite nonempty memory set, its initial element, a deterministic memory update \(\mu:M\times\Delta\to M\), and for each \((m,q,a)\) a probability distribution \(p_{m,q,a}\) on the outgoing transitions \(\Delta_{q,a}\). Its probabilities are arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one; some may be zero. At step \(i\), the resolver observes \(m_i,q_i,a_i\), samples \(\delta_i\) with distribution \(p_{m_i,q_i,a_i}\), follows that transition and sets \(m_{i+1}=\mu(m_i,\delta_i)\). For a fixed word, finite-run cylinder probabilities are the products of these step probabilities; their induced measure on infinite runs defines the displayed probability. The memory size is finite but has no prescribed bound and may depend on the input automaton. Neither the resolver nor its probabilities are part of the finite input. Requiring rational probabilities, a fixed memory bound or memorylessness would be an additional restriction, not imposed here. The automaton and its marked transitions are explicitly listed using binary indices and delimiters; the alphabet is part of the input. Decidability means one effective machine for all such finite descriptions of the specified acceptance type, with exact yes/no output and no running-time bound. The source uses complete automata; missing transitions may equivalently lead to a fresh rejecting sink.
answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proofs for each of the Büchi and coBüchi input classes. A decidability proof must supply an effective total algorithm and establish its correctness for the existential finite-memory, real-probability resolver semantics above. An undecidability proof must exclude every total computable decider for that class. A result for only one acceptance class settles only that component of the source question. Checking an already specified resolver, restricting its memory to one state, or replacing probability one by a smaller threshold does not settle either full existence question.
context:
A nondeterministic automaton may accept a word because one successful run exists, even if choosing that run requires knowledge of future letters. A resolver must commit to each transition when the current letter arrives. Stochastic resolvability allows these commitments to be random while requiring failure probability zero on every accepted word.

The order of choices matters. The same resolver is used on every word, but a word cannot react to the random transitions actually taken. Requiring success against an environment that sees those transitions is the stronger adversarial notion studied alongside stochastic resolvability. Probability one here is a separate assertion for each fixed word; it does not require one common set of random choices that succeeds simultaneously on all words.

Finite memory is part of the source definition, not a consequence silently assumed in this card. Memoryless resolvers are a strictly weaker class for Büchi and coBüchi automata. The source also leaves open whether the particular nonzero probability values can always be changed while preserving success, so the definition cannot be replaced by an unproved finite search over transition supports.

The source proves that checking a supplied finite-memory resolver is undecidable for both acceptance conditions. This concerns a pair consisting of an automaton and a prescribed resolver; the present input is just an automaton and asks whether any suitable resolver exists. A failed prescribed resolver may coexist with a successful alternative, which explains why the checking theorem is not already the requested negative answer.

Related positive results help locate the boundary. Recognition is polynomial-time for safety automata and PSPACE-complete for reachability and weak automata. A safety condition rejects as soon as a bad transition occurs; reachability requires eventually entering an accepting region, and weak automata do not mix accepting and rejecting recurrence within one strongly connected component. The unrestricted Büchi and coBüchi conditions allow behaviors beyond these subclasses.

The later quantitative paper studies memoryless resolvers with a fixed success threshold strictly below one. Its undecidability theorem is explicitly separate from almost-sure stochastic resolvability with finite memory. Treating the common word “resolvability” as identifying the two problems would incorrectly retire this card.
why: This problem asks when nondeterministic specifications can be executed online with finite memory and reliable random choices. It isolates a precise gap between deterministic resolution against an adaptive environment and probabilistic behavior on every fixed input. A decision procedure would recognize which existing automata admit such execution; an undecidability theorem would establish a limitation even for two elementary acceptance conditions on finite graphs.
status_note: Source-open in MFCS 2025 §6. The revised 31 March 2026 quantitative-resolvability paper still distinguishes this almost-sure problem as open for general infinite-word acceptance classes. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution for either acceptance condition. Cited proof bodies were consulted for scope, not independently formalized.
progress: 2025-08-20: The MFCS paper establishes the structural separation of memoryless and finite-memory stochastic resolvability. Theorem 24 gives polynomial-time safety recognition, PSPACE-complete reachability/weak recognition, and undecidability of checking a supplied Büchi or coBüchi resolver; §6 retains existence of a suitable resolver as an open question. | 2026-03-31: The revised quantitative-resolvability paper distinguishes its memoryless threshold model from probability-one resolvability and records the latter as open for the more general infinite-word acceptance classes. Its negative theorem therefore does not match the target. | 2026-09-16: The exact source definitions and the later quantitative paper were rechecked. A bounded search found no matching resolution for either Büchi or coBüchi finite-memory almost-sure recognition; this is a dated literature check, not proof that no resolution exists.
working_summary: A finite-memory stochastic resolver selects an automaton transition using the current letter, current state and a finite memory state. One resolver must produce an accepting run with probability one for every accepted infinite word fixed independently of its random choices. The question asks separately whether existence of such a resolver is decidable for Büchi and coBüchi automata. Undecidability of verifying a supplied resolver and results for memoryless thresholds below one concern different decision problems. A resolution would determine whether reliable randomized online execution can be recognized from a finite nondeterministic specification.

title: Two-dimensional cellular-automaton limit sets
importance_reason: This seeks a structural description of all persistent configurations generated by finite local rules, linking symbolic dynamics with computation. A whole-class characterization would explain which spatial constraints can emerge from arbitrary starting configurations, beyond results describing typical behavior or only computational invariants.
formal: Characterize exactly which two-dimensional subshifts are ordinary limit sets of cellular automata, allowing finitely many auxiliary states that disappear from the limit set. Equivalently, determine the realizability function \(R(q,S)\in\{0,1\}\) on the full domain of finite alphabet sizes \(q\ge1\) and subshifts \(S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) defined below. Its value is 1 exactly when some cellular automaton on a finite alphabet containing those \(q\) symbols has ordinary limit set exactly \(S\), and is 0 otherwise. This is a whole-class characterization, with no computability or time requirement on the answer function.
question_excerpt: Nevertheless, the problem of characterising which subshifts can be limit sets of CA remains open.
definitions: For \(q\ge1\), let \(A_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\). A configuration over \(A_q\) is a function \(x:\mathbb Z^2\to A_q\). Give \(A_q\) the discrete topology and the configuration space the product topology: specifying the states on any finite set of cells defines a basic open cylinder. For \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\), translation is \((\sigma_vx)(u)=x(u+v)\). A subshift \(S\) is any closed subset of \(A_q^{\mathbb Z^2}\) with \(\sigma_v(S)=S\) for every \(v\); the empty subshift is allowed. Equivalently, it is specified by the set \(\mathcal L(S)\) of all finite patterns that occur in some configuration in \(S\), where a finite pattern is a map from a finite subset of \(\mathbb Z^2\) to \(A_q\). This is an abstract mathematical domain; a subshift is not promised to have a finite forbidden-pattern description or a decidable language. To realize \(S\), one may choose any finite integer \(b\ge q\), use alphabet \(A_b\), choose any integer radius \(r\ge0\), and specify one local rule \(\phi:A_b^{[-r,r]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2}\to A_b\). The induced global map \(F:A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\to A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\) applies this same rule synchronously at every cell: \(F(x)(u)=\phi((x(u+v))_{v\in[-r,r]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2})\). All initial configurations in the full space \(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\) are allowed. Write \(F^0\) for the identity and \(F^t\) for \(t\) iterations, and define the ordinary limit set \(\Omega(F)=\bigcap_{t\ge0}F^t(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2})\). Thus \(x\in\Omega(F)\) means that for every \(t\ge0\), some initial configuration \(y_t\) satisfies \(F^t(y_t)=x\); the preimage may depend on \(t\). Identify \(S\) with its coordinatewise inclusion in \(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\). Define \(R(q,S)=1\) if there exist \(b\ge q,r\ge0,\phi\) with \(\Omega(F)=S\), and \(R(q,S)=0\) otherwise. Equality is exact: projecting away auxiliary states, applying a block code, matching only the occurring Turing degrees, or obtaining a superset is insufficient. No auxiliary symbol may occur in any configuration of \(\Omega(F)\). There is no bound on \(b,r\) and no uniform construction requirement across subshifts. Empty \(S\) has value 0 because every such full-space limit set is nonempty. No probability distribution on initial configurations is used.
answer_criterion: Supply a characterization, equivalently a function \(g(q,S)\in\mathbb R\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|g(q,S)-R(q,S)|\le1/100\) for every \(q\ge1\) and every subshift in the specified domain. A necessary-and-sufficient condition on the subshift or its finite-pattern language with proofs of both directions qualifies and determines \(R\) exactly. As for other function targets, merely renaming or unfolding the defining existential search over local rules and their iterated full-space images is not a determination of the function. No fixed grammar for the characterization and no computable decision procedure is prescribed. A classification only up to a factor map, only for a restricted family of subshifts, only by computational invariants, or only for a measure-based or generic limit-set notion does not meet the target.
context:
The selected source sentence concerns ordinary limit sets, while the article’s proved characterization concerns measure-based limit sets. This card makes the two-dimensional setting of the article explicit and selects exact realization with an arbitrary finite extension of the target alphabet. These conventions are part of the reviewed version of the broad source question.

Finite auxiliary alphabets are explicitly used in the source’s realization framework. Here they may be present during the dynamics but must be entirely absent from the ordinary limit set. Exact equality is stronger than simply reading a desired component of a larger persistent configuration.

An ordinary limit set consists of configurations having preimages at every finite time depth. A measure-based limit set instead retains patterns whose occurrence probabilities do not vanish under a chosen initial distribution. The article’s Theorem 9 characterizes the latter notion for a uniform Bernoulli initial measure and does not settle the ordinary-limit-set question.

Borello, Cervelle and Vanier characterize the possible sets of Turing degrees of configurations in one-dimensional limit sets. Equal sets of computational degrees do not imply equality of subshifts, so their theorem is not an exact realization classification of the configurations requested here.

Sabrié and Törmä’s 2026 study of elementary rule 18 proves that its ordinary, generic and measure-based limit sets are distinct. This is a one-dimensional example, not a two-dimensional classification, and illustrates why the three notions cannot be substituted for one another.
why: A cellular automaton has a finite local description but can retain complex global configurations indefinitely. An exact realizability classification would identify which translation-invariant spatial constraints can arise in that long-term behavior. It concerns every possible initial configuration, including exceptional configurations that probabilistic descriptions may discard.
status_note: The 2015 source explicitly leaves ordinary-limit-set characterization open and proves a measure-based theorem instead. The checked later computational-invariant and generic/measure-based results do not settle the precise two-dimensional exact-realization version stated here. Bounded searches through 2026-09-16 identified no general classification; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2014-02-16: Borello, Cervelle and Vanier state a complete characterization of the sets of Turing degrees of one-dimensional cellular-automaton limit sets. Theorem 1 concerns computational invariants rather than exact subshift equality. | 2015: Delacourt and Hellouin de Ménibus state that ordinary limit-set realizability lacks a general characterization. Their Theorem 9 gives a two-dimensional measure-based realization result with a finite alphabet extension. | 2026-04-20: Sabrié and Törmä’s article establishes distinct ordinary, generic and measure-based limit sets for elementary cellular automaton 18; it does not claim a general exact realizability classification.
working_summary: A cellular automaton updates every site of an infinite grid using one finite local rule. Its ordinary limit set contains configurations that can occur after arbitrarily many update steps from some initial configurations. The question classifies exactly which two-dimensional subshifts can arise in this way, allowing finitely many transient auxiliary states. The classification is represented by a realizability indicator on the full domain of subshifts, without assuming an effective decision procedure. Results for typical initial states, computational degrees or a different notion of limit set do not determine this exact ordinary-limit-set class.

title: Separating words problem
importance_reason: A basic state-complexity problem measuring finite automata’s ability to distinguish arbitrary strings and connecting to reconstruction questions.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), \[s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}\min\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\}.\]
definitions: The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton. A proposed positive comparison function \(f\) determines the requested asymptotic scale when constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) exist with \(a f(n)\le s(n)\le b f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). The source’s conjectured endpoint is \(s(n)=O(\log n)\); the card explicitly asks for the underlying worst-case scale rather than asserting this endpoint.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function \(f(n)\) and a Lean proof of both constant-factor inequalities in the definitions. A universal small-DFA upper bound must be accompanied by a matching worst-case lower bound. This is asymptotic state complexity; the numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to big-O bounds. Results for random words or selected families of pairs do not determine the unrestricted maximum.
context:
The original problem asks whether logarithmically many states always suffice to distinguish two equal-length binary words. This card develops that threshold question into determination of the worst-case state function.

The August 2026 primary abstract reports a general \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) upper bound and studies a stronger result only when one word is random. The September preprint supplies another proof at the general one-third exponent, not a logarithmic universal bound.
why: Determining this scale would quantify how little finite-state memory suffices to distinguish an arbitrary pair of long binary strings.
status_note: The checked 2026 preprints retain a general one-third-power upper-bound scale and do not give matching asymptotics or a universal logarithmic bound. Read on 13 September 2026; proofs were not independently verified and the literature search was bounded.
progress: 2019: The source poses a logarithmic upper-bound target and mentions a one-third-power bound as an intermediate scale. | 2026-08-28: Bathie reports the general one-third-power upper-bound frontier and proves a different guarantee for a random word against an adversarial comparison word. | 2026-09-08: Xu’s preprint abstract gives an elementary proof of an \(O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{7/3})\)-state upper bound.
working_summary: The problem measures the smallest deterministic automaton that distinguishes two binary words of equal length. A different automaton may be chosen for each pair and its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The target is the worst-case number of states as a function of the common word length. The original question proposes a logarithmic upper bound, while recent general bounds have a one-third power with logarithmic factors. The benchmark asks for matching constant-factor asymptotics across all pairs, not a random-input guarantee.

title: Recognizable separability of automatic relations
importance_reason: This is the unrestricted separation problem between two fundamental classes of word relations. Its equivalence to finite regular colorability links finite-state abstraction, automatic structures and relational constraints, while known fixed-bound undecidability leaves the central unbounded formulation unresolved.
formal: Is the following recognizable-separability problem undecidable, as asserted by Conjecture 7.1 of the source? Given a finite alphabet \(A\) and two nondeterministic finite automata representing binary automatic relations \(R_1,R_2\subseteq A^*\times A^*\), decide whether there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\) and regular languages \(L_1,\ldots,L_k,K_1,\ldots,K_k\subseteq A^*\) with \[R_1\subseteq S,\qquad S\cap R_2=\varnothing,\qquad S=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(L_i\times K_i).\] The number \(k\) and the sizes of all component automata have no prescribed finite bound. Undecidability means that no deterministic Turing machine halts and gives the correct answer on every finite input description of this kind.
question_excerpt: The Rec-separability problem – or, equivalently, the regular colorability problem – is undecidable.
definitions: For \(u,v\in A^*\), their convolution \(u\otimes v\) has length \(\max\{|u|,|v|\}\). Its \(j\)-th symbol is the pair of \(j\)-th letters, using a fresh padding symbol \(\bot\notin A\) when \(j\) exceeds one word's length. Padding occurs only at the end of the shorter component; \(\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon=\varepsilon\). An input automaton \(B\) over \((A\cup\{\bot\})^2\) represents \(R(B)=\{(u,v):B\text{ accepts }u\otimes v\}\). Only valid convolutions affect this relation. A nondeterministic finite automaton has a finite state set, designated initial and accepting state sets, and a finite letter-labeled transition relation; it accepts a finite word if some path with that label leads from an initial state to an accepting state. A language is regular if some such automaton accepts it. A recognizable binary relation is a finite union of Cartesian products of two regular languages, as displayed above; \(k=0\) gives the empty relation. All alphabets, state sets and transition lists are explicit finite input data, with symbol and state indices encoded as binary integers with delimiters. Both relations are binary, as in the source's main formulation; neither has to be symmetric. There is no promise that they are disjoint. The quantifier over candidate separators is inside the decision problem and ranges over all finite descriptions; it is not a fixed bound supplied to the deciding machine. One uniform machine would have to decide every instance, using finite computation and no advice or oracle. No complexity bound is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the defined input language is undecidable, or refute the conjecture by supplying a uniform total decision algorithm and proving its correctness and termination in Lean. A proof of undecidability must exclude every total computable decider for unrestricted finite recognizable separators. Undecidability when the number of Cartesian products is fixed, or when the input relations are asynchronous rational relations, does not prove this conjecture.
context:
A synchronous automaton can inspect matching positions in the two component words. In one Cartesian product, by contrast, the first component is checked independently of the second. Taking finitely many such products allows finitely many alternatives, while retaining independent tests within each alternative.

Separation permits an overapproximation: the separator may contain pairs outside both input relations. This differs from asking whether one automatic relation is itself recognizable, which is already decidable. The difference is the freedom to choose what happens on pairs not constrained by either input.

The source connects unrestricted recognizable separation to coloring an automatic graph with finitely many colors, each color class a regular language. An automatic graph has words as vertices and a synchronously recognized edge relation; adjacent vertices must receive different colors. The number of colors is existentially chosen and unbounded.

The published fixed-product-count and fixed-color-count undecidability results do not settle the unrestricted question. A pair with no separator of one prescribed size may have a larger separator. Morvan’s later thesis continues to identify this unbounded version as an open problem.
why: Automatic relations allow a finite machine to compare positions in two unbounded strings. Recognizable relations replace this synchronization with finitely many independent regular tests. Deciding whether such a replacement can separate two specifications is a basic abstraction question connected to regular colorings of infinite graphs and to simplifying relational constraints. Its answer would locate an effective boundary between two elementary finite descriptions of infinite relations.
status_note: Source-open: the MFCS 2023 statement is Conjecture 7.1, not a theorem. Morvan’s 22 May 2025 thesis retains the unrestricted question as Open Problem VII.1.10. The February 2026 automatic-structure dichotomy concerns a fixed finite target and does not resolve the existentially unbounded separator size. Checked on 15 September 2026 with a bounded later-work search; no cited proof was independently formalized.
progress: 2023: Theorem 3.1 gives polynomial-time reductions in both directions between binary recognizable separation and finite regular colorability of automatic graphs. Theorems 4.4 and 5.6 prove undecidability for each fixed color or product bound of at least two; Conjecture 7.1 proposes undecidability for unrestricted separation. | 2025-05-22: Morvan’s thesis, Open Problem VII.1.10 and Chapter X.1, explicitly says the unrestricted recognizable-separability problem remains open. | 2026-02-20: Cuvelier and Morvan’s preprint gives a decidability dichotomy for homomorphisms from automatic structures to a fixed finite target, including the regular-homomorphism variant. Fixing that target fixes the palette in coloring instances; the result does not decide whether some finite palette exists. | 2026-09-15: The conjecture, complete binary-relation definitions, and later thesis and preprint scopes were checked. A bounded search found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the source conjecture is not presented as an established undecidability theorem.
working_summary: Binary automatic relations are recognized by finite automata reading padded pairs of words synchronously. The question asks whether it is undecidable to separate two such relations by a finite union of products of regular languages. The number of products is existentially chosen with no prescribed upper bound. Fixed-bound separation is already undecidable, but the unrestricted problem remains explicitly open in the checked later thesis. A resolution would clarify when synchronized infinite relations admit effective separation by finitely many independent regular tests.

title: Polynomial-time universality for unambiguous context-free grammars
importance_reason: Universality for unambiguous context-free grammars is a canonical complexity question about a major language class.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that decides whether \(L(G)=\Sigma^{*}\) for every context-free grammar \(G\) promised to be unambiguous, in time polynomial in the bit length of its explicit description? The algorithm must have one polynomial running-time bound on all input strings; correctness is required on the promised grammars. The terminal alphabet is part of the input. This card selects the polynomial-time endpoint of the source’s broader question about the exact complexity.
definitions: ['A context-free grammar is a finite tuple \\(G=(V,\\Sigma,P,S)\\), where the finite sets of nonterminals \\(V\\) and terminals \\(\\Sigma\\) are disjoint, \\(S\\in V\\), and \\(P\\subseteq V\\times(V\\cup\\Sigma)^{*}\\) is a finite set of production rules. The alphabet is finite and nonempty. All symbols, productions and right-hand-side strings are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices; repeated identical rules are treated as a single rule. Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed.', 'A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \\(S\\). Each nonterminal node expands according to one production, with its children in the right-hand-side order; an empty production contributes no terminal. Its yield is the terminal string read from left to right. \\(L(G)\\) is the set of yields. The unambiguity promise says that each word has at most one such parse tree, including the empty word. It is a promise on the given grammar, not merely on its language.', 'Universality includes every finite word, including \\(\\varepsilon\\). Polynomial time means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine and constants \\(C,d\\geq1\\) whose runtime on every string of length \\(N\\) is at most \\(C(N+1)^{d}\\). It outputs a bit. On every well-formed unambiguous grammar this bit is 1 exactly for universal grammars; on other inputs either answer is allowed.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the specified uniform polynomial-time promise algorithm, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A faster superpolynomial algorithm, a conditional lower bound alone, or an algorithm limited to deterministic grammars does not meet this criterion.
context:
The 2019 problem asks to close the complexity gap for universality with a unique-parse promise. The benchmark’s yes/no polynomial-time endpoint is an editorial choice; a negative answer would leave finer complexity classification open.

Clemente’s 2020 paper proves a polynomial-space upper bound (Theorem 10). Its quantitative coin-flip-measure hardness theorem concerns a different problem and does not establish an equivalent hardness result for universality.

The 2023 paper improves the checked upper bound to \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\): randomized polynomial time with one-sided error and access to an oracle for majority acceptance of polynomial-time nondeterministic computations. This oracle-assisted bound does not provide the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm asked for here.
why: Unique parse trees suffice to make universality decidable, but they do not give deterministic control of parsing. A polynomial-time procedure, or a proof excluding one, would locate the computational cost of this fundamental coverage test between finite-state reasoning and general context-free behavior.
status_note: The 2019 question asks to close the complexity gap. Primary papers from 2020 and 2023 give successively stronger upper bounds, the latter in coRP with a PP oracle. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no resolution of the deterministic polynomial-time endpoint; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2019-07-01: The problem list asks for improved upper or lower complexity bounds under the unambiguity promise. | 2020-08-07: Theorem 10 gives a polynomial-space algorithm; the discussion leaves exact universality complexity open. | 2023-04-27: Corollary 4 and its stated consequence place universality of arbitrary-alphabet unambiguous grammars in \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\), improving the polynomial-space bound.
working_summary: An unambiguous context-free grammar gives each accepted word a unique parse tree. This card asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can test if such a grammar generates every finite word over its alphabet. Unambiguity is promised for the supplied grammar, and the alphabet and complete production rules are part of the input. The checked upper bound uses randomized polynomial time with a PP oracle; it does not yield the unconditional deterministic polynomial-time procedure sought here. The polynomial-time endpoint is an explicit editorial specialization of the source’s broader complexity question, with either answer requiring a Lean-checked proof.

title: Decidability of discounted-sum universality over infinite words
importance_reason: A central decision problem for quantitative automata with direct connections to verification and exact discounted-sum representability; the rational infinite-word case goes beyond established restricted algorithms.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a complete nondeterministic discounted-sum automaton \(\mathcal A\) with rational weights and a rational discount factor \(0<\lambda<1\), and a rational threshold \(t\), decides whether \(\mathcal A(w)\leq t\) for every infinite word \(w\in\Sigma^\omega\)? Here \(\mathcal A(w)\) is the infimum of the discounted sums of its runs on \(w\).
definitions: The input contains a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), finite nonempty state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and weight map \(g:E\to\mathbb Q\). Completeness means every state has at least one outgoing transition for each letter. There are no epsilon transitions, final-state restrictions or fairness conditions: every infinite run is eligible. On \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run is an infinite state sequence \(q_0,q_1,\ldots\) with \(e_i=(q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\in E\). Its value is \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i)\); finite weights and \(0<\lambda<1\) ensure absolute convergence. The word value is \(\mathcal A(w)=\inf\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i): (e_i)_{i\geq0}\text{ is a run on }w\}\). The run set is nonempty and finitely branching, and this infimum is attained, so universality is equivalently \(\forall w\,\exists r\) with run value at most \(t\). Different words may use different runs; a run is not required to be chosen by an online strategy. One common discount factor applies to every transition. It is an input rational, not restricted to the reciprocal of an integer. All finite sets and tables are explicit; rational numerators and positive denominators are binary integers. An algorithm means one ordinary deterministic Turing machine that halts on every encoded valid instance and answers the exact non-strict threshold question. No finite-word truncation, approximation tolerance or bound on running time is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for the stated infinite-word, non-strict universality problem, including its correctness on every rational input. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A procedure for deterministic or functional automata, integer-reciprocal discount factors, finite words, strict inequalities alone or thresholds separated by a promised positive gap does not meet this full target without a proved reduction.
context:
Discounting reduces the influence of distant transitions while retaining their exact contribution. For instance, an infinite run of weight one at every step has value \(1/(1-\lambda)\). A finite prefix determines an approximation, but equality to a rational threshold can depend on the entire continuation.

The 2014 source mentions universality as an unresolved problem related to exact-value discounted-sum games. This card fixes the standard non-strict infimum convention from the cited discounted-automata literature. The games problem is related but has different quantifiers and is not substituted for automaton universality.

Boker and Henzinger define universality by comparing every word value to a constant threshold. Their discount parameter is greater than one and divides the weight at each successive position; the present multiplier is its reciprocal. Their integral-parameter determinization result therefore covers integer-reciprocal multipliers, not all rational multipliers.

Nondeterminism is resolved separately for each complete word. Requiring one strategy to choose transitions from prefixes would impose an additional online restriction. Similarly, finding one favorable path in the underlying weighted graph would ignore the requirement to handle every input word.

The 2025 target-sum paper distinguishes strict from non-strict universality and finite from infinite words. Its universality and inclusion decidability theorem for functional automata appears in the finite-word part. Functional means that all accepting runs of each word have the same value; this is an additional restriction absent here.

For infinite words, the same paper develops connections to exact target discounted sums, including a hardness implication for strict universality and a result for instances where the corresponding generalized target sum has no solution. These are useful delineations of the remaining difficulty, rather than a decision theorem for every instance in this card.
why: Universality asks whether a quantitative finite-state specification can keep every possible infinite input below a threshold. Its decidability is a basic unresolved boundary for verification with rational discounting, where arbitrarily small tail contributions can still decide exact threshold equality.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2014 source records the general universality difficulty, and the November 2025 follow-up still separates finite-word functional results from the infinite-word problem. No general decision or undecidability theorem for the precise non-strict rational model was located in the bounded later-work check. The infimum and non-strict convention are made explicit rather than inferred from the isolated 2014 sentence.
progress: 2011: Integral divisor discount factors admit the determinization result of Boker and Henzinger; in the multiplier convention this means integer-reciprocal factors. | 2014: Hunter and Raskin identify discounted-sum universality as unresolved in their discussion of exact-value games. | 2025-11-28: Boker, Henzinger and Otop give finite-word functional-automaton universality results and separate partial connections for infinite words in Section 6.
working_summary: The input is a finite nondeterministic automaton whose transitions carry rational discounted costs. Each infinite word receives the minimum cost among its runs, using one rational discount multiplier. The problem asks whether every infinite word has value at most a supplied rational threshold. The chosen run may depend on the entire word, and threshold equality must be decided exactly. Known restricted discount factors and recent finite-word functional results do not supply the general algorithm requested here.

title: Zeroness of rational weighted context-free grammars
importance_reason: Zero and universality questions are basic algorithmic tests for the power of automata representations.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides whether \(f_G(w)=0\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), given a context-free grammar in the weighted normal form below with rational production weights? Here \(f_G(w)\) is the sum, over all parse trees with yield \(w\), of the product of their production weights. Rational weights may be negative. This card selects the rational weighted-grammar case of the source’s broader zeroness agenda.
definitions: ['The input has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \\(V\\) and terminals \\(\\Sigma\\), with \\(\\Sigma\\ne\\varnothing\\), a start nonterminal \\(S\\in V\\), and finitely many productions. Every production has one of the forms \\(A\\to BC\\) or \\(A\\to a\\), with \\(A,B,C\\in V\\) and \\(a\\in\\Sigma\\); additionally \\(S\\to\\varepsilon\\) is allowed. The start symbol never occurs on a right-hand side. Each production has a rational weight, explicitly encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. At most one production with each left- and right-hand side is listed. There are no unit productions or other empty productions. Zero weights are allowed.', 'A parse tree is a finite ordered tree rooted at \\(S\\). Each nonterminal node expands by a listed production; the terminal leaves in order give its yield, and the empty start production gives the empty yield. The weight of a tree is the product of all weights of the productions used at its nonterminal nodes. The same production used at several nodes contributes one factor for every occurrence.', 'For a nonempty word of length \\(m\\), a parse tree in this form has \\(m\\) terminal-producing nodes and \\(m-1\\) binary-producing nodes. Thus there are only finitely many parses for each word, even when the grammar is ambiguous. Their rational weights are summed to define \\(f_G(w)\\); an empty sum is zero. For the empty word the value is the weight of \\(S\\to\\varepsilon\\), or zero if that production is absent. No analytic convergence or infinite sums of derivations are involved.', 'Terminal order is preserved: words with the same numbers of letters can have different values. Zeroness concerns the full function on words, not its commutative generating function or sums over word lengths. Cancellation between positive and negative tree weights is part of the semantics; there is no nonnegativity or probabilistic normalization promise.', 'All symbols and productions are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices. The algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on finite descriptions, halting on every well-formed input and returning yes exactly for identically zero functions. No time bound is imposed; malformed descriptions can be rejected. The explicit binary normal form and coefficient field \\(\\mathbb{Q}\\) are editorial choices fixing one benchmark variant.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for this rational weighted-grammar zeroness problem, or a Lean-checked undecidability proof. Testing finitely many sampled words, deciding zero only on a unary or bounded language, or deciding a commutative generating-series identity does not settle the stated word-by-word problem.
context:
The seminar’s question lists several separate models: weighted grammars over a field, unary polynomial automata, weighted Parikh automata and weighted vector addition systems. This benchmark retains the grammar branch with rational coefficients and an explicit finite-parse normal form. It does not claim that solving this selected variant settles the other listed models.

Clemente’s 2024 paper still identifies rational weighted context-free grammar zeroness as beyond known techniques. It obtains decidability for weighted basic parallel processes, whose interleaving composition is different from sequential grammar concatenation.

The 2023 algebraic-series results concern commuting variables and multiplicity comparisons on restricted languages. Those results do not determine cancellation separately for every ordered word in an unrestricted alphabet.
why: This is an identity test for recursive numerical descriptions, extending finite-state weighted equivalence to context-free composition. It isolates the difficulty of exact cancellation across arbitrarily deep but finitely parsed derivations, a basic obstacle behind comparing quantitative grammars and counting their parses.
status_note: The 2021 seminar direction and 2024 primary paper identify weighted context-free zeroness as unresolved. The 2023 results concern commutative series or restricted word languages. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no decision theorem for the selected rational finite-parse grammar model; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2022-04-11: The seminar report lists weighted-grammar zeroness among the unresolved algorithmic questions. | 2023-04-27: The algebraic-series paper gives counting-hierarchy upper bounds for commuting-variable series and restricted multiplicity comparisons. | 2024-07-04: The weighted-parallel-process paper distinguishes its new decidability result from the still-unresolved weighted context-free grammar case.
working_summary: A weighted context-free grammar assigns each word the sum of the weights of its parse trees. This card asks whether an algorithm can always decide if that value is zero for every finite word. Production weights are signed rationals, and an explicit normal form ensures every word has only finitely many parses. The challenge is cancellation for each ordered word; results on commuting-variable series and weighted parallel processes address different models. The rational grammar variant is an explicit editorial choice from a broader source agenda, with decidability or undecidability to be proved in Lean.

title: A \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy for visibly pushdown languages
importance_reason: A structural circuit-complexity classification for an established automaton model; its scope connects language theory with the unresolved boundary between threshold and logarithmic-depth circuits.
formal: For every visibly pushdown language \(L\) of well-matched finite words, is \(L\in\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) or is \(L\) complete for \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under constant-depth truth-table reductions? The circuit families and reductions are nonuniform, as defined below; the alternatives are inclusive.
definitions: The alphabet is a fixed finite disjoint union \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{\mathrm{call}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{ret}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\). A word is well-matched when every prefix has at least as many calls as returns and the whole word has equally many. A deterministic visibly pushdown automaton has finite control states, a finite stack alphabet with a bottom marker, an initial state and designated final states. It reads one letter per step, starting with just the bottom marker. A call pushes one non-bottom symbol, a return pops one symbol, and an internal letter leaves the stack unchanged; the finite transition table may inspect the state, letter and stack top. Acceptance requires a final control state and a stack containing just the bottom marker. Words that are not well-matched are rejected. Missing transitions reject. A language recognized by such an automaton is a visibly pushdown language (VPL); the automaton is fixed, while word length grows. Letters use a fixed-length injective binary code, and invalid codes are rejected. A nonuniform circuit family has one Boolean circuit for each input length, with no requirement that a machine generate the circuits. In \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), circuits have polynomial size and constant depth and may use NOT and unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and majority gates. A majority gate returns one precisely when more than half its inputs are one. In \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\), circuits have polynomial size, depth \(O(\log(n+2))\), and AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two, together with NOT gates. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on the fixed language. The reduction \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) consists of nonuniform constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean circuits with AND, OR and NOT gates and polynomial-length oracle gates for membership in \(L\). No directed path goes from an oracle output to an oracle input. The circuit decides \(K\), and its size includes the oracle-query wires. Completeness means \(L\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) and \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) for every \(K\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated alternative for every VPL. Alternatively specify a VPL and prove in Lean both that it is outside \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) and that it is not \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-hard under the stated reductions. The target does not additionally require an algorithm assigning automata to the alternatives. A classification using a different reduction or uniformity convention must establish that it implies this proposition.
context:
The input itself prescribes when the machine uses its stack. Nested calls can therefore carry information that finite-state machines cannot store, while the matching structure remains visible before the control computation is performed. Well-matched words can nest arbitrarily deeply; the question does not impose a depth bound.

Every VPL is in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The unresolved issue is whether any VPL occupies an intermediate position: requiring more than constant-depth threshold computation while failing to represent every logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in computation. The known upper bound makes hardness and completeness equivalent here.

The 2024 paper classifies many VPLs relative to \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\), the constant-depth class without majority gates, and isolates a family whose \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) membership remains unresolved. That three-way outcome does not decide the present \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) question.

A lower bound against \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) is insufficient: majority and modular counting can require gates absent from \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) but still lie in \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Conversely, knowing that a language has a logarithmic-depth circuit is only an upper bound, not a completeness proof.

The source separately asks whether membership in the threshold-circuit class can be decided from an automaton. This card selects the stated dichotomy proposition itself, preserving that distinction.
