importance_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
focus_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.
context:
Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.
why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.
status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. Results with outer strict equality or display primitives use additional structure and are recorded separately.
progress: 2013: The HoTT book supplies the ordinary dependent-type, univalence and higher-inductive framework fixed for this card. | 2018: Kraus states the uniform finite-level semisimplicial family problem and explains its connection to higher categories and internal metatheory. | 2023: Annenkov and coauthors develop the two-level framework and distinguish outer-indexed constructions from inner semisimplicial universes. | 2025: Chen’s thesis develops internal-model methods but explicitly marks the classifier construction incomplete and the unrestricted ordinary-HoTT problem open. | 2025-12-17: The journal version of Displayed Type Theory gives semisimplicial types using additional modal/display primitives; the preprint dates from 2023–2024. | 2026-05-26: Two-Level Type Theory v5 updates typos and references while retaining the distinction between ordinary HoTT and enriched constructions.
working_summary: Semisimplicial types organize vertices, edges, triangles and higher-dimensional fillers with compatible shared boundaries. Ordinary homotopy type theory can describe any fixed finite collection of these stages externally. The project asks for one internal family indexed by natural numbers, together with compatible maps forgetting the highest stage. Higher identities carry data, so specifying all coherence requirements uniformly is harder than listing equations in ordinary set-based mathematics. Such a construction would provide an internal foundation for important higher-dimensional structures without extending the stated type theory.

title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
importance_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
focus_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to [D\to D]\) and \(\mathrm{L}:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction \(\lambda x\).M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (\(\lambda x\).M)\(N=M[N/x]\), with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. \([D\to D]\) consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as \(\rho (x), MN\) as F(⟦M⟧\(\rho\))(⟦N⟧\(\rho\)), and \(\lambda x\).M as L(\(d\mapsto\)⟦M⟧\((\rho [x:=d])\)). The desired condition is \(\forall M,N\): (\(\forall \rho\), ⟦M⟧\(\rho\)=⟦N⟧\(\rho\)) ⇔ \(M=\beta N\). Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.
context:
The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates \(\lambda x\).f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly \(\lambda \beta\) or \(\lambda \beta \eta\). They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly \(\lambda \beta\). Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.
why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?
status_note: The exact question is explicit in Honsell’s primary statement. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of its \(\lambda \beta\) alternative. The inspected 2025–2026 filter-model papers study unsolvables and other equational theories. Proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2007: Honsell records the exact \(\lambda \beta\) and \(\lambda \beta \eta\) continuous-model questions, tracing discussion to the 1980s. This card asks the \(\lambda \beta\) alternative. | 2007: Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra rule out exact \(\lambda \beta\) and \(\lambda \beta \eta\) theories for their class of effective models. | 2025: Dezani-Ciancaglini, Giannini and Honsell analyze nontrivial interpretations of unsolvable terms in filter models. | 2026-04-15: Lambda Galore constructs sensible continuously complete filter models not extending Böhm-tree theory; sensibility prevents these constructions from realizing exactly \(\lambda \beta\).
working_summary: Scott's continuous semantics interprets untyped lambda terms using mathematical domains and continuous functions. The project asks whether some model identifies exactly the pairs of terms related by beta-conversion. Beta-conversion expresses equality generated by applying functions to arguments and substituting those arguments into their bodies. Many semantic constructions validate additional equations, so soundness for beta-reduction alone does not answer the question. An exact model would show whether this influential notion of continuous meaning can distinguish every pair of terms that the basic operational equations keep separate.

title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
importance_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
focus_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
definitions: S is a set of sorts, \(A\subseteq S\times S\) is a set of axioms, and \(R\subseteq S\times S\times S\) is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions \(t ::= x | s | t u | \lambda x:B\).\(t | \Pi x:B\).C, with \(s\in S\) and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) generated by the following rules. Axiom: \(\varnothing \vdash s:t\) when \((s,t)\in A\). Start: \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash x:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s\) and x is fresh. Weakening: \(\Gamma ,x:C\vdash t:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and x is fresh. Product: \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).\(C:s_{3}\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s_{1}, \Gamma ,x:B\vdash C:s_{2}\) and \((s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})\in R\). Abstraction: \(\Gamma \vdash \lambda x:B\).\(t:\Pi x:B\).C when \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).C:s for a sort s. Application: \(\Gamma \vdash t u:C[u/x]\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:\Pi x:B\).C and \(\Gamma \vdash u:B\). Conversion: \(\Gamma \vdash t:C\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and \(B=\beta C\). All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (\(\lambda x:B\).t)u to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =\(\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) for some finite \(\Gamma ,B\). Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.
context:
A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let \(\Omega\)=(\(\lambda z\).zz)(\(\lambda z\).zz). The term (\(\lambda x\).y)\(\Omega\) reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce \(\Omega\) forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.
why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.
progress: 1993–1995: The conjecture appears in Geuvers’ thesis and is circulated by Barendregt; the TLCA list records it as Problem 9. | 1997: Sørensen proves the implication for specified typed calculi and generalized non-dependent systems under additional hypotheses. | 2001: Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend the known non-dependent class, recorded as a partial result in the problem statement. | 2023-07-28: Mull’s TYPES 2022 proceedings paper extends the known class to some systems with dependent rules, retaining the general conjecture.
working_summary: A pure type system specifies a typed lambda calculus through a uniform collection of formation rules. Weak normalization means that every well-typed term has some terminating reduction path. The conjecture asks whether that global property forces every reduction path of every well-typed term to terminate. A term may have both a normalizing route and a divergent route in less constrained rewriting settings, so the type-system hypothesis is essential. A proof would connect existence of normal forms with unrestricted evaluation termination across a broad family of typed calculi.

title: Parity games in polynomial time
importance_reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(L\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.
context:
The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.
why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).
status_note: Current status unverified as of 14 September 2026. arXiv:2511.03752v1 (4 November 2025) claims a full polynomial-time solution; the checked record has no later version. Suilen–Pérez arXiv:2604.26748v2 (24 June 2026, accepted at CONCUR) still treats the question as open. The review did not independently establish the claimed proof or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution, and later open-problem language is not itself a refutation. The mathematical formulation is complete; the card remains uncertain.
progress: 2017: Calude and coauthors give a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm for general parity games. | 2018-11-02: The second preprint version of the separating-automata work gives a quasipolynomial size barrier for the specified strong separating safety automata; the paper later appeared at SODA 2019. | 2025-11-04: Van der Heijden posts a claimed polynomial-time solution, with correctness and time bound asserted in Theorems 5, 7 and 8. This review has not independently verified that claim. | 2026-06-24: Suilen and Pérez’s revised CONCUR paper still treats polynomial-time parity-game solving as open and gives a reduction to robust discounted reward. This does not constitute a refutation of the earlier claim.
working_summary: A parity game is a finite arena in which two players choose an infinite path, and the least priority recurring infinitely often decides the winner. The target asks whether one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decides the winner from every specified starting vertex. The card specifies arbitrary vertex ownership, full-history strategies, binary priorities and the complete bit-cost model. Quasipolynomial algorithms are established, while known separating-automaton lower bounds concern restricted methods. A November 2025 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution, but its correctness remains unverified in this review despite later literature continuing to call the problem open.

title: Skolem problem
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.
formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
question_excerpt: Although the Skolem-Mahler-Lech Theorem is almost 90 years old, decidability of the Skolem Problem remains open.
definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.
context:
Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.
why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
status_note: The unrestricted integer Skolem problem is explicitly open in the corrected 17 July 2026 low-order paper, the 16 July general conditional paper and the joint survey dated 26 July 2026. Revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no unconditional resolution. The new general decidability argument is conditional on its stronger good-prime gap conjecture; density-one index coverage does not cover every possible zero. Source statements and their scopes were checked, not all cited proofs independently verified.
progress: 1930s–1950s: The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem describes zero sets as finitely many arithmetic progressions plus a finite set; the inspected primary papers explain why this is not an effective solution of the decision problem. | 2022: The MFCS paper gives a procedure for simple recurrences with unconditional correctness certificates upon termination, but termination on every input depends on two number-theoretic conjectures. | 2026-01–2026-07: The SODA low-order result places order at most four in coRP; the inspected third arXiv version of 17 July corrects Lemma 3.2. Its bounded-index result for each fixed order retains the index bound as input. | 2026-07-16: The general conditional decidability paper uses a strengthened Cramér–Granville hypothesis and separately gives an unconditional Universal Skolem Set of density one. | 2026-07-26: The new joint survey explicitly retains the unrestricted integer Skolem problem as open and separates Positivity, Bi-Skolem and other settings.
working_summary: The Skolem problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide if any given integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term. The input lists its order, coefficients and initial values in binary, with no restriction on order or repeated characteristic roots and no upper bound on the index. Every single term can be computed, but a decision procedure must also finish when the infinite sequence has no zero. The question is a basic exact reachability problem in linear dynamics with connections to program verification and automata. A complete Lean proof must establish decidability or undecidability for all inputs; conditional termination, low-order algorithms and density-one index sets do not settle that target.

title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
importance_reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.
formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm P\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm P\).
question_excerpt: The classical polynomial-time question for mean-payoff games concerns the bit length of binary weights, not their numerical magnitude. The July 2026 source restates this distinction explicitly in Section 3.7.2. This card retains its deterministic single-start, zero-threshold liminf winner problem and adds a concrete encoding and total decision-language convention.
definitions:
The edge set is a subset of \(V\times V\); self-loops are allowed and duplicate edges are not listed. Every listed edge has one arbitrary integer weight, possibly negative or zero. Either ownership set may be empty, and edges may connect vertices of the same owner. There are no chance vertices, additional agents, hidden information, simultaneous moves, fairness constraints, or extra payoff coordinates. Every vertex has a successor, so no finite-play convention is needed.

A finite history from \(s\) is a nonempty vertex sequence \(h=(s=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) following edges of \(E\). A strategy of Max assigns to every such history ending in \(V_{\mathrm{Max}}\) a successor \(v\) with \((v_t,v)\in E\); define a strategy of Min analogously. The sets of these total deterministic history-dependent functions are \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}}\). Neither player sees future choices. A strategy may depend on the complete known instance and entire finite history; the problem statement places no memory or computability restriction on strategies. For any pair, the play is uniquely determined by recursion. A positional strategy means that the selected successor depends only on the current vertex; positional optimality is an established theorem, not an additional promise on the instance.

For \(T\ge1\), set \(a_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\). The lower limit means
\[\liminf_{T\to\infty}a_T=\sup_{N\ge1}\inf_{T\ge N}a_T.\]
It is a finite real number because \(|a_T|\le W\), where \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|)\). The average need not converge for arbitrary history-dependent play. A negative finite prefix is allowed: this objective imposes no lower bound on the running cumulative sum and no prescribed initial energy budget. The payoff is not a discounted sum or a finite-window average.

For a concrete binary encoding, let \(b(u)\) be the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(u\), without leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Define \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Encode an integer \(z\) by \(B(\zeta(z))\), where \(\zeta(z)=2z\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(\zeta(z)=-2z-1\) for \(z<0\). This is a signed binary representation with a uniquely recoverable sign and magnitude; it is not unary in \(|z|\).

The input is \(B(n)B(m)B(s)\), followed by the \(n\) ownership bits in vertex order, and then \(m=|E|\) triples \(B(u)B(v)B(\zeta(w(u,v)))\), listing edges in increasing lexicographic endpoint order. Ownership bit one denotes Max and zero denotes Min. The complete string must satisfy the stated graph and encoding conditions, with no trailing bits. All other binary strings are rejected and are outside \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). Let \(L\) denote the complete input length. Input validation and the translation to ordinary explicit adjacency-list signed-binary representations are polynomial-time operations; these representation conventions do not impose a graph or weight promise.

Membership in \(\mathrm P\) means that there are a finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that for every binary string \(x\), \(A(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps, outputting one exactly when \(x\in\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). The same program and constants must work for every size, graph, weight assignment and start vertex. Input reading, validation, arithmetic, storage access and output all count. There is no advice, randomization, game-solving oracle or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily large integers. The polynomial may depend on the fixed program but not on \(n,m,W\) or the instance. The output is only the exact winner bit; the task does not require printing an infinite strategy or play.

There is no bound on \(W\) in terms of \(n\) or \(m\). Its contribution to the input is logarithmic, so a bound polynomial in \(n,m,W\) is pseudopolynomial and need not be polynomial in \(L\). A rational threshold \(a/b\), with binary integers \(a\) and \(b>0\), gives an equivalent decision model: the weights \(bw(e)-a\) have polynomial encoding length and their nonnegative mean threshold expresses the original threshold. Thus fixing the threshold to zero retains the binary-weight complexity question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
 A(x)\text{ halts within }C(|x|+1)^d\text{ steps and outputs }\mathbf1_{\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}}(x),\]
or its logical negation, with the machine and language definitions above. A positive proof must establish the exact game semantics, correctness on every valid instance, rejection of invalid encodings, and the full polynomial bit bound. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, rather than only a particular local-improvement rule, representation, certificate family or algorithmic framework.

A pseudopolynomial bound, a polynomial bound only after random perturbations, a randomized expected-time guarantee, or an algorithm for a restricted graph or weight family does not answer the full question. A polynomial number of arithmetic operations alone is insufficient if intermediate integers require superpolynomial bit length. A strongly polynomial algorithm with polynomially bounded bit representations would suffice but is more than required. There is no approximation tolerance or unproved complexity hypothesis in the target.
context:
A finite initial loss disappears from a long-run average. For example, an eventual repetition of weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one after any fixed finite prefix. Requiring every partial sum to stay nonnegative is a different objective. A play of weight zero forever is winning here because the threshold is nonnegative, not strictly positive.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players. With both such strategies fixed, a finite graph produces an eventually repeated cycle, whose average determines the payoff. The resulting certificates place the winner language in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): yes and no instances each have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. This does not provide a polynomial-time way to find them. Zwick and Paterson give the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games, which add random transitions.

Brim and coauthors' Theorem 8 gives \(O(nmW)\) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\). A weight of magnitude \(2^b\) requires only \(b+1\) magnitude bits. Thus this dependence can be exponential in the encoding length even before charging for arithmetic. Their theorem is pseudopolynomial; it is not a uniform polynomial bit bound for arbitrary weights.

Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish size bounds for universal graphs, auxiliary weighted graphs that represent all bounded-size graphs satisfying the mean-payoff objective through weight-preserving maps. Their lower bounds constrain the resulting family of value-iteration algorithms. They do not exclude algorithms outside that framework, so they do not prove that the winner language is outside P.

The published ICALP 2024 theorem of Loff and Skomra assumes an ergodic game graph and independent random perturbations of rewards. Ergodic means that for every reward assignment the game value is independent of the starting vertex; ordinary strong connectivity does not imply this property. For example, Theorem 1 gives time polynomial in \(n\) and the inverse perturbation scale for normalized rewards perturbed by independent Gaussians, with high probability over those perturbations. Both the input restriction and probabilistic guarantee remain part of the theorem.

Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies strategy improvement with simplex runs for a nondegenerate longest-shortest-path game formulation. Nondegeneracy excludes certain zero cycles and equal-weight competing paths. Section 5 explicitly warns that the constructed linear-program coefficients can have doubly exponential magnitudes, so writing them may require exponentially many bits. The existence of this linear program and its correspondence between iterations therefore do not supply a polynomial-bit-time solver.

Ohlmann’s March 2026 preprint gives a new deterministic recursive algorithm and a correctness argument. Its introduction and Section 7 explicitly leave a useful running-time analysis, including the hoped-for subexponential bound, unresolved. It does not claim a polynomial-time solution. Its presentation uses limsup and positional strategies; positional determinacy of these finite games preserves the game value, while the present definition retains its explicit liminf objective for arbitrary histories.

Adenwalla and coauthors’ July 2026 preprint relates mean-payoff games to tropical inequalities and graph classes defined by equality patterns among vertex labels. Tropical linear expressions replace ordinary addition and multiplication by maximum and addition. Section 7 gives a reduction using compact encodings of path clauses and functional constraints; it does not assume that an exponentially long clause is written out. This is a connection between decision problems, while Section 3.7.2 explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open.
why: Mean-payoff games model sustainable long-run rewards when an adversary controls part of a finite system. Their exact winner problem has short certificates for both answers, yet its unrestricted polynomial bit complexity remains an important question in quantitative verification and graph-game theory.
status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly leaves polynomial complexity in the binary weight length open; the March 2026 recursive solver also leaves its improved runtime analysis open. The inspected pseudopolynomial, universal-graph, ergodic smoothed-analysis, simplex-correspondence and restricted-signature results do not establish membership in P or exclusion from P for the exact language here. Bounded searches found no full matching resolution claim. The new smoothed-algorithm author-page title was not assigned a theorem beyond the inspected evidence. This review checks statement and source scope, not every cited proof or an exhaustive certification of present openness.

The published hypotheses are retained. | 2025-09-19: Maat’s preprint gives a nondegenerate strategy-improvement/simplex correspondence and records the large coefficient obstruction to polynomial bit complexity. | 2026-03-08: Ohlmann introduces a deterministic symmetric recursive solver, leaving its intended improved complexity bound open. | 2026-07-26: The set-defined graph-class preprint gives new reductions and explicitly retains the binary-weight polynomial-time question.
working_summary: Two players control different vertices of a finite integer-weighted graph and choose an infinite path from a specified start. Max wins when the lower limit of the average weight is nonnegative against every history-dependent strategy of Min, including exact equality zero. The question is whether the resulting binary-input winner language has one deterministic decider running in polynomial bit time on all inputs. Positional certificates and pseudopolynomial algorithms are known, but large binary weights leave a gap to the required complexity. Recent recursive, smoothed and linear-programming connections retain runtime, distributional or encoding limitations and do not settle the full target.

title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
importance_reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.
formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the card’s encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.
context:
Tarski’s decision theorem covers polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals with arbitrary first-order quantifiers. Adding the single function \(\exp\) asks whether that global decidability survives beyond polynomial arithmetic. The input remains a finite symbolic formula: a quantified real is part of the semantics, not a real number that must somehow be supplied as an infinite input string.

The target includes exact equalities and unrestricted quantifier alternation. For example, \(\forall x\,(x>0\Rightarrow\exists y\,\exp(y)=x)\) expresses surjectivity onto the positive reals; the implication here is an abbreviation for a disjunction in the specified syntax. Individual familiar identities are decidable, but they do not supply a machine for every sentence. Approximating an exponential value is also a different task: arbitrarily accurate approximations need not by themselves decide whether a given expression is exactly zero.

Wilkie proved model completeness of the real exponential theory in 1996: every formula is equivalent, in that theory, to an existential formula. The structure is also o-minimal, meaning that every definable subset of the real line is a finite union of points and intervals. These are strong finiteness properties, but neither statement alone certifies an algorithm for exact truth. The June 2026 paper recalls both results and distinguishes model completeness from completeness and effective axiomatization.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability assuming the real form of Schanuel’s conjecture. That hypothesis says that whenever \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the field \(\mathbb Q(a_1,\ldots,a_n,\exp(a_1),\ldots,\exp(a_n))\) has transcendence degree at least \(n\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Linear independence means that a rational linear combination is zero only when every coefficient is zero; transcendence degree is the maximum number of elements algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\), meaning that no nonzero rational polynomial in those elements vanishes. Wilkie’s 1997 exposition explicitly describes the decidability result as conditional. The stronger conjecture about complex tuples is not required for this real-theory implication.

The algorithmic survey distinguishes Schanuel’s transcendence conjecture from a weaker effective separation statement equivalent to decidability. For integer polynomials \(p,q_1,\ldots,q_n\) in \(2n\) variables, set \(F_p(x)=p(x_1,\ldots,x_n,\exp(x_1),\ldots,\exp(x_n))\), and define \(F_{q_i}\) similarly. The weak statement asks for a computable positive integer \(\eta\) such that every common zero \(\gamma\) of the \(F_{q_i}\) with invertible derivative matrix \((\partial F_{q_i}/\partial x_j)(\gamma)\) satisfies \(|F_p(\gamma)|\leq1/\eta\Rightarrow F_p(\gamma)=0\). The source explains that some such separation value exists; the unresolved requirement is its uniform computability. Consequently, failure of the stronger Schanuel conjecture would not by itself establish undecidability.

Berarducci and Gallinaro’s revision of 23 June 2026 gives a new axiomatization of the full real exponential theory under the real Schanuel hypothesis. Its unconditional theorem concerns model completeness for axioms of a restricted exponential function: this function equals \(\exp(x)\) on \((-1,1)\) and zero outside that interval. Completeness for their axiom systems, including the unrestricted exponential system, still uses the conjecture. Thus the unconditional theorem is not an unconditional decision procedure for the full language on this card.

One application comes from weighted automata assigning nonnegative rational values to finite words. The CONCUR 2020 source asks whether two initial states define functions \(f,g\) with \(f(w)\leq Cg(w)\) for every word \(w\) and some constant \(C>0\). The general problem is undecidable, but when both positive-weight languages are bounded—each contained in a product \(w_1^*\cdots w_k^*\) of repetitions of finitely many fixed words—the source reduces the comparison to real-exponential arithmetic and obtains conditional decidability. Decidability of the present card would make that application unconditional; the unrelated undecidability result for arbitrary automata does not refute this theory’s decidability.
why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.
status_note: Checked through 14 September 2026. The latest listed Berarducci–Gallinaro revision is 23 June 2026 and retains the real Schanuel assumption for full-theory completeness and decidability. Its unconditional restricted-exponential model-completeness result does not match the target. The full checked algorithmic survey separates the weaker effective hypothesis from Schanuel’s stronger transcendence assertion. Bounded later-work searches found no unconditional full-theory decider or undecidability result. This is a dated source review with explicit limits, not independent verification of all source proofs.

working_summary: Tarski’s exponential function problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide every first-order sentence about the standard real numbers with their full exponential function. The input is finite symbolic syntax with no arbitrary real constants or real-number oracle, and quantifiers range over all reals. Acceptance requires a complete Lean-checked proof of total correct decidability or a proof of undecidability, with no time bound and no unresolved extra hypothesis. The question extends decidable polynomial real arithmetic and already controls conditional verification results for restricted weighted automata. Macintyre–Wilkie’s conditional theorem and the checked June2026 axiomatization still rely on the real Schanuel hypothesis; restricted model completeness is a different conclusion.

title: Continuous Skolem problem
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in \mathbb Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in \mathbb Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
question_excerpt: Decide whether a rational linear differential system reaches a specified rational homogeneous hyperplane at some finite nonnegative real time.
definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is \(\exp (tA)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t^{j} A^{j}/j!\), and \(x(t)=\exp (tA)b\) is the unique real solution of \(x' (t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b\). The target is the hyperplane \(\{x:c^{T}x=0\}; c=0\) is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at \(t=0\) counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit \(t\to \infty\), the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional always-halting Turing decision algorithm for every finite rational input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must specify a computable classifier and prove equivalence with \(\exists t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0},\ c^T\exp(tA)b=0\), including tangencies and the initial time. A negative proof must establish undecidability for this exact rational matrix/vector representation. The formalization must cover the analytic semantics and all effectiveness claims, rather than merely postulating an exact real-number test. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may fail to halt, or a certificate requiring a nonzero-distance promise is partial progress. Hardness with arbitrary algebraic coefficients, nonlinear differential equations or a different target set needs a proved reduction into this rational linear model.
context:
Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output \(c^{T}x(t)\) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system \(x' =- x, x(0)=1\) has output \(e^{- t}\), which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial \((t- 1)^{2}\) touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is \(c^{T}b=0\). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when \(c^{T}A^{j} b=0\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,d- 1\). These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all \(t\ge 0\).

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at \(\pi /2\). The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.
why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.
status_note: The rational linear exact-reachability problem remains explicitly identified as unresolved in the checked November 2025 JACM discussion; the July 2026 survey discusses the continuous analogues and their distinct obstacles. Rechecked through 16 September 2026: no matching unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof was located. Conditional bounded results, low-order recurrence theorems, open/robust verification and nonlinear or algebraic-coefficient hardness do not by themselves settle this saved rational model. This is a bounded literature review, not proof of continuing openness.
