D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.
context:
Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.
why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.
progress: 2011 / 2012: Das Sarma and coauthors establish randomized communication lower bounds for exact and approximate distance problems, giving the \(\tilde\{\Omega\}(\sqrt{n}+D)\) lower-bound benchmark. | 2020 / 2022: Chechik–Mukhtar obtain \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\) rounds for exact weighted SSSP. | 2022: Rozhoň and coauthors give near-optimal deterministic distributed algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances, with accuracy-dependent complexity. | 2023: Cao–Fineman give \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\) rounds for polynomially bounded weights, including an improvement in the intermediate-diameter comparison. | 2026-04-18: The programmable-matter article retains a CONGEST gap in related work. Its own communication model and theorems are different, and that summary does not include the 2023 bound above.
working_summary: Single-source shortest paths asks every vertex to learn its exact distance from one source in a weighted network. In CONGEST, each edge carries only a logarithmic number of bits per communication round. The target is a randomized algorithm using roughly \(\sqrt{n}\) plus the hop diameter D rounds, ignoring polylogarithmic factors. The graph is undirected and connected, with nonnegative polynomially bounded integer edge weights. Achieving this bound would combine global distance propagation with the bandwidth limits of the network at the scale identified by the saved problem statement.

title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
importance_reason: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.
context:
Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.
why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
status_note: The checked primary literature leaves explicit superconstant unicast bounds as a central challenge. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this polynomial-time, one-bit target. The latest checked revision of the one-round MST result is January 2024; it is not presented as a new 2026 status theorem.
progress: 2014: Circuit simulations explain barriers to explicit lower bounds and separate unicast from broadcast communication. | 2018: A uniform congested-clique time hierarchy is proved through hard-function selection, without the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time guarantee. | 2023 / 2024: The MST lower bound excludes one round with logarithmic link bandwidth; it does not establish a diverging lower bound for a one-bit graph predicate.
working_summary: Can a graph predicate that is easy to compute centrally require a number of congested-clique rounds tending to infinity? Each processor initially knows its incident graph edges and can send a different logarithmic-size message to every other processor in each round. Only one decision bit is required, and local computation is unrestricted. Known hard-function counting and hierarchy arguments do not provide the required centrally polynomial-time predicate. Broadcast bounds and the known two-round MST limitation do not resolve this unicast one-bit target.

title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
importance_reason: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized priority-CRCW PRAM algorithm \(A_a\), constants \(C_a\ge1\) and \(B_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge a+3}\), and a function \(h_a:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to[1,\infty)\) with
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h_a(N)}{\log N}=0,
\]
such that the following holds? On every explicitly given directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le n^a\), the algorithm outputs an exact integral maximum flow with probability at least \(2/3\), and every execution satisfies
\[
 W\le C_a(m+n)h_a(m+n),\qquad
 D\le C_a h_a(m+n).
\]
Here \(W\) is total work and \(D\) is parallel depth in the word model below. In asymptotic notation the requested simultaneous bounds are \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth.
question_excerpt: The source explicitly identifies almost-optimal parallel algorithms for exact directed maximum flow as a major open target, where almost-optimal means almost-linear work and subpolynomial depth. Its graph conventions use polynomially bounded integer capacities. This card retains that endpoint and its previously fixed uniform priority-CRCW word model.
definitions:
The vertex set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Input memory contains \(n,m,s,t\) and an explicit ordered array of arcs \(E\), each with its two endpoint labels and integer capacity. There are no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. The range is \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\), and isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and zero capacities are permitted. No planarity, acyclicity, density or expansion promise is assumed. The fixed integer \(a\) specifies the admitted capacity regime and may be built into the program.

A feasible output is an integer \(f_e\) for every original arc, in input order, such that \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) and
\[
 \sum_{(v,z)\in E}f_{(v,z)}=
 \sum_{(z,v)\in E}f_{(z,v)}
 \quad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}).
\]
Its value is outgoing flow minus incoming flow at \(s\). It must maximize that value over all feasible flows. Integral capacities admit an integral maximum flow. Any maximizing flow is acceptable, but the entire arc vector must be output explicitly. A maximum-flow value, a cut or an implicit flow alone is not the required output. If no positive flow is possible, the exact optimum is zero.

The computational model is a synchronous parallel random-access machine with shared memory and priority concurrent reads and writes (priority CRCW PRAM). Simultaneous reads of one cell are allowed. If multiple processors try to write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes at most one word-RAM instruction per round, using its own local registers and the shared memory. Processor identifiers and memory addresses are word values. Processors follow one finite program with their identifiers available; there is no input-length advice or precomputed table. Processor activation and all program-controlled initialization count as work; a hidden computation cannot be assigned to an uncharged processor. Initially only the explicit input and fixed machine constants are present, and unused memory and registers are zero.

Words have length
\[
 w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Each processor may generate a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one instruction; all such random words are mutually independent. Operations on longer integers are implemented by multiple charged instructions. There are no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic operations or real-number oracles. The chosen \(B_a\) must accommodate every processor identifier and address used by the algorithm.

Work \(W\) is the sum of all executed processor instructions, including activation, input access, preprocessing, random generation and output writes. Depth \(D\) is the number of synchronous rounds until the complete output is available. Both resource bounds must hold on every execution, including executions returning an incorrect answer. Correctness means that the whole vector is feasible and exactly optimal, with probability at least \(2/3\) over the machine's coins for each fixed input. The success probability is not averaged over graphs, and resources are not merely bounded in expectation. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case.

The program, word constant, multiplicative constant and overhead function may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its input ordering or its capacities. One algorithm for the fixed \(a\) must achieve the asymptotic bounds over all sizes. In particular, for every \(\delta>0\), its work is eventually at most \((m+n)^{1+\delta}\) and its depth at most \((m+n)^\delta\), after increasing a size threshold depending only on \(a,\delta\). Allowing a different algorithm for each \(\delta\) would be a different claim. The overhead function is an analytic bound, not advice supplied to the machine.

Subpolynomial depth is the requested target; polylogarithmic depth would suffice but is not required. The same computation must have almost-linear total work. An algorithm with small depth and polynomially more work, or with almost-linear work and a fixed positive power of \(n\) in its depth, does not meet the simultaneous endpoint. Using \(m+n\) accounts explicitly for the vertex set even when the graph contains few arcs.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation.

A positive answer must cover every fixed capacity exponent \(a\), with a uniform algorithm for that exponent, the simultaneous worst-case work and depth bounds, and the per-input probability of an exact explicit integral maximum flow. A result with stronger bounds also qualifies if it supplies this full output and model guarantee.

A negative answer must prove that for at least one fixed \(a\) no admissible algorithm and constants satisfy the target. A conditional obstruction, a lower bound for one algorithmic framework, or a difficulty confined to a more demanding capacity model does not establish the unconditional negation. An approximation algorithm, a restricted graph-family result, or a reduction to another task alone is insufficient unless the remaining task is also solved with the required resources.
context:
Sequential almost-linear-time algorithms do not guarantee few dependent computation stages. This question asks whether exact directed flow can retain almost-linear total work while reducing those stages to subpolynomial depth.

The DAG-projection result gives efficient parallel reductions between exact directed flow and suitable approximation tasks on directed acyclic graphs. A reduction transfers a future algorithm; it does not itself supply the missing endpoint.

The August 2026 revision of the dense-instance result gives \(\widetilde O(m+n^{3/2})\) work and \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) depth. Its work is near-linear on sufficiently dense inputs, but its depth is still polynomial in graph size.

The separate strongly polynomial parallel result supports arbitrary real capacities with \(\widetilde O(mn)\) work and \(\widetilde O(m)\) depth. Neither bound supplies the almost-linear-work and subpolynomial-depth combination asked for here.

Approximate flow in undirected graphs is a different regime in the source’s classification. Exactness, direction and the simultaneous resource limits are essential parts of this card.
why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
status_note: The April 2026 source explicitly poses the almost-optimal parallel exact-flow endpoint. The checked August 2026 revision of the dense-instance algorithm and the strongly polynomial parallel theorem still have polynomial depth or superlinear work relative to this target. Bounded primary-source searches through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The review does not independently certify the complete proofs or exhaust all later literature.
progress: 2026-04-06: DAG projections relate the open exact directed-flow endpoint to approximation on DAGs. | 2026-08-19: The revised dense-instance algorithm retains near-linear work in the dense regime and square-root depth. | 2026-08-25: A strongly polynomial parallel algorithm improves the work/depth tradeoff for arbitrary real capacities.
working_summary: The task is exact maximum flow in an arbitrary directed graph with polynomially bounded integer capacities. Every arc must receive an explicit integral flow value, and the entire output must be correct with probability at least two thirds. The desired uniform parallel algorithm has almost-linear total work and subpolynomial depth on every execution. Recent DAG reductions and dense-instance algorithms clarify the problem without supplying this simultaneous endpoint. A complete Lean-checked answer must meet both resource bounds for every fixed polynomial capacity range, without restricting the graph family.

title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
importance_reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.
formal:
Does directed single-source reachability admit nearly linear work and polylogarithmic depth simultaneously in the uniform randomized CREW PRAM model specified below? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists A_c,K_c,a_c,b_c,q_c\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall G\ \forall s\in V(G),
\]
\[
\Pr\!\left[\begin{array}{l}
A_c(G,s)\text{ terminates with the exact reachability indicator,}\\
W\le K_c(n+m)L^{a_c}\ \text{and}\ D\le K_cL^{b_c}
\end{array}\right]\ge1-n^{-c},
\]
where \(G\) ranges over every directed graph on the labeled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)? Here \(K_c\ge1\), \(a_c,b_c\ge0\) and \(q_c\ge3\) are integers independent of \(n,G,s\); \(A_c\) is one finite program independent of input size. The word length is \(q_cL\). The required event jointly bounds total work \(W\), depth \(D\), and correctness of the entire output on each fixed input. The confidence exponent is requested as a fixed constant before choosing the program. The one-vertex case has the prescribed output consisting of a single 1 and is omitted only to avoid a vacuous probability bound.
definitions:
Graphs are unweighted and directed. Their edge sets satisfy \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\); loops are allowed and repeated copies of an edge are absent. A vertex is reachable from \(s\) when there is a finite directed path from \(s\) to it, including the length-zero path. No assumption of strong connectivity, acyclicity, bounded diameter or a lower bound on \(m\) is imposed.

The input is an outgoing adjacency-array representation in shared read-only word memory. Cells 0, 1 and 2 contain \(n,m,s\). The next \(n+1\) cells contain offsets \(o_0,\ldots,o_n\), with \(0=o_0\le\cdots\le o_n=m\). The next \(m\) cells contain target labels \(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}\). The outgoing neighbors of vertex \(v\) are exactly the distinct labels \(t_j\) for \(o_{v-1}\le j<o_v\). Neighbor order is arbitrary. The output occupies the next \(n\) cells, one word for each vertex in label order: its value must be 1 for a reachable vertex and 0 otherwise. Thus the answer is the entire exact set, represented by \(n\) Boolean values, and does not include distances or a transitive closure.

For the chosen program, words are unsigned \(w=q_cL\)-bit integers. Shared cells and processor identifiers are numbered from 0 to \(2^w-1\). Every processor has a fixed finite number of word registers and runs the same finite program, with its identifier available in a designated register. These register counts and the program may depend on \(c\), but not on the graph or its size. Noninput cells and all other registers initially contain zero. There is no advice, oracle, precomputed graph index or uncharged preprocessing. The polynomial address space is the only imposed working-space limit.

Execution is synchronous. One active processor executes one primitive instruction per round. Instructions read or write one shared cell by its word address; copy words; add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\); perform bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement; shift a word left or logically right by an integer between 0 and \(w-1\); compare unsigned words; branch; or obtain one fresh unbiased random bit. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Instructions use a constant number of registers. Reads observe the memory at the beginning of the round, and writes commit at its end. Several processors may read one cell, but at most one processor may write a given cell in a round, even if competing writes would contain the same value. Input cells cannot be written. Programs must obey these CREW access rules on every execution.

To account explicitly for activation, only processor 0 starts active. A unit-cost fork instruction activates one previously unused processor with a specified identifier, a program entry label and a constant number of copied registers; it starts in the next round. Two simultaneous forks may not name the same processor. Halting a processor costs one instruction; halted or not-yet-activated processors do no work. All input-independent setup, processor activation, data movement, auxiliary graph construction and output writes count toward work. Work is the total number of executed primitive instructions, and depth is the number of synchronous rounds until all activated processors halt. Nontermination gives infinite depth and does not satisfy the success event. The fork convention makes processor initialization explicit and allows ordinary parallel scheduling with polylogarithmic overhead.

All random-bit instructions draw mutually independent fair bits; the probability is over these bits for each fixed input representation. The required probability concerns correct output and both resource bounds together, not three expectations or an average over graphs. On the exceptional event, the program may return an incorrect answer, exceed a resource bound or fail to terminate. The notation \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) and polylogarithmic depth in the motivating question is replaced by the explicit logarithmic powers and constants in the statement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified algorithm-existence statement or its negation in the specified model. A positive answer must provide the uniform program witnesses and prove the joint correctness, work and depth guarantee on every admissible graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for every fixed confidence exponent. A negative answer must refute that entire existence statement without an additional unproved complexity assumption. A result restricted to a class of graphs, a particular representation of auxiliary information, or work measured by transitive-closure size does not establish either answer unless it entails the full statement.

Explicitly, a negative answer establishes an integer \(c\ge1\) such that for every legal finite program and every proposed integer constants \(K\ge1\), \(a,b\ge0\), \(q\ge3\), there are \(n\ge2\), a valid graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for which the joint probability in the formal statement is strictly below \(1-n^{-c}\). A legal program obeys the stated word and CREW rules on all executions. The failing instance may depend on the candidate program and constants.
context:
The target concerns arbitrary directed inputs and the full reachable set from one source. Near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth must be achieved in the same execution. Neither a low-work algorithm with polynomial depth nor a fast parallel algorithm with polynomially excessive work meets that requirement.

The input parameter is \(n+m\), including isolated vertices. The cited papers sometimes assume \(m\ge n\) or absorb one implicit self-loop per vertex into \(m\). This card makes the additive vertex term explicit. For a directed path, \(m=n-1\), whereas the reflexive transitive closure contains \(n(n+1)/2\) ordered pairs; a bound in closure size can therefore be much larger than a bound in input size.

The sources use the standard work/depth terminology but do not fully specify shared-memory write conflicts, word instructions or input layout. This card retains its previously selected CREW convention and makes word size, adjacency arrays, exact output, processor activation and the joint high-probability event explicit editorial model choices. It permits a program selected for each fixed confidence exponent; the program is uniform over input sizes. These details are not quotations of a particular source model.

The May 2026 full version explicitly identifies improving the sparse-graph regime as open. The August result gives polylogarithmic depth with work parameterized by \(T=|TC(G)|\), where \(TC(G)=\{(u,v):v\text{ is reachable from }u\}\). Since \(T\) may be quadratic on a sparse graph, that theorem does not provide the nearly linear input-work guarantee asked for here.
why: Directed reachability is a basic graph operation with a linear-work sequential solution. The unresolved issue is whether its dependencies can be processed in polylogarithmic parallel time while retaining nearly that work bound on every input. A resolution would determine whether a fundamental sequential graph task admits efficient use of many processors, rather than a speedup purchased with polynomially more computation.
status_note: The full May 2026 source retains the sparse-graph work/depth frontier. The checked August 2026 preprint claims polylogarithmic depth with work in transitive-closure size, which can be quadratic even on a linear-size graph. Individual primary-source reading and a bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of nearly linear input work with polylogarithmic depth on all directed graphs. This supports a dated source-open classification; it is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate or an independent verification of every cited proof.
progress: 2019-12-06: Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give directed single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth with high probability. This entry uses the corrected fourth arXiv version of their FOCS 2019 paper. | 2026-07-01: Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak give \(\widetilde O(m)\) work and \((n^{\omega+o(1)}/m)^{1/(2\omega-2)}\) span for \(m\ge n\). Here \(\omega\) is the exponent used for parallel matrix multiplication. Their dense-graph bound is \(n^{0.136}\); this is not a polylogarithmic bound on arbitrary inputs. | 2026-08-13: Kogan and Parter claim polylogarithmic-depth single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})\) work, where \(T\) is the number of ordered pairs in the reflexive transitive closure. The arXiv record reports FOCS 2026 acceptance. The claim concerns work in terms of \(T\), which need not be nearly linear in \(n+m\).
working_summary: Given a directed graph and a source, the task is to mark exactly all vertices reachable from that source. The question asks for a uniform randomized CREW parallel algorithm with nearly linear total work in the input size and polylogarithmic depth on every input. Correctness of the complete output and both resource bounds must hold together with high probability for each fixed graph. The 2026 density improvement retains polynomial depth, while the August polylogarithmic-depth result measures work by a potentially quadratic transitive closure. A complete Lean proof must decide whether the two desired resource guarantees can be achieved simultaneously in the specified model.

title: Depth-first search in NC
importance_reason: Asks whether the search structure produced by an apparently sequential graph traversal can be computed efficiently in parallel.
formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.
context:
Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.
why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves deterministic NC construction for general graphs open while proving results for restricted classes. Targeted searches found no later general resolution. Randomized NC, deterministic quasipolynomial resources, and the 2023 near-linear-work algorithm have distinct guarantees. The cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1988: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness. | 2023: Ghaffari, Grunau and Qu give a randomized algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\) depth; this addresses work efficiency with a larger depth bound. | 2025-12-09: Chauhan, Datta and Praveen prove deterministic parallel bounds for bounded-genus and undirected single-crossing-minor-free graphs, and a logspace bound for bounded treewidth. The general question remains open in their statement.
working_summary: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration. For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth. Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target. A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) rounds
importance_reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform quantum-LOCAL protocol \(A\) and a function \(T:\mathbb N_{\ge3}\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge3\) and every injective identifier assignment \(\lambda:V(C_n)\to\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), all nodes of the consistently oriented cycle \(C_n\) finish within \(T(n)\) communication rounds on every possible execution branch, and their classical outputs \(c_v\in\{1,2,3\}\) satisfy
\[
\Pr\bigl[\forall\{u,v\}\in E(C_n),\ c_u\ne c_v\bigr]\ge1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T(n)}{1+\log^{*}_2n}=0?
\]
The probability is over the protocol's quantum measurement outcomes. Initially the quantum state is a product of local zero states. Each node knows \(n\), its own identifier and the predecessor/successor ports, and communication in both directions is permitted.
definitions:
For specification only, \(C_n\) has vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\) and edges \(\{v_i,v_{(i+1)\bmod n}\}\). Its consistent orientation tells each node which port leads to its successor and which to its predecessor. The indices \(i\) are not inputs to the protocol. Identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), represented in binary. Nodes receive no distinguished leader, numerical position, neighbor identifiers, list of all identifiers, or other global information beyond \(n\). The identifier assignment is fixed before quantum randomness; the success bound holds for every such assignment.

All nodes execute the same fixed finite classical control program. Its initial classical input consists only of \(n\), the node's identifier and its two port labels. Classical computation manipulates finite binary strings by ordinary Turing-machine operations and may determine which local qubits to use next. There is no bound on local computation time, local storage or message length, but every local phase and every message must be finite on every possible branch. No advice depending on \(n\), the identifiers or the graph is supplied.

Local quantum storage is a finite tensor product of qubits. A node may append a fresh qubit in state \(\lvert0\rangle\), discard a local qubit, apply \(H\) or \(T\) to one local qubit, apply CNOT to an ordered pair of distinct local qubits, or measure a local qubit in the computational basis, with subsequent classical control depending on the outcome. The gates are
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{\mathrm i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert x,x\mathbin{\oplus}y\rangle
\quad(x,y\in\{0,1\}).
\]
Here \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. On a global density operator \(\rho\), a local gate acts by unitary conjugation on its chosen registers; discarding a register takes its partial trace. A computational-basis measurement with outcome \(b\in\{0,1\}\) has probability \(\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\) and, when that probability is nonzero, leaves normalized state \(P_b\rho P_b/\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\), where \(P_b\) projects the measured qubit onto \(\lvert b\rangle\). Classical random choices may be obtained by such measurements. There is no postselection that discards unsuccessful outcomes from the success probability.

A communication round consists of finite local processing followed by simultaneous noiseless transmission of finite quantum registers along the cycle edges. Each node may send registers to both neighbors and receives their sent registers before the next local phase. Sending transfers ownership of the qubits; it does not copy unknown states. Classical messages can be encoded as computational-basis registers. A final finite local phase may produce the node's color without another round. There is no communication between nonneighbors, no information conveyed by elapsed local computation time, and no additional inter-node channel. The initial global quantum state is the tensor product of all freshly initialized local \(\lvert0\rangle\) registers; there is no shared randomness or preshared entanglement. Entanglement created by the protocol through counted communication is allowed.

Every node must output one color and halt, including on branches where the resulting coloring is improper. A possible branch is one whose finite measurement outcomes have nonzero Born probability. The round bound holds on every such branch and uniformly over all identifier assignments of the same size, rather than merely in expectation or with high probability. Local operations, message lengths and numbers of qubits are not charged to round complexity. The program has no real-number oracle or arbitrary exact unitary as an extra primitive; the gate set above retains the card's existing concrete uniform interpretation.

For real \(x\ge1\), \(\log^{*}_2x\) is the least nonnegative integer \(r\) for which applying \(\log_2\) repeatedly \(r\) times reaches a value at most \(1\), stopping as soon as that occurs. The displayed limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(T(n)\le\varepsilon(1+\log^{*}_2n)\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The probability target is global correctness of all edges simultaneously, not separate correctness probabilities for individual nodes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a uniform protocol and a worst-case round-bound function satisfying every stated input, quantum-operation, termination and global-success condition, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of that existence statement. A conditional lower bound alone does not prove nonexistence. A lower bound limited to anonymous probability-one protocols, to one-way one-round communication, to two-coloring, or to growing-degree trees does not settle the stated protocol class.
context:
The primary problem list asks whether cycles can be 3-colored in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) quantum rounds and separately asks about a constant-round algorithm. This card retains the first question with its already chosen orientation, identifiers, known size, finite gate set and global error bound.

Classical deterministic and high-probability randomized cycle coloring both have \(\Theta(\log^{*}n)\) round complexity. The August 2026 paper summarizes those classical bounds and distinguishes them from the unknown quantum-LOCAL complexity.

Finitely dependent proper color distributions exist on finite cycles: collections of colors on vertex sets at sufficiently large graph distance are independent. This is a statement about distributions, not an implementation by the local quantum protocol specified here. The finite-cycle result is due to Holroyd, Hutchcroft and Levy, following the earlier integer-line construction.

The July 2026 preprint proves quantum lower bounds for 3-coloring rooted trees using growing degree, and for 2-coloring even cycles. It explicitly distinguishes the bounded-degree case; neither result resolves three-coloring cycles.

The August 2026 preprint proves a linear-round lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that color cycles with probability exactly one. Its Section 1.4 leaves high-probability correctness open. The identified, nonzero-error model here is retained.

The September 2026 preprint rules out high-probability four-coloring in the restricted one-way one-round quantum model. Section 1.4 explicitly leaves bidirectional communication and additional rounds as further questions; this does not resolve the sub-log-star target.

The cited quantum papers allow general finite-dimensional local operations in their mathematical models. This card preserves its pre-existing uniform finite-gate formulation; the review does not claim an exact compilation equivalence for probability-one results.
why: Cycle coloring is a basic distributed symmetry-breaking problem with a sharp classical locality threshold. Settling whether quantum communication beats that threshold would establish a concrete capability or limitation for coordinating neighboring processors with classical outputs.
status_note: Source-open: the August 2026 paper explicitly retains high-probability cycle coloring, and the September 8, 2026 preprint leaves bidirectional or multi-round quantum locality open. Its one-way one-round four-color lower bound does not settle this identified, uniform finite-gate, sub-log-star question. Primary sources and bounded later searches were checked on 2026-09-16; this is not exhaustive certification or independent verification of the preprint proofs.

working_summary: Processors on an oriented cycle must choose three classical colors with different colors at every edge. They may perform finite local quantum computations and communicate qubits with both neighbors in synchronous rounds. One uniform protocol must work for every cycle size and every distinct identifier assignment, starting without shared randomness or entanglement. The target is worst-case communication below the log-star scale with global success probability at least one minus one over the number of nodes. Recent zero-error and one-way one-round lower bounds cover restricted models and do not resolve this high-probability question.

title: Optimal one-pass randomized space for LIS length
importance_reason: A longstanding central streaming problem with a substantial unresolved benefit-of-randomness question. The fixed one-pass model and finite alphabet make a matching bit-space determination precise while retaining the main conceptual difficulty.
formal:
Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal randomized one-pass streaming space in bits for a factor-two estimate of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a length-\(n\) sequence over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

For every fixed input \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), let
\[L(x)=\max\{r:\exists\,1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n,\ x_{i_1}<\cdots<x_{i_r}\}.\]
An admissible algorithm reads \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) once in this order and, after the final item, outputs an integer \(\widehat L\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[L(x)/2\le\widehat L\le L(x)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
Find an explicit asymptotic function \(f(n)\) admitting a uniform algorithm with \(O(f(n))\) worst-case bit space and a matching \(\Omega(f(n))\) lower bound for every admissible randomized algorithm. Logarithmic factors are part of the requested answer.
question_excerpt: Chakrabarti asks for the randomized streaming space complexity of a factor-two LIS-length approximation and mentions both one pass and a constant number of passes. The user selected one pass, length-n sequences over the alphabet {1,…,n}, success probability at least two thirds and optimal bit space up to constant factors. The strict-increase convention and the multiplicative output interval are stated explicitly.
definitions:
The stream length \(n\ge1\) is known before the stream begins. The input contains exactly \(n\) integers, each in the ordered alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), represented in binary. Repetitions are allowed: the input is an arbitrary sequence and need not be a permutation. The asymptotic parameter is the number of items \(n\), whereas memory is measured in bits, not in stored items or machine words. An explicit input list occupies \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits.

An increasing subsequence retains selected positions in their original order; the positions need not be consecutive. Both inequalities in its definition are strict. In particular, repeated equal values cannot both appear in such a subsequence. The strictly decreasing sequence has LIS length one, while \((1,2,\ldots,n)\) has LIS length \(n\). The problem asks only for the length estimate. It does not require the positions or values of a witnessing subsequence.

A single pass gives sequential access to the items from first to last, with no rewind, rereading, permutation of the stream or random-access queries to earlier positions. The algorithm may retain information about previous items only in its working memory. Its output appears after the whole sequence has been processed. It need not approximate the LIS of every prefix or issue intermediate answers.

For each fixed valid sequence, the probability is taken over independent fair random bits used by the algorithm. The entire input is fixed independently of those bits. The guarantee is required separately for every sequence, including sequences with short LIS; there is no promise that the LIS contains a constant fraction of the input. The algorithm may fail on at most one third of its random executions for a particular sequence. No distribution on input sequences is imposed.

The output convention is an underestimate within a factor two, as in the later paper's multiplicative approximation definition. On successful executions it lies in \([L(x)/2,L(x)]\). This is not the wider interval \([L(x)/2,2L(x)]\). The output can be an integer: rounding up a real output in the chosen interval preserves both bounds because \(L(x)\) is an integer. No additive error is allowed.

Use one finite uniform streaming program at all lengths. Its persistent state and temporary working storage are measured in bits; stored input values, counters, indices, retained random choices and output preparation all count. There is no external scratch storage, reusable random tape containing uncharged information, advice string or oracle. The stream itself is read-only sequential input. Fresh random bits may be consumed during computation; information about past bits can be reused only if it was retained within the counted memory.

Space is the maximum number of working bits used at any time, over every valid input of length \(n\) and every random execution, including executions whose final answer is inaccurate. Call this quantity \(s_A(n)\) for algorithm \(A\). It is not expected space. The algorithm must terminate after processing its input, but the target imposes no separate update-time or total-time bound. Unlimited local computation does not permit additional storage or another pass. Knowing \(n\) does not provide the input's LIS length or any statistic of the sequence.

The requested optimum means matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds in this model. There must be one admissible algorithm \(A_*\), a constant \(C>0\) and a threshold \(n_0\) with \(s_{A_*}(n)\le C f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). For every admissible randomized algorithm \(A\), there must be constants \(c_A>0,n_A\) with \(s_A(n)\ge c_A f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_A\). The constants are independent of the input and its random bits. The answer must state \(f\) explicitly and establish both directions; merely defining \(f\) to be the unknown optimum is not an answer.

All factors growing with \(n\), including \(\log n\), iterated logarithms or a slowly growing multiplier, must be retained. Determining only an exponent in \(n\), or proving bounds that match only after hiding logarithmic factors, does not meet the selected precision. No numerical additive tolerance applies to an asymptotic space bound.

The white-box adversarial model is different: its input generator may inspect the algorithm's previous random choices and internal memory before selecting the next item. A lower bound against algorithms required to survive that stronger input generator need not hold when the sequence is fixed beforehand. Deterministic algorithms, multiple-pass algorithms, algorithms with reordered access and additive approximations are also separately specified variants. The original source mentions both one and constantly many passes; the user selected exactly one pass and the alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
answer_criterion: Give an explicit function \(f(n)\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of the matching uniform upper and randomized lower space bounds defined above. The algorithm must meet the factor-two interval and success probability on every fixed input, using one pass and counted worst-case bit space. The lower bound must apply to randomized algorithms in this same fixed-input model and alphabet, not only to deterministic or white-box adversarial algorithms. A single improved bound without a matching other direction, an additive approximation, an algorithm for a larger approximation factor or bounds differing by a logarithmic factor do not complete the selected constant-factor determination.
context:
The length of the longest increasing subsequence measures how much ordered structure survives inside a sequence. Computing or estimating it differs from sorting: only a number is requested, yet information from distant positions can determine which choices combine into a long subsequence.

Gopalan and coauthors give a deterministic one-pass approximation algorithm using \(O(\sqrt n)\) stored input symbols for fixed relative accuracy. With alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the corresponding bit bound is \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\). Their discussion explains how to handle strict rather than nondecreasing subsequences. This is an upper bound for randomized algorithms as well, because they may ignore randomness.

Deterministic lower bounds leave open whether randomness saves substantially more memory. Chakrabarti shows that the communication problems used in those lower bounds admit inexpensive randomized protocols. This establishes a limitation of those particular lower-bound arguments; it does not provide a small-space randomized LIS algorithm.

The ITCS 2026 paper proves a square-root space lower bound in the white-box model for a 1.1-approximation with an alphabet of size at least three times the stream length. Its theorem differs from this card in the adversary, accuracy and stated alphabet. Its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary randomized approximation problem as open.

An additive approximation to LIS length can be useful when \(L(x)\) is large. An additive error proportional to \(n\), however, can exceed the entire answer when \(L(x)\ll n\). Likewise, an approximation to the complementary quantity \(n-L(x)\), the number of deletions needed to leave a strictly increasing sequence, need not approximate a small \(L(x)\) multiplicatively.

This is an unusual streaming question in which a sublinear-space deterministic algorithm is known but the benefit of randomness remains poorly understood. Matching randomized bounds would explain whether the memory cost comes from the ordered structure of the input or from limitations of deterministic summaries.
why: This problem tests whether randomness can substantially reduce the memory needed to retain ordered structure in a sequence. The large gap between what is known for deterministic algorithms and what is proved necessary for ordinary randomized algorithms makes it a basic unresolved question about one-pass computation.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 44, Bertinoro 2011, updated 7 March 2013. The selected version uses one pass over length-n sequences from {1,...,n}, a factor-two underestimate and success at least 2/3. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the SODA 2007 upper bound, Chakrabarti’s 2010/2012 communication result and the published ITCS 2026 paper, whose introduction explicitly leaves ordinary randomized LIS approximation open. Its Theorem 1 is a white-box adversarial result for factor 1.1 and alphabet size at least 3n, so it does not resolve the selected model. A bounded later-work search found no verified matching randomized bounds; this does not certify the entire literature or supply a Lean proof.
progress: 2007: A deterministic one-pass approximation uses \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\) bits for the selected alphabet and fixed accuracy, giving a valid randomized upper bound. | 2010 preprint; 2012 journal: Chakrabarti proves that the communication problems behind earlier deterministic lower bounds have efficient randomized protocols. Those reductions therefore do not yield matching randomized lower bounds. | 2026: Gal, Kol, Saxena and Yu prove a square-root white-box lower bound with the additional model and accuracy conditions stated above; they still describe ordinary randomized LIS approximation as a longstanding open problem.
working_summary: The problem asks for optimal bit space to estimate the longest strictly increasing subsequence in one streaming pass. Inputs are arbitrary length-n sequences of numbers from one to n, fixed before the algorithm chooses its random bits. The final estimate must lie between half the true length and the true length with probability at least two thirds. Deterministic upper bounds and recent lower bounds against a stronger adaptive adversary leave the ordinary randomized optimum unresolved. The requested answer must match upper and lower bounds up to constants, including every logarithmic factor.

title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
importance_reason: A basic randomized symmetry-breaking question on arbitrary graphs whose resolution would sharpen the global locality frontier.
formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.
answer_criterion: Give one randomized LOCAL algorithm with a uniform \(o(\log  n)\) round bound and the stated success probability on all graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A degree restriction does not settle the proposition.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?
why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. General-graph sublogarithmic elapsed-round complexity remains open in the checked literature; awake-time and high-girth results have different guarantees.
progress: 2016: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$. | 2025: Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier. | 2025: Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.
working_summary: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent vertices and leaves every unselected vertex next to a selected one. The question asks for a randomized LOCAL algorithm that finds such a set in \(o(\log  n)\) rounds on every graph with high probability. Message sizes and local computation are unrestricted, so the resource measures the distance over which decisions must be coordinated. The running-time improvement must hold uniformly even for graphs of very large degree. Degree-sensitive algorithms already improve some cases, but the target requires a mechanism that also avoids logarithmically many phases on unrestricted graphs.

title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
importance_reason: A small connectivity promise problem serves as a basic round-complexity benchmark for low-memory massively parallel computation.
formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint \((n/2)\)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is \(O(n)\) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.
answer_criterion: Prove the logarithmic lower bound for every fixed sublinear-memory exponent and every admissible randomized algorithm, or refute that universal lower bound. An \(o(\log  n)\)-round algorithm for one fixed exponent would suffice for a refutation.
context:
Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.
why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.
progress: 2022: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here. | 2025: Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.
working_summary: The one-cycle-versus-two problem distinguishes a single n-vertex cycle from two disjoint cycles of half that size. In the low-memory MPC model, edges are spread across machines with sublinear local memory and linear total memory. The conjecture says randomized algorithms require \(\Omega (\log  n)\) communication rounds under these resource bounds. Both input types have identical vertex counts, edge counts, and degrees, so only their global connectivity distinguishes them. A lower bound must handle arbitrary communication between machines and arbitrary encodings, rather than assuming information can travel only along graph edges.

title: Deterministic LOCAL MIS in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds
importance_reason: Matching a logarithmic deterministic bound for MIS would settle a central gap in local symmetry breaking.
formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be \(O(\log  n)\) uniformly over degrees.
answer_criterion: Give one deterministic LOCAL algorithm with a uniform \(O(\log  n)\) bound over all graphs and valid identifiers, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Constants must not depend on maximum degree.
context:
Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.
why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An \(O(\log  n)\) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is solved; the \(O(\log  n)\) target remains open in the checked literature.
progress: 2019: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor. | 2020: Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS. | 2024: Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$. | 2026: Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve \(\Delta\)-coloring; their result does not give an \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{MIS}\) algorithm.
working_summary: Deterministic maximal independent set algorithms must coordinate their choices using the graph and vertex identifiers alone. The question asks whether \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{LOCAL}\) rounds suffice on every graph and every valid identifier assignment. The output must be independent and dominate all unselected vertices, without requiring maximum cardinality. Network decomposition already supports polylogarithmic deterministic algorithms, so the target is a sharper dependence on network size. Reaching the logarithmic bound would require organizing deterministic progress efficiently even when identifier patterns defeat simple greedy local rules.

title: Subquadratic metric TSP cost estimation below factor two
importance_reason: A longstanding question linking sublinear algorithms to a fundamental optimization problem, with a strong nearly linear baseline and several substantial recent special-case results. The fixed improvement below two exposes a general information barrier rather than a small adjustment to a known approximation ratio.
formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a classical randomized distance-query algorithm that estimates the minimum traveling-salesperson tour cost of every \(n\)-point metric within a factor \(2-\delta\), using \(o(n^2)\) distance queries?

For a metric \(d\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge3\), define
\[\operatorname{TSP}(d)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(j),\pi(j+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
The algorithm knows \(n\) and can request \(d(i,j)\) for any chosen pair of labels. Its output \(Z\) must satisfy
\[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le Z\le(2-\delta)\operatorname{TSP}(d)\right]\ge\frac23\]
for every input metric. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; the output is a cost estimate and need not describe a tour.
question_excerpt: Sublinear.info Problem 71 asks whether some positive constant improvement below approximation factor two is possible for metric TSP cost with fewer than quadratically many pair-distance queries. It presents a subquadratic total running time as an even stronger goal. This card retains the primary query-complexity question and makes the randomness and cost-estimation convention explicit.
definitions:
The input consists of a known integer \(n\ge3\), the labels \([n]\), and an oracle for a function \(d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). It is promised that \(d(i,j)=0\) exactly when \(i=j\), that \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), and that
\[d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in[n].\]
Thus all off-diagonal distances are finite positive real numbers. The triangle inequality and symmetry are input promises, not properties that the algorithm must verify. Metrics are arbitrary: no Euclidean embedding, dimension bound, integer-distance restriction, bounded aspect ratio or distribution on inputs is supplied.

One query consists of specifying labels \(i,j\in[n]\) and receiving the exact real distance \(d(i,j)\). It costs one oracle call. Queries may depend on earlier replies and on the algorithm’s private randomness. Repeated calls are charged again. Diagonal values are known to be zero; allowing a paid diagonal call gives no additional information. The metric remains fixed throughout the execution and is chosen independently of the random bits.

The algorithm is uniform: a single finite program works for every \(n\).
