To specify computation with exact real oracle replies, use a classical real-register machine with rational program constants, ordinary finite control, integer counters, and exact real arithmetic and comparisons. Allowed real operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value; registers may store queried distances and calculated real values. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, which may be used to select labels. Integer computation, local arithmetic, storage and random-bit generation are not charged to the query budget. They must define an algorithm that halts with probability one on each input. No advice depending on the metric or on \(n\), quantum queries, further metric oracle, precomputed spanning tree or access to unqueried matrix entries is available.

This is a query-complexity question, so there is no polynomial-time or subquadratic-time requirement on the computation between calls. In particular, the original source’s suggestion of subquadratic total time is a stronger aspiration, not an additional condition for answering its primary query question. A positive solution with such a time bound would also solve this card, provided it meets all the stated guarantees.

The output \(Z\) is one real value. On a successful execution it is an upper estimate at most \(2-\delta\) times the optimum. An equivalent lower-estimate convention would require \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)/(2-\delta)\le Z'\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\); multiplication by the fixed approximation factor converts between the conventions without oracle calls. The algorithm may fail to meet the interval on at most one third of its random executions. Success is required for each metric individually, not merely on average over an input distribution.

The query bound is worst case over inputs and random executions, apart from null-probability exceptional executions. Formally, there must exist \(q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every \(n\)-point input uses at most \(q(n)\) oracle calls with probability one, and
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{q(n)}{n^2}=0.\]
The constant \(\delta\), the program and this bound are independent of all distance values. There is no hidden dependence on the ratio of the largest to the smallest positive distance. For finitely many small \(n\), all pair distances may be queried without affecting the limit. The little-o condition is weaker than demanding \(O(n^{2-\gamma})\) for some fixed \(\gamma>0\); both a fixed polynomial saving and a genuine slower asymptotic saving would qualify.

The quantifier order is \(\exists\delta\;\exists A\;\exists q\;\forall n\ge3\;\forall d\), followed by probability over the execution of \(A\). The improvement \(\delta\) must be a positive constant; an approximation factor approaching two from below as \(n\) grows is insufficient. The card asks whether any such constant improvement exists, not for the largest possible improvement or a full approximation-query tradeoff.

A tour is a cyclic ordering of all labels, using each exactly once before returning to the start. The cost includes that closing edge. The oracle describes the complete metric, so each tour edge costs the queried distance itself; no separate underlying graph path needs to be output. \(\mathfrak S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). The finite minimum in the definition of \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)\) is attained and is strictly positive.

For background, a spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph on all labels, and \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\) is the minimum sum of its edge distances. The familiar inequalities \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le2\operatorname{MST}(d)\) explain the factor-two threshold. Estimating the weight of an MST does not give its edges. A graphic metric is the shortest-path distance metric of a connected unweighted undirected graph. A \((1,2)\)-metric has every off-diagonal distance equal to one or two. Both are special classes of the general metric inputs here.

This is not a streaming task: a stream reveals entries in an imposed order, whereas the algorithm here chooses each pair it queries. A result that is given a minimum spanning tree as additional input, or promises a spanning tree of unit-distance edges, concerns additional information or structure absent from the target. Full-input approximation algorithms may also use quadratically many distance entries, regardless of their approximation ratio.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of an absolute \(\delta>0\), a uniform classical randomized algorithm and a worst-case query bound \(q(n)=o(n^2)\) with the stated success probability for every metric. A positive answer must prove the cost guarantee, the uniform little-o bound independent of the metric’s scale and aspect ratio, and almost-sure halting in the specified oracle model. It need not output a tour or run in subquadratic total time. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence statement for randomized adaptive algorithms; a lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, near-exact approximation, or a specific algorithm is insufficient. Positive results restricted to graphic or \((1,2)\)-metrics, or assuming an MST is supplied, do not resolve the arbitrary-metric target. Experimental success rates, conditional computational hardness and an improvement that vanishes with \(n\) do not establish the required result.
context:
A distance matrix contains quadratically many entries. Estimating a global optimum after reading a vanishing fraction of these entries asks how much information about a metric is needed to recover a useful numerical summary, rather than an explicit combinatorial solution.

Czumaj and Sohler estimate metric MST weight within a factor \(1+\varepsilon\) using nearly linear oracle access for fixed \(\varepsilon\). The resulting TSP estimate approaches factor two. Their arbitrary-metric model does not assume a given geometric embedding or a bounded ratio of distances.

Classical tour algorithms can rely on an actual spanning tree and further global structure. The source emphasizes that obtaining the tree itself can require quadratically many distance queries even though estimating its total weight is much easier. This is an information-access distinction between value estimation and producing a witness.

Chen, Kannan and Khanna obtain below-two estimation for graphic and two-valued metrics. They also prove that sufficiently accurate approximation already requires quadratic query complexity on these special classes. That obstruction near factor one does not rule out every fixed improvement below two.

Chen, Khanna and Tan extend below-two estimation to positive integral metrics that either have a promised unit-edge spanning tree or are supplied with an MST. The query cost is \(\widetilde O(n^{3/2})\). Their paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted general-metric query question open.

The 2023 paper also gives streaming algorithms and lower bounds. Those theorems have different access rules and cannot be substituted for a pair-distance query theorem. In particular, a result with an extra pass over every matrix entry need not inspect only a subquadratic number of distances.

The requested estimate need not correspond to a tour produced by the algorithm. A positive answer would establish that useful information about tour cost is accessible with strictly fewer than all pairwise measurements, even where recovering the usual intermediate structures is expensive.
why: This is a central test of how well a global optimization value can be estimated from incomplete metric information. Resolving it would determine whether the factor-two barrier is inherent to sparse distance access or reflects limitations of current estimators, with a sharp separation between learning a value and constructing a tour.
status_note: Source-open in Onak’s Sublinear.info Problem 71 (Baltimore 2016) and explicitly retained as open for arbitrary metrics by Chen, Khanna and Tan, ICALP 2023, abstract and §1.1. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the arbitrary-metric oracle model in Czumaj–Sohler, the 2020 lower-bound scope and the exact promises of the 2023 algorithms. Bounded subsequent searches found no unrestricted subquadratic-query below-two estimator or impossibility theorem for the target. The 2023 paper’s positive results assume positive integral distances and either supplied MST information or a unit-tree promise; these are recorded as limited progress. This review did not independently audit every proof deferred from the conference papers to full versions and does not claim an exhaustive current-status certification.
progress: 2009: Czumaj and Sohler establish nearly linear-time approximation of metric MST weight, giving the near-two baseline for TSP value estimation. | 2016: Onak’s problem statement asks for a fixed improvement below two with a subquadratic number of distance queries. | 2020: Chen, Kannan and Khanna give subquadratic below-two algorithms on special metrics and quadratic-query lower bounds for sufficiently accurate estimation. | 2023: Chen, Khanna and Tan extend the positive results under a unit-tree promise or supplied MST, while explicitly retaining the unrestricted question.
working_summary: A metric TSP cost query algorithm asks for distances between selected pairs of labeled points. The question asks whether some fixed approximation factor below two is achievable with a subquadratic number of queries on every metric. The algorithm is randomized and only needs to output a cost estimate, with success probability at least two thirds. Nearly linear MST-weight estimation gives the factor-two baseline, while stronger TSP estimates are known for special metrics or with extra spanning-tree information. The target separates sparse access to a global optimum value from the information needed to construct an explicit tour.

title: Full random walks with near-linear streaming space
importance_reason: A central streaming sampling problem linking sequential access, memory and long-range graph dependence. The known-start full-trajectory version preserves a substantive unresolved tradeoff beyond the established two-pass and dense-graph results.
formal:
Can a randomized graph-streaming algorithm sample a whole \(L\)-step random walk, for every \(1\le L\le n\), with total-variation error at most \(1/100\), near-linear bit space and polylogarithmically many passes?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and fixed nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with the following property? For every unweighted directed graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every start \(s\), every \(1\le L\le n\) and every fixed ordering of its edges, \(A\), knowing \(n,L,s\) before reading the stream, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b\right\rceil\text{ passes}\]
and outputs a tuple \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_L)\) whose distribution \(\nu_{G,s,L}\) satisfies
\[\|\nu_{G,s,L}-\mu_{G,s,L}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/100?\]
Here \(\mu_{G,s,L}\) is the joint distribution of the ordinary directed random walk starting at \(s\), with the absorbing convention at a vertex of out-degree zero defined below.
question_excerpt: Panigrahy asks whether random-walk simulation can use near-linear space and only polylogarithmically many passes in the graph size and walk length. The source also asks separate questions about endpoint distributions. The user selected the entire trajectory of length at most n, a known initial vertex, unweighted directed graphs and total-variation error at most 1/100; the absorbing convention makes zero-out-degree inputs well defined.
definitions:
The graph has the known labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and edge set \(E\subseteq V\times V\). There are no multiple copies of an edge; self-loops are allowed. Both directions between distinct vertices may be present independently. Every edge has unit weight. The stream explicitly lists each directed edge once as a binary pair, in an arbitrary fixed order. Empty streams, isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and graphs with highly unequal degrees are allowed. The number of edges need not be known in advance.

For a vertex \(v\), its out-neighbor set is \(N^+(v)=\{w:(v,w)\in E\}\) and its out-degree is \(d^+(v)=|N^+(v)|\). A true random walk starts with \(X_0=s\). At every step, conditional on the complete history so far, if \(d^+(X_i)>0\), then \(X_{i+1}\) is chosen uniformly from \(N^+(X_i)\). New choices are independent conditional on the successive current vertices. Repeated visits and repeated traversal of an edge are permitted; this is not a simple path.

At a vertex of out-degree zero, define \(X_{i+1}=X_i\). This absorbing convention ensures that a length-\(L\) tuple is defined for every input. It is equivalent to adding a self-loop only at each zero-out-degree vertex. The convention is stated explicitly rather than leaving a uniform choice from an empty set undefined. It does not replace directed transitions elsewhere by undirected ones or add restarts from another vertex.

Equivalently, define the transition probabilities \(K_G(v,w)\) as \(1/d^+(v)\) when \(d^+(v)>0\) and \((v,w)\in E\), as one when \(d^+(v)=0\) and \(w=v\), and as zero otherwise. The desired law on \(V^{L+1}\) is
\[\mu_{G,s,L}(v_0,\ldots,v_L)=\mathbf1_{\{v_0=s\}}\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}K_G(v_i,v_{i+1}).\]
The integer \(L\) counts transitions, so the output lists \(L+1\) vertices including the start. The parameters \(n,L,s\) are explicitly available before the first pass. Only one sampled trajectory is requested.

For distributions \(\mu,\nu\) on this finite tuple space, total variation means
\[\|\nu-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\omega\in V^{L+1}}|\nu(\omega)-\mu(\omega)|.\]
This compares the complete joint distributions, including dependencies between visits. Correct endpoint probabilities or correct single-time marginals alone do not establish the requirement. The output law averages over all internal random choices. The bound is not a probability that a numerical estimate is accurate, so a separate two-thirds-success convention is not substituted for it. Any probability assigned to an impossible trajectory is part of the total-variation error.

The algorithm returns an explicit tuple in \(V^{L+1}\), with initial vertex \(s\), after processing its passes. It must include every intermediate vertex, not just the endpoint, selected checkpoints, transition counts, a random seed or a program for reconstructing a longer object. The tuple may be assembled in working memory and then written to a final output tape. Its \(O(L\log(n+2))\) bits fit inside the allowed near-linear class because \(L\le n\); all working storage used to assemble it is counted.

A pass reads the full edge sequence from beginning to end. Between passes the algorithm may rewind and keep its working memory, but the sequence and its order remain the same. It cannot change the edge list, jump to an old edge, query an adjacency list or ask for a random neighbor except through computations on information acquired from the stream. There is no uncounted external scratch storage. This is an insertion-only arbitrary-order stream, not a randomly ordered or deletion stream.

Use one finite uniform randomized program for all parameter values. It may draw independent fair random bits. All mutable information counts toward bit space, including edge samples, labels, counters, retained randomness, intermediate structures and the assembled output. Old random choices can be reused only through information retained within that space. Pass and memory bounds hold on all executions. The algorithm must produce its tuple with probability one; no additional bound on local running time is imposed. The input graph and its edge ordering are fixed independently of the random choices.

The constants and logarithmic exponents in the statement do not depend on \(n,L,s,G\), its edge order or the random choices. Since \(L\le n\), a fixed polynomial in \(\log(n+2)\) and \(\log(L+2)\) is bounded by a fixed power of \(\log(n+2)\). Thus the displayed pass bound expresses the source's polylogarithmic target in the selected length range. In background bounds, \(\widetilde O\) and \(\widetilde\Omega\) hide fixed logarithmic factors; the target itself specifies their permitted form.

Knowing the start before reading the graph is important. A preprocessing summary that must later support any as-yet-unknown start has a stronger requirement. A lower bound for that stronger preprocessing task does not automatically apply to the present algorithm. Likewise, a theorem with a fixed constant pass count cannot be evaluated at a growing polylogarithmic pass count unless its uniform dependence on that parameter is proved.

The source asks broadly for faster simulation and separately for endpoint-distribution estimation and the most likely endpoints. With the user's approval, this card selects the full trajectory, fixed total-variation accuracy, unweighted directed input and length range \(1\le L\le n\). It retains the known-start and near-linear-space, polylogarithmic-pass objective.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying every condition above exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that they do not. A positive answer must bound the total variation of the entire explicit output tuple and account for memory and passes on every graph and edge ordering. A negative answer must rule out all fixed logarithmic exponents \(a,b\) in the selected resource bounds, with the start known before streaming. Constant-pass lower bounds, lower bounds only for unknown-start preprocessing, endpoint-only samplers, results on dense graphs or bounds allowing a polynomial factor in \(L\) do not resolve this target. The tolerance \(1/100\) is the specified statistical distance between distributions, not an additive error on asymptotic resource bounds.
context:
Random walks are useful for sampling and exploring large graphs, but a streaming algorithm encounters edges in an order unrelated to the trajectory it will eventually follow. Limited memory prevents retaining all possible future choices, while rereading the graph can be expensive.

A distribution on endpoints discards the route taken to reach them. Two samplers can agree at the endpoint while assigning very different probabilities to intermediate visits. The full-trajectory target therefore explicitly checks the joint law of all visited vertices.

Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy obtain a near-linear-space simulation with roughly \(\sqrt L\) passes, up to logarithmic factors. Their basic procedure stores endpoints of walk segments; Remark 3.7 discusses reconstructing internal vertices, and §6 charges additional reconstruction space. The present output convention keeps that distinction visible.

Chen and coauthors give a two-pass sampler using \(\widetilde O(n\sqrt L\log(1/\delta))\) space and total-variation error \(\delta\). Choosing an inverse-polynomial \(\delta\le1/100\) meets the requested accuracy. For polynomially long walks, the extra factor \(\sqrt L\) can exceed every allowed logarithmic memory factor.

The same paper proves \(\widetilde\Omega(nL^{1/p})\) space lower bounds for each fixed pass count \(p\), with \(L=\lceil n^\beta\rceil\) and fixed \(\beta\in(0,1]\). These obstruct constant-pass near-linear-space simulation at such lengths, but do not rule out the growing polylogarithmic number of passes asked here. Its separate unknown-start result has a different quantifier order.

The 2026 dense-graph result gives much smaller one-pass memory when every vertex has sufficiently large out-degree. The minimum degree condition is essential to its guarantee; large average degree alone can leave a difficult region containing the chosen start. The result does not handle all directed graphs in the selected near-linear resource range.
why: Random-walk sampling is a basic graph primitive, and this question asks whether its full trajectory can be recovered with both modest memory and few sequential scans. It isolates a gap between known constant-pass tradeoffs and the possibility of polylogarithmically many passes.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 22, Kanpur 2009, with a 23 July 2021 update linking the two-pass result. The user selected a full trajectory for 1 <= L <= n, known start, unweighted directed graph and total-variation error at most 1/100. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the original 2011 reconstruction discussion, the 2021 full-version Theorems 1.1–1.3 and the published ITCS 2026 dense-graph result. Constant-pass lower bounds and the stronger unknown-start preprocessing lower bound do not exclude the selected polylogarithmic-pass algorithm; the dense-graph theorem assumes a minimum out-degree bound. A bounded later-work search found no verified resolution for the selected general-graph model. No new sampler, impossibility proof or Lean formalization is claimed.
progress: 2008 conference; 2011 journal: Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy establish the near-linear-space, roughly square-root-in-\(L\) pass baseline and discuss full-walk reconstruction separately. | 2021: Chen and coauthors establish a two-pass space tradeoff and lower bounds for every fixed constant number of passes. Their full-trajectory and starting-vertex conventions are explicit. | 2026: Efremenko, Kol, Saxena and Zhang obtain one-pass sampling bounds exploiting a lower bound on every vertex out-degree. This advances dense-graph instances without settling arbitrary directed graphs.
working_summary: The problem asks for one entire random-walk trajectory in a directed graph presented as an edge stream. The start is known in advance, and the number of steps is at most the number of vertices. The output distribution must be within 1/100 in total variation of the true joint distribution of all visits. Near-linear bit space and a fixed polylogarithmic number of passes must suffice for every graph and edge order. Known constant-pass tradeoffs and improved dense-graph samplers do not settle this general target.

title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
importance_reason: The existing high importance is retained for the broad conversion from sequential summaries to efficiently mergeable computation; the unresolved resource is explicitly time, after the known space simulation.
formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.
definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.
context:
The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. This is the time-sensitive refinement motivated by the paper cited on that page, rather than a claim that the already established space-only simulation remains unknown.

Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.
why: Fast merging would allow any efficiently maintained order-independent statistic to be computed from independently processed pieces without an expensive reconstruction step. A separation would expose an inherent computational cost of parallel aggregation even when communication and memory are small.
status_note: The cited paper establishes a space-preserving simulation but explicitly identifies its high running time as a limitation. This card selects a precise uniform polylogarithmic-time refinement, with no promise or randomness. No matching general simulation or separation was located in the bounded September 2026 check; the literal malformed source sentence is not treated as evidence.
progress: 2006: Sivakumar asks the general streaming-versus-sketching question. | 2008: Feldman and coauthors give the aggregation simulation, discuss its large running time, and identify time as the remaining possible source of separation. | 2026-04-23: A later turnstile simulation treats polynomial-length integer update streams, a different model from the one fixed here.
working_summary: The input statistic is a total Boolean function invariant under reordering the stream. A streaming program computes it using polylogarithmic memory and time per item. The selected question asks for equally efficient local summaries and merging on every binary aggregation tree. A known simulation preserves small space but can use superpolynomial merge time. The target excludes promise and randomness separations and does not require identical intermediate summaries.

title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
importance_reason: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.
formal:
Is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge3\quad
\exists A_n:\quad A_n\text{ implements a linearizable wait-free FIFO queue for }n\text{ processes}
\]
using only the atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set bits defined below? The queue is initially empty and has no capacity bound. Every process may perform arbitrarily many operations of either kind, with arbitrary finite binary strings as enqueued values. Each \(A_n\) is deterministic and has finite code; it may depend on \(n\). The quantifiers do not additionally require one compiler producing all \(A_n\).
definitions:
Fix \(n\ge3\). There are \(n\) named sequential processes with identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\), each knowing \(n\) and its own identifier. A process has unbounded private storage, initially containing only its identifier, \(n\), and its fixed program data. Its local computation is given by a deterministic finite Turing program on finite strings. Shared communication is confined to two countable arrays with natural-number addresses: registers \(R_0,R_1,\ldots\), initially containing the empty binary string, and bits \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\), initially zero. A register read atomically returns its whole current finite string; a write atomically replaces that string and returns an acknowledgement. The primitive \(\operatorname{TAS}(j)\) atomically returns the old value of \(B_j\) and changes it to one. A bit is never reset, and every later test-and-set on that bit returns one. Any process can access any address; using a previously unused address does not require an allocation oracle. There is no fixed bound on addresses used, register bit lengths, private storage or total operations over a whole execution. A finite execution prefix uses only finite data and finitely many primitive calls.

The scheduler interleaves individual local computation steps and atomic primitive calls. Each scheduled process chooses its next action from its private state, its current invocation and previous primitive responses. Processes receive no randomness, clock, failure detector, schedule information or noncomputable oracle. They can be delayed arbitrarily and can stop forever at any point. No fairness assumption constrains other processes. Local Turing steps, primitive invocations and operation responses count as that process's own steps; no bounded step complexity is demanded.

The sequential queue state is a finite sequence of finite binary strings, initially empty. \(\operatorname{Enqueue}(v)\) appends one occurrence of \(v\) at the end and returns a distinguished acknowledgement. \(\operatorname{Dequeue}()\) removes and returns the first occurrence if the sequence is nonempty; otherwise it returns a distinguished \(\mathsf{Empty}\) value without changing the state. Empty, acknowledgement and string-valued responses have separate tags, so the empty binary string is an ordinary possible item. Repeated equal values represent separate occurrences. Each process can invoke either operation whenever its previous invocation has returned, so it has at most one pending invocation. Clients may choose later invocations from earlier responses; there are no designated enqueuer or dequeuer roles, no bound on the number of calls and no promise that a dequeue finds an item.

Linearizability is required for every finite execution prefix. Take its history of queue invocations and responses. Append responses to any chosen subset of pending invocations and discard the other pending invocations. There must be a total order of the resulting completed operations that preserves each process's order, respects every real-time precedence in the completed history, and gives exactly their responses under the sequential queue specification. Here real-time precedence means that one operation's response occurs before the other's invocation. The choice of this total order may differ between different execution prefixes; it is not required to preserve earlier choices when a history is extended. Infinite executions must satisfy this safety condition at every finite prefix.

Wait-freedom is the following per-process termination property: from any reachable configuration with a pending operation of process \(p\), every continuation in which \(p\) takes infinitely many of its own steps contains a response to that operation after finitely many such steps, regardless of all other processes' delays, crashes or continuing operations. Thus an infinite execution in which one process's pending operation never finishes despite that process continuing to take steps is forbidden, even if other operations keep completing. These definitions specify ordinary linearizability and wait-freedom, with unlimited resource capacity; they impose neither strong linearizability nor a resource bound uniform over all histories.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed proposition, including both safety and per-process termination for every \(n\ge3\), or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: there is an integer \(n\ge3\) for which no permitted implementation exists. A result confined to restricted process roles, stronger primitives, a stronger correctness condition, or system-wide progress alone does not settle this proposition.
context:
The OPODIS 2015 paper, published in 2016, explicitly asks whether an \(n\)-process ordinary linearizable wait-free queue can be built from test-and-set and registers for every \(n\ge3\). This card retains that quantifier order and the unrestricted repeated-operation interface, with finite-string values and explicit deterministic computation conventions.

Requiring an implementation for every \(n\ge2\) gives the same existence question as requiring one for every \(n\ge3\). A three-process implementation can serve two processes while the third remains permanently inactive: wait-freedom already requires the continuing processes to finish independently of that process. The implementation may still depend on the fixed process count.

The consensus number of an object type is the largest number of processes for which copies of that type together with registers can solve wait-free consensus: every continuing process decides one proposed input value and all decisions agree. Test-and-set and queues have consensus number two. That agreement capability by itself does not supply a many-process queue implementation. Common2 is the historical class of types implementable in a wait-free manner from any object type of consensus number two.

Stacks admit Common2 implementations. This result concerns last-in-first-out removal and does not supply the first-in-first-out semantics of the target. The source also studies unbounded numbers of participating processes; the present question allows a separate implementation for each fixed finite process count.

Eisenstat gives a Common2 queue for at most two enqueuing processes and any number of dequeuing processes. The stated restriction on who can enqueue leaves the unrestricted interface in this card unanswered.

The OPODIS 2022 article, published in February 2023, explicitly repeats the open Common2 queue question. Its efficient exact queue uses compare-and-swap, which atomically checks an expected value and conditionally writes a replacement; that primitive is unavailable here. Its separate multiplicity variant relaxes removal semantics.

Strong linearizability requires one choice of linearizations that preserves prefixes across histories. The 2025 paper proves an impossibility for strongly linearizable queues from the relevant weak primitives. Its progress condition is lock-freedom, meaning that infinitely many steps yield infinitely many completed operations somewhere in the system. The stronger correctness requirement prevents this result from being an impossibility for ordinary linearizability.

The PODC 2026 paper extends impossibility results for strongly linearizable queues, including settings with additional primitives and at least four processes. Those results continue to assume strong linearizability. The checked full version therefore does not refute the ordinary wait-free target.

The OPODIS 2020 paper gives relaxed queues and stacks from read/write operations while repeating the exact Common2 queue question. System-wide nonblocking progress allows an individual process to starve; wait-freedom does not. Neither that weaker progress condition nor relaxed removal semantics answers the exact wait-free question.

The subsequent journal article retains the exact queue question in footnote 7. Its multiplicity and weak-emptiness variants alter the required responses: repeated removal of one occurrence or a weaker empty response does not meet the FIFO specification used here.
why: A queue orders work shared by concurrent processes. This question asks whether very weak synchronization suffices to guarantee that each continuing process finishes, even while others stop or interfere. It tests the distinction between consensus power and the ability to implement a reusable data type.
status_note: Explicitly open in the OPODIS 2015 article published in 2016 and again in the OPODIS 2022 article published in February 2023. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the unrestricted ordinary linearizable wait-free queue target. The checked 2025 and 2026 impossibility theorems assume strong linearizability; they are not refutations of this card. This status records dated source evidence, not exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2006: Stacks are shown to belong to Common2; the queue question is kept separate. | 2009-04-07: The revised preprint provides a queue with two enqueuers and any number of dequeuers. | 2016-10-13: The published OPODIS 2015 article explicitly states the unrestricted ordinary wait-free queue question. | 2020: The source supplies relaxed queue implementations and reiterates the open exact Common\(_{2}\) question for unrestricted finite process counts. | 2022-12-07: The later journal article retains the exact queue question in footnote 7. | 2023-02-15: The published OPODIS 2022 article still identifies Common2 queue membership as open while giving bounds with stronger primitives. | 2025-08-06: An impossibility theorem excludes strongly linearizable lock-free queues from the stated weak primitives. | 2026-07-01: The PODC paper extends strong-linearizability impossibilities; the checked full version retains that stronger hypothesis.
working_summary: Several named processes repeatedly insert arbitrary items into a first-in-first-out queue and remove the oldest remaining item. Only atomic read/write registers and initially unused test-and-set bits are available, with no fixed memory-capacity limit. For every fixed process count, the question asks for a deterministic implementation in which every continuing process finishes each operation despite arbitrary interference or crashes. Correctness requires ordinary linearizability, allowing a legal sequential explanation of every history without demanding one prefix-preserving choice across histories. Known restricted-role queues and impossibility theorems under strong linearizability do not settle this unrestricted target.

title: Deterministic volume gap
importance_reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.
formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with \(V_{A}(n)=o(n)\) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with \(V_{B}(n)=O(1+\log * n)\)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots ,|V(G)|^{2}\}\). Here \(V_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed \(\Delta \ge 2, a\) fixed verification radius \(r\ge 1\), finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, \(\Pi\) and the exact |\(V(G)|\), and visited set \(\{v\}\). It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. \(\log * n\) is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no \(O(\log * n)\)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every \(C>0\) and every \(n_{0}\), some \(n\ge n_{0}\) satisfies \(V_{B}(n)>C(1+\log * n)\). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.
why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.
status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2020: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume. | 2021: Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) can be sped up to deterministic \(O(\log * n)\). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL. | 2022: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above \(\log * n\) remains the issue here. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear. | 2026-07: Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity \(\Theta (\log ^{k} n)\) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.
working_summary: The VOLUME model measures how many graph vertices an adaptive local algorithm inspects to determine one requested output. Outputs from separate queries must still fit together into a single valid labeling. The conjecture says every deterministic locally checkable problem with sublinear worst-case volume actually has O(log-star n) volume. It concerns fixed bounded-degree graph families with exact size information and polynomially bounded identifiers. Proving the collapse would eliminate an entire intermediate range of deterministic local information complexity, despite the richer range available to randomized algorithms.

title: Factor-two graph distances in logarithmically many passes
importance_reason: A longstanding core graph-streaming problem with a sharply stated resource target inside a recently narrowed upper/lower bound gap. It tests the limits of repeated sequential access even for minimal single-pair output.
formal:
Can a randomized streaming algorithm estimate the distance between two specified vertices of an undirected, unweighted graph within a factor of two using \(O(\log n)\) passes and \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) bits of memory?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that the following holds for every simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every specified pair \(s,t\), and every ordering of its edges? The algorithm knows \(n,s,t\) before the stream begins, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\text{ passes},\]
and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs \(D\) satisfying
\[d_G(s,t)\le D\le2d_G(s,t).\]
For disconnected \(s,t\), success means outputting the symbol \(\infty\). All passes read the same edge order.
question_excerpt: McGregor asks how well the distance between two specified vertices can be estimated from an edge stream, particularly in O(log n) passes, and separately mentions random-order input. The user selected factor two, undirected unweighted graphs, arbitrary fixed edge order, success probability at least two thirds and semi-streaming bit space. These choices narrow the source to one decision question about algorithm existence.
definitions:
The input graph is finite, undirected, unweighted and simple: there are no self-loops or parallel edges. Its vertices have distinct binary labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\). Each edge appears exactly once as an unordered pair of labels. The stream lists these edges explicitly in an arbitrary order, with an end marker; it may be empty. Isolated vertices are included in the known vertex set even though they do not appear in any edge. No planarity, sparsity, degree or diameter restriction is imposed.

The vertices \(s,t\) belong to the known vertex set and are supplied before any edge is read. They may be equal. A path has length equal to its number of edges, and \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(s\) to \(t\). Set \(d_G(s,s)=0\) and \(d_G(s,t)=\infty\) if there is no connecting path. Every finite distance is an integer between zero and \(n-1\).

A pass scans the edge list once from beginning to end. After a pass the algorithm may rewind to the beginning and retain its memory, but it cannot reorder or change the stream. Within a pass it has only sequential access. There is no random access to old edges, adjacency-query oracle, external scratch file or separate stored copy of the graph. All passes encounter the same fixed order. The algorithm may stop after fewer passes than its bound; starting another scan counts as another pass.

The output is one integer \(D\) or the distinguished symbol \(\infty\). The algorithm need not output a path, a spanning tree, distances to other targets or a summary supporting later queries. Integer output loses no generality for this factor guarantee: rounding down a nonnegative real estimate in the permitted interval preserves both inequalities when the true distance is an integer. For a connected pair the successful output lies between \(d_G(s,t)\) and \(2d_G(s,t)\), with no additive error. For a disconnected pair the successful output is \(\infty\); for \(s=t\) it is zero.

For every fixed graph, edge ordering and pair, probability is over the algorithm's independent fair random bits. The input and its order are fixed independently of those bits. The success condition concerns the single requested output. It is not an average over graphs or stream orders, and it does not require one random seed to work for all inputs simultaneously.

Use one finite uniform program for every input size. Its memory consists of all mutable working information, including retained edge data, vertex labels, counters, stored random choices and output preparation. Every bit of that information counts. Fresh random bits may be read as needed, but old random bits cannot be revisited unless their information was retained within the space bound. The graph stream is read-only external input. The supplied parameters take only \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, so charging their storage does not change the target.

Both resource bounds hold throughout every execution, including unsuccessful random executions. The algorithm must halt and produce an output; no bound on local computation time is imposed beyond this termination requirement. Thus the question isolates memory and passes, as in the streaming source. Computationally expensive processing between edges cannot hide extra memory or reread the input. A polynomial local-time algorithm would suffice, but such a time requirement is not added to the target.

The constants \(C_s,C_p\) and the exponent \(k\) are fixed independently of \(n\), the graph, the stream order, the distance and the random choices. The memory notation \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) permits any fixed power of the logarithm. The pass bound permits only one power: an arbitrary \(O(\log^c n)\) bound for a fixed \(c>1\) is not the requested \(O(\log n)\) result. Binary logarithms with the harmless \(n+2\) offset avoid small-input exceptions.

The term semi-streaming refers to memory proportional to the number of vertices times a fixed power of the logarithm, even though a dense graph can have quadratically many edges. Papers often count \(O(\log n)\)-bit words rather than bits. This changes the permitted logarithmic power by one and therefore describes the same space class here. When a particular logarithmic space bound is quoted, its unit must still be stated.

The selected model is insertion-only and allows every fixed edge ordering. Edge deletions, random-order streams and a source or target revealed only after streaming are separately quantified variants. Likewise, all-pairs distances and single-source shortest-path trees ask for more output than this card. The original source combines several of these questions. With the user's approval, this card retains just factor-two estimation of one known pair in logarithmically many passes.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the algorithm and constants in the statement, including its success probability for every graph and order and its worst-case bit-space and pass bounds. Alternatively, provide a complete Lean-checked proof that no such uniform randomized algorithm exists. The negative direction must rule out every fixed polylogarithmic space exponent \(k\) together with an \(O(\log n)\) pass bound; a lower bound for one narrower space allowance does not suffice. A lower bound of only \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\), or an upper bound with \(O((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes, leaves the selected target unresolved. Improved constants, a larger approximation factor, an additive error, average-order correctness or correctness only for nearby vertices do not settle this exact resource-and-error question.
context:
A graph may contain far more edges than a small-memory algorithm can retain. One scan can reveal useful local connections, while a short path between distant vertices can depend on edges encountered in an inconvenient order. The question asks how much repeated access is needed even when only one numerical distance is requested.

The original discussion emphasizes spanners. An \((\alpha,\beta)\)-spanner is a subgraph \(H\) preserving all pairwise distances within \(d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\). Such a summary supports many pairs, whereas this card supplies its only pair in advance. Results that exploit all-pairs summaries do not by themselves characterize the best method for that smaller output requirement.

Exact distance can be obtained with a number of passes depending on the distance. That dependence can be large on arbitrary graphs. The selected target instead demands a logarithmic worst-case pass bound and permits a controlled multiplicative error.

The SODA 2026 result gives a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation in \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}(\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes using \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}n\log^3 n)\) words. Fixing \(\varepsilon=1/2\) meets the accuracy and bit-space requirements here, but the number of passes is asymptotically larger than \(O(\log n)\).

The same work proves a lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) passes for any constant approximation in semi-streaming space, even for one fixed pair in an unweighted graph. It also explains how its communication simulation accommodates the same order in every pass. This rules out substantially fewer passes while remaining compatible with the requested logarithmic upper bound.

A positive answer would improve the known number of scans for a basic distance query without requiring the whole graph in memory. A negative answer would establish a sharper limitation on what repeated sequential access can recover, even with a constant approximation and only one requested pair.
why: Shortest-path distance is a basic graph quantity whose global dependencies challenge small-memory sequential access. This question isolates the number of scans needed for a useful constant-factor estimate, between new near-logarithmic lower bounds and the best verified upper bounds.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 14, Kanpur 2006, updated 25 September 2016. The user selected factor-two single-pair estimation in O(log n) passes and O(n polylog n) bits. The SODA 2026 publication of Assadi–Hoppenworth–Sundaresan and its 21 October 2025 full version were checked on 16 September 2026. Their constant-factor upper bound uses O((log n/log log n)^2) passes; their lower bound is Omega(log n/log log n), including fixed-pair unweighted instances and a same-order simulation. These statements leave the selected target unresolved. A bounded later-work search found no verified closure of this gap. No new algorithm, lower-bound proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

title: Linear-sketch complexity of the nuclear norm
importance_reason: A long-standing quantitative question about a standard matrix norm in the general sketching model. Its importance comes from the gap between neighboring norms, applications of compact matrix summaries, and the need to distinguish arbitrary linear measurements from restricted sketches and bit-space bounds.
formal:
Determine the optimal number \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) of exact real linear measurements required to estimate the nuclear norm of an arbitrary real \(n\times n\) matrix with relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\), up to matching constant factors in \(n\), for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

The sketch is randomized and chosen independently of the input matrix. It must satisfy, for every fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\),
\[\Pr_\omega\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\le d_\omega(S_\omega A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\right]\ge\frac23,\]
where \(S_\omega:\mathbb R^{n\times n}\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(d_\omega\) is a decoder that receives only the sketch and the input-independent random choices. The quantity \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) is the smallest possible dimension \(m\).

Give an explicit asymptotic description \(g(n,\varepsilon)\) and prove that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) there exist \(0<c_\varepsilon\le C_\varepsilon<\infty\) and \(N_\varepsilon\) such that
\[c_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge N_\varepsilon).\]
The constants may depend on the fixed accuracy, but not on \(n\). Logarithmic factors in \(n\) must be resolved; determining only a polynomial exponent does not meet this target.
question_excerpt: Woodruff asks for the optimal dimension of a linear sketch that approximates the Schatten-1, or nuclear, norm within a constant factor. The question contrasts it with the much better understood Frobenius and spectral norms.
definitions:
Let \(n\) be any positive integer. For a real square matrix \(A\), its singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_n(A)\) are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\), with multiplicities and zeros included. Its nuclear norm, also called the trace norm or Schatten-1 norm, is
\[\|A\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i(A).\]
No symmetry, positive-semidefiniteness, rank, sparsity, integrality or bounded-entry promise is imposed. In particular, this is not the entrywise sum of absolute values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues, and for that restricted class the nuclear norm equals the trace; the target covers all real matrices.

An \(m\)-measurement randomized linear sketch for given \(n,\varepsilon\) is specified by an input-independent probability space of random seeds \(\omega\), a real linear map \(S_\omega\), and a decoding function \(d_\omega:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\). Equivalently, each measurement has the form
\[(S_\omega A)_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n B_{tij}(\omega)A_{ij},\qquad1\le t\le m,\]
where all coefficients are fixed once the seed is sampled, before inspecting any entry of \(A\). The map may depend on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(A\). The seed may also specify independent decoder randomness. The coefficient functions and the combined decoding map \((\omega,y)\mapsto d_\omega(y)\) are measurable with respect to their probability space and the usual Borel sigma-algebra on finite-dimensional real spaces, so every displayed success probability is defined.

All randomness is over the seed. The matrix is fixed before that seed is chosen, with the quantifier order \(\exists\text{ sketch distribution}\;\forall A\;\Pr_\omega[\text{success on }A]\ge2/3\). The same seed need not work simultaneously for all matrices. Conversely, a guarantee only for a random input matrix is insufficient. For \(A=0\), success requires the output to be exactly zero. For nonzero inputs the error bound is multiplicative, equivalently \(|d_\omega(S_\omega A)-\|A\|_*|\le\varepsilon\|A\|_*\).

The cost is the fixed number \(m\) of data-dependent real scalars retained. Coefficients, measurements and arithmetic are exact real objects. Their bit lengths, the description of the seed, evaluation time, and the decoder's auxiliary working space are not counted. No finite-precision or efficient-sampling requirement is added. The decoder can be nonlinear and have unbounded computational cost. This is an information measure for general linear sketches, not a claim of a Turing-machine implementation. Separate choices of distribution and decoder for each \(n,\varepsilon\) are allowed; an algorithm constructing them uniformly in polynomial time is not part of the target.

Define
\[m_\varepsilon(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{ an admissible }m\text{-measurement sketch satisfies the stated guarantee}\}.\]
This minimum is finite and attained as a minimum over integers: retaining all \(n^2\) entries is a linear sketch from which the norm is defined exactly. The target seeks a noncircular asymptotic description of this optimization, with upper bounds witnessed by admissible sketch distributions and lower bounds applying to every such distribution and decoder.

A restricted bilinear sketch retains a matrix \(UAV\) for input-independent matrices \(U\) and \(V\); its scalar entry count is one possible general linear-sketch dimension. General sketches are not restricted to this form. Lower bounds for one selected architecture do not automatically extend to all real linear maps. Likewise, bits of streaming memory and real measurement dimension are different resources. An entry update can be reflected linearly in the sketch, but this does not identify the number of exact counters with their finite binary storage cost.

The source asks for a constant-factor approximation without fixing the constant. This review spells out the family of fixed relative accuracies \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with constant success probability \(2/3\), in the standard model made explicit in the subsequent literature. Each accuracy is held constant while \(n\to\infty\); the answer need not optimize a joint regime where \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\). The requested precision for the optimal dimension is equality of asymptotic order up to multiplicative constants, including every unbounded logarithmic factor.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular asymptotic description of \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with the quantifiers and input domain above. An upper bound must give a valid input-independent sketch and decoder with the per-matrix success guarantee. A lower bound must apply to arbitrary measurable decoders and all general randomized real linear maps. Bounds matching only up to polylogarithmic factors, only the exponent in \(n^{\alpha+o(1)}\), a result confined to positive semidefinite matrices, or a finite-bit streaming bound alone do not determine the requested order. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the sketch's relative error; the benchmark's default additive numerical tolerance does not replace the required asymptotic precision.
context:
The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.
why: Determining this complexity would explain whether summing singular values permits a materially smaller linear summary than storing a general matrix, and exactly how much compression is possible. It would also locate a central matrix norm within the sharply differing sketching behavior of the Schatten family.
status_note: The exact asymptotic order up to constant factors remains source-open in the checked material. The original question is Woodruff’s 2014 survey Open Question 4. The 2019 journal article’s model and linear lower bound were checked. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found Yang’s arXiv:2608.22247v3, revised 27 August 2026: its stated near-quadratic lower and upper bounds leave logarithmic factors unresolved, as explicitly discussed in §6. This review inspected its model, theorem statement and remaining-gap discussion, not a full independent verification of its 94-page proof; no verified journal acceptance is asserted. The recent bounds are therefore identified as preprint claims, and even as stated they do not complete this card’s matching-constant-factor criterion.

The same paper distinguishes this statement from bilinear-sketch and finite-bit streaming results. | 27 August 2026: Preprint v3 of Yang claims bounds within polylogarithmic factors of \(n^2\), together with an upper bound saving a logarithmic factor up to iterated logarithms.
