working_summary: The nuclear norm of a matrix is the sum of its singular values. The question asks for the smallest number of randomized exact real linear measurements that suffice to approximate this norm for every fixed input matrix. The requested answer must give matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors for each fixed relative accuracy. Published results separate this matrix problem from ordinary vector norms, bilinear sketches and finite-bit streaming complexity. An August 2026 preprint claims near-quadratic bounds but leaves logarithmic factors unresolved, and its proof is not independently verified by this review.

title: One-pass semi-streaming depth-first search
importance_reason: A basic and broadly used graph primitive with a concrete pass-versus-memory barrier. Its significance comes from separating arbitrary connectivity certificates from DFS structure on dense streams, not from the age of the source; current status is explicitly uncertain.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm and fixed constants \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\) that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices, outputs a depth-first-search spanning tree using at most
\[C n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory, with probability at least \(2/3\) for every ordering of its edge stream?

The stream lists each edge once, contains no deletions, and can only be scanned from beginning to end. The algorithm may choose the root and neighbor order of the DFS tree. The question concerns the memory and pass bounds, with no additional polynomial-time requirement.
question_excerpt: The 2020 paper explicitly asks whether DFS-tree computation needs more than one pass with semi-streaming memory. It treats connected simple undirected graphs and distinguishes insertion-only lower bounds from stronger insertion-deletion upper bounds.
definitions:
The graph has labelled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is connected and undirected, and has no self-loops or parallel edges. The algorithm is given \(n\) in advance. Its input stream is an arbitrary permutation of the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\), represented by the two binary vertex labels, followed by an end marker. No adjacency lists, neighbor-query oracle, random access to the graph or second scan are available. The empty stream for \(n=1\) is valid. The requirement is a promise on these well-formed connected graph streams; recognition of the promise is not an additional task.

A rooted spanning tree \(T\) consists of a root \(r\in V\) and one parent in \(V\) for each other vertex, with every parent edge belonging to \(E\). Following parents must reach \(r\) and visit no cycle. A vertex \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) when it lies on the tree path from \(r\) to \(v\). The required DFS condition is
\[\forall\{u,v\}\in E:\quad u\text{ is an ancestor of }v\ \text{or}\ v\text{ is an ancestor of }u.\]
For undirected graphs this characterizes a spanning tree obtainable by depth-first search: start at the root, recursively finish exploring a newly discovered neighbor before exploring another, and retain the edges used for first discovery. The root and each vertex's order of neighbors may be chosen by the algorithm. No prescribed or lexicographic traversal must be reproduced, and the neighbor order need not equal edge-arrival order. An arbitrary spanning tree need not satisfy the ancestor condition.

The output is an explicit root and parent table on all \(n\) labels; for \(n=1\), the sole vertex is the root. It has \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits. The output may be produced after the stream ends using only retained memory and fresh randomness. A write-only output tape cannot be reread as extra storage. Deferring the output to the end does not change semi-streaming feasibility: an earlier root/parent output of this size could instead be retained within the same asymptotic memory regime.

The algorithm has a single finite description, independent of \(n\) and of the graph. It processes the input in one left-to-right pass and may keep at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^k\) bits at any time, including retained edges, summaries, counters, random seeds, temporary computation and postprocessing. The bound is worst case over valid streams and random choices. No advice or external writable storage is allowed. Fresh fair random bits are independent of the graph and edge order; old random bits can be accessed again only if retained within the memory bound. The algorithm must finish processing and produce an output with probability one, but no numerical bound on its processing time is imposed. In particular, the question does not silently add efficient offline computation to the streaming space restriction.

For every fixed \(G\) and every fixed edge permutation chosen before the random bits, the probability that the entire root/parent table is a valid DFS tree must be at least \(2/3\). An invalid tree or failure symbol counts as failure. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case. This is a guarantee on arbitrary graphs and orders, not on random graphs or random-order streams.

Semi-streaming space here means \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits with one fixed exponent. A word of \(O(\log n)\) bits changes only that exponent, but arbitrary-precision words do not have unit storage cost. The source studies both insertion-only and insertion-deletion streams and states its lower-bound convention for insertion-only streams. This card retains the one-pass question in that basic insertion-only setting. A result only for streams with deletions would not refute it, while an algorithm handling deletions would be a stronger positive result.

A negative answer means that no pair of constants \(C,k\) and no such randomized algorithm works on every promised stream. It need not establish a full quadratic-space lower bound: any lower bound excluding \(n(\log n)^k\) for every fixed \(k\) would suffice. Extra passes, a restriction to sparse graphs with \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) edges, or a prescribed traversal order change the problem.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its logical negation in the stated insertion-only streaming model. A positive answer must prove that one algorithm makes one pass, respects its worst-case bit-space bound including postprocessing, terminates with probability one, and outputs some valid DFS tree with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid graph and edge order. A negative answer must exclude all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and all allowed randomized algorithms, without relying on a processing-time limitation absent from the model. A lower bound only for a prescribed traversal, directed graphs, streams with deletions or deterministic algorithms does not suffice. Experiments, random-graph guarantees, and a many-pass algorithm do not settle the target. The output is exact; numerical tolerance does not apply.
context:
Ordinary depth-first search takes linear time when the entire graph is available in memory. The challenge here is that edges needed later in the traversal may have already passed by, and the full dense graph cannot be retained.

Finding some spanning tree is possible with near-linear memory in one pass. A DFS tree has the additional global ancestor condition: every edge must connect comparable vertices in the rooted tree. On a triangle, a star rooted at its center is a spanning tree but is not a DFS tree, because the two leaves are adjacent.

The source’s Theorem 4 gives a deterministic insertion-only algorithm with \(p\) passes and \(\widetilde O(n^2/p^2)\) bits, for \(1\le p\le\sqrt n\). At \(p\) of order \(\sqrt n\), this yields semi-streaming space, while at one pass its bound is quadratic. The quoted draft missed this improvement from the very paper containing the question.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.
why: DFS is a basic graph decomposition tool whose required ancestor structure is stronger than connectivity or an arbitrary spanning tree. Resolving its one-pass feasibility would explain whether near-linear memory can retain enough information for this globally constrained traversal without revisiting edges.
status_note: The exact one-pass question is explicitly open in the checked STACS 2020 source, and the 2024 engineering paper records the existing many-pass bounds rather than a general one-pass algorithm. Current status is uncertain: the introduction of Konrad–Trehan, ESA 2025 p.22:2 (also arXiv:2508.16022v1), states that subquadratic-space BFS/DFS algorithms do not exist, citing Cormode–Dark–Konrad 2019 and Assadi–Chen–Khanna 2019. On 16 September 2026 this review followed both citations; their inspected statements establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds, and text searches and relevant theorem readings did not locate a DFS lower bound or a reduction supporting the assertion. The 2025 statement is not used as a verified resolution, but the conflict prevents a confident current-open certification. Bounded additional searches located no matching theorem. This is a completed formulation and evidence review with its status limit retained.
progress: 2020: The paper explicitly leaves the one-pass question open and gives square-root-pass semi-streaming algorithms, including a deterministic insertion-only tradeoff. | 2024: The engineering study improves practical pass counts and distinguishes theoretical worst-case bounds from experiments and random-graph properties. | 2025 assertion checked in September 2026: The long-path paper contains a conflicting introductory DFS lower-bound assertion. Following its two citations located maximal-independent-set results, without identifying a theorem resolving this DFS question. This review does not certify that assertion.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary-order stream of edges of a connected undirected graph. The task is to output any DFS spanning tree in one pass using nearly linear bit memory. The tree must place the endpoints of every graph edge in an ancestor relationship, beyond ordinary connectivity. The original paper gives many-pass tradeoffs, while practical one-pass observations apply only to evaluated or special inputs. Current status remains uncertain because a later introductory lower-bound assertion was not substantiated by its cited results.

title: Local certificate size versus verification radius
importance_reason: The tradeoff asks whether increased local visibility can universally replace stored proof information, even for graph properties with constant-size certificates. This probes a basic resource relationship in distributed verification and the memory needed for locally checkable evidence, beyond any single graph problem.
formal: Determine the worst-case certificate-size function \[F(s,d)=\max\{c_d(P):P\text{ is a graph property and }c_1(P)\le s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\] in the anonymous local-verification model defined below. Here \(c_d(P)\) is the minimum number of certificate bits per vertex permitting sound and complete verification of \(P\) at radius \(d\), uniformly over all finite graphs. This asks for the whole numerical tradeoff, with pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\), rather than only a yes-or-no answer to the source’s proposed inverse-radius scaling.
question_excerpt: Is it true that if we allow the verification algorithm to look at distance d, then the optimal size is at most \(\alpha  \cdot  s/d [\ldots ]\)
definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.
context:
Open problem 2 asks whether allowing distance \(d\) reduces optimal certificate size \(s\) to at most a constant times \(s/d\), including dependence on the parameters of local properties. It does not specify all rounding and uniformity conventions for a numerical benchmark.

This card explicitly selects the source’s anonymous model and the branch of unlabeled graph properties admitting a constant certificate bound for all graph orders. It broadens the threshold question to the underlying worst-case function \(F(s,d)\), following the authorized quantity/function review. Determining this function is a stronger quantitative target, not an assertion that it is equivalent to every version of the source conjecture. Identifier-dependent models, properties with separate vertex inputs and bounds growing with graph order are outside this selected branch.

The radius view follows Definition 15, including the omission of edges between outer-boundary vertices. A finite terminating verification program fixes computational uniformity, while local running time is unrestricted.

The source proves that anonymous radius-one certification of \(k\)-colorability requires exactly \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) bits. Its larger-radius lower bound and upper bounds for selected properties illustrate the tradeoff, without establishing a universal compression theorem.

The later paper on decreasing verification radius studies how certificate sizes grow when a verifier must see less. Its bounds for that direction do not determine the cost of increasing the radius in the model of this card.

The 2025 complexity-landscape paper studies possible certificate growth rates on paths, cycles and trees, with distinctions involving identifiers and knowledge of graph order. These are different from the full worst-case function for constant certificate bounds on arbitrary graphs.
why: Local certificates let every vertex check a global claim using a small neighborhood. Understanding their dependence on verification radius would distinguish properties for which additional communication reliably reduces stored proof information from properties that retain an irreducible local memory cost.
status_note: The inverse-radius question is explicitly open in the 2024 source. This card documents a selected anonymous branch and a stronger full-function target. Checked later radius-reduction, certification-landscape and local-advice results do not determine it; later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.
progress: 2024: The STACS paper formulates the tradeoff conjecture, gives an exact anonymous radius-one bound for colorability, and proves radius tradeoffs for several specific properties. | 2024-08-20: The checked preprint on decreasing verification radius studies the reverse conversion and its dependence on degree, radius loss, certificate length and input size. | 2025: The DISC paper develops a complexity landscape on several graph classes. Its results do not identify the full function specified here.
working_summary: Local certification assigns a short proof string to every vertex so that a global graph property can be checked from nearby information. The selected model has no identifiers or input labels, and certificate bounds must hold uniformly over all finite graphs. For each initial bit budget and verification radius, the target is the largest minimum certificate size among properties certifiable within that budget at radius one. The source asks whether certificate size always scales inversely with radius; this card explicitly asks for the full underlying worst-case function. Determining the function would quantify when greater local visibility can replace stored proof information, with a Lean-certified error of at most one hundredth of a bit at every parameter pair.

title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.
formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. Gate descriptions use binary indices in topological order and specify the output gate. There is no advice or oracle. The constants, circuit generator and gate basis are independent of the instance. Randomized error is not allowed; no time \(t\) is supplied as part of the instance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of membership of this language in the specified uniform circuit class, or a complete Lean proof that no such circuit family and generator exist. Polynomial sequential simulation alone is insufficient. A proof of P-completeness under logspace reductions would imply nonmembership only with the additional assumption that P differs from NC; it is not an unconditional negative answer.
context:
The 2025 source defines eventual prediction from a finite stable configuration plus one grain on the infinite lattice. This card retains that decision question for the ordinary four-neighbor rule, with an explicit array encoding, and asks for its NC-membership branch. It does not ask for an entire final configuration or a toppling at a supplied time.

Moore and Nilsson establish \(\mathrm{NC}^3\) prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three, in their finite-lattice formulation. Their two-dimensional discussion remains a foundational motivation; the direct definition used here comes from the 2025 infinite-lattice source.

The June 2026 paper continues to describe ordinary planar prediction as unsettled while studying weighted and nonuniform variants. Its formal finite-grid model includes a sink at the boundary. That convention is distinguished from the zero-extended infinite lattice fixed here.

The March 2026 fungal-automaton result concerns alternating horizontal and vertical update rules. It does not provide a classification of the simultaneous four-neighbor dynamics in this card.
why: One extra grain can trigger a long deterministic cascade. Whether its eventual effect can always be computed in polylogarithmic parallel time is a canonical test of how much sequential dependence a simple physical process can express.
status_note: Source-open for the retained standard four-neighbor eventual-prediction question. The 2025 source explicitly gives its infinite-lattice definition; the June 2026 preprint still treats ordinary planar prediction as unresolved while using a different finite-grid model for its variant results. Checked on 2026-09-16 with a bounded later search. No exhaustive current-openness or independent proof-verification claim is made.

Adding one grain triggers simultaneous topplings, each sending one grain in each of the four cardinal directions. The question asks whether a specified cell ever topples, without giving a time bound in the input. The desired computation uses one uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth Boolean circuits on the full explicit input. Known results for other dimensions, weighted grids, boundary sinks or alternating update schemes do not settle this precisely specified planar question.

title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
importance_reason: A unifying classification problem for streaming dissimilarity estimation, extending both norm-based geometry and the known one-variable aggregation framework.
formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.
context:
The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.
why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.
status_note: The source asks for a broad characterization. This card explicitly fixes an effective separable streaming variant rather than attributing every resource convention to the source. The 2016 one-variable result is only a partial classification, and the later metric counterexample concerns another model. No full characterization for the specified domain was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2006: Guha and Indyk pose the broad distance-sketchability question and discuss separable coordinate costs. | 2016: Braverman and coauthors classify nearly all one-variable frequency aggregates and explicitly identify the result as a partial answer for difference-based dissimilarities. | 2019: Khot and Naor show that the norm-sketchability characterization does not extend to arbitrary metrics.
working_summary: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates. The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative. The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations. The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs. Known offset obstructions, difference-based aggregate classifications and norm-sketching results cover only parts of this domain.

title: Linear-round weighted APSP in CONGEST
importance_reason: Foundational exact distributed-distance task with a sharp information lower bound and a major near-linear upper bound. The remaining strict-linear question tests coordination overhead; it is a narrower residual gap than the original polynomial-gap challenge.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm and a constant \(C_b\) that, on every connected simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \(\{0,\ldots,n^b\}\), outputs all exact weighted distances at their respective vertices within \(C_b n\) communication rounds, with probability at least \(2/3\) that all outputs are correct simultaneously?

The bound must hold on every execution, for all \(n\ge2\). “Linear” means \(O(n)\) with no factor growing with \(n\); a bound \(\widetilde O(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) does not meet the target.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths can be computed in linear CONGEST time, after proving a linear lower bound and a limitation of the standard two-party lower-bound framework.
definitions:
The communication network is the input graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). It has \(n\ge2\) vertices, no loops or parallel edges, is connected, and has nonnegative integer edge weights. For a fixed \(b\), each weight lies between 0 and \(n^b\) inclusive and is represented in binary. A vertex is a processor with a unique identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It initially knows \(n\), \(b\), its own identifier, the identifiers of its neighbors and the weights of its incident edges, but no other part of the topology or other edge weights. The requirement holds for all labelled graphs and therefore all assignments of these identifiers. The usual polynomial-size identifier range is equivalent for this target because identifiers can be renamed in \(O(n)\) rounds.

Computation is synchronous. In each round each endpoint of each edge can send the other endpoint a message of at most \(B_b\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, for a fixed constant \(B_b\). Both directions operate independently and different neighbors may receive different messages. All messages sent in a round arrive before the next round. Communication is allowed only along edges of \(G\); there are no additional links between non-neighbors. Edge weights affect shortest-path lengths, not message latency or bandwidth. Local storage and finite local computation are unrestricted and uncharged; only the number of communication rounds is counted. The local rules form one finite, computable program, fixed for all \(n\) and inputs, with no topology-dependent advice or preprocessing.

Randomized processors use independent private fair random bits. For every fixed graph, weights and identifier assignment, probability is over these bits. By the prescribed worst-case round deadline every processor must halt and produce its output; an invalid or incomplete output counts as failure. The success event requires all vertices' entire distance tables to be correct in the same execution, with probability at least \(2/3\). Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. No average over graphs or identifier assignments is used.

For vertices \(u,v\), define
\[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e),\qquad d_G(u,u)=0.\]
The minimum may be taken over simple paths, since weights are nonnegative. Each vertex \(v\) must output the labelled table \(\{(u,d_G(u,v)):u\in V\}\). Distances are finite integers of at most \((n-1)n^b\); zero-weight edges and equal-length alternative paths are allowed. The output is the exact distance table, without a requirement to list every path. Output and retained local tables are local memory, not extra communication channels.

The constants, bandwidth bound and program may depend on \(b\), but not on \(n\), graph density, diameter, individual weights or the random choices. At most \(C_b n\) rounds are allowed on every execution. There is no message-count bound beyond the per-edge per-round bandwidth. The source's linear-time question is retained literally. The explicit bounded-error convention uses one fixed constant global success probability; it does not impose an additional failure probability tending to zero with \(n\). The source's nonnegative polynomially bounded integer-weight setting includes the zero-weight edges used in its lower-bound example.

The proposition's negation says that for some fixed \(b\), no such uniform bounded-error algorithm has a linear worst-case round bound on all instances. It does not demand an \(\Omega(n^{1+\delta})\) lower bound for a fixed positive \(\delta\); a rigorously unavoidable unbounded logarithmic or slower factor could already refute linear time. The notation \(\widetilde O(n)\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors and therefore must not be read as \(O(n)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated linear-round existence proposition. A positive answer must give, for every fixed weight exponent \(b\), a uniform protocol with the stated bandwidth, worst-case \(C_b n\) deadline and simultaneous exact correctness probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. A negative answer must rule out every such protocol for at least one fixed \(b\), preserving the communication and randomness conventions. A near-linear bound with an unbounded factor, approximate distances, a result only for unweighted graphs, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an algorithm with communication links outside the input graph is insufficient. Neither an expected-time bound alone nor a per-vertex success probability alone supplies the stated guarantee. The target is exact asymptotic linearity; numerical error tolerance does not apply.
context:
Every node needs an entire row of the distance matrix, yet communication occurs only through the original network. The task therefore combines many shortest-path computations that compete for the same bounded-capacity links.

The 2017 source proves an \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound even on a weighted graph with a constant hop diameter. Its example encodes many edge weights that must pass through one communication link. Thus dependence on the network diameter alone cannot describe the cost of this problem.

The same source shows that its standard two-party reduction with a fixed partition of the vertices cannot yield a superlinear weighted-APSP lower bound. This is a theorem about the scope of that reduction framework, not an \(O(n)\) algorithm or a general impossibility of stronger lower bounds.

Bernstein and Nanongkai subsequently obtain a randomized Las Vegas \(\widetilde O(n)\)-round algorithm for exact weighted APSP, with additional generality including directed inputs. Their analysis retains polylogarithmic overhead, so it resolves the near-linear question without establishing the literal linear bound of this card.

The 2025 message-complexity paper still cites that \(\widetilde O(n)\) randomized round bound. Its own weighted-APSP result uses \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) messages and \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) rounds. Minimizing total messages and eliminating the logarithmic overhead in rounds are different objectives.

A resolution would determine whether the information-transfer lower bound fully captures exact weighted distance computation, or whether coordinating distance information imposes an additional asymptotic cost. The remaining gap concerns factors suppressed by near-linear notation, rather than the large polynomial gap present in 2017.
why: Exact APSP is a central global task in bandwidth-limited networks. Closing the remaining logarithmic gap would identify whether transmitting the necessary information is the only asymptotic obstacle, while respecting the established near-linear breakthrough rather than treating its older polynomial gap as open.
status_note: Source-open for the literal O(n)-round question in the 2017 paper. On 16 September 2026 the source model, Theorems 9–10 and Lemma 11 were checked, together with Bernstein–Nanongkai’s STOC 2019 near-linear algorithm and its explicit polylogarithmic overhead. The April 2025 message-complexity preprint still records that near-linear round result; its own improvement concerns message count. Bounded later-result searches did not locate an O(n) protocol or a superlinear lower bound for the specified randomized model. The newer paper is evidence about the known near-linear bound, not an explicit exhaustive certification that the literal O(n) question remains open.
progress: 2017: The source proves the linear lower bound, establishes the fixed-partition two-party limitation, and asks for a linear-round algorithm. | 2019: The STOC result gives exact randomized APSP in \(\widetilde O(n)\) rounds. Its logarithmic factors are explicitly retained in the proof and do not certify \(O(n)\). | 2025: The message-complexity preprint records the near-linear round bound while giving a separate improvement in total messages.
working_summary: Every node in a weighted network must learn its exact distance to every other node. Messages are limited to logarithmically many bits per edge and round, with communication only along the input network. The target is a uniform randomized algorithm using a truly linear number of rounds and succeeding globally with constant probability. A linear lower bound and a randomized near-linear upper bound are known, leaving factors hidden by polylogarithmic notation. A complete answer must prove the literal linear bound or rule it out in this same model.

title: Optimal clique-detection rounds in CONGEST
importance_reason: Clique detection is a central distributed subgraph problem whose optimal communication cost remains distinct from the better-understood task of listing all cliques.
formal:
Determine the optimal randomized round complexity
\[
T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)
\]
of detecting an \(\ell\)-vertex clique in an \(n\)-vertex communication graph, when each directed use of an edge can carry \(b\) bits per round. The parameter domain is
\[
n\ge16,\qquad 4\le\ell\le\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad b\ge1,
\]
with all three parameters integers.

The requested answer is an explicit asymptotic expression \(F(n,\ell,b)>0\) and absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that, throughout this domain,
\[
cF(n,\ell,b)\le T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)
                 \le CF(n,\ell,b).
\]
The constants may not depend on \(n,\ell,b\). Polylogarithmic uncertainty is not sufficient. This full constant-factor target, rather than the historical question of whether a linear number of rounds is necessary, is the explicit user choice.
question_excerpt: The source leaves a gap between its bandwidth-dependent square-root lower bound for clique detection and the linear-round algorithm then known, and asks how much communication detecting cliques actually requires.
definitions:
The input is any finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|=n\); it need not be connected. A clique of size \(\ell\) is a set of \(\ell\) distinct vertices every two of which are adjacent. The communication links are exactly the edges of \(G\), with communication possible in both directions. Nodes have distinct identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\), under an arbitrary assignment. Initially a node knows \(n,\ell,b\), its own identifier and the identifiers of all its neighbors, but no other edges. There is no instance-dependent advice or free preprocessing.

In a synchronous round, each node performs arbitrary finite local computation and sends one \(b\)-bit word to each neighbor, possibly a different word on every incident edge. Padding permits shorter content; there is no additional uncharged message channel. All of these words arrive at the end of the round, so a word sent in that round cannot depend on a word received in the same round. Nodes use independent private random bits. Local memory, computation and random-bit generation are uncharged, but each local phase terminates. The algorithm is one finite effective program that operates for every valid \(n,\ell,b\) and every identifier assignment.

At termination each node outputs one bit. On each input, with probability at least \(2/3\), the disjunction of all output bits equals the indicator that \(G\) contains an \(\ell\)-clique. Equivalently, a clique-containing graph must cause at least one node to output one, and a clique-free graph must cause all nodes to output zero, each with the stated joint probability. Either kind of error is allowed outside the successful event. The node outputting one need not belong to a clique or output its vertices. Nodes are not required to enumerate cliques, decide their own membership in a clique, or all learn the answer.

For an admissible algorithm \(A\), let \(r_A(n,\ell,b)\) be the least nonnegative integer bounding its number of rounds on every \(n\)-vertex graph, every identifier assignment and every random execution for those parameters; put \(r_A=\infty\) when no such finite bound exists. Define
\[
T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)=\inf_A r_A(n,\ell,b),
\]
where the infimum ranges over all uniform algorithms satisfying the correctness requirement on the entire parameter domain. Cost is thus worst-case bounded rounds, not expected rounds. The infimum is pointwise in the displayed parameters; admissibility never permits an algorithm that is correct only for a selected graph or parameter tuple.

The bandwidth \(b\) is an explicit positive integer, including values outside the usual \(b=\Theta(\log n)\) specialization. Both directions of an edge have their own \(b\)-bit capacity in each round. This is ordinary CONGEST, with different messages permitted for different neighbors. There are no direct links between nonneighbors. An explicit expression for \(F\) must characterize the dependence on the three integers; merely renaming the optimization defining \(T_{\mathrm{det}}\) is not an answer.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds within absolute constant factors for the entire specified parameter domain. The upper bound must be realized in the stated detection model, and the lower bound must apply to every admissible randomized algorithm. A bound only for listing all cliques, for broadcast communication, for fixed \(\ell\) with constants depending on \(\ell\), or only at logarithmic bandwidth does not by itself determine the requested function. The selected acceptance tolerance is multiplicative by absolute constants; additive \(1/100\) error is not the criterion for this asymptotic resource function.
context:
The conference source proves a lower bound of \(\Omega(\sqrt n/b)\) in the range \(4\le\ell=O(\sqrt n)\), and a corresponding \(n/(\ell b)\) scale for larger cliques. At standard logarithmic bandwidth, it compares this with a linear-round upper bound.

The source also establishes a limitation of its two-party vertex-partition method for obtaining stronger clique lower bounds. That is a statement about the scope of the proof method, not an algorithm attaining the lower bound in a distributed network.

The SODA 2021 result lists all \(\ell\)-cliques in \(\widetilde O(n^{1-2/\ell})\) rounds for each fixed \(\ell\ge4\), at standard logarithmic bandwidth. It therefore also gives sublinear detection for every fixed clique size. The tilde hides polylogarithmic factors.

For \(\ell=4\), that upper bound matches the known detection lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. This does not establish a constant-factor formula even for this specialization.

For larger cliques, the paper’s matching general lower bound concerns listing, which requires reporting every occurrence. It cannot be transferred to existential detection merely because listing implies detection. Constants or other losses in a fixed-clique-size statement also cannot silently be taken as uniform when clique size grows.

The later journal presentation uses a high-probability detection convention. This card explicitly retains the constant-success convention of the original conference question and treats its full bandwidth dependence as the selected editorial continuation.
why: A network can contain a dense local pattern without any one processor initially knowing all of its edges. The question measures how much communication is intrinsically needed merely to detect that pattern. Resolving the full parameter dependence would distinguish the cost of establishing existence from the cost of enumerating every occurrence.
status_note: The historical possibility of sublinear rounds is settled positively for every fixed clique size at standard logarithmic bandwidth. The user instead selected a constant-factor characterization of detection complexity throughout the stated three-parameter domain. The checked tight listing theorem does not supply that characterization: its general listing lower bound is not a detection lower bound, and even its K4 comparison hides polylogarithmic factors. No resolution of the selected full target was found in this bounded review.
progress: 2018: The source proves the bandwidth-dependent detection lower bound and states the remaining gap. | 2020-11-14: The clique-listing preprint announces the fixed-size upper bounds and the K4 detection comparison. | 2021: The listing result appears at SODA, settling sublinear detectability for each fixed clique size at standard bandwidth. | 2026-09-16: The user selects the full optimal-rounds function within absolute constant factors; the review fixes detection, probability, initial-information and bandwidth conventions.
working_summary: The input graph is also the communication network, and each edge carries at most b bits in each direction per round. The task is for some processor to report that a clique of the requested size exists, with joint success probability at least two thirds. The selected question asks for the optimal number of rounds as a function of graph size, clique size and bandwidth, within absolute constant factors. Known clique-listing algorithms already give sublinear detection for every fixed clique size at logarithmic bandwidth. Their tightness for listing does not settle the full detection function, and even the known four-clique comparison retains polylogarithmic uncertainty.

title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
importance_reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the minimum worst-case round complexity \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) for computing an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected graph on \(n\) labelled vertices in the deterministic unicast congested clique defined below. The output is distributed: each processor outputs the membership bit of its own vertex in one common maximum independent set. Local computation and storage have no resource bound, but each local computation must terminate. Only synchronous communication rounds are charged.
definitions: For every integer \(n\ge2\), the vertices and processors have identifiers \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An input is a simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), represented at processor \(v\) by its \(n\)-bit incident-edge row. Initially each processor knows only this row, its own identifier, \(n\), all identifiers and the common protocol; it has no information about edges not incident to it. The communication network is complete, independently of \(E\). Let \(b(n)=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). In each round and for each ordered pair of distinct processors, the sender supplies one \(b(n)\)-bit string; shorter payloads must use a fixed padded encoding within that string. Different recipients may receive different strings. All messages for a round depend only on the initial state and messages from earlier rounds, and arrive simultaneously at its end. Local computations are deterministic, with finite descriptions and arbitrary finite local memory; no random coins, advice depending on the input graph, or additional communication channel are available. For fixed \(n\), a protocol may depend on \(n\), but it must work for every labelled graph of that size. All processors must produce their final bits after at most its round bound; their set \(S\) must satisfy both independence, \(\{u,v\}\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\), and optimality, \(|S|\ge |I|\) for every independent \(I\subseteq[n]\). Ties between maximum sets are unrestricted, provided the output bits describe one such set. Define \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) as the least integer round bound of any such protocol, taking the worst case over all input graphs. There is no promise on density or graph structure. This retains the earlier card’s deterministic, logarithmic-bandwidth specialization of the source’s broader question with bandwidth \(b\).
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous nonnegative asymptotic function \(f(n)\), a computably specified family of correct deterministic protocols, and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), the supplied protocol uses at most \(Cf(n)\) rounds on every input graph, while every correct protocol for that size needs at least \(cf(n)\) rounds on some graph. Thus \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)=\Theta(f(n))\) in precisely the stated model. The upper-bound family must be described by one finite procedure taking \(n\), whose local computation is uncharged. Logarithmically separated bounds, a conditional lower bound alone, approximate solutions, or maximal rather than maximum independent sets are insufficient. This is an asymptotic communication-complexity target; the numerical absolute-error convention does not apply to its big-Theta bounds.
context:
Each processor starts with a different overlapping portion of the same graph. A processor may talk directly to any other vertex, including vertices that are nonadjacent in the input. The output nevertheless has to describe a globally optimal set, so individually reasonable local choices need not be compatible.

The elementary general upper bound is \(O(n/\log n)\) rounds for this bandwidth. It uses the fact that local work is unrestricted: centralized NP-hardness does not turn into a round lower bound. This bound provides a scale for the question, without asserting optimality.

Maximum and maximal independent sets impose different requirements. A maximal set merely cannot be enlarged by adding a vertex; it may be much smaller than the largest independent set. The many fast maximal-set algorithms therefore do not supply the requested exact optimization guarantee.

Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman distinguish unicast communication from broadcast and establish connections between unicast protocols and Boolean circuit complexity. Their results explain why superconstant lower bounds for explicit functions in this network are difficult. Those connections are model context, not a tight maximum-independent-set theorem.

Chechik’s 2025 seminar question asks about maximum independent set with incident-edge input and communication to every other player. It leaves bandwidth as a parameter and does not specify a randomness convention. The present card preserves its previously selected deterministic logarithmic-bandwidth question; it does not claim to settle the broader bandwidth tradeoff.
why: Exact independent set separates the cost of learning a global optimum from the cost of computing it once the input is known. The complete communication network removes distances and narrow cuts, yet each link still carries only logarithmically many bits. A tight characterization would identify whether this canonical optimization problem intrinsically requires substantially more information exchange than easier graph tasks in the same network. The circuit connections also make it a meaningful test of the limits of current distributed lower-bound methods.
status_note: The 2025 source explicitly asks the broader round-complexity question. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 did not identify matching bounds for this card’s deterministic logarithmic-bandwidth maximum-set task. This is an individually reviewed formulation, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

The result does not determine the exact maximum-independent-set round complexity. | 2025: Chechik explicitly poses the maximum-independent-set round-complexity question in Section 5.8 of Dagstuhl Seminar 25191, printed pages 18–19.
