Each vertex initially knows its incident edges and can exchange a logarithmic number of bits with every other processor in a round. The target is the optimal worst-case number of deterministic communication rounds, with local computation uncharged. A tight bound would measure the information exchange needed for exact graph optimization in a network without distance barriers. The source leaves bandwidth and randomness broader, while this card preserves its explicit deterministic logarithmic-bandwidth specialization.

title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
importance_reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.
context:
Suomela’s problem list, updated 23 February 2026, explicitly asks whether maximal matching in bipartite graphs admits volume polynomial in the maximum degree. The supplied coloring and deterministic connected exploration are part of the model used here.

The list records a degree-only lower bound \(\Omega(\Delta)\) and an upper bound \((\Delta+1)^{O(\Delta)}\) for volume. These bounds leave open whether some fixed polynomial in \(\Delta\) is sufficient.

Rosenbaum and Suomela define volume by the number of distinct vertices seen through adaptive connected queries. This can differ substantially from the largest graph distance reached. The output of every rooted execution must still fit the same globally valid solution.

Suomela conjectures a \(2^{\Theta(\Delta)}\) dependence. This is a conjecture about the full degree dependence, and the cited page does not present it as a proved superpolynomial lower bound.

The degree parameter grows in this question. A bound that is constant in graph size for each separately fixed degree does not necessarily give one universal polynomial in the degree.
why: This asks how much graph information is needed to answer a single matching query while remaining consistent with all other answers. A polynomial degree bound would give a deterministic local oracle for a basic graph primitive with cost independent of graph size. A superpolynomial lower bound would separate this information requirement from the known linear dependence on degree in communication rounds.
status_note: The primary problem list updated 23 February 2026 explicitly leaves polynomial-in-degree deterministic volume open. The checked round bounds and the author’s exponential-volume conjecture do not settle the yes/no target. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution of the stated model; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2019: As reviewed in the checked 2020 paper, Balliu and coauthors establish the deterministic LOCAL lower bound \(\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})\) for bipartite maximal matching. This yields a degree-linear obstruction for degree-only volume bounds. | 2020: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive volume, and Brandt and Olivetti refine degree-dependent bipartite matching bounds in the round model. Their exact round constants are not asserted as exact volume constants. | 2026-02-23: Suomela’s updated list retains the explicit polynomial-in-degree volume question and states an exponential-degree conjecture.
working_summary: A maximal matching is a collection of disjoint edges to which no additional edge can be added. A vertex query may inspect the graph only by following ports from vertices it has already visited. The input supplies the two sides of the bipartite graph, and separate queries must describe one consistent matching. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm whose visited volume is polynomial in the degree bound and independent of graph size. The February 2026 primary list retains this question between known linear and superpolynomial degree-dependent bounds.

title: Superlinear local certificates for hereditary graph classes
importance_reason: A structural existence question about the amount of distributed evidence required by hereditary properties. It goes beyond one geometric family and separates a possible universal limitation from the known linear examples, with a precise information measure and a recent explicitly retained open formulation.
formal:
Does there exist an isomorphism-invariant hereditary class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, with connected members of arbitrarily large order, and a fixed real exponent \(c>1\), such that every correct one-round proof-labeling scheme for membership in \(\mathcal C\) has worst-case certificate size \(\Omega(n^c)\) bits per vertex on connected \(n\)-vertex inputs?

More explicitly, for the optimal accepting-certificate size \(s_A(n)\) of a fixed correct local verifier \(A\), as defined below, require
\[\exists\mathcal C\;\exists c>1\;\forall A\text{ correct for }\mathcal C\;\exists a_A>0\;\exists N_A\;\forall n\ge N_A:\ s_A(n)\ge a_A n^c.\]
The exponent and graph class are common to all verifiers. This asks for a polynomial gap above linear certificate size, not merely for a bound that grows faster than \(n\).
question_excerpt: After proving the first linear local-certificate lower bounds for nontrivial hereditary and monotone graph classes, the authors ask whether some hereditary class has a lower bound with a fixed exponent strictly greater than one, and ask additionally whether it can be monotone.
definitions:
A graph class is a set of finite simple undirected graphs invariant under relabelling of vertices. It is hereditary if \(G\in\mathcal C\) implies \(G[U]\in\mathcal C\) for every subset \(U\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[U]\) retains exactly the edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). The class is fixed independently of input size. Membership is certified only on nonempty connected input graphs, as in the source. Closure under induced subgraphs is a property of the full class, including disconnected graphs; it does not require certifying disconnected networks. Requiring arbitrarily large connected members excludes vacuous lower bounds. Such a hereditary class has connected members of every positive order, by taking connected induced subgraphs of larger connected members.

On an \(n\)-vertex input graph, each vertex has a distinct positive integer identifier from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), in binary. These are arbitrary identifiers, not part of the graph property. This fixes the source's polynomial-size identifier convention. Every completeness and soundness condition holds for every permitted identifier assignment. The prover knows the entire labelled graph and assigns a finite binary string \(\sigma(v)\in\{0,1\}^{*}\) to every vertex. Certificates may depend on the graph and its identifiers. Their cost is the maximum length at a vertex, \(\max_v|\sigma(v)|\), not the sum of all certificate lengths.

The same deterministic local verifier \(A\) is used at every vertex, on every input size and every certificate assignment. At a vertex \(v\), it sees its own identifier and certificate, and the identifiers and certificates of its immediate neighbors, with the center distinguished. It has no information about edges among neighbors, about more distant vertices, or about a geometric representation of the graph. It outputs either accept or reject. This is the one-round proof-labeling model: certificates are assigned once and examined locally, without further interaction with the prover. The graph order is not supplied as extra global information. There is no randomization or acceptance error.

As in the source's definition, a verifier and prover are mathematical functions with no computational resource bound. The quantity measures the amount of local information, not the running time of deciding a local predicate; no separate computability or recognition-time requirement is imposed on the graph class or those functions. This convention is what makes the source's universal quadratic upper bound applicable to arbitrary graph classes. A scheme must still satisfy both exact logical requirements:
\[G\in\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\sigma\;\forall v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept},\]
\[G\notin\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\sigma\;\exists v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{reject}.\]
These quantify over every connected input and every valid identifier assignment. In the second condition the adversarial strings may be of any finite length; soundness is not restricted to certificates obeying an advertised short length. The prover is untrusted, and acceptance means that every vertex accepts.

For a fixed correct verifier \(A\) and a connected yes-instance \((G,\mathrm{id})\), let
\[\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id})=\min_{\sigma:\ \forall v\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept}}\ \max_{v\in V(G)}|\sigma(v)|.\]
Completeness makes this a finite nonnegative integer. Define
\[s_A(n)=\max_{\substack{|V(G)|=n,\ G\in\mathcal C,\ G\text{ connected}\\ \mathrm{id}:V(G)\hookrightarrow\{1,\ldots,n^2\}}}\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id}).\]
Only finitely many labelled graphs and identifier assignments occur at a fixed \(n\), so the maximum is well-defined; if the set is empty it is defined as zero. The target's \(\Omega(n^c)\) means the displayed eventual bound for every sufficiently large integer \(n\). The verifier is fixed before taking the asymptotic limit; a different verifier for each size is not allowed. Since the prover may choose the shortest accepting certificates, this rules out cheap schemes rather than merely identifying inefficient choices of proof.

The source also asks whether the witnessing class can be monotone, meaning closed under all subgraphs obtained by deleting edges as well as vertices. Monotone classes are hereditary, so such an example would satisfy this card's main target, but edge-deletion closure is not required. The source's hereditary question is the main proposition; its stronger parenthetical variant remains context. The stronger locally-checkable-proof model additionally lets a vertex inspect the entire induced graph on its closed neighborhood. The known lower bounds in the paper hold even in that model, but the target here uses its stated proof-labeling model.

To refute the proposition, one must rule out a common positive polynomial gap for every hereditary class in the stated domain. Formally, for each such \(\mathcal C\) and each \(c>1\), there must be a correct verifier \(A\) for which \(s_A(n)\) is not \(\Omega(n^c)\): for every \(a>0\) and \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has \(s_A(n)<a n^c\). A universal near-linear upper bound would suffice, but the logical negation does not require that particular stronger result.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence statement. A positive answer must specify a hereditary class and one exponent \(c>1\), verify the closure and unbounded connected-member conditions, and prove the per-vertex lower bound against every correct verifier in the stated model, even when the prover chooses its best certificates. A negative answer must prove the logical negation for every admissible hereditary class and exponent. A linear lower bound, a bound such as \(n\log n\), a total-certificate lower bound spread over many vertices, or a lower bound for one selected verifier is insufficient. Computational hardness of centralized recognition alone is not a local certificate-size lower bound in this unrestricted-computation model. The target is an exact asymptotic proposition; numerical tolerance does not apply.
context:
A short global proof can be difficult to verify when its readers only see neighboring pieces. Local certification asks how much evidence must be copied or distributed to individual vertices so that all honest instances are accepted and every false instance is rejected somewhere.

Hereditary properties survive deleting vertices. Many geometric intersection classes have this stability: deleting objects leaves a representation of the induced subgraph. The closure condition distinguishes this question from large lower bounds for properties that depend on a particular global size or symmetry.

The source proves linear lower bounds for several geometric classes, including penny graphs, graphs that are subgraphs of the square grid, and 1-planar graphs. These supply substantial examples at the linear threshold but do not establish a fixed exponent \(c>1\).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the local complexity of a connected graph class by \(\log_2|\mathcal C_n|+O(\log n)\), where \(\mathcal C_n\) is its set of isomorphism types with \(n\) vertices. Thus the number of possible graphs in a class gives a general information bound, and every class has an \(O(n^2)\) upper bound. The question concerns where hereditary classes can lie inside this range.

The known examples illustrate how sensitive local evidence can be to the graph property: planar graphs have logarithmic-size certificates, whereas the source proves a linear bound for 1-planar graphs. A 1-planar graph admits a drawing with at most one crossing on each edge. This comparison concerns certificate size even though local computation is unrestricted.

The full February 2026 revision retains the superlinear question. It also keeps the stronger neighborhood-inspection model separate from ordinary proof labeling. This review fixes the latter and records the stronger known lower-bound scope without changing the target.
why: The question asks whether vertex-deletion stability imposes a fundamental information limit on distributed proofs. A polynomially superlinear example or a general obstruction would clarify how far local verification of structural graph properties can depart from the linear examples now known.
status_note: Explicitly source-open in MFCS 2024 and still explicitly asked in the full arXiv v5 revision of 24 February 2026. On 16 September 2026 the review checked both versions’ local-verifier definitions, Theorem 3.1 and the exact final superlinear question, with the current arXiv revision history confirmed. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no matching hereditary-class resolution. This is current source evidence through the checked revision, not an exhaustive certification of all later literature.
progress: 2024: The MFCS paper proves linear lower bounds for hereditary and monotone geometric classes and asks whether \(\Omega(n^c)\) is possible for any fixed \(c>1\). | 24 February 2026: The revised full paper retains the question and the same local-certification definitions. It does not claim a hereditary-class lower bound with exponent greater than one.
working_summary: A prover gives each vertex a binary certificate, and each vertex checks only its immediate certified neighborhood. The question asks for a hereditary graph class requiring a fixed polynomial factor more than linear certificate length at some vertex. The lower bound must hold against every correct proof-labeling verifier and every sufficiently large graph size. Known geometric examples require linear certificates, while a quadratic upper bound applies to all graph classes in the source model. The February 2026 revision still asks whether any hereditary class crosses this polynomially superlinear threshold.

title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
importance_reason: A broad proposed transfer of approximation resistance across both models and space thresholds, with implications for the classification of streaming CSPs.
formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.
context:
This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.
why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.
progress: 2024: Chou, Golovnev, Sudan and Velusamy publish the finite-CSP sketching dichotomy. | 2025: Singer poses the lifting implication as Conjecture 8 and explicitly allows that counterexamples may exist. | 2026-04-09: Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy establish LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, creating a stronger framework that must be compared with the conjecture’s premise.
working_summary: Each fixed predicate family defines a maximum constraint-satisfaction problem. A nontrivial approximation beats the best constant lower bound on the optimum by a fixed amount. The conjecture lifts resistance to small mergeable sketches into resistance to all sublinear-space streaming algorithms. Both the algorithm model and the space threshold change in the implication. The 2026 LP-gap lower bounds are recorded without claiming a verified resolution of this exact lifting statement.

title: Parallel sampling of planar perfect matchings
importance_reason: A representative unresolved separation between parallel counting and parallel sampling, with a precise combinatorial distribution and substantial general significance beyond one sampling implementation.
formal:
Do there exist constants \(C,k\ge1\) and a uniform family of randomized Boolean circuits \((A_{n,t})_{n\ge0,t\ge1}\) that, for every simple unweighted planar graph \(G\) on \([n]\) with at least one perfect matching, output a distribution \(\mu_{G,t}\) satisfying
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu_{G,t},U_G)\le2^{-t},
\]
with circuit size at most \(C(n+2^t+2)^k\) and depth at most \(C(\log_2(n+2)+t)^k\)?
Here \(U_G\) is uniform over all perfect matchings of \(G\), and the complete input, output, uniformity and failure conventions are defined below. The same constants and uniform circuit generator must work for every graph and precision. This is the user-selected approximately uniform RNC sampling target.
question_excerpt: The original source lists several determinant-counted combinatorial distributions and asks for parallel randomized sampling algorithms. This card selects its planar perfect matching example, as explicitly authorized by the user.
definitions:
A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and without parallel edges; its vertices are \([n]\). Planarity means it admits an embedding in the plane with edges meeting only at shared endpoints. The input is the upper-triangular Boolean adjacency matrix in the lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs. An embedding is not supplied. The promise is that the graph is planar and has at least one perfect matching. Inputs outside this promise still obey the resource bounds, but carry no distributional correctness requirement.

A perfect matching is a set of present edges incident to every vertex exactly once. Write \(\mathcal M(G)\) for this finite nonempty set and \(U_G(M)=1/|\mathcal M(G)|\) for \(M\in\mathcal M(G)\). The empty graph has the single empty perfect matching. Disconnected promised graphs are allowed; no bipartiteness, positive-degree lower bound or edge weights are assumed.

The accuracy parameter is a positive integer \(t\), defining error \(\varepsilon=2^{-t}\). These dyadic errors specify arbitrary requested accuracy up to a factor of two. Each circuit has the adjacency bits as ordinary inputs and independent unbiased random bits as additional inputs. Gates are AND and OR of fan-in two and NOT of fan-in one, together with constants; fan-out is unrestricted. Size counts gates, random inputs and output wires. Depth is the longest gate path and is a worst-case bound, independent of the random bits. The output consists of an edge-incidence vector indexed by all unordered vertex pairs and a failure flag. A nonmatching vector or a raised failure flag is interpreted as the single symbol \(\bot\).

Both output measures live on the finite set \(\mathcal M(G)\cup\{\bot\}\), with \(U_G(\bot)=0\), and
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,U_G)=\frac12\sum_{z\in\mathcal M(G)\cup\{\bot\}}|\mu(z)-U_G(z)|.
\]
Thus failure probability is charged to the error and the approximation is unconditional; conditioning on success cannot conceal a large failure probability. The graph itself is fixed when taking this distribution.

Uniformity means that one deterministic machine, given unary \(n\) and unary \(2^t\), generates the description of \(A_{n,t}\) using \(O(\log(n+2)+t)\) work space and polynomial time in \(n+2^t\). Padding the inverse-accuracy parameter states precisely the permitted polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\); it does not require a bound polynomial merely in its binary bit length. No graph-dependent advice, counting oracle or exact-real random primitive is free. The circuit must implement all needed computation. Boolean depth and size give a precise standard parallel model corresponding to polynomially many bit processors. For inverse-polynomial error, the displayed bounds are polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth in graph size.

The generator, constants and exponent are chosen before \(n,t,G\). An affirmative answer is one such family. A negative answer is the full negation over all uniform families and fixed constants. Finding one perfect matching or computing their number is not the requested sampling task. The source's broader list of determinant-counted objects has been narrowed to this one user-selected graph distribution.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of the asserted uniform circuit family, including worst-case depth, size, fair-bit implementation and the total-variation bound for every promised graph and every \(t\ge1\); or prove the full negation of that existence assertion. A result only about counting, finding one matching, a restricted graph family, conditional-on-success accuracy or sublinear but non-polylogarithmic depth is insufficient. The explicit sampling error \(2^{-t}\), not the default tolerance for numerical-value answers, governs this proposition. An experimental sampler or citation alone is not a Lean proof.
context:
Planar perfect matchings are among the combinatorial objects whose counts can be evaluated through determinants. Efficient parallel counting does not automatically give efficient parallel sampling, because the familiar conditional choices can depend sequentially on previous choices. The target asks whether this dependence can be removed for the entire matching distribution.

The selected question requires almost uniform random output, not simply the discovery of an arbitrary matching. It isolates one unresolved member of the source’s broader list; subsequent RNC results for other distributions do not answer it.

The 2023 work gives parallel planar matching sampling in roughly square-root time, suppressing logarithmic factors. The later autospeculation preprint reports an application with expected time \(\widetilde O(n^{1/4})\), and explicitly retains the polylogarithmic question. These bounds are recorded with their source conventions rather than promoted to the worst-case Boolean-depth target.

The June 2026 result on planar matching counting studies weighted arithmetic complexity relative to determinants. It provides neither the distributional sampler nor a lower bound ruling out the sampler requested here.
why: This is a concrete test of whether counting and sampling remain equivalent under strong parallel-time constraints. Planarity makes exact counting tractable, so the remaining issue isolates the cost of coordinating random choices rather than the hardness of evaluating the partition function. A resolution would clarify a central boundary in parallel randomized algorithms.
status_note: Open in the inspected November 2025 autospeculation preprint, which explicitly distinguishes parallel planar matching sampling from already parallelizable counting. The source reports a soft-O(n^(1/4)) expected parallel-time application, still above the polylogarithmic target. The 2024 RNC results for Eulerian tours and asymmetric determinantal processes resolve other parts of the inherited broad direction. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the selected planar approximate-sampling assertion. The June 2026 weighted counting paper concerns arithmetic operation counts and does not settle this target. This review checked model definitions and result scopes, not all source proofs or a Lean formalization.
progress: 2021: The arborescence paper lists planar perfect matchings among the outstanding determinant-based parallel sampling tasks. | 2023: Theorem 11 gives exact planar matching sampling in \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) parallel time using polynomially many processors. | 2024: RNC sampling results resolve the directed Eulerian-tour and asymmetric determinantal-process applications, not this selected planar matching task. | 2025-11: The autospeculation preprint reports an expected \(\widetilde O(n^{1/4})\) planar application and continues to identify polylogarithmic sampling as open. | 2026-09-16: The bounded update checked later weighted-counting work and found no resolution of the selected sampling target.
working_summary: The input is a planar graph with at least one perfect matching, and the desired output is an almost uniform random perfect matching. The sampler must use polynomially many Boolean gates and polylogarithmic depth, with explicit dependence on the requested total-variation error. Failure probability counts toward the error and the circuit uses only independent fair random bits. Parallel counting and finding one matching do not themselves produce this distribution, while known faster samplers still have non-polylogarithmic parallel bounds. The problem tests a central boundary between counting and sampling under parallel resource constraints.

title: Work-efficient parallel approximate flow
importance_reason: This asks for work-efficient polylogarithmic parallel time for fundamental flow primitives that combine cost or vertex congestion with capacity constraints.
formal:
Does at least one of the following two problems admit a uniform randomized parallel algorithm with nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth, in the precise regime below?

1. Edge-capacitated budgeted minimum-cost flow: given an undirected graph, terminals \(s,t\), edge capacities and nonnegative edge costs, and a total cost budget \(B\), output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow whose value is at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the largest flow value within both the capacities and budget.
2. Vertex-capacitated maximum flow: given an undirected graph, terminals \(s,t\), and vertex capacities, output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow whose value is at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the largest capacity-respecting value.

The assertion is a disjunction over the two entire problem classes. The algorithm may choose one class once and for all; choosing an easier alternative separately for each instance is not the assertion.
question_excerpt: The authors ask whether either undirected edge-capacitated minimum-cost flow or undirected vertex-capacitated maximum flow admits a parallel approximation scheme with nearly-linear total work and polylogarithmic depth.
definitions:
An input graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected, with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\), and distinct named terminals \(s,t\). It is supplied by an explicit edge list; disconnected graphs and zero capacities are allowed. For each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\), a flow has nonnegative values \(f_{uv},f_{vu}\). Put
\[
\mathrm{out}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{vw},\qquad
\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{wv}.
\]
Require \(\mathrm{in}_f(s)=\mathrm{out}_f(t)=0\) and \(\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). The value is \(F=\mathrm{out}_f(s)=\mathrm{in}_f(t)\). Fractional flows are allowed. Internal circulations may occur but consume the same capacities and costs as other flow.

For the edge problem, each edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) has capacity \(u_e\ge0\) and cost \(c_e\ge0\). Feasibility requires
\[
f_{uv}+f_{vu}\le u_e,\qquad
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}c_{\{u,v\}}(f_{uv}+f_{vu})\le B.
\]
There are no vertex constraints in this alternative. The source calls maximization under this cost budget approximate minimum-cost flow; the card uses that source convention.

For the vertex problem, each \(v\) has capacity \(U_v\ge0\). Its load is \(\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) if \(v\ne t\), and \(\mathrm{in}_f(t)\) if \(v=t\). Require load at most \(U_v\) for every vertex, including both terminals. There are no edge capacities or cost objective in this alternative. Equivalently, in a decomposition into directed simple terminal paths, every unit uses capacity at each vertex on its path, including its endpoints; removable internal circulations do not improve the optimum.

In each alternative \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum \(F\) over feasible real flows. Zero flow is feasible, and instances with \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\) must also be handled. The output explicitly lists rational values for both orientations of every edge. On a successful run all feasibility inequalities hold exactly and \(F\ge\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\); no capacity or budget violation is permitted.

Here is an explicit polynomial-data and inverse-polylogarithmic-accuracy convention. For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allow integral capacities and costs in \([0,n^a]\), and a budget \(B=b/d\) with integers \(0\le b\le n^a\), \(1\le d\le n^a\). Let
\[
L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\qquad
\varepsilon=1/q,\quad q\in\mathbb N,\quad 2\le q\le L^a.
\]
Input numbers, labels and \(q\) are encoded in binary. The same algorithm must cover every fixed \(a\); it receives the numerical instance and \(q\), not advice or a precomputed structure for the graph. Reciprocal-integer accuracies specify the source's inverse-polylogarithmic regime: intermediate accuracies can be met by requesting a smaller reciprocal accuracy. This does not require a fully polynomial bound for arbitrary inverse accuracy outside that regime.

Use a synchronous priority-CRCW word PRAM: processors execute one fixed finite program, have labelled shared-memory words, can read concurrently, and simultaneous writes to one location retain the value of the lowest-numbered writing processor. A step performs word arithmetic, comparison, a Boolean operation, a shift, a shared-memory access, or generation of one independent fair random bit. A word has \(C_a L\) bits for a fixed constant \(C_a\); larger integers and rational numerators or denominators use multiple words and their operations are charged accordingly. There is no exact-real or arbitrary-precision unit-cost primitive. Work counts all processor operations, including input handling and output; depth is the number of synchronous steps. The algorithm must halt within the stated bounds on every random tape and succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on each valid input.

Nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth mean that, for every fixed \(a\), there are constants \(K_a>0\) and \(k_a\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, its numerical data and \(q\), such that
\[
\mathrm{work}\le K_a(n+m)L^{k_a},\qquad
\mathrm{depth}\le K_a L^{k_a}.
\]
These are explicit editorial model conventions for the source's parallel resource question. They count the finite precision needed by an actual implementation. Polynomially many processors without the work bound, or a subpolynomial factor that is not bounded by a fixed power of \(L\), is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this disjunctive existence assertion. A positive answer must specify one uniform algorithm for at least one whole alternative and establish its feasibility, approximation, per-instance success probability and simultaneous work/depth bounds for every fixed data-and-accuracy exponent \(a\). A negative answer must rule out the asserted algorithm for both alternatives in the stated model. The question is binary; there is no additional numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. A theorem about the optimum value alone must also supply the required flow output, and a capacity-violating bicriteria result alone does not meet the stated feasibility guarantee.
context:
An undirected capacity bounds total flow through a resource; a cost budget bounds the sum of flow times edge cost. Vertex capacities instead constrain all traffic passing through a vertex. These impose different feasible regions even when the graph and terminals agree.

The source studies the more general setting with costs and capacities on both edges and vertices. Its single-commodity theorem achieves almost-linear work and subpolynomial depth for inverse-polylogarithmic accuracy. The open question asks for the sharper polylogarithmic factors, already on either restricted alternative.

The full version also treats concurrent and nonconcurrent multicommodity demands. Open Problem 1 is posed even for a single commodity. The broader multicommodity problem and its dependence on the number of commodities are not added to this target.

SODA 2024 gives an undirected edge-capacitated maximum-flow approximation using work O(m ε^{-3} polylog n) and depth O(ε^{-3} polylog n). That result has neither the cost budget of the first alternative nor the vertex capacities of the second.

The ICALP 2026 result concerns unit capacities and unit lengths on expanders. For conductance φ it gives work near m/(εφ) and depth near 1/(εφ), with approximate congestion and cost while routing prescribed demand exactly. Its restricted graph class and bicriteria guarantee leave the general question here unresolved.

The SPAA 2025 exact-flow algorithm has square-root, rather than polylogarithmic, depth. Its near m+n^{3/2} work is nearly linear on sufficiently dense instances; this does not supply the simultaneous bounds sought for all graphs.
why: A small depth bound makes an algorithm useful on many processors only when the total work also remains close to input size. The question asks whether cost budgets or vertex bottlenecks force an additional parallel cost for basic flow optimization. Its resolution would clarify the boundary between known efficient parallel flow primitives and more general constrained routing.
status_note: FOCS 2025 explicitly leaves nearly-linear work with polylogarithmic depth open for either alternative. The source’s general algorithm has subpolynomial overhead instead. The 2026 ICALP result concerns unit-data expanders with a bicriteria guarantee; it does not settle the general graph question. No matching resolution was found in the bounded review through 16 September 2026.
progress: 2024: Published work establishes nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth for approximate undirected edge-capacitated maximum flow. | 2025: FOCS gives the broader flow algorithm with subpolynomial overhead and explicitly poses the sharper resource target. | 2026-07-01: ICALP publishes a polylogarithmic-depth result for the restricted unit-data expander setting, with a bicriteria guarantee. | 2026-09-16: Individual review separates the two alternatives, the cost-budget meaning of approximation and the exact simultaneous work/depth requirements.
working_summary: The question concerns parallel approximation of single-commodity flow in undirected graphs. It asks for an algorithm for at least one of two full classes: edge-capacitated flow under a cost budget, or vertex-capacitated maximum flow. The output must be a feasible flow with value within a factor of one plus the requested inverse-polylogarithmic error of optimum. The target combines nearly-linear total work with polylogarithmic depth, improving on general results with subpolynomial overhead. The checked 2026 expander result addresses a restricted case and does not settle this general graph question.

title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
importance_reason: This measures a basic memory cost of synchronization and exposes a large gap between known impossibility arguments and protocols.
formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of shared atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) named processes with input domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in the model below. Supply a real-valued function approximating \(R\) with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers throughout this domain.
definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real-valued function \(g\) on all integer pairs \(n>k\ge1\), and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(n,k)-R(n,k)|\le1/100\) throughout the domain, with error measured in registers and \(R\) defined by the stated model. The approximation need not be integer-valued. A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. A finite table, an asymptotic estimate, or unmatched bounds outside this precision do not meet the criterion; merely restating the defining minimization does not specify a determination.
context:
The known bounds are \(\lceil n/k\rceil\le R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The lower bound applies to named processes; the upper bound is achieved even by anonymous processes, so it also applies here. Both ends of the parameter range are determined: \(R(n,1)=n\) and \(R(n,n-1)=2\). In the interior, the general bounds can leave a substantial gap.

The upper-bound algorithm uses exactly \(n-k+1\) physical read/write registers, including the implementation of the snapshots appearing in its presentation. The resource is the number of arbitrarily large registers, not their combined bit capacity. The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.
why: This measures how much shared memory is intrinsically needed for synchronization when processes may disagree on a bounded number of proposed values. Resolving the gap would connect the solvability of agreement tasks to their exact memory requirements, even under the weak guarantee of eventual progress in isolation.
status_note: The 2024 journal abstract explicitly describes determining register space as open. Two primary papers published on 7 January 2026 retain the same general bounds. A bounded primary-source and subsequent-result review through 16 September 2026 found no verified determination for all \(n>k\ge1\); this is not exhaustive certification of current openness. The 1/100 tolerance is the atlas acceptance rule, not a tolerance proposed by these papers.
progress: 2015: Bouzid, Raynal and Sutra give an anonymous obstruction-free one-shot protocol using \(n-k+1\) atomic read/write registers. Their repeated-task extension has the already optimal repeated-task register count. | 2018: The revisionist-simulation preprint establishes the lower bound \(\lfloor(n-x)/(k+1-x)\rfloor+1\) for \(1\le x\le k<n\). At \(x=1\) this equals \(\lceil n/k\rceil\); the preprint also states the conjecture that the upper bound is exact. | 2024-08-01: The journal publication states the \(\lceil n/k\rceil\) obstruction-free register lower bound and describes determining the required number of registers as open. | 2026-01-07: The published OPODIS 2025 related-work account retains the lower/upper gap for n-valued obstruction-free set agreement. | 2026-01-07: The paper on exhaustive extension-based proofs also retains these register bounds; its main theorems address proof-system limitations rather than a new register-space bound.
working_summary: Each process proposes a value and must decide one of the values proposed by participating processes. At most k distinct values may be decided, and a process must finish if it continues alone long enough. The resource is the number of atomic read/write registers, whose individual capacities are unrestricted. Known bounds range from the ceiling of n/k to n-k+1; consensus and (n-1)-set agreement have exact values. The target is the full register-space function for all n>k>=1, with the atlas's pointwise 1/100-register acceptance tolerance.

title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
importance_reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.
formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.
answer_criterion: Determine a function \(f(n)\) with an \(O(f(n))\)-round randomized algorithm and an \(Omega(f(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every randomized algorithm in the stated model, up to constant factors. Either a faster algorithm or a stronger lower bound alone is partial progress.
context:
Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.
progress: 2021: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound. | 2025: Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round. | 2025-10: Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks a distributed network to report whether any three vertices are pairwise adjacent. In CONGEST, each edge transmits only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per round, even though vertices initially know all their own neighbors. The saved card asks for the optimal randomized round complexity between the stated doubly logarithmic lower bound and roughly \(n^{1/3}\) upper bound. Detection needs only one positive witness somewhere in the network, unlike listing every triangle. The challenge is to exploit that smaller output requirement while still communicating enough information to discover an edge between two neighbors.

title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
importance_reason: A general space-versus-approximation barrier for a central geometric connectivity objective, separating polynomially small summaries from polylogarithmic ones as dimension grows.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of \(n\) distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), the algorithm uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate \(Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
definitions:
The point set \(X\) consists of the \(n\) distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters \(n,d\) and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, fresh independent fair random bits accessed sequentially, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, stored random bits or seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Random bits can be reused only if explicitly retained in charged memory. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer \(b\ge1\) and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows the dimension to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in \(d\) does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite \(C\). Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing \(C\). Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
context:
Pavel Veselý proposed this one-pass insertion-only question through the Atlas website. It asks for a constant-factor estimate of the cost, rather than a stored or output spanning tree. The current proposal explicitly allows either an algorithm or an impossibility result.

The central gap is between small memory and small approximation error. The STOC 2022 work gives a one-pass sketch with polylogarithmic space and an approximation factor of \(\widetilde O(\log n)\), which still grows with the number of points.

The STOC 2023 paper achieves a constant approximation for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), with ratio \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) and space \(n^{O(\varepsilon)}\) up to the stated dimension and logarithmic factors. Its sketches allow insertions and deletions. For fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), this is a larger memory budget than the one requested here.

The same paper excludes approximation below 1.1035 with \(o(\sqrt n)\) space for one pass in dimension at least a sufficiently large constant times \(\log n\). This does not rule out every constant approximation factor. Neither low-dimensional algorithms with exponential dependence on dimension nor the paper’s multiple-pass guarantees settle the target.

The finite input model uses integer coordinates and charges their bit length through \(\log(\Delta+2)\). This makes the representation explicit while retaining \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) memory when the coordinate range is polynomially bounded in \(n\). The proposal’s allowance for logarithmic dimension is retained as part of the general dimension-dependent target.
why: An MST measures the cost of connecting an entire geometric data set. A small summary that estimates this global quantity within a constant factor would clarify how much connectivity information survives a single streaming pass as dimension grows.
status_note: Individually reviewed on 17 September 2026 against the current community proposal, the full model and theorem statements in the STOC 2023 author preprint, and the earlier STOC 2022 result. Targeted later-work searches did not locate a resolution of the insertion-only, one-pass, polylogarithmic-space constant-factor target. Status remains source_open; this is a bounded source review, not an exhaustive literature audit or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2022: A one-pass streaming algorithm obtains a \(\widetilde O(\log n)\) approximation using polylogarithmic sketch space. | 2023: Constant-factor approximation is achieved in \(n^{O(\varepsilon)}\) space for each fixed positive accuracy parameter in the stated range; a separate lower bound excludes approximation below 1.1035 with \(o(\sqrt n)\) one-pass space. | 2026-09-14: The community proposal asks whether constant-factor estimation can use only memory polynomial in dimension and polylogarithmic in the number of points, already in insertion-only streams.
working_summary: Points arrive one at a time in Euclidean space, and the goal is to estimate the total cost of their minimum spanning tree. The algorithm gets one insertion-only pass and memory polynomial in the dimension and logarithmic input parameters. It must return a constant-factor estimate with probability at least two thirds for every fixed stream order. Known results obtain a growing approximation with polylogarithmic space or a constant approximation with a positive polynomial space exponent. Either a qualifying algorithm or an unconditional proof that no such algorithm exists would settle the question.

title: Optimal measurements and near-linear decoding for universal ℓ₂/ℓ₁ sparse recovery
importance_reason: A central universal compressed-sensing tradeoff between measurement count, robust mixed-norm error and decoding time; explicit matrix generation is a separate issue.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,B>0\), \(a\geq0\), and a deterministic recovery scheme such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq n\), one fixed matrix \(A_{n,k}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\leq Bk\log_2(en/k)\) permits recovery from \(A_{n,k}x\) in at most \(Bn\log_2^a(n+2)\) operations, with \[\|x-\widehat x\|_2\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\min_{z:\,|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\leq k}\|x-z\|_1\] simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)?
definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required. Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. Constants, the polynomial advice exponent and the decoding exponent are independent of \(n,k,x\). Measurements are noiseless; no additional post-measurement perturbation is included.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction or existence proof of a scheme meeting both resource bounds and the universal mixed-norm error guarantee in the specified arithmetic model, or prove that no such scheme exists. A guarantee holding with high probability separately for each input, an ℓ₁/ℓ₁ error bound, or optimal row count with slower decoding is insufficient.
context:
The source’s “deterministic” target is universal recovery from one matrix: the same measurements must work for every signal. Editorial model convention: this card makes the arithmetic-operation and preprocessing conventions explicit, without adding the separate challenge of efficient deterministic matrix generation. It also uses \(\log(en/k)\) and \(k\geq1\) to remove the source formula’s undefined or zero endpoint expressions.

For exactly \(k\)-sparse signals the right-hand side is zero, so the scheme must recover them exactly. For nonsparse signals, recovery quality depends on the entire tail and gains a factor \(1/\sqrt{k}\). Merely outputting a plausible support does not establish this robust guarantee.

The original question emphasizes achieving optimal measurement count and fast reconstruction together. Classical constructions achieve the two features separately for this error criterion, whereas some fast optimal-measurement schemes use a different norm on the reconstruction error.

The later for-all sparse-recovery work of Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improves measurements and decoding for the ℓ₁/ℓ₁ formulation, and explicitly lists mixed-norm recovery as a remaining direction. Its use of a matrix fixed for all signals is compatible with a nonconstructive probabilistic existence proof.

The inequality \(\|v\|_2\leq\|v\|_1\) does not convert an \(\ell_1/\ell_1\) theorem into the requested result: it loses the essential \(1/\sqrt{k}\) factor. Likewise, an input-dependent success probability does not imply that one random seed works simultaneously over the uncountable set of all real inputs.

When \(k\) is comparable to \(n\), storing the full vector is consistent with the measurement bound. The compression challenge lies in the sparse regime. Counting the output cost explains why near-linear decoding remains a meaningful target even when the number of measurements is much smaller than \(n\).
why: The target combines information-efficient sensing with fast, uniformly reliable reconstruction for arbitrary signals. Resolving it would show whether the strongest standard universal mixed-norm guarantee can be obtained without sacrificing near-optimal compression or practical asymptotic decoding time.
status_note: The 2009 source poses this universal mixed-norm tradeoff, and the checked later for-all recovery paper still distinguishes it from its ℓ₁/ℓ₁ result. No matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check. The arithmetic/preprocessing convention is explicit; efficient explicit matrix generation is not asserted to be part of the original target.
