working_summary: A fixed matrix compresses every real signal to a short vector of linear measurements. The decoder must work for all signals with error controlled by the best k-sparse ℓ₁ tail divided by √k. The conjecture combines O(k log(en/k)) measurements with near-linear deterministic decoding. The arithmetic model permits input-independent polynomial preprocessing but charges decoding accesses. Faster results with an ℓ₁ reconstruction error or only per-input randomized success do not meet this target.

title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
importance_reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.
formal: Does randomized maximal independent set admit a constant-round algorithm in the unicast Congested Clique? Precisely, for every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized distributed algorithm \(A_c\) and positive constants \(R_c,B_c\) such that, on every simple undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), the algorithm always terminates within \(R_c\) rounds, uses at most \(B_c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits per directed communication link per round, and outputs a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}\)? Constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\), the graph or its maximum degree.
definitions: There is one processor for each vertex \(v\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initially it knows \(n\), its own identifier \(v\), the common identifier set, and exactly the identifiers of its neighbors in the input graph. The physical communication network is complete: in each synchronous round every processor may send a separate message to every other processor, even when the corresponding input edge is absent. Messages sent in a round arrive by its end. Each directed link has the stated bit limit independently; processors may send different messages to different recipients. No extra processors or initially centralized graph description are provided. All processors run the same finite program, with their identifier and local input as parameters. Local computation and local storage have no asymptotic bound, but each local computation terminates and reads only finitely many independent private fair random bits on every execution. All communication, including initialization and distribution of any shared randomness, counts toward the round bound. No graph-dependent or size-dependent advice is supplied. At termination each processor outputs one bit, defining \(S=\{v:\text{processor }v\text{ outputs }1\}\). Correctness means both \(\forall\{u,v\}\in E(G):\{u,v\}\nsubseteq S\) and \(\forall v\notin S:\exists u\in S:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Thus maximality means that no additional vertex can be inserted while preserving independence; maximum cardinality is not required. The probability refers to the single global event that all output bits together define a valid set. The round and message bounds hold on every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Restricting the requested fixed failure exponent to positive integers is equivalent to allowing every fixed positive real exponent.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and proof of the quantified algorithmic statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every input graph and every requested fixed failure exponent with the uniformity, bandwidth and worst-case round bounds specified above. A negative answer must rule out the entire stated randomized algorithm class; a limitation of a particular algorithm family, of deterministic algorithms alone, or of broadcast communication is insufficient. Computing an independent set whose distance-two neighborhoods cover the graph does not fulfill maximal independence.
context:
The checked 2025 paper explicitly identifies constant-round MIS on arbitrary graphs as open. It records the general randomized upper bound \(O(1+\log\log(\Delta+2))\), where \(\Delta\) is the input graph’s maximum degree. The harmless offsets cover small degrees.

The 2025 result gives constant rounds on several substantial graph classes. One guarantee applies whenever average degree is at most \(2^{K\sqrt{\log n}}\) for a fixed constant \(K\); the running-time constant may depend on this fixed class parameter. These restricted guarantees leave arbitrary graphs outside their scope.

Section 5 of that paper exhibits limitations of the sampling procedures analyzed there. These are restrictions on those procedures and do not constitute a lower bound for all algorithms in the communication model of this card.

A 2-ruling set is independent and places each vertex within graph distance at most two of the selected set. The 2023 constant-round algorithm for this relaxation allows distance two, whereas MIS requires every unselected vertex to have a selected neighbor.
why: The question measures how much communication exact distributed symmetry breaking needs when every processor can directly contact every other processor. A constant-round solution would establish a sharp capability of this widely studied model. A general lower bound would expose a bandwidth limitation that survives unrestricted local computation and arbitrary global coordination.
status_note: The February 2025 source explicitly leaves constant-round randomized MIS on arbitrary graphs open. Its positive results concern restricted graph classes and its negative results concern specified procedures. The bounded later-work search through 2026-09-15 found no resolution of the exact model and probability target here; this is not an exhaustive certification of present openness.
progress: 2018: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović and Rubinfeld give the general \(O(\log\log\Delta)\)-round Congested Clique MIS bound; the checked arXiv version was revised in 2022. | 2023-10-05: Cambus, Kuhn, Pai and Uitto publish a constant-round Congested Clique algorithm for 2-ruling sets. | 2025-02-28: Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin and Halldórsson state the general constant-round question and prove constant-round results under restrictions on average degree and independence parameters.
working_summary: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent selected vertices and gives every unselected vertex a selected neighbor. Each processor starts with its own incident input edges and can send separate short messages to every other processor. The target is a uniform randomized algorithm using a constant number of rounds on every graph. Its output must be globally correct with an arbitrarily requested fixed polynomially small failure probability. The checked literature gives constant rounds for restricted graph classes and for distance-two coverage, leaving the general MIS target unresolved.

title: Constant-pass weighted matching with O(n log n) bits
importance_reason: A precise resource question for a fundamental graph optimization task; its historical RAM and broad semi-streaming components are separated from the stricter bit-space endpoint.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and fixed integer \(c\geq1\), is there a randomized insertion-only streaming algorithm that, on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with integer edge weights in \([1,n^c]\), outputs a matching of weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p_{\varepsilon,c}\) passes and \(B_{\varepsilon,c}n\log_2(n+2)\) bits of memory, where \(p_{\varepsilon,c},B_{\varepsilon,c}\) do not depend on \(n\)?
definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.
context:
The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.
why: The question asks whether near-optimal weighted matchings can be found with memory comparable to the explicit output and a fixed number of scans of a dense graph. It isolates the remaining strict memory requirement from the already established existence of constant-pass algorithms with polylogarithmic overhead.
status_note: The broad historical question is substantially resolved: linear-time RAM approximation and constant-pass near-linear-space streaming algorithms exist. This card explicitly retains the stricter O(n log n)-bit streaming variant with polynomially bounded integer weights. The checked general-graph theorems and 2025 overview do not state that precise memory endpoint; no matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check.
progress: 2006: McGregor poses the streaming approximation and separate RAM-time questions. | 2014: Duan and Pettie give a linear-time approximation scheme in the RAM model. | 2019: Gamlath and coauthors obtain constant-pass weighted approximation with near-linear memory. | 2023: Huang and Su obtain polynomial-in-accuracy pass complexity; Theorem 1.2 records its word-space dependence on the weight ratio. | 2025: Assadi’s journal overview compares the available pass-space tradeoffs for weighted and unweighted matching.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary-order insertion stream of a positively weighted general graph. The algorithm must output a nearly maximum-weight matching after a number of passes independent of graph size. The retained space target is O(n log n) bits with polynomially bounded integer weights. Linear-time RAM approximation and broader constant-pass semi-streaming results are already known. The card distinguishes those achievements from the exact bit-space endpoint it asks to settle.

title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
importance_reason: Breaking the square-root degree barrier for the canonical coloring task would improve a broadly reused distributed primitive.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\), and a constant \(C>0\) such that \(A\) properly colors every simple \(n\)-vertex graph with a supplied valid maximum-degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), using colors in \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\), within
\[C\bigl(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^* n\bigr)\]
synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct \(O(\log n)\)-bit identifiers and know \(n\) and \(\Delta\). Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The same \(\varepsilon,A,C\) must work for every admissible \(n,\Delta\), graph and identifier assignment.
definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target. The exponent saving is chosen before the graph parameters; it is not an accuracy input that must be handled uniformly by a family of algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting the stated uniform round bound, or of the logical negation of this existence statement. The improvement may be arbitrarily small but must be one positive constant independent of both \(n\) and \(\Delta\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant exponent saving in the stated model. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent \(1/2\), or allowing the saving to tend to zero with input size, does not meet the target. There is no prescribed minimum saving and no numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance for this proposition.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

Suomela's list gives the concrete exponent \(0.499\) as one example of crossing the square-root degree barrier. Following the user's 17 September 2026 formulation choice, this card asks for any fixed exponent \(1/2-\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\), rather than the particular saving \(0.001\). This broadens the original fixed-threshold question: a smaller positive saving also qualifies. The palette, determinism and additive \(\log^* n\) term remain part of the model.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is deterministic and uniform in both degree and graph size; fast randomized coloring is not a resolution.
progress: 2020: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence. | 2026-01: The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.
working_summary: A proper coloring with \(\Delta+1\) colors always exists for a graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\). The question asks whether a uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm can find one in \(O(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^* n)\) rounds for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Any positive constant saving in the degree exponent qualifies, however small, and it must be independent of both graph size and degree. Processors must reduce a large identifier-based palette without causing conflicts among adjacent vertices acting simultaneously. Crossing the square-root degree barrier would improve local coordination while preserving the small dependence on total network size.

title: Fractional-edge-cover load for general-message parallel joins
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: The question asks whether the central structural parameter governing worst-case join output can also govern communication for arbitrary schemas when messages may be coded.
formal:
For every fixed finite natural-join schema \(Q\), is there a randomized MPC algorithm computing its full join in a constant number of communication rounds with load
\[
\widetilde O_Q\!\left(\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}\right)
\]
on every database instance of total input size \(m\), using \(p\) machines with \(2\le p\) and \(p^3\le m\)?

Precisely, for every \(Q\) and every fixed word-size multiplier \(a\ge1\), must there exist one algorithm \(A_{Q,a}\), constants \(C_{Q,a}>0\), and integers \(R_{Q,a},d_{Q,a}\ge1\), such that it halts within \(R_{Q,a}\) rounds on every execution and, for each valid instance and initial distribution, with probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) both outputs exactly the join and has load at most
\[
C_{Q,a}\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}
       \bigl(\log_2(m+2)\bigr)^{d_{Q,a}}?
\]
Messages may encode arbitrary information; they are not restricted to complete input tuples. This broader model is the explicit user choice.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether arbitrary join schemas admit constant-round MPC algorithms matching the fractional-edge-cover load scale, up to the polylogarithmic factors used in its algorithmic bounds. It gives such an algorithm for binary-relation schemas.
definitions:
A schema is a finite nonempty attribute set \(V\) and a finite indexed list of nonempty subsets \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\subseteq V\) with union \(V\). Attribute names, arities, relation names and \(r\) are fixed independently of \(m,p\). Schemas may have repeated subsets. An instance supplies a finite set \(R_i\) of tuples on \(e_i\) for each \(i\). A tuple on \(e_i\) assigns one domain value to each attribute in \(e_i\). Relations have set semantics; duplicate copies within a relation do not contribute multiplicity. The total input size is \(m=\sum_i|R_i|\). The output is the full relation
\[
J_Q(R_1,\ldots,R_r)
=\{t:V\to\mathrm{dom}:\ \forall i,\ t|_{e_i}\in R_i\}.
\]
Every attribute is output; there is no projection, aggregation or bag multiplicity.

The fractional edge-cover number depends only on the schema:
\[
\rho(Q)=\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r x_i:
x_i\ge0,\quad
\forall v\in V,\ \sum_{i:v\in e_i}x_i\ge1\right\}.
\]
It is finite and at least one. The variables \(x_i\) are real weights on relation schemas, not data values or relation sizes.

For a precise finite encoding, fix an integer \(a\ge1\) and let a machine word contain \(w=a\lceil\log_2(m+2)\rceil\) bits. Domain values are arbitrary \(w\)-bit strings, with equality of strings deciding attribute matches. A tuple occupies a constant number of words depending only on \(Q\), including its relation tag. Quantification over every fixed \(a\) gives the usual polynomial-size-domain word convention. A message word can contain any \(w\)-bit string computed by its sender; its interpretation is not restricted to a tuple, identifier, count or comparison result.

There are \(p\) machines with distinct indices \(1,\ldots,p\), each able to communicate directly with every other machine. The total input is initially partitioned without replication, with each machine holding at most \(2\lceil m/p\rceil\) tagged tuples. The algorithm must work for every such partition. All machines know \(Q,a,m,p\), the encoding and their own index, but receive no other instance-specific advice, preprocessing or statistics for free.

Each synchronous round consists of arbitrary finite local computation followed by message transmission. All messages in the transmission phase must have been prepared before receiving any message from that phase. A machine may send different messages to different recipients, and later rounds may depend on earlier messages. The load is
\[
\max_{\text{round }j,\ \text{machine }u}
\{\text{number of words received by }u\text{ in round }j\}.
\]
Headers and transmitted metadata count; a word sent to several recipients is received separately by each. Local computation, local storage, outgoing traffic as a separate metric, and local output are uncharged. There is no additional memory cap or running-time requirement, but each local phase must terminate.

Output uses a local emission operation on an explicitly written full tuple. Every output tuple must appear on at least one machine, no non-result tuple may appear on any machine, and repeated emissions of a valid tuple are allowed. A factorized representation, tuple count or emptiness bit is not the required output. A machine may derive and emit a tuple from arbitrary received information; it need not have received all its witness input tuples as intact records.

The algorithm is a single finite effective program for each fixed \(Q,a\), with independent private random bits and no advice depending on \(m,p\) or the data. Its joint correctness/load event has probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) on every instance. All constants in the displayed bound may depend on \(Q,a\), but not on relation contents, input size, machine count or initial partition. The one-machine case is trivial and does not affect the target. The source's polynomial slack condition \(p^3\le m\) is retained rather than enlarged to all machine counts.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence assertion. A positive answer must cover every fixed schema, arbitrary data skew and every valid initial distribution, with the required full output and simultaneous round/load guarantee. A negative answer must show that the target fails for at least one fixed schema in the general-message model. An impossibility restricted to transmitting whole tuples or to a single round is insufficient. This is a binary resource-existence question; no numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention relaxes its bound or exact join output on successful runs.
context:
The source focuses on data complexity: a schema is fixed, while its input relations grow. It measures communication received by the busiest machine, and treats local processing and emission of output tuples as free. Its binary-relation result uses three rounds and the edge-cover load scale up to polylogarithmic factors.

The source distinguishes one-round bounds from constant-round algorithms. Its one-round structural parameter can exceed the fractional edge-cover number, so a one-round lower bound does not answer the multiround question.

The later JACM result gives a cyclic boat schema with \(\rho=2\) for which tuple-based algorithms need load \(\Omega(m/p^{1/3})\) in the relevant machine regime. This exceeds the proposed scale \(\widetilde O(m/p^{1/2})\). The restriction to tuple-based algorithms is explicit in both its model and theorem.

In that restricted model, input rows are atoms, and reporting an output tuple requires receiving all of its input witnesses. This card allows arbitrary encodings and inferences instead. Consequently the published restricted lower bound is not presented as a refutation of the selected target.

The same JACM article obtains the edge-cover scale for acyclic joins and distinguishes their behavior from cyclic queries in the tuple-based setting. Thus the failure of the universal tuple-based claim does not negate the established special cases.

The March 2026 κ-Join preprint gives a schema-dependent load bound based on a reduced quasi vertex-cover parameter. It conjectures matching lower bounds for tuple-based algorithms and explicitly says that general tightness remains unresolved. It does not establish the claimed edge-cover bound for arbitrary coded messages.
why: Parallel join processing must distribute related information so that machines can produce all compatible output tuples. The fractional edge-cover number captures a fundamental structural feature of the query. Whether it still suffices for communication with unrestricted messages separates a general information limit from limitations of algorithms that move database rows intact.
status_note: The source’s general edge-cover load target remains the selected question in unrestricted-message MPC. The 2024 JACM result refutes its atomic-tuple version, but expressly limits the lower bound to that model. The March 2026 kappa-Join preprint also states its lower-bound conjecture for tuple-based algorithms. No matching result for arbitrary message encodings was found in this bounded review.
progress: 2020-03-11: The source states the arbitrary-schema question and gives a three-round algorithm for binary relations. | 2021: PODS introduces stronger cyclic-query load lower bounds in the tuple-based framework. | 2024-02: The JACM article explicitly separates cyclic and acyclic behavior and states the boat-query lower bound for tuple-based MPC. | 2026-03-10: The κ-Join preprint proposes a new general schema parameter and a tuple-based tightness conjecture. | 2026-09-16: The user selects unrestricted messages; the review fixes word, output, load and round conventions and preserves the restricted status of known lower bounds.
working_summary: A natural join returns every assignment of values that belongs to all input relations on their shared attributes. The question asks whether every fixed schema can be processed in constant MPC rounds with load matching its fractional-edge-cover scale up to polylogarithmic factors. The selected model permits arbitrary encoded messages and requires explicit full output, with free local computation and receive-only communication cost. A published stronger lower bound rules out the analogous target for algorithms that treat rows as indivisible tuples. That restricted lower bound and the checked 2026 results do not settle the general-message assertion retained here.

title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
importance_reason: A broad structural comparison between randomized communication and parity measurements, with consequences for transferring sketching lower bounds to unrestricted one-way protocols.
formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.
definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.
context:
The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.
why: A positive result would justify proving lower bounds for arbitrary one-way XOR protocols by analyzing linear summaries, a much more structured class. A separation would identify Boolean information that a short nonlinear message preserves more effectively than nonadaptive random parities.
status_note: The primary CCC 2018 paper leaves the worst-input randomized comparison open. The checked April 2026 simulation is for a different streaming model and does not claim this one-way communication theorem. No matching resolution was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check; the precise polylogarithmic-loss convention is stated explicitly.
progress: 2017: Yaroslavtsev presents the conjecture at the Banff workshop. | 2018: The CCC paper proves the uniform-distribution comparison and records the general randomized conjecture. | 2026-04-23: Jiang, Liu and Yu give a polynomial-length integer-turnstile simulation and distinguish prior XOR-stream results from that model.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary Boolean function on a binary vector space. A parity sketch measures a fixed random collection of linear forms and then decodes their bits. A one-way protocol may instead send any randomized message about Alice’s vector to Bob. The conjecture asks whether parity sketches lose only a universal polylogarithmic factor for the associated XOR function. Known deterministic and uniform-input comparisons do not establish the required worst-input randomized bound.

title: Polynomial-state protocols for Presburger arithmetic
importance_reason: A structural succinctness question linking quantified logic and finite-state distributed computation; it isolates local state complexity beyond the established expressiveness and quantifier-free synthesis results.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(C,k\) such that every Presburger formula \(\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\), including arbitrary nested quantifiers, has a leaderless pairwise population protocol \(P_\varphi\) with
\[
|Q_\varphi|\le C(1+|\varphi|)^k
\]
that computes its truth value on every input \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb N^d\) with \(\sum_i a_i\ge2\), reaching permanent unanimous agreement under every fair execution?
The size is that of the original quantified formula, using the syntax and encoding below. The constants are independent of the formula and population size. No running-time bound is required for constructing the protocol or for reaching consensus.
question_excerpt: The conclusion asks whether polynomially many states suffice for every Presburger formula, possibly with quantifiers, and distinguishes this from the known quantifier-free construction and the difficulty of synthesis. The user selected the leaderless pairwise model with stable consensus under all fair executions.
definitions:
All variables range over \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Formulas are finite syntax trees built from linear comparisons \(\sum_i c_i z_i>b\) and congruences \(\sum_i c_i z_i\equiv b\pmod m\), Boolean connectives \(\neg,\wedge,\vee\), and quantifiers \(\exists z,\forall z\). Coefficients and thresholds are integers, and a congruence modulus is an integer \(m\ge2\). A congruence asserts integer divisibility of the difference by \(m\). Comparisons and sums are evaluated in the integers; quantified values remain nonnegative. Equality and other order relations are expressible using these primitives. Coefficient multiplication is by fixed encoded integers, not multiplication of two variables. Remainder atoms are the standard definitional extension used by the source.

The formula has a declared list of \(d\ge1\) free input variables. A sentence can be treated as independent of one dummy input variable. Encode the original syntax tree explicitly, with operator tags, parentheses or equivalent delimiters, variable binding/index information, and signed binary coefficients, thresholds and moduli. The size \(|\varphi|\) is the total bit length, including the free-variable list. Subexpressions are written at each occurrence; there are no shared circuit nodes, macros hiding large formulas, or uncharged quantifier elimination. Standard explicit encodings of this syntax are polynomially interconvertible, so the existence of some polynomial state bound is independent of their routine delimiter choices.

A leaderless pairwise population protocol consists of a finite state set \(Q\), an input map \(\iota:\{1,\ldots,d\}\to Q\), an output map \(o:Q\to\{0,1\}\), and a finite transition relation \(T\). A transition replaces a multiset of exactly two states by another multiset of exactly two states. Thus a rule may have the form \(\{p,q\}\to\{r,s\}\), allowing equal states; two occurrences of a state require two distinct agents in that state. Include the identity rule for every two-state multiset, so every configuration of at least two agents admits an infinite execution. Multiple rules with the same input multiset are allowed and are resolved by the scheduler. All agents are anonymous; there are no identifiers, order comparisons, extra leaders, initially supplied helper agents, or a known bound on the population.

A configuration is a multiplicity vector \(D:Q\to\mathbb N\). A rule with input multiset \(u\) and output multiset \(v\) is enabled when \(D\ge u\) coordinatewise and then produces \(D-u+v\). The input \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\) gives exactly
\[
D_{\mathbf a}(q)=\sum_{\{i:\iota(i)=q\}}a_i
\]
agents in each state \(q\), with no additive initial population. Total population size is conserved. As in the source, correctness is required for all inputs with at least two agents; the zero-agent and one-agent cases are outside this protocol convention.

Write \(D\to^*E\) for reachability by finitely many legal transitions, including zero transitions. An infinite execution \(D_0,D_1,\ldots\) is globally fair if, for every configuration \(E\), whenever the set \(\{j:D_j\to^*E\}\) is infinite, the set \(\{j:D_j=E\}\) is also infinite. This is the source's configuration-reachability fairness, not merely the requirement that each pair of agent identities meet infinitely often.

The protocol computes \(\varphi\) when, for every allowed input and every fair execution starting at \(D_{\mathbf a}\), there is a finite index \(J\) such that for every \(j\ge J\) and every occupied state \(q\), \(o(q)\) equals the Boolean truth value of \(\varphi(\mathbf a)\). All agents must agree thereafter; they need not detect stabilization or stop interacting. The stabilization index can depend on both input and execution.

The resource being minimized is the number of states available to one agent, \(|Q|\), not its bit logarithm, the number of agents, or the time to consensus. Protocol descriptions depend on \(\varphi\) but not on its input vector. All transition rules are explicit finite rules; pairwise state semantics cannot hide an oracle for the predicate. The same \(C,k\) work for all formulas. The assertion is purely existential and does not add an efficient uniform synthesis procedure.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated uniform polynomial bound. An affirmative proof must establish one pair \(C,k\) and the existence, for every original quantified formula, of a protocol with the required state count, leaderless initialization and correctness on every fair execution for every allowed input. A negative proof must establish the negation of that quantified assertion. A polynomial bound only after quantifier elimination, a protocol using extra leaders, or a lower bound only on construction time does not answer this target. No numerical tolerance changes the proposition, and no Lean proof is supplied merely by specifying a finite transition table.
context:
Population protocols distribute computation among anonymous agents with a fixed finite repertoire of states. They determine properties of the initial counts of input types. Presburger arithmetic describes exactly the predicates computable in this model, but that expressiveness theorem does not determine how many states a short logical specification requires.

The 2020 theorem gives polynomially many states for quantifier-free combinations of linear thresholds and congruences. A quantified formula can be much shorter than a formula obtained by eliminating its quantifiers. Consequently, applying the known theorem to an expanded quantifier-free formula does not establish a polynomial bound in the original input size.

The source also distinguishes small protocols from efficiently finding them. The present target asks whether small protocols exist; its affirmative answer would not include a polynomial-time synthesis algorithm or a convergence-time guarantee. Later fast-and-succinct results strengthen the quantifier-free case, and their input-size parameter remains crucial.

Recent protocols over ordered agents allow interactions to inspect extra positional information. That changes the anonymous model specified here and does not provide an answer to this state-complexity question.
why: The question compares the succinctness of logical descriptions with that of anonymous distributed computation. It asks whether quantifier compression forces an unavoidable increase in the number of local states, even when computation time is unrestricted. This separates representational power from synthesis and stabilization complexity.
status_note: Open in the precise source distinction: STACS 2020 §7 asks for polynomial states in the original possibly quantified formula, while its main theorem covers the quantifier-free representation. The inspected 2024 fast-and-succinct result still measures a quantifier-free formula and does not establish the present bound before quantifier elimination. On 16 September 2026 a bounded later-work check found no resolution; the 2026 ordered-agent paper concerns a different model. This is an existential state-size question, not an efficient synthesis claim: the source separately proves a synthesis-time obstruction. Definitions and theorem scopes were inspected; full source proofs, exhaustive literature coverage and Lean formalization are not claimed.
progress: 2020: Theorem 2 establishes succinct leaderless protocols for quantifier-free formulas; §7 explicitly leaves state bounds for original quantified formulas open. | 2024: Fast-and-succinct protocols improve the quantifier-free size/time tradeoff, without establishing a bound before quantifier elimination. | 2026: Ordered-agent protocols study additional interaction capabilities and therefore a different computational model. | 2026-09-16: The bounded update retained the quantified-formula state question as source-open and recorded the user-selected leaderless semantics.
working_summary: A population protocol uses anonymous finite-state agents whose pairwise interactions eventually decide a predicate of their initial counts. The question asks whether every quantified Presburger formula has such a leaderless protocol with polynomially many states in the original formula size. Correctness requires permanent unanimous agreement on every globally fair execution, without a time bound. Known succinct protocols for quantifier-free formulas do not control the expansion caused by eliminating quantifiers. A resolution would separate or equate the succinctness of quantified logical specifications and anonymous finite-state distributed computation.

title: Classification of robust chemical computation
importance_reason: An exact classification would identify which analog computations can depend only on reaction stoichiometry and initial concentrations, despite arbitrary kinetic constants.
question_excerpt: The authors conjecture that the classes constructed in their positive results exhaust robust predicate and numerical-function computation. The function class is the one defined in Definition 2.3, despite a shortened name in the conclusion.
definitions:
A chemical reaction network has a finite species set \(\Lambda\) and finitely many reactions indexed by \(R\). Reaction \(r\) has reactant and product vectors \(a_r,b_r\in\mathbb N^\Lambda\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), with \(a_r\ne b_r\). The vectors give integer stoichiometric multiplicities. Empty reactants or products are allowed; there is no restriction to reactions of a particular order.

Choose distinct input species \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), with \(\Sigma=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\), and a fixed initial context \(i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\Lambda\setminus\Sigma}\). For input \(x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{k}\), the initial concentration is \(c_{X_j}(0)=x_j\) and \(c_S(0)=i_S\) for \(S\notin\Sigma\). The context can contain arbitrary nonnegative real constants. It is fixed as part of the computing network and depends neither on the input nor on the rate constants.

For each assignment \(\kappa\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{R}\), the mass-action trajectory solves
\[
\frac{dc_S}{dt}
=\sum_{r\in R}(b_r(S)-a_r(S))\kappa_r
\prod_{T\in\Lambda}c_T(t)^{a_r(T)}
\qquad(S\in\Lambda).
\]
An exponent-zero factor is one, including at zero concentration. Each \(\kappa_r\) is a finite positive real constant, independent of time, with no common upper or positive lower bound assumed. The polynomial vector field has a unique maximal solution from the initial state. A network used in either robust computation definition must have a nonnegative solution defined for every \(t\ge0\), for every input and every \(\kappa\); finite-time blowup does not qualify. Species other than the output need not converge or remain bounded over infinite time.

For predicate computation choose disjoint voter sets \(\Upsilon_0,\Upsilon_1\subseteq\Lambda\). The network robustly decides \(\varphi\) when, for every \(x\) and \(\kappa\), writing \(b=\varphi(x)\),
\[
\liminf_{t\to\infty}\sum_{S\in\Upsilon_b}c_S(t)>0,
\qquad
\forall S\in\Upsilon_{1-b},\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}c_S(t)=0.
\]
The positive lower limiting value may depend on \(x,\kappa\). It is the total correct-voter concentration that must stay away from zero; individual correct voters need not converge. For numerical computation choose one output species \(Y\in\Lambda\). The network robustly computes \(f\) when, for every \(x,\kappa\),
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}c_Y(t)=f(x).
\]
Input and output species are not required to be disjoint. A predicate or function is called robustly decidable or computable if some finite network with the appropriate fixed data has this property. No bound on time, species, reactions or convergence rate is imposed. The network may depend on the entire predicate or function, but not on a particular input or rate assignment.

A threshold predicate has the form
\[
\theta(x)=\mathbf1\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^k q_jx_j>h\right\},
\qquad q_j\in\mathbb Q,\quad h\in\mathbb R,
\]
where \(\mathbf1\) is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. A multi-threshold predicate is a finite Boolean expression using such tests, constants, AND, OR and NOT. This defines boundary behavior at equality exactly.

A rational floor-affine function is
\[
g(x)=\max\!\left\{0,b+\sum_{j=1}^k q_jx_j\right\},
\qquad q_j\in\mathbb Q,\quad b\in\mathbb R.
\]
Here “floor” means clipping below zero, not rounding to an integer. A function \(f\) is threshold-piecewise rational floor-affine if there exist an integer \(\ell\ge1\), multi-threshold predicates \(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_\ell\), and functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_\ell\) of the displayed form such that, for every \(x\), exactly one \(\varphi_j(x)\) equals one and \(f(x)=g_j(x)\) for that index. The partition is finite; continuity across its boundaries is not required. Slopes are rational, while thresholds and offsets may be arbitrary real constants.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the joint classification. A positive answer must establish both equivalences for every input dimension, with the exact dynamics and convergence conventions stated here. A negative answer must prove the negation of at least one equivalence, for example by fully verifying a robustly computing network whose predicate or function lies outside the specified class. This is an exact yes/no classification, so the numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention does not replace equality of functions or exact Boolean decisions. A result for a single choice of rate constants, leaderless networks only, discrete molecule counts, or time-varying rate laws does not establish the claimed characterization.
context:
The continuous model represents molecular amounts by nonnegative real concentrations. Reactions give a polynomial differential equation. Different positive kinetic constants change trajectories, but robust computation requires their eventual output to agree for every such choice.

Stable chemical computation allows a more powerful adversary controlling reaction progress beyond fixed mass-action laws. The paper shows that stable Boolean decisions can inspect which inputs are zero, but cannot in general distinguish arbitrary positive magnitudes. Fixed-constant mass-action robustness admits more predicates.

Theorem 3.7 constructs robust deciders for every finite Boolean combination of rational-weight threshold tests. Initial context permits real threshold offsets. Exact behavior on the threshold itself is part of the predicate, even though the answer is obtained asymptotically.

Theorem 3.10 constructs robust computers for the finite threshold-defined partitions and rational floor-affine pieces in the question. The resulting functions may be discontinuous. Their values are concentration limits, rather than integer molecule counts.

The conclusion conjectures necessity of both constructed classes. It separately discusses removing initial context and representing signed inputs by differences of concentrations. Those alternatives are outside this card’s selected source conjecture.

The 2026 reverse-robust result allows discrete reactions to run backward until a cutoff and then only forward. Its semilinear classification concerns that different execution model and does not establish the continuous mass-action classification here.
why: Chemical implementations often have uncertain reaction speeds. This question isolates what can be computed when every positive choice of fixed kinetic constants must lead to the same answer. A classification would distinguish robust computational content from behavior that depends on carefully selected reaction rates.
status_note: The published DISC 2025 paper proves the sufficient directions and conjectures that they are necessary in §4. This review fixes the exact model from Definitions 2.1–2.7, with initial context and arbitrary fixed positive rate constants. The 2026 reverse-robust CRN result concerns a different discrete model. No resolution of the joint continuous-model classification was found in the bounded review.
progress: 2025-06-06: The original preprint gives constructive robust computation results for threshold predicates and piecewise affine numerical outputs. | 2025: The published paper states exact definitions, proves the sufficient directions in Theorems 3.7 and 3.10, and conjectures their necessity in §4. | 2026-04-15: A new preprint studies reverse robustness for discrete CRNs; its model does not resolve the mass-action classification. | 2026-09-16: Individual review recovers the complete joint conjecture and distinguishes all initial-context, rate and output conventions.
working_summary: A continuous chemical reaction network computes through the evolution of nonnegative species concentrations. Robust computation requires the same limiting answer for every assignment of positive reaction-rate constants fixed over time. The conjecture characterizes robust predicates by finite Boolean combinations of rational-weight threshold tests. It simultaneously characterizes numerical outputs by finite threshold-defined partitions with rational affine pieces clipped at zero. The constructive directions are known, while necessity remains unresolved in the sources checked.

title: Two-stage group testing with arithmetic progressions
importance_reason: A concrete query-design question connecting structured pools, sparse identification and limited adaptivity. Its contribution is narrower than unrestricted group testing, but the arithmetic-progression restriction captures a meaningful loss of query freedom and the source identifies a pattern-matching motivation.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C,D>0\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le n\), an unknown set \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|\le k\) can be identified exactly by the following deterministic two-stage scheme?

The first stage uses at most \(Ck\log_2 n\) tests. Each test asks whether \(S\) meets a finite arithmetic progression contained in \([n]\), and every first-stage test is fixed before any answers are received. After seeing all first-stage answers, the second stage chooses at most \(Dk\) individual indices and learns their membership in \(S\). All second-stage indices must be chosen before receiving any second-stage answer. The final output must equal \(S\) for every admissible hidden set.

The constants must work simultaneously for all \(n,k,S\). The resource being bounded is the number of tests in each stage; neither constructing the scheme nor decoding the answers is subject to a running-time bound.
question_excerpt: Porat asks whether two-stage exact group testing can use \(O(k\log n)\) first-stage pools when each pool is an arithmetic progression. Only \(O(k)\) individually chosen membership tests are allowed in the second stage. The listed benchmark for the progression-restricted first stage is \(O(k\log^2 n)\).
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input parameters \(n\) and \(k\) are known; only the subset \(S\) is hidden. The promise is an upper bound \(|S|\le k\), not knowledge of its exact size. In particular \(S=\varnothing\) is allowed. The elements have their fixed integer positions, and the arithmetic-progression constraint refers to these positions. There is no ability to permute the hidden input and then declare arbitrary pools to be progressions.

An admissible first-stage pool has the form
\[T=\{a,a+d,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)d\},\qquad a,d,\ell\in\mathbb N_{>0},\quad a+(\ell-1)d\le n.\]
Each pool may have its own start, step and length. Singletons are allowed. There is no wraparound modulo \(n\), no repeated item within a pool, and no requirement that the progression be extended to the ends of \([n]\). The answer is the noiseless bit \(b(T,S)=1\) if \(T\cap S\ne\varnothing\), and zero otherwise. It does not reveal the number or positions of the elements in the intersection.

For given \(n,k\), a scheme consists of a nonnegative integer \(m\), a list of admissible pools \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\), a selection function \(J\), and a final decoding function \(F\). The list depends only on \(n,k\); it is identical for every possible hidden set of the promised size. Write
\[y(S)=(b(T_1,S),\ldots,b(T_m,S))\in\{0,1\}^m.\]
The selection function takes any first-stage answer vector \(y\) to a set \(J(y)\subseteq[n]\) of indices with \(|J(y)|\le Dk\). Every selected index is queried separately, giving the function \(z_S:J(y(S))\to\{0,1\}\) defined by \(z_S(j)=1\) exactly when \(j\in S\). The final decoder knows the parameters, the entire first-stage design, \(y(S)\), the selected indices and their individual answers. Correctness means
\[\forall S\subseteq[n]\text{ with }|S|\le k:\quad F\bigl(y(S),z_S\bigr)=S.\]
The decoder may infer membership of unqueried indices from the complete transcript. It is not required to query every element that it finally reports. Queries in the second stage are individual membership tests only; no additional pooled tests or third stage are allowed. Unrealizable first-stage answer vectors can have arbitrary decoding behavior, subject to the same advertised second-stage query cap.

One test is one oracle answer, independent of the pool's cardinality. First-stage pools may be represented by their integer triples \((a,d,\ell)\), and individual indices and parameters in binary, but description length and computational time are not the costs asked about. No noise, random hidden-set distribution, random design, or probability of error is part of this formulation. This records the source's exact identification problem for an arbitrary set, as opposed to average-case recovery. An existence proof for the finite designs and functions suffices; a polynomial-time construction is not an extra requirement. Since all choices for fixed finite parameters can be enumerated and their correctness checked, this convention does not allow an undecidable query operation.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,D>0\;\forall n,k\;\exists(T_1,\ldots,T_m,J,F)\;\forall S\), with the stated size restrictions. In particular a separate design tailored to the unknown \(S\) is inadmissible. The upper bound uses \(\log_2 n\), not \(\log_2(n/k)\). The source's \(O(k\log n)\) and \(O(k)\) mean absolute constant factors independent of both parameters. Using \(n\ge2\) avoids the irrelevant zero logarithm at one item.

A negative answer is the logical negation: for every proposed pair of constants \(C,D>0\), there are admissible \(n,k\) for which every scheme satisfying both test caps fails on some hidden set. It need not establish a particular alternative asymptotic lower-bound formula. A lower bound for a single family of progressions, a chosen decoder, or a nonadaptive one-stage scheme would not by itself disprove the target.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of absolute constants and two-stage schemes with the stated bounds. A positive answer must prove the arithmetic-progression restriction, first-stage independence from answers, the \(O(k)\) cap on individual second-stage queries, and exact recovery for every hidden set of size at most \(k\), uniformly over the full parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out all allowed designs and decoders with every proposed pair of constant factors. Results allowing arbitrary first-stage pools, more rounds, non-individual second-stage tests, or error on some hidden sets do not settle this proposition. This is an asymptotic existence question, so additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.
context:
The hidden set represents a sparse collection of relevant positions. A pooled answer identifies whether an entire regular selection of positions contains any relevant element, so many positions can be checked with one bit of feedback.

The central restriction concerns which collections can be tested together. An arithmetic progression has a fixed spacing, as occurs when inspecting regularly sampled positions in pattern-matching applications. A result for arbitrary subsets does not automatically provide such regularly spaced pools.

The source permits one round of adaptation: pooled answers can determine which individual positions will be checked next. Its question asks whether this limited feedback compensates for the restriction on first-stage pools.

The 2009 question reports \(O(k\log^2 n)\) first-stage tests under the arithmetic-progression restriction and asks to remove one logarithmic factor. This is a dated benchmark reported by the problem proposer, not a newly verified 2026 optimality claim.

The unrestricted two-stage setting has order-optimal test-count results in the cited 2005 paper. Its publisher abstract confirms that the main theorem concerns unrestricted intersection queries, with other variants treated separately. This comparison explains why the geometry of the permitted pools is the substantive issue here.

The inherited card contained only the topic name. The full problem page supplies the two stages, the progression restriction and the desired bound. This review preserves that target and makes the worst-case, zero-error and test-count-only conventions explicit. It does not add efficient construction or a distributional recovery promise.
why: This question tests how much measurement restrictions can cost in sparse identification even when one follow-up round is available. A resolution would distinguish what arbitrary pooling achieves from what regularly spaced queries can support, a distinction motivated by pattern matching rather than by a new statistical noise model.

On 16 September 2026 the full problem page and its current collected-PDF reproduction were checked, together with the publisher abstract and metadata of the cited 2005 unrestricted two-stage paper. The page was last edited in March 2013. Bounded later-work searches using the arithmetic-progression restriction, two-stage target and proposer name found no matching resolution. The active status reflects that dated source and limited search, not a recent author confirmation or exhaustive literature certification.
