This is the baseline cited by Porat; it does not impose arithmetic progressions. | 2009: Problem 33 records the progression-restricted \(O(k\log^2 n)\) bound and asks for \(O(k\log n)\), retaining only \(O(k)\) individual queries after the first-stage results. | 16 September 2026: The original problem page still presents the question, with a last edit dated March 2013. A bounded search for subsequent arithmetic-progression group-testing results found no matching resolution; the age of this page limits the current-status evidence.
working_summary: A hidden set of at most k positions must be identified by noiseless yes/no tests. Every first-stage pool must be an arithmetic progression fixed before any answers are seen. After receiving those answers, the scheme may query only O(k) individual positions in one final stage. The question asks whether O(k log n) first-stage tests suffice for every hidden set, improving the bound reported in the 2009 source by one logarithmic factor. The restriction models regularly spaced queries motivated by pattern matching, and unrestricted pooling results do not settle it.

title: Polynomial-in-optimum graph matching in \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)
importance_reason: The problem isolates whether extremely shallow uniform Boolean computation can construct a growing set of compatible choices even when it can already estimate their attainable number.
formal:
Do there exist constants \(c,\alpha>0\) and a DLOGTIME-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits \((C_n)_{n\ge1}\), of constant depth and polynomial size, such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is mapped to a matching \(M(G)\subseteq E(G)\) satisfying
\[
|M(G)|\ \ge\ c\,\nu(G)^\alpha?
\]
Here \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum cardinality of a matching in \(G\). The same constants and circuit family must work for all \(n\) and all graphs. The output must identify the actual chosen edges. The scale \(c\,\nu^\alpha\), and the restriction to graph matching rather than general set packing, were explicitly selected by the user.
question_excerpt: The source leaves open whether AC0 circuits can construct approximate graph matchings, and then raises the more general set-packing question. Its positive approximation result concerns the optimum size alone.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. Its input is its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix \(A\), in row-major order, with \(A_{ii}=0\), \(A_{ij}=A_{ji}\in\{0,1\}\), and \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(\{i,j\}\in E(G)\). Thus \(C_n\) has \(n^2\) input bits. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted.

The circuit has \(n^2\) output bits, interpreted as a matrix \(B\) in the same order. It must satisfy \(B_{ii}=0\), \(B_{ij}=B_{ji}\le A_{ij}\), and, for every vertex \(i\), at most one \(B_{ij}\) is one. The represented matching is
\[
M(G)=\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ B_{ij}=1\}.
\]
A matching is any collection of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoint sets, and \(\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching in }G\}\). This counts edges, not covered vertices. For an edgeless graph \(\nu(G)=0\), and the output is the empty matching; use \(0^\alpha=0\).

The permitted internal gates are AND and OR of unbounded fan-in and NOT of fan-in one, together with constant zero and one. Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs; wires may fan out to many gates. There are fixed integers \(D,k\ge1\) and a constant \(K\ge1\) such that every \(C_n\) has depth at most \(D\) and at most \(K(n+1)^k\) gates and wires. Depth is the maximum number of internal gates on any input-to-output path. The circuits receive no randomness, advice or auxiliary graph information.

DLOGTIME uniformity means that the circuits admit gate addresses of \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits and a single deterministic random-access Turing machine describing their local wiring in \(O(\log(n+2))\) time. Given \(n\) in binary and gate addresses, it decides whether an address is valid, the gate type, and whether a directed wire joins two addressed gates; it also identifies the designated input and output gate for an addressed matrix coordinate. Random access means that the machine can query an input bit using its binary address. The machine and constants are independent of \(n\) and of the input graph. Hardwiring a separate arbitrary circuit description for each \(n\) is not uniformity.

The constants \(c,\alpha\) do not depend on \(n\) or on \(\nu(G)\). One may equivalently require rational \(0<c,\alpha\le1\): decreasing either positive constant preserves the assertion for integer \(\nu(G)\ge1\), and \(|M(G)|\le\nu(G)\) rules out a persistent exponent greater than one on graphs with unbounded optimum. The condition asks for a positive power of the optimum; it is not an assertion of a fixed ratio \(|M(G)|/\nu(G)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this exact existence assertion. A positive answer must specify the uniform circuit family and fixed constants and prove circuit size, depth, uniformity, output validity and the cardinality inequality for every graph. A negative answer must refute all choices of positive constants and all allowed circuit families. This binary question has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Producing only an estimate of \(\nu(G)\), proving a limitation of monotone circuits, or handling a restricted input class alone does not meet this target.
context:
The source uses the functional version of AC0: a circuit can have many output bits, but still has constant depth, polynomial size and DLOGTIME uniformity. Its Boolean basis includes negation. Threshold or majority gates belong to the stronger TC0 model used separately in the paper.

For hitting set, the paper gives AC0 circuits that output a hitting set with size polynomial in the optimum. The analogous passage for packing explicitly says that extracting a collection of disjoint sets remains an unresolved issue.

Theorem 5.6 estimates the size of an optimum packing in a bounded-rank hypergraph. For graphs its guarantee gives a numerical lower estimate on the order of the square root of the optimum. The returned number does not identify disjoint edges, so it does not solve the search question.

The source does not prescribe a matching approximation ratio. The selected target fixes a positive-power guarantee in the optimum, which can be substantially weaker than a constant-factor approximation. The source’s independent extension to general set packing remains provenance rather than a second task on this card.

The 2025 monotone lower bound concerns deciding whether a perfect matching exists using AND and OR without negation. Both the restricted gate basis and the exact decision objective differ from the construction problem here. It therefore supplies context, not a negative resolution.
why: A matching requires many output decisions to be mutually consistent: selected edges may not share vertices. This creates a concrete test of the constructive power of uniform constant-depth circuits. A resolution would clarify how much of combinatorial approximation survives when the number of sequential logical layers is bounded independently of input size.
status_note: The 2020 source leaves approximate matching construction in AC0 open without fixing a ratio. On 16 September 2026 the user selected the polynomial-in-optimum graph-search variant formalized here. The checked 2025 monotone exact-decision lower bound does not settle this variant. No resolution was found in the bounded review.
progress: 2020: The published paper gives uniform shallow-circuit packing-size estimates and leaves construction of approximate matchings open. | 2025-11-06: A revised monotone perfect-matching lower bound concerns a different gate basis and exact decision task. | 2026-09-16: The user selects graph matching with a positive-power-of-optimum output bound; the individual review specifies the complete circuit and output model.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary labelled simple graph, and the output must explicitly identify pairwise vertex-disjoint edges. One deterministic uniform AC0 circuit family must produce at least c times the optimum matching size to the power alpha, for fixed positive c and alpha. The circuits have constant depth, polynomial size and unrestricted-fan-in AND and OR gates together with negation. The source can estimate packing cardinality in this model but does not construct a corresponding packing. The selected search question remains unresolved in the checked sources and is distinct from recent monotone exact-matching lower bounds.

title: Streaming space for additive \(L_\infty\) estimation
importance_reason: A focused model comparison or resource frontier in distributed, parallel, or streaming computation.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal worst-case bit space for a one-pass randomized streaming algorithm that returns only an estimate \(z\) of \(\|f\|_\infty\), with \[\Pr\!\left[|z-\|f\|_\infty|\le\frac{\|f\|_p}{k}\right]\ge\frac23.\] The bound must describe its dependence on domain size \(n\ge2\), update budget \(M\ge2\), accuracy parameter \(k\ge4\), norm flag \(p\in\{1,2\}\), and update mode \(b\in\{\mathrm{insert},\mathrm{difference}\}\), in the model below.
definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.
context:
The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.
why: Separate the memory needed for one largest-magnitude estimate from the information needed to identify heavy coordinates, while accounting for error scale, domain size and cancellation.
status_note: Partially resolved historical source direction. The PODS 2016 paper explicitly reports an answer for insertion-only L1-relative maximum-frequency estimation, so that endpoint is not advertised here as a fresh open problem. The present full space characterization retains both source norms and update modes with explicit editorial conventions. Its complete current status was not established by the bounded 14 September 2026 search; source proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2006: Cormode asks for reduced bit space for scalar \(L_\infty\) estimates under \(L_1\)- or \(L_2\)-scaled additive error, discussing insertions and differences of streams. | 2016: Bhattacharyya–Dey–Woodruff report improved maximum-frequency space and a resolution of the insertion-only \(L_1\) variant in their formulation. This is a partial resolution of the broader source direction.
working_summary: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector. The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm. Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question. The target is a tight bit-space characterization in the domain size, update budget and accuracy. A 2016 paper reports resolving the insertion-only L1 part, while this review does not certify a complete characterization of all cases.

title: Query complexity of the graph degree distribution
importance_reason: A focused estimation, group-testing, or reduction question whose main consequences are within its specified model.
formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors, the function
\[
Q^\star(n,m,h,w)=
\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}\ 
\max_{G\in\mathcal G(n,m,h,w)}
\mathbb E[T_A(G)]
\]
on every feasible tuple defined below. Here \(\mathcal A\) consists of uniform randomized algorithms which receive only \(n\), access the graph through the three specified query types, and correctly estimate its entire complementary cumulative degree histogram with probability at least \(2/3\). The required simultaneous accuracy is
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\forall d\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\},\
\frac9{10}N_G\!\left(\frac{11}{10}d\right)
\le \widehat N(d)\le
\frac{11}{10}N_G\!\left(\frac9{10}d\right)
\right]\ge\frac23.
\]
The parameters \(m,h,w\) describe the graph on which cost is evaluated; their values, estimates and bounds are not supplied to the algorithm.
question_excerpt: The first question asks whether the SADDLES degree-distribution query bound can be improved and whether matching lower bounds can be proved. The user selected the full four-parameter complexity function, fixed ten-percent bicriteria error and constant-factor precision, with only n known in advance.
definitions:
The input graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\ge2\) and \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is finite, simple and undirected, with no loops or repeated edges. All labels in \([n]\) are valid query arguments; the edge set is hidden. Put
\[
m=|E|,\qquad
N_G(t)=|\{v\in[n]:\deg_G(v)\ge t\}|\quad(t\in\mathbb R).
\]
Thus a noninteger threshold means its ceiling, \(N_G(t)=n\) for \(t\le0\), and \(N_G(t)=0\) for \(t>n-1\). The output is a list of nonnegative rational estimates \(\widehat N(d)\) for integer \(1\le d\le n-1\); the value at zero is known to be \(n\). The event in the question must hold for all output thresholds together.

The h-index and the second tail parameter are
\[
h(G)=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{d\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}:N_G(d)\ge d\}\bigr),
\]
\[
w(G)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{dN_G(d):1\le d\le n-1,\ N_G(d)>0\},&m>0,\\
0,&m=0.
\end{cases}
\]
The \(z\)-index in the 2018 paper satisfies \(z=\sqrt{w}\). These are integer parameters, with the displayed empty-graph convention. A tuple \((n,m,h,w)\) is feasible precisely when some graph on \([n]\) has those values. Let \(\mathcal G(n,m,h,w)\) be the finite nonempty set of all such labeled graphs. The domain includes edgeless graphs.

Each of the following oracle calls costs one query:

- Vertex: return a uniformly random label in \([n]\).
- Degree(\(v\)): return the exact integer \(\deg_G(v)\).
- RandomNeighbor(\(v\)): return a uniformly random neighbor of \(v\), or a distinguished symbol \(\bot\) if its degree is zero.

Random replies are fresh independent samples conditional on the selected query and the fixed graph. An algorithm may adapt its calls and stopping rule to previous replies and its independent fair random bits. There is no indexed-neighbor, edge-existence or direct uniform-edge oracle. The initial input is the binary encoding of \(n\), without advice. Computation, memory, random-bit generation and output length are unrestricted and do not contribute to the query count.

An element of \(\mathcal A\) is one probabilistic Turing machine, uniform over all \(n\ge2\), which halts almost surely with finite expected query count on every input graph and meets the stated success guarantee on every such graph. Let \(T_A(G)\) count all its calls, including those on unsuccessful runs. Expectation includes both its internal randomness and the oracle randomness. The maximum in the question ranges over the exact parameter class, but membership in that class is not an input promise available to \(A\).

The infimum is taken pointwise over this same class \(\mathcal A\). A witness for an upper bound must still be a machine correct on every graph with only \(n\) supplied. The definition does not demand that one machine attain the infimum, or achieve optimal cost simultaneously for every tuple. In particular, a procedure justified only under a promised value of \(m,h,w\) is not automatically an admissible witness. Querying all \(n\) degrees provides an admissible finite baseline.
answer_criterion:
Supply an unambiguous, noncircular description of a nonnegative function \(F\) on the feasible tuples and absolute constants \(c,C>0\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
cF(n,m,h,w)\le Q^\star(n,m,h,w)\le CF(n,m,h,w)
\]
for every feasible tuple. Upper bounds must use admissible algorithms or an approaching family establishing the infimum bound; lower bounds must apply to all admissible algorithms. Merely repeating the optimization defining \(Q^\star\) is not a determination. Hidden logarithmic factors are not permitted in this constant-factor answer, and no additive \(1/100\) tolerance applies to the asymptotic target. Bounds for average degree alone, only the high-degree tail, a stronger query oracle, or algorithms given the hidden parameters do not settle the requested function.
context:
A cumulative degree histogram counts vertices above each degree threshold. Approximating only its normalization in an additive distributional distance can overlook a small but structurally important population of high-degree vertices. The bicriteria requirement controls this tail while allowing a small shift of the threshold.

Uniform vertices and random neighbors have different sampling biases. The model makes these access costs explicit and includes degree queries. The question therefore concerns information available through local graph access, rather than the cost of reading an adjacency matrix.

The 2018 paper introduces the \(z\)-index alongside the usual h-index. In its Standard Model, Theorem 3.1 gives expected cost \(O((n/h+m/w)\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))\), for positive parameters and sample budgets meeting the theorem’s hypotheses, with simultaneous success probability at least \(1-\delta\). This is a sourced algorithmic bound, not a matching characterization.

The sample-budget conditions in that theorem depend on graph parameters. Because this card supplies only the vertex count, an upper-bound proof must account for obtaining suitable information or otherwise justify its stopping rule. The source theorem is not silently promoted to an unknown-parameter guarantee.

The 2025 preprint gives nearly matching bounds on an \(m/h\) scale in a stronger query model, using direct random-edge samples. Its general interface also includes indexed neighbors and edge-existence tests. Those guarantees do not determine the cost when an edge sample must be obtained using only the three calls in this card.

The original entry also raises tail-only estimation, testing degree-distribution properties and replacing uniform vertex samples by other access. Those are separate variants. This card retains the full cumulative profile and the original three types of access.
why: The degree histogram distinguishes common low-degree vertices from rare hubs. Estimating its whole cumulative profile requires guarantees in the tail as well as where most vertices lie. A sharp query bound would identify which structural features permit reliable graph summaries with limited access.
status_note: The 2019 source asks for improved upper and matching lower bounds. Its displayed bicriteria shifts are reversed; this review uses the original 2018 Definition 1.1. The user selected all four performance parameters, fixed ten-percent error and constant-factor precision, then specified on 16 September 2026 that only n is supplied. The 2018 SADDLES theorem requires suitable parameter-dependent sample budgets. The 2025 preprint uses stronger direct random-edge access. Neither source establishes the full constant-factor, four-parameter minimax envelope for the selected information model. No matching resolution was found in the bounded current review.
progress: 2018-08-28: Version 3 states the simultaneous bicriteria guarantee and the h-index/z-index expected-query analysis of SADDLES. | 2019-08-26: Problem 98 asks for improved upper bounds and matching lower bounds for the whole cumulative degree distribution. | 2025-07-29: A preprint studies tighter bounds using direct random-edge access and streaming models; the stronger query interface matters. | 2026-09-16: Individual review applies the user’s four-parameter, constant-factor target with only n supplied and corrects the source display against its cited paper.
working_summary: A graph’s cumulative degree histogram counts vertices above each degree threshold. The task is to estimate the entire histogram with ten-percent bicriteria error and simultaneous success probability at least two thirds. The algorithm knows only the number of vertices and may sample vertices, query degrees or sample neighbors. The target is the optimal expected query complexity as a function of the vertex count, edge count, h-index and minimum positive degree-times-tail count. Known bounds and recent stronger-oracle results do not provide the full constant-factor characterization in this information model.

title: Deterministic linearizable objects for set agreement
importance_reason: A structural question about whether deterministic linearizable abstractions can express exactly the power of set agreement; relevant to classifications of shared-object coordination power. Existing score retained.
formal: Is it true that, for every pair of integers \(n>k>2\), no deterministic linearizable \((n,k)\)-set agreement object is computationally equivalent to the \((n,k)\)-set agreement task? The quantifier includes every proposal domain I with at least n values and every n-ported object satisfying the definitions below. Equivalence means mutual implementation with atomic read/write registers by deterministic wait-free algorithms. The object may depend on n,k and I, may use the chosen port in determining a response, and may be invoked repeatedly; it is not restricted to one call per port.
definitions: The system consists of asynchronous processes with distinct identities communicating through shared objects and atomic read/write registers. A process can crash by stopping permanently. Algorithms must be correct for every schedule and every pattern of such crashes. Wait freedom means each operation or task invocation of a process that continues taking steps completes after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of the speeds or failures of other processes; no fixed complexity bound is requested. Reductions are deterministic: randomization is not available. The one-shot task \(T(n,k,I)\) has at most n participating processes, each supplying an input in I and deciding once. Every decision is an input supplied by a participant, at most k distinct values are decided, and every participant that continues taking steps must decide. No sequential ordering constraint is added to these task guarantees. An \((n,k)\)-set agreement object O has ports \(1,\ldots ,n\) and an operation \(ProposeSA(v), v\in I\). Each process chooses a port for each call and waits for its response before making another call. Access is well formed if no two pending calls use the same port. Ports are not permanently assigned to process identities; arbitrarily many processes may use the object over its lifetime, but at most n calls may be pending simultaneously. Only well-formed access is required to be implemented. On every such execution, each response is the current call’s proposal or a proposal of a previously invoked call, and across the entire execution at most k distinct values are returned. This agreement bound does not reset after a round or after all processes become idle. All invocations are supported and are wait-free. A finite sequential history S is a sequence of completed triples (port,proposal,response). Determinism requires that for every allowed S, port p and proposal v there is a unique response extending S by a call at p with v; different histories or ports may give different responses. Linearizability requires every concurrent history to admit an ordering of its operations that obeys this sequential specification and preserves real-time precedence: an operation whose response precedes another’s invocation must come first. Incomplete calls may be discarded or assigned responses before ordering them. To implement an object means to produce only its allowed histories, with the required termination, for all well-formed client executions; reproducing every allowed history is unnecessary. O and T are computationally equivalent when copies of O and registers can solve T, and O can be implemented from registers and instances of any correct solver for T. A task instance has n one-shot participant roles; separate instances have independent state, and the implementation must rely only on the task guarantees, not on additional agreement power a particular solver might possess. This is the source’s equivalence to the black-box set agreement task. Any number of fresh instances and registers is allowed; a completed operation uses finitely many steps. The object’s specified initial state is fixed independently of client inputs. O already solves T by one proposal per participant on distinct ports, so the substantive issue is whether a reduction from the task to O can exist.
answer_criterion: Prove that no such object and reverse wait-free implementation exist for every \(n>k>2\), or refute the statement by giving a pair \(n>k>2, a\) proposal domain with at least n values, a deterministic linearizable object and a correct wait-free implementation from the set agreement task and registers. A positive proof need not exhibit a stronger set agreement task: that is an additional conjectured explanation in the source, not a required proof method. Restricting objects to port-independent behavior or proving only some parameter pairs does not establish the universal claim.
context:
Set agreement allows several proposed values to be decided. A linearizable object must additionally behave like an ordered sequence of operations. Computational equivalence asks whether these constraints change implementation power, even though the permitted histories differ.

The 2017 paper gives a linearizable object equivalent to the task, but its sequential specification allows nondeterministic choices. The OPODIS paper gives a deterministic equivalent object whose concurrent behavior is not linearizable. Requiring both properties is the remaining issue.

For \(n\ge 4\), the source proves that every deterministic linearizable \((n,2)\)-set agreement object can solve two-process consensus with registers, whereas the \((n,2)\) task alone cannot. It also proves the \(n=3\) case for objects whose sequential behavior is independent of the port. These theorems do not cover \(k>2\).

The 2020 journal paper constructs deterministic linearizable objects whose full set agreement power is insufficient to implement them. This demonstrates limitations of classifying objects by agreement tasks, but does not establish the claimed separation for every deterministic linearizable \((n,k)\)-set agreement object.
why: Tests whether deterministic sequential semantics inevitably add coordination power to reusable set agreement objects, clarifying the relation between one-shot tasks and composable shared-memory abstractions.
status_note: Read the OPODIS definitions and conclusion and the cited DISC 2017 implementation model. Checked the publisher’s 2020 Life beyond set agreement abstract and subsequent-work searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of the universal \(n>k>2\) statement was located. The later paper was checked at the abstract/model-note level, not by a full proof review; searches are not exhaustive.
progress: 2017-10-12: A linearizable, potentially nondeterministic object equivalent to each set agreement task is established. | 2020-02-11: OPODIS 2019 proceedings establish the \(n\ge 4,k=2\) deterministic separation and state the \(n>k>2\) conjecture. | 2020-04-21: The journal treatment of Life beyond set agreement establishes existential gaps between task-solving power and object implementation power; its statement does not resolve the universal conjecture here.
working_summary: Set agreement lets n processes decide at most k proposed values. Its task has an equivalent linearizable object and an equivalent deterministic object, but these known objects do not possess both properties. The conjecture says no object can possess both properties while retaining exactly the task’s implementation power whenever \(n>k>2\). Equivalence uses deterministic wait-free reductions with registers and allows repeated operations through n ports. The source proves the analogous separation for \(k=2\) and \(n\ge 4\); later existential object separations do not settle the universal higher-k question.

title: Subpolynomial detection of two-connected patterns
importance_reason: A structural existence question about the distributed complexity of cyclic graph patterns, encompassing the unresolved communication barrier for triangles. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a fixed finite simple 2-vertex-connected graph H, with at least three vertices, for which exact H-subgraph detection in the randomized CONGEST model can be solved in \(n^{o(1)}\) rounds on every n-vertex network? The pattern is fixed independently of n. Detection means that, with probability at least \(2/3\), every node outputs NO when the network contains no copy of H, and at least one node outputs YES when it does contain a copy.
definitions:
The pattern H is an undirected finite simple graph. It is 2-vertex-connected if it has at least three vertices, is connected and remains connected after deleting any single vertex and its incident edges. This excludes an isolated edge and includes triangles and longer cycles. The network G is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph on n vertices. A copy of H is an injective map \(\varphi :V(H)\to V(G)\) such that every edge uv of H maps to an edge \(\varphi (u)\varphi (v)\) of G. Extra edges among the images are allowed: the task is not induced-subgraph detection, homomorphism, minor containment or property testing with a distance promise.

There is one processor at each vertex. Each knows n, H, its own distinct identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors; identifiers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, and the guarantee must hold for every valid assignment of identifiers. Local edges have identifiable ports. In each synchronous round a node may send a different message of at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to each neighbor, for a fixed constant B independent of n. Messages are received before the next round, and later messages may depend on everything received so far. No communication is allowed across nonedges. Local computation and memory are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. This is ordinary CONGEST, with distinct messages permitted on distinct edges, not broadcast CONGEST or the congested clique.

The algorithm is a uniform distributed procedure fixed with H; it may use independent private random bits at the nodes. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. It halts within a worst-case bound \(T_{H}(n)\) on every network, identifier assignment and random tape. The success event concerns the joint vector of all node outputs, with probability over all random bits. In an H-free network all outputs must be NO simultaneously; in a network containing H one YES anywhere suffices. There is no requirement that the detecting node belong to a copy, identify its vertices, list all copies, or notify distant nodes. Disconnected networks are permitted and the same global output convention applies.

The required bound \(n^{o(1)}\) means that one such algorithm exists with \(\log (\max \{2,T_{H}(n)\})/\log  n\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty\). Equivalently, for every fixed \(\delta >0\) its worst-case round bound is at most \(n^{\delta}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants and the threshold length may depend on H and \(\delta\). A family of different algorithms, one for each \(\delta\), is not silently identified with that single-algorithm claim. A bound \(n^{\alpha _{H}}\) with a fixed positive \(\alpha _{H}\), even a very small one, is not subpolynomial. The size of H is a constant, not another growing complexity parameter.

The source also asks whether every 2-connected pattern instead requires a polynomial number of rounds. A theorem giving each fixed H a lower bound \(\Omega (n^{\delta _{H}})\) for some \(\delta _{H}>0\) would refute the existence question, but this stronger growth dichotomy is not assumed to be its logical negation. A negative answer here only needs to exclude the stated \(n^{o(1)}\) algorithms for every eligible H.
answer_criterion: A positive answer provides one fixed eligible H and proves a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm with the stated global success probability and \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case rounds. A negative answer rules out such an algorithm for every fixed eligible H. A lower bound for only one pattern, or a fast algorithm for induced copies, promised-far graphs, listing in another model or a pattern that grows with n, does not settle this existence question.
context:
The source contrasts constant-round detection of every fixed tree with polynomial lower bounds for cycles of length at least four and other pattern classes. Its reductions transfer hardness from a 2-connected block to larger connected patterns, motivating the focus on 2-connected graphs.

Standard distributed detection allows any one node to signal existence. Requiring every node to learn that a distant copy exists would add an unrelated distance cost and would change the constant-round comparison with trees.

The revised survey keeps the complexity of triangle detection open. Assadi and Sundaresan give an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) lower bound, while the known upper bounds are polynomial in n. This is significant progress, but a logarithmic lower bound does not exclude \(n^{o(1)}\) detection.

Listing requires every copy to be reported; detection needs only one existence signal. The known polynomial lower bounds for triangle listing therefore do not establish a polynomial detection lower bound or settle the all-pattern question.
why: Asks whether any cyclic pattern can be detected almost as quickly as trees under per-edge communication limits. A resolution would clarify a broad boundary in distributed graph algorithms, and its negative direction includes the difficult triangle-detection barrier.
status_note: Read the original question and surrounding graph-class interpretation; checked the 2025 survey’s standard output convention and the newer triangle lower bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no subpolynomial algorithm for an eligible pattern or a resolution excluding all of them. The reported logarithmic triangle bound does not prove polynomial hardness. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2017: The OPODIS source proves hardness transfers for pattern classes and asks whether any fixed 2-connected pattern admits subpolynomial detection. | 2025-04-02: Assadi and Sundaresan report the first general multi-round lower bound for triangle detection, \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\); the checked revision is from 13 August 2025. | 2025-08-27: The survey’s fifth revision incorporates this bound and retains the open triangle-detection question.
working_summary: The question asks whether any fixed 2-vertex-connected graph can be detected in subpolynomial CONGEST rounds. Nodes can exchange only logarithmically many bits per edge per round. Exact detection requires one node to signal an existing copy and all nodes to stay negative when none exists. Trees have constant-round algorithms, while many cyclic patterns have polynomial lower bounds. The newer logarithmic lower bound for triangles leaves the requested subpolynomial-versus-harder boundary unresolved.

title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
importance_reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.
focus_reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
question_excerpt: The Open Problems Project asks whether linear programming is strongly polynomial. This card retains its previously selected deterministic rational-input, exact-output formulation. The explicit scalar arithmetic and binary-size conventions fix the rational arithmetic/Turing variant discussed in Section 1.3 of the STOC 2024 paper; the card measures rational values in lowest terms and separately requires polynomial bit simulation. The paper additionally proves its special-case result under a stricter unreduced numerator-denominator representation convention. Neither that stronger representation result nor the arbitrary-real BSS formulation is silently substituted for this card’s retained target.
definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
context:
Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision directly claims a strongly polynomial algorithm for general LP; Lemma 7.1 asserts a linear bound on its iteration count. A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation. This review has not certified the proof or located independent primary validation in bounded searches.

Truffet’s current August 2026 revision also states a general strongly polynomial solution in Theorem 2.1. Its opening revision note acknowledges a logical error in earlier versions and asserts a correction; the current theorem remains a claim requiring verification. This review read that note, the theorem and the stated complexity conclusion, without certifying their proof or the full bit-complexity requirements. These unresolved claims are why the card retains uncertain status.
why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

working_summary: A rational linear program minimizes a linear objective subject to linear equalities and nonnegative variables. The question asks for one deterministic exact solver using polynomially many scalar arithmetic operations depending only on the numbers of variables and constraints. Intermediate rational values must have bit lengths polynomial in the full input length, and the computation must admit an exact polynomial-time bit implementation. The solver must distinguish infeasibility, an objective unbounded below and a finite attained optimum on every input, without matrix or conditioning promises. Strongly polynomial algorithms are established for major special classes, while current claims of a general solution remain unverified in this review.

title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
importance_reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.
focus_reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.
formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm P\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
question_excerpt: The retained target is unrestricted rational-data semidefinite feasibility in the ordinary bit model, as discussed by Ramana, Pataki–Touzov and the later duality literature. This card chooses the equivalent affine linear-matrix-inequality representation and explicitly makes the variables real. It asks for a decision bit, without adding an optimization or witness-output task. The zero-variable case fixes the harmless endpoint of the input domain.
definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm P\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.
context:
A semidefinite constraint requires a quadratic form to be nonnegative in every direction. Diagonal matrix inequalities include ordinary linear inequalities. Exact decision asks whether the feasible region is empty, which is different from obtaining a useful approximate optimizer on well-conditioned instances.

De Klerk–Vallentin’s inspected approximation theorem is supplied with a rational feasible center and quantitative inner and outer radius information. Its runtime also depends on requested accuracy. This is a polynomial bit-complexity result under explicit geometric assumptions, not an unrestricted exact emptiness test.

Approximate feasibility need not imply exact feasibility. For example,
\[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\]
has determinant \(-1\), so it is never positive semidefinite. Nevertheless its negative eigenvalue \((t-\sqrt{t^2+4})/2\) tends to zero as \(t\) tends to positive infinity. This infeasible affine family has distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone in the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries.

A rational input can also have only irrational feasible parameters. The rational affine block-diagonal matrix
\[\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\2&2x\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}2&x\\x&1\end{pmatrix}\right)\]
is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x=\sqrt2\). Replacing the real domain by rational substitutions would change the answer to this instance.

Even when rational feasible points exist, all of them can require exponentially many bits relative to the number of variables. Pataki–Touzov study the structural occurrence of such examples and questions about compact representations. This explains an obstacle to algorithms that must explicitly output a point; it does not itself lower-bound the complexity of the decision bit requested here.

General exact decision is possible through real-algebraic methods. Henrion–Naldi–Safey El Din develop symbolic algorithms accommodating degenerate feasible sets. Their optimization analysis retains generic auxiliary choices and objectives, and its displayed bounds count arithmetic operations. Bounds polynomial when one dimension is fixed do not establish one polynomial bit bound when both dimensions and coefficient lengths vary.

Ramana’s exact alternative replaces infeasibility by feasibility of another semidefinite system of polynomial description size. In the Turing model it implies that the problem lies in NP if and only if it lies in coNP; neither membership is thereby established on its own. The separate NP-intersect-coNP result over exact real-number machines uses a different model of computation.

Pataki’s October 2025 treatment retains this complexity distinction and gives a fuller description of the exact dual’s feasible set. A polynomial-size dual system is not automatically a polynomial-size binary certificate: its real variables still have to satisfy semidefinite constraints.

Slot–Steurer–Wiedmer obtain effective solution bounds and polynomial-time approximate minimization of convex polynomials over polyhedra. The constraints in that result are linear, and the authors explicitly contrast their result with general semidefinite programming. It does not make arbitrary linear matrix inequalities decidable in polynomial bit time.

The September 2026 higher-order Newton paper of ter Voert–de Klerk explicitly retains the unknown exact SDP complexity. Its iteration analysis uses a derivative oracle and real-number computation, and fixed-accuracy SDP subproblems require stated regularity. A reduction of an iteration to an SDP is therefore not a solution of this unrestricted Turing-model decision question.
why: Semidefinite constraints underlie many successful optimization relaxations, yet their unrestricted exact decision complexity is still unsettled. This problem isolates whether finite rational input admits a polynomial-time decision even when numerical separation and small explicit witnesses are unavailable.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The October/November 2025 primary texts and the September 2026 higher-order Newton paper explicitly retain the unknown exact SDP complexity. Current exact-duality, restricted approximation and symbolic results do not establish polynomial bit-time decision for all rational inputs. No verified full resolution was found in bounded searches. The card remains source_open; this pass does not independently certify all cited proofs.

working_summary: The input is a fully listed rational affine symmetric matrix whose dimension and number of real variables are both unbounded. The target is a deterministic polynomial bit-time decision of whether some real substitution makes the matrix positive semidefinite. Singular feasible points, irrational-only feasible parameters, unbounded sets and infeasible instances at zero distance from the cone are included. Known approximation and exact-duality results retain assumptions or model distinctions, and the September 2026 source still states the unrestricted exact complexity as open. A complete Lean proof must establish one polynomial-time decider or exclude all such deciders; it need not output a feasible point or optimization value.

title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
importance_reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.
focus_reason: The packing versus max-flow min-cut conjecture adds a fundamental combinatorial integrality question alongside continuous optimization and numerical computation.
formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.
context:
Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

For the member-by-element incidence matrix \(A\), whose entry \(A_{F,e}\) is one precisely when \(e\in F\), the corresponding fractional problems are \(\min\{w^{\mathsf T}z:Az\ge\mathbf1,\ z\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le w,\ y\ge0\}\). The conjectured equality concerns integer solutions, and hence is stronger than ordinary linear-programming duality. It asks for integral optima on both sides for every integer weight.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

Roy and Saha report a proof for \((n-2)\)-uniform clutters: every member has size exactly \(n-2\) when the ground set has \(n\) elements. Arbitrary clutters can have unrelated member sizes, so this subclass result leaves the stated universal implication unchanged.
why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. Abdi–Schwarcz v2 (9 July 2026) explicitly retains the general conjecture and reports verification on at most ten elements. Roy–Saha v2 treats only (n−2)-uniform clutters. No general resolution was located in the bounded search; neither the computational artifacts nor these source proofs were independently verified.

This is a restricted family. | 2026-07-09: Abdi–Schwarcz v2 reports finite verification through ten ground-set elements and an improved finite-weight test, while leaving the universal conjecture open.
working_summary: A clutter is a finite family of sets with no redundant containing member. Its packing property requires unweighted packing–covering equality in every deletion and contraction minor. The conjecture asks whether this already implies equality for every nonnegative integer capacity vector. Weighted packings may repeat members within those capacities. Recent source results cover finite ground-set sizes and restricted families, while retaining the general question.

title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
importance_reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.
focus_reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
question_excerpt: This is the retained editorial near-input-size variant of the general sparse-system complexity question. Polynomial conditioning, logarithmic input coefficient lengths, inverse-polynomial residual accuracy, an explicit rational output and the word-RAM cost convention make the broad direction precise. Peng–Vempala and Nie supply the general finite-precision context; the Simons workshop report asks narrower benchmark and numerical-analysis questions. The proposition is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report, and does not ask the already resolved question of beating matrix multiplication.
definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.
context:
Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.
why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The retained proposition is an explicitly editorial near-linear target, not a named conjecture or the already resolved faster-than-matrix-multiplication question. Inspected primary results improve general polynomial bounds or handle structured families; the August 2026 report retains narrower scalable-solver and finite-precision questions. Bounded later-work searches found no matching universal solver or unconditional impossibility proof. This status assessment does not independently certify the cited proofs.
