working_summary: A sparse linear system explicitly stores only the nonzero matrix entries and its right-hand side. The question asks whether every nonsingular rational system with polynomial conditioning can be approximately solved in nearly linear time in the number of nonzeros. Coefficient lengths and residual accuracy are bounded on a logarithmic scale, and the output must list every rational coordinate. The fixed word-RAM model charges preprocessing, precision, randomness and output, with a worst-case time bound and success probability at least two thirds. Known structured solvers and general improvements over matrix multiplication motivate the target but do not provide its universal near-linear guarantee.

title: Smale’s seventh problem
importance_reason: Smale's seventh problem asks for efficient construction of globally near-optimal configurations.
focus_reason: Smale's seventh problem asks for efficient construction of globally near-optimal configurations.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.
context:
Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?
why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No general deterministic polynomial-time construction with logarithmic total-energy excess was located. The March 2026 finite-cardinality classification and existing distributional energy guarantees do not establish the uniform algorithmic target. This source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.
progress: 1998: Smale specifies polynomial time in N in the real-number model and universal logarithmic excess energy. | 2018: The low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution attains logarithmic excess in expectation and with high probability; efficient generation is a separate issue. | 2022 / 2023: The generalized Diamond ensemble covers every N with an explicit asymptotic expected-energy estimate. | 2023 / 2024: A central limit theorem identifies \(\sqrt{N}\) energy fluctuations for random polynomial zeros. | 2026-03-22: Revised algebraic classification handles at most six points in all dimensions and a restricted seven-point case.
working_summary: Smale's seventh problem concerns placing N points on the unit sphere so that their logarithmic interaction energy is nearly minimal. The target is an algorithm running in time polynomial in N. Its output energy may exceed the global minimum by only a universal constant times log N. This is an additive energy guarantee, which requires more precise control than merely producing visually well-distributed points. A construction with a rigorous bound would connect efficient computation with the equilibrium behavior of many mutually repelling particles on a curved surface.

title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(L\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
question_excerpt: The retained target is the deterministic polynomial bit-time question for primal simplex from a supplied feasible basis. The standard equality form, full row rank, initial basis and positive reduced-cost pivots match Section 2 of the ranking-based work; the explicit ratio test and degeneracy convention also match Section 2.1 of Kukharenko–Sanità, with signs reversed from minimization to maximization. The card fixes a finite uniform algorithm and total bit costs. It does not silently strengthen polynomial bit time to a dimension-only strongly polynomial bound or require a shortest pivot sequence.
definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(L\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.
context:
General linear programming has polynomial-time algorithms measured in the binary input size. This card imposes the additional requirement that the computation reach its answer through legal simplex pivots on the given program from the supplied basis. The August 2026 full version of the ranking-based paper still poses the unrestricted pivot-rule question as open.

A short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short improving path to an optimum. A polynomial bit-time rule would bound both the number of its basis exchanges and the work required to choose them. Its bound may depend on coefficient bit lengths; it would not by itself establish a strongly polynomial LP algorithm or a polytope diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy allows many bases to represent one point. Kukharenko and Sanità bound consecutive degenerate improving pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n-m-1\), with efficient implementation when an improving feasible direction is available. Their result controls a block of stalling at that vertex; it does not give a dimension-independent or polynomial-in-input bound on the total number of distinct vertices visited by an arbitrary simplex run.

Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a two-phase shadow-vertex simplex method. The expectation is over Gaussian perturbations around an arbitrary input, with polynomial dependence on dimensions and on \(1/\sigma\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the relative perturbation scale. This does not bound the deterministic worst-case bit time on every unperturbed rational input.

The ranking-based results restrict the information a rule may use. One theorem gives a superpolynomial iteration lower bound in \(n\) for index-ranking rules with \(o(n/\log n)\) memory states. The other gives \(\Omega(2^{\sqrt K})\) iterations for the stated memoryless class based only on rankings by index, reduced cost and objective increase, where \(K\) counts nonzero constraint-matrix entries. The definitions also require choices to respect ranking-preserving relabelings. Memory states are not bits of memory, and \(K\) is not this card's binary input length \(L\). These restricted-information theorems do not exclude algorithms with full numerical access and general polynomial-time history.

Disser and Mosis obtain an all-pivot-rules lower bound for the active-set method with higher-degree polynomial objectives on a hypercube. Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen this to convex quadratic maximization. The objective is nonlinear and the optimization direction is maximization; neither theorem is an all-rules lower bound for the linear objective required here.

Black and Steiner’s April 2026 revision proves that finding a shortest monotone pivot sequence is NP-hard, already for simple polytopes where vertices are nondegenerate. Thus a polynomial-time algorithm for always finding a shortest sequence would imply P = NP. This card asks for some polynomial-time legal run and does not require its number of pivots to be minimum, so shortest-path hardness alone does not answer it negatively.
why: Simplex is a central optimization method whose practical effectiveness has long exceeded its general worst-case guarantees. The question isolates whether exact polynomial-time linear optimization is compatible with its required improving basis exchanges, including degeneracy, and with efficiently choosing every exchange.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected current ranking-based preprint (v2, 10 August 2026) still poses the general pivot-rule question as open. Its lower bounds restrict information and memory; the March stalling theorem is local, the April shortest-path result concerns minimum-length sequences, and the active-set lower bounds have nonlinear objectives. No verified resolution of the exact supplied-feasible-basis deterministic polynomial bit-time target was established in bounded searches. The card remains source_open; this does not claim an exhaustive proof audit.
progress: 2004: Spielman–Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex method, with an expectation over perturbed input and dependence on perturbation scale. | 2025: The hypercube lower bound applies to the active-set method with nonlinear polynomial objectives. | 2026: The convex-quadratic-maximization lower bound strengthens the nonlinear result; it still does not cover linear objectives. | 2026-03-23: The published degeneracy result limits a block of stalling at a nonoptimal vertex under its improving-direction condition. | 2026-04-08: Black–Steiner version 2 establishes NP-hardness of shortest monotone pivot sequences, a different requirement from a polynomial-time sequence. | 2026-08-10: The full ranking-based version 2 retains the unrestricted open question and the stated information, symmetry and memory restrictions of its lower bounds.
working_summary: Primal simplex maximizes a rational linear objective by exchanging one entering and one leaving basis column at a time. The question asks for one deterministic rule that reaches an optimality-certifying basis from every supplied feasible basis in polynomial total bit time. Each pivot must have positive entering reduced cost and follow the exact minimum-ratio test, with tied and zero-length degenerate pivots included. The rule may inspect all numerical data and use history, but every computation and basis exchange must fit the same polynomial input-length bound. Smoothed guarantees, local antistalling results, restricted-information lower bounds and hardness of shortest pivot paths do not settle this unrestricted rule-existence target.

title: Komlós conjecture
importance_reason: A defining vector-balancing conjecture with consequences for rounding, approximation and the geometry of linear constraints.
formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.
context:
Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.
why: Komlós asks whether controlling the Euclidean size of each vector is enough to balance all coordinates by signs with a dimension-independent error. This is a central link between vector geometry and simultaneous rounding of linear constraints. It would imply the Beck–Fiala bound for sparse set systems and strengthen discrepancy-based guarantees in optimization.
status_note: A full affirmative resolution is claimed by Guo, Fang and Lu in arXiv:2609.11189v1, submitted 10 September 2026. Theorem 1.1 matches every matrix, dimension and normalization in this card and gives discrepancy strictly less than 3 sqrt(2 pi), with no algorithmic requirement. This review checked the target match and stated scope, not the correctness of the complete new proof; the card therefore remains active with uncertain status. The preprint was still at v1 when checked on 14 September. This supersedes the earlier same-day search assessment that had found only the September 8 growing upper bound.
progress: 1998: Banaszczyk obtains the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) discrepancy bound, as recalled in the inspected 2019 and 2026 primary papers. | 2019: Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s Theorem 2 makes the \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound constructive for arbitrary real matrices with column Euclidean norms at most one. | 2025–2026: Bansal and Jiang’s 2025 preprint, followed by STOC 2026, improves the general bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\). This does not assert a fourth power of a logarithm or a dimension-independent bound. | 2026-08-28: The authors’ new exposition gives the explicit \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\) bound and still describes the constant Komlós conjecture as open. | 2026-09-08: Ercan’s Theorem 1.1 claims an explicit \(O((1+\log n)^{1/4})\) bound without the iterated-logarithm factor. The paper’s reported Lean formalization assumes the earlier covariance theorem; this review has not checked the new proof or built its files. A bound growing with \(n\) leaves the card’s target open. | 2026-09-10: Guo, Fang and Lu’s Theorem 1.1 claims a dimension-independent bound \(3\sqrt{2\pi}\), which would settle the full conjecture. The statement matches this card, but its new proof is not independently verified here; recorded as an uncertain claimed resolution.
working_summary: Komlós asks whether every collection of real vectors of Euclidean norm at most one can be assigned signs so that every coordinate of their sum is bounded by one universal constant. The dimensions and entries are arbitrary, and the same complete choice of signs must control all coordinates simultaneously. The positive answer requires some finite constant, without determining the best one or giving an efficient algorithm. Such a theorem would imply the Beck–Fiala discrepancy bound and strengthen rounding and optimization guarantees. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or unbounded discrepancy; the 10 September 2026 preprint claims the full positive bound, but this review has not independently verified its proof.

title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
importance_reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm that solves every rational P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial bit time? More precisely, are there a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded rational input
\[n\in\mathbb N_{>0},\qquad M\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad q\in\mathbb Q^n,\]
the machine halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below, and whenever \(M\) is a P-matrix it outputs \(z,w\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying
\[w=Mz+q,\qquad z_i\ge0,\quad w_i\ge0,\quad z_iw_i=0\quad(1\le i\le n)?\]
A P-matrix has strictly positive determinant for every nonempty principal submatrix. No certificate of this promise is supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize it. The constants \(B,k\) and the program are shared by all dimensions and all rational coefficients.
question_excerpt: The retained question is ordinary deterministic polynomial bit-time solution of rational LCP under the P-matrix promise. It asks neither for recognizing that promise nor for a strongly polynomial arithmetic algorithm. The literature’s unique-sink and total-search formulations supply context; they do not add an obligation to produce non-P-matrix certificates here.
definitions:
Matrix promise. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), the principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) consists of the rows and columns with indices in \(S\), both in increasing order. Thus the promise is
\[\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n],\ \det M[S,S]>0.\]
Here the determinant is the usual alternating sum of products, evaluated exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). Strict positivity is essential. There is no symmetry, sparsity, triangularity, positive-semidefiniteness or nondegeneracy assumption. In particular, a valid solution may have both \(z_i=w_i=0\) in some coordinate.

Equations and output. The matrix product is \((Mz)_i=\sum_{j=1}^nM_{ij}z_j\), and all inequalities use the ordinary rational order. With \(z,w\ge0\), coordinatewise complementarity is equivalent to \(z^Tw=\sum_{i=1}^n z_iw_i=0\). A solution is the complete pair of vectors, with exact rational coordinates. An interval, floating-point vector or small residual is not an exact solution under this task. The guarantee is a search guarantee: returning only a yes/no answer about existence is insufficient.

Binary encoding. To make the bit model definite, encode a nonnegative integer \(t\) by
\[u(t)=1^{b(t)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(t+1),\qquad b(t)=\lfloor\log_2(t+1)\rfloor+1,\]
where \(\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) is its binary expansion without leading zeroes, of length \(b(t)\). The initial run of ones specifies that length. A rational number is written uniquely as \(p/d\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\gcd(|p|,d)=1\), and is encoded by a sign bit, then \(u(|p|)\), then \(u(d)\). The sign bit is zero for nonnegative \(p\), including zero, and one for negative \(p\). Thus zero uses numerator zero and denominator one. The input concatenates \(u(n)\), all \(n^2\) entries of \(M\) in row-major order, and the \(n\) entries of \(q\). Every entry, including a zero entry, is explicitly present. A syntactically valid input has exactly this form and no trailing bits. Its total binary length is \(N\). The output concatenates the \(n\) rational encodings of \(z\), followed by those of \(w\), in index order; \(n\) is already known from the input. Other usual explicit binary rational encodings are polynomially equivalent to this convention.

Computation. The same finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program is used for every input. One transition costs one step. Reading input, rational arithmetic, comparisons, intermediate representations and writing the entire output are all charged. There are no oracles, real-number unit-cost operations, randomness, nonuniform advice or free preprocessing. The polynomial time bound applies to every syntactically valid rational input, including matrices that fail the P-matrix promise. On those nonpromised inputs any halting output is allowed; detecting a violated principal minor is not required. Behavior on malformed input strings is unrestricted. A polynomial bound only on promised inputs is equivalent for this existence question, since a known polynomial bound can be enforced with a clock and arbitrary output after timeout. The bound may depend polynomially on coefficient bit lengths through \(N\); this is not a demand for a strongly polynomial number of arithmetic operations independent of those lengths.

Quantifier order. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists B,k\,\forall(n,M,q)\) with the time guarantee above and correctness whenever \(\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\). Coefficient magnitudes, dimension, degeneracy and numerical conditioning may vary without restriction; they do not permit selecting a different program or polynomial for each input.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this algorithm-existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish one program, one polynomial bit-time bound and exact correctness on every promised input, including degenerate instances. Any internal approximation procedure must be proved to recover and output the exact rational solution within that bound. A negative answer must show that every uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs fails to output the required solution on some P-matrix instance. Exponential examples for one pivot rule, hardness of recognizing P-matrices, a lower bound in a restricted oracle model, or a conditional complexity-theoretic barrier alone do not prove that negation. An algorithm for a proper matrix subclass or with an uncontrolled condition-parameter factor does not establish the positive answer.
context:
Complementarity imposes a discrete choice within linear equations: each coordinate must have \(z_i=0\), or \(w_i=0\), or both. For \(M=I_n\), the solution is \(z_i=\max\{0,-q_i\}\) and \(w_i=\max\{0,q_i\}\). For a general P-matrix, the coordinates interact through \(Mz\), so this coordinate-by-coordinate formula no longer applies.

The classical P-matrix characterization states that the linear complementarity system has exactly one solution for every real right-hand side if and only if all principal minors are positive. Uniqueness concerns the vector pair, not the choice of a complementary basis; degenerate instances can have several bases representing the same solution. The existence and uniqueness theorem does not itself give the polynomial algorithm requested here.

Rational exact output does not require an exponentially long description. In a solution, let \(S=\{i:z_i>0\}\). Then \(z_{[n]\setminus S}=0\), \(w_S=0\), and \(M[S,S]z_S=-q_S\); this principal matrix is nonsingular. Clearing input denominators and applying determinant bounds shows that its rational solution and the resulting \(w\) have polynomial bit length. If \(S\) is empty, \(z=0\) and \(w=q\). The difficult part is finding a valid pattern efficiently.

P-matrix recognition is co-NP-complete, but this card supplies the property as a promise. Gordon and Shu give polynomial conversions between different certificates that a matrix violates the promise. Such certificate results do not make recognition part of this task, and recognition hardness does not prove that promised solution finding is hard.

Fearnley, Gordon, Mehta and Savani place the promised problem in a class based on finding the endpoint of a unique, implicitly represented path whose potential increases along it. Their total-search variants permit a certificate of a violated promise as an alternative output. These complexity-class containments organize the search problem but do not give polynomial-time solution finding. The present card requires a solution only on P-matrix inputs.

Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for Hessenberg P-matrices, which have zero entries beyond the first off-diagonal on one side; tridiagonal matrices are included. Their \(O(n^5)\) arithmetic-operation bound combines polynomially many basis tests with linear-system solves. Exact rational linear algebra gives polynomial bit complexity for these subclasses. The general matrix in this card has no such zero pattern.

The ICALP 2024 paper “Two Choices Are Enough” reduces generalized complementarity instances to the ordinary binary-choice problem and relates them to geometric search problems. This equivalence extends the reach of P-matrix LCP; it is not a polynomial solver for it. ETH’s 2025 activity report continues to list general polynomial-time solution finding as open.

E.-Nagy and Végh’s June 2026 revision gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input length and in the optimized handicap \(\widehat\kappa^\star(M)\), the best handicap attainable by positive diagonal row scaling. The handicap measures departure from the inequality \(x^TMx\ge0\). Their general upper bound on the unscaled handicap is exponential in input bit complexity, and the algorithmic theorem does not give a polynomial input-length bound on the optimized parameter. It therefore does not settle the all-P-matrix target.
why: The P-matrix promise guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side, and that solution has a short rational description. The remaining difficulty is finding it efficiently despite the coupled choices of which coordinates vanish. A polynomial algorithm would resolve a central structured search problem that sits between tractable linear optimization and more general complementarity systems.
status_note: Checked through16 September2026. The general rational P-matrix LCP polynomial-time search question remains open in the inspected sources. The June2026 algorithm retains dependence on an optimized handicap parameter; its theorem does not bound running time polynomially in input length alone. Hessenberg algorithms, promise-certificate conversions and search-problem reductions do not settle the general target. The review is bounded and does not independently certify every cited proof.

This concerns violated promises, not a general solution algorithm. | 2024-07-02: Polynomial reductions identify generalized P-LCP with its ordinary binary-choice form. | 2025: ETH’s activity report retains polynomial-time general P-matrix LCP as an unresolved question. | 2026-06-30: The revised handicap-reduction paper improves algorithmic dependence to the best value under positive diagonal scaling. Its theorem retains a parameter beyond input length.
working_summary: The problem asks for nonnegative rational vectors linked by a linear equation, with at least one zero in each paired coordinate. The input matrix is promised to have every nonempty principal minor strictly positive, which guarantees a unique solution for every right-hand side. The question is whether one deterministic algorithm always finds that exact solution in polynomial time measured in the full binary input length. A complete Lean proof must supply that uniform algorithm and bound or rule out every such polynomial-time algorithm without adding a promise-recognition task. The checked 2026 handicap-dependent algorithm and earlier restricted-matrix and reduction results do not establish this general polynomial-time guarantee.

title: Beck–Fiala conjecture
importance_reason: A central discrepancy conjecture governing how local incidence restrictions control global rounding error.
formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every three integers \(m,n,t\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}\le t\) for each column \(j\), there exists a single vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) satisfying \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C\sqrt t?\] The same constant must work for every dimension, frequency bound and matrix.
definitions: The underlying elements are \(1,\ldots,n\), and the \(i\)-th set is \(S_i=\{j:A_{ij}=1\}\). The ordered collection \((S_1,\ldots,S_m)\) may contain repeated or empty sets, and some elements may occur in no set. Each element is in at most \(t\) sets, counting repeated rows separately. This is a restriction on column sums, not on the cardinality of each set, the number of elements or the number of sets. The integer \(t\) is an allowed upper bound on frequency; it need not be attained or be at most \(m\). A two-coloring assigns each element exactly one sign \(x_j\in\{-1,1\}\). The imbalance of a set is the absolute difference between the numbers of its plus and minus elements, equal to \(|\sum_{j\in S_i}x_j|\). Define \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\max_{1\le i\le m}|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|\); the minimum exists because the set of complete colorings is finite. One coloring must control all sets simultaneously. The conjecture is the existence of some universal finite constant, with no requirement to minimize it. The coloring may depend on the entire matrix; no online order, random input distribution or efficient construction requirement is imposed. Every element is colored, and no fractional or partially unassigned coloring is a witness. Dimensions and \(t\) are positive; a zero-frequency matrix is still allowed and has discrepancy zero.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal bound, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist positive integers \(m,n,t\) and a binary matrix \(A\) with every column sum at most \(t\), such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there exists a row \(i\) with \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\sqrt t\). Thus a refutation establishes that \(\operatorname{disc}(A)/\sqrt t\) is unbounded over the stated instances. A fixed example with positive discrepancy, or a lower bound proportional to \(\sqrt t\), is consistent with the conjecture. A positive proof must use one constant independent of all parameters; constants depending on \(t\) or bounds restricted to a growing-frequency range do not settle the target. An unverified announced proof, experimental signing search or result conditional on an unproved conjecture is insufficient for Lean benchmark acceptance. No optimal numerical constant or construction-time bound is requested.
context:
A coloring partitions the elements into two classes while trying to divide every set evenly. The conjecture permits large sets and arbitrarily many constraints: only the participation of each individual element is bounded. Writing \(y=(\mathbf 1+x)/2\in\{0,1\}^n\), where \(\mathbf 1\) is the all-one vector, gives \(A(y-\mathbf 1/2)=Ax/2\). Hence a discrepancy bound also bounds the simultaneous error of rounding the all-one-half vector. This identity explains the optimization connection without adding a rounding algorithm to the target.

Beck and Fiala’s 1981 theorem gives discrepancy at most \(2t-1\), uniformly in the two matrix dimensions. Known examples require discrepancy of order \(\sqrt t\), so the conjecture proposes the correct order in frequency up to a constant. Bansal and Jiang recall these facts in §1; their review of the older Banaszczyk bound gives \(O(\sqrt{t\log n})\), which still depends on the number of elements.

The Komlós conjecture allows arbitrary real matrices whose individual columns have Euclidean norm at most one and asks for constant discrepancy. Scaling a Beck–Fiala matrix by \(1/\sqrt t\) makes it admissible for Komlós, since the squared Euclidean norm of a column becomes its number of ones divided by \(t\). A Komlós constant therefore implies the same Beck–Fiala constant. The reverse implication is not asserted; the general real-matrix question has a wider domain.

Bansal and Jiang’s Theorem 1.3 gives the square-root bound once \(t\) is at least a constant multiple of \((\log n)^2\), and Theorem 1.4 gives \(\widetilde O(\sqrt t+\sqrt{\log n})\) in the full range, with powers of \(\log\log n\) suppressed. Their 2025 preprint was followed by STOC 2026. The first result restricts the frequency range; the second retains growth in \(n\). Neither of these statements alone yields the uniform target.

Altschuler and Tikhomirov’s July 2026 Corollary 1.2 states that for each fixed \(\eta>0\), constants \(a_\eta,b_\eta>0\) and \(N_\eta\) exist such that \(\operatorname{disc}(A)\le b_\eta\sqrt t\) when \(n\ge N_\eta\) and \(t\ge a_\eta(\log n)(\log\log n)^{2+\eta}\). Here \(n\) is the number of elements, denoted \(T\) in that source, and the logs are natural. Its stronger online result chooses signs irrevocably as columns arrive and bounds every prefix for a sequence fixed in advance. The card instead asks only for a complete final coloring chosen with the whole input available. The preprint’s proof was not independently verified in this review.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full statement: Corollary 1.2 gives \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi t}\) for every allowed positive \(m,n,t\), with no frequency threshold. It follows there from their claimed Komlós theorem. This is an affirmative claim matching the exact card target, not another range-restricted improvement. The authors make no polynomial-time implementation claim. This review checked the statement and parameter match, but did not independently verify the complete new proof, so the scientific status is uncertain.
why: The conjecture asks whether a local bound on how many constraints involve one element controls the error of balancing all constraints by the square root of that frequency. It is a central sparsity question in discrepancy theory, with a direct interpretation as simultaneously rounding half-integral choices in many overlapping constraints.
status_note: Guo, Fang and Lu claim a full affirmative resolution in arXiv:2609.11189v1, submitted 10 September 2026. Corollary 1.2 covers every binary matrix and all positive dimensions and frequency bounds in this card, with constant 3 sqrt(2 pi). The statement and its derivation from the paper’s claimed Komlós theorem were inspected; the complete new proof was not independently verified. The preprint remained at v1 on 14 September, so the card is active with uncertain status. This supersedes the prior note that only range-restricted results had been found.
progress: 1981: The classical bound \(2t-1\) is uniform over dimensions, as recalled in the inspected Bansal–Jiang introduction. | 2025–2026: Bansal and Jiang obtain \(O(\sqrt t)\) for \(t\) at least a constant multiple of \((\log n)^2\), and a further all-range bound still involving \(n\). The extended abstract appears at STOC 2026. | 2026-07-15: Altschuler and Tikhomirov’s preprint extends the stated offline square-root bound to \(t\ge a_\eta(\log n)(\log\log n)^{2+\eta}\) for sufficiently large \(n\) and each fixed \(\eta>0\), via a stronger online result. | 2026-09-10: Guo, Fang and Lu claim the unrestricted bound \(3\sqrt{2\pi t}\) in Corollary 1.2. The claim matches the full target, but the new proof is not independently verified here; the card remains active with uncertain status.
working_summary: The Beck–Fiala conjecture asks whether bounded participation of each element in a set system guarantees a coloring with square-root imbalance in every set. If each element belongs to at most t sets, one complete assignment of signs must achieve imbalance at most a universal constant times the square root of t. The constant must work for every number of elements and sets, with no lower restriction on t or requirement for an efficient algorithm. The question is a central sparsity principle for simultaneous rounding and is implied by the more general Komlós conjecture. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or unbounded normalized discrepancy; a 10 September 2026 preprint claims the full positive bound, with its proof unverified in this review.

title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
importance_reason: Close the central dimension-dependence gap in a general-purpose optimization primitive used throughout parameterized algorithms.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one uniform classical deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge0\), every explicitly given rational matrix \(Q\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) and every rational vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), the machine correctly decides whether
\[
 \exists x\in\mathbb Z^n\quad Qx\le b
\]
within at most
\[
 2^{Cn}(L+1)^c
\]
bit operations, where \(L\) is the total binary encoding length of the input? The inequalities are componentwise, and there is no boundedness or coefficient-size promise beyond the finite explicit encoding.
question_excerpt: The survey asks whether general integer programming can be solved with single-exponential dependence on the number of variables and polynomial dependence on the full input encoding length. This card retains the approved deterministic decision formulation for explicit rational inequalities.
definitions:
The dimension parameter \(n\) is the number of integer variables, and \(m\) is the number of inequalities. Both are supplied with the input. The matrix entries and right-hand-side entries are given exactly as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators, with explicit lengths or delimiters; entries need not be reduced to lowest terms. The entire matrix is listed in row-major order, followed by \(b\). The encoding length \(L\) includes all coefficients, dimensions, signs, denominators and delimiters. There is no succinct circuit or oracle representation of the inequalities.

The inequality \(Qx\le b\) means
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}x_j\le b_i
 \quad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Every coordinate of \(x\) must be an integer, with no a priori bound on its magnitude or sign. Nonnegativity restrictions are present only if encoded among the inequalities. The underlying real polyhedron may be empty, unbounded, lower dimensional, or contain lines; the matrix may be rank deficient. No bound is imposed on the number of inequalities, determinant magnitudes or width of the feasible region. There is no objective function.

For \(n=0\), \(\mathbb Z^0\) contains the single empty vector, and feasibility means \(0\le b_i\) for every row. For \(m=0\), the conjunction of inequalities is empty and the instance is feasible. These conventions also cover the completely empty system.

The output is one exact Boolean answer: YES if an integer solution exists, and NO otherwise. Producing a feasible point or a separate infeasibility certificate is not required by this decision target. A positive answer cannot be based solely on real feasibility or on satisfying relaxed or numerically perturbed inequalities.

The computation uses a fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, independent of \(m,n,L,Q,b\). Time is the number of bit-level machine steps. All reading, parsing, exact integer or rational arithmetic, storage operations and output are charged. Arithmetic on an arbitrarily large number is not one operation. Randomness, nonuniform advice, real-number primitives and uncharged optimization or separation oracles are not available.

The constants \(C\) and \(c\) are universal for that one program. In particular, the polynomial exponent on \(L\) may not depend on \(n\), and the exponential base may not grow with \(n\), coefficient magnitude or the number of rows. A polynomial factor in numerical coefficient or determinant magnitude can be exponential in its binary encoding length and therefore is not automatically permitted. Any implementation that uses such a factor must prove that its full bit cost nevertheless meets the displayed bound on every input.

The phrase single-exponential dependence on dimension refers to the factor \(2^{Cn}\). Bounds of the form \((\log(n+2))^{Dn}\) with a fixed \(D>0\) have a growing base and do not meet that dependence as stated. A family of unrelated algorithms, one for each fixed dimension, also does not suffice without one uniform machine and the required universal bounds.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated deterministic algorithm's existence or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

A positive answer must establish exact feasibility decisions and the total bit-operation bound for every encoded rational system, including unbounded and lower-dimensional cases. If the method first converts the input to another formulation, its cost, encoding growth and dependence on the number of integer variables must all be accounted for. An optimization algorithm is sufficient only if its proved guarantees include this feasibility task and the specified bound.

A negative answer must rule out every admissible uniform deterministic program and all fixed constants \(C,c\) in the statement. A lower bound conditional on ETH, \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or another unproved assumption does not establish this unconditional negation. Excluding subexponential time \(2^{o(n)}\) does not exclude the requested single-exponential bound.

A randomized algorithm, an algorithm restricted to bounded coefficients or a special block structure, an approximate integer-feasibility procedure, or a bound exponential in a different parameter does not decide the selected target without a proved extension.
context:
Fixed-dimensional integer programming is tractable, but the dimension dependence controls how broadly that fact can be used. The survey explicitly separates the single-exponential target from the known growing-base bound.

The March 2026 Reis–Rothvoss version gives a randomized \((\log(2n))^{O(n)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\) algorithm. Its bound is general, but both its growing exponential base and its randomization must be distinguished from the deterministic target here.

The approximate-to-exact work gives a single-exponential procedure with additional information about a solution, and records the unrestricted single-exponential question as open. Those extra inputs are not supplied in this card.

The September 2026 standard-form revision states feasibility time \(2^{O(k)}\Delta\operatorname{poly}(L)\), where \(k\) is row rank and \(\Delta\) bounds full-rank minors. The numerical determinant factor can be large despite a short binary encoding, so this statement does not give the requested unrestricted bound.
why: Integer feasibility is a general optimization primitive. A fixed exponential base in the number of variables would sharpen the dimension dependence of a widely used fixed-parameter algorithmic tool without restricting the coefficients or constraint structure.
status_note: The bounded primary-source review through 17 September 2026 found no verified deterministic 2^{O(n)} poly(L) algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem for unrestricted rational integer feasibility. The March 2026 general result remains randomized with a growing exponential base, and the September 2026 standard-form result retains a numerical determinant factor. The full revised proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2023: The Reis–Rothvoss work improves general integer programming to a polylogarithmic-base exponential randomized bound. | 2025: The survey explicitly retains the single-exponential dimension target as open. | 2026-03-27: The revised general bound is checked with its randomized computation convention. | 2026-09-13: A refined standard-form bound gives a single-exponential row-rank factor while retaining determinant-magnitude dependence.
working_summary: The input is an explicit system of rational linear inequalities whose variables must all be integers. The task is exact feasibility, with no boundedness, rank or coefficient-size promise. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm with a fixed exponential base in the number of variables and a fixed polynomial dependence on input length. The checked general randomized bound and recent determinant-dependent bound do not supply that guarantee. An accepted answer must give a complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional impossibility proof in the bit-computation model.

title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
importance_reason: Identify a fundamental limitation of exact semidefinite optimization representations.
formal:
Is the semidefinite extension complexity of the perfect-matching polytopes of complete graphs unbounded by every polynomial in the number of vertices? Precisely, is
\[
\forall B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N\quad
\bigl(n\ge2\ \land\ 2\mid n\ \land\
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)>Bn^b\bigr)
\]
true, for the exact real semidefinite lifts defined below?

This is a statement about the existence of representations, with arbitrary real coefficients and no symmetry or efficient-construction requirement. The quantifiers ask whether no single polynomial bounds the entire family; they do not require a specified exponential rate or a lower bound holding at every sufficiently large even size. Integer constants express the same assertion as the inherited formulation with every pair of positive real constants \(C,c\).
definitions:
For each even integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let
\[
E_n=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i<j\},
\]
and let \(K_n=([n],E_n)\) be the finite simple undirected complete graph. A perfect matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E_n\) in which every vertex belongs to exactly one edge. Its incidence vector \(\chi^M\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has coordinate one on edges in \(M\) and zero on all other edges. Define
\[
P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }K_n\}.
\]
The convex hull of a finite set consists of all weighted sums of its elements with nonnegative real weights summing to one. Thus \(P_n\) includes exactly those convex combinations, with one coordinate for each of the \(\binom n2\) edges.

For a positive integer \(r\), let
\[
\mathbb S^r=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}:Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\},
\qquad
\mathbb S^r_+=\{Y\in\mathbb S^r:\forall z\in\mathbb R^r,\ z^{\mathsf T}Yz\ge0\}.
\]
An affine subspace of \(\mathbb S^r\) is a translate of a real linear subspace. An affine map into \(\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has the form \(\pi(Y)=A(Y)+a\), with \(A\) real linear and \(a\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\). A size-\(r\) semidefinite lift of \(P_n\) is a pair \((L,\pi)\), where \(L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\) is an affine subspace and \(\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\) is affine, satisfying the exact equality
\[
P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+).
\]
The quantity \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)\) is the least positive integer \(r\) admitting such a pair. Every finite polytope has a finite such representation, so this minimum exists. Restricting sizes to positive integers also fixes the convention for the singleton \(P_2\).

Size means the order of this single positive semidefinite matrix, not the number of scalar entries or inequalities. If several positive semidefinite blocks are used, their block-diagonal combination counts their total order. Coefficients of \(L\) and \(\pi\) may be arbitrary real numbers. No bit-length bound, computability condition, uniform algorithm producing the representations, or efficient numerical procedure is imposed. The lifted feasible set need not be bounded or strictly feasible. No invariance under permutations of graph vertices or matrix coordinates is required. The condition \(Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\) is ordinary matrix symmetry and does not impose such an invariance requirement. Approximate outer representations do not meet the exact equality.

The inherited card uses affine projection maps. The cited survey defines lifts using linear projection maps; these conventions differ by at most one in matrix order and hence give the same polynomial-boundedness question. The original thesis asks about the polytope of all matchings, including nonperfect ones. Its family has polynomial-size exact semidefinite lifts if and only if the complete-graph perfect-matching family does, so the retained target is a polynomially equivalent formulation of the source question, not a claim that those polytopes are identical.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its full logical negation, for exactly the objects and size convention above.

A positive answer must prove that for every \(B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) there is an even \(n\ge2\) for which no exact semidefinite lift has matrix order at most \(Bn^b\). This includes all real affine slices and affine projection maps, without imposing symmetry, uniformity, strict feasibility or coefficient restrictions.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\forall n\ge2\text{ with }2\mid n\quad
\exists r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\ \exists\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\quad
\bigl(r\le Bn^b\ \land\ L\text{ is affine}\ \land\pi\text{ is affine}\
\land\ P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+)\bigr).
\]
The polynomial is common to all sizes, while the representations may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); an efficient construction algorithm is not additionally required.

A lower bound for linear lifts, coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulations, a fixed relaxation hierarchy, or a restricted coefficient field is insufficient by itself. An approximation result or an efficient matching algorithm is not an exact semidefinite representation. Conditional results must also establish any extra hypothesis needed for the unconditional target. This is an asymptotic representation-existence proposition, so no additive numerical tolerance replaces its quantified bounds.
context:
Perfect matching admits polynomial-time optimization, while its exact linear extension complexity is exponential.

The source asks whether positive semidefinite lifts can give polynomial-size representations of the matching polytope, a question equivalent at the family level to the retained perfect-matching version.

The benchmark allows all exact real semidefinite lifts, including representations with no symmetry or efficient construction.

Known exponential bounds for coordinate-symmetric matching formulations and general semidefinite bounds for other polytopes do not establish the unrestricted matching claim.

The later survey explicitly retains the matching question, and the bounded subsequent review found no theorem settling the precise family and model here.
why: Perfect matching is a canonical problem with efficient optimization algorithms and strong combinatorial structure. Deciding whether it nevertheless lacks polynomial-size exact semidefinite representations would clarify the limits of a major convex-optimization model beyond the established limits of linear programming. A polynomial-size family would instead demonstrate a substantial representational advantage over linear lifts for this central tractable polytope.

A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. A semidefinite lift represents that polytope exactly as an affine image of an affine slice of a real positive semidefinite cone. The question asks whether the required matrix order is unbounded by every polynomial in the number of graph vertices, allowing arbitrary real coefficients and separate representations at each size.
