A method is one fixed finite real-arithmetic program supplied with \(p,q,L,z_0\), initialized with empty history and fixed rational constants. It uses scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero numbers, exact comparisons, branching, copying, and integer loop/address operations. Real registers cannot be inspected digit by digit. Oracle calls may be adaptive, at points computed from the supplied data and earlier replies. Finite differences or other numerical quantities computed from finitely many permitted replies are allowed; direct derivative queries above first order are not.

The program may retain finite history and use iteration-dependent or adaptively chosen parameters. On every permitted input and after every finite iteration count it must finish the finite work needed to produce the next iterate, using finitely many elementary operations, stored values and oracle calls. No infinite inner loop, exact limit operation, uncharged auxiliary oracle, function-dependent advice or external randomization is allowed. Auxiliary storage is finite at each finite stage but need not have a fixed bound over the infinite run. This is an asymptotic convergence question: no polynomial iteration bound, oracle-complexity rate or bit-complexity bound is requested. The real oracle and exact arithmetic are part of the model, not claims about finite-precision implementation.

For precision, let \(z_k^{f,L}(u)\) be the sequence produced from initial point \(u\), with dimensions understood and \(z_0^{f,L}(u)=u\). The first guarantee means that, for each \(p,q,f,L\), there exists a set \(E_{f,L}\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\) of Lebesgue outer measure zero such that
\[\forall u\notin E_{f,L}\ \forall z^*,\quad
 \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*
 \ \Longrightarrow\ z^*\text{ is a local minimax point of }f.\]
The one exceptional set must cover all possible bad limits, not a separate uncountable union of exceptions for individual points. Equivalently, the same implication must hold almost surely for every initialization distribution with a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The algorithm itself is deterministic.

The second guarantee means that for every strict local minimax point \(z^*\), there exists \(r>0\), depending on \(f,L,z^*\), such that
\[\forall u\in\mathbb R^{p+q},\quad
 \|u-z^*\|_2<r\ \Longrightarrow\ \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*.\]
Every start uses the same program initialization; no target point or attracting radius is supplied to it. The requirements permit divergent or nonconvergent runs outside these local basins. They concern limits of the full sequence, not every subsequential accumulation point, and do not require global convergence or attraction to every non-strict local minimax point.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a method meeting both guarantees, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must specify one finite oracle program, establish that it produces every next iterate after finite work, prove the common measure-zero exception statement for every permitted objective and every valid supplied \(L\), and prove local attraction at every point satisfying the strict Hessian conditions.

A negative proof must exclude every method in this specified oracle model from satisfying the conjunction. Counterexamples only to gradient descent-ascent, extragradient or another named update do not exclude every method. A method that never converges, convergence only to stationary points or second-order necessary-condition points, local linear stability without the stated limit guarantees, or a theorem assuming additional curvature or neighborhood-radius restrictions does not meet this target. No finite iteration rate is demanded, and the benchmark's numerical tolerance does not replace exact convergence or exact local minimaxity.
context:
Both \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) and \(g(x,y)=-x^2+y^2\) have zero gradient at the origin. For the prescribed minimization in \(x\) and maximization in \(y\), the first has a strict local minimax point there, while the second fails even the required local maximization in \(y\). Thus stationarity does not identify the intended local solution.

The local minimax definition allows the maximizing player’s response neighborhood to shrink at a different rate from the minimizing player’s neighborhood. It describes the sequential order of play. Requiring the minimizing player to keep the maximizer’s action fixed instead gives the stronger local Nash notion; reversing the players gives a different local optimization question.

The original convergence literature distinguishes sufficient strict curvature conditions from necessary second-order conditions. With degeneracy, satisfying the latter need not certify a local minimax point. A guarantee stated only for strict linearly unstable points also does not automatically exclude convergence to every other undesirable stationary point.

The ICLR 2024 two-timescale extragradient paper extends analysis beyond an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its theorems still retain conditions on the restricted Schur complement, the full saddle-gradient Jacobian or spectral thresholds. Its stable points are characterized using necessary second-order conditions in the relevant regimes; this is not the unrestricted true-minimax limit guarantee selected here.

The ICML 2024 double-step alternating extragradient work improves local stability for further non-strict cases and studies increasing timescale separation. Its local results retain nondegeneracy conditions on specified Hessian-derived matrices; the increasing-timescale stability theorem additionally assumes a third derivative. The paper’s separate global-convergence result assumes star-convex–star-concave structure. Those hypotheses are absent from this card’s objective class.

Follow-the-Ridge gives a related local fixed-point theorem using second-order information and an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its distinction between strict linear stability and weak spectral stability also matters. This is a useful comparison with the first-order question, but its Hessian-assisted theorem is not a solution for every objective in the model here.

Lu and Wang’s August 2026 constrained minimax paper proves complexity bounds for approximate stationary points under a local Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz condition on a lifted inner problem. That condition restricts the relation between objective residuals and generalized gradients. The assumptions and approximate-stationarity target differ from exact local-minimax limit selection for arbitrary smooth objectives.

The probability qualifier concerns the initial point. It allows, for example, an exceptional initialization exactly at an undesirable stationary point when such starts form a null set. The local-attraction condition supplies a positive guarantee near strict solutions. No convergence assertion is being made for every trajectory of a nonconvex–nonconcave game.
why: Sequential adversarial optimization needs the minimization and maximization roles to be respected at the limiting solution. Reaching a stationary point alone can select the wrong kind of equilibrium. A first-order selection theorem that remains valid with degeneracy would clarify what gradient information can guarantee beyond the curvature-restricted cases already analyzed.
status_note: Reviewed on 16 September 2026. The primary 2023 source poses a broad open direction; the complete oracle and convergence quantifiers on this card are an explicitly chosen benchmark variant. The inspected 2024 results retain derivative, matrix, spectral or global-structure hypotheses, and the August 2026 constrained result concerns approximate stationarity under a KL assumption. Bounded searches did not establish a validated solution of both guarantees here. A further OpenReview submission advertises calmness-based selection in indexed passages, but its full current text and status were inaccessible in this pass and have not been verified. The card remains uncertain and active; the formulation is complete, while the dated literature check is expressly limited.
progress: 2020: Jin, Netrapalli and Jordan formalize local minimax optimality for sequential games and connect two-timescale gradient dynamics with it subject to degeneracy qualifications. | 2023-07: The COLT open-problem contribution asks for first-order convergence to genuine local minimax optima and explains the remaining gap beyond necessary derivative conditions. | 2024-04-22: The current ICLR extragradient version extends the covered non-strict cases, while retaining matrix and spectral assumptions. | 2024-07: The ICML double-step alternating method improves local stability, including an increasing-timescale analysis under additional assumptions. | 2026-08-25: Lu–Wang establish constrained approximate-stationarity guarantees under a local KL assumption; this does not certify the selected unrestricted limit property.
working_summary: In sequential minimax optimization, one player minimizes a smooth function of x while a second player maximizes it in y. A local minimax point respects this order using shrinking neighborhoods whose radii may differ for the two players. The selected variant asks for one deterministic method with exact function-value and gradient queries whose finite limits are local minimax points for almost every initialization. The same method must converge locally to every strict local minimax point, so avoiding convergence everywhere is not a valid answer. Existing convergence theorems retain extra hypotheses or weaker derivative-based targets, and the exact variant and limits of the current source review are explicitly recorded.

title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
importance_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
focus_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
context:
Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.
why: KLS asks whether covariance normalization alone controls the relation between global variation and local change for every log-concave distribution. Its equivalent geometric expansion principle is central to concentration inequalities and the analysis of random walks used for sampling, integration and convex optimization.
status_note: The complete all-function KLS conjecture is explicitly open in Letwin’s 27 July 2026 preprint and Zhang’s 5 September 2026 sampling revision. The latter retains dependence on the KLS constant; its claimed mixing theorem does not resolve KLS. Live revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no primary full resolution. Thin-shell and quadratic-form results are separately scoped. The new July and September proofs were not independently verified; source statements, conventions and implication directions were checked.
progress: 1995: Kannan, Lovász and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in their study of convex-body algorithms, as recounted in the inspected Lee–Vempala survey. | 2022: Klartag and Lehec’s Theorem 1.1 bounds reciprocal expansion by \(O((\log n)^5)\). | 2023: Klartag’s Theorem 1.2 gives reciprocal expansion \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), equivalent up to constants to a Poincaré bound \(O(\log n)\). | 2025–2026: Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell target; the February 2026 revision still distinguishes it from full KLS. | 2026-07-25: Chen and Klartag’s preprint states the sharp radial variance bound \(8n\), a restricted-observable result rather than full KLS. | 2026-07-27: Letwin’s preprint states a dimension-free quadratic-form inequality and derives the general Poincaré bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\); this review has not independently verified the new proof. | 2026-09-05: Zhang’s revised hit-and-run paper explicitly retains KLS as open while reporting progress on a sampling theorem that still depends on its constant.
working_summary: The KLS conjecture asks for a universal Poincaré inequality for every log-concave probability distribution with zero mean and identity covariance. Every locally Lipschitz function of finite variance and gradient energy must have its variance bounded by that energy times one constant independent of the dimension and distribution. The target includes uniform distributions on convex bodies and requires no symmetry, independence or positive curvature assumption. Its equivalent expansion principle connects high-dimensional geometry and concentration with the analysis of sampling algorithms. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or its unbounded-counterexample negation; radial, quadratic and dimension-dependent improvements do not settle the full target.

title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
importance_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
focus_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite simple graph \(H\), there exists a real constant \(C_H\ge1\) such that, for every nonempty finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with no \(H\) minor and every edge-length function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
d_{G,w}(u,v)\le
\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f(u)_j-f(v)_j|
\le C_H\,d_{G,w}(u,v)
\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V?
\]
The constant may depend only on \(H\). The dimension and map may depend on the whole weighted graph, with no bound on dimension or on the time needed to construct them.
question_excerpt: Every family of graphs excluding a fixed minor has a uniform constant bound on the distortion needed to embed all its weighted shortest-path metrics into ell-one.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called edges. Connected means every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, followed by removal of loops and duplicate edges, can produce a graph isomorphic to \(H\). Exclusion concerns the underlying unweighted graph.

The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. The shortest-path distance \(d_{G,w}(u,v)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(d_{G,w}(u,u)=0\). Positivity and finiteness make this a finite metric. A one-vertex graph is allowed and satisfies the target trivially.

The target space is finite-dimensional \(\ell_1^m\): the vector space \(\mathbb R^m\) with distance \(\|a-b\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\). The first inequality fixes a noncontracting normalization, and the second allows expansion by at most \(C_H\). Allowing an arbitrary common scaling factor instead gives the same distortion notion.

All edge lengths are arbitrary positive real numbers. Neither graph size nor the ratio of the largest to the smallest edge length may affect \(C_H\). There is no requirement that the graph or its lengths be efficiently encoded, since this is a mathematical existence question. All pairs must satisfy the inequalities simultaneously for the same map.

The source also allows zero edge lengths and hence zero distances between different vertices. That convention is equivalent for this conjecture: contract each component of zero-length edges, retain the shortest parallel edge when necessary, and map the original vertices through this quotient. The quotient is still a minor of the original graph. The positive-length statement above avoids treating distinct points at distance zero as a metric space.

No Euclidean target, restriction to selected terminals, average-distance guarantee, or transformation of the distances by a power is part of this statement. Here a terminal, when used in the context, simply means a selected vertex whose distances must be preserved.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain a finite constant for every fixed excluded minor, uniformly over all weighted graphs in that class and all vertex pairs. It need not determine the best constant or construct the embeddings efficiently. A negative answer must give one fixed graph \(H\) such that for every real \(C\ge1\), some finite connected positively weighted \(H\)-minor-free graph admits no map into any finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) space satisfying both inequalities with factor \(C\). Failure at one fixed distortion value is insufficient if a larger uniform value remains possible. This binary existence claim has no additive numerical tolerance.
context:
The conjecture links a qualitative restriction on graph structure to quantitative preservation of every distance. Removing one fixed graph from the set of permitted minors is predicted to prevent any distortion that grows with graph size, despite arbitrary edge lengths.

Finite \(\ell_1\) metrics are exactly nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric has value one on pairs separated by a vertex subset and zero on other pairs. This connects distance representation to weighted separation of vertices and hence to graph partitioning.

In the equivalent routing formulation, capacities are attached to graph edges and demands to arbitrary vertex pairs. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every demand, allowing a demand to split among paths. The flow-cut gap compares the best achievable fraction to the upper bound imposed by the sparsest cut. The conjecture predicts a constant gap on every fixed-minor-free family.

Demands in this correspondence may join any pairs; they need not themselves form a planar or minor-free graph. The multiflow/multicut optimization studied in recent work has a different objective and gap, so its constant bounds do not resolve the conjecture.

The planar case is already unresolved in the checked 2026 account: the upper bound grows as the square root of the logarithm of the number of vertices, while no superconstant lower bound is known there. Trees and several other restricted families do have constant bounds.

Lee and Sidiropoulos establish a constant bound on every minor-closed family excluding a fixed tree. Their stronger random-tree result applies to bounded pathwidth, a restriction stronger than bounded treewidth.

A constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs is known using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. The authors explicitly distinguish its stronger relaxation from the ordinary concurrent-flow relaxation, whose gap is the relevant one here.

For planar graphs with a selected terminal set covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a drawing, Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log(\gamma+1)})\). The added one handles the single-face boundary case in asymptotic notation. The number of covering faces is unbounded in the general conjecture.

Mori’s February 2026 preprint states that the worst distortion over edge lengths of \(K_{2,n}\) is \((3k-2)/(2k-1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\) and \(n\ge1\). Here \(K_{2,n}\) has two independent parts of sizes two and \(n\), with all edges between them. These values tend to \(3/2\), so this is progress within a bounded-distortion family.
why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.
status_note: The original source poses constant distortion for every family excluding a fixed minor. The May 2026 notes still identify the planar constant bound as open. The checked pathwidth, face-cover and February 2026 complete-bipartite results impose additional restrictions. The fixed-treewidth approximation result uses a stronger relaxation, and recent multiflow/multicut results concern a different gap. A bounded primary-source review on 16 September 2026 found no settlement; the cited proofs have not all been independently verified.
progress: 1999–2004: The original work formulates the conjecture and proves constant distortion for restricted classes, including series-parallel graphs. | 2012: The checked final preprint establishes the bounded-pathwidth result and the consequence for families excluding a fixed tree. | 2010: A stronger relaxation gives constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class, without proving the ordinary flow-cut-gap conjecture. | 2024-11-22: The journal publication improves the planar terminal face-cover distortion bound. | 2026-02-27: The preprint states exact worst-weight distortion values for \(K_{2,n}\). | 2026-09-16: The individual review retained the general conjecture and checked the scope of the later restricted-family results.
working_summary: The GNRS conjecture asks whether weighted graphs excluding a fixed minor have shortest-path metrics that embed into \(\ell_1\) with bounded distortion. The bound may depend on the excluded graph but must be independent of graph size and all edge lengths. One map must preserve every pairwise distance, with no required algorithm or target-dimension bound. The equivalent routing formulation predicts a constant concurrent-flow versus cut gap for arbitrary demands. The checked restricted-family results leave the general conjecture, including its planar case, unresolved.

title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
focus_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
question_excerpt: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for unknot recognition?
definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The parameter \(N\) is the length of the supplied finite encoding. A standard indexing uses \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, with the crossing-free code handled separately. It is neither the smallest possible crossing number of the knot nor the length of a compressed program describing a larger diagram.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the algorithm’s correct answer on every valid diagram and one polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative proof must exclude every deterministic polynomial-time recognizer in this input model, rather than only a selected algorithm or simplification rule. Short certificates, polynomial-length move sequences and successful finite experiments do not by themselves prove deterministic polynomial running time. The existence statement is binary and has no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
A complicated knot diagram can represent a circle that has merely been drawn in an awkward way. The task is to distinguish such projections from actual knots, using a finite description of crossings and planar incidence. No physical model of rope or numerical geometry is involved.

Both positive and negative instances have short efficiently checkable certificates. The NP theorem certifies unknottedness, and the coNP theorem certifies knottedness. These are existence statements about verifiable evidence; they do not show how to find the evidence in deterministic polynomial time.

Thus the problem belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\). Here NP consists of decision problems with polynomial-size witnesses verifiable in polynomial time, and coNP contains their complements. NP-hardness of this particular problem under polynomial-time reductions would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\); a proof that it is outside P would in particular separate P from NP.

Lackenby proves that an unknot diagram with \(n\) crossings admits a simplification using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local changes of diagrams that preserve knot type. The theorem bounds a successful sequence’s length, while an algorithm must determine appropriate moves without an uncontrolled search.

The March 2021 Oxford announcement states a recognition algorithm with running time \(n^{O(\log n)}\). The checked SoCG 2025 article still describes that result as announced. Such a quasipolynomial bound allows a growing exponent and therefore does not give the fixed exponent requested here.

The SoCG 2025 factorisation work distinguishes practical performance from worst-case guarantees. It reports that Regina’s recognition algorithm behaves polynomially in experiments despite an exponential worst-case bound. Testing many diagrams cannot establish a bound for every possible input.

Lackenby’s July 2026 hierarchy algorithm gives another recognition method. Section 9 bounds iteration counts by \(L(g+1)^L\), where \(L\) is a hierarchy-length bound and \(g\) bounds surface pattern complexity. These parameters are not bounded there as functions of the original diagram size, and some operation costs also remain unspecified. The displayed iteration estimate is not a polynomial-time theorem for this card.

Musick’s September 2026 preprint claims a positive solution. A bridge presentation separates the knot into trivial arcs in two balls. The preprint claims to find a locally minimal bridge presentation in polynomial time using compressed data, then invokes the fact that a locally minimal presentation of the unknot has one bridge.

The claim’s key dependencies include completeness of the permitted simplifications for local bridge minimality and polynomial manipulation of arc multiplicities. This review read those arguments but did not independently certify them. The scientific status remains uncertain pending validation; no counterexample to the claim is asserted.
why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.
status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 v1 claims a deterministic polynomial-time solution. This review examined its statement and main proof dependencies but did not independently establish the local-minimality argument in Lemma 6 or all compressed-update bounds in Lemmas 8–10. No later revision or independent validation was located through 16 September 2026. The card therefore remains uncertain, rather than being declared resolved or unconditionally open. The July hierarchy paper, polynomial certificate theorems and earlier quasipolynomial announcement are recorded with their distinct scopes.
progress: 1997–1999: Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger prove NP membership using normal surfaces, with deterministic exponential-time algorithms; FOCS 1997, JACM 1999. | 2013–2015: Lackenby proves a polynomial bound on the number of Reidemeister moves needed to simplify an unknot, without a polynomial algorithm to find the sequence. | 2016–2021: Lackenby establishes unconditional NP certificates for knottedness, placing unknot recognition in coNP; journal publication 2021. | 2021: Lackenby announces quasipolynomial-time unknot recognition; retained as an announced result. | 2025: He–Sedgwick–Spreer present practical factorisation algorithms and explicitly distinguish empirical performance from worst-case polynomial unknot recognition. | 2026-07-25: Lackenby gives a new hierarchy-based recognition algorithm; its Section 9 does not establish polynomial input-size complexity. | 2026-09-06: Musick’s preprint claims polynomial-time recognition via locally minimal bridge presentations. This review has not independently validated the proof. | 2026-09-16: The individual review checks the input model and the recent claim’s central dependencies while retaining uncertain status.
working_summary: The input is an explicit finite crossing diagram of a tame knot. The question asks whether a deterministic algorithm can recognize the unknot in polynomial bit time. Both unknottedness and knottedness have polynomially verifiable certificates, which does not itself give such an algorithm. A September 2026 preprint claims a positive solution using locally minimal bridge presentations. The review has not independently certified that claim, so the card retains uncertain scientific status.

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
importance_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
focus_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
question_excerpt: Is the diameter of a polyhedron bounded by a polynomial in its dimension and number of facets?
definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
A linear program optimizes a linear function over a polyhedron. Moving between adjacent vertices is the geometric operation behind simplex pivots. The conjecture asks whether every pair of feasible vertices is joined by a short sequence of these moves, before any navigation rule or objective is chosen.

The facet count measures the number of essential inequalities. It can be much smaller than the number of vertices: the cube \([0,1]^d\) has \(2d\) facets and \(2^d\) vertices, but diameter only \(d\). Merely bounding distance by the number of vertices therefore does not give the desired polynomial.

A bound such as \(n^d\) allows the exponent to increase with the dimension. The conjecture demands one fixed exponent, and allows neither the multiplicative constant nor that exponent to depend on the particular polyhedron.

Santos’s 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets has diameter greater than 43, refuting the original Hirsch bound \(n-d\) for bounded polytopes. This leaves open all sufficiently large polynomial bounds. The bounded counterexample does not itself show superpolynomial growth.

Todd proves the general bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the single-vertex boundary cases treated separately. The earlier Kalai–Kleitman bound was \(n^{2+\log_2 d}\). These estimates are quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.

Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has exponent \(\log_2 d-\log_2\log d+O(1)\) for large \(d\). The exponent still grows without bound, so this improvement does not establish the conjecture.

The length of the best available path is different from the length of a path selected by a particular pivot rule. A positive answer would give geometric existence, without supplying a fast procedure for choosing the next edge or guaranteeing objective improvement.

Wulf proves that computing diameter is \(\Pi_2^p\)-hard even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, the convex hulls of incidence vectors of perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. This is a hardness classification at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It concerns finding the value, and is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on that value.

Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a circuit-diameter bound \(O(r^2\log r)\) for standard-form polyhedra \(\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank \(r\ge2\). A circuit direction is a nonzero kernel vector whose set of nonzero coordinates contains no smaller support of another nonzero kernel vector. A circuit step moves maximally in a feasible circuit direction and may pass through a higher-dimensional face. Such a walk need not follow graph edges.

A monotone path increases a chosen linear objective. A coherent monotone path is more restricted: it traces optimizers as a second linear objective varies along a line in objective space. Black and Xue’s July 2026 preprint gives polytopes for which every coherent monotone path for the chosen orientation is long. Their restriction is absent from ordinary graph distance.

More precisely, their Theorem 1.1 gives, for each \(q\ge3\), a polytope of dimension \(q+1\) with \((2q+1)(q+1)+1\) facets and an objective for which every coherent monotone path has length at least \(2^{q-1}-1\). The paper continues to list the unrestricted polynomial Hirsch question as open.
why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.
status_note: The reviewed July 2026 paper still poses the polynomial edge-diameter conjecture and proves a lower bound only for coherent monotone paths. Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a polynomial circuit-diameter bound, with moves beyond edges. Neither changes the unrestricted edge-path target, which includes pointed unbounded polyhedra. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for this target; recent cited proofs were not independently certified in full.
progress: 1992: Kalai and Kleitman establish a quasipolynomial general diameter bound. | 2010–2012: Santos announces and publishes a bounded counterexample to the original linear Hirsch inequality. | 2014-03-20: Todd’s revised preprint proves the bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\). | 2018–2019: Sukegawa publishes an asymptotic exponent improvement, still outside a uniform polynomial bound. | 2025-11-03: Wulf’s revised FOCS paper establishes stronger hardness of computing diameters. | 2026-02-10: Natura’s revised preprint states a polynomial bound for circuit walks, including monotone circuit walks. | 2026-07-13: Black and Xue state exponential lower bounds for coherent monotone paths, while retaining the unrestricted conjecture. | 2026-09-16: The individual review retains the full edge-diameter target and distinguishes these three path models.
working_summary: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture asks for a universal polynomial bound on the edge-graph diameter of every pointed polyhedron. The parameters are dimension and number of facets, with arbitrary real coordinates and both bounded and unbounded regions allowed. The original linear bound is false, while known general upper bounds remain quasipolynomial. Recent results give short circuit walks and long coherent monotone paths, neither of which settles unrestricted edge distance. The target concerns the existence of short paths and does not require an algorithm to find them.

title: Planar k-set extremal function
importance_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
focus_reason: A defining two-parameter extremal problem underlying levels and geometric selection; its source-defined asymptotic function is admissible under the restored numerical/function policy.
formal:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]
Determine a positive real-valued function \(F(n,k)\), together with universal real constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), such that
\[
cF(n,k)\le K_2(n,k)\le CF(n,k)
\quad\text{for every }n\ge2,\quad
1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor.
\]
question_excerpt: What is the largest number of k-element subsets of an n-point set that can be cut off by a hyperplane?
definitions:
The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

The domain of \(F\) consists of every integer pair specified in the statement. The constants \(c,C\) must not depend on \(n\), \(k\), the point set or its coordinates. In particular, \(k\) may grow with \(n\). Bounds for a single fixed \(k\), only the balanced case, or only a random model do not determine this whole function.

The upper inequality means that every permitted \(P\) has at most \(CF(n,k)\) k-sets. The lower inequality means that for every permitted pair \(n,k\), at least one such \(P\) has at least \(cF(n,k)\) k-sets. Different pairs may use different point sets. No efficient construction of these sets is required.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points.
answer_criterion: Supply \(F,c,C\) and complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean of both inequalities throughout the stated domain. The upper proof must cover all permitted point sets, and the lower proof must establish existence for every parameter pair. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required, but simply repeating the defining extremum under a new name is insufficient. Finite boundary cases must be covered; they may be absorbed by choosing larger universal constants when justified. This user-retained asymptotic target uses constant-factor precision, not additive \(1/100\). A one-sided bound, a halving-only result or constants depending on a growing parameter does not suffice.
context:
A linear cut realizes only a restricted collection of subsets of a point set. Fixing the subset size measures this restriction more precisely than counting all possible cuts together. The planar problem already exhibits the persistent gap in the broader higher-dimensional question.

For \(k=1\), the separable points are precisely the vertices of the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing \(P\). Their maximum number is \(n\). The unresolved part concerns how the count grows when the selected subset size grows too.

Point-line duality relates these counts to levels in arrangements of lines. A level follows the positions with a prescribed number of arrangement lines below them. Such complexity bounds occur in geometric selection and parametric optimization, where the preferred solution changes with a parameter.

Dey’s general upper bound is \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the domain of this card. Tóth’s constructions give \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets. Thus the existing upper and lower estimates do not differ by only a universal constant when \(k\) increases.

In the plane, k-sets correspond to directed \((k-1)\)-edges. For even \(n\), subsets of size \(n/2\) therefore correspond to the two orientations of undirected halving edges. Consequently \(K_2(n,n/2)\) is twice the maximum number of halving edges. The index \((n-2)/2\) counts points on one side of a halving edge, not the size of a halving subset.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves a subtractive term proportional to the number of points and some finite-size bounds. Its leading upper growth remains proportional to the four-thirds power. Better lower-order terms alone do not give the matching function requested here.
why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.
status_note: The TOPP entry revised in June 2025 still lists the planar extremal problem as open. The checked bounds leave an unbounded gap for growing k. The 2024 halving-line refinement does not change the upper exponent, and the cited improved halving construction changes a constant in its lower exponent. No matching general bound was found in the bounded review through 16 September 2026; this review does not independently certify all cited proofs.
progress: 1997–1998: Dey obtains the planar upper bound \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the nontrivial domain. | 2000–2001: Tóth constructs \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets for every \(n\ge2k>0\). | 2008: Nivasch improves the exponent constant in the known halving-edge construction. | 2024-07-22: The published halving-line refinement improves subtractive and finite-size upper bounds. | 2025-06-14: The revised TOPP entry retains the planar extremal gap. | 2026-09-16: The individual review checks the joint parameter domain, strict separation and the halving-edge indexing.
working_summary: A planar k-set is a k-element subset strictly separated from the remaining points by a line. The extremal function maximizes the number of these subsets over n distinct points with no three collinear. The task is to determine one function within universal constant factors for every n and every k between one and half of n. Acceptance requires both a bound for all point sets and matching examples for every parameter pair. The checked general bounds and newer halving-line refinements still leave the asymptotic function unresolved.

title: Lang–Plaut problem
importance_reason: A major metric-embedding characterization problem: whether doubling and Hilbert embeddability suffice for finite-dimensional Euclidean representation.
formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.
context:
Naor and Neiman state the Lang–Plaut question in Section 1.1 and justify its quantitative form in Section 4. This card uses that form so the dependence of dimension and distortion is explicit. The original question is attributed there to Lang and Plaut’s Question 2.4.

Every subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space is doubling, with a bound controlled by dimension, and is already a subset of Hilbert space. A positive answer would make these two necessary conditions sufficient for finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embeddability.

Naor and Neiman prove that for an arbitrary doubling metric \((X,d)\), every snowflake \((X,d^{1-\eta})\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), embeds into a Euclidean space whose dimension depends only on the doubling constant. The distortion still depends on \(\eta\). Letting \(\eta\) tend to zero therefore does not supply the uniformly controlled embedding asked for here.

Lafforgue and Naor construct, for every \(p>2\), a doubling subset of \(L_p\) that has no bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Their theorem explicitly leaves the Hilbert case \(p=2\) open, so replacing Hilbert space by a general Banach space changes the answer.

Usual finite-set dimension reduction allows dimension to grow with the logarithm of the number of points. Here arbitrarily large or infinite sets with the same doubling bound must share a finite target dimension and distortion bound. This is a geometric existence question rather than a request for a faster implementation of a known projection.
why: The problem asks whether intrinsic local metric dimension completely controls Euclidean dimensional reduction once Hilbert embeddability is available. Its resolution would clarify a central obstruction to finite-dimensional metric representation and the limits of geometry-based compression independent of dataset size.
status_note: Open in the checked Naor–Neiman and Lafforgue–Naor sources. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for the Hilbert case. Results for other Banach spaces or restricted families do not supply one; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.
progress: 2001: Lang and Plaut pose the finite-dimensional embeddability question. | 2012: Naor and Neiman obtain snowflake embeddings with dimension independent of the snowflake exponent and explain why the unsnowflaked Hilbert question remains. | 2013: Lafforgue and Naor give a negative answer for every Lp with p greater than two, while retaining the Hilbert case as open.
working_summary: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls. The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space. It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor. Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant. The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.

title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
importance_reason: A longstanding and precisely isolated computational-topology problem connecting finite combinatorial input with fundamental four-dimensional topology.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) with the following property? For every finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\), encoded by its facets as below and promised to be a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold, \(M\) halts and outputs a bit satisfying
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(K))=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}\partial\Delta^5.
\]
Here \(\partial\Delta^5\) is the standard PL \(4\)-sphere. Output zero is required on every promised input that is not PL homeomorphic to it. There is no running-time or space bound, and connectedness is not part of the promise.
question_excerpt: Is recognition of the standard piecewise-linear four-sphere algorithmically decidable?
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a finite family of finite subsets of a finite vertex set \(V\), containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its members are faces; inclusion-maximal faces are facets. The dimension of a nonempty face \(\sigma\) is \(|\sigma|-1\). Pure dimension four means that all facets have exactly five vertices.

Vertex labels are distinct nonnegative integers. The input lists each facet once, sorting labels increasingly within facets and sorting the facet lists lexicographically. Each label is written in binary with no leading zero except for the label zero itself. A fixed separator between labels and a second separator between facets make this a finite string over a fixed alphabet. The full complex is the family of all subsets of the listed facets, and its vertex set is their union. Renaming vertices does not affect the correct answer.

The geometric realization \(|K|\) is the subset of \(\mathbb R^V\) consisting of vectors \((t_v)_{v\in V}\) with \(t_v\ge0\), \(\sum_vt_v=1\), and \(\{v:t_v>0\}\in K\). Each face is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite simplicial subdivision is a finite triangulation of this realization by simplices contained in old simplices, whose union on each old simplex equals that simplex.

Two finite complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic, written \(K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}L\), when they admit finite subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection on vertices taking faces to faces in both directions. Equivalently, their realizations have a homeomorphism that is affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions.

The simplex \(\Delta^q\) is the complex of all subsets of a set of \(q+1\) vertices. Its boundary \(\partial\Delta^q\) consists of all proper subsets of that vertex set. The standard PL \(j\)-sphere is \(\partial\Delta^{j+1}\), up to PL homeomorphism.

The link of a vertex \(v\) is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
In this card, a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold means a finite pure four-dimensional complex for which every vertex link is PL homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^4\). Multiple connected components are allowed. No orientation, simple-connectivity, homology-sphere or prior topological-sphere promise is imposed.

A deterministic Turing machine has a finite transition rule, finite tape alphabet and finitely many tapes; it starts with the encoded complex on its input tape. Halting with output one means acceptance, and halting with output zero means rejection. Termination and correctness are required on all and only promised inputs; behavior on malformed strings or complexes outside the promise is unrestricted. The same finite machine must work for complexes of every size.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the stated machine or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish termination and the exact PL classification on every promised input, without additional unproved hypotheses. A negative answer must establish that every deterministic Turing machine has a promised input on which it either fails to halt with a bit or gives the wrong bit. A lower bound ruling out only polynomial time, a procedure that can return “unknown,” or a classifier proved correct only on a finite census does not settle this target. This is a binary decidability statement with no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
Finite input does not guarantee algorithmic decidability of a global geometric property. The question concerns existence of any always-terminating decision procedure, even one whose resource use is far beyond practical computation.

The PL sphere-recognition problem is decidable through dimension three and undecidable in dimensions at least five. The four-dimensional case is the exceptional gap in the checked account. This card fixes that dimension and promises a manifold rather than asking for manifold recognition itself.

The promise is local: links of vertices have the standard three-sphere type. The output concerns the entire four-dimensional space. Local manifold structure alone does not force the global space to be a sphere.

The topology category matters. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, whereas PL equivalence adds finite piecewise-affine structure. The standard PL sphere cannot be replaced silently by a merely topological sphere.

Pachner’s theorem characterizes PL equivalence of closed triangulated manifolds by finite sequences of bistellar moves, local replacements that preserve PL type. Such finite certificates are useful for individual positive instances. Existence of a certificate does not ensure a recognition procedure terminates on negative instances.

The 2022 computational study explicitly allows an inconclusive outcome. Its successful classifications establish properties of those tested triangulations, without proving that every permitted input will eventually be classified.

The 2026 census work examines closed orientable four-manifolds with at most six four-dimensional simplices. Among triangulations topologically equivalent to the four-sphere, it leaves at most four potentially distinct PL types and conjectures that all are standard. These are unresolved classifications, not a proof that four distinct structures exist.

That census uses generalised triangulations, permitting identifications among faces of a simplex. The card instead uses abstract simplicial complexes with the explicit vertex-set encoding. Neither the finite census limit nor its orientability restriction is added to the benchmark promise.

An algorithm here must reject disconnected promised manifolds as well as connected non-spheres. It must also answer correctly for any PL structures that actually exist, without assuming a conjectural classification of four-manifolds.
why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.
status_note: Joswig’s July 2025 presentation explicitly leaves PL-SPHERE(4) open. The February 2026 census paper treats bounded-size triangulations and retains unresolved PL types, rather than giving an all-input decision procedure. The card retains the approved standard PL sphere and closed combinatorial manifold promise. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no resolution; this is not an independent certification of every historical topological theorem.
progress: 1994–1995: Three-sphere recognition becomes decidable; the checked account identifies dimension four as the remaining gap. | 2022-05-19: The published computational study develops practical sphere-recognition heuristics with potentially inconclusive outcomes. | 2025-07-15: The research presentation explicitly marks PL-SPHERE(4) as open. | 2026-02-25: A larger finite-census classification is published with residual PL-type ambiguities. | 2026-09-16: The individual review retains unrestricted promised-input decidability and checks the scope of the newer census.
working_summary: The input is a finite simplicial complex promised to be a closed combinatorial four-manifold. The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can recognize the standard PL four-sphere on every such input. There is no time bound, but both termination and a correct binary answer are mandatory. Topological equivalence, finite experimental classifications and heuristics that may remain inconclusive do not supply this guarantee. The checked sources retain dimension four as the unresolved boundary in PL sphere recognition.

title: Optimal size of weak \(\varepsilon\)-nets for convex ranges
importance_reason: A foundational extremal problem in discrete geometry, with nonmatching upper and lower bounds already in dimension two and consequences for geometric transversals.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), determine the asymptotic order of \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(d\). Here \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest worst-case number of auxiliary points required to hit every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\).
definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(G_d(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that for each fixed \(d\geq2\) there are \(c_d,C_d,\varepsilon_d>0\) with \(c_dG_d(\varepsilon)\leq f_d(\varepsilon)\leq C_dG_d(\varepsilon)\) whenever \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_d\). Upper bounds must cover all finite configurations; lower bounds must establish configurations requiring the matching order. Constants may depend on dimension but not on accuracy or input size. The exponent alone, bounds missing logarithmic factors, or a solution only for the plane do not characterize the stated family.
context:
Rubin’s paper explicitly identifies the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension at least two as an outstanding problem. The cardinality function above is the source’s extremal target, with its counting, rounding and range conventions made explicit.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.
why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.
status_note: The extremal asymptotic question is open in the checked sources, including the higher-dimensional revision of December 2023. The bounded later-work review on 13 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the stated family. Publication and revision dates are distinguished from the date of this status check.
progress: 2011: Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch establish superlinear lower bounds in every fixed dimension at least two. | 2018: Rubin obtains the first improvement of the longstanding general planar upper bound. | 2023-12: The revised higher-dimensional work supplies further upper-bound improvements; matching growth rates remain undetermined.
working_summary: A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net places auxiliary points so that every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a given point set contains an auxiliary point. The auxiliary points may lie anywhere in the ambient Euclidean space. For each fixed dimension, the task is to determine the smallest worst-case net size as \(\varepsilon\) decreases. The challenge comes from hitting all sufficiently populated convex regions simultaneously, regardless of the original configuration. Sharp bounds would quantify how economically a finite set can represent its large convex subsets.

title: Dürer’s conjecture
importance_reason: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.
formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.
context:
A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.
