The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.
why: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The March 2026 prismatoid paper retains the general existence question; the July overlap construction does not refute it. This card uses its explicit disjoint-facet-interior convention with boundary contacts permitted, without asserting equivalence to a stricter simple-boundary requirement. The bounded source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.
progress: 2001: The problem source records the general convex edge-unfolding question as open and distinguishes known nonconvex obstructions. | 2026-03-23: The revised prismatoid paper retains the general prismatoid and convex edge-unfolding questions while analyzing a restricted subclass. | 2026-07-10: A preprint constructs selected unfoldings with arbitrarily high overlap; it does not show that every unfolding of any convex polytope overlaps.
working_summary: The input is a convex three-dimensional polytope. Its faces may be separated only along original edges. The output sought is one connected planar net. Distinct face interiors must not overlap. Allowing cuts across faces or disconnected pieces gives a different problem.

title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
importance_reason: A central distance-preserving graph compression question, now settled for fixed-minor-free families but still demanding a topology-independent constant in general graphs.
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
definitions: The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_G\) is the minimum path length between its endpoints. Zero-length edges are allowed, so distinct terminals can have distance zero; the displayed inequalities then require their distance in \(H\) to be zero too. To specify precisely the terminal-preserving minor condition, choose pairwise disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\), one for each \(t\in K\), with \(B_t\cap K=\{t\}\). The graph \(H\) is a simple graph on the labeled set \(K\); an edge \(st\) of \(H\) is permitted only if some edge of \(G\) joins \(B_s\) to \(B_t\). Not all such permitted edges have to be kept, and vertices outside the branch sets may be deleted. Thus vertices can be deleted, edges deleted or contracted, and parallel edges or loops removed, but no two terminals are identified and no surviving vertex is a nonterminal. Each edge of \(H\) may receive an arbitrary new nonnegative real length, independent of the original length of an edge witnessing its adjacency. This is a topological minor relation with allowed reweighting, not a requirement that contraction preserve inherited edge lengths. Define \(d_H\) by shortest paths and as infinity for disconnected pairs; the guarantee forces finite terminal distances. Both inequalities must hold simultaneously for all pairs in one chosen minor. The same \(C\) must work independently of the numbers of vertices, edges and terminals, graph topology, edge-length magnitudes and aspect ratio. The target is existential and imposes no construction-time, input-encoding or randomness requirement on a proof of existence.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a universal constant and the required rooted minor for every input in Lean, or prove its negation: for every finite \(C\), some graph and terminal set admit no minor meeting all the inequalities. A family with unbounded necessary distortion is a valid negative answer; a single fixed lower bound on the constant is not. Expected distortion for each pair, additional surviving Steiner vertices, or a guarantee only in a restricted graph class does not settle the statement.
context:
The source describes Steiner point removal for general graphs before solving the version excluding a fixed graph minor. This card retains the general-graph question from the inherited record. The word minor includes terminal identities and permitted edge reweighting, which are made explicit in the branch-set definition.

Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\log k)\) for arbitrary graphs with \(k\) terminals. This bounds the loss in terms of the size of the surviving vertex set, but does not provide a constant independent of that size.

For trees, the source recounts an upper bound of eight and examples with necessary distortion approaching eight. Thus even on trees exact preservation is not generally possible, and a universal positive answer must allow nontrivial distortion.

Chang, Conroy, Le, Milenković, Solomon and Than prove constant distortion for every class excluding a fixed complete graph minor. More specifically, for \(K_r\)-minor-free graphs their Theorem 1.4 gives \(2^{O(r\log r)}\) distortion. This settles the planar case and much more, but the constant depends on the excluded minor and is not uniform over all graphs.

If the minor condition is dropped, the complete graph on the terminals with original shortest-path distances as edge lengths preserves every terminal distance exactly. The scientific constraint is preserving a graph-minor representation while removing every other vertex. Distances alone would give a much easier problem.

Choosing a distribution over minors with a small expected stretch for each pair need not produce a single minor that has small stretch on every pair. Likewise, allowing a few extra vertices changes the compression target. Neither relaxation is silently included here.
why: Steiner point removal asks how much of a network’s geometry and topology can survive when only designated terminals remain. A universal constant would establish a strong form of graph compression; an unbounded lower bound would show that the topology of general graphs forces a growing loss even when edge lengths may be redesigned.
status_note: The checked 2024 source settles fixed-minor-free graphs and records logarithmic distortion for general graphs. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a universal constant for all graphs or a refutation. The solved planar question is not presented as still open.
progress: 2001: Gupta establishes constant-distortion removal on trees, as recounted in the source’s historical overview. | 2018: Filtser gives logarithmic distortion in the terminal count for arbitrary graphs. | 2024: Chang and coauthors settle the fixed-minor-free case, including planar graphs; their constant depends on the excluded minor.
working_summary: Steiner point removal starts with a weighted graph and a designated set of terminals whose mutual distances matter. The goal is to delete the other vertices through graph-minor operations, leaving a graph on exactly those terminals. Its edges may be reweighted, but terminal distances should never shrink and should grow by at most a universal factor. The same guarantee must work regardless of how many terminals the input contains. This asks whether graph topology and useful terminal geometry can both survive an extreme reduction in representation size.

title: Klee’s measure problem
importance_reason: A basic measure-computation problem underlying geometric union and coverage algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge 3\), determine the optimal deterministic worst-case running time, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\), for computing the exact d-dimensional volume of the union of n axis-aligned boxes in the arithmetic real-RAM model below. The dimension may affect constants and the algorithm, but is not an input parameter in this running-time question.
definitions: An input is a list of \(n\ge 0\) closed boxes \(B_{i}=\prod _{j=1}^{d} [a_{i},j,b_{i},j]\), specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with \(a_{i},j\le b_{i},j\). Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of ∪_\(i B_{i}\), returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. The requested precision is a \(\Theta\) bound: logarithmic factors count, and constants may depend on d. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied.
answer_criterion: For each fixed \(d\ge 3\), give a rate \(T_{d}(n)\), an exact algorithm with worst-case time \(O(T_{d}(n))\), and an unconditional lower bound \(\Omega (T_{d}(n))\) for every correct algorithm in the same model. If no single rate is attainable within constant factors, establishing that failure of asymptotic optimality also answers the stated optimal-time request. An improved upper bound alone, a conditional lower bound, a restriction to particular box shapes, or a result only for approximate or dynamic volume does not complete the classification.
context:
Two boxes may cover the same region, so adding their individual volumes overcounts their intersection. In three dimensions, \([0,2]^{3}\) and \([1,3]\times [0,2]^{2}\) each have volume 8, but their union has volume 12. The task requests this single total volume; it does not request a full description of the union boundary. In higher dimensions a box is simply a product of intervals.

Chan’s 2013 algorithm computes the union volume in \(O(n^{d/2})\) time for every fixed \(d\ge 3\). This gives \(n^{3/2}\) in dimension three and \(n^{2}\) in dimension four. The unresolved target is a matching classification of the fastest possible exact computation. The known relationship with clique problems supplies conditional evidence for the exponent, rather than a matching unconditional lower bound for all algorithms.

The real-RAM question counts an arithmetic operation on a coordinate as one step even when the coordinate would require many bits to encode. Chan also obtains logarithmic improvements for integer coordinates in a word-RAM setting. Those improvements do not automatically transfer to unrestricted real inputs, and the source explicitly discusses this distinction. The detailed primitive and worst-case conventions above make the inherited real-RAM target explicit.

The SoCG 2025 work speeds up approximation of union volume and proves a lower bound for algorithms restricted to certain object queries. A small relative error is permitted there. The ICALP 2026 work maintains exact volume under insertions and deletions and measures amortized update time. Both are significant results, but neither determines the unconditional optimal time of a single exact static computation in this card’s model.
why: A basic measure-computation problem underlying geometric union and coverage algorithms.
status_note: The general exact static bound remains \(O(n^{d/2})\) in the checked ICALP 2026 discussion; its optimality evidence is conditional. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching unconditional classification. Approximation, integer word-RAM and dynamic results have different guarantees.
progress: 2013: An exact \(O(n^{d/2})\) static algorithm is obtained for fixed \(d\ge 3\); separate word-RAM improvements use integer-coordinate assumptions. | 2025-06: Faster box-union approximation and a general object-query lower bound are published. | 2026: Exact dynamic data structures achieve near-optimal amortized update bounds under a stated combinatorial clique hypothesis, leaving the present unconditional static classification separate.
working_summary: Klee’s measure problem asks for the volume covered by a union of axis-aligned boxes. Overlapping regions count once, and only the exact total volume is required. For each fixed dimension at least three, the question seeks matching worst-case time bounds in a specified arithmetic real-RAM model. Chan’s general upper bound is \(O(n^{d/2})\), with no matching unconditional classification supplied by the checked later work. Recent approximation and dynamic advances answer different questions.

title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
importance_reason: Determine the complexity of a basic three-dimensional topological recognition problem.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial triangulation of a closed connected piecewise-linear \(3\)-manifold is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the standard \(3\)-sphere?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be the promised encodings below, and let \(S(x)\) assert that the encoded complex is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\). Does there exist one uniform deterministic Turing machine \(M\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists b\in\{0,1\}\
\left[
H_{M}\bigl(x,C(|x|+1)^{d},b\bigr)
\ \land\
\bigl(x\in\mathcal P\ \Rightarrow\ (b=1\Longleftrightarrow S(x))\bigr)
\right]?
\]
Here \(H_{M}(x,t,b)\) means that \(M\) halts within \(t\) transitions with output bit \(b\). The running-time bound holds on every binary string, including malformed encodings and inputs outside the manifold promise; correctness is required on \(\mathcal P\). The machine and both polynomial constants are fixed before the input is chosen.
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex on \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is a collection \(K\) of subsets of \([m]\), closed under taking subsets and containing every singleton. Its elements are simplices; a simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). A tetrahedron is a simplex with four vertices.

An input complex is given by integers \(m\ge4\) and \(N\ge1\), and \(N\) distinct tetrahedra
\(\tau_{j}=\{v_{j1},v_{j2},v_{j3},v_{j4}\}\), where
\[
1\le v_{j1}<v_{j2}<v_{j3}<v_{j4}\le m.
\]
The quadruples are listed in strictly increasing lexicographic order, and every vertex in \([m]\) occurs. Define
\[
K_{x}=\{\sigma\subseteq[m]:\ \sigma\subseteq\tau_{j}
\text{ for some }j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\}.
\]
All lower-dimensional faces are implicit. Thus the listed tetrahedra are exactly the maximal simplices. There are no coordinates, edge lengths or geometric drawings in the input.

Fix a binary encoding as follows. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(b(r)\) be the ordinary binary representation of \(r+1\), with no leading zero, and let \(\ell=|b(r)|\). Encode \(r\) by \(1^{\ell}0b(r)\). The input string is the concatenation of the codes of \(m,N\), followed by the codes of \(v_{11},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14},v_{21},\ldots,v_{N4}\) in that order, with no trailing bits. A syntactically valid string parses uniquely and obeys the preceding inequalities, ordering and vertex-coverage conditions. Set \(L=|x|\), the total number of input bits. Since every vertex occurs, \(m\le4N\); these explicit encodings have length \(O(N\log(N+2))\).

The geometric realization is the polyhedron
\[
|K|=\left\{(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m}:
\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}=1,\ 
\{i:a_{i}>0\}\in K\right\}.
\]
Each abstract simplex is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite geometric simplicial complex is a finite collection of convex hulls of affinely independent finite point sets, containing all their faces, with the intersection of any two simplices empty or a common face. A subdivision of a realization \(|K|\) is such a geometric complex with underlying set \(|K|\), each of whose simplices is contained in an original simplex, and for which every original simplex is the union of simplices of the subdivision. New vertices may be arbitrary real points; they are not additional input data.

Two finite complexes are PL-homeomorphic if they have finite subdivisions whose abstract simplicial complexes are isomorphic. An isomorphism is a bijection of their vertices carrying simplices to simplices in both directions; its affine extension on each simplex supplies the piecewise-linear homeomorphism. There is no required bound on the size of these subdivisions in the definition of the topological property. For \(r\ge1\), \(\Delta^{r}\) is the full simplex on \(r+1\) vertices and \(\partial\Delta^{r}\) consists of all its proper faces. The standard PL \(3\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{4}|\); the standard PL \(2\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{3}|\).

For a vertex \(v\) define its link by
\[
\operatorname{lk}_{K}(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
A link has as its vertex set the union of its simplices; when realizing it, use those vertices as the coordinate indices. The same definitions apply to any finite vertex set by replacing \([m]\) with that set. The promise set \(\mathcal P\) consists of syntactically valid strings such that the graph with vertex set \([m]\) and edges the two-element simplices of \(K_{x}\) is connected, and every vertex link is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{3}\). This is the simplicial formulation of a closed connected PL \(3\)-manifold: finite realization gives compactness, and the spherical-link condition gives the local manifold condition without boundary. No orientation, homology calculation, fundamental-group presentation or certificate of the promise is supplied. Nonorientable manifolds are permitted by the promise. For every binary string \(x\), define \(S(x)\) to be false if \(x\) is not syntactically valid, and otherwise to mean that \(K_{x}\) is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\).

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its tape alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tape cells have nonnegative integer indices and every head initially scans cell zero. The input tape initially holds exactly \(x\) followed by blanks. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at cell zero stays there. The two halting states output zero and one, respectively. Each transition costs one unit, so all parsing and arithmetic are charged at the bit level. The number of tapes, state set and transition table are independent of \(L\). There is no advice, randomness, oracle or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers.

An answer of one is required for every promised triangulation of the standard PL sphere, and an answer of zero for every other promised manifold. For all other binary strings either bit is permitted, but the same uniform polynomial time bound is mandatory. Neither efficient performance on sampled inputs nor an algorithm restricted to a proper subclass of the promised manifolds meets this definition.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including one machine, its uniform polynomial clock on all binary strings and both correctness directions on \(\mathcal P\), or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation.

Explicitly, the negative answer must prove
\[
\forall M\ \forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall d\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}
\]
such that, writing \(t=C(|x|+1)^{d}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(\neg H_{M}(x,t,0)\land\neg H_{M}(x,t,1)\bigr)\\
&\quad\lor\
\left[
x\in\mathcal P\ \land\
\left(
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,1)\land\neg S(x)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,0)\land S(x)\bigr)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every candidate machine and polynomial clock must fail either the total time bound or correctness on a promised input. The witness input may depend on the candidate and clock. A lower bound for one algorithm, a conditional complexity implication, NP or coNP membership, or a proof of decidability alone does not decide this unconditional target.
context:
Schleimer proves that 3-sphere recognition lies in NP: sphere instances have certificates of polynomial length that can be verified in polynomial time. The same source records earlier decision algorithms. These are different guarantees from finding the correct answer deterministically in polynomial time.

The source allows tetrahedra glued by face pairings and deliberately leaves the precise binary format unspecified. This card retains its existing finite simplicial-complex representation and closed connected PL-manifold promise, and now fixes a concrete explicit encoding and bit-cost machine model. Its local-link formulation states that promise precisely.

Zentner proves a conditional negative-certificate result under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. His Theorem 11.2 is stated for integer homology spheres represented by Heegaard diagrams; the 2026 problem list records the resulting coNP status for sphere recognition with the same hypothesis. Such a certificate statement does not imply membership in P.

Lackenby's unconditional theorem concerns certifying that a knot is nontrivial. It must not be substituted for an unconditional coNP theorem for 3-sphere recognition.

The 2026 K3 problem list asks explicitly whether 3-sphere recognition has a polynomial-time algorithm. It also records that such an algorithm would make unknot recognition polynomial-time when the knot is supplied by a diagram.
why: Recognizing the simplest closed three-dimensional manifold is a basic test of whether global topological structure can be determined efficiently from local combinatorial data. A polynomial-time algorithm would also give polynomial-time unknot recognition for diagram input, while separating decidability and short certificates from efficient decision in a central example of computational topology.
status_note: Source-open with a bounded status review through 16 September 2026. K3 (2026), Problem 3.27(b), explicitly asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for 3-sphere recognition. The checked primary sources establish decidability, NP membership, and a coNP result conditional on the generalized Riemann hypothesis, not a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm. No verified resolution was found in the bounded later search. The review checked formulations and the cited statements, not every proof and not a Lean formalization.
progress: 2004-07-05: Schleimer's initial preprint announces NP membership; the final 2011 publication has revised theorem numbering. | 2011: The published paper proves NP membership in Theorem 15.1 and specifies Turing computation and explicit triangulation-size conventions in Section 3. | 2018-02-02: Zentner's fourth arXiv revision includes Theorem 11.2, giving negative certificates under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. | 2026: K3, Problem 3.27(b), explicitly retains the polynomial-time sphere-recognition question; Remark (5) still states the GRH condition for coNP. | 2026-09-16: Checked the source editions and later status, retained the existing promise and score, and specified exact encodings, PL terminology, machine semantics and the full Lean negation.
working_summary: The input is an explicit finite simplicial complex promised to triangulate a closed connected PL three-manifold. The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can recognize the standard three-sphere in time polynomial in the total input bit length. The polynomial bound must hold on all binary inputs, while correct answers are required on the promised manifold inputs. Sphere recognition is decidable and has polynomially verifiable positive certificates, with the checked negative-certificate result depending on the generalized Riemann hypothesis. The 2026 K3 problem list retains the polynomial-time question, whose resolution would also affect the complexity of unknot recognition.

title: General unfolding of nonconvex polyhedra
importance_reason: A central longstanding question in geometric folding, explicitly highlighted by Demaine as a major open problem. It has a simple global existence target, substantial positive and negative results around its boundary, and a direct conceptual connection to producing three-dimensional surfaces from flat material.
formal:
Does every closed embedded polyhedral surface in \(\mathbb R^3\), including nonconvex surfaces, admit a general nonoverlapping unfolding into one connected planar piece?

Precisely, for every compact connected polyhedral two-dimensional manifold \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) without boundary, do there exist a finite union \(C\) of straight segments on its surface and a continuous injective map
\[f:P\setminus C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2\]
such that \(P\setminus C\) is connected and \(f\) is a rigid Euclidean placement on each triangle of a finite subdivision of the surface away from the cuts?

Cuts may cross original faces. They have zero width, no area of the surface is discarded, and the whole uncut surface must remain connected. Coincidence between copies of cut-boundary points in the planar closure is allowed; overlap between distinct uncut surface points is not. No restriction to genus zero is imposed.
question_excerpt: TOPP Problem 43 asks whether every closed polyhedron can be cut on its surface and flattened into a single planar piece without overlap. Its distinction between general, edge and vertex unfoldings is retained. The finite-cut model is made explicit from the foundational paper, with the boundary-contact convention of the cited orthogonal-unfolding work.
definitions:
The input is a compact connected surface \(P\) embedded in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. It is the union of finitely many closed nondegenerate straight triangles whose intersections are common edges, common vertices or empty. Each edge belongs to exactly two triangles, and every point of the union has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open disk. The latter condition excludes singular pinched vertices and surfaces connected only at isolated points. Thus \(P\) is a closed polyhedral two-manifold, not a solid volume. Its triangulation is a representation of the surface, rather than a restriction on where cuts may lie.

Coordinates are arbitrary real numbers. Neither convexity nor general position is required. The surface may have handles of any finite genus; genus zero means homeomorphic to a sphere. Faces of an original polygonal description may be subdivided into triangles without changing the geometric surface. Self-intersecting surfaces, overlapping copies of faces and surfaces with an existing boundary are outside this embedded closed-surface model.

A cut set \(C\) is a finite union of closed straight line segments contained in \(P\), with each segment lying in a planar face or triangle after subdividing at any face crossings. Intersections and endpoints of the segments can be added as subdivision vertices. The segments need not be original edges, need not lie on a prescribed grid and may have arbitrary real endpoints. There is no uniform upper bound on their number or on the fineness of a subdivision. Curved cuts with infinitely many bends and infinitely many cuts are not allowed.

The surface is cut along \(C\) by separating its two sides wherever present. Its uncut part is \(P\setminus C\); this set must be nonempty and connected in the surface topology. Because it is an open subset of a two-manifold, this requires genuine surface connectivity. It does not allow two otherwise separate pieces to be joined only at one vertex. The finite cut graph has area zero, so all two-dimensional material remains. Boundary copies of cut points are recovered by taking limits from each side.

A precise finite description of a flattening consists of a subdivision \(K\) of the surface triangulation, with every cut a union of edges of \(K\), and one affine Euclidean isometry \(g_\tau\) from the supporting plane of each triangle \(\tau\in K\) into \(\mathbb R^2\). For every \(x\in\tau\setminus C\), set \(f(x)=g_\tau(x)\). Whenever a point lies on two or more triangles and is not cut, these assignments must agree. The resulting map on \(P\setminus C\) must be continuous and injective. Reflections of individual triangle coordinate frames are permitted in specifying the placements; continuity and injectivity enforce a consistent planar surface across uncut adjacencies.

Being an isometry on each triangle means exactly preserving Euclidean distances within that triangle, and hence its lengths, angles and area. The assembled map preserves the lengths of surface paths. It is not required to preserve the three-dimensional straight-line distance between points in different faces. Nor is the intrinsic distance in a nonconvex planar piece generally the straight-line distance through its missing regions.

Nonoverlap is expressed by injectivity on \(P\setminus C\). Interiors cannot cover one another; two distinct uncut points cannot coincide even if each lies on an uncut triangulation edge. Distinct copies of points along the cuts may touch in the closure of the planar image. Such boundary contacts are not gluing operations and do not establish connectivity that the uncut surface lacks. This is the usual boundary-contact convention explicitly used by Damian, Flatland and O’Rourke. Requiring a positive clearance between every pair of boundary portions would impose a stronger condition.

The planar piece may be nonconvex and may have slits or holes. No additional simple-polygon requirement is imposed beyond the connected nonoverlapping flattening just defined; the foundational paper explicitly discusses this distinction. No disconnected dissection followed by rearrangement or new gluing is allowed. The finite subdivision merely expresses the original surface and the cuts; it does not permit stretching, shrinking, removing positive-area strips or covering a portion of the original surface twice.

The quantifiers are \(\forall P\;\exists C,K,(g_\tau)_{\tau\in K}\), subject to the stated geometric conditions. This is an exact existence question. There is no running-time, coordinate bit-length, bounding-box size, minimum strip width or approximation target. Only the final flattened configuration is required: a continuous collision-free physical motion from the original shape to that configuration is a separate question.

An edge unfolding restricts cuts to the original edges of the given polyhedral description. A general unfolding, the target here, permits additional cuts through faces. A vertex unfolding permits pieces to be connected only at vertices and therefore uses a weaker connectivity requirement. Neither the impossibility of an edge unfolding nor the existence of a vertex unfolding decides the general-unfolding question.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal existence statement for the specified closed embedded polyhedral surfaces. A positive proof must establish finite surface cuts, a connected uncut surface and a compatible collection of exact rigid planar triangle placements whose assembled map is injective on the entire uncut surface. No efficient construction or collision-free unfolding motion is required. A negative proof must give a valid surface in this model and show that every finite permitted cut set and every compatible planar placement fail the connectivity or nonoverlap requirement. Ruling out only original-edge cuts, a particular algorithm or a bounded number of cuts is insufficient. Results for convex surfaces alone, overlapping flattenings, disconnected pieces, or surfaces that already have boundary do not settle the target. A numerical mesh picture or approximate nonoverlap check does not replace the complete proof.
context:
The surface of a three-dimensional object can be fabricated from flat material by cutting a planar pattern and joining its boundary as prescribed. The question asks whether arbitrary surface cuts always suffice to produce one connected pattern, even when the desired object is nonconvex. It isolates a geometric existence obstruction before manufacturing constraints or algorithmic efficiency are considered.

Convex polyhedra have general nonoverlapping unfoldings. Nonconvex polyhedra can fail to have any edge unfolding, but this does not answer the present question because new cuts can run through faces. Bern and coauthors give a nonconvex example for which those additional cuts make a difference.

Bern and coauthors also construct a polyhedral surface with boundary that cannot be generally unfolded. This shows why “closed” is an essential input condition. Their discussion of cuts distinguishes connected planar pieces from the extra convention that the result must be a simple polygon.

Damian, Flatland and O’Rourke prove general unfoldability for every genus-zero orthogonal polyhedron, whose edges are parallel to three coordinate axes. Their construction can require very thin strips. TOPP’s abbreviated statement of this progress omits genus zero; the cited theorem does not justify removing that restriction.

The official description of Demaine’s Spring 2025 MIT lecture explicitly retains general unfolding of boundaryless polyhedra as an open question. This is a later dated statement of the same broad geometric problem, rather than a new theorem.

The December 2025 two-step refolding theorem concerns common unfoldings that may overlap in the plane. Its introduction and first footnote state that convention explicitly. Consequently the result does not establish a nonoverlapping general unfolding as required here.

General unfolding and convex edge unfolding ask for different extensions of a known convex result: one expands the permitted input shapes, while the other restricts the allowed cuts. The distinction makes nonconvex edge counterexamples relevant context without turning them into solutions of this card.
why: This asks whether nonconvex geometry can obstruct every possible connected planar net even when cuts are unrestricted within faces. Resolving it would identify a fundamental limit of cutting and flattening polyhedral surfaces, and distinguish geometric impossibility from the shortcomings of particular meshing or fabrication algorithms.
status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 43 (history through 24 July 2008) and explicitly listed as open in the official description of Demaine’s Spring 2025 MIT Lecture 16. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the foundational finite-cut model, boundary contact and the genus-zero restriction of the orthogonal result. It also checked the published December 2025 refolding paper, whose overlap-allowing definition does not resolve this question. Bounded later-work searches and the authors’ book-update pages revealed no resolution of the specified nonoverlapping target. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review; it is not an exhaustive current-status certification or an independent proof audit of every background theorem.
progress: 1987–1997: The source records general nonoverlapping unfolding results for convex polyhedra, including the source and star unfoldings. | 2003: Bern and coauthors exhibit nonconvex edge-ununfoldable polyhedra and show that crossing faces can enable a general unfolding; they also prove an obstruction for a surface with boundary. | 2007: A general unfolding is proved for every genus-zero orthogonal polyhedron, with potentially very fine subdivisions and thin strips. | Spring 2025: Demaine’s official MIT lecture description explicitly lists the boundaryless general-unfolding problem as open. | December 2025: The two-step refolding theorem uses possibly overlapping unfoldings. It therefore leaves the nonoverlap requirement in this card unproved.
working_summary: A general unfolding cuts a polyhedral surface along finitely many segments, including segments through faces. The goal is one connected planar piece with no overlap of its uncut surface. The question asks whether every closed embedded polyhedral surface admits such an unfolding, including nonconvex surfaces and surfaces with handles. Convex surfaces and genus-zero orthogonal polyhedra have positive results, while restrictions to original edges or inputs with boundary have counterexamples. A 2025 refolding theorem permits overlap and therefore does not settle this nonoverlapping existence question.

title: Optimal input-sparsity subspace embeddings
importance_reason: This is the precise optimal dimension-versus-sparsity conjecture for oblivious subspace embeddings, a central primitive in fast numerical linear algebra. Resolving the remaining growing factors while preserving failure-probability dependence would identify the attainable compression and application-cost frontier for an extensive class of matrix algorithms.
formal: Is the optimal-dimension sparse oblivious subspace-embedding conjecture true? Precisely, does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that for every pair of integers \(n\ge d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\), there are an integer \(m\) and a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) over real \(m\times n\) matrices with \[1\le m\le\left\lceil C\,\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil,\qquad s=\left\lceil C\,\frac{\log(d/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\] such that every matrix in the support has at most \(s\) nonzero entries per column and, for every \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pr_{\Pi\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\ \forall x\in W:\ (1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|\Pi x\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\ \bigr]\ge1-\delta?\] The row and column-sparsity bounds must hold simultaneously, with no additional growing factors.
definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.
context:
Woodruff’s survey, in the discussion after Theorem 10, records the proposed row bound \(O((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)\) and input-sparsity application cost involving \(\log(d/\delta)/\varepsilon\). The original title-level card omitted the concrete parameters.

Conjecture 2 of the 2025 ICALP paper states the underlying distributional question explicitly in terms of row dimension and nonzeros per column. This supplies the precise formulation used here, without imposing a particular embedding construction.

The 2025 result reaches optimal row dimension with sparsity \(\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)\) in its stated parameter regime, where that notation hides growing polylogarithmic factors. It therefore does not give the exact logarithmic sparsity bound required here.

The SODA 2026 paper improves the remaining losses to sub-polylogarithmic factors in \(d\) for inverse-polynomially bounded \(\varepsilon\), with a polynomially small failure probability in its headline theorem. Its more detailed Theorem 2.1 gives explicit dimension/sparsity tradeoffs. Neither statement removes all extra factors in the full parameter range of this card.

The preserved norm guarantee concerns one entire fixed subspace. An embedding for selected vectors alone or one constructed using the particular matrix is a different object from an oblivious subspace embedding.
why: Subspace embeddings compress a matrix’s column space while preserving the lengths of all its linear combinations. Small output dimension reduces later computation, and sparse embedding columns reduce the arithmetic needed to apply the map to sparse data. The conjecture asks whether these two advantages can be attained together at the stated dependence on accuracy and failure probability.
status_note: The checked ICALP 2025 and SODA 2026 sources retain the exact dimension/sparsity conjecture. The SODA improvement has sub-polylogarithmic losses and stated parameter restrictions, so it does not settle the all-parameter target here. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-15 found no exact resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-status certification.

title: Simultaneous embedding with fixed edges for two graphs
importance_reason: A central simultaneous graph-drawing problem about making overlapping structures geometrically consistent.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given any two finite simple planar graphs \(G_{1}=(V,E_{1})\) and \(G_{2}=(V,E_{2})\) on the same labeled vertex set, decides in polynomial time whether they admit planar topological drawings that coincide on every shared vertex and every shared edge?
definitions: The input gives \(n\ge 0, V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), and two symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is \(H=(V,E_{1}\cap E_{2})\), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points \(p(v)\in \mathbb{R} ^{2}\) to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints \(p(u),p(v)\), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same \(p(v)\) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in \(E_{1}\cap E_{2}\). Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) with at most \(C(N+1)^{c}\) bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.
context:
Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

Take \(G_{1}\) to be \(K_{5}\) with one edge deleted and \(G_{2}\) to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. \(G_{1}\) is planar, and \(G_{2}\) can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to \(G_{1}\). This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph \(K_{5}\). Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.
why: A central simultaneous graph-drawing problem about making overlapping structures geometrically consistent.
status_note: The general two-graph problem is explicitly open in the checked ISAAC 2025 and JGAA 2025 sources. The March 2026 path result concerns geometric optimization. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this topological decision problem; proofs were not independently audited.

working_summary: Two planar graphs share labeled vertices and possibly some edges. The question asks whether the existence of compatible planar drawings can be decided in polynomial time. Each shared vertex and edge must look identical in both drawings, while edges exclusive to different graphs may cross. The case with connected common graph is known to be efficiently solvable. The remaining target covers arbitrary common graphs and is distinct from straight-line or three-graph variants.

title: Euclidean minimum spanning tree complexity
importance_reason: A foundational geometric optimization problem with a linear-size answer but an implicit quadratic edge set, tied to bichromatic closest-pair complexity in higher fixed dimensions.
formal: For each fixed integer \(d\geq3\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic worst-case time for computing an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of \(n\geq2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\). The input is the array of coordinates of the points \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\); the output is a list of \(n-1\) pairs of indices forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) that minimizes \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\) over all spanning trees on these labels. Include logarithmic factors in the requested complexity, and use the real-arithmetic model below.
definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n)\) for every fixed \(d\geq3\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of matching uniform upper and lower bounds. For each \(d\), one correct deterministic program must have worst-case time at most \(C_dg_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Every correct program must have worst-case time at least \(c_{A,d}g_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(c_{A,d}>0\). The constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\) and, for the lower bound, on the program. An approximation scheme, an expected-time bound alone, or the polynomial exponent without matching logarithmic factors does not determine this target.
context:
The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. This card makes its resource question concrete by requesting optimal deterministic arithmetic complexity in every fixed dimension at least three. This is an editorial sharpening of the source’s informal word “close,” not an assertion that the source prescribed a particular logarithmic overhead.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.
why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.
status_note: The original exact-complexity gap is source-backed. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the specified deterministic fixed-dimensional family. The 1991 randomized results are dated partial progress, not asserted to be current deterministic records.

working_summary: A Euclidean minimum spanning tree connects the input points with minimum total edge length. The input gives coordinates, while the complete graph of candidate edges is implicit. The card asks for the optimal deterministic arithmetic running time in every fixed dimension at least three. Exact computation must be distinguished from approximation and from algorithms with predictions or random-input promises. A resolution would determine how much low-dimensional geometry can reduce the cost of this basic connectivity problem.

title: Exact planar Euclidean matching
importance_reason: A longstanding gap for a fundamental geometric pairing problem, connecting exact weighted matching with the algorithmic value of low-dimensional coordinates.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors including logarithmic factors, the optimal deterministic worst-case running time for computing a minimum-length perfect matching of \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for all integers \(n\geq1\), in the exact real-arithmetic model below. The output is a list of \(n\) unordered pairs of input indices, every index occurring exactly once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\) among all perfect matchings. The input consists only of the point coordinates; the complete graph is implicit.
definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(g:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds in the stated model. The upper bound must give one uniform deterministic algorithm with worst-case time at most \(C g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The lower bound must show that every correct uniform algorithm has worst-case time at least \(c_A g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), where \(c_A>0\) and the threshold may depend on the algorithm. Constants are independent of the point configuration and \(n\). Approximate matchings, a bound only for bipartite matching, or a polynomial exponent with unresolved logarithmic factors do not meet this criterion.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for the optimal complexity of exact Euclidean matching in the plane and mentions the bipartite problem separately. This card retains the unrestricted objective and makes the deterministic arithmetic and worst-case conventions explicit.

A matching contains only a linear number of edges, but the coordinate input describes quadratically many possible pairs. Its objective is the sum of their Euclidean lengths; replacing lengths by squared lengths can change the minimizing matching.

Varadarajan proves an \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) exact algorithm. The separator subroutine in the author manuscript has a deterministic implementation, so this is an upper bound for the deterministic target rather than merely an expected randomized bound.

Hougardy and Tammemaa’s April 2026 journal article still identifies Varadarajan’s bound as the fastest known exact algorithm. Their new results improve fast approximation guarantees and do not compute the exact optimum.

The same article recalls an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for deterministic geometric approximation algorithms with approximation ratio depending only on input size. Thus the exact task has a substantial known gap even before finer logarithmic factors are considered.

The arithmetic convention matters because the objective involves square roots and comparisons between sums of lengths. Counting each such arithmetic step is different from bounding the number of bit operations needed to certify every comparison for rationally encoded points. The requested output here is an optimal pairing, not a decimal expansion of its total length.
why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.
status_note: The exact complexity gap is explicitly present in the checked April 2026 article. The bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The real-arithmetic model is an explicit editorial specification of the geometric task; bit complexity and approximation are separate targets.

working_summary: Given an even number of planar points, a perfect matching pairs every point with exactly one other point. The Euclidean objective minimizes the sum of the lengths of all chosen segments. The question is the optimal complexity of computing that minimum exactly, with bipartite matching as a related restricted variant. Approximation algorithms can exploit geometry differently and do not by themselves settle the exact problem. Sharper algorithms would improve a central geometric pairing primitive whose implicit complete graph contains quadratically many candidate edges.

title: Flip graph connectivity in three dimensions
importance_reason: A longstanding central problem in computational geometry and triangulation theory, with direct relevance to local mesh transformations and a sharp distinction between geometric and abstract complexes. The simple local moves conceal a global connectivity question that remains unsettled beyond regular triangulations.
formal:
For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with \(|P|\ge4\) and no four points coplanar, is the graph of all geometric tetrahedralizations of \(P\) connected under \(2\leftrightarrow3\) bistellar flips?

A tetrahedralization must use exactly the vertices \(P\), consist of straight, nondegenerate tetrahedra meeting along common faces, and cover \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). A legal flip replaces two tetrahedra filling a convex triangular bipyramid by the three tetrahedra with the same five vertices and the same union, or performs the reverse replacement. Every intermediate tetrahedralization must retain all points of \(P\) as vertices.

Equivalently, for every such \(P\) and every pair \(T,T'\) of its tetrahedralizations, must there exist a finite sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m=T'\) in which each consecutive pair differs by one legal flip?
question_excerpt: TOPP Problem 28 asks whether tetrahedralizations of a general-position point set in three-dimensional space form a connected graph when adjacency is restricted to replacing two tetrahedra by three, or three by two. The source specifies general position as having no four coplanar points and distinguishes results that permit vertex insertion or deletion.
definitions:
The set \(P\) is finite and consists of distinct points with arbitrary real coordinates in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. General position here means that every four distinct points are affinely independent, equivalently that no four lie in a common plane. Together with \(|P|\ge4\), this ensures a three-dimensional convex hull and nonzero volume for every tetrahedron with four vertices in \(P\). Points may lie in the interior of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\); they are not assumed to be in convex position. No additional condition on cospherical points is imposed.

For a finite set of points \(A\), its convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is the set of all convex combinations of points of \(A\), with \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). A geometric tetrahedron with vertex set \(A\subset P\), \(|A|=4\), is the closed set \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\). Its faces are the convex hulls of subsets of its vertices, including vertices, edges, triangles, the tetrahedron itself and the empty face.

A tetrahedralization is a collection \(T\) of four-element subsets of \(P\) satisfying all of the following conditions. Every point of \(P\) belongs to some member of \(T\). The union of the corresponding closed tetrahedra is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). For every \(A,B\in T\),
\[\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B)=\operatorname{conv}(A\cap B).\]
Thus different tetrahedra have disjoint interiors and any intersection is their common face; overlaps, crossing faces and hanging vertices inside another tetrahedron are excluded. All faces of the tetrahedra are understood to belong to the resulting simplicial complex. This is a full geometric triangulation, not merely an abstract complex homeomorphic to a ball. No extra vertices, curved faces or gaps in the convex hull are allowed.

The local replacement can be specified by five distinct points \(a,b,c,d,e\in P\). They must all be vertices of their convex hull, and that hull must be the convex triangular bipyramid formed by the two tetrahedra \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and \(\{a,b,c,e\}\) sharing triangle \(abc\). In particular, \(d\) and \(e\) are on opposite sides of the plane of \(a,b,c\). Write
\[U_2=\bigl\{\{a,b,c,d\},\{a,b,c,e\}\bigr\},\qquad U_3=\bigl\{\{a,b,d,e\},\{b,c,d,e\},\{c,a,d,e\}\bigr\}.\]
These are the two tetrahedralizations of this bipyramid: \(U_2\) uses the interior triangle \(abc\), while \(U_3\) uses the interior edge \(de\). A \(2\)-to-\(3\) flip is allowed when \(U_2\subseteq T\) and
\[T'=(T\setminus U_2)\cup U_3\]
is a tetrahedralization of the same \(P\), with the replaced tetrahedra and the new tetrahedra having exactly the same geometric union. A \(3\)-to-\(2\) flip is the inverse operation under the same conditions. Requiring both configurations to be valid tetrahedralizations makes the local move compatible with all tetrahedra outside the replaced region.

The flip graph \(\mathcal F(P)\) is the finite undirected graph whose vertices are these tetrahedralizations and whose edges join pairs related by one such flip. Reversing a legal move is legal. Connectivity means that every pair of graph vertices can be joined by a finite path. The path may have length zero when the two tetrahedralizations coincide. No polynomial bound, sharp diameter, monotonicity condition or prescribed target triangulation is part of the proposition.

Only \(2\)-to-\(3\) and \(3\)-to-\(2\) moves are permitted. A \(1\)-to-\(4\) move inserts an interior vertex into a tetrahedron, and a \(4\)-to-\(1\) move removes a vertex; neither is allowed, even if the point is restored later. Points cannot be moved or perturbed along a path. Allowing such operations changes the graph under study.

The quantifier order is \(\forall P\;\forall T,T'\;\exists m\ge0\;\exists(T_i)_{i=0}^m\). All tetrahedralizations and all intermediate coordinates refer to the same fixed geometric point set. A negative answer consists of a set meeting the general-position hypothesis and two valid tetrahedralizations in different components, with a proof that no finite legal path joins them. Merely showing that one particular greedy rule gets stuck, or displaying an abstract nonrealizable tetrahedral complex, is insufficient.

Regular tetrahedralizations are a special class mentioned in the known results. A tetrahedralization \(T\) is regular if there is a height assignment \(w:P\to\mathbb R\) such that, for each \(A\in T\), an affine function \(\ell_A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) equals \(w\) on the four points of \(A\) and is strictly below \(w\) at every point of \(P\setminus A\). These are the tetrahedralizations obtained by projecting the simplicial lower hull of the lifted points. The target includes nonregular tetrahedralizations as well. It is an exact geometric existence question; there is no coordinate encoding, running-time or approximation tolerance to optimize.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of connectivity for every finite point set in the stated general position. A positive proof must establish a finite legal \(2\leftrightarrow3\) path between every pair of full geometric tetrahedralizations, with all intermediate complexes using the same point coordinates and vertex set. No efficient path-finding algorithm or polynomial path length is required. A negative proof must establish the general position and geometric validity of a counterexample and prove that two tetrahedralizations lie in different components of its full flip graph. A result only for regular triangulations, higher-dimensional point sets, abstract complexes, or paths that remove or add vertices does not settle the target. Numerical experiments and approximate coordinate pictures alone are insufficient.
context:
A tetrahedral mesh can be changed locally while leaving its boundary and vertex coordinates fixed. Connectivity asks whether these basic local changes can in principle reach every mesh of the same point set, or whether the space of meshes splits into inaccessible regions.

For planar point sets, diagonal flips connect all triangulations. This is an important structural basis for local triangulation algorithms. The analogous conclusion in three dimensions does not follow just from the existence of tetrahedralizations or from the planar argument.

For regular triangulations with a fixed vertex set, Pournin and Liebling prove connectivity by paths that preserve faces common to the two endpoints. TOPP explicitly notes that in the three-dimensional general-position setting this uses the required two-to-three and three-to-two moves. The unrestricted question is whether nonregular tetrahedralizations can also be connected within the full graph.

There are disconnected triangulation spaces in higher dimensions, and TOPP records nonrealizable abstract tetrahedral complexes with no allowed flips. These show why dimensional and geometric-realizability hypotheses matter, but neither gives a counterexample for the three-dimensional point sets in this question.

Wagner and Welzl’s 2022 paper proves stronger connectivity results in the plane and explicitly says in its introduction that connectivity remains open in dimensions three and four. It also carefully distinguishes full triangulations, which retain all points, from partial triangulations that may omit interior points.

A positive answer would establish reachability by the permitted local moves, rather than a running-time guarantee for a mesh optimization heuristic. Even a connected graph can have long routes, and connectivity does not ensure that an objective improves on every move.
why: This is a basic reachability question for three-dimensional meshes: can local bistellar moves explore every tetrahedralization without changing the underlying points? A resolution would identify a fundamental difference, or an essential commonality, between planar triangulation algorithms and their three-dimensional counterparts.

On 16 September 2026 the source’s fixed-vertex move restriction, the 2007 regular-triangulation consequence and the 2022 discussion were checked. The regular result was checked through its publisher abstract and the TOPP statement, not by independent verification of its full proof.
