working_summary: A tetrahedralization divides the convex hull of a fixed three-dimensional point set into tetrahedra. A local flip replaces two tetrahedra by three, or reverses that replacement, while retaining the same five vertices. The question asks whether every pair of tetrahedralizations can be joined by such moves when no four input points are coplanar. All intermediate meshes must keep every original point as a vertex at its original coordinates. Regular tetrahedralizations are known to be connected, but the unrestricted geometric question remains open in the checked sources.

title: NP certificates for homeomorphism of three-manifolds
importance_reason: A major unresolved verification bound for topological classification in dimension three, beyond decidability and the recognition of specific manifold classes.
formal: Does homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds, have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) of total encoded length \(N\), \[H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;V(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the NP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem below.
definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed existence of \(p,V\) with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer needs completeness for every homeomorphic promised pair and soundness against every candidate witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair, with polynomial worst-case verification time in \(N+|w|\). The verifier need not find the witness. A negative answer must exclude all polynomially bounded certificate systems in this model, not merely certificates made from a particular type of topological transformation. A result restricted to a fixed manifold, orientable closed manifolds, or one geometric class does not settle the full domain.
context:
Schleimer’s Question 3 asks whether Homeo(3) lies in NP. His standing domain is compact connected manifolds supplied by triangulations. The boundary, orientation and binary-verifier conventions above make that domain explicit.

Two very different tetrahedron lists can describe the same space. A positive certificate must establish equality of the represented topological types, rather than just exhibit a relabelling of the supplied pieces. Its form is unrestricted; the polynomial bound concerns the entire witness and its verification.

Kuperberg proves an elementary-recursive decision algorithm for closed oriented 3-manifolds: the running time has a fixed-height exponential-tower bound. This establishes a quantitative decidability result in that setting, not polynomial certificates for the broader domain.

Jackson proves NP recognition for compact orientable Seifert fibered spaces with nonempty boundary, together with NP and coNP certification for their naming problem. The paper explicitly asks about general homeomorphism, which its special-class results do not decide.

NP verification concerns yes instances. It does not imply a polynomial-time method for constructing a homeomorphism, nor provide short certificates when the manifolds differ. The latter is the separate coNP question.

The 2025 seminar report asks a related fixed-parameter tractability question measured by the treewidth of the input triangulations. A parameter-dependent algorithm with no global polynomial bound would not by itself resolve this certificate question.
why: Short certificates would separate the cost of discovering topological equivalence from the cost of checking it. An NP upper bound would place a fundamental classification problem within the standard theory of efficient verification.
status_note: The NP question is explicit in the 2024 report and Jackson’s 2024/2025 article. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no general certificate theorem. The stated target retains the source’s broad compact connected domain; closed-oriented and Seifert results are limited to their published hypotheses.
progress: 2019: Kuperberg establishes elementary-recursive decidability for the closed oriented setting. | 2024-02: Schleimer states the general NP question as Question 3. | 2024-06-20: Jackson’s first online publication proves NP recognition for Seifert fibered spaces with boundary; the journal volume is dated 2025.
working_summary: Two triangulations can describe the same three-dimensional manifold while looking combinatorially unrelated. This question asks whether every homeomorphic pair has a certificate whose size and verification time are polynomial in the input. Such a certificate need not be found efficiently by the verifier itself. The challenge is to encode the necessary topological equivalence without an excessively long sequence of transformations. An NP upper bound would distinguish the difficulty of discovering a homeomorphism from the difficulty of checking convincing evidence that one exists.

title: Minimum-weight triangulation in NP
importance_reason: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.
formal: Does the following language belong to NP? An instance consists of a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb{Q} ^{2}\) of explicitly given points and a rational bound B; it is a yes instance exactly when S has a triangulation whose total Euclidean edge length, counting every edge once, is at most B.
definitions: The input lists \(n\ge 0\) distinct points \((x_{i},y_{i})\), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight \(\mathrm{W}(T)=\sum _{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\sqrt{(x_{i}- x_{j})^{2}+(y_{i}- y_{j})^{2}}\). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality \(\mathrm{W}(T)=B\) is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if \(V(x,y)\) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.
context:
A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points \((0,0), (1,0), (0,1)\) have a single triangular boundary of total length \(2+\sqrt{2}\). A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.
why: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.
status_note: The original theorem establishes NP-hardness, not NP membership. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established membership or nonmembership resolution for this exact Euclidean decision problem. The checked 2025 source confirms the related radical-comparison gap but is not itself a triangulation-status theorem.
progress: 2008: Strong NP-hardness is proved, while NP membership for exact Euclidean costs remains explicitly unresolved. | 2018: Practical exact methods scale to very large tested point sets. | 2025: A later primary paper still records the unresolved NP placement of the related square-root-sum comparison problem.
working_summary: The input gives rational planar points and a rational limit on the total length of a triangulation. Every input point must be used, no extra points may be added, and Euclidean edge lengths are compared exactly. The question asks whether every feasible instance has a short certificate that can be checked in polynomial bit time. NP-hardness is known, but the sum of potentially irrational edge lengths prevents the usual edge-list argument from establishing NP membership. Practical exact solutions and rounded-cost variants do not settle the certificate question for arbitrary exact inputs.

title: Exact planar Euclidean maximum TSP
importance_reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem that distinguishes dimension, norm and bit complexity within a canonical tour problem. The gap between approximation and exact optimization gives it significance beyond one special geometric algorithm.
formal:
Is there a deterministic algorithm that finds an exactly longest Euclidean tour through any finite set of rational points in the plane in time polynomial in the full binary input length?

For an explicitly listed set \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^2\), with \(n\ge3\), define the length of a cyclic ordering \(\pi\) by
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(x_{\pi(i)}-x_{\pi(i+1)})^2+(y_{\pi(i)}-y_{\pi(i+1)})^2},\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(a\ge0\) such that, on every valid input of bit length \(B\), the machine returns a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\]
within \(C(B+1)^a\) bit operations?
question_excerpt: TOPP Problem 49 asks for the complexity of finding a maximum-Euclidean-length tour through a planar point set. It records approximation algorithms, easier polyhedral distances, hardness in three dimensions and the arithmetic issue caused by square roots. The user selected the narrower yes/no target of a deterministic polynomial bit-time algorithm returning an exact optimal tour from rational coordinates.
definitions:
The input is a finite list of coordinates \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\). Each coordinate is a signed binary integer numerator divided by a positive binary integer denominator. Use a fixed self-delimiting encoding of these integers and the list. The bit length \(B\) counts all numerators, denominators and delimiters, as well as the number of points. The coordinates may have arbitrarily many bits. There is no bound on their magnitude, denominators, aspect ratio or minimum separation beyond what the finite input specifies. Equivalent ordinary binary encodings change polynomial time only by polynomial factors.

The points are pairwise distinct. Collinear triples, an entirely collinear set and other degeneracies are allowed. No general-position or convex-position promise is imposed. The algorithm must work for all \(n\ge3\). A machine may reject malformed encodings, repeated points or lists shorter than three; this validation must also take polynomial time. These validity conventions do not permit rejecting any valid instance because its coordinates are numerically difficult.

The symbol \(S_n\) denotes the set of all permutations of the point indices. A tour visits every input point exactly once in that order and then returns to its starting point. Its edges are the straight segments between consecutive points, and its total length is the sum of their ordinary Euclidean lengths. Every pair of points is an available connection. There is no separate graph of allowed edges, and there are no obstacles.

The word “planar” restricts the locations of the points to two-dimensional Euclidean space. It imposes no noncrossing requirement on the tour. Segments may intersect, overlap on collinear inputs or pass through other points; the visits in the tour are specified by its permutation. Cyclic rotations and reversals represent the same undirected cycle, but the output may be any representing permutation. If several tours attain the maximum, any one is acceptable.

The output is the explicit list of \(n\) indices in a maximizing order. It need not include the optimum length, an approximation to that length, a square-root expression or a certificate independently checking optimality. Its size is polynomial in \(B\). Exactness refers to maximizing the real-valued sum in the statement, even though the output itself is a finite combinatorial object.

Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite alphabet and finite program. The constants \(C,a\) are fixed for the entire algorithm, independent of the input length, coordinates and arrangement. All arithmetic, storage, comparisons and output operations are charged by their bit cost. An operation involving arbitrarily large integers or algebraic numbers is not a unit-time primitive. The machine has no exact-real arithmetic oracle and no oracle comparing sums of square roots. Randomized algorithms, advice depending on input length and machines whose polynomial exponent depends on the input do not satisfy this definition.

Each squared edge length is rational, but its square root can be irrational. Distinct tours can also have equal total lengths. A proposed algorithm must justify any precision or exact arithmetic it uses within its polynomial bit bound. A polynomial bound on the number of real-arithmetic operations alone does not provide that justification. Conversely, returning an optimal permutation is not defined to include solving every separate comparison problem for arbitrary sums of square roots.

The objective is the sum of all edge lengths. It differs from minimum-length TSP, from finding a longest spanning path without the closing edge, and from maximum scatter TSP, which maximizes the shortest edge in the tour. Replacing Euclidean distance by squared Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance or a polygonal norm also changes the optimization problem.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme supplies, for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a tour of length at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(P)\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\). Its polynomial exponent or constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This does not give exact optimization by simply choosing an unspecified tiny error: the separation between unequal tour lengths and the resulting computation cost would both need proof.

The original source asks broadly for the complexity of finding a maximum tour and mentions a conjecture of NP-hardness. This card selects, with the user's approval, the specific existence question for a polynomial bit-time exact-tour algorithm on rational planar inputs. NP-hardness means that a polynomial-time reduction would make this optimization task at least as hard as every problem in NP, with the reduction and output access specified. Such a theorem can establish a conditional obstruction under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); NP-hardness alone does not prove the unconditional nonexistence quantified here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm in the statement, including correctness on every valid input, handling of exact ties and a polynomial bound in the full bit length. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A negative answer must quantify over every deterministic machine and every fixed polynomial bound. An approximation scheme, a real-arithmetic algorithm without a bit-cost analysis, a result only for a restricted point configuration or a three-dimensional hardness theorem does not settle this target. A planar NP-hardness reduction is substantial progress but gives an unconditional negative answer only together with a proved premise sufficient to rule out the algorithm. There is no additive or multiplicative tolerance: the returned permutation must attain the exact maximum.
context:
Maximizing a tour rewards long connections while requiring all selected edges to form one cycle. Geometry can make some versions unusually structured, but that structure depends on the distance function. This problem asks whether ordinary straight-line distance in two dimensions still permits an exact efficient optimization algorithm.

A longest tour is allowed to cross itself. Restricting the output to a simple polygon would discard valid candidates and could change the optimum. The 2025 work on noncrossing longest structures constructs particular point sets and studies their extremal geometry; it does not give a general optimization algorithm.

Polynomial-time approximation schemes were established for fixed-dimensional normed spaces, including Euclidean distance. They provide arbitrarily good fixed relative accuracy. The exact question retains the need to distinguish tours whose lengths may be extremely close.

Barvinok and coauthors prove polynomial-time exact solvability for fixed polyhedral norms and Euclidean NP-hardness in dimensions at least three. Their rational-input discussion accounts for bit costs in the polyhedral case. Neither result transfers directly to the Euclidean plane.

The arithmetic issue is separate from the number of candidate permutations. Even checking whether a specified tour exceeds a rational length threshold involves a sum of square roots. The present output is a permutation, so the card makes no unsupported equivalence between finding that permutation and every possible square-root comparison problem.

The comparison matters beyond this one tour objective: it isolates how changing only a norm or a dimension can alter the known complexity of an optimization problem. A positive answer would expose algorithmic structure special to the plane; a negative answer would delimit that structure despite the availability of close approximations.
why: This is a sharply focused boundary in geometric optimization: nearby versions are tractable under polygonal norms or hard in higher Euclidean dimension, while accurate approximation is available. Settling exact planar optimization would clarify how the geometry of a distance function and the arithmetic of exact lengths affect efficient computation.
status_note: TOPP Problem 49, revised 1 August 2003, presents the planar Euclidean problem as open. The 2003 JACM author manuscript, especially §1 and Conjecture 30, distinguishes planar Euclidean optimization from the solved polyhedral and hard higher-dimensional variants and notes the exact-arithmetic issue. The 2025 paper Noncrossing Longest Paths and Cycles still explicitly describes planar MaxTSP complexity as unknown. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no verified algorithm or unconditional negative answer for the user-selected rational-input exact-tour bit model. The narrower target and stronger arithmetic precision are stated explicitly; this is a source assessment, not an exhaustive status certification or a new Lean proof.
progress: 1996: Barvinok gives a polynomial-time approximation scheme for longest tours in fixed-dimensional normed spaces. This is an approximation result, not an exact-tour algorithm in the bit model selected here. | 2003: Barvinok and coauthors prove exact polynomial-time solvability for fixed polyhedral norms and NP-hardness for Euclidean dimension at least three. Conjecture 30 asks for planar Euclidean NP-hardness. | 2025: The introduction of Noncrossing Longest Paths and Cycles still describes the complexity of planar MaxTSP as unknown. Its results concern specially constructed point sets and the crossing behavior of their longest structures.
working_summary: The problem asks for an exactly longest closed Euclidean tour through rational points in the plane. The output is an ordering of all points, and edge crossings are allowed. One deterministic algorithm must run in time polynomial in the full binary length of all coordinates. Approximation schemes and exact algorithms for polygonal norms do not settle this Euclidean bit-complexity question. A resolution would clarify how the choice of geometry and exact arithmetic affects optimization complexity.

title: Output-sensitive convex hull complexity
importance_reason: A fundamental input/output tradeoff in higher-dimensional geometry; it asks whether the work needed to find a hull can be matched to its actual facial complexity.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq4\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic output-sensitive running time for constructing the convex hull of \(n\geq d+1\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in general position, as a function of \(n\) and the actual number \(f\) of hull facets. The coordinate array is the input. Output the complete facial structure of the hull, as specified below. The required complexity must cover every realizable pair \((n,f)\), including small hulls, and retain logarithmic factors.
definitions: General position means every subset of at most \(d+1\) input points is affinely independent. The convex hull is \(H=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Its proper nonempty faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes; a facet has dimension \(d-1\). The promise makes \(H\) full-dimensional and simplicial, with exactly \(d\) vertices per facet. Output each proper nonempty face by its set of input-vertex indices and list every containment incidence between faces of consecutive dimensions; also identify the facets. The total output size is \(O_d(f)\). Interior input points need not be output. Let \(\mathcal D_d\) be the pairs \((n,f)\) realized by a valid input, and let \(T_A(n,f)\) be the supremum of algorithm \(A\)’s steps over all such inputs with exactly these parameters. One finite deterministic program per fixed \(d\) must work for all \(n\); it is given neither \(f\) nor advice. The model has exact real registers with rational program constants and indexed memory; \(+,-,\times,/\), comparisons, copies and memory accesses cost one each. Integer indices and counters have \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits at time \(t\), with ordinary word arithmetic and comparisons charged. No floor, extraction of real digits, or free geometric query is available. Reading input and reporting faces are charged. Coordinates have no bounded-precision promise, and no randomization or input distribution is used.
answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n,f)\) on each domain \(\mathcal D_d\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds. For each fixed \(d\geq4\), give one uniform algorithm \(A_d\) with \(T_{A_d}(n,f)\leq C_dg_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). For every correct algorithm \(A\), prove \(T_A(n,f)\geq c_{A,d}g_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). Positive constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\), and in the lower bound on \(A\), but not on the feasible pair. A worst-case bound in \(n\) alone, listing only extreme vertices, or resolving only dimensions two and three is insufficient.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for the best output-sensitive hull algorithm. The general-position convention used here is explicit in Chan’s cited primary paper. Without it, a facet can contain many vertices, and the number of facets alone need not measure the amount of output.

Output sensitivity accounts for what the particular input produces. Many points may lie inside a hull with few facets, so a bound based solely on the largest possible hull of an equally large point set can greatly exceed the size of the actual result.

Chan’s 1996 theorem gives \(O_d(n\log f+(nf)^{1-1/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)}\log^{O_d(1)}n)\) time. The paper contrasts this with the \(\Omega_d(n\log f+f)\) lower bound and explains the range of small outputs where its upper bound is optimal. These are dated results, not a claim that every intervening bound has been exhaustively surveyed.

The same paper distinguishes the hull’s full facial structure from the task of finding only its extreme points, and records optimal \(O(n\log f)\) algorithms in dimensions two and three. In dimension four there are also stronger specialized bounds than a literal use of the general-dimensional expression.

The ESA 2025 work on universal optimality concerns planar hulls and additionally reports certificates for interior points. It addresses a refined form of input sensitivity but does not settle the higher-dimensional two-parameter target here.

The fixed dimension is allowed to affect constants; the input size and output size are not. General position is a substantive source assumption, not a license to perturb a degenerate input while pretending its output size remains unchanged.
why: Sharp output-sensitive hull bounds would connect the work of discovering a geometric boundary to its actual combinatorial size. This matters for hull construction, polyhedral representations and geometric computations whose input contains many nonextreme points.
status_note: The complexity question is open in the primary source and problem entry. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for the stated higher-dimensional family. The displayed general-dimensional bound is attributed to 1996 rather than presented as a verified current record.
progress: 1996: Chan obtains output-sensitive upper bounds in every fixed dimension under general position. | 2001: The Open Problems Project records the unresolved optimal output-sensitive complexity. | 2025: The ESA paper establishes a refined planar universal-optimality result, for a different dimensional and output setting.
working_summary: An output-sensitive convex hull algorithm charges for both its input points and the facets it actually produces. The question asks for the best such running time for point sets in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space. Small hulls should be cheaper than the worst-case hull complexity would suggest. The difficult target is to reconcile reading the input, identifying extreme structure, and listing the output with nearly optimal overhead. Progress would improve geometric optimization whenever many input points contribute little to the final convex boundary.

title: Earth mover distance sketching complexity
importance_reason: A central compression problem for optimal transport, with a consequential unresolved constant-approximation/polylogarithmic-space regime and a full information-versus-accuracy tradeoff.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the minimum sketch length \(s(n,c)\) for approximating planar earth mover distance for every integer \(n\geq2\) and real approximation factor \(c\geq1\). Inputs are subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]^2\) of equal cardinality, with unit mass at each occupied grid point, and \[\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)=\min_{\pi:A\to B\ \mathrm{bijection}}\sum_{a\in A}\|a-\pi(a)\|_1.\] Each set must be encoded independently using the same public randomness. From the two \(s\)-bit encodings the decoder must return \(\widehat d\) satisfying \(\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\leq\widehat d\leq c\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every fixed pair.
definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_1=|x-u|+|y-v|\); grid spacing and point mass are both one. Empty sets are allowed and their distance is zero. There are no repeated points, arbitrary real weights or bounds on cardinality beyond \(|A|=|B|\leq n^2\). A length-\(s\) scheme for parameters \((n,c)\) is a probability space of public seeds \(R\), encoders \(L_R:2^{[n]^2}\to\{0,1\}^s\), and decoders \(D_R:\{0,1\}^s\times\{0,1\}^s\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\), with all relevant events measurable. The estimate is \(D_R(L_R(A),L_R(B))\). The seed is independent of the inputs and available to both encoders and the decoder. Seed length and local computation are unrestricted and not charged; this is information-theoretic sketch length in bits, not streaming update time or the dimension of a real vector. The decoder knows \(n,c,R\), but receives no input-dependent information beyond the two sketches; any stored cardinality is charged. The same encoder works for both inputs. Success is required for each fixed pair chosen independently of \(R\), not simultaneously for all pairs under one seed or against adaptive exposure of the seed. When \(A=B\), success requires estimate zero. Define \(s(n,c)\) as the least integer \(s\geq0\) admitting such a scheme; it is finite because the entire \(n^2\)-bit incidence vector can be stored. The displayed interval fixes the usual one-sided multiplicative convention explicitly; it is not an additive-error guarantee.
answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g(n,c)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \(a g(n,c)\leq s(n,c)\leq b g(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\) and every \(c\geq1\). The upper bound must supply schemes with the stated probability and bit length; the lower bound must cover all allowed, possibly nonlinear, public-coin schemes. Constants and \(n_0\) cannot depend on \(c\), so varying approximation regimes and logarithmic factors must be accounted for. A single upper bound, a linear-embedding lower bound alone, or the answer for only one fixed approximation factor does not determine the requested tradeoff.
context:
Indyk’s 2011 question asks for the sketch-length/approximation tradeoff and highlights the possibility of constant \(c\) with \(s=\operatorname{polylog}n\). The card retains that full tradeoff and specifies the grid, masses, randomness and approximation convention.

A sketch must be computed without seeing the other set. The decoder then estimates one transport cost from two compressed descriptions. A fast algorithm that reads both complete inputs can exploit information that the sketch decoder does not have.

Andoni, Do Ba, Indyk and Woodruff prove that, for any fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), a sketch of polynomially sublinear grid-size dependence can obtain approximation \(O(1/\varepsilon)\). Their Theorem 1.1 uses \(O(n^\varepsilon)\) integer coordinates of polynomial magnitude; for sets this converts to \(O(n^\varepsilon\log n)\) bits. Thus constant-factor approximation is possible with more than polylogarithmic space in the stated construction.

Andoni, Krauthgamer and Razenshteyn prove that the full planar transportation norm cannot have both constant approximation and constant-size distance-threshold sketches. That norm allows general signed real mass vectors; the theorem neither identifies this subset-only bit tradeoff nor rules out polylogarithmic sketches.

The published STOC 2026 lower bound of Gartland and Ostrovskii closes the planar \(L_1\)-distortion gap for transportation cost spaces at order \(\log n\). An embedding theorem is not a theorem about every arbitrary decoder of two finite sketches, so this result does not automatically resolve the present question.

The number of grid locations and the number of occupied points are different parameters. Here the grid side length is the parameter and every equal-size pair is covered. Likewise, replacing the one-unit point masses by arbitrary weighted distributions would enlarge the input family.
why: EMD sketching asks how much information must be retained to compare geometric mass distributions without keeping the original data. Sharp tradeoffs would clarify the limits of metric compression and the distinction between embeddings, sketches and full-input transport algorithms.
status_note: The full tradeoff and highlighted constant-approximation/polylogarithmic-size question are open in the 2011 source. The bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for this exact subset and public-coin model. Full transportation-norm and L₁-distortion results have been checked separately and do not by themselves certify a resolution.
progress: 2009: Theorem 1.1 provides sublinear-size sketches with constant approximation when its parameter is fixed. | 2011: Indyk records the tradeoff question and specifically asks for constant approximation with polylogarithmic bit length. | 2015–2017: Sketching/embedding equivalences imply nonconstant resources for the full transportation norm, with a different input domain and threshold task. | 2026-06-09: The planar L₁-distortion gap is closed in the STOC publication; this is not a general sketch-decoder lower bound.
working_summary: Each planar grid subset must be compressed independently before the other input is available. The decoder uses the two bit strings to estimate the minimum Manhattan-cost matching of equal-size sets. The target is the optimal tradeoff between sketch length and multiplicative approximation, with constant success probability for every fixed pair. Known embedding and full transportation-norm results do not automatically characterize arbitrary decoders for these subset sketches. Sharp bounds would establish how much information optimal-transport comparisons must retain.

title: Counting simple polygonalizations
importance_reason: A longstanding and repeatedly studied counting problem in computational geometry, with recent progress on subexponential algorithms and enumeration but no settled polynomial-time classification. It tests the algorithmic power of noncrossing geometry in a broadly recognizable family rather than optimizing one construction.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite planar point set \(S\subset\mathbb Q^2\) in binary rational coordinates, outputs the exact number \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) of simple polygonalizations of \(S\)?

A simple polygonalization is a non-self-intersecting closed polygonal curve that visits every point of \(S\) exactly once and joins consecutive points by straight segments. Two cyclic orders count as the same polygonalization precisely when one is obtained from the other by changing the starting point or reversing the traversal. Collinear points are allowed, but crossings, overlapping edges and contacts between nonadjacent edges are forbidden.

The running time must be polynomial in the total binary input length, including the coordinate encodings, and the output count is written in binary.
question_excerpt: TOPP Problem 16 asks whether the number of simple polygonalizations of a planar point set can be computed in polynomial time, defining a polygonalization as a simple polygon with exactly the given vertices. The card retains that exact-counting existence question and spells out binary rational input, collinearities and the removal of cyclic-order multiplicities.
definitions:
The input is a finite list \(S=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb Q^2\). Each rational coordinate is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator in binary, in lowest terms, using a fixed self-delimiting encoding. Let \(N\) be the total length in bits of the encoded list, including the coordinates, signs, delimiters and list length. Input order supplies labels for describing cyclic orders; it does not change the answer. The exact bit model makes the source’s polynomial-time question explicit rather than treating arbitrary-precision arithmetic as a unit-cost operation.

For \(n\ge3\), choose a permutation \((i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its edges are the closed segments
\[e_j=[p_{i_j},p_{i_{j+1}}],\qquad j=0,\ldots,n-1,\]
where indices are read modulo \(n\). Each edge must have no point of \(S\) in its relative interior. Two adjacent edges must intersect in exactly their common endpoint. Two nonadjacent edges must be disjoint. These conditions say that the cyclic polygonal curve is simple: it is an embedded circle made of line segments. In particular, edges cannot cross, overlap along a segment, or touch a nonincident vertex.

Three successive vertices may be collinear if the path proceeds straight through the middle vertex. Such an input point is still counted as a vertex even though its interior angle is \(\pi\). Reversing direction along an already traversed segment is forbidden by the intersection conditions. No general-position promise is imposed, and an arbitrary perturbation that changes collinearities would change the input counting problem.

A polygonalization uses every point and no additional vertices. Its region need not be convex, and its boundary need not be monotone in any direction. There is no prescribed graph of allowed edges, no obstacle polygon, no additional forbidden region and no weight or length objective. Admissibility depends only on the geometry of the given points and the straight segments selected between them.

Cyclic permutations of a valid order and reversal of that order describe one unoriented polygonalization. Distinct geometric edge sets on the fixed point set are counted separately, even if a symmetry of the point set maps one to another. For example, one can count each polygon exactly once using the representative with \(i_0=1\) and \(i_1<i_{n-1}\). These conventions remove the \(2n\)-fold starting-point and orientation multiplicity; they do not quotient by translations, rotations or reflections of the input configuration.

Define \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) as the number of valid equivalence classes of cyclic orders. For \(n<3\), set \(\operatorname{poly}(S)=0\). A set with all points on one line also has count zero. For \(n\ge3\), the elementary bound
\[0\le\operatorname{poly}(S)\le (n-1)!/2\]
shows that the binary count has \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, despite potentially having many polygonalizations. The target is the count for each input set, not the maximum or minimum number over all \(n\)-point sets.

The computational model is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite description, ordinary bit operations and no oracle or advice. All input parsing, exact geometric predicates, integer arithmetic and output writing are charged to the running time. The requested quantifiers are
\[\exists A\;\exists a\ge1\;\exists k\in\mathbb N\;\forall S:\quad A(S)=\operatorname{poly}(S),\qquad \operatorname{time}_A(S)\le a(N+1)^k.\]
The constants and exponent are independent of the number, positions and encoding lengths of the points. The machine may return zero on malformed inputs; it can check the encoding and pairwise distinctness in polynomial time. There is no restriction on workspace beyond that implied by the time bound.

The task requires the exact integer count in binary. An estimate with bounded relative error, an approximation to the logarithm of the count, or a random polygon is a different computational task. This card asks a yes-or-no question about existence of an exact-counting algorithm, rather than asking the solver for a numerical value of a single instance or an unrestricted approximation to a function.

Writing down every polygonalization may require exponentially many symbols. An enumeration algorithm whose time is polynomial in that whole output length therefore need not run in time polynomial in \(N\), even though the binary count is short. Likewise, generating one simple polygon or listing only a particular geometric subclass does not compute the required count.

For complexity context, \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of integer-valued functions counting accepting branches of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines. A canonical cyclic order is a polynomial-size witness here, and its segment-intersection conditions can be verified exactly in polynomial bit time, placing the count in this class. \(\mathrm{FP}\) denotes functions computable by a deterministic polynomial-time machine. A conditional hardness theorem would describe consequences of a polynomial algorithm; it would not by itself refute the algorithm’s existence without proving the relevant separation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time exact-counting algorithm. A positive answer must establish correctness for every encoded finite rational point set, including collinearities and zero-count cases, and a single polynomial bound that includes arithmetic and output costs. A negative answer must prove that no such machine and polynomial bound exist. A #P-hardness result conditional on an unproved complexity separation is progress but does not by itself supply that unconditional refutation. A polynomial-time approximation, output-polynomial enumeration, a result only for general-position or convex-position sets, or a lower bound for one particular counting algorithm does not satisfy the full target.
context:
Finding one noncrossing polygon through a point set and counting all such polygons are different tasks. The latter asks whether a geometric restriction on Hamiltonian cycles permits efficient exact counting despite the large number of possible cyclic orders.

Marx and Miltzow give a subexponential algorithm for counting noncrossing Hamilton cycles on point sets in general position. Their Theorem 6 states a running time of \(n^{O(\sqrt{n})}\). This is substantial progress but is not a polynomial-time bound, and their stated general-position hypothesis must be retained.

The same paper gives a sharper constant in the exponent for counting triangulations. The TOPP progress paragraph compresses these statements too aggressively: this card does not attribute the triangulation constant to every graph family, nor does it treat a triangulation count as a polygonalization count.

Eppstein proves that all polygonalizations can be listed in time polynomial in the input size and the total output size, even when the input has collinearities. An exponential number of polygons still permits an exponential running time under that guarantee.

Eppstein’s polynomial-time estimates concern the logarithm of the number of polygonalizations. Such an estimate can allow a large multiplicative uncertainty in the count itself. The paper’s conclusion retains both stronger approximate counting and the #P-completeness question as open.

For points in convex position there is only one polygonalization, while other configurations have exponentially many. The difficulty lies in determining the exact count for arbitrary inputs, not in the bit length needed to write the resulting integer.

Uniform random generation on a fixed point set is a closely related theme in the source. Heuristic generation or a distribution that favors some polygons is not a counting algorithm, and no unconditional equivalence with the exact counting target is asserted here.
why: This is a basic exact-counting question for a geometric family of Hamiltonian cycles. A resolution would clarify whether planarity of the drawing and freedom to choose its edges make counting fundamentally easier than familiar hard graph-counting problems, and would separate compact numerical output from exhaustive geometric enumeration.
status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 16, revised 18 June 2025, and retained as unresolved counting complexity in Eppstein, Algorithmica 86 (2024), introduction and §6. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the 2016 published extended abstract’s general-position assumption and Hamilton-cycle theorem, and the full 2024 article’s enumeration model and counting discussion. Bounded 2025–2026 searches found no polynomial exact-counting algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem for this target. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review, not an exhaustive current-status certification; the omitted full-version proofs behind the 2016 extended abstract were not independently audited.
progress: 2001–2003: The original TOPP entry poses polynomial-time counting and records related monotone-polygon and random-generation work. | 2016: Marx and Miltzow obtain \(n^{O(\sqrt{n})}\)-time counting for noncrossing Hamilton cycles under their general-position assumption. | 2023–2024: Eppstein obtains output-polynomial enumeration, including degenerate point sets, and polynomial-time estimates for the logarithm of the count. The published conclusion still asks about exact counting hardness. | 18 June 2025: The revised TOPP entry retains the polynomial-time counting question as open while adding the subexponential result.
working_summary: A simple polygonalization connects all points of a planar set into one noncrossing closed polygon. The question asks whether its exact number can be computed in deterministic polynomial time from binary rational coordinates. Starting-point changes and reverse traversals count as the same polygon, and collinear input points are allowed. Subexponential counting in general position and output-polynomial enumeration are known, but neither gives a polynomial-time exact count for every input. The problem tests whether geometric noncrossing structure can make a large family of Hamiltonian cycles efficiently countable.

title: Near-quadratic Voronoi complexity of lines in three dimensions
importance_reason: This is a central unresolved complexity gap for a fundamental three-dimensional proximity structure, closely connected to lower-envelope and arrangement bounds.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that every regular Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\ge2\) distinct affine lines in \(\mathbb R^3\), under the exact stratum convention below, has total complexity at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\)?
definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.
context:
At each point of space, the nearest-line set describes which sites compete to be closest. Regions with one nearest line, interfaces with two, curves with three, and isolated points with four form the strata counted here. A stratum can have several connected components, and unbounded components count as well. Counting just the input lines would omit this geometric arrangement.

The question concerns Euclidean distance to complete affine lines in three dimensions. The source records a quadratic lower bound and an upper bound of \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), leaving a full exponent gap. A nearest-point diagram, a planar diagram, or a polyhedral distance function is a different object.

The conjectured guarantee is \(n^{2+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with a constant allowed to depend on that exponent slack. It does not require a single \(Cn^2\) bound. Conversely, a bound with one fixed exponent strictly above two does not meet the universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).

The source also distinguishes the full diagram from a fixed-distance level set, describable through a union of cylinders. Complexity controlled at one distance does not automatically count all strata of the nearest-site partition throughout space.

The March 2026 four-line classification describes a base case with zero through eight Voronoi vertices under general-position assumptions. The result clarifies local configurations, but fixes the number of sites and supplies no asymptotic bound for arbitrary input size.

The August 2026 regulus preprint claims quadratic total complexity when all lines lie in one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric: one of the two line families covering that surface. Its hypotheses strongly restrict the line configuration. It explicitly retains the broader quadratic-to-cubic gap for arbitrary Euclidean line sites. The present card spells out its own regular-stratum convention rather than leaving “general position” undefined.
why: This is a central unresolved complexity gap for a fundamental three-dimensional proximity structure, closely connected to lower-envelope and arrangement bounds.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The August 2026 regulus preprint still records the general quadratic-to-cubic gap; its quadratic theorem and the March four-line classification are restricted results. This benchmark retains the explicitly defined regular-stratum interpretation from the preceding individual development, without claiming that every source uses identical degeneracy conventions. No matching resolution was located; new proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2001: The problem source records the near-quadratic conjecture and the gap to the known general upper bound. | 2026-03-20: A preprint classifies general-position four-line diagrams; the cardinality is fixed. | 2026-08-27: A preprint claims quadratic complexity for one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric, while retaining the unrestricted gap.
working_summary: Each point in three-dimensional space has a set of nearest input lines. Connected regions with the same nearest-line set form the diagram’s cells. The question counts cells of all dimensions. The proposed bound is arbitrarily close to quadratic. The Euclidean metric and the specified nondegeneracy convention are essential parts of this formulation.

title: coNP certificates for three-manifold homeomorphism
importance_reason: A broad certificate question for distinguishing topological types, with a consequential implication for graph nonisomorphism via the known many-one reduction.
formal: Does nonhomeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Allow boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) with total input length \(N\), \[\neg H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;W(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the coNP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem.
definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(p,W\) exist, or that none exist. A positive answer needs a short accepted witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair and rejection of every candidate witness for every homeomorphic promised pair. Verification time must be polynomial in \(N+|w|\) on every binary input. A particular invariant that distinguishes only some pairs is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out all polynomial certificate systems, rather than showing the inadequacy of one invariant or representation. Conditional upper bounds qualify only if the additional hypothesis is also proved.
context:
Schleimer states this as Question 4, separately from NP membership and NP-hardness. Its quantifiers run over nonhomeomorphic pairs; changing the sign of the target changes which instances need certificates.

Different triangulations can share many familiar invariants without being homeomorphic. The card does not prescribe an invariant: an accepted certificate system may use any finite evidence, but it must be complete for every pair in the full domain.

Lackenby gives a polynomial-time many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Consequently a coNP certificate system for the domain here would also provide polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism. The implication runs from a manifold upper bound to a graph upper bound.

Jackson’s naming theorem provides both NP and coNP certificates within the compact orientable Seifert setting with nonempty boundary. These two-sided certificates apply to the specified naming problem, not arbitrary pairs of triangulated 3-manifolds.

A decidability theorem guarantees that a search eventually terminates. It does not bound the size of evidence for a negative answer by a polynomial. Similarly, an NP system for homeomorphic pairs supplies no general witness for the opposite answer.

If homeomorphism were both NP-hard under the valid-output reductions defined in the related hardness card and in coNP, then \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). This is a logical consequence of the two prospective results, not a proof that either is false.
why: The question asks whether topological difference always has efficiently checkable finite evidence. Its reduction from graph isomorphism ties the difficulty of distinguishing 3-manifolds to a central unresolved certificate problem in complexity theory.
status_note: The general coNP question is explicitly open in the 2024 report. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no general result meeting these unconditional quantifiers. Special Seifert naming certificates do not establish the full target.
progress: 2017: Lackenby proves the graph-isomorphism reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. | 2024-02: Schleimer poses the coNP question and discusses its connection to graph isomorphism. | 2024-06-20: Jackson proves two-sided certificates for a Seifert naming problem with boundary.
working_summary: The homeomorphism problem asks whether two triangulations represent the same three-dimensional space. This card asks for short certificates precisely when those spaces are not homeomorphic. Every nonhomeomorphic pair must have verifiable evidence, including pairs that agree on familiar invariants. A general positive result would imply polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism through a known reduction. It would clarify whether topological distinction has a uniformly efficient theory of verification.

title: Point location in three-dimensional subdivisions
importance_reason: A central static spatial-search problem asking whether linear representation size can coexist with logarithmic exact navigation in arbitrary three-dimensional subdivisions.
formal: Do there exist uniform deterministic preprocessing and query algorithms that, for every explicitly represented polyhedral subdivision of a three-dimensional box of total boundary complexity \(n\), store \(O(n)\) words and answer every point-location query in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time? A query gives an arbitrary point \(q\in\mathbb R^3\) and must return the label of a subdivision region whose closure contains \(q\), or the exterior label for points outside the box. Constants are universal, the guarantee is exact, and the subdivision may have nonconvex regions.
definitions: The input includes a bounded axis-aligned box \(B\) with nonempty interior, real coordinates of vertices, an embedded finite triangle mesh containing \(\partial B\), and the labels of the two incident regions of every triangle (one label is the exterior on \(\partial B\)). Nondegenerate closed triangles meet only in a common whole edge, a common vertex, or not at all. The input is promised to describe the boundaries of a partition: bounded regions are closures of the connected components of \(\operatorname{int}(B)\) minus the mesh, with disjoint interiors and no unrepresented boundary; the exterior region is \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(B)\). Arbitrary topology and collinear or coplanar incidences consistent with these conditions are allowed. Bounded regions have distinct labels \(1,\ldots,r\), with \(r\leq n\), and the exterior has label zero. All vertex coordinates, triangle vertex-index triples and incident labels are explicitly listed. Define \(n\) as their total number of real-coordinate and integer-index entries, including the box. Thus complicated polygon boundaries are charged through their triangulated representation. Any incident region is acceptable for a query on a shared face, edge or vertex, including the exterior on \(\partial B\). The algorithms are finite deterministic programs independent of the input, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each real \(+,-,\times,/\) operation on its domain, comparison, copy or memory access costs one step. Each stored word contains one real or one integer; query-stage integer words have \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged. Floor and digit extraction from reals, size-dependent advice and free geometric oracles are excluded. Storage includes the input retained for queries and temporary query workspace. Preprocessing must halt on every valid input but has no prescribed time or temporary-space bound; only the final stored structure and each query have the stated bounds.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such algorithms, or refute it, with a complete Lean-checked proof. Existence requires constants \(C_s,C_q\) and one pair of uniform algorithms such that every valid subdivision yields a structure of at most \(C_s n\) words and every query is answered correctly within \(C_q\log_2(n+2)\) steps. Refutation must exclude all such pairs in the defined model. Expected performance, a query-distribution promise, linear storage with slower queries, or logarithmic queries with superlinear storage do not establish the positive statement.
context:
The Open Problems Project asks for linear space and logarithmic point-location queries in a three-dimensional subdivision. Snoeyink’s 2017 handbook version states the question for a subdivision with a linear number of faces and vertices. This card makes the total boundary representation explicit; it does not count an arbitrarily complicated polygonal face as a constant-size input.

The source asks for a data structure: one preprocessing stage must support arbitrary later queries without knowing them in advance. Checking membership in every region can save storage but loses the logarithmic query requirement.

The 2017 handbook reports \(O(n\log n)\) space and \(O(\log^2 n)\) query time for general three-dimensional subdivisions, with \(O(n\log n)\) preprocessing. Its Section 38.6 then explicitly lists achieving both target bounds as open.

The same section distinguishes point membership in a single convex polyhedron and subdivisions into axis-aligned boxes, where stronger bounds are known. An algorithm restricted to those objects does not handle the arbitrary oblique subdivision boundaries in this card.

A boundary convention is necessary for exact inputs: a query may fall on a face shared by several regions. Returning any incident label avoids making the answer undefined while preserving the search task. No average over query positions or perturbation promise is used.

The target measures words and exact arithmetic operations. The finite representation and word operations prevent treating a real constant as a free oracle encoding answers to all queries; no claim about bounded coordinate bit lengths is implicit in the statement.
why: Point location is a basic spatial-search operation. Resolving the simultaneous storage and query bounds would establish whether arbitrary three-dimensional partitions admit the same asymptotic search economy as planar subdivisions.
status_note: The checked 2017 handbook explicitly retains the joint bound as open. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no resolution for the general subdivision model. The triangulated total-complexity representation and deterministic arithmetic conventions are explicit editorial specifications, rather than hidden assumptions about arbitrary face sizes.
progress: 2001: The Open Problems Project records the simultaneous linear-space/logarithmic-query target. | 2017-08-10: The third-edition handbook retains the problem and distinguishes known general bounds from convex and orthogonal special cases.
working_summary: A three-dimensional subdivision divides space into labelled polyhedral regions. After preprocessing the boundary representation, a query asks for the region containing an arbitrary supplied point. The target is simultaneous linear storage and logarithmic worst-case query time, measured in the total representation size. Queries on boundaries may return any incident region, and neither random queries nor convex cells are assumed. A resolution would determine whether arbitrary spatial partitions can support exact search as economically as planar ones.

title: Efficient constant-distortion cut-cone approximation
importance_reason: A uniformly tractable constant-distortion outer approximation would improve a central geometric relaxation for cut optimization and clarify the algorithmic limits of finite metric embeddings.
formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(C\ge1\), a family of closed convex cones
\[
K_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\qquad(n\ge2),
\]
and one uniform deterministic algorithm for exact membership and strong separation, as defined below, satisfying both
\[
\mathrm{CUT}_n\subseteq K_n\subseteq\mathrm{MET}_n
\]
and
\[
\forall d\in K_n\quad\exists\rho\in\mathrm{CUT}_n
\quad\forall\,1\le i<j\le n,\qquad
d_{ij}\le\rho_{ij}\le C\,d_{ij}?
\]
The constant \(C\) is independent of \(n\) and \(d\). The membership/separation algorithm must run in polynomial bit time for every rational query point, with a single polynomial bound independent of \(n\).
question_excerpt: The source asks for a computationally tractable convex cone approximating the cut cone with a constant loss in metric distortion. The user chose exact membership and separation on rational inputs with polynomial bit complexity.
definitions:
Write \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Coordinates of a vector \(d\in\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\) are indexed by unordered pairs \(\{i,j\}\). Extend it by \(d_{ji}=d_{ij}\) and \(d_{ii}=0\). The semimetric cone is
\[
\mathrm{MET}_n=\{d:d_{ij}\ge0,\quad d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}
\text{ for all }i,j,k\in V_n\}.
\]
Distinct vertices may have zero distance. This convention includes the zero vector and degenerate cut metrics.

For every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V_n\), let \((\delta_S)_{ij}=1\) when exactly one of \(i,j\) belongs to \(S\), and zero otherwise. The cut cone is
\[
\mathrm{CUT}_n=
\left\{\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V_n}\lambda_S\delta_S:
\lambda_S\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\right\}.
\]
The sum is finite. Equivalently these are the pairwise distances of finite configurations in a real \(\ell_1\) space: \(\rho_{ij}=\|v_i-v_j\|_1=\sum_t |(v_i)_t-(v_j)_t|\), with no fixed restriction on the finite dimension.

A closed convex cone contains zero, is closed under nonnegative linear combinations, and is closed in the Euclidean topology. The coordinatewise inequalities in the question define multiplicative distortion after choosing an overall scale for the \(\ell_1\) distances. They also require \(\rho_{ij}=0\) whenever \(d_{ij}=0\). No algorithm for producing \(\rho\) or its cut coefficients is required.

The algorithm receives \(n\) and every coordinate of \(d\in\mathbb Q^{\binom n2}\), each represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator in binary. Let \(L\) be the total bit length, including the parameter and delimiters in a fixed unambiguous encoding. The query may be outside \(\mathrm{MET}_n\). In at most \(B(L+1)^k\) Turing-machine steps, for constants \(B>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\), the algorithm must do exactly one of the following:

- If \(d\in K_n\), output the membership verdict IN.
- If \(d\notin K_n\), output a rational vector \(a\) such that \(\langle a,d\rangle<0\) and \(\langle a,z\rangle\ge0\) for every real \(z\in K_n\).

Here \(\langle a,z\rangle=\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}z_{ij}\). The output coordinates use the same binary rational convention, and writing them is included in the running time. The latter output is an exact separating hyperplane through the origin, appropriate for a cone. There is no precision parameter or permitted indeterminate boundary answer. The algorithm is uniform over \(n\), receives no advice and has no extra oracle. The cones need not have polynomially many defining inequalities or a prescribed semidefinite representation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence assertion. A positive answer must define the cones and the single algorithm, prove exact membership/separation and its bit-time bound, and prove the uniform distortion bound for all real semimetrics in every cone. A negative answer must rule out every family and algorithm meeting those conditions; disproving one candidate cone, or proving a lower bound for one representation format, is insufficient. This binary constant-factor target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Weak approximate separation or a distortion factor growing with \(n\) does not meet the requirement.
context:
A single cut records which vertex pairs lie on opposite sides of a partition. Adding such cut vectors with nonnegative weights yields the cut cone. This connects geometric distances with linear objectives measuring capacities crossing graph cuts.

The source describes cut optimization through convex optimization over a normalized section of this cone. It also records NP-hardness of exact cut-cone membership. This motivates a larger cone whose membership and separation are easier while its distances remain close to cut-cone distances.

The whole semimetric cone is a simple outer relaxation, defined by nonnegativity and triangle inequalities. General finite-metric embedding bounds provide a logarithmic distortion scale, rather than the constant scale requested here. The gap is in the guarantee for every dimension.

Negative-type semimetrics form the classical candidate relaxation: the square root of the distance admits a Euclidean realization. They contain cut-cone distances. The source already reports that a uniform constant-distortion embedding of every such metric into ℓ₁ is false, so that candidate cannot answer the broader question.

Chang, Naor and Ren prove that the Goemans–Linial semidefinite relaxation for Sparsest Cut with general capacities and demands has integrality gap \(\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})\). Their 2025 contribution is the matching upper bound; the lower bound comes from prior work. This is sharp for that relaxation and still grows with dimension.

The cone family in this card is unrestricted apart from its convexity, distortion and exact algorithmic guarantees. A limitation on negative-type metrics or on short linear formulations does not exclude other efficiently separable convex sets. Conversely, a fast optimizer without the required membership and separating outputs would not establish the user-selected formulation.
why: Cut metrics encode graph partitions, and their nonnegative combinations capture finite ℓ₁ distances. The question seeks a tractable convex domain that retains this geometry to constant distortion. It separates a broad algorithmic possibility from the limitations of the best-studied semidefinite candidate.
status_note: The source poses an efficiently separable cone approximation and separately proposes negative-type metrics. That particular proposal is already refuted in the source. The STOC 2025 theorem sharpens the performance of the Goemans–Linial relaxation to a growing square-root-logarithmic factor; it does not rule out every other cone. The user selected exact rational membership and separation in polynomial bit time on 16 September 2026. No resolution of this general target was found in the bounded review.

working_summary: The cut cone consists of nonnegative sums of the distance vectors defined by graph cuts. The target is an outer convex cone whose every semimetric lies within one absolute distortion factor of a cut-cone semimetric. One uniform algorithm must decide exact membership and return exact rational separating hyperplanes in polynomial bit time. title: NP-hardness of three-manifold homeomorphism
importance_reason: A major lower-bound question for topological equivalence, asking whether general NP computation can be encoded in valid pairs of 3-manifolds.
formal: Is homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\).
