The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning. The language \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) consists of encodings of satisfiable conjunctions of clauses containing at most three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variable indices and the entire clause list are explicitly encoded in binary; malformed strings are outside the language. A many-one reduction returns one pair, with its entire length and construction time bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). It does not query a homeomorphism oracle or obtain a sequence of adaptive answers. The verifier machinery in the common domain description is not an extra NP-membership assumption on homeomorphism. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, the stated valid-output reduction gives a reduction from every NP language to this promised problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a valid-output reduction exists, or that no such deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists. A positive result must establish the polynomial resource bound, validity of every output manifold and both directions of the satisfiability/homeomorphism equivalence. A negative result must exclude all reductions of this kind. NP-hardness of a related knot, embedding or triangulation-optimization task is insufficient without a reduction to this exact equivalence question. No proof that homeomorphism belongs to NP is required for the positive answer.
context:
Schleimer’s Question 5, attributed there to Burton, asks for NP-hardness of Homeo(3). This card fixes polynomial-time many-one reductions and requires valid triangulated manifolds on every output.

NP-hardness is a lower-bound comparison: any polynomial-time algorithm for homeomorphism would then decide every NP language in polynomial time. It does not assert NP membership, and hence does not by itself assert NP-completeness.

Lackenby establishes hardness relative to graph isomorphism through a many-one reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Graph-isomorphism hardness alone is not the required NP-hardness theorem.

Kuperberg’s elementary-recursive algorithm concerns closed oriented manifolds and provides an upper bound on decision complexity. Such an upper bound is compatible with NP-hardness; decidability and NP-hardness are not mutually exclusive.

The yes/no orientation of the reduction matters. A transformation that sends satisfiable formulas to nonhomeomorphic pairs would instead compare SAT with the complement problem. Likewise, allowing invalid geometric outputs would evade the promised decision task.

A positive answer together with a general NP certificate theorem would make the promised homeomorphism problem NP-complete under valid-output reductions. Combined instead with a coNP certificate theorem, it would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). These consequences explain why the three questions are retained separately.
why: NP-hardness would locate a central topological classification task relative to general combinatorial search. It would supply a stronger complexity obstruction than the currently known reduction from graph isomorphism.
status_note: The NP-hardness question is open in the checked 2024 report, and the 2025 discussion retains graph-isomorphism hardness as the known comparison. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no valid-output NP-hardness resolution for the stated target.
progress: 2017: Lackenby gives a many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. | 2024-02: Schleimer records Burton’s NP-hardness question separately from the two certificate questions. | 2025: The later seminar discussion continues to describe graph-isomorphism hardness while asking a parameterized homeomorphism question.
working_summary: Deciding whether two triangulated three-manifolds are homeomorphic has algorithms, but decidability alone says little about feasible running time. This question seeks an NP-hardness lower bound for the general decision problem. A reduction would have to encode arbitrary instances of a known hard problem into pairs of manifolds. Hardness of related knot or triangulation optimization tasks does not immediately supply that encoding. Such a result would locate manifold equivalence more precisely among familiar computational problems and constrain expectations for general-purpose recognition algorithms.

title: Lower-left anchored rectangle packing constant
importance_reason: A longstanding geometric extremal problem whose elementary input model hides a large unresolved gap between universal coverage guarantees. It links continuous packing choices with arbitrary finite point configurations, and the demonstrated limitation of the familiar greedy algorithm separates general existence from that algorithm’s performance.
formal: Determine the universal lower-left anchored rectangle packing constant \(\alpha\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). For each finite point set \(P\subseteq[0,1)^2\) containing \((0,0)\), let \(A(P)\) be the supremum of the total area of all valid packings of one positive-area axis-aligned rectangle per point, each anchored at that point as its lower-left corner and contained in the unit square. Rectangles must have disjoint interiors. Define \(\alpha=\inf_{P\subseteq[0,1)^2,\;P\text{ finite},\;(0,0)\in P}A(P)\). Area is measured as a fraction of the unit square, so the tolerance is one percentage point of its area.
definitions: Write \(p=(x_p,y_p)\). A valid packing chooses real coordinates \(u_p,v_p\) satisfying \(x_p<u_p\le1\) and \(y_p<v_p\le1\) for every \(p\in P\), and uses \(R_p=[x_p,u_p)\times[y_p,v_p)\). For distinct points \(p,q\), the open sets \((x_p,u_p)\times(y_p,v_p)\) and \((x_q,u_q)\times(y_q,v_q)\) must be disjoint; boundaries may touch. Its total area is \(\sum_{p\in P}(u_p-x_p)(v_p-y_p)\). All points are distinct, their number is arbitrary, and coordinates may be any real numbers in the stated domain. Points may share an x-coordinate or y-coordinate; there is no general-position assumption. The origin is mandatory. The other three corners of a rectangle need not belong to \(P\). Every point anchors exactly one positive-area rectangle, and no rotations, other anchor corners, squares-only restriction, or overlaps of positive area are permitted. Valid packings exist for every such finite set, and their areas are bounded by one. Thus \(A(P)\) and \(\alpha\) are well-defined real suprema and infima. No optimum-attaining point set or packing is demanded by the definitions. There is no computational running-time requirement and no rational-coordinate or finite-precision restriction.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha|\le1/100\), with the quantifiers, positivity and boundary conventions above. Equivalently, certify an interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) and take its midpoint. A lower bound \(L\) must hold for every finite allowed point set through its packing supremum; an upper bound \(U\) must bound the infimum over all allowed point sets, allowing a sequence of sets approaching the bound. A value of \(A(P)\) for one selected instance, an uncertified experiment, or only a performance guarantee for a particular algorithm is insufficient. Exact determination is welcome but not required. This numerical benchmark does not claim that a one-percentage-point approximation proves or refutes the exact half-coverage conjecture.
context:
Freedman’s original conjecture asks whether every permitted point set admits a packing covering at least \(1/2\) of the square. The ICALP 2021 source states this in its introduction and calls for algorithms reaching that guarantee in its conclusion. This card follows the authorized numerical formulation of extremal targets: it asks for the underlying universal coverage constant, retaining the exact conjecture here as the source question. The numerical acceptance criterion is a broadening, not a claim of logical equivalence to proving the conjecture.

The checked 2021 paper establishes a universal coverage guarantee of \(0.39\), while its introductory extremal comparison gives \(\alpha\le1/2\). Consequently the checked bounds are \(0.39\le\alpha\le0.5\). This interval is wider than the benchmark’s permitted \(1/50\) certified interval.

The same paper exhibits inputs on which its studied greedy packing algorithm covers less than \(0.433\). That is an upper bound on this particular algorithm’s worst-case guarantee. It is not an upper bound of \(0.433\) on the optimum packing constant \(\alpha\), and it does not refute Freedman’s conjecture.

A 2013 preprint announcing a proof was withdrawn on 28 April 2014 because its authors found a bug in Claim 5. Its unchanged abstract must be read together with the withdrawal notice; it is not a verified resolution.

Nölke’s 2023 dissertation still records the half-coverage conjecture as open and cites 0.39 as the best known universal guarantee. Its other anchored-packing variants have different allowed anchor positions and do not automatically settle the lower-left problem.
why: The question asks how much area arbitrary anchors inevitably permit one to occupy. Its mathematical interest comes from the universal guarantee over every finite configuration, including degeneracies, rather than the optimal value of one instance. The half-area conjecture would identify the extremal value, while rigorous estimates of the constant quantify the remaining gap.
status_note: The checked 2021 primary paper and 2023 dissertation leave Freedman’s exact conjecture open and give the interval 0.39 to 0.5 for the associated universal coverage constant. The 2013 proof announcement was explicitly withdrawn. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no verified resolution at the stated precision; this is not an exhaustive certification of all subsequent literature.
progress: 1969: Freedman poses the half-coverage question, as documented in the checked 2021 paper’s introduction and its reference to Tutte’s collection of unsolved problems. | 2014-04-28: The authors withdraw the announced existential proof because of an error in Claim 5. | 2021-07-02: Damerius, Kaaser, Kling and Schneider publish a 39 percent coverage guarantee and a below-43.3-percent limitation for their studied greedy algorithm. The half-coverage conjecture remains a separate general question. | 2023: Nölke’s dissertation, defended on 21 February 2023, retains the open conjecture and the 0.39 universal guarantee in its introduction and Chapter 3.
working_summary: The target is the worst possible optimal coverage by rectangles anchored at their lower-left corners at arbitrary points of the unit square. Every finite point set must include the origin, and each point receives a positive-area rectangle with no interior overlap. The numerical answer must locate the universal coverage constant within one percentage point, with a complete Lean proof. Freedman’s exact half-coverage conjecture remains the source question and is stronger than satisfying this approximation criterion. The checked universal bounds are 39 and 50 percent, while the smaller upper bound in the 2021 paper concerns only its particular greedy algorithm.

title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
importance_reason: A longstanding graph-realization problem whose difficulty persists even with the polygon boundary order fixed; it tests the boundary between combinatorial recognition and real-coordinate geometry.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm P\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.
context:
The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.
why: The problem is a central inverse question about geometric visibility: whether pairwise sight-line information and a boundary order can be tested for realizability efficiently. It connects graph recognition with geometric representation complexity.
status_note: The specified fixed-order recognition question remains explicitly open in the checked 2024 compendium. The bounded search through 13 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution. Closed visibility and permitted collinear labelled vertices are explicit formulation conventions; no unrestricted rational-witness assumption is used.
progress: 1995: Lin and Skiena investigate representation complexity and its bearing on short recognition certificates. | 2001: The Open Problems Project lists the fixed-boundary-order polynomial recognition question. | 2024-07-25: The compendium explicitly states that recognition remains open even with boundary order given.
working_summary: A polygon's visibility graph records which pairs of vertices can be joined by a segment lying inside the polygon. The source supplies both a candidate graph and a Hamiltonian cycle specifying the intended polygon boundary. It asks for an efficient decision procedure for whether a simple polygon realizes exactly that information. Choosing coordinates must satisfy visibility and obstruction requirements simultaneously. The problem tests whether a combinatorial record of sight lines contains enough accessible structure to reconstruct a genuine geometric environment.

title: Constant-factor streaming approximation of planar Earth Mover Distance
importance_reason: Estimating Earth Mover Distance concerns the efficient approximation of a widely used transportation metric.
formal:
Do there exist a uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm \(A\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(B>0\), and an integer \(q\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream consisting of \(n\) red and \(n\) blue point arrivals in \([\Delta]^2\), the algorithm uses at most
\[
B\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(\Delta+1)\rceil\bigr)^q
\]
bits of working memory and returns a nonnegative rational number \(\widehat E\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\operatorname{EMD}(R,B_{\mathrm{pts}})
\le\widehat E
\le C\,\operatorname{EMD}(R,B_{\mathrm{pts}})
\right]\ge\frac23?
\]
Here \(R\) and \(B_{\mathrm{pts}}\) are the red and blue multisets, respectively, and
\[
\operatorname{EMD}(R,B_{\mathrm{pts}})
=\min_{\pi:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\ \mathrm{bijection}}
\sum_{i=1}^n\|r_i-b_{\pi(i)}\|_1.
\]
The constants and algorithm are independent of \(n,\Delta\), coordinates and stream order.
question_excerpt: Is there a constant-approximation streaming algorithm for planar Earth Mover Distance using space polynomial in the logarithms of the point count and grid side length?
definitions:
The grid is \([\Delta]^2=\{1,\ldots,\Delta\}\times\{1,\ldots,\Delta\}\). A point has two integer coordinates, each given in binary. For points \(u=(u_1,u_2)\) and \(v=(v_1,v_2)\), the ground distance is \(\|u-v\|_1=|u_1-v_1|+|u_2-v_2|\). Each arrival contains a color and a point and inserts one unit of mass of that color. Coincident arrivals are allowed and count separately; there are no deletions. The letters \(r_i,b_i\) enumerate occurrences, so a matching pairs occurrences rather than only distinct occupied locations.

There are exactly \(2n\) arrivals, with \(n\) of each color, in an arbitrary order. The parameters \(n\) and \(\Delta\) are supplied in binary before the stream. No coordinates, matching, distance estimate or future updates are supplied in advance. The algorithm must work on every such stream, including ones with all red points before all blue points.

The Earth Mover Distance is the minimum total, unnormalised matching cost. It is an integer between zero and \(2n(\Delta-1)\). The algorithm outputs only an estimate of this value, not a matching. When the two multisets agree, the value is zero and the success condition requires output exactly zero.

Uniform means one finite randomized Turing-machine program for every parameter pair. It has a sequential read-only stream input, finite control, work tapes and access to independent unbiased random bits. It may finish processing an arrival before advancing but cannot reread an earlier arrival or the random-bit source. Every retained random seed, counter, coordinate and auxiliary data structure counts toward working memory. Its computation and final rational-output computation must fit the stated memory bound. Output is written only at the end and cannot be read back as storage.

The space bound is a worst-case bound over all times, all valid streams and all random-bit outcomes. The algorithm must finish processing and halt with an output for every valid stream and every random-bit outcome; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. Probability is over the algorithm’s coins for each fixed stream. The order need not be random, and cannot be chosen in response to private random bits.

The output rational is encoded by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The required approximation is multiplicative; no additive error depending on \(n\) or \(\Delta\) is allowed. No linearity, mergeability, independent red/blue sketches or embedding representation is imposed on the memory state.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,B,q\) satisfying every stated condition, or of the logical negation. A positive answer must prove the uniform memory guarantee and the success probability for all parameter pairs and all valid stream orders. A negative answer must exclude every constant approximation factor and every fixed polylogarithmic space exponent in this model; ruling out one particular sketch representation or constant-size sketches alone is insufficient. The proposition is binary. The approximation factor is an existential universal constant, not a numerical quantity subject to additive \(1/100\) tolerance.
context:
Earth Mover Distance measures the cheapest way to move one distribution of mass onto another. In this discrete model each point has unit mass, so transport becomes a minimum-cost red-blue matching. Nearby displacements can be cheap even when few coordinates match exactly.

The difficulty is retaining enough global transportation information while discarding almost all arrivals. Storing all points or a full grid histogram usually exceeds the requested memory. The task only asks for the total optimum cost, which may be much easier to summarize than an actual matching.

The source records an \(O(\log\Delta)\)-approximation in polylogarithmic space. Constant approximation requires removing the growing loss without allowing memory to grow as a positive power of the grid size. The two independent parameters are the number of arrivals and the coordinate range.

The 2009 algorithm achieves an \(O(1/\varepsilon)\)-approximation with space \(\Delta^\varepsilon\log^{O(1)}(\Delta n)\) for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Thus it gives constant approximation, but its positive power of \(\Delta\) exceeds a fixed polynomial in \(\log\Delta\). Allowing the exponent to shrink does not preserve a constant approximation under this tradeoff.

Its decoder is more general than taking an \(\ell_1\) distance between embedded vectors. This distinction matters: a geometric lower bound on embedding distortion does not automatically lower-bound the memory required by every possible decoder or streaming state.

The sketching/embedding theorem excludes constant-size, constant-approximation threshold sketches for the planar transportation norm and the related weighted-set metric. Constant-size is stricter than the polylogarithmic storage allowed here. That theorem is meaningful partial progress, without settling the displayed proposition.

Gartland and Ostrovskii’s 2026 result raises the planar-grid \(L_1\)-distortion lower bound to \(\Omega(\log\Delta)\), matching the logarithmic upper bound for embeddings of the full transportation space. Distortion compares all distances under one map into a space with distance given by an integral of absolute differences. The result sharpens this geometric obstruction, not a space bound for the unrestricted algorithm in this card.

The related independent-sketch problem gives each point set its own separately computed summary. Here the algorithm maintains one evolving state while receiving both colors. Restrictions or lower bounds for one representation model require an explicit reduction before they can be transferred to the other.
why: Determine whether transportation distance can be estimated from one scan using only polylogarithmic memory, beyond the limitations of standard metric embeddings.
status_note: The source explicitly asks for constant approximation with polylogarithmic memory. The 2009 result obtains constant approximation using a positive power of the grid side length in its space bound. The norm-sketching lower bound rules out simultaneously constant approximation and constant sketch size, while the February/June 2026 result sharpens L1 embedding distortion. Neither checked theorem rules out the allowed polylogarithmic memory for unrestricted streaming algorithms. No resolution of this target was found through 16 September 2026 in the bounded review; cited proofs were not all independently reconstructed.
progress: 2004–2006: The original question records logarithmic approximation in polylogarithmic streaming space and asks for constant approximation. | 2009: A grid-size versus approximation tradeoff yields the first sublinear-grid-space constant approximation. | 2014–2017: The sketching/embedding work rules out simultaneously constant-size and constant-approximation threshold sketches for planar EMD. | 2026-02-16: The new preprint states a matching \(\Omega(\log\Delta)\) lower bound for planar transportation-space \(L_1\) distortion; a conference version appears at STOC 2026. | 2026-09-16: The individual review specifies the original insertion stream target and separates known bounds by model.
working_summary: The stream contains equal numbers of red and blue unit-mass points on a planar integer grid. Earth Mover Distance is the minimum total L1 cost of matching red occurrences to blue occurrences. The question asks for one-pass constant-factor estimation with memory polynomial in the logarithms of the point count and grid side length. The guarantee must hold with constant success probability for every fixed arbitrary stream order. Known grid-space tradeoffs and embedding or constant-sketch lower bounds do not settle this unrestricted streaming target.

title: Linear-size universal point sets for planar graphs
importance_reason: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?
definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.
context:
A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.
why: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Gordon’s new preprint claims n^{1+o(1)} universal point sets for general planar graphs, but does not state the fixed-constant linear bound requested here. The new proof has not been independently verified. No proof or refutation of the O(n) target was located in the bounded source search.
progress: 2023: Linear-size constructions for restricted planar graph classes do not establish a universal linear bound for all planar graphs. | 2026-09-10: Gordon’s preprint claims an unrestricted \(n^{1+o(1)}\) upper bound. This is not a constant-factor linear bound, and the proof has not been independently verified in this pass.
working_summary: One point set is selected for each graph size. Every planar graph of that size must have a straight-line drawing using some of those points. Vertex assignments may depend on the graph. The question asks whether only linearly many points suffice. Results for subclasses do not settle the universal requirement.

title: Polynomial flip-distance bounds for three-manifold triangulations
importance_reason: Polynomial bounds for triangulation transformations would give quantitative control over topological equivalence representations.
formal:
Does every compact connected piecewise-linear three-manifold, with or without boundary, have a polynomial bound on the number of local moves needed to pass between any two of its finite simplicial triangulations?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal M_3\) be the finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulations defined below, let \(t(K)\) count tetrahedra, and write \(K\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}L\) when their realizations are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic. Prove or refute
\[
\forall R\in\mathcal M_3\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall T,U\in\mathcal M_3:\quad
\bigl(T\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\ U\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\exists\text{ a legal move sequence from }T\text{ to }U
\text{ of length at most }C\bigl(t(T)+t(U)\bigr)^k.
\]
The constants may depend on the fixed reference triangulation \(R\), equivalently on its manifold type, but must work for every pair \(T,U\) of that type. No common polynomial for different manifolds, effective procedure to obtain the constants, or efficient algorithm to find a move sequence is required. Intermediate triangulations may have more tetrahedra than either endpoint.

The card uses the standard combinatorial version: finite abstract simplicial complexes, interior bistellar moves, and elementary shellings and their inverses on the boundary. This explicitly repairs the boundary convention in the original question and specifies a simplicial representation. The source also discusses more general face-pairing encodings; no unproved equivalence between their quantitative move bounds and this specified version is part of the claim.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}=\{1,2,\ldots\}\) and \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a collection of subsets of a finite vertex set, containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its vertex set is exactly the union of its faces. A face with \(j+1\) vertices has dimension \(j\). The complex is pure of dimension three if it is nonempty and every maximal face has four vertices. These maximal faces are its tetrahedra, and \(t(K)\) is their number. A finite encoding labels the vertices by \([n]\) and lists each four-element maximal face once, in increasing lexicographic order; every other face is its subset. There are no face self-identifications, distinct simplices with the same vertex set, geometric lengths, or ideal vertices deleted from the realization.

The realization \(|K|\) is the union of the convex hulls of the standard basis vectors indexed by each nonempty face, inside Euclidean space with one coordinate for each vertex. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection between vertex sets that takes faces to faces in both directions. A subdivision replaces the linear simplices of a realization by finitely many linear simplices meeting along common faces, with the same union, each new simplex contained in an old one. Two complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic if they admit subdivisions related by a simplicial isomorphism. This defines \(\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}\); no chosen homeomorphism or boundary marking is included as input.

For a face \(A\in K\), its link is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(A)=\{B\in K:B\cap A=\varnothing\text{ and }A\cup B\in K\}.
\]
The set \(\mathcal M_3\) consists of finite pure three-dimensional complexes whose realizations are connected and whose link at every vertex is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic either to the boundary of a tetrahedron or to one filled triangle. These are the two-sphere and two-ball link conditions, respectively, for a compact combinatorial three-manifold with possibly nonempty boundary. Both orientable and nonorientable manifolds are allowed. The boundary subcomplex \(\partial K\) is generated by the triangular faces lying in exactly one tetrahedron. A manifold is closed when this subcomplex has no nonempty face. Connectivity means any two vertices can be joined by a sequence of edges. Quantification over reference complexes covers precisely the compact connected PL manifold types in this convention.

Here are the permitted moves. For a finite nonempty set of vertices \(A\), let \(\Delta A\) be the simplex consisting of all its subsets, and \(\partial\Delta A\) the complex of its proper subsets. For complexes on disjoint vertex sets, their join is the complex of unions of a face from each. An interior bistellar move chooses a nonempty face \(A\in K\) and a disjoint nonempty finite vertex set \(B\), allowing new vertices, such that
\[
|A|+|B|=5,\qquad B\notin K,\qquad
\operatorname{lk}_K(A)=\partial\Delta B.
\]
It replaces \(\Delta A*\partial\Delta B\) by \(\partial\Delta A*\Delta B\), retaining their common boundary. In set notation the result is
\[
K'=\bigl(K\setminus\{\sigma\in K:A\subseteq\sigma\}\bigr)
\ \cup\ (\partial\Delta A*\Delta B).
\]
Vertices no longer contained in any nonempty face are discarded. This is one move: according to the two set sizes it replaces one tetrahedron by four, two by three, three by two, or four by one. The link and missing-face conditions rule out accidental identifications or an already present replacement simplex. Only results in \(\mathcal M_3\) are admitted.

For a boundary attachment, choose a four-element vertex set \(\sigma\) whose tetrahedron is not already in \(K\), possibly introducing new vertices. Require that
\[
D=K\cap\Delta\sigma
\]
is exactly the union, including all their subfaces, of one, two, or three distinct triangular faces of \(\sigma\), and that \(D\subseteq\partial K\). This is a triangulated two-ball in the boundary. Replace \(K\) by \(K\cup\Delta\sigma\), requiring the result to belong to \(\mathcal M_3\). The reverse of any such legal attachment is an elementary boundary shelling and is also one move. It removes the tetrahedron and precisely those of its faces absent before the attachment; it does not leave isolated unsupported lower-dimensional faces. The conditions exclude attaching a tetrahedron along no face or along its entire boundary. These boundary moves preserve the PL manifold type and allow its boundary triangulation to change.

A legal sequence is a finite sequence \(K_0,\ldots,K_\ell\in\mathcal M_3\), with \(K_0\) isomorphic to \(T\) and \(K_\ell\) isomorphic to \(U\), in which each consecutive pair is related by one of the permitted moves, allowing a simplicial relabeling. Its length is \(\ell\); relabeling itself is free, so this is a distance on isomorphism classes. A zero-length sequence is allowed for isomorphic endpoints. Every intermediate complex has the same PL manifold type, but its vertex set, tetrahedron count and boundary triangulation may vary. There is no restriction to geometric hyperbolic triangulations, fixed vertices, or size-decreasing moves.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal assertion or its full logical negation, for the complexes and legal moves above.

A positive answer must prove that each reference \(R\) admits some constants \(C,k\) bounding the length of a connecting sequence for every pair of triangulations of its PL type. An existence proof is sufficient; the target does not require a polynomial-time search algorithm or a uniform polynomial across all manifold types.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists R\in\mathcal M_3\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists T,U\in\mathcal M_3:\quad
T\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\ U\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\
\forall\text{ legal sequences }(K_0,\ldots,K_\ell)\text{ from }T\text{ to }U,
\quad \ell>C\bigl(t(T)+t(U)\bigr)^k.
\]
The same fixed manifold type must defeat every polynomial; choosing a different manifold as \(C,k\) vary is insufficient. A lower bound for one prescribed simplification procedure, an upper bound on only the largest intermediate triangulation, or a theorem restricted to geometric triangulations does not settle the required distance statement. Conditional complexity consequences establish only the corresponding conditional claim. The assertion is exact; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not relax it.
context:
Question 8 permits a different polynomial for each fixed manifold. Question 9 separately asks for independence from the manifold, and Question 10 asks about the largest intermediate triangulation. Neither additional target is included here.

The original text permits manifolds with boundary but describes only interior bistellar flips, which preserve the boundary triangulation; its stated vertex-link definition also omits ball links. This card explicitly uses the standard compact-manifold convention with sphere or ball links and elementary boundary moves.

The 2026 K3 problem list supplies the combinatorial compact-manifold setting, explicitly adding boundary shellings and distinguishing fixed-manifold from uniform move bounds. The finite simplicial model in this card follows that convention; the scope choice is editorial.

Kalelkar and Phanse give bounds for geometric triangulations of closed constant-curvature manifolds. In dimension three their bound is cubic in the two tetrahedron counts when the geometric parameters are fixed, but its coefficient depends on edge-length and injectivity-radius data absent from arbitrary combinatorial inputs.
why: Polynomial move bounds would provide short, locally checkable certificates relating arbitrary triangulations of each fixed three-manifold. A counterexample would exhibit intrinsic superpolynomial reconfiguration distance in one fixed topological space. The question measures representation changes, rather than the performance of a particular recognition algorithm.
status_note: Open as the per-fixed-manifold question in Dagstuhl 2024 Question 8. The 2026 K3 problem list retains the general move-bound problem and supplies the boundary convention used here. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of this specified standard combinatorial version. The finite simplicial representation and inclusion of elementary boundary moves are disclosed editorial refinements of the original text. Geometric bounds have additional hypotheses. The review checked definitions and theorem scopes, not every proof, an exhaustive bibliography or a Lean formalization.

working_summary: A compact connected three-manifold can be represented by many finite simplicial triangulations. The question asks whether each fixed manifold admits a polynomial bound, in the two endpoint tetrahedron counts, on the number of local moves connecting any pair of its triangulations. The specified convention permits both interior bistellar flips and elementary boundary shellings and their inverses, explicitly repairing the boundary ambiguity in the original source. Such a bound would give short certificates connecting finite descriptions of the same space without requiring an efficient method to find them or a single polynomial for every manifold. A complete Lean answer must prove the bound for every fixed manifold type or exhibit one fixed type whose triangulation distances defeat every polynomial.

title: NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds
importance_reason: Short certificates for recognizing major three-manifold classes would refine the algorithmic structure of topological classification.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that, for every finite PL-triangulation T of a compact connected three-manifold M, M is closed and admits a hyperbolic metric if and only if there exists a binary certificate w with |\(w|\le p(|T|)\) and \(V(T,w)=1\)?
definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space \(M=|T|\). The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space \(H^{3}\); for example \(H^{3}\) is the upper half-space \(\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R} ^{3}:z>0\}\) with metric \(ds^{2}=(dx^{2}+dy^{2}+dz^{2})/z^{2}\). Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.
answer_criterion: Give a polynomial certificate bound and a uniform polynomial-time verifier that accepts some bounded-length certificate for every closed hyperbolic input and accepts none for every other promised manifold input. Alternatively, prove that no such bound and verifier exist. A terminating recognition algorithm alone, or certificates for non-hyperbolicity, do not establish this NP membership.
context:
The input says which faces of finitely many tetrahedra are glued together. It determines a topological space, but does not hand the verifier a hyperbolic metric. The question asks whether existence of that global geometric structure always has a short, efficiently checkable witness.

Two very different gluing descriptions can represent the same manifold. A successful verifier must accept every description of a closed hyperbolic manifold with some certificate polynomial in that description’s size. It cannot be limited to triangulations that visibly carry a convenient geometric structure.

Schleimer’s 2024 report records decidability of hyperbolic recognition and separately asks for NP membership. Decidability guarantees eventual termination; NP requires a polynomial bound on both the witness size and verification work.

Haraway and Hoffman study non-hyperbolicity certificates for orientable manifolds with torus boundary. Their results give coNP statements about hyperbolicity in that setting. The present question concerns positive certificates for closed hyperbolic manifolds, so it has both a different input class and a different answer direction.
why: Would show that a global constant-curvature geometry can always be certified using polynomially bounded discrete evidence from an arbitrary triangulation. It would sharpen the complexity of a central geometric recognition problem beyond mere decidability.
status_note: Original manifold and triangulation conventions recovered, and subsequent-work searches checked through 11 September 2026; no matching NP-resolution result located. Related cusped non-hyperbolicity results have different promises and answer direction. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2002: The 2024 report attributes decidability of hyperbolic recognition to Casson and Manning, while retaining the stronger NP question. | 2022-09: Haraway and Hoffman give non-hyperbolicity certificates in the cusped orientable setting; their Theorem 1 assumes \(S^{3}\) recognition lies in coNP, while their irreducible cusped case is unconditional. | 2024: Schleimer explicitly poses NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds as Question 12.
working_summary: The input describes a compact connected three-manifold by gluing faces of finitely many tetrahedra. The question is whether being closed and admitting a hyperbolic metric always has a polynomial-size certificate. A single deterministic verifier must check such certificates in polynomial time for every input triangulation. Recognition is decidable, but this does not give the required certificate-size and verification-time bounds. A positive answer would connect a global geometric structure with short, efficiently verifiable combinatorial evidence.

title: Efficient average-distortion embeddings of polyhedral norms
importance_reason: The problem concerns sparse or low-distortion representations of geometric distances, a reusable algorithmic resource.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time construction of a globally defined Euclidean embedding of the square-root metric of every rational polyhedral norm, with quadratic average distortion at most \(C\sqrt{\log_2 d}\) on any given finite rational point set, for one universal constant \(C\)? The construction must produce a finite description permitting polynomial-time evaluation to any requested precision. This is the explicitly encoded polyhedral-norm branch of the source’s algorithmic average-John question; the exact guarantees and complexity parameters are below.
definitions:
An input consists of integers \(d\ge2\), \(r\ge d\), \(n\ge2\), a matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{r\times d}\) of column rank \(d\), and a list \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^d\). Integers and rational coordinates are written in binary, with signed numerators and positive denominators; dimensions and lists are explicit. Let \(N\) be the total input bit length. Define a norm on the entire real space \(\mathbb R^d\) by
\[
\|x\|_A=\max_{1\le j\le r}|(Ax)_j|,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}_A(x,y)=\sqrt{\|x-y\|_A}.
\]
Full column rank makes \(\|\cdot\|_A\) a norm. There is no bound on \(r\), coordinate magnitudes or geometric aspect ratios except what their input lengths express. The norm is supplied by the matrix, not by a unit-cost oracle. All arithmetic and norm evaluations are charged at bit cost.

The assertion asks for two fixed deterministic multitape Turing-machine programs \(B,E\), constants \(C,K\ge1\), and an integer \(a\ge1\), independent of every input. On each valid input, \(B\) must output an integer \(m\ge1\) and a finite binary description \(\sigma\) in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps, with \(m\) and \(|\sigma|\) at most \(K(N+1)^a\). That description must specify one continuous function \(f_\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
\|f_\sigma(x)-f_\sigma(y)\|_2^2\le\|x-y\|_A
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R^d
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n
\|f_\sigma(p_i)-f_\sigma(p_j)\|_2^2
\ \ge\
\frac{1}{C^2\log_2 d}
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\|p_i-p_j\|_A.
\]
Here \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Euclidean norm. Both sums are over ordered pairs, including the zero diagonal. The average is with respect to the uniform distribution on \(P\); the factor \(n^{-2}\) cancels on both sides. The first inequality is nonexpansion for the square-root metric on the whole space, including points outside \(P\). The second controls squared Euclidean distances on average. No individual lower bound on a pairwise distance or injectivity is required.

The meaning of a finite description is fixed by the second program. On input \((\sigma,x,1^k)\), where \(x\in\mathbb Q^d\) has binary description length \(b\) and \(k\ge1\), \(E\) must output a dyadic rational vector \(v\in\mathbb Q^m\) satisfying
\[
\|v-f_\sigma(x)\|_2\le2^{-k}
\]
in at most \(K(N+b+k+1)^a\) bit operations. Dyadic rationals are represented by an integer numerator and a power-of-two denominator, both explicitly encoded in binary. The approximations for all rational \(x\) and all precisions must correspond to the same continuous map; they are not separate independently chosen embeddings. Continuity and density of rational points determine that map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\). Its displayed geometric inequalities are exact mathematical requirements; rounding pertains only to evaluation.

The description may include the original matrix and point set. Both construction and evaluation may depend polynomially on their total bit length; no storage or query-time bound independent of \(n\) is imposed. No random bits, advice, noncomputable real constants, free preprocessing or oracle is available. The problem asks for construction of a map, not just a table of images of the input points.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such uniform programs and constants, including their bit complexity, a single well-defined global map per output description, both geometric inequalities and the evaluation guarantee at every rational query and precision, or a complete Lean proof that the assertion is false. A nonconstructive embedding, a map defined only on \(P\), or a sketch whose decoder estimates distances without giving Euclidean coordinates does not meet this target. The distortion requirement is \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) with a common constant; \(2^{-k}\) specifies computational output precision. Neither is replaced by the numerical-benchmark \(1/100\) tolerance.
context:
Nikolov’s question in Section 4.3 starts with the square-root metric of a finite-dimensional normed space and asks for an explicit, efficiently computable average-distortion map from the given point set. The preceding existence theorem already supplies the geometric distortion bound.

The report does not specify how an arbitrary norm is encoded or how real-valued outputs are represented. This card explicitly selects rational polyhedral norms given by a full-rank matrix and rational data points, and uses finite descriptions with certified precision-dependent evaluation. This is a documented computational specialization, not a claim of equivalence to all norm-oracle formulations of the original question.

The selected efficiency requirement is polynomial in the full input bit length, including the norm description. It does not impose the stronger succinct storage and query bounds, independent of the number of data points, used by some near-neighbor-search reductions. Those bounds are a separate requirement.

Naor’s average John theorem gives a map from the whole normed space into a Hilbert space with quadratic average distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) for its one-half snowflake. The theorem and its discussion distinguish this existence statement from an explicit efficient construction.

Kush, Nikolov and Tang give explicit average-distortion embeddings for \(\ell_p\) spaces and a framework relating efficient embeddings to near-neighbor search. Their stated special-case constructions do not supply the full polynomial-time map required here for arbitrary input polyhedral norms.

The 2025 average-distortion sketching paper permits an arbitrary compressed representation and a pairwise distance decoder. Its nonexpansion guarantee is stated in expectation over sketches; this is distinct from one globally nonexpanding map into a Euclidean space.
why: Average-distance preservation can be much better than preservation of every distance from below. Constructing such maps would make a strong structural theorem in metric geometry algorithmically usable. The global nonexpansion requirement matters because a later query point need not belong to the original data set.
status_note: The broader constructive question is open in the 2021 seminar source. This card explicitly fixes a rational polyhedral bit-model specialization. Checked later sketching results have different output and nonexpansion guarantees, but bounded checks through 2026-09-16 do not independently establish current openness of this selected computational version.
progress: 2021: Naor’s published average John theorem establishes the geometric \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) bound through an existence argument. | 2021: The seminar report asks for an explicit efficient map, and the near-neighbor paper gives constructions for specified norm families. | 2025-04-10: Version 3 of the average-distortion sketching preprint develops a more general sketch-and-decoder model and results for discrete subsets of fixed norm families. These guarantees are not the global Euclidean-map target.
working_summary: The average John theorem preserves squared distances on average after taking the square root of a norm metric. The algorithmic question asks for an efficiently constructed map that is nonexpanding on the entire space, including future query points. This card explicitly selects rational polyhedral norms and rational data points so that the input and computational cost have finite bit encodings. The output must describe one continuous Euclidean map that can be evaluated to any requested precision in polynomial time. This would turn a structural existence theorem into an algorithmic object, while the present review keeps the current status of the selected computational specialization uncertain.

title: Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms for sparse vectors
importance_reason: A basic optimization, estimation, or encoding task serves as a concrete benchmark for streaming resource tradeoffs.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C_1,C_2>0\), an integer \(q\ge0\), and uniform sampling and application algorithms with the following property? For every integer \(d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), the sampling algorithm produces an input-independent representation of a random linear map \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\), where
\[
1\le k\le\min\{d,\lceil C_1\varepsilon^{-2}\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\}.
\]
For every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), its distribution satisfies
\[
\Pr_A\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|Ax\|_2
                 \le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\bigr]\ge1-\delta.
\]
Given a sampled representation and the list of the \(s\) nonzero coordinates of any \(x\), the application algorithm must return all coordinates of \(Ax\) in at most
\[
C_2(s+k)\bigl(\log_2(d+2)\bigr)^q
\]
operations in the arithmetic model below, for every sampled representation and input. The same constants and algorithms must work for all parameters. The matrix distribution is independent of \(x\), including its support.
question_excerpt: The source asks for a distribution of norm-preserving linear maps with the usual Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension bound, whose product with a sparse input can be evaluated in time proportional to input sparsity plus output dimension, apart from logarithms of the ambient dimension.
definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(s=\|x\|_0=|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|\) is input sparsity. The input is an arbitrary-order list of distinct indices in \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and their nonzero real values, together with \(d\). Coordinates absent from the list are zero. Reading this list and writing the dense length-\(k\) output count toward application time. The zero vector is included, with \(s=0\).

A sampled object represents one genuine linear map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), not a map chosen after seeing the support or magnitudes of the input. The application algorithm must evaluate that map exactly in real arithmetic. The approximation concerns preservation of length, not numerical evaluation of the matrix product. The probability statement is for each vector fixed independently of the sampled map; it does not claim that one dimension-reducing map preserves every vector simultaneously. No promise bounds the ratio of the largest coordinate to the norm.

Use an arithmetic RAM: a real value occupies one cell, and addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and comparison each cost one operation. Memory access and operations on integer indices of logarithmic size in the allocated storage also cost one. There is no floor operation on arbitrary real values, arbitrary real-to-integer decoding, or oracle for matrix-vector multiplication. The programs are finite and uniform, with rational built-in constants; \(\varepsilon,\delta\) are real parameter inputs. This is an arithmetic-operation question, not a bound on the bit complexity of arbitrarily precise real coordinates.

The distribution and its representation may be prepared before the input vector is provided. To fix the construction convention, the sampler uses independent fair bits, has expected time and storage bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(d+\varepsilon^{-1}+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\), and terminates with probability one. It outputs a finite read-only representation used by the application algorithm. Setup work is independent of the input vector and is not included in per-vector application time; any subsequent work on the vector, including an input-dependent transformation or preprocessing, is included. Application time is a worst-case bound, not an amortized bound over a favorable collection of vectors. All sampler outcomes with positive probability must define an evaluable map. No logarithmic bound on the number of random bits is requested.

The output dimension \(k\) is selected from the parameters and is fixed before drawing the map. The ceiling handles integer dimensions, and the cap at \(d\) allows the identity when the usual dimension bound would exceed the ambient dimension. The phrase optimal dimension refers to the order of the displayed upper bound, not its best leading constant. The exponent \(q\) and time constant are independent of error and failure probability. In particular, an extra factor depending on \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) or \(\log(1/\delta)\) cannot be hidden in the input-sparsity term unless it is absorbed by the displayed bound.

The source has a separate question about generating the map with \(O(\log(d/\delta))\) random bits. The user explicitly removed that additional objective. The setup convention above makes the retained application question precise without reinstating the short-seed target.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the uniform existence assertion, including the distribution, dimension bound, pointwise probability guarantee and worst-case sparse-input application bound in the stated model. An affirmative answer must cover every parameter choice and arbitrary real input vector; a result only for constant distortion, constant failure probability, dense inputs, or special coordinate distributions is insufficient. A negative answer is the full negation and must cover every allowed construction and application algorithm, rather than one chosen sparse-matrix family. A proof about the omitted seed-length objective does not answer this card. The benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not weaken the prescribed asymptotic guarantees.
context:
Dimension reduction can shorten later computations on high-dimensional data while approximately preserving distances. For sparse data, even scanning every ambient coordinate may waste most of the work. This question seeks a transformation whose application cost follows the amount of input actually present and the amount of output produced.

Sparse Johnson–Lindenstrauss matrices reduce multiplication work by limiting nonzeros per column. Their standard application bound still multiplies input sparsity by a factor of order \(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\). The existence of such matrices therefore does not establish the requested additive dependence on input sparsity and output dimension.

Fast structured transforms use a different route to rapid multiplication. The inspected 2023 improvement retains an ambient-dimension term, which can dominate when the input is sparse. Lower bounds on column sparsity alone do not rule out a different structured map with a faster evaluation algorithm.

Later sparse-embedding work refines parameter regimes, while the 2026 concentration result targets sharper confidence constants. These developments concern the same geometric primitive, but neither inspected statement supplies the full application-time bound selected here.
why: An affirmative answer would make optimal Euclidean dimension reduction almost as cheap as reading a sparse vector and writing its sketch. This would strengthen a general primitive used in similarity search, randomized linear algebra and high-dimensional geometry. A general obstruction would identify a computational cost that dimension bounds alone do not reveal.
status_note: The 2011 source poses the application-time question separately from its seed-length question. The latter was removed by explicit user choice. Known sparse transforms and the inspected 2023 fast-transform bound do not give the requested sparsity-plus-output bound across all parameters. The inspected June 2026 paper concerns concentration constants and does not assert such an application algorithm. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the selected target; this is a source-scope review, not an exhaustive open-status certificate or verification of every cited proof.
progress: 2011: The workshop list poses fast sparse-vector application and short random seeds as separate questions. | 2014: Sparse transforms achieve the optimal dimension order with an additional inverse-distortion factor in direct sparse-vector multiplication. | 2023: Fast-transform and sparse-embedding analyses improve different parameter regimes without supplying the complete selected guarantee. | 2026-06-20: A concentration refinement for sparse projections was published; its theorem does not assert the requested application-time bound. | 2026-09-16: The source and later theorem scopes were checked, and the approved removal of the seed-length objective was recorded.
working_summary: A Johnson–Lindenstrauss map reduces dimension while approximately preserving the length of each fixed vector with high probability. The question asks for the optimal output dimension together with application time proportional to input sparsity plus output length, up to logarithms of the ambient dimension. The map is chosen independently of the input, and the guarantee must hold for all distortion and failure-probability parameters. Known sparse and fast structured transforms do not by themselves provide this full combination, and the separate short-seed objective has been removed. A resolution would clarify whether geometric compression can be performed almost at the cost of reading and writing sparse data.

title: Minimum-Link Path in 2D
importance_reason: A focused question about a specified geometric class, representation, or variant; this category review assigns it a shared specialist priority.
formal:
Does there exist a single deterministic algorithm \(A\) in the real-RAM model specified below and a function \(T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every valid planar polygonal-domain input \((P,s,t)\) with \(n\) boundary vertices, \(A\) outputs a minimum-link polygonal path from \(s\) to \(t\) contained in \(P\), using at most \(T(n)\) operations, and
\[
\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:
\qquad T(n)\le\eta n^2?
\]
The source's word “subquadratic” is interpreted here literally as \(o(n^2)\). The target permits logarithmic-factor savings and does not require a fixed power saving \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\).
definitions:
A closed simple polygonal region is the bounded region enclosed by a non-self-intersecting polygonal cycle, together with its boundary. The input gives an optional closed simple outer polygon \(B\), and finitely many closed simple polygonal obstacle regions \(O_1,\ldots,O_h\). When the outer polygon is absent, set \(B=\mathbb R^2\). Each obstacle is contained in \(B\), their interiors are pairwise disjoint, and the free space is
\[
P=B\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{h}\operatorname{int}(O_i).
\]
The input is promised to have connected free space. Boundary contact between obstacles, or with the outer polygon, is allowed; it does not prohibit a path from using the remaining closed free space. The two specified points \(s,t\) belong to \(P\). There is no general-position promise: collinearities, boundary endpoints and tangencies are included. Each polygon is supplied as its cyclic list of real-coordinate vertices, with polygon lengths and delimiters, and \(s,t\) as coordinate pairs. The size \(n\) is the sum of the lengths of all polygon lists, including the outer polygon when present. Neither a triangulation, visibility graph nor preprocessed data structure is supplied.

A polygonal path is a finite list \(q_0,\ldots,q_k\in\mathbb R^2\), where \(q_0=s\), \(q_k=t\), and every closed line segment \([q_{i-1},q_i]\) lies in \(P\). Its number of links is \(k\); the one-point path has zero links and is available when \(s=t\). The required output attains the minimum of \(k\) over all these paths. All intermediate points may lie anywhere in \(P\), including its interior and boundary, and segments may have any orientation. Output consists of the full list of points with exact coordinates in real registers. Obstacle vertices are not the only permitted bends. Because \(P\) is closed, touching an obstacle or following its boundary is permitted, but entering its interior is forbidden.

For this card, a real RAM is a uniform finite program with exact real registers and random-access memory, together with integer control registers and addresses of \(w=c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed program-dependent integer \(c\ge1\). A real-register copy, an input/output operation on a register, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, square root of a nonnegative real, and comparison of two reals each cost one operation. Word reads, writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic each cost one operation; addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\), integer division by a nonzero word rounds down, and a shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Branching and memory addressing also cost one operation. The program has only finitely many rational real constants and no oracle or advice. Real values cannot be converted into integer addresses by a floor or arbitrary bit-extraction operation; comparisons can affect the finite control. All input processing, construction of auxiliary data and writing of the output are included in \(T(n)\). There is no randomness. The bound is worst-case over coordinates, degeneracies, number of holes, endpoints and all other valid inputs of size \(n\). This explicitly fixes a deterministic, exact-arithmetic real-RAM interpretation; it is not a bound on the bit complexity of rational coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that such a uniform algorithm exists, including exact path feasibility, minimum link count and the stated worst-case little-o operation bound, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of this proposition. A conditional lower bound, an approximation to the minimum number of links, a bound for a restricted direction set, or an algorithm only for polygons without holes does not settle this target.
context:
TOPP Problem 22 asks for a subquadratic algorithm for a minimum-link path among planar polygonal obstacles. Its entry is dated 2 August 2001. This card interprets subquadratic as little-o of the square of the input boundary size and makes the deterministic worst-case real-RAM convention explicit.

Mitchell, Rote and Woeginger give an exact algorithm in \(O(E\alpha(n)\log^2 n)\) time, where \(E\) is the number of visibility-graph edges and \(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function. Since \(E=O(n^2)\), this is nearly quadratic in the worst case. Their free space is closed, permits holes and may be unbounded.

Mitchell, Polishchuk and Sysikaski prove that exact link distance with unrestricted directions is 3SUM-hard, even for rectilinear obstacle boundaries. This is a reduction-based result, not an unconditional impossibility theorem. The rectilinear boundaries do not restrict path directions.

The distinction between little-o and a fixed power saving matters: Grønlund and Pettie gave deterministic algorithms for real-number 3SUM whose operation counts are already little-o of the input size squared. Their result is about 3SUM, and is not itself an algorithm for minimum-link paths. The older 3SUM-hardness result therefore does not refute the present little-o target.

The 2014 minimum-link paper also obtains an \(O(\sqrt{h})\)-approximation in subquadratic time, where \(h\) is the number of holes. The May 2025 Dagstuhl seminar report still asks for a better subquadratic approximation. These approximation results and questions do not establish an exact subquadratic algorithm.

The 2016 complexity study separates unrestricted planar bends from bends constrained to polygon boundaries, and from three-dimensional paths. Its NP-hardness results for boundary-reflection paths and three-dimensional paths concern different targets. The paper also explains why real-RAM operation counts and coordinate bit complexity must be distinguished.
why: The number of straight portions of a route captures the cost of changing direction, independently of how far the route travels. This question asks whether exact optimization of that basic geometric objective can avoid a quadratic operation count in environments with many obstacles, where the planar Euclidean shortest-path objective has a different complexity.
status_note: Source-open under an explicitly documented literal o(n²), deterministic real-RAM interpretation. TOPP Problem 22 labels the question open in its 2 August 2001 entry. The individual source review and bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching exact planar resolution; 3SUM-hardness is conditional evidence and does not refute this little-o target, especially given known logarithmic-factor improvements for 3SUM itself. The 2025 Dagstuhl report concerns the approximation frontier. This status is not a claim of an exhaustive current-openness check.
