working_summary: A minimum-link path connects two given points through closed planar free space while using the fewest straight segments. The environment may contain many polygonal holes, and the path may bend at arbitrary interior or boundary points and use arbitrary directions. The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose worst-case real-RAM operation count divided by the square of the total boundary size tends to zero. This interpretation includes logarithmic-factor savings, and known 3SUM-hardness does not by itself rule them out. The checked approximation results and hardness results for boundary bends or three-dimensional paths do not settle this planar exact-path target.

title: Half-snowflake embeddings into Wasserstein p-space
importance_reason: A structural universality conjecture about transport metrics that asks for a larger snowflake exponent with size-independent distortion. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed real \(p\in(2,\infty)\), does there exist a finite constant \(C_p\ge1\) such that every finite metric space \((X,d)\) admits a map \(F:X\to\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) and a scale \(s>0\) satisfying \(s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\le W_p(F(x),F(y))\le C_p s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\) for all \(x,y\in X\)? The constant may depend on p but must be independent of X, its number of points and its distances.
definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. Results allowing the distortion or base-space dimension to grow with |X|, or using exponent 1/p instead of 1/2, do not settle it. No optimal numerical value of C_p is requested.
context:
The source proves almost-isometric universality at exponent 1/p. Question 23 of the full journal paper asks for bounded distortion at the larger exponent 1/2 when p>2. This restores the mathematical expression lost from the saved extraction.

Allowing a different, arbitrarily large distortion bound for each finite metric would remove the central uniformity requirement. The proposed C_p depends only on the fixed Wasserstein exponent.

The source separately raises almost-isometric half-snowflake embeddings, embeddings of the entire Wasserstein-2 space into Wasserstein-p space, and sharp lower bounds above exponent 1/2. Those are not substituted for this finite-distortion conjecture.

The 2024 paper relates coarse embeddability and 1/p-snowflake universality for Wasserstein space over R² to persistence diagrams. Its stated results do not supply half-snowflake universality in R³ for p>2.
why: Asks how richly a fixed three-dimensional transport space can represent arbitrary finite metric geometry after taking square roots of distances. The proposed exponent would improve the known universality range beyond what follows directly from the transport-cost exponent.
status_note: Read the conference equation, the full journal definitions and Question 23, and the later publisher full-text results on planar snowflake universality. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of bounded-distortion half-snowflake universality for every p>2 in P_p(R³). The extraction’s apparent p before d was the square-root sign, not an exponent or coefficient.
progress: 2016: The ICALP paper proves 1/p-snowflake universality and states the bounded-distortion half-snowflake conjecture in equation (25). | 2018: The full journal treatment retains the conjecture as Question 23, equation (52), while proving sharpness of the known exponent for 1<p≤2. | 2024-06-26: Later work establishes planar Wasserstein/persistence-diagram relationships for coarse embeddings and 1/p-snowflake universality, a different target.
working_summary: The question asks whether every finite metric becomes a bounded-distortion subset of Wasserstein p-space over R³ after taking square roots of its distances. The exponent p is fixed above two, and the distortion bound must depend only on p. The known theorem works at snowflake exponent 1/p, which is smaller than one half in this range. Almost-isometric embeddings and embedding the entire Wasserstein-2 space are separate stronger questions. The later planar results checked here do not settle this three-dimensional half-snowflake conjecture.

title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
importance_reason: A foundational low-dimensional decidability boundary linking computational topology and balanced group presentations. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?
question_excerpt: Hence, any pair of contractible 2-complexes can be connected by a simple-homotopy equivalence of dimension at most four – but determining whether we can always […]
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.
context:
The source explicitly asks about deciding whether a two-dimensional complex admits a simple-homotopy equivalence to a point. Its separate parameterized problems bound expansions or ask to reach a graph; those are different computational tasks.

The source relates this decidability question to recognizing the trivial group from balanced finite presentations, which have the same number of defining relators and generators. Undecidability of the corresponding problem for arbitrary presentations cannot simply be transferred to this restriction. Likewise, a trivial fundamental group alone does not make every two-dimensional complex contractible.

The stable geometric Andrews–Curtis question asks whether every contractible two-dimensional complex can reach a point using moves of dimension at most three. Here the unknown is whether an algorithm can always decide contractibility, with higher-dimensional intermediate complexes allowed. The source recalls that dimension four already suffices when a contraction exists.

The 2023/2024 random simple-homotopy paper gives practical simplification methods and successful examples while explicitly retaining the open low-dimensional decidability question. A heuristic that finds reductions on many contractible inputs does not provide a halting, correct procedure for every input.
why: This is a basic boundary of algorithmic topology: whether a finite two-dimensional description admits any reliable procedure for recognizing a space with no nontrivial homotopy. It separates unrestricted computability from practical simplification and from resource-bounded versions of topological reduction.
status_note: Read the full source introduction, elementary-move definitions and the complete page-four continuation. Checked the full later random simple-homotopy introduction and searched through 12 September 2026. No decision or undecidability theorem for arbitrary finite two-dimensional contractibility was found. Search results on contracting a loop inside a fixed complex, general fundamental-group triviality and Andrews–Curtis examples concern different tasks.
progress: 2019: The source distinguishes open contractibility recognition from its parameterized expansion-budget problems. | 2023-10-28: Random simple-homotopy methods are published online, with the dimension-two and dimension-three decidability questions still stated as open.
working_summary: The input is a finite simplicial complex made of vertices, edges and triangles. Decide whether expansions and collapses can transform it into a single vertex. Intermediate complexes may be larger and higher-dimensional than the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct answer on every input, but no efficiency bound is imposed. This recognition problem differs from limiting expansions to dimension three or using collapses alone.

title: Linear-size sample compression
importance_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
focus_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
question_excerpt: Does every class of finite VC dimension admit sample compression whose number of retained labeled examples and side-information bits is bounded linearly in that dimension?
definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.
context:
The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.
why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The April 2026 primary graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture; its structured width-dependent results and the 2024 embedding obstruction do not settle this target. arXiv:2603.23561v4 remains withdrawn, with an incorrect Lemma 2 proof identified by the authors. A bounded later-work search found no matching resolution. The model retains unordered labeled subsets and counted side bits, with no computational or properness restriction.
progress: 1986–2003: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions. | 2015–2016: Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general \(2^{O(d)}\) bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016. | 2024: Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself. | 2026-04-03: Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open. | 2026-08-03: The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the unordered-kernel and side-information models, the 2016 theorem, the 2024 embedding obstruction, the April 2026 structured results and the current withdrawal notice. A bounded later-work search found no matching general linear bound or counterexample.
working_summary: Sample compression keeps labeled examples and a short side message from which a fixed decoder recovers every original training label. The conjecture asks for a bound linear in VC dimension, uniformly across all Boolean concept classes. This card counts both retained examples and side bits, and permits arbitrary predictors and unlimited computation. The general known upper bound is exponential, while recent structured results and an embedding obstruction do not close that gap. A complete Lean answer must prove the universal linear bound or rule it out for some classes, and the withdrawn 2026 claim supplies no resolution.

title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
focus_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
question_excerpt: Can the hidden binary parity vector be recovered in polynomial time from uniformly random examples with any fixed independent noise rate below one half?
definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.
context:
Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.
why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.
status_note: The checked classical and 2026 primary literature does not provide a matching polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional impossibility for every fixed rational constant noise rate. The May amplification changes parameters; the September worst-case reduction is conditional on a joint code/dual-code hardness premise. The 15 September optical paper’s publisher abstract reports finite structured sparse-constraint experiments, not the stated general guarantee; its full PDF was inaccessible through the publisher gateway. The rate-dependent polynomial convention, classical independent samples and exact every-secret recovery target are retained. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 justify uncertain current status rather than proof of continued openness.

title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
importance_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
focus_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
question_excerpt: Can every Boolean function depending on at most k unknown coordinates be learned from independent uniform examples in time polynomial in n, 2^k and inverse error?
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
context:
A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the user-approved consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.
why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

The inherited OpenReview pointer was identified on 16 September 2026 as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields; its full theorem has a positive random-smoothing premise, with probability over that perturbation and the stated graph/width conditions. The checked May 2026 theorem uses correlated lazy-random-walk examples. Neither matches the exact passive uniform model. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no general learner or unconditional lower bound for the retained universal polynomial target, so current status remains uncertain.

title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
importance_reason: A defining computational learning problem originating with the PAC framework, explicitly highlighted in successive surveys and connected to representation-independent learning hardness, decision-tree learning and junta learning. Selected for the Learning theory focus prefix after correcting the mislabelled junta record; the score reflects breadth and foundational significance, not the date of this review.
focus_reason: A defining improper PAC-learning question for compact Boolean rules under arbitrary input distributions, with broad consequences for decision-tree and junta learning. The general target and its conditional-hardness evidence are now stated precisely.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
question_excerpt: The inherited question comes from the first paragraph of Feldman’s 2012 introduction: polynomial-time PAC learning of polynomial-size DNFs from random examples under an arbitrary unknown distribution. The retained size-sensitive statement permits improper learning. The integer learning parameters, explicit circuit syntax and charged example-access convention specify that target rather than adding query access or restricting the hypothesis to DNF.
definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.
context:
A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.
why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 survey retains the distribution-free computational gap. The 2016 and 2021 improper-learning lower bounds retain random-SAT or local-PRG assumptions. Current 2025/2026 exact-query, property-testing and PQ-learning results have different access, output, distribution or runtime guarantees. No verified unconditional solution of the retained target was found in bounded primary-source checks; recent proofs were not independently certified.

working_summary: A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of possibly negated Boolean variables, with the number of terms bounded by the supplied size parameter. The learner sees only independent noiseless labeled examples from an arbitrary unknown distribution and must run in one polynomial in dimension, term bound and the stated accuracy/confidence parameters. Its output may be any explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit whose predictions have small distributional error with high probability. Polynomial sample complexity is available, while known improper-learning lower bounds remain conditional and recent positive results use restricted distributions, stronger query access or different output guarantees. A solution needs a complete Lean proof of the full uniform learner guarantee or a negation covering every allowed learner and polynomial bound.

title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
importance_reason: A central unresolved efficiency threshold for spherical mixture parameter learning, with a clear separation between global initialization and statistically efficient local refinement.
formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
question_excerpt: At the well-separated spherical-Gaussian regime of the paper, can parameter learning from unlabeled samples use both polynomial time and polynomial sample complexity?
definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.
context:
Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.
why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.
status_note: The source’s selected §4.3 question concerns a global polynomial-time algorithm at square-root-logarithmic separation, while Theorem9 supplies the parameter metric and a statistically efficient but potentially inefficient procedure. The strongest directly checked later polynomial-time identity-covariance result uses log^{1/2+c}(k) separation with fixed c>0. Low-dimensional Fourier results, the 2026 slow-characteristic-function family excluding Gaussians, and newer nonspherical clustering bounds do not match the full target. No matching resolution was found in this bounded review through 16 September 2026; current status remains uncertain rather than a proved assertion of openness. The public bound parameters and exact-real arithmetic convention are explicit and are not claimed equivalent to a finite-bit interface.

title: Fully polynomial learning of halfspace intersections under Gaussian and uniform inputs
importance_reason: A central distribution-specific learning problem for conjunctions of linear thresholds, connecting geometric prediction and Boolean learning; both variable intersection size and inverse accuracy are essential to the unresolved efficiency target.
formal: Resolve the following two distribution-specific questions, separately. For \(D_n=\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(D_n=U_n\), the uniform measure on \(\{-1,+1\}^n\), does there exist a uniform randomized learner \(A_D\) and constants \(B_D,C_D\ge1\) such that, for all integers \(n,k\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and all intersections \(f\) of at most \(k\) affine halfspaces, \(A_D(n,k,t)\), using only independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D_n\), outputs a predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23\] in total training, output-writing and evaluation cost at most \(B_D(n+k+t)^{C_D}\)? The Gaussian branch uses the explicit real-arithmetic convention below; the Boolean-cube branch uses bit computation. The learner may be improper. Both the number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy are variable parameters: a polynomial whose exponent depends on \(k\) or \(t\) does not answer either branch affirmatively. A full resolution reports an answer to each branch, rather than treating failure of one as a classification of both.
question_excerpt: Can intersections of a variable number of halfspaces be learned in time polynomial in dimension, number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy under Gaussian inputs or uniform Boolean-cube inputs?
definitions:
An affine halfspace has Boolean value \(+1\) when \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i+b\ge0\), and value \(-1\) otherwise, for arbitrary real \(w_1,\ldots,w_n,b\). Its boundary is included in the positive side. An intersection has value \(+1\) exactly when all its component inequalities hold; otherwise it has value \(-1\). The intersection with no components is the constant positive function. All coefficients and the number of nonredundant inequalities are hidden; only the upper bound \(k\) is supplied. No coefficient-size, margin, balance or homogeneity promise is added. On the cube, the function is simply the restriction of those inequalities to the finite domain; their real coefficients are not input strings whose sizes the learner must read.

\(\gamma_n\) has independent standard normal coordinates, with joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\). Under \(U_n\), each of the \(2^n\) sign vectors has mass \(2^{-n}\). The appropriate distribution is known to its learner, but the target is unknown. Each example is an independent draw with the exact noiseless target label. The learner cannot ask for labels at chosen points, inspect the target description, or query conditional distributions. The inner probability is disagreement on a fresh example; the outer probability includes training examples and the learner’s random coins. The error tolerance is \(\varepsilon=1/t\), with integer \(t\) supplied in unary together with \(n,k\). These reciprocal tolerances define arbitrary requested accuracy up to a constant factor without introducing an uncounted rational encoding length. Confidence is fixed at \(2/3\); neither branch promises perfect recovery of coefficients.

For the cube, \(A_U\) is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a source of independent fair bits and an example tape. Writing a labeled example costs \(n+1\) bit operations. The output is an ordinary finite acyclic Boolean circuit, using AND, OR and NOT gates and constants, evaluated on the input signs encoded as bits. Training, reading, output length, and worst-case output evaluation time are all counted. The polynomial bound must hold on every sample and coin history. The same program and constants must work for every \(n,k,t,f\), with no advice depending on input length.

For the Gaussian branch, use one finite real-register program whose fixed constants are rational. Copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with an explicit zero-denominator guard, comparison, branching, and generating a fair bit have unit cost; discrete control, register access and output writing are also charged. Loading one exact labeled Gaussian vector costs \(n+1\) units. Integer control and the unary public parameters do not supply any infinite advice. There is no floor or digit extraction, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or oracle deciding general real-number properties. The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit with constants computed during training and a total Boolean sign output. Every division must be guarded so evaluation is defined on every input. Its stored constants, instructions and worst-case evaluation operations are counted in the same polynomial bound; it requires no further target access. This permits any such efficiently evaluable predictor, including ones outside the intersection class. All these predictors are Borel measurable.

The real-arithmetic convention explicitly fills the source’s unspecified continuous-input cost interface. Exact Gaussian coordinates need not have finite binary representations, so this branch does not silently claim an equivalent finite-bit learning theorem. Conversely the discrete branch uses actual bit costs and Boolean outputs. A result stated in a different computational model must justify the transfer before it resolves the corresponding branch. Independent programs and constants for the two branches are allowed; each program must be uniform over its own parameters.
answer_criterion: Give Lean proofs deciding the displayed uniform-existence proposition for each of \(D=\gamma\) and \(D=U\). A positive proof supplies one learner, universal polynomial constants, termination/resource bounds, a valid finite predictor and the learning guarantee for every parameter and target. A negative proof negates that full existence statement: for every candidate learner and polynomial constants, show a violating parameter/target or resource requirement. A conditional lower bound proves only the corresponding implication unless its assumption is also established. A restriction to statistical-query learners, proper hypotheses, fixed \(k\), a positive margin or a different sample source does not by itself resolve these propositions. State the model transfer for any invoked bound. The answer is a pair of exact truth values; no numerical approximation or unspecified asymptotic exponent counts as a resolution.
context:
The selected question is in the related-work discussion of the 2025 paper. Its antecedent distributions are Gaussian inputs and the uniform Boolean cube. The original card title mentioned factorizable distributions, which describe the surrounding paper’s main two-halfspace margin theorem; that title did not describe the selected question. The revised title restores the source scope.

An individual linear inequality is a simple classifier. An intersection accepts only points satisfying every inequality, while a rejected example does not say which condition failed. The desired learner receives labeled examples and may output any efficient predictor, rather than having to reconstruct the hidden inequalities.

The 2025 paper’s main result assumes two component halfspaces, a positive data margin, and a factorization relative to the subspace of relevant directions. Those are additional promises. Its theorem therefore does not resolve the separate question about a variable number of arbitrary affine halfspaces under the two known distributions.

Alman–Patel–Servedio’s 2026 Theorem 1 learns arbitrary Boolean functions of \(k\) halfspaces from random examples under any distribution in time \(\operatorname{poly}(2^{\sqrt n(\log n)^{O(k)}},1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta))\). The paper specifically notes the previously missing subexponential bound for two halfspaces on the uniform cube at \(\varepsilon=1/n\). This is substantial progress, but the displayed bound is not polynomial in \(n,k,1/\varepsilon\).

The STOC 2026 Gaussian sparsification theorem has learning applications for intersections with bounded geometric width, meaning the defining hyperplanes have a bounded distance from the origin in its stated representation. Its constants depend on width and accuracy. That result does not supply a single polynomial bound for arbitrary thresholds and arbitrary accuracy in the current question.

The May 2026 proper agnostic learner for Gaussian functions of halfspaces also includes realizable labels as a special case. However its dimension exponent depends on the number of halfspaces and inverse error, and it has an additional parameter-dependent term. The output restriction is stronger than needed here, but the running-time guarantee does not meet the fully polynomial target.
why: Simple independent input coordinates do not identify which inequality caused a negative label. The question asks whether that ambiguity creates a computational barrier even when the distribution is completely known. Its uniform dependence on the number of inequalities and desired accuracy separates practical polynomial learning from algorithms efficient only for fixed parameters.

Through 16 September 2026, the checked primary results include Alman–Patel–Servedio’s subexponential distribution-free learner (v2, July), bounded-geometric-width Gaussian learning applications, and a proper agnostic Gaussian learner with nonconstant parameter-dependent exponents. None supplies a checked fully polynomial answer for both source questions. This is an uncertain current-status assessment, not a proof of openness. The Gaussian exact-real convention and discrete bit convention are explicit; a theorem in a different cost model requires a justified transfer.
