The learner receives independent noiseless examples under any input distribution and must output a small ordinary Boolean predictor. A one-way function is uniformly easy to evaluate but has negligible inversion probability for every efficient uniform adversary at all sufficiently large lengths. Known reverse connections impose efficiently sampled targets, low computational depth, different learning-length quantifiers or a different description-approximation problem. The completed card preserves the unrestricted implication and records those distinctions while leaving its current status uncertain.

title: Nontrivial agnostic membership-query learning of \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)
importance_reason: A foundational algorithmic boundary for ACC⁰, connecting expressive constant-depth modular circuits with strong agnostic query learning. The source identifies the class as beyond the current learning frontier even in the easier realizable uniform-input setting.
formal: Can polynomial-size constant-depth modular circuits be agnostically learned under uniform inputs using membership queries in time \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\)? Precisely, for every fixed depth bound \(d\ge1\), fixed modulus \(m\ge2\), and fixed integer size exponent \(k\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized oracle Turing machine \(A_{d,m,k}\), an integer \(n_0\), and a saving function \(\sigma:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\sigma(n)/\log_2 n\to\infty\) and the following holds? For every \(n\ge n_0\) and every joint distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\times\{-1,+1\}\) whose first marginal is uniform, \(A_{d,m,k}\), given \(1^n\) and the conditional-label oracle described below, runs in worst-case time at most \(2^{n-\sigma(n)}\) and outputs a hypothesis \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{corr}_D(h)\ge \max_{c\in\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)}\operatorname{corr}_D(c)-2^{-n^{99/100}}\right]\ge\frac13,\qquad \operatorname{corr}_D(g):=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim D}[g(x)y].\] All machine coins and oracle responses are included in this probability. The success constant \(1/3\) is the literal consequence of the source’s full-learning convention \(1-\delta\) and its assignment \(\delta=2/3\); it is recorded explicitly rather than silently exchanged with the separate weak-learning convention.
question_excerpt: Is there a nontrivial agnostic membership-query learner for ACC⁰, even with uniformly distributed unlabelled examples?
definitions:
An \(\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)\) circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with \(n\) input bits, constants, unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and unbounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gate returns one exactly when the number of its one-valued inputs is divisible by \(m\). There are at most \(d\) gates along each input-to-output path and at most \(n^k\) internal gates and wires in total. Its output bit is converted to \(-1,+1\) by \(b\mapsto2b-1\). Fix an effective binary encoding of gates and their ordered incoming wires. These fixed-depth, fixed-modulus, polynomial-size classes give the usual \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) target when the fixed parameters vary. Gate-count versus wire-count conventions change polynomial size exponents only; the question quantifies over every exponent. The parameters are fixed before input length and may determine the learner and its saving; neither depth nor modulus grows with \(n\). Hidden comparator circuits may be chosen independently at different lengths and need not form a uniformly constructible family. No target circuit description is given to the learner.

The joint distribution \(D\) is otherwise arbitrary. For each chosen query \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), the oracle returns one fresh label sampled from \(D(Y\mid X=z)\), independently of its earlier samples conditional on the submitted queries. Queries may adapt to previous answers, and repeated queries need not agree. The uniform marginal gives every \(z\) positive probability, so all conditional label distributions are defined. Labels may be deterministic, stochastic, noisy, or inconsistent with every comparator circuit; no realizability promise is made. The learner knows the uniform marginal and can itself draw uniform inputs. It has no sampler description for the label probabilities, equivalence oracle, circuit advice, or oracle access to an optimal comparator. Correlation lies in \([-1,1]\), and the maximum exists because the comparator set is finite and nonempty. For \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued functions, zero-one error equals \((1-\operatorname{corr})/2\); thus the displayed correlation slack is excess prediction error at most \(2^{-n^{99/100}}/2\), rather than a multiplicative approximation to optimum error.

The output is a finite description of an ordinary Boolean circuit with AND, OR and NOT gates, interpreted as \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,+1\}\). The hypothesis need not be an ACC circuit, have depth \(d\), or have size \(n^k\); this is improper learning. Its description is counted in the learner’s running time, and it is evaluated without further training queries. Using ordinary finite circuits makes the usual effectively evaluable hypothesis convention explicit. All query writing and reading, fair random bits, bit computation and output writing count toward worst-case running time; one submitted label is one oracle response, and the oracle’s internal generation cost is not charged. Consequently the number of queries is bounded by the same time. There is no real-arithmetic unit-cost computation in the learner. The exponential accuracy threshold is a mathematical success condition fixed by \(n\), not an exact irrational input that must be encoded or compared by the machine.

The expression \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\) means that a single learner for each fixed \((d,m,k)\) has a saving \(\sigma(n)\) whose ratio to \(\log_2 n\) tends to infinity: for every real \(B>0\), eventually \(\sigma(n)\ge B\log_2 n\). The saving is a runtime-bound witness, not an additional oracle or input. Finite exceptional lengths are allowed. A fixed-factor improvement or division by one fixed power of \(n\) is insufficient. Polynomial factors in an otherwise qualifying time can be absorbed into a smaller saving with the same limit. No efficient procedure for constructing the learner uniformly from the fixed depth, modulus and size exponent is additionally requested.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence statement, or of its full logical negation: some fixed \((d,m,k)\) admits no uniform learner with the stated eventual superlogarithmic saving and correlation guarantee simultaneously for all uniform-marginal label distributions. A positive answer must meet the specified shrinking accuracy, the literal full-learning success constant, the conditional-query interface and worst-case total time, including a finite evaluable output. Constant-error learning, realizable-only learning, a fixed polynomial-factor saving or a multiplicative optimum-error factor does not meet this agnostic target. A lower bound against a restricted query method or a conditional cryptographic obstruction is not the unconditional negation unless the additional assumption is also proved. This is an exact asymptotic yes/no statement, not a request to approximate a numerical quantity.
context:
Agnostic learning compares the returned predictor with the best member of a chosen circuit class, while allowing the observed labels to be generated by an arbitrary process. Membership queries let the learner choose which input is labeled; they do not reveal a target circuit or guarantee that an exact circuit representation exists. The original paper fixes both the extremely small correlation slack and the confidence parameter when defining its nontrivial-time problem.

The source explicitly states that the ACC⁰ problem is open even with uniform inputs and even without the agnostic requirement. This card retains the agnostic question selected in its title and records the source’s uniform-input version. It does not replace the comparator by only prime-modulus circuits or by a restricted family of symmetric-polynomial gates.

Carmosino–Impagliazzo–Kabanets–Kolokolova obtain quasipolynomial-time query learning for prime-modulus AC⁰[q] with a polylogarithmic multiplicative factor on optimum error. That is a meaningful earlier result, but both the restricted modulus and the multiplicative error criterion differ from full ACC⁰ agnostic learning with the additive slack specified here.

Karchmer’s positive results treat several circuit classes built from restricted low-degree threshold or symmetric-polynomial functions. Those classes include functions outside earlier families, but the published statement does not contain all polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuits. The paper separately identifies that missing full class as a frontier question.

The full-learning definition gives success at least 1−δ and then sets δ to 2/3. The separate weak-learner definition uses success at least 2/3. These are distinct displays in the source. This record preserves the literal full-learning guarantee 1/3 and marks the convention explicitly; it does not assume a typographical correction or silently use the weak definition as the target.

The original arXiv record still lists only its November 2023 version, and the checked published ALT 2024 text contains the question. Bounded later-work searches through September 2026 found no matching theorem, but that search is not a proof of continued openness. Current status is therefore recorded as uncertain.
why: Constant-depth circuits with modular gates are a central boundary class in circuit complexity. The question asks whether their predictive structure can be exploited even when labels need not come from that class and the learner may choose its queries. The requested saving must beat every fixed polynomial factor relative to the exponential scale while retaining the source’s high-accuracy guarantee.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked ALT 2024 source, including the easier realizable uniform-input case. The completed statement preserves the selected agnostic version and the source’s fixed epsilon=2^(-n^0.99), superlogarithmic saving and literal delta=2/3 assignment (success 1/3); its separate weak-learner display has success 2/3. The prime-modulus multiplicative-error result does not match. Live version history and bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain.
progress: 2017: Prime-modulus AC⁰[q] receives a quasipolynomial-time membership-query algorithm with a multiplicative polylogarithmic optimum-error factor. | 2023–2024: The source gives full agnostic nontrivial-time algorithms for restricted circuit classes and explicitly identifies ACC⁰ as beyond the known uniform-input learning frontier. | 2026-09-16: Checked the exact source query model, superlogarithmic saving, exponentially small correlation slack and the inconsistent-looking full/weak confidence conventions. The literal full-learning constant is retained, and no matching later resolution was located in bounded checks.
working_summary: The card asks whether constant-depth modular circuits admit agnostic membership-query learning with a superpolynomial-factor saving over exponential time. Inputs are uniform, labels may be arbitrary and stochastic, and each chosen query receives a fresh conditional label. The target keeps the source’s exponentially small correlation slack and its literal one-third full-learning success guarantee. Known positive results restrict the circuit class or relax the optimum-error comparison and do not establish the full ACC⁰ target. A Lean answer must prove the complete uniform algorithmic assertion or its unconditional negation under these exact resource and accuracy conventions.

title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
importance_reason: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
question_excerpt: Can every polynomial-size Boolean decision tree be learned in polynomial time from independent uniformly random labeled examples, with no restriction that the output remain a tree?
definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.
context:
Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.
why: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
status_note: Explicitly unresolved in the checked 2008 source and ITCS 2025 §6. The later 2025 survey retains the related uniform-example computational barriers. The checked May 2026 product-space paper uses chosen-input label queries and gives a depth-dependent size bound; its theorem is not the requested passive fully polynomial learner. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain. Existing all-node size, unrestricted circuit output, fixed confidence and the consolidated source scope are preserved.
progress: 2008: Kalai–Teng give a polynomial-time improper learner with high probability over perturbed product-distribution means, while explicitly retaining the fixed uniform-example question. | 2025-01: The backdoor-defense paper restates the sample-only question and proves a representation-aware defense theorem with a different input interface. | 2025-11: Servedio’s survey records the quasipolynomial uniform DNF upper bound and the junta obstacle for fully polynomial learning. | 2026-05: Decision Tree Learning on Product Spaces analyzes a query-based greedy learner with depth-dependent output size; §3 explicitly supplies chosen-input labels. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the two inherited sources and newer learning results, preserving all-node size, improper output and passive independent examples. No matching resolution was located in bounded later-work checks.
working_summary: The card asks for a polynomial-time learner for every small Boolean decision tree from independent uniform labeled examples. The tree is hidden and the learner receives neither chosen-input labels nor its representation. A successful learner may return any efficient Boolean circuit with the requested prediction error and two-thirds confidence. Known smoothed, query-based and representation-aware results provide different guarantees and do not settle this passive learning target. The completed card preserves its importance and scope while making the accuracy encoding, resource bounds and full Lean proof criterion explicit.

title: Sample-optimal Gaussian graphical model learning in polynomial time
importance_reason: A basic statistical-computational question for sparse Gaussian models, distinguished by the absence of spectral assumptions and the exact graph-recovery objective; it now has substantive conditional separation evidence.
formal: Can general Gaussian conditional-independence graphs be learned in uniform polynomial time using, up to a universal constant factor, the information-theoretically optimal number of independent observations? For integers \(p\ge2\), \(1\le d\le p-1\), \(r\ge2\), and rational \(0<\kappa<1\), let \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) be the Gaussian family defined below and let \(m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\) be its minimax sample count for exact graph recovery with failure probability at most \(2^{-r}\), allowing unrestricted measurable estimators. Is there one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,B,a\ge1\) such that, for every parameter choice and every \(P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\), \(A(p,d,\kappa,r)\) returns its exact graph with probability at least \(1-2^{-r}\), draws at most \(\lceil C m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\rceil\) independent samples, and uses at most \[B\bigl(p+d+\lceil\kappa^{-1}\rceil+r+L\bigr)^a\] real-arithmetic operations, including sample loading and output, where \(L\) is the binary encoding length of \(\kappa\)? The exponent and constants must be independent of every parameter and of the unknown distribution. This retains the general sample-optimal computational question from the source’s conclusion; bounded-degree recovery is already treated there. The minimax definition does not presume that the commonly quoted \(d\log p/\kappa^2\) sample scale is sharp in all joint parameter regimes.
question_excerpt: Can the information-theoretically optimal independent-sample count for general Gaussian graph recovery be attained by a polynomial-time algorithm?
definitions:
A member \(P\) of \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\) is arbitrary, \(\Sigma\) is a real symmetric positive definite \(p\times p\) covariance matrix, and \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is its precision matrix. Its undirected graph has vertices \([p]=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and an edge \(\{i,j\}\), for \(i\ne j\), exactly when \(\Theta_{ij}\ne0\). Every vertex has at most \(d\) neighbors, and every edge satisfies \[\frac{|\Theta_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\ge\kappa.\] This normalized precision entry is the magnitude of the corresponding partial correlation. For an empty graph the edge condition holds vacuously. The parameters are upper and lower promises, not assertions that degree equals \(d\) or minimum strength equals \(\kappa\). No eigenvalue, condition-number, variance, sign-pattern, incoherence, faithfulness, treewidth or walk-summability restriction is imposed. The learner is not given \(\mu,\Sigma,\Theta\), or a graph representation.

An observation is an entire vector \(X\in\mathbb R^p\) drawn from \(P\); observations are independent and identically distributed. The graph-recovery loss is zero exactly when all off-diagonal zero/nonzero decisions are correct, and one otherwise. Estimating covariance entries to a numerical tolerance is a different task. The probability in the guarantee includes the observations and internal randomness. The public failure tolerance is \(2^{-r}\); allowing all integers \(r\ge2\) keeps confidence variable. The graph output is its \(p\times p\) symmetric binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal.

For a fixed \((p,d,\kappa,r)\), define \(m^*\) as the least nonnegative integer \(m\) for which some Borel-measurable randomized estimator from \((\mathbb R^p)^m\) to the finite set of labeled undirected graphs satisfies \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)}\Pr_{X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P}[\widehat G(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=G(P)]\ge1-2^{-r}.\] Randomization is an independent infinite fair-bit sequence, and the estimator must be measurable jointly in data and that sequence. It may depend arbitrarily on the four public parameters and has no computation bound; this defines an information benchmark, not a computational oracle. If the set of such sample counts were empty, set \(m^*=+\infty\); known finite sample upper bounds exclude that case for this family. The target algorithm receives neither \(m^*\) nor an optimal estimator. Its sample limit must hold on every possible observation and coin history, even if it adaptively decides when to stop. Padding an early stop with unused observations makes comparison with fixed-size estimators unambiguous.

Computation uses an explicitly chosen standard exact-real arithmetic convention. One finite uniform register program has rational constants in its code, discrete control and fair random bits. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\), comparison, branching and each control or output operation cost one unit; any division must be guarded at a zero denominator. Loading one observed vector costs \(p\) units. The algorithm outputs only finite bits for the adjacency matrix. It has no access to conditional samples, a Markov transition trajectory, matrix entries of the unknown distribution, exact expectations, optimization oracles, arbitrary real advice, floor/digit extraction, or an oracle deciding general real-number properties. The positive integers \(p,d,r\) are public unary inputs and \(\kappa\) is supplied by positive coprime binary numerator and denominator, with total bit length \(L\). Reading and translating these inputs are counted. The displayed worst-case operation bound applies to all sample and random-bit histories, not just in expectation.

This convention makes the source’s continuous-observation computational question precise without asserting equivalence to finite-bit Gaussian data. Exact Gaussian coordinates are generally not finite binary strings; the source does not prescribe a rounding budget. In particular, allowing arbitrary condition numbers in the distribution is material to numerical implementation. Any finite-precision result, or computational hardness assumption in another machine model, needs a justified relation to this arithmetic convention before it resolves the displayed proposition. Polynomial time means a single fixed exponent for variable \(d\); \(p^{O(d)}\) is insufficient. Sample optimality means a universal multiplicative factor, with no suppressed dependence on \(d,\kappa,r\) or logarithmic loss.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the existence proposition or its full negation. An affirmative result must supply one uniform algorithm and constants, prove exact graph recovery over the entire promised Gaussian family, prove the universal constant-factor comparison with the defined information-theoretic minimum, and verify worst-case sample and arithmetic-time bounds. A negative result must rule out every such learner and constants on some allowed parameters or distribution. A conditional computational obstruction remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A \(p^{O(d)}\) method, a result only for a fixed degree, a polynomial-time method using more than a universal-factor sample overhead, or a theorem with extra spectral/sign assumptions does not suffice. Neither does learning from a Glauber trajectory establish the independent-observation guarantee. A closed form for \(m^*\) is useful but is not assumed in advance; any claimed closed form must be proved uniformly in its stated regime. The answer is an exact yes/no theorem, not a numerical estimate of a covariance matrix.
context:
The graph records conditional dependence, not merely pairwise correlation: an edge is determined by a nonzero entry of the inverse covariance matrix. Strong correlations and poor conditioning are allowed. This explains why guarantees depending only on dimension, sparsity and normalized edge strength are stronger than many familiar covariance-estimation results.

The source’s DICE theorem gives exact recovery when \(m>2d+192\kappa^{-2}d\log p+64\kappa^{-2}\log(4d/\delta)\). Its neighborhood-search cost is \(O(p^{2d+1})\). Thus fixed-degree graphs have a polynomial-time guarantee, but the exponent is not uniform over growing degree.

The source explicitly qualifies statistical tightness when degree grows while minimum edge strength shrinks. Therefore its motivating abstract sentence cannot be read as an unresolved bounded-degree theorem, or its sample bound as a universally matching minimax formula. The current question retains the general computational issue using an explicit minimax benchmark.

Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Moitra provide fixed polynomial-time algorithms without condition-number bounds for attractive and walk-summable Gaussian models. These are genuine positive results for additional structural subclasses. Their assumptions do not cover every signed precision matrix in the present family.

COLT 2024 Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Rohatgi, Remark 43, gives conditional evidence of a sample-computation gap. Under its Conjecture 33 relating low-degree likelihood tests to polynomial-time detection for a spiked Wishart model, efficient general recovery would need nearly quadratic rather than linear dependence on sparsity in the relevant regime, even at constant normalized edge strength. The conjecture is not a proved theorem about arbitrary algorithms.

The hard family in that remark has covariance equal to identity plus a negative rank-one perturbation supported on a hidden sparse set. Exact graph recovery would distinguish it from the independent-coordinate null model. This is a stated reduction under a specific detection-hardness conjecture, not an unconditional archive-worthy impossibility. Its computational convention must also match any use against the real-arithmetic target.

The 2026 Shen–Wu–Majid–Moitra paper gives a polynomial-time method observing one Glauber trajectory, where coordinates are successively resampled conditional on the others. Its introduction still identifies efficient recovery from few independent samples as unresolved. A trajectory exposes update information that independent observations do not provide, so the newer theorem does not automatically answer the present question.
why: Sparse conditional dependence can be statistically identifiable even when variables are extremely correlated. Recovering that graph from few observations is useful only if the necessary search is computationally affordable. The problem asks whether uniformly efficient computation must pay an extra sample cost without regularity assumptions on the covariance.
status_note: The source already gives sample-efficient polynomial-time recovery for bounded degree, but with a degree-dependent runtime exponent. Its p4 discussion qualifies the claimed information-theoretic matching when degree and minimum edge strength vary together. The residual general question is therefore stated using a defined minimax independent-sample count, not an assumed uniformly tight d log p / kappa² formula. COLT 2024 Remark 43 gives a conditional statistical-computational gap under Conjecture 33; that assumption is not asserted true. A 2026 primary paper still distinguishes the independent-sample difficulty while solving a different Glauber-trajectory problem. No unconditional resolution of the displayed uniform arithmetic-time target was checked through 16 September 2026. Numerical precision and cross-model hardness transfers are explicitly not certified.
progress: 2020: DICE proves an explicit sample upper bound independent of condition number; its degree-dependent search is polynomial for bounded degree, with a stated caveat about statistical tightness for joint degree/strength scaling. | 2020: Fixed polynomial-time recovery without condition-number assumptions is obtained for attractive and walk-summable subclasses. | 2024: Remark 43 derives a GGM statistical-computational separation conditional on the specific low-degree/spiked-Wishart detection conjecture. | 2026-06: A new polynomial-time result uses a Glauber trajectory; the paper distinguishes the unresolved independent-sample problem. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the source’s theorem, caveat and final question; retained the unrestricted model, minimax sample definition and conditional nature of later hardness evidence.
working_summary: The problem asks whether sparse Gaussian conditional-independence graphs can be recovered in polynomial time with an information-theoretically optimal number of independent samples. The statement allows arbitrary means and condition numbers and requires every edge and nonedge to be identified correctly. Sample optimality is defined by a minimax benchmark that retains degree, normalized edge strength and confidence without assuming a universally sharp formula. Known degree-dependent algorithms, structural-subclass results, conditional hardness and trajectory-based algorithms each address a different part of the question. A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform algorithm with both a universal sample factor and a fixed polynomial arithmetic-time bound.

title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
importance_reason: Determine whether combining two elementary classifiers already defeats efficient distribution-free learning.
formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof constructing and bounding a learner under all the stated quantifiers, or a Lean proof that none exists. Proper-learning hardness and statistical-query lower bounds do not exclude all allowed learners. A margin promise, a restricted input distribution or membership queries would change the problem.
context:
A single halfspace is efficiently learnable, but combining only two thresholds introduces a longstanding computational obstacle. Allowing an arbitrary output representation avoids the known hardness of proper learning.

The existing TCS-6544 explicitly assumes a positive margin and polynomial dependence on its reciprocal. This candidate instead concerns unrestricted integer-weight thresholds on the Boolean cube. The distinction affects the running time and cannot be hidden behind their similar titles.
why: Determine whether combining two elementary classifiers already defeats efficient distribution-free learning.
status_note: The 2026 TheoretiCS source explicitly retains the fixed-two-halfspace polynomial-time question. A July 2026 subexponential-time preprint does not establish the requested polynomial bound. Checked through 13 September 2026 within a bounded literature review.
progress: 2009: The source distinguishes proper-learning hardness from the unresolved unrestricted-output learning question. | 2026-04-28: Tiegel’s published hardness result still describes polynomial-time learning of two halfspaces as open; its lattice-based bound concerns a growing number of halfspaces. | 2026-07-30: A later preprint gives subexponential-time learning for arbitrary Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces, without establishing polynomial time for the present two-halfspace target.
working_summary: One threshold is efficiently learnable from labeled examples, but the target here combines two thresholds. Examples follow any fixed distribution on the Boolean cube and no positive margin is promised. The learner receives a bound on target description length and may output any efficiently evaluable classifier. Hardness for proper learners or growing numbers of halfspaces does not settle this two-halfspace target. The question asks for a uniform polynomial-time guarantee across all distributions and permitted target descriptions.

title: PAC learning of finite automata under the uniform distribution
importance_reason: A classical computational-learning question about a basic representation class. The later conditional hardness on the uniform hypercube is a major clarification, and the distinctions between random examples, active queries, hidden-state information and improper prediction are fundamental.
formal: Are deterministic finite automata efficiently PAC learnable from independent uniformly distributed words and their acceptance bits? Use the ordinary finite-word, fixed-length uniform model. Does there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(L\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every alphabet size \(q\ge2\), word length \(n\ge1\), state bound \(s\ge1\), integers \(a,b\ge3\), and deterministic finite automaton \(M\) with at most \(s\) states over \(\Sigma_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), the following holds? Given \(1^q,1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((w,M(w))\) with \(w\sim U_{q,n}\), \(L\) runs in worst-case time at most \(p(q+n+s+a+b)\), and outputs a finite predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{L,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{w\sim U_{q,n}}[h(w)\ne M(w)]\le\frac1a\right]\ge1-\frac1b?\] The predictor may use any efficiently evaluable representation; it need not be an automaton. A 2021 theorem rules out this guarantee under a specified local-pseudorandom-generator assumption, already for binary alphabets. This card retains the unconditional algorithm-existence question, while recording that published conditional negative answer explicitly.
question_excerpt: Can deterministic finite automata be PAC learned efficiently under uniformly distributed words?
definitions:
A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple \(M=(\Sigma_q,Q,q_0,F,\tau)\) with a nonempty finite state set \(Q\), \(|Q|\le s\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), and a total transition function \(\tau:Q\times\Sigma_q\to Q\). Starting at \(q_0\), it reads the letters of a finite word from left to right and updates its current state by \(\tau\); \(M(w)=1\) exactly when its final state lies in \(F\), and otherwise \(M(w)=0\). The target transition table, states and accepting set are hidden. The public value \(s\) is an upper bound on the number of states, not the full target description. The source’s size convention is state count. A complete transition-table encoding has length polynomial in \(s\) and \(q\), so the explicit polynomial dependence on both parameters accounts for that representation.

\(U_{q,n}\) assigns probability \(q^{-n}\) to every word in \(\Sigma_q^n\); equivalently its \(n\) letters are independent and uniform in \(\Sigma_q\). Each oracle request supplies a fresh independent word and its deterministic acceptance bit under the same fixed \(M\). The learner may request more independent examples adaptively but cannot select the word to be labeled. It sees neither the final state nor the sequence of intermediate states. There are no membership queries, equivalence queries, counterexamples, nonuniform advice or random-target assumption. The guarantee must hold for every automaton, including arbitrarily chosen transition graphs and accepting sets. Randomness in the outer probability comes only from examples and the learner’s independent fair coins; the inner probability is error on a fresh uniform word. This is the realizable PAC model with noiseless labels. Parameters \(1/a\) and \(1/b\) range over inverse integers, which suffice to express every desired positive accuracy and failure tolerance by rounding downward.

For a concrete hypothesis interface, encode each letter in \(\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits and let the output be an ordinary Boolean circuit on the resulting \(n\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits. Its output on valid word encodings is \(h(w)\); values on unused letter codes are irrelevant. The circuit may use two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates with a fixed effective binary encoding. Its description is written within the learning-time bound and is evaluated without examples or access to the target. This expresses unrestricted improper efficient prediction: the output is not constrained to at most \(s\) states or to a minimal consistent automaton. Uniformly polynomial-time evaluable finite predictors have ordinary polynomial-size circuit representations under the usual bit-computation convention. All bit operations, reading examples, fair random bits and output writing count toward the one polynomial bound, as does the number of example requests. The example oracle supplies the promised distribution; its own sampling computation is not charged. The same machine and polynomial work for all displayed parameters, lengths and targets.

Uniformity refers to words of the specified length, not to an impossible probability measure assigning equal mass to all of \(\Sigma_q^*\). The learner may depend on the public \(n\), and its guarantee is only over words of that length. Exact identification of the complete infinite regular language, prediction simultaneously at every length by one output, geometric length mixtures, and real-valued limit-average behavior on infinite words are different tasks. The arbitrary-finite-alphabet convention follows the source’s DFA and \(U^n\) definitions; the later hardness theorem applies already when \(q=2\). Computational efficiency is essential: the question does not merely ask for a finite or polynomial information-theoretic sample bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(L,p\) with the complete uniform guarantee in Lean, or prove its logical negation: for every proposed machine and polynomial, some allowed parameters and target violate the runtime, finite-output or PAC condition. A positive answer must allow every target automaton and observe only independent acceptance-labeled uniform words. A result for random transition graphs, additional state labels, membership queries or only a fixed bounded state count does not meet the statement. A negative answer under the local-PRG assumption is a conditional theorem and must retain that premise; it does not by itself prove the unconditional negation. Hardness of finding a smallest consistent DFA also does not exclude an arbitrary efficient predictor. The yes/no assertion has exact logical quantifiers and rational error/confidence tolerances; no numerical optimum is being approximated.
context:
The 2019 source studies weighted limit-average automata, but its related-work paragraph cites Pitt’s older question about ordinary deterministic automata. The imported card refers to that ordinary Boolean acceptance problem. The paper’s own infinite-word impossibility and minimization results concern a different model and do not answer the selected question.

Knowing that every finite automaton has a finite transition table does not imply a polynomial learning algorithm. There are only finitely many targets at a fixed state bound, but computationally finding a useful predictor is a stronger requirement than having enough examples to identify one statistically. The target permits improper prediction and therefore does not ask for minimum-state reconstruction.

Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 proves a conditional obstruction substantially stronger than failure of high-accuracy PAC learning: for every constants c, η>0, no efficient learner achieves error at most 1/2−1/n^c for all n^η-state DFAs under the uniform distribution on n-bit words, under their Assumption 1. The learning model allows arbitrary efficiently evaluable hypotheses. Consequently the obstruction is not merely a lower bound for proper automaton reconstruction.

Assumption 1 is the existence of Goldreich-style local pseudorandom generators with every constant polynomial stretch: for each constant \(t>1\), some constant locality \(k\) and Boolean predicate \(P\) make the length-\(N^t\) output formed by applying \(P\) to independent random ordered \(k\)-tuples of distinct seed positions computationally indistinguishable from uniform with advantage at most \(1/3\). The chosen tuples are public to the polynomial-time distinguisher. This is an unproved computational assumption, not a consequence of merely defining a finite automaton or a uniform distribution. The exact security convention is the named Assumption 1 of the cited paper; it is not added as a premise of this card’s unconditional target.

The official ALT 2026 paper on learning regular expressions explicitly lists uniform-distribution DFA PAC hardness under its local-PRG Assumption C and attributes that result to Daniely–Vardi. Its additional regular-expression results concern a different succinct representation: equivalent languages can require exponentially different description sizes. Thus the 2026 table corroborates the conditional status rather than proving the cryptographic premise.

Angluin–Chen’s 2015 positive result assumes a random transition graph and access to information about the terminal state reached by a sampled word. The acceptance bit does not identify that state. Likewise, the known polynomial algorithms with membership and equivalence queries use more information than the sampling-only oracle in this card. These distinctions prevent positive results in richer observation models from being substituted for the target.

The historical source described the question as open in 2019; that summary is incomplete after the 2021 conditional hardness theorem. The present record makes this development prominent and keeps current unconditional status uncertain. It does not claim that an unproved local-PRG assumption has been established or that a bounded literature check proves continued unconditional openness.
why: Finite-state machines give very small descriptions of potentially complicated behavior on long strings. This question isolates whether uniformly random training words make that behavior computationally learnable from acceptance labels alone. It separates the simplicity of the sampling distribution from the difficulty of recovering a useful predictor.
status_note: The 2019 source’s open-status sentence predates Daniely–Vardi (COLT 2021), whose Theorem 12 gives a conditional negative answer under Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators, already for weak improper learning over the uniform Boolean hypercube. The official ALT 2026 Table 1 retains that premise. These full primary statements were checked on 16 September 2026. The card preserves the unconditional existence question and therefore remains active with uncertain unconditional status; the assumption is neither silently adopted nor asserted proved. Bounded checks found no unconditional matching resolution.
progress: 1989; recalled in 2019: The original source attributes the ordinary-DFA uniform-distribution PAC question to Pitt and distinguishes it from active-query learning. | 2015: Angluin–Chen obtain a positive result for random transition graphs with terminal-state information, a stronger observation interface than binary acceptance labels. | 2021: Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 rules out even inverse-polynomial-advantage improper weak learning on the uniform Boolean hypercube under their local-PRG Assumption 1. | 2026: The ALT regular-expression paper’s Table 1 explicitly cites the local-PRG-dependent uniform DFA hardness, separate from its own regular-expression results. | 2026-09-16: Checked the original DFA and finite-word uniform definitions, the full 2021 learning model and assumption/theorem, and the official 2026 table. The conditional negative answer is recorded without converting it into an unconditional archival resolution.
working_summary: The card asks whether every finite automaton can be learned efficiently from uniformly sampled words labeled only by acceptance. The learner knows the word length, alphabet and state bound and may return any efficient predictor. It must achieve every requested accuracy and confidence using polynomial time without membership queries or state information. A published local-pseudorandom-generator assumption rules out even weak improper learning on uniform binary words, and a 2026 source retains that premise. The completed card records this conditional negative answer while preserving the original unconditional question and its exact Lean decision criterion.

title: Optimal multiclass regret versus Littlestone dimension
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: The minimax regret of every multiclass hypothesis family tests whether Littlestone dimension alone captures online prediction difficulty, even with infinitely many labels.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the function \[R(d,T)=\sup\bigl\{R_T(H):\ X,Y\text{ nonempty sets},\ \varnothing\ne H\subseteq Y^X,\ \mathrm L(H)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(T\ge d\ge1\). The supremum permits infinite instance sets, infinite label sets and arbitrary hypothesis classes. For the prediction game defined below, \[R_T(H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in X\times Y}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T(1-p_t(y_t))-\min_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\}.\] Here \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\) is a probability distribution on labels. The infimum ranges over all causal prediction rules, without computational restrictions. Retain all logarithmic factors. This is the previously authorized quantitative reformulation of the source conjecture, which predicts \(R(d,T)=\Theta(\sqrt{dT})\).
question_excerpt: Does every multiclass hypothesis class have optimal online regret \(\Theta(\sqrt{\mathrm L(H)T})\), with universal constants?
definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) assigns a label from \(Y\) to each instance in \(X\). A depth-\(r\) Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels from \(Y\) on that node's outgoing edges; the pair of labels may vary by node. The tree is shattered if every root-to-leaf path has one fixed hypothesis agreeing with all its edge labels on its instance points. The dimension \(\mathrm L(H)\) is the largest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. On each round the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner supplies \(p_t\), and the adversary then reveals \(y_t\). The learner observes the actual label before the next round and is charged expected zero-one loss \(1-p_t(y_t)\). It does not observe future instances. The adversary may react to \(p_t\); loss is the displayed expectation, not a reaction to a sampled label. The sequence need not be realizable by any hypothesis. The comparator is one fixed hypothesis chosen in hindsight, whose minimum loss exists since the possible losses are integers from zero to \(T\). A distribution here is a function \(p:Y\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{y\in Y}p(y)=1\), with this sum defined as the supremum of sums over finite subsets. It automatically has at most countable positive support. This atomic convention does not increase the best possible regret relative to arbitrary probability measures with measurable singletons: any missing atom mass can be assigned to one fixed label, increasing no zero-one loss. All histories and rules are arbitrary set functions, so no topology or measurability structure on \(X,H\) is required. Rules may know \(H\) and \(T\), need not be proper, and have no runtime, memory, computability or finite-description bound. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Dimension zero means all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The range \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime because cumulative regret cannot exceed \(T\). All requested comparison constants must be independent of the instance and label spaces, class, dimension and horizon.
answer_criterion: Supply an explicit positive rate function \(g(d,T)\) of the two integer parameters and universal constants \(a,A>0\), and prove in Lean that \[a\,g(d,T)\le R(d,T)\le A\,g(d,T)\qquad(T\ge d\ge1).\] The rate must describe the parameter dependence, rather than merely rename the original game optimization. An upper bound must hold for every class in the supremum; a lower bound may choose a class separately for each parameter pair. If an extremum is not attained, approaching rules or classes suffice. The criterion allows a different sharp rate if the source's square-root conjecture fails. A bound conditional on class regularity, a constant depending on the label-space size, or a remaining logarithmic gap does not determine this unrestricted function. This requests constant-factor asymptotic precision in cumulative expected regret, not additive numerical error.
context:
The learner sees the current instance and then receives the correct label after predicting. It can distribute its prediction among labels, and is scored by expected mistakes relative to the best fixed hypothesis. Labels can contradict every member of the class. The regret target is therefore different from a realizable mistake bound.

The 2023 paper proves that finite Littlestone dimension characterizes agnostic multiclass online learnability even for unbounded label spaces. This general learnability theorem does not require the separate minimax regularity assumption used in its sharper finite-label result. The remaining rate question asks how far a learner must fall behind the best fixed concept.

The unrestricted argument in §3 gives regret at most \(\mathrm L(H)+\sqrt{(T/2)\mathrm L(H)\ln(eT/\mathrm L(H))}\) for positive dimension. In the stated horizon range this yields \(R(d,T)=O(\sqrt{dT\log(eT/d)})\). A universal lower scale is \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\). The logarithm is part of the unresolved gap and cannot be suppressed when asking for constant factors.

For a finite label set, Theorem 9 gives \(O(\sqrt{\mathrm L(H)T\log|Y|})\) under the additional minimax regularity condition explicitly stated in p. 9 footnote 4 for those results. Under that condition a fixed label count yields the square-root scale, but the coefficient grows with the count. Even for two labels, removing the condition for unrestricted classes is a separate open issue recorded by the source and by the 2025 thesis.

The previously approved quantitative target takes the worst minimax regret over classes of dimension at most d. It asks for the complete function, allowing a rate different from the source conjecture if necessary. This change of answer form remains explicit; no equivalence between an arbitrary sharp-rate answer and proving the conjectured square-root bound is asserted.

The checked May 2026 oracle-complexity paper concerns binary classification and retains logarithmic factors in its dimension-dependent regret statement. It improves resource use within an online algorithm and does not resolve the unrestricted multiclass constant-factor rate.
why: Would determine whether Littlestone dimension alone controls the exact minimax cost of multiclass sequential prediction, beyond the already known learnability characterization.
status_note: The source’s 2023 universal multiclass conjecture is retained as context for the previously authorized full minimax-rate target. The sharper finite-label theorem is qualified by its explicitly stated minimax condition; Raman’s 2025 thesis retains the unrestricted binary issue. The checked May 2026 binary oracle result retains logarithmic factors, and no matching unrestricted multiclass resolution was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026.
progress: 2023: The source proves general learnability and the unrestricted upper scale \(O(\sqrt{dT\log(eT/d)})\), compared with lower scale \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\), and poses the sharp square-root conjecture. | 2023: Its sharper finite-label upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\mathrm L(H)T\log|Y|})\) uses the additional minimax regularity condition specified in p. 9 footnote 4. | 2025: Raman’s dissertation repeats the qualification and states that the unrestricted binary square-root question remains open. | 2026-09-16: Targeted re-review corrected the omitted finite-label qualification, checked the source’s general theorem and exact game, and retained the previously authorized quantitative target. The bounded later-work search found no matching unrestricted multiclass resolution.
working_summary: An online learner predicts a label distribution and then sees the correct label on each round. Regret compares its expected cumulative mistakes with the best fixed hypothesis on the same sequence. The card asks for the worst minimax regret among all classes of Littlestone dimension at most d, including infinite label spaces. The general upper and lower bounds differ by a square-root logarithm, while the sharper finite-label theorem needs an extra regularity condition. A complete Lean answer must give matching universal bounds on the two-parameter regret function under the unrestricted model.

title: Time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning
importance_reason: A central quantitative problem in computational learning theory. Strong modern SQ and cryptographic results clarify the error-dependent exponent, but exact optimization, label conventions, model of computation and uniform parameter regimes remain essential to interpreting the original question.
formal: Determine the optimal joint running-time dependence on dimension \(n\) and inverse excess error \(t=1/\varepsilon\) for agnostically learning affine halfspaces from Gaussian examples. Retain the source’s deterministic Boolean target-function model: for every measurable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\{-1,+1\}\), a learner sees independent \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\), and must output a predictor \(h\) such that \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{err}_f(h)\le\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)+\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{err}_f(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)],\] where \[\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n,\ b\in\mathbb R}\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\ne f(x)].\] The parameters range over \(n\ge2\), \(t\ge3\). More precisely, characterize the asymptotically attainable uniform time bounds \(T(n,t)\) defined below, with matching algorithmic upper and general lower bounds in each stated parameter regime. The source’s subsidiary question about \(n^{O(\log t)}\) is recorded in context; it does not replace the broader optimal-time target. The real-arithmetic convention and its distinction from a finite-bit implementation are explicit parts of this formulation.
question_excerpt: What is the optimal time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning; in particular, can the dimension exponent be only logarithmic in inverse excess error?
definitions:
\(\gamma_n\) is the Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure; its coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A halfspace predictor has the form \(x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sum_i w_i x_i+b)\), with real coefficients and threshold and \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\), otherwise \(-1\). Constant predictors are allowed by \(w=0\). Affine halfspaces follow the source’s introductory definition, which includes a constant term; its later notation sometimes suppresses that term. No margin, bounded coefficient encoding, sparsity or homogeneity assumption is added. The infimum in \(\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)\) does not presume an available optimum or supply its value to the learner.

The unknown target \(f\) is any Borel-measurable Boolean function, fixed before the examples and learner coins are drawn. It need not itself be a halfspace. Each oracle request returns an independent Gaussian vector with its exact value under the same \(f\); the learner cannot choose the sampled point, inspect code for \(f\), ask for a label at a selected point, or query the optimum. There is no independent stochastic label distribution conditional on \(x\) in this literal target-function formulation. The outer success probability includes all sample draws and internal randomness; error is measured on a fresh Gaussian input. The learner may output an improper predictor. The source uses \(L^1\) notation: for \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued \(h,f\), \(\mathbb E|h-f|=2\operatorname{err}_f(h)\). Thus excess disagreement \(1/t\) is excess \(L^1\) loss \(2/t\), not \(1/t\). This exact factor is kept separate from asymptotic runtime notation.

Computational convention: use one finite uniform real-arithmetic register program, with rational constants in its fixed code, integer control and rational public parameters \(n,t\). It can copy real registers, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) to a constant number of registers, compare their values, branch and generate a fair random bit, each at unit arithmetic cost. Division by zero must be handled by a comparison before division. Discrete control, register access and writing an output instruction each cost one step. Sampling and loading an \(n\)-coordinate labeled example costs \(n+1\) units. The oracle supplies exact real coordinates; no cost for internally generating a Gaussian real is attributed to the learner. There is no floor, digit-extraction primitive, arbitrary real advice, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or decision oracle for general properties of real numbers. Uniformity means the same finite program works for all \(n,t,f\), with no length-dependent constants or advice.

The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit on \(n\) real inputs, built from the same operations, Boolean choices and sign tests. Constants may be stored real values computed during training. It must define a total \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued predictor on every real input, with each division guarded when its denominator vanishes. Output writing and each stored real coefficient are charged one unit per written item. Evaluation cost is the number of circuit operations; it is included in the resource measure. Such circuits give measurable predictors and need no further examples or target access after training. There is no requirement that the output be a halfspace, and no fixed polynomial degree or circuit-size restriction beyond the stated time bound.

For a learner \(A\), let \(\tau_A(n,t)\) be the supremum over every allowed target, sample history and coin history of its training cost plus the evaluation cost of its output circuit, with nontermination or invalid output charged infinite cost. A computable nondecreasing positive integer function \(T(n,t)\) is an attainable asymptotic time bound if there are one such uniform learner \(A\) and a constant \(K\ge1\), independent of \(n,t,f\), such that the PAC guarantee holds for every \(n,t,f\) and \(\tau_A(n,t)\le K T(n,t)\) for every \(n\ge2,t\ge3\). Characterizing optimal complexity means an explicit description of which rates are attainable, up to constant factors, rather than a pointwise infimum over a different hard-coded algorithm for each parameter pair. The dependence on both parameters must remain visible; any restriction such as \(t\le n^c\) must be stated for that bound. No single asymptotically fastest uniform algorithm is assumed to exist in advance.

This exact-real arithmetic model is an explicitly stated convention completing the source’s continuous-example interface. It does not assert a theorem translating arbitrary real computations to the bit model. Exact Gaussian examples have no finite binary representation in general, and the 2014 question specifies neither a rounding oracle nor a coordinate-bit budget. A separate bit-complexity variant would need those definitions and a proof that rounding preserves the learning guarantee for arbitrary measurable targets. Numerical rounding is therefore not silently included as a free primitive in the present arithmetic target.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean-checked asymptotic classification of the attainable bounds just defined: explicit noncircular conditions on \(T(n,t)\), together with proofs of attainability for the asserted upper rates and impossibility for the excluded lower rates. An optimal-rate expression must have matching bounds with the same dimension/error regimes and cost convention. If a fastest uniform rate is not attained, describe and prove the resulting attainable-rate structure instead of assuming a pointwise optimum corresponds to one algorithm. An upper bound alone, a conditional obstruction alone, or a matching result only for statistical-query algorithms does not determine the unrestricted optimum. Computational assumptions must remain hypotheses of the relevant partial result. A lower bound with stochastic labels or a restricted proper output must establish its applicability to the deterministic-target, improper-output interface before being used here. A proof about finite-bit computation must likewise establish a relation to the specified real-arithmetic model. The requested precision is matching asymptotic rates up to constants, not an additive approximation to a numerical value.
context:
A halfspace classifies points by which side of a hyperplane they occupy. In an agnostic task, the labels need not be linearly separable: the benchmark is the least disagreement achievable by a halfspace, plus a requested excess error. A regular Gaussian input marginal does not itself constrain the complexity of the labeling rule.

The 2014 paper contrasts the known \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}\) algorithmic scale with a sparse-noisy-parity-based conditional \(n^{\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) obstruction. Its Question 3 asks for the optimal time and explicitly proposes \(n^{O(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) as a possibility. The quoted lower scale comes from a reduction and a hardness premise; it is not an unconditional time lower bound.

Definition 4 of the source labels examples by a deterministic target function and states an L¹ approximation guarantee; its halfspace discussion also uses Boolean classification language. Later papers often start directly from an arbitrary joint distribution on features and labels. An upper guarantee for all such joint distributions includes deterministic labels as a special case. A lower bound for the larger family does not automatically apply to the deterministic subfamily.

COLT 2021 Diakonikolas–Kane–Pittas–Zarifis proves essentially matching \(n^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)}\)-scale statistical-query hardness for halfspaces in its general joint-distribution model. Statistical queries return approximate expectations of bounded test functions instead of the actual independent examples. This is an important optimality theorem for that restricted access model, not a lower bound for every sample-based learner in the present formulation.

ICML 2023 Diakonikolas–Kane–Ren gives a stronger related cryptographic obstruction. Its Corollary 3.2, under Assumption 2.3 on subexponential LWE hardness, excludes time \(n^{O((1/(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log n}))^\alpha)}\) for every fixed \(0<\alpha<2\), in its stated range \(c/(\sqrt n\log n)\le\varepsilon\le1/(\log n)^\gamma\), with \(\gamma>1/2\) and the specified sufficiently large constant \(c\). Both the logarithmic loss in the exponent and the error range are material. The theorem uses arbitrary joint labels and a computational cryptographic reduction; it is not an unconditional constant-factor characterization of this real-arithmetic deterministic-label problem.

The 2023 hard-instance construction contains residual random noise in the labels even after conditioning on the Gaussian feature vector, and its null case has independent fair labels. This review has not established a conversion of that construction into a fixed deterministic target with the same computational costs. Nor does a finite-bit cryptographic assumption by itself give a lower bound against unit-cost exact-real programs. Those interface gaps are stated explicitly rather than hidden by a claim that the original question is fully resolved.

Tikhonov–Vasilyan’s May 2026 Theorem 3.14 outputs an affine halfspace with error \(\operatorname{OPT}+\varepsilon\) and time \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}+(1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^{2.5})}\) at constant confidence. Its general joint-label guarantee includes fixed deterministic targets, and proper output is allowed by an improper-learning task. The theorem advances proper learning and matches the known dimension exponent; its additional accuracy-only term and continuous computational conventions must remain visible in a joint optimal-time comparison. No finite-bit equivalence is claimed here.

The April 2026 Huang–Juba paper studies a further related problem with homogeneous halfspace output and general joint labels. Its LWE-based hardness is stated with those restrictions. Homogeneous proper learning is not substituted for unrestricted improper affine learning, and the computational assumption is not asserted true.

The original source does not fix coordinate precision or a universal elementary cost model for real samples. This card states a real-arithmetic convention so the resource question can be read precisely. Its current-status review remains uncertain: the inspected recent results explain substantial progress but do not certify a matching resolution with all the displayed label, computation and parameter conventions.
why: Gaussian inputs remove many distributional complications, yet arbitrary labels can still make even the best linear predictor difficult to match. The question asks for the precise computational cost of decreasing excess error, allowing any output representation. It separates the number of examples needed for learning from the much larger time used by current algorithms.
status_note: The broad optimal-time question remains without a checked matching resolution under the exact formulation given here. The 2014 Definition 4 uses a fixed target function and leaves real-input precision implicit; affine halfspaces are stated in its introduction. The completed record explicitly selects an exact-real arithmetic convention and preserves deterministic Boolean labels. COLT 2021 gives SQ optimality in a larger joint-label model. ICML 2023 gives conditional LWE hardness with stochastic labels, a sqrt(log n) exponent loss and a stated error range; a deterministic-label and exact-real lower-bound transfer was not established in this review. The 2026 proper and homogeneous results have their own output/runtime qualifications. These known theorems are substantive related progress, not a claimed constant-factor classification or unconditional resolution. Current status is uncertain after checks through 16 September 2026.

It preserves the original deterministic Boolean target-function model and permits any finite evaluable predictor.
