title: Memory–sample tradeoffs for noisy parity learning
importance_reason: The memory cost of noisy parity learning separates information retained from samples from computation time and exposes a basic resource cost of noise.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(c_{1},c_{2}>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\), every \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) and every one-pass learner recovering a uniformly random \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) from the noisy parity samples defined below, its worst-case memory S and maximum sample count T satisfy \(S\ge c_{1}n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\) or \(T\ge 2^{c_{2}n}\)? Constants are independent of \(n, \varepsilon\) and the learner, and \(\varepsilon\) may tend to zero with n. This states the bounded-error recovery interpretation of Conjecture 1; it does not additionally require a lower bound at exponentially small success probability.
definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽\(_{2}=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two; \(\langle a,x\rangle =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}x_{i}\) mod 2. First choose x uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose \(a_{t}\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and a noise bit \(Z_{t}\) with \(\Pr [Z_{t}=1]=1/2- \varepsilon\); observe \((a_{t},b_{t})\) with \(b_{t}=\langle a_{t},x\rangle +Z_{t}\) mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means \(\hat\{x\}=x\), and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose \(a_{t}\) or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with \(T+1\) layers and width at most \(2^{S}\), one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and \(\varepsilon\); its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, \(S=\lceil \log _{2}(\operatorname{width})\rceil\), and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\), or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ), a\) result only for constant \(\varepsilon\), or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.
context:
Without noise, every observation is a correct linear relation about the hidden vector. Here the relation is only slightly more likely to be right than wrong when \(\varepsilon\) is small. The question asks whether this forces a quadratic loss in the storage threshold as the bias tends to zero.

The source proves that a learner needs \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\) memory or exponentially many samples, and records an upper bound using \(O(n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) memory and \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) samples. The conjecture asks whether the stronger memory dependence is necessary below an exponential sample budget.

The lower bound concerns retained information, not the time needed to process it. It must hold for arbitrary state-transition rules and therefore would be unconditional even though efficient learning of noisy parity is also used as a computational hardness assumption.

For \(\varepsilon\) fixed away from zero, the two memory bounds differ only by constants. The unresolved content is their uniform dependence on \(\varepsilon\), together with an exponential sample threshold whose exponent does not shrink with \(\varepsilon\).

The 2024 DIMACS project abstract identifies the same \(n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\)-versus-exponential tradeoff as its long-term goal and describes intermediate observations in a modified model. It is evidence of continued study, not a proved lower bound or a fresh claim that all later work has been exhausted.
why: Would quantify how observation noise increases the storage needed for a central learning problem, strengthening unconditional limits relevant to streaming learning and bounded-storage cryptography.
status_note: Checked the complete conference statement and branching-program model, the arXiv version record, a 2024 follow-up abstract and the author’s 2026 publication list. No resolution was found through 12 September 2026. The listed 2026 planted-structure work has a different stated scope; its abstract, not its full proofs, was inspected.
progress: 2021: The published lower bound has memory dependence \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\); Conjecture 1 proposes \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) under a subexponential sample budget. | 2024: A subsequent research-project abstract reports partial investigations and keeps the full tradeoff as its goal.
working_summary: A hidden binary vector is observed through uniformly random parity equations with independent noise. Each equation is correct with probability one half plus \(\varepsilon\). The proposed lower bound requires either \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\) stored bits or exponentially many samples. The source proves the weaker \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon )\) memory threshold and gives a matching-to-the-conjecture space upper bound. The card fixes bounded-error exact recovery and requires constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\).

title: Learning PH/poly from learning NP/poly
importance_reason: A general structural implication for the polynomial hierarchy in computational learning, with uniform random-example algorithms and nonuniform target classes. It connects complexity-class collapses with a substantially different access model, rather than one isolated concept family.
formal: Does efficient distribution-free PAC learnability of \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\) from random labeled examples imply the same learnability for every fixed level of \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\)? In the size-parameterized model below, write \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) for efficient learning of Boolean concepts represented by circuits with \(r\) alternating witness blocks, starting existentially. The target is the single implication \[\mathsf{Learn}_1\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \mathsf{Learn}_r.\] The learner for each fixed \(r\) may be different and have a different polynomial running-time bound. This does not request one polynomial uniform over arbitrarily many alternations. Both sides use ordinary Boolean circuits as output hypotheses and only independent random examples of the unknown target.
question_excerpt: Does polynomial-time learnability of NP/poly imply polynomial-time learnability of PH/poly?
definitions:
Fix the ordinary Boolean circuit basis consisting of two-input AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and constants; circuits are acyclic and have one output bit. Fix a standard effective binary encoding. For \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), and fixed \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal C_r(n,s)\) contain every function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) of the form \[f(x)=\mathbf1\{\exists u_1\ \forall u_2\ \exists u_3\ \cdots Q_r u_r:\ C(x,u_1,\ldots,u_r)=1\},\] where \(Q_i\) alternates with \(i\), each \(u_i\) ranges over a specified finite Boolean cube, and the total number of input nodes, witness bits and gates of the deterministic matrix circuit \(C\) is at most \(s\). Zero-length witness blocks are allowed. The size is a combinatorial circuit-size bound; encoding such a circuit takes a polynomial number of bits in \(s\). At \(r=1\), these are nondeterministic circuits. Allowing size polynomial in \(n\) gives the usual nonuniform class \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\). The union over every fixed alternation depth gives \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\), the polynomial hierarchy with polynomial-length advice. Equivalently, advice can be included in the matrix circuit; it is not given to the learner. There is no requirement that the target descriptions at different input lengths be produced by one algorithm.

Precisely, \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) says that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A_r\) and one polynomial \(p_r\) such that the following holds for every \(n,s\) as above, every pair of integers \(a,b\ge3\), every \(f\in\mathcal C_r(n,s)\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Given the public unary parameters \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts on every execution in at most \(p_r(n+s+a+b)\) steps and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[\Pr_{A_r,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer probability includes the random training draws and the machine’s independent fair random bits. The inner probability uses a fresh test draw. Each requested example is an independent draw; requests count toward the time bound and reading its \(n+1\) bits is charged. The bound therefore also limits the number of examples, random bits and output bits. The predictor is evaluated without access to the example source, target or learner state. Its gates have no nondeterministic or higher-hierarchy oracle. It need not use the target’s representation or respect its size bound, but its printed description must fit the learner’s polynomial time.

The learner knows the size bound, not the unknown circuit, its advice, witness assignments, or the distribution. There are no membership queries asking for labels at chosen points, and no equivalence queries. All distributions are admitted; efficient sampling code is not required because the example source is part of the PAC interface. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed concept, so this is realizable rather than agnostic learning. Integer inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters specify the usual arbitrary accuracy and confidence guarantees without numerical-encoding ambiguity. Supplying \(s\) makes explicit the source’s standard polynomial-in-target-size convention: combining all polynomial-size representations at one \(n\) without any size bound would erase the intended computational restriction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, with a polynomial-time learner for every fixed alternation depth under the hypothesis \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\), or prove its negation \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\land\exists r\ge1,\neg\mathsf{Learn}_r\). All distribution, target-size, accuracy and confidence quantifiers must be preserved. The requested result is a qualitative implication about uniform learning algorithms; it does not ask for a particular optimal exponent. An oracle-relative separation by itself is evidence about relativizing arguments, not a refutation of the unrelativized implication. A theorem about average-case decision algorithms, membership-query learners, or existence of nonuniform hypothesis circuits alone does not establish this random-example learning implication.
context:
An NP/poly concept labels an input by whether some short witness makes a small verification circuit accept. Higher levels alternate existential and universal witness tests. The learner never performs those tests on the hidden target description; it sees only random correctly labeled examples and must produce an efficiently evaluatable prediction circuit.

The classical Karp–Lipton theorem concerns small circuit representations for NP and a resulting collapse of decision complexity. The question here is about finding useful predictors from limited observed data. A guarantee that some small circuit exists is weaker than a learning algorithm that discovers one under every distribution.

Uniformity applies to the learner: for a fixed level, one Turing algorithm must handle every input length, size bound and target circuit. The target class is nonuniform because its hidden descriptions may vary arbitrarily with input length. Neither target advice nor a circuit solving a higher-level decision problem is supplied as free advice to the learner.

The 2021 paper proves stronger equivalences for EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. In those classes it relates worst-case and average-case learning and shows that restricting the example distribution to uniform or allowing membership queries does not alter the qualitative polynomial-time learnability conclusion. These results concern stronger classes and do not prove the NP-to-PH implication.

The source separately studies restricted reductions from SAT to learning NP/poly. Its hierarchy-collapse consequence for such a reduction concerns a hardness proof with additional structural properties. The existence of that kind of reduction is not part of the premise of this card. The source’s additional question about an oracle-relative obstacle is also separate from the unrelativized implication.

The December 2021 full manuscript explicitly retains the hierarchy question. The January 2025 journal publication is confirmed by the publisher, whose accessible abstract states the paper’s stronger-class and reduction results. Its subscription-only full text was not available in this review. Bounded later-work searches found no checked theorem answering this exact implication, so current status remains qualified rather than certified from publication metadata.
why: The question asks whether solving one level of a powerful prediction task automatically solves every fixed level above it. An affirmative answer would give a structural collapse for efficient learning, beyond the familiar collapses for deciding languages or merely representing them by small circuits.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked 2021 conference and December 2021 full manuscript. The 2025 journal publication and abstract were checked, but subscription full text was not available and its question section is not claimed to have been rechecked. Bounded later-work searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching proof or refutation. The card remains active with uncertain current status; it retains distribution-free random-example PAC learning, public target-size bounds and a separate uniform polynomial-time learner for each fixed hierarchy level.

The publisher’s abstract and metadata confirm publication; the full question section was not accessible. | 2026-09-16: Completed the size, alternation, uniformity, output, accuracy, confidence and example-access model. A bounded later-work search found no matching resolution; the current-status check is recorded as uncertain.
working_summary: The question asks whether efficient PAC learning of NP/poly would imply efficient PAC learning at every fixed level of the polynomial hierarchy. Targets are small circuits with alternating witness tests, while the learner sees only independent labeled examples from an arbitrary unknown distribution. The output must be an ordinary efficiently evaluatable Boolean circuit, with polynomial time also accounting for samples, randomness and the public target-size bound. Known structural equivalences for stronger classes and ordinary circuit-representation collapses do not establish this learning implication. The full 2021 source explicitly asks the question, while the bounded later-status review supplies no matching resolution and leaves present status uncertain.

title: Proper decision-tree learning in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central proper-learning question, with a near-polynomial algorithm but no polynomial bound for the uniform membership-query setting; representation and access to labels both materially affect its complexity.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized membership-query algorithm that properly learns Boolean decision trees under the uniform distribution in polynomial time? For every \(n,s\geq1\), every integer \(m\geq2\), and every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a decision tree with at most \(s\) leaves, the learner is given \(n,s,m\) and oracle access to \(f\). It must output an explicitly represented decision tree \(h\), with probability at least \(2/3\), such that \[2^{-n}|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:h(x)\ne f(x)\}|\leq1/m.\] Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in \(n,s,m\).
question_excerpt: Design a \(\operatorname{poly}(n, s, 1/\varepsilon )\)-time membership query algorithm for properly learning size-s decision trees over n variables to error \(\varepsilon\) under the uniform distribution.
definitions: A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node queries one coordinate \(x_i\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its two outgoing edges correspond to values zero and one. Leaves are labelled zero or one; following the input’s path defines the output bit. Size means the number of leaves. Repeated coordinate tests are allowed. The unknown target need only admit a tree with at most \(s\) leaves; that tree is not supplied. A membership query may be any chosen bit string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and returns the exact noiseless bit \(f(x)\). The learner is one finite probabilistic multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice, and no other oracle. Writing the \(n\)-bit query costs ordinary bit steps; reading its returned label costs one. All random-bit generation, computation and output are charged. Its time is bounded by \(K(n+s+m+1)^a\) on every target and every random execution, for constants \(K,a\) independent of parameters. Integers are supplied in binary. The accuracy convention \(\varepsilon=1/m\) specifies the usual inverse-accuracy parameter without an arbitrary real input encoding; existence for these accuracies is equivalent to existence for arbitrary requested positive accuracy by rounding to a smaller reciprocal accuracy. Properness is weak properness: the output must be a decision tree, but need not have at most \(s\) leaves. Its full explicit description, with variable indices, children and leaf bits, must fit the polynomial time bound. The success probability concerns the learner’s randomness; prediction error is measured over a fresh uniform point and the guarantee holds for every promised target.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that a learner satisfying all these quantifiers exists, or that no such learner exists. The positive direction requires polynomial bit time, a proper explicit tree output and the uniform-distribution error bound with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative result must rule out all randomized learners of this kind, including those allowed polynomial-size trees larger than the target. An improper hypothesis, a random-examples-only result, distribution-free hardness alone, or a conditional obstruction whose assumption is unproved does not settle the stated existence question.
context:
Open Problem 1 asks for polynomial time in the number of variables, target size and inverse accuracy. The source explicitly distinguishes strict properness, which preserves the target size bound, from weak properness, which merely returns a tree; its question is open even for the latter.

The representation constraint matters: an efficient predictor need not come with a comparably small tree representation. Membership queries also matter because they let the learner choose inputs instead of relying only on the examples that a distribution happens to provide.

The source’s Theorem 2 reports an almost-polynomial proper query learner, with time \(\widetilde O(n^2)(s/\varepsilon)^{O(\log((\log s)/\varepsilon))}\). In the usual polynomial-size, constant-error regime this yields \(n^{O(\log\log n)}\), which still exceeds a fixed polynomial.

Koch, Strassle and Tan prove NP-hardness for distribution-free proper learning with queries in FOCS 2023. Their paper explicitly contrasts that result with the easier uniform-distribution setting. A lower bound obtained from a specially chosen distribution does not rule out this card’s learner.

Their FOCS 2024 coding-theoretic work gives further hardness connections for decision-tree learning. Its discussion distinguishes the remaining uniform-distribution problem from the distributions used in its reductions.

An empirical tree-fitting procedure and its success on a finite collection of datasets are not the universal learning guarantee. The error bound must hold for every small-tree target, even when the target’s structure is unknown and the output tree has a different topology.
why: The question tests whether efficient prediction can be achieved while retaining a decision-tree representation in a basic, well-specified query model. Its resolution would clarify the computational cost of proper learning beyond sample complexity alone.
status_note: The exact uniform-distribution proper query question is explicit in the 2022 source. Checked later hardness results do not cover this distributional setting. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no polynomial-time learner or unconditional impossibility theorem for the stated model.
progress: 2022: The open-problem paper records an almost-polynomial proper learner and asks for a polynomial bound. | 2023: Distribution-free proper query learning is shown NP-hard; this does not settle the uniform case. | 2024: New connections to nearest-codeword approximation give further learning hardness under different distributional/access assumptions.
working_summary: Proper learning of decision trees requires the learner to output a decision tree, preserving the target representation's simple branching structure. The source asks for a polynomial-time algorithm under the uniform input distribution with membership queries available. Those queries let the learner choose inputs and observe their target labels, making this different from learning from random examples alone. Existing algorithms in the source are faster than earlier quasipolynomial approaches but still fall short of polynomial time. A solution would provide an efficient way to recover an interpretable tree hypothesis without abandoning the tree representation during learning.

title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
importance_reason: A major hardness question for unrestricted polynomial-size hypothesis representations, linking worst-case NP difficulty, agnostic learning and cryptographic assumptions; substantially broader than hardness of proper learning for one representation.
formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.
context:
An improper learner may return a larger circuit than any circuit in the comparator class. Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The quantification over every fixed polynomial output-size bound makes this distinction explicit.

The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. These are substantive assumptions, so the result does not by itself give the unconditional reduction asked for here.
why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.
status_note: Open in the CCC 2025 source. The subsequent ECCC TR26-091 checked on 2026-09-14 establishes related conditional hardness under cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions, not the unconditional claim here. The selected formal oracle-reduction variant and its quantifier order are explicit; this bounded check is not an exhaustive literature or proof verification.
progress: 2025: Goldberg and Kabanets relate restricted forms of learning hardness to witness encryption and explicitly leave general improper circuit-learning NP-hardness open. | 2026-06-04: Goldberg, Juvekar and Kabanets give randomized reduction results for full-support PAC learning under additional cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions. The checked statement does not eliminate those assumptions.
working_summary: The question asks whether SAT reduces to agnostic learning of general polynomial-size Boolean circuits. The learning oracle receives a circuit sampling labeled examples and returns an approximately optimal hypothesis. The returned hypothesis may use an arbitrarily larger fixed polynomial size than the comparator circuits. The reduction must work with every valid oracle reply and without additional cryptographic assumptions. A June 2026 follow-up gives related conditional hardness, leaving the unconditional target unresolved.

title: Polynomial-time robust spectral estimation
importance_reason: A concrete computational gap for robust dimension reduction, separating guaranteed reconstruction from certification under perturbations affecting every data point.
formal: For every fixed \(q\in[2,\infty]\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that always recovers a robust low-rank representation of an unknown clean matrix from bounded perturbations to every data point, with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically in Proposition 27? Specifically, do there exist, for each fixed \(q\), a uniform algorithm \(\mathcal A_q\) and constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\ge1\) such that the following holds for all integers \(n,m\ge1\), \(0\le r\le n\), real \(\kappa,\delta\ge0\), and matrices \(A,\widetilde A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) satisfying \(\|\widetilde A_j-A_j\|_q\le\delta\) for every column \(j\)? Given only \((\widetilde A,r,\kappa,\delta)\), the algorithm must output an orthogonal projection \(\widehat\Pi\) with \[\operatorname{rank}(\widehat\Pi)\le r,\qquad \|\widehat\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le b_q\kappa,\] and, for every \(\eta>0\), \[\|(I_n-\widehat\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}\le C_q(1+\eta^{-1})\left(\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)+\sqrt m\,\delta\kappa\right)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\|A\|_{2\to2}.\] The same output must satisfy every \(\eta\); \(\eta\) is an analysis parameter, not an extra source of clean-data information. Require at most \(B_q(n+m+1)^{a_q}\) operations in the explicit fixed-\(q\) real-arithmetic model below. The output must be a projection, even when the observed matrix has large spectral distortion; reporting only that the input was poisoned is insufficient.
question_excerpt: Can a polynomial-time estimator always return a robust low-rank projection with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically under bounded perturbations to every training point?
definitions:
Columns \(A_j\in\mathbb R^n\) are the clean data points and columns \(\widetilde A_j\) are the supplied observations. An adversary may change every column, in any correlated way, subject only to the displayed per-column constraint. There is no distributional assumption, random design, fraction of uncontaminated points, spectral gap, incoherence or sparsity promise. For finite \(q\), \(\|v\|_q=(\sum_i|v_i|^q)^{1/q}\); for \(q=\infty\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). Thus the infinite-norm version permits a change of magnitude at most \(\delta\) to every entry.

For a matrix \(M\), \(\|M\|_{u\to v}=\sup_{\|x\|_u\le1}\|Mx\|_v\), with input and output dimensions determined by \(M\). The spectral norm \(\|M\|_{2\to2}\) is its largest singular value; it measures maximum Euclidean amplification, not the sum of squared entry errors. A real \(n\times n\) matrix \(\Pi\) is an orthogonal projection when \(\Pi^T=\Pi\) and \(\Pi^2=\Pi\). Its rank is the dimension of its range. The condition \(\|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\) means every input perturbation of \(q\)-norm at most \(\delta\) moves the projected point by at most \(\kappa\delta\) in Euclidean norm.

Define the clean benchmark by \[\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)=\min\{\|(I_n-\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}:\Pi^T=\Pi=\Pi^2,\ \operatorname{rank}(\Pi)\le r,\ \|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\}.\] The zero projection is feasible, so the class is nonempty; it is a closed bounded subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space and the minimum exists. The rank constraint is an upper bound, as in the source’s robust approximation framework and Theorem 25. The algorithm is not given the optimizer, its value, the clean matrix, its norm or the perturbation matrix. Only \(n,m\), the observed entries, rank budget and two corruption/robustness bounds are available. The output is the complete \(n\times n\) projection matrix. No extra data access is available at evaluation.

The constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\) may depend on the fixed norm exponent, consistently with the source’s \(q\)-dependent approximation constants, but not on dimensions, rank, matrix entries, \(\kappa,\delta\) or \(\eta\). For a fixed \(q\), the same finite algorithm works on all sizes. The recovery inequality is the source’s constant-factor spectral guarantee with its additive corruption term and \(\eta\)-tradeoff, not an exact recovery or squared-Frobenius guarantee. It is valid for every compatible clean matrix \(A\): the algorithm sees only \(\widetilde A\). In particular, \(\eta\) is universally quantified after the output; a different projection for each value is not silently substituted.

Computational convention: the observed matrix and real bounds are held in exact real registers. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\) with a zero-denominator guard, comparisons, branching, square roots of nonnegative reals, discrete control and register access each cost one unit. For finite fixed \(q\), the primitives \(x\mapsto x^q\) and \(x\mapsto x^{1/q}\) on \(x\ge0\) also have unit cost, with \(0^q=0\). For \(q=\infty\), maxima and absolute values use comparisons instead. These are explicit elementary-power conventions for each fixed real \(q\), including exponents that are not rational; no algorithm uniform in an encoded variable exponent is requested. Program constants otherwise are rational. Reading each observed entry and writing each output entry costs one unit. The stated bound is a worst-case arithmetic-operation bound on every input, and the algorithm must always return a valid output satisfying the guarantees. It has no optimization oracle, spectral-decomposition oracle, induced-norm oracle, digit-extraction operation, clean-data oracle or general-real decision oracle. The norms used in the target are mathematical definitions, not free computational queries.

The source formulates its algorithms on real matrices and does not fix an entry-bit or approximation budget. The displayed model is an explicit real-arithmetic interpretation of polynomial time; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity formulation. In particular, exact real output and the special fixed-\(q\) power operations must not be imported into a finite-bit claim without a separate numerical analysis. The full range of fixed exponents, including infinity, is preserved rather than restricting the question to the illustrative entrywise case.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the displayed existence statement for every fixed \(q\), or of its negation. An affirmative answer must construct the uniform algorithms, prove their polynomial arithmetic costs, exact projection/rank properties, constant-factor robustness and clean spectral-error bounds for every adversarially compatible input and every \(\eta>0\). A negative answer must exhibit an exponent for which no algorithm and constants with these guarantees exist; a lower bound for one heuristic is insufficient. A conditional complexity assumption must remain a hypothesis unless established. Returning a corruption certificate, controlling Frobenius error alone, allowing a larger rank, assuming Gaussian/spiked input, or giving an inefficient estimator does not meet the stated goal. The objective is the explicit approximation inequality, so a numerical eigenvector estimate without a proved error and robustness bound does not constitute a resolution.
context:
Ordinary principal component analysis minimizes reconstruction error without a robustness constraint. Here the projection must also limit how much a small change to one point can move its representation. Training data may already be corrupted, so the reconstruction guarantee concerns an unknown matrix rather than the observed matrix alone.

The source proves efficient recovery with Frobenius error and gives a different spectral algorithm that may return a certificate of substantial poisoning. Proposition 27 establishes that a robust projection satisfying the stronger spectral guarantee exists information-theoretically. The selected open question asks for efficient recovery with that guarantee, without the certification-only alternative.

The rank bound and robustness factor are separate requirements. The source’s worst-case spectral approximation theorem also has a variant trading increased rank for improved approximation, but that enlarged-rank variant does not by itself give the rank-at-most-r recovery requested here.

The additive term involving column count, corruption size and robustness is essential to the target. Small changes to all coordinates can collectively create a large matrix perturbation, so controlling each point is different from assuming the whole perturbation has small spectral norm.

The related COLT 2020 work studies principal-subspace estimation for Gaussian covariance models under per-sample adversarial perturbations. Its statistical assumptions supply structure absent from an arbitrary clean matrix. The 2021 source explicitly distinguishes that setting from its worst-case recovery question.

The live arXiv history lists a last revision in August 2021. Bounded later-work searches did not locate a checked theorem matching the full always-recover spectral interface; that search outcome is not a proof of openness. The card therefore keeps uncertain current status and states its computational convention explicitly.
why: A representation can be stable against future perturbations and still be difficult to learn from already corrupted data. This question asks whether worst-case robust spectral reconstruction is computationally attainable whenever it is information-theoretically possible. It isolates a gap that is hidden if an algorithm may simply report severe corruption.

The exact always-return-a-projection target, rank bound, robustness factor and eta tradeoff are retained. Related Gaussian principal-subspace results have extra distributional structure. The live original manuscript history and bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 did not yield a verified theorem resolving this full worst-case question. Status is uncertain, not a proof of openness. Polynomial time is explicitly interpreted in a fixed-q exact-real arithmetic model with unit-cost q-powers; neither finite-bit equivalence nor an unrestricted norm/optimization oracle is asserted.

working_summary: The card asks for polynomial-time recovery of a robust low-rank representation when every training point may have been adversarially perturbed. The output must approximate the unknown clean matrix in spectral norm while respecting the rank budget and induced-norm robustness bound. The source proves that such recovery is information-theoretically possible but its efficient spectral method may only certify severe poisoning. The statement preserves the full range of fixed norm exponents and the same-output error tradeoff in an explicit real-arithmetic model. A Lean resolution must prove or refute guaranteed recovery with the stated approximation and computational costs, without extra distributional assumptions.

title: Proper unlabeled compression of ample classes
importance_reason: Optimal proper unlabeled compression of every ample class is a substantial structural case of the central sample-compression programme.
formal: Does every nonempty ample concept class \(C\subseteq \{0,1\}\)ᵁ on a finite domain U admit a proper unlabeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(d=\operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Precisely, do there exist maps \(\kappa :RS(C)\to \{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\) and \(\rho :\{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\to C\) such that, for every realizable labeled partial sample \(s, \kappa (s)\subseteq dom(s)\) and \(\rho (\kappa (s))\) agrees with every label in s? The stored object is only an unordered subset of the sample’s input points. The bound is d, not an unspecified multiple of d.
definitions: A concept \(c\in C\) is a function \(c:U\to \{0,1\}\). A set \(A\subseteq U\) is shattered by C if \(\{c|_{A}:c\in C\}=\{0,1\}^{A}\). It is strongly shattered if some \(b:U\setminus A\to \{0,1\}\) has the property that, for every \(a:A\to \{0,1\}\), the combined labeling \(a\cup b\) belongs to C. Thus strong shattering requires a full cube of concepts with identical labels outside A. The class is ample when every shattered set is strongly shattered; ample classes are also called lopsided or shattering-extremal. Its VC dimension d is the maximum size of a shattered set. A labeled partial sample is a function \(s:A\to \{0,1\}\) on some \(A\subseteq U\), equivalently a set of pairs \((x,s(x))\) with distinct x. It is realizable if \(s=c|_{A}\) for some \(c\in C; RS(C)\) contains every such sample, including the empty sample. The compressor \(\kappa\) sees the entire labeled sample and may use its labels to choose a subset \(\kappa (s)\) of its domain, of size at most d. It sends only that subset. The reconstructor \(\rho\) receives no labels, ordering, multiplicities, sample size, omitted sample points or auxiliary bits; \(U,C,\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are fixed and shared beforehand. It returns a total concept belonging to C, which must agree with the original entire sample, including omitted labels. This is the proper convention explicitly used in the full source. Requiring \(\rho\) on all subsets of size at most d is equivalent to defining it only on \(Im(\kappa )\), because C is nonempty and unused inputs can be assigned any fixed concept. The existence of \(\kappa ,\rho\) is quantified separately for each finite C; no running-time bound for constructing or evaluating them, distributional assumption or probability of error is part of the statement. For \(d=0 a\) nonempty class has a single concept and the empty compressed set suffices. A maximum class of dimension d has cardinality \(\sum_{j=0}^{d} binomial(|U|,j)\); every maximum class is ample, but the converse need not hold.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the two maps with the stated d-point bound for every finite nonempty ample class, or give an ample class with a proof that no such pair of maps exists. A scheme retaining labels, returning a hypothesis outside C, storing extra information, or exceeding d points does not meet the target. A scheme that handles only full concepts rather than every realizable partial sample is also insufficient. Failure of a proposed corner-peeling construction alone does not refute existence of a compression scheme.
context:
The source constructs proper unlabeled schemes of size d for maximum classes. Its open extension concerns all ample classes, a strictly larger family.

Size-d labeled compression is already known for ample classes. The new requirement is that the reconstructor recover a consistent concept from selected input points after all their labels have been removed.

The source exhibits a maximum class of VC dimension three without a corner, refuting earlier corner-peeling arguments. It nevertheless proves the compression theorem for maximum classes. The absence of corners therefore does not imply the desired maps do not exist.

The 2024 paper proves proper unlabeled schemes for oriented matroids and for complexes of oriented matroids admitting corner peelings. It explicitly states that the general ample-class question remains open.
why: Would extend sharp label-free sample compression from maximum classes to the larger class characterized by equality of shattering and strong shattering, clarifying how far the VC dimension controls lossless reconstruction of consistent samples.
status_note: Read the full proper-compression definition and the distinction between maximum and ample classes, then checked the 2024 oriented-matroid theorem and its explicit remaining-question paragraph. Also checked the revised labeled-compression work for complexes of oriented matroids, whose retained labels make its result different. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for every finite ample class; searches are not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The source corrects earlier corner-peeling claims, proves size-d unlabeled compression for maximum classes and asks for an ample-class extension. | 2022: The journal treatment explicitly uses proper reconstruction and retains the ample extension as open. | 2024: Proper unlabeled compression is proved for additional oriented-matroid classes, while the general ample question is explicitly retained.
working_summary: An ample class strongly shatters every set of coordinates that it shatters. A compressor selects at most d input points from any realizable labeled sample, where d is the class’s VC dimension. A reconstructor must recover a concept in the original class consistent with all sample labels while receiving only the selected points. Maximum classes satisfy this exact bound, and labeled compression is known more generally. The 2024 oriented-matroid results still leave proper unlabeled size-d compression for all ample classes open.

title: Multiclass sample compression from binary compression
importance_reason: A quantitative reduction connecting the central binary sample-compression problem to arbitrary-label multiclass prediction. It could transfer every improved universal binary bound without label-cardinality loss, while existing results require additional structure.
formal: Is the following implication valid for every function \(f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0\)? Suppose every nonempty binary concept class \(B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{U}\) on every nonempty domain \(U\), with finite VC dimension \(v\), admits an exact realizable sample compression scheme of size at most \(f(v)\). Must there exist an integer \(A_f\ge1\) such that every nonempty multiclass concept class \(H\subseteq Y^X\), on arbitrary nonempty sets \(X,Y\) and with finite graph dimension \(d\), admits such a scheme of size at most \[A_f f(d)?\] The constant may depend on the chosen binary bound \(f\), but not on \(X,Y,H,d\), the sample size or the labels occurring in a sample. Label sets may be infinite. No properness, majority-vote form, stability, effectiveness or computational efficiency of the compression schemes is assumed. This restores the hypothesis omitted from the imported source sentence: the question concerns transfer of an arbitrary universal binary compression bound, not just existence of some graph-dimension bound.
question_excerpt: If every binary class admits compression of size f of its VC dimension, must every multiclass class admit compression of size O(f of its graph dimension)?
definitions: \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A concept is a function assigning a label to every instance. A finite labeled sample is a sequence \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\); repetitions and the empty sample are allowed. It is realizable by \(H\) if a single \(h\in H\) satisfies \(h(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). A compression scheme for the fixed class is a pair of deterministic set functions \[\kappa:(X\times Y)^*\to(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*,\qquad \rho:(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*\to Y^X.\] Writing \(\kappa(S)=(S',b)\), every labeled record in \(S'\) must occur in \(S\). Following the source’s explicit convention that subset notation for sequences means inclusion of their underlying sets, the retained list may be reordered and may repeat a retained record. Every occurrence counts toward its length. No new or relabeled record may be introduced. The bit string \(b\) is auxiliary information. Size at most \(s\) means \(|S'|+|b|\le s\) on every finite input sample. The reconstruction receives only \(S',b\), not the original sample, its length, or the original positions of retained records. One retained labeled record costs one unit; one auxiliary bit costs one unit. Domain points and labels are mathematical objects, not charged by bit length. Exact realizable consistency means \(\rho(\kappa(S))(x_i)=y_i\) for every record of every realizable \(S\). The reconstructed function need not belong to \(H\), and no accuracy requirement is imposed on unrealizable samples. Both functions may depend on the complete class, but the same pair must work at all sample sizes. There is no randomness or failure probability. A binary class has VC dimension \(v\) when \(v\) is the largest size of a set of distinct domain points on which all binary label patterns occur. A multiclass class graph-shatters distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) if there are reference labels \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\in Y\) such that every subset \(I\subseteq[r]\) has a hypothesis with \(h(x_i)=a_i\) exactly for \(i\in I\). The graph dimension is the largest such \(r\). Only classes of finite dimension enter the implication; dimension zero permits a size-zero scheme because all hypotheses agree pointwise. No monotonicity or computability assumption is placed on \(f\).
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer must show that every binary bound satisfying the premise transfers with a constant \(A_f\) uniform over all multiclass classes and all sample sizes; an effective black-box procedure is not required. A negative answer must exhibit one function \(f\) that really bounds compression for every binary class as stated, and prove that for every integer \(A\ge1\) some finite-graph-dimension multiclass class admits no compression scheme of size at most \(Af(d)\). Merely showing failure of a particular reduction does not refute the implication. A result with an extra label-count factor, an added structural requirement on the binary reconstruction, or a substituted dimension does not settle this question. The assertion concerns exact consistency and constant-factor size transfer; there is no numerical error tolerance.
context:
Sample compression retains a few labeled examples and a few auxiliary bits, from which a fixed reconstruction rule must recover a predictor agreeing with the entire original realizable sample. It compresses the information needed for consistency, not the literal binary encoding of all discarded data. The size bound must hold regardless of the original sample length.

VC dimension records which binary patterns a class can realize on a finite set. Graph dimension asks which agreement and disagreement patterns with chosen reference labels a multiclass class can realize. These dimensions coincide for binary classes. The target uses graph dimension, not the different dimension characterizing general multiclass learnability.

Theorem 4 of the proceedings paper transfers any binary bound \(f(d)\) to a finite-label multiclass bound \(O(f(d)\log|Y|)\). The question asks whether that extra label-count cost can be removed without assumptions on the binary compression scheme. In the April 2025 revision the same open question is numbered 3.3.

The source removes the extra factor if the available binary reconstruction is proper or is a finite majority vote of class members; that result also covers infinite label sets. Proper means that the reconstructed binary predictor belongs to the class, and majority vote means pointwise voting among finitely many members, with ties assigned zero. The existence of an unrestricted binary compression scheme does not supply either property.

A separate result removes the extra factor for finite label spaces if the binary compressor is stable: removing records outside its retained set leaves its compressed message unchanged. The source treats infinite labels in that direction using a stronger extension of compression to infinite samples. Those are extra premises, so none is silently inserted into this card’s general finite-sample question.

Finite graph dimension already guarantees bounded compression of size \(2^{O(d)}\), and the source also gives size one for graph dimension one. These results do not establish transfer of every potentially smaller binary bound. In particular, proving a new binary bound would answer this card only if its multiclass consequence preserved the requested order.

Pabbaraju’s counterexample concerns multiclass learnability with a different dimension and an infinite label space. The paper explicitly distinguishes finite graph dimension, where bounded compression is available. Thus the broad slogan that multiclass learnability does not imply compression does not refute this finite-graph-dimension reduction.
why: A general transfer theorem would carry any improvement in binary sample compression to multiclass prediction without a penalty for the number of labels. It would separate the combinatorial difficulty of binary compression from additional requirements imposed by multiclass reconstruction. This matters even though bounded compression at an exponential graph-dimension scale is already known.
status_note: Open Problem 5 in ALT 2025, retained as Open Problem 3.3 in the checked 7 April 2025 revision, asks for this general conditional transfer. The source proves it under additional reconstruction or stability assumptions and gives an extra label-count factor in the general finite-label case. Nearby impossibility results concern another dimension. No matching unrestricted transfer theorem or counterexample was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026; this is not a proof of current openness.

A bounded later-work search found no theorem or counterexample matching the unrestricted conditional transfer stated here.
working_summary: A compression scheme stores labeled examples and auxiliary bits so a fixed decoder can reproduce all labels of a realizable sample. The question assumes a universal binary compression bound f in terms of VC dimension. It asks whether every multiclass class then has compression of the same order in f of its graph dimension, independently of its label set. Known reductions either pay an extra label-count factor or require additional structure of the binary scheme. A complete Lean answer must establish the full conditional transfer or give an admissible binary bound for which that transfer fails.

title: Linear conditional-information bounds for VC learning
importance_reason: A central comparison between VC learning and information-based generalization, asking whether the logarithmic sample-size overhead can be removed for proper agnostic learners. The full-output and pointwise-accuracy requirements distinguish it from already optimal prediction-error analyses.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(c>0\) such that the following holds? For every nonempty Boolean hypothesis class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer \(n\ge d\), there is a proper randomized learner \(A:(X\times\{0,1\})^n\to H\) satisfying both \[\forall P,\quad \operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\le cd\] and \[\forall s\in(X\times\{0,1\})^n,\quad \mathbb E_{W\sim A(s)}\widehat L_s(W)\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat L_s(h)+c\sqrt{d/n}?\] The first quantifier ranges over all labeled-data distributions in the measurable model below, including nonrealizable distributions. The second ranges over every deterministic sample, including samples with conflicting labels. The same learner must satisfy both guarantees; it may depend on \(H,n\), but not on \(P\). This is the original source’s main agnostic Conjecture 6, recovered from the imported introduction excerpt, not its different realizable or improper variants.
question_excerpt: For every VC class, does there exist a proper learner with conditional mutual information linear in VC dimension and expected empirical loss within a universal constant times the square root of dimension divided by sample size of the best empirical loss?
definitions:
A hypothesis is a total function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\). A finite set \(V\subseteq X\) is shattered if every map \(V\to\{0,1\}\) is the restriction of a hypothesis in \(H\); the VC dimension is the supremum of sizes of shattered finite sets. For a labeled sequence \(s=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\), its empirical zero-one loss is \(\widehat L_s(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{h(x_i)\ne y_i\}\). Samples are ordered and may contain repeated points. Proper means that every output is a member of \(H\), rather than an arbitrary Boolean predictor. The expected empirical loss averages only the learner’s private randomness, with the input sequence held fixed. There is no running-time, finite encoding, efficient evaluation, or finite/countable-domain restriction.

The following explicit measurable-kernel convention makes the source’s probability notation meaningful. Equip \(X\) and the hypothesis space \(H\) with sigma-algebras for which evaluation \((h,x)\mapsto h(x)\) is jointly measurable; binary labels have all subsets. The statement quantifies over such measurable presentations of the classes. A randomized learner is a probability kernel from the product sample space into \(H\): for each input it assigns a probability distribution on \(H\), and probabilities of measurable output events vary measurably with the input. Deterministic learners are included. All distributions \(P\) on the labeled product space are allowed. This is a stated probability-interface convention, not a finite-domain specialization, a premise that a measurable empirical-risk minimizer exists, or a claim about nonmeasurable learning rules. It should be retained explicitly in a formalization.

For \(\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\), draw a supersample \(\widetilde Z=(Z_{i,b})_{1\le i\le n,\ b\in\{0,1\}}\) of \(2n\) independent labeled examples from \(P\), and independently draw a uniformly random selector \(B\in\{0,1\}^n\). Let \(\widetilde Z_B=(Z_{i,B_i})_{i=1}^n\), then draw \(W\) from the kernel \(A(\widetilde Z_B)\) using no access to the unselected examples. Define \[\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)=I(W;B\mid\widetilde Z)=n-H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)\] in bits. Here \(H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)=\mathbb E[-\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n}p_b\log_2 p_b]\), where \(p_b=\mathbb E[\mathbf1\{B=b\}\mid\sigma(W,\widetilde Z)]\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). This finite-selector definition uses conditional expectation and does not need pointwise conditional densities on arbitrary domains. The quantity lies between zero and \(n\). It measures the complete hypothesis-valued output \(W\) under its stated measurable structure, not merely the labels it predicts on the supersample and not the learner’s unreleased random seed. Changing logarithm base only rescales the universal constant. The learner cannot see \(P\), the supersample or selector as additional inputs. The accuracy slack and information constant are uniform over all classes, dimensions and sample sizes; a bound with an extra \(\log n\), or with a class-dependent constant, is a different assertion.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of Conjecture 6 in the explicitly stated probability convention, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer supplies one universal \(c\) and a proper probability kernel for every admitted \(H,n\), with the distribution-uniform CMI bound and pointwise empirical-loss bound both established. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(c>0\), some admitted class and sample size defeat every proper kernel: either some distribution violates the information bound, or some deterministic sample violates the expected empirical-loss bound. A counterexample only to exact consistency or to empirical loss \(O(d/n)\) does not refute the allowed \(O(\sqrt{d/n})\) slack here. A generalization bound using a different information quantity, an improper output, or a distribution-dependent learner does not prove this claim. The target is existence with universal constants, not a numerical quantity requiring additive approximation.
context:
Conditional mutual information exposes two candidates for each training position and measures what the final hypothesis reveals about which candidate was selected. Conditioning on both candidates avoids the unbounded information cost that can arise when an algorithm reveals a real-valued observation under ordinary mutual information.

The source’s Theorem 5 gives an empirical-risk minimizer with conditional information at most \(d\log n+2\), in its logarithm convention. Empirical-risk minimization chooses a hypothesis with the fewest training errors. Conjecture 6 permits a controlled excess in this empirical error while asking that the extra sample-size dependence disappear from the information bound.

The source also states Conjectures 7 and 8 for realizable samples. They demand expected empirical loss \(O(d/n)\), or zero, together with the linear information bound. Haghifam and coauthors’ Theorem 4.2 refutes those two proper-learning claims, even if the information bound is replaced by an arbitrary dimension-only function. Its smaller empirical-loss allowance is essential; that theorem does not supply a refutation of Conjecture 6 as displayed here.

The same lower-bound paper notes that chaining conditional-information analyses yields the optimal \(O(\sqrt{d/n})\) expected generalization scale. That fact concerns the resulting bound on prediction behavior. It does not assert that a single learner’s complete output has CMI at most \(cd\) while satisfying the present pointwise training guarantee.

The 2021 PAC-Bayes/CMI paper’s VC-class Theorem 13 retains an information term \(d\log(2n)\). This extends information-based generalization guarantees, but it does not remove the sample-size dependence required to answer Conjecture 6.

The 2025 projection paper controls an auxiliary compressed real-vector output and a distortion term. Its checked theorem does not state the present universal proper binary learning claim with dimension-only information about the complete output and a pointwise training guarantee.

The official FOCS 2026 list now includes Hanneke and Wang’s “The optimal information complexity of VC learning.” The author’s publication page confirms the entry, but the checked entries supply no manuscript or theorem statement. This is a concrete unresolved status lead: the title alone does not establish whether the proper agnostic Conjecture 6, a realizable variant, or another information model has been settled. The card therefore retains uncertain status rather than asserting current openness or a resolution.
why: Classical VC theory controls prediction error through the richness of a class. This question asks whether the same optimal scale can always be realized by a learner whose whole output reveals only a dimension-proportional amount about which examples were used. The joint information and empirical-accuracy requirements make it a statement about the learner itself.
status_note: Historical source: Steinke–Zakynthinou 2020 Conjecture 6, the proper agnostic statement. The known November 2020 negative theorem concerns Conjectures 7–8 with smaller realizable empirical error, and the checked 2021/2025 information analyses do not themselves match Conjecture 6. Crucially, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and Hanneke’s author page list “The optimal information complexity of VC learning” by Hanneke and Juexiao Wang. No theorem text or manuscript link was located in the bounded checks on 16 September 2026. Current status is therefore uncertain, with that specific comparison outstanding; this review does not assert that the conjecture remains open.

The same learner must achieve expected training error within a universal square-root dimension-to-sample-size term of the best hypothesis on every sample.
