title: Non-clashing teaching dimension versus VC dimension
importance_reason: The sharp universal relation between VC dimension and non-clashing teaching compares two basic notions of information needed to identify concepts.
formal: For every finite set X and every nonempty concept class \(C\subseteq 2^{x}\), is \(NCTD(C)\le \operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Equivalently, if C has VC dimension d, does there exist a teaching map assigning at most d correctly labeled examples to each concept such that no two distinct concepts are mutually consistent with one another’s assigned examples? Both positive and negative examples are allowed. The target constant is exactly one, not merely a bound \(O(d)\).
definitions: A concept \(C\in C\) is a subset of the finite instance set X, identified with its indicator function \(1_{C}:X\to \{0,1\}\). A labeled sample is an unordered subset of \(X\times \{0,1\}\). It is consistent with C if each \((x,y)\) in it has \(y=1_{C}(x)\). A teaching map T assigns a sample \(T(C)\) consistent with C to every concept C in the class. It is non-clashing if, for every distinct \(C,D\in C, T(C)\) is not consistent with D or \(T(D)\) is not consistent with C. Equivalently, some point appearing in either teaching set has different labels under C and D. The condition is pairwise: \(T(C)\) need not by itself distinguish C from every other concept. A positive example has label 1 and a negative example has label 0; both count as one example. The size of T is \(\max _{C\in C}|T(C)|\), and \(NCTD(C)\) is the minimum of that size over all non-clashing teaching maps. The minimum exists because X and C are finite and giving all labels is a valid map. No sample order, extra message or additional side information is part of this definition. A subset \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by C when \(\{C\cap S:C\in C\}=2\)ˢ. The VC dimension \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the maximum cardinality of a shattered set. For a singleton concept class it is zero, and the empty teaching set works. The statement quantifies over all finite X and nonempty C, including that case; it concerns existence of a map, without an efficiency or encoding-size requirement on constructing it. The positive-only parameter NCTD\(^{+}\) restricts \(T(C)\) to samples with label 1 and can be larger. It is not the parameter in this conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove the exact inequality for every finite concept class by establishing existence of a valid map of maximum size at most its VC dimension, or give a finite concept class and a proof that every non-clashing teaching map has larger maximum size. A quadratic bound or even a larger-constant linear bound is insufficient. A separation for positive-only maps, another teaching model, or an algorithmic hardness result for finding maps does not refute this existence statement.
context:
The source and journal article give a universal upper bound quadratic in VC dimension. Their conclusion asks for the sharper inequality with coefficient one, and reports no counterexample to that inequality.

If a class of VC dimension d on X attains Sauer’s size bound \(\sum_{i=0}^{d} binomial(|X|,i)\), the cited representation-map result supplies a non-clashing map of size d. Maximum classes are a special case, not all finite classes.

The COLT 2024 paper constructs small maps for balls in particular graph classes and explicitly repeats the general open question. A size-four upper bound together with a VC-dimension-three upper bound for another family does not prove NCTD exceeds VC there.

The journal article separately studies stronger restrictions on avoiding collusion. Their optimal teaching parameter need not equal NCTD. Likewise, a map for the concepts themselves is not automatically a sample-compression scheme that must reconstruct from arbitrary samples.
why: Would show that every finite concept class can be taught with at most its VC dimension many examples per concept in the non-clashing model, giving a sharp link between learning capacity and teaching complexity.
status_note: Read the finite-domain no-clash definition and conclusion, the expanded JMLR treatment, and the COLT 2024 special-case results. Later searches through 12 September 2026 also found work on computing positive graph-ball teaching maps, but no proof or counterexample to the universal signed NCTD\(\le\)VC inequality. Search is not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The ALT paper defines NCTD, proves general and special-case bounds, and asks for the exact inequality NCTD\(\le\)VC. | 2023: The expanded JMLR article retains the universal question and distinguishes stronger teaching restrictions. | 2024: COLT results establish additional bounds for graph-ball classes and explicitly preserve the general conjecture.
working_summary: A teacher assigns correctly labeled examples to each concept in a finite class. No two different concepts may both fit each other’s assigned examples. The conjecture asks whether at most d examples per concept always suffice when the VC dimension is d. A quadratic general bound and exact bounds for certain special classes are known. The sharp signed-example inequality remains distinct from positive-only teaching, computational map-finding and sample-compression questions.

title: Littlestone-dimension regret bounds for unrestricted classes
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: A foundational quantitative characterization of adversarial binary learning, with universal scope over concept classes. The outstanding gap concerns the validity of the sharp dimension-only bound without a technical minimax assumption, rather than practical computational efficiency.
formal: Do universal real constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) exist such that, for every nonempty set \(\mathcal X\), every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer horizon \(T\ge d\), the optimal adversarial online regret satisfies \[c\sqrt{dT}\le R_T(\mathcal H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Here \[R_T(\mathcal H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(p_t,y_t)-\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\},\] where \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\in[0,1]\), \(\ell(p,0)=p\), and \(\ell(p,1)=1-p\). The infimum ranges over all such causal prediction rules. No restriction of countability, topology, compactness, or measurability is imposed on \(\mathcal X\) or \(\mathcal H\). The unresolved issue in the source is whether the upper bound holds with this full generality; the matching lower scale is already known.
question_excerpt: Is \(\Theta(\sqrt{\operatorname{LD}(\mathcal H)T})\) the optimal adversarial binary online regret for arbitrary concept classes, without the extra minimax regularity condition?
definitions: A concept \(h\) assigns one binary label to every instance. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has one instance from \(\mathcal X\) at each internal node and its outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. The tree is shattered by \(\mathcal H\) if every root-to-leaf path has a concept whose labels on that path's nodes equal its edge labels. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the largest shattered depth. Each horizon-specific rule \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_T)\) is an arbitrary family of set functions from labeled histories and the current instance to \([0,1]\); it may depend on the whole class and on \(T\). The number \(p_t\) is a probability of predicting label 1, so \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\) is the expected zero-one mistake loss. No probability distribution on the arbitrary instance space is required: regret is defined directly by the displayed supremum of finite sums. Equivalently, the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner chooses \(p_t\), and the adversary then supplies \(y_t\); the charged loss is \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\), not an adversary's reaction to a sampled binary prediction. The learner sees the label before the next round. Future instances and labels are unavailable. The sequence need not be realizable by any concept; comparison is to the best single concept in hindsight. The minimum comparator loss exists because the class is nonempty and losses are integers in \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\). The infimum over rules and supremum over sequences need not be attained. Running time, memory, computability, and finite descriptions of the class or rules are unrestricted; the predictor need not choose a concept from the class. The constants must be independent of the domain, class, dimension, and horizon, and logarithmic factors may not be hidden. The restriction \(T\ge d\) is essential to this square-root formulation because regret is at most \(T\); the omitted dimension-zero case has a single distinct concept and zero regret.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal two-sided statement, or its logical negation, in Lean under the stated arbitrary-set prediction model. For a positive answer, supply universal constants and prove both bounds, using any previously formalized lower-bound result with matching hypotheses. If an optimal rule does not attain the infimum, rules approaching the upper bound arbitrarily closely suffice. A negative answer must refute the existence of universal constants: for every proposed pair \(0<c\le C<\infty\), some class and allowed horizon violate a bound. In view of the known universal lower bound, the outstanding mathematical task is the upper bound or classes with unbounded ratio \(R_T(\mathcal H)/\sqrt{dT}\). A result with a class-dependent constant, an extra logarithmic factor, or an added regularity hypothesis does not settle the question. This is an exact constant-factor asymptotic claim, not an additive numerical approximation.
context:
In agnostic online classification, labels can contradict every member of the reference class. Regret therefore subtracts the errors of the best fixed concept instead of requiring the learner to make few errors outright. Randomized predictions are represented by their probabilities, which gives the stated finite-sum game even when the instance set has no measurable structure.

Littlestone dimension measures how long a class can sustain every binary answer pattern along an adaptively chosen tree of instances. Finite dimension characterizes online learnability. Here the question is quantitative: can the optimal cumulative excess error always be bounded by a universal constant times the square root of dimension times horizon?

The standard unrestricted binary bounds have lower scale \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\) and an upper bound with an additional logarithmic factor. Alon and coauthors obtain the sharp square-root rate through a connection with sequential Rademacher complexity. The later sources explicitly point out that the minimax step supporting this connection assumes an additional regularity condition on the class.

The source paper studies self-directed learning, where the learner chooses the order of available instances. Its footnote asks a separate question about the ordinary adversarial game. This card preserves that footnote’s question: the adversary supplies each next instance, and the dimension is Littlestone dimension rather than the paper’s self-directed dimension.

The 2023 multiclass paper explicitly records the unresolved unrestricted binary question and carries the same regularity condition into its sharp finite-label bounds. Raman’s 2025 dissertation repeats that qualification. It would therefore be incorrect to treat the unrestricted-looking headline of the 2021 theorem as a checked unconditional resolution.

The theorem on randomized Littlestone dimension and nearly realizable sequences cites the same 2021 upper bound inside its proof. It supplies no independent justification for removing the regularity condition. Its different mistake-budget formulation is not silently substituted for the present arbitrary-sequence regret target.

The checked May 2026 work improves weak-consistency-oracle complexity and memory in agnostic online learning. Its dimension-dependent regret guarantee still hides logarithmic factors. Those resource improvements do not supply the universal constant-factor upper bound requested here.
why: Littlestone dimension already characterizes whether adversarial online classification is learnable. This question asks whether that single combinatorial number also controls the sharp regret for every class. Removing the remaining regularity assumption would complete that quantitative characterization; a counterexample would exhibit a genuine limitation of a purely dimension-based prediction theorem.
status_note: The 2024 source and Raman’s 2025 dissertation explicitly retain this unrestricted-class question. The checked 2021 sharp theorem relies on a minimax step later sources qualify; the May 2026 resource improvement retains logarithmic factors. No matching unrestricted resolution was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026. This records the available source evidence, not a proof of present openness.
progress: 2021: The square-root regret theorem is obtained using a sequential-complexity bound and an earlier minimax theorem; later primary sources identify the regularity condition needed in that step. | 2023: Hanneke and coauthors explicitly say that the unrestricted binary square-root rate remains open and qualify their related finite-label results accordingly. | 2024: The ALT source asks whether the optimal square-root Littlestone regret survives without restrictions on the concept class. The previous imported quotation had lost the square-root sign. | 2025: Raman’s dissertation retains the explicit unresolved unrestricted-class qualification. | 2026-05: A new regret-oracle tradeoff improves computational resources while retaining logarithmic factors in the dimension-dependent regret statement. | 2026-09-16: Checked the exact source footnote, later regularity qualifications and candidate follow-up results. No matching unrestricted constant-factor theorem or counterexample was found in this bounded search.
working_summary: A learner predicts binary labels while an adversary supplies instances and then labels. Its regret is the expected number of errors beyond those of the best fixed concept on the same sequence. The question asks whether every class of finite Littlestone dimension has regret of square-root order in dimension times horizon, with universal constants. The sharp known theorem uses a minimax regularity assumption, and later primary sources explicitly leave removal of that assumption open. A complete Lean answer must establish the universal two-sided bound for arbitrary classes or refute it under the same prediction model.

title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
importance_reason: A fundamental proposed relationship between two established learning-complexity measures, with a general quadratic bound and an unresolved universal linear target.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.
context:
Simon’s 2023 Open Problem 3 asks for precisely this universal linear relationship. The earlier Simon–Zilles open-problem paper is retained as provenance from the already consolidated duplicate; there is a single active target.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Recursive teaching measures the hardest easiest-to-teach concept that remains after restricting the candidate class; it is not the maximum ordinary teaching dimension of the original class.

Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.

Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

Compton, Pabbaraju and Zhivotovskiy give lower bounds for particular greedy teaching-set constructions in 2025. They describe the universal conjecture as unresolved; limitations of those constructions are not counterexamples to the existence of small teaching sets.

The conjecture permits any universal constant, so examples separating the two dimensions by a fixed factor are compatible with it. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.
why: A universal linear bound would connect sample-based combinatorial complexity with the number of examples needed for structured teaching. It asks whether recursive teaching can always be controlled at the same scale as VC dimension.
status_note: The conjecture is explicitly open in the 2023 source and the checked 2025 work. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no general linear upper bound or unbounded-ratio counterexample. The new results address special classes and particular construction rules.
progress: 2015: Simon and Zilles pose the linear RTD-versus-VC question. | 2017: A general quadratic upper bound is proved. | 2023: Simon explicitly retains the universal linear bound as Open Problem 3. | 2025: New graph-class theorems confirm special cases, while greedy-construction lower bounds do not refute the conjecture.
working_summary: A finite concept class can be studied through both its VC dimension and its recursive teaching dimension. VC dimension measures the ability to realize label patterns, while recursive teaching measures how examples can identify concepts through successive elimination. The question asks whether one universal constant always bounds recursive teaching dimension by that constant times VC dimension. The same constant must work for every finite class. The project seeks a direct quantitative link between the complexity of learning from samples and the information needed for structured teaching.

title: Statistical-query complexity of sparse halfspaces
importance_reason: Sparse-halfspace statistical-query complexity locates an important computational learning barrier.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge 2\) and \(a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}])\le C n^{b}\), where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function \(h:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,+1\}\) of the form \(h(x)=+1\) if \(\sum j w_{j}x_{j}\ge \theta\) and \(h(x)=- 1\) otherwise, where \(w\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) has at most r nonzero coordinates and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and \(0<\gamma <1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,\gamma )\) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions \(h_{1},\ldots ,hd\) in Hn,r satisfying |\(\sum x D(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)|\le \gamma\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(SQ-DIM(Hn,r,\gamma )\) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its \(O(1)\) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than \(Cn^{b}\) with pairwise absolute correlations at most \(1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}]\). The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.
context:
A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on \(x_{7}\) is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function \(\varphi (x,h(x))\in [- 1,1]\). A tolerance \(\tau\) allows any answer within \(\tau\) of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules \(2x_{1}- 1\) and \(2x_{2}- 1\) have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.
why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-\(\operatorname{poly}(r \log  n)\) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2014: Feldman states the precise sparse-halfspace correlation-dimension question and connects the parameter to attribute-efficient SQ learning.
working_summary: An r-sparse halfspace uses at most r of the n Boolean input coordinates. Statistical-query learning accesses approximate expectations instead of individual labeled examples. The source asks whether the worst-case number of nearly uncorrelated sparse halfspaces stays polynomial in n when correlation is inverse-polynomial in r log n. Both the sparsity dependence and the worst-case distribution are essential to the question. A resolution would clarify the informational limits of exploiting sparse structure through statistical queries.

title: Improper compression for Gaussian-mixture reconstruction
importance_reason: Tests whether allowing a learned improper representation removes a computational obstruction while preserving a compact per-point code; the bounded reconstruction target is distinct from estimating mixture densities or parameters.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learning procedure with the following guarantee? For all integers \(d\ge1\), \(k>d\) and \(t\ge2\), and every Borel probability distribution \(D\) on the closed Euclidean unit ball \(B_d\), it learns a shared model \(w\) and an encoder–decoder pair \(E_w:B_d\to\{0,1\}^{b}\), \(Q_w:\{0,1\}^{b}\to B_d\) such that, with probability at least \(2/3\), \[\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\|Q_w(E_w(x))-x\|_2^{2}\le\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)+1/t,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(D)=\inf_{\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\in B_d}\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\min_{i\in[k]}\|x-\mu_i\|_2^{2}?\] Training, sample count, model storage, encoding and decoding must all be polynomial in \(d,k,t\), while the number of bits per encoded point satisfies \(b\le C(1+\log_2 k+\log_2 t)^{q}\) for universal \(C,q>0\). This is the explicitly normalized, bounded-data version of the source's first reconstruction question, in the overcomplete regime \(k>d\).
definitions:
Here \(B_d=\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}:\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{2}\le1\}\), \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and \(\|x\|_2^{2}=\sum_jx_j^{2}\). The comparator is the best set of \(k\) reconstruction centers; repeated centers are allowed. The distribution need not itself be a Gaussian mixture. There is no separation, covariance or minimum cluster-weight promise. Accuracy is additive squared Euclidean reconstruction error in these unit-ball coordinates. The integer \(t\) requests error \(1/t\); all positive accuracy levels are covered by rounding to a smaller reciprocal-integer tolerance.

Fix three finite programs, for training, encoding and decoding. They use a real RAM with rational program constants, exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square roots of nonnegative values, comparisons and indexed memory access, each charged one operation. Integer counters and addresses use logarithmically many bits in \(d+k+t+2\), with a fixed constant factor allowed for each program. There is no floor operation, real-digit extraction, advice, or noncomputable real program constant. Training also has independent fair random bits and a sampling oracle returning independent points from \(D\). One sample request and reading each of its coordinates are charged. There must be one polynomial \(p\), independent of \(D,d,k,t\), bounding training operations, samples, and stored scalar or integer cells, and bounding operations for encoding any one point and decoding any codeword. All executions must halt within these bounds, even on the probability-of-failure event.

Training returns a finite shared parameter vector \(w\) and the integer code length \(b\); the two fixed evaluation programs use \(w,d,k,t,b\). They are deterministic after training. Every codeword has exactly \(b\) bits, with padding allowed. The decoder receives only that codeword and the shared model, and returns a point in \(B_d\). The original point and extra point-dependent information are unavailable to it. Model storage is charged to the polynomial storage bound, not again to each point's code length. Probability of training success is over its samples and random bits; the expectation in the successful guarantee uses a fresh independent point. No restriction to a nearest-center decoder or to \(k\) possible reconstructions is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of the three uniform procedures and universal polynomial and code-length bounds, with the stated error guarantee, or a proof that no such procedures exist in this model. A negative result for a proper Gaussian-parameter estimator or a decoder restricted to exactly \(k\) centers does not refute this improper target. A multiplicative constant greater than one in front of \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)\) does not meet the required additive guarantee.
context:
The Gaussian-mixture title motivates the comparator, but the source deliberately uses a non-generative reconstruction objective to permit improper learning. Recovering Gaussian densities or component parameters is a different task. A successful encoder and decoder need only achieve the specified squared-distance loss.

The 2018 note leaves normalization and the detailed computational model implicit. This card explicitly selects unit-ball data and real-arithmetic polynomial time, drawing on the normalized reconstruction framework it cites. This bounded-data target is not asserted equivalent to every distribution on unbounded Euclidean space. It retains the source’s first, spherical-comparator question; the additional general-covariance direction is not folded into it.

A nearest-center code for a known set of k centers needs only a logarithmic number of bits for the center index. The challenge includes learning from samples. The source’s linear-subspace comparison has a substantially larger pointwise representation when the number of retained coordinates is large.

The 2020 JACM paper proves sample-complexity bounds for approximating Gaussian-mixture densities in total variation, using compression of a distribution description. It explicitly does not optimize running time. Those results do not establish polynomial-time, short-code reconstruction of each new point in the model here.
why: The task asks whether efficient unsupervised reconstruction can compete with a small optimal codebook while using only a polynomial in the logarithms of its size and accuracy per point. It separates the cost of discovering original mixture parameters from the cost of learning a useful compact representation.
status_note: The first reconstruction question is open in the COLT 2018 source. The bounded-data real-RAM version is an explicit editorial specification, not a verbatim complete model supplied there. Bounded searches on 2026-09-14 found later Gaussian-mixture compression results for density estimation, whose objective and time guarantees differ. No matching resolution was verified, and the search is not exhaustive.
progress: 2016: Hazan and Ma formalize comparative unsupervised learning through encoding and decoding with reconstruction loss. | 2018: Hazan and Livni ask for polynomial-in-logarithms encoding length and efficient improper reconstruction in the overcomplete regime. Their PCA comparison does not attain the requested pointwise encoding length. | 2020-10: Ashtiani and coauthors obtain near-optimal Gaussian-mixture density-estimation sample bounds through distribution compression, a different objective and resource guarantee.
working_summary: The task is to learn short pointwise encodings that reconstruct bounded Euclidean data almost as well as the best k centers. It concerns the overcomplete regime, where the number of comparator centers exceeds the ambient dimension. The decoder may be improper and share a learned model, but each new point receives only polynomial-in-logarithms many bits. The card explicitly fixes unit-ball normalization, squared reconstruction loss and polynomial real-arithmetic training and evaluation. Density-estimation compression results use a different objective and do not by themselves settle this task.

title: Compression overhead for adversarial robustness
importance_reason: A structural transfer question between ordinary and adversarially robust sample compression, testing whether robustness imposes information overhead independent of perturbation-set size; more general than a bound for one attack family.
formal: Is there a universal constant \(K>0\) such that the following implication holds for every nonempty domain \(X\), every nonempty total binary concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension, every integer \(k\ge1\), and every perturbation map \(U:X\to2^{X}\) satisfying \(x\in U(x)\)? If \(\mathcal C\) admits an ordinary labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(k\), must it admit an adversarially robust labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(\lceil Kk\rceil\)? The constant is independent of the class, domain, perturbation sets and sample length. Perturbation sets may be infinite. This makes the size-overhead assertion in Open Problem 28 explicit, with \(k\) denoting the available ordinary compression bound.
definitions:
A sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\) is any finite sequence of points of \(X\) with labels in \(\{0,1\}\), including the empty sequence. A labeled compression scheme consists of fixed deterministic maps \(\kappa,\rho\). The compressor sends \(S\) to \((T,b)\), where \(T\) is a finite ordered sequence of labeled examples drawn from \(S\) and \(b\) is a finite binary string. Following the source's sequence convention, every entry of \(T\) must occur in \(S\); reordering or repetition is allowed, and every retained occurrence is counted. Size at most \(k\) means \(|T|+|b|\le k\) on every sample. The reconstructor maps only \((T,b)\) to a total binary predictor \(\rho(T,b):X\to\{0,1\}\). It does not receive the omitted examples, their original indices, or the original sample length for free. One labeled example counts as one unit regardless of its representation length; each auxiliary bit also counts as one unit. No computability or running-time restriction is imposed.

Ordinary realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). An ordinary scheme must reconstruct a predictor satisfying those equalities for every realizable sample. Robust realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(z)=y_i\) for every sample position \(i\) and every \(z\in U(x_i)\). A robust scheme must have \(\rho(\kappa(S))(z)=y_i\) for all these positions and perturbations whenever the sample is robustly realizable. The compressed examples must be original labeled examples, not freely chosen perturbed points. Each pair of maps may depend on \(\mathcal C\) and, in the robust case, on the entire fixed map \(U\), but is selected once for all samples. Reconstructed predictors can lie outside \(\mathcal C\). There is no correctness requirement on nonrealizable samples, although the size bound still applies. Empty samples impose no correctness constraints.

A finite set is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if all its binary labelings are restrictions of members of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the supremum of the cardinalities of shattered finite sets; it is required to be finite.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal constant-overhead implication, or a proof that no universal \(K\) works. A negative answer must establish ordinary compression of size \(k\) for its finite-VC class and a robust compression requirement exceeding \(\lceil Kk\rceil\), for arbitrarily large proposed constants \(K\); nonexistence of any bounded robust scheme for such a class also suffices. Bounds depending on perturbation-set size, or a conclusion for stable ordinary schemes alone, do not establish this implication.
context:
The source writes the available ordinary size as a function of VC dimension. Here the available bound is called k so that the constant hidden in its proposed overhead is explicitly universal. The printed phrase that the domain has a compression scheme is read as referring to the concept class; sample compression is a property of a class together with its reconstructor.

The decoder knows the fixed perturbation map, but it must recover a predictor from original examples and auxiliary bits. Retaining one original example does not by itself identify which of its potentially many perturbations an ordinary compressor selected. This distinction is part of the information requirement, even when computation is unrestricted.

For uniformly finite perturbation sets, Theorem 26 gives an additional logarithmic dependence on their maximum cardinality. Theorem 27 removes this factor under the stronger premise of a stable ordinary compression scheme. Stability requires that discarding unselected examples leave the compressor’s message unchanged.

Theorem 29 establishes that robust learnability alone need not give a bounded robust compression scheme. Its construction starts from a partial concept class. It does not supply the ordinary bounded-compression premise for the resulting total class required here; it is therefore not a resolution of Open Problem 28.
why: Sample compression asks how much of a training set determines a predictor consistent with all its constraints. Adversarial robustness replaces each example by an entire set of required predictions. A constant-overhead theorem would connect these two information requirements without charging separately for the number of possible perturbations.
status_note: Open Problem 28 in the ALT 2025 source. A bounded later-work search and the author bibliography checked on 2026-09-14 did not reveal a matching resolution. The finite-set and stable-scheme theorems and the separate robust-learnability counterexample have different hypotheses. No independent verification of all cited proofs is claimed.
progress: 2025: Attias, Hanneke and Ramaswami state Open Problem 28 after finite-perturbation-set and stable-compression results. They allow general perturbation maps in the question. | 2026-09-14: The checked primary paper and author bibliography do not supply a resolution of this general implication. The separate negative robust-learnability theorem has a different premise.
working_summary: The question asks whether ordinary sample compression can be made adversarially robust with only a universal constant factor in size. A message contains original labeled examples and a counted auxiliary bitstring. The reconstructed predictor must label every allowed perturbation correctly whenever the full sample is robustly realizable. Known reductions impose a perturbation-cardinality factor or a stability assumption on the ordinary scheme. The general question permits infinite perturbation sets and asks whether that overhead can be avoided.

title: Local regularization for multiclass learning
importance_reason: A general characterization of multiclass learning or direct-sum behavior would organize a broad family of learning problems.
formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer \(\psi :H\times X\to \mathbb{R} \ge 0\) such that every learner induced by \(\psi\), under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? This is the existence part of the source question; optimal sample complexity is a separate refinement.
definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and \(H\subseteq Y^{X} a\) nonempty class of predictors \(h:X\to Y\). A distribution D on labeled examples \(X\times Y\) is realizable by H if some \(h*\in H\) satisfies PrD\([h*(x)\ne y]=0\). The risk of a predictor g is \(LD(g)\)=PrD\([g(x)\ne y]\). A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor \(A(S)\), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), there is \(mA(\varepsilon ,\delta )<\infty\) such that for every H-realizable D and every \(m\ge mA(\varepsilon ,\delta ), a\) sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies \(\Pr [LD(A(S))>\varepsilon ]\le \delta\). Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space \(H[S]\) consists of all \(h\in H\) agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair \((h,x) a\) nonnegative real score \(\psi (h,x)\), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on \(H[S]\) is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by \(\psi\) when \(A(S)(x)\) belongs to {\(h(x): h\in\)argmin \(g\in H[S] \psi (g,x)\)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, \(D, \varepsilon\) or \(\delta\).
answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.
context:
A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.
why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. A negative answer would identify a limit of regularization even when improper prediction is allowed; a positive answer would give a common template for all learnable multiclass classes.
status_note: As of 11 September 2026, two checked preprints claim a negative resolution. Their theorem statements and local-regularization/PAC definitions match the main target, but the full impossibility proofs were not independently audited and no accepted publication was verified. Retained as uncertain rather than certified open or resolved.
progress: 2024: The COLT open-problem paper asks whether fixed local regularization characterizes realizable PAC learnability. | 2026-07-26: Hou posts a claimed negative resolution, explicitly addressing the original tie convention and nonvacuity of minimization. | 2026-08-27: Asilis and coauthors post another claimed PAC counterexample in Theorem 4.6 and acknowledge the independent July result.
working_summary: A local regularizer fixes a score for every hypothesis and test point before seeing the training sample. At prediction time it selects among the lowest-scored hypotheses consistent with the sample. The question asks whether every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass class admits such a rule that succeeds under every tie-breaking choice. Two preprints from July and August 2026 claim counterexamples under this definition. Their statements match the main question, while independent verification of the claimed negative resolution remains outstanding.

title: Agnostic direct-sum learning rates
importance_reason: A general question about how agnostic learning difficulty scales across multiple tasks and whether a single-instance minimax rate contains enough information; the source’s distinct compression and realizable questions are not bundled into this target.
formal: Does the single-instance agnostic learning rate determine all Cartesian-power learning rates up to constant factors? Precisely, for every two nonempty concept classes \(\mathcal C\subseteq Y^{X}\) and \(\mathcal D\subseteq Z^{W}\) on nonempty countable input and label sets, suppose there are \(a,b>0\) such that \[a\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C}(n)\le b\,e_{\mathcal D}(n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge1.\] Must there then be \(a',b'>0\), allowed to depend on the two classes but not on \(n\) or \(r\), such that \[a'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\le e_{\mathcal C^{r}}(n)\le b'\,e_{\mathcal D^{r}}(n)\qquad\text{for every }n,r\ge1?\] This is the constant-factor rate-determination form of the source's agnostic Open Question 3. The countable-domain convention and constant-factor interpretation are explicit editorial choices; the source paper also asks separate realizable-learning and compression questions.
definitions:
For a nonempty class \(\mathcal H\subseteq V^{U}\) on countable sets \(U,V\), and any probability distribution \(P\) on \(U\times V\), let \(L_P(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}[h(x)\ne y]\). Define \[e_{\mathcal H}(n)=\inf_{A_n}\sup_{P}\left(\mathbb E_{S\sim P^{n}}L_P(A_n(S))-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}L_P(h)\right).\] Here \(A_n:(U\times V)^{n}\to V^{U}\) ranges over all deterministic learning rules and is chosen before \(P\); it may depend on \(\mathcal H\) and \(n\). It need not be computable, and may output a predictor outside \(\mathcal H\). The training sample consists of \(n\) independent pairs from \(P\). The outer expectation is over that sample; the risk uses a fresh independent pair. All countable sets have their discrete sigma-algebras. The countable sample space makes these expectations well-defined even when the hypothesis class is uncountable. Labels may have arbitrary noise. Infima are not assumed to be attained. The rate is a dimensionless minimax expected excess probability of error in \([0,1]\).

For \(r\ge1\), \(\mathcal H^{r}\) consists of all maps \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mapsto(h_1(x_1),\ldots,h_r(x_r))\) with \(h_1,\ldots,h_r\in\mathcal H\). Its input set is \(U^{r}\) and its label set is \(V^{r}\). Apply the same learning-curve definition to this class. Each of the \(n\) examples is now an entire input–label tuple. Its coordinates can be arbitrarily correlated: \(P\) ranges over every distribution on \(U^{r}\times V^{r}\), not just product distributions. A tuple prediction incurs loss one whenever any coordinate differs from the label tuple, and zero otherwise. This is whole-tuple zero-one loss, not a sum or average of coordinate losses. The learner for the product may also be improper, so its output need not act separately on each coordinate.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the rate-determination implication. A refutation must give two admissible classes with comparable single-instance curves but prove that no positive constants independent of both \(n\) and \(r\) compare their product curves. A positive answer must cover every such pair of classes and all positive sample sizes and product multiplicities. The target is a proposition about constant-factor rate information; it does not ask whether exact numerical single-instance curves encode additional information.
context:
The inherited card contained the title of a paper posing several independent problems. This revision selects its agnostic rate question and makes the precision of the proposed relationship explicit. It does not assert that the other questions in that paper are equivalent or resolved.

The comparison is between expected error and the best predictor in the target class under the same distribution. Bounding the total error of separately learned coordinates does not automatically bound this excess error against the best whole-tuple predictor.

The order of quantifiers matters. Constants depending on the number of tasks would allow different behavior to be hidden as that number increases. This formulation requires a single pair of comparison constants for all sample sizes and multiplicities.

The August 2026 preprint claims a counterexample using \(X=Y=\{0,1\}\): one class contains the two constant functions, and the other contains the zero function and the identity function. It claims product rates respectively of order \(n^{-1/2}\) and \(\min\{1,\sqrt{r/n}\}\), while both single-instance rates are of order \(n^{-1/2}\). The claim concerns the exact whole-tuple, improper model used here, and would refute this implication.
why: A direct-sum law would explain whether learning several tasks together has a statistical cost determined by the difficulty of one task. In the agnostic setting, whole-tuple loss and unrestricted correlations can make that question depend on class structure not visible in its ordinary learning rate.
status_note: Uncertain pending assessment of the matching claimed refutation in arXiv:2608.06951v1 (7 August 2026). On 2026-09-14, the primary 2024 question and the preprint’s definitions and Theorem 1 were checked. The finite binary classes in that claim fall within the specified domain and would refute the displayed implication if the proof is correct; publication and independent proof verification were not established.
progress: 2024: Hanneke, Moran and Waknine ask how the agnostic learning curve changes under Cartesian powers, separately from their realizable-learning, uniform-convergence and compression questions. | 2026-08-07: More, Das and Gupta post Theorem 1 claiming a negative rate-level answer. Its model and theorem statement match the selected formulation, but this review has not independently verified the proof or established a peer-reviewed resolution.
working_summary: The question asks whether comparable single-instance agnostic learning rates force comparable rates for every number of simultaneous tasks. The learning curve is minimax expected excess zero-one error, with arbitrary distributions and improper deterministic learners. For a Cartesian power, each example is a complete tuple and any wrong coordinate makes the tuple prediction incorrect. The comparison constants must be independent of both sample size and number of tasks. An August 2026 preprint claims a finite binary counterexample, so the card records an unresolved verification status for that claimed refutation.

title: Dimension complexity of distribution-independent SQ learning
importance_reason: A source-defined connection between distribution-independent statistical-query learning and a shared exact linear representation; its universal quantifiers make it broader than a comparison of two chosen training implementations.
formal: Is there a universal constant \(C>0\) with the following property? For every nonempty set \(X\), every nonempty binary concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^{X}\), every integer \(m\ge1\), tolerance \(0<\tau<1\) and error \(0\le\varepsilon<1/4\), suppose a single randomized statistical-query learner makes at most \(m\) queries of tolerance \(\tau\) and, for every input distribution \(D\), target \(h\in\mathcal H\) and admissible oracle response rule, returns \(\hat h\) with \(\mathbb E[\Pr_{x\sim D}(\hat h(x)\ne h(x))]\le\varepsilon\). Must \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)\le C m/\tau^{2}\)? The learner is selected before the distribution, target and oracle replies. The constant is independent of all these objects and of the accuracy, domain size and class.
definitions:
Use the discrete measurable structure \(2^{X}\) on an arbitrary domain, and quantify over all countably additive probability measures on it. A tolerance-\(\tau\) query is an arbitrary bounded function \(q:X\times\{-1,+1\}\to[-1,1]\); its answer is any real \(v\) satisfying \(|v-\mathbb E_{x\sim D}q(x,h(x))|\le\tau\). Queries may depend on previous answers and an internal random seed independent of the instance. A response rule can depend on the public history, including the current query, but observes the hidden seed only through that history. It must obey the tolerance at every history that can occur for the fixed distribution and target. The guarantee holds for every such rule, with expectation over the learner's seed. Require the interactions and their resulting loss to be measurable, so that the stated expectations exist. These measurable-interaction conventions specify the source's abstract oracle model. Query count is the resource: there is no restriction on computation between queries, description length, adaptivity, or the class containing the output predictor. There are no free samples or additional distribution information.

The dimension complexity is the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which there is one map \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^{d}\) such that, for each \(h\in\mathcal H\), some \(w_h\in\mathbb R^{d}\) satisfies \(h(x)=\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(\langle w_h,\phi(x)\rangle)\) for every \(x\in X\). Here \(\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(z)=+1\) when \(z\ge0\), and \(-1\) otherwise, and the inner product is the sum of coordinatewise products. Put \(\operatorname{dc}=+\infty\) if no finite dimension works. The feature map is deterministic, shared by all targets, and independent of \(D\); no construction or efficiency requirement is imposed on it. Offsets require a coordinate of the feature map. The representation must be exact at every point, even though the learner's premise allows positive expected error.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must supply a universal finite \(C\). A negative answer must show that no such constant works: for every \(C>0\), exhibit or prove the existence of a class and admissible learner parameters satisfying the premise but with \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)>Cm/\tau^{2}\). An infinite dimension example also qualifies. A result assuming extra rank, margin or distribution conditions, or allowing only approximate or random feature representations, does not establish the stated implication.
context:
The source poses separate questions about a specified neural-network training procedure and about statistical queries. This card selects its formal Open Question 2. The broader deep-learning motivation is retained here; the card does not assert that this SQ question is equivalent to the neural-network question.

Learning may choose different predictors after observing different distributions. A low-dimensional representation has a stronger order of choices: the same features must work before either the distribution or the target is selected. Exact representation also concerns points that may have negligible probability in a particular learning instance.

The statistical-query interface permits queries that depend jointly on the example and its label. Restricting queries to a label multiplied by an example function gives a different model. Similarly, replacing the requested bound by an unspecified polynomial, or adding dependence on the domain size, changes the question.

The August 2026 preprint gives a conditional polynomial dimension statement. It assumes a bound on the dimension of a space of averaged terminal predictions; that bound is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence established for arbitrary SQ learners. Its authors explicitly describe the remaining gap to the original question.
why: This asks whether learning successfully from noisy expectation information under every distribution forces all targets to share a small linear representation. It connects a general information-access model with the geometric capacity of linear predictors, and tests whether known advantages of learned representations depend essentially on the input distribution.
status_note: Open Question 2 in the COLT 2026 source. Bounded primary-source search on 2026-09-14 found the August 2026 VALG theorem, whose explicit additional rank hypothesis and polynomial bound do not settle the stated implication. The source also reports a flaw in the earlier 2025 claimed bound. This review compares theorem scope; it does not independently verify either paper’s proofs.
progress: 2026-06–07: Feldman, Kamath and Srebro state the linear dimension bound as Open Question 2. Their Section 3 reports that the claimed upper bounds of Karchmer and Malach (2025) have a proof flaw, citing a 2026 communication with those authors. | 2026-08-13: The VALG preprint presents Theorem 4.9 under the additional polynomial mean-response-rank hypothesis of Assumption 4.42. Its explicit qualification prevents treating it as a resolution of the unrestricted question. The theorem has not been independently proof-checked in this review.
working_summary: The question asks whether successful distribution-independent statistical-query learning forces low dimension complexity. The learner may adapt bounded expectation queries to previous noisy answers. Its guarantee must hold for every distribution, target and valid response rule. The desired conclusion is one deterministic feature map representing the entire class exactly in dimension proportional to the query count divided by squared tolerance. Recent conditional results impose additional structure and do not establish the unrestricted implication.

title: Monotone empirical risk minimization
importance_reason: A basic structural question about empirical risk minimization and finite-sample learning curves, made distinct from known constructions of unrestricted monotone learners.
formal: Does every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\) of finite VC dimension on a countable domain \(X\) admit a possibly randomized empirical risk minimizer whose expected population error never increases with sample size, under every data distribution? Precisely, for each such \(X,\mathcal H\), require learning rules \(A_n\), \(n\geq1\), that always return an empirical risk minimizer in \(\mathcal H\), and for every distribution \(D\) on \(X\times\{0,1\}\) satisfy \[\mathbb E_{S\sim D^{n+1},R}L_D(A_{n+1}(S,R))\leq\mathbb E_{S\sim D^n,R}L_D(A_n(S,R))\quad(n\geq1).\] The learner may depend on \(\mathcal H\), but not on \(D\).
definitions: The population zero-one loss of \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\) is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). For an ordered sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\), its empirical loss is \(\widehat L_S(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1[h(x_i)\ne y_i]\). Each \(A_n\) maps a sample and an independent uniform seed \(R\in[0,1]\) to an element of \(\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\widehat L_S(h)\). This minimum exists because the attainable empirical errors form a nonempty subset of \(\{0,1/n,\ldots,1\}\). Ties may be resolved using the whole ordered sample and the seed; for every fixed sample and test point, the returned label is required to be a measurable function of the seed. With countable \(X\), these conditions make all displayed expectations well defined. No computational or storage bound is imposed. Samples are independent identically distributed draws from \(D\), repetitions are allowed, and the test observation defining population loss is independent of training and of the seed. Labels may be noisy: realizability by \(\mathcal H\) is not assumed. Finite VC dimension means a finite upper bound on the cardinalities of sets \(F\subseteq X\) for which \(\{h|_F:h\in\mathcal H\}=\{0,1\}^F\). The monotonicity compares expectations over samples and learner randomness; it is not a pathwise comparison for each particular sample extension, a statement only after a distribution-dependent threshold, or monotonicity of a generalization bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every class in the stated domain admits such a family of learning rules, or exhibit a class of finite VC dimension on a countable domain and prove that no family of randomized empirical risk minimizers has the displayed property for all \(D,n\). An affirmative proof must retain exact empirical minimization and membership of the output in \(\mathcal H\). For a negative answer, showing nonmonotonicity of one tie-breaking rule does not exclude all eligible ERMs. General monotone learners that need not minimize empirical risk, eventual monotonicity, or decreasing upper bounds on error do not meet this criterion.
context:
Viering, Mey and Loog’s original paper asks broadly when learning is monotone and whether it can be made so, emphasizing empirical risk minimization. This card selects the Boolean classification ERM question on countable domains, keeping the broader research direction as provenance instead of presenting it as one unspecified characterization request.

Bousquet, Daniely, Kaplan, Mansour, Moran and Stemmer formulate the remaining ERM question explicitly in their 2022 open-questions section: whether every learnable class admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer. Their general monotone-learning theorem permits rules outside this constraint.

Finite VC dimension controls statistical learning in this setting, but convergence to the best population error need not imply improvement at each consecutive sample size. The quantifier over all distributions includes misspecified or noisy data as well as realizable classification problems.

The 2019 paper provides monotone and nonmonotone examples using the same loss for fitting and evaluation. Such counterexamples show that particular familiar procedures may fail, but do not automatically rule out every permissible ERM rule for a given class.

The 2025 PAC perspective studies distributions constructed from generalization bounds. In its Section 3, a bound-derived expression is used as a distributional model. Monotonicity of that expression alone does not establish the actual expected-risk inequality required here.

Randomization and tie resolution are part of the existence question. The learner can choose among all empirically optimal hypotheses, but cannot replace exact minimization with an arbitrary predictor or select its rule after learning the unknown data distribution.
why: The problem asks whether exact empirical fitting is inherently compatible with the intuition that more independent data should improve expected predictions. It separates the behavior of ERM from general statistical consistency and from monotone wrappers that change the learning rule.
status_note: The ERM existence question is explicit in the checked 2022 paper. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no proof or refutation for the specified countable-domain Boolean finite-VC family. The broader source also asks about other losses and models. Later statements about monotone unrestricted learners, maximum likelihood in well-specified families, or bound-derived risk distributions are not treated as resolutions of this exact ERM claim.
progress: 2019: The source defines monotonicity of expected risk and poses the broader ERM question. | 2022: General monotone-learning constructions are proved, while the existence of monotone ERMs is retained as a separate open question. | 2025: The PAC perspective analyzes bound-derived distributions; the checked passage does not establish the exact expected-risk statement of this card.
working_summary: Expected prediction error can increase when a learner receives an additional independent training example. This card asks whether every finite-VC Boolean class on a countable domain nevertheless admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer. The learner may randomize and resolve ties, but must always output an empirically optimal hypothesis from the original class. Monotonicity is required for every data distribution and every consecutive positive sample size, using actual population error. A resolution would clarify whether exact empirical fitting can always be reconciled with monotone learning curves.

title: Identifiable elicitation complexity
importance_reason: A quantitative or model-specific learning frontier; resolving it would sharpen a useful guarantee but has more limited scope than a general learnability characterization.
formal: Determine the identifiable elicitation-complexity function \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) defined below, throughout its full domain of nonempty convex families of real-outcome distributions and finite-dimensional statistical properties. Its value is the smallest positive number of intermediate real reports needed to recover \(\Gamma\) through an elicitable, identifiable property, or \(\infty\) if no finite number suffices. The numerical benchmark requires a real-valued approximation with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite value, and a proof identifying exactly the infinite-value cases.
definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be the set of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\). A distribution family \(\mathcal P\) is any nonempty subset of \(\mathcal M\) that contains \(\lambda p+(1-\lambda)q\) whenever \(p,q\in\mathcal P\) and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). The domain consists of every such \(\mathcal P\), every positive integer \(d\), and every function \(\Gamma:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^d\). The dimension \(d\) is part of the specification of \(\Gamma\). No finite encoding, computability, continuity, moment assumption or uniform support bound is imposed on this domain.

For a positive integer \(k\), an admissible intermediate property consists of a nonempty report set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^k\), a surjective function \(h:\mathcal P\to R\), a loss \(L:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), an identification function \(V:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^k\), and a link \(\psi:R\to\mathbb R^d\). For each report \(r\in R\), the functions \(y\mapsto L(r,y)\) and every coordinate of \(y\mapsto V(r,y)\) must be Borel measurable and absolutely integrable with respect to every \(p\in\mathcal P\). Write \(\mathbb E_p u(Y)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(y)\,dp(y)\). Elicitation means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and every \(r\in R\) distinct from \(h(p)\), \(\mathbb E_p L(h(p),Y)<\mathbb E_p L(r,Y)\). Thus the expected loss has the unique global minimizer \(h(p)\), with no approximate minimization or tie-breaking convention. Identification means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and \(r\in R\), \(\mathbb E_p V(r,Y)=0\) if and only if \(h(p)=r\). Finally, \(\Gamma(p)=\psi(h(p))\) must hold for every \(p\in\mathcal P\).

Set \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) to the least positive integer \(k\) for which these objects exist, and to \(\infty\) when there is no such finite \(k\). The unit is the number of scalar real coordinates of the intermediate report. Constant properties therefore have value \(1\), under the positive-dimension convention used here. Requiring \(R=h(\mathcal P)\) makes identification apply exactly to attainable reports; unused reports can be removed without losing elicitation. Neither convexity nor smoothness of \(L\), nor continuity of \(h\) or \(\psi\), is required. The single observation \(Y\) is the sole outcome argument of the loss and identification functions; a loss on several independent observations defines a different model. Statistical sample complexity and computational time for optimizing a loss are not the quantity being measured.

The symbol \(\infty\) here records failure of every finite report dimension. It does not assert the existence of a countably infinite-dimensional elicitable intermediate property. This convention extends the finite complexity classes to a total extended-valued function, including cases that the 2021 source leaves undefined when no allowed intermediate property exists.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a full determination of \(E\) on the stated domain: specify an unambiguous function \(a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\in[0,\infty]\), prove \(a=\infty\) exactly when \(E=\infty\), and prove \(|a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)-E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)|\le1/100\) for every finite value, interpreting the integer \(E\) as a real number. A structural characterization of all finite complexity classes together with all infinite cases may specify the answer. The approximation need not be integer-valued, and no efficient algorithm or predetermined formula grammar is required. Merely repeating the defining minimum over admissible losses and intermediate properties, a one-sided bound, or a classification of only selected statistics does not meet the criterion.
context:
The 2016 paper poses three distinct questions: which properties are elicitable, which losses elicit a given property, and how to characterize elicitation complexity classes. This card selects Question 3. It makes the real-outcome, convex-distribution-family branch explicit and retains the source’s restriction to identifiable intermediate properties; it does not additionally demand a classification of every possible loss.

Without a restriction on intermediate properties, encodings of an entire distribution into one real report can make the dimension measure degenerate. Identifiability is part of the target definition, rather than an optional regularity assumption.

The later journal treatment distinguishes identifiable intermediates from other classes defined through linear expectations or smooth convex losses. Its theorems establish tight complexity values for several families, including suitable Bayes-risk examples, rather than a classification of all statistical properties.

The 2024 survey still records unresolved elicitation complexities for several statistical quantities, including higher central moments and financial risk measures. Results using multiple independent observations or a restricted class of losses concern different complexity functions.
why: A loss can recover a richer prediction than the statistic ultimately needed. The minimum dimension of that prediction measures an expressive limitation of loss-based estimation, independently of optimization time. A general classification would connect statistical functionals, forecast evaluation and the design of indirect prediction objectives.
status_note: Question 3 is open in the 2016 source. The checked 2021 journal framework proves important families of complexity bounds, and the 2024 survey still lists unresolved examples. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no classification over the full stated domain; restricted Lipschitz and calibration variants are not treated as resolving it.
progress: 2016: Question 3 asks for a characterization of the elicitation complexity classes, with identifiable intermediate properties specified in Section 3. | 2021-12-01: The journal study develops complexity relative to several classes of intermediates and gives upper and lower bounds that match for important families. Its Definitions 2, 4, 6 and 7 specify elicitation, relative complexity and identification. | 2024-06: A survey by Frongillo and Waggoner describes further open complexity questions and distinguishes ordinary single-observation elicitation from multi-observation and conditional variants.
working_summary: The question asks how many real-valued reports are needed to recover an arbitrary statistic by minimizing expected loss. The intermediate prediction must have a unique expected-loss minimizer and an identification function whose expected value vanishes exactly at the correct report. An unrestricted link may then turn that intermediate prediction into the desired statistic. The target covers every finite-dimensional property of a nonempty convex family of real-outcome distributions, with infinity meaning that no finite report dimension works. A full classification would determine the expressive limits of single-observation loss-based prediction beyond the statistic families whose complexities are already known.

importance_reason: A structural boundary for transferring VC uniform-convergence guarantees from independent samples to dependent data, with implications for empirical-risk validation. Existing score retained.

The paper proves learnability for finite-VC classes under the ordinary total-variation Dobrushin condition. A guarantee for the hypothesis returned by that learner does not assert that every hypothesis has an accurate empirical loss.

The source separately gives a Gaussian-complexity theorem for much more general real-valued losses. This card retains its explicit finite-VC classification question and asks for the same rate with ordinary Dobrushin dependence. It does not demand the full real-valued empirical-process theorem.

why: Would determine whether the standard weak-influence condition suffices for the uniform statistical guarantees that make finite VC dimension useful, beyond the already-known existence of a successful learner.

working_summary: A dependent training sample has identical marginal distributions and a bounded total influence on every coordinate. Uniform convergence requires every hypothesis’s empirical zero-one loss to approximate its population loss. The card asks whether every finite-VC class has the usual square-root rate when the ordinary Dobrushin coefficient stays below one. The source already proves learnability under that condition, but its uniform-convergence theorem requires stronger logarithmic influences.
