title: Learning speedups from random examples
importance_reason: A structural question about gaps in the running time of passive circuit learning and the power of chosen examples. Existing score retained.
formal: Does the low-end learning speedup hold using only independent uniform labeled examples? For each circuit family C specified below, suppose every polynomial-size subfamily has a randomized weak learner under the uniform distribution, with confidence \(1- 1/n\) and worst-case running time \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\). Must every polynomial-size subfamily then have, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and \(a\ge 1, a\) randomized learner with error at most \(n^{- a}\), confidence at least \(1- 1/n\), and worst-case running time \(O(2^{n^{\varepsilon}})\), still using only independent uniform labeled examples?
definitions:
The unknown target is a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\). One example request supplies \((X,f(X))\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and independent of all earlier examples and the learner’s private random bits. The learner receives \(1^{n}\) and the fixed parameters specifying the target class. It may decide when to stop sampling, but cannot choose, correlate, condition or relabel the oracle’s next input. Reading and storing examples, internal computation and writing the hypothesis all count toward the time bound. A standard randomized multitape Turing machine with an example tape suffices; polynomial overheads in n do not alter the time classes used here. On every run it halts within the bound, including runs with labels outside the target promise. Its output is an explicitly encoded Boolean circuit h, with no example oracle or target-function gates. The hypothesis may belong to a larger circuit family than the target.

The error of h is \(\Pr_{X\text{ uniform}}[h(X)\ne f(X)]\). Confidence is the probability, jointly over the sample and internal randomness, of obtaining a hypothesis satisfying the stated error bound, for every eligible f and every sufficiently large n. A weak learner has error at most \(1/2- n^{- b}\) for some fixed \(b\ge 1\). The exponent b and the learner may depend on the fixed target subfamily. A strong learner here means that for each fixed \(a\ge 1\) there is an algorithm attaining error \(n^{- a}\); this is not a claim of polynomial dependence on a variable accuracy input.

The circuit families are \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}, \mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) for a fixed prime \(p, \mathrm{ACC}^{0}, \mathrm{TC}^{0}, \mathrm{NC}^{1}\), Boolean formulas, and unrestricted Boolean circuits. Circuits have input bits and Boolean constants, and size is the number of wires. \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) uses \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) gates of unbounded fan-in and NOT gates; \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\) also permits gates testing whether the number of true inputs is 0 modulo p. \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) permits such modular gates for fixed moduli, with the choice of moduli independent of n. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) additionally permits unweighted majority gates, outputting 1 when at least half their inputs are 1. For these four families a subfamily fixes both a constant depth bound d and a size bound \(n^{k}\), where \(k\ge 1\) is constant; modular parameters are also fixed. Boolean formulas use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and NOT, have fan-out one except for input variables, and at most \(n^{k}\) wires. Unrestricted Boolean circuits use those same gate types, allow shared subcircuits and have at most \(n^{k}\) wires. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) uses bounded fan-in Boolean gates, polynomial size and depth at most \(d \log _{2}(n+2)\) for fixed d. Taking all fixed k,d covers the source’s polynomial-size \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) convention. Every circuit description is finite, with gate types and wire endpoints in binary.

For each fixed family C, the premise quantifies over ALL its fixed polynomial-size subfamilies: for each k and any fixed depth/modular parameters, there exist b, a uniform learner A and a time bound \(T_{A}(n)\) such that for every constant \(M>0, T_{A}(n)\le 2^{n}/n^{M}\) for all sufficiently large n. Thus \(2^{n}/n^{\omega (1)}\) means a superpolynomial saving, not just \(2^{n}/n^{10}\) and not a different algorithm for each M. The conclusion quantifies over every target subfamily and every fixed \(\varepsilon >0,a\ge 1\); the algorithm and the hidden constant may depend on these fixed choices, but not on n or f. There is no requirement that one algorithm accept descriptions of arbitrary target families. Learners are uniform algorithms across input lengths; the target circuits themselves need not be uniformly generated. The implication is unconditional and applies separately to each listed family.

This card makes explicit the low-end, polynomial-target branch of conference Lemma 24. The source also has a high-end branch relating learning subexponential-size targets to quasipolynomial-time learning of polynomial-size targets. The generic extracted question referred to that lemma as a whole; the present target selects its main low-end branch rather than asserting that this one implication is equivalent to both branches together.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated implication for the listed circuit families, with only independent uniform labeled examples in both the premise and conclusion. A positive result must supply the all-\(\varepsilon\), all-fixed-accuracy speedup whenever the weak-learning premise holds. A negative result must establish failure of that implication for an eligible family; a lower bound in a restricted learning model, or an algorithm that needs membership queries, does not by itself refute or establish it. The separate high-end branch is not required by this card.
context:
The source’s low-end theorem says that learning polynomial-size circuits slightly faster than their full truth-table scale already implies learning them in time \(2^{n^{\varepsilon}}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), with much better accuracy. Its theorem permits chosen membership queries.

The open-question paragraph asks about learning from random examples under the same uniform distribution. Here both sides use only independently sampled labeled points, so the faster learner cannot recover the missing power by choosing special inputs.

Pich’s 2025 Theorem 5.1 starts with nonuniform learning circuits supplied with random examples, but obtains a learner using nonadaptive membership queries. It is a related quantitative speedup, not the uniform random-example-to-random-example theorem stated here.
why: Tests whether the sharp gap in possible circuit-learning runtimes is a structural feature of passive learning, or relies on being able to choose labels to request. It connects the computational cost of statistical prediction with major circuit classes while keeping the distribution and available information fixed.
status_note: Read the conference model, low-end lemma and open-question passage, and the full preprint’s corresponding question. Read the later journal Theorem 5.1 and its access conventions. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of this precise passive low-end implication; they are not exhaustive and proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2017: Lemma 24 proves the low-end speedup with membership queries; Section 8 asks for a random-examples analogue. | 2025-03-27: Theorem 5.1 of Pich’s journal paper gives a generalized nonuniform speedup whose output learner uses nonadaptive membership queries.
working_summary: The question asks whether a weak passive learner with a superpolynomial saving over \(2^{n}\) must imply dramatically faster passive learners. Targets range over standard polynomial-size circuit classes, and all examples are independent and uniform. The desired learners attain every fixed inverse-polynomial error in time \(2^{n^{\varepsilon}}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). The source establishes this implication when learners may choose membership queries. A later generalized speedup still permits such queries in its conclusion, leaving the passive implication unestablished by that result.

title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
importance_reason: A central minimal-assumption question in cryptographic foundations, separating the known reach of generic one-wayness from public-key communication.
focus_reason: A central minimal-assumption question in cryptographic foundations, separating the known reach of generic one-wayness from public-key communication.
formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
context:
Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.
why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.
status_note: The full implication is explicitly open in the checked 2017 survey and Fall 2023 MIT lecture, but Li–Ni–Zan ePrint 2023/1260 explicitly claims a positive solution. This audit found the claim on 14 September 2026 and has not independently verified it or located a conclusive later verification or refutation. Status is therefore uncertain and the card remains active. The May 2026 MinRank result assumes a specific planted problem; oracle separations do not refute the unrelativized target.
progress: 1989: Impagliazzo–Rudich establish the oracle separation for key agreement, also obstructing public-key encryption. Corollary 6.1 of the checked 1994 author manuscript states the oracle-world conclusion. | 1999: Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby publish the equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators, supporting the private-key side of the comparison. | 2009-04-18: The corrected Barak–Mahmoody author version proves the quadratic random-oracle query bound with explicit success loss; it withdraws the same quadratic claim for random permutations from the earlier manuscript. | 2023-08-21: Li–Ni–Zan post a claimed positive solution. Its proof has not been independently verified in this audit. | 2023: MIT’s Fall 2023 Lecture 10, PDF page 55, explicitly lists public-key encryption from one-way functions as an open question. This lecture is a dated source, not a refutation of the 2023 preprint. | 2026-05-07: The planted-MinRank construction appears online in EUROCRYPT 2026, pp. 449–480. The checked arXiv version was submitted 4 October 2025 and displays 7 October on its title page.
working_summary: A one-way function is easy to evaluate and difficult for efficient classical algorithms to invert on a random input. Public-key encryption requires that anyone can encrypt with public information while a receiver can decrypt with a related secret key. The question asks whether the existence of any one-way function implies such a uniform classical scheme, allowing arbitrary non-black-box constructions. The scheme must have negligible average decryption error and hide an encrypted bit from every efficient chosen-plaintext observer. Oracle barriers do not settle the unrestricted implication, and a 2023 preprint claiming a positive solution remains unverified in this review.

title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
importance_reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.
focus_reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
question_excerpt: This retains the basic one-way-function implication from Wigderson’s multi-part cryptography question, Open Problem 4.10 in the August 2019 edition. The other parts ask about stronger average-case premises or trapdoor conclusions; they are not combined into this target. The card fixes its existing classical uniform, same-length inversion and eventual negligible-success convention. The textbook’s informal constant-success discussion is not substituted for these explicit security quantifiers.
definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
context:
Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.
why: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The original book and survey pose the implication, and the inspected January/April 2026 primary papers retain specialized hardness hypotheses or conditional primitives rather than deriving eventual classical one-wayness from P != NP alone. No verified complete implication or its full negation was found in bounded current searches. The card remains source_open, without claiming that all recent proofs were independently verified.

working_summary: The question asks whether P != NP alone guarantees a total efficiently computable function that is hard to invert on images of uniform inputs. One fixed function must defeat every fixed uniform classical polynomial-time inverter, even when finding any same-length preimage counts as success. Success must eventually be smaller than every inverse polynomial, with probability over the sampled input and the inverter’s independent coins. Current description-complexity characterizations and conditional-generator results retain specialized hardness premises or different guarantees. A complete Lean proof must establish the implication or its full negation, whose inversion guarantee is at arbitrarily large lengths rather than necessarily every sufficiently large length.

title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
importance_reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.
focus_reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.
formal:
Does ordinary polynomial-hard decisional Learning With Errors imply indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, circular-security or leakage-resilience hypothesis?

Precisely, let \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) be the fixed classical nonuniform decisional-LWE assumption below, with prime modulus \(q(n)\ge n^4\) and Gaussian width \(n\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) assert the existence of the uniform classical probabilistic obfuscator defined below, with security against all classical polynomial-size circuit families. The proposition to establish or refute is the implication
\[H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\ \Longrightarrow\ I_{\mathrm{circ}}.\]
All modulus, error, sample, correctness and security quantifiers are fixed in the definitions. Neither subexponential hardness nor additional information supplied about the LWE secret or errors is part of the premise.
question_excerpt: The source asks broadly whether LWE alone suffices for general iO. This card retains the explicit editorial variant selected on 10 September: least-prime modulus at least n^4, integer Gaussian width n, polynomial sample counts, ordinary negligible-advantage security against classical nonuniform polynomial-size circuits, and a uniform classical obfuscator with negligible probability of any functionality error. These exact parameters are a formulation choice, not parameters asserted by the source. The yes/no target is the mathematical implication itself, not a claim that every black-box construction exists or a task to prove LWE hardness. Importance remains 97.
definitions:
LWE assumption. For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(q(n)\) be the least prime at least \(n^4\), and let \(\mathbb Z_q\) mean integers modulo \(q=q(n)\). Define the probability distribution \(\chi_n\) on the integers by
\[\Pr_{e\leftarrow\chi_n}[e=t]=\frac{\exp(-\pi t^2/n^2)}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi j^2/n^2)}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).\]
The positive normalizing sum converges. This specifies an exact mathematical distribution; it is not an input consisting of real-number samples or a unit-cost real-arithmetic oracle.

For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(m=m(n)\), compare the following distributions:
\[X_n=(A,As+e\bmod q),\qquad Y_n=(A,u),\]
where \(A\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times n}\), \(s\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\), the \(m\) entries of \(e\) are independent samples of \(\chi_n\), and \(u\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). All these choices are mutually independent before forming \(As+e\); the same secret \(s\) is used in every row. Reduce each integer error modulo \(q\). Each residue is encoded as its canonical representative in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), using \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil\) bits, and the matrix and vector are fully listed. Public parameters \(n,m,q\) accompany the encoding. No leakage or other secret-dependent hint is given.

An ensemble pair is computationally indistinguishable if, for every family \((D_n)\) of classical Boolean circuits with description length bounded by some polynomial in \(n\),
\[\left|\Pr[D_n(X_n)=1]-\Pr[D_n(Y_n)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(n\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), there is \(n_0\) such that \(\nu(n)\le n^{-c}\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). Circuit families need not be uniformly computable and may hardwire polynomially many advice bits. Deterministic distinguishers suffice here; private random coins can equivalently be allowed. The assertion \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) is indistinguishability for every such sample count and every such distinguisher family. This is asymptotic polynomial security, not a bound on the cost of attacks at a single numerical parameter.

Circuit model. A circuit has \(a\ge0\) labelled input bits, \(g\ge0\) gates in topological order, and \(b\ge1\) designated output wires. Gates are binary AND or OR, unary NOT, or constants 0 and 1. Wires may be reused. Gate predecessors must be inputs or earlier gates; each output names an existing input or gate. This defines a total deterministic function \(C:\{0,1\}^a\to\{0,1\}^b\). Constant gates are allowed as part of the conventional Boolean basis.

Use the explicit encoding \(1^a0\), then length-delimited counts \(U(g),U(b)\), followed by every gate and every output index. Here \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\). Each gate has a fixed three-bit type tag and the appropriate zero, one or two \(U\)-encoded predecessor indices. Input nodes come first, then gate nodes; unused tags and out-of-range indices are invalid. Each output is a \(U\)-encoded index, and trailing bits are forbidden. Define \(|C|\) to be the total description length. Thus every input, gate and output is explicitly counted; exponentially many undeclared inputs or succinctly generated gate lists are not allowed. Two circuits are equivalent when their input/output arities coincide and their outputs agree on every input, exactly.

Obfuscator. There is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(O\) and positive integers \(K,d\). On \((1^\lambda,C)\), for every integer \(\lambda\ge2\), it halts within \(K(\lambda+|C|+1)^d\) bit steps on every sequence of independent fair random bits. On a valid circuit it always returns a valid circuit with the same input/output arities, of description length at most the same polynomial bound. Malformed descriptions may be rejected, within the clock. All input reading, randomness, arithmetic and output writing are charged. There is no advice, quantum state, oracle, trusted setup or free preprocessing.

Functionality requires a uniform error bound over all circuits at each size scale. For every positive integer polynomial bound \(p\), there exists a negligible function \(\mu_p\) such that for every \(\lambda\ge2\) and valid \(|C|\le p(\lambda)\),
\[\Pr_r[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^a:\ O(1^\lambda,C;r)(x)=C(x)]\ge1-\mu_p(\lambda).\]
One successful output must be correct on all inputs simultaneously; a separate high success probability for each input is insufficient.

Indistinguishability requires that for every pair of circuit sequences \((C_{0,\lambda},C_{1,\lambda})\) of polynomially bounded description length, with equal description lengths, matching arities and equivalent functions for each \(\lambda\), and every classical polynomial-size distinguisher family \((D_\lambda)\), the advantage
\[\left|\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{0,\lambda};r))=1]-\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{1,\lambda};r))=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). The sequences themselves need not be efficiently generated. Distinguishers can hardwire the circuit pair and arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information. Variable-length outputs are presented with their length and zero padding to a common polynomial bound determined by the pair's size bound and the clock; actual length remains visible. Probabilities use fresh independent obfuscator coins. No efficiently verifiable certificate of circuit equivalence is supplied or required. The assertion \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) is existence of one machine and clock meeting both functionality and security for every polynomial size scale.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{circ}}\), or of its full logical negation. A positive construction must prove the stated uniform efficiency, simultaneous all-input functionality, and security against all nonuniform polynomial-size classical distinguishers using only the specified LWE premise and proved mathematical facts. Any parameter changes used inside a construction must be justified from that premise. The literal negation is \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\land\neg I_{\mathrm{circ}}\). Refuting one candidate, excluding only black-box reductions, or separating the notions in an oracle world does not establish this unrelativized negation. A construction needing stronger quantitative hardness, circular security or auxiliary-leakage resilience does not prove the specified implication unless those properties are themselves derived from the fixed premise.
context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of the same function. It requires their obfuscations to be computationally indistinguishable when the original descriptions have equal size. It does not promise that a function hides information already revealed by its outputs, nor does it equate functionally different programs. These distinctions separate the mathematical notion from an informal claim that code is unreadable.

Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement: whatever can be learned from the code should be reproducible from oracle access to the function. Their revised full paper explicitly introduces the weaker indistinguishability comparison. Its impossibility result therefore does not supply a negative answer to this card.

LWE describes noisy linear equations over a finite residue field. The same hidden vector is used in all rows, while fresh independent errors perturb the products. Regev connects suitable LWE distributions to worst-case lattice problems by a quantum reduction. That historical foundation is evidence for studying LWE, not a proof of the exact classical nonuniform hardness hypothesis selected here. In particular, its rounded-Gaussian notation should not be silently identified with this card’s integer-Gaussian convention.

Jain, Lin and Sahai construct iO using four well-studied assumptions. The February 2026 journal theorem lists LWE, sparse-noise LPN over large prime fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and DLIN in bilinear groups. It requires subexponential security guarantees and a subexponential LWE modulus-to-noise ratio. Both the extra assumptions and the quantitative regime exceed the premise here. The journal publication follows earlier work; it is not a new LWE-only construction.

Their follow-up removes LWE from the sufficient set, leaving the other three assumptions. Its introduction explicitly raises the possibility that LWE alone might suffice. Removing one assumption from a conjunction does not show that the removed assumption implies the conclusion. The distinction between subexponential security for its iO theorem and polynomial security for its functional-encryption consequence also remains substantive.

The circular-security construction eliminates factoring and pairing assumptions, but its theorem still assumes subexponential LWE hardness together with a key-randomness circular form of shielded randomness-leakage security. The latter experiment provides structured information involving encryption keys and ciphertext randomness. Its Definition 7 is an additional security premise; plain noisy LWE samples do not contain these hints. The paper also repairs a gap in an earlier efficiency transformation.

Later lattice proposals continue to separate ordinary LWE from strengthened assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin explicitly introduce Circular Security with Random Opening, an LWE-with-hints assumption. Their abstract discusses attacks on earlier hint assumptions and presents the new proposal as a different target for cryptanalysis. No reduction from this card’s ordinary LWE premise is asserted in the inspected abstract.

Cini, Lai and Woo instead use NTRU and a new Equivocal LWE assumption alongside other lattice assumptions. Their abstract qualifies the post-quantum construction and identifies possible cryptanalytic targets. A construction based on lattice assumptions can be an important advance without establishing that plain LWE alone suffices.

The April 2026 authentication preprint, revised in June, likewise distinguishes several claims. Its lattice tool assumes decomposed LWE; its pseudorandom-obfuscation result additionally assumes subexponentially secure iO. A separate general-iO proposal is expressly labelled heuristic. Neither the extra-premise theorem nor that heuristic is a proof of the implication posed here.

The September 2026 trapdoor-function preprint assumes both iO and LWE for copy protection. Its separate LWE-only key-leasing result concerns another primitive. This recent application uses general iO as an input assumption rather than deriving it, so it does not close the source question.
why: General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

The February 2026 JACM theorem uses four assumptions and stronger quantitative security; circular, CRO and Equivocal-LWE proposals add premises. The April/June 2026 general candidate is explicitly heuristic, and the September copy-protection application assumes iO. No matching resolution of the fixed implication was identified in the bounded search. The exact modulus/error convention is editorial, and abstract-only or blocked-access review limits are recorded for each source.

working_summary: Indistinguishability obfuscation hides which of two equally sized implementations of the same function was supplied. This card asks whether one fixed ordinary polynomial-hard LWE assumption implies such obfuscation for every polynomial circuit size. It specifies classical nonuniform security, exact noisy-equation parameters, a uniform polynomial-time obfuscator and simultaneous correctness on all inputs. Known cited constructions require several assumptions, stronger security regimes, or additional circular and leakage-related properties. Recent lattice candidates and iO-dependent applications do not establish the selected implication; an oracle or black-box barrier would not prove its full negation either.

title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
importance_reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.
focus_reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.
formal:
Does the ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional Learning With Errors assumption specified below imply the existence of a classical compact fully homomorphic public-key encryption scheme whose keys are generated without a bound on the size or depth of the circuits subsequently evaluated?

The scheme must be secure against nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversaries given both its encryption and evaluation keys. Its only hardness assumption may be the stated ordinary LWE assumption; no independent circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption is allowed.
question_excerpt: The source distinguishes known leveled LWE constructions from fully homomorphic encryption with depth-independent keys and asks for the latter from comparable standard lattice assumptions. This card preserves its existing ordinary polynomial-modulus LWE specialization, classical nonuniform security, and fresh-input correctness convention.
definitions:
Fix the following precise LWE hypothesis. For every integer \(c\ge3\), let \(q_c(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^c\). For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(M(d)\), sample independently
\[
 A\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)\times d},\qquad
 s\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^d,\qquad
 u\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)}
\]
uniformly, and let the coordinates of \(e\) be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/(4d))\), reduced modulo \(q_c(d)\). Here \(\mathbb Z_q\) is the ring of integers modulo \(q\). The hypothesis is that the distributions
\[
 (A,As+e\bmod q_c(d))\quad\text{and}\quad(A,u)
\]
are computationally indistinguishable against every family of nonuniform classical randomized circuits of size polynomial in \(d\). That is, the absolute difference of their acceptance probabilities is negligible in \(d\). The integer \(c\) and the polynomial sample bound are fixed before \(d\) grows. A distinguisher may know them and \(d\). The noise is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{\mathbb Z,2\sqrt d}\); no encryptions of secrets, correlated auxiliary hints or circular-security statements are included in this assumption.

A nonnegative function \(\mu(t)\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge1\), there is \(t_a\) such that \(\mu(t)\le t^{-a}\) for every \(t\ge t_a\). Circuit size counts gates, input bits and private random bits, using fan-in-two Boolean gates and unary negation. Nonuniform means that each circuit may be chosen independently at each parameter value, with no efficient procedure producing the family. These are classical adversaries, not quantum ones.

The requested scheme has one fixed tuple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\to(pk,evk,sk),\quad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,b)\to c,\quad
 \operatorname{Eval}(evk,F,c_1,\ldots,c_t)\to c_F,\quad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to b.
\]
All algorithms may also receive \(1^\lambda\) implicitly. Generation, encryption and evaluation may use fresh independent fair random bits; decryption is deterministic. Generation and bit encryption have polynomial worst-case bit running time in \(\lambda\). Evaluation runs in time polynomial in \(\lambda\) and its complete input length. The model is an ordinary multitape Turing machine; no ideal cryptographic oracle is available.

Plaintexts are bits. The circuit \(F\) is explicitly given by its gate list, has \(t\) inputs and one output, and uses fan-in-two AND and OR and unary NOT. The generation algorithm receives no circuit, circuit-size bound or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial \(P\) bounding the lengths of \(pk,evk,sk\), fresh bit ciphertexts and evaluated one-bit ciphertexts, as well as the time for decrypting these ciphertexts, by \(P(\lambda)\). This bound is independent of \(F\), its input count and its depth. All auxiliary public material is included in \(pk,evk\).

For every fixed polynomial \(p\), there must be a negligible function \(\mu_p(\lambda)\) such that, for every circuit \(F\) with size and input count at most \(p(\lambda)\) and every vector of input bits, independently encrypting those bits, evaluating \(F\), and decrypting yields \(F(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\mu_p(\lambda)\). The probability includes all coins of generation, encryption and evaluation. Fresh bit decryption has negligible error as well. The algorithms and \(P\) are fixed before choosing \(p\). Thus one key-generation algorithm supports every polynomial circuit bound; choosing a large fixed polynomial depth during setup does not meet the quantifiers.

Security means that for every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family \(T_\lambda\),
\[
 \left|\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,0))=1]
       -\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,1))=1]\right|
\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Each experiment generates a fresh key tuple and fresh encryption and adversary randomness. Since the public key allows arbitrary further encryptions, this is bit-message chosen-plaintext indistinguishability. The requested theorem must derive this security from the precise LWE hypothesis above. It is not a request to prove LWE hardness unconditionally.

There is no external trusted setup, subsequent secret-key assistance, random oracle or additional hardness premise. Bootstrapping and public encryptions involving secret-key bits are permitted if their security is proved from ordinary LWE. In particular, the absence of a circular-security assumption is a requirement on the proof, not a ban on a syntactic form of evaluation key. Polynomial hardness of LWE is the assumption: subexponential hardness, functional encryption and obfuscation may not simply be assumed independently.

The correctness condition is evaluation of one arbitrary polynomial-size circuit on fresh ciphertexts. A stronger guarantee for indefinitely composing new evaluations on already evaluated ciphertexts is not an extra requirement here. The related TCS-6871 instead asks for an operational reduction from worst-case polynomial-factor GapSVP, allowing quantum computation in that reduction; it has a different stated foundation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one scheme, its uniform running-time and compactness bounds, the correctness guarantee for every polynomial circuit-size bound, and a proof of its security from exactly the specified LWE hypothesis; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of that implication.

An additional circular-security, functional-encryption, obfuscation or stronger-hardness assumption does not meet the positive target. A construction with depth-dependent setup, a quantum evaluator or noncompact decryption also does not qualify. Breaking one proposed scheme, or separating one restricted class of black-box reductions, does not refute the general existence implication. All assumptions of a conditional obstruction must remain explicit. Numerical approximation tolerance does not weaken these asymptotic security, correctness and resource requirements.
context:
Compactness requires the returned ciphertext and its decryption cost to stay independent of the evaluated circuit. Supporting any chosen polynomial depth after fixing that depth during setup gives a leveled scheme, which has different quantifiers from this target.

The functional-encryption construction removes the circular-security assumption but uses additional primitives. Its nonuniform-security extension also has a further complexity assumption, so it does not establish the sole-LWE proposition.

The February 2026 dynamic multi-key construction explicitly gives its setup the maximum depth. Removing a common reference string or permitting more keys does not remove that level parameter.

The April 2026 quantum proposal uses a quantum evaluator and a preselected number of independent key layers. Those features place it outside this classical, depth-independent target.

A June 2026 primary paper explicitly declines an optimization because it would need unleveled FHE, which its authors state is not known from plain LWE. This supports the recorded open status without certifying every possible later claim.

Fresh-input FHE correctness and full composability are separate definitional questions. The present card requires the former; the latter is not silently added as a stronger acceptance condition.
why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.
status_note: The June 2026 primary remark explicitly records unleveled FHE from plain LWE as unknown. Checked functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions; the examined 2026 dynamic multi-key and quantum proposals retain a depth bound. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the retained ordinary-LWE-only target. The full security proofs of the cited proposals were not independently certified.

working_summary: Fully homomorphic encryption evaluates Boolean computations on encrypted bits and returns a compact encrypted result. The question asks for one classical key-generation procedure that needs no advance bound on the depth of those computations. The only hardness premise is the specified ordinary polynomial-modulus LWE assumption, without independent circular security. Security must hold against polynomial-size nonuniform classical adversaries who also see the evaluation key. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish the entire implication and its uniform correctness and compactness guarantees, or refute it.

title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
importance_reason: The share size needed for general secret sharing is a fundamental efficiency limit for realizing arbitrary access structures.
focus_reason: The share size needed for general secret sharing is a fundamental efficiency limit for realizing arbitrary access structures.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.
context:
Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).
why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Nir’s August 2026 ECCC report, Theorem 1.5, claims a general scheme with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\), directly implying the stated strict threshold after adjustment of the universal constant. The target and theorem were compared; the proof was not independently verified. This remains an uncertain claimed resolution.
progress: 2021: Applebaum–Nir give a general upper exponent \(\log _{2}(3/2)\approx 0.585\). | 2022 / 2023: The Dagstuhl seminar poses the strict \(c<1/2\) target; the printed historical exponent differs from the cited construction. | 2026-08: Nir states a matching nonlinear upper bound with exponent 0.496 in Theorem 1.5.
working_summary: Secret sharing lets authorized groups reconstruct a secret while unauthorized groups learn nothing. The target asks for a universal bound \(K\cdot 2^{cn}\) bits per share for every n-party access structure, with \(c<1/2\) and a one-bit secret. Perfect reconstruction and privacy are required, and nonlinear schemes are allowed. Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\) bound that would meet this target. The claimed resolution is recorded with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified in this review.

title: Existence of one-way functions
importance_reason: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.
formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.
context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

One-way functions would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) nor any candidate’s hardness.

Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.
why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.
status_note: Open after the 11 September 2026 source and subsequent-work check. Levin’s complete function and the checked 2020–2026 complexity characterizations are conditional or equivalence results, not unconditional one-way-function constructions.
progress: 2003: Levin gives a combinatorial complete function, one-way if any one-way function exists. | 2020: Liu and Pass characterize one-way-function existence by average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. | 2026-06: Hirahara and Nanashima characterize the hypothetical Pessiland setting; neither existence nor impossibility of one-way functions follows unconditionally.
working_summary: Do classical one-way functions exist without an unproved hardness assumption? A polynomial-time function with negligible inversion success against every uniform classical polynomial-time adversary, or a proof that none exists. Complete candidates and complexity-theoretic equivalences are known; their required hardness has not been proved. An unconditional existence or impossibility theorem. Would establish or rule out the basic computational asymmetry behind many cryptographic primitives.

title: Existence of public-key encryption
importance_reason: Would establish the existence of secure public communication from a mathematical theorem rather than a computational assumption.
formal: Do there exist uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc and Dec forming a public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages with negligible correctness error and IND-CPA security against every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, with these properties proved without an unproved hardness assumption?
definitions: For security parameter \(n\ge 1, Gen(1^{n})\) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. \(Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\) takes a bit \(m\in \{0,1\}\) and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; \(Dec(1^{n},sk,c)\) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over \(m\in \{0,1\}\) of Pr[Dec(\(1^{n},sk,Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary \(A_{1}\) receives \((1^{n},pk)\) and outputs bits \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate \(c=Enc(1^{n},pk,m_{b})\), and give \((1^{n},pk,z,c)\) to its second stage \(A_{2}\), which outputs a bit \(b'\). For every pair \((A_{1},A_{2}), |\Pr [b' =b]- 1/2|\) must be negligible. A function \(\eta (n)\) is negligible if, for every integer \(d\ge 1, \eta (n)\le n^{- d}\) for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.
context:
A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success \(1/2\). Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.
why: Would establish the existence of secure public communication from a mathematical theorem rather than a computational assumption.
status_note: Open after the 11 September 2026 review of the standard security definitions and subsequent primary work. Checked lattice and March 2026 stabilizer-decoding constructions remain conditional on unproved hardness assumptions.
progress: 2004: Goldreich gives precise encryption security definitions, conditional constructions and relations to one-way functions. | 2005 / 2009: Regev constructs classical public-key encryption under learning-with-errors hardness. | 2026-03: Lu and coauthors obtain classical public-key encryption from assumed average-case hardness of stabilizer decoding.
working_summary: Can public-key encryption be proved computationally secure without an unproved hardness assumption? An efficient correct scheme with negligible IND-CPA advantage against every uniform classical PPT adversary, or a proof that none exists. Constructions from lattice and other hardness assumptions are known. No checked result proves an appropriate hardness assumption or establishes unconditional existence. Would give a mathematical foundation for secret communication using only an authenticated public key.

title: Key agreement from one-way functions
importance_reason: A foundational boundary between symmetric cryptographic hardness and secret establishment through public interaction. Distinct from the existing stronger PKE-from-OWF target, and supported by a long research line on black-box barriers.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol in the plain public-channel model below? The parties must output \(\lambda\)-bit keys with negligible disagreement, and either honest key must be computationally indistinguishable from an independent uniform key given the entire public transcript. This is the unrelativized existence implication, allowing arbitrary constructions and security proofs, including those that inspect the program implementing the one-way function.
definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\geq1\), given as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). Every algorithm has one finite program for all parameters and is a classical Turing machine operating on bits; no nonuniform advice or oracle is available. A probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) algorithm uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every input and every random tape. For standalone algorithms, the bound is in the total input length. Machine steps, reading and writing bits, and producing outputs all count. Each algorithm may have its own fixed polynomial bound. Tuples of bit strings use the prefix-free component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); a finite list is encoded by its number of components in the same encoding, followed by its encoded components, with integers represented in binary without leading zeros except for zero itself. Any explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encoding is acceptable.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\mu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform classical PPT inverter \(I\), the function \(\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\) is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability includes the independent coins of \(I\). A failure output or a string of the wrong length is an unsuccessful inversion; recovering any preimage of the stipulated length suffices. The function need not be injective or length preserving. Its program is public.

A candidate protocol consists of two uniform interactive machines \(A,B\). On the common input \(1^{\lambda}\), they start with independent private coins and no other secret or correlated input. They exchange finite classical bit strings through a noiseless public channel. Fix the conventional alternating-message execution, with \(A\) first and empty messages permitted; public termination flags indicate when each machine has finished. A polynomial in \(\lambda\), fixed for the protocol, bounds the combined computation, messages, message lengths, and execution length on every pair of honest random tapes. Both parties always terminate with strings \(K_A,K_B\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The public transcript \(T\) is the finite ordered list of messages with sender labels, message boundaries and termination flags, encoded as above. Private working tapes and private coins are not part of \(T\). Communication occurs only through these messages; there is no additional timing channel. No trusted setup, preshared secret, correlated randomness, random oracle, quantum computation or quantum communication is permitted.

Correctness means that \(\Pr[K_A\ne K_B]\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over independent honest coins. Passive secrecy means that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(D\) outputting a bit, the advantage
\[\left|\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,K_A)=1]-\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]\right|\]
is negligible, where each experiment runs the honest protocol and \(U_{\lambda}\) is an independent uniform element of \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The coins of \(D\) are independent of all other randomness. Correctness makes the same requirement with \(K_B\) equivalent. The eavesdropper sees the whole transcript and the public programs but does not modify messages.
