title: One-way functions from errorless average-case NP hardness
importance_reason: Whether general average-case computational hardness already provides one-wayness is a foundational gap between complexity theory and cryptography. Resolving this explicit source branch would determine whether useful cryptographic structure follows from broad distributional hardness, rather than requiring specially structured computational assumptions.
formal: Is the following implication true? \[(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\not\subseteq\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{there exists a classical one-way function}.\] Here the antecedent means that some fixed NP language, under some fixed polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble, has no deterministic exact decider with average polynomial running time in the moment sense below. The conclusion asks for a total polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every integer \(c\ge1\), there exists \(n_0\) for which, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\ I}\bigl[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\bigr]\le n^{-c},\qquad z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x)).\] The statement is unrelativized and has no additional hardness, derandomization or cryptographic assumption.
definitions: A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(R(x,u)=1\). A sampler is one probabilistic Turing machine \(S\) that, on the unary size parameter \(1^n\), uses independent unbiased random bits and halts within \(q(n)\) bit steps on every random tape, for a fixed polynomial \(q\). Its exact output distribution is \(D_n\), over finite strings of length at most \(q(n)\). The ensemble parameter \(n\) need not equal the output length. PSamp is the class of these ensembles. A deterministic exact decider \(A\), given \((1^n,x)\), must halt and return the membership bit of \(L\) correctly for every \(n\ge1\) and every finite \(x\), including inputs outside the support of \(D_n\). Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of bit steps. The pair \((L,D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist \(A\), constants \(\alpha>0,C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\alpha]\le C(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). These choices may depend on \(L,S\), but not on \(n\). This is an exact, deterministic moment-based notion, not merely a polynomial first moment or a heuristic allowed to misclassify a small fraction of inputs. The antecedent asserts the existence of one pair \((L,D)\) in the stated class failing this condition. In the conclusion, \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings, and the probability also includes the inverter’s independent unbiased coin flips. An inverter is a fixed finite probabilistic Turing program whose running time is polynomial in its input length on every random tape; all reading, writing and arithmetic are charged. It receives both \(1^n\) and \(f(x)\). It may output any preimage of \(f(x)\) of length exactly \(n\), not necessarily the original \(x\); malformed or wrong-length outputs fail. The function \(f\) is computed by one fixed finite deterministic polynomial-time program on all input strings, so output length is automatically polynomially bounded. All programs are uniform and have no advice or oracle. Security is required for all sufficiently large \(n\) for each inverter and exponent; security on only infinitely many lengths is a different guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must derive the existence of a function with the full uniform, all-sufficiently-large-length inversion guarantee from the stated distributional hardness alone. The implication does not require an efficient black-box transformation from a description of the hard pair. A negative answer must establish the antecedent together with nonexistence of every such function in the unrelativized model; an oracle world, a barrier to one type of reduction or failure of one candidate construction is insufficient. A result assuming randomized heuristic hardness instead of the specified deterministic exact hardness, or yielding only infinitely-often security or a fixed polynomial security gap, does not alone settle this formulation.
context:

The hardness assumption concerns exact deterministic decision under an efficiently samplable distribution, with average polynomial time defined by a runtime moment. title: Public-key quantum money from LWE alone
importance_reason: Ground publicly verifiable unclonable quantum states in a standard lattice assumption, resolving a central assumption gap in quantum cryptography.
formal: Does quantum hardness of the fixed decisional Learning with Errors distributions below imply the existence of a reusable, unforgeable public-key quantum money scheme in the plain computational model? The scheme must have a static classical public key, polynomial-time quantum minting and verification, and security against every nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary with classical advice.
question_excerpt: The sources construct public-key quantum money under stronger assumptions and study restricted barriers to obtaining it from standard cryptographic tools. This card selects the unrestricted implication from its explicitly fixed decisional LWE premise, with static public verification, repeated reuse and a many-note counterfeiting game.
definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\ge2\), supplied in unary. Let \(q_\lambda\) be the least prime at least \(\lambda^4\), let \(\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}\) denote integers modulo this prime, and define an integer error distribution by
\[
 \chi_\lambda(z)=\frac{\exp(-\pi z^2/\lambda^2)}{\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi a^2/\lambda^2)},\qquad z\in\mathbb Z.
\]
For every polynomially bounded function \(m:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), sample independently a uniform matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{m(\lambda)\times\lambda}\), a uniform vector \(s\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{\lambda}\), errors \(e_i\) independently from \(\chi_\lambda\), and a uniform vector \(u\in\mathbb Z_{q_\lambda}^{m(\lambda)}\). All field elements have their ordinary binary encodings. The LWE premise says that the two classical ensembles
\[
 (1^\lambda,A,As+e\bmod q_\lambda)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 (1^\lambda,A,u)
\]
are computationally indistinguishable against the quantum adversaries defined below. That is, every such distinguishing circuit has negligible absolute difference between its two acceptance probabilities, for every such sample-count function. The discrete Gaussian specifies a probability law, rather than granting an exact sampling oracle to any algorithm.

A nonnegative function \(\mu(\lambda)\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge1\) it is at most \(\lambda^{-a}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). The threshold may depend on \(a\). A different negligible function may be used for each fixed adversary, sample-count function or repetition bound.

Quantum computations use qubits, the fixed Clifford-plus-T gate set, zero-state ancillas and computational-basis measurements, with polynomial-time classical control. A quantum state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on the finite qubit register concerned; mixed states are allowed. A uniform polynomial-time algorithm has one finite classical program generating and controlling these operations, with a fixed polynomial bound on the number of gates, qubits and classical bit operations on every measurement branch. Classical random bits may be generated by fair quantum measurements. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of such circuits with polynomial-size classical descriptions and classical advice depending only on \(\lambda\). Its size and advice polynomial may depend on the adversary. There is no quantum advice or advice correlated with the fresh samples or keys. Uniform honest algorithms and nonuniform adversaries have no external oracle.

A money scheme is one fixed triple of uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\to(pk,sk),\qquad
 \operatorname{Mint}(sk)\to(\sigma,\rho),\qquad
 \operatorname{Verify}(pk,\sigma,\rho)\to(b,\rho').
\]
Both keys and the serial number \(\sigma\) are classical binary strings; the keys may encode \(\lambda\). The note \(\rho\) occupies a register whose size is bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(\lambda\), as are all honest classical lengths. A scheme specifies its admissible serial and register formats and rejects malformed inputs. The bit \(b=1\) means acceptance. Verification returns the residual note register in its prescribed format, so it can be verified again with the same serial number. Its public inputs are only \((pk,\sigma,\rho)\): it has no secret key, persistent verifier state, external time input or interaction with the bank. Each call uses fresh ancillas and randomness. Mint calls are independent conditional on the classical secret key; the bank retains no correlated quantum minting state. All banknotes have one unit of value.

Reusable correctness requires that for every polynomially bounded integer function \(t(\lambda)\ge1\) there is a negligible \(\mu_t\) such that the following experiment succeeds with probability at least \(1-\mu_t(\lambda)\): generate the keys, mint one honest note, and invoke Verify on that note \(t(\lambda)\) times in succession, feeding each residual register into the next invocation with the unchanged public key and serial. Success means all invocations accept. The probability includes key generation, minting and all verification measurements. The scheme and the original minted note's size are not chosen as a function of \(t\); there is no prescribed expiration time or replacement by the bank.

For security, fix any polynomially bounded integer function \(k(\lambda)\ge0\) and any nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary \(\mathcal A\). Generate \((pk,sk)\), mint \(k(\lambda)\) independent notes under this secret key, and give \(1^\lambda\), \(pk\), all serials and all note registers to \(\mathcal A\). It outputs \(k(\lambda)+1\) serial/register pairs. Measure its classical serial outputs and run fresh local copies of Verify on the respective registers. The output registers may be jointly entangled; the acceptance event is the joint outcome of these local tests, not a product of their marginal probabilities. Security requires
\[
 \Pr[\text{all }k(\lambda)+1\text{ output notes are accepted}]
 \le\mu_{\mathcal A,k}(\lambda)
\]
for a negligible function \(\mu_{\mathcal A,k}\). The probability includes all honest randomness and all quantum measurements. Wrong output syntax is a loss. The serials may repeat or differ from those received; no condition of distinct serials weakens the game. The case \(k=0\) forbids creating an accepted note from the public key alone. Since Verify is a public algorithm, the adversary can run it as often as its polynomial circuit size permits. One fixed scheme must satisfy correctness and security for every polynomial repetition count, note count and adversary.

The question is an unrestricted implication between this LWE hardness statement and existence of such a money scheme. No black-box restriction, security-tightness requirement or preservation of the LWE parameter's numerical size is imposed on the reduction; polynomial overhead and polynomial reparameterization are permitted. No ideal random oracle, generic group oracle, trusted hardware, externally supplied setup or additional unproved hardness, obfuscation or leakage assumption is available. The bank's own randomized generation of its public and secret keys is allowed. Anonymity, tracing, public minting and quantum-lightning security are not additional requirements.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated implication, including the uniform polynomial-time algorithms, reusable correctness and security reduction to the fixed LWE premise; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation in the ordinary computational model. The latter means the LWE premise holds while no scheme satisfying the full definition exists.

A broken candidate, a black-box barrier or an oracle separation alone does not refute this unrestricted existence implication. Schemes with private verification keys, changing public verification keys, expiring notes, a preselected polynomial transfer limit, generic oracles or additional unproved assumptions do not establish it. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no target.
context:
Public verification and unclonability must coexist: anyone can execute the verifier, while a holder of several valid notes cannot produce one additional accepted note. The definition counts notes even when they share a serial number.

The anonymous-money construction supplies additional privacy and tracing features under stronger assumptions. Its LWE-based auxiliary encryption primitive does not by itself give money from LWE alone.

The evasive-obfuscation obstruction limits the oracle access used by the mint and verifier. The current target allows arbitrary constructions and reductions, so that restricted barrier is not its negation.

The group-representation approach supplies money and lightning under group-action or specially structured homomorphism assumptions. These remain different premises from decisional LWE.

A reduction to group-action discrete logarithm can still retain an idealized group-action interface. The generic-model theorem does so, whereas this card requires ordinary finite quantum algorithms.

The 2026 time-dependent construction from post-quantum one-way functions uses public key announcements and banknotes that expire after their authentication layers are exhausted. Its transfer lifetime is chosen at minting and exhausted notes must return to the bank. The card instead requires a fixed note format reusable for every polynomial number of local verifications.
why: Ground publicly verifiable unclonable quantum states in a standard lattice assumption, resolving a central assumption gap in quantum cryptography.

This review does not independently certify the complete security proofs or exhaust the literature.

The same note must survive every polynomial number of verifications with that fixed key. An efficient quantum holder of k valid notes must have negligible probability of producing k+1 accepted notes. The question asks whether a fixed quantum-hard Learning with Errors assumption alone guarantees such a scheme. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove this unrestricted implication or its ordinary-model negation.

title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
importance_reason: Identify the computational assumption underlying one of the central public-key primitives.
formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof or refutation of the stated existence implication for this exact modulus ensemble and inverse-polynomial average-success convention. A refutation must establish the inverter premise together with failure of the factoring conclusion. Excluding only a chosen class of black-box reductions is insufficient; results for other exponents or worst-case oracles must first be related to the specified average-case problem.
context:
Factoring an RSA modulus gives the private exponent and hence breaks encryption, but the reverse reduction is a longstanding cryptographic question. It would identify whether RSA inversion rests on precisely the factoring assumption or on a potentially weaker computational task.

Boneh’s survey asks about factoring with an RSA inversion oracle. This card retains the imported fixed-exponent average-case specialization and explicitly compares inverse-polynomial average success on its balanced-prime ensemble. The implication permits arbitrary constructions; restricted-model separation results do not refute it.
why: Identify the computational assumption underlying one of the central public-key primitives.

Rechecked its formulation on 13 September 2026; the saved bounded status search found no resolution, and no exhaustive current-open claim is made.

This card asks for a converse implication with exponent 65537 on a specified ensemble of balanced prime products. Both inversion and factoring are measured by inverse-polynomial average success of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The implication allows unrestricted use of an inverter’s code and is not confined to black-box reductions. The fixed-exponent average-case question is an explicit specialization of the broader oracle question in Boneh’s survey.

title: Linear-seed pseudorandom generators from one-way functions
importance_reason: A linear seed with this quantitative security would connect strong average-case hardness to efficient derandomization without the polynomial seed overhead of the general conversion. It asks for substantially more than the foundational existence equivalence between one-way functions and cryptographic generators.
formal:
Can every efficiently evaluable length-preserving one-way function be converted into a fully explicit pseudorandom generator with seed length linear in the function's input length, while retaining the following quantitative security?

Precisely, for every integer \(b\ge1\), do there exist integers \(A,K,q,r\ge1\), \(\ell_0\ge4\), and one deterministic compiler \(\mathcal B_b\) such that the following holds? Its input is a Boolean circuit \(F:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) of size at most \(\ell^b\), integers \(\ell\ge\ell_0\), \(1\le s\le2^{2\ell}\), \(m>A\ell\), and \(1\le e\le2\ell\). Write
\[
 \varepsilon=2^{-e},\qquad
 t=\left\lfloor\frac{s}{K(m2^e)^q}\right\rfloor,
\]
and require \(t\ge1\). Suppose every inversion circuit \(I\) of size at most \(s\) satisfies
\[
 \Pr_{x\leftarrow U_{\ell}}[F(I(F(x)))=F(x)]\le\frac12.
\]
The compiler must produce a circuit \(G:\{0,1\}^{d}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\), with \(1\le d\le A\ell<m\), in at most \(K(m+1)^r\) bit operations, such that every Boolean distinguishing circuit \(T\) of size at most \(t\) satisfies
\[
 \left|\Pr[T(G(U_d))=1]-\Pr[T(U_m)=1]\right|\le\varepsilon.
\]
The construction may depend on \(s\) and \(\varepsilon\): a separate generator is permitted for each requested pair of these parameters.
question_excerpt: Vadhan asks whether the conversion from a general one-way function to a fully explicit pseudorandom generator can use a seed linear in the underlying input length while retaining a fixed-polynomial loss in the output length and inverse distinguishing advantage. The user selected this original quantitative target and allowed the construction to depend on the requested security and error.
definitions:
The uniform distribution \(U_j\) assigns equal probability to all binary strings of length \(j\). All random variables in the probability expressions are fresh uniform strings of their indicated lengths. The generator itself is deterministic once its seed is fixed.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic Boolean circuits with fan-in-two AND and OR gates, constants, and negations on wires. Size counts AND and OR gates; inputs, constants, fan-out and negations are free, following the source's nonuniform-time convention. A circuit is encoded by a topologically ordered gate list with binary wire indices and polarity bits, followed by the output wires. Negation chains are reduced to a polarity bit. This fixes a polynomial-length representation of a size-\(\ell^b\) function circuit. An inverter has \(\ell\) input and \(\ell\) output bits; a distinguisher has \(m\) input bits and one output bit. Their descriptions may depend arbitrarily on \(F,\ell,s,m,e\). They are not required to be generated by a uniform algorithm. Allowing additional independent random coins does not strengthen either hypothesis or conclusion, since averaging over the coins reduces the relevant bound to deterministic circuits.

Inversion succeeds on any preimage of \(F(x)\), not necessarily the particular sampled \(x\). There is no injectivity, regularity or preimage-size promise on \(F\). The hardness hypothesis is a finite-parameter implication: the compiler is not required to decide whether the supplied circuit really is hard to invert. It must halt with a well-formed generator and the stated seed and time bounds on every input satisfying the syntactic parameter conditions; pseudorandomness is required when the inversion hypothesis holds.

The exponent \(b\) fixes the polynomial evaluation bound of the underlying function. The constants and compiler may depend on \(b\), but not on the particular \(F,\ell,s,m,e\). The integers are supplied in binary and the circuit is explicitly listed. The resource bound is time on a classical multitape Turing machine, including reading the inputs and writing the entire generator circuit. Circuit evaluation consequently also takes polynomial time in \(m\). A uniformly polynomial-time family of functions supplies circuits with some fixed polynomial exponent, so this formulation gives the source's polynomial-output-time explicitness. It does not allow exponential preprocessing hidden in the generator description or polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) when that quantity is superpolynomial in \(m\).

The chosen parameter range states the nontrivial quantitative regime. At sufficiently large \(\ell\), every function on \(\ell\)-bit inputs has an inverse-selection lookup circuit smaller than \(2^{2\ell}\); greater claimed hardness would therefore have a false premise. With that upper bound on \(s\), errors smaller than \(2^{-2\ell}\) give a displayed time bound below one. Those cases are not additional positive-time security targets. Restricting error to dyadic values loses at most a constant factor when rounding any desired error downward, which can be absorbed in \(K\). The condition \(m>A\ell\) specifies output lengths beyond the allowed linear seed threshold and ensures genuine stretch. The target is asymptotic in \(\ell\), hence the fixed initial cutoff \(\ell_0\).

Both \(s\) and \(e\) are construction inputs, not only quantities used afterwards to assess a single generator. In particular, the question does not require one generator for a fixed \(F,m\) to satisfy all security-error pairs simultaneously. The compiler may inspect and use the full description of \(F\); no restriction to black-box oracle calls is imposed. The exponent \(q\) in the security loss is fixed before the varying parameters and cannot grow with them. Thus the bound is exactly of the form \(s(\varepsilon/m)^{O(1)}\), up to a fixed multiplicative factor and integer rounding.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of the compilers and their constants, together with the uniform polynomial bit-time bound, linear seed bound and stated security implication for every admissible input; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence statement.

A construction only for permutations, regular functions or another proper subclass is insufficient. Mere existence of some cryptographic generator from a one-way function does not meet the seed-length and quantitative-security requirements. A lower bound restricted to black-box constructions does not refute this unrestricted target. A larger-than-linear seed bound, a security-loss exponent that grows with the input, or unbounded preprocessing is insufficient. The yes-or-no proposition and asymptotic bounds have no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
importance_reason: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a deterministic uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction satisfying both stated promises, or a Lean proof that such a reduction does not exist. The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.
context:
Statistical zero knowledge asks whether a verifier can be convinced while learning only information that a simulator could reproduce. The unresolved equality asks whether interaction adds power when a noninteractive protocol has an honestly sampled public random string.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. The requested reduction therefore tests the original class equality with a fully discrete input and output contract.
why: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.

working_summary: Statistical zero knowledge studies proofs whose verifier learns no statistically distinguishable information beyond the assertion being proved. The question is whether every such interactive proof can be replaced by a noninteractive proof with public randomness. The primary source expresses the same issue as a reduction between two promise problems on sampling circuits. The reduction must transform close or far pairs into distributions respectively close to or far from uniform. A deterministic polynomial-time reduction with the specified promises would establish NISZK equals SZK.

title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
importance_reason: Determine whether computation over encrypted data requires fundamentally more than public-key confidentiality.
formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))

context:
Public-key encryption permits confidential communication; fully homomorphic encryption additionally permits computation over ciphertexts. A general implication would make the stronger capability follow from the existence of the basic public-key primitive.

The cited black-box separation rules out deriving fully homomorphic encryption from even hierarchical identity-based encryption by that restricted type of construction. It therefore supplies a barrier and motivation, not a negative answer to an arbitrary non-black-box implication. The existing LWE-to-FHE card starts from a specific stronger assumption.
why: Determine whether computation over encrypted data requires fundamentally more than public-key confidentiality.
status_note: The primary source proves a restricted black-box separation, not impossibility of arbitrary constructions. The later functional-encryption implication requires an additional premise. These scopes were checked on 13 September 2026; the bounded status review found no resolution of the stated general implication.
progress: 2015: The paper rules out specified fully black-box constructions; unrestricted implications remain distinct. | 2023: Bitansky and Solomon obtain a homomorphic-encryption implication with an additional functional-encryption premise. That premise is absent from this card.
working_summary: Fully homomorphic encryption permits evaluating Boolean circuits over encrypted input bits. The question asks whether its existence follows from ordinary public-key encryption alone. Key generation must work without a supplied circuit-depth bound, and decryption cost must remain independent of the evaluated circuit. The scheme must remain secure with its evaluation key public. Known black-box barriers and implications from additional primitives do not settle this unrestricted existence implication.

title: PZK versus SZK
importance_reason: A foundational comparison between two information-theoretic privacy notions, posed in a standard cryptography textbook, supported by a nontrivial oracle separation and explicitly retained in recent work on perfect zero knowledge.
formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.
context:
Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.
why: Determine whether allowing any negligible statistical simulation error increases the expressive power of information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
status_note: No unrelativized resolution was found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 paper explicitly retains the equality as open. Oracle separations and perfect-zero-knowledge results in PCP or multiprover models do not settle this target.
progress: 2001: Goldreich lists PZK versus SZK as open and distinguishes strict from expected-time simulation. | 2020: The journal paper proves an oracle separation of SZK from PZK, not an ordinary class separation. | 2024-03-18: The PCP paper explicitly retains the ordinary interactive-proof equality as unknown.

title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
importance_reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.
formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over \(F_{2}\) and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.
context:
LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.
why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-09-08: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
working_summary: Learning parity with noise asks for information about hidden binary linear equations when some answers have been flipped. This project asks whether worst-case hardness of the binary nearest-codeword problem implies average-case hardness for a specified low-noise LPN distribution. The chosen regime uses quadratically many samples and a noise rate inversely proportional to the square root of the secret dimension. A reduction must produce that particular random-instance distribution rather than merely another hard coding problem or a different noise level. Such a connection would strengthen the theoretical foundation of low-noise LPN in the way worst-case reductions support lattice-based assumptions.

title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
importance_reason: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
formal:
Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family? With the definitions below, the proposition is
\[
\bigl[\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists g\;\mathrm{OWF}(g)\land\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\bigr].
\]
Both sides require security against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family. The conclusion asks for the existence of some such \(g\), with some constant depth and some polynomial bounds. These constants may depend on \(g\), but not on its input length or on an adversary. There is no additional assumption on the starting function's circuit depth, no requirement that \(f\) and \(g\) have the same input or output lengths, and no requirement of a black-box construction or an efficient compiler from descriptions of \(f\).
definitions:
A candidate function is a family \(f=(f_n)_{n\ge1}\), with a length function \(m_f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\) and total maps
\[
f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m_f(n)}.
\]
The output length depends only on \(n\), and zero is an allowed length. Let \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) mean that there are a single deterministic machine \(M\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), the machine outputs exactly \(f_n(x)\) and halts within \(B(n+1)^k\) steps, with \(m_f(n)\le B(n+1)^k\). The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finitely many tapes, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary symbols, a separator and a blank, and one-cell head moves; each transition counts as one step. The input is the binary string on a read-only input tape with end markers, work tapes are initially blank, and output bits are written sequentially on an output tape. This fixes ordinary bit computation; the number of tapes, alphabet and program are fixed independently of \(n\). No advice, oracle or random coins are supplied to the evaluator.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose input nodes carry the input bits, whose constant nodes carry \(0\) or \(1\), and whose internal gates are binary AND, binary OR or unary NOT. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same predecessor may occupy both input positions. Outputs are an ordered list of references to nodes, with repetitions allowed. Size is the number of nodes plus the number of output positions. Depth is the largest number of internal gates on a path from an input or constant node to an output. Circuit descriptions list the nodes in a topological order, with gate tags and predecessor indices, followed by the output indices; indices and list lengths are in binary with separators from a fixed finite alphabet. No gates for arbitrary functions or oracle evaluation are present.

For a candidate \(f\), an allowed inverter is any family \(A=(A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of Boolean circuits of this basis, together with integers \(r(n)\ge0\), such that
\[
A_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m_f(n)+r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\exists C,c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,
\quad\max\{\operatorname{size}(A_n),r(n)\}\le C(n+1)^c.
\]
No uniform procedure for producing \(A_n\) is required, and its depth is unrestricted. The input blocks are \(1^n\), a proposed function value, and \(r(n)\) independent fair random bits. Thus the security parameter is given in unary, the adversary may depend on the input length nonuniformly, and it is not restricted to shallow circuits. For independent uniform strings \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\), put
\[
s_{f,A}(n)=\Pr\!\left[
f_n\bigl(A_n(1^n,f_n(X),R)\bigr)=f_n(X)
\right].
\]
Success means finding any preimage of the specified length \(n\), not necessarily the sampled \(X\). The function itself is deterministic; the probability is only over \(X\) and the adversary's coins \(R\). The negligible-success requirement is
\[
\forall A\text{ allowed}\ \forall a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists N\ge2\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad s_{f,A}(n)\le n^{-a}.
\]
The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(f,A,a\). Define \(\mathrm{OWF}(f)\) to mean \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) together with this requirement. Security holds at every sufficiently large length for each adversary and exponent, rather than merely on infinitely many lengths. There is no requirement of injectivity, length preservation, expansion, or any fixed ratio of output to input length.

The predicate \(\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\) means that there are a single deterministic circuit-generating Turing machine \(G\), integers \(B,k\ge1\), and an integer \(D\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\), the machine \(G\) outputs the full description of a circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(B(n+1)^k\) steps. That circuit has exactly \(n\) input bits, exactly \(m_g(n)\) outputs, size at most \(B(n+1)^k\), and depth at most \(D\), and satisfies \(C_n(x)=g_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Generation uses the same deterministic bit-computation convention as above. The depth bound is a single constant for the entire family; in particular, every output depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits. The question places no bound on how many outputs a given input bit may influence. Circuit generation has no random setup, randomly chosen graph, public key or advice. The two existentially quantified functions may have different length functions and polynomial bounds.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed implication or of its logical negation, using exactly the evaluation, uniformity and nonuniform-security conventions above. A positive proof must establish the existence of a secure family with one constant depth bound from the sole assumption that a one-way function exists. A negative proof must establish both
\[
\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall g,\quad\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\Longrightarrow\neg\mathrm{OWF}(g).
\]
Equivalently, for every candidate \(g\) with such a uniform constant-depth implementation, it must establish an allowed polynomial-size inverter family \(A\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) with
\[
\forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad s_{g,A}(n)>n^{-a},
\]
as well as the existence of an unrestricted one-way function. The inverter and exponent may depend on \(g\). A separation only relative to an oracle, an obstruction only to a selected kind of reduction, or failure of a particular local candidate does not prove this negation. A theorem under an additional computational assumption establishes only that conditional result.
context:
Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz explicitly ask whether an arbitrary one-way function implies a one-way function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\). A local function can expose many output bits, each depending on only a constant number of inputs, while inversion must remain difficult for general polynomial-size circuits.

Their theorems establish the implication when the starting one-way function has a polynomial-time uniform nondeterministic branching-program representation of polynomial size, which in particular covers logspace and uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

This card retains its existing editorial choices of deterministic polynomial-time uniform evaluation, length-dependent output size, same-length preimages, and nonuniform circuit security; the source uses polynomial-time uniformity by default and explicitly extends its security results to nonuniform adversaries.

The Ren–Santhanam revision of August 2025 still explicitly describes the general implication as open and gives a characterization through average-case Kolmogorov complexity in its stated uniform-adversary setting.
why: The question tests whether the minimal computational assumption underlying much of cryptography already guarantees functions with constant-depth local evaluation. A positive answer would make this extreme parallelism available under the general one-way-function assumption; a negative answer would separate local cryptographic hardness from unrestricted polynomial-time cryptographic hardness.
status_note: The general implication is explicit in AIK’s 2006 open questions and is still described as open in Ren–Santhanam’s ECCC revision of 25 August 2025. This card retains its declared P-uniform evaluation and nonuniform circuit-security conventions; AIK explicitly supports the latter extension, whereas the later paper states its main definitions using PPT adversaries. Individual primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated source-open assessment, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2006: Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz show that a one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size nondeterministic branching programs implies a one-way function with output locality four. Their general open question allows any constant output locality and starts from an arbitrary polynomial-time one-way function. | 2023-02-28: The Mao–Mazor–Zhang revision gives non-adaptive constructions of universal one-way hash functions from arbitrary one-way functions. Its constant-depth corollary still assumes that a one-way function exists in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\); treating oracle calls as gates does not remove that hypothesis. | 2025-08-25: Ren and Santhanam retain the general question in their revised introduction, alongside their characterization of local one-way functions by average-case hardness of \(\mathrm{KT}\) complexity. Their separate characterization of unrestricted one-way functions uses a different time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity measure, so these results do not establish the displayed implication.
working_summary: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but resists inversion on a uniformly chosen input by every polynomial-size adversary. The question asks whether the existence of any such function guarantees one whose Boolean circuits have a single constant depth bound. The circuits must be generated deterministically in polynomial time, while inversion security is required against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuits. Known theorems establish this implication under restricted computational assumptions, and a 2025 source still explicitly lists the general implication as open. A complete Lean proof must establish the implication or prove both that general one-way functions exist and that every eligible local family is insecure.

title: Identity-based encryption from arbitrary public-key encryption
importance_reason: Compare the assumptions needed for basic encryption and large-scale identity-based access control.

u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. e b]\le
u(\lambda)\) for one negligible \(
