working_summary: A local Hamiltonian describes a quantum system through bounded-strength interactions on a fixed number of qubits at a time. The question asks whether distinguishing two constant-separated ranges of its average ground energy is as hard as every problem with a quantum witness verifier. The saved variant requires deterministic classical reductions, a stronger requirement than the original survey’s formulation allowing quantum reductions. All global quantum states are allowed, and neither growing locality nor a vanishing normalized gap meets the target. Known low-energy state complexity, interactive verification and restricted gap-amplification results leave the stated hardness question unresolved in the checked sources.

title: BPP versus BQP
importance_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
focus_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
question_excerpt: The retained target is strict containment for total decision languages. In the inspected August 2019 edition of Wigderson, it is Conjecture 11.5, alongside Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2. Conjecture 11.4 in that edition concerns NP versus BQP; the older March 2018 numbering must not be carried over. The card keeps its finite H, T, CNOT basis and now gives explicit matrices, uniformity and measurement semantics.
definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
context:
Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.
why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.
status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.
progress: 1990s: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with the containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\); the inspected 2019 book states it as Theorem 11.2. | 1994 conference; 1996 preprint revision: Shor’s polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms give major candidate advantages without an unconditional classical lower bound. | 1999: Boykin and coauthors prove universality of the finite Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT basis used here. | 2018 preprint; 2019 conference; 2022 journal: Raz–Tal establish a separation from the polynomial hierarchy relative to an oracle, preserving that oracle restriction. | 2026-08-12: Quantum publishes the shallow-circuit sampling separation, with explicit classical randomness/fan-in restrictions and a different output task. | 2026-09-07: A new oracle separates the promise-class comparison from the total-language comparison even when the language classes coincide.
working_summary: BPP and BQP are classes of total decision languages with bounded error separately on every input, using classical randomness and quantum circuits respectively. The quantum model uses one polynomial-time classical generator for finite H, T and CNOT circuits with auxiliary qubits initialized to zero and one final measured bit. The question asks whether some quantum polynomial-time language has no classical randomized polynomial-time decider; the alternative is equality of the classes. Factoring algorithms, oracle separations and shallow sampling lower bounds retain assumptions or output/resource differences that do not establish this full separation. A September 2026 oracle result further distinguishes total-language equality from promise-class equality, while the ordinary total-language target remains unresolved in the inspected sources.

title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
importance_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
focus_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
question_excerpt: Does a nondegenerate ground state of a finite-range, uniformly gapped two-dimensional local Hamiltonian obey an entropy area law?
definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.
context:
A region containing \(m\) sites has entropy at most \(m\log_2q\). For a square block with side length \(\ell\), this volume bound is quadratic in \(\ell\), while the conjecture permits only a constant times its boundary length. Fixing both interaction norms and the gap prevents rescaling an increasingly gapless family from appearing uniformly gapped.

Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped one-dimensional local systems. An interval has only a constant number of boundary edges, so its entropy stays bounded as the chain grows. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not give a constant independent of width: each grouped site has dimension \(q^L\).

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.
why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the full 2D frustration-free introduction and theorem, official February 2026 article introduction and approximate-projector definition, April 2026 thermodynamic introduction and frustration-free section, primary historical abstracts and bounded later-work searches were checked. The newer area-law consequences retain extra assumptions; no proof or counterexample for the stated uniformly globally gapped, unique-ground-state two-dimensional family was identified. Entanglement-spread and area-law computational-hardness results address different claims. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2007: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters. | 2021: Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap. | 2022: Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar publish an area law for entanglement spread, rather than von Neumann entropy. | 2022–2023: Anshu, Arad, and Gosset give a nearly linear entropy bound for vertical cuts in locally gapped frustration-free systems. In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) at the end of §4. | 2026-02-05: Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector. | 2026-04-15: Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.
working_summary: An area law says that entanglement between a region and its surroundings grows with the region's boundary rather than its volume. This problem asks for such a bound for the unique ground state of a general two-dimensional local Hamiltonian with a fixed positive spectral gap. Interaction strength, local dimension, and interaction range are held fixed as the lattice grows. Known routes involving frustration-free systems or additional conditions do not automatically establish the unrestricted statement recorded here. A solution would clarify how strongly locality and an energy gap constrain many-body quantum states, without by itself supplying an efficient algorithm to find them.

title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
importance_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
focus_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
formal:
Can a completely classical verifier check arbitrary efficient quantum computation by interacting with one efficient quantum prover, with soundness against every computationally unbounded cheating prover?

The common input is an explicitly encoded quantum circuit \(C\) over \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), with all qubits initially zero and a designated output qubit. Write \(N\) for its description length and \(p(C)\) for the probability that measuring that output in the computational basis gives one. The promise is
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\iff p(C)\ge 2/3,\qquad C\in\mathrm{NO}\iff p(C)\le 1/3.\]
Does there exist one uniform interactive protocol \((P,V)\) and positive integer constants \(a,d\) with the following properties? The verifier \(V\) is a classical probabilistic machine; the honest prover \(P\) is a quantum machine with classical control. They exchange only classical messages with no setup or extra prover. Both honest computations, the verifier against every cheating strategy, the number of messages and total communication have the polynomial bounds specified below. For every promised circuit,
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P\text{ on }C]\ge2/3,\]
\[C\in\mathrm{NO}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall P^*\quad\Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P^*\text{ on }C]\le1/3.\]
Here \(P^*\) ranges over all adaptive response strategies, without any computational bound. The protocol and the constants precede the quantifiers over inputs and cheating strategies.
question_excerpt: Preserves the existing score 97, single-prover model, classical communication, efficient uniform honest prover, unbounded-cheater soundness and constant completeness/soundness gap. Aharonov–Ben-Or–Eban–Mahadev §1.8 and Aaronson–Natarajan–Tal–Villányi §1 explicitly pose this conjunction of requirements. The all-zero circuit promise is the already selected concrete BQP verification target. The encoding, gates, message interface and global clocks specify that target; no new physical or cryptographic assumption is added.
definitions:
A circuit consists of \(q\ge1\) labelled qubits, an ordered list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) of gates with \(m\ge0\), and an output index \(o\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The one-qubit matrices and two-qubit action are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|x,y\rangle=|x,x\mathbin\oplus y\rangle.\]
Here \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Each gate acts on its indicated qubit or ordered pair of distinct qubits and as the identity on the rest. Let \(U_C=g_m\cdots g_1\), with identity for an empty list. In the vector space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\), set
\[p(C)=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^q\\z_o=1}}|\langle z|U_C|0^q\rangle|^2.\]
These gate entries and probabilities are exact mathematical quantities, not floating-point input data. No correctness condition is imposed when \(1/3<p(C)<2/3\).

For a concrete bit encoding, write \(q\) as \(1^q0\), followed by \(U(m),U(o)\) and every gate in sequence. The length-delimited integer code is \(U(b)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(b\ge0\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero has expansion 0. A gate uses a two-bit tag for H, T or CNOT, followed by the \(U\)-encoded target indices; the fourth tag is invalid. All indices must be within the declared range and CNOT indices must be distinct. No trailing bits are allowed. Thus \(q\le N\) and all gates are explicitly listed. Both parties receive the same classical description; neither receives an additional quantum input or witness. Malformed descriptions are rejected by the verifier.

The two algorithms have fixed finite classical control programs, independent of \(N\) and \(C\). The verifier has ordinary classical work tapes, private independent fair random bits, and a classical message interface. It has no quantum register, quantum channel or ability to prepare, transform or measure qubits. The honest prover starts with zero qubits, may create zero ancillas, apply H, T and CNOT gates, measure qubits in the computational basis, and use outcomes in subsequent classical computation. Measurements follow the squared-amplitude rule; a measured qubit may be discarded. Its classical controller may also toss fair coins. Gate addresses, classical arithmetic and generation of the next instruction are computed and charged. There is no input-dependent or length-dependent advice, precomputed advice state or uncharged oracle for either honest party.

Put \(R(N)=a(N+1)^d\). On every input and every branch of its private randomness, the verifier uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps, reads at most that many received bits, and halts with accept or reject. This clock holds against every possible sequence of replies. In an honest execution, the prover uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps and elementary quantum operations in total, on every randomness and measurement branch. One elementary quantum operation acts on at most two addressed qubits; all classical bit operations and all written or read message bits are charged. The honest prover holds at most \(R(N)\) qubits. These bounds also apply to well-formed circuits outside the promise. The protocol allows at most \(R(N)\) messages and \(R(N)\) communicated bits in total; the verifier enforces the declared message lengths and aborts on a violation. A missing reply or an explicit abort is rejection. There is no constant-round requirement or uncharged preprocessing phase.

For soundness, an arbitrary prover strategy can be described by a conditional distribution on its next classical reply for each input and history of messages it has seen. It can have unlimited private memory and arbitrary input-dependent information, but cannot see the verifier's private coins except through sent messages. This description includes the observable behaviour of any quantum cheating prover through the classical interface; no bound on its computation, circuit size or internal state is assumed. Acceptance probabilities include all private randomness and measurement outcomes. There is no initial shared secret, correlated setup state, trusted third party, random oracle or enforced separation inside the single prover.

Completeness concerns the one fixed honest algorithm on all YES instances. Soundness concerns every strategy on each NO instance. The task is verification of this decision promise problem; it imposes no separate blindness, sampling-output or witness-preservation requirement. Fixed error constants are part of the specification, rather than a numerical approximation tolerance for the final answer.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a protocol or its full logical negation. A positive answer must give uniform algorithms and universal polynomial resource bounds, prove completeness on every YES circuit, and prove the stated bound against all unbounded response strategies on every NO circuit. A negative answer must rule out every protocol in this model: for each resource-bounded pair, some YES input violates completeness or some NO input and cheating strategy violate soundness. A cryptographic argument sound only against efficient attackers, a quantum verifier, extra isolated provers, an inefficient honest prover or an impossibility theorem restricted to particular protocols does not settle this proposition.
context:
The honest-prover condition matters as much as the classical-verifier condition. The standard containments of quantum polynomial time in polynomial space, and IP=PSPACE, provide classical interactive proofs with an unrestricted prover. They do not establish that the auxiliary answers needed by that prover can be generated by a quantum polynomial-time machine. A verification protocol that demands a substantially more powerful server would not meet this card.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev supply information-theoretically sound verification with an efficient quantum prover when the verifier retains a small quantum register. For a fixed error gap, a constant number of qubits suffices in their result. Although their class definition first restricts dishonest provers, they explicitly state that the protocol proof protects against unbounded provers. Eliminating the verifier’s remaining quantum capability is the open question highlighted in their §1.8.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani use separated entangled quantum subsystems. Their classical verifier can certify and control quantum operations under the noncommunication constraints of that model. A single freely communicating prover is allowed to coordinate its replies across all of its internal components, so combining the devices loses a condition used by the multiprover theorem.

Mahadev’s protocol achieves the classical verifier and single efficient quantum prover by using a computational assumption. The inspected version bases its construction on quantum hardness of Learning With Errors with the specified superpolynomial noise ratio. Its soundness quantifies over efficient quantum cheating algorithms. An unbounded strategy is outside that guarantee, even if the protocol is otherwise fully classical at the interface.

The February 2026 quantum-cat preprint addresses preservation of a quantum witness: the prover can reuse one copy while obtaining negligible errors. Its abstract retains the post-quantum LWE assumption. A QMA witness is an additional quantum input that is not present in the all-zero BQP computation here, and preserving it does not remove the computational soundness assumption.

Another February 2026 preprint gives a conditional barrier to quantum black-box reductions for non-interactive QMA verification from falsifiable assumptions. Its model has one message after instance-independent setup, and its premise is a QMA–QCMA gap problem. Both the task and the restrictions differ from this card’s arbitrary polynomial interaction for BQP. The checked abstract therefore supplies no general impossibility answer here.

The April 2026 paper proves \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\subseteq\mathrm{MIP}^{O}\) for every classical oracle \(O\). Its associated classical proof is exponentially long but checked at polynomially many adaptively chosen locations. The theorem concerns several classical provers without shared entanglement, and it does not promise that their honest work is quantum polynomial time. Section 2 separately asks for such an efficient-prover result. The paper presents relativization as a research perspective, not as an equivalence resolving single-prover verification.

The May 2026 trusted-gate article removes trusted state preparation and measurement from the client’s requirements while retaining trusted quantum transformations. Its first construction uses single-qubit rotations and bit flips; the inspected preprint explicitly sends qubits through the client. Removing two hardware capabilities is useful progress, but the client still has quantum operations and quantum communication. It is not the classical machine specified here.

For this question, “information-theoretic” is a quantifier about every cheating strategy. It does not require perfect completeness, zero soundness error, blindness or verification of an entire output distribution. Keeping these notions distinct prevents either a stronger unrelated task or a weaker computational guarantee from replacing the stated decision problem.
why: The question isolates the resources needed for a classical user to trust a quantum answer. Known protocols obtain trust by giving the verifier some quantum capability, separating several devices, or assuming that particular computations are hard for an attacker. Resolving the stated conjunction would determine whether any of those additional resources is necessary when the honest server itself remains efficient.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected April 2026 primary source explicitly leaves efficient, unconditional single-prover verification by a classical verifier open. Its relativizing MIP theorem does not supply one efficient honest prover. The February witness-preserving protocol retains LWE; the February non-interactive barrier concerns a restricted QMA model; and the May trusted-gate article retains quantum client operations. None meets or rules out the full conjunction specified here. No matching later resolution was found in the bounded search; individual cited proofs were not independently certified.

working_summary: A classical user wants to check whether an explicitly given quantum circuit accepts with high probability. One uniform quantum polynomial-time honest prover must convince the user on every YES circuit using only classical messages. The verifier must reject NO circuits with high probability even against an unbounded adaptive cheating strategy. Known positive results use limited quantum verifier resources, separated provers, or computational hardness assumptions. The inspected 2026 literature retains the full single-prover information-theoretic question as open; narrower new protocols and barriers do not settle it.

title: NPT bound entanglement
importance_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
focus_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
question_excerpt: Does a bipartite state with negative partial transpose exist that is undistillable for every finite number of copies?
definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.
context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The open problem therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal investigated NPT states whose one-copy behavior differs from their spectral negativity. Their evidence did not establish one fixed NPT state undistillable for every finite number of copies. The present question retains that full order of quantifiers.

The Werner family is \(\rho_{\mathrm W}(d,\alpha)=(I+\alpha F)/(d^2+\alpha d)\), for \(d\ge2\) and \(-1\le\alpha\le1\), where \(F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u\) swaps the two local systems and \(I\) is identity. Its members are NPT exactly for \(\alpha<-1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly for \(\alpha<-1/2\). Thus \(-1/2\le\alpha<-1/d\) is the NPT one-copy-undistillable interval when \(d\ge3\). This is a known subclass; the target is not restricted to Werner states.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

Bharti, Gajjala and Haug also obtain the two-copy threshold and several restricted finite-copy extensions, while explicitly leaving the general all-copy assertion open. A family of states indexed by the allowed number of copies does not give the single fixed state required by the existential target.

Wu and Zou prove three-copy endpoint nonnegativity for specified sectors, including normal rank-two coefficient operators. A coefficient operator is the matrix of a bipartite test vector in product bases; normal means that the matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. Other rank-two matrices are allowed in the full criterion, so these sector results do not settle unrestricted three-copy distillability or the all-copy question.
why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.
status_note: Source-open. The two-copy thresholds and restricted three-copy sectors do not prove or refute the all-copy target. No general resolution was identified; this review did not independently verify the cited proofs or formalize them in Lean.

working_summary: Entangled states can sometimes be converted into nearly perfect shared Bell pairs using many copies and local operations with classical communication. Bound entanglement means that this distillation remains impossible despite the presence of entanglement. The question asks whether such states can have a negative partial transpose, a spectral property associated with distillability in simpler settings. Failure of a protocol on one copy or any fixed number of copies does not establish the required obstruction for every number of copies. Resolving the question would sharpen the distinction between entanglement as a property and entanglement as a usable communication resource.

title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
importance_reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge1\), some stabilizer code on \(n\ge N\) qubits has an admissible list of checks as defined below and satisfies \[k\ge rn,\qquad d\ge\delta n,\qquad H\succeq\frac{s}{n}D_Q?\] Here \(k\) is its number of logical qubits, \(d\) its code distance, each listed check acts on at most \(w\) qubits, and each qubit occurs in at most \(b\) listed checks. All five constants are fixed for the unbounded family. This is the bounded-degree stabilizer version of asymptotically good quantum local testability.
question_excerpt: Do asymptotically good stabilizer codes exist with constant local-test soundness, bounded check weight and bounded check incidence?
definitions:
The physical Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). In the standard one-qubit basis, \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). The Pauli group consists of tensor products of \(I,X,Y,Z\), multiplied by phases from \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\). A Pauli's support is the set of positions with a nonidentity tensor factor, and its weight is the cardinality of that set; the scalar phase does not affect support.

An admissible stabilizer presentation is a finite nonempty list \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) of Hermitian Pauli checks of positive weight. Hermitian means \(S_j=S_j^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose. The checks commute pairwise, and the group they generate does not contain \(-I\). Its code space is \[Q=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_n:S_j\psi=\psi\text{ for every }j\}.\] This nonzero space has dimension \(2^k\); the target requires \(k\ge1\). The distance \(d\) is the minimum weight of a Pauli \(P\) that preserves \(Q\), meaning \(P(Q)=Q\), but whose restriction to \(Q\) is not a scalar multiple of identity. For a stabilizer code with \(k\ge1\), such logical Paulis exist. This distance concerns undetectable changes to encoded information. The rate is \(k/n\) and the relative distance is \(d/n\).

The checks need not be independent, and a list may contain repetitions. The bounds refer to that actual list: \(\operatorname{wt}(S_j)\le w\) for every \(j\), and each qubit belongs to the supports of at most \(b\) checks, counting repetitions separately. Both are maximum bounds, not average bounds. Define the normalized check Hamiltonian \[H=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{I-S_j}{2}.\] Each summand is the orthogonal projection onto the failing eigenspace of one check. If a check is selected uniformly, the rejection probability on a unit vector \(\phi\) is \(\langle\phi,H\phi\rangle\); on a density matrix \(\rho\) it is \(\operatorname{Tr}(H\rho)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one.

For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_t\) be the complex linear span of vectors \(E\psi\), where \(\psi\in Q\) and \(E\) ranges over Pauli errors of weight at most \(t\). Let \(\Pi_t\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(Q_t\). These spaces are nested, with \(Q_0=Q\) and \(Q_n=\mathcal H_n\). Define \[D_Q=\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(I-\Pi_t)=\sum_{t=1}^n t(\Pi_t-\Pi_{t-1}).\] The two expressions agree by telescoping. The eigenvalue \(t\) measures the error radius of the corresponding orthogonal layer. Using Pauli errors in the span is equivalent to using arbitrary operators supported on at most \(t\) qubits, since local Pauli products span all such operators. This is not trace distance between density matrices.

The inequality \(H\succeq(s/n)D_Q\) means its difference is positive semidefinite: \(\langle\phi,[H-(s/n)D_Q]\phi\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(\phi\in\mathcal H_n\), where \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Equivalently it holds in expectation for every density matrix. The number \(s\) is normalized soundness. The family may use an arbitrary unbounded sequence of lengths rather than every integer length. Checks may connect any qubits, without geometric locality. No CSS restriction, efficient construction, decoding algorithm or transversal-gate property is required.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that fixed constants and an unbounded family satisfying all conditions exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\), there is a finite length bound beyond which no admissible presentation satisfies all the conditions simultaneously. An existence proof need not provide a polynomial-time construction. A failure for one proposed family, one subclass such as CSS codes, or one geometry does not prove nonexistence. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance, a growing maximum check weight or incidence, and a soundness guarantee confined to selected error weights do not meet the target. The operator inequality must cover the entire physical Hilbert space. This is an exact existence question, not a numerical approximation task.
context:
A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

The distance operator measures distance from the entire code space, not the written weight of one chosen Pauli error. A stabilizer leaves every codeword unchanged, while a logical Pauli can change the encoded information and still stay inside the code space. Both therefore remain at distance zero from the code as a subspace. The nested spaces \(Q_t\) account for these identifications. The operator inequality also controls superpositions and mixed states, not only individual Pauli-corrupted codewords.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has \(k=\Omega (n)\), distance \(\Omega (n/\log ^{3}n)\), soundness \(\Omega (1/\log ^{3}n)\), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

Garg and Sengupta obtain a further constant-soundness result using algebraic-geometry codes. Their stated application has locality growing as the square root of code length. This still misses the maximum constant check weight required here.
why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.

No family simultaneously meeting constant rate, relative distance, maximum check weight, maximum incidence and normalized soundness was identified. Existing inverse-polylogarithmic losses and growing-locality results do not meet this target. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

working_summary: A locally testable quantum code should reveal a substantial error by checking only a few qubits. The desired family must also encode a linear amount of quantum information and tolerate errors on a linear number of physical qubits. Each check and each qubit's participation in checks must remain bounded as the code grows. These requirements strengthen ordinary good quantum LDPC codes by demanding a quantitative relation between distance from the code space and rejection probability. Such codes would connect robust quantum error detection with the complexity of low-energy states and the broader search for quantum PCP constructions.

title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions
importance_reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.
formal: Do there exist constants \(B,R>0\), a fixed finite inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), strictly increasing qubit counts \(n_j\to\infty\), local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians \(H_{n_j}\), and fixed encoding maps \(\operatorname{Enc}_{n_j}\), all satisfying the definitions below, for which \[\tau_{n_j}(\beta)\longrightarrow\infty?\] The dynamics couple every single-qubit Pauli error to the same specified positive-temperature bath, with no intervention during storage. This card retains a claimed affirmative resolution from May2026; the complete preprint proof has not been independently verified here.
question_excerpt: Can a local three-dimensional quantum memory protect an encoded qubit for unbounded time as size grows at one fixed positive temperature?
definitions:
Place the \(n\) qubits at points in \(\mathbb R^3\), with at most \(B\) qubits in every closed unit ball. Each Hamiltonian is \[H_n=\sum_{a=1}^{M_n}\frac{I-S_a}{2}.\] The operators \(S_a\) are commuting, nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks. Each has support contained in a ball of radius \(R\), and each qubit belongs to at most \(B\) checks. Support is the set of wires where a tensor factor is not identity. The common \(+1\) eigenspace of all checks must have dimension exactly two, so the Hamiltonian has a single encoded ground-space qubit. A check is a signed tensor product of \[I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\] with overall sign \(+1\) or \(-1\). The coefficient of each term is fixed as displayed, so local energy penalties cannot grow with \(n\). The geometry need not be translation invariant, a regular lattice, or connected. The constants \(B,R\) work for the entire sequence. No efficient construction of the sequence is required.

All states live in finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces. A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and is completely positive, meaning that its tensor product with the identity on every auxiliary register preserves positive semidefiniteness. Such channels model encoding, noise and recovery. Use units \(\hbar=k_B=1\), so physical temperature is \(1/\beta\). The same finite positive \(\beta\) is used for all sizes.

Here is the complete bath convention. Let \(\Pi_E\) denote the spectral projector of \(H_n\) at energy \(E\). For every site \(u\), every \(P\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), and every energy difference \(\omega\) for which the following operator is nonzero, define \[A_{u,P,\omega}=\sum_{E'-E=\omega}\Pi_{E'}P_u\Pi_E,\qquad g_\beta(\omega)=\min\{1,e^{-\beta\omega}\}.\] Thus positive \(\omega\) means an increase in system energy; its rate is suppressed by the Boltzmann factor. The generator on density matrices is \[\mathcal L_{n,\beta}(\rho)=-i[H_n,\rho]+\sum_{u,P,\omega}g_\beta(\omega)\left(A_{u,P,\omega}\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger-\frac{A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}\rho+\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}}2\right).\] The commutator is \([H,\rho]=H\rho-\rho H\). The evolution for real \(t\ge0\) is the channel \(\Phi_{n,\beta,t}=\exp(t\mathcal L_{n,\beta})\), the finite-dimensional linear-map exponential. All single-site \(X,Y,Z\) couplings are included; no symmetry forbids one of them. Rates for allowed transitions are positive, and their attempt-rate normalization does not depend on size. The opposite-frequency ratio ensures the Gibbs state \(e^{-\beta H_n}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_n})\) is stationary. Although the spectral formula uses global energy projectors, commuting finite-range checks make these frequency components local: only checks meeting the site can affect its energy change. With the fixed range and density bounds, their support and possible energy changes are bounded independently of \(n\).

For each size choose one completely positive trace-preserving encoding \(\operatorname{Enc}_n\) from one qubit to the \(n\)-qubit system. It must have a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse \(D_{n,0}\), so \(D_{n,0}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n\) is exactly the identity channel. This encoding may depend on the chosen temperature, and may initialize a thermal auxiliary state; it need not map entirely into the ground space or be efficiently preparable. It is chosen once for the device, independently of storage time and the unknown logical input. This retains the previous card’s thermal-encoding convention rather than adding a ground-state-only initialization requirement.

Let \(\|A\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}\) be the trace norm. For this fixed encoding define \[\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)=\inf_{D}\ \sup_{\rho}\left\|D\circ\Phi_{n,\beta,t}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n(\rho)-\rho\right\|_1.\] The supremum ranges over every one-qubit density matrix; the infimum ranges over recovery channels \(D\) from \(n\) qubits to one. One recovery channel must work for every logical input at the given time. It may depend on \(n,\beta,t\), but cannot depend on the unknown input \(\rho\). Recovery is not required to be efficient. Define \[\tau_n(\beta)=\inf\{t\ge0:\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)>1/10\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The trace norm here has no factor of one half. Encoding occurs before storage and recovery only at readout; no syndrome measurements, feedback, cooling procedure or active corrections are allowed during the evolution. Divergence means that for every finite \(T>0\) there is an index \(j_0\) such that \(\tau_{n_j}(\beta)>T\) for all \(j\ge j_0\), at the same fixed temperature and local parameter bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of the family, fixed temperature and encoding maps in the displayed statement, including the lifetime bound for this generator, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative side need only prove divergence; a lower bound \(\exp(c n^\eta)\) for fixed \(c,\eta>0\) is stronger than required. The negative side must cover every admissible sequence and encoding, including thermal encodings, rather than a particular candidate geometry. The May2026 preprint claims a stronger affirmative bound, but this review has not independently verified its full construction or supplied its Lean formalization. A finite-size numerical trend or lifetime growth only up to a temperature-dependent crossover does not establish the fixed-temperature limit. Changing the bath with size, increasing local energy scales, forbidding local errors, adding corrections during storage, or demanding ground-state-only initialization changes the target.
context:
This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some \(\eta >0\). Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

The current preprint’s Equation(5) prints a first-threshold condition with error at most \(1/10\), which already holds at time zero. The card instead defines lifetime by the first time the recovery error exceeds the threshold. The source’s substantive claim is the trace-norm estimate in Equation(3), supported by its stated stability theorem and §5.4; that estimate would imply the intended lower bound with this corrected convention.
why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.
status_note: Claimed affirmative resolution, not confirmed open. On16September2026 arXiv:2605.10943 remained v1 from11May2026. Its Theorems1.1–1.2 and3.16, §2.5 stability/thermal-encoding statements, §5.4 main probability bound and Corollary5.14, and initialization/perturbation caveats were checked alongside the2010 stability theorem and Davies discussion. The stated estimate would give the required lifetime for the retained bounded-rate local bath and thermal encoding; the complete102-page geometric and probabilistic proof has not been independently verified here. The card therefore retains uncertain status with the affirmative claim prominent. Current cored-code numerical and August2026 layer-code results have distinct guarantees. No Lean formalization is claimed.
