working_summary: Passive quantum memory aims to preserve an encoded qubit through the natural dynamics of a material without repeated active correction. The question here fixes a nonzero temperature and asks whether lifetime can grow without bound in a three-dimensional local stabilizer system. Protecting a qubit requires retaining phase information as well as distinguishing its classical basis states. The saved card records a May 2026 claimed affirmative construction, while distinguishing its proof claim from an independently verified conclusion. This makes the record a useful guide to the precise thermal model and remaining verification questions rather than an unqualified assertion that the original existence problem is still open.

title: Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
importance_reason: A benchmark capacity problem connecting quantum error correction, information-theoretic converses and the operational effect of entangled encodings.
formal: Determine the unassisted quantum-capacity function \(Q(q)=Q(\mathcal D_q)\) for every real \(q\in[0,1]\), where the qubit depolarizing channel is \[\mathcal D_q(\rho)=(1-q)\rho+\frac q3(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z).\] The parameter \(q\) is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error. Capacity uses the operational definition below and is measured in qubits per independent channel use. The quantitative benchmark accepts a function with absolute error at most \(1/100\) throughout the whole domain.
question_excerpt: Determine the quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel as a function of its noise parameter.
definitions:
For the standard basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\) of \(\mathbb C^2\), define \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). Each of the three nonidentity errors has probability \(q/3\), and identity has probability \(1-q\). The formula therefore defines a channel for every real \(q\in[0,1]\). On general matrices it extends complex-linearly. In the coding definition, take \(A=B=\mathbb C^2\) and \(\Phi=\mathcal D_q\). The parameter is fixed across a code block and across the sequence of block lengths; a different parameter may have a different code sequence.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
answer_criterion: Give an unambiguous real-valued function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof that \[|g(q)-Q(q)|\le\frac1{100}\qquad\text{for every real }q\in[0,1].\] The proof must establish both the lower and upper sides of this absolute error bound in qubits per channel use. Exact equality with \(Q\) also qualifies. A finite table, uncertified numerical plot, or restatement of the defining optimization or supremum does not determine the requested curve. There is no prescribed formula grammar, finite representation for the argument \(q\), or polynomial evaluation-time requirement. The inherited numerical acceptance is weaker than the source's exact-capacity question; a solution at this tolerance need not settle the exact positive-capacity threshold.
context:
Depolarizing noise treats the three Pauli errors symmetrically. Despite this short channel description, its quantum transmission limit allows arbitrary collective encodings over arbitrarily long blocks. The entanglement-fidelity criterion keeps the distinction between transmitting an unknown quantum state and sending only classical data.

Parameter conventions matter: the probabilities \((1-3p,p,p,p)\) correspond to \(p=q/3\). The expression \((1-\lambda)\rho+\lambda I/2\) has \(\lambda=4q/3\), with the usual convex-mixture interpretation only for \(q\le3/4\). Thus \(q=3/4\) is the completely depolarizing channel; \(q=1\) still specifies a valid channel, but is a different map. All thresholds here use total Pauli error \(q\).

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

A known lower bound is \(\max\{0,1-h_2(q)-q\log_2 3\}\), where \(h_2(q)=-q\log_2q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)\), with the endpoint convention \(0\log_2 0=0\). Its positive part vanishes near \(q=0.1893\). Multicopy results surpass this bound, so the one-use expression is not the capacity curve throughout the noise range.

Agarwal and coauthors report positive coherent information for a 45-copy symmetric rank-two input up to a numerically evaluated per-Pauli value \(p=0.064657\), corresponding to \(q=0.193971\). This is a lower bound from particular inputs, not optimality over all block lengths.

Krohn-Grimberghe supplies an exact-arithmetic certificate for a 45-copy state with positive coherent information at \(q=48717/250000=0.194868\). The paper also gives positivity below this point and distinguishes its certified witness from stronger numerical states in the earlier authors' repository. This review checked the statement, conventions and limitations; it did not rerun the supplied verification artifact.

The endpoints and a whole zero-capacity range are known: \(Q(0)=1\) and \(Q(q)=0\) for every \(q\ge1/4\). In that range the channel is antidegradable, meaning that a channel applied to the environment output can simulate the receiver's output. The certificate paper explicitly does not determine the true positivity threshold. Knowing that threshold alone would still not determine the positive-rate curve.

Leditzky, Leung and Smith determine low-noise capacities to leading orders. This controls an asymptotic regime near the noiseless channel and does not evaluate the whole parameter interval.

Zhu and coauthors give improved upper bounds for depolarizing channels. Their §3.4 retains a gap between achievable rates and upper bounds; a numerical comparison of bounds does not by itself certify the benchmark error throughout the domain.

The August 2026 strong-converse paper establishes fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels and additional upper bounds. It explicitly distinguishes those bounds from an exact capacity value. A strong converse therefore does not supply the missing depolarizing curve.

The source literature retains the exact-capacity question. The absolute 0.01 acceptance rule was already adopted by the atlas before this review. Openness of the exact question does not alone imply that approximation to this tolerance is open; the status records that distinction.
why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.
status_note: Uncertain for the inherited absolute 0.01 benchmark; the underlying exact-capacity question remains open in the checked primary literature. On 16 September 2026 the coding theorem, low-noise introduction, geometric bounds, May and August 2026 threshold results, and strong-converse statements were checked, together with current revision metadata and bounded later-work searches. No full curve meeting the benchmark was identified, but openness at that fixed tolerance was not independently established. The August certificate is a positivity lower bound, not an exact threshold or curve; its verification artifact was not run. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

working_summary: A depolarizing channel models a qubit subjected to randomly chosen Pauli errors. Its quantum capacity measures how much unknown quantum information can be transmitted reliably per channel use when many uses are encoded together. The goal is the capacity curve throughout the noise range under the unassisted coding convention fixed in the card. Coding across several uses can behave differently from optimizing a single use, which complicates attempts to match achievable rates with impossibility bounds. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: NP outside BQP
importance_reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\)? That is, does there exist a total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{with}\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BQP}?\]
Equivalently, is the total language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) defined below outside \(\mathrm{BQP}\)? The negation is that every language with polynomially bounded classical certificates and a polynomial-time classical verifier has a uniform bounded-error quantum polynomial-time decider. This is noncontainment, not merely inequality of two classes.
question_excerpt: The standard noncontainment target is retained. In the inspected 6 August 2019 Wigderson draft it is Conjecture 11.4; the inherited March 2018 edition used Conjecture 11.5. The nearby BPP-versus-BQP conjecture is a different class comparison. The explicit NP verifier, finite-gate BQP semantics and 3-SAT encoding clarify the existing question without replacing it by a promise, search or restricted-circuit problem.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. Put \(n=|x|\) and write \(\mathbf1_L(x)\) for its membership bit, allowing \(n=0\). The condition \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) means that there exist a finite deterministic classical multitape Turing-machine verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d,K,e\) such that
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad |y|\le C(n+1)^d\ \land\ V(x,y)=1.\]
For every pair of binary strings \((x,y)\), the verifier halts with a bit output within \(K(|x|+|y|+1)^e\) ordinary tape steps. The existentially quantified certificate is classical. It defines membership but is not supplied to the quantum decider, which receives only \(x\). All programs and exponents are fixed independently of the input length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Quantum computation is ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

For a concrete satisfiability language, a formula has variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\) and \(M\) explicitly listed clauses. Each clause has zero to three literals, each a variable or its negation. A truth assignment is a vector in \(\{0,1\}^{N}\); it satisfies a clause when at least one literal is true and satisfies the formula when every clause is satisfied. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false; repeated variables, repeated clauses and tautologies are allowed.

Here is one explicit binary representation. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Begin with \(1^N0B(M)\). For each of the \(M\) clauses, write \(B(k)\) for its length \(0\le k\le3\), followed by its \(k\) literals. A literal is a sign bit and \(B(j)\) for \(1\le j\le N\); sign zero denotes \(z_j\), sign one denotes \(\neg z_j\). There are no trailing bits. The language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) consists of the valid encodings with a satisfying assignment. Every malformed string is a no-instance. Input length counts every encoding bit, rather than only \(N\), and the unary variable-count field ensures that the full assignment has polynomial length in the encoding.

This encoding is polynomially equivalent to the usual explicit 3-CNF satisfiability problem, with variables relabeled consecutively when necessary. By NP-completeness and closure of BQP under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). A many-one reduction here is one deterministic polynomial-time map \(f\) with \(x\in L\) exactly when \(f(x)\) is a satisfiable valid encoding. This equivalence concerns total languages, with the required bounded error on every yes- and no-instance.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BQP},\]
or its full negation \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\).

A separation must establish the classical verifier and polynomial certificate bound for one fixed language and exclude every polynomial-time-uniform quantum circuit family with any fixed polynomial size/register bounds in the stated finite-gate model. Equivalently, it may prove that the full encoded 3-SAT language is outside BQP. A containment proof may instead give a uniform quantum decider for this 3-SAT language, including rejection of malformed encodings, and establish its complete resource and pointwise success guarantees together with the NP-completeness implication.

An oracle or unstructured-search lower bound does not exclude algorithms that inspect the explicit input. Neither a restriction to selected formula families nor a lower bound for one quantum architecture answers the full question. Merely proving \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{BQP}\) is insufficient if the argument only places a language in BQP outside NP. A proposed SAT algorithm must count all elementary operations and qubits, including state preparation and any subroutine implementation. Nonlinear dynamics, postselection, supplied witnesses or uncharged exponential resources are outside this BQP definition. There is no unproved hardness assumption or numerical approximation tolerance in the target.
context:
For a satisfiable formula, one assignment certifies a yes answer; for an unsatisfiable formula, every assignment fails. The quantum decider receives the formula without a certificate and must answer both cases reliably. Its input is the entire explicit syntax, so shared variables and clause structure are available to every algorithm being quantified over.

Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). A proof merely that classical deterministic computation is weaker than NP would not by itself establish this stronger noncontainment. The statement also differs from BPP versus BQP: quantum algorithms could be more powerful than classical randomization while still failing on some NP languages.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms are polynomial in the input bit length. These structured function tasks do not provide a general quantum decider for every NP language, and their quantum upper bounds do not prove any unrestricted classical lower bound. They are major algorithmic successes whose scope remains distinct from the NP-complete decision target.

For unstructured search over \(M\) candidates with one marked candidate, Grover’s bound is \(O(\sqrt M)\) oracle queries. With \(N\) binary assignment coordinates, the square-root search scale \(\sqrt{2^N}=2^{N/2}\) is still exponential in \(N\); evaluating a candidate also has a cost. This resource comparison does not establish a lower bound for all algorithms on an explicitly supplied formula.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove that relative to a randomly chosen length-preserving oracle, with probability one NP is not contained in bounded-error quantum time \(o(2^{n/2})\). Both the quantum algorithm and the NP verifier receive the oracle. The source expressly warns that its oracle theorem does not rule out unrelativized \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). Black-box evaluations reveal less structure than a full formula description.

Cifuentes’ June 2026 preprint studies whether a circuit-prepared state has a nonidentity Pauli observable with expectation magnitude at least \(\varepsilon\), promised against all such magnitudes being at most \(\varepsilon/2\). Pauli observables are tensor products of the standard one-qubit identity and Pauli matrices. Its reduction shows that an efficient quantum solver for this promise task would imply \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\), even for pure states and thresholds bounded below by a positive constant. The resulting hardness is conditional on this card’s conjecture; it does not prove the conjecture.

Kelly and coauthors’ June 2026 revision discusses efficient SAT solving with an added nonlinear quantum coprocessor. Its first section explicitly distinguishes those dynamics from the usual linear unitary circuit model and notes the exponential space cost of the discussed large-system simulation. Consequently, its proposed computational power is not a BQP algorithm under the gate and qubit bounds specified here.
why: This asks whether efficient classical verification always permits efficient quantum decision. Noncontainment would identify a limit even for ideal scalable quantum computers and would also imply P differs from NP. Containment would place all classically verifiable decision problems within quantum polynomial time.
status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states NP noncontainment in BQP as Conjecture 11.4, and the June 2026 Pauli-coefficient paper uses it as an unproved hardness assumption. The checked oracle lower bounds, formula-oracle synthesis and nonlinear-coprocessor results do not settle the stated total-language comparison in the standard finite-gate model. Bounded current searches located neither a matching unconditional noncontainment proof nor a general BQP SAT algorithm. This review does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all later literature.

working_summary: NP consists of total decision languages with polynomial-length classical certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. The question is whether at least one such language has no uniform bounded-error quantum polynomial-time decider, equivalently whether full 3-SAT is outside BQP. The quantum model has a fixed finite universal gate set, polynomially many zero-initialized auxiliary qubits and a final membership-bit measurement, with no supplied witness or oracle. Structured quantum algorithms and unstructured-search or oracle lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted explicit-input comparison. Recent Pauli-coefficient hardness remains conditional on this noncontainment, while nonlinear quantum computation adds operations outside the model.

title: QMA versus QCMA
importance_reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem that has a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with polynomially many quantum witness qubits also have such a verifier with only polynomially many classical witness bits, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The converse inclusion is available by measuring a purported classical witness in the computational basis, so the requested equality is exactly the inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\).
question_excerpt: Are quantum witnesses more powerful than classical witnesses for an efficient quantum verifier, without oracle access?
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

The class \(\mathrm{QCMA}\), quantum classical Merlin–Arthur, uses the same uniform quantum verifier model, but its witness is a binary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), loaded in the computational-basis state \(|w\rangle\). For every yes-input some such string must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every no-input every such string must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Lengths can be padded to a polynomial bound. Classical witnesses are untrusted and may depend on the individual input. They are not trusted advice shared by all inputs of a given length. A QCMA verifier may perform general quantum computation after receiving the classical witness. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems under these definitions, not equality of the two witness representations for a particular circuit.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation: there exists a disjoint promise pair in QMA for which no uniform polynomial-time QCMA verifier meets both guarantees. The affirmative direction must cover every QMA promise problem, with a possibly different verifier and polynomial witness bound. A negative proof must quantify over all eligible classical-witness verifiers. An oracle separation, a gap between two particular verifiers, or a quantum state's large classical description length does not alone settle the target. The output is a proof of class equality or strict containment, not an approximation to an acceptance probability.
context:
Both sides allow quantum computation. A classical certificate may tell the verifier which quantum experiment to perform; it need not describe a quantum witness state. Consequently, showing that some state needs many classical bits to describe does not establish a separation of the verification classes.

Soundness is essential: a verifier must reject a no-instance for every permitted witness. A proof that works only when the prover follows the intended preparation is not a QMA or QCMA verification guarantee. The mathematical model makes this universal quantifier explicit.

Aaronson–Kuperberg gave a separation after both verifiers are granted access to the same quantum black box. This supplied evidence about black-box methods while leaving the ordinary classes without that extra resource unresolved.

The November 2025 manuscript, published at STOC 2026, strengthens the oracle type to a standard classical function. Classical here describes the function encoded by the oracle, not a requirement to ask only classical queries: the quantum verifiers can query it in superposition. The result remains relative to an oracle.

The 2026 good-code construction gives a simpler classical-oracle separation and extends to quantum versus classical advice. Advice is trusted information that depends only on input length; a witness is untrusted information tailored to the individual input. The advice theorem is therefore recorded as related work, not as a replacement of this card’s witness question.

An ordinary separation would require an explicit promise problem and a lower bound against every uniform classical-witness quantum verifier. The checked oracle theorems do not remove their black box, so they do not justify marking the original class comparison resolved.
why: This asks whether an untrusted quantum state can certify something that no short classical message can certify, even when the recipient already has a quantum computer. It isolates the power of the evidence itself from the power of the verifier and is a basic boundary in quantum complexity.
status_note: Source-open for the ordinary QMA versus QCMA question. On 16 September 2026 the April 2026 ECCC revision’s definitions, original-question discussion and oracle theorem, the 2007 primary abstract, and the 2025/2026 classical-oracle manuscript abstract and metadata were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unrelativized resolution. Oracle type and quantum access are stated explicitly; advice results are kept distinct from witness results. The literature review does not independently verify the cited proofs or supply Lean formalizations.
progress: 2007: Aaronson–Kuperberg separate quantum and classical witnesses relative to a quantum oracle. | 2025-11-12: Bostanci–Haferkamp–Nirkhe–Zhandry post an unconditional separation relative to a standard classical oracle; the revised manuscript is dated 17 January 2026 and appears at STOC 2026. | 2026-02 to 2026-04: Bostanci–Huang–Vaikuntanathan give a simpler classical-oracle proof using good codes; the checked ECCC revision is dated 12 April and also separates quantum from classical advice in that oracle setting.
working_summary: QMA and QCMA use efficient quantum verifiers but allow quantum and classical witnesses respectively. A witness can depend on the entire input and is untrusted, so soundness must hold against every permitted message. The question is equality of the ordinary uniform promise classes without oracle access or shared advice. Quantum-oracle and, more recently, classical-oracle separations give evidence about the role of quantum witnesses without separating the ordinary classes. The revised card fixes the finite-circuit model and requires a complete Lean proof of containment or a universally valid separating problem.

title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
importance_reason: A foundational computability question about regularized information quantities, separating lack of efficient algorithms from the possible absence of any certified approximation algorithm.
formal: Does there exist a single deterministic classical Turing algorithm that, for every valid finite description of a memoryless finite-dimensional quantum channel \(\Phi\) specified below and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), halts and outputs a rational \(r\) satisfying \(|r-Q(\Phi)|\le\varepsilon\)? Here \(Q\) is unassisted, vanishing-error quantum capacity in qubits per channel use. The algorithm must work for all valid descriptions and all positive requested accuracies; there is no time or space bound beyond eventual halting.
question_excerpt: Is the quantum capacity of a finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channel computable?
definitions:
The input consists of positive integers \(d_A,d_B\), a finite program \(P\) for an ordinary deterministic Turing machine, and a positive rational \(\varepsilon\). Integers use binary notation and a rational uses a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. Programs use one fixed effective encoding over a finite alphabet; choosing a different standard encoding only changes effective translations. Write \(A=\mathbb C^{d_A}\), \(B=\mathbb C^{d_B}\). The program \(P\), on every positive integer input \(m\), is promised to halt and output a complex matrix \(J_m\) of order \(d_Ad_B\), with rational real and imaginary entries in this encoding. There is a matrix \(J\) such that, for every entry, both its real and imaginary parts differ from those of \(J_m\) by at most \(2^{-m}\). No additional time bound on \(P\) is promised. The approximating matrices themselves need not be positive or trace preserving.

Index matrix entries by pairs \((i,u)\), with \(1\le i\le d_A\) and \(1\le u\le d_B\). The limiting matrix is promised to be positive semidefinite and to satisfy \[\sum_{u=1}^{d_B}J_{(i,u),(j,u)}=\delta_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d_A),\] where \(\delta_{ij}\) is one if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. These conditions say \(\operatorname{Tr}_B J=I_A\). They make \(J\) the unnormalized Choi matrix of the unique CPTP channel defined on matrix units by \([\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)]_{u,v}=J_{(i,u),(j,v)}\) and extended complex-linearly. Equivalently, \(J=\sum_{i,j}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)\). The guarantee supplies effective approximation of arbitrary computable complex entries; algebraic-entry channels and ordinary finite circuits over computable gates are included. The algorithm receives the program's finite code and may execute it. It receives no oracle deciding equality, positivity or ordering of arbitrary computable real numbers.

All guarantees for the requested capacity algorithm apply only to inputs satisfying these promises. It need not recognize validity and has no prescribed behavior on invalid descriptions. Every valid program describing the same channel must yield an approximation to that channel's same capacity, though the output rational and running time may differ between programs. The description specifies the channel, not a particular encoder or decoder.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of such an algorithm, including its termination and additive error guarantee for every valid description and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such single algorithm exists in the specified input representation. The negative alternative means that every candidate algorithm fails termination or the error guarantee on at least one promised input and requested accuracy. The yes/no assertion quantifies over all requested accuracies; a fixed \(1/100\) error guarantee is not a replacement for it. A regularized formula without a finite stopping guarantee, polynomial-time hardness, or undecidability for an assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity does not answer this question. Nor would undecidability of the exact predicate \(Q(\Phi)=0\) alone rule out additive approximation.
context:
Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

The regularized formula gives approximable finite-dimensional objectives at every fixed block length. This yields lower semicomputability: certified rational lower bounds can approach capacity. Such a sequence alone need not tell an algorithm when its distance from the limit is below a requested tolerance.

Cubitt and coauthors prove that no fixed number of channel uses suffices uniformly over all channels even to detect positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there but whose capacity is positive. The channel can change with the chosen length. This does not rule out an algorithm with stopping time depending on the channel description and requested accuracy.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.
why: Determine whether the fundamental reliable quantum communication rate is algorithmically accessible even without efficiency constraints.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 selected full primary statements on coding, continuity, unbounded block lengths and the 2025 review were checked, together with the corrected March 2026 paper, its current revision metadata and bounded later-work searches. The 2026 paper explicitly leaves general quantum-capacity computability open. Its QMA-hardness is for succinct circuit input; its undecidability result concerns a restricted entanglement-assisted one-shot zero-error classical capacity. Neither resolves the retained uniform approximation question. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2003–2005: Devetak proves a quantum coding theorem yielding the regularized coherent-information expression for unassisted capacity. | 2009: Leung–Smith establish explicit continuity bounds for finite-dimensional unassisted quantum capacity. | 2015-03-31: Cubitt and coauthors prove that arbitrarily many channel uses may be needed before positive coherent information appears. | 2025: Undecidability in Physics reviews the open computability issue and distinguishes memoryful channels and zero-error capacities. | 2026-03-30: Bhattacharyya–Mehta–Zhao’s corrected v3 proves circuit-input QMA-hardness for quantum capacity and undecidability for a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity; ordinary quantum-capacity computability remains open.
working_summary: Quantum channel capacity describes the best asymptotic rate for transmitting quantum information through a noisy channel. This problem asks whether that number can always be approximated by an algorithm from an effective finite description of the channel. The algorithm may be slow, but it must halt and meet any requested rational accuracy. Optimizations involving arbitrarily many channel uses make the asymptotic definition harder to turn into a guaranteed finite computation. Establishing computability or an obstruction would separate the existence of an operational communication rate from our ability to calculate it even in principle.

title: Quantum query-to-communication lifting
importance_reason: A general quantum lifting theorem would transfer the full strength of quantum query lower bounds to two-party communication, including arbitrary promise problems. The gap persists despite powerful classical lifting theorems and partial quantum analogues, making it a central structural question about quantum information complexity.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), there is a total nonconstant Boolean communication gadget \(g_n:\{0,1\}^{a_n}\times\{0,1\}^{b_n}\to\{0,1\}\), with finite positive integers \(a_n,b_n\), for which every partial Boolean function \(f:D\to\{0,1\}\), \(D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), satisfies \[\frac{Q_{1/3}(f)}{C(\log_2n)^k}\ \le\ Q^*_{1/3}(f\circ g_n^n)\ \le\ C(\log_2n)^k Q_{1/3}(f)?\] Here \(Q_{1/3}\) is quantum query complexity and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is two-party quantum communication complexity with unrestricted prior entanglement. Both have worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The gadget depends on \(n\), but not on \(D\) or \(f\), and the constants are common to the entire family.
definitions: For \(z\in D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a query applies \(O_z:|i,b,w\rangle\mapsto|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}z_i,w\rangle\), where \(i\in[n]\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(w\) denotes an arbitrary finite workspace. A quantum query algorithm starts in an input-independent state, uses arbitrary input-independent local quantum operations and measurements between queries, and produces \(f(z)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised \(z\). \(Q_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum worst-case number of calls to \(O_z\), counting all branches. Computation between queries is free; there is no uniformity or finite-gate-set restriction. A function constant on its promise, including an empty promise, has query complexity zero. For the composed communication problem Alice receives \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}^{a_n}\), Bob receives \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}^{b_n}\), and the promise is that \(z=(g_n(x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\) belongs to \(D\). Bob must output \(f(z)\). A protocol has arbitrary finite-dimensional local registers and any finite-dimensional shared initial state independent of the inputs, with no bound on its entanglement. It may exchange messages in both directions, perform arbitrary local quantum operations and measurements depending on its own input and local history, and use shared or private randomness. All communicated qubits in both directions count; a classical bit sent as a message costs one qubit. Local computation, local memory, and the shared initial state are free. \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is the minimum worst-case total communication over protocols whose error probability is at most \(1/3\) for every promised input pair. The number of rounds is unrestricted, subject to finite protocol length; communication cost includes every branch. Query algorithms and protocols may depend on the particular finite function and promise and need not be uniformly constructible. The gadget family is existential: no efficient method to print its truth table, input-length bound on \(a_n,b_n\), or fixed gadget independent of \(n\) is required. Its communication cost is nevertheless constrained by the universal two-sided inequality, which includes coordinate functions \(f(z)=z_i\). All logarithms in the inequality are base two.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of this gadget family and common constants with both inequalities for all \(n,D,f\), or a complete Lean proof that no such family and constants exist. A theorem for a restricted class of outer functions, a fixed round bound, approximate polynomial degree instead of quantum query complexity, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not meet the stated affirmative target. The target is bounded-error lifting; a separate zero-error theorem is not also required.
context:
The source asks about both bounded-error and zero-error quantum lifting. This card selects its bounded-error branch, retaining partial outer functions and polylogarithmic losses. The source’s reductions between lifting statements are conditional implications, not a proof of the missing lifting theorem.

Ben-David’s lecture notes state a gadget-family conjecture in which the gadget may depend on the outer input length and has only polylogarithmic communication cost. This card does not add a constant-size, logarithmic-input-length or efficient-construction requirement.

The communication convention is made explicit as the entanglement-assisted model used in the later quantum lifting literature. This is a documented choice within the original general question, whose short extraction did not specify the shared-state convention. The quantification over partial functions follows the original paper’s Section 7.

The CCC 2021 work proves an unconditional bounded-round lifting result for a classical adversary measure and a conditional result for a simplified positive-weight quantum adversary bound. Neither is a general, unconditional lifting theorem for full quantum query complexity with unrestricted rounds.

The ICALP 2026 hybrid theorem lifts approximate degree within a model that begins with classical communication and then uses quantum messages. Its Introduction explicitly retains general quantum query-to-communication lifting as a major open problem. Approximate degree and full quantum query complexity are distinct targets.
why: Quantum query complexity captures information obtainable from an oracle, while communication complexity measures information exchanged between separated parties. A universal lifting theorem would tightly connect these two models across all Boolean promise problems. The demand for only polylogarithmic loss is substantially stronger than transferring a weaker lower-bound measure or obtaining an arbitrary polynomial relation.
status_note: The original question remains explicitly open in the checked ICALP 2026 primary discussion. The CCC 2021 and ICALP 2026 positive results have weaker lower-bound measures, additional hypotheses or model restrictions. Bounded checks through 2026-09-16 did not verify a full resolution; this is not an exhaustive survey of all subsequent work.
progress: 2019: Ben-David and Kothari state the missing bounded-error and zero-error lifting questions in Section 7.1; Theorem 18 gives an implication from a hypothetical zero-error lifting theorem to bounded-error lifting. | 2020: Ben-David’s CS 860 notes state Conjecture 8.6 with an input-length-dependent gadget of polylogarithmic communication cost. | 2021: Anshu, Ben-David and Kundu give bounded-round and conditional adversary lifting results, retaining the distinction from full quantum lifting. | 2026: Wu, Yang and Yao establish a hybrid classical-quantum lifting theorem at ICALP 2026 and still identify unrestricted quantum query-to-communication lifting as open.
working_summary: A lifting theorem would turn the quantum query complexity of a Boolean promise problem into the communication complexity of a composed two-party problem. The question asks for one gadget per input length that works for every partial outer function. Both complexity measures should agree up to common polylogarithmic factors. The communication model allows arbitrary prior entanglement and an unrestricted number of rounds. Known bounded-round, adversary and hybrid lifting results leave this general bounded-error transfer open in the checked 2026 source.

title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}_1\) over Clifford+T
importance_reason: A longstanding central question about one-sided quantum proof verification, exact gates and the boundary between satisfiability and approximate quantum verification.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) for the exact gate set \(\mathcal G=\{H,\mathrm{CNOT},T\}\) defined below? Both classes concern promise problems on finite binary strings and use polynomial-size, uniformly generated verification circuits with polynomially many witness qubits. In \(\mathrm{QMA}\), every yes-instance has a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\), it has a witness accepted with probability exactly \(1\). In both classes, every witness for a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The one-sided class in this question is explicitly the Clifford+T version.
question_excerpt: Can bounded-error QMA verification be made perfectly complete?
definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). The input length is \(n=|x|\). No acceptance condition is imposed on strings outside the promise. For a fixed problem, a deterministic classical algorithm, on input \(x\), produces a quantum verification circuit \(V_x\) in time polynomial in \(n\). Its witness register \(W\) has \(m(n)\) qubits and its private ancillary register \(A\) has \(a(n)\ge1\) qubits, where \(m,a\) are polynomially bounded integer functions. Circuit size is also polynomially bounded. All bounds and the generating algorithm are fixed for the problem, independently of the particular input.

A qubit is \(\mathbb C^2\) with basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\). A witness is any density matrix \(\rho\) on \(W=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m(n)}\): it is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and has trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\). Its entries may be arbitrary complex numbers; no efficient preparation or finite classical description of the witness is required. All private ancillas start in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a(n)}\), uncorrelated with the witness. There is one witness message and no interaction, oracle, preshared resource or nonuniform advice.

The allowed unitary gates, applied to specified wires, are \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,c\oplus b\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). These exact matrices define the finite gate set; arbitrary real rotations are not allowed as single gates. A circuit is a finite product of these gates, tensored with identity on all other wires. One designated output qubit is measured in the displayed basis, with outcome one meaning accept. Equivalently, with \(\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}\) the orthogonal projector onto output value one, its acceptance probability is \[p_x(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle\langle0^{a(n)}|\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right].\]

The verifier is a QMA verifier if \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\ \exists\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\ge2/3\) and \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\ \forall\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\le1/3\). Using this fixed universal gate set gives the usual bounded-error class QMA. The class \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) changes only the first acceptance requirement to \(p_x(\rho)=1\), retaining all other resources and the same exact gate set. The accepting witness can depend on the yes-input. It need not be accepted by the original QMA verifier with probability one; equality of classes permits a different verifier and polynomial witness length. All registers remain finite and polynomial in input length. Acceptance approaching one through a sequence of circuits is not perfect completeness unless one admissible circuit family attains one exactly.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that every QMA promise problem has a verifier in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) under these exact conventions, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem has no such verifier. The reverse inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\) is immediate from the acceptance bounds, so the issue is the stated containment or its failure. A negative proof must rule out every eligible one-sided verifier for the separating promise problem, not only one attempted amplification procedure. Exponentially or doubly exponentially small completeness error still differs from zero. Perfect completeness using an infinite register, extra interaction, a different exact gate set without a suitable equivalence proof, or an added oracle does not establish the target. Numerical approximation to the acceptance probability cannot replace this exact yes/no assertion.
context:
Editorial gate-set choice: the source treats a family of exact-gate versions of QMA with perfect completeness. This card now fixes Hadamard, CNOT and T, as explicitly selected on 16 September 2026. It does not assert that every other exact-gate version defines the same one-sided class.

A quantum witness can make a yes-instance convincing without being efficiently preparable. Perfect completeness asks whether at least one witness can be accepted with certainty, while keeping every no-instance resistant to all witnesses. The question is about the power of proof systems, not reliability of an experimental device.

Approximate gate synthesis preserves a bounded acceptance gap after allowing sufficiently small error. It does not automatically preserve an acceptance probability equal to one. This is why the source attaches an explicit exact gate set to the one-sided class.

The source proves containment and completeness results for finite gate sets with entries in specified cyclotomic fields, which are fields generated by selected roots of unity. These results clarify exact-gate conventions and quantum satisfiability, but explicitly leave equality with bounded-error QMA open in that earlier source; the September preprints make matching new claims.

Aaronson constructs a quantum oracle relative to which QMA and its perfectly complete version differ. An oracle supplies an additional unitary operation; that theorem does not separate the ordinary classes with only the gates in this card.

Jeffery and Witteveen obtain perfect completeness when the witness system includes an infinite counter register with shift access. Their finite-dimensional truncation instead yields exceptionally small positive completeness error. Neither conclusion gives exact acceptance one with polynomially many ordinary qubits in the selected model.

The source also recalls perfect-completeness results for classical-witness quantum verification and for interactive quantum proofs. A restriction to classical witnesses or the addition of verifier-prover messages changes the model, so those equalities do not settle this single-message quantum-witness question.

Grewal and Rudolph's preprint of 11 September 2026 claims \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G_2}\) for \(\mathcal G_2=\{X,\mathrm{CNOT},\mathrm{Toffoli},H\otimes H\}\). Corollary 1.2 transfers the claimed equality to any gate set implementing these gates exactly with clean ancillas, and the text explicitly includes Clifford+T. Thus this is a matching claim for the exact gate set in the card, not only an equality using arbitrary rotations or an infinite counter. The proof is not independently certified in this review.

Liu and Vidick's preprint of 14 September 2026 separately claims perfect completeness for QMA over \(\{H,X,\mathrm{Toffoli},S\}\), where \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\), in Theorem 1.3. The model uses finite polynomial resources. Its gates have exact Clifford+T implementations, preserving acceptance probability one; the claimed constant soundness gap permits the usual exact Boolean error reduction. The same paper treats two-message proof systems in separate theorems. Those stronger interaction claims should not be confused with, or substituted for, its one-message QMA theorem.
why: This determines whether certainty on yes-instances changes the power of efficient quantum proof verification. It separates arbitrarily reliable verification from exact acceptance and affects the relation between quantum satisfiability and general quantum witness problems.
status_note: Matching fresh solution claims found on 16 September 2026. Grewal–Rudolph arXiv:2609.13032v1, submitted 11 September, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 explicitly claim QMA with perfect completeness over a fixed finite gate set and its exact implementation in Clifford+T. Liu–Vidick arXiv:2609.15926v1, submitted 14 September, gives a second claimed construction over {H,X,Toffoli,S}; its stated fixed gates admit exact Clifford+T implementations. These are ordinary finite-register, single-witness claims, so the selected gate set does not protect this target from the new results. The full PDFs and theorem/model scope were inspected, but the complete proofs were not independently certified or checked in Lean. Status is uncertain pending verification, superseding the earlier source-open assessment.
progress: 2008: A quantum-oracle separation is established, giving a barrier to some proof methods without separating ordinary QMA from its one-sided version. | 2026-05-06: Perfect completeness is obtained with an infinite counter; finite truncation retains nonzero completeness error. | 2026: The MFCS source develops exact universal gate-set results within specified fields and explicitly retains the QMA-versus-QMA1 question. | 2026-09-11: Grewal and Rudolph post a claimed QMA perfect-completeness theorem, with an explicit exact-gate corollary covering Clifford+T. Full proof correctness is not independently certified here. | 2026-09-14: Liu and Vidick post a second claimed one-message perfect-completeness construction, alongside separate results for two-message quantum proof systems. The claimed one-message gate set is exactly implementable in Clifford+T.
working_summary: A perfectly complete quantum proof system accepts some valid witness with probability exactly one. This question asks whether every QMA proof system can achieve that guarantee without sacrificing efficient verification or soundness. Approximate gate synthesis creates a special difficulty because a tiny implementation error can destroy exact acceptance. Two September 2026 preprints now claim finite-register perfect completeness with fixed gates that cover this card’s exact Clifford+T model. Their stated results match the target, whose status is uncertain pending independent proof verification.

title: Quantum–classical communication gaps for total functions
importance_reason: A central communication-complexity separation target isolating totality from promises and information cost from local computation; current matching preprint claims require an explicit status qualification.
formal:
Do there exist real constants \(a\ge1\), \(\delta>0\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and an infinite set \(\mathcal N\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}\) such that, for every \(n\in\mathcal N\), some total Boolean function
\[f_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\]
has bounded-error communication complexities satisfying
\[Q^*_{1/3}(f_n)\le a(\log_2 n)^b,
\qquad R_{1/3}(f_n)\ge a^{-1}n^\delta?\]
Here \(R_{1/3}\) permits classical public randomness and unrestricted interaction, and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) permits quantum communication and arbitrary finite prior entanglement. Only communication is charged. The constants are fixed independently of the input length and the function chosen at that length.
question_excerpt: The imported passage is the background question on ITCS 2021 page 54:2 asking for exponential quantum advantage on total functions. This card makes its quantitative scale explicit as polylogarithmic quantum versus polynomial classical communication on an infinite family, matching the scale used in that source and in the new preprints. The source paper’s own main theorem additionally concerns efficient local players and partial functions; those extra restrictions are not part of the imported total-function question. Prior entanglement is permitted on the quantum side, and all classical interaction is allowed.
definitions:
For a fixed function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), Alice receives \(x\) and Bob receives \(y\). A protocol is fixed for the entire function before these inputs are chosen. Bob must output the bit \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every pair \((x,y)\). Total means all \(2^{2n}\) pairs are included; no joint promise or relation with several acceptable outputs is allowed.

In a classical protocol the parties exchange bits and may use a shared random seed and private random bits, independent of the inputs. They have no shared entanglement. Each message and the final output depend only on the sender's own input, random information and received history. In a quantum protocol the parties exchange finite-dimensional registers consisting of qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may initially share any finite-dimensional entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). Local operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Measurements may have classical outcomes stored locally. Transmitting a classical bit within a quantum protocol costs one qubit; communication is not hidden in a message's timing or length. Shared randomness and entanglement are not supplied as input-dependent advice, and postselection is not available.

Local computation, memory and preparation of input-independent shared resources are free. There is no bound on their complexity or on the finite dimension of prior entanglement. A protocol may depend nonuniformly on the full function \(f\). It uses a finite predetermined alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused messages if needed, so a choice of schedule cannot convey information for free. Arbitrarily many rounds are permitted, subject to finite termination. The cost is the maximum total number of transmitted bits or qubits, over all input pairs and all random or measurement branches. \(R_{1/3}(f)\) and \(Q^*_{1/3}(f)\) are the least costs of protocols with the stated per-input error bound. These costs are finite because transmitting an entire input gives a finite deterministic protocol.

The family need exist only for infinitely many, hence arbitrarily large, input lengths. The constants \(a,b,\delta\) are common to all of them; the functions and their protocols may vary with \(n\). The display defines the precise polylogarithmic-versus-polynomial meaning of the exponential-advantage question used here. It does not require efficient local players, a uniform generator for the functions, one-way communication or a fixed number of messages. A stronger construction with any of these properties is allowed but not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed family-existence proposition, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify admissible constants and an unambiguous infinite family, establish the quantum upper guarantee and prove the classical lower bound against every public-coin protocol in the stated model. A negative answer must establish that for every choice of the constants, only finitely many lengths admit a function satisfying both bounds. A separation only on promised input pairs, for relations, or against restricted-round classical protocols does not meet this target. A preprint theorem statement alone is not a checked proof.
context:
Communication complexity studies two parties who can process their own inputs without charge but must pay for information exchanged. Thus an advantage measures transmitted information, not execution time. Total Boolean functions require one specified answer for every input pair; partial functions can exclude some pairs, and relations can permit several valid outputs. These distinctions are essential to interpreting a separation.

Girish, Raz and Tal’s ITCS 2021 work supplies a partial-function separation with efficient quantum players given oracle access to their inputs. Its introduction separately states that exponential advantage for total functions is open. The paper’s efficient-player theorem is a different statement from this card: importing its title as an extra runtime requirement would change the background question.

The chosen scale requires a classical cost growing as a positive power of \(n\), while quantum cost grows as a fixed power of \(\log n\). A fixed polynomial relation between the two communication costs is incompatible with such a family. The converse implication is not automatic: disproving every universal polynomial relation need not, by itself, yield this particular input-length scale.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint states an explicit total family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the per-party input length. These stated bounds fit the displayed scale after absorbing logarithmic factors into a fixed power and a slightly smaller positive exponent. The claimed quantum protocol has two messages and needs no prior entanglement; its classical lower bound permits unrestricted rounds.

Le Gall's September 2026 preprint claims a larger two-message separation, with \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum cost and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized classical cost. It further states a classical lower bound \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\), with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Its definitions explicitly allow public classical randomness and require worst-case communication and error at most \(1/3\) on each input.

A protocol without prior entanglement is admissible in the entanglement-assisted model, so that stronger resource restriction does not obstruct the claimed upper bound here. If the protocol outputs at Alice, sending the final answer bit to Bob adds only one unit of communication. These convention checks establish that the fresh claims match the target; they do not independently validate the new lower-bound proofs.

The matching claims are recorded with uncertain status. The original source, new full PDFs, theorem statements and relevant model conventions were inspected, but no complete independent proof certification or Lean verification was performed. The question has not been replaced by a stronger optimal exponent or an efficient-player variant merely because the new papers claim to answer it.
why: This asks whether the large quantum savings known for promise problems can persist for a Boolean function defined on every input pair. A positive family would refute any universal polynomial simulation of quantum communication by randomized classical communication, even when local computation is unrestricted.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Gavinsky arXiv:2608.18784v1 and Le Gall arXiv:2609.16726v1 claim total Boolean families with the displayed polylogarithmic quantum and polynomial randomized-classical costs. Their stated protocols/lower bounds match the free-entanglement, unrestricted-classical-interaction, per-input-error and worst-case-cost conventions here, allowing a final answer bit to Bob. The full PDFs and relevant scope were inspected, but the complete proofs have not been independently certified or Lean-checked. Status remains uncertain pending verification; the 2021 source-open statement is historical.
