These statements match the retained quantitative target, pending independent proof verification.
working_summary: Alice and Bob must compute a Boolean function defined on every pair of their binary inputs. The target is an infinite family requiring polynomial randomized classical communication but only polylogarithmic quantum communication in the input length. Local computation is free, classical public randomness and arbitrary interaction are allowed, and the quantum side may share input-independent entanglement. The 2021 source’s separate efficient-player result concerns partial functions and does not impose an additional runtime condition here. August and September 2026 preprints make matching total-function separation claims whose complete proofs remain unverified in this review.

title: Entanglement without distillable secret key
importance_reason: A central unresolved boundary between entanglement and private communication, directly controlling assumptions in the resource theory of quantum secret key.
formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge2\) and an entangled density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) with zero distillable secret-key rate, \(K_D(\rho)=0\), under arbitrary local quantum operations and two-way public classical communication? The rate is the standard asymptotic, vanishing-error rate defined below. There is no restriction to one-way communication, perfect finite-block output, a chosen measurement, or efficient protocols.
question_excerpt: So far, it is known that separable, i.e., disentangled states, are useless [43], while it remains open if entangled but key-undistillable states exist.
definitions:
A state on a finite-dimensional complex vector space is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(X=X^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The state \(\rho\) is separable if \(\rho=\sum_jp_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) for some finite list of local states \(\sigma_j,\tau_j\) and real weights \(p_j\ge0\), \(\sum_jp_j=1\). It is entangled if no such decomposition exists. All matrix entries may be arbitrary complex numbers.

A local quantum instrument has finitely many outcomes \(t\). Outcome \(t\) sends a local matrix \(X\) to \(\mathcal E_t(X)=\sum_jA_{t,j}XA_{t,j}^\dagger\), where the rectangular matrices \(A_{t,j}\) obey \(\sum_{t,j}A_{t,j}^\dagger A_{t,j}=I\). On a normalized input, \(\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal E_t(X)\) is the outcome probability and division by this probability gives the conditional state. An LOCC protocol is a finite adaptive sequence of these instruments performed alternately in the two laboratories. An outcome may be sent as a classical message to the other party; later instruments may depend on the messages and local outcomes already available. Classical communication is public and can proceed in both directions. Local ancillary states, local randomness, public shared randomness and discarding local systems are allowed. No extra shared entangled state, preshared secret key or quantum communication is supplied. The resulting map \(\Lambda\), including all outcomes rather than conditioning for free on a success branch, is trace preserving. Each protocol may have arbitrarily many finite rounds and finite-dimensional ancillary systems; their sizes may grow with the number of input copies. There is no bound on local computation, no finite gate-set restriction and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of protocols. Finite-round approximations suffice for the vanishing-error rate, so allowing limits of LOCC maps on fixed finite systems does not change the target.

For an integer \(M\ge1\), a private state with key dimension \(M\) has the form \[\gamma=\frac1M\sum_{i,j=0}^{M-1}|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_A}\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_B}\otimes U_i\sigma U_j^\dagger.\] Here \(K_A,K_B\cong\mathbb C^M\) are the local key registers, \(\sigma\) is an arbitrary state on finite local shield systems \(S_A\otimes S_B\), and each \(U_i\) is a unitary matrix on the joint shield space. This is a mathematical description of the target state; applying these joint unitaries is not a free operation available to the two parties. The physical output partition is \((K_AS_A):(K_BS_B)\). Measuring both key registers in the displayed basis gives the same uniform symbol, independent of any purifying external system, hence \(\log_2M\) bits of secret key. The shields remain local output systems. For matrices on the same space, trace distance is \(D(X,Y)=\tfrac12\|X-Y\|_1\), where \(\|Z\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{Z^\dagger Z}\).

A real rate \(R\ge0\) is achievable from \(\rho\) if there are, for every integer \(n\ge1\), a protocol \(\Lambda_n\) acting on \(n\) independent copies \(\rho^{\otimes n}\), an integer \(M_n\ge1\), and a private state \(\gamma_n\) of key dimension \(M_n\) on the protocol's output systems, such that \[D\bigl(\Lambda_n(\rho^{\otimes n}),\gamma_n\bigr)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2M_n}{n}\ge R.\] The private states, shields and protocols can depend on \(n\) and \(\rho\). Define \(K_D(\rho)\) as the supremum of achievable rates. The zero rate is always available. Thus zero distillable key means no strictly positive rate with error tending to zero, not merely inability to produce one exact secret bit at a particular block size. The private-state formulation is equivalent to local quantum operations and public communication that produce classical keys secure against an eavesdropper holding a purification of the input state.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that some finite-dimensional entangled state has \(K_D=0\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that every such entangled state has \(K_D>0\). The same chosen state must defeat every allowed protocol sequence in an affirmative existence proof. Refuting existence may use a state-dependent strictly positive rate, with no rate uniform over all entangled states. Failure of one-way protocols, an exact-output no-go theorem, or zero key after one chosen local measurement is insufficient. Conversely, proving arbitrarily small positive rates for a sequence of different states does not exhibit a state of zero rate. The target is an exact yes/no assertion about positivity; an additive estimate of the rate cannot replace it.
context:
Secret-key distillation asks two parties to turn a noisy shared quantum resource into matching random data unavailable to an eavesdropper. Entanglement is necessary, but the open issue is whether it is always sufficient for some positive asymptotic rate.

The source develops a theory of the cost of creating quantum secret key under the explicit assumption that entangled states with zero distillable key do not exist. Its conditional theorems therefore do not answer this existence question.

Bound entanglement obstructs producing maximally entangled pairs. Horodecki and coauthors nevertheless show that certain bound-entangled states yield secret key, so zero distillable entanglement cannot be substituted for zero distillable key.

The March 2026 no-go theorem concerns heralded exact key and one-way classical communication. It explicitly exhibits a gap from approximate key distillation. The present target permits vanishing error and two-way messages, so that no-go theorem is not a counterexample here.

The July 2026 classical bound-information preprint concerns three classical random variables supplied to the parties and an eavesdropper. The abstract also distinguishes particular measurements of quantum states from the original states. Such a fixed classical distribution does not rule out all collective local quantum operations on an entangled input state.
why: This question determines whether every entangled bipartite state has some usable private correlation when arbitrary collective quantum processing is allowed. An entangled zero-key state would establish an additional form of irreversibility beyond ordinary bound entanglement; a universal positivity theorem would identify entanglement itself as the exact boundary for asymptotic key usefulness.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the full official May 2026 source and March one-way no-go paper, primary historical key abstract, July classical bound-information abstract and bounded later-work searches were checked. The source explicitly assumes the negative answer rather than proving it. One-way exact key obstructions and classical bound information do not establish an entangled zero-key state under the retained two-way vanishing-error model. No verified resolution was found; cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2005: Private-state methods demonstrate secret key from some states with no distillable entanglement. | 2026-03-10: A no-go theorem for heralded exact one-way key is published; its restrictions differ from the asymptotic two-way target. | 2026-05-06: The source explicitly retains the existence of entangled key-undistillable states as an open question and builds its cost theory under their nonexistence assumption. | 2026-07-28: A classical bound-information construction is posted; its classical source model does not settle unrestricted quantum key distillation.
working_summary: Shared quantum states can sometimes be converted into secret classical keys by local operations and public communication. This project asks whether there are entangled states from which no secret key can be distilled. Separable states provide a known class of useless resources, but entanglement alone does not immediately determine the distillable-key rate. The question is also different from asking whether an entangled state can produce maximally entangled pairs. Identifying an entangled key-undistillable state, or proving that none exists, would settle a basic boundary in the resource theory of private communication.

title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
importance_reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.
formal: Does there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), every integer \(\ell\ge1\), every subgroup \(H\le D_N\), and every function \(f:D_N\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) hiding \(H\) as defined below, the algorithm outputs a finite list generating exactly \(H\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+\ell+2)^c\) total operations? The only external quantum oracle is the reversible evaluation of \(f\). The bound is uniform over subgroup and hiding-function choices and includes both oracle calls and all other computation.
question_excerpt: Can the dihedral hidden subgroup problem be solved with polynomial total quantum and classical work in the logarithmic group size and oracle-label width?
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\) with addition modulo \(N\). The dihedral group \(D_N=\mathbb Z_N\times\{0,1\}\) has multiplication \[(x,b)(y,d)=\bigl((x+(-1)^by)\bmod N,\ (b+d)\bmod2\bigr).\] Its identity is \((0,0)\). A subgroup is a subset containing the identity and closed under products and inverses. For \(g\in D_N\), the left coset \(gH\) is \(\{gh:h\in H\}\). The hiding promise is \[f(g)=f(g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gH=g'H.\] Thus each coset has one label and distinct cosets have different labels; no structure in the label bits is promised. The classical input is \(N\) in binary and the register width \(\ell\) in unary, fixing input size at the parameter scale \(\log N+\ell\) used in the inherited bound. With \(m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\), an element is encoded by \(m\) bits for \(x\), followed by one bit for \(b\). Bit strings with \(x\ge N\) are invalid element encodings. The oracle acts on a group register and an \(\ell\)-bit register by \[U_f|g,z\rangle=|g,z\mathbin\oplus f(g)\rangle\] for valid \(g\), extended linearly to superpositions, and acts as identity on invalid group encodings. Here the XOR acts coordinatewise. Each invocation costs one operation; it is self-inverse. The algorithm has no classical truth table of \(f\), subgroup description, coset-state preparation oracle, subset-sum oracle or uncharged random-access-memory service. It may implement additional operations using the allowed gates and controller, with their full cost charged. Output is a classical finite list of valid encoded elements; success means that the smallest subgroup containing all listed elements is \(H\). The empty list generates the identity subgroup. Writing the list is charged, so its length is automatically bounded by the running time. The algorithm may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), but its running-time guarantee holds on every execution. Probability is over its measurements and internal randomness for each fixed legal \(N,\ell,H,f\). When \(\ell\) is polynomial in \(\log N\), as in the usual succinct oracle setting, the requested time is polynomial in \(\log N\).

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with all stated guarantees, or of the logical negation ruling out every eligible uniform algorithm and polynomial total-work bound. An affirmative proof must establish exact subgroup-generation correctness with the specified probability for every legal hiding function. A negative proof must apply to the full model, not merely a particular sieve, measurement family or recently proposed procedure. Polynomial query complexity with superpolynomial postprocessing, a method requiring an additional oracle, or uncounted parallel work is insufficient. The target is a yes/no algorithm-existence statement; subgroup generators on each input must be exact, and numerical approximation of a group element is not an alternative answer.
context:
Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

In the reflection case, a coset sample is a state \((|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle)/\sqrt2\) with an unknown random \(x\). Its Fourier representation includes a known random label \(k\) and a qubit with relative phase \(e^{2\pi i ks/N}\), for a chosen Fourier-sign convention. This phase encodes information about \(s\); it is not a classical register containing \(ks\). The sample interface and the hiding-function oracle interface are distinct.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).

Regev’s separate polynomial-space algorithm uses time \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}))\). Improving quantum memory alone and obtaining polynomial total running time are different achievements.

Kuperberg’s later collimation algorithm attains \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N}))\) time with logarithmic quantum space and subexponential classical storage. The paper explicitly separates quantum-addressable classical memory from ordinary memory: Proposition 4.2 analyzes the former, while Corollary 4.3 gives an implementation without quantum memory access, with its additional work counted. No free memory-access primitive is included in this card’s target.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.
why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.
status_note: Uncertain pending a verified resolution of the polynomial-time target. On 16 September 2026 the source model, Kuperberg’s full resource analysis, cached survey and restricted-group manuscript, and the current primary pages for Simon’s claim, Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry’s refutation and Guo–Yang’s lemma analysis were checked. The claim page still lists 17 August as its latest revision and the refutation page 1 September. The restricted no-go theorem is not a lower bound against all dihedral algorithms. No verified general polynomial-time solution was identified in the bounded search; cited proofs and the supplied Lean repository were not independently verified or rerun.

working_summary: The dihedral hidden subgroup problem presents a function that is constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup of a dihedral group. The task is to recover generators for that subgroup using quantum access to the function. The target is a uniform algorithm whose total running time is polynomial in the length of the group description and oracle values. Counting only a small number of oracle queries is insufficient if processing the resulting quantum information is expensive. An efficient solution would extend the reach of hidden-subgroup methods beyond the abelian setting and illuminate connections with lattice-related algorithmic problems.

title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
importance_reason: A central quantum-algorithm target linking graph algorithms, permutation groups and the computational use of entangled states.
formal: Does the ordinary graph-isomorphism decision problem belong to \(\mathrm{BQP}\), bounded-error quantum polynomial time? That is, do there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple graphs given by their complete binary adjacency matrices, the algorithm decides whether a vertex bijection preserves adjacency, with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(C(n+2)^c\) total elementary operations, where \(n\) is the larger vertex count? No distributional or structural promise is imposed on the graphs.
question_excerpt: Is ordinary graph isomorphism decidable by a uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm in polynomial total time?
definitions:
For an integer \(r\ge0\), write \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite simple graph on \([r]\) is an undirected graph with no loops or parallel edges. Its adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{r\times r}\) is symmetric with zero diagonal. Each input graph is encoded by its binary order with a self-delimiting length prefix, followed by all adjacency entries in row-major order; the two graph encodings are concatenated. A prefix can be encoded as \(1^t0\) followed by a \(t\)-bit binary order, using \(t\ge1\) and the usual minimal binary representation. Invalid encodings are rejected. Graphs of different orders are not isomorphic. If both have order \(r\), an isomorphism is a bijection \(\pi:[r]\to[r]\) such that \[A_{uv}=B_{\pi(u),\pi(v)}\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in[r].\] The two order-zero graphs are isomorphic. A yes-instance has at least one such bijection; a no-instance has none. The algorithm must accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(2/3\) and every no-instance with probability at most \(1/3\). Its probability is over its quantum measurement outcomes and any internal random bits, separately for each fixed input. It receives only the explicit classical input, with no witness, nonuniform advice, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle, promised rigidity, degree bound or typical-input assumption. Here GI denotes this ordinary permutation-based relation, not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory. The running time is polynomial in the graph order and hence in the explicit input length; malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their actual length.

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language lies in BQP, including uniformity, bounded error on every input and polynomial total work, or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not lie in BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm is a valid affirmative solution because it can be implemented within the quantum model with polynomial overhead. A negative proof must exclude all uniform bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms, rather than only coset-state, Fourier-sampling or photonic-sampling methods. A necessary invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic graphs, an efficient fixed relaxation, or uncharged preparation of a helpful state does not establish membership. The output is a proof of the yes/no complexity statement, not an approximate isomorphism score.
context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

A classical adjacency matrix is the entire input resource. Preparing a special quantum representation of its relabelings is additional computation and must be charged. Distinguishability of hypothetical states therefore cannot substitute for a complete uniform algorithm that prepares and processes its data within the required running time.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

The 2026 paper by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman concerns the different relation called quantum graph isomorphism. It gives randomized polynomial-time algorithms for exact feasibility at each fixed level of a hierarchy of noncommutative semidefinite relaxations. Neither the relation nor a fixed relaxation is the ordinary vertex-bijection decision problem posed here.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.
why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

working_summary: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge. This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs. The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle. Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm. title: Classical hardness of approximate Boson Sampling
importance_reason: A central quantum sampling-advantage question connecting linear optics, permanents and classical counting complexity. The explicit approximation model addresses the robustness gap separating exact probability calculations from distributional simulation.
formal: Is the following classical sampling impossibility statement true? There is no single probabilistic classical Turing machine \(M\) and polynomial \(p\) such that, for every valid ideal Boson Sampling input \(B\) defined below and every integer \(k\ge2\), the machine \(M(B,1^k)\) outputs an occupation vector with law \(Q_{B,k}\), always halts in at most \(p(|B|+k)\) steps, and satisfies \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q_{B,k},D_B)=\frac12\sum_{s\in\Omega_{m,n}}|Q_{B,k}(s)-D_B(s)|\le\frac1k?\] The target distribution is \[D_B(s)=\frac{|\operatorname{Per}(A_s)|^2}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_j!},\qquad A=\operatorname{GS}(B),\qquad \Omega_{m,n}=\{s\in\mathbb N_0^m:\sum_js_j=n\}.\] Thus the approximation must meet every requested error tolerance, in time polynomial in the explicit network description and the inverse tolerance. The claim is unconditional and concerns all valid inputs, rather than only typical random optical networks.
question_excerpt: Classical computers cannot efficiently sample the output of ideal Boson Sampling.
definitions:
There are \(n\ge1\) indistinguishable photons and \(m\ge n\) modes. A mode is one orthogonal single-particle state. Initially each of the first \(n\) modes contains one photon and every other mode is empty. The network is ideal passive linear optics: it preserves photon number and acts on the single-particle mode space by an \(m\times m\) unitary matrix \(U\). It has no loss, noise, distinguishability of photons, intermediate measurements, adaptive feed-forward or postselection. The output records the photon count in every mode. Collisions, meaning two or more photons in a mode, are included.

Only the first \(n\) columns of \(U\) matter for this input. Write these columns as \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\), so \(A^\dagger A=I_n\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. Any such column isometry can be completed to a unitary, and the distribution below is independent of that completion. The input therefore specifies this part of the optical network rather than an exponentially large many-photon transition matrix.

Here is an explicit finite encoding of the matrix convention in the source's footnote19. The input \(B\) contains \(m,n\) and every entry of an \(m\times n\) complex matrix. Real and imaginary parts are signed dyadic rationals, each stored as an integer numerator and a nonnegative denominator exponent in unary: \(a/2^b\). All numerator bits, signs, exponents and matrix entries count toward \(|B|\). Dimensions and lists are explicitly delimited. A valid input satisfies \[\|B^\dagger B-I_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac12,\] where the operator norm is \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Cv\|_2\). This promise ensures that the columns are linearly independent. It is a convenient fixed conditioning threshold for the finite encoding, not a physical noise parameter. Define the represented ideal isometry by exact ordered Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization: for the columns \(b_j\) of \(B\), set \[v_j=b_j-\sum_{i<j}a_i(a_i^\dagger b_j),\qquad a_j=v_j/\sqrt{v_j^\dagger v_j},\] using the positive square root, and let \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). These equations define the ideal mathematical distribution exactly; they do not give the classical sampler a real-arithmetic oracle or make numerical computation free. Finer explicit dyadic approximations can represent arbitrary optical isometries to arbitrary precision. The encoding spells out the source's correction of a finite-precision matrix to an isometry; its chosen threshold does not impose a restriction on the number of photons or on network depth.

For \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\Omega_{m,n}\), form the square \(n\times n\) matrix \(A_s\) by repeating row \(j\) of \(A\) exactly \(s_j\) times, in increasing row order. For an \(n\times n\) matrix \(C\), its permanent is \[\operatorname{Per}(C)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i)},\] where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The factorial convention is \(0!=1\). The bosonic transition rule gives the displayed \(D_B\); because \(A\) is an isometry, these nonnegative probabilities sum to one. The output lists all \(m\) occupation numbers in binary. No requirement to enumerate the whole distribution or to estimate each exponentially small probability is imposed.

The classical machine is a uniform multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. It receives the complete explicit finite input, has no advice, quantum operations or oracle, and its polynomial runtime bound holds for every input and every random tape. Correctness is required only on valid matrices. For each such input, its output must lie in \(\Omega_{m,n}\). The law \(Q_{B,k}\) averages over all its random bits; there is no separate high-probability event certifying closeness. Total variation compares this full output law with the target distribution. The polynomial and machine are fixed independently of \(m,n,B,k\).

The unary accuracy input \(1^k\) requests error at most \(1/k\). This gives the arbitrary-error convention \(\varepsilon>0\) with runtime polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\): choose \(k=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\). It does not require polynomial dependence on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Every \(m\ge n\) is allowed, with its full matrix encoding charged; in particular the class includes the dilute, polynomially many-mode families used in the original hardness results. It does not claim that every individual network is hard. Easy subfamilies are compatible with the universal-sampler impossibility statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the impossibility statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation by a uniform classical probabilistic machine with one polynomial bound satisfying all input, output and accuracy quantifiers above. A positive answer must rule out every such machine without assuming a separation of complexity classes or an unproved permanent conjecture. A conditional polynomial-hierarchy consequence, hardness of computing an individual probability, an exact-sampling lower bound, a multiplicative-error result, a fixed numerical error guarantee, or experiments on finitely many networks do not settle this total-variation question. This is an exact yes/no question about arbitrarily requested sampling accuracy; the benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not replace its quantified error requirement.
context:
The overview presents Boson Sampling as a restricted quantum experiment whose output distribution is conjectured to be difficult to reproduce classically. Its source paragraph does not choose an error model. On 16 September2026 the user selected approximate sampling to every requested total-variation error with polynomial inverse-error cost; this card records that specialization explicitly. The exact version remains distinct source context, not an asserted equivalent formulation.

Passive optics acts linearly on the single-photon modes, but the output probabilities for several indistinguishable photons involve squared permanents and factorial collision factors. Sampling asks for one random occupation pattern with the right distribution, rather than a list of all probabilities. The two computational tasks cannot be identified merely from that formula.

The 2013 paper proves that an efficient exact classical sampler would entail a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. Its route to a corresponding total-variation statement additionally uses conjectures about average-case Gaussian permanents and anticoncentration. These are conditional consequences; neither the noncollapse of the hierarchy nor all the required permanent statements are unconditional theorems.

The 2025 work substantially strengthens average-case probability-estimation hardness and proves a conditional multiplicative-error sampling theorem. Its Theorem1 still has an accuracy gap relative to the permanent conjecture, while Theorem3 assumes noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy and an anticoncentration conjecture. Multiplicative control of individual probabilities is stronger than the total-variation guarantee selected here.

The present claim concerns ideal indistinguishable photons and a sampler that works on every explicitly represented network. Typical-network hardness, constant-error hardness, loss-tolerant experiments and Gaussian Boson Sampling are separate variants. No measured experimental advantage or special family of classically simulable networks decides the stated universal-sampler question.
why: This asks for an unconditional boundary between classical sampling and a concrete, restricted quantum optical experiment. It would clarify whether reproducing an entire physically defined distribution can require superpolynomial classical resources even when universal quantum computation is not part of the device model.

title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
importance_reason: A central unresolved comparison in quantum proof complexity, connecting unentanglement, separable optimization and verification. The unusually broad known containment range and the new oracle separation make its ordinary-class target substantial; the score is for equality of QMA and QMA(2), not an unrestricted request to classify every multiprover model.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{QMA}\) for ordinary uniform promise problems without an oracle? A QMA(2) verifier receives two polynomial-length quantum witnesses that are promised to be unentangled across the two witness registers, even on a no-instance. A QMA verifier receives one arbitrary polynomial-length quantum witness. The easy inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) follows by ignoring a second witness; the question is whether every QMA(2) promise problem is also in QMA under the definitions below.
question_excerpt: Does the promise that two quantum witnesses are unentangled give more verification power than an unrestricted single quantum witness?
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some promise problem lies in QMA(2) but outside QMA. An equality proof must supply sound single-witness verification for every eligible two-witness problem; merely concatenating the intended honest witnesses is insufficient because the single-witness verifier must also resist entangled dishonest states. A separation must exclude every ordinary uniform polynomial-time QMA verifier for the same promise pair. A quantum- or classical-oracle separation, a result about a restricted-amplitude class, or a state-generation task does not alone settle this decision-class comparison.
context:
The two-witness condition changes which dishonest messages a verifier must handle. A verifier designed for a product state may be fooled by an entangled state on the same two registers. Treating both registers as one long witness preserves an honest proof but can invalidate soundness; this is why the class comparison is nontrivial.

There is no resource advantage just from having twice as many qubits: a single polynomial-length witness can already contain that many. Nor does the model provide two-way interaction or ask the verifier to certify that an arbitrary state is unentangled. The product-state restriction is part of the proof-system model.

The ordinary inclusions recorded in both the 2024 source and the September 2026 manuscript are \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\). Here NEXP is the class of promise problems decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\) for some polynomial \(p\), with an accepting branch on every yes-input and no accepting branch on any no-input. These inclusions alone neither prove nor refute equality of the first two classes.

Harrow–Montanaro establish error amplification and show that two unentangled proofs can simulate polynomially many. This explains why the two-proof class captures a broad finite-message regime, while still leaving comparison with one unrestricted quantum witness open.

The 2024 source studies witnesses whose relative phases are restricted, including nonnegative-amplitude variants at specified completeness and soundness parameters. It explicitly warns that those results do not immediately establish the relationship between ordinary QMA and QMA(2). A restriction on which dishonest states are allowed can increase verification power, so it cannot be transferred by treating it as an innocuous representation change.

The September 2026 manuscript gives the first separation relative to a unitary oracle. Both verifiers receive access to the same quantum black box, and the two-proof verifier gains power in that setting. This updates the 2024 paper’s statement that even such an oracle separation was unknown, but it does not separate the ordinary classes.

The new manuscript also draws consequences for approximate disentanglers and explicitly says a classical-oracle separation remains open. These are separate statements with their own parameters; neither is substituted for the unrelativized equality asked here. The recorded status is a manuscript claim checked for scope, not an independent validation of its proof.
why: This asks whether a promise of independence between two untrusted quantum messages can increase what an efficient quantum computer can verify. It connects computational verification with the geometry of entanglement and separates the value of unentanglement from simply supplying more qubits.

The latest manuscript updates the quantum-oracle status but explicitly retains the ordinary-class question. A bounded later-work search identified no unrelativized resolution. Cited proofs, including the new preprint, were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

working_summary: QMA(2) receives two quantum witnesses that are promised unentangled across a specified division, whereas QMA receives one unrestricted quantum witness. Both use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification with constant completeness and soundness error. The question is whether the promise of unentanglement adds power for ordinary promise problems without an oracle. Known amplification and restricted-phase results do not resolve this comparison, and concatenating honest witnesses does not preserve soundness automatically. A September 2026 manuscript separates the classes relative to a unitary oracle while explicitly leaving their ordinary relationship unresolved.

title: Quantum entropy inequalities beyond strong subadditivity
importance_reason: A foundational open boundary in quantum information theory, connecting multipartite correlations, entropy cones and universal information inequalities.
formal:
Is there an unconditional homogeneous linear inequality for finite-dimensional quantum subsystem entropies that does not follow from the standard von Neumann inequalities? Precisely, do there exist an integer \(n\ge4\), real coefficients \((c_J)_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}\), and a vector \(v\in\mathcal V_n\), as defined below, such that \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_J S(ho_J)\ge0\] for every choice of finite local dimensions and every \(n\)-party density matrix \(ho\), while \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_Jv_J<0?\] The same coefficients must work in every local dimension. The party count is any one finite \(n\ge4\); the target is not restricted to exactly four parties or to a special class of states.
question_excerpt: Do quantum subsystem entropies satisfy any universal linear inequalities beyond positivity, strong subadditivity and their purification consequences?
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Choose arbitrary positive integers \(d_1,\ldots,d_n\) and the Hilbert space \(\mathcal H=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathbb C^{d_i}\), with its standard product basis. A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) that is positive semidefinite, meaning \(z^\dagger\rho z\ge0\) for every complex vector \(z\), and has trace one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. Arbitrary complex matrix entries and mixed states are allowed.

For a subset \(J\subseteq[n]\), the marginal \(\rho_J\) is obtained by tracing out its complement. In product-basis indices its entries are \[(\rho_J)_{a,b}=\sum_z\rho_{(a,z),(b,z)},\] where \(a,b\) index the factors in \(J\), \(z\) ranges over all basis indices of the complementary factors, and the tuples are placed in the original order of the parties. If \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\) are the eigenvalues of a density matrix, define its von Neumann entropy in bits by \(S=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). Define the empty-system entropy to be zero. The entropy vector \(s(\rho)\in\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\) has coordinates \(s(\rho)_J=S(\rho_J)\), indexed by the nonempty subsets.

The standard comparison cone \(\mathcal V_n\) consists of all real vectors \(v=(v_J)_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq[n]}\), extended by \(v_\varnothing=0\), that satisfy \(v_J\ge0\) for every \(J\), and, for every pair of subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]\), both \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\cap B}+v_{A\cup B}\qquad\text{(strong subadditivity)}\] and \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\setminus B}+v_{B\setminus A}\qquad\text{(weak monotonicity)}.\] Disjoint, overlapping, equal and empty subsets are all included. Thus familiar subadditivity and the Araki–Lieb inequalities are already among the consequences. Weak monotonicity follows from strong subadditivity after purifying a quantum state with an additional party; it is explicitly included here so it cannot be counted as a new inequality. Every actual quantum entropy vector lies in \(\mathcal V_n\), but a vector in this cone is only a list of real numbers and is not promised to come from a state.

An inequality is homogeneous linear if its left side is the displayed linear combination with constant coefficients and zero right side. It is unconditional if it holds for all states and dimensions, without extra entropy equalities, independence assumptions or a restriction to stabilizer, classical or holographic states. Not following from the standard inequalities means exactly that it fails at some vector of \(\mathcal V_n\), as required by the strict inequality in the target. This is semantic nonimplication; no choice of syntactic proof system is involved. Equivalently, since the closure of the set of quantum entropy vectors is a closed convex cone, the question asks whether this closure is strictly smaller than \(\mathcal V_n\) for at least one finite \(n\ge4\). Closure means approximation to arbitrary accuracy in the finite-dimensional real coordinate space; it is not exact realization by a single finite-dimensional state. No running-time or algorithmic discovery requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence, including validity for every finite-dimensional state and an exact vector witnessing nonimplication by the standard cone, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The negative outcome must show that for every finite \(n\ge4\), every universally valid homogeneous linear entropy inequality is nonnegative on every vector in \(\mathcal V_n\). Equivalently it proves equality of the closed quantum entropy cone and \(\mathcal V_n\) for every such \(n\). A positive outcome needs only one party count, but a negative result for exactly four parties does not settle all larger counts. An inequality valid under additional constraints, a restriction to some states, or failure of exact realization of a boundary vector without excluding arbitrarily close realizations does not establish the requested separation. Numerical searches alone and approximate versions of the strict separation are insufficient.
context:
A multipartite state has one entropy for every nonempty subsystem. Universal linear inequalities limit which patterns of shared quantum information are possible, independently of the dimensions used to realize them. The question asks whether the familiar inequalities already exhaust these linear constraints.

Quantum entropy differs from classical entropy: adjoining a system can reduce entropy. For instance, a pure maximally entangled pair has zero joint entropy and positive one-party entropies. Classical monotonicity cannot be added to the comparison cone; the source uses weak monotonicity instead.

For at most three parties, the closure of the set of quantum entropy vectors is characterized by the standard inequalities. For four or more, the source explicitly distinguishes this closed-cone question from the exact set of realizable entropy vectors. Nonrealizability at a limiting boundary point alone is not a new universal linear inequality.

Classical non-Shannon inequalities demonstrate that the analogous classical outer cone is too large. That fact does not transfer directly to quantum states, because classical diagonal states form only a subclass and quantum conditional entropy can be negative.

The 2013 paper characterizes the four-party stabilizer entropy cone using an additional Ingleton inequality. General quantum states, including some classical diagonal states, need not satisfy Ingleton. The theorem therefore answers a restricted-state question and leaves the target here open.

Known constrained quantum entropy inequalities assume additional relations among entropies. Such a conclusion can fail to survive limits of states that only approach those relations. It does not automatically give an unconditional separating inequality for the closed entropy cone.

The 2025 Quantum Entropy Prover formalizes deduction from strong subadditivity and weak monotonicity using linear programming, and also handles supplied constraints. Its introduction explicitly retains existence of non-von-Neumann-type unconditional inequalities as an open question; an automated prover for the known cone does not characterize the actual quantum cone.

The 2026 holographic-cone paper also distinguishes the unresolved general quantum cone from the more restricted holographic setting. New graph realizations or inequalities for that restricted cone do not apply to every finite-dimensional quantum state.
why: This asks whether the established linear laws of quantum entropy are complete. A new unconditional inequality would reveal a universal restriction on sharing quantum information; completeness would characterize every finite-party entropy cone by finitely many standard inequalities, after taking closure.

working_summary: For a multipartite quantum state, the entropies of all subsystems form a vector subject to universal inequalities. Positivity and strong subadditivity give basic constraints on those vectors. This question asks whether additional inequalities are needed to describe the quantum entropy cone for four or more parties. The cited stabilizer-state analysis relates the problem to classical non-Shannon inequalities and to states violating the Ingleton inequality. New constraints or counterexamples would sharpen the mathematical description of how quantum information can be shared among several systems.

title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
importance_reason: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
formal: For every finite pair of local dimensions \(d_A,d_B\ge2\) and every entangled state \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}\), do there exist a finite integer \(k\ge1\), local filters with strictly positive joint success probability, and finite families of local measurements for which the successfully filtered state obtained from \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) has Bell-nonlocal correlations? Both filters act before the measurement settings are chosen. No auxiliary shared entangled state is supplied. The number of copies, filters, output dimensions and measurement families may depend on \(\rho\).
question_excerpt: Can local filtering of sufficiently many copies of every entangled bipartite state reveal a violation of some Bell inequality?
definitions:
A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(X=X^\dagger\) with \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for all complex vectors \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}X=1\). Dagger is conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination of product density matrices; entangled means not separable. No purity, rational-entry or efficient-preparation promise is imposed. The \(k\) copies are independent copies of the same state. Regroup the tensor factors of \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) into Alice's \((\mathbb C^{d_A})^{\otimes k}\) and Bob's \((\mathbb C^{d_B})^{\otimes k}\); each party may act jointly on all of its own copies.

A successful local filter is specified by finitely many rectangular complex matrices \(A_j\) from Alice's input space to a finite output space \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\), with \(\sum_jA_j^\dagger A_j\le I\). It maps \(X\) to \(\mathcal F_A(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j^\dagger\). Bob's filter \(\mathcal F_B\) is defined by matrices \(B_l\) and \(\sum_lB_l^\dagger B_l\le I\), with output \(\mathbb C^{r_B}\). Here \(S\le I\) means \(I-S\) is positive semidefinite. These are precisely finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing maps. Their joint success probability and conditional output are \[q=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})\bigr]>0,\qquad \sigma=\frac{(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})}{q}.\] No lower bound on \(q\) uniform over states or copy counts is required. The success flags may be compared before the measurement settings are chosen. The filters cannot depend on those settings. Local ancillary states are absorbed in the local maps; no entangled ancilla shared between the parties is permitted.

Let \(X,Y,O_A,O_B\) be finite nonempty sets of settings and outcomes. For each \(x\in X\), Alice's positive-operator-valued measurement is a family \((M_{\alpha|x})_{\alpha\in O_A}\) of positive semidefinite operators on \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\) summing to identity. Define Bob's \((N_{\beta|y})_{\beta\in O_B}\) similarly. The conditional correlation is \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sigma(M_{\alpha|x}\otimes N_{\beta|y})\bigr].\] Measurement settings are independently selected after successful preparation; no communication is allowed after they are supplied. All outcomes are retained in this distribution, with no further postselection on outcomes or settings.

The correlation is Bell-local if there are a finite set \(L\), nonnegative weights \(w_\lambda\) summing to one, and normalized conditional probability distributions \(u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)\), \(v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\), such that \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}w_\lambda u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\] for every setting and outcome. The weights cannot depend on \(x,y\). For finite settings and outcomes this includes all local hidden-variable models, since deterministic response tables have a finite convex hull. Bell-nonlocal means no such representation exists. Equivalently, the distribution violates some linear Bell inequality valid for all local distributions. The target permits every finite Bell scenario, not only two settings or the CHSH inequality. Public shared randomness may select local procedures, but cannot turn a convex combination of Bell-local correlations into a nonlocal one; existence can therefore be tested for fixed filters and measurements as above. There is no computation, sample or circuit-size bound on the chosen operations.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal finite-copy assertion, or of its logical negation: there is one finite-dimensional entangled state for which every finite \(k\), every allowed pair of filters with positive success probability, and every finite family of local measurements produces a Bell-local distribution. A positive proof need not bound \(k\), filter success probability or violation size uniformly over states. A one-copy local model, including a model surviving every one-copy filter, does not establish the negative all-copy assertion. Activation with a different auxiliary entangled state, a network with additional parties, or a test with quantum inputs does not establish the specified bipartite target. Bell violation and filter positivity are exact mathematical conditions; approximate numerical evidence alone is insufficient.
context:
Entanglement describes the shared state. Bell nonlocality describes observed correlations that cannot be reproduced by local response functions and shared randomness. The source explicitly asks whether collective use of repeated copies and preliminary local filtering always connects these two notions.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove that entanglement can activate a Bell violation when combined with a suitable auxiliary state. That auxiliary resource need not be a copy of the state being tested, so the theorem leaves the question in this card open.

Hirsch and coauthors exhibit entangled two-qubit states remaining Bell-local after every local filter on one copy, including general positive-operator-valued measurements. Their theorem rules out a universal one-copy claim; it does not give a state remaining local after arbitrary numbers of copies.

The December 2025 broadcast result places the original source in a four-party experiment and rules out quantum-realizable broadcast explanations with a separable source across the original cut. Its additional parties and causal assumptions differ from the ordinary two-party local hidden-variable definition here. Its universal entanglement-certification result therefore does not settle this repeated-copy question.

The original source also distinguishes arbitrary Bell inequalities from the CHSH test. The repeated-copy filtered CHSH criterion is tied to distillability, while the present target allows every finite setting and outcome configuration. Restricting the output test to CHSH would change the question.
why: A positive answer would give every entangled bipartite state an intrinsic Bell-nonlocal manifestation using only repeated access to that same state. A negative answer would exhibit entanglement that remains Bell-local under every finite collective local test and preliminary filter. This separates the mathematical resource of entanglement from the observable nonlocal correlations used in device-independent information tasks.

The broadcast theorem uses additional parties and quantum-realizable network explanations; it is not a general local-hidden-variable counterexample in this card’s scenario. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
