working_summary: Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are distinct properties of quantum states and measurement correlations. The question asks whether every entangled bipartite state becomes Bell-nonlocal after local filtering of some finite number of copies. The filter must succeed before measurement settings are selected, and no extra shared entangled state is provided. Single-copy counterexamples, auxiliary-state activation and four-party broadcast results address different resource models. A full answer would determine whether repeated copies of the state itself always make its entanglement observable through a conventional bipartite Bell violation.

title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus NEXP
importance_reason: A major class-comparison problem at the interface of quantum verification, unentanglement and exponential-time complexity. Nearby small-gap and restricted-amplitude models already reach NEXP, but neither supplies the ordinary constant-gap result. It is distinct from, though tightly related to, QMA versus QMA(2).
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{NEXP}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), admit a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with two polynomial-length unentangled witnesses, completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The known inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\) makes the reverse containment the unresolved direction. The verifier, its running time and both witness lengths must remain polynomial in the original binary input length.
question_excerpt: Does ordinary QMA(2), with a constant completeness–soundness gap, equal nondeterministic exponential time?
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.

A nondeterministic classical Turing machine has finitely many tapes, a fixed finite tape alphabet and a fixed finite transition relation. An execution chooses one permitted transition at each step, and one step is charged for each such transition. A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is in \(\mathrm{NEXP}\), nondeterministic exponential time, if there exist such a machine and an integer-valued polynomial \(p\) with the following properties. Every computation branch on every length-\(n\) binary input halts within \(2^{p(n)}\) steps; every yes-input has an accepting branch; and no no-input has an accepting branch. No correctness requirement is imposed outside the promise. The machine is fixed for the problem and has neither an oracle nor advice. The polynomial and machine may differ between promise problems. Here QMA(2) retains the constant error thresholds already defined. A class allowing an exponentially small difference between completeness and soundness is called a precise variant; that is not the class being compared in this card.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that a promise problem in NEXP is outside QMA(2). A positive proof must preserve polynomial verification and proof lengths with the fixed \(2/3\) versus \(1/3\) acceptance gap; a negative proof must exclude every ordinary uniform verifier with two unentangled polynomial-length witnesses. A protocol with an exponentially small gap, an exponentially long proof, extra oracle access, or a restriction to nonnegative dishonest witness amplitudes does not by itself satisfy this target. Equality or separation between QMA and QMA(2) alone does not answer their comparison with NEXP.
context:
The comparison is about how much computation can be verified, not the physical size of a state vector’s written description. A polynomial number of qubits has exponentially many amplitudes, but an efficient verifier can access them only through its permitted quantum computation. A constant completeness–soundness gap is a substantive part of the claim.

The original source records equality between NEXP and a precise version of QMA(2) whose gap may be exponentially small. Such a verifier may distinguish its yes- and no-cases by a probability difference too small for polynomially many repetitions to resolve. The present card retains the ordinary constant-gap definition.

Known amplification for ordinary QMA(2) and equivalence of two to polynomially many unentangled proofs do not convert every exponentially small-gap protocol into a polynomial-time constant-gap one. The initial gap is a parameter of the amplification cost.

Nonnegative-amplitude proof systems impose additional conditions on the witnesses allowed in the soundness case. Results reaching NEXP in such models therefore concern a different collection of dishonest proofs. The 2024 source explicitly distinguishes those results from ordinary QMA(2).

The August 2026 preprint reports stronger amplification for the nonnegative-amplitude variant, approaching the one-quarter soundness threshold from above as completeness approaches one. Its abstract distinguishes that regime from the stronger-gap comparison with ordinary or real-amplitude witnesses. It does not state the unrestricted equality asked here.

The September 2026 manuscript still records the chain from QMA through QMA(2) to NEXP as the general ordinary-class information available. Its new theorem separates QMA from QMA(2) relative to a unitary oracle; that theorem neither puts all NEXP problems in ordinary QMA(2) nor separates them from it.

The neighboring single-witness question concerns the lower end of the containment chain. This card concerns the upper end. Their logical relationship is worth retaining, but they ask different equalities and a result about one pair does not automatically settle the other.
why: Two short quantum messages may contain a highly structured encoding of a much longer computation, while their independence restricts how a dishonest prover can cheat. This question asks whether that resource reaches the full power of nondeterministic exponential time despite a polynomial-time verifier and a constant reliability gap. It locates the upper end of the unusually wide known range for QMA(2).
status_note: Source-open for ordinary constant-gap QMA(2) versus NEXP. On 16 September 2026 the full ITCS 2023 source and ITCS 2024 discussion, the August 2026 amplification abstract, and the September 2026 oracle manuscript introduction were checked. The latter explicitly retains the ordinary containment range. A bounded later-work search found no resolution of the stated equality. Recent preprint claims are reported with their amplitude, gap and oracle restrictions; their proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2013: Harrow–Montanaro establish amplification for ordinary unentangled proof systems and show that two proofs capture polynomially many. | 2023: Gharibian–Rudolph explicitly distinguish the open ordinary QMA(2) versus NEXP problem from the known exponentially small-gap equality. | 2024: Bassirian–Fefferman–Marwaha analyze relative-phase restrictions and explain why their effects do not immediately settle ordinary QMA(2). | 2026-08-08: Miyamoto posts a stronger amplification claim for nonnegative-amplitude witnesses, with the amplitude and acceptance-gap restrictions retained. | 2026-09-02: The new unitary-oracle separation manuscript explicitly retains the ordinary containment range QMA through QMA(2) to NEXP.
working_summary: The question asks whether polynomial-time verification of two unentangled polynomial-length quantum proofs captures nondeterministic exponential time. It compares ordinary promise classes with a fixed constant acceptance gap and no oracle or advice. NEXP already contains QMA(2), so the unresolved direction is verification of every NEXP promise problem by the two-proof model. Exponentially small-gap and nonnegative-amplitude variants have stronger known characterizations that do not automatically transfer to this model. Recent amplification and oracle results retain those distinctions and do not establish ordinary QMA(2) equals NEXP.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
importance_reason: Determines the strongest quantum query advantage when the function has no promise, a basic limit on quantum computation.
formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.
context:
Quantum algorithms can exploit a special promise to obtain enormous advantages over randomized algorithms. Total functions remove that freedom. Every input string must have a specified correct answer, so both the quantum algorithm and its classical competitors must handle adversarial inputs.

The quartic upper bound follows from \(R(f)\le D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)\), where \(D(f)\) is deterministic decision-tree depth. A matching separation between deterministic and quantum queries does not automatically give a matching separation against randomized algorithms.

The near-cubic lower-bound family comes from stronger promise-problem separations combined with a construction turning them into total functions. This establishes an exponent of at least three; it does not supply a quartic randomized separation.

The exponent formulation intentionally ignores subpolynomial factors. For example, an additional logarithmic factor in a universal cubic bound would still be compatible with exponent three. Establishing the exact bound with exponent three and no extra factor is a finer question.
why: This quantifies the greatest possible quantum query advantage when an algorithm must handle every input, without a promise. It tests a basic limitation on quantum speedups and distinguishes the role of classical randomization from that of deterministic computation.
status_note: Open in Aaronson’s 2021 survey. The near-cubic lower-bound family and universal quartic bound were checked in their primary papers on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search found no resolution of the displayed exponent; the September 2026 paper Quantum Query Advantage Requires Space concerns an additional workspace restriction and does not close this gap.
progress: 2021: Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal establish the universal quartic deterministic-versus-quantum query bound, giving the upper endpoint four. | 2021: Bansal and Sinha obtain total Boolean functions with a near-cubic randomized-versus-quantum separation, giving the lower endpoint three. | 2021: Aaronson explicitly asks to close the gap between the cubic separation and quartic universal upper bound.
working_summary: The question asks for the largest polynomial quantum query advantage over randomized algorithms on total Boolean functions. Both models must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input. Only queries to input bits are counted, with other computation and workspace unrestricted. Known results put the optimal separation exponent between three and four. The target is to certify that exponent within one hundredth, without resolving finer logarithmic factors.

title: One-way state generators versus EFI pairs
importance_reason: A basic comparison of minimal quantum cryptographic assumptions, connecting indistinguishability, search hardness and efficient verification; the distinction affects which primitives can be based on the weakest known quantum resources.
formal: Does the existence of EFI pairs imply the existence of efficiently verifiable one-way state generators in the ordinary quantum circuit model defined below? Both primitives have uniform polynomial-time honest algorithms and security against polynomial-size quantum circuits with classical nonuniformity. The implication is between existence assertions; no oracle is supplied to any algorithm.
definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\ge1\), supplied as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A negligible function is a map \(\nu:\mathbb N_{>0}\to[0,1]\) such that, for every integer \(c\ge1\), eventually \(\nu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\). Each security quantifier may have its own negligible function. Polynomial bounds have fixed constants and exponents independent of \(\lambda\).

An \(m\)-qubit state is a positive semidefinite complex matrix of trace one on \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}\). Algorithms use quantum circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), preparation of zero qubits, computational-basis measurement, classical control and discarding qubits. Here \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\). Classical inputs and outputs are bit strings. All gate applications, classical computation and input/output operations are charged. A uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm has one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator, and its circuit size and classical control time are polynomial in the input length on every branch. Honest algorithms receive no advice. Their security-parameter-dependent lengths are positive, polynomially bounded and polynomial-time computable.

An adversary is any family of polynomial-size circuits in this model, with arbitrary polynomial-size classical descriptions depending on \(\lambda\). Equivalently it may use polynomially many classical advice bits depending only on \(\lambda\), independently of the sampled secret or challenge bit. It may prepare quantum work registers from zero but receives no arbitrary quantum advice. There is no oracle or uncharged computation. The descriptions of all honest algorithms are public.

An EFI pair consists of one uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm \(G\) with output \(m(\lambda)\) qubits. Write \(\rho_{b,\lambda}\) for the mixed output of \(G(1^\lambda,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). The following two requirements hold:
\[
\exists p\ \exists\lambda_0\ \forall\lambda\ge\lambda_0:
\quad \frac12\|\rho_{0,\lambda}-\rho_{1,\lambda}\|_1\ge\frac1{p(\lambda)},
\]
where \(p\) is a positive polynomial, and, for every adversary \(D\), its distinguishing advantage
\[
\left|\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{0,\lambda})=1]
-\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{1,\lambda})=1]\right|
\]
is negligible. The trace norm is \(\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^\dagger X}\). The distinguishing experiment supplies one challenge state. Its preparation randomness and all measurements are included in the probabilities.

An efficiently verifiable one-way state generator consists of three uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms \(\mathrm{KeyGen},\mathrm{StateGen},\mathrm{Ver}\). The first, on \(1^\lambda\), samples a classical key \(k\in\{0,1\}^{\kappa(\lambda)}\). The second, on \((1^\lambda,k)\), outputs an \(m(\lambda)\)-qubit state \(\sigma_{k,\lambda}\), which may be mixed. The third, on \((1^\lambda,k',\sigma)\), outputs an acceptance bit; a key of the wrong length is rejected. Correctness requires
\[
\Pr_{k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda)}
 [\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k,\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1]\ge1-\nu(\lambda)
\]
for some negligible \(\nu\). This is averaged over the generated key, not a promise of correctness for every bit string.

Security requires that, for every positive integer-valued polynomial copy bound \(t(\lambda)\) and every adversary \(A\), the following success probability is negligible:
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k',\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1:
\ k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\
 k'\leftarrow A(1^\lambda,\sigma_{k,\lambda}^{\otimes t(\lambda)})
\right].
\]
Conditioned on \(k\), all copies are produced by independent runs of \(\mathrm{StateGen}\). The verifier's copy is fresh and independent of the copies supplied to \(A\). The probability includes key generation, state preparation and all measurements. The adversary wins by producing any accepted key, not necessarily the original key. In particular the verifier must be efficient; allowing it unlimited time defines a different primitive.

The proposition quantifies over existence of complete schemes, with their own polynomial lengths and running-time bounds. It does not prescribe a fixed transformation or loss of security from a given EFI generator. A counterexample relative to an added oracle, or impossibility for one restricted form of transformation, does not by itself negate this ordinary-model existence implication.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this existence implication, or a complete Lean proof of its negation in the stated ordinary model. All correctness, polynomial-time and asymptotic security requirements must match the definitions, including efficient verification and classical rather than quantum advice. An equivalence with generators whose verifier has unlimited running time, an oracle-relative separation or a restriction on black-box constructions alone is insufficient.
context:
Question 4 compares one-way state generators with EFI pairs and, separately, pseudorandom state generators. This card selects the EFI comparison. title: Locality-preserving quantum gap amplification
importance_reason: Preserving constraint arity while amplifying normalized quantum energy addresses a central structural obstacle in adapting the combinatorial PCP strategy. Even one such step would distinguish quantum soundness from the currently available locality-increasing or restricted-soundness constructions.
formal:
For every fixed integers \(k,q\ge2\), do there exist integers \(D\ge q\) and \(C\ge1\), a rational \(0<\gamma\le1\), and a deterministic classical polynomial-time transformation \(T_{k,q}\) with the following property? Given any explicit \(k\)-local projective Hamiltonian
\[
 H=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m P_j
\]
on \(n\) sites of local dimension \(q\), it outputs an explicit projective Hamiltonian
\[
 H'=\frac1{m'}\sum_{j=1}^{m'} P'_j
\]
with \(1\le m'\le Cm\), whose terms each act on at most \(k\) sites and whose site dimension is \(D\), such that
\[
 \lambda(H)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda(H')=0,
 \qquad
 \lambda(H')\ge\min\{2\lambda(H),\gamma\}.
\]
Here \(\lambda\) denotes the lowest eigenvalue of the normalized Hamiltonian. In particular, whenever \(0<\lambda(H)\le\gamma/2\), its normalized energy is at least doubled. All output-dimension, term-growth and energy-threshold constants are independent of the input instance and its size.
question_excerpt: The CCC paper identifies preservation of the number of variables in each constraint as a missing feature of attempted quantum versions of Dinur’s amplification. Its own repetition increases that locality. The user selected one energy-doubling step with constant-factor term growth, allowing a larger local dimension but requiring that dimension to remain independent of instance size.
definitions:
A site is a finite quantum system with state space \(\mathbb C^q\). An input has integers \(n,m\ge1\) and a list of \(m\) constraints. Constraint \(j\) specifies an ordered subset \(S_j\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(1\le|S_j|\le k\), and the full \(q^{|S_j|}\)-by-\(q^{|S_j|}\) matrix of an orthogonal projection \(P_j\). Thus \(P_j=P_j^\dagger=P_j^2\). It acts as the identity on sites outside \(S_j\). Zero projections are allowed, and identical repeated constraints count separately. Projections on overlapping sites need not commute; there is no input bound on how many constraints contain a site.

The normalized energy is
\[
 \lambda(H)=\min_{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle=1}\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle,
 \qquad |\psi\rangle\in(\mathbb C^q)^{\otimes n}.
\]
The minimum ranges over every unit vector, including arbitrarily entangled states, and lies in \([0,1]\). Equivalently it is the smallest eigenvalue of \(H\). Zero energy means that some state is simultaneously in the kernel of every \(P_j\). Energy is divided by the number of constraints before and after transformation, so increasing the number of identical constraints cannot by itself create the required amplification. This is ground-energy amplification, not enlargement of the difference between the two lowest eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian.

Each local matrix entry is an explicitly encoded complex algebraic number. Its real and imaginary parts are each represented by a nonzero integer polynomial, with all coefficients listed in binary, and rational isolating endpoints selecting one real root. The polynomial must have exactly one real root in the indicated interval. Rational numbers can be supplied by linear polynomials. This gives exact finite matrices, rather than a tolerance-dependent approximation oracle. Hermiticity and idempotence are promises about the exact entries. The total bit length \(L\) includes all matrix data, site lists, and unary encodings of \(n\) and \(m\); for fixed \(k,q\) this differs only polynomially from usual explicit input encodings.

The output uses the same exact algebraic-entry representation. It may introduce new sites and new constraints, and may change the interaction pattern. Every output site belongs to some declared output support; hence there are at most \(km'\) output sites. Output constraints are again orthogonal projections, supported on at most \(k\) sites, and \(H'\) is their equally weighted average. The normalization and unit-norm projection convention prevent amplification merely by multiplying the whole Hamiltonian by two.

The dimension \(D=D(k,q)\) may exceed \(q\), as selected by the user, but it is one fixed integer for the transformation. It cannot grow with \(n,m,L\), the coefficient degrees or precision, or any property of the particular instance. The same independence holds for \(C\) and \(\gamma\). The number of sites may change; what is preserved is the maximum number of sites touched by a single constraint. A bound of \(O(k)\) sites with a larger hidden constant is not the stated bound \(k\).

For each fixed \(k,q\), \(T_{k,q}\) is one finite deterministic program and there exist constants \(A,b\ge1\) such that it halts within \(A(L+1)^b\) elementary steps of a classical multitape Turing machine on every input encoding. This includes computing and writing all output matrices. Its guarantees apply to valid promised inputs; there is no requirement to recognize all invalid encodings. The constants and program may depend on \(k,q\), and no bound on an effective compiler from \(k,q\) to that program is requested.

The completeness condition is exact preservation of zero energy. The soundness condition holds on every valid input, with a constant plateau \(\gamma\) once the input energy is no longer small. This fixes a one-step, perfect-completeness version of the source’s broader template question. It does not ask for alphabet reduction, a complete quantum PCP theorem, or a bound uniform over an unbounded number of iterations. Enlarging the constant local dimension again in a later separate step is not part of the present guarantee.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of the transformations and their constants, polynomial bit-time bounds, exact zero-energy preservation, output arity and term-count bounds, and the displayed normalized-energy inequality for all states; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of the existence statement for some fixed \(k,q\).

A lower bound proved only for product states, computational-basis states or another restricted witness class is insufficient. A locality-increasing construction, dimension growing with input size, superconstant multiplicative term growth, or an increase caused only by rescaling constraints does not meet the target. A single step does not by itself establish the other ingredients of a full quantum PCP theorem. The exact propositions and asymptotic resource bounds do not receive a numerical approximation tolerance.

working_summary: The input is a collection of local quantum projection constraints, and its energy is the smallest possible average violation over all quantum states. The task is one polynomial-time transformation that preserves zero energy and at least doubles sufficiently small positive normalized energy. Each output constraint must still involve at most the original number of particles, and the number of constraints may grow only by a constant factor. The local quantum dimension may increase to a larger constant but cannot grow with the size of the input instance. A complete Lean-checked proof or refutation must control entangled states as well as all stated representation and resource bounds.

title: Bosonic quantum computation in PP
importance_reason: A substantive comparison between infinite-dimensional quantum computation and classical counting complexity, exposing energy and numerical representation as computational resources. The restricted-energy PP theorem makes the distinction from the unrestricted target particularly consequential.
formal: Does \[\mathrm{CVBQP}[X^3]\subseteq\mathrm{PP}\] hold for the Gaussian-and-cubic bosonic model below, with no additional restriction on energy during the computation? For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) decided by the stated polynomial-time uniform bosonic circuit family with polynomial total evolution time and the separated output intervals below, must there be a classical probabilistic polynomial-time machine accepting each \(x\in L\) with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) and each \(x\notin L\) with probability at most \(1/2\)? The target is the inclusion itself, rather than an unspecified improvement of an exponential-space upper bound.
question_excerpt: Can the upper bound for bosonic computation with Gaussian and cubic phase gates be improved, in particular to \(\mathrm{CVBQP}[X^3]\subseteq\mathrm{PP}\)?
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. PP consists of languages for which one classical multitape probabilistic Turing machine, using independent fair random bits, runs in polynomial time on every random tape and has acceptance probability greater than \(1/2\) on exactly the strings in the language. No inverse-polynomial gap from \(1/2\) is required. The machine has no advice or oracle. Its polynomial may depend on the language, but not on the individual input.

For an input of length \(n\ge1\), the bosonic state space is \(L^2(\mathbb R^n)\), the square-integrable complex functions of \(n\) real coordinates. Equivalently it has the orthonormal occupation basis \(|r_1,\ldots,r_n\rangle\) indexed by nonnegative integers. On the usual Schwartz domain, position acts by \((X_j f)(q)=q_jf(q)\), and momentum by \(P_jf=-i\,\partial f/\partial q_j\), with \(i^2=-1\) and units fixed by \([X_j,P_k]=i\delta_{jk}I\). The single-mode number operator is \[N_j=(X_j^2+P_j^2-I)/2,\qquad N_j|r_1,\ldots,r_n\rangle=r_j|r_1,\ldots,r_n\rangle.\] The vacuum is \(|0,\ldots,0\rangle\). These are genuine infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; there is no finite photon-number cutoff in the model.

For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), the source's input \(|x\rangle\) means a product of coherent states with real amplitudes \(x_j\), not the occupation state with photon counts \(x_j\). In coordinates its normalized wavefunction is \[\psi_x(q)=\pi^{-n/4}\exp\!\left(-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^n(q_j-\sqrt2x_j)^2\right).\] Preparing this state is the prescribed input convention. Equivalently, input-dependent displacement gates can be placed before a vacuum-input circuit; the displacements have polynomial total cost.

The allowed unitaries are Gaussian gates and single-mode cubic phase gates. A Gaussian gate is \(e^{-itH}\) for a self-adjoint quadratic Hamiltonian \(H\) in the positions and momenta: a real linear combination of \(I,X_j,P_j\) and symmetrized products \((R_aR_b+R_bR_a)/2\), where \(R=(X_1,P_1,\ldots,X_n,P_n)\). A cubic gate is \(e^{-itH}\) with \(H=\pm X_j^3\). Quadratic Hamiltonians and \(\pm X_j^3\) use their standard self-adjoint closures; their exponentials are defined by the spectral calculus. The coefficients of the quadratic Hamiltonians have absolute value bounded by a family-dependent constant. The signs of Hamiltonians may be reversed. Durations are nonnegative; allowing a signed duration is the same convention after moving its sign into the Hamiltonian. Thus total physical evolution time is \(\sum_j|t_j|\), not a signed sum that can cancel. No other non-Gaussian Hamiltonian, intermediate measurement, postselection, feed-forward or non-Gaussian input is allowed.

Uniformity and scalar representation are made explicit as follows. One deterministic classical algorithm on \(1^n\) produces the finite gate list, mode addresses, polynomial lists for the Gaussian Hamiltonians, and the output interval descriptions in polynomial time. The number of listed gates and total description length are polynomial in \(n\). Every real gate parameter is specified by a finite description with one uniform deterministic evaluation algorithm: given \(n\), its location in the list and a unary precision request \(1^b\), the algorithm outputs a dyadic rational within \(2^{-b}\) of that parameter in time polynomial in \(n+b\). Rational parameters and fixed polynomial-time computable constants are included; arbitrary uncomputable real advice is not. These descriptions denote exact real numbers; replacing them by rounded numbers is not a free simulation step. This is the explicit effective-real interpretation of the source's polynomial-time uniformity. In particular, it does not assume that polynomially many precision bits suffice to simulate a circuit whose intermediate energy is very large.

There is a polynomial \(p\), depending only on the family, which bounds the list length, description length, total evolution time and output interval endpoints in magnitude. Write \[|\psi_{n,x}^{\mathrm{out}}\rangle=e^{-it_{\ell(n)}H_{\ell(n)}}\cdots e^{-it_1H_1}|x\rangle.\] At the end, only \(N_1\) is measured. The integer outcome \(Y\in\mathbb N_0\) has probability \[\Pr[Y=r]=\langle\psi_{n,x}^{\mathrm{out}}|\bigl(|r\rangle\langle r|\otimes I\bigr)|\psi_{n,x}^{\mathrm{out}}\rangle.\] Fix polynomial-time computable rational threshold functions \(a(n),b(n),E(n)\), with polynomial-length binary encodings, \(E(n)\ge0\), \(a(n)-E(n)\ge0\), \(b(n)-a(n)\ge1/p(n)\), and all interval endpoints at most \(p(n)\). The family decides \(L\) if, for every input \(x\), \[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[Y\in[b(n),b(n)+E(n)]]>2/3,\] \[x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[Y\in[a(n)-E(n),a(n)]]>2/3.\] The intervals are inclusive and only their integer points are measurement outcomes. Outcomes outside the indicated interval are part of its error probability. The empty input can be assigned a fixed constant-time decision. All bounds and algorithms are independent of the individual input string.

This is the separated-interval formulation of Definition4.4. Its concentration requirement for the final measurement is retained. It does not itself bound the expectation of that outcome: a small tail at very large photon number can make an expectation large. No promise is added that the total mean energy \(\sum_j\langle N_j\rangle\) remains polynomial or exponential at intermediate times. In particular, no promise of exponentially accurate approximation by exponentially bounded-energy states is imposed. Such a promise is a substantive extra hypothesis in a later PP theorem, not a consequence of the interval acceptance rule.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the inclusion for every language and uniform family in the specified model, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some such language is outside PP. A positive result must cover all allowed polynomial-length Gaussian-and-cubic circuits without adding an intermediate energy or energy-approximation promise. A negative result must establish nonmembership in PP, rather than merely lower bounds for a particular simulation algorithm. The existing EXPSPACE upper bound, a PSPACE upper bound, a PP simulation under extra energy assumptions, or simulation only of low-degree observables does not settle this target. The answer is an exact class-inclusion decision, with no numerical-value approximation tolerance substituted for it.
context:
The source asks broadly for a better bound on bosonic computation and explicitly singles out containment in PP. On 16 September2026 the user selected that particular inclusion, with no new energy restriction. This narrows the requested outcome from any improvement of the upper bound to one concrete class comparison; it is not presented as equivalent to the broader objective.

The formal model combines coherent inputs, Gaussian and cubic phase gates, a polynomial total evolution time and a final number measurement with separated acceptance intervals. Its infinite-dimensional state space permits very high occupation numbers during a short computation. The source proves an EXPSPACE upper bound for its Gaussian-and-cubic simulation problem and documents doubly exponential energy growth.

The source uses polynomial final-output energy language in its informal Definition1.2, but its formal Definition4.4 states probability concentration in polynomial-size intervals. Concentration alone does not bound the expectation of a tail. This card explicitly follows the latter formal decision model and does not silently supply a stronger intermediate-energy condition.

The published 2026 PSPACE simulation restricts intermediate energy to at most exponential size. That condition is explicit in the published abstract, introduction and Methods, even though the older arXiv abstract describes a less qualified upper bound. The restricted theorem cannot by itself settle the present inclusion for the original unrestricted-energy model.

The June2026 energy paper goes further and states a PP simulation under an effective exponential-energy approximation promise. Its formal Theorem5.27 also uses constant-bit gate parameters and explicitly says that the promise does not cover the entire Gaussian-and-cubic class. The same paper retains EXPSPACE as the known general simulation bound for polynomial-depth circuits. These qualifications are essential when comparing it with the selected target.

The family here has no adaptive intermediate measurements or additional non-Gaussian input states. Results about richer continuous-variable models, other polynomial Hamiltonians, or expectation values of low-degree observables have different hypotheses or outputs and do not establish this precise inclusion.
why: This tests whether an infinite-dimensional optical model with cubic nonlinearity still fits within a familiar classical counting class. Its answer would clarify how much computational power can be hidden in very high intermediate photon numbers despite polynomial evolution time and a bounded-error final decision.

Both follow-ups impose conditions absent from the selected target. No resolution of the unrestricted-energy inclusion was identified. The model uses coherent input states, polynomial evolution time and a final number measurement with separated acceptance intervals. No exponential bound on intermediate energy is added to the original formal decision model. Later PSPACE and PP simulations require additional energy assumptions and therefore do not settle this target. A resolution would clarify the computational significance of high photon numbers in infinite-dimensional quantum computation.

title: Remote state preparation from quantum-secure one-way functions
importance_reason: A broad cryptographic foundations question about whether the weakest standard classical computational primitive can support classical control of an untrusted quantum system. Parallel hidden-state preparation supports several distinct quantum cryptographic applications, and the assumption gap connects to the limits of classical-communication secure computation. The precise retained target is the source’s inverse-polynomial rigidity form, not an automatically strengthened composable primitive; score 87 is a new individual editorial assessment replacing an unassessed 50.
formal:
Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against quantum polynomial-time inversion with quantum advice imply the existence of a protocol for parallel remote preparation of BB84 states with the inverse-polynomial rigidity guarantee defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists\Pi\;\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi)\bigr).
\]
The protocol has one classical client and one quantum server, uses only classical communication, and has no trusted setup or initially shared resource. The client chooses a basis string \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and upon acceptance obtains a string \(v\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). For an honest server, its designated output register contains the corresponding BB84 product state
\[
|\psi_{v,\theta}\rangle=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}H^{\theta_{i}}|v_{i}\rangle,
\qquad H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
with uniformly random \(v\), up to negligible correctness error. Against any efficient malicious server, the accepted joint output must satisfy the computational rigidity condition below, up to an efficient isometry on the server’s space and an auxiliary state independent of \(v,\theta\). A unary accuracy parameter \(t\) permits soundness error \(1/t\) plus a negligible term, with resources polynomial in the security parameter \(\lambda\), \(n\), and \(t\).

This is a documented selection of the original paper’s own inverse-polynomial, isometry-based guarantee from its broader question about an RSP-like protocol. The target is an implication between existence statements, not a prescribed black-box reduction or a requirement for negligible simulation error.
definitions:
A function \(\nu:\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(c\ge1\), there is \(\lambda_{0}\) such that \(\nu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for every \(\lambda\ge\lambda_{0}\). All negligible errors below are with respect to \(\lambda\).

Classical computation uses ordinary multitape Turing machines over a fixed finite alphabet, with unary security and public size parameters and binary strings as data. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Classical randomness consists of independent fair bits, each charged as a step. A uniform quantum computation has a classical polynomial-time machine that, on the unary public parameters, prints its polynomial-size circuit description. Circuits use the finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4})\), controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements, and classical Boolean control; ancillas start in \(|0\rangle\). Controlled-NOT maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\), and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Gates and wire indices have finite binary descriptions. Adaptive operations are controlled by recorded classical measurement results. Circuit generation, classical steps, quantum gates, measurements, output writing and communication are all charged. An interactive quantum strategy is a uniform sequence of these operations between messages, with total operations and qubits bounded by a fixed polynomial in the public input length on every branch. An inverse unitary can use the same gate set since \(T^{-1}=T^{7}\). The choice of this particular universal finite gate set is a modeling convention.

For adversarial computation and the auxiliary efficient procedures in the rigidity condition, allow quantum advice: a polynomial number of extra qubits in an arbitrary density operator depending on the public parameters but independent of the private challenge, client coins and hidden input. The advice need not be efficiently preparable. An advice family is fixed together with the algorithm before an experiment is sampled. Different public parameter tuples may have different advice, and all such families are quantified over. This uses the original full paper’s explicit advice convention, including in the hardness assumption. Honest protocol algorithms use no advice. An isometry is a linear map \(J\) satisfying \(J^{\dagger}J=I\); efficient implementation means a circuit of the preceding kind acting unitarily on the input with additional pure ancillas, retaining all output qubits. Pure quantum advice independent of the private input is permitted for such an auxiliary isometry. Mixed advice may be purified by enlarging the ancillary space. An efficiently preparable auxiliary state means the output of an efficient procedure under this same advice convention, not that its advice can itself be generated from a classical description.

The one-way-function premise \(\operatorname{QOWF}(F)\) has the following meaning. There are an output-length function \(\ell(\lambda)\ge1\), bounded by a fixed polynomial, and a single deterministic polynomial-time classical algorithm evaluating
\(F_{\lambda}:\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\)
on input \((1^{\lambda},x)\). For every uniform quantum polynomial-time inverter \(I\), with any polynomial-size quantum-advice family \((\eta_{\lambda})\), there is a negligible \(\nu_{I,\eta}\) such that
\[
\Pr_{x\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{\lambda}}\!\left[
z\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\ \land\ F_{\lambda}(z)=F_{\lambda}(x)
\ :\ z\leftarrow I(1^{\lambda},F_{\lambda}(x);\eta_{\lambda})
\right]\le\nu_{I,\eta}(\lambda).
\]
The probability includes the inverter’s measurements and random bits. Any preimage is a successful inversion; injectivity, a trapdoor, length preservation and hardness of recovering the particular sampled preimage are not required. The evaluator’s public program is available to the inverter, which may implement it coherently. There is no random oracle in this assumption.

The remote-state-preparation protocol \(\Pi=(A,B_{\mathrm{hon}})\) consists of a single probabilistic classical client algorithm \(A\) and a single uniform quantum honest-server algorithm \(B_{\mathrm{hon}}\). Their public inputs are \((1^{\lambda},1^{n},1^{t})\), with \(\lambda,n,t\ge1\), and only the client receives \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Inputs are encoded as the unary blocks separated by the fixed symbol \(\#\), followed on the client’s input tape by the binary basis string. The number of rounds, total communicated bits, client runtime, honest-server operations and honest-server qubits are bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(\lambda+n+t\). Communication is a reliable classical channel; any message produced by a quantum party is measured in the computational basis before delivery. Private classical coins are independent, and the honest parties initially share no secret, randomness or entanglement. There are no oracles, quantum messages, auxiliary devices, additional servers or trusted setup. The protocol specifies polynomial message-length and round limits, with a malformed or overlong message, missing prescribed response, or limit violation causing the client to abort. The client finally outputs an accept/reject flag and, when accepting, the classical string \(v\). The server may retain its entire transcript and private quantum workspace.

For fixed \(\lambda,n,t,\theta\), define the ideal classical–quantum state on registers \(WQ\) by
\[
\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}
=2^{-n}\sum_{v\in\{0,1\}^{n}}|v\rangle\langle v|_{W}
\otimes|\psi_{v,\theta}\rangle\langle\psi_{v,\theta}|_{Q}.
\]
Here \(W\) is a classical register represented in its computational basis, and \(Q\) contains \(n\) qubits. A density operator is a positive semidefinite operator of trace one; a subnormalized state has trace at most one. The trace norm is \(\|X\|_{1}=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^{\dagger}X}\), and trace distance is \(\tfrac12\|X-Y\|_{1}\).

Completeness and honest correctness mean the following. For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), there is a negligible function \(\mu_{c}\) such that for all \(\lambda\), all \(1\le n,t\le\lambda^{c}\), and every basis string \(\theta\), the honest run accepts with probability at least \(1-\mu_{c}(\lambda)\). Let \(\rho^{\theta,\mathrm{hon}}_{WQ,\mathrm{acc}}\) be its accepted joint output, after tracing out other registers and weighting by the acceptance probability. Require
\[
\tfrac12\bigl\|\rho^{\theta,\mathrm{hon}}_{WQ,\mathrm{acc}}-
\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}\bigr\|_{1}\le\mu_{c}(\lambda).
\]
Thus no exact correctness or perfect acceptance is imposed, and uniformity of the honest value string is included in the guarantee.

For soundness, let \(B^{*}\) be any quantum polynomial-time interactive server, including a fixed quantum-advice family independent of \(\theta\). Let \(P\) be all its final registers, including classical transcripts, and write
\[
\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}
=\Pr[\mathrm{acc}\mid\theta]\,
\rho^{\theta}_{WP\mid\mathrm{acc}},
\qquad p_{\theta}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}.
\]
The accepted operator is defined as zero when acceptance has probability zero, so conditional normalization is never needed. There must exist a family of efficiently implementable isometries
\(J_{\lambda,n,t}:P\to QB\)
and efficiently preparable normalized states \(\alpha_{\lambda,n,t}\) on the residual register \(B\). Their algorithms, dimensions and polynomial resource bounds may depend on \(B^{*}\) and its fixed advice family, and their values may depend on the public tuple \((\lambda,n,t)\). They must be chosen before the distinguisher, must not depend on \(\theta\) or \(v\), and act only on the server’s systems and independent ancillas. All advice used by these auxiliary procedures is independent of \(\theta,v\) and the sampled protocol randomness.

Define the two subnormalized operators
\[
R^{\theta}=(I_{W}\otimes J_{\lambda,n,t})\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}
(I_{W}\otimes J_{\lambda,n,t})^{\dagger},
\qquad
S^{\theta}=p_{\theta}\,\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}\otimes\alpha_{\lambda,n,t}.
\]
For every quantum polynomial-time distinguisher \(D\), including its independent polynomial-size quantum advice, and every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), there must be a negligible function \(\nu_{B^{*},D,c}\) such that, simultaneously for every \(\lambda\), every \(1\le n,t\le\lambda^{c}\), and every \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\),
\[
\left|\Pr[D(R^{\theta})=1]-\Pr[D(S^{\theta})=1]\right|
\le\frac1t+\nu_{B^{*},D,c}(\lambda).
\]
The distinguisher receives the public tuple and \(\theta\), as well as registers \(WQB\), but no additional client workspace, private randomness or secret data. Allowing the fixed basis as a test parameter makes explicit the source’s statement for each basis choice; it is not information sent to the server during the protocol. Its advice is independent of the sampled run. For a subnormalized operator \(X\), the expression \(\Pr[D(X)=1]\) denotes the linear acceptance functional \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_{D}X)\), where \(0\le E_{D}\le I\) is the effect implemented by \(D\), including its fixed advice. This convention applies without dividing by \(\operatorname{Tr}X\).

The soundness quantifier order is: choose the protocol, then quantify over the malicious server and its advice, then choose its common extraction isometry and auxiliary-state procedures, then quantify over distinguishers and polynomial parameter ranges, then choose the negligible errors, and finally quantify over parameters and basis strings. No lower bound on a malicious server’s acceptance probability is required. Only accepted mass is constrained, and its weight \(p_{\theta}\) is retained; no additional claim about the rejected output is imposed. The adjustable accuracy has polynomial cost in \(t\), and security is required when \(n,t\) are polynomially bounded in \(\lambda\). It therefore specifies arbitrarily adjustable inverse-polynomial soundness, not a single polynomial-time protocol with negligible soundness, and not a composable simulation definition.

The selected guarantee follows the roles, output states, efficient-isometry form and quantum-advice convention of the source’s Theorem 4.33 and Corollary 4.35. Packaging accuracy as a unary input and giving explicit uniform parameter-range and gate conventions are editorial precisions. The original question also discusses RSP with sufficiently strong parameters for further cryptographic applications; this card does not identify that stronger possibility with the guarantee selected here.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
(\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F))
\Rightarrow(\exists\Pi\;\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi))
\]
or its logical negation, for exactly the definitions above.

A positive answer must establish the existence of the client and honest-server algorithms, their uniform polynomial bounds, negligible honest correctness error, and the accepted-state rigidity property with its full malicious-server, advice, isometry, auxiliary-state, distinguisher and parameter quantifiers, using only the stated existence of a quantum-advice-secure classical one-way function. No efficient compiler taking an arbitrary one-way-function description as input, black-box use of that function, or preservation of a supplied security parameter is required beyond the definitions.

A negative answer must prove both
\[
\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall\Pi\;\neg\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi).
\]
The second quantifier ranges over all finite descriptions of protocol pairs in the stated standard model; failure may concern uniform efficiency, completeness, correctness or the entire quantified soundness property. Merely showing that one proposed construction fails, that a black-box reduction is impossible relative to an oracle, or that a stronger perfect-correctness, negligible-error or composable functionality is impossible does not refute this implication. Conversely, a protocol under a stronger cryptographic assumption or for only an honest or classical server does not establish the positive implication. No numerical-answer tolerance replaces any error bound in this criterion.

title: Efficient approximation of the optimal dihedral measurement
importance_reason: A concrete implementation barrier for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem, connecting optimal quantum measurements to subset-sum structure and lattice-related quantum algorithms.
formal: Can the specific pretty good measurement \(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1},E_{\bot}\}\) defined below be approximated by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits to every requested inverse-polynomial accuracy? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic circuit generator and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), number of copies \(k\ge1\), and precision parameter \(m\ge2\), it runs in time at most \(p(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+k+m)\) and produces a circuit with at most that many gates and ancilla qubits whose output distribution satisfies \[\sup_{\sigma}\frac12\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z_N\cup\{\bot\}}\left|\Pr[C_{N,k,m}(\sigma)=j]-\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\right|\le\frac1m?\] The supremum ranges over all input density matrices on \((\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The circuit receives one such state and returns one classical outcome. The selected target concerns this concrete measurement, without requiring a particular unitary realization or a Subset Sum algorithm.
question_excerpt: Can the optimal dihedral measurement be implemented efficiently without requiring the known coherent subset-sum-sampling construction?
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), with addition modulo \(N\). For a hidden shift \(s\in\mathbb Z_N\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_N\), let \[|c_x^{(s)}\rangle=\frac{|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \rho_s=\frac1N\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_N}|c_x^{(s)}\rangle\langle c_x^{(s)}|.\] Thus \(\rho_s\) is the mixed state obtained by a uniform unknown coset offset. For \(k\) independent samples with the same shift, the state is \(\tau_s=\rho_s^{\otimes k}\) on \(\mathcal H_{N,k}=(\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The discrimination ensemble assigns prior probability \(1/N\) to each shift \(s\). Both this prior and the average over coset offsets are part of the definition; neither \(s\) nor the offsets are supplied to the implementing circuit.

For this ensemble define \[G=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z_N}\tau_s,\qquad E_s=G^{-1/2}\tau_sG^{-1/2},\qquad E_{\bot}=I-P_G.\] The inverse square root is the inverse on the support: if \(G=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda\) is its spectral decomposition, then \(G^{-1/2}=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1/2}P_\lambda\), with value zero on the kernel, and \(P_G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda\). Every \(E_s\) is positive semidefinite and \(\sum_sE_s=P_G\). Adding \(E_{\bot}\) makes the sum the identity on the entire input space. A positive operator-valued measure is such a finite collection of positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; its outcome probabilities on state \(\sigma\) are \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one. Hermitian means \(\sigma=\sigma^\dagger\), with dagger conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\sigma v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\). The above expression, including its kernel convention, fully specifies the measurement even when \(G\) is singular. On each \(\tau_s\), outcome \(\bot\) has probability zero. The source associates that complementary outcome with the trivial hidden subgroup, but optimality is asserted for the uniform ensemble of order-two subgroups.

The classical generator receives \(N\) in binary and \(k,m\) in unary. This makes the error tolerance \(1/m\) and the polynomial dependence on its reciprocal explicit. The target does not demand polynomial dependence on \(\log m\). Each \(N\)-dimensional register is embedded in \(q=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) qubits by the binary basis encodings of \(0,\ldots,N-1\); the input therefore uses \(k(q+1)\) qubits. No correctness condition is imposed on states outside that valid encoded subspace. The given state can be mixed, entangled across copies, and unrelated to an actual hidden shift; the error bound specifies the measurement on its whole valid input space. The circuit receives no further copies or a state-preparation oracle. It may consume the input, and no condition is imposed on the remaining quantum state after it outputs the label. In particular, this is a guarantee for classical outcome distributions, not for a prescribed post-measurement state or a particular coherent circuit extension.

Ancillas start in zero, and the circuit uses the fixed gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] These act on the indicated wires and as identity elsewhere; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i^2=-1\). A final computational-basis measurement produces a binary outcome label, with \(0,\ldots,N-1\) interpreted as shifts and every remaining label mapped to \(\bot\). Ordinary finite gates and classical bit operations have unit cost, so no arbitrary real matrix is supplied as one free gate. There is no nonuniform advice, extra oracle, postselection or unbounded repeat-until-success loop. The displayed half-sum is total variation distance between the actual and specified outcome distributions; it is the largest difference in probabilities of an event defined by a set of labels. The requirement is uniform in the input state and every finite \(N,k,m\), with one polynomial and generator for the whole family. It asks for a sample from the distribution, not an explicit list of its \(N+1\) probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the displayed uniform approximation family exists, including the circuit-generation and gate bounds and its total-variation guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such polynomially bounded family exists. A negative proof must cover all implementations of these outcome probabilities, not merely a prescribed subset-sum-basis unitary or a chosen extension to a larger Hilbert space. A different measurement with a good success probability for recovering the hidden shift does not by itself implement the specified POVM. Agreement only on the average success rate, or only on the coset ensemble without the uniform-input error guarantee, is insufficient for this precise implementation target. Exponential dependence on \(\log N\), \(k\), or the unary precision parameter does not meet the resource bound. This is a yes/no efficiency question with accuracy quantified in its definition, not a numerical output problem requiring only a fixed additive tolerance.
context:
The imported card combined implementation of an optimal measurement with the broader relation between the dihedral problem and random Subset Sum at different densities. On 16 September 2026 the user selected efficient approximation of the specific measurement. The present target records that narrowing and explicitly fixes its statistical error criterion and unary inverse-accuracy parameter. The wider reduction question is not claimed answered.

Bacon, Childs and van Dam prove that the displayed pretty good measurement maximizes the probability of identifying a uniformly random hidden shift from the coset-state ensemble. Optimality is an information-theoretic statement: it does not bound the number of elementary gates needed to carry out the measurement.

Their Theorem 2 gives success probability at least \(1/8\) once \(k\ge\log_2N+4\), and bounds it above by \(2^k/N\) for every \(N,k\). Thus enough copies can contain useful information even while extracting that information efficiently remains difficult. The chosen implementation target permits all copy counts and does not select a random Subset Sum density.

The earlier implementation analysis connects coherent uniform sampling of subset-sum solutions with an implementation of the optimal measurement. Its converse imposes a particular refinement and unitary realization. The 2016 source studies further restricted types of subset-sum-basis unitaries and derives consequences for subset-sum collision problems. Those statements do not prove a lower bound for every possible circuit with the same measurement statistics.

The later dihedral survey continues to separate the existence and success rate of an optimal measurement from its efficient implementation. Its exact-recovery no-go statements concern deterministic recovery from nonorthogonal samples, not approximation of the probabilistic measurement defined here.

The August 2026 semidirect-product algorithms apply under explicit restrictions on the abelian factor and the acting prime. For the dihedral action that prime is two, and the required ratio condition does not cover arbitrary cyclic order. Those results therefore do not supply this general measurement implementation.
why: This isolates the cost of extracting the information already present in dihedral coset states. An efficient implementation would turn a provably optimal measurement into an algorithmic resource, while a general impossibility theorem would distinguish measurement optimality from computational feasibility.

No uniform polynomial-size approximation meeting the stated full-input distribution guarantee, or general nonexistence theorem, was identified. Restricted coherent-implementation hardness is not claimed for all POVM realizations. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

working_summary: The selected question asks for efficient approximation of one explicitly defined optimal quantum measurement. Its input space contains several dihedral coset-state registers, and its outcomes are candidate hidden shifts plus a complementary outcome. The measurement is defined by the inverse square root of the sum of the ensemble states, with an explicit convention on its kernel. The required circuit must reproduce its outcome distribution uniformly on valid inputs to any requested inverse-polynomial accuracy. Known subset-sum connections constrain particular unitary implementations and do not establish hardness for every measurement circuit.

title: Parity versus \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) with shallow quantum preprocessing
importance_reason: A concrete hybrid circuit lower-bound challenge for a canonical function, connecting shallow quantum processing with a major classical circuit barrier while avoiding the ambiguity of unrestricted quantum gate arity.
formal: Does every polynomial-size constant-depth classical \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) circuit with polynomial-size constant-depth quantum preprocessing have asymptotically zero correlation with parity? Precisely, for every polynomial \(p\), constant \(d\in\mathbb N\), and sequence \((C_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the model and bounds below, is \[\left|2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\ \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}}\Pr[C_n(x)=y]f_n(y)(-1)^{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad(n\longrightarrow\infty)?\] Here \(m(n)\le p(n)\) zero-initialized ancillary qubits are allowed, both circuit stages have depth at most \(d\), and both have polynomial size bounded by \(p(n)\). There is no geometric locality, uniformity or clean-ancilla condition.
question_excerpt: \(\mathrm{AC}^0\circ\mathrm{QNC}^0\) cannot maintain constant correlation with parity as the input length grows.
definitions:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), parity in the sign convention is \(\operatorname{Par}_n(x)=(-1)^{x_1+\cdots+x_n}\). The quantum circuit \(C_n\) begins in the computational-basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{m(n)}\rangle\). A qubit is a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the full register has state space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes(n+m(n))}\). A gate is any unitary on one or two qubits, acting as identity on the others. Unitary means \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Gates are arranged in layers, with disjoint supports in each layer. The number of layers is the quantum depth, at most \(d\); the total number of nonidentity gates is at most \(p(n)\). Any two wires may interact. The ancillary count is separately bounded by \(p(n)\), including ancillary wires that are only measured.

All output wires are measured once in the computational basis. If the product of the layers is \(U_n\), the resulting bit string \(y\) has probability \[\Pr[C_n(x)=y]=|\langle y|U_n|x,0^{m(n)}\rangle|^2.\] There are no intermediate measurements, adaptive gate choices or postselection. No ancillary wire has to return to zero, and garbage is allowed. The initial ancillas are zeros, not arbitrary input-dependent advice states. Gates may depend on \(n\) and may have arbitrary complex entries satisfying unitarity: this is the source's nonuniform circuit lower-bound model, not a uniform algorithm with free real-number input. Consequently no fixed finite gate alphabet or efficient gate-description requirement is imposed.

The classical postprocessor \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}\to\{-1,1\}\) is a finite Boolean circuit of unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and fan-in-one NOT gates, with constants permitted. Its underlying output bit \(b\) is interpreted as \((-1)^b\). Classical depth is the greatest number of gates on an input-to-output path and is at most \(d\). Its number of gates is at most \(p(n)\); repeated identical incoming wires can be omitted. Including wires in the size instead gives an equivalent polynomial-size family, since the vertex count is polynomial. There are no parity gates, arbitrary Boolean lookup-table gates, threshold gates or extra classical advice inputs. The entire classical circuit is allowed to depend nonuniformly on \(n\).

The two stages are composed once: measure the quantum output, then apply the deterministic classical circuit to that outcome. The correlation is the expectation of \(f_n(Y)\operatorname{Par}_n(X)\) when \(X\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) follows the Born probabilities above. There is no promise on the input Hamming weight. The average success probability at computing sign parity is \((1+\operatorname{Corr}_n)/2\). Correlation is signed; the displayed limit of its absolute value is equivalent to the source's limit \(\operatorname{Corr}_n\to0\). It also rules out a persistent advantage after negating the output.

The polynomial, depth and circuit sequence are fixed before taking the limit, but are otherwise arbitrary. Equivalently, for each such choice and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an \(N\) such that \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\). No particular rate of decay is requested. A refutation can consist of one polynomially bounded sequence and one \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|\ge\varepsilon\) at infinitely many input lengths; constant correlation at every length is sufficient but is not necessary for a negative answer.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified zero-correlation limit, or a complete Lean-checked refutation under the same gate, ancilla, depth, size and average-input conventions. A positive result must allow every polynomially bounded number of zero ancillas and every polynomial-size classical postprocessor. Ancilla-free preprocessing, linear-size classical circuits, geometric restrictions, uniform families, a finite restricted gate set or a worst-case statement about one input do not cover the whole conjecture. A negative result must supply a circuit sequence with a proved failure of convergence; search or sampling advantages for another task do not suffice. This is an exact asymptotic proposition, not a request to estimate a correlation at finitely many sizes.
context:
A single output qubit of a shallow bounded-fan-in quantum circuit depends on only a bounded number of input wires. The hybrid model instead measures all wires and lets the classical circuit use their joint outcome. The source asks whether this combination can overcome the classical constant-depth limitation on computing parity.

Conjecture3 is a correlation statement over uniformly random classical inputs and quantum measurement outcomes. It is stronger than ruling out exact computation. The source uses arbitrary two-qubit unitaries, polynomially many zero ancillas and no locality or clean-computation restriction; those choices are preserved here.

The source proves a bound of the form \(2^{-n/\operatorname{polylog}n}\) for ancilla-free preprocessing and general polynomial-size classical postprocessing. Its separate linear-classical-size theorem permits general shallow quantum preprocessing, even with quantum advice. Neither theorem covers both polynomially many ancillas and arbitrary polynomial-size classical postprocessing at once.

The ITCS2026 follow-up studies unconditional pseudorandomness against shallow quantum and hybrid circuits. Its introductory comparison repeats the ancilla-free and linear-classical-size parity results. Its broader ancilla allowance for QNC0 alone and its restricted-ancilla hybrid pseudorandomness theorem are different statements from this full parity-correlation conjecture.

This model does not insert unbounded quantum fanout or other large-arity quantum gates. Results about such QAC0 models cannot be substituted solely because both circuit families have constant depth. Likewise, a quantum advantage for a promise search relation does not directly supply a parity decision circuit.
why: Parity is a basic test of global information processing. Resolving this conjecture would show whether very shallow quantum preprocessing can give weak classical decision circuits a persistent advantage on a canonical Boolean function, beyond known quantum search and sampling separations.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September2026 the original full Conjecture3, Definitions1/12, Theorems4/6 and corresponding formal corollaries were checked. The ITCS2026 pseudorandomness paper was checked for its introduction, hybrid model, parity comparison and ancilla-qualified statements, alongside bounded later-work searches. No full polynomial-ancilla, polynomial-classical-size parity correlation resolution was identified. Neither cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
