working_summary: Parity is a basic function that small constant-depth classical circuits cannot approximate well on uniformly random inputs. This project asks whether a shallow quantum preprocessing stage can remove that limitation when its measured output is passed to a classical AC0 circuit. The conjecture concerns constant-depth quantum circuits with bounded-fan-in gates, followed by the specified classical postprocessing. Any approximation guarantee must account for both the random input and the randomness of quantum measurement. Establishing the conjecture would place a concrete limit on hybrid computation and help clarify the power of weak classical procedures that use shallow quantum devices.

title: A finite quantum gate set with decision power strictly between P and BQP
importance_reason: A fundamental structural question about quantum computational resources. The selected strict decision-class target is exceptionally strong and entails P differing from BQP; sampling evidence must therefore be kept separate.
formal:
Does there exist a finite set \(G\) of constant-arity unitary quantum gates with algebraic complex matrix entries such that
\[
\mathrm P\subsetneq Q_G\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP},
\]
and \(G\) is not contained in any common one-qubit conjugate of the Clifford gates? The bounded-error decision class \(Q_G\), the circuit interface, and the conjugation exclusion are defined below. Both strict containments are unconditional parts of the assertion.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether gate sets other than conjugated stabilizer gates can have complexity neither contained in P nor equal to BQP. Its surrounding examples also involve sampling. The user explicitly selected a decision class strictly between P and BQP. Finite algebraic gates, input-dependent uniform circuit generation, basis-state initialization and a single final output qubit specify that interpretation; they are editorial model conventions rather than a verbatim theorem from the source.
definitions:
A \(k\)-qubit gate is a \(2^k\)-by-\(2^k\) complex unitary matrix, for an integer \(k\ge1\). The set \(G\) is finite and independent of input length; its maximum arity is therefore a constant. Each matrix entry is algebraic over \(\mathbb Q\), and each gate can be specified exactly by its minimal polynomials and isolating data for the real and imaginary parts. These fixed descriptions are not input-dependent advice. Algebraicity is an explicit editorial finite-description convention.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is in \(Q_G\) if one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on each input \(x\), produces a polynomial-size circuit description \(C_x\) with polynomially many qubits, a computational-basis initial string \(b_x\), and one designated output qubit. Initialize the state to \(|b_x\rangle\). A gate from \(G\) may be applied to any ordered tuple of distinct qubits of the correct arity, with identity on all other qubits. There are no geometry or depth restrictions beyond the polynomial size bound. At the end, measure only the designated output qubit in the computational basis. Require
\[
x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\ge2/3,
\qquad
x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\le1/3.
\]
The generator and polynomial bound may depend on \(L\) and \(G\), but not nonuniformly on input length. They count all classical bit operations. The generator may prepare additional \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) qubits by specifying them in \(b_x\), but no other initial states. Wires may be named arbitrarily. Only gates listed in \(G\) are available: inverses, controlled variants, and arbitrary one-qubit gates are not free. Intermediate measurements, postselection, classically controlled quantum branches, quantum advice, and joint-output sampling followed by unrestricted classical postprocessing are not part of this interface. The final single-bit output convention makes the selected decision target precise.

The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decidable by one deterministic polynomial-bit-time Turing machine. Define \(\mathrm{BQP}\) by the same uniform bounded-error circuit convention using the universal gates
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad
\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle.
\]
Classical preprocessing and basis preparation imply \(\mathrm P\subseteq Q_G\). Fixed algebraic gates are efficiently approximable, so \(Q_G\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). The strictness requirements mean that some language in \(Q_G\) is not in \(\mathrm P\), and some language in \(\mathrm{BQP}\) is not in \(Q_G\). Merely failing to densely generate every unitary is insufficient, since encoded computation can still give full BQP power.

For the Clifford exclusion, let
\[
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and let \(\mathcal P_k=\{i^j P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_k:j\in\{0,1,2,3\},\ P_i\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}\}\) be the Pauli group. The Clifford group consists of the unitaries \(V\) satisfying \(V\mathcal P_kV^\dagger=\mathcal P_k\); global phase is immaterial. Require that there is no one-qubit unitary \(U\) such that, for every \(g\in G\) of arity \(k\),
\[
U^{\otimes k}g(U^\dagger)^{\otimes k}
\]
is Clifford. The same \(U\) must be tested for all gates, but it may be any complex unitary, not only an algebraic one. The condition is a structural exclusion, not an additional allowed operation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of existence of a finite algebraic gate set satisfying both strict decision-class containments and the common-conjugate Clifford exclusion. Conditional sampling hardness, universality only after postselection, a separation for nonuniform circuits, or physical nonuniversality alone does not settle the statement. A positive proof must establish both strictness assertions in the specified uniform single-output model.
context:
The classical reversible-gate classification motivates a quantum analogue. The source distinguishes dense unitary generation from universality through an encoding, and asks whether other finite gate sets support intermediate computational behavior.

Conjugated Clifford circuits illustrate why the output interface matters: their full output distribution can be difficult to sample under complexity assumptions, while individual output-bit probabilities have an efficient classical strong simulation. They therefore do not supply the required decision separation in this card’s single-output model.

The October 2025 revision classifies weak multiplicative simulation for additional conjugated Clifford fragments, including commuting cases. Its quantum-advantage statements concern sampling and use a noncollapsing polynomial-hierarchy assumption; they do not establish either unconditional strict decision-class containment here.

A positive answer would in particular prove P distinct from BQP. Conversely, simply assuming that separation, excluding Clifford conjugates, or showing a generated group is not dense does not prove the displayed intermediate-class assertion.
why: A genuine intermediate decision class generated only by a finite gate set would expose a computational regime beyond deterministic classical computation but below universal quantum computation. It would distinguish gate-induced limitations from restrictions on depth, state preparation or geometry.
status_note: The source’s gate-set program remains unresolved for this user-selected strict decision-class interpretation in the bounded checks through 18 September 2026. The displayed model is an explicit specialization of an informal question. The reviewed 2018 and October 2025 classifications concern classical simulation, often of joint samples under assumptions; they do not prove P strictly contained in Q_G strictly contained in BQP. No exhaustive current-status or independent full-proof validation is claimed.
progress: 2017-01: The source poses the intermediate-gate-set question as part of the program of classifying quantum gate resources. | 2018-06: The conjugated-Clifford classification separates joint sampling hardness from easy simulation of a single output marginal. | 2025-10: The revised postselected-advantage criterion extends sampling classifications to additional Clifford fragments without resolving the selected decision-class problem.
working_summary: A finite quantum gate set determines which polynomial-size uniform circuits can be built from its operations. The user-selected question asks for a bounded-error decision class strictly larger than P and strictly smaller than BQP. The gates must also escape every common one-qubit conjugate of the Clifford group. The card fixes algebraic gates, computational-basis inputs and one final measured output bit to make the computational model precise. Known hardness results for sampling restricted circuits do not establish this stronger unconditional decision-class separation.

title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
importance_reason: Asks whether quantum information can encode useful nonuniform computational advice beyond classical advice of comparable size.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) as classes of languages without an oracle? Explicitly, for every language decidable by a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm supplied with a polynomial-size quantum advice state depending only on input length, does some uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm with polynomial-length classical advice decide the same language with error at most \(1/3\) on every input? The algorithm and polynomial advice bound may change. The reverse inclusion follows by encoding a classical advice string in the computational basis.
question_excerpt: Can every language decidable with polynomial-size quantum advice also be decided with polynomial-length classical advice, using an efficient quantum algorithm?
definitions: A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\); here every binary string must be decided, with no promise excluding some inputs. For each \(n\ge0\), let \(m(n),a(n)\) be nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed polynomial. A single deterministic classical Turing machine, given an input string \(x\) of length \(n\), generates in polynomial time a quantum circuit \(U_x\) with an \(m(n)\)-qubit advice register, \(a(n)\) ancillary qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), polynomially many gates, and one designated output qubit. The generating machine has no advice and no oracle. It uses the fixed exact gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), with \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit outputs the computational-basis measurement of its output qubit. The quantum advice family is a sequence \((\rho_n)_{n\ge0}\) of density matrices on \(\mathbb C^{2^{m(n)}}\). A density matrix is positive semidefinite with trace one; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho_nv\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The probability of output 1 is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1U_x\bigl(\rho_n\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a(n)}\bigr)U_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output 1 and is identity on the remaining qubits, and dagger denotes conjugate transpose. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\) if some such generating machine, polynomial bounds and advice family satisfy output-1 probability at least \(2/3\) for every \(x\in L\) and at most \(1/3\) for every \(x\notin L\). The same fixed \(\rho_n\) must work for all \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\). A fresh copy of that state is supplied for each independent computation; no cloning or repeated reuse of a consumed copy is promised. Advice is trusted: the requirement concerns the selected family, not all possible advice states. There is no computability or efficient-preparation requirement on the family, and its preparation cost is not charged. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) if the advice can instead be a binary string \(b_n\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), supplied as the basis state \(|b_n\rangle\). Its length may have a different polynomial bound and the circuit may be different, but \(b_n\) still depends only on \(n\), need not be computable, and must work for every length-\(n\) input. Both classes use uniform quantum computation in addition to the explicitly allowed nonuniform advice. BQP abbreviates bounded-error quantum polynomial time; poly and qpoly indicate classical-bit and quantum-qubit advice of polynomial length.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP/poly}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language has quantum advice as defined but no eligible classical-advice algorithm and family. An affirmative proof need not produce the classical advice efficiently, but must establish one length-indexed family and a uniform algorithm that work for all inputs. A negative proof must rule out every polynomial advice length, every classical advice family and every uniform quantum algorithm. A separation of promise problems alone does not automatically meet this card’s retained total-language target. Oracle separations, a difficult-to-describe state, or an advantage for advice selected after seeing the input do not suffice.
context:
Advice is fixed before the particular input is seen and is trusted to be the chosen length-specific information. It must support every input of that length. A witness, by contrast, may be selected for one instance and must be checked against dishonest alternatives. Neither comparison is obtained simply by changing the name of the auxiliary register.

Quantum advice is supplied as a fresh copy on each run. The definition does not assume the algorithm can clone an unknown state or preserve it for unlimited reuse. Classical advice can be copied, but the class comparison allows either algorithm to consume the supplied resource during its computation.

The advice families can be uncomputable in both models. The question concerns what polynomial-size information makes possible for the uniform computation, not how to construct that information. Allowing input-specific advice would remove the crucial requirement that one message works for all strings of a given length.

Aaronson proved \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{PP/poly}\). PP permits polynomial-time classical randomized computation with acceptance probability strictly greater than one half on yes-inputs and at most one half on no-inputs, without an inverse-polynomial margin; poly again permits length-specific classical advice. This upper bound uses a different computation model from bounded-error BQP, so it is not the desired simulation in BQP/poly.

The 2007 quantum-oracle separation demonstrated an advice advantage when both computations share a quantum black box. This supplies evidence in that augmented computation model and retains the oracle as an essential part of its statement.

The 2024 result separates the advice classes with an oracle encoding a classical function, but restricts even quantum algorithms to classical queries. This is a genuine precursor to the later standard classical-oracle theorem. Permitting superposition queries gives the classical-advice algorithm more power, so the access conventions must not be conflated.

The February 2026 construction, checked in its April revision, separates the advice classes using a standard classical oracle that both quantum algorithms may query in superposition. It resolves that oracle question while leaving the ordinary language equality asked here unresolved.
why: This compares the computational value of quantum and classical information stored in advance for an entire input length. It asks whether a short quantum state can support useful computations that no polynomial-length classical record can support, even when preparing either kind of advice is free. The shared-advice requirement makes this a different resource comparison from per-instance witnesses.
status_note: Source-open for the ordinary total-language advice comparison. On 16 September 2026 the April 2026 ECCC revision’s definitions, Theorem 1.2 and advice discussion, Aaronson’s primary PP/poly upper-bound abstract, and the primary 2007 and 2024 oracle results were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unrelativized language-class resolution. The classically accessible, quantumly accessible classical, and unitary oracle models are distinguished. The review does not independently verify the cited proofs or provide Lean formalizations.
progress: 2004–2005: Aaronson places quantum-advice bounded-error quantum computation inside PP with polynomial classical advice. | 2007: Aaronson–Kuperberg separate quantum and classical advice relative to a quantum oracle. | 2024: Li–Liu–Pelecanos–Yamakawa separate the advice classes relative to a classical oracle with classical-only access. | 2026-02 to 2026-04: Bostanci–Huang–Vaikuntanathan give the first standard classical-oracle advice separation; the checked revision is dated 12 April.
working_summary: Quantum and classical advice supply information fixed for an entire input length to an efficient quantum computation. The selected advice must decide every binary input of that length correctly with bounded error, and can be arbitrarily hard to prepare. The question asks whether quantum advice increases the resulting ordinary class of total languages. A known simulation by PP with classical advice uses a different error and computation model, while successive oracle separations retain their black boxes. The latest standard classical-oracle separation does not resolve the ordinary equality, and fresh-copy advice remains distinct from untrusted per-instance witnesses.

title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
importance_reason: Relates quantum query algorithms to polynomial approximation, connecting two core tools for quantum upper and lower bounds.
formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the extremal function \[M(n,d)=\max\bigl\{Q(f):\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ f:D\to\{0,1\},\ \operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le d\le n\). The bounded approximate degree \(\operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\) is the least total degree of a real polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[|p(x)-f(x)|\le1/3\quad(x\in D),\qquad 0\le p(x)\le1\quad(x\in\{0,1\}^n).\] The query measure \(Q\) has worst-case error at most \(1/3\). This makes the source's largest-gap question a two-parameter extremal query bound. The source's additional question of whether an exponential gap exists was answered affirmatively in 2023.
definitions:
A partial Boolean function has a nonempty promise domain \(D\) of valid inputs, with one prescribed output bit for each valid input. An algorithm knows the function and promise but receives the actual input only through its bit oracle. Correctness is required on \(D\). Its fixed query budget applies on every input, including inputs outside the promise, where the output bit may be arbitrary.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

A real polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in \(n\) real variables; its total degree is the largest sum of variable exponents in a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Multilinear polynomials suffice because \(x_i^j=x_i\) on Boolean inputs for \(j\ge1\). Their real coefficients have no bit-length or computability restriction. Boundedness is imposed only on the entire Boolean cube, not on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), and includes inputs outside the promise. Every partial Boolean function has a bounded exact representing polynomial of degree at most \(n\): extend its values to a total Boolean function and interpolate.

There are finitely many partial Boolean functions on a fixed cube, so the displayed maximum is over a finite set. It is nonempty and satisfies \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain, using a single input-bit function for the lower bound and reading all bits for the upper bound. The parameter \(n\) counts individual Boolean oracle bits. A symbol from a larger alphabet is not available in one query. Neither the promise nor the polynomial is supplied as an additional input-dependent oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified positive function \(H(n,d)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(cH(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le CH(n,d)\) throughout the stated integer domain. The answer must identify the asymptotic dependence on \(n,d\), not merely rename the defining optimization over functions or algorithms. Both a universal upper bound and matching worst-case examples are required. Exponential separation alone is already known and does not settle this full extremal target.
context:
A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.
why: Bounded approximate degree is the main numerical object behind the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds. Determining its worst possible discrepancy from actual quantum query complexity would quantify how much algorithmic difficulty this method can miss under promises.
status_note: The exponential-separation part of the 2021 question was resolved by Ambainis and Belovs at CCC 2023. The card retains the broader maximum-gap target as the explicit extremal curve M(n,d). The source, published separation and 2024 follow-up were checked on 2026-09-14; their checked theorems do not determine this curve, and a bounded later-work search found no complete characterization.
progress: 2021: Aaronson asks for the largest bounded-degree-versus-quantum-query gap for partial Boolean functions and whether it can be exponential. | 2023: Ambainis and Belovs prove an exponential separation, with full-cube boundedness retained after encoding the alphabet into Boolean bits. | 2024-10-21: Ben-David and Kundu reprove the partial-function exponential separation and establish related separations for stronger measures and total search problems.
working_summary: The question compares quantum query complexity with polynomials that approximate a promised Boolean function. The polynomial must remain between zero and one even on inputs outside the promise. The target is the largest quantum query complexity possible at each input length and bounded-degree budget. A 2023 theorem already proves that the gap can be exponential, so that subquestion is no longer open. The remaining task is to determine the full extremal bound up to universal multiplicative constants.

title: Limiting optimized QAOA energy in the SK model
importance_reason: The limiting optimized energy of QAOA asks whether a central quantum optimization ansatz can reach the statistical-mechanics optimum after taking the infinite-instance limit.
formal: Determine \(A=\sup _{p\ge 1} \sup _{\gamma ,\beta \in \mathbb{R} ^{p}} a_{p}(\gamma ,\beta )\), where \(a_{p}(\gamma ,\beta )=\lim _{n\to \infty} n^{- 1} E_{J}[\langle \psi _{p,J}(\gamma ,\beta )|H_{J}|\psi _{p,J}(\gamma ,\beta )\rangle ]\) for the Gaussian Sherrington–Kirkpatrick Hamiltonian and QAOA state defined below. The benchmark requires absolute error at most \(1/100\) in energy per spin.
question_excerpt: Encouraged by our findings, we conjecture that the large p performance of the QAOA will achieve the optimal cut fraction on large random D-regular graphs, […]
definitions: For \(n\ge 2\) let \(J_{ij}, 1\le i<j\le n\), be independent real normal random variables of mean 0 and variance 1. On \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes n}\), let \(Z_{i}\) and \(X_{i}\) act on the i-th qubit by the Pauli matrices \(Z=diag(1,- 1)\) and X with off-diagonal entries 1 and diagonal entries 0. Put \(H_{J}=n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_{i} Z_{j}\) and \(B_{n}=\sum_{i} X_{i}\). Let |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). For integer depth \(p\ge 1\) and fixed real angle vectors \(\gamma ,\beta \in \mathbb{R} ^{p}\), define |\(\psi _{p,J}\rangle =e^{- i\beta _{p} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{p} H_{J}}\cdots e^{- i\beta _{1} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{1} H_{J}}|+\rangle ^{\otimes n}\). Matrix exponentials have their usual convergent-series meaning; states have unit norm. Expectation is over J. The n limit exists for each fixed p and angles as established for this model in the source. Angles may depend on p but are fixed independently of n and J. First take the infinite-n ensemble limit for fixed angles, then optimize those angles, then take the supremum over finite depths. Supremum need not be attained. Identity layers imply that the optimized depth values are nondecreasing. They are bounded by \(\Pi *=\lim _{n\to \infty} E_{J}[\max _{z\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}} n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_{i} z_{j}]/n\), the finite Parisi ground-state value in this normalization. Maximization, rather than minimization, fixes the sign convention.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous value a and a Lean proof that |\(a- A|\le 1/100\), or certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) with the midpoint as answer. Exact determination also qualifies. Merely restating the defining supremum, reporting floating-point optimization at finitely many depths, or interchanging depth and instance-size limits is insufficient. Equality with \(\Pi\)* is a stronger possible answer, not assumed by the target.
context:
QAOA alternates evolution under an objective Hamiltonian and a simple mixing Hamiltonian. Here its optimized energy is measured on a standard random spin-glass ensemble after the number of spins tends to infinity.

Theorem 1 identifies this fixed-depth ensemble performance with the high-degree limit of the normalized MaxCut performance on large-girth regular graphs. This supplies a precise model for the original MaxCut question without assuming an interchange of limits.

Section 5 conjectures that the limiting optimized performance equals \(\Pi\)*, approximately 0.763166 in the source normalization. Asking for A with the benchmark numerical tolerance is a quantitative reformulation and is not logically equivalent to exact equality.

Letting depth grow on one fixed finite instance before taking the size limit gives a different question. The retained target fixes the ensemble-limit-first convention.
why: The limiting optimized energy of QAOA asks whether a central quantum optimization ansatz can reach the statistical-mechanics optimum after taking the infinite-instance limit.
status_note: The source conjectures the exact limiting optimum. The retained numerical task keeps its ensemble-limit-first convention; no rigorous determination within 0.01 was located.
progress: 2022: The source proves the fixed-depth SK/large-girth MaxCut equivalence and states the limiting Parisi-value conjecture in Section 5.
working_summary: QAOA is a widely studied quantum optimization ansatz using alternating objective and mixing operations. The SK model provides a canonical random quadratic objective with a known limiting optimum. The question asks for the best limiting energy reachable by finite-depth QAOA when depth is subsequently allowed to grow. Angles are optimized only after taking the infinite-size ensemble limit. The source conjectures that this limiting value reaches the Parisi optimum, and the card now accepts a proved numerical determination within 0.01.

title: Optimal quantum query complexity of uniformity testing
importance_reason: Uniformity is a canonical statistical testing task; its full quantum query tradeoff measures a fundamental advantage of coherent sample access.
formal: Determine \(Q(d,\varepsilon )\), the optimal worst-case quantum query complexity of distinguishing \(p=u_{d}\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})>\varepsilon\) with success probability at least 0.99, up to universal constant factors jointly for all integers \(d\ge 2\) and real \(0<\varepsilon \le 1/4\). Access is to an arbitrary distribution synthesizer with the precise oracle convention below.
definitions: Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots ,d\}, u_{d}(i)=1/d\) and \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})=(1/2)\sum_{i}|p_{i}- 1/d|\). The algorithm receives d and \(\varepsilon\) and oracle access to a unitary \(U_{p}\) satisfying \(U_{p}|0^{k}\rangle =\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}|i\rangle |\psi _{i}\rangle\), where each garbage state |\(\psi _{i}\rangle\) is normalized. The extension of \(U_{p}\) away from |\(0^{k}\rangle\) and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of \(U_{p}, U_{p}\dagger\) or controlled-\(U_{p}\); intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let \(Q(d,\varepsilon )\) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with \(p=u_{d}\) or \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})>\varepsilon\), taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,\varepsilon )\) and absolute constants \(a,A>0\) such that a \(g(d,\varepsilon )\le Q(d,\varepsilon )\le A g(d,\varepsilon )\) throughout the stated domain. Prove both bounds uniformly over its two parameters and all valid oracle implementations. A formula or certified evaluation rule may specify g; merely renaming Q is insufficient. This is an asymptotic query bound up to multiplicative constants, not pointwise additive 0.01 accuracy.
context:
Ordinary sample access reveals only independent outcomes. Coherent access to a sampler and its inverse permits interference between executions. This can reduce the number of calls needed to detect a departure from uniformity; a classical sample lower bound therefore does not automatically apply.

The paper establishes \(O(\min \{d^{1/3}/\varepsilon ^{4/3},\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon\})\) queries. The terms cross at \(\varepsilon =d^{-1/2}\): the first governs larger errors and the second smaller errors. The question asks whether any quantum tester can improve this full dependence.

The source recalls \(\Omega (d^{1/3})\) queries for constant \(\varepsilon\) and \(\Omega (1/\varepsilon )\) already on a two-element domain. Knowing both separately does not yield their conjectured joint dependence. For example, at \(\varepsilon =d^{-1/2}\) the target is \(\Omega (d)\).

For a string \(x\in [d]^{m}\), the standard oracle maps |\(j,z\rangle\) to |\(j,z\oplus x_{j}\rangle\) and defines \(p_{i}=|\{j:x_{j}=i\}|/m\). The authors also conjecture the same lower bound even with this structure available, in the worst case over m and x. This is a stronger claim than the arbitrary-synthesizer target selected here; fixed small m can cap the cost through reading the entire string.

The original conjecture predicts \(Q(d,\varepsilon )=\Theta (\min \{d^{1/3}\varepsilon ^{- 4/3},d^{1/2}\varepsilon ^{- 1}\})\), with its upper bound proved by the source. The retained target asks for the optimal joint function even if that candidate lower bound is false; it is not asserted to be logically equivalent to the conjecture.
why: Would identify the optimal joint dependence on domain size and accuracy for one of the basic distribution-testing tasks with coherent sampler access, clarifying the extent of quantum advantage over classical samples.
status_note: Conjecture, access definitions, version record and later-result searches checked through 12 September 2026. No matching general quantum-query lower bound was located; classical uniformity and quantum-state measurement results use different access models.
progress: 2025: The TQC paper supplies the matching candidate upper bound and states its optimality as Conjecture 2.
working_summary: Uniformity testing distinguishes a perfectly uniform distribution from one separated in total variation distance. The tester can coherently call a unitary preparing the distribution, its inverse and its controlled version. Its guarantee must hold for arbitrary garbage states and arbitrary valid unitary extensions. The target is the optimal query count jointly in domain size and distance, up to universal factors. The source supplies a candidate upper bound whose matching lower bound remains conjectural.

title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\)
importance_reason: Locating QMA(2) in a standard time class tests the computational effect of unentangled quantum witnesses.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{BQEXP}\)? In promise-problem terms, does every pair \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of binary strings that has a polynomial-time quantum verifier with two unentangled polynomial-size proofs also admit a uniform quantum algorithm running in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every promised input? The algorithm receives no proofs. The polynomial may depend on \(\Pi\) and its verifier, but not on the individual input of length \(n\).
definitions:
A promise problem specifies yes-inputs \(Y\) and no-inputs \(N\); on inputs outside \(Y\cup N\), a deciding algorithm has no correctness requirement but must still obey its resource bound. A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A pure state on \(w\) qubits is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\). Two unentangled proofs have the tensor-product form \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\), where each vector describes at most \(w(n)\) qubits for some polynomial \(w\). Arbitrary entanglement within either proof is allowed, but entanglement between the proofs is excluded.

Membership in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) means that one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on input \(x\), generates a quantum circuit \(V_x\) of polynomial size. The circuit takes the two proof registers and zero-initialized work qubits, and finally measures an output bit. Write \(a_x(\psi,\phi)\) for its acceptance probability. Its guarantees are \[x\in Y\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\ge2/3,\qquad x\in N\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\le1/3.\] The two proofs are sent once; there is no later interaction. The same definition results if mixed product states or convex mixtures of product states are permitted, by linearity of acceptance probability. The verifier need not certify that an arbitrarily supplied entangled pair is a product: unentanglement is the proof model's assumption.

Use the fixed finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT, acting on named wires. Circuit size counts every gate; every initialized or proof qubit counts toward the relevant qubit bound. Uniform generation outputs the full gate and wire list.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\) means that one deterministic circuit generator, on input \(x\) of length \(n\), runs in at most \(2^{p(n)}\) steps and outputs a circuit with at most \(2^{p(n)}\) gates and qubits, using the same finite gate set. The circuit begins with zero-initialized qubits, receives no proof or advice, and accepts yes-inputs with probability at least \(2/3\) and no-inputs with probability at most \(1/3\). Classical dependence on \(x\) is through the generator. Polynomial overheads in the generator and circuit can be absorbed into \(p\). No oracle or postselection is available. Probability in both models is ordinary quantum measurement probability.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. Inclusion requires a bounded-error, uniform exponential-time quantum decision procedure for every problem satisfying the stated two-proof verification definition. Separation requires a promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) with no such decision procedure. Simulations only for restricted verifiers, shorter proofs, or a different completeness-soundness gap do not suffice.
context:
Classically, two existential witnesses can simply be concatenated. In this quantum model, allowing an arbitrary joint state would remove the product restriction and give the ordinary single-proof model. That restriction is therefore part of the computational resource, rather than an incidental communication detail.

A known upper bound is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\), where \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) allows nondeterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). Guessing sufficiently accurate classical descriptions of the two states and verifying them explains this bound. Enumerating all such descriptions is much more expensive, so this does not give a deterministic or quantum exponential-time algorithm.

The 2026 hierarchy result gives a structural upper bound using competing quantifiers over pure quantum states. Its stated containments still end at nondeterministic exponential time. An existential/universal characterization does not itself implement a bounded-error quantum decision procedure.

The July 2026 work obtains exponential-time algorithms for a stoquastic restriction, designed to remove destructive interference. Its verifier restrictions are substantive, so those algorithms do not yield the requested simulation for general quantum verifiers.
why: Unentangled quantum proofs add a nonconvex constraint to quantum verification. An exponential-time quantum simulation would place a meaningful algorithmic limit on this model and clarify whether its power can be explained without nondeterministic exponential-time witness search.
status_note: The source explicitly asks this inclusion in January 2026. Primary definitions and the NEXP upper bound were checked together with July 2026 hierarchy and stoquastic results on 2026-09-14. None of those checked results supplies a BQEXP simulation for general QMA(2); this is a bounded literature check.

The verifier is polynomial-time and may process both proofs jointly, but the proofs must initially be a product state. The deciding algorithm must be uniform and have bounded error on every promised input. The standard upper bound uses nondeterministic exponential time, which does not give the requested algorithm. Recent quantified and stoquastic results concern different upper-bound models and leave this inclusion unresolved.

title: Polynomially many EPR pairs for bounded-error Boolean communication
importance_reason: A universal polynomial entanglement bound would control a resource currently left free in a central quantum communication model; a failure would show that even Boolean computation can require more shared quantum memory at essentially optimal communication.
formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C\ge1\), \(A\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n\ge1\), every promise set \(D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\), every Boolean function \(f:D\to\{0,1\}\), and every two-party quantum protocol computing \(f\) with worst-case error at most \(1/4\) using at most \(Q\ge1\) communicated qubits and arbitrary prior entanglement, there exists a protocol computing \(f\) with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(CQ\) communicated qubits and at most
\[
 \lfloor A(n+1)^d\rfloor
\]
shared EPR pairs initially? Both protocols may use arbitrary two-way interaction. The replacement may change all local operations and the message pattern; it need not reproduce the original shared state or its internal evolution.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether a large shared entangled state can be replaced by a smaller one if the communication protocol may also change. Its theorem shows that maximally entangled resources suffice as a type, while leaving the amount unresolved. The user selected a polynomial number of EPR pairs in the input length, constant communication overhead and a fixed constant error increase.
definitions:
Alice receives only \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), Bob receives only \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\), and the pair is promised to belong to \(D\). Both know the function, promise and protocol. Bob outputs one classical bit, which must equal \(f(x,y)\) with the stated probability on each promised pair. Total functions are the case \(D=\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\). Every promised input has one correct bit; the task is not to generate any of several jointly valid output pairs. There is no accuracy condition outside the promise.

A protocol uses finite-dimensional quantum registers divided between Alice and Bob. A state is a positive semidefinite complex matrix of trace one. The original shared resource may be any finite-dimensional bipartite state, fixed independently of the actual inputs. Its dimension may depend on \(n,f\) and the protocol without an a priori upper bound. Pure shared states suffice as a convention: a mixed state can be purified by assigning its purifying register to one party, with no initial communication charge. Private ancillas and private randomness are allowed, and local storage is unrestricted.

Local quantum operations act only on the acting party’s registers and may depend on its own input and its available classical outcomes. They are arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum channels or measurements, with no computational gate-count restriction. Concretely a channel is a map \(\rho\mapsto\sum_jK_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_jK_j^\dagger K_j=I\); a measurement may retain the outcome \(j\), which occurs with probability \(\operatorname{Tr}(K_j\rho K_j^\dagger)\). The matrices may have arbitrary complex entries. Input-independent protocol design is nonuniform in the function and input length; no efficient or effective compilation from the old protocol to the new one is required.

Sending a register of \(q\) qubits costs \(q\), summed in both directions over the whole execution. One transmitted classical bit also costs one, as an orthogonal qubit encoding. Messages, their lengths and whose turn it is must follow the prescribed protocol or be communicated through charged registers; timing and silence are not extra channels. There is no restriction to one message, simultaneous messages or a fixed number of rounds. The protocol has finite local dimensions and finitely many rounds, with the communication bound holding on every branch of its measurement outcomes. All communication used to prepare an auxiliary resource after the initial state is supplied counts toward this bound. Unlimited classical communication is not free.

An EPR pair is the pure two-qubit state
\[
 |\Phi^+\rangle=(|0\rangle_A|0\rangle_B+|1\rangle_A|1\rangle_B)/\sqrt2.
\]
The replacement begins with exactly a tensor product of at most \(\lfloor A(n+1)^d\rfloor\) such pairs, together with local product ancillas; it has no other shared quantum state or separate free shared random string. The parties may measure pairs to obtain shared random bits. The bound counts pairs, or equivalently initially entangled qubits held by either party, rather than the dimension of the shared Hilbert space. With \(e\) pairs, each entangled local register has dimension \(2^e\), so the selected polynomial-qubit bound permits an exponential Hilbert-space dimension. Entanglement need not be returned at the end and may be consumed.

The constants \(C,A,d\) are universal, independent of the function, promise, input length, original protocol, communication cost and original state dimension. The replacement protocol itself may depend on all of those except the private inputs. The polynomial bound concerns initial entanglement; entanglement subsequently generated by charged messages is allowed. The positive-cost convention \(Q\ge1\) avoids an irrelevant zero-cost normalization case. The chosen errors \(1/4\) and \(1/3\) specify a constant increase below one half; they do not ask for an arbitrarily accurate simulation or for a bound uniform in an additional accuracy parameter.

Only the computed Boolean answer and its worst-case error are to be preserved. In particular, the new protocol need not approximate the old transcript distribution, the parties’ final quantum states, their individual measurements or the original entangled state. Bounds that forbid changing those objects are different statements.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial-EPR simulation statement, including its communication, entanglement and per-input error bounds, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must rule out every choice of universal constants and polynomial exponent: for each candidate bound, there must be a Boolean function with an allowed original protocol but no allowed replacement meeting both budgets and the final error.

A lower bound for keeping the old operations fixed, for classical communication alone, for one-way or simultaneous-message protocols, for noisy entanglement, or for a relation with multiple valid outputs is insufficient. A lower bound excluding logarithmic or sublinear entanglement alone is also insufficient to rule out every polynomial amount. Numerical tolerance does not weaken these asymptotic resource and probability requirements.
context:
The 2019 theorem allows arbitrary prior entanglement to be replaced by EPR pairs at a constant-factor communication cost for fixed error. Its guarantee does not limit how many such pairs are supplied, which is the extra requirement here.

The 2023 partial-function separations impose classical communication or simultaneous-message restrictions on the replacement model. They demonstrate sensitivity to entanglement in those settings but do not rule out a fully interactive quantum replacement with a universal polynomial budget.

The revised 2026 separation uses relation problems with several valid joint outputs and distinguishes linear shared entanglement from sublinear or absent entanglement. It explicitly treats zero-communication function problems separately; this does not settle a polynomial entanglement bound for Boolean functions.

The September 2026 paper studies noisy shared resources. Even a polynomial lower bound on the number of noisy copies for a function does not refute the present allowance of polynomially many perfect EPR pairs.
why: Communication complexity counts the messages but usually gives the parties their shared entangled state for free. This question asks whether that hidden resource can always be bounded polynomially while keeping almost the same communication cost.
status_note: The checked source leaves reducing the amount of prior entanglement open while proving that EPR pairs suffice as its type, with constant communication overhead at fixed error. The 2023 restricted-model tradeoffs, April 2026 relational separation and September 2026 noisy-resource results do not settle the selected polynomial bound for unrestricted two-way quantum protocols computing Boolean functions. This is a bounded later-work check, not a certification of every cited proof.
progress: 2019: The CCC theorem establishes universality of EPR pairs as a resource type for partial and total Boolean communication, while leaving their required amount open. | 2023-07-10: CCC publishes entanglement-versus-communication separations for specified classical and simultaneous-message models. | 2026-04-17: The revised preprint gives a maximal relation-problem separation between entangled and unentangled two-way quantum communication. | 2026-09-04: A preprint studies noisy-entanglement communication and nonlocal games, a distinct resource model.
working_summary: The target is to replace arbitrary prior entanglement in a Boolean quantum communication protocol by polynomially many perfect EPR pairs. One universal polynomial in the input length must work for all functions and promises, with only a constant factor more qubit communication. The selected constant-error convention allows error to increase from one quarter to one third on every promised input. Both parties may change the entire protocol and interact freely, while local computation and storage remain unbounded. Known EPR-type universality and later restricted-model separations do not settle this amount bound; a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation is required.

title: Universal quantum stability of seeded extractors with output-linear error loss
importance_reason: A universal stability theorem would transfer a broad class of classical randomness extractors to quantum side-information settings with controlled parameter loss; a refutation would expose a structural limit on that transfer.
formal:
Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every classical \((k,\varepsilon)\) seeded extractor
\[
 F:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^d\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^m
\]
is quantum-proof with conditional min-entropy requirement
\[
 K=C\bigl(k+\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)
\]
and trace-distance error at most \(C m\sqrt{\varepsilon}\)? Quantify over all integers \(n,m\ge1\), \(d\ge0\), real \(0\le k\le n\), and \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Use the general, or weak, seeded-extractor definition below: the uniform independent seed is averaged out, and \(m\) counts the entire retained classical output.
question_excerpt: The TQC source asks whether arbitrary multi-bit seeded extractors retain security with quantum side information and points to the operator-space work. That work makes a quantitative conjecture: increasing the entropy requirement by a universal factor and a logarithmic error term should suffice for an error bounded by output length times the square root of the classical error, up to a universal constant.
definitions:
Write \(U_t\) for the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^t\), including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). The min-entropy of a distribution \(P_X\) is \(H_{\min}(X)=-\log_2\max_x P_X(x)\). A function \(F\) is a classical \((k,\varepsilon)\) seeded extractor if, for every distribution \(X\) on \(n\) bits satisfying \(H_{\min}(X)\ge k\), and an independent seed \(S\sim U_d\),
\[
 \frac12\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^m}
 \left|\Pr[F(X,S)=z]-2^{-m}\right|\le\varepsilon.
\]
The same function must work for all such input distributions. The question imposes no construction time, circuit-size, seed-length or output-length bound beyond these definitions. In particular, the quantified class includes arbitrary finite truth tables, not only named or efficiently evaluable extractors.

A classical-quantum input with side information \(E\) is a density matrix
\[
 \rho_{XE}=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|x\rangle\langle x|\otimes\rho_E^x,
 \qquad \rho_E^x\succeq0,\qquad
 \sum_x\operatorname{Tr}\rho_E^x=1,
\]
on the classical register \(X\) and an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space \(E\). Here the matrices \(\rho_E^x\) include their probability weights, and \(\rho_E=\sum_x\rho_E^x\). There is no bound on the dimension of \(E\), computational restriction on the adversary or rational-entry assumption. Define
\[
 p_{\mathrm{guess}}(X\mid E)_\rho
 =\max_{\substack{M_x\succeq0\\\sum_xM_x=I_E}}
   \sum_x\operatorname{Tr}(M_x\rho_E^x),\qquad
 H_{\min}(X\mid E)_\rho=-\log_2p_{\mathrm{guess}}(X\mid E)_\rho.
\]
The maximization is over all measurements with an outcome labeled by each possible input string: each \(M_x\) is positive semidefinite and their sum is the identity. This is unsmoothed conditional min-entropy, measuring the best probability of guessing the whole input.

The seed is uniform and independent of the entire state \(\rho_{XE}\), so the initial joint state is \(\rho_{XE}\otimes\tau_d\), where \(\tau_t=2^{-t}\sum_y|y\rangle\langle y|\) is the uniform classical state on \(t\) bits. After evaluating \(F\) and discarding \(X,S\), the retained state is
\[
 \rho_{ZE}=2^{-d}\sum_{s\in\{0,1\}^d}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}
 |F(x,s)\rangle\langle F(x,s)|\otimes\rho_E^x.
\]
Being quantum-proof at parameters \((K,\eta)\) means that every such input with \(H_{\min}(X\mid E)_\rho\ge K\) satisfies
\[
 \frac12\|\rho_{ZE}-\tau_m\otimes\rho_E\|_1\le\eta,
 \qquad \|A\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}.
\]
Thus the ideal output is uniform and independent of all side information, and security is measured against unrestricted measurements, not efficient distinguishers.

The entropy requirement is literally \(C(k+\log_2(1/\varepsilon))\), without rounding or truncation to \(n\). If it exceeds \(n\), no normalized classical-quantum input meets the premise and the implication is vacuous. If \(Cm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ge1\), the error bound is automatic because trace distance between states is at most one. The same constant \(C\) must work across all nonvacuous parameter regimes and all dimensions. Allowing separate universal constants for entropy and error would be equivalent by taking their maximum and then increasing to an integer.

For comparison, a strong seeded extractor \(G\) retains its seed and asks that \((S,G(X,S))\) be close to a uniform pair, also independent of \(E\) in the quantum case. It is represented here by \(F(x,s)=(s,G(x,s))\). In that representation \(m=d+m'\), where \(m'\) is the number of newly extracted bits. A stronger bound depending only on \(m'\) while revealing an arbitrarily long seed is not silently substituted for the general output-length formulation above. No independent-source or Markov condition is imposed on the single weak source and its quantum side information.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one universal constant satisfies the stated implication, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish that for every candidate constant there are parameters, a classically valid extractor and an allowed classical-quantum input meeting the increased entropy threshold whose output exceeds the claimed error. Failure at the original entropy threshold or with unchanged error is insufficient.

The theorem must cover arbitrary side-information dimension and arbitrary extractor functions. Proving it only for a particular construction, bounded quantum storage, one output bit, very high input entropy or a multi-source Markov model does not settle the question. There is no requested numerical approximation; the quantified error inequality itself is the exact target.
context:
Classical side information can be accommodated by a modest loss in entropy and error for any extractor. Quantum side information does not admit that immediate transfer, and known examples already rule out simply keeping the original parameters. The present question explicitly allows larger losses.

The operator-space paper gives generic quantum bounds for small outputs and for input entropy very close to its maximum. Their dependence on output length or the entropy deficit leaves the selected all-parameter estimate unresolved.

Several structured constructions, including suitable hashing and Trevisan-based extractors, have quantum-security proofs. Their existence does not establish the same guarantee for every function that passes the classical extractor test.

The corrected Cryptomite paper provides practical implementations and parameter analyses for specific extractors. Its construction and source-model guarantees illustrate useful positive results without supplying the universal stability statement here.
why: An adversary can store information about a weak random input in a quantum state. The question asks whether a classical extractor’s guarantee alone controls how much this changes the quality of its output, with a loss that grows only linearly in output length.
status_note: The checked operator-space source states this quantitative classical-to-quantum stability question as open. Its generic small-output and high-entropy bounds do not imply the requested estimate in all parameter regimes. The checked later construction literature, including the corrected November 2025 Cryptomite version, does not supply a resolution of this universal statement. Known failures of parameter-preserving quantum security do not by themselves refute the allowed entropy and error losses.
progress: 2016: The TQC paper identifies the general seeded multi-bit security question while proving a separate result for multi-source extractors in the Markov model. | 2017-05-04: The published operator-space version states the quantitative open question and records generic small-output and high-entropy bounds. | 2025-11-26: The corrected Cryptomite preprint supplies implementations and construction-specific quantum guarantees, without a universal classical-to-quantum stability theorem.
working_summary: The question asks whether every classical seeded extractor remains secure against arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum side information with a universal quantitative loss. The selected target increases required min-entropy to C times the sum of k and log base two of one over epsilon, and allows trace-distance error at most C times m times the square root of epsilon. One constant must work for every extractor and all parameters, without a bound on the adversary’s computation or storage dimension. The seed is averaged out in the general formulation; if retained as part of a strong extractor’s output, its bits count toward the output length m. Specific quantum-proof constructions and known parameter-preserving counterexamples do not settle this claim, which requires a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation.

title: Succinct entangled proofs with efficient provers
importance_reason: A broad quantum verification question for a canonical QMA-complete promise problem, joining information-theoretic soundness, two-prover separation, short communication and polynomial honest resources. The tension between succinctness and witness-dependent prover efficiency connects quantum complexity with feasible verification, beyond a single protocol’s parameter optimization.
formal: Does quantum circuit acceptance admit a uniform two-prover, one-round proof with a classical polynomial-time verifier, total classical communication \(O((\log(N+2))^k)\) for some fixed \(k\), completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\) against arbitrary entangled provers, such that the honest provers can prepare and execute their strategy in quantum polynomial time given polynomially many copies of an accepting witness? Here \(N\) is the explicit circuit-instance length, and the instance, efficiency and soundness requirements are defined below.
question_excerpt: The best of both worlds The essential reason that two-prover succinct verification remains an open problem is that nonlocal answer reduction is hard.
definitions: An instance is an explicitly listed quantum circuit \(U\) with \(w\) witness qubits, \(a\) auxiliary qubits initially in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a}\), and a designated output qubit. The wire counts are included in unary and each gate and its wire indices are explicitly encoded in binary, so the total bit length \(N\) bounds the numbers of gates and wires. Use the fixed universal gate set \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle\), for bits \(b,c\). Acceptance means measuring output one in the computational basis. A YES instance has a normalized witness \(|\psi\rangle\) for which acceptance is at least \(2/3\); a NO instance has acceptance at most \(1/3\) for every witness density matrix, meaning every positive semidefinite trace-one matrix on the witness register. The input is promised to satisfy one of these cases. All parties know the circuit. The verifier uses private independent random bits, sends one classical question to each of two separated provers, receives one classical answer from each, and accepts or rejects in worst-case polynomial time in \(N\). Each prover sees only its own question. The worst-case sum of both question lengths and both answer lengths is at most \(C(\log_2(N+2))^k\), for constants \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) independent of the instance and strategy. The verifier rejects overlong messages, and no uncharged timing or message-length channel is permitted. For completeness there must be fixed uniform quantum algorithms for setup and for each prover, and a fixed polynomial \(p\). For every YES instance some accepting witness \(|\psi\rangle\) enables the setup algorithm, given at most \(p(N)\) independent copies of \(|\psi\rangle\) and clean auxiliary qubits, to prepare the provers’ joint state using at most \(p(N)\) gates and qubits. Setup occurs before the verifier samples its questions and distributes the two shares of this state. Each local response then takes at most \(p(N)\) gates, qubits and classical computation steps. Uniform means that circuit descriptions and classical control are generated from the public instance and available local messages by fixed polynomial-time algorithms; arbitrary input-dependent advice is not supplied in addition to the witness copies. These algorithms may use the stated universal gates, computational-basis measurements and classical randomness and control. The resulting acceptance probability must be at least \(2/3\). For soundness, on every NO instance, acceptance must be at most \(1/3\) for every finite-dimensional shared state and every pair of local quantum measurement strategies, regardless of dimension or computational cost. In particular, a cheating strategy need not obey the honest resource bound. Its initial entanglement may depend on the instance but not on the verifier’s private questions. Neither honest nor cheating provers communicate after setup. All probabilities include the verifier’s randomness and measurement outcomes. This is an information-theoretically sound proof; no computational hardness assumption or security parameter is part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a verifier and uniform honest algorithms exist with some universal constants and polynomial bounds, or prove that no such protocol exists for the stated circuit promise problem. A positive answer must establish both efficient witness-dependent setup and local execution as well as soundness against unrestricted entangled cheating. Short questions with polynomial-length answers, a protocol with more than two provers or more rounds, an inefficient honest strategy, or a single-prover computational argument does not meet this particular target. The negation rules out every choice of the verifier, honest algorithms and fixed bounds; a limitation of one construction alone is insufficient.
context:
The circuit asks whether some quantum witness makes a known computation accept. The verifier sees the circuit description but receives only a very short classical exchange with two quantum devices. The witness itself need not have an efficiently computable classical description.

Entangled provers may share a joint quantum state before the test, even though they cannot exchange information while answering. Soundness must hold for every such cheating strategy. This is a stronger security demand than an argument whose guarantee assumes that cheating computations are efficient.

The honest side has a different resource requirement. Copies of a valid witness are allowed as input, but a vast precomputed state or an exponential computation hidden in setup is not. Natarajan and Nirkhe explicitly distinguish efficient setup from efficient responses, and explain why membership in a larger complexity class does not supply a witness-preserving efficient strategy.

Metger, Natarajan and Zhang identify succinct two-prover verification with efficient honest provers as unresolved. Their discussion distinguishes protocols with short questions from those with short total communication and distinguishes efficient honest strategies from general entangled proofs.

This card fixes the one-round nonlocal-game interpretation and ordinary polynomial verifier time. It expresses the quantum claim as an explicit circuit-acceptance promise problem and requires preparation from copies of an accepting circuit witness. It asks only for polylogarithmic total communication; it does not add the sharper logarithmic-question, constant-answer target of a quantum games PCP.

Fu, Mastel and Zhang’s 2025 paper gives two-prover, one-round succinct perfect-zero-knowledge proofs for every recursively enumerable language, a class that includes undecidable problems. Its main theorem does not supply polynomial-time honest preparation from QMA witness copies. An efficient simulator for zero knowledge is also not a pair of separated efficient provers.

Bartusek, Liu and Malavolta’s 2026 result broadens the assumptions under which succinct classical-verifier arguments for QMA exist: it assumes oblivious state preparation and collapsing hash functions. It remains a computational argument system. Its small communication therefore does not establish the unconditional two-prover proof requested here.
why: This asks whether a classical verifier can check general quantumly provable claims using very little communication while keeping the honest quantum resources polynomial. It joins three substantial demands—two separated provers, unconditional soundness and succinct communication—and would clarify the practical content of entangled proof systems beyond their unconstrained complexity-class power.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The 2024 primary sources explicitly retain this efficient-honest-prover target. Checked 2025 and 2026 results improve general MIP* zero knowledge or computational QMA arguments, without supplying this conjunction of requirements. No matching resolution was found in the bounded search, and the cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2024: The source identifies the simultaneous two-prover succinctness and honest-efficiency requirement as open, while constructing a single-prover argument under cryptographic assumptions. | 2025-10-01: Fu–Mastel–Zhang give succinct perfect-zero-knowledge entangled proofs for recursively enumerable languages without the honest witness-efficiency guarantee required here. | 2026-06-03: Bartusek–Liu–Malavolta broaden the assumptions for succinct classical-verifier QMA arguments. The guarantee remains computational rather than unconditional.
working_summary: The question asks a classical verifier to check a quantum circuit’s acceptance using two separated quantum provers. Both the questions and answers together must use only polylogarithmically many bits in the circuit description length. Honest provers must prepare and execute their shared strategy efficiently from polynomially many copies of a valid quantum witness. Cheating provers may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and unlimited computation, but cannot communicate while answering. Known succinct computational arguments and entangled proofs without efficient honest preparation do not supply all of these requirements.

title: Zero-free quantum partition functions with a tensor-product perturbation
importance_reason: This asks whether analytic absence of zeros still yields efficient deterministic approximation when a structured global perturbation breaks the multiplicativity used by existing counting methods. It isolates a barrier beyond ordinary noncommuting local Hamiltonians.
formal:
For every fixed integers \(q\ge2\), \(k,d\ge1\), positive rational \(J\), and rational \(R>1\), does there exist a deterministic classical algorithm with the following guarantee? Its input specifies a bounded-occurrence local Hamiltonian \(H=\sum_{j=1}^m h_j\) on \(n\ge1\) sites of dimension \(q\), a tensor-product Hermitian perturbation
\[
 H'=A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_n,\qquad \|H'\|\le1,
\]
and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Each \(h_j\) acts on at most \(k\) sites, has operator norm at most \(J\), and each site occurs in at most \(d\) terms. Under the promise
\[
 Z(z):=\operatorname{Tr}\exp(-zH+H')\ne0
 \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb C\text{ with }|z|<R,
\]
the algorithm must output a rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[
 |\widehat Z-Z(1)|\le\varepsilon Z(1)
\]
in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\). The polynomial may depend on the fixed parameters \(q,k,d,J,R\), but not on the instance or its accuracy.
question_excerpt: Section 3.4 asks for polynomial-time approximation of Tr exp(-beta H+H-prime) from zero-freeness. It shows that the multiplicative framework of the paper fails even when H-prime is a tensor product of one-site operators. The user selected this tensor-product case with operator norm at most one; the card fixes a zero-free disk, a bounded local input model and relative-error bit complexity.
definitions:
The Hilbert space is \((\mathbb C^q)^{\otimes n}\), with the standard tensor-product basis. A matrix is Hermitian when it equals its conjugate transpose. Its operator norm is \(\|B\|=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Bv\|_2\). The trace is the sum of diagonal entries, and the matrix exponential is the convergent series \(\exp(B)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}B^r/r!\). Thus the value \(Z(1)\) is a strictly positive real number, although \(Z(z)\) is generally complex for nonreal \(z\).

For each interaction the input lists a nonempty set \(S_j\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of at most \(k\) sites, in increasing order, and the full \(q^{|S_j|}\)-by-\(q^{|S_j|}\) matrix of \(h_j\) on those sites. It is extended by the identity on all other sites. Each site belongs to at most \(d\) of the listed supports; duplicate terms count separately. The empty list of terms is allowed, giving \(H=0\). An interaction is allowed to be the identity on some of its listed sites; this does not reduce the declared occurrence count.

Each \(A_i\) is supplied as a full Hermitian \(q\)-by-\(q\) matrix. The real and imaginary parts of every matrix entry are rational numbers, encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. All matrices are given explicitly on their listed local spaces; neither a succinct circuit for a full exponentially large matrix nor a matrix-entry oracle is used. The total input length \(L\) includes these entries, supports, \(n\), and the rational \(\varepsilon\). The bounds on Hermiticity, interaction norms, occurrence and \(\|H'\|\) are promises on the input.

The norm condition concerns the full tensor product. The individual factors need not each have norm at most one. The term \(H'\) may act on every site and is represented only by its supplied one-site factors. It is not an additional bounded-locality term, not a sum \(\sum_i A_i\), and not an operator multiplied outside the exponential. No commutation between the \(h_j\), between different interactions, or between \(H\) and \(H'\) is assumed.

The zero-free disk has a fixed positive margin around the target point \(1\): its radius \(R>1\) is fixed before choosing an input. Its promise ranges over every complex point of the disk, not merely real temperatures. No proof of zero-freeness, exact partition value at zero, Taylor coefficients or auxiliary evaluation oracle is supplied. In particular, the algorithm must obtain all numerical information from the explicit local input. Zero-freeness is promised only for \(Z\) of the full input; it is not separately required after deleting sites or interactions. A result based on a stronger high-temperature condition does not by itself cover this entire promise class.

Polynomial time means that for every fixed \(q,k,d,J,R\) there exist an algorithm and constants \(C,a\ge1\) whose running time is at most \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1)^a\) elementary steps of a deterministic multitape Turing machine. The bound includes finite-precision arithmetic and writing the rational output. The machine must terminate within its polynomial clock even on encodings outside the promises, but its approximation guarantee is required only on promised inputs. No efficient uniform dependence on the fixed parameters, in particular as \(R\) tends to one, is required. This fixes a precise disk version of the source’s broader question about zero-free regions.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated approximation scheme exists for every fixed parameter tuple, including the promised input class, relative error and classical bit-time bound, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. An algorithm for a single fixed accuracy, a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm, or a quantum algorithm alone does not establish the target.

A negative answer must refute this existence statement for at least one fixed parameter tuple. Conditional hardness may document progress, but without the needed hardness assumption it is not an unconditional refutation. A lower bound for unrestricted global perturbations, an input oracle model, or instances whose zero-free margin shrinks with input size does not refute this card. The benchmark’s numerical absolute-error convention does not replace the relative-error guarantee of the algorithmic proposition.
context:
The source proves a deterministic approximation theorem for bounded-occurrence local quantum Hamiltonians, also allowing a tensorized measurement outside the exponential. The selected additive perturbation lies inside the exponential and is explicitly identified as beyond that theorem.

The source’s two-site example shows failure of the relevant factorization even for diagonal matrices. This is a barrier to the given framework, not a hardness proof and not evidence that commutation alone resolves the selected target.

The 2024 cluster-expansion paper gives algorithms for specified high-temperature systems and thermal expectations. Its checked abstract does not assert an algorithm for every tensor-product perturbation satisfying only the disk promise here.
why: Zero-free complex regions often turn a difficult counting problem into an efficient approximation problem. A tensor-product perturbation has a short description but disrupts the factorization behind the known algorithm, testing whether zero-freeness alone remains sufficient.
status_note: The primary source explicitly leaves the additive-perturbation extension open. Its proved tensorized-measurement theorem and the checked 2024 high-temperature cluster-expansion abstract do not settle the selected tensor-product, bounded-norm disk formulation. Bounded later-work checks through 17 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2022: ICALP publishes the zero-free approximation theorem and the separate open question for additive perturbations inside the exponential. | 2024-01-16: A cluster-expansion framework provides further high-temperature quantum approximation results; its stated scope differs from the selected promise class.
working_summary: The input describes local quantum interactions together with one global tensor product of one-site operators. The task is to approximate the trace of the exponential after adding that product inside the exponent. The only analytic promise is that this partition function has no zeros in a fixed complex disk extending beyond the target temperature. The requested deterministic classical algorithm must achieve every relative accuracy in polynomial bit time for fixed local parameters. The known theorem treats a different position of the tensorized operator, and a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this extension is required.

title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
importance_reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.
formal: Does every QMA promise problem have a strong quantum interactive oracle proof with polynomial communication, constantly many messages and a constant total number of queried message qubits? More precisely, for every \(L\in\mathrm{QMA}\), do there exist a polynomial \(p\), constants \(r,q\in\mathbb N\), and one uniform verifier under the strong access rules below such that, on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), its running time and total incoming prover-message length are at most \(p(n)\), the total number of messages is at most \(r\), the total query cost is at most \(q\), and \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\le1/3?\] Here \(P\) ranges over all allowed prover strategies, with no computational bound. Strong means that the verifier returns each incoming quantum register in full and sends no additional quantum register of its own.
question_excerpt: Can strong quantum interactive oracle proofs for QMA have polynomial communication?
definitions:
A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is a pair of disjoint subsets of finite binary strings; inputs outside these sets have no correctness requirement. QMA is the class of such pairs with a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier receiving one polynomial-size quantum witness. For every yes-input there is a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); on a no-input every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Uniform means that a single deterministic classical algorithm generates the input-dependent circuit in polynomial time. Its private ancillas start in zero. Gate count, number of qubits and witness length are polynomial in the classical input length. The witness can be any density matrix and need not be efficiently preparable.
