A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and remains positive when tensored with the identity on an arbitrary auxiliary register. Verifier operations are uniformly described polynomial-size circuits of fixed elementary gates, zero-state preparations and computational-basis measurements with classical control. For a concrete universal gate convention take \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) means addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). No arbitrary numerical matrix is a free gate. Channel descriptions include their finite circuit realization; all uniform classical computation and elementary gate operations count toward running time.

An interactive proof has one verifier and one prover, exchanging a bounded sequence of registers and classical messages. They begin with no shared entanglement. The verifier has private workspace \(R\) initialized in zero, containing both its quantum memory and classical records. The prover has an unrestricted private register and may apply any quantum channel to its own memory and the messages it receives; its strategy can depend on \(x\) and the prior interaction. It may entangle different messages with its private memory and with returned registers. Soundness must hold against every such strategy, even computationally unbounded ones. The honest prover is also allowed to be unbounded, as in the source's formal Definitions5.14–5.15. Neither efficient preparation of an honest quantum witness nor a bound on the honest prover's computation is part of this question.

In one verifier turn, let the incoming prover register be \(W=(W_1,\ldots,W_\ell)\). It can contain quantum data or classical data encoded in the computational basis; reading a bit in such a message is still a query. The verifier first applies a channel only to its private register \(R\), then measures an address register in \(R\) to obtain a classical list specifying a set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,\ell\}\) of at most \(q_i\) positions. Conditioned on these addresses, it applies a circuit channel only to \(R\) and the qubits \(W_S\). Its operation is identity on the other incoming wires. This is the query-channel structure of Definitions5.1–5.2: the addresses may depend on private randomness and earlier rounds, but are classical measurement outcomes before the current message is touched. Coherent querying in a superposition of addresses, or choosing a second set adaptively after inspecting the same message within this turn, is not this one-batch query operation. Repeated local gate operations on the already selected qubits affect running time but do not add new positions to that turn's query set.

After its turn the verifier returns the entire \(W\) register to the prover and retains only its own private register. It may also send polynomially many classical bits, but no additional quantum register. The returned qubits may have changed through the allowed interaction; their original state need not be restored. Keeping information acquired in private workspace is allowed, including quantum information transferred through the queried-qubit channel. The restriction forbids keeping incoming message wires between turns, not all changes to private memory. The verifier's own quantum workspace may be polynomial: the formal strong model does not impose a constant bound on all its private qubits. Merely forwarding the unqueried wires counts as communication, but is not counted as inspecting them. At its final turn the verifier produces an accept/reject bit, returning the message if a return is needed to respect the same convention; a final unused return changes the constant message bound only by one.

The incoming message lengths \(\ell_i\), the query budgets \(q_i\), and the protocol's uniform circuit descriptions are fixed by the input and protocol; branchwise budgets may be bounded by fixed worst-case values. Total prover-message length is \(\sum_i\ell_i\), including every incoming copy or retransmission of a register. Total query cost is \(\sum_iq_i\), counting access again if a position is queried in a later message. All resource bounds hold on every branch, not only in expectation or for the honest prover. Returning the full registers adds at most the same quantum communication again. Classical messages generated by the polynomial-time verifier are also polynomially bounded. The constants \(r,q\), the polynomial \(p\) and the verifier may depend on the promise problem but not on \(n\) or the individual input. A polynomial bound on communication does not permit polynomially many queried qubits: the latter must remain a constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated inclusion of QMA in the constant-message, constant-query strong class with polynomial communication, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem admits no such verifier. An affirmative construction must prove uniform resource bounds, completeness and soundness against arbitrary entangled adaptive prover strategies. A negative result must quantify over all eligible verifiers and all constants and polynomials in the definition. Exponential communication, polylogarithmic queries or messages, retaining part of an incoming register between rounds, or sending extra verifier-generated quantum registers does not meet the target. No computational hardness assumption can replace the required unconditional soundness. A protocol with constant private quantum space would suffice, but that extra condition is not necessary in the selected formal model. This is an exact class-inclusion question, not a numerical approximation target.
context:
An interactive oracle proof distinguishes the amount of information transmitted from the amount inspected. A verifier may receive a long register while touching only a few of its qubits. The question requires a polynomial bound on the first resource and a constant bound on the second, together with a constant number of interactions.

The source distinguishes general, restricted and strong access models. Strong protocols return the whole incoming quantum register and send no additional verifier-generated quantum register. These restrictions still allow private workspace. The existing exponential-communication construction happens to operate on constantly many total qubits, but that stronger property is not built into formal Definition5.13.

The source obtains polynomial communication and constantly many queries in its general model. That construction distributes verifier-generated entanglement, which the strong rules forbid. Its separate strong construction uses exponentially many communicated qubits. Question1.9 asks whether polynomial communication can be obtained in the strong model.

The June2026 paper obtains polynomial communication with polylogarithmically many queries and interaction rounds. Its description also retains an initial prover witness and returns successive blocks across rounds, rather than returning the entire incoming register each turn. These parameters and access rules do not establish the selected constant-query, constant-message strong statement.

The June paper discusses conditional improvements from quantum codes with stronger parameters. Such a conditional parameter discussion is not an unconditional construction satisfying all the present access and resource requirements. The card therefore retains the original open question.

A quantum proof need not remain unchanged after inspection, and the prover may keep entanglement across the interaction. Consequently, soundness concerns the complete sequence of allowed strategies, rather than independent checks of fixed classical strings.
why: This asks whether very local interactive verification of quantum evidence can avoid enormous communication while obeying the strong return rules. Resolving it would clarify the joint limits of proof length, local access and interaction for QMA.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September2026 the full January2026 Question1.9, query-channel and strong-protocol definitions, both construction scopes, current version metadata and the June2026 introduction/main theorem/formal-model statements were checked, with bounded later-work searches. The later result uses polylogarithmic queries and rounds and retains incoming witness blocks, so it does not establish this constant-message constant-query strong target. No resolution under all stated restrictions was identified. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2026-01-19: The source proves polynomial communication in the general model and exponential communication in the strong model, both with constant query and message bounds; Question1.9 asks for polynomial communication in the strong model. | 2026-06-08: The later construction achieves polynomial communication with polylogarithmic queries and rounds in a model retaining parts of the initial witness. These bounds do not settle the stated strong constant-query question.
working_summary: Interactive oracle proofs let a verifier inspect only selected parts of much larger prover messages. This question asks for constant-round quantum versions that verify all QMA promise problems with polynomial total communication and only constantly many queries. The strong quantum access model is part of the target, because different ways of querying quantum messages permit different verification strategies. Soundness must cover arbitrary prover behavior, while the verifier remains efficient and has a constant completeness-soundness gap. The project probes how far proof compression and local checking can extend when the evidence itself is quantum.

title: Oracle separation of BQP from IP
importance_reason: A model-relative separation probing the relation between quantum computation and classical interactive proofs.
formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}^{A}\)?
definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.
context:
A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq MIP^{A}\) for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.
why: Determines whether classical single-prover verification of efficient quantum computations survives arbitrary oracle access. The distinction is sharper than a quantum speedup over direct classical computation: even an unrestricted interactive helper must fail in the separating world.
status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.
progress: 2021: Aaronson states the oracle separation as Problem 7 and defines the distinction between IP and its efficient-quantum-honest-prover variant. | 2026-04: The preprint A Relativizing MIP for BQP states containment in classical MIP for every classical oracle and explicitly leaves the single-prover oracle separation open. The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.
working_summary: A classical interactive proof lets a verifier check answers supplied by a prover through a polynomial-length conversation. This problem asks for one oracle relative to which a quantum polynomial-time language has no such proof, even with an unrestricted prover. The quantum algorithm may query the oracle in superposition, whereas the classical verifier queries ordinary strings. The 2026 relativizing containment in the multiple-prover class MIP leaves the single-prover question open in that source. A separation would demonstrate a limit on classical verification of quantum computations through arbitrary oracle interfaces.

title: Quantum query–space tradeoffs for collisions and distinctness
importance_reason: Characterizes simultaneous time and memory limits for basic quantum collision tasks, beyond query complexity alone.
formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the functions \(T_b(n,m,S)\) for \(b\in\{\mathrm{collision},\mathrm{distinctness}\}\): the minimum worst-case number of quantum queries needed by an algorithm with at most \(S\) qubits of total retained memory to solve the specified decision problem with error at most \(1/3\). The input is an oracle for \(f:[n]\to[m]\). In the collision problem, \(n\) is even and \(f\) is promised to be either injective or exactly two-to-one; distinguish these cases. In element distinctness there is no promise; decide whether \(f\) is injective. The full parameter domain is \(m\ge n\ge2\) and \(S\ge4(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil)+10\), with integer parameters. This card selects the source's total-memory tradeoff, allowing all retained memory to be quantum; separating classical and quantum memory budgets is a further variant.
definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Injective means that distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Exactly two-to-one means that every value in the image has exactly two preimages; unused output values have none. The required output is one bit, not a pair of colliding indices.

Let \(a=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) and \(v=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\). A query maps \(|i,y,z\rangle\) to \(|i,y\mathbin{\oplus}\operatorname{enc}(f(i)),z\rangle\), with \(a\) address qubits, \(v\) answer qubits and a remaining work register. Here \(\operatorname{enc}\) is the length-\(v\) binary encoding and \(\oplus\) is bitwise addition modulo two. For address zero or an address larger than \(n\), use the all-zero answer. One call returns one entire output symbol and costs one query. The address and answer registers are included in \(S\).

An algorithm begins with an input-independent state on at most \(S\) qubits, alternates a fixed finite sequence of input-independent quantum channels with oracle calls, and ends with a two-outcome measurement. A density matrix describes its state. An allowed intervening channel has the form \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\), where the finitely many matrices satisfy \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\); it maps the retained memory back into the same bounded space. This allows measurement, randomization and resetting memory. Discarded information cannot be retrieved later. Any measurement outcomes, classical work bits, or tables that remain accessible must occupy the counted memory. Input-dependent classical control is therefore also stored in that memory. There is no external input-dependent advice, second oracle, or uncounted read/write storage.

The channels and measurement may depend on \(b,n,m,S\), but not on \(f\). Their descriptions and the input-independent instruction index are not workspace, and no uniformity, gate-count or computation-time restriction is imposed between queries. Arbitrary computation on the stored memory, including coherent access to stored tables, is free. All oracle calls count, including preprocessing and calls on branches later discarded. The finite query budget is worst-case, and correctness must hold on every valid oracle, with probability at least \(2/3\). The stated space floor allows elementary repeated scans, so both minima are finite; no upper limit on \(S\) is imposed.
answer_criterion: Supply positive functions \(H_b(n,m,S)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(cH_b(n,m,S)\le T_b(n,m,S)\le CH_b(n,m,S)\) for both tasks throughout their parameter domains. Both algorithms and matching lower bounds must respect the stated memory budget; an unrecorded increase in space is not allowed. The functions must describe the asymptotic dependence on the parameters, not simply repeat the optimization defining \(T_b\). Bounds for collision search, random inputs, or label-symmetric algorithms alone do not establish the required worst-case decision tradeoffs.
context:
Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.
why: Quantum collision and distinctness algorithms gain speed while retaining substantial information about queried values. Their optimal time/space tradeoffs would quantify how much memory is necessary for those advantages and develop lower-bound methods for problems whose output contains only one bit.
status_note: Open in the 2021 source. Checked on 2026-09-14: the February 2026 work concerns nested collision finding; the September 2026 preprint gives claimed search bounds under label symmetry and explicitly leaves removal of symmetry open. Neither checked statement settles the unrestricted, worst-case decision tradeoff formulated here. The total-memory convention is explicit.
progress: 2021: Aaronson lists the two query/space tradeoffs as open, distinguishing them from the already established unrestricted-query complexities. | 2026-02-27: Hao, Huang and Liu give space-sensitive lower bounds for nested collision finding, addressing a related short-output barrier. | 2026-09-09: Magniez and Zur post claimed tight search tradeoffs under label symmetry and explicitly retain the unrestricted-algorithm question. These are restricted-model progress, not a resolution of the displayed decision curves.
working_summary: The question asks for the optimal quantum query cost of collision testing and element distinctness at every allowed memory budget. The oracle returns an output symbol, and the algorithm must decide the answer with bounded worst-case error. All retained storage counts, including classical tables and query registers. Recent lower bounds concern nested collision tasks or search algorithms restricted by label symmetry. The target remains matching upper and lower bounds for unrestricted algorithms solving the two decision problems.

title: Sequential randomness certification against non-signaling adversaries
importance_reason: A substantial foundational question about the relation between finite entanglement resources, sequential measurements and device-independent randomness. The difference between quantum and post-quantum no-signaling adversaries tests the assumptions behind an unbounded resource claim, with consequences for the conceptual limits of randomness certification.
formal: Is the randomness certifiable from a single pure entangled pair of qubits universally bounded against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries, even when Bob measures his qubit arbitrarily many times? Precisely, does a real constant \(B\ge0\) exist such that \[H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=-\log_2 G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)\le B\] for every finite sequence length, every experiment in the single-pair model below, and every fixed generation input string \(\mathbf y^0\)?
definitions: Fix an integer \(N\ge1\) and a nonempty finite set \(X\) of Alice’s measurement choices. Initially Alice and Bob share one normalized pure entangled state \(|\psi\rangle\in\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2\), and no other shared quantum resource. Alice receives \(x\in X\), performs one binary measurement and outputs \(a\in\{-1,+1\}\). Its effects are positive semidefinite matrices \(A_a^x\) on \(\mathbb C^2\) with \(A_{-1}^x+A_{+1}^x=I\). Bob performs \(N\) binary instruments successively on his same qubit. At step \(i\), he receives \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and produces \(b_i\in\{-1,+1\}\). His instrument may depend on all his earlier inputs and outputs. It consists of maps \(\mathcal M^{h,y_i}_{i,b_i}\) from two-by-two matrices to two-by-two matrices, where \(h=(y_1,b_1,\ldots,y_{i-1},b_{i-1})\). Each map is completely positive and trace-nonincreasing, and their sum over \(b_i\) is trace-preserving. Completely positive means that tensoring with the identity map on matrices of any finite size preserves positive semidefiniteness. The output quantum register passed to the next step is only the same two-dimensional system. Local auxiliary systems may implement an instrument but are discarded within that step; no extra persistent quantum register or fresh shared entanglement is supplied. The recorded classical history is available to later Bob steps. There is no communication between Alice and Bob during the experiment. Inputs are chosen independently of the preparation and of any adversarial side information. Let \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\), \(\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)\), and let \(\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y}\) denote the composition of the corresponding history-dependent Bob maps. The exactly known observed distribution is \[P(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(A_a^x\otimes I)(\operatorname{id}\otimes\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\right].\] The size of \(X\), the state and the instruments may vary with \(N\); in particular Alice’s input set is not fixed to two settings. Define \(\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\) to be all nonnegative conditional arrays \(Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\), normalized for each input, with the following marginal constraints. The sum over \(\mathbf b\) is independent of \(\mathbf y\); the sum over \(a\) is independent of \(x\); and, for every \(0\le j<N\), \(\sum_{b_{j+1},\ldots,b_N}Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\) is independent of \(y_{j+1},\ldots,y_N\). The last condition includes the joint Alice outcome and Bob prefix and forbids signaling from later Bob inputs to earlier outputs. Forward dependence on earlier Bob inputs and outputs is permitted. Members of this set need not be quantum correlations or admit any qubit realization. For a fixed publicly known \(\mathbf y^0\in\{0,1\}^N\), set \[G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=\sup_{P=\sum_e q_e Q_e}\ \sum_e q_e\max_{\mathbf b\in\{-1,+1\}^N}\sum_a Q_e(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y^0),\] where the supremum runs over all finite convex decompositions with \(q_e\ge0\), \(\sum_e q_e=1\), and \(Q_e\in\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\). The mixture identity holds at every input and output, and the weights are independent of inputs. The expression is independent of \(x\) by no-signaling. Eve knows the label \(e\), may choose a decomposition for the fixed generation input, and guesses the entire Bob string. Alice’s outcome is not revealed or conditioned upon. The certified randomness here is this raw conditional min-entropy, without smoothing, postselection or an extractor; all \(N\) Bob outcomes belong to the string. The two-qubit restriction constrains which observed distributions the honest experiment can generate, not the adversary’s decomposition. Exact correlations are assumed; finite sampling and a noise tolerance uniform in \(N\) are not additional requirements.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of a universal finite bound \(B\), or prove that the certified min-entropy is unbounded in this model. A negative answer to the boundedness question must establish that for every real \(M\ge0\) there exist a finite \(N\), finite \(X\), one entangled qubit pair, allowed measurements and instruments, and \(\mathbf y^0\) with \(H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)>M\). Different experimental designs may be used for different \(M\). Equivalently, a positive answer requires a uniform constant \(c>0\) with \(G_{\mathrm{NS}}\ge c\). The optimal numerical value of a finite bound is not requested. Security only against quantum adversaries, a bound depending on the sequence length, or accumulation using an increasing supply of entangled systems does not resolve this fixed-single-pair question.
context:
A quantum measurement can produce an unpredictable outcome while leaving a state that can be measured again. The question is how much unpredictability can be certified from the observed input-output statistics of this repeated experiment, when only one entangled pair was initially supplied.

An ordinary random-looking output is not enough: Eve may know which hidden component of the observed distribution occurred. The guessing probability maximizes her success over all allowed decompositions, and min-entropy measures the resulting unpredictability of the whole Bob string.

Curchod and coauthors show that one pure entangled qubit pair can certify any finite amount of randomness against quantum adversaries using a sufficiently long sequence. Their concluding question asks whether a finite upper limit returns when the adversary is constrained only by no-signaling.

Their sequential construction increases Alice’s number of possible measurement settings as the sequence grows. Fixing Alice to two settings would impose an extra restriction absent from that result. The present card permits every finite input set while keeping Alice’s output binary and her quantum system a single qubit.

The adversary model is made explicit here by replacing the source’s quantum decomposition with the full time-ordered no-signaling set. Each component preserves separation of Alice and Bob and the causal order within Bob’s sequence. Its dimension and physical realization are unrestricted: the honest qubit promise is not trusted as a constraint on Eve.

Padovan and coauthors’ 2024 work studies one Alice and two sequential Bobs, with a quantum correlation boundary and improved robustness of randomness certification. Its quantum-adversary guarantee does not answer the post-quantum boundedness question.

Ramanathan, Liu and Wu’s 2025 preprint reports linear min-entropy accumulation against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries when Alice and Bob run a Bell test repeatedly with a prescribed nonlocal value in each round. That theorem does not impose this card’s single-qubit-per-wing resource and single Alice output. General sequential Bell-test accumulation therefore cannot by itself be treated as a resolution of the single-pair question.

Unboundedness would mean that experiments can be designed to certify any chosen finite amount. It does not demand infinitely many outputs in one finite experiment, nor a fixed noise tolerance as the target amount grows.
why: The question tests how much repeated randomness certification depends on quantum theory beyond no-signaling. It separates the physical resource available to the honest experiment—a single pair of qubits—from assumptions about an adversary. A universal bound or unbounded family would clarify whether recycling one entangled system can retain its qualitative advantage under this stronger adversarial model.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly conjectures boundedness against no-signaling adversaries. The 2024 quantum-security result and 2025 no-signaling accumulation preprint do not establish a resolution with this single-pair resource and measurement model. No matching proof or counterexample was found in the bounded search; the new proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2017: The source proves unbounded certification against quantum adversaries and conjectures boundedness against post-quantum no-signaling adversaries for its sequential setting. | 2024-09-30: Padovan and coauthors obtain quantum correlation and robustness results with two sequential Bobs; they do not establish security against the full no-signaling set. | 2025-06-20: Ramanathan–Liu–Wu report linear no-signaling min-entropy accumulation in repeated Bell tests. The single-pair resource condition needed to apply it to this question is not supplied.
working_summary: A single entangled pair of qubits is measured once by Alice and repeatedly by Bob. The question asks whether the certified unpredictability of Bob’s entire outcome string has a universal finite bound against an adversary constrained only by no-signaling and causal order. The honest experiment uses just one qubit per wing, but the adversary is not assumed to be quantum or dimension-limited. Alice may have more possible measurement choices as the sequence grows, and the full observed correlations are assumed known. Unbounded randomness against quantum adversaries and general repeated Bell-test accumulation do not by themselves settle this fixed-resource post-quantum question.

title: Constant-round quantum refereed games versus \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
importance_reason: Bounding constant-round quantum refereed games compares two basic verification models.
formal: Does \(\mathrm{QRG}_{\mathrm{const}}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? For every promise problem \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) admitting a quantum refereed game with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, two competing provers and some fixed constant \(k\) of interaction cycles, must there be a deterministic algorithm deciding \(\Pi\) using polynomial space? For \(x\in Y\), a yes-prover must have a strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) against every no-prover strategy. For \(x\in N\), a no-prover must have a strategy that makes it reject with probability at least \(2/3\) against every yes-prover strategy. The constant \(k\) and the polynomial bounds may depend on the problem and verifier, but not on input length.
definitions:
A promise problem is a pair of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\); no answer is prescribed outside their union. Both provers know the classical input \(x\) and the verifier's complete specification. The yes-prover seeks acceptance and the no-prover seeks rejection. They cannot communicate directly and do not initially share an entangled state or correlated private randomness. Each may retain private quantum memory throughout the interaction, use randomness, and perform arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum operations without a time or memory bound.

The verifier is generated from \(x\), of length \(n\), by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. Its total gate count, workspace, and total communicated qubits are polynomial in \(n\). It starts with zero-initialized registers. In each of at most \(k\) cycles, it applies a quantum circuit, sends one message register privately to each prover, and receives both response registers. Each prover acts only on its current message and its own retained private memory. The verifier then proceeds to the next cycle or its final two-outcome measurement. Messages to the two provers may be entangled through the verifier's preparation; this is part of the specified protocol. Empty messages are allowed. Sequential exchanges can be scheduled in separate cycles, so allowing every fixed \(k\) includes any constant-length message pattern. The verifier never gives a prover access to the other prover's private channel unless its own prescribed operations deliberately convey information from it.

Use a fixed universal finite gate set: Hadamard maps \(|0\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|1\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\); \(T\) multiplies \(|1\rangle\) by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) and fixes \(|0\rangle\); include \(T^{-1}\) and controlled NOT. The verifier's measurements, randomness and adaptive choices may be implemented coherently with polynomially many ancillary qubits. Prover operations are unrestricted quantum channels, expressible as \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\), on their message and private registers. Initial private states can be prepared by those channels. All winning probabilities are over the resulting quantum measurement outcomes and private randomization. Each winning strategy may depend on \(x\), but must work against every opposing strategy on that input.

The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists here of promise problems decided by a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape and at most \(C(n+1)^r\) work-tape cells for fixed constants \(C,r\). It must halt on all inputs and give the correct answer on \(Y\cup N\). It has no oracle or advice. The simulator need only decide which side can force a win; it need not output either prover's strategy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. An inclusion proof must cover every fixed constant number of interaction cycles and every polynomial-time uniform verifier in the stated private-message model. A negative proof must exhibit a promise problem in this class with no deterministic polynomial-space decision algorithm. An exponential-time simulation, or a polynomial-space simulation only for one exchange pattern, does not suffice.
context:
The winning-strategy requirements contain opposite quantifier orders on yes- and no-inputs. A prover must force its preferred outcome against all opposing strategies. This is different from two cooperating proof providers or a verifier receiving two unentangled existential witnesses.

Gutoski and Wu prove a polynomial-space simulation when all interaction with one prover is completed before interaction with the other begins. This includes their class QRG(2). Their result does not cover arbitrary repeated interleaving of the two private conversations.

Different papers count individual messages, turns and full send/receive rounds differently. This card fixes a complete interaction cycle explicitly. Since it asks about every constant cycle count, a constant change of counting convention does not change its scope.

With polynomially many messages, quantum refereed games capture \(\mathrm{EXP}\), deterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). This gives an upper bound for constant-length games, but it does not supply a polynomial-space simulation. The constant-length question remains meaningful even for classical messages.
why: These games combine efficient quantum verification with competition between two powerful provers who have different information. Locating constant-length games would clarify whether repeated alternation of private interaction can increase computational power beyond polynomial space, even when only a few exchanges are allowed.
status_note: The July 2026 source asks the general constant-round question. The primary game definitions, polynomial-length EXP characterization and bounded-turn PSPACE results were checked on 2026-09-14, with a bounded later-work search. The one-switch/DQIP result does not settle arbitrary constant interleaving, and no full resolution was identified.
progress: 2005: Gutoski and Watrous establish the competing-prover model and short quantum games, emphasizing private messages and interaction order. | 2007: Gutoski and Watrous characterize polynomial-length quantum refereed games by EXP. | 2013: Gutoski and Wu prove DQIP = QRG(2) = PSPACE for their specified one-switch interaction pattern and leave more general bounded-turn games outside that characterization. | 2026-07-27: The source problem list reiterates the question for a general constant number of rounds.
working_summary: A quantum refereed game has two competing provers trying to make an efficient verifier accept or reject. The provers exchange private quantum messages with the verifier and may keep private memory. The question asks whether every game with a constant number of interaction cycles can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space. Polynomial-space simulations are known for specific patterns in which interaction switches from one prover to the other only once. Polynomially many general rounds capture exponential time, leaving the full constant-round boundary open.

title: Black-box unitary synthesis
importance_reason: A basic quantum transformation problem under black-box access, clarifying what an oracle interface permits.
formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.
context:
Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.
why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.
status_note: The source question is retained in Rosenthal’s May 2026 revision and the July 2026 Dong–Lombardi–Ma paper. Checked on 2026-09-14. Their bounds concern exponential-time upper bounds or restricted-query lower bounds, not a resolution of the displayed general polynomial-time, constant-diamond-error formulation.
progress: 2021: Aaronson lists general black-box unitary synthesis as open and distinguishes it from the easier state-preparation task. | 2024: Lombardi, Ma and Wright prove a one-query lower bound for general unitary synthesis, with related cryptographic consequences. | 2026-05-04: Rosenthal’s revised author manuscript presents the exponential-time oracle upper bound and explicitly retains polynomial-time synthesis as Question 1.1. | 2026-07-29: Dong, Lombardi and Ma give additional one-query separations and approximation results for structured unitaries; the general polynomial-query question remains outside their claimed resolution.
working_summary: The problem asks whether every quantum unitary can be implemented efficiently using an appropriately chosen Boolean oracle. One fixed circuit family must work for all unitaries, with the desired unitary encoded only in the oracle. The implementation must work on arbitrary inputs, including states entangled with an untouched reference. Both total computation and coherent oracle access must remain polynomial in the number of input qubits. Known exponential-time implementations and restricted-query lower bounds leave the general question unresolved.

title: Complement of quantum approximate counting in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
importance_reason: A complexity classification for a natural quantum Hamiltonian or counting task would clarify the reach of core quantum complexity classes.
formal: Is the following complementary quantum approximate-counting promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)? The input is a finite quantum verification circuit \(V\) with \(w\) witness qubits, together with a binary integer \(1\le K\le2^w\). Let \(A_V\) be its acceptance operator on the witness space and let \(D_a(V)\) count its eigenvalues at least \(a\), with multiplicity. Distinguish \[\text{YES: }D_{1/3}(V)\le K/2\qquad\text{from}\qquad\text{NO: }D_{2/3}(V)\ge K,\] promised that one of these conditions holds. Membership asks for one uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier using two polynomial-size, mutually unentangled witnesses, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\). The two spectral thresholds deliberately leave a buffer; the selected target is the complement of this buffered counting problem.
question_excerpt: Does the complement of quantum approximate counting belong to QMA(2)?
definitions:
Use a conventional explicit binary circuit encoding. It specifies the ordered list of gates and their wire indices, which wires hold the \(w\) input witness qubits, which \(a\ge1\) ancillary qubits start in \(|0\rangle\), and one measured output wire. Wire counts are written in unary, so both \(w\) and \(a\) are bounded by the input length. The allowed gates are the fixed exact unitary matrices \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle,\] acting as identity on the other wires. Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). The sole measurement of \(V\) is its final computational-basis output, with value one interpreted as acceptance. The input includes the complete gate list, not an oracle or a succinct generator of an exponentially long circuit. Let \(N\) be the total bit length of the circuit description and the binary encoding of \(K\). Malformed inputs and inputs outside the promise have no correctness requirement. The bound \(K\) varies with the input and may be exponential in \(w\); it is not a universal constant.

A state of the witness register is a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\): a Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every complex vector \(v\). With \(\Pi_1\) the projector onto output one, define \[A_V=(I\otimes\langle0^a|)V^\dagger\Pi_1V(I\otimes|0^a\rangle).\] It satisfies \(0\preceq A_V\preceq I\) and \(\Pr[V\text{ accepts }\rho]=\operatorname{Tr}(A_V\rho)\). Its \(2^w\) eigenvalues lie in \([0,1]\). For \(a\in[0,1]\), \(D_a(V)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf1_{[a,1]}(A_V)\): the dimension of the span of eigenvectors with eigenvalue at least \(a\). Eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity, including equality at the threshold. This is neither the number of individual normalized states nor the dimension of an arbitrarily chosen accepting basis. There are continuously many possible witnesses, but the spectral count is a finite integer.

Since \(D_{1/3}\ge D_{2/3}\) and \(K>0\), the two promised cases are disjoint. The YES bound means \(D_{1/3}\le\lfloor K/2\rfloor\). Eigenvalues strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are allowed; the promise does not say the entire spectrum avoids this interval. They contribute to the larger count, but not the smaller one. The uncomplemented buffered counting problem labels \(D_{2/3}\ge K\) as YES and \(D_{1/3}\le K/2\) as NO. Complementation swaps these two sets and retains the promise; it does not replace \(A_V\) by \(I-A_V\) or count all eigenvalues below a single threshold.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), there must exist one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator and a fixed polynomial \(p\) such that, on every input \(x=(V,K)\) of length \(N\), it produces a circuit \(W_x\) with at most \(p(N)\) gates and private zero-initialized ancilla qubits. Two additional witness registers \(R_1,R_2\) each have at most \(p(N)\) qubits. Their supplied joint state must have the form \(\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\); each factor may itself be mixed and internally entangled, with arbitrary complex entries and no efficient-preparation requirement. The verifier may act jointly on the two registers and its ancillas, using the gate convention above, and measures a final output bit. Write its acceptance probability as \(p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\). The requirements are \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\exists\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\forall\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\le1/3.\] Product witnesses suffice to specify soundness; by linearity the same bound then holds for every separable mixture of products. Soundness is not required against arbitrary entangled states across the two supplied registers. There are no additional messages, advice or oracle calls. Polynomial running time is measured in \(N\), including the length of \(K\), not in its numerical value or in \(2^w\). The spectral count describes the problem; no eigenbasis is supplied to the verifier.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that this exact promise pair belongs to \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not. An affirmative answer must supply a uniform verifier with polynomial resources and prove both quantified acceptance conditions for all promised circuit inputs and all allowed witnesses. A negative answer must rule out every such verifier, rather than one proposed protocol. A result for a single spectral threshold, a verifier given an eigenbasis, exponentially large witnesses, entangled witnesses without the stated product restriction, or a model with interaction or an oracle does not establish the claim. Quantum-oracle separations alone do not give an unrelativized nonmembership theorem. This is an exact class-membership question; the fixed counting promise and verifier error are part of the model, not a request to estimate a number to additive precision.
context:
The imported card broadly asked for the complexity of quantum approximate counting. The source separately asks whether its complement is in QMA(2). On 16 September 2026 the user selected that narrower target and authorized repairing the brief single-threshold description to the standard version with two separated spectral thresholds. This scope change is explicit; the broad classification programme is not claimed complete.

An ordinary quantum witness can demonstrate the existence of a state that a verifier accepts. Approximate counting asks how large the accepting eigenspace is. The selected complement instead asks for efficient verification that even the lower-threshold accepting space is small.

Definition 17 of the ITCS 2026 paper uses two thresholds \(b<a\) separated by at least an inverse polynomial, and allows a returned estimate between \((1-\varepsilon)D_a\) and \((1+\varepsilon)D_b\). The present decision formulation fixes the spectral thresholds to \(2/3\) and \(1/3\) and keeps the original source's factor-two count gap. It does not assume an absence of eigenvalues between the thresholds.

The two witnesses in QMA(2) are separate resources. They may be compared by a joint quantum verifier, but cannot arrive entangled with one another. The requested membership is therefore different from supplying one larger arbitrary witness, and from asking two provers to participate in an interactive protocol.

The ITCS 2026 authors prove a quantum-oracle separation between quantum approximate counting and quantum verification with a QMA oracle, ruling out a black-box analogue of the classical approximate-counting algorithm in that setting. Their statement concerns an additional oracle and a different verification model. It does not settle this ordinary two-witness complement question.

The phrase quantum approximate counting also occurs for counting marked inputs of a classical Boolean oracle using quantum queries, or for estimating the acceptance probability of a computation with no witness. The cited paper explicitly distinguishes those tasks from counting the accepting eigenspace of a quantum verifier.
why: This asks whether two unentangled quantum certificates can verify that a quantum verifier has only a small accepting space. It connects the power of independent quantum witnesses to approximate counting and distinguishes proving scarcity from merely proving existence.
status_note: Source-open for the user-selected complementary two-threshold formulation. The full 12 March 2026 question and ITCS 2026 Definition 17, introduction, main oracle separation and open-problem discussion were checked on 16 September 2026, together with bounded later-work searches. No ordinary QMA(2) containment or noncontainment resolving this selected promise problem was identified. The authorized spectral buffer is recorded as a repair of the source’s brief definition, not asserted to be identical to a sharp single-threshold problem. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2026-01-23: The ITCS paper states the buffered spectral-counting definition and proves a quantum-oracle lower bound against a QMA-oracle verification model. | 2026-03-12: The source explicitly asks whether the complement belongs to QMA(2). | 2026-09-16: Editorial scope selection retains the complement question and makes the two spectral thresholds explicit; the source-open status is based on the cited question and bounded later-work checks.
working_summary: The selected task asks whether two unentangled quantum witnesses can certify a small accepting eigenspace. The input is an explicitly described quantum verification circuit and a binary threshold for its spectral count. A low count at acceptance threshold one third must be distinguished from a count at least twice as large at threshold two thirds. The spectral buffer permits intermediate eigenvalues and avoids treating the source’s shortened one-threshold description as the full model. The target is ordinary QMA(2) membership of the complementary promise problem; known quantum-oracle lower bounds concern different models.

title: Oracle separation of BQP from efficient-prover interactive proofs
importance_reason: An oracle benchmark for the reach of efficient-prover interactive verification of quantum computation.
formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\), where \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) requires a polynomial-time quantum honest prover and classical interaction with a polynomial-time classical verifier?
definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover. \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) is the subclass of \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) whose languages admit such an \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol with one uniform quantum polynomial-time oracle algorithm as the honest prover. Its total local work and oracle queries across all rounds are polynomial in n, under the same quantum access convention as \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\). Only the honest prover is restricted: soundness still quantifies over all computationally unbounded cheating strategies. Polynomial bounds and machines may depend on A and the language, but must work for all input lengths; they cannot depend on the particular input through advice.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) language L for which no classical interactive proof has an honest quantum polynomial-time oracle prover. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}=\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. All negative instances must rule out arbitrary polynomial bounds on rounds and honest-prover work, and the positive alternative must retain soundness against unbounded cheating provers.
context:
A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq MIP^{A}\) for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.
why: Distinguishes the existence of a classical interactive proof from the ability of an efficient quantum device to carry out its honest strategy. It tests whether verification can match the computational resources of the device while retaining soundness against all cheating provers.
status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.
progress: 2021: Aaronson states the oracle separation as Problem 8 and defines the distinction between IP and its efficient-quantum-honest-prover variant. | 2026-04: The preprint A Relativizing MIP for BQP states containment in classical MIP for every classical oracle and explicitly leaves the single-prover oracle separation open. The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.
working_summary: An efficient quantum computation can have a classical interactive proof whose honest prover is too expensive for the quantum device to execute. This problem asks for an oracle relative to which some quantum polynomial-time language has no classical interactive proof with a quantum polynomial-time honest prover. The verifier and honest prover access the same classical oracle, with quantum queries available only to the quantum computation. Soundness must hold even against an unbounded dishonest prover, so computationally sound cryptographic arguments have a different guarantee. A separation would expose an oracle obstruction to classical verification using only the computational power of an efficient quantum device.

title: Exact quantum fanout in constant depth with unrestricted circuit size
importance_reason: Isolates a basic exact-unitary expressiveness question in constant-depth quantum computation even when finite size and ancilla count are unrestricted. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer d such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), some finite QAC circuit of depth at most d exactly implements FANOUT\(_{n}\) on one control qubit and n target qubits, allowing arbitrarily many clean ancillas and no size bound?
definitions: For bits \(s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\in \{0,1\}\), FANOUT\(_{n}|s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\rangle =|s,s\oplus x_{1},\ldots ,s\oplus x_{n}\rangle\), extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on \(n+1+a(n)\) qubits for some finite \(a(n)\ge 0\). Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over \(\mathbb{C}\) and generalized Toffoli gates: for any \(k\ge 1\) distinct controls and a distinct target, |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\rangle\) maps to |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\oplus (z_{1}\cdots z_{k})\rangle\). Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase \(e^{i\varphi _{n}}\), independent of the input state \(\psi , C_{n}(|\psi \rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n))=e^{i\varphi _{n}}\)(FANOUT\(_{n}|\psi \rangle\))⊗|\(0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n)\) for every unit vector \(\psi\) in \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes}(n+1)\). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.
context:
On a basis input, the control flips every target when it is one and leaves them unchanged when it is zero. The same circuit must act correctly on superpositions, including inputs entangled with other systems. Agreement only on measured classical outputs would be weaker.

For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|\(00\rangle\) yields \((|000\rangle +|111\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

A Toffoli gate may inspect many controls in one layer, but a qubit cannot participate in several gates in that same layer. The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

The ITCS paper discusses approximate implementations and records exact fanout as open even without a size bound. Its known parity/fanout equivalence and later 2026 equivalence results connect the task to other shallow quantum operations, but do not constitute the exact implementation or impossibility theorem requested here.
why: Determines whether unbounded-arity quantum AND operations and one-qubit gates can express coherent fanout in bounded depth at any finite size. It isolates a basic limitation of shallow unitary computation that cannot be explained solely by insufficient circuit width.
status_note: Exact implementation definition, gate set and arbitrary-size footnote checked, with later August 2026 abstracts searched through 11 September 2026. No matching exact constant-depth construction or all-size impossibility result was located.
progress: 2026-01: The ITCS paper explicitly records arbitrary-size exact fanout as open and distinguishes it from approximate constructions. | 2026-08-25: The revised Fourier-concentration preprint still describes the related parity question as open while proving additional equivalences.
working_summary: Quantum fanout coherently flips every target qubit according to one control qubit. The problem asks whether one constant depth bound can implement it exactly using arbitrary one-qubit and generalized Toffoli gates. The circuit may have any finite size and any finite number of clean ancillas. Superposition inputs must be handled correctly and the ancillas must return to zero. An exact construction or an impossibility theorem would determine whether this basic operation lies beyond the expressive power of the shallow gate model.

title: Quantum games PCP with efficient honest provers and short messages
importance_reason: A succinct verification question connecting QMA, entangled games and quantum PCP. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Does every promise problem \(\mathrm{L}=(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) in QMA admit a one-round entangled multiprover proof with a uniform classical polynomial-time verifier, a constant number r of provers and polylogarithmic-length classical questions and answers, such that: \((i)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some polynomial-size quantum witness permits uniform quantum polynomial-time preparation and local execution of an honest strategy accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); and \((ii)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every entangled strategy, with no computational bound on the dishonest provers, is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\)?
definitions: Write \(n=|x|\). QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least \(2/3\), while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most \(O((\log (n+2))^{a})\) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state \(\psi _{x}\), prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state \(\psi _{x}\) is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\cup \mathrm{L}_{no}\). The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.
context:
The verifier has an n-bit instance but exchanges only polylogarithmically many bits with each prover. Quantum information stays with the provers. The task is to check a quantum witness through these short classical exchanges, with a constant separation between acceptance on YES and NO instances.

It is insufficient for a prover to answer quickly after receiving an arbitrarily difficult-to-prepare entangled state. The setup itself must take polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness. Conversely, cheating provers receive no time or entanglement-size restriction.

Very powerful entangled proof systems already exist when honest provers are unrestricted. The 2024 status note explains why these results do not establish efficient-prover quantum games PCP and identifies an error in an earlier claimed QMA construction.

The status note proposes \(O(\log  n)\)-bit questions and \(O(1)\)-bit answers. The selected CCC passage explicitly asks for polylogarithmic questions and answers. Resolving this card would settle that weaker efficient-prover benchmark, without automatically establishing the stronger message lengths.

The 2026 paper proves a streaming Hamiltonian verification result. It discusses a possible game application with short questions but polynomial-size answers; that application is not a theorem in the checked passage, and even those parameters would not meet this card’s answer bound.
why: Would connect efficient verification of quantum witnesses to succinct classical interaction with entangled provers. The honest-prover requirement preserves the computational meaning of the witness, which unrestricted entangled proof-system containments do not ensure.
status_note: The full CCC 2026 question and the 2024 status note were checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching efficient-prover protocol or impossibility theorem was located. The stronger logarithmic-question/constant-answer conjecture is distinguished explicitly.
progress: 2024-03-19: The status note formalizes witness-assisted efficient provers and explains why the earlier claimed quantum games PCP construction does not establish the conjecture. | 2026: The CCC paper proves streaming gap amplification and explicitly leaves efficient-prover games with polylogarithmic questions and answers open.
working_summary: The question asks whether every quantum-verifiable problem has a short classical game with entangled provers. Both questions and answers must have polylogarithmic length, with a constant completeness–soundness gap. Honest provers must prepare their entanglement and answer in polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness. Soundness must hold even against computationally unrestricted cheating provers. Existing unrestricted entangled proof systems and the source’s streaming Hamiltonian result do not establish this efficient-prover communication target.

title: Completeness and soundness amplification in StoqMA
importance_reason: A foundational robustness question for stoquastic proofs, equivalent to a central equality between quantum-inspired and classical verification classes. Existing score retained.
formal: For every pair of efficiently computable threshold functions \(a(n),b(n)\) with \(1/2\le b(n)<a(n)\le 1\) and \(a(n)- b(n)\ge 1/q(n)\) for some polynomial q, and every integer-valued polynomial \(\ell\)\((n)\ge 2\), is \(StoqMA(a,b)\) contained in \(StoqMA(1- 2^{- \ell (n)}, 1/2+2^{- \ell (n)})\)? Here n is the classical input length. The new verifier must remain in the same one-witness stoquastic circuit model, with polynomially many gates, witness qubits and ancillas.
definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in \(StoqMA(a,b)\) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit \(V_{x}\) on \(m(n)+r(n)+s(n)\) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |\(w\rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes r}\otimes |+\rangle ^{\otimes s}\), where |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the \(\{|+\rangle ,|- \rangle\}\) basis, with |−⟩=\((|0\rangle - |1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least \(a(n)\). If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most \(b(n)\). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within \(2^{- t}\) in time polynomial in \(n+t\). The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description.
