Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and \(\ell\). Soundness approaches \(1/2\) from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and \(\ell\), or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above \(1/2\) while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.
context:
The computation is classically reversible, but its ancillas and final measurement allow a nonnegative quantum witness to affect acceptance. This restricted verification model arises in the complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonians. Familiar error-reduction statements for unrestricted quantum verification do not automatically give the required stoquastic verifier.

The source’s Theorem 5 maps thresholds \((1/2+u/2,1/2+v/2)\) to \((1/2+u^{r}/2,1/2+v^{r}/2)\) for polynomial r. This improves excess soundness but can also lower completeness. Conjecture 6 asks for simultaneous amplification towards completeness one and soundness one half.

The 2025 published paper proves that negligible completeness error with a suitable inverse-polynomial gap is already contained in MA, the class of promise problems verified in polynomial time with a classical witness and random bits. Its Corollary 1.5 makes general StoqMA error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA.

The July 2026 preprint still explicitly calls general one-witness error reduction open. Its restricted repetition results do not supply the two threshold limits required here for arbitrary original completeness.

The May 2026 preprint claims that the number of stoquastic provers can be reduced while retaining an inverse-polynomial gap. It explicitly avoids assuming general amplification. This preprint claim is not recorded as a solution of the one-witness error-reduction question.
why: Would determine whether the stoquastic verification model has ordinary exponential error reduction and, through the published equivalence, whether its proof power collapses to classical Merlin–Arthur verification.
status_note: Read Conjecture 6, the verifier definition and soundness-only theorem, the 2025 published equivalence, and the relevant statements in the May and July 2026 preprints. No full one-witness amplification theorem was found through 12 September 2026. The July 2026 source explicitly still calls the general question open.
progress: 2021: Soundness-only error reduction is established, while Conjecture 6 states the simultaneous completeness/soundness target. | 2025-09-11: A published theorem establishes that general StoqMA error reduction is equivalent to StoqMA=MA. | 2026-07-12: A revised preprint on unentangled stoquastic proofs retains the general error-reduction problem as open and studies more restricted amplification guarantees.
working_summary: A StoqMA verifier uses classical reversible gates, special initial ancillas and one final measurement in the plus/minus basis. It accepts a suitable nonnegative quantum witness on yes instances and must reject arbitrary witnesses with the prescribed soundness bound on no instances. The question asks whether every inverse-polynomial gap can be amplified to completeness exponentially close to one and soundness exponentially close to one half. Soundness-only repetition is known, but it does not provide this simultaneous improvement. A published theorem makes full error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA, and July 2026 work still states the general problem as open.

title: Simulation or postselection universality for algebraic two-qubit interactions
importance_reason: A broad classification question for the computational power of restricted quantum interactions; an exact simulation convention is needed for a benchmark-ready dichotomy. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed Hermitian \(4\times4\) matrix \(H\) with complex algebraic entries, does at least one of the following hold: all of its basis-input, basis-output circuits admit polynomial-time classical sampling to arbitrary inverse-polynomial total-variation accuracy; or \(\mathrm{PP}\subseteq\operatorname{Post}(H)\), with the circuit, uniformity and postselection conventions below?
definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. Conditional on it, the output is 1 with probability at least \(2/3\) for \(x\in K\) and at most \(1/3\) otherwise. Circuit descriptions, including the unary time bound, have polynomial length in \(|x|\). The postselection list and values may depend on the input through the compiler. PP consists of languages for which a uniform polynomial-time fair-coin Turing machine accepts with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) on members and at most \(1/2\) on nonmembers. The second branch is the source’s postselected-computation criterion expressed via PP; the algebraic-entry, accuracy and exponentially bounded postselection conventions are explicit editorial choices. The alternatives need not be disjoint. No commutativity promise is imposed on \(H\).
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the disjunction for every allowed fixed interaction, or a Lean counterexample interaction for which both branches fail. The proof must use the supplied finite-precision sampling and uniform postselection conventions. A classification with free local gates, arbitrary analog reductions, a commutativity promise or a different sampling error does not automatically settle this variant.
context:
The original question asks whether every fixed two-qubit interaction is classically simulable or universal with postselection. Its circuit model starts and ends in the computational basis and permits oriented interactions and inverse evolution.

The authorized editorial variant fixes algebraic matrix entries, rational gate times with a charged physical-time bound, total-variation sampling accuracy and an exponential lower bound on the conditioning event. These choices specify a discrete benchmark; they are not asserted to be the source’s only interpretation.

The later analog-universality theorem classifies a different simulation model with closed Hamiltonian families and faithful reductions.
why: Seeks a boundary between classically manageable quantum dynamics and postselection universality using only one fixed two-qubit interaction. The restriction to basis preparation and measurement makes computational power depend on more than ordinary unitary controllability.
status_note: A user-authorized precise variant of the 2016/2017 general interaction question. The primary commuting theorem and the later analog theorem have different scopes and do not establish this selected general dichotomy. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the model choices are editorial and no exhaustive current-status claim is made.
progress: 2016: The source proves its commuting-interaction sampling dichotomy and asks for an extension to arbitrary two-qubit H. | 2017-09: The author’s thesis retains the same general conjecture in Section 4.8. | 2022-01-13: A later analog-universality characterization concerns faithful reductions and closed Hamiltonian families, a different model.
working_summary: A fixed two-qubit interaction generates circuits by evolving selected ordered pairs for specified times. Every circuit begins in a computational-basis state and ends with computational-basis measurement. The chosen dichotomy asks for efficient classical approximate sampling or full PP decision power with postselection. The variant makes all matrix constants, time encodings, sampling accuracy and conditioning probabilities explicit. Commuting-interaction results and analog Hamiltonian simulations do not by themselves classify this unrestricted circuit model.

title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
importance_reason: A general soundness-amplification question central to the power of entanglement in nonlocal games and interactive proofs. Current status must account for a directly relevant new claimed proof. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.
question_excerpt: The results of Bavarian, Vidick and Yuen show that, while we do not know if the Quantum Parallel Repetition Conjecture holds for all games \(G, [\ldots ]\)
definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.
context:
Yuen proves \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})=O_{G}(n^{-1/4}\log n)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence the repeated value cannot stay bounded away from zero. The surrounding text explicitly leaves exponential decay as the full conjecture; the previous working summary conflated these two targets.

The source describes anchoring and fortification transformations that add auxiliary questions and give exponential decay for the resulting game while preserving quantum completeness. This supplies useful gap amplification but does not bound standard repetition of every original game.

Chapter 6, Theorem 1.1, claims a universal \(c>0\) with \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq\exp\!\left(-c\,\frac{\varepsilon^{13}}{\varepsilon+\ln(|A||B|)}\,n\right),\qquad\varepsilon=1-\omega^{*}(G)>0.\] Its definitions allow arbitrary finite-dimensional joint strategies and correlated question distributions for the unchanged game. If valid, this resolves the displayed conjecture; the exponent \(13\) is not claimed optimal.

This review checked the manuscript’s version date, theorem and model against the original conjecture. It did not independently verify the proof or establish an independently reviewed publication of this result. The card therefore records an uncertain claimed resolution rather than labeling the conjecture securely open or verified resolved.
why: Determines how reliably independent challenges amplify soundness against quantum players who may coordinate across all copies. The universal question isolates the effect of entanglement without adding auxiliary tests or restricting the form of the game.
status_note: Claimed resolution found. Read the complete 2016 question and its polynomial-decay theorem, checked the author-version history, and read the August 2026 manuscript’s Chapter 6 Theorem 1.1 and Definitions 2.1–2.2. Its statement matches the full conjecture, but its proof and independent acceptance were not verified. Searches through 12 September 2026 do not justify either a confidently open label or a verified-resolved label. The old working summary’s “source-resolved” description applied only to convergence to zero.
progress: 2016-04-15: The full author paper announces polynomial decay for all two-player entangled games, resolving nonconvergence but leaving exponential decay open. | 2016: The conference introduction distinguishes the full exponential conjecture from amplification through game transformations. | 2026-08-06: The updated manuscript claims an exponential bound for every finite two-player game in the required tensor-product strategy model. Independent proof verification was not completed in this review.
working_summary: Two quantum players must win every copy of a fixed game repeated independently by the referee. They may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and joint local measurements across the copies. The target is exponential decay whenever the original optimal value is below one. The original paper establishes only polynomial decay, while game transformations give a different amplification guarantee. An August 2026 manuscript claims the full exponential theorem, but this review has not independently verified its proof.

title: Martin’s conjecture
importance_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
focus_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
context:
A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.
why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.
status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey, Conjecture 6.4. The corrected Lutz–Siskind preprint and the February 2026 Day–Marks revision address restricted or conditional variants. The checked survey erratum withdraws a separate claimed equivalence at limit ordinals; it is not a solution of this target. Bounded follow-up checks through 14 September 2026 found no full determinacy-model proof or refutation. Cited full proofs were not independently verified.

Its revision note corrects the proof of Theorem 4.12; this audit uses the corrected version. | 2026-02-16: Day–Marks version 2 records conditional structural results for a related decomposition question and many-one output degrees; it does not settle the unrestricted Turing-degree target. | 2026-03: Walsh’s Bulletin of Symbolic Logic survey presents the full target as Conjecture 6.4 and summarizes distinct partial cases in Theorems 6.6–6.7; the article first appeared online on 4 December 2025. | 2026-09-14: The survey’s author erratum was checked. The withdrawn Theorem 1.8 is not used to replace or simplify the full two-part target.
working_summary: Turing-invariant functions send mutually computable reals to mutually computable outputs. Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin’s conjecture predicts a rigid hierarchy for these operations when they are compared on Turing cones. Part I says every invariant function is constant in degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II says all operations above the identity are prewellordered, with the Turing jump increasing their ordinal rank by exactly one. Known uniform and order-preserving cases, choice-based counterexamples and conditional results for other output degrees leave the full stated conjecture unresolved in the checked sources.

title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
importance_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
focus_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96 and the inherited fair-coin KLR⇒MLR question, rather than replacing it with a finite-family uniformity assertion from the source’s open-set game. The operational rational multiplier formulation is the standard scan-rule/stake-function model of Merkle and coauthors and Kastermans–Lempp. The review specifies partial computations and explicitly permits permanent omission of coordinates; neither computational resource bounds nor oracle access is added.
definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
context:
Martin-Löf randomness and betting randomness concern individual infinite objects. Effective tests describe events of arbitrarily small fair-coin probability, while a gambler uses observed bits to determine future bets. Neither definition is a confidence score for a finite sample. Every finite binary string can occur at the start of a Martin-Löf random sequence, so a finite unusual-looking prefix alone cannot settle membership in either class.

Adaptivity changes the information available to a strategy. It may inspect coordinate 100, then choose between coordinates 3 and 7 based on that value. Reading a bit with no money at risk still reveals it and makes it unavailable for later betting. The strategy must choose its next fresh position and wager using only its current history; otherwise it could exploit information it has not legitimately obtained.

The established implications are \(\operatorname{MLR}\subseteq\operatorname{KLR}\subseteq\operatorname{CR}\), where computable randomness \(\operatorname{CR}\) rules out successful total computable fair gamblers that read bits in their original order. The first inclusion is the known direction; the card asks whether it is equality. Kolmogorov–Loveland stochasticity instead controls limiting frequencies of adaptively selected bits and is a different, weaker requirement than defeating all fair betting strategies.

Partiality must be separated from which bits are eventually visited. The standard theory permits partial computations, and using total nonmonotonic procedures yields the same randomness class. However, a total procedure can still leave infinitely many coordinates unseen. Requiring a total strategy to visit every coordinate changes its power: the classical source shows that such a strategy can be matched by a monotonic gambler on every sequence where it succeeds.

Kastermans and Lempp separate Martin-Löf randomness from randomness against predetermined computable permutation orders, and against the more general predetermined computable injective orders. A permutation visits every position; an injection may omit positions. In both cases the query order is fixed independently of revealed bit values. These separations therefore do not decide what fully adaptive strategies can detect.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan show that a Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequence has Martin-Löf random subsequences on computable sets of coordinates with densities arbitrarily close to one. Their Theorem 12 says that splitting at any infinite co-infinite computable set leaves at least one Martin-Löf random part. These are substantial proximity results, but randomness of a subsequence does not establish randomness of the whole interleaving.

Petrović’s universal-pair result concerns a generalized half-betting game. Such games allow richer computable partitions of the remaining possible sequences than asking for the value of one fresh coordinate. A pair of generalized strategies can cover all failures of Martin-Löf randomness, but this theorem does not turn them into strategies in the more restricted query model of the card.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.
why: Determines whether adaptive computable fair betting detects every effective measure-theoretic failure of randomness in an individual infinite sequence. Equality or separation would connect two foundational ways to formalize unpredictability.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 primary paper and journal record retain KLR=MLR as open. Its open-set result concerns level-dependent witnesses and is not a separating sequence. Restricted query orders, generalized partitions and pairwise nonuniversality results do not settle the full stated class. No matching resolution was found in the bounded later-work search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

working_summary: Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies make computable fair bets while adaptively querying previously unseen coordinates of an infinite binary sequence. The problem asks whether defeating every such strategy implies passing every uniform effective null test for fair-coin measure. Strategies may be partial and may omit coordinates forever, but they cannot borrow, revisit observed bits or inspect them through an oracle. A complete Lean answer must prove the implication or exhibit one non-Martin-Löf-random sequence on which every strategy has bounded capital. Known subsequence theorems, nonadaptive-order separations and the 2025 open-set obstruction leave that exact comparison unresolved.

title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
importance_reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.
formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.
context:
Two oracle decision problems represent the same Turing degree precisely when each can compute the other. Their degree records computational power without committing to a particular set of integers as its encoding. This question asks whether all degrees can be consistently relabeled, changing at least one point while preserving every reducibility comparison. A nontrivial symmetry must work simultaneously across the whole structure.

The computable degree \(\mathbf 0\) and the join operation are fixed by every order automorphism. Shore and Slaman proved the stronger fact that the graph of the Turing jump is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Thus \(\pi(a')=\pi(a)'\) for every degree \(a\), and all finite jumps of \(\mathbf 0\) are fixed. Preservation of the jump is an established restriction, not a proof of full rigidity.

Slaman and Woodin proved that every automorphism fixes every degree at least \(\mathbf 0''\); their automorphism group is also at most countable. These are statements about restrictions of global automorphisms. They do not assert that an arbitrary automorphism of the upper cone extends to the full structure, and they do not cover degrees incomparable with its base. The underlying set of all degrees has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

The same structural analysis connects rigidity with the Slaman–Woodin bi-interpretability conjecture: the degree structure and full second-order arithmetic would recover one another through logical interpretations, with the correspondence to degrees definable without parameters. The survey states equivalence with rigidity in its precise sense of bi-interpretability. This concerns the expressive power of the whole order.

Rigidity does not mean that every degree has its own parameter-free first-order definition. There are only countably many finite formulas in this language and uncountably many degrees. Most degrees therefore cannot be individually defined that way, even if the entire order is rigid.

Kjos-Hanssen proves that a coordinate permutation \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), acting on characteristic sequences by \(F_p(A)(n)=A(p(n))\), can induce an automorphism of all Turing degrees only when that automorphism is the identity; in fact \(p\) must be computable. He also excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by homeomorphisms of \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) preserving every Bernoulli product measure. Here the topology is generated by finite initial segments, and the measure with parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) makes coordinates independent bits with probability \(t\) of being one. These representation and measure restrictions are absent from the main question.

Slaman and Soskova study the separate structure of degrees at most \(\mathbf 0'\), equivalently the \(\Delta^0_2\) degrees. They prove that this local structure has a finite automorphism base: agreement on a fixed finite tuple determines an automorphism. They obtain a countable automorphism group and an equivalence between local rigidity and bi-interpretability with first-order arithmetic. None of these conclusions states that the group is trivial. Their local arithmetic comparison is distinct from the full structure’s second-order comparison.

Ongay-Valverde’s 2021 preprint gives restrictions on the action of a hypothetical automorphism on generic degrees under the continuum hypothesis \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). Theorem 7.4 additionally concerns families meeting a relative genericity condition above every degree, with jointly generic representatives for each degree and its image. Its Section 8 explicitly keeps the continuum-hypothesis assumption. This conditional restriction neither constructs a nontrivial automorphism nor proves that all automorphisms are trivial, even under that hypothesis.

Cooper’s 1999 Theorem 1.1 claims a nonidentity global automorphism fixing every degree at least \(\mathbf 0'\). This is a claim of a full negative answer, rather than merely a local example. The present review checked the statement in the author-uploaded text but did not verify its long construction.

Slaman’s later survey explicitly reports that Cooper’s construction had not been independently verified and treats the general problem as unresolved. The subsequent permutation paper also states the full question as open. The card therefore keeps the historical full-solution claim visible and uses uncertain status; it does not infer either correctness or a proved error from the announcement alone.
why: Rigidity asks whether the entire ordering of relative computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. Its connection with intrinsic definability and second-order arithmetic makes it a central structural question in computability, beyond the classification of individual computable problems.
