Bounded later-work searches found no independently verified resolution or checked refutation of Cooper’s construction. This review does not certify every cited proof or infer current openness from the absence of a search result.
progress: 1980; summarized in 2016: Nerode and Shore proved that each automorphism is the identity on some upper cone. Kjos-Hanssen’s introduction distinguishes this from the later common \(\mathbf 0''\) cone bound. | 1999: Shore and Slaman proved order-theoretic definability of the Turing jump; the inspected author manuscript states the conclusion as Theorem 1.15. | 1999: Cooper announced a nontrivial automorphism of the full degree order. The later survey reports its construction as not independently verified; this review does not certify the claim. | 2008: Slaman’s published survey states rigidity on the cone above \(\mathbf 0''\), countability of the automorphism group and equivalence between full rigidity and its bi-interpretability conjecture. It retains the global question as open. | 2018: Slaman and Soskova’s journal article gives finite automorphism bases and related definability results for \(D_T(\le_T\mathbf 0')\), without proving local or global rigidity. | 2016-03-02; journal 2018-08-07: Kjos-Hanssen’s preprint and later journal publication exclude nontrivial automorphisms induced by coordinate permutations or by homeomorphisms preserving all Bernoulli measures. The preprint record remains version 1. | 2021-06-23: Ongay-Valverde’s version 1 gives a conditional restriction on genericity of degrees and their images; Theorem 7.4 and its Section 8 consequences assume the continuum hypothesis. The complete proof was not independently certified in this review.
working_summary: Turing degrees identify oracle sets that compute one another, and their order compares relative computational power. The question asks whether every bijection of all degrees that preserves and reflects this order fixes every degree. The target allows arbitrary set-theoretic automorphisms and requires a complete Lean proof of rigidity or of a nontrivial global automorphism. Known jump, cone, representation and local-structure results impose substantial restrictions without settling the entire order. Cooper’s historical full-solution claim remains explicitly separated from verified partial results, and the card records uncertain status because its construction was reported as unverified.

title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
importance_reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.
formal:
Determine the exact six-state binary Busy Beaver runtime \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) by giving a concrete machine \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\) and proving
\[M_*\text{ halts on the blank tape},\qquad
\forall M\in\mathcal M_6:\ M\text{ halts on the blank tape}\ \Longrightarrow\ T(M)\le T(M_*).\]
Here \(\mathcal M_6\) is the finite class of deterministic six-nonhalting-state, two-symbol Turing machines defined below, and \(T(M)\) is the number of transitions through the first entry into the separate halting state. The complete transition table of \(M_*\), together with proofs of its halting and universal maximality, specifies the answer exactly as \(S(6)=T(M_*)\).
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96, BB(6)=S(6), the full six-state binary machine class and the user-approved exact machine-witness answer. Explicit state/tape/step semantics clarify the existing target. The primary proof paper uses partial tables and counts the attempted undefined transition as the last step. Replacing every undefined entry by any write/move transition into Z, or conversely forgetting the write/move on a Z-entry, preserves halting time exactly; therefore this total-table convention agrees for S(6), without an off-by-one change.
definitions:
Machine. Fix the nonhalting states \(Q=\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\), one additional halting state \(Z\notin Q\), and the tape alphabet \(\{0,1\}\). A machine is a total transition function
\[\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\times(Q\cup\{Z\}).\]
Thus its description has exactly twelve entries. The three outputs specify the symbol to write, a move of exactly one cell left or right, and the next state, respectively. There are no stationary moves, extra tapes or transitions out of \(Z\). Unreachable states and entries are allowed. Different tables need not have different behavior; no symmetry reduction is imposed on the quantified class \(\mathcal M_6\).

Execution. The tape is indexed by all integers. A configuration consists of a state \(q\), a head position \(h\in\mathbb Z\), and a tape function \(\tau:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}\). At time zero, \(q=A\), \(h=0\), and \(\tau(i)=0\) for every integer \(i\). If \(q\ne Z\) and \(\delta(q,\tau(h))=(b,d,q')\), one transition replaces \(\tau(h)\) by \(b\), leaves every other tape cell unchanged, replaces the head position by \(h+d\), and enters \(q'\). Execution stops immediately on entering \(Z\); that final write-and-move transition is included in the count. Each transition costs one step, irrespective of head position or time elapsed. There is no external input, randomness or resource limit.

Halting time and maximum. A machine halts if its unique execution first enters \(Z\) at some positive integer time. Only for such a machine, \(T(M)\) denotes this least time. Let \(\mathcal H_6\subseteq\mathcal M_6\) be the halting machines. Define
\[S(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal H_6\}.\]
There are \(28^{12}\) tables in \(\mathcal M_6\), since each entry has \(2\cdot2\cdot7\) choices. The halting subset is nonempty, since a table can send \((A,0)\) directly to \(Z\). Hence the maximum exists as a finite positive integer. No value of \(T\) on a nonhalting machine is used in the statement or the submitted certificate.

Answer representation. The runtime of a specified, proved-halting table defines an exact integer through a terminating step-counting computation, even when actually evaluating it is infeasible. The accepted answer need not separately evaluate that computation. In this card, \(\mathrm{BB}\) always means the runtime maximum \(S\), not the distinct extremal function \(\Sigma\) that maximizes the number of ones on the final tape.

Notation in the context. For positive integer \(k\), \(2\uparrow\uparrow k\) is a tower of \(k\) twos, equivalently \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2^{(2\uparrow\uparrow k)}\). Three arrows mean iteration of this tower operation: \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)\).
answer_criterion:
Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\), with complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that it halts from the stated blank initial configuration and that every halting \(M\in\mathcal M_6\) has \(T(M)\le T(M_*)\). These two proofs must establish the exact equality \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_*)\). This is the user-approved exact witness criterion, superseding the default numerical tolerance for this card only.

The witness runtime is an accepted exact finite description of the integer. A simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. A candidate machine without both proofs, an estimated runtime, a one-sided bound, a list of undecided machines or a restatement of the defining maximum is insufficient. Any reduction to representative transition tables must itself be justified as covering the full stated class. A result for a different alphabet, state count, tape convention or final-tape score does not settle this target.
context:
Radó introduced Busy Beaver functions in 1962 as concrete examples of noncomputability. The runtime function takes a maximum over finitely many halting programs at each state count, but there is no algorithm computing all its values. That statement about the entire sequence does not make every individual value unknowable. The first five binary runtime values have now been determined.

Finiteness alone does not supply an effective stopping rule for the search: a machine still running may halt much later or may run forever. Conversely, a proved value of \(S(6)\) would decide blank-tape halting for every table in this finite class in principle, by checking whether it halts within that many steps. The enormous possible duration makes this a mathematical consequence, not a practical promise.

The collaboration proves \(S(5)=47{,}176{,}870\) in Coq, now called Rocq. Its 2026 revised paper proves coverage of the relevant five-state machines as well as their halting classifications. The total number of representatives examined by that proof is \(181{,}385{,}789\); it is not a count of six-state holdouts or of all syntactically distinct tables in this card.

The formal paper presents halting entries as undefined transitions. Its convention counts the final attempt to execute such an entry, so even an immediately halting machine takes one step. Replacing an undefined entry by a write/move transition into the separate state Z preserves its runtime exactly. The card retains total twelve-entry tables to make a submitted witness fully explicit.

For six states, the paper records the lower bound \(S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5\). Appendix B carefully separates two kinds of evidence: the champion’s halting is proved in Coq, while the stated enormous step lower bound is estimated mathematically from its verified abstract evolution rules. The paper does not claim a formally verified exact runtime for that champion or a proof of universal six-state maximality.

Runtime and final output are different objectives. The function \(\Sigma(n)\) maximizes the number of ones present when a machine halts; \(S(n)\) maximizes the duration. Even their maximizing machines need not coincide: the paper records this already for three states. Approximate final-output formulas in a champion table therefore cannot simply be used as an exact answer for runtime.

One unresolved six-state behavior is Antihydra. Its halting question has an equivalent arithmetic form: start at \(a_0=8\) and iterate \(a_{j+1}=\lfloor3a_j/2\rfloor\). It halts exactly when some finite prefix of \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\) contains strictly more than twice as many odd terms as even terms. This is a particular recurrence question; resemblance to the classical Collatz problem is not an equivalence with that conjecture.

The Antihydra page discusses a probabilistic model suggesting nonhalting. The machine itself is deterministic, and a heuristic probability is not a halting or nonhalting proof. More generally, the six-state project distinguishes proved halters from unresolved machines, including examples heuristically expected to halt. Those expectations cannot certify a Busy Beaver upper bound.

The holdout table records 964 remaining six-state representatives in the entry dated 8 September 2026, attributed to mxdys. Some equivalent machines are omitted. The page warns that contributed lists are not uniformly independently verified, and this particular entry does not yet link a downloadable list. The number is therefore a dated project progress report, not a checked exhaustion theorem.

Holdout counts need not decrease monotonically: when an incompletely specified representative reaches a previously undefined transition, further completions of its table may need to be considered. Counts also depend on which equivalences have been removed. A smaller list measures progress in classification but is neither the Busy Beaver value nor a substitute for a universal proof.

The accepted answer isolates exactly what must be established: one explicit halting machine attaining the maximum, with a proof that every halting machine in the stated class takes no more steps. It can name an integer far beyond feasible decimal expansion through that certified runtime. Neither the general noncomputability theorem nor speculation about axiomatic independence supplies this requested witness.
why: The halting behavior of a finite set of exceptionally short programs is still beyond complete classification. This problem makes the boundary of current computability knowledge concrete: one additional nonhalting state separates the established five-state maximum from an unresolved maximum with enormous certified examples and difficult residual halting questions. A solution would give a universal exact upper bound for every halting program in this precisely fixed class.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The primary project page revised 15 September still lists BB(6) as unsolved. The 2026 revised proof paper settles the five-state value and records a six-state lower bound, not universal six-state maximality. The 8 September report of 964 holdouts is explicitly treated as a dated project count with verification limits. This editorial review checked the full paper and primary project explanations but did not rebuild the formal proofs, enumerate machines or independently certify the champion’s numerical lower bound.
progress: 1962: Radó introduces the Busy Beaver functions as concrete noncomputable functions. | 2024-07-02: The project reports completion of the formally verified five-state case; the later paper gives the theorem and proof framework. | 2025-06: The project credits mxdys with the six-state champion behind the bound \(S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5\). This is a lower bound, not an exact determination. | 2025-09-15; revised 2026-03-23: The proof paper establishes \(S(5)=47{,}176{,}870\) in Coq and records the different evidence scopes for the six-state champion’s halting and huge runtime lower bound. | 2026-09-08: The latest dated BB(6) entry inspected in the project holdout table reports 964 representatives after equivalence reductions. | 2026-09-15: The project page still marks \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\) unsolved and lists unresolved six-state halting behaviors.
working_summary: \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) is the maximum number of steps taken by a halting six-state binary Turing machine from the blank tape. The required answer supplies one complete transition table and Lean-checked proofs of its halting and universal runtime maximality. That proved-halting machine’s runtime names the exact integer without requiring a decimal expansion, closed form or execution trace. The five-state value is established, while six-state machines already exhibit enormous halting runtimes and unresolved arithmetic behavior. The September 2026 project pages still report the value as unknown; lower bounds, heuristics and a shrinking holdout list do not certify the requested maximum.

title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
importance_reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.
formal:
Does the following formal provability statement hold?
\[
\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\ \vdash\
\forall X\,\exists Y\,
\bigl[Y_0=X\ \wedge\ \forall j\,(Y_{j+1}=Y_j')\bigr].
\]
Here \(\mathrm{HT}\) is Hindman's theorem for every finite coloring of the positive integers and all nonempty finite sums of distinct members of one infinite set. The conclusion says that every set has its coded \(\omega\)-jump. Equivalently, does full Hindman's theorem imply \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) over \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\)?
question_excerpt: The inherited introduction places Hindman’s theorem between arithmetic comprehension and closure under the omega-th Turing jump over RCA0 and identifies its exact strength as a major open problem. The card retains the specific upper-bound reversal already selected in its previous formulation.
definitions:
Use classical two-sorted first-order logic, with number variables, set-of-number variables, equality, membership, \(0\), successor \(S\), addition and multiplication. Set equality is extensional. Models may have nonstandard numbers, and their set sort need not contain every subset of their number domain. Thus the logical semantics is Henkin semantics, not full second-order semantics.

The number axioms are Robinson arithmetic: \(Sx\ne0\), \(Sx=Sy\Rightarrow x=y\), \(x\ne0\Rightarrow\exists y\,x=Sy\), \(x+0=x\), \(x+Sy=S(x+y)\), \(x\cdot0=0\), and \(x\cdot Sy=x\cdot y+x\). Write \(1=S0\), define \(x<y\) by \(\exists z\,x+S(z)=y\), and define \(x\le y\) by \(x<y\) or \(x=y\).

A bounded arithmetic formula has only number quantifiers bounded by number terms; set membership and free set parameters are allowed, but quantified set variables are not. A \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula consists of a finite block of existential number quantifiers followed by a bounded formula; a \(\Pi^0_1\) formula uses a universal block instead. The base theory \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) adds the universal closures of the following schemes, allowing number and set parameters. For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\varphi(0)\wedge\forall n(\varphi(n)\Rightarrow\varphi(Sn))]
\Rightarrow\forall n\,\varphi(n).
\]
For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\) and \(\Pi^0_1\) formula \(\psi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\forall n(\varphi(n)\leftrightarrow\psi(n))]
\Rightarrow\exists Z\,\forall n\,[n\in Z\leftrightarrow\varphi(n)],
\]
where \(Z\) is not free in either defining formula. This is \(\Delta^0_1\) comprehension.

Functions and finite sequences are represented by their usual arithmetic codes. Fix the pairing \(\langle j,e\rangle=(j+e)(j+e+1)/2+e\), whose division is exact, and a standard effective coding of finite sequences and oracle Turing computations. All statements about a coded finite computation or sequence are interpreted inside the theory. In particular, finite lengths and color counts range over its number sort, rather than only over externally standard integers.

In \(\mathrm{HT}\), quantify over every number \(k\ge1\) and every set coding the graph of a total function \(c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\). There must exist a set \(H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}\) and a number \(i<k\) such that \(\forall b\,\exists h>b\,(h\in H)\) and
\[
c(h_0+\cdots+h_{r-1})=i
\]
for every coded strictly increasing finite sequence \(h_0<\cdots<h_{r-1}\) from \(H\) with \(r\ge1\). There is no fixed bound on \(r\), no repeated summand and no extra separation condition on the binary supports of the integers in \(H\).

Fix a standard enumeration of oracle Turing machines. For a set \(A\), the notation \(A'\) denotes the halting set
\[
\{e:\text{the }e\text{-th machine with oracle }A\text{ halts on input }e\}.
\]
The assertion \(B=A'\) is the arithmetic formula saying that membership of \(e\) in \(B\) is equivalent to existence of a coded finite halting computation using the answers supplied by \(A\). It does not assume that the jump set already exists in the model. For a single set \(Y\), define its sections by \(Y_j=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle\in Y\}\). The target requires one such \(Y\) simultaneously recording every finite jump iterate, beginning with \(Y_0=X\). The theory \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) is \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) plus this closure axiom.

The symbol \(\vdash\) means existence of a finite formal derivation in a sound and complete classical two-sorted first-order proof calculus using the stated axioms and schemes. Equivalent standard encodings of syntax and computation do not alter the question. This is an exact provability proposition, with no bound on proof length or computational resources.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that a finite formal derivation of the displayed closure axiom exists from \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such derivation exists. For the latter, a fully verified Henkin model of \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\) omitting the coded \(\omega\)-jump of some set suffices, together with the soundness argument. A model with standard natural numbers is sufficient but is not required.

Proving the closure axiom in the ambient logic of Lean without verifying the restriction to the stated object theory does not prove this reversal. Neither the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\) lower bound, the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) upper bound, nor a claim about one computable coloring decides it. A negative answer need not establish equivalence with \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\); any valid separation from the displayed closure axiom settles the question.
context:
A finite coloring may be arbitrary. Hindman’s theorem supplies one infinite set whose single elements, pair sums, triple sums and every larger finite sum all have the same color. The theorem itself is established; this card asks which axioms its assertion forces.

The classical bounds are \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\Rightarrow\mathrm{HT}\Rightarrow\mathrm{ACA}_0\) over \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\). Ordinary arithmetic comprehension gives each set its next Turing jump. The stronger closure principle collects all finite iterates into one set.

Restricted sum lengths can have different strengths. The inherited paper obtains the arithmetic-comprehension lower bound already for sums of at most two elements. Such a lower bound does not supply the whole coded sequence of jumps required here.

Liu and Patey prove that, for every non-arithmetical set \(C\) and every arithmetical finite coloring, some full Hindman solution \(H\) satisfies \(C\not\le_T H\). Here arithmetical means definable using only number quantifiers, and \(C\le_T H\) means computable with oracle \(H\). In particular, an individual such coloring cannot force every solution to compute \(\emptyset^{(\omega)}\).

The same authors explicitly state that this does not rule out equivalence with omega-jump closure through multiple applications of Hindman’s theorem. Their result does not construct a model closed under every required instance while omitting the target jump.

The July conservation paper concerns a different one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle. Its introduction distinguishes the additional block-order condition associated with Hindman’s theorem, so its weaker axiomatic bounds do not settle this card.
why: The problem asks how much set existence is forced by a basic theorem about finite sums. A reversal would identify unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity with closure under all finite Turing jumps recorded in one set; a separation would show that this known upper theory is stronger than necessary.
status_note: The checked July 2026 papers retain ACA0+ as the best known upper theory for full Hindman. The new non-arithmetic cone-avoidance result explicitly leaves equivalence by multiple applications possible. No proof or separation for RCA0+HT proving omega-jump closure was found in the bounded later-work check; the cited proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1987: The classical reverse-mathematical bounds place full Hindman between ACA0 and ACA0+, as recalled in the inherited introduction. | 2017–2020: The inherited work sharpens lower bounds for bounded-length sums while retaining the full reversal gap. | 2026-07-02: New variable-word results still distinguish their principles from the full Hindman upper-bound question. | 2026-07-20: Non-arithmetic cone avoidance shows a limitation of one application; the authors explicitly leave the multiple-application reversal open. | 2026-07-30: A conservation theorem for a neighboring one-variable principle preserves the distinction from full Hindman.
working_summary: Hindman’s theorem finds an infinite set whose nonempty finite sums of distinct elements all have one color. This card asks whether that theorem forces every set’s complete sequence of finite Turing jumps over the weak base theory RCA0. The question concerns a formal implication between theories, not whether Hindman’s theorem is true in ordinary mathematics. A July 2026 result limits what one arithmetic coloring can force a solution to compute but explicitly leaves the full implication undecided. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish the stated formal derivation or its nonexistence, for example through a verified separating model.

title: Universality of Turing equivalence
importance_reason: A classical universality question with consequences for Martin’s conjecture and for the distinction between definable and uniform computational encodings.
formal: Is unrestricted Turing equivalence universal among countable Borel equivalence relations? Precisely, is the following proposition true: for every standard Borel space \(X\) and every Borel equivalence relation \(E\subseteq X\times X\) whose equivalence classes are at most countable, there exists a Borel map \(f:X\to2^{\mathbb N}\) such that \[\forall x,y\in X,\qquad x\,E\,y\ \Longleftrightarrow\ f(x)\equiv_T f(y)?\] The map may depend on \(X\) and \(E\); both implications must hold on every pair.
question_excerpt: Retains the ordinary Borel-universality question in Caicedo–Löwe Question 6 and Kechris Problem 12.5. The free-group shift is an explicitly defined equivalent universal test relation, not a restriction to computable or uniform reductions. No conditional Martin-conjecture consequence is promoted to an unconditional answer.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) contains all infinite binary sequences, with the product topology of the discrete two-point space; its basic open cylinders specify a finite initial segment. Fix an effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs. For \(a,b\in2^{\mathbb N}\), define \(a\le_T b\) by \(\exists e\,\forall n\in\mathbb N\,[\Phi_e^b(n)\text{ halts with output }a(n)]\). One program must work for every coordinate; its index may depend on the ordered pair \((a,b)\). It may query individual bits of \(b\), with no time or space bound and no additional oracle. Define \(a\equiv_T b\) by \(a\le_T b\) and \(b\le_T a\). Finite strings and machine descriptions are encoded by any fixed effective encoding, which does not change this reducibility.

A Polish topology is a topology induced by a complete separable metric. A standard Borel space is a set equipped with the Borel sigma-algebra of some Polish topology; the Borel sigma-algebra is the smallest family containing the open sets and closed under complements and countable unions. Equip \(X\times X\) with the product Borel structure. The relation \(E\) is a Borel subset of this product and is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Each class \([x]_E=\{y\in X:x\,E\,y\}\) must be finite or countably infinite; \(X\) itself may be uncountable. A map is Borel if the inverse image of every Borel set is Borel. For a map to Cantor space it suffices to check inverse images of its basic cylinders. The notation \(E\le_B F\) means that a Borel map preserves both equivalence and inequivalence between \(E\) and \(F\) on all pairs.

An equivalent single-relation formulation uses the following fixed \(E_{\infty}\). Let \(F_2\) be the free group on two generators \(a,b\): its elements are finite reduced words in \(a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1}\), with no adjacent inverse letters; multiplication concatenates words and cancels adjacent inverse pairs, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses the word and inverts each letter. Give \(2^{F_2}\), the set of all functions \(F_2\to\{0,1\}\), the product topology, whose basic cylinders prescribe values at finitely many group elements. Define \[x\,E_{\infty}\,y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists g\in F_2\,\forall h\in F_2,\ y(h)=x(g^{-1}h).\] This particular countable Borel equivalence relation is known to be universal, so the main target is equivalent to \(E_{\infty}\le_B\equiv_T\).

The question concerns ordinary classical mathematics, with no additional determinacy or unproved conjectural assumption. The requested reduction need not be computable, continuous or injective on individual points; its induced map on equivalence classes must be injective. There is no requirement for an algorithmic transformation from a code for \(E\) to a code for \(f\), no prescribed dependence of output program indices on input equivalence witnesses, and no exception on a null or meager set. Neither a probability measure nor a resource bound is part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universality proposition or its negation, including all necessary definitions and background results. A positive answer establishes the existence of a Borel reduction for every stated \((X,E)\); an equivalent positive theorem gives a Borel reduction of the explicitly defined \(E_{\infty}\), together with the theorem establishing its universality. No effective construction of all reductions is required. A negative answer establishes one countable Borel equivalence relation \(E\) for which every Borel map \(f:X\to2^{\mathbb N}\) fails the biconditional for at least one pair \(x,y\); equivalently, prove this failure for every Borel map on the stated \(E_{\infty}\) domain. The counterexample pair may depend on \(f\). A theorem conditional on Martin’s conjecture, failure only of uniform or computable reductions, or universality of a different degree relation does not settle the target. This is an exact yes/no question, with no numerical tolerance.
context:
Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of \(f(x)\) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

The explicitly defined shift relation \(E_{\infty}\) is a universal countable Borel equivalence relation: every such relation reduces to it. This theorem of Dougherty, Jackson and Kechris makes the single question \(E_{\infty}\le_B\equiv_T\) equivalent to the full target. The space here includes all binary labelings of the free group, including labelings with nontrivial stabilizers.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Universality does not automatically pass from a finer relation to a coarser one. Two encoded outputs that are inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may nevertheless be equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. That collapses distinct source classes and violates the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction.

A related negative theorem concerns uniform universality with respect to specified generating maps. When Turing equivalence is generated by its usual oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Uniformity would require the two output computation indices to depend only on the indices witnessing the input equivalence, independently of the input objects. This extra requirement is absent from the target.

The choice of generators matters for uniform universality. Marks shows that a universal countable Borel relation can always be given some generating family for which it is uniformly universal. Consequently, the negative result for the standard Turing-program generators does not itself rule out an arbitrary Borel reduction.

The Borel form of Martin’s conjecture implies nonuniversality of Turing equivalence: it even rules out a Borel reduction of two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. This is a conditional consequence, not an unconditional answer.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies whether Turing equivalence is an increasing union of Borel equivalence relations whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. These are conditional consequences of a different open decomposition question. The article is published in Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, Series B 13 (2026), 379–402.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey identifies an incorrect equivalence assertion in Theorem 1.8 concerning formulations of Martin’s conjecture. That characterization is not used as an established theorem on this card.
why: A central bridge between computability and descriptive set theory, asking whether equality of computational power can encode every countable Borel classification problem.

Arithmetic and polynomial-time universality, nonuniversality for specified uniform generators, the conditional Martin-conjecture obstruction and the conditional February 2026 Day–Marks consequences concern distinct statements. The erroneous equivalence characterization in MSS Theorem 1.8 is excluded following the author erratum.

working_summary: Turing equivalence groups all infinite binary sequences according to mutual oracle computability, without time or space restrictions. The question asks whether every Borel equivalence relation with countable classes can be encoded by Turing degrees using a Borel map. The encoding must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence for every input pair, but need not be computable, continuous or uniform on computation indices. The explicitly defined binary shift of the free group on two generators gives an equivalent single universal relation whose reducibility would settle the whole question. A complete Lean proof must establish or refute this exact universality statement; neighboring universality theorems and conditional Martin-conjecture or 2026 decomposition consequences do not suffice.

title: Mortality of \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
importance_reason: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\) of \(2\times 2\) integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist \(\ell\)\(\ge 1\) and indices \(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{\ell}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(A_{i_{1}} A_{i_{2}} \cdots  A_{i_{\ell}}=0_{2}\)?
definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.
context:
A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.
why: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.
status_note: The checked 2024 primary manuscript explicitly leaves unrestricted \(2\times 2\) integer mortality open. The 2020 determinant-restricted algorithm and April 2026 embedding results do not settle it. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established general resolution; proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2012: The two-dimensional integer mortality problem is shown NP-hard; lower-bound attribution checked in later primary papers. | 2020-07: The revised affine-reachability paper proves NP-completeness under the determinant promise {0,+1}. | 2024: The same authors explicitly retain general two-dimensional mortality as open while resolving membership complexity for \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\). | 2026-04: New results concern word representations and embeddings in complex matrix structures rather than unrestricted integer mortality.
working_summary: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition. The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix. Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted. NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case. Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.

title: Computability of the Mandelbrot set
importance_reason: This classical question asks whether a basic explicitly defined fractal admits a single rigorous algorithm for approximation at every precision.
formal:
Is the Mandelbrot set a computable compact subset of the plane?

Precisely, does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that for every integer \(k\ge0\), \(A(k)\) halts and outputs a finite nonempty set \(S_k\) of points with dyadic rational coordinates satisfying
\[
d_H(S_k,M)\le 2^{-k},
\]
where
\[
M=\{c\in\mathbb C:\ (z_j(c))_{j\ge0}\text{ is bounded}\},\qquad
z_0(c)=0,\quad z_{j+1}(c)=z_j(c)^2+c?
\]
The assertion is unconditional and places no complexity bound on \(A\).
question_excerpt: The source identifies the computability of the Mandelbrot set as an unresolved question in the study of effectively approximable planar sets and relates it to complex dynamics.
definitions:
Identify \(\mathbb C\) with \(\mathbb R^2\) and use the Euclidean norm \(|\cdot|\). Boundedness of the orbit means that there exists a finite real \(R\ge0\), depending on \(c\), such that \(|z_j(c)|\le R\) for every integer \(j\ge0\). For this family, equivalently,
\[
M=\{c:\ \forall j\ge0,\ |z_j(c)|\le2\}.
\]
The set \(M\) is nonempty, closed and contained in the closed disk of radius two, hence compact.

A dyadic rational is an integer divided by a nonnegative integer power of two, encoded by signed binary integers for numerator and exponent. The output \(S_k\) is an explicit finite list of pairs of such numbers; repetitions may be removed. No bound on the list length is imposed. The accuracy input \(k\) has its ordinary finite binary encoding.

For two nonempty compact subsets \(X,Y\) of the plane, their Hausdorff distance is
\[
d_H(X,Y)=\max\left\{
\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{y\in Y}|x-y|,
\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}|x-y|
\right\}.
\]
Thus every reported point must be within the stated accuracy of \(M\), and every point of \(M\) must be within that accuracy of a reported point. A close picture on a selected finite grid without a proved global error guarantee is insufficient.

The machine is an ordinary algorithm operating on finite strings. It receives only \(k\); it has no oracle for complex numbers, set membership, the halting problem or a dynamical conjecture. One finite program must work at every precision, rather than a separately chosen program or advice string for each \(k\).

This is the standard computable-analysis notion for a fixed compact set. Equivalently, its distance function
\[
\operatorname{dist}(q,M)=\inf_{c\in M}|q-c|
\]
must be uniformly computable: a machine, given any rational point \(q\in\mathbb Q^2\) and \(k\ge0\), returns a rational number within \(2^{-k}\) of this distance. The equivalence uses the fixed compact bound on \(M\). The question does not ask for a total exact membership decision on arbitrary real inputs, for a polynomial running time, for the area of \(M\), or for its boundary alone.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of \(A\) with the stated all-precision Hausdorff guarantee. A positive answer must prove both termination and the approximation bound for every \(k\). A negative answer must rule out all ordinary Turing programs with this behavior. An implication from an additional unproved conjecture or an undecidability result for exact real membership does not settle the assertion. This is a binary computability question: a fixed numerical tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the requirement to handle every \(2^{-k}\).
context:
The source uses this question as motivation for computable geometry. Its main results concern semicomputable triangles, so the existence of that paper does not constitute progress resolving the Mandelbrot question.

The author’s later handout distinguishes one-sided information from a complete approximation algorithm: the exterior can be effectively enumerated as an open set, while the boundary and hyperbolic components satisfy other enumerability properties. These individual statements do not by themselves provide the target distance computation.

The relevant hyperbolicity conjecture asserts that every \(c\) in the interior of \(M\) gives a quadratic map with an attracting periodic cycle. Here a periodic point \(z\) of period \(r\) is attracting when \(|(f_c^r)'(z)|<1\), for \(f_c(z)=z^2+c\). Hertling shows that this conjecture would imply computability, including a stronger two-sided distance notion. The conjecture is not an assumption of this card.

The 2021 handout lists ordinary distance computability separately from the stronger two-sided assertion. Accordingly this card asks only for the ordinary compact-set approximation target and does not add a requirement to recognize the entire interior.

The 2025 escape-problem paper supplies an alternative conditional result for the quadratic family. Its Theorem 22 identifies the robust instances reached by its reduction and retains the hyperbolicity condition; it does not claim an unconditional approximation algorithm for the whole Mandelbrot set.

The 2025 paper also distinguishes the bit-based approximation question from exact membership in the Blum–Shub–Smale real-computation model. A negative result for the latter is not a negative answer to the finite Hausdorff-approximation question specified here.
why: The defining iteration is simple and finite images are ubiquitous, yet those facts do not establish a uniform algorithm with certified error at every resolution. The problem tests whether the global geometry of a natural dynamical parameter set is effectively recoverable from its definition.
status_note: The source’s ordinary compact-set computability question remains the selected target. Hertling’s conditional result is restated in his 2021 problem-session handout, and Neumann’s 2025 quadratic-family result still invokes the hyperbolicity conjecture. No unconditional resolution was found in this bounded review; exact membership in a different real-computation model does not decide this question.
progress: 2005: Hertling publishes computability results for associated sets and a conditional positive result under hyperbolicity. | 2018: The source records Mandelbrot computability as an open motivating problem. | 2021-04-27: Hertling’s problem-session handout explicitly separates ordinary and two-sided distance computability. | 2025-08-20: The MFCS escape-problem application retains a hyperbolicity condition for the quadratic family. | 2026-09-16: The review fixes an unconditional, all-precision Hausdorff target and finds no unconditional resolution in the checked primary sources.
working_summary: The Mandelbrot set consists of complex parameters whose quadratic iteration starting at zero remains bounded. The question asks for one ordinary program that approximates the entire set to every requested accuracy. Its output must be a finite set of dyadic points with a proved Hausdorff error bound, and no running-time bound is imposed. Known positive results depend on a hyperbolicity conjecture, including the checked 2025 application to escape problems. The selected unconditional approximation question differs from exact real membership, computing area and producing images without certified error.

title: NP-hardness of conditional polynomial-time pKt
importance_reason: The proposed hardness transfer connects a concrete description-length problem to the gap between average-case NP hardness and one-way functions.
formal:
Does conditional probabilistic time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity admit the following unconditional, uniform padding-compatible NP-hardness reduction in the polynomial-time regime?

For every integer \(\kappa\ge1\), there must exist one randomized polynomial-time map \(R_\kappa\) such that for every integer \(c\ge2\), there exist polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable length functions \(n_c,m_c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge2}\) with the following property. For every Boolean 3-CNF formula \(z\) of encoded length \(v\ge2\),
\[
R_\kappa(z,1^{n_c(v)},1^{m_c(v)})=(x,y,1^s),
\qquad |x|=n_c(v),\quad |y|=m_c(v),
\]
and, with probability at least \(1-v^{-\kappa}\) over the reduction's random bits,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 z\text{ satisfiable}
 &\ \Longrightarrow\
 \mathrm{pK}_{2/3}^{\,\tau_c(|x|,|y|)}(x\mid y)\le s,\\
 z\text{ unsatisfiable}
 &\ \Longrightarrow\
 \mathrm{pK}_{1/3}^{\,\tau_c(|x|,|y|)}(x\mid y)>s,
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\tau_c(n,m)=(n+1)^c(m+1)^c.
\]
The same \(R_\kappa\) must work for all \(c\); \(c\) affects the chosen output-length schedules and is not a separate input or advice string to the reduction. The schedules may also depend on \(\kappa\). This is the quantified polynomial-regime target underlying the source's Corollary 55.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether computing conditional probabilistic Kolmogorov complexity is NP-hard in the polynomial-time regime and links such hardness to excluding Pessiland.
definitions:
Fix a standard time-optimal universal machine \(U\) for binary programs with a read-only random input and random access to a finite conditional string \(y\). A query specifies a bit position in binary and returns that bit, or an end marker for a position outside the string. Writing a query and all ordinary computation count toward time; an oracle query itself takes one step. The machine has no other oracle or advice. Programs use a fixed paddable binary encoding. Polynomial simulation overhead is allowed in the universal-machine convention.

For strings \(x,y\), an integer time bound \(t\ge1\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1]\), let
\[
\mathrm{pK}^{t}_{\lambda}(x\mid y)
=\min\left\{k\in\mathbb N:
\Pr_{r\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{t}}\!
\left[\exists p\in\{0,1\}^{\le k}:
 U^y(p,r)\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps and outputs }x
\right]\ge\lambda
\right\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) if no such \(k\) exists. The existential program is inside the probability: it may depend on the public random string \(r\). This is not the private-randomness measure that chooses one program before its coins. No probability is taken over \(x\) or \(y\).

For a fixed \(c\), the promise problem \(\operatorname{Cond\text{-}pK}[\tau_c]\) has instances \((x,y,1^s)\), with \(s\ge0\), and disjoint parts
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{YES}_c
 &=\{(x,y,1^s):
       \mathrm{pK}^{\tau_c(|x|,|y|)}_{2/3}(x\mid y)\le s\},\\
\mathrm{NO}_c
 &=\{(x,y,1^s):
       \mathrm{pK}^{\tau_c(|x|,|y|)}_{1/3}(x\mid y)>s\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Disjointness follows because achieving probability \(2/3\) requires at least as much description length as achieving \(1/3\). Inputs in neither set carry no required answer. The problem is called computing conditional probabilistic complexity in the source, but its specified task is this promise decision problem, not evaluation of the exact integer \(\mathrm{pK}^t\).

Use a fixed ordinary binary encoding of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause. Satisfiability asks whether an assignment makes every clause true. This standard NP-complete source problem makes NP-hardness concrete. Finitely many shorter encodings can be handled separately.

For each \(\kappa\), \(R_\kappa\) is one uniform probabilistic Turing machine whose time on every input \((z,1^n,1^m)\) and every random tape is bounded by a polynomial in \(|z|+n+m\). It always outputs a finite triple; for the length schedules selected in the statement, the displayed output lengths hold on every execution. The bound counts writing \(x,y,1^s\), so the output threshold is polynomially bounded as well. For a fixed \(\kappa,c\), composing with its length schedules is a randomized polynomial-time many-one reduction. There are no adaptive calls to a solver and no nonuniform advice depending on \(v\).

Requiring all \(c\ge2\) specifies arbitrarily generous polynomial decoding times at which the entire conditional string can be read. It also gives a cofinal explicit family of the source's polynomial time bounds; the required reduction is uniform across the family, as in its formal corollary. A different unrestricted reduction chosen independently for each exponent is not the full uniform assertion made here. The unary length arguments permit the padding dependence that the corollary expressly allows.

The reduction's probability is separate from the inner public-randomness probabilities defining the target promise. A successful reduction must land in the correct promise part. Landing outside the promise counts against its permitted failure probability.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified reduction statement. An affirmative answer must supply the uniform reduction family, the polynomial length schedules, the running-time bounds, and both promise-preservation guarantees for every required exponent. A refutation must disprove that assertion in the stated unrelativized model. A sublinear decoding-time result, an additional cryptographic assumption, or a limitation of one reduction technique does not settle it. This is a binary existence question; \(1/100\) numerical tolerance does not replace the two promise thresholds or the reduction error bound.
context:
The source proves randomized NP-hardness for a regime in which the allowed time is sublinear in the length of the conditional string. A program may still run polynomially long in the output length, so sublinear here refers to the side input.

Its polynomial regime instead permits time growing as a product of powers of the two string lengths. The decoder can inspect its entire conditional input, and the sublinear theorem does not extend automatically.

The task has a probability gap between two public-randomness description thresholds. It is not a request to output an exact Kolmogorov-complexity number and does not exchange the order of the random tape and program quantifiers.

The full corollary places one randomized reduction before the time-bound quantifier and permits the output lengths to vary polynomially with the chosen bound. This uniformity is part of the precise target used to support the claimed consequence.

Under that reduction, the proof sketch combines average-case easiness of conditional probabilistic complexity with the non-existence of infinitely-often one-way functions to obtain average-case randomized tractability for NP. This is the direction relevant to excluding Pessiland.

The March 2026 chain-rule report still separates the unconditional sublinear result from polynomial-regime hardness assumptions. A cited polynomial-regime result for deterministic conditional complexity uses witness encryption and concerns a different measure.
why: When a short program cannot inspect most of its conditional input, there is a provable source of hardness. Allowing it polynomial time to read and process the whole input removes that obstruction. Establishing the stated uniform hardness reduction would make a major connection between worst-case reductions and the existence of cryptographic hardness.
status_note: The source proves randomized NP-hardness when the decoding program cannot read the entire conditional input, and asks for the polynomial-time regime. The full version specifies a padding-compatible reduction sufficient for its average-case consequence; that is the target expanded here. The checked March 2026 report retains the distinction, and no later unconditional construction or refutation was found.

working_summary: Conditional probabilistic Kolmogorov complexity measures how short a program can be when it sees a conditional string and public random bits. The question asks for randomized NP-hardness even when decoding is allowed arbitrarily large polynomial time. The target is a promise decision problem with two success-probability thresholds, rather than an exact numerical evaluation. One reduction per error exponent must work across the time bounds through the permitted polynomial output-length padding. The known sublinear-time theorem and later conditional hardness statements do not establish this uniform polynomial-regime target.

title: Unconditional coding theorem for randomized Kolmogorov complexity
importance_reason: The question asks whether a basic information-content coding principle survives polynomial-time decoding with private randomness for the full class of efficient samplers.
formal:
Is the following coding statement true without a computational hardness or derandomization assumption?
\[
\forall D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ \exists c,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge2\ \forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_n):
\quad
\mathrm{rK}^{(n+2)^d}(x)
\le
\left\lceil\log_2\frac1{D_n(x)}\right\rceil
+c\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil .
\]
Here \(D=\{D_n\}_{n\ge2}\) ranges over uniformly polynomial-time samplable distributions on \(n\)-bit strings, and \(\mathrm{rK}^t\) uses private random bits and success probability at least \(2/3\), as defined below. The constants \(c,d\) may depend on the fixed sampler but must work for every length and every string in its support.

The target is existence of short polynomial-time randomized descriptions. No efficient algorithm for finding a description from \(x\) is required.
question_excerpt: The source leaves open whether all polynomial-time samplable distributions admit an existential coding theorem for polynomial-time randomized Kolmogorov complexity without assumptions.
definitions:
Fix one standard efficiently universal probabilistic Turing machine \(U\), with a binary program, a one-way tape of independent fair random bits and an output tape. Its simulation of any fixed machine has polynomial time overhead and a constant program-description overhead. The program receives no input string, length, advice, shared random tape or oracle for the sampler's distribution.

For \(t\in\mathbb N\), define
\[
\mathrm{rK}^{t}(x)=
\min\left\{
 |p|:
 \Pr_{r\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{t}}
 [U(p;r)\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps with output exactly }x]
 \ge\frac23
\right\}.
\]
A computation uses at most \(t\) random bits in \(t\) steps; unused bits are ignored. Failure to halt in time or outputting another string is failure. The minimum is \(+\infty\) if there is no such program. The same program \(p\) must succeed for the indicated fraction of random tapes. It may depend on \(D,n,x\), but it is chosen before the random tape. A description can encode the length and a sampler description within its counted program bits.

Membership \(D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) means that there is one deterministic algorithm \(S\), a polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer function \(a(n)\), and a polynomial time bound, such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every \(r\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), the computation \(S(1^n,r)\) outputs exactly \(n\) bits within that bound. The law of \(S(1^n,R)\) for uniform \(R\) is \(D_n\). Thus \(D_n(x)\) is an exact rational probability and \(\operatorname{supp}(D_n)=\{x:D_n(x)>0\}\). The sampler is uniform and has no length-dependent advice.

The expression \(\log_2(1/D_n(x))\) is the information content, in bits, of the particular string. The inequality is pointwise on the entire support, including very unlikely strings. It is not only an expected-length bound or a guarantee outside a small exceptional set. There is one polynomial decoding-time exponent and one logarithmic-overhead constant for the whole sampler family.

For comparison, probabilistic complexity \(\mathrm{pK}^{t}(x)\) permits the short deterministic program to be chosen after seeing public random bits: its quantifiers have the form \(\Pr_r[\exists p\text{ short}:U(p;r)=x]\ge2/3\). That is a different measure from the single-program private-randomness measure in the question. Likewise, an efficient coding theorem would additionally require an efficient encoder that finds a short description; this card does not impose that requirement.

No assumption about one-way functions, average-case hardness or circuit lower bounds is part of the statement. The fixed universal-machine convention is harmless for this existential polynomial-time and logarithmic-overhead target, since the constants and exponent may change.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal coding statement. An affirmative answer must cover every uniformly polynomial-time sampler and every supported string with the stated quantifier order. A negative answer must establish a sampler family for which no pair of constants \(c,d\) works. A conditional result, a coding theorem only for public-randomness complexity, an expected-length bound, or a theorem allowing exceptional strings does not suffice. This is a binary question; numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not relax the coding inequality or its universal quantifiers.
context:
The classical coding principle bounds description length by information content when no decoding-time restriction is imposed. The card asks for a polynomial-time private-randomness version for arbitrary efficient samplers.

Public-randomness descriptions may choose a different short program after seeing the shared random tape. The cited literature supplies stronger coding results in that model; they do not give the single fixed randomized program required here.

The source proves efficient coding for next-bits predictable distributions, where conditional next-bit probabilities can be estimated to arbitrarily small inverse-polynomial accuracy. An efficient sampler alone is not that additional prediction guarantee.

Theorems I.1–I.2 give conditional and average-case coding consequences under the non-existence of infinitely-often one-way functions. Their assumptions and allowance of exceptional instances differ from the unconditional pointwise statement.

Theorem I.7 identifies a cryptographic obstruction to efficient encoding for all samplable distributions. It does not show that short descriptions fail to exist when the encoder is unrestricted.

The December 2025 boundary-hardness paper still identifies the unconditional theorem for every string in the sampler support as missing, and explains why an average-case coding result does not supply that requirement.
why: A sampler may assign a string high probability without providing an obvious short description that a fast decoder can use. The question asks whether information content nevertheless always predicts description length, allowing private randomness and logarithmic overhead. A resolution would clarify a recurring gap between information-theoretic coding and computational descriptions.
status_note: The FOCS 2024 paper leaves existential coding for all polynomial-time samplable distributions open. The December 2025 boundary-hardness paper again identifies the all-support theorem as unavailable. Its conditional average-case substitutes and the efficient-coding equivalences do not resolve the statement below; no later resolution was found in the bounded check.

working_summary: An efficient sampler assigns a probability to each string it can produce. The question asks whether every such string has a short randomized description close to its information content. One fixed description must reconstruct the string in polynomial time with probability at least two thirds using private random bits. The guarantee must cover the whole sampler support, while the encoder that finds a description may be inefficient. Known conditional, average-case and public-randomness coding results do not establish the stated unconditional theorem.

title: Scaling joint Kolmogorov-complexity profiles
importance_reason: Scaling complete algorithmic-information profiles asks whether shared information has a universal homogeneous geometry, across arbitrary tuples rather than one example.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\) and real \(\lambda >0\), does there exist a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every tuple of binary strings \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}\) of length at most n, there are finite binary strings \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{k}\) satisfying |\(C(b_{S})- \lambda  C(a_{S})|\le c \log _{2} n\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,k\}\)? The same tuple b must satisfy all \(2^{k}- 1\) inequalities simultaneously.
definitions: Fix one optimal plain Kolmogorov machine U: an optimal partial computable map from finite binary programs to finite binary strings. \(C(x)\) is the minimum program length with U(program)=x. For \(S=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{r}\}\), encode the tuple \(x_{S}\) as \(1^{r}0\) followed, in that order, by the strings \(1^{|x_{i}|}0x_{i}\), and let \(C(x_{S})\) mean the complexity of this encoding. This is a fixed computably decodable encoding. The strings \(b_{i}\) have no prescribed lengths and need not be computable from the \(a_{i}\) by a fixed transformation. Only joint unconditional complexities of all nonempty subtuples are required. The constants may depend on \(k, \lambda\) and U but not on n, the input strings or S. The additive slack is measured in bits. This uses the original length normalization \(O(\log  n)\); it does not silently replace it by the potentially smaller \(O(\log  C(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}))\).
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal statement, or its logical negation with the same quantifier order. Failure of one algorithm for producing b, or failure of obtaining the scaling by conditioning the original strings on an auxiliary string, is not a refutation. The logarithmic slack is part of the proposition, not a numerical-estimation tolerance.
context:
Scaling each component separately can destroy its shared-information pattern with other components. The target scales the entire joint profile, retaining those dependencies.

The original card asked for \(\lambda =1/2\). The retained question asks for every fixed positive \(\lambda\), as in Question 1 of the 2025 paper. It is a broader formulation; no equivalence to the single halving case is asserted.

The 2025 paper separates freely choosing a new tuple from conditioning the original tuple on one auxiliary string. Its negative conditioning result does not settle the new-tuple problem. Its discussion retains nonintegral scaling for general tuples as open.
why: Scaling complete algorithmic-information profiles asks whether shared information has a universal homogeneous geometry, across arbitrary tuples rather than one example.
status_note: The 2025 primary source retains the general scaling question; its conditioning obstruction is a different target.
progress: 2025: Question 1 retains arbitrary joint-profile scaling as a problem, while distinguishing the conditioning formulation addressed by the paper.
working_summary: Every tuple of strings has a profile of complexities of its nonempty subtuples. The question asks whether that whole profile can be multiplied by any fixed positive real factor. One new tuple must realize all the scaled quantities within logarithmic additive error. No fixed algorithm mapping the old tuple to the new one is required. The target concerns the homogeneous geometry of shared algorithmic information.

title: Shannon feasibility from algorithmic network coding
importance_reason: Equivalence of Shannon and algorithmic network coding would connect two general frameworks for distributed information.
formal: For every fixed finite acyclic directed network with correlated finite-alphabet sources and specified source-reconstruction demands, does high-probability algorithmic feasibility on independent source blocks imply Shannon achievability at the same edge rates? The algorithmic model permits sample-dependent local programs of length \(O(\log N)\) and \(O(\log N)\) extra bits on each edge for a block of \(N\) samples. The Shannon model requires fixed local encoding and decoding maps for each block length, with vanishing error and arbitrarily small rate slack, as defined below.
definitions: Fix a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(m\ge1\), nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\), and any joint probability law \(P\) for \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\) on their product. The law is fixed as block length varies; its coordinates may be arbitrarily correlated, and no computability assumption is imposed on its probabilities. Each vertex \(v\) has fixed sets \(S_v,T_v\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\): it initially receives the source coordinates in \(S_v\) and must reproduce the coordinates in \(T_v\). Require \(\bigcup_v S_v=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Several vertices may know or demand the same source, and a vertex may both receive sources and relay messages. Each edge \(e\) has a fixed finite real rate \(r_e\ge0\), measured in bits per joint source sample. For \(N\ge1\), take \(N\) independent copies of the entire vector \(X\); write \(X_j^N\) for the resulting length-\(N\) word of coordinate \(j\). The block law is \(P^{\otimes N}\), not independence between different coordinates. All finite words, integers and tuples use fixed computable binary encodings; tuple components and incident edges are ordered once with the network. Let \(C(u\mid v)\) be plain conditional Kolmogorov complexity: the least length of a binary program for a fixed optimal interpreter that halts with output \(u\) on auxiliary input \(v\). There is no time bound. Optimal means that this interpreter simulates every other partial computable interpreter with an additive program-length overhead independent of \(u,v\). Let \(L_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). For a realized source block and an integer \(K\ge1\), algorithmic feasibility means that there exist edge-message strings \(M_e\) with \(|M_e|\le\lfloor Nr_e\rfloor+K L_N\), such that at every vertex \(v\), \[C\bigl(( (M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{out}(v)}, (X_j^N)_{j\in T_v})\mid N,(X_j^N)_{j\in S_v},(M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{in}(v)}\bigr)\le K L_N.\] The demanded outputs in this formula are the true source words, so reconstruction is exact on a feasible realization. Messages and witnessing programs may depend on the whole realized source block; only their lengths and the displayed local conditional complexities are constrained. They need not arise from one choice of encoding functions used for every realization. Call the rate vector algorithmically feasible with high probability if there exists one \(K\) such that, for every \(\eta\in(0,1)\), some \(N_0\) makes the probability of this feasibility event at least \(1-\eta\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). The same \(K\) works for every block length, realization and error threshold. Shannon achievability means that for every rate slack \(\delta>0\) and every error tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\), there is \(N_0\) such that for every \(N\ge N_0\) there exist deterministic local encoding and decoding maps with the following properties. In a topological order, each vertex computes its outgoing edge messages from only its local source words and incoming messages; each demand is decoded from the same local information. Each edge message belongs to the finite set of binary strings of length at most \(\lfloor N(r_e+\delta)\rfloor\). For each edge this bounded-string alphabet is shared by the parties and the receiver observes the whole message, including its length; the same convention is used for algorithmic messages. The probability, under \(P^{\otimes N}\), that every demanded word is reconstructed correctly is at least \(1-\eta\). The local maps are fixed before observing the source realization; they may depend on the network, law, rates, block length and tolerances, and have no computational time or description-size bound. There is no feedback, extra channel, shared sample-dependent advice or communication other than the edge messages. This is an asymptotic rate-region converse. It does not assert equivalence with logarithmic finite-block overhead in the Shannon model.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every network, source law, demand pattern and finite rate vector just defined, or refute it. A refutation requires a fixed admissible network, joint law and rate vector for which algorithmic feasibility holds with one logarithmic-overhead constant and probability tending to one, but Shannon achievability fails. In particular, failure at a single block length or at a rate boundary without accounting for arbitrarily small positive rate slack is insufficient. Results for only one source, independent sources, one terminal, particular network shapes, or only information-cut inequalities do not settle the general converse. An inefficient Shannon code is allowed; the target is coding feasibility, not efficient construction.
context:
A network code chooses how each relay transforms its received messages and local source data. The same code must handle many possible source realizations. Several correlated sources and several destinations can make compatibility between these local choices a substantial constraint.

The algorithmic version instead asks whether a particular tuple of strings admits suitable edge messages. A short program may certify each local transformation, and a different realized tuple may use different programs. Their permitted logarithmic length is small compared with the transmitted source block, but this nonuniform freedom is exactly what the converse must address.

Shen’s 2006 framework defines algorithmic requests on finite acyclic directed graphs, with message-length capacities and logarithmic conditional-complexity allowances. The graph, local-information and program conventions in this card make that model explicit.

The 2021 problem list compares the two settings by taking independent repeated samples of a joint source law. Question 13 asks whether algorithmic feasibility with high probability can occur even when the corresponding Shannon transmission is impossible. The earlier direction from Shannon codes to algorithmic requests is discussed with an explicit warning that logarithmic precision may be lost.

Accordingly, the main target here is the converse actually asked in Question 13. It fixes logarithmic algorithmic overhead and the standard Shannon closure under vanishing error and positive rate slack. It does not claim a two-way finite-block equivalence, and it keeps arbitrary correlation within each source sample.

The source surveys networks where both theories have strong positive coding theorems, including transmission with side information and the two-sender Slepian–Wolf problem. It also discusses networks where elementary cut constraints do not suffice. Agreement in these special cases does not supply a general translation between the models.

The distinction is operational rather than a change of terminology for entropy. The conclusion requires one collection of local maps that succeeds on almost all realizations, while the premise only asserts the existence of compatible short local descriptions separately for those realizations.
why: The question compares information transmission for random sources with transmission of their individual realized strings. A positive answer would show that logarithmic sample-dependent algorithmic descriptions cannot create new asymptotic network rates. A negative answer would expose a concrete operational distinction between Shannon and Kolmogorov descriptions of distributed information.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. Question 13 explicitly leaves the converse unresolved in the 2021 source, reposted in 2022. The 2006 source grounds the algorithmic model but does not settle the general comparison. No matching proof or counterexample was found in the bounded later-work search; current openness is not exhaustively certified.
progress: 2006: Shen states the acyclic algorithmic-network model with logarithmic local complexity allowances and relates several classical information-theoretic examples to it. | 2021: The problem list explicitly asks whether high-probability algorithmic feasibility for independent joint-source samples can exceed Shannon feasibility. | 2022-03-28: The authors deposit the problem list on arXiv; this is a later source version, not a new coding theorem.
working_summary: Several correlated sources must be transmitted through a fixed directed acyclic network to designated recipients. Shannon coding chooses local encoding and decoding maps that work with high probability for random source blocks. Algorithmic coding instead allows each realized block to have its own short local programs and compatible edge messages. The question asks whether high-probability algorithmic feasibility with logarithmic overhead always implies Shannon feasibility at the same asymptotic rates. The target is this general converse, with vanishing error and rate slack defined explicitly, rather than a finite-block equivalence inferred from the title.

title: Existence of strings without simple optimal hypotheses
importance_reason: A substantial structural question connecting algorithmic statistics, exact randomized sampling and resource-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. It probes the existence of explanatory models beyond a specific estimator, while its immediate consequences are concentrated in this specialist framework. This individually replaces the unassessed midpoint and evaluates the significance of the research direction; selection of an exact variant does not certify that it remains open.
formal:
For every polynomial sampling budget, do infinitely many lengths contain a string with no simple optimal statistical hypothesis, when its reference description is allowed a larger polynomial time budget?

The selected unconditional proposition is
\[
\forall U\in\mathcal U\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\exists d\in\mathbb N_{>c}\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}\quad
\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n).
\]
Here \(\mathcal U\) is the explicitly defined class of polynomially universal finite machines below. Write
\[
\begin{split}
\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n\ \forall\mu\in\mathcal D_n\quad
\bigl[
&\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;n^c,c\log_2 n)\\
&\Longrightarrow\
\mu(x)\le n^{-c}2^{-C_U^{n^d}(x)}
\bigr].
\end{split}
\]
The set \(\mathcal D_n\) consists of rational probability distributions on \(n\)-bit strings. Simplicity requires an exact sampler with description length strictly less than \(c\log_2 n\), halting within \(n^c\) steps on every choice of its fair random bits.
