The quantity \(C_U^{n^d}(x)\) is the length of a shortest deterministic description producing \(x\) within \(n^d\) steps. Optimality requires the strict reverse likelihood inequality, so the displayed weak inequality expresses its failure.

The exponent \(d\) may depend on \(U,c\), but must be chosen before the length threshold \(N\), the witness length \(n\), and the string \(x\). The same exponent \(c\) sets the sampling time, logarithmic description budget and inverse-polynomial likelihood slack. No algorithm generating the witness strings is required.

This is the explicitly selected editorial formulation of the source question. The original Question 3 does not state this quantifier order or tie these three budgets to one exponent, and its presentation also invites conditional results. The target here is the displayed unconditional proposition, not a claim that the source already states exactly this variant.
definitions:
A binary string is a finite sequence of symbols from \(\{0,1\}\); \(|x|\) denotes its length and \(\Lambda\) the empty string. All logarithms have base two. For \(n\ge2\), define
\[
\mathcal D_n=
\left\{\mu:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}:
\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}\mu(z)=1\right\}.
\]
A hypothesis is a mathematical distribution \(\mu\in\mathcal D_n\). Values in likelihood inequalities are regarded as real numbers. The distribution is not supplied as an oracle to a program, and the definition does not require efficient computation of its point probabilities.

Use the following explicit completion of the source's one-tape machine convention. A deterministic machine has a finite set of control states, a designated initial state and halt state, and one tape with cells indexed by the integers and alphabet \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), where \(\square\) is blank. On the triple of binary arguments \((p,y,r)\), the tape initially contains \(p\#y\#r\#\) starting at cell zero and is blank elsewhere. The head starts at cell zero, and a separate write-only binary output stream is empty. Each nonhalting transition reads the current state and symbol, writes one tape symbol, moves the head by \(-1,0\), or \(1\), changes the state, and appends either no bit or one bit to the output stream. The transition table is finite, deterministic, and defined on every nonhalting state and tape symbol. The stream cannot be read. Entering the halt state returns exactly the emitted binary string. A nonhalting computation has undefined output.

One transition costs one step, including transitions emitting output. Initial input placement is not charged. Space is the number of distinct tape cells visited by the head, including its initial cell. The finite transition table is the machine's entire fixed control; it receives no oracle, advice or additional real-valued parameter. All input strings, programs and random strings are finite.

Let \(\mathcal U\) be the class of machines in this convention satisfying the following polynomial universality property. For every machine \(V\) in the same convention, there are integers \(a,b,k\ge1\) such that
\[
\forall p\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ \exists q\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\quad
|q|\le |p|+b
\]
and \(U(q,y,r)=V(p,y,r)\) as partial functions for every pair of binary strings \(y,r\). The same \(q\) must work for all \(y,r\). Whenever the latter computation halts in \(s\) steps using \(h\) tape cells, the former halts in at most
\[
a(1+|y|+|r|+s)^k
\]
steps and uses at most
\[
a(1+|y|+|r|+h)^k
\]
tape cells. The constants may depend on \(U,V\), but not on \(p,y,r\); the translated program \(q\) may depend on \(p\). Equality as partial functions includes agreement on divergence. This is the usual constant-description-overhead, polynomial-resource universality condition, and the class is nonempty. No prefix-free restriction is imposed on programs. Quantifying over this defined class avoids leaving an unspecified universal transition table as a parameter of the question.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), define plain time-bounded description complexity by
\[
C_U^t(x)=
\min\{|p|:U(p,\Lambda,\Lambda)
\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps with output }x\}.
\]
If the set is empty, define \(C_U^t(x)=+\infty\) and \(2^{-\infty}=0\). This is complexity of producing the string, rather than recognizing it, and is plain rather than prefix complexity.

A randomized description is a pair \((p,m)\), where \(p\) is a binary program and \(m\ge1\) is an integer. Independently choose \(m\) fair bits, giving each \(r\in\{0,1\}^m\) probability \(2^{-m}\), and execute \(U(p,\Lambda,r)\). The charged description length is the real number
\[
\ell(p,m)=|p|+\log_2 m,
\]
as in the source; it is not the bit length of a self-delimiting encoding of the pair. The random-string choice and initial placement specify the probability experiment. Time counts the subsequent machine transitions and must be bounded on every one of the finitely many random strings. Requiring \(m\ge1\) makes \(\log_2 m\) defined; a bit may be unused.

The pair samples \(\mu\in\mathcal D_n\) within \(t_0\) steps when every run on \(r\in\{0,1\}^m\) halts within \(t_0\), outputs a string in \(\{0,1\}^n\), and satisfies
\[
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^n\quad
\mu(z)=2^{-m}
\left|\{r\in\{0,1\}^m:U(p,\Lambda,r)=z\}\right|.
\]
Here the vertical bars on the set denote its cardinality. Sampling is exact and total on all random strings, with no failure symbol. Such samplers realize dyadic probabilities; the broader hypothesis domain is still all rational distributions. No requirement to evaluate \(\mu(z)\) efficiently is added.

For \(t_0\in\mathbb N\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the predicate \(\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;t_0,\alpha)\) means that some pair samples \(\mu\) within \(t_0\) steps and has \(\ell(p,m)<\alpha\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), define
\[
\operatorname{Optimal}_U(\mu,x;t,\varepsilon)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mu(x)>\varepsilon\,2^{-C_U^t(x)}.
\]
The strict inequality follows the source's Definition 11. In the target, \(t_0=n^c\), \(\alpha=c\log_2 n\), \(t=n^d\), and \(\varepsilon=n^{-c}\). There are no suppressed multiplicative constants or further asymptotic terms in these predicates. Each candidate distribution and sampler may depend on the particular string and length; the assertion ranges over all of them within the stated budgets. Infinitely many lengths means precisely that for every integer \(N\ge2\) a witnessing integer \(n\ge N\) exists.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed unconditional proposition or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must prove that for every \(U\in\mathcal U\) and integer \(c\ge2\), some fixed integer \(d>c\) has witnessing strings at arbitrarily large lengths. At each witnessing length, the same string \(x\) must satisfy the likelihood upper bound for every distribution having any qualifying exact sampler. The proof need not construct these strings by one effective procedure.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists U\in\mathcal U\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\forall d\in\mathbb N_{>c}\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}\quad
\neg\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n).
\]
Equivalently, for every such \(d\), after its permitted threshold \(N\), one must prove
\[
\forall n\ge N\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n\
\exists\mu\in\mathcal D_n\quad
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;n^c,c\log_2 n),\\
\mu(x)>n^{-c}2^{-C_U^{n^d}(x)}.
\end{cases}
\]
The distribution and sampler may depend on \(n,x,d\), while the same fixed \(c\) bounds their sampling time and description length. The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(d\). This negation requires existence of the hypotheses with these budgets; it does not require a uniform algorithm finding them from \(x\).

Both directions must use the specified finite-machine, description and probability conventions, and prove all of the stated quantifiers. Restricting a positive nonexistence result to uniform distributions on sets, efficiently evaluable probabilities or a chosen sampler family does not cover the full hypothesis class. A theorem about the distinct source notions of acceptable or plausible hypotheses is insufficient unless it establishes the defined optimality assertion. A result depending on an additional unproved complexity assumption is conditional progress, not a proof of this unconditional proposition or its negation. This is an exact existence question; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace its likelihood comparisons or quantifiers.
context:
The original paper distinguishes acceptable, plausible and optimal hypotheses under computational limits. Question 3 asks about strings lacking simple optimal hypotheses; it does not fix how the polynomial time bounds depend on one another.

This card adopts an explicit unconditional variant: for each sampler exponent \(c\), the reference-description exponent \(d>c\) may depend on \(c\), and strings without a qualifying optimal hypothesis must occur at infinitely many lengths. This specified regime is an editorial choice, not an equivalence attributed to the source.

The relative time budgets matter. The source establishes existence of simple optimal hypotheses when the sampler receives sufficiently more time than the reference description, so those budgets cannot be omitted or reversed without changing the question.

The official presentation asks under which assumptions such strings exist. The present target is unconditional; the presentation does not certify this precise quantified variant as an established conjecture.

The 2018 follow-up studies polynomial-time prediction in indexed families of distributions using another optimality definition. Its prediction-neighborhood comparisons do not resolve the selected finite-string existence statement.

The 2024 paper explicitly distinguishes its uncomputable predictor from an effective prediction algorithm. This prevents its unbounded-computation guarantee from being read as a polynomial-time resolution here.
why: This target asks whether computation limits can create an intrinsic gap between descriptions of individual data and simple probabilistic models of that data. It concerns existence of explanatory models, beyond the success of one model-selection or learning algorithm. A resolution would clarify how exact randomized sampling and time-bounded algorithmic information constrain statistical explanation. The selected asymptotic regime makes this structural question precise while leaving its scientific status separate from the editorial choice.
status_note: The 2017 primary source asks whether strings without simple optimal hypotheses exist, but does not state the selected forall-sampler-exponent/exists-larger-reference-exponent regime. The user selected this unconditional editorial variant on 16 September 2026, and its machine model, predicates and full logical negation are now specified. A bounded primary-source review through that date, including the source preprint and slides, the 2018 prediction follow-up and the 2024 infinite-sequence work, found no verified resolution or later source certifying this exact quantifier combination as open. Scientific status therefore remains uncertain independently of the completed formulation review. No exhaustive literature or Lean proof verification is claimed.
progress: 2017-08-01: CCC 2017 publishes exact finite-parameter definitions of simple and optimal hypotheses, the dependence on the relative time bounds, and the open question about strings lacking both properties. | 2018: The prediction follow-up introduces indexed distribution families and a related prefix-complexity optimality definition. Its prediction comparisons do not settle the present plain-complexity existence target. | 2024-05-20: The infinite-sequence prediction paper appears online. Its computable-measure setting and uncomputable predictor have a different scope from exact polynomial-time samplers for finite strings. | 2026-09-16: The user selected the unconditional formulation in which every sampler exponent admits a larger reference exponent and witnesses at infinitely many lengths. Completed the machine and quantifier specification while retaining scientific status uncertain for this precise editorial variant.
working_summary: The question asks whether some binary strings lack every simple probabilistic explanation satisfying a specified time-bounded likelihood comparison. For each polynomial sampling budget, a simple explanation must be sampled exactly by a logarithmically short randomized program that halts within that budget on every random choice. The selected target permits a larger polynomial time bound for describing the string and asks for strings without such explanations at infinitely many lengths. This is an explicit unconditional editorial formulation because the source did not fix the order of its polynomial time bounds. A complete Lean answer must prove the quantified existence statement or its full negation, clarifying how computational limits constrain statistical explanations of individual data.

title: Strong extractors for infinite sequences
importance_reason: Relating randomness, extraction, computational bounds, and logical strength would clarify general principles in algorithmic information.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(F\) such that for every pair of infinite binary sequences \(x,y\) with
\[\dim(x)=\dim(y)=\tfrac12\]
and global algorithmic independence as defined below, all computations \(F^{x\oplus y}(i)\), \(i\ge0\), halt with a bit, and the resulting sequence \(z(i)=F^{x\oplus y}(i)\) satisfies
\[\dim^x(z)=\dim^y(z)=1?\]
Here \(\dim^a\) is effective Hausdorff dimension measured with the entire sequence \(a\) available as an oracle. The same machine must work for all promised pairs; it receives no description of their independence constants.

This card takes the explicit dimension-one-half instance in the 2012 question and uses “independent” in the global oracle sense of Calude–Zimand's Definition 2.1. The weaker finitary prefix-independence notion is distinguished below; it is not silently substituted for this premise.
definitions:
An infinite binary sequence is a function \(a:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), with positions starting at zero. Its length-\(n\) prefix is \(a{\upharpoonright}n=a(0)\cdots a(n-1)\). The join is the interleaving \((x\oplus y)(2i)=x(i)\), \((x\oplus y)(2i+1)=y(i)\).

Fix an optimal plain universal Turing machine and an optimal plain universal oracle Turing machine. For a finite binary string \(u\), let \(C(u)\) be the minimum number of program bits required by the first machine to halt with exactly \(u\) as output. Let \(C^a(u)\) be the corresponding minimum for the oracle machine with access to the entire sequence \(a\): a query at index \(i\) returns \(a(i)\). No time, space or oracle-use bound is imposed. Programs are finite binary strings and are not required to form a prefix-free set. Optimality means simulation of every fixed machine of the same type with an additive constant in program length, uniformly in the oracle for the oracle version. Changing the chosen optimal machines changes the complexities only by constants and does not change the dimensions or independence condition here.

Define
\[\dim(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\qquad
\dim^b(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C^b(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\]
where \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Both dimensions lie in \([0,1]\). The input requirement is equality to one half, not a uniform finite-prefix lower bound with a supplied deficiency. In particular the point at which a lower estimate begins to hold may depend on the sequence and on the estimate's accuracy.

Global algorithmic independence means that there exists a finite constant \(c\ge0\), depending on the pair but not on prefix length, such that for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[C^y(x{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2),\qquad
C^x(y{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(y{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2).\]
An additive constant can be absorbed into \(c\), so this fixes the logarithmic-loss convention also at small lengths. These are requirements about individual infinite sequences; there is no probability distribution from which inputs must be sampled.

For comparison only, finitary independence requires a constant \(d\ge0\) such that for every \(n,m\ge1\),
\[C((x{\upharpoonright}n)(y{\upharpoonright}m))\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)+C(y{\upharpoonright}m)-d\bigl(\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(m+2)\bigr).\]
Juxtaposition here is finite-string concatenation. Global independence implies this condition, but the converse fails; the finitary condition alone is not this card's input promise. The 2007 extraction paper uses “independent” for that weaker condition, whereas the 2010 paper explicitly distinguishes both.

The machine \(F\) has a finite program and input the binary representation of the output position \(i\). It may adaptively query either sequence through the join and use arbitrarily much finite time and space on each halting computation. Each output bit must halt for every promised pair. The machine may diverge on pairs outside the promise, and no computable uniform bound on oracle positions queried is required. There is no additional oracle, random seed or input-dependent advice. A truth-table reduction, which halts on all oracles, would qualify, but that stronger requirement is not imposed.

The output condition means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an onset \(N\), allowed to depend on \(x,y,\varepsilon\), such that for every \(n\ge N\), both \(C^x(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) and \(C^y(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) are at least \((1-\varepsilon)n\). The two conditionings are separate: the output need not retain dimension one relative to the join, from which it is computable. Ordinary dimension one alone is insufficient, as is a high limsup ratio achieved only along selected prefix lengths. The word “strong” refers here to resistance to either input oracle, not to the distinct limsup notion called effective strong dimension.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform extraction claim. A positive answer must supply one finite oracle-machine program, prove termination for every output bit on every promised pair, and prove both relative liminf-dimension guarantees for its full infinite output. A negative answer must show that every candidate machine has a promised pair on which some bit fails to halt with a bit or one required relative dimension is less than one. Failure of one proposed construction, or an impossibility restricted to finite-state or truth-table transformations, does not by itself refute existence of the general Turing reduction. A finite-string conditional extraction theorem does not meet the infinite-oracle target.
context:
The 2012 report explicitly asks for dimension one relative to either source after recalling ordinary two-source dimension amplification. The card preserves its concrete half-dimensional case and makes the oracle meaning of both conditioning and independence explicit.

The 2007 theorem supplies one transformation whose output has every randomness rate below one, hence effective dimension one. Its stated conclusion is ordinary output complexity, without either entire input supplied as side information. It therefore establishes the baseline rather than the strong conclusion.

Calude and Zimand distinguish global and finitary independence, prove that the notions differ, and give a positive independence-production result when the two sources are already fully random. That restricted source class does not cover the half-dimensional inputs required here.

The finite-string result permits high-complexity output even conditional on either finite input. Such finite conditioning does not give free access to all future bits of an infinite input oracle.

The July 2026 finite-state impossibility concerns a different computational model and a different dimension. It is recorded as related later work, not as a resolution of the unrestricted Turing question.
why: The question asks whether two imperfectly random infinite sources can yield information of full asymptotic density that remains incompressible even after either entire source is disclosed. It tests how far the strong-extraction principle from finite information extends to arbitrary individual sequences. The distinction matters because an infinite oracle can expose information beyond any fixed pair of input prefixes.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the full 2012 question, the 2007 ordinary extraction theorem, and Calude–Zimand’s global/finitary independence definitions and restricted positive result. The published finite-string abstract and July 2026 finite-state extraction abstract were checked for their scope. A bounded search found no matching strong global-oracle extractor or general impossibility for the fixed half-dimensional promise. The independence interpretation is explicit; source-open does not claim exhaustive present-status certification.
progress: 2007-12-11: The revised two-source preprint states its uniform ordinary dimension-amplification theorem. | 2010: The independence paper separates global and finitary notions and treats the already-random source case. | 2012: Section 4.13 asks for the strong, input-relative dimension-one guarantee. | 2026-07-09: The LICS paper proves an impossibility for finite-state extraction, outside the computational model of this card.
working_summary: The question asks for one computable transformation of two independent infinite binary sequences of effective dimension one half. Its output must have effective dimension one even when either entire input is available as an oracle. Independence is the global oracle condition, which is stronger than comparing only finite input prefixes. The transformation may use unbounded computation but must produce every output bit on every promised input pair. Known ordinary extraction, finite-string strong extraction and finite-state impossibility results do not settle this stated target.

title: An algorithmic Ahlswede–Körner lemma
importance_reason: A substantive structural question about information transformations, reducibility, or logical strength, with consequences beyond one concrete machine.
formal: Is there a constant \(a>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and all finite binary strings x,y,z with \(C(x,y)\le n\), some finite binary string \(z'\) satisfies \(C(z' |x,y)\le a \log _{2} n\) and |\(C(w|z)- C(w|z' )|\le a \log _{2} n\) for each \(w\in \{x,y,\langle x,y\rangle\}\)?
definitions: Fix an optimal plain conditional universal machine U. Define \(C(u|v)=\min\){|\(p|:U(p,v)\) halts with output u}; there is no prefix-free restriction or time bound on programs p. Set \(C(u)=C(u|\varepsilon )\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty string. Use the computable, uniquely decodable pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle =1^{|}x|0xy\), and write \(C(x,y)=C(\langle x,y\rangle )\) and \(C(u|x,y)=C(u|\langle x,y\rangle )\). The integer n bounds joint description length, not the bit lengths of x or y; z has no length or complexity bound. The single constant a may depend on U and the fixed encoding, but not on n,x,y,z. Choosing a larger constant absorbs the additive effects of different fixed optimal machines or computable tuple encodings. The auxiliary string \(z'\) may depend on all three strings. No bound on \(C(z' |z)\), and no efficient procedure for finding \(z'\), is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniformly logarithmic bounds for every permitted triple, or refute them by showing that every constant a fails for some n,x,y,z with \(C(x,y)\le n\). An example that only violates a particular small constant does not refute the asymptotic assertion.
context:
C(x|z) measures how many program bits still describe x when z is already available. The question asks whether one can replace z while preserving the remaining description lengths of x, of y and of their pair. The replacement must itself have a short description when the pair is given.

The three quantities impose more than separate compression of x and y. They also constrain how much information remains shared between them. For example, when z is empty, taking \(z'\) empty satisfies the preservation requirements and makes \(z'\) describable by a fixed program.

The algorithmic statement concerns fixed strings rather than repeated samples of random variables. The source reports the assertion for stochastic pairs: pairs that have almost maximal complexity inside a simply describable finite set. That promise is absent from the general question.

Requiring a short program for \(z'\) given z would impose an additional common-information extraction condition. Q10 explicitly omits it. Its accompanying runtime question is separate from whether a suitable replacement exists.
why: Tests how far a central information-theoretic replacement principle extends to individual strings, including highly non-stochastic data. Preserving the whole two-string conditional profile would clarify which information relationships can be represented by side information determined almost entirely by the data itself.
status_note: Primary formulation recovered and subsequent-work searches checked through 11 September 2026; no matching resolution located. The 2025 MFCS paper on halving algorithmic information concerns different conditional scaling requirements. General proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2021: Q10 poses the general logarithmic-precision existence question; the following paragraph records a positive result under a stochastic-pair promise. | 2023-09-27: Romashchenko discusses one-shot common-information analogues in a later seminar. The checked abstract does not claim a solution to the general string problem.
working_summary: For individual binary strings x and y, side information z can shorten descriptions of either string and of their pair. The question asks whether another string \(z'\) can preserve those three conditional description lengths to logarithmic accuracy. The replacement must have a logarithmically short description when x and y are both given. It need not be easy to obtain from z, and no fast construction is required. The source establishes a special case for stochastic pairs, while the general question tests the scope of an algorithmic analogue of the Ahlswede–Körner lemma.

title: Algorithmic networks characterized by cut inequalities
importance_reason: A substantive structural question about information transformations, reducibility, or logical strength, with consequences beyond one concrete machine.
formal:
Characterize the finite directed acyclic network patterns \(\mathcal N\) for which the information-flow inequalities across all cuts are sufficient, with logarithmic precision, for transmitting arbitrary correlated input strings to their requested destinations.

Precisely, determine a necessary-and-sufficient condition on \(\mathcal N\) for the property
\[
\forall a\in\mathbb N\ \exists b,B\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge2\ \forall x_1,\ldots,x_k\
\forall (u_e)_{e\in E_{\rm fin}}:
\quad
\operatorname{Cut}_a(\mathcal N,x,u,n)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{Code}_{b,B}(\mathcal N,x,u,n),
\]
where \(|x_i|\le n\) and \(u_e\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The definitions below specify both predicates. The constants \(b,B\) may depend on the fixed pattern and on \(a\), but not on \(n\), the strings or the capacities.

Equivalently, determine the Boolean characteristic function that assigns one exactly to patterns with this property. The characterization must be a condition on the finite network pattern, including source placement and demands, rather than a restatement of the quantification over strings and codes.
question_excerpt: After explaining cut conditions and examples where they do or do not suffice, Q12 asks which networks have information transmission completely characterized by those conditions.
definitions:
Fix an optimal universal machine for plain conditional Kolmogorov complexity:
\[
C(s\mid t)=\min\{|p|:\ U(p,t)\text{ halts with output }s\}.
\]
Use a fixed effective self-delimiting encoding of finite tuples and let \(C(s)=C(s\mid\epsilon)\), where \(\epsilon\) is the empty string. All complexity quantities here refer to this one fixed machine. There is no running-time restriction on the programs in the definition.

A pattern \(\mathcal N\) consists of a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), a fixed integer \(k\ge1\) of input labels, two sets \(P_v,D_v\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}\) for each vertex \(v\), and a partition \(E=E_{\rm fin}\mathbin{\dot\cup}E_\infty\). The union of the \(P_v\) is all input labels. Vertex \(v\) initially possesses \(x_{P_v}\), the tuple of strings with indices in \(P_v\), and must recover \(x_{D_v}\). A label may be supplied at more than one vertex or requested at several vertices. Empty possession or demand sets are permitted. Vertices and edges have fixed orders for encoding tuples. The graph size, label count, placement and demand sets are not growing parameters.

An instance chooses any correlated binary strings \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) of lengths at most \(n\) and nonnegative integer capacities \(u_e\le n\) for the finite channels. The scale \(n\) bounds both input lengths and finite capacities; all such scales and choices are quantified. Edges in \(E_\infty\) have no capacity constraint. Put \(L_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\).

For \(W\subseteq V\), write
\[
P(W)=\bigcup_{v\in W}P_v,\qquad
D(W)=\bigcup_{v\in W}D_v,\qquad
\delta^-(W)=\{(v,w)\in E:v\notin W,\ w\in W\}.
\]
The cut predicate \(\operatorname{Cut}_a\) requires, for every \(W\) whose entering edges all lie in \(E_{\rm fin}\),
\[
C\!\left(x_{D(W)}\mid x_{P(W)}\right)
\le \sum_{e\in\delta^-(W)}u_e+aL_n.
\]
The empty sum is zero. A cut with an unlimited entering edge imposes no inequality. These are ordinary incoming-cut bounds, not the family of all possible Shannon or non-Shannon information inequalities.

The code predicate \(\operatorname{Code}_{b,B}\) asserts the existence of a binary message \(m_e\) on every edge, each of length at most \((n+2)^B\), such that
\[
|m_e|\le u_e+bL_n\qquad(e\in E_{\rm fin})
\]
and, at every vertex \(v\),
\[
C\!\left(
  (m_e)_{e\in\operatorname{out}(v)},\,x_{D_v}
  \ \middle|\
  (m_e)_{e\in\operatorname{in}(v)},\,x_{P_v}
\right)\le bL_n.
\]
In particular, an internal processor can create only logarithmically much information beyond what it receives, and the terminal’s demanded strings must be recoverable from its local information with the same tolerance. The polynomial message-length convention is the source’s finite-scale convention; no polynomial-time encoding or decoding is required. Unlimited channels still carry finite messages.

Messages and the short local programs may depend on the entire instance. This is an existential coding question with logarithmic nonuniform descriptions, not a demand for one computable protocol that finds the messages from the strings alone. The acyclic graph specifies that incoming messages are available before outgoing messages are formed. There are no private random tapes, extra shared strings or uncharged side information beyond what is allowed in the displayed conditional descriptions.

The joint outgoing-tuple convention is equivalent, up to a pattern-dependent logarithmic constant, to bounding each outgoing message and requested output separately, because the pattern is fixed. Measuring finite capacity by message length is the explicit convention of the formal network model; its short-description formulation gives the same logarithmic-scale information interpretation. Allowing the constants to change absorbs the fixed universal-machine and tuple-encoding choices.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked necessary-and-sufficient characterization of the finite source-demand patterns satisfying the quantified cut-sufficiency property. Equivalently, for its Boolean characteristic function \(\chi\), a real-valued function \(g\) is accepted if a complete Lean proof establishes \(|g(\mathcal N)-\chi(\mathcal N)|\le1/100\) for every finite pattern \(\mathcal N\). This approximation determines the classification by thresholding at \(1/2\); the supplied function need not itself be Boolean. Establish both directions of the classification. Classifying only a chosen special family, assuming independent source strings, restricting messages to linear codes, or replacing the model by Shannon block coding does not answer the full question. No algorithmic complexity requirement is imposed on the structural characterization. The numerical acceptance tolerance does not replace the separately quantified logarithmic tolerances inside the coding property.
context:
The question concerns individual finite strings. Their correlations are measured by conditional Kolmogorov complexity; no probability distribution on source strings is supplied.

The formal network framework uses a directed acyclic graph and allows logarithmic descriptions at processors. It asks for the existence of compatible messages, so it is more permissive than requiring uniformly computable encoders with prescribed running time.

The conditional-code network and the Slepian–Wolf source-reconstruction network are positive examples in the source: their cut constraints suffice at logarithmic precision. The source also records stronger efficient randomized encoding results for Slepian–Wolf with their own overhead conventions.

The Gray–Wyner pattern is a negative example in general. Its three cut bounds only constrain the total information sent and the amounts reaching each receiver; for some correlated pairs these bounds do not guarantee the required common description.

The placement and identity of requested strings are part of the pattern. Asking two terminals for different source strings can behave differently from broadcasting one common source, even when part of the underlying graph is similar.

The source asks separately, in Q13 and Q14, about comparisons between Shannon and algorithmic coding. Those comparisons are not assumed by Q12 and are not folded into this characterization.
why: A cut counts how much information must enter a group of processors, but it does not describe whether the information can be packaged consistently for all destinations. The requested characterization would identify precisely when these numerical constraints capture the whole coding problem for individual correlated strings.
status_note: The 2021 source asks for the general classification after exhibiting both sufficient and insufficient network patterns. The explicit target below retains its existential algorithmic-information interpretation and logarithmic tolerance. No general characterization was found in the bounded later-source check; this review does not assert that every special-case result has been exhaustively surveyed.
progress: 2006-07-31: The formal algorithmic network framework records cut necessity and contrasting positive and negative network examples. | 2021: The survey poses the general classification as Q12, after the conditional-code and Slepian–Wolf examples. | 2026-09-16: The review specifies source-demand patterns, all cuts, local descriptions and logarithmic tolerance, and finds no general classification in the bounded later-source check.
working_summary: A network distributes correlated finite strings through directed channels with limited capacities. Each cut imposes a necessary bound on the information that must enter its vertices to meet their demands. The question asks exactly which fixed network patterns make all of these bounds sufficient for a coding solution. Codes are existential per-instance assignments with logarithmic local descriptions, without an efficient uniform-encoder requirement. The source gives both positive examples and networks where the cut bounds fail, leaving the general structural characterization open.

title: Communication rate for secret-key agreement at fixed Hamming distance
importance_reason: A focused quantitative or structural problem in computability and algorithmic information.
formal:
Determine the function
\[
 R:[0,1]\longrightarrow\mathbb R_{\ge0}
\]
to pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\). Here \(R(\theta)\) is the optimal asymptotic public-communication rate, in bits per input bit, for two parties with independent private randomness to agree on a secret key of maximal algorithmic-information length. Their inputs are pairs of \(n\)-bit strings at distance \(\lfloor\theta n\rfloor\) with nearly maximal joint Kolmogorov complexity in that Hamming layer. The precise family, secrecy condition and rate quantifiers are defined below.
question_excerpt: Question 17 asks for optimal communication in important examples of algorithmic secret-key agreement, explicitly suggesting strings at a given Hamming distance. The user selected nearly maximally complex pairs in that layer, a key of maximal information length, and the leading communication rate with pointwise absolute accuracy 1/100.
definitions:
Fix an optimal universal plain description machine \(U\) and effective binary encodings of finite tuples. Write \(C(a\mid b)\) for the length of the shortest program making \(U\), with auxiliary input \(b\), output \(a\); write \(C(a)\) when there is no auxiliary input. Joint complexity uses the fixed tuple encoding. All logarithms are base two. The algorithmic mutual information of two strings is
\[
 I(x:y)=C(x)+C(y)-C(x,y).
\]
Let \(\ell_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\).

For every real \(\theta\in[0,1]\), integer \(n\ge1\) and fixed integer \(c\ge1\), put \(t=\lfloor\theta n\rfloor\). The promised family \(\mathcal F_{n,\theta,c}\) consists of all ordered pairs \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{dist}_H(x,y)=t,\qquad
 C(x,y\mid n,t)\ge
 \left\lfloor\log_2\!\left(2^n\binom nt\right)\right\rfloor-c\ell_n.
\]
The Hamming distance counts coordinates where the bits differ. There are exactly \(2^n\binom nt\) pairs in the layer; the displayed condition makes the permitted complexity deficiency explicit. The constant \(c\) is fixed as \(n\) grows, and the rate must cover every such constant. The input pair is fixed, not sampled by the protocol from a probability distribution.

Alice receives \(x\), Bob receives \(y\), and both receive the public data
\[
 q=(n,t,C(x),C(y),C(x,y)).
\]
These exact complexity values are supplied as a promise, not computed by the parties. An eavesdropper also knows \(q\) and the full finite description of the protocol \(\Pi\), but receives neither private input nor either private random tape. There is no other shared secret or correlated resource. Each party has an independent tape of independent fair random bits. Random bits sent over the channel become public.

A protocol is a pair of uniform classical algorithms with unrestricted finite computation. One fixed finite program works over all input lengths; it has no oracle for Kolmogorov complexity or for a real parameter. The parties communicate by a public binary protocol: the next speaker and public termination are determined by the public data and the transcript so far, while each sent bit can depend on the sender's private input and coins. All transmitted bits count, including any control or framing bits. Timing supplies no extra information. There is no bound on the number of rounds, on local running time or on the number of private random bits, but every execution on finite inputs and every pair of random tapes must terminate after finitely many steps. Each party then outputs a finite binary string or a failure symbol. Totality is required even outside the promise; correctness is required only on promised pairs with the true profile.

For fixed \(\theta,c\), a protocol is valid if there is a constant \(K>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \((x,y)\in\mathcal F_{n,\theta,c}\), with probability at least \(2/3\) over the private coins the two outputs are the same string \(Z\) and simultaneously
\[
 \bigl||Z|-\max\{0,I(x:y)\}\bigr|\le K\ell_n,
 \qquad C(Z\mid T,q,\Pi)\ge |Z|-K\ell_n.
\]
Here \(T\) is the complete public transcript. Thus the key has maximal length up to logarithmic loss and remains nearly incompressible given everything public. Agreement, length and secrecy are one joint success event for each input pair. Secrecy is defined by description length, without a computational bound on the observer. It is not a claim of statistical uniformity for a distribution of inputs.

Let \(W_{\Pi,\theta,c}(n)\) be the supremum of the total number of transmitted bits over all pairs in \(\mathcal F_{n,\theta,c}\) and all private random tapes, including unsuccessful executions. The supremum of an empty family is taken as zero. Communication is a worst-case cost, not an expectation or a cost conditioned on successful agreement.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable at \(\theta\) if, for every integer \(c\ge1\) and every real \(\eta>0\), there exist a valid uniform protocol \(\Pi\) and an integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[
 W_{\Pi,\theta,c}(n)\le(r+\eta)n\quad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0.
\]
Set \(R(\theta)=\inf\{r\ge0:r\text{ is achievable at }\theta\}\). General secret-key agreement bounds ensure this set is nonempty and the infimum is finite. This definition does not assume that a finite-length optimum divided by \(n\) has a limit, or that the infimum is attained.

The protocol, its logarithmic-loss constant \(K\) and the threshold \(n_0\) may depend on the fixed parameters \(\theta,c,\eta\). They cannot depend on \(n\) or the particular input pair. Even for irrational \(\theta\), an admissible protocol has a finite description and sees the integer \(t\), not a real-number oracle. No effective procedure for selecting protocols from these fixed parameters is required. The unit of the requested function is total bits sent in both directions divided by the length \(n\) of one party's input, not by the combined length \(2n\).

The \(O(\log n)\) key and secrecy allowances are fixed by the constant \(K\) in each protocol. They do not permit losing a positive linear fraction of the key. Conversely, the requested accuracy \(1/100\) is in the asymptotic communication rate; it does not request a finite-length communication estimate with additive \(O(\log n)\) error.
answer_criterion:
Supply a mathematically specified function \(a:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
 |a(\theta)-R(\theta)|\le1/100\qquad\text{for every real }\theta\in[0,1].
\]
Pointwise certified bounds \(L(\theta)\le R(\theta)\le U(\theta)\), with width at most \(1/50\) everywhere, qualify via their midpoint. An exact formula or another certified mathematical characterization meeting the accuracy also qualifies; a closed form, decimal table or efficient evaluation procedure is not required.

Upper and lower control must use the stated family, maximal-key criterion, private randomness and worst-case communication. Bounds up to unspecified multiplicative constants, a proof at just one distance, numerical evidence, a different key-length tradeoff, or a result that averages success over random inputs does not suffice. Merely restating the defining infimum is not a determination. Any transfer from a Shannon-source theorem or a different pair family must itself be proved for this model.
context:
The source makes maximal key length operational: the parties can turn their algorithmic mutual information into a shared secret, provided they receive the small complexity profile as auxiliary data. It separately asks how much communication particular input families require.

The general upper bound is \(\min\{C(x\mid y),C(y\mid x)\}+O(\log n)\) communicated bits. Worst-case examples over all pairs make this bound tight, but that does not automatically establish the optimal rate for the Hamming family.

For a representative fixed Hamming distance, the 2024 source proves order-of-growth tradeoffs between communication and key length and explicitly leaves a gap between their constants. Such \(\Theta(n)\) information does not determine the normalized rate within \(1/100\).

The model is about individual input strings: every promised pair must have a high probability of success over the parties’ private coins. An average guarantee for independent samples from a probability distribution is a different quantifier.

The later graph-incidence results show that full-key communication can be forced onto one side in certain families. Their hypotheses do not establish the same conclusion for Hamming layers.

The algebraic results concern balanced communication for incidences in finite projective planes. Their stated deterministic or public-random setting and geometric input family differ from the private-random Hamming-rate target.
why: Determine how the geometry of correlated binary data controls the public communication needed to realize all of its algorithmic mutual information as a shared secret. A sharp rate distinguishes inputs with the same information profile but different communication requirements.
status_note: The 2024 full paper explicitly leaves the sharp Hamming-family communication tradeoff unresolved. The checked 2025–2026 developments concern other input families or related information inequalities. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified determination of the selected private-random maximal-key communication-rate function within pointwise absolute error 1/100. This does not certify an exhaustive literature search or independently verify every cited proof.
progress: 2021: The open-problems column explicitly asks for the communication cost on Hamming-distance input pairs. | 2024-05-09: The extended paper removes the polynomial restriction on private randomness and records a remaining constant-factor gap in its Hamming example. | 2025-09-09: The revised graph-incidence paper gives additional full-key communication lower bounds for its stated graph families. | 2025: Balanced communication is further analyzed for finite projective-plane inputs.
working_summary: Alice and Bob hold binary strings at a specified Hamming distance and may communicate on a channel observed by an eavesdropper. The input pair must have nearly the largest Kolmogorov complexity possible in that distance layer, and its complexity profile is public. Using independent private randomness, they must agree on a key whose length is their mutual information up to logarithmic loss and which remains nearly incompressible given the transcript. The target is the smallest asymptotic worst-case number of communicated bits per input bit, as a function of relative distance. An answer must prove the whole rate function within absolute error 1/100 in Lean, with success guaranteed separately for every promised input pair.

title: Random-oracle invariance of fully extractable common information
importance_reason: A focused quantitative or structural problem in computability and algorithmic information.
formal:
Is the following implication true? For every integer \(c\ge1\) there exists an integer \(d\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every pair of binary words \(x,y\) with \(|x|,|y|\le n\), put \(\ell_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). If
\[
 \Pr_{X}\!\left[\exists b\in\{0,1\}^*:\
 \begin{array}{l}
 C^X(b\mid x)\le c\ell_n,\quad C^X(b\mid y)\le c\ell_n,\\
 |C^X(b)-I^X(x:y)|\le c\ell_n
 \end{array}\right]\ge2/3,
\]
where \(X\) is an infinite fair random binary oracle, must there exist a finite binary word \(z\) such that
\[
 C(z\mid x)\le d\ell_n,\qquad C(z\mid y)\le d\ell_n,\qquad
 |C(z)-I(x:y)|\le d\ell_n\ ?
\]
The coefficient \(d\) may depend on \(c\) and the fixed description conventions, but not on \(n,x,y\).
question_excerpt: Shen asks whether two words having fully extractable mutual information relative to a random oracle implies that the same holds without an oracle. The user selected success for at least two thirds of the infinite fair oracles and logarithmic losses in the finite input lengths.
definitions:
Fix one optimal plain universal oracle description machine \(U\). Its inputs are a finite binary program \(p\), a finite binary auxiliary word \(v\), and access to an oracle \(X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\). It can query any natural-number position of \(X\); a halting computation makes finitely many queries and prints a finite word. There is no running-time, query-count or largest-query bound. Plain programs need not form a prefix-free set.

Optimality is uniform over oracles: for each other oracle description machine, a fixed finite compiler prefix simulates it under every \(X\), with additive program-length overhead independent of \(X,p,v\). Fix the ordinary no-oracle machine to be \(U\) with the all-zero computable oracle. Define
\[
 C^X(u\mid v)=\min\{|p|:U^X(p,v)=u\},\qquad C^X(u)=C^X(u\mid\epsilon),
\]
where \(\epsilon\) is the empty auxiliary word. Write \(C\) for the same definitions with the fixed all-zero oracle. Thus ordinary complexity is not measured using a different machine chosen for each input pair.

Fix a computable injective encoding \(\langle u,v\rangle\) of pairs, with computable decoding, and set
\[
 I^X(x:y)=C^X(x)+C^X(y)-C^X(\langle x,y\rangle),\qquad
 I(x:y)=C(x)+C(y)-C(\langle x,y\rangle).
\]
These are the stated integer expressions; small negative values caused by description conventions are not silently truncated. The permitted logarithmic errors absorb the usual fixed-machine changes. Bit length is denoted by \(|u|\), and every logarithm here is to base two.

The random oracle has independent unbiased bits: for every fixed binary prefix of length \(r\), the probability of that prefix is \(2^{-r}\). It is sampled independently of the fixed words \(x,y\). Probability refers to this product measure, not a finite random string, a random permutation or a computably generated sequence. The probability event in the statement is interpreted as an ordinary measurable event on this space; complexities and halting outputs are defined by the oracle computations just specified.

The existential witness \(b\), and the short programs showing its conditional complexities, may depend on \(X,x,y\). In particular, \(\Pr_X[\exists b\,\cdots]\) does not mean that one fixed \(b\) works for two thirds of the oracles. No uniform extractor must produce these witnesses. Their finite lengths and the positions queried from \(X\) can be arbitrarily large. What is required to be near the mutual information is the oracle-relative complexity \(C^X(b)\), not the unrelativized complexity or literal length of \(b\).

The conclusion asks only for existence of an ordinary common-information word \(z\). It need not equal any oracle-dependent witness. Its short descriptions from \(x\) and \(y\) receive no oracle and no transcript of communication. In both premise and conclusion the slack is measured by the original input-length bound \(n\), even if a witness or a finite prefix of the oracle used by a computation is much longer. The quantifier over \(d\) is outside the choice of inputs, so a constant chosen separately to cover each finite example does not establish the statement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication with quantifiers \(\forall c\,\exists d\,\forall n,x,y\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must give some fixed \(c\) such that every proposed \(d\) fails on some pair meeting the two-thirds oracle-extraction premise but lacking an ordinary witness with that \(d\)-logarithmic loss.

Exact changes of a complexity value or information profile on a single fixed pair do not refute this asymptotic statement: the failure must survive every allowed output coefficient. Nor is it sufficient to alter some other part of a profile without changing full extractability. A theorem for finite auxiliary strings whose error depends on their complexity, or a conclusion with merely sublinear rather than logarithmic loss, does not meet the target. The assertion and the selected probability threshold require proof, not numerical tolerance.
context:
For a fixed finite tuple, adding independent random oracle access ordinarily changes its complexity values only by small amounts with high probability. The source asks whether the existence of a further common-information witness has the same stability.

The 2010 paper proves finite-auxiliary-word results, including a sublinear-loss theorem and stronger statements for stochastic tuples. Its error parameter includes the auxiliary word’s complexity, and its conclusion explicitly says it has no results about infinite oracles.

The 2021 survey asks the broader stability question for Gray–Wyner and other profiles. Changing an arbitrary profile coordinate is not automatically the same as changing whether all mutual information can be extracted.

An August 2026 manuscript claims a random-oracle counterexample for Gray–Wyner profiles using a pair of words and a universal machine. Only its indexed abstract was accessible in this review. It is not established here that the claim survives the quantified logarithmic tolerance or resolves this particular full-extraction question.
why: Mutual information is a number; representing it by a word recoverable from either input is a stronger property. This asks whether an unlimited independent random resource can change that property, even though ordinary complexity values are stable up to small losses with high probability.
status_note: The original infinite-oracle full-extraction question is distinct from the proved finite-auxiliary-word results. A related August 2026 manuscript claims a Gray–Wyner-profile counterexample, but only its abstract was accessible and no implication for this quantified logarithmic-loss target was verified. The card remains active with uncertain current status; this review neither certifies nor rejects the uninspected proof.
progress: 2010: Published finite-auxiliary-word stability results leave infinite-oracle relativization untreated. | 2012: The Dagstuhl report poses the full-extraction question for a random oracle. | 2021: A survey records the broader random-oracle information-profile question. | 2026-08-13: SSRN posts a claimed result on broader Gray–Wyner-profile questions; only the abstract was checked, so it is not accepted as a resolution of this target.
working_summary: Two words have fully extractable common information when a word containing almost all their mutual information has short descriptions from either one. The premise allows such an extraction for at least two thirds of independent infinite fair random oracles. The question is whether an extraction must then exist without any oracle, with losses still logarithmic in the input lengths. Oracle-dependent witnesses may vary and use arbitrarily many oracle positions, so finite auxiliary-word results do not directly supply the required bound. A complete Lean-checked proof or refutation must respect the uniform loss constants; a recent broader profile claim has not been verified to settle this statement.

title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
importance_reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.
focus_reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.
formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
context:
Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.
why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.
status_note: The June 2026 algebraic paper explicitly distinguishes its theorem from the unresolved classical EF problem, and the checked cryptographic paper likewise treats EF hardness as an unresolved issue. The August 2026 preprint concerns different logics. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified classical EF resolution. The checked Pich–Santhanam version is the 2023 preprint, not its inaccessible journal version; the cited proofs have not been independently recertified.
progress: 1979-03: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit. | 2019-08-06: Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF. | 2023-12-13: Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound. | 2026-06-14: Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target. | 2026-06-21: Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies. | 2026-08-31: Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.
working_summary: Extended Frege is a classical propositional proof system that can introduce reusable names for previously specified formulas. The question asks whether no single polynomial bounds the shortest proof of every tautology by its statement length. The target counts the full encoded proof and allows arbitrary depth and reuse of earlier lines. Its negation would give short proofs for every tautology without necessarily making them easy to find. Recent conditional, algebraic and intuitionistic results do not supply the unrestricted classical lower bound.

title: Frege versus Extended Frege
importance_reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.
focus_reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.
formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.
context:
Frege proofs model a finite list of ordinary propositional deductions. Extended Frege adds named definitions, allowing a long expression to be referenced by a variable after paying for its definition. Chains of these definitions describe shared Boolean circuits. Every assignment to the ordinary variables extends uniquely through an acyclic sequence of definitions, so the extension rule preserves truth of conclusions that contain no extension variables. This explains the systems' common set of theorems while leaving their proof lengths potentially different.

Proof reuse and subformula sharing are different resources. Both systems may cite an earlier proof line many times; ordinary Frege still pays for every occurrence inside each newly written formula. Extended Frege also has names for intermediate expressions. This representational distinction does not itself show that any tautology lacks a short Frege proof. The question compares the best proofs available in the two systems, irrespective of how those proofs were discovered.

The usual robustness theorem compares finite sound and complete Frege presentations with polynomial overhead. Cook and Reckhow also define fresh extension variables and establish the analogous robustness of Extended Frege. The card preserves the saved size-simulation target while making its syntax and bit accounting explicit. It restores the source convention allowing auxiliary ordinary variables; restricting such variables to those of the conclusion gives a polynomially equivalent convention. A bounded-depth, tree-like or otherwise restricted Frege system would be a different question.

A polynomial bound on the existence of translated proofs is distinct from a polynomial-time translator. Buss's work separates these notions and relates size simulation to short finite consistency proofs. His 1991 result characterizes Frege simulation of Extended Frege by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the corresponding partial EF consistency statements: finite propositional assertions that a contradiction has no proof up to a specified length. Frege already has polynomial-size partial self-consistency proofs. This comparison is a stated theorem about the systems, not a resolution of Frege versus EF. The current review checked the author and publisher abstracts; the author's downloadable copy is headed 11 July 2002, although the journal publication is from 1991.

Buss's Stanford tutorial of 27 February 2014 explicitly presents the formula-versus-circuit proof comparison as a longstanding open question. Its discussion of proposed separating principles is historical context, not a current lower-bound theorem. Quasipolynomial upper bounds for particular families must remain distinct both from polynomial upper bounds and from a separation of the unrestricted systems.

A concrete example is the Kneser–Lovász coloring principle. The graph has the \(k\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) as vertices and joins disjoint subsets; for \(n\ge2k\), its propositional principle rules out a proper coloring with \(n-2k+1\) colors. Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs for each fixed \(k\). Constants and exponents may depend on that fixed parameter. Their 2015 conference version states these as Theorems 4 and 5; the 2018 expanded journal abstract retains the fixed-parameter condition. These are upper bounds for particular tautologies, not a superpolynomial Frege lower bound or a uniform bound with both parameters growing.

Krajíček's 11 June 2026 preprint describes circuit-equivalence reasoning by local circuit rewrites. Its relation is polynomial-time recognizable, and each rewrite may delete gates and add at most seven; a short EF proof yields a polynomially bounded chain. The intermediate objects retain circuit sharing. The concluding discussion also distinguishes existence of a small chain from a polynomial-time construction of it by the presented proof. This normal-form statement therefore supplies neither the polynomial-size formula proof nor the polynomial-time translator that could be mistakenly inferred from the abstract.

The September 2026 report by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay states a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted Ideal Proof System over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), the field with two elements. Certificates are algebraic formulas. The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.
why: This asks whether naming and reusing intermediate formulas can shorten rigorous propositional proofs by more than every polynomial factor. It is a central comparison between strong proof systems and between reasoning with formula trees and shared circuit representations. A separation would yield superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege; an equivalence would show that the extension rule changes shortest-proof lengths by at most polynomial factors.
status_note: Explicitly open in the 2014 source. Bounded primary-source checks through 15 September 2026 did not identify a polynomial-size Frege simulation of unrestricted EF or a superpolynomial separation. The checked June circuit-rewriting and September restricted formula-IPS results have different representations or overhead. The oldest consistency characterization was verified at the author/publisher abstract level in this pass because full-PDF retrieval failed. This individual model and source review is not an exhaustive certification of current openness or an independent verification of new proofs.
progress: 1979: Cook and Reckhow formalize Frege rules, fresh extension definitions and polynomial robustness of standard presentations. Their size accounting distinguishes total proof length from the number of lines. | 1991-04-15: Buss characterizes Frege size simulation of EF through polynomial-size partial EF consistency proofs in Frege, and proves polynomial-size partial Frege self-consistency proofs. The 2002 date on the downloadable typescript is not a new publication. | 2014-02-27: The Stanford mini-tutorial explicitly presents Frege versus Extended Frege as an open comparison between strong propositional systems. | 2015–2018: Aisenberg and coauthors establish polynomial EF and quasipolynomial Frege upper bounds for the Kneser–Lovász principles for each fixed \(k\); no lower-bound separation follows. | 2026-06-11: Krajíček states a polynomial-size local circuit-rewriting characterization of EF reasoning.
