The intermediate representations remain circuits; the concluding discussion does not assert a polynomial-time construction by the displayed argument. | 2026-09-05: ECCC TR26-166, submitted 4 September and published 5 September, reports quasipolynomial Frege simulation of two-group partially commutative formula IPS over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), under its explicit placeholder and axiom conventions.
working_summary: Extended Frege permits named definitions that share intermediate formulas within an otherwise ordinary propositional proof. The question asks whether every such proof has an ordinary Frege proof of the same conclusion with only polynomially larger total encoded size. The statement fixes the formula syntax, inference rules, freshness conditions and binary accounting while allowing unrestricted depth and reuse of proof lines. Known finite-consistency characterizations, fixed-parameter combinatorial upper bounds and restricted algebraic simulations do not settle this universal comparison. A complete Lean proof must establish either one universal polynomial size bound or its logical negation, without imposing a polynomial-time procedure for finding translated proofs.

title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
importance_reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.
formal:
For every prime integer \(p\), does there exist a single polynomial-time constructible family of DNF tautologies \((\tau_{p,n})_{n\ge1}\) of length polynomially related to \(n\), such that its proofs in the fixed modular Frege calculus below exceed every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth? Precisely, require for each \(p\) a finite deterministic machine \(M_p\) and integers \(C_p,k_p\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) the machine outputs a DNF \(\tau_{p,n}\) within \(C_p(n+2)^{k_p}\) bit steps, this formula is a tautology, and
\[n\le |\tau_{p,n}|\le C_p(n+2)^{k_p}.\]
The required lower bound is
\[\forall d,r,N\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau_{p,n})\Rightarrow |\pi|>n^r\bigr).\]
The machine and the family may depend on \(p\) but not on \(d,r,N\); the witness \(n\) may depend on all three. No effective procedure producing \(M_p\) from \(p\) is required. The family consists of genuine tautologies, not formulas whose lack of short proofs might be due to falsity. The lower bound is infinitely often, not necessarily eventually for every \(n\).
definitions:
Fix a prime \(p\ge2\). Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees built from constants \(0,1\), variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary \(\neg\), binary \(\land,\lor\), and gates \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(A_1,\ldots,A_t)\) for \(0\le j<p\) and any finite arity \(t\ge0\). Under an assignment of Boolean values to the variables, the usual connectives have their ordinary truth tables, and a modular gate is true exactly when the number of its true arguments is congruent to \(j\) modulo \(p\). A tautology is true under every assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation. A DNF is a finite disjunction of finite conjunctions of literals, written as a binary formula with any parenthesization; an empty conjunction is \(1\), an empty disjunction is \(0\), and a singleton conjunction or disjunction is its sole member. Target DNFs contain no modular gates.

The notation \(A\Rightarrow B\) is an abbreviation for \(\neg A\lor B\), and \(A\Leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((A\Rightarrow B)\land(B\Rightarrow A)\). Both are expanded fully before checking syntax, depth or size. Fix the following finite ordinary Frege axiom schemes, in the order displayed:
\[\begin{gathered}
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow A),\\
 (A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow C))\Rightarrow((A\Rightarrow B)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow C)),\\
 (\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow B),\\
 (A\land B)\Rightarrow A,\qquad (A\land B)\Rightarrow B,\\
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow(A\land B)),\\
 A\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\qquad B\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\\
 (A\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((B\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((A\lor B)\Rightarrow C)),\\
 1,\qquad \neg0.
\end{gathered}\]
The metavariables \(A,B,C\) may be replaced consistently by arbitrary formulas of the full modular language. The sole inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\Rightarrow B\), infer \(B\). There are no hypotheses. Besides these eleven schemes, allow the modular axioms
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,0}(),\qquad \neg\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}()\quad(1\le j<p),\]
and every instance of
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma,A)\Leftrightarrow
 \bigl((\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma)\land\neg A)\lor
 (\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j-1}(\Gamma)\land A)\bigr),\]
where \(\Gamma\) is any finite ordered list of formulas, including the empty list, and \(j-1\) is reduced modulo \(p\) to \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). These are the modular schemes of the cited source, attached to the specified finite complete classical Frege basis. An axiom line must match its indicated scheme syntactically after expansion, using the same substituted formula at each occurrence of a metavariable. A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom or modus-ponens lines ending with the claimed formula. Earlier lines may be reused without restriction. There are no extension-variable definition axioms, no separate substitution rule for previously derived lines, and no restrictions of regularity or tree shape.

Define the logical depth \(\delta\) of constants and variables to be zero. Negation has depth \(1+\delta(A)\), and a modular gate has depth \(1+\max(0,\delta(A_1),\ldots,\delta(A_t))\). For a conjunction, flatten its maximal connected subtree of conjunction nodes and collect the boundary subformulas whose roots are not conjunctions; its depth is one plus the maximum depth of those subformulas. Use the same rule for disjunctions. Flattening does not cross a negation, modular gate or different Boolean connective. It defines the depth measure only: the actual binary syntax tree is still written and counted in full. A depth-at-most-\(d\) proof must have \(\delta\le d\) for every line, including instantiated axioms and the conclusion. This bounds individual formulas, not the length of an inference path in the proof graph. Such paths and the total number of lines are unrestricted.

All sizes are bits in a fixed prefix encoding. For \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. Formula tags 000 and 001 encode constants \(0\) and \(1\); 010 followed by \(E(i)\) encodes \(x_i\); 011 followed by the child encodes negation; 100 and 101 followed by both child encodings encode conjunction and disjunction. Tag 110 followed by \(E(j)E(t)\) and all \(t\) ordered child encodings represents \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}\). Tag 111 is invalid. The prime is fixed by the system, not supplied as an oracle. A proof starts with \(E(m)\), its positive number of lines. Each line contains \(E(q)\) followed by its complete formula encoding. Rule labels \(q=1,\ldots,11\) refer to the ordinary schemes in their displayed order; labels 12, 13 and 14 refer respectively to the empty-zero-residue, empty-nonzero-residue and recursive modular schemes. Label 15 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): on line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a=A\) and line \(b=A\Rightarrow B\), with the current line exactly \(B\). Other rule labels and malformed strings are invalid. The length \(|\pi|\) includes every variable index, gate, repeated formula occurrence, line count and inference reference. Formula length uses the same formula encoding. Nothing is given by a compressed circuit, advice or a program for generating a larger proof.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau)\) means validity under all these rules, conclusion \(\tau\), and line depth at most \(d\). Construction time for the target family is measured on a standard deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet containing input/output bits and blank. A transition reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; all transitions and output writes count. Each \(M_p\) is one finite program, with no oracle or length-dependent advice. Its constants \(C_p,k_p\) may depend on that program and the fixed prime. The formula-size lower bound \(|\tau_{p,n}|\ge n\) and polynomial upper bound make size in \(n\) polynomially comparable with size in the conclusion. Quantifying over positive integer exponents \(r\) is equivalent to exceeding every polynomial bound, including bounds with arbitrary fixed multiplicative constants.
answer_criterion: Supply the stated families, their construction machines and bounds, together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that all outputs are DNF tautologies and that the displayed lower-bound quantifiers hold for every prime and every fixed line depth. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of the logical negation: some prime \(p\) has no family satisfying all the stated requirements. Equivalently, for that prime, every polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family of the prescribed length scale has some fixed depth \(d\), exponent \(r\) and threshold \(N\) for which every \(n\ge N\) admits a valid depth-\(d\) proof of size at most \(n^r\). A negative answer does not require an efficient proof-finding algorithm. Unproved tautologicity, one fixed polynomial lower bound, a bound only at restricted derivation depth, or a result for only one prime does not establish the full positive claim. All assumptions, construction bounds, depth and size conventions must match the card. This binary asymptotic claim retains its polynomial precision; the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not a replacement for a proof-size lower bound.
context:
A modular gate states that a count has a particular residue. The case \(p=2\) includes parity, while other primes give other fixed modular tests. A bounded-depth proof may make arbitrarily many deductions, each of which uses only a bounded number of logical layers. Krajíček's §5 explicitly defines the modular recurrence axioms and the depth convention that flattens consecutive conjunctions or disjunctions. The card fixes a finite ordinary basis and a complete binary encoding within that presentation.

The saved benchmark asks for one efficiently generated DNF family for each prime that defeats all fixed line depths, with the same family at every exponent. This explicit construction and quantifier order are retained as the card's chosen formulation of the broad modular-Frege frontier; they are not silently replaced by a family chosen separately for each depth. A method for selecting the program uniformly from the prime is not an additional requirement. Hard instances may occur on different infinite subsequences at different depths and exponents.

Without modular gates, the bounded-depth comparison has established lower bounds. Ajtai's 1988 work proves superpolynomial bounds for propositional pigeonhole formulas, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo's 1993 paper strengthens them to exponential-type size bounds at each fixed depth. These are statements about ordinary bounded-depth Frege. Adding all modular axiom instances enlarges the set of possible proofs, so an ordinary-Frege lower bound does not itself establish the present one.

Circuit lower bounds and proof lower bounds measure different things. Prime-modulus circuit lower bounds concern nonconstant Boolean functions that cannot be computed by small circuits. Every tautology in this card instead computes the constant true function. The object required to be large is a syntactically verified deduction of that tautology in a fixed calculus. The February 2026 source explicitly retains modular Frege lower bounds as open while distinguishing the circuit results.

Resolution over parities permits disjunctions of linear equations modulo two as proof lines. It is a restricted proof system within the modular-Frege setting. Efremenko and Itsykson's CCC 2025 Theorems 3 and 4 give a tree-like lifting statement and a size-versus-derivation-depth tradeoff, respectively. For their lifted Tseitin family with \(m\) variables, the latter requires either size \(2^{\Omega(m/\log m)}\) or derivation depth \(\Omega(m\log m)\). These results leave open proofs of polynomial size with sufficiently long inference paths; the present card permits such paths.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov's February 2026 result gives a stronger tradeoff for parity resolution. After the specified fixed-gadget lifting, resolution width \(w\) of the original CNF forces derivation depth \(\Omega(w^2/\log S)\) in a size-\(S\) parity-resolution refutation, and also an unconditional size bound \(\Omega(w^2)\). Here width is the maximum number of literals in a clause, minimized over ordinary resolution refutations. The construction and gadget conditions remain part of the source theorem. The depth tradeoff and quadratic bound each fall short of a superpolynomial bound on unrestricted derivation size.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret's full version states in Corollary 5.7 that, for every prime, an explicit DNF sequence has no polynomial-size modular Frege proofs. Crucially, the same corollary describes the formulas' validity as unknown. A false formula has no proof in a sound calculus, so lack of short proofs alone cannot certify a hard tautology. The ITCS 2026 published abstract retains this distinction and discusses conditional evidence for tautologicity. Those conditions have not become unconditional theorems in the versions checked here.

Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret's May 2026 report states exponential-type lower bounds for actual Boolean CNF instances in \(\mathrm{roABP}\text{-}\mathrm{IPS}_{\mathrm{LIN}}\), where the algebraic certificate representation is restricted to read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs in the linear-certificate model. The stated bound holds for every variable order and every field. It is stronger in instance scope than earlier purely algebraic examples, but it retains its restriction on certificate representation. It therefore does not supply lower bounds against arbitrary modular-Frege deductions. The report's new complete proof was not independently verified in this card review.

The target excludes hardness arising merely from an enormous conclusion or an unbounded search for its description: every output has polynomial length and a polynomial-time construction, and its truth must be proved. It also excludes confusing a fixed bound such as \(n^{10}\) with growth beyond every polynomial. The depth, prime and uniform-family conventions are part of the mathematical question rather than implementation details that can be decided after submitting a proof.
why: This is a central unresolved comparison between the expressive power of shallow formulas and the length of rigorous deductions. Ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds are known, but modular gates permit compact reasoning about arithmetic counts, including parity. Proving the stated lower bounds would move a major proof-complexity frontier beyond shallow reasoning without modular counting.
status_note: Explicitly open in Krajíček’s 2023/2024 source and the checked 2025/2026 primary literature. Bounded checks through 15 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the retained uniform DNF-family target for every fixed prime. The ITCS 2026 candidate DNFs still have unproved tautologicity in the listed full version; the checked ECCC results restrict derivation depth, give polynomial size bounds, or restrict algebraic certificates. These checks do not independently certify all new proofs or exhaust the literature.
progress: 1988–1993: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for pigeonhole formulas; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo publish exponential-type improvements in 1993. These systems do not contain modular gates. | 2023–2024: Krajíček gives the explicit modular Frege schemes and flattened logical-depth convention in §5 of the preprint, revised 27 September 2023 and published in November 2024. The modular lower-bound frontier remains open there. | 2025-07-29: Efremenko and Itsykson publish tree-like lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth tradeoffs for resolution over parities. Derivation depth is not the logical depth of each line. | 2026-01-23: Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish an unconditional no-short-proof result for explicit candidate DNFs while leaving their tautologicity unresolved. The full arXiv version is v1 of 20 September 2025. | 2026-02-12: Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov report near-quadratic derivation-depth lifting and an unconditional quadratic size lower bound for parity resolution, under their stated lifting conditions. | 2026-05-10: Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret publish ECCC TR26-070, submitted 5 May, reporting hard Boolean CNF instances for the restricted linear-certificate roABP fragment of IPS, for all variable orders and fields.
working_summary: Modular Frege proofs can reason with shallow Boolean formulas containing gates that count true inputs modulo a fixed prime. The problem asks for one polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family per prime that requires superpolynomial total proof size at every fixed logical line depth. The statement fixes a complete finite classical calculus, the modular recurrence axioms, all encodings and the distinction between formula depth and unrestricted derivation depth. Ordinary bounded-depth lower bounds and recent parity-resolution or restricted algebraic results do not establish this stronger modular-Frege target. A complete Lean proof must supply genuine tautologies and all construction and lower-bound guarantees, or prove the logical negation of the specified family-existence claim.

title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
importance_reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.
formal:
Is ordinary Frege not polynomially bounded? For the fixed calculus and complete binary encoding below, determine whether
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\land\forall\pi\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over finite propositional formulas, and \(\pi\) over finite binary strings. Equivalently, for every fixed polynomial bound, some tautology has minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) exceeding that bound in its own encoded length. Neither a polynomial-time construction of hard tautologies nor any algorithm for finding their shortest proofs is required. The depth and length of intermediate formulas and the reuse of previous lines are unrestricted.
definitions:
Ordinary propositional formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by variables \(x_i\), where \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary negation \(\neg A\), and binary material implication \(A\to B\). A Boolean assignment gives every variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses it, and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. The predicate \(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\) means that \(\varphi\) evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables. Formulas are fully written trees: repeated occurrences of a subformula are counted separately.

Fix exactly three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each instance consistently replaces the metavariables \(A,B,C\) by arbitrary formulas. The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom instances and such inferences, with its last formula the conclusion. There are no hypotheses, no extension axioms naming other formulas, and no separate rule substituting into a previously derived line. Variables absent from the final formula may appear in ordinary intermediate formulas. Earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily often, so the dependency graph need not be a tree. There is no cap on line size, logical depth, dependency-path length or number of lines.

Use the following explicit prefix encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. The formula \(x_i\) is encoded by tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\); a negation by tag 01 followed by the child formula; an implication by tag 10 followed by the antecedent and consequent formulas in order. Formula tag 11 is invalid. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then has a two-bit justification tag followed by its complete formula encoding. Tags 00, 01 and 10 identify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be a syntactic instance of the indicated scheme. Tag 11 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\). On line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) to be some \(A\), and line \(b\) to be exactly \(A\to B\), where the current line is \(B\). Malformed strings are not proofs. This makes \(\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\) a specific syntactic validity predicate with final formula \(\varphi\), rather than a claim that unspecified inference rules are sound.

The lengths \(|\varphi|\) and \(|\pi|\) are their entire binary encoding lengths. Every connective, variable index, repeated subformula, line count and inference reference is included. A huge formula is not a constant-cost proof line; proof-size bounds are measured against the full conclusion length, not just its number of distinct variables. This finite Hilbert calculus is sound and complete for classical propositional tautologies. Therefore every tautology has some finite proof, and \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) is the minimum bit length among its valid proof strings. Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so this explicit convention fixes the meaning without changing polynomial boundedness. Restricting the coefficients and exponents of candidate polynomial bounds to positive integers also does not change the question.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. For an affirmative answer, prove that for every pair \(C,k\ge1\) there exists a genuine tautology for which every valid proof exceeds the specified size; an efficiently generated hard family is welcome but is not required. A negative answer must establish one fixed pair \(C,k\ge1\) such that every tautology has some valid Frege proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^k\). It need not supply a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. All formula semantics, syntactic verification and size claims must match the given model and be justified in Lean. A fixed-degree lower bound, an independent cap on line size or depth, a bound for a subsystem, or hardness of finding proofs does not answer the full question. The numerical 1/100 convention does not replace this binary asymptotic comparison.
context:
Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof can derive intermediate lemmas, combine them and cite them again. Checking a proposed step is a syntactic task with polynomial cost in its written size. The question asks whether some short true statements inevitably require much larger certificates in this particular language, even when no restrictions are placed on intermediate formulas.

The distinction between statement length and variable count matters. A formula on \(n\) variables can itself have exponential length in \(n\), so an exponential bound expressed only in the variable count need not be large compared with the actual input. This card compares total proof bits directly with \(|\varphi|\). It also distinguishes the number of proof lines from their combined size: a single enormous intermediate assertion is fully charged.

Cook and Reckhow show that some polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here, and polynomial boundedness of Frege would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). A lower bound for this one fixed proof language does not by itself establish that no other proof language is polynomially bounded. The card asks for an unconditional answer and does not assume a complexity-class separation.

Short proofs and efficient proof discovery are separate resources. The positive statement quantifies over all candidate polynomial size bounds, then permits a different hard tautology for each bound. It does not impose a construction algorithm for those tautologies. Conversely, a universal polynomial upper bound would assert that short certificates exist, without by itself giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them.

The propositional pigeonhole principle asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into \(n\) holes. Its familiar CNF encoding requires exponential-size resolution refutations, while Buss proved polynomial-size Frege proofs in 1987. This is a concrete separation between a weaker clause-based system and Frege. It also explains why a hard family for one proof system cannot automatically be treated as hard for every stronger system. The original author abstract and theorem statements were checked, together with Wigderson's textbook account.

Wigderson states the unrestricted question as Open Problem 6.10 in the author draft of 6 August 2019, on printed page 66, following the pigeonhole upper bound in Theorem 6.9. The older cached March 2018 draft has different pagination; the 2019 file was checked separately in this review. Arbitrary intermediate formulas are part of this problem even when the final tautology is shallow. A theorem limiting only bounded-depth proofs does not cover deductions using deeper formulas.

De Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse's April 2026 preprint states average-case superpolynomial refutation-length bounds for tree-like semantic Frege with a separate line-size cap. Corollary 1.6 considers \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\le s(n)\le2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}}\), with source-prescribed fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and an explicit family of CNFs of size at most \(s(n)^{1+\varepsilon}\); a uniformly sampled member is hard with probability tending to one for tree-like proofs whose individual lines have size at most \(s(n)\). The conclusion concerns that capped system and the stated distribution, not every member or every unrestricted Frege proof. The arXiv submission is dated 30 April; the downloaded typescript is headed 1 May.

The line cap is material. Without a separate line-size cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The cited paper explains that the known conversion increases individual formula sizes, so it does not preserve the capped model used by its lower bound. In the stronger semantic setting, allowing a line large enough to represent the entire inconsistent input even permits an immediate semantic contradiction. None of this supplies a lower bound for unrestricted syntactic Frege.

Davis and Robere's 10 April 2026 report concerns proofs of statements about proof lengths. Its refutation-principle formula asserts that a specified pigeonhole CNF has a depth-\(d\) Frege refutation with a prescribed number of lines, each of polynomially bounded size. Theorem 1.3 gives refutations of those assertions in \(\operatorname{Res}(\log)\), where lines are DNFs with logarithmically bounded conjunction width. The bound is quasipolynomial in the length of the encoded refutation-principle assertion; it is not a polynomial upper bound in the original pigeonhole parameter. The depth and line-size restrictions on the asserted proofs remain essential.

Alekseev's journal paper, published 21 June 2026 after a CCC 2021 precursor, proves an exponential bit-size lower bound over \(\mathbb Q\) for Polynomial Calculus with extension and square-root rules. Its Binary Value Principle instance consists of \(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i-1}x_i=0\) and \(x_i^2-x_i=0\). The paper explicitly notes that this algebraic input is not the relevant polynomial-size propositional CNF translation, so the theorem does not yield Frege or EF lower bounds. This is a limit on transferring that specific lower bound, not a claim that no Boolean encoding of the arithmetic condition can exist.

Extended Frege additionally permits variables naming intermediate formulas. A lower bound for EF would imply one for Frege, while a Frege lower bound need not persist in the presence of those definitions. Separating Frege from EF is also a different question: Frege could have hard tautologies that are equally hard for EF. The present target requires only failure of a universal polynomial bound for Frege itself.

The September 2026 report on partially commutative Ideal Proof Systems again records that unrestricted Frege has no known superpolynomial lower bound. Its own theorem is an upper bound: a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted algebraic formula system over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\). This fresh source supplies dated context, not a proof of the present conjecture. The model restrictions and complete new proof have not been independently validated beyond the source-scope review.
why: This asks whether a standard, robust language of propositional deduction must sometimes use certificates larger than every polynomial in the statement proved. It is a central unresolved lower-bound question for formal reasoning, beyond the restricted proof systems for which strong size lower bounds are known. It concerns the size of the best possible proof, independently of the resources used to discover it.
status_note: Open in Wigderson’s checked 6 August 2019 draft and reiterated in the September 2026 primary literature. Bounded checks through 15 September 2026 identified no unconditional superpolynomial bit-size lower bound for unrestricted Frege and no universal polynomial upper bound. The April tree-like result has a separate line cap, the refutation-principle result has bounded-depth/line parameters and quasipolynomial overhead, and the June algebraic theorem does not transfer its hard instance to the required propositional setting. New proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: Ordinary Frege is a fixed finite calculus for propositional reasoning that allows arbitrary intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of earlier deductions. The question asks whether every proposed polynomial bound fails to cover the shortest Frege proofs of some genuine tautologies. Both the conclusion and the entire proof are measured by explicit binary encodings, including repeated formulas and inference references. Known lower bounds with depth, tree or line-size restrictions and recent algebraic lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted comparison. A complete Lean proof must establish failure of every universal polynomial bound or prove one bound for all tautologies, without an additional proof-search or hard-family construction requirement.

title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
importance_reason: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}*\to\)TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(\mathrm{P}(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists \mathrm{P} \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |\(\pi |\).
answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.
context:
Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\).

Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.
why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
status_note: Primary definitions and the 1989 equivalence theorem were checked, together with February and ICALP 2026 primary sources. The latter retain the propositional optimality questions; their oracle results do not resolve this unrelativized target. A search through 11 September 2026 found no full resolution, and proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1989: Theorem \(2.1(ii)\) relates polynomial simulation of all propositional proof systems to optimal tautology recognition and finite-consistency proof construction; \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) implies this existence. | 2026-02-02: Q1 explicitly retains (p-)optimality for TAUT as open. New oracle constructions show barriers for relativizing answers even with assumptions about the polynomial hierarchy. | 2026-07: ICALP work on recursive jump operators gives oracle barriers and results for other languages, while retaining the propositional optimality questions.
working_summary: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system? The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length. Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial. This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology. The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
importance_reason: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
formal:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), and let
\[
\mathcal D=\{(A,B):A,B\subseteq\Sigma^{*},\ A,B\in\mathrm{NP},\ A\cap B=\varnothing\}.
\]
Does there exist a disjoint NP pair that is complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions of pairs? Precisely, is
\[
\exists(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \forall(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \exists f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\forall x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\Rightarrow f(x)\in A)\land(x\in D\Rightarrow f(x)\in B)\bigr]
\]
true? Here \(\mathrm{FP}\) consists of total polynomial-time functions \(\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\), as specified below. The target pair is fixed before the source pair is chosen; the reduction and its polynomial running-time bound may depend on the source pair.
definitions:
\(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) denotes the number of bits of \(x\). A language is an arbitrary subset of \(\Sigma^{*}\). The pairs are ordered, and disjointness means that no string belongs to both components. Empty component languages are permitted. The quantifiers range over all pairs that are actually disjoint, without requiring their disjointness to be provable in any particular theory.

Computations use uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite control, a fixed finite number of tapes per machine, and tape alphabet \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), where \(\square\) is blank. Each tape has cells indexed by nonnegative integers and one head, initially at cell zero; a left move at cell zero leaves the head there. There is one read-only input tape and finitely many initially blank work tapes. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, and moves each head by at most one cell. A transducer additionally has an initially empty output string and may append at most one output bit per transition. Each transition costs one step. Verifiers halt in an accept or reject state; transducers halt with their accumulated binary output. The finite program and tape count are independent of input length. There is no advice, random input or oracle access.

A language \(L\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there exist such a verifier \(V\), integers \(a,b\ge1\) and \(k,\ell\ge0\), with the following properties. For every \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\), the verifier on input \(x\#y\) halts within \(b(|x|+|y|+2)^{\ell}\) steps, and for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\),
\[
x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\Sigma^{*}\ \bigl(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^{k}\ \land\ V(x\#y)\text{ accepts}\bigr).
\]
The string \(y\) is a certificate. These verifier and polynomial constants may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\) or \(y\).

A function \(f:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{FP}\) if there exist one deterministic transducer \(M\), an integer \(c\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\), \(M\) on input \(x\) halts within \(c(|x|+1)^{d}\) steps and outputs \(f(x)\). Thus \(f\) is defined and polynomial-time computable on every binary input, including strings outside the source promise. Its output length is charged through bit writing and is consequently polynomially bounded.

A reduction from \((C,D)\) to \((A,B)\) is one such function \(f\) satisfying both displayed implications. The same function handles both sides. For \(x\notin C\cup D\), its output may lie anywhere in \(\Sigma^{*}\), including inside \(A\cup B\), but the same totality and time bound still apply. Neither surjectivity nor reverse membership implications are required. For a fixed source pair the transducer, coefficient and degree must work for every input length; they need not be shared by different source pairs. The target does not require a computable procedure that takes descriptions of source pairs and produces their reductions.

The mathematical target concerns the ordinary, unrelativized classes \(\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathrm{FP}\). Completeness for a restricted family of pairs, or completeness or noncompleteness after supplying machines with an oracle, is a different assertion.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including the target languages' NP membership and disjointness and the total polynomial-time reductions for every source pair, or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation:
\[
\forall(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \exists(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \forall f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\exists x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\land f(x)\notin A)\lor(x\in D\land f(x)\notin B)\bigr].
\]
In the negative statement the witness source pair may depend on the candidate target pair but must defeat every eligible reduction; the witness string may depend on the reduction. All computational classes and reductions must have the definitions above. A conditional implication, an oracle construction, or failure of one candidate pair does not alone decide this unconditional target.
context:
Pudlák's 2017 revision defines precisely these pair reductions and conjectures that no complete disjoint NP pair exists. The card preserves its yes-or-no existence question, so proving that conjecture gives a negative answer.

A propositional proof system is a polynomial-time map whose range is exactly the Boolean tautologies. A p-optimal system can translate proofs from every such system in polynomial time; its existence would imply a complete disjoint NP pair. Pudlák's Proposition 5.2 in fact obtains this implication from the weaker requirement that one system polynomially bounds the shortest proof lengths of every other system. No converse implication is asserted.

Dose's 2019 result constructs an oracle relative to which no complete disjoint NP pairs exist even though every NP language has a p-optimal proof system. The proof systems in that result concern NP languages, whereas the propositional implication concerns tautologies; the results do not contradict one another.

Egidy's ICALP 2026 paper constructs an oracle relative to which disjoint NP pairs have no complete pair and the polynomial-time hierarchy remains infinite. An oracle supplies membership answers for a fixed auxiliary language to the machines defining both the classes and reductions. This result concerns those modified classes and does not establish nonexistence for the ordinary classes on this card.
why: A complete pair would be a universal promise problem for two disjoint cases that each have efficiently checkable certificates. The question links the structure of promise problems to the possible existence of a strongest propositional proof system and to feasible versions of incompleteness.

title: PSPACE-completeness of resolution clause space
importance_reason: A long-standing structural question about a central propositional proof system, with a precise gap between an established space upper bound and unresolved hardness. It connects intrinsic proof memory, reuse of deductions and the difficulty of predicting proof-search resources.
formal:
Is the following language \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) PSPACE-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
\[\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}=\{\langle F,s\rangle:\ F\text{ has a general resolution refutation in clause space at most }s\}.\]
Here \(F\) is any finite CNF formula, with no fixed bound on input clause width, and \(s\ge0\) is an integer encoded in binary. A refutation starts with no stored clauses and may download an input clause, derive a resolvent or weakening of currently stored clauses, or erase a stored clause. It succeeds when the empty clause is stored. Its clause space is the largest number of simultaneously stored distinct clauses, counting a new conclusion together with its still-stored premises. Proof length and clause width during the derivation are unrestricted.

The question is about general resolution, allowing a retained clause to be reused in arbitrarily many inferences. PSPACE membership is known; the unresolved target is whether the full problem is PSPACE-hard. Satisfiable inputs have no refutation and are no-instances for every finite \(s\).
question_excerpt: Open Problem 3 asks whether deciding the existence of a resolution refutation with at most a given number of simultaneously retained clauses is PSPACE-complete, preferably even for bounded-width CNF inputs. The adjacent Open Problem 2 asks the separate question for total literal space. The user selected the clause-space question without imposing bounded input width.
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes a value in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\). A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a conjunctive normal form formula, or CNF, is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction. Repeated literals and repeated clauses in an input list are identified. A clause containing both signs of a variable is permitted and is always true. The empty clause \(\bot=\varnothing\) is always false; a formula with no clauses is always true.

Variables are labeled by positive binary integers in the input. Let \(V(F)\) be the finite set of variables actually occurring in \(F\), and let \(n=|V(F)|\). All proof clauses use only variables in \(V(F)\). Relabeling these variables consecutively is harmless and does not provide extra information. No extension variables or extension axioms are allowed. The formula is given as an explicit list of literal lists, with a sign bit and binary variable label for each literal and delimiters for lists. Include the binary representation of \(s\) and a delimiter separating the two components. The input length \(N\) is the total number of bits. Any fixed conventional self-delimiting encoding of this format is allowed; these explicit encodings are polynomial-time interconvertible. Malformed encodings are no-instances.

A memory configuration \(\mathcal C\) is a finite set of clauses over \(V(F)\). A proof is a finite sequence \(\pi=(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T)\) with \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). Each transition applies exactly one of the following operations.

Input download: for a clause \(C\in F\), replace \(\mathcal C\) by \(\mathcal C\cup\{C\}\). The full input formula remains available in a read-only source, but its clauses can be used as inference premises only after being downloaded. Downloaded clauses count toward space just like derived clauses.

Resolution: choose stored clauses \(C,D\in\mathcal C\) and a variable \(x\) such that \(x\in C\) and \(\neg x\in D\). Add the clause
\[R=(C\setminus\{x\})\cup(D\setminus\{\neg x\})\]
to the configuration. Both premises must already be present. Set union removes duplicate literals. Tautological resolvents are allowed. The rule uses one complementary pair, with the displayed set removal defining its exact result.

Weakening: from a stored clause \(C\in\mathcal C\), add any clause \(D\) over \(V(F)\) with \(C\subseteq D\). This is the source's standard optional weakening rule. Weakening is sound and can be eliminated from resolution refutations without increasing clause space, but including it here fixes the proof system explicitly.

Erasure: for a stored clause \(C\in\mathcal C\), replace \(\mathcal C\) by \(\mathcal C\setminus\{C\}\). An erased input clause can later be downloaded again. An erased derived clause can later be obtained again only through legal inferences or because it is also an input clause. There is no free access to a previously erased derived clause.

An inference adds its conclusion without simultaneously deleting its premises. Thus the configuration immediately after the inference is counted before any later erasure. A rule that overwrites a premise with the conclusion in the same step would have a different exact space convention; it is not used in this definition. Adding an already stored clause leaves the set unchanged, and multiple identical copies carry no extra information or storage charge. These conventions follow the general configuration model in Definitions 2.1–2.4 of the source.

A refutation is a proof with \(\bot\in\mathcal C_T\). It need not erase other clauses before it ends. Define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal C_t|,\qquad
\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi\text{ refutes }F}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\]
with \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)=+\infty\) when no refutation exists. The input is accepted precisely when \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le s\). The bound is exact, including its additive constants. For example, space zero never permits the empty clause to be stored, while a formula already containing the empty clause has clause space one.

Clause space counts clauses, regardless of their widths. It is not total space, which counts the sum of literal occurrences in all stored clauses, nor variable space, which counts distinct variables present in memory. It is also not the number of bits used by an algorithm searching for a proof. These are separate resources. The clause-space limit here constrains the proof witness; PSPACE classifies the computational problem of deciding whether such a witness exists.

General resolution permits any stored clause to serve as a premise any number of times before erasure. No tree-like, regular, read-once or input-resolution restriction is imposed. Resolution may use a variable repeatedly along a chain of inferences. There is no bound on \(T\), on the total number of downloads or rederivations, or on any proof clause's width beyond its being a set of literals over \(V(F)\). A short proof is not required as an additional certificate. The input has no satisfiability promise, bounded-width promise, special graph structure or sparsity condition.

PSPACE is the class of languages decided by a uniform deterministic Turing machine that always halts and uses at most \(p(N)\) work-tape bits on inputs of length \(N\), for some fixed polynomial \(p\). The read-only input is not charged to workspace. There is no polynomial-time bound in this class definition. Membership of \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) requires one such machine for all inputs \(\langle F,s\rangle\), counting \(s\)'s binary encoding as part of \(N\).

A deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) to \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) is a total function \(f\), computed by one finite deterministic program in time polynomial in \(|z|\), such that
\[z\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(z)\in\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\]
for every binary input string \(z\). It produces one encoded instance, without oracle calls or nonuniform advice. PSPACE-hardness means such a reduction exists for every language \(L\) in PSPACE; the reduction and its polynomial may depend on \(L\). PSPACE-completeness means both this hardness condition and membership in PSPACE. The card asks for this class-completeness assertion, not a proof that PSPACE differs from P.

Scope decision: the imported record joined Open Problems 2 and 3 of the source, concerning total literal space and clause space respectively. On 16 September 2026 the user selected clause space alone, with no extra input-width restriction. This card records that narrowing. The phrase preferably of fixed width in the source motivates a possible stronger hardness theorem but is not an additional acceptance requirement here.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation that \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\), with the exact configuration transitions, binary threshold encoding and unrestricted CNF inputs above, is PSPACE-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. An affirmative answer must establish both PSPACE membership and hardness with the required uniform reductions and bit-cost bounds. A negative answer must prove that the full completeness assertion is false. Merely placing the language in a smaller complexity class does not refute completeness without the needed separation from PSPACE. A classification for tree-like resolution, total literal space, approximate thresholds or a more restricted class of proofs does not answer the stated question. No numerical benchmark tolerance changes the exact decision predicate. A source citation, experimental proof search or an unformalized reduction is not a substitute for the complete Lean proof.
context:
Resolution derives contradictions by combining clauses. Its memory requirement measures how much derived information must coexist during a proof, even when the proof may be very long. The question asks how difficult it is to determine whether this intrinsic memory requirement fits a supplied budget.

The survey places the general clause-space decision problem in PSPACE and asks whether the corresponding hardness can be proved. This is a decision problem about the existence of an entire proof, rather than about verifying one explicitly supplied proof or measuring one prescribed derivation.

Hertel and Urquhart establish PSPACE-completeness for the tree-resolution space problem. Tree-like derivations restrict reuse of intermediate conclusions. Allowing unrestricted reuse can lower the least required space, so that theorem does not automatically give the claimed hardness for general resolution. Their exact configuration convention also permits deleting parents in the inference step.

The early total-space completeness claim by Hertel and Pitassi was withdrawn after a proof error, as documented in the survey. It concerns a different measure in any event. Neither that withdrawn claim nor the valid tree-like result is recorded as resolving this card.

The 2021 Handbook of Satisfiability chapter still describes PSPACE-completeness of deciding space as a likely classification. It discusses why knowing intrinsic width and space would help interpret proof-search experiments, while distinguishing such proof measures from all of a practical solver's behavior.

Papamakarios and Razborov give later comparisons and trade-offs among several proof measures. Their diagram distinguishes ordinary general clause space from tree-like and regularized quantities, and the comparisons permit polynomial and logarithmic losses. They do not supply an exact-threshold PSPACE-hardness theorem for the language defined here.
why: The target asks whether predicting the minimum memory needed by a resolution proof is as hard as arbitrary polynomial-space computation. This would sharpen the distinction between checking a supplied logical derivation and determining whether any derivation fits a memory budget. It also tests how unrestricted reuse of learned information changes the complexity landscape beyond tree-like proof search.

The inspected 2023 Papamakarios–Razborov comparisons address different proof-measure relationships and do not classify this exact threshold language. A bounded later-work search found no applicable resolution. This is a source-backed open status with later checks, not an exhaustive certification that no result exists. working_summary: Resolution clause space counts how many clauses must coexist while a contradiction is derived. The selected decision problem takes an arbitrary CNF formula and a binary space budget and asks whether any general resolution refutation fits that budget. Intermediate clauses may be reused and proof length is unrestricted. The problem is known to lie in PSPACE, while the established tree-like completeness result does not settle hardness for general resolution. title: Linear versus general resolution
importance_reason: Individual assessment: a longstanding universal comparison between a fundamental sequential proof discipline and unrestricted resolution, with direct consequences for the structural hierarchy of propositional proof systems. Both outcomes identify what proof reuse and deduction order can accomplish. Its breadth is substantially greater than a bound for one formula family; the score reflects that foundational role, not practical use of linear resolution in current SAT solvers or merely the age of the question. This replaces the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.
formal:
Is linear resolution strictly weaker than general resolution in polynomial refutation size, for the same input CNF formula? Here linear resolution has no restarts, and the size \(\ell\) is one plus the number of resolution inferences. More precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \exists\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\ \land\
\forall\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\Longrightarrow
\ell(\lambda)>c\,\ell(\pi)^{k}\right)
\right].
\]
The classes of formulas and the two syntactic refutation predicates are defined below. This asserts failure of every polynomial bound on the extra proof length needed by linear resolution. The constants \(c,k\) range independently over positive integers; \(n,F,\pi\) may depend on them. The comparison concerns existence of proofs, with no requirement that a conversion between proofs be computable in polynomial time. It does not prescribe an exponential separation or an effectively generated family of formulas.
definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), put \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), for \(i\in[n]\). A clause is a finite set of literals containing at most one of \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for each \(i\); thus all clauses are non-tautological and repeated literals are identified. A formula \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\) is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A valuation \(v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\) makes \(x_i\) true when \(v(i)=1\) and makes \(\neg x_i\) true when \(v(i)=0\). A clause is true if it contains a true literal. The empty clause \(\varnothing\) is false, while the empty conjunction is true. A formula is unsatisfiable if no valuation makes all its clauses true.

The sole inference rule is resolution. If \(i\in[n]\), neither \(x_i\) nor \(\neg x_i\) occurs in clauses \(A,B\), and \(A\cup B\) is non-tautological, the rule is
\[
\frac{A\cup\{x_i\}\qquad B\cup\{\neg x_i\}}{A\cup B}.
\]
The two premises may be interchanged. The variable \(x_i\) is the pivot. Every input and derived clause uses variables in \([n]\). There is no weakening rule, additional axiom, introduction of a new variable, or permission to add tautological clauses. Equality of clauses is equality of their literal sets.

A general resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\) is a finite nonempty directed acyclic graph of clause occurrences with one sink, labelled \(\varnothing\). Every vertex reaches that sink. Each source vertex is labelled by a clause of \(F\); every other vertex has exactly two parent vertices and is labelled by the resolvent of their labels under the displayed rule. Each such vertex records its pivot and premise orientation. A clause occurrence may be used as a parent arbitrarily many times. Distinct vertices may have equal labels. This defines \(\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\). A single vertex labelled \(\varnothing\) is allowed exactly when \(\varnothing\in F\).

A linear resolution refutation \(\lambda\) of \(F\) is a finite main sequence
\[
C_0,C_1,\ldots,C_t,\qquad
t\in\mathbb N_0,\quad C_0\in F,\quad C_t=\varnothing,
\]
together with the following annotations. For every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j<t\), the next clause \(C_{j+1}\) is the resolvent of \(C_j\) and a side clause \(D_j\). The side clause is either an input clause \(D_j\in F\), or an earlier main clause \(D_j=C_i\) for a specified integer \(i\) with \(0\le i<j\). The annotation records which alternative is used, its clause or index, and the pivot and premise orientation. This defines \(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\).

Every step after the first main clause must therefore use the immediately preceding main clause as a premise. One cannot insert a new input clause as the next main clause without deriving it by that rule: such an insertion would be a restart. An input clause can nevertheless be used as a side clause whenever needed, whether or not it appeared previously in the main sequence. Earlier main clauses can be reused as side clauses without a limit on the number of uses. All such earlier main clauses are ancestors of the current main clause along the main sequence; no further ancestor test is imposed. Side clauses are not restricted to input clauses. There is no regularity requirement forbidding repeated use of a pivot along a proof path, and no subsumption requirement that a conclusion be contained in its preceding main clause.

For either type of refutation, define
\[
\ell(\Pi)=1+\text{the number of resolution inferences in }\Pi.
\]
Thus \(\ell(\pi)\) for a general refutation is one plus its number of non-source vertices, and \(\ell(\lambda)=t+1\) for the displayed linear refutation. Reusing a parent is not a new inference; deriving a new occurrence is. Input clauses used as side premises do not themselves count as resolution inferences. The additive one includes a refutation with no inference. This is a count of deductions, not the binary length of the whole formula or of its serialized proof.

For a finite representation, label variables by their integer indices, store clauses as sorted lists of signed indices without repetitions, and store formulas as sorted lists of distinct clauses. In a general proof, index vertices in a topological order and store their clause labels and source or two-parent annotations; in a linear proof store the main sequence and its side-clause annotations. All integer indices have ordinary finite binary encodings. These representations specify finite proof objects; the cost remains \(\ell\), without charging literal, index or annotation bits. The same \(F\) must be used in both proof systems. No formula transformation, additional input clause, width bound, clause bound, or proof-search time bound is part of the comparison.

In this card, polynomial simulation means that there are single constants \(c,k\ge1\) such that every general refutation of every \(F\) has some linear refutation of that same \(F\) of size at most \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\). This is ordinary proof-size simulation. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm producing the latter proof would be the stronger notion of \(p\)-simulation and is not required here. Every linear refutation is a particular general refutation when its main and input occurrences are represented as a graph, so only the converse simulation is at issue.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the assertion in the formal statement or of its full negation, using exactly the formulas, inference rule, proof predicates and size measure above.

A positive answer must show that for every pair \(c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), there is a finite formula with a general refutation \(\pi\) for which every linear refutation has size greater than \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\), with all the quantifiers of the displayed assertion. No particular exponential rate or uniformly generated counterexample family is required.

A negative answer must prove the polynomial simulation statement
\[
\exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \forall\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\Longrightarrow
\exists\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\land
\ell(\lambda)\le c\,\ell(\pi)^k\right)
\right].
\]
The same \(c,k\) must work for every formula and every general refutation; the linear refutation may depend on the formula and proof. An efficient proof-conversion algorithm would suffice if its size guarantee meets this statement, but is not an additional obligation. Comparisons allowing restarts, changing the input formula, using resolution over linear equations, or imposing extra regularity or input-only restrictions do not answer the stated question. A separation at one fixed polynomial degree also does not prove the universal separation assertion. This is a yes/no comparison of asymptotic proof lengths, so numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not alter the quantifiers or polynomial bounds.
context:
Nordström's 2013 survey poses the unresolved strength comparison in Section 3.2. Its preceding definition permits restarting the main sequence from an input clause. This card preserves the intended open question while explicitly correcting that definition to linear resolution without restarts, using the later direct definition of Buss and Johannsen.

Buss and Johannsen distinguish the two systems: allowing restarts gives a polynomial-time simulation of general resolution, whereas the strength of linear resolution without restarts remains open in their account. They also prove that regular resolution does not simulate linear resolution; that different comparison does not settle the question here.

Johannsen's 2018 Dagstuhl contribution again gives the no-restarts definition and asks about superpolynomial separation or polynomial-time simulation of unrestricted resolution. This card fixes the original proof-size comparison, distinguishing ordinary polynomial simulation from the additional efficient-conversion requirement in the latter alternative.

An ECCC correction dated November 2002 withdraws the earlier claimed separation: its author identifies a failed lemma and unproved separation theorems. The old report title must therefore not be treated as a solution of this problem.

The later primary results checked in the bounded review include effective simulation, which permits changing the input formula, and a separation for resolution over parity equations. Their models differ from the unchanged-formula, classical-clause comparison in this card.
why: This compares two longstanding, complete refinements of a foundational propositional proof system. It isolates the effect of how deductions are organized and reused, with the inference rule and input formula held fixed. A separation would identify an intrinsic proof-length cost of the linear discipline; a polynomial simulation would show that arbitrary resolution structure can always be reproduced within polynomial length. The result would clarify the strength hierarchy of resolution refinements, independently of how efficiently a solver can discover the proofs.

title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) lower bounds
importance_reason: A repeatedly identified major proof-complexity barrier: one of the simplest parity-aware systems without known general superpolynomial lower bounds, with substantial recent progress on restricted fragments.
formal:
Is resolution over parities not polynomially bounded on unsatisfiable Boolean CNF formulas? Precisely, is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists F\quad
\bigl[F\text{ is an unsatisfiable CNF}\ \land\
L_{\oplus}(F)>C\bigl(N(F)+1\bigr)^k\bigr].
\]
Here \(L_{\oplus}(F)\) is the minimum number of lines in any unrestricted \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) refutation of \(F\), with the rules below, and \(N(F)\) is its full combinatorial input size. Earlier proof lines may be reused arbitrarily. There is no restriction on depth, width, regularity or space.
question_excerpt: Do some unsatisfiable formulas require refutations longer than every universal polynomial bound in unrestricted resolution over linear equations modulo two?
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two. A Boolean assignment to \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is an element of \(\mathbb F_2^n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\); a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction, with the empty clause false. A CNF formula \(F\) is a finite conjunction of clauses. It is unsatisfiable if no assignment makes every clause true. Relabel its distinct occurring variables consecutively as \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\); no unused declared variables are counted. Put
\[
N(F)=n+\#\{\text{clauses of }F\}+
       \sum_{D\text{ a clause of }F}|D|.
\]
The empty conjunction and empty clauses are allowed. Clauses are listed explicitly, with signs and binary variable indices. This input measure is polynomially equivalent to the length of this ordinary explicit binary encoding, so the existence of a polynomial bound does not depend on that encoding choice.

A linear form is \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb F_2\), including the zero form. A linear equation is \(f=b\), for \(b\in\mathbb F_2\). A linear clause is a finite disjunction of these equations, again allowing the empty disjunction. Its truth value is given by evaluating all equations over \(\mathbb F_2\). Ordinary positive and negative literals are represented respectively by \(x_i=1\) and \(x_i=0\).

A refutation is a finite sequence of linear clauses ending with the empty clause. Each line is either an input clause of \(F\), translated as above, or follows from earlier lines by one of exactly these rules:

Parity resolution:
\[
\frac{A\vee(f=0)\qquad B\vee(f=1)}{A\vee B},
\]
where \(A,B\) are linear clauses and \(f\) is any linear form in the input variables. Disjunction is taken modulo order and repeated identical disjuncts.

Semantic weakening: from a linear clause \(A\), infer any linear clause \(B\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb F_2^n,\quad A(x)=1\Longrightarrow B(x)=1.
\]
This rule is implication from one previous line, not arbitrary implication from all input clauses jointly.

All equations use only the variables of \(F\); there are no extension variables, additional axiom schemes or unlisted inference rules. A previous line can serve as a premise arbitrarily many times, giving a directed acyclic proof graph. Size is the total number of lines, including occurrences of input clauses and weakening steps. It is not the sum of the lengths of the equations. Define \(L_{\oplus}(F)\) as the minimum such size. Every unsatisfiable CNF has a refutation since the system contains ordinary resolution.

The constants \(C,k\) are proposed universal bounds; the witnessing formula may depend on both. The question imposes no separate running-time condition on constructing these witnesses and fixes no particular family of formulas. It asks for unconditional non-polynomial boundedness of this fixed proof system, not for a conditional statement assuming a complexity separation.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its negation. An affirmative answer must rule out every uniform polynomial line-count upper bound for unrestricted refutations. A negative answer must prove that there are fixed \(C,k\ge1\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF \(F\) has a refutation of at most \(C(N(F)+1)^k\) lines; no efficient proof-finding algorithm is additionally required. Lower bounds confined to tree-like, regular, reversible or bounded-depth proofs do not meet the affirmative target, and a conditional lower bound does not settle the unconditional proposition. No additive numerical tolerance changes this binary asymptotic claim.
context:
Ordinary resolution reasons with disjunctions of individual literals. \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) also permits equations asserting the parity of an arbitrary subset of variables. These equations provide compact algebraic information that ordinary resolution may express inefficiently.

This system lies within constant-depth Frege reasoning augmented with parity gates, commonly denoted \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\)-Frege. The absence of general lower bounds even for this restricted proof language isolates an important boundary in understanding short propositional proofs. A lower bound here alone would not automatically prove one for the stronger Frege system.

Regular refutations and proofs of bounded depth have received much stronger lower bounds. They still exclude possible short proofs with more complicated reuse and longer dependency chains. The unrestricted question must allow those proofs as well.

The 2026 polynomial-depth paper separates conditional results for the general system from unconditional results for reversible proofs. Its unrestricted polynomial-depth claim cannot be cited without its combinatorial hypothesis.

A February 2026 result gives a quadratic unrestricted lower bound together with stronger size-depth tradeoffs. Quadratic growth remains polynomial, and a tradeoff can be satisfied by a short proof with sufficient depth.

Resolving it would establish whether this algebraic ability suffices to give short refutations of every unsatisfiable CNF, or whether even unrestricted reuse of parity information leaves an unavoidable superpolynomial proof-size barrier.
