The question asks whether unsatisfiable CNF formulas can require more proof lines than every universal polynomial bound in their input size. Proofs may reuse earlier lines without any restriction on depth, width, regularity or space. Recent strong lower bounds for restricted proofs and the known unrestricted quadratic bound do not settle this question. A resolution would locate a central limitation, or unexpected strength, of propositional reasoning with parity.

title: Linear-space Cutting Planes refutations
importance_reason: Individual assessment: this asks for the universal memory capacity of Cutting Planes once integer magnitudes are charged, bridging a sharp constant-line-space phenomenon and a persistent linear-versus-quadratic total-space gap. Its scope is an entire established proof system, and it distinguishes arithmetic compression from genuine simultaneous storage. The score reflects this foundational breadth and relevance to proof complexity, rather than merely the presence of an open-problem paragraph; it replaces the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.
formal:
Does there exist one constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF formula on \(n\) Boolean variables has a Cutting Planes refutation using total space at most \(C(n+1)\), with the exact rules and space measure below?
\[
\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\
\left(\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\ \Longrightarrow\
\exists\Pi\
\left[\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)
\land\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)\le C(n+1)\right]\right).
\]
Here \(n\) counts variables, rather than clauses, literal occurrences or the binary length of the whole input. There is no restriction on the number of clauses, proof length or coefficient magnitudes. The same constant \(C\) must work for every \(n\) and \(F\); the finite refutation \(\Pi\) may depend on \(F\). The \(n+1\) convention includes formulas with no variables and is equivalent to the source's asymptotic linear bound.
question_excerpt: Can every unsatisfiable CNF be refuted in CP in linear total space?
definitions:
Put \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and let the variables be \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A clause is a pair of subsets \(P,N\subseteq[n]\), representing the disjunction of the positive literals \(x_i\), \(i\in P\), and negative literals \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in N\). Repeated occurrences of a literal are removed. A CNF \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\) is a finite set of such clauses, interpreted as their conjunction; tautological clauses are allowed. A valuation is a map \(v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\). It satisfies \((P,N)\) exactly when some \(i\in P\) has \(v(i)=1\), or some \(i\in N\) has \(v(i)=0\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\ \exists(P,N)\in F\
\left[(\forall i\in P,\ v(i)=0)\land
(\forall i\in N,\ v(i)=1)\right].
\]
The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. Allowing unused variables in \([n]\) does not change the universal assertion, since one can also take \(n\) to be the number of variables that occur and rename them.

A line is a pair \(J=(a,b)\), where \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z\), denoting \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ge b\). Terms are collected, zero coefficients are omitted, and the constant is on the right. Equality of lines means equality of these integer data, not logical equivalence. There are no extension variables, semantic inference rules or implicit rescaling operations.

The input line for clause \((P,N)\) is
\[
\sum_{i\in P}x_i-\sum_{i\in N}x_i\ge 1-|N|.
\]
Let \(A(F)\) be the set of these lines after collecting coefficients. Besides downloading a line in \(A(F)\), the permitted rules are exactly the following.

1. For each \(i\in[n]\), introduce either Boolean axiom \(x_i\ge0\) or \(-x_i\ge-1\).
2. Choose any integer \(k\ge1\), currently stored lines \((a^{(1)},b_1),\ldots,(a^{(k)},b_k)\), and positive integers \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\), and derive
\[
\left(\sum_{j=1}^k s_j a^{(j)},\ \sum_{j=1}^k s_j b_j\right).
\]
There is no fixed upper bound on the number \(k\) of premises. A premise may be selected more than once, equivalently by increasing its multiplier.
3. From a currently stored line \((a,b)\), choose an integer \(d\ge1\) dividing every \(a_i\), and derive
\[
\left(a/d,\ \left\lceil b/d\right\rceil\right).
\]
Division of \(a\) is coordinatewise. The ceiling is the least integer greater than or equal to the rational number \(b/d\), also when \(b\) is negative.

A memory configuration \(M\) is a finite set of lines. A refutation \(\Pi=(M_0,\ldots,M_T)\) is a finite sequence, with \(T\in\mathbb N_0\), starting with \(M_0=\varnothing\) and ending with \((0,1)\in M_T\), the contradiction \(0\ge1\). At each step, either \(M_{t+1}=M_t\cup\{J\}\), where \(J\in A(F)\), \(J\) is a Boolean axiom, or \(J\) follows by one permitted rule using premises in \(M_t\); or \(M_{t+1}\subsetneq M_t\), an erasure. This defines \(\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)\). In particular, premises and a new conclusion coexist before a later erasure; overwriting a premise is not a free operation. An erased input line may be downloaded again. The full input need never be present simultaneously.

For \(z\in\mathbb Z\), let its unsigned binary length be
\[
\beta(z)=
\begin{cases}
1,&z=0,\\
1+\lfloor\log_2|z|\rfloor,&z\ne0.
\end{cases}
\]
This uses the one-digit representation of zero and omits leading zeroes. Define
\[
\operatorname{size}(a,b)=\beta(b)+
\sum_{\substack{i\in[n]\\a_i\ne0}}\beta(a_i),\qquad
\operatorname{sp}(M)=\sum_{J\in M}\operatorname{size}(J),\qquad
\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}\operatorname{sp}(M_t).
\]
This is the source's numerical-symbol measure: count binary digits of nonzero coefficients and the right-hand constant, ignoring signs, variable names or indices, punctuation and arithmetic symbols. It is not the bit length of a fully serialized proof or machine memory. The conceptual vector \(a\) does not charge for its zero entries. Each distinct stored line is counted once. Input lines count while stored; the separate input, previous erased lines, proof history and rule annotations or multipliers do not count. There is no running-time, randomization or effective proof-search requirement: the target concerns existence of finite syntactically valid refutations.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed assertion or of its full negation, using exactly the CNF encoding, inference rules, configurations and total-space measure above.

A positive answer must establish a single universal constant \(C\ge1\) and a finite refutation meeting \(C(n+1)\) for every unsatisfiable \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\). No uniform polynomial-time procedure for finding the refutations is required.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\
\left(\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\land
\forall\Pi\
\left[\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)>C(n+1)\right]\right).
\]
The final universal quantifier includes proofs of every finite length and every integer coefficient magnitude. The counterexample formula may depend on \(C\); a fixed power-law lower bound is not required. A bound only for short proofs, bounded coefficients, a restricted inference system or a different space measure does not establish this negation. This is an asymptotic existence question with a constant-factor linear bound, so the numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not replace its quantifiers or inequalities.
context:
Galesi, Pudlák and Thapen's 2015 Problem 2 asks precisely whether every unsatisfiable CNF has a Cutting Planes refutation in linear total space. Their parameter is the number of variables, and their Section 2 ignores variable-name length while charging coefficient magnitudes in binary.

The same paper proves that five simultaneously stored inequalities suffice without coefficient restrictions, and gives an \(O(n^2)\) total-space upper bound. The former result counts lines, so it does not already give the linear total-space conclusion.

Buss and Nordström's 2021 handbook chapter records a linear lower bound and a quadratic general upper bound for total space, with no known superlinear lower bound at the time of that account. These are dated statements, not a claim that all later literature has been exhausted.

The later papers checked here establish length-space tradeoffs, a bounded-coefficient length-space separation, size-depth tradeoffs, and a 2026 proof-length lower bound. Their resource restrictions differ from this card's unrestricted-length total-space question, and none of their inspected statements settles it.
why: The question tests a basic memory limit of a central arithmetic proof system used to study pseudo-Boolean reasoning. Counting only inequalities hides the cost of large coefficients, whereas total space records that cost. A resolution would determine whether the known constant-line-space phenomenon extends to a linear numerical representation budget, or whether some Boolean contradictions force additional simultaneous information even when arbitrarily long proofs are permitted. This is a universal structural question about the proof system, with a separate meaning from lower bounds on proof length.
status_note: Open as stated in CCC 2015, Section 7, Problem 2. A bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The 2021 handbook account still describes a linear-versus-quadratic total-space gap; inspected 2020/2021 length-space and coefficient tradeoffs, the November 2024 size-depth result, and the July 2026 clique proof-length result do not settle the unrestricted-length total-space target. This is not an exhaustive literature review, an independent verification of the cited proofs, or a Lean verification. The apparent linear-space claim in Corollary 6 of an older 29 October 2014 author draft conflicts with its own introduction and is corrected to quadratic space in the final 2015 proceedings; it is not treated as a resolution.

working_summary: Cutting Planes refutes a Boolean CNF by deriving integer linear inequalities until it obtains a contradiction. Total space counts the binary digits of coefficients and right-hand constants stored simultaneously, with the source's convention that variable names and signs are not charged. The question is whether one constant times the number of variables always suffices, with no limit on proof length or coefficient magnitude. The source gives a quadratic universal upper bound, and the bounded later-source review found no resolution of the remaining linear-space question. An accepted answer must prove the universal linear bound or its fully quantified failure in Lean for the exact rules and space measure stated here.

title: Effective polynomial simulation of Extended Frege by Resolution
importance_reason: Tests whether conventional proof-size separations remain meaningful when hard instances themselves must be found efficiently.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer \(s\ge 1, R\)(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
definitions:
A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation \(
eg\) and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent \(C\lor D\) of earlier clauses \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor 
eg x\). Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), or follow by modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\). One may also introduce an extension axiom \(z\leftrightarrow B\), where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here \(z\leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((z	o B)\land (B	o z)\). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.
context:
Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

From \(x\lor y\) and \(\neg x\), Resolution derives y. Together with the clause \(\neg y\), it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.
why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.
status_note: Checked the original simulation definition and subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The checked 2024 simulation theorem concerns two Resolution systems and does not settle the EF target. No unconditional resolution of the stated question was located; paper proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2010: Pitassi and Santhanam define effective polynomial simulation and explicitly pose the Resolution-versus-Extended-Frege question. | 2024: Regular and unrestricted Resolution are shown equivalent under effective simulations, with the auxiliary proof-size parameter retained.
working_summary: Resolution refutes inconsistent clauses, while Extended Frege permits named intermediate Boolean formulas. Ordinary proof-size comparisons keep the statement fixed and separate these systems. This question allows a polynomial-time transformation of the statement, given a unary bound on an EF proof’s length. Whenever that bound is sufficient, the transformed CNF must have a comparably short Resolution refutation, while correctness must be preserved for every input. An answer would clarify whether efficient preprocessing can overcome the proof-size gap between these systems.

title: Polynomial resolution length from logarithmic clause space
importance_reason: A basic unresolved relation between two central resolution resources, with a precise logarithmic threshold and a gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial guarantees. It helps separate intrinsic proof complexity from the stronger demand to optimize time and memory in the same proof.
formal:
Does logarithmic clause space imply polynomial refutation length for every fixed input clause width in general resolution?

Precisely, for every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and real constant \(a>0\), do there exist constants \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), depending only on \(k,a\), such that every unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(F)\le B\,N(F)^d?\]
Here \(N(F)=2+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) is formula size, \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\) is the minimum number of clauses simultaneously retained in a resolution refutation, and \(L(F)\) is its minimum number of axiom downloads and inference steps. These two minima are taken independently over all general resolution refutations. The short refutation whose existence is requested has no space restriction.
question_excerpt: Nordström records Esteban and Torán’s question whether an unsatisfiable CNF with a fixed bound on input-clause width and a resolution refutation in logarithmic clause space must also have a polynomial-length resolution refutation.
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. Clauses contain no repeated literal and no complementary pair \(x,\neg x\). The empty clause \(\bot\) is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction; it is unsatisfiable if no assignment to its variables makes every clause true. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals in every input clause. The fixed input-width parameter \(k\) does not bound clauses derived during a proof.

The variable universe for a proof is the finite set of variables occurring in \(F\). Renaming these variables has no cost. The size \(N(F)\) counts input clauses and literal occurrences, with the added constant two ensuring that its logarithm is positive. Input clauses are a set, so padding by duplicate clauses does not change the formula or its size. If a concrete binary encoding is needed, number the occurring variables consecutively, encode each literal by its index and sign, and list clauses with delimiters. For fixed \(k\), this encoding and the stated combinatorial size are polynomially related; the logarithmic-space versus polynomial-length question is invariant under this choice of size convention.

A resolution refutation is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal D_0,\ldots,\mathcal D_T\), each a set of clauses over the input variables. Initially \(\mathcal D_0=\varnothing\), and the final configuration contains \(\bot\). Each step performs exactly one of the following operations. It may download one input clause \(C\in F\) into memory, adding it to the current set. It may erase one currently retained clause. It may add a resolvent \(C\cup D\) from two currently retained premises \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\), where neither \(C\) nor \(D\) contains the pivot variable and the resolvent is non-tautological. It may also weaken a retained clause by adding literals, provided the result is a clause over the same variables. These are the ordinary syntactic resolution and weakening rules. Arbitrary semantic consequence is not an additional inference rule.

Premises must be present before an inference, and they remain present after it unless erased in subsequent steps. An inference adds its conclusion before any such erasure, so the temporary memory needed to hold the conclusion is counted. An erased clause must be downloaded or derived again before reuse. The input formula itself is available for downloads without occupying working memory. Resolution proofs may share intermediate results arbitrarily; neither the tree-like restriction nor the regularity restriction forbidding repeated pivots on a proof path is imposed. No extension variables, stronger proof rules, randomization or error are allowed.

For a refutation \(\pi\), define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal D_t|,\]
and let \(L(\pi)\) be its number of axiom-download and inference steps, with repetitions counted. Erasures are not counted in length. One can instead count all steps without changing polynomial-length bounds, because useful erasures can be bounded by the number of additions. Clause space counts each stored clause as one object regardless of its width. It is different from total literal space \(\max_t\sum_{C\in\mathcal D_t}|C|\), from the number of distinct variables in memory, and from the number of stored bits.

For an unsatisfiable formula, resolution completeness guarantees that the following finite integer minima exist:
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\qquad L(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}L(\pi).\]
The refutation attaining the first minimum may have very large length. The question is whether a possibly different refutation of polynomial length must nevertheless exist whenever that minimum space is logarithmic.

The full quantifier order is \(\forall k\ge1\;\forall a>0\;\exists B>0,d\ge1\;\forall F\). The exponent \(d\) may depend on the input-width bound and the constant multiplying the logarithm, but not on the individual formula or its size. The proposition does not demand one exponent uniform in all \(k,a\), a procedure finding the short proof, or a transformation that keeps the original space bound.

A negative answer means that for some fixed \(k\) and \(a>0\), no polynomial bounds the minimum length throughout this class: for every \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), some unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF \(F\) has \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\) but \(L(F)>B N(F)^d\). Thus it must establish genuinely superpolynomial unrestricted resolution length despite the small-space refutation. Merely proving that all proofs which retain small space are long does not refute the proposition.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified implication. A positive answer must establish a polynomial length bound for all promised formulas, with its dependence on fixed \(k,a\) explicit or provably existent. A negative answer must prove the stated logical negation against all polynomial length bounds, including unrestricted-space refutations. A quasipolynomial upper bound, a theorem for constant clause space only, a result for tree-like resolution only, or a simultaneous length–space tradeoff does not settle the target. The statement is an exact asymptotic proposition; additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.
context:
Resolution combines clauses to certify that a Boolean formula is inconsistent. Its proof length is a basic lower bound on the work needed by resolution-based proof search, while clause space records how many learned facts must be retained together.

The memory measure here treats a clause as one object even when it is long. This makes logarithmic clause space fundamentally different from logarithmic bit space of an ordinary machine computation; a small number of clauses may encode many bits.

For constant-width input CNFs, the known space-to-width relation and the width counting bound imply \(L(F)\le N(F)^{O(\operatorname{Sp}(F)+k)}\). In particular, constant clause space implies polynomial length, whereas logarithmic clause space gives only a quasipolynomial bound \(N(F)^{O(\log N(F))}\). The question asks whether that remaining gap can always be removed.

The reverse implication behaves differently: the survey documents families with short refutations but large minimum clause space. Those examples do not decide whether small clause space forces short refutations.

A simultaneous-resource question asks whether a single proof can be both short and economical in memory. This card asks only whether a short proof exists at all. A tradeoff forcing a memory-limited proof to be long is compatible with a polynomial proof that uses more memory.

The 2023 work organizes connections among clause space, other space measures and tree-like proof size, and leaves major simultaneous-resource questions open in its concluding section. Those developments supply recent structural context but are not a solution or a newly restated confirmation of the precise logarithmic-space implication in this card.
why: The question asks whether a resolution proof that can be checked with only logarithmically many retained clauses necessarily has a short certificate somewhere in the same proof system. Resolving it would sharpen the relation between proof memory and proof length beyond the known constant-space case, without conflating proof existence with an efficient search algorithm.

title: Frege lower bounds from circuit hardness
importance_reason: Would connect circuit hardness with the power of propositional proof systems, transferring progress between two difficult lower-bound areas.
formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
definitions:
A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary string \(y\), with \(|y|\le p(|x|)\), satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). A Boolean circuit has input bits, constants zero and one, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one output. Its size is its number of gates, and its depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The class P/poly consists of languages decided at each input length \(n\) by a circuit \(D_n\) of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for fixed \(C,k\). These circuits need not be produced by an algorithm: they may be chosen nonuniformly. Thus NP not contained in P/poly asserts that at least one NP language has no such circuit family.

Fix the following classical Hilbert presentation of Frege. Formulas are finite trees built from propositional variables \(p_0,p_1,\ldots\), negation \(\neg\), and implication \(\to\). Under a Boolean assignment, negation reverses the truth value and \(A\to B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is true and \(B\) false. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its finitely many variables. The axiom schemes, allowing arbitrary formulas \(A,B,D\), are
\[A\to(B\to A),\]
\[(A\to(B\to D))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to D)),\]
\[(\neg A\to\neg B)\to(B\to A).\]
The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an instance of an axiom scheme or obtained by this rule; its last formula is the theorem proved. No extension axioms introducing a new variable as an abbreviation for a formula are allowed.

Choose a fixed uniquely parsable binary tree encoding with constant-length tags for connectives and binary, self-delimited variable indices. Let \(|\varphi|\) be its bit length. Encode a proof by its full sequence of formula strings, with line delimiters; let \(|\pi|\) be that total bit length. Identical subformulas are written out each time they occur, not stored as a shared circuit. Earlier proof lines may be reused in multiple inferences. Including explicit rule tags and premise indices changes these sizes by at most polynomial factors and does not affect polynomial boundedness. The source recalls that standard finite complete Frege presentations polynomially simulate one another, so fixing this presentation does not change its lower-bound question.

Frege is polynomially bounded if there exist \(C,k\) such that every tautology has at least one proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\). Its negation does not require a polynomial-time generator for the hard tautologies or a single explicit family: existence of arbitrarily hard tautologies with the displayed quantifiers suffices. Formula size, proof size and circuit-input length are different parameters and are not silently identified.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication or of its negation. A positive proof may use exactly the circuit-hardness premise, without assuming additional cryptographic hardness, a feasible-interpolation property of Frege, or a lower bound for another system. A proof of the negation must establish both NP not contained in P/poly and polynomial boundedness of the fixed Frege system. An oracle separation or an obstruction to one reduction technique is not itself a negation of the stated unrelativized implication.
context:
Feasible interpolation turns short proofs in some weaker systems into small circuits, permitting circuit lower bounds to imply proof lower bounds there. The source emphasizes that such interpolation is not available for general Frege under the same assumptions; granting it for free would change the question.

The source asks about ordinary Frege, with unrestricted formula depth. Lower bounds for bounded-depth Frege do not settle it. Extended Frege permits abbreviation variables and is a stronger system; the names should not be interchanged.

Pich and Santhanam study connections in the direction from proof lower bounds to circuit hardness, using additional witnessing or provability conditions. These results do not supply the source’s implication from the bare NP circuit-hardness premise to ordinary Frege lower bounds.

The September 2026 report extends simulations between Frege and algebraic proof systems with partially commutative formulas. Its identity-testing and algebraic-model restrictions do not yield the general Boolean-circuit implication asked here.
why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

title: Simultaneous polynomial-length constant-space refutations
importance_reason: A basic unresolved compatibility question between two central resolution resources. Constant clause space already implies the existence of polynomial-length proofs separately, while known severe trade-offs at growing space do not determine whether the two bounds can always coexist at constant space.
formal: Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and every family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas of size polynomial in \(n\), if there is a constant \(s\) such that every \(F_n\) has a resolution refutation using at most \(s\) clauses simultaneously, then there are constants \(S\ge1\), \(C>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(F_n\) has a single resolution refutation \(\pi_n\) with \[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi_n)\le S\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\pi_n)\le C(n+1)^d.\] The constants may depend on the family and on \(k,s\), but not on \(n\). In particular, the conclusion may use a larger constant space bound \(S\) than the original bound \(s\).
definitions: Variables are drawn from a countable set. A literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a CNF formula is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals per input clause; derived clauses have no width bound. Define the size of \(F\) to be \(\sum_{A\in F}(1+|A|)\). Polynomial size means that some \(a>0,b\in\mathbb N\), fixed for the family, satisfy this size bound \(\le a(n+1)^b\) for every \(n\). The parameter \(n\) indexes the family; it need not equal the number of variables. There is no computability or uniform generation requirement on the family. A proof is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_t\), each a finite set of clauses, starting at \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). One step may add an input clause from \(F\); add the resolvent \(A\cup B\) when \(A\cup\{x\}\) and \(B\cup\{\neg x\}\) are both currently present, with \(x\) absent from \(A\) and \(\neg x\) absent from \(B\); add a weakening \(A\cup B\) when \(A\) is present and \(B\) is any finite clause; or erase one currently present clause. An inference adds its conclusion before any separate erasure, so premises and conclusion coexist in that configuration. The proof ends with the empty clause present. The clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_j|\mathcal C_j|\), counting input clauses only while they have been downloaded and retained. The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of input-clause downloads and inference steps, including weakenings and rederivations, but excluding erasures. Erased clauses may be downloaded or derived again; their reappearance is charged again. There is no read-once, tree-like, regularity or restriction on reuse. Space counts clauses regardless of how many literals they contain: it is not total literal space, variable space, bit memory or width. Length counts proof lines as specified, not the bit cost of manipulating a long clause. The target concerns existence of proofs with the two simultaneous bounds, not an efficient algorithm that finds them.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication for every fixed width and every polynomial-size family, or prove its negation. A positive answer must produce or establish existence of refutations satisfying both resource bounds at once. Separate witnesses for polynomial length and constant clause space do not suffice. A negative answer must exhibit a fixed \(k\) and a polynomial-size family with a common constant-space refutation bound, but such that for every \(S\ge1,C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) some member has no refutation satisfying both \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)\le S\) and \(L(\pi)\le C(n+1)^d\). A polynomial length lower bound, a lower bound only for tree-like proofs, or a trade-off that disappears after increasing space by a fixed constant does not refute this statement.
context:
Nordström’s Open Problem 16 asks this simultaneous length–clause-space question for polynomial-size fixed-width CNF families. It is distinct from the neighboring question about trade-offs when space is at least linear in formula size, whose later resolution is already noted in the survey.

The survey records that a constant clause-space bound guarantees some polynomial-length refutation, but that conclusion does not bound the clause space of the short refutation. The missing simultaneous guarantee is precisely the present target.

With total literal space in place of clause space, the corresponding simultaneous constant-space and polynomial-length statement is already known. A constant number of clauses may nevertheless contain many literals, so that result does not apply to this measure.

Papamakarios and Razborov’s ICALP 2022 paper revisits the same constant-clause-space question explicitly in Section 5. Theorem 4.7 gives formulas of linear size with clause-space-four tree-like refutations for which all tree-like refutations have a nearly quadratic length lower bound. A polynomial lower bound in that restricted proof system does not contradict the present unrestricted polynomial-length conclusion.

Their broader equivalences relate proof-space measures to tree-like proof size and identify stronger separation questions. The checked journal metadata places the expanded publication in November 2023; the theorem numbering quoted here is from the fully read ICALP version.
why: Proof length measures how many lines a refutation generates, and clause space measures how many it must retain at once. The question asks whether a formula that is easy in each measure separately can be hard when both restrictions apply to the same proof. Its constant-space regime makes it a sharp structural question about resolution and the interpretation of proof-memory bounds.

title: Cutting Planes versus polynomial-coefficient Cutting Planes
importance_reason: A central unresolved comparison in proof complexity: whether large integer coefficients provide a superpolynomial advantage in proof length after memory restrictions are removed. It isolates a fundamental resource of arithmetic reasoning rather than a parameter change in one solver.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(C,k\) such that, for every CNF formula \(F\) and every Cutting Planes refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), there is a Cutting Planes refutation \(\pi'\) of the same formula satisfying
\[
L(\pi')\le C\bigl(N(F)+L(\pi)\bigr)^k,\qquad
M(\pi')\le C\bigl(N(F)+L(\pi)\bigr)^k?
\]
Both refutations use exactly the rules and variables defined below. The original coefficients are unrestricted, proof lines may be reused, and there is no space restriction. A negative answer is the full quantified negation: for every pair \(C,k\ge1\), some \(F,\pi\) admit no replacement satisfying both bounds. The violating instance may depend on \(C,k\).
question_excerpt: The source asks whether arbitrary coefficients increase the strength of Cutting Planes over its polynomial-coefficient restriction. The user selected an existential, uniform polynomial bound in formula size plus original proof length, simultaneously on replacement length and coefficient magnitude, without a memory restriction.
definitions:
A CNF formula \(F\) is a finite list of clauses over Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), each taking values in \(\{0,1\}\). Each clause is a finite set of positive or negative literals. Duplicate literal occurrences are removed; tautological clauses and the empty clause are allowed. Variables are consecutively relabeled, and only variables occurring in the formula are counted. The empty conjunction is true and the empty clause is false. Fix the combinatorial input size
\[
N(F)=1+n+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|.
\]
This measure is polynomially equivalent to the bit length of an explicit clause-list encoding with binary variable indices. The choice fixes the size parameter, rather than granting a succinct circuit encoding of the input.

A Cutting Planes line is a normalized integer inequality \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i x_i\ge b\), with every \(a_i,b\in\mathbb Z\). Zero coefficients may be omitted in writing, but the coefficient vector is defined on all \(n\) variables. A clause with positive-variable set \(P\) and negative-variable set \(M\) contributes the input inequality \(\sum_{i\in P}x_i-\sum_{i\in M}x_i\ge1-|M|\). If both signs occur, their coefficients cancel. Boolean axioms are \(x_i\ge0\) and \(-x_i\ge-1\); the harmless constant axiom \(0\ge0\) is also permitted. No extension variables, semantic inference rules, or extra assumptions are allowed.

A proof is a finite sequence of lines. Each line is an input inequality, a Boolean or constant axiom, or follows from earlier lines by one of these rules: addition of two inequalities; multiplication of one inequality by a positive integer; or division by a positive integer \(d\) that divides every coefficient on its left side, replacing \(\sum_i a_i x_i\ge b\) by \(\sum_i(a_i/d)x_i\ge\lceil b/d\rceil\). All sums are put in normalized form by collecting coefficients. Earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily many times, so these are general directed-acyclic proofs, not tree-like proofs. A refutation ends with \(0\ge1\). Its length \(L(\pi)\) is its number of lines, including input and axiom occurrences. No bound is placed on the number of lines simultaneously retained. In particular, proof length is not algorithmic runtime, total coefficient bit length, or a memory measure.

Define the magnitude of a proof by
\[
M(\pi)=\max\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{|a_i|,|b|:\text{a line }\sum_i a_i x_i\ge b\text{ occurs in }\pi\}\bigr).
\]
The original proof may have arbitrarily large integer coefficients, written in binary. The replacement proof must bound the numerical magnitudes of all line coefficients and right-hand sides, not merely their bit lengths. Multiplication and division annotations are required to make the displayed inferences valid; the magnitude measure concerns the inequalities themselves. Every inference, including intermediate multiplication lines, counts toward length and is subject to the replacement bound.

The common polynomial bound in this card can equivalently be written \(C(N+L)^k\), for positive integers \(C,k\) independent of the formula and original proof. The same \(C,k\) bound both replacement length and coefficient magnitude. This is an existential comparison of proofs: it does not additionally require a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs the replacement proof from the original one. The parameter \(N+L\), one common polynomial, and the absence of a space bound are the user's explicit specification of the source question. Literature also discusses bounds polynomial only in input size and polynomial-time proof transformations; those additional requirements are not silently imposed here.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universally quantified simulation assertion or its full negation, for the precise syntactic proof system, \(N\), \(L\), and \(M\) defined here. An affirmative answer must establish one pair \(C,k\) working simultaneously for every input formula and every unrestricted-coefficient refutation. A negative answer must establish failure for every such pair; failure of one transformation or a lower bound with an additional memory restriction is insufficient. No numerical tolerance changes this proposition. A bibliography, experimental proof search, or a proof only for tree-like refutations does not substitute for the full theorem.
context:
Cutting Planes expresses Boolean constraints as integer linear inequalities. Its ability to add and round inequalities connects propositional proof complexity with integer programming and pseudo-Boolean reasoning. Numerical coefficients may compress information that takes many separate clauses to express. The question asks whether this numerical magnitude provides an indispensable advantage in the number of proof lines.

The selected comparison permits a replacement proof to reorganize all inferences and to use arbitrary memory. It is consequently a statement about the existence of short bounded-magnitude certificates, rather than the runtime of a particular solver or conversion procedure. The uniform polynomial and its input parameter are fixed explicitly so that the benchmark has a definite truth value.

Buss and Clote showed that an exponential bound on numerical magnitudes suffices after a polynomial increase in length. Exponential magnitude can require only polynomially many bits, so this normalization does not supply the polynomial magnitude required here. The 2021 handbook still presents the general coefficient-strength comparison as an open question.

The 2020 lifting result separates unrestricted and bounded coefficients when length and memory are constrained together. The relevant formulas still have short proofs when more memory is permitted, so that result does not answer this card. Later tree-like lower bounds likewise impose a restriction absent from the stated proof system.
why: A resolution would determine whether the numerical size of coefficients is an essential resource for concise integer-inequality proofs, independently of memory. This is a central comparison among propositional proof systems and clarifies what short pseudo-Boolean certificates can express. It does not by itself guarantee an efficient algorithm for discovering those certificates.

title: Lovász–Schrijver simulation of Cutting Planes
importance_reason: This comparison would locate the relative power of two central geometric proof systems and determine whether Boolean quadratic reasoning can always match short cutting-plane refutations.
formal:
Does the basic Lovász–Schrijver system \(\mathrm{LS}\) polynomially simulate Cutting Planes \(\mathrm{CP}\) in the following real-coefficient, line-count sense?

There exist a real constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every \(m\ge0\), every finite initial system
\[
\Phi=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j\ge b_i:1\le i\le m\right\},
\qquad a_{ij},b_i\in\mathbb R,
\]
and every CP refutation \(\Pi\) of \(\Phi\), there is an LS refutation \(\Lambda\) of the same initial system satisfying
\[
|\Lambda|\le C\bigl(n+m+|\Pi|+1\bigr)^k.
\]
All variables are Boolean. The proof systems and the length measure are defined below. The constants are independent of the initial coefficients and both proofs.
question_excerpt: After separating LS from Cutting Planes in one direction, the source asks whether every short Cutting Planes refutation admits a polynomially bounded LS refutation. The user selected existence measured in lines, with the source’s real coefficients.
definitions:
A line is an inequality \(f(x)\ge0\). Polynomials are over \(\mathbb R\) in the original variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\); algebraically identical polynomials are identified by collecting coefficients. The initial lines are the members of \(\Phi\), written with the right-hand side moved to the left. Boolean axioms \(x_j\ge0\) and \(1-x_j\ge0\) are available. The harmless constant axioms \(0\ge0\) and \(1\ge0\) are also permitted; they can be derived from the Boolean axioms with constantly many steps.

Both systems permit nonnegative linear combination: from earlier lines \(f\ge0\) and \(g\ge0\), derive \(\alpha f+\beta g\ge0\) for any \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Coefficients are exact real numbers. Combining any finite number of earlier lines instead of two changes length by at most a polynomial factor, so the binary version fixes a definite convention.

CP contains only affine-linear lines. Its additional rounding rule is
\[
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j\ge d}
{\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j\ge\lceil d\rceil},
\qquad c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb Z,\ d\in\mathbb R.
\]
The rounding premise must have integer variable coefficients; the right side and intermediate combination coefficients may be real. Rounding is justified by the Boolean, hence integer, values of the variables.

Basic LS contains lines of degree at most two. In addition to the common rules and axioms it permits both \(x_j^2-x_j\ge0\) and \(x_j-x_j^2\ge0\). From an earlier affine-linear inequality \(f\ge0\), it may derive \(x_jf\ge0\), or \((1-x_j)f\ge0\), as one line each. Multiplication is permitted only for an affine-linear premise. Nonnegative combination may combine linear or quadratic lines. The source’s linear weakening rule \(a\cdot x\ge d\Rightarrow a\cdot x\ge d'\) for \(d'\le d\) is permitted; it is also obtainable by adding a nonnegative multiple of \(1\ge0\). There is no unrestricted multiplication rule, no rule freely adding arbitrary squares, and no rounding rule in LS. Boolean reduction of quadratic monomials must be justified by the displayed axioms; equality merely on Boolean assignments is not free algebraic rewriting.

A refutation is a finite sequence of justified lines ending with \(-1\ge0\), equivalently \(0\ge1\). Any negative constant conclusion can be normalized by a positive scalar in one further step. An earlier line may be used any number of times: proofs are directed acyclic graphs, not necessarily trees. There are no auxiliary extension variables. Length \(|\Pi|\) is the number of listed lines, counting each occurrence of an initial inequality or axiom that appears, and each derived line. Reuse adds no copy unless a new line is written.

No bound is imposed on the magnitude or bit representation of real coefficients, and no effective transformation from \(\Pi\) to \(\Lambda\) is requested. The statement quantifies mathematically over finite systems of real inequalities; its size parameters count variables, initial inequalities and proof lines. This is the convention selected by the user, not a bit-size or polynomial-time simulation assertion.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the uniform polynomial line-count assertion. A positive answer must prove the existence of the LS refutation bound for every allowed CP refutation and initial system. A negative answer must show that every candidate polynomial bound fails for some allowed initial system and CP proof. A lower bound restricted to tree-like LS, a simulation only with restricted coefficients, or the already known separation in the opposite direction does not decide this statement. No numerical \(1/100\) tolerance applies to this binary assertion.
context:
An inconsistent zero-one system has no assignment of zeros and ones satisfying all its inequalities. A refutation proves this by deriving an impossible inequality. Two complete systems may both refute every inconsistent system while requiring very different numbers of steps.

The systems exploit integrality differently. CP rounds a lower bound upward when its left side is integer-valued. LS uses products with a variable or its Boolean complement, together with the identities for zero-one values. Keeping all intermediate degrees at most two is part of the basic LS model.

title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
importance_reason: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic would clarify the proof-theoretic strength of basic theories of feasible computation.
formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.
context:
Open Problem 5.5 asks to separate some two levels with positive indices. This is not a request to select one predetermined pair or to give proof-length lower bounds. The survey places it alongside the question of whether feasible arithmetic can prove that P equals NP.

The complete finite axiom list matters because the target concerns formal provability, not only the intended meaning of addition and binary length. The model above uses the book’s first-order language without its optional sequence-function extension.

The 2026 preprint extends conditional comparisons between theories with different induction and bounded collection principles. Its introduction recalls the implication from noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy to noncollapse of bounded arithmetic, and Section 1.3 expressly leaves unconditional separations open. This is progress on related conditional statements, not a claimed unconditional witness for this card.
why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

Ježil–Tsintsilidas, arXiv:2602.19934v1 (February 2026), explicitly retain removal of assumptions in their hierarchy separations as an open problem. A bounded subsequent search found no matching unconditional separation or proof that all positive levels coincide. This records the checked sources and search limits, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

Each level has the same basic arithmetic axioms but permits induction for a different class of bounded formulas. A solution may choose any two distinct positive levels and must prove an unconditional difference in their deductive strength. The full axiom list, formula grammar and induction scheme specify the theories without relying on an unstated standard model. Recent conditional separations do not provide the unconditional nonprovability witness required here.

title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
importance_reason: An unprovability result for circuit or proof bounds would expose the limits of formal theories used to reason about efficient computation.
formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]

To specify the polynomial-time predicate without leaving its formal representation implicit, let \(\eta(x,y)\) range over \(\Sigma_1^b\) formulas whose only free variables are among \(x,y\) and for which
\[S_2^1\vdash\forall x\,\exists y\bigl(\eta(x,y)\land\forall z(\eta(x,z)\to z=y)\bigr).\]

By the definability/witnessing characterization of \(S_2^1\), these provably total \(\Sigma_1^b\) graphs represent polynomial-time functions. This is a base-language presentation of the source's polynomial-time function symbols in a conservative definitional extension. The formula \(\eta\), rather than just its extension in the standard natural numbers, is part of the witness being quantified over.

Here is an explicit arithmetic encoding of the circuits used in the upper-bound sentence. An \(n\)-input circuit has constants at nodes zero and one, inputs at nodes \(2,\ldots,n+1\), and \(g\ge0\) computational nodes \(n+2,\ldots,n+g+1\) in evaluation order. Each computational node has a two-bit operation tag: zero is AND, one OR, two NOT of the first predecessor, and three a copy of the first predecessor. It also has two predecessor indices, both less than its own index; the second is ignored for the last two tags. The output is any node. Shared values and unrestricted depth are allowed, with exact correctness on all inputs. Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

Let \(w=\ell(n+g+2)\), \(q=2+2w\), and \(d=gq+w\). The circuit number \(C\) has binary length \(d+1\); its highest bit is a delimiter. In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For fixed positive integers \(c,k\), let \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) be the following closed \(L\)-sentence, with the defined predicates expanded:
\[\begin{split}
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\ \forall y\bigl((\ell(x)\le n\land\eta(x,y))\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow y\ne0)\bigr)\bigr),
\end{split}\]
where every \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). The fixed numeral \(c\) and fixed power \(n^k\) are expanded using multiplication. This is the source's Log convention: lengths come from the length of an arbitrarily quantified number, instead of treating their unary encodings as separately available objects. definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

The theory \(T_2^1\) consists of BASIC together with the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[
\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land
\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)
\longrightarrow \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a)
\]
for every \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula \(\varphi\). This is successor induction. It differs from the halving induction used in \(S_2^1\). No true-sentence oracle or additional complexity assumption is included among the axioms.

Let \(\theta(x)\) range over all \(\Sigma_1^b\) formulas of this language whose only free variable, if any, is \(x\). In the standard natural numbers each such formula defines an NP predicate: a yes-instance has a polynomial-length binary witness checkable in polynomial time. Conversely NP predicates on binary-encoded natural numbers have such representations. There is no requirement that \(\theta\) be a total function graph. The formula itself is part of the witness in the main question; two formulas agreeing in the standard model need not be treated as interchangeable inside a theory that has not proved their equivalence.

Here is an explicit arithmetic encoding of the circuits used in the upper-bound sentence. An \(n\)-input circuit has constants at nodes zero and one, inputs at nodes \(2,\ldots,n+1\), and \(g\ge0\) computational nodes \(n+2,\ldots,n+g+1\) in evaluation order. Each computational node has a two-bit operation tag: zero is AND, one OR, two NOT of the first predecessor, and three a copy of the first predecessor. It also has two predecessor indices, both less than its own index; the second is ignored for the last two tags. The output is any node. Shared values and unrestricted depth are allowed, with exact correctness on all inputs. Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

Let \(w=\ell(n+g+2)\), \(q=2+2w\), and \(d=gq+w\). The circuit number \(C\) has binary length \(d+1\); its highest bit is a delimiter. In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. All field and bit occurrences use the preceding formulas, with Boolean auxiliary variables bounded by one and extracted indices bounded by \(n+g+4\). The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For external fixed integers \(c,k\ge1\), define the closed upper-bound sentence
\[
\begin{split}
\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\theta]\ \equiv\
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&
\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\,[
\ell(x)\le n\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow\theta(x))]\bigr),
\end{split}
\]
where every occurrence of \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). All auxiliary predicates have the arithmetic expansions specified above. The fixed coefficient and exponent are written as a numeral and a fixed finite product in the language. Quantification over \(N\) implements the source's Log convention: a length is supplied as the binary length of a number, not via an assumption that arbitrary exponential-size truth tables exist in the theory.

Inputs are numbers represented as zero-padded \(n\)-bit strings. The same number therefore has the same membership value at different padded lengths. The circuit can depend on \(n\), but must be correct on every input at that length. It is a deterministic nonuniform circuit, with no witnesses or random bits; NP describes the target predicate rather than the gates.

The formula, coefficient and exponent quantified in the main question are standard finite syntactic objects or standard positive integers outside the theory. For each \(k\), the same \(\theta\) must work for every \(c\). Nonprovability means absence of any finite first-order proof of the displayed upper-bound sentence. It does not mean that \(T_2^1\) proves its negation, and does not by itself assert a circuit lower bound in the standard model.

The explicit circuit description is an editorial serialization of the source's usual finite Boolean circuits. Circuit bit length and gate count are polynomially related, so the all-exponents target is unchanged after adjusting the exponent and coefficient; no exact fixed-exponent equivalence between the two size measures is asserted. The card uses the base arithmetic language rather than the conservative extension by symbols for polynomial-time functions.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed unprovability statement or its logical negation, for the exact theory and sentence scheme. A positive result must be unconditional and obtain one \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for each exponent that works against every coefficient. It need not give an efficient algorithm constructing these formulas. A negative result must establish that for some fixed \(k\), every \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula \(\theta(x)\) has some \(c\) for which \(T_2^1\) proves its stated upper bound. Proving a result only for a weaker theory or for a larger class of predicates does not settle this target. This is a claim about finite formal proofs, not a requirement to exhibit a standard-model circuit lower bound; numerical tolerance does not apply.
context:
A nonuniform circuit upper bound allows a different finite circuit at each input length. A proof of such an upper bound is a stronger demand on a formal theory than the mere possibility that the circuits exist. This question studies that formal provability boundary.

The theory \(T_2^1\) supports successor induction with NP-definable hypotheses. The related theory \(S_2^1\) uses halving induction. These theories formalize substantial reasoning about efficient computation, but their different induction principles matter for unprovability.

The 2020 result establishes nonprovability of infinitely-often circuit upper bounds for NP in \(S_2^1\), and for \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) in \(T_2^1\). Here \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) allows a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm to query an NP-complete oracle. Neither result gives the requested NP predicate in the stronger theory.

The 2026 student-teacher work strengthens some upper-bound unprovability results beyond the basic polynomial-time theory PV. Its stated upper-bound theorem still concerns a theory weaker than the one selected here and does not resolve this NP question.

For each represented predicate and coefficient, nonprovability of an upper-bound sentence is equivalent to consistency of its negation with the theory. Such a model may be nonstandard. This explains why an unconditional unprovability theorem can be meaningful without already proving the corresponding ordinary circuit lower bound.
why: This asks whether a theory that supports induction over NP predicates can certify fixed-polynomial circuits for every NP language. An unconditional negative limitation on its proving power would strengthen a central connection between bounded arithmetic and circuit complexity, beyond the known weaker-theory or larger-language-class cases.
status_note: Oliveira v1 states the NP-versus-fixed-polynomial upper-bound unprovability question for T-two-one as Open Problem 5.2. The 2020 theorem uses NP for the weaker S-two-one theory and the larger class P with an NP oracle for T-two-one. The checked 2021 and 2026 developments do not supply the missing theory/class pair. A bounded primary-source search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The common arithmetic axioms and explicit serialization were checked; this review does not independently certify the cited proofs.
