working_summary: For each fixed polynomial exponent, the question asks for an NP predicate whose circuit upper bounds cannot be proved in T-two-one. One represented predicate must resist every fixed multiplicative coefficient at that exponent. The theory uses successor induction for NP formulas, and the card fixes its axioms and the precise circuit upper-bound sentence. Known results concern NP in a weaker theory or a larger complexity class in T-two-one. A resolution would clarify limits on formal proofs about efficient nonuniform computation without itself asserting a standard-model circuit lower bound.

title: \(PV_1\) nonprovability of polynomial-time SAT solvers
importance_reason: An unprovability result for circuit or proof bounds would expose the limits of formal theories used to reason about efficient computation.
formal: Is it true that, for every unary function symbol \(g\) in the syntactically generated language \(L_{PV}\) below, \[PV_1\not\vdash\Phi_g,\qquad \Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\bigl(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))\bigr)?\] The theory, admissible symbols and arithmetic formula \(\operatorname{Sat}\) are fixed in the definitions. This is an unconditional assertion about finite first-order proofs.
definitions:
The theory is one-sorted classical first-order arithmetic with equality. We use Jeřábek's explicit presentation of \(PV_1\), cited as an alternative axiomatization by the source survey. Its base language is
\[
L=\{0,S,+,\cdot,\le,\#,\operatorname{len},M\}.
\]
In the intended structure on the nonnegative integers, \(S(x)=x+1\), \(\operatorname{len}(x)=\lceil\log_2(x+1)\rceil\), \(M(x,y)=\lfloor x/2^y\rfloor\), and \(x\#y=2^{\operatorname{len}(x)\operatorname{len}(y)}\). In particular \(\operatorname{len}(0)=0\). Write \(1=S(0)\), \(2=S(S(0))\), \(H(x)=M(x,1)\), and \(x<y\) for \(x\le y\land x\ne y\). These intended interpretations do not supply additional axioms.

The base theory has the universal closures of the following arithmetic axioms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+0&=x,& x+S(y)&=S(x+y),\\
x\cdot0&=0,&x\cdot S(y)&=x\cdot y+x,\\
0&\le x,& S(y)\le x&\ \longleftrightarrow\ y<x,\\
M(x,0)&=x,&
M(x,y)&=2M(x,S(y))\ \lor\ M(x,y)=S(2M(x,S(y))),\\
\operatorname{len}(0)&=0,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\ \operatorname{len}(x)=S(\operatorname{len}(H(x))),\\
0\#1&=1,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\
\bigl(x\#1=2(H(x)\#1)\ \land\
y\#x=(y\#1)(y\#H(x))\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
It also has ordinary induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(x,\vec z)\to A(S(x),\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every base-language formula \(A\) all of whose quantifiers are sharply bounded. A sharply bounded quantifier is \(\forall v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\) or \(\exists v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\), where \(t\) has no free occurrence of \(v\). A bounded universal quantifier expands to an implication, and a bounded existential quantifier to a conjunction. All induction parameters \(\vec z\) are universally closed.

Generate \(L_{PV}\) syntactically from \(L\) by finitely iterating two rules. For every existing term \(t\) with free variables among \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\), add an \(r\)-ary symbol \(f_t\). For every tuple of existing symbols \(g(\vec x),h_0(\vec x,y,z),h_1(\vec x,y,z),b(\vec x,y)\), add a new symbol \(R_{g,h_0,h_1,b}(\vec x,y)\). Arity is finite, the parameter tuple may be empty, and distinct construction trees are distinct symbols even when their intended functions agree. Include the universal closure of \(f_t(\vec x)=t(\vec x)\). For each recursion symbol, abbreviating it by \(R\), include exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\vec x,y)&\le b(\vec x,y),\\
g(\vec x)\le b(\vec x,0)&\to R(\vec x,0)=g(\vec x),\\
y\ne0\land h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,2y)
&\to R(\vec x,2y)=h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)),\\
h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,S(2y))
&\to R(\vec x,S(2y))=h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are bounded-recursion constraints; no unconditional recursion equation is added when its bounding test fails.

Finally include polynomial induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(H(x),\vec z)\to A(x,\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every quantifier-free \(L_{PV}\)-formula \(A\). Together with the base theory and the symbol axioms, these schemes define \(PV_1\) here. A proof is a finite derivation in classical first-order logic with equality from finitely many instances of these schemes. No true-universal arithmetic sentences, consistency assumptions, or external correctness axioms are added. The outer quantifier over unary symbols \(g\) ranges over their finite syntactic construction trees, not over an oracle for deciding which arbitrary programs run in polynomial time.

The SAT relation is fixed arithmetically, rather than by selecting an unspecified polynomial-time evaluator symbol. All abbreviations in this paragraph and below expand into formulas of the base language \(L\). Set \(\ell=\operatorname{len}(F)\), and define
\[
\operatorname{Bit}(x,i)\ \longleftrightarrow\
M(x,i)=2M(x,S(i))+1.
\]
Every auxiliary quantifier over a node, field, index or width is bounded by \(\ell\), with any smaller displayed bound imposed as a guard. Thus these quantifiers are sharply bounded. The one truth-table witness below has a separate bound.

The natural number \(F\) encodes an ordinary propositional formula tree whose nodes are numbered \(0,\ldots,m-1\), with children before their parents. Its variables are \(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\), with unused variables allowed. To define \(\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\), require \(w,d,m\le\ell\), \(w\ge2\), \(m\ge1\), \(w+d=\ell\), and
\[
\ell=w+2+(1+3m)w.
\]
The least significant \(w\) bits of \(F\) are all one and bit \(w\) is zero. Starting at bit \(w+1\) are \(1+3m\) fields of \(w\) bits, followed by the high sentinel bit one; the exact bit-length equality enforces that sentinel and forbids further bits. Put \(P=M(1\#F,d)\), whose intended value is \(2^w\). Field \(j\) has value \(r\) exactly when
\[
D(F,w,d,j,r)\ \longleftrightarrow\
r<P\ \land\
M(F,w+1+jw)=P\,M(F,w+1+(j+1)w)+r.
\]
Require field zero to have value \(m\). For each node \(i<m\), its fields \(1+3i,2+3i,3+3i\) have values \(\tau_i,u_i,v_i\), respectively. This notation abbreviates existentially quantified numbers at most \(\ell\) satisfying their three \(D\) relations, not new function symbols. Every record must satisfy exactly the relevant one of these four cases:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\tau_i & \text{record restrictions} & \text{meaning}\\
0 & u_i<m,\ v_i=0 & x_{u_i}\\
1 & u_i<i,\ v_i=0 & \neg\text{ child }u_i\\
2 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\land\text{child }v_i\\
3 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\lor\text{child }v_i .
\end{array}
\]
Every node \(i\) with \(S(i)<m\) must occur in exactly one child slot of all records, and the node \(r\) with \(S(r)=m\) in no child slot. Specifically, slot \((j,0)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{1,2,3\},u_j=i\); slot \((j,1)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{2,3\},v_j=i\). Denote this relation by \(C(j,s,i)\), with other slot values false. Exactly one means
\[
\exists j,s\le\ell\
[C(j,s,i)\land
\forall k,t\le\ell\,(C(k,t,i)\to(k=j\land t=s))].
\]
Together the record restrictions, field conditions and child-slot conditions define \(\operatorname{Form}\). In particular this encodes a tree, with no shared subtrees or circuit gates.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\) by requiring, at every node \(i<m\), the following biconditional for the indicated record type:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\tau_i & \operatorname{Bit}(v,i)\text{ is equivalent to}\\
0 & \operatorname{Bit}(a,u_i)\\
1 & \neg\operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\\
2 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i)\\
3 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\lor\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i).
\end{array}
\]
Here \(v\) is the numeric table witness and \(v_i\) the second child field; their names designate different bound variables when the abbreviations are expanded. Now set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists w,d,m,e\le\ell\ \exists v<1\#F\
[&\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\land e+m=\ell\\
 &\land a<M(1\#F,e)
 \land\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\\
 &\land\exists r\le\ell\,(S(r)=m\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,r))].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a\) is an assignment of \(m\) bits, allowing leading zeroes, and the first \(m\) bits of \(v\) are the values of the formula nodes with true root. The bound \(1\#F\) is \(2^\ell\), so the table has only linearly many bits in the input bit length. Malformed formula codes make \(\operatorname{Sat}\) false. No unrestricted exponentiation symbol or semantic SAT predicate is added to the theory.

For each syntactically generated unary symbol \(g\), let
\[
\Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\,
(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))).
\]
It asserts search correctness on every satisfiable formula. It imposes no required output on an unsatisfiable formula. The claim concerns absence of finite \(PV_1\) proofs of these sentences, not absence of semantically correct polynomial-time solvers as a separate assumption.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that no generated unary symbol has a finite first-order derivation of its displayed SAT-search correctness sentence from the stated PV1 axioms, or a complete Lean proof of the negation, exhibiting a particular symbol and a valid finite derivation. The formalization must implement the stated syntactic theory and arithmetic SAT relation; any substitute SAT encoding or axiomatization must be proved to preserve the relevant provability claim. Neither assuming P differs from NP, adding all true universal arithmetic axioms, checking finitely many proofs, nor proving only a conditional statement settles this target.
context:
Open Problem 5.3 states this nonprovability schema using polynomial-time symbols and a standard SAT verifier. It is a formal weakening of the conjecture that polynomial-time algorithms cannot solve SAT: even if a solver existed, the theory might fail to prove its correctness. The card is not asking whether the assertion that P differs from NP is itself unprovable.

The explicit theory presentation is Jeřábek’s Definitions 2.1–2.2, which the survey cites when discussing alternative axiomatizations. Its language is generated by term formation and bounded recursion, and its induction schemes are specified above. True universal sentences are not automatically axioms.

The record encoding and local evaluation-table relation make the SAT predicate precise without selecting an arbitrary semantically equivalent function symbol. Its formula trees have polynomial-size descriptions, and their bottom-up evaluation has polynomial cost. The table relation is provably equivalent in the stated theory to the usual polynomial-time verifier; this is a concrete encoding convention for the source schema, not a change to its computational target.

The February 2026 paper formalizes probabilistic reasoning and proves a parity lower bound for constant-depth circuits inside the base theory. That result concerns a restricted computational model and does not show that the theory cannot prove the correctness of any polynomial-time SAT solver.
why: The question isolates whether reasoning restricted to efficiently computable concepts can certify a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete search task. It is a foundational test of the strength of feasible mathematics and separates the truth of an algorithmic assertion from the existence of a proof in a particular theory.

Checked on 2026-09-16 against the exact theory definition and bounded later primary sources, including February2026 formalized lower-bound progress. No matching unconditional nonprovability result was located; this is not an exhaustive current-status certificate.

working_summary: A polynomial-time SAT search algorithm would return a satisfying assignment whenever one exists. The question asks whether the theory PV1 fails to prove correctness for every such polynomial-time function symbol. This is a statement about finite formal proofs, with the theory and formula encoding specified explicitly. It can hold even if a polynomial-time solver exists but its correctness has no proof in this particular theory. The benchmark requires a complete Lean proof of the nonprovability schema or a verified counterexample consisting of a symbol and a finite correctness proof.

title: Sharp resolution length bounds at fixed width
importance_reason: A precise quantitative refinement of a central width-versus-length phenomenon in propositional proof complexity, with direct relevance to the limits of resolution-based search; narrower than the already settled qualitative tradeoff.
formal:
Do there exist integers \(c\ge1\) and \(w_0\ge\max\{3,c+1\}\) such that, for every integer \(w\ge w_0\), there are constants \(a_w,b_w,d_w>0\), an integer \(n_w\ge1\), and a family of unsatisfiable 3-CNF formulas \((F_{n,w})_{n\ge n_w}\) satisfying, for every integer \(n\ge n_w\),
\[
a_wn\le s(F_{n,w})\le b_wn,\qquad
W(F_{n,w})\le w,\qquad
L(F_{n,w})\ge d_wn^{\,w-c}?
\]
Here \(W\) is minimum refutation width and \(L\) is minimum refutation length without a width restriction. The absolute constant \(c\) is common to every width. The family and the other constants may depend on \(w\), which is fixed before \(n\) tends to infinity.
question_excerpt: The survey asks how close a fixed-width refutation can come to requiring length with exponent equal to that width. The selected version seeks linear-size 3-CNFs admitting width at most w but requiring unrestricted length at least a constant times n to the power w-c, for a common absolute c.
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes a value in \(\{0,1\}\); a literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. Its width is its cardinality; the empty clause is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction. A 3-CNF has clauses of width at most three, not necessarily exactly three. Tautological clauses, containing both signs of one variable, may be omitted. The formula is unsatisfiable if no assignment to its occurring variables makes every clause true.

Write \(v(F)\) for the number of distinct occurring variables and use the combinatorial formula size
\[
s(F)=v(F)+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|.
\]
Variable names have no semantic significance. This is the customary variable/clause/occurrence size, rather than the bit length of a variable-index encoding or the size of a succinct description. For 3-CNF formulas the three displayed counts are bounded by constant multiples of the number of clauses. The parameter \(n\) indexes a family of linear combinatorial size; it is not an extra width or a proof-length parameter.

A resolution refutation is a finite sequence of clauses ending with the empty clause. Each line is an input clause of \(F\) or follows from two earlier clauses \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\) by deriving \(C\cup D\), where \(C,D\) contain neither sign of the pivot \(x\). No extension variables, semantic inference, or additional axioms are allowed. Duplicate literals in a resolvent are merged. Reusing any earlier line arbitrarily often is allowed, so the underlying proof is a directed acyclic graph and need not be a tree. Weakening is not an additional rule in this convention.

The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of clause lines, including input-clause occurrences. The width \(W(\pi)\) is the maximum width of any line, including input lines. Define \(L(F)\) as the minimum length of any resolution refutation of \(F\), and \(W(F)\) as the minimum width. For unsatisfiable formulas these minima exist by completeness of resolution. The two minima need not be attained by the same proof. There is no bound on space, depth, or regularity.

In particular, the lower bound in the target ranges over all refutations, including those much wider than \(w\). Merely showing that every width-\(w\) refutation is long is insufficient. The family is not required to have a uniformly efficient construction. Requiring \(c\) to be a positive integer loses no positive-real-constant version, since it can be increased to its ceiling. The threshold \(w_0\) excludes widths with a vacuous nonpositive exponent.

This is the user's selected precise form of the survey's sharp fixed-width question. The original imported card also mentioned the separate short-proof-to-narrow-proof tradeoff question; that second direction is now background. No assertion that the present statement is equivalent to every phrasing in that broader source entry is made.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed quantified existence assertion, using the formula size and resolution rules above. An affirmative answer must establish one absolute \(c\) and all sufficiently large fixed widths, with a lower bound on unrestricted minimum length. A lower bound \(n^{\alpha w}\) for a fixed \(\alpha<1\), a tree-like lower bound, a restriction on proof depth, or a result for a single width does not suffice. A negative answer is the full logical negation of the assertion, not merely failure of a proposed construction. This is an asymptotic proposition, so the numerical-value tolerance does not replace its exponent requirement.
context:
Width limits how many literals a proof line can mention together. For fixed \(w\), counting the possible clauses gives an \(n^{O(w)}\) length upper bound whenever a narrow refutation exists. The selected question asks whether nearly the whole width can be forced into the exponent, even when the shortest proof may use unrestricted width.

Atserias, Lauria and Nordström established \(n^{\Omega(w)}\) hardness for narrow 3-CNF refutations. This makes the exponential dependence on width unavoidable. The coefficient hidden in that exponent is significant here: the selected target asks for \(w-c\), not an unspecified positive fraction of \(w\).

Thapen established that forcing an already short proof to become narrow can require an exponential increase in length. That settles the different conversion direction grouped in the old draft. It does not supply the present fixed-width, nearly full-exponent lower bound.

Recent supercritical tradeoffs impose tree structure or a depth restriction on proofs. Those are substantial results about other combinations of resources. The present lower bound must survive unrestricted reuse, width and depth in the proof whose length is being minimized.

It would distinguish the optimal dependence on width from the already known qualitative exponential dependence, and sharpen what resolution-based proof search can achieve even when it is free to use wider clauses.

title: \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) proof systems for directed reachability
importance_reason: Restricting the computational cost of proof systems isolates a focused proof-encoding model question.
formal:
For \(n\ge2\), let
\[
R_n=\{A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}:
\text{the directed graph encoded by }A\text{ has a path from }1\text{ to }n\}.
\]
Does there exist an integer \(D\ge0\) such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) there are a nonnegative integer \(m_n\) and a Boolean circuit
\[
C_n:\{0,1\}^{m_n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n^2}
\]
of depth at most \(D\), using AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two and NOT gates, for which
\[
\{C_n(z):z\in\{0,1\}^{m_n}\}=R_n?
\]
The right side is identified with row-major adjacency-matrix encodings. Equivalently, every proof string must produce a graph with the required directed path, and every graph with that path must be produced by some proof string.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether the directed graphs with a path between two distinguished vertices can be exactly generated by a family of bounded-fan-in circuits of constant depth.
definitions:
The graph has labeled vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with distinguished vertices \(s=1\) and \(t=n\). The entry \(A_{ij}=1\) means that the edge \(i\to j\) is present. There are no parallel edges; self-loops are allowed. The output is the \(n^2\)-bit string \(A_{11},A_{12},\ldots,A_{nn}\), in row-major order. A directed path from \(1\) to \(n\) is a sequence \(v_0=1,v_1,\ldots,v_\ell=n\) with \(A_{v_{i-1},v_i}=1\) for every step. Existence is unchanged if one requires the vertices of the path to be distinct.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph of input nodes, gates and designated outputs. Constants zero and one are allowed. AND and OR have at most two incoming wires, NOT has one, and an output may copy an input, constant or gate. Fan-out is unrestricted. Depth is the maximum number of gates on a path from an input or constant to an output. The same bound \(D\) must work at every \(n\).

This is the nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^0\) convention: circuits may be chosen separately for each \(n\), with no required running time for constructing their descriptions. After gates and proof bits that influence no output are removed, bounded fan-in and depth imply at most \(O(2^D n^2)\) gates and relevant input bits. Thus the family has linear size in its output length, without an extra size hypothesis. Each output bit depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits, possibly a different set for each output position.

A proof system here is a total generating map whose range is exactly the target language at the relevant output length. All \(2^{m_n}\) proof strings are allowed. There is no promise that an input is a valid path encoding and no separate test that may reject malformed proofs. Soundness is the universal requirement \(C_n(z)\in R_n\); completeness is surjectivity onto \(R_n\). The graph is the output, not an input to a one-bit acceptance circuit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence assertion. A positive answer must establish one fixed depth bound and soundness and completeness of the circuit family for every graph size. It may be nonuniform. A negative answer must show that every fixed depth fails at some size, for all circuits in this model. A depth lower bound for deciding reachability, or failure of one generating construction, is insufficient. This is an exact binary target; no error probability or numerical \(1/100\) tolerance is permitted.
context:
Ordinary reachability algorithms receive a graph and search for a path. Here a proof string produces the entire graph. The generator must arrange that even arbitrary, inconsistent input bits produce a yes-instance, while retaining enough flexibility to produce every graph containing the distinguished path.

Constant depth with bounded fan-in makes each output edge depend on only a constant number of proof bits. Different edge positions may depend on different bits, and a proof bit may influence many edges. This local dependence is the substantive restriction; the proof need not be a list of path vertices.

The published paper constructs such proof systems for undirected reachability. Thus the mere fact that paths are global objects does not prove that a local generating map is impossible. Direction of edges remains an essential distinction in the open case.

It also constructs a proof system for directed unreachability: graphs having no path from the first distinguished vertex to the second. Complementing the output bits of that generator would complement individual edges, not complement the reachability property of the graph. The positive unreachability result therefore does not immediately transfer.

The class of languages with these proof systems is not determined simply by the difficulty of ordinary membership testing. The paper gives a depth obstruction even for the regular language of strings with exactly one one, alongside positive results for more complex languages.

The seminar report additionally asks for a characterization of regular languages admitting these systems. The user chose the directed graph problem as this card’s single target, so that separate classification task is recorded only as provenance.
why: The question asks whether a global directed-path property can be guaranteed by generating each edge from only constantly many proof bits, while still representing every yes-instance. The contrast with known local proof systems for undirected reachability and directed unreachability isolates the role of direction and global consistency in very weak proof systems.

Their positive results concern undirected reachability or directed unreachability, which are different output languages. No later resolution was found in the bounded primary-source check through 16 September 2026. The user selected this directed-reachability target on that date.

An NC⁰ proof system must generate exactly these matrices from arbitrary input bit strings. Each output edge depends on only constantly many proof bits, with one constant depth bound for all graph sizes. Such generators are known for undirected reachability and for directed unreachability. title: Short tree-like resolution from small proof space
importance_reason: A structural relationship between proof memory, reuse and tree size, with direct consequences for strong proof size-space trade-offs. Existing score retained.
formal: For \(\mu\) equal to resolution clause space CSpace or PCR monomial space \(MSpace_{K}\), does there exist a constant \(a\ge 1\) and \(C>0\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF F on \(n\ge 2\) variables satisfies \(\log _{2}(S_{T}(F)+1)\le C((\mu (F)+1)\log _{2}(n+1))^{a}\)? Determine the validity of this comparison in each of the two cases in the source’s Problem 5.1. For monomial space, K is an arbitrary fixed field and the constants may depend on K, but not on F or n. Here \(S_{T}\) is minimum tree-like resolution leaf count. The opposite comparison, bounding each space measure by logarithmic tree-like size up to these polynomial/logarithmic losses, is known.
definitions:
A literal is \(x_{i}\) or its negation \(
eg x_{i}\). A clause is a disjunction of literals and a CNF F is a finite conjunction of clauses over variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\); unsatisfiable means no Boolean assignment satisfies every clause. Resolution derives \(C\lor D\) from \(C\lor x_{i}\) and \(D\lor 
eg x_{i}\), and allows weakening from C to \(C\lor D\); input clauses can be used as axioms. A refutation derives the empty clause. A tree-like proof uses each derived occurrence as a premise at most once, duplicating occurrences when necessary; \(S_{T}(F)\) is the minimum number of leaves, rather than total literal count. A configuration proof starts with no stored clauses and at each step downloads an input clause, erases a stored clause, or adds a resolvent/weakening of clauses currently stored; it ends with the empty clause stored. \(CSpace(F)\) is the minimum, over such proofs with unrestricted length, of the maximum number of simultaneously stored clauses. For PCR fix K and use the polynomial ring \(K[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n}]\), where \(y_{i}\) represents \(
eg x_{i}\). A line P means \(\mathrm{P}=0\). Logical axioms are \(z^{2}- z\) for each z among \(x_{i},y_{i}\) and \(x_{i}+y_{i}- 1\). The encoding of a clause is the product of its false-literal indicators: \(x_{i}\) contributes \(y_{i}\) and \(
eg x_{i}\) contributes \(x_{i}\). From P,Q derive \(\alpha \mathrm{P}+ eta Q\) for \(\alpha , eta \in K\); from P derive zP for any literal variable z. A PCR refutation derives 1. Its configurations may download axioms, erase lines or add an inference whose premises are stored. The monomial space of a configuration is the number of distinct formal monomials with nonzero coefficients occurring anywhere in its stored polynomials, counted once across all lines; coefficients and exponents are not separately charged. \(MSpace_{K}(F)\) is the minimum maximum monomial space over all PCR refutations. Every proof is finite and minima concern the specified syntactic systems. The source’s relation \(A\preceq B\) permits \(A(F)\le ((B(F))\log  n)^{O(1)}; \approx\) means both directions. The harmless +1 terms here cover one-leaf or other constant-size cases. No polynomial-length restriction is imposed on the space-minimizing proof.
answer_criterion: For each stated space measure, prove the universal polynomial/logarithmic simulation bound or refute it by showing that no constants C,a work for all unsatisfiable formulas (with K fixed in the PCR case). The two variants must be reported separately. A polynomial separation between raw measures does not refute a comparison that explicitly permits arbitrary polynomial and logarithmic factors.
context:
A configuration refutation can retain a clause, use it many times and discard it later. A tree-like refutation must duplicate reused derivations. The question asks how much tree size can grow when only a small working memory is needed.

The source proves equivalence when a proof’s space is multiplied by the logarithm of its length and then minimized over proofs. Removing that length penalty is precisely the missing step in this comparison; it is not the product of two separately minimized quantities.

The symbol ≈ does not mean equality or equality up to constants. A gap by a fixed polynomial, or by a polylogarithmic factor in n, is allowed. This convention is essential for understanding what would constitute a separation.

The source exhibits formulas with clause space four and quadratic tree-like size. Their logarithmic tree size is only \(O(\log  n)\), so that example does not violate the proposed comparison.
why: Would determine whether low working memory in propositional refutations fundamentally limits repeated work, clarifying strong size-space trade-offs and the cost of converting reusable proofs into trees.

No resolution of these exact coarse comparisons was located. The journal full text was inaccessible; current openness is therefore recorded as source-open rather than certified by a new theorem audit.

Its two memory measures are stored clauses in resolution and distinct monomials in polynomial calculus with resolution. The comparison allows polynomial losses and powers of log n, so it is much coarser than a constant-factor identity. A length-penalized version of space is already known to satisfy the comparison. The unresolved issue is whether ordinary space can be substantially smaller on this scale.

title: Does uniform randomized circuit learning imply P equals NP?
importance_reason: A fundamental proposed connection between worst-case hardness and learning; the source’s introductory scope needs additional resource conventions. Existing score retained.
formal: Does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time learner for arbitrary Boolean circuits under the uniform input distribution, with membership queries and the resource bounds below, imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\)?
question_excerpt: However, while some progress on the opposite implications has been made, they remain open, cf. \([2, 33]\).
definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. The target description explicitly lists gates and wire indices; its binary length is at most a supplied bound \(s\). A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. It outputs an explicit deterministic Boolean circuit \(H\) over the same basis. For every permitted input and target it must satisfy \(\Pr_{A\text{ coins}}[2^{-n}|\{x:H(x)\ne f(x)\}|\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). There is one fixed polynomial \(p\) bounding its time, queries and output length on every random tape by \(p(n+s+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)+\operatorname{len}(\delta))\). The hypothesis need not lie within the target’s size bound; its encoding must obey this output bound. The quantifiers range over every \(n,s\ge1\) and every function with a target description of size at most \(s\). P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. NP consists of languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Equality concerns languages on all binary inputs, not promise classes. The conclusion is deterministic P equals NP even though the learner is randomized. The implication allows arbitrary proofs and use of the fixed learner code; it is not restricted to black-box reductions.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of this exact implication, or a Lean refutation proving the learning premise together with P different from NP. A proof only of NP containment in BPP or a nonuniform circuit inclusion would not establish the displayed deterministic conclusion. Proper-learning, agnostic-learning or restricted-reduction hardness alone does not refute the premise.
context:
The source asks whether efficient circuit learning is equivalent to P equals NP, and separately asks about the absence of strong pseudorandomness. This card addresses the first converse only.

The user-authorized completion selects a single uniform randomized learner with polynomial dependence on target size and the stated accuracy and confidence parameters. It keeps the source’s P equals NP conclusion, without identifying it with a randomized or nonuniform inclusion.

The 2025 follow-up concerns different learning and representation restrictions; its result is not a blanket hardness theorem for the unrestricted improper learner specified here.
why: Asks whether the difficulty of predicting efficiently computable functions follows from worst-case NP hardness alone. The question probes the gap between worst-case complexity, learning and the average-case hardness used in cryptography; its significance depends on keeping their models and quantifiers distinct.

Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the exact resource specialization is editorial and the inaccessible journal text is not claimed to have been checked.

Accuracy is measured on uniformly random Boolean inputs, and the output may be any suitably small Boolean circuit. The learner is uniform and randomized, with explicit polynomial dependence on target size, error and confidence. The chosen conclusion is the deterministic class equality P equals NP. title: Optimal proof systems outside NP
importance_reason: A basic existence boundary for optimal proof systems, connecting proof-length comparison to NP membership and known relativization barriers. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a nonempty language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) that has an optimal Cook–Reckhow proof system, where optimality compares proof lengths and does not require an efficient translation between systems?
question_excerpt: Hence, for most sets we do not know whether they have optimal proof systems and proving their existence would require to overcome at least the […]
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. Such a language is automatically computably enumerable, because it is the range of \(f\); decidability is not an additional requirement.
answer_criterion: Give an unconditional example of a language \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) and prove that it has an optimal system under the stated simulation relation, or prove that every language admitting such an optimal system belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). A conditional existence theorem, an oracle construction, or an example using advice or a weaker simulation relation does not by itself settle this question.
context:
Every nonempty language in \(\mathrm{NP}\) has an ordinary optimal proof system. This does not imply \(p\)-optimality. The source also reviews languages outside \(\mathrm{NP}\) for which optimal systems provably do not exist; these examples do not cover every language outside the class.

Egidy and Glaßer construct one oracle with no optimal systems for languages in \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), and another with no optimal systems for computably enumerable languages outside nondeterministic quasipolynomial time. The first also has an infinite polynomial hierarchy; the second has \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\). These are limitations on arguments that remain valid relative to arbitrary oracles, rather than a universal negative answer in the ordinary computational model.

A recursive jump operator would effectively turn each proof system for a language into one it cannot simulate. Its existence rules out an optimal system. The source investigates the converse relationship, while explicitly retaining the general existence question outside \(\mathrm{NP}\).
why: Determines whether a proof language can be best up to polynomial proof-length overhead even when membership has no uniformly short certificates. It separates optimality relative to all competing proof systems from the existence of short proofs themselves.
status_note: Read the 2026 conference and full-version introduction and formal simulation definitions, and the full July 2025 STOC-paper introduction and oracle result statements. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution. Explicitly selected the any-language-outside-NP question from the source; the stronger arbitrarily-complex-language question and the specialized tautology question remain separate.

working_summary: The question asks whether any language outside NP has an optimal proof system. Each system is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps proofs to exactly the statements in its language. Optimality means that every competing system’s proofs can be matched with at most polynomial growth in length. A fast algorithm for translating proofs is a separate, stronger requirement. Recent oracle barriers and jump-operator results do not decide the ordinary existence question.

title: Weak automatability of Resolution
importance_reason: A central remaining distinction between proof search in Resolution and recognizing formulas with short refutations, directly relevant to the limits of SAT-solving proof systems. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?
question_excerpt: While it is now known and well understood that fully automating propositional Resolution as a proof system for propositional logic is NP-hard, it remains an […]
definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. A conditional obstruction must state its hypothesis explicitly. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.
context:
Atserias and Müller show that finding a Resolution refutation in time polynomial in the formula size and the shortest available refutation length would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their proof-length gap distinguishes short refutations from very long or nonexistent ones. The latter side may include unsatisfiable formulas, so it does not give the SAT-versus-short-refutation promise required here.

Buss and Yolcu show that weak automatability of regular Resolution would imply weak automatability of general Resolution. Their definition allows the output proof to use another system. This relation between systems is not an algorithm or a hardness result for the full promise problem.

The May 2026 full version of The Proof Analysis Problem develops algorithms that analyze supplied proofs of Resolution lower bounds. Section 1.4 still treats weak automatability of Resolution as open. Having such an additional proof as input is a different task from receiving only a formula and a unary budget.
why: Asks whether the existence of a short familiar refutation can make unsatisfiability efficiently recognizable even when finding a refutation in that same calculus is hard. This isolates an unresolved limitation of proof search and the theoretical analysis of SAT solvers.
status_note: Read the complete original abstract, the full regular-Resolution definitions and weak-automatability corollary, the Atserias–Müller author-version main theorems, and the May 2026 full-paper weak-automatability discussion and definitions. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The unary-budget promise formulation makes the original distinction precise; no strong-automatability hardness claim has been transferred to it.
progress: 2019-09-03: The author version proves NP-hardness of strong Resolution automatability and of distinguishing short from sufficiently long refutations. | 2025: The STACS invited talk explicitly leaves SAT-versus-short-Resolution-refutation separation open. | 2026-05-19: The revised full Proof Analysis Problem paper continues to discuss weak automatability as an open question.
working_summary: The input is a CNF formula and a proof-length budget written in unary. The algorithm must distinguish satisfiable formulas from those having a short general Resolution refutation. The proof is not supplied, and the algorithm need not produce a Resolution proof. Unsatisfiable formulas whose shortest refutations exceed the budget can receive either answer. Known hardness for finding Resolution proofs does not settle this weaker recognition problem.

title: Log-rank conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
focus_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.
why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.
status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.
progress: 1988: Lovász and Saks pose the relation between real matrix rank and deterministic communication, as traced in the checked source papers. | 2014–2016: Lovett establishes the general upper bound \(O(\sqrt r\log(r+2))\), substantially improving the linear-rank upper bounds. | 2015–2018: Göös, Pitassi and Watson prove a nearly quadratic lower bound in log-rank. Their Theorem 2 first concerns one-sided partition number, with the real-rank consequence stated separately. | 2023–2025: Sudakov and Tomon obtain \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r(f)})\). The preprint dates from November 2023, the article appeared online in July 2024, and the journal volume is dated 2025. | 2026-08-03: Song reports \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) for an explicit construction. This is a preprint claim with a specific quantitative comparison, not an independently verified catalogue assertion of the strongest bound over all constructions. | 2026-08-14: The checked third revision of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley proves the signed-rectangle decomposition theorem and equivalent formulations, and explicitly retains the general conjecture as open.

working_summary: Alice and Bob must exactly evaluate a total Boolean function while each receives only one part of its input. The conjecture asks whether their minimum worst-case deterministic communication is bounded by one universal polynomial in logarithmic real matrix rank. The protocol may use arbitrary interaction and local computation, but all input pairs must be handled correctly. A refutation must defeat every universal polynomial, rather than a single proposed constant or exponent. Known square-root-rank upper bounds, nearly quadratic logarithmic lower bounds and signed-partition equivalences leave the central gap unresolved.

title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
focus_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and give each \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) probability \(2^{-n}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), with empty product one, and \[\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x),\qquad q_S=\widehat f(S)^2.\] These are real coefficients and \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}q_S=1\). Define \(\eta(0)=0\) and \(\eta(t)=t\log_2(1/t)\) for \(0<t\le1\), where \(\log_2 t=\ln t/\ln2\). Then \[H(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\eta(q_S).\] The sum includes the empty set and is not conditioned on nonempty spectral subsets or divided by the variance. For each \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) negate coordinate \(i\) and retain all other coordinates. Set \[I_i(f)=2^{-n}\bigl|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}\bigr|,\qquad I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n I_i(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|q_S.\] Influence uses an actual bit flip, with no additional probability of leaving that coordinate unchanged. All scalar Boolean functions are allowed; no balance, monotonicity, circuit-size, degree or efficient-computability promise is imposed. Constant functions satisfy \(H(f)=I(f)=0\). The inequality is non-strict, so it includes them.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal inequality for some positive finite constant, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must use the specified uniform measure, full squared spectrum, base-two Shannon entropy and total bit-flip influence for every \(n\) and every scalar Boolean function. A negative proof must establish \[\forall C>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\},\quad H(f)>C I(f).\] The dimension and function may depend on \(C\); equivalently, the entropy-to-influence ratios of nonconstant Boolean functions must be unbounded. Defeating one numerical constant or checking finitely many truth tables is insufficient. No optimal value of \(C\), algorithm for finding counterexamples or numerical approximation is required.
context:
A Fourier coefficient records correlation with a parity of selected input bits. Squaring these correlations gives a probability distribution on subsets of the coordinates. Its Shannon entropy measures dispersion among subsets; total influence is the expected cardinality of a subset from that distribution. The conjecture asks whether being the spectrum of a Boolean-valued function forces a universal linear relation between these two quantities.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s revision of 9 June 2026 reports FEI for the defined \(\delta\)-tribes class and for classes with recursive separation properties. The separation theorems retain hypotheses on their terminal functions and constants; they are not assertions for all monotone functions or unrestricted decision trees. The paper also exhibits failure of a stronger inequality involving a prescribed splitting coordinate. Those examples satisfy FEI, so that failure is not a counterexample to this card’s target.

Slote’s 2 August 2026 preprint reports a counterexample to the quantum extension, whose inputs are Hermitian unitary operators and whose coefficients come from tensor products of Pauli matrices. Theorems 1 and 5 give operators supported on degree-\(d\) Pauli terms with entropy \(\Theta(d^2)\) and influence \(d\). Classical Boolean functions form a restricted diagonal case of that operator setting. The operators constructed in the theorem therefore do not supply scalar Boolean counterexamples. The full new construction was not independently verified in this review.

A follow-up by Slote, Volberg and Zhang, revised 6 August 2026, also treats quantum counterexamples. Its §6.6 reports Hermitian involutions with total influence below two and spectral entropy \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) in its family parameter. The underlying auxiliary scalar functions take complex values of modulus one, rather than only the real values \(-1\) and \(1\). That domain change is essential, and §6 still describes classical FEI as open. These theorem scopes were checked without independently certifying the full proofs.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.
why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.
status_note: Open in the checked classical primary literature, explicitly reiterated in both August 2026 quantum papers. Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of the universal scalar Boolean Shannon-entropy inequality. The June separated classes impose extra hypotheses, the coordinate-entropy estimates retain an extra term, and the August counterexamples are operator-valued or use non-Boolean complex phases. Li–Han’s December 2025 weaker-bound preprint was withdrawn for prior appearance of its result. Complete new preprint proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1996: Friedgut and Kalai propose FEI; the historical attribution is recorded in the checked O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou primary paper. | 2011: O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the symmetric and read-once decision-tree cases and detail the consequence for fixed-accuracy DNF Fourier concentration. | 2011-05-13: Keller, Mossel and Schlank post the coordinate binary-entropy upper bound in Claim 4.1. | 2024-12-20: Han’s bound with an additional coordinate-entropy term appears online in Combinatorica; the journal volume is dated 2025. | 2025-12-09: Li and Han withdraw their weaker-bound refinement, citing the result already present in Keller–Mossel–Schlank Claim 4.1. | 2025-12-10: Xiao Han’s v2 adds a note acknowledging related earlier work. | 2026-06-09: González, MacManus and Pereyra revise results for \(\delta\)-tribes and separated classes while retaining the unrestricted conjecture. | 2026-08-02: Slote reports a quantum counterexample with quadratic entropy and linear influence in its degree parameter; it does not settle scalar Boolean FEI. | 2026-08-06: Slote, Volberg and Zhang revise further quantum examples, including bounded influence with growing Pauli entropy, and explicitly retain the classical question.
references: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~jswright/papers/fei.pdf | https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08271 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00246 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01424 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2651 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03117 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04411
working_summary: A scalar Boolean function has a Fourier spectrum whose squared coefficients form a probability distribution on sets of input coordinates. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture asks whether its Shannon entropy is at most a universal constant times the expected size of a spectral set. Every dimension and every Boolean function are included, with uniform inputs, base-two entropy and exactly normalized bit-flip influence. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove the universal bound or show that the ratio is unbounded over nonconstant Boolean functions. The conjecture would imply fixed-accuracy Fourier concentration for DNF formulas, while weaker coordinate-entropy estimates and quantum counterexamples leave its classical target unsettled.

title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.
formal:
Does there exist a positive integer \(C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(1\le d\le n\), and every real multilinear polynomial \(f\) in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\),
\[\bigl[\forall x\in\{-1,1\}^n,\ 0\le f(x)\le1\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists i\in[n]:\ \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)\ge\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C?\]
Variance and squared \(L_2\) influence use the uniform distribution on the entire Boolean cube, with the normalization below. The same exponent \(C\) must work for all dimensions, degrees, coefficients and variances.
question_excerpt: The inherited ITCS 2025 Conjecture 4 and Aaronson–Ambainis’s original Conjecture 6 ask for polynomially large influence in terms of variance and inverse degree. This card preserves its full scalar-polynomial scope, output interval [0,1], uniform sign cube, squared L2 influence, category and importance 96. The original source uses the bit cube and omits the factor 1/4 in its influence; changing cube coordinates preserves degree and this fixed normalization factor is absorbed by the unspecified exponent. Restricting the exponent to positive integers is equivalent, not an additional mathematical restriction.
definitions:
Polynomials and domain. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\) for \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(\chi_{\varnothing}=1\). A real multilinear polynomial is a finite sum
\[f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\chi_S(x),\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R.\]
Multilinear means that each variable has exponent at most one in each monomial. Degree at most \(d\) means \(a_S=0\) whenever \(|S|>d\). The range restriction \(0\le f(x)\le1\) is required at every one of the \(2^n\) sign vectors. No range condition away from this cube is imposed.

Uniform averages and Fourier coefficients. For any real-valued function \(h\) on the cube, define \(\mathbb E h=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}h(x)\). The characters \(\chi_S\) give the unique multilinear representation on the cube, with
\[\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E[f(x)\chi_S(x)]=a_S.\]
In particular \(\widehat f(\varnothing)=\mathbb Ef\). Variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}(f)=\mathbb E[(f-\mathbb Ef)^2]=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
For the stated range, \(0\le\operatorname{Var}(f)\le1/4\).

Influence. Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be obtained from \(x\) by negating its \(i\)-th coordinate and leaving all others fixed. Set
\[D_if(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=\mathbb E[(D_if)^2]=\frac14\mathbb E[(f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i}))^2]=\sum_{S\ni i}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
This is a mean squared difference, not the probability that the two function values differ, their mean absolute difference, or the maximum change over inputs. All sums and expectations in the target use this same uniform measure.

Scope and quantifiers. Coefficients are arbitrary real numbers, without a rationality, description-length or computability restriction. The statement is an existence inequality, not a demand for an algorithm finding the coordinate. The coordinate may depend on the whole polynomial. No sparsity, block decomposition, common coefficient magnitude, Boolean-output, nonnegativity-of-coefficients or realizability-by-quantum-algorithms promise is present. There is no positive lower threshold on variance. Constant polynomials have zero variance and all influences zero, so every coordinate satisfies the inequality for them. The degree parameter is a positive upper bound, so division by zero never occurs.

Normalization of the exponent. Allowing any real \(C\ge1\) gives an equivalent assertion: for \(0\le v/d\le1/4\), increasing the exponent to a positive integer only decreases the right-hand side. A bound of the usual form \(c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^a/d^b\), with fixed positive constants \(c,a,b\), also yields this formulation after increasing \(C\). Thus the one-exponent statement records polynomial dependence without selecting a particular best exponent or a hidden constant depending on \(n\).
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must prove one exponent works simultaneously for every allowed \(n,d,f\), including arbitrarily small positive variance. No optimal exponent or algorithm for computing an influential coordinate is required.

A negative answer must prove that for every positive integer \(C\) there exist integers \(n\ge1\), \(1\le d\le n\), and an admissible polynomial of positive variance such that
\[\forall i\in[n],\quad\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)<\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C.\]
The dimension, degree and polynomial may depend on \(C\). A rigorously specified family with those properties qualifies; a counterexample to just one proposed exponent does not negate the existence of another universal exponent. Numerical estimates must be certified strongly enough to establish the exact pointwise range and strict influence inequalities they assert.

A theorem only for Boolean-valued outputs, completely bounded forms, boundedly many quantum-query rounds, or a positive fraction of randomly restricted functions does not by itself cover the full polynomial class. An exponential dependence on degree is also weaker than the requested polynomial bound. This is a yes-or-no conjecture with an exact inequality, not a numerical target subject to additive 1/100 tolerance.
context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

A \(t\)-query quantum algorithm has acceptance probability represented on the Boolean cube by a real polynomial of degree at most \(2t\), with values in \([0,1]\). Aaronson and Ambainis prove that the influence conjecture would imply a classical estimate of this probability within additive \(\varepsilon\) on at least a \(1-\eta\) fraction of uniformly distributed inputs using \(\operatorname{poly}(t,1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)\) queries. The classical algorithm may depend on the quantum algorithm. This gives a concrete reason why a dimension-independent inequality for bounded polynomials matters to quantum computation.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

Complete boundedness imposes more than scalar boundedness. In a block-multilinear polynomial, each monomial contains at most one variable from each of several fixed blocks. Replace variables by square matrix contractions, meaning matrices whose Euclidean operator norm is at most one, and multiply factors in block order. The completely bounded norm is the supremum of the resulting operator norm over all such matrices and dimensions. Requiring this norm to be at most one can support influential-variable theorems, but it is an extra hypothesis not imposed on the polynomials in this card.

The published ITCS 2025 restriction theorem assumes \(d\ge2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\ge1/d\). Each coordinate is independently left free with probability \(\log(d)/(C_1d)\), and otherwise fixed to an independent uniform sign. For universal positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), the resulting function has a coordinate with influence at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)^2/d^{C_2}\) with probability at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\log(d)/(50C_1d)\). These are influences of the restricted function. The March 2026 revision retains both the restriction and original-variance assumptions; it does not establish the unrestricted claim.

Blanc, Docter, Strassle and Tan’s August 2026 theorem concerns quantum query rounds. A round applies parallel input queries between input-independent operations; the number \(r\) of rounds is distinct from the total \(t\) queries and from polynomial degree. Their classical query bound is \(2^{O(r^2)}(t\log(1/\eta)/\varepsilon)^{O(r)}\) for approximation error \(\varepsilon\) outside an \(\eta\) fraction of inputs. This is polynomial for fixed \(r\), but its exponent is not uniform over an unbounded number of rounds. The theorem neither treats every scalar bounded polynomial nor proves the full influential-variable conjecture.

The September 2026 theorem gives \(\sum_i\sqrt{\operatorname{Inf}_i(a)}\le t\|a\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\) for a polynomial with \(t\) blocks, summed over all variables. The constant is optimal, and the result permits nonadaptive classical queries in the associated restricted simulation. The authors expressly retain the unrestricted scalar conjecture as open. A small scalar norm does not supply the completely bounded norm hypothesis, so this sharper inequality is not a general resolution.

The 2019 Keller–Klein preprint once claimed a general proof, but the authors withdrew it on 2 December after a flaw in Lemma 5.3 invalidated the argument. The original abstract still contains the affirmative claim; its withdrawal notice is the controlling status information. It is not evidence that the conjecture has been established.
why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

working_summary: The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture concerns real multilinear polynomials whose values lie between zero and one on every point of the Boolean cube. It asks for a variable whose mean squared influence is bounded below by a fixed power of variance divided by degree, independent of the number of variables. The universal claim includes arbitrary real coefficients and arbitrarily small positive variance, with one normalization and one exponent throughout. A complete Lean proof must establish that claim or provide violations for every proposed exponent, rather than only a particular numerical power.
