title: Mansour’s conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.
formal:
Does there exist an absolute real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), integer \(s\ge2\), function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, and real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), there is a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) for which
\[
 |\mathcal F|\le\left\lceil s^{C\log_2(1/\varepsilon)}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 \sum_{S\subseteq[n],\ S\notin\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)^2\le\varepsilon?
\]
The coefficients are the ordinary Walsh–Fourier coefficients under the uniform distribution. The same constant \(C\) must work for every dimension, term count, formula and accuracy.
question_excerpt: The 2011 source states polynomial Fourier concentration for DNF formulas and explicitly notes Mansour’s stronger proposed exponent proportional to the logarithm of inverse accuracy. This card preserves that stronger dependence from its existing formulation.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. A literal is either the condition \(x_i=1\) or the condition \(x_i=-1\). A term is a conjunction of literals; a disjunctive normal form (DNF) is an OR of terms. Its represented function has value \(+1\) when at least one term is satisfied and \(-1\) otherwise. The number of terms, rather than the total number of literal occurrences, is the size parameter \(s\). Each term may contain any number of variables; variables may occur in arbitrarily many terms, and terms may overlap. Empty conjunctions and an empty disjunction have their usual constant meanings. The statement asks only for existence of some representation with at most \(s\) terms.

For every \(S\subseteq[n]\), define the parity character and its coefficient by
\[
 \chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad \chi_{\varnothing}(x)=1,
 \qquad
 \widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x).
\]
These characters form an orthonormal basis for real functions on the uniform Boolean cube, with inner product \(\mathbb E[g(X)h(X)]\) for uniform \(X\). In particular,
\[
 f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x),
 \qquad \sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)^2=1.
\]
The empty-set coefficient is included in these sums and may belong to \(\mathcal F\).

Keeping the coefficients indexed by \(\mathcal F\) gives the real multilinear polynomial
\[
 g_{\mathcal F}(x)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x),
\]
whose mean squared error is exactly
\[
 \mathbb E[(f(X)-g_{\mathcal F}(X))^2]
   =\sum_{S\notin\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)^2.
\]
Thus \(\varepsilon\) measures discarded squared Fourier mass, without an additional normalization factor. The approximant need not be Boolean-valued. The bound concerns the number of retained characters, not their maximum degree, pointwise error or disagreement probability.

The family \(\mathcal F\) may depend on the function and on \(\varepsilon\). No efficient algorithm for discovering it, producing the coefficients or learning the function is required. There is no promise on a DNF’s read number, which is the maximum number of its terms containing any one variable, and no random distribution on formulas. The only input distribution in the approximation is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}^n\).

This is the strong accuracy-dependent form of the conjecture. Allowing \(s^{K(\varepsilon)}\) characters for an arbitrary function \(K\) of the error would be a weaker target. Here that exponent must be bounded by one constant times \(\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\), uniformly even when \(\varepsilon\) decreases with \(n\) or \(s\).
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed statement with one universal \(C\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation.

A negative answer must show that for every \(C>0\) there are admissible \(n,s,\varepsilon,f\) for which every family of at most \(\lceil s^{C\log_2(1/\varepsilon)}\rceil\) characters leaves discarded squared mass greater than \(\varepsilon\). Defeating only one proposed constant does not refute existence of another. A theorem only for random DNFs, bounded-read formulas, fixed width or a different input distribution does not cover the target. A polynomial concentration bound with unspecified dependence of its exponent on \(\varepsilon\) establishes only the weaker form. This is an exact universal proposition; the benchmark’s numerical \(1/100\) tolerance is not a replacement for its full range of error parameters.
context:
DNF size counts sufficient conditions for acceptance; Fourier sparsity counts parity correlations needed for approximation. The conjecture asks whether a short representation of the first kind always yields an approximately short representation of the second, independently of the ambient dimension.

The source distinguishes the stronger \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) exponent from a general error-dependent exponent. Its stated FEI implication yields \(O(1/\varepsilon)\), which does not establish the stronger bound selected here.

Random-formula and fixed-read-number theorems give important subclasses, but neither hypothesis is part of the universal target.

The 2021 work improves dependence on the read number and proves a polynomial fixed-accuracy bound for a growing small-read range. Its full small-read estimate has base \(s/\varepsilon\), which matters when comparing varying accuracies.

The June 2026 FEI preprint concerns additional classes satisfying structural conditions. Its checked abstract does not claim the strong concentration theorem for arbitrary DNFs.

The June 2026 learning revision changes the Fourier representation to fit Bayesian-network distributions. Learning DNFs in that model and agnostically learning decision trees are different conclusions from uniform Walsh concentration of every DNF.
why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.
status_note: The checked general DNF bounds and subclass theorems do not establish the universal strong accuracy-dependent concentration bound. The June 2026 works concern restricted FEI classes or a different distribution-adapted learning framework. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified proof or refutation of the retained strong form; the full cited proofs were not independently certified.

working_summary: A short DNF describes a Boolean function using a small number of conjunctions. Mansour’s conjecture asks whether such a function can always be approximated by retaining only a small number of its ordinary Fourier coefficients. The permitted discarded squared mass is epsilon under uniformly random Boolean inputs. The retained number must be at most the term count raised to a universal constant times log of inverse epsilon, with no dependence on the ambient dimension. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove or refute this strong bound for all DNFs and all stated accuracies, without an algorithmic recovery requirement.

title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.
formal:
Determine, up to universal multiplicative constant factors jointly in \(n\) and \(d\), the function
\[M(n,d)=\max\{I(f):f\in\mathcal F_{n,d}\},\qquad n,d\in\mathbb N,\quad n\ge1,\quad1\le d\le n,\]
where \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is the class of Boolean functions represented by the sign of a real polynomial of total degree at most \(d\) with no zero on \(\{-1,1\}^n\), and \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution, defined below. The answer must give a positive growth function \(h(n,d)\) and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of both parameters, such that \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall d\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad c\,h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C\,h(n,d).\] No particular formula for \(h\) or extremizing Boolean function is prescribed.
question_excerpt: Preserves the user-authorized quantitative reformulation recorded on 12 September 2026: determine the joint extremal influence function within universal constant factors. The original asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture proposes the upper bound O(d sqrt(n)); the stronger exact symmetric-extremizer claim was disproved. The main target permits a different matching growth rate rather than asking only whether that proposed formula is true.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A real multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(d\) has the form
\[p(x)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le d}}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R,\]
with empty product \(1\). All coefficients are unrestricted reals; there is no bound on their magnitude, bit length, the number of nonzero monomials, or the minimum nonzero value of \(|p|\) on the cube. Require \(p(x)\ne0\) at every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\). Its threshold function is \(f(x)=+1\) when \(p(x)>0\), and \(f(x)=-1\) when \(p(x)<0\). The class \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) contains every function with at least one such representation, not just those whose least possible threshold degree is exactly \(d\). Starting with arbitrary real polynomials gives the same class: reducing powers using \(x_i^2=1\) preserves the cube values and does not increase degree. Excluding zeros fixes the tie convention; any representation using one fixed value of sign at zero can be perturbed by a sufficiently small constant to remove its cube zeros without changing the function.

Choose \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) cube points, with independent equally likely coordinates. For \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) have coordinate \(-x_i\) at \(i\) and agree with \(x\) elsewhere. Define
\[\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\quad s_f(x)=|\{i\in[n]:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\]
\[I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}s_f(x).\]
Thus total influence is average sensitivity, not maximum pointwise sensitivity and not influence divided by \(n\). There is no biased input distribution or additional probability over polynomials. The maximization is over Boolean functions; different coefficient choices representing the same function have the same influence. It is a maximum rather than merely a supremum because only finitely many Boolean functions exist on a fixed cube, and \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is nonempty. Constants belong to the class with influence zero, while a dictator \(f(x)=x_1\) has influence one; hence \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain.

The constants in the answer must be absolute: they cannot depend on degree, dimension, a representation, or an asymptotic path through the parameter pairs. The estimates must hold throughout the domain, including small dimensions and growing degrees; finite exceptional cases must be covered by the proved constants. This is a mathematical extremal-growth problem, with no evaluation-time requirement or finite encoding assumption for real coefficients. The omitted degree-zero case has value zero, and degrees larger than \(n\) give no additional Boolean functions, so the displayed domain covers all nontrivial regimes.
answer_criterion: Give a specified growth function \(h\) and universal positive constants \(c,C\), together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both inequalities for every stated \((n,d)\). The upper bound must cover every realizing polynomial in the defined class. The lower bound must establish, for each pair, the existence of a degree-at-most-\(d\) threshold function with influence at least \(c h(n,d)\); an algorithm for producing its coefficients is not required. The answer must determine joint growth, including the large-degree saturation regime. Merely renaming \(M\), repeating its defining maximization, or giving an equivalent optimization is not such a determination. A degree-dependent hidden factor, a polylogarithmic gap in \(n\), a result only for fixed \(d\), or a counterexample to one proposed formula without matching replacement bounds is insufficient. No exact symmetric maximizer is required. The accepted precision is universal constant factors, not additive error \(1/100\).
context:
The target is the maximum total influence as a joint function of dimension and threshold degree, within universal constant factors. It retains the quantitative formulation selected in the earlier review. The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture is a proposed answer at a particular scale; the stronger claim prescribing an exact symmetric maximizer is a separate, disproved statement.

A polynomial threshold function evaluates a real polynomial and keeps its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority and weighted voting rules; degree two also permits pairwise interactions. Threshold degree measures the degree needed to represent the sign pattern, rather than the degree needed to equal the Boolean function numerically on every input.

Total influence is the expected number of sensitive coordinates at a uniformly random input. If \(D(f)\) is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2^{1-n}D(f)\). By contrast, the probability that flipping one uniformly chosen coordinate changes the output is \(I(f)/n\). The normalization in the target is the former, which ranges from zero to \(n\).

For odd \(n\), majority has \[I(\operatorname{MAJ}_n)=n\,2^{1-n}\binom{n-1}{(n-1)/2}\sim\sqrt{2n/\pi}.\] Thus influence already grows with dimension at degree one. At the opposite endpoint, parity \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) has degree \(n\) and influence \(n\), so \(M(n,n)=n\).

The classical symmetric examples change sign across consecutive central Hamming layers. Their total influence has order \(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\}\), with constants uniform in the two parameters. This supplies the standard lower scale, including saturation at large degree. Gotsman and Linial conjectured that such an example actually maximizes influence exactly; the remaining asymptotic question permits different maximizers.

Chapman’s counterexamples refute that exact assertion for \(d=2\) in every odd dimension \(n\ge5\), and for \(n\ge7\) with \(3\le d\le n-3\). They do not rule out a universal \(O(d\sqrt n)\) upper bound. Combined with the elementary upper bound \(I(f)\le n\) and the standard lower scale, that surviving conjecture would give \(M(n,d)=\Theta(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\})\).

The common constants are part of the mathematical target. Bounds \(M(n,d)\le C_d\sqrt n\) with an unspecified degree-dependent constant \(C_d\) do not determine the joint dependence on \(n,d\). Nor does an estimate only as \(n\to\infty\) with \(d\) fixed cover sequences of increasing degree. The requested bound must also cover the transition to influence of order \(n\).

Kane’s Theorem 2 gives \(I(f)\le\sqrt n\,(\log n)^{O(d\log d)}2^{O(d^2\log d)}\) for \(d\ge2\). For every fixed degree this has the correct power of \(n\), up to logarithmic factors. Those factors still grow with dimension, and the bound’s dependence on degree is much larger than linear, so it does not give matching universal factors in the requested joint regime.

For quadratic threshold functions, Kim, Maldonado and Wellens study the graph whose edges mark nonzero coefficients of pairwise monomials. Their Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 give bounds in terms of the graph’s fractional chromatic number and its number of edges. These are structural estimates for a prescribed representation, not a matching bound for all dense quadratic representations.

The April 27, 2026 revision by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a fixed-degree polylogarithmic bound on Boolean surface area, defined by \(\operatorname{BSA}(f)=\mathbb E_x\sqrt{s_f(x)}\). Its Theorem 1.1 has constants depending on degree. The paper explicitly distinguishes this fractional sensitivity moment from total influence \(\mathbb E_x s_f(x)\).

The two quantities satisfy \((\operatorname{BSA}(f))^2\le I(f)\le\sqrt n\,\operatorname{BSA}(f)\). In particular, an upper bound on Boolean surface area cannot be squared to obtain an upper bound on influence. The checked 2026 surface-area theorem therefore still leaves dimension-dependent logarithmic factors when applied to this target.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision establishes a polynomial relationship between rational degree and ordinary degree. Its §5.2 restates the asymptotic influence conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue. Neither that main degree theorem nor the proposed weaker conjecture determines the maximum influence of arbitrary polynomial threshold functions.

A matching joint bound would quantify how strongly a low-degree sign representation constrains the edge boundary of a Boolean function. This connects algebraic representation to sensitivity, noise behavior and learning-theoretic complexity. A solution may establish the surviving conjectured scale or a different scale, but disproving one particular candidate without determining the extremal growth does not complete the task.
why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture is false, but no universal joint constant-factor determination of M(n,d) was found in the bounded primary-source review. The surviving O(d sqrt(n)) influence bound is explicitly still a conjecture in the checked April2026 revisions. The Boolean surface-area theorem bounds a different sensitivity moment with degree-dependent logarithmic factors, and the rational-degree theorem concerns a different degree comparison. New proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 2012–2014: Kane proves the \(\sqrt n\) exponent up to logarithmic factors depending on degree; the preprint, CCC presentation and journal version have different dates. | 2017: Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs. | 2018: Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question. | 2022: Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations. | 8 April 2026: Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2. | 27 April 2026: Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.
working_summary: A polynomial threshold function records the sign of a real polynomial on the uniformly distributed Boolean cube. Total influence is the expected number of individual coordinate flips that change the function’s value. The target is the largest influence possible as a joint function of dimension and degree bound, within constants independent of both parameters. A complete Lean proof must give a matching universal upper bound and a lower example for every parameter pair, including the regime where influence is of order the dimension. The disproved exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture, fixed-degree logarithmic bounds and the separate 2026 surface-area and rational-degree theorems do not determine this joint growth.

title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A basic lower-bound question about whether symmetry prevents any edge query from being avoided.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}; a\) graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |\(U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.
context:
Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.
why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The October 2025 revision of Elekes, Kátay and Kocsis explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. No later resolution matching the full graph-property model was located. The June 2026 topological counterexample announcement concerns a broader symmetry condition; only its abstract and an in-preparation listing were accessible, so no claim about its proof or graph specialization is made. Source/model review is not an independent proof audit.

title: Interactive compression with logarithmic input-length overhead
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A central structural question connecting interactive information, compression and direct-sum lower bounds across communication complexity. The general correlated-input case captures a broad barrier, beyond one protocol family or a multiparty implementation detail. The selected logarithmic-loss regime is an explicit editorial specification of the substantial source question, and this importance judgment does not certify that exact variant as a verbatim later conjecture.
formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) such that every two-party protocol \(\pi\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, under every joint input distribution \(\mu\), has a simulation \(\rho\) with distributional error at most \(1/100\) and worst-case communication at most
\[
K\bigl(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1\bigr)\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil\quad\text{bits}?
\]
Here \(n\ge1\), the protocol and simulation model, internal information cost \(I_{\mu}\), and joint-transcript error are defined below. There is no restriction on the finite communication cost of \(\pi\), and \(K\) must be independent of \(n,\mu,\pi\).

This is an explicitly selected editorial version of the source's proposed logarithmic-loss question. The source's surrounding paragraph concerns two-party internal information, despite the article's multiparty title. It already reports that compression without an overhead is impossible. The particular logarithmic factor, constant error, additive regularization and worst-case transcript-simulation guarantee below are specified here rather than attributed verbatim to its informal sentence.
question_excerpt: Put differently, is it always possible to compress the communication cost of a protocol to its information cost?
definitions:
Alice has \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), Bob has \(y\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and the pair \((X,Y)\) has an arbitrary probability distribution \(\mu\) on this finite product. The inputs may be correlated. Both parties know \(n\), the description of \(\pi\) and \(\mu\). Neither party is initially given the other party's realized input. No promise is placed on the support of \(\mu\).

A protocol uses one finite string \(R\) of shared fair random bits and two finite strings \(R_A,R_B\) of private fair random bits. The three strings are mutually independent and independent of \((X,Y)\). Their finite lengths may depend on the protocol and are not charged as communication. A length of zero is allowed. For each fixed public string, the protocol is a finite rooted binary communication tree: every internal node designates Alice or Bob, and the selected player sends one bit determined by their own input, private string, public string and the earlier messages. That bit selects the next child. A leaf terminates communication. The owner of the next message and termination are therefore determined by the public string and common message history, rather than by an uncharged timing channel. The transcript of communicated bits is \(M\), and the augmented transcript is \(T=(R,M)\). Both parties observe every communicated bit. A protocol is defined on every input pair and every coin choice. Its worst-case communication \(\operatorname{CC}(\pi)\) is the maximum number of transmitted bits over all these executions; it is finite but may be arbitrarily large.

All local computation, protocol descriptions and shared randomness are free. There is no restriction on the number of rounds or the local running time, and no privacy requirement. No advice depending on the other party's realized private input or quantum resources are supplied; all initial resources are exactly those specified above. Protocols for different \(n,\mu,\pi\) may be unrelated. This is an existence statement about finite communication protocols, not an efficient compiler for producing one from a table of \(\mu\).

For a finite random variable \(U\), its base-two Shannon entropy is
\[
H(U)=-\sum_{u}\Pr[U=u]\log_2\Pr[U=u],
\]
where \(0\log_2 0=0\). Conditional entropy \(H(U\mid V)\) is the average of \(H(U\mid V=v)\) weighted by \(\Pr[V=v]\), with zero-probability terms omitted. The conditional mutual information is
\[
I(U;W\mid V)=H(U\mid V)-H(U\mid V,W).
\]
The internal information cost in bits is
\[
I_{\mu}(\pi)=I(X;T\mid Y)+I(Y;T\mid X).
\]
All variables use the joint law of \(\mu\) and the three independent coin strings of \(\pi\). Including \(R\) in \(T\) accounts for public randomness; private coins are not included in that transcript. This is internal information, not the external quantity \(I(X,Y;T)\), and not the distinct multiparty public-information measure introduced in the source. The quantity is finite, nonnegative and at most \(2n\).

A simulation \(\rho\) is another finite protocol in the same model, with its own independent shared and private fair coins. At its terminal leaf Alice outputs a value \(T_A\) determined by her local view and Bob outputs \(T_B\) determined by his. These values lie in the finite set of augmented transcripts possible for \(\pi\), together with a failure symbol \(\bot\). Output descriptions and their lengths are not communication costs. The simulated public string of \(\pi\) is part of these output values; it need not equal \(\rho\)'s actual public string.

Let \(P\) be the law of \((X,Y,T,T)\) produced by drawing \((X,Y)\sim\mu\) and executing \(\pi\). Let \(Q\) be the law of \((X,Y,T_A,T_B)\) produced by drawing the same input distribution and executing \(\rho\). Regard both as distributions on the same finite product space, assigning zero mass to impossible original outcomes and to original failures. The simulation error is their total variation distance
\[
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)=
\frac12\sum_{x,y,t_a,t_b}|P(x,y,t_a,t_b)-Q(x,y,t_a,t_b)|.
\]
Thus the requirement preserves correlation with the inputs and agreement between the parties' reconstructed transcripts, except for total variation at most \(1/100\). It is stronger than reproducing only an output bit of a particular function or only the unconditioned marginal law of \(T\). Error is averaged under \(\mu\) and the coins, whereas communication is worst case over every input pair and every coin string, including pairs of \(\mu\)-probability zero. There is no joint simulation of many independent copies. The \(+1\) in the cost bound avoids a zero-information boundary convention, and the logarithm is of the input bit length \(n\), not the number of possible inputs, the transcript length or the number of rounds.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal compression statement or its full negation. Equivalently, a positive answer gives one absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) and proves
\[
\forall n\ge1\ \forall\mu\ \forall\pi\ \exists\rho:\quad
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)\le\frac1{100}
\ \land\
\operatorname{CC}(\rho)\le
K(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
A negative answer must prove that for every proposed \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\), there are \(n,\mu,\pi\) in the stated domain for which every simulation with error at most \(1/100\) has communication strictly larger than that bound. A positive theorem only for product input distributions or public-coin original protocols does not cover the universal domain, although a matching lower bound within either subclass can refute the universal statement. Refuting only constant-overhead compression does not refute the logarithmic allowance. An expected-communication upper bound must be converted to the specified worst-case guarantee; error slack and an increased absolute constant can permit such a conversion. A theorem for external or multiparty public information must establish the claimed conclusion for the internal-information measure defined here to qualify. Likewise, failure of one simulation construction is not a lower bound for all simulations. The chosen constant simulation error is part of the mathematical proposition; the benchmark asks for a proof of that proposition or negation, rather than an approximate numerical verdict.
context:
Interactive information measures what two participants learn about each other’s inputs during a conversation. The number of transmitted bits can be much larger. The source asks whether most of that discrepancy can always be removed while retaining the relevant behavior.

Reading the complete source paragraph changes the interpretation of the imported excerpt. It discusses the two-party question and says that compression with no loss is already ruled out. The open direction permits a small loss, giving logarithmic input-size dependence as an example.

The paper subsequently introduces a different public-information measure for multiparty computation and proves a compression theorem for it with logarithmic factors. That theorem cannot be substituted for a solution to the preceding two-party internal-information question.

Internal simulation reconstructs the original transcript for both participants while retaining its joint distribution with their inputs. The survey explicitly distinguishes this stronger requirement from merely computing the same total Boolean function. This card selects the transcript-simulation version.

Known exponential separations rule out compression solely to a fixed constant times information in general. Such statements must be compared with input size before treating them as a refutation of a logarithmic-input-length allowance.

Product-distribution compression assumes independent inputs. Compression to external information uses another information measure. These important positive results concern different domains or benchmarks from the present arbitrary-distribution internal target.
why: The question asks how much communication is forced by interaction beyond the information actually transferred. A general small-overhead simulation would strengthen the connection between information-theoretic lower bounds and communication complexity, with consequences for direct-sum phenomena. A matching obstruction would show why correlated inputs prevent a near-information-cost account of interactive communication.

This card spells out a particular logarithmic-input-length, internal-information, joint-transcript simulation variant. Because the source does not uniquely select all of those conventions, the exact editorial combination is labeled uncertain rather than represented as a verbatim source conjecture. The dated later-result checks and explicit editorial scope decision are recorded in the individual audit; no exhaustive current-status certificate or Lean verification is claimed.

Its input tables are sufficiently large that the low-information protocol itself uses only a constant times their logarithmic bit length. | 2018: Braverman–Kol establish compression with a different external-information benchmark and original-communication dependence. | 2026-08-04: A preprint gives many-copy amortized characterizations using zero-error information; these are not the stated simulation of every prescribed one-copy transcript.
working_summary: The underlying question concerns two-party interactive communication, even though its source article studies multiparty protocols. A protocol can transmit many more bits than its internal information cost under the input distribution. The proposed precise target allows a logarithmic factor in input bit length and a fixed total-variation error when both parties reconstruct the transcript. Exact compression without loss is already known to fail, while results for external information or independent inputs address different targets. A complete Lean answer must prove this explicitly specified universal simulation bound or a lower bound refuting every proposed universal constant.

title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.
formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and Bob must output \(F(x,y)\). A protocol is agreed in advance for the entire function \(F\). Local computation and storage are unrestricted and free; only communication is charged. The protocol may depend on \(F\), but its shared resources are independent of the actual inputs. In the classical model the parties exchange bits and may use shared public randomness and private randomness. In the quantum model they exchange qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may start with any finite-dimensional shared entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). There is no fixed upper bound on the amount of this prior entanglement; its preparation is not charged. Local quantum operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, with measurement outcomes retained in local registers, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Classical bits sent by a quantum protocol count as transmitted qubits. Neither model receives free input-dependent advice or any communication through timing, message length, silence or postselection. One may use a fixed finite alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused transmissions; local branches cannot signal through the schedule. Arbitrarily many rounds are allowed, with no input-length-dependent round restriction imposed by the question. The cost is the worst-case total number of bits or qubits transmitted, including all rounds and all randomness or measurement branches. In either model the output must equal \(F(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every pair \((x,y)\). The quantities \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\) and \(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)\) are the least costs among protocols with this guarantee. Total means that all of \(X\times Y\) is the correctness domain; no additional joint promise is allowed. The additive one in the polynomial handles zero-communication functions. The constants \(C,k\) must be independent of the function, the domains, any bit encoding of the inputs, and the amount of shared entanglement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal polynomial bound or of its negation. A negative answer must show that for every \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\), some finite total Boolean function satisfies \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)>C(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1)^k\). A superpolynomial separating family can witness this; one fixed polynomial separation cannot. A bound with an extra input-length factor, a promise-problem or relation separation, or a comparison imposing a fixed round limit does not resolve the stated all-functions, unrestricted-round target.
context:
Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.
why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

Le Gall arXiv:2609.16726v1, submitted 15 September, Theorems 2–3 claim stronger separations with explicit public-coin, worst-case, per-input error conventions. If correct, either family refutes every universal polynomial relation in this card: allowing free prior entanglement only decreases quantum cost, and moving the final output to Bob costs at most one bit. Full PDFs and theorem/model statements were inspected, not independently certified or Lean-checked. Status is uncertain pending verification, superseding the earlier search that had located only a polynomial gap.

working_summary: Two parties must evaluate a Boolean function when each holds one part of the input. The question asks whether randomized classical communication is polynomially bounded by quantum communication with shared entanglement for every total function. Both models allow bounded error on each input, and their costs count transmitted bits or qubits rather than local computation. August and September 2026 preprints claim total-function families with polylogarithmic quantum cost and polynomial randomized classical cost. Those stated results would refute the conjecture even with the quantum side allowed free entanglement, but their proofs are not independently certified in this review.

title: Fourier Min-Entropy–Influence conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A broad structural conjecture connecting sensitivity with a guaranteed spectral coefficient for every Boolean function. It is a consequential weakening of Fourier entropy–influence with an independent connection to KKL, and recent lower bounds on its universal constant emphasize a substantial unresolved barrier rather than a single construction parameter.
formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\), some set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfies \(\widehat f(S)^2\ge 2^{-C I(f)}\)? Here \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution. Equivalently, the conjecture asserts \(H_\infty(f)\le C I(f)\), with Fourier min-entropy defined below. The same constant must work for every dimension and every function.
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define the parity \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\), with \(\chi_\varnothing(x)=1\), and the normalized Fourier coefficient \(\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x)\). Set \(p_f(S)=\widehat f(S)^2\); these nonnegative masses sum to one. Define \(H_\infty(f)=-\log_2\bigl(\max_{S\subseteq[n]}p_f(S)\bigr)\), measured in bits. The maximum is positive, so this logarithm is always defined, even if some coefficients vanish. If \(x^{\oplus j}\) is obtained by changing the sign of coordinate \(j\), define \(I_j(f)=2^{-n}|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus j})\}|\) and \(I(f)=\sum_{j=1}^n I_j(f)\). Equivalently \(I(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|p_f(S)\). Quantification includes constant functions, for which \(I(f)=H_\infty(f)=0\), as well as unbalanced, nonmonotone and arbitrarily complex functions. The witnessing set may be empty and may depend on the entire function. There is no algorithmic requirement to find it. In particular, the target is the largest squared Fourier coefficient, not the entropy of the truth table, the largest individual coordinate influence, or the Shannon entropy \(H(f)=\sum_{S:p_f(S)>0}p_f(S)\log_2(1/p_f(S))\). Changing the base from two to the natural exponential only rescales the universal constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated universal-constant inequality or its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C>0\) for every dimension and Boolean function, with the normalized Fourier distribution and uniform influences above. A negative answer must prove that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) with \(H_\infty(f)>C I(f)\). Disproving one proposed constant, checking finitely many truth tables, or establishing a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not settle this existence question. Determining the smallest possible constant is not required.
context:
The named conjecture is stated explicitly as Conjecture 4.1 by Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Koucký, Saurabh and de Wolf. The draft’s saved O’Donnell book locator instead points to the Kahn–Kalai–Linial theorem and its surrounding influence theory. That book remains background provenance; the explicit research statement is anchored to the conjecture in the checked paper.

The full Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture implies this one because \(H_\infty(f)\le H(f)\). A proof of the present target would not by itself establish the full Shannon-entropy inequality. Conversely, a refutation of this target would also refute that stronger conjecture.

The same paper verifies the conjecture for DNFs in which each variable occurs only a fixed bounded number of times. This supplies a representation-restricted result; the universal conjecture allows every Boolean truth table.

Biswas and Sarkar obtain a Boolean function with \(H_\infty(f)/I(f)=128/45\). Li and Tang’s 2026 paper reports a family with ratios tending to \(4\) from below, which forces any universal constant to be at least \(4\). These are lower bounds on a possible constant, not an unbounded sequence of ratios and hence not a refutation.

Han’s general Fourier-entropy bound contains the additional term \(\sum_j I_j(f)\log(1/I_j(f))\), with zero terms omitted. Its dependence on the separate coordinate influences does not supply the universal multiple of \(I(f)\) asked for here.
why: Total influence measures how often individual bit changes alter an output, while Fourier min-entropy measures how weak even the strongest parity correlation can be. A universal relation would constrain all Boolean functions without representation or balance assumptions. Its distinction from full Fourier entropy matters: controlling a single coefficient asks for less than controlling the entire spectral information, yet retains a connection to fundamental influence inequalities.
status_note: The unrestricted conjecture is explicit in the 2021 primary paper and is still treated as a conjecture in the checked July 2026 Li–Tang publication. Their reported constant lower bound and Han’s general bound do not settle existence of a finite universal FMEI constant. This bounded source review does not independently verify every later proof or certify an exhaustive literature search.

working_summary: The FMEI conjecture says that every Boolean function has a parity whose squared Fourier correlation is exponentially large in minus its total influence. Both influence and Fourier coefficients use the uniform distribution on the Boolean cube. One universal constant must cover every dimension and truth table, including constant and unbalanced functions. The conjecture is weaker than full Fourier entropy–influence and remains meaningful because of its connection to fundamental influence inequalities. Recent constructions force the universal constant to be at least four, while leaving the existence of any finite constant unresolved.

title: Number-on-forehead disjointness complexity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Multiparty set disjointness is a central explicit test problem for randomized communication with overlapping information; a sharp characterization would resolve a substantial general lower-bound gap even for small player counts.
formal:
Determine, up to absolute constant factors, the randomized number-on-forehead communication complexity
\[
R(n,k)=R_{1/3}^{\mathrm{pub}}(\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k})
\]
for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(k\ge2\).

The input consists of \(k\) arbitrary subsets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\). Player \(i\) sees every set except \(S_i\). The common output must be
\[
\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k}(S_1,\ldots,S_k)
=\mathbf 1\!\left[\bigcap_{i=1}^k S_i=\varnothing\right].
\]
Players use public randomness and unrestricted interactive broadcasts, with error at most \(1/3\) on every input and communication measured by the maximum total number of broadcast bits.

The requested characterization is a specified noncircular asymptotic function \(g(n,k)>0\) and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of both \(n\) and \(k\), such that
\[
c\,g(n,k)\le R(n,k)\le C\,g(n,k)
\qquad(n\ge1,\ k\ge2).
\]
question_excerpt: The early draft describes the overlapping-input k-party intersection problem, compares deterministic and randomized communication bounds, and asks whether the randomized lower bound is tight.
definitions:
The universe \([n]\) is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Each \(S_j\) is represented by its characteristic vector \(x^{(j)}\in\{0,1\}^n\), where \(x^{(j)}_t=1\) means \(t\in S_j\). There is no restriction on set sizes, intersections, repeated sets, or the number of players relative to \(n\). In particular, \(k\) can exceed \(n\). The predicate asks for an empty intersection of all sets, not pairwise disjointness. Equivalently, the complementary predicate asks whether some row of the \(n\)-by-\(k\) incidence matrix is all ones; complementing the common output leaves the communication complexity unchanged.

All players know \(n,k\), their labels and the protocol. Player \(i\)'s initial view is the ordered tuple \((x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(i-1)},x^{(i+1)},\ldots,x^{(k)})\). No player initially sees its missing column. This is the number-on-forehead model; it is different from giving player \(i\) only \(S_i\).

A deterministic protocol is a finite binary tree. An internal node specifies which player broadcasts the next bit. That bit can be any function of that player's visible input and the preceding public transcript. The bit is written once on a blackboard and is seen by all players; broadcasting one bit costs one bit, not \(k\) bits. Each leaf specifies a common output bit. The speaker and the decision to stop are determined by the public node, so they cannot transmit an uncharged input-dependent signal. The players may speak in any order prescribed by the tree and may return arbitrarily often; neither the number of rounds nor the number of messages is separately bounded.

A public-coin randomized protocol is a distribution over deterministic protocols, selected using shared randomness independent of the inputs. Its cost is the maximum depth of any tree in the support. This bound is over all inputs and all random outcomes, not an expectation. For every full input tuple, the probability that the common output equals \(\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k}\) must be at least \(2/3\). No private communication, pre-shared secret or quantum resource is provided.

Local computation, storage and the complexity of the protocol description are free. Protocols may be chosen independently for each pair \((n,k)\); there is no uniform algorithm for generating them or local running-time requirement. The model therefore asks about communication alone.

Define \(R(n,k)\) to be the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which such a randomized protocol of cost at most \(d\) exists. This set of costs is nonempty: one player can transmit a missing column to another, who can broadcast the answer, using at most \(n+1\) bits. Both output values occur for every allowed \((n,k)\), so a zero-communication output independent of the input cannot attain error \(1/3\) on all inputs. Thus \(1\le R(n,k)\le n+1\).

The lower-bound part must apply to every allowed randomized interactive protocol. Restricting to one-way protocols or simultaneous messages gives a different lower-bound target. An upper bound may of course use a simpler protocol. All logarithms used to describe a proposed answer are base two. Constants hidden in the requested characterization cannot depend on the number of players.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked constant-factor characterization over the full domain \(n\ge1,k\ge2\), including both a protocol upper bound and a matching lower bound against every protocol in the stated model. The function \(g\) must describe the dependence on the parameters rather than merely rename the defining optimum over protocols. Bounds with a growing logarithmic or player-dependent gap, or a characterization only for a selected player-count regime, do not meet the target. Known regimes may be used as components of a full proof. This is an asymptotic-complexity question with the displayed multiplicative tolerance; additive \(1/100\) numerical tolerance is not the answer criterion.
context:
The overlapping views are essential: with two players this recovers the usual two-party problem, while additional players see different nearly complete views. A lower bound for private-input message passing cannot simply be substituted.

For every fixed \(k\ge3\), the directional-derivative theorem yields a randomized lower bound of order \(\sqrt n\). Its explicit dependence is \(\Omega(\sqrt n/(2^k k))\). This does not match the general linear upper bound at a fixed small player count.

For \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge\max\{2,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}\), the 2020 result determines the answer as \(\Theta(1+\log_2 n/\log_2(1+k/\log_2 n))\). Its constants are uniform in this regime. The full question also includes fewer players.

The consolidated Jukna question only asks for a three-party deterministic lower bound growing faster than \((\log n)^3\). The known randomized polynomial lower bound already implies that historical threshold. It is not a second unresolved target here.

The July 2026 revision revisits disjointness with a deterministic one-way lower bound. Arbitrary randomized interaction is more powerful than that restricted protocol model, so the result is not a matching lower bound for this card.

The requested bounds must be uniform as the number of players changes. Hiding a player-dependent constant in a fixed-player estimate can conceal precisely the dependence that the question asks to determine.
why: Each player knows almost the entire input, which makes communication lower bounds much harder than in the ordinary split-input model. Set disjointness gives a concrete way to measure how this overlap and additional players change the power of randomized interaction. A full answer would clarify a basic limitation used in several connections between communication, circuits and proofs.
status_note: Known results determine the constant-factor answer when the number of players is at least logarithmic in the universe size, and give strong lower bounds in smaller-player regimes. The bounded source review found no matching characterization over the full parameter domain. The consolidated historical three-player lower-bound threshold is already resolved, and the 2026 one-way deterministic result does not settle the active randomized target.

title: Multiparty Clique lower bounds in compression games
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: The model isolates whether interaction with unrestricted computation can overcome constant-depth limitations at low communication cost. The conjectured Clique bound would separate NP from nonuniform logarithmic-depth circuits, giving this precise communication question consequences far beyond a single compression scheme.
formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and an integer round bound \(r(N)\to\infty\) such that every nonuniform, deterministic, polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)-compression protocol family deciding Clique with at most \(r(N)\) rounds has cost \(\Omega(N^\varepsilon)\)? Here \(N\) is the graph’s number of vertices. In each round, Alice sends messages to independent computationally unrestricted Bobs, receives their replies, and eventually computes the answer herself with an \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuit. Cost is the sum over rounds of the maximum length of an Alice-to-Bob message in that round.
question_excerpt: We conjecture that such a lower bound holds for the Clique function.
definitions: For each integer \(N\ge2\), the input consists of the \(\binom N2\) adjacency bits of a simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([N]\), listed in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\), followed by \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\) bits encoding a nonnegative integer \(k\) in ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. The input length is \(L_N=\binom N2+\ell\). Clique is 1 if \(0\le k\le N\) and some \(k\)-vertex set has every pair joined by an edge; it is 0 when \(k>N\). The empty set makes the answer 1 for \(k=0\). Alice receives all input bits, while \(b_N\ge1\) Bobs receive no input. A protocol has a fixed number \(R_N\le r(N)\) of rounds. In round \(t\), Alice simultaneously sends a fixed-length binary string \(a_{t,j}\) to each Bob \(j\). Each Bob replies with a fixed-length binary string \(z_{t,j}\). Message lengths and all strategies are fixed before the input is known; empty strings are permitted. Bob \(j\)’s reply is an arbitrary deterministic function of the sequence \(a_{1,j},\ldots,a_{t,j}\), with no computational restriction. Bobs cannot communicate with each other or observe other Bobs’ messages. Each message \(a_{t,j}\) is computed by a Boolean circuit using the original input and all messages in earlier completed rounds. After the final replies, an additional circuit at Alice computes the single output bit from the input and the complete transcript. All of Alice’s circuits use only AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in, unary NOT gates, and constants. There are constants \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(A>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N\), fixed across \(N\) for the protocol family, such that every Alice circuit has depth at most \(d\), and the sum of their gate, wire, input and output counts, the number \(b_N\) of Bobs, and the total number of transmitted bits are each at most \(A(N+1)^a\). Reply bits are not charged to communication cost, but remain subject to these polynomial length bounds. Alice’s circuits and all Bob functions may depend arbitrarily on \(N\); no uniform construction is required. No player uses randomness. Correctness means the output equals Clique on every input of length \(L_N\). Define \(c_\Pi(N)=\sum_{t=1}^{R_N}\max_{1\le j\le b_N}|a_{t,j}|\). The target quantifiers are \(\exists\varepsilon>0\;\exists r:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with \(r(N)\to\infty\) and \(r(N)\le\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), such that \(\forall\Pi\) in the specified model deciding Clique, \(\exists C_\Pi>0\;\exists N_\Pi\ge2\;\forall N\ge N_\Pi,\ c_\Pi(N)\ge C_\Pi N^\varepsilon\). The constants governing polynomial circuit size, constant depth and the number of parties are arbitrary and may depend on \(\Pi\), while \(\varepsilon,r\) are chosen before \(\Pi\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified lower-bound statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative proof must cover every polynomial-size constant-depth Alice family and every collection of unrestricted Bob strategies, for the stated growing round budget and some exponent independent of the protocol family. A fixed-round lower bound whose exponent tends to zero as the chosen round count grows does not establish the target. Bounds on the total sum of all parties’ message lengths, a single-Bob model, average-case correctness or a different function do not establish this Clique statement.
context:
The selected sentence follows the source’s conjecture of a polynomial communication lower bound with a growing number of rounds. This card interprets it as the existence of one growing round budget and one positive exponent that work against every polynomial-size constant-depth protocol family, with the lower-bound constant and starting length allowed to depend on the family.

The source uses input-bit length \(n\). This statement fixes a standard graph-and-threshold encoding and uses vertex count \(N\), with \(L_N=\Theta(N^2)\); a fixed positive polynomial exponent remains a fixed positive polynomial exponent under this normalization. The growing budget is capped at \(\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\): existence of a lower bound for any growing budget also entails it for a smaller growing budget. Aggregate polynomial circuit and transcript bounds agree with the source’s polynomial resources in this round range.

In the multiparty model, Alice computes the final answer. An unrestricted Bob does not act as a referee who receives everyone’s messages. The Bobs are independent helpers with access only to their respective conversations with Alice, and only messages from Alice contribute to the stated cost.

Corollary 5.6 states that every function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) has polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) compression games of cost \(n^{O(1/r)}\) for each fixed positive integer \(r\). Here \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) means Boolean functions computed by nonuniform polynomial-size, bounded-fan-in circuits of depth \(O(\log n)\).

The paper consequently identifies the conjectured Clique lower bound as sufficient to separate \(\mathrm{NP}\) from \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\). Its Majority bounds have round-dependent exponents and do not establish the required fixed exponent for Clique with an unbounded round budget.
why: This asks whether many unrestricted helpers can compensate for Alice’s constant-depth computation using short messages and an increasing number of interactions. The source connects a positive answer for Clique to a major nonuniform circuit lower bound. The unusual communication measure makes precise model recovery essential to that connection.
status_note: The conjecture is explicit in the 2015 primary source. Its proved fixed-round Majority results and logarithmic-depth simulation do not settle the selected growing-round Clique bound. Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 identified no resolution, but this dated review does not certify present openness exhaustively.
progress: 2015: Oliveira and Santhanam define the multiparty model in Section 2 and state the growing-round Clique conjecture on printed page 129. | 2015: Corollary 5.6 gives the \(n^{O(1/r)}\) compression upper bound for nonuniform logarithmic-depth functions for every fixed \(r\). The paper’s established Majority lower bounds do not close the selected Clique question.
working_summary: Alice sees a graph and a requested clique size, but her computation is limited to polynomial-size constant-depth Boolean circuits. She can exchange messages with polynomially many unrestricted helpers, each of whom sees only its own conversation. Alice must compute the correct final answer on every input. Communication cost sums the longest message from Alice in each round, and the question asks for a polynomial lower bound even under a growing round budget. The source shows that such a Clique lower bound would separate NP from nonuniform logarithmic-depth circuits.

title: Zero-error query complexity of recursive majority-of-three
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A longstanding benchmark problem in randomized query complexity, with a simple complete specification, nontrivial adaptive behavior and connections to composition and communication complexity. The remaining gap concerns the intrinsic cost of unrestricted exact algorithms, rather than a technical constant in one prescribed procedure.
formal:
Determine, up to multiplicative constants independent of the height \(h\), the zero-error randomized query complexity \(Q(h)\) of the complete height-\(h\) recursive majority-of-three function \(M_h\).

Set \(M_0(x)=x\). For \(h\ge0\), divide an input of length \(3^{h+1}\) into three consecutive blocks \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},x^{(3)}\) of length \(3^h\) and define
\[M_{h+1}(x)=\operatorname{Maj}_3\bigl(M_h(x^{(1)}),M_h(x^{(2)}),M_h(x^{(3)})\bigr),\]
where \(\operatorname{Maj}_3(a,b,c)=1\) exactly when at least two of its three Boolean arguments are one.

An algorithm adaptively queries individual input bits and must always output the correct value. Its cost is the maximum over inputs of its expected number of queries, with expectation only over its internal randomness. If \(\mathcal T_h\) is the finite set of deterministic decision trees computing \(M_h\) without repeating a query on a path, then
\[Q(h)=\min_{\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal T_h)}\ \max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{3^h}}\ \mathbb E_{T\sim\mu}\bigl[q_T(x)\bigr].\]
Here \(q_T(x)\) is the number of queried bits on the input path, and \(\Delta(\mathcal T_h)\) is the set of probability distributions on these trees. The target is matching upper and lower bounds for this full function as \(h\to\infty\), including any nonconstant factors beyond its exponential growth rate.
question_excerpt: In Example 8.64, O’Donnell identifies estimating the zero-error randomized decision-tree complexity of recursively composed majority-of-three as a well-studied open problem. Definition 8.61 measures the maximum, over inputs, of the expected number of queries.
definitions:
The input domain is all bit strings of length \(n=3^h\), with \(h\) any nonnegative integer. Equivalently, bits label the leaves of a known, complete ternary tree, every internal node applies majority to its three children, and the requested output is the root value. The tree shape and the height are known to the algorithm. There is no promise on leaf values, no random input distribution and no promise that a subtree is close to a tie. Recursive majority is not ordinary majority of all \(3^h\) leaves.

A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a leaf-coordinate index \(i\in\{1,\ldots,3^h\}\), its outgoing edges are labeled zero and one, and each terminal node is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), querying a node reveals exactly \(x_i\), costs one unit, and selects the correspondingly labeled edge. Every reachable terminal node must output \(M_h(x)\). One may query coordinates from different subtrees in any order and interleave their evaluation arbitrarily. No requirement to finish one subtree before beginning another is imposed.

Only queries to individual leaf bits are available. Querying an internal majority value, the parity of a set of bits, or a linear combination of bits is not a unit-cost operation. All calculations based on already revealed bits, storage, random sampling and the description of the decision tree are free in this query model. It is a classical model, with no quantum queries. Repeated queries can be answered from the previous reply and removed without increasing cost, so it is harmless to require no repeated coordinate along a path. All such trees have depth at most \(3^h\), and there are finitely many of them for each fixed height.

A randomized decision tree is an input-independent probability distribution \(\mu\) on deterministic trees that each compute the whole function correctly. Its probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, all nonnegative and summing to one. Sampling a tree at the start is equivalent to making random adaptive choices during execution: the algorithm's random choices can be fixed in advance to determine a tree. Zero error requires correctness for every input and every tree assigned positive probability, with no allowed failure output. Since the family of input strings is finite, the almost-sure correctness convention gives the same quantity.

The cost on a fixed input is \(\mathbb E_{T\sim\mu}q_T(x)\). The maximum over \(x\) is taken after these expectations, not inside the expectation. Thus \(Q(h)\) differs from both the uniform-input average cost and the worst query count over all random outcomes. It is also different from bounded-error randomized query complexity, where the output may be wrong with some fixed probability. The minimization over a finite probability simplex attains its value, so \(Q(h)\) is a finite real number; in particular \(Q(0)=1\).

The optimization is performed separately for every height. No bound on the time or description size needed to specify the distribution is part of this model; in particular, no polynomial-time uniform construction of the optimal decision trees is demanded. Both the upper-bound algorithm and the lower bound must address all input strings. An algorithm restricted to a particular traversal order does not define the optimum in this card.

To determine the asymptotic complexity, supply a positive comparison function \(g\) on the nonnegative integers and prove that there are constants \(c,C>0\) and an integer \(h_0\) such that
\[c\,g(h)\le Q(h)\le C\,g(h)\quad\text{for every integer }h\ge h_0.\]
The constants are independent of \(h\). An equivalent statement in the leaf count \(n=3^h\) is acceptable on that domain. A mathematical expression or independently characterized rate may specify \(g\); simply renaming the minimization that defines \(Q\) is not a determination of its growth.

In particular, knowing only a limiting base \(\alpha=\lim_{h\to\infty}Q(h)^{1/h}\) or an exponent \(\log_3\alpha\) need not yield constant-factor bounds on \(Q(h)\): subexponential factors in \(h\) can still matter. Approximating \(\alpha\) within a fixed additive tolerance is weaker still, since distinct fixed bases differ exponentially after raising them to the power \(h\). The requested precision is asymptotic order up to constant factors, not absolute numerical error.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked determination of a positive asymptotic comparison function \(g(h)\), with upper and lower bounds matching up to constants for all sufficiently large integer heights. The upper bound must establish the existence of valid zero-error randomized decision trees with the stated worst-input expected query cost, and the lower bound must hold against every distribution on valid decision trees. It must account for arbitrary adaptive query orders and interleaving. Bounds with different exponential bases, a limiting exponent alone, experiments on finitely many heights, an average-input bound or a lower bound only for restricted traversal algorithms do not settle the target. No efficient uniform algorithm construction is additionally required. The default absolute \(1/100\) tolerance is not applied to this asymptotic complexity target.
context:
Recursive majority is a small, symmetric rule repeated through a deep tree. Although the rule is simple, choosing which leaf values to reveal can exploit information collected in distant parts of the tree. This makes the family a basic test case for the power of adaptive randomization in exact function evaluation.

The deterministic query complexity is \(3^h\), whereas the book records a zero-error upper bound \((8/3)^h\). Thus randomization saves a polynomial factor in the number of leaves even though the algorithm must never make a mistake. The book explicitly notes that this elementary bound is not optimal.

Magniez and coauthors give the upper bound \(Q(h)\le 1.007\cdot 2.64944^h\), as well as improved lower bounds. The journal article appeared online in 2015 and in the 2016 volume; its full author version provides the precise expected-query model and constants.

Göös and Jayram prove a stronger lower bound for bounded-error randomized decision trees, stated in particular as \(\Omega(2.59^h)\). It also lower-bounds the present zero-error expected-cost model up to a constant factor. Their more precise exponential base is \((35/2)^{1/3}\), with a logarithmic loss in converting their theorem to constant-error queries; the lower and upper exponential rates still do not match.

Al-Dhalaan and Ben-David’s 2026 work equates the zero-error and bounded-error composition limits for recursive majority. These limits describe the bases of exponential growth as height increases. The same work explicitly says that their value remains unknown; equality of these limits does not supply matching constant-factor bounds for the query-complexity function on this card.

The source separately discusses average cost under uniformly random inputs. That quantity is not the minimax expected cost retained here. Likewise, results for parity-query trees or quantum algorithms use different access to the input and cannot be substituted for the requested model.
why: Determining this complexity would explain the full power of random adaptive evaluation on one of the simplest recursively defined Boolean functions. It is a canonical setting where exact computation gains substantially from randomization, but the best possible savings are still not understood despite decades of improved bounds.
status_note: Source-open in O’Donnell’s Example 8.64 and still explicitly unresolved in §1.2 of Al-Dhalaan–Ben-David, arXiv:2601.08073v1, submitted 12 January 2026. On 16 September 2026 the original zero-error definition, the 2015/2016 quantitative bounds, the Göös–Jayram improvement, and the 2026 composition-limit statement were read. The 2026 result equates the bounded-error and zero-error exponential rates without determining their value, so it does not resolve this stronger constant-factor asymptotic target. Bounded later-work searches found no matching resolution. This status distinguishes the checked statements from an independent verification of all their proofs or an exhaustive literature search.

The author version’s model, theorem and open-status passage were checked; its full proof was not independently reverified.

working_summary: Recursive majority-of-three evaluates a complete ternary tree whose internal nodes take majority votes. An algorithm may adaptively inspect leaf bits in any order, but it must always return the exact root value. The cost is its largest expected number of queries over all possible inputs.
