title: Sharp low-degree Fourier weight of halfspaces
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A sharp universal low-degree Fourier inequality for all halfspaces describes the spectral structure of a foundational Boolean function class.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every linear threshold function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\), is \(\mathrm{W}^{\le 1}(f)=\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat\{f\}(\{i\})^{2}\ge 2/\pi\)?
definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. Constant functions are included. Under the uniform measure on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), define \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with empty product 1. Thus \(\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )\) is the mean and \(\hat\{f\}(\{i\})\) is the correlation with the i-th coordinate. The displayed squared coefficients are the Fourier weight in degrees zero and one. There is no bound on dimension, weights or bias, and no regularity assumption on the halfspace. The constant \(\pi\) is the usual circle constant.
answer_criterion: Prove the exact universal inequality or give a threshold function with a rigorous proof that its low-degree weight is strictly less than \(2/\pi\). Approximation of the extremal constant to 0.01 would not settle this universal proposition. An algorithm for approximating that constant is already known; the retained target is the source’s sharp inequality.
context:
The low-degree coefficients describe how much of a halfspace is visible through its mean and individual-coordinate correlations. The proposed lower bound holds across all dimensions and all weight vectors.

The source conjectures the bound \(2/\pi\), approached by odd-variable majority functions as dimension increases. The question is not a dimension-dependent numerical experiment.

De, Diakonikolas and Servedio give a lower bound strictly above \(1/2\) and an algorithm approximating the infimum over all halfspaces. Keeping only numerical approximation would weaken this already studied task, so the exact universal inequality is retained.

An August 2026 preprint claims the improved lower bound 0.53317, still below \(2/\pi\). Its proof has not been independently verified in this editorial review.
why: A sharp universal low-degree Fourier inequality for all halfspaces describes the spectral structure of a foundational Boolean function class.
status_note: The universal \(2/\pi\) inequality remains conjectural in the checked sources. The August 2026 preprint gives a claimed partial lower bound, not a resolution.

working_summary: A halfspace is the sign of a weighted sum of input bits and a threshold. Its degree-zero and degree-one Fourier coefficients measure its mean and coordinate correlations. The question asks whether their squared weight is always at least \(2/\pi\). Majority functions approach that proposed universal constant as dimension grows. title: Removing low-influence directions from convex sets
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Dimension-free stability of negligible Gaussian influence would give a general geometric meaning to an irrelevant direction in a convex set.
formal: Does there exist a function \(\tau :(0,1)\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\tau (\varepsilon )=0\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge 1\), every centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), every unit vector v and every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\)? If \(Inf_{v}[K]\le \varepsilon\), then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(C\subseteq v\perp\) such that \(\gamma _{n}(K \triangle  (C+\mathbb{R} v))\le \tau (\varepsilon )\). The same \(\tau\) must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.
definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.
context:
The approximating set is unrestricted along v. Moving any distance parallel to v cannot change membership, although membership may depend arbitrarily on the orthogonal projection.

title: Deterministic communication versus monochromatic partition size
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A basic structural comparison in two-party communication complexity, connecting arbitrary rectangle partitions to realizable protocols and many lower-bound methods. The large exponent gap is resolved by the nearly quadratic separation; the retained target concerns the complete extremal growth rate and must not be presented as though that progress had not occurred.
formal:
Determine the largest deterministic two-party communication complexity possible for a total Boolean function with a given bound on its monochromatic partition size, up to multiplicative constants.

For a total function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) on finite nonempty sets, let \(D(f)\) be its minimum worst-case deterministic communication cost in bits. Let \(\chi(f)\) be the smallest number of pairwise disjoint monochromatic combinatorial rectangles whose union is all of \(X\times Y\). Define, for integers \(t\ge0\),
\[H(t)=\max\bigl\{D(f): X,Y\text{ finite and nonempty},\ f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\},\ \chi(f)\le2^t\bigr\}.\]
The target is the asymptotic order of \(H(t)\) as \(t\to\infty\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to constants independent of \(t\). This includes any nonconstant factors below the known quadratic upper bound; determining only the optimal power exponent does not meet this precision.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 1.12 cites a superlinear separation between deterministic communication and the logarithm of a monochromatic partition size, and asks for the best parameters in the quadratic protocol upper bound. This card retains the two-sided partition comparison explicitly named in that question and in the imported title.
definitions:
Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know the entire function \(f\), the domains and the protocol before receiving their inputs. A deterministic protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies which party sends the next bit and gives a function from that party's private input to \(\{0,1\}\). The node itself encodes the preceding transcript, so each transmitted bit can depend on all previous messages as well as the sender's input. The bit determines the outgoing edge. Every leaf is labeled by an output bit, and on every input pair the reached leaf must be labeled \(f(x,y)\). In this convention both parties know the final output.

The cost of a protocol is the largest number of transmitted bits on any input pair, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost among all correct protocols. Arbitrarily many rounds and either order of speaking are allowed. Local computation, local storage and the advance description of the function or protocol are free. There is no public or private randomness, no error, no nondeterministic witness and no quantum communication. Domains can be named \(\{1,\ldots,|X|\}\) and \(\{1,\ldots,|Y|\}\); transmitting an index uses its binary bits, not a unit-cost unbounded alphabet symbol.

A combinatorial rectangle is a nonempty set \(A\times B\) with \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\). The subsets can be arbitrary; they need not be intervals in a chosen row or column ordering. The rectangle is monochromatic for \(f\) when \(f\) is constant on it. A monochromatic partition is a finite collection of pairwise disjoint such rectangles that covers every input pair exactly once. Rectangles of both output colors are counted. The minimum size \(\chi(f)\) is a positive integer, and \(\chi(f)=1\) exactly for constant functions.

This is a partition of both the zero and one entries of the communication matrix. It is different from a cover that may overlap, from a partition of only the one entries, and from the minimum number of leaves in an actual protocol tree. An arbitrary monochromatic partition is not required to arise by successive row and column splits chosen by a communication protocol. The distinction between these combinatorial and protocol partitions is central to the question.

The parameter \(t\) is an integer bound on \(\lceil\log_2\chi(f)\rceil\); every logarithm here has base two. There is no bound on \(|X|\) or \(|Y|\) other than finiteness, and the maximum defining \(H(t)\) ranges over all their choices and all total Boolean functions. One may restrict to numbered finite sets to make this a set-indexed definition. Partial functions with unspecified or promised-away matrix entries are not included.

The universal upper bound \(D(f)=O((\log_2\chi(f))^2)\) for nonconstant functions shows that the set of integer costs in the definition of \(H(t)\) is bounded for each \(t\). It is nonempty because constant functions are allowed, and thus its maximum exists and is attained by at least one finite function. In particular \(H(0)=0\). No unique extremizing matrix is presumed.

An asymptotic answer supplies a positive comparison function \(g\) on the positive integers and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(t_0\ge1\) such that
\[c\,g(t)\le H(t)\le C\,g(t)\quad\text{for every integer }t\ge t_0.\]
The constants do not depend on \(t\), the matrix dimensions or the function. The upper bound must apply to every total Boolean function with \(\chi(f)\le2^t\). The lower bound must establish, for every sufficiently large \(t\), a finite total function with that partition-size bound and deterministic cost at least \(c g(t)\). No efficient algorithm for constructing the lower-bound examples or for finding an optimal protocol is imposed.

The target is the full worst-case rate up to constant factors. For instance, separating the measures by a power arbitrarily close to two establishes the optimal exponent against any fixed smaller power, but does not distinguish a quadratic rate from a quadratic rate divided by an unbounded slowly growing factor. Simply repeating the maximum that defines \(H\), or computing it for finitely many parameters, is not an asymptotic determination.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic order of \(H(t)\), giving a comparison function and matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants for all sufficiently large integer \(t\). The proof must use arbitrary-round, deterministic, worst-case bit communication for total Boolean functions and the two-sided disjoint rectangle partition defined here. An upper bound for all functions and a lower-bound family must establish the same rate; a separation merely approaching the optimal exponent is insufficient if nonconstant factors remain unresolved. A result about overlapping covers, one-color partitions, randomized communication or partial functions does not by itself settle this target. No uniform efficient construction is required. The default absolute numerical tolerance does not apply to this asymptotic question.
context:
A deterministic conversation identifies its input pair by following a sequence of decisions, each based on one participant’s knowledge. Every terminal transcript corresponds to a monochromatic rectangle, so a short protocol necessarily provides a small partition of the communication matrix.

The converse asks how much more communication is needed to turn a compact combinatorial description into an actual conversation. A partition may describe where every output occurs without providing either participant with a cheap way to determine which rectangle contains their private pair of inputs.

The standard bounds are \(\log_2\chi(f)\le D(f)\le O((\log_2\chi(f))^2)\) for nonconstant total functions. The upper theorem in the draft even allows overlapping monochromatic covers; disjoint partitions satisfy its hypothesis. The present target is specifically the partition variant in the source’s separation question.

The draft cites the 2015 separation of Göös, Pitassi and Watson. Ambainis, Kokainis and Kothari subsequently establish families with \(D(f)\ge(\log_2\chi(f))^{2-o(1)}\), showing that no fixed power below two can be a universal upper bound. This settles the power-exponent aspect of the earlier gap, but the theorem is described as nearly optimal and does not give a constant-factor determination of \(H(t)\).

The partition number is a structural lower bound on communication, rather than an algorithmic cost of finding the partition. Both parties may know the partition and still need a substantial conversation to locate their input. Computational hardness of discovering an optimal partition is therefore a different issue.

The inherited draft asks for the optimal gap without defining a comparison function. Writing the extremal envelope H(t) makes that quantitative target explicit and avoids replacing it by a single threshold assertion. The requested asymptotic precision retains slowly varying factors that an exponent-only formulation would discard.
why: This tradeoff measures how much information a small monochromatic partition fails to capture about an executable communication protocol. Determining it sharply would delineate the power and limitations of a central combinatorial lower bound on deterministic communication, beyond knowing only its quadratic exponent.

The 2016 Ambainis–Kokainis–Kothari theorem resolves optimality of the quadratic exponent via a lower bound with exponent 2−o(1), but does not determine the finer constant-factor asymptotic rate required here. On 16 September 2026 the draft definitions/question and the 2016 theorem were read, and bounded later-work searches found no constant-factor matching result for the two-sided partition envelope. A checked August 2026 preprint on optimal unambiguous DNFs gives one-sided partition/cover and log-rank statements, which are different comparisons. This status is based on dated sources and a limited literature review, not an exhaustive current-openness certification.

The exponent approaches two, matching the universal upper-bound exponent while leaving the finer constant-factor rate undetermined by that theorem.

working_summary: Alice and Bob must compute a Boolean function of their separate inputs by exchanging bits. A monochromatic partition divides its entire communication matrix into disjoint rectangles on which the output is constant. The question asks for the greatest possible deterministic communication cost when the logarithm of that partition size is at most t. A quadratic upper bound and nearly quadratic separations determine the optimal exponent, but do not by themselves settle all nonconstant factors. This card asks for upper and lower bounds on the full worst-case rate that match up to multiplicative constants.

title: Optimal time exponent for truth-table decision-tree depth
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A well-motivated meta-complexity question for a fundamental computational model: complete input-output information still leaves an optimization problem whose sharp sequential exponent is unknown in the source. It connects query complexity with algorithm design and separates sequential efficiency from parallel hardness. Its scope is more specialized than a general complexity-class separation, but the full-truth-table setting makes it a clean and consequential test case rather than a parameter adjustment to one algorithm.
formal:
Determine the real number
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}=\inf\mathcal E,
\]
where \(\mathcal E\) is the set of real \(a\ge0\) for which one deterministic word-RAM program computes the minimum decision-tree depth of every Boolean function, from its complete truth table of length \(N\), in worst-case time \(O(N^a)\). The input, output, machine and quantifiers defining \(\mathcal E\) are specified below. Give a real answer \(v\) and a complete Lean proof of
\[
|v-\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
This is the user-selected optimal-exponent refinement of the source's broader request for exact sequential time complexity. It measures the exponent in truth-table length \(N=2^n\), not in the number \(n\) of variables. It does not ask for a constant-factor characterization of the entire running-time function, or for the depth of a parallel circuit solving the task. The infimum need not be attained by any one algorithm.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), a Boolean function is a map \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\). Its truth table is the binary array \(X\) of length \(N=2^n\), with positions numbered from zero, in increasing lexicographic order of the input strings; thus the binary expansion of the array index, padded to \(n\) bits, is the argument of \(f\). All \(2^N\) truth tables at each length are valid inputs.

A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree with an input-coordinate label in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) at each internal node, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and a Boolean output at each leaf. On input \(x\), it follows the edge labeled \(x_i\) at a node labeled \(i\), and returns the reached leaf's value. It computes \(f\) if that value equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\). Its depth is the largest number of internal nodes on a root-to-leaf path. Define \(D(f)\) to be the least depth of a tree computing \(f\); it is an integer between zero and \(n\). The required algorithmic output is exactly this integer, not a tree, its number of leaves, an average depth, or an approximation to \(D(f)\).

The computational model is the following explicit deterministic word RAM. Its description contains a finite program, a finite number of named registers, finitely many nonnegative integer constants written in binary, and a positive integer \(d\). These are fixed independently of the input. On an \(n\)-variable instance the word width is
\[
w=d(n+2).
\]
Registers and memory cells hold unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The read-only input array contains one truth-table bit per word, in the order just defined. Separate read-only registers give \(n,N,w\). Work memory is an array indexed by all \(w\)-bit addresses, initially zero, and the program's writable registers initially contain zero. There is no other precomputed data. Initial input placement and provision of the three size registers are not charged; examining input values is charged.

One instruction may load a fixed constant reduced modulo \(2^w\), copy a register, read one input cell at a register address, read or write one work-memory cell at a register address, or apply one of the following operations to at most two register operands: addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement on \(w\) bits; logical left or right shift by the unsigned value of a register; equality or unsigned-order comparison. Shifted-out bits are discarded, vacated bits are zero, and a shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Conditional branches use the comparison result and jump to one of the finitely many program labels. A halt instruction returns one designated register. Every instruction costs one step, including every memory access, comparison, branch and halt. Instructions have fixed register operands and labels in the finite description; arbitrary code, tables or computations cannot be supplied as a constant-time instruction. A zero divisor or out-of-range input-array access is a failure, not a permitted oracle result. Addresses for work memory are always \(w\)-bit unsigned integers. There is no randomness, advice, real arithmetic, unbounded-precision unit-cost operation, parallelism or access to a tree oracle. All preprocessing must use the same charged instructions.

For a program \(A\), including its declared \(d\), let \(\tau_A(X)\) be its step count if it halts normally on \(X\), and \(+\infty\) if it does not halt or incurs a failure. Let \(f_X\) denote the function with table \(X\). Precisely,
\[
\mathcal E=\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\
\exists A\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall X\in\{0,1\}^{2^n},\quad
\tau_A(X)\le C(2^n)^a\ \land\ A(X)=D(f_X)\right\}.
\]
The output equality requires normal halting with that value. The exponent and program are chosen before all input lengths and tables. The multiplicative constant \(C\) is independent of them. This all-length convention is equivalent to allowing a finite initial range of exceptional lengths and changing the fixed program and constant there. Different candidate exponents may use different finite programs and word-width constants.

The set \(\mathcal E\) is nonempty and bounded below. In this model the elementary input-reading lower bound and the source's sequential upper bound give
\[
1\le\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\le\log_2 3.
\]
The upper endpoint is an infimum bound: the known running time includes a polynomial factor in \(n\), and need not belong to \(O(N^{\log_2 3})\) itself. The source states its sequential bound on a random-access machine; the finite word width, instruction set and explicit input layout above make that convention precise. No exact equivalence of running times on all machine models is asserted.
answer_criterion:
Supply an unambiguous real value \(v\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|v-\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}|\le1/100\). Alternatively, supply a certified real interval \([\ell,u]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\) with width at most \(1/50\). The interval's midpoint is then an admissible real approximation. The answer need not be an integer or an exact closed form. Merely repeating the defining infimum without establishing its location does not determine the requested value.

Bounds must control the full algorithm class. An upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\le u\) can be certified by showing that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed program and constant achieve correct worst-case time \(C N^{u+\varepsilon}\) on every truth table; the program and constant may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No single program attaining exponent \(u\) is required. A lower bound \(\ell\le\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\) must exclude every exponent \(0\le a<\ell\): for every candidate program and constant, some length and table must exceed its proposed \(C N^a\) bound or violate exact correctness. A lower bound for one algorithm does not give this conclusion.

Both sides needed for the numerical tolerance must be proved. A conditional lower bound settles only the conditional statement unless the extra assumption is also established. Faster evaluation of a supplied decision tree, computation from a succinct circuit, approximation to \(D(f)\), optimization of leaf count, and parallel-circuit depth are different targets. The numerical tolerance applies to the optimal time exponent; the algorithms in its definition must still compute \(D(f)\) exactly.
context:
The input lists every value of a Boolean function, while the desired output is the minimum worst-case number of bit queries needed to evaluate that function.

The source gives a sequential random-access algorithm taking \(O(3^n n)\) time for a truth table of length \(2^n\).

Its parallel circuit upper bound and hardness result concern a different resource and do not determine the best sequential exponent.

The source explicitly asks whether the sequential algorithm can be improved and whether meaningful lower bounds can be proved.

This card selects the optimal exponent with real numerical acceptance, preserving the source task while making the requested precision and machine model explicit.
why: This is a basic question in the complexity of optimizing a computational model when its entire input-output behavior is already explicit. It separates knowing every value of a Boolean function from finding its best adaptive query depth. The source establishes polynomial-time solvability and parallel hardness, leaving a substantial gap in the sequential exponent; narrowing that gap would sharpen our understanding of decision-tree optimization and this form of meta-complexity.
status_note: The 2025 source explicitly asks for improved sequential time and lower bounds for the exact truth-table depth task. The user selected its optimal deterministic time exponent as a precise numerical refinement. A bounded primary-source check through 16 September 2026 found no determination to the stated tolerance; checked 2026 results concern restrictions or average-cost approximation instead. This is a source-open assessment with a disclosed model and precision choice, not an exhaustive literature certificate.

Proposition 9 and Theorem 11 separately bound parallel depth and give NC1 hardness. | 2026-09-16: The user selected the optimal sequential time exponent as the precise numerical target. Checked later primary works on restriction-based hardness condensation and average-cost decision-tree approximation concern other tasks and do not determine this exponent.
working_summary: Given the complete truth table of a Boolean function, the task is to compute the minimum worst-case depth of a decision tree evaluating it. The known sequential upper bound is polynomial in the table length but has an exponent larger than one. This card asks for the infimum deterministic time exponent in a fixed finite-word random-access model, allowing different uniform algorithms for different candidate exponents. That exponent separates the cost of optimizing query depth from the query depth itself and from parallel complexity. An accepted answer must give a real approximation within 1/100 and a complete Lean proof, without assuming that an algorithm attains the infimum.

title: Two-sided versus one-sided randomized communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: The question compares the full polylogarithmic power of two-sided randomized communication with deterministic adaptive use of every one-sided randomized test, across all total functions.
formal:
For total Boolean two-party function families, is
\[
\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{RP}^{\mathrm{cc}}}\,?
\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}\) consists of families with public-coin randomized protocols using a polylogarithmic number of communicated bits and error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The class on the right consists of families computed exactly by deterministic protocols with adaptive access to ideal one-sided-error communication oracles, with polylogarithmic total charged cost as defined below.

Equivalently, does every total family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\), where \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with
\[
R_{1/3}^{\mathrm{pub}}(F_n)\le C(\log_2(n+2))^a
\]
for some fixed \(C\ge1,a\ge0\), admit deterministic oracle protocols of cost at most
\[
C'(\log_2(n+2))^b
\]
for some fixed \(C'\ge1,b\ge0\) and every \(n\)? The latter constants may depend on the family. There are no promised or undefined inputs.
question_excerpt: The introduction asks whether two-sided-error communication and deterministic adaptive access to one-sided-error communication oracles have the same power for total functions.
definitions:
Alice receives \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), Bob receives \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\), and both know \(n\), the target function and their protocol. A deterministic protocol is a finite binary tree. At an internal node, the designated party sends one bit determined by that party's entire input and the public transcript. A leaf has a common output bit. Its cost is its maximum depth. Local computation, local storage and the size of the protocol description are unrestricted.

A public-coin randomized protocol is a distribution over such deterministic protocols, sampled using shared randomness independent of the inputs. Its cost is the maximum communication cost over its support, rather than an expected cost. It computes a total function \(G\) with two-sided error \(1/3\) if, on every pair \((x,y)\), its output equals \(G(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Define \(R_{1/3}^{\mathrm{pub}}(G)\) as the least possible cost.

For a total function \(G\) on the same input domain, define \(R_{\mathrm{RP}}^{\mathrm{pub}}(G)\) using public-coin protocols that satisfy
\[
G(x,y)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[\text{output }1]=0,\qquad
G(x,y)=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[\text{output }1]\ge\frac12 .
\]
Only false negatives are allowed. Every deterministic protocol in the support must obey the same worst-case communication bound. The constant \(1/2\) can be replaced by another fixed positive success probability using amplification. The cost is finite because exchanging both inputs computes any \(G\) exactly.

An ideal deterministic RP-oracle protocol is a finite binary tree with two permitted kinds of internal node. An ordinary communication node sends one locally determined bit and costs one. An oracle node is labelled by an arbitrary total Boolean function \(G_v(x,y)\). It reveals the exact bit \(G_v(x,y)\) to both parties and costs
\[
1+R_{\mathrm{RP}}^{\mathrm{pub}}(G_v).
\]
Its label and the next node may depend on the previous transcript and previous oracle answers. A leaf has a common output bit. The protocol must output \(F_n(x,y)\) exactly on every input, when all oracle answers are exact. Its charged cost is the maximum sum of node costs over root-to-leaf paths. In particular, the number of queries is counted and can grow polylogarithmically; it is not required to be a fixed constant.

Each \(G_v\) is defined on all \(n\)-bit input pairs, including those that never reach node \(v\). Private local transformations of an input can be included in \(G_v\), and their local computation is free. The oracle computes a joint function; it does not reveal the other party's input. Oracle answers are ideal exact answers to functions that possess one-sided-error protocols, not individual noisy samples from those protocols. Neither party has private information about an oracle's answers beyond the public returned bits.

This weighted-tree description is the communication-cost formulation of adaptive access to RP oracles: the cost of each requested computation is charged, and the extra one charges the query itself. Fixing any constant-factor variation in this charging convention gives the same polylogarithmic class. The oracle functions, ordinary protocol and public-coin distributions may depend on \(n\). There is no uniform algorithmic-generation or running-time requirement on these objects; the resource is communication.

A family belongs to either displayed class only if one fixed polynomial in \(\log_2(n+2)\) bounds its respective cost for all \(n\). The oracle class is contained in \(\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}\): each test can be amplified and simulated with enough accuracy for the polylogarithmic sequence. Thus the substantive direction is the containment from two-sided randomized protocols to deterministic RP-oracle protocols.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal total-function containment in the formal question. A positive answer must cover every total family with polylogarithmic public-coin two-sided-error communication. A negative answer must establish a total family in \(\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}\) for which no polylogarithmic charged-cost deterministic RP-oracle family exists. A separation only for partial functions, only against one particular oracle, or only for a fixed constant number of queries is insufficient. The target is a binary class equality; numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not relax it.
context:
Equality admits a very short public-coin fingerprinting protocol. The source explains that this particular oracle does not account for every efficient randomized communication problem. Enlarging the oracle class to all RP functions leads to the target here.

An ideal oracle answer is exact even though the function is characterized by a one-sided-error protocol. Treating every oracle call as a fresh unamplified random answer would change the deterministic oracle model.

The source proves that allowing successively more constant numbers of queries gives a strict hierarchy. This does not rule out a simulation using a growing polylogarithmic number of queries.

Totality is a substantive restriction. The source distinguishes this open equality from known separations that use input promises.

The August 2026 preprint studies stronger oracle and pseudodeterministic distinctions with partial functions. Its stated separation involving deterministic RP-oracle access therefore does not settle the all-total-input formulation.

The 2025 Hamming-distance separation rules out a specific family of constant-cost oracle simulations. It does not exclude polylogarithmic adaptive access to arbitrary RP functions.
why: Many randomized communication algorithms use a few kinds of tests that can be wrong in only one direction. The question asks whether arbitrary two-sided randomized interaction can always be organized around such tests while retaining efficient communication. Either outcome would clarify the role of randomness in the structural hierarchy of two-party protocols.
status_note: The ICALP 2020 source explicitly leaves the total-function equality open. The checked August 2026 oracle-separation paper works in a partial-function setting, while recent Hamming-distance results restrict the oracle or change the resource bound. No resolution of the stated total-function equality was found in the bounded source review.
progress: 2020: The ICALP paper states the total-function equality as open and separates every fixed level of the randomized Boolean hierarchy. | 2025-05-06: The revised Hamming-distance paper gives a separation for constant-cost reductions to those specific oracles. | 2026-08-26: A new preprint separates further communication classes in an ambient partial-function setting. | 2026-09-16: The review fixes totality, public randomness, adaptive exact oracle answers and polylogarithmic cost; no resolution of this target is found.
working_summary: Two parties want to compute a total Boolean function using little communication. The question asks whether every efficient two-sided randomized protocol can be replaced by deterministic adaptive queries to one-sided randomized tests. Oracle answers are exact, and each query is charged the communication needed by its one-sided-error protocol. The total communication and query cost may grow polynomially in the logarithm of the input length. Known constant-query hierarchy separations and partial-function results do not resolve this total-function equality.

title: A randomized-communication characterization of ordinary KW games
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A structural bridge between total search, communication and Boolean circuit games. The selected candidate makes a broad characterization program falsifiable, while its status must remain explicitly separate from the source’s established monotone theorem.
formal:
Is the following candidate characterization true? For every family of total two-party search relations \((R_n)_{n\ge2}\) with polynomially bounded input and answer lengths and deterministic polylogarithmic communication for verifying a proposed answer, the following are equivalent:

1. \(R_n\) has a public-coin randomized protocol with polylogarithmic communication and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair.
2. \(R_n\) is equivalent, under deterministic polylogarithmic-communication mapping reductions in both directions, to the ordinary Karchmer–Wigderson game of a partial Boolean function on at most quasipolynomially many variables.

All bounds, quantifiers, models and reductions are specified below. This is a user-selected editorial candidate, not a conjecture asserted verbatim by the source.
question_excerpt: The source asks for a communication characterization of nonmonotone KW games after proving the analogous monotone representation theorem. It does not propose the equality with cheaply verifiable randomized-polylogarithmic search. The user explicitly selected that editorial candidate, with deterministic polylogarithmic mapping equivalence and the quasipolynomial dimension convention made precise here.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(X_n,Y_n\) be nonempty subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{n^{a}}\), let \(1\le\ell_n\le n^{a}\), and let
\[
R_n\subseteq X_n\times Y_n\times[\ell_n],\qquad [\ell]=\{1,\ldots,\ell\},
\]
where the integer \(a\ge1\) is fixed for the family. Totality means that for every \((x,y)\in X_n\times Y_n\), at least one \(i\in[\ell_n]\) satisfies \(R_n(x,y,i)\). Alice receives \(x\), Bob receives \(y\), and both must output a common valid \(i\).

A deterministic verification protocol is given \(i\) publicly, in addition to the split input \((x,y)\), and both parties determine exactly whether \(R_n(x,y,i)\) holds. Assume there are constants \(K>0\) and an integer \(b\ge1\), independent of \(n\), such that this uses at most \(K(\log_2(n+2))^b\) communicated bits on every input and every proposed answer. These are the communication analogues of total, efficiently verifiable search relations. There is no algorithmic uniformity, local-computation, or finite-description requirement on the family or its local operations; this is a communication-complexity assertion, not ordinary Turing-machine TFNP.

In condition 1, for each \(n\) a protocol has access to a finite public string of independent fair random bits. Its length is unrestricted and uncharged. Its worst-case number of communicated bits, over every input and random string, is at most \(K'(\log_2(n+2))^{b'}\) for constants \(K',b'\) fixed for the family. On every input pair, the probability that both parties output one common \(i\) satisfying \(R_n(x,y,i)\) is at least \(2/3\). The error is over the public randomness, not an input distribution. Local computation is free. Communication is by the ordinary binary protocol-tree model; speaker identity and termination are determined by the public transcript and randomness and do not transmit extra information for free.

An ordinary KW game is specified by two nonempty disjoint sets \(A_n,B_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^{m_n}\). Equivalently, a partial Boolean function \(f_n\) is zero on \(A_n\), one on \(B_n\), and undefined elsewhere. Alice receives \(u\in A_n\), Bob receives \(v\in B_n\), and a valid answer is any \(j\in[m_n]\) with \(u_j\ne v_j\). No order between these two bits is required. Neither set must be monotone, and no circuit-size, computational-uniformity or decidability bound is imposed on \(f_n\).

A deterministic \(t\)-bit mapping reduction from a relation \(S\subseteq X\times Y\times I\) to \(S'\subseteq X'\times Y'\times I'\) consists of local maps \(M_A:X\to X'\), \(M_B:Y\to Y'\), and a deterministic two-party decoder. Given \(x,y\) and any publicly supplied \(j\in I'\) with
\[
S'(M_A(x),M_B(y),j),
\]
the decoder uses at most \(t\) bits of communication and both parties output one common \(i\in I\) satisfying \(S(x,y,i)\). Correctness is required for every valid target answer, not just answers chosen by one preferred target solver. The decoder halts within its communication bound for all candidate \(j\), even if the target relation does not hold. The local maps incur no communication cost; their description and evaluation times are unrestricted. There is one mapped target instance and one returned answer, with no adaptive oracle calls.

Precisely, condition 2 says that there exist constants \(K''>0\), an integer \(b''\ge1\), and for every \(n\) an integer
\[
1\le m_n\le2^{K''(\log_2(n+2))^{b''}},
\]
a partial function \(f_n\) as above, and reductions in both directions between \(R_n\) and \(\operatorname{KW}(f_n)\), each with at most \(K''(\log_2(n+2))^{b''}\) bits of decoding communication. The two pairs of local maps need not be inverse functions. All choices may depend on the relation family and \(n\), but the constants and exponents must work for the entire family. The quasipolynomial dimension convention matches the exponential-in-verification-cost expansion in the source's monotone comparison. Merely representing an arbitrary relation with exponentially many coordinates in \(n\) does not meet this bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of this candidate equivalence for all relation families meeting the stated conditions. A proof must supply the quantified communication bounds and both mapping reductions, valid for every target answer. A refutation may give a family with cheap verification and randomized solution but no such ordinary-KW equivalence, with a complete impossibility proof. Proving only the necessary randomized upper bound, the monotone version, or a weaker one-way or randomized reduction does not settle the assertion.
context:
The source’s Lemma 12 represents a total relation with t-bit answer verification as a monotone KW game on at most 2ᵗ times the number of answers coordinates, with t-bit mapping reductions in both directions. For polylogarithmic verification this allows a quasipolynomial number of coordinates.

Ordinary KW asks only for a differing coordinate. Randomized fingerprinting can locate one with polylogarithmic communication, independently of the complexity of the underlying partial function; the cited discussion records an even sharper logarithmic bound. This gives a necessary randomized upper bound for relations reducing to such games.

Monotone games impose a direction on the differing bits and can have polynomial randomized communication complexity. The ordinary-game characterization therefore cannot simply repeat the source’s unrestricted monotone TFNP representation.

The difficult direction of the selected candidate is sufficiency: cheap verification and a randomized protocol would have to yield deterministic mapping equivalence to an ordinary game of the stated dimension. The reviewed sources neither state nor prove this exact assertion.

The source’s next question concerns reductions between games versus low-depth reductions between Boolean functions. That is a separate target and is not substituted for the characterization selected here.
why: An intrinsic characterization would explain which total communication search tasks arise from ordinary Boolean function separation. It would connect randomized communication with the structural reductions behind circuit-depth games, while distinguishing ordinary games from their monotone counterparts.

working_summary: An ordinary Karchmer–Wigderson game asks two parties to find a coordinate where their differently classified Boolean inputs disagree. The selected candidate says these games capture exactly total search tasks with cheap answer verification and cheap randomized communication. Capture means deterministic mapping reductions in both directions, with polylogarithmic communication and at most quasipolynomially many target coordinates. Ordinary games have cheap randomized protocols, whereas the known monotone representation theorem covers a broader class of total search tasks. title: Formula size versus partition complexity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Comparing representation sizes for circuits, formulas, or partitions probes a general source of succinctness.
formal: Are there universal constants \(C\ge1\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every nonconstant Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every \(n\ge1\), satisfies \(L(f)\le C\,\chi(f)^d\)? Here \(L(f)\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size, and \(\chi(f)\) is the minimum number of disjoint coordinate-monochromatic rectangles partitioning \(f^{-1}(1)\times f^{-1}(0)\). The polynomial bound must depend only on \(\chi(f)\), with no additional factor depending on \(n\).
definitions: A De Morgan formula on \(n\) variables is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is AND or OR; each leaf is one literal \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Evaluation uses the usual Boolean operations. Repeated occurrences of the same literal count as separate leaves, and subtrees cannot be shared. The leaf size is the total number of leaves. Define \(L(f)\) as the minimum leaf size among formulas evaluating to \(f(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Formulas need not be monotone, balanced, depth-bounded or uniformly constructible. Let \(A=f^{-1}(1)\) and \(B=f^{-1}(0)\), both nonempty because \(f\) is nonconstant. A rectangle is a nonempty Cartesian product \(U\times V\) with \(U\subseteq A\) and \(V\subseteq B\). It is coordinate-monochromatic if there are a coordinate \(i\in[n]\) and a bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(u_i=b\) for every \(u\in U\) and \(v_i=1-b\) for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, a single literal separates the two sides, with either orientation permitted. A partition is a finite collection of such rectangles whose union is all of \(A\times B\), with distinct rectangles pairwise disjoint as subsets of ordered pairs. Row sets may overlap across rectangles, and column sets may overlap, provided the products do not. Define \(\chi(f)\) as the minimum number of rectangles in any such partition; coordinate labels and the descriptions of the row and column sets have no additional cost. Every pair \(a\in A,b\in B\) differs in some coordinate, so a singleton partition exists and \(\chi(f)\ge1\) is finite. No recursive or protocol-tree condition is imposed on a partition. The statement quantifies \(\exists C,d\;\forall n\;\forall f\) with the domains above. Both measures are nonuniform finite mathematical minima; no algorithm converting a partition into a formula is required. Restricting to nonconstant functions removes the empty-rectangle convention for constants without changing the substantive comparison.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a universal polynomial bound \(L(f)\le C\chi(f)^d\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\forall C\ge1\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\exists n\ge1\;\exists f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) nonconstant with \(L(f)>C\chi(f)^d\). Refuting one proposed exponent or giving a constant-factor gap is insufficient to refute all polynomial bounds. A result for arbitrary communication relations, overlapping covers, positively oriented monotone partitions or algebraic tilings does not automatically establish the target for the defined partitions of total Boolean functions.
context:
The imported early draft states the question as Research Problem 6.24 after Rychkov’s lemma. Its tiling number is a coordinate-labelled partition of accepting versus rejecting inputs, rather than a partition of the Boolean input cube or a tiling by constant output bits.

Rychkov’s lemma gives \(\chi(f)\le L(f)\). The question asks whether the reverse comparison holds with one fixed polynomial for every Boolean function. The known bound recorded by the source is \(L(f)\le\chi(f)^{2\log_2\chi(f)}\), which is quasipolynomial rather than polynomial.

Disjointness is essential to the measure: overlapping coordinate rectangles can cover every accepting–rejecting pair using only twice the number of variables. The task concerns the minimum disjoint partition, not the size of such an unrestricted cover.

Neither the formulas nor the functions are required to be monotone. Both orientations of a differing coordinate are allowed in a partition rectangle. The source separately defines positively monochromatic partitions for monotone formula questions.

Jukna’s second expanded edition draft dated 14 September 2026 retains the exact question as Research Problem 6.1 on printed page 277. It again states that the polynomial inverse is unknown and records the same quasipolynomial upper bound. This is a dated author draft, not a claim of publication of the second edition.
why: A formula organizes computation hierarchically, whereas a rectangle partition only gives a disjoint collection of valid local distinctions between accepting and rejecting inputs. The question asks whether this absence of an imposed hierarchy can yield more than polynomial savings. A resolution would determine how closely a central combinatorial lower-bound measure captures general formula size.

Bounded checks through 2026-09-16 found no newer resolution of the exact measure. The draft’s date and status are recorded without implying publication or an exhaustive proof audit.

working_summary: A De Morgan formula computes a Boolean function with an expression tree whose leaves are literals. Its partition measure counts disjoint rectangles pairing accepting and rejecting inputs, each certified by one differing coordinate. The question asks whether formula leaf size is always bounded by a fixed polynomial in that rectangle count. The partition need not already be organized as a recursive communication protocol, which is the source of the possible gap. title: Linearization conjecture for depth-two circuits
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Efficient linearization would relate unrestricted computation to the more tractable model of linear circuits.
formal:
Is there an absolute integer \(C\ge1\) with the following property?

For every \(n\ge1\), every matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\), and all integers \(w,d\ge0\), if the linear map \(x\mapsto Ax\) is computed exactly by a depth-two circuit with arbitrary Boolean gates, width at most \(w\), and degree at most \(d\), then it is computed exactly by a linear depth-two circuit with width at most \(Cw\) and degree at most \(Cd\).

Width counts middle-layer gates. Degree counts, for each output separately, only the direct wires from the original input variables; it does not count wires through middle-layer gates. Both notions and the gate models are defined below. The constant \(C\) is independent of the matrix, dimensions and resource bounds.
question_excerpt: Research Problem 13.14 asks whether a linear operator computed with arbitrary depth-two gates can also be computed with linear gates while increasing both degree and width only by constant factors.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition modulo two and ordinary bit multiplication. For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), the required output has coordinates
\[
(Ax)_i=\bigoplus_{j:A_{ij}=1}x_j .
\]
The circuit is deterministic and may depend arbitrarily on \(A\); no uniformity requirement is imposed.

A depth-two circuit of width \(r\) has \(n\) input bits, \(r\) middle-layer gates computing arbitrary functions \(h_j:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), and \(n\) output gates. For each output \(i\), choose a fixed set \(S_i\subseteq[n]\) and an arbitrary Boolean function \(g_i\) such that the output is
\[
g_i\bigl(x_{S_i},h_1(x),\ldots,h_r(x)\bigr).
\]
The set \(S_i\) lists its direct input wires. Its middle-gate inputs can be any subset of the displayed values; unused arguments can be ignored. Gates have unrestricted fan-in and arbitrary truth tables. There are no edges between gates in the same layer. Input bits may connect directly to output gates. The width is \(r\), and the degree is \(\max_i|S_i|\). Neither the number of input-to-middle wires nor the number of middle-to-output wires is included in degree.

Such a circuit computes \(Ax\) exactly if every displayed output equals \((Ax)_i\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Agreement only on the standard basis vectors, or on most inputs, is not sufficient. An arbitrary gate may compute a nonlinear Boolean function even though the final map is linear.

A linear depth-two circuit has the same graph convention, but each gate computes a linear form over \(\mathbb F_2\): a parity of some of its inputs, including the empty parity zero. No nonzero constant term is needed. Thus, with \(r\) middle gates, its transformation has the form
\[
Ax=L(Rx)+Ex,\qquad
R\in\mathbb F_2^{r\times n},\quad
L\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times r},\quad
E\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}.
\]
Its direct-input degree is the maximum number of nonzero entries in a row of \(E\). Equivalently, the desired conclusion is that
\[
A=B+E,\qquad
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(B)\le Cw,\qquad
\max_i|\{j:E_{ij}\ne0\}|\le Cd.
\]
A rank factorization of \(B\) gives the middle-layer linear forms, so this is precisely the same existence target.

The conclusion may choose new direct-input sets and a new middle layer; it need not preserve the input circuit graph. It must bound both width and degree simultaneously. The cases \(w=0\) and \(d=0\) use the displayed multiplicative bounds without additive slack. One may restrict \(0\le d\le n\), since larger direct degree adds no power. There is no restriction on truth-table description size, total circuit wire count or the time needed to find the linear circuit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal constant-factor linearization statement. A proof may use either the circuit formulation or the equivalent rank-plus-row-sparsity formulation, with the equivalence justified. A refutation must show that no universal \(C\) works. A conversion with a growing factor, a result only for selected matrices, or agreement on a restricted set of inputs is insufficient. This is a binary proposition; \(1/100\) numerical tolerance does not alter either resource bound.
context:
This degree measure ignores the wires through the shared middle layer. Bounding ordinary gate fan-in, all graph degrees or total wires would give a different conjecture.

A middle gate is an arbitrary one-bit summary of the whole input. Each output can inspect the shared summaries and its fixed collection of direct input bits. The question asks whether linear summaries are always comparably effective.

For a linear circuit, the shared summaries correspond to a low-rank matrix, while direct input wires give a matrix sparse in every row. This connects the resource tradeoff to matrix rigidity.

The source distinguishes representing a matrix on unit input vectors from computing its linear operator on every Boolean vector. Nonlinear circuits can behave quite differently in the representation problem, which does not refute this conjecture.

The 2020 report restates the same conjecture and proves an implication from a stronger rigidity comparison. That conditional implication supplies additional motivation, not a proof of linearization.

The 2022 report studies related linearization assumptions for data structures and derives consequences for the Multiphase Conjecture. Its extra model and hypotheses are not part of this card.
why: A short nonlinear summary of the input might help answer many linear queries even when no equally short linear summary is available. The conjecture asks whether that advantage disappears up to constant factors when the only other resource is a few direct input bits per output. It would connect matrix-based lower bounds more closely to unrestricted Boolean computation.
status_note: The author-hosted book draft poses this constant-factor linearization problem, and the checked later work restates it or studies strengthened data-structure variants. No general proof or counterexample was found in the bounded later-source review. The target concerns existence, without a running-time requirement on finding the linear circuit.
