working_summary: A depth-two Boolean circuit computes a linear transformation using shared middle-layer gates and direct input wires. The question asks whether all its gates can be made linear with only constant-factor increases in width and direct-input degree. Middle-layer gates may initially compute arbitrary Boolean functions, and every input vector must be handled exactly. The linear conclusion is equivalent to decomposing the matrix into a low-rank part and a part sparse in each row. The target is existence of such circuits, without a requirement to find the conversion efficiently.

title: PSPACE-hardness of a factor-two gap in decision-tree depth
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Robust hardness of deterministic query depth is a substantive metacomplexity question linking succinct representations, adaptive query algorithms and PSPACE beyond exact threshold computation.
formal:
Is the following promise problem PSPACE-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? The input is an explicitly given Boolean circuit \(C\) on \(n\ge1\) input variables and an integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n\). Writing \(f_C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) for the function computed by \(C\), the two promised cases are
\[
\text{YES}:D(f_C)\le k,\qquad
\text{NO}:D(f_C)>2k,
\]
where \(D(f_C)\) is the minimum worst-case depth of a deterministic decision tree that computes \(f_C\) exactly on every input.
question_excerpt: The source asks about approximating decision-tree complexity after treating both truth-table and circuit representations. It already gives hardness for any constant additive error. This card selects the circuit representation and a factor-two PSPACE-hardness promise under polynomial-time many-one reductions. The fixed factor is an editorial specialization; the optional choice received no reply and the recommendation was announced before application. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Circuit input and PSPACE-hardness of distinguishing exact decision-tree depth at most k from depth greater than 2k.
definitions:
A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node names an input variable \(x_i\), its two outgoing edges are labeled zero and one, and each leaf carries an output bit. On input \(x\), the tree follows the edge labeled \(x_i\) at a node querying \(x_i\). Its depth is the maximum number of internal nodes on a root-to-leaf path. The tree computes \(f_C\) if its output is \(f_C(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). The minimum depth over such trees is \(D(f_C)\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\); constant functions have depth zero. Queries are adaptive, but the tree has no randomness or computational error. The objective is depth, not number of leaves or total number of nodes.

The circuit is a directed acyclic graph over AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, optional Boolean constants, and one specified output. Its input variables are explicitly listed, including any unused variables. Encode it by a topologically ordered node list with gate types and binary predecessor indices, followed by the output index. Encode \(k\) in binary. The input size \(L\) is the total number of bits in this description. No bound polynomial in \(n\) on circuit size is promised; computational resources for a reduction are measured in the length of its own input, and its entire output description must be polynomially long.

For the promise problem, a pair \((C,k)\) with \(k<D(f_C)\le2k\) lies outside the promise. A solver may behave arbitrarily there. Invalid encodings are also outside the promise.

PSPACE is the class of languages \(A\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) decidable by a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input and uses at most polynomially many work-tape cells. The asserted hardness means that for every \(A\in\mathrm{PSPACE}\), there exists one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(R_A\) that maps every string \(z\) to a valid pair \((C_z,k_z)\) within the promise and satisfies
\[
z\in A\Longrightarrow D(f_{C_z})\le k_z,\qquad
z\notin A\Longrightarrow D(f_{C_z})>2k_z.
\]
The reduction may depend on \(A\), but not on \(z\) except through its computation. It has no advice or oracle. This is a many-one promise reduction, not a Turing reduction allowed multiple adaptive calls to an approximation oracle.

The selected gap is multiplicative and fixed independently of \(n\). An additive constant gap does not establish it. An algorithm outputting an integer \(a\) with \(D(f_C)\le a\le2D(f_C)\) on all circuits would distinguish the promised cases by comparing \(a\) with \(2k\), but the card asks specifically for the displayed hardness assertion, not for a complete classification of every approximation guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of PSPACE-hardness for the stated factor-two promise problem under polynomial-time many-one reductions. Exact hardness or hardness for a constant additive error alone is insufficient. A conditional consequence such as “a polynomial-time approximation would imply P = PSPACE” must be supported by a reduction meeting the stated gap, rather than assumed.
context:
The paper distinguishes the truth-table input of length 2ⁿ from a circuit that may describe the same function much more succinctly. For an explicit truth table, dynamic programming computes exact depth in polynomial time in that table length.

For circuit input, the source proves PSPACE membership and PSPACE-hardness of exact depth computation. Its truth-table lower bound instead concerns NC¹-hardness under a much weaker reduction model. Those two statements must not be interchanged.

The final open-question discussion explains that constant additive approximation retains the exact problem’s hardness. It asks for stronger approximation results without fixing a multiplicative factor. The factor-two gap here makes one such direction explicit.

The lower-bound task concerns the minimum depth of an exact tree. Hardness for learning a tree from samples, minimizing its leaf count, or allowing classification mistakes would concern other problems.
why: The exact decision-tree depth of a succinctly represented function is PSPACE-hard. A multiplicative-gap result would show that this difficulty survives coarse approximation of the number of input bits that must be inspected, rather than depending on a single critical query.
status_note: The 2025 source proves exact circuit-input PSPACE-hardness and retains stronger approximation as an open direction. The selected factor-two many-one promise specialization was not found resolved in the bounded review through 18 September 2026. It is an explicit editorial target rather than a factor stated verbatim in the source. The known constant-additive-error observation does not establish it. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Circuit input and PSPACE-hardness of distinguishing exact decision-tree depth at most k from depth greater than 2k.
progress: 2025-02: STACS 2025 establishes exact circuit-depth PSPACE-hardness and records the stronger approximation question, beyond constant additive error.
working_summary: Given a Boolean circuit, decision-tree depth is the fewest input-bit queries needed in the worst case to compute its function exactly. The question asks whether distinguishing depth at most k from depth greater than 2k remains PSPACE-hard. The function is supplied by a circuit, whose binary description is the input-size measure. Exact computation and constant additive approximation are already hard in the cited source, while a multiplicative gap needs a stronger result. The card fixes a factor-two many-one promise and keeps this distinct from truth-table algorithms and tree-size minimization.

title: Near-linear communication for exact maximum flow with local outputs
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Communication lower bounds for flow could provide tools for proving dynamic resource limitations.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), does there exist a randomized two-party protocol and constants \(K_a\ge1\), integer \(r_a\ge0\), such that for every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge capacities in \([0,n^a]\), whose edges are partitioned between Alice and Bob, the protocol computes an exact maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with success probability at least \(2/3\) and communicates at most
\[
 K_a n\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil^{r_a}
\]
bits on every execution? Each party must output the flow on its own edges. Interaction is unrestricted, and local computation, storage and local output are free; all transmitted bits are charged.
question_excerpt: Blikstad asks for the communication complexity of maximum flow when graph edges are split between Alice and Bob, with arbitrarily many interactive rounds, and singles out a near-linear-in-vertex-count protocol as a concrete target. The user chose that target for directed graphs with polynomially bounded integer capacities and flow output on each party’s own edges.
definitions:
The common vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and the distinct terminals \(s,t\in V\) are public. The graph is loopless and has at most one edge for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; both opposite directed edges may be present. Alice privately receives a list \(E_A\) of edges and their nonnegative integer capacities, and Bob receives \(E_B\) and its capacities. The promise is \(E_A\cap E_B=\varnothing\), and \(E=E_A\cup E_B\). The partition is arbitrary. Apart from their own edges and the public vertex/terminal data, neither party is initially given the other party’s edge set, its cardinality or its capacities. Missing edges have no flow variable. Zero-capacity edges and isolated vertices are allowed, and there is no connectivity promise.

Each local input is the explicit finite list of endpoint labels and capacities in binary; its storage and local reading cost are not communication. The exponent \(a\) is a fixed public parameter, not a number growing with \(n\). A separate protocol and constants may be used for each fixed \(a\), but must work uniformly over every \(n\), graph, capacity assignment and edge partition in that regime. The question does not replace the polynomial capacity bound by arbitrary real numbers whose encodings could hide uncharged information.

A feasible flow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) for every edge and
\[
 \sum_{(v,w)\in E} f_{(v,w)}-
 \sum_{(w,v)\in E} f_{(w,v)}=0
 \quad\text{for every }v\notin\{s,t\}.
\]
Its value is the net outflow at \(s\),
\[
 \operatorname{val}(f)=
 \sum_{(s,w)\in E}f_{(s,w)}-
 \sum_{(w,s)\in E}f_{(w,s)}.
\]
An exact maximum flow attains the largest such value among all feasible flows. The zero flow is always feasible, including when no directed terminal path exists. Edges entering \(s\) or leaving \(t\) are permitted and are accounted for by the net-flow definition. Integral capacities ensure that an integral optimum exists, but any exactly represented rational optimum is an acceptable output.

At termination Alice outputs a rational value \(f_e\) for each \(e\in E_A\), and Bob does so for each \(e\in E_B\). Rational numbers use finite signed-integer numerator and positive-integer denominator encodings. The two local outputs together must be one feasible optimal flow in the union graph. A party may compute its output from its private graph and the transcript, using unlimited local time and storage. Neither party is required to learn the other party’s edges or output values. Requiring both parties also to know the maximum-flow value would cost only \(O_a(\log n)\) additional bits after successful local outputs; it is not a substitute for them.

An admissible protocol consists of two fixed classical algorithms, for the chosen \(a\), that may use a shared sequence of independent fair random bits and private fair random bits, all independent of the input. Communication follows the standard bit-transcript model: each transmitted bit costs one, and message framing, lengths and termination signals must be encoded in charged bits or determined by the already shared transcript and public randomness. Silence, local running time and the choice of message length do not provide an additional uncharged channel. For each fixed public random tape, the speaking order is determined by the protocol and transcript. Messages may be interactive, with no separate limit on the number of rounds. There is no quantum communication, shared entanglement, oracle, input-dependent advice or prior correlation carrying information about the graph.

The algorithms must terminate on every input satisfying the promise and every random tape. All transmitted bits, in both directions and including preprocessing communication and failure cases, count toward the stated worst-case bound. Local computations and output lengths need not satisfy a time or space bound. For each fixed valid input and edge partition, probability at least \(2/3\), over all protocol randomness, must yield a jointly valid optimum. This is a simultaneous success guarantee for the whole flow, not a separate per-edge probability or average over random graphs. On failure the outputs may be invalid. A worst-case communication bound is required, not merely expected communication.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, including the protocol’s exact local-output correctness, per-instance success probability, termination and worst-case bit bound for every fixed capacity exponent. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation in this same model, ruling out all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and constants for at least one fixed polynomial-capacity regime.

Computing only the optimum value or a minimum cut is not sufficient for the selected output task. A result for approximate flows, undirected graphs alone, bounded interaction or a different output convention must not be treated as resolving it. An \(n\log^b n\) lower bound for one fixed \(b\) would still be compatible with the requested bound for a larger exponent. The question is a binary asymptotic existence claim; numerical tolerance does not relax flow feasibility or optimality.
context:
The seminar question distinguishes communication from sequential computation: a fast centralized maximum-flow algorithm need not have a cheap simulation when the two parties hold different edges. It also allows arbitrary interaction, so this is not a fixed-round lower-bound question.

The October 2025 protocol computes an exact integral maximum flow using soft-O(n^(3/2) log U) bits, where U bounds the integer capacities. For polynomial capacities this is a subquadratic bound, but still larger than the selected near-linear target.

The July 2026 theorem explicitly gives each participant the flow on its own edges. Its local decoding uses the participant’s input graph, explaining why a full flow can be produced with less communication than would be needed to transmit a stand-alone encoding of all its edge values.

The same paper provides a finite-bit implementation of its real-word analysis. Its abstract states soft-O(n^(3/2) log-squared W) communicated bits for min-cost flow, which includes maximum flow after the usual polynomially bounded reduction. Counting arbitrary real words as single bits would not justify this card’s target.
why: A dense flow may assign values to quadratically many edges, yet each participant already knows its own part of the graph. The question asks whether this local knowledge lets them coordinate an exact optimum while exchanging only about as many bits as there are vertices.
status_note: The checked 2025 and 2026 papers give subquadratic randomized communication protocols, with soft-O(n^(3/2)) bits when capacities are polynomially bounded. Their guarantees include determining the flow on each party’s own edges, but do not reach n*polylog(n) bits. The near-linear existence question remains unresolved in this bounded source check. A lower bound for communicating an entire flow to a party without its graph does not settle the local-output model here.
progress: 2022-11: The seminar asks whether maximum flow admits near-linear communication with an unrestricted number of interactive rounds. | 2025-10-03: A preprint gives a randomized subquadratic-bit protocol for maximum flow and minimum-cost flow. | 2026-07-01: The ICALP paper proves a subquadratic communication theorem with exact flow outputs on each party’s own edges and explains its finite-bit cost.
working_summary: Alice and Bob hold disjoint parts of a directed graph and want an exact maximum flow between public terminals. For every fixed polynomial bound on integer capacities, the target is a protocol using n times a fixed power of log n communicated bits. Each party outputs the flow only on its own edges, using free local computation and storage, with joint success probability at least two thirds. The bit bound is worst-case over inputs and randomness, while the number of interactive rounds is unrestricted. The checked recent protocols use roughly n to the three-halves power bits; a complete Lean-checked near-linear protocol or refutation is required.

title: Optimal one-bit cryptogenography success for every number of players
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A focused communication problem or restricted lower-bound target, with narrower scope than general information-versus-communication comparisons.
formal:
Determine the function \(p:\{2,3,4,\ldots\}\to[0,1]\), where
\[
 p(k)=\sup_{\Pi}\ \inf_{e}\Pr\bigl[Y_\Pi=X\ \text{and}\ e(T_\Pi)\ne J\bigr].
\]
Here \(X\) is a uniformly random secret bit, \(J\) is an independent uniformly random owner in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(\Pi\) ranges over the private-randomness public-communication protocols defined below, \(T_\Pi\) is the entire public transcript, and \(Y_\Pi\) is the protocol’s public output bit. The observer’s strategy \(e\) maps the transcript to one accused player and is chosen after the protocol is known. The requested answer is a function \(a\) with
\[
 |a(k)-p(k)|\le1/100\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge2.
\]
There is no restriction on the time needed to evaluate or specify the answer.
question_excerpt: The Banff problem asks how well a group can publicly reveal one secret bit while concealing its original owner, giving separate bounds for two players and for large groups. The user selected the optimal-success function for every number of players, with absolute accuracy one hundredth.
definitions:
There are \(k\) labeled cooperating players and one passive observer. Player \(J\) initially knows that it is the owner and knows \(X\). Every other player initially knows only that it is not the owner; it does not receive \(X\) or the identity of \(J\). The prior distribution of \((X,J)\), the number of players and the whole protocol are common knowledge. All players follow the protocol. They have independent private randomness, independent also of \((X,J)\), and have no private communication, prior secret keys, prior shared random string or quantum resources.

A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node \(v\) specifies the next speaker \(i_v\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and three numbers \(r_{v,*},r_{v,0},r_{v,1}\in[0,1]\). If the speaker is not the owner, it sends the bit \(1\) with probability \(r_{v,*}\). If it is the owner with secret \(x\), it sends \(1\) with probability \(r_{v,x}\). Otherwise it sends \(0\). The corresponding child is then visited. The conditional random choices can be made using fresh independent private coins. The parameters may be arbitrary real numbers: no effective sampling or local running-time constraint is imposed in this information-theoretic model.

The node is determined by the public prefix, so both the speaker schedule and the transmitted bits are visible to every player and the observer. A leaf \(t\) specifies a single output \(y_t\in\{0,1\}\), which is also public. All messages are broadcast; there is no anonymous channel, hidden timing signal or private preparatory phase. The tree can have arbitrarily large finite size and depth. There is no common upper bound on communication or number of rounds across the protocols in the supremum. This tree formulation records precisely the dependence on the speaker’s local input and the transcript; maintaining private state gives the same conditional-message description.

The observer knows the tree and all its probabilities and sees the full transcript, including its public output. It has unlimited computational power. It chooses one index \(e(t)\) for each possible transcript. The cooperating players win only when the public output is the actual secret and the accused player is not its original owner. If the output is incorrect, they lose regardless of the accusation. Their success probability is averaged over the uniform initial input and their private random choices; it is not a worst-case success guarantee for each owner or bit.

For clarity, put
\[
 w_{t,j}=\Pr[T_\Pi=t,\ X=y_t,\ J=j].
\]
The value of a fixed protocol is exactly
\[
 s(\Pi)=\sum_{t\text{ leaf}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^k w_{t,j}-\max_{1\le j\le k}w_{t,j}\right).
\]
Thus an optimal observer at \(t\) maximizes the joint posterior contribution of owner \(j\) and correctness of the public output. It need not maximize the marginal probability of \(J=j\) alone if the output can be wrong. Randomizing the accusation cannot improve the observer’s optimum. This formula also handles zero-probability transcripts without conditioning on them.

The target is the supremum \(p(k)=\sup_\Pi s(\Pi)\), not an assumption that a best finite protocol exists. Allowing protocols that terminate almost surely after an unbounded number of messages does not enlarge this supremum: their finite truncations can lose at most the probability of not yet terminating. The function includes every finite integer \(k\ge2\); it is not merely the two-player value, a large-\(k\) limit, a many-bit secret problem or a model with several original owners.
answer_criterion:
Specify a real-valued function \(a\) on every integer \(k\ge2\) and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a(k)-p(k)|\le1/100\) throughout that domain. Equivalently, a supplied interval for each \(k\), of width at most \(1/50\), with a complete Lean-checked containment proof, qualifies by taking its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies, but neither a decimal expansion nor an efficient evaluation algorithm is required.

The argument must bound the supremum over all allowed protocols against the optimal observer. A list of experimental values, an uncertified optimization program, bounds only for finitely many player counts, or the defining supremum repeated without a determination does not satisfy the target. Matching the tolerance just for two players or just in the limit does not establish the function-wide requirement. If protocols approaching the lower bound are used, finite attainment of the supremum is not required.
context:
The original work gives a one-third two-player protocol, a success probability of at least 0.5644 for sufficiently large groups, and an upper bound of three quarters for every group size. These do not determine the full function at the requested accuracy.

The 2016 work improves the two-player lower bound to 0.3384. The 2019 work improves the upper bound to 0.35183 after accounting for numerical error in its sum-of-squares calculation. These published bounds already leave a two-player interval narrower than 1/50; they do not cover every k.

The upper-bound paper explicitly leaves convergence of its optimization hierarchy to the true optimum as an open question. Its numerical search should therefore not be treated as a certified approximation procedure for the full function.

A protocol can be required to reveal the bit correctly with certainty without changing the best joint success probability, by the original paper’s Lemma 2.1. The card keeps the direct joint-success definition so both correctness and anonymity are explicit.
why: This model separates revealing information from revealing who supplied it, without relying on computational secrecy or a private channel. The function measures the best anonymity that cooperation alone can achieve as the group size changes.
status_note: The checked published bounds already determine the two-player value to absolute error below 1/100, but no checked source establishes that accuracy for every k. The selected whole-function question remains a source-grounded open target after bounded later-work searches through 17 September 2026. Published numerical certificates have not been independently Lean-verified here.
progress: 2014: The original paper establishes the one-bit model and nontrivial two-player and general-group bounds. | 2016: ICALP publishes an improved two-player protocol and upper bound. | 2017: The Banff problem asks for improved bounds for two players and for larger groups. | 2019-11-28: ISAAC publishes a corrected two-player upper bound of 0.35183, which is already close enough to the known lower bound for the card’s two-player tolerance alone.
working_summary: One uniformly chosen player knows a uniformly random secret bit and the group can communicate only in public. The players succeed when their public output is correct and an optimal observer accuses someone other than the original owner. The target is the best achievable success probability as a function of every number of players from two onward. Private randomness and arbitrarily long finite interaction are allowed, without computational secrecy or a private channel. A complete Lean-checked approximation within one hundredth is required at every player count, even though existing bounds already meet that precision for two players alone.

title: Large zero rectangles in low-rank real matrices
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A significant algorithmic question under particular parameters or graph restrictions, with more specialized consequences than a general parameterized-complexity principle.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) of rank \(r\) with at least \(n^2/2\) zero entries, there are nonempty sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \[A_{ij}=0\quad(i\in I,\ j\in J),\qquad |I|\,|J|\ge n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)?\]
definitions: The rank is the dimension over \(\mathbb R\) of the span of the columns. A zero entry means exact equality to zero. Apart from the zero-density condition, entries may be arbitrary real numbers of either sign and magnitude; there is no finite-alphabet or integrality assumption. A rectangle is a Cartesian product \(I\times J\) of row and column index sets, and its size is its number of entries \(|I||J|\). The sets need not be consecutive, equal, or of the same cardinality. This is an area guarantee, with no separate lower bound prescribed for each side. The exponential is the real exponential function and \(\sqrt r\) is the nonnegative square root. The same constant must work for all dimensions, ranks, entries and zero patterns. When \(r=0\), the entire matrix is zero and the displayed bound asks for the whole matrix. The target is an existence theorem about matrices, not an algorithm with a specified input representation or running time.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal statement, or of its negation. A negative answer must establish that for every real \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and an admissible real matrix of rank \(r\) such that every all-zero rectangle has area strictly below \(n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). One finite example violating a chosen constant does not refute the conjecture. A result restricted to Boolean, nonnegative integer, bounded-entry or intersection matrices does not settle the stated arbitrary-real target. No numerical approximation of matrix entries or of a zero test substitutes for exact equality.
context:
A matrix can have many zero entries without those entries forming a large Cartesian block. The question asks whether a small dimension of the column span forces such a block, and specifies how much of the matrix it must occupy.

The conjectured area fraction is \(\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). It depends only on rank, even when the number of rows and columns is much larger. The constant is uniform: allowing it to depend on the particular matrix would remove the quantitative content of the question.

Lovett posed this precise half-zero-density, real-matrix, rectangle-area version in the 2013 Dagstuhl report. That report also states that the square-root dependence in the exponent would be best possible. The present formulation keeps its area target rather than requiring a balanced square.

For Boolean communication matrices, a constant rectangle is a collection of input pairs on which the answer is fixed. Low-rank real matrices allow a much wider range of entry values, so a theorem for Boolean matrices alone does not cover this question.

Hunter, Milojević, Sudakov and Tomon retain a broader sparse-real-matrix conjecture as Conjecture 1.8: when at most an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of entries are nonzero, a zero square of side \(n\exp(-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon r}))\) is predicted. That additional density parameter and square-side target are useful context, not replacements for the fixed-density area statement here.

Their Theorem 1.12 proves a related bound for nonnegative matrices whose nonzero entries are at least one and whose average entry is at most one half. In particular it gives the desired rank dependence for Boolean matrices with at least half their entries zero. A density of zeros does not impose the required average-entry bound on an arbitrary real matrix, and arbitrary signed entries fall outside the theorem.

Their Theorem 1.10 also resolves a related cross-disjoint-set-family conjecture, with its exponent measured by the size of the ground set. This result does not identify the ground-set size with the real rank of every matrix. Sudakov’s 2025 Oberwolfach report continues to list the general sparse-real-matrix statement as Conjecture 5.
why: The question asks whether low real rank forces a large exact combinatorial pattern when zeros are dense. This connects linear-algebraic complexity to the rectangles that control communication protocols, while extending beyond Boolean matrices. Its value is the proposed general structural principle; the question is not merely to speed up a search for a rectangle.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The original target is explicit in the 2013 source. The 2024 primary paper and 2025 Oberwolfach report retain the broader real-matrix conjecture; the checked positive results have additional restrictions. No proof or refutation of this precise half-density area bound was located in the bounded search. Cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2013: Lovett poses the half-zero-density real-matrix rectangle conjecture and records optimality of the proposed exponent. | 2024-11-20: Hunter and coauthors prove zero-submatrix bounds under nonnegative-entry and average-entry restrictions, and a related set-system result; their Conjecture 1.8 retains arbitrary real matrices. | 2025: Sudakov’s Oberwolfach report continues to state the sparse-real-matrix question as Conjecture 5.
working_summary: The question concerns square real matrices with low rank and at least half their entries equal to zero. It asks for a Cartesian block consisting entirely of zeros whose area is a square-root-exponential fraction of the whole matrix. The constant in that guarantee must be the same for every matrix and dimension. The rank is over the real numbers, and entries may have arbitrary signs and magnitudes. Recent results establish related guarantees under additional entry restrictions, while the checked sources retain the general real-matrix question.

title: Quadratic decision-tree bounds from block sensitivity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A concrete question about a restricted function family, representation, or resource bound; useful for techniques but narrower than the category's central separations.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every integer \(n\ge1\), satisfies \[D(f)\le C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2?\] Here \(D(f)\) is deterministic worst-case bit-query complexity and \(\operatorname{bs}(f)\) is block sensitivity, with both measures defined below. The constant must be independent of \(n\) and of the function, and no logarithmic or dimension-dependent multiplier is allowed.
definitions: A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by an input coordinate \(i\in[n]\), with its two outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), the tree queries the bit \(x_i\) at the current node and follows the matching edge until it reaches a leaf. It computes \(f\) if the reached leaf equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Its worst-case query cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited on any input, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost over all trees computing \(f\). Repeated coordinate queries are permitted and count again. A leaf-only tree has cost zero. The tree may be chosen separately for each known function, and its number of leaves or total nodes is not the measured resource. No efficient construction of the optimal tree from a truth table or circuit is required. For \(B\subseteq[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus B}\) denote the input obtained from \(x\) by flipping exactly the bits in \(B\). A nonempty block \(B\) is sensitive at \(x\) if \(f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus B})\). Define \(\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\) as the largest number \(t\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) that are each sensitive at this same input \(x\), and let \(\operatorname{bs}(f)=\max_x\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\). Each block is tested by flipping it alone from the common input, not by a cumulative sequence of flips. Blocks need not be singletons or have a specified size. This maximum disjoint collection is different from the number of all minimal sensitive blocks and from fractional block sensitivity. All total Boolean functions are included: monotonicity, symmetry, graph invariance, bounded alternation, balanced output and succinct circuit representation are not assumed. Constant functions have \(D(f)=\operatorname{bs}(f)=0\) and satisfy the proposed bound. Randomized and quantum queries are outside the definition of \(D(f)\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal quadratic inequality or of its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) that works for every dimension and every total function. A negative answer must establish that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a total nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) for which \(D(f)>C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\). Thus disproving the coefficient-one inequality is insufficient unless the ratios \(D(f)/\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\) are unbounded. A result for a subclass, a bound on decision-tree size instead of depth, or a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not meet the criterion. The smallest possible constant and an efficient tree-construction algorithm are not required.
context:
Jukna’s early draft poses \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) as Research Problem 14.10 after Corollary 14.9 gives the general cubic upper bound. This card retains that constant-factor universal inequality, rather than asking only whether some polynomial relation exists.

Chugh, Podder and Sanyal’s 2023 paper states that the known general upper bound is cubic and the widest known separation is quadratic. Their Question 1 keeps the unrestricted gap open. Polynomial equivalence among measures, including the sensitivity theorem, does not by itself fix this exponent.

Their Theorem 4 establishes the quadratic bound for zebra functions, defined by having the same number of output changes along every increasing path from the all-zero input to the all-one input. This includes monotone and symmetric functions but is a restriction on the truth table. Their Theorem 5 also gives the quadratic bound when the maximum number of such changes is bounded by a fixed constant.

Chakraborty and Gál’s February 2026 paper improves bounds for the number of minimal sensitive blocks, and obtains consequences for the total size of decision trees. Those quantities differ from both the maximum number of disjoint sensitive blocks and the worst-case query depth in the present target. Its stated results do not establish the unrestricted quadratic inequality here.
why: The two quantities measure different aspects of the information needed to determine a Boolean output: the worst adaptive query cost and the number of disjoint ways to change the output at one input. Their known cubic general upper bound and quadratic examples leave a basic gap. A uniform quadratic relation would sharpen the structure of query complexity across every total Boolean function.
status_note: The unrestricted inequality is posed in the checked Jukna draft and remains explicitly unresolved in the 2023 primary paper. The 2026 primary result checked here concerns block number and decision-tree size, not this general depth bound. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no resolution; this does not independently certify an exhaustive later literature review.
progress: 2012: Jukna records the universal \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) question immediately after the cubic upper bound. | 2023-12-12: Chugh, Podder and Sanyal publish quadratic bounds for zebra functions and fixed-bounded-alternation functions, while explicitly retaining the general cubic-versus-quadratic gap. | 2026-02-01: Chakraborty and Gál post improved bounds on block number and decision-tree size. The main theorem and stated size consequences concern different measures from the proposed quadratic depth inequality.
working_summary: The target is a universal quadratic upper bound on deterministic decision-tree depth in terms of block sensitivity. A decision tree adaptively reads individual bits and must compute a total Boolean function correctly on every input. Block sensitivity counts disjoint blocks whose separate flips all change the value at one common input. The known general bound is cubic, while quadratic bounds hold for several restricted classes. The proposed constant must work for every function and dimension, and recent results on tree size or counts of minimal blocks do not settle this depth question.

title: Sign-rank bounds from constant margin
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A qualitative relationship between two fundamental geometric complexity parameters, with consequences for learning and communication. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every real \(\rho \in\)(0,1], does there exist a finite integer \(d(\rho )\), independent of matrix dimensions, such that every finite sign matrix A with margin \(m(A)\ge \rho\) has sign-rank at most \(d(\rho )\)? This is the dimension-free bounding-function question written in the source as rank±\((A)\le \eta (m(A)^{- 1})\); no polynomial or computable bound on \(\eta\) is requested.
definitions: A sign matrix \(A\in \{- 1,+1\}^{r\times s}\) has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±\((A)\) is the least \(D\ge 1\) for which there are unit vectors \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{r},v_{1},\ldots ,v_{s}\in \mathbb{R}\)ᴰ with \(A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle >0\) for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying \(A_{ij}B_{ij}>0\) entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin \(m(A)\) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of \(\min _{i,j} A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle\). It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as \(\rho\) tends to zero, but for each fixed positive \(\rho\) it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function \(\eta\):[\(1,\infty\))→\(\mathbb{N}\). This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound \(d(\rho )\) for every positive margin threshold \(\rho\), or prove there is a fixed \(\rho >0\) and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least \(\rho\) and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.
context:
Rows can be represented as points and columns as oriented hyperplanes through the origin. Sign-rank minimizes the ambient dimension; margin instead maximizes the smallest normalized separation from any hyperplane.

The source recalls a bound of order \(m(A)^{- 2}\log  N\) for an \(N\times N\) matrix. The open question is whether any dependence on N can be removed, even at the cost of an arbitrarily worse dependence on margin.

Small sign-rank need not imply a large margin. Thus the card concerns the particular direction from a positive margin lower bound to bounded dimension.

The later theorem shows that exact k-Hamming-distance matrices have sign-rank bounded by \(2^{O(k)}\), independently of input length. It refutes the particular growing-rank conjecture proposed alongside Question 1.4, while restating the general question as open.

The April 2026 work obtains strong lower bounds for a Gap Hamming Distance promise problem. Its matrix leaves intermediate distances unspecified, so it does not give a fully specified constant-margin counterexample to the present statement.
why: Asks whether robust high-dimensional point–halfspace representations can always be replaced by bounded-dimensional representations, connecting geometric learning parameters with communication complexity.
status_note: The primary definitions and question were matched to the explicit open restatement in the March 2026 conference-version revision. April 2026 partial-matrix progress was checked separately. No total-matrix resolution was located through 12 September 2026.
progress: 2022: The source presents the qualitative margin-to-sign-rank bound as Question 1.4 and separately conjectures growing sign-rank for a hypercube family. | 2025: The Hamming-distance family is proved to have constant sign-rank for fixed distance, refuting that proposed counterexample. | 2026-03-31: The revised conference version still explicitly asks the full margin-versus-sign-rank question. | 2026-04-12: New topological lower bounds treat partial Gap Hamming Distance matrices, not a total constant-margin counterexample.
working_summary: A sign matrix can be represented by points and separating hyperplanes. Its margin measures how far every point stays from every relevant hyperplane after normalization. Its sign-rank is the smallest dimension of any representation with the correct signs. The question asks whether a fixed positive margin forces a dimension bound independent of matrix size. Recent work disproves a proposed Hamming-distance counterexample but explicitly leaves the general question open.

title: Fourier rank versus sparsity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Asks for the exact qualitative relation between two fundamental Boolean Fourier complexity measures. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers \(n_{j}\ge 1\) and Boolean functions \(f_{j}:\{- 1,1\}^{n_{j}}\to \{- 1,1\}\) such that \(k(f_{j})\to \infty\) and \(r(f_{j})/\sqrt{k}(f_{j})\to \infty\) as \(j\to \infty\), where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over \(F_{2}\)? Equivalently, is the ratio \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.
context:
Fourier sparsity counts the nonzero parity coefficients. Rank counts how many independent parity directions are needed to contain their support. The question asks how far these two structural measures can diverge at the square-root scale.

Sanyal’s published Theorem 1.2 gives \(r(f)=O(\sqrt{k}(f) \log (k(f)+1))\). Addressing functions attain the square-root scale up to constants. The 2021 paper explicitly asks whether that scale can be exceeded by an unbounded factor.

The 2026 linear-invariance-testing paper describes a square-root bound up to constants in a background sentence and cites Sanyal’s 2019 result. Checking that cited theorem shows that it includes log k. This citation therefore does not establish the stronger universal bound that would negatively resolve the present question.
why: Would determine whether sparse Boolean Fourier support necessarily occupies only square-root-many independent parity directions, or whether the familiar quadratic relation misses a growing separation.
status_note: Checked the 2021 question, the exact published 2019 theorem, and the 2026 property-testing paper and its cited bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the unbounded-ratio question. The 2026 background wording is not treated as a new rank theorem.
progress: 2019: The published upper bound is \(O(\sqrt{k} \log  k)\), within a logarithmic factor of addressing examples. | 2021: The source explicitly asks whether \(r=\omega (\sqrt{k})\) occurs for any family of Boolean functions. | 2026: A later property-testing paper cites the 2019 dimension bound in its background; checking the cited theorem preserves the logarithmic gap.
working_summary: A Boolean function has a Fourier expansion in parity characters. Its sparsity counts nonzero coefficients, while its rank is the \(F_{2}\) dimension spanned by their index sets. The question asks whether rank can exceed the square root of sparsity by an unbounded factor. Known addressing examples attain the square-root scale, and the published universal upper bound allows an additional logarithmic factor. The answer requires either an asymptotically separating family or a universal square-root bound with an absolute constant.

title: Constant-factor randomized direct sums for total Boolean functions
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A central question about economies of scale in interactive computation, linked to communication lower bounds and compression. Its importance does not remove the need to fix the precise variant. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty finite input sets \(X,Y\), every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R_{1/3}(f^{\otimes k})\ge c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f),\] where communication is public-coin, worst-case and measured with one global error probability?
question_excerpt: A classic example is the case of direct sum in communication complexity: a near-perfect direct sum result holds in the non-deterministic case \([49, 38]\), but […]
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the universal constant-factor inequality, or a Lean proof of its negation: for every positive proposed constant there are a total Boolean function and copy count violating it. Refuting a version for relations, partial functions, distributional inputs or per-coordinate error alone does not refute this selected assertion. Expected communication is not the cost used here.
context:
The source identifies randomized direct sums as an open direction. The authorized variant fixes total Boolean functions, public coins, worst-case communication and global error.

A 2026 preprint claims a global-error amortization characterization and counterexamples for relations, while explicitly retaining a question for total functions. Its relation claim is not transferred to the selected Boolean-function target.
why: Direct sums ask whether communicating about many tasks together can save a substantial fraction of the single-task cost. They connect communication lower bounds with interactive compression and the distinction between information revealed and bits transmitted. The exact error and task conventions determine which savings are possible.
status_note: A user-authorized precise total-Boolean-function variant. The August 2026 primary preprint explicitly distinguishes relations from the remaining total-function question. Rechecked on 13 September 2026; its new theorem is a reported preprint claim, not an independently verified result or a refutation of this target.
progress: 2010: Information cost is related exactly to amortized distributional communication with error allowed separately in each copy. | 2019: The source describes randomized direct sums as an open setting without fixing one complete conjecture. | 2026-08-04: A preprint claims a global-error amortization characterization and relation counterexamples, while retaining a total-function question.
working_summary: Alice and Bob must jointly compute a total Boolean function of their private inputs. The question compares the communication needed for one input pair with the communication needed for many pairs together. A single universal constant would force cost to grow proportionally with the number of copies. The protocol uses public randomness and must produce the entire answer vector correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input tuple. Recent claimed counterexamples for relations do not resolve the chosen total-function version.

title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
importance_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
focus_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
context:
Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.
status_note: The precise deterministic statement remains an unproved hypothesis in the checked sources. The July 2026 preprint improves a fixed-width randomized analysis and does not supply the quantified deterministic refutation. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; its imported inequalities and numerical certificates were not independently verified.
progress: 2001-01-21: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates of fixed-width satisfiability and their limiting rate, proving relations among widths under ETH. They do not prove the limiting rate equals one. | 2015: The textbook states deterministic SETH as Conjecture 14.2, distinguishes separate fixed-width algorithms from a single unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm, and proves that SETH implies ETH. | 2018: Vassilevska Williams surveys fine-grained reductions from satisfiability hypotheses to polynomial-time problems, explicitly tracking the relevant models and forms of hypotheses. | 2026-07-12: Jiang and Cai report the randomized general-3-SAT bound \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) and a separate stronger Unique-3-SAT bound. Their Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 concern fixed width; these preprint claims do not settle the deterministic all-width hypothesis.
