working_summary: SETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rates for fixed-width satisfiability approach one as the allowed width grows. Every proposed constant saving from exhaustive search must fail at some fixed width. To refute it, one saving must work at every fixed width, although the algorithms and polynomial factors may vary with that width. Faster algorithms for width three, including recent randomized ones, do not meet that requirement. The hypothesis underlies many precise conditional lower bounds, including problems whose algorithms already run in polynomial time.

title: Truly subcubic APSP
importance_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
focus_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
question_excerpt: This retains the existing arbitrary-real-weight randomized APSP question and its comparison-addition model with ordinary logarithmic-size word operations. It makes uniformity, primitive operations, the graph promise and joint output guarantee explicit. The cited equivalence literature also states integer-weight theorems with a logarithmic dependence on the weight range; its strongly polynomial reduction is identified separately rather than silently equating all weight and machine conventions.
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
context:
If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.
why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.
status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The published July 2026 node-weighted-triangle introduction and July prediction-assisted APSP preprint explicitly retain the general fixed-exponent challenge. The inspected few-weight algorithms, extra-prediction bounds and August black-box reduction barriers do not resolve the uniform randomized comparison-addition real-RAM question stated here. Bounded current searches located no full matching solution claim. This is an individual formulation and source-scope review, not exhaustive certification of every cited proof or all later literature.
progress: 2010; journal 2018: Subcubic equivalences connect APSP to min-plus products, negative triangles and several other tasks; the full manuscript distinguishes integer-range reductions from its strongly polynomial randomized reduction. | 2013-12; revised 2014-05: Williams obtains randomized time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) on the real RAM; STOC publishes the result in 2014 and an expanded journal version appears in 2018. | 2025-06-24: The few-weights manuscript gives deterministic improvements under restrictions on the number of outgoing weights per vertex, with explicit weight-model conventions. | 2026-07-01: ICALP publishes the matrix-multiplication-time node-weighted zero-triangle result; independently weighted edges remain a different target. | 2026-07-01: The prediction-assisted APSP preprint gives a fixed exponent saving when its supplied certificate has sufficiently few erroneous or unverifiable pairs. | 2026-08-19: The black-box-reduction preprint establishes barriers for reductions uniform over arbitrary triangle relations; it does not establish an unrestricted APSP lower bound.
working_summary: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary exact real edge weights and no negative cycle, and the output gives the shortest distance for every ordered vertex pair. The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed positive saving below the cubic exponent, correct on the entire output matrix with probability at least two thirds. Time is charged in a specified comparison-addition real RAM that also permits ordinary logarithmic-size word operations, including all preprocessing and output. Known general algorithms achieve subpolynomial savings, while faster restricted results concern node weights, few outgoing weights, or supplied predictions. Recent restrictions on black-box reductions do not rule out all APSP algorithms, and the inspected sources retain the full target as unresolved.

title: Randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
importance_reason: A defining hardness hypothesis for randomized exact exponential-time and fine-grained algorithms, with consequences for fundamental satisfiability, set-system and polynomial-time problems. Its significance lies in excluding a uniform positive saving across all fixed clause widths and in strengthening deterministic hardness to bounded-error algorithms. This individual assessment follows that mathematical breadth, not the age of the survey or the inherited unassessed midpoint.
formal:
Is the following randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis true?
\[
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge3:
\quad\text{there is no bounded-error randomized algorithm for }k\text{-SAT}
\text{ with time }O\!\left(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\operatorname{poly}(L)\right).
\]
Here \(n\) is the number of variables, \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and algorithms are uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machines with worst-case running time over both inputs and coin outcomes, as defined below.

More precisely, for each \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed width \(k\ge3\) must exclude every machine \(M\) and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) satisfying, for every valid \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
\Pr_r[M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23,
\qquad
\forall r:\quad
t_M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d.
\]
The machine returns a decision bit. The width may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed before the machine and the input are quantified.

This card uses the standard bounded-error Turing-machine formulation explicitly named RSETH in the later primary source’s \(\mathrm{BPTIME}\) definition. The original 2018 survey states its hypothesis under a logarithmic-word RAM convention. The choice of the later formulation is explicit; equivalence to a literal logarithmic-address-space interpretation of that earlier RAM convention is not asserted.
definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\ge3\). A \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most \(k\) literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\). The distinct variables occurring in the entire formula are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so \(n\) counts variables, not clauses or encoding bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment is a map \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1\}\); it satisfies \(F\) when every clause has at least one true literal. The empty clause is false, the empty conjunction is true, and the empty conjunction has \(n=0\). Define \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)=1\) if some assignment satisfies \(F\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Use the following explicit binary encoding. For each integer \(a\ge0\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\) be the binary expansion of \(a+1\) with no leading zeros, let \(b\) be its length, and put \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\). Encode the number \(n\) of variables and the number \(m\) of clauses using this code. Then encode each clause by its coded length, followed by its literals in their listed order. Encode a literal by one sign bit, \(0\) for positive and \(1\) for negated, followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\) for its variable index. Require \(1\le i\le n\), all declared lists to be fully present, every declared variable to occur, no trailing bits, and every clause length to be at most \(k\). Let \(L=|\operatorname{enc}(F)|\).

The inputs range over all such formulas. There is no promise of linearly many clauses, bounded variable occurrences, a unique satisfying assignment, a gap in the optimum number of satisfied clauses, or a random input distribution. The clause width is a fixed constant for each language \(k\)-SAT; it does not grow with the input length. The model allows arbitrarily many explicitly listed clauses, including duplicates, and the displayed polynomial factor in \(L\) includes their processing.

A machine has one finite program, finitely many tapes and finite tape alphabets, with these choices fixed independently of input length. Its tapes have cells indexed by the nonnegative integers, all heads start at cell zero, and an attempted left move from cell zero leaves that head there. The read-only input tape contains the encoding starting in cell zero, followed by an end marker and blanks; work tapes are initially blank. The finite control starts in a fixed initial state and has halting states labelled by the decision bits \(0\) and \(1\). At each transition the machine reads or writes only the symbols under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one fresh fair random bit during a transition. The random source \(r\) is an infinite sequence of independent unbiased bits; a run reads a finite prefix before halting. All transitions, including input access, random-bit generation and internal computation, count toward \(t_M\). There is no unit-cost random access, unbounded-integer arithmetic, quantum operation, oracle or advice depending on input length.

A \(k\)-SAT algorithm in the quantified class halts with output \(0\) or \(1\) on every input and every random sequence. It rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their bit length, with a fixed polynomial for that machine. On each valid formula its answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\), independently of whether the formula is satisfiable. Thus errors on both yes-instances and no-instances are permitted. The runtime bound is required for every random sequence, not only in expectation or with high probability. There is no additional space bound.

The constants \(C,d\) and the program may depend on the fixed width \(k\) and on a proposed saving \(\varepsilon\), but cannot depend on \(F\), \(n\), \(L\) or the realized random bits. Any finite exceptional set of input lengths can be covered by increasing \(C\). Every algorithm is uniform across input lengths. A different algorithm may be considered for each width; no computable procedure selecting those algorithms from \(k\) is built into the hypothesis.

The quantifier over \(\varepsilon\) asks about every fixed positive saving in the exponent. It does not assert a \(2^{n-o(n)}\) lower bound for a single fixed width, and it does not preclude a width-dependent saving tending to zero as \(k\) increases. The claim also does not replace bounded-width satisfiability by arbitrary-width CNF-SAT. The randomness belongs to the algorithm while correctness and time are worst-case over formulas.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed hypothesis or of its full negation in the stated machine and input model.

A positive answer must establish that, for every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed integer \(k\ge3\) excludes all machines and constants satisfying both the correctness and runtime conditions. It must cover all uniform bounded-error randomized algorithms, not only a selected algorithm or a restricted family.

A negative answer must establish the quantifier order
\[
\exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\ \forall k\ge3\
\exists M_k,\ C_k\ge1,\ d_k\ge0\
\forall F\in k\text{-CNF}:
\]
\[
\Pr_r[M_k(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall r:\ 
t_{M_k}(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C_k\,2^{(1-\varepsilon_0)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_k}.
\]
Here \(C_k,d_k\) are integers and each \(M_k\) meets all machine, termination and malformed-input requirements above. The same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work for every fixed width; programs and polynomial factors may vary with the width. Proving these existential witnesses for every width suffices without an additional requirement of one algorithm that accepts the width as input.

An improvement only for one width, a saving that vanishes as the width grows, average-case performance, or a result under an additional unproved hypothesis does not settle this statement. A proof only about deterministic algorithms establishes a different claim unless it also yields the required randomized statement. Numerical evidence about running-time bases and a Lean definition of the hypothesis alone are insufficient.
context:
The 2018 survey explicitly extends the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis to randomized algorithms in Hypothesis 1. The later definition by Ron-Zewi and Rothblum names the hypothesis RSETH and states it using bounded-error probabilistic time. This card adopts that standard Turing-machine formulation and records the original survey’s different global RAM convention rather than silently identifying the two models.

Exhaustive search examines \(2^n\) assignments. For any particular fixed clause width, randomized algorithms can improve its exponential base. The hypothesis concerns whether the savings can be kept bounded away from zero across every fixed width, so improvements for \(3\)-SAT are compatible with it.

Cygan and coauthors formulate the randomized growth rate with error probability at most \(1/3\) and a polynomial factor in the complete input size. They distinguish the hypothesis for all fixed widths from the weaker assertion that unrestricted-width CNF-SAT has no fixed improvement over exhaustive search. Their work also connects the bounded-width hypothesis to corresponding exponential-time barriers for Hitting Set, Set Splitting and Not-All-Equal SAT.

The randomized claim excludes a larger class of algorithms than deterministic SETH in the same bit model, so it implies that deterministic hypothesis. Randomized ETH asks instead for a positive exponential-time barrier already for \(3\)-SAT; it does not demand that the optimal exponent approach one with increasing width. Nondeterministic SETH, parity hypotheses and assumptions about randomly sampled formulas concern other algorithmic or input models.

The July 2026 preprint on PPSZ reports improved randomized bounds for Unique-\(3\)-SAT and general \(3\)-SAT. Its theorems address that fixed width and do not supply the common positive exponent saving for every width that would negate rSETH. This bounded literature check records the preprint’s scope without treating it as a verified resolution of the hypothesis.
why: This hypothesis is a central proposed barrier for randomized algorithms: it specifies whether exhaustive assignment search becomes essentially optimal as clause width increases. It supports fine-grained conditional lower bounds where randomized target algorithms must also be excluded, and links exact satisfiability complexity to tight complexity questions for other fundamental problems. A proof or refutation would change a major foundation of modern algorithmic hardness, well beyond the performance of one SAT solver.

The original survey’s different word-RAM convention is disclosed rather than declared equivalent. working_summary: Randomized SETH asks whether every fixed positive saving in the exhaustive-search exponent fails at some fixed clause width. Inputs are arbitrary explicitly encoded \(k\)-CNF formulas, with the number of variables in the exponent and a polynomial factor in input length. The developed formulation uses uniform fair-coin Turing machines, error at most \(1/3\) on every input, and worst-case time over random bits. title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
importance_reason: A core fine-grained hardness hypothesis for a basic graph problem, including randomized algorithms and polynomial integer weights. Its extensive graph and matrix equivalences and consequences for other algorithmic problems make a resolution foundational. This individual assessment is based on that breadth and the precise target, not the inherited provisional score or the existence of a survey entry.
formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
definitions:
For fixed integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order, with a presence flag for each ordered pair and, for each present edge, a signed integer weight \(w(u,v)\) satisfying \(|w(u,v)|\le n^c\). There is at most one edge per ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges are indicated by their flags. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle with negative total weight. Negative edges, zero-weight cycles and ties between shortest paths are allowed. For vertices \(u,v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum total weight of a finite directed walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or a separate unreachable symbol \(+\infty\) if there is no such walk. The empty walk has weight zero. Under the promise every reachable minimum is attained, \(d_G(u,u)=0\), and each finite distance has absolute value at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output consists of these \(n^2\) exact integers or unreachable flags in vertex-pair order; listing all path vertices is not required.

The machine is a word RAM with one fixed finite program. For a fixed integer \(a\ge c+4\), its word length on \(n\)-vertex inputs is \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each memory address and memory cell is one word. The input is one word for n followed in row-major order by two words for each matrix entry: its zero-or-one presence flag and its signed weight, with zero in the weight word when the flag is zero. The output uses the same row-major order and two words per entry: a zero-or-one finite-distance flag and its signed distance, with zero in the second word for unreachable pairs. Signed integers use two's-complement encoding; distances fit in a constant number of words. Word load, store, copy, comparison, conditional branch, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) each cost one step. Unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step. Division by zero is invalid; shifts by at least \(b(n)\) positions return zero. Algorithms may use several words for larger quantities, charging all operations. All accessed addresses must fit in a word. Work memory initially contains zero, and no input-dependent precomputed tables, advice or oracle are supplied. All preprocessing, table construction, memory operations and output writing count toward the time bound. One random instruction yields one fresh independent fair bit in one step. The input graph is fixed before the coins are drawn. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring random bits.

Precisely, \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) asserts the existence of a finite program \(A\), an integer word-size factor \(a\ge c+4\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every promised graph, every run halts within \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps, and with probability at least \(2/3\) its entire output matrix equals \((d_G(u,v))_{u,v\in[n]}\). Correctness is joint for the matrix, rather than a separate bound for each entry. The program, \(a\) and \(C\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. There is no requirement to classify or detect inputs that violate the promise. The exponent in the time bound concerns the number \(n\) of vertices; the input has \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and \(O(n^2\log n)\) bits for each fixed \(c,a\). Rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) capture every possible fixed positive exponent saving.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed hypothesis, or of its full logical negation \[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] A refutation must therefore establish one common positive exponent saving for every fixed polynomial weight bound; programs and runtime constants may depend on \(c\). A proof of the hypothesis must rule out all uniform randomized algorithms in the specified model for a suitable \(c\) at each saving \(\varepsilon\). A deterministic-only lower bound, a barrier for a particular algorithm or reduction technique, or a truly subcubic algorithm only for one restricted weight regime does not settle the statement. Neither do approximate distances, random input distributions, single-source bounds, distributed round bounds or extra accurate predictions. A subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time alone is insufficient. This yes/no target concerns exact APSP algorithms; an unproved APSP hypothesis cannot be assumed as the proof of itself.
context:
The 2018 survey treats APSP as one of the central hypotheses used to explain polynomial-time barriers. Its model permits randomization and logarithmic machine words, and its graph weights are polynomially bounded signed integers with no negative cycle.

Fischer's 2026 formulation explicitly places the requested exponent saving before the weight exponent: for every saving there is a polynomial weight range that remains hard. Its footnote distinguishes the stronger hypothesis with one absolute weight exponent for all savings. The paper uses nonnegative weights and explicitly states equivalence with the signed, no-negative-cycle convention retained here.

Williams gives a randomized word-RAM algorithm for nonnegative integer weights bounded by \(M\) in time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}+n^{2+o(1)}\log M\). For polynomial \(M\), this achieves a substantial improvement over cubic time while the saving remains subpolynomial in \(n\), so it does not provide a fixed exponent improvement.

The 2025 few-weights algorithms exploit a bound on the number of distinct edge weights associated with each vertex. Their truly subcubic results concern those restricted instances, whereas this hypothesis imposes no such bound.

The 2026 universe-reduction paper connects APSP to stronger hypotheses for small-weight and unweighted graphs. Its full equivalence is conditional on the matrix-multiplication exponent being two and on an additional algorithmic assumption from additive combinatorics; it proves neither the APSP hypothesis nor its negation.

The August 2026 lower bound concerns a class of black-box triangle reductions. It limits those reductions' ability to preserve precise running-time exponents, and does not establish a general lower bound for APSP algorithms.
why: The randomized APSP hypothesis is a principal foundation of fine-grained complexity. Resolving it would determine whether exact distances in general integer-weighted graphs admit a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic time, and would affect a large network of conditional bounds for graph, matrix, sequence and dynamic problems.
status_note: The original 2018 source states the randomized polynomial-integer-weight hypothesis. Fischer's 29 March 2026 full preprint explicitly states the modern forall-epsilon/exists-c formulation adopted here as Hypothesis 1.1, describes truly subcubic APSP as a major open question, and fixes the randomized word-RAM model. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026, including the 2025 few-weight results, the conditional 2026 universe reduction, July 2026 node-weighted-triangle work and the August 2026 reduction barrier, found no verified resolution of this exact statement. This does not exhaustively certify current openness. The stronger quantifier order with one absolute c for every epsilon is not silently substituted for this target.

working_summary: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a directed graph. The graph has polynomially bounded signed integer edge weights and no negative-weight cycle. The hypothesis says that for every fixed improvement over the cubic exponent, some polynomial weight bound rules out every randomized algorithm with that running time. Computation uses logarithmic-size machine words, and the whole distance matrix must be correct with probability at least two thirds on every input. Known general algorithms save a subpolynomial factor, while recent restricted algorithms and conditional equivalences do not settle this hypothesis.

title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
importance_reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.
formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
question_excerpt: Rohatgi’s inherited source states a randomized OV conjecture for a superlogarithmic dimension function. The existing card selected the standard logarithmic-dimension formulation with the order “for every exponent saving, some fixed dimension constant”; July 2026 Conjecture 1 states exactly that order and explicitly includes randomized algorithms. This review retains that selected variant, bichromatic lists, packed inputs, worst-case running time, category and importance 96. It makes the word-RAM operations and parameter dependencies explicit, without claiming that the different dimension formulations are identical solely by renaming parameters.
definitions:
Decision problem. For \(n\ge2\), the input consists of ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of binary vectors of common dimension \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\). Repeated vectors, zero vectors and overlap between the lists are allowed. Output YES exactly when
\[\exists r,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad\sum_{j=1}^{d}a^{(r)}_j b^{(s)}_j=0.\]
The sum is an ordinary nonnegative integer sum. Equivalently, the two supports are disjoint. Orthogonality modulo two is a different predicate. The selected pair must come from opposite lists, but the task only asks for a decision bit, not for a witness. There is no promise on Hamming weights, intersections, number of solutions or input distribution.

Words and encoding. A machine fixes an integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses unsigned words of
\[w=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil\]
bits. Input headers supply \(n,d\), followed by the two lists in order. Each vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) consecutive words, with its coordinates packed from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. Thus for fixed \(c\) one vector occupies a constant number of words as \(n\) grows. The input is explicit, not supplied by a membership or inner-product oracle. Changing between ordinary explicit bit arrays and this packing costs at most a logarithmic factor; the stated acceptance bound itself uses the packed model.

Instruction set and cost. The program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and random-access memory addressed by single words. One step may read or write a constant number of addressed words; perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT; shift logically left or right; compare words; or branch using a comparison. Shifts discard overflow and give zero when their shift count is at least \(w\). A fresh uniform random \(w\)-bit word costs one step and is independent of all previous random words. A compound operation on several words must be built from these instructions and charged accordingly. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, real arithmetic, vector instruction of input-dependent width, or additional oracle.

Uniformity, memory and preprocessing. Outside the explicit input, memory initially contains only zeros. Programs may contain fixed finite constants, but receive no advice, precomputed tables or extra data depending on \(n\). Any such tables must be produced during the charged computation. The program and \(\lambda\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), as may constants in the running-time bound; none may vary with \(n\). Single-word addressing bounds available memory by \(2^w\) words. Reading input, constructing tables, preprocessing either list, generating randomness and producing the answer are all charged. There is no separate free preprocessing phase.

Time and error. To solve the problem, the program must halt with a decision bit on every allowed input and random execution. For each fixed input, over its independent internal random words, the bit must equal the predicate above with probability at least \(2/3\). Either type of error is allowed within this bound. The claim \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) means that there exist a real \(K>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\), and every sequence of random choices, takes at most \(K n^{2-\varepsilon}\) steps. An expected-time or average-input bound is not itself this worst-case guarantee. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring the random instruction.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every allowed uniform randomized program in the specified instruction model, with the quantifier order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) and the per-input success requirement. A proof conditional on an unproved version of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is evidence for the conjecture, not an unconditional resolution.

A refutation must establish
\[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists A_c,\lambda_c,K_c,n_{0,c}:\quad A_c\text{ meets the stated time and correctness conditions}.\]
The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\). The programs, word-size constants, multiplicative constants and asymptotic thresholds may depend on \(c\). Each \(A_c\) must be uniform in \(n\); no additional uniform algorithm taking \(c\) as input is demanded. A deterministic family would also refute the randomized hypothesis.

An exponent saving \(\varepsilon_c>0\) that shrinks with \(c\), a bound for a fixed small dimension, logarithmic improvements over quadratic time, success only on random instances, or a lower bound restricted to monotone circuits, formulas or branching programs does not settle the full proposition. A fast online query bound with separate preprocessing must satisfy the total charged offline time before it qualifies. This is an asymptotic yes-or-no claim, with no additive numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on \(c\) is the main subtlety. Abboud, Williams and Yu’s SODA 2015 algorithm runs in \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time in the relevant large-\(c\) regime. Thus a positive exponent saving is already known for every fixed dimension constant, but the saving decreases as that constant increases. This is compatible with the hypothesis, which excludes one positive saving shared by all constants. The conference year is 2015, even though some later bibliographies label the paper 2014.

Randomness is not necessary for the existing dimension-dependent saving. Chan and Williams’s SODA 2016 result obtains deterministic \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time, including counting orthogonal pairs and batched bichromatic detection. It still allows the saving to decrease with \(c\). The hypothesis therefore does not assert that randomization is the only obstacle to a universal subquadratic algorithm.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm has a one-sided-error running-time bound \(\widetilde O(1.25^d n)\), with a reported computer-aided improvement to \(O(1.16^d n)\). Here the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors in the input size, including polynomial factors in \(d\) in the stated logarithmic regime. The finite parameter evaluation was not independently rerun in this review. Exponential dependence on dimension becomes a power of \(n\) after substituting \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\), so this bound does not give the uniform exponent saving excluded by the hypothesis.

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this randomized OV hypothesis through the standard satisfiability reduction and sparsification. That supplies a conditional explanation for the proposed barrier, not an unconditional lower bound. A deterministic-only satisfiability assumption cannot by itself rule out randomized OV algorithms. The current primary literature continues to separate these assumptions from the restricted-model theorems it proves.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

The May 2026 online-OV paper deterministically refutes a different conjecture about preprocessing space and later query time. Its logarithmic-dimensional query saving depends on \(c\), and preprocessing has its own stated cost. The offline decision problem here is charged for both lists and every preprocessing step. The word “refutation” in that paper consequently does not mean the present OV hypothesis was refuted.
why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. July 2026 Conjecture 1 explicitly retains the unrestricted randomized OV hypothesis while proving circuit, formula and branching-program restrictions. Deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent algorithms remain compatible with its quantifier order. The May online-OV refutation addresses a different space/query conjecture, and average-case algorithms do not cover every input. No matching unrestricted resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; external proofs were not independently formalized.
