The retained hypothesis says that every proposed fixed saving over quadratic time fails at some fixed logarithmic-dimension constant. It concerns uniform randomized word-RAM algorithms with all preprocessing charged, worst-case running time and bounded error on every input. A complete Lean refutation must provide one positive exponent saving valid for every dimension constant, although its individual programs and time constants may depend on that constant. Known deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent savings, average-case improvements and restricted-model lower bounds leave this full hypothesis unresolved.

title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
importance_reason: A principal fine-grained benchmark connecting clique detection, matrix multiplication, dynamic data structures, and constraint optimization.
formal:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), let \(\tau(k)\) be the infimum worst-case time exponent for uniform classical randomized algorithms deciding whether an \(n\)-vertex graph contains a \(k\)-clique, in the word-RAM model defined below. Let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\). Is
\[
 \liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\tau(k)}{k}=\frac{\omega}{3}?
\]
The input size \(n\) tends to infinity with \(k\) fixed when defining \(\tau(k)\); only afterwards does \(k\) grow in the displayed limit inferior.
question_excerpt: The inherited ISAAC source states graph k-clique hardness with exponent omega*k/3 minus a sublinear term in k, allowing randomized and deterministic algorithms. This card retains the corresponding leading-coefficient formulation and makes its machine conventions and quantifier order explicit. Stronger versions that assert the exact exponent for every fixed k are separate.
definitions:
A graph is simple and undirected, with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge k\), and an explicitly given symmetric Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Its \(n^2\) entries are stored in row order, one per word, together with \(n\). A \(k\)-clique is a set of \(k\) distinct vertices with all pairs adjacent. The algorithm outputs a YES or NO bit; it is not asked to list or count cliques.

For fixed \(k\), call a real \(a\ge0\) admissible if there exist a finite uniform randomized program, an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), real \(C>0\) and integer \(N\ge k\), such that for every graph on \(n\ge N\) vertices every execution takes at most \(Cn^a\) instructions and the answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The program must also terminate and meet the same probability guarantee on each valid smaller input. Constants and program may depend on \(k\) and \(a\), but not on \(n\) or the graph. Define
\[
 \tau(k)=\inf\{a\ge0:a\text{ is admissible for }k\}.
\]
Exhaustive enumeration makes this set nonempty. Its infimum need not itself be achieved. There is no requirement for an efficient compiler taking \(k\) to its program; uniformity here means one program handling every \(n\) for each fixed \(k\).

At size \(n\), words contain \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. One instruction may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), divide two unsigned words with nonzero divisor and return quotient or remainder, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, compare two unsigned words, or branch. Logical shifts discard bits beyond the word; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word may also be obtained in one instruction. All other memory is initially zero, and every preprocessing operation is charged. No nonuniform advice, free table depending on \(n\), arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic or external oracle is allowed. The constant \(B\) may be chosen with the algorithm so that its polynomially many addressed cells fit in a word. The time bound holds on every random tape, not only in expectation, while success probability is over that tape on each fixed graph.

To define \(\omega\), for each integer \(N\ge1\) let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates in an arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb C\) that computes every entry of the product of two formal \(N\)-by-\(N\) matrices. The \(2N^2\) entries of those matrices are independent indeterminates. Circuits may share intermediate results and use arbitrary complex constants, but not division or branching; they must compute the required polynomial identities exactly. Put
\[
 \omega=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\ \forall N\ge N_0,
                       \ M(N)\le CN^a\}.
\]
This is the characteristic-zero arithmetic exponent, not a particular currently published numerical upper bound. The complex constants used to define it are not free constants or arithmetic oracles supplied to the word-RAM graph algorithm.

For a real sequence \(u_k\), its limit inferior is \(\sup_K\inf_{k\ge K}u_k\). Thus the question concerns the leading coefficient of clique size in the optimal exponent. The standard matrix-multiplication benchmark gives the upper asymptotic coefficient \(\omega/3\); the hypothesis asserts the matching lower coefficient. The inherited leading-exponent formulation does not separately assert the precise optimum for each small fixed \(k\). Nor does it invoke an informal restriction to algorithms described as combinatorial: all classical algorithms in the specified machine model are included.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed equality or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation, with exactly the models and order of limits defined above.

In view of the matrix-multiplication upper benchmark, an affirmative result must establish that for every real \(\delta>0\) there is \(K\) such that \(\tau(k)\ge(\omega/3-\delta)k\) for every integer \(k\ge K\). A negative result can establish one fixed positive saving \(\delta\) for arbitrarily large clique sizes, with proved algorithms and resource bounds, so that the limit inferior is strictly smaller than \(\omega/3\).

An improvement confined to a single fixed \(k\), logarithmic factors in \(n\), or an additive \(o(k)\) saving in the exponent does not by itself refute this formulation. Beating an outdated numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) is also insufficient. Lower bounds only for a restricted algorithm family, or only conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis, do not prove the unrestricted proposition. This is an exact yes-or-no hypothesis about exponents; numerical accuracy within \(1/100\) is not a substitute for the equality or its negation.
context:
The hypothesis concerns the exponent of a polynomial-time problem for each fixed clique size. Ordinary NP-hardness when the clique size varies with the input does not give the requested sharp leading coefficient.

Matrix multiplication supplies the asymptotic benchmark. Divisibility by three and rectangular refinements affect individual clique sizes, so the source’s leading-coefficient target should not be silently replaced by a stronger statement for every small size.

The 2024 graph-detection improvements save logarithmic factors. Those do not change the leading coefficient tested here; its hypergraph and clique-listing results concern different tasks.

The August 2026 preprint reports \(\omega<2.371177\). Such progress improves the matrix-based upper benchmark but does not prove its optimality for clique decision. The target uses the true exponent, with no numerical estimate substituted.

The source applies clique hardness to dynamic Boolean-formula problems. A precise form of the assumption therefore matters beyond clique detection itself. Conditional applications and exponent-preserving reductions are not unconditional proofs of the hypothesis.
why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.
status_note: The checked sources and 2026 conditional applications continue to use clique hardness as a hypothesis. Logarithmic combinatorial improvements, regularization reductions and the August 2026 matrix-exponent announcement do not resolve this leading-coefficient formulation. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified proof or refutation; the numerical matrix certificate was not independently replayed.
progress: 2021: The source explicitly states the leading-exponent clique hypothesis with randomized and deterministic algorithms. | 2024-08-03: The revised combinatorial-algorithms paper records logarithmic graph-detection improvements. | 2025: Regularization reductions preserve the relevant clique and hyperclique exponents. | 2026-08-17: A matrix-multiplication preprint reports a smaller numerical upper bound, without resolving clique optimality.
working_summary: For each fixed clique size, the task is to decide whether an arbitrary graph contains that many pairwise adjacent vertices. The hypothesis compares the leading coefficient of the optimal randomized time exponent with one third of the true matrix-multiplication exponent. The graph algorithm uses logarithmic-size words, and its time bound must hold on every random tape. The graph size tends to infinity first, while the clique size is fixed; the outer limit then considers growing clique sizes. A complete Lean-checked proof or refutation must address that full asymptotic comparison, rather than only logarithmic savings or one fixed clique size.

title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
importance_reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.
formal: Is the following bounded-error randomized Hyperclique Hypothesis true? For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge3\) and \(k>h\), and every constant real \(\epsilon>0\), there is no uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and constant \(T\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge k\) and every simple \(h\)-uniform hypergraph \(H\) on \([n]\), \(A\) outputs one bit deciding whether \(H\) contains a \(k\)-clique, runs for at most \(Tn^{k-\epsilon}\) steps on every execution, and is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on that input. The dense representation, permitted instructions and word size are fixed below. The program and constants may depend on \(h,k,\epsilon\), but not on \(n\), the input hypergraph or the random outcomes.
question_excerpt: Retains the explicitly selected randomized classical version of the h≥3 branch of Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß Hypothesis 2.2, with the clique-size/uniformity notation translated consistently. Its partite and the card’s general-input forms are equivalent for fixed parameters. The dense word-RAM representation, two-sided per-input error and worst-case runtime are editorially explicit; no claim is made that every cited paper separately spells out this randomization convention.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\binom{[n]}h=\{e\subseteq[n]:|e|=h\}\). The hypergraph is \(H=([n],E)\) for an arbitrary set \(E\subseteq\binom{[n]}h\): hyperedges are unordered sets of distinct vertices, with no weights, repetitions, colors or other promises. A \(k\)-clique is a subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(k\) satisfying \(\binom Sh\subseteq E\). Only existence is queried; a witness, count or list is not required. Inputs with \(n<k\) have answer zero and may be handled separately. Uniformity \(h\) and clique size \(k\) are fixed constants for each algorithm under consideration, not growing input parameters.

The input stores \(n\) and a dense read-only membership array with one word for each increasing tuple \(1\le v_1<\cdots<v_h\le n\), ordered lexicographically. That word is exactly \(1\) if \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_h\}\in E\), and \(0\) otherwise, with all unused bits zero. There is no auxiliary input index or precomputed data structure. The RAM may access this array at a computed address; each probe is charged. All preprocessing, auxiliary table construction, arithmetic and output are charged. The algorithm is not required to scan the entire array if it can obtain the answer with fewer probes.

For a fixed algorithm choose an integer \(D\ge h+1\) and let the word length be \(w=D\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. The constant \(D\) can depend on the fixed \(h,k,\epsilon\), but not on \(n\) or \(E\). Registers, addresses and memory cells contain unsigned \(w\)-bit words; initially work memory is zero. In one step the machine may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare words, branch, use a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or take unsigned integer quotient or remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Each random instruction produces a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one step. Computations involving larger integers require charged multiword operations. There is no unit-cost real or arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle or quantum operation, and no advice depending on \(n\). The program has one finite description for all sizes; input-independent constants in that fixed description are allowed, but generated tables cost time.

Success probability is over these random words for each fixed hypergraph. It may have two-sided error, but must be at least \(2/3\) on every positive and every negative input. The time bound holds on all random executions, including erroneous ones; expected time alone is a different guarantee. No separate space bound is imposed beyond the addressed-word model and charged computation. The exclusion concerns every fixed pair \((h,k)\) separately and every fixed positive exponent saving, not only a limit as \(k\) grows. Writing the time bound for all \(n\ge k\) is equivalent to the asymptotic big-O convention: finitely many exceptional sizes can be handled by a finite modification of the algorithm and its constant. One may restrict to rational positive savings without changing the hypothesis, since any positive saving implies a smaller rational saving.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the entire stated exclusion, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A proof of the hypothesis must cover every fixed \(h\ge3,k>h\), every positive saving and every randomized algorithm in the specified model; a conditional lower bound alone is insufficient. A refutation supplies one fixed pair \((h,k)\), one \(\epsilon>0\), a finite algorithm and constants, and proves its worst-case bound and per-input success probability for all hypergraphs of every size. It need not improve all parameter pairs and need not print a clique. Saving only a logarithmic factor, using expected time without the required worst-case guarantee, exploiting a proper promised subclass, or proving a restricted or nonuniform algebraic circuit bound does not settle this statement. This is an exact yes/no hypothesis about asymptotic resources, with no additive numerical tolerance.
context:
A graph records pairwise compatibility; an \(h\)-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of \(h\) vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4\), a positive instance has four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Having each pair participate in some hyperedge elsewhere does not establish these four triples on the same vertex set. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed \(h,k\), direct inspection of all \(k\)-vertex sets gives \(O(n^k)\) time, since each set has only \(\binom{k}{h}\) hyperedges to check. The task is therefore polynomial-time for every fixed parameter pair. The hypothesis concerns a constant reduction in that polynomial exponent; NP-hardness with a variable clique-size parameter is a different assertion.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding has \(\binom nh=\Theta(n^h)\) Boolean entries for fixed \(h\). Since \(k>h\), conversions taking \(n^h\) times logarithmic factors do not erase every positive exponent saving: a claimed saving can always be weakened to a smaller positive constant. There is no promise that the input has few hyperedges, few nonedges or a particular distribution.

The inherited hypothesis is stated for \(k\)-partite hypergraphs. In that setting vertices are divided into \(k\) parts and each hyperedge uses distinct parts; a clique has one vertex in each part. For fixed \(h,k\), standard conversions between general and partite instances have a constant-factor vertex increase and preserve a positive exponent saving after charging their input-processing time. The card states the equivalent general-input detection task.

Fischer, Künnemann, Redžić and Stieß prove a stronger regularization theorem. For each fixed \(h<k\), their Theorem 3.1 converts an arbitrary hypergraph to a \(k\)-partite one with only a parameter-dependent constant-factor vertex increase, preserving whether a \(k\)-clique exists. The output has equal extension counts for transversal subsets of each size below \(h\). Thus this strong regularity promise does not by itself remove the conditional fine-grained difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work relates \((k-1)\)-uniform \(k\)-hypercliques to detecting \(k\)-term arithmetic progressions in a bounded integer universe. For the smallest case and a fixed \(0<\epsilon<1\), an \(O(n^{4-\epsilon})\)-time hyperclique algorithm would give an \(O(N^{2-\epsilon/2})\)-time algorithm for four-term progression detection in \(X\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N\}\), by Lemma 5.7. Here \(N\) is the universe bound, not merely \(|X|\). This is a conditional connection; neither side is proved hard unconditionally.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The February 2026 report Beyond Bilinear Complexity states a separate nonuniform algebraic hyperclique conjecture about circuit families computing a hyperclique tensor. Its Theorem 4 derives a failure of circuit-complexity submultiplicativity from that assumption. The authors explicitly distinguish this circuit hypothesis from a uniform algorithmic consequence. It is not a proof of the randomized word-RAM lower bound on this card.

Brand, Kaski and Wang’s August 2026 revision relates partition ranks to multiplicative complexity of multilinear maps. Its hyperclique discussion concerns potential algebraic circuit lower bounds; it does not establish the required exponent bound even for the hyperclique polynomial, nor does it give an exponent-saving classical detection algorithm. The computational models and the conjectural status remain separate.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.
why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No classical bounded-error word-RAM algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving on all inputs for a covered pair, or unconditional proof of the full exclusion, was found in the bounded primary-source review. The 2025 regularization and 2026 arithmetic-progression and sparsity papers state conditional consequences. The February 2026 nonuniform algebraic variant and August partition-rank result do not prove this randomized algorithmic hypothesis. External proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 2017–2018: Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams develop hyperclique hypotheses, their Max-h-SAT connections and conditional graph-algorithm lower bounds. | 2025: Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß prove regularization preserving fine-grained clique complexity and apply it to Boolean CSP optimization. | 30 March–June 2026: Dudek and coauthors relate the 3-uniform 4-hyperclique hypothesis to arithmetic-progression detection in their STOC 2026 study of algebraic identities. | July 2026: Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß analyze when sparsity helps for hypergraph independent sets and use hyperclique assumptions for matching lower bounds. | February 2026: A tensor-complexity report states and uses an explicitly nonuniform algebraic hyperclique assumption; it does not prove the classical algorithmic hypothesis. | 5 August 2026: The revised partition-rank paper gives general connections to algebraic circuit lower bounds while leaving its hyperclique application conjectural.
working_summary: A k-clique in an h-uniform hypergraph is a set of k distinct vertices containing every possible h-element hyperedge. The hypothesis excludes a fixed positive improvement over the exhaustive-search exponent for every fixed uniformity at least three and every larger fixed clique size. The chosen model is a uniform classical randomized word-RAM on a dense membership table, with worst-case time and success probability at least two thirds for each input. A complete Lean proof must establish the full exclusion or give one fixed parameter pair and a proved exponent-saving algorithm that refutes it. Conditional reductions, sparse-input improvements and nonuniform algebraic circuit results from the 2026 literature do not settle this all-input randomized hypothesis.

title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
importance_reason: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.
context:
The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.
why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
status_note: The checked primary literature gives conditional exact-distance lower bounds and a March 2026 approximation advance. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established deterministic truly subquadratic exact algorithm or unconditional exclusion in this model.
progress: 2015 / 2017: Backurs–Indyk prove a SETH-based obstruction to truly subquadratic exact edit distance; the 2017 full revision also records subsequent developments. | 2015-04: Bringmann–Künnemann establish the conditional lower bound already on binary strings. | 2026-03: A randomized approximation scheme obtains a quasi-polynomial speedup; it does not compute exact distances.
working_summary: Can exact edit distance between two length-n binary strings be computed in truly subquadratic time? Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum. The requested deterministic worst-case bound has a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n. Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved. The 2026 approximation improvement has different accuracy and randomness guarantees.

title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
importance_reason: A widely reusable fine-grained hardness hypothesis underlying trade-offs for many dynamic problems; its consequences reach well beyond matrix-vector multiplication.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every integer \(n\ge2\), every Boolean matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and every sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n\) supplied online, the algorithm outputs each \(Mv_t\) before receiving \(v_{t+1}\), and outputs \(Mv_n\) at the end, using at most
\[
 K n^{3-\varepsilon}
\]
word-RAM instructions in total on every execution, including preprocessing of \(M\), with probability at least \(2/3\) that all \(n\) output vectors are correct? Products are over the Boolean semiring:
\[
 (Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j\bigr).
\]
The OMv conjecture asserts a negative answer.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 1.1 rules out a fixed polynomial saving over cubic total time for online Boolean matrix-vector multiplication with error at most one third. The card asks for an algorithm with such a saving, so its conjectured answer is no, and makes the charged uniform word-RAM and complete-sequence error conventions explicit.
definitions:
The input initially supplies \(n\) and all \(n^2\) entries of the fixed matrix \(M\), in row-major order. After the algorithm's initial preprocessing, vectors arrive one at a time in the order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Each vector is an arbitrary length-\(n\) bit string. The next vector is unavailable until the algorithm has finished returning the current vector's complete answer. The algorithm may preserve its computed state and earlier vectors, but cannot postpone an output to use future inputs. There is no per-query time bound beyond the total bound and these deadlines.

Both the matrix bit string and each input vector are explicitly packed into consecutive words with known zero padding. An output vector contains its \(n\) bits in coordinate order; an explicit array with one Boolean value per word is an allowed canonical output representation. Returning an implicit circuit, a pointer to uncomputed answers, a count of nonzero entries or just one queried coordinate is insufficient. All input access and output writes are charged. The matrix never changes. The operations \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) mean Boolean AND and OR; this is neither arithmetic multiplication over the reals nor multiplication over the field of two elements.

The computation is a sequential word RAM with
\[
 w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
\]
bits per word and one fixed finite program for all \(n\). Memory cells, registers and addresses are word-sized. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Multiword computations cost their component instructions. An independent uniform random \(w\)-bit word can be generated in one instruction. This permits deterministic algorithms as a special case. There are no quantum instructions, nonuniform advice, free precomputed tables or input-dependent oracles. Unused memory initially contains zero.

All instructions are counted, including construction of auxiliary tables, allocation or initialization performed by the program, preprocessing before the first vector, work between vectors, generation of random words, copying and output. There is no separate allowance for an arbitrary polynomial preprocessing phase. Space has no additional sublinear or near-linear restriction, but every address must fit in a word and writing any used state costs instructions. Only the currently supplied input is made available by the online interface; it supplies no information about a future vector.

For the success guarantee, the matrix and complete vector sequence are fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. The probability is over the program's random words, and the successful event requires every bit of every output to be correct. A separate success probability of \(2/3\) for each individual query is not the specified joint guarantee. The time bound holds for every random execution, including erroneous executions. Every output deadline and eventual termination must likewise be met on every execution.

The constants \(\varepsilon,K,B\) and the program are chosen once, independently of the input dimension and contents. Any fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) suffices. A merely logarithmic or subpolynomial improvement in total time is not a fixed exponent saving. No restriction to combinatorial algorithms is imposed: every algorithm implementable by the specified word-RAM instructions is allowed.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated algorithm exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist.

A positive answer must establish the fixed exponent saving after charging preprocessing and all input/output work, the online deadlines, and joint success for every fixed input. It refutes the OMv conjecture in this model. A negative answer must exclude every admissible uniform randomized program, every fixed word-size constant and every positive exponent saving. It proves the conjecture in this model and cannot assume the conjecture itself or another unproved hardness hypothesis.

An algorithm for structured matrices, an offline matrix product, a query bound after uncharged preprocessing, or a cell-probe bound with free computation does not meet the target without a proved extension. Neither does a speedup of the form \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), which supplies no fixed positive saving in the exponent.
context:
The online requirement separates this task from ordinary matrix multiplication: each answer must be committed before a future query arrives. The original work develops reductions from this task to many dynamic problems.

Larsen and Williams obtain a randomized total bound of \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\). Its speedup is larger than any fixed polylogarithmic factor but does not supply the fixed exponent saving requested here.

The same work gives a genuinely subquadratic query bound in the cell-probe model, where computation between memory accesses is free. This separates a known information-access bound from the charged computation required by the card.

Hu and Polak establish subcubic equivalences with existential equality and dominance products, min-witness, min-max and bounded monotone min-plus variants. These equivalences transfer algorithmic breakthroughs or hypotheses; they do not prove the hypotheses.

The February 2026 revision gives faster queries when the matrix has bounded VC dimension, with corresponding extensions to other structured inputs. Arbitrary Boolean matrices are not subject to that promise.

title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
importance_reason: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.
context:
Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.
why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The ICALP 2026 paper still states the unrestricted min-plus convolution hypothesis, records a subpolynomial unrestricted speedup, and proves faster results for monotone bounded-range inputs. No fixed-saving algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this explicit integer formulation was located. Source proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2014: Convolution algorithms exploit pair-sum structure without establishing a fixed exponent improvement for general min-plus convolution. | 2026: Deterministic faster algorithms handle the monotone structured variant; they do not settle arbitrary polynomially bounded arrays.
working_summary: Min-plus convolution returns the minimum sum of two array entries for each possible sum of their indices. The input arrays contain polynomially bounded integers and need not be monotone. The question asks for a fixed improvement in the quadratic running-time exponent. Bounded-error randomization is allowed and every output entry must be correct simultaneously. Faster algorithms for monotone instances do not settle this unrestricted fine-grained barrier.

title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
importance_reason: Truly subquadratic 3SUM is a central fine-grained hypothesis with consequences for a large family of geometric and combinatorial problems.
formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.
context:
Known algorithms beat \(n^2\) by logarithmic factors. Such bounds are \(o(n^2)\), but they do not give \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The modern conjecture concerns this latter, truly subquadratic improvement.

The three-set input convention follows the source. The integer word-RAM and polynomial-universe choices distinguish this target from real-RAM variants and from decision trees that charge only selected comparisons. The lower-bound claim is not restricted to a comparison-only instruction set.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat formulate the modern conjecture even for expected running time and use Las Vegas complexities in their reductions. The zero-error convention here follows that formulation; it is made explicit rather than silently identifying different randomized models.

Recent work improves time–space tradeoffs after sets have been preprocessed. This is useful progress for data structures, but the present input arrives from scratch, so the entire preprocessing time must be included in its complexity.
why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.
status_note: The source problem list and Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat’s modern expected-time formulation were checked on 2026-09-14, together with 2026 preprocessed-3SUM work. A bounded later search found no from-scratch Las Vegas algorithm or general lower bound resolving the explicitly selected polynomial-universe variant.
progress: 2005: Subquadratic integer algorithms with logarithmic-factor savings are among the results reviewed by the source; they leave a fixed polynomial saving open. | 2016: Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat develop reductions from the modern expected-time 3SUM conjecture to set-intersection, graph and data-structure tasks. | 2026: ICALP work obtains improved subquadratic-space tradeoffs for preprocessed 3SUM; the model retains a preprocessing phase and does not establish a truly subquadratic from-scratch algorithm.
working_summary: 3SUM asks whether a value in one integer list is the sum of values from two other lists. The target is a fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic running time on a precisely specified word RAM. The selected variant allows every fixed polynomial integer universe and requires a common exponent saving. Randomization may change the running time but must never produce an incorrect answer. Known logarithmic savings and faster queries after preprocessing do not meet the from-scratch target.

title: Hitting Set conjecture
importance_reason: A standard hardness hypothesis behind fine-grained diameter and graph-distance barriers.
formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length
\[
w=\max\!\left\{\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\ \lceil\log_2(2nd+n+d+8)\rceil\right\}.
\]
The second term ensures that the full explicit input and its headers fit in the address universe even for small \(n\) and a large fixed dimension constant \(c\). For every fixed \(c\), it is eventually dominated by the first term, so this finite-input correction leaves the stated asymptotic time hypothesis unchanged. Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.
context:
For fixed \(c\), comparing every pair of packed vectors gives an \(O(cn^2)\)-time baseline. The conjecture permits savings that vanish as dimension grows; it rules out one fixed polynomial saving valid across all dimension constants.

Orthogonal Vectors asks whether some pair has zero inner product. Here one supplied vector must have nonzero inner product with every vector on the other side. Exchanging these quantifiers changes the question, just as finding a graph center differs from finding a distant pair of vertices.

The 2021 source transfers this hypothesis to model checking with an existential–universal–existential quantifier pattern. Such reductions establish consequences of the conjecture, not an unconditional lower bound for Hitting Set.

The card retains the randomized bounded-error convention of the saved formulation and specifies its machine model. Restricted-dimensional algorithms and expected-time-only guarantees should be compared against these exact quantifiers and resources.
why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.
status_note: The original 2016 conjecture and the 2021 logarithmic-dimension formulation were checked on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search, including 2026 graph-center work, found continuing conditional applications and no resolution of the selected randomized bounded-error hypothesis.
progress: 2016: Abboud, Vassilevska Williams and Wang introduce the conjecture to formulate radius and related graph-distance barriers. | 2021: An and coauthors use the logarithmic-dimensional Hitting Set problem to obtain conditional quadratic lower bounds for multi-dimensional ordering properties.
working_summary: Two lists contain subsets of a logarithmic-size universe. The task is to find whether one supplied set in the first list intersects every set in the second. The conjecture rules out a single fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic time across all constant multiples of logarithmic dimension. The selected model permits randomization with bounded error and counts all word-RAM computation. Its existential–universal structure makes it useful for graph-radius and quantified-ordering lower bounds.

title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
importance_reason: Clarify whether a major approximation-hardness assumption adds strength to the standard exact exponential-time hypothesis.
formal:
Is the implication
\[
 \mathsf{ETH}_{\mathrm{det}}\ \Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathsf{GapETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
\]
true for the following precise hypotheses?
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf{ETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
   &:\quad \exists\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ 
           \neg\operatorname{FastSAT}(\eta),\\
 \mathsf{GapETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
   &:\quad \exists B\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
           \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ 
           \exists\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ 
           \neg\operatorname{FastGapSAT}(B,\delta,\eta).
\end{aligned}
\]
The fast-algorithm predicates below use deterministic bit computation, exponent parameter equal to the number of variables, and a fixed polynomial factor in the whole binary input length. The gap predicate concerns formulas with at most \(Bn\) clauses and the promise of full satisfiability or value at most \(1-\delta\).
question_excerpt: The dot-product-proof paper obtains ETH-based exponential approximation hardness for dense linear-equation constraints and explicitly distinguishes that result from the open implication ETH ⇒ Gap-ETH for local constraint problems. The card isolates the deterministic implication with fixed positive exponential rates and sparse 3-CNF inputs on the gap side.
definitions:
A 3-CNF formula \(F\) is a finite list of clauses on Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), each clause being a disjunction of at most three signed variables. The indices are in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and each of these variables occurs somewhere unless \(n=0\). Clauses and literals may repeat, and tautological and empty clauses are allowed. Satisfiability means that one assignment makes every clause true. A list with no clauses is satisfiable, while an empty clause is false under every assignment.

For definiteness, encode a nonnegative integer \(z\) by \(1^t0\operatorname{bin}(z)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\) and \(t\) is the length of the usual binary expansion. The input contains the codes of \(n\) and the clause count \(m\), then each clause length in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) followed by its literals, each a sign bit and a coded positive variable index. There is no trailing data. The full encoded length is \(L\); the exponent parameter is \(n\), not \(L\) or \(m\). The variable-naming convention prevents a large binary index from declaring unused variables. Invalid encodings are outside the mathematical input domain.

For \(m>0\), define
\[
 \operatorname{val}(F)=
 \max_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}
 \frac{\#\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\text{clause }j\text{ is true under }z\}}{m}.
\]
Clause occurrences are counted with their multiplicities. Put \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) when \(m=0\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) is precisely satisfiability, including the empty conjunction.

For a fixed rational \(\eta>0\), \(\operatorname{FastSAT}(\eta)\) means that there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every valid formula \(F\), the machine halts within
\[
 K2^{\eta n}(L+1)^d
\]
bit operations and returns 1 exactly when \(F\) is satisfiable, returning 0 otherwise. There is no bound on the clause count in this predicate. The existential machine and constants may depend on \(\eta\), but not on \(n,m,L\) or the particular input.

For fixed \(B\ge1\), \(0<\delta<1\) and \(\eta>0\), \(\operatorname{FastGapSAT}(B,\delta,\eta)\) means that there exist a single deterministic machine \(A\), a constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) with the same displayed bit-time bound on every valid formula with \(m\le Bn\). It must return 1 when \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) and 0 when \(\operatorname{val}(F)\le1-\delta\). For formulas strictly between those values, either answer is allowed, but the time bound still holds. There is no required behavior for valid formulas violating \(m\le Bn\). The fixed parameters \(B,\delta,\eta\) specify which algorithm is under discussion and are not additional variable input parameters. The machine and its polynomial factors may depend on them, but not on a formula.

All machines are uniform classical deterministic bit machines with finite programs, no advice, no oracle, no random bits and no quantum operations. Input processing, intermediate computation and output are charged. In each predicate the polynomial exponent and multiplicative constant are fixed independently of input size. The assertion of a positive exponential lower-bound rate means that at least one fixed positive \(\eta\) admits no such algorithm; it does not merely rule out one chosen algorithm. Restricting the fixed rate and gap constants to rational values and the density bound to integers does not change these existential positive-rate conventions.

The implication is between these particular mathematical propositions. It does not assert either hypothesis separately, and it does not request a proof specifically by a chosen reduction. It retains a perfectly satisfiable YES case. Randomized hypotheses, other completeness thresholds, other computational models and hardness of other approximation problems are not substituted without a proof connecting them to these definitions.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication, with no unproved premise besides its stated antecedent, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

The negation is \(\mathsf{ETH}_{\mathrm{det}}\) together with \(\neg\mathsf{GapETH}_{\mathrm{det}}\). Under the definitions above the latter says that, for every fixed \(B\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and rational \(\eta>0\), \(\operatorname{FastGapSAT}(B,\delta,\eta)\) holds. Different fixed parameters may have different uniform machines and polynomial factors; no effective compiler from these parameters to programs is demanded. Ruling out one reduction method or giving a relativized separation does not prove this unrelativized negation.

An ETH-based lower bound for a different gap problem, a parameterized inapproximability theorem, or a PCP construction with a superlinear increase that loses the required positive exponential rate does not by itself prove the implication. If a reduction is used, its completeness, soundness, size, running time and deterministic conventions must suffice for the exact hypotheses here. Further unproved assumptions establish only a more conditional statement.
context:
Exact satisfiability permits an unsatisfiable formula whose assignments each violate only a tiny fraction of clauses. The gap hypothesis asks for exponential hardness even when the NO instances have a fixed positive fraction of unavoidable violations.

The dot-product-proof result removes the need for a gap assumption in a dense linear-equation approximation problem. The source expressly distinguishes that accomplishment from establishing Gap-ETH for sparse local constraints.

ETH is known to imply the Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis. Its parameterized constraint model and alphabet bounds do not yield the particular sparse Boolean exponential-rate assertion on this card.

The quasi-linear-size PCP construction gives strong ETH-based approximation consequences, but its stated bound retains a polylogarithmic loss in the exponent.

The April 2026 lattice work obtains further consequences from dense MAXLIN, distinguishing deterministic and randomized reductions. These are results for specific applications, not a proof that the two general hypotheses coincide.
why: The implication would show that exponential hardness of exact satisfiability already supplies the sparse constant-gap hardness used in many fine-grained approximation lower bounds.
status_note: The bounded source check through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the deterministic positive-exponent ETH-to-sparse-Gap-ETH implication. The December 2025 source explicitly retains the distinction; ETH-implied PIH, quasi-linear PCPs and April 2026 lattice consequences have different models or quantitative guarantees. Full proofs of the later results were not independently audited.
progress: 2024: Dot-product proofs give ETH-based hardness for dense MAXLIN while distinguishing the ETH-to-Gap-ETH question. | 2025-06-15: The quasi-linear PCP construction improves size-efficient approximation hardness with a remaining polylogarithmic exponent loss. | 2025-10: The JACM version proves ETH implies PIH in the parameterized setting. | 2025-12-30: The revised dot-product-proof source retains the distinction between its dense consequence and Gap-ETH. | 2026-04-21: The revised lattice paper gives further ETH-based consequences through MAXLIN.
working_summary: ETH asserts a fixed positive exponential-time lower bound for exact 3-SAT. The selected Gap-ETH asserts such a lower bound for sparse formulas promised to be satisfiable or to leave a fixed fraction of clauses unsatisfied under every assignment. The question asks whether the deterministic exact hypothesis implies this deterministic gap hypothesis. All exponential rates and polynomial input-length factors have explicit quantifiers, and the YES case requires perfect satisfiability. A complete Lean-checked resolution must establish the implication or its actual logical negation, rather than hardness for a different approximation problem.

title: Disjunction of randomized SETH, integer APSP and 3SUM hypotheses
importance_reason: A proof would supply one shared foundation for many fine-grained lower bounds without deciding which of the three core problems is hard; a refutation would require major algorithmic improvements for all three.
formal:
Is the following disjunction true in the uniform randomized word-RAM models defined below?
\[
H_{\mathrm{SAT}}\ \lor\ H_{\mathrm{APSP}}\ \lor\ H_{\mathrm{3SUM}},
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_{\mathrm{SAT}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists k\ge3:
 \neg\operatorname{FastSAT}(k,\varepsilon),\\
H_{\mathrm{APSP}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists c\ge1:
 \neg\operatorname{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon),\\
H_{\mathrm{3SUM}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1):
 \neg\operatorname{Fast3SUM}(\varepsilon)?
\end{aligned}
\]
The quantified \(k,c\) are integers. The predicates assert algorithms with respective time bounds \(K2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}(L+1)^d\), \(Kn^{3-\varepsilon}\), and \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\), and success probability at least \(2/3\) on each input. Each time bound holds on every random tape.
question_excerpt: The survey asks for a more robust foundation for fine-grained hardness by considering the conjecture that at least one of SETH, the APSP Hypothesis and the 3SUM Hypothesis holds. The primary paper states this as Conjecture 1 and explicitly allows randomized algorithms.
definitions:
For \(\operatorname{FastSAT}(k,\varepsilon)\), an input is an explicit Boolean CNF formula on exactly its \(n\) occurring variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). It is a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most the fixed \(k\) literals; a literal is a variable or its negation. Empty clauses are false and an empty conjunction is true. Repeated clauses and literals are allowed, with no density, occurrence or satisfiability promise. The output is one exactly specified bit: whether an assignment in \(\{0,1\}^n\) makes the formula true. The encoding explicitly lists \(n\), the number of clauses, each clause length and its signed variable indices. To fix its bit length \(L\), encode each nonnegative integer \(a\) by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(a+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\); a sign uses one bit. All records must be present, with no trailing bits, all variable indices valid and every declared variable occurring. The input bits are supplied as an explicit array. A fast SAT predicate asserts existence of one finite program, integers \(d\ge1,B\ge8\), and \(K\ge1\) giving the stated bound on all such formulas. These choices may depend on \(k,\varepsilon\). Malformed strings are rejected in polynomial time. Cases with no occurring variables are decided directly.

For \(\operatorname{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\), an input is an explicit adjacency matrix of a directed graph on \(n\ge2\) numbered vertices, with a presence flag and a signed integer weight for each ordered vertex pair. Present weights belong to \([-n^c,n^c]\). The graph is promised to have no negative-weight directed cycle. Absent edges have a flag rather than a large finite cost; self-loops, negative edges, equal distances and zero-weight cycles are allowed. The output is the entire \(n\times n\) matrix of exact shortest-walk distances, using a separate unreachable flag. Empty walks have cost zero. Under the promise each finite distance is attained and has magnitude at most \((n-1)n^c\). The algorithm succeeds only when the whole matrix is correct. The fast predicate asserts existence of a finite program, a word-size factor \(B\ge c+4\), and \(K\ge1\), all depending at most on \(c,\varepsilon\). No path listing or behavior on a graph violating the promise is required.

For \(\operatorname{Fast3SUM}(\varepsilon)\), an input is an explicit list of \(n\ge2\) distinct integers from \([-n^4,n^4]\). The required bit is whether three distinct indices \(i,j,\ell\) satisfy \(a_i+a_j+a_\ell=0\), using ordinary integer addition. For \(n<3\) the answer is no. The program, \(K\ge1\) and word-size factor \(B\ge8\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the list or \(n\). This fixes the single-set, polynomial-universe integer formulation; it is not a question about arbitrary real inputs or solely the number of comparisons.

For SAT set \(N=L+2\); for APSP and 3SUM set \(N=n+2\). A word has \(w=B\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) bits. Programs are sequential classical word RAMs with a fixed finite instruction list, one-word addresses and initially zero work cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero is invalid. Larger quantities use multiple words with every constituent operation charged. Signed input integers use two's-complement encoding; the chosen word-size bounds accommodate all input values and required outputs. A random instruction supplies one fresh independent fair bit. Every access, random bit, preprocessing step, lookup-table construction and output write counts. There is no advice, oracle, unit-cost arbitrary-precision operation or quantum operation. The address space contains \(2^w\) cells; the logarithmic-word convention is explicit also for SAT, rather than silently allowing exponential-space address words.

For every fixed input, the required correctness probability is over the algorithm's coins, not an input distribution. The time guarantee holds for every coin sequence. Deterministic algorithms are included. Constants and programs in each fast predicate are fixed before choosing an input. The exponent saving is any positive fixed constant; rational savings below one capture existence of any such saving by decreasing it if needed. The SAT polynomial factor may depend on the fixed clause width. In \(H_{\mathrm{APSP}}\), the hard weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\); one absolute \(c\) working for every saving is not required.

The disjunction permits any one, two or all three hypotheses to hold. Its negation requires all three to fail: one SAT saving that works for every fixed clause width, one APSP saving that works for every fixed polynomial weight exponent, and one 3SUM saving. The three savings may differ, and the algorithms for different fixed widths or weight exponents may differ. No effective compiler from a width or weight exponent to its algorithm is required.

These are the source's randomized integer variants. In particular, \(H_{\mathrm{SAT}}\) is not defined by copying the deterministic Turing-machine SETH card, and \(H_{\mathrm{3SUM}}\) is not defined as the literal negation of the separate Las Vegas expected-time, three-list card. The polynomial-integer APSP quantifier order agrees with the explicitly stated modern convention on its separate hypothesis card.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this disjunction or its logical negation. A positive proof need not identify a particular true disjunct constructively, but must establish that at least one holds in the specified models. A refutation must establish failure of all three hypotheses with their full quantifier order and correctness/time requirements; the algorithms and positive savings need not be the same for the three tasks.

Proving only a conditional lower bound from the disjunction, relating two hypotheses, or improving algorithms by logarithmic or other subpolynomial factors does not resolve this target. There is no additive numerical tolerance and no requirement of a prescribed minimum saving such as one hundredth.
context:
A disjunction is a weaker assumption than choosing any one of its component hypotheses. Consequently, a consequence proved separately from each component also follows from the disjunction.

The original work supplies common hard triangle problems and derives conditional consequences. These reductions motivate the joint assumption; they do not prove that it is true.

Later work obtains related hardness from a different disjunction involving real-number inputs and Orthogonal Vectors. That variation must retain its own model and is not substituted here.

The 2026 universe-reduction paper compares three APSP variants under additional assumptions. Its title does not refer to establishing equivalence among SETH, APSP and 3SUM.
why: Many precise algorithmic lower bounds rest on one of these three separate assumptions. Establishing their disjunction would support results that are hard under all three while requiring less than any individually chosen hypothesis. Refuting it would require fixed-exponent algorithmic advances across satisfiability, weighted shortest paths and integer sum detection.
