working_summary: The permanent of a binary matrix counts its perfect matchings exactly. The source asks whether its exponential-time difficulty can be related to SETH in either direction. This card makes that comparison precise using deterministic oracle reductions that preserve a constant saving in the exponential rate. A reduction from SAT must preserve a saving uniform across clause widths, while the reverse direction may choose a fixed width for each saving. The preferred binary-matrix case and exact counting oracle are distinguished from general matrix variants, ordinary completeness and counting SAT.

title: Time exponents for multiple-string LCS over fixed alphabets
importance_reason: A sharp parameterized or exponential-time bound for a reusable graph, string, or satisfiability problem.
formal: Determine the optimal deterministic polynomial-time exponent function \(\tau(\sigma,k)\) for longest common subsequence of \(k\) strings over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\), on the entire domain \(D=\{(\sigma,k)\in\mathbb N^2:\sigma\ge2,\ k\ge2\}\). For each fixed pair, let \[\tau(\sigma,k)=\inf\bigl\{c\ge0:\ \exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \forall(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\in(\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}^{\le n})^k,\ A\text{ outputs an LCS within }Cn^c\text{ operations}\bigr\},\] where \(A\) ranges over the correct uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithms defined below, and \(n,n_0\) are integers. Supply a function \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|g(\sigma,k)-\tau(\sigma,k)|\le1/100\) for every \((\sigma,k)\in D\). This explicitly broadens the source’s proposed constant-fraction exponent improvement into determination of the underlying exponent function; it is not claimed to be equivalent to that yes/no question.
definitions: A subsequence of a string \(s\) is any string obtained by deleting positions while preserving the order of the retained symbols. An LCS of \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) is a string that is a subsequence of every input and has maximum possible length. The algorithm must output one such string exactly, with arbitrary tie-breaking; inputs may have unequal lengths or be empty. The input includes an integer bound \(n\ge2\), the \(k\) lengths and all symbols, stored explicitly in a read-only array with one length or symbol per word; each length is at most \(n\). Output symbols and output length are written explicitly. For each fixed \((\sigma,k)\), the algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), with no nonuniform advice or tables supplied as a function of \(n\). Its word width is \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed integer \(d\ge\sigma+k+4\), allowed to depend on the program and the fixed pair. A constant number of word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, additions, subtractions, multiplications modulo \(2^W\), or unsigned divisions with quotient and remainder by a nonzero word each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(W\) returns zero. Work memory starts at zero; all input access, preprocessing, addressing and output are charged. Each local operation accesses only constantly many words, and no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or random coins are allowed. Running time is worst-case over all valid tuples for the stated length bound. The constants \(C,n_0,d\) and program may depend on \(\sigma,k\), but not on \(n\) or the input strings. An admissible algorithm must be correct and terminate on every valid input, including sizes below \(n_0\). The alphabet and string count remain fixed when taking the exponent; neither is hidden as a growing function of \(n\). The infimum is finite: exact multiple-string LCS has an \(O(n^k)\) algorithm for each fixed pair, while explicitly outputting a length-\(n\) common string requires linear time. Thus \(1\le\tau(\sigma,k)\le k\). No algorithm attaining the infimum is assumed to exist.
answer_criterion: Provide one unambiguous mathematical function \(g\) on all of \(D\), together with a complete correct proof checked in Lean of the pointwise absolute bound \(1/100\) in exponent units. A family of certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) covering every pair qualifies through their midpoints. The answer may be an expression or certified evaluation rule; merely repeating the defining infimum is not a determination. Bounds on the infimum must respect its possible nonattainment: a claimed endpoint need not be achieved by one algorithm with exactly that exponent. A result only for one alphabet, one number of strings, average-case inputs, approximations, or substring variants does not meet the entire criterion. Conditional bounds alone do not give an unconditional determination. The tolerance concerns the real-valued exponent function, not an approximation to the output subsequence or a constant-factor characterization of the full running time.
context:
Bringmann’s Open Problem 3 asks whether \(k\)-LCS has an \(O(n^{(1-\varepsilon_\Sigma)k})\) algorithm for a fixed alphabet \(\Sigma\). The surrounding paragraph contrasts this with conditional \(n^{k-o(1)}\) hardness when the alphabet can grow linearly with \(k\). Recovering this alphabet dependence is essential; the inherited title alone omitted it.

The benchmark’s permitted quantitative broadening is used here to ask for \(\tau(\sigma,k)\). The original proposed fractional saving remains a separate sourced question. In particular, approximating every exponent to \(1/100\) need not decide whether an arbitrarily small strict exponent improvement exists or whether an infimum is attained. No equivalence between those targets is asserted.

Subsequences retain order while allowing gaps. Requiring a contiguous substring, an increasing sequence, a compressed representation, or a multiplicative approximation changes the task. The unrestricted worst case also differs from parameter bounds that become fast only when the optimum is very close to the input length.

Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams give conditional exponent lower bounds when the alphabet size is allowed to depend linearly on the number of strings. Their result does not supply the same uniform exponent barrier while one alphabet is held fixed and the number of strings varies. The source also records weaker parameterized hardness for constant alphabets, which leaves room between different linear coefficients in the exponent.

Golan, Kraus, Porat and Shalom review exact multiple-string LCS in CPM 2026 and study a hybrid subsequence–substring requirement. The faster algorithm for that hybrid does not solve unrestricted multiple-string LCS. Their discussion also distinguishes exact algorithms from recent two-string approximation results.
why: Multiple-string alignment has a rapidly growing dependence on the number of sequences, even though it is polynomial-time solvable when that number is fixed. A small alphabet may constrain the combinatorial choices enough to change the leading exponent. Determining the full exponent function would separate the cost of coordinating many strings from the expressiveness supplied by a growing alphabet, and would sharpen the fine-grained limits behind exact sequence comparison.
status_note: The 2017 source explicitly poses the fixed-alphabet exponent-saving question. This card records a transparent quantitative broadening to the underlying exponent function, not an equivalent reformulation or a claim that every parameter pair is unresolved. Bounded later-work checks through 14 September 2026 found conditional bounds and different string variants, but no unconditional determination of this entire function.
progress: 2015: Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams, Theorem 2, show that an exponent improvement for k-LCS with alphabet size proportional to k would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. The alphabet dependence is part of the result. | 2017: Bringmann poses the fixed-alphabet fractional-exponent improvement in Section 4.3, Open Problem 3, printed page 120. Section 4.2 defines the common-subsequence task and asks a different time-space question. | 2026: Golan et al., CPM 2026, review the multiple-string worst-case bounds in Section 1 and obtain algorithms for a hybrid that also imposes a substring requirement. Their result does not determine the exponent function here.
working_summary: Multiple-string LCS finds a longest string that occurs as a subsequence of every input. The target is the optimal deterministic time exponent for every fixed alphabet size and fixed number of strings. It makes the source’s question about a fractional exponent saving into an explicitly broader quantitative function. Resolving the function would identify how alphabet size changes the computational cost of coordinating many sequences. Acceptance requires a Lean-certified error of at most one hundredth at every parameter pair, while retaining the source question separately.

title: P versus BPP
importance_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
focus_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
question_excerpt: The target is the standard total-language P versus BPP question, stated as Open Problem 7.6 in the inspected August 2019 book draft. Its Definition 7.3 supplies the pointwise bounded-error convention. The earlier March 2018 draft used Open Problem 7.5; the numbering here is tied to the actual edition read. The explicit clock, finite probability space and machine quantifiers clarify the retained problem without changing its scope.
definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm P\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C',d'\) such that for every binary string \(x\), the program halts within \(C'(|x|+1)^{d'}\) steps and outputs \(\mathbf1_L(x)\). Reading, writing, arithmetic and tape access all count toward time. The deterministic program and its constants may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or its length.

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm P.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.
why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

working_summary: P contains total decision languages with a deterministic polynomial-time decider, while BPP allows fair random bits and error at most one third separately on every input. The randomized machine must obey one polynomial time bound on every random tape, and the deterministic decider must work correctly at every input length. The question is whether these classes are equal, allowing a different deterministic algorithm and a different polynomial exponent for each language. Nonuniform simulation and equality under strong circuit-hardness assumptions are established results, while recent insensitivity bounds retain additional hypotheses. A current preprint claims a full separation, but this review has not independently validated its proof and therefore retains uncertain status.

title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
importance_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
focus_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
question_excerpt: The general target is the space-efficient ordinary PRG frontier described in the introduction of Chen et al., RANDOM 2026, and in the earlier Hoza and Cheng–Hoza papers. This card retains its binary, fixed-order, arbitrary-width formulation and the previously stated polynomial-in-\(n,w,1/\varepsilon\) time bound. The explicit tape convention, binary parameters, dyadic errors and uniform constants make that retained target precise; the source papers use asymptotic explicitness conventions.
definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.
context:
A branching program models a stream computation that remembers only its current state. Its width \(w\) permits roughly \(\log_2 w\) memory bits, while its length \(n\) counts inspected input bits. The quantifiers require one distribution that works simultaneously for every allowed transition table. Computing a favorable distribution after seeing a particular table would answer a different question.

Short-seed distributions exist nonconstructively; in particular, seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) is known for width-\(n\), length-\(n\) programs. The unresolved issue is explicit computation with the required space bound. An optimal ordinary generator of the kind requested here would imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\), the equality of deterministic and bounded-error randomized logarithmic-space decision classes. The card does not assert the converse implication.

The classical general bound is \(O(\log n\cdot\log(nw/\varepsilon))\) seed bits. For polynomial width and constant error, this becomes \(O(\log^2 n)\), whereas the requested bound is \(O(\log n)\). The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.
why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

title: L versus BPL
importance_reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm L?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
question_excerpt: The card retains the total-language equality and fresh one-way randomness convention. The inspected August 2019 edition of Wigderson’s book states Conjecture 14.7 and discusses the input/work-tape and one-way-randomness models in Chapter 14. The earlier 2018 draft remains in provenance. Explicit endmarkers, finite clocks, the exact coin probability, small-input convention and universal machine constants complete the retained model without replacing the question by a particular PRG or promise-problem target.
definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm L\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm L.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.
context:
Logarithmic memory is enough for a constant number of input-position counters but not for storing an arbitrary long random history. Fresh coins can guide the computation without remaining available afterward. Allowing the machine to freely revisit an entire random string changes the resource model, which is why the random-access convention is part of the question.

Saks and Zhou obtained deterministic simulation in \(O((\log n)^{3/2})\) space. Hoza’s Theorem 1.6 improves this to
\[O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\). This remains larger than \(O(\log n)\). These are space bounds; they do not assert that the improved-space simulation also runs in polynomial time.

A read-once branching program is a finite layered computation: each newly read random symbol selects a transition to the next layer, and a designated final state determines the answer. Its width is the number of states per layer and its length is the number of symbols read. This represents the random part of a bounded-space computation after the ordinary input is fixed. Restricted transition structures or unusually short programs need not capture every BPL computation.

An ordinary pseudorandom generator approximates acceptance probabilities using a genuine distribution generated from a short uniform seed. A weighted generator instead associates possibly negative real weights with seeds and approximates acceptance through a signed weighted average. Such estimates can be useful for derandomization, but they are not themselves sampling probabilities. Improving weighted generators does not automatically supply an ordinary generator with identical parameters.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.
why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected May 2026 ECCC revision 3 and July 2026 Cheng–Wu version 5 retain the unrestricted BPL versus L problem as open. Hoza’s general simulation remains superlogarithmic; the newer results reviewed here improve weighted generators or impose regularity/length restrictions. No verified resolution of this total-language equality was established in the bounded searches. The card remains source_open, with no claim of an exhaustive audit of all later proofs.

working_summary: L contains languages decided by one deterministic machine using logarithmic work space, while BPL permits fresh fair random bits and bounded error. Random bits are read once unless stored in counted memory, and the randomized machine obeys uniform logarithmic-space and polynomial-time bounds on every run. The question asks whether every BPL language has a deterministic logarithmic-space decider that is correct on every input. The best general simulation reviewed here uses more than logarithmic space, and recent weighted-generator and regular-program results retain distinct guarantees or restrictions. A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the inclusion or a single total language separating the two classes under the stated uniform model.

title: P versus RP
importance_reason: A defining derandomization question for a standard complexity class, with consequences for all one-sided-error polynomial-time algorithms. Its scope and asymmetric relationship with P versus NP justify a separate landmark card alongside the stronger P versus BPP question.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\)? In other words, can randomness be removed from every polynomial-time decision algorithm that never accepts a false instance and accepts each true instance with probability at least one half?

Let \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be any language for which there is one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\), with a polynomial worst-case time bound on every random tape, such that
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]\ge\tfrac12,\qquad x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]=0.\]
Must there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(D\) and constants \(C>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[D(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)\qquad\text{within }C(|x|+1)^a\text{ steps}?\]
The machine and constants may depend on the language, but not on its particular input.
question_excerpt: Vadhan’s Open Problem 2.10 asks whether P equals RP immediately after defining one-sided-error randomized polynomial time. This card retains that ordinary language-class equality and its worst-case time convention.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings, including the possible empty string. The indicator \(\mathbf1_L(x)\) is one when \(x\in L\) and zero otherwise. A decision algorithm must terminate with one of these two answers on every input; there is no promise excluding some binary strings from its correctness requirement. Input length \(n=|x|\) is the full number of input bits.

Use classical multitape Turing machines with a fixed finite alphabet and finite transition description. Polynomial time means that there are an integer \(a\ge0\) and a constant \(C\ge1\) for which the running time is at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every input of length \(n\). All bit operations and all random-bit requests take time. Uniformity means that one finite machine works at every input length. No advice string depending on \(n\), oracle, quantum operation or real-number register is supplied.

The class \(\mathrm P\) contains exactly the languages decided correctly by deterministic polynomial-time machines. A probabilistic machine additionally obtains independent fair random bits during its execution. It has a polynomial time bound on every input and every sequence of random choices, not merely in expectation or with high probability. Thus only polynomially many random bits can be read. Shorter random computations may be padded with ignored bits without changing their acceptance probabilities.

More explicitly, the probabilistic definition can be written using a deterministic machine \(A(x,r)\), a polynomially bounded integer function \(p(n)\), and a uniform string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\). The machine runs in time polynomial in \(n\) for all such pairs, and unused bits of \(r\) are ignored. Each tape \(r\) has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). The probability in the statement is over this finite sample space separately for each fixed \(x\); it is not an average over an input distribution. The function \(p\) is computable in polynomial time and may be taken to be an integer-coefficient polynomial bound by padding.

The class \(\mathrm{RP}\) consists of languages satisfying the two displayed probability conditions. A no-instance has no accepting random tape. A yes-instance has accepting tapes occupying at least half the sample space. The machine may reject some yes-instances on unlucky tapes; it never accepts a no-instance. Replacing the acceptance threshold one half by another fixed constant strictly between zero and one gives the same class. An arbitrarily small positive acceptance probability, without an inverse-polynomial lower bound, does not give this definition.

The deterministic inclusion \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{RP}\) follows by ignoring randomness. The question is therefore whether \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm P\). Equality requires a deterministic polynomial-time decider for every language in \(\mathrm{RP}\). A negative answer requires some language \(L\in\mathrm{RP}\) for which no deterministic decider has any polynomial worst-case time bound. The negative claim must quantify over all deterministic machines and all fixed polynomial exponents; it is not a separation at one selected exponent.

The deterministic polynomial exponent may depend on the language or on a chosen randomized decider for it. It may not depend on the particular input. In particular, a construction that handles each encoded randomized or deterministic machine within a time whose exponent is encoded in the input need not have one polynomial bound. Nor does showing that a language is an increasing union of polynomial-time languages put that union in polynomial time. The target is a single machine with a single polynomial bound for each whole language.

Equality of these language classes does not require a computable compiler that takes every description of an RP machine and produces a deterministic simulation. A proved universal transformation would be sufficient, but the acceptance criterion is the class inclusion itself. The deterministic machine need only decide membership; it need not reproduce the randomized machine’s output distribution, internal choices or running-time exponent.

For comparisons, \(\mathrm{coRP}\) consists of the complements of RP languages. Its machines always accept yes-instances and accept a no-instance with probability at most one half. Since deterministic polynomial time is closed under complementation, \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{coRP}\). The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) permits two-sided error: yes-instances are accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and no-instances with probability at most \(1/3\), with the same worst-case polynomial time convention. The stronger equality \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\) would imply the equality asked here; the card does not replace one-sided error by two-sided error.

A promise problem specifies disjoint sets of yes-instances and no-instances and imposes correctness only on their union. Derandomizing all promise versions of RP is a separately quantified stronger task. The promise-class implication connecting one-sided and two-sided derandomization must not be presented as an equivalence of the ordinary language equalities without further justification.

For another comparison, \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. An accepting random tape is a certificate, so \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\), whereas \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{RP}\) would imply \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The positive answer to this card does not itself assert that every NP language has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

The conditional result in the progress section uses \(\mathrm E=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{cn})\). An exponential circuit lower bound there means that some language in \(\mathrm E\) and some constant \(\alpha>0\) require Boolean circuits of size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large input length \(n\). Circuits use the fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, with size measured by gates; they may differ freely with \(n\). This circuit-hardness assumption is background for a conditional theorem, not an assumption of the question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm P\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language belongs to \(\mathrm{RP}\) and not to \(\mathrm P\), with the machines, probability conventions and uniform worst-case time bounds specified here. Equality must cover all RP languages; a deterministic algorithm for only one example does not suffice without a proved reduction covering the entire class. A separation must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, not just a proposed simulation or one polynomial exponent. Conditional derandomization, nonuniform circuits, oracle separations, average-input guarantees and correctness at only infinitely many input lengths do not settle the unconditional language comparison. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this exact class-equality target.
context:
An RP computation has a useful asymmetry: any observed acceptance is trustworthy, yet an observed rejection may be a missed opportunity to accept. A substantial fraction of random choices succeeds on each yes-instance. The question asks whether that availability of successful choices always translates into deterministic polynomial-time decision.

Repeating the randomized algorithm can make its failure probability very small, while retaining a polynomial running time. This reduces error but still uses randomness. Likewise, the existence of good advice for each input length does not by itself give one uniform deterministic algorithm.

Polynomial identity testing is a representative algebraic example. Given an arithmetic circuit, it asks whether the computed polynomial is identically zero. Vadhan’s Theorem 2.12 places identity testing over the integers in coRP, and therefore its nonidentity complement in RP. A deterministic identity test would be a substantial special-case advance, but no completeness equivalence with all RP languages is assumed.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove that exponential circuit hardness for a language in \(\mathrm E\) implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\), and hence \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\). This connects removing random choices to proving strong computational lower bounds. The hardness premise remains an assumption of that theorem.

The logical relation to P versus NP is asymmetric. A deterministic solution of every NP language would also cover RP, while a proved RP separation would give an NP separation. An equality between P and RP can still leave open the possibility of harder NP languages whose accepting certificates are too sparse to be found by the original random-tape guarantee.

Derandomization for restricted algebraic computations, special graph problems, shorter random tapes or promise classes concerns useful neighboring questions. This card asks for the entire uniform language class with one-sided error, without an input distribution or a special form of algorithm.
why: This is a central question about whether random choices enlarge efficient decision power even when false acceptances are forbidden. It tests a basic source of randomized algorithmic speed and connects the construction of deterministic algorithms with strong circuit lower bounds and the broader boundary between finding and verifying solutions.

This is a bounded source and claim assessment, not an exhaustive literature certification or a new Lean proof.

working_summary: RP consists of languages decided in worst-case polynomial time using fair random bits, with no false acceptances. The question asks whether every such language also has a uniform deterministic polynomial-time decider. Each language may have its own fixed polynomial bound, but the exponent cannot vary with the input. Strong circuit-hardness assumptions imply derandomization, while deterministic algorithms for individual examples do not settle the whole class comparison. A resolution would determine whether one-sided-error randomness increases efficient decision power.

title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
importance_reason: An optimal derandomization problem connecting compressed sensing, pseudorandomness, additive combinatorics and explicit geometric constructions.
formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,B\ge1\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(\mathcal A\) with the following property? For every integer pair \(N\ge2\), \(2\le s\le N\), given the pair in binary, \(\mathcal A\) outputs an explicitly listed rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times N}\), with an integer row count \(m\ge1\), in at most \(BN^b\) Turing-machine steps, such that
\[m\le C s\ln(eN/s)\]
and
\[\forall x\in\mathbb R^N\text{ with }|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le s,\qquad \frac23\|x\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|_2^2\le\frac43\|x\|_2^2?\]
The complete binary output must also have length at most \(BN^b\). The constants and the algorithm are common to every pair \((N,s)\).
question_excerpt: Retains the saved optimal deterministic RIP construction question motivated by Fickus–Lake and the cited construction literature. The fixed squared-norm distortion 1/3, all-input row bound C s ln(eN/s), real signal space and explicit rational output are the previously selected variant. The finite encoding and uniform Turing-machine convention make that target precise without replacing it by coherence, statistical recovery or a restricted parameter family.
definitions:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\), set \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:x_j\ne0\}\) and \(\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^N x_j^2\). A vector is \(s\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(s\), including the zero vector and all smaller supports. Matrix multiplication has its usual exact real meaning, \((Ax)_i=\sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij}x_j\), with rational entries viewed as reals. The displayed inequalities are the restricted isometry property of order \(s\) with distortion \(\delta=1/3\), for squared Euclidean norms. They must hold simultaneously for every support and every real choice of coefficients; no input distribution, typical-signal exception or probability of correctness is permitted. Columns need not be individually normalized to exactly one, provided the inequalities hold. The matrix is real, not complex.

Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(e=\exp(1)\), so \(\ln(eN/s)=1+\ln(N/s)\), which equals \(1\) when \(s=N\). The real-valued row upper bound is an inequality on the integer chosen by the algorithm; no additional rounding convention is needed. Constants \(C,B,b\) cannot depend on dimension, sparsity, a signal or a support. The case \(s=1\), excluded from the main domain, has the trivial single-row all-ones construction; at \(s=N\), the identity matrix satisfies the geometric requirement. No compression promise such as \(m<N\) is imposed in the dense regime.

Use one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite alphabet, no advice, randomness or oracle, and ordinary bit-level computation. Time is polynomial in the ambient dimension \(N\), not necessarily in the length of its binary input. In particular, the full matrix must be written; a succinct circuit for entries, an existential matrix description, or a real-number computation with unit-cost exact arithmetic is not the stated output model. All computation and output steps count toward the bound.

For a concrete self-delimiting binary encoding, let \(u(t)=1^k0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) for \(t\ge0\), where \(k\) is the length of the binary expansion of \(t+1\) without leading zeroes. The input is \(u(N)u(s)\) with no extra bits. The output is \(u(m)\) followed in row-major order by the \(mN\) rational entries. Encode \(p/q\) by one sign bit, \(u(|p|)\) and \(u(q)\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\ge1\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), and zero has numerator zero, denominator one and sign bit zero. The sign bit is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative numerators. No trailing bits are allowed. This represents every output entry exactly and counts its denominator and numerator lengths. Requiring reduced fractions is an encoding convention, since integer gcd computation is polynomial time. Invalid binary inputs can be rejected without changing the valid-input target; no asymptotic bound is required on malformed encodings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a uniform deterministic construction exists, or an unconditional proof that it does not in the stated model. A positive answer supplies the finite algorithm and fixed constants and proves termination within the bit-time and output-length bounds, the row inequality and exact RIP for all permitted inputs and all real sparse vectors. The Lean proof must justify any rounding of other representations to the rational output actually printed. A negative answer must rule out every polynomial-time algorithm and choice of universal constants, not just one matrix family or verification method. A conditional lower bound alone is not an unconditional negative answer. Random existence, shorter random seeds, successful numerical recovery, statistical restricted isometry, a different norm, or an asymptotically larger row count does not suffice. This asks whether an algorithm meets the specified exact distortion guarantee; the numerical-target tolerance of 1/100 does not enlarge that guarantee.
context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The condition has an equivalent spectral formulation. For a set \(S\) of column indices, let \(A_S\) denote those columns. Every eigenvalue of the real symmetric Gram matrix \(A_S^{\mathsf T}A_S\) must lie in \([2/3,4/3]\) whenever \(1\le|S|\le s\). Thus the target controls every linear combination within every small column set, not only column lengths or pairwise inner products.

Restricted isometry of order \(2t\) implies that different \(t\)-sparse signals have different measurements, since their difference has at most \(2t\) nonzero entries. At distortion \(1/3<\sqrt2-1\), the recovery theorem recorded by Bandeira and coauthors also gives robust reconstruction through \(\ell_1\) minimization. The reconstruction problem and its additional sparsity parameter are consequences, not extra outputs required of this construction task.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

The standard existence benchmark is compatible with rational entries. Normalized Bernoulli matrices with a square number of rows \(m=t^2\) have entries \(\pm1/t\), and rounding a positive row target up to a square changes its size by at most a constant factor. Thus the rational representation requirement does not itself obstruct optimal-order existence. The remaining demand is one deterministic algorithm with the proved time bound.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova give explicit matrices beyond the square-root bottleneck. Their Theorem 1 specifies a restricted relation between row count and column count, with sparsity slightly above the square root of the row count. This is a positive construction theorem in that regime, but does not give the required optimal row order uniformly over all ambient dimensions and sparsities.

Rao’s construction attains the optimal row order using \(O(s\log(N/s)\log s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime stated in the paper, with distortion fixed. Its guarantee remains probabilistic and still uses a seed whose length depends on sparsity and dimension. Reduced randomness is distinct from a deterministic rule whose single output is proved to satisfy RIP on every allowed input.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The parameter range matters. For \(s\) comparable to \(N\), the identity matrix is compatible with the requested row order. The problem also includes all intermediate sparse regimes and arbitrary integer dimensions, whereas many algebraic constructions only give particular dimension sequences or sparsity ranges. Statistical guarantees for typical signals and restricted isometries in \(\ell_1\) are different targets.

The August 2026 preprint by Moonchaisook, Kumam and Sriwongsa gives further deterministic incidence matrices from finite orthogonal spaces. Its guarantee uses \(\delta_s\le(s-1)\mu\), where \(\mu\) is the normalized column coherence, and evaluates particular geometric parameter families. It does not claim the uniform \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\)-row construction required here. Numerical recovery comparisons in that paper are separate from the all-vector RIP theorem.
why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. Rao’s optimal-row result still uses randomness; the older explicit result and the August2026 orthogonal-space construction have restricted parameter guarantees. Coherence and statistical sparse-recovery results do not establish this all-vector RIP target. New preprint proofs were not independently certified.

The question asks for one deterministic algorithm producing an explicit rational matrix with \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\) rows and distortion \(1/3\). Its bit running time and complete output length must be polynomial in the ambient dimension, with constants common to every dimension and sparsity. A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm, its resource bounds and the simultaneous guarantee for all real sparse vectors, or prove unconditional nonexistence in the fixed model. title: AM versus NP
importance_reason: A major comparison between standard proof-system complexity classes, isolating the role of public randomness and interaction. It has a compelling concrete consequence for graph nonisomorphism and a substantial body of conditional and recent structural results.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{NP}\)? Equivalently, does every language having an Arthur–Merlin protocol admit polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time?

For a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), an Arthur–Merlin protocol is specified by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and polynomially bounded lengths \(p(n),q(n)\). Arthur draws a uniform public string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\); after seeing \(x\) and \(r\), Merlin may choose a reply \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\). With \(n=|x|\), require
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\ge\tfrac23,\]
\[x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\le\tfrac13.\]
Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomially bounded length \(s(n)\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(|x|)}:\ W(x,z)=1?\]
The resulting verifier and its polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but must work uniformly at all input lengths.
question_excerpt: Vadhan discusses removing randomness from Arthur–Merlin verification and identifies AM = NP as the general class comparison. Graph nonisomorphism in NP is given as a consequence. This card retains the full class equality and treats the graph problem as motivation, correcting the inherited page locator.
definitions:
Languages are subsets of the finite binary strings. Every input string is either a yes-instance in the language or a no-instance outside it; the target is an equality of ordinary language classes. There is no omitted promise domain. Input size \(n\) is the full bit length of \(x\), and the empty input is allowed.

Use classical uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions. A polynomial time bound means \(C(n+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(a\ge0\). In a verifier taking several strings, time is polynomial in their total encoded length; the stated polynomial message bounds make this polynomial in \(n\) on protocol inputs. The verifier terminates on every such tuple, including misleading messages. It has no advice depending on the input length, oracle or quantum operation. All communication consists of ordinary binary strings.

The functions \(p,q,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable in polynomial time and bounded by fixed polynomials. They may be taken to be integer-coefficient polynomial bounds, with unused bits ignored. Messages have the indicated exact lengths. Permitting shorter messages with a length encoding and padding gives the same class. Malformed messages are rejected according to the chosen verifier; they cannot provide an extra form of communication or uncounted computation.

The protocol has two messages: Arthur’s random challenge followed by Merlin’s reply. Arthur samples \(p(n)\) independent fair bits, so each challenge has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). All of these bits are public before Merlin replies. The verifier’s final computation \(V(x,r,y)\) is deterministic; there is no additional hidden random tape. A zero-length challenge or reply is permitted. The polynomial defining each length is fixed for the protocol, not chosen separately for individual inputs.

Merlin is computationally unbounded. He knows the entire input and challenge and may choose a different reply for every pair \((x,r)\). Thus the existential quantifier over \(y\) is inside the probability over \(r\). Completeness says that on each yes-instance an accepting reply exists for at least two thirds of the challenges. Soundness says that on each no-instance an accepting reply exists for at most one third of them, even with an unbounded dishonest prover. Randomizing Merlin’s reply cannot increase the set of challenges for which some accepting reply exists.

These two probability conditions define \(\mathrm{AM}\). They are per-input guarantees. Neither the inputs nor Merlin’s strategy are averaged over an external distribution. The soundness bound is information-theoretic: it is not limited to efficient cheating provers. The fixed gap between two thirds and one third is part of the chosen standard definition; ordinary amplification yields equivalent constant-gap conventions. Perfect completeness is not an added requirement of this card.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with a verifier \(W\) and certificate length \(s\) satisfying the displayed exact equivalence. On yes-instances at least one certificate is accepted, and on no-instances every certificate is rejected. The verifier is deterministic and has no random challenge. The certificate itself need not be found in polynomial time. A proof of AM containment in NP must establish existence of these certificates and their efficient verification, not efficient deterministic decision or witness generation.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{AM}\) is immediate by letting the AM verifier ignore its challenge. Thus equality asks for the converse inclusion. A positive answer must cover every AM language. A negative answer must exhibit, or prove the existence of, an AM language that has no polynomially bounded deterministic certificate system. Failure of one proposed verifier, one circuit family or one polynomial exponent does not establish such a separation.

The quantifier order is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{AM}\;\exists W\;\exists s\;\forall x\), with a fixed polynomial running-time bound for each \(W\). There is no common required exponent for all languages. Equality of language classes does not additionally require a computable compiler from protocol descriptions to NP verifiers, although a proved general transformation would suffice. A certificate system whose exponent changes with the individual input is not polynomially bounded in this sense.

The related class \(\mathrm{MA}\) reverses the message order: Merlin supplies a certificate before Arthur’s fresh random choices. Moving \(\exists y\) outside the probability changes the condition and must not be done here. Standard results identify AM with constant-round interactive proofs, but the explicit two-message public-coin definition above is the target model. Protocols with an input-dependent polynomial number of rounds are not the target.

A promise problem consists of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), with no correctness requirement outside \(Y\cup N\). The notation \(\mathrm{prAM}\) refers to the analogous promise-protocol class. A claim that every promise-AM problem has a separating NP language is stronger than the ordinary language inclusion asked here and is not assumed equivalent. This distinction matters for the neighboring targeted-generator question TCS-1135 and for several recent derandomization theorems.

Graph nonisomorphism is an example consequence, not a completeness reformulation. A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges; two such graphs are isomorphic if some bijection between their vertex sets preserves adjacency. Graph nonisomorphism asks whether no such bijection exists, for explicitly encoded graph pairs. An NP certificate for nonisomorphism would be a polynomial-length binary witness of that negative assertion checked in polynomial time. Since graph nonisomorphism has an AM protocol, AM equality with NP would supply such certificates. Solving only that graph problem would not establish the full class equality without an additional proved completeness reduction.

For the conditional progress cited below, \(\mathrm{NE}=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{cn})\) and \(\mathrm{coNE}\) is its complement class. A single-valued nondeterministic Boolean circuit has ordinary input bits, auxiliary choice bits, and two outputs: a flag and a value bit. For every input some choice must set the flag to one, and every choice with flag one must give the correct value of the function. Choices with flag zero are ignored. Circuit size counts gates in a fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, together with auxiliary input bits. Circuits may vary nonuniformly with the input length. An exponential lower bound means that some \(\alpha>0\) requires size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large length \(n\). This hardness hypothesis belongs to the cited conditional result and is not a premise of the question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{AM}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language lies in \(\mathrm{AM}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), with the specified verifier, message-order, uniformity and probability conventions. Equality must supply the existence of polynomial-length certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification for every AM language on every input. It need not supply a deterministic decision algorithm or an efficient way to find the certificates. A separation must rule out every NP verifier and polynomial certificate bound for the chosen language. Conditional collapses, oracle results, simulations with advice, average-input correctness, larger time bounds and a certificate system only for graph nonisomorphism do not settle the unconditional class comparison. The default numerical approximation tolerance does not apply to this exact proposition.
context:
An NP proof is one static certificate that a deterministic verifier can check. In an Arthur–Merlin protocol, the prover first sees a fresh public challenge and can tailor the proof to it. The question asks whether this additional use of randomness and interaction changes which languages have efficient proofs.

The placement of the existential reply inside the probability is the defining feature. Different challenges may need different valid replies. A deterministic certificate system must verify the same membership claim without asking for that random challenge, while retaining polynomial certificate length and verification time.

Graph nonisomorphism illustrates why this matters. A relabeling certifies that graphs are isomorphic, while certifying that no relabeling works is a different verification task. The known AM protocol for nonisomorphism gives an interactive justification; equality with NP would guarantee static, efficiently checkable certificates.

Miltersen and Vinodchandran show that an exponential lower bound against single-valued nondeterministic circuits for a language in the intersection of nondeterministic and co-nondeterministic exponential time implies AM equality with NP. The published theorem weakens earlier circuit-hardness hypotheses, but does not establish the required hardness premise.

The 2025 work of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski develops conditional connections between Arthur–Merlin derandomization and uniform hardness or constructive refutation. Its main near-equivalences carefully distinguish ordinary protocols from promise protocols and account for advice. These are refinements of the conditions under which derandomization follows, not an unconditional collapse.

The same paper gives an unconditional weaker simulation in a different resource model: it uses a second-level quantified machine, subexponential time and a short advice string, and is guaranteed on most inputs at infinitely many lengths. Its theorem therefore leaves several requirements of ordinary NP verification unmet, including the time bound, lack of advice and correctness on all inputs.

A positive answer would eliminate random interaction as a source of additional polynomial-time proof power for this class. It would not make NP membership efficiently decidable. A negative answer would establish that some efficiently verifiable interactive claims inherently lack static polynomial-time certificates.
why: This asks whether short randomized interaction gives more verification power than static certificates. It is a fundamental derandomization question beyond decision algorithms, with consequences for certifying graph nonisomorphism and with close links to nondeterministic circuit hardness.
status_note: Source-open in Vadhan’s 2012 monograph and explicitly retained as open in van Melkebeek–Mocelin Sdroievski, Computational Complexity 34, article 15 (23 October 2025), introduction. On 16 September 2026 this review checked the original definition and graph consequence, the exact hardness hypothesis of Miltersen–Vinodchandran Theorem 1.5, and the model and scope of the 2025 Theorems 1.6 and 1.12. The latter unconditional result is an average-case, infinitely-often simulation with advice in a stronger quantified model and does not place AM in NP. Bounded subsequent searches found no unconditional equality or separation for the stated ordinary-language target. The review checks theorem statements and applicability, not every technical proof in the 86-page journal article.

title: Uniform PRGs from exponential-time hardness
importance_reason: This is the high-end uniform hardness-versus-randomness gap: it asks whether strong algorithmic hardness in EXP yields a single short-seed generator against uniform algorithms. It would sharpen a central connection between lower bounds and derandomization without assuming circuit hardness.
formal: Does \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPSUBEXP}\) imply the following generator statement? There are integers \(C,k,a\ge1\), a constant \(A\ge1\), and a single deterministic generator algorithm which, for every \(m\ge2\), maps \(d(m)=C\lceil\log_2m\rceil^k\) seed bits to \(m\) output bits in time at most \(A(m+2^{d(m)})^a\), and has this security property: for every fixed uniform probabilistic distinguisher \(T\) running in time \(O(m)\), there are infinitely many \(m\) such that \[\left|\Pr[T(G_m(U_{d(m)}))=1]-\Pr[T(U_m)=1]\right|\le \frac1m.\] The generator is independent of \(T\), and the infinitely many successful lengths may depend on \(T\).
definitions: All machines are multitape Turing machines with a fixed finite program and no advice. Time counts every transition, including input and output processing. Randomized machines use independent fair bits and have their time bound on every random tape. For a time function \(t\), \(\mathrm{DTIME}(t(n))\) consists of languages decided on every input of length \(n\) by a deterministic machine in \(O(t(n))\) time, and \(\mathrm{BPTIME}(t(n))\) uses a randomized machine that is correct on each input with probability at least \(2/3\). Define \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{j\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^j})\) and \(\mathrm{BPSUBEXP}=\bigcap_{j\ge1}\mathrm{BPTIME}(2^{n^{1/j}})\). The intersection permits different algorithms for different \(j\), but each must solve the language on all input lengths. Noncontainment means that some language in the union is absent from that intersection. The generator receives \(1^m\) and an independent seed \(s\in\{0,1\}^{d(m)}\), and produces exactly \(m\) bits \(G_m(s)\). Its one finite program, constants and seed-length exponent are common to all \(m\) and all distinguishers. Integer powers of \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) are a concrete normalization of polylogarithmic seed length; extra seed bits may be ignored. The displayed generator running time is the meaning of mildly explicit and may exceed the distinguishing time. A distinguisher \(T\) receives only an \(m\)-bit string, returns one bit, and has a constant \(K_T\) with running time at most \(K_Tm\) on every input and random tape. It receives no input-dependent advice, seed, hard-language oracle or additional auxiliary input. Here \(U_j\) is the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^j\); in each displayed probability the seed or uniform input is independent of the distinguisher’s internal fair random bits. The security quantifiers are \(\forall T\,\forall M\ge2\,\exists m\ge M\) satisfying the inequality. They neither require security at all sufficiently large lengths nor a single length at which every possible finite program is fooled.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated implication, with a uniform generator and all seed-length, construction-time and distinguishing guarantees under its hypothesis, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation. A result assuming nonuniform circuit hardness, hardness only for a smaller complexity class, nonuniform advice for the generator, or a different exceptional-length quantifier does not by itself prove this implication. A limitation on a restricted kind of reduction alone is not a refutation of the implication.
context:
This is Open Problem 8.7 with its polylogarithmic-seed, mildly explicit and infinitely-often conventions made explicit. The printed phrase about the generator’s “input” being pseudorandom is read as referring to its output distribution, consistently with the surrounding generator definitions. The inverse-linear advantage is a stated conventional security normalization; the seed is not revealed to the distinguisher.

Trevisan and Vadhan define uniform distinguishing success at all sufficiently large lengths, so failure of every such distinguisher means that each fixed program is fooled infinitely often. Their paper also studies a stronger seed-visible convention; this card does not add that stronger requirement to the textbook’s output-only question.

The textbook distinguishes its known low-end uniform tradeoff from the open high-end implication. It records the corresponding stronger-assumption result when EXP is replaced by PSPACE; that replacement is not the hypothesis asked for here.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell obtain stronger uniform tradeoffs for hard functions with additional uniform-circuit depth structure. Their high-end theorem also uses advice for its BPP simulation. These are material differences from a single advice-free generator derived solely from the EXP noncontainment in this card.

Sdroievski’s 2024 dissertation still describes the high-end uniform equivalence as open. This is a later primary discussion of the gap, rather than a claim that every subsequent manuscript has been exhaustively checked.
why: Hardness against algorithms is a weaker kind of premise than hardness against arbitrary circuits. A generator with only polylogarithmically many seed bits would turn strong uniform hardness into correspondingly fast average-case derandomization. The remaining gap tests how much of the familiar nonuniform hardness-versus-randomness tradeoff survives with uniform assumptions.

The question asks whether this uniform hardness yields a single generator with only polylogarithmically many seed bits.
