title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
importance_reason: Reach the information-theoretic entropy threshold for a foundational seedless randomness primitive.
formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
definitions:
Write \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) for all binary strings of length \(n\). A probability distribution on this finite set is any function \(p:S_n\to[0,1]\) with real values and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\). Its min-entropy is
\[
H_\infty(p)=-\log_2\!\left(\max_{x\in S_n}p(x)\right).
\]
Thus the required entropy condition means \(p(x)\le 1/(2^C n)\) for every string \(x\). Distributions need not be uniform on their support, rational, computable or efficiently samplable. Independence means that the joint distribution is \(\Pr[X=x,Y=y]=p(x)q(y)\). The output probability in the question is the finite sum
\[
\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]=\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\,\mathbf1_{\{E_n(x,y)=1\}}.
\]
The indicator is one when its subscripted condition holds and zero otherwise. For a single output bit, the displayed bias is its statistical distance from the uniform bit, where statistical distance between distributions \(r,s\) on a finite set is \(\frac12\sum_z|r(z)-s(z)|\). There is no conditioning on either source in this guarantee.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and fixed finite tape alphabet. Its read-only input is \(1^n\#x\#y\), where \(|x|=|y|=n\), and its work tapes initially contain blanks. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol on each tape and moves each tape head by at most one cell, costing one step. There are no random coins, oracle calls, auxiliary seed, advice or length-dependent precomputed tables. The machine must halt and output exactly one bit on every such input. There must be integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that this takes at most \(K(n+1)^d\) transitions for all \(n,x,y\), including inputs at lengths with no eligible sources. The input contains no distribution description or samples other than \(x,y\); \(C,K,d\) and the machine are fixed existential choices, independent of both distributions and of \(n\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be the class of all machines meeting this total polynomial-time evaluation condition, and write \(E^A_n\) for the function computed by a member \(A\).

Only the probability bound concerns the random choice of the two input strings; the evaluator itself is deterministic. When \(\log_2n+C>n\), no eligible distribution exists, so the extraction requirement at that length is vacuous. Using a nonnegative integer for the existential additive constant fixes a harmless convention: any fixed real constant can be increased to such an integer. The task has one output bit and fixed error \(1/100\); it does not demand arbitrarily small error, more output bits or resilience to tampering.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence proposition, including one finite machine, its uniform polynomial-time bound and the probability guarantee for all eligible distributions. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: for every integer \(C\ge0\) and every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there exist \(n\ge1\) and distributions \(p,q\) on \(S_n\), each having min-entropy at least \(\log_2n+C\), for which
\[
\left|\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\mathbf1_{\{E^A_n(x,y)=1\}}-\frac12\right|>\frac1{100}.
\]
In this negation the length and distributions may depend on the machine and additive constant. A construction requiring \(c\log_2n\) entropy for an unspecified constant \(c>1\), nonuniform existence alone, or a conditional implication does not establish the displayed unconditional target.
context:
Li’s introduction and concluding open questions explicitly distinguish the optimal additive threshold \(\log_2n+O(1)\) from the achieved asymptotic order \(O(\log n)\). This card retains its existing one-bit, error-\(1/100\), uniform polynomial-time version of that question; it does not interpret the paper’s title as claiming the additive threshold.

The source records nonconstructive existence at \(\log_2n+O(1)\). Its Theorem 1.6 gives polynomial-time extraction for every fixed positive constant error when each source has at least \(c\log_2n\) entropy for a suitable fixed \(c>1\), even when the two sources’ bits are interleaved. The remaining distinction is the coefficient of the logarithm.

Extraction from arbitrary independent sources is stronger than merely requiring a function to take both values on every sufficiently large Cartesian product. The latter property is a two-source disperser and yields a bipartite Ramsey graph. The fixed small-bias guarantee here requires approximate balance, not only nonconstancy.

Li and Zhong’s 2024 construction adds resistance to separate tampering of the sources. Its constant-error, one-bit theorem still has an entropy requirement \(c\log n\), with a constant \(c>1\); it does not assert the additive threshold.

Oh and Shaltiel’s July 2026 revision constructs extractors under a computational hardness assumption for distributions generated by small circuits. It concerns a restricted source class and a conditional result, whereas the present target is unconditional and covers arbitrary independent distributions.
why: The additive threshold asks whether polynomial-time evaluation can match the entropy scale available without an efficiency restriction, including its leading coefficient. It is a basic question about converting two independent imperfect sources into a nearly unbiased bit and has consequences for explicit Ramsey constructions.

The card retains its existing one-bit, error-1/100 version. title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
importance_reason: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP would remove randomness in a broad regime without hardness assumptions.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.
context:
Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.

If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.
why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

working_summary: BPP contains decision problems solved efficiently using random bits with bounded error on every input. The question asks whether all of them have exact deterministic simulations in the class SUBEXP. Here SUBEXP requires a simulation in time two to the n-to-epsilon power for every fixed positive epsilon. The simulator may depend on the chosen exponent, but it must work on every input without advice or assumptions. Known general brute-force simulations take larger exponential time, while stronger derandomization theorems rely on unproved hardness.

title: Does arithmetic formula hardness derandomize identity testing?
importance_reason: A central structural question joining algebraic formula lower bounds to derandomization in the same computation model. It probes the scope of a foundational hardness–randomness principle and has consequences for deterministic polynomial identity testing beyond a narrow circuit subclass. The score reflects this broad conceptual reach, not the venue or the former provisional midpoint.
formal: Does \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\) hold over \(\mathbb Q\)? Here \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\) asserts that there exists an explicit family \(f_m\in\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\) of multilinear polynomials with \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\), in the precise sense below. The assertion \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) is that, for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), polynomial identity testing for unrestricted arithmetic formulas has a uniform deterministic algorithm taking time \(2^{O(N^{\varepsilon})}\), where \(N\) is the input's bit length. This card selects the hardness-to-derandomization branch of the source's two-direction question; it asks for subexponential time, without requiring polynomial time.
question_excerpt: For example, does super-polynomial lower bounds for arithmetic formulas imply non-trivial deterministic algorithms for PIT for arithmetic formulas, and vice-versa?
definitions:
An arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb Q\) is a finite rooted binary tree. Each leaf is labeled by a rational constant or a variable, and each internal node by addition or multiplication. It computes its polynomial in commuting variables by the indicated operations; there are no division or exponentiation gates and no shared internal subcomputations. Negative rational constants are allowed. Its size is its number of edges. Let \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f)\) be the minimum size among formulas computing exactly \(f\). Rational constants of arbitrary bit length are permitted in this minimum, and their bit lengths are not charged to this algebraic size. The lower bound is against every formula, with no depth, read-count, homogeneity or intermediate multilinearity restriction. A polynomial is multilinear when each variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. Explicitness of \((f_m)_{m\ge1}\) means that there are positive integers \(a,b,C\) and one deterministic Turing machine which, on unary input \(1^m\), outputs the ordered list of all \(2^m\) rational coefficients of \(f_m\) in time at most \(2^{a m+C}\), and every coefficient has numerator/denominator bit length at most \(C(m+1)^b\). The order is lexicographic on exponent vectors in \(\{0,1\}^m\); zero coefficients are included. Coefficients are written as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in reduced form. The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\) means \(\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists m_0\ \forall m\ge m_0:\ L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)>m^k\). Thus the hard family is uniform in its coefficient generation, while the competing formulas are nonuniform. For PIT the input is an arbitrary formula, with its tree and gate labels explicitly supplied, variable indices in binary, and rational constants in binary numerator/denominator form. Use the following prefix encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\) and write \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary representation of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(p\) is represented by this code for \(2p\) when \(p\ge0\), and for \(-2p-1\) otherwise. A rational is its signed-numerator code followed by its positive-denominator code, with numerator and denominator coprime. The four two-bit formula tags are 00 for a rational leaf (followed by that rational code), 01 for a variable leaf (followed by its positive integer index), 10 for addition and 11 for multiplication. Each internal-node tag is followed recursively by the encodings of its left and right children. No trailing bits are permitted. Let \(N\) be the total encoding length. The hard-family coefficient list uses the same rational encoding, concatenated in the specified order. The required output is whether the computed formal polynomial has every coefficient zero. The tester may examine the formula description (white-box access); a black-box hitting-set construction is not required. There is no promise that the input computes a multilinear polynomial. Time is measured in bit operations of a deterministic Turing machine, including reading constants, and the tester uses neither randomness nor advice nor an oracle. More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there must be a machine \(A_\varepsilon\), constants \(c_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon>0\), and a threshold \(N_\varepsilon\) such that it is correct on every valid formula and takes at most \(C_\varepsilon 2^{c_\varepsilon N^\varepsilon}\) steps on every formula of length \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). Machines and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the input. The implication concerns existence of these algorithms; it does not additionally require a uniform compiler from descriptions of hard families to testers.

For the stated bit costs, a deterministic multitape Turing machine has one read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes, fixed finite control and alphabet, and one head on each tape. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; it may append at most one output bit. Each transition costs one. Tape cells are indexed by nonnegative integers and a left move at zero stays there. The program and tape count are independent of input length. Malformed encodings may be rejected; correctness and the displayed clocks are required on every valid encoded instance.
answer_criterion:
Give a mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full implication \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\), or a Lean-checked refutation establishing \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\land\neg D_{\mathrm{form}}\) under exactly the definitions above. A positive answer must cover unrestricted rational arithmetic formulas and every \(\varepsilon>0\). A result assuming lower bounds against general circuits, exponential formula hardness, a particular stronger border-complexity hypothesis, or hardness only for an additionally constrained polynomial family does not by itself prove this implication. A restricted-depth, bounded-read or noncommutative PIT algorithm alone is insufficient. This is a logical implication; proving the hard-family hypothesis unconditionally is not required for a positive answer.

Equivalently, failure of \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) means there is an \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every uniform deterministic machine \(A\) that halts with the correct PIT answer on every valid formula, all positive constants \(c,C\), and every length threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid formula \(F\) of encoding length \(N\ge N_0\) on which \(A\) takes more than \(C2^{cN^\varepsilon}\) transitions. A refutation must establish this failure together with the hard-family hypothesis.
context:
The 2018 source asks about both directions between formula lower bounds and nontrivial deterministic PIT. The chosen branch tests whether the usual superpolynomial hardness-to-subexponential-time principle for circuits also holds for formulas. The source's formal coefficient-list definition supplies the explicitness condition used here.

For general arithmetic circuits, Kabanets and Impagliazzo establish the corresponding forward tradeoff: superpolynomial hardness of an explicit multilinear family gives deterministic PIT in time with arbitrarily small positive powers in the exponent. A stronger hardness assumption gives quasipolynomial time. Circuit hardness is a stronger hypothesis than formula hardness.

The reverse direction depends on how the tester accesses its input. A black-box hitting set is a finite set of evaluation points on which every nonzero polynomial in the specified formula class is nonzero somewhere. Such constructions imply algebraic lower bounds. An arbitrary white-box tester need not provide a hitting set. The known white-box formula-PIT consequence in Kabanets–Impagliazzo is a disjunction: either a nondeterministic exponential-time language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuits, or the permanent has no polynomial-size division-free integer arithmetic formulas. It is not stated as the converse of this card's single explicit-family hypothesis.

The 2019 survey explicitly poses a stronger forward formula question with a polynomial-time conclusion. The present target retains the weaker subexponential conclusion from the 2018 question.

The 2025 polynomial-time PIT equivalence uses hardness against uniform arithmetic networks with PIT gates on almost all individual inputs. Its model and hardness condition differ from the nonuniform formula-size hypothesis here.

Another 2025 theorem gives a hitting-set generator for formulas assuming a stronger, specific lower bound: superpolynomial border-formula complexity of the determinant. Border complexity permits polynomials arising as limits of computations, and its lower bound is not supplied merely by the hypothesis in this card.

The 2026 read-4 result supplies deterministic PIT algorithms when each variable occurs at most four times in a formula. The target here permits an unbounded number of occurrences and arbitrary depth.
why: This asks whether hardness against arithmetic computation without shared subexpressions already suffices to remove randomness from identity testing in that same fundamental model. A resolution would clarify whether the central circuit hardness–randomness principle survives the restriction to formulas, connecting algebraic lower bounds with deterministic symbolic computation.

A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the stated unrestricted-formula implication. The checked 2025 uniform-network and border-determinant results, and the 2026 read-4 algorithm, have materially different hypotheses or models. This records bounded review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The source quotation retains its original two-direction wording; the formal target explicitly selects the forward subexponential branch.

working_summary: An arithmetic formula is a tree of additions and multiplications with rational constants and commuting variables. Assume a coefficient-explicit multilinear polynomial family eventually requires formulas larger than every fixed polynomial in its variable count. Must there then be deterministic identity testers for every unrestricted formula in time 2^{O(N^epsilon)} for every epsilon > 0? The selected target is the forward, subexponential branch of the original two-direction question. Known later results change the hardness assumption or restrict the formula model; the bounded review found no verified resolution of this implication.

title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
importance_reason: A canonical explicit-construction problem seeking random-like small-set vertex expansion at a sharp additive threshold, beyond the already achieved vanishing relative loss. Its central graph-theoretic target and broad connections justify high importance; current open status of the exact sharp form remains separately uncertain.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or multiple edges. It is \(d\)-regular if each vertex has exactly \(d\) distinct neighbors. Its labeled vertex set is \([n_j]=\{1,\ldots,n_j\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n_j]\), define
\[
\Gamma_{G_j}(S)=\{v\in[n_j]:\ \exists u\in S,\ \{u,v\}\in E(G_j)\}.
\]
The left side in the target counts distinct neighbors outside \(S\), not edges leaving \(S\), not neighbors counted with multiplicity, and not neighbors inside \(S\). The cutoff \(\eta n_j\) is a real number; the condition is imposed on every integer set size satisfying the displayed inequality. Empty sets impose no requirement. The same positive \(\eta\) works for the entire family at the fixed values of \(\delta,d\).

The output of \(A\) is \(n_j\) in binary followed by an explicit list of the edges, each an unordered pair of distinct binary vertex labels, with delimiters. Isolated vertices would still be specified by \(n_j\), although none occur for \(d\ge3\). Reading the unary index, all computation and every output bit count in the bound. The machine has a finite program, no random bits, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. It must work on every \(1^j\), not merely on infinitely many selected indices. The integers \(n_j\) must increase strictly, so the construction gives arbitrarily large graphs; an allowed family need not contain every admissible vertex count.

The degree threshold \(d_0\) may depend on \(\delta\). After \(d\) is fixed, the machine \(A\) and constants \(\eta,K,a\) may depend on both \(\delta,d\), but not on \(j\) or \(S\). No algorithm uniform in \(\delta,d\) is required. The construction requirement is the survey's mild explicitness convention, polynomial time in the family index, with full output charged. It does not additionally require computing one neighbor in time polynomial in \(\log n_j\). Restricting positive \(\delta\) and the small-set fraction to rationals loses no expansion guarantee: a smaller positive rational tolerance or fraction can be chosen when needed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the entire proposition, including the explicit algorithm families, their cost bounds and the expansion inequality for all indicated sets, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. Random existence alone is insufficient. A construction with a relative loss tending to zero as degree grows does not meet this additive-loss target without a proof of the displayed bound with the stated quantifier order. A result for one degree or a one-sided bipartite expansion promise does not by itself establish the proposition.
context:
The saved survey explicitly asks for \(d-2-\delta\) external vertex expansion for every sufficiently large degree, with a positive small-set fraction depending on \(d,\delta\). This card preserves that additive target. Definitions 2.3 and 4.6 supply the mild explicitness and external-neighborhood conventions; it does not replace the question by a relative \((1-\varepsilon)d\) target.

Theorem 4.16 shows that random regular graphs have the displayed small-set expansion asymptotically. This establishes the combinatorial feasibility of the bound, not a deterministic polynomial-time family.

Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner and Zhang give explicit lossless expanders: for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large degrees admit a \((1-\varepsilon)d\) distinct-neighbor guarantee. Their introduction cites the survey question as a longstanding problem addressed by their construction.

The two quantitative formulations are not identical. A degree threshold depending on \(\varepsilon\) does not by itself justify taking \(\varepsilon\) proportional to \(1/d\) at the same degree. Moreover, counting all distinct neighbors and counting only external neighbors differ. The review therefore does not infer the exact additive \(d-2-\delta\) proposition from the stated relative-loss theorem.

The retained status is uncertain because the limited review has not established the present status of this sharper literal survey formulation after the lossless-expander breakthrough. The formulation is precise, and the original source question is preserved; the uncertainty concerns current resolution, not a license to claim the broader historical problem remains unsolved.
why: Random regular graphs have almost the largest possible external neighborhood for every small set. Matching that additive guarantee by deterministic constructions would sharpen a central benchmark for expanders, with consequences for combinatorial structures underlying coding, routing and pseudorandomness.

The 2025 lossless-expander paper cites that historical problem while its displayed main theorem establishes arbitrarily small fixed relative loss at sufficiently large degree. The review did not verify a theorem meeting the literal additive target and quantifier order. This card therefore neither claims the target resolved nor certifies its continued openness.

title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
importance_reason: Individually assessed as a foundational equivalence question about cryptographic pseudorandomness: it compares two natural security primitives and bears directly on the gap between errorless and error-prone average-case hardness and on the role of one-way functions. The selected statement is about unrestricted polynomial-size Boolean tests, not a narrow generator family or a parameter optimization. The score is editorial judgment based on these connections and the precise source questions, replacing the inherited unassessed midpoint.
formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.
question_excerpt: There are proof techniques that enable derandomizing two-sided-error randomized algorithms using a hitting set generator [12]; however, it is unknown if a hitting set generator […]
definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge 0\), let \(U_m\) denote the uniform distribution on the \(2^m\) binary strings of length \(m\). Output lengths are integers \(N\ge 2\). An admissible generator family \(F=(F_N)_{N\ge 2}\) has a seed-length function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) with \(1\le s(N)<N\) and maps \(F_N:\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\). One deterministic multitape Turing machine computes \(s(N)\) from \(1^N\), and another computes \(F_N(z)\) from \((1^N,z)\) for every seed \(z\). Here \(1^N\) is the unary encoding of \(N\). There are constants \(A,b\ge 1\), depending only on the family, such that each computation takes at most \(A(N+1)^b\) steps. In particular, time is polynomial in the output length. A machine has finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes with a fixed finite alphabet. In one step each head reads and may move by at most one cell, each work head may write one symbol, and at most one output bit may be appended. All tapes start at their first cell and are indexed by nonnegative integers; a left move at zero stays at zero. The generator input is the literal string \(1^N\#z\), and the seed-length output is the binary encoding of \(s(N)\). The machine programs and tape counts are independent of \(N\). These machines receive no advice, oracle or randomness. The output need not contain the seed, and different seeds may have the same output.

A test at length \(N\) is an arbitrary deterministic Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{N}\to\{0,1\}\), with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, constant gates, unrestricted fan-out and unrestricted depth. Its size is its number of gates, excluding the input nodes. There is no uniformity requirement on tests at different lengths. Security against polynomial-size circuits means the quantifier \(\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\) followed by a threshold length that may depend on \(c\), and then a guarantee for every circuit of size at most \(N^c\) at every larger length.

A function \(\nu:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to(0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge 1\) there is an integer \(N_a\) such that \(\nu(N)\le N^{-a}\) for all \(N\ge N_a\). No computability assumption is imposed on a security-bound function.

For an admissible family \(H\) with seed length \(s\), the property \(\operatorname{HSG}(H)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists N_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge N_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\ge\varepsilon(N)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\; C(H_N(z))=1.
\]
The hit is an existence guarantee; it need not occur with any specified fraction of seeds.

For an admissible family \(G\) with its own seed length \(t\), the property \(\operatorname{PRG}(G)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\eta\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists M_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge M_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{t(N)}}[C(G_N(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\eta(N).
\]
Thus generated outputs are sampled by a uniform seed, with multiplicity when seeds collide. The same generator and the same negligible function must serve every circuit-size exponent. In the implication, all generator, seed-length, time-bound and security-bound witnesses are existentially quantified separately on the two sides.
answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated existence implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish the existence of a generator satisfying the full PRG definition whenever a generator satisfying the HSG definition exists. A negative answer must establish that an HSG as defined exists while no PRG as defined exists, in the stated ordinary model. A theorem restricted to a smaller test class, additional hardness assumptions, infinitely many lengths, or the impossibility of a particular conversion method does not decide this implication.
context:
A hitting-set generator guarantees that every sufficiently dense efficiently recognizable set contains at least one generated string. A pseudorandom generator controls each test's acceptance probability under a uniformly selected seed. The question asks whether the first kind of efficiently generated object already entails the existence of the second.

The 2022 source raises a broad conversion question in its introduction and footnote 2. This card explicitly selects the cryptographic existence question stated earlier as Question 6 in Santhanam's 2020 paper, which the 2022 discussion cites. The defaults in Section 2.2 of that paper specify polynomial time in output length, arbitrary polynomial-size circuit tests and negligible error. The seed may have any nontrivial length; neither a prescribed stretch nor preservation of parameters is part of the target. Unary output-length input and polynomial-time computation of the seed length make the uniform-family convention explicit.

The 2022 paper proves a different positive result for seed-extending generators tested by polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. Seed-extending means that the seed is a prefix of the output. The restrictions on both generator form and test class are part of that theorem. It does not settle the cryptographic implication above.
why: This asks whether hitting dense sets and reproducing acceptance probabilities have the same existential power when a uniform efficient generator must withstand arbitrarily stronger polynomial-size tests. Pseudorandom generators are foundational cryptographic objects connected to one-way functions, while the weaker hitting guarantee arises naturally from errorless average-case hardness. A resolution would clarify whether these two notions represent distinct assumptions about computational randomness, rather than merely improve the parameters of one construction.
status_note: The selected cryptographic question is explicitly open in Santhanam 2020 and is highlighted again in the 2022 source. The 2022 positive theorem has seed-prefix and NC1/poly restrictions. The checked 2023 conditional equivalence and 2024–2026 results use different assumptions, adversaries or targets. Individual primary-source reading and a bounded later-work search completed on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated existence implication. This supports a dated source-open classification, not a claim of exhaustive current verification.

working_summary: A hitting-set generator produces strings that intersect every sufficiently dense set accepted by a polynomial-size Boolean circuit. A pseudorandom generator must instead approximate every such circuit’s acceptance probability when its seed is chosen uniformly. The selected cryptographic question asks whether the existence of the first kind of uniform polynomial-time generator entails the existence of the second, with negligible security bounds and any nontrivial stretch. The generators may have different parameters, and the known seed-extending result for logarithmic-depth circuits does not establish the unrestricted implication. A complete Lean proof must decide this existence implication, clarifying the relationship between two basic forms of computational randomness.

title: Deterministic linear representations of transversal matroids
importance_reason: A central derandomization problem for translating ubiquitous bipartite matching constraints into one exact linear representation. Its connections to gammoids, representative sets, cut representations and several important kernelization problems give it broad algorithmic consequences. The 2025 quasipolynomial construction highlights a substantial remaining polynomial-time barrier. This assessment replaces the unassessed midpoint and reflects those consequences rather than the textbook source or age alone.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm that, given any finite bipartite graph with its two sides specified, constructs a rational matrix representing its transversal matroid in polynomial bit time?

Precisely, let \(a,b\) be nonnegative integers and let
\[
G=([a],[b],E),\qquad E\subseteq[a]\times[b],
\]
where the two labeled sides are disjoint copies and \([0]=\varnothing\). Let \(r(G)\) be the maximum size of a matching in \(G\). The required output is one explicit matrix
\[
M\in\mathbb Q^{\,r(G)\times a}
\]
whose column \(j\) corresponds to vertex \(j\) on the first side, such that
\[
\forall S\subseteq[a]\quad
\left[\exists\text{ injective }f:S\to[b]\ 
       \forall j\in S\ (j,f(j))\in E\right]
\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\left[\text{the columns }(M_{\ast j})_{j\in S}
       \text{ are linearly independent over }\mathbb Q\right].
\]
The same matrix must satisfy this equivalence for all subsets simultaneously.

With the encodings and deterministic machine model below, the algorithmic assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall a,b\in\mathbb N\ \forall E\subseteq[a]\times[b]\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,\operatorname{enc}(G),y,C(L(G)+1)^d)
\land \operatorname{Correct}(G,y)
\bigr).
\]
Here \(A\) is one fixed finite deterministic program, \(L(G)\) is the input's bit length, and \(\operatorname{Correct}\) checks the full matrix requirement above. The constants do not depend on the graph or its rank. This formulation makes explicit the rational-field and bit-complexity setting surrounding the source question; it does not ask for representations over every finite field or permit unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded numbers.
definitions:
A finite bipartite graph has two disjoint labeled vertex sets, here \([a]=\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and a separate copy of \([b]=\{1,\ldots,b\}\). An edge is a pair in \(E\subseteq[a]\times[b]\), so there are no parallel edges. A matching is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is its number of edges, and \(r(G)\) is the maximum matching size, including zero for an edgeless graph.

A subset \(S\subseteq[a]\) is independent in the transversal matroid of \(G\) when some matching covers every vertex in \(S\). Equivalently, there is an injective function \(f:S\to[b]\) with \((j,f(j))\in E\) for each \(j\in S\). These independent subsets form the matroid; the task does not receive an explicit list of all such subsets or an additional oracle.

For a matrix \(M\in\mathbb Q^{r(G)\times a}\), its columns indexed by \(S\) are linearly independent precisely when
\[
\forall(\lambda_j)_{j\in S}\in\mathbb Q^S\quad
\left[
 \forall i\in[r(G)]\ \sum_{j\in S}\lambda_jM_{ij}=0
\right]
\ \Longrightarrow\
\left[\forall j\in S\ \lambda_j=0\right].
\]
The empty family of columns is independent. A zero-row matrix is allowed when \(r(G)=0\); its nonempty column families are dependent. In particular, empty sides and isolated vertices are valid inputs. Matrix columns remain labeled by all \(a\) first-side vertices, including isolated ones. The required representation is an actual rational matrix, with no indeterminates, unevaluated expressions or collection of alternative matrices.

Encode \(G\) by the binary string \(1^a0\,1^b0\) followed by its \(ab\) adjacency bits, ordered first by the first-side label and then by the second-side label. Thus
\[
L(G)=a+b+2+ab.
\]
This explicit encoding includes isolated vertices. Polynomial time in this encoding is polynomial time in the size of an explicit graph presentation; it is not time in a compressed specification of exponentially many vertices.

To specify the output encoding, for a nonnegative integer \(k\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Let \(\ell(k)\) be this expansion's length and put
\[
\operatorname{code}(k)=1^{\ell(k)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(k).
\]
A signed integer \(p\) is encoded by one sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|p|)\), where the sign bit is one exactly for a negative integer; zero has sign bit zero. A rational number is encoded as such a signed numerator \(p\) followed by \(\operatorname{code}(q)\) for a positive denominator \(q\), and denotes \(p/q\). Fractions need not be reduced. A matrix output consists of \(\operatorname{code}(r(G))\), then \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), then the \(r(G)a\) rational entries in row order, with no further bits. The predicate \(\operatorname{Correct}(G,y)\) means that \(y\) has this valid encoding and its decoded matrix satisfies the independence equivalence for every \(S\subseteq[a]\). Thus the polynomial running-time requirement includes writing every numerator and denominator bit.

The computational model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes, and a binary output stream. The finite program, finite tape alphabets, and number of work tapes are fixed independently of the input. Tape cells are indexed by nonnegative integers; initially the heads are at cell zero, work tapes are blank, and the input string is followed by blanks. A step reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite control, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, moves each head by at most one cell, and appends at most one bit to the output. A requested move left from cell zero leaves that head at zero. A designated halt state ends the computation. There is no randomness, advice or oracle access. All preprocessing and output steps count. The predicate \(\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,x,y,T)\) means that \(A\), on input \(x\), halts after at most \(T\) steps with exactly output \(y\). Invalid input strings impose no requirements.

Requiring integer constants \(C,d\ge1\) expresses the usual polynomial-time existence condition: larger integer constants cover any fixed polynomial bound. The row count \(r(G)\) fixes a standard representation convention; the source notes that representations can be taken to have one row per rank. The question requires no prescribed numerical upper bound on individual matrix entries beyond the polynomial number of bits that can be written in polynomial time.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal algorithmic assertion or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must specify one deterministic finite program \(A\) and constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and prove that for every encoded bipartite graph it halts within \(C(L(G)+1)^d\) bit steps and outputs one correctly encoded rational matrix. Correctness must prove both directions of the independence equivalence for every subset of first-side vertices in the same output matrix. Existence of a suitable matrix for each graph without a uniform polynomial-time construction is insufficient, as is a bound counting only arithmetic operations without controlling bit costs and output length.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall A\ \forall C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists a,b\in\mathbb N\ \exists E\subseteq[a]\times[b]\quad
\neg\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,\operatorname{enc}(G),y,C(L(G)+1)^d)
\land\operatorname{Correct}(G,y)
\bigr).
\]
Thus, for each proposed program and polynomial bound, some valid graph makes it run too long, fail to halt, produce an invalid encoding, or produce a matrix violating the required equivalence. The defeating graph may depend on the program and bound. The negative claim is computational; it does not assert that a transversal matroid lacks a rational representation.

A randomized construction, a quasipolynomial-time construction, or a construction only for bounded rank does not by itself establish the requested positive assertion. A lower bound for one method or a conditional obstruction does not prove the unrestricted negative assertion unless it also proves the missing general claim or hypothesis. This is an exact algorithm-existence target; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace the required proof.
context:
The textbook defines the independent sets by bipartite matchings and gives a randomized polynomial-time construction over the rationals. Immediately after discussing the polynomial bit length of its integer entries, it asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction. This card fixes that rational, bit-complexity interpretation explicitly.

The representation must preserve every independent set in a single matrix. The existence of rational representations is known; the unresolved issue is constructing them deterministically within polynomial bit time from the bipartite graph.

The MFCS 2025 paper gives a deterministic construction in quasipolynomial time. In terms of the total vertex count \(N\), its construction has time and output length bounded by \((N+2)^{O(\log(N+2))}\), while the polynomial-time question remains open in that source.

The same paper documents applications to gammoid representations, cut representations and deterministic quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several parameterized problems. These results make the representation question useful beyond testing a single matching constraint, while leaving polynomial time as a distinct endpoint.
why: This asks whether randomness can be removed from a basic translation between matching constraints and linear algebra. Such representations support matroid algorithms and, through related gammoid representations, several central preprocessing and cut-representation results. A polynomial-time construction would supply one exact algebraic representation of all independence relations without random choices. A negative result would establish a computational obstruction to this widely used translation, despite the existence of small rational representations.

The MFCS 2025 primary paper still calls this a longstanding open problem and proves a quasipolynomial-time construction instead. The public progress uses a quasipolynomial bound supported by the 2025 proof without inheriting its inconsistent sharper rank-only entry-bit statement. This is a formulation and theorem-scope review, not an exhaustive literature certificate or Lean proof verification.

working_summary: A bipartite graph defines a transversal matroid by declaring a subset on its first side independent when it can be matched to distinct vertices on the second side. The task is to construct one explicit rational matrix whose corresponding columns are linearly independent exactly for those subsets. The question asks for one uniform deterministic algorithm with polynomial bit running time, including the full binary output. Randomized polynomial-time representations and deterministic quasipolynomial-time representations are known, while polynomial-time derandomization would support important matroid and preprocessing algorithms. A complete Lean answer must prove such a construction works on every bipartite graph or prove that no deterministic algorithm meets the stated polynomial bound.

title: Subpolynomial-seed pseudorandom generators for \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\)
importance_reason: A standard unconditional derandomization challenge for a canonical circuit class beyond AC0, exposing the gap between known lower bounds and the stronger average-case hardness needed for short seeds.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), is there an unconditional, mildly explicit generator family
\[
G_{k,m}:\{0,1\}^{d_k(m)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m}\qquad(m\ge1)
\]
whose integer seed length satisfies \(d_k(m)=m^{o(1)}\), and which fools every depth-at-most-\(k\), size-at-most-\(m\) \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\) circuit on \(m\) input bits with error at most \(1/4\)?

Precisely, for every such circuit \(C\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{s\sim U_{d_k(m)}}[C(G_{k,m}(s))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_m}[C(x)=1]\right|\le1/4.
\]
The generator for a given \(k,m\) must work simultaneously for all the indicated circuits and cannot depend on \(C\). “Mildly explicit” means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(m\) and \(2^{d_k(m)}\), with the polynomial permitted to depend on \(k\).
question_excerpt: Open Problem 7.33 asks for a mildly explicit, error-one-quarter generator with subpolynomial seed length against every fixed-depth AC0[2] circuit, using output length as the circuit-size bound.
definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output bit. Input nodes carry literals \(x_i\), their negations \(\neg x_i\), or constants \(0,1\), for \(1\le i\le m\). Every computation node is an AND, OR or parity gate with arbitrarily many predecessors. AND is one exactly when all its input bits are one; OR is one exactly when at least one is one; parity is the sum of its inputs modulo two. For no predecessors, AND is one and OR and parity are zero. Fan-out is unrestricted. Gates may be used at any depth, and parity gates may feed other parity gates or either Boolean gate type.

Size counts computation nodes only. Input literals and constants are free input nodes. Depth is the maximum number of computation nodes along a directed path from an input to the output; a literal or constant output has depth zero. There is no restriction on wires beyond a finite circuit description, and no requirement that the testing circuit descriptions be generated uniformly over lengths. Negations are available at inputs as in the source definition. Allowing complemented parity outputs or internal NOT gates gives the same all-fixed-depth target after routine constant changes in resources, but the formal statement uses the specified basis.

For an integer \(\ell\ge0\), \(U_\ell\) is the uniform distribution on all \(\ell\)-bit strings; \(U_0\) is concentrated on the empty string. Randomness consists only of the uniformly chosen seed. The generator is a deterministic map, may have collisions and outputs exactly \(m\) bits. The two probabilities use independent draws from the stated uniform domains.

For each fixed \(k\), a single function \(d_k:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge0}\) must satisfy
\[
\forall a>0\ \exists M_{k,a}\ \forall m\ge M_{k,a}:\ d_k(m)\le m^a.
\]
This defines the subpolynomial seed requirement. It does not ask merely for one fixed sublinear power, nor permit choosing a different generator family separately for each \(a\).

Uniform mild explicitness requires deterministic algorithms for computing \(d_k(m)\) and evaluating \(G_{k,m}(s)\). There are constants \(A_k\ge1,b_k\ge1\) such that on input \(1^m\) the first algorithm outputs the binary encoding of \(d_k(m)\), and on input \((1^m,s)\), with \(|s|=d_k(m)\), the second outputs \(G_{k,m}(s)\), each within
\[
A_k\bigl(m+2^{d_k(m)}+1\bigr)^{b_k}
\]
steps. Use the ordinary uniform deterministic multitape Turing model: finitely many tapes and finite alphabets, initially blank work tapes, and one-cell head moves per transition. Input access and output writing are charged. There is no advice, random construction, oracle, unbounded unit-cost arithmetic or assumed computational hardness. The programs and constants may depend on the fixed \(k\); no efficient procedure producing them from \(k\) is required. A fully explicit polynomial-in-\(m\) evaluation algorithm also qualifies, but is not required.

The size parameter is the source's number of computation gates and is set equal to the output length. The requested error bound is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities, with no averaging over circuits. It must hold at every positive \(m\); only the seed-length estimate is asymptotic.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction or a proof that the asserted family cannot exist. A positive answer must prove the uniform evaluation bound, the subpolynomial seed condition and the \(1/4\) fooling guarantee for every fixed depth and every circuit in the stated class. A construction using a hardness assumption, treating only one depth, restricting the locations or number of parity gates, or providing only a fixed sublinear seed exponent does not suffice. This is an existence question with its own exact error threshold; numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance does not replace the \(1/4\) pseudorandomness condition.
context:
The monograph first constructs short-seed generators for circuits without parity gates. Parity itself provides useful hardness for that construction, but becomes directly computable once parity gates are allowed.

The source discusses known worst-case lower bounds for the larger circuit class and explains that their available average-case form does not immediately give this generator.

Mild explicitness permits evaluating a seed in time polynomial in the whole seed-space size. Enumerating all seeds still takes subexponential time when the seed length is subpolynomial.

The 2025 work improves generators and correlation bounds for circuits with restricted symmetric or threshold gates, including a symmetric gate above AC0. This does not furnish the requested guarantee for unrestricted parity composition.

The 2026 polynomial-generator result assumes a field and characteristic regime that excludes the binary-field case required here. It is a related advance, not a construction for this card.
why: Adding parity gates is a basic step beyond constant-depth AND/OR circuits, yet existing worst-case lower bounds do not supply the strong average-case guarantees used by standard generator constructions. A generator with the requested seed would permit deterministic seed enumeration in subexponential time for the entire fixed-depth class. The question probes a central gap between proving circuit lower bounds and turning them into useful pseudorandomness.
status_note: The 2012 source poses the stated mildly explicit construction. Checked 2025 results cover restricted uses of symmetric or threshold gates and structured polynomials; checked 2026 results concern larger fields or individual modular sums. None supplies the all-circuits construction below, and no resolution was found in the bounded later-work check.

working_summary: The question asks for pseudorandom bits that fool constant-depth circuits built from AND, OR and parity gates. For each fixed depth, one generator family must work against every circuit with at most as many computation gates as output bits. The difference in acceptance probabilities must be at most one quarter for every permitted circuit. The seed length must eventually be smaller than every positive power of the output length. title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
importance_reason: Optimal hardness-to-randomness generators would strengthen a central bridge between lower bounds and deterministic algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
definitions:
\(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on \(t\)-bit strings. The probabilities in the premise and conclusion use fresh independent uniform strings of the indicated lengths. They are computational distinguishability guarantees, not statistical closeness against unbounded tests.

A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input wires, free Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one output wire. Size counts computation gates, including NOT gates, but not input wires or constants. The circuits \(B\) and \(D\) are deterministic and completely nonuniform; \(B\) has \(\ell\) inputs and \(D\) has \(m\). Their choices may depend on all parameters and on \(f\). They have no oracle access to \(f\). Allowing additional independent random input wires does not change these guarantees, because fixing the random bits gives a deterministic circuit of no greater size and averaging preserves the displayed inequalities. The premise means that even the best size-\(s\) predictor has advantage at most \(1/s\) over a fair guess.

Explicitness is uniform deterministic polynomial-time computation of the sampler. There are fixed multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that the parameter machine on \((1^{\ell},s)\), with \(s\) binary, outputs integer lengths \(d,m\), and the evaluation machine on \((1^{\ell},s,z)\) writes the ordered list of all \(m\) sampled \(\ell\)-bit strings. Each runs in at most \(K(\ell+s+1)^q\) steps on valid inputs. Equivalently the time can be polynomial in \(\ell+m\), because of the polynomial relationship between \(s\) and \(m\). All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, hard-function description or hard-function truth table available to these machines.

The constants and the machines precede the parameters, and \(H_{\ell,s}\) precedes the universal quantifier over \(f\). The family must be computed even for parameter pairs at which no function satisfies the hardness premise; its implication is then vacuous. No algorithm recognizing hard functions is required. The function \(f\) need not itself be efficiently computable: this is a transformation guarantee conditional on its finite-length circuit hardness, not a claim that such hard functions have been constructed. When \(f\) is also computable within a suitable exponential-time bound, the transformation has the usual derandomization applications.

The normalization \(m\le s\) and the lower bound using \(\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\) express the source's polynomially many output bits. A larger qualifying output can be truncated, and fixed multiplicative factors in a polynomial lower bound can be absorbed by reducing \(\beta\) and handling finitely many small hardness parameters. The single-evaluation requirement excludes encoding or otherwise transforming the truth table of \(f\) before producing the output bits.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated sampler-family claim. A positive proof must supply the uniform sampler and constants and establish the implication for every promised \(f\), including the linear seed bound, polynomial output length and size-\(m\), error-\(1/m\) guarantee. A negative proof must rule out all such families, not merely one combinatorial-design construction or one kind of security reduction. A general hardness-to-randomness generator that encodes the hard function or combines several evaluations per output bit does not answer this sampling question.
context:
The Nisan–Wigderson construction evaluates the hard function at correlated points determined by a combinatorial design. The source obtains a seed bound of order \(\ell^2/\log s\) while keeping polynomially many output bits. This is linear in \(\ell\) when \(s\) is exponential in \(\ell\), but not throughout the lower-hardness range.

General hardness-to-randomness constructions already improve the seed dependence to linear in the relevant hard-function input length. Vadhan explains that their output bits can depend on an encoding of the entire hard function. Open Problem 7.25 asks for the more restrictive point-evaluation form written here, so those results do not directly settle it.

The 2022 Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman theorem refines quantitative derandomization under hardness for randomized single-valued nondeterministic circuits. It uses pseudoentropy and extraction and assumes a different, stronger type of circuit hardness. Its nearly optimal parameters are not a theorem for every ordinary average-case-hard function under the one-evaluation-per-bit requirement.

A lower bound for one construction or for a specified reconstructive proof technique would not refute the semantic existence statement. Conversely, merely assuming that a hard function exists is not the desired answer: the question requires one uniform sampler with the stated implication for every function meeting the premise.
why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.

title: Super-bits from demi-bits
importance_reason: A long-standing implication between foundational nondeterministic pseudorandomness primitives, with consequences for natural-proof barriers and proof-complexity generators; generic stretching still falls short of the requested security upgrade.
formal:
Does existence of a demi-bit imply existence of a super-bit?

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuit families \(G=(G_n)_{n\ge1}\) with
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n+1}.
\]
For a nondeterministic circuit \(D\) on \(n+1\) ordinary input bits, write
\[
\alpha(D)=\Pr_{y\sim U_{n+1}}[D(y)=1],\qquad
\beta(D,G_n)=\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[D(G_n(x))=1].
\]
Define the two positive-integer hardness measures
\[
H_{\mathrm{dh}}(G_n)=\min\{s:\exists D,\ |D|\le s,\ 
\alpha(D)\ge1/s,\ \beta(D,G_n)=0\},
\]
\[
H_{\mathrm{nh}}(G_n)=\min\{s:\exists D,\ |D|\le s,\ 
\alpha(D)-\beta(D,G_n)\ge1/s\}.
\]
Is the following implication true?
\[
\bigl[\exists G\in\mathcal G\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\
\forall n\ge N:\ H_{\mathrm{dh}}(G_n)\ge2^{n^\varepsilon}\bigr]
\ \Longrightarrow\
\bigl[\exists H\in\mathcal G\ \exists\delta>0\ \exists N'\
\forall n\ge N':\ H_{\mathrm{nh}}(H_n)\ge2^{n^\delta}\bigr].
\]
The premise defines a demi-bit and the conclusion a super-bit. The two families, hardness exponents and cutoffs may differ.
question_excerpt: After defining demi-hardness and the demi-bit existence conjecture, the source asks whether the existence of this weaker primitive implies existence of a super-bit.
definitions:
For \(m\ge1\), \(U_m\) is the uniform distribution on all binary strings of length \(m\). The seed is sampled uniformly even if several seeds give the same output; generated outputs therefore have their actual multiplicities, not a uniform distribution on the range.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant \(0\) and \(1\) nodes, unary NOT gates and fan-in-two AND and OR gates. Fan-out is unrestricted. Outputs are designated nodes. Size counts all nodes, including ordinary input nodes, witness input nodes and constants; designating an output does not create an extra node. This fixes a bounded-fan-in basis for the source's gate-count convention.

A family belongs to \(\mathcal G\) if there are fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) such that every \(G_n\) is a deterministic circuit of size at most \(C(n+1)^d\), with exactly \(n\) ordinary inputs and \(n+1\) output bits. Different lengths may have unrelated circuit descriptions. No algorithm generating these descriptions is required, so a polynomial-time-uniform construction is a stronger optional conclusion.

A nondeterministic circuit is represented by a deterministic single-output circuit \(D_0(y,z)\), with \(n+1\) ordinary input bits \(y\) and some finite number \(w\ge0\) of witness bits \(z\). Its acceptance predicate is
\[
D(y)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{w}\ D_0(y,z)=1.
\]
The witness is existential, not random; there is no averaging over witnesses. The size \(|D|\) is the size of \(D_0\), including all its witness inputs. The adversary may depend arbitrarily on \(n\) and on the generator. There are no oracle gates or restrictions on its depth.

Each minimum ranges over integers \(s\ge1\) and all such finite circuits. It exists: the range has at most \(2^n\) elements, so its complement in \(\{0,1\}^{n+1}\) has density at least one half and is recognized by some finite Boolean circuit. Taking a sufficiently large \(s\) makes that circuit an admissible witness for either minimum.

A demi-hardness witness must reject every generated string, while accepting at least a \(1/s\) fraction of uniformly random strings. A super-hardness witness may accept generated strings, but must accept uniform strings more often by at least \(1/s\). The order of subtraction is part of the definition. There is no absolute value and no symmetric requirement on the opposite difference. Nondeterministic acceptance is not closed under complementing the circuit's output gate.

The lower bound \(2^{n^\varepsilon}\), for some fixed positive real \(\varepsilon\), is required for every sufficiently large \(n\), with one exponent for the whole family. Neither hardness only against polynomial-size circuits nor hardness at merely infinitely many lengths is the premise in this question. The card asks about existence of the two families; it does not demand that every demi-bit already be a super-bit or impose a black-box or uniform conversion procedure.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential implication. An affirmative answer must obtain a polynomial-size one-bit-stretch super-bit family with some positive hardness exponent from the existence of a demi-bit family as defined. A negative answer must establish existence of a demi-bit and nonexistence of every super-bit family in the same ordinary model. Showing only that one particular demi-bit is not itself a super-bit, or proving a limitation of one conversion method, is insufficient. The proposition is binary; numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not change the signed advantage, zero-error condition or eventual hardness bounds.
context:
Every demi-hardness distinguisher also witnesses super-hardness, so \(H_{\mathrm{nh}}(G_n)\le H_{\mathrm{dh}}(G_n)\). Consequently every super-bit is a demi-bit. The question asks for the reverse implication at the level of existence.

With the subtraction reversed, a nondeterministic test could guess a seed and check whether the input is its generated output. It would accept all generated strings and at most half of uniformly random strings. This explains why standard absolute-value indistinguishability is not the target.

The 2024 stretching theorem increases the number of demi-bits by a sublinear amount. Increasing output length while retaining demi-hardness does not establish the super-hardness guarantee.

The source relates super-bits to pseudorandom function generators secure against nondeterministic adversaries and to barriers for nondeterministic natural properties. Obtaining these consequences directly from demi-bits remains a separate question.

The 2026 range-avoidance theorem uses demi-bit generators with larger stretch and superpolynomial hardness. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes the stretch it assumes from the generic stretching available from a single demi-bit.
why: The problem compares two basic notions of pseudorandomness against nondeterministic tests. Resolving the implication would determine whether a hitting requirement with no false positives on generated strings can yield the stronger distributional guarantee used in nondeterministic natural-proof barriers. It connects foundational generator assumptions, circuit lower-bound methods and proof complexity, rather than only improving a parameter in one construction.
status_note: The 2024 paper explicitly leaves the demi-bit-to-super-bit implication open. Its stretching theorem preserves the weaker demi-hardness notion. The checked ITCS 2026 work assumes larger stretch and derives different consequences. No resolution of the existential implication was found in the bounded later-work check.

working_summary: A demi-bit is a polynomial-size generator that adds one output bit and resists nondeterministic tests rejecting every generated output. A super-bit also resists tests that accept generated outputs but accept uniformly random strings noticeably more often. Both notions here require hardness at least exponential in a fixed positive power of the seed length for every sufficiently large length. The question asks whether existence of the weaker generator guarantees existence of the stronger one, allowing different nonuniform circuit families. Known stretching and range-avoidance results give consequences of demi-bits without supplying this security upgrade.

title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
importance_reason: Optimal seeded extraction parameters concern one of the central universal tools for converting weak randomness into usable randomness.
formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.
context:
The probabilistic existence bounds in the source permit logarithmic seed length and constant total entropy loss at fixed error. The obstacle in this question is a single efficiently evaluable construction, rather than the existence of a suitable finite table for each pair of parameters.

Vadhan contrasts logarithmic-seed constructions that extract a constant fraction of the source entropy with constructions extracting all but a constant number of source bits using a polylogarithmic seed. Neither parameter guarantee by itself gives \(m\ge k+d-O(1)\) with \(d=O(\log n)\).

The 2026 revised Doron–Ribeiro paper improves evaluation time for short-seed strong extractors. Its Theorem 1 gives \(m\ge(1-\eta)k\) and \(d=O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for fixed \(\eta>0\), with stated entropy and preprocessing conditions. Even after counting the seed as part of an ordinary output, the theorem allows a loss proportional to \(k\); it does not establish the constant-loss target.

The adjacent seed-length question TCS-1016 instead fixes the leading coefficient of the logarithm and allows only a constant fraction of source entropy as output. These two additive-precision questions have different required guarantees.
why: This asks whether an efficient general randomness purifier can preserve all but a constant number of the available random bits while using only a logarithmic seed. In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.
