title: Optimal-size highly unbalanced lossless expanders
importance_reason: Near-optimal explicit expansion is a reusable resource for coding, pseudorandomness, and algorithms.
formal:
Do there exist two fixed deterministic algorithms \(P,Q\) and positive integers \(C,c\) with the following properties for every pair of integers \(N,K\) satisfying \(N\ge2\) and \(1\le K\le N\)? Write \(L_{N}=1+\lceil\log_{2} N\rceil\). Algorithm \(P\), on input \((N,K)\), must output positive integers \(D=D(N,K)\) and \(M=M(N,K)\) such that
\[
D\le C L_{N}^{c},\qquad M\le CKD.
\]
Algorithm \(Q\), on input \((N,K,x,j)\) with \(x\in[N]\) and \(j\in[D]\), must output an element \(\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j)\in[M]\). Both the parameter computation and each neighbor computation must take at most \(C L_{N}^{c}\) steps in the uniform bit model defined below. The resulting bipartite multigraph must satisfy
\[
\forall S\subseteq[N],\quad |S|=K\ \Longrightarrow
\left|\{\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j):x\in S,\ j\in[D]\}\right|
\ge\frac{99}{100}DK.
\]
Thus the target is a fully explicit family with polylogarithmic left degree, a right side of size at most a constant times \(KD\), and expansion for every left set of size exactly \(K\). The algorithms and constants are chosen before \(N,K\); they must work uniformly over the entire stated parameter range. Prove this existence statement or its negation.
definitions:
For a positive integer \(t\), \([t]=\{1,\ldots,t\}\). The two vertex classes are disjoint labeled copies of \([N]\) and \([M]\). Each left vertex \(x\) has precisely \(D\) edge slots, indexed by \(j\in[D]\), whose right endpoints are \(\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j)\). Repeated right endpoints in different slots are allowed, so degree counts edges with multiplicity. In contrast, a neighborhood is a set of distinct right vertices, and its cardinality counts each right vertex once. No degree condition is imposed on right vertices.

For fixed \(N,K\), the graph must have the displayed expansion property simultaneously for all sets \(S\) with exactly \(K\) elements. It is not required to satisfy the same expansion factor for every smaller cardinality in that same graph. Different values of \(K\), including those with the same \(N\), may produce different graphs, degrees and right-side sizes. The factor \(99/100\) is fixed, not an input parameter. The target does not ask for an optimal exponent in the degree bound. There is no extra condition \(M<N\); the full source parameter range includes values of \(K\) for which such an imbalance cannot hold.

Use ordinary binary representations of nonnegative integers, with no leading zeros and with zero represented by the single digit 0. Encode a tuple by these representations separated by the symbol \(\#\), with no trailing separator. Input and output alphabets contain the fixed symbols 0, 1 and \(\#\); the number of symbols is a bit-length measure up to a fixed constant factor. Algorithm \(P\) outputs the tuple \((D,M)\), and \(Q\) outputs one binary integer. Inputs are supplied between end markers on a read-only input tape. Each algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes and an output tape. Each transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; one transition is one time step. All parameter selection, arithmetic, work-tape access and output writing count toward the time bound. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or uncharged preprocessing.

The running-time requirements are worst-case bounds on every valid input just specified, including every valid vertex and edge-slot query. No behavior is required on malformed tuples or tuples outside the promises. Each neighbor query starts with blank work tapes and may recompute parameters within its time allowance; no graph-sized data structure is supplied. Thus the representation is an implicit neighbor function, not a demand to output all \(ND\) edge slots in polylogarithmic time.

The positive constants \(C,c\) do not depend on \(N,K,x,j\), or on the set \(S\). Using one constant and one exponent for the degree and both computation bounds, and the same constant in \(M\le CKD\), is a normalization: separate fixed polynomial and multiplicative bounds can all be enlarged to bounds of this form. The finite case \(N=1\) can be handled separately and has no effect on the construction question. The word lossless refers here to preserving at least the fraction \(99/100\) of the maximum possible \(DK\) distinct neighbors, rather than requiring that all edge endpoints be distinct.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed uniform existence statement or its logical negation, using the specified machine model, graph representation and quantifier order.

For a positive answer, supply finite descriptions of \(P,Q\), constants \(C,c\ge1\), and proofs of the parameter-output requirements, both time bounds, valid neighbor outputs and the expansion inequality for every admissible \(N,K\) and every exact-size set \(S\). All constants must be uniform in the input parameters.

For a negative answer, define \(\operatorname{Good}(P,Q,C,c;N,K)\) to mean all the displayed parameter, computation and expansion requirements for that pair \((N,K)\), and prove
\[
\forall P,Q\ \forall C,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists N,K\in\mathbb Z,
\quad N\ge2\ \land\ 1\le K\le N\ \land\
\neg\operatorname{Good}(P,Q,C,c;N,K).
\]
The quantifiers over \(P,Q\) range over all deterministic machines of the defined kind. The failure can be in the uniform construction or resource requirements; it need not show that a graph with those numerical parameters fails to exist. A nonconstructive family, a slower construction, a construction for only selected parameter pairs, or a guarantee of only one distinct neighbor per left vertex does not meet the full positive criterion. The fixed fraction \(99/100\) is part of the proposition, not a numerical-answer tolerance.
context:

The checked September 2026 two-sided and one-expansion results concern different parameter guarantees, and the bounded review found no construction or refutation meeting the full target.

A construction with this right-side size and fast neighbor computation would provide lossless condensers with constant entropy overhead, improving a basic resource used in randomness extraction, coding and related algorithms.

working_summary: The problem asks for an explicit bipartite graph for every left-side size and every prescribed exact subset size. Each such subset must reach at least ninety-nine percent of the maximum number of distinct neighbors allowed by the left degree. The left degree must be polynomial in the logarithm of the left-side size, and the right side must have size at most a fixed constant times the subset size times that degree. A single deterministic construction must compute its parameters and any requested neighbor in polylogarithmic time, making the graphs useful as lossless condensers. A complete Lean proof must establish this uniform construction or its negation, while the checked later results do not meet all of its requirements.

title: Optimal PRGs for high-dimensional combinatorial rectangles
importance_reason: An explicit construction meeting a sharp randomness or extremal target would improve a widely used pseudorandom primitive.
formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) and a uniform explicit family
\[
G_{n,d,q}:\{0,1\}^{s(n,d,q)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\]
such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\), and every integer \(1\le q\le n\),
\[
s(n,d,q)\le C\left(\frac nd+q+L(n)\right),
\qquad L(n)=1+\left\lceil\log_2\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil,
\]
and every \(d\)-dimensional combinatorial rectangle \(R\) on \(n\) bits satisfies
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n,d,q)}}[G_{n,d,q}(Y)\in R]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[X\in R]\right|\le 2^{-q}?
\]
The constant and the algorithms are independent of all parameters and of \(R\). This is the source’s seed target \(O(n/d+\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log\log n)\), with dyadic error \(\varepsilon=2^{-q}\).
question_excerpt: The source asks for an explicit generator fooling products of arbitrary tests on \(d\) equal blocks, with seed bounded by a constant times \(n/d+\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log\log n\).
definitions:
Put \(b=n/d\). Split an \(n\)-bit string into its \(d\) consecutive, disjoint blocks \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(d)}\), each with exactly \(b\) bits. A combinatorial rectangle is a product
\[
R=A_1\times\cdots\times A_d,\qquad A_i\subseteq\{0,1\}^{b}.
\]
Every subset \(A_i\), including the empty and full sets, is allowed. Membership in \(R\) means that every block lies in its corresponding set. Equivalently its Boolean indicator is \(\prod_{i=1}^d f_i(x^{(i)})\), where \(f_i\) is any Boolean function of \(b\) bits. No succinctness or computational restriction is imposed on these functions. Under uniform input the membership probability is \(\prod_i |A_i|/2^b\).

\(U_r\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(r\)-bit strings, with the usual singleton convention for \(r=0\). A seed supplies exactly \(s(n,d,q)\) independent fair bits. The displayed error is additive, including for rectangles of very small or zero uniform measure.

Uniform explicitness requires fixed deterministic Turing machines \(S,G\), a constant \(B>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\). On parameters \((1^n,d,q)\), with the latter two integers in binary, \(S\) computes \(s(n,d,q)\); on these parameters and a seed \(y\), \(G\) computes \(G_{n,d,q}(y)\). Both take at most \(Bn^k\) bit operations on valid inputs. Neither receives the sets \(A_i\), nonuniform advice or an oracle.

The dyadic convention loses no part of the source’s error range. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), take \(q=\lceil\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil\). If \(q\le n\), the displayed error is at most \(\varepsilon\), with only a constant additive change in the seed expression. If \(q>n\), the identity generator on \(n\) seed bits has zero error and meets the required bound because \(n<q\). For larger errors use \(q=1\). The nonnegative function \(L\) only regularizes the small-\(n\) logarithms. The dimension may grow with \(n\); no parameter is treated as a fixed hidden constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence assertion. A positive answer must provide the uniform algorithms and establish their running time, the seed bound with one absolute constant, and the additive error for every allowed rectangle and parameter triple. A negative answer must refute this unrestricted construction target. A nearly optimal bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic factor does not suffice. Neither a hitting set nor a generator restricted to one fixed dimension or to special coordinate subsets meets the full assertion. This binary asymptotic target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance.
context:
The word rectangle denotes a Cartesian product of finite sets, not a geometric region with real coordinates. The tests on separate blocks are arbitrary. The generator must coordinate the blocks so that every such product has almost its uniform probability.

The alphabet has \(2^{n/d}\) possible values per coordinate. Thus \(n/d\) is its logarithm, while \(d\) is the number of coordinates. Confusing alphabet size, dimension and total bit length changes the seed target substantially.

For two blocks the source records seed \(n/2+O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\). The open problem asks for one guarantee valid in arbitrarily high dimension, with only a doubly logarithmic contribution from total length in addition to block size and error.

Gopalan and Yehudayoff’s Theorem 1.9 gives seed \(O((\log\log d+\log(M/\varepsilon))\log\log(M/\varepsilon))\) for alphabet size \(M\) and \(d\) coordinates, with logarithms regularized at small parameters. Taking \(M=2^b\) and \(\varepsilon=2^{-q}\) leaves an extra factor of order \(\log(b+q+2)\) beyond the requested additive scale.

Min-wise hashing asks that each element of a selected set have approximately the right probability of receiving the smallest hash value. It is related to rectangles but is a different family of probability tests, with a relative-error requirement. The newer optimal-size hashing construction explicitly discusses the absence of an optimal general rectangle generator in the small-error regime. Its title does not settle this card.

The guarantee is stronger than merely outputting some point in every sufficiently large rectangle. It controls the frequency of membership among all uniformly chosen seeds. Conversely, the card does not require relative accuracy for exponentially rare rectangles; its error is the specified additive quantity.
why: Combinatorial rectangles express simultaneous constraints on separate blocks and occur in pseudorandomness, hashing and communication. The question asks for the full dependence on alphabet size, dimension and error, so removing an extra factor would improve a reusable construction across several parameter regimes.
status_note: The source asks for an absolute-constant optimal seed bound uniformly over block size, dimension and additive error. Gopalan–Yehudayoff’s published construction retains an additional logarithmic factor. The November 2025 revision of the SODA 2026 min-wise hashing paper still distinguishes the missing optimal rectangle generator from its hashing result. No resolution of the full target was found through 16 September 2026 in the bounded review.

working_summary: A combinatorial rectangle requires each of several disjoint input blocks to belong to an arbitrary chosen subset. The generator must preserve every rectangle’s probability to a prescribed additive error. The requested seed is proportional to block length plus logarithmic inverse error plus doubly logarithmic total length. The same polynomial-time algorithm and absolute seed constant must work in every dimension and accuracy regime. Checked near-optimal rectangle generators and recent optimal min-wise hashing results do not establish the full target.

title: Polynomial-time derandomization of randomized \(\mathrm{AC}^0\)
importance_reason: A generator or simulation improvement for a restricted computational model would sharpen a concrete derandomization frontier.
formal: Does \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\) hold for polynomial-time-uniform circuit families? Equivalently, must every Boolean function on finite binary strings that is computed with error at most \(1/3\) on each input by a uniform polynomial-size, constant-depth randomized AND–OR circuit family admit an exact deterministic polynomial-time algorithm?
definitions: A Boolean function here is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}\). A randomized circuit \(C_n(x,r)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output, \(n\) data input bits \(x\), and \(m(n)\) random input bits \(r\). Input nodes may contain these bits, their negations, and constants zero and one. Internal nodes are unbounded-fan-in AND or OR gates. There are no parity, majority, threshold or oracle gates. The depth is the maximum number of internal gates on an input-to-output path, and the size is the number of internal gates. Repeated wires into one gate are omitted. The entire circuit is encoded by an explicit ordered list of nodes, labels and predecessor lists with binary indices. A family witnesses \(f\in\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) if there exist fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(M\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\), \(M\) given \(1^n\) outputs the circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) Turing-machine steps; its depth is at most \(d\), and both its size and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+2)^b\). On every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), independent fair random bits \(R\), uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), satisfy \(\Pr[C_n(x,R)=f(x)]\ge2/3\). The constants, circuit-generation algorithm and random-bit bound may depend on the family but not on \(n\), \(x\) or the random choices. Polynomial-time uniformity is required; merely having a circuit at each length is insufficient. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of the functions computed correctly on every binary input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(K_0(n+2)^{b_0}\) worst-case steps, for some constants \(K_0,b_0\). That machine has no random bits, advice or oracle. It may depend on the randomized family, and its polynomial exponent need not be the same for all families. The target concerns class containment, with no additional demand for an algorithm that takes arbitrary family-generating programs and produces their deterministic simulators. The notation \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), used in the context below, means the analogous polynomial-time-uniform family with no random inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\), or of its negation under the stated uniformity convention. A positive answer must give exact, all-input polynomial-time simulation for every such family. A negative answer requires a total function in uniform \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) with no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Average-case correctness, quasipolynomial simulation, deterministic circuits without a uniform construction, or a failure to build one particular pseudorandom generator is insufficient. A proof of the stronger uniform equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\) also answers the stated containment question, but preservation of constant depth is not required.
context:
The randomized computation is shallow, but its random input can contain polynomially many bits. Trying every possible random string can therefore require far more than polynomial time. The desired simulator need only compute the same final bit; it is not required to retain the shallow circuit shape.

Uniformity is essential. A polynomial-time algorithm must be able to obtain the description for each length from that length alone. An existence theorem for a separately chosen circuit or separately chosen good random strings at every length does not provide such an algorithm.

Vadhan’s Definition 7.26 explicitly permits polynomial-time uniform construction. Open Problem 7.31 asks for the stronger equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\), or at least containment in \(\mathrm P\). This card selects the latter, already stated alternative, matching its original polynomial-time title.

The source’s Corollary 7.30 gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time simulation: time \(2^{(\log(n+2))^{O(1)}}\), with constants depending on the fixed family. It also records a quasipolynomial-size constant-depth simulation. Neither guarantee supplies polynomial time.

Shaltiel’s work gives uniform weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, where the deterministic result is correct on most inputs. It also notes that the nonuniform randomized and deterministic constant-depth classes coincide. Those statements leave this card’s simultaneous uniformity and all-input correctness requirement unresolved.

Lyu’s 2022 Theorem 1 constructs generators fooling depth-\(d\), size-\(S\) circuits within error \(\varepsilon\), with seed length \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\), for fixed \(d\) and \(S\) large enough. Here “fooling” means that every circuit’s acceptance probability changes by at most \(\varepsilon\). This is a substantial quantitative improvement, but its general fixed-depth seed bound is not \(O(\log S)\).

A pseudorandom generator is a useful comparison point, but its optimal construction is a separate, stronger-looking formulation. This question permits any deterministic simulator meeting the stated time and correctness requirements, without prescribing a generator or any other proof method.
why: Constant-depth AND–OR circuits are a central restricted model for which strong lower bounds are known, yet fully eliminating their randomness in uniform polynomial time remains a distinct challenge. The question tests whether those structural restrictions suffice to remove random choices while allowing a much more flexible deterministic simulator.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly poses the polynomial-time-uniform containment. The checked later generator and earlier weak-derandomization results have different quantitative or correctness guarantees. No proof or refutation of the stated containment was found in the bounded search; this does not certify exhaustive current openness.

Each randomized circuit must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input. A single polynomial-time procedure constructs the family’s circuit descriptions from the input length. The deterministic simulator may use arbitrary polynomial-time computation and need not remain a constant-depth circuit. Quasipolynomial simulation, correctness on most inputs and nonuniform deterministic circuits do not meet the full target.

title: Nontrivial PRGs for logarithmic-degree binary polynomials
importance_reason: A generator or simulation improvement for a restricted computational model would sharpen a concrete derandomization frontier.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform explicit generator family
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{s(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\]
and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\),
\[
s(n)\le n-1
\]
and every polynomial \(p:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2\) of total degree at most \(d(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\) satisfies
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n)}}[p(G_n(Y))=1]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[p(X)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}?
\]
The same generator must fool all such polynomials at that length. The seed saving is required at every sufficiently large length, not merely infinitely often.
question_excerpt: The source asks for a polynomial-time explicit generator for binary polynomials of logarithmic degree that uses fewer random bits than its output. The user fixed the benchmark to one saved bit eventually, at error \(1/10\).
definitions:
\(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) is the field with addition modulo two and ordinary bit multiplication. On Boolean inputs every polynomial has a unique multilinear representation
\[
p(x)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|S|\le d(n)}}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,
\qquad a_S\in\mathbb F_2,
\]
where the empty product is one and the sum is computed modulo two. The test class consists of all coefficient choices in this display, including the zero and constant polynomials. There is no bound on the number of nonzero monomials or on the size of a circuit computing the test. “Degree” is the largest monomial size in this multilinear representation; the zero polynomial is included by convention.

\(U_r\) is uniform on the \(r\)-bit strings, also allowing \(r=0\). The input bits and polynomial values are identified with field elements. Because a test has two possible outputs, the displayed absolute difference is also the total-variation distance between its two output distributions.

Uniform explicitness means that fixed deterministic Turing machines \(S,G\) compute \(s(n)\) from \(1^n\), and \(G_n(y)\) from \((1^n,y)\), respectively, in at most \(Cn^k\) bit operations for some fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\). The polynomial \(p\) is not an input. Neither machine receives advice or an oracle, and the generator has no random bits beyond its seed. The machines and seed lengths are defined for every \(n\ge2\); the probability and saving requirements apply for \(n\ge n_0\).

The threshold \(n_0\), running-time constants and machines are existentially quantified once for the whole family. Saving at least one bit is the user-selected meaning of nontrivial. It does not impose \(s(n)=o(n)\) or a bound \(n^{1-\delta}\) with fixed \(\delta>0\). Unused seed bits may be added, so a shorter qualifying seed may equivalently be padded to length \(n-1\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this existence assertion. A positive answer must specify the uniform algorithms and a threshold, and prove the running time, seed saving and error simultaneously for every allowed polynomial at every sufficiently large length. A negative answer must rule out the full family of such algorithms, not just sums of small-bias generators or another selected template. This binary question has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Smaller constant degrees, sparse polynomials, larger fields, or infinitely many successful lengths do not meet the stated target.
context:
Linear tests are parities of subsets of the input bits. Higher-degree tests can also multiply bits before taking their parity. The degree bounds how many distinct variables appear in one monomial, while the number of monomials can still be very large.

Viola’s construction has seed \(O(d\log n+d\,2^d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) in the displayed analysis. For fixed degree and error this is logarithmic in \(n\). At \(d=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\), the exponential degree term prevents that guarantee from proving even a one-bit saving. This is a limitation of the bound, not a general lower bound on generators.

The 2020 fractional-generator analysis provides a different construction while retaining exponential dependence on the degree. Its comparison with the earlier bound highlights the same logarithmic-degree obstruction. It does not prove impossibility beyond that regime.

Over larger finite fields the relationship between degree and field size is different. The February 2026 paper reduces the field size needed for an optimal-seed construction, but retains a sufficiently large characteristic assumption. Since this card fixes characteristic two, that theorem does not provide a solution.

A distribution supported on fewer than all bit strings can still approximate every test in a restricted class. The hard part here is producing such a distribution uniformly in polynomial time with a proof covering every logarithmic-degree polynomial. A separate generator chosen for each individual test would have a different quantifier order.

The source’s qualitative word “nontrivial” allows several stronger interpretations. This card records the user’s least-demanding seed-saving choice explicitly, so future progress can be assessed against one definite statement rather than a moving asymptotic target.
why: Binary polynomial tests describe algebraic correlations of increasing order. At logarithmic degree the standard seed bounds stop giving a guaranteed saving, even though they are very effective at fixed degree. Resolving the selected minimal saving would cross that precise boundary without assuming the much stronger goal of a polylogarithmic seed.
status_note: The source leaves “nontrivial” quantitative conventions unspecified. On 16 September 2026 the user selected saving at least one bit at error 0.1 in uniform polynomial time. The checked binary-field constructions do not achieve that guarantee at degree floor(log2 n). The February 2026 optimal-seed theorem concerns fields of sufficiently large characteristic, not GF(2). No resolution of this precise selected target was found in the bounded review.

working_summary: The tests are all binary polynomials of degree at most the floor of log₂ n, without a sparsity restriction. One uniform polynomial-time generator must preserve every test’s output probability within one tenth. The user-selected goal is to save at least one random bit at every sufficiently large output length. Known binary-field constructions in the checked sources retain exponential dependence on degree. The 2026 optimal-seed construction over larger-characteristic fields does not settle this binary-field target.

title: Sublinear-seed generators for AC0 with parity gates
importance_reason: A generator or simulation improvement for a restricted computational model would sharpen a concrete derandomization frontier.
formal:
Do there exist two deterministic multitape Turing machines \(R,G\) with the following properties? For all integers \(d,a,n\ge1\), the machine \(R(1^n,1^d,1^a)\) outputs an integer \(r(n,d,a)\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and, for each seed \(z\in\{0,1\}^{r(n,d,a)}\), the machine \(G(1^n,1^d,1^a,z)\) outputs a string \(G_{n,d,a}(z)\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). For each fixed pair \(d,a\), both computations take at most \(K_{d,a}(n+1)^{b_{d,a}}\) bit steps for some constant \(K_{d,a}>0\) and integer \(b_{d,a}\ge1\), uniformly over all seeds. The seed length satisfies
\[
\forall d,a\ge1\ \forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:
\qquad r(n,d,a)\le\eta n.
\]
For every \(n,d,a\ge1\) and every circuit \(C\) on \(n\) input variables with depth at most \(d\), at most \(n^a\) gates, and the gate types defined below, require
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{r(n,d,a)}}[C(G_{n,d,a}(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}.
\]
Here \(U_t\) is the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{t}\). The constant distinguishing error is the documented interpretation of the source question.
definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output. Each input node is labeled by a literal \(x_i\) or \(1-x_i\), for \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), or by a constant \(0\) or \(1\). Every other node is an AND, OR or PARITY gate with a positive, finite, unrestricted number of incoming wires. A PARITY gate outputs the sum of its incoming Boolean values modulo two. Gates and inputs may have unrestricted fan-out, and variables may be used repeatedly. The size counts AND, OR and PARITY gates, including the output if it is a gate, but not the literal or constant nodes. Depth is the maximum number of gates on a path from an input node to the output; a literal or constant output has depth zero. There is no restriction on the number, placement or successive layers of parity gates beyond the total size and depth bounds. The circuit class is nonuniform: the guarantee is for every individual circuit, with no requirement that its description be produced by an algorithm.

The generators receive unary \(n,d,a\), separated by delimiters, and \(G\) also receives the seed as an ordinary binary string. The seed-length machine \(R\) writes \(r(n,d,a)\) in binary. There is one finite program for \(R\) and one for \(G\), shared by every parameter triple; choosing a separate program or advice string for each output length is not allowed. All input reading, seed-length computation, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing of all \(n\) output bits are charged in the bit-cost bound. There is no oracle, advice or additional randomness. The polynomial runtime constants may depend on the fixed circuit depth \(d\) and size exponent \(a\), but not on \(n\), the seed or the particular circuit. The machines are not given a circuit description.

The seed condition is little-\(o\) for each fixed \(d,a\): the ratio \(r(n,d,a)/n\) tends to zero with no prescribed rate. It does not demand a bound \(n^{1-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), nor a bound uniform when \(d\) or \(a\) grows with \(n\). The probability spaces in the displayed guarantee consist solely of the independent uniform choices indicated in their respective experiments. The seed is not exposed to the circuit. The required error is the fixed rational number \(1/10\), rather than an error tending to zero or an additional small-error parameter.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of the two finite algorithms, their polynomial bit-cost bounds for each fixed depth and size exponent, the entire little-o seed guarantee and the fooling inequality for every permitted circuit, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of this proposition. A conditional construction, a nonuniform existence argument, a construction requiring superpolynomial time for fixed depth and size exponent, or guarantees only for a restricted arrangement or number of parity gates do not settle this target.
context:
Open Problem 4.3.1 asks for an explicit sublinear-seed generator for constant-depth polynomial-size circuits with parity gates. The source leaves the error unspecified in that sentence; its immediately preceding discussion identifies the constant-error regime. This card fixes error 1/10 as an explicit interpretation and does not claim an inverse-polynomial-error version. Definition 1.4.1 and Section 1.4.1 supply full-output polynomial-time computation and a single uniform generator across parameter values.

The 2013 construction of Fefferman, Shaltiel, Umans and Viola uses seed length \(n-n/(\log n)^c\) for an appropriate constant \(c\), with error tending to zero against the relevant bounded-depth circuits. Although this saves many random bits, its seed-to-output ratio tends to one, so it does not satisfy the present little-\(o\) target.

The 2025 extractor-based results treat several structured models, including circuits with a restricted budget of symmetric gates. Parity is a symmetric operation, but those restrictions are not the unrestricted polynomial-size parity-gate model of this card.

The February 2026 optimal-seed result for polynomials imposes sufficiently large field size and characteristic. Its theorem does not cover the binary field, and the paper separately identifies the binary-field regime as a major remaining challenge; it is not a resolution for these Boolean circuits.
why: This asks whether an explicit generator can save an asymptotically complete fraction of the random bits against shallow circuits that freely combine Boolean operations and parity. It isolates a substantial gap between lower bounds for a well-studied circuit class and unconditional, efficiently generated pseudorandomness for that same class.
status_note: Source-open under the explicitly documented constant-error interpretation. Hatami–Hoza revision 2 of 14 April 2023 states the sublinear-seed challenge; its numbered sentence omits an error value, and this card selects error 1/10 from the surrounding constant-error setting. The individual source review and bounded later-work check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Restricted-gate and large-field results do not establish this target; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.

working_summary: These shallow Boolean circuits may combine AND, OR and parity gates throughout the circuit, with arbitrary reuse of input variables. The question asks for one uniform generator that fools every circuit of each fixed depth and polynomial size with distinguishing error at most one tenth. The generator must write all its output bits in polynomial time and use a seed whose length divided by the output length tends to zero. The fixed error is an explicit interpretation of the source’s constant-error discussion because the numbered question does not specify an error value. Known linear-seed savings and generators for restricted gate patterns or large-field polynomials do not meet this unrestricted parity-circuit target.

title: Universal traversal sequences under arbitrary labels
importance_reason: A focused structural or construction-efficiency question within pseudorandomness, with less general scope than eliminating randomness from an entire complexity class.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(C,b\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n,d\ge1\), on input \((1^n,1^d)\) the algorithm outputs in at most \(C(n+d+2)^b\) steps a word \(w=w_1\cdots w_T\in[d]^T\), with \(T\le C(n+d+2)^b\), satisfying the following universal property? For every connected undirected \(d\)-regular port-labeled multigraph on \(n\) vertices in the convention below and every starting vertex \(s\), the walk that successively takes absolute port numbers \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) visits all vertices.
definitions:
Use \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A port-labeled multigraph is specified mathematically by a map \(h:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\). The \(d\) ports at each vertex are distinct local labels; different ports may lead to the same neighbor. Undirectedness means \[ \forall u,v\in[n]:\quad |\{i:h(u,i)=v\}|=|\{j:h(v,j)=u\}|.\] This represents equal directed multiplicities in opposite directions. A self-loop is allowed and consumes one port, following the textbook’s directed-edge convention. A graph is connected when any two vertices are joined by a finite walk through its ports. No compatibility between the port numbers at opposite ends of an edge is imposed.

formal: Does the uniform-distribution heuristic assumption \[\forall L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \forall k\ge1\ \exists A_{L,k}\in\mathrm P\ \exists N_{L,k}\ \forall n\ge N_{L,k},\quad \Pr_{x\sim U_n}[A_{L,k}(x)\ne\mathbf1_L(x)]\le n^{-k}\] imply \[\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname{Perm}\text{ has no polynomial-size arithmetic circuits over }\mathbb Z\] in the constant-free arithmetic-circuit model below?
definitions: A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\); \(U_n\) is uniform on length-\(n\) binary strings. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial worst-case time on every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input and independent fair coins. Each \(A_{L,k}\) is one deterministic Turing machine with no advice and a worst-case polynomial time bound; its code, exponent and sufficiently-large-length threshold may depend on \(L,k\). No joint polynomial dependence on \(k\) is required. The displayed error is an input fraction at every sufficiently large length, not a probability over simulation coins. NEXP consists of languages recognized by nondeterministic Turing machines in time \(2^{n^a}\) for some fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allowing constant factors and finitely many small lengths. P/poly consists of languages whose length-\(n\) characteristic functions have polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no uniformity between lengths. Boolean circuits are finite acyclic networks of fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and constants, with one output. Circuit size is the length of an explicit binary gate-and-wire encoding. For \(m\ge1\), \(\operatorname{Perm}_m(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\prod_{i=1}^m X_{i,\pi(i)}\) is a formal polynomial in \(m^2\) indeterminates, where \(S_m\) is the set of permutations of \([m]\). Arithmetic circuits use fan-in-two addition, subtraction and multiplication, variable leaves and only the constants 0 and 1; there are no divisions or other field constants. They must compute the permanent as a formal polynomial over the integers, not merely on Boolean matrices. Polynomial size means one polynomial bound in \(m\) for all sufficiently large dimensions; the individual circuits need not be uniformly constructible. Thus a non-polynomial circuit conclusion excludes every fixed polynomial bound, rather than demanding an eventual exponential lower bound. The assertion is an ordinary logical implication, with no restriction to a black-box proof.

title: Pseudodeterministic construction of primes at every length
importance_reason: A foundational explicit-construction challenge and concrete test of pseudodeterministic search, with a major infinitely-often theorem leaving a consequential uniform length-coverage gap. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a constant \(c\), and a sequence of primes \((p_{n})_{n\geq2}\), with \(2^{n-1}\leq p_{n}<2^{n}\), such that \(A\) runs in time \(O(n^{c})\) on input \(1^{n}\) and \[\Pr[A(1^{n})=p_{n}]\geq 2/3\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq2?\]
question_excerpt: In the context of polynomial time pseudo-determinism, there are many fundamental problems with polynomial time randomized algorithms where the existence of pseudodeterministic polynomial time algorithms […]
definitions:
The input \(1^{n}\) is unary: a string of \(n\) copies of the symbol 1. The output is the ordinary binary representation of an integer. An \(n\)-bit prime is an integer \(p\) in \([2^{n-1},2^{n})\) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \(p\). The domain begins at \(n=2\), since there is no one-bit prime.

The machine is a single classical probabilistic Turing machine, with independent unbiased random bits and a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every random tape. There is no advice depending on \(n\), precomputed table of primes, oracle, or free preprocessing. All computation, including any primality tests, counts toward its time bound.

Pseudodeterminism means that for each fixed length there is one fixed prime \(p_{n}\) returned with the stated probability across independent executions. The prime may depend on the algorithm and on \(n\), but not on the execution’s random bits. It need not be the smallest \(n\)-bit prime or a prime prescribed in advance. The remaining probability mass may produce a failure symbol, another prime, or an invalid output.

The guarantee is required at every length. Success on infinitely many unbounded lengths alone does not suffice. A guarantee for all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, since finitely many shorter lengths can be handled by a fixed finite part of the algorithm.

The constant success probability is the usual bounded-error convention for pseudodeterminism. Independent repetitions followed by a majority output can amplify concentration on the same canonical prime with polynomial overhead. Merely finding some prime with high probability, while different runs usually return different primes, does not meet the requirement.

The source lists several distinct search tasks. This card explicitly selects prime generation as its main target; it does not assert that solving it is equivalent to making every randomized search problem pseudodeterministic.

title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
importance_reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.
focus_reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose input-size exponent is constant while a computable multiplier absorbs all dependence on k. Polynomial time separately for each fixed k does not establish that uniform bound. Clique completeness makes the question equivalent to FPT equalling W[1]. title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
importance_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
focus_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.
why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.
status_note: The original sources and the July 2026 ICALP paper continue to use ETH as an unproved hypothesis. The optimal-rate definition and cited algorithmic upper bound were checked against the full relevant source passages. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; bounded searches do not independently verify the cited proofs or exhaust all later literature.

working_summary: ETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rate for 3-SAT is strictly positive. The exponential parameter is the number of distinct variables, while polynomial factors account for the complete encoded input. One positive rate must obstruct every algorithm, and refutation permits different algorithms for arbitrarily small positive rates. Known exponential-time algorithms provide upper bounds but no positive lower bound on the optimum. title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
importance_reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.
formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+L)^c.\]
Here \(L\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96 and the existing editorial choice of complete symmetric TSP with arbitrary nonnegative binary integer weights, bounded-error classical randomization, a worst-case clock and polynomial bit-length overhead. Retains the random-access model with word length proportional to n+log(L), so the statement does not silently replace exponential-space random access by a slower sequential machine. Stoian’s 2024 question concerns the prefactor of the historical bound; the broader fixed-base question is explicitly discussed as open in Dallant–Kozma and the July 2026 follow-up.
definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(L\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(L+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,L\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+L\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(L\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
context:
In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.
why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

Recent improvements concern prefactors, structurally restricted weight sets, interior time-space tradeoffs, or quantum algorithms. Framework and local-search lower bounds do not prove the full negation. No fixed-base classical algorithm with polynomial dependence solely on arbitrary input bit length was found in the bounded search; abstract-only checks and proof-review limits are recorded separately.

This question seeks a uniform classical algorithm with a fixed exponential time base below two. Weights are arbitrary nonnegative integers written in binary, and only polynomial dependence on their total encoding length is allowed. Bounded-error randomization and exponential memory are permitted, but every execution must satisfy the stated worst-case clock. Recent prefactor, structured-weight, time-space and quantum improvements do not establish the full classical guarantee.

title: Set Cover conjecture
importance_reason: One of the few central exact-algorithm barriers not simply interchangeable with SAT hypotheses.
formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.
context:
A subset dynamic program solves the problem in \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\) time. The target asks whether the base two can be reduced by a constant independent of the maximum allowed set size. Polynomial factors are explicitly permitted and may grow with that fixed size bound.

The family is given explicitly and each set has at most d elements. This is distinct from requiring exactly d elements, requiring a partition into disjoint sets, or bounding how many sets contain each element. The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

Cygan and coauthors use the Set Cover assumption for tight conditional bounds on several exact algorithms. Their work does not prove that the ordinary Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this Set Cover conjecture.

Björklund and Kaski prove that Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture would yield a randomized sub-two-base algorithm and hence refute SCC. Pratt strengthens the conditional algorithm. These are incompatibility and conditional-algorithm theorems, not unconditional resolutions of either conjecture.
why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.
status_note: The 2024 SCC formulation and both STOC 2024 asymptotic-rank connections were checked on 2026-09-14, together with a bounded later-work search. The rank-based algorithms are conditional; no unconditional proof or refutation of the selected randomized SCC was identified.
