title: FPT approximation of twin-width
importance_reason: A central algorithmic access problem for a major graph-width parameter, with consequences for the applicability of logical algorithms on bounded twin-width classes.
formal:
Do there exist total computable functions \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) and \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every nonempty finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices and every integer \(k\ge0\), the machine halts within
\[
 f(k)(n+1)^c
\]
bit operations and either correctly reports \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\), or outputs a contraction sequence of \(G\) of width at most \(g(k)\)? Only the graph and \(k\) are supplied, with no helpful vertex order, decomposition or contraction sequence.
question_excerpt: The first project question asks for an algorithm which, given a graph and k, runs in fixed-parameter time, correctly declares twin-width greater than k, or constructs a sequence whose width depends only on k. The card makes computability, input representation and the contraction certificate explicit.
definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The graph has vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), and is given by its symmetric \(n\times n\) Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. The input also includes \(n\) and \(k\) in binary. Arbitrary disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. Vertex labels are just part of the explicit representation and carry no promise about a useful ordering.

A partition of \(V\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets, called parts, whose union is \(V\). Two distinct parts \(X,Y\) form a mixed pair if there exist \(x,x'\in X\) and \(y,y'\in Y\) such that \(\{x,y\}\) is an edge of the original graph and \(\{x',y'\}\) is not. The two witness pairs need not have distinct endpoints within each part. A pair is not mixed when all possible cross pairs are edges, or when none are edges. Relations are always evaluated in the original graph.

For a partition \(\mathcal P\) and part \(X\in\mathcal P\), its red degree is
\[
 r_{\mathcal P}(X)=
 |\{Y\in\mathcal P\setminus\{X\}:(X,Y)\text{ is mixed}\}|.
\]
This counts mixed neighboring parts, not individual edges or vertices. Adjacency inside a part does not contribute to its red degree.

A contraction sequence is a list of partitions \(\mathcal P_n,\mathcal P_{n-1},\ldots,\mathcal P_1\). The first partition consists of all singleton vertices and the last is \(\{V\}\). Each \(\mathcal P_{j-1}\) is obtained from \(\mathcal P_j\) by merging exactly two distinct parts and leaving the others unchanged. The merged parts need not be adjacent. The width of a sequence is
\[
 \max_{1\le j\le n}\ \max_{X\in\mathcal P_j} r_{\mathcal P_j}(X).
\]
The twin-width \(\operatorname{tww}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such sequences. In particular, a one-vertex graph has width zero and its sequence has no merge steps.

The output encodes the \(n-1\) merges explicitly. Initially labels \(1,\ldots,n\) refer to singleton parts. At step \(t\), two distinct currently active labels are listed, their parts are replaced by their union, and the new part receives label \(n+t\). This list determines every partition and is a complete certificate, not just an upper-bound number or a promise that a sequence exists.

The two permitted outputs have the following meaning on every input. If the output is the rejection symbol, then \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\) must be true. If the output is a merge list, that list must always be a valid complete sequence of width at most \(g(k)\). Consequently, when \(\operatorname{tww}(G)\le k\) the machine must return a bounded-width sequence. When \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\), either output is allowed if its respective guarantee is true. There is no input promise that the parameter is an actual upper bound.

The deterministic machine has one finite program independent of \(k,n,G\), no advice and no oracle. The running time counts all bit-level computation, reading the binary parameter and the graph, constructing auxiliary information, and writing the output. The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are fixed total computable functions; their growth is unrestricted and may absorb the cost of reading the parameter. They depend only on \(k\), while the exponent \(c\) is a single constant independent of \(k\). No separate efficient evaluation bound on these functions is imposed, but any evaluation performed by \(A\) must fit the total running-time bound.

This is a fixed-parameter approximation with arbitrary computable width loss, not a specified multiplicative approximation ratio. A bound with a polynomial exponent depending on \(k\), such as \(n^{h(k)}\), is not the required fixed-parameter running time. Dependence on another graph parameter is insufficient unless it is bounded by a function of the supplied \(k\) on the inputs in question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(A,f,g,c\) exist, including total computability of the functions, all-input termination, the running-time bound and both output guarantees, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A negative answer must exclude all total computable width-loss functions and all fixed-parameter running-time bounds in the stated deterministic model. NP-hardness of exact recognition at a fixed twin-width, or a lower bound for a fixed approximation ratio, is not by itself such a negation: the card permits arbitrarily large computable \(g(k)\). A conditional result under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved assumption does not unconditionally decide the target.

An algorithm receiving a helpful ordering or a contraction sequence, restricted to one fixed width or a special graph class, or running in fixed-parameter time for a different unbounded structural parameter does not settle the whole statement without a proved extension.
context:
The project question permits any computable loss in output width. The challenge is already to obtain a bounded-width certificate with the required parameter dependence, before optimizing a numerical approximation ratio.

Twin-width-one recognition can construct the needed sequence in linear time under the source representation. This establishes a special case while the same paper explicitly leaves general approximation open.

Exact recognition is NP-hard already at a small fixed width. That fact obstructs exact algorithms under the usual complexity assumption but does not rule out the arbitrarily large width loss allowed here.

The 2026 work obtains approximation in time parameterized by treedepth and exact computation in time parameterized by vertex integrity. Its introduction still identifies approximation parameterized by twin-width itself as open; the theorem statements retain the stronger structural runtime parameters.
why: Many algorithms exploiting twin-width need a low-width contraction sequence as part of their input. Finding such a certificate from an ordinary graph would make these methods applicable without requiring the structural witness in advance.

The desired algorithm receives a graph and a proposed width bound without an accompanying structural certificate. It must either reject that bound correctly or return a complete merge sequence whose width is bounded by a computable function of the parameter. title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
importance_reason: A central graph-cut kernelization problem: whether arbitrarily large instances can be compressed to size polynomial in the edge-deletion budget.
formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.
context:
The source contrasts polynomial kernels for each fixed terminal count with the open case of arbitrary terminal sets. For a bound \(|T|\le s\), the earlier kernel has a size exponent depending on \(s\); that dependence is exactly what the present question must avoid.

Wahlström proves a randomized quasipolynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut in the revised 2021 manuscript, with size \(k^{O(\log^3 k)}\) in the displayed bounds. The same work distinguishes a smaller nonconstructive mimicking-network bound from the network size achievable by randomized polynomial-time preprocessing.

The source’s mimicking networks preserve a richer family of terminal cut values. The benchmark asks only for an equivalent Edge Multiway Cut decision instance, so a solution does not need to construct such a stronger universal network.

The 2025 MFCS paper obtains deterministic kernels using quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several problems whose randomized polynomial kernels were already known. It explicitly treats Multiway Cut with deletable terminals and separately mentions quasipolynomial-size Edge Multiway Cut kernels. Neither changing the deletion model nor allowing more preprocessing time resolves this card.
why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.
status_note: The full March 2021 Wahlström revision and its kernelization corollaries were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search through 2026 and inspection of the 2025 MFCS comparison found no polynomial-size randomized kernel for the arbitrary-terminal edge-deletion problem. The status remains source-open; the check does not claim exhaustive literature coverage.
progress: 2012: Kratsch and Wahlström obtain polynomial kernels for Multiway Cut with a fixed number of terminals; the 2021 source states the dependence on that fixed number. | 2021-03: Wahlström’s revised full manuscript establishes randomized polynomial-time construction of quasipolynomial-size multicut-mimicking networks and, as a consequence, a randomized quasipolynomial Edge Multiway Cut kernel. | 2025-08-20: Gurjar and coauthors publish quasipolynomial-time derandomization of several matroid-based kernels, distinguishing those results from the unrestricted Edge Multiway Cut size question.
working_summary: Edge Multiway Cut removes a small number of edges so that no two designated terminals remain connected. The question asks whether polynomial-time preprocessing can reduce any instance to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in the deletion budget alone. The number of terminals is unrestricted, and the size exponent must not depend on it. Randomized preprocessing is allowed with a per-instance equivalence guarantee of at least two thirds. Known fixed-terminal kernels and quasipolynomial-size kernels leave the unrestricted polynomial-size target open in the checked sources.

title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
importance_reason: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(L\) is the total binary input length?
definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.
context:
Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.
why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The SODA 2026 paper retains the worst-case classical exponential question; the August 2026 preprint improves a quantum bound instead. No classical fixed-saving worst-case algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this model was located. The new quantum proof was not independently verified.

The question asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent with polynomial dependence on binary input length. Bounded-error classical randomization is allowed, with no random-instance promise. Quantum, pseudopolynomial and polynomial-factor improvements do not establish this fixed exponent saving.

title: Strictness of the W-hierarchy
importance_reason: A foundational structural conjecture for parameterized complexity, interpreting the distinction between canonical complete problems and every higher level of the W-hierarchy.
formal:
Is the \(W\)-hierarchy strict at every positive level?
\[
\forall\,t\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad
W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1].
\]
The classes use uniform deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions and exact-weight satisfiability of bounded-depth Boolean circuits, as defined below. Equivalently, for every \(t\ge1\), is there a parameterized decision problem in \(W[t+1]\) that does not belong to \(W[t]\)?
question_excerpt: The textbook states the expectation that every positive level of the W-hierarchy differs from its next level. It illustrates the first pair with Independent Set and Dominating Set.
definitions:
A parameterized decision problem is a set \(P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\mathbb N\). An input is a finite binary string \(x\) together with a nonnegative integer \(k\), its parameter. The input length \(L\) includes both \(x\) and the binary encoding of \(k\), with delimiters. Membership is an exact yes/no question.

A fixed-parameter many-one reduction from \(P\) to \(Q\) is one uniform deterministic algorithm \(R\), total computable functions \(f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that \(R(x,k)\) halts in at most \(f(k)(L+1)^c\) steps and outputs a pair \((y,\ell)\) satisfying
\[
(x,k)\in P\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (y,\ell)\in Q,
\qquad \ell\le g(k).
\]
The algorithm, functions and exponent are fixed for the reduction; in particular, \(c\) cannot grow with \(k\). Functions \(f,g\) may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Time is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine over fixed finite alphabets, counting input access, arithmetic and output writing. No random bits, length-dependent advice or oracle are available. This is a single-output reduction, not an adaptive sequence of queries to \(Q\).

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with at least one input node and a designated output node of outdegree zero. Nodes of indegree zero are distinct Boolean input variables. Each other node is either a NOT gate of indegree one or an AND or OR gate of indegree at least two, with the usual Boolean semantics. Gates have unrestricted fan-out. A gate is large if its indegree exceeds two. The depth of the circuit is the maximum number of edges on a path from an input node to the designated output. Its weft is the maximum number of large gates on such a path. Unused input nodes are allowed and still count among the input variables.

For an explicit encoding, order all \(N\) nodes topologically, put the \(n\) input nodes first, and give the integers \(n,N\) and the output-node index, followed by each remaining gate's type, indegree and list of distinct predecessor indices. Predecessors must have smaller indices. Encode each integer \(u\ge0\) by \(1^{h}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary representation of \(u+1\) and \(h=|w|\); encode gate types NOT, AND, OR by integers \(1,2,3\). All listed integers use this code, and there are no trailing bits. Invalid encodings are no-instances in the circuit problems below.

For fixed integers \(t,d\ge1\), let \(\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\) be the parameterized problem consisting of pairs \((C,k)\) where \(C\) is an encoded circuit of weft at most \(t\) and depth at most \(d\), and some assignment to its input nodes has exactly \(k\) ones and makes its output one. The parameter is \(k\) alone. Circuits exceeding either structural bound, or having fewer than \(k\) input nodes, are no-instances.

Define
\[
W[t]=\{P:\ \exists\,d\ge1\text{ such that }P
\text{ has a fixed-parameter many-one reduction to }
\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\}.
\]
The integer \(d\) may depend on the problem \(P\) and level \(t\), but it is a fixed constant independent of the input and its parameter. The reduction may also depend on \(P,t,d\). This quantifier does not allow depth growing as a function of \(k\).

The inclusions \(W[t]\subseteq W[t+1]\) follow directly from the weft bounds. Strict inclusion means that at least one problem belongs to the larger class and not the smaller one. The formal target quantifies over all fixed positive integers \(t\); it does not require an algorithm that constructs witnesses from \(t\).

For comparison, FPT consists of parameterized problems decidable within \(f(k)(L+1)^c\) deterministic time for some computable \(f\) and constant \(c\). Separating FPT from \(W[1]\) is a distinct statement and does not by itself establish the requested adjacent-level separations.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1]\) for every integer \(t\ge1\), with the classes and reductions above; or supply a complete Lean-checked refutation, proving \(W[t]=W[t+1]\) for at least one particular \(t\ge1\). A proof for just finitely many strict inclusions does not establish the universal positive answer. Completeness or hardness for one of these classes, an oracle-relative separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle the target. No claim about collapse of all other levels is required for a negative answer.
context:
With the desired solution size as parameter, Independent Set is \(W[1]\)-complete and Dominating Set is \(W[2]\)-complete. The source gives a reduction from the former to the latter. A reduction in the reverse direction would identify these two classes.

For higher levels, the source supplies complete weighted satisfiability problems using alternating layers of conjunctions and disjunctions. Completeness describes their position in the hierarchy without proving that the positions are distinct.

The unrestricted target is stronger in scope than separating one chosen pair. It asks whether every adjacent positive pair differs, while leaving the separate FPT boundary to its own question.

Bottesch constructs, for each level, a suitable oracle separating the relevant adjacent relativized classes. The oracle may depend on the level, and such results do not prove a separation without an oracle.
why: Parameterized completeness places many natural problems into different levels of a common hierarchy, but a level label alone does not prove a difference in computational power. Establishing strictness would show that these levels capture distinct forms of parameterized intractability. An equality would instead identify a new general reduction principle connecting problems currently treated as having different complexity.
status_note: The textbook explicitly conjectures strictness at every positive adjacent level. Later oracle constructions provide only relativized evidence and do not prove the unrelativized conjecture. No proof or counterexample to the full target was found in the bounded review through 2026-09-17.

working_summary: The W-hierarchy groups parameterized decision problems by reductions to exact-weight satisfiability for restricted Boolean circuits. The question asks whether each positive level is strictly contained in the next. The circuit depth is fixed for each target problem, and reductions may spend arbitrary computable time in the parameter times a fixed polynomial in input length. Independent Set and Dominating Set illustrate the first two levels, whose known completeness does not itself separate them. A solution must prove all adjacent separations or prove equality at one particular adjacent pair; oracle-based evidence is insufficient.

title: General Formula-SAT with a fixed exponential saving
importance_reason: A fixed saving for arbitrary Boolean formulas would substantially improve a basic NP-complete search problem and refute deterministic SETH, going beyond algorithms exploiting bounded width, density or small formula size.
formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), constants \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that every explicitly given Boolean formula \(F\) over AND, OR and NOT is correctly decided for satisfiability in at most
\[
K\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}\bigl(L(F)+1\bigr)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(n(F)\) is the number of distinct variables occurring in \(F\), \(L(F)\) is its full binary encoding length, and no restriction is placed on its size or depth. The same algorithm, positive saving and constants must work for every formula.
question_excerpt: Fortnow describes general formula satisfiability as lacking algorithms that substantially improve exhaustive assignment search, unlike some restricted satisfiability problems. The passage does not specify a saving. This card adopts a deterministic fixed positive exponential saving with a polynomial factor in the full formula encoding length as an explicit editorial target.
definitions:
A Boolean formula is a finite rooted ordered tree. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or one of the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). An internal node is a unary NOT gate or a binary AND or OR gate. Each nonroot node has exactly one parent; subexpressions are supplied in full and cannot be shared by pointers as in a circuit. The same variable may label any number of different leaves. Every declared variable must occur, so \(n\) counts distinct variables rather than leaves, literal occurrences, gates or input bits. If no variable occurs, \(n=0\). Negations may appear anywhere, with the usual Boolean semantics. No monotonicity, bounded occurrence, normal-form, clause-width, density, balancing or satisfying-assignment promise is imposed.

An assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\) determines every leaf value and then the root value by the gate operations. The formula is satisfiable exactly when at least one assignment gives root value one. The output is this yes/no bit. Finding an assignment or counting assignments is not required. Constants and formulas that do not use any variable are included.

For a fixed explicit encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\) for an integer \(a\ge0\) be \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary representation of \(a+1\), with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Begin with \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), then traverse the tree in preorder. Each node has a three-bit tag specifying constant zero, constant one, variable, NOT, AND or OR. A variable tag is followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\), \(1\le i\le n\); other tags determine their arity and have no extra payload. There must be exactly one complete tree, no unused tags or trailing bits, and all declared variables must occur. The full length of this encoding is \(L(F)\). This includes every copy of a repeated subexpression. A succinct generator, truth-table oracle or circuit with shared gates is not an alternative input encoding.

The algorithm is one fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and finite tape alphabets. One transition reads or writes only the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell; its cost is one bit step up to a fixed machine-dependent factor. It halts on every input, rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their length and returns the exact satisfiability answer for every valid formula. Parsing, input access, preprocessing and internal computation are included in the runtime. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, quantum computation or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. No separate workspace restriction is imposed.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(\varepsilon,K,d,A)\,\forall F\). In particular, neither the exponent saving nor the polynomial exponent may deteriorate with formula size, depth, variable-occurrence count or a chosen size bound. The target includes formulas of every polynomial size as well as larger explicit formulas; their input length remains charged through the displayed factor. For a fixed polynomial relation \(L\le n^q\), any polynomial overhead is absorbed into a smaller fixed exponential saving for sufficiently large \(n\), but no separate size-dependent algorithm is substituted for the single program demanded here.

Exhaustive evaluation gives a bound \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(L)\). The question asks to replace its exponential base by some fixed smaller value. A bound \(2^{n-n^\alpha}\operatorname{poly}(L)\), \(0<\alpha<1\), or a polynomial-factor improvement over \(2^n\) does not meet the target: its saving divided by \(n\) tends to zero. No particular numerical saving is prescribed. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1)\) preserves existence of a positive fixed saving.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply an exact deterministic decision algorithm and a fixed positive saving valid for every allowed formula, with all input and computation costs counted. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms and constants in the proposition unconditionally; a lower bound assuming SETH, ETH or another unproved hardness hypothesis is only a conditional result.

Results restricted to fixed clause width, bounded variable occurrences, linear-size or subcubic-size formulas do not establish the universal positive answer. A counting algorithm could establish it only if it satisfies the full stated size, time and machine requirements. There is no additive numerical tolerance or minimum required saving of one hundredth.
context:
The input is a formula tree, but the exponent is measured in distinct variables. Repetition can make a formula much larger without introducing new assignment bits, which is why its full encoding length appears separately.

Tal gives deterministic counting for formulas with at most \(n^{3-16\eta}\) leaves in time \(2^{n-n^\eta}\operatorname{poly}(n)\), for sufficiently small fixed \(\eta>0\). This is significant restricted-size progress but has neither the universal size range nor the linear-in-\(n\) exponent saving required here.

The 2024 work connects further improvements for small-formula counting to stronger formula lower bounds. Those conditional connections illustrate the importance of the algorithmic problem without deciding this general existence question.

Fixed-width CNF formulas are a special case with the same variables. Consequently, the proposed algorithm would refute deterministic SETH; that implication is not an equivalence or an unconditional negative answer.
why: Boolean formulas are more general than bounded-width CNF instances while still lacking arbitrary circuit sharing. A fixed exponential saving across all formula sizes would reveal algorithmic structure beyond exhaustive search and would also improve every fixed-width SAT problem with one common saving.

The source itself is qualitative, so the exact target is an announced editorial default after an optional user question, not a claimed verbatim source formulation or confirmed user choice. The reviewed restricted-size algorithms and conditional lower-bound connections do not settle it.

working_summary: The input is any explicit Boolean formula tree, and the task is to decide exactly whether some assignment satisfies it. The time target is 2^((1-epsilon)n) times a fixed polynomial in the full formula length, for some fixed positive epsilon. One uniform deterministic algorithm must work for all sizes, depths and variable-occurrence patterns. title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
importance_reason: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central cycle-deletion problem whose fixed-parameter tractability is established but whose factorial-versus-single-exponential parameter dependence remains unresolved. A single-exponential algorithm or an impossibility theorem would identify a major boundary in parameterized exact algorithms for directed graphs.
formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.
context:
Open Problem 3.3 groups the general vertex-deletion and arc-deletion questions and separately asks about planar vertex deletion. This card selects the unrestricted vertex-deletion question and makes the deterministic algorithm convention explicit. A positive answer also covers planar digraphs; a negative answer for unrestricted inputs alone would not settle that subclass.

The general unweighted vertex and arc versions have parameter-preserving polynomial reductions between them, so their single-exponential fixed-parameter existence questions are equivalent. Planarity is an additional restriction and is not presumed to be preserved by those general reductions.

The survey records the established \(k^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) parameterized running time and asks whether it can become \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\). Both are fixed-parameter bounds, but the exponent \(k\log k\) in the former is not bounded by a constant times \(k\).

Xiong and Xiao’s SOSA 2025 result improves the bound to \(O(k!\,2^{o(k)}(n+m))\), where \(m\) is the number of arcs. The factorial term remains, so this result is not a single-exponential algorithm in the deletion budget.

The June 2025 Acta Informatica paper still calls improving the general \(2^{O(k\log k)}\) dependence to \(2^{o(k\log k)}\) a major open problem. Its positive results exploit additional graph structure, and bounds exponential in a treewidth or cycle-length parameter are not bounds exponential only in the deletion budget.
why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.
status_note: The checked 2025 primary papers retain the general single-exponential parameter question or the stronger unresolved subfactorial improvement. The SOSA 2025 bound retains k! and does not settle the target. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
importance_reason: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.
context:
Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

Polynomial-time recognition is known through \(k=3\), with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain \(k=4\) as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

A procedure that returns an expression with \(f(k)>k\) labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.
why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.
status_note: The fixed-threshold question is explicitly open in the checked 2009 primary paper and 2012 recognition abstract. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. The checked July 2026 algorithmic result assumes an input expression and is not a current-status theorem about recognition. No independent proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2009: The variable-threshold recognition problem is proved NP-complete; the paper explicitly leaves recognition at each fixed threshold open. | 2012: The full polynomial-time recognition algorithm for clique-width at most three is published. | 2026-07: New graph algorithms exploit a supplied clique expression; they do not determine whether such an expression exists at an exact threshold.
working_summary: Clique-width measures how many reusable vertex labels are needed to build a graph with four specified operations. Even a complete graph of arbitrary size needs only two labels. The question asks whether graphs of width at most k can be recognized in polynomial time for every fixed k. The polynomial exponent may depend on k, so known NP-completeness when k is input does not settle it. Small thresholds are understood, while approximate or supplied decompositions do not give exact recognition at every threshold.

title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
importance_reason: A general algorithm-versus-representation question connecting graph structure, dynamic programming and automatization beyond one decomposition family.
formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every finite simple graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) labeled vertices and every nonnegative integer weight vector \(w\), the machine outputs the exact value \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,w)\) within \(K(\tau(G)+n+L+1)^a\) bit operations? Here \(L\) is the total encoded length of the weights and \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum tropical-circuit size defined below. The input contains only \(G,w\), without a circuit, a decomposition or the value of \(\tau(G)\).
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is supplied as \(n\) in binary and its explicit \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix. The weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) are listed in binary with delimiters, including one zero bit for a zero weight. Let \(L\) include all those weight bits and delimiters. A set \(I\subseteq[n]\) is independent if no two distinct vertices of \(I\) are adjacent. For every real vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{MWIS}(G,x)=\max_{\substack{I\subseteq[n]\\ I\text{ independent}}}\ \sum_{v\in I}x_v.
\]
The empty set is allowed and has weight zero. The required output of \(A\) is the nonnegative integer \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,w)\), in ordinary binary notation.

A tropical circuit on variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output gate. Each input gate has no incoming wires and is labeled by one variable or by the constant \(0\). Every other gate has two input wires and is labeled either \(\max\) or \(+\), interpreted as ordinary maximum or addition of real numbers. Input wires may carry the same previously computed value; fan-out is unrestricted. No other constants, comparisons with branching, multiplication, subtraction or oracle gates are allowed. Size is the total number of gates, including input and constant gates. A circuit for \(G\) is valid if its output equals \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Its topology and labels depend on \(G\) alone, not on the weight assignment. Define \(\tau(G)\) as the minimum size of such a valid circuit. This finite integer exists for every graph.

The machine \(A\) may perform arbitrary deterministic Turing-machine computation; it is not restricted to the operations allowed in the circuits that define \(\tau\). Its program and the constants \(K,a\) are independent of \(G,w,n\). All graph reads, arithmetic on binary weights, preprocessing and output writing are charged. The \(n\) term in a fixed polynomial also accounts for the \(n^2\)-bit adjacency matrix. There are no random bits, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing. The guarantee is a worst-case bound for each valid input. Only the optimum value is requested, not a witnessing independent set or a tropical circuit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform algorithm and fixed constants meeting the exact computational task and bound for all graphs and weights, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. A quasipolynomial dependence on the circuit-size parameter, a construction that is supplied a circuit, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not establish the stated polynomial target. A conditional lower bound retains its condition and alone does not give an unconditional negative answer.
context:
The author’s current problem list asks for polynomial or quasipolynomial running time in the smallest circuit size. This card retains its previously selected polynomial branch and exact value output; it does not require constructing a circuit. The binary model makes weight arithmetic part of the cost.

The paper defines the circuit parameter using all real weights. The card retains its approved nonnegative-weight convention. Section 2.2 observes that these conventions have linearly related circuit sizes, so they give the same polynomial-automatization question.

Corollary 4 establishes polynomial-overhead circuit construction for bounded-degree graphs and for graphs excluding a fixed minor. The unrestricted graph class is the remaining scope of the author’s question.

The paper’s lower bounds on tropical circuits do not themselves lower-bound an unrestricted algorithm given the graph and weights. The target concerns how quickly that algorithm can exploit small circuit complexity, rather than requiring its computation to use only maximum and addition.
why: A compact circuit can express a dynamic program for every weight assignment to one graph without explaining how to discover it. This question asks whether the existence of that compact representation always yields an effective uniform algorithm, connecting nonuniform computation with exact graph optimization.

Corollary 4 of the 2021 paper applies only to bounded-degree or fixed-minor-free graph classes. A bounded later search found no resolution of the retained uniform polynomial bit-cost target.

working_summary: A tropical circuit combines vertex weights using only maximum and addition. For each graph, its minimum circuit size measures how compactly maximum independent-set weight can be represented for every nonnegative weight assignment. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm whose bit cost is polynomial in that circuit size and the input parameters. The algorithm receives only the graph and weights, and may use unrestricted computation to output the exact optimum value. The known construction for restricted graph classes leaves the author’s general polynomial-automatization question open in the sources checked.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
importance_reason: Resolve a major parameterized isomorphism boundary for a broad graph-decomposition measure.
formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs \(G,H\), \(A\) decides whether \(G\cong H\) within \[f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^c\] bit operations, where \(k=\max\{\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H)\}\)? Graphs are supplied by their explicitly encoded adjacency matrices; neither a rank decomposition nor a width bound is supplied.
definitions:
A graph of order \(n\ge0\) has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and an \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-one adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Thus there are no loops, parallel edges, colors or vertex labels that an isomorphism must preserve. For graphs of orders \(n,m\), the assertion \(G\cong H\) means that there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) satisfying
\[
\{u,v\}\in E(G)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\{\pi(u),\pi(v)\}\in E(H)
\quad\text{for every }u,v\in[n].
\]
The required output is one decision bit; an isomorphism, canonical labeling or canonical graph is not required.

For \(X\subseteq V(G)\), let \(M_G(X)\) be the adjacency submatrix whose rows are indexed by \(X\) and columns by \(V(G)\setminus X\). Define the cut-rank
\[
\rho_G(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}M_G(X),
\]
where \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two, and rank is the dimension of the row space over this field. A matrix with no rows or no columns has rank zero.

For \(n\ge2\), a rank decomposition consists of a finite tree \(T\) of maximum degree at most three and a bijection between its leaves and \(V(G)\). Removing any edge \(e\) partitions the leaves into two sets; write \(X_e\subseteq V(G)\) for either side. The width of the decomposition is \(\max_{e\in E(T)}\rho_G(X_e)\). This is independent of the chosen side because the two cut matrices are transposes. The rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such trees and leaf bijections. For \(n\le1\), set \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\). The unrooted decomposition convention here gives the same width as a rooted binary decomposition whose nodes represent the descendant leaf sets.

For a concrete input encoding, let \(\mathrm{bin}(n)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with \(\mathrm{bin}(0)=0\), and set \(b=|\mathrm{bin}(n)|\). Encode \(n\) by \(1^b0\,\mathrm{bin}(n)\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order. Concatenate the two graph encodings. The machine must reject malformed strings; the displayed parameterized bound is required on valid graph pairs. The model charges every input access, tape move, arithmetic operation as its bit-level implementation, preprocessing step and output bit. No decomposition, parameter value, advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing is available.

The program \(A\) and exponent \(c\) are fixed for all graph sizes and widths. The function \(f\) must be computable by an ordinary halting algorithm on every nonnegative integer, although it need not be polynomial, elementary or explicitly evaluated by \(A\). It may grow arbitrarily rapidly with the parameter. An algorithm with exponent depending on \(k\), or a separate nonuniform algorithm for each width without the stated common computable bound, is not the claimed fixed-parameter algorithm.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including uniform correctness and the computable parameter factor, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation. A conditional lower bound alone does not establish the unconditional negation. Polynomial time separately for each fixed width, efficient computation of a rank decomposition, or an algorithm for a more restrictive graph parameter is insufficient.
context:
Question 6.2 contains two separate targets: fixed-parameter tractability and a smaller parameter-dependent polynomial exponent. This card retains the first branch. The survey defines fixed-parameter tractability with one algorithm and a computable parameter factor; the explicit bit encoding here makes that uniform convention concrete.

Grohe and Neuen give a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm at every fixed rank-width, with running time \(O(n^{3k+5}\log n)\) for the stated bounded-width setting. The exponent still grows with \(k\). The revised paper corrects a proof issue in its earlier version; the cited revision is the July 2022 version.

The parallel canonization result gives small-depth circuits for each fixed rank-width, but their size has an exponent depending on the width. It does not supply the fixed exponent required by this card.

The 2026 connectivity-function result improves computation of rank-width and its decomposition. This is a different task from determining whether two graphs are isomorphic. The card charges any decomposition work done by its algorithm and does not assume one is given.

The survey also discusses isomorphism parameterized by rank-depth, which restricts the depth as well as the cut structure. Its cited fixed-parameter result is nonuniform and concerns the more restrictive parameter; it does not establish this rank-width target.
why: Rank-width captures dense graphs with structured adjacency cuts, extending the reach of graph decomposition beyond sparse settings. A uniform fixed-parameter isomorphism test would make the polynomial exponent independent of this structural complexity and settle a central boundary in parameterized graph isomorphism.

Checked on 2026-09-16 against its explicit uniformity convention, the revised bounded-width algorithm, parallel canonization, 2026 decomposition computation and restricted twin-width progress. No matching resolution was found in the bounded search; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.

working_summary: Rank-width measures the ranks of adjacency cuts in an optimally chosen decomposition tree. Graph isomorphism asks whether a bijection of vertices preserves all edges. This card asks for one deterministic algorithm whose polynomial exponent is independent of the rank-width. The parameter-dependent multiplier may be any total computable function, and no decomposition is supplied. Known fixed-width polynomial algorithms and faster decomposition methods do not by themselves give the required uniform isomorphism bound.

title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
importance_reason: A basic conceptual comparison of two central preprocessing notions. A rigorous separation would determine whether freedom to change representation yields a substantive advantage beyond polynomial kernelization for NP-complete problems.
formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
definitions:
The parameter \(k\) is a nonnegative integer supplied in unary. Encode a pair \((x,k)\) by
\[
\langle x,k\rangle=1^{|x|}0\,x\,1^k,
\qquad
\widetilde Q=\{\langle x,k\rangle:(x,k)\in Q\}.
\]
The prefix determines the end of the binary string \(x\); the remaining symbols must all be one. Strings that fail this syntax are outside \(\widetilde Q\). Input length is \(2|x|+k+1\), equivalent within fixed constants to \(|x|+k+1\).

The property \(\operatorname{PC}(Q)\) holds when there exist a fixed language \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\), such that for every binary string \(x\) and every \(k\ge0\), \(A\) on \(\langle x,k\rangle\) halts within \(C(|x|+k+2)^a\) bit steps and outputs a binary string \(y\) satisfying
\[
|y|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ y\in R.
\]
The target language \(R\) is fixed across all inputs and parameters. No decidability or NP-membership condition is imposed on \(R\). The compressor has no membership oracle for \(R\); it only computes the string. The machine, exponents and constants may depend on the selected \(Q\) and compression scheme, never on \(x,k\).

The property \(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\) holds when there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(B\), a constant \(D\ge1\), and integers \(c,d\ge1\), such that, for every \((x,k)\), \(B\) outputs an encoded pair \(\langle x',k'\rangle\) within \(D(|x|+k+2)^c\) bit steps, with
\[
|x'|+k'\le D(k+1)^d,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ (x',k')\in Q.
\]
The output language is the same \(Q\), and the bound includes the new parameter in unary. In both definitions all input reading, computation and output writing count. Algorithms have finite fixed programs, no advice, no oracle and no randomness. They must be correct on every valid pair, without a promise on \(x\) beyond the language membership being decided.

For completeness, a binary language \(L\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial bound \(p\) such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}\ V(x,z)=1.
\]
The notation \(\{0,1\}^{\le r}\) denotes all binary strings of length at most \(r\). A language \(L\) is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\), a polynomial bound \(p\), and a sequence of advice strings \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) with \(|\alpha_n|\le p(n)\), such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}
\ W(x,\alpha_{|x|},z)=1.
\]
Advice may depend on input length but not on the particular input, and need not be computable. It belongs only to this comparison class, not to the compression or kernel algorithms. Each language may have its own verifier, polynomial and advice sequence. The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) means every NP language belongs to that advice class.

A language is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every NP language reduces to it by one deterministic polynomial-time many-one map preserving membership. This is ordinary polynomial-time completeness of the unary-encoded language \(\widetilde Q\), not parameterized hardness of \(Q\).

The main proposition quantifies over a single fixed \(Q\), with an unconditional compression scheme and the displayed implication for every possible polynomial kernel. It does not require proving the hypothesis that NP is not contained in the advice class. It also does not assert unconditional nonexistence of a kernel. The informal adjective “natural” is not a further uncheckable requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the language and encoding, prove NP-completeness of its unary form, establish an unconditional deterministic compression with all size and running-time guarantees, and prove that any deterministic polynomial kernel would imply the displayed complexity-class inclusion. Absence of a known kernel, a randomized compression alone, or an output language merely not known to belong to NP does not establish the proposition. The lower-bound implication must be proved; the assumed noninclusion itself need not be proved.
context:
The textbook asks for a separation on “natural problems” without defining a mathematical class for that adjective. On 16 September 2026 the user explicitly selected a precise NP-complete source-language branch. This card records that selection and uses the usual conditional kernel-lower-bound interpretation with the displayed advice-class assumption. This is a documented formulation of the research direction, not a claim that NP-completeness is equivalent to the original informal requirement.

Definition 15.8 permits an arbitrary compression target, including languages not known to be decidable. Restricting the target to NP would materially change this question. The algorithms themselves are ordinary effective polynomial-time machines and receive no target-language oracle.

The kernelization monograph proves that an NP-hard unary source language has a polynomial kernel whenever its polynomial compression targets a language in NP. The unresolved comparison therefore concerns the possibility of more general compressed representations.

For a nontrivial NP source language, proving unconditional absence of polynomial kernels would in particular prove that P differs from NP, since a polynomial-time decider could output fixed yes and no instances. The selected implication gives the conventional conditional distinction without importing that stronger demand.

The motivating cycle-through-terminals example has a randomized compression to a matrix problem whose NP-membership is not known. The cited sources do not turn either fact into a proof of a deterministic compression-versus-kernel separation. Later boundaried-kernel lower bounds also impose a different preservation requirement.

title: Job-shop approximation parameterized only by machines and accuracy
importance_reason: A general approximation-scheme question for a central scheduling model, testing whether machine count and accuracy suffice despite arbitrarily long reentrant job routes. Its significance is the removal of an entire structural parameter, not a small improvement to one approximation ratio.
formal:
Do there exist a total computable function \(F:\mathbb N_{\ge1}^2\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every number of machines \(m\ge1\), accuracy parameter \(q\ge1\), and job-shop instance \(I\) defined below, \(A(I,q)\) returns a feasible schedule \(S\) satisfying
\[
C_{\max}(S)\le(1+1/q)\operatorname{OPT}(I)
\]
in at most \(F(m,q)(L+1)^c\) Turing-machine steps, where \(L\) is the complete binary input length? The number of operations per job is unbounded and may not be an additional parameter of \(F\).
question_excerpt: Open Problem 13 asks whether general job-shop makespan admits a (1+epsilon)-approximation in f(m,epsilon) times a polynomial, removing the maximum number of operations per job from the known parameter dependence. The source’s model expressly permits repeated visits to a machine. This card specifies the full explicit binary input length and a reciprocal-integer accuracy parameter to make its resource claim precise.
definitions:
An instance has machines \(1,\ldots,m\) and jobs \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(m,n\ge1\). Job \(j\) is an explicitly listed sequence of \(\ell_j\ge1\) operations. Its \(h\)-th operation has a prescribed machine \(\mu_{j,h}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a positive integer processing time \(p_{j,h}\), encoded in binary. Let \(N=\sum_{j=1}^n\ell_j\) be the total number of operations. A job may use the same machine repeatedly and may skip other machines. Neither \(\ell_j\) nor \(\max_j\ell_j\) is bounded as a function of \(m\). All jobs are available at time zero.

A schedule assigns a nonnegative real start time \(s_{j,h}\) to every operation. Each operation runs without interruption for exactly \(p_{j,h}\) time units on its prescribed machine. Job order must be respected:
\[
s_{j,h+1}\ge s_{j,h}+p_{j,h}
\qquad(1\le h<\ell_j).
\]
For any two distinct operations assigned to the same machine, their half-open processing intervals \([s_{j,h},s_{j,h}+p_{j,h})\) are disjoint. Equivalently, one operation must finish no later than the other starts. These are all feasibility constraints. Jobs may wait between consecutive operations; operations cannot be split, migrated to another machine or processed in parallel. There are no release dates, deadlines, setup times, inter-job precedence constraints or extra conflict-resource requirements.

The makespan and optimum are
\[
C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j,h}(s_{j,h}+p_{j,h}),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).
\]
A feasible serial schedule exists. For these integer durations an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the displayed minimum is attained and is positive. The optimization domain nevertheless permits real start times. The algorithm must output one rational start time for each of the \(N\) operations, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, in the input operation order. The output itself must be feasible and obey the approximation ratio; merely estimating the optimal value is insufficient.

The input contains binary encodings of \(m,n,q\), every \(\ell_j\), and all pairs \((\mu_{j,h},p_{j,h})\), with unambiguous separators. Their entire bit length is \(L\). Jobs and operations are listed individually; multiplicities, long repeated routes and durations are not expanded into unit-time jobs, and routes are not supplied by a succinct grammar. Processing times can be arbitrarily large relative to \(N\), so a bound polynomial in their numerical sum is not by itself a polynomial bound in \(L\).

The algorithm is one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a constant number of cells and moves each head by at most one cell. All preprocessing, exact rational/integer arithmetic on individual bits, input reading and output writing are counted. There is no advice, uncharged parameter preprocessing, oracle or randomness. The function \(F\) is total computable, meaning that some fixed machine halts on every positive pair \((m,q)\) and outputs its value; no particular growth bound on \(F\) is imposed. The exponent \(c\) is one absolute constant, independent of \(m,q,I\).

The reciprocal-integer accuracy grid specifies an approximation scheme: for any desired rational \(0<\epsilon\le1\), choosing \(q=\lceil1/\epsilon\rceil\) gives ratio at most \(1+\epsilon\). This does not restrict the scheme to one fixed approximation ratio. The parameter-only factor may depend on machines and accuracy, but not on the number of jobs, maximum route length, processing-time magnitudes or other input features. Those features can contribute to the fixed polynomial in the full bit length. “Fixed-machine” means that each fixed \(m,q\) yields a polynomial-time guarantee; one uniform algorithm must still handle all \(m,q\).
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one uniform algorithm, a total computable parameter bound \(F\), an absolute polynomial exponent, and prove feasibility, approximation and running time for every valid instance and every \(q\ge1\).

A scheme whose nonpolynomial factor also depends on the maximum number of operations per job, or whose input-length exponent depends on \(m\) or \(q\), does not meet the target. Neither exact optimization hardness, a heuristic with good observed schedules, a scheme only for nonreentrant routes, nor an algorithm for a different shop model settles it. A conditional impossibility theorem establishes only its conditional conclusion. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this algorithm-existence question.
context:
General job-shop routes are ordered lists of machine-specific operations. A small number of machines does not limit the number of times a job can return to them.

Jansen, Solis-Oba and Sviridenko obtain an approximation scheme when both the machine count and the maximum number of operations per job are fixed. This additional route-length parameter is exactly what the question seeks to remove.

The survey contrasts the job-shop dependency with schemes for open-shop and flow-shop models. Their different ordering and route assumptions prevent those guarantees from automatically answering the job-shop question.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme for each fixed machine count can still have an input exponent depending on accuracy. The requested bound places all machine-count and accuracy dependence in one computable multiplicative factor.

Exact optimization hardness does not exclude an approximation scheme. Likewise, exact fixed-parameter tractability for different parameter combinations does not establish the requested dependence.
why: Machine count alone is a natural measure of shop complexity, but long job routes can still encode difficult interactions. An approximation scheme with no separate route-length parameter would clarify whether near-optimal schedules remain tractable on a fixed shop even when individual jobs revisit machines many times.
status_note: The 2018 accepted survey explicitly poses this parameter-dependence question. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution for arbitrary reentrant job routes. The 2003 scheme fixes an extra route-length parameter; checked recent transaction and conflict-graph papers use different constraints and do not supply the required scheme. This review verifies statements and model scope without independently checking every cited proof.
