title: Sub-base-two exact maximum acyclic subgraph
importance_reason: A significant algorithmic question under particular parameters or graph restrictions, with more specialized consequences than a general parameterized-complexity principle.
formal: Do there exist constants \(1<c<2\), \(K\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every unweighted directed graph on \(n\) vertices, outputs a maximum-cardinality acyclic spanning subgraph in at most \(Kc^n(n+1)^a\) bit operations? The exponent parameter is the number of vertices, and the graph class and computational model are specified below.
definitions:
An input consists of \(n\ge0\) and an \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. It represents \(D=([n],A)\), with one possible arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices. Both opposite arcs between a pair may occur. There are no parallel copies, loops, weights, bounds on degree or density, connectivity promises, or restrictions to tournaments or planar graphs. The vertex number is encoded in binary along with the full matrix; the empty graph is allowed.

For \(B\subseteq A\), the spanning subgraph \(([n],B)\) is acyclic when it contains no directed cycle: there are no pairwise distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) with \(k\ge2\) and arcs \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in B\) for every cyclic index \(i\). All original vertices remain, including isolated vertices. Define
\[
\operatorname{mas}(D)=\max\{|B|:B\subseteq A,\ ([n],B)\text{ is acyclic}\}.
\]
The output is the binary incidence vector of a subset \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|=\operatorname{mas}(D)\). Merely producing an inclusion-maximal acyclic set does not meet this task.

An algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, with ordinary bit-cost input access, computation and output. Its worst-case running time, including all preprocessing, is bounded as stated on every valid graph. It has no oracle, random instructions or advice depending on \(n\), and there is no independent polynomial-space requirement. The constants \(c,K,a\) and the program are independent of the graph and its order. Polynomial factors in the input size can be written as polynomial factors in \(n+1\), since the matrix has \(n^2\) entries.

The required improvement is a fixed exponential base below two. Equivalently one can absorb the polynomial factor into a slightly larger base still below two and require a bound \(K'(c')^n\) with \(c'<2\). A factor saving that leaves exponential base two is insufficient. Exact output is part of this computational task, rather than an invitation to estimate a numerical benchmark value.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such an algorithm, its exact optimal output and the worst-case bit-complexity bound for all valid inputs, or a complete Lean proof that no such constants and algorithm exist. Conditional lower bounds do not prove this unconditional negation. Algorithms for a proper graph subclass, approximation algorithms, or bounds exponential in the number of deleted arcs rather than vertices do not by themselves settle the assertion. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance applies to the asymptotic running-time target.
context:
The inherited title did not specify the missing resource bound. Section 6.4 of the 2013 seminar report asks for an exact algorithm with exponential base strictly below two, parameterized by the number of vertices. This card makes the deterministic, unweighted adjacency-matrix branch explicit.

The 2012 vertex-ordering paper gives \(O^*(2^n)\) time and space for directed feedback arc set, where the star suppresses polynomial factors. Its complementary arc set is a maximum acyclic subgraph, so the exact optimization objectives have the same running-time baseline.

The retained arcs need only be consistent with some vertex ordering; deleting vertices is a different optimization problem. Similarly, the nearby arity-three ordering question in the seminar report is distinct from this card’s binary precedence constraints.

The 2026 spanning-tree paper gives algorithms parameterized by the amount \(k\) above a spanning-tree lower bound. Its dependence \(2^{k^{O(1)}}\) for integral weights does not provide a fixed base below two as a function of the vertex count on arbitrary inputs.

The requested bound allows exponential storage. Adding a polynomial-space condition or substituting a faster algorithm on a restricted degree class would change the target.
why: Many ordering problems admit exact algorithms whose time grows like two to the number of vertices. Maximum acyclic subgraph is a basic test of whether directed precedence constraints permit a fixed exponential improvement, without restricting the input graph or accepting an approximate ordering.

title: Converting CNF to DNF
importance_reason: A focused parameterized or exact-algorithm problem for a specified model, parameter, or restricted input family.
formal:
Determine the worst-case minimum DNF term count of a Boolean function representable by a \(k\)-CNF on \(n\) variables. More precisely, for integers \(1\le k\le n\), let \(\mathcal C_{n,k}\) be the set of Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) representable as a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most \(k\) literals. Define
\[
d(f)=\min\{\text{number of terms in }D:D\text{ is a DNF on the same variables and }D(x)=f(x)\text{ for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n\},
\]
\[
M(n,k)=\max_{f\in\mathcal C_{n,k}}d(f).
\]
Supply a mathematical description of a real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathcal D=\{(n,k)\in\mathbb Z^2:1\le k\le n\}\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[
\forall(n,k)\in\mathcal D,\qquad
|g(n,k)-M(n,k)|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The error is measured in the unnormalized number of DNF terms. The approximation need not be integer-valued. This finite-parameter determination is an editorial extension of the source’s request to close the gap between exponential upper and lower bounds.
definitions:
The variables are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), with values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\); at an assignment \(a\), these have values \(a_i\) and \(1-a_i\), respectively. A clause is a disjunction of literals and a term is a conjunction of literals. A CNF is a finite conjunction of clauses; a DNF is a finite disjunction of terms. Width at most \(k\) bounds the number of literals in each CNF clause, not the number of clauses. Both positive and negative literals are permitted, and no monotonicity, occurrence bound or bound on the number of clauses is assumed.

For a concrete finite representation, identify literals with signed indices \((i,b)\), where \(1\le i\le n\), \(b=1\) denotes \(x_i\), and \(b=0\) denotes \(\neg x_i\). A clause is a set of at most \(k\) such signed indices with at most one sign per variable, and a CNF is a set of these clauses. Repeated literals and clauses have no effect; clauses containing both signs of a variable are tautological and may be omitted. A term is likewise a set of signed indices with at most one sign per variable, with no width bound other than \(n\), and a DNF is a set of terms. A contradictory term may be omitted. These normalizations do not change the represented functions or their minimum DNF term counts.

An empty conjunction has value one and an empty disjunction has value zero. Thus an empty CNF represents one, an empty clause makes a CNF zero, an empty DNF represents zero, and the singleton DNF consisting of the empty term represents one. In particular, \(d(0)=0\) and \(d(1)=1\). The ambient variable set has size \(n\), but a represented function need not depend on every variable. Equivalence means equality of Boolean values on all \(2^n\) assignments. No auxiliary variables, projection, merely equisatisfiable encoding or approximation of the Boolean function is allowed. Distinct DNF terms may be satisfied simultaneously.

The size being minimized is the number of terms, irrespective of their lengths. It is not the number of literal occurrences, the serialized bit length, the number of satisfying assignments, or the number of all inclusion-minimal implicants. There are finitely many functions and normalized formulas at each \((n,k)\), and every function has a DNF, so the stated minima and maximum exist. This is a structural extremal question. It imposes no computational model, running-time or space bound for converting an individual formula or evaluating the supplied mathematical answer; the signed-index representation fixes the objects being counted rather than an algorithmic resource promise.
answer_criterion:
Supply \(g\), a formula, certified evaluation rule or other unambiguous mathematical description of its values in terms of \(n,k\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed pointwise error bound throughout \(\mathcal D\). The proof must establish both the universal upper bound for every permitted \(k\)-CNF function and the corresponding extremal lower bound at every admissible parameter pair. Equivalently, certified real bounds \(L(n,k)\le M(n,k)\le U(n,k)\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination is welcome but is not required, and the answer need not be integer-valued.

Merely renaming the defining maximum and minimum, or giving exhaustive enumeration of all CNF and DNF representations as the answer, does not determine the requested extremal law. Finite tables, one-sided estimates, bounds only for monotone formulas, or asymptotic estimates with unspecified constants do not meet the full-domain tolerance. This numerical acceptance precision belongs to the editorial extension and is not attributed to the 2013 source.
context:
Schneider’s 2013 question asks how large the smallest equivalent DNF of a \(k\)-CNF can be and explicitly measures size by the number of terms. It asks to close an exponential upper/lower gap; it does not pose an output-sensitive algorithmic problem or state that a particular lower-bound example is always extremal.

The source reports the upper bound \(2^{n(1-1/(100k))}\) and the block-parity lower bound \(2^{n(1-1/k)}\) when \(k\) divides \(n\). Block parity here is the conjunction of prescribed parity conditions on disjoint blocks of \(k\) variables. These estimates agree in the order of the exponent saving while leaving its precise value undetermined.

The current card makes the underlying extremal function \(M(n,k)\) explicit and asks for a pointwise determination within \(1/100\) term on all \(1\le k\le n\). This is the authorized quantitative extension used by the catalogue, stronger than closing only the source’s asymptotic gap. The source is retained as provenance for the quantity, not presented as having demanded this finite-parameter precision.

Miltersen, Radhakrishnan and Wegener’s December 2003 report defines DNF size by the number of terms and proves the bounded-width upper estimate in Lemma 4. Their main parameterized result instead constrains the number of CNF clauses; that parameter is distinct from the clause-width parameter \(k\) used here.

Mossé, Sha and Tan obtain the bound \(n\,2^{n(1-0.282/k)}\) for monotone \(k\)-CNFs with \(k\ge2\), where monotone means that no variable is negated. Their more general results count all prime implicants: terms implying the function from which no literal can be removed while retaining that implication. In general these terms need not all be present in a smallest equivalent DNF, so that counting problem is distinct from \(M(n,k)\).

A June 2026 Isabelle formalization proves exponential size blowup for specific CNF and DNF families. Its lower-bound examples and formula-size measure do not determine the full extremal term-count function asked for here.
why: The same Boolean function can have very different sizes in conjunctive and disjunctive normal form. This question measures the largest unavoidable number of DNF terms when only the input clause width and number of variables are fixed, separating an inherent representation cost from the performance of any particular conversion algorithm.
status_note: The checked 2013 primary source leaves the general minimum-DNF-term exponential gap open. The 2022 primary paper improves a monotone special case and counts general prime implicants, while the June 2026 formalization concerns classical exponential-blowup examples. The individual review and bounded later-work check on 16 September 2026 found no determination of the full general extremal term-count function. This card explicitly extends the source’s asymptotic question to pointwise approximation of M(n,k) within 1/100; that acceptance target is not itself a historically sourced conjecture. The review is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.
progress: 2003-12-11: The December BRICS report gives a bounded-width DNF upper bound in Lemma 4 and defines size as the number of terms. Its printed lemma assumes \(1\le k\le n/100\); the seminar later summarizes the bound without that displayed regime. | 2005-11-30: On converting CNF to DNF appears in Theoretical Computer Science 347(1–2), pages 325–335; the 2013 question cites this journal version. | 2013: Schneider poses the problem of closing the gap between the upper bound and the block-parity lower bound in Seminar 13331, Section 6.19. | 2022: SAT 2022, Corollary 34, proves \(d(f)\le n\,2^{n(1-0.282/k)}\) for monotone \(k\)-CNFs; the general signed-clause extremal function is not determined. | 2026-06-15: An Archive of Formal Proofs entry formalizes classical exponential blowup examples in Isabelle; it does not supply matching full-domain extremal bounds for the present quantity.
working_summary: For each variable count n and clause width k, the target is the largest minimum number of DNF terms needed to represent an n-variable k-CNF function. The DNF must agree on every assignment using the same variables, while its terms may overlap and may have arbitrary width. The source leaves a gap between exponential upper and lower bounds, and later improvements for monotone formulas do not determine the general case. The card explicitly extends that asymptotic question to a real-valued description of the extremal function within one hundredth of a term at every admissible pair. A complete Lean proof must certify the universal upper and extremal lower bounds, thereby identifying the inherent representation cost rather than a conversion algorithm’s running time.

title: Slice-wise Polynomial Space Conjecture
importance_reason: A class-wide hypothesis about simultaneous memory and time, with consequences for many parameterized graph algorithms. Existing score retained.
formal: Is it true that no XNLP-hard parameterized decision problem has a single deterministic algorithm with both worst-case time \((n+2)^{f(k)}\) and working space \(f(k)(n+2)^{c}\), for any total computable function \(f:N\to N\) and any absolute constant c? Here k is the parameter, n is the bit length of the ordinary input, and both resource bounds must hold on the same execution. Hardness uses parameterized logspace many-one reductions defined below.
definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of \(\{0,1\}*\times N\), with input \((x,k), n=|x|\) and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time \(g(k)(n+2)^{a}\) and working space \(g(k)\log _{2}(n+2)\) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction \(Q_{1}\le Q_{2}\) is a deterministic halting transducer mapping \((x,k)\) to \((y,k' )\), preserving the yes/no answer, with \(k' \le h(k)\) for a total computable h and space \(h(k)+C \log _{2}(n+2)\) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by \(n+2\) only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.
context:
Parameterized dynamic programs often store tables of size \(n^{O(k)}\) and run in a comparable amount of time. Allowing a larger exponent in time does not automatically show whether the memory exponent can be made independent of k.

Its machines use only a parameter-dependent multiple of log n working space while running in fixed-parameter polynomial time. Many problems on graphs with linear decompositions are complete for this class.

The target would prohibit all deterministic algorithms with a fixed polynomial space exponent while retaining polynomial time on each fixed-parameter slice. It is a simultaneous tradeoff conjecture, not a claim that the problems cannot be solved in polynomial space with unrestricted time.

The Algorithmica paper establishes XNLP-completeness for several familiar graph problems and explicitly retains this time-space assertion as Conjecture 1. Such classifications transfer the conjectured obstruction; they do not prove it.
why: Would explain a broad barrier to reducing the memory of parameterized dynamic programming while keeping polynomial time for each fixed parameter, connecting practical table-size tradeoffs with a uniform complexity-class obstruction.

The conjecture forbids deterministic algorithms for XNLP-hard problems with both slice-wise polynomial time and a fixed polynomial space exponent. One algorithm must meet both guarantees on every input. The parameter may affect the time exponent and the space multiplier, but not the space exponent. Later completeness results retain this as a conjecture that would explain memory barriers in dynamic programming.

title: Disjoint-union closure of tractable forbidden patterns
importance_reason: Would organize the parameterized complexity dichotomy for forbidden induced subgraphs by showing that disconnected obstructions introduce no new tractability barrier beyond their components. Existing score retained.
formal: For every pair of fixed nonempty finite simple graphs \(H_{1},H_{2}\), is the following implication true? If Independent Set parameterized by the requested set size k is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{1}\)-free graphs and is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{2}\)-free graphs, then it is fixed-parameter tractable on \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free graphs. Here exclusion is as an induced subgraph, ⊔ is disjoint union of the forbidden patterns, and fixed-parameter tractability has the deterministic meaning defined below. The two forbidden graphs may themselves be disconnected and may be isomorphic.
definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), under the promise that no subset of \(V(G)\) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|\ge k\) and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{H}, a\) total computable function \(f_{H}:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) and a constant \(c_{H}\ge 0\) such that \(A_{H}\) correctly decides every promised input in at most \(f_{H}(k)(n+1)^{c_{H}}\) bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while \(c_{H}\) cannot depend on k or n. For \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\). The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of \(H_{1},H_{2}\) or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \(H_{1},H_{2}\) satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free problem in \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.
context:
Every \(H_{1}\)-free or \(H_{2}\)-free input is automatically \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free, but the latter class can also contain both patterns. The conjecture asks whether this enlargement preserves parameterized tractability. It is not the elementary decomposition of Independent Set across disconnected input components.

When the forbidden graph is a disjoint union of cliques, the paper gives an FPT algorithm. The concluding conjecture asks whether the same closure principle holds for all tractable forbidden patterns, not only clique components.

The author-hosted Algorithmica manuscript repeats the disjoint-union implication in its conclusion. It also distinguishes this question from another proposed closure operation, adding false twins, which the paper shows does not preserve the hoped-for tractability classification under the usual complexity separation.

The ISAAC 2019 follow-up provides additional tractable forbidden patterns and randomized FPT algorithms for dart- and cricket-free graphs. These results concern individual patterns and do not prove the general disjoint-union implication. In particular, a randomized result is not silently substituted for the deterministic premises here.
why: A closure theorem would reduce the classification of parameterized Independent Set with one forbidden induced pattern to its connected components. It would organize many currently separate tractability results through one general structural principle.
status_note: Read the original conjecture, induced-exclusion definition and parameter convention, the expanded journal manuscript’s conclusion, and the later ISAAC paper’s individual-pattern results and randomness qualification. Searched subsequent work without finding a resolution of the full closure implication. This is a source-grounded open status, not an exhaustive absence proof. No independent proof verification.
progress: 2018: Work presented at IPEC 2018 proves the disjoint-clique special case and states the general disjoint-union conjecture; proceedings appeared 5 February 2019. | 2019-11-28: ISAAC follow-up obtains more individual-pattern algorithms, including randomized dart- and cricket-free cases. | 2020-06-17: Journal version published; the expanded author manuscript retains the general closure conjecture.
working_summary: Independent Set asks whether a graph contains k pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Suppose the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when either one of two fixed induced patterns is forbidden. The conjecture asks whether tractability persists when only their disjoint union is forbidden. This is already known when the forbidden components are cliques, and the 2020 journal manuscript retains the general conjecture. The problem concerns the forbidden pattern, not whether the input graph itself is disconnected.

title: Expected FPT delay from small-witness decision
importance_reason: A general relationship between parameterized decision and enumeration complexity, with a substantive gap between total work and responsiveness. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every self-contained \(k\)-witness problem whose decision version is fixed-parameter tractable admit an always-correct randomized enumeration algorithm with expected delay \(f(k)L^{O(1)}\), where \(L\) is the encoded input length and \(f\) is a computable function? The algorithm must output every distinct witness exactly once and terminate, with the same expected bound before the first output and after the last. This selects the expected-delay branch of the source question; deterministic delay and the weaker incremental bounds are distinct companion questions.
definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated implication for all self-contained k-witness problems, or exhibit a problem satisfying its decision premise and prove that no enumerator with the stated expected-delay guarantee exists, with any complexity assumption made explicit. A bound only on final expected running time, a delay allowed to grow polynomially with the number already output, a randomized list that can omit witnesses, or a result assuming an efficient extension oracle does not settle this selected branch. The source’s deterministic and incremental companion questions require separate conclusions.
context:
A decision algorithm applied to restricted universes provides an inclusion test. The question asks what control that information gives over the pauses while listing all distinct witness subsets.

The journal Theorem 1.1 gives an always-correct randomized enumerator with expected work e^{k+o(k)}g(k)|U|^{O(1)}N when N is positive and inclusion queries take g(k)|U|^{O(1)} time. One initial inclusion test handles N=0. This is an expected-output guarantee, and the conclusion still asks about delay and incremental guarantees.

The source supplies examples where efficient inclusion queries do not yield FPT extension queries unless FPT=W[1]. That obstruction to one standard route does not itself prove a lower bound against every possible enumerator.

The later version formulates its broader question in terms of an FPT inclusion algorithm. For the self-contained problems retained on this card, ordinary decision supplies that operation by restriction. The paper’s approximate-enumeration results with fallible oracles have a different correctness guarantee.
why: Tests how far an efficient existence test can be converted into a reliably responsive generator of all small solutions. The distinction between total work and delays matters when a solution set is large and users need successive answers before enumeration finishes.
status_note: Read the IPEC definitions and complete conclusion, the January 2018 author-final v4, and the publisher’s corresponding definitions and conclusion. Targeted later-work searches through 12 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the expected-delay implication. This card explicitly selects that branch from the source’s several alternatives; it does not claim that solving it negatively settles the weaker incremental branch.
progress: 2016: The IPEC paper proves expected-output-FPT enumeration and explicitly asks about expected delay, expected incremental time and their deterministic versions. | 2018-01-16: The expanded journal article sharpens the total-work dependence and treats fallible inclusion oracles, but Section 7 retains the delay and incremental questions.
working_summary: A self-contained witness is a k-element subset whose validity survives restriction to any universe containing it. An FPT decision algorithm can therefore test whether a chosen subset contains a witness. The selected question asks whether this always yields exact enumeration with expected FPT time between outputs, including startup and termination. The source already controls expected total work but leaves the stronger delay guarantee open. Incremental time, deterministic delay and enumeration with possible omissions are separate variants.

title: Polynomial kernels for forbidden-minor vertex deletion
importance_reason: A major generic preprocessing question for graph-minor deletion, with vertex planarization among its unresolved instances. Existing score retained.
formal: Does vertex deletion to exclude any fixed finite family of graph minors admit a polynomial kernel, parameterized by the number of vertices allowed to be deleted? Precisely, for every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\), is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation of \((G,k)\) into an equivalent instance \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same \(\mathcal F\)-deletion problem whose total encoding length and parameter are bounded by \((k+1)^{O_{\mathcal F}(1)}\)?
definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.
context:
The source observes that every fixed-family problem is fixed-parameter tractable. This guarantees preprocessing to a size depending only on the solution budget, but does not guarantee polynomial dependence.

The FOCS 2012 work obtains polynomial kernels when the forbidden family contains a planar graph. The 2026 introduction explains how a later deterministic approximation removes the randomized ingredient from that kernel construction.

For \(\mathcal F=\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}\), the output after deletion must be planar. Both obstructions are nonplanar, so the preceding theorem does not apply. The later constant-factor approximate kernel does not preserve the exact decision threshold.

Theorem 1 transfers an existing solution-size kernel to a different parameterization for connected forbidden families. It does not supply the missing kernel for every family, and its introduction explicitly retains the general and planarization questions.
why: Would give a general guarantee that graphs close to a minor-closed class can be reduced efficiently to a polynomial amount of relevant information. It unifies preprocessing questions for vertex cover, feedback vertex set, bounded-width deletion and planarization.
status_note: Read the original minor and kernel definitions and full concluding question; checked the full planar-family theorem, the full 2022 lossy-planarization version and its 2025 journal status, and the 2026 structural theorem and open-status passage. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for arbitrary fixed families. The deterministic requirement, family-dependent exponent and exact solution-budget parameter are explicit.
progress: 2011: The source gives kernels for selected forbidden families and asks whether every fixed-family vertex-deletion problem has a polynomial kernel. | 2012: The planar-obstruction condition yields a broad polynomial-kernel theorem. | 2025: The journal version of lossy planarization gives a constant-factor approximate kernel, preserving the distinction from exact preprocessing. | 2026: STACS work extends structural parameterizations while explicitly retaining the general solution-budget question.
working_summary: Delete at most a specified number of vertices to eliminate every minor from a fixed finite family. The question asks for polynomial-time preprocessing to one equivalent instance of polynomial size in that budget. The polynomial may depend on the forbidden family. Families containing a planar obstruction are covered, while planarization remains a key open case. Later lossy and structural-parameter results do not establish the full exact-kernel claim.

title: Degeneracy-sensitive classification of homomorphism counting
importance_reason: Importance has not been individually assessed. This draft shares the provisional midpoint with other unassessed drafts; its position is not evidence that the question is less important.
formal: A short source quotation appears below. The model definitions are on the linked page of the paper.
question_excerpt: Find an explicit criterion on computable graph classes C such that #\(H OM D (C)\) is FPT if the criterion is satisfied and #\(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard otherwise.
context:
Exact computation as a function of structure or input size. Bounds must be compared in the same parameter regime.

Source of the specific model: Exact and Approximate Pattern Counting in Degenerate Graphs: New Algorithms, Hardness Results, and Complexity Dichotomies (FOCS, 2021). Question location: Open Problem 1.
why: The question asks for an object to exist or to be constructed efficiently. Bridging existence and explicit computation is often essential for using the structure.
status_note: Question recorded in a source from 2021; subsequent results and present open status have not been individually checked.
progress: 2021: The source contains an explicitly unresolved question or conjecture. This entry dates the formulation; it is not a newly verified upper or lower bound.
working_summary: Pattern homomorphism counting measures adjacency-preserving maps from a pattern into a host graph. The source asks for an explicit criterion on computable pattern classes in its degeneracy-sensitive counting framework. The intended dichotomy places every satisfying class in FPT and every remaining class on the #\(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard side. Such a criterion would explain a broad tractability boundary rather than only catalog individual easy patterns. The saved notation does not fully define the host restrictions or parameter combination, so those model details must be supplied before presenting the classification as self-contained.

title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
importance_reason: A central long-standing kernelization problem separating fixed-parameter solvability from polynomial-size preprocessing for directed cycle deletion. Existing score retained.
formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.
question_excerpt: Directed Feedback Vertex Set has a kernel of exponential size \(k O(k)\) , as the problem was shown fixed-parameter tractable by Chen et al. \([4], [\ldots ]\)
definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
answer_criterion: A complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof is required. Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.
context:
The 2016 source recalls a \(k^{O(k)}\)-size kernel following from fixed-parameter tractability, while explicitly leaving a polynomial-size kernel open. The missing improvement concerns how small a polynomial-time preprocessing can make every instance, rather than whether exponential dependence on the solution budget is possible.

The source proves polynomial kernels when deletion must leave an out-tree, an out-forest, or a directed pumpkin. These are stronger conditions than merely destroying directed cycles, so the results do not constitute a kernel for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set.

The WADS 2019 result, subsequently published in the 2025 journal article, gives a polynomial kernel with parameter \(k+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the size of a supplied vertex set whose removal leaves an underlying undirected graph of fixed bounded treewidth. Here treewidth at most \(\eta\) means that there are vertex bags indexed by a tree, each of size at most \(\eta+1\), covering all vertices and both endpoints of every edge, with the bags containing each vertex forming a connected subtree. The constant \(\eta\) is fixed. The extra \(\ell\) need not be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\); the general question therefore remains distinct.

The same work distinguishes the combined parameter \(k+\ell\) from parameterization by \(\ell\) alone. Its conditional obstruction for the latter does not rule out a polynomial kernel in the solution budget \(k\).

The edge-modification survey lists both Directed Feedback Vertex Set and Directed Feedback Arc Set in Open Problem 3.1. In the arc version, one deletes at most the budgeted number of arcs to destroy all directed cycles. The survey records polynomial-time reductions in both directions that preserve the solution-size parameter, so these two formulations have the same answer to the polynomial-kernel existence question. The separate imported survey record TCS-7033 is consolidated here.

The June 2025 study still identifies kernelization by the solution budget alone as a central open problem. Its positive results bound induced cycle length or use additional structure; those promises are absent from the present target.
why: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central test of how much efficient preprocessing can compress a fixed-parameter tractable cycle-hitting problem. A polynomial kernel would reduce every large instance with a small deletion budget to a polynomial amount of relevant information. A rigorous obstruction would distinguish directed cycle constraints from many successful kernelization settings.
status_note: Checked the full 2016 source and WADS 2019 author manuscript, plus the 2025 journal abstract, institutional publication record and author publication listing. The publisher blocked access to its full journal text, so detailed theorem scope is attributed to the checked conference manuscript. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the unrestricted solution-budget kernel. No independent proof verification.
progress: 2016: The source explicitly records the unrestricted polynomial-kernel question as open, alongside polynomial kernels for stricter deletion targets. | 2019: A combined-parameter polynomial kernel is proved using solution budget plus the size of a modulator to fixed treewidth. | 2025: The journal publication continues to identify the kernel parameterized only by solution size as a central open problem. | 2026-09-17: Consolidated the equivalent vertex/arc kernel question from the published edge-modification survey and checked the scope of the 2025 restricted-class progress.
working_summary: Directed Feedback Vertex Set asks whether deleting at most a given number of vertices destroys every directed cycle. The question is whether polynomial-time preprocessing can always replace an instance by one of size polynomial in that deletion budget. The replacement must preserve the exact yes or no answer. Known kernels with extra structural parameters or more restrictive deletion targets do not give this guarantee. Resolving the general question would clarify the limits of efficient compression for directed cycle problems.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
focus_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
question_excerpt: Retains the already selected deterministic, all-graphs, exactly-k constant-factor target and its importance score of 97. The cited literature studies several nearby approximation, gap and randomized formulations. This card fixes the deterministic variant explicitly, as in its 10 September formulation; the bit encoding and output convention make that existing target precise without imposing an extra graph promise.
definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation for this card.

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
context:
The exact cardinality makes the objective distinctive. A large region of moderate density can be an excellent answer when size is unrestricted or only bounded below, yet it need not contain a k-vertex region with a comparable fraction of the optimum for exactly k. The card asks for the actual selected vertices, so evaluating a continuous objective or estimating an optimum is insufficient.

Bhaskara and coauthors give an \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Their paper includes a deterministic combinatorial algorithm. Its title’s \(O(n^{1/4})\) endpoint requires quasipolynomial \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time in that analysis. The 2026 AAAI paper still describes the quarter-power-plus-epsilon bound as the general polynomial-time benchmark; neither bound is a universal constant.

Manurangsi proves that the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out polynomial-time approximation within \(n^{1/(\log\log n)^c}\) for some universal \(c>0\). The paper states ETH as the absence of a deterministic \(2^{o(m)}\)-time algorithm for 3SAT with \(m\) clauses. Its hard YES instances contain a \(k\)-clique, a property called perfect completeness. The result already excludes every fixed approximation constant if ETH holds, but ETH is an unproved assumption stronger than \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

The corresponding conclusion under only P≠NP remains a different issue. The May 2026 at-least-k paper explicitly says that even NP-hardness of a 1.001 approximation for Densest k-Subgraph is not known. This is consistent with the ETH lower bound: different hypotheses support different conclusions. A proof of conditional hardness is significant evidence, but does not establish the unconditional negative answer required by the card.

Chuzhoy and coauthors propose a Low-Degree CSP conjecture. Together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), it would exclude a polynomial-time \(2^{(\log n)^\varepsilon}\)-approximation for some \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Their stated consequence uses Cook-type reductions, which may make multiple oracle queries. The work also connects graph partitioning, dense coloring and other graph objectives, sometimes with quasipolynomial reductions. These are qualified conditional relationships rather than constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences.

The 2012 integrality gaps demonstrate limitations of specified strong semidefinite relaxations. They exhibit a separation between what a relaxation permits and the objective attained by genuine selected vertices. Such a separation constrains approximation arguments based on that relaxation; it does not rule out every polynomial-time algorithm.

Jones and coauthors give further Sum-of-Squares lower bounds in a planted-subgraph distinction model for \(k\le\sqrt n\). Their Theorem 1.1 constructs high-degree pseudoexpectations on random graphs, with approximately correct first-moment cardinality and normalization. These are the theorem’s particular relaxation constraints; they should not be silently replaced by all exact cardinality identities. This adds evidence about a broad algorithmic framework without proving unrestricted constant-factor hardness.

The AAAI 2026 continuous formulation is exact in a different sense. Under a sufficient penalty, its global optima correspond to the combinatorial problem, with an additional local-optimum correspondence. The accompanying convergence result controls a criticality residual under its stated algorithmic conditions. It does not guarantee a global optimum or a fixed approximation ratio on every input. Practical optimization progress can therefore coexist with the unresolved worst-case target.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi show that the absence of every constant-factor DkS approximation would rule out a \((3/2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for the at-least-k density problem, for each \(\varepsilon>0\). Their latter objective is edges per selected vertex and permits more than \(k\) vertices. Its known constant-factor algorithms do not solve the exactly-k problem.

The August 2026 preprint of Grigorescu and Taziki claims a linear-time approximation scheme for the unrestricted density objective. It also gives a near-linear-time at-least-k result with value at least \((1/2-\varepsilon)\) of that objective’s optimum. Both statements permit a different feasible cardinality from this card. They are relevant recent progress, but neither is a claimed resolution of its constant-factor question.
why: Densest k-Subgraph asks whether a prescribed number of vertices can capture a constant fraction of the greatest possible internal connectivity. Its approximation landscape is a central gap between available algorithms, conditional hardness and what follows from the usual P-versus-NP assumption. The answer also matters for several graph optimization objectives linked to its approximability.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The deterministic constant-factor question remains source-open in the inspected literature. The bounded later-work check is not an independent certification of every cited proof or an exhaustive absence-of-results claim.

title: Unique Games Conjecture
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
focus_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.
context:
Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. The conclusion leaves the near-one completeness in UGC unresolved. The 2025 journal publication of one part of the proof sequence records the historical role of its conditional intermediate theorem and still states full UGC separately as Conjecture 1.4.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims the \(4\)-to-\(1\) Games Conjecture with perfect completeness. Its constraints are projections in which each right-hand label has four preimages, rather than bijections. Theorem 1.6 is a major related hardness claim, with graph-coloring consequences, but does not prove the permutation-constraint UGC. The same introduction retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 and identifies completeness \(1/2\) as the existing Unique Games hardness frontier. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Yoshida’s May 2026 tolerant-testing preprint concerns adjacency-list queries and distinguishes small from larger optimum violation fractions. Its Theorem 1.1 requires \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\), where \(\rho\) is the larger violation threshold and \(c_q>0\) depends on the fixed alphabet. For the UGC gap, \(\rho=1-\delta\); the displayed assumption does not hold for every input size when the positive errors and alphabet are fixed. Thus the tester’s sublinear query bound does not refute this fixed-parameter, all-instance hardness statement.
why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The 14 September Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint explicitly retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 while claiming perfect-completeness 4-to-1 hardness in Theorem 1.6; that theorem has different constraints and does not settle this card. The May tolerant tester has a size-dependent error restriction and does not cover the full fixed-gap target. No matching proof or refutation of UGC was found in the bounded primary-source search. The formulation is complete; the recent preprint proof and historical proof sequences were not independently certified.
