working_summary: A Unique Games instance consists of explicitly listed vertices and permutation constraints between pairs of labels. UGC asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing almost completely satisfiable instances from those with arbitrarily small optimum value. The alphabet and deterministic reduction may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but must be independent of the growing input formula. A complete Lean proof must establish the full reduction statement or its negation over every alphabet and polynomial-time candidate reduction. The September 2026 perfect-completeness 4-to-1 claim and the known half-completeness Unique Games theorem do not establish this near-one-completeness permutation-constraint conjecture.

title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,C,K,q\) and one uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A\) such that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance \(I\) of encoding length \(N\) with \(k\ge1\) terminals, every execution halts within \(K(N+1)^q\) bit steps and outputs a feasible arc subset \(F\), and
\[\Pr\!\left[c(F)\le a\bigl(\log_2(k+2)\bigr)^C\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness, separately for each input. The graph is arbitrary and directed, with exactly represented nonnegative rational arc costs. All four constants and the program must be independent of the instance.
question_excerpt: The inherited 2024 Laekhanukit entry once claimed a general polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation. That claim was withdrawn, and the October 2025 replacement expressly assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation. This card retains the underlying general approximation question, not the restricted replacement theorem. The existing terminal-count factor, randomized success convention, always-feasible output, nonnegative rational costs, category and importance 96 are preserved; the review specifies the bit model and complete quantifier order.
definitions:
Instance. The vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge2\). A finite list of \(m\) indexed arcs specifies their tails and heads in \(V\); different indices denote different arcs even when their endpoints coincide. Loops and parallel arcs are allowed. The root is \(r\in V\), and the terminal set is \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), with \(k=|T|\ge1\). Every arc \(e\) has cost \(c_e=u_e/v_e\), where \(u_e\) is a nonnegative integer and \(v_e\) a positive integer, both supplied in binary. Zero costs and arbitrarily long cost descriptions are allowed. There is no planarity, acyclicity, degree, treewidth, depth or metric promise.

Reachability and feasibility. A directed path follows arc orientations from its first vertex to its last; it may be taken without repeated vertices. The input is promised feasible: every terminal is reachable from \(r\). A feasible output is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of arc indices such that the subgraph \((V,F)\) has a directed \(r\)-to-\(t\) path for every \(t\in T\). Nonterminal vertices may be used freely as intermediate vertices. Arc cost is paid once, regardless of how many terminal paths use it:
\[c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min\{c(F):F\subseteq E\text{ is feasible}\}.\]
The minimum exists because there are finitely many subsets and at least one is feasible. It may equal zero. The name “tree” does not impose an additional output-syntax condition: a feasible directed subgraph qualifies. Nonnegative costs also permit deletion of redundant arcs to obtain a rooted outward branching without increasing cost. Terminals are not required to be leaves.

Encoding and size. The graph, root, terminal list and every arc cost are explicit. One fixed encoding lists \(n,m,r,k\), all vertex labels \(1,\ldots,n\), the \(k\) distinct terminal labels in increasing order, and, for each indexed arc in order, its tail, head, numerator and denominator. Encode each nonnegative integer by its binary expansion preceded by its length in unary and a zero delimiter; the expansion of zero is the single bit zero. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. In particular \(N\ge n\), and every bit of every cost contributes to \(N\). Output identifies the selected arc indices, or equivalently their \(m\)-bit indicator vector.

Computation and randomness. Use an ordinary uniform multitape Turing machine with a finite program, read-only input, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. A step reads and updates a constant number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; a random step additionally supplies one independent fair bit. Reading the input, writing the entire solution, exact rational arithmetic and all preprocessing count in the bit time. No nonuniform advice, free optimization oracle, supplied fractional solution or unit-cost exact-real operation is available. The required bound holds for every random bit sequence, not just on average.

Guarantee. On each feasible input, every execution must return a feasible subset; on an event of probability at least \(2/3\), its cost must also satisfy the displayed ratio. On other executions the cost may be larger but feasibility is still required. When \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\), the successful output must have cost zero; an additive positive error is not allowed. The \(k+2\) convention makes the factor defined and positive also at one terminal. Choosing positive integer constants rather than arbitrary real constants at least one does not change existence, since the logarithm is greater than one and rounding constants upward only relaxes the bound. No behavior is prescribed on malformed encodings; infeasible well-formed instances may be detected and reported in polynomial time before applying the feasible-instance algorithm.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify an algorithm and fixed constants, and prove its bit running time on every execution, feasibility of every output, and the per-instance probability and cost bound throughout the full class. The proof must account for binary rational costs and zero optimum. A procedure with a variable time exponent depending on \(k\), or with uncharged access to a special fractional solution, does not meet the statement.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed power \(C\) of \(\log_2(k+2)\), every factor \(a\), every polynomial time bound and every permitted randomized program. For example, for every uniformly polynomial-time program that always returns feasible outputs and for every \(a,C\), it suffices to prove the existence of a feasible instance on which the probability of the requested ratio is less than \(2/3\). A lower bound for deterministic programs alone is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem must identify its unproved assumptions and does not by itself give an unconditional negative answer.

A polylogarithmic ratio in quasipolynomial time, an \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) ratio for each separately fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a theorem for planar graphs, or an integrality gap for one chosen relaxation is partial progress. Hardness below a particular logarithmic power leaves larger fixed powers possible. Expected-time or expected-cost analyses must be converted into the stated execution-time and success guarantees in the checked proof; they cannot simply replace those requirements.
context:
The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li prove a randomized \(O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)\) approximation with running time \(n^{O(\log^5 k)}\), in the asymptotic range where this expression is used. This is quasipolynomial: its exponent grows with the input parameter. The target here permits a larger fixed power of the logarithm, but requires one polynomial time exponent for every instance. The old classical paper’s original quasipolynomial \(O(\log^2 k)\) claim was corrected to \(O(\log^3 k)\) because of a height-reduction lemma; the 2019 paper explicitly records that correction.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The December 2024 general approximation claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, calls itself a rectification and assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation: for each terminal and arc, its flow is either zero or the whole purchased capacity. Theorem 1 states an expected-polynomial-time rounding result under this extra hypothesis. This is neither an algorithm that supplies the needed solution on every ordinary input nor a proof for arbitrary standard flow-LP optima. The live record still carries the reachability-proof withdrawal comment. The restricted result is recorded as a reported claim, not an independently verified general approximation.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s length-constrained work appeared on arXiv in July and was published on 9 September 2026. The published introduction still explicitly identifies the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question as open. For planar graphs, Theorem 2 gives logarithmic cost approximation with logarithmic length slack, while Theorem 3 gives a log-squared bound against a fractional relaxation with the same length slack. Removing the path-length constraint does not remove their planarity assumption. The related directed-forest theorem has multiple source–sink demands, a different target from one-root DST.
why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

working_summary: Directed Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost directed subgraph connecting one root to every designated terminal. The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed polynomial bit running time and a fixed polylogarithmic approximation factor in the number of terminals. Every output must be feasible, and each input must achieve the cost guarantee with probability at least two thirds, including instances with zero optimum. A complete Lean proof must establish those guarantees or rule out all permitted randomized algorithms and all fixed logarithmic powers. The September 2026 published literature still leaves this general problem open; planar algorithms, quasipolynomial results and the corrected fractional-solution claim have additional restrictions.

title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).
definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.
context:
Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.
why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
status_note: No proof or refutation located through 11 September 2026. The original exact-size regular-graph promise was checked separately from later weighted, volume and randomized variants. The August 2026 least-squares result is conditional on such a variant.
progress: 2010: Raghavendra–Steurer introduce the exact-size expansion promise and relate its hardness to Unique Games. | 2010 / 2012: Raghavendra–Steurer–Tulsiani establish reductions and conditional hardness for Balanced Separator and Minimum Linear Arrangement. | 2026-08: A sparse least-squares lower bound is obtained assuming a randomized weighted exact-volume SSE variant.
working_summary: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size? The target set occupies a fixed fraction \(\delta\) of the graph, with \(\delta\) chosen after the gap parameter \(\eta\). Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set. A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size. Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for metric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.
formal:
Determine, to absolute accuracy \(1/100\), the universal subtour-LP integrality gap for the symmetric metric traveling-salesperson problem:
\[
 \Gamma=\sup_{n\ge3}\ \sup_{c\in\mathcal M_n}
 \frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)}.
\]
Here \(\mathcal M_n\) is the set of all metrics on \(n\) labeled vertices, and the two optima are defined below. The target is this one dimensionless real number over all finite sizes, not the gap for one fixed number of vertices or for a restricted metric family.
question_excerpt: The source describes the four-thirds conjecture for the integrality gap of the symmetric metric subtour relaxation and writes the degree, cut and box constraints explicitly. This card retains the broader numerical task of determining that gap, with the project’s absolute 1/100 acceptance precision.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge3\), put \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E\) contain one undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\) for each pair of distinct vertices. A metric \(c\in\mathcal M_n\) is a real matrix satisfying
\[
 c_{uu}=0,\qquad c_{uv}=c_{vu}>0\ (u\ne v),\qquad
 c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\quad(u,v,w\in V).
\]
Costs may be arbitrary real numbers. No Euclidean embedding, graph-metric representation, sparsity or bound on the ratios of positive distances is assumed. Write \(c_{\{u,v\}}=c_{uv}\).

A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph: it visits each vertex once and returns to its start. Its cost is the sum of its \(n\) edge costs. The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)\) is the minimum of this cost over all such tours.

For a subset \(S\subseteq V\), let \(\delta(S)\) be the edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). For an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) and a real vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\), write \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_e\). The fractional optimum is the finite-dimensional linear program
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)=\min\quad &\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\\
 \text{subject to}\quad &x(\delta(\{v\}))=2 &&(v\in V),\\
 &x(\delta(S))\ge2 &&(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\\
 &0\le x_e\le1 &&(e\in E).
\end{aligned}
\]
All cut constraints are included. They enforce connectivity conditions in addition to the degree equations; this is not merely a fractional cycle-cover relaxation. A tour's incidence vector is feasible, so the LP is nonempty. Its feasible region is closed and bounded, hence the optimum exists. Positivity of the metric and the degree equations make both optima positive and the ratio well-defined.

The supremum ranges over every integer \(n\ge3\) and every such metric. It need not be achieved by a single finite instance. Multiplying all distances by the same positive scalar leaves the ratio unchanged. The known general upper bounds make \(\Gamma\) finite.

This is a numerical extremal question, with no running-time requirement on evaluation of a submitted mathematical expression for the answer. It does not ask for a fast tour-finding algorithm or for the worst ratio attained by any particular algorithm. A ratio proved against the integral tour optimum is not automatically a ratio against the possibly smaller LP optimum. Half-integral LP vectors, cycle-cut instances, graph metrics, Euclidean metrics and bounded vertex counts are proper restrictions of the domain unless a separate theorem proves they suffice for this supremum.

The classical four-thirds conjecture proposes \(\Gamma=4/3\). That exact equality would answer this card, but a different certified approximation meeting the stated accuracy also answers it. The benchmark tolerance is absolute error in the ratio itself, not a relative error and not an additive error in tour cost.
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
 |a-\Gamma|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
Equivalently, give explicit bounds \(L\le\Gamma\le U\) with \(U-L\le1/50\), proved in Lean, and take their midpoint. An exact value with a complete proof also qualifies. A certified finite expression can specify the answer; a decimal expansion or efficient evaluation algorithm is not required.

The upper control must cover every size and every metric in the domain. The lower control must establish an actual lower bound on the universal supremum; a family of increasingly large examples is allowed, and attainment is not required. An unevaluated restatement of the defining supremum, an unproved numerical estimate, a one-sided improvement, or finite enumeration without a theorem covering the remaining sizes is insufficient. Proving only the behavior of one rounding algorithm or one restricted family is insufficient unless accompanied by a reduction covering the full target. Accuracy within \(1/100\) does not by itself prove the exact four-thirds conjecture.
context:
The classical general bounds put the gap between \(4/3\) and \(3/2\). The conjecture proposes the lower endpoint. The numerical benchmark still requires substantially tighter two-sided control than that interval.

The 2022 improvement is explicitly LP-relative, so it bounds the integrality gap as well as an algorithmic approximation ratio. The distinction matters because the integral optimum and the LP optimum are different denominators.

The 2024 analysis records the universal bound \(\Gamma\le3/2-2.18\cdot10^{-34}\). This is progress below the historical threshold but does not determine the gap within \(1/100\).

The July 2026 \(10/7\) theorem analyzes a particular algorithm on half-integral cycle-cut instances. That restricted class already has gap at most \(4/3\), so the new algorithmic theorem neither worsens that class gap nor determines the unrestricted gap.

The September 2026 enumeration covers all metric instances through \(n=16\) and half-integral extreme points through \(n=18\). It supplies finite-size evidence; no reduction from all larger sizes is claimed here.

A September preprint claims a larger universal saving above \(2.05522\cdot10^{-30}\) below \(3/2\). Its theorem statement was checked, but its proof and certificate were not audited. Even the claimed improvement remains far short of the numerical precision required here.
why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.
status_note: The latest checked September 2026 primary sources still present the four-thirds gap as unresolved. The verified scopes of special-class results and finite enumeration do not yield a universal numerical determination within 1/100. The new explicit-saving preprint is recorded as an unaudited claim, and even its stated bound would not meet this card’s precision. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution.
progress: 2022: The general LP-relative guarantee improves strictly below three halves. | 2024: An improved explicit universal saving is established in the cited analysis. | 2026-07-03: The revised source studies an algorithm on the restricted half-integral cycle-cut class. | 2026-09-02: A preprint claims a larger, still very small, universal saving; not independently proof-audited. | 2026-09-08: The revised computational study extends general finite-size coverage to sixteen vertices.
working_summary: The metric traveling-salesperson problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. Its subtour linear program permits fractional edges while retaining degree and connectivity constraints. The target is the supremum of the tour optimum divided by the LP optimum over every finite symmetric metric. The four-thirds conjecture proposes an exact value, but this benchmark accepts absolute error at most 1/100. A complete Lean-checked answer must control the unrestricted supremum from both sides, without assuming it is attained or restricting the number of vertices.

title: Breaking two for metric k-Median
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,b\ge1\) such that, for every valid metric k-Median input \(I\) of bit length \(L\), every execution of \(A\) finishes within \(KL^b\) bit steps and returns a nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|\le k\), while
\[\Pr[\operatorname{cost}(S)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)]\ge2/3?\]
The input, cost and computation model are specified below. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial constants must work for every input, facility budget, metric size and distance precision. No unproved complexity assumption is included.
question_excerpt: The source asks for a tight metric k-Median approximation. Following the user's 17 September 2026 choice, this card selects the binary question of a fixed positive improvement below factor two, motivated by the standard LP gap and algorithms approaching two from above. This is an editorial choice of barrier, not a claim that the source conjectures two is optimal for every algorithm. The bounded-error randomized polynomial bit model, rational full metric and mandatory feasibility are retained. The coverage threshold remains conditional context, not an assumed value or an additional hypothesis of the target.
definitions:
An input is \(I=(v,C,F,k,d)\), with \(v\ge1\), \(V=[v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\), nonempty \(C,F\subseteq V\), \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). The sets may overlap. The full table \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is promised to be a metric: \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\), \(d(x,y)=0\) if and only if \(x=y\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points. There are no weights or capacities: each client in \(C\) has unit demand, and facilities must be chosen from the supplied \(F\).

For a nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), let \[\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min_{s\in S}d(c,s),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}=\min_{S\subseteq F,\ 1\le|S|\le k}\operatorname{cost}(S).\] Both minima are over finite nonempty sets. The output need only specify the selected facilities; no assignment or optimality certificate is required. Feasibility is mandatory even on random executions where the approximation inequality fails. No extra facilities are allowed in such executions or merely on average. Zero optimum is included: in that case the successful executions must have exactly zero cost. In a metric this case occurs precisely when \(C\subseteq F\) and \(|C|\le k\); a quotient by the optimum is never used in the definition.

Fix a concrete binary encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(t\), write \(u(t)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}\) has no leading zeros and \(a\) is its length. The input concatenates \(u(v)\), \(u(k)\), the two \(v\)-bit membership masks for \(C,F\), and the \(v^2\) rational entries in row-major order. An entry is a reduced pair \(p/q\) with integers \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), encoded by \(u(p)u(q)\); zero uses \(p=0,q=1\). The total length of this entire string is \(L\). A facility set is output as a \(v\)-bit membership mask. No bound on numerators or denominators is assumed beyond their finite encoding.

The model is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape, initially blank work and output tapes, and ordinary charged tape transitions. A random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. Running time counts every transition, including preprocessing, arithmetic, random-bit generation and output; the stated polynomial bound holds on every random execution. There is no advice depending on input length, oracle, quantum operation or unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Behavior on strings outside the input promise is irrelevant. Success probability is over the random bits for each fixed input, not over an input distribution, and no single choice of coins must work for all inputs.

The positive improvement is fixed before the input and is not an input parameter. The program and its time polynomial may depend on that fixed improvement, but cannot vary with the input size, facility budget or distance precision. There is no extra geometric or structural promise.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\) be the factors \(r\ge1\) achievable by one uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm per factor with the same all-executions feasibility and per-input \(2/3\) success convention. Put \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\mathcal R\). Known constant-factor algorithms make this set nonempty. The current target asks whether \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}<2\), not for a numerical determination of the infimum or its attainment.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting all stated guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies; there is no prescribed \(1/100\) improvement or numerical answer tolerance. Every execution must obey the polynomial bit-time bound and the facility budget, and each fixed input must satisfy the approximation inequality with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant saving for the allowed randomized algorithms. An expected-only facility budget, a fixed-parameter running time in \(k\), restricted metrics, or a result only about an LP integrality gap does not settle the target. A hardness conclusion under an unproved complexity assumption remains conditional.
context:
The source asks for a tight approximation result. The current card selects the strict-below-two question under the user's 17 September 2026 barrier rule. The standard LP has gap approaching two, while the established true-budget algorithms approach two from above. This makes a fixed improvement below two a concrete barrier question without assuming that two is the optimal ratio for unrestricted algorithms.

Metric k-Median chooses service locations and minimizes the sum of client travel distances. It also models selecting representatives for clustering. Clients and candidate facilities may be different sets, and the metric need not have Euclidean coordinates. The unresolved ratio measures how much optimization quality is lost when an arbitrary metric instance must be processed in polynomial time.

The known unconditional bounds give \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\le2\). The upper endpoint follows from the \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); it does not assert a factor-two algorithm. Under \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), the coverage hardness below gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\ge1+2/e\approx1.73576\). These are different kinds of bounds. In particular, \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=1\).

Feige’s Theorem 5.3 gives an NP-hard coverage gap: all elements can be covered by \(k\) sets, or every such collection covers at most a \(1-1/e+\eta\) fraction, for any fixed \(\eta>0\). The associated client–facility metric uses separate copies of elements and sets, with cross distances one for incidence and three otherwise, and distance two between distinct points on the same side. Covering a fraction \(p\) corresponds to cost \((3-2p)|U|\), where \(U\) is the universe. Thus the gap becomes \(1\) versus \(1+2/e-2\eta\) per client.

This gap also explains the randomized assumption. A returned feasible solution of sufficiently small cost certifies the positive side; on a negative instance no such solution exists. Consequently a bounded-error algorithm beating the threshold would put the underlying NP-hard decision problem in \(\mathrm{RP}\), the class with polynomial time, one-sided error and no false acceptance. The exclusion for this card is therefore conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than justified by \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 Theorem 10 instead derives the classical k-Median lower bound from a Set Cover approximation barrier. The historical complexity assumption stated there is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{O(\log\log n)})\). Feige’s ordinary NP-hardness theorem for Max k-Cover and its metric gap distinguish the stronger coverage-based conclusion from the assumption in that earlier Set Cover argument.

Theorem 1.1 of the STOC 2025 paper, retained in its May 2026 full revision, gives a randomized polynomial-time \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with a feasible facility budget. The separate Theorem 1.2 allows extra centers, but this is not the budget of the final theorem. Lemma 1.4 relates bounded integer distances to general distances, so the result is not confined to a fixed distance precision.

Byrka and coauthors’ April 2026 paper supplies another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for metric k-Median, in Corollary 1.2. Its intermediate guarantee opens \(k\) facilities only in expectation; the final approximation restores the facility budget with an \(\varepsilon\) loss. This distinction matters: an expected budget permits some outcomes with too many facilities and does not meet the card’s all-executions feasibility requirement. The new result does not narrow the interval between the known conditional lower endpoint and two.

The standard linear relaxation has fractional openings \(0\le y_s\le1\), assignments \(0\le x_{c,s}\le y_s\), \(\sum_s x_{c,s}=1\) for every client, and \(\sum_s y_s\le k\), minimizing \(\sum_{c,s}d(c,s)x_{c,s}\). Its integrality gap approaches two. For a unit-edge star with \(q\ge3\) leaves, all vertices as facilities, leaves as clients and \(k=q-1\), the integral optimum is two. A feasible fractional solution has center opening \(1/(q-1)\), each leaf opening \((q-2)/(q-1)\), and each client assigned to its own leaf and the center in those proportions. Its cost is \(q/(q-1)\), yielding a gap at least \(2(q-1)/q\). This is a barrier for that relaxation, not an unconditional computational lower bound against the true integral optimum.

Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 Theorem 1 attains \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in time \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\). That fixed-parameter guarantee allows a dependence on \(k\) which need not be polynomial. Here \(k\) is part of the unrestricted input, so the parameterized result does not establish the corresponding polynomial-time factor.

The March 2026 low-dimensional Euclidean work improves approximation-scheme running times by using geometric structure. Its guarantees do not apply to arbitrary metric tables.

The July 2026 spectral dual-fitting preprint improves k-Means guarantees in Euclidean and general metrics. That objective sums squared distances, which changes both approximation and hardness constants; the paper does not give a smaller general k-Median ratio.

A polynomial-time factor \(2-\varepsilon\), for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), would cross the selected barrier for general metric clustering. Feasibility, probability and runtime must refer to the same input model. A restricted metric theorem, an LP gap or an expected-budget guarantee addresses a different question.
why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.
status_note: The source review through 16 September 2026 recorded true-budget \(2+\eta\) approximations for every fixed \(\eta>0\), and a \(1+2/e\) lower bound conditional on NP differing from RP in the randomized model. The standard LP has integrality gap approaching two; that is not general computational hardness. On 17 September the target was changed to existence of any fixed-factor improvement below two. The primary May 2026 revision was checked for this barrier context; no new exhaustive later-work or proof certification is claimed.
progress: 1998: Feige proves the \(1- 1/e\) hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the \(1+2/e\) metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction. | 2002: Jain–Mahdian–Saberi give the classical k-Median lower bound via Set Cover approximation; Theorem 10 states the historical reduction. | 2019: Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li reach \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k, not unrestricted polynomial time. | 2025–19 May 2026: Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time \(2+\varepsilon\) approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem. | 10 March 2026: Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting. | 16 July 2026: Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective. | 7 April 2026: Iterative randomized rounding yields another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with the true facility budget (Corollary 1.2); its intermediate expected-budget guarantee is distinct.
working_summary: Metric k-Median selects at most \(k\) supplied facilities and minimizes the sum of distances from clients to their nearest selected facility. The question asks for a uniform randomized polynomial-time approximation with factor \(2-\varepsilon\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Every execution must return a feasible set within polynomial bit time, and the cost guarantee must hold with probability at least two thirds on each input. The same improvement must apply to all facility budgets and arbitrary finite rational metrics, however small the chosen positive constant is. Algorithms approaching two from above and the standard LP's gap approaching two do not supply such a strict improvement.

title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Resolve a basic approximation threshold for a widely used covering primitive.
formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G\) of input bit length \(L\), the algorithm halts within \(B(L+1)^k\) Turing-machine steps and returns a vertex cover \(S\) satisfying
\[|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G),\qquad
\tau(G)=\min\{|T|:T\subseteq V(G),\ T\text{ is a vertex cover of }G\}?\]
The same positive improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the same algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no structural promise. Vertices have unit cost. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm-existence theorem or its unconditional negation.
definitions:
Graphs and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). For \(n=0\), the vertex set and edge set are empty. Edges are unordered pairs, with no loops or multiplicities. A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover if every \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has \(u\in S\) or \(v\in S\). The quantity \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of such a set; the minimum exists because the finite set \(V\) itself covers every edge. All vertices have weight one, so the cost is the number selected. If \(E=\varnothing\), then \(\tau(G)=0\), and the approximation inequality requires the output \(S=\varnothing\). Isolated vertices are allowed. The class includes disconnected, bipartite, nonbipartite, sparse and dense graphs without imposing any of those promises.

Input and output. The input is the full \(n\)-by-\(n\) binary adjacency matrix, preceded by a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\). One fixed encoding is \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(n+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(n+1)\rfloor+1\), followed by the matrix entries in row order. A valid input has a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal, and entry \((u,v)\) equals one exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Its bit length is \(L=n^2+2b+1\). This explicitly includes all vertices, including isolated ones; there is no succinct matrix generator or graph oracle. The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector, with entry one exactly at selected vertices. Reading the input and writing this output count toward time. No guarantee is required on malformed encodings. Every labeling of the vertices by \([n]\) is a valid input order on which the guarantees must hold.

Computation. The algorithm is one deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step reads and writes one symbol on each tape, changes finite control and moves each head by at most one position. Work tapes are initially blank. No randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. Integer or rational arithmetic, if used internally, is performed on finite binary representations with all bit operations charged. The time bound is worst-case over every valid input, rather than expected or amortized time. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once with the algorithm, not supplied as a graph-dependent accuracy parameter.

Quantifiers and accuracy. The order is
\[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists A\ \exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G.\]
The time constants may depend on this chosen algorithm and improvement but not on the input graph. Requiring a rational improvement does not change the original real-constant question: any positive real improvement implies a smaller positive rational one. The objective inequality is multiplicative, with no additive error, asymptotic slack or exceptional small graphs. A guarantee strictly below two separately on each finite graph, such as \(2-1/n\), does not give one improvement valid for all sizes. The numerical benchmark tolerance of 0.01 is not an additive tolerance on this approximation-ratio existence question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the formal statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), one deterministic program and common polynomial time constants, and prove termination, valid-cover output and \(|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\) on every valid adjacency-matrix input, including empty and edgeless graphs. A negative answer must prove that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every deterministic program having a polynomial running-time bound on all valid inputs, some graph produces an invalid cover encoding, an uncovered edge, or a cover larger than \((2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\). It must rule out all such algorithms, not merely one rounding scheme or restricted family. A conditional result under UGC, \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved hypothesis does not establish this unconditional negation. A vanishing improvement, experiments, an estimate of the optimum without a cover, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not meet the stated universal guarantee.
context:
A cover chooses vertices so that every edge is touched. A star with many leaves has optimum one, while a triangle has optimum two. The complement of a vertex cover is an independent set, but the identity between their optimum sizes does not preserve multiplicative approximation factors. This card uses unit vertex costs, retaining the unweighted target selected at admission.

The original seminar source discusses weighted Vertex Cover, its factor-two approximation, and its role in the primal-dual framework. The event was on 11 December 2000, and the online account is a summary by Claire Kenyon. It motivates the approximation barrier; it does not supply a contemporary status check or specify the full deterministic bit model used here.

Polynomial-time approximation bounds of the form \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\) improve on two at each sufficiently large fixed size. The improvement nevertheless tends to zero as \(n\) grows. Karakostas’s result therefore does not answer whether one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) works on all inputs. The present deterministic target also requires the stated worst-case bit-time and output guarantees.

The 2-to-2 Games line of work proves NP-hardness of approximation within \(\sqrt2-\eta\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\). The 2025 Khot–Minzer–Safra journal account explains how later work proved the combinatorial hypotheses in its original reduction. This hardness gives an algorithmic impossibility consequence under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), but leaves a gap up to two and does not unconditionally rule out the algorithms quantified here.

Khot and Regev prove NP-hardness below every fixed factor \(2-\varepsilon\), assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. Thus UGC together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would imply a negative answer to this card. Conversely, a deterministic improvement would contradict that conjunction; it would not by itself unconditionally refute UGC. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), an exact polynomial-time cover algorithm would give a positive answer.

Claimed improvements require version and quantifier checks. The latest Salvador preprint, version 3 posted 6 July 2026, labels its universal \(7/4\) ratio as Conjecture 1, supported by finite experiments. The earlier version’s asserted \(7/5\) theorem is not the current conclusion. The latest version therefore supplies no proved fixed improvement for every graph.

The inspected March 2026 Hallelujah preprint states \(|S|<2\tau(G)\) for each finite nonempty graph, not a graph-independent positive gap. Its explicit lexicographic selection rule also has a direct limiting example: on \(K_{r,r}\) with the two parts labeled by alternating odd and even numbers, all degrees tie and the selected union has \(2r-1\) vertices while the optimum is \(r\). Its ratio is therefore \(2-1/r\). This observation concerns that preprint’s stated rule; the separately published version was accessible only through its abstract. Neither this pointwise claim nor its stated UGC interpretation certifies the target here.

The 6 September 2026 Karthik–Minzer preprint reports stronger NP-hardness for vertex cover in hypergraphs: factor \(1+\sqrt2-\eta\) for three-element edges, and \(k-\eta\) for fixed edge size \(k\ge4\). Ordinary graphs have two-element edges and are outside those new parameter ranges. The recent perfect-completeness four-to-one-games result likewise continues to list \(\sqrt2\) as the graph Vertex Cover hardness frontier in its introduction.
why: Vertex Cover is a basic covering problem with a long-standing gap between its factor-two algorithmic benchmark and known unconditional hardness thresholds. A fixed improvement would distinguish the true computational limit from a barrier shared by many methods. Ruling out every such algorithm would require an unconditional complexity separation, so the logical strength of the chosen question must remain explicit.

Salvador version 3 explicitly leaves its 7/4 ratio conjectural; earlier version-2 claims do not represent its current result. The inspected Hallelujah preprint states a pointwise strict ratio, and its specified selection rule has ratios 2-1/r on alternating-labeled complete bipartite graphs, so it does not supply a fixed improvement. working_summary: A vertex cover selects at least one endpoint of every edge of a finite simple undirected graph. The problem asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm always finds a cover within a fixed factor strictly below two of the minimum size. The positive improvement must be independent of graph size, and the output and worst-case bit-time guarantees apply to every explicitly listed graph, including edgeless ones. A complete Lean proof must establish such an algorithm or unconditionally rule out every polynomial-time candidate, rather than assume an unproved hardness hypothesis. Known vanishing improvements, Unique-Games-based hardness, recent hypergraph results and the checked heuristic claims do not provide the required unconditional fixed-gap resolution.

title: Does a fixed d-to-1 Games conjecture imply Unique Games?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central implication between hardness hypotheses with broad approximation consequences, now directly connected to the claimed perfect-completeness four-to-one theorem. Its exact gap quantifiers are essential.
formal:
Is the following implication true for the classical constraint games and deterministic polynomial reductions defined below?
\[\bigl(\exists\,d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge2\text{ and }D_d\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{UGC}.\]
Here \(D_d\) is the perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one Games conjecture with \(d\) fixed independently of the soundness parameter; \(\mathrm{UGC}\) is the full near-perfect-completeness Unique Games conjecture. Equivalently, for every fixed \(d\ge2\), does \(D_d\) imply \(\mathrm{UGC}\)? The card retains the forward implication singled out in the saved source excerpt.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether the d-to-one conjecture implies the Unique Games conjecture, and separately whether the reverse implication holds.
definitions:
A constraint game has two finite disjoint vertex sets \(U,V\) and a nonempty finite list of edges \(e=(u_e,v_e)\in U\times V\). Repeated edges, with their own constraints, are allowed and count separately. Every edge has equal weight in the list. No regularity or bounded-degree promise is imposed. All vertices, edges and constraint tables are explicitly encoded with binary integers; there is no succinct representation or compressed multiplicity.

For integers \(d\ge2\) and \(r\ge1\), a \(d\)-to-one game gives left vertices labels in \([dr]\), right vertices labels in \([r]\), and every edge a surjective map \(\pi_e:[dr]\to[r]\) with exactly \(d\) preimages of every right label. Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). An assignment is a pair of maps \(\alpha:U\to[dr]\) and \(\beta:V\to[r]\); it satisfies edge \(e\) when \(\pi_e(\alpha(u_e))=\beta(v_e)\). Its value is the fraction of list entries it satisfies. The optimum \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the maximum of this fraction over all assignments. It lies in \([0,1]\) and is a finite rational maximum. Perfect completeness means the YES instance has optimum exactly one.

A Unique Game has the same bipartite constraint format, a common alphabet \([k]\) on both sides, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[k]\to[k]\) on each edge. Assignment, satisfaction and optimum are defined by the same equality. This is a classical combinatorial optimum; no entangled, interactive, nonsignalling or quantum strategy is used.

For a promised pair of disjoint YES and NO sets of such instances, NP-hard means that Boolean 3-SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to that pair. Specifically, a single finite Turing program maps every explicitly encoded Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause to a valid game. It maps satisfiable formulas into YES and unsatisfiable formulas into NO and uses at most \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps on every length-\(L\) input, for fixed constants \(K,c\). Literal indices, signs, clauses, vertex names and table entries use ordinary explicit binary encodings. An algorithm for the promised game need have no specified behaviour outside YES and NO. NP-hardness here asserts the existence of a reduction; it does not assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

For a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \(D_d\) to mean:
\[\forall\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1),\ \exists r\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapD}_{d,r}(1,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard},\]
where the YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\) and the NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The integer \(d\) is outside the quantifier over \(\gamma\). The alphabet size \(r\), reduction program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(d,\gamma\), but not on the formula length. Allowing \(d\) to increase as \(\gamma\) decreases would be a different antecedent.

Define full \(\mathrm{UGC}\) by
\[\forall\eta,\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/4),\ \exists k\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapUG}_{k}(1-\eta,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard}.\]
Its YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\eta\) and its NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The constants \(k\) and the polynomial reduction may depend on both gap parameters. The rational, small-gap convention gives disjoint promises and is equivalent to requesting all arbitrarily small positive gaps: smaller rational gaps imply the less stringent real gaps. There is no demand for one alphabet or one polynomial degree working for all gap choices, or for a uniform algorithm generating all the reductions from their parameters.

The target is the implication between these mathematical hardness propositions. It is not a question about formal unprovability in a separately chosen axiom system, nor is it limited to one specified family of gadget or oracle reductions. The reverse implication from UGC to perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one hardness is a separate question mentioned in the source, not an additional requirement on this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative answer must establish full UGC from the assumption that \(D_d\) holds for some fixed \(d\ge2\), respecting the gap quantifiers and the deterministic polynomial reductions. An unconditional proof of UGC would also establish the implication. A negative answer must prove the conjunction \((\exists d\ge2\ D_d)\land\neg\mathrm{UGC}\); showing only that a particular reduction loses completeness, or that some restricted reduction class cannot work, does not refute the implication. Hardness of Unique Games with a fixed YES value such as \(1/d\) or \(1/2\) is not the required near-one YES value for every \(\eta>0\). Exact asymptotic proof is required; the numerical approximation tolerance does not alter these logical statements.
context:
Both games ask for globally consistent labels subject to local compatibility rules. Unique Games has one allowed right label for each left label and also one allowed left label for each right label. A d-to-one constraint keeps the first property but permits d compatible left labels for a given right label. This additional freedom changes which perfect-completeness gaps are possible.

The source already proves a weaker implication: its Appendix B gives one-sided Unique Games hardness with completeness 1/d. This is one fixed positive completeness constant. Full UGC instead requires a YES value arbitrarily close to one while keeping soundness arbitrarily close to zero. The weaker implication therefore does not answer the source question.

Perfectly satisfiable Unique Games can be checked efficiently by trying a starting label in each connected component and propagating the forced labels. The conjecture deliberately permits a small positive fraction of unsatisfied constraints in the YES case. Substituting exact satisfiability for near-satisfiability would change the problem.

The 2025 journal account explains the sequence that proved almost-perfect-completeness two-to-one hardness. It retains exact perfect completeness as a separate conjecture and states full UGC separately. These distinctions matter even though all the parameters may be described informally as almost satisfiable games.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness for every positive soundness constant. If correct, its Theorem 1.6 establishes D₄ and hence the antecedent of this card. Under that theorem, the forward implication is equivalent to UGC itself: an implication proof would give UGC, while UGC immediately implies the implication. This is a logical consequence of the claimed theorem, not a claim that UGC has been proved. The new full proof has not been independently audited here.

This connection would turn a hardness theorem with several compatible labels into the general Unique Games hypothesis underlying many sharp approximation thresholds. Keeping alphabet size, constraint multiplicity, completeness and soundness explicit prevents a useful weaker hardness theorem from being mistaken for that conclusion.
why: An implication would connect exact satisfiability in many-to-one constraint games with the near-satisfiable permutation games used to predict sharp approximation thresholds. The new perfect-completeness four-to-one claim makes this relationship especially consequential: accepting that theorem would make the requested implication as strong as full UGC.
status_note: Source-open as a full implication to UGC. The 2016 source’s exact definitions and complete one-sided implication proof were checked, as were the 2025 journal definitions and historical theorem scope. The 14 September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness D₄, making the antecedent true if its proof is correct; its stated theorem does not settle the forward implication or UGC. Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The recent full proof and the other external proof sequences have not been independently audited or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2016: The source explicitly leaves both conjecture implications open and proves the forward implication only to its weaker one-sided Unique Games conjecture, with completeness 1/d. | 2018–2025: The two-to-one proof sequence establishes an almost-perfect-completeness result; the 2025 journal account continues to distinguish full UGC and perfect-completeness d-to-one hardness. | 2026-09-14: A new preprint claims D₄ with exact perfect completeness. Its stated main theorem establishes the antecedent if correct, but does not establish the Unique Games conclusion.
working_summary: The question asks whether perfect-completeness d-to-one hardness for any fixed d implies the full Unique Games conjecture. Every game is an explicit finite classical constraint system, and hardness means deterministic polynomial reductions from Boolean satisfiability. Known direct conversion gives a fixed positive Unique Games completeness rather than a value arbitrarily close to one. A September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness, which would establish the antecedent if correct. The implication remains a separate target and, conditional on that theorem, is equivalent to proving full UGC.

title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for asymmetric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Would identify the fundamental relaxation gap for asymmetric travelling salesman.
formal: Determine \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=\sup\){\(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c): n\ge 2, c\) is a nonnegative directed metric on n vertices, \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)>0\)}, using the tour and linear program below.
definitions:
A directed metric is a function \(c:V	imes V	o R\ge 0\) with \(c(i,i)=0\) and \(c(i,k)\le c(i,j)+c(j,k)\) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc \((i,j)\) for each \(i
e j\) and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) is the minimum over all such cycles. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta ^{+}(S)=\{(i,j):i\in S,j
otin S\}\) and \(\delta ^{-}(S)=\{(i,j):i
otin S,j\in S\}\); for a set of arcs F write \(x(F)=\sum_{(i,j)\in F} x_{ij}\). \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) minimizes \(\sum_{i
e j} c(i,j)x_{ij}\) over real variables \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) subject to \(x(\delta ^{+}(\{v\}))=x(\delta ^{-}(\{v\}))=1\) for every v, and \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\). The degree equalities imply \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))=x(\delta ^{-}(S))\), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. Zero-LP instances are excluded from the ratio; they also have zero tour optimum. Indeed, the positive support of a zero-cost feasible solution is strongly connected by the cut constraints, and directed triangle inequalities then give zero distance between every ordered pair. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path. The supremum is over every finite size and is not required to be attained. The usual factor-two conjecture asserts \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), taking account of known approaching lower-bound families.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
context:
This card determines the universal subtour-LP integrality gap. The factor-two conjecture is a proposed exact answer; refuting that factor alone would not determine a larger gap.

A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.
why: Would identify the fundamental relaxation gap for asymmetric travelling salesman.

Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established factor-2 proof or counterexample. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

working_summary: Asymmetric TSP finds a cheapest directed Hamiltonian tour in a directed metric. The subtour relaxation has fractional arcs with unit incoming and outgoing degree and at least one outgoing arc across each cut. The target is the supremum tour-to-LP ratio over all positive-LP finite instances. The familiar factor-two conjecture supplies one candidate for the value, and zero-LP metrics cause no division convention ambiguity. The Lean acceptance tolerance is absolute error 0.01 for the universal ratio.

title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine whether a central graph-decomposition objective admits approximation independent of instance size.
formal:
Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\) and \(K>0\), an integer constant \(d\ge1\), and one uniform classical randomized Turing machine \(A\) with the following property? For every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge2\) vertices, every execution halts within \(K(n+1)^d\) bit operations and outputs a nonempty proper vertex set \(S\). For each fixed input graph,
\[
 \Pr\!\left[\varphi_G(S)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\right]\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne T\subsetneq V(G)}\varphi_G(T),
 \qquad
 \varphi_G(T)=\frac{|E(T,V(G)\setminus T)|}{|T|\,|V(G)\setminus T|}.
\]
The same machine and constants must work for all these graphs.
question_excerpt: The notes define the uniform cut objective as boundary capacity divided by the number of separated vertex pairs and present the square-root-logarithmic ARV approximation. This card asks whether a constant factor is possible on all simple unweighted graphs, retaining the input restriction of the admitted card.
definitions:
The vertex set is \(V(G)=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input consists of \(n\) in binary and the explicit symmetric \(n\times n\) Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices and has unit capacity; there are no parallel edges, additional weights or demand inputs. All finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge2\) are allowed, including disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and graphs with no edges.

For a set \(T\), the boundary \(E(T,V(G)\setminus T)\) consists of the edges with exactly one endpoint in \(T\). Every edge is counted once. The denominator counts unordered vertex pairs separated by the cut, each with demand one. It is positive for every allowed nonempty proper set. Thus all objective values and the minimum are well-defined nonnegative rational numbers. The word uniform refers to these equal pair demands, not to equal degrees or to a random input graph.

The output is the length-\(n\) Boolean membership vector of \(S\). On every execution it must encode a nonempty proper subset. The approximation guarantee, which may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), is required separately for each input graph; it is not an average over graphs. Since every output is feasible, its value is automatically at least the optimum. If the graph is disconnected, the optimum is zero, so success requires an output cut with no crossing edge, not merely an additive approximation. There is no balance requirement on the sizes of the two sides, and either a set or its complement represents the same cut value.

The machine uses independent unbiased random bits and otherwise has a fixed finite deterministic program. The total bit-operation bound holds on every possible random tape and includes reading the input, generating and processing random bits, all numerical computations and preprocessing, and writing the membership vector. There is no advice, oracle, uncharged preprocessing, exact real-arithmetic primitive or quantum computation. Intermediate numbers must have finite encodings and their manipulation is charged. The polynomial bound in \(n\) is equivalent to a polynomial bound in the specified explicit input length. All constants are absolute and independent of the input; the target does not prescribe their numerical values.

The output requirement is a cut, not merely an estimate of its optimum value. The denominator is the product of cardinalities above; replacing it by degree volumes gives a different objective. General unequal pair demands, a promised balanced cut and restrictions to regular, dense or algebraically structured graph families are not part of this input model.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a machine and constants exist, including output feasibility, the per-input approximation probability and the worst-case bit-time bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of their logical negation.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed finite approximation factor and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm in this model. A growing integrality gap for one linear or semidefinite relaxation does not by itself do this. Conditional inapproximability under an unproved complexity hypothesis establishes only that conditional assertion, with its assumptions and randomized-algorithm implications stated explicitly.

A factor growing with \(n\), an additive-error estimate, a number without a cut, or a result only on a special graph class does not establish the positive target. Results for arbitrary weighted capacities or demands must be shown to cover the selected unweighted uniform instances; hardness for a broader class alone is insufficient.
context:
The ARV approximation gives a factor \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\). The target asks whether the dependence on graph size can be removed entirely, while retaining polynomial running time and an explicit cut output.

The 2025 algorithm simplifies and parallelizes the existing approximation framework; the stated quality guarantee still grows with graph size.

Near-optimal approximation is known for low-degree Abelian Cayley graphs with a running-time dependence on degree and accuracy. The algebraic and degree restrictions prevent that statement from covering all input graphs here.

The September 2026 preprint states new exactness and gap bounds for the Goemans–Linial relaxation on finite Abelian Cayley graphs. These are recent restricted-model claims, not a verified general constant-factor algorithm or impossibility theorem.

The sharp 2025 rounding result concerns arbitrary capacities and demands and the performance of a particular SDP. Its tight relaxation gap does not characterize the best possible algorithm for unweighted uniform Sparsest Cut.
why: A constant approximation would bound the quality loss for finding sparse graph separations independently of graph size, addressing a central question connecting approximation algorithms and metric geometry.
status_note: The bounded primary-source check through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of general constant-factor approximation for the selected simple unweighted uniform objective. The 2025 improvements and September 2026 preprint retain graph-class, approximation-factor or relaxation restrictions. The full proof of the recent preprint was not independently audited.
progress: 2016-07-04: The source notes present the uniform objective and the ARV approximation. | 2025-09-15: A near-optimal approximation is obtained for low-degree Abelian Cayley graphs. | 2025-10-01: A simpler, parallelizable algorithm retains a square-root-logarithmic approximation factor. | 2026-09-04: A new preprint studies integrality gaps on finite Abelian Cayley graphs; its scope does not settle general constant approximation.
working_summary: Uniform Sparsest Cut minimizes the number of crossing edges divided by the number of separated vertex pairs. The input is an arbitrary explicitly given simple unweighted undirected graph. The question asks for one randomized polynomial-time algorithm returning a cut within an absolute constant factor of optimum. Success is required separately on every graph, including finding a zero-boundary cut with the required probability when the optimum is zero. A complete Lean-checked resolution must settle the all-graph algorithmic target rather than the performance of one relaxation or a special graph class.

title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine whether a defining semidefinite approximation threshold follows from ordinary NP-hardness alone.
formal:
Let
\[
 \alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=
 \min_{0<\theta\le\pi}\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}.
\]
Is the following statement true? For every rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1-\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\), there exist rational constants \(0<b<a\le1\), with
\[
 \frac ba<\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon,
\]
and a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R_\varepsilon\) from 3-SAT to simple unweighted Max-Cut such that, for every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), its output graph has at least one edge and satisfies
\[
 \varphi\text{ satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow
       \operatorname{val}(R_\varepsilon(\varphi))\ge a,
 \qquad
 \varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow
       \operatorname{val}(R_\varepsilon(\varphi))\le b?
\]
The statement assumes no hardness conjecture.
question_excerpt: The source proves optimal Max-Cut inapproximability at the Goemans–Williamson ratio under the Unique Games Conjecture. The card asks whether ordinary unconditional NP-hardness can yield gaps arbitrarily close to that same ratio, retaining its approved simple-graph formulation.
definitions:
A graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected: there are no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. Write \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and \(m=|E|\ge1\). A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), representing the bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\). Its size is the number of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). Define the normalized optimum by
\[
 \operatorname{val}(G)=\frac1m\max_{S\subseteq V}
       |\{\{u,v\}\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}|.
\]
