The constants \(a\) and \(b\) are fractions of all edges, not numbers of edges. The gap promise consists of YES graphs with value at least \(a\) and NO graphs with value at most \(b\). A procedure distinguishing these cases has no required behavior on graphs with value strictly between \(b\) and \(a\). The reduction must map every input formula into one of the two promised cases according to its satisfiability.

A 3-CNF formula is an explicit finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean literals, with each literal a variable or its negation. Satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values makes every clause true. Empty clauses are false and an empty conjunction is true. Variables and signs are listed in a standard binary encoding; let \(L\) be the full encoding length. Equivalent explicit encodings related by polynomial-time translations give the same reduction notion.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program, uniform over all input lengths. There must exist constants \(K\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that it halts within \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every valid formula. It outputs the graph explicitly, for example by its vertex count and binary adjacency matrix. Thus its output size is also polynomial in \(L\). A single output graph is required; oracle calls, a randomized reduction and a succinct implicit graph do not meet this definition.

The rationals \(a,b\), the program and its polynomial bound may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(\varphi\) or \(L\). The question does not require one reduction with polynomial dependence on the bit length of \(\varepsilon\), or an algorithm that constructs the reduction from \(\varepsilon\). Once chosen, each reduction itself is uniform and efficient in its formula input.

The constant \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) is defined by the exact real expression above, with angles in radians and the usual constants \(\pi\) and cosine. Its approximate value \(0.878567\) is only explanatory; substituting a rounded decimal does not define the target. A multiplicative retained-fraction guarantee \(r\) for this maximization problem means a cut of size at least \(r\) times the optimal size. A gap with \(b/a<r\) separates satisfiable and unsatisfiable reductions for such a guaranteed approximation.

Here NP-hardness means precisely the displayed reduction from 3-SAT. It is a claim about the existence of polynomial-time reductions, not an assumed inequality between complexity classes. Proving those reductions does not itself prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The Unique Games Conjecture, Gap-ETH and other unproved hardness assumptions are not premises of the proposition.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or of its logical negation.

A positive answer must establish the reduction for every specified rational \(\varepsilon\), with rational thresholds, polynomial output size, deterministic polynomial bit complexity, and both correctness implications for all formulas. If an intermediate construction uses weighted graphs, parallel edges or a different constraint problem, its conversion to the required simple unweighted graph must be included with the required gap bound.

A negative answer must prove that some rational \(\varepsilon\) in the stated interval admits no pair of thresholds and deterministic polynomial-time reduction satisfying all the conditions. It is not enough to refute one proposed reduction or one conjecture used by a known construction.

An implication conditional on an unproved Unique Games assumption does not settle the unconditional proposition. An integrality gap for a particular relaxation, or an approximation algorithm without the further theorem needed to exclude NP-hardness, likewise does not alone establish either answer. No fixed additive numerical tolerance replaces the universal epsilon quantifier.
context:
The Goemans–Williamson algorithm supplies the approximation benchmark through semidefinite programming and randomized rounding.

Håstad establishes unconditional hardness for retained fractions strictly above \(16/17\). This leaves a gap to \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\); the reciprocal convention in that paper should not be confused with the fraction used here.

The source reaches the Goemans–Williamson threshold assuming Unique Games. The present target asks for the same limiting hardness scale without that conjectural premise.

The 2025 improvement assumes a structural abundance of edge-disjoint triangles. It does not assert a better approximation for every graph or settle unconditional hardness.

The July 2026 preprint states sharp hardness for three-part cuts and for a quantum product-state objective. Both statements explicitly retain the Unique Games assumption, so even their stated scope does not resolve this classical two-part question.
why: An unconditional reduction at this threshold would explain the limit of a landmark semidefinite approximation algorithm using ordinary NP-hardness, without adding a separate hardness conjecture.
status_note: The checked primary sources give unconditional hardness at the weaker 16/17 scale and matching Goemans–Williamson hardness under Unique Games. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified unconditional resolution of the exact simple-unweighted-graph gap statement. Recent special-graph and three-part or quantum results do not cover it; full new-preprint proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1995: Semidefinite rounding establishes the Goemans–Williamson approximation benchmark. | 2001: Unconditional Max-Cut hardness reaches the 16/17 retained-fraction threshold. | 2007-02-07: The source theorem matches the Goemans–Williamson ratio assuming Unique Games. | 2025-09-15: A better ratio is proved for graphs with sufficiently many edge-disjoint triangles. | 2026-07-31: New sharp-hardness claims concern different cut objectives and retain Unique Games.
working_summary: Max-Cut asks for a bipartition crossing as many edges of a graph as possible. The question asks for unconditional NP-hardness of approximation arbitrarily close to the Goemans–Williamson ratio. The requested proof must reduce every 3-SAT formula deterministically to a simple unweighted graph with a fixed satisfiable-versus-unsatisfiable gap. Matching known hardness uses Unique Games, while the checked newer cut results have different graph restrictions or objectives. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish the full reduction statement or its exact logical negation.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine the fundamental efficient-approximation limit of the canonical routing problem, beyond the guarantees of any one linear relaxation or rounding algorithm.
formal:
Determine, to absolute accuracy \(1/100\), the optimal expected polynomial-time approximation ratio for symmetric metric traveling-salesperson problems:
\[
 \rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}=\inf\mathcal R,
\qquad
 \mathcal R=\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge1\text{ and }r\text{ is achievable as defined below}\}.
\]
The infimum ranges over all uniform classical randomized algorithms in the stated bit model and all finite input metrics. It is an unconditional real constant; no unproved complexity assumption is part of its definition.
question_excerpt: The original breakthrough gives an expected polynomial-time approximation strictly below three halves for every metric TSP instance. The hardness source describes determination of the best approximation ratio as the broader open problem. This card retains its numerical version: the infimum over all uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, with the project’s absolute 1/100 tolerance.
definitions:
An input \(I\) consists of an integer \(n\ge3\) and the full explicitly listed matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), with
\[
 d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)=d(j,i)>0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad
 d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}).
\]
Integers are binary encoded, and a rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L(I)\) be the full binary encoding length, including all entries and their delimiters. There is no promise of an embedding, a graph representation, bounded aspect ratio or a restricted metric family.

A feasible output is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its tour cost includes the closing edge:
\[
 \operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)),
 \qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).
\]
The positive number \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum of this cost over all permutations.

An algorithm is one uniform classical randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. For some polynomial \(p\), on every valid input and every random tape it halts within \(p(L(I))\) steps and outputs a feasible tour. Its program is finite and independent of the input length; no input-length advice, external oracle or uncharged real arithmetic is available. The runtime bound is worst-case over the coins, although approximation quality is measured in expectation over those coins. Deterministic algorithms are included.

A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and polynomial bound \(p\) with
\[
 \mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)
 \quad\text{for every valid }I.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial may depend on the fixed value \(r\), but not on the particular input or its unknown optimal tour. There is no requirement of an effective procedure that takes \(r\) and produces the algorithm. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty by known constant-factor algorithms, so its infimum is a finite number at least one. The infimum need not itself be achievable.

This quantity compares efficient algorithms with the integral tour optimum. It is distinct from the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the optimum of the subtour linear program. An integrality-gap example is not by itself a lower bound against every algorithm. A result for one rounding method, a bounded number of vertices, graph metrics, Euclidean metrics or a special class of fractional solutions does not determine this unrestricted algorithmic infimum.

The accuracy requirement is absolute error in the dimensionless ratio. No runtime bound is imposed on evaluating a submitted mathematical expression for the answer. If \(P=NP\), exact optimization gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}=1\); conditional inapproximability results must therefore keep their assumptions and cannot silently be substituted for unconditional lower bounds.
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
 |a-\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}|\le1/100.
\]
A Lean-proved interval \(L\le\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}\le U\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. A certified finite mathematical expression may specify the answer; a decimal expansion or efficient evaluation algorithm is not required.

Upper control must establish achievable guarantees approaching the proposed bound, or an equivalent proof about the infimum; an algorithm attaining the infimum is not required. Lower control must concern every admissible algorithm. Merely improving a single algorithm, proving an LP integrality gap, giving conditional hardness under an unproved assumption, or restating the defining infimum is insufficient. A proof using an unproved complexity assumption answers only that conditional variant, not this card's unconditional target.
context:
The 2021 breakthrough establishes a universal expected approximation strictly below \(3/2\), after decades at that threshold. Its theorem compares the returned tour with the optimal integral tour, matching this card’s denominator.

The later derandomization gives a deterministic guarantee below \(3/2\). Thus the current progress is not confined to algorithms with only an expected runtime bound.

The 2024 analysis records the explicit ratio \(3/2-2.18\cdot10^{-34}\). This improves a universal upper bound, but does not determine the best achievable ratio to absolute precision \(1/100\).

Approximating within any fixed factor strictly below \(123/122\) is NP-hard in the cited theorem. Such a hardness statement does not itself prove an unconditional numerical lower bound on the infimum over randomized polynomial-time algorithms.

The July 2026 \(10/7\) guarantee applies to half-integral cycle-cut instances. It does not give that ratio for every metric in this card.

A September 2026 preprint claims a larger universal saving above \(2.05522\cdot10^{-30}\) below \(3/2\). Its statement was checked, but its proof and numerical certificate were not independently audited. Even the claimed upper bound is far from a two-sided determination within \(1/100\).
why: Determine the fundamental efficient-approximation limit of the canonical routing problem, beyond the guarantees of any one linear relaxation or rounding algorithm.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified numerical determination of the unrestricted polynomial-time approximation infimum within 1/100. General approximation improvements, restricted-instance theorems and conditional hardness statements do not supply this unconditional two-sided estimate. The September explicit-saving preprint is recorded as an unaudited claim, whose stated bound would also leave the target unresolved.
progress: 2021: The expected approximation threshold improves strictly below three halves. | 2022-12-13: A deterministic polynomial-time guarantee below three halves is announced. | 2024-05-09: The revised analysis gives an improved explicit universal approximation constant. | 2026-07-03: A revised theorem improves an algorithm on half-integral cycle-cut instances. | 2026-09-02: A preprint claims a further small universal saving; its proof was not independently audited.
working_summary: Metric TSP asks for a cheapest closed tour visiting every point in a finite metric. This card asks for the infimum of expected approximation ratios achieved by uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. All inputs are explicit rational metrics, every execution must finish in polynomial time, and every output must be a valid tour. Known improvements below three halves and conditional hardness results leave the unconditional optimal ratio undetermined. An answer needs a complete Lean-checked estimate within absolute error 1/100, controlling the algorithmic infimum on both sides.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A defining approximation problem for directed cycle hitting.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for minimum-weight Directed Feedback Vertex Set on arbitrary finite directed graphs?

Precisely, do there exist one machine \(A\) and integers \(C,K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid input \((D,w)\) of bit length \(L\), the machine halts within \(K(L+1)^d\) transitions and outputs a set \(F\subseteq V(D)\) satisfying
\[
D-F\text{ is acyclic},\qquad
\sum_{v\in F}w(v)\le C\,\operatorname{OPT}(D,w)?
\]
The same \(C,K,d,A\) must work for every graph and every allowed assignment of weights.
question_excerpt: The source records a polylogarithmic approximation for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set and asks whether the approximation can be improved. The approved proposal selects the precise constant-factor existence question and its minimum-weight version.
definitions:
A directed graph is \(D=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge0\) and \(E\subseteq\{(u,v)\in[n]^2:u\ne v\}\). There are no loops or parallel copies of an arc, but both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may be present. There is no promise of planarity, bounded degree, bounded genus, quasi-transitivity or tournament structure.

A directed cycle consists of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\), with \(r\ge2\), and arcs \((v_i,v_{i+1})\) for \(1\le i<r\) and \((v_r,v_1)\). The induced digraph \(D-F\) deletes the vertices in \(F\) and all their incident arcs. It is acyclic if it contains no directed cycle. A directed feedback vertex set is any \(F\) for which this holds. In particular, the two opposite arcs between a pair of vertices form a cycle.

Each vertex has a nonnegative rational weight \(w(v)\). Define
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(D,w)=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in F}w(v):
F\subseteq[n]\text{ and }D-F\text{ is acyclic}\right\}.
\]
The minimum always exists because deleting all vertices is feasible. Zero weights are allowed. If the optimum is zero, the output must have weight zero as well; the guarantee has no additive slack. The empty graph has optimum zero.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(b(a)\) be the length of the ordinary binary expansion of \(a+1\), and encode \(a\) by \(1^{b(a)}0\) followed by those \(b(a)\) binary digits. Encode an instance by \(1^n0\), then the adjacency bits for all ordered pairs \((u,v)\), \(u\ne v\), in lexicographic order, then \(n\) pairs of integer codes \((p_v,q_v)\), where \(p_v\ge0\), \(q_v\ge1\) and \(w(v)=p_v/q_v\). A reduced fraction is not required. No trailing bits are allowed. All these bits contribute to \(L\); the running time may not depend polynomially on the numerical weights while ignoring their bit lengths.

The output is the \(n\)-bit incidence vector of an actual set \(F\). Feasibility is required on every input, as is the stated multiplicative cost guarantee. An estimate of the optimum without a feasible set, an expected-cost bound or a success probability below one is a different target.

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and an append-only output tape. A transition accesses the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. All transitions, including arithmetic, parsing and output, count toward the polynomial bound. There is no randomness, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. Malformed encodings must be rejected in polynomial time. No complexity conjecture is assumed. Restricting the approximation constant to an integer loses nothing: any finite real factor can be rounded upward to an integer.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of \(A,C,K,d\), proving polynomial bit complexity, feasibility and the constant-factor guarantee on every weighted digraph; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such machine and constants exist. A conditional inapproximability theorem based on an unproved complexity conjecture does not establish the unconditional negative answer. An algorithm for a proper class of digraphs or for only unit weights does not establish the full positive answer. The target concerns existence of a fixed multiplicative approximation factor, not numerical estimation of the optimal possible factor.
context:
The source discusses the general \(O(\log n\log\log n)\) approximation and the open gap in approximation quality. Its polynomial-kernel question concerns a separate parameterized resource target.

Svensson proves Unique-Games hardness of approximation within any fixed constant, already in the unweighted case. This gives a major conditional barrier, but it is not an unconditional proof that the algorithm asked for here does not exist.

The ICALP 2026 result gives a deterministic \(9/4\)-approximation for nonnegative node weights on quasi-transitive digraphs. Quasi-transitivity requires that whenever distinct vertices have arcs \(u\to v\to z\), at least one of \(u\to z\) and \(z\to u\) is present. Arbitrary digraphs need not satisfy this condition.

The September 2026 preprint claims a deterministic \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) on tournaments and, more generally, on node-weighted quasi-transitive digraphs. This improves the special-class factor without providing the all-digraph guarantee.
why: Deleting vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic optimization problem for cyclic dependencies. Its approximation behavior differs sharply from the undirected version: special directed graph classes admit constant factors, while the general case has resisted them and has strong conditional hardness. Resolving the unrestricted weighted target would clarify a central boundary of efficient approximation for directed graphs.
status_note: The weighted constant-factor approximation question for arbitrary digraphs remains open in the checked sources. The general polylogarithmic guarantee and Unique-Games hardness leave this unconditional existence target unsettled. The 2026 constant-factor improvements require quasi-transitivity; the September improvement is a versioned preprint claim, not a general-digraph result.
progress: 2013-09-26: The published hardness result establishes the conditional barrier to every constant factor. | 2016-02-16: The source records the polylogarithmic general guarantee and the unresolved approximation gap. | 2026-07-01: The quasi-transitive result supplies a deterministic 9/4 guarantee on that graph class. | 2026-09-15: A preprint claims a factor arbitrarily close to two on the same broader class containing tournaments. | 2026-09-17: The review preserves the arbitrary weighted-digraph target, specifies its bit model and distinguishes conditional hardness and graph-class progress.
working_summary: A directed feedback vertex set deletes vertices so that no directed cycle remains. The question asks for one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm whose output weight is at most a fixed constant times the minimum possible weight. The guarantee must hold for every directed graph and every nonnegative rational assignment of vertex weights. General approximation remains polylogarithmic in the checked sources, and every constant factor faces a conditional Unique-Games hardness barrier. Recent constant-factor improvements apply to quasi-transitive digraphs and do not settle the unrestricted question.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for asymmetric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine the efficient-approximation threshold for directed routing, a central remaining question after the constant-factor ATSP breakthrough.
formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for the asymmetric metric traveling salesman problem, under worst-case polynomial running time. Let \(\mathcal I\) be the set of valid rational distance-matrix instances and \(\mathcal A\) the class of uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms defined below. Put
\[
\mathcal R=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:\ r\ge1\ \land\ \exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,
\quad\mathbb E_{\omega}\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\bigr]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=\inf\mathcal R.
\]
Supply a real value \(a\) with a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on the achievable ratio \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. No complexity assumption is included in the target. The requested accuracy is additive error in the dimensionless approximation ratio.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge3\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,d)\) consists of the complete matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), satisfying
\[
d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)>0\ (i\ne j),\qquad
d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in[n]).
\]
No symmetry condition is imposed. Every directed distance is finite and explicitly given; the input is not an oracle for distances or a succinctly represented graph. A feasible tour is a permutation \(\pi:[n]\to[n]\), represented by the ordered list \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\). With \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\pi\text{ a permutation of }[n]}\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi).
\]
This is a closed directed Hamiltonian tour, with no prescribed start vertex or pair of distinct endpoints. Strictly positive off-diagonal distances ensure \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).

The encoding fixes the full bit cost. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), with no leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Express every entry uniquely as \(d(i,j)=p_{ij}/q_{ij}\), where \(p_{ij}\ge0\), \(q_{ij}\ge1\), and \(\gcd(p_{ij},q_{ij})=1\). Form the list consisting of \(n\), then \(p_{11},q_{11},p_{12},q_{12},\ldots,p_{nn},q_{nn}\), with matrix entries in row order. Write each list element as \(b(t)\), place one separator \(\#\) between consecutive elements, and encode each resulting symbol by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). There is no trailing separator. Let \(L(I)\) be the number of bits in this string. The output list of vertex labels uses the same integer and separator encoding. All numerator and denominator bits count; arithmetic and comparison are not unit-cost operations on arbitrary rational numbers.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and a sequential output tape. Input is between end markers, and each tape head moves by at most one cell per transition. A transition may read at most one fresh independent fair random bit; it otherwise performs the machine's finite transition rule, and counts as one step. The number of tapes and the program do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-number instruction, or uncharged preprocessing. Deterministic algorithms are included by ignoring random bits.

The class \(\mathcal A\) consists of precisely those machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input string \(z\) and every infinite random-bit sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) transitions, and on every valid instance and every such sequence it outputs a feasible tour. On invalid encodings it may output any finite string within that same time bound. Constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\) but not on the instance or its random sequence. Time is bounded on every execution, not only in expectation. Output cost is averaged over the independent fair coins; there is no distribution on the input instances and no allowed probability of infeasibility. Since the runtime is bounded, the expectation is a finite average over sufficiently long random-bit prefixes.

Every \(r\in\mathcal R\) bounds expected tour cost on every instance, with no additive error term or exception for small instances. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty because constant-factor polynomial-time approximation algorithms are known, and it is bounded below by \(1\). Its infimum is therefore a finite real number. An algorithm achieving exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=1\) means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm has ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring a ratio-one algorithm or one program taking \(\varepsilon\) as input.

For the conditional hardness statements in the context, \(\mathrm{NP}\) denotes the languages with polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{RP}\) denotes the languages decided by uniform randomized polynomial-time machines that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). Neither a separation nor an equality of these classes is assumed in the definition of \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of \(|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le1/100\) for the specified instance class and algorithm model. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) and \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. The supplied value need not be rational or a decimal expansion, and exact equality is welcome but not required.

Bounds must concern the infimum with its correct endpoint convention: an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) permits achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above and need not provide an algorithm attaining \(u\); a lower bound must apply to every eligible algorithm. A lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption establishes only that conditional statement and does not by itself certify this unconditional constant. A gap for one linear-programming relaxation, a lower bound for one chosen algorithm, or results only on finitely many input sizes do not determine the target. Merely renaming the defining infimum is not a determination.
context:
The first constant-factor approximation for general asymmetric TSP established that directed routing admits a uniform constant guarantee, despite the long gap between known algorithms and hardness results.

This card retains the explicit numerical interpretation of the optimal-approximation question: rational positive directed metrics, worst-case polynomial time, always-feasible outputs and a ratio measured by expected cost over the algorithm’s coins.

Vygen’s March 2026 preprint proves a ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and a subsequent remark reports a further improvement below \(14.7\).

Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied prove NP-hardness of approximation below \(75/74\); for the randomized expected-cost model here, the corresponding exclusion is conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than an unconditional lower bound.

The separate subtour-relaxation question concerns the strength of a specified linear program, whereas this constant ranges over all eligible algorithms and the known bounds do not determine it within the benchmark’s absolute tolerance \(1/100\).
why: Asymmetric TSP is a central model of directed routing, where travel costs can depend on direction. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would measure how much optimality must be sacrificed for polynomial computation, beyond the breakthrough establishing that some constant factor is possible.
status_note: The optimal-ratio question is supported by the primary approximation and inapproximability literature. Vygen’s 15 March 2026 preprint supplies improved upper bounds, while the checked hardness result is conditional for the card’s randomized expected-cost model. Individual primary-source reading and bounded later checks through 16 September 2026 found neither a determination of the stated infimum nor bounds meeting the absolute 1/100 acceptance tolerance. This is a bounded source-open assessment, not exhaustive verification of current openness; the preprint’s reported refinements are not presented as independently verified proofs.
progress: 2015: Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied establish NP-hardness of approximation within every constant strictly below \(75/74\). In this card’s randomized, always-feasible expected-cost model, the reduction gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\ge75/74\) assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). This conditional inference does not supply an unconditional bound above one. | 2020-09-15: The full Svensson–Tarnawski–Végh version gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with ratio \(506\), establishing a finite upper bound on the optimal constant. Its main theorem compares the produced tour to the standard relaxation, and therefore also to the minimum tour cost. | 2026-03-15: Vygen’s Theorem 1 gives an approximation ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), which yields an upper bound \(12+2\sqrt2\) on the infimum without asserting attainment. The remark after the main proof reports a further guarantee below \(14.7\), using additional results from the Traub–Vygen book. These are reported preprint bounds, not a determination of the optimal ratio.
working_summary: An asymmetric metric TSP instance specifies positive rational directed distances and asks for a minimum-cost tour through all vertices. The target is the infimum of all expected approximation ratios achieved by uniform randomized algorithms that always return a tour and run in polynomial time on every execution. The algorithm and polynomial may depend on the ratio, and an algorithm attaining the infimum need not exist. Known constant-factor algorithms and conditional hardness results leave a substantial gap, even after the improvements reported in March 2026. The benchmark requires a supplied real estimate and a complete Lean proof of absolute error at most one hundredth for the unconditional constant.

title: Better-than-two approximation for weighted 2ECSS
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Breaking the factor-two barrier would resolve a central approximation question in survivable network design with arbitrary costs. It would close a basic gap between weighted and unweighted connectivity problems and improve our understanding of the limits of network-design relaxations.
formal:
Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that, for every finite undirected 2-edge-connected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative rational edge costs \(c\), the algorithm returns a 2-edge-connected spanning subgraph \((V,F)\), with \(F\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[\sum_{e\in F}c(e)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G,c)?\]
definitions: The input is a finite loopless undirected multigraph on a labeled vertex set \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), given by an explicit list of edge identities and their endpoints. Parallel input edges are allowed and remain distinct. Each edge has a nonnegative rational cost, encoded by a binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. The graph is promised to remain connected after deletion of any one edge. A feasible output is a subset \(F\) of the input edge identities such that \((V,F)\) has the same property; equivalently every nonempty proper vertex set has at least two selected edges crossing its cut. All vertices must be spanned. An input edge may be selected at most once; the algorithm cannot create extra copies. The cost of \(F\) is the sum of its edge costs, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,c)\) is the minimum cost over all feasible subsets. Running time is worst-case polynomial in the full binary input length, including all cost encodings, on a deterministic Turing machine. The algorithm and polynomial may depend on the single fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on the instance. The guarantee includes instances with optimum zero and is unconditional.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence of a deterministic algorithm and a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). A positive proof must establish polynomial worst-case time, feasibility and the cost guarantee on every valid weighted instance. A negative proof must rule out every such constant and algorithm, unconditionally; hardness based on an unproved complexity assumption only establishes a conditional result. An improvement that vanishes with input size, applies only to unit costs, or permits repeated purchases of an input edge does not qualify.
context:
The weighted 2-edge-connected spanning subgraph problem asks for the cheapest spanning network that survives any single edge failure. The factor-two guarantee applies to arbitrary nonnegative edge costs, while substantially better bounds are known when every edge costs one.

Hommelsheim, Lindermayr and Liu give a \((5/4-\eta)\)-approximation for the unweighted problem, for a fixed \(\eta\ge10^{-6}\). In Section 1.1 they explicitly identify obtaining a better-than-two approximation for weighted 2ECSS as a major open problem.

Traub and Zenklusen obtain a \((1.5+\delta)\)-approximation, for every fixed \(\delta>0\), for weighted connectivity augmentation. That problem starts with an existing connected graph and pays for added links. Its theorem does not provide the same guarantee when the whole spanning network must be purchased.

The distinction between a subgraph and a multiset of purchased edges is essential. Reusing an edge can produce a different feasible network, and does not satisfy this card unless separate copies were already present in the input.
why: Breaking the factor-two barrier would resolve a central approximation question in survivable network design with arbitrary costs. It would close a basic gap between weighted and unweighted connectivity problems and improve our understanding of the limits of network-design relaxations.
status_note: Primary-source statements and a bounded search for subsequent work were checked on 16 September 2026; the formulation was individually reviewed on 17 September 2026. No resolution of this precise target was located. This records source-supported openness, not an exhaustive literature certification or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2022: Traub’s TCS+ talk presents weighted 2ECSS among the open barriers for connectivity approximation. | 2023: Weighted connectivity augmentation admits a \((1.5+\delta)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\delta>0\); this concerns adding links to an existing network. | 2026: The unweighted approximation drops below \(5/4\), while the same paper explicitly retains the factor-two barrier for weighted 2ECSS.
working_summary: The task is to buy a minimum-cost spanning network that survives deletion of any single edge. Costs are arbitrary nonnegative rational numbers, and each input edge may be selected only once. The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time approximation beating factor two by one fixed constant. Better unweighted and connectivity-augmentation guarantees concern different instance models. A solution would break a central barrier in approximation algorithms for survivable networks.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Euclidean k-means
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Resolve the fundamental computational approximation limit of a central clustering objective, beyond successive improvements to particular algorithms.
formal:
Determine the real constant
\[
 \rho_{\mathrm{EucKM}}=
 \inf\left\{r\in[1,\infty):\begin{array}{l}
 \text{there is one uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm }A\\
 \text{such that }\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]
 \le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\text{ for every valid instance }I
 \end{array}\right\}
\]
to absolute error at most \(1/100\), using the explicit rational-input, arbitrary-center and worst-case polynomial bit-time model below. Neither the number of clusters nor the dimension is fixed.
question_excerpt: Recent work improves polynomial-time approximation algorithms for high-dimensional Euclidean k-means, whose centers may be arbitrary points. The card asks for the best achievable approximation ratio across all uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, not the ratio of a particular method.
definitions:
An instance \(I\) consists of integers \(n,d\ge1\), \(1\le k\le n\), and an explicitly listed sequence of points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb Q^d\). Repeated points are allowed and contribute separately to the objective. Every integer is in binary, and each rational coordinate is represented by an integer numerator and a positive integer denominator in binary, with explicit delimiters. The full lengths of all \(nd\) coordinates and headers count toward the input length \(L\).

A feasible output is a list \(C=(c_1,\ldots,c_k)\in(\mathbb Q^d)^k\) of exactly \(k\) centers. Centers may be repeated and may lie anywhere in the space; they need not be input points or belong to a supplied candidate set. Its cost is
\[
 \operatorname{cost}_I(C)=
 \sum_{i=1}^n\min_{1\le j\le k}\|x_i-c_j\|_2^2,
 \qquad
 \|v\|_2^2=\sum_{t=1}^d v_t^2.
\]
Every point is assigned to a nearest center for purposes of this minimum; ties have no effect. There are no outliers, fairness constraints, capacities or permission to exceed the center budget. Returning fewer distinct centers can be represented by repeating entries in the length-\(k\) list.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum of the same expression over \((\mathbb R^d)^k\). This minimum exists and has a rational attaining center list: for any nonempty cluster its mean is optimal, and only finitely many assignments of the \(n\) points to \(k\) labels need be considered. Empty clusters may use arbitrary repeated rational centers. Thus the rational-output convention does not increase the exact optimum.

An admissible algorithm is one finite classical multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice and no external oracle. There must be constants \(K>0\) and an integer \(b\ge1\) such that, for every valid input and every random tape, it halts within \(K(L+1)^b\) steps and outputs a feasible rational center list. All computation, random-bit generation and output bits are charged; exact real arithmetic is not a unit-cost primitive. The expectation in the formula is over the algorithm's own coins on each fixed input. It is a bound on expected cost, not merely a success probability or an expected running-time guarantee.

A ratio \(r\ge1\) is achievable precisely when some such algorithm satisfies the displayed inequality on every instance. Its algorithm and polynomial constants may depend on this fixed \(r\), but cannot depend on the input, \(k\), \(d\) or coordinate precision. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the inequality requires zero cost almost surely; no division by zero defines the guarantee. Known constant-factor algorithms make the set of achievable ratios nonempty, and it is bounded below by one. The infimum need not itself be achieved by a single algorithm. No computational complexity hypothesis is included in this definition.
answer_criterion:
Supply a real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
 |a-\rho_{\mathrm{EucKM}}|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
A proved interval \([\ell,u]\) containing the defined constant with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualifies by taking its midpoint. A finite mathematical expression is allowed; a decimal expansion is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum is not a determination.

The proof must concern the unrestricted randomized polynomial bit-time class above. An upper bound alone, a lower bound for one relaxation or method, a result for fixed dimension or fixed cluster count, or a solution using more than \(k\) centers does not determine the constant. A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity assumption settles only that conditional statement. The benchmark tolerance applies to the supplied value, not to feasibility or to the meaning of the approximation ratio.
context:
Euclidean k-means minimizes the sum of squared distances. This differs both from k-median, which uses unsquared distances, and from a general finite metric problem with a supplied list of possible centers.

Polynomial-time approximation schemes with a fixed dimension or fixed number of clusters do not give a scheme whose time is polynomial uniformly in both parameters.

The STOC 2026 result gives randomized ratios approaching four. Its final algorithm respects the center budget, although an intermediate result permits extra centers.

The July 2026 preprint states a \((3+\ln 2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). This improves algorithmic guarantees but does not prove a matching lower bound for all algorithms.

Determining the infimum requires control from both sides in the stated bit model. A conditional hardness theorem has to retain its assumption; it cannot silently become an unconditional lower bound on this constant.
why: Locate the computational approximation limit of a central clustering objective when neither dimension nor cluster count is a fixed parameter. This separates what any efficient algorithm can achieve from the performance of the current best technique.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified determination of the unconditional expected polynomial-time approximation constant within 1/100. The July preprint improves the stated algorithmic ratio; parameterized and fair-clustering results have different guarantees. This review checked statements, model distinctions and final budget scope, not complete proofs or every bit-level implementation detail.
progress: 2026-05-27: The SoCG result studies parameter-dependent approximation time and lower bounds under a separate hypothesis. | 2026-06: The STOC randomized algorithm gives approximation ratios approaching four. | 2026-07-16: The spectral dual-fitting preprint reports ratios approaching 3 + ln 2 for unrestricted Euclidean centers.
working_summary: Euclidean k-means chooses k arbitrary centers to minimize the sum of squared distances from the input points. The dimension, number of clusters and rational coordinate lengths are all part of the input. The target is the infimum of expected ratios achievable by uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. The latest reviewed upper-bound improvement does not determine that unrestricted infimum. An accepted answer needs a complete Lean-checked value within 0.01, without silently assuming an unproved hardness hypothesis.

title: Optimal approximation for nonmonotone submodular maximization over a matroid
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Individual assessment: the optimal approximation for nonnegative submodular maximization under one arbitrary matroid is a central structural question in approximation algorithms, unifying many independence-constrained objectives. It asks for the frontier of an entire oracle model, with implications extending beyond a single algorithm or application. The score reflects that breadth and the unresolved algorithm-versus-information gap, and replaces the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.
formal:
Determine the optimal expected approximation ratio for maximizing a nonnegative, not necessarily monotone submodular set function subject to one matroid independence constraint, in the polynomial-time oracle model specified below.

For an instance \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\), write
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(J)=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr A\) be the class of uniform randomized oracle algorithms defined below: each always outputs an independent set and has a polynomial bound on its total number of elementary operations, on every valid instance and every random tape. Define
\[
\mathcal R=\left\{\alpha\in[0,1]:
 \exists A\in\mathscr A\ \forall J\
 \mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[f\!\left(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega)\right)\right]
 \ge \alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(J)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}=\sup\mathcal R.
\]
The universal quantifier ranges over every finite ground-set size, every nonnegative submodular function on that ground set, and every matroid on it. The approximation constant and algorithm are chosen before the instance. The target is the real number \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\); it is not assumed that an algorithm attains the supremum. Supply a real answer \(a\) with a Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}.
\]
question_excerpt: On the other hand, the best achievable approximability for general CSM remains open; the best known inapproximability factor is 0.478 due to Oveis Gharan and […]
definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_{0}\), the ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and \(2^{[n]}\) denotes its power set. The objective is a function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying
\[
f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)
\quad\text{for all }S,T\subseteq[n].
\]
This is submodularity. Monotonicity would additionally require \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\); no such requirement is imposed. Nonnegativity applies to every subset, including infeasible ones. No normalization \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is required.

A matroid independence family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) satisfies three axioms: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); every subset of an element of \(\mathcal I\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\); and if \(S,T\in\mathcal I\) with \(|S|<|T|\), then some \(t\in T\setminus S\) satisfies \(S\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal I\). An output is any set in \(\mathcal I\), and need not be maximal. The rank, defined as \(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}|S|\), is unrestricted. A cardinality constraint is the special case \(\mathcal I=\{S:|S|\le k\}\).

The input explicitly supplies the integer \(n\) in binary, with zero represented by the single bit zero. Sets supplied to or returned by an oracle are represented by their \(n\)-bit incidence vectors. Two exact oracles are available: a value oracle returns the real number \(f(S)\), and an independence oracle returns the bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). The oracles remain fixed throughout a run. Neither the full table of \(f\) nor a list of all independent sets is supplied, and there is no oracle for a continuous extension, its derivatives, or an optimum.

Fix the following exact-real oracle computation convention. An algorithm is one finite program with finite control, finitely many ordinary bit tapes and finitely many tapes of exact real cells. It may contain finitely many rational constants, each specified by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator. Initially work tapes are blank or zero. Elementary instructions are ordinary bit-tape read/write and one-cell head moves; one-cell real-tape head moves; copying or loading a real cell; addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of a fixed finite number of currently addressed real cells; exact comparison of two such cells; obtaining one independent fair random bit; or one of the two oracle calls. Each instruction costs one operation. Division must have a nonzero divisor on every valid run. The query incidence vector must already have been written on the query tape; reading and writing its bits are charged by the bit-tape instructions. An oracle answer is deposited in a designated real cell or bit cell in one operation. Outputting the final incidence vector is also charged. Real cells have no instruction for inspecting a binary expansion or converting an arbitrary real directly into an integer.

This is a unit-cost exact-arithmetic oracle model: the size parameter is \(n\), and real answers are not charged by a bit length. All computation between queries is counted. Programs have no advice depending on \(n\) or the instance, no arbitrary real constants, and no other oracles. This explicit convention completes the source's polynomial-time/value-oracle formulation; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity model for rational objectives.

Formally, \(A\in\mathscr A\) means that there are integers \(C\ge1\) and \(q\ge0\), fixed for that program, such that for every valid \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\) and every random tape \(\omega\), the program makes only valid operations and queries, halts within \(C(n+1)^q\) elementary operations, and outputs an \(n\)-bit vector encoding a member of \(\mathcal I\). Thus both its number of oracle queries and its other work are polynomially bounded. No feasibility error is allowed. The expectation in the guarantee concerns objective value, not feasibility or running time.

The random tape consists of independent fair bits, so each specified prefix of length \(r\) has probability \(2^{-r}\). For a program with the above clock, at most \(C(n+1)^q\) bits are read; its expected value is consequently a finite average over that many fair bits, with unused bits ignored. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(J)=0\), the multiplicative guarantee is automatically satisfied; no quotient by zero is used. Always returning the empty set guarantees factor zero, so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and its supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\).
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}
\]
for exactly the instance class and algorithm class above. Merely restating the supremum that defines \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\) is not a determination.

A certified interval is sufficient: give \(l,u\in[0,1]\), prove
\[
l\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le u,\qquad u-l\le\frac{1}{50},
\]
and use \(a=(l+u)/2\). To make explicit what both sides mean, the lower bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists A\in\mathscr A\
\forall J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
\ge(l-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
The upper bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall A\in\mathscr A\
\exists J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
<(u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
Membership in \(\mathscr A\) includes the full program, uniform polynomial clock and unconditional feasibility requirements from the definitions. In the lower statement the program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(J\); the upper statement ranges over every such program and all possible polynomial degrees. This permits approaching a supremum without attaining it.

Exact determination is welcome but is not mandatory. A guarantee for a subclass of matroids or objectives, for deterministic algorithms alone, or for polynomially many queries with unrestricted computation does not by itself determine this target. Nor does an upper bound assuming an unproved complexity separation constitute the unconditional upper certificate above.
context:
Qi's original question concerns general constrained submodular maximization: a single nonnegative submodular objective over independent sets of one matroid. Although the paper mainly studies a sum with a linear function, that linear term is absent from the extracted open question. The source measures approximation in expectation and running time polynomially in ground-set size.

The 2022 source records a \(0.385\) approximation and a \(0.478\) oracle inapproximability threshold. Qi also proves the latter threshold already for the cardinality-constrained special case. The upper bound therefore applies to algorithms for all matroids, but does not make the special case and general case identical problems.

Buchbinder and Feldman's STOC 2024 result improves the approximation guarantee to \(0.401\) for a matroid constraint. Their Corollary 1.3 is stated directly for the discrete set-function problem; the result is not merely a guarantee for a continuous objective with stronger oracle access.

The checked results give the conservative bracket \(401/1000\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le239/500\). Its width is \(77/1000\), larger than the benchmark's sufficient interval width \(1/50\). These bounds therefore do not already meet this card's numerical acceptance criterion.

A March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap as open while improving a deterministic guarantee to \(0.385-\varepsilon\). A September 2026 online continuous-optimization preprint explicitly says its \(0.401\) result does not claim optimality. Neither supplies the requested determination in this card's offline randomized model.
why: This is a central approximation question for a general combinatorial optimization model, rather than a guarantee for one application or a running-time refinement. Matroids include cardinality, partition and linear-independence constraints, and submodularity encompasses many cut, coverage and information objectives. Determining the optimal guarantee would identify the inherent cost of combining diminishing returns, potentially harmful additions and independence constraints. Unlike several neighboring monotone or unconstrained models, the known algorithmic and information-theoretic bounds still leave a substantial gap.
status_note: Open in the 2022 source, with a bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026. The checked discrete matroid approximation improved to 0.401 in Buchbinder–Feldman (preprint 2023; STOC 2024), while the checked oracle barrier remains 0.478. Chen and coauthors' March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining gap as open. The September 2026 online continuous result does not claim optimality and is a different model. No verified resolution or interval meeting the card's 1/100 answer tolerance was found. The review inspected model definitions, theorem statements and limited supporting arguments; it is not an exhaustive literature review, a full proof audit or a Lean verification.
progress: 2011: Oveis Gharan and Vondrák prove that a \(0.478\) approximation under a matroid independence constraint would require exponentially many value queries. | 2022-12-14: Qi's ISAAC paper explicitly asks for the best achievable approximation for general matroid-constrained submodular maximization and proves \(0.478\) oracle hardness already under a cardinality constraint. | 2023-11-02: Buchbinder and Feldman's preprint gives the \(0.401\) guarantee; the work subsequently appears at STOC 2024. | 2026-03-16: The second revision of Chen and coauthors' preprint improves a deterministic approximation while explicitly retaining the general \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap. | 2026-09-16: Recovered the background CSM target, specified its exact oracle and computation conventions, updated the known bounds, and defined numerical Lean acceptance without requiring attainment of the optimal ratio.
working_summary: The input is a nonnegative submodular set function and one matroid, accessed through exact value and independence oracles. The goal is to choose an independent set with a large objective value, even though adding elements can reduce that value. The target is the supremum of expected approximation factors achievable by a uniform randomized algorithm using polynomially many total oracle-model operations. The checked literature gives a 0.401 approximation and a 0.478 value-query barrier, with the general gap explicitly retained in a March 2026 source. A benchmark answer must determine that optimal real ratio within 1/100 and prove the claimed accuracy in Lean without assuming that the supremum is attained.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine the efficient-approximation limit of the basic network-design problem that underlies many more general connectivity objectives.
formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for undirected weighted Steiner Tree under worst-case polynomial running time. For the valid instances \(\mathcal I\) and the uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms \(\mathcal A\) defined below, put
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:
r\ge1\ \land\
\exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\
\mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\right]
\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=\inf\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}.
\]
Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. The expectation concerns output cost, not running time. No complexity assumption is part of the definition. The requested error is additive in this dimensionless approximation ratio.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,E,R,w)\) consists of a connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), a set of terminals \(R\subseteq[n]\) with \(2\le |R|\le n\), and nonnegative rational weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices; each pair occurs at most once. Connected means every two vertices are joined by a finite path. The whole graph, terminal list and all weights are explicitly given. There is no restriction on the topology, number of terminals, weight magnitudes, or ratio between positive weights.

A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that the graph on vertex set
\[
W=R\cup\bigcup_{\{u,v\}\in F}\{u,v\}
\]
with edge set \(F\) is connected and has no cycle. Thus the output is one tree containing all terminals; its other vertices may be any subset of the available nonterminals. Its cost and the optimum are
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(F)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=
\min\{\operatorname{cost}_I(F):F\text{ is a feasible solution of }I\}.
\]
Every valid instance has a feasible solution, so the minimum is over a nonempty finite set and is attained. Output edges must be original input edges. Neither new Steiner points outside \([n]\), a separate cost for selected vertices, a set of pairwise connection demands, nor directed edges are part of this problem.

The following encoding fixes the full bit cost. Write each weight uniquely as \(p_e/q_e\), where \(p_e\ge0\), \(q_e\ge1\), and the integers are relatively prime, so a zero weight is encoded as \(0/1\). Order edges lexicographically by their endpoints \(u<v\), obtaining \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and order terminal labels increasingly, obtaining \(r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Form one list of integers consisting of \(n\), the explicit vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), \(m\), the four entries \(u,v,p_{e_j},q_{e_j}\) for each edge \(e_j=\{u,v\}\) in order, then \(h,r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Encode each integer in ordinary binary without leading zeros, with \(0\) represented by one zero. Put a separator \(\#\) between consecutive integers and no trailing separator. Finally encode the three symbols by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). The length of the resulting binary string is \(L(I)\). A valid output is the list consisting of \(|F|\) followed by the strictly increasing indices of the selected edges in \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), using the same integer, separator and binary-symbol encoding. All numerator, denominator, endpoint and output bits count; arithmetic on rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and a sequential output tape. The input is delimited by end markers. Each transition reads the scanned symbols, can write one symbol per writable tape, and moves each head by at most one cell; it counts as one step. A transition may additionally read at most one fresh independent fair random bit. The program and tape count do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-arithmetic instruction or uncharged preprocessing. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the random bits.

The set \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly the machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input \(z\) and every random sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) steps, and on every valid instance and every such sequence its output encodes a feasible solution. Invalid inputs may receive any output within that same bound. The constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\), but not on the instance or the random bits. This is a bound on every execution, not merely an expected-time bound.

The random sequence \(\omega\) has the product distribution of independent fair bits; there is no probability distribution on inputs. Since at most \(C(L(I)+1)^k\) bits can be read, the expected cost is the finite average over all bit strings of that length, each with equal probability, disregarding unused bits. Infeasibility has no permitted error probability. The multiplicative bound must hold on every valid instance, with no additive cost term or exception for small inputs. Instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\) are included: their expected output cost must be zero. As every finite random execution has positive probability and costs are nonnegative, this requires zero output cost on every execution of such an instance.

Known polynomial-time approximations make \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}\) nonempty; it is bounded below by \(1\), so its infimum is a finite real number. An algorithm attaining exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=1\) would mean that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm achieves ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring an exact algorithm or one program that takes \(\varepsilon\) as an additional input.

For the conditional results in the context, \(\mathrm P\) is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary certificates checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class \(\mathrm{RP}\) consists of languages decided by randomized machines with polynomial running time on every random tape that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). No equality or separation among these classes is assumed in \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\).
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}
\]
for precisely the instance class and machine model above. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with
\[
\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u,\qquad u-\ell\le\frac1{50}
\]
qualifies through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The value need not be an integer, rational number or decimal expansion; exact determination is welcome but is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum does not specify an answer.

The proof must respect the infimum's endpoint convention. To establish an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u\), achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above suffice; an algorithm achieving \(u\) itself is not required. Equivalently, one may prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an eligible algorithm whose expected cost on every instance is at most \((u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). A lower bound \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) must exclude every eligible algorithm from achieving each ratio \(r\) with \(1\le r<\ell\). For every such \(r\) and algorithm, this requires some valid instance with expected cost strictly greater than \(r\operatorname{OPT}\).

A hardness bound under an unproved complexity assumption proves only the corresponding conditional statement. It does not by itself certify the unconditional constant requested here. A gap for a particular linear-programming relaxation, the worst case of one selected algorithm, a guarantee only for a restricted graph family, or computations on finitely many input sizes do not determine this infimum over all eligible algorithms and all valid instances.
context:
The source model is an undirected weighted graph with a terminal subset; passing to shortest-path distances preserves the approximation problem. This card retains the canonical graph input with nonnegative rational weights, explicit binary encoding, worst-case polynomial time and expected feasible-output cost. These machine and encoding conventions make the inherited numerical target precise.

Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß and Sanità obtain a polynomial-time \((\ln 4+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and their full account derandomizes the algorithm. Consequently the infimum satisfies the unconditional bounds \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le\ln 4\), without an assertion that the upper endpoint is attained.

Traub and Zenklusen obtain the same limiting guarantee by a combinatorial algorithm, first presented in their 2021 preprint and SODA 2022 paper and incorporated into their 2025 journal article. Their model discussion explicitly explains the compatibility of positive and nonnegative edge weights.

Chlebík and Chlebíková prove NP-hardness of achieving factors below \(96/95\). For the always-feasible randomized expected-cost model of this card, their gap reduction excludes those factors assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\); that randomized-model consequence is an editorial inference, not an unconditional lower bound.

The 2024 result bounding the bidirected cut relaxation's integrality gap by \(1.9988\) settles a different question about a specified relaxation.

A July 2026 primary paper still reports \(\ln 4+\varepsilon\) as the best known general Steiner Tree approximation guarantee. The checked bounds do not determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\).
why: Steiner Tree is a basic network-design problem and a recurring subproblem in more general connectivity objectives. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would establish how closely polynomial-time algorithms can approach optimal connection cost in unrestricted weighted graphs. The target compares all algorithms, making it broader than the accuracy of one method or the strength of one relaxation.

A bounded review through 16 September 2026 found no verified value or certified interval meeting this card's absolute error tolerance of one hundredth.
