title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-means
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Determine the computational limit of squared-distance clustering in arbitrary metrics, a central network and data-clustering approximation problem.
formal:
Determine, to absolute error at most \(1/100\), the constant
\[
 \rho_{\mathrm{MetKM}}=
 \inf\left\{r\in[1,\infty):\begin{array}{l}
 \text{some uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm }A\text{ always returns}\\
 \text{a feasible solution and satisfies }
 \mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\\
 \text{for every valid explicitly encoded metric instance }I
 \end{array}\right\}.
\]
The metric, squared cost, candidate-center constraint and worst-case polynomial bit-time model are defined below.
question_excerpt: Metric k-means minimizes squared distances to a fixed number of centers from an explicitly given candidate set. Recent primary work improves approximation ratios; this card asks for the infimum across all uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, with the source-compatible convention that clients are eligible centers.
definitions:
An instance contains a nonempty finite labelled set \(U\), its full rational distance matrix \(d:U\times U\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), nonempty subsets \(D,F\subseteq U\) with \(D\subseteq F\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). The distance function satisfies \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all triples. Thus it is a genuine metric, not merely a squared-distance table or an arbitrary cost matrix. The sets are explicitly listed; each rational distance has a binary integer numerator and positive binary denominator. All matrix entries, labels and headers count toward the input bit length \(L\).

The elements of \(D\) are distinct unweighted clients, each counted once; the elements of \(F\) are the allowed center locations. The inclusion \(D\subseteq F\) is part of this card's model, so every client is itself eligible to be a center. Points of \(U\) outside these sets carry no demand and cannot be selected unless they belong to \(F\). A feasible solution is a set \(S\subseteq F\) of exactly \(k\) distinct centers. Its cost and optimum are
\[
 \operatorname{cost}_I(S)=\sum_{x\in D}\min_{s\in S}d(x,s)^2,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq F\\ |S|=k}}
 \operatorname{cost}_I(S).
\]
The minimum exists because the feasible family is finite and nonempty. Squared distances need not themselves satisfy a triangle inequality. An output lists the center labels, not a fractional solution or a distribution over center sets. Selecting fewer centers can be padded with unused eligible locations without increasing cost, but opening more than \(k\) centers is never feasible.

The metric is unrestricted and fully supplied. No Euclidean embedding, bounded dimension, geometric coordinates, shortest-path oracle or input distribution is assumed. The parameter \(k\) is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. There are no fairness constraints, capacities, client weights, outliers or facility-opening charges.

An admissible algorithm is one finite classical multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice and no external oracle. It has constants \(K>0\) and integer \(b\ge1\) such that, on every valid input and every random tape, it halts within \(K(L+1)^b\) steps and returns a feasible set. Reading, rational arithmetic, random-bit generation, auxiliary computation and output are all charged. Expected polynomial time or unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrary reals is not this model.

A fixed real \(r\ge1\) is achievable when some admissible algorithm satisfies the displayed expected-cost bound for every fixed input. The program and polynomial constants may depend on \(r\), but not on the input, its center count or its coordinate bit lengths. Expectation is over internal randomness. Zero optimum requires zero expected cost, hence zero cost almost surely; no cost ratio with a zero denominator is used. Known constant-factor algorithms make the set of achievable ratios nonempty. The infimum need not be attained by one algorithm. The definition is unconditional and assumes no unproved complexity hypothesis.
answer_criterion:
Supply a real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
 |a-\rho_{\mathrm{MetKM}}|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
A proved containing interval \([\ell,u]\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. A finite mathematical expression is acceptable; a decimal expansion is not required. Merely restating the defining infimum is insufficient.

The result must concern all admissible algorithms on the full metric input class with \(D\subseteq F\). A guarantee opening \(k\) centers only in expectation, a larger center budget, one algorithm's ratio, a relaxation gap, or a geometric or fixed-parameter special case does not determine this constant. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption and is not an unconditional lower bound. The \(1/100\) tolerance concerns the supplied value, not feasibility or distance preservation.
context:
The objective squares the underlying metric distances. This is different from k-median, whose objective uses the unsquared distances, and from a continuous Euclidean model with freely chosen center coordinates.

A solution using too many centers may have artificially low cost. The exact budget must hold on every execution; an expected count of k centers is not enough.

The April 2026 iterative-rounding paper explicitly converts an intermediate expected-budget result into a true approximation and reports ratios approaching five.

The July 2026 spectral paper reports ratios approaching 4.9. Its final theorem respects the center budget even though parts of the construction temporarily use additional centers.

A best-known algorithmic ratio is an upper-bound contribution to the approximation landscape. Determining this infimum to a narrow interval also requires an appropriate lower bound for the full randomized class, without silently assuming a hardness conjecture.
why: Determine the computational approximation limit of squared-distance clustering in general finite metrics. This isolates the cost of clustering without geometric assumptions while requiring an exact center budget on every execution.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified determination within 1/100 of the unconditional expected polynomial-time approximation infimum. The April and July papers improve algorithmic guarantees without a matching unconditional lower bound. This review checked model and final feasibility scope, not complete proofs or every bit-level implementation detail.
progress: 2026-04-07: Iterative randomized rounding gives a true approximation with ratio 5 + epsilon after converting the intermediate expected-budget guarantee. | 2026-07-16: Spectral dual fitting reports the improved metric ratio 4.9 + epsilon.
working_summary: Metric k-means chooses exactly k distinct centers from an explicit candidate set that includes every client. Its objective is the sum of squared metric distances to the nearest selected center. The target is the infimum of expected ratios achievable by uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. The July 2026 result reports an improved algorithmic ratio approaching 4.9 without determining the infimum. Acceptance requires a complete unconditional Lean-checked approximation to that constant within 0.01.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: The principal approximation barrier for a foundational objective in hierarchical clustering, with links to graph partitioning and metric optimization.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\), \(K>0\), an integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine which, on every explicitly encoded nonnegative rational similarity graph \(G\), outputs a hierarchy \(T\) with \(\operatorname{cost}_G(T)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) within \(K(N+1)^a\) bit operations, where \(N\) is the total input bit length and the cost and allowed hierarchies are defined below?
definitions:
An input is an integer \(n\ge2\) and a finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E,w)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:1\le u<v\le n\}\), and \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). The encoding explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and all edges with their endpoints and weights. Integers use ordinary binary notation with delimiters; each rational weight is a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. The explicit vertex list ensures \(N\ge n\). There are no loops or repeated edges. An absent edge has weight zero. The graph need not be connected and has no metric, clusterability, density or sampling promise.

A hierarchy is a finite rooted full binary tree whose leaves are labeled bijectively by \([n]\); every internal node has exactly two children. For a node \(z\), let \(L_T(z)\subseteq[n]\) be its descendant leaf labels. For distinct leaves \(u,v\), let \(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v)\) be their least common ancestor. Define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w(\{u,v\})\,|L_T(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v))|,
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_T\operatorname{cost}_G(T).
\]
Each unordered edge contributes once. The minimum is over all such trees, with no restriction on height or balance. The output explicitly lists the root, child edges and leaf labels of one tree. If all weights are zero, the required cost is zero and any valid hierarchy qualifies.

The same finite machine and constants must work for every \(n\), graph and weight encoding. All input reads, binary arithmetic, preprocessing and output writes count in the worst-case running time. The machine has no random bits, advice, external comparison or cluster-label oracle, or uncharged preprocessing. The factor \(C\) is independent of \(n\), the number of edges and the sizes or ratios of the weights; it is not an input parameter. Only the tree is required as output, and its stated cost guarantee is mathematical, using exact rational weights.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a machine and fixed constants satisfying every stated guarantee, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. An approximation factor growing with the input size, a result for a promised graph class, or a guarantee with an additional oracle does not settle this target. A conditional hardness result establishes its implication but does not by itself prove the unconditional negative answer.
context:
The source defines a cost for a complete hierarchy of pairwise similarities. This card retains the previously selected deterministic polynomial-time, constant-factor question. The explicit rational encoding and vertex list fix bit complexity and output size; they do not impose a structural promise.

The general approximation guarantee of Charikar and Chatziafratis is \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\). Their Theorem 3.4 proves Small-Set-Expansion hardness of approximation within every constant factor, already on unweighted graphs. This is a conditional complexity barrier, not an unconditional proof that the requested machine cannot exist.

The ICALP 2025 sublinear result assumes a clusterable graph and access to cluster labels of sampled seeds. Its input model and guarantee do not supply the unrestricted algorithm asked for here.

The July 2026 generalized clustering paper permits a leaf cluster to remain a whole graph from a specified class, such as a tree. Its objective can consequently vanish on inputs for which singleton-leaf hierarchies have positive cost. Those results concern a different stopping rule.

A constant-factor guarantee for the complementary revenue-maximization objective does not, just from that guarantee, give a constant-factor bound for this minimization objective. The target here is the displayed cost itself.
why: A hierarchy must represent similarity at every scale, so optimizing a single flat partition is insufficient. A constant approximation for this canonical objective would give a uniform quality guarantee on arbitrary similarity data and would cross a major graph-partitioning hardness barrier.
status_note: Source-open under the retained unrestricted deterministic interpretation. Checked on 2026-09-16: the established general approximation and Small-Set-Expansion hardness leave the unconditional constant-factor proposition unsettled in the sources inspected. The 2025 seeded clusterable-graph result and July 2026 generalized terminal-cluster result do not meet this target. This is a bounded literature check, not an exhaustive certificate of current openness.
progress: 2015-10-16: The initial preprint defines the hierarchy cost; the work appears at STOC 2016. | 2016-09-29: The Charikar–Chatziafratis preprint gives the \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound and Small-Set-Expansion hardness; the work appears at SODA 2017. | 2025-06-30: A sublinear-time approximation result is published for clusterable graphs with sampled seed labels. | 2026-07-14: A preprint studies a generalized objective allowing nonsingleton terminal clusters. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the objective, encoding and conditional-hardness scope. A bounded subsequent-literature search found no matching unconditional resolution.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary graph whose nonnegative edge weights express pairwise similarities. A hierarchy repeatedly separates its vertices until every leaf contains one vertex. An edge pays its weight times the size of the smallest cluster containing both endpoints. The question asks for one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with a fixed approximation factor on every such graph. Known general guarantees grow with the number of vertices, while Small-Set-Expansion hardness and results for richer inputs or different objectives do not unconditionally settle this question.

title: Min-CSP approximation at the SDP integrality gap
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A universal bridge between SDP integrality gaps and polynomial-time multiplicative approximation would organize minimization across all finite-domain cost languages, including near-satisfiable instances where the existing additive theory loses its guarantee.
formal:
For every fixed finite domain \(D\), positive arity \(k\), and finite set \(\Lambda\) of nonnegative rational cost functions \(f:D^k\to[0,1]\), is the following true? For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, on every \(n\)-variable minimization \(\Lambda\)-CSP instance \(I\) with finite \(n\)-variable SDP integrality gap \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\), returns an assignment \(\sigma\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)\leq (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_\Lambda(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\bigr]\geq\tfrac23?\]
The same algorithm handles all \(n\); it also halts and returns an assignment on the sizes where the gap is infinite, but no multiplicative guarantee is imposed there. The gap and the basic SDP are defined below.
question_excerpt: If the minimization SDP gap at n variables is α_n, can a polynomial-time algorithm attain approximation factor (1+ε)α_n for every positive ε?
definitions:
Fix \(D=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \(q\geq1\), and a finite nonempty \(\Lambda\). Its rational cost tables and \(k\geq1\) are fixed, not input. The nonnegative rational convention gives a finite effective version of the source’s generalized nonnegative predicates; negative costs do not define the multiplicative approximation question. An instance has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq1\), and a finite list of \(m\) constraints \(C=(f_C,(i_1,\ldots,i_k))\). Every \(f_C\in\Lambda\), and each \(i_j\in[n]\). Repeated coordinates and repeated occurrences are allowed, with each occurrence having unit weight. There are no hard constraints, infinite costs, extra unary pins or input-dependent predicates. For an assignment \(\sigma:[n]\to D\), set
\[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)=\frac1m\sum_C f_C(\sigma(i_1),\ldots,\sigma(i_k)),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_\sigma\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma).\]
For \(m=0\), cost and optimum are zero. A zero-one cost table records violation by value one and satisfaction by value zero. Different arities can be represented by a common maximum arity with unused arguments; the question is not restricted to Boolean predicates.

Define the basic semidefinite relaxation as follows. Choose real vectors \(v_0,u_{i,a}\in\mathbb R^{1+nq}\), for \(i\in[n],a\in D\), satisfying
\[\langle v_0,v_0\rangle=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in D}u_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle u_{i,a},u_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b).\]
For each constraint occurrence \(C\), let \(S_C\) be its set of distinct variables and choose a local distribution \(\mu_C:D^{S_C}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with total mass one. Impose
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{i,a}\rangle\quad(i\in S_C),\]
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a,\ z(j)=b}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{j,b}\rangle\quad(i,j\in S_C,\ i\ne j).\]
Thus all local one- and two-variable marginals agree with the common vector inner products. Repeated occurrences of a variable in a constraint use the same value \(z(i)\). The SDP value \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) is the minimum of
\[\frac1m\sum_C\sum_{z\in D^{S_C}}\mu_C(z)f_C(z(i_1),\ldots,z(i_k)),\]
with value zero when \(m=0\). This is a finite semidefinite program via its Gram matrix; the stated vector dimension suffices for every such matrix. It is feasible and compact in Gram-matrix and distribution coordinates. Every assignment gives a feasible point, so \(0\leq\operatorname{SDP}(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). No higher level of an SDP hierarchy is included.

For a fixed instance define its gap ratio as \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) if the denominator is positive, as one if both values are zero, and as \(+\infty\) if only the denominator is zero. Let \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\) be the supremum of these ratios over all lists of constraints on exactly \(n\) labelled variables; unused variables are counted. Then \(1\leq\alpha_\Lambda(n)\leq+\infty\), and the gap may grow with \(n\). The algorithm is not supplied with its value or an oracle for it. This is an instance-size gap, not a single constant supremum over every size.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary and each constraint by its fixed-table index and its \(k\) variable indices in binary; the total bit length is \(L\). The algorithm is a finite probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair coin bits. For each fixed \(D,k,\Lambda,\varepsilon\), one program has worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\) on every input and every coin sequence; \(C,c\) may depend on these fixed parameters. Malformed strings may be rejected. The output explicitly gives all \(n\) labels. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common exponent across languages or effective algorithm for finding the program from \(\Lambda\) is required. The probability convention is the explicit bounded-error interpretation of the source’s randomized approximation framework.

The guarantee is multiplicative, relative to the actual optimum. When that optimum is zero and the size-dependent gap is finite, the algorithm must find a zero-cost assignment with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no additive error term, and no assertion that it must round a supplied SDP point or achieve the stronger bound with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) in place of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal algorithmic assertion, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one polynomial-time machine for every fixed language and positive accuracy, working at all input sizes with the stated success probability, size-dependent gap and zero-optimum convention. A negative proof must establish a fixed finite language and positive accuracy for which no such machine exists. A constant additive guarantee for normalized cost, an algorithm restricted to one predicate family, or a conditional obstruction to one rounding scheme does not settle the universal statement. An unproved complexity assumption may support partial progress but is not part of this unconditional target.
context:
The integrality gap measures a relaxation’s worst discrepancy from a genuine assignment. In minimization, the SDP can make local constraints appear cheaper than any global assignment. This question asks whether an efficient algorithm can always match the resulting size-dependent benchmark to arbitrarily small relative slack; it does not ask to compute the gap itself.

The source distinguishes maximization and minimization with nonnegative predicates. For maximization, a random assignment provides a positive baseline for each nonzero fixed predicate, allowing additive approximation losses to become relative losses. For minimization, satisfiable or nearly satisfiable instances can have optimum zero or arbitrarily close to zero, so the same argument fails.

Raghavendra and Steurer’s universal rounding theorem obtains the integrality-gap curve with an additive error in both its argument and its returned objective. Its running-time dependence on that additive accuracy can be very large. Taking the accuracy to shrink with the instance size therefore does not yield the polynomial-time multiplicative guarantee asked here.

The source explicitly permits α_n to depend on n. Replacing it by one global constant would discard major minimization examples, while a generic additive approximation to a normalized objective would leave zero and very small costs unprotected. These are essential parts of the question, not presentation choices.

The 2026 robust-satisfiability work obtains quantitative guarantees for specified majority and plurality preservation classes, along with separate conditional hardness for a particular promise problem. Those results concern selected families and loss curves. They do not assert a universal algorithm matching the exact n-variable multiplicative SDP gap for every finite nonnegative cost language.
why: A universal theorem would extend the general SDP approximation framework to multiplicative minimization guarantees, including instances whose optimum vanishes with input size. It would connect a geometric obstruction of a standard relaxation to actual polynomial-time approximation across all finite cost languages. A counterexample would identify a limit to interpreting integrality gaps as achievable algorithmic benchmarks.
status_note: The 2017 chapter explicitly poses this n-dependent multiplicative question after distinguishing it from the 2009 additive rounding theorem. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper supplies results under additional template hypotheses, not the universal statement. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this does not establish that the historical question remains open beyond the checked sources.
progress: 2009: Raghavendra and Steurer prove a universal rounding result for the integrality-gap curve, with additive accuracy losses. | 2017: Makarychev and Makarychev explain why the additive theorem does not give the corresponding minimization ratio, then pose the n-dependent multiplicative question as Open Problem 4. | 2026-02-10: New robust-satisfiability guarantees are proved under specified algebraic preservation hypotheses; they provide special-family progress rather than a matching theorem for every finite cost language.

working_summary: A minimization CSP assigns finite-domain values to variables to minimize the average of fixed local nonnegative costs. Its basic SDP can achieve a lower cost using consistent local distributions and vectors than any actual assignment. The question asks whether a randomized polynomial-time algorithm can match the SDP’s worst gap at each number of variables within every factor 1+ε. The multiplicative guarantee must also protect zero or very small optimum values, which existing additive universal rounding does not do. title: Square-root logarithmic approximation for metric labeling
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Close a major gap for a general labeling objective linking metric geometry and approximation.
formal: Does a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist giving an \(O(\sqrt{\log (k+2)})\) approximation for every metric-labeling instance with k labels?

title: Hardness of coloring 2-dicolorable digraphs with any fixed number of colors
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Tests constant-factor approximation hardness for partitioning a digraph into acyclic sets under a two-colorability promise, a structural counterpart of hard coloring problems. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 4\), is it NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions to distinguish digraphs with dichromatic number at most 2 from digraphs with dichromatic number greater than k?
definitions: A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), no loops, and at most one arc in each direction between distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) and arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\), with indices modulo \(\ell\). A k-dicoloring is a map \(c:V\to \{1,\ldots ,k\}\) such that each color class induces an acyclic digraph, equivalently no directed cycle is monochromatic. The dichromatic number is the least k admitting such a map. The promise problem for k accepts inputs with dichromatic number at most 2 and rejects those with dichromatic number greater than k; inputs with values \(3,\ldots ,k\) are outside the promise. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm \(R_{k}\) and constants \(c_{k},C_{k}\) such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length \(N, R_{k}\) outputs a digraph in time at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c}_{k}\), with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed \(k\ge 4\), or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Hardness for \(k=3\), bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.
context:
In a directed path \(u\to v\to w\), all three vertices may receive the same color because there is no directed cycle. In a directed triangle \(u\to v\to w\to u\) they may not all receive the same color. This differs from ordinary graph coloring, which forbids any monochromatic edge.

The promise guarantees that two acyclic color classes exist. The algorithm is allowed more colors to make the search easier. If the two-coloring itself were supplied, the task would already be solved; it is deliberately absent from the input.

The paper asks about every constant k greater than three and then suggests that the problem may be NP-hard for every such k, as in a related hypergraph setting. This card adopts that explicit conjectural gap-hardness formulation, making the intended yes/no proposition reviewable.

The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm using at most \(2\sqrt{n}\) colors for a 2-dicolorable n-vertex digraph. It also records three-color hardness, even on tournaments. Neither result answers whether any larger fixed palette changes the complexity on general digraphs.
why: Tests how much approximation helps when searching for a partition into acyclic subgraphs. Constant-color hardness would establish a strong obstruction even when an optimal two-part partition is promised to exist.
status_note: Published Question 2, its following conjectural sentence and the coloring model checked through 11 September 2026; the May 2026 full-version record and later searches yielded no matching resolution for every fixed k.
progress: 2026-07: The ICALP paper supplies a \(2\sqrt{n}\)-color algorithm, records known three-color hardness and asks about every larger constant palette.
working_summary: A dicoloring partitions a directed graph into color classes containing no directed cycle. The input is promised to admit two colors, but that coloring is not supplied. The source conjecturally asks whether producing any fixed larger number of colors remains NP-hard. Its polynomial-time algorithm uses a number of colors growing as the square root of the vertex count. Settling the constant-color hardness claim would clarify whether a bounded relaxation of the optimum can overcome the search difficulty.

title: Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis from \(\mathrm{FPT} \ne  \mathrm{W}[1]\)
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A general bridge from exact parameterized hardness to constant-gap approximation hardness. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\), is there an absolute constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that no deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm can distinguish a satisfiable binary constraint satisfaction instance on k variables from an instance in which every assignment violates at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the constraints, with k as the parameter?
definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )=1\) or \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\le 1- \varepsilon\); no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.
context:
Exact unsatisfiability only says every assignment fails somewhere. PIH asks for a constant fraction of failures on every assignment. If an instance has many constraints, the existence of just one unavoidable violation need not give any fixed gap.

The alphabet is allowed to grow with the input. Exhaustive search takes \(n^{k}\) time, whose exponent depends on k; that is not fixed-parameter tractable. A running time such as \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) would qualify despite its very large dependence on k.

Baby PIH distinguishes satisfiable instances from instances for which even a constant-size list of values at each variable cannot satisfy every constraint. This is a different guarantee from saying that every ordinary assignment violates a constant fraction of constraints.

The Guruswami–Lin–Ren–Sun–Wu theorem derives PIH from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. ETH imposes a quantitative subexponential-time obstruction for 3SAT and is a stronger assumption than the parameterized separation sought here. The February 2026 survey still separates these targets.
why: Would supply a parameterized analogue of the PCP theorem from the standard exact-hardness assumption, giving a common basis for constant-gap inapproximability across many parameterized optimization problems.
status_note: Source definitions, the ETH theorem and the February 2026 survey checked with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No proof under only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) was located.
progress: 2024: Baby PIH is established under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\); the full PIH implication is left open. | 2025: The journal version of PIH under ETH records the stronger-assumption theorem, whose preprint already appeared in 2023. | 2026-02: The survey explicitly retains the distinction between PIH under ETH and PIH under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
working_summary: The hypothesis \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) says exact parameterized problems such as k-Clique do not admit fixed-parameter algorithms. The question asks whether it also rules out distinguishing satisfiable binary constraint systems from systems that force a constant fraction of violations. The parameter is the number of variables, while the alphabet may grow with the input. PIH is already known under the stronger ETH assumption, and Baby PIH is known under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\). A proof of the full implication would provide a broad foundation for parameterized inapproximability.

title: Almost 3-colorable graphs versus graphs with no large independent set
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A graph-coloring hardness strengthening with a concrete consequence for the Vertex Cover approximation threshold. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every fixed pair of constants \(0<\eta <1\) and \(0<\varepsilon <(1- \eta )/3\), is it NP-hard to distinguish graphs G on N vertices in which an induced subgraph on at least \((1- \eta )N\) vertices is properly 3-colorable from graphs G with independence number \(\alpha (G)<\varepsilon N\)? This is the nonoverlapping promise range of the source’s Conjecture 23, whose intended demand is hardness for arbitrarily small positive \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\).
definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; \(\alpha (G)\) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by \(U\subseteq V(G)\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map \(U\to \{1,2,3\}\) gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol\(_{3}(G)=N^{- 1}\max\){|\(U|:G[U]\) is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol\(_{3}(G)\ge 1- \eta\), and the no case is \(\alpha (G)/N<\varepsilon\). Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters \(\varepsilon ,\eta\) are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\). An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible \(\varepsilon ,\eta\), with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.
context:
Deleting at most an \(\eta\) fraction of vertices must leave a properly 3-colorable graph. The input need not be exactly 3-colorable.

Every independent set must occupy less than an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the entire graph. Merely proving that no almost-spanning subgraph can be colored with a fixed number of colors does not give this guarantee.

For every fixed k, the paper obtains a positive \(\delta\) such that it is hard, under randomized reductions, to distinguish almost 3-colorability from failure to k-color all but a \(\delta\) fraction of vertices. Conjecture 23 asks for the substantially stronger independent-set soundness condition.

The complement of an independent set is a vertex cover. The requested gap would imply hardness of approximating minimum Vertex Cover within \(3/2- \zeta\) for every fixed \(\zeta >0\), as the source explains. This consequence is motivation, not an additional target.
why: Would strengthen almost-coloring hardness enough to improve a central Vertex Cover approximation barrier, linking graph coloring promises with independent-set soundness.
status_note: The full conjecture, its definition of induced coloring and the weaker proved theorem were checked. Subsequent-result searches through 12 September 2026, including the publisher abstract of the related MFCS 2025 matrix-completion paper, did not locate this stronger independent-set gap. That later abstract is not evidence of a resolution.
progress: 2023: Theorem 1 establishes the almost-coloring gap under randomized reductions; Conjecture 23 asks for no independent set of any prescribed small positive fractional size.
working_summary: The yes instances become 3-colorable after deleting an arbitrarily small fixed fraction of vertices. The no instances have no independent set occupying a prescribed small fixed fraction of all vertices. The conjecture asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing these two cases. The source proves a weaker almost-coloring gap with randomized reductions. The stronger independent-set gap would improve hardness of approximating Vertex Cover toward a factor of three halves.

title: Subquadratic factor-three edit-distance approximation
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A consequential accuracy-versus-runtime boundary for a fundamental sequence problem, contrasting strong approximation with fixed polynomial improvements over quadratic computation. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm and constants \(\eta>0\) and \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given strings \(X,Y\) of total length \(n\), the algorithm runs in at most \(C(n+2)^{2-\eta}\) time and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs an estimate \(\widehat d\) satisfying \[\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\leq\widehat d\leq3\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)?\]
question_excerpt: Recent developments in designing fast approximation algorithms \([2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 25]\) culminated in an \(O(1)\)-approximation in near-linear time [3], but the existence […]
definitions:
The unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(X\) into \(Y\). Each operation costs one, including substitution. There are no transpositions, moves of blocks, or cheaper substitution costs. The two strings can have different lengths or be empty.

The input consists of both strings in full, with their lengths. Let \(n=|X|+|Y|\). Characters can be encoded by integer labels in \(\{1,\ldots,\max\{1,n\}\}\); only equality of labels matters. This allows arbitrary alphabets occurring in the input, rather than a binary-alphabet promise. Renaming polynomially bounded integer symbols takes only a near-linear preprocessing cost, which is included.

Use the usual sequential random-access model with \(O(\log(n+2))\)-bit words: a word read or write, comparison, Boolean operation, shift, or arithmetic operation on a constant number of words costs one step. Memory is initially empty except for the input; reading the input, all preprocessing and writing the output are charged. The algorithm has independent fair random bits, but no advice or uncharged preprocessed strings, distance oracle, parallel processors or quantum operations.

One uniform algorithm and fixed constants must work at every input length, for every input pair and every distance regime. Its running-time bound holds for every random tape. The probability of meeting the approximation guarantee is over its internal randomness alone; the inputs need not be random or generated by a mutation model.

The estimate may be an integer: rounding a valid nonnegative rational estimate down preserves the inequalities because the true distance is an integer. No edit script or alignment has to be returned. When the strings are identical, a successful estimate must be exactly zero.

Truly subquadratic means a fixed positive exponent saving \(\eta\), independent of \(n\). A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log n\), or a stated improvement of the form \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{c}}\) with fixed \(0<c<1\), does not supply such a saving. A polylogarithmic overhead on an already fixed-power saving can be absorbed by decreasing \(\eta\).

The approximation factor is at most three, uniformly over the input size. A guarantee of \(3+\varepsilon\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), or \(3+o(1)\), does not itself establish this endpoint. The main question is existence of some positive runtime saving, not its optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm meeting the factor-three guarantee and some fixed positive exponent saving for all inputs in the stated model, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. State any hypothesis of a conditional negative result explicitly. An arbitrary constant approximation, a factor exceeding three, an average-case result, or a subpolynomial rather than fixed-power runtime saving is insufficient.
context:
Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.
why: Tests how much accuracy can be retained while obtaining a fixed polynomial speedup for a basic sequence-comparison problem. It separates the power of approximation from the quadratic barrier for exact computation, with relevance to algorithms for aligning and comparing strings.
status_note: Read the complete original introductory question and its full author counterpart, the Andoni–Nosatzki full-version main theorem, the Goldenberg–Rubinstein–Saha ordinary-input result, and the full March 2026 paper’s tradeoff table and Theorem 6.1. Verified the STOC 2026 publisher date. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no fixed-power-time factor-three resolution. The sequential model and constant success probability make explicit the randomized algorithmic target; no near-linear-time requirement is imposed.
progress: 2020: Near-linear time becomes possible with an arbitrary parameter-dependent constant factor, while another result reaches factor 3+o(1) in truly subquadratic time. | 2023: The source explicitly retains a truly subquadratic factor-three approximation as open. | 2026-06-09: The STOC approximation-scheme result achieves factors arbitrarily close to one, with a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time.
working_summary: The task compares two arbitrary explicit strings using unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions. The estimate must lie between the true edit distance and three times that distance. The algorithm must save a fixed positive power over quadratic time on every input. Known truly subquadratic algorithms approach factor three from above. The 2026 approximation scheme achieves better accuracy, but its proved time saving is smaller than a fixed power of the input length.

title: Constant-factor approximation of graph crossing number
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximability gap for a classical graph-layout objective, with a large separation between known general guarantees and constant-factor hardness. Existing score retained.
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\geq1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite undirected graph \(G\), outputs a drawing \(D\) in the plane satisfying \[\operatorname{cr}(D)\leq C\,\operatorname{cr}(G)\] with probability at least \(2/3\)?
question_excerpt: There exists a \(c > 1\) such that \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) cannot be approximated within a factor c in polynomial time [4], but we do not know […]
definitions:
The input explicitly lists the vertices and edges of an unweighted graph. Parallel edges are permitted and counted separately, as in the source. Self-loops can be omitted because they can be drawn locally without crossings. There is no bound on degree, genus or crossing number, and no planar subgraph or embedding is provided. Running time is polynomial in the full input length on every random tape.

A drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple polygonal curve joining its endpoints, without passing through any other vertex. The objective \(\operatorname{cr}(D)\) is the total number of pairwise edge crossings, summed over the entire drawing. The crossing number \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) is its minimum over all drawings. One may restrict to good drawings: adjacent edges do not cross, two edges cross at most once, and no three edges cross at one point.

The output must specify a drawing, rather than only an unsupported estimate of its value. A finite combinatorial representation suffices: list crossings in order along each original edge and give a planar embedding of the graph obtained by replacing crossings with degree-four vertices. At each such vertex, the two segments of each original edge must be opposite in the cyclic order. This records the original curves and their crossings without requiring real-number coordinates.

Randomization with bounded error is explicitly allowed, in keeping with the later approximation literature; a deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The success probability is over internal coins for each fixed graph. The constant \(C\) and the polynomial time bound are independent of the graph. In particular, a factor depending on its maximum degree does not meet the target. When \(\operatorname{cr}(G)=0\), the approximation guarantee requires a drawing with no crossings.

This is ordinary topological crossing number. Edges need not be straight, there is no prescribed rotation system, and the objective is not the maximum number of crossings on any one edge. The source’s Multiple Edge Insertion problem additionally keeps a specified subgraph planar; that constraint is absent here.
answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm and prove its running time and universal constant-factor guarantee, or prove that none exists. A conditional impossibility result must state its complexity assumption and cover randomized algorithms in the stated model. Hardness for a particular small approximation factor alone does not exclude all constant factors.
context:
Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

The 2023 paper studies maximizing the number of retained edges subject to a crossing budget. Its conditional hardness for Maximum Bounded-Crossing Subgraph should not be read as hardness of every constant approximation for the minimum total crossings of the entire input graph.
why: Crossing minimization is a basic graph-layout optimization problem with applications to drawing networks and circuit layouts. A constant approximation would establish a general algorithmic guarantee across sparse and dense inputs, beyond the degree-dependent and additive-error bounds currently available.
status_note: Checked the original full question and drawing model, the 2022 full approximation theorem, the distinct 2023 hardness variant, and the 2025/2026 dense-graph theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no universal constant-factor approximation or impossibility covering all constants. The randomized convention is explicit; the historical P ≠ NP hardness is stated only for deterministic algorithms.
progress: 2013: A fixed-factor inapproximability result establishes an obstruction to arbitrarily accurate polynomial-time approximation. | 2022: A subpolynomial approximation factor is obtained for bounded-degree graphs. | 2025-10-21: An additive-error approximation and drawing theorem yields asymptotically optimal approximation for dense graphs.
working_summary: Draw every graph in the plane using at most a fixed constant times its minimum possible number of crossings. The constant must be independent of the graph size and maximum degree. The algorithm must construct a drawing in polynomial time; bounded-error randomization is allowed. Existing low-degree and dense-graph results do not provide this guarantee for all graphs. Hardness for one fixed ratio above one leaves open the possibility of a larger universal constant.

title: Optimal general-domain CSP approximation under Unique Games hardness
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A broad quantitative approximability question for general finite-domain constraints, linking algorithms and PCP hardness across two independent parameters. Existing score retained.
formal: Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture and \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\), determine up to universal constant factors the optimal expected approximation ratio \(\rho(k,d)\) for every fixed arity \(k\ge2\) and domain size \(d\ge2\). The source proposes the scale \[q(k,d)=\frac{\max\{k,\log d\}}{d^{k-1}},\] which is retained as context rather than assumed to equal the answer.
definitions: An instance has an explicit finite list of variables with values in \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and an explicit finite list of constraints. Each constraint names at most \(k\) distinct variables and gives the full Boolean truth table of its predicate on those variables. A repeated constraint counts separately. All variables, indices, delimiters and table entries count in the input bit length \(L\); there is no succinct predicate circuit or implicit list. The value of an assignment is the number of satisfied constraints, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the maximum value. For fixed \((k,d)\), an admissible algorithm is a uniform fair-coin Turing machine that outputs an assignment and halts within \(C_{k,d}(L+1)^{a_{k,d}}\) steps on every input and random tape, including output time. Its code and constants may depend on the fixed parameters, but not on the instance. Define \(\rho(k,d)\) as the supremum of \(r\in[0,1]\) for which some admissible algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}(A(I))]\ge r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every instance; zero-optimum instances impose no additional ratio condition. The supremum is not presumed attained. Logarithms in \(q\) are natural. A constant-factor answer consists of a positive function \(g(k,d)\) and one \(C\ge1\) such that \(C^{-1}g(k,d)\le\rho(k,d)\le Cg(k,d)\) for all \(k,d\ge2\). No hidden constant may depend on either parameter. Here the Unique Games Conjecture means: for every rational \(0<\eta,\gamma<1/2\), there is a fixed label count \(R\ge2\) for which it is NP-hard to distinguish unique-game instances of optimum satisfied fraction at least \(1-\eta\) from those of optimum at most \(\gamma\). A unique-game instance is an explicitly listed finite bipartite multigraph with at least one edge, a label in \([R]\) at each vertex, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[R]\to[R]\) at each oriented edge; an edge is satisfied when its endpoint labels obey that permutation. The objective is the fraction of satisfied edges, counting multiplicity. NP-hardness of this promise problem means that every language with polynomial-time verifiable polynomial-length witnesses has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping members to the first promise and nonmembers to the second. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized polynomial-time machine with error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The additional assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) makes the NP-hardness premise exclude bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decision procedures. Both assumptions and the fixed-parameter algorithm convention are explicit editorial choices.
answer_criterion: Supply a positive comparison function and a Lean proof, conditional only on the two stated hypotheses, of both universal constant-factor bounds for the entire arity/domain range. A ratio established for each fixed parameter with uncontrolled parameter-dependent comparison constants does not suffice. Bounds only for Boolean domains or only for one parameter regime do not determine this target. The answer concerns a supremum of achievable expected ratios and does not require an optimum-attaining algorithm. Numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to the asymptotic scale.
context:
The source asks whether the combined arity-and-domain approximation scale is optimal. The authorized variant makes the hardness assumptions and the dependence of algorithms on fixed parameters explicit.

The checked primary papers identify \(k\ge d\) as a regime of matching bounds. The concluding survey sentence reverses that inequality; the card follows the primary theorem statements.

The 2016 paper gives improved bounds for large domains, while the August 2026 preprints concern the Boolean leading constant. Neither supplies matching dependence over the full two-parameter range.
why: The question asks how arity and the number of labels jointly control the best efficient approximation of arbitrary local constraints. Matching bounds would explain the transition between Boolean-like behavior and large-domain instances, with consequences for the quantitative strength of probabilistically checkable proofs.

The checked bounds and Boolean-only preprint claims do not determine the full joint scale. The model and explicit hardness hypotheses were reviewed on 13 September 2026; new preprint proofs were not independently verified.

The task maximizes the number of satisfied constraints using randomized polynomial time for each fixed arity and domain size. The target is the best expected approximation ratio, compared across both parameters with universal constants. The chosen hardness framework assumes Unique Games hardness and that NP is not contained in BPP. Known matching regimes and recent Boolean leading-constant claims do not determine the full general-domain scale.

title: Breaking two for unrelated-machine makespan
importance_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
focus_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+2)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same fixed-factor approximation-existence question.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside the valid input domain. The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

Choose \(\varepsilon\), the program and its polynomial constants once, before all inputs. They cannot depend on machine count, job count, processing times or encoding precision. There is no additive slack or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; the empty instance is included.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\) be the set of universal multiplicative factors achievable by one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm per factor in this exact model, and put \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R\). The established factor-two algorithm makes this set nonempty. The current proposition is equivalent to \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}<2\), but does not require determining that infimum or attaining it.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic algorithm with some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and the stated worst-case polynomial bit-time and feasibility guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies. A factor such as \(2-1/m\), whose improvement vanishes as the input machine count grows, does not qualify. Neither a guarantee for a fixed number of machines nor a restricted family of processing times settles the full target. A negative answer must exclude all positive constant improvements for all uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in this model. A conditional hardness result is only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. There is no minimum improvement of \(0.01\), and the task does not ask to determine the optimal ratio.
context:
The original source asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. The 12 September numerical reformulation asked for the full optimal ratio. The user's 17 September choice restores the barrier question: any positive constant improvement suffices, including an improvement smaller than \(1/100\).

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.
why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.
