working_summary: Jobs have machine-dependent processing times, and every job must be assigned wholly to one eligible machine. The objective is to minimize the maximum total load on any machine. The question asks whether a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee factor \(2-\varepsilon\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The same improvement must hold for every input machine count and processing-time matrix, however small the chosen constant is. Instance-dependent savings and guarantees for restricted machine models do not establish this universal improvement.

title: Breaking two for precedence-constrained makespan
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+1)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
question_excerpt: The 17 September 2026 formulation asks whether a uniform deterministic polynomial-time approximation can improve factor two by any fixed positive constant. This supersedes the previous numerical infimum target and its absolute 1/100 tolerance. The saved bit encodings and integer output starts, including equivalence with real-start optima, are retained. Arbitrary input machine count and arbitrary positive integer processing times remain part of the model; the improvement cannot depend on the machine count. Importance 96 is unchanged.
definitions:
Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and improvement. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is in the full input bit length, including durations and machine count. All computation and output costs count. Invalid encodings may be rejected. The same algorithm, positive \(\varepsilon\) and polynomial constants must work for every valid input; \(\varepsilon\) is not an input accuracy parameter. In particular, the improvement cannot shrink as the number of machines or jobs grows.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\) be the universal approximation factors achievable by uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithms for this model, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R\). Graham's list-scheduling guarantee gives \(2\in\mathcal R\). The present question asks whether \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}<2\); it does not require finding the infimum or an algorithm attaining it.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic algorithm with some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and the stated worst-case polynomial bit-time and feasibility guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies. A factor such as \(2-1/m\), whose improvement vanishes as the input machine count grows, does not qualify. Neither a guarantee for a fixed number of machines nor a restricted family of processing times settles the full target. A negative answer must exclude all positive constant improvements for all uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in this model. A conditional hardness result is only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. There is no minimum improvement of \(0.01\), and the task does not ask to determine the optimal ratio.
context:
The input is an entire task graph, not a stream of arrivals. A scheduler may inspect all durations and dependencies before choosing assignments and start times. It must place every job, keep each job uninterrupted, and minimize the last completion time. Changing to an online rule, preemption, machine-dependent durations or total completion time changes the problem.

Total work \(W=\sum_j p_j\) gives the lower bound \(W/m\) on any feasible makespan. The total duration \(D\) of a longest directed path in the precedence graph gives another lower bound, since that chain runs sequentially. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.

Graham’s list scheduling starts available jobs according to a priority order when machines become free. A job is available after all its predecessors finish. The established bound is \(C_{\max}\le W/m+(1-1/m)D\le(2-1/m)\operatorname{OPT}\). Although this is below two for each finite \(m\), its supremum over input machine counts is two. It therefore gives the universal bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), not a fixed improvement below two.

A priority example separates a poor list from algorithmic impossibility. For \(m\ge2\), take \(m(m-1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length \(m\). Listing the long job last gives makespan \(2m-1\), whereas starting it immediately and distributing the units over the other machines gives makespan \(m\), which also equals the work lower bound. This shows tightness for that list order; it has no precedence edges and does not prove hardness for every algorithm.

Classical NP-hardness excludes every factor strictly below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(4/3\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The word “unless” is essential: NP-hardness is not an unconditional proof that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot exist.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), feasible integer schedules of polynomial bit length can be found optimally in polynomial time, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\). Here all optimum starts lie at most at total processing time, whose binary length is polynomial in the input length. Thus an unconditional lower bound strictly above one would in particular separate P from NP. Conditional hardness must remain distinguished from an unconditional negative answer to the algorithm-existence question.

Svensson proves a transfer from the approximability of a different objective: total weighted completion time on a single machine with precedences. Hardness arbitrarily close to two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit jobs. The transferred loss tends to zero, but the two scheduling objectives and their approximation parameters are not identical.

His Corollary 1 uses the Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant in Appendix Hypothesis 1. It requires a satisfiable large bipartite portion in the completeness case and an extra expansion condition in the soundness case. The paper explicitly distinguishes it from ordinary UGC and does not establish their equivalence. Together with P different from NP, this hypothesis gives inapproximability for every fixed factor below two and hence the conditional value two.

The user-authorized numerical target of 12 September asked for the entire infimum. The 17 September choice instead asks for any fixed factor strictly below two. Although \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\) remains useful background notation, approximating it to \(1/100\) is no longer the answer criterion: a smaller proved positive improvement also resolves the existence question.

For unit jobs on a fixed number of machines, approximation schemes with quasipolynomial running time represent substantial progress. Das and Wiese give a simpler such scheme at ESA 2022, following earlier results. Its runtime is still not polynomial in the sense required here, and the fixed-machine, unit-duration promises do not cover all inputs in this card.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki give an exact unit-job algorithm running in \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) time; this is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\). They also improve the exponential base in the regime \(m=\Theta(n)\). The work appeared at SODA 2025 and online in TALG in January 2026. Faster exact exponential-time algorithms do not supply a polynomial-time universal approximation ratio.

The July 2026 unique-machine preprint proves NP-hardness of every constant approximation factor for unit jobs when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. This removes assignment flexibility and is an additional input restriction on allowable schedules, absent from the present model. Its stronger hardness therefore does not contradict the factor-two algorithm for freely assignable identical machines.

The factor-two upper bound, the classical conditional lower bound and the stronger hypothesis-based hardness address different conclusions. The current target accepts any uniform polynomial-time factor \(2-\varepsilon\) with fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or an unconditional proof that no such algorithm exists. A vanishing saving as the machine count grows is insufficient.
why: Precedence constraints make scheduling depend on both how much work can run in parallel and which completions unlock later jobs. A fixed improvement below factor two would show that these two effects can be coordinated more efficiently than the classical worst-case guarantee, uniformly over all machine counts.
status_note: The individual source review of 16 September 2026 recorded Graham's universal factor-two guarantee, classical conditional hardness below \(4/3\), and hardness below two under the specific stronger Bansal-Khot hypothesis together with P different from NP. Fixed-machine schemes, exact unit-job algorithms and predetermined-machine hardness have different scope. On 17 September the formulation was changed to the strict-below-two algorithm-existence question. The prior later-work search was bounded and long source proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: The problem schedules positive-duration jobs on an input number of identical machines while respecting all precedences and minimizing the last completion time. The question asks whether a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can achieve approximation factor \(2-\varepsilon\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Any positive constant improvement qualifies, and the same improvement must hold for all job counts, machine counts and precedence graphs. Graham's \(2-1/m\) guarantee approaches two as the machine count grows and therefore does not give the requested fixed saving. Known conditional hardness and restricted-instance algorithms do not themselves settle this unconditional existence question.

title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
importance_reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\ge0\), a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), and absolute integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance \(I\), of binary input length \(L\), satisfies all three conditions below?

Every execution of \(A(I)\) takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations and outputs a feasible packing into bins of capacity one; and, writing \(B_A(I)\) for its number of nonempty bins,
\[
\Pr[B_A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+C]\ge\frac23.
\]
The constants do not depend on the number of items, their sizes or precision, the number of distinct sizes, or the optimum. The entire input is available before any packing decisions are made.
question_excerpt: Bansal asks whether ordinary one-dimensional bin packing admits a polynomial-time algorithm using OPT+O(1) bins, and separately mentions the stronger OPT+1 target. This card retains the constant-additive alternative and its previously selected explicit rational input and randomized guarantee.
definitions:
An instance is a finite list \(I=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), with \(n\ge1\) and rational sizes \(0<s_i\le1\). Write each size as \(s_i=a_i/b_i\), where \(1\le a_i\le b_i\) are positive integers given in canonical binary. The numerator and denominator need not be relatively prime. A fixed unambiguous encoding includes \(n\) and every pair \((a_i,b_i)\); \(L\) is its full bit length, including boundaries. Repeated items are separate entries. Binary multiplicities, an oracle, a circuit or a program generating a larger item list are not alternative input encodings. Malformed strings may be rejected in polynomial time.

A packing assigns each item to exactly one bin, without splitting or discarding any item. It is output as a list \(b(1),\ldots,b(n)\) of labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its nonempty-bin count is \(B=|\{b(i):1\le i\le n\}|\); unused labels do not count. It is feasible if
\[
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad
\sum_{i:b(i)=j}s_i\le1.
\]
All these inequalities use the exact rational input values. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) as the minimum of \(B\) over all feasible assignments. A singleton bin for each item is feasible, so \(1\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le n\).

The algorithm is a single classical multitape Turing machine that may read independent fair random bits. Reading random bits, reading the input, arithmetic on binary integers and rationals, preprocessing and writing every output label count toward bit time. The polynomial time bound must hold on every random tape for every valid input. Feasibility must also hold on every tape. Only the additive-quality bound is probabilistic, and its probability must be at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed input, not merely on average over an input distribution. On unsuccessful tapes the algorithm may use more than \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)+C\) bins, but must still produce a feasible assignment.

The algorithm is offline and can inspect all sizes before assigning any item. Bins all have exactly capacity one; there is no augmentation of capacity, additional cardinality constraint, packing order requirement, restriction on the number of item types or lower bound on item size beyond positivity. It cannot call an optimum oracle or use uncharged instance-dependent advice. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.

The additive constant \(C\) is existentially chosen once for all instances. The question does not require \(C=1\), a prescribed value of \(C\), or finding the smallest possible constant. The benchmark \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the integral packing optimum, not the value of a fractional relaxation. This is an exact algorithm-existence proposition; the numerical tolerance for a separate value-estimation problem does not alter the displayed approximation guarantee.
answer_criterion:
Supply \(A,C,K,d\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of worst-case bit time, feasibility on every random tape and the per-input probability bound. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no choices of a uniform randomized algorithm and such absolute constants meet these conditions.

An additive loss growing with the instance or optimum, a fixed multiplicative approximation ratio, increased bin capacity, a guarantee only for a restricted family, or an existential fractional integrality-gap bound without the required algorithm does not settle the question. Impossibility of one rounding method is not impossibility of all algorithms. A negative answer restricted to deterministic algorithms would not exclude the permitted randomized algorithms.
context:
Every item must fit completely in one bin, and feasibility can be checked from the output assignment. The unknown optimum is only the comparison benchmark; it is not supplied to the algorithm.

A guarantee of \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_\varepsilon\) can still waste an unbounded number of bins as the optimum grows. The requested \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) guarantee instead limits the absolute loss by one universal constant.

Hoberg and Rothvoss obtain a logarithmic additive guarantee with a randomized expected-polynomial-time algorithm. Their comparison is even to the fractional configuration optimum, obtained by allowing nonnegative fractional weights on feasible bin patterns. The logarithmic loss still grows.

A constant integrality gap for a relaxation would be a structural statement about fractional and integral optima. The card asks for a polynomial-time algorithm outputting the near-optimal assignment itself. Neither statement should be substituted for the other without the needed algorithmic argument.

The 2025 support theorem bounds how many different bin patterns some solutions need. Its introduction also records an OPT+1 algorithm whose dependence on the number of item types is not polynomial. These address other aspects of the problem.

High-multiplicity input stores large numbers of equal items by binary counts. The 2026 lower bound concerns exact optimization measured in that compressed length. Here every item is listed and the algorithm is allowed a fixed additive loss.
why: The question asks whether the absolute loss in a basic packing problem can be bounded independently of instance scale. Such a result would go beyond a ratio tending to one by controlling the number of extra bins itself, and would sharpen a longstanding boundary in approximation algorithms.
status_note: The inherited constant-additive algorithm question remains unresolved in the checked sources. The logarithmic additive randomized result does not give a constant loss. The ESA 2025 support theorem and ICALP 2026 exact high-multiplicity lower bound concern different targets and do not rule out the explicitly listed randomized formulation here.

The question asks for a polynomial-time algorithm using at most a fixed constant more bins than the optimal integral packing. title: Optimal competitive ratio for convex body chasing
importance_reason: A canonical geometric model of online optimization with movement costs.
formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as a function of \(d\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\mathcal C(d)\) for general convex body chasing in Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^d\). The domain is every integer \(d\ge1\).

An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]
The strategy may depend on \(d\), but must serve all horizons and request sequences in that dimension. The target is the asymptotic order of this dimension-dependent ratio, resolving the source's gap between order \(\sqrt d\) and order \(d\).
definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound. Determination up to universal factors means providing a noncircular positive function \(h\) on the positive integers and constants \(a,b>0\), independent of dimension, such that \(a h(d)\le\mathcal C(d)\le b h(d)\) for every \(d\ge1\). Equivalent eventually valid asymptotic bounds may be extended over the finitely many smaller dimensions by adjusting constants. The question does not require an exact ratio or an additive \(1/100\) estimate of that ratio.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic growth of \(\mathcal C(d)\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors. The upper bound must cover arbitrary finite, possibly non-nested request sequences with one horizon-independent deterministic strategy in each dimension. The lower bound must apply to every permitted strategy. A nonattained infimum may be handled by arbitrarily approaching bounds. Merely renaming the optimization defining \(\mathcal C\), proving a bound for nested requests, allowing the ratio to grow with the horizon, or establishing a lower bound in another norm does not meet the criterion.
context:
The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.
why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.
status_note: The 2025 source slides and the full November 2021 Sellke revision were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded search through 2026 found work on nested feasible regions and related chasing variants but no matching dimension-only upper and lower bounds for general Euclidean requests. The card records the established bounds and source-open gap without claiming an exhaustive current-status review.
progress: 1993: Friedman and Linial introduce convex body chasing; the later sources describe its finite-competitiveness conjecture and the square-root Euclidean obstruction. | 2020: The SODA results give linear dimension dependence for general requests, and a nearly square-root Euclidean bound for the nested variant. Sellke’s revised full manuscript separately states the horizon-dependent Euclidean improvement. | 2025: Gupta’s Winter School slides continue to distinguish the linear general bound, the nearly square-root nested bound, and the square-root Euclidean lower bound.
working_summary: Convex body chasing requires an online player to move into each newly revealed convex set. The player pays Euclidean movement while an offline comparator knows all future requests. This question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as dimension grows, up to universal constant factors. The strategy must work for arbitrary finite request sequences without knowing the horizon. The checked sources leave a gap between square-root and linear dimension dependence for general requests, with stronger results only in restricted settings.

title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
importance_reason: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret \(R*(d,T)\) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in \([0,1]\). Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function \(g(d,T)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) with a \(g(d,T)\le R*(d,T)\le b g(d,T)\) for all \(d,T\ge 1\). Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate \(g(d,T)\) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.
context:
On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.
why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
progress: 2020: A general information-theoretic upper bound \(O(d^{2.5} \sqrt{T} \log (T \operatorname{diam}(K)))\) is proved for the oblivious exact-feedback model. | 2026-03: The book’s Outlook retains the gap between dimension-linear lower bounds and higher-degree general upper bounds. | 2026-06: Budgeted-perturbation results concern smooth underlying losses, including in the unperturbed case. | 2026-07: The revised two-point strongly convex result has a different feedback and comparator model.
working_summary: What is the optimal expected regret for adversarial convex losses when only one value is observed per round? The learner competes with the best fixed point in hindsight over a known convex body. The losses lie in \([0,1]\) and are chosen before the learner’s random actions, with no smoothness assumption. General upper and lower bounds still have different polynomial dependence on dimension. Two-point, strongly convex, smooth-loss and computational-efficiency results address different guarantees.

title: Matroid secretary conjecture
importance_reason: A central online-selection benchmark spanning arbitrary matroids and arbitrary fixed weights; the new claimed resolution changes its status without changing its mathematical significance.
formal:
Does there exist a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), there is a randomized online selection strategy \(\mathcal A_M\) satisfying
\[\forall w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0},\qquad
\mathbb E_{\pi,U}\!\left[\sum_{e\in S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)}w(e)\right]
\ge\frac1C\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)?\]
The element weights are fixed adversarially before a uniformly random arrival permutation \(\pi\) and the strategy's independent randomness \(U\) are chosen. Each acceptance decision is irrevocable and must preserve independence. The same \(C\) must work for all matroids and all weights.
question_excerpt: The retained target is the classical constant-competitive matroid secretary conjecture in the model where the matroid is known beforehand. It is not the stronger question of attaining the best universal constant, nor an efficient-oracle implementation question. The September 2026 preprint claims a guarantee in the more restrictive model with only the size known beforehand and independence access to arrived elements, which would also cover this formulation.
definitions:
A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set \(E\) and a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) of independent sets with two properties. First, \(B\subseteq A\in\mathcal I\) implies \(B\in\mathcal I\). Second, if \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). In particular, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\). Loops, zero weights, ties and the empty ground set are allowed. The matroid rank is \(\max_{I\in\mathcal I}|I|\).

The strategy knows \(E\) and \(\mathcal I\) in advance, including all element identities and \(n=|E|\), but has no information about the weights of unarrived elements. At step \(t\), it sees the identity \(\pi(t)\) and its finite real weight \(w(\pi(t))\). Before the next arrival, it chooses to accept or reject that element. Its decision may use only the known matroid, the revealed prefix, its previous decisions and its random seed. An accepted element cannot subsequently be discarded, and a rejected element cannot subsequently be accepted. Every accepted prefix must belong to \(\mathcal I\), for every input, arrival order and seed. The notation \(S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)\) denotes the final accepted set.

A randomized strategy is a measurable nonanticipating decision rule; one may model its private randomness by \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), independent of \(\pi\). The permutation is uniform among the \(n!\) permutations of \(E\) and independent of the fixed weight assignment. Expectations include these two sources of randomness. For every fixed assignment the optimum is finite, so the expected reward is well-defined and finite. If all feasible weights are zero, the inequality still applies with a zero right-hand side.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C\;\forall M\;\exists\mathcal A_M\;\forall w\). A strategy cannot be selected after seeing the weight assignment. The guarantee has no additive loss, no dependence of \(C\) on size or rank, and no high-probability requirement beyond the stated expectation. There is no restriction on computation, preprocessing or independence queries. This is the competitive-existence question in the known-matroid model, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights; no finite encoding or polynomial running time is appended.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed constant-competitiveness proposition, or of its full logical negation. A positive proof must give a finite universal constant and admissible strategies with the expected guarantee for every matroid and weight assignment. A negative proof must show that for every proposed finite constant some matroid defeats every admissible strategy on some fixed nonnegative weight assignment. A result for a restricted matroid family, randomly assigned weights, or a constant depending on rank does not settle this target. A newly posted proof claim is not itself a Lean-checked answer.
context:
The classical secretary task chooses one item whose unknown value is revealed on arrival. Matroids extend the feasibility rule to collections of items. For example, a uniform matroid permits any set up to a prescribed size, while a graphic matroid permits sets of edges containing no cycle. The offline optimum knows every weight; the online strategy sees only a random prefix at each decision.

Random arrival order and random assignment of weights are distinct sources of information. In the random-assignment variant, a multiset of weights is distributed uniformly among ground-set elements. Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen obtain a constant guarantee for that variant even without advance knowledge of the matroid. Their May 2023 preprint explicitly leaves the adversarial-assignment conjecture open. Its theorem cannot by itself justify the general claim here.

Before the new September claim, the cited general guarantee was \(O(\log\log r)\), with the small-rank cases treated separately, where \(r\) is the matroid rank. A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, this card's advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.
why: This is a central question about the power of random arrival order in online selection under general independence constraints. A universal bound would apply across all matroids and is equivalent, through established reductions, to a general random-order contention-resolution guarantee.
status_note: Matching claimed resolution found on 16 September 2026: Singla, arXiv:2609.14555v1, submitted 13 September, Theorem 3.1, would establish the whole target with C=4 and less advance matroid information. The full PDF and relevant theorem/model were inspected, but the complete proof has not been independently verified or Lean-checked here. The status is therefore uncertain pending verification, superseding the previous source-open assessment. No stronger optimal-constant or efficient-implementation target is substituted.
progress: 2007: The classical conjecture asks for one constant competitive ratio for all matroids and all fixed nonnegative weight assignments. | 2022-01-25: Dughmi establishes equivalence with universal random-order contention resolution for arbitrary known prior distributions. | 2023-05-09: Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen post a constant guarantee for random assignment without knowing the matroid upfront, distinguishing it from the general conjecture. | 2026-09-13: Singla posts a claimed resolution: Theorem 3.1 gives per-optimum-element acceptance probability at least \(1/4\), hence a claimed universal factor 4. The current record is version 1; proof correctness has not been independently certified in this review.
working_summary: Elements of a known matroid arrive in a uniformly random order with fixed nonnegative weights revealed only on arrival. The strategy must accept or reject each immediately while keeping its selected set independent. The target is one universal constant fraction of the offline optimum in expectation, with no running-time restriction. Singla’s September 2026 preprint claims a factor-four guarantee even with only arrived-element independence access. The claimed theorem matches this target, so the record is uncertain pending verification rather than still classified as an unchallenged open conjecture.

title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
importance_reason: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
formal:
Determine the growth, up to universal multiplicative constants, of the optimal randomized competitive ratio for \(k\)-server on all finite metrics against an oblivious adversary. For each integer \(k\ge2\), define
\[R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where \(\mathcal R_k\) is the set of real \(r\ge1\) such that
\[\forall (X,d)\in\mathcal M_k\;\forall C_0\in X^k\;\exists\mathcal A\;\exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\;\forall\sigma\in X^{<\omega},\qquad
\mathbb E_U[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathcal A}(\sigma;C_0,U)]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite metric spaces with at least \(k+1\) points, and \(\mathcal A\) is an online randomized strategy as defined below. Give an unambiguous positive function \(h\) on the integers \(k\ge2\) and fixed real constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\) such that
\[a h(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le b h(k)\qquad\text{for all integers }k\ge2.\]
The requested precision is matching asymptotic bounds, including any logarithmic dependence.
question_excerpt: The saved September 12 quantitative formulation broadened the polylogarithmic-in-k question to the asymptotic order of the universal randomized competitive ratio. That constant-factor target is retained, including finite known metrics, oblivious adversaries, no computation restriction and sequence-independent additive cost. The earlier logarithmic conjecture is false; the weaker question of any fixed polylogarithmic bound is distinct from both that conjecture and the full quantitative target. The September deterministic conjecture claim does not replace this randomized question.
definitions:
A metric on a finite set \(X\) is a finite-valued function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry and the triangle inequality. The number \(n=|X|\) is unbounded relative to \(k\). The strategy knows the full metric and initial configuration before any request. Distances may be arbitrary real numbers: no rational encoding, finite-precision cost or computability restriction is imposed on this information-theoretic question.

Exactly \(k\) identical servers serve the requests. For bookkeeping write a configuration as a tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in X^k\); repeated locations are allowed and the labels confer no different costs. A finite sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\) is revealed one request at a time. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay and this step costs zero. Otherwise the strategy chooses one server, moves it from its current position \(x_i\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_i,q_t)\). All other servers stay. The total cost is the sum over the \(T\) steps. This lazy convention has the same attainable competitive guarantees as the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances model. It is not a simultaneous maximum-movement objective.

An online strategy is a measurable rule whose move depends on the known metric, \(k,C_0\), the revealed request prefix, its past choices and its private randomness. One may model the randomness by a uniform seed \(U\in[0,1]\). It must make a legal move for every prefix and seed, and serve the current request before observing the next. No future request, request horizon, prediction or advice depending on the sequence is supplied. There is no time, space, number-of-random-bits or finite-program bound. The same seed law and nonanticipating rule serve all finite sequences on the chosen instance.

The adversary is oblivious: each sequence \(\sigma\) in the guarantee is fixed independently of \(U\). It may know the strategy and its distribution, but may not choose the next request from observed random moves. Expectation is over \(U\), for that fixed sequence. Every finite-sequence cost is bounded by \(T\) times the finite metric diameter, so the expectation is finite. The offline comparator starts at the identical tuple \(C_0\), knows all of \(\sigma\), and minimizes total movement under the same serving convention. This minimum exists because there are finitely many possible server choices for a finite sequence. The empty sequence has online and offline cost zero.

For fixed \(k,r\), the strategy and finite additive term \(\beta\) may depend on the metric and initial tuple, but neither may depend on the future sequence or its length. The ratio \(r\), and ultimately the comparison constants \(a,b\), cannot depend on \(n\), distances or initial placement. The same chosen strategy and \(\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all lengths and contents. Classical deterministic bounds imply \(1\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le2k-1\), so the infimum is a finite dimensionless number. No strategy attaining the infimum is presumed to exist.

An upper bound on this infimum need not give an algorithm attaining its endpoint: for every positive slack, strategies with ratios at most the proposed upper bound plus that slack suffice on every metric and initial placement. A lower bound must exclude every smaller universal ratio; for such a smaller ratio some metric and initial placement must defeat every eligible strategy and every fixed additive constant on a sequence independent of the realized seed. The unknown function \(h\) must specify the asymptotic scale, rather than merely rename the defining infimum.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both displayed inequalities for some unambiguous \(h\) and universal \(a,b\). This is the retained constant-factor asymptotic-complexity target, not an additive numerical approximation requirement. Upper bounds must cover all finite metrics, all initial placements and all obliviously chosen finite request sequences with the permitted additive term. Lower bounds must cover every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics and cannot rely on an adversary observing its random outcomes. Respect possible nonattainment of the infimum. A one-sided improvement, a bound depending on \(|X|\), or a determination restricted to one metric family does not establish the full scale.
context:
On the uniform metric, all distances between distinct points equal one, and the server positions represent pages held in a cache. General metrics give different costs for replacing one location by another. Randomization can protect an online strategy from a fixed request sequence, but the comparator sees the whole sequence and has the same number of servers.

The old randomized conjecture proposed an \(O(\log k)\) ratio on every metric. Bubeck, Coester and Rabani refute it with \((k+1)\)-point metrics requiring \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) randomized competitiveness. Their definition permits an arbitrary fixed additive constant and compares expected online cost to offline cost, matching the relevant convention here. The obstruction still leaves possible larger polylogarithmic ratios.

The \((k+1)\)-point special case has order \(\Theta(\log^2 k)\) through its connection with metrical service and task systems. This does not determine the card's function, which takes the worst case over every finite number of metric points. Allowing \(n\) much larger than \(k\) is an essential part of the remaining target.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 paper gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on hierarchically separated trees. These are a structured class of leaf metrics of weighted rooted trees whose edge scales decrease geometrically by a fixed factor along root-to-leaf paths. Theorem 1 also bounds the amount of randomness independently of request-sequence length. The geometry restriction matters to the competitive guarantee.

Their Corollary 2 gives \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\) competitiveness on arbitrary \(n\)-point metrics. This is a computational improvement, but the factor \(\log n\) cannot be hidden in a universal function of \(k\). The same paper explicitly states that even an \(o(k)\) ratio on arbitrary metrics remains open. Its separate advice-assisted consequence has additional future-dependent information and is not the oblivious randomized model here.

The classical deterministic \(2k-1\) guarantee is also a randomized upper bound, because a randomized strategy may ignore its coins. Together with the squared-logarithmic lower bound, it leaves a gap between \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) and \(O(k)\). The quantitative question is to determine the entire asymptotic scale within this gap, not just to improve one endpoint.

The September 2026 preprint by Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński claims that the deterministic work-function algorithm attains ratio \(k\) on every metric. If correct, it also gives \(R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le k\); it does not supply a randomized lower bound of \(k\), or improve the order \(O(k)\). Its theorem therefore does not settle this card's matching-asymptotics target. The new proof has not been independently certified in this review.
why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The final ICALP 2026 primary source retains the arbitrary-metric o(k) randomized question and gives a log n-dependent general guarantee; the 2023 lower bound is squared-logarithmic in k. The September deterministic factor-k claim, arXiv:2609.15979v1, would improve a constant in the available linear upper bound but does not determine the randomized asymptotic scale. No matching randomized resolution was located in the bounded search. The card remains source_open for its explicitly quantitative constant-factor target; the fresh deterministic proof is not independently certified here.

title: Constant-factor online contention resolution for matroids
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: A general random-order selection principle for correlated inputs, with a published equivalence to the matroid secretary conjecture and a fresh matching implication requiring verification.
formal:
Is there a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that the following holds? For every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), every real \(\alpha\ge1\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(2^E\) that admits an offline \(\alpha\)-competitive contention-resolution map, there exists a randomized online random-order strategy \(\mathcal A\) which always returns an independent subset \(S\subseteq R\) and satisfies
\[\forall e\in E,\qquad \Pr[e\in S]\ge\frac{\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R]}{C\alpha}.\]
Here \(R\sim D\) is the active set, the elements of \(E\) arrive in an independent uniformly random order, and the strategy learns whether an element is active only when it arrives. The strategy knows \(M,D,\alpha\) in advance; \(C\) is independent of all of them. The target is unconditional existence, without assuming the matroid secretary conjecture.
question_excerpt: Dughmi’s ICALP 2020 §6 asks whether the unconditional conclusion of Theorem 4.1 holds: a universal online contention-resolution scheme losing a constant factor compared with offline balance. The complete target here uses the definitions in §3 and the random-order model of §4. Full knowledge of the prior and no computation restriction are retained. This replaces the previously truncated source excerpt with a fully specified statement, without turning it into a prior-independent or efficient-oracle question.
definitions:
The ground set \(E\) is finite, and \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) contains \(\varnothing\), is closed under taking subsets, and satisfies augmentation: if \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) and \(|I|<|J|\), some \(e\in J\setminus I\) has \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). These are the matroid axioms. Elements, including loops that belong to no nonempty independent set, have fixed identities known to the strategy. Empty ground sets are allowed.

An arbitrary distribution \(D\) specifies probabilities \(D(R)\ge0\) for every \(R\subseteq E\), summing to one. Activations may be correlated in any way. An offline contention-resolution map \(\phi\) chooses a random independent subset \(\phi(R)\subseteq R\), after seeing the entire active set. Formally, it is a probability kernel from the finite set \(2^E\) to \(\mathcal I\), supported on subsets of its input. It is \(\alpha\)-competitive for \(D\) when
\[\forall e\in E,\quad \Pr_{R\sim D,\phi}[e\in\phi(R)]\ge\frac1\alpha\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R].\]
The premise requires the existence of such a map; the online strategy is not given its realized output or the realized set \(R\). This premise is called \(\alpha\)-uncontentiousness in the source.

First draw \(R\sim D\), a permutation \(\pi\) uniform among all permutations of \(E\), and private randomness \(U\), independently. One may represent \(U\) by a uniform seed on \([0,1]\) with measurable decisions. At step \(t\), the strategy sees only \(\pi(t)\) and the bit indicating whether \(\pi(t)\in R\), in addition to its revealed history. It must decide before the next arrival whether to select this element. Inactive elements cannot be selected. Every selected prefix must be independent, and neither acceptance nor rejection can later be reversed. The full stream contains inactive as well as active elements. The same strategy, selected from \(M,D,\alpha\), must work over all possible realized sets, orders and seeds, and may not use their future contents.

The target probability includes the active set, arrival order and private randomness. For an element with positive activation probability it is equivalently a conditional acceptance probability at least \(1/(C\alpha)\) given that the element is active; zero activation probabilities make the displayed inequality automatic. One strategy must meet the guarantee simultaneously for every element, rather than choosing a different strategy for each element. Universal means a family of strategies for all known distributions with one loss factor \(C\), not a single strategy ignorant of the prior. The model imposes no running-time, representation, sampling or oracle restriction. Exact distributional knowledge is part of the mathematical instance, and arbitrary preprocessing is permitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal constant-factor proposition or its full logical negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) and admissible online strategies for every promised matroid, distribution and \(\alpha\). A negative answer must show that every finite \(C\) fails on some such instance despite the existence of the stated offline map. The guarantee must hold for all elements simultaneously and all possibly correlated distributions. A theorem conditional on an unproved secretary conjecture, or a guarantee only for product distributions, does not alone establish the unconditional target. A fresh preprint claim is not itself a checked benchmark answer.
context:
Contention resolution takes a random active subset of a ground set and retains a feasible subset while protecting the inclusion probability of every element. In a matroid, feasibility means independence. The balance guarantee is per element, so a scheme that obtains a large total cardinality while systematically discarding one active element may still fail the requirement.

The offline benchmark matters when activations are correlated. For a rank-one matroid on \(n\) elements, let \(R=E\) with probability \(1/n\) and \(R=\varnothing\) otherwise. Every element has marginal activation probability \(1/n\), but at most one element can be selected on the rare nonempty event. Even offline, simultaneous balance requires \(\alpha\ge n\). The target asks for only a constant additional loss relative to this intrinsic offline obstruction.

For product distributions, all activation indicators are independent, and classical contention-resolution results provide constant guarantees under suitable marginal feasibility. The source studies a larger class characterized by the existence of a balanced offline map, including distributions with positive correlations. Neither independent activation nor a marginal feasibility condition alone is the definition of the premise here.

Dughmi's ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 proves that a \(\gamma\)-competitive secretary algorithm for a matroid gives an online \(\gamma\alpha\)-competitive map for every \(\alpha\)-uncontentious distribution on that matroid. The theorem assumes the distribution is known. The paper separately discusses the difficulties of removing that knowledge and of obtaining efficient implementations; those are different questions.

The ITCS 2022 sequel proves the converse at the level of universal constants: known-prior random-order contention resolution matching offline balance up to a constant would establish the matroid secretary conjecture. Thus the unconditional target is an equivalent formulation of that conjecture, rather than merely a special case for independent random activations.

Singla's September 2026 preprint claims a secretary algorithm with factor 4 for every matroid. Combined with the published 2020 implication, this would establish this card's target with \(C=4\). This consequence uses the claimed main secretary theorem, not the separate single-sample and matroid-intersection extensions whose detailed proofs are deferred in that preprint. The current status is uncertain because this review has not independently certified the complete new proof.
why: This question isolates the additional cost of making feasible selections online when the active set can have arbitrary correlations. Comparing with the best available offline balance avoids charging the online algorithm for distributional obstructions that already exist offline. Its constant-factor form is equivalent to the matroid secretary conjecture.
status_note: Current status checked on 16 September 2026. Singla’s arXiv:2609.14555v1, submitted 13 September, claims the general factor-four matroid secretary theorem. Through Dughmi’s published ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 it would imply this entire known-prior correlated contention-resolution target with C=4. The theorem/model match was checked, but the complete new proof has not been independently certified or Lean-checked here. The record is uncertain pending verification rather than source_open. The 2022 equivalence and 2025 journal abstract corroborate the relationship; efficient and prior-independent variants are separate.
progress: 2020-06-29: The source proves the secretary-to-contention implication and asks for its unconditional conclusion. | 2022-01-25: The sequel establishes the converse constant-factor implication, giving equivalence with the secretary conjecture. | 2026-09-13: A new preprint claims a universal factor-four secretary algorithm. If correct, the existing implication supplies a factor-four loss relative to offline contention balance. The new proof is not independently certified here.
working_summary: A random set of active elements is drawn from an arbitrary known distribution on a finite matroid. An offline map can inspect the whole active set before selecting an independent subset while preserving each element’s probability up to a factor alpha. The question asks whether an irrevocable strategy seeing activity in uniformly random arrival order can always match that balance within one universal extra constant. This known-prior correlated model is equivalent at the constant-factor level to the matroid secretary conjecture. A September 2026 secretary proof claim would settle the target with extra factor four, so its current status awaits independent verification.

title: Constant-factor related-machine precedence scheduling
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation question at the boundary between identical and arbitrary machine environments. It asks whether speed heterogeneity and precedence alone force a growing loss, connecting a canonical scheduling model to substantial structural inapproximability conjectures rather than tuning an isolated ratio.
formal: Does nonpreemptive precedence-constrained makespan minimization on uniformly related parallel machines admit a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a universal constant factor? Precisely, do there exist one algorithm \(A\), constants \(K\ge1,C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge1\), such that for every instance of binary encoding length \(L\) specified below, \(A\) returns a feasible schedule of makespan at most \(K\,\mathrm{OPT}\) in at most \(C(L+1)^b\) Turing-machine steps? All constants are independent of the numbers of jobs and machines, processing requirements, machine speeds and precedence graph.
definitions: An instance consists of integers \(n,m\ge1\), jobs \(J=[n]\), machines \(M=[m]\), positive rational job requirements \(p_j\), positive rational machine speeds \(s_i\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,E)\) of precedence requirements. Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). A job \(j\) assigned to machine \(a(j)\in M\) occupies one uninterrupted interval \([t_j,t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\), with start \(t_j\ge0\). Two intervals on the same machine must be disjoint, and every edge \((j,\ell)\in E\) imposes \(t_\ell\ge t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)}\). Every job executes exactly once on exactly one machine; it cannot be split, migrated or duplicated. Every job is eligible on every machine, and all jobs and the entire precedence graph are supplied before scheduling. There are no communication delays, release times, job weights or additional restrictions. The makespan is \(C_{\max}(a,t)=\max_{j\in J}(t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\). Define \(\mathrm{OPT}\) as the infimum of this makespan over all feasible assignments and nonnegative real start times; it is finite and positive. The input explicitly lists \(n,m\), the graph’s edge pairs, and each positive rational as a binary positive numerator and denominator in lowest terms. Counts and edge endpoints are binary integers with fixed separators; \(L\) is the total bit length of this list. No bound on numerical magnitudes or speed ratios is imposed beyond this finite encoding. The output explicitly lists each machine assignment and a nonnegative rational start time, again in binary rational form. The algorithm is one finite deterministic program with ordinary work tapes, and its time includes parsing, exact arithmetic and writing the complete output. Polynomial dependence on the numerical values rather than their bit lengths does not qualify. Randomized or expected-only guarantees are outside this stated deterministic target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the stated universal constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove the negation of that existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove feasibility, the multiplicative makespan guarantee and the polynomial bit-complexity bound for every input. A negative answer must exclude every finite universal factor and every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. A theorem conditional on an additional unproved scheduling or complexity hypothesis does not establish that unconditional negation. Bounds growing with \(m\), algorithms restricted to a fixed number of machines or speed values, and results for a different scheduling objective do not meet the target.
context:
Williamson and Shmoys list this as Problem 8 among the book’s highlighted open approximation questions. The surrounding discussion contrasts the constant guarantee for identical machines with the then-known logarithmic guarantee when speeds vary. The target remains existence of a constant approximation, with the ordinary deterministic finite-input model made explicit.

Shi Li’s Theorem 1.3 improves the general upper bound to \(O(\log m/\log\log m)\) as \(m\) grows; the guarantee can be written \(O(1+\log(m+2)/\log\log(m+3))\) to include small \(m\). Although the paper title emphasizes total weighted completion time, its theorem explicitly covers makespan as well. The 2011 book’s logarithmic bound is therefore historical rather than the latest checked upper bound.

Bazzi and Norouzi-Fard obtain nonconstant hardness under an additional structural hypothesis about multipartite graphs. Davies and coauthors subsequently derive a growing lower bound for related-machine precedence scheduling from their Unique Machine Precedence Scheduling conjecture together with the exclusion of quasipolynomial algorithms for NP. Those assumptions remain part of the cited results.

The unconditional reduction in the latter work is often encountered under a title about communication delays. Its main communication-delay hardness result concerns a different model; its consequence for the delay-free related-machine problem here still requires the additional scheduling conjecture. Neither consequence is recorded as an unconditional resolution of this card.

Su, Ren, Vardi and Wierman study related machines with machine-dependent communication effects. Their bound also refers to a communication-free optimum, and specializes to a nonconstant approximation when the extra communication contribution vanishes. It does not supply a universal constant for arbitrary speed ratios.
why: Identical machines already allow nontrivial parallelism constrained by a dependency graph, and different speeds add a global allocation choice. A universal constant approximation would show that this extra heterogeneity can be handled with bounded worst-case loss. A negative resolution would identify a basic source of approximation difficulty even though every job can run on every machine and execution times have the simple requirement-divided-by-speed form.
status_note: Explicitly highlighted in the 2011 book. The checked later upper bound is Li’s nonconstant approximation, and the checked 2022 inapproximability result for this exact model depends on additional unproved assumptions. The 2023 communication-aware result and bounded 2025–2026 searches through 2026-09-15 did not yield a constant approximation or an unconditional refutation of its existence. This review does not certify an exhaustive literature search.

working_summary: The problem asks for a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the makespan of precedence-constrained jobs on machines with different speeds. Every job may use every machine, and its uninterrupted execution time is its processing requirement divided by the selected machine’s speed. The approximation factor must remain fixed as the number of machines and the range of speeds grow. The checked general upper bound grows logarithmically divided by an iterated logarithm, while known stronger hardness uses extra unproved hypotheses.
