title: Minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
importance_reason: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
formal: Determine \(C(T)=\inf _{A} \sup _{B} E[\sum _{p\in \mathrm{P}_{A}}|\sum _{t:p_{t}=p}(y_{t}- p)|]\) up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set \(\mathrm{P}_{A}\subseteq [0,1]\), which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects \(p_{t}\in \mathrm{P}_{A}\) and adversary B selects \(y_{t}\in \{0,1\}\) simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history \((p_{s},y_{s})_{s<t}\), and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.
answer_criterion: Determine the stated minimax quantity up to universal multiplicative constants, including all logarithmic factors, with matching upper and lower bounds. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing \(T^{2/3}\) upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above \(\sqrt{T}\) is also known. Thus neither the old two-thirds barrier nor a square-root target is an appropriate new open question. The remaining problem is the optimal rate itself.
why: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Ordinary calibration is distinct from multicalibration and from simultaneous regret bounds for all proper scoring rules. The source’s finite forecast-set convention is preserved.
progress: 2024: The paper proves an upper bound \(O(T^{2/3- \varepsilon})\) for an absolute \(\varepsilon >0\) and a lower bound \(\Omega (T^{0.54389})\); these do not match.

title: Optimal randomized competitive ratio of weighted k-server
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: The optimal randomized cost of heterogeneous servers is a central online resource-allocation question; the recent singly-exponential breakthrough leaves a substantial quantitative frontier.
formal: Determine the asymptotic growth of \(R_{w}(k)\), the optimal randomized competitive ratio of the weighted k-server problem over all finite uniform metrics, up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer k tends to infinity. Use an oblivious request adversary and expected online cost, as defined below.
question_excerpt: Closing the exponential gap between the 1.62 upper bound and the \(\Omega (2k )\) lower bound on the randomized competitive ratio is still an open problem.
definitions: For \(k\ge 1\) an instance environment consists of a finite set X with |\(X|\ge k+1\), uniform distance \(d(x,y)=1\) if \(x\ne y\) and 0 otherwise, positive real weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\), and an initial location \(c_{i}\in X\) for each labeled server i. Co-location is permitted. These data are known to the online algorithm. A finite request sequence \(\sigma \in X\)* is revealed one request at a time. Before proceeding, at least one server must occupy the requested location. Moving server i from x to y costs \(w_{i} d(x,y)\); all movements count. The algorithm may use arbitrary computation but cannot inspect future requests. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum cost of an offline execution with the same weights and initial locations. A real \(c\ge 1\) is universally achievable for k if, for every environment, there are a randomized online strategy A and \(b\ge 0\) such that for every finite \(\sigma , E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le c \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+b\). The strategy and b may depend on the environment; b may not depend on \(\sigma\) or its length. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random choices, and expectation is over those choices. Define \(R_{w}(k)\) as the infimum of universally achievable c. It is finite by known upper bounds and need not be attained. Metric size and the ratios between server weights are unbounded independently of k. No running-time bound or bit encoding of the real weights is imposed; the target measures online movement cost.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(k)\) and constants \(a,A>0,k_{0}\) such that a \(g(k)\le R_{w}(k)\le A g(k)\) for every integer \(k\ge k_{0}\), proving both bounds in the specified randomized model. Constants must not depend on metric size or weights. An improvement for one algorithm, fixed weight ratios or a bounded number of locations does not by itself determine this worst-case function. Precision is multiplicative constant factors in \(R_{w}\), not additive 0.01 and not merely constant factors in its logarithm.
context:
Even with all locations equally far apart, deciding when to move an expensive rather than a cheap server creates a substantial online uncertainty cost.

The SODA 2026 result gives an \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\)-competitive randomized algorithm. Thus merely asking whether randomization can beat a doubly-exponential bound would now retain an answered target.

The exponential lower bound and the \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) upper bound leave the optimal randomized ratio undetermined. The retained card asks for that full function, independently of the decomposition method motivating the older occurrence.

The 2023 source contains an earlier randomized weighted-k-server question. The 2026 upper bound supersedes the qualitative doubly-exponential barrier; its bibliography is retained here under the current optimal-ratio target.
why: The optimal randomized cost of heterogeneous servers is a central online resource-allocation question; the recent singly-exponential breakthrough leaves a substantial quantitative frontier.
status_note: Updated through the SODA 2026 breakthrough; the task is the remaining optimal ratio, not the superseded request to beat a doubly-exponential upper bound.
progress: 2022: Ayyadevara and Chiplunkar prove an exponential randomized lower bound. | 2026: Bijoy, Mondal and Chiplunkar give an \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) randomized upper bound on uniform metrics.
working_summary: Weighted k-server assigns a separate movement-cost multiplier to each server. All distinct locations are at unit distance, isolating uncertainty about which weight to move. The target is the optimal randomized competitive ratio as a function of the number of servers. It takes the worst case over finite metric sizes and arbitrary positive weights against oblivious requests. The recent \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) upper bound removes the old doubly-exponential barrier but leaves a substantial gap above exponential lower bounds.

title: Sublinear-in-q prophet inequalities for q-matroid intersection
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: This asks whether intersecting many independent feasibility constraints forces an essentially linear loss from sequential decisions even with full distributional knowledge and unlimited computation. Closing the gap would clarify a basic limitation of prophet inequalities and their use in stochastic allocation and mechanism design.
formal: Is there a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to[1,\infty)\) with \(\lim_{q\to\infty}g(q)/q=0\) such that, for every sequence of independent nonnegative random values and every feasibility constraint given by the intersection of \(q\) matroids, some online irrevocable selection strategy obtains expected reward at least \(1/g(q)\) times the expected offline optimum? The arrival order is fixed in advance, all value distributions and constraints are known to the strategy, and the guarantee is independent of the number of elements.
question_excerpt: Are there asymptotically better algorithms for the matroid intersection prophet inequality?
definitions: Fix integers \(q,n\ge1\). The ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with elements arriving in the known order \(1,\ldots,n\). For each \(j\in[q]\), a matroid independence family \(\mathcal I_j\subseteq2^{[n]}\) contains \(\varnothing\), is hereditary, and satisfies augmentation: whenever \(A,B\in\mathcal I_j\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(b\in B\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{b\}\in\mathcal I_j\). The feasible sets are \(\mathcal I=\bigcap_{j=1}^q\mathcal I_j\); repetitions among the matroids are allowed. For each \(t\), let \(D_t\) be an arbitrary Borel probability distribution on \([0,\infty)\) with finite first moment, and draw \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) independently with laws \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\). The offline optimum is \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)=\max_{S\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in S}X_t\), after all values have been revealed. An online strategy knows \(q,n,\mathcal I_1,\ldots,\mathcal I_q,D_1,\ldots,D_n\) in advance. Upon seeing \(X_t\), it accepts or rejects element \(t\) irrevocably. Its decision is a measurable function of \(t\), the observed prefix \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\), previous decisions and an internal random seed \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\) and independent of all \(X_t\). Deterministic strategies may ignore \(U\). Every accepted prefix must be feasible, for every value sequence and seed, and previously accepted elements cannot be removed. Let \(S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)\) be the final accepted set and \(\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}(X,U)=\sum_{t\in S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)}X_t\). No bound on computation, distribution access or preprocessing is imposed; this is the information-theoretic online model. Exact distributions are part of the mathematical instance, not an implicit finite encoding or a sampling oracle. The target quantifiers are \(\exists g\;\forall q\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\forall(\mathcal I_j)_{j=1}^q\;\forall(D_t)_{t=1}^n\;\exists\mathcal A\) such that \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}]\ge\mathbb E[\operatorname{OPT}]/g(q)\). Expectations include both the independent values and the independent internal seed. The first-moment assumption makes both expectations finite. The inequality also applies when the offline expectation is zero. The limit requirement means that for every \(\eta>0\), some \(q_0\) satisfies \(g(q)\le\eta q\) for all \(q\ge q_0\). The fixed arrival order represents any adversarially chosen order known before the random values are drawn; the order cannot adapt to their realizations.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence statement for one function \(g=o(q)\), including a policy with the stated guarantee for every instance, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation over all permitted strategies. Improving the constant in a linear \(Cq\) guarantee is insufficient. An \(o(q)\) result only for partition matroids, identical distributions, random arrival order or a bounded number of elements does not prove the full positive statement. A super-square-root lower bound that is itself \(o(q)\) does not refute it. There is no additional polynomial-time requirement.
context:
The 2023 source asks whether asymptotically better matroid-intersection prophet inequalities exist. This card selects the \(o(q)\) improvement asked by the imported title, using the source’s unrestricted online-strategy benchmark rather than adding a polynomial-time computation requirement.

The source’s Theorem 7 records a general upper bound \(e(q+1)\) on the ratio of expected offline reward to expected online reward, where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm. The ratio compares two expectations, not an expectation of a ratio or a pointwise competitive guarantee.

The paper proves a lower bound \(q^{1/2+\Omega(1/\log\log q)}\), already for intersections of partition matroids with identical Bernoulli values. This improves a square-root obstruction while leaving room between the proved lower bound and linear upper bounds.

Footnote 3 explicitly corrects an earlier claimed \(\Omega(q)\) lower bound in Kleinberg and Weinberg’s work: that construction yields an \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) obstruction. The correction does not invalidate their linear upper bound. Thus the earlier linear lower-bound claim cannot be used as a resolution of this question.

Velusamy’s June 2024 open-problem note again asks for an asymptotic improvement in online stochastic hypergraph matching with Bernoulli values, a partition-matroid subcase. That note supports the persistence of a restricted version and does not claim a general-matroid solution.
why: A prophet knows all random values before choosing a feasible set, while an online selector must commit before later values arrive. Matroid intersections capture many simultaneous resource constraints. Determining whether the approximation loss can grow sublinearly in their number would distinguish a limitation imposed by lack of future information from the performance of existing selection guarantees.
status_note: The 2023 source leaves the general asymptotic improvement open, and the author’s June 2024 note retains a corresponding restricted stochastic-matching question. The checked lower bound is sublinear and does not refute the target. Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive guarantee of current openness.
progress: 2012: As checked against the 2023 source’s explicit correction, Kleinberg and Weinberg provide a linear-in-\(q\) upper guarantee and a square-root lower-bound construction; their originally claimed matching linear lower bound was erroneous. | 2023: Saxena, Velusamy and Weinberg improve the lower bound to \(q^{1/2+\Omega(1/\log\log q)}\), retain the linear upper bounds, and ask in Section 6 for asymptotically better algorithms. | 2024-06-07: Velusamy’s stochastic-matching note poses asymptotically beating the linear approximation in the Bernoulli hypergraph-matching special case as Question 2.
working_summary: Independent random element values arrive one at a time in a fixed known order. The selector must irrevocably choose a set that is independent in each of q given matroids. It knows the value distributions, while the offline comparator sees all realized values before making its choice. The question asks whether the ratio of their expected rewards can always be bounded by a function growing sublinearly in q. The checked source improves a square-root lower obstruction but corrects an earlier erroneous linear lower-bound claim and leaves the gap open.

title: Sublogarithmic competitiveness for online metric TSP
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: The question isolates the cost of irreversible online ordering in arbitrary metrics after computational and storage limits are removed. Breaking the longstanding logarithmic bound would separate this canonical geometric online problem from superficially similar irrevocable-edge problems and clarify how much adaptivity a growing tour retains.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic online insertion algorithm \(A\), in the unrestricted-space model below, and a function \(\rho:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) such that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n)/\log_2 n=0\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)\le\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(D)\) for every \(n\ge2\) and every valid sequence of \(n\) metric arrivals? The algorithm knows \(n\), but receives distances only as points arrive and does not know the final offline optimum. Earlier relative-order decisions are irrevocable.
definitions:
An instance of length \(n\) is a real symmetric matrix \(D=(d_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) with \(d_{ii}=0\), \(d_{ij}\ge0\), and \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\). Distinct arrival indices may have distance zero, representing repeated occurrences of the same point. Equivalently, this is a sequence of points in an arbitrary metric space, with repetitions permitted. There is no bound on the number of distinct points, metric dimension, nonzero distance ratios or magnitude of distances. Arrival indices carry no information beyond their order.

The integer \(n\) is given initially. At step \(t\), the algorithm receives exactly the vector \((d_{t1},\ldots,d_{t,t-1})\), in addition to the prefix information and its stored state. It must then choose a position for the new index \(t\) in its current ordered list. If \(\pi_{t-1}\) is the list before this step, \(\pi_t\) must be obtained by inserting \(t\) in one of its \(t\) gaps, including before its first and after its last element. The order of all earlier indices is preserved. The algorithm must finish this choice before receiving step \(t+1\). It has no access to distances involving future arrivals, a description of the ambient metric, future points, the final optimum, predictions or advice. There is no limit on the number of available insertion positions imposed by a fixed array, and no memory bound.

For a permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), define
\[
\ell_D(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}d_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}.
\]
The final cost is \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)=\ell_D(\pi_n)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(D)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\ell_D(\pi)\), where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). Endpoints are free, and no return edge is charged; this follows the online-ordering source’s path-length convention. Costs at intermediate stages are not separately accumulated. There is no additive allowance in the competitive guarantee. When all arrivals coincide, \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\) and the multiplicative inequality still applies.

For explicit uniformity, an algorithm is a single finite deterministic program with ordinary binary integer control and exact real registers. It may copy real values, use \(0,1\), addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, and order or equality comparisons; its integer control may perform arbitrary finite bit computation. The revealed distances are exact real input values, rather than numerical approximations. Arbitrary real constants, advice indexed by \(n\), an oracle for unreceived distances and random instructions are unavailable. Each insertion decision must halt after finitely many operations on every valid prefix, but there is no running-time or storage bound. The quantity being compared is solely the length of the final ordering. This fixes an ideal exact-distance model; it does not impose polynomial-time optimization between arrivals.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such a uniform deterministic algorithm and a sublogarithmic competitive bound for every valid input, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. The proof must cover unrestricted metrics and all arrival orders, with a common \(\rho(n)=o(\log n)\). A constant-factor improvement to an \(O(\log n)\) bound, a lower bound for one particular insertion rule, or a lower bound requiring a restricted array capacity does not settle this target. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance is attached to this asymptotic resource comparison.
context:
The selected sentence concerns improving the \(O(\log n)\) guarantee even with unlimited space. This card makes the deterministic branch in the surrounding paragraph explicit and interprets “improving” asymptotically as \(o(\log n)\). It does not require constant competitiveness or a near-linear array.

The model is online construction of an ordering. It is different from a traveling server that moves while new requests are released: here there are no release times, movement before the final ordering, deadlines or service constraints.

The ESA 2024 definition charges distances between consecutive occupied positions and allows repeated points. With arbitrary insertions and no fixed array capacity, only the relative order of previous arrivals is committed. Closing the path into a tour changes costs by at most a factor two in a metric, so that endpoint convention does not change the sublogarithmic existence question.

The 2026 source reports the classical \(O(\log n)\) guarantee for unrestricted insertion. Its new lower bound requires an array of limited size and therefore does not establish a logarithmic lower bound in the unrestricted-space model.

For \(m=(1+\varepsilon)n\), the 2026 paper gives a deterministic \(O(\log^3 n/\varepsilon)\) guarantee in its stated parameter range. This is progress on the space tradeoff, while the unlimited-space sublogarithmic question remains explicitly open in its closing remarks.
why: An online tour can insert new points between old ones while keeping the old relative order. The question asks how costly that one irreversible choice is when future distances are unknown. Its resolution would identify whether the logarithmic guarantee reflects an inherent online limitation or a limitation of known ordering rules.
status_note: Explicitly open in ICALP 2026 Section 4 and the checked 7 August 2026 full version. The capacity-dependent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted insertion model. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.
progress: 2024: The ESA paper specifies online ordering through the distances between consecutive array entries, with repeated points allowed. Its fixed-capacity results concern a stricter insertion model. | 2026: The ICALP paper improves the upper bound with a small amount of extra array capacity and proves a capacity-dependent deterministic lower bound. Section 4 explicitly leaves improving logarithmic competitiveness with unlimited space open. | 2026-08-07: The full arXiv version repeats the unlimited-space open question and the distinction between known and unknown offline optimum.
working_summary: Points arrive with distances to earlier points and must immediately be inserted into an evolving order. Each insertion preserves the relative order of all previous arrivals, but there is no fixed array capacity or computational resource bound. The final cost is the sum of distances between consecutive points, compared with the best offline ordering. The question asks whether a deterministic algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio smaller than logarithmic by an asymptotic factor on every metric input. This would isolate how much performance is lost through irreversible ordering alone, beyond the additional losses caused by limited storage.

title: Polynomial-time unit-job precedence scheduling on fixed machines
importance_reason: The complexity of unit-job precedence scheduling tests how much difficulty remains in a highly simplified canonical scheduling model.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), can the minimum makespan of unit-duration jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints be computed in deterministic polynomial time on \(k\) identical machines?

For a finite directed acyclic graph \(G\), let \(\mu_k(G)\) be the least number of time slots needed to execute all its vertices as jobs, using at most \(k\) jobs per slot and executing every job strictly after its predecessors. The precise target is
\[
\forall k\ge3\ \exists A_k,C_k,c_k\ \forall G,
\]
where \(A_k\) is one uniform deterministic algorithm, \(C_k,c_k\ge1\) are integers, and on every valid \(L\)-bit encoding of \(G\), \(A_k\) halts in at most \(C_k(L+1)^{c_k}\) steps and outputs a rational number \(a\) satisfying
\[
|a-\mu_k(G)|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The numerical output convention is equivalent here to computing the optimum integer exactly, by rounding in polynomial bit time.
question_excerpt: The source fixes a number k of processors, repeatedly removes at most k currently available vertices from a precedence DAG, and asks whether the minimum number of rounds can be computed in polynomial time for k greater than two.
definitions:
The input graph is \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\ge0\). It has no loops, parallel arcs or directed cycles. An arc \((u,v)\) means that job \(u\) must finish before job \(v\) starts. All transitive consequences are enforced; the input need not already be transitively closed. There is no restriction on the height, width, indegrees or outdegrees of this graph.

Each job has duration one and can run on any of \(k\) identical unit-speed machines. For an integer \(T\ge0\), a schedule of length \(T\) is a function
\[
s:[n]\to\{0,\ldots,T-1\}
\]
such that \(|s^{-1}(t)|\le k\) for every slot \(t\), and \(s(u)<s(v)\) for every arc \((u,v)\). Job \(v\) executes throughout the half-open interval \([s(v),s(v)+1)\). Distinct jobs in the same slot are assigned to distinct machines; such assignments always exist because of the cardinality bound. A successor may start when a predecessor finishes, but they cannot execute in the same slot.

The makespan optimum \(\mu_k(G)\) is the minimum \(T\) admitting such a schedule. Idle capacity is allowed. For the empty graph it is zero; for \(n>0\) it is an integer between one and \(n\), since a topological order yields a sequential feasible schedule. The model is offline: the whole graph is supplied before computation. There are no release dates, extra deadlines, communication delays, machine eligibility restrictions, setup costs, preemption or migration during a job.

The graph is encoded by \(1^n0\) followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, including zero diagonal entries. Require no trailing bits. Its length is \(L=n+1+n^2\). Invalid encodings, including cyclic graphs, must be rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine count \(k\) is fixed for the algorithm and is not another input field.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one fixed finite program, fixed finite tape alphabets, read-only input and initially blank work tapes. Each transition accesses the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. All parsing, arithmetic and output are charged. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed.

An output rational is specified by a signed integer numerator \(p\) and a positive integer denominator \(q\), with value \(a=p/q\). Use one sign bit for \(p\), followed by self-delimiting binary codes for \(|p|\) and \(q\); the code for a nonnegative integer \(b\) is the binary representation of \(b+1\), prefixed by its bit length in unary and a zero separator. All output bits count toward the running time. Rounding \(p/q\) to its unique nearest integer can be performed in polynomial time in these bit lengths, and the \(1/100\) error bound guarantees that this integer is \(\mu_k(G)\). An exact integer output also qualifies by taking denominator one.

The quantifiers permit the program, multiplicative constant and polynomial exponent to depend on \(k\). Each program must work on every graph size and every permitted graph. The card does not require one exponent independent of \(k\), a polynomial bound when \(k\) is part of the input, or an effective compiler producing \(A_k\) from \(k\). A positive result only for \(k=3\) would settle the first unresolved case but would not by itself establish the displayed assertion for all larger fixed counts.

The requested output is the optimum value; outputting an optimal schedule is sufficient but is not an additional requirement. A multiplicative approximation with a fixed nonzero relative error is generally too coarse to recover this integer optimum.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the all-fixed-\(k\) algorithm-existence proposition, with the full correctness, output precision and polynomial bit-time bounds; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation. A negative answer must identify one fixed \(k\ge3\) for which no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. NP-hardness with the machine count supplied as input is insufficient. NP-completeness for one fixed count gives only a conditional negative answer unless \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is also proved. A subexponential exact algorithm or a quasipolynomial approximation scheme does not meet the polynomial-time requirement.
context:
One machine needs exactly one slot per job. Two machines admit a polynomial-time exact algorithm. The source asks about every larger fixed count, with three as the first unresolved case.

The checked exact-algorithm preprint proves a running time of \((1+n/k)^{O(\sqrt{nk})}\). For fixed \(k\), this is subexponential in the number of jobs, but its exponent is not bounded as required for polynomial time. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and online in journal form in January 2026.

Quasipolynomial-time approximation schemes for fixed machine counts provide schedules whose lengths are close in relative terms to optimum. They neither give polynomial running time nor determine the exact optimum from a fixed relative error.

When the number of machines is unrestricted input, the decision problem is NP-hard. That theorem does not settle polynomial solvability separately at every fixed machine count.

The July 2026 unit-job hardness paper studies a different model in which the machine for every job is prescribed. Here a job may use any identical machine, so that hardness does not resolve this target.
why: With unit-duration jobs and identical machines, the only remaining source of scheduling difficulty is the interaction between a partial order and limited parallel capacity. Polynomial solvability for each fixed machine count would identify a major tractable boundary in precedence scheduling. The three-machine case has resisted classification since the classical scheduling complexity literature, despite the recent subexponential advance.
status_note: Amarilli’s current source retains the fixed-machine polynomial-time question. The exact subexponential advance appeared at SODA 2025 and online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026; it does not give polynomial time even for three machines. No resolution of the all-fixed-machine-count target was found in the bounded later-work review.
progress: 2022: The checked approximation paper records exact solvability on two machines and the open fixed-machine question. | 2023-12-06: The preprint gives the subexponential exact algorithm and explicitly retains the three-machine classification question. | 2025-01-07: The subexponential result is published in the SODA proceedings. | 2026-01-03: Publisher-deposited metadata dates the journal version online. | 2026-09-17: The live source still asks for polynomial time at each fixed larger count; the review makes that quantifier order and numerical output criterion explicit.
working_summary: Every job takes one time slot, and a directed acyclic graph specifies which jobs must finish before others start. At most k jobs may run simultaneously on k identical machines. The question asks for polynomial-time computation of the minimum number of slots for every fixed k greater than two. The polynomial and algorithm may depend on k, but must handle all job counts and precedence graphs. The recent exact subexponential algorithm improves the general upper bound without establishing the requested polynomial time.

title: Randomized competitive ratio of list update
importance_reason: Even for an elementary self-organizing list, the optimal benefit of randomization in competitive performance is unknown.
formal: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio of online list update against an oblivious adversary in the full-cost model: \[\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}=\inf\{r\in[1,\infty):r\text{ is achievable under the definition below}\}.\] Give its value to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The same competitive factor must work for lists of every finite size, with an additive constant allowed to depend on the size and initial order. No predictions or advice about future requests are supplied.
definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the item set is \([n]\) and an initial list \(L_0\) is a permutation of these items. A request sequence \(\sigma=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\in[n]^T\) has arbitrary finite length \(T\ge0\), is fixed independently of all online randomness, and is revealed one request at a time. The online rule must finish serving \(x_t\) before learning \(x_{t+1}\); it is not told the remaining sequence or its length. Accessing an item in current position \(j\), counting from one, costs \(j\). After this access, that item may be moved any distance toward the front at zero cost. Each other exchange of adjacent items costs one. Paid exchanges may be performed between accesses, including before serving a revealed request, and every such exchange is charged. The free move changes only the accessed item’s position and preserves the relative order of all other items. Items are never inserted or deleted. The total cost is the sum of access costs and paid exchanges. The offline optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)\) is the minimum cost of a legal schedule starting from the same \(L_0\), with advance knowledge of all of \(\sigma\), under exactly these access and exchange rules. A randomized online rule chooses each finite legal service action using only the revealed request prefix, its previous actions and its private random state. Abstract probability distributions over actions are permitted, with no bound on computational work or memory; all expectations must be well defined. Each request is served with finitely many exchanges on each realization. A real \(r\ge1\) is achievable if \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall L_0\ \exists A_{n,L_0,r}\ \exists\beta_{n,L_0,r}\in[0,\infty)\ \forall T\ge0\ \forall\sigma\in[n]^T:\quad \mathbb E[\mathrm{cost}_{A_{n,L_0,r}}(\sigma)]\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)+\beta_{n,L_0,r}.\] The rule and finite additive constant are chosen before the future requests, so neither may depend on \(\sigma\) or \(T\). Expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness alone. The infimum is over such common factors \(r\); it need not be attained. This is the full-cost convention \(j\), not the partial-cost convention \(j-1\). All costs and the ratio are dimensionless.
answer_criterion: Provide an unambiguously specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}|\le1/100\). Certified upper and lower bounds that imply this error are sufficient, even if no algorithm attains the infimum. The proof must use full access costs, an oblivious adversary, all list sizes and sequence lengths, and the permitted additive constant. Bounds for a restricted family of online rules, for a fixed bounded list size, for algorithms given predictions or for the partial-cost convention do not by themselves certify the requested value.
context:
The 2025 primary source states the classical randomized bounds \(1.5\le\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}\le1.6\) and defines access cost by the position counted from one. This interval has width \(0.1\), so it does not certify the required absolute error \(0.01\).

The same paper investigates algorithms assisted by predictions. Their guarantees involve additional information unavailable in the ordinary online problem specified here; those results do not settle the classical optimal ratio.

A related lower bound of \(1.50084\), proved by Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel, is explicitly for the partial-cost model, where the first item costs zero to access. Changing the charge by one on every request can change a competitive ratio, so that theorem is not asserted here as a stronger full-cost lower bound.

The additive constant is independent of the entire request sequence and its length. It permits a fixed initial-order cost but cannot absorb a cost that grows with the number of requests. The infimum formulation also permits a limiting optimal ratio without assuming that a best online rule exists.
why: List update is a basic model of a data structure adapting to changing demand without knowing future accesses. Its optimal randomized ratio would quantify the value of randomization in a simple online problem whose deterministic analogue is well understood. The unresolved constant gap makes it a precise long-standing benchmark in competitive analysis.
status_note: The April 2025 source records the unresolved full-cost randomized 1.5–1.6 gap. The checked 1.50084 theorem concerns partial costs and is not used as a stronger bound for this card. A bounded later-work search through 2026-09-15 found no result certifying the specified optimal constant to absolute error 1/100; no exhaustive current-status claim is made.
progress: 1995: The 2025 source attributes the randomized upper bound 1.6 to Albers, von Stengel and Werchner. | 2001: Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel publish a lower bound of 1.50084 for the distinct partial-cost model; the checked author manuscript is dated 21 June 1999. | 2025-04-11: List Update with Prediction records the classical 1.5–1.6 gap while proving guarantees for algorithms supplied with predictions.
working_summary: An online list serves each request before seeing the next, and access costs the item’s position counted from one. The accessed item may move forward for free, while other adjacent exchanges cost one. Randomized performance is compared with an optimal offline schedule under the same rules and initial order. The checked full-cost bounds leave the optimal competitive factor between 1.5 and 1.6. The benchmark asks for a Lean-certified approximation of this factor to absolute error at most one hundredth.

title: Pinwheel Packing in NP
importance_reason: A long-standing complexity-class boundary for a basic recurrent scheduling model, connecting infinite behavior, succinct numerical input and finite certificates. The recent NP-hardness theorem makes the unresolved gap between NP membership and the PSPACE upper bound particularly concrete.
formal:
Does ordinary Pinwheel Packing belong to \(\mathrm{NP}\)?

An instance is an explicit finite list of positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\), written in binary, with \(k\ge1\). It is feasible if there exists a schedule \(\sigma:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1,\ldots,k\}\) such that
\[
\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\ \forall t\in\mathbb Z\
\exists j\in\{0,\ldots,a_i-1\},\qquad \sigma(t+j)=i.
\]
Thus one machine must execute task \(i\) at least once in every \(a_i\) consecutive time slots, forever.

Precisely, do there exist one uniform deterministic verifier \(V\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that every valid encoded instance \(x\), of bit length \(L\), satisfies
\[
x\text{ is feasible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(|z|\le C(L+1)^c\ \text{and}\ V(x,z)=1\bigr),
\]
and \(V\) halts on every pair \((x,z)\) within \(C(|x|+|z|+1)^c\) steps?
question_excerpt: The ISAAC source records a PSPACE upper bound for Pinwheel Packing and explicitly leaves membership in NP open. The card asks this question for its ordinary infinite packing model, with the full explicit list of binary periods.
definitions:
Time is discrete and indexed by all integers. The value \(\sigma(t)=i>0\) means that the machine executes task \(i\) during slot \(t\); the value zero denotes an idle slot. At most one task executes in any slot. A task has unit execution time, may be executed arbitrarily many times, and must obey its recurrence requirement on every window, including windows crossing any chosen origin of time. There is no finite horizon, initial-state input, release date or online sequence of unknown tasks.

The number \(a_i\) is an upper bound on the gap between successive executions of task \(i\). Gaps need not equal \(a_i\), and executions may be more frequent. Every task is distinct, even if several periods coincide. Idle slots can be filled with task 1 without harming any recurrence requirement, so allowing them does not change feasibility for \(k\ge1\).

The instance contains the whole list of periods, with no compressed multiplicities. Encode it by \(1^k0\), followed in order by a code for each \(a_i\). For a positive integer \(a\), let \(b\) be the bit length of its ordinary binary representation; its code is \(1^b0\) followed by those \(b\) bits. Require a leading one in each binary representation and no trailing bits. Then
\[
L=k+1+\sum_{i=1}^k(2\lfloor\log_2 a_i\rfloor+3).
\]
Malformed strings are not feasible instances and must be rejected by the verifier for every certificate. The chosen encoding is polynomially interconvertible with the usual explicit binary-list encodings; periods are not written in unary.

There is no promise on the density \(\sum_i 1/a_i\), the number of distinct periods or their magnitudes. For example, all instances whose density exceeds one are infeasible, but the verifier must handle them as well. Restricting attention to density exactly one, a fixed number of tasks or finitely many required executions would change the scope.

The verifier is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, fixed finite tape alphabets, read-only inputs \(x,z\) and initially blank work tapes. Each transition accesses only the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Parsing, arithmetic and all verification work are charged. There is no advice, randomness, oracle or free preprocessing.

The certificate \(z\) may be any finite binary string. A positive answer may use any sound certificate representation; it is not required to list the entire period of a schedule, or to provide a polynomial-time procedure for finding a certificate. The running-time guarantee applies to every supplied certificate, including incorrect and overlong ones. The membership equivalence only quantifies over certificates of the displayed length bound.

Feasibility is an exact decision property, so the numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention does not relax a recurrence deadline or permit any fraction of violated windows.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of a verifier and constants satisfying the polynomial certificate, running-time, completeness and soundness conditions; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such verifier and constants exist. An NP-hardness proof alone does not refute NP membership. A polynomial-space algorithm, an exponentially long explicit periodic schedule, an approximation that relaxes the periods, or an NP verifier for a finite-visit or restricted-density variant does not meet this target.
context:
The inherited question concerns membership in NP, independently of whether the problem is NP-hard. The source gives PSPACE as the established general upper bound.

Every feasible integer-period instance has a periodic feasible schedule with period at most \(\prod_i a_i\). The state graph used to prove this has one coordinate for the elapsed time of each task. This bound can be exponential in the binary input length, so the existence of a periodic schedule alone does not provide a polynomial-length certificate.

The April 2026 preprint proves NP-hardness for the ordinary explicit-list encoding, including instances of density one. Earlier hardness results for exact spacing or binary-encoded multiplicities did not establish this ordinary-encoding theorem.

The same preprint gives an approximation scheme that permits multiplicative relaxation of the recurrence limits. Such a relaxation is different from verifying feasibility with every original deadline unchanged.

The September 2026 finite-covering paper explicitly separates perpetual scheduling from finite-visit problems. NP-completeness of a model requiring only finitely many executions does not supply certificates for an unbounded schedule.
why: A compact list of recurring service requirements describes an infinite scheduling obligation. NP membership would show that feasibility always has a short, efficiently checkable finite explanation, even when a directly listed repeating schedule may be very long. Together with the 2026 hardness result, a positive answer would classify this long-studied perpetual scheduling problem as NP-complete.
status_note: The 2025 source explicitly asks whether ordinary Pinwheel Packing belongs to NP. Kleinberg and Mishra’s April 2026 preprint proves NP-hardness for the ordinary explicit-list encoding, but retains the gap to the PSPACE upper bound. September 2026 work distinguishes this perpetual problem from NP-complete finite-visit variants. No resolution of NP membership was found in the bounded review.
progress: 2025: The source explicitly records ordinary Pinwheel Packing membership in NP as open. | 2026-04-15: A preprint proves NP-hardness with the ordinary explicit list of periods and also gives an approximation scheme for relaxed recurrence limits. | 2026-09-07: The revised finite-covering preprint retains the distinction between perpetual scheduling and NP-complete finite-visit variants. | 2026-09-17: The review states the exact binary-input NP-membership target and updates the hardness context without treating NP-hardness as a negative answer.
working_summary: Pinwheel packing asks one machine to execute every recurring task often enough to meet all of its sliding-window deadlines. The input is an explicit list of positive recurrence limits written in binary, while the schedule extends indefinitely. The question is whether every feasible instance has a polynomial-length certificate checkable in polynomial time. A polynomial-space algorithm and finite periodic schedules are known, but the available period bound can be exponential in the input length. An April 2026 preprint proves NP-hardness, while the checked literature leaves membership in NP unresolved.

title: Adaptive regret in misspecified linear bandits
importance_reason: A substantial robustness and adaptation question for a foundational sequential-learning model. The simultaneous guarantee tests whether useful linear structure can be exploited without sacrificing controlled performance when that structure is inaccurate, across arbitrary known action geometries. Its importance is broader than optimizing a bound for one fixed action set.
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and an integer \(p\ge0\) such that, for every \(d,k,T\in\mathbb N\) with \(d,T\ge1\) and \(k\ge d^2\), and every known feature matrix \(\Phi\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\), there is one bandit policy \(\pi\) satisfying, simultaneously for every unknown mean-reward vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\max_i\mu_i-\min_i\mu_i\le1\), \[R_T(\pi,\mu)\le C[\log(2kdT)]^p\min\left\{T,\ d\sqrt T+\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)T\sqrt d,\ \frac{k}{d}\sqrt T\right\}?\] Here \(\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\|\Phi\theta-\mu\|_\infty\). The policy may depend on \(\Phi,d,k,T\), but cannot be given \(\mu\), a fitting parameter \(\theta\), the misspecification level \(\varepsilon\), or an upper bound on that level. Use the Gaussian-noise model below.
definitions: There are \(k\) indexed arms, with \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\); row \(\Phi_i\) gives the known feature vector of arm \(i\). Different arms may have the same feature vector, and no full-rank assumption or bound on the entries of \(\Phi\) is imposed. The mean vector is fixed before play and does not change with time or the learner’s choices. In round \(t\in[T]\), the policy chooses \(A_t\in[k]\), then observes only \(Y_t=\mu_{A_t}+Z_t\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) are independent standard real Gaussian random variables with mean zero and variance one, independent of the learner’s randomness. A policy for fixed known \((\Phi,d,k,T)\) is a collection of Borel-measurable maps from the history \(([k]\times\mathbb R)^{t-1}\) to the probability simplex \(\Delta_k=\{q\in[0,1]^k:\sum_iq_i=1\}\), one for each round; the selected arm is sampled from that distribution using fresh private randomness. These maps do not take the unknown environment as an argument. Thus the same policy must work for all allowed \(\mu\) for that fixed known instance. Expected regret is \(R_T(\pi,\mu)=\mathbb E_{\pi,\mu}[\sum_{t=1}^T(\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i-\mu_{A_t})]\), with expectation over observation noise and policy randomness. It compares to the best fixed arm’s mean, not the largest realized noisy reward. For \(v\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The infimum in the misspecification definition ranges over all real \(\theta\), with no norm constraint. The reward-range normalization bounds regret by \(T\); it does not bound the realized Gaussian observations. Logarithms in the displayed guarantee are natural. The single exponent \(p\) and multiplicative constant \(C\) are chosen before all instance parameters, so all hidden logarithmic losses are uniform powers of \(\log(2kdT)\). This is an information-theoretic policy-existence question: the number of reward observations is the resource, and no running-time, finite-precision representation or efficient implementation requirement is imposed on the measurable policies.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this policy-existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must provide the policy family and prove the simultaneous expected-regret bound with one universal \(C,p\), over the entire stated domain and without access to the misspecification level. title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
original_area: Online algorithms, bandits and stochastic optimization
importance_reason: A general adaptation question for online forecasting across unknown downstream proper losses. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For each fixed number \(K\ge 2\) of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss \(\ell\) its worst-case expected regret satisfies \(R_{A},\ell (T)\le C_{\ell},K\cdot (1+R*_{\ell},K(T))\cdot (\log (T+2))^{c_{\ell},K}\) for all \(T\ge 1\), for some constants \(C_{\ell},K>0\) and \(c_{\ell},K\ge 0\) independent of T? Here \(R*_{\ell},K\) is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
definitions: The prediction space is the simplex \(\Delta _{K}=\{p\in \mathbb{R} ^{K}:p_{i}\ge 0,\sum p_{i}=1\}\). At round t, A chooses a possibly random \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\in \Delta _{K}\) from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes \(y_{t}\in \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\), where \(e_{i}\) is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes \(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{T}\) in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss \(\ell\):\(\Delta _{K}\times \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\to [- 1,1]\), propriety means \(E_{Y\sim p}\ell (p,Y)\le E_{Y\sim p}\ell (q,Y)\) for every \(p,q\in \Delta _{K}\); the minimizer need not be unique. Define \(Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)=E_{A}[\sum _{t=1}^{T} \ell (\mathrm{P}_{t},y_{t})]- \inf _{p\in \Delta _{K}}\sum _{t=1}^{T}\ell (p,y_{t})\). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set \(R_{A},\ell (T)=\sup _{y_{1}:T}Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)\), and \(R*_{\ell},K(T)=\inf _{B} R_{B},\ell (T)\), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know \(\ell ,K\) and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{T})\) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.
context:
A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\) before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order \(\sqrt{T}\) can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

The paper gives one efficient algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((K^{5/4}\sqrt{T})\) regret for every bounded proper loss and \(O(\beta  \log  T+\beta \sqrt{K} \log  K)\) for bounded \(\beta\)-smooth proper losses. It also extends logarithmic guarantees to a broader relative-smoothness class. These are substantial simultaneous guarantees, but do not characterize every individual proper loss.

The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal \(p_{t}\) on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.

For each fixed loss, average regret over A’s own randomization must have the required rate against every fixed outcome sequence. The statement does not claim that a single realized random trajectory satisfies all loss bounds with high probability.
why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.
status_note: Full forecasting model, proven simultaneous bounds and concluding question checked with the June arXiv record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No loss-universal minimax-rate result or impossibility was located. The displayed minimax comparison makes the asymptotic target explicit.
progress: 2026: The paper simultaneously achieves logarithmic regret for smooth proper losses and nearly square-root regret for every bounded proper loss, leaving individual-rate optimality for all proper losses open.
working_summary: One online forecaster must issue predictions before knowing which proper loss a downstream user cares about. The question asks it to match each loss’s own optimal regret rate up to logarithmic factors in the horizon. The benchmark is the best fixed probability prediction in hindsight, with expectation over the forecaster’s randomness. The source already combines logarithmic regret for smooth losses with nearly square-root regret for all bounded proper losses. The remaining task is to adapt to the individually optimal rate of every bounded proper loss.

title: Additive-one approximation for bin packing
importance_reason: A major additive-approximation question for a foundational packing problem: whether efficient algorithms can remain within one bin of the integer optimum on every instance. Existing score retained.
formal:
Is there a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for one-dimensional offline bin packing that uses at most one more bin than optimum? Explicitly allowing randomization, the target is one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every finite input list \(I=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n})\) of rational sizes \(0<s_{i}\le1\), \(A\) runs within \(p(L)\) steps for every coin sequence, always outputs a feasible packing, and satisfies
\[
\Pr\bigl[B(A(I))\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+1\bigr]\ge\tfrac23.
\]
Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, \(B\) is the number of bins used, and probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits for each fixed input. A deterministic algorithm with the same bound on every input also qualifies.
definitions:
All items and their sizes are given before computation starts. Each item is listed separately, including repetitions. Write \(s_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i},b_{i}\) are positive binary integers and \(a_{i}\le b_{i}\). Input length includes the item list, numerators, denominators and separators; arithmetic precision is not free.

A packing partitions the item indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty bins \(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q}\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in B_{j}}s_{i}\le1\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Items are indivisible and must each appear in exactly one bin. The output explicitly assigns every item to a bin. The integer \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum feasible number \(q\); the empty input has optimum zero and can be packed in zero bins. Zero-size items, if allowed by an alternative convention, can be handled separately without changing the existence question.

Running time is worst-case bit complexity on a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine. There is no input advice, supplied optimal packing or promise on the size distribution, number of distinct sizes or optimum. The input is an explicit list, not binary multiplicities representing exponentially many separate output items.

The additive allowance is exactly one bin with capacity exactly 1. It does not grow with the instance, and it is not a multiplicative factor \(1+\varepsilon\). Neither larger bin capacities nor discarding an item is permitted. The target concerns the integer optimum of the packing problem, not the optimum of a fractional relaxation.

The probability convention makes explicit an algorithmic interpretation that includes randomized approximation algorithms, as in the later logarithmic-additive result. Its theorem gives expected polynomial runtime with its quality guarantee; that is a separately reported form of the known result. For the target here, the output must always be feasible and only the one-extra-bin guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\).
answer_criterion: Give one algorithm and a proof of all stated time, feasibility and probability guarantees, or refute the existence of such an algorithm. A conditional impossibility result must expose its assumption, including any assumption needed to exclude randomized algorithms. An \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) bound with unspecified constant \(C>1\), an asymptotic approximation scheme, or a nonconstructive fractional-integrality-gap bound alone does not meet the target.
context:
Problem 3 asks whether bin packing can join problems that admit polynomial-time solutions within one unit of their integer optimum. The book separately highlights a constant number of extra bins as significant progress. This card keeps the one-bin endpoint as its main target.

The book recalls the Karmarkar–Karp additive \(O((\log n)^{2})\) guarantee. Hoberg and Rothvoss later give a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial runtime and at most \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+2))\) bins, where \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is the fractional packing optimum. In particular this gives \(\operatorname{OPT}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}+2))\) bins, without establishing a constant additive bound.

The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Its objective is the total fractional number of bins. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

Bounds of the form \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_{\varepsilon}\) can approach multiplicative ratio 1 while retaining an unbounded or larger additive loss. They therefore do not imply the requested one-extra-bin guarantee on every instance.
why: A one-extra-bin algorithm would show that a strongly NP-hard packing problem can nevertheless be solved to a uniformly tiny additive error. The question tests a much sharper notion of approximation than a ratio tending to one and is a long-standing benchmark for understanding the structure of feasible packings.

title: Planted clique conjecture
importance_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
focus_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
context:
The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.
why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.
status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

working_summary: A detector receives one random graph and must tell whether a uniformly chosen set of exactly k vertices was made into a clique. The selected conjecture excludes a uniform randomized polynomial-time detector with balanced success at least two thirds at all sufficiently large sizes when k is a fixed power below the square-root scale. The input, all sources of randomness, the complete bit-time clock and the precise order of quantifiers are specified. Known recovery algorithms reach the square-root scale, while sum-of-squares integrality gaps and other method restrictions do not exclude every detector. Conditional distinguishing results and newer inference reductions remain evidence about the hypothesis, with differing planting conventions and guarantees identified explicitly.

title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
importance_reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.
focus_reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.
formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
question_excerpt: The retained question is Wigderson’s worst-case-to-average-case implication, made precise using Bogdanov–Trevisan’s strict exact sampling and deterministic positive-moment convention. In the August 2019 book edition it is Open Problem 4.6, not the numbering in the earlier 2018 draft. The conclusion is existence of an intractable distributional NP problem; this card does not additionally require a named natural distribution or a completeness reduction.
definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
context:
Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the card’s single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.
why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The original book/survey explicitly pose the implication; inspected January and April 2026 results retain specific description-problem hardness assumptions or different distributional guarantees. The July nondeterministic-description abstract does not claim this general implication. No verified derivation from P != NP alone, or proof of its full negation, was found in bounded primary-source checks. The card remains source_open; the cited proofs were not independently certified.
