working_summary: The premise P != NP only states a worst-case separation between efficient decision and verification. The conclusion asks for one fixed NP language and one strict polynomial-time sampler whose generated inputs defeat every deterministic exact decider under a positive-moment runtime bound. The ensemble parameter is supplied to the decider, while correctness is required even on inputs outside the sampler’s support. Known reduction barriers concern restricted proof methods, and recent description-complexity results retain specialized hardness premises or different average-case conventions. A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the implication from the stated premise alone or of its full negation in the ordinary uniform model.

title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
importance_reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.
formal: Is the following computational impossibility statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), rational \(0<\varepsilon<(k-2)/4\), and rational \(0<c<1\), no uniform randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm can, for all sufficiently large \(n\), recover a vector with absolute correlation at least \(c\) with a uniformly random hidden unit direction from the single rounded tensor observation \[Y=\lambda_n v^{\otimes k}+Z,\qquad \lambda_n=n^{k/4-\varepsilon},\qquad v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{n-1}),\] where all \(n^k\) ordered entries of \(Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables. Recovery must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\), averaged over the hidden direction, noise and algorithm coins. Rounding, output normalization and the uniform bit-cost model are defined below. The fixed power saving \(n^\varepsilon\) and the spherical prior are parts of the existing target, not replaced by a threshold for one algorithm family.
question_excerpt: Does a fixed-power signal reduction below the conjectured tensor-PCA computational scale prevent every polynomial-time algorithm from obtaining constant correlation with a hidden spherical direction?
definitions:
\(S^{n-1}=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i v_i^2=1\}\), with its rotation-invariant probability measure. A tensor is an array indexed by all ordered tuples \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in[n]^k\), including repeated indices. Its rank-one signal has entry \(\lambda_n v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_k}\). The Gaussian noise entries, the direction and learner coins are independent. In particular the noise is not symmetrized: entries indexed by different permutations remain independent. The learner has exactly one tensor observation, with no labeled coordinates, informative starting vector, auxiliary graph or additional independent noise samples. The fixed constants \(k,\varepsilon,c\) are known to its program, but \(v\) and \(Z\) are hidden.

For \(n\ge2\), put \[b_n=\lceil10k\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad Q_b(x)=2^{-b}\left\lfloor2^b\max\{-2^b,\min\{x,2^b\}\}\right\rfloor.\] The actual input is \(n\) and the complete list \((Q_{b_n}(Y_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}))_{[n]^k}\) in lexicographic tuple order. Each entry is encoded by its signed integer numerator with the common denominator \(2^{b_n}\); the numerator has at most \(2b_n+2\) bits. The clipping interval and rounding direction are fixed, not chosen adaptively by the algorithm. The exact real tensor exists only in the sampling experiment; the machine receives no oracle for its discarded digits. The input length is \(O(n^k\log n)\) at fixed \(k\). This is the previously adopted explicit finite-precision version of the Gaussian question, not a theorem asserting equivalence to every exact-real formulation.

An allowed algorithm is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. There exist constants \(B,a\ge1\), possibly depending on the fixed triple, such that it terminates within \(Bn^a\) bit operations on every encoded input of this dimension and every random tape. Reading, storage operations, arithmetic, writing the output and its rational encodings are included. The single program and polynomial work for all \(n\), with no advice depending on dimension. Since \(k\) is fixed, this is polynomial in the complete input length. There are no exact-real or quantum operations.

The output is a list of \(n\) rational coordinates \(w_i\), each a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. A malformed vector or \(w=0\) fails. Otherwise interpret \(u=w/\|w\|_2\), where \(\langle w,v\rangle=\sum_i w_i v_i\) and \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). The success event is the mathematically defined inequality \[|\langle w,v\rangle|\ge c\|w\|_2.\] The learner need not compute that event, since it does not know the planted direction. Absolute correlation permits a global sign flip, including the inherent even-order ambiguity. The output need not encode the irrational normalized vector exactly; its rational representative determines the direction.

Write \(p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)\) for the probability of this event in the specified experiment. The target is \[\forall(k,\varepsilon,c)\ \forall A\text{ of polynomial bit cost}\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:\quad p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)<2/3.\] Thus the conjecture rules out eventual success on all dimensions; it does not claim that every algorithm fails at every large dimension, or that its success probability must tend to zero. Conversely, a refutation needs one fixed triple and one machine with eventual success at least \(2/3\). The range of \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(\lambda_n/\sqrt n=n^{(k-2)/4-\varepsilon}\to\infty\), placing the signal above the usual statistical scale in the unrounded model.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the full quantified impossibility statement, or a Lean-verified counterexample consisting of one fixed triple, a single algorithm, polynomial worst-case bit/output bounds and an \(N\) for which \(p_A(n)\ge2/3\) for every \(n\ge N\). A lower bound against low-degree estimators, one iterative method, or a different prior is not the universal statement. Detection and recovery must not be interchanged without a proved reduction. Any normalization, symmetrization, multiple-sample or precision transfer must be justified in the same success and resource model. A conditional hardness reduction is partial progress until its premise is proved. Logarithmic threshold improvements or a constant-prefactor improvement at \(n^{k/4}\) do not supply the fixed exponent saving. The desired output quality is a fixed absolute correlation, not coordinatewise numerical recovery.
context:
Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Randomly initialized power iteration has a different benchmark from the best known general methods: Wu–Zhou analyze its scale \(n^{(k-1)/2}\) and improve it by a polylogarithmic factor. For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.
why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.
status_note: No checked result through16 September2026 settles the displayed unrestricted finite-bit spherical recovery statement. The 2024 cumulant reconstruction theorem is restricted to odd order and low-degree estimators; the May2026 general-prior result assumes independent coordinates and both of its degree conditions. Random-start power iteration has scale n^{(k−1)/2}, while multiple-observation gradient and constant-prefactor critical-scale improvements do not produce a fixed power saving below n^{k/4}. The 2026 XOR reductions use Boolean spikes and conditional hardness premises. The checked Hastings2026 paper proves detection guarantees with a stated spectral-property caveat, not this recovery theorem. All such results remain context, and unrounded-to-rounded equivalence is not claimed.

title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
importance_reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.
formal:
Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge5\), fixed rational numbers \(a>b>0\), a fixed real \(\delta>0\), and one uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that
\[(a-b)^2<q\bigl(a+(q-1)b\bigr)\]
and, for every sufficiently large integer \(n\), the symmetric stochastic block model defined below satisfies
\[\mathbb E\bigl[\operatorname{ov}(A(G),\sigma)\bigr]\ge\frac1q+\delta?\]
All model parameters and the algorithm are chosen once, independently of \(n\). The expectation is over the planted labels, the graph and the algorithm's random bits.
question_excerpt: The Kesten–Stigum boundary is conjectured to be the computational threshold for sparse symmetric community recovery. The inherited card asks whether any fixed assortative parameters with at least five groups permit polynomial-time recovery strictly below it.
definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), draw the hidden labels \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n\) independently and uniformly from \([q]\). Conditional on these labels, independently include each unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\), \(i\ne j\), as an edge with probability \(a/n\) when \(\sigma_i=\sigma_j\), and with probability \(b/n\) otherwise. The graph is simple and undirected. Take integer \(n\ge\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}\), so these probabilities are valid. Groups have equal prior probabilities; their sizes are not conditioned to be exactly equal.

The input to \(A\) is this single graph on the named vertices \([n]\), encoded by its explicit binary adjacency matrix together with \(n\). The constants \(q,a,b\) are known to the algorithm and may be incorporated into its finite description. No hidden labels, correlated side information or auxiliary sample graphs are supplied. On every graph input and every random tape, the algorithm halts within \(K(n+1)^k\) ordinary Turing-machine bit steps for some fixed constants \(K,k\), and outputs a vector \(\widehat\sigma\in[q]^n\). Randomness consists of independent unbiased bits. Uniform means one finite program for all input lengths, with no length-dependent advice. The program, runtime constants and recovery advantage may depend on the chosen \(q,a,b\), but not on \(n\).

For label vectors \(u,v\in[q]^n\), set
\[\operatorname{ov}(u,v)=\max_{\pi\in S_q}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{u_i=\pi(v_i)\},\]
where \(S_q\) is the finite set of all permutations of \([q]\) and the indicator is one exactly when its condition holds. Relabelling communities does not change their quality. Output labels may be unused. The maximum is part of the mathematical performance measure; the algorithm does not know \(\sigma\) and is not asked to compute this maximum. The chance baseline \(1/q\) is the limiting baseline for fixed \(q\), not a claim that the finite-sample expectation of a maximized random overlap equals exactly \(1/q\).

Write
\[d=\frac{a+(q-1)b}{q},\qquad \theta=\frac{a-b}{a+(q-1)b}.\]
Here \(d\) is the limiting expected degree; the finite graph has expected degree \((1-1/n)d\). The Kesten–Stigum threshold is \(d\theta^2=1\), and the required strict inequality is \(d\theta^2<1\). The case \(a>b\) is assortative: edges are more likely within a group. The card asks for a fixed positive expected recovery advantage for all \(n\ge n_0\), for one finite \(n_0\); it does not replace that requirement by a probability tending to one, a statement only on a subsequence, or a community count growing with \(n\). There is no separate promise of information-theoretic recoverability: a successful algorithmic example would itself prove it.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the exact existential proposition. A positive answer must give one fixed eligible \(q,a,b,\delta,A\), a uniform worst-case polynomial runtime bound, and a finite \(n_0\) for which the expected-overlap inequality holds for every eligible \(n\ge n_0\). A negative answer must exclude every such choice: for every eligible fixed parameter triple, uniform polynomial-time randomized algorithm and positive \(\delta\), and every proposed \(n_0\), some eligible \(n\ge n_0\) must violate that expected-overlap inequality. Information-theoretic recovery with unlimited computation, conditional computational hardness, lower bounds for a restricted estimator class, and results with growing \(q\) do not settle the proposition. This is exact yes/no acceptance, with no numerical tolerance applied to the threshold or the quantifiers.
context:
Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity \(d\theta ^{2}\) compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and \(\theta\) describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case \(a>b\).

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer derive recovery hardness from a restricted, unproved low-degree conjecture about testing. Their recovery statistic correlates an estimated matrix with the centred matrix of community co-membership. Theorem A.1 uses integer average-degree parameters and a signal parameter in [0,1], so it should not be quoted as an unconditional theorem for every rational pair a,b allowed here. Under its hypotheses it supplies strong evidence for a computational barrier, not a proof excluding every polynomial-time algorithm.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

The August 2026 revision of Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein proves efficient recovery in some regimes below the usual threshold when the number of communities grows as n^χ with χ greater than one half by a fixed margin. In that scaling, within-community edge intensity also grows. Here q,a,b are fixed before n tends to infinity. The new algorithm therefore does not provide the example requested by this card. Their accompanying lower bounds apply to low-degree polynomial estimators, not to all algorithms.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.
why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the four primary papers were checked at the definition and main-theorem passages identified in their references, including the 23 August 2026 revision. Above-threshold algorithms, below-threshold information-theoretic recovery, restricted conditional hardness and growing-community algorithms leave the stated fixed-parameter unconditional question open in these sources. Bounded current-work searches found no matching settlement. Full cited proofs have not been independently verified or formalized in Lean.

This recovery need not run in polynomial time. | 2025-04-28: The revised conditional lower-bound paper relates restricted low-degree testing conjectures to matrix recovery hardness, retaining explicit model and parameter assumptions. | 2026-08-23: The revised many-community paper gives below-threshold polynomial algorithms when the number of groups grows sufficiently quickly, and separate bounds on low-degree estimators. Neither is an unconditional settlement for all algorithms at fixed q,a,b.
working_summary: A sparse stochastic block model hides a fixed number of equally likely community labels in a random graph. The question asks whether any fixed assortative parameters below the Kesten–Stigum threshold allow polynomial-time recovery with a constant expected advantage over chance. The algorithm receives one graph, and success is measured after the best permutation of the community names. Information can survive below the threshold, but known computational barriers retain conjectural or restricted-estimator assumptions. Recent algorithms with a growing number of communities do not supply the fixed-parameter example required here.

title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
importance_reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\geq6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that \(A\) never outputs \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) on any satisfiable \(3\)-CNF formula, and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{F\sim R_3(n,Cn),\,\rho}
 [A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]=1?
\]
The distribution \(R_3\), exact soundness, and worst-case time bound are defined below. The constant \(C\), machine and its time polynomial must be fixed before \(n\); the probability includes the algorithm’s independent random bits \(\rho\).
question_excerpt: Can a sound polynomial-time algorithm refute almost all random 3-SAT instances already at some constant clause density?
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. General inputs are explicitly listed \(3\)-CNF formulas, with at most three literals in each clause; repeated clauses, repeated literals and empty clauses are allowed. The empty clause is false. The number \(n\) of named variables and the list length are encoded in binary, followed by binary indices and sign bits with delimiters. Valid indices lie in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); unused variables are allowed. Let \(L\) be the complete encoded length. Malformed encodings receive \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\) in polynomial time.

For \(n\geq3\), the random distribution \(R_3(n,m)\) is an ordered list of \(m\) independent clauses sampled with replacement. For each clause choose a uniformly random three-element subset of \([n]\), and independently negate each selected variable with probability \(1/2\). Write its three variables in index order. Thus each random clause has three distinct variables, duplicate clauses may occur, and signs in all clauses are independent. This fixed-size distribution is not a planted distribution or a distribution conditioned on unsatisfiability.

The algorithm always outputs either \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) or \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). Exact soundness means that for every satisfiable input formula \(F\) and every sequence \(\rho\) of its random bits, \(A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). On an unsatisfiable formula it may also return \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\); the required frequency of success applies only to the stated random distribution. Even on exceptional input formulas or random choices there is no allowed false assertion of unsatisfiability.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine with independent fair bits and no advice or external oracle. There must be integers \(K,d\geq1\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence, including adversarial formulas. Reading random bits and producing the answer are charged, so only polynomially many bits may be used. This is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time bound on random formulas. Deterministic machines are included.

The probability limit requires that for every real \(\eta>0\) there is an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n\geq\max\{3,n_0\}\), the probability of \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) is at least \(1-\eta\). The rate of convergence need not be supplied as an algorithm. The density \(C\) is an absolute constant, not a function tending to infinity with \(n\). Choosing integer \(C\geq6\) loses no successful smaller constant-density regime: on a denser input the algorithm can run a lower-density refuter on the appropriate clause prefix, whose distribution is exactly the lower-density model. Unsatisfiability of a prefix implies unsatisfiability of the full formula, preserving soundness.

No named proof system or explicit derivation format is imposed. The output \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) must be justified by the proven soundness of the algorithm; the machine need not print a resolution or sum-of-squares proof. Existence of short unsatisfiability certificates without an efficient way of finding them does not meet this definition.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply one constant \(C\), one uniform algorithm, its worst-case polynomial time bound, exact soundness for every satisfiable input and every random-bit sequence, and the success limit for \(R_3(n,Cn)\).

A negative answer must rule out every such constant and every such algorithm. Equivalently, for every proposed sound polynomial-time \(A\) and every integer \(C\geq6\), there must be some \(\eta>0\) such that failure probability is at least \(\eta\) for arbitrarily large \(n\). Showing failure for a single algorithm, proof system or finite set of inputs is insufficient. A conditional theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. Algorithms requiring a growing clause density, allowing erroneous refutations on rare satisfiable inputs, or merely distinguishing a planted distribution do not satisfy the criterion.
context:
Typical unsatisfiability has a short counting proof. For any fixed assignment, a random clause is satisfied with probability \(7/8\), so the expected number of satisfying assignments in \(R_3(n,Cn)\) is \(2^n(7/8)^{Cn}\). For \(C\geq6\), this tends to zero exponentially. Markov’s inequality therefore shows that the formula is unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Always printing UNSAT would exploit that statistical fact but would violate soundness on satisfiable inputs.

The task asks for a certificate on a particular input while exploiting its typical structure. Search and proof existence are separate: a family of short refutations does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds one. The 2015 source explicitly separates these possibilities in its comparison of efficient refutation algorithms and nondeterministically available certificates.

Spectral and semidefinite methods give efficient refutation at much higher clause counts, around \(n^{3/2}\) for random \(3\)-SAT in the source’s historical account. The relevant density is the number of clauses divided by \(n\), so this regime grows like \(\sqrt n\), in contrast to the constant required here. A bound for other predicates, such as not-all-equal clauses, cannot be substituted for ordinary disjunction clauses.

Gap refutation proves that every assignment violates a positive fraction of clauses. It must therefore remain silent even on suitable nearly satisfiable formulas. Barak’s cited formulation of Feige’s hypothesis uses this stronger soundness requirement. The present target retains the previously approved requirement of soundness only on satisfiable formulas, so consequences of a gap hypothesis must be checked separately.

The 2026 work extends the density, relaxation degree and refutation-strength tradeoff to more general random CSP distributions without uniformly random literals. Its sum-of-squares lower bounds restrict a particular family of algebraic relaxations; its generalization of the upper bounds does not supply the unrestricted constant-density algorithm asked for here. The paper treats binomial random-instance models in its displayed theorems, another reason to avoid identifying them verbatim with this fixed-size target.

The August 2026 ECCC report states stronger lower bounds for resolution extended to bounded-width disjunctions of conjunctions. Such a result blocks algorithms restricted to those refutations, but it does not rule out a different sound polynomial-time computation. The claim is recorded at the abstract level rather than as an independent full-proof audit.

If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a deterministic polynomial-time SAT decision algorithm can refute every unsatisfiable input, and the elementary counting argument gives the required average-case success. Consequently an unconditional negative answer here would imply \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\). A positive answer would be a distribution-specific algorithm and would not itself decide worst-case SAT.
why: This problem isolates the gap between knowing that a typical sparse formula is unsatisfiable and efficiently proving unsatisfiability without ever making a false claim. A resolution would identify a major limit of average-case certification or produce an algorithm beyond the methods underlying existing refutation barriers.
status_note: The 2015 primary source poses efficient random-3-SAT refutation as a major challenge and explicitly defines exact soundness. The 30 April 2026 paper and the August 2026 ECCC abstract concern SoS/spectral tradeoffs and k-DNF resolution, respectively; neither states a solution for unrestricted sound polynomial-time refutation at constant density. Checked 16 September 2026. This is a bounded source review, not a proof of universal current openness or an independent verification of every cited lower bound.
progress: 2012: Barak records a Feige-hypothesis formulation with soundness on nearly satisfiable instances, which is stronger than the exact-satisfiability condition retained here. | 2015: Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer give general random-CSP refutation algorithms and separate exact-sound refutation, gap refutation, planted detection and existence of short certificates. | 2026-04-30: Chan, d’Orsi and Xu extend SoS and spectral tradeoffs to predicates without uniformly random literals; the displayed results concern these algorithmic families and their density requirements. | 2026-08-30: An ECCC report states improved constant-density lower bounds within k-DNF resolution; this is proof-system evidence, not a lower bound against every sound refuter.
working_summary: A random 3-SAT formula at sufficiently large constant clause density is almost surely unsatisfiable. The question asks for one polynomial-time randomized refuter that recognizes almost all such formulas while never rejecting a satisfiable formula. The density, algorithm and time bound must be fixed independently of the number of variables. Gap refutation, planted detection and lower bounds for particular proof systems do not settle this exact-sound unrestricted target. An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility with the full quantifiers in Lean.

title: Infinitely-often one-way functions from average-case NP hardness
importance_reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.
formal:
Does
\[
 \mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \text{an infinitely-often one-way function exists}
\]
hold under the uniform classical definitions below? In this card \(\mathrm{DistNP}\) uses exactly polynomial-time samplable input distributions, and infinitely-often security means that for every polynomial-time inverter and every inverse-polynomial success threshold there are arbitrarily large lengths at which the inverter's success falls below that threshold.
question_excerpt: The revised source asks whether average-case NP hardness implies one-way functions, and explicitly uses infinitely-often one-way functions in Theorem 1.5. This card retains that weaker security target, with all quantifiers written out, rather than silently imposing security at every sufficiently large length.
definitions:
All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial worst-case running-time bound over every random tape. Its polynomial can depend on its fixed program. No nonuniform advice, quantum computation or external oracle is allowed.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that
\[
 x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}\ V(x,w)=1.
\]
Write \(L(x)\in\{0,1\}\) for its membership bit. An exactly polynomial-time samplable ensemble is a sequence \(D=(D_n)_{n\ge1}\) of distributions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) for which one probabilistic polynomial-time sampler \(S\), on unary input \(1^n\), always outputs an \(n\)-bit string with distribution exactly \(D_n\). Samplability does not require efficiently computing the probability assigned to a given output string. Here \(\mathrm{DistNP}\) is the class of all pairs \((L,D)\) with these properties; conventions using efficiently computable cumulative probabilities are not the definition of this card.

A pair \((L,D)\) belongs to \(\mathrm{HeurBPP}\) if there are one randomized algorithm \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every integer accuracy parameter \(k\ge2\), and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), the computation \(A(x,1^k)\) always returns a bit in at most \(p(n+k)\) steps, and
\[
 \Pr_{x\sim D_n}\!\left[
   \Pr_{\omega}\bigl[A(x,1^k;\omega)=L(x)\bigr]\ge\frac23
 \right]\ge1-\frac1k.
\]
The inner probability is over the fresh coins of \(A\); the outer probability is over the input distribution. The unary parameter makes polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy explicit. The same program works for every \(n,k\); separate unrelated algorithms for different accuracies do not constitute this scheme. It may depend on the fixed language and sampler, but has no membership oracle for \(L\). No guarantee is required on the exceptional input fraction of size at most \(1/k\). This is an error-prone heuristic scheme, not an algorithm required to detect all its mistakes or output an explicit failure symbol.

Consequently, the premise states that there exist a language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and one such sampler \(S\) for which no scheme satisfying all these bounds exists. It does not assume that every NP language, every sampler or every individual input is hard, or that hardness is present at all sufficiently large lengths.

A candidate one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*\). Its output length is therefore polynomially bounded in its input length; injectivity and length preservation are not required. For a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(J\), define
\[
 s_{f,J}(n)=
 \Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n,\,\omega}\!\left[
 z\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad
 z=J(1^n,f(x);\omega)
 \right],
\]
where \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings and is independent of the inverter's coins. Any preimage of the sampled image with length exactly \(n\) counts as success; recovering the particular sampled \(x\) is not required. Failure symbols or outputs of another length count as unsuccessful inversion. The unary length is supplied, so inversion is not made hard by concealing the input length. Running time is polynomial in the full inverter input length and hence polynomial in \(n\) in this experiment.

The function \(f\) is infinitely-often one-way if
\[
 \forall J\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\quad
 \exists n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge N}:\quad s_{f,J}(n)<n^{-c},
\]
where \(J\) ranges over all the uniform polynomial-time inverters just defined. The function \(f\) is chosen once and works against all of them. Hard lengths may depend on \(J\) and \(c\); this does not require one common infinite set of hard lengths for every inverter. Replacing the final quantifiers by a guarantee for every sufficiently large \(n\) would impose the stronger, eventual security target and is not this question.

The desired conclusion is existence of at least one such function from the stated average-case hardness premise alone. A positive answer may use any mathematical argument; it is not restricted to a black-box construction or a reduction with a predetermined number of oracle calls. The question is about ordinary unrelativized computation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication, with the stated sampler, heuristic and inversion quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

A negative answer must establish both that some \((L,D)\) satisfies the average-case hardness premise and that no total polynomial-time function has the specified security. The latter means that for every candidate \(f\) there are a uniform polynomial-time inverter \(J\), an integer \(c\ge1\) and a threshold \(N\ge2\) with
\[
 s_{f,J}(n)\ge n^{-c}\quad\text{for every }n\ge N.
\]
Showing only that a particular proposed construction is insecure, or giving an oracle separation, does not prove this unrelativized negation. A result requiring a special language, a special sampler or an additional cryptographic premise suffices only if the stated general assumption is proved to imply those extra hypotheses. Strengthening the premise to hardness at all sufficiently large lengths answers a different implication unless a reduction from the retained premise is supplied.
context:
The premise concerns difficulty of deciding membership on efficiently sampled inputs. The conclusion concerns finding preimages of an efficiently computed function on uniform inputs. The possibility of the former without the latter is the Pessiland question.

A heuristic scheme has two distinct probability levels: it must answer reliably on most inputs, and it receives an accuracy parameter controlling the exceptional fraction. A fixed average error bound or worst-case NP hardness is not the premise defined here.

The June 2026 revision relates average-case NP hardness and one-way functions to two nearby approximation factors for a learning task, \(\ell^{1-o(1)}\) and \(O(\ell)\). It leaves that gap open. Its valid parameter regime uses sufficiently large fixed advice-complexity constants; the stronger regime asserted in April was corrected.

Infinitely-often security is deliberate: the hard input lengths can recur sparsely and depend on the inverter. The source separately notes a route to eventual security when its average-case premise is strengthened to eventual hardness.

The August 2026 quantum results construct relativized worlds with average-case hardness but absent cryptographic primitives. Their oracle qualifications prevent interpreting them as a negative solution in the ordinary classical model.

The September information-density characterization gives another condition implying infinitely-often one-way functions. Its hypothesis is a particular separation over sampled infinite sequences, not the unrestricted average-case NP premise of this card.
why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.
status_note: The latest listed June 2026 revision explicitly retains the Pessiland question. The checked August oracle separations and September information-density characterization do not establish either direction of the requested unrelativized resolution. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified solution to this precise infinitely-often implication; the cited proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 2026-06-23: The revised learning characterization records a remaining quantitative gap and corrects the parameter regime of the April version. | 2026-08-30: Quantum and classical oracle separations are announced for related cryptographic primitives. | 2026-09-09: A further information-density characterization yields infinitely-often one-way functions from its specific separation hypothesis.
working_summary: Some NP problems may remain hard to decide on inputs generated by an efficient sampler. This card asks whether such distributional hardness alone guarantees a polynomial-time function that is hard to invert at infinitely many lengths. The premise rules out one randomized heuristic scheme that works at every requested accuracy. The conclusion requires each polynomial-time inverter to have arbitrarily small inverse-polynomial success at arbitrarily large lengths, with those lengths allowed to depend on the inverter. A complete Lean-checked answer must settle the unrelativized implication, rather than a stronger eventual-hardness variant or an oracle-world separation.

title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
importance_reason: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(\mathrm{W}_{w}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(uv\in E\): exactly one of u,v lies in S} \(w_{uv}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(\mathrm{L}(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(\mathrm{L}=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(\mathrm{L}\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[\mathrm{L}(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.
context:
The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.
why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
progress: 2019 / 2020: Theorem 1.1 gives the general upper bound \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) with high probability, controlling every directed path in the improvement graph. | 2024-09-23: The sparse-graph theorem gives polynomial expected and high-probability bounds for arboricity \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\), with any fixed \(\delta \in\)(0,1]. The paper retains arbitrary graphs as an open case. | 2024-09-26: The author manuscript gives a smoothed superpolynomial lower bound for 3-FLIP and unperturbed exponential single-FLIP examples; both have a different scope from this target.
working_summary: Does FLIP for Max-Cut have polynomial expected path length on every graph under independent bounded-density edge weights? Each step moves just one vertex and must strictly increase the cut weight. The expectation controls the longest path after the weights are sampled, including all starting cuts and improving choices. Polynomial bounds for sparse graph families and a general high-probability bound do not finish this target. The known smoothed superpolynomial example permits three-vertex moves, while its single-vertex analogue is unperturbed.

title: Polynomial simplex complexity under zero-preserving perturbations
importance_reason: Individual judgment: preserving the structural zeros of linear programs addresses a central limitation of a foundational explanation of simplex performance. The question has broad relevance to algorithm analysis and optimization, while the exact chosen two-phase variant remains an explicitly disclosed editorial interpretation rather than a sourced universal conjecture.
formal:
Does there exist one randomized two-phase simplex algorithm \(\mathcal A\), in the exact model below, and fixed integers \(C,k\ge1\), such that for every \(m,d\ge1\), every real matrix \(\bar A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), vectors \(\bar b\in\mathbb R^m,c\in\mathbb R^d\) with
\[
\max_{i\in[m]}\| (\bar A_{i,*},\bar b_i)\|_2\le1,
\qquad\|c\|_2\le1,
\]
and every \(0<\sigma\le1\),
\[
\mathbb E_{G,R}\,[T_{\mathcal A}(A,b,c,\sigma)]
\le C(m+d+\sigma^{-1}+1)^k?
\]
For each nonzero entry of \((\bar A,\bar b)\), independently add \(\sigma\) times a standard normal random variable; entries initially equal to zero remain exactly zero. The resulting data are \((A,b)\), and \(c\) is unchanged. The task is to solve \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb R^d\}\) exactly, including infeasibility and unboundedness. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions, centers, zero patterns and noise scales. Expectation includes both the perturbations \(G\) and independent algorithmic fair coins \(R\). This is an explicitly disclosed specialization of the source's general direction to the fixed artificial-variable initialization and fair-bit program class below. It is not a claim about every pivot rule, and the specified class is not asserted to include all published shadow-vertex implementations.
definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). A standard normal variable has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All perturbations are independent of each other and the algorithm's coins. No independence assumption is imposed on the entries of the fixed center. There is no bound on the number of nonzero entries per row: preserving sparsity here means preserving each prescribed zero entry. There is no conditioning on feasibility, boundedness or nonsingularity. The algorithm receives only \(m,d,A,b,c,\sigma\), not the center or the realized perturbation values separately.

Here is the precise allowed two-phase simplex class. All vectors and matrices below are formed after perturbation. Represent \(x=x^+-x^-\) with \(x^+,x^-\ge0\), introduce slacks \(s\ge0\), and let \(p=2d+m\). Let \(D\) be diagonal with \(D_{ii}=1\) if \(b_i\ge0\) and \(-1\) otherwise. Put
\[
E=D[A,-A,I_m],\qquad h=Db=|b|.
\]
The original problem has the standard-form constraints \(Eu=h,u\ge0\), where \(u=(x^+,x^-,s)\), and objective \(q^{\mathsf T}u\) for \(q=(c,-c,0_m)\). The structural identity matrix and the signs and duplicate columns introduced in this conversion are not independently perturbed. The matrix \(E\) always has row rank \(m\).

Phase I uses \([E,I_m](u,z)=h\), \(u,z\ge0\), and maximizes \(-\sum_i z_i\). It starts at the artificial-variable basis with \(u=0,z=h\). Phase II uses \(Eu=h,u\ge0\) and objective \(q^{\mathsf T}u\). A basis for a rank-\(m\) constraint matrix \(H\) is an ordered set \(B\) of \(m\) column indices whose matrix \(H_B\) is invertible. Its basic vector has nonbasic coordinates zero and basic coordinates \(H_B^{-1}h\); it is feasible when these coordinates are nonnegative. For current objective vector \(w\), the reduced cost of a nonbasic column \(j\) is
\[
\bar w_j=w_j-w_B^{\mathsf T}H_B^{-1}H_j.
\]
A legal improving pivot chooses a nonbasic \(j\) with \(\bar w_j>0\), computes \(v=H_B^{-1}H_j\), and, if some \(v_i>0\), exchanges \(j\) with any basic position attaining
\[
\theta=\min_{i:v_i>0}(H_B^{-1}h)_i/v_i.
\]
Ties may be chosen by the algorithm; \(\theta=0\) is allowed. The resulting basis must be the actual next basis. If all \(v_i\le0\), this column instead supplies a feasible unbounded improving ray. A basis with all nonbasic reduced costs nonpositive certifies optimality for its current phase. All computations to select a pivot, solve linear systems, check costs or maintain auxiliary data count toward the running time.

During Phase I only these improving pivots are permitted. If all artificial variables become zero, the algorithm may finish Phase I immediately, since the objective cannot exceed zero. It then removes basic artificial columns one at a time by basis exchanges with columns of \(E\), retaining a feasible basis with every artificial coordinate zero after each exchange. These cleanup exchanges need not have positive reduced cost; each must reduce the number of basic artificial columns by one. Once none remain, all artificial columns are discarded and Phase II starts from exactly that basis. If instead Phase I reaches an optimal basis with \(\sum_i z_i>0\), it returns infeasible. Phase II permits only the improving pivots just defined and ends with an optimal feasible basis or a feasible unbounded improving ray. No auxiliary constraints, additional variables beyond this initialization, jumps to a different feasible basis, changes to the objective within a phase, or interior-point moves are allowed.

An eligible algorithm is a single finite classical program with fixed rational constants. It must obey these rules, terminate and return a correct certificate on every real input \(A,b,c\) of the stated dimensions, every \(0<\sigma\le1\), and every sequence of coin outcomes. An optimum is returned as the final basic vector and basis; an unbounded outcome includes its feasible basic vector and improving ray; infeasibility includes the terminal Phase-I basis with positive artificial sum and nonpositive reduced costs. The representation \(x=x^+-x^-\) translates standard-form optimum points and rays back to the original problem. Arbitrarily small numerical gaps are handled exactly, with no feasibility or optimality tolerance.

The computation model has ordinary binary work tapes and exact real work tapes, all initially blank apart from the input. Dimensions are given in binary; real input data are stored in row-major order with dimensions delimiting the arrays. The program has finitely many heads and registers, independent of the dimensions. Each bit operation, fair-coin request, head move by one cell, real-cell copy/read/write, rational-constant load, real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and real comparison has unit cost. Branches use the comparison or bit outcomes. All instructions and memory access are charged. There is no integer-part operation on reals, transcendental-function primitive, infinite table, arbitrary real program constant, oracle, nonuniform advice, parallel processor, or free linear-system solver. Noise is sampled externally to form the input; its generation is not charged. This exact arithmetic model is specified because Gaussian input numbers have no finite exact binary encoding. The number \(T_{\mathcal A}\) is the total operation count, not merely the number of pivots or bit precision. Its expectation is an extended nonnegative real and may be infinite. The rational program constants, internal states and number of tapes are fixed once for \(\mathcal A\); the machine has no length-dependent advice. Internal coin requests read independent uniform bits from an infinite binary sequence.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed universal expected polynomial bound for some eligible algorithm, or of its full negation. A positive proof supplies one program and constants \(C,k\), establishes exact correctness and compliance with the two-phase pivot rules for every input and coin sequence, and proves the expectation bound for every permitted center and noise scale. A negative proof establishes
\[
\forall\mathcal A\text{ eligible}\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists m,d,\bar A,\bar b,c,\sigma\text{ as above}:\quad
\mathbb E_{G,R}T_{\mathcal A}>C(m+d+\sigma^{-1}+1)^k.
\]
The bad dimensions, center and noise scale may depend on the algorithm and proposed bound. A bad example for one pivot rule does not establish this negation. A theorem with dense noise, additional geometric assumptions, a different allowable algorithm class, or numerical feasibility tolerances must establish the full proposition above to count. This is an asymptotic resource question; the benchmark's numerical \(1/100\) acceptance tolerance does not weaken exact LP correctness or replace the polynomial bound.
context:
Roughgarden explicitly identifies sparsity-preserving perturbations as a missing extension of smoothed simplex analysis in a footnote to the standard Gaussian model.

The source describes existing positive bounds for shadow pivot rules, while Spielman and Teng distinguish additive zero-preserving Gaussian perturbations from multiplicative relative perturbations.

This card chooses the additive model, fixed artificial-variable Phase I and a fair-bit program class with exact optimization; the original shadow initialization uses other auxiliary programs and continuous internal random vectors, so equivalence with that algorithm class is not asserted.

Bach, Black, Huiberts and Kafer's June 2026 revision explains why exponential examples survive zero-preserving perturbations for Bland's rule.

Their positive sparse-matrix analysis uses right-hand-side noise together with scaling parameters and numerical tolerances, so it does not by itself establish the universal exact statement here.
why: Zero coefficients encode much of the structure that makes large linear programs usable. A guarantee stable under preserving those zeros would test whether random-data explanations of simplex efficiency extend beyond dense perturbations. The question concerns the existence of an exact simplex implementation with a universal expected resource bound, and therefore separates a limitation of one pivot rule from a limitation of the whole specified algorithm class.
status_note: The source states a broad open direction in 2018. The bounded primary-source review through16September2026 found later results for particular rules and other sparse models, but no checked source explicitly certifies this exact combined two-phase formulation as open. It is therefore an uncertain, explicitly editorial interpretation rather than a claim of verified present openness.

That model does not give the zero-preserving existence statement here.

working_summary: Smoothed analysis asks how a simplex algorithm behaves on a worst-case linear program after independent random perturbations. This version keeps every original zero coefficient fixed and adds Gaussian noise only to nonzero matrix and right-hand-side entries. The target asks whether some explicitly defined two-phase simplex algorithm solves every such family exactly in expected polynomially many arithmetic operations. The algorithm class and additive noise convention are disclosed editorial choices completing a broader source question. A complete Lean answer must prove the universal expected bound or refute it for every algorithm in the stated class.

title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
importance_reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational threshold question for a canonical random constraint model, connected to discrepancy algorithms, solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness; its scope concerns all efficient algorithms rather than a single construction.
formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
question_excerpt: As \(\kappa  \to  0\), the algorithmic threshold for the 2 ). SBP is at \(\Theta\)(\(\kappa\) In particular, we conjecture that up to factors that are […]
definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.
context:
The source conjectures a \(\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\) scale. The logarithmic allowance is part of that conjecture, while the separate question of removing a logarithmic factor and the sharper overlap-threshold prediction are not added to this card’s acceptance criterion.

The full source gives the \(\Theta(\kappa^2)\) algorithmic benchmark via Bansal–Spencer for Rademacher entries and expressly describes transfer of the same guarantee to Gaussian entries as expected. This distribution qualification is preserved; the card does not cite that corollary as a proved Gaussian lower bound.

The source’s geometric obstruction rules out classes of stable algorithms. A bound for a specified stable class is evidence for the conjecture, while a proof of the upper inequality must cover every program allowed here.

Vafa and Vaikuntanathan give worst-case lattice reductions for a margin specified as a function of the inverse aspect ratio. Their stronger logarithmic-scale hardness conclusion uses a stronger lattice assumption. These are conditional results with their own algorithm and parameter conventions; they do not by themselves prove this unconditional fixed-margin real-arithmetic threshold statement.

The January 2026 preprint proposes parametric threshold predictions and reports practical performance of an algorithm. Its abstract does not state a universal lower bound excluding every polynomial-time search algorithm in the model above.
why: The symmetric binary perceptron is a basic random constraint model in which many solutions can exist while known algorithms reach much smaller densities. Locating the small-margin search scale tests whether the observed computational obstruction captures all efficient algorithms or only particular algorithm families. Its links to discrepancy, random solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness make the threshold a substantial average-case complexity question.

Read the full 2022 Gaussian model, tilde-scale conjecture and Rademacher qualification; checked the July 2025 lattice paper’s Theorem 3, Corollary 2, Remark 1 and reduction conventions, and the January 2026 prediction preprint’s abstract. The explicit real-arithmetic convention resolves a specification omitted in the source; no equivalence with every finite-precision formulation is asserted. The checked later works do not establish the unconditional full-class statement here. A bounded search found no matching proof or refutation; source-open records these limits rather than certifying all cited preprint arguments.
