working_summary: The symmetric binary perceptron seeks a sign vector satisfying many random Gaussian two-sided constraints. The conjecture places the efficient-search density at the scale of the squared margin, allowing fixed powers of its reciprocal logarithm. The card defines a supremum over uniform polynomial-time algorithms and states its exact real-arithmetic convention. The input dimension tends to infinity at each fixed margin and density before the margin approaches zero. Stable-algorithm barriers, a sign-matrix algorithm and conditional lattice reductions each have limits that prevent treating them as a full resolution.

title: Optimization and certification of Max-Cut in random cubic graphs
importance_reason: A canonical sparse random optimization problem separating the ability to find good solutions from the ability to certify their quality, with concrete links to average-case hardness, spectral relaxations and statistical physics.
formal:
Determine the two-valued function \(F:\{\mathrm{optimization},\mathrm{certification}\}\to\mathbb R\) for Max-Cut on a uniformly random simple labeled \(3\)-regular graph:
\[
F(\mathrm{optimization})=a_*\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(\mathrm{certification})=b_*.
\]
Here \(a_*\) is the supremum of asymptotic cut sizes achievable with high probability by uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, and \(b_*\) is the infimum of asymptotic upper bounds obtainable with high probability by uniform randomized polynomial-time producers of always sound, polynomial-time-verifiable certificates. Both values count crossing edges per vertex. The definitions below fix the quantifiers without assuming that either computational optimum is attained.

This is the user-approved specialization, recorded on 16 September 2026, of the source’s broader program for unspecified sparse random CSP models. The general model parameter is deliberately replaced by this single distribution and this pair of optimal computational thresholds.
question_excerpt: For a sparse random CSP model, how close to its optimal value can efficient algorithms construct assignments and efficiently certify upper bounds?
definitions:
For every even integer \(n\geq4\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on the labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with degree exactly three at every vertex. There are no loops or parallel edges, and disconnected graphs are allowed. Let \(\mu_n\) be the uniform distribution on \(\mathcal G_n\). All limits below run through even \(n\) tending to infinity. The graph is given explicitly by a unary size header and the upper triangle of its adjacency matrix, so its input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2\). Algorithms receive this graph, without access to a sampling oracle. Invalid encodings are rejected in polynomial time.

A cut is any vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\), with no balance constraint. Its value and the maximum cut value are
\[
q_G(x)=\frac{|\{\{i,j\}\in E(G):x_i\ne x_j\}|}{n},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}q_G(x).
\]
Thus values belong to \([0,3/2]\). A cut containing a fraction \(\theta\) of all edges has value \(3\theta/2\), since \(|E(G)|=3n/2\). The benchmark tolerance is applied in these per-vertex units, not to an approximation ratio and not to the fraction of edges.

Polynomial time means worst-case bit complexity on a uniform multitape Turing machine: for each algorithm there are fixed integers \(C,k\geq1\) bounding its steps by \(C(L+1)^k\) on every valid graph and every random-bit sequence. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, at most as many as the time bound allows, independently of the input graph. Finite programs have no advice or oracles. Deterministic algorithms are included. Reading and writing rational numbers, outputting a cut or a certificate, and all precision used in numerical computation count toward the bound. Constants and exponents may depend on the algorithm, but not on \(n\), the graph or its random bits.

An optimization algorithm \(A\) always outputs a valid cut. A level \(a\in[0,3/2]\) is achievable if there is one such polynomial-time algorithm satisfying, for every rational \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\ \mathrm{even}}}
\Pr_{G\sim\mu_n,\,\rho}\big[q_G(A(G;\rho))\geq a-\varepsilon\big]=1.
\]
Define \(a_*\) as the supremum of these levels. Here \(\rho\) denotes the algorithm’s random bits. The tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is a performance quantifier, not an additional input. The definition optimizes over all finite uniform algorithms; it does not require the supremum to be achieved by one algorithm.

A certification scheme is a pair \((P,V)\). The producer \(P\) is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a rational number \(u\in[0,3/2]\) and a binary certificate \(\pi\). Write rationals as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. Both output lengths are polynomial in \(L\). The verifier \(V\) is deterministic and runs in time polynomial in the total bit length of \((G,u,\pi)\). It rejects malformed encodings. Soundness is universal:
\[
V(G,u,\pi)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{OPT}(G)\leq u
\]
for every valid cubic graph \(G\), every rational \(u\in[0,3/2]\) and every finite certificate \(\pi\). In particular, soundness cannot fail on rare graphs or rare random choices. The producer must always return an accepted pair on every valid input and every random-bit sequence; the trivial bound \(u=3/2\) may be used as a fallback. Producing the certificate efficiently is part of the target, not just verifying an existentially supplied short certificate.

A level \(b\in[0,3/2]\) is certifiable if there is one such scheme satisfying, for every rational \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\ \mathrm{even}}}
\Pr_{G\sim\mu_n,\,\rho}\big[u(P(G;\rho))\leq b+\varepsilon\big]=1.
\]
Define \(b_*\) as the infimum of these levels. The notation \(u(P(G;\rho))\) selects the numerical bound from the producer’s output. No particular proof system, semidefinite relaxation or local algorithm is imposed. The algorithms and their verifiers can vary when taking the infimum, which need not be attained.

These extrema are well defined. The all-edge upper bound gives a certification scheme. Repeatedly moving a vertex that has fewer than two crossing incident edges strictly increases the cut; after at most \(3n/2\) moves the resulting cut has at least \(n\) crossing edges. This gives a polynomial-time baseline \(a_*\geq1\). Every cut is at most every accepted upper bound on the same graph, and the two high-probability events intersect with probability tending to one. Consequently \(1\leq a_*\leq b_*\leq3/2\). No existence theorem for a limit of \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) is needed to define the two computational extrema.
answer_criterion:
Supply an explicit function \(g:\{\mathrm{optimization},\mathrm{certification}\}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|g(\mathrm{optimization})-a_*|\leq\frac1{100},\qquad
|g(\mathrm{certification})-b_*|\leq\frac1{100}.
\]
Two rational approximations or two unambiguous mathematical expressions are valid ways to supply \(g\). Certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) for both extrema qualify through their midpoints. A restatement of the definitions of \(a_*\) and \(b_*\) without determining approximations or certified intervals is not an answer. Exact evaluation is welcome but not required.

Both sides of each interval must be justified for the full algorithm classes and the specified graph distribution. Constructing a good cut only gives a lower bound on \(a_*\); constructing a good certificate only gives an upper bound on \(b_*\). Their opposite bounds require valid limitations, possibly derived from information-theoretic bounds, on every algorithm or scheme in the class. All claims must be unconditional: an unproved complexity or detection conjecture does not discharge the Lean target. Simulations, predictions for the typical true optimum, the exact value of one SDP relaxation, or hardness confined to one algorithm family do not alone determine both entries of \(F\). Numerical estimates must retain enough exact or certified arithmetic to prove the stated absolute error.
context:
The original source leaves the random CSP model unspecified. This card formerly recorded that missing choice as pending specification. The user selected Max-Cut on random 3-regular graphs and asked for the best asymptotic polynomial-time construction and certification quality. The fixed distribution, normalization, randomization convention and certificate model above make that approved narrower objective explicit; other CSP predicates, densities and degree distributions remain part of the broader source program.

Finding a cut and certifying an upper bound solve different computational tasks. A proposed cut is easy to evaluate. A claimed upper bound must rule out every possible cut, so an algorithm that finds excellent solutions can coexist with a much weaker efficiently obtainable upper certificate. The true typical optimum lies between these kinds of guarantees, but knowing its typical value alone does not produce an always sound certificate on a particular input.

The standard spectral bound uses the adjacency matrix \(A_G\). If a rational \(t\) satisfies \(tI+A_G\succeq0\), then \(x^\top A_Gx\geq-tn\) for every cut vector, and \(q_G(x)\leq3/4+t/4\). Positive semidefiniteness means that the symmetric matrix has nonnegative quadratic form on every real vector; it can be checked with exact rational linear algebra and polynomial bit complexity. Rational approximation from above to \(-\lambda_{\min}(A_G)\) therefore gives a sound, efficiently produced certificate. The random regular spectral theorem yields the asymptotic level \(3/4+\sqrt2/2\), approximately \(1.457107\). The source also records that the basic SDP relaxation has this limit; a tight value for that relaxation is not optimality among all certification methods.

Information-theoretic bounds concern the maximum cut itself. Coja-Oghlan and coauthors prove a variational upper bound whose displayed cubic numerical value is approximately \(0.9241\) of all edges, or \(1.38615\) per vertex. The variational theorem, not an unqualified rounding of that decimal, is the rigorous statement. It bounds the quality of any constructed cut on typical inputs, but the probabilistic theorem does not by itself certify a bound for every individual input graph.

Kunisky and Yu propose that it is hard to distinguish a uniform random regular graph from a slightly perturbed random lift of a suitable small Ramanujan graph. A lift replaces each base vertex by a fiber and each base edge by a matching between fibers; a Ramanujan graph has its nontrivial adjacency eigenvalues bounded in magnitude by \(2\sqrt{d-1}\). Their detection conjecture gives a conditional obstruction to certifying cubic Max-Cut below \(17/18\) of the edges, namely \(17/12\) per vertex. This is a conjecture-dependent computational lower bound, not an unconditional lower bound proved here. Applying a detection hypothesis to the randomized producer class above requires its randomized-test version; a deterministic-only hypothesis cannot silently replace it.

The March 2026 version of Nagda, Raghavan and Thakurta reports a polynomial-time certification upper bound of \(0.953\) of the edges, or \(1.4295\) per vertex, using local cut distributions and spectral constraints in a fixed finite linear program. Its cubic lower bound remains the earlier conjecture-dependent one. The numerical linear-program certificate was not independently verified in this review. Moreover, the printed discretized lower inequality in Lemma B.3 fails for an empty cut with grid value zero and positive discretization width: it asks for a correlation larger than one. This is a local defect in the displayed argument that may be repairable; it is not a refutation of the reported theorem. The number is recorded as reported progress, not as an independently certified conclusion or a determination of \(b_*\).

Degree three stays fixed as the number of vertices grows. Results that become near-optimal only as the degree tends to infinity, bounds for dense random graphs, and worst-case approximation guarantees have different quantifiers. Likewise, a certificate whose correctness only holds with high probability over the graph is weaker than the always sound, efficiently obtainable certificates required here.
why: Random cubic Max-Cut is a concrete sparse optimization model in which excellent solutions and convincing upper certificates may have different computational limits. Determining both thresholds would measure that gap in a fixed distribution, test the limits of spectral and local methods, and clarify which information about a typical optimum can be made into an efficient proof for an individual instance.

title: Algorithmic threshold for random k-SAT
importance_reason: A central statistical-versus-computational gap in random constraint satisfaction, with rigorous algorithms and restricted barriers but no general matching lower bound. Existing score retained.
formal: Does the randomized polynomial-time satisfying-assignment threshold for random \(k\)-SAT satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)}{2^{k}\ln(k)/k}=1?\] For each fixed \(k\), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) is the supremum of constant clause densities at which some polynomial-time algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with probability tending to one as the number \(n\) of variables tends to infinity. The distribution and quantifiers are specified below.
question_excerpt: Given the existence of satisfying assignments for \(\alpha  = Ok (2k ), a\) natural algorithmic question arises: can we find such an assignment efficiently?
definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.
context:
For sufficiently large fixed \(k\), the satisfiability threshold is known and is asymptotic to \(2^{k}\ln 2\). This is about existence of an assignment; it does not provide an efficient way to find one throughout that range.

Coja-Oghlan’s Fix algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with high probability below \((1-\varepsilon_{k})2^{k}\ln(k)/k\), where \(\varepsilon_{k}\to0\). Thus the conjecture asks whether its leading asymptotic scale is optimal among all polynomial-time algorithms.

Bresler and Huang prove a low-degree obstruction above a constant multiple of this scale; their main stated constant is about \(4.911\), and their appendix discusses improvements. Theorem 2.6 concerns a specified normalized polynomial representation and requires a quantitatively small failure probability, stronger than an arbitrary \(o(1)\) failure rate. Their local-algorithm theorem rules out much smaller success probabilities within a narrower class. Neither theorem covers all polynomial-time algorithms.

The 2025 source explicitly retains the algorithmic conjecture. Its sharp geometric results for random SAT use growing clause width in the relevant exact-solution regime. They do not establish the fixed-width, all-algorithm upper bound asked here.
why: Pinpoints a possible computational barrier inside a regime where satisfying assignments typically exist. A resolution would clarify whether the geometry of random constraint problems predicts the power of arbitrary efficient algorithms, beyond individual heuristics and restricted computational models.
status_note: Read the conference source and full July 2025 version, the Fix publisher abstract and author introduction, and the full low-degree definitions and principal theorem statements. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for arbitrary polynomial-time assignment finding. The supremum definition spells out the source’s asymptotic algorithmic-threshold question. The source’s damaged saved density and its separate incidental logarithm typo are not used as mathematical definitions.
progress: 2010: Fix reaches density \((1-o_{k}(1))2^{k}\ln(k)/k\) with high-probability assignment finding. | 2021-10-29: The full low-degree paper provides restricted hardness results and explicitly conjectures a sharper constant. | 2025-07-07: The revised full source still states the all-polynomial-time threshold as a conjecture while proving sharp overlap-gap results.
working_summary: The input is a random conjunction of fixed-width clauses, with all literal positions sampled independently. The algorithm must find an assignment satisfying every clause with probability tending to one. The conjectured leading threshold is two to the clause width times its natural logarithm, divided by the width. Known algorithms reach this scale, while satisfying assignments exist at substantially higher densities. Existing overlap-gap and low-degree barriers do not establish optimality against every polynomial-time algorithm.

title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.
focus_reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
question_excerpt: For every graph, Glauber dynamics on proper colourings with at least \(\Delta+2\) colours should mix in polynomial time.
definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

For probability laws \(\mu,\nu\) on the finite state space, total variation is \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)=\frac12\sum_{\tau\in\Omega_{G,q}}|\mu(\tau)-\nu(\tau)|\). Define \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min\left\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_{G,q}}\frac12\sum_{\tau\in\Omega_{G,q}}|P^t(\sigma,\tau)-\pi(\tau)|\le\frac14\right\}.\] One may set this minimum to infinity if the set is empty; ergodicity in the stated range ensures that it is finite. The maximum is over arbitrary initial proper colourings, with no warm-start or random-initial-state assumption.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.
context:
The source poses polynomial mixing at the degree-plus-two threshold. This card retains the already adopted heat-bath update rule and the explicit requirement of one polynomial for all degrees and palettes. The source’s initial update description uses proposal-and-rejection; that clock is stated separately rather than silently identifying its transition matrix with this one.

At one fewer colour, a clique on Δ+1 vertices can be frozen: every vertex already sees every other colour. Thus ergodicity itself can fail at q=Δ+1. At q≥Δ+2 the basic chain is ergodic, but eventual convergence alone supplies no polynomial bound on how long it takes.

The2020 source proves polynomial mixing for bounded-treewidth graphs at the additive threshold and for chordal graphs with fixed multiplicative slack. Its treewidth-dependent exponent and the extra hypotheses do not establish the all-graph uniform statement.

The2024 flip-dynamics theorem applies for Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ. Its comparison gives polynomial Glauber mixing in that range; the sharper O(n log n) corollary permits a constant depending on degree and palette. Neither the larger palette ratio nor that parameter dependence is the selected degree-plus-two theorem.

The August2026 girth-seven revision treats Metropolis updates with q≥(1+δ)Δ, for fixed δ and degree sufficiently large in terms of δ. The separate girth-five preprint gives a heat-bath theorem under analogous fixed-slack and large-degree conditions. The latter’s general bound is Oδ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); its optimal-order corollary has further bounded-degree qualifications. Both retain structural assumptions absent here.

The ICALP2026 paper repeats the ordinary colouring-sampling conjecture before studying prescribed colour-class sizes. Fixing class sizes changes the stationary state space and the allowed moves, so those refined sampling results do not settle the chain defined here.
why: This tests whether the simplest local update rule samples proper colourings efficiently throughout the full range where it is guaranteed to move between all solutions. It connects random sampling, approximate counting and antiferromagnetic spin systems at a longstanding boundary for general graphs.

Their added graph, palette-slack and parameter assumptions do not establish the all-graph degree-uniform heat-bath Δ+2 statement. No matching resolution was identified in bounded later-work checks. No cited full proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

It asks for one polynomial mixing bound for every graph and every palette with at least two more colours than the maximum degree. The stationary law is uniform on all proper labelled colourings and the bound must hold from the worst initial colouring. title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A central obstruction to a general theory of uniform sampling with fixed combinatorial marginals.
focus_reason: A central obstruction to a general theory of uniform sampling with fixed combinatorial marginals.
formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.
context:
Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.
why: A general guarantee for a basic sampler that preserves individual degrees, with applications to network and fixed-margin statistical models. The reported solution would close the gap between eventual convergence and a uniform polynomial sampling bound.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Fu–Qin–Wang, arXiv:2606.22636v2, Theorem 2.2 claims the required general polynomial bound for this lazy chain. The theorem statement and model match; this pass has not independently verified the proof or built the authors’ Lean artifact. The active card therefore retains an uncertain claimed resolution, rather than an unqualified open status.

working_summary: The lazy switch chain samples binary matrices while preserving every row and column sum. Each attempted move chooses a two-by-two rectangle and may exchange its two checkerboard patterns. The target is polynomial convergence to the uniform distribution for every feasible choice of margins and every starting matrix. Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 preprint states an explicit bound meeting this target and supplies a Lean formalization. The card records that claimed resolution with uncertain status because its proof and formalization were not independently verified here.

title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A fundamental question about efficient sampling at a phase transition in the standard three-dimensional Ising model.
formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

For distributions on \(\Omega_L\), \(\operatorname{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\frac12\sum_{\sigma\in\Omega_L}|\nu(\sigma)-\pi(\sigma)|\). Define
\[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_L}\operatorname{TV}(P_L^t(\sigma,\cdot),\pi_L)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes every deterministic initial spin configuration. The question concerns this exact mathematical Markov chain; approximating its transition probabilities on finite-precision hardware is not an additional task. Rates in a continuous-time convention with one rate-one clock per site have an extra factor of the volume relative to individual updates; that normalization does not affect polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.
context:
Bauerschmidt and Dagallier relate functional inequalities for Ising dynamics to susceptibility bounds. Their critical finite-volume application uses mean-field susceptibility behavior and yields polynomial control on free-boundary lattice boxes in dimensions at least five. The checked result does not establish the needed hypothesis or conclusion in dimension three.

The source also distinguishes the earlier two-dimensional critical theorem from the higher-dimensional argument. Having polynomial mixing in dimension two and in dimensions at least five leaves the three-dimensional target separate; interpolation between dimensions is not a stated theorem.

The 2024 Prodromidis–Sly note proves polynomial mixing at the uniqueness threshold of the infinite regular tree for bounded-degree graphs. At degree six its parameter is \(\operatorname{arctanh}(1/5)\). The word critical in that title refers to the tree threshold, not to the infinite cubic lattice threshold defined in this card.

Boundary conditions materially affect low-temperature dynamics. The source contrasts slow mixing with free boundaries and a different conjecture under all-plus boundaries. Keeping the free-boundary convention is necessary to preserve this card’s specific critical-lattice question.
why: This is a basic question about whether a standard local sampling dynamics remains efficient at a phase transition in three dimensions. The equilibrium system has correlations on many scales, so high-temperature mixing guarantees do not directly apply. A polynomial bound or a superpolynomial obstruction would clarify the computational cost of critical fluctuations in one of the central lattice models.
status_note: The full November 2022 Bauerschmidt–Dagallier manuscript (published in 2024) and the November 2024 Prodromidis–Sly note were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search through 2026 found no polynomial mixing proof or superpolynomial obstruction for the exact critical three-dimensional free-boundary model. Higher-dimensional, tree-threshold and different-initialization results do not resolve this target.

The parameter in their theorem is distinguished from the cubic-lattice critical point.
working_summary: This question concerns local heat-bath sampling of the Ising model at the critical point of the infinite cubic lattice. The finite system is a three-dimensional box with free boundaries and zero external field. It asks whether every initial spin configuration becomes close to equilibrium after polynomially many individual updates. The critical inverse temperature is specified by the infinite-volume magnetization threshold, without relying on a numerical estimate. Known critical results in other dimensions and at the regular-tree threshold do not settle this three-dimensional lattice problem.

title: Polynomial mixing of planar Ising dynamics with plus boundaries
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A long-standing model question about whether boundary phase selection makes local sampling efficient throughout the planar Ising model’s low-temperature regime. It connects geometric interface relaxation with worst-state Markov-chain mixing and remains explicitly open in 2026 primary work.
formal:
For every fixed finite inverse temperature \(\beta\in[0,\infty)\), does random-site heat-bath Glauber dynamics for the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\), with all exterior boundary spins fixed to \(+1\), mix in time polynomial in \(n\)? Precisely, is it true that
\[\forall\beta\in[0,\infty)\ \exists C_\beta,a_\beta>0\ \forall n\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}^+(n,\beta,1/4)\le C_\beta(n+1)^{a_\beta}?\]
The mixing time is worst-case over every initial configuration inside the box and counts individual site-update attempts. The constants may depend on the fixed temperature, but not on \(n\). The finite-temperature convention and the update rule are specified below.
definitions:
Vertices are adjacent when their lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=|u_1-v_1|+|u_2-v_2|\) is one. Let \(E_n\) consist of the unordered adjacent pairs inside \(V_n\), and let \(\partial V_n\) be the vertices outside \(V_n\) adjacent to it. A state is \(\sigma\in\Omega_n=\{-1,+1\}^{V_n}\). Extend it to \(\widetilde\sigma\) by assigning \(+1\) to every vertex of \(\partial V_n\). The Gibbs measure is
\[\pi_{n,\beta}^+(\sigma)=\frac1{Z_{n,\beta}^+}\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_n}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in V_n,\ v\in\partial V_n\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right),\]
where the normalizing constant is the sum of this weight over \(\Omega_n\). Internal and crossing edges are each counted once and all interaction strengths are one. There is no external field beyond the effect of the fixed boundary spins. A corner vertex has two crossing edges; each contributes to its local field.

At each discrete step choose \(v\in V_n\) uniformly and independently, and replace \(\sigma_v\) by \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\qquad h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\|u-v\|_1=1}\widetilde\sigma_u,\]
and by \(-1\) otherwise. The other interior spins are unchanged and exterior spins are never updated. An update that retains the old value counts as a step. For every finite \(\beta\), the chain has strictly positive conditional probabilities, is irreducible and aperiodic, and has stationary measure \(\pi_{n,\beta}^+\). Denote its transition matrix by \(P_{n,\beta}^+\).

Total-variation distance between distributions \(\nu,\pi\) on the finite state space is \(\operatorname{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\frac12\sum_{\sigma\in\Omega_n}|\nu(\sigma)-\pi(\sigma)|\). Define
\[t_{\mathrm{mix}}^+(n,\beta,1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_n}\operatorname{TV}((P_{n,\beta}^+)^t(\sigma,\cdot),\pi_{n,\beta}^+)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes the all-minus interior configuration; it is not restricted to typical or mostly-plus starts. The boundary is plus throughout, regardless of the interior initial state.

Inverse temperature is measured in units with interaction strength and Boltzmann constant equal to one. The domain includes \(\beta=0\), the independent-spin infinite-temperature limit, and every positive physical temperature, but not the separate zero-temperature limit \(\beta=\infty\). The quantified statement is pointwise in fixed \(\beta\); it does not demand common constants for temperatures varying with \(n\). In the continuous-time convention with one rate-one clock per interior site, the typical update count per unit time is \(n^2\). This polynomial factor preserves the question of a polynomial mixing bound, but matters when comparing exact exponents. This card studies the exact mathematical chain, not finite-precision implementation of its probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed all-finite-temperatures polynomial bound or its negation. A positive answer must cover every fixed finite \(\beta\) and every interior initial state with all-plus boundaries. A negative answer must establish at least one fixed finite inverse temperature for which no polynomial in box side length bounds the specified mixing time. Bounds only from biased initializations, only in the zero-temperature limit, or of quasipolynomial size do not meet the target.
context:
Question 1 of the source is explicitly two-dimensional: an n by n grid with all-plus boundaries. Its remarks about higher dimensions are related context, not an enlargement of this card’s quantifiers.

The published Lubetzky–Martinelli–Sly–Toninelli bound is \(n^{c(\beta)\log n}\) in the low-temperature regime. It is a substantial improvement over earlier subexponential bounds, but its exponent grows with \(n\), so it is not polynomial.

The May 2026 Gheissari–Sly preprint still identifies polynomial plus-boundary mixing as a long-standing open problem. Its Theorem 4 strengthens control of the temperature dependence in a quasipolynomial bound. Its rapid phase-ordering theorem uses biased initial configurations and a different convergence target, rather than providing the worst-state polynomial mixing bound here.

Zero-temperature interface dynamics and finite-temperature mixing are distinct statements. The new preprint discusses the known zero-temperature polynomial bounds as supporting evidence, while retaining the finite-temperature question. The card fixes finite inverse temperature to avoid treating a non-irreducible limiting chain as the same ergodic model.
why: This question asks whether fixing a coherent boundary phase is enough to make local sampling efficient at every positive temperature. At low temperature, convergence from an opposing interior phase is controlled by the disappearance of large interfaces. A polynomial bound would quantify how boundary information removes the slow phase switching that occurs under other boundary conditions.

A bounded search found no subsequent matching resolution; this is source-open with a recent direct source.

title: Cutoff for bounded-degree transitive expanders
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A central cutoff conjecture connecting expansion, spatial symmetry and abrupt equilibration. It asks for a general principle on sparse graphs used throughout theoretical computer science, rather than another estimate for one random-walk family.
formal:
Does every sequence of bounded-degree vertex-transitive expander graphs exhibit total-variation cutoff for lazy simple random walk? More precisely, consider any sequence \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) of finite connected undirected simple graphs, with \(N_k=|V(G_k)|\to\infty\). Assume each \(G_k\) is vertex-transitive, that there is a fixed integer \(D\ge3\) with \(3\le d_k\le D\) for its vertex degree \(d_k\), and that the lazy-walk spectral gaps satisfy \(\gamma_k\ge\delta\) for some constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). Must
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{t_k(\varepsilon)}{t_k(1-\varepsilon)}=1?\]
The transition rule and worst-start mixing times \(t_k\) are defined below. The constants \(D\) and \(\delta\) may depend on the sequence. No quantitative cutoff window or common leading constant for different sequences is demanded.
definitions:
A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. Vertex-transitive means that for any vertices \(x,y\) there is a bijection of the vertex set preserving adjacency in both directions and mapping \(x\) to \(y\). Consequently all its vertices have the same degree \(d_k\). The graph sequence is deterministic and need not come from a particular construction or a random-graph model.

One lazy-walk step stays at the current vertex with probability \(1/2\), and otherwise chooses a neighbor uniformly and moves there. Its transition matrix is
\[P_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2&y=x,\\1/(2d_k)&\{x,y\}\in E(G_k),\\0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The stationary probability is \(\pi_k(y)=1/N_k\). List the real eigenvalues in decreasing order as \(1=\lambda_{1,k}>\lambda_{2,k}\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_{N_k,k}\ge0\), and set \(\gamma_k=1-\lambda_{2,k}\). A uniformly positive lower bound on \(\gamma_k\), together with bounded degree, is the expander assumption used here. Laziness includes bipartite graphs without periodicity problems.

At an integer time \(t\ge0\), let
\[d_k(t)=\max_{x\in V(G_k)}\frac12\sum_{y\in V(G_k)}\left|P_k^t(x,y)-\frac1{N_k}\right|,\qquad t_k(\eta)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_k(t)\le\eta\}\quad(0<\eta<1).\]
The maximum is over every starting vertex. Times count discrete lazy steps, including steps that stay put. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the denominator \(t_k(1-\varepsilon)\) is positive for all sufficiently large \(k\); the limit uses this eventual tail. The displayed ratio condition defines total-variation cutoff. It asks that the transition between distance near one and distance near zero occupy a vanishing fraction of the mixing time.

The source first states the question with one fixed degree. Allowing degree to vary in a fixed finite range is equivalent at the level of this universal conjecture: each degree occurring infinitely often gives a fixed-degree subsequence. Neither degrees growing without bound nor expansion constants tending to zero are admitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every sequence satisfying the hypotheses has the displayed cutoff property, or a Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must establish a sequence satisfying every hypothesis for which the ratio limit fails for at least one fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\). A single finite graph cannot refute an asymptotic cutoff statement. Logarithmic mixing-time bounds alone, cutoff in a different distance, or a result only for a special class of expanders do not meet the criterion.
context:
The textbook asks this question for a fixed degree and explicitly chooses lazy random walk. The card retains that walk and the total-variation meaning of cutoff, while making the graph-sequence and uniform-gap quantifiers explicit.

Salez’s 2025 notes state the vertex-transitive expander conjecture as Problem 2.3. The notes explain that expansion already gives mixing time of logarithmic order in the graph size; cutoff asks for substantially finer asymptotic information.

Lubetzky and Peres prove cutoff for simple random walk on non-bipartite \(d\)-regular Ramanujan graphs, where all adjacency eigenvalues other than \(d\) have absolute value at most \(2\sqrt{d-1}\). This is a much stronger spectral condition than an arbitrary fixed positive gap. Their result supplies a major special case, not a proof for every transitive expander.
why: Expanders combine sparse connectivity with fast random-walk mixing and are central objects in algorithms and pseudorandomness. This conjecture asks whether spatial symmetry forces their approach to equilibrium to be abrupt. A resolution would separate the role of expansion in the speed of mixing from the role of symmetry in the shape of convergence.

This question asks whether vertex symmetry forces a sharp transition to equilibrium in every bounded-degree expander sequence. title: Weakly negatively regressive sampling of matroid bases
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A general matroid rounding question connecting prescribed marginals, negative dependence and submodular optimization; its scope covers all matroids and its consequences extend beyond a particular objective or sampling construction.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every finite matroid \(M\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) given by an independence oracle and every rational point \(p\) of its base polytope, samples a basis \(B\) with exact marginals
\[\Pr[i\in B]=p_i\quad(i\in[n])\]
and a weakly negatively regressive output distribution, in expected time polynomial in \(n\) and the binary encoding length of \(p\)?

Here weak negative regression (WNR) requires, simultaneously for every \(i\in[n]\) and every increasing function \(f:2^{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\to\mathbb R\),
\[\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{i\in B\}} f(B\setminus\{i\})]\le p_i\,\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})].\]
The algorithm receives no objective function \(f\). One output law must satisfy all these inequalities.

This card selects WNR, the weakest of the three alternative dependence requirements in the source question. Negative association or negative regression would also suffice by implying WNR. The independence-oracle, rational-input and exact expected-time sampling conventions below make the source's efficiency question precise; they are explicit editorial conventions.
definitions:
A matroid \(M=([n],\mathcal I)\), with \(n\ge1\), consists of a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) of independent sets. If \(A\in\mathcal I\) and \(A'\subseteq A\), then \(A'\in\mathcal I\). If \(A,D\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|D|\), some \(e\in D\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). A basis is an inclusion-maximal member of \(\mathcal I\); all bases have the same cardinality. Let \(\mathcal B(M)\) be their family, including the singleton family containing the empty set for a rank-zero matroid.

The base polytope is
\[P_B(M)=\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B(M)}\lambda_B\mathbf 1_B:\lambda_B\ge0,\ \sum_B\lambda_B=1\right\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1_B\in\{0,1\}^n\) is the incidence vector. This is the convex hull of bases, as specified by the source's maximal-independent-set convention. It is distinct from the convex hull of all independent sets.

An oracle query supplies an \(n\)-bit incidence vector for a set \(A\) and receives the exact bit indicating whether \(A\in\mathcal I\). The oracle is fixed throughout a run and is promised to describe a matroid. The input gives \(n\) in binary and \(p_i=a_i/b_i\), with binary integers \(0\le a_i\le b_i\) and \(b_i\ge1\). Let \(L\) be their total encoding length. The promise is \(p\in P_B(M)\); membership testing is not an additional required output. A convex decomposition of \(p\), an explicit list of bases and a sampling oracle are not supplied.

Use a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with this independence oracle and independent fair random bits. All ordinary bit operations, random-bit generation, oracle-query preparation and output writing count toward time; obtaining the answer to a completed oracle query costs one additional step. There must be fixed constants \(C,d\) such that expected total work is at most \(C(n+L+1)^d\) on every promised input and every matroid oracle. These constants and the machine are independent of the instance. No arbitrary real-arithmetic operations or nonuniform advice are available.

The machine must halt with probability one, and every terminating run must output the incidence vector of a basis. Its probability law over outputs must have the exact stated marginals and satisfy WNR without an additive tolerance. There is no failure output or exceptional probability on which feasibility or the distributional guarantees may fail. Expected time permits exact sampling with rational probabilities whose denominators are not powers of two. Independent invocations use fresh random bits; a joint coupling across different inputs is not required.

Increasing means \(f(A)\le f(D)\) whenever \(A\subseteq D\). The domain is finite, so each real-valued \(f\) has finite expectation. For \(0<p_i<1\), the displayed WNR inequality is equivalent to
\[\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\in B]\le\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\notin B].\]
For \(p_i=0\) or \(p_i=1\), the unconditional inequality is automatically an equality and does not invoke undefined conditional probabilities. WNR concerns all increasing functions of the remaining coordinates, not just pairwise covariances or linear functions.

For context, a set function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular when \(F(A)+F(D)\ge F(A\cup D)+F(A\cap D)\) for all sets \(A,D\). Submodular dominance at marginals \(p\) means \(\mathbb E[F(B)]\ge\mathbb E[F(R_p)]\) for every such \(F\), where \(R_p\) includes each element independently with probability \(p_i\). This consequence of WNR is not a substitute for the stronger specified distributional target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement in the declared oracle and bit-computation model. A positive answer must establish one uniform sampler, exact feasibility and marginals, all WNR inequalities, almost-sure termination and the expected polynomial resource bound for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such sampler exists; it need not show that a WNR law is nonexistent for any individual input. A theorem that only supplies a distribution nonconstructively, approximate marginals, pairwise negative correlation, submodular dominance, or a sampler for a restricted class of matroids does not by itself meet the full criterion.
context:
The 2022 question asks about sampling for arbitrary matroid marginals with WNR, negative association or negative regression. The latter two properties each imply WNR. This card adopts the first listed branch and retains arbitrary matroids; it does not impose one particular rounding procedure.

WNR implies submodular dominance: every submodular objective has expectation at least that under independent inclusion with the same marginals. Matching marginals alone fixes linear objectives, but does not establish this nonlinear guarantee.

The source reports a gap in an earlier claimed negative-association sampler for general matroids. It also observes that maximum-entropy matroid distributions need not have the required negative dependence, because even uniform distributions can have positively correlated coordinates.

The 2026 journal paper proves dimension-free submodular lower-tail bounds under one-negative association, equivalent to WNR for binary variables. Its introduction continues to flag the gap in the earlier general-matroid sampling claim and leaves the dependence properties of standard matroid rounding procedures open. These are conditional consequences of the dependence property, not a construction for every matroid.

The 2026 correlated-sampling paper gives cardinality-constrained rounding with preserved marginals and submodular dominance. Its discussion of negative association includes a known hypersimplex sampling law, and the introduction mentions a partition-matroid extension. Cardinality and partition constraints are special cases of matroids; the paper does not establish the arbitrary-matroid target here.
why: Randomized rounding must reconcile combinatorial feasibility with the dependence created by exact marginal requirements. This question asks whether every matroid base point has an efficiently accessible law controlling all monotone effects of conditioning on one coordinate. Such a general sampling theorem would support objective-independent rounding and strong guarantees for nonlinear submodular objectives, beyond the linear expectations fixed by marginals alone.

The output law must satisfy weak negative regression for every increasing function of all coordinates except one. The chosen model uses an independence oracle and a uniform exact sampler with expected polynomial bit complexity. This dependence property implies favorable submodular expectations and supports known concentration guarantees. A reported gap in an older general-matroid claim remains acknowledged in the 2026 literature, while newer special-case rounding results do not settle this target.

title: Monotonicity of Ising spectral gaps
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A general comparison principle for the relaxation of ferromagnetic sampling, combining temperature and graph modifications. Its significance lies in a universal relation between interactions and dynamics, beyond bounds for one lattice or one parameter regime.
formal:
Does strengthening any collection of ferromagnetic interactions always weakly decrease the spectral gap of zero-field random-site heat-bath Ising dynamics on a fixed finite vertex set? For every integer \(n\ge1\), put \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Let \(J=(J_{uv})_{u<v}\) and \(J'=(J'_{uv})_{u<v}\) be finite nonnegative real interaction strengths on the unordered vertex pairs. Is the following statement true?
\[\bigl[\forall u<v,\ 0\le J_{uv}\le J'_{uv}\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\gamma(J')\le\gamma(J).\]
Here \(\gamma\) is the spectral gap per individual uniformly chosen site update, defined below. There is no external magnetic field or fixed boundary spin. This is the common interaction-strength generalization explicitly asked in Question 2 of the source.
definitions:
The state space is \(\Omega=\{-1,+1\}^{V}\). Use the symmetric convention \(J_{vu}=J_{uv}\) and \(J_{vv}=0\). The Gibbs probability of a configuration is
\[\pi_J(\sigma)=Z_J^{-1}\exp\!\left(\sum_{u<v}J_{uv}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\qquad Z_J=\sum_{\tau\in\Omega}\exp\!\left(\sum_{u<v}J_{uv}\tau_u\tau_v\right).\]
Each unordered pair is counted once. A zero interaction means the corresponding edge is absent, so arbitrary finite graphs, isolated vertices and edge additions are included. Inverse temperature is absorbed into the interactions. All couplings are finite; the infinite-coupling limit is not a separate input.

At each step choose \(v\in V\) uniformly, independently of previous choices. Set \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u\ne v}J_{uv}\sigma_u\). Replace the spin at \(v\) by \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-h_v(\sigma))},\]
and by \(-1\) otherwise; all other spins stay fixed. Retaining the current spin counts as one update. Write \(P_J(\sigma,\tau)\) for this transition probability. The chain is finite, irreducible and reversible with stationary distribution \(\pi_J\).

For \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), set \(\overline f_J=\sum_\sigma\pi_J(\sigma)f(\sigma)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)=\sum_\sigma\pi_J(\sigma)(f(\sigma)-\overline f_J)^2\). Define
\[\gamma(J)=\inf_{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)>0}\frac{\frac12\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Omega}\pi_J(\sigma)P_J(\sigma,\tau)(f(\sigma)-f(\tau))^2}{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_J}(f)}.\]
Equivalently, this is \(1-\lambda_2(P_J)\), with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly and the stationary eigenvalue \(1\) first. The heat-bath matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues because it averages conditional-expectation projections. Thus the spectral and absolute spectral gap agree for this update rule. The relaxation time is \(1/\gamma(J)\).

Both compared chains have exactly the same \(n\) sites and site-selection probabilities. Adding an edge does not add a vertex or rescale the clock. The assertion uses a non-strict inequality and does not assume differentiability of eigenvalues. The question is about exact real transition matrices; numerical simulation or a choice of finite-precision implementation does not define the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal implication, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may specify a finite vertex set and two allowed interaction arrays \(J\le J'\) and prove \(\gamma(J')>\gamma(J)\). A positive answer must cover arbitrary graph structure and independent changes in edge strengths, including edges of initial strength zero. A theorem only for common rescaling of all interactions, or for a restricted family of graphs, does not establish the universal claim. Approximate eigenvalue calculations require rigorous bounds certifying the claimed strict reversal.
context:
For fixed nonnegative physical edge weights \(K\), changing inverse temperature replaces \(J\) by \(\beta K\). The proposed interaction-wise inequality therefore implies that the spectral gap increases with physical temperature. Allowing zero strengths also includes the edge-addition question. The source separately asks about monotonicity of total-variation distances at fixed times; that stronger question is not part of this card’s answer criterion.

Nacu proves monotonicity in each individual coupling on a cycle. The argument also permits zero strengths by a limiting convention, including the path obtained by removing a cycle edge. This remains a graph-family result.

Kargin proves temperature monotonicity for the complete graph when all interaction strengths are equal and varied together. The theorem allows a uniform fixed external field, and hence includes zero field. Its one-parameter comparison does not establish independent edge-wise monotonicity on general graphs.

Salez’s 2023 theorem identifies the spectral gap of an order-preserving Markov chain with its optimal curvature. In that work, monotone means preservation of increasing functions of the state. It is distinct from the proposed comparison between chains with different interaction arrays.
why: The conjecture asks whether stronger attractive interactions universally slow the relaxation of local sampling. A positive answer would give a comparison principle across both temperature and graph structure, while a counterexample would expose a limit of that basic physical intuition. The difficulty is a global dynamical property, even though each update uses only the neighboring spins.

title: Mixing of the self-avoiding-walk pivot chain
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A substantial gap between a widely used polymer-sampling method and rigorous control of equilibration from arbitrary starts. The target connects geometric constraints, nonlocal Monte Carlo moves and worst-state mixing, beyond implementation tuning.
formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\) of the following pivot chain on rooted \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks in the square lattice. The target is an asymptotic order \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) for which there exist constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[c\,h(n)\le t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\le C\,h(n)\qquad\text{for every }n\ge n_0.\]
A step is one attempted pivot, including a rejected proposal. The exact proposal distribution and the distance threshold \(1/4\) are fixed below. This is an explicitly selected asymptotic mixing-time formulation of the source’s broader request to analyze convergence.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), the finite state space \(\Omega_n\) consists of sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\) such that \(\omega_0=(0,0)\), \(\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1\) for \(0\le i<n\), and \(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Here \(\|(x,y)\|_1=|x|+|y|\). Walks are ordered, rooted at the origin and not identified under rotation, reflection or reversal. There is no confining box or additional energy weight. Let \(\pi_n\) give equal probability \(1/|\Omega_n|\) to each walk.

In one step independently choose \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S\) uniformly from these five maps:
\[(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).\]
These are the three nontrivial quarter-turn rotations and the two coordinate-axis reflections in Example B.5. Propose
\[\omega'_i=\begin{cases}\omega_i&i\le k,\\\omega_k+S(\omega_i-\omega_k)&i>k.\end{cases}\]
If the proposal belongs to \(\Omega_n\), accept it; otherwise keep \(\omega\). In either case the time increases by one. Fresh choices are independent at subsequent steps. In particular \(k=n\) always leaves the walk unchanged. Denote this transition matrix by \(P_n\).

The proposal maps occur with the same probabilities as their inverses, so the chain is reversible for \(\pi_n\). The irreducibility established in the source, together with the positive holding probability, gives a unique stationary law and convergence to it. Define
\[d_n(t)=\max_{\omega\in\Omega_n}\frac12\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_n}\left|P_n^t(\omega,\eta)-\pi_n(\eta)\right|,\qquad t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_n(t)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes every valid walk, not just a straight walk, an equilibrium start, or a numerically typical configuration.

The clock counts proposals rather than CPU operations or accepted pivots. Testing whether a proposed walk intersects itself is part of implementing a transition, but its computational cost is not multiplied into this mathematical mixing time. The textbook’s instruction to repeat after rejection is interpreted as proceeding to the next proposal with the old state retained, as explicitly specified in Clisby’s standard pivot dynamics. Discarding all rejected attempts from the clock would define a different chain and is not the convention here.
answer_criterion: Supply a non-circular asymptotic description \(h(n)\) and complete mathematically correct Lean-checked upper and lower bounds establishing the displayed inequalities for the specified chain. The constants must be independent of \(n\). A function defined merely by renaming the unknown mixing time is not a determination. A polynomial upper bound alone is a partial result unless it comes with a matching-order lower bound. Average cost per update, autocorrelation estimates for selected observables, empirical equilibration tests and a different sampling algorithm do not establish worst-state total-variation mixing of this chain.
context:
Example B.5 fixes the square lattice and five allowed symmetries, proves irreducibility, and leaves convergence behavior open. The card preserves that geometry and proposal set. It makes asymptotic worst-state mixing the concrete target rather than requiring an unspecified convergence analysis.

Clisby explicitly retains the old walk on a rejected pivot and identifies detailed balance with the uniform law. The card uses that standard rejection convention to specify exactly what a Markov-chain step means.

Clisby’s work substantially improves the computational implementation of individual pivots. Its introduction and autocorrelation study distinguish heuristic and numerical performance evidence from a rigorous worst-state bound on total-variation mixing. A fast transition implementation by itself does not establish the mixing-time order requested here.

The source also mentions the Randall–Sinclair approximate sampler, which uses a different underlying Markov chain. Existence of another sampler does not determine the convergence rate of the fixed pivot chain.
why: The pivot algorithm is a major sampling method for self-avoiding walks, a basic model of polymers with excluded volume. Its practical efficiency makes the absence of a matching rigorous convergence analysis especially consequential. Determining its mixing order would quantify when samples have forgotten an arbitrary initial shape, beyond the behavior of a few measured observables.

title: Deterministic approximation scheme for graph cover times
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times
importance_reason: A persistent deterministic-versus-randomized approximation question for a fundamental global exploration statistic. Arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on all graphs asks for more than the known universal constant-factor comparison or special-family algorithms.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the expected cover time of simple random walk from a specified starting vertex of an arbitrary finite connected undirected simple graph? Specifically, does there exist one deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every integer \(q\ge2\), there are constants \(C_q,a_q>0\) for which every allowed \(n\)-vertex input \((G,v,q)\) is processed within \(C_q(n+1)^{a_q}\) bit operations and the output rational number \(\widehat C\ge0\) satisfies
\[\left|\widehat C-C(G,v)\right|\le\frac{C(G,v)}q?\]
Here \(C(G,v)\) is defined below. The runtime is polynomial in graph size for every fixed accuracy \(1/q\); its exponent may depend on \(q\). This restores the relative-approximation question actually stated by Aldous and Fill, rather than the unsupported exact-output wording in the imported draft.
definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. It is promised connected. Its encoding consists of \(n\) in unary followed by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix, a binary starting label \(v\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the integer accuracy parameter \(q\ge2\) in binary, with standard self-delimiting integer fields. All graph families and degrees are allowed; in particular there is no bounded-degree or rapid-mixing promise.

For \(n\ge2\), let \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the discrete-time walk with \(X_0=v\). At each step it independently chooses a uniformly random neighbor of its current vertex. It has no added holding probability. Define
\[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=V(G)\},\qquad C(G,v)=\mathbb E_v[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}].\]
The initial vertex is already visited at time zero, and time counts edge traversals. There is no requirement to return to \(v\) after the last new vertex is visited. For \(n=1\), put \(C(G,v)=0\). Connectedness guarantees finite expectation. The quantity \(\max_v C(G,v)\), often called the graph’s cover time, is related but is not substituted for the supplied-start expectation.

The algorithm is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no random bits, advice or sampling oracle. Input processing, rational arithmetic and output writing count toward the runtime. Its output is a pair of binary integers representing a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. The required inequality holds for every input, not merely with high probability. When \(n=1\), it requires output zero.

The integer \(q\) represents reciprocal relative accuracy. This discretization covers any fixed requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). The constants \(C_q,a_q\) are independent of the graph and the starting vertex. No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is demanded; that would be the stronger fully polynomial scheme. Nor is an exact numerator and denominator for the unknown expectation demanded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that an algorithm with the displayed correctness and runtime guarantees exists, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must work at arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on every allowed graph and starting vertex. A constant-factor estimate, a randomized approximation, a theorem restricted to trees or a promise on hitting times, and a procedure that computes only the worst-start maximum do not establish the stated scheme. An exponential-time exact formula by itself does not establish the polynomial-time guarantee.
context:
Section 6.8.3 explicitly introduces numerical evaluation of the supplied-start expectation up to a fixed factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\), then asks for deterministic polynomial time. The older imported title “exact cover time” omitted this convention. This review restores the original accuracy and starting-vertex scope; exact computation remains a stronger possible route to a positive answer, not a requirement.

The 2017 textbook notes describe exponential-size exact computation and then cite Aldous–Fill’s question in compressed form. They also record the later constant-factor approximation. Reading the original accuracy convention avoids treating those sentences as a new explicitly exact-output conjecture.

Ding, Lee and Peres give a deterministic constant-factor approximation for the maximum expected cover time over starting vertices. Their theorem resolves that weaker approximation question; neither the precision nor the starting-vertex guarantee is the full target of this card.

Feige and Zeitouni obtain a fully polynomial approximation for trees. Their main theorem concerns cover and return, and Section 3.2 extends the method to ordinary cover time from a specified vertex. The tree restriction is essential to the scope of the cited result.

Meka’s 2015 Gaussian-process approximation theorem has a cover-time application on bounded-degree graph sequences satisfying \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}=o(t_{\mathrm{cov}})\), as specified in Section 1.1. Here \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}\) is the maximum expected time to hit one vertex from another and \(t_{\mathrm{cov}}=\max_v C(G,v)\). The application is qualified by that assumption and does not assert this card’s all-graph, supplied-start guarantee.
why: Cover time is a global measure of how efficiently a random walk explores a network. It is readily estimated by randomized simulation, while deterministic evaluation must account for the distribution of entire exploration histories. A scheme for arbitrary graphs would resolve a concrete derandomization question about an important graph parameter, with accuracy beyond universal constant-factor estimates.
