title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
importance_reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.
focus_reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(L\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(L\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.
context:
Finding a perfect matching is possible in deterministic polynomial time on general graphs, but exact counting is #P-complete even on bipartite graphs. A relative approximation can be much easier than exact counting, as the permanent demonstrates. This question asks whether that distinction persists on all simple graphs, making it one of the central missing cases in the theory of randomized approximate counting.

For an \(m\times m\) nonnegative matrix \(B\), its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_{m}\) is the set of permutations. When \(B\) is a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings between the two specified vertex classes. Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda prove an FPRAS for every nonnegative permanent, solving the bipartite matching case. Their theorem does not require the matrix entries to be strictly positive.

For a general graph on an even number of vertices, the corresponding expression is the hafnian of its symmetric adjacency matrix: the sum, over partitions of the vertices into unordered pairs, of the product of the selected entries. It is different from the permanent of that same square matrix. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine, because the latter also counts directed cycle covers. This example identifies the mathematical distinction between the two targets.

Jerrum and Sinclair’s 1989 Corollary 4.5 gives an FPRAS for the number of matchings of all sizes in arbitrary unweighted graphs. The related weighted monomer–dimer statement has a weight-encoding qualification; no unrestricted binary-weight theorem is needed here. Total matching count can differ exponentially from perfect-matching count: a disjoint union of \(j\) edges has \(2^{j}\) matchings but only one perfect matching. Thus the two quantities are not interchangeable even on elementary graphs.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes identify a precise obstruction for a family of chains on perfect and near-perfect matchings. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly two vertices uncovered, and its hole pattern records those vertices. For the specified JSV-type transitions and any weighting depending only on the hole pattern, their Theorem 2.2 gives graphs on which either perfect matchings have exponentially small stationary probability or the mixing time is exponential. The disjunction matters: the theorem does not assert slow mixing for every weighting, nor impossibility of every FPRAS. Their positive result treats bounded ear complexity of factor-critical subgraphs; a factor-critical graph remains perfectly matchable after deleting any one vertex, and ear count is not its vertex count.

The relevance extends to statistical counting models. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s Proposition 1.2 recalls that, for fixed rational equal interaction parameters \(\beta=\gamma<-1\), approximation of the corresponding two-state spin partition function is equivalent to general perfect-matching approximation under reductions preserving the existence of an FPRAS. The source states this equivalence in both directions and explicitly identifies the perfect-matching question as open. Its other tractable parameter regimes therefore do not settle this one.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s preprint of 27 August 2026 reports an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(m\times m\) zero–one matrix with \(m\ge2\), its Theorem 1 states time \(O(m^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}m\log(2/\delta))\) for relative error \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\); the trivial and zero-permanent cases are handled separately. The state space remains bipartite. This is a reported preprint running-time improvement within the solved neighboring case, not a general-graph theorem; its full proof and bit-level implementation were not independently verified here.

Zihong Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic approximation scheme for weighted hafnians when the support graph has minimum degree at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) and nonzero weights lie in \([\theta,1]\), for fixed \(\gamma>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The unweighted case takes \(\theta=1\), but it still has the fixed density margin. The polynomial’s exponents depend on these fixed margins. The paper explicitly retains the general nonbipartite FPRAS question as open and separately discusses its limitations at the exact Dirac threshold. The reviewed statement does not cover every graph, and the full new proof has not been independently verified.

A positive answer would extend a landmark success of randomized counting beyond bipartiteness. A negative answer would establish a separation between the ease of finding these objects and the existence of arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number. The source-specific Markov-chain obstruction explains part of the difficulty without deciding this algorithm-independent question.
why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.
status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. General unweighted perfect-matching FPRAS existence is explicitly open in Štefankovič–Vigoda–Wilmes, Fei–Goldberg–Lu v3 (17 August 2025), and Yi v1 (3 September 2026). Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 (27 August 2026) reports a faster permanent algorithm on bipartite graphs, while Yi’s new deterministic hafnian approximation requires a fixed positive density margin. Neither claims the unrestricted target. Their complete new proofs and implementations have not been independently verified. The 2017 lower bound concerns a specified Markov-chain family and gives a stationary-mass-or-mixing disjunction, not impossibility of every FPRAS. Bounded later-work searches found no matching full resolution; retained as source_open with these verification limits.

working_summary: A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one neighbor. The question asks for one randomized algorithm giving arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number on every finite unweighted simple graph. Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in the full input length and inverse accuracy, with success probability at least three quarters for each input. Bipartite perfect matchings and all matchings have approximation schemes, but the checked 2026 dense-graph and permanent results retain restrictions absent from this target. A complete Lean proof must establish such a uniform scheme with exact zero behavior or prove that no scheme meeting all requirements exists.

title: FPRAS for #BIS
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.
focus_reason: #BIS is the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem: an FPRAS would resolve a central boundary shared by many spin-system and combinatorial counting tasks.
formal: Does \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), counting all independent sets in an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Precisely, do there exist one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,k\geq1\) such that, for every encoded bipartite graph \(G\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the machine outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) within \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^k\) steps on every random tape and satisfies \[\Pr\big[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\big]\geq\tfrac34?\] Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of independent vertex subsets, \(L\) is the complete encoded input length, and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair coin bits.
definitions: For an integer \(n\geq0\), the vertex set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), partitioned into disjoint specified sets \(U,V\), either of which may be empty. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices with one endpoint in each part; there are no loops or parallel edges. An independent set is a subset \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) that contains no complete edge, and \(Z(G)=|\{I\subseteq U\cup V:I\text{ is independent}\}|\). Every independent set is counted once, with weight one, irrespective of its size or the number of its vertices in either part. The empty set is included, so \(Z(G)\geq1\), and the graph with no vertices has \(Z(G)=1\). Graphs may be disconnected and have isolated vertices, arbitrary degrees and parts of unequal sizes. Fix the following explicit finite-alphabet encoding. Write bin(j) for the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer j, with no leading zeros except in bin(0). An input is the string bin(n)#b#a#bin(r)#bin(s), where b has exactly n bits specifying part membership, a has exactly n(n−1)/2 bits specifying adjacency for pairs (i,j), i<j, in increasing lexicographic order, and integers r,s satisfy 0<r<s. Every adjacency bit equal to one must join vertices whose membership bits differ. The accuracy is \(\varepsilon=r/s\); the fraction need not be reduced. Thus isolated vertices are represented explicitly, and L counts all bits and separators, including both accuracy integers. The ceiling \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\) is taken after real division. An output encodes \(\widehat Z=p/q\) as bin(p)#bin(q), with integers \(p\geq0\), \(q\geq1\). The machine has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, with a stream of independent unbiased random bits. All input reading, bit computation, random-bit access and output writing are charged as Turing-machine steps; exact arithmetic on unbounded integers or reals is not a unit-cost operation. There is no oracle, advice, quantum resource or random input-graph assumption. The same program and constants C,k must work for all graph sizes, degrees, bipartitions and accuracies. Malformed strings are rejected by returning 0/1 within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps on every random tape, after increasing the common constants if needed. Deterministic algorithms are permitted as the special case that ignores the random bits.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a single algorithm and constants C,k meet the stated worst-case bit-cost bound, rational-output requirement and per-instance relative-error guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The negative direction must rule out every uniform fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme. Equivalently, every candidate satisfying the polynomial runtime and output conditions must have some valid input \((G,\varepsilon)\) on which its probability of a correct relative approximation is strictly less than \(3/4\). Showing a failure of a particular sampler, a finite running-time lower bound, or difficulty of exact counting does not establish this universal impossibility. A conditional lower bound, for example one assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), is not an unconditional negative resolution unless the assumed separation is also proved. The positive direction must cover every input graph and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with a polynomial degree independent of those inputs; expected runtime alone does not match the specified bound without a proof yielding the required always-bounded scheme. The target is existence of an approximation algorithm with its requested accuracy parameter, so a fixed numerical tolerance of 1/100 does not replace the quantified relative-error requirement. A deterministic fully polynomial scheme would meet the target, but is not required.
context:
An independent set need not be maximal or maximum. For an edgeless graph on \(n\) vertices the count is \(2^n\), whereas a complete bipartite graph with part sizes \(a,b\) has \(2^a+2^b-1\) independent sets: any subset of either part is allowed, with the empty set counted only once. In every bipartite graph all subsets of each part are independent, so the count can be exponentially large even though the instance and the binary representation of its count have polynomial length. The requested error is relative to that count, not to the number of vertices.

Exact counting and approximate counting have different known boundaries. The 2019 primary source recalls that exact \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete even at maximum degree three, while efficient relative approximation is known when all degrees on one side are at most five. It also recalls that allowing maximum degree six already recovers the full approximation difficulty. Here \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of counts of accepting computation paths of nondeterministic polynomial-time machines; hardness of computing such counts exactly does not itself rule out an FPRAS.

Approximation-preserving reductions allow a counting problem to be solved using relative approximations for another, with polynomial overhead and polynomially controlled requested precision. The literature contains many problems equivalent to \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) under such reductions, including problems about constrained assignments and statistical-mechanics models. The 2019 authors describe the family as conjecturally intermediate: neither an FPRAS nor NP-hardness of approximation is known for the unrestricted target. This is a description of the open complexity landscape, not a proved impossibility theorem.

The hard-core partition function is \(Z_G(\lambda)=\sum_{I\text{ independent}}\lambda^{|I|}\), for a positive parameter \(\lambda\) called fugacity. It normalizes the probability distribution assigning each independent set probability \(\lambda^{|I|}/Z_G(\lambda)\). The card fixes \(\lambda=1\), so every independent set has equal weight. Results for other fugacities or for distributions conditioned on a prescribed set size must be checked against this unweighted total count.

Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for almost every \(\Delta\)-regular bipartite graph when the fixed degree \(\Delta\geq53\), including the unweighted count. Regular means that every vertex has the same degree. Their probability is over a uniformly chosen graph with \(n\) vertices on each side, and tends to one as \(n\to\infty\); the approximation algorithm itself is deterministic. This is a substantial result for typical inputs, but it does not guarantee success on every bipartite graph as required here.

The ICALP 2024 dense-graph theorem gives an FPRAS for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\) on graphs with \(2n\) vertices that are \(\lfloor\delta n\rfloor\)-regular. Its constants and polynomial running-time degree may depend on the fixed density \(\delta\). Consequently, allowing \(\delta\) to decrease with the input size does not turn the stated theorem into a fully polynomial bound for all bipartite graphs. The paper’s exponential-form relative error and the card’s \(1\pm\varepsilon\) convention are equivalent for the existence of an FPRAS after a constant-factor change in the accuracy parameter.

The August 2026 preprint studies a different count: only independent sets occupying the two sides equally, or prescribed numbers of vertices on the two sides. Theorem 1.2 reports an approximation hardness threshold for the balanced partition function. In particular, at fugacity one and maximum degree six, it reports no FPRAS unless \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}\). Here NP is nondeterministic polynomial time, and RP is randomized polynomial-time decision with no false positives and acceptance probability at least one half on positive instances. The balance restriction changes which sets are counted, so this conditional result does not establish hardness of the unrestricted total count on this card. The new proof has not been independently verified in this review.

The same August preprint explicitly states that ordinary \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is neither known to admit an FPRAS nor known to be NP-hard to approximate. A slow-mixing Markov chain is likewise an obstruction to that chain, rather than to all possible randomized approximation algorithms. The remaining question concerns the existence of any uniform scheme satisfying the full worst-case guarantee.
why: The canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting: many counting problems share its approximation difficulty, while exact counting hardness does not settle whether a randomized relative approximation is efficient. A general scheme would transfer to problems reducible to it with preserved approximation guarantees; an impossibility proof would separate this central family from the counting problems with known fully polynomial schemes.

Bounded subsequent searches located no full FPRAS or unconditional impossibility for the present all-graph target. This remains the only listed version as checked on 14 September 2026.
working_summary: The #BIS problem counts all independent vertex subsets of an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, including the empty set. The question asks for one uniform randomized bit algorithm with polynomial runtime in the complete input length and inverse requested relative accuracy, succeeding with probability at least three quarters on every instance. Acceptance requires a full Lean-checked construction with an every-random-tape runtime bound, or a proof excluding every such scheme without an unresolved extra assumption. The problem represents a central approximation class whose apparent intermediate complexity is not settled by hardness of exact counting. The checked2026 literature still leaves the total count open, while typical regular inputs, dense regular graphs and balanced or fixed-size counts have distinct known results.

title: FP versus #P
importance_reason: A foundational complexity-class equality governing exact computation of all polynomially verifiable witness counts and strengthening the algorithmic consequences of P versus NP.
formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm P\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm P=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
question_excerpt: Can all #P functions be computed efficiently, so that FP and #P coincide under the binary-integer convention?
definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm P\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm P\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm P\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists of languages decidable using polynomially many working-tape cells, with no polynomial time restriction. A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm P\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.
context:
A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

A polynomial-space computation can enumerate all witnesses while keeping only a polynomial-length counter. The textbook therefore notes that P = PSPACE would imply a positive answer. This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.
why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.
status_note: The January 2007 draft and the checked 2017 primary teaching sources pose the exact-counting equality as open. Bounded source searches through 16 September 2026 found no verified proof of either equality or inequality. A March 2026 preprint claiming only the conditional P = NP implication is discussed on TCS-6821; it neither asserts this unconditional equality nor supplies a valid resolution in the local proof check recorded there. This review does not certify exhaustive present openness.

working_summary: The question asks whether every polynomially verifiable witness count can be evaluated exactly in deterministic polynomial time. Witnesses are binary strings of a fixed polynomial length, and different witnesses retain their multiplicities. The exact count is output in binary, so even an exponentially large value needs only polynomially many output bits. An affirmative answer would imply P = NP, but efficient existence testing or relative approximation does not establish exact counting. A resolution would settle the basic computational boundary for counting satisfiability, permanents and all other functions in #P.

title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
importance_reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.
formal:
Does there exist one finite deterministic algorithm \(D\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every explicitly encoded matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(D(A,\varepsilon)\) halts within
\[C\bigl(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and returns a nonnegative rational \(z\) satisfying
\[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)\le z\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)?\]
Here \(L\) is the full binary input length, and the permanent is defined below. The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(S_{n}\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. For a nonnegative rational matrix define
\[\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}.\]
Zero entries, zero rows, reducible matrices and arbitrarily large or small positive rational entries are permitted. There is no density, expansion, degree, rank, stochastic-scaling, or positive-entry lower-bound promise. This is the usual unsigned permutation sum, not the determinant or the hafnian. For a zero–one matrix it counts perfect matchings in the bipartite graph having one vertex for each row and each column, with an edge exactly where the entry is one. For a weighted matrix, each matching contributes the product of its edge weights.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion, with \(b(0)=0\), and set \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Encode \(n\) as \(E(n)\), then encode all \(n^{2}\) entries in row-major order. Each entry is a reduced pair \(u/v\), with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), encoded by \(E(u)E(v)\). Encode \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms, \(0<r<s\), by appending \(E(r)E(s)\). The length of this complete string is \(L\). It is not a succinct circuit or oracle description of a larger matrix. Output \(E(p)E(q)\), with \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), represents \(z=p/q\); the output need not be reduced.

Computation uses one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets and an output tape. Each transition costs one step, including all arithmetic, reading, writing, storage and output costs. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or unit-cost exact-real operations. The machine and the two clock constants are independent of the dimension, entries and requested accuracy. The exponent is fixed independently of \(\varepsilon\); polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\) is permitted in addition to dependence on its encoding length. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

The approximation is relative to the permanent itself, not additive relative to \(n!\), a matrix norm, or a rescaled quantity. Nonnegativity makes the permanent positive precisely when the positive-entry bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. Thus the zero case is deterministically recognizable in polynomial time, and the displayed inequality requires \(z=0\) exactly in that case. Arbitrarily small positive permanents must still receive the same relative guarantee. This is a genuine algorithm-existence question, not a numerical-value target at the catalogue’s absolute \(1/100\) tolerance.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite deterministic machine and constants \(C,k\), and prove termination, the full bit-cost bound, the rational output and both inequalities for every valid nonnegative rational matrix and every valid accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such machine and clock, rather than just one approximation formula or family of algorithms. A conditional lower bound remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A randomized FPRAS, a scheme restricted to positive dense matrices, a fixed dimension-dependent approximation factor, or running time \(n^{h(1/\varepsilon)}\) with an unbounded accuracy-dependent exponent does not qualify. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a negative answer: an exponentially small requested error may legitimately require exponential time under an FPTAS clock.
context:
The permanent is a basic counting polynomial whose nonnegative entries remove cancellation. Its zero–one specialization counts bipartite perfect matchings, while weighted inputs total the contributions of all such matchings. Existence of a matching and accurate estimation of their total weight are different tasks. The input’s full bit encoding matters when weights vary over many orders of magnitude; floating-point proximity to zero is not a substitute for the required relative guarantee.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda establish a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all nonnegative matrices. This makes the permanent a particularly explicit test of the power of randomness: the desired relative approximation is already possible with bounded error, and the question asks whether it can always be obtained deterministically with the same fully polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy.

Anari and Rezaei prove the tight comparison \(\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le2^{n/2}\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\). Here the Bethe permanent is a particular variational estimate over nonnegative matrices with all row and column sums equal to one. Block diagonal matrices with \(2\times2\) all-ones blocks attain the factor. This proves a limitation of that estimate, not a lower bound on all deterministic approximation algorithms. The result was first posted in 2018 and presented at FOCS 2019; the journal’s later issue date does not make it a new 2025 algorithm.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s 27 August 2026 preprint reports an improved permanent FPRAS, with \(O(n^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}n\log(2/\delta))\) time for zero–one inputs of dimension at least two, where \(\delta\) is the failure probability. The theorem also states an extension to nonnegative matrices. This is a reported improvement on the randomized side; it does not remove randomness or establish this deterministic target.

Anari’s preprint, first posted on 28 August 2026 and revised on 1 September, claims a deterministic polynomial-time factor \(c^{n}\) for an absolute \(c<\sqrt2\). Its main theorem explicitly treats rational matrices, with zero entries and certified finite precision discussed in Appendix A. Narang and Perkins independently claim the same type of improvement in their 31 August preprint. These are bounds for estimates different from the unmodified Bethe value, so they do not contradict its tight example. The new proofs and any associated formalization were not independently checked in full by this review.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint states a stronger general result: positive rational endpoints \(L_{A}\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le U_{A}\), after separate zero detection, with
\[\log(U_{A}/L_{A})=O\!\left(\frac{n(\log\log n)^{2}}{\log n}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\), using a polynomial number of bit operations on arbitrary nonnegative rational inputs. This is a subexponential multiplicative interval width, not subexponential running time. Its Theorem 1.2 makes the error/time tradeoff explicit, and the introduction still distinguishes its guarantee from a fully polynomial relative approximation scheme. The full new proof has not been independently verified here.

Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic FPTAS on another substantial subdomain: nonzero matrix entries must lie in \([\theta,1]\), and every row and column of the support must contain at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) nonzero entries, for fixed \(\theta>0\) and \(\gamma>0\). Its polynomial exponents may depend on those margins. The statement includes some matrices with zeros, but it does not cover unrestricted rational inputs or margins that shrink with the input size. Its full proof was not independently verified in this review.

The remaining question is a uniform relative approximation guarantee with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent and arbitrary requested accuracy. Improving an exponential factor, making its logarithm sublinear in dimension, and solving a restricted dense case are all meaningful advances, but none of their stated guarantees is the full requirement. A resolution would settle a central concrete derandomization problem in approximate counting.
why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.
status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. The current Kudria–Luo–Majid v1 of 9 September explicitly distinguishes its subexponential-factor approximation from an FPTAS; Narang–Perkins v1 also identifies the FPTAS as unknown even for zero–one matrices. Anari v2 (1 September), Narang–Perkins v1 (31 August), the randomized Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 (27 August), and Yi v1 (3 September, fixed-density and weight margins) report narrower advances. Their statements, versions and relevant model restrictions were checked, but complete new proofs and any linked Lean formalization were not independently verified. Bounded later-work checks found no matching unrestricted deterministic FPTAS. Retained as source_open with these limits; exact #P-hardness does not establish a negative answer.

working_summary: The permanent of a nonnegative matrix sums the weights of all perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm approximating this value to any requested relative accuracy on every nonnegative rational matrix. Its running time must be polynomial in the full binary input length and inverse accuracy, with a fixed exponent and exact output zero when the permanent is zero. Randomized approximation is established, while checked 2026 deterministic results have dimension-dependent error factors or fixed density and weight restrictions. A complete Lean proof must establish the unrestricted deterministic scheme or prove that none meets the stated guarantees.

title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
importance_reason: A canonical open problem of enumeration complexity connecting polyhedral computation and optimization. The bounded versus unbounded distinction and long-running algorithmic work give it a separate scientific role from counting or approximate optimization.
formal:
Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every rational matrix \(M\) and rational vector \(b\) for which
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Mx\leq b\}
\]
is bounded, \(A\) lists every vertex of \(P\) exactly once and halts in at most \(p(L+S)\) bit operations? Here \(L\) is the complete binary input length and \(S\) is the length of the required exact vertex list in the canonical encoding below. The dimension \(d\) is part of the input. Empty, lower-dimensional and degenerate polytopes are included.
question_excerpt: Can the vertices of a bounded polyhedron given by linear inequalities be enumerated in time polynomial in the combined input and output size?
definitions:
The input consists of integers \(m,d\geq1\), an explicitly listed matrix \(M\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d}\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\). The inequality \(Mx\leq b\) is coordinatewise. Every rational is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive denominator in binary, in lowest terms, with no leading zeros; zero has numerator zero and denominator one. Fixed delimiters separate dimensions, entries and rows. The input length \(L\) includes all these symbols. Dimensions are unbounded, and no rank, sparsity, integrality or conditioning restriction is imposed.

A polyhedron is a set described by finitely many closed linear inequalities. The promise here is that it is bounded: there exists a finite real number \(B\) such that \(\|x\|_2\leq B\) for every \(x\in P\). An empty set satisfies this promise. The number \(B\) is neither supplied nor assumed to have a given value. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope. Redundant inequalities, repeated inequalities and a non-full-dimensional affine hull are allowed; no nondegeneracy or general-position promise is made.

A vertex is an extreme point. A vector \(v\in P\) is a vertex if, for all \(x,y\in P\), the equality \(v=(x+y)/2\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex of a rational polyhedron is rational. The output must contain the coordinate vector of each distinct vertex, exactly once, in arbitrary order, with all \(d\) coordinates in the same reduced rational encoding. It ends with a fixed end marker. An empty polytope produces only that marker. A singleton produces its unique point even if its affine dimension is zero.

Define \(S\) as the sum of the canonical lengths of the distinct required coordinate vectors, including fixed separators and the end marker. Permuting the list does not change its length. Extra padding, duplicate vectors, alternative descriptions of the same vertex and extraneous certificates do not enlarge \(S\). At a vertex, a full-rank selection of active equations determines its coordinates; Cramer’s rule bounds their binary lengths by a polynomial in \(L\). Thus every individual output has polynomial length even though the number of outputs can be exponential.

Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with bit-operation cost, no advice and no oracle. The same finite program and the same polynomial \(p\) must work for every input satisfying the boundedness promise. Arithmetic precision, preprocessing, writing all coordinates, duplicate handling and the final termination signal are charged. The bound is on total time from start to termination. No polynomial-delay, incremental-polynomial-time or input-polynomial-working-space requirement is added. The algorithm may use space up to its total time bound. Its behavior outside the boundedness promise is immaterial; malformed encodings can be rejected.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and polynomial exist, or a proof in Lean of their nonexistence. A positive proof must establish exactness of every rational output, completeness, absence of duplicates, termination and one uniform \(p(L+S)\) bit bound for all bounded rational input polyhedra, including the empty and lower-dimensional cases.

A negative proof must rule out every correct uniform deterministic enumerator with every polynomial total input-plus-output bound. It is not enough to exhibit an input on which a particular pivot rule or intermediate-representation algorithm is slow. A conditional hardness theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional existence question. Approximate vertices, a fixed dimension, bounded branch-width, nondegeneracy, or enumeration measured against all bases or all arrangement intersections does not meet the full criterion.
context:
An inequality system describes a convex region implicitly, while its vertices describe the extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without listing every vertex. The question asks whether converting the whole description requires only polynomial overhead beyond the size of the answer.

A polytope can have exponentially many vertices, so polynomial time in the input alone is not the intended goal. Output-polynomial time allows this unavoidable output cost. It still demands fast termination on instances whose final vertex list is short, even when a natural algorithm encounters a large collection of intermediate objects.

One direct method chooses sets of tight inequalities, solves the resulting linear systems and tests feasibility. Degeneracy can make many different sets identify the same vertex. The total number of bases examined can therefore be much larger than the number of distinct vertices. A total-polynomial bound in the number of such bases would not establish the required output-polynomial bound.

Reimers and Stougie obtain a total-polynomial algorithm when a branch-width parameter of the linear matroid of the constraint matrix is bounded by a fixed constant. This parameter measures how the columns can be recursively divided while limiting the overlap of the spans on either side. Their result supplies a structural tractable case, while their introduction explicitly retains the general bounded-polytope question.

The same source recalls that total-polynomial vertex enumeration for arbitrary unbounded polyhedra would imply P equals NP. Boundedness is therefore a substantive promise. Intersecting an unbounded polyhedron with a large box can introduce additional vertices; the number of these new outputs is not automatically controlled by the original required list, so this operation does not simply transfer the unbounded lower bound.

The arrangement paper, revised in March 2025, enumerates intersections arising throughout a family of hyperplanes. Most such intersections may be infeasible for the chosen orientations of the corresponding inequalities. Its output count can thus be much larger than the number of vertices of one polytope, so enumerating the entire arrangement and filtering it does not give the claimed bound in this card’s output size.

The numerical coordinates are part of the computational model. Their polynomial bit-length bound permits exact rational output and prevents an apparently short geometric answer from hiding unbounded precision costs. Conversely, no compact symbolic description of a vertex replaces the explicitly required coordinate vector.
why: This is a basic unresolved question about converting between implicit and explicit representations of convex feasible regions. A general output-polynomial algorithm would make degeneracy and intermediate representation growth manageable at the level of total complexity, while an impossibility result would separate efficient linear optimization from full exact enumeration.
status_note: The full 2016 primary source explicitly poses total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polytopes as unresolved. The checked March 2025 arrangement revision concerns a different output set. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the exact variable-dimension rational bounded-polytope target. This is a dated literature review, not an exhaustive proof of current openness.
progress: 2016-07-09: The revised Reimers–Stougie paper gives a total-polynomial algorithm under bounded branch-width and explicitly retains the unrestricted bounded-polytope question. | 2024–2025: The arrangement-enumeration work gives algorithms for all intersections of a hyperplane arrangement; version 2 was posted on 25 March 2025. That output set differs from a single polytope’s vertex set.
working_summary: The input describes a bounded rational polyhedron by linear inequalities in variable dimension. The task is to list every distinct extreme point exactly once and then halt. The requested total time is polynomial in the combined binary lengths of the input and the required vertex list. Degeneracy, exponentially many bases per vertex and infeasible arrangement intersections obstruct straightforward enumeration strategies. An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility of the full uniform algorithm in Lean.

title: FPRAS for counting undirected Euler tours
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved approximate-counting problem for natural graph traversals, distinct from the tractable approximation of Eulerian orientations.
formal:
Does the number of Euler tours of an arbitrary connected Eulerian undirected graph admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Using the labelled-edge, fixed-first-traversal normalization below, let \(Z(G)\) be the tour count. The question is whether there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,a>0\) such that, for every allowed graph \(G\) and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) in at most \(C(N+q+1)^a\) bit operations on every random tape and
\[\Pr\!\left[\left|\widehat Z-Z(G)\right|\le\frac{Z(G)}q\right]\ge\frac34.\]
Here \(N\) is the input encoding length and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits. The constants are independent of the graph and accuracy. There is no degree bound, planarity promise or prescribed sampling chain.
definitions:
A graph has labelled vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and labelled edges \(E=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. Parallel edges are permitted and remain distinct by their labels; there are no loops. The graph is promised connected, and every vertex has even degree, counting parallel edges with their multiplicities. The input explicitly lists every edge, rather than encoding a multiplicity by a large binary number. One encoding uses unary \(n\), self-delimiting binary \(m\), the endpoint pair of each edge in label order, and self-delimiting binary \(q\). Graphs are unweighted.

If \(m>0\), write the endpoints of edge 1 as \(a_1<b_1\). Define \(Z(G)\) to be the number of sequences
\[v_0,e_1,v_1,e_2,v_2,\ldots,e_m,v_m\]
such that \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) is a permutation of all edge labels, \(e_1=1\), \(v_0=a_1\), \(v_1=b_1\), \(v_m=v_0\), and edge \(e_i\) joins \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\) for every \(i\). Vertices may be revisited; edges may not. This fixes the starting point and traversal direction by the first labelled edge. It counts one representative of each closed tour modulo cyclic rotation and reversal, while retaining vertex and edge labels. No quotient by graph automorphisms is taken. For the single-vertex graph with no edges, put \(Z(G)=1\), counting the empty tour.

The allowed nonempty graphs have Euler tours. Allowing explicit parallel edges is compatible with the usual simple-graph formulation: replacing each labelled edge by a path through its own new degree-two vertex preserves the tour count under the corresponding first-edge convention and increases the input size only polynomially. Thus this representation choice does not demand a different approximation complexity.

The output is a pair of binary integers specifying a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. Its writing and all arithmetic are charged in the standard multitape Turing model; neither large integers nor rational operations have unit cost. All choices of random bits terminate within the stated bound. A bad random tape may give an inaccurate estimate, but the displayed success probability holds separately for every graph and accuracy input.

The accuracy \(1/q\) is relative to the count. It covers arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). Runtime is polynomial in \(q\), not merely polynomial in graph size for each fixed accuracy. The fixed success threshold \(3/4\) is the convention inherited from the card. No particular estimator, Markov chain or proof technique is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm meeting all displayed guarantees, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must approximate the normalized tour count on every allowed Eulerian graph in fully polynomial time. An exact-counting hardness theorem alone does not refute an FPRAS. Counting balanced orientations, solving a fixed-degree or fixed-grid-width subcase, or proving convergence of a sampler without a fully polynomial approximation guarantee is insufficient.
context:
Cryan’s 2024 abstract says that an FPRAS remains unknown even for undirected 4-regular graphs. It discusses rapid mixing for a particular two-row toroidal-grid chain, a restricted graph family. The full card asks for an algorithm on arbitrary Eulerian graphs.

Ge and Štefankovič explicitly state the general-graph FPRAS question. Their exact-counting results include hardness on planar 4-regular graphs, but exact hardness is not an approximation lower bound. Their introduction carefully separates exact reductions from approximation-preserving reductions.

The same paper gives an approximation-preserving reduction to counting A-trails in 4-regular maps. Such a map supplies a cyclic order of incident edges, and an A-trail requires consecutive traversed edges to be adjacent in that order. That additional model is distinct from ordinary tours on a 4-regular graph and is not silently substituted into this question.

An Eulerian orientation assigns one direction to each edge so that indegree equals outdegree at every vertex. The cited sampling notes prove an FPRAS for these orientations. An orientation records edge directions but not their traversal order, so its count is a different target from the number of tours.
why: Euler tours are elementary graph traversals whose existence is easy to decide, yet approximate enumeration remains a major counting question. A solution would clarify how much harder it is to impose one globally connected traversal than to satisfy local balance constraints on edge directions. This is a test case for the reach of randomized approximate counting beyond problems with tractable orientation or matching formulations.

A bounded later-work search found no FPRAS or matching impossibility result for general undirected Euler tours. Orientation and hypergraph results were not treated as solutions. Source-open status is limited to these checked sources and searches.

working_summary: An Euler tour traverses every edge of an undirected graph exactly once and returns to its start. This question asks whether the number of such tours can be approximated by a randomized algorithm in fully polynomial time. The count uses labelled edges and a fixed first traversal to remove rotation and reversal ambiguity. The accuracy is multiplicative, and the success probability must be at least three quarters on every input. Known orientation-counting algorithms and restricted graph results do not resolve the general tour-counting question.

title: FP = #P from \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\)
importance_reason: This isolates whether exact counting has computational power beyond NP decision even under a complete decision collapse, a central relation among uniform complexity classes.
formal:
Does the following implication hold for ordinary uniform Turing computation?
\[\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}.\]
The conclusion means exact deterministic polynomial-time computation of every polynomially verifiable witness count, output as a binary nonnegative integer. Since \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm P\) holds unconditionally, the conclusion is also written \(\#\mathrm P=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\).
question_excerpt: Would P = NP imply polynomial-time exact computation of every #P function?
definitions:
All language inputs are finite binary strings, of bit length \(n=|x|\). A deterministic polynomial-time machine has a finite program and halts on every input within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps of a multitape Turing machine, for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Each tape read, write and head move is charged; writing an output is part of the bound. There is no advice, randomness or oracle. The program and constants may depend on the fixed problem, but not on the input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm P\) when such a machine outputs its exact membership bit.

For a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients and a deterministic verifier \(V(x,y)\) running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), put
\[W_{V,p}(x)=\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\},\qquad f_{V,p}(x)=|W_{V,p}(x)|.\]
The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages \(\{x:W_{V,p}(x)\ne\varnothing\}\). The class \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of the total numerical functions \(f_{V,p}\). The verifier is required to halt on every pair of binary strings. Witnesses have exactly the specified length; each distinct witness string contributes one, even when several describe the same object. The hypothesis \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) asserts equality of these language classes, with a separate polynomial-time decider permitted for each language.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) computed by deterministic polynomial-time machines under the same bit-cost convention. The output is the exact binary integer, with 0 represented by a single zero and no leading zeros for positive integers. Every \(\#\mathrm P\) function satisfies \(f_{V,p}(x)\leq2^{p(n)}\), so polynomially many output bits suffice. Conversely, a polynomial-time numerical function is in \(\#\mathrm P\): choose a fixed polynomial witness length longer than its output bound, regard witnesses as binary integers, and accept exactly those smaller than its value. This explains the numerical FP equality convention in the source.

In the conclusion the quantifiers are \(\forall V,p\ \exists M,C,d\ \forall x\): one exact counting program for every fixed witness-counting function. No common exponent or effective transformation from arbitrary existence deciders to counting machines is required. The proposition is an implication about these unrelativized classes. It does not assert that P = NP actually holds, introduce access to a SAT oracle, or restrict the algorithms to a specified proof technique.

The logical negation of the target is \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) together with \(\#\mathrm P\not\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). In particular, a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would prove the implication through its false antecedent, not refute it. Here and below exact computation differs from relative approximation: an approximation \(a\) with parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1\) need only satisfy \(|a-f(x)|\leq\varepsilon f(x)\), which forces \(a=0\) when the count is zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication, or of its logical negation. A direct affirmative proof may assume \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) and derive an exact deterministic polynomial-time counting machine for every fixed verifier; a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) also settles the literal implication affirmatively. A negative answer must establish both \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) and a \(\#\mathrm P\) function outside numerical FP. An oracle-relative counterexample, a limitation of one proposed reduction, or an error in a claimed affirmative proof does not establish that negation. Approximation, finding a single witness and time polynomial in the numerical count do not meet the exact-computation conclusion.
context:
The known reverse implication is immediate: an exact count decides whether a witness exists by testing whether the value is positive. This card asks whether decision tractability forces counting tractability as well. It is separate from the unconditional question whether all counting functions are already efficiently computable.

Under P = NP, one can find a witness by fixing its bits successively and testing whether each chosen prefix still extends to an accepted witness. The number of prefix queries is polynomial. Running that process for every witness can still require exponential time, because polynomial-time verification allows exponentially many witnesses.

A tempting binary search asks whether \(f(x)\geq k\), with \(k\) encoded in binary. Listing \(k\) distinct witnesses certifies the threshold only at a cost proportional to \(k\), which can be exponential in the input length. Therefore this certificate does not place all binary-threshold questions in NP. An efficient threshold procedure would recover the count with polynomially many comparisons, but P = NP alone does not supply that procedure.

The source and Aaronson’s survey record a substantial weaker consequence: P = NP gives polynomial-time relative approximation at every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy. Such accuracy need not distinguish adjacent exponential-size counts. Requesting exponentially small relative error can destroy a running-time guarantee polynomial in inverse accuracy, so this known result does not settle exact computation.

The stronger hypothesis P = PSPACE suffices for exact counting. Here PSPACE means decision problems solvable with polynomial working space: exhaustive counting stores a witness and a binary counter of polynomial length, and individual output-bit questions use only polynomial space. The source explicitly separates this implication from the P = NP question.

A March 2026 preprint claims the affirmative implication. A direct editorial check finds an internal obstruction: §2.4 defines \(S(F)\) using precisely the satisfying assignments of a formula, so an unsatisfiable formula gives the empty complex and has \(\beta_2(S(F))=0\), where the second Betti number is the dimension of second homology. Yet §3.2 uses unsatisfiable instances in a family with \(\beta_2=2^{\Omega(N)}>0\). That step cannot hold under the stated definition. This identifies a defect in the presented argument; it neither disproves the implication nor substitutes for a community assessment of the preprint.
why: The implication isolates the computational gap between learning that solutions exist and determining their exact number. A proof from the decision-collapse hypothesis would connect two central forms of computational tractability, while a negative answer would show that exact counting can remain hard even after all NP existence problems become easy.
status_note: The checked 2007 draft and 2017 author survey explicitly treat the implication as unresolved. Alasli’s 23 March 2026 v1 claims a positive proof. A direct editorial check on 16 September 2026 finds that its §3.2 uses unsatisfiable formulas with positive second Betti number, incompatible with the solution-complex definition in §2.4. The claim is therefore not accepted as establishing resolution here; this observation does not refute the mathematical conclusion. No independent validation or exhaustive current-status certification is claimed, so status remains uncertain.

The local September 2026 check records a contradictory use of unsatisfiable instances and positive homology in its main argument, so this card does not accept the claim as a resolution.

working_summary: The question asks whether P = NP forces exact polynomial-time computation of every #P witness count. Each counting function has its own uniform deterministic machine, and its exact value must be output in binary. Finding one witness or approximating an exponential count to inverse-polynomial relative accuracy does not give its exact value. The literal negative answer would require P = NP together with a counting function outside numerical FP. A 2026 preprint claims the implication, but a directly checked internal defect prevents this review from accepting it as a resolution.

title: Output-polynomial hypergraph transversal enumeration
importance_reason: A central longstanding enumeration problem and a reference point for the complexity of many other complete-output tasks.
formal: Do a deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph \(H\), \(A\) outputs every inclusion-minimal transversal exactly once and terminates within \(C(L(H)+L_{\mathrm{out}}(H)+1)^c\) bit steps?
definitions: \(H=([n],E), n\ge 0\), is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges \(e\subseteq [n]\), each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. \(\mathrm{L}(H)\) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq [n]\) intersecting every \(e\in E\); it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for \(T=\varnothing\). If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is \(\varnothing\). If E contains \(\varnothing\), there is no transversal and \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}=0\). Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

The target imposes no polynomial-delay or polynomial-space bound. A lower bound for one enumeration algorithm does not establish nonexistence of all algorithms.
context:
