working_summary: The input asks how many homomorphisms map a source structure A from a fixed class C into an arbitrary target structure B. The conjecture says a fixed-parameter randomized approximation scheme exists exactly when C has bounded Gaifman treewidth. Relation arity is uniformly bounded, C is recursively enumerable, and the parameter is the size of A. The source proves this under a further fan-class condition and asks to remove it. The 2020 journal version retains that restriction, so exact-counting and fixed-target classifications do not settle the missing approximation direction.

title: Decision versus approximate counting for fixed-width SAT
importance_reason: A fundamental decision-versus-counting comparison in fine-grained satisfiability, isolating the cost of multiplicative estimation at fixed clause width. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed clause width \(k\geq3\), do randomized decision \(k\)-SAT and randomized multiplicative approximation of \(\#k\)-SAT have the same optimal exponential running-time rate in the number of variables? With \(d_k\) and \(a_k\) defined below, the target is \(a_k=d_k\) for every fixed \(k\geq3\). This makes “close the gap” precise at the exponential-rate level, as in the later source’s fixed-width question.
definitions:
An input is a Boolean CNF formula \(F\) on an explicitly declared set of \(n\) variables, with at most \(k\) literals in each clause. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(N(F)\) be the number of assignments to all declared variables satisfying every clause. Variables absent from clauses still contribute their two possible values. There is no promise of satisfiability or sparsity.

Decision asks whether \(N(F)>0\). Approximate counting receives a rational accuracy parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and must output a nonnegative binary-encoded rational \(Z\) such that
\[
(1-\varepsilon)N(F)\leq Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)N(F)
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. When \(N(F)=0\), a successful output is exactly zero. Probability is over algorithmic randomness. Decision also has success probability at least \(2/3\), allowing two-sided error.

Use ordinary classical randomized algorithms and worst-case bit-operation running time, over both inputs and random tapes. Let \(L\) be total input bit length, including the formula and, for approximate counting, the rational accuracy. Define \(d_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which decision has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}L^C)\) for some fixed \(C\). Define \(a_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which an approximation scheme has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}(L+\varepsilon^{-1})^C)\) for some fixed \(C\), for every admissible accuracy. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and hidden constants may depend on the fixed \(k\) and \(\alpha\), but not on the input or accuracy.

The infima need not be attained. Equality asks that every exponential decision rate can be matched for approximation with any arbitrarily small positive addition to that rate and polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy. It does not demand a single optimal algorithm at an unattained infimum, identical polynomial factors, or an effective compiler transforming all decision programs.

Already \(d_k\leq a_k\): a constant-relative-error estimate distinguishes zero from a positive count. The unresolved direction compares approximation with decision at the same fixed clause width. Taking a supremum or a limit over all widths is a different statement. A reduction whose decision queries add parity constraints or increase clause width must account for their cost before it can establish this comparison. The source uses an \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplicative convention; changing to the displayed relative-error convention only rescales accuracy by constant factors in this range.
answer_criterion: Prove equality of the two defined infimum rates for every fixed integer width at least three, or prove a strict separation for at least one such width. A reduction preserving the width and adding arbitrarily small exponential overhead would suffice for equality. Improved individual upper bounds, a result only as width tends to infinity, or hardness for exact counting alone does not settle this comparison.
context:
Thurley obtains a randomized approximation scheme substantially faster than the exact counting bounds cited in 2012. Schmitt and Wanka later improve the three-literal upper bound to \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}1.51426^n)\). These are historical upper bounds, not claims about the optimal rates or the latest decision record.

Dell and Lapinskas show that a common exponential saving for decision at every constant width transfers to approximate counting with arbitrarily small loss. Their Theorem 8 therefore matches the all-width saving, but its hypothesis is stronger than having a fast algorithm at one selected width.

The full journal version explicitly leaves the fixed-width exponential comparison open. Its main SAT reduction uses a decision problem with sparse parity constraints; encoding those constraints into CNF may require larger width. It also relates subexponential decision and approximation, without settling each fixed positive exponential rate.
why: Tests whether estimating the number of satisfying assignments intrinsically requires more exponential work than finding out whether any exist. Equality would transfer the leading exponential savings in fixed-width SAT to a broader counting task.
status_note: Read the original approximation convention and question, the 2013 authors’ reported improvement, and the full November 2020 author version of the 2021 journal paper, especially its explicit fixed-width question and Theorem 13. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The chosen target is equality of infimum exponential rates with polynomial accuracy cost, not a requirement of polynomial-overhead reduction or identical lower-order running time.
progress: 2012: The source asks whether the exponential gap between approximate counting and decision can be closed. | 2013: An improved approximation scheme lowers the known counting upper bounds without matching the decision bounds. | 2021: The journal reduction preserves common all-width savings and states that the fixed-width comparison remains open.
working_summary: A fixed-width CNF formula has a finite number of satisfying assignments. Decision tests whether that number is positive; approximation estimates it to relative error. The question asks whether the optimal exponential rates in the variable count coincide for each fixed width. Polynomial accuracy costs and arbitrarily small losses in the exponential rate are allowed. Later all-width and subexponential equivalences do not settle this fixed-width comparison.

title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.
focus_reason: A central unresolved graph decision problem whose polynomial-time complexity remains a foundational algorithmic target.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.
why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.
status_note: Neuen’s survey, published online 5 February 2026, explicitly retains the unrestricted polynomial-time problem as open. The author correction and both consolidated primary-source passages were checked. Targeted subsequent searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified general polynomial-time result; this bounded search and formulation audit do not independently verify every cited proof.

The available arXiv versions predate the later correction. | 2017-01-09: Babai reports a replacement for the recursive call whose analysis had invalidated the original runtime claim, restoring quasipolynomial time. Its newer upper bounds concern specified graph parameters.
working_summary: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite simple graphs agree after a bijective relabeling of their vertices. The target is a single deterministic algorithm that answers correctly on every explicitly encoded pair in polynomial time. A proposed relabeling is easy to verify, while ruling out all relabelings can require substantially more structure. The checked general upper bound is quasipolynomial, and efficient algorithms for restricted graph classes do not establish the unrestricted polynomial bound. A resolution would settle a central structural comparison problem whose position between P and NP-completeness remains unresolved.

title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
importance_reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.
focus_reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
question_excerpt: The inherited card selects the classical uniform sequential comparison question: all connected simple graphs, arbitrary opaque real weights and deterministic worst-case O(n+m) total time. Karger–Klein–Tarjan explicitly distinguish this weight-access model from the integer representation model, and Pettie–Ramachandran distinguish optimal comparison complexity from a known linear time bound. The review specifies the exact machine instructions, output, constants and complete Lean criterion while preserving the target, category and importance.
definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.
why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No matching deterministic worst-case linear-time comparison-RAM result was found in the bounded primary-source search. The May 2026 pseudorandomness manuscript explicitly treats MST as motivation and does not improve the known deterministic frontier. Integer-weight access, randomized expectation, high-girth restrictions, unknown optimal decision-tree complexity and distributed message bounds do not settle this card. Source limitations and inspected locators are recorded; external proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1994: Fredman–Willard obtain deterministic linear time in a stronger integer-word model. | 1995: Karger–Klein–Tarjan obtain randomized linear time for arbitrary comparison weights. | 2000: Chazelle achieves deterministic \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) comparison-based time. | 2002: Pettie–Ramachandran match the optimal decision-tree complexity with a uniform deterministic algorithm, without determining that complexity. | 2008: Pettie–Ramachandran develop alternative randomized MST algorithms using far fewer random bits; complete deterministic linear time remains unresolved. | 2026-05-17: Doron and coauthors discuss MST in a pseudorandomness framework, explicitly distinguishing this illustration from an improved deterministic MST running-time bound.
working_summary: The problem asks for an exact minimum spanning tree of every connected simple undirected graph with arbitrary real edge weights. The target is one uniform deterministic sequential algorithm whose worst-case total running time is linear in the explicitly listed vertices and edges. Weights are opaque comparison keys, while ordinary logarithmic-word computation, preprocessing and writing the output are all charged. A complete Lean proof must establish every correctness and running-time guarantee or rule out all correct algorithms in this model. Randomized linear time, integer-weight algorithms and uniform decision-tree optimality are known, but the checked 2026 literature does not settle deterministic linear time for arbitrary comparison weights.

title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
importance_reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
question_excerpt: The inherited question asks for almost-linear exact maximum-cardinality matching on arbitrary explicitly represented simple undirected graphs. It already permits randomized success probability two thirds, expected running time, almost-sure termination and feasible output on every terminating run. These conventions are retained. The review specifies the word operations, graph/output encoding, isolated-vertex cost and same-program quantifier order. The 2024 implementation source distinguishes this general-graph frontier from the almost-linear bipartite consequence of flow algorithms.
definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.
context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.
why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No valid almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the bounded primary-source search. The June catalytic result gives a different polynomial-time/space guarantee; almost-linear flow applies to the bipartite consequence, and fixed-accuracy matching is weaker than exact optimality. The old Glauber-dynamics O(m log² n) claim is expressly invalidated by the authors in the current arXiv record. The retained target allows bounded-error randomization and expected word-RAM time; external proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1980: Micali–Vazirani obtain the classical \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound, plus input reading for explicitly listed isolated vertices; later work supplies a full correctness theory. | 2004: Mucha–Sankowski construct maximum matchings using fast algebraic operations. | 2011-08-17: The authors of the Glauber-dynamics preprint acknowledge an incorrect coupling; its claimed almost-linear maximum-matching result does not hold. | 2011: Duan–Pettie–Su obtain linear-time approximation for each fixed accuracy parameter in general weighted graphs. | 2022: Chen and coauthors achieve almost-linear exact flow algorithms, giving the corresponding bipartite matching consequence. | 2024-09-23: Ansaripour–Danaei–Mehlhorn publish a detailed implementation and experimental study of Gabow’s general matching algorithm. | 2026-06-01: The catalytic-logspace revision constructs general maximum matchings with a polynomial-time bound, a different resource guarantee.
working_summary: Maximum-cardinality matching selects as many pairwise vertex-disjoint edges as possible in an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph. The target is one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that constructs an optimum matching with probability at least two thirds on every input. It must halt almost surely, always return a valid matching when it halts, and have expected time within every fixed positive exponent slack above the full explicit input size. A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm and all these guarantees or rule out every permitted randomized program with this expected-time behavior. Known almost-linear bipartite algorithms, approximation schemes and catalytic-space results do not settle the general exact target, and the older Glauber-dynamics claim has an acknowledged error.

title: Optimal bounds in the Excluded Grid Theorem
importance_reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.
formal:
For every integer \(r\ge2\), define
\[f(r)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\ \forall\text{ finite simple undirected graphs }G,\ \operatorname{tw}(G)\ge t\ \Longrightarrow\ Q_r\text{ is a minor of }G\},\]
where \(Q_r\) is the square grid of side length \(r\). Determine the asymptotic order of \(f(r)\) up to universal constant factors, including all logarithmic or other unbounded factors. In particular, supply an independently specified positive function \(h\) and prove
\[\exists a,b>0\ \exists r_0\ge2\ \forall r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge r_0}:\quad a\,h(r)\le f(r)\le b\,h(r).\]
The constants and the threshold \(r_0\) are independent of the host graph and of \(r\). The problem asks for the actual asymptotic order; it does not assume a quadratic or cubic conjectured answer.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96 and determination of the all-graphs excluded-grid threshold up to universal constant factors, including logarithmic dependence. The parameter is grid side length, not its vertex count. The threshold convention tw(G)≥f(r) is equivalent to one plus the maximum treewidth among excluding graphs. The 2016 paper uses the inverse parameterization, guaranteed side length from treewidth; its bounds are translated accordingly. No polynomial-time construction requirement is added.
definitions:
Graphs and grids. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; there are no loops or parallel edges. The vertex set of \(Q_r\) is \(\{1,\ldots,r\}^2\), and two vertices \((i,j)\) and \((i',j')\) are adjacent exactly when
\[|i-i'|+|j-j'|=1.\]
Thus \(r\) counts the side length, while the grid has \(r^2\) vertices. Host graphs may be disconnected and have arbitrary order, degree and genus.

Minor containment. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if there are nonempty vertex subsets \((B_v)_{v\in V(H)}\) of \(V(G)\) such that they are pairwise disjoint, each induced graph \(G[B_v]\) is connected, and for every edge \(uv\in E(H)\) an edge of \(G\) joins \(B_u\) to \(B_v\). These subsets are called branch sets. Extra edges inside or between branch sets are allowed. Equivalently, one may delete vertices and edges and contract edges, then remove loops and merge parallel edges. This is ordinary minor containment, with no prescribed roots, induced-subgraph condition or topological-minor requirement.

Treewidth. A tree decomposition of \(G\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and bags \(X_t\subseteq V(G)\) for its nodes such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of every edge lie together in a bag, and for each vertex the nodes whose bags contain it form a nonempty connected subtree of \(T\). A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. The decomposition width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|X_t|-1\). The treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions. In particular, the empty graph has treewidth \(-1\) under this convention and has no effect on thresholds \(t\ge0\).

Extremal threshold. The qualitative Grid-Minor Theorem ensures that the defining set of thresholds is nonempty. Since treewidth is integer valued,
\[f(r)=1+\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G):G\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph with no }Q_r\text{ minor}\}.\]
This maximum exists: its set of integer values is nonempty and bounded above by the qualitative theorem. It is a maximum of widths, not a bound on the number of vertices of a grid-excluding graph. Arbitrarily large trees, for example, do not contain \(Q_r\) for \(r\ge2\).

Asymptotic convention. The domain of \(h\) is the integers \(r\ge2\), with values in \(\mathbb R_{>0}\). Bounds must hold at every sufficiently large integer side length. Write \(\log r=\log_2 r\); another fixed logarithm base only changes constant factors. The notation \(\operatorname{polylog}r\) in known bounds denotes \((\log r)^c\) for some fixed nonnegative constant \(c\). It may be suppressed when stating historical progress, but not when claiming matching bounds for this target. This is an extremal existence question, with no algorithm, input encoding, grid-finding time or random-error guarantee imposed on an answer.
answer_criterion:
Give an explicit asymptotic description \(h\) and complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that there are constants \(a,b>0\) and an integer \(r_0\ge2\) for which \(a h(r)\le f(r)\le b h(r)\) at every integer \(r\ge r_0\). The upper bound must apply to all finite simple undirected host graphs; the lower bound must establish grid-excluding graphs with sufficiently large treewidth to give the matching order. No efficient construction of these graphs or of grid models is required.

The description must determine the growth rate rather than rename the defining minimum or maximum. A residual factor that tends to infinity, even a logarithm, fails the constant-factor criterion. Improving only the polynomial exponent, proving a bound with unspecified logarithmic loss, obtaining the result only on planar or fixed-minor-free host graphs, or replacing ordinary minors by another containment relation is insufficient. The numerical tolerance used elsewhere in the atlas is not an additive tolerance on asymptotic notation. A conditional estimate qualifies only if the additional assumption is also proved.
context:
Treewidth records the smallest possible largest bag in a tree decomposition, minus one. Many graph algorithms can process small bags efficiently even when the whole graph is large. A grid is a canonical obstruction to small treewidth. The qualitative theorem says that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed grid as a minor; the unresolved issue is the optimal dependence on grid size.

The grid \(Q_r\) itself has treewidth \(r\), but this does not imply a linear threshold for arbitrary host graphs. The complete graph on \(r^2-1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^2-2\), yet cannot contain a minor with \(r^2\) vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^2-1\). Branch sets can contract large parts of a host, but they must remain pairwise disjoint and nonempty.

The established lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega(r^2\log r)\). The cited work attributes it to Robertson, Seymour and Thomas using constant-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs combine treewidth proportional to their order with long shortest cycles; a large grid minor forces many disjoint cycles in the host. The extra logarithmic obstruction survives even for sparse graphs.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy first made the relationship polynomial. Their theorem is stated in the reverse direction: treewidth \(k\) guarantees grid side length at least a constant times \(k^{1/98}\) divided by a fixed power of \(\log k\). Equivalently, it gives an upper bound \(f(r)=O(r^{98}\operatorname{polylog}r)\). Confusing side length with vertex count, or the threshold with this inverse guarantee, changes the exponents.

That first polynomial result is constructive and gives a randomized polynomial-time procedure for finding a grid model at its guaranteed scale. The present question asks for the best existence threshold. An improved structural bound would answer the mathematical upper-bound side even without a matching grid-finding algorithm; algorithmic guarantees must be assessed separately.

Chuzhoy and Tan prove \(f(r)\le C r^9(\log r)^c\) for absolute constants \(C,c>0\). The 2026 revised product-structure paper and the SODA 2026 fixed-minor paper still cite this general quantitative result. It remains far above the quadratic-logarithmic lower bound. Knowing the leading polynomial exponent alone would also leave the card unfinished if an unbounded logarithmic gap remained.

The literature records different predictions. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas conjectured that the \(r^2\log r\) lower bound is tight, whereas Demaine and coauthors conjectured cubic growth. The target here is the true asymptotic order. Even an upper bound of the form \(r^2\) times an unspecified power of \(\log r\) would not by itself establish the required matching constant-factor characterization.

The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a finer structural description: graphs excluding a fixed planar graph embed as subgraphs of clique blow-ups of graphs of controlled treewidth. A clique blow-up replaces each vertex by a fixed-size complete graph and every original edge by all edges between the corresponding cliques. The factor controlling the clique size may depend on the excluded graph, so the theorem does not determine this card’s optimal numerical dependence on grid side length.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs proves that excluding both a fixed graph \(H\) and \(Q_r\) gives treewidth \(O(g_H r+t^{2304})\), where \(t=|V(H)|\) and \(g_H\) is the Euler genus of \(H\). Euler genus is the minimum value \(2-\chi\) of a closed connected surface admitting an embedding, with \(\chi\) its Euler characteristic. Since \(g_H=O(t^2)\), the paper also gives \(O(t^2r+t^{2304})\). For fixed \(H\), the dependence on \(r\) is linear.

The additional exclusion in that theorem matters. General host graphs do not avoid a common fixed \(H\). Choosing \(H=Q_r\) is allowed for a grid-excluding graph, but then \(H\) varies with \(r\) and \(t=r^2\); it cannot yield a linear universal threshold. This distinction prevents a sharp special-class result from being mistaken for a solution of the all-graphs problem.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies a designated set of vertices and grid models whose every branch set meets that set. It obtains polynomial bounds for the corresponding structural decomposition. Those bounds concern an annotated generalization and are not a matching estimate of the ordinary threshold defined here. Additional structure in a decomposition and an optimal numerical treewidth bound are different conclusions.

The May 2026 disjoint-paths preprint sharpens bounds for vital linkages and for vertices whose deletion preserves bounded-size rooted-minor information. Its parameters include the number of terminals and the size of a grid rooted on an annotated set. Despite the phrase “Optimal Bounds” in the title, its theorems do not claim a constant-factor characterization of the unrestricted excluded-grid threshold.

Sharper general grid bounds affect the quantitative consequences of routing, packing-versus-covering results and parameterized algorithms. Their role is to turn sufficiently large treewidth into a usable grid, or to bound treewidth when such a grid is absent. Matching lower bounds would also identify an unavoidable limitation of that structural implication.
why: The Grid-Minor Theorem connects an abstract measure of graph connectivity with a concrete planar pattern. Its quantitative loss controls the strength of many structural and parameterized-algorithm results. Determining the optimal loss would identify how much treewidth is inherently needed to force a grid in unrestricted graphs, including whether the remaining logarithmic obstruction captures the whole difficulty.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected primary literature supports the general bounds \(\Omega(r^2\log r)\) and \(O(r^9\operatorname{polylog}r)\). The June 2026 revision of the product-structure paper still cites the latter general bound. The SODA 2026 fixed-minor result, ICALP 2026 annotated result and May 2026 linkage preprint have different additional promises or targets; none inspected supplies matching bounds for f(r). No general resolution was found in the bounded later-work search. This review checked theorem statements and their scope, without independently verifying the long proofs.

working_summary: The excluded-grid threshold is the least treewidth that forces a square grid of a specified side length in every finite simple undirected graph. The question asks for its true asymptotic order up to universal constant factors, including logarithmic dependence. A complete answer needs a universal grid-forcing bound and grid-excluding examples of matching treewidth, certified in Lean. The known quadratic-logarithmic lower bound and exponent-nine upper bound leave a large gap in this fundamental structural theorem. Recent product-structure, fixed-minor, annotated-grid and disjoint-paths results refine related questions while leaving the all-graphs target open.

title: Almost-linear triangle detection
importance_reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.
formal: Does one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm exist that, for every finite simple undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges given by explicit adjacency lists, returns whether a triangle exists with probability at least \(2/3\), while every execution takes at most \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) word instructions? The running-time guarantee must cover all graph densities, all valid adjacency-list orders and every random tape.
question_excerpt: Abboud and Vassilevska Williams ask about linear-time triangle detection and state Conjecture 4 as a positive power lower bound in the number of edges on a logarithmic-word RAM. This card retains the existing precise positive target of a single almost-linear algorithm, charges isolated-vertex input explicitly, and fixes worst-case time over its random tapes. Its negation is not identified with the source’s stronger common-exponent lower-bound conjecture.
definitions:
Let \(n\ge0\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \(V\). Set \(m=|E|\). There are no loops or multiple edges. A triangle is a set \(\{u,v,z\}\) of three distinct vertices for which all three pairs are edges. The output is YES exactly when such a set exists, and NO otherwise; the algorithm need not output a witness or list triangles.

The input supplies \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) list offsets, and a contiguous array of \(2m\) vertex labels. The segment for vertex \(v\) contains precisely its neighbors, in an arbitrary order. Each undirected edge occurs once in each endpoint's list. Validity of this representation is promised. Vertex labels, counts and offsets occupy single words. Thus the input occupies \(O(n+m+1)\) words. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed; graphs with fewer than three vertices are legitimate NO-instances.

The word length is
\[
 w=\left\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil.
\]
Memory consists of addressable \(w\)-bit words; addresses are unsigned words. Input is initially stored in its specified arrays, and other memory is initially zero. A fixed finite program may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare unsigned words, branch, perform bitwise Boolean operations, shift logically, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or take the integer quotient and remainder of unsigned division by a nonzero word, at unit cost per instruction. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. It may also obtain one independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word in one instruction. Longer integers and algebraic operations must be implemented using these instructions. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, matrix-product oracle, input-dependent advice or free precomputed table. All input access and preprocessing count toward time. The fixed word length permits the explicit graph representation at every \(n\).

Precisely, set \(S=n+m+2\). The algorithm must halt on every valid graph and every random tape. For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an integer \(S_\varepsilon\) such that, on every valid input with \(S\ge S_\varepsilon\), every execution uses at most \(S^{1+\varepsilon}\) instructions. The same program works for every \(\varepsilon\); it does not receive \(\varepsilon\) as input. This convention absorbs fixed multiplicative constants and defines the displayed almost-linear bound. Thresholds may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, its list order or the random tape.

For each fixed input separately, the probability over internal random words of a correct YES/NO output must be at least \(2/3\). There is no average-case input distribution, degree bound, forbidden-subgraph promise, triangle-count promise or restriction to combinatorial methods. Algebraic algorithms are allowed with their actual implementation cost. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of an algorithm satisfying the exact uniformity, word model, all-input time and per-input probability guarantees; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in this model.

A bound with any fixed exponent greater than one is insufficient. A quadratic bound in \(n\) alone need not be almost linear on sparse inputs. Restricted graph classes, counting or listing results, average-case guarantees, and conditional lower bounds do not settle the target by themselves. An expected-time or high-probability-time result needs a proved conversion to the stated all-tapes bound and success guarantee. A separate program for each exponent slack requires a justified uniform combination. The negation of this target need not supply one common positive exponent gap against every algorithm. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to the decision.
context:
The output is only one bit. The large number of triangles in a dense graph therefore creates no output-size lower bound for this question. Correctly rejecting graphs with no triangle remains part of the requirement.

The classical sparse bound has exponent \(2\tau/(\tau+1)\) in the edge count for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), plus input reading. This is an upper bound, not a proof that a better unrestricted algorithm is impossible.

Arboricity-sensitive listing takes \(O(m\,a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests covering the edges. Bounded arboricity gives useful special cases but is not promised here.

The 2026 weighted improvement and restricted-graph dichotomies answer related questions. They do not supply the required almost-linear algorithm on every explicit graph.

The local-sketching preprint claims \(O(m\log^2 n)\) time and high-probability correctness. Its displayed amplification step in §7 equates \(\exp(-\theta c_G/c_T)\), for positive absolute constants, with \(n^{-\Omega(1)}\). The former is constant, so that inference does not establish the stated decay. This limited check is not a proof that no repair is possible; the claim remains unverified here.

The 2024 combinatorial proposal was withdrawn after an invalid case analysis was identified. It is not an established upper bound.

The older parent-edge rule fails on the path \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6\) with added edges \(\{0,3\},\{3,6\},\{0,6\}\). Its only triangle uses none of the path’s DFS tree edges. This counterexample concerns the stated 2025 rule, not every subsequent implementation.

The replacement posted on 14 September 2026 claims an expected \(O(n^{2.5}\log n)\) dense bound with separate sparse processing. Even a verified result at that bound would not provide the target all-density almost-linear guarantee; its proof was not independently certified.
why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.
status_note: Current status is uncertain: Duan–Zhang arXiv:2509.03215v1 claims a directly relevant near-linear high-probability algorithm, but the displayed amplification inference in §7 does not establish its claimed decaying error and no full proof or corrected implementation has been verified here. The old parent-edge proposal has a checked counterexample, the 2024 proposal is withdrawn, and the September 2026 Aegypti replacement has a different claimed bound. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 do not justify either declaring a resolution or asserting unqualified present openness.

working_summary: The input is an explicit undirected graph, and the output says whether three distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. One fixed randomized program must work on every graph and every adjacency-list order. Every execution must take almost linear time in the number of vertices plus edges, with a correct answer on each input with probability at least two thirds. A relevant local-sketching preprint remains unverified, so the card records current status as uncertain. A complete Lean-checked answer must supply this algorithm and its guarantees or prove that none exists in the specified model.

title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
importance_reason: A central static graph optimization primitive with broad algorithmic consequences. The precise remaining overhead separates the established almost-linear breakthrough from the longstanding nearly linear target; this is a general problem rather than a refinement of one fixed algorithm.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_a\), integers \(B_a\ge a+3\), \(k_a\ge0\) and \(C_a\ge1\) with the following property? On every explicitly represented directed graph \(G\) with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integer arc capacities
\[0\le u_e\le n^a,\]
the algorithm uses words of \(w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, halts on every random execution within
\[C_a(m+n)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{k_a}\]
word operations, and outputs an exact integral maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with probability at least \(2/3\)?
The output must give a flow value on every original arc. The algorithm, constants and logarithmic exponent may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its capacities, its terminal choices or its input ordering. The complete graph, flow and machine conventions are specified below.
question_excerpt: The retained target is the user-selected fixed-polylogarithmic overhead for exact directed maximum flow with capacities at most n^a, for every fixed a. The cited exact-flow papers provide almost-linear benchmarks, not statements that their subpolynomial overhead is already a fixed logarithmic power. The m+n convention, per-a word length and worst-case randomized time are explicit editorial model choices preserved from admission.
definitions:
Graph and representation. The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An ordered arc list \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) consists of distinct ordered pairs \(e_j=(x_j,y_j)\in[n]^2\) with \(x_j\ne y_j\), so \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\). Opposite arcs may both occur and have independent capacities; parallel copies of the same ordered pair and loops are excluded. The graph may be disconnected and may contain isolated vertices and zero-capacity arcs. The terminals \(s,t\in[n]\) are distinct. The input is an array of machine words containing the header \((n,m,s,t)\), the list \(1,\ldots,n\) of vertices, and the triples \((x_j,y_j,u_{e_j})\) in the given arc order. Correctness and time bounds hold for every ordering. Capacities and labels are unsigned integers, each in one word. The explicit vertex list fixes the \(m+n\) convention even when \(m=0\). There is no succinct representation, adjacency oracle or precomputed index.

Feasible flow and optimum. A flow is a list \(f=(f_{e_1},\ldots,f_{e_m})\) of integers with \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) on every arc and
\[\sum_{e=(x,v)}f_e=\sum_{e=(v,y)}f_e\qquad\text{for every }v\in[n]\setminus\{s,t\}.\]
Each sum ranges over the arcs actually present. Its value is the net flow leaving the source,
\[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{e=(s,y)}f_e-\sum_{e=(x,s)}f_e.\]
Incoming arcs at \(s\), outgoing arcs at \(t\), and circulations are allowed. Conservation implies that this equals the net flow entering \(t\). Define \(F(G,u,s,t)\) as the largest value among the feasible integral flows. The set of such flows is finite and nonempty because the all-zero list is feasible, so the maximum is attained and nonnegative. Also \(F\le(n-1)n^a\). The usual integral-flow theorem identifies this optimum with the real-valued maximum flow for integral capacities. A successful output is the list of exactly \(m\) integers in original arc order that forms a feasible flow with value \(F\). No prescribed tie-breaking between different optimal flows is required. If \(m=0\), the empty list is the correct output.

Machine model. Put \(L_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), so each word contains \(w=B_aL_n\) bits. A word stores an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The random-access machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite set of registers and word-addressed memory; input words occupy the initial array and other memory is initially zero. Each executed instruction costs one operation. Allowed instructions are word reads and writes, moves, conditional branches, comparisons, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer division with a nonzero divisor. A logical shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A memory address must fit in one word. Input, output and all memory used must fit within the address space, with \(B_a\) chosen as part of the algorithm's fixed constants. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented using these operations and charged accordingly. Exact real arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

Randomness and resources. A random-word instruction returns a fresh independent uniform element of \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\) at cost one; equivalently its bits are independent fair bits. The success probability is over this sequence for each fixed valid input. A run outside the successful event may return a failure marker or an incorrect result, but must obey the same time bound. All graph preprocessing, memory accesses, random generation and writing of output words are charged. The bound is on the total running time of every run of this one static computation, not merely on expected time or on typical executions. An amortized analysis of internal operations is permitted if it establishes this total bound. There are no oracles, quantum operations, input-dependent advice or free preprocessing. Behavior outside the stated input promises is unrestricted.

Uniformity and quantifiers. For each fixed \(a\), one finite program works for all \(n,m,G,u,s,t\); it cannot contain a table or different advice indexed by \(n\). The quantifier order is
\[\forall a\ge1\ \exists A_a,B_a,k_a,C_a\ \forall(G,u,s,t).\]
The selected target does not additionally require an effective procedure that constructs \(A_a\) from \(a\), a common logarithmic exponent for all \(a\), or a bound polynomial in \(a\). For each fixed \(a\), however, \(k_a\) is a single integer independent of input size. The explicit running-time expression is precisely the meaning of the title's \(O((m+n)\operatorname{polylog}n)\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, for each fixed capacity exponent \(a\), one program and fixed constants satisfying both the every-run time bound and the per-input success probability, including exact integral feasibility and optimality of all output arc values. A deterministic algorithm with that bound also qualifies. A negative proof must establish a fixed \(a\ge1\) for which every uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm in this model having any such fixed-polylogarithmic worst-case bound has some valid instance with success probability strictly below \(2/3\). A lower bound for one flow framework, an oracle-only algorithm, or a conditional conjecture does not prove that universal negation. A \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate flow, the optimum value alone, an algorithm for a restricted graph class, or a bound of \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) without the required fixed logarithmic overhead is insufficient. The algorithmic exact-flow requirement is retained; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace its output specification.
context:
Capacity constraints bound how much can travel along each arc, while conservation couples choices throughout the network. Exactness asks for the largest transferable amount, not merely a feasible routing. Because capacities are integral, an integral optimum exists, but the algorithm still has to find an optimal routing among many interacting possibilities.

The logarithmic overhead is the unresolved guarantee. For example, \(h(n)=2^{\sqrt{\log_2(n+2)}}\) satisfies \(h(n)=n^{o(1)}\), yet exceeds \((\log_2(n+2))^k\) for every fixed \(k\) once \(n\) is sufficiently large. Thus almost-linear and fixed-polylogarithmic time bounds are different. In this simple directed-graph format, \(n\le m+n\le n^2\), so logarithms of input word count and vertex count differ by only a constant factor.

Chen and coauthors’ 2022 breakthrough computes exact maximum flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\log U\) time with high probability for integral capacities bounded by \(U\). For \(U\le n^a\), the capacity term is logarithmic, while the subpolynomial graph-size overhead remains. Their analysis uses fixed-point quantities with polynomially many logarithmic bits; charging multiword arithmetic does not turn that overhead into a fixed logarithmic power.

The 2023 deterministic algorithm of van den Brand and coauthors also obtains exact almost-linear flow. The 2024 duality paper further improves the stated static bounds: its Theorem 6.17 gives randomized \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{3/4}\log\log m)}\) time and deterministic \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{5/6}\log\log m)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral minimum-cost flow. These are still guarantees with subpolynomial overhead, rather than the fixed logarithmic bound requested here.

Li and Wice’s August 2026 manuscript removes the outer interior-point loop from another almost-linear maximum-flow framework. Its deterministic pseudo-circulation subroutine is combined with a randomized balanced-graph flow routine, and the stated final result remains almost-linear. The deterministic nature of an intermediate step does not make the full reduction deterministic, and removing the outer loop does not itself establish fixed-polylogarithmic overhead.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm of Fleischmann, George Z. Li and Jason Li has fixed-polylogarithmic overhead for constant-accuracy approximate flow on undirected graphs. Both qualifications matter: the present task concerns arbitrary directed graphs and exact integral output, and that approximation theorem has additional inverse-error dependence. It does not directly establish the target here.

An approximation with a fixed relative error need not determine an integer optimum whose magnitude grows with the input. Likewise, finding only an optimal value does not fulfill the requested output list. Polynomially bounded capacities ensure each input capacity and output arc value fits in a logarithmic number of bits; the question does not hide arbitrarily long integers behind unit-cost input access.
why: Maximum flow is a central primitive for routing, cuts and combinatorial optimization. Almost-linear algorithms have already removed a polynomial overhead. This question asks whether exact directed flow can be computed with only a fixed power of a logarithm beyond explicit input size, on all polynomial-capacity instances and with a complete flow as output.

The inspected exact-flow sources give almost-linear bounds, including deterministic2023 and improved static2024 results and Li–Wice’s August2026 framework. None of their stated guarantees establishes the fixed-polylogarithmic overhead required here. The ICALP2026 near-linear approximation theorem is for undirected graphs and has inverse-error dependence. This is a bounded source review; external proofs were not independently certified.
