The algorithm must find the cheapest outgoing cut over all nontrivial vertex partitions and output its exact value. The target is one uniform almost-linear randomized algorithm, with bounded error and a time limit on every execution. Recent almost-linear approximations pay for inverse precision, while threshold-dependent exact results retain an extra connectivity factor. A complete Lean-checked exact construction or unconditional refutation is required.

title: Almost-linear directed vertex connectivity
importance_reason: A uniform almost-linear algorithm would settle the remaining general exact running-time gap for directed vertex robustness, a classical network problem.
formal:
Do there exist one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\), an integer word-size constant \(d\ge4\), and a function \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h(N)}{\log N}=0,
\]
such that, on every simple unweighted directed graph \(G\) with \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\) arcs, every execution uses at most \(C(m+n)h(m+n)\) word-RAM instructions and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs the exact vertex connectivity \(\kappa(G)\) together with an attaining vertex set? Define
\[
\kappa(G)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq V(G),\ G-S\text{ is not strongly connected or }|V(G)\setminus S|\le1\}.
\]
Both density and connectivity are unrestricted.
question_excerpt: Recent work improves exact directed vertex-cut algorithms and obtains almost-linear relative approximation. This card retains the editorial endpoint of exact almost-linear computation for every unweighted directed graph, including all intermediate density and connectivity regimes.
definitions:
The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. For \(S\subseteq V\), remove \(S\) and all incident arcs. Define \(\kappa(G)\) as the smallest \(|S|\) for which the remainder is not strongly connected or contains at most one vertex. Strong connectivity means reachability for every ordered pair of remaining vertices. Thus an input that is not strongly connected has value zero, and a complete bidirected graph has value \(n-1\). Output the value and an attaining \(S\). Whenever at least two vertices remain, failure of strong connectivity is equivalent to a partition \((L,S,R)\) with nonempty \(L,R\) and no arc from \(L\) to \(R\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Write \(N=m+n\). Almost-linear time means that there exist one algorithm, a constant \(C\) and a function \(h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), independent of the input graph, with \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h(N)/\log N=0\), such that the time is at most \(CNh(N)\) for every input. All hidden constants are independent of the graph.

The explicit input consists of \(n,m\) and an array of \(m\) ordered endpoint pairs, one word per endpoint. The output separator is an \(n\)-bit incidence vector packed into words, and the reported connectivity is an integer word. Output writing is charged. A successful output satisfies both \(|S|=\kappa(G)\) and the displayed separator condition. Failed executions may return a failure symbol or an incorrect result, but must obey the same instruction limit. The word-size constant is at least four and may be larger if needed for the fixed algorithm’s addressing.

For a complete bidirected graph the answer is \(n-1\), achieved by leaving one vertex. Every noncomplete graph has two vertices missing at least one directed arc between them, so deleting the others supplies a separator leaving at least two vertices. Thus the stated convention agrees with the nonempty-left-and-right cut formulation throughout the noncomplete case. No strong-connectivity promise is imposed on the input.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(A,C,d,h)\,\forall G\). In particular, neither the program nor its almost-linear overhead can depend on the unknown \(\kappa(G)\), an edge-density promise or a requested fixed exponent. There is no separate space restriction beyond charged computation and word-addressable memory. Approximation of \(\kappa(G)\) is not an alternative output guarantee.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one uniform algorithm, exact value and separator correctness with the required probability, and the subpolynomial-overhead time bound on every execution for every input. A negative proof must rule out the full statement unconditionally; an assumption-based lower bound is only a conditional result.

An almost-linear approximation, an exact bound with an unrestricted extra connectivity factor, or a result confined to undirected graphs does not settle the target. An expected-time algorithm is sufficient only with a justified conversion to the stated bounded-error worst-case time guarantee. The at-most-one-remaining-vertex convention must also be handled. No numerical tolerance in the answer is allowed.
context:
Directed vertex connectivity measures resilience to vertex removals when reachability is asymmetric. The task asks for the most vulnerable separator anywhere in the graph.

The SODA 2026 theorem gives randomized expected time \(O(\min\{m^{1+o(1)}\kappa,n^{2+o(1)}\})\), with its stated success probability at least one half. It covers useful low-connectivity and dense regimes, but does not give almost-linear time everywhere.

Almost-linear relative approximation schemes are known. Their exact integer versions retain a connectivity-dependent cost, which is not uniformly subpolynomial.

The July 2026 revision supplies another vertex-cut scheme with inverse-precision dependence. Its noncomplete-graph requirement is separate from the easy complete-graph convention used here.

Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified almost-linear exact algorithm for all unweighted directed inputs in the stated uniform model. This is an explicit editorial endpoint, not a verbatim conjecture or independent certification of all cited proofs.

working_summary: The input is any simple unweighted directed graph, with no connectivity or density promise. The output is the smallest number of vertices whose removal destroys strong connectivity, together with such a set. Leaving at most one vertex is allowed, so a complete bidirected graph has value n minus one. The target is exact almost-linear randomized computation on every input; known expected and approximation bounds have additional limitations. A complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional refutation must respect the worst-case time and bounded-error guarantees.

title: Boolean dimension of posets with planar cover graphs
importance_reason: A constant-size Boolean description of every order with a planar cover graph would explain how planar local structure controls global order information.
formal:
Does there exist an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every finite poset \(P=(V,<_{P})\) whose undirected cover graph is planar, there exist strict total orders \(L_1,\ldots,L_d\) on \(V\) and a Boolean function \(\varphi_P:\{0,1\}^{d}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[
\forall x,y\in V\ (x\ne y\Longrightarrow
\bigl[x<_{P}y\iff
\varphi_P(b_1(x,y),\ldots,b_d(x,y))=1\bigr]),
\]
where \(b_i(x,y)=1\) if \(x<_{L_i}y\), and \(b_i(x,y)=0\) otherwise? The integer \(d\) must be independent of the poset. The total orders and the Boolean function may depend on \(P\).
definitions:
A finite poset consists of a finite set \(V\) and an irreflexive, transitive relation \(<_P\). An element \(y\) covers \(x\) if \(x<_P y\) and no \(z\in V\) satisfies \(x<_P z<_P y\). The undirected cover graph is the simple graph with vertex set \(V\) and one edge \(\{x,y\}\) for each such cover relation, with the direction forgotten. It is planar if its vertices can be assigned distinct points of the plane and its edges drawn as simple curves between their endpoints so that edge interiors are disjoint from every vertex and two edge curves meet only at a shared endpoint. The drawing need not place greater elements above smaller ones or make cover edges increase vertically. Planarity of the undirected cover graph, rather than the existence of an upward planar order diagram, is the required hypothesis.

A strict total order \(<_L\) is an irreflexive, transitive relation that, for every two distinct elements, contains exactly one of \(x<_L y\) and \(y<_L x\). Each \(L_i\) orders all of \(V\). The orders may repeat and are auxiliary encodings: they are not required to extend \(<_P\). A Boolean function here is an arbitrary map on the finite set of \(d\)-bit strings; no restriction on its formula size or method of computation is imposed. A sequence of orders and a function satisfying the displayed equivalence is a Boolean realizer of size \(d\). Boolean dimension measures the smallest size of such a realizer; the present question asks only whether these sizes have a universal finite bound.

For each fixed \(P\), the same function \(\varphi_P\) must work for every ordered pair of distinct elements. It cannot depend additionally on the queried pair. An incomparable pair must produce output zero in both orders of its two elements. The equality case is excluded from the equivalence; for empty or one-element ground sets the pair requirement is vacuous. The universal bound applies without restrictions on the number of elements, the size of the largest chain, or the number of minimal or maximal elements. In particular, the poset is not assumed to have a least element. This is an existential structural question with no algorithmic, input-encoding, running-time or randomness requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed proposition, including a universal finite bound and the existence of the required realizers for every permitted poset, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation. The negation means that for every integer \(d\ge1\) there exists a finite poset with a planar undirected cover graph admitting no Boolean realizer of size at most \(d\). A bound depending on the poset size, height or another unbounded parameter, or a bound only for posets with a least element or an upward planar diagram, does not establish the universal positive statement. A conditional result alone does not settle the unconditional target.
context:
Problem A explicitly asks this question for planar undirected cover graphs. Its footnote records that the question originally posed by Nešetřil and Pudlák in 1989 concerned the more restricted class admitting planar order diagrams. This card retains the broader formulation stated in the later primary papers; it does not attribute the two scopes as identical.

Blake, Micek and Trotter prove \(\operatorname{bdim}(P)\le13\) when the cover graph is planar and \(P\) has a unique minimal element. In a finite nonempty poset, this is a least element, meaning an element below every other element. The additional hypothesis is absent from the general question.

Ordinary order dimension requires total orders that extend the partial order and reconstruct it by taking their intersection. Boolean realizers allow arbitrary auxiliary total orders and an arbitrary Boolean decoder. The known examples of large ordinary dimension with planar cover graphs do not automatically have large Boolean dimension.

Joret, Micek, Pilipczuk and Walczak prove bounded Boolean dimension for posets of bounded cliquewidth. This parameter concerns construction of the full directed order relation using a bounded set of vertex labels and uniform operations on label classes; it is not a hypothesis supplied merely by planarity of the cover graph. Their October 2025 revision explicitly retains the planar-cover-graph question as open.

The reachability connection concerns labels assigned to vertices of a directed graph, from which one fixed decoder decides whether a directed path joins the two queried vertices. Bounded Boolean dimension for all posets in this question would imply labels of \(O(\log n)\) bits for planar directed graphs with \(n\) vertices. This is a consequence motivating the target, not an additional required theorem.

The March 2025 revision of Boolean Dimension of a Boolean Lattice independently lists planar-cover-graph boundedness as open. Its results about inclusion orders on subsets do not settle this planar question.
why: This asks whether planar local cover relations force a uniformly bounded comparison description of the entire partial order, despite arbitrarily large ordinary order dimension. A positive answer would also give logarithmic-size reachability labels for planar directed graphs, connecting a structural question about orders with concise representations of global reachability.
status_note: Source-open in the checked primary formulations. Problem A in Blake–Micek–Trotter revision 2 (17 December 2022) states the broader planar-cover-graph target; Joret–Micek–Pilipczuk–Walczak revision 3 (18 October 2025) still lists it as open, and the related journal publication is dated 7 January 2026. The individual source review and bounded later-work check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The unique-minimum bound 13 and bounded-cliquewidth theorem concern additional hypotheses. This is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.

working_summary: The cover graph records which pairs in a finite partial order are immediately comparable, with edge directions forgotten. The question asks whether planarity of that graph guarantees a universal constant number of total orders encoding every comparability. One Boolean function decodes the comparison bits for all distinct ordered pairs, and both that function and the auxiliary orders may vary with the poset. The orders need not extend the partial order, and no upward planar diagram or unique minimal element is assumed. Known bounds with additional structural hypotheses leave the general question open in the checked sources and motivate its connection to concise reachability labels.

title: Strongly explicit Ramanujan families for every degree
importance_reason: Combine extremal spectral quality with efficient local access for arbitrary constant-degree expanders.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge 3\), is there one deterministic algorithm that computes the port rotation map of connected d-regular Ramanujan graphs for an unbounded set of vertex counts n in time polynomial in log n, with the effective family and graph conventions below?
definitions: The graphs are undirected multigraphs on \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); parallel edges and loops are permitted, as in the source’s graph convention. Each vertex has ports \([d]\). A rotation map \(Rot_{n}:[n]\times [d]\to [n]\times [d]\) is an involution: if \(Rot_{n}(v,i)=(w,j)\), then \(Rot_{n}(w,j)=(v,i)\). Paired ports encode an undirected edge; a fixed port encodes a loop. Define the symmetric integer adjacency matrix A by \(A_{vw}=|\{i\in[d]:\operatorname{first}(\operatorname{Rot}_n(v,i))=w\}|\), so every row sum is d and a fixed-port loop contributes one to the diagonal and degree. Connectivity means the underlying undirected graph is connected. List the real eigenvalues with multiplicity in decreasing order \(d=\lambda _{1}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{n}\). Require \(|\lambda_i|\le2\sqrt{d-1}\) for \(i\ge 2\), except that the single eigenvalue −d is permitted when the graph is bipartite. For each fixed d the answer supplies a decidable infinite set \(N_{d}\) of positive integers, a single total deterministic bit algorithm \(R_{d}\), and constants \(C_{d},a_{d}\). On input \((n,v,i)\) in binary, \(R_{d}\) runs in at most \(C_d(1+\log_2 n)^{a_d}\) steps for valid \(v\in [n],i\in [d]\). For every \(n\in N_{d}\) its outputs constitute the rotation map of such a graph. No graph-dependent advice, preprocessing or tables are supplied to \(R_{d}\); its fixed program may depend on d. The family’s size-membership decider must halt on all binary n but has no prescribed running-time bound. No bound on gaps between successive \(n\in N_{d}\) is required. Outputs at n outside \(N_{d}\) carry no graph promise. This retains the imported infinite-family target, which is weaker than requiring every admissible size; it does not impose simple-graph or non-bipartite restrictions.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified family construction, including a size-membership decider, the uniform local rotation algorithm, infinitely many sizes, connectivity and the exact spectral bound for every fixed degree. Alternatively provide a Lean refutation for some degree. Spectral slack, graph-specific advice or polynomial time in the vertex count does not satisfy strong explicitness.
context:
Ramanujan families attain the limiting optimal spectral bound for their fixed degree. Strong explicitness requires computing local connections in time polynomial in the vertex-label length.

The source distinguishes exact Ramanujan families for certain degrees from constructions with spectral slack for general degrees. This question retains an unbounded effective family for each fixed degree, without requiring every admissible graph size.
why: Combine extremal spectral quality with efficient local access for arbitrary constant-degree expanders.
status_note: The primary source distinguishes available exact special-degree families from arbitrary-degree constructions with slack. The statement and a bounded later-work search were reviewed on 13 September 2026 without finding a general exact strongly explicit construction. This is not a claim of an exhaustive status audit.

working_summary: A regular Ramanujan graph meets the optimal asymptotic bound on nontrivial adjacency eigenvalues. The question asks for an infinite family at every fixed degree at least three. One algorithm must compute each local port connection in time polynomial in the vertex-label length. The family may use only a decidable unbounded set of sizes and permits the stated multigraph conventions. Constructions with positive spectral slack or slower global access do not meet the exact strong-explicitness target.

title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
importance_reason: Exact Matching is a central derandomization test even on bipartite graphs. Its importance remains high while the recent claimed solution is assessed.
formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) with \(|L|=|R|=n\ge0\), every red/blue coloring of its edges, and every integer \(0\le k\le n\), the machine decides within \(C(\ell+1)^d\) bit steps whether \(G\) has a perfect matching with exactly \(k\) red edges? Here \(\ell\) is the full explicit input encoding length. The answer must be correct on every allowed instance, with no randomness or additional promise.
question_excerpt: Exact Matching asks for a perfect matching with a prescribed number of red edges. The historical deterministic polynomial-time question includes arbitrary bipartite graphs; a 2026 preprint claims a solution, whose verification status is recorded separately.
definitions:
The left vertices are \(L=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\) and the right vertices are \(R=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\), with the two lists disjoint. Every edge has the form \(\{u_i,v_j\}\). There are no loops, edges within a side or parallel edges. Each present edge has exactly one color, red or blue. Missing edges are permitted, and the graph need not be connected, complete, regular, planar or of bounded degree.

A perfect matching is a subset of edges containing exactly one edge incident to every vertex. Equivalently, it is specified by a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that every \(\{u_i,v_{\pi(i)}\}\) is present. It satisfies the additional requirement precisely when
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1[\{u_i,v_{\pi(i)}\}\text{ is red}]=k.
\]
There is no tolerance, interval or parity relaxation in this equality. For \(n=0\), the empty matching is perfect and the only allowed \(k=0\) has answer YES.

For an explicit encoding, code a nonnegative integer \(z\) as \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). Supply the codes of \(n,k\), followed by the \(n\)-by-\(n\) matrix in row order, with two bits per position: 00 for absence, 01 for blue and 10 for red. The tag 11 and trailing data are invalid. The matrix lists every potential cross-edge, so this is not a succinct graph representation. The total bit length is \(\ell\).

The machine is one finite classical deterministic multitape Turing program, with no advice, random bits, oracle or quantum operation. Reading, arithmetic on encoded numbers, intermediate storage manipulation and the final yes/no output are all charged. The same \(A,C,d\) must work for every size and color pattern. No separate space bound is imposed. The output need not exhibit a matching or count all matchings. An algebraic algorithm may be used, but polynomially many arithmetic operations alone do not replace a polynomial bit-time analysis. Only sequential polynomial time is requested; a polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithm is a stronger requirement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed deterministic polynomial-time existence claim, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its unconditional negation. A positive answer must prove exact decision correctness on every bipartite input and one common polynomial bound in the full bit length. A negative answer must prove that this decision language does not belong to \(\mathrm P\), rather than assuming a complexity hypothesis.

If the April 2026 proposed algorithm is used, every necessary mathematical ingredient must be proved, including any structural assertion supplied as a hypothesis to an existing formalization, and the bit complexity must be justified. The presence of a machine-checked conditional theorem is not a proof of its unproved premises. A flaw in that particular proposal would not by itself prove that no other algorithm exists. Randomized algorithms, restricted graph classes, approximate red counts and ordinary perfect matching do not answer the full target.
context:
The equality constraint adds information that minimum-cost or maximum-cost matching does not supply. In a complete graph with two vertices on each side, color the two diagonal edges red and the others blue: the only perfect matchings have zero or two red edges, so the intermediate count one is impossible.

The 2023 bipartite result permits a red count between one half and three halves of the target on feasible instances. Such a relaxation is useful but does not decide exact equality.

Du’s preprint claims a deterministic solution. Its third version identifies eight remaining assumptions in the top-level Lean theorem, while asserting mathematical arguments for them in the paper or prior work. This review has not independently verified that full argument.

The August 2026 all-count improvement uses randomness and counts field operations. It applies to general graphs and does not validate or invalidate the separate deterministic bipartite proposal.

The historical question remains the existence of a complete deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Its current status is marked uncertain because of the unresolved verification of the claimed advance, rather than being presented as a confirmed open problem.

title: Polynomial-time computation of planar treewidth
importance_reason: Treewidth computation is a central structural primitive, so tight complexity bounds influence many parameterized algorithms.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that computes the exact treewidth of every finite planar graph?

Precisely, do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that \(M\) halts on every binary input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and, for every finite simple planar graph \(G\) in the encoding below,
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))=\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G))?
\]
The output is the exact integer treewidth in the specified signed binary encoding. Graph size and treewidth are unrestricted; the polynomial is fixed independently of both. No planar embedding, tree decomposition or bound on treewidth is supplied with the graph.

This is the polynomial-time existence question stated in §4.6 of the 2016 seminar report. It asks for an exact algorithm, not an optimal numerical running-time exponent. A negative answer is the full negation of that existence assertion, not merely an NP-hardness theorem conditional on a separate complexity-class separation.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) for an integer \(n\ge0\), and \(E\) a set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Loops and parallel edges are absent; isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and the empty graph are allowed. Graphs are unweighted. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices joined by edges. A cycle is a closed sequence of at least three edges visiting no vertex twice except its starting and ending vertex. A nonempty finite tree is a finite simple connected graph with no cycle; it has a unique path between each pair of its vertices.

A graph is planar if its vertices can be mapped injectively to points of \(\mathbb R^2\), and each edge can be represented by a continuous injective curve \([0,1]\to\mathbb R^2\) whose endpoints are the points of its two vertices, such that no interior point of a curve is a vertex point and distinct edge curves intersect only at common endpoint vertices. The existence of such a drawing is a promise on the input graph; its curves and coordinates are not part of the input. The algorithm is not required to output a drawing.

A tree decomposition is a nonempty finite tree \(T\) with a bag \(B_t\subseteq V\) at each node \(t\in V(T)\), satisfying
\[
\bigcup_{t\in V(T)} B_t=V,
\qquad
\forall\{u,v\}\in E\ \exists t\in V(T):\{u,v\}\subseteq B_t,
\]
and the connectedness condition: for every \(v\in V\), the set \(\{t\in V(T):v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Equivalently, every node on the unique path between two bags containing \(v\) also has \(v\) in its bag. Empty bags are allowed. The width of this decomposition is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\), and
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)=
\min_{(T,(B_t))\text{ a tree decomposition of }G}
\left(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\right).
\]
The one-node tree with bag \(V\) is a decomposition, so the minimum exists. For the empty graph this convention gives \(-1\); for any nonempty graph it is an integer between \(0\) and \(n-1\). The convention on the single empty graph does not affect polynomial-time solvability.

Encode \(G\) as the bitstring \(1^n0\) followed by exactly \(n(n-1)/2\) bits. These final bits list the indicators of \(\{i,j\}\in E\) in lexicographic order of pairs \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<j<n\). Thus the encoding length is
\[
L(G)=n+1+\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
The empty graph is encoded by the single bit 0. The unary prefix includes every vertex, even if isolated. This explicit adjacency encoding and the ordinary explicit adjacency-list encoding are polynomially interconvertible, so the chosen representation does not alter the polynomial-time question.

The output encoding \(\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(z)\) for an integer \(z\) is one sign bit, 0 for a nonnegative integer and 1 for a negative integer, followed by the usual base-two representation of \(|z|\), with no leading zero except that zero has magnitude string 0. Negative zero is forbidden. For example, the output for the empty graph's treewidth is the sign bit 1 followed by the magnitude bit 1. Exact numerical equality is part of the algorithm's task; it is not an additional demand for an exact-value benchmark answer.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has one finite program, a finite tape alphabet, a read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes initially blank, and a binary output tape. A transition inspects or changes only the scanned symbol on each tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including reading the graph, arithmetic, preprocessing and writing the answer. There is no oracle, random tape, advice depending on input length, unbounded-word unit-cost arithmetic or free preprocessing. The polynomial clock is worst case and applies to every bitstring, including malformed encodings and encodings of nonplanar graphs. On those inputs, correctness and the output format are unrestricted. Imposing this total clock does not change the promised polynomial-time question, because a candidate machine with fixed bounds can be stopped at its own polynomial clock.

An algorithm returning only the exact minimum width suffices; an optimal tree decomposition need not be printed. Conversely, any polynomial-time algorithm producing an optimal decomposition would also answer this question. Fixed-parameter algorithms whose dependence on treewidth is superpolynomial do not give the required single polynomial bound when treewidth is unrestricted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the exact algorithm-existence proposition, or its full logical negation, using the definitions and encoding above.

A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic machine and fixed polynomial bound, prove the total clock, and prove that its output is the exact treewidth for every encoded planar graph. It must cover all sizes, components and treewidth values, without an embedding or decomposition in the input.

A negative answer must prove that for every finite deterministic machine \(M\) and every pair of integers \(C,k\ge1\), at least one of the following holds:
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad
M(x)\text{ does not halt within }C(|x|+1)^k\text{ transitions},
\]
or
\[
\exists G\text{ finite, simple and planar}:\quad
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))\text{ fails to halt with output }
\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G)).
\]
Failure includes a malformed output, an incorrect integer or nontermination. The graph or failing input may depend on the machine and its proposed bound. Refuting one particular algorithm is insufficient.

An NP-hardness proof together with a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would give a negative answer; NP-hardness alone is not the negation of polynomial-time solvability. Here \(\mathrm P\) is uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) is uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time decision, with acceptance on at least one branch and polynomial clocks on all branches. A result for branchwidth, a proper subclass of planar graphs, an approximation guarantee, or a polynomial-time procedure per output object with potentially superpolynomially many output objects does not establish the positive assertion by itself. This is a yes/no running-time question. The numerical \(1/100\) benchmark tolerance does not change the exact integer function computed by its hypothetical algorithm.
context:
The 2016 seminar report explicitly asks whether the treewidth of a planar graph can be computed in polynomial time. It does not prescribe a fixed exponent, an approximation ratio, a bounded-width promise or a space restriction.

The 2025 potential-maximal-clique paper defines the standard tree decomposition and still describes exact planar treewidth as a long-standing question. Its graph convention is simple, undirected and unweighted; the present card spells out the finite encoding and computational model.

The related branchwidth parameter is polynomial-time computable for planar graphs. The cited sources emphasize that this does not by itself determine exact treewidth, though it supports approximation results.

The 2023 hardness result covers cubic graphs and certain three-dimensional grid subgraphs. Those input classes are not restricted to planar graphs, and its conclusion explicitly retains the planar question as open.

The 2025 algorithm has time polynomial in the graph size multiplied by the number of potential maximal cliques. Its polynomial delay guarantee controls the time between consecutive generated objects, and does not assert that every planar graph has only polynomially many such objects.

A September 2026 preprint improves a structural bound: a planar graph excluding a \(t\times t\) grid minor has treewidth at most \(4t+4\). This is a width-versus-grid theorem, not an exact polynomial-time computation theorem.
why: Treewidth is a central measure connecting graph structure with algorithms for otherwise difficult graph problems. An exact polynomial-time algorithm on planar graphs would make optimal width accessible on a large and important sparse graph class. A negative answer would locate a fundamental limitation of planarity despite efficient algorithms for the related branchwidth parameter. The issue is distinct from using a decomposition once one has already been supplied.

working_summary: Treewidth is the minimum largest-bag size minus one among all tree decompositions of a finite graph. The question asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can compute that integer exactly for every planar graph. The input is only the finite graph, without a planar embedding, a tree decomposition or a bound on its width. Inspected results on cubic-graph hardness, polynomial-delay enumeration and planar grid bounds do not establish that polynomial-time algorithm or its nonexistence. title: 3-colorability of diameter-two graphs
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph \(G\) of diameter at most \(2\), decides whether \(G\) has a proper vertex coloring with three colors? The input does not promise that such a coloring exists. Precisely, there must be one Turing machine and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, whose worst-case running time on every valid \(n\)-vertex graph is at most \(C(n+1)^b\), and whose output is correct on every such graph.
definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is the ordinary binary encoding of \(n\), a delimiter, and an \(n\times n\) matrix of bits in row order. Valid graph matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal; a one in position \((u,v)\) means that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge. Edges are unweighted, and distance is the number of edges in a shortest path. The graph is connected if every pair has a path, and its diameter is the maximum distance over all vertex pairs; a singleton has diameter zero. A proper three-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,2,3\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) whenever \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge; use of fewer than three colors is permitted. The decision output is one exactly when the input is a connected graph of diameter at most two admitting such a map, and zero otherwise. Malformed encodings, nonsimple graph matrices, disconnected graphs and graphs of larger diameter are rejected. Thus the problem is a total language; checking the structural promise does not change its polynomial-time classification. The machine has one finite deterministic program, ordinary finite-alphabet tapes, no oracle or advice, and no random choices. Costs include reading the explicit adjacency matrix and writing the answer, and are worst-case over all encodings with the given vertex count. There are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, restrictions on degrees, triangle exclusions or four-cycle exclusions. The number of colors and the diameter bound are fixed, while the number of vertices is unbounded. The source’s diameter-exactly-two version has the same polynomial-time question, because connected graphs of diameter zero or one are complete and constitute a polynomial-time decidable additional class.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that this total language belongs to deterministic polynomial time, or prove that it does not. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its worst-case polynomial bound and exact correctness on all permitted graphs, including those with no proper three-coloring. A negative answer must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. An NP-completeness theorem is a meaningful conventional hardness classification, but by itself gives a negative answer only under the additional assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); it is not an unconditional proof of nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\). A subexponential upper bound or an algorithm on a narrower forbidden-subgraph class does not settle the stated target.
context:
Paulusma’s 2019 open-problem discussion identifies three colors and diameter two as the outstanding tractability boundary. The same section contains further questions with extra graph restrictions or a variable number of colors. Those are distinct targets; this card keeps the existing unrestricted three-color decision problem.

The boundary is striking because diameter-one connected graphs are complete, whereas three-colorability is NP-complete already for diameter-three graphs, including triangle-free inputs. Requiring every pair of vertices to be at distance at most two leaves considerable global structure available, and its effect on the fixed three-color decision problem remains unresolved in the checked sources.

Dębski, Piecyk and Rzążewski’s Theorem 3 gives a \(2^{O(n^{1/3}\log^2 n)}\)-time algorithm for list three-coloring of diameter-two graphs, and hence for ordinary three-colorability. The statement is subexponential, not polynomial. No methods from its proof are part of the problem’s answer requirements.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list three-coloring when the graph has diameter two and contains no four-cycle as a subgraph. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly leave the unrestricted diameter-two case open. Forbidding a four-cycle as a subgraph is stronger than excluding only induced four-cycles, and neither restriction is present in this target.
why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.
status_note: The unrestricted problem is explicitly left open in Murakami’s 1 July 2026 primary preprint, and bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no subsequent general resolution. The preprint’s special-case proof is not independently certified here; its four-cycle exclusion does not apply to the present unrestricted domain.
progress: 2013–2016: Mertzios and Spirakis give a \(2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}\)-time diameter-two algorithm and NP-completeness at diameter three. The 2021 paper recalls these results in its introductory classification. | 2019: Paulusma’s Section 4.3 records the unrestricted diameter-two three-color question separately from additional restricted-graph questions. | 2021-04-28: Dębski et al., Theorem 3, improve the diameter-two list-coloring time to \(2^{O(n^{1/3}\log^2 n)}\); the journal publication follows in 2022. | 2026-07-01: Murakami’s arXiv v2 proves a polynomial-time result with a four-cycle subgraph exclusion and explicitly retains the unrestricted case as open.
working_summary: The problem asks whether three-colorability is decidable in deterministic polynomial time for every graph of diameter at most two. The graph is given explicitly, and it is not promised to be colorable. No sparsity, forbidden-cycle, degree or vertex-list restriction is imposed. The best general bound identified in the checked sources is subexponential, while a July 2026 polynomial-time result needs an additional four-cycle exclusion. The question isolates a precise structural boundary between easy complete graphs and the known hardness at diameter three.

title: Optimal exact-distance label length for planar graphs
importance_reason: Closing this polynomial gap would identify the information needed to distribute an entire planar graph metric into independent vertex labels.
formal: Determine the asymptotic growth of \(\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\) up to universal constant factors, where \(\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\) is the least integer \(b\ge0\) permitting labels of \(b\) bits that determine every pairwise distance in every connected unweighted simple planar graph on \(n\ge2\) vertices using only the two labels.
definitions: For fixed \(n,b\), a permitted decoder is a function \(D:\{0,1\}^b\times\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). The same \(D\) must work for every connected unweighted simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\): there must be a label assignment \(\lambda_G:[n]\to\{0,1\}^b\) such that \(D(\lambda_G(u),\lambda_G(v))=\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) for all vertices, where distance counts edges on a shortest path. The decoder may depend on \(n\) and \(b\), but not on \(G\), and receives no shared graph data, vertex identifiers or additional input. Both the decoder domain and graph class are finite for fixed \(n,b\); no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing labels or decoding. The target measures label information alone, with arbitrary values on label pairs never used by an assignment. Known efficient schemes provide upper bounds in this unrestricted model as well. Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); simple means no loops or parallel edges, and planar means admitting a drawing by nonintersecting arcs except at shared endpoints. Labels have the common fixed length \(b\); the target is the largest per-vertex bit length, not the sum over vertices. A finite admissible \(b\) always exists: each label can contain the whole finite graph description together with its vertex index, and a common decoder can recover graph distances from that description. Thus the least integer in the definition is well-defined.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified asymptotic rate \(f(n)>0\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\), \(n_0\), such that \(cf(n)\le\ell_{\mathrm{planar}}(n)\le Cf(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Both bounds must use the same unrestricted exact-decoder model. Merely renaming the defining optimum, a one-sided improvement, or conditional hardness without its assumption proved does not meet this target. The accuracy requirement is constant-factor asymptotic matching, not an additive 0.01 error on big-O notation.
context:
A label is the information a vertex carries when the graph itself is unavailable. To answer a distance query, the decoder sees exactly the two endpoint labels. Its rule is common to the whole graph family, so it cannot have a different hidden graph stored for every labeling assignment.

Even the diagonal query constrains labels: a vertex is at distance zero from itself, while two distinct vertices in a connected unweighted graph are at positive distance. Two different vertices therefore cannot share a label. This simple observation only forces \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits, far below the known polynomial lower bound.

The reviewed upper bound is \(O(\sqrt n)\) bits per vertex, while the general lower bound is \(\Omega(n^{1/3})\). The gap is polynomial in \(n\), not just a missing logarithmic factor. An exact constant-factor answer must identify a rate that is both attainable and necessary for the same two-label model.

Decoding speed is a separate resource. The 2023 paper also gives a variant with polylogarithmic decoding time and \(O(\sqrt{n\log n})\)-bit labels. This card permits an arbitrary finite decoder for each \(n,b\), so a lower bound that applies only to fast decoders would not establish its information-theoretic optimum.

A shared distance oracle can distribute information between vertex identifiers and one common data structure; that common structure is absent here. Approximate distances, weighted graphs, and distances after a failure similarly change the information a pair of labels must provide. This target fixes connected, simple, unweighted planar graphs and exact edge counts.

The graph can determine its entire label assignment, but it cannot determine the decoder. The order of these choices permits graph-dependent labels while preventing the graph from being supplied for free through a query routine. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the labels or evaluating the decoder.
why: Closing this polynomial gap would identify the information needed to distribute an entire planar graph metric into independent vertex labels.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The reviewed author and journal sources give the square-root upper bound and cube-root lower bound for exact unweighted planar distance labels. The faster-decoding variant uses larger labels. No constant-factor matching resolution of the unrestricted decoder model was located in the bounded later-work check; proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2021 / 2023: The improved scheme removes a logarithmic factor from the previous upper bound, leaving the exponent gap between \(n^{1/3}\) and \(n^{1/2}\).
working_summary: Each vertex receives a short binary label. The exact distance between two vertices must follow from their labels alone. The same decoder serves every graph of the chosen size. The target is the optimal asymptotic number of label bits. Current lower and upper bounds differ by a polynomial factor.

title: Erdős girth conjecture
importance_reason: A general extremal obstruction underlying sharp routing and distance-sparsification tradeoffs. Existing score retained rather than raised by this formulation review.
formal: For every integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(c_{k}>0\) and \(N_{k}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N_{k}\), some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least \(c_{k} n^{1+1/k}\) edges and contains no cycle of length less than \(2k+2\)? Equivalently, is \(M_{2k+2}(n)=\Omega _{k}(n^{1+1/k})\) for every fixed k, where \(M_{s}(n)\) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.
context:
Known extremal upper bounds give \(M_{2k+2}(n)=O_{k}(n^{1+1/k})\). The conjecture asks whether forbidding all these short cycles still permits that many edges up to a constant factor.

Using threshold \(2k+1\) instead of \(2k+2\) gives an equivalent asymptotic conjecture: a graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least half its edges, and that subgraph has no odd cycles. This equivalence changes neither the exponent nor the fixed-k target.

The cases \(k=1,2,3,5\) are known. The July 2026 spanner paper still lists exactly those cases; the next missing parameter \(k=4\) asks for \(\Omega (n^{5/4})\) edges with girth at least 10.

The source uses these graphs to establish conditional lower bounds on the memory needed by routing schemes with small stretch. More generally, the conjecture controls sharpness of size-versus-stretch bounds for graph spanners.

The 2026 preprint removes this assumption for a particular model of spanners tolerating edge failures of bounded degree. It explicitly distinguishes that result from constructing graphs of the girth and density required here.

This additional occurrence comes from the same compact-routing paper. The retained formal statement fixes its own girth threshold and graph-size quantifiers; a differently quantified girth conjecture is not automatically identified with it.
why: A central extremal graph question with direct consequences for compact routing and graph sparsification: it asks whether the standard density obstruction from short cycles is asymptotically tight at every fixed scale.
status_note: Read the source definitions and routing use, then checked the July 2026 primary discussion and subsequent searches through 12 September 2026. The later spanner result does not resolve the girth conjecture; no further settled k was found.
progress: 2022: The routing paper records the known \(k=1,2,3,5\) cases and uses the full conjecture for higher-stretch space lower bounds. | 2026-07-08: A new spanner preprint still states the full girth conjecture as open and proves a separate degree-fault-tolerant lower bound unconditionally.
working_summary: The girth conjecture asks for dense graphs with every short cycle forbidden. For each fixed k, the target is \(\Omega (n^{1+1/k})\) edges and girth at least \(2k+2\). The lower bound must hold for every sufficiently large n, with constants depending on k. The known cases are \(k=1,2,3,5\), as still recorded in July 2026. A resolution would sharpen fundamental lower bounds for routing and graph spanners.

title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
importance_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
focus_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.
why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint gives a growing competitive factor and still distinguishes its theorem from constant dynamic optimality. The primary text and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026; no complete resolution was found in that check. This review does not independently verify the new proof.
progress: 1985 / background: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree. | 2007: Tango trees give an online BST with an \(O(\log\log n)\) competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying. | 2026-07-20: The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.
working_summary: Splay trees reorganize a binary search tree after each access using local rotations. The question asks whether this simple rule is always within a constant factor of the best tree strategy that knows the entire request sequence. An additive linear allowance pays for the initial tree. Frequency and locality guarantees cover useful patterns but do not establish this universal comparison. Understanding this gap would show whether local adaptation can exploit every advantage available to an offline search tree.

title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
importance_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
focus_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.
why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.
status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.
progress: 2018: Larsen–Weinstein–Yu cross the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean data structures; the journal version appeared in 2020. This does not settle the static question. | 2025-05-28: Revision 1 of Korten–Pitassi–Impagliazzo improves cell-probe space/time tradeoffs using local PRGs and studies conditional barriers. | 2025-10-22: Ko proves stronger bit-cell bounds for random linear operators, including regimes with superpolynomially many queries. | 2026-03-26: Ko’s preprint claims a nearly log-squared lower bound for dynamic Boolean multiphase problems. No independent proof audit of that claim is supplied here. | 2026-06: Koucký–Loff–Molli–Saks appears at STOC 2026, with conditional natural-proofs barriers and an explicit statement of the static challenge.
working_summary: A static data structure preprocesses a database and later answers queries by reading stored memory cells. This question seeks an explicitly computable Boolean query problem forcing more than logarithmically many reads despite unrestricted preprocessing. The saved formulation fixes short queries, logarithmic word size, near-linear space, and deterministic adaptive access. Free computation between reads makes this an information-access lower bound. Such an example would expose a fundamental limit on making useful information locally accessible through clever storage alone.

title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
importance_reason: A foundational derandomization question for exact lookup: linear construction, linear storage and constant worst-case queries would give many algorithms an optimal deterministic dictionary primitive. The 2024 and 2026 string-indexing applications show concrete dependencies on dictionary construction costs.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
definitions: The universe is \(U_{w}\)={\(0,\ldots ,2\)ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.
status_note: The primary dictionary results, later applications and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No complete resolution of the specified logarithmic-word deterministic construction target was found. The accessible 2025 draft Slightly more practical deterministic static dictionaries was also inspected; it contains unfinished statements and does not claim the required linear construction, so it is not used to certify a new bound.
progress: 1999-12: Pagh gives deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction with linear space and constant lookup for \(w=O(\log  n)\); the paper contrasts this with randomized expected linear construction. | 2008: Ružić brings deterministic construction within a log log n factor of sorting time while retaining linear space and constant lookup. | 2024-10-14: The internal-pattern-matching journal paper uses general deterministic dictionaries with \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction and distinguishes restricted small instances. | 2026: Kosolobov’s CPM paper records a construction slowdown when replacing randomized dictionaries in a compressed index. This is an application, not a solution of the present static target.
working_summary: A static dictionary stores distinct integer keys together with associated values and supports exact membership queries. The question asks for deterministic linear-time construction, linear space, and constant worst-case query time on the stated word RAM. All preprocessing work must be included in the construction bound. Random hashing motivates the desired efficiency but does not itself provide a deterministic construction. A solution would give other algorithms a dependable dictionary primitive without making their preprocessing randomized or increasing their asymptotic running time.

title: Constant-time deterministic dynamic dictionaries
importance_reason: This is a basic possible separation between the power of randomization and determinism in a general-purpose data-structure primitive.
formal:
Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), there exist a uniform deterministic word-RAM program \(A_c\) and a constant \(C_c\ge1\) such that, for every integer capacity \(N\ge2\), with word size
\[
 w=\lceil c\log_2(N+2)\rceil,
\]
the program maintains a dictionary of at most \(N\) word-sized key–value pairs, starting empty, and satisfies all of the following guarantees for every valid online operation sequence: initialization costs at most \(C_cN\) instructions; at most \(C_cN\) words of space are used at any time; every lookup costs at most \(C_c\) instructions; and initialization together with every finite prefix containing \(q\) lookups and \(u\) insertions or deletions costs at most \(C_c(N+q+u)\) instructions? All answers must be exact.
question_excerpt: The research statement asks whether deterministic dictionaries must take more than constant time and describes this as a possible fundamental advantage of randomization. The card keeps its approved concrete version: logarithmic words, linear capacity space, constant worst-case lookup and constant amortized updates.
definitions:
The key and value universe is \(U_w=\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). A dictionary is a partial function \(D:U_w\rightharpoonup U_w\) with at most \(N\) keys in its domain. The capacity \(N\) and word size \(w\) are supplied at initialization and do not change during a sequence. Initially the domain is empty.

An operation is one of the following. \(\operatorname{Insert}(x,v)\) requires \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(D)\) and \(|\operatorname{dom}(D)|<N\), and changes \(D\) by assigning \(D(x)=v\). \(\operatorname{Delete}(x)\) requires \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(D)\) and removes that key. \(\operatorname{Lookup}(x)\), with any \(x\in U_w\), returns its exact stored value if present and otherwise a distinguished absent marker. The marker is separate from every word value, for example represented by a presence bit and a value word. Replacing a value can be expressed by deletion followed by insertion; it is not an extra operation requiring a separate guarantee.

A valid finite sequence respects the operation preconditions at every step. There is no bound on its length, and the same keys may be inserted and deleted repeatedly. Operations arrive one at a time. Each must terminate and return its result before the next arrives; the program has no advance access to later operations. The guarantee is for every such sequence, including one whose next operation is chosen after observing earlier answers or execution costs. Lookup may modify the internal representation, but must preserve the represented partial function.

The program has a fixed finite instruction list for the chosen \(c\), independent of \(N\), the keys, values and operation sequence. Registers and addressed memory cells contain unsigned \(w\)-bit words. Addresses must fit in one word. Unit-cost operations are reading, writing and copying words, comparisons, branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and logical shifts.
