Shifting by at least \(w\) positions yields zero. Computation involving multiple words costs the corresponding instructions. No random instruction, random seed, nonuniform advice, input-dependent oracle or uncharged table is available.

Only the current operation and its constant number of words are newly supplied. The program cannot reread a history of earlier operations from external storage; any retained information must be in its counted memory. Initialization begins with zero memory and the supplied parameters. Constructing constants that depend on \(w\), choosing hash functions, preparing lookup tables, copying records, rebuilding representations, managing memory, and writing answers all count toward the instruction cost. Fixed constants in the finite program are allowed, but a different table or program for each word size is not.

Space includes every live register, retained input word, auxiliary table and temporary workspace, including both old and new structures during rebuilding. It is measured by the number of simultaneously used words. The \(C_cN\) bound applies during initialization and all operations, not just between operations. Memory outside the retained state conveys no information from earlier operations. In particular, a table indexed by every possible key counts in full if retained or used as allocated storage.

The initialization bound, individual lookup bound, space bound and total prefix bound must all hold with constants depending only on \(c\). The aggregate prefix bound is the precise amortized convention in this card: costly individual updates are allowed, but cannot violate the bound on any prefix. No average over sequences or inputs is taken. No constant worst-case bound is required for a single insertion or deletion. Space is linear in the fixed capacity \(N\), rather than in the possibly smaller current number of keys.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed statement or its logical negation.

A positive answer must provide, for each fixed \(c\ge2\), a uniform program satisfying the exact interface, every individual lookup bound, every aggregate prefix bound and the simultaneous space bound. A family whose constants depend on \(c\) is allowed; size-dependent programs or free precomputation are not.

A negative answer must establish that for at least one fixed \(c\ge2\), no admissible uniform deterministic program and constant \(C_c\) satisfy all of the guarantees for all capacities and valid sequences. It need not prove a superconstant bound for every operation or every value of \(c\). A lower bound restricted to one hashing scheme or a comparison-only machine is insufficient, as is a conditional impossibility result under an unproved conjecture.

A static dictionary, a randomized expected-time implementation, or an algorithm with constant amortized lookup cost but occasional slow queries does not alone settle the target.
context:
Dynamic perfect hashing gives constant worst-case lookup and expected amortized constant updates with randomization. The same paper proves deterministic lower bounds for a restricted class of hashing schemes, so those lower bounds cannot be applied to every word-RAM program.

The source singles out a superconstant deterministic dictionary lower bound as an open problem. The target here keeps its concrete capacity, word-size and amortization conventions.

Uniform deterministic dictionaries are known with query/update tradeoffs. The cited construction avoids free word-size-dependent constants, but its stated tradeoff does not provide constant bounds for both operations.

The STOC 2025 succinct dictionary result concerns static sets and includes random hash bits. Its worst-case constant lookup guarantee does not supply fully deterministic dynamic maintenance.

The 2026 fully indexable dictionary supports rank and select as well as updates. Its stated time includes \(\log_w n\), where \(n\) is the current number of stored keys, and therefore does not give constant update time throughout the logarithmic-word capacity regime.
why: A fully deterministic dictionary with these guarantees would match the basic operation bounds of randomized dynamic hashing in linear space. An unconditional obstruction would establish a substantive limitation of determinism for this central data-structure interface.
status_note: The bounded primary-source review through 17 September 2026 found no verified deterministic implementation or unconditional impossibility result for the selected fixed-capacity word-RAM target. Restricted hashing lower bounds, static succinct dictionaries and the checked 2026 rank/select result do not resolve it. This is not exhaustive certification of openness or an independent audit of every cited proof.
progress: 1994: Dynamic perfect hashing provides the randomized benchmark; deterministic lower bounds are proved for restricted hashing schemes. | 2007: The research statement highlights the unresolved deterministic constant-time regime. | 2008: Uniform deterministic dictionaries provide explicit query/update tradeoffs. | 2025-03-26: The revised static succinct dictionary result provides worst-case constant lookup. | 2026-03-24: A deterministic dynamic fully indexable dictionary improves redundancy while retaining a nonconstant time term in the general logarithmic-word regime.
working_summary: A dictionary stores word-sized keys and values while keys are repeatedly inserted and deleted. Every lookup must return its answer in constant worst-case time, and updates share a constant amortized budget. The question asks whether a uniform deterministic program can achieve these bounds using space linear in a fixed capacity. Randomized hashing gives the basic benchmark, while restricted deterministic lower bounds do not cover every permitted program. A solution must give a complete Lean-checked construction or impossibility proof with the specified machine and online guarantees.

title: Multiphase conjecture
importance_reason: The multiphase conjecture is a central candidate for proving polynomial operation lower bounds for dynamic data structures.
formal:
Do there exist real constants \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) such that every admissible uniform, always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm for the following three-phase problem, with \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\), satisfies
\[
 \tau_A(n)=\Omega(n^\delta)?
\]
Phase I receives \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\) and preprocesses them. Phase II receives \(T\subseteq[n]\) and updates the retained state. Phase III receives \(i\in[k]\) and answers whether \(S_i\cap T=\varnothing\). The normalized expected overhead is
\[
 \tau_A(n)=\max\left\{1,\frac{t_1(n)}{kn},\frac{t_2(n)}n,t_3(n)\right\},
\]
where \(t_j(n)\) is the worst-input expected number of instructions used in Phase \(j\), as defined below. The lower bound must hold for all sufficiently large integer \(n\), with no restriction on query adaptivity.
question_excerpt: Conjecture 1 asks for fixed exponents gamma>1 and delta>0 forcing polynomial overhead in a three-phase word-RAM set-disjointness problem, when the number of stored sets is polynomial in the universe size. This card keeps the previously selected exact number of sets, zero-error expected costs and explicit uniform machine convention.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\). All subsets, including the empty set and the full universe, are permitted, and repetitions among the \(S_j\) are allowed. The first input is the concatenation of the \(k\) length-\(n\) incidence vectors in index order. The second input is the length-\(n\) incidence vector of \(T\). Each bit string is packed consecutively into words, with known zero padding in the last word. Phase III supplies the integer \(i\). The integer size parameters \(n,k\) are public from Phase I onward; the program is not required to compute \(\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\) from a real constant supplied as an oracle.

A candidate uses a fixed integer \(a\ge2\) and words of
\[
 w=\lceil a\log_2(n+k+2)\rceil
\]
bits. One finite program, with a fixed entry point for each phase, works for every \(n\) in this regime. The program may depend on the fixed regime \(\gamma\); it has no size-dependent advice or free precomputed table. The claim quantifies over every fixed \(a\) and every such uniform program.

The machine has word-sized registers and memory cells, with addresses fitting in one word. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and logical shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Producing an independent uniform random \(w\)-bit word also costs one instruction. Multiword computations cost their component instructions. Inputs are presented in explicit memory arrays at the start of their phase; all accesses, initialization performed by the program, table construction, copying, control and output are charged. Other memory initially contains zero. There is no extra free oracle for the sets.

Memory persists between phases. Phase I cannot see \(T\) or \(i\); Phase II cannot see \(i\). Phase III receives only \(i\), public size parameters and the retained memory, including any retained input arrays. Access to that state is charged in the usual way. Every phase may choose its next address adaptively using all information it has read. In particular, the query may alternate arbitrarily between information from the first two phases. There is no layering or nonadaptivity restriction.

Fix the entire input \((S_1,\ldots,S_k,T,i)\) independently of all random words. Each phase must terminate almost surely, and every terminating execution must return the correct disjointness bit. Deterministic algorithms are included. Let \(C_j\) be the random number of instructions in Phase \(j\). Define
\[
 t_1(n)=\max_{S_1,\ldots,S_k}\mathbb E[C_1],\qquad
 t_2(n)=\max_{S_1,\ldots,S_k,T}\mathbb E[C_2],\qquad
 t_3(n)=\max_{S_1,\ldots,S_k,T,i}\mathbb E[C_3].
\]
Each expectation includes the randomness in all preceding phases that determines the retained state, as well as new randomness in the current phase. There is no averaging over inputs and no conditioning on a favorable previous state. Infinite expectations are allowed and make the corresponding overhead infinite. The maxima range over all valid fixed inputs at that size.

The notation \(\tau_A(n)=\Omega(n^\delta)\) means that there exist \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that \(\tau_A(n)\ge c n^\delta\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). These two constants may depend on the program and the fixed parameters. In contrast, \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) must be chosen before quantifying over all programs and word-size constants. Preprocessing is part of the overhead; unrestricted preprocessing with only memory probes charged is a different, stronger-model conjecture.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of this existence claim or of its logical negation in the stated model.

A positive answer must choose universal \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) and prove the eventual normalized lower bound against every admissible program and fixed word-size constant, including unrestricted adaptive Las Vegas algorithms.

For a negative answer, prove that for every \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) there are an admissible program \(A\) and fixed \(a\ge2\) for which \(\tau_A\) is not \(\Omega(n^\delta)\): for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), some integer \(n\ge N\) satisfies \(\tau_A(n)<c n^\delta\). The counterexample program may depend on \(\gamma,\delta\). A single algorithm with subpolynomial overhead is sufficient when established in every required regime, but is not the definition of the negation.

A conditional consequence of 3SUM hardness, a lower bound confined to semi-adaptive queries, or a polylogarithmic bound for the Inner Product variant does not alone settle this target. The Lean proof must cover the specified inputs, costs, zero-error convention and quantifier order.
context:
The source charges preprocessing as well as the later update and query, and gives reductions transferring a polynomial overhead to several dynamic problems. It also supplies conditional support from 3SUM hardness.

Ko and Weinstein prove a polynomial lower bound when queries have layered adaptivity: after moving to the update layer, they cannot return to the preprocessing layer. The card permits unrestricted alternation.

The 2025 linear-operator preprint states partial progress for an Inner Product communication variant with superpolynomially many queries. Both the predicate and the parameter regime differ from this card.

The 2025 dynamic preprint states a superlogarithmic bound for Inner Product. This is progress at a different asymptotic scale from the required polynomial overhead.

The 2026 report states an \(\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) Inner Product bound and explicitly excludes Disjointness from its lifting criterion. The theorem statement was checked; its full proof was not independently audited. It does not announce a resolution of this card.
why: This staged problem is a candidate for unconditional polynomial operation lower bounds for dynamic data structures, including directed reachability. Its conjectured overhead is much larger than the logarithmic bounds accessible in general models.
status_note: The original word-RAM conjecture remains unresolved in the bounded primary-source review through 17 September 2026. The checked semi-adaptive theorem and 2025–2026 Inner Product claims do not supply an unrestricted polynomial SetDisjointness bound or a counterexample. This records the scope of the checks, not exhaustive certification of openness or independent verification of all preprint proofs.
progress: 2010: The three-phase word-RAM conjecture and its dynamic-problem consequences are proposed. | 2019-10-29: A polynomial lower bound is obtained for queries with layered adaptivity. | 2025-10-22: Two preprints state progress for communication and dynamic Inner Product variants. | 2026-04-05: A report states a nearly log-squared Inner Product lower bound while excluding Disjointness from its lifting criterion.
working_summary: First, a data structure receives a polynomial-size family of subsets of a finite universe. It later receives another subset, and only afterward learns which stored set must be tested for disjointness. The conjecture requires polynomial overhead in at least one of the three normalized expected phase costs. The model permits arbitrary adaptive memory access, and recent restricted or Inner Product lower bounds do not cover the full target. An accepted resolution must be unconditional and completely checked in Lean with the stated quantifiers and zero-error guarantees.

title: Superlinear cell-probe lower bounds for succinct Boolean matrix-vector products
importance_reason: A fundamental unconditional lower-bound target for a central matrix-query problem. Its importance lies in handling general succinct encodings and adaptive word probes, beyond strong but representation-specific known results.
formal:
For every family of deterministic exact static cell-probe data structures representing arbitrary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) in \(n^2+o(n^2)\) bits, with word length
\[w_n=\left\lceil\log_2(n^2+1)\right\rceil,\]
must its worst-case number \(T(n)\) of word probes for answering a Boolean matrix-vector query satisfy
\[T(n)=\omega(n)?\]
The representation may encode the whole matrix arbitrarily; it need not retain the original matrix as a separately readable array. Computation between probes and preprocessing time are uncharged, as specified below.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether succinct data structures for Boolean matrix-vector multiplication must use more than a linear number of cell probes per query.
definitions:
For \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and a query \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\), the required answer is the entire vector \(y=Mv\in\{0,1\}^n\) over the Boolean semiring:
\[y_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^n(M_{ij}\wedge v_j),\qquad i\in[n].\]
Here \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) are logical AND and OR. This is not multiplication over the two-element field, where addition would instead be parity. Every matrix and every query vector is allowed.

For each integer \(n\ge2\), choose an integer number of memory cells \(S_n\), with \(1\le S_n\le2^{w_n}\), and an encoding map
\[E_n:\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\longrightarrow(\{0,1\}^{w_n})^{S_n}.\]
The stored memory on input \(M\) is exactly \(E_n(M)\). All persistent matrix-dependent information must be in these cells. The space bound includes padding to complete words: define \(r_n=S_nw_n-n^2\), and require \(r_n\ge0\) and \(r_n/n^2\to0\). This is the meaning of succinct storage. No particular rate such as \(r_n=n^{7/4}\), and no smaller fixed redundancy budget, is imposed.

The query gets \(n\) and \(v\) for free, plus access to the stored cells at addresses \(0,\ldots,S_n-1\). One probe reads one entire \(w_n\)-bit word. The next address may depend on the query and all words previously read. Arbitrary finite computation and temporary workspace between probes cost nothing; reading the query vector and producing the output vector also cost nothing. Temporary state starts empty apart from the query and public size parameters, so there is no free matrix-dependent advice. The representation is static and read-only, and each query starts afresh; no state left by earlier queries is available.

Equivalently, for each \(n\) and query \(v\), the query rule is a finite decision tree whose internal nodes specify cell addresses, whose outgoing edges are indexed by possible word contents, and whose leaves specify an output vector. Its leaves must give the correct \(Mv\) on every stored encoding. The trees and their computations may depend on \(n\) and \(v\), but not on \(M\) except through the probed words. There is no restriction on their description size or on the encoding's preprocessing time. Thus the lower bound is in the usual permissive, nonuniform cell-probe model; restricting the query computation to an efficient word-RAM program would be a different target. The formulation fixes the deterministic exact version: no random coins or error probability are allowed in the data structures quantified over here.

For one such family \(\mathcal D\), let
\[T_{\mathcal D}(n)=\max_{M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n},\ v\in\{0,1\}^n}
\#\{\text{word probes on query }v\text{ after storing }M\}.\]
Repeated reads count repeatedly. The assertion means that for every eligible family \(\mathcal D\) and every real \(C>0\), some \(n_0\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal D}(n)>Cn\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on the family and \(C\). The fixed choice \(w_n=\Theta(\log n)\) makes words large enough for cell addresses without allowing one word to hold the whole matrix.

A systematic representation stores the unchanged matrix and separate redundant bits. That is a restriction on \(E_n\), not part of this general succinct target. The source page does not require that restriction; its example upper bound happens to have it. The distinction matters for applying later lower bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal superlinear lower bound. An affirmative answer must cover every deterministic exact representation and adaptive query family with the stated \(n^2+o(n^2)\) total storage. A negative answer must exhibit an eligible family, a constant \(C>0\), and arbitrarily large \(n\) with \(T(n)\le Cn\); a bound holding at all sufficiently large sizes is sufficient but not necessary to negate the displayed limit. A lower bound only for systematic encodings, nonadaptive queries, smaller redundancy, individual matrix-entry probes, or charged word-RAM computation does not establish this statement without the needed conversion. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance, not an approximation of a finite running time.
context:
The matrix contains n² independent bits, but one query asks only for n Boolean answers. Preprocessing can reorganize the information before any query arrives. The question asks whether nearly minimal storage still forces substantially more than n memory accesses on a worst-case query, even when all arithmetic and logical work is free.

The source contrasts this model with the online matrix-vector conjecture for ordinary computation. A time lower bound in a word-RAM model charges operations that the cell-probe model ignores. The online conjecture therefore cannot simply be substituted for an unconditional memory-access lower bound.

Larsen and Williams give a deterministic cell-probe structure using \(O(n^{7/4}/\sqrt w)\) probes per query and only \(O(n^{7/4}\sqrt w)\) bits beyond the stored matrix. With logarithmic words this is succinct and polynomially faster in probe count than scanning all matrix entries. It remains superlinear and hence does not refute the proposed lower bound.

The 2018 paper proves a much stronger tradeoff for systematic representations. Its Theorem 1.2 gives \(t_{\rm bit}r=\Omega(n^3)\) when \(n\le r\le n^2/4\), even for queries correct with probability at least \(1-1/n\), and permits reading all redundant bits. Here \(t_{\rm bit}\) counts original matrix entries, not words. A word-probe consequence loses a factor of \(w\), yielding \(\Omega(n^3/(rw))\) in that restricted representation model.

Two qualifications prevent that theorem from settling this card as stated. It retains the matrix in its original layout, whereas a general succinct representation may encode every bit differently. Moreover, even its word-probe consequence is superlinear only for suitably smaller redundancy; arbitrary o(n²) redundancy need not be o(n²/w). The title of a succinct-data-structure theorem alone does not establish the general claim.

The same paper improves the systematic upper bound to roughly n³ᐟ² probes and redundant bits, up to logarithmic factors at logarithmic word size, using randomized queries. This is useful progress on the tradeoff, while the exact deterministic lower-bound question here remains a separately specified target.
why: A superlinear lower bound with almost no storage overhead would go beyond the standard static-data-structure barriers for this central problem. It would isolate an information-access obstruction independently of how much computation is performed between memory reads.
status_note: Source-open for the explicitly stated general succinct deterministic cell-probe model. The complete 2017 problem page and the original upper-bound theorem were checked; the 2018 paper’s main results explicitly concern systematic representations, with the stated lower theorem counting original matrix entries. Its unrestricted-redundancy word-probe conversion and representation restriction do not establish this exact target. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. This is a source/formulation and theorem-scope review, not independent verification or Lean formalization of every cited proof.
progress: 2017: Problem 75 asks for an unconditional superlinear query lower bound for succinct Boolean matrix-vector structures. | 2017: The cell-probe upper bound accompanying faster online matrix-vector multiplication uses subquadratic probe complexity and subquadratic redundancy. | 2018: The STOC paper proves near-matching systematic space–probe tradeoffs, explicitly distinguishing them from unrestricted succinct encodings and from word-probe bounds.
working_summary: The input is an arbitrary Boolean matrix, stored using only a vanishing fraction of extra bits beyond its n²-bit information content. A query asks for the entire Boolean product with one vector, charging only logarithmic-word memory probes. The target asks whether every deterministic exact adaptive structure needs a worst-case probe count growing faster than n. Known strong tradeoffs retain the original matrix layout and count individual entries, so their scope and word-size conversion matter. The card keeps arbitrary succinct encodings and all subquadratic redundancies rather than substituting a narrower solved model.

title: Randomized complexity of online labeling
importance_reason: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal amortized expected number of relabelings per insertion or deletion for randomized online list labeling with at most \(n\) live items and labels in \([2n]\), against an oblivious adversary. The target is one asymptotic rate \(f(n)\) with a matching upper bound and lower bound in the model below.
definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. An upper rate \(f\ge1\) means a uniform online algorithm and a constant \(C\) satisfy expected total cost at most \(C(n+M f(n))\) for every capacity and every finite valid sequence of \(M\) updates. For tightness, every algorithm and every rate \(g\) permitting such a bound must have \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\). Constants are independent of the sequence and capacity. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update. Here \(f(n)\) and competing rates \(g(n)\) concern integer capacities \(n\ge2\), and the asymptotic lower comparison is as \(n\to\infty\).
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously defined rate \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) and complete Lean-checked upper and matching lower bounds up to constant factors in the stated expected amortized movement model. The upper bound must provide one uniform online algorithm with expected total cost \(O(n+Mf(n))\) for every capacity and oblivious valid sequence. The lower bound must establish the stated \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\) requirement for every competing permitted algorithm and achievable rate. An unbounded polylogarithmic factor or a lower bound only for a restricted algorithm family does not meet the target.
context:
List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.
why: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The reviewed See-Saw theorem gives the stated cubic-log-log upper factor and records the logarithmic general randomized lower bound. The independent near-logarithmic writes result also retains growing factors. No constant-factor matching resolution of the selected oblivious constant-slack model was located in the bounded subsequent-work search.
progress: 2017: The randomized online-labeling question is posed in the seminar report. | 2024-05-01: See-Saw Theorem 1 achieves \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) at constant slack, while the recorded general randomized lower bound is \(\Omega(\log n)\).
working_summary: An ordered list is stored using a fixed range of numerical labels. Insertions and deletions must preserve label order while keeping spare labels available. The cost counts how many existing items receive a different label. Randomization achieves nearly logarithmic expected amortized cost in the cited result. The remaining task is to determine the optimal asymptotic rate for constant slack.

title: Amortized decrease-key complexity of standard pairing heaps
importance_reason: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.
formal:
Determine an explicit asymptotic growth rate \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to[1,\infty)\) that is a tight amortized decrease-key charge for the standard two-pass pairing heap. For every finite legal operation sequence \(\mathcal S\) starting from empty heaps and having at most \(N\) live items in all heaps combined, require
\[
W(\mathcal S)\le C\bigl(a(\mathcal S)+b(\mathcal S)\log_2(N+2)+c(\mathcal S)f(N)\bigr)
\]
for one absolute \(C\). Here \(a\) counts make-heap, insert, meld and find-min operations, \(b\) counts delete-min operations, and \(c\) counts decrease-key operations. Tightness means that every charge function satisfying such an inequality is \(\Omega(f(N))\), with the quantifiers specified below. The algorithm itself and the other-operation charges are fixed.
question_excerpt: The long-standing question is the tight amortized complexity of decrease-key in the standard pairing heap. The 2026 pure-heap paper explicitly separates the standard algorithm and retains the gap between known lower bounds and its announced improvement. This card fixes the other-operation charges and asks for the complete asymptotic rate.
definitions:
Each heap is empty or is a single rooted tree of items. Every item has an opaque key in a totally ordered set and a stable identity. Ties are resolved by a fixed total order on identities, so every comparison has a deterministic winner. A parent’s key, including this tie-breaking order, is no greater than a child’s. Children form a left-to-right list. A link of two disjoint trees compares their roots and makes the losing root the new leftmost child of the winner. A cut removes one parent-child edge and detaches the entire child subtree while preserving the order of remaining children.

Make-heap creates an empty heap. Find-min returns its root, or an empty marker. Insert creates a new singleton item, links it with the heap’s root if present and returns a stable item handle. Meld takes two distinct item-disjoint heaps, links their roots when both are nonempty and returns the resulting heap, invalidating the old heap handles. If either is empty, the other tree is returned. Item handles remain valid until their items are deleted, including through melds.

Decrease-key receives a heap handle, a handle to an item in it and a new key no larger than its old key. Replace the key. If the item is not the root, cut its entire subtree and link that subtree to the heap root, even if no heap-order violation would have occurred without the cut. If it is the root, no link or cut is needed. The operation’s inputs and membership promises are supplied, so searching for the item is not required.

Delete-min requires a nonempty heap. Remove its root and detach its children into their existing ordered root list. In the pairing pass, link the first and second roots, then the third and fourth, and so on from left to right, leaving a final unpaired root unchanged. The resulting trees retain their pair order. In the assembly pass, start with the rightmost resulting tree and repeatedly link it to the next tree to its left, moving right to left until one tree remains. This becomes the heap. If the deleted root had no children, the result is empty. Changing the order of either pass, omitting the assembly pass, adding rank-driven restructuring or using multiple retained trees defines a different heap.

A direct pointer implementation stores a constant number of fields per item, including the key and enough child, sibling and parent information for a cut given a handle in constant time. Comparisons of keys or identities, pointer reads and writes, branches and allocating or releasing a constant-size record are unit-cost primitives. There is no arithmetic on keys and no hidden balancing operation. Let \(\lambda\) be the number of links and \(\chi\) the number of edges cut, including child edges detached during delete-min. Define
\[
W(\mathcal S)=a(\mathcal S)+b(\mathcal S)+c(\mathcal S)+\lambda+\chi.
\]
This is within constant factors of the work of the specified direct implementation. Only this fixed sequential deterministic algorithm is being analyzed.

The integer \(N\ge1\) is a global upper bound on simultaneously live items throughout the sequence, not its total insertions, length, number of heap objects or final size. Sequences may create arbitrarily many heaps, interleave operations on them, merge them and leave items undeleted at the end. Every operation contributes to its count, even if it returns an empty result or changes no key value. The inequality must hold for every \(N\) and every sequence obeying that live-item bound, with no uncharged initial nonempty heaps or additive credit depending on the sequence.

Call any function \(d:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to[1,\infty)\) admissible if there exists a constant \(C_d\ge1\) such that the displayed inequality holds with \(d\) in place of \(f\), for all \(N\) and all permitted sequences. A tight answer consists of an explicit rate \(f\) which is admissible and satisfies
\[
\forall d\text{ admissible}\ \exists k_d>0\ \exists N_d\ge1\ \forall N\ge N_d:\quad d(N)\ge k_d f(N).
\]
The lower-comparison constants may depend on \(d\) and its admissibility constant, but not on \(N\) or a chosen sequence. Requiring one fixed lower-comparison constant for every rescaling of every admissible function would be inappropriate. No specific conjectured rate is imposed.
answer_criterion:
Supply an explicit asymptotic rate and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of both admissibility and the matching universal lower statement. A characterization that merely renames the worst sequence cost or repeats the definition of admissibility is not a determination of the rate. Constants hidden by asymptotic notation must have the dependencies specified above.

A better upper bound without matching tightness does not complete the task. Neither does a tight bound for another heap variant, or an analysis that increases the allowed insert or meld charge without proving the displayed inequality. Amortized bounds for individual operations from separate analyses cannot be combined without a simultaneous total-cost proof. This is an asymptotic classification up to constant factors, not a finite numerical approximation task.
context:
The immediate decrease-key operation uses only a constant number of pointer changes. Its amortized charge measures the extra work these changes can cause during later delete-min operations.

A logarithmic-logarithmic lower bound rules out the original constant-amortized expectation under the relevant other-operation charges. This review records it through the later primary papers’ statements of Fredman’s result.

Iacono’s analysis gives constant insert and meld charges with logarithmic delete-min and decrease-key. Its comparison table explicitly warns against combining operation charges from unrelated amortized analyses.

Pettie’s sublogarithmic analysis also charges insert and meld a nonconstant amount. That result alone is not a simultaneous upper bound under this card’s constant-charge convention.

The July 2026 paper proves \(O(\log\log N\,\log\log\log N)\) for pure heaps and announces \(O((\log\log N)^2\log\log\log N)\) for standard heaps in forthcoming work. The announcement and the remaining tightness question are distinct; no companion proof was independently checked.
why: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.
status_note: The July 2026 source explicitly retains the tightness gap and distinguishes its proved pure-heap analysis from an announced standard-heap improvement. Bounded primary-source searches through 17 September 2026 found no verified tight analysis under the stated simultaneous charges. No independent verification of the announced companion proof or Fredman’s full lower-bound proof is claimed.
progress: 1999: Fredman establishes a logarithmic-logarithmic decrease-key obstruction, as described in the later primary sources. | 2000: Iacono’s work establishes constant insert/meld charges while allowing logarithmic decrease-key; the expanded account appears on arXiv in 2011. | 2005: Pettie obtains sublogarithmic charges for insert, meld and decrease-key, retaining logarithmic delete-min. | 2026-07-25: Pure heaps receive a near-log-log analysis; an improved standard-heap bound is announced, and a matching bound remains open.
working_summary: The standard pairing heap performs a left-to-right pairing pass and a right-to-left assembly pass when deleting the minimum. The question asks for the tight asymptotic amortized cost of decrease-key while keeping the stated charges for all other operations. The bound must hold on every finite sequence from empty heaps, in terms of the maximum simultaneous live-item count. Different heap variants and operation charges from separate analyses cannot be substituted; a 2026 improvement for standard heaps is recorded as an announcement. A complete Lean-checked upper analysis and matching lower bound are required, not just another improvement.

title: Space-query exponent curve of 3SUM indexing
importance_reason: The curve asks how much information about a quadratic family of sums must be stored to support reusable membership queries, a general representation barrier underlying several string indexes.
formal: Determine \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) for every real \(s\in[1,2]\), where \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) is the infimum of real \(t\ge0\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform randomized 3SUM index uses \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and answers queries in \(O(n^{t+\eta})\) worst-case time.
definitions: The input is two sets \(A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n^4-1\}\), each of size \(n\ge2\), supplied explicitly. A query \(z\in\{0,\ldots,2n^4-2\}\) asks whether \(z=a+b\) for some \(a\in A,b\in B\), using ordinary addition. Set \(L=n\) and fix \(d=10\) in the word-RAM model below. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing may take arbitrary time but must terminate almost surely; this preserves the preexisting card’s space-hardness convention. Every retained input, table and random seed is counted. Each fixed input/query is answered correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) over preprocessing and query randomness, and space and query time bounds hold on every random outcome. Queries cannot communicate input-dependent state for free. For each chosen \(s,t,\eta\), one finite program pair and constants handle every \(n\); there is no per-size choice of advice. Parameters select programs and are not real-number computational inputs. The infimum need not be attained. The quantity is a dimensionless query exponent, and it ignores subpolynomial factors only through the displayed quantifiers.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire stated domain and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(|g(x)-\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(x)|\le 1/100\) at every point. Uniform certified upper and lower bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify via their midpoint. Exact equality also qualifies. A plot, finitely many sample points, one-sided improvement, or a renamed copy of the defining infimum is insufficient. This numerical acceptance tolerance does not establish a separate exact threshold conjecture.
context:
An index is built once for all future sum-membership queries. Storing every potential sum and scanning one input set occupy very different points of the space-query frontier.

The original framework separates different 3SUM-indexing hardness hypotheses; its strongest old tradeoff should not be treated as a theorem.

The revised 2026 paper improves intermediate space regimes without determining the entire frontier.

The previous card asked specifically for genuinely subquadratic space with polylogarithmic queries. The present curve broadens the target; a query exponent of zero or a numerical approximation to it does not by itself establish a polylogarithmic bound.
why: The curve asks how much information about a quadratic family of sums must be stored to support reusable membership queries, a general representation barrier underlying several string indexes.
status_note: Primary sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the precise target was located; this is a bounded literature review, not exhaustive certification of current openness. User-approved consolidation broadens TCS-7333 from its binary polylogarithmic-query endpoint to the underlying exponent curve. Its old statement is preserved in formulation history. Unrestricted preprocessing and the polynomial universe are retained; 0.01 accuracy does not decide every exact endpoint.
progress: 2017: The space-hardness framework distinguishes weak and strong 3SUM-indexing conjectures. | 2026-04-23: The revised work improves the tradeoff in intermediate space regimes.
working_summary: Two integer sets are stored before membership queries arrive. A query asks whether its number belongs to their sumset. The target is the best query exponent at each allowed storage exponent. All retained information is charged even though preprocessing time is unrestricted. The numerical curve target is broader than the saved polylogarithmic-query existence question.

title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
importance_reason: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.
formal: Is the following statement true? For every admissible uniform static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness, with worst-case retained space \(S(N)\) words and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) steps, there exist constants \(c>0\), \(b\in\mathbb N\), and \(N_0\ge2\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log_2(N+2))^b\) for every integer \(N\ge N_0\). For every integer \(N\ge2\), the input is a list \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) of nonempty subsets of \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with \(1\le m\le N\) and total size \(N=\sum_{i=1}^m|A_i|\). A query supplies indices \(i,j\in[m]\) and must return whether \(A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\).
definitions:
The input gives \(N\), \(m\), the lengths of the sets, and each set's elements explicitly as words, without repetitions within a set. Different listed sets may be equal. The indices of two stored sets are the whole query; there is no new query set. The case \(i=j\) is allowed. Each admissible data structure is a fixed pair of finite programs, one for preprocessing and one for queries, working for every input size. The word length is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). The sequential word RAM has word-sized registers and addressed memory cells; each read, write, comparison, branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero integer, Boolean bit operation, or logical shift costs one step. Arithmetic stored in a word is modulo \(2^w\), and a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Addresses fit in one word. Outputting the answer and all memory operations are charged.

Preprocessing must halt on every valid input and random execution, but its finite running time is unrestricted. Only the resulting stored representation is accessible to a query; the original input is not available for free. The representation includes all retained input-dependent tables, seeds, pointers and metadata. A query begins with its two indices, the input-size metadata and that representation, with no input-dependent private state inherited from earlier queries. It leaves the representation unchanged. Temporary query storage starts empty; accessing or filling it costs time. There is no advice, oracle, input-specific code, or uncharged precomputed table.

The two programs may generate independent uniformly random words in one step. For every fixed input and fixed valid query, the probability of the correct empty/nonempty answer, over preprocessing randomness and independent query randomness, is at least \(2/3\). The query bound holds for every random outcome, including erroneous ones. Let \(s(N)\) be the maximum retained word count over all valid inputs of total size exactly \(N\) and preprocessing outcomes, and let \(T(N)\ge1\) be the maximum query step count over those inputs, their produced representations, all valid queries and all query outcomes. These maxima are required to be finite. Use the saved card's space normalization \(S(N)=\max\{N,s(N)\}\), and restrict to structures with \(S(N)\le N^2\). Unused cells may be padded. All constants in the asserted bound may depend on the fixed programs, but not on \(N\), the input family, or the query. The displayed bound is the precise meaning of \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\); it suppresses only fixed powers of a logarithm, not an arbitrary \(N^{o(1)}\) factor.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal lower bound or its logical negation in the specified model. A refutation must violate every admissible polylogarithmic lower-bound factor for one fixed admissible data structure; a fixed logarithmic improvement alone is not a refutation. The negation is an asymptotic assertion and need not have a finite counterexample. Results conditional on Strong SetDisjointness, or lower bounds only for preprocessing time, do not establish this lower bound.
context:
Goldstein, Kopelowitz, Lewenstein and Porat formulate the Strong SetDisjointness conjecture as \(S=\widetilde\Omega(N^2/T^2)\). Their \(N\) is total set incidence count, not the number of sets. The source explicitly uses the tilde notation to suppress polylogarithmic factors.

A matching upper tradeoff has retained space \(O(N+N^2/t^2)\) words and query time \(O(t)\), in particular \(S T^2=O(N^2)\) in the relevant range \(1\le t\le\sqrt N\). This upper bound does not establish the conjectured universal lower bound.

The 2020 algorithms of Kopelowitz and Vassilevska Williams improve the tradeoff between preprocessing time and query time. Their analysis measures preprocessing time separately from retained storage, so its improved preprocessing bound does not refute this space-query conjecture.

Huang, Tao and Wang use the same space-query conjecture in their 2026 work on join sampling, in a word-RAM with logarithmic word length. Their Lemma 21 relates an expected-query-time formulation for exact answers to the formulation with deterministic query time. They assume the conjecture rather than prove its lower bound.

This review retains the card's explicitly chosen uniform, bounded-error word-RAM convention and normalized space range. The 2017 conjecture itself does not spell out these machine, uniformity and error details. Relabelling the elements of the union into \([N]\) preserves every intersection; empty sets and self-pair queries are trivial.

The Strong 3SUM-Indexing conjecture mentioned alongside SetDisjointness in the original paper was subsequently refuted. The 2019 bounded-universe paper explicitly distinguishes that development and continues to assume Strong SetDisjointness for its conditional results.
why: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.
status_note: Strong SetDisjointness is conjectured in the 2017 source and is still assumed in the checked ICDT 2026 paper. The bounded primary-source review on 16 September 2026 found no matching proof or refutation of the saved bounded-error word-RAM target; later use of the conjecture is not an exhaustive current-status certificate.
progress: 2017: The source proposes the full \(S T^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\) lower-bound conjecture and records its matching upper tradeoff. | 2019: The bounded-universe results assume Strong SetDisjointness. The paper separately records that the stronger 3SUM-indexing conjecture has been refuted. | 2020: Improved algorithms address the preprocessing-time/query-time tradeoff, while retaining the distinction between preprocessing work and stored space. | 2026: The join-sampling paper still uses Strong SetDisjointness as a conjecture and proves a transfer to its expected-query-time variant for exact answers.
working_summary: A family of sets is stored before the queries arrive. Each query names two stored sets and asks whether their intersection is empty. The conjecture says that retained space times squared query time cannot beat the squared total input size by more than polylogarithmic factors. Known upper bounds attain that tradeoff, while recent work still uses its lower-bound direction as an assumption. Preprocessing time is unrestricted and remains a separate resource from retained storage.

title: Superconstant word-RAM time for prefix-\(U_1\)
importance_reason: A minimal dynamic set primitive whose superconstant word-RAM lower bound would establish a basic computational barrier and settle conditional constant-time classifications for regular word and tree languages.
formal:
Is it impossible to maintain a length-\(n\) bit sequence under substitutions and answer prefix-AND queries using a deterministic uniform word-RAM data structure with \(O(n)\) preprocessing and \(O(1)\) worst-case time for each update and each query?

An update \(\operatorname{set}(i,b)\) replaces the bit at position \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(b\in\{0,1\}\). A query at \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) must return
\[\operatorname{prefix}(k)=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}b_i,\qquad\operatorname{prefix}(0)=1.\]
The word length is \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer constant \(c\ge1\). The impossibility is to hold for every such fixed constant and every correct data structure in the model below.

This retains the source's worst-case time convention. The target is absence of any constant bound, not a prescribed logarithmic lower-bound rate or the stronger exclusion of amortized constant time.
question_excerpt: There is no structure for prefix-U1 with complexity \(O(1)\).
definitions:
The sequence length \(n\ge1\) remains fixed for the lifetime of the structure. Its initial bits are supplied explicitly, one per input cell. Preprocessing receives \(n\) and that sequence and must run in at most \(K(n+1)\) word operations for one fixed constant \(K\). It builds the state from which all subsequent operations are served. The two-element monoid \(U_1=\{0,1\}\) has multiplication Boolean AND, with identity one and absorbing element zero. Hence a nonempty prefix has product zero exactly when it contains a zero.

Equivalently, the zero positions form a changing subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Substitution adds or removes a supplied position, and the complemented prefix answer says whether \(S\cap\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is nonempty. Repeating a substitution with the present value is allowed and must also meet the cost bound. Queries do not ask for the minimum element itself or a predecessor of the query position. No insertion or deletion of sequence positions, change of \(n\), or restriction on which positions may change is included.

Use a finite-program unit-cost random-access machine whose cells and addresses are unsigned \(w\)-bit words. One operation can read or write one addressed cell, copy a word, compare two words or branch, apply word addition, subtraction or multiplication, apply unsigned integer division or remainder by a nonzero word, apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT, or shift a word left or right by a supplied integer amount. Arithmetic results are reduced modulo \(2^w\), except that division and remainder have their usual unsigned integer meanings; left shifts discard overflowing bits, right shifts insert zeros, and shifts by at least \(w\) give zero. Division by zero must be avoided or handled as an error, not an extra operation. Constant literals are fixed by the finite program. The program can use \(n\) and \(w\); both are supplied at initialization. Each listed operation has unit cost. No other arbitrary word function or input-dependent instruction is provided.

There are at most \(2^w\) addressable cells, all initially zero except the supplied input. Every read, write and table construction counts; no nonuniform precomputed table or advice depending on \(n\) is supplied free of charge. There is no additional linear-space requirement: the machine may use its polynomially many addressable cells, even if many were populated by previous updates. The fixed program, positive integer \(c\) and preprocessing constant \(K\) may depend on the data structure, but never on the input length, initial bits or future history. These explicit word operations instantiate the source's unit-cost arithmetic RAM convention, with only logarithmically many bits per word.

Updates and queries arrive one at a time. The answer to each query must be exactly correct for the state after all earlier updates, before a later operation is revealed. Every finite operation history is allowed, including histories selected using earlier answers and histories much longer than \(n\). All operation invocations must terminate. The structure is deterministic, with no error probability and no random or expected-time convention.

A constant-time structure would have one constant \(T\) bounding the work of every individual update and query, for every initial sequence, every length and every history. The work done by one operation cannot be charged to earlier or later operations. Allowing an onset \(n_0\) rather than all lengths gives the same existence question, since the finitely many smaller lengths can be handled separately. Consequently a positive impossibility result can be expressed as follows: for every correct linear-preprocessing structure, every proposed bound \(B\) and every onset \(N\), there is a length \(n\ge N\), an initial sequence and a finite operation history in which an individual operation takes more than \(B\) steps. No particular function tending to infinity is prescribed in advance.

The cell-probe model, mentioned in the context, charges only memory accesses and allows arbitrary computation on values already read at no cost. It is more permissive than the word-operation model just defined; a counting argument that ignores all such computation cannot automatically establish the requested word-RAM barrier.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the claimed nonexistence. A proof must exclude every correct deterministic uniform structure with linear preprocessing and fixed logarithmic word-length constant from having a common constant worst-case bound for both operations. It may give a quantitative lower bound, but must justify that it excludes all constants in this model. A refutation must give a single finite-program structure, some fixed word-length constant, linear preprocessing and exact constant worst-case bounds for both updates and queries on every history. An amortized or expected constant upper bound alone does not refute the specified worst-case conjecture. A lower bound for a stronger query task, larger monoid, smaller instruction set or stricter space limit does not alone prove it.
context:
Section 2 explicitly uses worst-case operation cost and linear preprocessing. The question concerns the two-element AND monoid. The separately discussed three-element monoid has a stronger predecessor-type task and a different known lower bound.

The source records an \(O(\log\log n)\) deterministic upper bound and a better expected bound when randomness is allowed. It emphasizes that this does not provide the superconstant lower bound and distinguishes the word-RAM problem from unrestricted local computation in the cell-probe model.

The 2022 string-data-structure paper formulates a stronger amortized constant-time hardness conjecture. Its conditional consequences are evidence of the primitive’s relevance, but this card retains the original worst-case question rather than silently changing the cost convention.

The 2025 tree-language paper still states prefix-U-one hardness as a conjectural premise. Under that premise it classifies constant-time maintainability for its specified class of regular tree languages with a neutral letter; it does not prove the premise.
why: This small dynamic problem isolates whether maintaining even threshold information about a changing minimum requires more than a constant number of actual word operations. Its hardness would complete conditional classifications of dynamic regular-language membership, and newer work extends that connection to tree languages. The challenge concerns computation inside the machine as well as memory access, making it a foundational word-RAM question.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: ICALP 2021 Section 2 and Conjecture 2.3, the 2022 amortized variant, and MFCS 2025 Section 6. The latter continues to use the original hardness premise conditionally. A bounded later-work search found no matching worst-case constant-time structure or proof of its nonexistence in the declared logarithmic-word model. The source-open label records these search and model limits, not exhaustive verification of current openness.
progress: 2021-07-02: The ICALP paper states Conjecture 2.3 and the worst-case, linear-preprocessing RAM model. | 2022-05-01: The string-data-structure preprint uses an explicitly amortized version as a hardness assumption. | 2025-08-20: The MFCS paper extends conditional classification consequences to regular tree languages and retains the prefix conjecture.
working_summary: The prefix-U-one problem maintains a fixed-length bit sequence under substitutions and returns the AND of any requested prefix. The conjecture rules out a deterministic data structure with linear preprocessing and constant worst-case time for both operations. Its machine has logarithmic-size words and explicitly charged arithmetic, bit operations and memory accesses. Amortized constant time, expected constant time and stronger predecessor queries are separate questions. A resolution would settle a basic dynamic set barrier underlying conditional classifications for regular word and tree languages.

title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
importance_reason: This asks whether complete access to a changeable operation history can cost only as much asymptotically as an ordinary priority queue.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic comparison pointer-machine program \(A\), with fixed constants \(C_t,C_s>0\), that implements the fully retroactive priority queue defined below on every valid finite sequence of commands? Starting with an empty history, it must insert and remove historical insertion or extract-min records, and return the minimum item immediately after any queried historical time. Write \(m_j\) for the number of historical records after command \(j\), \(m_0=0\), and \(M_j=\max\{m_{j-1},m_j\}\). For every \(q\ge0\), require
\[
T_A(q)\le C_t\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\log_2(2+M_j)\right),
\]
where \(T_A(q)\) counts initialization and all steps through the first \(q\) commands. During command \(j\), at most \(C_s(1+M_j)\) records may be allocated and not yet reclaimed; after it finishes, at most \(C_s(1+m_j)\) may remain. Initialization uses at most \(C_s\) records. Thus time is amortized over all edits and queries, while space is linear in the currently maintained history, including working storage.
definitions:
Fix three opaque totally ordered domains: priorities, item identities and historical times. The same program and constants must work for every choice of these domains and every valid input sequence. An item is a pair \((p,\iota)\) of priority and identity, ordered lexicographically: compare priorities first and use identities to break ties. Identities of items whose insertion records are currently in the history are distinct. Atoms in each domain can be copied and compared in constant time, with no access to their representation.

The history is a finite set of records with pairwise distinct timestamps. A record is either \(\operatorname{InsertItem}(t,p,\iota)\) or \(\operatorname{ExtractMin}(t)\). Its meaning is obtained by sorting the records by time and replaying them from an empty queue. An insertion adds its item; an extraction removes the least surviving item in the lexicographic order. The history after every edit is promised valid: no extraction is encountered with an empty queue. There is no monotonicity promise on priorities. The data structure need not detect invalid commands or histories.

An input command has one of four forms. \(\operatorname{AddInsert}(t,p,\iota)\) adds an insertion record at an unused timestamp. \(\operatorname{AddExtract}(t)\) adds an extraction record at an unused timestamp. Either addition returns a constant-size stable handle for the new historical record. \(\operatorname{Remove}(h)\) removes the existing historical record named by its valid handle; a handle becomes invalid after that removal. \(\operatorname{Minimum}(t)\) returns the identity and priority of the least item after replaying all current records with timestamp at most \(t\), or a distinguished empty marker. The supplied query time may coincide with a record, lie between records, or precede or follow all records. Thus an insertion at \(t\) is already effective at \(t\), and an extraction at \(t\) has already removed its item. Edits change the interpretation of all subsequent historical records. An extraction record is not a request to remove a named item, and a removal command deletes a historical operation rather than executing an extra queue extraction.

The computation is online: each command arrives only after the preceding response, and its response must be completed before the next command is seen. Commands may depend on earlier responses. Input atoms and a removal handle occupy only constantly many input registers; earlier inputs remain available to the program only if it stores them in its charged memory. The client may retain returned handles, but gives the program only the handle named by the current command, with no auxiliary stored computation.

A program has finite control and a fixed finite number of registers. Memory consists of records with a fixed finite number of pointer fields and data fields. A pointer is null or the address of an allocated record. A data field contains one input atom or a symbol from a fixed finite alphabet. Each step may read or write a fixed field of a record reached by a register, copy a register or field, follow a stored pointer, compare two pointers for equality, compare two atoms from the same ordered domain, test a finite-alphabet symbol, branch, allocate or reclaim one record, or emit one output field. Each such primitive costs one step. Allocation supplies a fresh available address; addresses cannot be ordered, converted to data, used in arithmetic, or used for computed array access. Pointer access starts from the fixed registers or follows stored pointers. Unbounded integers and bit strings, if needed, must be represented by charged records and manipulated through these primitives; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on counters. There are no random bits, advice, oracle operations or uncharged preprocessing.

Every allocated record counts toward space until reclaimed, including historical records, handle records, indexes, temporary storage and unreachable garbage. Rebuilding and reclamation count toward time. The parameters \(m_j,M_j\) are used to state the guarantee and are not free machine inputs or unit-cost counters. A query does not change \(m_j\), and an edit changes it by exactly one. The bounds hold for every finite prefix, including arbitrarily long sequences that repeatedly add and remove records while keeping the current history small. They do not use the cumulative number of commands as a replacement for history size. The record format, register count, program and resource constants are fixed independently of all inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic implementation and constants satisfying the exact replay semantics, total-prefix time bound and space bounds for every valid command sequence, or a complete Lean proof of their logical negation in the stated comparison pointer-machine model. All representation, correctness and resource claims must be included. A conditional lower bound alone does not establish unconditional nonexistence, and a result confined to monotonic histories or using a different machine model does not settle this target.
context:
The original retroactive model distinguishes edits to a history from queries about its states and promises that edited histories remain consistent. Its partially retroactive priority queue has logarithmic update time, but queries concern only the present.

The 2015 general fully retroactive structure has \(O(\log^2m)\) amortized update time, \(O(\log^2m\log\log m)\) query time and \(O(m\log m)\) space. These are the reported bounds in that paper’s computational setting.

Version 3 of the monotonic-priority-queue paper, dated 14 April 2026, reports \(O(\log m)\) time and \(O(m)\) space for the restricted variant and explicitly retains the unrestricted logarithmic and linear-space question. Here the relevant monotonic restriction forbids inserting a key smaller than the most recently extracted key.

The card retains its previously specified strict comparison pointer machine, including charged counter manipulation. The original paper generally uses RAM or real RAM, and the 2026 result states comparison-model bounds without an explicit analysis under this stricter instruction set. The cited upper bounds are therefore context, not verified implementations in the card’s model.

The existing valid-history and post-operation query conventions are retained. The minimum is requested at arbitrary supplied times, while deletion uses a handle to a currently represented historical operation. The explicit before-and-after history sizes remove ambiguity in amortized accounting when operations are erased.
why: A single change to the past can alter which items many later extractions remove. Matching ordinary priority-queue costs despite this dependence would show that unrestricted historical access can be maintained without an asymptotic time or space penalty in the stated model.
status_note: Source-open: arXiv2508.09892v3, dated14April2026 and rechecked on 2026-09-16, explicitly retains the general logarithmic-time, linear-space question. Its optimal result has a monotonicity restriction. The card preserves its existing stricter comparison pointer-machine interpretation; the cited upper bounds were not independently transferred to that instruction set. Bounded subsequent searches found no verified resolution.
progress: 2007-05: The journal paper defines retroactive histories and consistency promises and establishes the logarithmic partially retroactive priority queue. | 2015-08: The WADS paper gives a general fully retroactive priority queue with \(O(\log^2m)\) amortized updates, \(O(\log^2m\log\log m)\) queries and \(O(m\log m)\) space. | 2026-04-14: The third revision reports logarithmic time and linear space for monotonic priority queues and explicitly leaves the general target open. | 2026-09-16: Checked the current revision and the earlier operation definitions; made handles, tie-breaking, boundary semantics, uniformity, and changing-history resource accounting explicit.
working_summary: A fully retroactive priority queue permits inserting and erasing queue operations anywhere in its current history. Every edit changes the queue obtained by replaying later historical operations, and minimum queries may refer to any time. The target is one deterministic comparison pointer-machine implementation with logarithmic amortized time and linear storage in the currently maintained history. All temporary storage and counter manipulation are charged, and histories remain valid without a monotonicity promise. The 2026 logarithmic result covers monotonic priority queues in its stated comparison model and leaves the general question open in that dated source.

title: Optimal randomized memory-reallocation overhead
importance_reason: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.
formal: Determine, up to absolute constant factors as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the optimal worst-case expected reallocation overhead \(F(\varepsilon)\) for online allocators with load at most \(1-\varepsilon\). The allocator stores objects in contiguous intervals of a fixed array and may relocate live objects after each insertion or deletion.
definitions: For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\) and integer array length \(M\ge1\), a request inserts a fresh object of positive integer size \(s\), or deletes a named live object. Valid finite sequences start empty and have total live size at most \((1-\varepsilon)M\) after every request. At each operation boundary, every live object occupies one contiguous interval of its size in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), and these intervals are disjoint. On an update involving an object \(x\), cost is \(1+\sum_y s(y)/s(x)\), where the sum is over objects live both before and after the update whose starting addresses change. This counts allocation changes at operation boundaries; local computation and allocation metadata are uncharged. The online rule may know \(M,\varepsilon\) but no future requests, and may use private randomness. A sequence is fixed independently of that randomness; allocations must always be valid. For a family of rules covering all \(M\), its overhead is the supremum, over all capacities, valid finite request sequences and individual update indices, of expected update cost. \(F(\varepsilon)\) is the infimum of those overheads over all such families. No history-independence or resizability constraint is imposed. The target measures each update’s expectation, rather than expected amortized cost or a high-probability bound.
answer_criterion: Supply an explicit function \(f(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(c f(\varepsilon)\le F(\varepsilon)\le C f(\varepsilon)\) for absolute positive constants \(c,C\) and all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). Bounds only for resizable or history-independent allocators, or only for amortized expectation, do not establish the required matching result.
context:
The 2024 work studies low-overhead memory reallocation and its relationship with stronger resizability and history-independence guarantees. Those extra guarantees are not required for the target here.

Jin’s February 2026 paper gives an upper bound \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^4(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^2)\) and a lower bound \(\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for general allocators. The new general lower bound improves the scope of earlier bounds restricted to resizable allocators.
why: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2026-02-17: Polylogarithmic overhead is achieved, and a logarithmic lower bound is proved for general allocators.
working_summary: Objects of different sizes share one nearly full memory array. Every object must occupy a contiguous interval. An insertion or deletion may require moving other live objects. Cost compares the total moved volume with the size of the updated object. The remaining problem is the tight expected overhead as the unused fraction tends to zero.

title: Deque conjecture
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete stress test for splay-tree adaptivity, already on the elementary deque interface; less sweeping than dynamic optimality.
formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite binary search tree \(T_0\) with \(n\ge0\) distinct ordered keys and every legal sequence \(\mathcal S\) of \(m\ge0\) deque operations, the specified bottom-up splay implementation satisfies
\[
W(T_0,\mathcal S)\le C(n+m)?
\]
The operations are insertion of a new minimum or maximum and deletion of the current minimum or maximum. Insertions make the new key the root; deletions splay the requested extremum to the root and remove it. The cost \(W\) counts operation overhead, search edges and rotations as defined below.
question_excerpt: Tarjan’s deque conjecture, as stated by Pettie, says that splay-tree deque operations take constant amortized time. Pettie specifies new-root insertions and deletion by splaying the appropriate extremum. This card includes the initial-tree size explicitly, as in Pettie’s upper-bound theorem.
definitions:
A binary search tree is a finite rooted tree with at most one left child and one right child per node. Each node carries a key; all keys in its left subtree are smaller, and all keys in its right subtree are larger. Keys are opaque elements of a totally ordered set and are used only through order comparisons. The initial tree may have any shape and is supplied as a tree, rather than built by charged insertions. The \(n\) term in the target is its allowed initial credit.

Insert-min supplies a key smaller than every currently present key. Allocate a new node with that key, no left child, and the former root as its right child; it becomes the root. Insert-max is symmetric. Both operations are allowed on an empty tree. Legality is promised, so no search to verify the new key’s extremal status is performed. A key that was deleted may be inserted again whenever the current extremal-order condition permits it.

Delete-min is allowed only on a nonempty tree. Follow left-child pointers from the root until reaching the leftmost node \(x\), splay \(x\) to the root, remove it and make its right child the root of the remaining tree. Delete-max follows right-child pointers, splays the rightmost node and retains its left subtree. Removing the only node leaves the tree empty. There are no searches for internal keys, other update operations, balance conditions or promises about the order of deletions.

A right rotation at a node \(p\) with left child \(x\) makes \(x\) replace \(p\), makes \(p\) the right child of \(x\), and makes the former right subtree of \(x\) the left subtree of \(p\), preserving all other attachments. A left rotation is the mirror image. Parent pointers and the root pointer are updated as needed. To splay \(x\), repeat until it is the root: if its parent \(p\) is the root, rotate \(x\) above \(p\) (zig); if \(x,p\) are both left children or both right children of their respective parents, first rotate \(p\) above its parent and then \(x\) above \(p\) (zig-zig); otherwise rotate \(x\) above \(p\) and then above its new parent (zig-zag). These are the standard bottom-up rules; the algorithm is fixed, not a choice among tree heuristics.

Let \(e\) be the total number of child edges traversed while finding extrema for deletions, and \(r\) the total number of single rotations performed by all splay steps. Define \(W=m+e+r\). A node has a constant number of child and parent pointers. Reading or changing one such pointer, comparing keys, allocating or deleting one node and executing a branch are constant-cost primitives. The standard direct implementation takes time within constant factors of \(W\), since each search edge, rotation and operation uses only a constant amount of additional work. Key bit lengths, memory-allocation system overhead and an alternative implementation’s avoidable extra work are not part of this combinatorial cost model.

The conjecture is a bound on the entire sequence, including sequences with insertions and deletions interleaved arbitrarily. It does not assert a constant worst-case cost for an individual deletion.
