The constant \(C\) must be independent of \(n,m\), all keys, the initial shape and the operation sequence. The empty sequence has cost zero.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal bound or its logical negation. A negative proof must show that for every proposed constant \(C\) there is a legal finite initial tree and sequence with \(W>C(n+m)\); equivalently, the cost ratio is unbounded over nonempty instances.

A constant-cost deque implemented by a different data structure does not answer this question. A slowly growing nonconstant amortized factor, a guarantee for only deletion sequences or special initial shapes, and a nonconstant competitive ratio against an optimal search tree do not establish the full linear bound. No additive approximation tolerance is allowed.
context:
A deque uses only the two extremes of an ordered set. Although a dedicated deque supports these operations easily, the conjecture concerns the behavior of the fixed splay-tree algorithm on every such sequence.

Pettie proves \(O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))\) total time, where \(\alpha^*\) counts repeated applications of an inverse-Ackermann function until a fixed threshold is reached. Its growth is extremely slow but is not an absolute constant.

The arbitrary initial tree matters: the first extremal deletion may traverse a long path. The additive initial-size allowance permits that cost while still asking for a linear bound over the whole sequence.

The July 2026 preprint obtains a near-double-logarithmic competitive ratio for general splay accesses and separately records the deque conjecture. A nonconstant general competitiveness guarantee is not itself the constant amortized deque bound.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint separately records the deque conjecture and the known iterated-inverse-Ackermann upper bound. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified proof or counterexample for the exact linear target. The recent general competitiveness theorem is not treated as a resolution of this specific conjecture.
progress: 2007-07-14: The initial-tree-plus-sequence upper bound is reduced to a linear term times an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor; the result appears at SODA 2008. | 2026-07-20: A preprint proves substantially improved general splay competitiveness while separately retaining the deque conjecture and its known nonconstant-factor bound.
working_summary: Start with any binary search tree and update only the minimum or maximum end. New extrema become roots, while deleting an extremum first moves it to the root by standard bottom-up splaying. The conjecture asks whether total search and rotation work is linear in the initial size plus the number of operations. A known bound has an extremely slowly growing extra factor, and the 2026 general competitiveness result does not remove it here. A complete Lean-checked proof of the linear bound or an unbounded family of counterexample ratios is required.

title: Constant-update working-set heaps on pointer machines
importance_reason: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that every legal sequence \(\sigma\) of \(M\ge1\) operations, starting with an empty queue, has total charged cost
\[
W_A(\sigma)\le C\left(M+\sum_{x\text{ extracted in }\sigma}\log_2\Gamma_\sigma(x)\right)?
\]
The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key and extract-min, and
\[
\Gamma_\sigma(x)=1+\#\{\text{insertions strictly between the insertion and extraction of }x\}.
\]
Those later insertions count even if their items were already removed. All answers must be exact, and the same program and constant must work for every finite sequence and every ordered key domain.
question_excerpt: The seminar asks for a pointer-model heap combining a working-set extraction guarantee with constant decrease-key. The later ESA paper makes the insertion-age convention explicit and leaves removal of its inverse-Ackermann decrease-key overhead open.
definitions:
An insertion creates a new item carrying a supplied opaque key and returns a handle to it. A handle is a pointer identifying that live item; subsequent decrease-key requests supply it directly. Decrease-key replaces the key by a supplied no-larger key and does not change the item’s original insertion time. It is legal only for a live handle. Find-min returns a minimum live item without removing it. Extract-min returns and removes a minimum live item, invalidating its handle. On an empty queue either minimum operation returns an empty symbol. Melding queues, arbitrary deletion and increasing keys are not requested.

Keys have a total-order comparison interface. If application priorities can coincide, a fixed tie label may be included in the supplied opaque key so comparisons also settle ties. The queue can copy references to supplied keys and compare them, but cannot inspect their representation, extract an integer from them or manufacture auxiliary keys for storing counters. Item identity is separate from priority; repeated insertions create distinct items. Each operation must finish and return its answer before the next request is supplied. The program receives neither future requests nor the total sequence length.

A pointer machine is a finite program with a fixed constant number of pointer registers and finite control. Memory consists of records, each with at most a fixed constant number of pointer fields, auxiliary bits and references to supplied keys. These constants belong to the implementation and are independent of the sequence length and heap size. Pointers may be copied, compared for equality, followed or changed; the null pointer is allowed. A primitive step performs one such constant-size action, one comparison of two supplied keys, a Boolean operation on constantly many auxiliary bits, allocation or disposal of one record, or a constant-size input/output action. A request supplies its constant number of key references and handles to the registers. New records have fixed initial contents. The machine begins with a fixed constant-size empty representation.

No address arithmetic, array indexing by a computed integer, unbounded integer operation or word-parallel bit operation is available. A large counter may be represented by multiple records, but traversing and changing its bits is charged. There is no separate space bound; allocating and manipulating every auxiliary record costs time. All initialization and maintenance work is included in \(W_A\), including work between requests. The empty sequence has zero operation cost.

The number \(\Gamma_\sigma(x)\) is a performance parameter defined from the history, not supplied free to the program. It is always at least one. The \(M\) term pays the constant part of each extraction and all other operations. The inequality is a joint amortized guarantee, not a worst-case constant bound on each update. It must hold even if many items remain in the queue at the end; future deletions cannot be used to pay for already completed work.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence claim or its unconditional logical negation. A positive proof must specify the pointer-machine implementation, establish the exact online interface, and prove the one total-cost inequality for every legal finite sequence. Any potential argument must justify its initial and final contributions, including sequences that leave items in the queue.

A negative proof must rule out every deterministic implementation in this model, not just a particular heap design. A word-RAM solution, a guarantee without decrease-key, an unbounded inverse-Ackermann update factor, or a nonconstant insertion overhead does not satisfy the joint target. Any use of a different working-set definition must prove the required transfer while preserving all operation charges. No lower bound under an unproved assumption is an unconditional refutation.
context:
The extraction charge depends on how recently the item entered the queue. Keeping many old items while repeatedly inserting and immediately extracting a new minimum should cost only a constant per pair of operations.

A priority decrease can concern an old item and must coexist with this temporal adaptivity. Efficient extraction without cheap priority changes does not meet the goal.

The final ESA 2026 construction gives constant insertion and an insertion-age extraction bound, but its decrease-key cost retains an inverse-Ackermann factor. Its Introduction explicitly identifies removal of that factor as open.

The July comparison-model construction gives constant decrease-key and a stronger stack-like extraction guarantee. It pays a slowly growing insertion cost for every fixed depth of its iterated construction, so the stated theorem does not provide simultaneous constant updates.

The July equivalence theorem relates several amortized working-set definitions while preserving other operation charges. The card fixes insertion count directly and does not require the stronger stack-like property.
why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.
status_note: The exact joint constant-update target remains open in the final ESA 2026 publication and was not resolved by the checked July comparison-model tradeoff. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution. This review checks formulations, models and theorem scopes, not every implementation proof.
progress: 2025: The pointer-model working-set/decrease-key problem is stated at Dagstuhl. | 2026-07-27: A comparison-model heap combines constant decrease-key with stack-like extraction and a nonconstant iterated-log-star insertion overhead. | 2026-08-25: The final ESA publication gives the inverse-Ackermann pointer-machine update bound and explicitly retains the overhead-removal question.
working_summary: The queue must support insertion, minimum lookup, priority decrease and minimum extraction online. An extraction is charged logarithmically in the number of insertions since that item arrived. The target combines that adaptive extraction cost with constant amortized charges for every other operation. The computation uses pointers, constant auxiliary bits and key comparisons; the checked recent results retain a growing factor in an update bound. A complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional refutation must cover every finite operation sequence.

title: Buffered fully persistent search trees
importance_reason: Efficient historical branching together with buffered writes would combine two major capabilities of storage indexes without sacrificing their I/O savings.
formal:
For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon<1\), does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-based external-memory data structure and a constant \(c\ge1\) that maintain the fully persistent ordered-set interface below, for every integer block size \(B\ge2\), internal-memory capacity \(M\ge2B\), and every online operation history? Require correctness and termination, worst-case at most \(c\) I/Os for each explicit \(\operatorname{Clone}\), and the following joint amortized bound on every finite history \(H\):
\[
\operatorname{IO}(H)\le c\!\left(1+C_H+\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_H}B^{\varepsilon-1}L_j+\sum_{j\in\mathcal Q_H}L_j+\sum_{j\in\mathcal R_H}\frac{K_j}{B}\right),
\qquad L_j=1+\log_B(2+N_j).
\]
Here \(\mathcal U_H\) indexes insertions and deletions, \(\mathcal Q_H\) indexes successor and range queries, \(\mathcal R_H\subseteq\mathcal Q_H\) indexes range queries, \(C_H\) counts explicit clones, \(N_j\) is the size of the version accessed by operation \(j\), and \(K_j\) is that range query’s output size. At every point require at most
\[
c\!\left(1+\frac{U+C}{B}\right)
\]
external-memory blocks, including metadata and temporary storage, where \(U,C\) count update and clone operations begun by that point. The constants and program may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the block parameters, history, keys or version sizes. This retains the card’s stated simultaneous quantitative sharpening of the source’s broader question about buffered full persistence and efficient cloning.
definitions:
Keys are indivisible atoms from an arbitrary totally ordered set. A version stores a finite set of keys, without multiplicities. Initially version \(0\) is empty. Each insertion, deletion and explicit clone creates a distinct new immutable version, assigned the next unused nonnegative integer handle. Every existing version remains available indefinitely. Operations are:

\(\operatorname{Insert}(v,x)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\cup\{x\}\). It creates a version even if \(x\in S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Delete}(v,x)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\setminus\{x\}\). It creates a version even if \(x\notin S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Clone}(v)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Search}(v,x)\) returns \(\min\{y\in S_v:x\le y\}\), or a distinguished empty marker when that set is empty.

\(\operatorname{Range}(v,a,b)\), for \(a\le b\), reports every key in \(S_v\cap[a,b]\) once, in increasing order. An empty result is permitted.

In every operation, \(v\) can be any previously returned handle, including an ancestor or a version used many times before. The sizes \(N_j=|S_v|\) are measured before the operation. No version is overwritten or merged with another. In particular, an update already preserves its parent and must meet its update charge without an additional explicit clone charge. An explicit clone is a separate requested operation. Every operation must finish and return its full answer before the next is received. Later requests may depend on earlier answers; no future operations or length of the history are known to the data structure.

The I/O model has at most \(M\) internal cells and an initially blank external array partitioned into blocks of \(B\) consecutive cells. A cell holds one key atom or one metadata word. Data can be inspected or changed only in internal memory. One I/O transfers one entire block between internal and external memory and costs one. Reads and writes both count, including all preprocessing, rebuilding, buffer flushing and version metadata access. Computation on resident data is free for the I/O measure but must terminate. Keys may only be copied, stored, output or compared for order/equality; their bit representation cannot be inspected, arithmetically manipulated, packed with other keys into one cell or used as an address. Metadata words encode integers, addresses, handles and finite tags; each contains at most \(d\lceil\log_2(t+M+B+2)\rceil\) bits during the \(t\)-th operation, for one fixed integer \(d\ge1\) chosen with the program. All program work storage and persistent metadata count toward the stated memories. Fixed finite control is not a source of growing storage. Apart from the supplied current operation, the program cannot read past inputs, old outputs or the caller’s collection of handles without having stored the needed information itself.

The program knows \(B,M\), so cache obliviousness is not required. It is a finite deterministic algorithm, with no advice, randomness, oracle or input-dependent precomputed tables. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there must be a single such program for all \(B,M\); no algorithm taking an arbitrary real \(\varepsilon\) as input is requested. There is no separate internal computation-time bound or prescribed B-tree layout.

Operation arguments and a constant-size returned handle/key are presented through the interface without an extra compulsory I/O. A range answer is written to an output-only stream in blocks; each flushed full or final partial output block counts as an I/O. The stream is unavailable for later reads and is excluded from retained data-structure space. Internal output buffering counts toward \(M\). Allocated external storage, including partially filled blocks, is charged; freed blocks cease to count. The space bound holds throughout an operation using the number of updates/clones already begun, and at every completed prefix. No deletion of historical versions or garbage collection of their logical contents is allowed.

\(\operatorname{IO}(H)\) counts all transfers from initialization through completion of \(H\). The displayed single inequality defines amortization jointly across operation types and every prefix. Its additive constant covers initialization and rounding; it does not add one to the charge of each update. The clone bound is additionally a per-operation worst-case bound. The space bound concerns the whole retained history, not the sum of the sizes of its sets, and is independent of the number of queries.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed universal existence statement, supplying for every \(0<\varepsilon<1\) a finite algorithm and constants that satisfy correctness, termination, the memory model, the prefix I/O inequality, the individual clone bound and the space bound for every admissible \(B,M\) and online history. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its negation: there is a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no finite algorithm and fixed constants satisfy all these requirements. The negative result must quantify over all algorithms in the specified comparison model, not just a particular representation. Partial persistence, a bound in terms of the total history in place of \(N_j\), an additive constant I/O per update, or a theorem requiring more than \(M\ge2B\) does not alone establish the positive target.
context:
The ESA 2025 paper permits queries at every old version while allowing updates only at the newest version. Its Theorem 1 proves buffered update cost \(O(B^{\varepsilon-1}\log_B N_v)\), successor-query cost \(O(\log_B N_v)\), range-reporting cost \(O(\log_B N_v+K/B)\), and space linear in the update history for fixed \(\varepsilon\). Its model needs only \(M\ge2B\).

The source’s Section 4 explicitly leaves efficient cloning with buffered full persistence open. It does not conjecture the entire numerical combination on this card. The retained editorial target adds the exact per-version bounds, worst-case constant cloning, immutable versions after every update and linear total history space. In particular, it does not hide a constant clone charge inside each subconstant amortized update.

The STOC 2023 result provides full persistence with \(O(1)\) worst-case cloning, \(O(\log_BN_v)\) amortized updates and \(O(\log_BN_v+K/B)\) worst-case range reporting. It has no buffering factor in its update bound. Its interface uses mutable leaves and explicit cloning to preserve a version before modifying it.

Svenning’s dissertation, dated 4 October 2025, includes the buffered partial-persistence work and repeats the open question about efficient cloning. This is a later copy of the same research question rather than an independent proof of the combined target.

A July 2026 paper on a retroactive buffer tree describes batched edits to a temporal history using partial persistence. Its inspected publisher abstract does not claim the immutable branching interface and simultaneous bounds required here. Retroactivity changes later states along a history, whereas this card preserves every existing version.
why: Buffering reduces storage transfers for updates, while full persistence permits new branches from historical states. Combining them with queries measured by the accessed version’s size and space measured by the update history would provide both capabilities in one comparison-based storage index.
status_note: The broad question of buffered full persistence with efficient cloning is explicitly open in ESA 2025 Section 4 and repeated in Svenning’s October 2025 dissertation. The exact simultaneous target retained here is an editorial sharpening, including immutable versions after every update, the subconstant amortized update charge, constant worst-case cloning and linear history space. A bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of that combination. Status is uncertain for this precise formulation; source openness is not an independent certificate of every sharpened requirement, and the 2026 retroactive-paper check was limited to publisher metadata and abstract.
progress: 2023-06: The STOC paper gives fully persistent unbuffered search trees with constant worst-case cloning and per-version logarithmic updates. | 2025-10-01: The ESA paper proves the buffered bounds for partial persistence and explicitly leaves the combination with efficient cloning open. | 2025-10-04: Svenning’s dissertation repeats the buffered full-persistence cloning question in its included paper. | 2026-07-06: The later retroactive buffer-tree abstract concerns batched temporal-history edits with partial persistence, not this immutable branching target.
working_summary: The data structure stores every version of an ordered set and permits a new immutable version to be created from any old one. The target combines buffered insertions and deletions, queries charged by the size of their accessed version, and constant worst-case I/O cost for explicit cloning. All operation bounds must hold jointly over every finite online history with only two blocks of internal memory required and space linear in updates and clones. The 2025 source achieves buffered partial persistence and leaves efficient full-persistence cloning open, while the exact numerical combination here is explicitly editorial. A solution would unite efficient historical branching and buffered storage access without charging an extra constant transfer to every update.

title: Combined depth and size bounds for confluently persistent tries
importance_reason: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does there exist a deterministic uniform functional trie representation and a constant \(C_k>0\) that supports the version, finger-navigation and subtree-copy interface below, with worst-case navigation time \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\), no new permanent records from navigation, and both worst-case modification time and newly permanent record count at most \(C_k[1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}]\) for every valid operation sequence?
definitions:
A logical trie is a finite rooted tree, including its root, with distinct totally ordered labels on the outgoing edges of each node and one constant-size data atom per node. Logical occurrences are counted separately even when their physical representations share records. For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), every stored version has \(k\) finger positions, possibly coincident. Selecting a version restores those positions in at most \(C_k\) operations; navigation changes a working copy of them. Reading a node’s data also costs at most \(C_k\) operations. These calls do not permit uncharged preprocessing. It can reset a finger to the root, move it to its parent, follow a child with a supplied label, or read the data at a finger. A failed parent or child move reports failure and leaves the finger unchanged. A modification creates a new stored version and leaves every previous version usable. It can change data at a finger, add a new leaf with an unused child label, remove the non-root subtree at a finger, or copy the subtree at a finger of any source version as a child with an unused label at a destination finger. The source and destination versions may coincide. The copy is a logical duplicate, so later changes to either occurrence do not change the other. Surviving destination fingers keep their logical positions; fingers in a removed subtree reset to the root. A copy may replace any specified subset of the resulting finger slots by counterparts of source fingers inside the copied subtree. Thus at most \(k\) fingers are stored in the resulting version. All parameters are supplied through version handles, finger indices and constant-size atoms; arbitrary logical nodes cannot be addressed directly.

Use a deterministic uniform pointer program with a fixed number of fields per record. A field holds a pointer, an opaque label or data atom, or an integer counter. Reading a field, comparing or copying atoms or pointers, comparing labels, and adding, subtracting or comparing counters cost one operation. New records may be initialized, but a previously initialized record is never overwritten. There is no pointer arithmetic, address-indexed array lookup, arithmetic on labels, random choice, oracle or nonuniform table. Counters have magnitude polynomial in the largest logical version size and operation count so far; costs count record operations, not their bit implementation. The program and field count are independent of all versions and operation sequences; constants may depend on the fixed finger bound \(k\). The initial version is a single root and costs \(O(k)\) operations and records.

For a modification, let \(N\) be the sum of the logical node counts of its participating input versions and its output version, counting a shared input only once. Let \(\Delta\ge2\) be the maximum of two and all node outdegrees in those versions. Let \(D=1+\sum_f\operatorname{depth}(f)\), summing the depths of the \(k\) stored or working fingers in each participating input version; root depth is zero. Define \(B=1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}\). For navigation, \(\Delta\) is instead the maximum of two and the outdegrees in the selected logical version. Navigation must cost at most \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\) operations, and a modification at most \(C_kB\) operations, in the worst case for every individual call in every finite valid sequence.

A record is permanent when reachable from any stored version handle, including that version’s stored finger representation. All stored versions remain available. Navigation may allocate temporary records but must leave the set of permanent records unchanged. A modification is charged every record newly made permanent by its result, including records allocated during earlier navigation; this count must be at most \(C_kB\). Existing permanent records shared by the new version are not charged again. Temporary allocation time is always charged to the call performing it; the permanent-space guarantee is not a bound on peak temporary storage. All logarithms and bounds use logical version sizes, not the number of previously allocated physical records.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that representations and constants with every stated interface, persistence, worst-case time and permanent-space property exist for all fixed \(k\ge2\), or prove the logical negation in Lean. A positive proof must charge navigation records subsequently retained by an update and preserve all prior versions. Separate representations attaining the two bounds, an amortized guarantee, or a theorem only for point changes without subtree copies does not meet the combined specification.
context:
Version control must preserve old directory trees while allowing a whole directory to be copied between branches. A logical subtree copy can contain very many nodes, yet a representation can initially share their unchanged contents. Confluent persistence requires both source versions and all older versions to remain usable after this operation.

The source gives two functional representations. One exploits locality of finger operations with \(O(\log\Delta)\) time and allocation per call; navigation records can later become permanent. The other uses \(O(\log n)\) time and permanent space per modification, with \(O(\log\Delta)\) navigation time and no permanent navigation space. These are different guarantees because navigation may be followed by either another query or a modification.

An arbitrarily long path illustrates the size/depth distinction. A change near its root has small root depth even when the version is enormous, whereas a change near the bottom has large depth. The requested minimum would retain a shallow-update bound and also cap deep-update costs logarithmically in logical size. The question concerns one representation with simultaneous guarantees, not choosing a separate representation after seeing the next operation.

Charging only the records allocated inside the final update would conceal part of the first representation’s cost. Records produced by earlier finger moves count against the update if the new stored version retains them. Conversely, a navigation-only sequence produces no new stored versions, so discarded temporary work does not count as permanent history.

Editorial specification: Section 6 states the combined depth/size goal but leaves the multi-finger parameters implicit. This benchmark uses the sum of participating finger depths, a maximum degree over participating versions, and the sum of input/output logical sizes. With a fixed number of fingers these specify a single bound for copies and deletions; a one-finger point modification retains the root-depth scale \(1+d\). They are explicit conventions for the combined variant, not definitions quoted verbatim from the authors.

The source’s constant-time comparison of labels and functional pointer-record model are retained. This is not a claim about the cost of comparing arbitrary file-name strings, storing file contents, or implementing large counters in a bit machine. The documented temporary/permanent distinction is part of the target, rather than an unrecorded memory exemption.
why: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.
status_note: The combined goal is explicitly open in the source’s Section 6. A bounded 13 September 2026 search did not locate a later resolution. The complete benchmark makes its multi-finger parameters and space accounting explicit editorial conventions; it does not claim that the source spelled out this entire interface or that absence of a later result was exhaustively established.
progress: 2010: The conclusion asks to combine the two functional bounds in one representation.
working_summary: Confluent persistence lets a subtree be copied between historical trie versions while retaining all old versions. The question asks for one functional representation combining a shallow-update bound with a logarithmic bound in logical version size. Navigation has its own worst-case time bound and may not extend permanent version history. An update must pay for any earlier navigation records that its new stored version retains. The model and parameters explicitly cover multiple fingers, logical sharing, subtree copies and temporary versus permanent memory.

title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
importance_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
focus_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
question_excerpt: The introduction and Theorem 1.3 discussion of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 paper explicitly identify deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case dynamic connectivity as an open target. This card retains its existing exact pair-query, polynomial-space word-RAM formulation and makes its machine and sequence quantifiers explicit. A newer FOCS 2026 title was found during the current review, but its theorem scope was not available in the inspected announcement.
definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
context:
Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

Probst Gutenberg’s publication page independently lists the same FOCS 2026 title and coauthors, again without a manuscript link in that entry. The conference is scheduled for November 2026; its acceptance announcement is distinct from an inspected proceedings paper. A complete statement is needed to decide whether the result meets this exact deterministic target.
why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.
