title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
importance_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
focus_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon,a}\) and constants \(K,d,B\ge1\) with the following guarantees?

For every \(n\ge2\) and every valid oblivious sequence of \(T\le n^a\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty graph on \([n]\), the expected total initialization and update cost is at most
\[
K\left[n+T\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\right].
\]
With probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\), after every update the algorithm maintains an explicit matching \(M\) in the current graph \(G\) such that
\[
|M|\ge\frac{\nu(G)}{1+\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality. The same constants apply to every \(n,T\) and sequence for the fixed \(\varepsilon,a\).
question_excerpt: The inherited Dynamic Matching section describes maintaining a (1+epsilon)-approximate matching with polylogarithmic update time as a central long-term objective and distinguishes it from maintaining only an estimate of the optimum size. This card retains its previously selected fixed-accuracy, oblivious-adversary, randomized expected-amortized version.
definitions:
At all times the graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, with the fixed vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Initially there are no edges. One update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge; only valid update sequences are required to be handled. The graph need not be bipartite or have bounded degree.

A matching is a subset of the current edges in which no vertex belongs to more than one edge. The integer \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum possible number of edges in a matching, and it is zero for an edgeless graph. The algorithm stores a mate array \(\operatorname{mate}[1..n]\): zero means unmatched, while a nonzero value \(\operatorname{mate}[v]=u\) must have \(u\ne v\), \(\operatorname{mate}[u]=v\) and \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Together with its stored cardinality, this explicitly represents \(M\). A size estimate or a fractional assignment to edges is not this representation.

After each completed update, reading the mate of any specified vertex or reading \(|M|\) takes at most a fixed constant number of word operations. Listing the full matching may scan the array in \(O(n)\) time, and need not be performed after every update. All work needed to modify the representation, including every changed array entry and the cardinality, counts toward update cost. External requests to read or list the maintained matching are charged their stated query costs separately; they do not excuse extra update work.

The update sequence is oblivious: for each guarantee it is any fixed sequence independent of the algorithm’s random bits. Updates are delivered one at a time, and the algorithm must finish processing one before seeing the next. It knows \(n\) and has the fixed parameters \(\varepsilon,a\), but the future sequence and its actual length are not supplied in advance. This is distinct from a computation receiving all updates at once, and it makes no guarantee against an adversary choosing updates from observed random-dependent outputs.

Use a word-RAM with word length \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with \(B\) a fixed positive integer for the algorithm. Memory cells have word addresses and initially contain zero; every access or write costs an operation, and untouched cells require no initialization work. The instruction set consists of word reads and writes, indirect addressing, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one operation. Stored random words and intermediate values use ordinary memory. Larger integers must use multiple words, with all operations charged; no arbitrary-precision operation, graph oracle or precomputed instance advice is available. No additional linear-space restriction is imposed.

Expectation is over the algorithm’s private randomness on each fixed sequence and includes the entire initialization and all \(T\) updates. The bound is amortized over that sequence, not a worst-case bound on each individual update. The required finite expectation includes termination with probability one. Separately, one event of probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\) must ensure the valid mate representation and approximation inequality after every update in the sequence simultaneously. A separate probability bound at each time without this joint guarantee is insufficient.

The parameters \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\) are fixed independently of \(n\). The machine and constants may depend on both; no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) and no uniform compiler taking \(\varepsilon,a\) as inputs is required. Integer \(a\) covers every polynomial sequence-length regime. There is no demand for an infinite update sequence with one global success event. This is an exact existence proposition for the stated approximation scheme and resources, not a numerical question about \(\nu(G)\).
answer_criterion:
Supply algorithms and a complete Lean-checked proof covering every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\), every fixed polynomial horizon, every \(n\), and every valid oblivious sequence, including the expected total cost, representation-access costs and simultaneous success event. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation of these quantified guarantees; failure for one fixed accuracy and one fixed horizon exponent, for every admissible algorithm and constants, suffices.

An estimator without explicit matching edges, a fixed approximation factor bounded away from one, a partially dynamic algorithm, an algorithm receiving future updates, or an update bound larger than every fixed power of \(\log n\) does not prove the proposition. A lower bound requiring accuracy to shrink with \(n\), polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), or an adaptive adversary does not by itself refute this weaker stated target. Conditional lower bounds require their hypotheses and are not unconditional negative answers.
context:
The maintained object must contain compatible graph edges. Reporting a good estimate of how many such edges could be chosen leaves a separate search and maintenance task, which the source explicitly distinguishes.

Azarmehr, Behnezhad and Roghani improve the approximation achievable in polylogarithmic update time for estimating matching size. Their result does not maintain the mate array required here.

Assadi, Khanna and Kiss obtain explicit near-optimal matching bounds governed by the density of ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Those graphs decompose into ordered matchings, each induced in the union of itself and the later matchings. The resulting structural dependence does not supply a universal polylogarithmic bound.

Pratt relates the density of those ordered graphs to the older unordered variant. The theorem resolves a comparison between two combinatorial quantities, rather than completing the dynamic matching algorithm target.

The fixed-accuracy convention matters: an algorithm may have very large dependence on the chosen accuracy. Lower bounds that require one polynomial dependence as accuracy shrinks with graph size cannot simply be transferred to this formulation.

A maximal matching cannot be extended by adding another edge, but it may be much smaller than a maximum matching. The 2026 deterministic maximal-matching result improves a different maintenance guarantee and does not yield approximation arbitrarily close to one.
why: A single insertion or deletion can change which edges should be used together in a large matching. The question asks whether a near-optimal explicit solution can be kept current at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically with graph size, combining approximation quality with efficient dynamic maintenance.
status_note: The checked work distinguishes matching-size estimation, maximal matching, fixed-accuracy explicit approximation and algorithms given the full update sequence in advance. ORS-dependent bounds and the 2026 deterministic maximal-matching improvement do not give the selected polylogarithmic expected amortized explicit-matching guarantee. No resolution was found in the bounded later-work search.
progress: 2023: The inherited report distinguishes explicit matching from size estimation and identifies the near-optimal polylogarithmic-update objective. | 2024-01-04: A stronger constant approximation for matching-size estimation is published with polylogarithmic updates. | 2024-10-18: The revised ORS-based algorithm gives improved structural bounds for explicit matching at fixed accuracy; published at SODA 2025. | 2025–2026: The ORS–RS density comparison appears as a 2025 preprint and a SOSA 2026 paper. | 2026-06-09: The STOC maximal-matching algorithm improves deterministic update time for its distinct target.
working_summary: The graph undergoes online edge insertions and deletions, and the algorithm must maintain the actual edges of a near-maximum matching. For every fixed accuracy it must have polylogarithmic expected amortized update time, including linear initialization in the total cost. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s randomness, and one high-probability event must guarantee correctness throughout each polynomial-length sequence. The matching is stored explicitly with constant-time mate and cardinality access, and every change to that representation is charged. A complete Lean-checked solution must establish all these guarantees or refute them; size estimation and maximal matching solve different tasks.

title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
importance_reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.
formal:
For every fixed pair of integers \(a,b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized data structure that maintains the exact canonical minimum spanning forest of the graph below, with polynomial preprocessing and space and polylogarithmic worst-case time for each edge insertion or deletion? For every valid update sequence \(\sigma\) of length \(T\le n^a\) fixed independently of its randomness, require
\[\Pr_R\bigl[\widehat F_t=F(G_t)\text{ for every }0\le t\le T\bigr]\ge1-n^{-b}.\]
The event also requires every edge-change report to be valid as defined below. Here \(G_t\) is the graph after update \(t\), \(F(G_t)\) is its specified exact forest, and \(\widehat F_t\) is reconstructed from the reported edge changes. Each update must finish within its time bound on every execution, including executions on which the answer is wrong. The data structure receives no future updates in advance.
question_excerpt: The card preserves the previously selected randomized, oblivious-adversary, exact weighted-forest question, its importance score, the weight range \(\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\), canonical tie-breaking and polynomial sequence horizon. The original imported ICALP 2021 link concerned matching and was already identified as a citation mismatch; the MSF target is grounded instead in the sources listed here. The present review makes the standard RAM convention and probability/resource quantifiers explicit without adding deterministic or adaptive-adversary requirements.
definitions:
Graph and updates. Fix an integer \(n\ge2\), with labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is simple and undirected: no loops or parallel edges. Initially \(G_0\) has no edges. An insertion supplies distinct endpoints \(u,v\) of an absent edge and an integer weight \(w\in\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\); a deletion supplies the endpoints of a present edge. A weight stays fixed until its edge is deleted. Reinsertion may assign a different weight. A valid sequence respects these rules at every prefix; disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and repeated insertions after deletions are allowed. Vertices are never inserted or deleted. The exponent four is the retained concrete choice of polynomial weight range.

Exact target and ties. A spanning forest has one spanning tree in each connected component, with an isolated vertex contributing no edges. Its cost is the sum of its edge weights, and a minimum spanning forest minimizes that sum. To specify one answer when several forests have the same cost, order edges by the triple \((w,\min(u,v),\max(u,v))\), in increasing lexicographic order. Define \(F(G)\) by starting with no edges, scanning the present edges in this order, and retaining an edge exactly when adding it does not create a cycle. This is the canonical minimum spanning forest; the scan defines the target and is not a required implementation. In particular \(F(G_0)=\varnothing\).

Required output. After each update, before receiving the next one, report a list \(D_t\) of forest edges removed and a list \(A_t\) of forest edges added, using unordered endpoint pairs represented with their smaller endpoint first. Starting from \(\widehat F_0=\varnothing\), the reported forest is \(\widehat F_t=(\widehat F_{t-1}\setminus D_t)\cup A_t\). On a correct execution these lists must be exactly \(F(G_{t-1})\setminus F(G_t)\) and \(F(G_t)\setminus F(G_{t-1})\), respectively. Each contains at most one edge for a single valid update. Printing all current tree edges is not required. Duplicate or invalid reports count as a correctness failure; they never excuse exceeding the time or space bound. No later query or background computation may postpone completing the report.

Machine and costs. Use a classical sequential word RAM, with word length \(w_n=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed positive integer \(\lambda\) chosen with the data structure. Unit-cost operations are direct or indirect word reads and writes; word comparisons, branches and copies; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w_n}\); integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor; bitwise Boolean operations; and shifts with zero fill and truncation to one word. A shift by at least the word length produces zero. One instruction may generate one independent uniformly random word. Larger integers require multiple words and their actual operations are charged. Endpoints and allowed weights occupy a constant number of words. Addressable memory cells contain words and have word-sized addresses. Input reading, output writing, random generation, memory access and all computation count. There is no rank oracle, free query to another graph algorithm, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, parallel computation or uncharged lookup table.

Uniformity and resource bounds. For each fixed \(a,b\), choose one finite program, constants \(K\ge1\), integers \(C,D\ge1\), and \(\lambda\). These choices are independent of \(n\) and of the sequence. On input \(n\), initialization of the empty graph finishes within \(Kn^D\) steps and uses at most \(Kn^D\) words; all later memory use has the same bound. Initialized tables must be computed within this preprocessing budget. There is no advice or precomputed table varying with \(n\). For every valid sequence in the stated horizon and every realization of all random choices, update \(t\) finishes in at most
\[K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^C\]
steps, including its report. Choose the word-length constant large enough to address the permitted memory. Randomness may be used in preprocessing and updates. The parameters \(a,b\) tune the allowable polynomial horizon and failure probability; the program and constants may depend on them. No uniform bound on that dependence is requested.

Probability convention. The entire input sequence is fixed before the data structure draws any random bits, so it is an oblivious sequence. The probability is over all random words \(R\), including initialization, and covers simultaneous correctness of every report throughout the sequence. Separate per-update probability bounds without a simultaneous bound are insufficient. The time and memory bounds themselves have no exceptional random outcomes. This is the retained Monte Carlo formulation: a small probability of a wrong answer is permitted, whereas an always-correct deterministic data structure would be a stronger positive answer.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify the programs for every fixed \(a,b\), their resource constants and randomization. Prove initialization, exact canonical forest maintenance, online reporting, worst-case time and space on every random execution, and the simultaneous probability bound for every valid oblivious sequence of length at most \(n^a\).

A negative answer must refute the stated quantified claim: for some fixed \(a,b\), no allowed uniform program and constants meet all requirements. It must cover randomized data structures with polynomial preprocessing and space in this word-RAM model. Failure of one technique or one logarithmic exponent, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an impossibility limited to a more restrictive access model does not suffice. A conditional lower bound must retain its assumptions and does not by itself refute this unconditional proposition.

Amortized polylogarithmic time, subpolynomial worst-case time, an expected-time bound alone, an approximate forest or a deferred expensive query does not meet the criterion. A result with probabilistic time bounds needs an explicit conversion satisfying the stated hard time cap and simultaneous correctness guarantee. A rank-query count or parallel span is not the sequential running time specified here.
context:
One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log^4 n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization bounds the total cost across a sequence and permits individual updates to be much slower. The present target requires the current answer within the same polylogarithmic time budget after every single update, including a deletion chosen to expose a difficult replacement search.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain a Las Vegas algorithm: its answers are always correct, while each update has subpolynomial time in expectation and with high probability. These probability guarantees concern time. This card instead places a hard limit on time and allows a small probability of an incorrect forest. The two conventions must be distinguished even before comparing their asymptotic bounds.

Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case time for exact dynamic MSF. Subpolynomial remains weaker than polylogarithmic: \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\), for example, grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\) but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Thus the deterministic theorem is a major improvement without meeting this card’s sharper running-time target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

The dependence on \(\varepsilon\) prevents reading the approximate theorem as an exact polylogarithmic-time result. Integer forest costs differ by at least one, but a forest may have total weight as large as \((n-1)n^4\). Requiring multiplicative error small enough to certify exact cost in every instance introduces a polynomial, rather than polylogarithmic, overhead in the displayed guarantee. Exact cost would also still have to respect this card’s fixed choice among tied optima.

The ESA 2026 paper on dynamic matroids gives a deterministic algorithm maintaining a minimum-weight base with \(O(\log N)\) rank queries per update, where \(N\) is the matroid ground-set size. A rank query asks for the maximum size of an independent subset of an arbitrary supplied set. For a graph this requires determining the largest forest inside that edge set. The paper expressly distinguishes its oracle-query count from update time: it does not bound the cost of implementing these rank queries on a concrete matroid. Its proposition therefore does not settle the ordinary RAM problem here.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.
why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Inspected primary sources retain the gap between exact polylogarithmic amortized updates and exact subpolynomial worst-case updates. The SODA 2026 weighted extension is approximate, and ESA 2026 minimum-weight-base maintenance counts rank queries without bounding their implementation time. No matching exact polylogarithmic worst-case RAM resolution was found in the bounded source search; cited proofs were not independently formalized.
progress: 1998–2001: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates. | 2014–2015: Holm–Rotenberg–Wulff-Nilsen improve amortized bounds; the \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) option uses randomized priority queues in the stated RAM model. | 2017: Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. | 2020: Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition. | 2026-01-07: Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate with inverse-\(\varepsilon\) overhead. | 2026-08-25: De Vos–Grilnberger give logarithmically many rank queries per dynamic minimum-weight-base update, without a corresponding RAM update-time guarantee.
working_summary: The data structure receives insertions and deletions of weighted edges in an initially empty simple graph. After every update it must report the changes to the exact minimum spanning forest with fixed tie-breaking. The target combines a hard polylogarithmic update-time cap with simultaneous high-probability correctness over every polynomial-length oblivious sequence. A complete Lean proof must cover the charged word-RAM computation, polynomial initialization and space, and all program and probability quantifiers, or refute the full allowed class. Amortized bounds, subpolynomial worst-case bounds, approximate forests and logarithmic rank-query counts do not settle this exact maintenance question.

title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
importance_reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized data structure maintaining the exact global minimum-cut value of a fully dynamic simple unweighted undirected graph with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time, polylogarithmic worst-case query time and polynomial space? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) and fixed integers \(b\ge1,c\ge0\) such that, for every fixed integer confidence parameter \(a\ge1\), there is a constant \(C_a\ge1\) for which the following holds? For every \(n\ge2\), initialize on the empty graph on \([n]\). For every legal operation sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the random bits, with \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries and \(U+Q\le n^a\), require all of:
\[\text{space on every execution}\le C_a n^b\text{ words},\qquad \mathbb E[T_{\rm init}+T_{\rm updates}]\le C_a\bigl(n^b+U L^c\bigr),\]
\[\text{each query takes at most }C_aL^c\text{ steps on every execution},\qquad \Pr[\text{all }Q\text{ answers equal the current }\lambda(G)]\ge1-n^{-3},\]
where \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the machine model and costs are defined below. The exponents \(b,c\) and program are independent of \(a,n,\sigma\) and all cut values; constants may depend on \(a\).
question_excerpt: Retains the polylogarithmic exact fully dynamic global-minimum-cut question from the OMv open-problem discussion, using the previously selected simple unweighted, expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention. Makes the inherited polynomial horizon, common exponents, polynomial initialization/space, worst-case value queries and oblivious-sequence joint correctness explicit. The specified RAM instructions and integer confidence parameter fix the model; no weighted, terminal-cut or small-connectivity variant is substituted.
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), fixed throughout the sequence. Each edge is an unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) of distinct vertices and occurs at most once. A legal update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge. There are no loops, weights, parallel edges or vertex changes. For \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]\), put \(\delta_G(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E(G):|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and
\[\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]}|\delta_G(S)|.\]
Thus \(0\le\lambda(G)\le n-1\), and \(\lambda(G)=0\) precisely for disconnected graphs, including the initial empty graph. A query returns just this integer, not a minimizing vertex set, edge list or prescribed-terminal cut. Isolated vertices are not discarded. There is no upper bound on connectivity other than \(n-1\).

The algorithm receives \(n\) and \(a\) at initialization. It then receives one operation at a time, represented by a query tag or an insertion/deletion tag with the two vertex indices. It is not given future operations. The external sequence is fixed in advance independently of the algorithm’s randomness, including any answers or internal state; its prefixes are legal. Correctness is simultaneous over all queries in each fixed sequence, not simultaneous over all possible sequences for one random seed. No correctness obligation is imposed on invalid update sequences. Initialization and updates must finish almost surely before the next operation is provided; the finite expectation bound applies to every legal sequence and hence to each prefix. Queries have the stated worst-case bound for every choice of random bits. Expected cost includes unsuccessful executions, not only those with correct answers.

Use a uniform word-RAM. For each fixed \(a\), the word length is \(w=B(a)L\) bits, where \(B(a)\ge1\) is an integer determined by a fixed computable function chosen with the algorithm, independently of \(n\) and the operations. Words represent unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). One step may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare two words, branch, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. A random instruction returns one fresh independent uniformly distributed \(w\)-bit word in one step. Arithmetic requiring more than one word is charged for its word operations; there are no real-number, unbounded-integer or oracle primitives. The finite program and computable word-length rule are common to all inputs, with no nonuniform advice or free precomputed tables.

Space counts all stored words, including tables and temporary work. Initialization work, random choices, rebuilding and all other computation belong to the operation during which they occur; there is no uncharged background work. The expectation bound includes initialization once and all update work. Query work is separately bounded, so expected total time is also at most \(C_a(n^b+(U+Q)L^c)\). The additive initialization allowance is polynomial, not an allowance repeated at each update. Amortization concerns the total over the supplied sequence, with no average over random input graphs. A query answer that differs from the exact integer is an error. The fixed failure bound \(n^{-3}\) applies to the entire sequence of length at most \(n^a\); \(a\) is supplied to set the horizon and confidence, not to reveal the actual sequence.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a data structure satisfying every displayed requirement, or an unconditional proof of the negation in the same model. A positive answer must define one program and its computable word-length rule, establish fixed exponents, and prove the space, expected total update/initialization cost, worst-case query cost and joint correctness probability for every allowed parameter and oblivious sequence. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of program and exponents; a theorem conditional on a conjecture alone does not do so. An insertion-only algorithm, an approximation, a bounded-connectivity guarantee, superpolylogarithmic update time, or polylogarithmic updates accompanied by slower queries is insufficient. Lower bounds for weighted graphs or terminal cuts require a proved transfer preserving this exact model. The output is exact because the question asks for an exact-maintenance algorithm; there is no additive 1/100 approximation option.
context:
The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. Stability of the value alone does not specify whether an update changes it. The all-input guarantee includes long sequences in which different vertex partitions attain the minimum.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup give a deterministic algorithm with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. Its permitted updates only insert edges. The present target permits both insertions and deletions, including repeated removal and reinsertion of the same edge.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors give a randomized exact algorithm with \(\widetilde O(n)\) worst-case update time and a deterministic algorithm with \(\widetilde O(m^{29/31}n^{1/31})\) amortized time. Their March 2024 revision corrects an expander-decomposition running time. These bounds are substantial improvements over recomputing from scratch, but do not give the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. Here \(m\) denotes the current edge count and \(\widetilde O\) hides logarithmic factors.

The final June 2026 Algorithmica article by de Vos and Christiansen gives the deterministic exact amortized bound \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple unweighted graphs. This is Theorem 6 in the journal version; the article distinguishes it from an erroneous earlier cited exponent. Returning a full cut has a separate output-sensitive bound. The theorem does not establish polylogarithmic maintenance for all graph densities.

The inherited SODA 2026 theorem of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li gives deterministic exact \(n^{o(1)}\) amortized update time within a cut-size range bounded by \(2^{\Theta((\log n)^{3/4-\eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta<3/4\) in its parameter regime. It extends the earlier small-connectivity range. Both restrictions matter: the theorem does not cover every value up to \(n-1\), and a subpolynomial time bound need not be a fixed power of \(\log n\).

The word “subpolynomial” permits bounds that are larger than every polylogarithm; for example, \(2^{\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{o(1)}\) eventually exceeds \((\log_2 n)^c\) for every fixed \(c\). Thus replacing “polylogarithmic” by “subpolynomial” would change the target even if exactness and the cut-size range were otherwise identical.

El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm instead maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. A multiplicative estimate with relative error \(\epsilon\) can have additive error \(\epsilon\lambda\). Integrality does not turn such a guarantee into exactness uniformly over large \(\lambda\); the approximation accuracy and its effect on running time remain essential.

Kenneth-Mordoch’s February 2026 preprint reports a canonical exact minimum-cut algorithm with polylogarithmic worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n)\) queries. Its query procedure constructs a sparse contracted graph and computes a cut on that graph before reporting the result. Consequently, its stated query bound is not just the cost of printing the cut’s vertices, and the theorem does not provide the polylogarithmic value query required here.

The SOSA 2026 paper by Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer gives another tradeoff: its publisher abstract states \(\widetilde O(n/\lambda)\) worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n^2/\lambda^2)\) worst-case queries for positive connectivity. This becomes efficient in the high-connectivity range, but it is not a polylogarithmic bound uniform over all positive values of \(\lambda\). Disconnected graphs are also part of the present target.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.
why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No algorithm satisfying both polylogarithmic expected-amortized updates and worst-case value queries for unrestricted exact connectivity, or unconditional impossibility theorem in the chosen model, was found in the bounded primary-source review. The SODA2026 exact result restricts cut size; the final June2026 tree-packing bound is not polylogarithmic. The February2026 pseudo-deterministic result has nearly linear queries, and the SOSA2026 tradeoff depends on connectivity. These are distinct guarantees; new proofs were not independently certified.

working_summary: The global minimum cut is the minimum number of edges crossing any nonempty proper vertex subset, with value zero for a disconnected graph. The question asks for one randomized data structure returning that exact value while arbitrary legal edge insertions and deletions arrive online. It requires polylogarithmic expected amortized updates, polylogarithmic worst-case queries and polynomial space, with explicit initialization cost and uniform exponents. For each fixed oblivious polynomial-length operation sequence, all answers must be simultaneously correct with error probability at most \(n^{-3}\). A complete Lean proof must establish the whole guarantee or its unconditional impossibility; approximate, small-cut, insertion-only and fast-update/slow-query results do not suffice.

title: Logarithmic Las Vegas dynamic connectivity
importance_reason: Closing the remaining iterated-logarithm gap would pin down a central dynamic graph primitive near its information-theoretic lower bounds.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(K>0\), integers \(a\ge4\) and \(c\ge0\), and one uniform randomized online word-RAM data structure \(A\) with the following guarantees for every \(n\ge1\)?

Starting with the empty undirected simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), it processes every finite valid operation sequence \(\sigma\), fixed independently of its randomness, consisting of edge insertions, edge deletions and connectivity queries. It is always correct, all operations terminate almost surely, and, writing \(u\) and \(q\) for the numbers of updates and queries and \(\lambda_n=\log_2(n+2)\),
\[
 \mathbb E[T_A(n,\sigma)]\le
 K\bigl(n\lambda_n^c+(u+q)\lambda_n\bigr).
\]
Every individual query uses at most \(K\lambda_n\) instructions on every execution. The structure uses at most \(K(n+m)\lambda_n^c\) words when the current graph has \(m\) edges, with workspace counted as specified below. Its word length is \(w=a\lceil\lambda_n\rceil\).
question_excerpt: The 2023 Las Vegas dynamic-connectivity result has amortized expected update time O(log n (log log n)^2) and logarithmic-or-smaller worst-case query time. This card asks whether the remaining squared iterated-logarithm update overhead can be removed while retaining exact answers and near-linear space.
definitions:
An insertion \(\operatorname{Insert}(v,z)\) adds one absent edge \(\{v,z\}\), with distinct endpoints in \([n]\). A deletion \(\operatorname{Delete}(v,z)\) removes one present edge. Loops and parallel edges are excluded. A query \(\operatorname{Connected}(v,z)\) returns one Boolean value indicating whether a finite path connects its endpoints in the current graph. A path of length zero is allowed, so \(\operatorname{Connected}(v,v)\) is true. No assumptions are made about degrees, components, planarity or update order.

Operations are supplied one at a time and answered before the next operation is supplied. The algorithm knows \(n\) at initialization but has no advance access to future operations or to their total number. The guarantee holds for every finite valid sequence and every prefix of that sequence, with no polynomial upper bound on sequence length. The sequence is chosen independently of the internal random words: this is an oblivious adversary. Access to hidden random state, response times or an exposed spanning forest is not supplied to the chooser. No public spanning forest is required as output.

The variable \(T_A(n,\sigma)\) counts initialization and all instructions used to process the sequence, including query and update outputs. The expectation is over independent uniform random words generated by the data structure. Every answer produced must be exact, not merely correct with high probability. Updates may have random unbounded running time on exceptional random tapes, but terminate almost surely; the displayed finite expectation is required for every finite sequence. Queries obey their deterministic instruction bound whenever invoked from a reachable state. The empty sequence imposes the stated expected initialization bound. Amortization permits an individual update to cost more than a logarithm.

Space is the total number of live stored words, including the graph representation, tables, copies, counters and temporary workspace, on every execution. Between operations, \(m\) is the current edge count. During one update, the bound uses the larger of the edge counts immediately before and after that update; these differ by one. During a query it uses the unchanged count, and during initialization it uses zero. Released storage cannot retain information accessible to the program without being counted. Space is not measured by a maximum edge count from the distant past.

The uniform sequential word RAM is a fixed finite program with unsigned \(w\)-bit registers and word-addressed memory, with no advice, oracle or free precomputed tables. Its unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words. Multiword computations pay for each constituent instruction. Generating an independent uniform random word costs one instruction. All initialization, table construction, memory management, auxiliary computation and output are charged. The same program and constants \(K,a,c\) work for every \(n\) and sequence.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a data structure and constants exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof of their logical nonexistence with the same online model, space bound and correctness and cost quantifiers.

A larger polylogarithmic update bound, a guarantee allowing erroneous answers, an offline algorithm or a special graph class does not establish the proposition. A lower bound on deterministic algorithms, worst-case updates or a stronger adversary does not by itself refute this Las Vegas amortized target. A conditional hardness result proves only its conditional conclusion. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
context:
An edge deletion can split a component, so fast insertion alone does not solve fully dynamic connectivity. The structure must detect whether another path still connects the endpoints.

The 2023 theorem achieves \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^2)\) amortized expected update time with always-correct answers. The target removes the factor \((\log\log n)^2\); it does not demand a worst-case bound for each update.

General cell-probe lower bounds already give a logarithmic obstruction for dynamic connectivity and tradeoffs between update and query costs. They motivate the endpoint without proving an additional superlogarithmic update requirement.

The SODA 2026 result guarantees a polylogarithmic expected bound for each update, a stronger temporal guarantee than amortization. Its unspecified polylogarithmic exponent does not give the particular logarithmic bound requested here.

Both cited upper-bound papers tolerate adversaries stronger than the fixed-sequence adversary in this card. That robustness is useful progress but is not an extra requirement on a solution here.
why: Determine the logarithmic endpoint for a basic graph property under arbitrary edge insertions and deletions. It would close the remaining update-time gap to general information-access lower bounds under a precise, always-correct randomized guarantee.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified logarithmic amortized expected Las Vegas solution with the stated query and space guarantees, or unconditional impossibility result. The SODA 2026 expected worst-case theorem is polylogarithmic and does not state the logarithmic endpoint. Cited complete proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2006: Logarithmic randomized amortized cell-probe lower bounds and update/query tradeoffs establish a natural benchmark. | 2023-04-28: The full Las Vegas algorithm gives logarithmic updates times a squared iterated logarithm. | 2026: The SODA result gives polylogarithmic expected worst-case updates, addressing a different guarantee.
working_summary: An undirected graph changes by single-edge insertions and deletions. Connectivity queries must always return the exact answer. The target is logarithmic amortized expected update time and logarithmic worst-case query time. Known guarantees either retain an iterated-logarithm update overhead or use a larger polylogarithmic bound. A complete Lean-checked answer must respect online access, the fixed-sequence adversary and near-linear current-graph space.

title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
importance_reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist integers \(a,d\ge1\) and \(B\ge c+3\), a real constant \(K\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic word-RAM data structure with the following guarantees for every \(n\ge2\) and supplied integer capacity \(n\le m\le n^2\)?

The data structure maintains a simple directed graph on the fixed vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with at most \(m\) live edges and edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots,n^c\}\), under online single-edge insertions, deletions and weight changes. It returns the exact current distance for every queried ordered vertex pair. Write \(\ell=\log_2(n+2)\). Preprocessing an arbitrary initial graph uses at most \(Kn^d\) instructions, and space is at most \(Kn^d\) words at every time. Every individual query uses at most \(K\ell^a\) instructions. After preprocessing, every finite valid sequence containing \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries uses at most
\[
K\bigl(Um\ell^a+Q\ell^a\bigr)
\]
instructions in total. The constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n,m\), the initial graph or the operation sequence.
question_excerpt: The seminar asks for a fully dynamic all-pairs shortest-path algorithm with update cost proportional to the edge count and constant query cost, allowing polylogarithmic factors in both. This card retains the previously selected deterministic, directed, bounded-integer-weight version with amortized edge updates and a supplied edge capacity.
definitions:
The initial graph is explicitly given as a list of ordered endpoint pairs and integer weights, together with \(n\) and \(m\). There are no self-loops, and each ordered pair has at most one edge. An insertion supplies an absent edge and its allowed weight, a deletion names a present edge, and a weight change supplies a new allowed weight for a present edge. Every resulting graph must have at most the fixed supplied capacity \(m\) edges. The algorithm must support all such valid sequences, however long. The value \(m\) is neither the number of updates nor the current number of edges.

A query supplies \(s,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and requests the minimum sum of edge weights along a directed path from \(s\) to \(t\), with distance zero when \(s=t\) and a distinguished symbol \(\infty\) when no path exists. Positive weights imply that every finite distance is at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output is this one distance, not a shortest path or a full matrix. Every answer must be correct. Operations arrive one at a time, and each must finish before the next is supplied; future operations are unavailable.

For a given \(n\), a machine word has exactly \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Memory is indexed by unsigned words, and \(B\) must also be large enough to address the allowed \(Kn^d\) words. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, unsigned comparisons and conditional branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Finite distances and the infinity marker must have an unambiguous constant-word encoding. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented and charged through these operations. The program is finite and independent of \(n,m\); it receives no advice or uncharged precomputed tables.

Preprocessing includes reading and constructing all initial data. After it finishes, the displayed total bound applies to every finite prefix, including prefixes with no updates or no queries. There is no extra additive \(n^d\) allowance in that post-preprocessing bound. Individual updates may exceed their amortized charge, but each query also satisfies the stated worst-case bound, regardless of the preceding operations. All instruction counts include maintenance work and any rebuilding performed during the operation sequence. The space bound applies throughout preprocessing and all operations.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic data structure for every fixed \(c\), prove all exact query answers and the capacity-sensitive bounds for every allowed graph and operation prefix, and account for word size and polynomial space.

A negative answer must disprove the existence proposition in the stated model; a result conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis remains a conditional obstruction and must identify that assumption. An update bound near \(n^2\) only has the requested dependence on \(m\) for sufficiently dense graphs. Approximate distances, offline sequences, planar graphs, insertion-only updates, or an amortized query bound alone do not establish the stated target. The fact that one edge change alters many pairwise distances is not by itself a lower bound on an implicit distance oracle.
context:
The data structure must combine cheap updates with immediately available exact answers. The requested update scale follows a supplied bound on live edges, so it asks for a substantial saving on sparse graphs even though the number of possible queried pairs is quadratic.

Changing one edge can change many shortest-path distances. An oracle may represent those changes implicitly and expose only one distance per query, so counting changed entries in a materialized matrix does not settle its update cost.

The classical journal result achieves \(O(n^2\log^3 n)\) amortized updates and constant distance queries. Its theorem has its own initialization, sequence-length and tie-handling conventions. It supplies the near-quadratic baseline, while the selected card asks for a bound that scales with the edge capacity even when it is close to \(n\).

The ESA 2025 sparsification theorem achieves near-linear total processing for its bounded update sequence with a subpolynomial multiplicative distance approximation. Both the approximation and the meaning of its update-budget parameter must be kept explicit when comparing that theorem with exact capacity-sensitive maintenance.

The planar result posted to arXiv in June 2026 was already a SODA 2022 result according to its metadata. Its main fully dynamic guarantee is offline, and its query cost is near square-root rather than polylogarithmic. It does not resolve the general online target.
why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.
status_note: Source-open target, retaining the inherited deterministic positive-integer-weight specialization. Bounded searches through 17 September 2026 did not locate an exact general-digraph algorithm satisfying all the selected capacity-sensitive update, worst-case query, online and prefix guarantees. The 2025 approximate theorem and the planar offline paper posted in 2026 do not meet these requirements. This search does not establish unconditional current openness.
progress: 2004: The journal algorithm establishes the classical near-quadratic amortized-update and constant-query baseline under its stated initialization and sequence conventions. | 2021: The seminar asks for edge-linear updates and constant queries up to polylogarithmic factors. | 2025: The sparsification theorem gives very fast dynamic approximate distances for a bounded-length update sequence. | 2026-06-01: The SODA 2022 planar offline result is posted to arXiv; its model and query bound differ from this target.
working_summary: The data structure maintains exact directed distances while individual weighted edges change. The supplied capacity m bounds the number of live edges throughout an arbitrary online operation sequence. The requested update charge is m times a fixed polylogarithmic factor, with polylogarithmic worst-case distance queries. The deterministic model allows polynomial preprocessing and space but requires the operation bound after preprocessing for every finite prefix. The review separates this sparse exact target from near-quadratic, approximate and planar offline results.

title: Worst-case logarithmic dynamic planar convex hulls
importance_reason: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic data structure and an absolute constant \(K\ge1\) that maintain a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\), initially empty, with the following guarantees on every finite valid online sequence? Each point insertion, point deletion and extreme-point query takes at most \(K\log_2(n+2)\) worst-case real-RAM steps, where \(n\) is the larger set size immediately before and after that operation. The stored representation uses at most \(K(1+|P|)\) cells. Given any \(u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\), an extreme-point query returns a point \(p\in P\) maximizing \(\langle u,p\rangle\), or an empty marker if \(P=\varnothing\).
question_excerpt: The full version leaves open whether logarithmic worst-case update time can coexist with fast extreme-point queries. This card retains the precise extreme-point-only interface, linear-space budget and deterministic exact real-arithmetic conventions already selected for that question.
definitions:
Insert receives the two exact real coordinates of a point not currently in \(P\), adds it and returns a stable handle. Delete receives a valid handle for a currently present point and removes that point; the handle then becomes invalid. A previously deleted coordinate pair may be inserted again with a new handle. A handle is only a reference to an item, not an encoding of free auxiliary information. Each live handle must remain usable until its item is deleted, including across internal restructuring.

For \(u=(u_x,u_y)\) and \(p=(p_x,p_y)\), the objective is \(\langle u,p\rangle=u_xp_x+u_yp_y\). Any maximizing point is acceptable, chosen deterministically by the algorithm. All finite sets are allowed: no general-position, distinct-x-coordinate, noncollinearity, convex-position or bounded-coordinate promise is made. Updates may occur in arbitrary order. A query returns only one point or an empty marker, not a cyclic list of the entire convex hull, its edges, or all changes caused by an update.

Use an algebraic real RAM with a fixed finite program. A cell stores an exact real scalar, a pointer or a constant-size control value. Copying a cell, reading or writing an addressed cell, following or changing a pointer, comparison, branching, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value each cost one step. Allocating or releasing a constant-size record also costs one step. The program contains only fixed rational numerical constants and uses ordinary discrete address bookkeeping; a real coordinate is not an address encoding. No floor, bit extraction from a real, arbitrary-precision packing primitive, unbounded parallel operation, randomness, advice or oracle is supplied. There is no charge for coordinate bit length: these are exact real-arithmetic costs, not rational-input bit complexity.

All stored points, handles, indexes, auxiliary records and retained historical information count toward space. All comparisons, rebuilding, initialization and query work count toward time. Initialization on the empty set takes constant time and space. Between operations at most \(K(1+|P|)\) cells are retained; during an operation at most \(K(1+n)\) cells, including its workspace, are used, after enlarging the same universal constant if necessary. The client holds input coordinates and handles but supplies no uncharged index or preprocessing. Deleted data may be retained only within the current space bound.

The algorithm must finish each operation and return its answer before seeing the next. It has no advance knowledge of the sequence length, future operations, maximum eventual set size or coordinate values. The one program and constant \(K\) work for every sequence and every direction. Both time and space are measured against current size; an occasional expensive update cannot be paid for by averaging over other operations. Reading two input coordinates or returning one stored point takes constant work.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish exact answers, linear total storage and a logarithmic bound for every individual insertion, deletion and query, with all rebuilding and workspace charged. A negative proof must rule out all data structures in the stated model unconditionally; a conditional lower bound is only a conditional result.

Logarithmic amortized updates, expected bounds, ordered or one-sided update restrictions, and data structures requiring superlinear storage do not meet the full target. An argument that explicitly reporting a changed hull can have linear output size does not refute this one-point query interface.
context:
The known linear-space structure achieves logarithmic amortized update time and logarithmic extreme-point queries. The unresolved distinction is whether every individual update can satisfy the logarithmic time bound.

One update may change many hull vertices. A query interface avoids having to list those changes, so an output-size argument for explicitly reporting a hull is not a lower bound for this target.

The 2026 engineering paper develops a practical fully dynamic implementation with amortized logarithmic-times-log-log updates and logarithmic-squared queries. Its performance guarantees address a different endpoint.

The same recent discussion distinguishes general updates from simple-path and ordered-update settings. Bounds for those restricted settings do not by themselves give the unrestricted guarantee here.
why: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.
status_note: The 2019 full version explicitly leaves worst-case logarithmic updates open. The 2026 engineering paper has different amortized guarantees and does not settle this extreme-point target. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review is not an independent audit of every geometric data-structure proof.
progress: 2002: The conference result achieves linear space and logarithmic amortized updates with logarithmic extreme-point queries. | 2019-02-28: The full version supplies the detailed analysis and explicitly retains worst-case logarithmic updates as an open question. | 2026-06-15: A new implemented fully dynamic structure improves practical performance, with amortized update guarantees.
working_summary: Maintain an arbitrary changing set of exact points in the plane, starting from the empty set. Insertions and deletions may occur in any order, and a query asks for one point farthest in a supplied direction. The target is deterministic logarithmic worst-case time for each operation and linear total space. Known optimal amortized bounds and recent practical implementations do not provide that per-operation guarantee. The answer must be a complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional refutation in the specified real-arithmetic model.

title: Near-linear incremental topological ordering
importance_reason: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.
formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas randomized algorithm maintain a topological ordering of an initially empty directed graph on \(n\) named vertices during edge insertions in expected total time \((n+m)^{1+o(1)}\), with \(O(1)\) worst-case order-comparison queries and \(O((n+m)(\log(2+n))^C)\) words of space for some constant \(C\)? Here \(m\) is the number of edges inserted so far, and every graph in the sequence is promised acyclic.
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. For each \(n\ge2\), vertices are \([n]\), no parallel edges or loops are inserted, and the complete finite insertion/query sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Word length is \(\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed algorithm-chosen constant \(a\) large enough for its storage addresses. After every insertion there must be a total order of all vertices with every edge directed forward. A query on \((u,v)\) returns whether \(u\) precedes \(v\) in that maintained order, with all queries between insertions referring to the same order. It is not a reachability query, and printing a fresh list of all vertices after every insertion is not required. Answers are always correct, and operations terminate almost surely. The update bound means that for every constant \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(C_\eta\) such that expected initialization plus update time is at most \(C_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}\) for every prefix; \(q\) order queries add \(O(q)\) time. No predictions, special graph family or advance edge information are supplied. The target allows the full stated RAM, without an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the same inputs, computation model, space allowance, quantifiers and cost guarantees. A result for a restricted input family or a different model does not decide the full target.
context:
The 2025 report distinguishes maintaining a topological order from cycle detection, which already has almost-linear total update time. It records the dense-graph work of Bender and coauthors and sparse-graph bounds with a polynomial overhead.

The report also poses a more specific combinatorial improvement. This card instead formalizes the broader almost-linear ordering target discussed in the researcher list. Prediction-dependent graph maintenance does not establish this guarantee for arbitrary insertion sequences.
why: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.
status_note: Open in the cited dated sources. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 13 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2025: The report explicitly separates almost-linear cycle detection from the still-slower maintenance of a topological order. | 2026: Prediction-based incremental graph results concern additional input assistance and leave the stated unassisted target unchanged.
working_summary: Directed edges arrive one at a time without creating a cycle. The algorithm maintains a total vertex order consistent with every edge. Queries compare two vertices in the maintained order. The target is almost-linear total update time over the whole insertion sequence. Fast cycle detection by itself does not maintain the order required here.

title: Polylogarithmic dynamic maximal matching against adaptive updates
importance_reason: Dynamic maximal matching is a fundamental update-time benchmark and a building block for other dynamic graph algorithms.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that explicitly maintains a maximal matching in a fully dynamic \(n\)-vertex simple graph against an adaptive adversary, with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time? More precisely, are there an algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every horizon \(T\ge1\), and every valid adaptive update strategy, the algorithm is always correct and its expected total update work is at most
\[C T(\log_2(n+2))^c,\]
after initialization in at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) expected time? The graph starts empty and each update inserts or deletes one edge. The model and adversary are defined below. A deterministic algorithm is permitted as a special case.

This card selects the polylogarithmic question expressly included in the 2022 source. Its earlier sublinear-time question has since received positive answers; that weaker threshold is retained as dated progress rather than presented as open.
definitions:
The fixed vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is undirected, loopless and simple, with no sparsity, degree or bipartiteness promise. An insertion gives two distinct vertex labels whose edge is currently absent; a deletion specifies a currently present edge. Both kinds may occur in any order, and the next update is unavailable until the current one is finished.

A matching \(M\subseteq E\) has no two edges sharing an endpoint. It is maximal if no edge of \(E\setminus M\) can be added while preserving this condition; equivalently, every edge of the graph has at least one endpoint incident to \(M\). The requirement is inclusion-wise maximality after every update. No maximum-cardinality optimality requirement is imposed.

Explicit maintenance means retaining an array \(\mathrm{mate}[1..n]\) with value zero for an unmatched vertex and value \(v\) at \(u\) when \(\{u,v\}\in M\). Array changes are charged to update time; reading one mate entry takes constant time. The whole matching need not be printed after each update.

Use a word-RAM with words of \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(c_w\) chosen with the algorithm, polynomially many addressable words of persistent memory, and unit-cost word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Each independent uniform random word also costs one operation. All preprocessing, memory management and changes to the maintained matching are charged. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\), with no graph-dependent advice or uncharged table depending on the input. Its memory bound and word-size constant are fixed independently of the update horizon.

Before selecting update \(t+1\), the adversary may inspect the complete current matching, all previous updates and all observed update runtimes. It has unbounded computation and may use its own independent randomness. It does not see hidden algorithm state, past unexposed random choices or future random bits. Correctness and expected cost must hold for every such adaptive strategy, with the horizon \(T\) fixed before the experiment. The expectation includes randomness of both parties. Allowing the adversary to inspect the matching is an observation convention, not a requirement to print the array at every step.

Always correct means that every completed update returns a valid maximal matching, and every finite valid adaptive experiment terminates with probability one. Randomness may affect running time and which maximal matching is chosen, but may never permit an incorrect answer. This is a Las Vegas guarantee. The total-time inequality is amortized: a single update may cost more than a polylogarithm, provided every finite prefix obeys the stated expected total bound. All constants are independent of \(n,T\), the graph and the adversary.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of an algorithm with these guarantees. A positive answer must maintain an explicit maximal matching for all valid adaptive insertion/deletion sequences, with the stated uniformity, always-correct behavior and expected prefix-total bounds. A bound only against an oblivious adversary, a maintained estimate of maximum matching size, or a matching that is approximately maximum but not maximal is insufficient. A merely sublinear polynomial update bound does not reach the polylogarithmic target. A negative answer must rule out randomized algorithms in this model, not just one deterministic implementation.
context:
The original problem paragraph asks several related questions. This review takes its explicit polylogarithmic target and fixes the permissive expected-amortized, always-correct randomized setting against an adversary observing the matching. It does not combine the separate lower-bound question into the answer criterion.

The 2026 paper reports earlier oblivious-adversary algorithms with constant amortized update time and polylogarithmic worst-case update time. Those guarantees assume that the update sequence cannot adapt to the maintained matching.

Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak’s STOC 2025 results, summarized in the 2026 introduction, achieve \(\widetilde O(n^{3/4})\) randomized adaptive update time and \(\widetilde O(n^{8/9})\) deterministic update time, both amortized. Thus the source’s basic sublinear threshold is no longer the open target.

Chuzhoy, Khanna and Song’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic fully dynamic algorithm with amortized update time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\). This also tolerates adaptive updates, but its guarantee does not supply polylogarithmic update time. Here \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors, and \(o(1)\) in the exponent tends to zero as \(n\) grows.
why: Maximal matching is a basic dynamic graph primitive whose current answer can influence the next change to the graph. This problem asks whether the cost of responding to that feedback can be reduced to a polylogarithm. It would clarify a major difference between algorithms that assume an independently chosen update sequence and algorithms whose guarantees survive interaction.
status_note: The original Section 4.6 and Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song arXiv:2605.00797v1, including its introduction and Theorem 1.1, were read on 2026-09-14. The 2025 results resolve the source’s sublinear threshold, and the 2026 theorem improves the deterministic exponent. The selected polylogarithmic target is expressly asked in the source and is not established by these results. A bounded later-work search found no matching general adaptive polylogarithmic algorithm or impossibility theorem. The 2026 reference records the checked manuscript and its stated STOC venue rather than claiming a separately checked proceedings version.
progress: 2022-11: The workshop asks for sublinear and then polylogarithmic update time in the deterministic or adaptive-adversary setting. | 2025: The first sublinear adaptive and deterministic amortized bounds are obtained by Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak, as recorded in the checked 2026 introduction. | 2026-05-01: The Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song manuscript states a deterministic \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized bound in Theorem 1.1.
working_summary: A graph changes through edge insertions and deletions while an explicit maximal matching must remain available. The next change may depend on the matching the algorithm has just produced. The question asks for an always-correct algorithm with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against this adaptive feedback. Deterministic algorithms now achieve a square-root-scale amortized bound, resolving the older sublinear threshold. The much stronger polylogarithmic target remains distinct from constant-time results for update sequences fixed independently of the algorithm.

title: Dynamic spanning trees with polylogarithmic average stretch
importance_reason: Dynamically maintaining low-stretch spanning trees would provide a reusable primitive for graph optimization and numerical methods.
formal:
Is there a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains a spanning forest \(F_t\) of an unweighted simple graph \(G_t\) with polylogarithmic expected average stretch and sublinear expected amortized update time? Precisely, do there exist such an algorithm, constants \(C,a,c>0\), and a function \(u:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u(n)}n=0,\]
such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every finite oblivious sequence of \(T\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty \(n\)-vertex graph,
\[\mathbb E[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)]\le C(\log_2(n+2))^c\quad(0\le t\le T),\]
and the expected total work for the updates is at most \(T u(n)\), after at most \(C n^a\) expected initialization work? The maintained object must always be an actual spanning forest using current graph edges.

For a connected graph, a spanning forest is a spanning tree. The componentwise convention below makes the target meaningful when a deletion disconnects the graph, as in the original dynamic low-stretch algorithm. This card chooses the first question in the workshop source, with the expectation and amortization conventions of that prior work; it does not also require resistance to adaptive updates.
definitions:
The graph \(G_t=([n],E_t)\) is finite, undirected, loopless and simple, with unit edge lengths. Its vertex set remains fixed. An insertion specifies an absent edge between two distinct labels, and a deletion specifies a present edge. No maximum-degree or sparsity promise is imposed, and components may split or merge. A valid spanning forest \(F_t=([n],E_t^F)\) has \(E_t^F\subseteq E_t\), is acyclic, and connects every pair of vertices that lie in the same connected component of \(G_t\). Thus it contains one spanning tree for each nontrivial component and all isolated vertices.

For \(\{v,w\}\in E_t\), let \(d_{F_t}(v,w)\) be the number of edges on the unique path between its endpoints in \(F_t\). Put
\[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)=\begin{cases}|E_t|^{-1}\displaystyle\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E_t}d_{F_t}(v,w),&|E_t|>0,\\0,&|E_t|=0.\end{cases}\]
All current edges participate in the average, including forest edges, whose distance is one. The target bounds this absolute stretch quantity, not its ratio to the best possible forest. The expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness at each fixed time, after averaging over the graph edges; a bound for every individual edge is not required.

The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is revealed one operation at a time. The algorithm is not given future updates. Its guarantee covers every finite sequence length, and hence every finite prefix of any fixed infinite valid sequence. The same constants and function \(u\) work for all graphs, edge counts, times and sequences.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed constant \(c_w\) large enough to address the algorithm's polynomially many persistent words. Unit-cost operations are word reads/writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, and independent uniform random words. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\); no input-dependent advice or uncharged precomputed table is allowed. Initialization starts with no graph edges and is charged separately as specified.

The forest is maintained explicitly as its edge set: a linked list or equivalent enumerable collection of its current edge records is stored, and each current graph edge record indicates whether it belongs to the forest. Given an existing edge-record handle, this flag is readable in constant time, and all forest edges can be enumerated in time proportional to their number plus one. Finding graph-edge records from endpoint labels, changing forest membership, random choices, rebuilds and memory management are included in update work. No full forest printout or rooted-parent array is required after every update.

Every completed update must produce a valid spanning forest, and each finite execution must terminate with probability one. Only the quality and runtime guarantees are in expectation.
