title: Fully functional suffix trees in BWT-run-linear total space
importance_reason: This asks whether an entire general navigation structure can be retained at the scale of repetitive input, rather than supporting only a single search operation.
formal:
Do there exist constants \(C,K>0\), integers \(c\ge0\), \(p\ge1\), \(B\ge8\), and one uniform deterministic static data structure such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly given text
\[
T\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}\#,
\]
it constructs a representation of the compact suffix tree in at most \(Kn^p\) word-RAM instructions, retains at most \(Cr\) words, and answers each operation specified below exactly in at most
\[
K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^c
\]
worst-case instructions, while the retained representation together with all temporary query work uses at most \(Cr\) words? Here \(r\) is the number of runs in the Burrows–Wheeler transform of \(T\), including its unique sentinel, and the word length is \(B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). All constants and programs are chosen once, independently of the text and its length.
question_excerpt: The full r-index treatment asks which text-access and suffix-array/tree capabilities can be supported in O(r) space, having obtained full tree functionality in O(r log(n/r)) words. This card retains the previously imported binary-text specialization and exact list of required operations; it does not assert equivalence to every possible suffix-tree interface.
definitions:
Text positions and suffix ranks are zero-based. The alphabet is ordered \(\#<0<1\); the sentinel \(\#\) occurs only at position \(n-1\). For \(0\le i<n\), the suffix beginning at \(i\) is \(T[i]\cdots T[n-1]\). The suffix array \(\operatorname{SA}[j]\) is the starting position of the suffix of lexicographic rank \(j\), and \(\operatorname{ISA}[i]\) is the unique rank \(j\) with \(\operatorname{SA}[j]=i\). Define
\[
\operatorname{BWT}[j]=T[(\operatorname{SA}[j]-1)\bmod n].
\]
The residue lies in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). A run is a maximal nonempty interval of equal symbols in this BWT array; \(r\) is its number of runs. The sentinel is counted in both \(n\) and \(r\).

The suffix trie contains the paths spelling all \(n\) suffixes, with the empty string at its root. Contract maximal paths whose intermediate vertices have just one child, concatenating their edge labels. The resulting compact suffix tree retains the root, branching vertices and leaves. Every edge has a nonempty string label. A node's path label is the concatenation of edge labels from the root to that node. Leaves are ordered by suffix rank. Every node is represented externally by the pair \([l,h]\) of smallest and largest ranks among its descendant leaves. These intervals uniquely identify explicit nodes; an interior point of an edge is not an additional queryable node. In particular, the root is \([0,n-1]\) and leaf rank \(j\) is \([j,j]\).

The complete required interface consists of the following operations. Node arguments are valid node intervals of the indexed text; ranks and positions lie in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\).

- Return the root, or return the leaf of a supplied suffix rank.
- Given a node, return its parent, its lexicographically first child, or its next sibling in its parent's child order. Children are ordered by the first symbols of their edge labels. Return a distinguished marker \(\bot\) when the requested parent, child or sibling does not exist; in particular the root has no parent or sibling.
- Given a node and a symbol \(a\in\{\#,0,1\}\), return its child whose edge label begins with \(a\), or \(\bot\) if there is no such child.
- Given any node, return its tree depth, the number of edges from the root, or its string depth, the number of symbols in its path label. Both root depths are zero. A leaf for suffix position \(i\) has string depth \(n-i\).
- Given two nodes, return their lowest common ancestor, namely their common ancestor of maximum tree depth. A node is its own ancestor.
- Given a nonroot internal node with path label \(aU\), return its suffix link: the explicit node whose path label is \(U\). This node exists in this suffix tree; \(U\) may be empty, in which case the answer is the root. No suffix-link query on a leaf or on the root is required.
- Given \(j\), return \(\operatorname{SA}[j]\); given \(i\), return \(\operatorname{ISA}[i]\) or \(T[i]\).

Every query returns only a constant number of words. Arbitrary valid node intervals can be supplied directly; handles are not required to originate from a preceding traversal. Every operation must work after construction with no access to an uncounted input copy or external text-access service. All retained text, suffix samples, lookup tables, oracle implementations and internally retained handles count toward the space bound. Temporary query memory, including registers, also counts. Externally supplied arguments and the constant-size returned result may be excluded. Construction starts from the explicitly supplied text, one symbol per word, and may use additional temporary memory; construction instructions and initialization are charged to its polynomial time bound. That temporary memory is discarded before queries begin.

The machine is a sequential word RAM with a fixed finite program and the stated word length. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Values and addresses fit in words, and multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. There is no randomness, nonuniform advice, uncharged preprocessing, free size-dependent table or input-dependent oracle. A static query starts without input-dependent private state outside the counted representation. The bounds hold for every text and every valid query, without amortization over a query sequence.

The binary alphabet and this explicitly enumerated interface are the retained editorial specialization of the broader suffix-tree question. “Fully functional” here means exactly these operations; no unlisted operation is silently required.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must provide the uniform construction and all query algorithms, prove their exact behavior, and prove the simultaneous polynomial construction, run-linear total space and polylogarithmic worst-case query bounds.

A structure supporting only pattern counting, occurrence reporting or a proper subset of the required interface is insufficient. Space charged in addition to a separately stored text or access oracle does not establish the total-space target unless that additional representation is also included in the proved \(Cr\) bound. An extra logarithmic space factor does not meet the target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this existence question.
context:
Repeated text can have a small number of BWT runs even when its expanded suffix tree is large. The run-linear search index and the full navigation structure have different space guarantees.

The checked full suffix-tree theorem uses \(O(r\log(2+n/r))\) words and supports the relevant operations in polylogarithmic time. The harmless 2 in the logarithm makes the bound explicit also when the run count is close to the text length.

The ICALP 2026 path-decomposition result supports several tree operations with O(r) additional words. Its theorem assumes a separate text-access and longest-common-extension oracle and does not state all operations required here.

A July 2026 application to compact word graphs still invokes the earlier full suffix-tree representation as a black box with its logarithmic space overhead.

The September 2026 suffixient-array publication provides a different sampling and pattern-location interface with text-access assumptions. Its guarantees alone do not supply the combined tree interface and total-space bound on this card.

Non-overlapping occurrence reporting is another useful run-linear indexing task. The conference paper appeared in 2023, its repository posting in 2024, and its journal version in 2025; those dates do not denote a full-tree resolution.
why: A complete navigation index lets algorithms work directly on highly repetitive text without retaining an expanded tree. The question is whether this general interface, including direct suffix and text access, can fit at the same run-count scale as more specialized search indexes.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the exact binary-text interface in O(r) total words. The July 2026 theorem charges its O(r) words in addition to a text oracle and states a narrower interface; the September sampling result also has distinct access assumptions. This review checks theorem scope and dates, not complete proofs of all cited work. The binary specialization and operation list remain editorial choices already present in the imported card.
progress: 2019-07-04: The full revision gives the compressed suffix-tree theorem and records remaining O(r)-space access questions. | 2025-11-21: The non-overlapping reporting work appears in journal form; its task is narrower than the required suffix-tree interface. | 2026-07-01: Path decompositions reduce the additional space for a specified subset of tree operations to O(r), under separate text-oracle assumptions. | 2026-09-11: The suffixient-array journal paper develops another compressed pattern-location interface requiring access to the underlying text.
working_summary: A binary text with a sentinel determines a suffix tree and a run count in its Burrows–Wheeler transform. The target stores the entire specified navigation and direct-access interface in space proportional to that run count. Every query must be exact and take polylogarithmic worst-case time after deterministic polynomial-time construction. The space budget includes the text representation and any access oracle, which distinguishes the target from recent partial-interface results. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish or refute all of these guarantees simultaneously.

title: Certifying Karp–Rabin fingerprints
importance_reason: Efficient certification could turn a widely used probabilistic string primitive into a reliable one while preserving a chosen fingerprint representation.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), do there exist a constant \(K\ge1\) and one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) with this guarantee? Its input is \(n\ge2\), an alphabet size \(2\le\sigma\le n^c\), a string \(T\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^n\) and a supplied prime \(2\le p\le n^c\). Every execution takes at most \(Kn\log_2(n+2)\) word-RAM instructions. It outputs CERTIFIED or REJECT for the single fingerprint
\[
h_p(T[i..i+\ell-1])=\sum_{a=0}^{\ell-1}T[i+a]\sigma^a\pmod p.
\]
If any two unequal equal-length substrings collide, every execution must output REJECT. If no such pair exists, the probability of CERTIFIED must be at least \(2/3\). All lengths \(1\le\ell\le n\) are included; the supplied base and prime remain fixed.
question_excerpt: Farach-Colton asks how quickly a supplied prime can be checked for collisions between unequal, equal-length substrings of a supplied string. The source seeks linear time or at least n log n time, and permits small-probability false rejection. This card retains the latter time target with an explicit one-sided probability and word-RAM model.
definitions:
Positions of \(T\) are numbered \(0,\ldots,n-1\). For each \(1\le\ell\le n\), the valid starts are \(0\le i\le n-\ell\). A collision is a triple \((i,j,\ell)\) of valid starts and a length such that the strings \(T[i..i+\ell-1]\) and \(T[j..j+\ell-1]\) are unequal but have equal displayed fingerprints. Overlapping occurrences are included. Distinct starting positions that spell the same string are not a collision. Equal fingerprints of different-length strings are irrelevant. Collision-free means there is no collision at any valid length and pair of starts.

The base is exactly the supplied alphabet size \(\sigma\), not a new random evaluation point. The modulus is exactly the supplied prime \(p\). There is no promise that \(p>\sigma\), that \(p\) is coprime to \(\sigma\), or that this fingerprint is good. Primality is an input promise. Internal auxiliary fingerprints or indexes are allowed if their construction is charged, but their validity cannot replace certification of the specified \(h_p\). A REJECT output does not have to contain a collision witness.

Use a uniform sequential word RAM with \(w=\lceil(4c+10)\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit unsigned words, a fixed finite program and word-addressed memory. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, comparisons, branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and logical shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. An independent uniform random word may be generated in one step. Addresses must fit a word. No unbounded-integer primitive, advice, external oracle or quantum operation is provided.

The input is a read-only array containing \(n,\sigma,p\) and the \(n\) symbols, one per word. All input-dependent computation, preprocessing, table construction and auxiliary representations count toward the time bound. Initially there is no supplied suffix index or other precomputed information. Apart from the input and a fixed number of registers, at most \(Kn\log_2(n+2)\) working words may be used, after increasing the same constant \(K\) if necessary. This is the ordinary space allowance implied by the time budget, not a separate linear-space target.

The quantifier order is \(\forall c\,\exists(K,A)\,\forall(n,\sigma,p,T)\) satisfying the promises. The program and constant may depend on \(c\) but not on the input length, string, base or prime. The instruction bound holds for every random execution, not merely in expectation. For each fixed collision-free input, probability is taken only over the algorithm's independent random words. False rejection has probability at most \(1/3\); false certification is never allowed. Checking only a prescribed family of lengths or only the pairs queried by some other algorithm is a different task.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the uniform algorithm, the bound on every execution, and both one-sided correctness requirements for every allowed input. A negative proof must rule out the full stated proposition unconditionally; a conditional lower bound is only a conditional result.

Finding a different good modulus, selecting another base, or constructing a tuple of fingerprints does not certify the input fingerprint. A result limited to power-of-two lengths, sampled positions, a restricted class of strings or only the comparisons made by an index is insufficient. The stricter linear-time alternative mentioned by the source is not required here.
context:
A fingerprint speeds up equality tests by replacing a string with a small residue. This question concerns a guarantee about every equal-length comparison inside one text, even if no particular index ever makes that comparison.

The original problem records a quadratic-time baseline and asks for a linear or n log n bound. Allowing false rejection means the procedure may occasionally decline to certify a good input; it may never approve a collision.

The 2015 LCE construction verifies selected pairs required by its query procedure and can choose another fingerprint when verification fails. Its deterministic construction also permits tuples of fingerprints. Those scope choices differ from this fixed single-fingerprint task.

The 2026 compressed-index paper explicitly discusses n log n verification for power-of-two lengths. Its own new index avoids Karp–Rabin fingerprints. Neither statement establishes all-length certification for the supplied base and modulus.
why: Efficient certification could turn a widely used probabilistic string primitive into a reliable one while preserving a chosen fingerprint representation.
status_note: Open in the May 2025 seminar source. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the all-length fixed-base, fixed-prime target. The reviewed selected-comparison verification and 2026 compressed-index construction have different guarantees; this review is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2015-04-10: LCE structures verify selected comparisons and construct suitable fingerprints or fingerprint tuples. | 2025-05: The seminar asks for faster certification over all substring lengths with one supplied prime and allows one-sided false rejection. | 2026-06-08: A new compressed index avoids Karp–Rabin fingerprints; its background discussion still distinguishes verification for power-of-two lengths.
working_summary: The input is a string, its alphabet size and a fixed prime modulus. The algorithm must certify that unequal substrings of every common length have different polynomial fingerprints. The target is worst-case n log n time with all preprocessing included. A bad fingerprint must always be rejected, while every good fingerprint must be certified with probability at least two thirds. Verification of selected lengths or construction of a different fingerprint does not settle the target; a complete Lean-checked answer is required.

title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.
focus_reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.
formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96, universal truthfulness, expected welfare and the saved arbitrary-communication question. The inherited papers also study query-efficient or computationally efficient mechanisms; this card deliberately measures bits of communication while permitting unrestricted terminating local optimization. The previously selected public per-value precision parameter is retained and its domain, message costs, transcript convention and fixed-tape incentive quantifiers are made explicit. No individual-rationality or nonnegative-payment restriction is silently added.
definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.
context:
A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this card, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.
why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected general upper guarantee remains \(O((\log\log m)^2)\) with universal truthfulness and expected welfare. Value-query lower bounds do not cover arbitrary communication. The February 2026 graph-auction theorem and August procurement claims have distinct restrictions or type spaces. No matching constant-factor resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.
progress: 2009: Dobzinski–Dughmi distinguish universal truthfulness from truthfulness in expectation and separate their power in a restricted multi-unit setting. | 2010–2011: Dobzinski proves exponential value-query requirements for universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation; arbitrary communication remains outside this lower bound. | 2019: Assadi–Singla obtain expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomially many queries. | 2020–2021: Assadi–Kesselheim–Singla improve the submodular and XOS factor to \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\); Theorem 2 uses at most n value and demand queries. | 2026-02-25: Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács–Vlachos establish constant truthful guarantees under graph eligibility restrictions, without solving unrestricted submodular auctions. | 2026-08-07: The budget-feasible procurement preprint has a different private-cost model; its constant claim is not a general welfare-auction mechanism.
working_summary: The auction allocates indivisible items to bidders with private normalized monotone submodular bundle valuations. The question asks for a constant expected-welfare approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomial communication in bidders, items and per-value bit precision. Local computation is unrestricted, but every query description, price, reply, allocation and payment must fit the bit bound. A complete Lean proof must establish the fixed-random-tape incentive inequality and all-profile welfare guarantee, or rule out every protocol in this full class. Value-query impossibility, graph eligibility results, growing approximation factors and budget-feasible procurement do not settle the selected target.

title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
focus_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.
context:
Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.
why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the complete-allocation question for unrestricted nonnegative additive valuations was located. The August 2026 result covers four agents and at most nine goods; nonadditive counterexamples do not meet this model. The certificate corpus and cited proofs were not independently rerun.
progress: 2020: Complete EFX existence proved for three additive agents. | 2022: For four additive agents, all but at most one good can be allocated while preserving EFX. | 2026-05: Counterexamples for nonadditive valuation classes leave the additive question unresolved. | 2026-08: A computationally supported theorem gives complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) for four additive agents and at most nine goods.

working_summary: The problem asks whether every instance with at least four agents and nonnegative additive values admits a complete EFX allocation of indivisible goods. Complete means that each good is assigned to exactly one agent, with empty bundles allowed. For every potentially envious agent i and other bundle \(A_{j}\), removing any good that i values positively must leave a bundle worth at most i’s own bundle. The statement permits zero values and fixes the positive-good EFX convention, without requiring payments or an efficient algorithm. Universal existence would establish this fairness guarantee despite the inability to divide individual goods.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Santa Claus
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
importance_reason: A major approximation barrier in fair allocation and scheduling, linked by reductions to beating two for unrelated makespan and by relaxation gaps to the limits of fractional methods.
formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\), one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), and constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), such that for every explicit nonnegative rational additive valuation matrix \(I=(v_{ij})\) of bit length \(L\), the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within \(K(L+1)^d\) steps and
\[\Pr\!\left[\min_{i\in[n]}\sum_{j:\,A(I)(j)=i}v_{ij}
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{C}\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal fair random bits and concerns one allocation serving all agents simultaneously. The constants and program must work for every number of agents and items and every permitted valuation matrix. The optimum is the largest achievable minimum agent value under the same indivisibility constraints.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96 and the saved constant-factor existence target for general additive max-min allocation. The term Santa Claus is used in this general sense, as in the inherited Bamas and coauthors reduction, not only for restricted assignment. The selected randomized convention retains simultaneous probability at least 2/3 and a worst-case polynomial time bound on every tape. Explicit encodings, actual assignment output and unconditional proof/refutation semantics are added; neither agents nor items are fixed.
definitions:
Instances and values. There are \(n\ge1\) agents, \(m\ge1\) indivisible items, and an explicit matrix \(v\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\). Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Agent \(i\) values any bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) by
\[v_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S}v_{ij},\qquad v_i(\varnothing)=0.\]
Entries are finite and may be zero; their magnitudes, denominators and ratios are unrestricted. An item can have different positive values for different agents. The input has no identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-degree, bounded-agent-count or bounded-number-of-values promise. Values are known centrally and are used in their given common units. Rescaling different agents’ rows separately generally changes the objective and the optimal allocation.

Encoding. For an integer \(z\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(z+1\) and let \(U(z)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)\), followed in row-major order by \(U(p_{ij})U(q_{ij})\), where \(p_{ij}\ge0\), \(q_{ij}\ge1\) and \(v_{ij}=p_{ij}/q_{ij}\). Fractions need not be reduced. The total bit length of this encoding is \(L\); polynomial time includes reading these bits and performing arithmetic. This is an explicit matrix, not a value oracle or a succinct circuit.

Feasibility and objective. An allocation is a function \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), where zero means that the item is unallocated. Each item can belong to at most one agent and cannot be split. The bundle of agent \(i\) is \(S_i(a)=\{j:a(j)=i\}\), and
\[F_I(a)=\min_{i\in[n]}v_i(S_i(a)),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}F_I(a).\]
The maximum exists because there are finitely many allocations. It is a nonnegative rational number. Unallocated items are permitted; requiring all items to be assigned would leave the optimum unchanged because every value is nonnegative. No capacity limits, payments, incentives, entitlement weights or other constraints are imposed. The algorithm must output the actual assignment, encoded as \(U(a(1))\cdots U(a(m))\), rather than only an estimate of its value.

Algorithm and randomness. The computational model is a finite multitape Turing machine with independent unbiased random bits and no advice or oracle. A deterministic algorithm is allowed. A single polynomial bound must hold for every valid input and every random tape, including unsuccessful tapes. On every tape the output must be feasible. The program and its constants are fixed independently of \(n\), \(m\), \(L\) and the values; polynomial dependence on numeric values instead of their bit lengths does not qualify. Invalid encodings may be rejected. The probability in the formal statement concerns only the machine’s random bits, with the input fixed adversarially in advance.

Guarantee. The event \(F_I(A(I))\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/C\) says that every agent simultaneously receives at least that amount in the returned allocation. Separate expectation bounds for individual agents are different. There is no input distribution, additive loss, supplied optimum value or promise that the optimum is positive. On a zero-optimum instance any feasible allocation meets the multiplicative requirement, but the time bound still applies. The approximation constant can be arbitrarily large but finite and independent of all inputs; equivalently it can be an integer by rounding a real constant upward. No accuracy parameter is part of the input.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify a finite algorithm and a fixed constant \(C\), establish polynomial running time in the full binary input length on every random tape, establish feasibility on every tape, and prove the simultaneous \(2/3\)-probability guarantee for every valid matrix.

A negative answer must rule out every universal constant and every uniform randomized algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial bound. Ruling out only deterministic algorithms or one chosen constant, proving a gap for a particular relaxation, or exhibiting an instance defeating one method is insufficient. This is an unconditional proposition: hardness derived from a complexity assumption remains conditional unless that assumption is also established. In particular, a deterministic inapproximability statement under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) cannot silently be applied to randomized algorithms; a suitable randomized complexity assumption and reduction must be identified.

A factor growing with agents, items or bit length; a constant approximation in quasipolynomial time; a numerical estimate without an allocation; or an expectation guarantee for each agent separately does not meet the target. Neither do results restricted to identical values, restricted assignment, a bounded input parameter or different access to valuations.
context:
The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value \(w_{j}\) and \(v_{ij}\) is either \(w_{j}\) or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna obtain \(O(m^\varepsilon)\)-approximation in polynomial time for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), where \(m\) counts items here. Their more precise tradeoff includes logarithmic factors and has an exponent depending on \(1/\varepsilon\); it also gives a polylogarithmic approximation in quasipolynomial time. The result does not give a polynomial-time constant factor by making \(\varepsilon\) depend on the instance size.

The standard configuration relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by an unbounded factor on general additive instances. For a target value \(T\), its variables fractionally select bundles worth at least \(T\) for each agent while limiting the total fractional use of each item. The gap means that a feasible fractional target need not correspond to a comparable actual allocation. This limitation of one relaxation is distinct from an impossibility theorem for all polynomial-time algorithms.

Haxell and Szabó’s published 2025 theorem bounds the restricted-assignment configuration-LP integrality gap by \(53/15\), reported as less than 3.534. This compares fractional and integral optima in that particular model. A good integral allocation’s existence is also different from a polynomial-time procedure constructing it. The theorem supplies neither a general additive approximation nor a matching impossibility result.

Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter connect this question to unrelated-machine makespan. A polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for that scheduling problem, for fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields an \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation here for every fixed \(\delta>0\). Thus any fixed improvement below two in general unrelated makespan would give a constant allocation factor. Their general implication is one-way; the reverse equivalence in the paper has a two-value restriction.

The SODA 2025 submodular result extends the small-power polynomial-time and polylogarithmic quasipolynomial-time guarantees to monotone submodular preferences. Submodularity means diminishing marginal returns when a bundle grows. Those more general preferences are accessed through value queries, whereas the current card gives an explicit additive matrix. The improvement in preference scope leaves a growing factor on general additive instances.

Boehmer’s SWAT 2026 result guarantees at least \(2/5\) of optimum for identical monotone submodular valuations. In the approximation-factor convention used here this would be a factor \(5/2\), but only for that restricted input class. Allowing diminishing returns does not remove the separate assumption that every agent has the same preferences.

The distributed paper’s September 2026 revision gives each gift one intrinsic value and represents which children desire it by a bipartite graph. It measures communication rounds in CONGEST, where messages have bounded size. Its restricted model, communication cost and growing approximation factor differ from this centralized target; the paper’s separate discussion still identifies unrestricted allocation as open.
why: The central unresolved max-min allocation question: can all agents be protected to within a constant factor when indivisible resources have arbitrary heterogeneous additive values?
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected SODA papers and the 14 September distributed-paper revision retain the unrestricted additive approximation gap. Constant guarantees and integrality-gap bounds checked here apply to restricted assignment or identical valuations; communication-round results do not settle centralized polynomial time. No matching general constant-factor algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof was found in the bounded search. Full cited proofs were not independently formalized.
progress: 2009: Chakrabarty–Chuzhoy–Khanna achieve an arbitrarily small fixed power of the number of items in polynomial time, and a polylogarithmic approximation in quasi-polynomial time. | 2023–2024: Bamas and coauthors show that any fixed improvement below two for unrelated makespan implies a constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus. | 2024–2025: Bamas–Morell–Rohwedder extend the additive problem’s approximation–time tradeoff to monotone submodular valuations; the work appears at SODA 2025. | 2022–2023; journal 2025-03-27: Haxell–Szabó prove a restricted configuration-LP gap at most \(53/15\); this is not an arbitrary-value allocation algorithm. | 2026-04-14; SWAT 2026: Boehmer proves the \(2/5\)-of-optimum guarantee under identical submodular valuations. | 2026-09-14: The distributed Santa Claus revision treats restricted assignment and discusses unrestricted allocation separately as open.
working_summary: General Santa Claus allocation distributes indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values to maximize the least agent value. The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a constant approximation factor and polynomial running time in the full binary input length. It must output a feasible allocation on every tape and meet the common value threshold for all agents simultaneously with probability at least two thirds. A complete Lean proof must establish that guarantee or refute the entire stated algorithm class, retaining any complexity assumptions explicitly. Restricted-assignment constants, identical-preference results, relaxation gaps and distributed round bounds leave the general heterogeneous problem open in the inspected sources.

title: Randomized truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The central randomized counterpart of the resolved Nisan–Ronen conjecture, with a constant-versus-linear gap independent of computational restrictions.
formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as the integer number of machines \(m\to\infty\), the optimal worst-case expected-makespan ratio \(R(m)\) of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms for unrelated-machine scheduling. For each \(m\ge2\), the mechanism must handle every finite job count \(n\ge1\) and every matrix of finite nonnegative real processing times. It may use payments and arbitrary correlated random assignments, with no computational or communication restriction.
\[R(m)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_m}\ \sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0}}
\frac{\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(t)}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_m\) consists of the families satisfying the incentive and zero-optimum conditions below. The question includes deciding whether \(R(m)=\Theta(1)\), but a negative answer to that special possibility alone does not determine the requested asymptotic order.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96, the user-retained game-theory category and the saved asymptotic target over unrestricted truthful-in-expectation mechanisms. The source asks about the power of randomization after deterministic Nisan–Ronen; this card fixes the optimal expected-makespan ratio as a function of the machine count. Nonnegative real types, all job counts, unrestricted payments and no computational restriction are retained. The review makes the probability kernel and infimum semantics explicit without specializing to universal truthfulness.
definitions:
Jobs, machines and private costs. Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). There are \(m\ge2\) machines and \(n\ge1\) indivisible jobs. Machine \(i\) has a private type \(t_i=(t_{i1},\ldots,t_{in})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Executing a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). All entries are finite; zero is allowed. The times on different machines and jobs have no promised relation. Every job is assigned exactly once, and all jobs assigned to one machine are executed sequentially. There are no release times, precedences, eligibility restrictions, migration, preemption or interactions between different jobs' costs.

Direct mechanisms. Reports have the same domain as types. For each report matrix \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), a mechanism specifies numbers
\[q_\sigma(b)\ge0\quad(\sigma:[n]\to[m]),\qquad\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(b)=1,\]
and a finite real expected payment \(p_i(b)\in\mathbb R\) to each machine. Thus the outcome at each fixed report is a distribution on the finite set of \(m^n\) assignments. Define the marginal assignment probability
\[x_{ij}(b)=\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(j)=i}q_\sigma(b).\]
The numbers \(q_\sigma(b)\) may be arbitrary reals, and assignments of different jobs need not be independent. Payments can be deterministic amounts \(p_i(b)\): allowing random payments with finite expectations makes no difference to the risk-neutral utility or objective here. Positive payments are received by the machine. No individual rationality, budget balance, sign restriction, transfer bound, anonymity or task-independence condition is imposed.

Truthfulness in expectation. For every machine \(i\), true type \(t_i\), alternative report \(b_i\), and fixed reports \(b_{-i}\) of all other machines, require
\[p_i(t_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{-i})
\ \ge\ p_i(b_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{-i}).\]
This is the dominant-strategy condition for expected payment minus true processing cost. Only one agent's report changes in this comparison. There is no prior distribution on types, expectation over other players' reports, or assumption that those reports are honest. The expectation is over the mechanism's own allocation randomness. Truthfulness of each deterministic rule obtained by fixing a random seed is not required.

Performance. When the report matrix equals the true matrix \(t\), an assignment has makespan
\[C(\sigma,t)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}t_{ij},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min_{\sigma:[n]\to[m]}C(\sigma,t).\]
The expectation in the formal statement is the finite sum \(\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(t)C(\sigma,t)\). It is the expected maximum load, not the maximum of the expected loads. Payments do not enter the makespan. The optimum uses the same machines and jobs with full knowledge of the true processing times. For every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\), an admissible mechanism must have expected makespan zero; division by zero is omitted from the displayed supremum. All positive-optimum instances and all job counts are included, with no additive error term.

Optimization over mechanisms. For a fixed \(m\), a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_m\) precisely when each member has the stated domain and satisfies truthfulness and the zero-optimum condition at every report profile. Its supremum ratio may be infinite. The infimum is finite because a truthful minimum-total-cost allocation has ratio at most \(m\), so \(1\le R(m)\le m\). A single family must meet its ratio simultaneously for every \(n\) and \(t\); it cannot be chosen after the true instance is known. Different job counts and machine counts may have different rules, and no uniform finite program, computability, representation or time bound is required. The selected problem is an incentive-theoretic extremum over mathematical rules on real reports. A bit encoding or efficient sampling requirement would change that class.

Attainment and asymptotics. The infimum need not be attained. To establish \(R(m)\le u\), it is enough to have admissible families with ratios at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The constants in the requested asymptotic comparison must be independent of \(m\), \(n\), and all processing times. The finite distribution on assignments at each individual report must not be confused with a report-independent finite or countable distribution over entire deterministic truthful mechanisms; the latter is an additional restriction.
answer_criterion:
Supply a positive asymptotic scale \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), constants \(a,b>0\), and an integer \(m_0\ge2\), with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[a f(m)\le R(m)\le b f(m)\qquad\text{for every integer }m\ge m_0.\]
The scale must specify the growth rate by an unambiguous mathematical description, not merely rename \(R\) or its defining optimization. Both bounds must apply to the full stated type domain, every job count and the full truthful-in-expectation class. Upper bounds may use families approaching an unattained infimum; lower bounds must constrain all admissible mechanisms, with no hidden computational, independence or distributional hypothesis.

A constant upper bound would suffice together with the universal lower bound one. Proving only unboundedness, improving one bound without a matching scale, or settling universal truthfulness, a fixed machine count, a fixed job count, fractional makespan or a Bayesian variant does not meet this criterion. Constant-factor asymptotic precision is the selected target; the numerical absolute-error convention is not an additive tolerance on asymptotic notation.
context:
A machine can report a different processing-time vector to reduce the work it receives. Payments give the scheduler a way to counteract that incentive. Because a machine can be fast on one job and slow on another, its type is multidimensional; a single reported speed describes a substantially different model. The goal here measures the schedule at honest reports, while honesty must be optimal even when other machines report arbitrary vectors.

Total processing cost and makespan impose different objectives. A truthful minimum-total-cost allocation assigns each job to a cheapest machine, with appropriate payments. Its makespan is at most its total cost, which is at most the total cost of an optimal makespan assignment and hence at most \(m\operatorname{OPT}(t)\). This explains a universal factor \(m\). With complete information and unlimited computation, an optimal makespan assignment exists; the issue in this card is the additional incentive constraint.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that no deterministic truthful mechanism improves the worst-case factor \(m\). The result was posted in 2023 and published online in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It settles the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture without a computational hardness assumption. It does not give the same lower bound for truthfulness in expectation.

Universal truthfulness means that the mechanism samples a deterministic truthful rule from a report-independent distribution. Truthfulness in expectation asks only that honest reporting maximize expected utility and permits a larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\) for this larger class. Their theorem allows arbitrary finite processing times, including zero, and is independent of computational limitations.

Lu and Yu give the general truthful-in-expectation guarantee \((m+5)/2\). Together with the deterministic upper bound and the unrestricted randomized lower bound, the inspected literature gives
\[2-\frac1m\le R(m)\le\min\left\{m,\frac{m+5}{2}\right\}.\]
Thus the general gap remains between a constant and a linear function. The same WINE paper reports a linear lower bound under its task-independence restriction; that restricted conclusion cannot be transferred to the whole class defining \(R\).

Correlations matter even when every individual assignment probability is fixed. Take \(m\) unit jobs on \(m\) machines, with every processing time equal to one. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly chosen machine gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\) and makespan \(m\). Assigning the jobs by a uniformly chosen bijection also gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\), but makespan one. Both have expected load one on every machine. Expected utilities depend only on the marginal probabilities and expected payments, whereas expected makespan also depends on the joint assignment distribution.

The 11 September 2026 preprint of Anastasiadis and coauthors claims a lower bound \((3/2-\sqrt2)(m-1)\) for universally truthful mechanisms given by countably supported distributions over deterministic rules, and a universal upper bound \(m/2+o(m)\). The authors discuss extension to uncountable support as an expectation, not a proved theorem. These claims concern a stricter incentive model than this card. In particular, finitely many possible assignments at any fixed report do not imply a countably supported mixture of truthful rules over all reports. The new proof has not been independently certified here.

Small-instance bounds concern different extrema. Kuryatnikova and Vera place the optimal ratio for two machines and two jobs within their randomized monotone, task-independent, scale-free class between \(1.5059953\) and \(1.5059964\). Their scale-free restriction means that multiplying all processing times by one positive constant leaves an allocation rule unchanged. Their mechanisms permit correlated random choices; task independence of a fixed rule is not the same as statistical independence of job assignments. Neither that interval nor the selected restricted mechanism class determines the full \(R(m)\).

A bounded answer would show that randomization keeps the incentive cost of private processing times under control as the system grows. An unbounded answer would show a persistent efficiency loss even with risk-neutral agents and unrestricted transfers. Matching bounds would quantify that loss. Extra assumptions about independent types, Bayesian incentives, fractional execution or computational efficiency describe other questions and cannot be used silently in this one.
why: Quantifies how much load-balancing efficiency must be lost solely to multidimensional private costs when randomization and unrestricted payments are available. Matching asymptotic bounds would show whether expected-utility incentives can overcome the linear loss now known for deterministic truthful scheduling.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected unrestricted TIE bounds remain \(2-1/m\le R(m)\le\min\{m,(m+5)/2\}\), leaving its asymptotic order open. The September universal-truthfulness claim has narrower scope; its full proof was not independently certified. The deterministic JACM theorem and restricted two-machine results do not determine this target. The later-work search was bounded.
progress: 2007; full version 2017: Mu’alem–Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\), including truthfulness in expectation in §3.4, Theorem 4. | 2008: Lu–Yu establish the \((m+5)/2\) truthful-in-expectation upper bound; their linear lower bound has an additional task-independence hypothesis. | 2019–2020: Kuryatnikova–Vera nearly determine the optimum for a restricted two-machine, two-job mechanism class. | 2023-01-27; online 2026-02-11: The proof of the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture identifies its optimal ratio as \(m\). | 2026-09-11: A new preprint claims linear lower bounds for countably supported universally truthful mixtures; the broader truthfulness-in-expectation target remains separate.
working_summary: Machines privately know an unrelated processing time for each job and receive payments for their assigned work. The target is the asymptotic optimal expected-makespan ratio of mechanisms truthful in expectation, with no computational restriction. Every job count and every finite nonnegative real cost matrix is allowed, and the approximation compares the expected maximum load with the fully informed optimum. A complete Lean proof must give matching constant-factor bounds, accounting for the possibility that the infimum is not attained. Existing general bounds leave a constant-to-linear gap; deterministic, universal-truthfulness and small-instance results have narrower scope.
