original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.
formal:
Do there exist absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) and one uniform deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol which, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every profile of \(n\) nonatomic additive cake valuations, makes at most \(Cn^d\) queries and produces a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the entire cake satisfying
\[
 \mu_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_j)\qquad\text{for every }1\le i,j\le n?
\]
Every allocated piece may be a finite union of intervals. The allocation must be complete and exactly envy-free on every profile and for every valid choice of cut-query responses.
question_excerpt: The September 2026 preprint improves the general exact complete-allocation query bound to a single exponential and explicitly asks whether subexponential or polynomial protocols are possible. This card retains the inherited polynomial worst-case target; the separate average-case result in its original reference does not answer that target.
definitions:
The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent \(i\)'s valuation \(\mu_i\) is an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure: it is nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu_i([0,1])=1\), and \(\mu_i(\{x\})=0\) for every point \(x\). A piece is a finite union of intervals, with endpoints assigned consistently to make the pieces disjoint. Endpoints have zero value for every agent. Measures need not have densities, and there is no bound on density, number of breakpoints or description complexity. No distribution over profiles is assumed.

The protocol receives \(n\) and accesses valuations only through these exact oracles:

\(\operatorname{Eval}(i,x,y)\), for known marks \(0\le x\le y\le1\), returns \(\mu_i([x,y])\).

\(\operatorname{Cut}(i,x,\alpha)\), for a known mark \(x\) and a requested real value \(0\le\alpha\le\mu_i([x,1])\), returns some \(y\in[x,1]\) such that \(\mu_i([x,y])=\alpha\). This returned coordinate becomes a known mark. Initially only \(0\) and \(1\) are known. Nonatomicity guarantees existence of an answer. If an interval has zero value, a cut may have several valid positions; every such response must preserve the guarantee. The protocol must issue only valid queries.

Each evaluation or cut call counts as one query. The protocol may combine interval values by additivity and use previously learned values without paying again. It may query one agent at a mark obtained from another. The final allocation must use endpoints among the known marks; arbitrary newly guessed endpoints are not available as free cuts.

Uniformity means one finite program for all \(n\). Between queries it may use integer computation, store and copy exact real answers, perform real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero number, and compare real numbers exactly. Its program has rational real constants and may perform arbitrary finite loops and finite searches. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; no time, memory or bit-precision bound is imposed on this local computation. It must nevertheless terminate after finitely many operations on every allowed execution. This specifies a query model with exact real arithmetic, not a Turing computation of the digits of arbitrary valuation reals.

The output lists, for each agent, finitely many intervals with known endpoints. Their union covers \([0,1]\), and no interior point belongs to two agents' pieces. Shared boundary points are assigned to one incident piece. Empty pieces are allowed, but no positive-length residue may be discarded, even if all agents value it at zero.

Envy-freeness compares all pieces using the evaluating agent's own measure. It requires every displayed inequality exactly, with no additive or multiplicative fairness error. It does not require a connected piece per agent or impose any incentive-compatibility condition. The query bound is worst-case over both valuation profiles and valid oracle responses. There is no randomization or favorable-profile exception.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one protocol and constants satisfying the statement, with proofs of query validity, termination, complete allocation, exact envy-freeness and the uniform polynomial query bound; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence claim in the specified model.

A protocol with an arbitrary finite bound depending on \(n\), a polynomial average-case or approximate-fairness guarantee, or a protocol leaving cake unallocated is insufficient. A lower bound for one particular procedure does not rule out all polynomial-query protocols. This is an existence question about an exact fairness property and an asymptotic resource bound, so numerical approximation of envy does not meet the answer criterion.
context:
The reported September 2026 bound is a fixed polynomial times two to the number of agents. It handles complete exact allocations and arbitrary nonatomic valuations, but remains exponential. The preprint itself keeps polynomial query complexity as an open direction.

The quadratic lower bound is compatible with the polynomial target. It concerns general query protocols rather than merely showing that one historical procedure asks many questions.

The inherited high-probability result measures probability over a specified random valuation model. It does not ensure polynomially many queries for every fixed profile.

Exactness, completeness and permission to allocate disconnected pieces all matter. Approximate allocations and connected allocations have different query-complexity questions. Counting only final cuts also differs from counting all preference queries used to find them.
why: The question asks how much preference information is necessary to divide a continuous resource exactly without anyone preferring another person’s share. A polynomial query bound would separate the information needed for fairness from the enormous bounds in existing general protocols.
status_note: The September 2026 primary preprint explicitly retains polynomial query complexity as open after reporting a single-exponential general upper bound. The inherited polynomial result concerns random valuation profiles, and the general quadratic lower bound does not rule out the target. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the full new preprint proof has not been independently certified.
progress: 2009: A general quadratic query lower bound is proved. | 2022: The query-complexity study distinguishes exact and approximate fairness and the role of connected allocations. | 2025-09-26: The average-case polynomial-query result is published online. | 2026-09-04: A preprint reports a single-exponential general bound and retains polynomial complexity as an open question.
working_summary: The cake is a continuous interval whose value may differ arbitrarily between agents. The task is to allocate all of it exactly without any agent preferring another agent’s piece. Preferences are learned only through exact value and cut queries, and disconnected pieces are allowed. One deterministic protocol must use polynomially many queries on every profile, although computation between queries is unrestricted. A complete Lean-checked solution must prove the full protocol guarantee or rule out every such polynomial query bound.

title: Randomized metric distortion in social choice
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
formal: Determine the infimum D* of the universal worst-case metric distortion achievable by any randomized ordinal voting rule, when the rule sees every voter’s full ranking and minimizes expected total distance to voters. The infimum ranges over all rules for all finite positive numbers of voters and candidates, with the model and zero-cost convention below.
definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of \(n\ge 1\) voters and C of \(m\ge 1\) candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each \(v\in V\). A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on \(V\cup C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)\ge 0\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points, with a≻_v b implying \(d(v,a)\le d(v,b)\). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair \((E,d)\). The social cost \(SC_{d}(a)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,a)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=\min _{a}\in C SC_{d}(a)\). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery \(p=f(E)\), where \(p_{a}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{a} p_{a}=1\). Its expected cost is \(\sum_{a} p_{a} SC_{d}(a)\). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define \(Dist(f)=\inf\){\(D\ge 1\): for every E and every consistent \(d, \sum_{a} f(E)_{a} SC_{d}(a)\le D\cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{d}\)}, taking \(\inf \varnothing =+\infty\). This inequality requires zero expected cost if \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=0\) and avoids dividing by zero. Set \(D*=\inf _{f} Dist(f)\), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- D*|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
context:
Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively \(3- 2p\) and \(1+2p\). At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.
why: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
status_note: The latest checked preprint, dated 8 September 2026, states upper bound 2.13713 against a general lower bound of about 2.11264. The exact value remains unresolved. These fresh upper bounds were matched to the model but their proofs and computational certificates were not independently audited; no full-resolution claim was found through 11 September 2026. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 2021 / 2022: The former \(D*=2\) conjecture is disproved; a general randomized lower bound approaches approximately 2.11264. | 2025: Tournament and fuller-ranking models are explicitly separated; the source’s numerical gap is now historical. | 2026-08-18: A preprint gives the general upper bound \(5/2\). | 2026-09-06: The revised random-size-stable-lottery paper states upper bound 2.1441 and a separate family-specific lower bound 2.136. | 2026-09-08: Theorem 1 of a new preprint states the unrestricted upper bound 2.13713; it does not identify D* exactly.
working_summary: What is the smallest universal expected metric distortion achievable from full voter rankings? The voting rule selects a lottery without seeing the distances that produced those rankings. The former value-two conjecture is false, with a general lower bound around 2.11264. A preprint dated 8 September 2026 states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a nonzero gap. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: Nonemptiness of the approval core
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Core nonemptiness is a foundational feasibility question for proportional representation: can all voter coalitions be satisfied simultaneously when seats are indivisible? A resolution would identify whether the strongest basic coalition-stability demand is universally compatible with approval committee selection.
formal:
For every pair of integers \(n,m\ge1\), every integer \(1\le k\le m\), and every approval profile \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) with \(A_i\subseteq[m]\), is there a committee \(W\subseteq[m]\) of size \(k\) such that no nonempty coalition \(S\subseteq[n]\) and alternative committee \(T\subseteq[m]\) satisfy both
\[n|T|\le k|S|\quad\text{and}\quad\forall i\in S,\ |A_i\cap T|>|A_i\cap W|?\]
definitions: For an integer \(r\ge1\), \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\). There are \(n\) equally weighted voters and \(m\) distinct, indivisible candidates of unit cost. Voter \(i\) approves exactly the set \(A_i\) and assigns utility \(u_i(U)=|A_i\cap U|\) to a committee \(U\). Approval sets may be empty. The chosen committee contains exactly \(k\) distinct candidates. A nonempty voter coalition \(S\) can afford any set of candidates \(T\) with \(|T|\le k|S|/n\), using the Hare quota without additional rounding beyond this inequality. It blocks \(W\) if every one of its members obtains a strictly larger approval count from \(T\) than from \(W\). The two committees may overlap; \(T\) need not be contained in \(W\) or in its complement. Each candidate may appear at most once. The core is the collection of committees with no such blocking coalition and alternative. The question concerns existence, without an efficiency requirement for finding or certifying a committee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every allowed finite election has such a committee, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A finite counterexample must specify the entire approval profile and committee size, and prove that every committee of the required size has a blocking coalition and affordable alternative with strict improvement for each member. Fractional committees, repeated candidates, approximate stability or weak improvement by only some coalition members do not meet the stated target.
context:
The core formalizes proportional group representation: a coalition should not be able to use its share of the available seats to make all its members better represented. Because a selected candidate serves all voters who approve it, this is a public committee problem rather than a partition of goods among individual recipients.

The fractional core is known to be nonempty, but fractional selection can split candidates. Allowing unlimited copies changes the model as well. Neither guarantee establishes existence for a set of indivisible candidates, each selected at most once.

Goel, Jiang and Zhou explicitly state that unrestricted discrete-core nonemptiness remains open. Their August 2026 preprint reports a positive result for at most eight equally weighted voters using exhaustive computational verification; that reported result is a restricted case and its computations were not independently audited here.

The TCS+ talk by Gölz presents proportional representation and highlights the unit-cost approval setting as a central unresolved existence question.
why: Core nonemptiness is a foundational feasibility question for proportional representation: can all voter coalitions be satisfied simultaneously when seats are indivisible? A resolution would identify whether the strongest basic coalition-stability demand is universally compatible with approval committee selection.
status_note: Primary-source statements and a bounded search for subsequent work were checked on 16 September 2026; the formulation was individually reviewed on 17 September 2026. No resolution of this precise target was located. This records source-supported openness, not an exhaustive literature certification or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2023: Gölz’s TCS+ presentation identifies the existence problem for unit-cost approval elections among the outstanding questions in proportional representation. | 2026: The Nash-core preprint reports discrete-core existence for at most eight equally weighted voters and explicitly retains the unrestricted existence question.
working_summary: Each voter approves some candidates, and exactly a prescribed number of candidates must be selected. A voter coalition blocks the selection if its proportional share of seats can buy a committee that every member strictly prefers. The question is whether an unblocked committee always exists. Candidates are indivisible, have unit cost and cannot be selected more than once. A positive answer would establish universal feasibility of proportional coalition stability in approval voting.

title: Polynomial-time EFX for three additive agents
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,k\ge 1\) such that, for every finite set of goods and every three nonnegative rational additive valuations, A returns a complete EFX allocation in at most \(C(N+1)^{k}\) steps, where N is the binary input length and EFX has the all-goods convention below?
definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and \(m\ge 0\) goods indexed by \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\). The input gives m and each value \(v_{i},g=p_{i},g/q_{i},g\) with integers \(p_{i},g\ge 0\) and \(q_{i},g>0\) encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle \(S\subseteq [m], v_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}v_{i},g\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_{1},A_{2},A_{3})\) of \([m]\); bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in \(\{1,2,3\}\). It is EFX if \(v_{i}(A_{i})\ge v_{i}(A_{j}\setminus \{g\})\) for every \(i,j\in \{1,2,3\}\) and every \(g\in A_{j}\), including goods with \(v_{i},g=0\). The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty \(A_{j}\) gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.
context:
Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

A value as large as \(2^{\mathrm{L}}\) needs only \(\mathrm{L}+1\) binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.
why: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.
status_note: The exact polynomial-time three-agent question is explicitly unresolved in the checked 2025 primary paper. The May 2026 work gives relaxed guarantees, not an exact algorithm. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution; no proof was independently audited.
progress: 2020: Complete EFX existence for three additive agents is proved constructively, with a pseudopolynomial algorithm. | 2025: Polynomial-time EF2X for three agents is obtained, while the paper explicitly retains the exact EFX computational gap. | 2026-05: A preprint reports polynomial-time approximate EFX for up to eight agents, a different guarantee from exact EFX.
working_summary: Three agents must receive all indivisible goods under nonnegative additive valuations. An allocation is EFX when removing any one good from another agent’s bundle would eliminate the first agent’s envy. Such allocations are known to exist for three agents, including when values are zero or tied. The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the binary valuation table’s length. Pseudopolynomial constructions and polynomial algorithms for weaker fairness guarantees do not settle this target.

title: Polynomial-time approximation of EFX
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.
formal: Determine \(\alpha _{\mathrm{alg}} = \sup\){\(\alpha \in [0,1]\) : there is a deterministic algorithm that, on every finite instance of nonnegative rational additive goods, returns a complete \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) allocation in time polynomial in the binary input length}. The number of agents is unbounded and part of the input.
definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) goods and an explicit table of values \(v_{i},g=p_{i},g/q_{i},g\), with integers \(p_{i},g\ge 0\) and \(q_{i},g>0\) in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For \(S\subseteq [m], v_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}v_{i},g\). An allocation \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) partitions \([m]\) into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) if \(v_{i}(A_{i})\ge \alpha \cdot v_{i}(A_{j}\setminus \{g\})\) for every pair i,j and every \(g\in A_{j}\), including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty \(A_{j}\) imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed \(\alpha\) in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most \(C(N+1)^{k}\) on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on \(\alpha\), but not on n, m or the valuations. \(\alpha\) is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since \(\alpha =0\) is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must remain explicit and yields only a conditional bound.
context:
Higher \(\alpha\) means a stronger guarantee, with \(\alpha =1\) giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when \(\alpha \le 4/5\). This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\approx 0.618\). Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\le \alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}\le 1\); the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

The May 2026 preprint reports a \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even \(\alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}=1\) would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.
why: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.
status_note: The checked May 2026 primary preprint still gives about 0.618 as the best known general EFX factor. The exact polynomial-time supremum is not identified by the checked sources; searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. No independent proof audit is claimed. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
progress: 2020: A polynomial algorithm achieves the universal factor \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\). | 2023: The survey retains the gap beyond this general EFX approximation and distinguishes exact existence from computation. | 2026-05: A preprint improves the \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) guarantee to eight agents, while retaining about 0.618 as the known general frontier.
working_summary: All indivisible goods must be allocated among agents with nonnegative additive values. An \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) allocation lets each agent retain at least an \(\alpha\) fraction of the value she assigns to any other bundle after any one good is removed. The question asks for the supremum factor guaranteed by deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for arbitrarily many agents. A general factor of about 0.618 is known, while recent \(2/3\) guarantees cover only bounded numbers of agents. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: Multiplicative MMS guarantee for chores
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Seeks the intrinsic loss required for fair allocation of indivisible burdens.
formal: Determine the smallest real \(\alpha \ge 1\) such that, for every finite instance of nonnegative additive chores with any number of agents, there is a complete allocation \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) satisfying \(c_{i}(A_{i})\le \alpha \mu _{i}\) for every agent i, where \(\mu _{i}\) is that agent’s minimax share. Denote this universal factor by \(\alpha\)*.
definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) indivisible chores, and finite real costs \(c_{i},g\ge 0\). Agent i assigns a bundle \(S\subseteq [m]\) the additive cost \(c_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}c_{i},g\); lower cost is better. Let \(\Pi _{n}([m])\) be the finite set of ordered partitions of \([m]\) into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define \(\mu _{i}=\min _{(\mathrm{P}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{P}_{n})\in \Pi _{n}([m])} \max _{1\le j\le n} c_{i}(\mathrm{P}_{j})\). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to \(\Pi _{n}([m])\): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when \(\mu _{i}=0\), without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha *|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
context:
Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and \(\{3,3\}\); the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus \(\alpha *\ge 44/43>1\).

Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor \(13/11\) always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are \(44/43\le \alpha *\le 13/11\), approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a \(15/13\) multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses \(13/11\) as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.
why: Seeks the intrinsic loss required for fair allocation of indivisible burdens.
status_note: The checked sources leave a gap between \(44/43\) and \(13/11\). A primary preprint dated 8 September 2026 still describes \(13/11\) as the general frontier. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established determination of the optimal universal factor; restricted-cost results do not settle this question. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

working_summary: Chores are indivisible tasks whose costs add, and each agent prefers a smaller burden. Her minimax share is the lowest worst-bundle cost she can obtain by partitioning all chores among the agents. The question asks for the smallest universal factor by which every agent’s share must be relaxed to make a complete allocation possible. The checked general bounds are \(44/43\) and \(13/11\), while stronger guarantees for restricted costs do not close this gap. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.

title: Optimal universal approximation factor for EFX
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: The best universal EFX approximation factor quantifies how close fair allocation can get to a central unresolved fairness guarantee.
formal:
Determine the universal additive-goods EFX approximation constant
\[\alpha_* = \sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists A\in\mathcal A_{n,m},\ A\text{ is }\alpha\text{-EFX for }v\}.\]
Here \(n,m\) are integers, \(\mathcal A_{n,m}\) is the set of complete allocations of \(m\) goods to \(n\) agents, and \(\alpha\)-EFX uses the positive-good convention defined below. The requested benchmark precision is absolute error at most \(1/100\): supply a real number \(a\) and prove \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). This is an existence constant with unrestricted allocation computation, not a polynomial-time approximation threshold.
definitions:
Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) for integers \(k\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is a finite nonnegative real number giving agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\). For a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\), its value is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). No normalization, strict positivity, integrality, rationality, number-of-types or agreement-on-ordering assumption is imposed on values.

A complete allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is an ordered partition of \([m]\): the bundles are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of \([m]\). Empty bundles are allowed. There are no payments, negative-valued chores, fractional goods, discarded goods or additional efficiency constraints.

For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), the allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX if
\[\forall i,j\in[n]\ \forall g\in A_j:\quad v_{ig}>0\ \Longrightarrow\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\}).\]
Both the test of whether the removed good has positive value and the bundle comparison use the potentially envious agent \(i\)'s values. If every good of \(A_j\) has value zero to \(i\), there is no constraint for that pair. If the remaining bundle has value zero, the inequality is automatically satisfied. This is Definition 6 of the source survey. The stronger per-allocation convention often called EFX-zero tests also removed goods of zero value; the card does not silently substitute that convention.

The universally feasible set in the supremum is nonempty, because it includes zero, and is bounded above by one by definition. The constant is dimensionless. Its quantifier order allows a different allocation for each valuation matrix; no single common partition must serve all profiles. Neither an efficient algorithm nor any oracle-access restriction is part of the existence guarantee.

For a fixed finite instance \(v\), one can equivalently define \(\beta(v)\) as the largest \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) for which some complete allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX. This maximum exists: there are finitely many allocations, and each has a closed interval of feasible factors. Then \(\alpha_*\) is the infimum of these \(\beta(v)\) over all permitted instance sizes and profiles. There need not be one instance attaining this infimum. This equivalent definition makes the universal lower-bound and worst-instance upper-bound meanings explicit.

Exact equality \(\alpha_*=1\) is equivalent to existence of a complete EFX allocation for every additive instance: for each fixed instance, finitely many allocations and closed inequalities prevent loss of the endpoint. A numerical answer within \(1/100\) need not decide that exact equality. The present acceptance tolerance measures the numerical constant and does not relax the definition of \(\alpha\)-EFX itself.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) containing \(\alpha_*\) qualifies via its midpoint; an exact value also qualifies. Bounds must concern all finite nonnegative additive instances and complete allocations under the stated positive-good convention. A universal construction proves only a lower bound on the constant unless accompanied by sufficient upper information. An upper bound may be established without a worst instance attaining the infimum. Restricted numbers of agents, partial allocations, nonadditive counterexamples, or guarantees allowing removal of multiple goods do not by themselves determine this constant. A simulation or an unproved decimal estimate is insufficient.
context:
Open Problem 3 asks for the best factor guaranteeing existence. The survey separately asks about efficient computation, and this card retains the existence interpretation. The related exact EFX card asks whether the endpoint one is universally attainable.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos prove a universal factor \((\sqrt5-1)/2\), approximately \(0.618\), in Theorem 4.4. Their definition tests every removed good, including zero-valued goods, so their guarantee also implies the positive-good condition here. This supplies a lower bound on \(\alpha_*\), not its proved optimal value.

The EC 2024 work establishes \(2/3\)-EFX under restrictions including at most seven agents or at most three common value levels. Its July 2026 revision still identifies the golden-ratio bound as the general all-agent additive guarantee. Those restricted \(2/3\) theorems do not establish \(\alpha_*\ge2/3\).

The May 2026 paper extends the \(2/3\)-EFX guarantee to eight agents. It also gives all-agent results for EFkX with \(k\ge2\), where the comparison permits removing a set of \(k\) goods; it expressly states that this general theorem does not apply when \(k=1\). These are distinct from the universal single-good constant.

The numerical tolerance belongs to benchmark acceptance. It allows a certified approximation of the constant without claiming that the exact EFX existence question has been decided.
why: This constant measures how much of the demanding EFX fairness comparison can always be guaranteed when all indivisible goods must be assigned. It gives a quantitative target even if exact EFX existence is unresolved. Its scope is every number of agents and every additive valuation profile, so improvements for special structures do not alone determine the universal guarantee.
status_note: The source survey v2, Amanatidis–Markakis–Ntokos v2 Theorem 4.4, the frontier paper v3 dated 29 July 2026, and Filos-Ratsikas–Kalantzis–Wang v1 Section 1.1 and Definition 2.1 were read on 2026-09-14. The checked recent work retains a distinction between unrestricted additive EFX, restricted agent classes, and removal of multiple goods. A bounded search through this date found no determination of the universal constant to the requested tolerance or exact all-agent additive EFX resolution. The source-open status is limited by this literature check, and does not assert independent verification of the cited algorithmic proofs.
progress: 2020: A universal \((\sqrt5-1)/2\)-EFX guarantee is established for additive goods. | 2022-03-04: The source survey asks for the best universal existence factor in Open Problem 3. | 2024: The frontier paper obtains \(2/3\)-EFX for several restricted instance families. | 2026-05-11: A preprint gives \(2/3\)-EFX for eight agents and separate all-agent guarantees when more than one good may be removed. | 2026-07-29: The revised frontier paper continues to distinguish the general golden-ratio guarantee from stronger restricted results.

working_summary: The target is the best multiplicative EFX fairness factor that every finite additive-goods instance admits. Every good must be allocated, and the comparison removes any good that the potentially envious agent values positively. There is no bound on the number of agents and no computational-time restriction on choosing the allocation. Known universal guarantees reach the golden-ratio factor, while stronger results impose instance restrictions or allow removal of more goods. title: Bounded protocols for connected envy-free proportional cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Asks whether discarded cake permits exact fairness together with geometric simplicity in finite interaction.
formal: For every fixed integer \(n\ge 4\), does there exist a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) and a finite integer \(B_{n}\) such that, for every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations and all valid query answers, \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) uses at most \(B_{n}\) queries and returns disjoint connected bundles \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n}\) satisfying \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for all i,j and \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for all i, while permitting unallocated cake?
definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\), and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a)\), for \(0\le a\le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns \(y\ge x\) with \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=a\). Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each \(A_{i}\) must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue \([0,1]\setminus \bigcup _{i}A_{i}\) may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound \(B_{n}\) depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require \(B_{n}\) to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\).
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed \(n\ge 4\), or prove that for at least one fixed \(n\ge 4\) no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.
context:
A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length \(1/(2n)\), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact \(1/n\) requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once \(n\ge 3\). This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is \(1/7\) instead of the required \(1/4\). Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a \(1/(3n)\) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all \(n\ge 4\).

The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.
why: Asks whether discarded cake permits exact fairness together with geometric simplicity in finite interaction.
status_note: Checked source models and subsequent work through 11 September 2026. No bounded exact proportional connected-disposal protocol for every \(n\ge 4\), or impossibility covering this disposal model, was located. The recent complete-allocation bound allows disconnected bundles. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2008: Finite exact envy-free protocols are ruled out for complete connected allocation with \(n\ge 3\). | 2016: Bounded partial-allocation protocols achieve exact proportionality for three connected recipients, and weaker connected guarantees for larger n. | 2016: General bounded protocols give connected partial allocations worth at least \(1/(3n)\) per agent. | 2026-09: A preprint reports single-exponential queries for complete allocation with possibly fragmented bundles.
working_summary: The cake is a divisible interval valued differently by each agent. The desired division gives every agent one interval, eliminates envy, and guarantees at least one n-th of her value for the whole cake. Unallocated cake is allowed, but it cannot reduce that proportionality guarantee. Known connected partial protocols provide weaker guarantees for larger numbers of agents, while recent complete protocols allow fragmented shares. The question is whether a fixed finite query bound can achieve all the requested properties for every fixed \(n\ge 4\).

title: Universal Condorcet dimension
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: This determines the smallest universally sufficient relaxation of a Condorcet winner in ranked elections. The recent constant-size existence results leave a small but fundamental gap about how many representatives are needed to obtain majority acceptance independently of election size.
formal:
Determine the universal Condorcet dimension \(d_*\): the least positive integer \(d\) such that for every pair of integers \(n,m\ge1\) and every profile \((\succ_1,\ldots,\succ_n)\) of strict total orders on \([m]\), there exists a nonempty set \(W\subseteq[m]\) with \(|W|\le d\) and
\[\forall a\in[m]\setminus W,\qquad\bigl|\{i\in[n]:\ \forall w\in W,\ a\succ_i w\}\bigr|<\frac n2.\]
The target is measured in number of candidates, with absolute acceptance error at most \(1/100\).
definitions: For \(r\ge1\), \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\). There are \(n\) equally weighted voters and \(m\) distinct candidates. Each voter ranks all candidates without ties, and \(a\succ_i w\) means that voter \(i\) places \(a\) above \(w\). A Condorcet winning set in this card is a nonempty committee \(W\) such that, for each outsider \(a\), strictly more than half the voters prefer at least one member of \(W\) to \(a\). Different voters may prefer different committee members. Equivalently, strictly fewer than half rank the outsider above every member, as in the displayed formula. The strict inequality is intentional, including for an even electorate. The chosen committee may depend on the entire profile and need not be found efficiently. The least universal bound \(d_*\) ranges over all finite electorate and candidate sizes. Its existence as a finite positive integer follows from the known bound of five; if \(m\) is smaller, taking all candidates is allowed. This is a numerical universal bound, not a function of a fixed election and not a tournament domination number.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-(d_*:\mathbb R)|\le1/100\), with error measured in candidates. A certified containing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. The approximation need not be integer-valued. The proof must determine the universal least bound to that accuracy, including both the guarantee for all finite ranked profiles and the obstruction to any smaller value that the certification excludes. Merely reporting the known interval from three to five or restating the defining minimum does not qualify.
context:
A single Condorcet winner may fail to exist because majority preferences can cycle. Allowing a small set changes the comparison: each voter compares an outsider with that voter’s own most preferred selected candidate. The question asks for the smallest committee size that always provides a strict voter majority against every outsider.

Charikar, Lassota, Ramakrishnan, Vetta and Wang prove that six candidates always suffice and describe examples for which two do not. Their Question 1 uses the strict-majority convention retained in this card; the exact universal threshold remains undetermined.

The 2025 preprint A few good choices improves the upper bound to five. Although it defines undominance with a weak inequality, its Theorem 1 gives a five-candidate bound at most \(1/3+(2/3)^5=113/243<1/2\) for the fraction preferring any outsider. Thus the stated theorem also gives the strict guarantee used here.

The April 2026 study Is Four Enough? still reports the gap \(3\le d_*\le5\). It supplies further evidence for smaller bounds, rather than a proof that determines the universal dimension.
why: This determines the smallest universally sufficient relaxation of a Condorcet winner in ranked elections. The recent constant-size existence results leave a small but fundamental gap about how many representatives are needed to obtain majority acceptance independently of election size.
status_note: Primary-source statements and a bounded search for subsequent work were checked on 16 September 2026; the formulation was individually reviewed on 17 September 2026. No resolution of this precise target was located. This records source-supported openness, not an exhaustive literature certification or an independent verification of the cited proofs.
progress: 2025: Charikar and coauthors prove a universal upper bound of six, the result featured in Ramakrishnan’s TCS+ talk. | 2025: A few good choices gives an improved upper bound of five through a theorem whose guarantee is strictly below one half. | 2026: Is Four Enough? reports the remaining lower bound of three and upper bound of five without resolving the universal value.
working_summary: A Condorcet winning set is a committee that a strict majority prefers to any single outsider. Each voter may prefer a different committee member when making that comparison. The question asks for the smallest committee size that is sufficient for every finite ranked election. The checked bounds are three and five, improving on the six-candidate result presented at TCS+. An accepted answer supplies a Lean-certified numerical estimate within 0.01 candidates of the universal minimum.

title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: The best universally achievable maximin-share approximation is a central quantitative fairness threshold.
formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.
context:
An agent can imagine partitioning the goods into as many bundles as there are participants and then receiving a least-valued bundle. Optimizing that personal partition defines the maximin share. Actual allocation must respect all agents at once, although their best partitions and their rankings of the goods can be different.

The source asks for the best universal approximation and points to results for additive goods. Those linked papers fix the intended valuation class and distinguish it from chores or more general set valuations. The card makes this source-supported interpretation explicit and retains an existence target, without adding a demand for an efficient allocation algorithm.

Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-good instance in which every allocation leaves someone with at most \(39/40\) of their maximin share. This bounds the universal constant from above even though its definition includes arbitrarily large instances. Their tight result for that particular pair of agent and item counts is not a tight universal guarantee.

Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin and Shahrezaei prove a \(10/13\) guarantee. Huang and Zhou’s revised September 2026 manuscript states a \(7/9\) existence guarantee and a fully polynomial approximation scheme for slightly smaller ratios. These are distinct results: the problem-list entry groups their citations under \(7/9\), but the Heidari et al. paper itself states \(10/13\).

The Huang–Zhou revision explicitly reports correction of a bug and substantial rewriting of the proof. Its version and theorem scope are recorded here, without certifying the full proof independently. Computational approximation schemes and stronger results under restrictions on the number of agents remain different from determining the unrestricted existence constant.
why: Maximin share gives each agent a fairness benchmark determined by their own values, independent of how the other agents evaluate the goods. These personal guarantees can conflict when objects are indivisible. The universal constant measures the unavoidable loss from satisfying all agents simultaneously, separating a limitation of fairness itself from a limitation of available algorithms. It is a central quantitative threshold for additive fair division, with significance across instances and arbitrary numbers of participants.
status_note: The January 2026 source explicitly poses this constant. Checked primary statements through 14 September 2026 give the published upper bound 39/40 and a revised-preprint lower-bound claim of 7/9, still far apart at benchmark precision. The 7 September 2026 revision reports a corrected bug; this review verifies its stated scope, not every step of its proof. No matching determination was found in the bounded search.
progress: 2021-10-19: Feige, Sapir and Tauber, Theorem 1, prove the universal upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\le39/40\) using three agents and nine goods. Their Theorem 3 is tight only within that restricted instance size. | 2025-10-12: Heidari et al., Theorem 3.1, establish the \(10/13\) additive-goods guarantee. This is the value stated in their own manuscript, rather than the \(7/9\) value grouped with the citation on the problem-list page. | 2026-01-15: The TCS Open Problems entry asks for the best universal maximin-share approximation and links the additive-goods literature. | 2026-09-07: Huang and Zhou’s arXiv version 2 states a \(7/9\) guarantee through Theorem 3.1 and the general-instance correspondence in Lemma 2.4; Theorem 10.4 concerns \((7/9-\varepsilon)\)-MMS computation. The revision notice reports a corrected bug. The claimed interval still does not determine the benchmark constant within \(1/100\).
working_summary: Each agent’s maximin share is the best value they can secure by partitioning the goods and receiving a least-valued bundle. The target is the largest fraction of those personal shares that can always be met simultaneously for nonnegative additive valuations. It ranges over all finite numbers of agents and indivisible goods, with equal entitlements and no sharing. Determining this constant would quantify the inherent loss of fairness caused by indivisibility, independently of computational efficiency. The card requires a Lean-certified absolute error of at most one hundredth and records the precise versions and limits of the known bounds.

title: Polynomial-time EF1 and Pareto-optimal goods allocation
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: Efficiently combining EF1 with Pareto optimality would reconcile fairness, efficiency, and computation for a basic goods model.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicitly given instance of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations, outputs an allocation that is both envy-free up to one good (EF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)?

Precisely, do there exist one algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), and matrix
\[
(v_{ig})_{i\in[n],\,g\in[m]}\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times m},
\]
\(A\) outputs a complete integral allocation satisfying the two conditions below in at most \(C(L+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(L\) is the full binary input length? The same program, constant and exponent must work for every number of agents and goods.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 1 asks whether an EF1 and Pareto-optimal allocation can be computed in polynomial time. The survey’s global setting specifies complete allocations of indivisible goods and nonnegative additive valuations.
definitions:
Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) distinct goods. Each good is indivisible and must be assigned to exactly one agent. An allocation is a tuple \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) of disjoint subsets of \([m]\) whose union is \([m]\). Empty bundles are permitted.

Agent \(i\)'s value for a bundle \(S\) is
\[
v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}.
\]
All entries are nonnegative; zero entries, zero-valued agents and goods valued at zero by everyone are allowed. Values depend only on the agent's own bundle. There are no monetary transfers, capacities, equal-bundle-size requirements, unequal entitlements or restrictions on which agent may receive which good.

The allocation \(X\) is EF1 when
\[
\forall i,j\in[n]\ \exists S\subseteq X_j,\quad
|S|\le1\quad\text{and}\quad v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus S).
\]
The removal is only hypothetical and does not discard an allocated good. The set \(S\) may depend on the ordered pair \(i,j\). Allowing \(S=\varnothing\) covers the case of no envy and empty envied bundles. The condition asks for some removable good, rather than every removable good; the latter is a stronger fairness condition.

The allocation \(X\) is PO if there is no other complete integral allocation \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\) such that
\[
\bigl(\forall i\in[n],\ v_i(Y_i)\ge v_i(X_i)\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\exists j\in[n],\ v_j(Y_j)>v_j(X_j)\bigr).
\]
The competing allocation may reassign any number of goods, and need not be EF1. PO therefore excludes every integral Pareto improvement, not just a local exchange or another fair allocation. The target uses integral alternatives. Fractional Pareto optimality, which also excludes improvements obtained by splitting goods, is stronger and is not separately required.

The input explicitly lists \(n,m\) and every matrix entry in row-major order. Use unary headers \(1^n0\,1^m0\), followed by each rational as \(p_{ig}/q_{ig}\) with integers \(p_{ig}\ge0\), \(q_{ig}\ge1\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), encode \(a+1\) by its \(b\)-bit binary representation preceded by \(1^b0\). Use this code for every numerator and denominator, requiring no trailing bits. Fractions need not be reduced. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits, including all headers and rational entries.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one fixed finite program, read-only input and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. All parsing, arithmetic, preprocessing and output are charged; no valuation oracle, advice or randomness is available. The output lists the receiving agent for each good, in increasing good order, using \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits per label. For \(m=0\), the empty output denotes the unique allocation. Malformed inputs must be rejected within the same polynomial bound.

Polynomial time is measured in the bit length, not in the magnitudes of the values. A bound polynomial in a largest integer value can be exponential in \(L\). Conversely, the target does not demand strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. Rational inputs do not add an essential promise: multiplying all values of an agent by the product of that agent's denominators produces nonnegative integers of polynomial bit length and preserves both EF1 and PO.

The requested output must satisfy both conditions exactly. This is an algorithm-existence proposition, not a numerical target, so absolute \(1/100\) accuracy does not allow an envy violation or a Pareto improvement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial bit-time bound and proofs that every output is a complete allocation satisfying EF1 and PO; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence theorem for allocations without the running-time guarantee, a pseudo-polynomial algorithm, an algorithm for each fixed number of agents with a growing exponent, or an approximation to either output condition is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem is only a conditional obstruction unless its required complexity separation is also proved. Hardness of maximizing Nash welfare or of verifying PO does not by itself prove hardness of finding some EF1 and PO allocation.
context:
The survey records existence of EF1 and PO allocations via Nash welfare and an earlier pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm. Neither establishes a polynomial bit-time bound for arbitrary binary values.

An algorithm may return any allocation satisfying both conditions. It is not required to maximize Nash welfare, maximize total utility, or provide a separate efficiently checkable certificate of Pareto optimality. Hardness of these different tasks does not settle the requested search problem.

Mahara’s result, published online in May 2026, finds an allocation satisfying EF1 and the stronger fractional Pareto optimality when the number of agents is fixed. The same publication explicitly retains the general polynomial-time question.

The March 2026 balanced-allocation paper studies equal bundle sizes and restricted valuation families. Its introduction also states that the unrestricted general-case computation question remains open; those constrained special cases do not resolve the present all-matrices target.
why: Fairness and efficiency can each be obtained quickly, and an allocation satisfying both always exists. The unresolved computational question asks whether the two can be reconciled without time proportional to numerical value magnitudes or an exponent growing with the number of participants. It is a basic boundary between existence and efficient construction in discrete fair division.
status_note: The 2022 survey asks for polynomial-time EF1 and PO allocation under additive goods valuations. The May 2026 publication of Mahara’s fixed-agent algorithm explicitly retains the general question, as does the March 2026 balanced-allocation paper. No unrestricted polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem was found in the bounded later-work review.

working_summary: The task is to divide indivisible goods among agents whose nonnegative values add across goods. EF1 allows each agent’s envy of another bundle to disappear after the hypothetical removal of at most one good. Pareto optimality forbids any reassignment that improves one agent without hurting another. Allocations satisfying both properties exist, but the card asks for one polynomial-time algorithm on explicitly encoded rational values and arbitrary numbers of agents.
