title: EF1 and Pareto optimality for additive mixed items
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: EF1 and Pareto optimality for mixed goods and chores tests the compatibility of two fundamental allocation requirements.
formal: Does every finite instance of indivisible mixed-item allocation with \(n\ge3\) agents and arbitrary real additive utilities admit a complete allocation that is both envy-free up to one item (EF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)? The item removed to eliminate an agent’s envy may come from the envied bundle or from the envious agent’s own bundle, with at most one item removed in total.
definitions: The agents are \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the items are \([m]\) for any integer \(m\ge0\). Each agent \(i\) has values \(v_{i,g}\in\mathbb R\), with no restrictions on their signs or magnitudes, and \(u_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{i,g}\) for every \(S\subseteq[m]\). The same item may have positive, zero or negative value to different agents. Agents have equal entitlements; no normalization of utility totals is imposed. An allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is a partition of all items into pairwise disjoint bundles, which may be empty. Every item must be assigned exactly once. No disposal, monetary transfers or fractional assignment is permitted. Allocation \(A\) is EF1 if for every ordered pair of distinct agents \(i,j\), at least one of the following holds: \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j)\); there exists \(g\in A_j\) such that \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\); or there exists \(g\in A_i\) such that \(u_i(A_i\setminus\{g\})\ge u_i(A_j)\). These alternatives remove at most one item from one of the two bundles for this comparison only; they do not change the allocation. In particular, removing one item from each bundle is not allowed. Allocation \(A\) is PO if no other complete integral allocation \(B\) satisfies \(u_i(B_i)\ge u_i(A_i)\) for every \(i\) and \(u_j(B_j)>u_j(A_j)\) for at least one \(j\). The quantifiers are \(\forall n\ge3\;\forall m\ge0\;\forall v\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\;\exists A\), with both properties required of the same \(A\). The target is existence; there is no polynomial-time computation or representation requirement for an allocation-selection rule.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may specify a finite real-valued instance and prove that none of its complete integral allocations satisfies both defined properties. An existence theorem confined to pure goods, pure chores, two agents, restricted value magnitudes or a different envy relaxation does not prove the general statement. A computation-time bound is not additionally required.
context:
Open Question 2 of the August 2024 survey asks for existence of an EF1 and PO allocation for at least three agents with additive utilities. Its subsequent question about polynomial-time computation is a separate issue. This card selects the stated existence question and uses the survey’s mixed-item EF1 convention.

The survey defines mixed-item EF1 by allowing deletion of at most one item either from the envied bundle or from the envious agent’s own bundle. All utility comparisons use the envious agent’s valuation. For purely nonnegative values the useful deletion is from the other bundle; for purely nonpositive values it is from the agent’s own bundle.

Mahara’s November 2025 revision establishes EF1 together with PO, and also fractional PO, for arbitrary additive chores. Consequently, the survey’s 2024 observation that even the chores case was unresolved is no longer an appropriate current-status description.

Barman and Verma’s January 2026 revision explicitly retains the general mixed-manna EF1-and-PO question. It proves PO together with introspective EF1, a different condition that modifies an agent’s own bundle. That result does not assert standard mixed-item EF1 together with PO.

Teh’s September 2026 revision establishes complete weighted EF1 existence for unrestricted additive mixed manna. Its joint fractional-efficiency guarantee applies to restricted value magnitudes, so the results checked there do not establish the unrestricted EF1-and-PO statement.
why: Fairness and efficiency can conflict when an indivisible item benefits one participant and burdens another. This question asks whether one standard minimal relaxation of envy is always compatible with the absence of a Pareto improvement. Resolving it would determine whether a central fairness–efficiency guarantee survives unrestricted mixed valuations beyond the now-understood pure-goods and pure-chores existence settings.
status_note: The January 2026 Barman–Verma revision explicitly leaves standard EF1 together with PO open for unrestricted additive mixed manna. The checked September 2026 weighted-fairness results and November 2025 pure-chores theorem do not settle this target. The search through 2026-09-15 was bounded and does not certify that no later resolution exists.
progress: 2024-08-12: The survey’s Open Question 2 asks whether EF1 and PO allocations always exist for additive mixed items and at least three agents. | 2025-11-26: Mahara’s revised preprint states general additive-chores existence in Theorems 1.1–1.2, including the stronger fractional Pareto requirement. These theorems concern the pure-chores subcase. | 2026-01-02: Barman and Verma’s v3 establishes introspective EF1 with PO for mixed manna while explicitly identifying standard EF1 with PO as open. | 2026-09-04: Teh’s v2 gives weighted EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed additive values and separate efficiency results under restricted magnitudes; the checked results do not close the general joint guarantee.
working_summary: Each participant may value an indivisible item positively, negatively or at zero. Every item must be assigned, and the participants have additive utilities and equal entitlements. EF1 permits eliminating each envy comparison by removing at most one item from one of the two bundles. The question is whether an allocation with this fairness guarantee can always also be Pareto optimal for at least three agents. Recent results settle pure chores and some alternative mixed-item fairness guarantees, but the checked 2026 sources do not resolve the unrestricted combination.

title: EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed-item utilities
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: Existence or optimal approximation for broad fairness guarantees would organize a substantial family of allocation problems.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\), every finite item set M and every profile of utility functions \(u_{i}:2^{M}\to \mathbb{R}\) with \(u_{i}(\varnothing )=0\), does there exist a complete allocation \(A=(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) such that for every ordered pair of agents i,j there is a set \(X\subseteq A_{i}\cup A_{j}\) with |\(X|\le 1\) satisfying \(u_{i}(A_{i}\setminus X)\ge u_{i}(A_{j}\setminus X)\)?
definitions: The n agents are indexed by \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when \(u_{i}(A_{i})<u_{i}(A_{j})\). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item \((\mathrm{EF}1)\) for mixed items. If there is no envy, \(X=\varnothing\) works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every \(n\ge 3\) and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.
context:
With desirable goods, envy can disappear after ignoring a valuable item held by someone else. With burdens, it can disappear after ignoring a costly item in the envious agent’s own bundle. For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

An arbitrary utility can satisfy \(u(\{a\})=u(\{b\})=1\) but \(u(\{a,b\})=- 3\). Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.
why: Tests whether one-item envy relief remains possible when item values have unrestricted interactions and may change sign across bundles. A positive answer would extend a basic fairness guarantee far beyond additive goods and chores; a negative answer would identify a limit of that guarantee itself.
status_note: Survey v4 question and definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The relevant AAAI 2026 work concerns a weaker two-removal guarantee and restricted valuation signs. No resolution of the general EF1 existence question was located; no exhaustive literature or independent proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2024-08: The extended survey states Open Question 1 for at least three agents with arbitrary utilities, noting that even identical arbitrary utilities remain unsettled in that source. | 2026-03: Bilò, Loebl and Vinci establish existence for the weaker up-to-one-good-and-one-chore comparison under sign-restricted valuations. The stated model and guarantee do not resolve unrestricted one-item EF1.
working_summary: Agents divide a finite set of indivisible items, and each agent may assign an arbitrary real utility to every bundle. The question asks whether a complete EF1 allocation always exists for three or more agents. For each envy comparison, EF1 permits ignoring at most one item from either the envious agent’s own bundle or the other bundle. An item’s effect may depend on its companions, so the model does not assume a fixed division into goods and chores. The 2026 existence results allowing one removal from each bundle do not settle this stricter one-item question.

title: Polynomial-time mixed equilibria in coordination polymatrix games
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: A complexity classification for a natural equilibrium or consensus task clarifies a substantive computational frontier.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every finite rational coordination-only polymatrix game, outputs an exact mixed Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the complete binary input length?
definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and for each player \(i\) a nonempty explicitly enumerated action set \(A_i=\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\). Each edge \(\{i,j\}\), with \(i<j\), carries an explicitly listed matrix \(M_{ij}\in\mathbb Q^{k_i\times k_j}\). If its endpoints choose \(a\in A_i\) and \(b\in A_j\), both receive the same edge payoff \(M_{ij}(a,b)\). Set \(M_{ji}(b,a)=M_{ij}(a,b)\) for reverse orientation. Each player selects one action for all its incident edges and receives the sum of those edge payoffs; nonedges contribute zero. A mixed profile \(p=(p_i)_{i\in V}\) uses independent probability vectors \(p_i\) on \(A_i\). For a pure deviation \(a\in A_i\), write \[v_i(a,p_{-i})=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\sum_{b\in A_j}p_j(b)M_{ij}(a,b),\qquad u_i(p)=\sum_{a\in A_i}p_i(a)v_i(a,p_{-i}).\] It is an exact Nash equilibrium when \(v_i(a,p_{-i})\le u_i(p)\) for every player \(i\) and every action \(a\). The required output explicitly lists nonnegative rational probabilities summing to one for each player. A pure profile is allowed as a degenerate mixed profile; neither full support nor a genuinely randomizing player is required. Vertices, edges and all actions are listed, and each payoff is encoded by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with delimiters. Thus the input length \(N\) includes the action lists, graph and every payoff bit; no succinct payoff circuit is allowed. Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, no advice or oracles, and a bound \(C(N+1)^d\) on all valid inputs for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Charge every bit operation and output bit. The target is exact equilibrium, with no approximation parameter or promise on payoff magnitudes, graph degree or action counts.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of the stated uniform polynomial-time algorithm, including termination, the full bit bound and exact equilibrium correctness, or of its logical negation. A hardness reduction under an unproved separation establishes only a conditional conclusion. A polynomial bound in numerical payoff magnitudes, a fixed graph or action-count special case, or an approximate-equilibrium algorithm without an exact guarantee does not meet the target.
context:
Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.
why: Locate the tractability boundary for exact mixed equilibrium when every pairwise interaction has common payoffs, distinguishing the complexity of network coordination from general games and from pure local-search equilibria.
status_note: The exact coordination-only tractability question is open in the checked primary sources. A bounded later-work search on 14 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Pure-equilibrium hardness and the 2025 two-team result concern different tasks; they are not treated as a refutation or an unconditional lower bound for this proposition.
progress: 2011: Cai–Daskalakis establish pure-equilibrium PLS-completeness and mixed-equilibrium membership in PLS and PPAD, leaving polynomial-time mixed-equilibrium tractability open. | 2014: Savani poses the coordination-only mixed-equilibrium complexity question in the Dagstuhl report. | 2025: The two-team hardness result allows zero-sum interactions between teams and hence does not settle this coordination-only restriction.
working_summary: Each player uses one action across several pairwise interactions in a graph. The two endpoints of each edge receive equal payoffs from that interaction. The target is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returning any exact mixed Nash equilibrium. Pure equilibria are permitted outputs, but an algorithm may also use genuinely mixed profiles. Known pure-equilibrium and adversarial two-team hardness results do not settle this coordination-only mixed search task.

title: Pure positional Nash equilibria in reachability games
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
importance_reason: Memory, equilibrium, or model-checking complexity for a natural game or logic variant informs the design of verification methods.
formal:
Does every finite deterministic turn-based multiplayer game with a designated initial vertex and a reachability objective for each player admit a pure positional Nash equilibrium?

The equilibrium is evaluated from that one initial vertex. A unilateral deviating strategy may depend on the complete finite history, even though every strategy in the proposed equilibrium must depend only on the current vertex.
question_excerpt: Casares asks whether multiplayer graph games with reachability, Büchi or parity objectives always have Nash equilibria whose strategies are positional. The user selected reachability for every player, finite deterministic turn-based arenas and equilibrium from one designated start, with unrestricted unilateral deviations.
definitions:
Fix any integer \(k\ge1\). An arena consists of a nonempty finite vertex set \(V\), a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_k\), and an initial vertex \(v_0\in V\). Empty parts are allowed. Every vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. At a vertex in \(V_i\), player \(i\) chooses the next vertex along one outgoing edge. All players observe the full history. There are no simultaneous moves, random transitions or hidden information.

Player \(i\) has any target set \(T_i\subseteq V\), which may be empty or overlap other targets. Targets are not required to be absorbing: play may leave a target after reaching it. An infinite play \(\rho=v_0v_1v_2\cdots\) follows edges of \(E\). Its payoff to player \(i\) is
\[
u_i(\rho)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }v_t\in T_i\text{ for some integer }t\ge0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus a visit at time zero counts, and visiting a target once suffices forever. No player has a safety, recurrence or parity objective.

A pure strategy for player \(i\) assigns a legal successor to each finite path whose last vertex lies in \(V_i\). It can use the entire path and has no memory or computability restriction. A pure positional strategy is a function \(\sigma_i:V_i\to V\) satisfying \((v,\sigma_i(v))\in E\) for every \(v\in V_i\); at every occurrence of that vertex it makes the same choice.

A profile \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)\) determines one infinite play \(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\). It is a Nash equilibrium from \(v_0\) when, for every player \(i\) and every pure history-dependent strategy \(\tau_i\),
\[
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\bigr)
\ge
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\bigr).
\]
Here \((\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\) replaces only player \(i\)'s strategy; every other player keeps the originally specified strategy, including at vertices not reached by the original play. A player already winning cannot improve. A losing player must have no unilateral way to reach its target.

The question quantifies over all finite arenas, all target sets, all player counts and every designated start, and asks for the existence of a positional profile for each such instance. The profile may depend on the start. It need not be an equilibrium from every vertex simultaneously or following every history, and no particular payoff vector is prescribed. No running-time bound or algorithm to find the profile is required. Randomized positional profiles do not meet the pure-strategy requirement. Allowing randomized deviations with expected binary payoffs would give the same equilibrium condition against a fixed pure profile: a positive probability of reaching a target entails a finite legal reaching history that can be followed by a pure deviation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every instance in the stated class has such a pure positional equilibrium, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may provide one finite arena, target sets and initial vertex together with a proof that every pure positional profile has a profitable unilateral deviation.

A counterexample using other objective types, stochastic transitions, a required payoff vector, or equilibrium simultaneously from every vertex does not settle this proposition. Existence of randomized memoryless profiles or pure profiles with memory does not prove it. Positive results restricted to absorbing targets do not cover the full target.
context:
A Nash equilibrium does not require everyone to win. It requires that each losing player remain unable to win by changing only their own choices while the other players keep theirs. The restrictions on equilibrium strategies and on deviations must therefore be stated separately.

The current vertex does not generally record which targets the play visited earlier. Even with a finite arena and simple reachability goals, forgetting that history can affect which continuation is stable.

The 2026 theorem allows randomization in memoryless strategies and establishes a stronger continuation-based equilibrium notion for its stated objective classes. Randomization is a resource absent from this card’s proposed profile.

The same paper proves a pure positional result when all relevant targets are absorbing. Its conclusion still leaves the all-reachability question without that restriction open. Examples mixing reachability with safety, or using other infinite-play objectives, do not settle the selected class.
why: A positional strategy stores no history and is directly implementable as one choice per vertex. The question asks whether all players can always make mutually stable choices of this form when their goals are to reach target sets, despite the extra power available to a deviating player who remembers the past.
status_note: The MFCS 2026 paper gives randomized memoryless equilibria for a wider combination of objectives, but its conclusion explicitly leaves pure positional equilibrium existence open when all objectives are reachability. Its absorbing-target positive theorem imposes an extra restriction absent here. The selected ordinary equilibrium is required from one initial vertex, not simultaneously from all vertices.
progress: 2024-07-01: The source asks about positional equilibria for reachability, Büchi and parity games. | 2026-08-21: MFCS 2026 publishes randomized memoryless equilibrium results and a restricted absorbing-target positional result, while retaining the general pure all-reachability question.
working_summary: Every player in a finite deterministic turn-based game wants to visit their own target set at least once. The question asks for a Nash equilibrium in which each player always makes the same choice at the same vertex. A player testing a unilateral improvement may remember the entire play history while all other players keep their original choices. Equilibrium is required from one designated start, targets need not be absorbing, and neither a particular winning vector nor randomized strategies are allowed. A complete Lean-checked solution must prove universal existence or verify a counterexample; the 2026 randomized theorem leaves this pure all-reachability target open.

title: Polynomial-time stable matching in unimodular hypergraphs
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
importance_reason: Tests whether a strong integrality promise can turn guaranteed coalition stability into an efficient algorithm. It extends the computational perspective of classical stable matching while keeping the target independent of optimization over stable outcomes. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Is there one deterministic algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge1\) as below that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph with totally unimodular incidence matrix and strict vertex preferences, returns a stable matching in at most \(C(L+1)^k\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input bit length?
definitions: The input explicitly lists vertices \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge0\), distinct nonempty hyperedges \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\subseteq2^V\), and, for each vertex, a permutation of its incident edge indices from most to least preferred. Vertex and edge indices are binary encoded with ordinary length-delimited list syntax; the input length \(L\) counts every listed vertex, incidence and preference entry. The incidence matrix is \(A_{v,j}=1\) for \(v\in e_j\) and zero otherwise. The promise is total unimodularity: every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) consists of pairwise disjoint edges. Every vertex prefers any incident edge to remaining unmatched. An edge \(e\notin M\) blocks \(M\) if every \(v\in e\) is unmatched or strictly prefers \(e\) to the unique edge of \(M\) containing \(v\). Stability means no edge blocks. There are no ties, capacities above one, edge-size bounds or optimization objective. Use one deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, randomness or an oracle, running within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) on every input string. It must return a list of edge indices forming a stable matching on every well-formed promised instance; its answer outside that promise is unrestricted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a uniform polynomial-time algorithm satisfying the stated search specification on all promised instances, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A hyperedge represents a group that could cooperate. Selected groups cannot share members. Stability forbids an unselected group whose members would all prefer forming it to their current situation. The input includes each participant’s ranking, so merely finding disjoint groups is insufficient.

An August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs. In that class the ground elements are arcs of an oriented tree and each hyperedge is a directed tree path. title: Nash equilibria in concurrent terminal-reward games
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division

importance_reason: A basic exact-equilibrium existence question for concurrent infinite-duration games, distinguishing nonnegative terminal objectives from finite normal-form and approximate existence theorems. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every finite two-player concurrent game with nonnegative terminal rewards admit an exact Nash equilibrium in randomized strategies that depend on the history of visited states? Play may continue forever, in which case both players receive zero. Existence is required from every specified initial state; strategies may use unbounded memory.
definitions:
A game has a finite nonempty state set \(S\), a specified initial state \(s_0\), and two players \(i\in\{1,2\}\). At each state \(s\), player \(i\) has a finite nonempty action set \(A_i(s)\). Both players choose actions simultaneously. A deterministic transition function maps \((s,a_1,a_2)\) to the next state. There is no additional random transition mechanism.

Terminal states are absorbing: every legal action pair leaves their state unchanged. Each terminal state \(f\) has a fixed finite real reward \(r_i(f)\geq0\) for each player. A play that first reaches \(f\) gives player \(i\) the one-time payoff \(r_i(f)\). A play that never reaches a terminal state gives zero. There are no intermediate rewards, discounting or repeated payments after absorption. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed.

A strategy \(\sigma_i\) assigns a probability distribution on \(A_i(s_t)\) to every finite visited-state history \(s_0s_1\cdots s_t\). At each round, actions are drawn independently for the two players according to these distributions. The strategy has access to state history, not the history of either player's chosen actions. This is the source's action-insensitive behavioral model, called “mixed strategies” there. It permits arbitrary history dependence and real probabilities; neither finite memory nor computability is required.

The transition rule and strategies induce a probability distribution on infinite plays. Let \(u_i(\sigma_1,\sigma_2;s_0)\) be the expected one-time payoff, including zero on nontermination. Rewards are bounded because the game is finite, so this expectation is well defined. A profile is an exact Nash equilibrium from \(s_0\) if
\[
u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)\leq u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)
\]
for both players and every alternative strategy \(\tau_i\) in the same state-history model. The other player's strategy stays fixed.

The question quantifies over every such finite game and initial state. It asks for an equilibrium against all permitted deviations, not merely stationary deviations, and does not require an equilibrium after every possible history as subgame perfection would. No payoff threshold, welfare guarantee or algorithm for constructing the profile is part of the target. Positive scaling of a player's rewards preserves the question, but adding a constant only at terminals need not: infinite plays still receive zero.
answer_criterion: Prove that an exact equilibrium exists for every game and initial state in the specified two-player, nonnegative, state-history model, or give a finite game in that model and prove that no permitted strategy profile is an exact equilibrium from its initial state. A failure of stationary or finite-memory equilibria alone is insufficient. Approximate equilibria and equilibria under imprecise deviations do not meet the exact criterion.
context:
Nash’s theorem for finite normal-form games does not directly settle this setting. A finite state graph can generate arbitrarily long histories, and never reaching a terminal can change the payoff discontinuously.

The source gives a two-player counterexample when negative terminal rewards are allowed. Its conclusion explains why an earlier claimed nonnegative counterexample does not work: shifting terminal rewards changes their comparison with nontermination.

The 2016 paper still lists exact existence for two players as open, even for binary terminal rewards. It proves existence under imprecise deviations, where a deviation must remain profitable throughout a neighborhood to count. This is distinct from both exact Nash equilibrium and the usual tolerance on payoff improvement.
why: Tests whether nonnegative eventual rewards suffice for exact strategic stability in the simplest concurrent infinite-duration setting. It separates the existence of stable behavior from restrictions on memory, computation or approximate incentives.

The question asks whether an exact Nash equilibrium always exists in randomized state-history strategies with unrestricted memory. Negative terminal rewards already admit counterexamples. A later existence theorem uses imprecise deviations and does not settle the exact question.

title: Matrix multiplication exponent
importance_reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.
focus_reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.
formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
context:
The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).
why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.
status_note: The checked source states the exponent-two conjecture, and the August 2026 papers report improved upper bounds without determining omega. The known interval displayed here remains wider than the requested numerical tolerance. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified determination at that precision. The optimization certificate was not independently replayed, and its repository was still described as in preparation in the checked version.

This is a method-specific barrier. | 2025-01-07: The SODA publication of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication states \(\omega<2.371339\). | 2026-08-17: Dupont and coauthors report \(\omega<2.371177\). The target permits a separate circuit for every size and counts all addition, subtraction and multiplication gates. Its infimum may be approached without an algorithm attaining the endpoint exponent. The accepted answer must locate the exponent with a Lean-certified absolute error of at most 0.01. title: Permanent versus determinant
importance_reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.
focus_reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.
formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
context:
The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.
why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

Symmetry restrictions, real-field bounds, border upper bounds and Boolean-sum simple projections are not substituted for this card’s exact model.

The question asks whether its representation as a determinant of affine-linear forms can be bounded in dimension by any polynomial in the original matrix size.
