title: Shub–Smale \(\tau\)-conjecture
importance_reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(C\geq1\), independent of the polynomial, such that every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfies \[z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq(1+\tau(f))^C,\] where \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\) is the number of distinct integer roots and \(\tau(f)\) is the minimum number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct \(f\) from only \(1\) and \(x\)?
definitions:
The ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) consists of formal univariate polynomials with integer coefficients. A straight-line program of length \(s\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) starts with registers \(g_0=1\) and \(g_1=x\). For each \(i=2,\ldots,s+1\), it chooses \(j_i,k_i<i\) and one operation from \(\{+,-,\times\}\), and sets \(g_i=g_{j_i}\mathbin{\circ_i}g_{k_i}\). Operands may coincide, and an earlier register may be used arbitrarily many times. One register is designated as output. The program computes \(f\) if this output equals \(f\) as a formal polynomial. Define \(\tau(f)\) to be the least possible \(s\) among such programs. Every integer polynomial can be constructed in finitely many operations, so this minimum exists. When \(s=0\), only \(1\) or \(x\) can be output.

Every new arithmetic register costs one operation, including operations used to build integer constants. In particular \(2\), \(0\) and \(-1\) are not additional free inputs. There is no division, primitive exponentiation, comparison, conditional branch or access to a supplied coefficient list. The finite program may be chosen separately for each polynomial; there is no uniformity requirement on these choices. Intermediate degrees, coefficient sizes and integer magnitudes are unrestricted. Cost measures arithmetic operations, not the number of bits in coefficients, a formula without shared registers or the bit length of the program encoding.

For \(f\ne0\), define \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)=|\{a\in\mathbb Z:f(a)=0\}|\), counting negative roots, zero and positive roots once each, regardless of multiplicity. This cardinality is finite because a nonzero univariate polynomial has at most its degree many roots; a nonzero constant has no roots. The zero polynomial is excluded. The exponent \(C\) must be one constant for all \(f\), without dependence on degree, coefficients, root sizes or the choice of an optimal program. The question asks only for a bound, not for an efficient root-counting or root-finding algorithm.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the universal bound or its logical negation, \(\forall C\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists f\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus\{0\}:z_{\mathbb Z}(f)>(1+\tau(f))^C\). A positive answer may use any one absolute exponent; a negative answer must exclude all such exponents. No computable rule for choosing the counterexample polynomials is required. A counterexample to just one proposed exponent, bounds for a restricted program class, multiplicity counts, or results only about real or complex roots do not settle this full target. Conditional consequences of the conjecture are not proofs of it.
context:
After \(s\) squarings, the program for \(x^{2^s}\) has only \(s\) operations but exponential degree. In general \(\deg f\leq2^{\tau(f)}\), giving only \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq2^{\tau(f)}\). The example has just one distinct integer root, although that root has multiplicity \(2^s\). This is why both the arithmetic compression and the word “distinct” matter.

The corresponding unrestricted real-root assertion is false. Let \(q_0(x)=x\) and \(q_{j+1}(x)=q_j(x)^2-2\). Building 2 once and using two operations per iteration gives \(\tau(q_j)\leq2j+1\). The identity \(q_j(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(2^j\theta)\) shows that \(q_j\) has \(2^j\) distinct real roots. Integer roots impose a substantially different constraint.

Smale’s Problem 4 records the root-count question, and Rojas gives exactly the \((1+\tau)^C\) convention used here. Allowing the fixed constants \(-1,0,1\) for free changes operation counts by at most two relative to the present convention; it does not change whether some polynomial root bound exists. Exact small-length records do depend on the convention. Arbitrary free integer constants constitute a different cost model.

Shub and Smale’s work connects short integer computations with feasibility of polynomial systems over \(\mathbb C\). Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly states that the root conjecture implies \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb C}\ne\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb C}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model. This model has exact complex arithmetic and equality tests at unit cost. The implication is about that algebraic model; it does not itself assert Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Rojas’s Theorem 1 proves that a polynomial bound just for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime already implies the full conjecture. His Theorem 3 gives a bound \(\exp(O(s\log(s+1)))\) on rational roots in terms of additive complexity \(s\), a measure charging additions while allowing powers and multiplicative expressions more freely. This does not give a polynomial bound in the full operation count \(\tau\).

Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch and Tzameret record the implication \(\mathrm{VP}^0\ne\mathrm{VNP}^0\) for constant-free algebraic complexity, and obtain conditional lower bounds in the Ideal Proof System for a binary-value variant over rational functions. Their separate hypothesis about nonzero multiples of factorials yields a different lower bound over the rationals. These hypotheses and coefficient domains are distinct, and the results do not directly give Frege lower bounds for Boolean formulas.

Santibañez-Leal’s Zenodo preprint, version 0.03 dated 20 August 2026, reports an exhaustive census through eight operations using free constants \(-1,0,1\). The computation has not been independently reproduced for this card. A finite census, even if correct, does not establish or refute a bound with one exponent for every program length.
why: The conjecture asks whether a polynomial compressed into a short arithmetic computation can nevertheless have very many distinct integer zeros. Its elementary statement links arithmetic structure to fundamental lower bounds in algebraic computation. A proof would imply separation of polynomial-time nondeterministic and deterministic computation over the complex numbers, as well as important constant-free circuit separations; neither consequence is presently supplied by the conjecture itself.
status_note: The universal bound for distinct integer roots remains unresolved in the checked sources. A bounded later-work check through 14 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of this exact statement. The August 2026 finite census is an unreproduced computational claim with different free constants, and recent conditional algebraic-complexity implications do not settle the root bound. No cited proof or computation is represented as independently formally verified.
progress: 1995: Shub and Smale connect the complexity of integer computations to infeasibility testing over the complex numbers. Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly records the distinct-integer-root conjecture and its complex P versus NP consequence. | 2003-04-09: Rojas’s second arXiv version states the full root conjecture, proves the fixed-prime residue-class implication, and bounds rational roots using additive complexity. The latter bound is not polynomial in \(\tau\). | 2024-06-05: The SIAM paper on semialgebraic proofs publishes conditional IPS lower bounds from the root conjecture over rational functions and from a distinct factorial-multiple hypothesis over the rationals. | 2026-08-20: A Zenodo preprint reports a finite census through eight operations with free constants -1,0,1. Its computation is unverified here and its finite scope does not resolve a universal exponent.
working_summary: A straight-line program constructs an integer polynomial using only one, a variable, addition, subtraction and multiplication. The conjecture asks for one fixed polynomial bound on the number of distinct integer roots in terms of the shortest program length. All operations constructing constants count, shared registers are allowed, and the zero polynomial is excluded. A short program can already create exponential degree or exponentially many distinct real roots, so neither supplies the desired integer-root bound. The conjecture has major conditional consequences in algebraic computation and proof complexity, while finite censuses and bounds in other complexity measures leave its universal claim unsettled.

title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
importance_reason: A basic class equality linking general arithmetic circuits, algebraic branching programs and determinant universality; current symmetry and multilinearity results remain model-specific.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.
context:
Circuits combine previously computed polynomials by both addition and multiplication, with unrestricted reuse. An ABP records sums of products along paths with affine labels. ABPs are polynomially equivalent to skew circuits, where each multiplication gate has at least one operand that is an input variable or constant. The conjectural gap concerns the size of exact representations under these two forms of computation, rather than which individual polynomials can be represented at all.

The polynomial-degree condition is essential. Small general circuits can have output degree exponential in their size, whereas an ABP with affine labels has degree at most its longest source-to-sink path. Such degree alone cannot separate the classes in this card because it is explicitly required to stay polynomial. The stated bounds concern the final polynomial; intermediate cancellations and degrees in a competing circuit are allowed.

Determinants give an equivalent structural description of \(\mathrm{VBP}\): a family belongs to this class exactly when it has representations \(f_n=\det(A_{n,0}+\sum_j x_j A_{n,j})\) with polynomially bounded matrix dimension and complex constant matrices. The determinant itself admits polynomial-size ABPs. Thus \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VBP}\) would make determinants universal for the circuit families in the statement. This is distinct from permanent versus determinant: the permanent is not known to have the polynomial-size general circuits required on the easy side of a separation here.

The classical Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations among formulas, ABPs and circuits for polynomial-degree families. The ITCS 2024 paper recalls that their quasipolynomial versions coincide, where a quasipolynomial bound means \(n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\). A polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is stronger. Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.
why: The question compares unrestricted arithmetic circuits with path-sum computation inside the class of efficiently representable polynomials. Equality would make polynomial-size determinants of affine matrices sufficient to express every polynomial-degree circuit family. Inequality would establish a fundamental separation within efficient algebraic computation, isolating power supplied by general multiplication together with reuse of intermediate results.
status_note: Open in the checked June 2026 factoring survey, Remark 7.3. Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no resolution for unrestricted commutative exact nonuniform computation over C. The January/June symmetry separation uses orbit complexity, prescribed variable symmetries and no degree bound; the multilinear report studies a syntactically restricted model; min-plus-semiring results have different operations. Characteristic-zero factor closure and quasipolynomial simulations do not imply the required polynomial simulation. Complete new proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1983: Valiant, Skyum, Berkowitz and Rackoff establish classical depth reduction; the checked ITCS 2024 exposition records the resulting quasipolynomial equivalence of the algebraic models. | 2020: Sinhababu and Thierauf prove polynomial ABP factor closure over characteristic-zero fields at CCC. | 2021-10-15: The factor-closure result is published in Computational Complexity. It does not identify ABPs with general circuits. | 2026-01-01: Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff study the power of min-partition rank for syntactically multilinear ABPs and recover a restricted formula–ABP separation. | 2026-01-14: Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt post the symmetric-class separation and separate completeness results; the work appears at STOC 2026. | 2026-06-12: The revised factoring survey retains \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) with no strict containment known, in Remark 7.3.
working_summary: VP versus VBP asks whether every polynomial-degree family with small arithmetic circuits also has small algebraic branching programs over the complex numbers. The branching programs compute exact sums of affine-label products along paths, with all coefficients and variable occurrences included in the algebraic size. Both models are nonuniform and allow arbitrary complex constants, with no imposed symmetry, width or multilinearity restriction. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish the universal polynomial simulation or one circuit-easy family requiring superpolynomial branching-program size. The question would decide whether determinant-like computation captures general efficient algebraic computation, beyond the known quasipolynomial simulations and restricted-model results.

title: VP versus VNP
importance_reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.
formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
context:
The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. This card concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this card, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this card; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).
why: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No polynomial-size general permanent circuits or matching superpolynomial lower bound were found in the bounded primary-source review. The August OpenAI chapter reports a general permanent lower bound of order n^2 log log n and formula lower bounds, with released Lean certificates; these remain polynomial and the certificates were not independently replayed here. Narayanan’s depth/degree-qualified results and the September numerical approximation theorem have different guarantees. The full VP-versus-VNP question over C remains source-open in the inspected literature.

The modern formulation makes polynomial-size permanent circuits equivalent to VP=VNP over C. | 2021–2025: Limaye–Srinivasan–Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds for every fixed depth in characteristic zero; the journal version appears in 2025. Unrestricted circuits are outside that lower bound. | 2026-08-01: OpenAI reports \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) general division-free circuit size and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) formula size for the permanent, with released Lean certificates. These polynomial lower bounds do not settle VP versus VNP; certificates were not replayed in this review. | 2026-08-09: Narayanan’s July-submitted manuscript is published on ECCC with improved sublogarithmic-depth lower bounds and exponential-degree elusive curves; its parameters do not yield the full separation. | 2026-09-09: Kudria–Luo–Majid report a subexponential multiplicative approximation factor in deterministic polynomial bit time for nonnegative rational matrices, a distinct numerical target.
working_summary: The permanent sums one product of matrix variables for each permutation of the columns. The question is whether exact division-free arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers compute these polynomials with one polynomial size bound for all matrix dimensions. The selected model permits arbitrary complex constants, cancellations, unrestricted reuse and a different circuit at each dimension without a uniform generator. A complete Lean proof must establish such circuits or rule out every polynomial size bound, equivalently settling VP versus VNP in this model. The checked August polynomial lower bounds, constant-depth separations and September numerical approximation result do not settle the required general exact-circuit question.

title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
importance_reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(K,C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) there is an arithmetic formula \(F_n\) over \(\mathbb C\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{size}(F_n)\le K n^C,\qquad \llbracket F_n\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n(X),\]
where \(\llbracket F_n\rrbracket\) is its output as a formal commutative polynomial and
\[\operatorname{Det}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
The formula is a binary expression tree with arbitrary complex constants and addition, subtraction and multiplication. Computations may use cancellations, but intermediate expressions cannot be shared. The same constants \(K,C\) must work for all dimensions.
question_excerpt: The inherited Raz source treats general arithmetic formulas over fields and separately proves a multilinear lower bound. This card retains the previously chosen complex-field specialization, nonuniform arbitrary constants, binary operations, total-node size, polynomial-existence target and importance 96. The review makes evaluation and size recursive, spells out the exact quantifier negation, and does not import intermediate multilinearity or symmetry from restricted lower-bound results.
definitions:
Polynomial and parameters. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) has \(n^2\) distinct commuting indeterminates as its entries. The positive integer \(n\) is the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. The set \(S_n\) consists of all permutations of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}\), where \(\operatorname{inv}(\pi)\) counts pairs \(i<j\) with \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). All calculations take place in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\). In particular \(\operatorname{Det}_1=x_{11}\); no invertibility or numerical-entry promise is imposed.

Formula syntax and evaluation. A formula is a finite rooted binary tree with ordered children. A leaf is labelled by one input variable or one constant in \(\mathbb C\). Each internal node is labelled \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\) and computes the corresponding operation on the two child polynomials; subtraction uses left child minus right child. The root’s polynomial is denoted \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\). Every node other than the root has exactly one parent. Repeated uses of an expression therefore require separate copies of its entire subtree. No powers, determinants, summations or other compound expressions are primitive gates: any such shorthand in a proposed family must expand to allowed binary nodes.

Size. Every node counts once, including each occurrence of a variable or constant. Equivalently, a leaf has size one and a node with children \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). Distinct leaves carrying the same value count separately. Define
\[L_{\det}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n\}.\]
The set is nonempty by the finite permutation expansion, so this positive-integer minimum exists. The question is whether \(L_{\det}(n)\) is bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). Allowing real constants in a size bound rather than positive integer \(K,C\) would give the same polynomial-boundedness claim.

Constants and nonuniformity. Each constant leaf has unit size regardless of its magnitude, algebraic degree or description length. Constants and the tree may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and complex constants need not be computable or rational. They cannot depend on the values later substituted for input variables. There is no algorithmic or efficiency requirement for generating the family, and no bit-cost bound on its representation: the resource is algebraic tree size. The field \(\mathbb C\) is fixed throughout; the target is not a simultaneous assertion for all fields.

Exact unrestricted computation. The equality at the root is an exact polynomial identity, coefficient by coefficient. Approximation of coefficients, a limit of formulas or correct evaluation only on a restricted input set does not meet it. Division, inverses, comparisons, branching, input-dependent constants and additional input variables are not allowed. There is no restriction on depth, homogeneity, signs or coefficient magnitudes. Intermediate polynomials may have powers or monomials absent from the determinant, provided they cancel in the final identity. A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. The output determinant is multilinear, but the formula is not required to be multilinear at intermediate nodes.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, prove the existence of allowed formula trees for every dimension, their exact determinant identity, and one common polynomial size bound. A uniform construction is welcome but is not required by this nonuniform target. Count all copied subtrees and constant occurrences.

A negative answer must prove
\[\forall K,C\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\det}(n)>K n^C.\]
It must cover arbitrary complex constants and all unrestricted intermediate computations permitted above. Equivalently, for every \(K,C,N\ge1\), there must be some \(n\ge N\) violating that polynomial bound; finitely many exceptional dimensions can always be absorbed into its constant. It is not necessary to prove that every sufficiently large dimension violates every given polynomial, a stronger eventual-growth claim.

A fixed-power lower bound, such as \(\Omega(n^3)\), leaves larger polynomial bounds possible. Lower bounds only for multilinear, homogeneous, symmetric, monotone, bounded-depth, bounded-coefficient or noncommutative computations do not refute the stated unrestricted commutative claim. An exact identity using a small circuit with shared intermediate results is not yet a small formula, and a large size for one particular determinant expansion is not a lower bound for all formulas. A proof conditional on an unresolved separation must keep that assumption explicit and does not settle this unconditional question.
context:
The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The permutation expansion has \(n!\) summands, but this does not prove that every formula is large. A product of short sums may represent many expanded monomials. For example, the \(2\times2\) determinant is \(x_{11}x_{22}-x_{12}x_{21}\), represented by seven nodes in the stated model. The challenge is one size bound for all dimensions, not finding finite expressions for individual matrices. Numerical Gaussian elimination also does not directly answer the symbolic tree-size question: its usual implementation reuses intermediate entries, divides and chooses pivots.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size \(2^{O(\log ^{2} n)}=n^{O(\log  n)}\). This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is complete for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs. Such a program is a directed acyclic graph with a source and sink; affine-linear edge labels are multiplied along paths and the path products are summed. The class \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially many variables, polynomial degree and polynomial-size branching programs, while \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) uses formula trees. Every formula has a polynomial-size branching program, and every such branching program has a polynomial-size determinant representation. Thus the existence claim here is equivalent to \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\).

The larger class \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) permits polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, where gates may have several consumers, while retaining polynomially many variables and polynomial degree. The June 2026 factoring primer records \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) without a known strict containment. It includes recent closure results for factoring formulas and still expressly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved. A positive answer here would identify the first two classes; it would not alone identify either with \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\).

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are \(n^{2}\) independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power \(3/2\) in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, \((x+y)^{2}- x^{2}- y^{2}\) equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries whose determinants still require \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense \(n^{2}\)-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.
why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The June 2026 factoring revision explicitly leaves polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas unknown. The July CCC sparse-determinant theorem restricts intermediate computations to multilinear formulas, while other inspected 2026 separations impose symmetry or noncommutativity. No matching unrestricted complex-field resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; full external proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1984: Berkowitz gives division-free polynomial-size, \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-depth determinant circuits; unfolding yields quasipolynomial-size formulas. | 1985: Kalorkoti proves an unrestricted \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula lower bound for an n by n determinant, also allowing division. | 2003–2009: Raz establishes \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bounds for formulas that remain multilinear at every gate; the original ECCC report precedes the journal publication. | 2019-11-28: Chaugule and coauthors relate formula complexity of Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to the generic determinant. | 2026-06–07: Boyapati–Chillara–Vempati retain the \(n^{\Omega(\log n)}\) multilinear lower bound with \(\Theta(n\log^6 n)\) nonzero entries; ECCC in June, CCC publication on 23 July. | 2026-06-12: The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.
working_summary: The symbolic determinant has n² commuting input variables for an n-by-n matrix. The question asks whether its exact polynomial can be expressed by arithmetic trees of size bounded by one fixed polynomial in n. Every occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subexpression is charged, while arbitrary fixed complex constants and cancellations are allowed. A complete Lean proof must establish such formulas for all dimensions or refute every polynomial size bound in the full nonuniform model. Cubic unrestricted lower bounds and superpolynomial multilinear lower bounds do not settle this equivalent formulation of VF versus VBP over the complex field.

title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
importance_reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.
formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
question_excerpt: Does a uniform algorithm decide equality of two words in an ordinary monoid whose single defining relation is supplied as input?
definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.
context:
This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

An equality has a finite certificate: a sequence of contextual applications of the defining relation connecting the two words. Inequality has no analogous certificate supplied by the presentation itself. A long search with no successful derivation does not decide whether one exists, since intermediate words can have unbounded length.

Length-preserving relations, where \(|u|=|v|\), form a decidable special case. The general problem allows length-changing replacements. Termination of an oriented shortening rule is not sufficient by itself: different irreducible words may still represent the same element. The requested algorithm has no efficiency requirement, so a large computable time bound would still be a positive answer.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.
why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?
status_note: Gray–Reilly, 5 August 2026, explicitly retain the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Their inverse-monoid theorem, the 2025/2026 submonoid-membership results and the August 2026 Diophantine theorem do not decide equality of two supplied words in the card’s ordinary presentation model. The saved card asks for one uniform machine; the source’s per-presentation wording is distinguished. Bounded checks through 16 September found no matching uniform resolution, not an exhaustive proof of openness.
progress: 1932 and later: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure. | 2021-08-10: Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments. | 2022-09-07: The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure. | 2022-10-28: Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability. | 2026-08-05: Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open. | 2025–2026: The published membership results concern existential membership in generated submonoids, rather than equality of two specified words. | 2026-08-03: The Diophantine preprint proves undecidability of equation solvability with unknown elements in some one-relation monoids, a broader predicate than this card. | 2026-09-16: The audit preserves the uniform ordinary-monoid target and score 96, fixes complete word notation and encodings, and adds full Lean acceptance and later-result scope checks.
working_summary: An ordinary one-relation monoid identifies words using one fixed reversible literal replacement rule in arbitrary surrounding contexts. The question asks whether a single algorithm can decide equality of any two words when the alphabet and defining relation are also supplied. Empty words and length-changing relations are allowed, and the algorithm must halt on unequal pairs as well as equal ones. Recent undecidability results for inverse monoids, submonoid membership and equations with unknowns concern different or broader problems. A resolution would locate a central decidability boundary for equality under minimal finite algebraic presentations.

title: Superpolynomial arithmetic formula lower bounds
importance_reason: A defining unrestricted algebraic lower-bound challenge, separating the basic expression-tree model from VNP. Its reach comes from the permanent completeness theorem and the gap between known restricted-model bounds and general formulas, with consequences for the fundamental algebraic complexity hierarchy. This individually replaces the unassessed midpoint; the score reflects scope rather than recency of this review.
formal:
Is the permanent family outside polynomial-size arithmetic formulas over \(\mathbb C\)? Precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\forall F,\qquad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{size}(F)>K n^C,
\]
where \(F\) ranges over the arithmetic formulas defined below and
\[
\operatorname{Perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}
\in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:i,j\in[n]]?
\]
This card fixes the standard complex-field \(\mathrm{VNP}\)-versus-formula interpretation of the source’s broadly phrased explicit lower-bound challenge. By the permanent’s completeness under polynomially bounded projections, this asks whether some family in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) lacks polynomial-size formulas; it does not impose a separate uniform construction condition on the family of small formulas being ruled out. The source’s Open Problem 8 does not itself name a field or a particular hard family, so this precise choice is an explicit editorial specification.

Superpolynomial means that no single polynomial bound works for all dimensions. It does not demand one particular exponential rate or an eventually pointwise lower bound exceeding every polynomial. There are \(n^2\) input variables; \(n\) in the displayed size bound is the matrix dimension.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \([n]\), and let \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) be a matrix of distinct commuting indeterminates. The permanent is the displayed sum with coefficient one on every permutation monomial. Equality of outputs is equality of formal polynomials, including all coefficients; there is no numerical input distribution, approximation error or promise on matrix entries.

An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted ordered binary tree. Each leaf is labelled by one variable \(x_{ij}\) or one constant in \(\mathbb C\); each internal vertex is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Its output \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\) is defined recursively by the corresponding operations in the polynomial ring. Every vertex other than the root has exactly one parent. Reusing an expression requires another copy of its subtree. A sum or product with more than two operands must be expanded into binary operations and its full tree is counted.

The size is the total number of vertices, including every occurrence of each constant and variable. Thus a leaf has size one and a binary node with subformulas \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). This is one plus the edge count used by the original survey, an equivalent convention for polynomial boundedness. Arbitrary negative and nonreal constants are allowed; subtraction can be expressed using a constant \(-1\) and the permitted operations. There is no division gate, exponentiation gate, Boolean operation, test, conditional branch or determinant gate.

Constants have unit size regardless of their magnitude, algebraic degree, computability or description length. The finite tree and its constants may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); no algorithm for generating them and no finite binary encoding of arbitrary complex constants is required. A formula is a finite mathematical object with complex labels, not a bit-cost algorithm for evaluating a numerical matrix. There is no restriction on depth, cancellation, intermediate degree, repeated variables, monotonicity or homogeneity of intermediate polynomials. The output permanent is multilinear, but its subformulas need not be multilinear.

Define
\[
L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n\}.
\]
A finite formula exists by expanding the defining sum, so this integer minimum is well defined. The assertion is \(\forall K,C\ge1\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)>K n^C\). All finite initial exceptions to a prospective polynomial upper bound can be absorbed by increasing \(K\). Replacing \(n\) by the variable count \(n^2\) in the phrase polynomial size gives the same class of bounds.

For clarity, the class interpretation uses the following nonuniform algebraic definitions. A polynomial family \((f_t)_{t\ge1}\), with \(f_t\in\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_{v(t)}]\), is in \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable counts, degrees and formula sizes are bounded by fixed polynomials in \(t\). It is in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable count is polynomially bounded and there is a polynomially bounded witness count \(w(t)\) and a family \(g_t(z,y)\) of polynomial degree and polynomial-size arithmetic circuits such that
\[
f_t(z)=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{w(t)}}g_t(z,b).
\]
Here a circuit uses the same inputs and binary operations as a formula, but may share intermediate results in a finite directed acyclic graph. All bounds in these class definitions use constants independent of \(t\), while circuits and constants may depend on \(t\). The zero polynomial may be assigned degree zero for these bounds. A polynomially bounded projection substitutes variables or field constants into a member of another family whose index is polynomially bounded in \(t\). The direct permanent assertion is the acceptance target; these definitions explain its class-theoretic scope without adding an algorithmic requirement.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed assertion or its full negation for the specified formula model.

A positive answer must prove failure of every polynomial upper bound, with the quantifier order \(\forall K,C\ \exists n\ \forall F\) in the statement. A proof for another family suffices only if its implications for this exact target are also proved. One fixed polynomial lower bound, even with a larger exponent than all currently cited bounds, does not establish the assertion.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\exists F:\quad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \land\ \operatorname{size}(F)\le K n^C.
\]
The same constants work for every dimension; individual formulas and complex constants may vary with the dimension. A uniform construction is sufficient if it meets the size guarantee, but is not an additional obligation.

A lower bound only for fixed depth, monotone formulas, multilinear subformulas, bounded coefficients, or noncommuting variables does not by itself cover the formulas in this card. A polynomial-size circuit permitting shared intermediate results does not by itself provide the required formula upper bound. The numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not change this asymptotic class-separation question.
context:
Shpilka and Yehudayoff’s Open Problem 8 asks broadly for a superpolynomial arithmetic-formula lower bound; this card explicitly specifies the standard complex-field VNP-versus-formula version using the permanent.

The survey defines formulas as trees and proves that every VNP family over a field of characteristic different from two is a polynomially bounded projection of the permanent, supporting the chosen concrete representative.

The January 2026 Rossman–Zhu paper still identifies separating polynomial-size unrestricted formulas from VNP as a major open problem and distinguishes it from known restricted-model lower bounds.

Forbes’s 2024 result extends low-depth algebraic lower bounds to all fields, while the unrestricted depth of formulas here remains outside that guarantee.

An August 2026 report claims a permanent formula lower bound of order \(n^4/\log n\), including a version with division; this is still polynomial in the matrix dimension, and this review checks its statement rather than independently verifying its proof.
why: Separating polynomial-size formulas from VNP would establish a basic limit of unrestricted algebraic expression trees for an explicit central polynomial. Formulas already allow arbitrary constants and cancellations, so their limitations are considerably harder to prove than those of many restricted algebraic models. This is a foundational lower-bound target within the hierarchy of algebraic complexity and is weaker than separating unrestricted circuits from VNP.
status_note: The 2010 survey poses the broad lower-bound challenge, and the January 2026 primary paper explicitly identifies the standard VNP-versus-unrestricted-formula separation as open. The card fixes its complex-field permanent representative and discloses that choice. The MFCS paper published on 21 August 2026 continues to discuss this general separation as a lower-bound challenge. Bounded later checks through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the inspected August report claims a polynomial lower bound, while other recent results retain depth, representation or conditional restrictions. This does not independently verify all cited proofs or certify exhaustive present openness.

working_summary: The question asks whether the permanent requires arithmetic expression trees larger than every fixed polynomial bound. The trees compute formal polynomials over the complex numbers using addition and multiplication with arbitrary constants and unrestricted cancellations. This is the explicitly selected standard separation between polynomial-size formulas and VNP, represented by the permanent through its completeness theorem. Known bounds for restricted models and the inspected recent polynomial lower-bound claim do not establish the required unrestricted superpolynomial separation. A complete Lean answer must rule out every polynomial formula bound or prove that one polynomial bound suffices in every dimension.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
importance_reason: A defining open problem in algebraic computation: randomized polynomial-time search is known, while uniform deterministic polynomial bit complexity remains unresolved even for basic root-finding cases.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit field representation \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\) and every dense polynomial \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\ge1\), the algorithm outputs the complete irreducible factorization of \(f\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\bigr)^d
\]
bit operations?

The input includes the prime \(p\), the supplied monic irreducible field modulus \(h\), and every coefficient of \(f\). The algorithm and the constants are independent of \(n,p,h\) and \(f\), and no unproved number-theoretic assumption is allowed.
question_excerpt: Altman’s introduction asks for deterministic factorization into irreducibles in time polynomial in the degree and the logarithm of the prime, and states that no such general algorithm is known. Guo’s introduction states the corresponding complete-factorization question over arbitrary finite fields. The card makes their input-size convention explicit for a supplied polynomial-basis field representation.
definitions:
Let \(p\ge2\) be a prime, let \(e\ge1\), and let \(h(t)\in\mathbb F_p[t]\) be a monic irreducible polynomial of degree \(e\). The field \(\mathbb F_p\) is the integers modulo \(p\), and \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\), where \(q=p^e\), is the field of residue classes modulo \(h\). Its elements are represented uniquely by polynomials of degree less than \(e\), with each coefficient in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). Addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication followed by reduction modulo \(p\) and \(h\).

The input writes \(p,e,n\) in binary, all coefficients of \(h\), and all \(n+1\) coefficients of \(f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jx^j\), with \(a_n\ne0\). Each field coefficient uses its full \(e\)-tuple of residues, each residue occupying \(\lceil\log_2p\rceil\) bits. Integer and array boundaries use a fixed unambiguous encoding. In particular, the polynomial is dense: zero coefficients are present, and neither a circuit nor an evaluation oracle substitutes for the coefficient list. The field representation is also part of the counted input, rather than fixed advice. Primality of \(p\) and irreducibility and degree of \(h\) are promises; constructing \(h\) from \(p,e\) is not an additional output task. No correctness condition is imposed on malformed or unpromised inputs.

A nonconstant polynomial \(g\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) is irreducible if it cannot be written as the product of two polynomials of positive degree over this same field. Monic means that its leading coefficient is one. A complete factorization consists of a nonzero field element \(u\), a list of pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) of positive degree, and positive binary integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), satisfying the exact polynomial identity
\[
f=u\prod_{i=1}^r g_i^{m_i}.
\]
All factors are written as dense coefficient lists in the supplied field representation. The order of factors is irrelevant. Multiplicities are required, including for repeated factors in positive characteristic; there is no square-free or separability promise. Merely deciding irreducibility, returning a proper factor, or finding roots when they exist is not the specified output.

Time is worst-case deterministic bit time on a standard multitape Turing machine. Reading, arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factorization all count. The full input length is polynomially related to \(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\), so the displayed bound is equivalent to a single polynomial bound in that length. It is not polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(p\) or \(q\). There is no random tape, oracle, uncharged field operation or family of field-specific algorithms. Extension degree and characteristic may both grow with the input.

The target is an existence proposition about an exact symbolic factorization algorithm. Absolute numerical approximation does not replace the polynomial identity or irreducibility conditions.
answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and a complete Lean-checked proof that it terminates with the specified complete factorization on every valid input and obeys one bound of the displayed form. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no deterministic algorithm with any such absolute polynomial bound exists.

An expected-time randomized algorithm, an average over inputs or primes, polynomial dependence on the field cardinality or characteristic, a restriction on degree or Galois group, or a bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle this proposition. The failure of a particular method is not a proof of the negative answer.
context:
The field representation tells the algorithm how to perform exact arithmetic. Factoring the supplied polynomial asks for its irreducible building blocks over that field, including multiplicities. Factors over a larger extension field would be a different output.

Randomized polynomial-time factorization is classical. Unconditional deterministic bounds can depend polynomially on the characteristic, which is too costly when the characteristic is large relative to its binary encoding.

Altman factors reductions of one integer polynomial across many primes with an amortized guarantee depending on its splitting-field degree. This does not give the requested worst-case bound for an arbitrary polynomial over one input field.

The general problem also remains open under the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis in the inherited account. Conditional quasipolynomial or special-Galois-group algorithms therefore should not be described as a full conditional solution.

The 2026 Reed–Solomon decoding result removes randomness for the special factorization instances arising there by using information from the received word. It explicitly retains arbitrary univariate factorization as an open problem.

The recent sparse-polynomial result states that its bounds must include the cost of univariate factorization. Its finite-field preliminary theorem gives polynomial dependence on the characteristic, not only on its logarithm.
why: Finite-field factorization is a basic operation in computer algebra and coding theory. Randomized polynomial-time algorithms are available, while a deterministic algorithm must handle every coefficient list and every characteristic without trying a number of possibilities proportional to the field size. The question isolates a central derandomization gap in an exact algebraic task.
status_note: The checked sources retain unconditional deterministic polynomial-time factorization over arbitrary finite fields as open. The 2026 list-decoding algorithm solves specially structured factorization instances with extra information. The recent sparse-factorization theorem retains characteristic or univariate-oracle costs, and neither gives the uniform bound required here.
