working_summary: The input is a densely written polynomial over a finite field whose polynomial-basis representation is supplied. The requested output is every monic irreducible factor, its multiplicity, and the original leading scalar. One deterministic algorithm must run in time polynomial in the degree and the logarithm of the field size for all valid inputs. Randomized methods, special decoding instances, averages over primes and characteristic-dependent bounds do not provide that guarantee. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish both universal correctness and the uniform bit-time bound, or prove their impossibility.

title: Conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
importance_reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.
formal:
Does there exist a single total deterministic Turing algorithm which, given any finite presentation with one relator
\[
G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_k\mid r=1\rangle
\]
and two finite words \(u,v\) in those generators and their inverses, decides whether
\[
\exists w\in\{x_1,x_1^{-1},\ldots,x_k,x_k^{-1}\}^*,
\qquad w^{-1}uw=_Gv?
\]
The presentation is part of the input. There is no prescribed time or space bound, but the algorithm must halt correctly on both conjugate and nonconjugate pairs for every such presentation.
question_excerpt: The survey states that the conjugacy problem remains open for one-relator groups, despite the established word algorithm and positive conjugacy results for important subclasses. This card retains its previously selected uniform version, in which the finite presentation and the two words are all inputs to one machine.
definitions:
An input consists of an integer \(k\ge1\) and three explicitly written finite words \(r,u,v\) over the alphabet
\[
\Sigma_k=\{x_i,x_i^{-1}:1\le i\le k\}.
\]
Encode \(k\), word lengths and generator indices in binary with unambiguous boundaries, and encode the sign of each letter by one bit. Every letter occurrence is listed; exponents, circuits or other descriptions do not stand for omitted repetitions. Empty words and words with adjacent inverse pairs are allowed. An invalid encoding or an index outside \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is rejected. The requirement of totality also covers these invalid strings.

The free group \(F_k\) consists of reduced words, with adjacent pairs \(x_ix_i^{-1}\) and \(x_i^{-1}x_i\) cancelled. Its multiplication is concatenation followed by reduction; its identity is the empty word. The inverse of a word reverses its letters and changes each letter to its formal inverse.

Let \(N_r\) be the normal closure of \(r\) in \(F_k\). Explicitly, it consists of products
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{m} a_j r^{\varepsilon_j}a_j^{-1},
\qquad m\ge0,\quad a_j\in F_k,\quad\varepsilon_j\in\{-1,1\},
\]
interpreted as free-group elements; the empty product is included. The presented group is the quotient \(G=F_k/N_r\). Two words \(s,t\) satisfy \(s=_Gt\) exactly when \(st^{-1}\in N_r\). Thus the equation in the target is equality in this quotient, rather than literal string equality or equality only after free reduction. The one relator may reduce to the empty word, in which case the quotient is the free group.

The elements represented by \(u,v\) are conjugate if some finite word \(w\) satisfies the displayed equation. There is no bound on its length, no restriction to a subgroup and no requirement to output it. Every finite one-relator presentation is included: the number of generators and all three word lengths are unbounded, the relator may be a proper power, and no torsion, geometric or residual-finiteness promise is imposed.

Uniform means that the same finite machine receives all these inputs and outputs a bit, with one meaning conjugate and zero meaning nonconjugate. Its code and termination guarantee cannot depend on a separately fixed group. There is no oracle, advice or randomization. Separate decision procedures for each fixed presentation do not suffice unless there is an effective way to obtain and run them from the input presentation. No efficiency requirement is imposed beyond termination.

This is an exact algorithm-existence proposition. A routine that halts only on positive instances is a semidecision procedure, not the requested decision algorithm.
answer_criterion:
Supply a total uniform algorithm and a complete Lean-checked proof of its correctness and termination on every encoded input, with the group equation interpreted exactly as above. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of valid conjugate tuples \((k,r,u,v)\) is undecidable.

A fixed one-relator group with a proved undecidable conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer, but the uniform language could also be shown undecidable without such a fixed-group example. A result for a restricted family, a solution only of word equality, or undecidability of arbitrary systems of equations, subgroup membership or inverse-monoid problems does not settle this target.
context:
A presentation gives generators and equations that may be reused in arbitrarily long products. A single defining equation does not force the resulting group to be finite or simple. The card includes all finite strings describing that equation.

Conjugacy is different from equality even in a free group: \(ab\) and \(ba\) are conjugate because \(a^{-1}(ab)a=ba\). The identity is conjugate only to itself, so conjugacy includes deciding whether a word represents the identity.

Magnus’s word algorithm handles every one-relator group. The survey explains that the structural operations used for word equality do not automatically preserve decidability of conjugacy. Its harder examples in larger presentation classes do not give a one-relator counterexample.

Newman’s classical theorem settles conjugacy for one-relator groups with torsion, and further special classes are also known. Here torsion means that some nonidentity element has finite order. The full target includes groups without that property.

The August 2026 Diophantine theorem proves undecidability of arbitrary systems of equations in certain one-relator groups. It explicitly states that this does not prove conjugacy undecidable, and even notes a studied example whose conjugacy problem is decidable.

The separate August inverse-monoid result changes either the algebraic structure or the decision task. Its group prefix-membership example asks for membership in a specified submonoid, rather than existence of an unrestricted conjugator.
why: One defining relation permits complicated infinite groups while still allowing ordinary word equality to be decided. Conjugacy adds an unrestricted search for a change of representative. Resolving its uniform decidability would locate a basic boundary between effective equality and effective existential questions in finitely presented algebra.
status_note: The checked 2025 survey and August 2026 primary paper retain general one-relator conjugacy as open. The latter explicitly states that its Diophantine undecidability results do not imply conjugacy undecidability. The card keeps the uniform presentation-input question; no solution of that target was found in the bounded later-work check.
progress: 1932: Magnus’s word-equality algorithm supplies a positive result for a simpler decision problem, as recalled in the survey. | 1968: Newman establishes conjugacy decidability in one-relator groups with torsion, as recorded in Theorem 1.6.3 of the survey. | 2025-01-30: The comprehensive survey retains the general conjugacy question and describes positive subclasses and structural obstacles. | 2026-08-03: Diophantine undecidability is proved for one-relator examples, with an explicit statement that conjugacy remains unaffected. | 2026-08-05: Two-generator inverse-monoid word and group prefix-membership undecidability provide related results for different targets.
working_summary: A one-relator group is specified by finitely many generators and a single word required to equal the identity. Two input words are conjugate when an unrestricted finite word transforms one into the other by conjugation inside that group. The question asks for one always-terminating algorithm receiving both the presentation and the two words, with no efficiency bound. Known word algorithms and recent undecidability of more general equation systems do not decide this particular task. A complete Lean-checked solution must verify a uniform decision algorithm or prove that the full input language is undecidable.

title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
importance_reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, for every pair of finite one-relator presentations \[P=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_k\mid r=1\rangle,\qquad Q=\langle y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\mid s=1\rangle,\] where \(k,\ell\ge1\) and \(r,s\) are arbitrary explicitly written words in their respective generators and inverses, halts and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(G_P\cong G_Q\), and outputs \(0\) otherwise? Isomorphism is of abstract groups, with no condition on the images of the displayed generators. There is no running-time bound, promise on the presented groups, or restriction on the number of generators.
question_excerpt: Retains the unrestricted one-relator presentation-isomorphism question recorded in the survey, with arbitrary finite generator counts and abstract group isomorphisms. The empty-relator convention and concrete finite encoding make inputs explicit; they do not impose torsion, geometric or generic promises. No complexity bound is added.
definitions:
For \(k\ge1\), a word is a finite sequence of letters \(x_i^{\epsilon}\), where \(1\le i\le k\) and \(\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}\). The empty word is allowed. The free group \(F_k\) consists of freely reduced words: adjacent inverse letters cancel, multiplication is concatenation followed by cancellation, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses a word and inverts each letter. The given relator need not be freely or cyclically reduced and may be a proper power. Its normal closure is
\[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle=\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{t} w_j r^{\epsilon_j}w_j^{-1}:t\ge0,\ w_j\in F_k,\ \epsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}\right\}.\]
Define \(G_P=F_k/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle\), with two words \(u,v\) representing the same element exactly when \(uv^{-1}\) belongs to this normal closure; define \(G_Q\) in the same way. This specifies the meaning of a single relation \(r=1\) and the group operation on the quotient. A bijection \(\phi:G_P\to G_Q\) is a group isomorphism if \(\phi(gh)=\phi(g)\phi(h)\) for every \(g,h\in G_P\). It need not preserve a chosen generating tuple or lift to an automorphism of an ambient free group. The two presentations can have different numbers of generators, and all finite and infinite groups described by these presentations are included. The empty relator presents \(F_k\); the trivial group is included, for example by \(\langle x\mid x=1\rangle\).

Use the following concrete computable binary input encoding. For \(n\ge0\), let \(b\) be the length of the binary expansion of \(n+1\) with no leading zeroes, and encode \(n\) by \(u(n)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(n+1)\). If \(r\) has \(t\) letters, encode \(P\) by \(u(k)u(t)\) followed by, for each letter in order, one sign bit (\(0\) for \(+1\), \(1\) for \(-1\)) and \(u(i)\) for its generator index. Concatenate the encodings of \(P\) and \(Q\). Require \(k,\ell\ge1\), all indices in range, and no trailing bits. Thus validity is decidable from the finite string. Relators are explicit letter lists, with no compressed-word or binary-power notation in the input. A displayed power in mathematical examples denotes its fully expanded word in this encoding. Empty lists and unused generators are legal.

The machine has a finite description, ordinary read/write work tapes, and no oracle, advice or randomness. It must halt on every valid input pair and give the exact answer; it may be required to halt and output \(0\) on malformed strings without changing the question. There is no imposed time or space bound. One machine must handle all generator counts and relator lengths. No hyperbolicity certificate, torsion assumption, nontrivial-center promise or genericity assumption is supplied, and no explicit isomorphism witness need be printed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the specified isomorphism language is decidable or that it is undecidable. A positive answer supplies one finite algorithm and proves its termination and exact correctness for every valid pair in the stated encoding; all invoked decision subroutines require matching proved guarantees. A negative answer proves that every deterministic machine fails to halt with the correct bit on some valid pair, either through nontermination or an incorrect answer. A proved reduction from an undecidable problem qualifies only if it effectively produces pairs of the specified one-relator presentations and establishes both directions of the answer correspondence. Positive-instance semidecision, finite testing, a result for a proper subclass, or generic-case correctness is insufficient. A runtime lower bound alone is not undecidability. This is an exact yes/no question, without numerical tolerance.
context:
A finite presentation describes an abstract group, which may be infinite. Its displayed generators are names rather than a preferred basis intrinsic to the group. For example, \(\langle a,b\mid ba^{-2}=1\rangle\) and \(\langle x\mid\varepsilon=1\rangle\), with \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, both present the infinite cyclic group. The number of displayed generators and the spelling of the single relation therefore do not determine the isomorphism type.

Isomorphism is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality concerns two elements in one group, conjugacy concerns a particular relation between elements, and isomorphism compares the groups themselves. The single-relator restriction is strong enough for a uniform word algorithm, but the 2025 survey still records the general isomorphism question as unresolved.

An isomorphism between two finitely generated groups has a finite description by the images of the generators, and the inverse has such a description as well. This makes positive isomorphism instances semidecidable for finite presentations. Semidecidability provides no total decision procedure: the target also requires termination with a correct negative answer on every nonisomorphic pair.

Abelianization illustrates the difference between an invariant and a complete classification. The groups \(\langle a,b\mid\varepsilon=1\rangle\) and \(\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b^{-1}=1\rangle\) have the same abelianization \(\mathbb Z^2\), but the first is the nonabelian free group of rank two and the second is abelian. Thus even these elementary one-relator presentations agree on a natural algebraic invariant while representing different groups.

An automorphism of the ambient free group carrying one relator to the other, up to inversion, gives isomorphic quotient groups. Whitehead’s algorithm decides this free-group orbit problem. The converse fails: the Magnus conjecture was disproved, and Brunner exhibited a group with infinitely many pairwise inequivalent one-relator presentations. Abstract isomorphism is therefore a strictly broader comparison than that orbit test.

Dahmani and Guirardel give a uniform decision algorithm for isomorphism between presentations of hyperbolic groups, allowing torsion. Their Corollary 2 applies it to all one-relator groups with nontrivial torsion, because these groups are hyperbolic. This is a complete positive result for that subclass, not a resource-bound conjecture.

The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center. Nevertheless, arbitrary torsion-free one-relator groups are not covered by these results. The one-relator condition by itself does not imply hyperbolicity: the abelian group \(\mathbb Z^2\) already gives an example.

Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain prove strong isomorphism rigidity for an exponentially generic class of one-relator presentations with a fixed generator count. Here genericity refers to the proportion of long reduced relators in specified finite word models. A small exceptional set in that distribution can still contain inputs on which an all-input decision problem is unresolved.

Kapovich’s August 2026 preprint extends generic rigidity to fixed numbers of generators and relators. Theorem B describes polynomial-time recognizable generic classes with finite auxiliary data fixed separately for each parameter pair. Theorem C gives a quadratic-time algorithm comparing one fixed generic presentation with suitable small-cancellation presentations, and a linear-time comparison when both inputs are promised to belong to the stated generic classes. These hypotheses exclude arbitrary one-relator input pairs; the generic-family result does not supply the uniform total algorithm asked for here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 2026 preprint reports undecidability of solving systems of equations with coefficients in specified one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its input consists of equations inside a fixed group, whereas this card compares two group presentations. The theorem does not by itself provide an undecidability reduction for the isomorphism problem.

A positive resolution would establish effective classification of all groups in this concise presentation format, even if the algorithm were extremely slow. A negative resolution would show that abstract group type remains undecidable within a class whose word problem is decidable. Both outcomes concern a computability boundary rather than the practical speed of existing group software.
why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No uniform all-input isomorphism algorithm or undecidability theorem for arbitrary finite one-relator group presentations was found in the bounded primary-source review. The 2026 generic algorithms have explicit restrictions and fixed-parameter qualifications; the August Diophantine undecidability result concerns equations in fixed groups. Neither settles this unrestricted isomorphism question. New preprint proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1970–1976: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture separate abstract group isomorphism from free-group equivalence of relators; the 2025 survey describes the original examples and Brunner’s infinite family. | 1974: Pietrowski proves decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center; the survey records it as Corollary 1.7.3. | 2003–2006: Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain establish generic rigidity for random one-relator groups. | 2010–2011: Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups; their Corollary 2 covers one-relator groups with torsion. | 30 January 2025: The survey retains the unrestricted torsion-free one-relator isomorphism problem as open. | 3 August 2026: A new preprint reports undecidability of the separate Diophantine problem in specified Baumslag–Gersten groups. | 18 August 2026: Kapovich’s preprint reports generic few-relator rigidity and restricted isomorphism algorithms with explicitly stated input hypotheses.
working_summary: A finite one-relator presentation describes a group using finitely many generators and one explicitly written relation. The question asks for one algorithm deciding whether any two such presentations define isomorphic abstract groups, even with different generator counts. The answer must be exact and the algorithm must always terminate, but there is no running-time bound or geometric promise. A complete Lean proof must establish this uniform decision procedure or prove undecidability for the exact input class. Known hyperbolic and center subclasses, generic rigidity algorithms and the 2026 undecidability result for equations in fixed groups do not resolve the all-input comparison.

title: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing
importance_reason: A defining derandomization problem for unrestricted arithmetic circuits, with broad algebraic-algorithm applications and proved consequences for Boolean or arithmetic circuit lower bounds. The general explicit-circuit target is substantially broader than the many restricted circuit classes for which deterministic tests are known.
formal: Is polynomial identity testing for explicitly represented arithmetic circuits over the integers in deterministic polynomial time? More precisely, do a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, on every valid circuit encoding of bit length \(N\), \(A\) decides whether the output is the zero formal polynomial and halts within \(C(N+2)^k\) steps?
definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Each input node is either one of the explicitly listed variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or a signed integer constant given in binary. Each internal gate has two ordered predecessors and computes addition, subtraction or multiplication over \(\mathbb Z\). Intermediate results may be used by several later gates; the graph need not be a formula. A topological list of all nodes, their labels, predecessor indices and the output index is supplied, with the full variable list and all bits of every constant included in the input length \(N\). Repeated use of a variable or predecessor is allowed. Gates compute in the commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and the zero polynomial means that every coefficient is exactly zero. No division, exponentiation, comparison, oracle or approximate-arithmetic gate is present. There is no depth restriction, multilinearity promise or bound on the number of nonzero monomials. No separate polynomial bound on total degree is promised: repeated multiplication can give a degree exponential in the circuit description length. The algorithm has access to the complete graph and labels, not only an oracle for evaluations. Its running time counts bit-level Turing-machine operations, including all work on constants and any integers it computes; unbounded-size integer operations are not free. Correctness is exact on every valid encoding, with no randomness or advice. Malformed encodings are rejected within the same polynomial bound. One fixed machine and one fixed polynomial bound must work for all numbers of variables, circuits, degrees and integer constants.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated bit model. A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm correct for every allowed circuit, including those of exponential degree. A negative answer must exclude every deterministic machine with any fixed polynomial time bound; a lower bound for one procedure does not suffice. Results only for formulas, restricted depth, bounded-read circuits, sparse polynomials or a restricted degree regime do not resolve the full target. An evaluation-only lower bound without the explicit circuit-description promise also does not refute it. Numerical agreement at sampled inputs does not establish a formal identity.
context:
Two very different circuit expressions can represent the same polynomial. For instance, \((x+y)^2-x^2-2xy-y^2\) is zero as a formal polynomial. Identity testing asks for this conclusion without first expanding an expression that may contain exponentially many monomials.

The circuit description is part of the input. Its reuse of intermediate values can compress a large polynomial into a small graph, but the algorithm may inspect that graph. This differs from access only to a polynomial’s values, without any representation-size promise.

Strozecki’s enumeration survey explicitly identifies deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for arithmetic-circuit representations as a major unresolved step. The discussion explains why identity tests arise in procedures that generate the monomials of an implicitly represented polynomial.

The card adopts the standard integer-circuit, bit-complexity version of that direction, as explicitly defined in the 2026 STACS paper. Binary integer constants are included with their encoding cost. The target neither gives free arbitrary field constants nor silently bounds the circuit’s degree.

Randomized polynomial-time identity testing is known with one-sided error: the zero polynomial is always recognized as zero, while a nonzero polynomial is rejected with a fixed probability bounded away from zero. The requested change is a fully deterministic, all-input guarantee in polynomial time.

Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove that a polynomial-time deterministic identity test would force a major lower bound for Boolean circuits or for arithmetic circuits computing the permanent. This implication explains why removing randomness here is consequential. It does not make the task identical to proving any one chosen arithmetic lower bound.

Černý and Seppelt’s 2026 work shows that the same general identity-testing problem governs certain equivalence questions for graphs and weighted tree automata. Their reductions retain identity testing as a derandomization condition; they do not supply the requested deterministic test.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives deterministic identity tests for special expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} f_i^d\), where the \(f_i\) are sparse low-degree polynomials and the common power \(d\) is sufficiently large relative to \(r\). The input structure and parameter conditions are essential, and its polynomial bounds in those degree parameters do not cover all circuits in time polynomial in their bit length.
why: Polynomial identity testing is a central concrete derandomization problem: a polynomial may be identically zero because of cancellations invisible in the circuit syntax. A deterministic polynomial-time test would affect symbolic computation and numerous algebraic algorithms, and is known to imply major circuit lower bounds. This places the question at the intersection of efficient verification of algebraic identities and fundamental complexity limitations.

The 2026 primary papers retain the general PIT question and supply reductions or restricted-model progress, rather than a general deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. No matching proof or refutation was found in the bounded search; cited proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: An arithmetic circuit may compute the zero polynomial even when cancellation is difficult to see from its graph. The question asks for an exact deterministic polynomial-time test given the entire circuit over binary-encoded integer constants. Circuits may reuse intermediate results, have arbitrary depth and compute polynomials of exponential degree. Randomized polynomial-time tests are known, while removing their randomness would have major circuit lower-bound consequences. Recent deterministic results for restricted circuit shapes do not provide the requested algorithm for all explicit circuits.

title: Bit complexity of integer multiplication
importance_reason: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\), the optimal worst-case running time for exactly multiplying two n-bit nonnegative binary integers by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine. The target is an attainable asymptotic upper bound with a matching lower bound for every correct machine in this model.
definitions: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate \(g(n)>0\) means some correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=O(g(n))\), while every correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=\Omega (g(n))\); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).
answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate \(g(n)\) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in \(O(g(n))\) worst-case time and an \(\Omega (g(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.
context:
For example, \(11_{2}\) multiplied by \(11_{2}\) is \(1001_{2}\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes \(O(n \log  n)\) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.
why: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted multitape lower bound open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching bound or faster general algorithm; the August 2026 OBDD result concerns a different model.
progress: 2021: An \(O(n \log  n)\) deterministic multitape upper bound is published. It does not include a matching lower bound. | 2025-03: A conjectured optimal matrix-transposition lower bound is shown to imply the corresponding multiplication lower bound. | 2026-08: New OBDD-width bounds concern a restricted branching-program model and do not close the multitape time gap.
working_summary: What is the optimal worst-case bit complexity of multiplying two n-bit integers? The model charges individual steps of a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine. An \(O(n \log  n)\) algorithm is known, but only a linear general lower bound is established. A 2025 theorem connects the conjectured matching lower bound to the unresolved cost of matrix transposition. Bounds for restricted branching programs do not determine the optimal cost in this model.

title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
importance_reason: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.
formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
question_excerpt: The retained card asks the general cubic concise asymptotic-rank equality over C, as discussed by Christandl–Hoeberechts–Nieuwboer–Vrana–Zuiddam and Alman–Li–Pratt. Some sources, including Lee’s Conjecture 1, state a version restricted to tight concise tensors. That additional hypothesis has not been silently added to the selected target.
definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.
context:
A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.
why: The conjecture asks whether every bilinear operation attains, in the exponential growth rate of jointly processed copies, the elementary lower bound already visible from matrices. A positive answer would force matrix multiplication exponent two and impose a simple common asymptotic law on all concise tensors. A negative answer would exhibit an obstruction that survives arbitrarily many grouped copies, beyond the familiar difficulty of decomposing a single tensor.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The general cubic concise equality over C remains open in the inspected primary sources. The June structural characterization and April edge-spectrum results do not prove it. The checked September exact-rank, border-rank and stabilizer-dimension theorems address different guarantees, and the January numerical census is not a universal proof. This is a bounded source review, not a certification that no resolution exists.

working_summary: A three-factor tensor can be decomposed into elementary products, and its rank is the least number of those products. The question asks whether every concise complex tensor of equal factor dimension has asymptotic rank exactly that dimension when corresponding factors of many copies are grouped. The dimension and tensor stay fixed during the limit, and no tightness, symmetry, computability or uniform convergence promise is imposed. A complete Lean proof must establish the equality for all such tensors or a counterexample whose grouped powers all require a strictly larger exponential base. The inspected 2026 structural, numerical, finite-rank and symmetry results do not settle this general asymptotic equality.

title: Polynomial-time finite-group isomorphism in the Cayley-table model
importance_reason: The fundamental outstanding algorithmic isomorphism problem for finite algebraic structures in explicit representation.
formal:
Is isomorphism of finite groups given by their complete multiplication tables decidable in deterministic polynomial time?

Precisely, do there exist one uniform deterministic machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, on every binary input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps and outputs YES exactly when the input encodes two finite groups \(G,H\) and there is a bijection \(\varphi:G\to H\) satisfying
\[
\forall x,y\in G,\qquad
\varphi(x\cdot_G y)=\varphi(x)\cdot_H\varphi(y)?
\]
The constants and program are independent of the orders and structure of both groups.
question_excerpt: The FSTTCS 2024 introduction explicitly identifies whether Group Isomorphism belongs to P as an open question in the multiplication-table representation.
definitions:
A table of order \(n\ge1\) is a function \(T:[n]\times[n]\to[n]\), given by listing every one of its \(n^2\) entries. It defines a group precisely when the following three conditions hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall x,y,z\in[n],\quad T(T(x,y),z)=T(x,T(y,z));\\
&\exists e\in[n]\ \forall x\in[n],\quad T(e,x)=x=T(x,e);\\
&\forall x\in[n]\ \exists y\in[n],\quad T(x,y)=e=T(y,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The identity \(e\) in the inverse condition is the same identity supplied by the second condition. All entries already belong to \([n]\), so closure is part of the table definition. Commutativity is not required. A group of order one is allowed; an empty group is not.

The input contains tables \(T_G\) and \(T_H\) of orders \(n\) and \(m\), respectively. If \(n\ne m\), they cannot be isomorphic. When \(n=m\), an isomorphism uses one bijection on elements in all three positions of the multiplication equation. Independent permutations of table rows, columns and entries are not the definition of the predicate. The labels \(1,\ldots,n\) have no mathematical significance, and the identity need not have label one.

Encode a table by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) entries in row-major order, each in exactly \(\ell_n=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, using ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. Each entry must be in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Concatenate exactly two such encodings, with no trailing bits. The input bit length is
\[
L=n+m+2+n^2\ell_n+m^2\ell_m.
\]
Malformed encodings, entries outside the indicated range and tables failing any group axiom are NO instances. Group axioms can be checked in polynomial time, so this total-language convention does not add a new algorithmic obstacle to the promised-group version.

The output is only the decision bit. An explicit isomorphism, a canonical table and generators of an automorphism group are not required. There is no restriction to abelian, solvable, nilpotent or prime-power-order groups, and no distinguished subgroups, generators or decompositions are supplied.

The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite tape alphabets. Its input tape is read-only; work tapes begin blank. Each transition accesses only the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Parsing, checking the group axioms, accessing table entries, computing auxiliary data and returning the answer all count. There is no randomness, advice, oracle or free preprocessing.

Polynomial time is measured in the full explicit bit length \(L\). For equal-order groups this is polynomially equivalent to polynomial time in \(n\), since the table already has \(n^2\) entries. It is not polynomial time in \(\log n\), the length needed merely to name the group order. An input consisting only of generators, a presentation, matrices, permutations or oracle access to multiplication would define a different representation model.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of \(A,C,c\), proving exact correctness and the polynomial worst-case bound on all encoded pairs and invalid strings; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such deterministic polynomial-time decider exists. A lower bound for bounded-depth circuits or a restricted algorithmic method is not a lower bound for this entire machine class. An algorithm for only a proper family of groups, an average-case guarantee, a quasipolynomial bound or an unverified claimed general algorithm does not settle the target.
context:
The inherited source studies dynamic membership and isomorphism for abelian groups, but its introduction separately states the unrestricted static P-membership question. The card keeps that general question.

The standard general upper bound is \(n^{O(\log n)}\) for groups of order \(n\). The August 2026 paper explicitly distinguishes improvements in circuit depth from an improvement to polynomial sequential time. Its lower bound also concerns a restricted circuit depth.

The March 2026 preprint gives polynomial-time tests for several families of extensions of abelian groups, including abelian-by-cyclic groups. An abelian-by-cyclic group has an abelian normal subgroup whose quotient group is cyclic. This is a proper structural promise, absent from the target.

The corrected September 2026 result requires solvable groups with abelian Sylow subgroups. The solvability restriction is explicit in version 2; the broader wording of the first version is not the current theorem. The restricted family does not contain all finite groups.

A separate March 2026 preprint claims polynomial-time algorithms for broader isomorphism problems and explicitly draws a polynomial-time group-isomorphism consequence. Its proof was not verified or refuted in this review. This unresolved claim is the reason for uncertain status, while the checked later specialist literature continues to state the general problem as open.
why: Group isomorphism asks whether two complete finite algebraic structures differ only in their element names. Even with every multiplication available explicitly, a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary groups has resisted decades of work. Resolving it would clarify both the complexity of finite algebra and a central algebraic special case of graph isomorphism.

A separate March 2026 preprint explicitly claims a polynomial-time solution through broader matrix and quasigroup isomorphism algorithms; this review did not verify or refute that proof. The card is therefore active with uncertain resolution status. The special-class algorithms and restricted-depth circuit bounds do not by themselves settle the target.

working_summary: Two finite groups are isomorphic when one bijection of their elements preserves every product. The input supplies both complete multiplication tables, and the target is deterministic polynomial-time decision in their explicit bit length. The algorithm must cover all finite groups without additional structural information. Recent algorithms for restricted families and lower bounds for shallow circuits do not settle this general target. A separate claimed general solution remains unverified in this review, so the card stays active with uncertain resolution status.

title: Explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank
importance_reason: A central explicit lower-bound challenge for tensor rank and arithmetic computation: the gap between generic quadratic rank and explicit linear lower bounds persists even for three-way tensors and relates directly to unrestricted arithmetic circuit barriers.
formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) it outputs all entries of a rational tensor \(T_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) within \(K(n+1)^a\) bit operations, and \[\forall B\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)\ge Bn?\] Here rank is ordinary tensor rank over the complex numbers. Thus the required ratio \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)/n\) tends to infinity, with no prescribed rate.
definitions:
A tensor \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) is the array \((T_{ijk})_{1\le i,j,k\le n}\), regarded as an element of \(\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\) through the usual inclusion of the rationals into the complex numbers. Its ordinary rank is the smallest integer \(r\ge0\) for which there are vectors \(u^{(s)},v^{(s)},w^{(s)}\in\mathbb C^n\), for \(1\le s\le r\), satisfying
\[
T_{ijk}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u^{(s)}_i\,v^{(s)}_j\,w^{(s)}_k
\quad\text{for every }1\le i,j,k\le n.
\]
An empty sum is the zero tensor. The factors in a rank decomposition may be arbitrary complex vectors, although the constructed tensor entries are rational. No symmetry is required. The target is not matrix rank of an array rearrangement, slice rank, border rank, or an asymptotic tensor-power rank.

The machine outputs the \(n^3\) entries in lexicographic order of \((i,j,k)\). Each entry is an explicitly written signed binary integer numerator and positive binary integer denominator, with delimiters. All bits are charged, so their total length and each individual entry's bit length are polynomially bounded in \(n\). A symbolic power, root-of-unity description, unevaluated arithmetic expression or arbitrary real constant is not a rational-entry output under this convention. All input reading, integer arithmetic, preprocessing and output writing count. The finite program and \(K,a\) are independent of \(n\); there is no advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing.

The algorithm is required on every positive integer dimension, and the rank guarantee holds for all sufficiently large dimensions for each \(B\). The integer threshold \(N\) may depend on \(B\) and the fixed family; it is not required to be computed. No rank decomposition, rank value or lower-bound certificate is an output requirement for \(A\); the rank-growth guarantee must instead be established by the submitted proof. Explicitness here means polynomial time in the dimension to write the whole tensor, not a separate polylogarithmic-time entry-query requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of such a finite construction algorithm, its uniform polynomial bit-cost bound and the entire eventual superlinear rank guarantee, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence proof without the construction cost, a fixed constant multiple of the dimension, growth only along an unspecified subsequence, or a conditional lower bound alone does not meet this target. Any growth rate tending to infinity in the displayed normalized rank suffices; a fixed positive power improvement is not required.
context:
Open Problem 15 asks for explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank after explaining their connection to arithmetic circuits. The survey writes the ground field generically and leaves representation details implicit. This card selects the characteristic-zero branch with rationally encoded entries and rank over the complex numbers; it does not claim equivalence to every possible field or algebraic-number encoding.

The full-output polynomial-time convention follows the explicitness discussion in Definition 1.1 of Landsberg and Michałek. Their construction uses integer coordinates, and their border-rank lower bound grows linearly with the dimension. Such a result is meaningful progress but does not make the rank-to-dimension ratio tend to infinity.

The July 2026 sumset-expansion paper explicitly distinguishes efficiently constructible tensor entries from short algebraic descriptions. Its high-border-rank tensors use number-field coordinates and are described as semi-explicit; they do not constitute the rational bit-output construction fixed here. Its Remark 5 still states the explicit superlinear-rank challenge.

The target asks for ordinary rank. A superlinear lower bound on border rank would be sufficient, but proving that stronger property is not required. Conversely, improved linear bounds for either notion do not settle the superlinear target.
why: Tensor rank measures the number of independent bilinear products needed to express a computation. Explicit superlinear-rank families would turn generic hardness into concrete examples and yield lower bounds for the corresponding constant-degree arithmetic computations.

working_summary: A three-way tensor is a cubic array, and its ordinary rank is the fewest rank-one arrays whose sum equals it. The selected branch asks for rational entries written by one deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in the dimension. Rank is measured over the complex numbers, and its ratio to the side length must tend to infinity. The algorithm must produce every dimension without advice, symbolic number-field entries or uncharged output bits. Known explicit linear border-rank bounds and recent semi-explicit high-rank constructions do not meet this superlinear rational-output target.

title: Derandomizing black-box depth-four PIT
importance_reason: A central derandomization target in algebraic complexity. Depth four already captures a decisive barrier connected by depth reduction to general arithmetic identity testing, while black-box uniformity requires explicit evaluation sets rather than access to circuit syntax. Recent progress on restricted depth-four families leaves the unrestricted challenge substantial.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic uniform polynomial-time construction of hitting sets for all size-\(s\), \(n\)-variable \(\Sigma\Pi\Sigma\Pi\) arithmetic circuits, in the field-operation model specified below? Precisely, one algorithm and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\) must work for every \(n,s\ge1\), every working field \(K\), and every supplied list \(T\) of \(2s^2+1\) distinct elements of \(K\). In at most \(C(n+s+1)^b\) operations it must output a list \(H\subseteq K^n\) such that every nonzero formal polynomial computed by any allowed circuit over \(K\) has a nonzero evaluation at some point of \(H\). The algorithm receives no circuit description, coefficients, or evaluation oracle for a particular polynomial.
definitions: An allowed circuit is a finite directed acyclic arithmetic circuit with one output, four alternating layers of unbounded-fan-in arithmetic gates, and input leaves labeled by variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or arbitrary constants of \(K\). From output to inputs the operations are sum, product, sum, product. Fan-in-one gates may pad smaller depth. Gates and subexpressions may be shared; the size is the total number of wires, including wires from input leaves and with repeated uses counted separately. There are at most \(s\) wires. Addition and multiplication are the only polynomial operations; division gates, exponentiation gates with compressed exponents, and tests inside the hidden circuit are excluded. In expression form the output is a sum of products of sparse polynomials, with no fixed bound on the top fan-in or on the bottom monomial degrees beyond the wire budget. The total degree is at most \(s^2\), since each bottom product has degree at most \(s\) and each upper product has at most \(s\) factors. Homogeneity, multilinearity, and bounded variable occurrence are not assumed. A nonzero polynomial means one with at least one nonzero coefficient, not merely a function that is nonzero somewhere on the original base field. The construction uses one finite program with ordinary discrete control and registers holding opaque elements of \(K\). A field addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a tested nonzero element, equality test, copy, or access to a supplied field element costs one operation; discrete control is charged by its ordinary bit operations. The only initial field values are zero, one and the entries of \(T\). Field representations carry no readable extra advice. The constants \(C,b\) are independent of characteristic, field, \(T,n,s\) and all circuit coefficients. The cost includes writing every coordinate of every output point; existence of a small set without an efficient construction does not qualify. No randomness, parameter-dependent advice, or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. The input list \(T\) makes the source’s sufficiently-large-field convention explicit. For a smaller base field \(F\), evaluations may instead take place in a supplied extension \(K\supseteq F\) with such a list; the circuit is then viewed over \(K\). Constructing or encoding that extension is outside this field-operation target. This is not a claim about bit complexity over arbitrary field presentations or an algorithm confined to evaluations inside a too-small field.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the uniform hitting-set construction and its polynomial resource bound, or prove that no such construction exists in the stated model. A positive proof must handle every allowed coefficient assignment, every working field with the supplied distinct elements, and every size and variable count. It must establish that evaluating on all of \(H\) distinguishes the zero polynomial from every nonzero polynomial in the class. A negative proof must rule out every finite uniform algorithm and polynomial bound; failure of one candidate hitting set is insufficient. A white-box algorithm, a nonconstructive existence proof, a construction with superpolynomial running time, or a construction restricted to bounded top fan-in or bottom degree does not meet this target.
context:
Open Problem 18 explicitly asks to derandomize black-box depth-four PIT. Definition 1.1 counts wires and permits unbounded fan-in at bounded depth; Remark 1.1 uses arbitrary fields by default. Section 4 permits extension-field evaluations, while Section 4.1 defines hitting sets. These conventions are made explicit in the field-operation target here.

Theorem 4.9, attributed to Agrawal and Vinay, relates polynomial-time explicit hitting sets for depth-four circuits to quasipolynomial-size explicit hitting sets for general arithmetic circuits. This is a stated consequence of solving the restricted-depth target; the card does not add a general-circuit result to the required answer.

Dutta, Dwivedi and Saxena’s 2021 Theorem 2 gives quasipolynomial-time black-box testing for bounded-top-fan-in depth-four circuits with either sums of univariates or bounded-degree bottom polynomials. Their polynomial-time theorem is white-box and for the sums-of-univariates subclass.

Garg, Oliveira, Sengupta, Shalmon and Shpilka’s 2026 Corollary 1.4 gives polynomial-time black-box PIT in characteristic zero when top fan-in is fixed and bottom degree is at most two. Its polynomial dependence is for each fixed top fan-in; it is not a polynomial-time guarantee uniform in unrestricted fan-in.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives explicit hitting sets for sums of \(r\) powers of sparse polynomials when the common power \(d\) satisfies \(d>r^2\), over characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic. Upper product gates in the present card may multiply unrelated factors, so the powering result covers a different restricted family.
why: Identity testing asks whether a compact arithmetic computation represents the zero polynomial. A uniform collection of evaluations would remove randomness without inspecting the computation itself. The depth-four case is especially consequential because of its established relationship to much more general arithmetic circuits, and its unrestricted fan-ins distinguish it from several recent positive results.
status_note: The unrestricted problem is posed in the 2010 survey. The checked 2021 and 2026 primary results give restricted-family algorithms and do not cover the target’s unrestricted fan-ins and arbitrary working fields. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution. This records the scope of sources checked, not an independent certification of every later proof.

working_summary: The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of evaluation points that detect every nonzero polynomial computed by a size-bounded depth-four arithmetic circuit. The same generated set must work for every circuit of the given size without seeing its coefficients or gates. title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
importance_reason: Tests whether the central FFT upper bound is inherently necessary in unrestricted arithmetic computation.
formal: Let \(S(n)\) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. Do constants \(c>0\) and N exist such that \(S(n)\ge c n \log _{2}n\) for every power of two \(n\ge N\), with no bound on the magnitudes of the constants used in the program?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.
context:
For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.
