working_summary: Must the discrete Fourier transform take order n log n exact arithmetic operations when constants are unrestricted? The target covers every sufficiently large power-of-two input length and all straight-line programs in the stated model. The FFT achieves this cost by sharing intermediate computations. Known matching lower bounds impose coefficient, gate, storage or conditioning restrictions. Normalization, bit precision and quantum state transformations require care because their computational models differ.

title: Uniform exact permanent circuits below base two
importance_reason: A canonical exponential-time algebraic computation barrier dating to Ryser's formula.
formal:
Does there exist a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and one deterministic circuit generator \(G\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(G(1^{n})\) outputs a division-free rational arithmetic circuit \(\mathcal C_{n}\) with at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) nodes, within at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) Turing-machine steps, and
\[\forall K\text{ of characteristic zero}\ \forall A\in K^{n\times n},\qquad \mathcal C_{n}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
Here \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and every rational circuit constant is interpreted through the canonical embedding \(\mathbb Q\to K\). This fixes the uniform rational-circuit version of the saved characteristic-zero arithmetic-operation question.
definitions:
A field \(K\) has characteristic zero when the sum of any positive number of copies of its multiplicative identity is nonzero; this gives a unique injective field homomorphism \(\mathbb Q\to K\). The domain contains every square matrix over every such field, including rational, real and complex matrices, with no sign, magnitude, sparsity, rank, symmetry or integrality promise. The permanent is the unsigned permutation sum above; it is not the determinant. All evaluations must be exact.

An arithmetic circuit is a finite list of nodes in topological order, with the last node the output. Each node is either an input variable \(x_{i,j}\) with \(0\le i,j<n\), a rational constant, or a binary \(+\), \(-\), or \(\times\) gate whose two ordered parent indices refer to earlier nodes. Repeated use of the same parent is allowed, so shared intermediate values and squaring are permitted. Unused nodes may be omitted. The size counts all nodes, including constants and variable nodes. On a matrix \(A\), an input node evaluates to its entry, constants are embedded in \(K\), and internal gates perform the indicated field operations. Each internal gate costs one arithmetic operation, independently of the sizes of field elements; a rational constant is a permitted circuit input. There is no division by an input-dependent value, branching on an input entry, rounding, bit extraction, transcendental gate, oracle gate, or limit computation. Subtraction is equivalently addition using the constant \(-1\), so it does not introduce an extra algebraic operation type beyond the source circuit convention.

The generator is one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine over fixed finite alphabets, given only \(1^{n}\). It receives neither matrix entries nor a description of the field. Its program and clock constants are fixed independently of \(n\). For definiteness, for a nonnegative integer \(t\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion with \(b(0)=0\), and encode \(t\) by \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). The output begins with the encoded positive node count. Each node then has a three-bit tag: 000 for a variable followed by \(E(i)E(j)\); 001 for a constant followed by a sign bit and \(E(u)E(v)\), representing \((-1)^{s}u/v\), with \(u\ge0,v\ge1\) in lowest terms and zero having sign zero; 010, 011 or 100 for addition, subtraction or multiplication followed by the two encoded parent indices. Indices start at zero, and the output must be a well-formed list with no trailing bits. Every generator transition, including writing every constant and index bit, is charged. Thus a separate unbounded search or arbitrary nonuniform circuit choice is not hidden outside the construction bound.

Circuit generation and field evaluation are different costs: the first is bounded binary computation on the dimension, while the second counts exact field operations on abstract entries. There is no claim of a bit-time bound independent of entry length when evaluating on encoded integers or rationals. The same generated rational polynomial must work in all characteristic-zero fields; no field-dependent or noncomputable constants are allowed. This is a specified uniform circuit model, not an assertion that all branching arithmetic algorithms or all field-specific circuit models are equivalent to it. The fixed base saving is uniform in dimension. Polynomial prefactors may be absorbed by a smaller positive base saving, but \(2^{n-o(n)}\) alone does not meet the target. This is an exact complexity-existence question, so absolute numerical tolerance does not apply.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite generator, rational \(\varepsilon\), integer \(C\), valid output circuits and their two bounds for every dimension, and prove their exact evaluation identity for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field. A polynomial identity proof over \(\mathbb Q\), together with its transfer under the canonical field embedding, can establish the required universal identity. A negative answer must exclude every permitted generator and every fixed positive base saving, rather than one construction, bounded circuit depth or coefficient pattern. It need not be a single finite counterexample matrix. A conditional implication is only conditional unless its hypotheses are also proved. Approximate permanent values, algorithms only for bounded integer entries or finite rings, a sublinear saving in the exponent, and small circuits with no generator meeting the bound do not suffice. A negative result for this precise circuit model is not automatically a lower bound for every stronger arithmetic model.
context:
Ryser’s classical upper bound uses \(O(n2^{n})\) field operations to compute the permanent. A fixed improvement from exponential base two would change the scale of exact algebraic counting, while still allowing exponential running time. Exact #P-completeness on zero–one integer matrices explains the absence of an expected polynomial-time counting algorithm, but it does not rule out a fixed exponential-base improvement in this arithmetic model.

For a \(2\times2\) matrix with rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the permanent is \(ad+bc\), whereas the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Removing alternating signs changes the algebraic complexity substantially. On nonnegative entries the permanent also counts weighted bipartite perfect matchings, but this card allows every field entry and asks for exact evaluation. The randomized or deterministic relative approximations in the neighboring cards do not give this circuit family.

The proposal cited the uniform-circuit results of Björklund, Kaski, Koana and Nederlof. Their Section 2.2 uses division-free arithmetic circuits, and Theorem 1.3 bounds both construction time and circuit size. This card makes the previously unstated coefficient and uniformity conventions concrete by choosing a finite generator of rational circuits that works throughout characteristic zero. This portable rational model and the fixed exponential-base target are explicit editorial choices; they are not presented as identical to every possible reading of Knuth’s broader arithmetic-operation question quoted in that source.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves that a sufficiently low rank growth rate for a sequence of balanced tripartitioning tensors yields a uniform permanent circuit construction with a fixed exponential improvement. It relates the needed rank bounds to Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture. A tensor rank here is the least number of products of three linear forms needed to express the associated trilinear form. These are conditional upper bounds with a specified underlying field; the paper does not establish the required rank hypothesis unconditionally or identify every coefficient model. Its result is relevant evidence about the barrier, not a completed positive answer.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.

This card asks whether exact division-free rational circuits can beat exponential base two while being generated uniformly within the same exponential bound. The generated polynomial must work for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field, with bit costs for circuit construction separated from field-operation costs for evaluation. Checked recent results give conditional circuit improvements, finite-ring algorithms, bounded-entry bit-time savings or lower bounds for restricted formula classes. A complete Lean proof must establish the specified uniform circuit family with a fixed positive base saving or rule out every family meeting these conventions.

title: NP-hardness of PosSLP
importance_reason: PosSLP is a central bridge between exact arithmetic computation and discrete complexity, yet no general NP-hardness result is established in the checked literature. An unconditional reduction would materially clarify the computational strength of succinct integer sign testing and the interpretation of many PosSLP-hard numerical tasks.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{PosSLP}\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Concretely, does there exist one deterministic Turing-computable map \(g\) and constants \(C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) such that \(g\) runs in time at most \(C(N+1)^d\) on every input of bit length \(N\), outputs a valid integer straight-line program, and for every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\), \[F\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{value}(g(F))>0?\] The reduction must be unconditionally correct on all inputs, with no algebraic conjecture, randomness, oracle or advice. Malformed input encodings are treated as no-instances and must also map to nonpositive outputs.
question_excerpt: And finally, can we prove unconditional hardness results for PosSLP?
definitions: An integer straight-line program consists of an implicit initial value \(b_0=1\) and a finite sequence of \(m\ge0\) instructions. Instruction \(i\), for \(1\le i\le m\), is a triple \((j_i,k_i,\circ_i)\), where \(0\le j_i,k_i<i\) and \(\circ_i\in\{+,-,\times\}\); it defines \(b_i=b_{j_i}\circ_i b_{k_i}\). The output value is the exact integer \(b_m\), with output one when \(m=0\). Values may be negative or zero, and previous values may be reused arbitrarily. The program contains no input variables, divisions, roots, sign tests, branches, loops, separately supplied integer constants or compressed repetition instructions. The program is encoded by a self-delimited binary encoding of \(m\), followed in order by binary predecessor indices and an operation symbol for each instruction. All delimiters use a fixed finite alphabet; standard binary encodings of that alphabet are equivalent within constant factors. The PosSLP language accepts exactly valid encodings with positive output, and rejects valid zero or negative outputs and malformed programs. There is no promise on the sign or magnitude. A 3-CNF input is an explicit finite list of clauses, each containing at most three signed positive binary variable indices, with delimiters; repeated occurrences are allowed. Satisfiability means that some Boolean assignment to all occurring variables makes at least one literal in every clause true. An empty clause is false, and a conjunction with no clauses is true. The source input size \(N\) is its full encoded bit length. The reduction is one finite deterministic program on ordinary finite-alphabet Turing tapes; all reading, writing and index manipulation are charged by ordinary bit steps. Its time bound includes writing the entire straight-line program. It need not output the exponentially long binary expansion of the integer represented by that program. A many-one reduction makes one output instance with the displayed exact equivalence; it is not an adaptive oracle computation or a randomized transformation. Since 3-SAT is NP-complete under these reductions, this specific reduction is equivalent to NP-hardness, meaning that every language accepted by a polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machine has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to PosSLP.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must specify one reduction and prove its polynomial bit complexity, output validity and exact preservation of both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. It must discharge every assumption needed for correctness. A negative answer must rule out all reductions of this form; failure of one construction does not suffice. NP-hardness is a relationship between decision problems and by itself does not establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), membership in NP, or NP-completeness of PosSLP. A conditional implication about randomized algorithms, an oracle reduction with no conversion to many-one form, or hardness for a polynomial-positivity variant does not meet this specified target.
context:
The imported FSTTCS 2024 conclusion asks broadly for unconditional hardness results for PosSLP. To make that direction a single reviewable target, this card selects the concrete NP-hardness question explicitly posed in Bürgisser and Jindal’s earlier SODA 2024 conclusion, and fixes deterministic many-one reductions. It does not equate every possible hardness advance in the source direction with this particular target.

Bürgisser and Jindal show that a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for PosSLP would yield randomized polynomial-time algorithms for all NP languages, assuming an unproved constructive univariate-radical conjecture. This is a conditional complexity consequence and does not itself provide the unconditional deterministic reduction asked for here.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal prove unconditional coNP-hardness for a variant whose input represents a univariate polynomial and whose question is positivity at every real point. The quantification over real points changes the problem from testing the sign of one fixed integer. Their conclusion retains unconditional hardness of PosSLP as an open direction.

Miltzow’s March 2026 introduction to real computation again defines PosSLP by constant-one integer straight-line programs and describes the known NP-hardness results as conditional on assumptions that are far from resolved. Its informal discussion is used as a later status check; the complete input and reduction conventions here are stated independently.
why: A short sequence of elementary integer operations can represent numbers whose binary expansions are enormous. PosSLP isolates the task of deciding the sign of such a number. Its connections to numerical computation make a conventional hardness classification consequential well beyond the particular instruction format.
status_note: The checked 2024 primary papers leave unconditional PosSLP hardness open, and Miltzow’s March 2026 discussion still describes the NP-hardness evidence as conditional. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the specified deterministic many-one NP-hardness target. The source’s broader hardness direction is preserved separately and is not claimed equivalent to this concrete specialization.

working_summary: The target is unconditional NP-hardness of deciding whether a succinctly represented integer is positive. The integer is produced by a straight-line program starting from one and using only addition, subtraction and multiplication. The required reduction must deterministically convert each 3-SAT instance to one such program in polynomial bit time. Known conditional consequences for randomized algorithms and unconditional hardness of polynomial variants do not supply this reduction. A complete answer would clarify the discrete complexity of exact sign testing without also requiring a proof that P and NP differ.

title: Permanent lower bounds from black-box identity testing
importance_reason: A central unresolved strengthening of algebraic hardness-versus-randomness: replace hardness for less explicit polynomial families or a Boolean/arithmetic disjunction by nonuniform permanent hardness in the same circuit model. The source survey poses it explicitly, and an independent 2019 survey restates the general-circuit black-box instance; later uniform equivalences demonstrate continued relevance without settling this conclusion. The score is a new individual editorial assessment, replacing the unassessed midpoint, not a numerical theorem about importance.
formal:
Does the following implication hold over the rational field \(\mathbb Q\)?
\[
\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}.
\]
The premise \(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\) says that there are a single deterministic algorithm \(G\) and positive integers \(A,a\) such that, for every \(n,d,s\ge1\), on unary input \((1^{n},1^{d},1^{s})\), algorithm \(G\) outputs a finite list \(H_{n,d,s}\) of points in \(\mathbb Q^{n}\) within \(A(n+d+s)^{a}\) bit operations, with the property
\[
\forall f\in\mathbb Q[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}],\quad
\bigl(f\ne0\ \land\ \deg f\le d\ \land\ L_{\mathbb Q}(f)\le s\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\
\exists h\in H_{n,d,s},\quad f(h)\ne0.
\]
Here \(L_{\mathbb Q}(f)\) is the minimum number of edges in a division-free arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb Q\) computing \(f\), in the model below; rational constants of arbitrary bit length are allowed in those circuits.

The conclusion \(\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\) says that the permanent polynomial family has no polynomial-size circuits in that same algebraic model. Explicitly, with
\[
\operatorname{Perm}_{m}(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}x_{i,\pi(i)},
\]
the conclusion is
\[
\forall B,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall m_{0}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\exists m\ge m_{0},\qquad
L_{\mathbb Q}(\operatorname{Perm}_{m})>Bm^{b}.
\]
Prove this implication or its logical negation. The source asks a more general question about circuit classes; this card selects its explicitly published general-circuit black-box instance and fixes the rational field and bit-cost convention as disclosed below.
definitions:
A circuit has a finite directed acyclic graph, a single designated output gate, and commuting variables. Each input gate is labeled by one of the allowed variables or by an arbitrary rational number. Each other gate has two ordered incoming edge slots and is labeled by addition or multiplication. Both slots may refer to the same predecessor, and edges count with multiplicity. Values may be reused at arbitrarily many gates. Only gates lying on a path to the output need be retained. The polynomial at an input gate is its label; the other gates compute the sum or product of their predecessors. Equality is equality of formal polynomials, not agreement on a selected finite set. Division gates, tests, branching and approximation are not allowed. A negative rational constant is allowed, so subtraction needs no extra primitive. The algebraic size is the number of edges, independently of the bit lengths of rational labels. The minimum defining \(L_{\mathbb Q}\) is over all such circuits, with no uniformity requirement.

For an \(n\)-variable polynomial, the circuit may use any subset of \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\). Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient, with the zero polynomial assigned degree zero for this statement. The bound \(d\) applies to the polynomial at the output; no syntactic-degree bound or bound on intermediate degrees is imposed. The parameter \(s\) is an algebraic edge bound, not a bit-length bound on a circuit encoding. Thus the hitting-set requirement covers circuits with arbitrary rational constants, including constants whose binary encodings are longer than \(s\). A circuit is not supplied to \(G\): the output list depends only on \(n,d,s\), and must work simultaneously for every polynomial satisfying the displayed conditions. Repeated points in the list are harmless.

To fix the bit model, \(G\) is an ordinary deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, a read-only input tape and an output tape. One transition reads or writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The input word is \(1^{n}\#1^{d}\#1^{s}\). All transitions, integer and rational arithmetic, memory access and output writing are charged; there are no random bits, advice, oracles or uncharged preprocessing. A fixed finite alphabet changes the bit cost only by a constant factor.

Each rational coordinate in the output is represented uniquely by a sign followed by the binary magnitude of its numerator, a slash, and its positive binary denominator. Numerator and denominator are coprime, there are no leading zeros, and zero is represented as \(+0/1\). Coordinates within a point are separated by commas, and points by semicolons, with no trailing separators; the empty word denotes the empty list. Every point must contain exactly \(n\) coordinates. The output is the explicit list, not a circuit or an oracle for its entries. The running-time bound therefore also bounds its total encoding length, the number of points and their coordinate bit lengths by a fixed polynomial in \(n+d+s\). The machine must halt and satisfy that bound on every valid unary input; no promise about other inputs is needed.

The hitting property is the precise black-box testing premise used here. It asserts an efficiently generated universal set of evaluation points. It does not grant a procedure that can inspect the circuit description, and it does not charge arbitrary-size rational evaluations as unit-cost Boolean operations. The premise is stated directly as a hitting-set construction so that field-operation cost and the bit cost of circuit evaluation are not conflated. Dependence polynomial in \(d\) is permitted; there is no requirement polynomial in \(\log d\).

In the permanent definition, \(S_{m}\) is the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and \(X=(x_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le m}\) consists of \(m^{2}\) independent commuting variables. The conclusion concerns exact computation of this formal polynomial for all rational assignments. Different matrix dimensions may use unrelated circuits and unrelated rational constants, with no algorithm required to print those circuits. The constants \(B,b\) in a putative polynomial upper bound must be independent of \(m\). The displayed hardness condition means infinitely many violations of each fixed polynomial bound; it does not impose an additional almost-everywhere lower-bound rate. It is equivalent to the absence of constants \(B,b\) for which every \(\operatorname{Perm}_{m}\) has size at most \(Bm^{b}\), since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed by increasing \(B\).

The implication is the sole mathematical target. Its premise is the existence of one uniform hitting-set generator with fixed constants before all three parameters, and its conclusion is a nonuniform arithmetic size lower bound with no restriction on constant bit lengths. Choosing \(\mathbb Q\), specifying bit-time generation, output encoding and output-degree bounds are explicit refinements of the source question, which is stated in algebraic-complexity terminology over characteristic-zero fields.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\Rightarrow\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\)
or of its logical negation, with all the circuits, encodings, machine resources and quantifiers defined above.

For a positive answer, the theorem must derive the displayed permanent lower bound from precisely the hitting-set existence premise, with no additional hardness, complexity-class, number-theoretic, constant-bit-length or uniformity assumption. The premise is an assumption of the theorem, not an additional construction task that must be solved unconditionally.

For a negative answer, prove \(\mathsf{HIT}_{\mathbb Q}\) together with \(\neg\mathsf{PERMHard}_{\mathbb Q}\). Equivalently, provide the generator \(G\), its constants \(A,a\) and their complete uniform correctness and runtime proof, together with constants \(B,b\ge1\) and a nonuniform family \((C_{m})_{m\ge1}\) of the specified circuits such that
\[
\forall m\ge1,\qquad |C_{m}|\le Bm^{b}
\quad\text{and}\quad C_{m}(X)=\operatorname{Perm}_{m}(X).
\]
Here \(|C_{m}|\) counts edges, and circuit equality is formal polynomial equality. A generator for only a restricted circuit class, a lower bound for some other polynomial family, a Boolean-or-arithmetic disjunction, a bound against only uniform or constant-free circuits, or a relativized obstruction to a particular proof method does not establish either answer for this implication. There is no numerical tolerance in this yes-or-no target.
context:
Shpilka and Yehudayoff pose the implication for a circuit class, and Kumar and Saptharishi explicitly restate its general-circuit black-box instance as Question 3.2.

This card selects that published instance, fixing \(\mathbb Q\), an explicit hitting-set generator with unary parameters, bit-time generation and unrestricted rational constants as stated modeling refinements.

The standard consequence of efficient black-box testing gives arithmetic hardness for polynomials described through polynomial-space coefficient computations, without identifying such a hard family with the permanent.

The Kabanets–Impagliazzo theorem instead gives a disjunction of Boolean and arithmetic lower bounds under its encoding conventions, so it does not by itself establish the conclusion here.

The checked later results concern different lower-bound classes or restricted identity tests, and the bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated implication.
why: This question asks whether derandomizing algebraic identity testing forces hardness for the permanent, a canonical polynomial encoding counting, rather than merely for less explicitly describable polynomials. A resolution would clarify the strength of the connection between algorithms for detecting algebraic cancellation and nonuniform arithmetic lower bounds, a central barrier in algebraic complexity.

title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
importance_reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.
formal:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(K_n\) be the complete undirected graph on vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), with an arbitrary finite nonnegative real weight \(x_{ij}=x_{ji}\) on each edge \(\{i,j\}\). Let
\[
f_n(x)=\min_{P:\,1\leadsto n\text{ a simple path}}\sum_{e\in P}x_e.
\]
Write \(s(n)\) for the smallest number of binary gates in a circuit using only \(\min\) and addition, with optional constants \(0,+\infty\), that outputs \(f_n(x)\) exactly for every such weight assignment. Do there exist constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that
\[
\forall n\ge n_0:\quad s(n)\ge c n^3?
\]
There is one output, with unrestricted circuit depth and reuse of intermediate values.
question_excerpt: The seminar asks whether the cubic upper bound is optimal for a circuit representing the sum over simple 1-to-n paths in complete undirected graphs. It expressly leaves the matching lower bound open for the tropical semiring.
definitions:
A simple path from 1 to \(n\) is a vertex sequence \((v_0,\ldots,v_t)\) of distinct vertices with \(v_0=1\), \(v_t=n\) and \(1\le t\le n-1\). Its weight is \(\sum_{a=0}^{t-1}x_{v_a v_{a+1}}\). Every pair of different vertices is an edge of \(K_n\), so the family of paths is finite and nonempty. In particular, \(f_n(x)\) is finite. Zero weights are permitted. There are \(\binom n2\) independent edge inputs, not separate variables for the two directions of an edge.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph. Its input nodes are the variables \(x_{ij}\), \(1\le i<j\le n\), and optional constant sources \(0\) and \(+\infty\). Each operation gate has two incoming arguments and returns either their numerical minimum or their sum. Computation is in \([0,+\infty]\), with \(\min(a,+\infty)=a\) and \(a+(+\infty)=+\infty\). One designated node is the output. Size counts operation gates; input nodes, constant sources, wires and repeated use of a computed value are free. Fan-out and depth are unbounded.

The topology may depend on \(n\) but cannot depend on the numerical weights. No uniform procedure for generating the circuit descriptions is required. There are no other arithmetic operations, negative constants, Boolean comparison outputs, conditional gates, input-dependent routing, or addressable memory. A minimum gate returns a number; it does not expose which argument attained that number for use as a control bit. Arbitrary real weights are evaluated exactly by the specified operations; the resource measure is gate count, not finite-precision bit time.

Correctness means equality with \(f_n\) as a function on the whole nonnegative real input domain. It does not require that a formal expansion contain exactly one monomial for each simple path or exclude additional terms that never lower the numerical value on this domain. Requiring formal polynomial production, or correctness also for negative weights, would strengthen the model’s obligations and is not imposed. Only the distance from 1 to \(n\) is output, not an attaining path, all distances from 1, or all-pairs distances.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed cubic lower bound or its logical negation. A positive proof must apply to every correct circuit in the stated nonuniform model and use one positive constant \(c\) for every sufficiently large \(n\).

The negation is
\[
\forall c>0\;\forall n_0\ge2\;\exists n\ge n_0:\ s(n)<cn^3.
\]
A correct \(o(n^3)\)-size family at all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, but the negation does not require that stronger all-length upper bound. A lower bound for multiple outputs, negative weights, formulas, branching programs or formal polynomial production does not establish the selected claim without a valid transfer. An algorithm with weight-dependent control flow is not automatically a circuit of comparable size. No numerical approximation tolerance or additional unproved assumption is allowed.
context:
The numerical task asks for just one shortest-path distance. The restricted computational model is a fixed network of minimum and addition operations, so ordinary graph algorithms with data-dependent choices need not give circuits of comparable size.

The checked source records an \(O(n^3)\) construction and only the elementary \(\Omega(n^2)\) input-dependence lower bound. Closing that gap is the selected conjecture.

Tropical circuits can compute the correct numerical function without reproducing its exact formal polynomial expansion. This distinction matters for path families containing different lengths and is part of the source’s lower-bound discussion.

The cubic all-pairs lower bound uses the requirement to produce many distances. The author’s related single-source problem still requests several outputs. Neither statement may simply be relabeled as a lower bound for the one output here.
why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.
status_note: The exact single-output nonnegative min-plus question is explicitly open in the 2025 seminar and consistent with the 2015 conclusion. Bounded primary-source searches through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The author’s current linked single-source question has multiple outputs and is cited only as related evidence, not as the same formulation.

title: Superpolynomial noncommutative circuit lower bounds
importance_reason: A central explicit algebraic circuit lower-bound challenge with unrestricted depth and sharing, still substantially beyond the polynomial unrestricted-circuit progress reported in 2026.
formal:
Does there exist a family
\[
f_n\in\mathbb Q\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\qquad(n\ge2)
\]
of polynomial degree with uniformly polynomial-time computable word coefficients, such that
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:
\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f_n)>n^k?
\]
Here \(k,N,n\) are integers and \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}\) is minimum size among unrestricted noncommutative arithmetic circuits with arbitrary complex constants. The family can be chosen freely subject to the explicitness and degree requirements below; it is not required to be a particular permanent or determinant family.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 10 asks for superpolynomial noncommutative circuit lower bounds in the surrounding discussion of explicit polynomial-degree families. This card specifies efficient rational coefficient access and lower bounds over C. The 2021 source occurrence reiterates the general circuit challenge before addressing different restricted-model questions. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Some explicit polynomial-degree family with efficiently computable rational word coefficients, against circuits with arbitrary complex constants.
definitions:
The free associative algebra \(\mathbb C\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\) consists of finite complex linear combinations of words in the symbols \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Addition adds the coefficients of equal words. Multiplication concatenates words and distributes over sums; it is associative. Scalars commute with every word, but variable symbols do not commute. The empty word has value 1. Thus \(x_1x_2\) and \(x_2x_1\) are different monomials, and polynomial equality is exact equality of every word coefficient. This is not a problem about functions on scalar inputs or on matrices of one fixed dimension.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Input gates are variable symbols or arbitrary complex constants. An internal gate adds or multiplies two predecessor values. Each multiplication gate specifies a left and a right input; the same predecessor may occur in both positions. The size is the total number of gates, including inputs. There are no division gates, tests, approximation operations or limits. Fan-out, reuse of intermediate values and depth are unrestricted. Each scalar costs one input gate without a description-length restriction. Intermediate polynomials can have arbitrarily large degree and need not be homogeneous. \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f)\) is the minimum size of any such circuit whose formal output is \(f\), with rational coefficients embedded in \(\mathbb C\).

Polynomial degree and uniform explicitness mean that there are fixed integers \(a,b\ge1\), a fixed real \(K>0\), and one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(M\) with the following properties. Every nonzero \(f_n\) has degree at most \(n^a\), where degree is the largest length of a word with nonzero coefficient; the zero polynomial is allowed. Given \(1^n\) and any explicitly listed word \(w\) of length \(\ell\) over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(M\) outputs the exact coefficient \([w]f_n\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+(\ell+1)\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^b
\]
Turing steps. Word symbols are written as fixed-width binary indices. The output is a reduced fraction \(p/q\) with binary integers \(p\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\); zero is \(0/1\). Words of length greater than \(n^a\) have coefficient zero. The empty word is included. The bound includes writing the output and thus also limits coefficient bit lengths. No advice depending on \(n\) is supplied to \(M\).

The explicitness requirement prevents choosing arbitrary hard coefficient tables by counting. It concerns an algorithm to compute any one coefficient, not an algorithm to list all coefficients or a small arithmetic circuit for the full polynomial. Conversely, the circuits being ruled out are nonuniform and may use complex constants even though the target family has efficiently computable rational coefficients. The lower-bound quantifiers mean absence of every polynomial family-size upper bound, witnessed at arbitrarily large indices; they do not require an eventual lower bound at every index.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must define the family and its coefficient algorithm, prove the degree and uniform running-time bounds, and exclude every polynomial circuit-size upper bound in the stated unrestricted model. A negative answer must prove that every family meeting these requirements has a polynomial-size noncommutative circuit family over \(\mathbb C\). An exponential formula or branching-program lower bound does not suffice. Nor does a circuit lower bound for bounded depth, homogeneity, restricted syntactic degree, or a fixed polynomial exponent.
context:
The order of symbols gives a coefficient matrix method that proves exponential formula and branching-program lower bounds. A circuit can reuse an intermediate computation, so such a formula lower bound need not imply a comparably large circuit.

Uniform coefficient computation is a precise way to require an explicit family. Allowing only polynomial degree also prevents repeated squaring of a huge-degree monomial from masquerading as a meaningful circuit lower bound.

The January 2026 low-syntactic-degree result improves polynomial lower bounds under an intermediate-degree restriction. Later work must be considered before treating its stated unrestricted frontier as current.

The May 2026 preprint states a tight \(\Omega(nd)\) bound for the palindrome polynomial on two groups of \(n\) variables and degree \(2d\), with no syntactic-degree restriction. At \(d=n\), this is quadratic in the number of variables. Its matching \(O(nd)\) recursive circuit makes that particular family insufficient for the superpolynomial target.

The July revision of the concurrent Raz paper states \(\Omega(d\sqrt n)\) non-scalar multiplication lower bounds and discusses the stronger total-size palindrome result. These 2026 advances change the polynomial frontier without proving the superpolynomial statement.
why: Noncommutative computation retains the order of products and already supports strong formula lower bounds. Proving a superpolynomial bound that survives unrestricted reuse would establish a major circuit lower-bound milestone for an explicitly specified family.

title: Superpolynomial multilinear circuit lower bounds
importance_reason: A central unrestricted-depth algebraic lower-bound target for structured polynomial families, beyond known formula, depth-restricted and polynomial syntactic-circuit bounds.
formal:
Does there exist a family of multilinear polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(n\ge2\), belonging to \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), such that
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:
\operatorname{MC}(f_n)>n^k?
\]
All three quantified parameters are integers, and \(\operatorname{MC}(f_n)\) denotes the minimum size of a semantically multilinear arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb C\) computing \(f_n\). Thus the target is a VNP family for which no polynomial-size family of gatewise multilinear circuits exists. The family is not required to be the permanent.
question_excerpt: The survey asks for a superpolynomial multilinear circuit lower bound. Its preceding theorem concerns an explicit family in VNP. The user selected some multilinear VNP family over the complex numbers as the precise target, without fixing the permanent.
definitions:
An arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb C\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output gate. Input gates are variables or arbitrary complex constants. Every internal gate adds or multiplies two supplied predecessor values; a predecessor can supply both operands. Gate values are formal polynomials in commuting variables. There are no division gates, tests, approximations or limit operations. Output correctness is exact coefficientwise polynomial equality. The size is the total number of gates, including inputs. Depth and fan-out are unrestricted, and intermediate computations may be shared. A complex constant costs one gate, with no bound on its description length. These are nonuniform algebraic size measures, not bit-operation counts.

A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in each monomial with nonzero coefficient. Constants and zero are multilinear. A circuit is semantically multilinear when the actual polynomial computed at every gate has this property. Merely having a multilinear output is insufficient. Conversely, semantic multilinearity does not require the variable labels appearing in the two input subcircuits of a multiplication gate to be disjoint: intermediate cancellation can remove a variable’s dependence. Syntactic multilinearity imposes that extra disjointness condition and is a separate restriction.

For a multilinear polynomial \(f\), \(\operatorname{MC}(f)\) is the smallest gate count of any semantically multilinear circuit computing it. It is finite because a finite sum of multilinear monomials can be evaluated by such a circuit. The definition permits every possible circuit with the stated properties, not just a particular normal form or depth.

For this card, \((f_n)\in\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) means that there are an integer \(b\ge1\), integers \(0\le m(n)\le n^b\), and polynomials
\[
g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_{m(n)}]
\]
such that every \(g_n\) has total degree at most \(n^b\), is computable by an unrestricted arithmetic circuit of size at most \(n^b\), and
\[
f_n(x)=\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}}g_n(x,u)
\qquad(n\ge2).
\]
For \(m(n)=0\), the sum has one term. The witness bits \(u\) are substituted by the corresponding elements 0 and 1 of \(\mathbb C\). The circuits for \(g_n\) need not be multilinear. Requiring these polynomial size and degree bounds rules out arbitrary unstructured families; merely counting hard coefficient tables does not establish VNP membership.

The VNP representation and the circuits may be chosen separately at each length. No uniform algorithm for generating them or their complex constants is additionally required. Both the representation and the lower bound use the fixed field \(\mathbb C\). The lower-bound quantifiers mean that every proposed exponent fails at arbitrarily large indices. They do not require an eventual lower bound at all sufficiently large indices. Membership in VNP alone does not assert that the outputs themselves have small unrestricted circuits.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must rigorously define a family, prove its multilinearity and its VNP representation with the stated polynomial bounds, and prove the superpolynomial lower bound against every semantically multilinear circuit over \(\mathbb C\).

A negative answer must show that every multilinear family in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) has a polynomial-size family of semantically multilinear circuits. Showing that one candidate has small circuits does not refute the existential target. A counting argument without the VNP membership proof, or a lower bound only for formulas, branching programs, bounded-depth circuits or syntactically multilinear circuits, is insufficient. Unlike the separate unrestricted-versus-multilinear comparison, a positive answer here need not prove a polynomial-size unrestricted circuit upper bound for the chosen outputs.
context:
Multilinearity limits the exponent of each variable at every gate, but a circuit can still reuse values many times. This sharing makes unbounded-depth circuit lower bounds substantially different from formula lower bounds.

The VNP condition expresses each output as a sum of a polynomial-size computation over polynomially many Boolean witness coordinates. It gives a precise algebraic restriction on the family while allowing the output sum itself to contain exponentially many terms.

The published almost-quadratic lower bound is \(\Omega(n^2/\log^2 n)\) for syntactically multilinear circuits. Its size growth remains polynomial, and its circuit model imposes an additional syntactic restriction. Both distinctions matter for this target.

The January 2026 rank-method paper retains related lower-bound questions for multilinear branching programs and explicitly uses syntactic models. The later April claim of a polynomial-size full-rank construction was withdrawn in May and supplies no established resolution.

TCS-6883 asks for a separation using outputs that already have small unrestricted circuits. This card permits any multilinear VNP family, so it seeks a general lower-bound milestone without that additional upper-bound requirement.

title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
importance_reason: A basic arithmetic operation supplies a concrete candidate for a central circuit-lower-bound barrier. The question is explicitly highlighted in Goldreich’s textbook and retained in Viola’s current manuscript; its nonuniform target is distinct from the catalogue’s machine-time question.
formal: Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), some Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates computes the exact product of every pair of unsigned \(n\)-bit integers, outputting all \(2n\) product bits? The gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT; fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and the circuit family need not be uniform.
question_excerpt: Goldreich asks whether the exact product of two binary integers can be computed by linear-size Boolean circuits. Viola’s current author manuscript explicitly retains the same question.
definitions:
The \(2n\) inputs are bits \(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1},b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}\), representing
\[
a=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i2^i,\qquad b=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i2^i.
\]
The ordered output bits \(c_0,\ldots,c_{2n-1}\) must satisfy
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}c_j2^j=ab
\]
on every input, including inputs with leading zeros. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose internal gates apply the stated Boolean operations. Constant sources 0 and 1 are available. Size counts operation gates, excluding input nodes, constant sources and output wires. Wires may copy a bit to arbitrarily many gates or outputs without an additional charge. There is no randomness, approximation or restriction on depth.

Write \(M(n)\) for the minimum gate count of such a circuit at width \(n\). The proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). The same \(C\) bounds all sufficiently large widths, but each width may use a different circuit, with no requirement to compute the family’s descriptions. A machine instruction multiplying entire words is not one Boolean gate. Any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes this linear-size question only by constant factors.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one constant \(C\), a threshold \(n_0\), and the existence of correct circuits at every \(n\ge n_0\). It need not give a uniform algorithm constructing their descriptions.

A negative proof must establish
\[
\forall C>0\;\forall n_0\ge1\;\exists n\ge n_0:\ M(n)>Cn.
\]
It may give a stronger asymptotic lower bound, but such a stronger bound at every sufficiently large length is not required. A fixed linear lower bound, a bound only for restricted depth or wiring, or the failure of one multiplication construction does not settle the target. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional statement.
context:
Binary addition has linear gate complexity. Whether multiplication enjoys the same bound is an explicit candidate for separating two elementary arithmetic tasks in an unrestricted circuit model.

The full product is required. Computing only a residue or selected output bits, or counting whole-word multiplication instructions, measures a different task.

The 2019 paper reports an \(O(n\log n)\) multiplication construction and proves a matching lower bound under the undirected network-coding conjecture, in its bounded-degree circuit model. The hypothesis is essential to that lower bound.

Viola’s current manuscript still asks whether linear-size multiplication is possible and establishes equivalence with linear-size squaring. The manuscript’s revision year is not the date when this longstanding question originated.

The target allows a different circuit at each input width. It therefore differs from TCS-7174, which asks about uniform running time on a multitape Turing machine.
why: Determine whether multiplication has the same order of Boolean hardware complexity as addition, or provide an explicit superlinear lower bound in the unrestricted circuit model.

The network-coding lower bound cited here is conditional, and the review does not independently validate its full proof.

title: Optimal multilinear-formula size of the permanent
importance_reason: The optimal multilinear formula size of the permanent concerns a canonical explicit algebraic lower bound with a qualitative quasipolynomial-to-exponential gap.
formal:
Determine the asymptotic growth of \(\log_2 F(n)\), up to universal multiplicative constants, where \(F(n)\) is the minimum size of a multilinear arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb C\) computing the permanent of an \(n\times n\) matrix of independent variables.

More precisely, give an explicitly characterized positive scale \(g:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and prove that there exist constants \(a,A>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that
\[
2^{a g(n)}\le F(n)\le2^{A g(n)}
\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0.
\]
The scale must determine the growth rate, rather than restating \(F(n)\) or another unresolved minimum-formula-size quantity.
question_excerpt: After presenting Raz’s quasipolynomial lower bound, the survey asks about strengthening it to an exponential lower bound. The retained card asks for the actual logarithmic growth rate, allowing intermediate scales, as previously authorized by the user.
definitions:
Let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) have \(n^2\) independent commuting variables, and let \(S_n\) be the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The permanent is the polynomial
\[
\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
Here \(n\) is the number of rows and columns, not the number of variables.

An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted binary tree. Leaves are labeled by an entry variable \(x_{ij}\) or an arbitrary complex constant. Each internal node adds or multiplies the polynomials of its two children. There are no division gates, tests, limits or approximation operations. The size is the total number of nodes, including leaves and all repeated occurrences. Intermediate computations cannot be shared, so every reuse of a subexpression requires a new copy. No depth restriction is imposed, and constants have no numerical-description or magnitude bound. Negative and nonreal constants are allowed.

A polynomial is multilinear when every variable has exponent at most one in each of its monomials with nonzero coefficient. A formula is multilinear when the actual polynomial computed at every node is multilinear. Constants and zero are multilinear. This semantic definition permits cancellations, and does not demand disjoint syntactic variable sets as an additional condition. Correctness means equality in \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\), equivalently equality on all complex input matrices, not merely on Boolean matrices.

For each \(n\), \(F(n)\) minimizes the all-node size over exactly these formulas computing \(\operatorname{perm}_n\). The minimum exists: the defining sum of monomials is one valid multilinear formula and possible sizes are positive integers. The model is nonuniform; the formula and its constants may depend on \(n\), with no efficient generator requirement.

The requested precision is constant factors in the logarithm of the optimum. Thus an answer \(g(n)\) permits different positive constants in the lower and upper exponents. It does not require constant-factor approximation of \(F(n)\) itself, an exact leading constant in its exponent, or a numerical approximation at one fixed \(n\). The two bounds must hold at every sufficiently large integer \(n\), not only on an infinite subsequence.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of an explicit asymptotic scale \(g(n)\), together with the two displayed bounds for the exact formula model. The upper bound must establish formulas of the claimed size and account for duplicated subexpressions; the lower bound must cover all allowed complex constants, cancellations and depths.

Defining \(g(n)=\log_2 F(n)\), or replacing it by an equivalent search over formulas whose growth has not been determined, is not an answer. A lower bound alone, an upper bound alone or bounds at different asymptotic scales do not settle the task. A bound only for monotone, non-cancelling, row-set-multilinear or bounded-depth formulas does not automatically apply to the full model. The original exponential conjecture would establish \(g(n)=n\) when combined with the known exponential upper bound, but any other rigorously matched scale is an admissible resolution.
context:
The permanent is a canonical explicit polynomial for algebraic lower bounds. Requiring every intermediate polynomial to be multilinear creates a restricted model where a superpolynomial lower bound is already known, even at unrestricted depth.

Raz’s theorem gives \(F(n)\ge n^{\Omega(\log n)}\), or \(\log_2 F(n)=\Omega((\log n)^2)\). This leaves room for several very different growth rates above the known lower-bound scale.

Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion formula gives \(F(n)\le O(n^2 2^n)\). Each product combines linear forms from different rows, preserving multilinearity, and explicitly copying the expression still gives that formula-size bound. Consequently \(\log_2 F(n)=O(n)\).

An exponential lower bound would close the gap at the linear logarithmic scale. The full determination target also allows an intermediate answer, provided upper and lower bounds match. It is therefore broader than proving or refuting the source’s suggested endpoint.

The 2026 sparse-determinant paper shows that the quasipolynomial formula lower-bound phenomenon persists with substantially fewer variables. Its polynomial family and parameter improvement differ from determining the exponent for the full permanent.
why: Establish a qualitatively stronger explicit algebraic lower bound in one of the few models already admitting superpolynomial separations.

title: Semantic versus syntactic multilinear circuits
importance_reason: This tests whether the structural multilinearity restriction used in major arithmetic lower-bound models faithfully captures all circuits whose intermediate polynomials are multilinear. A superpolynomial gap would expose a fundamental loss caused by the restriction, while equality would justify its reach beyond formulas.
formal: Is there a field \(F\), fixed independently of \(n\), and a family \(f_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(n\ge1\), that has polynomial-size semantically multilinear arithmetic circuits over \(F\) but has no polynomial-size family of syntactically multilinear arithmetic circuits over that same field? Semantic multilinearity is required at every gate. The question uses nonuniform circuit size and allows arbitrary field constants.
definitions: A field is a commutative field with \(0\ne1\); it may be finite or infinite and is chosen once for the entire family. An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Input gates are labelled by variables in \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) or by arbitrary elements of \(F\). Every internal gate has two input wires and is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Wires may reuse gate outputs, including as the two inputs of a gate, and both wires are then counted. Every gate lies on a path to the output. Size is one plus the number of wires; a field constant occupies one input gate irrespective of any representation length. There is no bound on depth or fan-out, no division gate, and no requirement that a circuit or its constants can be computed from \(n\). Each gate computes its formal polynomial in the polynomial ring \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A polynomial is multilinear if every monomial with nonzero coefficient has exponent at most one in each variable; the zero polynomial is multilinear. A circuit is semantically multilinear if every gate computes such a polynomial, after all cancellations in \(F\). For each gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Var}(g)\) be the set of variable labels occurring at input gates from which there is a directed path to \(g\), whether or not those variables cancel from its polynomial. A circuit is syntactically multilinear if \(\operatorname{Var}(g_1)\cap\operatorname{Var}(g_2)=\varnothing\) at every product gate with children \(g_1,g_2\). No such disjointness is required at addition gates. Let \(s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f)\) and \(s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f)\) be the minimum sizes of the respective circuits computing exactly \(f\). Equality means equality of formal polynomials, including over finite fields. Both minima are finite for a multilinear polynomial. Precisely, the target asks for \(F,(f_n)_{n\ge1},C>0,k\in\mathbb N\) such that \(\forall n\ge1,\ s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^k\), while \(\forall B>0\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\forall N\ge1\;\exists n\ge N,\ s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f_n)>B(n+1)^d\). Thus superpolynomial separation means failure of every polynomial bound for the family, with violations arbitrarily far out; an eventually exponential lower bound is not required. The field and family are existentially quantified before these asymptotic bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated fixed-field family separation, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must establish polynomial semantic size and failure of every polynomial syntactic size bound for one family over one fixed field. A negative answer must show that over every field, each polynomial-size semantically multilinear family also has polynomial-size syntactically multilinear circuits, with polynomial constants allowed to depend on that field and family. No effective circuit-conversion algorithm is additionally required. A separation involving unrestricted intermediate polynomials, formulas only, bounded-depth circuits only or Boolean-function equality does not settle this comparison.
context:
Open Problem 4 in the 2010 survey compares multilinear circuits with syntactically multilinear circuits. The adjacent Open Problem 3 compares unrestricted circuits with multilinear circuits and is a different question. Semantic multilinearity here follows the gate-by-gate definition used by the survey.

The survey leaves the ground field implicit under its arbitrary-field convention. This card makes the fixed-field interpretation explicit: a separation may occur over some field, but that field must remain the same at every family size. It does not require separation over every field or allow the field to vary with the input length.

Syntactic multilinearity implies semantic multilinearity. The reverse implication for the given circuit need not hold, because a variable may occur in a subcircuit without occurring in its resulting polynomial. The question concerns the minimum sizes of alternative circuits computing the same polynomial.

The survey’s Theorem 2.4, attributed to Raz, states that a multilinear formula can be made syntactically multilinear without increasing its wire count. The open comparison concerns circuits with shared intermediate outputs, where that formula statement does not settle polynomial-size equivalence.

A January 2026 paper by Borém Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff still describes semantic multilinearity as potentially more powerful for circuits and branching programs. Its main results concern syntactic multilinear branching programs and a lower-bound method; they do not claim the semantic-versus-syntactic circuit separation.
why: Many arithmetic lower bounds are proved under syntactic restrictions that make the variables entering a multiplication disjoint. Semantic multilinearity permits the same polynomial property to hold after cancellation and sharing of intermediate computations. Determining whether this distinction changes polynomial circuit power would clarify the scope of a central restricted model of algebraic computation.

Semantic multilinearity requires this property at every arithmetic-circuit gate after cancellation. title: Explicit rigidity at rank n over log log n
importance_reason: Explicit matrix rigidity is a central construction problem connected to strong linear-circuit lower bounds.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(K>0\), \(b\in\mathbb N\), and one deterministic Turing machine which, for every integer \(n\ge4\), outputs a matrix \(A_n\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\) within \(Kn^b\) steps, such that
\[
\forall c>0\ \exists N_c\ge4\ \forall n\ge N_c:
R_{A_n}^{\mathbb F_2}\!\left(
\min\!\left\{n,\left\lfloor\frac{cn}{\log_2\log_2 n}\right\rfloor\right\}
\right)\ge n^{1+\varepsilon}?
\]
Here \(c\) is real, \(N_c,n\) are integers, and \(R^{\mathbb F_2}\) is the minimum number of entries that must be changed to reduce rank to the indicated value. The same matrix family and the same \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\).
question_excerpt: Jukna asks for an explicit Boolean matrix with rigidity at least n^(1+epsilon) at rank O(n/ln ln n). This card fixes the field F_2, deterministic full-matrix construction, and a guarantee for every fixed constant in that rank scale, using one positive epsilon. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: One family and one positive epsilon working for every fixed rank-scale constant c>0, over F_2.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo 2. For a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\) and an integer \(0\le r\le n\), define
\[
R_A^{\mathbb F_2}(r)=
\min\left\{
\bigl|\{(i,j):A_{ij}\ne B_{ij}\}\bigr|:
B\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n},\ \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(B)\le r
\right\}.
\]
Rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb F_2\), not over the reals. Every entry of \(B\) can be chosen independently. The cost counts changed positions in the whole matrix, not a maximum or average per row, a norm of the changes, or their numerical magnitude. The minimum exists because the candidate set is finite and contains the zero matrix. This is ordinary matrix rigidity, not a separately constrained row/column version.

The construction algorithm receives \(1^n\) and outputs all \(n^2\) bits of \(A_n\), in row-major order, on a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine. Its time bound includes writing those bits. It has no random bits, advice, noncomputable constants or oracle access. It outputs one matrix at each length, rather than a list containing an unspecified rigid member. Polynomial time in \(n\) is required; logarithmic-time computation of an individual entry is not additionally required.

All logarithms in the rank threshold are base 2. For \(n\ge4\), the iterated logarithm is positive. The minimum with \(n\) makes the rank parameter valid even before the eventual guarantee begins. For each fixed \(c\), sufficiently large \(n\) have \(\log_2\log_2 n>c\), so the clipping eventually disappears. The threshold length \(N_c\) may depend on \(c\); the algorithm, \(K,b\) and \(\varepsilon\) may not. The comparison with \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) is an ordinary real inequality against an integer rigidity value, equivalently a lower bound by its ceiling.

The target is unconditional existence of an explicit family and a proof of its rigidity. The algorithm is not required to compute rigidity or output a certificate with each matrix. The same \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed for the whole family, with no prescribed numerical lower bound such as \(1/100\). A rank guarantee for just one fixed \(c\), or for ranks much smaller than \(n/\log\log n\), is not the quantified target here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the explicit-family existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify and verify the deterministic construction and prove the rigidity inequality against every binary matrix of the allowed rank, for all fixed \(c\) and all sufficiently large lengths. A random-matrix existence proof, an unselected candidate list, an oracle construction, a conditional construction, or a rigidity bound over a different field is insufficient. A negative answer must exclude all constructions with the stated properties, not merely refute a familiar proposed family.
context:
The rank of a matrix can fall after some of its entries are changed. Rigidity asks how many changes are unavoidable, and a lower bound must cover every low-rank replacement matrix.

The surrounding source discusses Boolean linear maps and parity circuits, so the relevant field here is F_2. The same bit matrix can have different rank and rigidity over other fields.

Random-matrix counting proves strong existential bounds. The open construction target requires the matrix itself to be output deterministically in polynomial time, which a counting proof alone does not provide.

The STACS 2026 conditional result constructs small families with a rigid member at a rank scale near the square root of the dimension, under a hardness assumption. The premise, rank regime and selection of one member all distinguish it from this card.

The 2026 spiky-rank paper develops a new route to rigidity bounds and explicitly leaves strong explicit constructions open. Its proposed matrix parameters are tools toward rigidity, rather than a construction meeting the present binary near-linear rank requirement.
why: A sufficiently rigid explicit binary matrix gives a linear transformation whose computation resists linear-size logarithmic-depth circuits. Random matrices have strong rigidity, but obtaining the required guarantees from a uniform deterministic construction remains a central explicit lower-bound challenge.

title: Decidability of freeness in automaton groups
importance_reason: A longstanding structural decision problem for automaton groups, explicitly retained after the 2024 semigroup/monoid breakthrough and in a specialist March 2026 presentation.
formal: Is abstract freeness of an automaton group decidable? Does one deterministic Turing machine, given any finite complete deterministic invertible Mealy automaton \(\mathcal A\), always halt and return YES exactly when \[\exists r\in\mathbb N\quad G(\mathcal A)\cong F_r,\] where \(G(\mathcal A)\) is generated by all state transformations and their inverses and \(F_r\) is the free group of rank \(r\)? Rank zero, the trivial group, is included. The question does not require the supplied state transformations themselves to be a free basis.
question_excerpt: Is there an algorithm deciding whether the group generated by a given complete invertible finite automaton is a free group?
definitions:
A finite complete deterministic Mealy automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,\lambda)\), with finite nonempty state set \(Q\), finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and total tables \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\), \(\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Sigma\). Invertibility means that for each state \(q\), the map \(a\mapsto\lambda(q,a)\) is a permutation of \(\Sigma\). No reversibility assumption is made on the maps \(q\mapsto\delta(q,a)\), and the numbers of states and letters are unbounded parts of the input. There are no designated initial or accepting states: all states are generators. The input is the full finite table, with binary state/letter indices and cardinalities. Invalid or noninvertible tables may be rejected.

The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Each state defines a transformation recursively by \(T_q(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and \(T_q(aw)=\lambda(q,a)T_{\delta(q,a)}(w)\). Invertibility makes each \(T_q\) a bijection of \(\Sigma^*\), preserving lengths and prefixes. The group \(G(\mathcal A)\) consists of all finite compositions of these functions and their inverses, including the empty composition, with function composition as multiplication. Equality means agreement on every finite input word of every length. This uses synchronous, total, one-letter-in/one-letter-out machines, rather than partial or asynchronous transducers.

The free group \(F_r\) has generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) and their formal inverses. Its elements are finite reduced words, meaning adjacent inverse pairs have been cancelled; multiplication concatenates words and cancels such pairs, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses the word and flips each sign. Freeness of \(G(\mathcal A)\) means existence of a bijection to this group preserving multiplication and identity. A possible free basis may consist of arbitrary group elements rather than the given state list, which can contain identities, duplicates or dependent generators. Since the group is finitely generated, allowing all finite ranks is sufficient; no basis, rank, isomorphism or bound on relation length is supplied as an input promise or required as output.

The target is exact uniform decidability on every valid automaton table, with termination on both free and nonfree cases and no resource bound. One ordinary algorithm must work for all input sizes. No oracle, nonuniform advice, randomness, numerical tolerance or restriction to bounded input-word lengths is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this predicate admits a total computable decider on the encoded complete invertible Mealy tables, or prove that it does not. The formalization must connect the state recursion, generated group of all-word transformations and existence of an abstract free-group isomorphism, including rank zero, to the algorithm's correctness and termination. A negative reduction must preserve complete deterministic invertibility. Deciding whether the named states freely generate, checking absence of a positive relation, or proving semigroup freeness undecidable does not by itself meet the abstract group target. Failure of one bounded relation search is not a proof that every total algorithm is impossible. The card review does not claim a verified Lean resolution.
context:
A state table supplies a compact recursive description of transformations on a rooted tree of all finite words. Deciding equality of two specified products is possible in this representation, but recognizing the abstract structure of the entire infinite group is a separate problem.

The original 2000 list asks about the group’s structural properties, and the March 2026 handout defines freeness as isomorphism to a free group over some basis. This confirms that the target is not an injectivity test for the map from the free group on the names of all states.

For example, the usual adding machine generates an infinite cyclic group together with an identity state. The group is free of rank one, while the given state list is not a free basis and already contains a positive relation because the identity state acts trivially. Redundant state generators must therefore not force a NO answer.

Theorem 3.7 of the 2020 paper proves undecidability of checking absence of positive relations, which are nonempty products of state generators acting as the identity without using inverses. The same paper explicitly distinguishes this presentation-dependent property from abstract group freeness. Its appended erratum retracts other freeness claims, and was checked with the theorem.

The MFCS 2024 result proves undecidability of freeness for general complete automaton semigroups and monoids. Its final section still lists automaton group freeness as open. Allowing noninvertible state actions in the negative construction is not the promised group input class.

The 12 March 2026 specialist handout again records group freeness as open while listing semigroup/monoid freeness as undecidable. A bounded search through September found no checked later resolution; the card reports this dated evidence rather than claiming an exhaustive status proof.
why: Automata give finite descriptions of groups that can have complex infinite structure and need not have finite presentations by relations. Recognizing a free group tests a fundamental structural property in this representation. The problem isolates the effect of invertibility on decidability and distinguishes structural recognition from equality of individual represented elements.
status_note: The MFCS 2024 final section and the 12 March 2026 St Andrews handout explicitly retain abstract automaton group freeness as open. The original §7.2.1(b) and current definition quantify over some free basis, not necessarily the input states. Positive-relations undecidability and general semigroup/monoid freeness do not resolve this predicate. The search through 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution and is not exhaustive.
