working_summary: The target is a deterministic polynomial-time construction of rigid complex square matrices with algebraic entries. All entries must lie in one common number field of polynomial degree, supplied by an exact polynomial-size representation. Reducing rank to any fixed multiple of n divided by log log n must require at least n^(1+epsilon) changed entries for one fixed positive epsilon. The low-rank replacement may use arbitrary complex values, so its coefficients are not confined to the original number field. The answer must include complete Lean-checked construction, representation and rigidity proofs or prove the exact negation.

title: Linear-time unit-Monge distance multiplication
importance_reason: This is a reusable algebraic primitive for semi-local alignment and compressed-string comparison, so a linear bound would affect more than a single query interface.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(K,C>0\), an integer \(B\ge8\), and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm which, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and all permutations \(\pi,\tau\) of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), outputs a permutation \(\rho\) of that set in at most \(Kn\) instructions using at most \(Cn\) working words, such that
\[
 A_\rho(i,j)=\min_{0\le h\le n}
 \bigl(A_\pi(i,h)+A_\tau(h,j)\bigr)
 \qquad(0\le i,j\le n),
\]
where
\[
 A_\nu(i,j)=|\{t\in\{i,\ldots,n-1\}:\nu(t)<j\}|?
\]
The input and output are permutation arrays, not explicitly written dense matrices. The word length is \(B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\).
question_excerpt: Tiskin asks whether implicit distance multiplication of simple unit-Monge matrices can be performed in linear time, attributing the question to Landau. The input and output density matrices are permutations. The explicit counting convention here states that implicit problem with zero-based array indices.
definitions:
A permutation array contains exactly once each of the integers from zero to \(n-1\). Each input array has \(n\) entries, with one entry per word, and the output consists of the \(n\) entries of \(\rho\). The input size parameter is this permutation length. No data structure answering arbitrary matrix-entry queries is supplied for free.

The displayed formula defines an \((n+1)\)-by-\((n+1)\) integer matrix from a permutation \(\nu\). For each row boundary \(i\) and column boundary \(j\), it counts the permutation points strictly below that column boundary and at or after that row boundary. In particular,
\[
 A_\nu(i,0)=A_\nu(n,j)=0,
 \quad A_\nu(0,j)=j,
 \quad A_\nu(i,n)=n-i.
\]
All entries lie between zero and \(n\). Its discrete density satisfies
\[
 A_\nu(i+1,j)+A_\nu(i,j+1)-A_\nu(i,j)-A_\nu(i+1,j+1)
 =\mathbf 1_{\{\nu(i)=j\}}
 \qquad(0\le i,j<n).
\]
This fixes the orientation of the simple unit-Monge representation without relying on an unstated convention. Here the indicator is one if its condition holds and zero otherwise.

For equally sized matrices, their distance product, or min-plus product, has entry \((i,j)\) equal to the minimum over \(h\) of the sum of entry \((i,h)\) in the first and entry \((h,j)\) in the second. It is neither ordinary matrix multiplication nor composition of the two input permutations. The class of matrices defined above is closed under this product, so a suitable output permutation exists; its density determines it uniquely. The task is to compute that permutation, not to prove closure alone or output the quadratic array of product entries.

The RAM is sequential and executes a fixed finite program independent of \(n,\pi,\tau\). Allowed unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparison, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Stored values and addresses fit in words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. There is no randomness, advice, external oracle, uncharged preprocessing or free size-dependent lookup table. All initialization, intermediate representations, arithmetic, input access and output writes are included in the \(Kn\) bound. Working memory includes registers and temporary tables but excludes the supplied input arrays and the output array. Including those arrays changes the space bound only by a constant factor.

The constants and word-size factor are chosen once for the algorithm. Every valid input must satisfy the same worst-case time and space bounds. Expected time, amortization over a batch of products and constant-round massively parallel computation are different requirements.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive result must specify the uniform algorithm and prove exact correctness of all product entries through the output permutation, as well as the linear worst-case resource bounds in the stated model.

An \(O(n\log n)\), \(n^{1+o(1)}\), or other superlinear algorithm does not meet the target. Neither approximate multiplication, a restricted family of permutations, a dense-input model nor a parallel round bound suffices. An assumed conjecture can justify a conditional lower bound only; it cannot serve as an unconditional refutation. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this exact existence question.
context:
Dense matrices have quadratic output size, but a simple unit-Monge matrix is represented by one permutation. The implicit representation makes a genuinely linear-time multiplication question meaningful.

The simple boundary convention and permutation density are part of the problem. General Monge matrices have different representation costs and need not admit a permutation-sized description.

Tiskin proves closure under distance multiplication and an O(n log n)-time algorithm. His source explicitly identifies the remaining linear-time question.

The 2025 core-sparse algorithm broadens the matrix class and refines its complexity in terms of the number of nonzero density entries. In the permutation case it matches the earlier logarithmic overhead.

The separate constant-round MPC result measures distributed rounds. Such a bound does not establish that the same product can be computed using only linearly many sequential instructions.
why: This compact matrix operation combines many sequence-comparison values and is reused in alignment, subsequence and compressed-string algorithms. Removing its logarithmic overhead would improve an underlying primitive while matching the linear size of its representation.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the exact linear-time deterministic sequential target. The latest checked core-sparse theorem retains the logarithmic factor for this special case, and the MPC theorem concerns round complexity. The review verifies statement and representation scope without independently certifying full cited proofs.

The question asks for one deterministic algorithm taking only linear worst-case time and space. The checked sequential algorithms retain a logarithmic factor, while constant-round parallel results use a different model. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove or refute the linear-time proposition for every pair of input permutations.

title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
importance_reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.
formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption; hardness of forming several prescribed targets is a different problem.
context:
Erickson’s exponentiation discussion distinguishes asymptotically short multiplication programs from computing the absolute minimum number of multiplications. The current book chapter still states the latter question. This card retains the earlier length-only target and does not infer an unproved equivalence with constructing an optimal chain.

The elementary bounds are \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le\ell(n)\le2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\), including \(n=1\). Thus an optimal chain has \(O(b)\) entries of at most \(b\) bits. The existence of short certificates does not supply a deterministic polynomial-time optimizer.

The cryptographic arithmetic paper distinguishes single-target optimality from multiple-target addition sequences. Its procedures for selected exponents are not a proof of the general exact polynomial-time claim.

The 2025 assembly-theory article describes the shortest-addition-chain complexity as unknown. Only that dated observation is used here; its broader claims about complexity classes and assembly models are not part of this card’s mathematical premises.

Wallner’s 2026 result concerns the expected decompressed size of restricted chain structures, including Brauer chains. An average over chains of a fixed length does not compute the unrestricted minimum length for a supplied target.

The separately catalogued Scholz–Brauer conjecture concerns a structural inequality for special exponents. That conclusion differs from a uniformly efficient computation of the optimum on every binary input.
why: Addition chains express reuse in multiplication-only exponentiation. Their optimal length is small enough to have short certificates, yet finding that length for an arbitrary binary exponent has resisted a general complexity classification.

working_summary: An addition chain starts at one and repeatedly forms a new integer by adding two earlier entries. Its shortest length is the fewest such additions needed to reach a specified positive target. The target is given in binary, and the requested algorithm must output the exact optimum in time polynomial in that bit length. This is a question about computing the minimum count, without additionally requiring an optimal chain as output. Known short chains, restricted families, heuristics and hardness for multiple targets do not establish the requested general deterministic algorithm or its impossibility.

title: Arithmetic circuit closure under pth roots
importance_reason: A fundamental positive-characteristic circuit closure question with consequences for factoring and algebraic derandomization; the degree-independent target goes beyond the known few-variable construction.
formal:
For every prime \(p\), do there exist constants \(K_p>0\) and integers \(a_p\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every polynomial \(g\in\overline{\mathbb F_p}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\),
\[
\operatorname C_p(g)\le K_p\bigl(\operatorname C_p(g^p)+n+1\bigr)^{a_p}?
\]
Here \(\operatorname C_p\) is division-free arithmetic circuit size over the algebraic closure of the prime field, with arbitrary constants from that same field. The constants may depend on \(p\), but not on \(n\), \(g\), its coefficients or its degree. There is no degree parameter in the size bound.
question_excerpt: Andrews states that obtaining a small circuit for g from a small circuit for g^p remains open, while giving a construction that is polynomial when the number of variables is sufficiently small. This card fixes algebraically closed fields of each prime characteristic and asks for degree-independent polynomial overhead. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: No degree restriction; for each fixed prime p, require root-circuit size polynomial in s+n over the algebraic closure of F_p.
definitions:
For a prime \(p\), \(\mathbb F_p\) is the field of integers modulo \(p\), and \(\overline{\mathbb F_p}\) is its algebraic closure. It has characteristic \(p\), so the sum of \(p\) copies of 1 is zero. Every element has a unique \(p\)-th root in this field. This field choice removes the separate obstruction that a scalar root might not belong to the coefficient field. All coefficients and circuit constants belong to this one fixed field for the chosen \(p\).

The variables commute. Polynomials are formal finite sums of monomials with field coefficients. Equality means coefficientwise equality, not equality as functions on a finite set of field elements. In characteristic \(p\),
\[
\left(\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}\right)^p
=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}^p x_1^{p\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{p\alpha_n}.
\]
This is the polynomial \(g^p\) in the question. For example, even over \(\mathbb F_p\), the formal polynomials \(x^p\) and \(x\) differ although they induce the same function on that finite prime field.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Input gates are variable symbols or arbitrary field constants. Each internal gate adds or multiplies two predecessor values; a predecessor may serve both operands. The size is the total number of gates, including inputs. Fan-out, reuse, depth and intermediate degrees are unrestricted. There are no division gates, root gates, coefficient-extraction gates, tests or limit operations. A field constant costs one gate irrespective of the degree of the finite extension in which it lies. This is a nonuniform algebraic size measure, not a bit-complexity measure. \(\operatorname C_p(h)\) is the minimum size of such a circuit whose exact formal output is \(h\), including \(h=0\) and constant polynomials.

The question is about existence of small circuits. It does not require an efficient procedure to discover \(g\), extract its coefficients, or convert a given circuit for \(g^p\). In particular, allowing scalar constants with roots already in the field does not supply a polynomial-root operation on a circuit's entire output. A circuit for \(g^p\) may use cancellations between intermediate polynomials that are not themselves \(p\)-th powers.

There is no bound on the degree of \(g\) in terms of \(n\). It can be exponentially large in the supplied circuit size. A bound polynomial in \(\operatorname C_p(g^p)+n+\deg(g)\) would be a different, weaker assertion. The displayed quantifier order permits a different fixed polynomial size overhead for each prime; it does not ask for uniform dependence on a variable characteristic.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated inequality for every fixed prime or of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover all numbers of variables and all degrees while using only the allowed arithmetic gates. A negative answer must exhibit a prime \(p\) for which every proposed pair \(K_p,a_p\) fails on some polynomial. Bounds only for a fixed number of variables, for degree-bounded inputs, or for polynomial functions rather than formal polynomials are insufficient. No efficient conversion algorithm is required, but proving its existence with the same size guarantee would suffice.
context:
The scalar Frobenius map raises coefficients to the p-th power and multiplies all monomial exponents by p. Its simple expanded form does not itself give a small-circuit inverse when the output is available only as a shared arithmetic computation.

Andrews constructs a root circuit of size at most \(3s p^{2n}+2^n\) over the perfect closure of the coefficient field. This is polynomial in \(s\) when \(n=O(\log_p s)\), but is exponential in an unrestricted number of variables.

The chosen algebraically closed field is already perfect, so the scalar-extension requirement in that construction is automatically met. The unresolved issue here is the number of gates, not the mere existence of coefficient roots.

The finite-characteristic discussion of the branching-program factoring paper also identifies removal of p-th powers as a missing step for several arithmetic models. A result for one of those restricted models should not be silently identified with the present general-circuit assertion.

The June 2026 survey retains positive-characteristic factor closure as open and discusses the small-variable progress. That degree-sensitive factorization question does not automatically establish this stronger degree-independent root bound.
why: In positive characteristic, taking a power can conceal the coefficient structure needed for circuit factorization and hardness-to-randomness arguments. Removing such powers with polynomial size overhead would eliminate a basic inseparability obstacle in algebraic complexity.
status_note: Source-open for degree-independent polynomial circuit-size overhead for p-th roots over the algebraic closure of each fixed prime field. Andrews explicitly states the small-circuit question and gives an exponential-in-variable-count bound; the 2023 and June 2026 primary discussions retain the associated inseparability obstruction. No resolution of this precise stronger degree-independent target was identified in bounded checks through 17 September 2026. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: No degree restriction; for each fixed prime p, require root-circuit size polynomial in s+n over the algebraic closure of F_p.
progress: 2020: Andrews provides the exponential-in-variable-count root construction and explicitly retains the general small-circuit question. | 2023-03-08: The updated branching-program manuscript reiterates the p-th-power obstacle in finite characteristic. | 2026-06-12: The revised factorization survey retains the positive-characteristic closure frontier and the limited-variable progress.
working_summary: For each fixed prime p, the question compares the circuit sizes of g and its p-th power over the algebraic closure of the prime field. The desired size overhead is polynomial in the original size and number of variables, with no degree dependence. Circuits may share arbitrary intermediate computations and use arbitrary constants, but may not use root gates. The target is formal polynomial computation and existence of small circuits, not equality of finite-field functions or efficient reconstruction. A complete Lean-checked universal size bound or a counterexample to every such bound in some fixed characteristic is required.

title: Membership in \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
importance_reason: A longstanding low-dimensional decidability boundary for algebraic reachability, including matrix mortality and unrestricted mixtures of singular and nonsingular transitions.
formal:
Does there exist an algorithm which, for every finite list \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\mathbb Z^{2\times2}\), with \(k\ge1\), and every target \(B\in\mathbb Z^{2\times2}\), decides whether
\[
\exists \ell\ge1\ \exists i_1,\ldots,i_\ell\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:
A_{i_1}A_{i_2}\cdots A_{i_\ell}=B?
\]
All matrix entries are arbitrary signed integers; singular and nonsingular generators may occur together. The algorithm must halt on both positive and negative instances.
question_excerpt: The source explicitly leaves open decidability of membership for arbitrary 2 by 2 integer matrix semigroups, with nonempty generator products.
definitions:
A \(2\times2\) integer matrix is an array of four integers, with multiplication
\[
(XY)_{ij}=\sum_{h=1}^{2}X_{ih}Y_{hj}.
\]
Equality requires equality in every entry. A matrix is singular when its determinant \(X_{11}X_{22}-X_{12}X_{21}\) is zero; no determinant restriction is imposed here.

The generated semigroup consists of all nonempty finite products of the listed generators. Their order matters, generators may be reused arbitrarily often, and there is no bound on the product length. Inverses are not automatically available. The identity matrix is an admissible target, but is accepted only if a nonempty product equals it. In particular the empty word is not a witness. The zero matrix and all rank-one matrices are also admissible as generators or targets. Duplicate generators are harmless. Allowing an empty input list would just add instances whose answer is always no.

Input uses explicit lists of all four entries of each matrix, encoded as signed binary integers with fixed length delimiters. The number of generators is part of the input and is unbounded. A decider means one deterministic Turing machine acting on these finite encodings, with no oracle or advice, which always terminates and gives the exact yes/no answer. No polynomial or other prescribed time bound is requested. The entries, generators and product length are not parameters that may be hardcoded into different machines.

Enumeration of all nonempty words gives a procedure that eventually accepts every positive instance. The requested decider must additionally terminate and reject when no product reaches the target. This is semigroup membership, not subgroup membership or membership in the topological closure of the generated set.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a decider exists, including termination and both directions of correctness, or a proof that this exact decision problem is undecidable. A semidecision procedure, a bound applying only to nonsingular matrices, or a solution for determinants restricted to 0 and plus or minus 1 is insufficient. No efficient complexity bound or explicit product witness is required for an affirmative answer.
context:
The 2019 account distinguishes decidability when all generators are nonsingular from decidability when every determinant is 0 or plus or minus 1. Neither restriction is imposed by this card.

General integer matrix membership becomes undecidable in dimension three, whereas the unrestricted dimension-two case is left open in the source.

The 2024 journal extension develops decidability for flat rational sets over specified matrix submonoids. Its Introduction still identifies open integer dimension-two problems, including mortality.

Those flat-set theorems constrain how matrices outside the underlying submonoid may occur. They do not provide a decider for unrestricted products of every possible integer generator.

Taking the target to be zero gives matrix mortality, a special case of this question. Taking an invertible target instead prevents singular factors from appearing in a successful product; allowing arbitrary targets is consequential.
why: Dimension two is a sharp unresolved boundary for exact reachability by integer matrix products. The combination of rank loss and determinant growth escapes algorithms for several important restricted matrix classes.
status_note: Source-open for unrestricted 2 by 2 integer matrices and nonempty products. The 2024 structured rational-set extensions do not remove the determinant and product-form restrictions needed to decide the general case. Bounded status review through 17 September 2026.
progress: 2019: The source records decidable determinant-restricted cases and states the general integer dimension-two problem as open. | 2024: The journal treatment extends structured rational-set decidability without claiming the unrestricted integer semigroup problem solved.
working_summary: The input is a finite list of integer matrices of size two by two and a target matrix of the same size. The question asks whether any nonempty finite product of the listed matrices equals the target exactly. Generators may repeat and may include both singular and nonsingular matrices with arbitrary determinants. The desired algorithm must terminate on every input, without any prescribed running-time bound. A complete Lean-checked decision procedure or undecidability proof must cover the unrestricted input class.

title: A qAC⁰ versus NL-complete dichotomy for Cayley semigroup membership
importance_reason: A broad algebraic complexity classification at the boundary of shallow circuits and nondeterministic logarithmic space, with a precise representation and fresh structural progress.
formal:
For every pseudovariety \(\mathcal V\) of finite semigroups, does its Cayley-table membership promise problem \(\operatorname{Memb}_{\mathrm{CT}}(\mathcal V)\), defined below, satisfy at least one of these two alternatives?
\[
\operatorname{Memb}_{\mathrm{CT}}(\mathcal V)\in\mathrm{qAC}^{0}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\operatorname{Memb}_{\mathrm{CT}}(\mathcal V)\text{ is NL-complete under uniform AC}^{0}\text{ many-one reductions}.
\]
Use uniform circuit classes and reductions that always output valid promised instances. The pseudovariety is fixed separately for each problem, not part of the input.
question_excerpt: The selected target is Question 39 of the STACS 2026 source already consolidated into this record. The 14 September 2026 full revision retains it as Question 41. It is a precise Cayley-table target within the older broader classification request. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: The qAC^0 versus NL-completeness dichotomy for Cayley-table semigroup membership.
definitions:
A finite semigroup is a nonempty finite set \(S\) equipped with an associative binary operation \(\cdot:S\times S\to S\). An identity element or inverses are not required. A pseudovariety is a nonempty isomorphism-closed class of finite semigroups closed under nonempty subsemigroups, homomorphic images and finite nonempty direct products. A homomorphism preserves multiplication, and multiplication in a direct product is coordinatewise. No effective description of the class is assumed.

An instance gives the full multiplication table of \(S=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), a nonempty set of generators \(\Sigma\subseteq S\), and a target \(t\in S\). Table entries and the target are binary indices of the same fixed width \(\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\); the generator set is given by its length-\(N\) incidence vector. Use a standard explicit length-delimited encoding of the dimension, table, vector and target, and let \(L\) be its total length. Thus the entire table, not a circuit or transformation representation of multiplication, is included in the input.

Write \(\langle\Sigma\rangle\) for all products \(s_1\cdots s_\ell\) with \(\ell\ge1\) and each \(s_i\in\Sigma\), allowing repetitions. The promise is that the supplied table is a semigroup and
\[
\langle\Sigma\rangle\in\mathcal V.
\]
The ambient semigroup \(S\) need not itself lie in \(\mathcal V\). A yes-instance has \(t\in\langle\Sigma\rangle\), and a no-instance satisfies the promise but has \(t\notin\langle\Sigma\rangle\). There is no required behavior on inputs violating the promise. Recognizing whether the generated semigroup belongs to \(\mathcal V\) is not part of this problem.

For this question, \(\mathrm{qAC}^{0}\) means Boolean circuits with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constant depth, and size at most
\[
2^{K(\log_2(L+2))^c}
\]
for some constants \(K,c\ge1\). They must be \(\mathrm{DTIME}(\operatorname{polylog}L)\)-uniform: a random-access deterministic Turing machine, given the binary input length and gate indices, determines gate types, input labels, output gates and wire incidence in time polynomial in \(\log(L+2)\). Circuit depth, size constants and the uniformity machine may depend on the fixed \(\mathcal V\), but not on an individual instance. The circuits must give the correct answer on every promised instance of length \(L\).

The class NL consists of languages decided by nondeterministic Turing machines with a read-only input and \(O(\log L)\) work space. NL membership for the promise problem requires correct acceptance and rejection on promised inputs. NL-hardness means that every NL language has a many-one reduction to it computed by \(\mathrm{DTIME}(\log L)\)-uniform, polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean circuits with the same gate types. Each reduction outputs a promised instance on every source input and preserves its answer. Equivalently it suffices to reduce directed graph reachability, with a specified start and target, under these reductions. NL-complete means both membership and hardness. No logarithmic-space reduction is substituted for the finer circuit reduction.

The question asks for the dichotomy for all fixed pseudovarieties. It does not ask for an algorithm which, given a description of a pseudovariety, selects an alternative.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the dichotomy, including the promised-input interpretation and uniform complexity bounds, or a proof of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must cover every pseudovariety. A negative proof must establish a pseudovariety whose promise problem is neither in the stated uniform qAC⁰ class nor NL-complete under the stated promise-preserving reductions. Classifying only groups, inverse semigroups or efficient-compression classes is insufficient.
context:
The Cayley table is an essential part of the target. Giving generators as transformations can succinctly describe a far larger semigroup and leads to a different complexity classification.

The 2026 work classifies pseudovarieties admitting short straight-line descriptions of generated elements. This gives qAC⁰ upper bounds for those classes, but the paper leaves the full membership dichotomy open.

General table membership is in NL: nondeterministically follow right multiplication by generators through the finite set of elements. The difficult classification distinguishes which promised classes also admit shallow quasipolynomial circuits.

The September revision retains uniformity and promises membership of the generated subsemigroup, not of the ambient table semigroup. These conventions are part of the card.

The older record also asked for a broad classification of arbitrary semigroup varieties. This card selects the concrete dichotomy rather than claiming to classify all representation models.
why: Finite semigroup membership ranges from very shallow parallel computation to directed reachability. A dichotomy would organize this complexity landscape by algebraic closure properties, extending the structural understanding beyond known compression-friendly classes.

The selected target is the Cayley-table dichotomy with uniform qAC⁰ and promise-preserving uniform AC⁰ hardness, not the older unrestricted classification across representation models. The target selection was an announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: The qAC^0 versus NL-completeness dichotomy for Cayley-table semigroup membership.

working_summary: The input gives a finite semigroup by its complete multiplication table, a generator set and a target element. The promise places the generated subsemigroup in one fixed pseudovariety, and the task is to test whether it contains the target. The question asks whether every such class has either uniform shallow quasipolynomial circuits or an NL-complete membership problem. Hardness uses uniform constant-depth polynomial-size reductions that preserve the input promise. The September 2026 source retains this dichotomy as open; a complete Lean-checked universal proof or counterexample is required.

title: Polynomial-time dimension expansion over finite fields
importance_reason: Dimension expansion is a basic algebraic analogue of graph expansion used in rank condensation, coding and pseudorandomness. Efficiently evaluating arbitrary input maps would separate constructive existence results from a general algorithmic understanding of the invariant.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given an explicitly represented finite field \(\mathbb F_q\), integers \(n\ge2,d\ge1\), and arbitrary matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_d\in\mathbb F_q^{n\times n}\), computes the rational number \[\alpha(A_1,\ldots,A_d)=\min_{\substack{V\le\mathbb F_q^n\\1\le\dim V\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}\frac{\dim(A_1V+\cdots+A_dV)}{\dim V}\] exactly? Polynomial time is measured in the total input bit length, uniformly over the field, dimension and number of maps. This is the finite-field polynomial-time branch of the source’s broader computation-complexity question.
definitions:
Write \(q=p^e\), where \(p\ge2\) is prime and \(e\ge1\). The field is supplied as \(\mathbb F_p[X]/(h(X))\), with a monic irreducible polynomial \(h(X)=X^e+\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h_jX^j\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). Its elements are the coefficient vectors of representatives of degree less than \(e\), with coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\); addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication modulo \(p\) and \(h\). Primality and irreducibility are promises, not extra input-search tasks. Fix the following bit encoding. Give \(n,d,e\) as three unary strings terminated by zero, then the bit length \(\ell\) of \(p\) in unary terminated by zero, then the \(\ell\)-bit ordinary binary expansion of \(p\). Give \(h_0,\ldots,h_{e-1}\), followed by the entries of \(A_1,\ldots,A_d\) in matrix order and row-major order, each residue coefficient as an \(\ell\)-bit unsigned block. Matrix entries use their \(e\) coefficients in increasing degree. Let \(L\) be the length of this complete representation. All arithmetic cost is bit cost; field operations are not free unit-cost oracle calls.

A subspace \(V\) is any linear subspace over this supplied field, not merely the span of a subset of coordinate vectors. \(A_iV=\{A_iv:v\in V\}\), and the sum \(A_1V+\cdots+A_dV\) is their linear span, not a union or the intersection of their images. All dimensions are over \(\mathbb F_q\). The range \(1\le\dim V\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) is nonempty because \(n\ge2\); the finite field makes the minimum range finite. Each candidate ratio has numerator between zero and \(n\) and denominator between one and \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Hence the output has a polynomial-length exact representation as a reduced nonnegative fraction with positive denominator, both in binary. No subspace attaining the minimum needs to be output. The original subspace is not automatically added to its image: \(V+\sum_iA_iV\) would be a different quantity unless an identity map were included. Matrices need not be invertible, contain the identity, be distinct, or already form an expander. The value can be below one, including zero; in that case the tuple meets none of the source’s expander conditions requiring an expansion factor at least one.

The algorithm is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, random bits or external oracles. Ask for constants \(C,c\ge1\) independent of \(p,e,n,d,h,A_i\) such that it halts on every valid promised input, returns the exact specified fraction and uses at most \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions, including preprocessing, field arithmetic and output. No claim for characteristic-zero fields or a black-box field representation is included.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked algorithm and proof of exact output and the stated uniform polynomial bit bound, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The numerical output here is part of an exact computational task; the question asks for polynomial-time solvability, not the value on one input. A construction of particular expanding matrix families, a spectral sufficient condition, or an approximation to a different expansion parameter does not meet this target. A hardness result under an additional unproved complexity assumption establishes only a conditional negative answer.
context:
Question 5 in the original paper asks for the complexity of computing the largest half-dimension expansion factor over a field. This card specifies its finite-field setting and asks the polynomial-time existence question. It is a documented branch of that broader question, not a claim that all field representations or exact running-time classifications are equivalent.

Definition 11 uses the span of all image subspaces. It reserves the word expander for factors at least one; the displayed minimum extends the evaluation task to arbitrary tuples, returning a value below one when no such factor exists.

The source develops explicit matrix families and rank-condensation constructions. Those guarantees concern the constructed families and do not themselves compute the optimum expansion of arbitrary input maps.

The 2025 work of Li, Qiao, Wigderson, Wigderson and Zhang separates dimension expansion from quantum expansion and compares linear-algebraic analogues of vertex, edge and spectral expansion. Its dimension parameter includes the original subspace and subtracts its dimension, so it must not be silently substituted for the original paper’s image-span ratio.
why: The expansion guarantee quantifies over every low-dimensional subspace, including subspaces with no coordinate description. Explicit constructions can prove that certain families expand without yielding an efficient procedure to evaluate arbitrary supplied matrices. The question asks whether this global algebraic property has a polynomial-time exact evaluation algorithm.
status_note: The broader computation question is open in the checked 2015 source. This card explicitly selects the finite-field polynomial-time branch. The checked 2025 structural paper does not settle that branch, and bounded later searches through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution; its present open status is not exhaustively certified.
progress: 2015: Forbes and Guruswami define dimension expanders in Definition 11 and ask about computing the largest half-dimension expansion factor in Section 5, Question 5. | 2025-04-12: Li and coauthors publish structural separations and comparisons among linear-algebraic expansion notions. The checked statements do not provide a general exact evaluator for the finite-field parameter in this card.
working_summary: Dimension expansion measures how much a collection of linear maps enlarges every subspace of dimension at most half the ambient dimension. This card asks for exact evaluation on arbitrary matrices over an explicitly represented finite field. The desired algorithm must use polynomial time in the complete input bit length, including the field representation. The output is the minimum ratio of image-span dimension to original dimension over all eligible nonzero subspaces. Explicit constructions and spectral expansion tests remain distinct from a general exact evaluator.

title: Explicit univariate arithmetic circuit lower bounds
importance_reason: A concrete explicit arithmetic lower-bound target that tests the strength of current algebraic complexity techniques.
formal: Does there exist a family \(f=(f_d)_{d\ge2}\in\mathcal E\) whose arithmetic circuit complexity over \(\mathbb C\) is not \(O(\log d)\)? Precisely, \[\exists f\in\mathcal E\ \forall K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall D\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge D:\ S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)>K\log_2 d.\] Every \(f_d\in\mathbb Z[x]\) has degree exactly \(d\); \(\mathcal E\) is the class with the uniform coefficient-bit algorithm and polynomial coefficient-length bound defined below. Circuits are unrestricted binary addition/multiplication circuits with arbitrary complex constants, and \(S_{\mathbb C}\) counts wires. This is a disclosed editorial specialization of Wigderson's Open Problem 12.1: it retains the not-\(O(\log d)\) threshold, selects the complex field permitted by the source, and makes explicitness precise using ITCS 2021 Definition 1.
definitions:
The index \(d\) ranges over all integers at least two. Write
\[f_d(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{d,i}x^i,\qquad a_{d,i}\in\mathbb Z,\quad a_{d,d}\ne0.\]
Integer coefficients are embedded in \(\mathbb C\) in the usual way. All identities are exact formal polynomial identities in \(\mathbb C[x]\).

An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output. Input nodes are labeled by \(x\) or arbitrary elements of \(\mathbb C\). Every other node has two operand slots and is labeled \(+\) or \(\times\), computing the sum or product of its operand polynomials. The operands may coincide, in which case both wires are counted. Intermediate results may be reused arbitrarily often. Only nodes used by the output are retained. Size is the total number of wires, equivalently twice the number of binary arithmetic gates. Define \(S_{\mathbb C}(g)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit computing \(g\); every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum exists.

Constant labels may depend on \(d\) and the circuit, with no restriction on magnitude, computability or binary length and no cost for constructing them. Their uses as operands contribute wires. There are no division, primitive power, comparison, branch, bit-extraction or coefficient-query gates. Negative constants permit subtraction to be expressed with the allowed operations. Depth, fan-out, intermediate degrees and intermediate coefficients are unrestricted; cancellation is permitted. Circuits are nonuniform: they may be chosen separately at each degree, without an algorithm constructing the sequence.

For \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(q\in\mathbb N\), define
\[\mathrm{query}(a,q)=\begin{cases}1,&q=0\text{ and }a<0,\\0,&q=0\text{ and }a\ge0,\\\lfloor |a|/2^{q-1}\rfloor\bmod2,&q\ge1.\end{cases}\]
Thus query zero is the sign bit, and queries \(1,2,\ldots\) give magnitude bits starting with the least significant bit. Zero has sign zero, and leading magnitude bits are zero.

The family belongs to \(\mathcal E\) if there exist fixed integers \(B,A,k\ge1\) and one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) such that, for all \(d\ge2\) and \(0\le i\le d\),
\[|a_{d,i}|<2^{d^B},\]
and, for every additional index \(0\le q\le d^B\), \(M\) on input \(\mathrm{bin}(d)\#\mathrm{bin}(i)\#\mathrm{bin}(q)\) outputs exactly \(\mathrm{query}(a_{d,i},q)\) within
\[A(1+\lceil\log_2 d\rceil)^k\]
steps. Binary representations have no leading zeroes, with zero represented by \(0\); \(\#\) is a separator. The coefficient bound permits at most \(d^B\) magnitude bits, and this query range includes them all and the sign. Every valid input therefore has length \(O_B(\log d)\). The same machine and constants work for every degree and query. They may depend on the family.

Here \(M\) is an ordinary deterministic multitape bit Turing machine: it has a fixed finite alphabet, a fixed finite number of work tapes initially blank and a read-only input tape; each transition reads and updates only the symbols under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Output is charged. No randomization, advice, oracle, unbounded-precision primitive or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. No behavior is required outside the stated valid query domain. Any fixed standard Turing-machine convention yields the same class because arbitrary fixed polynomial time bounds are allowed.

The explicitness requirement gives access to individual coefficient bits; it does not require printing whole coefficients or the entire coefficient list in time polynomial in \(\log d\). This bit-computation algorithm is separate from the complex arithmetic circuits whose size is measured. The target says that \(S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)/\log_2 d\) is unbounded on every tail, not that it tends to infinity at all sufficiently large degrees.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full logical negation \[\forall f\in\mathcal E\ \exists K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists D\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\ \forall d\ge D:\ S_{\mathbb C}(f_d)\le K\log_2 d.\] A positive answer must specify one family, its coefficient-query machine and constants \(B,A,k\), prove exact degree \(d\), coefficient lengths, and query correctness and running time, and prove the lower-bound quantifiers against all allowed complex-constant circuits. A negative answer must cover every family in \(\mathcal E\); its \(K,D\) may depend on the family, and its small circuits may vary nonuniformly with \(d\). Showing that one proposed family has small circuits does not refute this existential target. Mere nonconstructive existence, a lower bound only for restricted constants, formulas, bounded depth, monotone or noncommutative circuits, or a weighted sum-of-squares bound alone is insufficient. The target retains not-\(O(\log d)\), without demanding a stronger superpolylogarithmic or almost-everywhere bound. An implication from an additional unproved complexity assumption is conditional progress rather than an unconditional resolution.
context:
The original source contrasts the \(\Theta(\log d)\) complexity of \(x^d\), the \(O(d)\) upper bound for arbitrary degree-\(d\) polynomials and nonconstructive \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bounds before posing the explicit not-\(O(\log d)\) question.

The 2021 deterministic coefficient-bit definition makes a family efficiently specified while excluding descriptions whose coefficients require more than polynomially many bits in the degree.

The 2024 journal work connects strong weighted sum-of-squares lower bounds to broader algebraic complexity separations, but its support-sum measure and broader coefficient-bit explicitness differ from this wire-count target.

Raz's July 2026 revision proves new bounds for noncommutative circuits and certain noncommutative rings, which does not establish the present claim over the commutative complex field.

Narayanan's July 2026 preprint constructs vector-valued elusive curves and improves lower bounds at restricted depths, while identifying exponential curve degree as an obstruction to the desired general lower-bound consequence.
why: This target asks whether efficiently accessible integer coefficients force unrestricted arithmetic computation beyond the elementary logarithmic degree bound, even with one variable and arbitrary complex constants. A solution would expose a source of circuit hardness that survives sharing and cancellation, providing a focused test of algebraic lower-bound techniques.
status_note: Wigderson's 2018 Open Problem 12.1 asks for an explicitly described univariate family of size not O(log d), without fixing algorithmic explicitness. This card adopts the disclosed integer-coefficient, deterministic coefficient-bit specialization based on ITCS 2021 Definition 1, with arbitrary complex circuit constants. Status remains uncertain because no checked source explicitly certifies this same combined formulation as open; the search is not an exhaustive current-status audit.

working_summary: The question asks for a family of one-variable integer polynomials whose smallest arithmetic circuits cannot all be bounded by a constant times the logarithm of their degree. Each polynomial must have polynomially many bits per coefficient, with any requested coefficient bit and sign computable by one uniform algorithm in time polynomial in the logarithm of the degree. The competing circuits may share intermediate computations and use arbitrary complex constants for free, while every wire into a binary addition or multiplication gate contributes to their size. This explicitness requirement is a disclosed specialization of the original question, whose wording did not fix a coefficient-generation model. A resolution would clarify how far efficiently specified coefficients can force arithmetic complexity beyond the elementary degree bound in a single variable.

title: Bounded-interval zero testing for exponential-trigonometric polynomials
importance_reason: A precise computability boundary for linear differential systems, linking effective algebra and exact analytic reachability; the broader coefficient-field scope distinguishes it from algebraic-coefficient results.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every computable discrete subfield \(K\subseteq\mathbb R\) with a fixed effective presentation, there exists an algorithm which, given a constant-coefficient homogeneous linear differential equation with coefficients and initial values in \(K\), together with \(T\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), decides whether its unique solution \(f\) satisfies
\[
\exists t\in[0,T]\quad f(t)=0.
\]
The order of the equation is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The algorithm may depend on the presented field, but must halt correctly on every valid equation and endpoint over that field. No unproved number-theoretic hypothesis is assumed.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether bounded zero existence is decidable over an arbitrary computable discrete real subfield. Its input functions are specified by linear differential equations and initial values.
definitions:
A computable discrete subfield is a countable subfield \(K\subseteq\mathbb R\) equipped with a decidable set of integer codes \(D_K\subseteq\mathbb N\) and a surjective interpretation \(p_K:D_K\to K\). Codes need not be unique. Its presentation supplies computable operations on codes for addition and multiplication, a partial computable inverse defined exactly on codes of nonzero elements, and decidable equality of interpreted elements. Fixed codes for 0 and 1 are available. It also supplies a computable function \(E:D_K\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) such that
\[
|E(a,r)-p_K(a)|<2^{-r}.
\]
Thus both symbolic equality and arbitrarily accurate rational approximation are available. “Discrete” refers to effective exact equality, not to a discrete topology on \(K\). Negative elements can be found by enumerating codes and testing their sum with the given element for zero.

An instance gives an integer \(m\ge1\), codes for \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\in K\) and \(u_0,\ldots,u_{m-1}\in K\), and a nonnegative rational \(T\). These specify
\[
f^{(m)}(t)+c_1 f^{(m-1)}(t)+\cdots+c_m f(t)=0,
\qquad f^{(j)}(0)=u_j\quad(0\le j<m).
\]
The unique real solution is analytic on all of \(\mathbb R\). This differential-equation representation defines an exponential-trigonometric polynomial over \(K\) for this card; characteristic roots are not required to belong to \(K\), and no separate input representation of those complex roots is needed. The supplied order need not be minimal.

All codes, list lengths and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs are finite binary strings in a fixed length-delimited encoding. A decider is an ordinary deterministic Turing machine using the computable procedures of this fixed field presentation; there are no noncomputable oracles. It outputs 1 exactly when a real zero exists in the closed interval and outputs 0 otherwise. It must handle zeros at either endpoint, zeros without a sign change, identically zero solutions and \(T=0\). No quantitative running-time bound is requested.

The quantifiers are \(\forall\) fixed presented fields \(K\), \(\exists\) a decider \(A_K\), \(\forall\) valid finite instances over \(K\). A single algorithm taking arbitrary field presentations as additional input is not required. Conversely, choosing a new machine separately for each equation or each order is insufficient. The coefficient field need not contain \(\pi\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish termination and exact correctness for every valid input over every fixed presented field. A negative answer must exhibit a computable discrete subfield with a specified effective presentation for which the bounded zero problem is undecidable. Numerical approximations, a procedure that halts only on one answer, conditional decidability, or undecidability solely on an unbounded interval does not settle this question.
context:
The source’s field model supplies exact arithmetic, equality testing and a computable real embedding. Arbitrary computable real numbers without decidable equality would be a different input model.

The differential equation keeps all input data in the given field while allowing its solution to involve complex characteristic roots. The exact root expression is not additional advice.

For real algebraic coefficients and initial values, bounded zero existence is decidable assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. Theorem 3.5 uses factorization and control of repeated zeros. Its hypothesis remains essential to the stated result.

An even-multiplicity zero can occur without a sign change. This explains why testing finitely many sample signs alone does not prove exact correctness.

The 2026 article separates its unbounded-interval hardness results from this bounded-interval question, which it explicitly leaves open.
why: Exact zero detection is a basic reachability question for linear continuous dynamics. A bounded interval removes long-term behavior but still requires deciding tangential contact with zero, which numerical approximation alone need not certify.
status_note: Source-open as explicitly stated in MFCS 2026, Open Problem 1. The question retains every fixed computable discrete real coefficient field and arbitrary equation order. The algebraic-coefficient theorem depends on Schanuel’s conjecture, while the source’s unbounded-interval hardness is a separate result. Bounded review through 17 September 2026.
progress: 2023: Conditional bounded zero decidability is established for algebraic data in Theorem 3.5. | 2026-08-21: MFCS 2026 states the arbitrary computable discrete field version as Open Problem 1.
working_summary: The input specifies a linear differential equation with constant coefficients, initial values and a nonnegative rational endpoint. The task is to decide exactly whether its real solution has any zero in the closed bounded interval. The question ranges over every fixed computable real subfield with effective arithmetic, equality and rational approximation. A decider may depend on the field but must handle every equation order, including endpoint zeros and zeros without sign changes. A complete Lean-checked unconditional decidability proof or a field-specific undecidability counterexample is required.

title: Polynomial-time feasibility of integer min-plus linear systems
importance_reason: The complexity of tropical linear feasibility lies at an important boundary between algebra, optimization, and game solving.
formal:
Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that, given arbitrary integer matrices \(A=(a_{ij}),B=(b_{ij})\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with \(m,n\ge1\) and all entries in binary, decides in polynomial bit time whether there is \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfying
\[
\min_{1\le j\le n}(a_{ij}+x_j)
=\min_{1\le j\le n}(b_{ij}+x_j)
\qquad(1\le i\le m)?
\]
question_excerpt: Grigoriev asks for polynomial complexity in the two matrix dimensions and the logarithm of the integer coefficient bound, for min-plus equations over the integers.
definitions:
The additions and the order used in each minimum are ordinary integer addition and order. Each row imposes equality of its two minimum values; a minimum may be attained at one or several indices. This is the min-plus equality presentation of the source question. It does not impose the different tropical convention that each single minimum be attained at least twice.

All coefficients and all solution coordinates must be finite integers. The value \(+\infty\) is not an allowed coefficient or solution coordinate. Both matrix dimensions vary with the input. Matrices are given explicitly by all their entries, each as a signed binary integer, with fixed length delimiters for the entries and dimensions. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length.

The target is one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(D\) and constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) such that every valid input is processed within \(K(L+1)^a\) steps, and the output is 1 exactly when an integer solution exists. There is no randomness, advice or oracle. The machine and constants are independent of \(m,n,A,B\). Arithmetic is charged at its actual bit cost, not as unit-cost operations on unbounded integers.

Equivalently for these dense inputs, the time must be polynomial in \(m,n,\log_2(H+2)\), where \(H=\max_{i,j}\{|a_{ij}|,|b_{ij}|\}\). A time bound polynomial in \(H\) itself is not sufficient. No strongly polynomial bound independent of coefficient bit length is requested. The output is a feasibility decision; the full solution set, its dimension, or the number of solutions is not requested.

Adding a common integer to every coordinate of a solution preserves all equalities, so feasibility has no prescribed coordinate normalization. Negative coordinates are allowed. Unsatisfiable instances must be rejected within the same running-time bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that the stated feasibility language is in deterministic polynomial time, or a proof that it is not. A positive answer must establish exact equivalence to integer feasibility, termination and the polynomial bit bound. Pseudopolynomial algorithms, a result with a fixed matrix dimension, or numerical approximate feasibility do not suffice.
context:
The source distinguishes polynomial dependence on the numeric coefficient bound from polynomial dependence on its logarithm. Only the latter resolves the binary-input target.

Integer min-plus feasibility, tropical linear solvability and mean-payoff games are polynomial-time equivalent in the cited work. Their syntactic definitions still differ.

The feasibility problem lies in NP and coNP. Those certificate bounds do not give the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm asked for.

The July 2026 account again states polynomial complexity in binary weight length as open. Its graph-class reduction transfers the problem instead of supplying the missing solver.

This card retains the source’s finite-integer equality model. The corresponding game formulation is recorded separately in TCS-6568; the connection is an equivalence of algorithmic questions.
why: Min-plus linear equations connect algebraic feasibility to two-player mean-payoff games. The challenge is to obtain a running time polynomial in the written input rather than in the magnitudes of its coefficients.
status_note: Source-open for exact integer min-plus feasibility in deterministic polynomial bit time. The July 2026 primary source still identifies the corresponding tropical/mean-payoff binary-weight problem as open. Finite integers and the equality presentation are retained; pseudopolynomial algorithms do not answer this target. Checked through 17 September 2026.
progress: 2012: The preprint relates integer tropical and min-plus feasibility to mean-payoff games. | 2015: The Dagstuhl question explicitly asks for polynomial dependence on coefficient bit length. | 2026-07-26: The newer tropical-algebra account retains this algorithmic gap.
working_summary: Each input row equates two minima of integer coefficients plus unknown integer coordinates. The question asks whether a single deterministic algorithm can decide feasibility in polynomial time. Time is measured in the full binary input length, with both matrix dimensions allowed to grow. The problem is polynomial-time equivalent to mean-payoff games, while known pseudopolynomial bounds depend on coefficient magnitudes. An answer must include a complete Lean-checked polynomial-bit-time decider or a proof that none exists.

title: VP factor closure in positive characteristic
importance_reason: Closure under factors in positive characteristic would clarify a basic structural property of arithmetic complexity classes.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) closed under polynomial factors for every field \(F\) of positive characteristic? Explicitly, quantify first over every prime \(p\), every field \(F\) with \(\operatorname{char}(F)=p\), every function \(m:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\), and every two polynomial families
\[
f_n,g_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
Does the following implication always hold?
\[
\begin{split}
&\left[\ \forall n\ge1,\ f_n\ne0\text{ and }g_n\mid f_n\ \right]\\
&\quad\land\left[\ \exists A,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
\max\{m(n),\deg(f_n),L_F(f_n)\}\le A(n+1)^k\ \right]\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow\left[\ \exists B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
L_F(g_n)\le B(n+1)^{\ell}\ \right]?
\end{split}
\]
Here \(L_F\) is exact algebraic circuit size as defined below, and degree means total degree. The field is fixed throughout each family. Constants in the polynomial bounds may depend on the field and the families but not on \(n\). There is no restriction on factor multiplicities, including multiplicities divisible by \(p\).
definitions:
A field has characteristic \(p\) when \(p\) is the smallest positive integer such that the sum of \(p\) copies of \(1_F\) is zero. The statement includes finite and infinite fields, including fields that are not perfect or algebraically closed. A field of characteristic \(p\) is perfect if every element has a \(p\)-th root in that same field. This property is not an assumption of the question.

The variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}\) commute. Polynomial equality and divisibility are identities in the formal polynomial ring over \(F\), not equality only as functions on \(F^{m(n)}\). Thus \(g_n\mid f_n\) means that some \(h_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\) satisfies the identity \(f_n=g_nh_n\). The requirement \(f_n\ne0\) implies that both factors are nonzero. Constant factors and the whole polynomial are allowed. For a nonzero polynomial, total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; nonzero constants have degree zero. The ring with zero variables is \(F\). Since \(F\) is a field and \(f_n\ne0\), a divisor has total degree at most \(\deg(f_n)\).

An algebraic circuit over \(F\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output gate. An input gate is labeled by a variable or by any element of \(F\). Every other gate has two ordered input positions, each referencing an earlier gate in a topological ordering, and is labeled by addition or multiplication. A predecessor may be used in both input positions. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same intermediate polynomial may be reused. Evaluation is formal addition and multiplication in \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\). The circuit size is the total number of gates, including variable and constant gates. The quantity \(L_F(u)\) is the minimum such size among circuits computing \(u\) exactly.

No division, root-extraction, oracle or approximation gates are allowed. Arbitrary constants from the fixed base field each occupy one constant gate; their bit descriptions or computability are not charged. This is algebraic size complexity, not bit complexity. A circuit can equivalently be recorded as a topologically ordered finite list of gate labels and predecessor indices. The representation carries actual field elements as labels and is not required to encode them as finite binary strings. There is no restriction on circuit depth or on degrees of intermediate gates, and no randomness or permitted error in the circuit's output.

A family belongs to \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) when its number of variables, output total degree and minimum circuit size have polynomial bounds in the family index, precisely as in the antecedent. The circuits for distinct indices may be unrelated: neither the circuit family nor its field constants must be generated uniformly. The desired circuits for \(g_n\) are over the same \(F\), and may use any constants from \(F\). The target is the existence of a polynomial-size circuit family for every factor family. It does not request a deterministic or randomized algorithm producing those circuits from circuits for \(f_n\), a common exponent valid for every field and family, or a complete factorization as an algorithmic output.

For a nonconstant irreducible polynomial \(u\), its multiplicity in a nonzero polynomial \(f\) is the largest integer \(e\ge0\) for which \(u^e\mid f\). The question includes every choice of a divisor, with any collection of such multiplicities permitted by \(f_n\). No square-free, separability or multiplicity-coprime-to-characteristic promise is imposed.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed universal implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish a polynomial bound for circuits computing the actual factor family over the same base field, for every admissible family and every field of positive characteristic. A negative answer must establish a fixed positive-characteristic field and admissible families with \((f_n)\in\mathrm{VP}_{F}\), \(g_n\mid f_n\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\forall B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge1,\quad L_F(g_n)>B(n+1)^{\ell}.
\]
No efficient method for generating a counterexample family is additionally required. A bound only for a positive-characteristic power of the factor, a circuit over an extension field without a proved return to the base field, or membership in a larger class does not settle the question. A proof of the failure of one factoring algorithm is not a refutation of this nonuniform closure statement.
context:
Kaltofen established the corresponding factor closure in characteristic zero. The source question asks whether this structural property of \(\mathrm{VP}\) persists without that characteristic restriction. Polynomial bounds on the original family’s output degree are part of the question; low-degree factors of circuits whose outputs have unbounded degree form a different, stronger factoring problem.

The source defines \(\mathrm{VP}\) as a nonuniform family class over a fixed field. This card expands that definition into explicit quantifiers. It makes the conventional exclusion of zero input polynomials and the requirement of formal polynomial identity explicit. Binary addition and multiplication gates fix a concrete size convention; the survey’s unrestricted-fan-in circuit convention gives the same polynomial-size class. These are declared modeling refinements, not a restriction to finite fields or a demand for a uniform factoring algorithm.

In characteristic \(p\), the identity \((a+b)^p=a^p+b^p\) creates a distinction between obtaining a small circuit for a factor and obtaining one for its \(p\)-power. Known positive-characteristic statements can retain such powers or enlarge the constant field. The present target requires the original factor over the original field, with arbitrary multiplicities.

The original June 2025 survey poses Question 3 on page 27. Its revision of 12 June 2026 retains the question as Open Problem 4.4.1 on page 29, after adding newer formula and bounded-depth factoring results. The finite-field result placing factors in \(\mathrm{VNP}\) is relevant partial progress, but does not assert the requested membership in \(\mathrm{VP}\).
why: Factor closure asks whether multiplication can conceal a polynomial that is substantially harder to compute than the resulting product, even when all output degrees remain polynomially bounded. It is a structural question about the standard class of efficiently computable polynomial families. Its positive-characteristic form is also relevant to the scope of algebraic hardness-versus-randomness results, where extracting factors from circuit identities connects lower bounds with polynomial identity testing.
status_note: The original Question 3 remains explicitly open as Open Problem 4.4.1 in the survey revision accepted 12 June 2026. Checked finite-field VNP closure and recent small-characteristic factoring theorems do not give the required VP circuits for the actual factors over the same arbitrary base field. Individual primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated source-open assessment, not exhaustive verification of present-day openness or of all cited proofs.
progress: 2020: Andrews proves a circuit-size bound \(3sp^{2r}+2^r\) for extracting a \(p\)-th root from a size-\(s\) circuit on \(r\) variables, over the perfect closure of the base field. This is polynomial in \(s\) when \(r=O(\log_p s)\); it does not give polynomial overhead for unrestricted polynomially many variables. | 2024: Bhargav, Dwivedi and Saxena prove factor closure for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over every finite field. Consequently, factors of \(\mathrm{VP}\) families over finite fields belong to \(\mathrm{VNP}\). This larger-class conclusion leaves the requested \(\mathrm{VP}\) closure unresolved. | 2025-06-28: Bhattacharjee and coauthors prove formula and bounded-depth circuit factor closure in characteristic zero. Their small-characteristic statement yields powers \(g^{p^{\ell}}\) of factors. A companion result places these powers over a sufficiently large base finite field, retaining the distinction between the power and the factor itself. | 2026-06-12: The revised Bhargav–Dwivedi–Saxena survey explicitly retains positive-characteristic \(\mathrm{VP}\) factor closure as Open Problem 4.4.1.
working_summary: VP consists of polynomial families whose variable count, output degree and algebraic circuit size are polynomially bounded. The question asks whether every factor family of a nonzero VP family also belongs to VP over each fixed field of positive characteristic. Circuits are nonuniform, may use arbitrary constants from that same field, and must compute the formal polynomials exactly. The target includes arbitrary factor multiplicities, whereas several known small-characteristic results compute only powers of factors or place the factors in a larger complexity class. A complete Lean proof must establish this universal closure or exhibit a fixed-field factor family without any polynomial circuit-size bound.

title: VBP factor closure in positive characteristic
importance_reason: Closure under factors in positive characteristic would clarify a basic structural property of arithmetic complexity classes.
formal:
For every field \(F\) of positive characteristic, do there exist a real constant \(K_F>0\) and an integer \(a_F\ge1\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) and all nonzero polynomials \(f,g\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) with \(g\mid f\),
\[
\operatorname{ABP}_F(g)\le
K_F\bigl(\operatorname{ABP}_F(f)+n+1\bigr)^{a_F}?
\]
Here \(\operatorname{ABP}_F\) denotes minimum size of a commutative arithmetic branching program over the same field \(F\), as defined below. Factors of arbitrary multiplicity are included. The constants may depend on the fixed field, but not on the polynomials, their coefficients, the number of variables, or their degrees.
question_excerpt: The revised survey explicitly asks whether VBP is closed under taking factors over fields of positive characteristic. The card retains the full field scope and all factors, and spells out the nonuniform size guarantee and the dependence on the fixed field.
definitions:
A field \(F\) has positive characteristic if there is a prime \(p\) for which the sum of \(p\) copies of its multiplicative identity is zero. The question quantifies over all such fields, finite or infinite, with no perfectness or algebraic-closure assumption. The same field is used for the input polynomial, its factors and every branching-program coefficient. No extension of the field is permitted in the conclusion.

An arithmetic branching program is a finite layered directed acyclic graph with a distinguished source in its first layer and a distinguished sink in its last layer. The source and sink are distinct. Each edge goes from one layer to the next and is labeled by an affine linear polynomial
\[
c_0+c_1x_1+\cdots+c_nx_n\qquad(c_i\in F).
\]
There is at most one edge between any ordered pair of vertices. The polynomial of a path from source to sink is the product of its edge labels, and the output polynomial is the sum of these products over all such paths. Variables commute throughout. Edge labels can include constants or the zero polynomial; an empty path sum is zero. There are no division, root, approximation or test gates. Width and number of layers are unrestricted, and a variable may occur on many edges and repeatedly along a path.

Size is the total number of vertices. A size-\(s\) program has at most \(s^2\) edges and \((n+1)s^2\) coefficient positions, so linear labels do not hide an exponential description. All constants are arbitrary elements of \(F\), with no bit-description charge. Counting coefficients or replacing affine labels by individual constant/variable edges changes the relevant bounds by polynomial factors. A path has at most \(s-1\) edges, so a nonzero output has total degree at most \(s-1\). Layering a general acyclic branching program also costs only polynomial size.

The value \(\operatorname{ABP}_F(h)\) is the minimum vertex count of any such program computing the formal polynomial \(h\) exactly. It is finite, since a polynomial is a finite sum of monomials. Polynomial equality is coefficientwise equality, not equality merely on points of a finite field. The divisibility condition \(g\mid f\) means that \(f=gh\) for some polynomial \(h\) over \(F\) in the same commuting variables. The input \(f\) is nonzero to exclude the vacuous fact that every polynomial divides zero. A constant factor is allowed, as are products of distinct irreducible factors and repeated factors. No circuit for the complementary factor is supplied or assumed small.

For a fixed field, \(\mathrm{VBP}_F\) is the class of polynomial families in polynomially many variables admitting polynomial-size arithmetic branching programs, with no uniformity requirement. Their degrees are automatically polynomially bounded by their sizes. The displayed statement expresses closure of this class under taking factors. It is an existence assertion for small programs, not a request for a deterministic or randomized factoring algorithm, and it does not ask for bounds uniform over changing fields. A bound for unrestricted arithmetic circuits computing the factor would not establish an ABP bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal factor-size assertion or of its logical negation. A positive proof must cover each fixed positive-characteristic field and all multiplicities, and return a branching-program size bound over that same field. A negative proof must establish a fixed field for which no polynomial size overhead works; merely showing that one factoring procedure fails is insufficient. Characteristic-zero closure, a theorem restricted to square-free inputs or favorable multiplicities, field-extension results, and unrestricted-circuit factor bounds do not settle the stated question.
context:
The sum over paths lets a small graph represent a polynomial with many monomials. A factor may have a much less obvious path representation, so its degree bound alone does not give a polynomial-size branching program.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure in characteristic zero. Their main theorem concerns all factors and a polynomial ABP-size bound; the underlying field assumption is essential to interpreting the theorem.

In characteristic p, derivatives of p-th powers vanish. The factoring manuscript explains that this obstructs reducing certain repeated factors to multiplicity one and may leave a power of a desired factor instead of the factor itself.

The June 2026 survey still lists positive-characteristic VBP factor closure as open. Its discussion of newer factor-closure techniques retains a qualification involving powers of the characteristic.

The separate p-th-root circuit card concerns unrestricted circuits and a degree-independent size bound over algebraically closed fields. This card concerns branching programs, whose degree is bounded by their path length, and retains all positive-characteristic fields.
why: Branching programs are a central algebraic model between formulas and unrestricted circuits. Understanding whether taking factors preserves their polynomial size in positive characteristic would complete an important structural closure property beyond the characteristic-zero theorem.
status_note: Source-open in the 12 June 2026 survey revision, Open Problem 4.5.1. The established ABP factor-closure theorem is stated for characteristic zero; the author manuscript identifies a repeated-factor obstruction to unrestricted positive-characteristic closure. The card preserves all fixed positive-characteristic fields, exact factors over the same field and all multiplicities. No resolution was found in bounded checks through 17 September 2026.

working_summary: The question asks whether taking any factor preserves polynomial-size commutative arithmetic branching programs in every fixed field of positive characteristic. A branching program sums products of affine edge labels along its source-to-sink paths. The factor must have a small program over the original field, including when its multiplicity is divisible by the characteristic. This is a nonuniform existence question and does not require an efficient factorization algorithm. A complete Lean-checked polynomial size bound or a counterexample field and superpolynomial factor-size separation is required.

title: Polynomial-time sign testing of matrix powers in every fixed dimension
importance_reason: A focused exact-arithmetic complexity question connected to recurrence positivity and succinct integer computation; it distinguishes fixed-dimensional spectral methods from general arithmetic circuits.
formal:
