Is it true that for every fixed integer dimension \(d\ge1\), there is a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm which, given matrices \(M,W\in\mathbb Z^{d\times d}\) and an exponent \(n\ge0\), all in binary, decides whether
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d} W_{ij}(M^n)_{ij}\ge0?
\]
The algorithm and the degree of its polynomial running-time bound may depend on \(d\), but not on the entries of \(M,W\) or on \(n\).
question_excerpt: The source leaves the complexity of PosMatPow in higher dimensions open. This card selects deterministic polynomial bit time separately for each fixed dimension, with all entries and the exponent in binary. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: A deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm for every fixed matrix dimension, with exponent allowed to depend on dimension.
definitions:
Matrix multiplication is the usual operation over the integers, and \(M^0=I_d\). The input matrix \(W\) represents the integer linear functional \(f_W(X)=\sum_{i,j}W_{ij}X_{ij}\). Its coefficients are arbitrary signed integers, just like those of \(M\). The decision concerns this one scalar value at the supplied exponent, not entrywise nonnegativity of every matrix power or positive semidefiniteness.

For each fixed \(d\), encode \(M\) and \(W\) by their full lists of signed binary entries and encode \(n\) in binary, using fixed length delimiters. Let \(L\) be the total bit length of this representation. The statement asks for
\[
\forall d\ge1\ \exists A_d\ \exists K_d>0\ \exists a_d\in\mathbb N\ \forall(M,W,n):
\operatorname{time}_{A_d}(M,W,n)\le K_d(L+1)^{a_d},
\]
with the stated exact yes/no output. Each \(A_d\) is a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine without advice, randomness or an oracle. It must handle singular matrices, negative entries, repeated eigenvalues and exact zero values. Every arithmetic operation is charged at its bit cost. The output is a single bit; neither \(M^n\) nor \(f_W(M^n)\) must be printed in full.

The quantifiers impose no common exponent \(a_d\), no common multiplicative constant \(K_d\), and no effective procedure for converting \(d\) into the code of \(A_d\). They ask for polynomial-time membership separately in every fixed dimension. Requiring one polynomial-time machine for all input dimensions would be a stronger target. Conversely, fixing \(M\) or \(W\) in addition to \(d\) would be weaker than this question. The case \(n=0\) is included by the identity convention and is directly decidable.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must provide the algorithms and polynomial bit-time analyses for every fixed dimension. A negative proof must establish a fixed dimension at which no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists. An arithmetic-operation bound with unit-cost unbounded integers, a unary exponent algorithm, or a result only for matrices whose entries are supplied in unary does not establish the requested statement.
context:
The source proves polynomial-time decidability in dimension two with binary data. Its dimension-three theorem requires the base matrix in unary, while the exponent and functional remain binary.

Repeated squaring uses few matrix multiplications but can create exponentially long integers. A polynomial arithmetic-operation count therefore does not by itself answer the bit-complexity question.

The 2017 paper records a reduction of general PosMatPow to integer arithmetic-circuit sign testing, PosSLP, and hence an upper bound in the counting hierarchy. This is not a deterministic polynomial-time upper bound.

That paper also uses PosMatPow hardness in the study of counting words with prescribed letter multiplicities. Its general-dimension application should not be mistaken for a lower bound ruling out this fixed-dimension target.

The selected statement asks about a single input exponent. Universal nonnegativity over all exponents is a different recurrence problem.
why: Matrix powering compactly describes integers with exponentially many output bits. Deciding one exact sign tests whether low-dimensional algebraic structure permits efficient computation without expanding those integers.
status_note: Source-open for deterministic polynomial bit time in every fixed dimension with binary matrix and functional entries. The dimension-three theorem cited in the source assumes a unary base matrix. The per-dimension polynomial-time target is an announced editorial precisification of the broader source question. Bounded status review through 17 September 2026. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: A deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm for every fixed matrix dimension, with exponent allowed to depend on dimension.
progress: 2015: The source proves the dimension-two result and the unary-base-matrix dimension-three result, then asks about higher dimensions. | 2017: PosMatPow is used as a hardness benchmark for counting problems, with its exact complexity still left open.
working_summary: The input specifies an integer matrix, an integer linear functional and a nonnegative binary exponent. The task is to decide whether applying the functional to that matrix power gives a nonnegative integer. The question asks for deterministic polynomial bit time separately in every fixed matrix dimension. The polynomial bound may depend on the dimension, while all matrix and functional entries remain part of the binary input. A complete Lean-checked affirmative algorithmic proof or a fixed-dimensional impossibility proof is required.

title: Exact Kronecker-polytope membership in polynomial time
importance_reason: Kronecker-polytope membership connects representation-theoretic geometry with computational complexity.
formal:
Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm which, given three partitions \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) of the same positive integer \(k\), each as a list of \(n\) nonnegative binary integers, decides whether
\[
\left(\frac{\lambda}{k},\frac{\mu}{k},\frac{\nu}{k}\right)\in\Delta_n,
\]
where \(\Delta_n\) is the Kronecker polytope defined below? The dimension \(n\) is part of the input, and membership is exact, including points on the boundary.
question_excerpt: Bürgisser asks for polynomial-time membership when the three partitions have a varying number of binary-encoded parts. The source already records membership in NP and coNP.
definitions:
A partition in this representation is a list \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\) of integers with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=k\). Trailing zeros are allowed. The lists \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) obey the same conditions and have the same sum. Division by \(k\) is coordinatewise. All entries and list lengths use binary encoding with fixed length delimiters; the complete lists are given explicitly. Let \(L\) be the total input bit length. In particular the number of parts grows with the input, while \(k\) may be exponentially large relative to its bit length.

Here is a self-contained spectral definition of \(\Delta_n\). For an array \(z=(z_{abc})_{a,b,c=1}^n\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1\), form three \(n\times n\) matrices
\[
R^{(1)}_{aa'}=\sum_{b,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{a'bc}},\quad
R^{(2)}_{bb'}=\sum_{a,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{ab'c}},\quad
R^{(3)}_{cc'}=\sum_{a,b}z_{abc}\overline{z_{abc'}}.
\]
The bar denotes complex conjugation. These matrices are Hermitian positive semidefinite and have trace 1. Write \(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R)\) for the length-\(n\) list of real eigenvalues, with multiplicity, in nonincreasing order. Define
\[
\Delta_n=\left\{
\bigl(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(1)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(2)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(3)})\bigr):
z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n},\ \sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1
\right\}.
\]
This is the usual rational convex Kronecker polytope. The spectral definition is equivalent to the representation-theoretic definition in the source and specifies the question without requiring a representation-theory oracle. The tensor \(z\) is existentially quantified in the definition; it is not part of the input, need not have rational coordinates and need not be output by the algorithm.

The target algorithm is one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(A\) with constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which halts on every valid input within \(K(L+1)^d\) steps and returns the exact membership bit. There is no advice, randomness, supplied list of facets, or oracle. All integer and rational arithmetic has its actual bit cost. No positive distance from the boundary is promised and no additive tolerance is allowed. A different precomputed algorithm for each fixed \(n\) is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that this exact membership language is in deterministic polynomial time, or a proof that it is not. A positive answer must establish the full variable-dimension bit bound and exact correctness on boundary points. An approximate tensor-scaling result polynomial in inverse error, a nondeterministic certificate bound, or a fixed-dimension polytope computation does not suffice.
context:
The original question varies the number of parts. Fixing the dimension would permit precomputation of a single polytope and would miss the requested uniform complexity.

The certificate theorem gives polynomially verifiable evidence for both membership and nonmembership. It does not supply a deterministic polynomial-time search for those certificates.

Membership corresponds to positivity after some common positive integer stretching of the three partitions. Positivity of the single unstretched Kronecker coefficient is a different problem.

The spectral model identifies the polytope with triples of reduced-state eigenvalue lists of a pure tripartite state. This gives an exact analytic formulation of the same input question.

The 2025 treatment records tensor-scaling time polynomial in inverse tolerance and a separation bound involving the partition denominator and dimension-dependent facet sizes. Combining them does not yield a polynomial bound in the binary input length.
why: Kronecker polytopes connect representation-theoretic multiplicities with possible spectra of quantum subsystems. Exact efficient membership would go beyond known certificate bounds and numerical scaling methods while avoiding the harder task of evaluating individual multiplicities.
status_note: Source-open for exact Kronecker-polytope membership with a varying number of binary parts. NP and coNP certificates are known; the inspected tensor-scaling and explicit-polytope results do not establish this deterministic polynomial-bit-time target. Bounded status review through 17 September 2026.
progress: 2015: The Dagstuhl question asks for a polynomial-time algorithm beyond NP and coNP certificates. | 2017: The revised certificate paper proves the NP and coNP upper bounds and the spectral membership formulation. | 2025-10-09: The later computational treatment gives explicit polytope methods and explains scaling precision needed for exact certification.
working_summary: The input consists of three integer partitions of the same size, written as binary lists whose length may grow. The task is to decide exact membership of their normalized triple in the Kronecker polytope. Equivalently, the three lists must occur as spectra of the reduced matrices of some unit complex three-dimensional array. The desired algorithm is deterministic and polynomial in the full bit length, including arbitrarily close boundary cases. A complete Lean-checked complexity proof must go beyond known certificates and algorithms whose time depends polynomially on inverse approximation error.

title: Efficient LRS evaluation
importance_reason: A substantive complexity or decidability question for a standard quantitative, timed, string, or language model.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm that, given a rational linear recurrence and a nonnegative index \(n\) in binary, decides whether its \(n\)-th term is exactly zero in time polynomial in the total input bit length? Both the recurrence and its initial values are part of the input, and its order is unrestricted.
question_excerpt: Clemente asks for polynomial-time testing of a rational recurrence term at a binary-encoded index. This review makes the varying recurrence and deterministic bit model explicit. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Both the rational recurrence and binary index are input to one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm.
definitions:
An input consists of an integer \(k\ge1\), rational numbers \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\) and \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), and an integer \(n\ge0\). They define the unique sequence \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) by
\[
f(i)=u_i\quad(0\le i<k),\qquad
f(t+k)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}c_i f(t+i)\quad(t\ge0).
\]
The supplied order need not be minimal; zero coefficients, repeated characteristic roots and degenerate recurrences are allowed.

Integers are encoded in binary, with a sign bit when needed. Each rational is a reduced numerator/positive-denominator pair. Use a fixed explicit length-delimited encoding for the two lists and all integers, and let \(L\) be its total length. In particular, \(n\) is not written in unary and the coefficient and initial-value bit lengths count toward \(L\).

The quantified algorithm is a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(M\). There must be constants \(K>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N\) such that on every valid input it halts within \(K(L+1)^a\) steps and outputs 1 if and only if \(f(n)=0\). The machine and both constants are independent of \(k\), all rational data and \(n\). No randomness, advice or oracle is supplied. Arithmetic operations must be implemented and charged at their actual bit cost.

Only a decision bit is required, not the value \(f(n)\). For example, the sequence \(f(n)=2^n\) can require exponentially many output bits relative to the length of its index, without making its zero test difficult. The question concerns the specified index alone: it does not ask whether a zero exists at some index below \(n\), or anywhere in the sequence.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence of the stated deterministic polynomial-bit-time decider, including correctness and the uniform running-time bound, or a proof of its logical negation. A polynomial arithmetic-operation count with unbounded unit-cost integers, a randomized decider, or a separate hardcoded algorithm for each fixed recurrence does not establish the affirmative statement.
context:
Binary addressing makes generating every preceding term potentially exponential in the input length. The formal target therefore counts all coefficient bits and allows the order to vary.

Repeated matrix squaring gives a small arithmetic circuit for an indexed integer term. Testing its output for zero lies in coRP. This randomized result does not give the deterministic algorithm requested here.

Editorial extension to rational inputs: maintain numerator and nonzero denominator as integer arithmetic circuits at each rational gate. The numerator zero test preserves the same randomized upper bound.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech description of zero sets implies, for each fixed recurrence separately, an efficient test with its finite exceptional set and arithmetic progressions hardcoded. This editorial implication does not provide a uniform way to obtain that data.

The SODA 2026 bounded Skolem result instead searches an interval and has a fixed-order randomized polynomial bound. Its quantifiers differ from this single-index deterministic question.
why: A single term of a rational recurrence has a compact arithmetic representation even when its expanded numerator is enormous. This question isolates whether exact zero testing for that representation can be performed efficiently without randomness.
status_note: Source-open for the specified uniform deterministic bit model. Randomized circuit zero testing and fixed-sequence nonuniform existence do not resolve this formulation. The source’s short question is made precise by an announced editorial default, not an unreceived user confirmation. Status checked through 17 September 2026. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Both the rational recurrence and binary index are input to one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm.
progress: 2025-07-01: Clemente contributes the binary-index evaluation question. | 2026: The SODA paper records randomized arithmetic-circuit zero testing as a subroutine for recurrence problems.
working_summary: The input gives a rational linear recurrence, its initial values and an index written in binary. The target is one deterministic algorithm that decides whether exactly that indexed term is zero. Its running time must be polynomial in the combined input bit length, including the recurrence order and coefficient descriptions. Randomized testing of a compact arithmetic representation is known, while printing the full term may take exponentially many bits. An answer must provide a complete Lean-checked uniform algorithm and time analysis or prove that no such algorithm exists.

title: Does real Zariski-closure membership belong to ∃R?
importance_reason: Pinning down the complexity of this concrete realizability problem would extend the map of real-algebraic computation; the individual variant is narrower than a general model separation.
formal:
Does the following language belong to \(\exists\mathbb R\)? An input is a quantifier-free Boolean formula \(\varphi\) in real variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), with explicitly encoded integer polynomial equations and inequalities. It is accepted exactly when
\[
0\in\overline{S_\varphi}^{\,Z},\qquad
S_\varphi=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\varphi(x)\}.
\]
Here \(\overline{S_\varphi}^{\,Z}\) is the real Zariski closure. The target is a deterministic polynomial-bit-time many-one reduction to the existential theory of the reals, for arbitrary input dimension and polynomial degree.
question_excerpt: Entry A37 asks for the complexity of the Zariski version of adherence. This card selects the concrete membership-in-∃R target, with finite-bit input and an explicit polynomial representation. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Membership in existential real arithmetic for finite binary inputs to real Zariski-closure membership.
definitions:
The input specifies an integer \(n\ge1\) and a finite formula tree built with AND, OR and NOT from atoms \(p(x)=0\) and \(p(x)>0\). Thus weak inequalities and disequalities can also be expressed. Each \(p\in\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is given by a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an exponent vector in \(\mathbb N^n\). Exponents and the declared dimension are written in unary; use an explicit length-delimited encoding for lists and the formula. Repeated monomials are added with their displayed coefficients. Let \(L\) be the complete binary encoding length, including all coefficients, exponents and Boolean connectives. No polynomial is supplied as a succinct arithmetic circuit. There is no fixed bound on dimension, degree, coefficient size or formula size.

For any \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\overline S^{\,Z}=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:
\forall p\in\mathbb R[X_1,\ldots,X_n],
[(\forall x\in S,\ p(x)=0)\Rightarrow p(z)=0]\}.
\]
The universal quantifier in this definition ranges over all finite real-coefficient polynomials, with no degree bound. It is a mathematical definition, not an additional part of the input. The closure is taken in real affine space. In particular the closure of the empty set is empty. The question concerns the origin, whose coordinates need not be supplied.

ETR is the language of true sentences \(\exists y_1\cdots\exists y_m\,\psi(y)\), where \(\psi\) is a finite Boolean formula in integer polynomial equalities and strict inequalities with the explicit encoding just described. A language belongs to \(\exists\mathbb R\) if it has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to ETR. Accordingly, the requested reduction is one Turing machine and constants \(K,a>0\) which, on every well-formed \(\varphi\) of length \(L\), output such an existential sentence in at most \(K(L+1)^a\) bit operations and satisfy
\[
0\in\overline{S_\varphi}^{\,Z}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb R\models\exists y\,\psi(y).
\]
The time bound includes writing the output; hence its length is polynomially bounded. Ordinary deterministic multitape Turing-machine time is used. Invalid encodings may be rejected directly. This is a finite-bit complexity question, not a unit-cost real-machine bound or an approximate closure test.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that the specified language belongs to ∃R, including a uniform reduction, its bit complexity and both directions of its correctness, or a proof that it does not belong to ∃R. Proving hardness alone, giving an unrestricted-time closure algorithm, or resolving the corresponding Euclidean-closure problem does not meet this target.
context:
The source classifies origin membership in the Euclidean closure as ∃R-complete, then separately leaves the complexity for the Zariski topology open. The card asks for the missing existential upper bound in that second problem.

These closures can differ even in one dimension: the real interval (1,2) has Zariski closure all of the real line, because a nonzero univariate polynomial cannot vanish throughout an interval. Its Euclidean closure is [1,2], which excludes the origin.

The homogenization reduction in Proposition 5.1 gives Zariski adherence hardness. Applying it to explicitly encoded integer feasibility instances also yields a polynomial-bit reduction: if the feasible set is nonempty its homogenized cone approaches the origin, and otherwise its closure is empty. This discrete application is an editorial consequence of the displayed reduction.

The input retains inequalities and Boolean combinations. Replacing the feasible set by the complex zeros of its displayed equations would change the problem. Nor is the target restricted to additive descriptions of semilinear sets.
why: This asks whether algebraic consequences of a real feasible region have existential real certificates of polynomial description length. It isolates a concrete boundary in real algebraic complexity that is not determined by the known classification for ordinary metric limits.
status_note: Source-open as the Zariski variant in compendium entry A37. This card chooses the precise ∃R-membership question within that broader complexity request; the choice was an announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question. The 2005 hardness reduction and known Euclidean closure classification do not provide this upper bound. Later-work search through 17 September 2026 was bounded. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Membership in existential real arithmetic for finite binary inputs to real Zariski-closure membership.
progress: 2005: The ECCC preprint proves adherence hardness using homogenization; the final journal version appeared in 2009. | 2024: The compendium explicitly lists the Zariski-topology complexity question as open, separately from Euclidean closure.
working_summary: The input describes a real semialgebraic set by a Boolean formula of explicitly written integer polynomial constraints. Its real Zariski closure consists of the points satisfying every real polynomial relation that vanishes on the set. The question asks whether testing that the origin lies in this closure belongs to the existential theory of the reals complexity class. A positive answer needs one polynomial-bit-time transformation to an equivalent existential real sentence for all input dimensions and degrees. The source leaves Zariski adherence open, and the known Euclidean result does not settle this target; a complete Lean-checked answer is required.

title: Deterministic divisibility testing by a constant-degree polynomial
importance_reason: A basic derandomization question linking sparse divisibility and low-degree factorization. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(\delta \ge 2\), is there a deterministic algorithm using \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s,d)\) arithmetic operations over Q that, given an explicitly s-sparse polynomial \(f\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most d and a nonzero polynomial \(g\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most \(\delta\), decides whether g divides f?
definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because \(\delta\) is fixed, it has at most \(binomial(n+\delta ,\delta )\) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial \(h\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) exists with \(f=gh\). The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed \(\delta\), but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases \(f=0\) or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed \(\delta\), or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.
context:
This problem verifies one supplied potential divisor. It does not ask to discover all irreducible factors or to decide whether f itself is irreducible. The nonlinear candidate can already be quadratic.

For example, \(x^{D}- 1\) is sparse and divisible by \(x- 1\), but its quotient has D terms. Sparsity of f therefore gives no promise that a quotient has few monomials relative to the sparse input length.

Deterministic polynomial-time testing is available for linear divisors; for arbitrary fixed-degree nonlinear divisors, the cited general sparse-dividend result is quasipolynomial. The target removes that quasipolynomial overhead.

The 2026 result gives polynomial time when every variable’s degree in the dividend is a fixed constant. Here only the divisor g has fixed total degree: the dividend can have arbitrarily large individual degrees up to d.
why: Tests whether even a supplied low-degree factor of a sparse multivariate polynomial can be verified efficiently without randomness, a basic obstruction in deterministic factorization.
status_note: Source field, cost model and missing predicate checked, together with the 2024 full-version record, the 2026 bounded-individual-degree result and arXiv:2606.12130 on finite-field sparse divisibility. The latter uses a different field and unrestricted divisor degrees. No resolution of this fixed-degree-divisor rational-arithmetic target was located through 12 September 2026.
progress: 2015: Forbes gives deterministic quasipolynomial-time divisibility testing for constant-degree divisors of sparse polynomials. | 2024: Dutta, Sinhababu and Thierauf retain polynomial-time testing as open even for quadratic divisors. | 2026: Chuyoon and Shpilka give new factorization guarantees under bounded individual degree of the dividend, while distinguishing the unrestricted case.
working_summary: The input is a sparse multivariate polynomial f and a proposed low-degree divisor g. The question is whether divisibility can always be decided deterministically in polynomially many rational arithmetic operations. Even quadratic g remains the key case. The time bound may be polynomial in the numerical degree of f, and no sparse quotient is promised. New results for dividends of bounded individual degree do not settle the unrestricted dividend case here.

title: Algebraic branching programs versus formulas
importance_reason: A basic separation in the algebraic complexity hierarchy, comparing formulas with reusable path computations. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For a fixed field F, is \(VF_{F} a\) proper subclass of \(VBP_{F}\)? Equivalently, is there a family \((f_{n})\) of polynomials of polynomially bounded degree in polynomially many commuting variables that has polynomial-size algebraic branching programs over F but no polynomial-size algebraic formulas over F? The field is a parameter of the question, as in the source; a result must state the fields to which it applies.
definitions: A polynomial family has \(f_{n}\in F[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m(n)}]\), where \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_{n}\) are at most \(n^{a}+a\) for some fixed a. An algebraic formula is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are variables or constants in F and whose internal gates are binary addition or multiplication. Its output is a formal polynomial; equality means coefficientwise equality in \(F[x]\), also when F is finite. Its size is its number of nodes. An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated source and sink and affine-linear polynomial labels on edges. It computes the sum, over all source-to-sink paths, of the product of the labels on that path. Count vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients used to describe edge labels as its size; these choices differ only polynomially from the usual size conventions. Field constants have unit algebraic cost, with no bit-length bound. \(VF_{F}\) and \(VBP_{F}\) consist respectively of the polynomial families with formula size and branching-program size bounded by \(n^{b}+b\) for some constant b independent of n. These are nonuniform classes: a different finite computation may be chosen for each n, with no requirement to generate it algorithmically. The separation asks for one family in \(VBP_{F}\) for which, for every b, some n requires formula size greater than \(n^{b}+b\). There is no restriction to multilinear computation, bounded depth, homogeneous intermediate gates or noncommuting variables.
answer_criterion: For the stated field F, prove \(VF_{F} \subsetneq  VBP_{F}\) by exhibiting a family in \(VBP_{F}\) and proving that its formula sizes are not polynomially bounded, or prove \(VF_{F}=VBP_{F}\) by showing that every polynomial-size branching-program family has polynomial-size formulas. Any characteristic or field restriction must be stated as part of the scope of the answer. A lower bound only for bounded-depth or multilinear formulas does not resolve the unrestricted question.
context:
A formula is a tree: an intermediate result used in two places must be copied. A branching program can share subpaths, and its output combines the products along all paths.

Every polynomial-size algebraic formula has a polynomial-size branching program. The question is whether this containment hides a strict difference in expressive power.

The source discusses a branching-program family that already requires more than a particular small depth in polynomial-size formulas. That does not rule out polynomial-size formulas of unrestricted depth.

The January 2026 paper recalls a known separation between syntactically multilinear formulas and branching programs. An unrestricted formula computing a multilinear output need not itself be syntactically multilinear, so that theorem does not settle VF versus VBP.
why: Separates two fundamental models of algebraic computation and asks whether sharing path computations gives a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic trees.
status_note: Recovered the exact containment from the source and checked subsequent work through 12 September 2026, including the January 2026 multilinear paper. No unrestricted resolution was located. The May revision notice for ECCC TR26-043 reports a gap in that separate barrier claim, which is not used as an established result here.
progress: 2023: The source explicitly records \(VF \subseteq\) VBP as a containment whose strictness is unknown and distinguishes it from depth-restricted lower bounds. | 2026-01-01: The later paper studies the restricted multilinear hierarchy and recounts its known formula-versus-branching-program separation; it does not claim the general separation.
working_summary: Algebraic formulas compute polynomials using arithmetic trees. Algebraic branching programs compute sums of products along paths and can share subcomputations. Every polynomial-size formula can be represented by a polynomial-size branching program. The question asks whether some branching-program family requires superpolynomial formula size over the specified field. Known results for bounded-depth or syntactically multilinear formulas do not settle this unrestricted separation.

title: A uniform exponent saving for arbitrary generalized convolution
importance_reason: A general exact-computation primitive whose improvements can transfer across many dynamic programs, rather than a speedup for one chosen operation. Existing score retained.
formal: Does there exist an absolute \(\varepsilon >0\) such that, for every fixed finite domain D with \(d=|D|\ge 2\) and every fixed function \(f:D\times D\to D\), the entire f-convolution of two integer tables on \(D^{n}\) can be computed exactly in \(\widetilde{O}\)\((d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(2+M))\) time? The same \(\varepsilon\) must work for all domains and operations; n is unbounded and M bounds the absolute input values. No associativity, commutativity or algebraic structure of f is assumed.
definitions: Identify D with \(\{0,\ldots ,d- 1\}\). For \(u,w\in D^{n}\) set \((u\oplus _{f} w)_{j}=f(u_{j},w_{j})\) for \(1\le j\le n\). Input tables \(g,h:D^{n}\to \{- M,\ldots ,M\}\), with \(n\ge 1\) and \(M\ge 1\), list every signed integer in binary. The output is the full table \(C:D^{n}\to Z\), where \(C(v)=\sum_{u,w\in D^{n}: u\oplus _{f} w=v}g(u)h(w)\); an empty sum is zero. All arithmetic is ordinary integer arithmetic. In the source’s fixed-operation convention, D and the finite \(d^{2}\)-entry table of f specify the convolution problem; the growing inputs are g,h. More explicitly, the requested bound means a deterministic algorithm, uniform in n and the input tables, taking at most \(C_{D,f} d^{(2- \varepsilon )n}(1+n \log  d+\log (2+M))^{a_{D,f}}\) bit operations, for constants \(C_{D,f},a_{D,f}\) depending only on D,f. Any finite preparation of that fixed table can be included in \(C_{D,f}; \varepsilon\) is chosen before D,f. This states the fixed-domain asymptotic question from the source, not a bound for reading an arbitrary operation table when \(n=1\). Standard random-access storage of the listed tables is permitted, with arithmetic charged for operand bit length; addressing costs are absorbed in the displayed polynomial factor. Each output has \(O(n \log  d+\log (2+M))\) bits. The target concerns every output entry, not a query for a single specified v.
answer_criterion: Establish the bound with one positive \(\varepsilon\) independent of D and f, for all fixed finite operations and all input tables, or refute that universally quantified existence claim in the stated deterministic exact-computation model. An exponent saving that tends to zero with d, a theorem restricted to selected operations, or a faster single-entry query algorithm does not suffice.
context:
Many exact algorithms combine two tables of partial solutions coordinate by coordinate. The function f specifies how one pair of coordinate states combines; the convolution sums the contributions of every compatible pair.

There are \(d^{n}\) entries in each input table and in the output, whereas there are \(d^{2n}\) pairs of input indices. The question asks for a fixed saving in this exponent for arbitrary coordinate-combination rules.

The journal theorem computes the full convolution in \(\widetilde{O}\)\((((3/4)d^{2})^{n} \operatorname{polylog} M)\) for even d; for odd d the base is \((3/4)d^{2}+(1/4)d\). This improves the conference constant \(5/6\).

For even d the known bound corresponds to \(\varepsilon _{d}=\log _{d}(4/3)\). It is positive for each fixed d but approaches zero as d grows. The open question requires a single positive \(\varepsilon\) valid for all d.

The paper also obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((d^{\omega n/2} \operatorname{polylog} M)\) for one requested output entry, where \(\omega\) is the matrix-multiplication exponent. The card requires all \(d^{n}\) entries within the total time bound.
why: Would give a broadly applicable improvement for table-merging computations without requiring an algebraic law on the state-combination operation, strengthening a common primitive in exact and parameterized algorithms.
status_note: Read the IPEC question and the improved Algorithmica version, including its retained Section 6 question. Checked the January 2023 arXiv revision and later exact-title/generalized-convolution searches through 12 September 2026; no result meeting the uniform exponent target was found.
progress: 2022: The conference paper beats brute force by a factor \((6/5)^{n}\) for even d and asks for an absolute saving in the d-exponent. | 2023-01-30: The revised preprint improves the constant to \(3/4\); the Algorithmica version retains the absolute-exponent-saving question.
working_summary: Generalized convolution combines two integer tables using an arbitrary operation on each coordinate. The card asks to compute the entire output table with a fixed saving over the brute-force exponent. The saving must be independent of the size of the coordinate domain. The improved journal algorithm reduces the exponential base by a constant factor, which gives a domain-dependent exponent saving only. A faster algorithm for one output entry does not meet the full-table target.

title: Efficient equations for VP with unrestricted complex coefficients
importance_reason: Tests the reach of algebraic natural-proof certificates for general polynomial-size circuits, with coefficient freedom as the unresolved boundary. Existing score retained.
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do there exist nonzero polynomials \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) in \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+n^{c},n)\) coefficient variables, with degree and algebraic circuit size at most \(C_{c} N_{n}^{a_{c}}\), such that for every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\) there is \(n_{0}(c,b)\) for which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\)(\(coeff(f)\))=0 whenever \(n\ge n_{0}(c,b)\) and \(f\in \mathbb{C} [x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) has total degree at most \(n^{c}\) and an algebraic circuit of size at most \(n^{b}\)? Constants \(C_{c},a_{c}\) and the family \((\mathrm{P}_{n})\) may depend on c, but not on b. Coefficients of f may be arbitrary complex numbers. This expresses the source’s eventual vanishing on every polynomial-size family, without demanding a common finite threshold across all circuit-size exponents.
definitions: An algebraic circuit over \(\mathbb{C}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and arbitrary complex constants, binary addition and multiplication gates, and one output. Subtraction is allowed via multiplication by −1; there are no division gates. Its size is its number of vertices. It computes an exact formal polynomial, and each constant is one field element regardless of its bit description. \(VP_{\mathbb{C}}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded total degree and polynomially bounded nonuniform algebraic circuit size. For \(d=n^{c}\), list all monomials \(x_{1}^{\alpha _{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha _{n}}\) with \(\alpha _{i}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i}\alpha _{i}\le d\) in a fixed lexicographic order of exponent vectors. There are \(N_{n}=\operatorname{binom}(n+d,n)\) such monomials. \(coeff(f)\) is the full vector of their coefficients, including zeros. \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a polynomial over \(\mathbb{C}\) whose variables are these \(N_{n}\) coordinates. Nonzero means not the zero formal polynomial; over \(\mathbb{C}\) it is equivalent to being nonzero at some coefficient vector. Both degree and circuit size of \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(N_{n}\), not in n. The equations themselves are nonuniform: there is no additional requirement to construct their circuits in polynomial time from n. Vanishing must hold for all circuits under each fixed polynomial size bound eventually; the threshold can depend on that bound. Restricting c,b to positive integers covers arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents by increasing them. The statement imposes no bound on output coefficients of f or on constants used inside its circuit, and requests no explicit hard polynomial on which \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is nonzero.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a nontrivial polynomial-degree, polynomial-circuit-size family for every c, or refute the universal existence statement for at least one c. Vanishing only on polynomials with bounded integer coefficients, or only on a fixed restricted circuit architecture, does not establish the claim. Nonexistence of equations for VNP alone does not refute existence for VP.
context:
The input to \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is the description of another polynomial by all its coefficients. An equation vanishes on easy polynomials and is nonzero somewhere else. Its efficiency is measured against this much larger coefficient-vector dimension.

The known positive result restricts the final polynomial’s coefficients, for example to \(\{- 1,0,1\}\). Its computing circuit may still use arbitrary complex constants internally. Removing that semantic restriction is the question here.

The source’s phrase “efficiently constructible equations” is formalized by membership in VP. The checked revision explicitly describes its upper-bound proofs as existential; the card therefore does not add a uniform circuit-generation algorithm.

Under sufficiently strong permanent hardness, the source rules out efficient equations for VNP over characteristic-zero fields. Since VP is a smaller class, an equation vanishing on VP need not vanish on VNP, so the theorem does not answer this card.

The February 2025 full version explicitly keeps Question 1.4 open while generalizing its positive and conditional negative results. The work was published in August 2026; the checked publisher abstract does not claim a resolution of unrestricted-coefficient VP.
why: Would clarify whether a broad family of algebraic lower-bound certificates can recognize all efficiently computable polynomials once arbitrary coefficients are allowed.
status_note: Checked the original question, complete February 2025 combined revision and August 2026 publisher record/abstract. No resolution of the unrestricted-complex-coefficient VP target was found through 12 September 2026. The full journal PDF was unavailable; the detailed current formulation is grounded in the checked author revision.
progress: 2020–2022: Efficient equations are known for bounded-output-coefficient subclasses; the STACS paper gives a conditional obstruction for unrestricted-coefficient VNP while leaving VP open. | 2025-02-03: The combined full revision states the unrestricted VP problem as Question 1.4 and distinguishes it from its expanded positive and conditional results. | 2026-08-07: The combined work is published in computational complexity, volume 35, article 7.
working_summary: An equation for VP is a nonzero polynomial that eventually vanishes on coefficient vectors of all polynomial-size arithmetic computations. Its own degree and circuit size should be polynomial in the coefficient-vector dimension. The question removes the bounded-integer-coefficient restriction from known positive results. Efficient equations here are nonuniform circuit families, without a separate construction-time requirement. The checked combined revision and new journal publication retain the distinction between this VP question and conditional hardness for VNP.

title: Uniform compressed word problem for graph groups
importance_reason: A uniform algebraic-computation question separating general compressed inputs from fixed-group and power-word algorithms. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there a single deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple graph \((A,I)\) and a straight-line program \(S\) over \(A^{\pm1}\), decides whether \(\operatorname{val}(S)=1\) in the graph group \(G(A,I)=\langle A\mid ab=ba\text{ for }(a,b)\in I\rangle\)? The time bound must be polynomial in the combined encoded size of the graph and the program, uniformly over all graphs. This is the polynomial-time branch of the source question; membership in NP is its separate, weaker intermediate target.
definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.
context:
The source already uses polynomial-time compressed identity testing for each fixed graph group. Remark 10 identifies the missing uniform guarantee when the graph and alphabet also become input.

The expanded journal treatment proves a coRP upper bound in Theorem 3.12 while leaving deterministic polynomial time and NP membership open. The distinction is about the kind of efficient verification available, rather than basic decidability.

The 2024 paper solves the uniform power word problem for graph groups in polynomial time and obtains NP-completeness of their uniform uncompressed knapsack problem. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes the still-open arbitrary-SLP compressed word question.

Remark 10 explains that NP membership would suffice for an NP upper bound on solvability of compressed exponent equations when the graph group is input. That consequence involves SLP-encoded coefficients and is different from the later uncompressed knapsack result.
why: Asks whether efficient algebraic computation survives when both a compressed group element and the commutation structure of its ambient group vary. It isolates a uniformity obstacle that remains after fixed-group algorithms and more restricted compressed representations have been handled.
status_note: Read the conference definitions and Remark 10, the indexed primary author-manuscript Section 3.6, and the 2024 publisher full-text introduction. The old journal-manuscript PDF redirect prevented a local full download; journal dates were checked against publisher-deposited metadata. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the uniform arbitrary-SLP question. The formal question explicitly selects P-membership and retains NP as a weaker branch, not an equivalent formulation.
progress: 2016: Remark 10 formulates the uniform P-or-NP question after using the fixed-group polynomial-time algorithm. | 2017-09-12: The expanded journal treatment supplies a coRP upper bound for uniform compressed identity testing. | 2024-05-07: The power-word paper gives uniform polynomial-time algorithms for that restricted representation and explicitly retains the arbitrary-SLP question.
working_summary: The input gives both a graph group and a compact straight-line program representing a word in its generators. The main question is whether one deterministic algorithm can test identity in polynomial time in the combined input size. Polynomial time for each fixed graph group does not provide that uniform guarantee. Randomized one-sided polynomial-time testing is known, while NP membership is a separate weaker target. A 2024 result handles uniform power words but explicitly leaves arbitrary straight-line programs open.

title: Collapse of rational recurrence systems to single recurrences
importance_reason: A structural expressive-power boundary for rational recurrence systems, tied to algebraic dynamics and equivalence questions for weighted sequence models. Existing score retained.
formal: Does every rationally recursive sequence \(u:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) admit a single finite-depth rational recurrence? Explicitly, for every such \(u\), must there exist an integer \(d\geq1\) and polynomials \(A,B\in\mathbb Q[y_{0},\ldots,y_{d-1}]\) such that, for all \(n\geq0\), \[B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})\ne0,\qquad u_{n+d}=\frac{A(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}{B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}?\]
question_excerpt: Unlike in the case of polynomial updates, we conjecture that for rational updates we do have such a collapse.
definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A sequence \(u\) is rationally recursive if there are an integer \(k\geq1\), rational initial values \(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\), and rational functions
\[F_{i}=P_{i}/Q_{i}\in\mathbb Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\qquad(1\leq i\leq k)\]
that generate a state sequence \(\mathbf z_{n}\in\mathbb Q^{k}\) by
\[\mathbf z_{0}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}),\qquad
z_{n+1,i}=F_{i}(\mathbf z_{n}),\qquad u_{n}=z_{n,1}.\]
All components are updated simultaneously from the preceding state. Each \(P_{i},Q_{i}\) is a finite polynomial with rational coefficients, \(Q_{i}\) is not the zero polynomial, and \(Q_{i}(\mathbf z_{n})\ne0\) for every \(i,n\). The other coordinates are auxiliary sequences.

The proposed scalar recurrence uses only the last \(d\) values of \(u\), in their stated order. Its coefficients are rational constants. It has no separate access to the index \(n\), the hidden coordinates, an externally supplied clock, or a rule that changes with \(n\). The first \(d\) actual values of \(u\) are its initial data.

The quantifiers permit \(d,A,B\) to depend on the entire sequence, including the original rational initial values. They must then work at every step. There is no requirement for one scalar recurrence to work uniformly for all initial vectors of a given mutual-update system, and no prescribed bound on \(d\), degree or coefficient size.

Denominators must be nonzero at every state or scalar window where the chosen fraction is evaluated. Algebraic cancellation may be used when choosing a fraction representation, but a recurrence is not allowed to evaluate \(0/0\), assign it an arbitrary value, or switch formulas to handle exceptional windows. The scalar recurrence must hold from \(n=0\), after its initial \(d\) values, rather than only on an unspecified eventual tail.

The claim is semantic existence of a finite recurrence over \(\mathbb Q\). It does not require an algorithm for finding one, a time bound for conversion, or an algorithm that checks whether an arbitrary proposed rational-update system avoids division by zero. The input class already consists of systems whose entire orbit is defined.

A scalar recurrence can always be expressed as a finite mutual system by retaining its finitely many preceding values as state. Thus the displayed direction is precisely the missing direction in the source’s equality of the two sequence classes.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed recurrence exists for every well-defined rationally recursive sequence over \(\mathbb Q\), or give such a sequence and prove that no finite \(d\) and no rational function with nonvanishing denominators along its windows can generate it in this way. A recurrence only for generic initial conditions, an implicit polynomial relation, or a rule with exceptional undefined evaluations does not settle the conjecture.
context:
For linear updates, finite mutual systems can be represented by single finite-depth linear recurrences. For polynomial updates the corresponding statement fails: the source recalls polynomially recursive sequences that have no single polynomial recurrence. Allowing division gives a distinct conjecture about expressive power.

Theorem 6 establishes a scalar rational recurrence when the original initial values are independent formal variables and the evolving values are rational functions of those variables. This is a theorem over a function field. It does not cover every fixed rational specialization of the initial vector.

The source explicitly explains why its symbolic result does not prove Conjecture 1: a denominator in the resulting scalar recurrence may vanish after substituting particular rational initial values, even when the original mutual system remains well-defined. An identity obtained by clearing denominators also need not specify a valid next value at those windows.

The source relates an effective version of the collapse to checking whether polynomially recursive sequences are identically zero and whether two such sequences agree everywhere. Those consequences require a suitable constructive conversion; they should not be built into this purely existential conjecture.
why: Asks whether auxiliary state increases the expressive power of rational recurrences, or whether finite memory of the observed sequence always suffices. It is a basic structural question about discrete algebraic dynamics and the sequence models underlying weighted and polynomial automata.
status_note: Read the full conference Conjecture 1, rational-recursion definitions, Theorem 6 and its specialization discussion, and the corresponding author-version formulation. Checked arXiv revision history and searched through 12 September 2026 for subsequent work; no resolution of the rational-initial-value collapse was found. The symbolic theorem, implicit polynomial identities and efficient conversion are kept distinct from the stated existence claim.
progress: 2022-10-04: The author preprint states the collapse conjecture and proves a variant with symbolic initial conditions. | 2023: The STACS paper publishes the symbolic theorem while retaining the rational-initial-value conjecture and explaining the specialization obstruction.
working_summary: A rationally recursive sequence is one coordinate of a finite system whose next state is a rational function of its current state. The conjecture asks whether finitely many past values of that coordinate always suffice to generate its next value. All coefficients and initial values are rational, and every denominator must remain nonzero along the sequence. A scalar recurrence may depend on the particular initial vector, but must work at every step. The known theorem with symbolic initial values does not settle the numerical case because specialization can make its denominators vanish.

title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
importance_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
focus_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
context:
Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.
why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.
status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.
progress: 1970: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem. | 2016: Koenigsmann’s Annals paper gives a universal definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\), implying undecidability of the universal-existential fragment but not the purely existential fragment. | 2023-09-26: Anscombe and coauthors explicitly record Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb Q\) as open and review its relation to existential definability. | 2025-11: The height-comparison undecidability paper appears in Journal of Number Theory after its 2023 preprint. It settles an expansion by height predicates, while retaining the ordinary rational question as open. | 2025-12-01: The Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman article appears online, proving a negative answer over the ring of integers of every number field; its print issue is March 2026. | 2026-07-03: Poonen’s account reviews the rings-of-integers breakthrough and gives an alternative proof of the relevant Diophantine-definability implication. Its domain restriction remains essential.
working_summary: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals asks whether an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial has a zero consisting of exact rational numbers. The target requires one deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides this for every number of variables, degree and coefficient size. There is no efficiency requirement, and merely enumerating rational solutions does not decide instances with no solution. Undecidability over integers, universal definitions and results with extra height predicates have different logical or arithmetic scope. Recent advances over rings of integers preserve that distinction, and the checked sources do not settle the rational-solvability question.

title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
importance_reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.
focus_reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.
context:
For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.
why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The survey’s unrestricted classical polynomial-factor search gap remains the saved target. The checked Shenoy expression is basis-dependent, PotBKZ counts costly enumeration calls, and the 2026 hardness results concern smaller factors, explicit assumptions or a different oracle model. Wan’s 8 September revision expressly withdraws its first version’s dimension-dependent claims. No full solution of this card was found in bounded later-work checks; cited new proofs and Shenoy’s convergence claim were not independently verified. The disputed quantum DCP claim on TCS-7234 is not a classical algorithm.
