working_summary: The shortest vector problem asks for a nonzero integer combination of a rational lattice basis with minimum Euclidean length. This card asks whether one uniform classical randomized algorithm can approximate that length within some fixed power of the rank on every basis. It must return a nonzero vector on every run, achieve the length bound with probability at least two thirds per input, and count all input, arithmetic and output bits in a polynomial clock. Known general upper guarantees, conditional hardness at smaller factors and basis-dependent approximation expressions do not settle this target. The September 2026 review retains the distinctions between search and decision, classical and quantum computation, and current theorems and withdrawn claims.

title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
importance_reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
context:
Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.
why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.
status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.
progress: 1994–1997: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this card. | 2004-09: Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery. | 2021-05-24: Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length. | 2026-06-05: Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.
working_summary: Integer factorization recovers the ordered primes and positive multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer. The question asks for one classical randomized algorithm taking polynomial time in the number of input bits on every random sequence. Its full factor list must be correct with probability at least two thirds separately on every positive input. Efficient primality testing and verification do not resolve the task of finding the factors. Known quantum algorithms, heuristic sieve estimates and improved deterministic subroutines each leave a different gap to this target.

title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
importance_reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
context:
For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.
why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.
status_note: The original number-theory survey leaves the classical prime-field problem open. The same generator-input problem is explicitly assumed classically hard in Wu et al., arXiv:2608.15545v1 of 16 August 2026, still its sole version on 14 September. The reviewed 2026 small-characteristic publication and quantum results do not resolve this target. A bounded later-work search found no matching classical polynomial-time solution or unrestricted impossibility proof; source proofs and new conditional reductions were not independently certified.

Those historical estimates are distinct from proven expected-time bounds and from a lower bound against arbitrary algorithms. | 1994–1997: Shor supplies a quantum polynomial-time discrete-logarithm algorithm; §6 of the inspected manuscript uses the same prime-field and supplied-generator mathematical problem. | 1997: Shoup’s Theorem 1 proves a generic-encoding lower bound parameterized by the largest prime divisor of the group order. It does not apply to unrestricted computation on concrete residues. | 2019–2022: Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s fixed-characteristic theorem appears in the inspected 18 November 2019 version and the 2022 JAMS article. The expected-time bound and extension-degree parameter do not give a prime-field polynomial-bit algorithm. | 2024: Discrete Logarithm Factory analyzes shared preprocessing for a constant proportion of fields of a given approximate size and degree, with individual-target costs separated. Its publisher abstract and full introduction were checked. | 2026-03: Lido’s Finite Fields and Their Applications article concerns small characteristic. The inspected preprint’s Theorem 1.1 requires \(d>p\), so its quasipolynomial guarantee does not settle the prime-field question. | 2026-08-16: Wu and coauthors explicitly assume worst-case classical hardness of prime-field DLP in a new quantum-complexity preprint. Version 1 remains the sole version on 14 September; its conditional reduction is not a resolution of the assumption.
working_summary: Given a prime p, a generator g and a nonzero residue h, the task is to recover the unique exponent x between zero and p minus two with g to the x congruent to h modulo p. The question asks whether one classical randomized algorithm can do this in polynomial time in the full binary input length on every promised input. All preprocessing is charged, and the running-time bound must hold for every random sequence while success is at least two thirds separately on each instance. This would invert a basic arithmetic operation used in finite-field cryptography and match a known quantum capability. A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm or rule out all algorithms in this model; generic lower bounds, quantum algorithms and small-characteristic extension-field results do not suffice.

title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
importance_reason: A foundational quantum-algorithm question with broad relevance to lattice complexity and computational cryptography. The model and accuracy combination is distinct from both existing classical approximation and quantum exact-search cards.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), a real constant \(K>0\), and one uniform quantum algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly given matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, the algorithm terminates within \(K(N+1)^k\) charged operations on every execution and outputs a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23.\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1(L(B))\) is the length of its shortest nonzero vector. The probability is over the computation’s measurement outcomes on this fixed classical input. All constants and the program are chosen before the input; the approximation exponent depends on neither rank nor coefficient size.
definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every execution on a valid input. An unsuccessful execution may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

A uniform quantum algorithm means one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine controller with classical input, work and output tapes and a collection of initially zero qubits. In addition to ordinary bit-machine steps, it may apply a gate from \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\) to explicitly addressed qubits, or measure an addressed qubit in the computational basis and receive its classical result. Qubit indices are written in binary on control tapes; writing and processing them take ordinary charged steps. Initializing a fresh zero qubit is charged, so the number of qubits is also polynomially bounded. The input is supplied as classical bits, not as a quantum state-preparation oracle. Classical input bits may be transferred to qubits through charged computation.

For computational basis states \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\), the gates are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4}),\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle,\]
where \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A register of \(q\) qubits has state a unit vector in \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\). A gate acts on its addressed factors and as the identity elsewhere. Measurement outcome \(a\) has probability equal to the squared norm of the projection onto the subspace whose measured bit is \(a\), after which the state is that normalized projection. Classical control may depend on all earlier outcomes. Probabilities of complete executions are defined by these conditional Born probabilities. Fair classical random bits can be generated by a Hadamard gate followed by measurement; their cost is included.

Each classical Turing-machine step, gate, initialization, measurement and output-bit write costs one operation; any fixed overlap in bookkeeping changes only the constant \(K\). The stated bound holds on every possible measurement branch, including unsuccessful branches. There is no quantum advice, computational oracle, free input oracle, postselection on rare outcomes or arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic. The program is independent of input length and of the particular basis. All classical control, including input parsing and generation of the quantum operations, contributes to the same bound.

The approximation parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(d\) or the bit length \(N\). In rank one the factor is exactly one. Coefficients may have arbitrary binary length, subject only to being part of the input. There is no promised gap between successive vector lengths, random input distribution, special ring structure, modular form or bound on the basis conditioning. Success is required separately on every valid basis, not on average over bases.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants \(C,K,k\) satisfying the entire statement, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every constant polynomial approximation factor and every uniform quantum algorithm with any fixed polynomial clock in the full bit length; an impossibility for one exponent, one circuit family, one oracle model or classical algorithms alone is insufficient. A valid positive answer must prove the actual nonzero-vector output and success probability on all valid inputs, with every-execution cost including classical processing. A decision algorithm for a length threshold, an algorithm assuming a unique shortest direction, a conditional cryptanalytic reduction, or a numerical experiment is not by itself an answer. Conditional results establish only their conditional conclusions unless the additional assumptions are proved. This is an exact existence proposition; the benchmark’s numerical tolerance does not weaken its approximation or probability requirements.
context:
Long basis vectors need not imply a large lattice minimum. The two columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\), with integer \(M\geq1\), generate a lattice containing \((1,0)\), although both input columns are long. The objective concerns all nonzero integer combinations. It differs from finding the shortest input column and from minimizing over real coefficients, where arbitrarily small nonzero combinations exist.

Bennett’s survey defines approximate search SVP by the same multiplicative comparison with \(\lambda_1\). It records the classical polynomial-time LLL guarantee \(2^{O(n)}\). The factor \(n^C\) requested here is a much stronger bound for every fixed \(C\), while allowing any such constant is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search. Small-dimensional experiments or guarantees for a particular basis family do not cover this quantifier order.

The decision problem \(\gamma\)-GapSVP is given a basis and a threshold \(r>0\), with a promise of either \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), and asks which case holds. It does not output a vector. Bennett’s §4.2 explicitly records the unresolved general search-to-decision connection with polynomially controlled approximation. This card does not silently identify those two tasks. Likewise, unique-SVP assumes that every vector linearly independent of a shortest vector is longer by a promised factor; unrestricted SVP has no such promise.

Regev’s original worst-case-to-average-case theorem says that an efficient solver for specified Learning With Errors parameters yields quantum algorithms for the stated GapSVP and shortest-independent-vectors tasks. Learning With Errors supplies random linear equations with a controlled noise distribution; it is not the classical arbitrary-basis input specified here. The direction, task and parameter losses of a reduction matter. In particular, this theorem is not an unrestricted equivalence between polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE family.

The Brakerski–Kirshanova–Stehlé–Wen paper explicitly describes Regev’s dihedral-coset reduction as a reduction for unique-SVP, then establishes an LWE connection with extrapolated dihedral cosets under parameter losses. Such coset problems supply particular quantum samples as input. Their efficient solution is a separate claim whose consequences for an arbitrary classical basis require a proved reduction with the appropriate target.

The April 2024 Chen manuscript initially claimed new polynomial-time quantum lattice and LWE algorithms. Its archive entry includes an explicit April 18 author correction: a bug in Step 9 invalidates the stated polynomial-modulus LWE claim, with no repair then known. The surviving old abstract is therefore not evidence of a verified breakthrough.

Zhang’s May 14, 2026 revision analyzes a conditional replacement for part of that procedure. Its current statement requires additional front-end conditions and access to a run-dependent offset residue; the introduction explicitly says the resulting LWE conclusion is conditional. These assumptions do not form a complete arbitrary-basis algorithm in the model of this card. Earlier stronger-looking descriptions are not substituted for the latest revision.

Simon’s ePrint 2026/1591, first posted August 3 and last revised August 17, explicitly advertises a polynomial-time dihedral-coset algorithm and polynomial-factor SVP consequences. The archive also records a correction to the first draft’s Lemma 3 and the author’s acknowledgment of a subsequent refutation. The available abstract alone does not verify the asserted unrestricted search consequence or its bit-complexity conventions. The claim is recorded as disputed, not as a resolution.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, states that Simon’s August 11 algorithm cannot recover even the secret’s least-significant bit with nonnegligible advantage. They provide accompanying Lean 4 code. The repository describes precise rounding and register conventions, and a theorem about the specified bit-output procedure and controllers of its coarse outcomes; it explicitly distinguishes this from a formalization of the full-secret recursion. This audit read those scope declarations but did not build or independently verify the proofs, and could not retrieve either ePrint PDF. The rebuttal is evidence against that proposed algorithm, not a lower bound against all algorithms on this card.

The accompanying repository explicitly states that its full-secret solver recursion is not formalized and that its controller theorem observes prescribed restart/bit outcomes rather than every internal measurement record. Those declared limits must be retained when describing what has been machine checked by its authors.

A classical solution of TCS-6667 with the matching factor would also solve this quantum existence target, and an exact quantum solution of TCS-7169 would supply the stronger approximation guarantee. Neither implication reverses automatically. An algorithm here would be a major lattice-complexity advance, but declaring a particular cryptosystem broken would require checking its problem variant, parameters and reductions.
why: This isolates whether quantum computation changes the polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Euclidean lattice search. A positive answer would improve the guarantee from a superpolynomial loss to one fixed power of rank on every lattice. A negative answer would establish an unconditional limitation on general quantum computation, far beyond the failure of any particular quantum lattice algorithm. Its cryptographic implications depend on the exact lattice task and approximation exponent.
status_note: Uncertain after the 14 September 2026 audit. The historical unrestricted search question remains the target, but Simon’s August 2026 ePrint abstract advertises a matching-looking polynomial-factor SVP consequence and acknowledges the Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response. That response, revised 1 September, states a refutation of the specified 11 August DCP algorithm and links Lean code. Neither full ePrint PDF was retrievable, neither proof was independently verified, and the full search-SVP consequence and cross-version coverage were not certified. The card records the disputed claim and rebuttal without declaring a solution, a verified global lower bound or an exhaustive current-openness check.

working_summary: A lattice consists of all integer combinations of a linearly independent rational basis, and its shortest nonzero vector can be much shorter than every basis column. The question asks whether one uniform quantum algorithm finds a nonzero vector within a fixed power of the rank of that optimum on every explicitly given basis. Its probability of meeting the length bound must be at least two thirds per input, with polynomial total bit cost on every execution and classical vector output. Known reductions for decision or uniqueness-promised lattice problems do not by themselves establish this unrestricted search guarantee. An August 2026 claimed lattice consequence and its September algorithm-specific rebuttal are recorded as disputed evidence with explicit verification limits.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
importance_reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.
formal:
Do there exist one randomized classical algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every rational lattice basis \(B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) with linearly independent columns and total binary encoding length \(L\), the algorithm finds an exact shortest nonzero vector of \(\Lambda(B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), while using simultaneously at most
\[
2^{Cn}L^d\quad\text{bit operations}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
L^d\quad\text{bits of working space}?
\]
Both bounds must hold on every random tape. The exponent parameter \(n\) is lattice rank, and every \(m\ge n\ge1\) and every valid coefficient encoding are included.
question_excerpt: The inherited paper’s open-problems section asks for an algorithm using single-exponential time and polynomial space simultaneously. Micciancio’s SVP problem page singles out that question for shortest-vector search. The card retains exact Euclidean SVP and its previously selected randomized, worst-case resource convention.
definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(m,n\) and every entry of \(B\), in column or row order fixed by the encoding. A rational entry is a signed binary numerator divided by a positive binary denominator, using canonical integer encodings and unambiguous boundaries. Reduction to lowest terms is not required. The bit length \(L\) includes all entries and dimension data; the input is not a generating circuit or an oracle. Full column rank and \(m\ge n\ge1\) are promises. No behavior on unpromised inputs is required for the target.

The rank-\(n\) lattice is
\[
\Lambda(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m.
\]
The columns are linearly independent over the rationals, equivalently over the reals, so \(Bz\ne0\) for every nonzero integer coordinate vector \(z\). With the Euclidean norm \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i^2)^{1/2}\), define
\[
\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))=
\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.
\]
Full rank makes this a discrete lattice in its linear span, so the positive minimum is attained.

Successful output is a finite binary encoding of a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))\). Equivalently, it satisfies the exact rational inequalities
\[
\forall u\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m(Bz)_i^2\le\sum_{i=1}^m(Bu)_i^2.
\]
Any minimizer is acceptable, including either sign and any of several shortest vectors. The integer coordinates refer to the input basis. An approximate length, a short vector with a factor greater than one, or a real-valued coordinate approximation is not this output. The algorithm may report failure or return a nonoptimal vector on unsuccessful executions; all executions remain subject to both resource bounds.

Use a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a one-way stream of independent fair random bits. Working space counts every used work-tape bit, including saved random bits, counters, intermediate vectors, basis transformations and precision data. The random source cannot be revisited as free writable storage. No external writable memory, preprocessing oracle or nonuniform advice is available. Input and final output tapes are not counted as working storage, but every operation reading or writing them counts toward time. All arithmetic is charged in bit operations; arbitrary-precision arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

The success probability is at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed valid input, over the machine’s internal random bits. The time and space bounds are worst-case over those bits, including unsuccessful executions, and include preprocessing and all precision management. The same constants \(C,d\) apply to all ranks, ambient dimensions and coefficient lengths. Different fixed polynomial exponents for time and space can be absorbed into one \(d\). A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.

No uniqueness, reduced-basis, random-lattice or special-lattice promise is imposed. The desired exponential base is any absolute constant \(2^C\); no particular base such as two is required. The task is an exact search-algorithm existence proposition, not a separate numerical approximation of \(\lambda_1\).
answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and complete Lean-checked proofs of both simultaneous resource bounds and its exact success probability on every valid rational basis. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no algorithm and absolute constants \(C,d\) satisfy the displayed requirements.

A single-exponential algorithm using exponential space, a polynomial-space algorithm with \(2^{\Theta(n\log n)}\) time, a heuristic or average-case guarantee, or an approximation algorithm does not settle the question. A counterexample to one enumeration or sieving procedure does not rule out all algorithms. A lower bound conditional on an unproved lattice-hardness assumption is not an unconditional negative resolution.
context:
A lattice contains all integer combinations of its basis vectors. Those combinations may be much shorter than any input column, so finding the shortest nonzero combination is not the same as inspecting the basis.

The inherited Voronoi-cell algorithm achieves deterministic single-exponential time with exponential storage. Its open-problems section explicitly asks whether the same broad time scale can be combined with polynomial space.

Polynomial-space enumeration has proved bounds of the form \(n^{O(n)}=2^{O(n\log n)}\). Practical pruning can improve observed performance but does not supply the missing universal \(2^{O(n)}\) bound.

The January 2026 sheaf-based proposal describes a memory-saving regime and an iteration scheme. The inspected sections do not specify and prove an all-input stopping bound with exact success probability while retaining polynomial bit space, so they do not establish this card’s theorem.

The 2026 hinted-ISIS work relates cryptographic assumptions to conjectured time-space hardness of lattice problems. It provides conditional evidence and implications, rather than a proof that the algorithm on this card cannot exist.
why: The problem asks whether exact lattice search can retain a single-exponential time bound while avoiding an exponentially large stored collection. It separates two major resource regimes in lattice algorithms and helps clarify which memory assumptions matter when interpreting lattice-based computational hardness.
status_note: The checked primary sources continue to distinguish single-exponential algorithms using exponential space from polynomial-space enumeration. The January 2026 proposal does not provide the universal exact-success and bit-resource theorem required here, and the CRYPTO 2026 result relies on conjectured time-space hardness. No resolution of the stated target was found in the bounded search.

working_summary: An input basis generates a lattice by taking all integer combinations of its rational columns. The algorithm must output coordinates of an exactly shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector, with success probability at least two thirds. One uniform algorithm must use single-exponential time in the lattice rank and polynomial working space in the full input length simultaneously. Both resource bounds include preprocessing, arithmetic precision and unsuccessful random executions. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish those guarantees or their impossibility; exponential storage, approximation and heuristic memory savings do not meet the target.

title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
importance_reason: A classical barrier in effective number theory governing the deterministic search for basic finite-field witnesses.
formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.
context:
Tao states the conjecture with a constant depending on the chosen exponent and records the general unconditional Burgess bound \(n(p)=O_\eta(p^{1/(4\sqrt e)+\eta})\) for every \(\eta>0\), where \(e=\exp(1)\). That fixed positive base exponent does not imply the conjecture.

The introduction records Ankeny’s stronger \(O((\log p)^2)\) bound under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It also notes results for almost all primes. Both are separated from the unconditional all-primes target.

Tao’s Theorem 1.3 proves that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture on primes in arithmetic progressions implies Vinogradov’s conjecture. This is a conditional implication, not an unconditional resolution.

Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides continue to display the Burgess exponent as the unconditional bound. The following slide discusses a better constant in a logarithmic-square estimate and explicitly assumes GRH. That improvement therefore does not settle the statement here.
why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.
status_note: Tao’s Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 and Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides 14–15 were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter retains the unconditional Burgess bound and explicitly labels its stronger recent bound as conditional on GRH. A bounded search including 2026 work found no matching unconditional all-primes resolution. This is source-open status with those limits.
progress: 1952: Ankeny’s conditional logarithmic-square upper bound, as recorded in Tao’s introduction, shows that GRH implies substantially more than the target. | 2015: Tao publishes the implication from Elliott–Halberstam to Vinogradov’s least-nonresidue conjecture. | 2025-06: Quesada-Herrera distinguishes the unconditional Burgess bound from a new GRH-conditional improvement in the logarithmic-square constant.
working_summary: A quadratic nonresidue is a nonzero residue that is not a square modulo the prime. Vinogradov’s conjecture says that the least positive one eventually lies below every fixed positive power of the prime. The threshold may depend on the exponent, but the bound must cover every sufficiently large odd prime. Conditional logarithmic-square estimates and almost-all-prime results do not establish this unconditional statement. A refutation would require one fixed positive exponent and arbitrarily large primes violating its bound.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
importance_reason: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.
formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every integer matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Z} ^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs \(z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}\) satisfying ||\(Bz||_{2}=\min _{y\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}}||\)By||\(_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) elementary steps on every execution? L is the total binary encoding length of m, d and all entries of B.
definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.
context:
The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.
why: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.
status_note: No polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the exact-search target was found through 11 September 2026. The checked August exact-SVP preprints claim exponential improvements, and the disputed DCP proposal concerns approximate SVP. Classical NP-hardness does not resolve the quantum target. Recent proofs and the response’s linked Lean development were not independently audited.

The output must be a classical integer combination of the basis, with success probability at least two thirds on every valid input. Randomized NP-hardness would make such an algorithm a major quantum complexity result, but is not a quantum impossibility proof. August 2026 exact-SVP preprints claim faster exponential algorithms with additional memory details. The disputed dihedral-coset proposal has an approximate-SVP consequence and does not settle this exact target.

title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
importance_reason: Standard-assumption hardness at cryptographic approximation factors would strengthen the foundations of lattice-based cryptography.
formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
definitions:
An instance consists of an integer \(n\ge1\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational threshold \(r\). The columns of \(B\) form a full-rank lattice basis. Its lattice and shortest-vector length are
\[\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad \lambda_1(B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum exists and is positive for a nonsingular basis. No ideal-lattice, module-lattice, random-lattice or special-basis promise is imposed.

The promise problem has YES instances with \(\lambda_1(B)\le r\) and NO instances with \(\lambda_1(B)>\gamma_k(n)r\). Either condition is promised. For \(r<\lambda_1(B)\le\gamma_k(n)r\), either answer is allowed. This preserves the source’s strict inequality on the NO side. The task is deciding the promise, not outputting a short vector. The dimension in the approximation factor is \(n\), not the bit length of the matrix entries.

Use a binary encoding of \(n\), the matrix entries and \(r\), each rational represented by its signed reduced numerator and positive denominator, with self-delimiting lengths. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length. A quantum polynomial-time solver is one finite uniform quantum algorithm, for the fixed chosen \(k\), which uses at most \(C(L+1)^a\) elementary operations for constants \(C,a\) on every branch, and returns the correct promise answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every YES and every NO instance. It must halt on all inputs within the time bound; malformed encodings, singular matrices and inputs outside the promise require no particular answer. This is the meaning of \(\mathrm{PromiseBQP}\) here. The program and polynomial may depend on \(k\), which is not an instance parameter.

For definiteness, uniform quantum computation uses a classical Turing controller, qubits initially in computational-basis states, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), and computational-basis measurements with the Born probabilities. On one qubit, \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\). The controlled-not gate maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Classical tape work, input reading, generation of gate instructions, gate applications and measurements are charged. The algorithm has no advice, external oracle, uncharged quantum state or postselection. Adaptive classical control and classical randomization obtained by measurement are allowed.

Quantum ETH in this card is a statement about classical Boolean satisfiability. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three signed Boolean variables. It is satisfiable if some assignment makes every clause true. Let \(N\) be its number of variables and \(s\) its binary encoding length. The assumption asserts that there exists \(\delta>0\) for which no uniform quantum algorithm decides satisfiability on every such formula, with error at most \(1/3\), in time \(C2^{\delta N}(s+1)^a\) for any fixed constants \(C,a\). Time is worst-case over inputs and measurement outcomes, in the same uniform quantum model. This uses the positive exponential-rate formulation of Definition 4.25 in the cited quantum complexity paper; it is not a hypothesis about the quantum satisfiability or local-Hamiltonian problem.

The exponent increment is fixed before instances or candidate solvers are considered. Writing it as \(1/k\) loses no existence case from an arbitrary constant \(\varepsilon>0\): choosing \(1/k\le\varepsilon\) only reduces the approximation factor, and a solver for the smaller factor also solves the larger-factor promise. The source’s alternative LWE target is not bundled into this card. No lattice-hardness or cryptographic-security assumption is available in addition to the stated quantum ETH premise.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed conditional assertion with these encodings, norm, approximation factor and uniform quantum model. A positive answer may assume quantum ETH as defined but must establish the claimed exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms, rather than assume hardness of GapSVP or LWE. It must obtain a fixed positive exponent increment and cover all promised rational-basis inputs. A lower bound only for classical algorithms, a constant-factor approximation problem, another norm, or exact SVP alone does not establish this target. Refuting the conditional assertion requires more than showing that one proposed reduction fails; likewise, refuting quantum ETH alone would make the implication vacuously true rather than false.
context:
Open Problem 4.11 distinguishes cryptographic approximation factors \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) from smaller powers of the dimension and explicitly includes quantum algorithms. The named assumption is left open by the author; selecting the quantum 3-SAT hypothesis makes this card’s proof obligation concrete.

The cited quantum complexity paper defines a positive-exponential-rate quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT. Its assumption provides the premise used here, rather than an already known reduction to lattice problems.

The source surveys worst-case-to-average-case reductions connecting sufficiently large-factor Euclidean GapSVP hardness to appropriate Learning with Errors parameters. The direction relevant here is that an efficient LWE algorithm would give an efficient worst-case lattice algorithm; these reductions do not themselves derive lattice hardness from SAT hardness.

The source also describes certificate-based obstacles to ordinary NP-hardness at large approximation factors. This helps explain why a standard-assumption hardness theorem in the cryptographic range remains a distinct question from constant-factor NP-hardness.

Hecht and Safra’s STOC 2026 deterministic hardness results assume norms strictly above two. Their displayed factors and norm hypotheses do not establish the Euclidean, cryptographic-factor, quantum conclusion.

Wan’s July 2026 preprint claims deterministic Euclidean hardness within constant factors below \(\sqrt2\), as a special case of its Theorem 1.8. Even if that claim is verified, its approximation scale does not yield hardness for \(n^{3/2+1/k}\). It is recorded as a preprint claim, not as an independently verified resolution of the target.
why: This question asks whether a familiar quantum satisfiability assumption can support hardness of lattice approximation at a scale relevant to worst-case-to-average-case cryptographic reductions. That scale is much larger than constant-factor approximation, and hardness at a small factor does not automatically persist as the promise gap grows. A proof would connect lattice-based security foundations to a separate complexity assumption while addressing quantum algorithms explicitly.

title: A classical same-dimension reduction from SIVP to polynomial-modulus LWE
importance_reason: A same-dimension classical SIVP-to-LWE reduction would remove a central quantum step in the worst-case foundations of lattice cryptography while retaining the approximation and parameter scales that make the connection useful.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), an integer \(b\ge0\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm \(\mathcal R_c\) with the following property?

For all \(n\ge2\), all admissible parameters \(q,\alpha,m,t\) below, every rank-\(n\) integer lattice basis \(B\), and every admissible search-LWE oracle \(A\), the algorithm \(\mathcal R_c^A(B,q,\alpha,m,t)\) outputs \(n\) linearly independent lattice vectors of length at most
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_n(\mathcal L(B)),\qquad
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac n\alpha\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input basis, using at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) bit operations and oracle calls on every run? Every LWE query must have dimension exactly \(n\), modulus exactly \(q\), and exactly \(m\) samples with the noise parameter \(\alpha\) in the oracle guarantee. Here \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and the constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), not on the instance.
question_excerpt: Question 1 asks whether a classical worst-case hardness reduction fully subsumes the quantum LWE reduction. This card selects its SIVP branch with polynomial modulus and unchanged dimension. The rounded Gaussian, finite sample interface and polynomial parameter bounds make that selected branch precise. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Classical same-dimension SIVP-to-LWE with polynomial modulus and the soft-O(n/alpha) approximation scale.
definitions:
Let \(B\in\mathbb Z^{h\times n}\) have full column rank, where \(h\ge n\). The lattice is \(\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), endowed with \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). Its last successive minimum \(\lambda_n\) is the least radius of a closed Euclidean ball about zero containing \(n\) linearly independent lattice vectors. The output is a tuple of nonzero integer coefficient vectors \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\) such that \(Bz_1,\ldots,Bz_n\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\) and each meets the stated length bound. They need not form a basis of the entire lattice. This is the shortest independent vectors problem (SIVP), not a shortest-vector decision problem.

The matrix entries, dimensions and all rational and integer parameters are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters. Admissible parameters have prime \(q\le(n+2)^c\), integers \(1\le m\le(n+2)^c\) and \(2\le t\le(n+2)^c\), and a positive rational \(\alpha=u/v\le1/2\) in lowest terms with \(u,v\le(n+2)^c\), satisfying \(\alpha q>2\sqrt n\). Thus both the modulus and inverse noise rate are polynomially bounded for fixed \(c\).

Define an integer noise variable by drawing a real random variable \(E\) with density
\[
\frac{1}{\alpha q}\exp\left(-\frac{\pi x^2}{(\alpha q)^2}\right),
\]
rounding it to the nearest integer, and reducing modulo \(q\). Denote its exact distribution on \(\mathbb Z_q\) by \(\chi_{q,\alpha}\). Ties have probability zero. This is the rounded Gaussian convention from the original LWE reduction, not an assertion that rounding gives the exact discrete Gaussian on the integers.

A search-LWE test instance is sampled by first choosing a uniformly random secret \(s\in\mathbb Z_q^n\). Independently choose \(m\) uniform vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_q^n\) and \(m\) errors \(e_i\leftarrow\chi_{q,\alpha}\), and give the ordered list
\[
(a_i,\langle a_i,s\rangle+e_i\bmod q)_{i=1}^m
\]
to the oracle. The oracle is any fixed randomized map from such lists to \(\mathbb Z_q^n\cup\{\bot\}\), using fresh independent randomness on each invocation, which outputs the actual sampled \(s\) with probability at least \(1/t\), averaged over the uniformly random secret, all samples and its randomness. There is no per-list guarantee; on other lists it may behave arbitrarily. The reduction must work for every such map, with no access to the secret or the oracle's internal random bits. It may make arbitrary adaptive list queries; their correctness is controlled only by this distributional guarantee.

The reduction is a classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair random bits. Its cost includes preparing and writing every finite query, reading the returned vector, processing its input and producing its output, but excludes computation inside the oracle. The exact Gaussian distribution defines the oracle promise. The reduction must implement any sampling or numerical approximation it needs in finite bit time, with its errors included in the final failure probability; it receives no exact-real or Gaussian-sampling primitive. It has no quantum computation, advice or other oracles. The all-run polynomial bound and per-basis success guarantee hold even when the admissible oracle gives adversarial replies away from its average-case guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and proof of the stated classical reduction for every fixed c, or prove the logical negation of this quantified statement. A positive solution must include the same-dimension query interface, noise convention, approximation factor, average-to-worst-case success analysis and finite-bit running time. A quantum reduction, a classical reduction only from GapSVP, an exponential modulus, or a polynomial-modulus reduction that enlarges the LWE dimension does not settle this target.
context:
The source explicitly separates the quantum SIVP and GapSVP guarantees from the classical GapSVP-only connection and its modulus–dimension tradeoff. Retaining the SIVP branch avoids conflating those different conclusions.

Regev’s quantum reduction iterates a lattice Gaussian-sampling procedure and then extracts sufficiently many short independent vectors. The resulting approximation factor is Õ(n/α) while the LWE dimension remains n.

The 2013 classical modulus reduction reaches polynomial-modulus LWE but increases the dimension. Its informal theorem relates an n-dimensional LWE solver to a worst-case lattice problem in dimension approximately √n; the open-question discussion also explicitly identifies the missing SIVP connection.

Polynomial modulus alone is therefore not the target. The card simultaneously preserves the rank, the SIVP output and the quantum theorem’s approximation scale, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed polynomial parameter range.

The prime-modulus and at-most-one-half noise restrictions are stated editorial specializations. The source asks a still broader question that also includes GapSVP and other modulus regimes; solving this card need not settle every branch of that larger request.
why: LWE is a classical noisy linear problem, yet the strongest known worst-case connection to SIVP uses quantum computation. Matching that connection classically at polynomial modulus and unchanged dimension would clarify which parts of the hardness foundation actually depend on quantum operations.
