title: Polynomial-factor approximation of cyclotomic ideal SVP
importance_reason: A core structured-lattice algorithmic barrier underlying widely used families of cryptographic assumptions. The all-ideals, polynomial-approximation target is substantially broader than a prime splitting subclass or a practical speedup, while the explicit classical specialization is narrower than the entire ideal-lattice research program.
formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds a polynomial-factor approximate shortest nonzero vector in every ideal of every power-of-two cyclotomic ring?

More precisely, do there exist one probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,C,d\) such that, for every \(n=2^k\) with integer \(k\ge1\), and every nonsingular matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) whose column lattice \(I_B=B\mathbb Z^n\) is an ideal of \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\), the following holds? On the explicit binary input \((n,B)\) of length \(L\), every run of \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and
\[\Pr\!\left[A(n,B)\text{ outputs }v\in I_B\setminus\{0\}\text{ with }\|v\|_2\le n^c\lambda_1(I_B)\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad
\lambda_1(I_B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.\]
The constants and program are chosen before the dimension and ideal. The approximation factor depends on dimension, not on coefficient bit lengths. The output must be the full integer coefficient vector \(v\).
question_excerpt: Peikert's 2016 Question 3 asks broadly whether ideal-lattice algorithms, possibly quantum, can substantially outperform general-lattice algorithms, and whether such advances extend to ring-SIS/LWE. It does not choose a field family, approximation scale or running time. Following the user's instruction to replace broad directions by concrete variants, this card selects the standard search-SVP problem with polynomial approximation and classical randomized polynomial time on power-of-two cyclotomic ideals. This is a documented editorial specialization, not a quotation or equivalent restatement of all of Question 3. It does not ask for a proved separation from every general-lattice algorithm or for a direct cryptographic attack. Existing conditional quantum speedups at larger approximation factors answer other parts of the historical direction without deciding this target.
definitions:
Identify \(R_n\) with the integer polynomials of degree less than \(n\), with addition and multiplication reduced modulo \(X^n+1\). Coordinates are ordered as the coefficients of \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\). The coefficient Euclidean norm is \(\|a\|_2=(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j^2)^{1/2}\). For these dimensions, \(X^n+1\) is the cyclotomic polynomial of conductor \(2n\), so \(R_n\) is the full ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2n})\). The dimension varies without an upper bound.

An integral ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by every ring element. In the supplied coordinates, the input promise is exactly that \(B\) is nonsingular over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(S(B\mathbb Z^n)\subseteq B\mathbb Z^n\), where
\[S(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})=(-a_{n-1},a_0,\ldots,a_{n-2}).\]
Closure under \(S\) and under integer linear combinations gives closure under every ring element. Equivalently, all entries of \(B^{-1}SB\) are integers. Every nonzero integral ideal has a full additive basis of this form. The basis need not be reduced, canonical, circulant or generated by one ring element. Arbitrary prime and composite ideals are included, and no factorization, short generator or special distribution of ideals is promised. Nonsingularity makes \(I_B\) a discrete full-rank lattice, so its positive shortest length is attained.

The input is a dense, explicitly written integer matrix. To fix a binary convention, encode a nonnegative integer \(a\) by \(U(a)=1^\ell 0b\), where \(b\) is the usual binary expansion of \(a\), without leading zeros, and \(\ell\) is its length; use \(b=0\) for zero. Encode a signed integer by a sign bit followed by \(U(|a|)\), with sign zero for zero. Write \(U(n)\) followed by the signed entries of \(B\) in row-major order. Their total length is \(L\). No omitted zeros, succinct matrix circuits or unit-cost large integers are available. Valid outputs list the \(n\) signed coordinates in the same integer encoding; writing every output bit is charged.

The machine has a fixed finite program, alphabet and number of tapes. Each transition reads and writes finitely many tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; an independent fair random bit can be drawn at a charged transition. Time includes reading, arithmetic, any preparation depending on \(n\), and writing the output. The time bound holds on all input strings of length \(L\) and all coin sequences. Mathematical success is required only on promised inputs. Outside the promise, any output is permitted. On a promised input, a failure marker, malformed vector or vector violating the displayed conditions counts as failure. Success probability is over the independent coins for each fixed input, not over a distribution of bases.

No quantum computation, oracle, nonuniform advice, precomputed table depending on the field, unit-group basis or ideal factorization is supplied for free. Such information may be computed only within the stated classical time bound. Polynomial exponents may be large but must be universal. Allowing a fixed multiplicative constant in the approximation would be equivalent after increasing \(c\), since \(n\ge2\).

The norm is fixed explicitly to avoid an embedding ambiguity. For \(\zeta_{2n}=\exp(\pi i/n)\), the canonical embedding lists the \(n\) values \(a(\zeta_{2n}^{2j+1})\), \(0\le j<n\). Its squared Euclidean norm is \(n\sum_j a_j^2\). Thus, in this selected family, canonical and coefficient norms differ by the common factor \(\sqrt n\), which cancels in the relative approximation guarantee. This statement does not identify the two norms in arbitrary number rings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full negation. A positive answer must specify one finite classical program and universal constants, with a proved bound on every execution and at least \(2/3\) success on each promised basis. A negative answer must rule out every program and every choice of polynomial approximation and time bounds in this model. In particular, for each machine with a global polynomial clock and each fixed exponent \(c\), some promised input must have success probability below \(2/3\). A conditional consequence under an unproved complexity assumption is not an unconditional negative answer. Algorithms for selected ideals, quantum algorithms, superpolynomial approximation factors, or uncharged field preprocessing do not establish this target. Producing or estimating only the shortest length does not satisfy the required search output.
context:
The 2016 survey frames the question as a tradeoff between the efficiency gained from ring structure and possible additional algorithmic weaknesses. Its search problem asks for an actual short vector. This distinction is essential: the same survey explains that certain polynomial-gap decision versions on ideals can be easy even when finding an adequately short vector is not known to be efficient.

Multiplication by \(X\) gives a signed rotation of every coefficient vector in the selected ideal. For example, \(q\mathbb Z^n\) is an allowed ideal with shortest length \(|q|\) for each nonzero integer \(q\). Such easy instances do not determine the worst-case question, which also includes ideals without a short generator supplied in the input. A change of additive basis describes the same ideal; the guarantee must hold for every explicit basis and charges its actual bit length.

General lattice algorithms already give polynomial-time approximations whose factors are much larger than polynomials in dimension. Peikert's §2.2.2 records that historical time–approximation landscape. Restricting to ideal lattices is useful here only if the output quality and full running time meet both polynomial requirements. The earlier broad phrasing “outperform general lattices” is replaced by this testable threshold, without claiming a lower bound for all generic algorithms.

Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski give a quantum algorithm with approximation factor \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) for cyclotomic conductor \(m\). Their Theorem 5.1 assumes GRH and a class-group generation hypothesis, and its running time also depends polynomially on the real-subfield class number. Polynomial boundedness of that class number is an additional hypothesis used for the advertised polynomial-time consequence. This important advance has a different computation model and a superpolynomial approximation guarantee.

Pan, Xu, Wadleigh and Cheng prove classical polynomial-time exact SVP for prime ideals above rational primes \(p\equiv3,5\pmod8\) in the power-of-two family, and for a specified class of products of such primes. Their introduction stresses that the proportion of easy instances depends on how ideals are sampled. The result does not cover every ideal, and the paper explicitly distinguishes these algorithms from a break of ring-LWE.

The CRYPTO 2022 work of Boudgoust, Gachon and Pellet-Mary extends the easy-instance analysis using ideals preserved by many field automorphisms. Its cryptographic application concerns particular partial Vandermonde knapsack instances. The publisher/ePrint abstract was checked for this scope; it is not evidence of a general polynomial-time algorithm for every ideal.

Cui, Li and Zhuang's January 2026 revision studies further prime-ideal classes. In particular, its Theorem 2 describes shortest lengths above primes \(p\equiv7,9\pmod{16}\). Its hypotheses still restrict the ideals, and a formula for a shortest length is distinct from the full uniform search guarantee. No claim that this preprint resolves the all-ideals target is made here.

Martin’s September 2026 preprint claims a dimension-preserving reduction from generic lattices to ideals in varying totally real monogenic number rings. Theorem 1.1 does not force a chosen cyclotomic field; the surrounding discussion explicitly preserves the possible advantage of field-specific methods. Its separate full-ring-of-integers extension has additional conjectural qualifications. This new hardness claim is not a hardness theorem for the fixed cyclotomic family selected here.

Wan’s September 2026 preprint claims exact Euclidean SVP hardness for ideals of \(\mathbb Z[X]/(X^N-1)\), with \(N=q-1\) for varying odd primes \(q\). That quotient has a different rational algebra from \(\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). The paper explicitly makes neither a fixed-factor approximation claim nor a cryptographic key-distribution claim. Even if its proof is correct, the stated exact cyclic result does not determine this polynomial-factor cyclotomic search question.

A worst-case-to-average-case security reduction has a direction: an algorithm for the average-case cryptographic problem would solve an associated worst-case lattice problem with stated parameters. An algorithm for the worst-case lattice problem does not automatically run that implication backwards. The historical second question about direct ring-SIS/LWE attacks therefore remains separate from this card’s selected algorithmic target.
why: The central issue is whether the algebraic structure used to make lattice cryptography compact also makes a core worst-case search problem efficiently solvable at polynomial approximation. The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
importance_reason: A canonical explicit construction at the interface of number theory, randomness and algorithmic information.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that constructs a prime of every requested bit length in polynomial bit time?

The input is the unary string \(1^n\), for any integer \(n\ge2\). The output must be the binary expansion of some prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2^{n-1}\le p<2^n.
\]
The prime may be any one in this interval; no particular choice, such as the smallest prime, is prescribed.

With the finite machine model and output predicate below, the precise assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
One fixed deterministic program and one polynomial bound must work for every requested length. This retains the source's unary-input prime-construction question and makes its bit-computation convention explicit.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), the unary string \(1^n\) consists of exactly \(n\) consecutive copies of the symbol one. Its length, rather than the binary length of the integer \(n\), is the input size. Valid inputs are precisely these strings; other input strings impose no requirements.

A positive integer \(p\) is prime when \(p\ge2\) and every positive integer dividing \(p\) is either one or \(p\) itself. A binary output string \(y=y_0y_1\cdots y_{n-1}\) of length \(n\), with \(y_0=1\), represents
\[
\operatorname{val}(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i2^{n-1-i}.
\]
Here each symbol \(y_i\) is identified with the integer zero or one. The predicate \(\operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)\) means that \(y\) has exactly this length, its first bit is one, and \(\operatorname{val}(y)\) is prime. No leading zeros, additional bits, compressed description or separate certificate form part of the output. This predicate is equivalent to requiring the ordinary binary expansion of a prime in the displayed interval.

An algorithm \(A\) is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and a binary output stream. Its finite control, finite tape alphabets and number of tapes are fixed independently of the input. Tape cells have nonnegative integer addresses. Initially all heads are at cell zero, work tapes are blank, the input tape contains the input followed by blanks, and the output is empty. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite control, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, moves each head left, right or not at all by at most one cell, and appends at most one bit to the output. A move left from cell zero leaves the head there. The transition rule is a finite deterministic table, defined on every nonhalting state and tuple of scanned symbols, and a designated halt state ends the computation.

One transition costs one bit-computation step. All computation, preprocessing, reading and writing count, including production of all \(n\) output bits. There are no random bits, quantum operations, oracle calls, input-dependent advice or unbounded integers with unit-cost operations. The finite program may contain fixed constants, but receives no additional information depending on \(n\).

The predicate \(\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,x,y,T)\) means that the computation on input \(x\) reaches its halt state after at most \(T\) transitions and has produced exactly the finite output string \(y\). Requiring positive integer constants \(C,k\) expresses ordinary polynomial time: increasing them covers any fixed polynomial bound. Both constants and the whole finite program precede the universal quantifier over \(n\). The assertion is unconditional; an unproved hypothesis about primes or computational hardness is not an additional assumption.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence assertion or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must supply one finite deterministic program \(A\) and positive integers \(C,k\), and prove for every \(n\ge2\) that it halts on \(1^n\) within \(Cn^k\) bit steps and outputs exactly the binary expansion of an \(n\)-bit prime. The output prime need not be the first prime in its interval.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall A\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\neg\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
Thus each proposed deterministic program and polynomial bound must fail at some length, which may depend on both. Failure includes running longer than the bound, never halting, or producing an invalid prime output. This does not assert that some bit length contains no prime.

A randomized or pseudodeterministic construction, success only at infinitely many lengths, or a bound that is polynomial in the numerical value of the output instead of its bit length does not establish the positive assertion. A conditional result establishes the target only if its additional hypothesis is also proved. A lower bound for one search procedure does not establish the unrestricted negative assertion. This is an exact algorithm-existence question, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation is not a substitute for the required proof.
context:
The MFCS 2018 paper explicitly asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can output an n-bit prime from the unary input specifying n. It distinguishes this construction task from deterministic polynomial-time primality testing and from probabilistic prime generation.

The 2022 survey formulates deterministic prime construction for every bit length at least two and explains its relationship with short time-bounded descriptions of primes. This card retains that all-length construction requirement and specifies the complete finite bit model.

The revised Chen–Lu–Oliveira–Ren–Santhanam manuscript proves an unconditional polynomial-time randomized algorithm that outputs a fixed prime with high probability for infinitely many requested bit lengths. Its Corollary 1.2 is a pseudodeterministic result: it permits random choices and does not give the deterministic construction required here.

The same manuscript records an unconditional deterministic upper bound of \(2^{(1/2+o(1))n}\) time, still exponential in the requested bit length. Its discussion of conditional polynomial-time construction uses stronger unproved hypotheses, including Cramér’s prime-gap conjecture; these are not assumptions of this card.
why: Prime generation is a canonical example where recognizing a suitable object is efficiently possible but constructing one deterministically remains unresolved. A positive answer would remove randomness from this basic number-theoretic construction at every bit length. A negative answer would establish an unconditional computational lower bound for a concrete total search problem. The connection with succinct descriptions of primes also makes the question central to research on derandomization and time-bounded information.

The question asks whether one fixed deterministic algorithm can do this for every length at least two in polynomial bit time. title: A classical SIS reduction from sublinear-factor GapSVP
importance_reason: Stronger worst-case reductions to SIS and LWE would connect cryptographic assumptions more tightly to general lattice hardness.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(C\ge1\), polynomially bounded computable modulus parameters as defined below, and a classical randomized polynomial-time worst-case-to-average-case reduction
\[
\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma(n)}\ \longrightarrow\
\operatorname{SIS}_{n,m(n),q(n),\sqrt{m(n)}},
\qquad \gamma(n)=\max\{1,Cn^{1-\varepsilon}\},
\]
in the Euclidean norm? The reduction must solve every promised rank-\(n\) GapSVP instance from a SIS oracle that succeeds on only an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random matrices. It must have polynomial overhead in the inverse of that success probability.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 4.1 gives separate SIS, classical-LWE and quantum-LWE targets. This card selects the classical SIS target with factor O(n^(1−ε)) and fixes a polynomial-modulus compressing family and a black-box average-success convention. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: The classical SIS reduction from GapSVP with approximation factor O(n^(1-epsilon)) for some fixed positive epsilon.
definitions:
The modulus is one integer-valued function \(q(n)\), for \(n\ge2\), computed from \(1^n\) by one deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in \(n\). For some fixed integer \(d\ge3\), require
\[
n^3\le q(n)\le(n+1)^d,\qquad
m(n)=2n\lceil\log_2 q(n)\rceil+1.
\]
The function, its algorithm, and \(d\) are existentially chosen once. Primality is not required. These conventions select a polynomial-modulus, compressing SIS family, without fixing one numerical modulus schedule.

An SIS instance is a matrix \(A\in(\mathbb Z/q(n)\mathbb Z)^{n\times m(n)}\), with entries sampled independently and uniformly from the residues \(0,\ldots,q(n)-1\). A valid solution is a nonzero vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^{m(n)}\) satisfying
\[
Az=0\pmod{q(n)},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{m(n)}z_i^2\le m(n).
\]
This is an exact Euclidean norm bound, not an infinity-norm bound or a restriction to binary solutions. Encode each coordinate with a sign bit and \(\lceil\log_2(m(n)+1)\rceil\) magnitude bits, allowing unused encodings to be rejected. The trivial vector with a coordinate equal to \(q(n)\) is too long. Every matrix has a valid solution: since \(2^{m(n)}>q(n)^n\), two distinct binary vectors have the same image under \(A\), and their difference meets the displayed bound.

A worst-case input is an explicit full-column-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{h\times n}\), with \(h\ge n\ge2\), and a positive rational radius \(r\). Entries, dimensions, and the numerator and denominator of \(r\) are given in binary; their complete length is \(L\). Write
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bv:v\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{v\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bv\|_2.
\]
The promise is either \(\lambda_1\le r\), a yes-instance, or \(\lambda_1>\gamma(n)r\), a no-instance. The algorithm need not decide inputs between these thresholds.

The oracle formulation makes the average-case guarantee precise. For any integer \(t\ge1\), a permitted SIS oracle at parameter \(n\) is a fixed, possibly randomized map from matrices to either a valid solution in the stated encoding or a failure symbol \(\bot\), with
\[
\Pr_{A,\,O}[O(A)\ne\bot]\ge1/t
\]
when \(A\) is uniform. Calls use fresh independent oracle coins; the oracle has no mutable state between calls. It may fail on any selected set of inputs consistent with this average guarantee. No distributional assumption is made about its valid solutions, and the oracle need not be efficiently computable.

The desired reduction is one uniform classical probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine \(R\) and constants \(K,a>0\). On input \((B,r,1^t)\), it may make adaptive queries to this rank-\(n\) SIS oracle, all with the parameters above. For every \(n,t\), every promised \((B,r)\), and every permitted oracle, it must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\), over its own independent fair coins and the oracle coins. Every execution takes at most \(K(L+t+1)^a\) bit operations, including parameter computation, queries and responses; only the oracle's internal computation is free. For \(t\) polynomial in \(n\), this is the usual polynomial overhead for a non-negligible average success probability. There is no advice, quantum computation, auxiliary short-vector hint or other oracle.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a reduction with some fixed ε > 0 and the stated SIS parameters, overhead and universal oracle guarantee, or a proof that no such choice exists. Improving only the modulus, assuming a solver correct on every SIS matrix, supplying hints with the matrices, or allowing superpolynomial reduction time does not establish this target. The two LWE alternatives in the source are not substitutes for the selected SIS branch.
context:
The source reports classical SIS reductions at approximation scale roughly n times polylogarithmic factors for meaningful parameters, and asks for a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n.

The SIS modulus, number of columns and solution norm are part of the problem. The chosen family has more input bits than output residues, guarantees a short solution by counting, and excludes the immediate q-multiple solution.

The hardness theorem must use an oracle that works on random matrices with noticeable probability. Requiring correctness on every matrix would replace the requested worst-case-to-average-case connection by a different claim.

The known refinements improve modulus requirements and related parameters. The selected target instead lowers the approximation factor of the worst-case input by a fixed power of its rank.

The survey also discusses reductions using superpolynomial time. Such results can improve tradeoffs but do not meet the polynomial overhead required here.
why: Current worst-case guarantees for SIS rely on roughly linear approximation factors when parameters support nontrivial compression. A fixed exponent improvement would base average-case short-integer-solution hardness on a weaker worst-case lattice assumption.

working_summary: A random SIS instance is a matrix modulo a polynomial-size integer, and the goal is a short nonzero integer vector in its modular kernel. The question asks for a classical reduction from every Euclidean GapSVP instance with approximation factor O(n^(1−ε)) for some fixed ε > 0. The chosen matrix dimensions ensure that a solution exists while excluding the trivial modulus-sized vector. The reduction must work even when its SIS oracle succeeds only on an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random matrices. Polynomial overhead includes the inverse success probability, and a complete Lean-checked reduction or impossibility proof is required.

title: NP-hardness of Euclidean covering radius
importance_reason: Exact covering radius is a basic geometric invariant of lattices, yet even NP-hardness in the Euclidean norm is unresolved in the 2026 source. A classification would settle a central lattice-complexity question and clarify the contrast with large-norm hardness; the question also sits within the geometry underlying lattice cryptography and integer programming.
formal: Is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time map sending each Boolean 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a rational full-column-rank matrix \(B\) and a positive rational threshold \(r\), such that \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu_2(L(B))\le r?\] Unsatisfiable formulas must map to instances with \(\mu_2(L(B))>r\). This is the exact decision problem, with approximation factor one and no promised gap between the two cases.
question_excerpt: In particular, we reiterate that the problem of showing NP-hardness of exact GapCRP in the l2 norm (the most important special case) remains open.
definitions: The input basis is a matrix \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), where \(m\ge n\ge1\) and the \(n\) columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\). Its lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^m v_j^2)^{1/2}\). Define \[\mu_2(L(B))=\sup_{t\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(B)}\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|t-Bz\|_2=\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|B(w-z)\|_2.\] The points \(t\) range over the real linear span of the lattice, not the whole ambient space when \(n<m\). The compact fundamental parallelepiped \(B[0,1]^n\) gives the equivalent finite-radius maximum. The minimum ranges over all integer combinations, including coefficients outside \(\{0,1\}\). The exact decision language contains precisely valid pairs \((B,r)\) with \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(\mu_2(L(B))\le r\); equality is a YES instance and any strict excess is a NO instance. Encode dimensions and signed rational numerators and positive denominators in binary, with explicit delimiters and all matrix entries listed. Complexity is measured in total encoding length, including entry precision and the threshold, not just dimension. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations, with variable indices encoded in binary; it is satisfiable when some Boolean assignment makes every clause true. The requested reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed polynomial bit-time bound. It must output a valid instance on every valid formula, and the equivalence must hold for all formulas. All output bits and exact rational arithmetic costs count. No oracle, advice, randomness, real-number oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost arithmetic is available. NP-hardness here is deterministic many-one hardness for every language with a polynomial-time verifier and polynomial-length witnesses, equivalently hardness for the specified 3-SAT language.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a reduction exists, including polynomial bit complexity, valid output bases and both directions of the satisfiability equivalence, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation. A proof of a polynomial-time algorithm would refute NP-hardness only with an appropriate complexity separation; it is not by itself a negative answer. Hardness in another norm, hardness of linear discrepancy or of coding-theoretic covering radius, randomized reductions alone, and a reduction that reverses YES and NO do not establish this target. The task does not require NP membership or a quantitative approximation gap.
context:
Bennett and Ly explicitly single out NP-hardness of exact \(\ell_2\) covering radius in Section 1.4 of their September 2026 proceedings paper. Definition 4 specifies the decision orientation: small covering radius is YES, while radius strictly above the threshold is NO.

Their new hardness theorem applies for fixed \(p>p_0\), where \(p_0\approx35.31\), in the norm \(\|v\|_p=(\sum_j|v_j|^p)^{1/p}\). It gives approximation hardness with factors greater than one for suitable parameters. The Euclidean value \(p=2\) lies outside that theorem.

The paper distinguishes covering radius from linear discrepancy, \(\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}\|B(w-z)\|_p\). Restricting the nearest point to binary combinations can change the value, even when the generated lattice is unchanged. The present question uses all lattice points.

The introduction relates approximate covering radius to worst-case lattice problems and integer programming. These connections motivate the complexity question but do not supply a hardness proof for the exact Euclidean decision language.
why: The covering radius measures how far a point can be from its nearest lattice point. It is a central lattice invariant with connections to integer programming and to worst-case lattice problems used in cryptography. Establishing even exact Euclidean NP-hardness would close a basic gap in the complexity classification of lattice problems, without requiring the stronger approximation-hardness results known in other norms.
status_note: The proceedings paper published on 9 September 2026 explicitly lists exact Euclidean covering-radius NP-hardness as open. Its new large-norm hardness theorem does not cover p=2. The bounded search through 2026-09-15 found no verified resolution of this exact deterministic many-one decision target; it is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2006: As reviewed in the 2026 paper, Haviv and Regev obtain stronger hierarchy hardness for the infinity norm and sufficiently large finite norms; a 2012 journal version follows. | 2026-09-09: Bennett and Ly publish explicit finite-\(p\) hardness thresholds while retaining exact Euclidean NP-hardness as an open question in Section 1.4.
working_summary: A lattice covering radius is the largest distance from a point in its span to the nearest lattice point. The input here is a rational basis and a positive rational threshold in the Euclidean norm. The exact decision problem accepts precisely when the covering radius is at most the threshold. The question asks whether satisfiability reduces to this decision problem by one deterministic polynomial-time map. A September 2026 paper proves hardness for sufficiently large norms while explicitly leaving the Euclidean case open.

title: Classical ideal-SVP hardness of ring-LWE in power-of-two cyclotomic rings
importance_reason: A classical worst-case connection for cyclotomic ring-LWE would address a foundational gap for structured lattice cryptography; the search ideal-lattice starting point avoids an easy decision surrogate.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), integers \(b\ge0,n_0\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm that, for every power of two \(n\ge n_0\), reduces worst-case ideal-SVP in \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\) to the same-ring search-LWE problem defined below, with approximation factor
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac{\sqrt n}{\alpha}\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b?
\]
The reduction must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input ideal basis, for every admissible oracle, and use at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) classical bit operations and oracle calls on every run. Its queries must retain the degree \(n\), modulus \(q\), noise-family bound \(\alpha\) and sample count \(m\). The constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), but not on the ideal or the other parameters.
question_excerpt: Question 4 asks for a meaningful classical worst-case hardness reduction for ring-LWE and explains why the ordinary GapSVP starting point is insufficient on ideal lattices. This card selects approximate search-SVP in power-of-two cyclotomic rings and the elliptical error family of the known quantum reduction, with explicit finite rounding. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Classical reduction for ideal lattices in power-of-two cyclotomic rings in the stated quantum-reduction parameter range.
definitions:
Put \(K_n=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). Since \(n\) is a power of two, this is a number field with ring of integers \(R_n\). A nonzero integral ideal \(I\subseteq R_n\) is given by a full-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\): its columns are the power-basis coefficient vectors of a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(I\). The input is promised to generate a set closed under multiplication by \(X\), hence by every element of \(R_n\). All entries, dimensions and parameters are encoded explicitly in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is their total length.

Let \(\sigma_j\) be the embeddings sending \(X\) to the roots of \(X^n+1\). Use the canonical Euclidean norm
\[
\|v\|_{\rm can}^2=\sum_{j=1}^n|\sigma_j(v)|^2,
\qquad \lambda_1(I)=\min_{v\in I\setminus\{0\}}\|v\|_{\rm can}.
\]
The required output is a nonzero integer vector \(z\) such that the ideal element with coefficient vector \(Bz\) has norm at most \(\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_1(I)\). A short vector must actually be produced; deciding whether one exists is not the task. In this ring the canonical norm is \(\sqrt n\) times the coefficient Euclidean norm. Also, multiplying a shortest nonzero element by \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\) gives independent vectors of the same length, so the first and last successive minima of an ideal agree.

Admissible parameters have a prime \(q\le(n+2)^c\), integers \(1\le m\le(n+2)^c\), \(2\le t\le(n+2)^c\), and a rational \(\alpha=u/v\in(0,1/2]\), in lowest terms with \(u,v\le(n+2)^c\), satisfying \(\alpha q\ge(\log_2(n+2))^2\). Let \(R_{n,q}=R_n/qR_n\); its elements are encoded by \(n\) coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\).

Here is the exact finite-output family of error distributions. Extend the power-basis coefficient space to \(K_{n,\mathbb R}=\mathbb R[X]/(X^n+1)\). Choose one embedding from each complex-conjugate pair and define the real isometry
\[
\tau(v)=\bigl(\sqrt2\operatorname{Re}\sigma_j(v),\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\sigma_j(v)\bigr)_{j=1}^{n/2}\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
For any vector \(\rho=(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_{n/2})\) with \(0<\rho_j\le\alpha\), sample independently two real Gaussian coordinates for pair \(j\), each of density \(\rho_j^{-1}\exp(-\pi x^2/\rho_j^2)\). Let \(e\in K_{n,\mathbb R}\) be their inverse image under \(\tau\). Expand \(nq e\) in the power basis, round each real coefficient to its nearest integer and reduce modulo \(q\). The resulting element of \(R_{n,q}\) has distribution \(\chi_\rho\). Ties occur with probability zero. The factor \(n\) is intentional: it converts rounding in the dual ring \(R_n^\vee=n^{-1}R_n\) to this ordinary-ring representation.

An admissible oracle \(A\) is a fixed randomized map from ordered lists of \(m\) pairs in \(R_{n,q}^2\) to \(R_{n,q}\cup\{\bot\}\). For every fixed \(\rho\) in the family, choose a uniformly random secret \(s\in R_{n,q}\), independently sample uniform \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in R_{n,q}\) and errors \(\eta_i\leftarrow\chi_\rho\), and form
\[
(a_i,a_i s+\eta_i)_{i=1}^m.
\]
On this input the oracle must output the sampled \(s\) with probability at least \(1/t\), averaged over the secret, samples and oracle randomness. The same oracle must satisfy this for every \(\rho\); neither the secret nor \(\rho\) is given as side information. It has fresh independent randomness on every invocation. Away from these distributional guarantees its answers are arbitrary. The reduction may make adaptive finite-list queries and must work for every such oracle.

Computation uses a classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine with fair independent random bits. Query construction, input reading, oracle-answer reading, all numerical approximations and output writing are charged; only the oracle's internal computation is excluded. Exact real Gaussians define probability distributions, not computational primitives available to the reduction. Its implementation must use finite arithmetic and include sampling errors in its total failure probability. There are no quantum operations, advice or additional oracles. This is a family-of-noises search target, not the stronger fixed spherical-noise or decision target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked classical reduction with the stated approximation factor, finite sample distributions, same-degree queries, bit cost and per-ideal success guarantee, or prove the logical negation of the quantified claim. A quantum worst-case reduction, a classical search-to-decision reduction, a decision GapSVP starting point, or a generic-to-ideal reduction whose number field varies with the input does not settle this target.
context:
The source calls the classical reduction question meaningful only when its worst-case premise carries useful ideal-lattice hardness. It explicitly notes that the decision GapSVP problem is easy at the relevant polynomial factors.

The quantum theorem first reduces an ideal Gaussian-sampling problem to search ring-LWE for an entire family of elliptical errors. It yields an Õ(√n/α) factor for independent vectors, and hence also short vectors in cyclotomic ideals.

The power-of-two dual ring is exactly n⁻¹R. Scaling its secrets to R and rounding the noise in a dual basis explains the n in this card’s finite sample definition. Treating the ordinary coefficient Gaussian as though it had the same canonical parameter would change the problem.

The known search theorem requires a solver for every bounded elliptical shape. A fixed spherical error distribution is a distinct stronger hardness target; classical search-to-decision conversions do not remove the quantum worst-case step.

The September 2026 generic-to-ideal preprint changes the ambient number field with the input and allows monogenic orders. Its abstract qualifies the full-ring-of-integers extension. It does not establish a classical reduction to ring-LWE in the fixed cyclotomic family used here.
why: Ring structure makes LWE-based constructions more compact, but the useful worst-case ideal-lattice connection uses quantum computation. A classical reduction at comparable approximation and modulus scales would strengthen the theoretical understanding of that connection.

title: A classical reduction from semiprime factoring to polynomial-gap SVP
importance_reason: A reduction from factoring or discrete logarithms to approximate SVP would connect major families of computational hardness assumptions.
formal:
Do there exist an absolute rational constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and one classical randomized polynomial-time oracle algorithm that factors every integer \(N=pq\), where \(p\ne q\) are primes, using an oracle for Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{n^{2+\varepsilon}}\)?

Here \(n\) is the rank of the lattice in each oracle query, and the algorithm must output the two prime factors with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised input \(N\). The oracle may answer arbitrarily inside its approximation gap.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 4.10 asks for a classical reduction from factoring or discrete logarithms to polynomial-gap SVP and singles out the factor n^(2+ε). This card selects factoring of two distinct primes and a bounded-error polynomial-time oracle reduction. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Classical randomized reduction of factoring a product of two distinct primes to decision GapSVP at the stated n^(2+epsilon) scale.
definitions:
The factoring input is just the binary representation of an integer \(N\ge6\), promised to be the product of two distinct primes. The factors, their bit lengths and any auxiliary information are not supplied. They need not have equal bit length, and the target is worst-case correctness over all such products, not only randomly sampled or balanced ones. Put \(s=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\). A valid output is a pair of binary integers \((a,b)\), in either order, with \(1<a,b<N\), \(ab=N\), and both entries prime. Under the promise any nontrivial factor determines the required pair.

A well-formed lattice query is an explicit integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with linearly independent columns and \(m\ge n\ge1\), together with a positive rational \(r\). Matrix entries are signed binary integers; \(r\) is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The dimensions and all entries are included in a length-delimited encoding. Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\]
where \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). An admissible \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{n^{2+\varepsilon}}\) oracle \(O\) is any total Boolean function obeying
\[
O(B,r)=1\quad\text{if }\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\le r,
\qquad
O(B,r)=0\quad\text{if }\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))>n^{2+\varepsilon}r.
\]
For \(r<\lambda_1\le n^{2+\varepsilon}r\), either answer is permitted. No oracle correctness is required on malformed queries. The real-valued factor in this definition is an exact promise threshold; no numerical approximation oracle is supplied.

The reduction is one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(R\), with independent fair random bits, and constants \(K,c>0\), such that for every promised \(N\) and every admissible \(O\), every execution of \(R^O(N)\) uses at most \(K(s+1)^c\) bit operations and outputs the prime factors with probability at least \(2/3\). Writing queries, reading their one-bit answers and writing the factors count toward the running time; the oracle's internal computation does not. Adaptive polynomially many queries are allowed. In particular query rank, ambient dimension and full bit length are all polynomially bounded in \(s\). The same fixed \(\varepsilon,K,c,R\) must work for all \(N\) and every completion of the oracle's gap answers. There is no quantum computation, advice, factoring hint or additional oracle.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence of the stated classical randomized reduction, including its query encodings, bit complexity and success guarantee for every promised semiprime and every admissible oracle, or a proof that no such fixed ε and reduction exist. An unproved heuristic lattice embedding, an exponential-time reduction, a reduction to exact SVP only, or a quantum factoring algorithm does not establish this target.
context:
The source offers factoring and discrete logarithms as alternative starting problems. This card fixes semiprime factoring, so a proof need not also establish a discrete-logarithm reduction.

The target is the decision promise problem with a large multiplicative gap. An oracle for exact shortest vectors is substantially stronger and cannot simply be substituted for this oracle.

The source highlights n^(2+ε) because known classical reductions connect this approximation regime to learning with errors. The input parameter in that factor is the queried lattice rank, not the number of bits of the integer being factored.

Quantum reductions would give no comparable evidence: a quantum algorithm can already factor without a lattice oracle. Requiring a classical reduction is therefore essential to the requested connection.

Using lattices as a heuristic component of a factoring algorithm does not by itself prove a worst-case reduction to this approximate decision oracle. Both the embedding guarantee and the polynomial bound must hold for every promised input.
why: This would connect two major sources of computational hardness: factoring integers and approximating shortest lattice vectors by a large polynomial factor. The selected approximation regime is strong enough to connect onward to classical worst-case-to-average-case reductions used for lattice cryptography.

title: Baillie–PSW pseudoprimes
importance_reason: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.
formal: Does there exist a composite integer n that passes the strong base-2 probable-prime test and the strong Lucas probable-prime test with Selfridge’s Method A, including the parameter-search rejection rule specified below?
definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.
context:
A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

The 2021 paper reports that no base-2 Fermat pseudoprime below \(2^{64}\) also passes its Lucas test, giving correctness through that finite range and hence ruling out smaller counterexamples to the strong combination. It reports no known larger counterexample. Such a bound leaves the existence question over all integers unanswered.

A January 2026 preprint reports that all 200 selected composites in its experiment fail the strong Lucas test despite passing several Miller–Rabin bases. This does not establish correctness for arbitrary integers or a rigorous independence theorem for the two tests. With the specified parameters, the test’s outcome on a fixed n is deterministic; “probable prime” describes the strength of the conclusion, not random choices made here.
why: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.
status_note: The 2021 primary paper records no known counterexample; targeted searches through 11 September 2026 found no established counterexample or universal correctness proof for the specified strong Selfridge variant. The checked January 2026 preprint provides only finite empirical evidence.
progress: 1980: The Fermat/Lucas combination originates in the work recounted by Baillie, Fiori and Wagstaff. | 2021: The paper records verification below \(2^{64}\), proves Method \(A/A\)* equivalences and proposes additional checks. | 2026-01: A selected-composite experiment reports no strong-Lucas survivors and does not resolve the universal question.
working_summary: The Baillie–PSW combination checks a prime-like modular power pattern and a prime-like Lucas sequence pattern. The question asks whether any composite integer passes both strong tests with the specified Selfridge parameters. All recurrences, congruences and parameter-search rejection rules are fixed in the statement. Exhaustive verification through a large finite range and later experiments have produced no counterexample in the checked sources. A single rigorously verified composite would answer yes, while answering no requires a proof covering integers of every size.

title: Scholz–Brauer conjecture
importance_reason: The Scholz–Brauer conjecture is a longstanding universal law proposed for optimal addition chains, linking a basic arithmetic complexity measure across all exponents.
formal: For every positive integer n, is \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell (n)\), where \(\ell\)\((m)\) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.
context:
An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.
why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. Wallner’s April 2026 paper still presents the unrestricted inequality as open. Later May and August 2026 preprints located in the search make density-one or restricted-optimal-chain claims, rather than covering every positive integer. No general resolution was found. Published special-case statements and preprint claims were read at the recorded depth; proofs were not independently verified.

working_summary: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values. Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation. The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for \(2^{n}- 1\) is always at most \(n- 1\) plus the minimum length for n. The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources. Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.

title: Polynomial-factor Euclidean SVP hardness assuming NP is not contained in RP
importance_reason: Polynomial-factor SVP hardness would extend the known hardness frontier toward algorithmically and cryptographically significant regimes.
formal:
Is the following implication true?
\[
\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{RP}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q,\ 0<\varepsilon<1/2:
\operatorname{GapSVP}^{(2)}_{n^\varepsilon}\notin\operatorname{PromiseBPP}.
\]
Thus the target is a fixed positive power of the lattice rank in the Euclidean norm, with no classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm under the specified standard assumption. The exponent may be arbitrarily small but must be independent of the input.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 2.3 asks for hardness at a fixed polynomial approximation factor under a standard assumption, in a discussion allowing different norms. This card selects the Euclidean case and the precise antecedent NP ⊄ RP. The August 2026 polynomial-factor theorem for p > 2 is recorded separately. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Retain Euclidean p=2 and the assumption NP is not contained in RP; the separate August 2026 p>2 result does not close this selected question.
definitions:
An input is an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) of full column rank, with \(m\ge n\ge2\), together with a positive rational \(r\). All dimensions, matrix entries and the numerator and denominator of \(r\) are explicitly given in binary with delimiters. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length. Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), the yes-instances have \(\lambda_1\le r\), the no-instances have \(\lambda_1>n^\varepsilon r\), and the inputs with \(r<\lambda_1\le n^\varepsilon r\) are outside the promise. The task is to output the correct yes/no bit; it does not ask for a lattice vector. The approximation factor is an exact mathematical threshold and depends on rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient bit length.

Membership in PromiseBPP means that there are one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), with independent fair random bits, and constants \(K,a>0\), such that every run on a well-formed input halts within \(K(L+1)^a\) bit operations, every yes-instance is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every no-instance is rejected with probability at least \(2/3\). Behavior inside the approximation gap is unrestricted. There are no quantum operations, advice or additional oracles. The machine and its constants may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(B,r\).

The class NP consists of finite-bit decision languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class RP consists of languages with a uniform randomized polynomial-time decision algorithm that never accepts a no-instance and accepts each yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). The antecedent says that at least one NP language has no such RP algorithm. This is an ordinary decision-complexity hypothesis, not an assumption that a lattice problem is hard.

The conclusion requires one rational exponent for which no machine with the stated bounded-error guarantee exists. It does not merely rule out deterministic algorithms or one particular family of reduction algorithms. Restricting the existential exponent to rational values below \(1/2\) does not remove a possible positive-power hardness result: a solver for a smaller gap would also solve the promise problem for any larger gap. No common algorithm is required across different exponents if the conclusion fails.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication, with an explicit rational exponent or a rigorous existence proof and all claimed algorithmic guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A refutation must establish NP ⊄ RP together with PromiseBPP membership for every rational exponent in (0,1/2). Hardness only in a norm p > 2, only for constant factors or for subpolynomial factors, or only under a stronger subexponential-time hypothesis does not settle this target.
context:
The survey separates constant-factor hardness under NP ⊄ RP from stronger, still subpolynomial factors obtained under stronger running-time assumptions. The selected target asks for a fixed rank exponent under the former assumption.

The April 2026 result covers the Euclidean norm through a deterministic subexponential-time reduction. Its stated hardness assumption and approximation regime do not establish this polynomial-factor, standard-assumption implication.

Wan’s September revision states deterministic hardness for every fixed constant approximation factor. It explicitly removes the first version’s dimension-dependent claims, so those older claims are not used to close this card.

The August 2026 theorem establishes fixed polynomial factors for every p > 2. Its allowed exponent is smaller than min{(p−2)/(4p),1/8}; the bound does not yield a positive exponent at p=2. The paper also explains directly why its Euclidean norm estimate fails to produce the required gap.

Consequently the historical request interpreted as allowing any norm now has positive progress that answers that broad variant. This card deliberately retains the Euclidean specialization, rather than presenting the whole any-norm question as still open.
why: Constant-factor Euclidean lattice hardness does not explain whether even a small fixed power of the rank remains difficult to approximate. Establishing this from the standard randomized NP-hardness assumption would close a major qualitative gap in the approximation landscape.

The question asks whether NP ⊄ RP rules out a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for some fixed factor n^ε. The card retains that precise open specialization and requires a complete Lean-checked implication or refutation.

title: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring
importance_reason: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring asks whether a canonical arithmetic search problem has the recursive structure common to complete problems.
formal: Is there one deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every integer \(N\ge 2\) of binary length n, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N within \(p(n)\) steps, using a factoring oracle only on integers \(M\ge 2\) whose binary length is strictly less than n?
question_excerpt: It is an open problem whether there exists an algorithm for factoring that uses oracle calls on smaller numbers.
definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two expansion of N without leading zeroes, and \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\). The output is the list of distinct increasing primes \(q_{1}<\cdots <q_{r}\) and positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), all in binary, with \(N=\prod _{i} q_{i}^{e_{i}}\). A prime input has the single pair \((N,1)\). The oracle returns the same unique prime-factorization representation on M. Queries may be adaptive but must all satisfy \(\lfloor \log _{2}M\rfloor +1<n\) relative to the original input length. Merely requiring \(M<N\) would be weaker and is not the target. The ordinary Turing-machine cost includes writing queries, reading answers and writing the output; supplying a correct oracle answer is the sole oracle operation. The output length of prime factorization is polynomial in n. There is no randomness, advice or nonuniform family of reducers. The reduction must work for every input, with one polynomial bound independent of its factorization.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform polynomial-time reduction or its logical negation. Factoring using smaller numerical values of the same bit length, arbitrary smaller circuits for a factoring relation, or an exponential-time recursion does not meet the stated definition. The output need not be a decimal expansion of the input; its prime-power representation is explicit.
context:
Downward self-reducibility asks whether oracle solutions to strictly shorter instances suffice to solve the current instance with only polynomial additional work.

Definition 2.17 compares binary input lengths. The source separately defines a circuit-based notion, which is not substituted here. The retained card makes the shorter-input convention explicit.

The source shows that downward self-reducibility of factoring would place it in UEOPL, linking arithmetic factorization with a unique structured total-search class. This consequence does not decide whether the reduction exists.
why: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring asks whether a canonical arithmetic search problem has the recursive structure common to complete problems.
status_note: The source explicitly leaves downward self-reducibility of factoring open. The shorter-bit-length definition was checked; no later resolution was located in the bounded search.
progress: 2023: The source defines downward self-reductions in Definition 2.17 and gives the UEOPL consequence for factoring while leaving existence of such a reduction open.
working_summary: Factoring is a central arithmetic search problem whose complete output is a unique prime-power decomposition. The question asks whether one can factor an n-bit number in polynomial time given oracle answers only on shorter numbers. All queries must have fewer than n bits, not merely a smaller numerical value. The reducer is deterministic and uniform, with polynomially many ordinary computation steps. A positive answer would place factoring in a more structured total-search class and reveal a basic recursive property of the problem.

title: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions for SVP
importance_reason: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions would sharpen a fundamental equivalence used throughout lattice algorithms.
formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
definitions:
The input lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with a rational full-rank square basis whose columns generate it. The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|v\|_2:v\in L,\ v\ne0\}\). The output is an exact integer coefficient vector \(z\), so its nonzero lattice vector is unambiguously represented even when coordinates are rational. There is no norm other than \(\ell_2\), target point, uniqueness promise, preprocessing of a fixed lattice, or ideal-lattice restriction.

An oracle query is \((\widetilde B,r)\), where \(\widetilde B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). An admissible \(O_\gamma\) is any total Boolean function on these valid queries satisfying \[ \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=1,\qquad \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))>\gamma r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=0.\] When \(r<\lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le\gamma r\), its answer can be either bit. The reduction must succeed for every such total completion of the promise problem, including completions with no computability assumption. Repeated identical queries have the same answer because the oracle is a function. The same input value \(\gamma\) applies to every query. At \(\gamma=1\) there is no gap.

Dimension preservation means every oracle lattice has exactly the original dimension \(n\), including its ambient dimension and rank. Queries may use different bases and thresholds, but cannot increase dimension even by an additive constant. This follows the explicit same-\(n\) statement of Open Problem 4.5. Adaptively chosen queries are allowed; this is a Cook (oracle Turing) reduction, not a requirement of one nonadaptive query.

Integers, rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary with signs and delimiters; \(N\) includes the entire basis and \(\gamma\). Use a probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine with independent unbiased coin flips, a read-only input tape, work tapes and a query tape. Writing a query and reading its one-bit answer are charged; the oracle itself returns that bit in one oracle step. All arithmetic is implemented on binary tapes and pays its full bit cost. The displayed polynomial bounds total time on every random tape and every admissible oracle, and therefore bounds the number and bit lengths of queries and output. Only valid full-rank rational queries are allowed. There is no additional oracle, advice, quantum computation, or free real arithmetic.

The constants and the finite program are fixed before \(n,B,\gamma\) and the oracle are chosen. A bound \(C(n\gamma)^a\) expresses an unspecified polynomial loss uniformly over the domain \(n,\gamma\ge1\); replacing it by any fixed polynomial in these two parameters gives the same polynomial-loss existence target after increasing \(C,a\). The chosen reduction is allowed bounded-error randomness. This makes explicit the classical randomized reduction convention used by the cited near-exact results, rather than adding a deterministic-only requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction and uniform polynomial bounds exist, with correctness against every admissible completion of the promise oracle, or prove their nonexistence. A positive result must bound the output norm, bit complexity, and dimension of every query. Preserving dimension only up to an unbounded factor, obtaining an approximation loss exponential in \(n\), assuming special lattices, or giving only a quantum reduction does not meet the target. The known exact case or approximation factors approaching one alone do not establish the quantified statement.
context:
The source asks for polynomial loss in the approximation factor, not exact preservation of that factor. It also explicitly retains dimension. This matters for lattice algorithms whose costs depend exponentially on dimension, and for distinguishing an algorithm that recognizes short vectors from one that actually finds them.

The search and decision versions are known to be equivalent under dimension-preserving reductions in the exact case \(\gamma=1\). The 2016 randomized reduction has search loss \(\gamma^{n/s}\) and running time \(2^{O(s)}\gamma^{O(n)}\), for \(s\ge\log(n+1)\), with input-bit polynomial factors suppressed in that summary. Choosing \(s\) logarithmic gives an efficient useful guarantee when \(\gamma\) is very close to one; it does not give a polynomial-loss polynomial-time reduction for all approximation factors.

Bennett’s 2023 problem is phrased using rational square bases and Euclidean length. The older reduction map uses a relaxed convention that permits an additive constant in dimension, while the card follows the later explicit same-dimension wording. The distinction is recorded so that a looser reduction is not silently counted as satisfying the target.

The source relates a solution at polynomial approximation factors to worst-case search-SVP foundations for lattice cryptography. The Simons list also discusses search-to-decision questions for closest vectors and independent short vectors, including quantum variants. Those questions have different outputs, oracles or computational models and do not settle the reduction here.
why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.
status_note: The target is explicitly open in Bennett’s 24 January 2023 source. The near-exact 2016 theorem and the older reduction-map convention were checked directly, as were the dated June 2022 workshop questions. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no verified matching same-dimension classical reduction with polynomial loss. Recent LWE/LPN search-to-decision results concern different average-case problems and were not treated as resolutions. This is a limited source review, not exhaustive current-status or Lean proof certification.
progress: 2016: Dimension-preserving randomized reductions are proved for near-exact approximation factors with a substantially larger loss outside that regime. | 2022-06-06: The Simons Lattices Program lists related approximate search-to-decision questions for CVP and SIVP, with separate classical and quantum conventions. | 2023-01-24: Open Problem 4.5 explicitly asks for same-dimension SVP-to-GapSVP reduction with search approximation factor \(\operatorname{poly}(\gamma,n)\).
working_summary: The input is a rational lattice basis, and the search task is to produce a nonzero vector whose length approximates the shortest possible length. The available oracle only distinguishes short-vector lengths across a multiplicative gap. The question asks for a classical polynomial-time reduction that keeps every query in the original dimension and loses only a polynomial in dimension and approximation factor. Known exact and near-exact reductions do not supply this guarantee across the full approximation range. A resolution would clarify whether approximate lattice decision algorithms can be converted efficiently into search algorithms without an exponential dimensional penalty.

title: NP-hardness of Euclidean unique SVP with a fixed gap greater than one
importance_reason: Hardness for unique or structured lattices tests whether strong restrictions preserve the difficulty needed by algorithms and cryptography.
formal:
Is there an absolute rational constant \(\gamma>1\) such that the search problem \(\gamma\text{-uSVP}_2\) is NP-hard under classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reductions?

The input is an explicitly encoded integer lattice basis \(B\), promised to satisfy
\[
\lambda_2(\mathcal L(B))>\gamma\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B)).
\]
The required answer is an exact shortest nonzero lattice vector. The uniqueness gap \(\gamma-1\) must be a positive constant independent of the input dimension and bit length.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 4.6 asks for randomized NP-hardness of Euclidean unique SVP for some constant uniqueness factor greater than one. The card spells out a bounded-error polynomial-time oracle reduction for the search formulation.
definitions:
A lattice basis is a matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) with \(m\ge n\ge2\) and linearly independent columns. Dimensions and all entries are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters; let \(L\) be the total input length. Its lattice is
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m.
\]
All lengths use the Euclidean norm \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The first successive minimum \(\lambda_1\) is the minimum length of a nonzero lattice vector. The second successive minimum \(\lambda_2\) is the smallest radius of a closed ball centered at zero containing two linearly independent lattice vectors. Independence is over \(\mathbb R\). Rank \(n\), ambient dimension \(m\), and coefficient bit length can all grow with the input.

Under the strict gap promise there are exactly two shortest vectors, differing by sign. A valid answer is a binary integer coefficient vector \(z\ne0\) such that \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\). Either sign is allowed. The gap concerns independent directions, not merely the second distinct vector, which would always include the negative of a shortest vector. The output target is exact recovery, not an approximation of the shortest length.

Use the following randomized Cook-reduction meaning of NP-hardness for this promise search problem. An admissible oracle is any total function which, on a basis satisfying the promise, returns a valid shortest-vector coefficient vector and, on any other query, can return an arbitrary string or a distinguished failure symbol. Bound every response to a query of length \(L\) by \(4(L+1)^3\) bits. This is only an encoding convention: shortest-vector coefficients for an explicit integer basis have a polynomial bit bound of this size, by bounding an invertible minor and using a basis column as an upper bound on shortest length. The oracle need not be computable or choose the same sign on different bases.

NP-hardness here means that there exist one classical probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine \(R\) and constants \(K,a>0\) such that for every Boolean 3-CNF formula \(F\) of encoded length \(s\), and for every admissible oracle \(O\), every execution of \(R^O(F)\) uses at most \(K(s+1)^a\) bit operations and
\[
\Pr[R^O(F)=1]\ge2/3\quad\text{if }F\text{ is satisfiable},\qquad
\Pr[R^O(F)=0]\ge2/3\quad\text{otherwise}.
\]
The probability is over independent fair random bits of \(R\). A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations. The reduction may make adaptive queries; writing them and reading oracle responses are charged, while the oracle's internal computation is not. On well-formed lattice queries outside the gap promise no correctness is presumed of the oracle, and the reduction must tolerate every permitted response. The constants and \(\gamma\) are fixed before any formula is received. Thus a polynomial-time solver for the promise problem would yield a bounded-error polynomial-time algorithm for every NP language.
