answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of such randomized oracle NP-hardness for some fixed γ > 1, including the reduction, its bit complexity and its guarantee for every admissible oracle, or a proof of the negation of this existence claim. Hardness only for a dimension-dependent gap tending to one, a non-Euclidean norm, a superpolynomial-time reduction or a separate nonstandard lattice-hardness hypothesis does not establish the target. Failure of one proposed reduction does not refute it.
context:
The 2023 source distinguishes ordinary approximate shortest-vector hardness from unique shortest-vector hardness. Its explicitly open target is a fixed Euclidean uniqueness factor greater than one.

Aggarwal and Dubey obtain randomized hardness with a uniqueness gap of 1+1/poly(n). Such a gap tends to one and therefore does not supply the fixed positive separation in this card.

The rotation-lattice reduction proves hardness for constant uniqueness factors if finding shortest vectors in rotations of the integer lattice is hard. Its authors explicitly label that source assumption nonstandard; it is not a reduction establishing NP-hardness.

The October 2025 paper gives new unique-SVP hardness for norms with p>2 under hypotheses on subexponential or quasipolynomial algorithms. Its theorems do not cover p=2. Its related-work discussion also distinguishes fine-grained constant-gap results from polynomial-time NP-hardness.

The two signs of a shortest vector cannot be separated by a uniqueness promise. The promise instead compares the first two successive minima, and the oracle convention retains arbitrary behavior whenever that promise fails.
why: A constant separation between the shortest lattice direction and every independent competitor is a strong geometric promise. Proving NP-hardness despite that promise would show that isolating a shortest vector does not remove the worst-case difficulty of Euclidean lattice search.
status_note: Source-open in Bennett’s 2023 Open Problem 4.6. The checked 2025 work excludes the Euclidean norm and uses stronger running-time assumptions. Known inverse-polynomial uniqueness gaps, rotation-lattice assumptions and fine-grained reductions do not supply this fixed-gap polynomial-time oracle NP-hardness statement. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no matching resolution.
progress: 2016: Randomized NP-hardness is established for a gap greater than one by an inverse polynomial, rather than by a fixed constant. | 2023: The source explicitly retains the constant-gap Euclidean NP-hardness question; the rotation-lattice result supplies a different conditional hardness statement. | 2025: Deterministic unique-SVP hardness is strengthened in norms p>2 under stronger running-time assumptions; this leaves the selected Euclidean NP-hardness target untouched.
working_summary: The input is an explicit integer lattice basis in Euclidean space. It promises that every independent direction is longer than a shortest vector by one fixed factor greater than one. The task is to recover an exact shortest vector, with either sign allowed. The question asks whether this promise search problem is NP-hard under classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reductions. Shrinking uniqueness gaps and hardness in other norms do not establish this target, whose full proof or refutation must be Lean-checked.

title: SVP hardness for fixed-rank cyclotomic modules
importance_reason: Hardness for unique or structured lattices tests whether strong restrictions preserve the difficulty needed by algorithms and cryptography.
formal:
Does exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision remain NP-hard on cyclotomic module lattices when the module rank is an absolute constant?

For each fixed integer \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal D_r\) be the decision problem defined below. A valid instance consists of a conductor \(m\ge3\), finitely many generators \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\in R_m^r\) spanning \(K_m^r\) over \(K_m\), and an integer squared threshold \(S\ge0\), where
\[K_m=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m),\quad R_m=\mathbb Z[\zeta_m],\quad M=\sum_{j=1}^s R_m y_j.\]
It is a YES instance exactly when \(\lambda_1(M)^2\le S\), using the canonical product norm below.

The target is the existence of a fixed \(r\), a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(F\), and positive integer constants \(C,d\) such that \(F\) runs in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) bit steps on every input string of length \(N\), and for every well-formed 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance of \(\mathcal D_r\) satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_1(M_{F(\varphi)})^2\le S_{F(\varphi)}.\]
Thus one rank and one uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction must work for all formulas; the conductor, generators and threshold may depend on the formula.
question_excerpt: Bennett’s Open Problem 4.9 asks for NP-hardness at some constant module rank over some family of base rings, with power-of-two cyclotomics given as an example. The example is not a mandatory restriction. This card makes the cyclotomic-family variant precise by allowing all conductors, choosing the canonical Euclidean product embedding, integral finite generator lists, exact squared thresholds and deterministic many-one reductions. It retains the existential fixed-rank quantifier, rather than requiring rank two, rank one or hardness for every fixed rank. The family/embedding choice is an explicit editorial specification of the source’s choices. Hardness on the prime-conductor rank-two subfamily would answer this variant affirmatively; it would not establish the separate power-of-two or rank-one questions.
definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge3\), let \(\zeta_m=\exp(2\pi i/m)\). The degree \(n=\phi(m)\) is the number of integers \(a\) with \(1\le a\le m\) and \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Define the monic cyclotomic polynomial
\[\Phi_m(X)=\prod_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}(X-\zeta_m^a)\in\mathbb Z[X].\]
The ring \(R_m\) is identified with \(\mathbb Z[X]/(\Phi_m(X))\); it is the full ring of integers in \(K_m\). Every ring element is written uniquely by its \(n\) integer coefficients in the basis \(1,\zeta_m,\ldots,\zeta_m^{n-1}\).

A module generated by \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\) is the set of all sums \(\sum_j a_jy_j\) with \(a_j\in R_m\). Here \(s\ge r\) is finite and may vary. The input promise is that the columns have rank \(r\) over the field \(K_m\). Hence the generated additive group has integer rank \(rn\) and is a full lattice in the real span of its canonical embedding. The ring rank \(r\) stays fixed, while the integer dimension \(rn\) can grow. Generators may be redundant; the module is not promised free over \(R_m\) or principal in rank one. Integral coordinates are required, with no supplied factorization or pseudo-basis oracle.

For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\in K_m^r\), the canonical product norm is
\[\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}^2=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}|\sigma_a(x_i)|^2,\qquad\sigma_a(\zeta_m)=\zeta_m^a.\]
Equivalently it is \(\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}_{K_m/\mathbb Q}(x_i\overline{x_i})\), where conjugation sends \(\zeta_m\) to \(\zeta_m^{-1}\). All embeddings, including both members of each conjugate pair, are included. The real lattice dimension is \(rn\), despite representing it with complex coordinates. Set \(\lambda_1(M)=\min\{\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}:x\in M\setminus\{0\}\}\). Discreteness and full rank make this a positive attained minimum. Squared norms of integral module vectors are integers. The comparison includes equality at the threshold and requires no approximation or gap promise. A threshold of zero gives a valid NO instance.

To specify the bit model, encode each nonnegative integer \(a\) as \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is its binary expansion without leading zeros and \(\ell=|b|\); zero uses \(b=0\). Encode signed integers by one sign bit and \(U\) of the absolute value, using the positive sign for zero. A module input writes \(U(m),U(s),U(S)\), then all \(rsn\) signed coefficients, ordered by generator, module coordinate and power-basis coefficient. All coefficients, including zeros, are explicitly present. The fixed \(r\) is a parameter of the language, not part of the input. Invalid encodings, conductors less than three and rank-deficient lists are rejected in \(\mathcal D_r\). The reduction must produce valid inputs on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable well-formed formulas.

A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with exactly three signed variable occurrences each; repetitions are allowed. Use an encoding consisting of a unary number of declared variables, a binary length-delimited clause count, and three sign/index pairs for each clause, with every index in the declared variable range. The empty conjunction is satisfiable. All clauses and occurrences are written explicitly. Malformed formula strings need not have a correctness guarantee for \(F\), but the global polynomial clock still applies.

The reduction uses one finite classical program and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step has the usual bounded-symbol read/write and one-cell head movement cost. Arithmetic, construction of the conductor and ring data, and every written output bit are charged. No randomness, quantum computation, advice, hard-instance table depending on input length or uncharged oracle is allowed. The output length is bounded by the same polynomial clock. The chosen rank and constants are independent of formula size. The statement asks for hardness at at least one fixed rank over the specified family, not at every rank or at a fixed conductor. This exact decision language is a yes/no target; it is not a request to estimate a shortest length numerically.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence or its full negation. A positive answer must supply a fixed rank, a uniform deterministic reduction and universal polynomial clock, and prove validity and the YES–NO equivalence for every well-formed formula. A negative answer must rule out such a reduction for every fixed rank, rather than refute a proposed construction or fail to establish hardness at one rank. A randomized reduction, a Turing reduction making several oracle queries, growing module rank, hardness for a non-Euclidean norm, or a security assumption about random keys does not establish this specified claim. It is not necessary to prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) in order to prove a reduction.
context:
A fixed module rank is compatible with an unbounded geometric dimension: rank \(r\) over a degree-\(n\) number field gives integer dimension \(rn\). The hard-instance family must therefore vary the underlying field as inputs grow. Treating “rank two” as a two-dimensional integer lattice would erase the central distinction in the question.

Rank-one modules include ideals, whereas higher rank permits interactions between several ring coordinates. Bennett presents the fixed-rank module question after the ideal-lattice hardness question as a broader target. The distinction between module rank and the number of listed generators also matters: redundant generators do not increase the rank over the field.

The original survey distinguishes exact decision SVP from approximate decision and search variants. Its use of GapSVP does not itself require an approximation gap: factor one is the exact threshold decision problem. The card therefore uses an exact squared threshold and asks for a deterministic reduction, with the norm and representation fixed explicitly.

Felderhoff, Pellet-Mary and Stehlé relate a promised module unique-SVP problem to NTRU and give a random self-reduction with an ideal-SVP oracle qualification. Those are reductions between structured lattice problems with an exceptional-short-vector promise. The checked abstract does not claim a deterministic reduction from an NP-complete problem to the exact decision language in this card.

De Boer, Page, Toma and Wesolowski’s 2025 preprint, presented at STOC 2026, gives a worst-case-to-average-case self-reduction for approximate SIVP at fixed module rank. Its abstract specifies the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, a discretized invariant distribution, and a polynomial loss in approximation. SIVP seeks independent short vectors; a self-reduction of that task does not establish NP-hardness of exact SVP.

Liu, Feng and Pan’s 1 September 2026 preprint claims NP-completeness of exact decision SVP for full-rank free modules of rank two over \(\mathbb Z[\zeta_q]\), where the conductor \(q\) ranges over primes congruent to three modulo four. Theorem 1.1 specifies deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, integral generators, a nonzero determinant and an integer squared threshold under the canonical product norm. These instances belong to the card’s family with \(r=2\).

If that claim is correct, it answers the selected existential-rank question affirmatively even with two generators. Its Corollary 1.2 separately states search hardness under Turing reductions. The paper explicitly excludes conclusions about a fixed cyclotomic ring, the power-of-two family, average-case hardness or a cryptographic security reduction. The theorem and model were matched here, but the complete new proof was not independently certified; the card is therefore uncertain.

The earlier ideal-SVP algorithmic advances give an additional reason to distinguish rank one from rank two. Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski’s cyclotomic ideal result is quantum, has a \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) approximation scale, and has stated number-theoretic hypotheses for its polynomial-time consequence. It is neither an exact decision algorithm for all fixed-rank modules nor a contradiction to an exact hardness claim.
why: Module lattices retain algebraic structure while permitting much larger families than single ideals. Establishing hardness with a fixed number of module coordinates would show that this compact structure can support a fundamental worst-case geometric obstruction as the field degree grows. The problem tests the boundary between algebraic organization and computational difficulty; exact worst-case hardness alone does not establish the security of cryptographic parameter distributions.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Bennett’s 2023 source poses the constant-rank hardness question. Liu–Feng–Pan arXiv:2609.01469v1, submitted 1 September 2026, now claims a matching positive answer for a prime-conductor cyclotomic rank-two subfamily under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The theorem’s norm, rank, representation and exact decision threshold were checked against this explicit variant. Its full proof was not independently certified, so the card remains uncertain rather than being archived as a verified resolution. The result does not assert the separate power-of-two, rank-one or average-case cryptographic statements.
progress: 2022-09-15: The revised module unique-SVP/NTRU work describes related structured reductions with a promise and an oracle qualification; it does not provide the NP-hardness reduction requested here. | 2023-01-24: Bennett’s full survey explicitly asks for NP-hardness at some constant module rank and some ring family; power-of-two cyclotomics are an example. | 2025-11-17; presented 2026: The fixed-rank SIVP work gives a conditional worst-case-to-average-case self-reduction, as distinct from an NP-hardness reduction for exact SVP. | 2026-09-01: Liu–Feng–Pan claim deterministic exact decision hardness already at rank two for a prime-conductor cyclotomic subfamily. Scope matches the selected target; complete proof independently unverified.
working_summary: Cyclotomic module lattices combine integer lattice geometry with multiplication by an algebraic number ring. The question asks whether exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision is NP-hard at some fixed module rank while the conductor and field degree grow. The card specifies the canonical product norm, integral generators and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction. A September 2026 preprint claims this hardness already for rank two over a prime-conductor subfamily, matching the selected formulation. The complete new proof is independently unverified here, and its claim does not imply hardness for every ring family or cryptographic distribution.

title: Unconditional exponential hardness of \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP
importance_reason: Unconditional exponential hardness would be a major complexity result, though the saved cryptographic target needs a precise model and formulation.
formal: Do there exist explicit positive constants c and \(\varepsilon\) such that no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm solves Euclidean \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP on n-dimensional rational lattices in time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\), for any fixed k, where N is the input bit length? The lower bound must be unconditional; deterministic and randomized classical algorithms are included among the algorithms ruled out.
definitions: An instance is an invertible rational matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{n\times n}\) and a positive rational threshold r, all represented explicitly in binary with numerator, denominator, sign and delimiters included in N. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\). Its shortest nonzero Euclidean length is \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{(\sum i v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\); the minimum exists because B is invertible and the lattice is discrete. The promise problem \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP asks for YES when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})\le r\) and NO when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})>n^{1+\varepsilon}r\), promised that one holds. There is no correctness requirement in the gap between those cases. The same \(\varepsilon\) is used at every dimension. A bounded-error algorithm must give the correct answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised instance. Use a uniform quantum computation with a fixed finite universal gate set, such as Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements and classical control; qubits begin in the input state and zero auxiliary states, without advice, oracles or special quantum input access. Gate operations, classical control and input handling all count toward total worst-case running time, with the bound applying to every measurement branch. A single machine must work for all dimensions and bit lengths. The factor \(N^{k}\) explicitly accounts for the ordinary polynomial input-processing overhead suppressed in the source’s dimension-based exponential notation. Constants \(c,\varepsilon\) are chosen before the algorithm and may be specified as positive rational numbers, with their values part of a positive resolution; k and the hidden running-time constant may depend on the algorithm. The task is worst-case promise decision, not a claim about a supplied random distribution of bases.
answer_criterion: Specify positive constants \(c,\varepsilon\) and prove, without a complexity-theoretic or cryptographic hardness assumption, that no correct bounded-error quantum algorithm has running time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\) for any fixed k. Alternatively, refute the proposition by proving that for every \(c,\varepsilon >0\) there is an algorithm with such a running-time bound for some fixed k. Conditional hardness, exact-SVP hardness with approximation factor 1, and hardness in a different norm do not settle the stated target.
context:
The input gives a lattice basis and a radius. A yes instance contains a nonzero lattice point within that radius; a no instance has every nonzero point farther away by a factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\). The question asks whether distinguishing these widely separated cases still requires exponential time in the dimension.

As the gap factor increases, fewer inputs satisfy the promise and the decision task can become easier. A lower bound for exact shortest vectors therefore does not establish hardness for the polynomially growing gap used here. Bennett’s Problem 4.12 combines a large approximation factor with an exponential lower bound.

The STOC 2023 work connects exponential hardness of worst-case approximate lattice problems to average-case problems used for cryptography. Its abstract states that hardness at an approximately linear factor, up to logarithmic factors, would imply public-key cryptography. The survey’\(s n^{1+\varepsilon}\) target is chosen in this regime; the card itself asks for a concrete worst-case theorem.

The desired result would establish a lower bound without assuming another problem is hard. It would also rule out bounded-error quantum algorithms. A 2025 result called deterministic hardness in other norms still assumes hardness of SAT-related problems; deterministic reductions and unconditional lower bounds are distinct notions.
why: Combines worst-case exponential hardness, a cryptographically relevant approximation gap and resistance to quantum computation in one unconditional theorem. A resolution would turn a central type of lattice-security assumption into a proved complexity bound and would go well beyond establishing \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
status_note: Full original formulation and model read; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution. Related reduction results were checked at abstract level and do not remove their hardness assumptions. Proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2023: Bennett poses Open Problem 4.12 with explicit \(c,\varepsilon >0\) and approximation factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\), including quantum algorithms. It is distinct from the conditional polynomial-time hardness question immediately before it. | 2023: Lattice Problems Beyond Polynomial Time supplies quantitative worst-case-to-average-case reductions underlying the cryptographic motivation; its consequences depend on an appropriate lattice-hardness premise. | 2025-10: Hecht and Safra state deterministic-reduction hardness results for \(\ell p\) norms with \(p>2\) under complexity assumptions. Their abstract does not resolve the unconditional Euclidean quantum-time target.
working_summary: The input is a rational basis for an n-dimensional lattice and a positive radius. The task distinguishes a nonzero vector within that radius from the promise that every nonzero vector is farther away by a factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\). The source asks for explicit \(c,\varepsilon >0\) and an unconditional lower bound excluding \(2^{cn}\)-time algorithms, up to polynomial input-processing factors. The bound must also exclude randomized and quantum computation with bounded error. Such a theorem would establish a powerful worst-case hardness foundation for lattice-based cryptography.

title: coNP certificates for GapSVP at the square-root n/log n scale
importance_reason: Improved short certificates for approximate SVP would constrain both algorithms and possible hardness reductions.
formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge2\) such that Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_C(n)}\) belongs to coNP, where
\[
\gamma_C(n)=C\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log_2(n+2)}}\ ?
\]
Concretely, must every input lattice whose shortest nonzero vector has length greater than \(\gamma_C(n)r\) admit a polynomial-length, deterministically polynomial-time verifiable certificate, with no accepted certificate when the lattice has a nonzero vector of length at most \(r\)?
question_excerpt: Open Problem 4.2 offers improvements to coNP or coAM. Its following paragraph specifically asks whether the coNP approximation scale can reach O(√(n/log n)); this card selects that concrete target. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: coNP membership for Euclidean GapSVP at C times sqrt(n/log_2(n+2)).
definitions:
The input consists of an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge1\) and linearly independent columns, and a positive rational radius \(r\). Dimensions, signed matrix entries and the numerator and positive denominator of \(r\) are written in binary using an explicit length-delimited encoding. Let \(L\) be its full bit length. The rank \(n\), ambient dimension \(m\), and all coefficient lengths are part of the input.

Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The GapSVP promise distinguishes yes-instances with \(\lambda_1\le r\) from no-instances with \(\lambda_1>\gamma_C(n)r\). Inputs between those thresholds are outside the promise. The constant restriction \(C\ge2\) ensures \(\gamma_C(n)\ge1\) at every positive rank; changing finitely many small ranks does not affect the intended asymptotic scale. The logarithm is to base two, and the approximation factor depends on lattice rank, not total bit length.

Membership in coNP for this promise problem means that there are one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(V\), constants \(K>0\) and integers \(a,b\ge1\), with the following properties on every well-formed input. A certificate is a finite binary string \(w\) with \(|w|\le K(L+1)^a\), and verification takes at most \(K(L+1)^b\) bit operations for each such certificate. The same verifier and constants must satisfy
\[
\lambda_1>\gamma_C(n)r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists w:\ |w|\le K(L+1)^a\ \land\ V(B,r,w)=1,
\]
\[
\lambda_1\le r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall w:\ |w|\le K(L+1)^a\ \Longrightarrow\ V(B,r,w)=0.
\]
Longer strings can be rejected. Verification behavior is unconstrained inside the gap. There is no required efficient algorithm for finding certificates, but verification is uniform, classical and deterministic. Certificates contain only finitely many bits; exact real numbers, randomness, quantum states, interaction with a prover and auxiliary oracles are not supplied. Both the choice of \(C\) and all resource bounds are fixed independently of each input.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a constant and verifier exist, including certificate length, deterministic bit complexity, completeness and soundness on the promise, or a proof of the negation of this existence claim. A randomized interactive coAM protocol, a polynomial-time verifier only at factor C√n, or a smaller-factor protocol with superpolynomial running time does not establish this target.
context:
Aharonov and Regev prove coNP membership at approximation factor C√n. Their argument provides succinct classical evidence that no sufficiently short vector exists; merely exhibiting a short vector certifies the opposite side.

The better scale √(n/log n) is known for a randomized interactive coAM protocol. The selected question asks whether deterministic checking of one polynomial-length certificate can reach the same scale.

The 2005 paper already discusses the corresponding refinement for the closest-vector problem as Speculation 1.5. Its approximation-preserving reduction would also transfer that stronger result to shortest-vector certification.

The source’s broader question also permits unspecified smaller improvements or a stronger coAM protocol. This card selects the explicit coNP target stated directly after Open Problem 4.2.

Protocols with larger running time or proof length can trade resources for approximation quality. Such a tradeoff does not imply membership in coNP, which requires both resources to be polynomial in the encoded input length.
why: A short certificate that no sufficiently short lattice vector exists would strengthen the known upper bounds on lattice complexity. Matching the better approximation scale of interactive proofs with a single classical certificate would clarify the role of interaction in certifying lattice distance.
status_note: Source-open in Bennett’s Open Problem 4.2 and its explicit following coNP target. The selected refinement was announced as an editorial default after an unanswered optional question. Existing coAM protocols and superpolynomial-time tradeoffs do not provide the required deterministic polynomial verifier. Bounded later-work checks through 17 September 2026 found no matching resolution. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: coNP membership for Euclidean GapSVP at C times sqrt(n/log_2(n+2)).
progress: 2005: Aharonov and Regev establish the C√n certificate bound and discuss a possible logarithmic refinement for closest-vector certification. | 2023: The survey retains the coNP improvement as open and singles out the √(n/log n) target.
working_summary: GapSVP asks whether an input lattice has a vector of length at most a threshold or all nonzero vectors are longer by a promised factor. This card asks for short classical certificates of the second alternative at factor C√(n/log n). One deterministic verifier must check the certificates in polynomial time in the complete binary input length. Known certificates work at the larger scale C√n, while the smaller scale is known for an interactive randomized proof. The requested improvement and all promise guarantees require a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation.

title: A quantum 2^(0.2075n) lower bound for exact Euclidean SVP from QSETH
importance_reason: Sharper exponential-time bounds or reductions would refine the quantitative complexity and security landscape of lattice problems.
formal:
Does the Quantum Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that there are no constants \(K,a>0\) and no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm which, for every explicitly given integer lattice basis of rank \(n\) and total binary input length \(L\), outputs an exact shortest nonzero vector using at most
\[
K\,2^{83n/400}(L+1)^a
\]
elementary operations on every execution? The exponent is the exact rational number \(83/400=0.2075\), and the norm is Euclidean.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 2.6 asks for the absence of a 2^(0.2075n)-time quantum algorithm for exact Euclidean SVP under a standard complexity assumption. The preceding discussion describes quantum SETH. This card selects that hypothesis and an explicit uniform gate-cost convention, with a polynomial factor in the full binary input length. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Quantum SETH with the exact Euclidean SVP lower-bound exponent 0.2075.
definitions:
An instance is a full-column-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge1\). The dimensions and all signed entries are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the complete encoding length. The lattice is
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
An acceptable classical output is a binary integer coefficient vector \(z\ne0\) with \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\). Either sign and any shortest vector are acceptable. The success probability must be at least \(2/3\) on each individual basis, over all internal measurements and randomness. No average-case or unique-shortest-vector promise is imposed. Reading the input and writing the output count toward the running time. The exponential parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(m\) or the bit length \(L\).

Use the following uniform finite-gate quantum model for both the lattice problem and the hypothesis. A fixed classical multitape Turing machine controls qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), applies gates from \(\{H,T,T^{-1},\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), prepares fresh zero qubits, measures in the computational basis and finally writes a classical answer. Here \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and CNOT maps \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin\oplus v\rangle\). The controller has the explicit classical input and may adapt to measurement outcomes. Each classical bit step, gate, preparation and measurement costs one operation. Gates may act on arbitrary finitely indexed qubits, but computing and writing their binary indices costs classical bit steps. There is no advice, postselection, external oracle or unit-cost coherent memory-lookup operation; any such lookup used by an algorithm must be implemented with counted gates. All classical control time is counted, and time is bounded on every measurement branch.

For an integer \(k\ge3\), a \(k\)-CNF formula is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most \(k\) literals on \(N\) named Boolean variables. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(M\) be the complete binary encoding length. The Quantum Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (QSETH) here is:
\[
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\ \exists k\ge3:
\text{there is no uniform quantum algorithm deciding }k\text{-SAT}
\text{ in time }O\!\left(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)N}(M+1)^b\right)
\]
for any constant \(b\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every formula. The algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on \(k,\varepsilon\). The cost model is exactly the one above. Thus the reference exponent is \(1/2\), reflecting quantum search, rather than the classical exponent 1.

The card asks for the full logical implication from this specific hypothesis. It does not restrict a proof to many-one, nonadaptive or black-box reductions. Its conclusion excludes the displayed running time itself; it is not merely a statement that all still smaller exponents are impossible. The polynomial factor permits arbitrary explicit coefficient lengths.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated implication from QSETH, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must establish QSETH together with an algorithm meeting the displayed time and per-input correctness guarantee. A barrier for a restricted family of reductions, a heuristic sieve cost, a lower bound only against classical algorithms, or an unspecified positive exponent does not settle this exact target.
context:
The source motivates 0.2075 from the space scale of plausible quantum sieving attacks. That motivation is an estimate for algorithmic approaches, not a lower bound against every quantum algorithm.

The survey records exponential fine-grained hardness for several non-Euclidean norms and explains how quantum hypotheses change the SAT baseline by a factor of two. These results do not provide the requested Euclidean exponent.

Its discussion already identifies obstacles to SAT-based proofs in the Euclidean norm. Selecting QSETH makes the target a particular conditional assertion rather than a search over unspecified assumptions.

The ICALP 2026 paper extends a barrier to polynomial-size nonadaptive quantum reductions from SAT to Euclidean closest-vector problems, unless NP has the indicated quantum statistical zero-knowledge protocols. The theorem restricts reduction methods; it does not refute every QSETH implication or give a fast exact-SVP algorithm.

The explicit finite-gate model counts coherent memory access when implemented and keeps the hypothesis and target in the same model. Consequently the card does not silently import an uncharged quantum-memory primitive from a heuristic algorithm estimate.
why: Quantum attacks on lattice problems are often estimated from particular sieving algorithms. A rank-sensitive exponential lower bound under an independent SAT hypothesis would provide a much firmer basis for those estimates and would have to overcome substantial limitations of current reductions.
status_note: The exact Euclidean quantum lower-bound target remains unresolved in the checked sources through 17 September 2026. The choice of QSETH was an announced editorial default after no reply to an optional question. The July 2026 barrier concerns restricted nonadaptive reductions and does not refute the unrestricted implication. The precise gate model and polynomial input-length factor are editorial specifications. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Quantum SETH with the exact Euclidean SVP lower-bound exponent 0.2075.
progress: 2023: The source poses the explicit Euclidean quantum exponent as Open Problem 2.6, with quantum SETH discussed immediately beforehand. | 2026-07: The ICALP result adds a no-go theorem for a restricted class of quantum reductions to Euclidean CVP; it leaves the full selected implication unresolved.
working_summary: Exact Euclidean SVP asks for a shortest nonzero vector of an explicitly given integer lattice. This card asks whether quantum SETH rules out time 2^(0.2075n) times a polynomial in the binary input length. The quantum SAT hypothesis uses the search baseline 2^(N/2), and both sides use the same uniform finite-gate model. Known barriers obstruct important families of reductions without resolving the full implication. A complete Lean-checked proof or refutation must establish the stated numerical exponent and computational guarantees.

title: ETH hardness of constant-factor shortest-vector approximation for \(1\le p\le 2\)
importance_reason: Seeks an ordinary-ETH exponential barrier for constant-gap shortest-vector approximation in the central ℓ1-to-Euclidean norm interval. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: Does deterministic ETH imply that for every fixed real \(p\in [1,2]\) there is a constant \(\gamma >1\) for which the gap shortest-vector problem \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) has no deterministic algorithm running in time \(2^{o}(d)N^{O}(1)\), where d is the ambient lattice dimension and N is the explicit input bit length?
definitions: An input consists of integers \(d\ge r\ge 1, a\) rational \(d\times r\) matrix B with linearly independent columns, and a positive rational threshold R. All rationals are given by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators with delimiters; N is the total bit length. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{r}\}\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{d}\). For fixed \(p\in [1,2]\), the norm is \(\Vert x\Vert _{p}=(\sum _{i=1}^{d}|x_{i}|^{p})^{1/p}\), and \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{p}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\). \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) accepts if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})\le R\) and rejects if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})>\gamma R\). Inputs between these thresholds are outside the promise; either answer is permitted there. The requested task is gap decision, not output of a lattice vector. The norm parameter and gap are fixed mathematical constants, not part of the input, and one finite deterministic Turing-machine program must solve all promised inputs for them. A subexponential bound means time at most \(2^{h(d)}N^{c}\) for some fixed c and nonnegative h with \(h(d)/d\to 0\). Bounds and programs may depend on p and \(\gamma\). The dimension convention follows the source’s lower-bound statements for lattices in \(\mathbb{R} ^{d}\); rank \(r\le d\) is displayed separately. ETH here asserts that for some \(\delta >0\) there is no deterministic algorithm deciding 3-CNF satisfiability on v variables in \(O(2^{\delta v}M^{c})\) time for any fixed c, where M is the formula’s bit length. It is the ordinary satisfiability assumption, not a promise that unsatisfiable instances have a constant fraction of violated clauses. Randomized ETH instead excludes bounded-error randomized algorithms and is a different premise. The card follows the literal deterministic-ETH version of Open Problem 1.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the implication from ordinary deterministic ETH to the stated constant-gap subexponential lower bound for every fixed \(p\in [1,2]\). The constant \(\gamma\) may depend on p but must be strictly greater than one and independent of dimension. A result using GapETH, or only randomized ETH, does not by itself prove this precise implication.
context:
The zero vector belongs to every lattice and is excluded from the minimum. In \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) the shortest nonzero vector has norm one for every p in this range. A YES instance has such a vector within radius R; a NO instance has none within the larger radius \(\gamma R\).

The desired factor \(\gamma\) is fixed once the norm is chosen. A hardness result whose factor approaches one as dimension grows would not meet the question. Conversely, the target does not require hardness for every constant factor, only for some factor greater than one at each p.

The paper proves ordinary-ETH hardness for constant-gap closest vector in all finite \(\ell p\) norms. Its shortest-vector result for \(p>2\) uses randomized ETH. Closest vector has a specified target point, while shortest vector looks for a short nonzero vector around the origin; the two tasks and the two ETH variants are kept separate.

At \(p=1\) the norm sums absolute coordinates, while at \(p=2\) it is Euclidean length. The source leaves this whole interval as an open shortest-vector hardness target. Its result outside the interval therefore does not establish the displayed claim.

Hair and Sahai give deterministic hardness of approximation in every finite \(\ell p\) norm, including \(p=2\), in a work accepted at FOCS 2026. Their reduction uses a subexponential-size/time regime relative to the SAT instance. This is substantial progress on removing randomization, but its stated hardness does not exclude every \(2^{o}(d)\)-time algorithm in the output lattice dimension, as this card requests.
why: Would strengthen the fine-grained hardness basis for constant-factor lattice approximation in the most familiar norm range, using an ordinary satisfiability assumption. It separates a genuine exponential obstruction from lower bounds relying on a stronger gap or randomized premise.
status_note: Published source and definitions checked through 11 September 2026. Hair–Sahai’s 2026 deterministic hardness result was also checked: its subexponential reduction does not supply the displayed \(2^{o}(d)\) lower bound in output lattice dimension. No matching resolution of the ordinary-ETH target for \(1\le p\le 2\) was located.
progress: 2026-07: The paper establishes ordinary-ETH constant-gap CVP hardness and randomized-ETH SVP hardness for \(p>2\), while explicitly leaving \(p\in [1,2]\) open. | 2026-04-06: Hair and Sahai’s revised preprint gives deterministic hardness for all finite norms; its reduction-size regime is different from the dimension-linear fine-grained requirement here. The work is accepted at FOCS 2026.
working_summary: The shortest-vector problem asks how short a nonzero lattice vector can be. This card asks for constant-factor gap hardness in every norm \(\ell p\) with \(1\le p\le 2\). The proposed lower bound excludes subexponential dependence on ambient dimension, with polynomial dependence on input encoding length. Its premise is ordinary deterministic ETH, and the approximation factor must stay bounded away from one as dimension grows. The source’s shortest-vector hardness theorem for \(p>2\) uses randomized ETH and does not settle this stated interval or premise.

title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
importance_reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.
focus_reason: A central continuous-alphabet interference tradeoff, with a fully specified weighted-capacity target and the saved uncertainty about recent claims preserved.
formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.
context:
Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

The user explicitly restored this real-parameter supporting-function target on 12 September 2026. The present review retains its full domain, average-power convention, and absolute \(1/100\) numerical acceptance. It does not add a requirement for a particular finite-letter characterization, and it does not infer fixed-tolerance unsolvability from sources discussing exact capacity.
why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.
status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026; retained as uncertain. Khandani 2501.14941v12, dated 7 September 2026, claims Gaussian Han–Kobayashi optimality for weak interference. The current primary PDF’s statement and §§7–8 were read, but its full proof for unrestricted codes was not independently validated; the scope is not an all-real-parameter capacity function. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and proves only a restricted single-phase Gaussian-suboptimality result without power control, not a refutation of v12 or of the full power-controlled region. Other checked 2025–2026 work supplies special inner-region and outer-bound results. The original Huleihel–Merhav reference was withdrawn in April 2018. Bounded later-work checks found no verified full answer at this card’s 1/100 tolerance; dated discussion of exact capacity alone is not a certification that this numerical benchmark is unsolved.
progress: 1981: Strong-interference capacity and the Han–Kobayashi achievable region establish fundamental benchmarks; later exact sum-rate results cover additional regimes without giving every rate tradeoff. | 2007-02-09: The checked v2 of Etkin–Tse–Wang states and proves the universal one-bit approximation in its complex-channel formulation; the journal version appeared in 2008. | 2018-04-08: Huleihel–Merhav withdraw the preprint originally used in this card’s provenance, acknowledging that Gaussian memory does not improve the power-controlled comparison region. | 2019-03: Nair–Ng’s published temporal-correlation invariance theorem concerns the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region with time sharing. | 2025: Nair–Zhao establish a parameter condition removing multiplexing from an optimized Gaussian Z-channel inner region. | 2026-01: Nair–Zhao give restricted Gaussian-suboptimality examples without power control and retain the full power-controlled Gaussian-capacity conjecture. | 2026-02: Gohari–Nair–Zhao present an auxiliary-receiver outer bound; its full Gaussian specialization gives the stated very-weak-interference and one-sided conclusions. | 2026-09-07: Khandani v12 claims weak-interference capacity optimality of Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling. The complete proof has not been independently validated in this review.
working_summary: Two separately informed transmitters communicate through real Gaussian noise while interfering with each other’s receivers. The target is the weighted support function of the capacity region for every real gain, nonnegative power budget and weight between zero and one. The model permits deterministic time sharing and averages each transmitter’s power over messages and time, with vanishing joint average decoding error. Known special cases and approximation results leave the general tradeoff unresolved in the checked sources, while a September 2026 weak-interference capacity claim remains unverified here. A complete Lean proof must certify one function within absolute error 1/100 bit per real channel use throughout the entire domain.

title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
importance_reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.
focus_reason: The fundamental asymptotic binary coding tradeoff; its well-defined rate curve is restored as a distinct coding-theory focus alongside multiuser communication.
formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.
context:
A code represents messages by selected bit strings. More codewords carry more information per transmitted bit, while greater pairwise separation permits correction of more adversarial errors. This question asks for the best possible asymptotic compromise over every binary code, independently of algorithmic restrictions.

The repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, and corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The complete set of three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, and cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. In general, correction of every pattern of at most \(t\) substitutions requires and is guaranteed by pairwise distance at least \(2t+1\), for an integer \(t\ge0\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\ge1-h_2(\delta)\), whereas the elementary Hamming bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\le1-h_2(\delta/2)\). Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.9 asks for the largest asymptotically attainable binary rate at a fixed relative distance. Its infinite-family formulation is represented here by the explicit limsup and subsequence convention.

The 1977 McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bounds sharpen the upper side. The first gives \(R_2(\delta)\le h_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\); the second is never weaker. These were the long-standing general upper bounds, but the August 2026 preprints report strict improvements, so the 1977 frontier must not be described as current.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s 10 August 2026 preprint reports strict improvements to the first and second MRRW bounds at every \(0<\delta<1/2\). The theorems concern arbitrary classical binary codes, including nonlinear ones; quantum states occur in the analysis and do not change the code alphabet. The introduction still identifies the GV curve as the best general asymptotic lower bound.

The requested tolerance needs a separate check from exact openness. At relative distance one quarter, the GV rate is approximately 0.18872, while Table 2 of the August preprint reports a numerical upper-bound estimate near 0.35038. The authors explicitly label the table as floating-point evaluations, not certified global optima. These reported values illustrate the remaining difference between the displayed lower and upper estimates; they are not a certified interval or a proof that no different approximation theorem exists. The checked sources do not supply the requested error of 0.01 throughout the domain.

Barg’s 1 September 2026 note compares the new channel bound with the concurrent Delsarte-certificate result. Its Section 2 identifies the coinciding variational formulas for the improvement of the first MRRW bound. The note provides a mathematical relation between those results, rather than a determination of the full rate–distance function.

Finite-length improvements can leave the limiting rate unchanged. Jiang and Vardy obtain a factor of order \(n\) over the binary Gilbert bound for each fixed \(0<\delta\le0.499\). Such a multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log n/n)\) after taking the logarithm and dividing by block length. It does not constitute an increase in the asymptotic rate exponent.

Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a probabilistic proof of a square-root block-length improvement for linear codes and an extension to quantum codes. The paper acknowledges the earlier classical square-root improvement. These polynomial factors do not by themselves alter \(R_2\), and the quantum-code statement has different objects and constraints.

Capacity under independent random bit flips, list decoding, and codes over larger alphabets have different targets. This card asks for worst-case pairwise separation over the binary alphabet. A construction above the GV curve at even one distance would address the separate beyond-GV question, while this card requires two-sided accuracy over the entire distance interval.
why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.
status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The primary August and September papers report stronger general upper bounds but do not determine the curve or supply the requested absolute 1/100 approximation throughout (0,1/2). The August table is expressly numerical rather than a certificate of its optimization. Bounded later-work searches found no matching approximation result; exact openness alone is not treated as proof of openness at the selected tolerance. Finite-length polynomial factors, other alphabets and other decoding models do not settle this target. New proofs were not independently certified.
