working_summary: The input is one rational linear inequality involving the Shannon entropies of subsets of variables. It must be tested against every joint distribution on arbitrary finite alphabets, with no conditional premises. The question asks whether one algorithm can always halt and decide exact validity, including equality cases. Decidability for restricted inequalities and undecidability for conditional statements concern different problems. A complete Lean-checked answer must provide a total decision procedure or prove undecidability of this precise input language.

title: Capacity of the general two-user interference channel
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with independent private messages and no feedback.
definitions: A channel has nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2,\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\) and arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Conditional on input sequences, an \(n\)-use output sequence has law \(\prod_{t=1}^n W(y_{1,t},y_{2,t}\mid x_{1,t},x_{2,t})\). Messages \(M_1,M_2\) are independent and uniform on \([K_{1,n}]\) and \([K_{2,n}]\), where \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and message counts are positive integers. Encoder \(i\) is a deterministic map \([K_{i,n}]\to\mathcal X_i^n\); its decoder is a deterministic map \(\mathcal Y_i^n\to[K_{i,n}]\). Error means at least one incorrectly decoded message, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A pair \((R_1,R_2)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2\) is achievable if there are codes with block lengths \(n_j\to\infty\), error tending to zero, and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both users. The capacity region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)\) is the closure of these achievable pairs. The channel and both codebooks are known to all terminals. There is no common message, feedback, terminal cooperation, input cost or computational bound. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed, so all its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. The function is measured in weighted bits per joint channel use. Channel laws and weights are mathematical real objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on the entire stated domain and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) for every channel and weight. The proof must control both sides of the error; exact determination also qualifies. The guarantee concerns the support value in bits per joint use, with the coding model unchanged. Sample values, a plot or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit are insufficient. No prescribed formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is required.
context:
Two sender–receiver pairs share one channel while each sender knows only its own independent message. The full rate tradeoff records how the two communications constrain each other.

Han and Kobayashi provide a fundamental achievable region. The historical model reference states that the general capacity region is not known. The support-value formulation expresses the full tradeoff without requiring a particular single-letter form.
why: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.
status_note: Open in the cited historical model reference. The code definition was rechecked on 13 September 2026 and a bounded follow-up search did not identify a general resolution. The 2010 notes are used for the model, not as current-status evidence; neither exact capacity nor the weaker numerical benchmark is certified as exhaustively searched.
progress: 1981: Han and Kobayashi establish an achievable region for the interference channel. | 2010: The model notes define the separate encoders, average error and capacity region, and explicitly state that the general region is unknown.
working_summary: Two independent senders communicate with their own receivers through one interfering channel. Each sender knows only its own message and receives no feedback. The capacity region contains the asymptotically reliable pairs of rates under average block error. Its weighted upper support values describe the entire tradeoff in bits per joint channel use. The benchmark asks for these values on every finite channel with a Lean-certified absolute error at most 0.01.

title: Positive-rate binary codes against adversarial deletions
importance_reason: Individual assessment: the binary adversarial deletion threshold is a central and broadly motivated coding-theoretic limit, not a tuning question for one construction. It asks when any positive-rate unique-decoding scheme can exist, connects code design to extremal subsequence structure, and survives a major qualitative upper-bound breakthrough with a substantial numerical gap. The score reflects this foundational role and scientific reach, replacing the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.
formal:
Determine the real zero-rate threshold
\[
p^*=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\operatorname{Ach}(p)\},
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Ach}(p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists r\in(0,1]\ \forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[n\ge N\ \land\ |C|\ge 2^{rn}\ \land\
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right].
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\) means that every codeword in \(C\) can be recovered uniquely, with zero error, after any choice of at most \(t\) deleted positions. Deleted positions are not revealed, and the adversary may know the entire code and transmitted word. The positive rate \(r\) may depend on \(p\), but must remain fixed along the unbounded sequence of block lengths. This is a question about arbitrary code families, with no efficiency, linearity or uniform construction requirement. Benchmark acceptance is absolute error at most \(1/100\) in \(p^*\).
definitions:
A binary word of length \(n\) is a sequence \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), with each symbol represented by one bit. A code \(C\) is a nonempty subset of these words. It may be represented by its duplicate-free lexicographically ordered list of words; no bound on the size of this representation is imposed. A message can be identified with an integer in \(\{1,\ldots,|C|\}\), encoded as the corresponding word in this list. The information rate, in bits per transmitted bit, is
\[
R(C)=\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}.
\]
Only positive block lengths \(n\ge1\) are used.

A word \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is a subsequence of \(x\) if there are indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(y_j=x_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). The empty word is a subsequence. No surviving bit is changed or reordered. For \(0\le t\le n\), define the possible received words
\[
\mathcal D_t(x)=
\{y:\ y\text{ is a subsequence of }x,\quad n-t\le |y|\le n\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall x,x'\in C,\quad x\ne x'\Longrightarrow
\mathcal D_t(x)\cap\mathcal D_t(x')=\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, a deterministic decoder from the binary words of lengths \(0,\ldots,n\) to \(C\cup\{\bot\}\) can satisfy \(D(y)=x\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(y\in\mathcal D_t(x)\), where \(\bot\) denotes failure on other inputs. The decoder may know \(C,n,t\), but receives no deletion locations. Its computation time and storage are unrestricted. Success is required for every transmitted word and every allowed deletion pattern, rather than with a small average or probabilistic error.

For two words \(x,x'\), their longest-common-subsequence length \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')\) is the largest integer \(m\ge0\) for which some length-\(m\) word is a subsequence of both. The correction condition is equivalent to
\[
\forall x\ne x'\in C,\qquad
\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<n-t.
\]
For \(t=\lfloor pn\rfloor\), this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<(1-p)n\), since the LCS length is an integer and \(n-\lfloor pn\rfloor=\lceil(1-p)n\rceil\). This fixes the source's suppressed rounding conventions exactly.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Ach}(p)\) uses infinitely many, equivalently arbitrarily large, block lengths. It does not require a code at every sufficiently large length. The quantified codes may be arbitrary nonlinear subsets and need not be generated by a single algorithm. The model has no shared secret, public key, feedback, random channel, stochastic encoder or list output. It is the information-theoretic unique-decoding model.

The supremum exists as a real number: the achievable set is contained in \([0,1]\) and contains \(0\), witnessed by the full binary codes. Correcting a larger deletion budget implies correcting every smaller one, so achievability is downward closed. The definition does not assert that \(p^*\) itself is achievable, or that one fixed positive rate works for fractions approaching it.
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|a-p^*|\le\frac{1}{100}
\]
for the exact model and quantifiers above. The answer need not be an integer or an exactly attained deletion fraction. Merely repeating the supremum that defines \(p^*\) does not determine it.

One sufficient form is a certified interval: supply reals \(0\le l\le u\le1\), prove \(l\le p^*\le u\) and \(u-l\le1/50\), and take \(a=(l+u)/2\). The two bounds can be made fully explicit as follows:
\[
\forall p\in[0,l)\ \exists r\in(0,1]\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\ge N\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[|C|\ge2^{rn}\land
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right],
\]
and
\[
\forall p\in(u,1]\ \forall r>0\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge N\ \forall\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)
\Longrightarrow |C|<2^{rn}\right].
\]
All block-length variables in these statements are integers. The lower statement allows rates and families to depend on \(p\), and the upper statement ranges over every code. Neither requires attainment at an endpoint. The Lean development must establish the stated correction property and its asymptotic quantifiers, not merely verify codes at finitely many lengths.

Exact determination is welcome but is not required. A one-sided estimate, a result for efficient or linear codes alone, a different alphabet, list decoding, or probabilistic deletion errors does not by itself meet this criterion.
context:
The original 2015 question asks for the value of the supremum \(p^*\), and then separately asks whether it equals \(1/2\). The present numerical target preserves that first question; it does not reinterpret the later resolution of the equality question as a determination of \(p^*\).

Bukh, Guruswami and Håstad construct positive-rate binary code families correcting every fixed deletion fraction below \(\sqrt{2}-1\). This proves \(p^*\ge\sqrt{2}-1\), without requiring that the endpoint itself be achievable.

Guruswami, He and Li prove \(p^*\le1/2-\delta_0\) for an absolute constant \(\delta_0\ge10^{-40}\). Thus the source's subsidiary question about equality with one half is resolved negatively, while the value of the threshold remains undetermined.

An ICALP 2025 primary paper explicitly retains the interval \([\sqrt{2}-1,\,1/2-10^{-40}]\) among open binary coding questions. Its width \(3/2-\sqrt{2}-10^{-40}\), approximately \(0.085786\), exceeds \(1/50\), so these checked bounds alone do not provide the benchmark's required \(1/100\) approximation.
why: This threshold is a basic information-theoretic limit for synchronization errors over the smallest nontrivial alphabet. It links the geometry of large code families to unavoidable common subsequences in binary words and separates worst-case synchronization loss from substitution and erasure models. Determining it would settle the maximum deletion fraction compatible with nonvanishing binary communication rate, independently of implementation constraints. The numerical question remains significant after the qualitative discovery that the threshold is strictly below one half.
status_note: The numerical threshold remains open in the checked primary literature. The original subsidiary question whether p*=1/2 was resolved negatively by Guruswami–He–Li (2021; inspected expanded arXiv revision 15 November 2022), but their conclusion still asks for the value of p*. An ICALP 2025 paper explicitly retains the bracket [sqrt(2)-1, 1/2-10^-40], whose width is about 0.085786 and therefore exceeds the 1/50 sufficient interval width for this benchmark. A bounded later-source search through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution or certificate meeting absolute error 1/100 for this precise model. The review inspected definitions, theorem statements and status passages, with abstract-level scope checks of newer neighboring models; it is not an exhaustive literature review, a full proof audit or a Lean verification.
progress: 2015: Guruswami and Wang explicitly ask for the positive-rate binary adversarial-deletion threshold and, separately, whether it equals \(1/2\). | 2016-03-01: The inspected second arXiv revision of Bukh–Guruswami–Håstad gives positive-rate constructions approaching deletion fraction \(\sqrt{2}-1\); the journal publication is in 2017. | 2021-06-09: Guruswami–He–Li announce the first constant improvement below the \(1/2\) upper bound; the checked expanded revision is dated 15 November 2022. | 2025-06-30: A primary ICALP paper continues to list determining the binary zero-rate threshold as an open question and records the remaining numerical interval. | 2026-09-16: Recovered the exact unique-decoding target, specified the infinitely-many-blocklength convention and rounding, audited the numerical tolerance, and checked later results within a bounded search.
working_summary: A binary deletion code must identify every transmitted word after an adversary removes an allowed fraction of its bits without revealing their positions. Positive rate means that codebook size grows exponentially along infinitely many block lengths with one fixed positive exponent. The target is the supremum deletion fraction for which such zero-error uniquely decodable code families exist, with no efficiency requirement. The checked bounds run from the square root of two minus one to one half minus ten to the minus fortieth power, and are too far apart to supply the required approximation. An accepted answer must determine this real threshold within 1/100 and prove the accuracy in Lean, without requiring that the supremum be attained.

title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
importance_reason: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.
definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is \(k/n\) and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants \(r, \delta\) and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple \((x,z,i)\); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.
context:
A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.
why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated ordinary binary query model; this is a bounded literature check, not an independent proof audit.
progress: 2000 / 2017: As summarized in the April 2026 source, constant-rate local decoding has an \(\Omega (\log  n)\) query lower bound and a binary high-rate upper bound of \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\). | 2026-01-30: HDX constructions improve approximate local list decoding and give logarithmic-depth list decoding, in a distinct model. | 2026-04-02: The revised large-alphabet LDC paper explicitly retains the ordinary binary constant-rate \(O(\log  n)\)-query question as open.
working_summary: Can a binary code protect arbitrarily long messages at constant rate while recovering any requested bit with only logarithmically many bit queries? A fixed positive fraction of the stored bits may be corrupted adversarially. The local decoder must return the requested bit with probability at least two thirds for every admissible received word and index. Large-alphabet and list-decoding results satisfy different guarantees. The target asks for existence, without an extra requirement that the code be efficiently constructed.

title: Rate–distortion tradeoff for distributed lossy source coding
importance_reason: The basic unresolved limit of compressing correlated information without coordination between encoders.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{RD}}(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2,\lambda)=\inf_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal R(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet memoryless source pair, finite distortion tables, feasible distortion targets and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the rate region for separate encoders and a joint decoder.
definitions: The source alphabets \(\mathcal X_i\) and reproduction alphabets \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\), for \(i=1,2\), are nonempty finite sets. The pairs \((X_{1,t},X_{2,t})\) are independent identically distributed draws from an arbitrary real probability table \(P\) on \(\mathcal X_1\times\mathcal X_2\). Distortions are finite-valued functions \(d_i:\mathcal X_i\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Write \(P_i\) for the marginal source law and \(D_{i,\min}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_i}P_i(x)\min_{z\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_i}d_i(x,z)\). The domain requires finite real \(D_i\ge D_{i,\min}\). An \(n\)-block code consists of deterministic encoders \(f_{i,n}:\mathcal X_i^n\to[M_{i,n}]\), where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and \(M_{i,n}\ge1\), and a deterministic decoder from the pair of indices to \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_1^n\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_2^n\). Each encoder sees only its own source block. For the resulting reproductions define \(\Delta_{i,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[d_i(X_{i,t},\widehat X_{i,t})]\). A nonnegative pair is achievable if, along some \(n_j\to\infty\), codes satisfy \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2M_{i,n_j}\le R_i\) and \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\Delta_{i,n_j}\le D_i\) for both sources. The region \(\mathcal R\) is the closure of achievable pairs. There is no interaction, extra side information, computational restriction or variable-length encoding; distortion is expected per-symbol distortion. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. Transmitting both source blocks and selecting minimum-distortion reproductions establishes feasibility on the stated domain; smaller distortion targets, which would give an empty region, are excluded. The region is convex and upward closed. Its nonnegative lower supporting values describe its lower rate boundary. The target is finite and nonnegative, in weighted bits per source pair. All tables are mathematical real objects, with no algorithmic representation requirement.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the whole source, distortion and weight domain above and a Lean proof of \(|g-F_{\mathrm{RD}}|\le1/100\) pointwise. This is an error bound on the weighted rate in bits per source pair; the distortion constraints remain exact. Prove both sides of the bound, or determine the function exactly. A finite sample of values or a restatement of the operational infimum or limit is insufficient. No specified formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed.
context:
Separate encoders describe correlated source blocks to one decoder. Correlation can reduce the total communication even though the encoders cannot inspect each other’s data. Allowing distortion changes the problem from lossless reconstruction.

The historical notes give inner and outer bounds and identify the general two-source lossy region as unresolved. This card measures its lower boundary by the minimum weighted rate and explicitly excludes infeasible distortion targets.
why: The basic unresolved limit of compressing correlated information without coordination between encoders.
status_note: Open in the cited 2010 model notes. The definition and the numerical benchmark were rechecked on 13 September 2026. The available later-work review is bounded and did not identify a general solution; the historical notes do not establish current open status.
progress: 2010: The model notes present Berger–Tung inner and outer bounds and state that the general distributed lossy rate–distortion region is not known.
working_summary: Two encoders separately compress correlated source blocks for one joint decoder. Each reconstructed source must satisfy its own expected per-symbol distortion limit. The function records the smallest weighted sum of the two description rates. Only feasible distortion targets are included, so every requested value is finite. The benchmark keeps the distortion constraints exact and requires a Lean-certified rate error of at most 0.01 on the whole domain.

title: Shannon capacity of \(C_{7}\)
importance_reason: The smallest odd-cycle zero-error capacity left unresolved after Lovasz's pentagon theorem.
formal: Determine the zero-error Shannon capacity \[\Theta(C_7)=\sup_{t\ge1}\alpha(C_7^{\boxtimes t})^{1/t}\] of the seven-cycle, in distinguishable symbols per channel use, with the graph power defined below.
definitions: \(C_{7}\) has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}\), with distinct vertices adjacent when their difference modulo 7 is 1 or 6. For an integer \(t\ge 1\), the strong power has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}^{t}\). Two distinct tuples are adjacent when, in every coordinate, their entries are equal or adjacent in \(C_{7}\). An independent set contains no adjacent distinct pair, and \(\alpha\) is its maximum cardinality. The capacity is measured in distinguishable symbols per channel use, rather than its logarithm in bits. It lies between 3 and 7; the supremum need not occur at a finite power. There is no computational restriction on independent sets or their construction.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a Lean proof that \(|a-\Theta(C_7)|\le1/100\). Certified lower and upper bounds \(\ell\le\Theta(C_7)\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). An exact value with proof also qualifies. A restatement of the defining supremum, a one-sided bound or an estimate without certified error does not suffice. This tolerance concerns the benchmark value, not an exact-capacity conjecture.
context:
The seven-cycle is the first odd cycle after the pentagon whose exact zero-error capacity remains unresolved in the cited literature. Independent sets in its strong powers represent collections of mutually distinguishable codewords.

The August 2026 preprint reports a lower bound of \(3.25883262\ldots\), while the Lovász upper bound is \(7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\approx3.31766720\). Their gap is still larger than \(1/50\), so these bounds do not yet meet this card’s acceptance tolerance.
why: The smallest odd-cycle zero-error capacity left unresolved after Lovasz's pentagon theorem.
status_note: The 31 August 2026 preprint explicitly leaves the exact capacity unresolved. Its reported lower bound and the primary-source upper bound still leave a gap exceeding 0.02, so they do not settle this card’s 0.01 acceptance target. Checked on 13 September 2026; the new construction was not independently verified.
progress: 2019: Polak and Schrijver give \(\Theta(C_7)\ge367^{1/5}\) and state the Lovász upper bound \(7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\). | 2026-08-31: Tandon’s preprint abstract reports a code in the 500th strong power giving \(\Theta(C_7)\ge3.25883262\ldots\). This is a reported preprint result; the construction and proof were not independently verified.
working_summary: The seven-cycle describes which pairs of seven channel symbols can be confused. Its Shannon capacity is the supremum of independence numbers of strong graph powers raised to the reciprocal power. The card asks for this real number in distinguishable symbols per use, rather than bits per use. No finite graph power is assumed to attain the supremum. The Lean benchmark accepts an explicit value with certified absolute error at most 0.01.

title: Capacity of the general two-way channel
importance_reason: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{TW}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-way channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with both terminals allowed to adapt their transmissions to past received outputs.
definitions: The channel has nonempty finite input alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2\), output alphabets \(\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\), and a table of arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for every input pair. In an \(n\)-use code, terminal \(i\) holds a message \(M_i\) uniform on \([K_{i,n}]=\{1,\ldots,K_{i,n}\}\), with positive integer message counts and independent messages. At time \(t\), its input is \(X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})\), where \(f_{i,t}\) is deterministic and \(Y_i^{t-1}=(Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,t-1})\). Given the current inputs and full past history, the current output pair has distribution \(W\). Terminal 1 estimates \(M_2\) from \((M_1,Y_1^n)\), and terminal 2 estimates \(M_1\) from \((M_2,Y_2^n)\), by deterministic decoders. Error is the probability that either estimate is wrong, averaged over messages and channel draws. A nonnegative rate pair is achievable if codes along \(n_j\to\infty\) have error tending to zero and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both terminals. Thus \(R_1\) is the rate from terminal 1 to terminal 2, and \(R_2\) is the reverse rate. The region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)\) is the closure of achievable pairs. The law and all coding functions are public. There are no extra communication links, shared messages, input constraints or computational bounds. The received outputs provide the permitted feedback. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The capacity region is compact, convex and downward closed, so its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. Rates are in bits per simultaneous joint channel use, without an extra factor of two. The channel table and weight are mathematical real objects, not finite-precision algorithmic inputs.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on every channel and weight above and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{TW}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) everywhere. Certify both sides of the error in bits per joint channel use; exact determination also qualifies. The adaptive coding model must be retained. A finite set of examples, an uncertified plot or a restatement of the operational optimization or limit is insufficient. No specified formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is imposed.
context:
Both terminals send their own independent messages and receive the other terminal’s transmissions. Each may use past received outputs to choose its next input, making interaction part of the capacity question.

Shannon’s two-way channel model comes with lower and upper bounds. The historical model notes retain the general capacity problem as unresolved. The weighted upper support function records the full directional rate tradeoff.
why: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.
status_note: Open in the historical model notes. The full adaptive model was rechecked on 13 September 2026. The later-work search was bounded and did not yield a verified general resolution; neither the notes nor that search provide exhaustive current-status evidence.

Reliable rates therefore include the possible benefit of adaptation and interaction. The target gives the weighted upper support values of the complete two-direction capacity region. title: Computability of graph Shannon capacity
importance_reason: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer \(k\ge 1, A\) on input \((G,k)\) halts and outputs integers a and \(b>0\) with |\(a/b- \Theta (G)|\le 2^{- k}\)? No bound on running time is imposed.
definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.
context:
Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

This source raises the computability of graph Shannon capacity. The retained target asks for a uniform halting procedure at arbitrary requested precision, not just one fixed numerical tolerance.
why: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.
status_note: General computability remains explicitly unknown in the checked October 2025 primary paper. January 2026 work supplies special-family results and nonattainment examples, not a general algorithm or noncomputability proof. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution.
progress: 2006: Alon–Lubetzky demonstrate large later increases beyond arbitrarily long fixed prefixes of the independence series. | 2025-10: A primary paper on spectral bounds explicitly states that general Shannon capacity is not known to be computable. | 2026-01: New special-family values and connected examples of finite-power nonattainment are published; they do not decide general effective approximation.
working_summary: A graph records which transmitted symbols can be confused. Its Shannon capacity is the limiting number of distinguishable messages per use when arbitrarily long blocks are allowed. The question asks for one terminating algorithm that approximates this quantity to any requested absolute accuracy on every finite graph. Known examples show that fixed finite prefixes and finite-power attainment do not supply a general stopping guarantee. The target concerns computability itself, with no required running-time bound.

title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
importance_reason: A central unrestricted existence question about whether constant bit-query locality and constant adversarial error tolerance can coexist with polynomial blocklength; distinct from the constant-rate logarithmic-query and relaxed-decoding questions.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(q\ge1\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\), such that for every integer message length \(k\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\) with \(k\le n\le Ck^d\), an injective encoding
\[
 E_k:\{0,1\}^k\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,
\]
and randomized local decoders \(D_{k,i}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), satisfying
\[
 \Pr[D_{k,i}^{\,z}=x_i]\ge\frac23
\]
for every message \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) and every received word \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) differing from \(E_k(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) coordinates, while each decoder reads at most \(q\) bits of \(z\) on every execution?
question_excerpt: Are there binary locally decodable codes with a constant number of queries, a fixed positive decoding distance and blocklength polynomial in the message length?
definitions:
Here \(k\) counts message bits and \(n\) counts stored codeword bits. The Hamming distance between two length-\(n\) words is the number of coordinates where they differ. The allowed corruptions are precisely the words at Hamming distance strictly less than \(\delta n\), as in the source definition. In particular the uncorrupted codeword is included. The constants \(q,C,d,\delta\) are fixed before \(k\); they do not depend on the message, requested coordinate, corruption or code length. The blocklength \(n=n(k)\), encoding and decoder descriptions may depend on \(k\). Polynomial blocklength does not require constant rate or a polynomial of any prescribed degree.

This is an existence question in the classical randomized bit-query model. For fixed \(k,n,i,E_k\), a deterministic query procedure is a finite binary decision tree of depth at most \(q\). Each internal node is labelled by a coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\); the oracle returns the single bit \(z_j\), and this chooses the next child. Each leaf is labelled by the output bit zero or one. A randomized decoder is a probability distribution over such trees, fixed independently of \(x\) and \(z\). This describes adaptive queries: later coordinates may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries count toward the same bound, and early stopping is allowed. The tree distribution may depend on the requested index and the code, but the only information it learns about the actual received word is through the queried bits.

The probability in the statement is solely over that decoder's private randomness. The guarantee holds separately for every triple \((x,z,i)\); a single random choice need not decode all message coordinates at once. Corruptions may depend on the full encoding and message and are computationally unrestricted, but \(z\) is fixed before the decoder draws its randomness. There is no secret key or randomness shared with the channel. The output is one bit: an erasure symbol, a candidate list or success only averaged over requested indices does not meet the definition.

Encoding linearity, systematic form and local correction of every codeword coordinate are not required. There is no bound on encoding time, decoder computation between queries or description length, and no additional requirement that one efficient uniform program construct the family. The finite decision-tree formulation makes the query resource explicit without granting access to any unqueried received bits. Codes must be available for every message length under one set of constants; a finite catalogue or a query bound growing with \(k\) does not suffice.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this existence statement, specifying or proving the existence of the encodings and decoders and verifying the common constants, polynomial blocklength, worst-case query bound and all corruption/success quantifiers; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

An efficient explicit construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative proof must rule out every fixed query count and every polynomial degree, including nonlinear codes and the unrestricted decoder model. A lower bound only for two or three queries, only for matching-vector constructions, or only for locally correctable codes does not establish that negation. Relaxed, approximate, list or amortized decoding and growing-alphabet symbol queries require a proved conversion meeting the exact binary single-bit requirements. No approximation tolerance applies to the yes/no target.
context:
Local decoding retrieves one chosen message bit without scanning the stored codeword. The positive constant corruption fraction prevents a direct read of a systematically stored bit from meeting the requirement.

The textbook gives polynomial-length binary codes with polylogarithmic query complexity and asks whether the query count can be constant. Its cited constant-query constructions instead have superpolynomial blocklength.

The general odd-query lower bounds apply even to nonlinear binary codes. For each fixed query count their blocklength bounds are polynomial, so they leave open a sufficiently large polynomial exponent in this existence question.

The August 2026 matching-vector bound yields superpolynomial length within a particular three-query construction framework at fixed modulus. The target permits other encodings and any fixed query count.

The subsequent August preprint also bounds three-restricted matching-vector families, without claiming a lower bound for every binary locally decodable code.

Relaxed decoders may report failure on some corrupted inputs. Their shorter codes and theorems comparing relaxed and full decoding do not automatically give the required success on every requested message bit.

The September 2026 construction combines relaxed outputs with amortizing queries over a consecutive block of message symbols. Constant queries per recovered symbol in that model are different from a constant total number of probes to recover any one requested bit.
why: Determine whether a constant number of bit probes can recover any requested message bit despite a constant fraction of adversarial corruptions using only polynomial storage. This is a central locality-versus-redundancy question with connections to private information retrieval and complexity theory.
status_note: Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of polynomial-length constant-query binary local decoding in the unrestricted model. General fixed-query lower bounds remain polynomial, the August matching-vector bounds restrict the construction class, and the September constant-rate result permits amortized relaxed decoding. This is not an independent full audit of those results.

title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
importance_reason: Efficient explicit tree codes would give a fundamental construction for reliable interactive communication.
formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.

Fix an integer \(q=|\Sigma|\ge2\) and identify \(\Sigma\) with \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), represented by fixed-length binary symbols. For each height \(N\), an encoder defines maps \(C_N:\{0,1\}^{\le N}	o\Sigma^{\le N}\) with \(|C_N(x)|=|x|\), \(C_N(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\), and prefix consistency: if \(u\) is a prefix of \(x\), then \(C_N(u)\) is the prefix of \(C_N(x)\) of length \(|u|\). Thus an output symbol cannot depend on future input bits. For every \(N\ge1\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and distinct \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\), let \(j\) be the first input position where \(x_j

e v_t\}|}{\ell-j+1}.\] A decoder receives \(1^N\) and any \(w\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and returns a binary string of length \(\ell\), or a failure symbol. For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\ell\), if \(d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(w,C_N(x))\le\alpha\), the output must be exactly \(x\). No correctness requirement is imposed outside this promise, but the decoder must still halt within its time bound. The promise bounds errors in every suffix of the received prefix. It is not a bound on total Hamming error alone, which would not separate paths that diverge close to their end. The encoder and decoder are two fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine programs, with constants \(K,k\), each using at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit steps per invocation on valid inputs. Encoding receives \(1^N\) and the currently available input prefix \(x\), and outputs \(C_N(x)\). The known horizon \(N\) is allowed; the code families for distinct horizons need not agree. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.
context:
Wigderson’s Open Problem 15.34 explicitly requests efficient encoding and decoding, constant rate and constant relative distance. The card keeps all four requirements and uses the standard finite-height binary-input formulation.

The 2018 interactive-coding paper defines efficient tree-code decoding through suffix distance: a received prefix is decoded when every suffix has sufficiently few errors. This supplies a concrete promise for the otherwise unspecified decoding clause in the source question.

The checked May 2026 version of Cohen, Schulman and Srivastava records that constant-rate positive-distance tree codes exist nonconstructively, while the explicit constructions discussed there achieve rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) at constant distance. That rate tends to zero as the horizon grows.

Their rate–immediacy theorem rules out constant rate for codes satisfying an additional immediacy property under the theorem’s hypotheses. General tree codes need not satisfy that property, so the result does not prove impossibility of the encoder and decoder requested here.
why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.

Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 found no unconditional construction or impossibility result for the precise efficient-encoding-and-decoding target here; the review does not certify exhaustive current openness.

working_summary: A binary tree code assigns output labels to every possible input history as that history unfolds. After two histories first differ, their output suffixes must disagree on a fixed positive fraction of positions. A fixed output alphabet keeps the information rate bounded below by a positive constant. The requested uniform algorithms must encode efficiently and recover any received prefix satisfying the stated suffix-error promise. The checked 2026 literature still leaves this constant-rate construction open, and its new barrier concerns an additional restricted property.

title: Explicit binary codes with efficient list decoding up to capacity
importance_reason: A central constructive coding question: attain the full binary adversarial list-decoding capacity with deterministic explicit encoding and efficient decoding. The inherited score is retained while correcting its obsolete beyond-Gilbert–Varshamov rationale.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\delta,R\) satisfying
\[
 0<\delta<\frac12,\qquad 0<R<1-H_2(\delta),
 \qquad H_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
there are uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and list-decoding algorithms for binary codes
\[
 E_m:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{N(m)}
 \quad(m\ge1),\qquad \frac{m}{N(m)}\ge R,
\]
such that every \(E_m\) is injective and the decoder, on every received word \(y\in\{0,1\}^{N(m)}\), outputs exactly
\[
 \{x\in\{0,1\}^{m}:d_H(E_m(x),y)\le\lfloor\delta N(m)\rfloor\}?
\]
The binary alphabet is fixed even as the gap to capacity tends to zero. The algorithms may depend on the two fixed constants but must handle all message lengths.
question_excerpt: Construct explicit binary code families with polynomial-time list decoding at every fixed rate strictly below 1 minus the binary entropy of the error fraction. The printed Open Problem 5.26 reverses this rate inequality. The corrected direction here is an editorial interpretation supported by its preceding capacity discussion and the 2026 survey, not a literal quotation.
definitions:
A binary word is a finite sequence of zeros and ones. Hamming distance \(d_H(u,v)\) counts the coordinates at which equal-length words differ. A code here is an injective encoding of every \(m\)-bit message into a word of a common length \(N(m)\ge m\); it need not be linear or systematic. Its rate is the number of message bits divided by the number of encoded bits.

For each fixed admissible pair \((\delta,R)\), the claimed construction consists of finite deterministic classical multitape Turing programs for an encoder and decoder, constants \(K>0\) and integer \(b\ge1\), and an integer length function \(N(m)\). On an input message \(x\) of length \(m\), the encoder outputs \(E_m(x)\) in at most \(K(m+1)^b\) steps; the output length depends only on \(m\). Thus the length and code construction are effective. On input \((1^m,y)\), where \(y\) has length \(N(m)\), the decoder halts in at most \(K(N(m)+1)^b\) steps. It explicitly lists all qualifying messages, once each, and no others; an empty list is allowed. All reading, code construction, arithmetic, auxiliary computation and output are charged. There is no nonuniform advice, free block-length-dependent code table, external oracle or uncharged preprocessing.

The polynomial output-time bound also bounds the list size polynomially in the block length. No constant list-size bound is imposed. Requiring an exact list is equivalent to allowing additional candidates that can be removed within polynomial time using the encoder and a distance check, provided every qualifying message is included.

The decoder must work for every received word, so the errors may be adversarial. The task is global list decoding, not unique decoding, local decoding, erasure correction or reliable communication only under a random-noise distribution. The code must be binary; a larger alphabet whose size grows as the capacity gap shrinks is insufficient.

The constants, programs and polynomial exponent may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pair \((\delta,R)\). No polynomial dependence on the inverse capacity gap and no single algorithm taking these constants as variable input is requested. Rational constants give a precise countable formulation without changing the strict-slack capacity target: any real pair strictly inside the region is dominated by rational parameters with a slightly larger permitted error fraction and a slightly larger rate. A family is supplied for every message length; it need not attain every possible block length.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply the uniform algorithms, encoding injectivity, rate bound, exhaustive decoding correctness and polynomial running-time bounds for every fixed admissible parameter pair. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence assertion; an unproved hardness assumption establishes only a conditional obstruction.

A randomized code construction, inefficient exhaustive decoding, capacity over a variable alphabet, success only on randomly corrupted words, or a construction for only one rate/radius pair does not meet the target. The goal approaches the binary capacity from below; it does not ask to exceed that information-theoretic limit. No numerical tolerance is applied to this existence question.
context:
List decoding permits multiple plausible messages. Its achievable rate versus error fraction is different from the unique-decoding rate versus minimum-distance problem; the old beyond-Gilbert–Varshamov title conflated those targets.

The entropy expression is the binary list-decoding capacity. The intended construction stays strictly inside that region for each fixed pair of constants; the printed reversed inequality is explicitly corrected.

The February 2026 survey still singles out fixed-alphabet capacity, including binary capacity, as a major construction and efficient-decoding problem. Allowing the alphabet to depend on the gap gives a different target.

The August 2026 paper improves time and space for capacity-approaching codes over a parameter-dependent constant alphabet. Its theorem does not specialize to the fixed binary guarantee on this card.

The September 2026 Reed–Solomon announcement uses fields at least as large as the block length. Even if its stated result is accepted, that alphabet regime does not resolve this question.
why: Explicit binary codes with efficient adversarial list decoding throughout the capacity region would close a central gap between information-theoretic existence and deterministic usable constructions. Fixing the smallest alphabet prevents larger-symbol constructions from bypassing the main difficulty.

Bounded later-work checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the deterministic binary target. The correction to Vadhan’s printed inequality is editorially documented, and recent complete proofs were not independently certified.

title: Linear-length locally testable proofs for CircuitSAT
importance_reason: Linear proof length with robust constant-query verification is a central size question linking PCPs, testing and hardness of approximation; the precise stronger proof-testing condition deserves independent treatment.
formal:
Does CircuitSAT have binary locally testable proofs of length linear in the circuit size? More precisely, do there exist an integer \(K\ge1\) and a polynomial-time decidable proof relation \(P\) such that, for every Boolean circuit \(C\) of size \(N\), the set
\[
\Pi_C=\{\pi\in\{0,1\}^{KN}:P(C,\pi)=1\}
\]
is nonempty exactly when \(C\) is satisfiable, and this one family of proof sets has the following property: for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there is a uniform randomized verifier that makes a constant number of nonadaptive bit queries to \(\pi\), accepts every \(\pi\in\Pi_C\) with probability one, and rejects every \(\pi\) at relative Hamming distance at least \(\varepsilon\) from \(\Pi_C\) with probability at least \(1/2\)? The computational and randomness bounds are specified below.
question_excerpt: Open Problem 13.12 combines linear-length locally testable codes and proofs. The code branch is resolved, so this card retains the proof branch. Definitions 13.5–13.6 require rejection of far proofs also on true assertions; this stronger condition is retained. CircuitSAT with size measured by node count, logarithmic randomness and the displayed uniformity conventions make the chosen branch precise. The optional branch choice received no reply and was applied as an announced editorial default. definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, optional constant-zero and constant-one nodes, AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, and one specified output node. Every input node denotes one independently assignable Boolean variable. Its size \(N\ge1\) is the number of nodes, including inputs and constants; fan-out is unrestricted. The circuit is satisfiable if some assignment to its input nodes makes its output one. Circuits are explicitly encoded by a topologically ordered node list with gate types, predecessor indices in binary and an output index. The binary description has length \(O(N\log_2(N+2))\). The requested proof length is \(KN\) bits, measured against node count, rather than binary description length.

The relation \(P\) is decided by a single deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the explicit input length \(|C|+|\pi|\). For every circuit, it specifies all accepted proof strings of the prescribed length. There is no advice depending on the instance or its size. No algorithm for producing a proof without a satisfying assignment is required.

For \(\Pi_C\ne\varnothing\), define
\[
\operatorname{dist}(\pi,\Pi_C)
=\min_{\sigma\in\Pi_C}\frac{|\{j\in\{1,\ldots,KN\}:\pi_j\ne\sigma_j\}|}{KN}.
\]
If \(\Pi_C=\varnothing\), set this distance to one, so every alleged proof of an unsatisfiable circuit must be rejected with probability at least one half.

For each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there must be constants \(q_\varepsilon,r_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon,b_\varepsilon>0\) and one probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(V_\varepsilon\), uniform over all circuits and sizes. On input the explicit circuit \(C\), and oracle access to any fixed \(KN\)-bit string \(\pi\), every run uses at most \(q_\varepsilon\) proof-bit queries, at most \(r_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) independent unbiased random bits, and at most \(a_\varepsilon(N+2)^{b_\varepsilon}\) Turing-machine steps. Query addresses must lie in \(\{1,\ldots,KN\}\); preparing an address counts toward time and its oracle answer costs one step. Nonadaptive means that all proof addresses depend only on \(C\) and the random bits, not on proof answers. The verifier has ordinary unrestricted polynomial-time access to the explicit circuit; only proof queries are limited by \(q_\varepsilon\).

For every circuit and every proof, the probability is over the verifier's coins alone. Completeness is \(\Pr[V_\varepsilon^\pi(C)=1]=1\) whenever \(\pi\in\Pi_C\). Soundness is \(\Pr[V_\varepsilon^\pi(C)=1]\le1/2\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(\pi,\Pi_C)\ge\varepsilon\). There is no condition on other proofs.

The same \(K\) and proof relation \(P\) must work for all accuracies. The verifier and its resource constants may depend on the fixed accuracy; no algorithm converting \(\varepsilon\) to a verifier, and no particular dependence of these constants on \(\varepsilon\), is required. Proof lengths shorter than \(KN\) may be padded consistently, so exact length here fixes an interface rather than imposing a lower bound on necessary proof length.

The rejection condition also applies to satisfiable circuits with alleged proofs far from all valid proofs. Merely rejecting every proof of an unsatisfiable circuit, as in an ordinary PCP, is a weaker condition. This card retains the source's local proof-testability requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence of a common linear-length proof relation and its constant-query testers. A positive answer must include the computational bounds, perfect completeness and rejection of far proofs even for satisfiable circuits. A linear-length error-correcting code or an ordinary PCP without the additional proof-testing property does not alone meet the criterion.

title: Explicit positive-rate codes below the Plotkin point
importance_reason: This asks whether the general information-theoretic criterion for positive-rate communication against a fixed adversarial channel has an efficient deterministic realization. A universal answer would explain the gap between random existence and explicit error-correcting objects across many channel models while preserving a fixed small list bound.
formal: For every fixed finite adversarial channel \(A\) with rational polyhedral input and noise constraints, and every fixed integer \(L\ge2\), does the existence of a nonconfusable completely positive order-\(L\) distribution with admissible input marginal imply a uniform deterministic polynomial-time encodable family of positive-rate \((L-1)\)-list-decodable codes for that same channel? The alphabets, transition rule, constraints and list bound are fixed as blocklength grows; all terms and the allowed blocklength convention are defined below.
definitions:
A channel \(A=(X,\Lambda_X,S,\Lambda_S,Y,W)\) has finite alphabets \(X=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(S=\{1,\ldots,b\}\), \(Y=\{1,\ldots,c\}\), where \(a\ge2\) and \(b,c\ge1\). Its deterministic transition rule is a table \(W:X\times S\to Y\). For a finite set \(T\), write \(\Delta(T)=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{T}:\sum_{t\in T}p(t)=1\}\). The nonempty sets \(\Lambda_X\subseteq\Delta(X)\) and \(\Lambda_S\subseteq\Delta(S)\) are closed rational polytopes, each given by finitely many linear equalities and non-strict inequalities with rational coefficients. The table, alphabet sizes, signed integer numerators and positive denominators have ordinary binary encodings. These are fixed channel data, independent of blocklength.

The type of \(u\in T^n\) is \(\tau_u(t)=|\{j:u_j=t\}|/n\). An input word \(x\in X^n\) is admissible if \(\tau_x\in\Lambda_X\). Given \(x\), any \(s\in S^n\) with \(\tau_s\in\Lambda_S\) is allowable noise, and the output is \(y_j=W(x_j,s_j)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). The adversary may choose the entire noise word with knowledge of the entire input word. There is no causality restriction, random channel transition, feedback, shared randomness, insertion or deletion.

A code \(C\subseteq X^n\) consists of admissible input words. It is \((L-1)\)-list-decodable when, for every \(y\in Y^n\), at most \(L-1\) distinct words \(x\in C\) admit an allowable noise word producing \(y\). Different candidate input words may use different noise words. This is a zero-error combinatorial guarantee over every output; it imposes no running-time bound on finding the list.

The promise on \(A,L\) is that there exist a probability vector \(p\in\Lambda_X\), a finite integer \(h\ge1\), probability vectors \(p_1,\ldots,p_h\in\Delta(X)\), and real numbers \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_h\ge0\) with \(\sum_j\lambda_j=1\), such that
\[
Q(x_1,\ldots,x_L)=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_j\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_j(x_i),
\qquad p=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_jp_j,
\]
is nonconfusable. This is the completely positive distribution condition. The component distributions \(p_j\) need not individually satisfy the input constraints; their common resulting marginal \(p\) must.

Precisely, \(Q\) is confusable if there exists a joint probability distribution \(Z\) on \(X^L\times S^L\times Y\) whose marginal on \(X^L\) is \(Q\), whose \(i\)-th noise-coordinate marginal belongs to \(\Lambda_S\) for every \(1\le i\le L\), and which gives probability one to \(y=W(x_i,s_i)\) simultaneously for all \(i\). Nonconfusable means that no such \(Z\) exists. These distributions are real probability vectors; the promise does not require their entries to be rational or supplied to an encoder.

An explicit positive-rate family means that there exist a rational \(R>0\), an infinite set \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) of blocklengths, two finite deterministic Turing-machine programs \(H,E\), and constants \(K,t\ge1\), with the following properties. On unary input \(1^n\), \(H\) decides whether \(n\in B\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations. For every \(n\in B\), set \(k_n=\lceil Rn\rceil\). On input \((1^n,m)\), with \(m\in\{0,1\}^{k_n}\), the encoder \(E\) outputs \(E_n(m)\in X^n\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations, using binary encodings for output symbols. The map \(E_n\) is injective and its image \(C_n\) is an admissible \((L-1)\)-list-decodable code. Thus the rate \(\log_2|C_n|/n\), measured in information bits per channel use, is at least \(R\).

The programs, constants, rate and infinite length set may depend on the fixed \(A,L\), but not on the particular blocklength or message. Both programs are uniform across lengths and have no advice, oracle, random bits or precomputed codebook supplied as input. The cost bound includes all preprocessing done on that input. No polynomial dependence on the binary description length of a varying channel is required, and there is no demand for a uniform algorithm that produces the programs from the channel. An infinite decidable set of lengths permits divisibility restrictions from exact type constraints; no positive density of those lengths is assumed. The output alphabet is exactly \(X\); replacing it or changing the channel is not allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this universal explicit-construction assertion, including polynomial bit complexity, positive rate and the fixed \((L-1)\) list bound, or a complete Lean proof of its negation for the stated class of channels. A random existence proof, exhaustive construction taking time polynomial only in the exponentially large codebook, or a construction after changing the alphabet does not meet the assertion. Efficient list decoding is not an additional requirement. The asymptotic polynomial-resource and positive-rate requirements do not carry a \(1/100\) numerical tolerance.
context:
Section 18, item 4 asks for explicit positive-rate codes whenever a nonconfusable completely positive distribution exists. Theorem 47 already establishes positive-rate existence; the unresolved part is explicit construction.

This card specifies the deterministic finite-alphabet channel branch used in the paper. It explicitly restricts the convex type constraints to fixed closed rational polytopes, so that the channel has finite exact data. It does not claim to cover arbitrary real, length-dependent constraints or stochastic transition rules.

“Explicit” is interpreted as one polynomial-time encoder per fixed channel and list bound, on an infinite polynomial-time recognizable set of lengths. The source’s positive-rate convention permits an infinite sequence of blocklengths. The length-set and Turing-machine clauses make that convention algorithmic, without requiring a code for every length or an efficient list-decoding procedure.

The completely positive condition involves mixtures of independent equal-marginal products. Confusability allows a different noise explanation for each of the candidate codewords, provided that all explanations yield the same output. This is more general than a single Hamming-distance threshold.

The 2025 zero-rate result bounds code size above the list-decoding or list-recovery threshold. Its matching constructions in that regime do not provide positive-rate families for every channel below the threshold.

Later explicit constructions reproduce broad classes of local properties of random linear codes. The checked AEL-based theorem increases the alphabet, and the checked folded Reed–Solomon construction uses an alphabet growing with length. These statements do not by themselves supply codes for every fixed channel and fixed alphabet in this card.
why: The information-theoretic criterion identifies when a channel permits a linear amount of information with a fixed ambiguity bound. Making that criterion explicit would turn a broad existence theorem into efficiently usable encoders without changing the channel or relaxing the list bound.
status_note: Explicit construction is open in the ITCS 2020 source. The 2025 zero-rate theorem and checked 2025 revised derandomization results, including the work published at STOC 2026, do not by their stated guarantees settle this fixed-channel formulation. Later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

The source gives a completely positive distribution criterion ensuring that positive-rate codes with a fixed list bound exist. The question asks whether every channel satisfying that criterion also admits deterministic encoders running in polynomial time in blocklength. The card fixes a finite-description channel model, preserves its alphabet and list bound, and specifies uniformity and the permitted infinite set of blocklengths. A resolution would connect a general information-theoretic feasibility criterion with explicit error-correcting constructions across many adversarial channel models.

title: Do nonlinear binary codes have a strictly better asymptotic rate?
importance_reason: A positive-rate separation or universal equality would resolve a fundamental structural comparison in binary coding theory, beyond any particular efficient construction.
formal:
Does there exist a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) such that
\[
R_2(\delta)>R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta),
\]
where these are the optimal asymptotic rates of arbitrary binary codes and binary linear codes, respectively, at relative minimum Hamming distance \(\delta\), as defined below? Any fixed strictly positive gap qualifies.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether optimum codes are far from linear, then discusses a weaker bounded-sum condition relevant to its LP hierarchy. This card selects the binary asymptotic rate comparison at fixed relative distance, with any positive gap. The optional choice received no reply; the recommended specialization was announced and applied as an editorial decision. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: A strict asymptotic rate advantage for general binary codes over linear codes at some fixed relative distance, with any positive gap.
definitions:
For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), let
\[
A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,
\ \forall x\ne y\in C,\ \Delta(x,y)\ge d\},
\]
where \(\Delta(x,y)=|\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_j\ne y_j\}|\). Let \(A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d)\) be the same maximum restricted to vector subspaces \(C\le\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The one-word code is allowed, and its pairwise distance condition is vacuous. Both finite maxima are well defined.

For a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), define
\[
R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n},\qquad
R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n}.
\]
These bounded-sequence limit superiors are real numbers in \([0,1]\), measured in message bits per transmitted bit. The limsup of \((a_n)\) means \(\inf_{N\ge1}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\). No assumption that the ordinary limits exist is made. The distance fraction is fixed before taking either limit superior.

All finite codes are eligible regardless of encoding, decoding, description or construction complexity. The arbitrary-code side includes linear codes. The linear side permits every binary subspace and every dimension. Affine translates do not change attainable cardinality and distance, so permitting affine codes on that side gives the same maximum.

A positive answer establishes \(R_2(\delta)\ge R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)+\eta\) for some fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and \(\eta>0\). Neither constant has a prescribed magnitude. A negative answer proves equality of the two rates for every \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), since the reverse inequality always follows from inclusion. An isolated finite-block advantage, a subexponential size advantage, or a comparison with one particular linear construction is not sufficient. This is a binary existence question, not a request to approximate the two entire rate curves.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of a fixed relative distance with a strictly positive asymptotic rate gap. A positive result must compare with all binary linear codes, and a negative result must establish equality throughout (0,1/2). No minimum improvement such as 1/100 is imposed.
context:
The 2022 work gives a complete hierarchy of linear programs for optimum linear-code size. Its comparison with a collapsing hierarchy for broader codes motivates the question about how much linearity can cost.

The bounded-sum condition in the source is weaker than full linearity and supports a separate hierarchy question. The selected target compares actual binary subspaces with unrestricted binary codes, rather than feasibility in a relaxation.

The classical Gilbert–Varshamov lower bound applies to linear codes as well as general binary codes. Therefore, showing that a nonlinear family meets that lower bound alone would not separate the two optimum rates.

The 2026 paper gives a new proof of the first LP upper bound and explicitly states that it obtains the same asymptotic bound. It also reports that the exact binary rate is unknown at every fixed distance strictly between zero and one half. This is broader rate-distance context, not a proof that the two optimum rates coincide.
why: Linearity makes coding algebraically tractable, but it is unknown in this regime whether it sacrifices a positive fraction of information per transmitted bit. Resolving the comparison would distinguish a fundamental cost of linearity from limitations of known constructions and bounds.
status_note: The selected asymptotic binary linear-versus-unrestricted rate comparison remains unresolved in the checked sources through 18 September 2026. The 2022 source motivates this specialization without stating its exact quantifiers, and the 2026 LP-bound result does not settle it. This is a bounded source review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
