At each fixed relative minimum distance, compare their largest possible asymptotic information rates. The question asks whether arbitrary codes have a strictly higher rate at even one distance between zero and one half. Any fixed positive rate gap counts, but a finite-block advantage or a comparison with one construction does not. The source motivates the comparison through linear-programming hierarchies, and the checked later bound does not resolve it.

title: Full-length Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond Johnson
importance_reason: List decoding full-length Reed-Solomon codes beyond Johnson concerns a basic algebraic code family; the exact parameters and current status require separate checking.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(\varepsilon,\rho\in(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\), a constant \(K\ge1\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and infinitely many prime powers \(q\), such that for every function \(r:\mathbb F_q\to\mathbb F_q\), \[\left|\left\{f\in\mathbb F_q[X]:\deg f\le\lfloor\rho q\rfloor,\;\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb F_q:f(x)=r(x)\}\bigr|>\varepsilon q\right\}\right|\le Kq^c?\] The zero polynomial is included among the degree-bounded polynomials. All four constants are fixed independently of \(q\) and of the received function \(r\). This is the combinatorial full-length Reed–Solomon question from Open Problem 5.20, without a requirement for an efficient decoding algorithm.
definitions: A prime power is \(q=p^m\), where \(p\) is a prime and \(m\ge1\) is an integer; the characteristic may vary along the infinite set. The field \(\mathbb F_q\) has exactly \(q\) elements. Let \(d=\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\). The code consists of evaluations of all formal polynomials \(\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jX^j\), with \(a_j\in\mathbb F_q\), at every element of the field. Its block length and alphabet size are both \(q\), its dimension is \(d+1\), and its rate is \((d+1)/q\), which tends to \(\rho\) as \(q\) grows. Because \(d<q\), distinct allowed polynomials give distinct codewords. Coordinates are indexed by field elements, so no ordering choice matters. A received word is an arbitrary function on this entire field and need not be a low-degree polynomial. Its agreement fraction with a codeword is \(q^{-1}|\{x:f(x)=r(x)\}|\); the normalized Hamming distance is one minus this fraction. The displayed list uses strict agreement \(>\varepsilon\), equivalently distance \(<1-\varepsilon\), following the source’s LIST convention. Thus a boundary with exactly \(\varepsilon q\) agreements is excluded. The list is a set of distinct polynomials, not a list with repetitions. The polynomial bound \(Kq^c\) is uniform over all received words and all selected field sizes. Infinitely many prime powers means an unbounded set of distinct values of \(q\); it does not mean every sufficiently large prime power. No efficient method for selecting that infinite set, constructing field representations, finding the list, or encoding its members is required. The evaluation set may not be punctured or replaced by a random proper subset; neither folded symbols, derivatives, restricted message spaces, nor an average over received words is part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive proof must establish one fixed admissible pair \((\varepsilon,\rho)\), one polynomial list bound and infinitely many field sizes, and the bound must hold for every received word at each of those sizes. It need not supply a decoder. A negative proof must show that for every admissible pair and every \(K\ge1,c\ge1\), only finitely many prime powers have the uniform list bound. Equivalently, beyond a threshold depending on those constants, every prime power must admit some received word with more than \(Kq^c\) qualifying polynomials. Hard instances for only one rate, one characteristic, or an infinite but not exhaustive subsequence do not by themselves refute the existence statement. Results for randomly punctured codes, list recovery with multiple candidate symbols per coordinate, or only algorithmic hardness do not settle this combinatorial full-length target.
context:
Vadhan’s Construction 5.14 defines the full-length code by evaluating every degree-at-most-\(d\) polynomial over the entire field. Definition 5.18 uses strict agreement, and Open Problem 5.20 asks for fixed \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\) with degree \(\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\) and polynomial list size along an infinite sequence. The rate convention differs slightly from writing the degree as the dimension.

The Johnson bound and the algorithms recalled in the textbook provide the familiar square-root threshold. The open question asks whether some fixed constant parameters can do strictly better at the level of list cardinalities, including with inefficient decoding.

The 2025 joint journal paper of Alrabiah, Guo, Guruswami, Li and Zhang establishes capacity results for randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes over fields whose sizes are linear in the block length. “Linear-sized” does not mean equal to the block length. Theorem 1.1 explicitly requires a field size strictly greater than the block length when the dimension is positive, so it does not apply to the full-length codes here.

That paper’s introduction distinguishes combinatorial obstructions for some full-length parameter regimes, due to Ben-Sasson, Kopparty and Radhakrishnan, from the later positive puncturing results. A restriction in some regimes does not refute the present existence quantifiers over parameters and infinitely many field sizes.

Li and Shagrithaya’s 2025 paper addresses list recovery, where each received coordinate may specify several acceptable symbols. Its discussion of full-length Reed–Solomon lower bounds concerns that stronger task. Ordinary list decoding here has exactly one received symbol at each coordinate.
why: Reed–Solomon codes are a central algebraic code family, and their list size expresses an intrinsic information limit even when computation is unrestricted. The full-length requirement fixes the evaluation set completely. Determining whether any constant-rate infinite family surpasses the Johnson threshold would resolve a basic distinction between this rigid algebraic family and the punctured variants for which capacity results are known.
status_note: The precise target is open in Vadhan’s 2012 source. The checked 2025 primary papers explicitly distinguish full-length codes from the punctured families covered by their positive results. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the displayed full-length existence statement. This review does not claim that all later parameter regimes or proofs were exhaustively checked.

The code evaluates every polynomial of degree at most a fixed fraction of the field size at every field element. title: Polyhedrality of linear-rank inequality cones
importance_reason: The geometry of linear-rank inequality cones controls the possible linear information profiles.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge6\), is the cone \(L_n\) of linear rank inequalities valid over every commutative field polyhedral? Equivalently, for each fixed \(n\ge6\), do finitely many valid coefficient vectors generate every universally valid homogeneous linear inequality on the dimensions of all nonempty sums of \(n\) subspaces by nonnegative real linear combination? The finite generating family may depend on \(n\); no common bound on its size as \(n\) varies is assumed.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\mathcal S_n=\{S\subseteq[n]:S\ne\varnothing\}\). A subspace arrangement consists of a commutative field \(F\), a nonnegative integer \(m\), and subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\) of \(F^m\). Finite and infinite fields, every characteristic, arbitrary ambient dimension, repeated subspaces and the zero subspace are all allowed. Its rank vector \(r\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal S_n}\) has coordinate \(r_S=\dim_F(\sum_{i\in S}V_i)\), where the sum denotes the linear span of the listed subspaces and each finite dimension is embedded in \(\mathbb R\).

A real vector \(a=(a_S)_{S\in\mathcal S_n}\) is a universally valid linear rank inequality if \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_n}a_Sr_S\ge0\) for every such arrangement, including every choice of \(F\). Define \(L_n\) to be the set of all these coefficient vectors. All inequalities are homogeneous and non-strict; no additive constant, normalization, integrality constraint on coefficients or restriction to a fixed characteristic is included. The empty-set coordinate is omitted because its dimension is always zero. In particular \(L_n\) is a closed convex cone in the finite-dimensional real vector space \(\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\).

Here a cone is polyhedral if it is the intersection of finitely many closed homogeneous real halfspaces. For \(L_n\), this is equivalent to finite generation: there exist a nonnegative integer \(M_n\) and vectors \(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(M_n)}\in L_n\) such that
\[
L_n=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{M_n}\lambda_j a^{(j)}:\lambda_j\in\mathbb R,\ \lambda_j\ge0\right\}.
\]
The empty sum is zero. These generators may have arbitrary real coordinates. No effective procedure for finding them, rationality of a generating family or computational bound is requested.

For clarity, the coefficient cone \(L_n\) is the dual of the closed conic hull \(C_n\) of all rank vectors: \(C_n\) is the Euclidean closure of the set of all finite nonnegative real combinations of arrangement vectors, allowing different fields for different arrangements. Then \(L_n=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in C_n\}\). Polyhedrality of \(C_n\) and \(L_n\) is equivalent. The question does not assert that every point of \(C_n\) is itself the rank vector of one arrangement, or that the unclosed conic hull is already closed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(L_n\) is polyhedral for every integer \(n\ge6\), or a complete Lean proof that \(L_n\) is not polyhedral for at least one fixed integer \(n\ge6\). A positive answer may establish the existence of finite generating families without an efficient construction. A growing number of required inequalities as \(n\) increases does not by itself refute polyhedrality at any fixed \(n\). Neither a result for unrestricted entropy inequalities nor a result confined to one field characteristic settles the stated all-fields target by itself.
context:
Problem (4.4), attributed to Alexander Shen in the 2022 seminar report, asks about the inequality cones for \(n\ge6\). This card uses the field-independent convention for linear rank inequalities from the subspace-arrangement literature. The report separately asks about field-size and characteristic dependence in Problem (8.3); those restricted cones are not silently substituted for \(L_n\).

The coefficient cone of valid inequalities and the closed cone of admissible rank profiles are dual objects. Making the closure and dual convention explicit prevents a claim about a discrete set of integer rank vectors from being mistaken for the polyhedrality question.

Dougherty, Freiling and Zeger give a complete finite set of inequalities on five variables, including 24 additional types beyond the Shannon and Ingleton inequalities. Their six-variable discussion gives further inequalities without a complete finite description.

Later work studies additional rank inequalities and distinctions between representability and common-information conditions, including in the broader setting of skew fields. Such results about individual inequalities or proof methods do not alone determine whether the full all-fields cone is polyhedral.
why: Dimensions of subspace sums describe the information profiles available to linear coding and linear secret-sharing systems. Finite generation would give a finite complete system of universal linear constraints for each fixed number of subspaces. Nonpolyhedrality would show an intrinsic need for infinitely many constraints even after that number is fixed.

This is distinct from a polyhedrality resolution.
working_summary: Linear rank inequalities constrain the dimensions of every nonempty sum in a collection of subspaces. The target cone contains the coefficient vectors of inequalities valid over every commutative field. The question asks whether this cone is polyhedral for each fixed number of subspaces at least six. A finite description is known through five subspaces, while increasing families of inequalities for larger collections do not themselves settle the fixed-dimension question. A resolution would determine whether linear information profiles admit a finite complete set of universal linear constraints at each fixed arity.

title: The maximal error fraction for constant-rate binary two-way codes
importance_reason: The threshold isolates a fundamental benefit and limitation of interaction in adversarial binary communication, with a precise distinction from noiseless feedback and general protocol simulation.
formal:
Determine, with certified absolute error at most \(1/100\), the constant
\[
\rho_* = \sup\{\rho\in[0,1]:\ \rho\text{ is achievable by a constant-rate deterministic binary two-way code}\}.
\]
Here Alice must transmit an arbitrary \(n\)-bit string to Bob; the speaking schedule is fixed before communication, and an adversary can flip up to a \(\rho\) fraction of all bits sent in both directions. Achievability and the cost model are defined below.
question_excerpt: The source asks for maximal noise tolerance at constant rate or even zero rate. This card selects constant rate, retaining the source’s deterministic fixed-schedule message-transfer model and applying the catalogue’s numerical accuracy criterion. The optional rate choice received no reply; the previously recommended constant-rate branch was announced and applied as an editorial decision. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Constant positive rate: O(n) total communicated binary bits with a predetermined speaking order and a joint error budget.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), a protocol consists of an integer \(T_n\ge1\), a fixed sequence \(p_n\in\{A,B\}^{T_n}\) specifying who sends each bit, deterministic local message functions, and a deterministic output function for Bob. Alice initially knows \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\); Bob has no private input. Both know \(n\), the protocol and the schedule. They have no shared secret, private randomness or public randomness.

Initially each party's local transcript is empty. At step \(t\), the designated sender computes a bit from its local transcript and, for Alice, her input \(x\). The sender appends that sent bit to its transcript. The receiver appends the received bit, which the adversary may replace by its complement. Both transcripts therefore have length \(t\), but may differ. After exactly \(T_n\) steps Bob outputs an \(n\)-bit string determined by his transcript. The speaking sequence and stopping time cannot depend on the input, received bits or adversary.

The adversary knows the input and protocol, sees the bits being sent, and may adapt its flips to the entire execution. It can corrupt either direction, with one shared budget of at most \(\lfloor\rho T_n\rfloor\) flips. Correctness requires Bob's final output to equal \(x\) for every input and every permitted corruption pattern. There are no erasures, insertions or deletions. A feedback bit from Bob costs one transmitted bit and is subject to the same corruption rule as a bit sent by Alice. Local computation, storage and protocol description size are unrestricted.

A fraction \(\rho\) is achievable at constant rate if there exist a real \(K>0\), an integer \(n_0\ge1\), and a family of such protocols, one for every \(n\ge n_0\), with
\[
T_n\le Kn
\]
and the stated exact correctness against \(\lfloor\rho T_n\rfloor\) flips. The rate is \(n/T_n\), including communication in both directions. The constants and protocol family may depend on \(\rho\), but \(K\) does not depend on \(n\). No efficient or uniform algorithm for producing the family is required. There is no fixed bound on the number of alternations between the parties.

The supremum exists: zero is achievable by transmitting the message directly, and the defining set is contained in \([0,1]\). It is a supremum, so a protocol family attaining exactly \(\rho_*\) is not required. The target is an explicit real number \(a\) with \(|a-\rho_*|\le1/100\), or an enclosing interval \([\ell,u]\) of width at most \(1/50\). Its midpoint then meets the requested absolute accuracy. An unambiguous mathematical expression is acceptable; no running-time bound for finding or evaluating it is imposed.

A lower certificate must establish that the supremum is at least \(\ell\), by an achievable fraction or rigorously approaching achievable fractions. An upper certificate must bound all constant-rate protocol families in the model. Allowing \(T_n/n\) to grow without bound, making Bob's feedback noiseless or free, allowing an adaptive speaking order, or simulating an arbitrary two-input communication task would change the quantity.
answer_criterion: Supply a concrete real approximation and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of absolute error at most 1/100, or a Lean-checked interval containing ρ_* with width at most 1/50. The bounds must apply to the full fixed-schedule, deterministic, constant-rate message-transfer model with one corruption budget for both directions. A single improved lower or upper bound need not meet the criterion.
context:
Theorem V.1 supplies deterministic protocols of length Kn tolerating a fraction 1/4 + 10⁻⁵ of bit flips. This shows that interaction improves the attainable resilience even when the communication rate stays bounded away from zero.

The source fixes the order of speaking and counts errors over both parties’ transcripts. Its task is transmission of Alice’s message to Bob, not simulation of every two-input protocol.

The 2023 Theorem 3 rules out resilience above 13/47 for sufficiently long messages. It improves the earlier upper bound 2/7 and applies without needing a constant-rate restriction. Hence it also bounds the selected supremum.

The verified interval [1/4 + 10⁻⁵, 13/47] has width greater than 1/50, so these two results alone do not meet the selected absolute-error criterion. A precise threshold or a narrower certified interval would.

Noiseless feedback has a different threshold and cost model. The 2025 feedback paper explicitly distinguishes it from two-way codes with noisy feedback; the older upper bound recalled in its discussion is not used as the best available bound here.
why: Interaction already allows binary message transmission beyond the classical one-way quarter-error threshold. Locating its ultimate constant-rate resilience measures the benefit of a dialogue when the feedback itself is costly and corruptible.
status_note: The checked sources give 1/4 + 10⁻⁵ ≤ ρ_* ≤ 13/47. This interval is wider than 1/50 and therefore does not yet certify the requested 1/100 approximation. No resolution matching the selected constant-rate deterministic fixed-schedule model was found in the bounded review through 18 September 2026. Results for erasures, free noiseless feedback, separate corruption budgets or general interactive-protocol simulation concern different targets. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Constant positive rate: O(n) total communicated binary bits with a predetermined speaking order and a joint error budget.
progress: 2022: A constant-rate deterministic construction exceeds one-quarter bit-flip resilience. | 2023: The universal upper bound is improved from 2/7 to 13/47. | 2025: Work on noiseless-feedback rounds emphasizes the distinction from the two-way noisy-feedback model.
working_summary: Alice sends an arbitrary binary message to Bob, and Bob may send costly, corruptible feedback bits. The speaking order is fixed, and an adversary may flip a bounded fraction of all transmitted bits in both directions. The target is the largest tolerable fraction with linear total communication, to certified absolute error 1/100. A construction tolerates slightly more than one quarter, while the checked upper bound is 13/47. Those bounds still leave too wide an interval, and noiseless-feedback results do not settle this model.

title: Bounded-alphabet approximation of the β = 0 entropy face
importance_reason: Understanding entropy regions and the strength of methods that prove information inequalities would clarify general limits on information-theoretic inference.
formal:
Does there exist an integer \(K\ge2\) such that every point \(z\) on the face
\[
F=\{(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)\in S:\beta=0\}
\]
can be approximated arbitrarily closely by points of the relative interior of \(S\) obtained from normalized entropy vectors of four jointly distributed variables, each taking at most \(K\) values? The body \(S\), its coordinates and normalization are defined below. One common \(K\) must work for the entire face and for every positive accuracy.
question_excerpt: Problem (2.2) asks whether the β = 0 face in Csirmaz’s visualization can be approximated from the interior with bounded alphabets. This card selects a common bound for the entire face, uses entropy rays normalized by joint entropy, and interprets interior as relative interior of the specified body. The optional uniform-versus-pointwise choice received no reply; the announced recommendation is an editorial choice, not a user confirmation. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: One finite alphabet bound K must work for the entire specified beta=0 entropy face.
definitions:
For a joint distribution of four finite-valued variables \(A,B,C,D\), its entropy vector is the 15-tuple \(h=(H(X_U))_{\varnothing\ne U\subseteq\{A,B,C,D\}}\). Entropy is in bits, \(H(Y)=-\sum_y p_y\log_2p_y\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). All joint probabilities may be arbitrary nonnegative reals. Let \(\Gamma_4^*\subseteq\mathbb R^{15}\) be the set of these entropy vectors over all finite alphabets, and let \(\overline{\Gamma_4^*}\) be its Euclidean closure.

For any real vector \(h\), use the linear expressions
\[
H(U\mid V)=H(UV)-H(V),\quad
I(U;V\mid W)=H(UW)+H(VW)-H(W)-H(UVW),
\]
where juxtaposition denotes union of coordinate sets and \(H(\varnothing)=0\); write \(I(U;V)=I(U;V\mid\varnothing)\). Define the following linear coordinate map \(N:\mathbb R^{15}\to\mathbb R^{15}\), in this exact order:
\[
N(h)=\bigl(J,I(A;B\mid C),I(A;C\mid B),I(B;C\mid A),
I(A;B\mid D),I(A;D\mid B),I(B;D\mid A),
I(C;D\mid A),I(C;D\mid B),I(C;D),I(A;B\mid CD),
H(A\mid BCD),H(B\mid ACD),H(C\mid ABD),H(D\mid ABC)\bigr),
\]
where \(J=I(A;B\mid C)+I(A;B\mid D)+I(C;D)-I(A;B)\). This is an invertible linear coordinate map; its expressions also apply to vectors that are only almost entropic.

For \(z=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)\), put
\[
v(z)=(-\alpha,2\beta,\delta,\delta,2\beta,\delta,\delta,\gamma,\gamma,0,0,0,0,0,0).
\]
The body in the question is exactly
\[
S=\{z\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^4:\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=1,
\ N^{-1}(v(z))\in\overline{\Gamma_4^*}\}.
\]
These are the coordinates of the source's visualization. In particular, its \(\beta=0\) requires both \(I(A;B\mid C)=0\) and \(I(A;B\mid D)=0\) in the core vector. Its labels must not be replaced by similarly named coordinates in another presentation. This normalization makes the joint-entropy coordinate of \(N^{-1}(v(z))\) equal to 4.

The relative interior \(\operatorname{relint}S\) means the interior in the affine hull of \(S\), using the Euclidean topology. Explicitly, \(y\in\operatorname{relint}S\) if some open ball around \(y\), intersected with that affine hull, is contained in \(S\). Distances in the question use the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb R^4\).

For an integer \(K\ge2\), let \(E_K\) consist of those \(y\in S\) for which there is a joint probability table on \(\{1,\ldots,K\}^4\), with entropy vector \(h\) and \(h(ABCD)>0\), such that
\[
N\!\left(\frac{4h}{h(ABCD)}\right)=v(y).
\]
Unused alphabet symbols and zero-probability atoms are allowed. Thus normalization rescales the actual entropy vector along its ray; it does not require the unscaled distribution to have exactly four bits of joint entropy. The equalities defining the core must hold exactly. Applying a projection, convolution or other entropy-region transformation to a bounded-alphabet table does not alone establish membership in \(E_K\).

The assertion is precisely
\[
\exists K\ge2\ \forall z\in F\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists y\in E_K\cap\operatorname{relint}S:
\quad\|y-z\|_2<\varepsilon.
\]
The distributions may depend on \(z\) and \(\varepsilon\), but \(K\) may not. There is no computability, running-time or rational-probability requirement. Allowing \(K\) to depend on the point or the accuracy is a different question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed quantified assertion. A positive answer must establish one finite alphabet bound for the whole face. A negative answer must show that every proposed bound fails for some face point and some positive accuracy. Numerical gaps in a sampled visualization alone prove neither direction.
context:
The seminar reports entropic points on the face with at most eight states per variable and an apparent gap to the interior in numerical experiments. It asks whether bounded alphabet size obstructs approaching the face.

The visualization defines a symmetric core by setting six natural coordinates to zero and equating several others. Its β coordinate is attached to I(A;B | C) and I(A;B | D); the exact displayed coordinate order removes ambiguity with the article’s notation.

The core is a closed convex cone inside the almost-entropic region, and fixing joint entropy gives the three-dimensional body. Almost-entropic closure membership must be distinguished from realization by a particular bounded-alphabet distribution.

The article’s numerical experiment starts with finite probability tables and then applies entropy-region transformations and symmetrization before normalizing. Those operations justify almost-entropic core points but do not assert preservation of the original alphabet size or exact entropic realization of every transformed point.

The selected uniform quantifiers require one alphabet bound for all points on the face. This is explicitly stronger than allowing a separate bound for each target point and is the recorded editorial interpretation of the broad wording.
why: This question tests whether the boundary geometry of a four-variable entropy region can be captured uniformly with bounded finite probabilistic models. It distinguishes genuine restrictions on alphabet size from gaps created by numerical exploration.
status_note: The 2022 report poses the bounded-alphabet approximation problem as open. No resolution matching the selected uniform, normalized-realization formulation was found in the bounded source review through 18 September 2026. The report does not explicitly settle uniform versus pointwise alphabet bounds; the selected quantifiers and normalization are documented editorial choices. Numerical pictures and almost-entropic transformations are not treated as certificates of bounded-alphabet approximation. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: One finite alphabet bound K must work for the entire specified beta=0 entropy face.
progress: 2013: The checked preprint defines and numerically investigates a symmetrized three-dimensional slice of the almost-entropic region. | 2022: The seminar records the bounded-alphabet approximation question and directs readers to the visualization’s coordinates.
working_summary: A symmetric three-dimensional slice of the four-variable almost-entropic region has a distinguished face labeled β = 0. The question asks whether every point of that face is a limit of interior points represented by normalized entropy vectors of bounded-alphabet distributions. One finite bound on the alphabet size must work for the whole face and for every requested accuracy. The source reports small-alphabet points on the face but an apparent gap in numerical exploration of the interior. The card fixes the visualization’s coordinate convention and distinguishes actual entropy realizations from transformed almost-entropic samples.

title: Entropic matroid approximations approaching unit ratio
importance_reason: Connecting entropy inequalities, rank, and matroid structure would transfer tools across coding, combinatorics, and information theory.
formal:
Does every finite integer-valued entropic polymatroid admit entropic matroid approximations with retention ratio arbitrarily close to one?

Precisely, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every normalized, monotone, submodular function \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) that is exactly the joint Shannon entropy function of finite-valued random variables in bits, and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1\), must there exist integers \(m,k\) and a set \(T\) satisfying
\[
m\ge1,\qquad 1\le k\le m,\qquad \frac{k}{m}>1-\varepsilon,
\qquad T\subseteq U_m,
\]
\[
|T\cap X_i|\ge k\,g(\{i\})\quad(i\in[n]),
\qquad \operatorname{EntMat}(T,r_m|_{2^T})?
\]
Here the disjoint blocks, their union and the free-expansion rank function are
\[
X_i=\{i\}\times[mg(\{i\})],\qquad U_m=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}X_i,
\]
\[
r_m(A)=\min_{S\subseteq[n]}
\left(mg(S)+\left|A\setminus\bigcup_{i\in S}X_i\right|\right)
\qquad(A\subseteq U_m).
\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{EntMat}\) below permits one common positive scaling of the entropy function. In contrast, the input polymatroid \(g\) must be exactly entropic without a scaling factor. The ratio measures how many elements survive in each block of a free expansion; it is not a relative error in approximating a rank table. The integers, retained set and entropy representation may depend on \(g\) and \(\varepsilon\).
definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge0\), write \([a]=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and write \(2^E\) for the set of all subsets of a finite set \(E\). A polymatroid on \(E\) is a set function \(g:2^E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) such that \(g(\varnothing)=0\), \(g(A)\le g(B)\) whenever \(A\subseteq B\), and
\[
g(A)+g(B)\ge g(A\cup B)+g(A\cap B)
\qquad(A,B\subseteq E).
\]
An integer polymatroid has all values in \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). No upper bound on these integers or on \(n\) is imposed.

Specify a finite joint distribution on a finite index set \(E\) by positive integers \(a_e\) for \(e\in E\) and a probability table
\[
p:\prod_{e\in E}[a_e]\longrightarrow\mathbb R_{\ge0},
\qquad \sum_z p(z)=1.
\]
The coordinate variables are jointly distributed according to \(p\). For \(A\subseteq E\), let \(p_A(u)=\sum_{z:z|_A=u}p(z)\) be the marginal distribution and put
\[
H_p(A)=-\sum_{u\in\prod_{e\in A}[a_e]}p_A(u)\log_2 p_A(u),
\]
using \(0\log_2 0=0\). The product over an empty index set is a singleton, so \(H_p(\varnothing)=0\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, not only rational numbers or equal weights. A function \(g\) is entropic in the input sense exactly when some such finite table satisfies \(g(A)=H_p(A)\) for every \(A\subseteq E\). These equalities use the same distribution and logarithm base for all subsets. Countably infinite alphabets, limits of entropy functions and entropy multiplied by an unspecified constant are not included in this input predicate.

A matroid rank function on a finite set \(E\) is an integer polymatroid \(r\) with \(r(A)\le |A|\) for every \(A\subseteq E\). Its restriction to \(T\subseteq E\) is the function on \(2^T\) with the same values \(r(A)\). There is no contraction or quotient operation in that restriction. The displayed minimum defines the matroid rank function of the free expansion of \(mg\); its domain is all subsets of \(U_m\). Blocks with \(g(\{i\})=0\) are empty and their retention requirement is vacuous. In every other block, \(|X_i|=mg(\{i\})\), so the required lower bound is exactly the retention fraction \(k/m\) times its size, without a rounding convention.

For a matroid \((E,r)\), define \(\operatorname{EntMat}(E,r)\) by the existence of finite alphabets, one probability table \(p\) on their product, and a single real number \(\lambda>0\) such that
\[
\forall A\subseteq E,\qquad r(A)=\lambda H_p(A).
\]
The same \(\lambda\) applies to every subset. It may depend on the matroid and on its representation. The table and alphabets may differ from those representing the input \(g\). There is no bound on their sizes, no prescribed field or alphabet cardinality, and no linear representation requirement. The empty matroid satisfies this predicate using the singleton probability space. Finite alphabets give a concrete convention for exact entropic matroid representations; the distinction from almost-entropic representations is essential.

An almost-entropic rank function can be approached arbitrarily closely by scaled joint entropy functions without being equal to any one of them. Such a limiting representation does not satisfy \(\operatorname{EntMat}\) unless an exact representation as above also exists. Likewise the retained set must be a restriction of the particular free expansion \(E(mg)\), not an arbitrary matroid with approximately matching ranks.

This is a mathematical existence question. The input integer function can be represented by its complete table on the subsets of \([n]\), in bit-mask order, and the finite retained set by its labelled elements. The entropy witnesses are finite real probability tables. There is no algorithm, computability condition, effective rate, bound on \(m\) as a function of \(\varepsilon\), or requirement to encode arbitrary real probabilities by finite binary strings. Different approximation precisions may use unrelated witnesses. The question does not require retention ratio one to be attained.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal existence assertion or its full negation, with the stated entropy conventions and free-expansion restriction.

A positive answer must establish the required witnesses for every finite integer entropic input and every \(0<\varepsilon<1\), including an exact proportional entropy representation of the retained matroid. An approximation theorem merely placing its rank function in the closure of the entropy region is insufficient.

A negative answer must establish a single integer \(n\ge1\), a finite integer polymatroid \(g\) with an exact finite joint-entropy representation, and a real \(0<\varepsilon_0<1\) such that
\[
\forall m\ge1\ \forall k\in[m]\ \forall T\subseteq U_m,
\quad
\left[
\frac{k}{m}>1-\varepsilon_0\ \land\
\forall i\in[n],\ |T\cap X_i|\ge k g(\{i\})
\right]
\Longrightarrow \neg\operatorname{EntMat}(T,r_m|_{2^T}).
\]
The failure must cover every denominator, retained set, finite probability table and positive entropy scaling permitted by the definition. Failure at one fixed denominator or one fixed alphabet does not establish this negation. No construction algorithm for the counterexample or for the positive witnesses is an additional obligation. The target is an arbitrarily-close existence assertion, so the numerical \(1/100\) acceptance tolerance does not replace its universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).
context:
Geva Yashfe posed Problem 5.2 in the 2022 Dagstuhl seminar report, defining an approximation by retaining a prescribed fraction of every block in the free expansion of a scaled integer polymatroid.

The input is an entropic polymatroid, while the output is an entropic matroid; the same author’s representability paper explicitly distinguishes exact entropy for polymatroids from entropy up to a common positive factor for matroids.

The finite-alphabet, base-two convention is made explicit here, and exact entropic representations are kept separate from limits of such representations.

The standard free-expansion construction preserves almost-entropic membership in both directions, which is a closure statement and does not provide the exact retained matroid demanded by this question.

The source motivates the question through matroids whose entropy representations could exceed the power of multilinear representations; its proposed retention target is preserved here without replacing it by unrestricted rank approximation.
why: The question asks whether information represented by a finite entropy function can be organized into exact matroid dependencies while losing an arbitrarily small fraction of each expanded coordinate. Such a bridge would connect entropy constraints with combinatorial independence and clarify the expressive power of entropic matroids beyond linear representations. Its approximation notion preserves the specific free-expansion structure, making it substantially more demanding than membership in the closure of an entropy region.
status_note: Problem 5.2 was posed at the July 2022 seminar and published in its report on 3 February 2023. Individual primary-source review recovers the retained-free-expansion target, exact finite input entropy and common-scale output representation. Bounded later checks through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of this target; the checked closure, algebraic-approximation, fixed-alphabet and representation-separation results have different guarantees. This is a source-open assessment with those review limits, not exhaustive current-openness certification or completed Lean verification.

working_summary: The input is an integer-valued polymatroid exactly represented by the joint entropies of finite random variables. After multiplying its values by an integer, the free expansion replaces each coordinate by a block of independent matroid elements. The question asks whether an arbitrarily large fraction of every block can be retained so that the resulting matroid has an exact entropy representation up to one common scaling factor. This would connect entropy functions with exact combinatorial independence while preserving the specific expansion structure. A complete Lean proof must establish this approximation for every admissible input and every precision or give an input with a fixed positive retention gap.

title: Are characteristic sets of linear-rank inequalities finite or cofinite?
importance_reason: Connecting entropy inequalities, rank, and matroid structure would transfer tools across coding, combinatorics, and information theory.
formal:
For every integer \(r\ge1\) and every family of rational coefficients \((c_S)_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[r]}\), is the set
\[
P(c)=\left\{p\text{ prime}:\ \forall d\ge0\ \forall V_1,\ldots,V_r\le\mathbb F_p^d,\quad
\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[r]}c_S\dim_{\mathbb F_p}\!\left(\sum_{i\in S}V_i\right)\ge0\right\}
\]
either finite or cofinite in the set of all primes?
question_excerpt: Problem (8.3) asks broadly how linear-rank inequalities depend on field size and characteristic. The finite-or-cofinite classification of the valid prime characteristics of each fixed rational homogeneous inequality is an editorial specialization of that broad question, not a conjecture explicitly stated in the report. The optional choice remained unanswered; this previously proposed default was announced before application. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: For every fixed rational linear-rank inequality, the valid prime characteristics form a finite or cofinite set.
definitions:
Here \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), \(\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), \(d\) is an arbitrary nonnegative integer, and each \(V_i\) is a linear subspace of the same ambient vector space. The sum of subspaces is the span of their union. There is no bound on ambient dimension or on the dimensions of the subspaces. The coefficients are fixed independently of \(p\), \(d\), and the subspace configuration. Coefficients may have either sign or be zero. The expression is homogeneous: no constant term or additional premise is allowed.

Write \(\mathcal P\) for the set of positive primes. Cofinite means that \(\mathcal P\setminus P(c)\) is finite. Thus the proposed assertion is
\[
\forall r\ge1\ \forall c\quad
\exists\text{ finite }F\subseteq\mathcal P:\quad
P(c)=F\ \text{or}\ P(c)=\mathcal P\setminus F.
\]
The exceptional set may depend on the entire inequality. No effective procedure, computable bound on the exceptional primes, fixed number of variables, or uniform dimension bound is requested. Empty and full characteristic sets are allowed.

Restricting to prime fields does not select a particular extension degree: validity of a homogeneous inequality over \(\mathbb F_p\), with all dimensions allowed, is equivalent to validity over every finite field of characteristic \(p\). This equivalence uses extension and restriction of scalars. The target concerns all subspace configurations, rather than representations of one specified matroid or solvability of one specified network.

A negative answer must supply a fixed rational inequality whose valid characteristic set and invalid characteristic set are both infinite. Examples with an arbitrarily large but finite exceptional set do not refute the assertion. Characteristic zero is outside the domain of this question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal assertion, or a Lean-checked refutation by a fixed number of variables and fixed rational coefficients with infinitely many valid and infinitely many invalid prime characteristics. A construction for each finite or cofinite set alone does not establish the classification.
context:
The seminar poses field size and characteristic dependence as a research direction without choosing one exact classification theorem. This card isolates a characteristic-set question and records that specialization explicitly.

For homogeneous inequalities with unbounded ambient dimension, passing from a finite field to its prime subfield multiplies every dimension by the same extension degree; extending scalars preserves dimensions. This elementary observation removes extension degree from this particular validity question.

The 2019 paper reviews constructions realizing finite and cofinite characteristic sets. Its Theorems 7 and 9 give inequalities valid when the characteristic divides a fixed integer and when it does not, respectively. Existence of these examples does not show that every inequality has one of those forms.

The 2023 theorem obtains characteristic-dependent inequalities from binary matrices of determinant t > 1, separating primes dividing t from those not dividing t; the following configurations witness failure in the opposite cases. The determinant-based theorem still treats finite or cofinite sets.

A theorem about the characteristics in which a single matroid is representable would concern a different quantifier pattern. Here validity ranges over every finite-dimensional subspace configuration, with no fixed rank bound.
why: Rank inequalities constrain what linear coding can accomplish over different alphabets. This question asks whether one such constraint can distinguish two infinite classes of prime characteristics, beyond the finite exceptional sets occurring in known constructions.

working_summary: Fix a rational homogeneous linear inequality in the dimensions of sums of finitely many subspaces. For each prime, test whether that inequality holds for every subspace configuration over its prime field, in every finite dimension. The question is whether the set of primes where it holds must be finite or have finite complement. Known characteristic-dependent constructions realize finite and cofinite sets but do not by themselves classify every inequality. This is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader field-dependence question, and its exact current status remains uncertain.

title: The infimal normalized Ingleton score
importance_reason: A structural question about attainable information profiles or entropy inequalities, with a more specific target than a general coding limit.
formal:
Determine, with certified absolute error at most \(1/100\), the real constant
\[
\iota_*=
\inf_{\substack{X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\ \text{finite-valued}\\H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)>0}}
\frac{I(X_1;X_2\mid X_3)+I(X_1;X_2\mid X_4)+I(X_3;X_4)-I(X_1;X_2)}
{H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)}.
\]
The infimum ranges over all finite alphabet sizes and all joint probability distributions, with no common bound on the alphabets. Negative values represent violations of the Ingleton inequality.
question_excerpt: Problem (2.1) asks how far the four-atom conjecture was from the infimal Ingleton score and additionally asks whether the infimum is algebraic and which distributions reach it. This card retains the value question, with the catalogue’s numerical acceptance tolerance; it does not combine the algebraicity and attainment questions.
definitions:
Choose arbitrary positive integers \(k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4\), and a joint probability table \(p\) on \(\prod_{i=1}^4\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\), with arbitrary nonnegative real entries summing to one. The variables \(X_i\) are its coordinate projections. For any tuple \(Y\) of these variables, use its marginal distribution and define Shannon entropy in bits by
\[
H(Y)=-\sum_y\Pr[Y=y]\log_2\Pr[Y=y],\qquad 0\log_2 0:=0.
\]
For tuples \(U,V,W\), define
\[
I(U;V)=H(U)+H(V)-H(U,V),
\]
\[
I(U;V\mid W)=H(U,W)+H(V,W)-H(W)-H(U,V,W).
\]
No independence, uniformity, symmetry, group representation or linearity is assumed. Zero-probability atoms are permitted. The only exclusion is zero joint entropy, which would make the displayed quotient undefined.

The infimum is the greatest real lower bound of this nonempty set of scores. It exists as a finite real number: all three positive terms in the numerator are nonnegative and \(I(X_1;X_2)\le H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)\), so every score is at least \(-1\). The infimum need not be attained by any single finite probability table. An approximating sequence may use growing alphabets. The normalization is by joint entropy, not by a Euclidean norm of the entropy vector or by a modified denominator; the resulting score is dimensionless and invariant under a common change of logarithm base.

The requested answer is a specified real number \(a\) with \(|a-\iota_*|\le1/100\), or a certified interval \([\ell,u]\) containing \(\iota_*\) and of width at most \(1/50\), whose midpoint supplies such an answer. The number may be given by an unambiguous mathematical expression; a decimal expansion is not mandatory. There is no running-time requirement for finding or evaluating it.

For interval certification, a lower bound must hold uniformly for every finite joint table: equivalently, the displayed numerator is at least \(\ell\,H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)\). An upper bound can be certified by a concrete joint table with score at most \(u\), or by a rigorous sequence whose limiting score is at most \(u\). A local numerical minimum or a search over any fixed alphabet does not certify a global lower bound.
answer_criterion: Supply a concrete real approximation a and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that |a−ι_*| ≤ 1/100, or a Lean-checked enclosing interval of width at most 1/50. Both sides of any interval must be justified over the full unrestricted finite-alphabet domain. Exact determination is welcome but unnecessary. Proving algebraicity, exhibiting an attaining distribution, or merely disproving the four-atom conjecture is not required and does not by itself meet this numerical criterion.
context:
The seminar identifies the score as a global geometric question and points to a reduction of the infimum to a symmetrized part of the four-variable almost-entropic region. It separately asks about algebraicity and attainment.

Matúš and Csirmaz prove that the infimum can be minimized on a compact three-dimensional slice of the almost-entropic closure. Their Example 2 yields a value near −0.09243 and refutes the four-atom conjecture. Closure membership is not the same as finite-alphabet attainment.

Boston and Nan use the opposite sign: positive values measure violations. Translating their convention gives the reported upper estimate near −0.0925000777 for this card’s infimum. Their Theorem 2.6 explains how an optimized modified-denominator score is approached by ordinary scores.

Their discussion reports the universal lower bound −3/19 after sign conversion. Together with the displayed examples it leaves a gap substantially wider than 1/50, so those bounds do not meet this card’s acceptance criterion.

The 2024 neural optimization reports −0.0925001031 after the entropy transformation and describes the tiny difference from the earlier estimate as numerical stability. Its approximation theorems concern a fixed finite alphabet; neither those theorems nor the numerical table certify the unrestricted global infimum.

The Ingleton violation index optimized elsewhere in that paper uses a different normalization. An improved index is therefore not automatically an improved bound on the score in this card.
why: The normalized Ingleton violation measures how far general entropy vectors can depart from an inequality obeyed by linear-rank models. Locating its global infimum would give a concrete quantitative constraint on the poorly understood four-variable entropy region.
status_note: The unrestricted normalized infimum, including a certificate meeting the selected 1/100 accuracy, remains unresolved in the checked sources through 17 September 2026. The four-atom conjecture is already false, and numerical examples near −0.0925 give only one side. The reviewed universal lower bound and reported upper estimates do not enclose the infimum within width 1/50. No claim of exact arithmetic certification is made for the final decimal digits of numerical experiments.

working_summary: The Ingleton score divides a particular linear combination of four-variable entropies by their joint entropy. Negative scores measure violations of an inequality satisfied by linear-rank configurations. The target is the infimum over all finite joint distributions, with no fixed alphabet bound, to certified absolute error 1/100. Known examples near −0.0925 disprove the four-atom conjecture but do not supply the needed global lower bound. A complete Lean-checked answer must certify both sides and need not prove algebraicity or attainment.

title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
importance_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
focus_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
question_excerpt: The source asks which finite forbidden induced-subgraph families have polynomial sample complexity; this card retains the previously selected additional requirement of a terminating decision procedure on the finite family.
definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
context:
Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.
why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.
status_note: Uncertain for the explicitly retained effective decidability target. On 15 September 2026, the finite-family theorem and counterexamples, the 2025 structural classification problem, the later induced-four-cycle manuscript and the August 2026 ECCC container characterization were checked. The source asks a structural characterization; that does not itself certify openness of the additional decision-procedure requirement. The checked quantitative theorem does not provide such a classifier, and a bounded later-work search did not verify a resolution. Source proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

Their path notation counts edges. | 2016–2021: Gishboliner–Shapira establish the checked finite-family sufficient and necessary conditions, including examples showing that they do not coincide. | 2018–2019: The checked author revision and Combinatorica publication give a single-exponential induced-four-cycle bound and state the polynomial conjecture separately. | 2025-08-23: The survey states the finite-family structural classification as Problem 3.14, with the four-cycle as the first key open case. | 2026-08-16: The ECCC container characterization provides explicit tester/container parameter conversions. No total classifier from an arbitrary finite forbidden list is established in its inspected main results.
working_summary: A finite family of forbidden induced graphs specifies a hereditary graph property. The question asks whether a total algorithm can decide from that family whether its canonical one-sided test has polynomial reciprocal-distance sample complexity. Every query is an adjacency check, while rejection must exhibit a forbidden pattern with both its edges and its nonedges. Known structural conditions and quantitative container equivalences do not give the total finite-input classifier required by this card. Algorithmic decidability is the inherited editorial specification, and its status is uncertain rather than attributed verbatim as a conjecture of the structural survey.

title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
importance_reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.
focus_reason: A universal polynomial tester-to-estimator implication would convert robust graph-property recognition into quantitative distance measurement across the dense model.
formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
question_excerpt: Does polynomial query complexity for testing a dense graph property imply polynomial query complexity for estimating its edit distance?
definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
context:
A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.
why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

A bounded later-work search did not identify a resolution. The source’s stronger Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to this card; neither the literature check nor the completed formulation is an independent verification of the cited proofs in Lean.

Theorem 1.9 still has a double-exponential loss and does not prove polynomial preservation. | 2025-08-23: The survey records the stronger quantitative conversion as Problem 5.4 and describes positive special cases after it.

title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
importance_reason: Tests the fundamental power of sublinear access to compare two sparse graphs without reading the entire input.
formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.
context:
Open Problem 2.4 explicitly separates testing against a known fixed graph from testing a pair of oracle inputs. This card chooses the latter, as in its saved formulation, and retains two-sided error.

Goldreich proves upper and lower query bounds of order \(n^{2/3}\), up to polylogarithmic factors and proximity dependence, when connected components have polylogarithmic size. The lower bound also applies to general inputs, but the upper bound retains its component-size restriction.

Goldreich and Tauber obtain a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) tester for almost all fixed regular target graphs, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Their model supplies the target graph in advance; it neither supplies both graphs only by oracle nor covers every possible target.

The relevant resource here is query complexity. A tester may perform extensive finite computation on its observations. Therefore a fast algorithm for explicit graph isomorphism does not, by itself, meet the oracle-query target, and a query bound does not by itself assert fast total runtime.
why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
importance_reason: The remaining induced four-cycle case is a central concrete obstacle in classifying which single forbidden induced patterns admit polynomial dense-graph testers. Its resolution would complete that single-pattern boundary up to graph complementation; the previously assessed score 88 is preserved.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
question_excerpt: Does induced four-cycle freeness have query complexity polynomial in reciprocal proximity?
definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. An induced four-cycle consists of four distinct vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\) whose edges among those vertices are exactly \(\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_2,v_3\},\{v_3,v_4\},\{v_4,v_1\}\); the two diagonals are absent. Let \(\mathcal P_n\) be the graphs on \([n]\) with no such induced subgraph. Define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min_{([n],E')\in\mathcal P_n}|E\mathbin{\triangle}E'|.\] Here \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference, so both edge additions and deletions are allowed and each undirected edit is counted once. The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. The graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. This uses the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention of the selected survey; it is half the adjacency-matrix-entry distance in the original Goldreich question. The tester is given \(n\) and rational \(\varepsilon\), and has oracle access to the adjacency bit of any unordered vertex pair. For a positive integer \(s\), the canonical test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries every unordered pair in \(S\), and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced four-cycle. All \(\binom{\min\{n,s\}}{2}\) adjacency queries count; the property check on the finite sampled graph has no additional query cost, and no running-time bound is requested. Uniform subset sampling is the stated finite probability distribution, with sampling and local computation not charged as adjacency queries. If \(n\le s\), the entire graph is inspected. In particular, orders below four are always accepted and never far. No behavior is required for nonsatisfying graphs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). Every host graph is allowed; no degree, density, chordality or other promise is imposed. The deterministic sampling-size formula and rejection rule specify a single uniform family of tests once \(C,a\) are fixed.
answer_criterion: Prove the formal proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must exhibit fixed polynomial constants and establish rejection probability at least \(2/3\) for every far input and every permitted proximity parameter. A negative answer must show that for every choice of \(C,a\) there are a proximity parameter and a graph at the stated distance for which that sampling test rejects with probability less than \(2/3\). A merely exponential sample bound, a result for ordinary four-cycle freeness, or a tester with an additional host-graph promise does not meet the target.
context:
An induced four-cycle is a cycle without either diagonal. A complete graph on four vertices contains ordinary four-cycles, but no induced four-cycle. This distinction changes both the set of valid graphs and the repair task: adding a diagonal can destroy an induced cycle, while adding edges cannot eliminate an ordinary subgraph copy.

The tester does not try to find every violation or to reconstruct a repaired graph. It distinguishes graphs satisfying the property from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon n^{2}\) edits. A polynomial sample bound would mean that the number of queried adjacencies remains polynomial in reciprocal proximity even when the host graph is arbitrarily large.

The induced removal lemma relates edit distance to the number of forbidden induced copies. For a fixed pattern, polynomial bounds on that density and polynomial bounds for canonical one-sided sampling are equivalent up to changes in polynomial exponents. The known four-cycle removal bound is exponential in a power of reciprocal distance, which is far larger than the polynomial dependence conjectured here.

Alon and Shapira classified the polynomial and superpolynomial cases for single forbidden induced graphs apart from a few small patterns. Alon and Fox settled the four-vertex-path case, leaving the induced four-cycle and its complement as the remaining case. Complementing all adjacencies preserves edit distance and transfers the sampling question between those two patterns.

It asks whether a globally expensive repair necessarily leaves violations visible in a polynomial-sized random sample. The answer would separate two very different quantitative regimes of dense-graph testing for one small and fully specified pattern.
