title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
importance_reason: A concrete local-to-global question linking planar graph structure, approximate isomorphism and sparse property testing beyond bounded degree.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
question_excerpt: Do identical sufficiently large rooted local-neighborhood multisets force two planar graphs of the same order to be close to isomorphic under edge edits?
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that for every positive integer \(D\), there are some \(n\ge1\) and simple planar \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G,H\) with identical radius-\(D\) neighborhood multisets but edit distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon_0 n\). The counterexample graphs and their orders may depend on \(D\); the same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work throughout. A proof restricted to bounded maximum degree or to outerplanar graphs does not establish the assertion for all planar graphs. Equality of the set of neighborhood types without multiplicities is a different hypothesis. A radius growing with \(n\) or maximum degree is insufficient. This is an exact yes/no implication, not a numerical approximation problem.
context:
The broad imported question asked for a classification of graph properties testable with sublinear query complexity. This card now adopts the separate, concrete planar local-neighborhood question from the same source. The change of scope was explicitly selected on 16 September 2026; it does not claim to complete the original general classification programme.

The structural issue is whether sufficiently large local views determine a sparse planar graph up to a small linear number of edge edits. The neighborhoods carry no consistent global labels. Matching their multiplicities therefore supplies statistical local information, not a ready-made global correspondence.

For planar graphs with a fixed maximum degree, earlier local-to-global results provide a radius depending on both the error tolerance and that degree bound. The selected question asks whether the degree dependence can be removed completely. Planarity bounds average degree, but permits individual degrees growing with the graph order.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.
why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.

working_summary: The question compares two planar graphs through the rooted neighborhoods around all their vertices. It asks whether a radius depending only on the allowed error makes identical neighborhood multisets imply closeness under edge edits and vertex relabeling. No maximum-degree bound is imposed, so even a small-radius neighborhood may be large. The source proves the analogous result for outerplanar graphs, while bounded-degree planar theorems allow the radius to depend on the degree bound. This specific structural question replaces the original broad classification target by an explicitly selected yes/no assertion.

title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
importance_reason: Sharp removal bounds for fixed graph patterns govern the quantitative efficiency of many graph testers.
formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
question_excerpt: Goldreich, Open Problem 8.17, asks for relatively tight bounds on the minimum number of copies of a connected fixed graph in a graph far from ordinary subgraph-freeness. The constant-factor precision and finite feasible-domain conventions are explicit editorial specifications of that quantitative request.
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.
context:
For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.
why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.

title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
importance_reason: A central statistical–computational question for a widely used distribution family: polynomial sample sufficiency contrasts with strong restricted-model and conditional hardness evidence. The unconstrained joint dependence is substantially broader than fixed-component or separated-mixture algorithms; the score concerns this density-learning target, not every private-learning problem in the source.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.
question_excerpt: Can Gaussian mixtures be learned in running time polynomial in both the number of components and the ambient dimension, even without privacy?
definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.
context:
A mixture combines several Gaussian populations without telling the learner which population generated an observation. Density learning asks for a distribution that predicts the whole population well. Two different lists of components can describe the same, or nearly the same, distribution; therefore success does not require reconstructing the original list.

The source defines proper PAC learning and unbounded positive-definite Gaussian components. Its highlighted computational question appears in a paper about private learning, but explicitly remains a question even when privacy is removed. The present target has no privacy requirement.

Section 9.3 recalls near-optimal nonprivate sample complexity \(\widetilde\Theta(kd^2/\alpha^2)\) at accuracy \(\alpha\), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A statistical existence bound does not make the search for a suitable mixture polynomial-time. The private construction also uses a nonconstructive cover, a separate obstacle discussed on page 6.

The statement fixes proper output, exact arithmetic primitives and the order of quantifiers explicitly. The source says polynomial in the two structural parameters and does not specify a bit model in its open-question sentence. Allowing the exponent to depend on fixed accuracy avoids silently strengthening that sentence to a fully polynomial accuracy guarantee.

Statistical-query lower bounds restrict algorithms that obtain information through approximate expectations of bounded test functions. They explain an obstruction for a broad family of learning methods, but alone do not exclude every algorithm with direct sample access.

There is also conditional evidence beyond statistical queries. Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan derive hardness of Gaussian-mixture density estimation from Learning with Errors assumptions. Those assumptions concern the difficulty of recovering or distinguishing hidden linear structure from noisy modular observations. The reductions and computational assumptions belong to their stated model; the card does not promote them to an unconditional theorem for its exact-real machine.

The score-matching theorem assumes a bounded conditioning/size parameter \(\tau\) and minimum positive weight at least inverse-polynomial in \(k\). It uses \(d^{\operatorname{poly}(k\tau/\alpha)}\) samples, runs in time polynomial in that sample count, and returns a sampler. The dimension exponent grows with the number of components, so this guarantee does not supply the joint polynomial bound sought here.

The 2025 parallel-pancake work studies shared-covariance structure and gives statistical-query limitations even with uniform weights, alongside a quasipolynomial testing guarantee. Its restrictions and model remain explicit.

The August 2026 manuscript concerns unit covariances, bounded means and a fixed component count. Its claimed sharp polynomial-time risk bound for that family does not settle arbitrary covariances or joint polynomial dependence. The card records the claim and its scope without asserting independent verification of the manuscript.
why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.
status_note: Source-open in ALT 2024 for joint polynomial dependence on component count and dimension. On 16 September 2026 the full source definitions and question, the 2017 and 2022 hardness manuscripts, the November 2024 score-matching theorem, and the April 2025/August 2026 primary abstracts were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution of the stated target. Proper output follows the source definition; fixed-accuracy quantifiers and exact-real primitives are explicit editorial computational conventions, not a claimed bit-complexity theorem. Conditional hardness and restricted-model lower bounds remain qualified. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2017: Diakonikolas–Kane–Stewart establish statistical-query obstacles to general Gaussian-mixture density estimation. | 2022: Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan strengthen conditional density-estimation hardness using reductions from Learning with Errors. | 2024: Afzali–Ashtiani–Liaw obtain polynomial sample sufficiency under privacy and explicitly retain efficient joint dependence on component count and dimension as a question even without privacy. | 2024-11-19: The second score-matching manuscript version gives a sampler with a dimension exponent depending on component count and accuracy, under its bounded-parameter assumptions. | 2025-04-21: Parallel-pancake work supplies additional statistical-query lower bounds and a restricted quasipolynomial testing result. | 2026-08-13: A work-in-progress manuscript claims sharp proper estimation for fixed-component, bounded-mean, unit-covariance mixtures.
working_summary: The learner receives independent observations from a mixture of at most k nondegenerate Gaussians in d dimensions. It must output another such mixture whose whole distribution is close in total variation, without reconstructing the original components. The question asks for a uniform algorithm with time polynomial jointly in k and d for each fixed accuracy, using explicitly specified exact-real arithmetic. Polynomial sample sufficiency coexists with statistical-query lower bounds and conditional computational hardness, neither of which is silently treated as an unconditional resolution. Newer positive results with bounded parameters, fixed component counts or growing dimension exponents do not establish the full target.

title: Query complexity of Max-CSP testing
importance_reason: A broad structural classification problem across finite CSP templates and approximation gaps in a central sublinear-query model. It connects local access to global optimization and contrasts constant, intermediate and linear inspection costs, with meaningful links to streaming approximation beyond a single predicate or parameter improvement.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the randomized query complexity \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) of distinguishing bounded-degree constraint instances with optimum satisfied fraction at least \(c\) from those with optimum at most \(s\). The target ranges over every fixed finite predicate template \((D,\Gamma)\), degree bound \(d\), density lower bound \(\alpha\), and gap \(0\le s<c\le1\), under the variable-query model defined below. Taking \(\alpha=0\) includes unrestricted bounded-degree inputs; positive \(\alpha\) includes the source’s density-bounded model.
question_excerpt: Determine the query complexity of \(MaxCSP(\Gamma )[c, s]\) in the bounded-degree model, for all predicate families \(\Gamma\) and parameters c and s.
definitions: The domain \(D\) is a nonempty finite set, and \(\Gamma\) is a finite collection of predicates \(R:D^{k_R}\to\{0,1\}\), with positive integer arities \(k_R\). A predicate is specified by its full finite table and ordered coordinates; these tables are fixed parameters known to the tester. For an integer \(n\ge1\), an instance has variable set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a finite multiset \(\mathcal C\) of \(m\) constraint occurrences. An occurrence consists of a predicate \(R\in\Gamma\) and an ordered tuple of \(k_R\) distinct variable labels. Identical occurrences may be repeated and each copy is counted separately. The degree of a variable is the number of occurrences containing it. Fix an integer \(d\ge0\) and a real \(\alpha\in[0,d]\); admissible instances have maximum degree at most \(d\) and \(m\ge\alpha n\). Thus \(\alpha=0\) permits empty or very sparse instances, while \(\alpha>0\) enforces a linear number of constraints. For an assignment \(\tau:[n]\to D\), an occurrence \((R,(v_1,\ldots,v_{k_R}))\) is satisfied when \(R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R}))=1\). If \(m>0\), define \[\operatorname{val}(I)=\frac{1}{m}\max_{\tau:[n]\to D}\sum_{(R,\mathbf v)\in\mathcal C}R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R})).\] Put \(\operatorname{val}(I)=1\) when \(m=0\). Fix real constants \(0\le s<c\le1\). YES instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\ge c\), NO instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\le s\), and no correctness condition is imposed between the two thresholds. The tester knows \(n,D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s\), but receives neither the constraint list nor its actual length \(m\). A query specifies a variable \(v\in[n]\). If an as-yet-unrevealed constraint occurrence involving \(v\) exists, the oracle reveals one such occurrence, giving its predicate and full ordered variable tuple. Otherwise it returns \(\bot\). Revealing an occurrence marks that copy as seen globally, including at its other variables. Distinct identical copies remain distinct possible future responses. Which available occurrence is returned may be chosen adversarially as a function of past queries and replies, subject to one fixed input instance; the oracle cannot depend on unrevealed future random choices. Every oracle call, including one returning \(\bot\), costs one query. Arbitrary variable labels may be queried without first being discovered. Local computation, storage and private random choices are free; there is no direct uniform-constraint sampling oracle, no degree oracle and no free inspection of \(m\). Query complexity is defined by finite randomized adaptive decision trees: finite probability distributions over deterministic query-and-answer trees, with rational probabilities, whose leaves output accept or reject. Each deterministic tree can choose its next variable from the preceding transcript. No time, space or tree-size bound is imposed. A tester is valid if it accepts every YES instance and rejects every NO instance with probability at least \(2/3\), for every valid oracle response policy. Its cost is the maximum number of queries on any branch. Let \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) be the minimum integer cost of a valid tester. If one promise side is empty, including when no admissible instance exists, this minimum can be zero. All parameters in the subscript are held fixed as \(n\) grows; they are not growing input-length parameters. A matching asymptotic classification must retain their effects on which growth regime occurs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct characterization checked in Lean of the asymptotic query growth for all fixed parameter tuples in the definition. In particular, specify nonnegative comparison functions \(f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\), with corresponding upper and lower bounds, such that for each fixed tuple some constants \(A,B>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \[A f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le B f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\qquad(n\ge n_0).\] Constants may depend on the fixed tuple, but not on \(n\), the instance or the oracle order. Zero-query cases must be correctly included. The classification need not consist of a prescribed finite list of cases, but it must establish growth rates rather than merely rename or repeat the defining decision-tree optimization. Polylogarithmic gaps between upper and lower bounds do not meet the requested constant-factor precision. Results only for perfect completeness \(c=1\), one template, a special gap, or a positive-density subclass do not cover the full target. A streaming-space or polynomial-time approximation classification is not a query classification.
context:
A Max-CSP instance asks for an assignment satisfying as many local predicates as possible. A query tester is allowed to inspect only selected incident constraints and must distinguish two separated ranges of the optimum value, even though it has unlimited ability to process what it has seen.

The fraction satisfied is normalized by the actual number of constraint occurrences. This differs from ordinary bounded-degree property-testing distance, which counts edits relative to the degree bound times the number of variables. The difference matters when most variables are isolated.

Fei therefore introduces \(\mathrm{BD}^{*}(d,\alpha,n)\), requiring at least \(\alpha n\) constraints for fixed positive \(\alpha\). The present density parameter includes both that model and \(\alpha=0\), the original bounded-degree regime. It keeps the sparse-instance issue visible rather than silently assuming linear density.

Question 13 asks for the complexity of all predicate families and completeness–soundness pairs. This card makes the degree, density and oracle conventions explicit and chooses constant-factor matching bounds as its asymptotic acceptance precision. No claim is made that a previously proved dichotomy already supplies those bounds.

Even the perfect-completeness satisfiability setting displays several behaviors. The source surveys constant-query languages, square-root lower bounds with nearly matching upper bounds for graph bipartiteness, and linear lower bounds for graph 3-colorability. These examples do not classify every imperfect-completeness gap.

Fei’s Theorem 8 proves a linear lower bound at some fixed gap, degree and positive density for every unbounded-width template. Here bounded width means that some fixed level of local consistency suffices to decide satisfiability for all instances; unbounded width means that no such fixed level suffices. The theorem does not determine the optimal hardness gap or the growth at all other parameter choices.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s April 2026 preprint strengthens related streaming lower bounds and extends the unbounded-width obstruction to that model. Its Section 1.4 explicitly still refers to the full query-complexity question as unresolved. The streaming results therefore provide relevant progress without completing the requested query classification.

Reading the entire bounded-degree instance gives a linear-query upper bound for fixed degree, irrespective of local computation time. The substantive issue is which templates and value gaps allow substantially less inspection and what the precise intermediate rates are.
why: This asks for a general account of how much of a sparse constraint system must be inspected to distinguish high from low optimum value. It covers different predicates, value gaps and densities in one query model, and could identify broad structural boundaries between local testing and essentially complete inspection. Its complexity bounds are information-based and need not assume computational hardness conjectures.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The 2026 published primary source retains the full query classification as Question 13. The April 2026 streaming paper explicitly refers to that query question as open while solving a different streaming extension. No full all-template, all-gap constant-factor classification was located in the bounded search; cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2025-10-30: Fei’s initial full preprint gives the unbounded-width linear query lower bound and poses the broader template-and-gap classification. | 2026-04-01: Fei–Minzer–Wang improve related streaming-space bounds, while Section 1.4 retains the general query classification as an open problem. | 2026: The published APPROX/RANDOM version states the density-aware Theorem 8 and the all-template, all-gap query problem as Question 13.
working_summary: A tester must distinguish constraint systems whose optimum satisfied fractions lie on opposite sides of a fixed gap. It can query variables to reveal incident constraint occurrences, with only a constant number of occurrences per variable. The target is the asymptotic query complexity for every finite predicate template, gap, degree bound and density regime. The actual number of constraints matters because value is normalized by constraints rather than by all possible incidence slots. Known linear lower bounds and related streaming results leave the complete query classification unresolved.

title: Sample complexity of symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
importance_reason: A foundational dependent-data testing problem with a single uncontrolled trajectory, a carefully motivated spectral discrepancy and a substantial unresolved joint parameter gap. It probes whether validation needs global exploration and connects information-theoretic testing with Markov dynamics.
formal: Determine the minimax trajectory-length complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) of identity testing for symmetric Markov chains in the model below, up to universal multiplicative constants. Both the state-space size \(n\) and reciprocal proximity \(1/\varepsilon\) vary. Give an explicit positive comparison function \(B(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[cB(n,\varepsilon)\le M(n,\varepsilon)\le CB(n,\varepsilon)\] for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). Constants must be independent of the reference chain, the starting state, \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\); logarithmic factors in these parameters may not be suppressed. If the complexity is infinite on part of this domain, identify that part and prove infinitude there instead of assigning it a finite bound.
question_excerpt: Determine the optimal sample complexity for identity testing of symmetric Markov chains; the source proposes order n/epsilon and asks whether explicit hitting-time dependence can be removed.
definitions: A chain on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has a transition matrix \(P\in[0,1]^{n\times n}\) with \(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). Symmetry means \(P_{ij}=P_{ji}\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros, holding probabilities and disconnected state spaces are allowed. For two such matrices set \[R(P,Q)_{ij}=\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}},\qquad \Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho(R(P,Q)),\] where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius, the maximum absolute value of an eigenvalue. The square root is entrywise; it is not a matrix square root. The resulting discrepancy lies in \([0,1]\), but it need not be a metric. The tester receives \(n\), rational \(\varepsilon\), the complete reference matrix \(Q\), and observations from one trajectory of an unknown symmetric matrix \(P\). For every initial state \(x\in[n]\), \(X_0=x\) and \[\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_t]=P_{X_t,j}.\] The tester sees \(X_0\) without a transition cost; each subsequent observed transition costs one. It cannot choose the initial state, reset the chain, request a transition from an arbitrary state, or inspect entries of \(P\). It may stop early, but it must stop within the claimed worst-case number of transitions. It accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(P=Q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(\Delta(P,Q)>\varepsilon\), for every starting state. No guarantee is imposed for other unequal pairs. Probabilities include both the Markov trajectory and independent internal fair random bits. Correctness for every fixed starting state also covers every starting distribution. The tester is one finite uniform program across all \(n,\varepsilon,Q\), with integer and bit-string work storage and exact real registers holding the supplied entries of \(Q\). It has rational constants, exact arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) with division by zero forbidden, nonnegative square root, and exact order/equality comparisons; it has no advice or other oracle. The integer and rational parameters use binary encodings. These conventions specify exact numerical access; no bit-time guarantee for arbitrary real input is being requested. Local computation, memory and access to the explicitly supplied \(Q\) are uncharged, but every execution terminates. For each \(n,\varepsilon\), let \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(m\) attained as a worst-case transition bound by a uniform tester correct for every permitted parameter value, reference and unknown chain. The worst case includes every \(Q,P\), starting state and execution. Set \(M=+\infty\) if no finite bound exists. This is a worst-reference minimax quantity, rather than a reference-dependent hitting-time or mixing-time complexity. The full symmetric class in the original boxed problem is retained; irreducibility, aperiodicity and stationary initialization are not extra promises.
answer_criterion: Supply the comparison function and a complete Lean-checked proof of the matching bounds, including correctness and trajectory cost of one uniform upper-bound tester and a lower bound against every tester in the stated model. Any asserted infinite values require a Lean proof that no finite uniform bound exists there. Merely repeating the defining minimization, suppressing unbounded logarithmic factors, or proving a bound only for fast-mixing or irreducible inputs does not meet the full target. The source's proposed \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) answer is a conjectured value of this complexity, not an assumption that an accepted answer must confirm.
context:
Independent distribution samples can be collected from scratch. Here the next observation is constrained by the current state, so revisiting an uninformative region may consume many observations. The reference matrix is fully known; only the transition rule that generated the trajectory is unknown.

A worst-case start makes some unequal chains indistinguishable: they may share a closed component with identical transitions, and the trajectory may never leave it. The source chooses a spectral discrepancy that vanishes in such cases. Replacing it with a maximum row distance would impose rejection obligations that a single trajectory might never be able to meet.

The square-root overlap matrix compares both transition rules on the same labeled state space. Its leading spectral behavior measures how quickly the distributions of long trajectories can separate. Testing equality of stationary distributions alone would not test this object; in particular, symmetric chains all admit the uniform stationary distribution.

The original sample complexity is trajectory length in observed states. This card counts transitions after the initial state, a difference of one. It retains the original strict farness inequality and asks for matching joint dependence on state count and proximity, with constants and the minimax reference convention made explicit.

The original upper bound includes a reference hitting-time term, and its lower bound is \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\). The hitting time is the largest expected time to reach a specified state from another state; it may be very large or infinite. Section 6 conjectures that a matching order-\(n/\varepsilon\) bound should avoid that dependence.

The 2019 paper removes hitting-time dependence in its stated irreducible symmetric setting, with bound \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\). Its Section 5 still asks whether the reciprocal-distance gap can be closed. This review records the irreducibility assumption from Section 2.1 rather than silently treating that theorem as an unrestricted statement about every reducible input.

Later work extends this line to reversible chains with additional stationary-distribution conditions, and develops a geometric reduction. Those extensions address broader types of transition matrix under promises; the checked results do not establish matching joint bounds for the full original symmetric problem.

Bounds in a matrix norm, experiments with a controlled restart interface, or results stated after assuming stationary initialization solve distinct testing problems. The source also asks other questions about its discrepancy and more general chains; those directions are not additional targets of this card.
why: This asks how much dependent data is needed to validate an entire stochastic transition rule when the experiment cannot be restarted or directed toward unvisited states. Sharp bounds would separate the intrinsic information cost of testing dynamics from the cost of fully exploring the reference chain, extending the foundations of distribution testing beyond independent samples.
status_note: Source-open as the optimal trajectory-complexity question in COLT 2018 Section 6. On 15 September 2026, the full original model and bounds, the 2019 irreducibility convention and theorem, and the 2022/2023 reversible extensions were checked. A bounded later-work search did not identify matching joint bounds for the retained full symmetric model. The minimax precision and exact-real computational primitives are explicitly recorded model specifications, not proof certification. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2018: The COLT paper defines the single-trajectory spectral-discrepancy model, proves a hitting-time-dependent upper bound and an \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\) lower bound, and proposes \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) in its first open question. | 2019: Cherapanamjeri–Bartlett Theorem 10 gives a \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) tester under the irreducible symmetric setting stated in Section 2.1; the conclusion retains the optimal reciprocal-distance dependence as an open question. | 2022: Fried–Wolfer extend testing to irreducible reversible chains under a stationary-distribution proximity promise. Their symmetric specialization recovers the \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) scale. | 2023: Wolfer–Watanabe give a geometric reduction under additional conditions, explicitly separating this discrepancy-based problem from testing under the matrix infinity norm.
working_summary: The tester observes one trajectory from an unknown symmetric Markov chain and receives a complete known reference transition matrix. It must distinguish equality from positive spectral discrepancy for every uncontrolled starting state, without resets or chosen-state sampling. The target is matching joint dependence of the worst-case required trajectory length on the number of states and the proximity parameter. Later testing results remove hitting-time dependence under their stated irreducibility assumptions, but the checked bounds still leave a reciprocal-distance gap. The card preserves the full original symmetric model and distinguishes its transition discrepancy from stationary-distribution or matrix-norm testing.

title: Polylogarithmic-query pattern-freeness testing
importance_reason: A uniform structural question over all fixed permutation patterns, with a major adaptive versus nonadaptive gap and links to monotonicity and sequence estimation. The first difficult nonmonotone patterns already have length four; the target goes beyond optimizing one tester.
formal: For every integer \(k\ge2\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \([k]\), is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error value-query tester \(A_\pi\) such that, for each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there are integers \(C_{\pi,\varepsilon},a_{\pi,\varepsilon}\ge1\) for which the tester uses at most \[C_{\pi,\varepsilon}\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^{a_{\pi,\varepsilon}}\] queries on every execution for every \(n\ge1\)? On input \(n,\varepsilon\) and access to any \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\), it must accept with probability one if \(f\) is \(\pi\)-free, and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) if the normalized Hamming distance to \(\pi\)-freeness is at least \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(k\) or \(1/\varepsilon\) is required; those parameters are fixed when measuring the growth in \(n\).
question_excerpt: We conjecture, however, that the query complexity is \(\operatorname{polylog} n\) for all constant \(k\).
definitions: For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A permutation \(\pi:[k]\to[k]\) is a bijection. A \(\pi\)-appearance in \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\) consists of indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) satisfying \[f(i_s)<f(i_t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\pi(s)<\pi(t)\qquad(s,t\in[k]).\] The comparisons are strict, so all values in an appearance are distinct. The function is \(\pi\)-free if it has no such appearance. Inputs may have repeated values, and there is no monotonicity, bounded-range, integrality or permutation promise on \(f\). Let \(\mathcal F_{\pi,n}\) be all \(\pi\)-free real-valued functions on \([n]\), and define \[d_0(f,\mathcal F_{\pi,n})=\frac1n\min_{g\in\mathcal F_{\pi,n}}|\{i\in[n]:f(i)\ne g(i)\}|.\] For \(k\ge2\), the class is nonempty because a constant function is free, and a minimum exists among finitely many possible disagreement counts. When \(n<k\), every input is free. A query chooses an index \(i\) and returns the exact value \(f(i)\); every such call costs one. Queries may adapt to all earlier returned values and random bits. The tester is one finite program for the fixed \(\pi\), receiving \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers. Its work storage consists of integers, bit strings and exact real registers, with rational constants, copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, and exact equality and order comparisons. It uses independent fair random bits, has no real advice or other oracle, and must terminate on every execution. There is no cost bound on local computation or storage. This specifies the exact-value oracle model, not a bit-time or noisy-value model. The stated query bound is a worst-case bound over input functions and all random executions. Probabilities are over the program's random bits for a fixed function. Behavior at positive distance below \(\varepsilon\) is unrestricted. The program may depend on \(\pi\), and both the multiplicative constant and logarithmic exponent may also depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\); neither may depend on \(n\) or \(f\).
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must work for every fixed permutation pattern, arbitrary real-valued input functions and every positive rational proximity parameter, with one tester per pattern and the stated polylogarithmic-in-\(n\) worst-case query bound. A negative answer must rule out this guarantee for at least one pattern. A bound of \(n^{o(1)}\), a lower bound restricted to nonadaptive algorithms, or a result on a higher-dimensional domain does not settle this proposition.
context:
A pattern specifies relative ranks rather than prescribed values. For example, \(\pi=(1,3,2)\) occurs at increasing positions when the first value is smallest, the second largest and the third between them. Equal values cannot form this occurrence. Avoiding \((2,1)\) is exactly being nondecreasing.

The repair distance counts how many entries must be changed, independently of how far their numerical values move. It is different from distances on permutations that charge the movement of points or inversions. Restricting the input itself to be a permutation would also change the model.

The source studies fixed pattern length and fixed proximity. This card therefore allows arbitrary dependence on those parameters and asks only for a polylogarithmic bound in sequence length. The one-sided convention follows the source algorithms and its separate discussion of whether two-sided error can help.

An adaptive tester can use values already seen to decide which positions to inspect next. A nonadaptive tester must select all query positions without their answers. The paper’s strongly sublinear adaptive bound and the much larger known worst-pattern nonadaptive bounds expose the importance of this distinction.

The best general bound in the checked source is \(\widetilde O_{k,\varepsilon}(n^{o(1)})\). A subpolynomial function of \(n\) can still grow faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\), so this does not establish the conjecture. The source separately records polylogarithmic bounds for patterns of length at most three and stronger bounds for monotone patterns.

The SODA 2026 hypergrid paper explicitly restates the one-dimensional conjecture. Its new polynomial lower bound concerns nonmonotone patterns on a two-dimensional partially ordered domain, where positions are not all comparable. It does not refute the conjecture on the line considered here.
why: A fixed order pattern is a basic obstruction in sequences and generalizes monotonicity. The conjecture asks whether adaptive access makes every such obstruction testable from only a polylogarithmic number of values, despite large lower bounds for predetermined queries. Its resolution would clarify the reach of adaptivity in ordered property testing and its connection with sublinear sequence analysis.

working_summary: A permutation pattern specifies the strict relative order of values at increasing positions of a real-valued sequence. The question asks whether every fixed pattern has an adaptive one-sided tester using only a polylogarithmic number of queries in the sequence length. Distance is the fraction of entries that must change to remove all occurrences, and the query bound may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pattern and proximity. The checked general adaptive upper bound is subpolynomial but not polylogarithmic, while newer lower bounds on hypergrids concern a different domain. Resolving the conjecture would clarify how much adaptive observations can improve the testing of ordered obstructions.

title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
importance_reason: Testing submodularity concerns a fundamental structural property used throughout combinatorial optimization and learning.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
question_excerpt: The source explicitly singles out polynomial query complexity in n and 1/epsilon within its broader request for the optimal testing complexity. This card retains that threshold, uses the cited foundational paper’s one-sided Hamming-distance convention, and specifies the exact-real value-oracle computational model. The source’s special cases are retained as provenance rather than imposed as input promises.
definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.
context:
A set function assigns a value to each possible subset of a ground set. Submodularity says that adding an element cannot become more valuable merely because the receiving set has grown. Equivalently, it satisfies the union/intersection inequality in the definitions. With \(n\) elements there are \(2^{n}\) values, so inspecting a polynomial number of them is a small fraction of the complete object.

Testing allows an unresolved band of nearby nonsubmodular inputs. The tester must accept genuinely submodular functions and reject functions that disagree with every submodular function on at least an \(\varepsilon\)-fraction of subsets. It is not required to reconstruct the closest submodular function or to decide exact membership for every oracle.

Hamming distance treats any changed entry as one disagreement. In contrast, an \(\ell_p\) distance for finite \(p\) averages the magnitudes of changes. Many tiny discrepancies can therefore contribute little to that norm while affecting a large fraction of the table. The published constant-query result for bounded functions in an \(\ell_p\) metric does not imply polynomial-query testing in the Hamming metric used here.

The saved problem asks both for optimal query complexity and, specifically, whether polynomially many queries suffice. This card selects that explicitly posed polynomial threshold as its single yes/no target. The one-sided-error convention is taken from Definition 1.2 of the cited foundational paper. The finite-program exact-real convention makes the value-oracle interpretation explicit; it is not a claim about bit complexity or noisy measurements.

The existing upper and lower bounds leave a substantial gap: known general testing uses a subexponential number of queries for fixed distance, while a nearly quadratic lower bound rules out much smaller sample budgets. Neither result decides whether some fixed polynomial suffices. Bounds on the frequency of a particular kind of local violation also have a narrower scope than a lower bound against every adaptive tester.
why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.
status_note: Source-open under the explicitly recorded one-sided Hamming-distance interpretation. On 15 September 2026, the foundational journal definitions and bounds, Hatami–Vondrák’s manuscript theorem, Blais–Bommireddi’s ITCS 2017 result and Haris–Palit’s published 9 September 2026 work were checked. The later work still records the ordinary-submodularity gap. The original problem page was recovered from its saved full text when live requests failed. This is a bounded status review, not an independent verification of the cited proofs or a Lean formalization.
progress: 2011: Seshadhri's Bertinoro problem explicitly asks whether \(\operatorname{poly}(n/\varepsilon)\) queries suffice. The listed matroid-rank and coverage directions are separate special questions, not promises imposed on the general target. | 2012–2014: Seshadhri–Vondrák give a one-sided tester with query complexity \((1/\varepsilon)^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) in the small-distance regime. Their Theorem 1.4 also gives examples with few violated squares; that obstruction to this particular local test is not a superpolynomial lower bound for all testers. | 2016: Hatami–Vondrák's author manuscript proves an \(\Omega(n^{2}/\log n)\) query lower bound for constant distance in Theorem 1.2. This is still compatible with a polynomial-query tester of larger degree. No later publication venue is inferred for this manuscript. | 2017: Blais–Bommireddi prove dimension-independent query bounds for testing \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1]\) under \(\ell_p\) distance for each fixed finite \(p\ge1\) and fixed positive proximity parameter. Theorem 1.1 uses a different distance metric from this card. | 2026-09-09: Haris–Palit's published k-submodularity paper records the remaining gap for ordinary submodularity. Its constant-query theorem concerns bounded functions in \(\ell_p\) distance; its Hamming-distance results test separate component properties with subexponential bounds. These results do not supply the polynomial Hamming tester asked for here.
working_summary: Submodularity expresses diminishing returns for a real-valued function on all subsets of a finite ground set. The question asks whether a polynomial number of exact value queries can test this property with one-sided error. Distance is the fraction of table entries that must change to obtain a submodular function, regardless of change magnitude. Known general upper and lower bounds leave the polynomial-query question unresolved, and constant-query norm-distance results concern a different task. A resolution would determine how efficiently an oracle’s global diminishing-returns structure can be checked from limited access.

title: Query complexity of conditional equivalence testing
importance_reason: Comparing proof or conditional-sampling interfaces tests the computational power of alternative distribution-testing models.
formal: Determine, up to multiplicative constant factors, the dependence on domain size \(n\) of the randomized adaptive conditional-query complexity \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) of testing equality of two unknown distributions, for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). The task is to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\ge\varepsilon\) with error at most \(1/3\), using the model below. The answer must give a positive comparison function \(F(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and for every fixed permitted \(\varepsilon\) constants \(c_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon}>0\) and \(n_0(\varepsilon)\) such that \[c_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\le Q(n,\varepsilon)\le C_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)).\] Multiplicative factors depending on \(n\), including iterated logarithms, must be resolved rather than suppressed.
question_excerpt: For constant positive proximity, determine the exact dependence of conditional equivalence-testing sample complexity on the domain size.
definitions: A distribution on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for an integer \(n\ge2\), is a function \(p:[n]\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p(i)=1\); probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers and may vanish. Neither input distribution is explicitly known. Their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}|p(i)-q(i)|.\] The tester receives \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers. A query specifies one of the two oracles and a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), represented by its full \(n\)-bit membership vector. For oracle \(p\), write \(p(S)=\sum_{i\in S}p(i)\). If \(p(S)>0\), the response is an element \(i\in S\) with probability \(p(i)/p(S)\). If \(p(S)=0\), the response is a uniformly random element of \(S\), with no failure flag. The same rule applies to \(q\). Each call uses fresh randomness conditional on its selected oracle and set; no probability value or set mass is revealed. Drawing from both distributions counts as two queries. Unconditional sampling is allowed by taking \(S=[n]\). All nonempty subsets are allowed, and later queries may depend on every previous response and internal random choice. The tester is a finite probabilistic Turing oracle program using independent fair random bits and no advice or other oracle. It must terminate on every execution; its local computation, subset-description length and storage have no imposed bound. Query cost is the worst-case total number of calls to both oracles, over input distributions, internal randomness and oracle responses. A correct tester accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) whenever \(p=q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) whenever \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\ge\varepsilon\); either answer is allowed at intermediate positive distance. Probabilities include both sources of randomness. Let \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least worst-case query bound at these parameters among uniform testers correct on every permitted parameter pair and every input pair. Such finite bounds exist, for example from ordinary finite-domain distribution testing. The target studies \(n\to\infty\) separately at each fixed \(\varepsilon\); constants and the starting order may depend on \(\varepsilon\). It does not ask for optimal joint dependence when \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\).
answer_criterion: Provide the matching bounds and uniform upper-bound tester specified in the formal statement, with complete Lean-checked correctness and complexity proofs. The lower bound must apply to every randomized adaptive tester in the stated conditional model. Bounds differing by unbounded functions of \(n\), even powers of \(\log\log\log n\), do not meet the constant-factor precision. A restatement of the defining optimum, fixed-size experiments, or results requiring a known reference distribution, a prover, probability evaluation or restricted conditioning sets are insufficient.
context:
In identity testing one of the two distributions is supplied explicitly. In equivalence testing both distributions are hidden behind sampling oracles. This information difference remains significant even when samples can be conditioned on arbitrary subsets: a comparison against a known reference and a comparison between two unknown sources need not have the same sample cost.

A conditional query requests a fresh draw from the original probability law restricted to a chosen set. It does not return the probability of reaching that set. The rule for zero-mass sets matters because the tester does not know either support in advance. This card adopts the uniform-response convention stated explicitly in the 2024 lower-bound paper.

The source fixes a positive proximity parameter and asks how complexity grows with the domain. Accordingly, this card permits constants depending on that fixed parameter, while requiring matching dependence on domain size. The worst-case query convention includes both oracles and permits unrestricted adaptivity; it is not an expected query budget or a limit on the number of adaptive rounds.

The 2015 upper bound and 2024 lower bound both have double-logarithmic main terms, with additional iterated-logarithmic factors hidden by soft asymptotic notation. The later paper explicitly describes its result as resolving the earlier gap. That is a major resolution at the soft-asymptotic scale, but it does not establish matching constant factors. This card records that progress rather than carrying forward the obsolete square-root gap from the 2017 problem page.

The COLT source uses unnormalized \(\ell_1\) distance, twice total variation, and a different constant error probability. Those constant changes do not change the fixed-proximity asymptotic question. By contrast, suppressing a factor that grows with the domain would change the requested precision, so the problem page's displayed upper bound is recorded here with its missing soft-asymptotic qualification restored.
why: Conditional sampling exposes relative probabilities inside chosen parts of a domain and can dramatically reduce the amount of data needed for comparison. The remaining dependence on domain size measures the cost of comparing two wholly unknown laws even with this strong access. The central gap is now closed up to iterated-logarithmic factors; the exact growth requested by the source still requires distinguishing those factors.
status_note: The main gap posed in 2017 was resolved at the soft-asymptotic scale by the published SODA 2024 lower bound. The source’s exact-dependence request is interpreted here as constant-factor matching, which is not established by the checked upper and lower bounds because they retain iterated-logarithmic factors. On 15 September 2026, the source page, original model, upper bound, 2024 theorem/proof scale and distinct 2026 interactive setting were checked. A bounded later-work search did not verify a full constant-factor resolution; the status is uncertain rather than an unqualified claim that the old gap remains open. Complete proofs were not independently verified in Lean.
progress: 2015: Falahatgar and coauthors obtain \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-5}\log\log n)\) queries in their closeness-testing formulation. For fixed proximity this is double-logarithmic up to further logarithmic factors, not an established ordinary \(O(\log\log n)\) bound. | 2015–2018: Acharya–Canonne–Kamath establish an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) lower bound for adaptive equivalence testing, proving that domain-independent conditional identity testing does not extend to two unknown distributions. | 2017: Problem 87 asks for the exact dependence on domain size at constant proximity, continuing the earlier question about the gap between the known upper and lower bounds. | 2024-01-04: Chakraborty–Chakraborty–Kumar prove \(\widetilde\Omega(\log\log n)\) queries are necessary. Their Theorem 1.1 explicitly hides factors polynomial in \(\log\log\log n\), and Section 4.3 works at the scale \(\log\log n/\log\log\log n\). The construction uses total variation distance \(1/4\); it is also a valid lower-bound instance for each smaller fixed proximity. This closes the main gap while leaving the constant-factor target unestablished by these bounds. | 2026: The ITCS work on interactive proofs adds a data-rich prover and conditional comparison queries. It does not give the matching unassisted equivalence-testing bound required here. A bounded later-work search was completed on 15 September 2026.
working_summary: Two unknown distributions must be distinguished as equal or separated by a fixed positive total variation distance. Each conditional query selects one distribution and a nonempty subset, then receives a fresh sample restricted to that subset. The target is matching constant-factor query bounds as the domain grows, allowing arbitrary adaptive queries and constants depending on the fixed proximity. The main gap was closed in 2024 up to iterated-logarithmic factors, which are not hidden by this card’s answer criterion. The result would pin down the remaining domain-size cost of comparing two unknown distributions under powerful conditional access.

title: Query complexity of directed acyclicity testing with bidirectional access
importance_reason: A sharp testing or correction bound for a specific distance, property, or sampling regime.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed degree bound \(d\ge 1\) and fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), the minimum worst-case number \(Q(n,d,\varepsilon )\) of incidence-list queries needed by an adaptive randomized two-sided-error tester to distinguish acyclic n-vertex digraphs from digraphs more than \(\varepsilon dn\) edge deletions away from acyclic, when every indegree and outdegree is at most d and both incoming and outgoing queries are allowed.
definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,d\}\); it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and \(\varepsilon\) are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}, k\ge 2\), with arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\) and \(v_{k}\to v_{1}\); acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let \(\tau (G)\) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(\tau (G)>\varepsilon dn\). Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least \(2/3\) and reject each \(\varepsilon\)-far graph with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational \(\varepsilon\); there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested \(\Theta\) bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and \(\varepsilon\). One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound \(F(n,d,\varepsilon ), a\) uniform tester using \(O(F)\) queries, and a matching \(\Omega (F)\) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed \(d,\varepsilon\) in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.
context:
A long directed cycle can remain invisible in a small explored neighborhood. The tester sees only chosen incident edges, so even the ability to move both forward and backward does not directly reveal whether some distant portion closes a cycle.

A directed cycle on n vertices becomes acyclic after deleting one arc. Its normalized distance is \(1/(dn)\), so for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) and large n it is outside the promised far case. Property testing asks for reliable rejection only when many arc deletions are unavoidable.

The source records an \(\Omega (n^{1/3})\) query lower bound for adaptive two-sided testing at suitable fixed parameters. Reading every outgoing list uses at most nd queries and determines the whole graph. The gap between such lower bounds and the linear bound motivates the sharp query question.

The 2023 model comparison distinguishes access to both directions from access only to outgoing arcs. A lower bound against the less informative oracle cannot automatically rule out an algorithm with incoming queries.

Yoshida’s preprint states stronger one-sided and two-sided lower bounds when queries only reveal outgoing neighbors and indegree is unrestricted. These hypotheses differ from the fixed bidirectional bounded-degree setting of the original question.
why: Measures how much local information is needed to certify the absence of global directed cyclic structure up to a proximity promise. It would clarify the power of adaptive two-direction exploration in sparse directed graphs.
status_note: Original access model, distance convention and subsequent related bounds checked through 11 September 2026; no matching sharp query classification found. The card explicitly chooses query complexity as the measure of the source’s best-algorithm question. The 2026 paper was checked at introductory-statement level, not independently proved.
progress: 2011: Ron asks for the best tester in the directed bidirectional bounded-degree model and reports the earlier \(\Omega (n^{1/3})\) two-sided lower bound. | 2023: Peng and Wang explicitly retain that historical bidirectional acyclicity lower bound while studying the relation between two graph-access models. | 2026-04-15: Yoshida states improved lower bounds for outgoing-only access with bounded outdegree but unrestricted indegree. They are not transferred to this model.
working_summary: The graph is directed and has bounded incoming and outgoing degree. A tester can ask for individual incoming or outgoing neighbors of any labeled vertex. It must distinguish graphs without directed cycles from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon dn\) arc deletions to remove all directed cycles. The target is the optimal number of adaptive queries with error probability at most one third on either promised case. Recent lower bounds for outgoing-only access use a different model and do not by themselves settle this bidirectional question.

title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
importance_reason: A quantitative or model-specific learning frontier; resolving it would sharpen a useful guarantee but has more limited scope than a general learnability characterization.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and \(\Delta_d=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d}:\sum_i p_i=1\}\). The input lists every entry of \(q\in\Delta_d\cap\mathbb Q^d\), including zeros, and the rational number \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\). Rationals are represented by binary nonnegative numerators and positive denominators in lowest terms, with delimiters; let \(B\) be the total bit length, including the length encoding of the list. No oracle or compressed description replaces this list. The alternative \(p\) ranges over all of \(\Delta_d\), including irrational probabilities and mass on coordinates where \(q_i=0\). Total variation is
\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d}|p_i-q_i|.\]

For a nonnegative integer \(s\), a possibly randomized statistical test is specified by a function \(\tau:[d]^s\to[0,1]\); \(\tau(x)\) is its conditional probability of rejecting the null on sample sequence \(x\). There is no time, space or representation constraint on this finite table of real probabilities. The product law \(p^{\otimes s}\) means that all \(s\) observations are independent and have law \(p\). A valid test satisfies
\[\mathbb E_{q^{\otimes s}}\tau\le1/3,\qquad
