\forall p\in\Delta_d\text{ with }d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_{p^{\otimes s}}\tau\ge2/3.\]
The same test must work for every alternative at that fixed \((q,\varepsilon)\); it cannot be chosen after learning \(p\). The minimum such \(s\) defines \(n_*\). It is finite on every permitted input. The sample count is fixed in advance, not an expected stopping time, and the two errors are bounded separately. Cases with \(0<d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\le\varepsilon\) impose no condition.

The zero-sample case is included: \([d]^0\) is a singleton. The alternative is empty exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge1-\min_iq_i\), since the largest possible distance from \(q\) in this simplex is \(1-\min_iq_i\). In that case \(n_*=0\); otherwise \(n_*\ge1\). Thus the claimed multiplicative guarantee requires the evaluator to return exactly zero in empty-alternative cases, including \(d=1\). The strict inequality in the alternative is intentional.

The evaluator is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine. It outputs a nonnegative integer in binary and halts within \(K(B+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(K,a\), independent of \(d,q,\varepsilon\); input reading, bit arithmetic and output writing all count. It has no advice or oracles, and must halt within the same bound on malformed encodings, whose outputs are irrelevant. The quantifier order is existence of the evaluator and constants, followed by all valid inputs. There is no permission for polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) in place of polynomial dependence on its encoded length. The statistical tester whose existence defines \(n_*\) is a separate object and need not be produced by this evaluator.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence claim. A positive answer must specify the evaluator and prove its uniform polynomial running time and both bounds with one universal finite factor \(C\). A negative answer must refute the existence of every such evaluator and constant; failure of one proposed expression is insufficient. Neither defining \(\Phi\) by the minimum over all statistical tests without proving efficient evaluation, nor comparing upper and lower bounds at different multiples of \(\varepsilon\), satisfies this target. A conditional computational obstruction alone does not prove the unconditional negative claim. Countably infinite or implicitly described references are outside this explicitly selected variant.
context:
The source explicitly offers efficient evaluation from an explicit reference description as one meaning of a succinct functional. Binary rational inputs and polynomial bit complexity make that meaning a precise mathematical predicate. The broader closed-form and infinite-domain versions remain part of the source direction, and are not claimed equivalent to this variant.

Valiant and Valiant give reference-dependent bounds using the \(2/3\)-quasinorm of a vector after removal of its largest coordinate and a small-probability tail. Their theorem and following discussion explicitly permit constant-factor changes in the distance parameter as well as in the sample count. That is a different guarantee from a characterization at fixed \(\varepsilon\).

Canonne explains that the differing tail cutoffs can cause an arbitrarily large ratio between the resulting bounds, with harmonic probability profiles as an example. Section 2 discusses a second characterization using an interpolation functional, which has an analogous mismatch. Section 3 explains why bounds on the optimal separation radius up to constants do not automatically provide the requested fixed-distance sample characterization.

The source separately raises a proof-coverage issue for the earlier lower bound near point masses, and separates that repair as Open Question 3. It does not claim the lower-bound theorem false. Repairing that corner case alone would not close the characterization gap in Open Question 1. The present finite-domain definition also treats empty alternatives explicitly.
why: Two reference distributions on the same domain can require very different numbers of samples to test. A computable characterization at the exact requested distance would identify the information needed for each reference profile, including distributions for which existing bounds disagree by unbounded factors. It would also separate the statistical cost of testing from the cost of evaluating that cost.
status_note: The full COLT 2024 open-problem paper and FOCS 2014 Definition 1, Theorem 1 and its distance-rescaling discussion were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded search for 2025–2026 work did not locate a matching fixed-distance efficient characterization or impossibility theorem. A July 2026 personal-webpage claim concerns only the separate Question 3 and identifies its proof as entirely AI-generated and in need of expert review; it was not used as a verified mathematical result. The card remains source-open under this limited literature check. The finite rational bit-model selection is editorial, not an assertion that the source fixed precisely this representation.
progress: 2014: The FOCS paper establishes instance-dependent bounds, with constant-factor changes allowed in the distance threshold. | 2024: The COLT open-problem paper identifies the unbounded possible gap at a fixed distance and asks for a succinct characterization; it distinguishes two further related questions.
working_summary: The problem asks for an efficiently computable estimate of the optimal sample count for testing equality to a particular known distribution. The selected variant gives the reference probabilities and distance threshold explicitly as binary rational numbers. The estimate must match the information-theoretic optimum within one universal factor at exactly the requested distance. Existing instance-dependent bounds can disagree by arbitrarily large factors because their distance parameters differ. The card makes efficient evaluation precise while keeping the computation of the statistical test unrestricted.

title: A dimension-free directed \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) Poincaré inequality
importance_reason: A dimension-free analytic relationship between local violations and global distance from monotonicity, with significance for property testing. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Lipschitz function \(f:[0,1]^{n}\to \mathbb{R} , d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f) \le  C \int _{[0,1]^{n}} (\sum_{i=1}^{n} \max \{- \partial _{i}f(x),0\}^{2})^{1/2} dx\)? Here \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)\) is the \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance to the coordinatewise nondecreasing functions. The same C must work for every dimension and every finite Lipschitz constant.
definitions:
Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]^{n}\) has total mass one. A function \(g:[0,1]^{n}	o \mathbb{R}\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x_{i}\le y_{i}\) for all i. Define \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)=\inf _{g} \int |f(x)- g(x)|dx\), over measurable integrable coordinatewise nondecreasing g; g need not have the same Lipschitz constant as f. A function f is Lipschitz if there is a finite L with |\(f(x)- f(y)|\le \mathrm{L}\Vert x- y\Vert _{2}\) for all x,y in the cube. Its gradient exists almost everywhere; its values on the exceptional null set may be set to zero without changing any integral. The negative gradient is \(
abla ^{-}f(x)=(\max \{- \partial _{1}f(x),0\},\ldots ,\max \{- \partial _{n}f(x),0\})\). The right-hand side is \(C\cdot E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}]\) for a uniform point X in the cube. It is not \(C\cdot (E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}^{2}])^{1/2}\). No boundary condition, mean-zero assumption or fixed bound on the range of f is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequality with one universal finite C, or refute the existence of such a C by showing that the ratio \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)/E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}\) is unbounded across the stated functions and dimensions (including a function with positive distance and zero denominator, if one existed). A bound whose constant grows with n, or a bound using the \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) norm of the gradient over the cube, is insufficient.
context:
A negative partial derivative witnesses a local decrease in one coordinate. The left-hand side measures the least average change to the entire function needed to remove all monotonicity violations.

The 2023 source proves a directed inequality using \(E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{1}\). Comparing \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) and \(\ell\)\(_{2}\) norms yields a bound with a factor \(\sqrt{n}\), whereas the conjecture asks to remove all dependence on dimension.

The later theorem bounds squared \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) distance to monotonicity by \(C\cdot E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}^{2}\). Even though \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) distance dominates \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance, the square root of this second moment can be much larger than \(E\Vert \nabla ^{-}f\Vert _{2}\). The author explicitly leaves the present conjecture open.

The 2025 thesis restates the inequality after obtaining a tester with sublinear dimension dependence from the \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) theorem. Thus the motivating algorithmic progress and the analytic conjecture have distinct statuses.
why: Would connect local directional decreases to global distance from monotonicity with a universal constant, extending a central isoperimetric principle to real-valued functions on continuous cubes.
status_note: The full 2023 conjecture, October 2024 preprint revision and July 2025 thesis were checked, including the explicit statement that the later norm inequality does not resolve this one. Searches through 12 September 2026 located no resolution of the full continuous-cube claim.
progress: 2023: The directed \((\mathrm{L}^{1},\ell _{1})\) inequality is proved; the dimension-free \((\mathrm{L}^{1},\ell _{2})\) version is Conjecture 1.8. | 2024: The directed \((\mathrm{L}^{2},\ell _{2})\) theorem yields improved testing bounds but explicitly does not settle this conjecture. | 2025-07-03: The thesis retains the same statement as Conjecture 4.43.
working_summary: The conjecture concerns every Lipschitz real-valued function on a continuous unit cube. It asks whether average distance to a monotone function is controlled by the average Euclidean magnitude of the negative gradient. The multiplicative constant must be independent of the dimension and the Lipschitz constant. A known inequality using the sum of coordinate decreases loses a square-root dimension factor. Later work proves a different inequality using squared quantities and explicitly leaves this conjecture open.

title: Optimal query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
importance_reason: A general resource tradeoff for adaptive Boolean property testing; a precise quantitative target is needed to distinguish a substantive advance from the existing simulations. Existing score retained.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors over all integers \(q,k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell<k\), \[F(q,k,\ell)=\sup\{q_\ell(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon):n\ge1,\ \varnothing\ne\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ 0<\varepsilon\le1,\ q_k(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\le q\},\] the worst query cost of reducing a Boolean property tester from \(k+1\) batches to \(\ell+1\) batches.
definitions: An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is available through queries to individual coordinates. Its distance to the known property \(\mathcal P\) is \(n^{-1}\min_{y\in\mathcal P}|\{i:x_i\ne y_i\}|\). A tester accepts every member with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects every input at distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\); other inputs have no correctness requirement. Under the source convention, \(j\) rounds of adaptivity mean \(j+1\) batches \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_j\). All coordinates in one batch are chosen before their answers are revealed. The coordinates and size of every later batch may depend on all earlier answers; empty batches are permitted. A randomized tester is a finite probability distribution over deterministic batch-query trees, each of which returns a bit on every input. Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers; this is the nonuniform query-complexity model, without a computational or randomness-generation cost. Each selected tree’s total queries are bounded on every input, and cost is their worst case over the support and inputs. Let \(q_j(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\) be the least such bound among all valid testers. Reading every coordinate shows \(q_j\le n\). The tester may depend arbitrarily on the fixed property, length and proximity parameter; no uniform synthesis from a property description is requested. Querying a coordinate already read gives no additional information and can be omitted. The same property, distance and error convention occur on both sides of \(F\). The source’s complete nonadaptive simulation shows \(F(q,k,\ell)\le2^q-1\), so the supremum is finite; since all values are integers, it is a maximum. The desired precision is a positive function \(g(q,k,\ell)\) and one absolute \(C\ge1\) with \(C^{-1}g\le F\le Cg\) for every admissible triple. The comparison constant must not depend on a parameter or on a hidden property.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function and a Lean proof of both universal constant-factor bounds on the full parameter domain. The upper bound must cover adaptive batch sizes, and the lower bound must be witnessed by permitted properties and proximity parameters. A bound only for deleting one round, fixed-size batches or a selected regime does not determine this tradeoff. Numerical 0.01 error is not the precision for this asymptotic-complexity target.
context:
The source asks how query complexity changes when a tester may use fewer adaptive batches. Its general question does not prescribe a particular exponent improvement.

The authorized editorial completion defines the extremal simulation cost and asks for matching constant-factor bounds. This is a quantitative development of the broader upper-bound question, not a claim that the source already asks for matching lower bounds.

The source already proves a one-round reduction bound and stresses that later batch sizes may depend on previous answers.
why: Quantifies the general price of replacing sequential information gathering by fewer batches. A substantive universal bound would apply across Boolean property testing, beyond the behavior of one particular property.
status_note: The source’s general round-reduction question is unresolved in the checked text; its known one-round bound does not determine the newly explicit full extremal tradeoff. This user-authorized editorial development was reviewed on 13 September 2026. The saved later-source check is bounded and does not certify exhaustive current status.
progress: 2017: Fact 25 gives complete nonadaptive simulation with at most \(2^q-1\) queries. Proposition 26 gives a one-round reduction using at most \(q(1+2^{q/k})\) queries; Open Problem 3 asks for the general tradeoff.
working_summary: A property tester probes bits in batches and may choose later batches using previous answers. The source counts one more batch than the number of adaptive rounds. The target is the largest query budget needed after reducing the number of rounds, among properties testable with the original budget. Both the property and its proximity and error guarantees remain fixed during the reduction. The benchmark asks for matching bounds with constants independent of all three resource parameters.

title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
importance_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
focus_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
formal: Do there exist universal integers \(A,k\ge1\) such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) on a nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal X\), with \(v=\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal C)\ge1\) and \(d=\operatorname{LD}(\mathcal C)\ge1\), has a positive integer sample size \[m\le A\bigl(1+v+\log^{*}d\bigr)^{k}\] and a possibly improper learner \(L\) that is \((1,1/(100m^{2}))\)-differentially private and realizes the following PAC guarantee? For every distribution \(D\) on \(\mathcal X\) and every target \(h^{*}\in\mathcal C\), when \(L\) receives \(m\) independent samples \((x_i,h^{*}(x_i))\) with \(x_i\sim D\), its output \(\widehat h\) satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[\widehat h(x)\ne h^{*}(x)]\le1/10\right]\ge9/10.\] The same \(m,L\) must work for all \(D,h^{*}\) for the chosen class. Their choice can depend on the complete class, but \(A,k\) cannot. Computation is unrestricted. This is the previously selected concrete polynomial-overhead version of the source question; the constant accuracy, confidence and sample-dependent privacy parameters are editorial specifications, not parameter values asserted in the source.
question_excerpt: Is there a generic private PAC sample bound polynomial in VC dimension and the iterated logarithm of Littlestone dimension?
definitions: A concept is a binary function; the learner knows \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension \(v\) is the largest cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) on which the restrictions of \(\mathcal C\) realize every binary labeling. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has an instance point at each internal node and its two outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. It is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is produced by one fixed concept on that path's instance points. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the greatest shattered depth. For \(z\ge1\), \(\log^{*}z\) is the least number of successive base-two logarithms needed to obtain a value at most one; in particular \(\log^{*}1=0\). The dimension-zero case is excluded only to avoid a logarithm convention: on a fixed nonempty domain such a class contains a single distinct concept and has a data-independent exact predictor. A learner is an arbitrary probability kernel from \((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\) to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\). It need not return a member of \(\mathcal C\). For every pair of labeled sample lists \(S,S'\) differing at one position and every subset \(E\) of output hypotheses, require \[\Pr[L(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[L(S')\in E]+1/(100m^{2}).\] Privacy holds even on samples not realizable by the class. The sample size is chosen before the target and distribution; the probability in the PAC guarantee includes both independently drawn examples and the learner's randomness. There are no runtime or representation bounds, and no uniform program across classes is required. The integer-power bound is equivalent to an unspecified universal polynomial in \(1+v\) and \(1+\log^{*}d\). A finite class on an arbitrary domain can be reduced to the finite domain of distinct label vectors \((h(x))_{h\in\mathcal C}\), of which there are at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|}\); both dimensions and these unrestricted learning/privacy requirements are preserved. Thus the finite-domain convention introduces no additional sample-complexity restriction on finite classes.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial bound or its logical negation under the exact privacy and PAC conventions above. A positive answer must supply, for every class, a sample size and private learner satisfying the guarantee simultaneously for all targets and distributions. A negative answer must show that for every proposed pair of universal integers \(A,k\), some finite class admits no such learner at any positive integer sample size within the proposed bound. Computational lower bounds, proper-learning obstructions that disappear for improper learners, or a result only for one fixed VC dimension do not refute the statement.
context:
Nonprivate PAC learning at constant accuracy and confidence has sample complexity governed by VC dimension. Approximate private learnability instead has a qualitative connection to finite Littlestone dimension. This equivalence says that a finite sample bound exists; it does not identify how large the bound must be.

For finite classes, the 2026 source summarizes a lower scale \(\Omega(v+\log^{*}d)\) and upper scales \(\min\{O(\log|\mathcal C|),\widetilde O(d^{5})\}\), suppressing privacy and learning parameters. The proposed bound depends polynomially on \(v\) and \(\log^{*}d\), so replacing \(d\) by another fixed power does not answer it. The source presents this as one concrete formulation following its broader characterization question.

Lyu’s improved PAC learner has a bound \(\widetilde O(d^{5}\log(1/\delta)/(\varepsilon\alpha))\), with the remaining confidence and logarithmic factors specified in the paper. Its dependence on \(d\) is polynomial but is still much larger than a polynomial in \(\log^{*}d\). The result was published at STOC 2026; the checked detailed theorem is in the 2025 author manuscript.

Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The 2026 problem paper also discusses thresholds, rectangles and halfspaces where the privacy overhead is relatively small. These positive special cases do not supply a bound uniform over unbounded VC dimension.

The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.
why: The theorem characterizing whether private learning is possible leaves an enormous quantitative gap. This question asks whether the extra data needed for privacy is controlled by ordinary statistical complexity and an exceptionally slowly growing function of sequential complexity. A positive answer would put a uniform bound on that privacy overhead across all finite concept classes.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked COLT 2026 source, which names the polynomial VC/log-star-LD bound as a concrete version of its broader characterization question. The full cited 2025/2026 upper-bound results cover general fifth-power-LD learning and the VC-one special case, not this universal target. Bounded later-work checks on 15 September 2026 found no matching resolution; source parameter suppression is kept separate from the card’s existing fixed normalization.
progress: 2019–2020: Lower and upper results establish the equivalence of finite Littlestone dimension and approximate private PAC learnability, as summarized in Theorem 1 of the 2026 source. | 2025-07: Yan’s Theorem 1 gives a nearly optimal private sample bound for VC-dimension-one classes; the result includes an explicit accuracy, confidence and privacy-parameter formula. | 2025–2026: Lyu’s Theorem 2 improves the general private PAC bound to a fifth power of Littlestone dimension up to the stated logarithmic and privacy/accuracy factors; the paper appears at STOC 2026. | 2026-06–07: The COLT 2026 invited open problem explicitly proposes a polynomial VC/log-star-LD upper bound and states that the general characterization remains open. | 2026-09-15: Checked the full COLT 2026 source, Lyu’s theorem and publication record, and Yan’s parameter-explicit theorem. A bounded later-work search found no proof or refutation of the universal polynomial-overhead target.
working_summary: A private PAC learner must predict a Boolean concept accurately while protecting every individual labeled example. The card asks for sample size polynomial in VC dimension and the iterated logarithm of Littlestone dimension for every finite class. It retains fixed accuracy and confidence and privacy slack shrinking quadratically with the actual sample size. The latest checked general upper bound is polynomial in Littlestone dimension itself, while the proposed much smaller dependence is known in important special cases. A solution must prove the universal bound or a superpolynomial obstruction for unrestricted improper private learners, with its full quantifiers checked in Lean.

title: Optimal error for pure-DP continual counting
importance_reason: Continual counting is a basic privacy primitive; the target is the optimal price of pure privacy across the entire stream.
focus_reason: The saved target asks for optimal worst-time error when releasing every prefix sum under pure differential privacy. It complements sample-complexity bounds for private learning with a fundamental sequential data-release problem.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(T\to \infty , E(T)=\inf _{M} \max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{T}} E_{Y\sim M_{x}}[\max _{1\le t\le T}|Y_{t}- \sum_{i=1}^{t} x_{i}|]\), where the infimum is over all causal \((1/2,0)\)-differentially private mechanisms defined below.
definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.
answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.
context:
Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.
why: Determines the minimax cost of repeatedly publishing a running count while protecting each individual event under pure privacy. It separates guarantees for the whole observed trajectory from per-time or average accuracy.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No matching order for the stated unrestricted causal pure-DP expected-maximum error was located. The July source records \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\) versus \(O(\log ^{2}T)\); later factorization results use restricted mechanisms and different error criteria. New preprint proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2023: Continual-observation work formalizes the difference from batch release and develops error bounds. | 2026-07: Bairaktari–Larsen strengthen the expected-maximum lower benchmark, retaining a pure-privacy gap. | 2026-07: Arkhipov–Kalinin improve squared-error constants within matrix mechanisms. | 2026-08: New exact-order and near-optimal factorization claims address narrower error objectives and mechanism classes.
working_summary: Continual counting releases prefix sums of a binary stream as its bits arrive. The target is the smallest worst-input expected maximum absolute error over all timestamps under pure differential privacy with privacy parameter one half. Every output prefix must depend only on the input prefix already observed, and privacy protects the whole transcript when one bit changes. The checked literature leaves a gap between logarithmic powers three halves and two, while newer matrix results concern different squared-error criteria. Matching bounds would quantify the unavoidable accuracy loss of this basic stream-release primitive.

title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
importance_reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete and widely used query family. It complements existing sample-complexity questions and has an explicit specialist open-problem formulation, while allowing non-synthetic outputs avoids a known source of misleading hardness claims.
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
question_excerpt: Is private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error possible in polynomial time from polynomially many Boolean records?
definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
context:
A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.
why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.
status_note: The source explicitly poses this all-marginal computational question in 2017. The retained synopsis/privacy conventions are the card’s previously documented editorial choices. Checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; the inspected recent factorization result is polynomial in explicit workload/output size and has a different optimality criterion. This bounded search does not establish current openness conclusively.
progress: 2013–2014: The checked 2013 manuscript, published at ITCS 2014, gives subexponential per-query private marginal answers for small databases at fixed absolute error. | 2017: Open Problem 7.8 in the March author manuscript explicitly asks for polynomial-time estimation of every higher-order marginal with vanishing error and polynomially many records. | 2025-12: Weighted Fourier factorizations give optimal Gaussian-factorization variance for arbitrary specified marginal workloads with runtime polynomial in explicit output size; this does not bound the time or synopsis size polynomially in dimension for all marginals. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the source’s exact open question, the older interactive theorem and the recent output-size-dependent algorithm. No matching polynomial all-marginal synopsis or unconditional impossibility was found in the bounded later-work search.
working_summary: A marginal query asks what fraction of database rows match a pattern on selected attributes. The card asks for one private synopsis that answers all exponentially many such queries with error tending to zero as the dimension grows. Both creating the synopsis and evaluating a short query must use polynomial time, with only polynomially many input rows. Known interactive, synthetic-data and Gaussian-factorization results impose different resource or output requirements and do not settle this target. A complete Lean answer must prove the specified uniform existence statement or rule out every mechanism and evaluator satisfying it.

title: Optimal regret for private stochastic online learning
importance_reason: Optimal private stochastic online-learning rates would identify the statistical price of privacy in a broad decision model.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal expected pseudo-regret \(R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\) for pure differentially private stochastic full-information online learning. The domain is integers \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), and real parameters \(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\Delta\le1\). For independent loss distributions \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) on \([0,1]\), let \(\mu_j=\mathbb E_{P_j}[L]\); require a unique minimizer \(j^{*}\) and \(\mu_j-\mu_{j^{*}}\ge\Delta\) for every \(j\ne j^{*}\). At round \(t\), select \(I_t\in[K]\) using only earlier observations and private randomness, incur loss \(L_{I_t,t}\), and then observe the entire vector \(L_t\), where all \(L_{j,t}\sim P_j\) are independent across actions and rounds. Put \[R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)=\inf_A\sup_{(P_1,\ldots,P_K)}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mu_{I_t}-\mu_{j^{*}})\right],\] where the supremum ranges over the promised product distributions and the infimum over the causal \(\varepsilon\)-private strategies defined below. The requested rate retains every dependence on \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\), including logarithmic factors and the small-horizon regime.
question_excerpt: Determine matching-order bounds for gap-dependent pseudo-regret under pure differential privacy in stochastic full-information decision-theoretic online learning.
definitions: \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\). The public parameters are \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\); the gap bound \(\Delta\) is a promise supplied to the strategy, while the distributions, their means, and the best-action index are unknown. This is the minimax interpretation of the source's gap-dependent optimal-rate question: the worst case is over all instances whose minimum gap is at least the supplied threshold, rather than one specified vector of means. A strategy is a family of Borel-measurable probability kernels for \(I_t\), given the public parameters, earlier actions, and earlier full loss vectors. It may retain arbitrary private state and use correlated internal randomness; equivalently use the conditional kernels of its observable history. No running-time, memory, or properness restriction is imposed. The output available to a privacy observer is the complete action sequence, not the privately observed losses. For every pair of deterministic sequences \(s,s'\in([0,1]^K)^T\) differing in at most one entire loss vector, and every event \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), require \[\Pr[A(s)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(s')\in E].\] This requirement applies to all loss sequences, including nonstochastic ones, and has no additive privacy slack. Its prefix versions follow by projection. The utility expectation includes both the stochastic losses and the strategy's independent initial randomness. Pseudo-regret compares against the smallest expected loss, not the smallest realized cumulative loss. The first action is selected before any losses are revealed. There is no adversarial dependence of later losses on released actions. Infima need not be attained; approaching strategies qualify.
answer_criterion: Supply a nonnegative rate function \(B(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\), an explicit family of admissible private strategies, and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), with a Lean-checked proof that \(cB\le R^{*}\le CB\) throughout the stated domain. The upper bound must hold for every promised product distribution; the lower bound must apply to every causal private strategy and allow a worst-case promised distribution. If an infimum is not attained, certify arbitrarily close upper bounds instead of requiring an optimal strategy. Constants cannot depend on any of the four parameters. A bound only for deterministic losses, bandit feedback, approximate privacy, or only one side of the rate does not meet this criterion. This is asymptotic precision in unnormalized cumulative pseudo-regret, not an additive \(1/100\) approximation.
context:
After each decision, the learner sees how every action performed. This makes the problem different from a bandit problem, where it sees only the chosen action. In a stationary environment, the mean-loss gaps measure how much evidence separates the best action from its competitors. The total error from exploring those competitors can remain bounded as the number of rounds grows.

Privacy treats one complete observed loss vector as one record and protects the joint distribution of all released actions. Protecting each action separately would not suffice: an observer can combine decisions across many rounds. Pure privacy also excludes a small additive exceptional-event term, which is explicitly outside the source question.

The 2024 paper compares an upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K\log T/\varepsilon)\) with a long-horizon lower scale \(\Omega(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K/\varepsilon)\). Its authors expressly do not conjecture that this lower scale is optimal. Those displayed rates describe the nontrivial parameter regime; a lower bound independent of \(T\) cannot hold for arbitrarily short horizons because regret is at most \(T\).

Wu and Wang prove the improved stochastic upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log^{2}K/\varepsilon)\). It removes dependence on \(T\) from the gap-dependent upper bound. A logarithmic factor in \(K\) remains between the stated upper and lower privacy terms. Their matching \(\Theta(\log K/\varepsilon)\) result applies to the separate model with deterministic loss vectors and does not settle the stochastic question.

The card makes the minimax quantifier convention explicit by supplying a lower gap promise \(\Delta\) and retaining finite \(T\). An upper bound using only the actual minimum gap also applies to this promise class. Sharp finite-horizon transitions and boundary gaps are part of the stated rate; the displayed long-horizon literature bounds are not claimed uniformly tight there.
why: This asks how protecting one round of observations changes the achievable accuracy of sequential decisions even when the environment is stationary and all actions are observed. A sharp rate would identify the statistical price of pure privacy and whether the remaining dependence on the number of actions is necessary.
status_note: The original question is open in Hu–Mehta 2024; the checked final ALT 2026 paper explicitly reports only a partial solution and retains a logarithmic stochastic gap. No matching complete rate was found in the bounded later-work search on 15 September 2026. This formulation is a stated minimax interpretation of the original gap-dependent question.
progress: 2024: Hu and Mehta pose the matching-order pure-privacy problem and explain why unequal suboptimality gaps leave uncertainty about the best privacy term. | 2026-02: Published ALT 2026 Theorem 3 gives a horizon-independent stochastic upper bound with privacy contribution \(\log^{2}K/\varepsilon\); §4 resolves its deterministic-loss comparison problem only. | 2026-09-15: Checked the 2024 definition and the final ALT 2026 paper, including its retained stochastic gap. A bounded search found no later theorem supplying the complete matching stochastic rate. This is a source-status check, not independent verification of the paper proofs.
working_summary: A learner repeatedly chooses an action and then observes the losses of every action. The losses are independent draws from fixed unknown distributions, and one action has strictly smallest mean loss. The card asks for matching-order expected pseudo-regret under pure privacy protecting one entire round of observations. A published 2026 upper bound removes the time-horizon factor but leaves a logarithmic gap in the number of actions. A solution must identify the rate throughout the stated parameter domain and certify both achievable guarantees and unavoidable loss in Lean.

title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
importance_reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.
focus_reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.
formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
context:
A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.
why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.
status_note: An open general classification question in the 2022 survey and the published July 2026 Krokhin–Vagnozzi article. The latter resolves a restricted three-element target family; the May 2026 Promise MMSNP preprint gives a logical correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full unconditional finite-pair dichotomy or counterexample. Individual theorem statements and scopes were checked, but their full proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2017: Bulatov proves the ordinary finite-template CSP dichotomy, covering the special case \(A=B\). | 2017: Zhuk independently proves the same ordinary CSP dichotomy; the final arXiv revision is dated 2 October 2020. | 2018: Brakensiek and Guruswami give a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations; the checked revised manuscript is dated 6 May 2021. | 2019: Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz classify all symmetric Boolean promise CSPs without requiring negations. | 2019: Barto establishes a tractable finite promise pair whose every finite intermediate exact CSP is NP-complete. | 2022-08-29: Krokhin and Opršal survey the open general classification and distinguish decision from search. | 2026-05-10: The Banakh–Barsukov–Nakajima preprint proves the Promise MMSNP correspondence and states a monochromatic-clique dichotomy with conditional hardness; it subsequently appears at LICS 2026. | 2026-07-01: The published Krokhin–Vagnozzi theorem proves NP-hardness for \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) and completes the three-element symmetric ternary target classification for approximations of exactly-one satisfaction.
working_summary: A finite promise CSP distinguishes inputs satisfying stronger local constraints from inputs failing even weaker constraints. The question asks whether every fixed finite template pair has a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm or is NP-hard under promise-preserving many-one reductions. The algorithm or reduction may depend on the pair, and no effective procedure for classifying input templates is required. The ordinary CSP dichotomy and several promise subclasses are known, but relaxing the constraints changes the classification problem substantially. The checked 2026 results concern restricted families and leave this full unconditional decision dichotomy open in the cited sources.

title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
importance_reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.
focus_reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.
formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm P\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
question_excerpt: Every finite-signature first-order reduct of a finitely bounded homogeneous structure has a CSP in P or an NP-complete CSP.
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.
context:
The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain. Homogeneity over a finite relational signature also gives quantifier elimination, so each fixed first-order reduct relation can be tested on that finite pattern by a fixed quantifier-free formula.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification. A model-complete core is a homomorphically equivalent template in which every endomorphism agrees, on each finite subset, with some automorphism; an endomorphism is a homomorphism from the template to itself.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open. Here first-order definability means that one fixed first-order sentence on finite inputs decides the CSP, and L denotes deterministic logarithmic work space.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card. The Ramsey condition says that for every pair of finite patterns P,Q and every finite number of colours, a larger finite pattern exists in which every colouring of embeddings of P has a copy of Q whose internal P-embeddings all receive one colour.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.
why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026 against the January 2026 book postprint and exact primary revisions: Three Fundamental Questions v4 (6 May), FO/L-hard v3 (14 July), and Decidability of Interpretability v2 (5 August). Their introductions explicitly retain the full dichotomy as open. The July theorem has an expansion hypothesis and a lower complexity boundary; the August theorem concerns effective comparison and cores under a homogeneous Ramsey hypothesis. This is a bounded source review, not independent verification of those preprint proofs or exhaustive certification of present openness.
progress: 2017: Bulatov and Zhuk independently prove the finite-domain CSP dichotomy; infinite domains require additional structural arguments. | 2020: Barto–Pinsker give a purely algebraic characterization of the relevant hardness obstruction for model-complete cores. The general tractability implication remains conjectural. | 2021–2026: Bodirsky’s monograph develops the framework; the checked author postprint is dated 31 January 2026. | 2026-05-06: The revised Three Fundamental Questions paper reduces the conjecture to templates without algebraicity and strengthens links with finite-domain promise CSPs. | 2026-07-14: Dorochko–Wrona’s v3 establishes an \(FO/\mathrm{L}\)-hard dichotomy for expansions of homogeneous model-complete cores, not the full \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy. | 2026-08-05: Feller–Pinsker’s v2 provides decidability and computable-core tools under additional structural hypotheses.
working_summary: The conjecture asks for a P-versus-NP-complete dichotomy for all finite-signature first-order reducts of countable finitely bounded homogeneous structures. Inputs are finite constraint systems, while their possible values lie in a fixed domain that may be infinite. Homogeneity provides symmetry, and finitely many forbidden induced patterns provide polynomial-size certificates despite the infinite domain. Recent results simplify the conjecture’s scope or classify lower complexity boundaries, while the full tractability implication remains open in the checked sources. A resolution would determine whether this broad structural framework rules out intermediate NP complexity.

title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
importance_reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.
formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
question_excerpt: Can three-colourable graphs be coloured in polynomial time with some constant number of colours?
definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.
context:
The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).
