The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.
why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.
status_note: The exact randomized constant-palette algorithm question remains source-open in this review. A new14September2026 preprint, Fei–Minzer–Wang ECCC TR26-179, claims in Corollary1.7 unconditional NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k decision gap. On16September2026 its introductory definitions, main theorem and exact corollary were checked; its95-page proof was not independently audited. Even if that claimed theorem is established, ruling out the randomized algorithms quantified here additionally requires NP different from RP. Thus it is important new claimed hardness evidence, not an unconditional resolution of this algorithm-existence target. Older references describing six-colour decision hardness as open are historical accounts superseded by this claim.

The question asks whether one fixed larger palette permits a randomized polynomial-time algorithm on every such graph. Successful outputs must colour every vertex properly, with probability at least two thirds for each input. A14September2026 preprint claims all-constant decision hardness, which would still require NP different from RP to exclude the randomized algorithms in this question. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish such an algorithm or exclude every constant palette in the full randomized model.

title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
importance_reason: A foundational search-versus-decision question spanning graph colouring, satisfiability and the algebraic classification of finite PCSPs.
formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
question_excerpt: For finite templates, does efficient solution of the decision promise always imply efficient construction of a weak solution on the original stronger promise?
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(L\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.
context:
The strong template A describes the constraints guaranteed to be simultaneously satisfiable; B describes the weaker constraints an answer must satisfy. The map from A to B proves that a weak answer exists whenever a strong one exists, but the input supplies only that existence promise. A decision algorithm recognizes the promised gap, whereas search must actually construct the weaker assignment.

For graph colouring, one may take A and B to be complete graphs on three and six vertices. Search then asks for a six-colouring of a graph promised to admit a three-colouring. Decision only separates three-colourable graphs from graphs admitting no six-colouring; it has no required behaviour on graphs with chromatic number four, five or six. This example illustrates the promise and does not assert tractability for that particular pair.

A polynomial-time search algorithm implies decision by returning a proposed weak assignment that can be checked. The reverse implication is known for ordinary fixed finite CSPs, where A=B. With two templates, fixing a variable to a weak-domain value can destroy the stronger promise, so ordinary decision self-reducibility does not automatically apply.

Known constructive cases include templates admitting a fixed finite intermediate structure C with A→C→B and tractable CSP(C). The survey also discusses tractable promise problems whose explanation requires more than such a finite intermediate problem, under the usual separation assumptions. Thus the ordinary CSP case does not supply the general statement.

Larrauri studies rounding for three standard decision relaxations: the basic linear program using consistent local distributions, an affine integer program, and their combination. Finding a weak assignment on every input accepted by one of these relaxations can encode arbitrary total NP search problems. A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.
why: Many applications need an assignment rather than recognition that an assignment must exist. A universal implication would connect tractability classifications of promise decision problems to actual construction across finite local constraint languages. A separation would identify a fixed finite promise problem whose decision gap is efficiently recognizable while its promised solutions resist every deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm.
status_note: The fixed-template question is explicitly open in §10 pp. 59–60 of Larrauri v4, 25 May 2026. Its relaxation-accepted rounding hardness and varying-template undecidability do not settle the promised search problem. A bounded primary-source search and revision check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability results apply under additional preservation hypotheses; cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2019–2022: The algebraic framework and survey distinguish finite-template decision from search and describe constructive special cases. | 2026-02-10: The robust-satisfiability paper establishes new constructive guarantees for Boolean majority-preserved templates and related larger-domain classes, under explicit structural hypotheses. | 2026-05-25: Larrauri’s v4 proves hardness for rounding relaxation-accepted inputs and undecidability of template meta-problems, but §10 explicitly retains the original per-template tractability implication.
working_summary: A finite promise CSP distinguishes strong constraints whose satisfiability is guaranteed from weaker constraints an output must satisfy. The decision problem separates strongly satisfiable inputs from those with no weak solution. The question asks whether every fixed template with a deterministic polynomial-time decider also permits deterministic polynomial-time construction on the original stronger promise. Hardness of rounding arbitrary relaxation-accepted inputs and undecidability of template recognition leave this implication unresolved. A resolution would clarify whether tractability of finite promise constraints always extends from recognizing feasibility to producing assignments.

title: Logarithmic-color approximation of 3-colorable graphs
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation challenge seeking a qualitative improvement from polynomially growing to logarithmic palettes under the simplest nontrivial colouring promise.
formal:
Is there a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every \(n\)-vertex graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, produces a proper colouring using \(O(\log n)\) colours in expectation? More precisely, do there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and an absolute integer \(K\geq1\) for which
\[
\mathbb E_{\rho}\big[\kappa(A(G;\rho))\big]\leq K\max\{1,\log_2 n\}
\]
for every nonempty \(3\)-colourable graph \(G\), where \(\kappa\) counts distinct colours used? Randomization and expected performance follow the source’s approximation-algorithm convention; deterministic algorithms are included. Properness is always required, and the time bound is worst case as specified below.
question_excerpt: Find a polynomial-time algorithm that uses only logarithmically many colours on every graph known to be three-colourable.
definitions:
The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An explicit unary size header is followed by its adjacency matrix, so the input length \(L\) includes isolated vertices and is of order \(n^2+1\). There are no loops or parallel edges and no restriction on degree, connectedness, density or induced subgraphs. The promise says only that some proper colouring with at most three colours exists. The colouring is not supplied, and the input need not be randomly generated.

A proper colouring is an explicit vector \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\) with \(c_i\in[n]\) and \(c_i\ne c_j\) whenever \(\{i,j\}\in E\). Its palette size is \(\kappa(c)=|\{c_i:i\in[n]\}|\). Colour names can be relabeled without changing \(\kappa\). Output the colour indices in vertex order in binary with delimiters. On the empty graph, the algorithm outputs the empty colouring with palette size zero. The logarithm in the bound has base two; changing its base only changes the absolute constant. Using \(\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\) fixes the cases \(n=1,2\) without imposing an asymptotic exception.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine. There are fixed integers \(C,d\geq1\) bounding the number of bit operations by \(C(L+1)^d\) on every graph and every random-bit sequence. Independent fair bits are the only random resource, so there are polynomially many random bits per run. There is no advice, oracle, exact-real arithmetic or free infinite-precision sampling. All numerical approximations, verification and output writing count toward time. The program, \(K,C,d\) are independent of \(n\) and \(G\).

The algorithm must output a proper colouring on every valid graph and every random-bit sequence; the palette-size guarantee applies only to the promised \(3\)-colourable graphs. Requiring universal properness introduces no new approximation obstruction: a candidate colouring can be checked in polynomial time, and any failure can be replaced by the trivial colouring assigning a different colour to each vertex. On malformed graph encodings the algorithm may reject in polynomial time. The expectation is over the internal random bits for each fixed promised graph, not over an input distribution.

The asymptotic existential target is equivalent to allowing a polynomial-time randomized algorithm to return a proper \(K'\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\)-colouring with probability at least \(2/3\) for every promised graph, for some absolute \(K'\). An expected bound implies this by Markov’s inequality after multiplying its constant by three. Conversely, a bounded-error algorithm can be run independently \(O(\log n)\) times, retaining a verified small colouring if one appears and otherwise using the \(n\)-colour fallback. Reducing failure probability to at most \(1/n\) makes the expected number of colours at most the successful palette bound plus one. The constant and running-time exponent remain fixed. This equivalence does not require derandomization and does not permit a small fraction of incorrectly coloured edges.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and absolute constants exist, or a proof in Lean that no algorithm in the stated class exists. A positive proof must cover every promised graph, always return a proper colouring, account for worst-case bit complexity and prove the expected logarithmic palette bound with one constant \(K\). The equivalent bounded-error formulation may be used if its conversion to the stated guarantee is proved.

A negative proof must rule out every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm and every absolute logarithmic-bound constant, rather than only a particular SDP relaxation, local procedure or deterministic subclass. Hardness conditional on an unproved assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. A bound \(O(n^\alpha)\) for fixed \(\alpha>0\), a bound \(O((\log n)^c)\) for \(c>1\), a colouring of only part of the vertices, or a guarantee for random or structurally restricted graphs does not meet the required logarithmic bound. This is an algorithm-existence question, so there is no replacement of the asymptotic palette guarantee by an additive numerical tolerance.
context:
The promise guarantees a partition into three independent sets but does not reveal any of them. Finding that exact partition is computationally hard. The question allows a growing palette, asking whether that relaxation is enough to reduce the output from a power of the graph size to a logarithm.

A standard way to build a colouring is to repeatedly remove a large independent set and assign it a fresh colour. Every induced subgraph of a three-colourable graph is still three-colourable. If one could efficiently find an independent set containing a fixed positive fraction of the remaining vertices at every stage, the number of stages would be logarithmic. This is a useful sufficient route, not an asserted equivalence between logarithmic colouring and a particular independent-set approximation.

The textbook develops Wigderson’s combinatorial ideas and semidefinite relaxations with randomized rounding. Its §13.2 analyses the expected size of independent sets produced by such rounding, and Problem 9 isolates the \(O(\log n)\) palette goal. Making randomization explicit preserves this surrounding algorithmic context; it does not demand that an eventual solution also be derandomized.

The February 2026 theorem of Bansal, Huang and Lee reports \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours, improving the previously stated growing-palette bounds. Its analysis combines combinatorial progress in dense graphs with semidefinite methods in sparse graphs and uses deeper neighborhoods in the rounding argument. For any fixed positive exponent, a power of \(n\) eventually exceeds every constant multiple of \(\log n\), so that improvement leaves the target’s asymptotic form unchanged.

The unconditional three-versus-five hardness theorem concerns a fixed output palette. A logarithmic palette eventually has more than five colours, so that theorem does not rule it out. Conversely, a logarithmic colouring algorithm would not give any fixed constant palette. The constant-colour and logarithmic-colour questions therefore remain distinct despite sharing the same input promise.

Properness is an exact combinatorial condition that can be checked directly. The uncertainty in the randomized formulation concerns the number of colours and is averaged over the algorithm’s coins for each input. A procedure that succeeds only on typical random graphs or leaves a few monochromatic edges would change the mathematical task.
why: Logarithmic colouring would be a major improvement for a canonical approximation problem whose positive guarantees still grow as powers of the input size. It would show that a hidden partition into three independent sets can be replaced efficiently by a very small exact partition without needing to recover the original three classes.
status_note: The textbook explicitly poses the logarithmic-colour target as Problem 9. Its randomized approximation convention and colouring chapter support the expected-performance model fixed here. The February 2026 primary paper still gives a power-of-n palette guarantee and records the constant-palette hardness frontier. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the logarithmic target; this source-open assessment is dated evidence rather than an exhaustive proof of present openness.

title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
importance_reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R\) from Boolean \(3\)-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every \(3\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
F\text{ is satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))\leq3,
\qquad
F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))>6?
\]
Equivalently, is the promise decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? This is the previously approved gap-decision formulation of the six-colouring hardness question.
question_excerpt: How hard is it to find a six-colouring when the input graph is promised to be three-colourable?
definitions:
A Boolean \(3\)-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables and clause lists are explicitly encoded with binary indices and fixed delimiters; repeated literals and clauses are allowed. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length.

The reduction is one deterministic multitape Turing machine. On every valid formula it outputs one graph \(G=R(F)\) on a labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), allowing \(n=0\). Encode \(n\) by an explicit unary size header and then list unordered pairs of distinct binary vertex indices as edges, without repeated edges. Thus isolated vertices are included explicitly in the input size and the graph is not a succinct exponentially large object. There are fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the entire computation, including writing the graph, takes at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations. There are no random bits, advice or oracle calls. Malformed formulas may be rejected. The graph need not come with any colouring, satisfying assignment or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring of a graph is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), with \(\chi\) of the empty graph defined as zero. For \(k\geq1\), \(K_k\) is the loopless complete graph on \([k]\). A graph homomorphism maps vertices to vertices and sends each edge to an edge, so a proper \(k\)-colouring is exactly a homomorphism to \(K_k\).

The promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) requires YES on graphs with \(\chi(G)\leq3\) and NO on graphs with \(\chi(G)>6\). Graphs of chromatic number four, five or six lie outside the promise; a decision algorithm may answer either way on them. The reduction itself must send every satisfiable formula to the YES region and every unsatisfiable formula to the NO region, so its valid outputs never lie in this middle region. It is a many-one reduction: it produces a single instance and does not query a colouring oracle.

The two reduction implications must hold without a Unique Games, Label Cover, or other unproved hypothesis. NP-hardness here denotes the existence of this unconditional reduction; it is not itself the assertion that the problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. Since Boolean \(3\)-SAT is NP-complete, the displayed reduction is equivalent to the standard deterministic many-one NP-hardness requirement for all NP languages.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction exists, or a proof in Lean that no such reduction exists. A positive answer must specify the construction, prove its uniform polynomial bit complexity and verify both chromatic-number implications for every input formula. Hardness only under an unproved conjecture, a reduction with weaker completeness or soundness, or hardness for a different pair of palettes does not settle this target.

A negative answer must rule out all deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions satisfying the two implications. In particular, a polynomial-time algorithm for the promise problem alone does not unconditionally prove nonexistence of the reduction: combining both would imply \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\). If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a SAT decider could itself construct such a reduction by returning \(K_3\) or \(K_7\) according to satisfiability. Failure of one algebraic gadget construction, inability to find a particular polymorphism, or a finite list of unsuccessful reductions is insufficient for the negative answer.
context:
A promise of three-colourability guarantees that a small partition into independent sets exists but does not reveal it. Allowing six colours relaxes the requested output. The associated decision gap separates graphs admitting three colours from graphs that do not admit even six. This is a small fixed-template promise CSP with no growing palette parameter.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove hardness for distinguishing \(k\)-colourable graphs from graphs not colourable with \(2k-1\) colours, for every \(k\geq3\). At \(k=3\), the result gives a gap from three to five colours. Its NO-instances may still be six-colourable, so the theorem does not imply the three-versus-six gap.

The algebraic PCSP framework relates the available reductions to operations that preserve the promised constraint relations, called polymorphisms. The source demonstrates the strength of this approach with the five-colour theorem and explains that moving to larger palettes requires additional analysis. A limitation of one reduction family does not by itself show that the requested polynomial-time reduction cannot exist.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 theorem reports a polynomial-time algorithm using \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours on an \(n\)-vertex three-colourable graph. Their introduction still identifies five colours as the unconditional hardness frontier in its account. A growing-palette algorithm supplies neither a six-colouring algorithm nor a reduction proving hardness at six colours.

A deterministic polynomial-time six-colouring search algorithm on three-colourable inputs would yield a decision algorithm for this gap: run it with a polynomial time cutoff and check whether its output is a proper six-colouring. Every YES-instance would be accepted, while no NO-instance could pass the check. This one-way implication explains the relevance to search without identifying all possible notions of search hardness with the chosen decision reduction.

The separate question of whether some fixed constant palette allows polynomial-time colouring has a different quantifier. Hardness at six colours would not exclude an algorithm using seven, one hundred or another fixed number. Likewise, logarithmically many colours eventually exceed every fixed palette, so that algorithmic target is distinct from this hardness threshold.

The14September2026 preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game hardness theorem. Its Corollary1.7 explicitly gives the three-versus-k decision gap for every fixed k; taking k=6 would answer the present question affirmatively. This is an exact target match, not merely search hardness or an almost-satisfiable completeness statement. The full proof has not been independently verified in this review, so the result is recorded as a claimed resolution.
why: The three-versus-six gap is a concrete fixed-template question in approximate colouring and promise constraint satisfaction. An established reduction would supply a fundamental obstruction to algorithms producing six-colour solutions on promised three-colourable inputs; the newly claimed all-constant result directly addresses this target.

title: NP-intermediate \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
importance_reason: Determines whether omega-categoricity alone permits intermediate NP complexity, testing the reach of the main algebraic framework beyond currently conjectured infinite-template dichotomy classes.
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that its fixed-template constraint satisfaction problem is NP-intermediate? Explicitly, the required three conditions are
\[\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP},\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\notin\mathrm P,\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\text{ is not NP-complete}.\]
Completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, as in the source’s hardness constructions. No effective presentation or uniform construction of the infinite template is required.
question_excerpt: Assuming P differs from NP, is there an NP-intermediate CSP with an omega-categorical template?
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A template \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and a relation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for every \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) preserves all positive relation tuples: if \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\), then \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^\Gamma\). It need not be injective or preserve missing tuples.

An automorphism is a domain bijection preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on ordered \(k\)-tuples coordinate by coordinate. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical when, for each fixed positive integer \(k\), this action has finitely many orbits on \(\Gamma^k\). For a countably infinite finite-signature structure, this is equivalent to its complete first-order theory having exactly one countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite templates satisfy the orbit convention too. The number of orbits may depend on \(k\), and no procedure computing them is assumed.

The language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) accepts encodings of finite \(\tau\)-structures \(I\) exactly when there is a homomorphism \(I\to\Gamma\). Encode the instance domain \([n]\) by unary \(n\), then in signature order the explicitly listed relation tuples, each list preceded by a unary length and with binary indices separated by delimiters. This polynomial encoding counts isolated elements; repeated coordinates and duplicate tuples are allowed. The empty domain maps by the empty function. Malformed inputs are rejected. Let \(L\) be the full bit length. The signature and template are fixed before instances arrive and are not supplied as an infinite table or an oracle.

A language is in \(\mathrm P\) when some deterministic multitape Turing machine decides it on every bit string in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) when membership has a certificate of polynomially bounded length checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. No randomness or advice is used. Importantly, a certificate for this infinite-template CSP need not list actual domain elements of \(\Gamma\); it can use any finite encoding and verifier proving the same language is in NP. Omega-categoricity alone does not guarantee NP membership.

A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(K\) to a language \(Q\) is a total polynomial-time computable function \(r\) on binary strings such that \(x\in K\) if and only if \(r(x)\in Q\). A language \(Q\) is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP language reduces to it in this sense. These reductions make one target instance and do not make adaptive oracle queries. A language is NP-intermediate if it lies in NP but satisfies neither tractability nor completeness. The constants and programs in these class definitions can depend on the fixed language or reduction; no common exponent for all templates is intended.

The question is existence of a mathematical template with all the stated properties, not a metaproblem receiving descriptions of arbitrary infinite structures. No finite list of forbidden patterns, homogeneous expansion, finite domain or algorithm deciding the relations of \(\Gamma\) is imposed. For context, coNP is the class of complements of NP languages; coNP-intermediate means in coNP but neither in P nor coNP-complete under the same reduction convention.
answer_criterion: Under the hypothesis \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either that such a template exists or that none exists. A positive proof must establish omega-categoricity, a finite relational signature, NP membership, absence of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, and absence of polynomial-time many-one NP completeness. An abstract NP-intermediate language or an unrestricted infinite template without omega-categoricity is insufficient. A negative proof must show, under the hypothesis, that every permitted template whose CSP lies in NP has a CSP in P or is NP-complete. CoNP intermediacy, completeness at a higher complexity level, or a dichotomy only for a narrower subclass does not settle this question.
context:
Ladner’s theorem gives NP-intermediate languages if P differs from NP, but it does not automatically place them inside every structured family of computational problems. The issue here is whether an intermediate NP language can be realized as a fixed CSP while retaining finitely many symmetry types at every tuple length.

Finite-template CSPs satisfy the P versus NP-complete dichotomy, so a finite template cannot witness the desired intermediate behavior under the hypothesis. Allowing an infinite domain admits new CSP languages, while omega-categoricity retains the symmetry property supporting many algebraic methods.

Bodirsky and Grohe already construct omega-categorical CSPs in coNP that are neither tractable nor coNP-complete, assuming P differs from coNP. Their construction adapts Ladner’s diagonalization by choosing a suitable infinite family of forbidden tournaments. This demonstrates intermediate complexity on the complementary side, but does not provide NP membership for the required example.

Taking the complement of a coNP-intermediate language produces an NP-intermediate language, but complementing a CSP language need not produce another CSP language. Every CSP is closed under inverse homomorphisms and disjoint unions of finite instances. Such closure properties constrain representation and do not automatically survive complementation.

The 2026 paper constructs omega-categorical CSPs complete for every level of the polynomial hierarchy, the decision classes described by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal blocks of polynomial-length certificates. Its constructions extend the known complementary-side examples, yet Question 3 explicitly retains NP intermediacy as a separate problem.

The Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concerns the narrower class of first-order reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. In that setting a homogeneous structure has all finite induced partial isomorphisms extend to automorphisms, finite boundedness specifies its finite induced substructures by finitely many forbidden patterns, and a first-order reduct retains finitely many parameter-free definable relations. None of these restrictions is imposed here; a dichotomy for that subclass would not rule out an intermediate template elsewhere.
why: This asks whether the principal symmetry condition for infinite-domain CSP algebra allows intermediate NP complexity at all. An example would locate a precise limit of tractability-versus-completeness classifications; a negative answer would establish a much broader NP dichotomy than the currently conjectured finitely bounded homogeneous framework.
status_note: Question 3 of the checked MFCS 2026 publication explicitly restates the conditional NP-intermediate existence question. The April 2026 preprint version history and bounded later primary-source searches were checked on 16 September 2026; no matching solution was found. The new polynomial-hierarchy completeness results and the older coNP-intermediate construction do not resolve it. This is a dated, bounded status review, not exhaustive certification of present openness.
progress: 2008: Bodirsky and Grohe prove conditional coNP-intermediate examples and explicitly distinguish the still unresolved NP-intermediate question. | 2021/2026: Bodirsky’s monograph poses Question 49; its January 2026 postprint retains the distinction between complementary-side constructions and NP intermediacy. | 2026: Guzmán-Pro and Rydval obtain omega-categorical CSPs complete for all polynomial-hierarchy levels and restate this exact question as Question 3 in the MFCS publication.
working_summary: Assuming P differs from NP, the question asks whether an omega-categorical fixed-template CSP can have intermediate NP complexity. Omega-categoricity means finitely many symmetry orbits at each fixed tuple length, and the template has a finite relational signature. The CSP must lie in NP while being neither polynomial-time decidable nor NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. CoNP-intermediate examples and completeness at every polynomial-hierarchy level are known, but they do not supply the required NP-intermediate example. A resolution would determine whether this broad symmetry condition alone rules out intermediate complexity inside NP.

title: VCSP tractability over the countable random graph
importance_reason: A concrete next test of a general algebraic classification program for infinite-domain optimization, asking whether the known hardness obstruction is also a complete tractability criterion.
formal:
Let \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\) be the countable random graph. Is it true that for every valued structure \(\mathcal A=(D;f_1,\ldots,f_s)\) with a finite signature and \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb R)\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal A)\),
\[
\mathcal A\text{ does not pp-construct }K_3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\in\mathsf P?
\]
All cost functions take values in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The valued decision problem and the precise pp-construction condition are defined below. The template \(\mathcal A\) is fixed for each decision problem; the claim is not a uniform algorithm taking arbitrary templates as part of its input.
question_excerpt: For every finite-signature valued structure preserved by all automorphisms of the countable random graph, does the absence of a pp-construction of K3 imply polynomial-time solvability of its VCSP?
definitions:
The countable random graph \(\mathbb R=(D;E)\), also called the Rado graph, is the countably infinite simple undirected graph with the extension property: for any disjoint finite sets \(U,V\subseteq D\), there is a vertex outside \(U\cup V\) adjacent to every vertex in \(U\) and to no vertex in \(V\). This property determines the graph up to isomorphism. The symbol \(\mathbb R\) denotes this graph here, not the real-number field. Its automorphisms are bijections \(\alpha:D\to D\) preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. No random graph is sampled in the algorithmic input.

A valued template consists of finitely many symbols \(f_i\), each with a fixed nonnegative finite arity \(k_i\), interpreted as \(f_i:D^{k_i}\to\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\). The automorphism requirement says that \(f_i(\alpha(a_1),\ldots,\alpha(a_{k_i}))=f_i(a_1,\ldots,a_{k_i})\) for every automorphism \(\alpha\) of the graph and every tuple. Equivalently, a cost depends only on the equality pattern of its arguments and the adjacency pattern between their distinct entries. There are finitely many such patterns at each fixed arity, so each cost has a finite table of rational values and possible infinities. Negative rational costs are permitted. There are no distinguished domain constants or input vertex names.

For fixed \(\mathcal A\), an instance of \(\operatorname{VCSP}(\mathcal A)\) is an explicit finite set of variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), a sum \(\Phi\) of atomic costs applied to these variables, and a rational threshold \(u\). An atomic cost is \(f_i(x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_{k_i}})\), the equality cost \(\operatorname{eq}(x,y)\) which is zero for equal arguments and infinity otherwise, or the always-infinite unary cost \(\bot(x)\). Variables may repeat within an atom, and atoms may repeat in the sum. The empty sum has value zero. Summands are explicitly listed with unit multiplicity; there are no binary-encoded external weights multiplying atoms. The question is whether there exists an assignment \(h:\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\to D\) with \(\Phi(h)\leq u\). Any infinite summand makes the sum infinite.

Encode the variable list explicitly, the sum as symbols with binary variable indices, and \(u\) by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L\) be the total length. The template’s finite tables are fixed and may be built into a machine. Membership in \(\mathsf P\) means that some uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine decides this threshold language correctly on every valid input in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Malformed encodings are rejected. There is no randomness, numerical error, advice or oracle access to the infinite graph. The machine and its constants may depend on \(\mathcal A\); a common exponent, a template-classification algorithm and an assignment-output algorithm are not additionally required.

Here is an explicit equivalent form of the source’s valued pp-construction criterion. First define the valued relational clone \(\langle\mathcal A\rangle\): the smallest collection of finite-arity functions on \(D\) containing the template costs, equality and the always-infinite unary cost, and closed under the following operations. One may form finite sums of functions applied to variables with any repetitions, identifications or permutations, including the zero empty sum; add a rational constant; multiply by a nonnegative rational; or project by
\[
g(\mathbf a)=\inf_{\mathbf b\in D^r} f(\mathbf a,\mathbf b).
\]
Use \(0\cdot\infty=0\), \(c\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(c>0\), and \(c+\infty=\infty\). Only functions valued in \(\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}\) are allowed. In this invariant setting every function produced has finitely many orbit values, so these projection infima are attained and remain rational or infinite.

Two further closure operations turn a function \(f\) into a crisp cost, meaning a function taking only zero and infinity. The feasibility cost is zero on \(\operatorname{Feas}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\}\) and infinity outside it. The optimality cost is zero on
\[
\operatorname{Opt}(f)=\{\mathbf a:f(\mathbf a)<\infty\text{ and } f(\mathbf a)\leq f(\mathbf b)\text{ for every }\mathbf b\},
\]
and infinity outside it. If no tuple has finite cost, both sets are empty. The feasibility and optimality operations are part of the definition; using only sums and projection would give a different expressive closure. Membership in the clone requires a finite expression using these operations; arbitrary limits are not added.

Let \(K_3\) have vertices \(\{1,2,3\}\) and the binary adjacency relation consisting of all ordered pairs of distinct vertices. The template pp-constructs \(K_3\) precisely when there exist a positive integer \(d\), a crisp cost \(r\in\langle\mathcal A\rangle\) of arity \(2d\), and functions
\[
h:D^d\to\{1,2,3\},\qquad g:\{1,2,3\}\to D^d
\]
with the following properties. Define the binary relation \(H\) on \(D^d\) by \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\) if and only if \(r(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=0\). Whenever \(H(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\), require \(h(\mathbf a)\ne h(\mathbf b)\); and whenever \(i\ne j\), require \(H(g(i),g(j))\). These are homomorphisms in both directions between \((D^d;H)\) and \(K_3\). The functions need not be computable or definable, and \(H\) need not be assumed symmetric in advance. This criterion includes arbitrary finite dimension and arbitrary expressible crisp costs, not only one graph relation from the original signature. Its equivalence with the source’s definition using valued pp-powers and fractional homomorphisms follows from Proposition 25 and the crisp homomorphism lemma in the full version.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must prove polynomial-time decidability for every invariant finite-signature template that has no pp-construction of \(K_3\), under the full cost and input model above. The algorithm may depend on the fixed template, as membership of its language in \(\mathsf P\) permits.

A negative answer must establish a qualifying fixed template with no such pp-construction and prove that its threshold language is not in \(\mathsf P\). Merely proving NP-hardness gives a conditional counterexample under \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\), not an unconditional refutation of the implication. A dichotomy without the specified pp-construction condition, a result only for temporal templates, or a result only for crisp or nonnegative finite-valued costs does not by itself settle this target. No decision procedure for recognizing the tractable templates is required beyond the source’s per-template assertion.
context:
The short imported question omitted the ambient class stated immediately before it. The countable random graph supplies that class: all costs are invariant under its automorphisms. Restoring this condition recovers the source’s exact scope. Arbitrary infinite-domain valued problems need not share the same tractability behavior.

Despite the infinite domain, every instance has a finite witness format for NP membership. Guess which variables are equal and the adjacency relation among their distinct assigned values. Every resulting finite simple graph embeds into the Rado graph by the extension property. The fixed pattern table evaluates every atomic cost, and exact rational arithmetic checks the threshold. This places each template’s language in NP without treating infinite-domain assignments as input strings or oracle answers.

The source’s pp-construction notion identifies a general reduction mechanism. Expressible costs can be implemented without changing polynomial-time solvability, finite powers encode tuples of domain elements, and homomorphisms transfer feasibility. Constructing the triangle in this way gives NP-hardness of the valued problem. The question asks whether absence of that obstruction always supplies tractability in this particular invariant class.

Feasibility alone discards relative preferences between assignments, while optimality singles out the tuples of minimum finite cost. Their separate presence in the expressive closure matters for the valued hardness criterion. The equivalent crisp construction above uses all crisp relations obtainable from the costs, not merely the feasibility relations of the originally supplied functions.

The temporal theorem concerns cost functions on the rationals invariant under every order-preserving bijection. It proves the corresponding polynomial-time versus NP-complete classification for that class, including the pp-construction criterion. The group of automorphisms of the countable random graph describes a different class, so the temporal theorem motivates the question but does not answer it.

The original Question 44 asks first for a complexity dichotomy and then for this sharper tractability implication. The imported card selects the second question. Combining its positive answer with the known hardness direction and the finite-pattern NP witness would give the broader dichotomy, while merely establishing a dichotomy would not identify its tractable side by this exact criterion.

In the general framework, the authors formulate a related conjecture for valued templates associated with reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. The random graph is a concrete highly symmetric test case. The January 2026 full version still explicitly poses this case after proving the temporal classification.
why: This asks whether the known expressibility obstruction completely determines tractability for a major new class of infinite-domain optimization problems. A positive answer would extend the algebraic classification of valued CSPs beyond ordered domains to graph-invariant costs; a counterexample would expose a failure of the proposed general obstruction.
status_note: Question 44 of the complete MFCS 2025 paper, repeated as Question 59 in arXiv:2409.07285v2 dated 20 January 2026, explicitly poses this random-graph tractability implication. Checked the full versions and foundational definitions on 16 September 2026; a targeted later-work search did not identify a resolution. This supports the dated source-open label without asserting an exhaustive proof of current openness or independent verification of all cited theorems.
progress: 2023–2025: The resilience framework develops valued pp-expressibility, fractional homomorphisms, hardness reductions and a general classification conjecture. | 2025: The MFCS paper proves the temporal valued-CSP dichotomy and poses the countable-random-graph extension as Question 44. | 2026-01-20: The full version retains the random-graph question as Question 59 and proves the equivalence used here to express the triangle obstruction through crisp relations.
working_summary: The question concerns valued constraint problems whose costs depend only on equality and adjacency patterns in the countable random graph. It asks whether every fixed finite-signature template is polynomial-time solvable whenever it cannot pp-construct a triangle. The expressive closure includes sums, projection, scaling, feasibility and optimality, and the construction can use arbitrary finite powers. The temporal classification proves an analogous result for ordered rationals but the January 2026 source still poses the random-graph case. An accepted answer proves the full implication or an unconditional counterexample with its complexity lower bound in Lean.

title: Super-log-logarithmic colouring hardness for two-colourable triple systems
importance_reason: A precise longstanding frontier in promise colouring and hardness of approximation: improve a growing palette gap while retaining exact two-colourable completeness and three-vertex constraints.
formal:
Is there an integer-valued function \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge2}\) with
\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{f(N)}{\log_2\log_2(N+4)}=+\infty\]
and a deterministic quasipolynomial-time many-one reduction from Boolean 3-SAT to the following promise problem on explicitly represented \(N\)-vertex three-uniform hypergraphs \(H\):
\[\text{YES: }\chi(H)\le2;\qquad \text{NO: }\chi(H)>f(N)?\]
This accepts either hardness level offered in the source: a polynomial-time reduction is a stronger special case of the permitted quasipolynomial-time reduction. No particular growth function \(f\) is prescribed in advance.
question_excerpt: The source asks whether colouring a two-colourable three-uniform hypergraph with \(\omega(\log\log n)\) colours can be shown NP-hard, or even quasi-NP-hard.
definitions:
A finite three-uniform hypergraph is \(H=(V,E)\), where \(V=[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), \(N\ge1\), and \(E\) is a set of three-element subsets of \(V\). Each edge has three distinct vertices. There are no repeated edges or singleton edges. A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V\to[k]\) such that no edge is monochromatic: for every \(\{u,v,w\}\in E\), the three values \(c(u),c(v),c(w)\) are not all equal. They need not all be different. Colours may be unused. The chromatic number \(\chi(H)\) is the least positive \(k\) allowing such a map. Thus two-colourability means that every triple meets both parts of some bipartition, not that a graph formed from its pairs is bipartite. The input contains no such bipartition.

Represent \(H\) explicitly by its list of all \(N\) vertex names and a list of its triples, with vertex names as binary integers. Isolated vertices count towards \(N\) and are explicitly listed. Output length is therefore at least \(N\); succinctly describing an enormous vertex set is not allowed. The parameter inside \(f\) is this output vertex count, not the length of the Boolean formula or the number of edges.

A 3-SAT input is a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form, each clause having at most three literals. A literal is a variable or its negation; satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values makes every clause true. Use an explicit finite binary encoding of the clause list and variable indices, and let \(L\) be its bit length. One deterministic Turing program \(R\) must, on every such formula \(\varphi\), output a hypergraph \(H_\varphi\) in at most
\[2^{C(\log_2(L+2))^c}\]
bit steps for fixed constants \(C,c\ge1\). Both constants and the program are independent of the input. Satisfiable formulas must produce a hypergraph with \(\chi(H_\varphi)\le2\); unsatisfiable formulas must produce one with \(\chi(H_\varphi)>f(|V(H_\varphi)|)\). Both promises are disjoint because \(f(N)\ge2\). The reduction must satisfy these implications on every input, with no randomness or error. A solver for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on hypergraphs satisfying neither promise.

The displayed limit means that for every real \(M>0\) there is an integer \(N_0\) such that \(f(N)>M\log_2\log_2(N+4)\) for every \(N\ge N_0\). The shift by four only makes the denominator well-defined for small sizes and does not change the source's \(\omega(\log\log N)\) requirement. A witness must specify one function \(f\) and prove this property. No fixed formula family, monotonicity condition or runtime for evaluating \(f\) is separately imposed; \(f\) states the soundness gap, and the reduction itself must have the stated uniform runtime.

Here quasi-NP-hardness means the existence of exactly the reduction above from the standard NP-complete satisfiability problem. It is a statement about reductions and does not take \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), or the stronger assertion that NP has no deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithms, as an extra premise. Such complexity separations would be needed to turn the reduction into an unconditional exclusion of fast colouring algorithms. A polynomial reduction is the special case with a polynomial runtime bound in \(L\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existential proposition. A positive answer must specify \(f\), one reduction program and fixed quasipolynomial runtime constants, prove the super-log-logarithmic limit, and prove both completeness and soundness for every Boolean formula. A negative answer must rule out every such function and reduction, including polynomial-time reductions. Hardness for each fixed palette with no quantitative control as the palette grows, hardness with four-element edges, or a completeness promise of three colours does not by itself establish this target. An algorithmic result refutes the reduction statement only if the needed complexity separation is also justified. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance; the numerical approximation tolerance does not weaken the growth or hardness requirements.
context:
With ordinary graph edges, a promised two-colouring can be found by exploring connected components. Triple constraints permit two equal colours within an edge and only forbid all three being equal. That small change produces a very different approximation problem: the task permits many more colours than the hidden solution uses.

The source’s two main results concern four-uniform hypergraphs: one gives polylogarithmic palette hardness under polynomial reductions, and another reaches a ratio of logarithms under a slightly larger reduction budget. Its first concluding question explicitly asks for three-uniform hypergraphs and permits quasipolynomial reductions. These distinctions are retained.

The historical table records a cube-root-of-log-log palette gap for two-colourable three-uniform hypergraphs. The question seeks a gap growing faster than log log N itself. Merely increasing the constant in an existing bound does not satisfy that asymptotic request.

Stronger-looking bounds can have different completeness promises. Guruswami, Håstad, Harsha, Srinivasan and Varma obtain an almost-polylogarithmic palette bound for three-uniform hypergraphs promised three-colourable, alongside stronger results at larger edge sizes. Their stated three-uniform theorem does not retain the hidden two-colouring required here.

A 14 September 2026 preprint claims hardness of finding an independent set of any fixed positive density even in two-colourable three-uniform hypergraphs. Since a colour class is independent, this implies fixed-palette colouring consequences. Obtaining the growing function required here additionally needs uniform quantitative control of the reduction as that density shrinks with input size. The fixed-parameter corollary alone supplies no such bound; its proof has not been independently audited here.

A hardness reduction certifies a gap between fully satisfiable instances and instances requiring many colours. Its output size matters twice: writing the instance consumes time, and that same size determines the allowed palette. The specified quasipolynomial budget makes this tradeoff part of the question rather than leaving the word hardness ambiguous.
why: This asks for a quantitative hardness barrier at the smallest hyperedge size where even a hidden bipartition can be difficult to find. It separates the three-vertex constraint frontier from much stronger results for larger edges and tests how far approximation hardness can grow with input size.
status_note: Source-open. The full ICALP 2018 source question and main statements were read, together with the primary low-degree-code abstract and the September 2026 perfect-completeness preprint’s definitions, theorem and relevant corollaries. Bounded searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching super-log-logarithmic palette reduction for the exact two-colourable three-uniform promise. The new fixed-density theorem is reported as a preprint claim, not a verified growing-parameter result. No full external proof was independently audited or formalized in Lean.
progress: 2013–2017: Low-degree-code results give stronger palette gaps with larger edge sizes or a three-colourable completeness promise in the three-uniform case. | 2018: The source proves its four-uniform results and explicitly leaves the super-log-logarithmic three-uniform gap as an open question. | 2026-09-14: A new preprint claims fixed-density independent-set hardness for exactly two-colourable three-uniform hypergraphs. The checked statement does not give the required input-size-dependent palette bound.
working_summary: The question concerns colouring hypergraphs whose edges contain exactly three vertices and whose vertices admit a hidden two-colouring. It asks for a hardness reduction ruling out a palette that grows faster than log log of the output vertex count. A deterministic quasipolynomial reduction from Boolean satisfiability suffices, and a polynomial reduction is a stronger permitted answer. Known larger palette gaps often change the edge size or allow three colours in the completeness promise. The latest fixed-density independent-set hardness claim does not by itself give the required quantitative growing-palette gap.

title: Boolean decision-Holant dichotomy
importance_reason: This is the full tractability classification for Boolean edge constraints, with matching and general delta-matroid structure forming a major unresolved algorithmic boundary beyond ordinary Boolean CSP.
formal:
Classify the polynomial-time solvable Boolean decision-Holant problems for all fixed finite families of Boolean relations. More precisely, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), determine the entire characteristic function
\[\chi_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal F)=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\in\mathrm P,\\0,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\notin\mathrm P,\end{cases}\]
with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite family \(\mathcal F\). The answer must give a substantive structural criterion on the allowed relations, with algorithms and complementary lower bounds, rather than merely restating the definition of polynomial-time solvability. The model is the source’s Boolean edge-CSP interpretation of decision Holant, specified below.
question_excerpt: Classify Boolean decision-Holant problems; the remaining general obstacle is the complexity of delta-matroid relations.
definitions:
A Boolean relation of arity \(r\geq1\) is a subset \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), equivalently its zero-one indicator function \(f_R\). A signature family \(\mathcal F\) is a finite ordered list of such relations given by their full finite truth tables; empty relations and the empty family are allowed. For each decision problem the family and all arities are fixed before inputs are supplied. Arbitrarily large fixed arities are covered across the classification.

A signature grid is a finite undirected loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), together with a label \(R_v\in\mathcal F\) at each vertex and an ordering \((e_{v,1},\ldots,e_{v,r_v})\) of its incident edges, where \(r_v\) equals the arity of \(R_v\). Parallel edges are permitted and are separate variables. The graph need not be planar or bipartite. Each edge has two distinct endpoints and appears exactly once at each endpoint. The incidence order is part of the input, since relations need not be symmetric. This is the explicit convention of Definitions 1–3 in the cited edge-CSP paper: a variable is in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without a repeated coordinate within one scope.

A Boolean assignment is a map \(\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}\). It is satisfying when \((\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v}))\in R_v\) for every vertex. Define
\[H_{\mathcal F}(G)=\sum_{\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{v\in V} f_{R_v}(\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v})).\]
The task \(\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\) accepts exactly the grids with \(H_{\mathcal F}(G)>0\). It asks for one yes/no answer, not the number or a list of satisfying assignments. The empty graph has value one, by the empty-product convention. A grid containing an empty relation is unsatisfiable. Nullary indicators, if included, can be processed separately: zero rejects the instance and one is deleted, so restricting the signature tables to positive arities loses no tractability class.

Encode the numbers of vertices and edges in unary; list binary endpoint indices for each numbered edge, the fixed-family index at each vertex, and its ordered list of edge indices. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Validity of the encoding is checked in polynomial time; malformed strings are rejected. A polynomial-time algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with the correct answer on every input in at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps, for positive constants \(C,k\) depending on \(\mathcal F\). There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Programs may depend on the fixed family, and no common running-time exponent across all families is requested.

No unary relation, pinning constant, equality relation, edge weight or graph restriction is freely added to \(\mathcal F\). The at-most-two-occurrences decision model used in the survey has the same complexity under this scope convention: remove unused variables, take two copies of the instance, and identify corresponding variables that occurred only once. This gives exactly two occurrences and preserves satisfiability without new relations. The target does not impose a uniform input-template algorithm or require a polynomial-time procedure for recognizing the tractable families from their truth tables.

Here \(\mathrm P\) is deterministic polynomial time and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages whose membership has polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. Every fixed-family problem above is in NP, with the edge assignment as certificate. NP-hardness, when used in the classification, means deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions from every language in NP; NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP. This is an explicit reduction convention. The separation assumption makes a tractability classification nontrivial; if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the function is identically one. A rational answer within \(1/100\) of a zero-one value determines that value, but the requested result is the structural description of the whole function, not numerical experiments on selected families.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of an exhaustive structural characterization of \(\chi_{\mathrm H}\) with the stated absolute \(1/100\) accuracy, under the explicit \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis. Prove correct polynomial-time decision algorithms for every family assigned one and a matching exclusion of polynomial time for every family assigned zero; NP-hardness under the stated reductions is a sufficient exclusion. The result must cover all finite Boolean signature families, including arbitrary delta-matroid relations, with the graph and occurrence conventions above. A characterization cannot simply rename the existence of a polynomial-time machine. Classifying only symmetric signatures, only even delta-matroids, planar inputs, weighted counting, or a language enlarged by freely available unary signatures does not answer the full question. If additional complexity cases arise instead of the expected polynomial-time/NP-complete dichotomy, identify and justify them rather than asserting that every nontractable case is NP-complete without proof.
context:
In ordinary CSP a variable may constrain many locations. In a Holant grid each variable is an edge linking two local constraints. This restriction creates new algorithms: an ExactOne relation accepts precisely tuples with one coordinate equal to one, and using it at every vertex asks for a perfect matching. Thus tractability is not exhausted by the familiar Boolean CSP cases.

For a nonempty relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), the delta-matroid exchange property says: if \(x,y\in R\) differ at coordinate \(i\), then either flipping \(i\) in \(x\) stays in \(R\), or there is a different coordinate \(j\) at which \(x,y\) differ such that flipping both \(i,j\) stays in \(R\). An even delta-matroid additionally has the same parity of Hamming weight for all its tuples; that parity may be odd. Empty relations are handled separately by immediate rejection when used.

The source’s Theorem 8 records Feder’s boundary: if a family contains a relation failing the delta-matroid exchange property, its decision-Holant complexity agrees with that of ordinary CSP on the family. Schaefer’s Boolean CSP dichotomy then supplies a polynomial-time algorithm or NP-completeness. The remaining general region consists of families whose relations all satisfy the exchange property.

For symmetric relations, membership depends only on the number of one coordinates. The delta-matroid condition then says that between consecutive permitted weights there is at most one forbidden integer. Such families are tractable as general factor problems. This permits relations with both parities; it is a different sufficient condition from the even delta-matroid algorithm.

Kazda, Kolmogorov and Rolínek generalize the matching blossom algorithm to arbitrary even delta-matroid relations given by tuple lists, and extend it to a further class they call efficiently coverable. Their planar Boolean CSP classification is a consequence. It does not classify arbitrary delta-matroid constraints in general edge-CSP grids.

The 2023 general-factor paper explicitly retains the general Boolean edge-CSP classification as open, while proving a strongly polynomial algorithm for particular weighted symmetric constraints. It records the conjecture that every delta-matroid family is tractable. The card retains the full classification question, so it does not assume this conjectured answer in its target.

A counting dichotomy concerns computing the entire sum H, which can be harder than deciding whether H is positive. Counting Holant results for real or complex signatures therefore cannot by themselves classify this zero-one decision task. Availability of all unary signatures and restrictions to planar grids also define different problems.
why: A full classification would explain exactly which local Boolean constraints remain tractable when each variable has two incidences. The unresolved region contains broad generalizations of matching rather than only the standard Boolean CSP algorithms. Resolving it would connect delta-matroid structure with the boundary between polynomial-time graph algorithms and NP-hardness.

working_summary: Boolean decision Holant asks whether edges of a graph can be assigned zero or one so that every local relation is satisfied. The question seeks a structural classification of all fixed finite relation families that admit polynomial-time decision. The source’s edge-CSP model makes each variable occur in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without freely adding constants or unary relations.
