title: Exact exponential-time equivalence for nonnegative Boolean Max-CSP
importance_reason: A degree-based exact-time classification would organize all finite NP-hard Boolean Max-CSP languages with nonnegative weights under one invariant.
formal: Does the following extension of the source’s degree-based classification hold? For every fixed finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) that is neither 0-valid, 1-valid, nor 2-monotone, let \(d=\deg (\Gamma )\). For every fixed real \(\alpha >1\), if Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) has an exact deterministic algorithm running in \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\) time for every fixed constant \(c\ge 1\), must Max d-CNF-SAT with nonnegative integer weights of total weight at most \(n^{c}\) also have an exact deterministic \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for every fixed \(c\ge 1\)? The same base \(\alpha\) is required. Algorithms and polynomial factors may depend on \(\Gamma ,\alpha ,c\). This formulates the conclusion’s speedup question as extending Theorem 6.2 to all NP-hard nonnegative-weight languages; tractable languages are explicitly excluded.
definitions: A Boolean predicate f of arity r is a map \(\{0,1\}\)ʳ→\(\{0,1\}\). A language \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of such predicates, not part of an input instance. An instance \(\Phi\) has variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and weighted applications \((f,(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{r}),w)\), where \(f\in \Gamma\), each \(i_{j}\in [n]\) and w is a nonnegative integer. Indices may repeat. Arguments are variables themselves: constants and negated literals are available only if the corresponding predicate can already be expressed by a member of \(\Gamma\) with variable arguments. The value \(\Phi (x)\) is the sum of weights whose predicate applications evaluate to 1. Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) asks whether \(\max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{n}}\Phi (x)\ge t\) for an input integer t, under the promise that total weight is at most \(n^{c}\). Weights, indices and t use binary encoding; duplicate applications can be combined and zero-weight applications discarded. Trivial thresholds outside the possible objective range are handled during input reading. Polynomial-time normalization is included; equivalently the runtime has an additional input-reading term for a redundantly listed representation. The normalized input has polynomial length for fixed \(\Gamma ,c\). The algorithm must answer every promised instance correctly, and n denotes variables, not clauses, total weight or bit length. For each f there is a unique multilinear real polynomial \(\mathrm{P}_{f}\) agreeing with f on its Boolean cube. Its degree is the largest number of variables in a monomial with nonzero coefficient; \(\deg (\Gamma )=\max _{f\in \Gamma}\deg (\mathrm{P}_{f})\). This is neither maximum predicate arity nor polynomial degree over \(F_{2}\). Constants can be removed with a threshold adjustment. Disregarding constant predicates, a language is 0-valid if every predicate accepts its all-zero input, and 1-valid if every predicate accepts its all-one input. It is 2-monotone if each predicate has a DNF representation with at most two terms, one consisting only of positive variables and one only of negated variables. The excluded three cases are the source’s polynomial-time cases for nonnegative weights; the remaining cases are NP-hard and have \(d\ge 2\). Max d-CNF-SAT is the same threshold maximization problem for disjunctions of at most d literals, with both signs of variables allowed, and nonnegative integer clause weights. Equivalently one may use the source’s d-ary clause language and repeated variables. All complexity statements are worst-case exact running times in an ordinary discrete computation model, up to polynomial factors. The premise is quantified over every fixed polynomial weight bound c; a result for only one small weight range does not supply that premise.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every eligible fixed language \(\Gamma\) and every \(\alpha >1\), retaining the same exponential base and the all-c weight convention, or refute it by a language and a rigorously established failure of that implication. A theorem comparing only whether both problems are NP-hard, or comparing compression sizes or exponential rates after a constant-factor increase in variable count, does not establish the stated base-preserving classification.
context:
Theorem 6.2 places all degree-d signed-weight languages in the same exact exponential-base class as weighted Max d-CNF-SAT. The forward implication from Max d-CNF-SAT algorithms also covers its nonnegative-weight restrictions.

The same theorem covers nonnegative languages closed under predicate-output negation, \(f\mapsto 1- f\), or under substitution of literals for arguments. An arbitrary NP-hard language need not have either closure.

The source’s additive reductions introduce only \(O(1)\) variables, so \(\alpha ^{n+O(1)}\) preserves \(\alpha\). Its general conversion to nonnegative weights can instead introduce a linear number of variables. That suffices for transferring a polynomial compression exponent but can change an exponential base.

The March 2024 version repeats the nonnegative-weight speedup question after the exponential-time theorem. Its complete compression classification does not itself resolve the exact-time classification.
why: Would show whether the algebraic degree of a Boolean constraint language determines its exact exponential-time complexity even when every constraint has the usual nonnegative weight.
status_note: Checked the conference statement against the March 2024 version of record, including the exact-base quantifiers, all-c convention and tractability dichotomy. Subsequent searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The displayed statement is the NP-hard-language extension of the source’s Theorem 6.2; this editorial interpretation of the shorter conclusion is explicit. Search is not exhaustive.
progress: 2020: The ESA paper proves the signed-weight and closure-restricted exact-base classification, leaving general nonnegative languages open. | 2024-03: The full TOCT article retains both Theorem 6.2 and the missing nonnegative-weight question.
working_summary: A Boolean Max-CSP instance asks for an assignment satisfying constraints of maximum total nonnegative weight. Each fixed language has a degree defined by the real multilinear polynomials of its predicates. The question asks whether an exact algorithm with exponential base \(\alpha\) for any NP-hard degree-d language yields the same base for weighted Max d-CNF-SAT. The known classification allows negative weights or imposes closure properties on the language. The remaining issue is preserving the exponential base when removing the sign restriction; the 2024 journal article still asks it.

title: Universal representation of NP by \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
importance_reason: This asks whether the main symmetry-based framework for infinite-domain CSP algebra can represent every NP computational problem, clarifying a fundamental boundary beyond finite-template classifications.
formal:
For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\), does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that
\[L\equiv_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\ ?\]
The relation \(\equiv_T^p\) means deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions in both directions. This reduction convention follows the source’s accompanying non-dichotomy results and the explicit definition in the later monograph; Question 2 itself abbreviates it as polynomial-time equivalence.
question_excerpt: Is every problem in NP polynomial-time equivalent to a CSP with an omega-categorical template?
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and an interpretation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) maps elements of \(I\) to domain values and preserves every positive relation tuple. It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples.

An automorphism of \(\Gamma\) is a bijection of its domain preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on an ordered tuple by applying the same bijection to all coordinates. Two tuples are in the same orbit if some automorphism maps one to the other. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical here if for every positive integer \(k\), there are only finitely many orbits of ordered \(k\)-tuples. For countably infinite structures in a finite signature, this is equivalent to their complete first-order theory having a unique countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite structures are admitted by the same orbit convention. The bound on the number of orbits can depend on \(k\); no fixed global bound, algorithm for orbits, homogeneity or finite list of forbidden patterns is assumed.

A CSP instance is a finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\) with domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. It is accepted exactly when \(I\to\Gamma\). Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; duplicate tuples are harmless. The empty structure has the empty homomorphism. Encode \(n\) in unary, then in signature order each relation’s unary list length and its tuples of binary indices, with delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. This defines a total language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) of finite bit strings. The signature and structure are fixed for this language; no infinite table, presentation algorithm or value from \(\Gamma\) is supplied with an instance.

A language lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is witnessed by a certificate of length polynomial in the input bit length and checked by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. A reduction \(K\leq_T^p Q\) is a deterministic oracle Turing machine deciding membership in \(K\) using exact yes/no membership queries to \(Q\). On every input \(x\), all its computation, query writing and answer processing take at most \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive constants \(C,d\). Thus query lengths and their number are polynomially bounded. The oracle supplies each membership bit at unit query cost; its own computation is not part of the reduction. Queries may depend on earlier answers, and answers may be negated. No randomness or advice is available.

Polynomial-time Turing equivalence means \(L\leq_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\leq_T^p L\). The two programs and their constants may depend on \(L,\Gamma\), but each works on every finite input. The quantifiers are \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\tau,\Gamma,M_1,M_2,C_1,C_2,d_1,d_2\). No uniform algorithm turning an NP verifier into a template or into these reductions is requested. The source explicitly permits defining a fixed CSP without fixing an effective representation of its infinite template.

This is equivalence of computational problems, not equality of their input classes or their logical definitions. Turing equivalence is also weaker than requiring many-one reductions, which produce one target instance with the same membership answer. No additional hypothesis \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP}\) is inserted: Turing equivalence to an NP language alone implies membership in \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\), the class decided by polynomial-time machines with an NP oracle, rather than closure inside NP. The original question does not separately impose that extra condition. Trivial languages are included and cause no difficulty under Turing reductions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every language in NP and produce existence of a finite-signature omega-categorical template with both deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. A negative answer must establish a language in NP for which no permitted template has the required equivalence. Giving an arbitrary infinite template, only one reduction direction, a weaker oracle-complexity upper bound, or a representation for only NP-complete languages does not settle the question. No unproved complexity separation is assumed; conditional constructions or obstructions settle only their conditional statements.
context:
Infinite templates vastly enlarge the class of possible CSPs, but omega-categoricity retains finitely many symmetry types at each tuple length. It is the structural hypothesis behind many preservation theorems used in algebraic CSP theory. The question asks whether imposing this symmetry still permits representation of every NP computational problem up to the stated reductions.

Bodirsky and Grohe prove that every decision language has a polynomial-time Turing equivalent CSP with an unrestricted infinite template. Their construction is not omega-categorical. Thus arbitrary-template universality is an established starting point, and the symmetry condition is the entire additional issue.

For omega-categorical templates their Theorem 2 instead gives, for any decision language \(L\), a template with \(L\leq_m^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\). Here the first relation is a polynomial-time many-one reduction and \(\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\) means complements of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time machines with exact oracle \(L\). This upper bound does not supply the required deterministic polynomial-time oracle reduction back to \(L\).

The same work constructs omega-categorical templates with coNP-complete CSPs and, conditionally, coNP-intermediate CSPs. These results demonstrate broad complexity within the symmetry class, but they do not establish equivalence to each prescribed NP language. The later book separately retains the question of NP-intermediate omega-categorical CSPs; that question explicitly requires NP membership, unlike bare Turing equivalence.

The stronger restrictions in the Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concern reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. They ensure finite-pattern certificates and hence NP membership. The present target quantifies over all omega-categorical templates and imposes neither restriction; proving that narrower dichotomy would not settle this representation question.

Logical representation is also a different issue. Two templates may define different finite-instance CSPs yet have polynomial-time equivalent decision problems. The source’s neighbouring question about whether a particular SNP-definable CSP has an omega-categorical template asks for the same accepted input class, which is stronger than computational equivalence and has separate counterexamples.
why: The question tests whether the symmetry framework that supports infinite-domain algebraic CSP methods is computationally universal for NP under the source’s equivalence convention. A positive answer would place every NP degree into that framework; a negative answer would exhibit a complexity limitation imposed by omega-categoricity itself.

The accompanying theorem and the January 2026 book postprint establish unrestricted-template universality but not the required omega-categorical Turing equivalence. Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general representation theorem or refutation; the 2026 scope results concern a narrower template class. This is a limited status check, not exhaustive certification of present openness. The Turing reduction convention is explicitly recovered from the related theorem and later monograph rather than attributed as verbatim wording of Question 2.

working_summary: The question asks whether every NP language is polynomial-time Turing equivalent to a CSP with a fixed omega-categorical template. Omega-categoricity means that each finite tuple length has only finitely many symmetry orbits, even when the domain is infinite. The reductions may use adaptive exact membership queries, and no uniform template-construction algorithm or effective template presentation is required. Universality is known for unrestricted infinite templates, while the known omega-categorical construction gives a weaker oracle upper bound. A resolution would determine whether this symmetry condition limits computational representation of NP problems.

title: Dichotomy for finite-domain restricted CSPs
importance_reason: The question tests how far the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives decidable infinite input promises and whether homomorphism-defined restrictions can produce intermediate complexity.
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). For every finite relational signature \(\tau\), every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(A\), and every possibly infinite \(\tau\)-structure \(B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is decidable, must \(\operatorname{RCSP}(A,B)\) be either polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard in the source’s completion sense? Explicitly, let
\[\mathcal S_{A,B}=\{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^*:S\text{ is decidable and }S\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)=\operatorname{CSP}(A)\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)\}.\]
Is it always true that
\[\bigl(\exists S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\in\mathrm P\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(\forall S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\text{ is NP-hard}\bigr)?\]
The input is a finite structure \(X\) promised to map homomorphically to \(B\); on that promise the decision is whether \(X\) maps to \(A\).
question_excerpt: Under P≠NP, do finite-domain restricted CSPs satisfy a polynomial-time versus NP-hard dichotomy when their restriction structures may be infinite?
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of positive integer arities. A \(\tau\)-structure \(D\) has a domain and a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. The target \(A\) is finite; the restriction \(B\) may have an arbitrary infinite domain. A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function preserving every relation tuple: \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\). Write \(D\to E\) for existence of such a map. Maps need not be injective. Neither \(A\to B\) nor \(B\to A\) is assumed.

Input structures have domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed tuples for each relation. Encode \(n\) in unary, then the relation lists in signature order with unary list lengths and binary coordinate indices. Let \(L\) be the total bit length. Empty relations, repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; repeated listed tuples are harmless. Define \(\operatorname{CSP}(D)\) as the set of valid encodings of finite \(X\) with \(X\to D\). Invalid encodings do not belong to this set. Empty template domains may be included; their trivial boundary cases do not alter the question.

For each problem \(A,B,\tau\) are fixed, and only \(X\) is supplied. An input in \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) must be accepted exactly when it lies in \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\); outside the promise either answer is allowed. A completion \(S\) is a total decidable language with precisely this behaviour on the promise. Since \(A\) is finite, \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\) is a decidable completion, so \(\mathcal S_{A,B}\) is never empty. Decidability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is a hypothesis recovered from the source, not a polynomial-time promise-recognition assumption. No description, relation-table algorithm, homomorphism into \(B\), or oracle for \(B\) is supplied. Infinite restrictions are not limited to finitely presented or categorically specified structures.

A completion is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic multitape Turing machine accepts exactly it and halts on every string of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). The machine and constants may depend on \(A,B\). Decidable means a deterministic machine halts and decides membership, without any time bound. No uniform procedure for constructing these machines from templates, common polynomial exponent, advice or randomness is requested.

A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has polynomially bounded certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A language \(S\) is NP-hard here under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a total polynomial-time function \(f_K\) with \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f_K(x)\in S\). Equivalently, it suffices to reduce Boolean three-clause satisfiability, where each clause has at most three literals. This is hardness of the total language \(S\), not a claim that \(S\) itself lies in NP.

The promise-hardness quantifiers are \(\forall\text{ decidable completions }S\ \exists\text{ suitable reductions to }S\). Reductions may depend on \(S\); no single reduction whose images always satisfy \(X\to B\) is required by this definition. A uniform reduction landing inside the promise would suffice, but is not silently substituted for the source’s definition. Under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) the two displayed alternatives are disjoint. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the first alternative already holds for every finite \(A\), since its ordinary CSP is in NP.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, under the stated \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis, that the displayed dichotomy holds for every permitted \(A,B\), or that it fails. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\) and a permitted possibly infinite \(B\) such that no completion is in P and at least one decidable completion is not NP-hard under the stated reductions. A positive answer must cover every infinite restriction with decidable CSP, retaining the completion quantifiers. Proving only the already known finite-restriction case, treating an arbitrary input class that is not \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\), or disproving a stronger uniform hardness requirement does not settle this question. No additional unproved hypothesis may replace the explicitly stated separation assumption.
context:
Restricted CSPs impose a promise on which input structures must be handled. For example, RCSP(K₃,K₄) asks whether a graph promised to be four-colourable is three-colourable; Kᵣ is the complete loopless graph on r vertices. Unlike a promise CSP, the promise here restricts the input class on both yes and no sides rather than relaxing which assignments count as solutions.

The source proves that a finite restriction B permits a reduction to an ordinary CSP on the exponential structure A^B. Its elements are functions from B to A, with relations defined by preservation along relation tuples of B. If A and B are both finite, this is again a finite structure, so the ordinary finite-domain decision dichotomy applies. Theorem 18 records the resulting restricted dichotomy.

An infinite B can impose familiar global input conditions. For directed graphs, the structure on rational numbers with the strict-order relation admits a homomorphism from exactly the finite acyclic digraphs. Such a restriction remains decidable even though its representing structure is infinite. This illustrates why finite assignment domains do not make the promise finite.

The general question preserves arbitrary decidable homomorphism restrictions. It is separate from the source’s neighbouring conjecture asking for a particular algebraic criterion for tractability. The finite exponential construction does not remain a finite template when B is infinite, so the known finite-restriction reduction alone does not prove the target.

The completion definition is essential: an algorithm must be correct only on the promised class, yet it must halt on every input. Hardness quantifies over every decidable total extension of that promised behaviour. Saying merely that the intersection of two CSP languages is NP-hard would describe one particular extension and would not prove the required universal hardness.
why: This asks whether the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives every decidable restriction described by homomorphisms into a fixed, possibly infinite structure. A positive answer would sharply constrain the complexity introduced by such promises. A counterexample would demonstrate intermediate promise behaviour even though all satisfying assignments still use a fixed finite domain.
status_note: The ICALP 2025 source poses this exact question in §10 after proving the finite-restriction case. Section 3 supplies the decidability and completion-hardness conventions omitted by the imported excerpt. A bounded primary-source search and full-version metadata check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is not exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2017–2020: The finite-domain decision dichotomy supplies the classification for ordinary finite CSPs used in the finite-restriction argument. | 2025: Theorems 16 and 18 reduce finite restrictions to finite exponential templates and establish the polynomial-time/NP-hard dichotomy in that case. | 2025: Section 10 explicitly asks whether the same complexity dichotomy extends to possibly infinite restrictions; the definition in §3 requires the restriction CSP to be decidable.
working_summary: A restricted CSP asks whether a finite input maps to a fixed finite target, under the promise that it maps to another fixed structure. The restriction structure may be infinite, but the source requires its finite-input CSP to be decidable. The question asks whether every such promise problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard when P differs from NP. Hardness must hold for every decidable completion of the promised answers, and the known dichotomy only covers finite restrictions. A resolution would determine whether decidable homomorphism promises preserve the finite-domain dichotomy or allow intermediate behaviour.

title: Search tractability of BLP-solvable promise CSPs
importance_reason: Equivalence of search and decision for LP-solvable promise CSPs concerns a basic algorithmic distinction in the promise framework.
formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite relational structures of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), suppose that the basic linear programming relaxation solves the decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\). Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite input structure \(X\) promised to satisfy \(X\to A\), outputs a homomorphism \(X\to B\)? The algorithm and its polynomial bound may depend on \(A,B\); the promised homomorphism to \(A\) is not supplied.
definitions:
A finite signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^{D}\subseteq D^{r}\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map such that \((d_1,\ldots,d_{r})\in R^{D}\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_{r}))\in R^{E}\) for every relation. It need not be injective. Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists. Templates \(A,B\), including their relation tables and signature, are fixed before inputs are supplied.

An input \(X\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. For a definite encoding, write \(n\) in unary followed by the relation lists in signature order, each prefixed by its tuple count in unary; each coordinate uses exactly \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. The total bit length \(L\) counts isolated variables and all tuples. Duplicate listed tuples are harmless. An output is the list of the \(n\) images in the fixed numbered domain of \(B\), or a distinguished failure symbol. The empty instance has the empty homomorphism.

For each \(x\in X,a\in A\), introduce a rational variable \(p_{x}(a)\). For each constraint \(C=(R,(x_1,\ldots,x_{r}))\) of \(X\) and tuple \(t\in R^{A}\), introduce \(q_{C}(t)\). The basic linear programming relaxation, abbreviated BLP, is feasibility of
\[p_{x}(a)\geq0,\quad \sum_{a\in A}p_{x}(a)=1,\qquad q_{C}(t)\geq0,\quad \sum_{t\in R^{A}}q_{C}(t)=1,\]
\[\sum_{\substack{t\in R^{A}\\t_{i}=a}}q_{C}(t)=p_{x_{i}}(a)\qquad\text{for every }C,\ 1\leq i\leq r,\ a\in A.\]
An empty sum is zero. These conditions are imposed at every coordinate even when a variable repeats in a constraint; no extra constraint forces its coordinates to be equal inside each tuple of a local distribution. Rational and real feasibility coincide for this finite rational system. A homomorphism to \(A\) gives an integral feasible point, but feasibility alone need not give such a homomorphism.

BLP solves the decision problem for \((A,B)\) precisely when, for every finite \(X\), feasibility of the displayed system implies \(X\to B\). This makes feasibility a valid test distinguishing \(X\to A\) from \(X\not\to B\). The search guarantee in the question applies only when \(X\to A\). An input that is BLP-feasible but has no homomorphism to \(A\) is outside that search promise, even though it necessarily has a homomorphism to \(B\).

Polynomial-time search means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no oracle or advice, that halts on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^{k}\) bit steps, for positive integers \(C,k\). On valid promised inputs it returns a \(B\)-homomorphism; on other inputs any output is allowed, and malformed inputs may be rejected. The machine and constants depend only on the fixed template. No common exponent across all templates, algorithm for recognizing BLP-solvable templates, or particular rounding procedure is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish a polynomial-time search machine for every fixed finite BLP-solvable template, with the stated promise, output and worst-case bit bound. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\to B\) satisfying the BLP-solvability hypothesis for which no such polynomial-time promised search machine exists. Difficulty rounding arbitrary feasible LP solutions, undecidability of recognizing templates, or a conditional obstruction to one prescribed algorithm does not prove this negation. An unproved complexity assumption may describe partial progress but does not settle the unconditional target.
context:
A promise CSP separates a stronger local requirement from a weaker one. Decision only distinguishes instances satisfying all strong constraints from those failing even the weak constraints. Search must actually assign weak-domain values when a strong assignment is guaranteed to exist. This distinction is absent from the familiar fixed-template CSP case, where decision and search are polynomial-time equivalent.

BLP replaces each variable value by a probability distribution and each constraint by a compatible local distribution. Compatibility checks one-variable marginals, so different constraints may agree locally without yielding a joint strong assignment. The BLP-solvability hypothesis guarantees the existence of a weak assignment whenever these local checks succeed; the question asks for a polynomial-time construction on the stronger promise.

The quantifier over fixed templates matters. A separate finite program may use all the information in its particular template, and its polynomial exponent may depend on that template. Consequently, the question is different from recognizing the class of BLP-solvable pairs from their relation tables.

Larrauri’s May 2026 preprint establishes hardness of finding weak assignments for every BLP-accepted input, with reductions from arbitrary total NP search problems. Its discussion explicitly leaves open whether search is tractable on inputs promised to map to the strong template. A total NP search problem has polynomially bounded, polynomially checkable witnesses and at least one witness for every input; its hardness is a statement about this broader input guarantee.
why: BLP is a central general-purpose tractability criterion for promise constraints. Determining whether its decision power always entails efficient promised search would clarify when an efficiently recognizable relaxation gap can also support construction of the relaxed object. A separation would expose a basic limitation of decision-to-search equivalence even for finite local relations.
status_note: The source poses the BLP-specific search question in 2024. Larrauri v4, 25 May 2026, §10 explicitly explains why its rounding hardness does not resolve it. A bounded primary-source search checked on 15 September 2026 found no matching resolution; the preprint proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2022: The survey distinguishes decision and search for finite promise templates and records the unresolved general relationship. | 2024: Mottet states this BLP-specific search question after defining the relaxation and its decision-solvability condition. | 2026-05-25: Larrauri’s v4 preprint proves TFNP hardness for rounding all BLP-accepted inputs and undecidability of recognizing BLP-solvable templates; §10 explicitly retains the narrower promised-search question. These are different assertions from a separation for this card.
working_summary: A finite promise CSP asks for weakly satisfying assignments when a strongly satisfying assignment is promised. BLP can recognize the decision gap using compatible local probability distributions. The question asks whether every fixed template solved by that relaxation also has a deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm on the original promise. The algorithm may depend on the template and need not round every feasible point of the relaxation. A resolution would determine whether this major decision tractability criterion always yields efficient construction of promised solutions.

title: Characterizing CSP languages with linear non-redundancy
importance_reason: Characterizing linear non-redundancy would give a structural explanation for which constraint languages admit compact instances.
formal: Characterize all finite constraint languages \(\Gamma\) over arbitrary finite nonempty domains for which every \(n\)-variable formula has a subformula with at most \(C_\Gamma n\) constraints and exactly the same set of satisfying assignments, for some constant \(C_\Gamma\) independent of the formula and \(n\). Equivalently, determine the class-membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) on all such finite languages, taking value \(1\) when this property holds and \(0\) otherwise. The target is the full classification from Question 8; it is not restricted to Boolean domains or to a proposed sufficient condition.
question_excerpt: Which finite constraint languages allow every formula to be reduced to linearly many of its own constraints while preserving all satisfying assignments?
definitions:
A language \(\Gamma\) consists of a finite nonempty domain \(D=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq D^{r}\), each with a positive integer arity \(r\). Empty and full relations, and the empty list of relations, are permitted. The domain, arities and relation tables give the entire description. A formula \(F\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\geq1\), is a finite conjunction of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) from this language. Variable repetitions and repeated constraints are permitted. An assignment \(a:V\to D\) satisfies the constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\in R\), and satisfies \(F\) when it satisfies every constraint. Write \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\subseteq D^{V}\) for this set; it may be empty.

A subformula \(F'\subseteq F\) is obtained only by deleting constraint occurrences, keeping the same variables and domain. It may have isolated variables and no constraints. The preservation requirement is \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\), as sets of assignments on the original \(V\). It is stronger than merely preserving whether a satisfying assignment exists. No new constraints, new variables, weights or relaxation of relations are allowed.

Define
\[\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)=\max_{F}\ \min_{\substack{F'\subseteq F\\\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)}} |F'|,\]
where \(F\) ranges over all formulas on these \(n\) variables and \(|F'|\) counts constraint occurrences. This maximum is finite: duplicate occurrences do not change solutions, and there are at most \(\sum_{R\in\Gamma}n^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\) distinct constraints. An equivalent definition is the maximum size of a formula in which every constraint is non-redundant. A constraint \(C\) is non-redundant when there is an assignment satisfying all other constraints but violating \(C\). Unsatisfiable formulas are included; no satisfiability promise is made.

The numerical function being classified is
\[\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)=\begin{cases}1,&\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\ \forall n\geq1:\ \operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)\leq Cn,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
Its domain consists of every finite language just defined, with no global bound on domain size, arity or number of relations. The hidden constant may depend on the whole fixed language. Requiring the bound at all positive \(n\) is equivalent to asymptotic \(O(n)\), since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed in the constant. A bound of \(n\log n\) or \(n^{1+o(1)}\) does not meet it.

This is a mathematical classification of an extremal property. No polynomial-time procedure for finding \(F'\), recognizing languages, or deciding satisfiability is built into the target. A structural criterion or another substantive unambiguous mathematical description of the membership function can specify an answer without a predetermined syntactic form. Introducing the characteristic function records the same classification target, rather than replacing it with an optimal-growth problem for \(\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma\).
answer_criterion: Supply a real-valued function \(g\) on the stated full domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every finite language \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient characterization of class membership also qualifies. The supplied description must determine membership substantively; merely renaming the defining optimization or repeating that a language is linear exactly when it has linear non-redundancy is not an answer. No efficient recognition algorithm is required. Prove both membership and nonmembership sides of the characterization, including all domains and arities. A sufficient algebraic condition, a finite table of small languages, a near-linear bound or a decision-preserving kernel alone does not settle the full target.
context:
A constraint can be logically unnecessary even when its relation occurs many times. For example, equality constraints connecting a set of variables can often be deleted while preserving the same equality requirements on all assignments. Non-redundancy asks how large a collection can remain when every member has its own witness to being essential.

This is a question about the amount of information in a system, not the difficulty of finding a satisfying assignment. Some NP-hard fixed predicates have linear non-redundancy. Conversely, the binary positive-OR relation has quadratic non-redundancy despite the simplicity of deciding its satisfiability. These contrasting examples separate this classification from the usual tractability dichotomy.

The 2020 Boolean work supplies linear sparsification through representations by degree-one equations over integer rings. The December 2025 manuscript identifies the Boolean languages admitting the more general Mal’tsev embedding condition with the corresponding balanced class, while exhibiting genuinely noncommutative behavior on larger domains. This clarifies known sufficient conditions without proving that they capture all languages with linear non-redundancy.

The 2025 manuscript realizes every rational non-redundancy exponent at least one over suitable finite domains. The resulting range is much richer than a choice between linear growth and the trivial maximal-arity bound. It does not supply a complete description of the languages at the linear endpoint.

The 2026 shrinking paper develops further superlinear lower bounds while retaining the general linear or near-linear classification as an open question.

The CP 2026 paper almost classifies Boolean arity four, leaving one predicate unresolved and exhibiting non-polynomial asymptotics. This is a restricted family within the all-language target.
why: A full classification would explain which systems of local relations always have a linear-sized exact description using their own constraints. It would organize connections among logical redundancy, sparsification, preprocessing and algebra across all finite domains. The distinction between existence of a small subformula and efficiently finding it is essential to interpreting the result.
status_note: Question 8 in the July 2024 workshop source poses the full classification. The December 2025 Richness revision and May 2026 shrinking manuscript retain it, and the published July 2026 arity-four paper gives only a restricted near-classification. These primary sources were checked on 15 September 2026; bounded later-work searches did not find a full resolution. Proofs and computational classifications were not independently reproduced.
progress: 2020: Chen, Jansen and Pieterse establish ring-based linear sparsification results for Boolean languages and classifications in important restricted cases. | 2022: Carbonnel develops an algebraic framework for non-redundancy and characterizes when the trivial maximal-arity bound is tight. | 2024-07-07: PACS Question 8 asks for the full linear classification and distinguishes the Boolean candidate condition from the general finite-domain problem. | 2025-12-01: The revised Richness manuscript relates Boolean Mal’tsev embeddings to balanced relations and explicitly leaves the complete linear classification open. | 2026-05-18: The shrinking-instances manuscript advances superlinear lower bounds and again identifies the linear or near-linear classification as open. | 2026-07-13: The CP 2026 paper gives a near-complete four-ary Boolean classification, including non-polynomial asymptotics and one remaining predicate; this is a restricted-domain result.
working_summary: Non-redundancy measures how many constraints can remain individually essential in a formula. The question asks which finite languages always allow a subformula with linearly many constraints and the identical set of satisfying assignments. The number of variables is the size parameter, and the linear constant may depend on the language. The classification includes all finite domains and does not require an efficient algorithm to find the subformula. A solution would identify the structural boundary for compact exact descriptions of constraint systems.

title: Common polynomial exponent for tractable digraph CSPs
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: Uniform algorithms across tractable CSPs test whether separate tractability results can be realized by a single effective procedure.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\geq1\) such that, for every fixed finite digraph \(H\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) is in \(\mathrm P\), there are a deterministic algorithm \(M_{H}\) and a constant \(C_{H}\geq1\) that decide whether an input digraph \(G\) admits a homomorphism to \(H\) in at most \(C_{H}(L+1)^{c}\) bit steps, where \(L\) is the input encoding length? The exponent must be independent of \(H\), while both the machine and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\).
question_excerpt: Is there one polynomial degree sufficient for every tractable fixed digraph CSP, with the template held fixed when input complexity is measured?
definitions:
A finite digraph \(G=(V_{G},E_{G})\) has a finite vertex set and a relation \(E_{G}\subseteq V_{G}\times V_{G}\); loops and both orientations of a pair are permitted. A homomorphism \(h:G\to H\) is a map such that \((u,v)\in E_{G}\) implies \((h(u),h(v))\in E_{H}\). It need not be injective or preserve nonedges. The problem \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) asks whether such a map exists. The target \(H\) is finite and nonempty, and is fixed before inputs are supplied. Including the empty target adds only a trivial decision problem and does not change existence of a common exponent.

Number the vertices of \(G\) by \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(n\geq0\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by the number of listed edges in unary, each terminated by a zero, and then their endpoint pairs, with \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits per coordinate. Duplicate listed edges denote the same edge and still count toward the bit length \(L\); all labels must be valid. This representation counts isolated vertices. Algorithms reject malformed encodings. They are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite programs and no oracle or advice; all reading, writing and intermediate bit operations count. Bounds are worst-case and answers must always be correct.

By \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\in\mathrm P\) we mean existence of such a decider with a polynomial bound whose exponent may depend on \(H\). The question's quantifier order is \(\exists c\geq1\;\forall H\;\exists M_{H},C_{H}\), restricted to tractable \(H\), with correctness and the stated time bound for every input. No procedure producing \(M_{H}\) from \(H\) is required. The graph \(H\) is not part of the varying input or its length \(L\).

The author separately asks for one machine receiving \(G,H\), running in \(f(|H|)(L+1)^{c}\) time for a computable function \(f\) under the tractability promise. That fixed-parameter tractability assertion implies this card's assertion but is stronger. Polynomial time in the combined descriptions is stronger still. The inherited label “uniform” left these distinctions unresolved; this formulation recovers the main fixed-template source question.

The source permits conditional refutation by fine-grained assumptions. This card admits deterministic SETH as one explicitly specified assumption: for every real \(\delta>0\) there is an integer \(k\geq3\) such that Boolean \(k\)-SAT has no deterministic algorithm running in \(O(2^{(1-\delta)v}S^{d})\) time for any constant \(d\). Here \(v\) is the number of variables, \(S\) the explicit input bit length, and \(k\)-SAT asks satisfiability of a conjunction of clauses containing at most \(k\) signed Boolean variables. The assumption concerns worst-case inputs of unbounded size.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the common-exponent assertion or its negation. Following the source's express allowance, a Lean proof that deterministic SETH implies the negation is also an accepted answer and must be labelled conditional on SETH. No other unproved assumption is implicitly accepted. A negative answer must establish that for every proposed exponent \(c\), some tractable finite digraph template \(H\) has no correct deterministic \(O((L+1)^{c})\) decider, even with a template-specific machine and multiplicative constant. Refuting one algorithm or showing superpolynomial dependence on template size is insufficient. An affirmative proof need not give one algorithm receiving arbitrary template tables.
context:
A graph homomorphism assigns each input vertex a target vertex while respecting every directed edge. Holding the target fixed defines one decision problem. The finite CSP dichotomy says that each problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete, but the existence of separate polynomial algorithms does not itself supply a common exponent.

The question concerns a quantitative distinction within tractability: whether separate template-dependent polynomial degrees can always be replaced by a single constant. The programs and hidden multiplicative factors may remain different, and those factors need not be practical.

Bodirsky and Weiß’s 2026 paper studies the stronger question of time polynomial in both explicitly listed structures and its relationship to finding operations that preserve relations. Its introduction says this fully uniform problem is open even for important subclasses. That does not by itself prove that the weaker common-exponent problem here is open or false.

The source explicitly allows a fine-grained conditional lower bound. Such a result would have to establish unbounded input-exponent requirements among tractable templates, with each individual template fixed while its input graphs grow. A lower bound arising only because the target itself grows has different quantifiers.
why: The finite CSP dichotomy classifies each fixed set of local relations qualitatively. A common exponent would add a quantitative uniformity principle to this classification. Its failure would show that polynomial-time digraph CSPs can require arbitrarily large exponents even though every individual template is tractable.
status_note: The live author entry checked 15 September 2026 still poses the common-exponent question, with its own caveat that the list is not an exhaustive investigation. Checked the CSP dichotomy abstracts and the ICALP 2026 paper on the stronger uniform problem; bounded searches found no matching resolution of this exact target.
progress: 2017: Bulatov proves the finite-template CSP dichotomy; its fixed-template statement does not assert a common exponent. | 2017–2020: Zhuk independently proves the dichotomy, with the journal result published in 2020. | 2026-07: Bodirsky and Weiß study the stronger template-input uniform CSP and related metaproblems. General uniform polynomial time remains open in their model. | 2026-09-15: The live author entry still poses the common-exponent question and distinguishes its separate FPT question. The list carries an author caveat about incomplete investigation.
working_summary: Each fixed finite digraph defines a constraint satisfaction problem through graph homomorphisms. The question asks whether all polynomial-time cases can be solved with one common polynomial exponent. The algorithm and its multiplicative constant may still depend on the fixed target digraph. This is weaker than requiring one algorithm whose input includes an arbitrary target table. A resolution would determine whether qualitative fixed-template tractability admits a shared quantitative time bound.

title: Polynomial kernels for Boolean MinCSP
importance_reason: Polynomial-kernel classification for Boolean MinCSP concerns the general preprocessing power of constraint languages.
formal: Classify all fixed finite Boolean constraint languages \(\Gamma\) for which \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\), parameterized by the allowed number \(k\) of violated constraints, admits a randomized polynomial kernel. Equivalently, determine the membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)\in\{0,1\}\) of this class for every finite Boolean language. Deterministic kernels also qualify; the target retains the full language classification and the allowance for randomization in PACS 2024 Question 9.
question_excerpt: For which Boolean constraint languages can instances be reduced in polynomial time to equivalent instances of size polynomial in the permitted number of unsatisfied constraints, allowing randomized reductions and standard conditional lower bounds?
definitions:
A finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) is a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{r}\), each of positive integer arity \(r\), described by its complete finite table. Empty relations, full relations and the empty language are allowed. For each individual decision problem \(\Gamma\) is fixed, including its maximum arity. There is no global bound on arity or on the number of relations when classifying languages.

An instance is \((F,k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(F\) is a finite set of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\). Coordinates may repeat. The set convention follows §1.1 of the cited dichotomy; repeated listings of the identical named constraint do not create extra cost. An assignment \(a:V\to\{0,1\}\) violates a constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\notin R\). Let \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\) be the minimum number of violated constraints over all assignments. The instance is yes exactly when \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\), equivalently when deleting at most \(k\) constraints makes the rest satisfiable. All constraints have unit cost and may be deleted; there are no separately undeletable constraints or freely supplied constant assignments.

Use an explicit binary input encoding: unary \(n\) and constraint count, each followed by zero; each constraint has a relation index in the fixed language and a tuple of variable indices of width \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\); finish with the length-prefixed binary representation of \(k\). The full length \(L\) includes isolated variables and the parameter bits. Output instances use the same convention. Encodings can be normalized to remove duplicate constraints in polynomial time.

A randomized polynomial kernel for a fixed \(\Gamma\) is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(K_\Gamma\) using independent fair coin flips, with no oracle or advice. There are positive integer constants \(C,d,e\), depending on \(\Gamma\) only, such that on every valid input \((F,k)\), and for every sequence of coin outcomes, it halts within \(C(L+1)^{e}\) bit steps and outputs a valid instance \((F',k')\) of the same \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\) with total encoding length at most \(C(k+1)^{d}\). Require
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F')\leq k'\bigr]\geq 2/3.\]
This is a worst-case guarantee for each input over the kernel's internal randomness; both kinds of error are allowed. The original workshop permits randomized kernels without fixing an error convention; bounded two-sided error and an all-runs size bound are recorded here explicitly. A deterministic kernel has probability one. The machine may create new variables and constraints from the same fixed language. It need not preserve the optimum or the entire solution set, and need not be a subformula reduction.

Define \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)=1\) if such a machine and constants exist, and \(0\) otherwise. Its classification is over all finite language tables. No uniform machine for recognizing the class is demanded. A polynomial kernel is different from an algorithm taking \(f(k)(L+1)^{e}\) time for an arbitrary computable function \(f\), and from a compression to an instance of a different decision problem. A bound in the variable count \(n\) alone is not a bound in the parameter \(k\).

The source allows standard complexity assumptions for the lower-bound side. This card fixes the customary hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) as an admissible conditional premise. Here \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of binary languages with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable by deterministic polynomial-time machines. A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when such a verifier may also receive an arbitrary advice string of polynomial length depending only on input length; advice need not be computable. A language is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when its complement is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\). The stated noncontainment means that some NP language lacks such a complement verifier. It is an assumption, not a proved theorem or a conclusion automatically obtained from any parameterized hardness result.
answer_criterion: Give a substantive mathematical characterization, represented by a real-valued function \(g\) on all finite Boolean languages, and prove in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient classification also qualifies. For every class identified as admitting a kernel, establish the stated machine, runtime, size and per-input error guarantees without an unproved assumption. For every excluded class, prove nonexistence of such a randomized kernel either unconditionally or under the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\), labelling the classification conditional when used. The required lower bounds must cover the allowed randomized model. Merely renaming the defining kernel-existence predicate, classifying only fixed-parameter tractability, excluding only deterministic kernels, or solving finitely many languages does not settle the question. No algorithm efficiently recognizing the class from language tables is required.
context:
A small number of violated constraints represents a small repair to an otherwise feasible system. Fixed-parameter tractability permits expensive work that depends only on that repair budget. A polynomial kernel asks instead for polynomial-time preprocessing that compresses all subsequent difficulty into a number of bits bounded polynomially in the budget. These demands can have different boundaries.

Almost 2-SAT is the language consisting of all Boolean clauses with at most two literals, viewed as individual relations. Its randomized polynomial kernel is an established positive example. The workshop includes it explicitly to allow randomization; requiring deterministic kernels would add a further unresolved issue from that example.

The completed FPT dichotomy of Kim, Kratsch, Pilipczuk and Wahlström distinguishes which Boolean MinCSPs admit algorithms with parameter-dependent overhead. It also distinguishes weighted and unweighted variants. This card uses the unweighted problem and asks the subsequent preprocessing classification, which their revised manuscript still presents as a further question.

The SWAT 2026 essential-constraint theorem concerns identifying constraints that occur in all sufficiently good repair sets. That preprocessing can improve the effective search parameter, but does not assert that the entire instance shrinks to polynomial size in the original violation budget. The same paper distinguishes results about compression measured by the number of variables.
why: This would classify the full preprocessing power of finite Boolean constraint languages after the fixed-parameter solvability boundary is known. It asks which nearly satisfiable systems admit a compact equivalent core whose size depends only polynomially on the repair budget. The source allows randomization so that the classification addresses this compression boundary without also demanding derandomization of established kernels.
status_note: The July 2024 workshop poses the full polynomial-kernel classification. The April 2025 full dichotomy manuscript still treats it as a future classification, and the checked SWAT 2026 theorem concerns a different preprocessing guarantee. Bounded primary-source searches on 15 September 2026 found no full kernelization classification. This is a sourced open-status assessment, not an exhaustive proof that no later resolution exists.
progress: 2012–2020: Kratsch and Wahlström establish a randomized polynomial kernel for Almost 2-SAT; the result appears in JACM in 2020. | 2023–2025: The flow-augmentation work classifies fixed-parameter tractability of Boolean MinCSP and its weighted variant; the April 2025 full revision still identifies kernelizability as a separate classification direction. | 2024-07-07: PACS Question 9 asks for this language-wide polynomial-kernel classification and explicitly permits randomized kernels and standard complexity assumptions. | 2026-06: Jansen and Verhaegh classify essential-constraint detection, a different preprocessing task, and distinguish kernelization by solution cost from variable-based compression.
working_summary: Boolean MinCSP asks whether an assignment can violate at most a specified number of constraints. The question seeks all finite Boolean languages admitting polynomial kernels in that violation budget. A kernel must run in polynomial time and output a same-problem instance with polynomially many parameter-dependent bits. Randomization is allowed, and the recorded complexity assumption may support lower bounds for the excluded languages. A classification would reveal which nearly feasible constraint systems admit efficient compression beyond their known fixed-parameter algorithms.

title: Polynomial-time tractability testing for core crisp CSP languages
importance_reason: A central effective-classification question for CSP templates, separating fixed-template tractability from uniform recognition. Existing score retained.
formal: Is there one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite crisp constraint language \(\Gamma\) over an explicitly given finite domain D and promised that \(\Gamma\) is a core, decides whether \(\Gamma\) admits an idempotent Siggers polymorphism? Equivalently on the core promise, decide whether \(\Gamma\) is solvable in the algebraic sense of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy. The polynomial must be uniform in the entire input, including |D|, the number of relations, their arities and their listed tuples; neither a polymorphism nor a tractability certificate is supplied.
definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D\)ʳ of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has |\(D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.
context:
Testing tractability for arbitrary crisp languages is NP-complete, and testing core status is itself difficult. The question assumes core status from the start; neither hardness result alone classifies the promised problem.

Theorem 16 gives a polynomial algorithm for the relevant binary symmetric fractional polymorphism of a core finite-valued language. Crisp relations use forbidden assignments with infinite cost, so that finite-valued theorem does not provide this Siggers test.

The source states that a uniform polynomial-time solver for all solvable core crisp languages would imply the desired test. The fixed-template dichotomy alone does not give a polynomial uniform in the varying input language.

Bodirsky and Weiß explicitly distinguish idempotent Siggers testing from the unrestricted NP-complete metaproblem and note the equivalence under the core promise. Their results on coset-generating and promise metaproblems do not give the general Siggers test.
why: Would make the finite-domain CSP tractability criterion efficiently recognizable when the core is already given, connecting the structural dichotomy to algorithms whose template also varies as input.
status_note: Checked the source’s encoding, core definition and algebraic solvability convention, its complete April 2019 version, and the explicit ICALP 2026 discussion following Theorem 4. Broader searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial core-crisp Siggers test or matching promised-core hardness result. The 2026 primary source directly supports continued openness; search is not exhaustive.
progress: 2019: The ICALP paper contrasts the solved core finite-valued test with the open core crisp test and records the uniform-solver implication. | 2026: The ICALP metaproblem article explicitly keeps idempotent Siggers testing open and explains why unrestricted Siggers hardness does not cover it.
working_summary: A crisp constraint language lists the allowed tuples over a finite domain, and the input is promised to be a core. The question asks for a polynomial-time test for an idempotent four-ary Siggers polymorphism. Both the domain and every relation are part of the input, so one uniform polynomial bound is required. The known finite-valued test and unrestricted-language NP-hardness do not answer this promised-core question. An ICALP 2026 article explicitly retains the relevant Siggers testing problem as open.

title: SNP definability of CSPs in NP
importance_reason: Importance has not been individually assessed. This draft shares the provisional midpoint with other unassessed drafts; its position is not evidence that the question is less important.
formal: Which constraint satisfaction problems in NP admit an exact definition in SNP? The source states this as a classification direction without prescribing a structural criterion. A known equivalent description by reducts of finitely bounded structures is recorded below, but it does not by itself identify what further classification the historical question seeks.
question_excerpt: Which constraint satisfaction problems in NP are in SNP?
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of fixed positive integer arities. A template \(\Gamma\) interprets these symbols as relations on a nonempty domain, which may be finite or infinite. A finite input structure \(I\) has domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) preserves all listed positive relation tuples; it need not be injective or preserve absence of tuples. The language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) accepts exactly such inputs with a homomorphism. Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed, and the empty structure maps to every template.

Encode \(n\) in unary and then each relation’s unary list length followed by binary tuple indices, in signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length; invalid encodings are rejected. Membership in NP means that there is a deterministic Turing verifier and a polynomial \(p\) such that a valid input is accepted exactly when it has a binary certificate of length at most \(p(L)\) accepted by the verifier within \(p(L)\) bit steps. The template and signature are fixed; no effective presentation or homomorphism oracle for the infinite domain is an input. No complexity separation is assumed.

An SNP sentence over the input signature \(\tau\) has form
\[\Phi=\exists S_1\cdots\exists S_t\ \forall x_1\cdots\forall x_q\ \psi,\]
where the \(S_j\) are fresh relation symbols of fixed finite positive arities and \(\psi\) is a quantifier-free first-order formula using input relations, the new relations, equality, Boolean connectives and the displayed individual variables. Truth constants are allowed. The formula, the numbers \(t,q\) and all arities are fixed independently of input size. On \(I\), the existential quantifiers choose relations on the same domain \([n]\); the universal quantifiers range over all tuples of input elements. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, constant naming input elements, or auxiliary larger universe. General arities are allowed: SNP is not restricted to unary second-order predicates. The empty-domain convention is the usual one for universal sentences, consistent with accepting the empty CSP input.

Exact SNP definability means \(I\models\Phi\) if and only if \(I\to\Gamma\) for every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\). There is no reduction or change of input signature hidden in this equivalence. A fixed SNP sentence has polynomial-size guessed relation tables and polynomially many universal tuples to check, so it always defines an NP problem. Arbitrary existential second-order sentences may contain alternating first-order quantifiers; restricting that part to a universal block is the additional requirement here.

For the known structural reformulation, a finite-signature structure \(C\) is finitely bounded if a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature satisfies
\[D\text{ embeds into }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D\]
for every finite \(D\). An embedding is an injective map preserving both relation membership and nonmembership, so the bounds are forbidden induced patterns. The age of \(C\) is the class of its finite induced substructures up to isomorphism. For signatures \(\tau\subseteq\sigma\), the reduct \(C\upharpoonright\tau\) forgets the symbols in \(\sigma\setminus\tau\) and keeps the same domain and remaining relations. No homogeneity or omega-categoricity is required. The representing reduct may differ from the original template; equality of their finite-instance CSPs is what matters.

The source classification direction concerns templates, or equivalently their finite-instance CSP classes. It does not specify an algorithm receiving finite descriptions of infinite structures. A countable representative suffices: choose one solution image for each satisfiable finite instance and take the induced substructure on their countable union.
answer_criterion: A precise completion criterion still requires selecting the additional structural characterization or effectiveness requirement intended beyond the known logical-to-forbidden-pattern representation. The source does not prescribe such a requirement. Merely restating SNP definability by existence of a finite universal expansion is insufficient to certify that this historical research direction is resolved; no particular stronger criterion is selected here.
statement_review_issue: The source asks which NP CSPs are SNP-definable, but gives no proposed structural invariant or required form of classification. Exact representation by reducts of finitely bounded structures is already known through a translation of the universal existential expansion; no checked later source identifies that reformulation as resolving the historical question. A completion criterion must specify what substantive new invariant or effectiveness requirement is sought beyond this known equivalence. Selecting one would add a target absent from the source.
context:
The following exact representation theorem is known:
\[\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{SNP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\sigma\supseteq\tau\ \exists C\ \bigl[C\text{ is countable and finitely bounded over finite }\sigma\ \land\ \operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)=\operatorname{CSP}(C\upharpoonright\tau)\bigr].\]
This equivalence is a structural reformulation of SNP definability, not a separately stated solution of the historical classification question. The equality is on all finite structures in the original signature. The LICS 2026 introduction explicitly identifies this class correspondence. It allows arbitrary finite bounds and auxiliary relations; homogeneity is not an extra condition.

For the forward direction, every CSP is closed under inverse homomorphisms and under disjoint unions. The monograph shows that an SNP sentence defining such a class can be chosen monotone and connected. Monotone means that input relations occur only negatively in clauses; connected means that each clause’s variables are connected through its negative relation literals. These are normal-form transformations of the given problem, not changes to the accepted inputs.

Consider all finite expanded structures satisfying the universal first-order part of that connected sentence. This class is closed under induced substructures, and connectedness makes it closed under disjoint unions. The disjoint union of one representative of each finite isomorphism type is therefore a countable structure whose age is exactly this class. Since the universal formula mentions only finitely many variables, its failures have finitely many minimal finite induced patterns, giving a finite bound list. Forgetting the guessed relations produces a template with exactly the original CSP.

Conversely, a CSP of a reduct of a finitely bounded structure is described in SNP by guessing equality classes for variables and the missing relational pattern on their prospective values. Universal clauses enforce congruence, the original positive constraints and avoidance of the finitely many forbidden induced patterns. The resulting quotient pattern embeds into the representing structure precisely when those constraints pass. This supplies finite universal certificates even when the domain of the representing template is infinite.

The representation concerns some template with the same CSP. It does not assert that the particular supplied template has a finitely bounded expansion, nor provide a uniform recognition algorithm for arbitrary infinite presentations. The 2008 question specifies neither of these stronger requirements. Choosing one, or choosing a particular algebraic invariant, would supply a new completion target rather than merely unpack its notation.

The monograph’s integer-successor example shows why omega-categoricity must not be added to this answer. Its CSP is definable in connected monotone SNP, but cannot be represented by an omega-categorical template with the same accepted finite structures. Thus SNP definability and the symmetry assumptions of infinite-domain dichotomy conjectures are distinct.

The 2026 paper separately studies extensional SNP and CSPs of finitely bounded structures before forgetting relations. These are distinct settings. Its discussion supplies the exact representation theorem above, but does not explicitly identify it as a resolution of the 2008 classification question. The distinction between a structural reformulation and the intended new classification therefore remains material.
why: This direction seeks to explain when general NP verification for a CSP can be replaced by finitely many guessed relations and universal local checks. The known forbidden-pattern reformulation connects syntax to infinite templates. The intended further classification must be specified before its exact significance and completion criterion can be assessed.
status_note: The 2008 source poses a broad classification direction. The checked 2021/January 2026 monograph and July 2026 LICS paper give an exact normal form and finite-pattern representation, but do not explicitly identify that reformulation as resolving this historical question. The intended substantive criterion beyond the known equivalence has not been specified, so neither resolved status nor a precise remaining open theorem is certified.
