title: Word equations with linear length constraints
importance_reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.
focus_reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
question_excerpt: Is satisfiability of word equations with linear constraints on total solution lengths decidable?
definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.
context:
The two ingredients are separately decidable: plain word equations by Makanin’s theorem and integer linear arithmetic by Presburger’s theorem. Their combination constrains both letter alignment and numerical size, and neither theorem alone settles their interaction.

Length identities can omit crucial content. For distinct letters \(a,b\), the word equation \(Xa=bX\) has no finite-word solution, although its induced length equality \(|X|+1=1+|X|\) is always satisfied. This illustrates why the target concerns a common word substitution, not merely a consistent length vector.

Restrictions on counts of individual letters, full Parikh vectors or additional quantifier alternation can yield different decidability results. Those predicates do not occur in the present input language. The distinction is explicit in Ciobanu’s survey.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on their solution lengths. Quadratic means each unknown appears at most twice across the equation. Their RP 2025 paper appeared online in November 2025; its proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. This restricted theorem does not cover an arbitrary system with unrestricted variable occurrences.

The IJCAR 2026 paper gives a sufficient termination condition and a partial converse for extended Nielsen transformations. The theorem concerns a specific procedure and a graph condition on an extended equation; it does not establish that every input of the unrestricted satisfiability problem is decidable. Its full preprint explicitly retains the general open question.

The checked July 2026 preprint states NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints over two letters. Its NEXP-completeness theorem concerns existential arithmetic with divisibility. These are distinct claims, and neither is a decision procedure or an undecidability proof for the current card.

The saved target is a conjunction, while that lower-bound corollary permits disjunctions. Finite expansion relates their decidability questions, but need not preserve polynomial input size; the corollary is therefore not presented here as a checked NEXP lower bound for the exact conjunction encoding. Allowing empty substitutions is likewise kept distinct from the preprint’s nonerasing convention.
why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.
status_note: The checked DLT 2024 survey and IJCAR 2026 paper/full preprint explicitly retain unrestricted decidability as open. The RP 2025 theorem is limited to quadratic two-unknown equations. July 2026 preprint v3 claims NEXP-hardness of a nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation, not decidability or a matching complexity upper bound for the current conjunction problem. The 16 September 2026 audit verified these scopes and found no matching resolution in its bounded search.
progress: 1977 onward: Makanin establishes decidability of plain word equations. Adding linear length constraints remains outside that theorem; the distinction is reviewed by Ciobanu. | 2024: Ciobanu’s survey explicitly separates the open length-constraint problem from undecidable letter-count and Parikh-image extensions. | 2025-11-05: Day and Konefal’s RP 2025 paper appears online, giving decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on solution lengths. The proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. | 2026-07-19: Version 3 of Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez claims NEXP-hardness for the nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation. Only its arithmetic-with-divisibility problem is asserted NEXP-complete. | 2026-07-24: Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 paper gives partial termination criteria for extended Nielsen transformations and explicitly retains general decidability as open. | 2026-09-16: Rechecked the original existential conjunction target, primary source models, restricted two-variable result, IJCAR termination theorem and July preprint’s separate Boolean/nonerasing lower-bound scope.
working_summary: Word equations require substitutions of finite strings that make all supplied concatenations identical. Here the same substitution must also satisfy a conjunction of integer linear constraints on total string lengths. The target is one always-terminating decision algorithm for arbitrary finite inputs, including empty substitutions and unrestricted variable occurrences. Known restricted decision results and partial termination criteria do not settle this combination, and stronger letter-count predicates describe a different problem. A resolution would establish whether complete exact solving is possible for this basic fragment of string constraints, before imposing efficiency requirements.

title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
importance_reason: The basic unresolved decidability boundary in modal unification, already in the minimal normal modal logic.
focus_reason: The basic unresolved decidability boundary in modal unification, already in the minimal normal modal logic.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.
context:
A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.
why: Determines whether automated reasoning can decide the existence of a validity-making substitution in the basic normal modal logic, despite the decidability of checking each individual instance and the poorly behaved structure of its unifiers.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No decision procedure or undecidability theorem for this exact basic-K problem was located. Beklemishev’s 2025 introduction explicitly states it as open. Nullary unification type, undecidability with extra modalities and 2025 decidability for K5 extensions do not settle it.
progress: 2006 / 2008: Unification is shown undecidable for K extended with a universal modality. | 2011 / 2015: Jeřábek proves nullary unification type for K, without deciding unifiability. | 2025: Most general unifiers become effectively computable for K5 extensions. | 2025: Beklemishev explicitly retains the basic-K decidability question as open.
working_summary: Basic modal logic K interprets formulas on arbitrary accessibility relations between possible worlds. The problem asks whether it is decidable that a finite formula has a substitution instance valid at every world of every such model. Substitutions act simultaneously on all input variables, may introduce new variables, and leave no designated parameters fixed. Frames may be finite or infinite, and no reflexivity or transitivity condition is imposed. The requested algorithm must halt on every input; its time and the size of a possible substitution have no prescribed bounds.

title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
importance_reason: A longstanding and foundational decidability boundary between tame additive arithmetic and number-theoretic predicates, with conditional definability of multiplication and direct links to prime-distribution conjectures.
formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
question_excerpt: Is Presburger arithmetic extended by the predicate for positive prime numbers decidable?
definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.
context:
Presburger arithmetic allows arbitrary first-order quantification but restricts its numerical operations to addition, order and fixed integer coefficients. Adding one decidable predicate can still change decidability of the full theory: the issue is the interaction with unbounded quantifiers, not the cost of evaluating that predicate at a known integer.

The source works over integers and writes an order-based twin-prime sentence. Accordingly, this card includes order and takes primes to be positive. For example, the twin-prime assertion is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\le y\land\mathrm{Pr}(y)\land\mathrm{Pr}(y+2))\).

The source also invokes Goldbach’s conjecture. Its even-input restriction must be explicit: one correct sentence is \(\forall n\,(n\ge2\Rightarrow\exists p\,\exists q\,(\mathrm{Pr}(p)\land\mathrm{Pr}(q)\land p+q=n+n))\). The printed illustrative sentence on p. 29 omits that restriction; the open decision question itself does not depend on this typo.

Bateman, Jockusch and Woods prove, assuming the linear case of Schinzel’s hypothesis, that multiplication is definable in the natural-number structure with addition and primes, yielding undecidability. The nonnegative integers are definable in the ordered integer structure, so this conditional obstruction applies to the present target too. The hypothesis is essential to the stated theorem.

Dickson’s prime-tuples conjecture is the assertion that finitely many integer affine forms with positive leading coefficients take simultaneous prime values infinitely often whenever no prime divides their product for every integer argument. The card does not assume this conjecture.

Kaplan and Shelah prove conditional decidability for the unordered additive integer structure whose predicate includes both primes and their negatives. Their introduction explicitly retains the number-theoretic assumption on the ordered undecidability result, although the abstract abbreviates that qualification. The absence of order and the symmetric prime convention are substantive differences.

The 2024 survey explicitly retains the present decision question. The September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; this is dated evidence and a search limit, not a proof that the question remains open.
why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.
status_note: The FSTTCS 2024 survey explicitly leaves this full decision problem open. The checked 1993 theorem is conditional on linear Schinzel/Dickson prime-tuples assumptions, and the 2017 conditional positive result uses the different unordered symmetric-prime structure. The 16 September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; source-open is a dated attribution, not certification of present openness.
progress: 1993: Under the linear Schinzel hypothesis, multiplication is definable over natural numbers with addition and primes, giving conditional undecidability. | 2017: Kaplan–Shelah publish conditional decidability for the different unordered additive integer structure with the symmetric prime predicate. | 2024: Chistikov explicitly records decidability of Presburger arithmetic with the prime predicate as open. | 2026-09-16: Checked the ordered positive-prime convention, the conditional hypotheses and the natural/integer transfer; no matching unconditional resolution was verified.
working_summary: Presburger arithmetic describes the standard integers using addition and order and has a decidable first-order theory. This question adds a predicate for positive primes and asks for one algorithm deciding every sentence, with arbitrary quantifier alternation. The resulting language can express prime-pattern claims such as twin primes and Goldbach’s conjecture. A classical undecidability result is conditional on a prime-tuples conjecture, while a conditional decidability theorem concerns a different unordered structure. An unconditional resolution would locate a major boundary between effective additive arithmetic and quantified number-theoretic reasoning.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
importance_reason: A basic unresolved operation in knowledge compilation, with consequences for checking and comparing compiled knowledge.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.

Equivalence concerns the same assignment in the two circuits; it does not allow renaming variables separately to obtain isomorphism. The inputs may have different numbers of gates and may mention different subsets of \(X\). Logical nonequivalence means that at least one assignment makes their outputs differ. Equal numbers of satisfying assignments do not by themselves establish equivalence. The only required output is the decision bit; construction of a distinguishing assignment is not an additional task.

For comparison with the known randomized result, a one-sided randomized equivalence test can always accept equivalent circuits while rejecting each nonequivalent pair with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time using independent random bits. The target here removes randomness entirely. A probabilistic test, even with arbitrarily small failure probability, does not meet its guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the deterministic polynomial-time existence claim in the stated promise model. A positive answer must give one uniform algorithm, prove exact equivalence decisions on all promised pairs, and establish a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm; it need not produce a single pair that defeats every algorithm. A randomized algorithm, a procedure requiring a common variable tree, or a hardness result for arbitrary DNNFs without determinism does not by itself settle this problem. Neither does hardness of verifying a proposed conjunction of two circuits, which is a different input-output relation.
context:
The 2026 source explicitly leaves equivalence across different variable trees open even for structured representations. This card retains the broader general d-DNNF question, independently stated in the knowledge-compilation map; it does not attribute that broader formulation solely to the structured-circuit paper.

Darwiche and Huang give a one-sided randomized polynomial-time equivalence test for general d-DNNFs. Their analysis includes a polynomial bound on the bit length of arithmetic values; the algorithmic claim is stronger than merely bounding the number of unit-cost arithmetic operations.

The knowledge-compilation map distinguishes exact model counting, equivalence and entailment. Efficient counting does not automatically decide whether two represented sets of assignments coincide, and a common variable order or compatible structured decomposition is an additional restriction.

The 2026 paper establishes efficiently checkable restricted restructuring steps while leaving the one-shot comparison across arbitrary trees open. Its hardness discussion for checking a conjunction relation concerns three representations and does not establish hardness of the two-circuit equivalence problem.
why: Equivalence testing checks whether two compiled representations express the same Boolean knowledge despite different decompositions. A deterministic polynomial-time test would support exact comparison and verification of representation changes without a probabilistic failure event. The gap between known randomized testing and the deterministic target also links this concrete compilation task to broader derandomization questions.
status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: Darwiche–Marquis definitions, Definition 4.3 and Table 5; Darwiche–Huang Theorems 2.1 and 3.1 and bit-length analysis; Berkholz–Micun arXiv v2 Sections 2.1, 3 and 6. The known general test is randomized, and the 2026 paper retains a restricted cross-tree version as open. A bounded subsequent-work check found no matching deterministic general algorithm or impossibility theorem.
progress: 2002-06-07: Darwiche and Huang’s technical report establishes randomized polynomial-time testing for general d-DNNFs. | 2026-06-23: The second arXiv submission of the structured-circuit proof-system paper retains unrestricted cross-tree equivalence as open; the accessible manuscript is dated 24 August 2026.
working_summary: The problem asks whether two explicit d-DNNF circuits can be tested for exact Boolean equivalence in deterministic polynomial time. Decomposability requires disjoint variable sets at conjunctions, while determinism requires mutually exclusive inputs at disjunctions. The circuits may use unrelated internal decompositions and need not share a variable tree. Randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing is known, but its possibility of error does not satisfy this target. A resolution would clarify the cost of comparing and verifying succinct compiled Boolean representations.

title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
importance_reason: A concrete bridge between SAT solving and proof complexity: it isolates the computational role of restarts while allowing helpful search choices. The significance comes from the unresolved comparison with general resolution and explicit specialist discussion, not from an unspecified explanation of solver performance.
formal: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution in the asserting-learning model below? Precisely, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a constant \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every finite CNF formula \(F\) and every valid resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), on the explicit binary input \((F,\pi)\) of length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same \(F\), without restarts, of at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bits? The single program and polynomial must work for all formulas and supplied proofs.
question_excerpt: Can greedy clause learning without restarts polynomially simulate general resolution?
definitions:
Literals are \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\); clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives \((C\setminus \{x\})\cup (D\setminus \{\neg x\})\) from clauses C containing x and D containing \(\neg x\). A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially \(D=F\) and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with \(\pi\); mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

The input promise is that the explicitly recorded resolution derivation is a valid refutation of the supplied formula; correctness is required for every promised input, including a formula already containing the empty clause. Invalid encodings or derivations may be rejected. All computation and output costs use ordinary sequential bit time. Choices made by the translator are deterministic and fully recorded, with exact clause and Boolean semantics; no randomness, numerical approximation, oracle or nonuniform advice is available. The model permits a conflict-justified backjump to level zero, which does not count as an independent restart.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed uniform p-simulation or its logical negation. A positive answer must formalize the finite clause encoding and resolution proof checker, the stated CDCL state and transition system, and a computable translator with a polynomial bit-time bound, proving that every valid input proof yields a trace on the original formula ending in the permitted UNSAT state. The trace must obey conflict and propagation priority, trivial asserting analysis, assertion-level backjumps, deletion restrictions and the absence of restarts. A negative answer must rule out all such uniform polynomial-time translators; a lower bound for one fixed heuristic or a different backtracking policy is insufficient. Existence of polynomial-size traces alone does not supply the required efficient translator. Conditional theorems settle only their stated conditional variants unless their premises are also proved. No proof-assistant verification of either answer is claimed by this editorial review.
context:
Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes no-restart simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the greedy comparison. Such changes alter which search traces are legal, so those positive results do not satisfy the transitions written here.

Buss–Thapen construct formulas with short resolution proofs whose height must nevertheless be large. They discuss these as candidates for separating pool resolution from general resolution, explicitly state that they cannot prove that separation, and give polynomial-size pool proofs for a simpler variant. This is related progress, not a checked identification of pool resolution with every operational CDCL model.

The SAT 2026 graph-backtracking paper proves correctness and termination of a generalized solver and shows how suitable weights reproduce chronological and nonchronological backtracking. Its more general repair operation can retain assignments outside the ordinary retained prefix. These are simulations between backtracking policies; they do not supply the requested translation of arbitrary resolution proofs into the unchanged greedy no-restart model.

The bounded search through 16 September 2026 found no checked proof of the stated p-simulation or its negation. The dated specialist open discussion and subsequent related papers support retaining the target; this search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.
why: Restarts are a central operation in modern clause-learning SAT solvers. This target isolates whether their removal causes an unavoidable loss in proof generation even when the solver may choose decisions, propagation order and learned asserting clauses with full knowledge of a supplied resolution proof. A resolution would connect an exact operational restriction of search with the polynomial simulation structure studied in proof complexity.
status_note: The 2022 specialist discussion leaves the greedy no-restart comparison unresolved. The checked Buss–Thapen report explicitly does not prove its proposed related separation; its journal issue is 2026 but the report dates to January 2024. July 2026 graph-backtracking results concern a generalized policy and do not give the requested p-simulation on the retained model. A bounded search through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is dated source-based status, not exhaustive certification.
progress: 2017: The Vinyals thesis specifies a greedy operational CDCL proof system with explicit conflict analysis, deletion and restart policies. | 2022: The specialist exposition distinguishes the no-restart question from known non-greedy and preprocessing simulations. | 2024-01-02: The Buss–Thapen ECCC report studies resolution size–height tradeoffs and unproved candidate pool-resolution separations; its later journal issue is dated 2026. | 2026-07-16: The SAT paper proves properties of generalized graph backtracking and policy simulations, without a resolution simulation for this unchanged model. | 2026-09-16: The audit preserves every operational restriction and the assessed score, makes the uniform bit-time quantifiers and Lean criterion explicit, and checks the distinct scope of newer results.
working_summary: A resolution refutation derives the empty clause by repeatedly combining clauses on opposite literals. This card asks whether any such supplied proof can be translated in deterministic polynomial time into a greedy clause-learning search on the same formula without restarts. The legal search must process conflicts and unit clauses immediately and may backjump only as justified by a learned asserting clause. Known simulations with relaxed propagation or preprocessing, and newer generalized backtracking results, do not establish this exact claim. A resolution would show whether restarts change the polynomial proof-generating power of idealized greedy SAT search.

title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
importance_reason: A minimal and longstanding unresolved termination problem in rewriting theory.
formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
definitions: ['The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \\(\\varepsilon\\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.', 'One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \\(\\ell\\) and replaces it with \\(r\\), preserving the prefix \\(x\\) and suffix \\(y\\). If \\(\\ell=\\varepsilon\\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \\(\\ell=r\\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \\(\\ell\\).', 'Global termination means that for every \\(w_0\\in\\Sigma^{*}\\) there is no function \\(w:\\mathbb{N}\\to\\Sigma^{*}\\) with first value \\(w_0\\) and \\(w_i\\to w_{i+1}\\) for all \\(i\\geq0\\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.', 'Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.']
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.
context:
Geser’s paper gives decidability for grid rules: there is a letter \(b\) occurring on the left whose count on the right is no larger. It explicitly distinguishes this substantial subclass from the unresolved arbitrary one-rule problem.

RTA Problem 21 distinguishes the string case from the more general question for a single linear term-rewriting rule. This card asks only about replacements of contiguous substrings.

Kfoury’s August 2026 note restates global one-rule termination as Open Problem 8. It is a source-status update, rather than a new proof of either answer.
why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.
status_note: The 2002 primary paper and the August 2026 authored note present arbitrary one-rule termination as unresolved. A bounded check on 13 September 2026 found no later resolution. The note and historical proofs have not been independently verified; source-open status is not an exhaustive certification.
progress: 2002: Geser proves decidability for grid rules, while retaining the general one-rule question. | 2026-08-19: Open Problem 8 of the new note again asks for decidability of arbitrary one-rule global termination.
working_summary: A one-rule string system repeatedly replaces one fixed substring by another. The question is whether an algorithm can decide if every reduction sequence from every finite starting word eventually stops. Replacement positions are unrestricted, and the rule and alphabet are part of the input. Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open. The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.

title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
importance_reason: Would bound the hidden size of solutions and support efficient compressed certificates for a central string-constraint problem.
formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
definitions:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) consists of all finite sequences of its letters, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Multiplication is concatenation, and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity. The length \(|w|\) is the number of letters in the sequence \(w\), with \(|\varepsilon|=0\). Distinct constant letters are distinct symbols, not variables or numbers. The alphabet may have any finite cardinality; if it is empty, its only word is \(\varepsilon\).

An equation is a pair of explicitly written words \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Each variable and each constant occurrence counts as one symbol in the equation size \(n\). No compressed input, binary-encoded repeat operator, regular-language membership condition, length constraint, inequality, involution or cancellation operation is supplied. Exponent notation in an example of an equation is only shorthand for its fully expanded string, and its expanded length is charged. Variables may occur arbitrarily many times and may appear on either or both sides.

A solution is a monoid morphism \(h:(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every \(a\in\Sigma\) and satisfies \(h(u)=h(v)\). Equivalently, choose one word \(h(x)\in\Sigma^*\) for each variable, substitute the same word at every occurrence, and concatenate in the original order. Empty substitutions are allowed, and no letter outside \(\Sigma\) may occur in a substitution. This is solving an equation in a free monoid, not in a free group or a semigroup with mandatory nonempty substitutions.

For a satisfiable equation, define
\[m(u,v)=\min_{h:\,h(u)=h(v)}\ \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|.\]
The minimum exists because the feasible lengths form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers. The claim is \(m(u,v)\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\) for all satisfiable equations. It asks for at least one bounded solution to each equation, not for a bound on every solution. An equation can have infinitely many solutions with unbounded lengths and still satisfy the proposed shortest-solution bound.

The source also measures a solution by the length of the common expanded word \(h(u)=h(v)\). For each solution with \(M=\max_x|h(x)|\), every occurring variable image is a factor of that common word, and
\[M\le |h(u)|\le n\max(1,M).\]
These inequalities also cover the no-variable case using \(M=0\). Thus existence of a singly exponential bound on the shortest common-word length and the displayed variable-image bound are equivalent after changing the universal polynomial in the exponent. The card does not assert equality of these two minimum-length quantities.

The negative answer is the quantified assertion that for every pair of positive integers \(c,k\), some satisfiable equation has no solution meeting \(\max_x|h(x)|\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\). It is not enough to exhibit an exponential-length solution when a shorter one exists, or to beat one chosen polynomial exponent. No efficient construction of a solution or of a counterexample family is part of this nonconstructive length question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the universal singly exponential bound. A proof must provide fixed positive integers \(c,k\) and prove the bound for all satisfiable equations under the free-monoid and explicit-symbol conventions. A refutation must prove that every such polynomial-exponent bound fails. Bounds for a fixed number of variables, bounded occurrence counts, a restricted equation family or only compressed solution sizes do not settle the general claim. Proving membership of satisfiability in NP by an unrelated argument does not by itself establish this specific length bound.
context:
Conjecture B concerns the length of a shortest solution. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 establish that this conjecture would imply the separate NP-membership conjecture for satisfiability. The implication depends on the proved compression property; an exponentially long explicit witness alone is not a polynomial-size certificate.

The source fixes letters and permits variable substitutions in the free monoid, hence allows erasing substitutions. The card retains its explicit occurrence-based equation size and uses a universal polynomial exponent to resolve the phrase singly exponential.

Jeż gives an independent proof of a doubly exponential general bound on the shortest common-word length. A bound of that scale does not establish the single-exponential claim, and bounds on repeated periodic blocks are not automatically bounds on the full solution length.

The 2026 paper gives stronger parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. It still describes membership in NP as open for unrestricted word equations. The fixed-variable, constant-free structural result does not cover the arbitrary equations in this card.
why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

working_summary: A word equation asks for consistent substitutions of finite strings that make two concatenations identical. The conjecture says that every satisfiable equation of size n has some solution whose variable images have length at most two to a fixed polynomial in n. The bound must hold uniformly over all finite alphabets and arbitrarily many variable occurrences, with empty substitutions allowed. title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
importance_reason: The exact complexity of word equations is a foundational boundary for string constraints, combinatorics on words, and automated reasoning.
formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
question_excerpt: The original sources ask for the complexity of satisfiability of equations between words with variables. The user selected the specific remaining question of NP membership and consolidated the overlapping word-unification record here.
definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge1\), the constant alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{a_1,\ldots,a_a\}\). Its free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as the operation. Concatenation is associative and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity; distinct letters do not commute by assumption.

The variable set is \(\mathcal X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_r\}\), disjoint from \(\Sigma\), where \(r\ge0\). An equation is a pair \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Both sides are explicitly written token sequences. A solution assigns one word \(\sigma(X_i)\in\Sigma^*\) to each variable, fixes every constant letter, and extends by concatenation. The equation is satisfiable exactly when \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\) for some assignment. All occurrences of a variable receive the same word. Empty words, repeated variables, variables on both sides, and equations with empty sides are allowed. There are no length constraints, regular-language restrictions, inverse symbols or inequalities.

One precise binary encoding is as follows. Write \(1^a0\,1^r0\,1^{\ell_u}0\,1^{\ell_v}0\), where \(\ell_u=|u|\) and \(\ell_v=|v|\) count tokens. Follow this header by all tokens of \(u\) and then all tokens of \(v\). Each token is encoded in \(b=\lceil\log_2(a+r+1)\rceil\) bits: code \(i\) for \(a_i\) and code \(a+j\) for \(X_j\). Codes outside \(1,\ldots,a+r\) are invalid. There must be exactly \(\ell_u+\ell_v\) token blocks and no trailing data. Thus
\[
N=a+r+\ell_u+\ell_v+4+b(\ell_u+\ell_v).
\]
This explicit encoding fixes bit complexity without allowing compressed input equations.

\(\mathrm{NP}\) is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates accepted by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier, with precisely the soundness and completeness quantified above. A certificate is any finite binary string. It need not contain the substituted words explicitly, and no particular compressed representation is prescribed. A satisfiable input must have some short accepting certificate; an unsatisfiable input must have none.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must specify the verifier and prove the polynomial time and certificate bounds together with soundness and completeness for every input. A negative answer must prove that no such verifier exists; failure of one certificate format or long explicit solutions is insufficient. This binary target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Results only for boundedly many variables, bounded occurrences, or added constraints do not decide the full statement.
context:
A variable stands for an entire finite word, not for one letter. For example, an equation can require two occurrences of the same unknown word to match material appearing at different positions on the other side. Concatenation couples the lengths and contents of all substitutions.

Makanin established decidability, and later work reduced the space needed to decide satisfiability. The 1998 RTA question predates the polynomial-space improvement, so its much larger upper bound is historical provenance rather than the current frontier.

Jeż’s 2017 theorem places satisfiability in nondeterministic linear space measured in input bits. This implies membership in PSPACE, the class decidable using polynomial working space. A space bound alone need not limit the number of computation steps to a polynomial, so it does not supply NP membership.

An explicit substitution may be much longer than the input equation. The NP question is therefore about succinct evidence that can be checked quickly, not about requiring a short fully expanded solution. Existing work on compressed solutions explains this distinction, but the card does not mandate any particular evidence format.

Saarela’s 2026 theorem simplifies parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. Its introduction still lists NP membership for general word equations as open. A result about the structure of that restricted solution set does not settle the unrestricted decision problem.

The June 2026 preprint claims stronger hardness for formulas that combine word equations with length constraints. Those extra arithmetic constraints change the input language. The claim therefore does not establish a lower bound excluding NP for plain equations, and its full proof was not independently audited in this review.

The earlier two atlas records used different historical names for overlapping complexity questions. This card is now the single active NP-membership target. The duplicate’s source and provenance remain available, while the broader request for an exact complexity classification is no longer the benchmark question.
why: Word equations are a basic model of string constraints and associative unification. Their decidability is established, but the gap between NP-hardness and polynomial-space algorithms leaves the complexity of short verifiable evidence unresolved. NP membership would place the unrestricted satisfiability problem at the familiar NP-complete boundary.
status_note: Ordinary word-equation satisfiability is NP-hard and decidable in nondeterministic linear space, hence in PSPACE. Saarela’s STACS 2026 introduction explicitly identifies membership in NP as open. The newer length-constraint hardness claim concerns a larger problem. The user selected NP membership and merged TCS-0171 into this card on 16 September 2026. No resolution was found in the bounded review through that date.

The selected target is whether satisfiability of unrestricted plain word equations belongs to NP. A positive answer needs polynomial-size certificates and one polynomial-time verifier, without prescribing how a solution is represented. title: Decidability of fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching
importance_reason: The remaining fixed-order boundary between known decidability and undecidability for pure higher-order beta matching, sharpened by a recent mechanized undecidability construction and an explicit 2026 open statement.
formal: Is fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching decidable in the source's closed range formulation? Given finite simple types \(\sigma,\tau\) and closed simply typed lambda terms \(F:\sigma\to\tau\) and \(N:\tau\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\), decide whether \[\exists M\;\bigl(\varnothing\vdash M:\sigma\ \land\ F\,M=_\beta N\bigr).\] The unknown \(M\) is a finite closed term. One deterministic Turing machine must halt and decide this predicate for every such input, with no time bound. Type order starts at one, exactly as in the source.
question_excerpt: With the ground type assigned order one, is beta-matching decidable when the unknown term has type of order at most five?
definitions:
Simple types are the finite trees \(A::=\iota\mid A\to A\), over one fixed ground atom \(\iota\); arrows associate to the right. Their order is \(\operatorname{ord}(\iota)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(A\to B)=\max(\operatorname{ord}(A)+1,\operatorname{ord}(B))\). Thus \(\iota\to\iota\) has order two. The bound five applies to the type \(\sigma\) of the term to be instantiated, rather than to \(\sigma\to\tau\) or to every type in the input derivations; \(\tau\) has no independent order bound. This is the convention made explicit for the order-six construction in the August 2026 source. A convention starting at zero shifts all these order numbers down by one.

Terms are finite expressions \(t::=x\mid(t\,t)\mid\lambda x.t\), up to consistent renaming of bound variables. There are no constants, recursion operators, polymorphic types, additional rewrite rules or extensional equations. A typing context \(\Gamma\) assigns simple types to finitely many distinct variables. Typing has exactly the variable rule \(x:A\in\Gamma\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash x:A\), application \(\Gamma\vdash t:A\to B,\ \Gamma\vdash u:A\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash tu:B\), and abstraction \(\Gamma,x:A\vdash t:B\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.t:A\to B\). Closed means no free variables, as witnessed by the empty context. The input includes finite type trees, term trees and typing derivations for \(F\) and \(N\); the finite encodings use binary variable/de Bruijn indices and explicit trees. A purported input failing typing, closedness or the order bound may be rejected. These syntactic conditions are decidable.

A beta step replaces \((\lambda x.t)u\) by the capture-avoiding substitution \(t[x:=u]\) in any subterm, including underneath lambda abstractions. The relation \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps, modulo bound-variable renaming. The eta equation \(\lambda x.f x=f\), where \(x\) is not free in \(f\), is not an allowed additional equation. The known equivalence of beta convertibility with equality of beta normal forms does not require candidate terms to be eta-expanded. The substitution occurs only at the unknown argument of \(F\); the closed target \(N\) is fixed. The same machine handles all allowed types and all finite term sizes, including types with no closed inhabitant. It returns exact YES/NO answers, with no oracle, random error or numerical tolerance.
answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete Lean proof of existence of a total computable decider for the displayed predicate or a proof that none exists. A positive answer must formalize the pure simply typed syntax, typing, the order-one ground convention, capture-avoiding beta conversion and the algorithm's termination and correctness for every allowed instance. A negative answer must prove noncomputability while keeping \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\); undecidability using order-six candidate types does not qualify. Neither a beta-eta decision theorem nor a restriction to eta-long candidates answers the beta-only question. This review does not claim to port or rerun the cited Rocq/Coq development in Lean.
context:
Ordinary matching holds the target fixed and chooses values only for the unknown part of the pattern. In the source’s range presentation, the pattern is the supplied function F, and the unknown is its closed argument M. This avoids changing the problem into two-sided unification.

The 2025 paper proves unrestricted beta-matching undecidable and reports that the construction reaches candidate type order six. The 2026 extended version makes this precise in Remark 3.24 as an equation for the order of σ_R. Applying the number five to F’s whole function type would therefore use a different convention.

The August 2026 conclusion records fourth-order beta-matching as decidable, citing Padovani, and expressly leaves fifth order open. The present review checked that source attribution and its numbering; it does not claim an independent proof audit of the older low-order theorem.

Stirling proves decidability of higher-order matching with beta-eta equivalence. That equality identifies a function with its eta expansion, so the theorem does not resolve the beta-only target. Both the 2025 and 2026 sources explicitly warn about this distinction.

The recent undecidability proof is reported as mechanized in the Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs, using the Rocq prover in the extended version. A certified theorem at order six is relevant progress and still does not settle the lower order-five case. No verification run of that artifact was performed during this review.

The 11 August 2026 revision is a more recent explicit open-status source than the imported conference passage. The bounded September search found no checked subsequent resolution; absence from that search is not an independent theorem of openness.
why: Matching is a central restricted form of higher-order unification, with uses in rewriting and symbolic reasoning. The fifth-order boundary asks exactly how much higher-order functional structure is needed for beta-only matching to encode undecidable behavior. It also exposes the substantive effect of extensional eta equality: a change in the equality relation, rather than just the input size, changes the general decidability result.
status_note: The FSCD 2025 source and its 11 August 2026 extended v2 explicitly leave beta-matching at order five open, with ground type order one. Remark 3.24 identifies σ, the candidate term type, as the bounded order in the order-six negative construction. The bounded 16 September search found no matching subsequent resolution. Older low-order decidability is reported with the source attribution; the cited formal development was not rerun.

working_summary: Beta-matching asks whether a supplied simply typed lambda function maps some closed term to a fixed target up to beta conversion. This card bounds the unknown term’s type at order five, counting the ground type as order one. It asks for a total decision procedure over all finite inputs in this class. The August 2026 source retains this case between a reported decidable order-four case and mechanized undecidability at order six, while beta-eta matching is a different decidable problem. A resolution would locate the exact fixed-order boundary for beta-only higher-order matching.

title: Polynomial-time equivalence of free binary decision diagrams
importance_reason: A longstanding knowledge-compilation and branching-program question, separating deterministic exact equivalence from a known one-sided randomized polynomial-time algorithm and from stronger circuit classes.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for equivalence of two explicitly given free binary decision diagrams? In full quantifiers, are there a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), constants \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid pair \((B_1,B_2)\), of total binary encoding length \(L\), the machine halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and returns YES exactly when \[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_{B_1}(a)=f_{B_2}(a),\] where \(X\) is the union of the variable labels appearing in the two inputs? No shared variable order is promised.
question_excerpt: Does the FBDD representation support polynomial-time equivalence testing?
definitions:
A free binary decision diagram (FBDD) is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph. Each nonterminal vertex is labelled by a Boolean variable and has exactly two outgoing edges, one marked 0 and one marked 1; their targets may coincide. A terminal vertex has no outgoing edge and is labelled by the output bit 0 or 1. All vertices can be taken reachable from the root. On every directed root-to-terminal path, each variable occurs at most once. Different paths, and the two different input diagrams, may inspect variables in different orders. In particular no fixed global linear order or common graph ordering is part of the input. Redundant tests and shared subgraphs are permitted; the diagrams need not be reduced or isomorphic.

For an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\), start at the root and at a vertex labelled \(x\) follow its edge marked \(a(x)\); acyclicity leads to a terminal, whose label is \(f_B(a)\). Variables absent from a diagram do not affect its value. Constant diagrams consisting of one terminal and the case \(X=\varnothing\) are included. The input is an explicit finite vertex table giving the root, each node's type and label, and its two successor indices when present. Identifiers, labels and indices are binary encoded, and \(L\) counts all bits in both tables. Inputs are promised to meet the graph and path conditions. All arithmetic, preprocessing and reading costs belong to the ordinary sequential deterministic bit-time bound; no unit-cost manipulation of unbounded integers, oracle, random coins or nonuniform advice is allowed. One program and one polynomial work for all pairs. Correctness is exact on every assignment, not agreement on most assignments or numerical approximation. Only the YES/NO equivalence answer is required; canonicalization or construction of a combined diagram is not an additional output.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that such a uniform polynomial-time equivalence decider exists, including the graph semantics, input encoding, runtime and both correctness directions, or prove the negation of the displayed quantified claim. The negative target rules out every deterministic polynomial-time machine on the promised FBDD input class; failure of one graph comparison or one representation-conversion method is insufficient. A randomized polynomial-time test or a deterministic test requiring a common ordering does not meet the full target. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional version unless its premise is proved. This review supplies no Lean proof of either answer.
context:
An FBDD records a branching computation that tests a variable at most once on each path. It generalizes an ordered binary decision diagram by allowing the order to vary between branches. Shared subgraphs make its explicit representation potentially much smaller than the full truth table.

Darwiche–Marquis Table 5 marks equivalence for FBDDs as unknown. This is distinct from entailment between diagrams and from constructing their conjunction; the map treats these as separate operations. The card retains equivalence alone.

Darwiche–Huang give randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing for FBDDs and even for general d-DNNFs. For every fixed equivalent pair the test accepts with certainty; for every fixed inequivalent pair it incorrectly accepts with probability at most one half. This is the one-sided-error class coRP, and their bit-length analysis makes the polynomial-time claim an ordinary finite-arithmetic claim.

That error statement is conditioned on the fixed input, not a posterior probability that the input is equivalent after a positive answer. The source’s informal confidence wording is therefore expressed here as the precise one-sided algorithmic guarantee. The requested deterministic answer admits no such error.

The 2026 structured-circuit paper discusses hardness of verifying a join rule for FBDDs: testing whether a third represented function equals the conjunction of two others. That is a different, three-diagram operation. Its hardness is not presented as a lower bound for the two-diagram equivalence question.

Every FBDD has a polynomial-size translation into deterministic decomposable negation normal form. Thus a deterministic general d-DNNF equivalence algorithm would also solve this card; an FBDD-only algorithm would not by itself settle that broader question. The related cards retain those different targets.

The September 2026 bounded search checked the foundational map, the randomized theorem and the newer proof-system discussion, without finding a matching deterministic solution or impossibility theorem. The dated unknown table cell is not an exhaustive certificate of present openness.
why: FBDDs allow different branches to choose different variable orders and can be much more compact than ordered diagrams. Reliable equivalence testing is needed to compare independently compiled representations or optimized versions of a Boolean function. The question asks whether that representational flexibility can coexist with deterministic exact polynomial-time comparison, beyond the known randomized guarantee.

The 2026 proof-system discussion concerns stronger join verification and different structured formats, not a checked resolution of two-FBDD deterministic equivalence. A bounded primary-source search through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; source-open records the dated question, not exhaustive present-status certification.
