working_summary: First-order model checking evaluates a vertex-quantified logical sentence on an explicitly given finite graph. The question asks for a uniform deterministic algorithm on each hereditary effectively monadically dependent class, with computable parameter dependence and a sentence-independent graph-size exponent. Effective monadic dependence bounds the powerset graphs obtainable through short formulas with arbitrary unary vertex markings. The algorithm receives no graph decomposition or class-membership certificate, and must work for all sentences on its fixed class. Hereditary independent classes have a hardness theorem and effectively stable classes have algorithms, while the July 2026 radius-one results leave the full positive direction open.

title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.
focus_reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.
formal:
Does there exist a total deterministic algorithm which, given any finite conjunctive query \(q\), decides whether all distinct answers to \(q\) can be enumerated on every finite database \(D\) with \(O_q(N)\) preprocessing time and \(O_q(1)\) worst-case delay?

Self-joins and projection are allowed. Here \(N\) is the database size defined below; the enumeration model is the specified deterministic word-RAM. The classifier has no prescribed running-time bound.
question_excerpt: The source asks for a fine-grained understanding of enumeration for conjunctive queries with self-joins, extending the classical self-join-free tractability picture. This card retains the explicit effective question of deciding which fixed queries admit linear preprocessing and constant delay, in the source’s permissive memory model.
definitions:
A conjunctive query is finite syntax
\[
q(\bar x)=\exists\bar y\;\bigwedge_{i=1}^{s}R_i(\bar z_i).
\]
The head \(\bar x\) is an ordered list of distinct variables, and \(\bar y\) lists the other variables. Each variable occurs in an atom. Each relation symbol has one fixed positive integer arity within the query, and the length of each argument list agrees with it. A symbol may occur in several atoms (a self-join); a variable may repeat within an atom. There are no constants, negation, disequalities, aggregation, or additional constraints on the database. All relation arities and the complete formula are part of the classifier input, not fixed globally. An empty conjunction has no variables and is the constantly true Boolean query.

A database for the query has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for any integer \(n\ge0\), and explicitly lists each relation \(R^D\subseteq[n]^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\). Each tuple occurs at most once in its relation list; list order is arbitrary. Domain elements outside all relations are permitted. Define the word size of the data by
\[
N=1+n+\sum_R\operatorname{arity}(R)\,|R^D|.
\]
All tuple entries and \(n\) are provided as binary integers. In particular, the domain-size contribution to the resource parameter is \(n\), not merely its binary encoding length. No succinct relation representation or data-access oracle is provided.

An assignment maps query variables to domain elements. It satisfies an atom exactly when the resulting tuple belongs to that relation. The answer set \(q(D)\) consists of head tuples having at least one satisfying extension to \(\bar y\). Different witnesses for the same head tuple give just one answer. An empty head gives either no answer or the one empty tuple, according to whether the query is false or true.

For a fixed query, an enumerator is a finite deterministic word-RAM program, with constants \(B,C\ge1\) independent of the database; \(B\) is an integer. Its word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits. The address universe contains \(2^w\) initially zero cells. Each read, write, indirect access, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient or remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or shift costs one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return results modulo \(2^w\); a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger values occupy multiple words with all operations charged. No random instruction, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, database-specific advice or oracle is available.

Every accessed cell and every output operation is charged. Unused addresses require no initialization. There is no further requirement that memory used in preprocessing be linear, or that enumeration use only constant additional memory. The fixed exponent implicit in the address universe may depend on the query and algorithm. Writing an answer writes its head coordinates, or one marker for the empty tuple; the output is append-only.

The program first finishes a preprocessing phase of at most \(CN\) operations, then enumerates exactly \(q(D)\) in any order without repetition and halts. After preprocessing, the time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to halting is at most \(C\). If there are no answers, it must halt within \(C\) operations after preprocessing. The same constants and program must work on every database for that query.

The classifier is a deterministic Turing machine on a full finite encoding of query syntax, with relation names, variable names and arities encoded by finite binary strings. It halts on every valid query and says yes exactly when an enumerator and constants as above exist; malformed encodings may be rejected. Its input is \(q\), not a database. It need not produce an enumerator or the constants, and its running time has no required bound. The property being classified is actual, unconditional existence of an enumerator. A classification under an unproved complexity hypothesis is not silently substituted for that property. This effective existence proposition is the previously selected precise version of the source’s broader classification request.
answer_criterion:
Give a total classifier and a complete Lean-checked proof of its correctness for every query in the stated syntax and enumeration model, or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such total classifier exists. A positive answer need not effectively construct the enumerators whose existence it classifies.

An algorithm for only a restricted query family, or sufficient and necessary conditions leaving other queries unclassified, is not complete. Exhibiting a query without efficient enumeration does not refute the existence of a classifier: a correct classifier may reject that query. Conditional exclusions must retain their hypotheses and do not by themselves establish an unconditional answer.
context:
For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y\,R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for endpoint pairs linked through some intermediate element. Many choices of the intermediate element can witness the same answer, which still has to be printed just once.

The query is fixed while the database varies. Query-dependent constants are therefore allowed, even though the separate classifier receives the query as its input. Its task is to decide an algorithm-existence property, rather than to enumerate answers itself.

A query hypergraph has variables as vertices and the variable set of each atom as a hyperedge. It is acyclic if the hyperedges have a join tree in which those containing each variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex acyclicity additionally requires this after adding the head-variable set as an edge. The source recalls the classical linear-preprocessing, constant-delay algorithm for this condition.

The corresponding hardness statements for self-join-free queries use hypotheses about Boolean matrix multiplication or hyperclique detection. They should not be read as unconditional proofs that all other queries are intractable.

Self-joins permit further tractable structures: §7.1 gives cyclic mirror queries with constant-delay enumeration. Their memory during enumeration may grow with output size. Imposing constant additional workspace would therefore change the class under consideration.

The preliminary 2025 report studies acyclic queries with unary or binary atoms, including projections. It develops partial conditions and explicitly leaves queries outside the classified cases. That atom-arity restriction does not cover the arbitrary-arity input of this card.

The author’s 2026 announcement of joint work on self-joins and projections still reports unclassified examples. Its unavailable manuscript is not treated as a verified complete classification.
why: Database queries can have far more answers than input tuples. Constant delay after linear preprocessing gives both output-sensitive total time and a bounded wait for each answer. A complete effective classification would identify exactly which query patterns allow this guarantee, including repeated uses of the same relation.
status_note: The checked self-join results supply partial positive and conditional negative classifications. The preliminary 2025 report and the author’s 2026 announcement retain unclassified examples. No resolution of the full effective classifier was found. The exact target retains the existing deterministic RAM and permissive polynomial-address-space convention; unconditional membership is not replaced by membership conditional on a fine-grained conjecture.
progress: 2023: The PODS paper develops partial classifications and cyclic mirror-query algorithms in a model allowing polynomial memory. | 2025-05-02: A preliminary report studies further projected, acyclic self-join queries with unary or binary atoms, leaving cases unclassified. | 2026: The author’s BDA26 announcement still describes partial conditions and unclassified examples; checked on 17 September.
working_summary: The input to the proposed classifier is any finite conjunctive query, allowing repeated relation symbols and existentially hidden variables. It must decide whether the query has a deterministic enumerator with linear preprocessing and constant worst-case delay on every database. Answers use set semantics, are printed without repetition, and the delay includes the first answer and final termination. The specified RAM permits polynomial address space without a separate linear-memory restriction, and all enumeration constants may depend on the fixed query. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish a total classifier or prove that none exists; partial or conditional classifications do not finish the target.

title: A logic capturing polynomial time
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.
formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.
context:
A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.
why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly states that no logic is known to capture PTIME on arbitrary finite structures. The review through 11 September 2026 found no general existence or impossibility result. Candidate-specific, ordered and structured-output results are distinguished.
progress: 2008: Grohe surveys the general capturing question and positive results for particular classes of structures. | 2015: Grädel–Grohe make the effective compiler and decidable-syntax requirements explicit in their survey of choiceless computation. | 2022 / 2023: Witnessed symmetric choice yields capture on classes with definable isomorphism in the extended formalism. | 2026-08: Group-order logic research retains the general question and studies restricted generating-set operations.
working_summary: Is there an effective logic for all polynomial-time properties of finite unordered structures? Its sentences must describe properties unchanged by renaming domain elements. Each sentence must compile effectively to an evaluation algorithm with a polynomial time bound. Fixed-point logic captures polynomial time when an order is supplied, but that is a different input model. Current candidate and restricted-class results leave the general existence question open.

title: Asser’s problem
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.
formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
question_excerpt: Preserves importance 96 and Asser’s general complement question, with nonempty finite models, positive-integer complement and a new unrestricted finite vocabulary for the representing sentence. No effective complementation algorithm or bounded-length representative is added. The three-variable reductions in the cited papers require the complement to be an unrestricted first-order spectrum; they do not require its representative to remain in the restricted fragment or prove that every spectrum already belongs to that fragment.
definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.
context:
Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The primary sources retain the general complement question and its equivalence with NE=coNE. The 2015–2018 reductions narrow input sentences while allowing an unrestricted complement representative; the 2024 result concerns a two-variable extension. No general resolution was found in the bounded later-work search. This is not an exhaustive literature check: the latest technical result inspected in full is the 2024 restricted-logic paper, and a later historical article could not be accessed in full.
progress: 1952–1955: Scholz introduces the spectrum question and Asser asks whether the class is closed under complement. | 1972–1974: The nondeterministic exponential-time characterization connects complement closure to NE versus coNE. | 2012: The comprehensive survey retains the unrestricted complement question as open. | 2015: Two-variable logic with counting receives an exact semilinear spectrum characterization and complement closure. | 2015: The general complement question reduces to three-variable binary-relation inputs despite an infinite variable hierarchy. | 2018-04-25: The reduction is refined to three-variable inputs whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. | 2024-07-08: The journal article on ultimately periodic counting gives an effective Presburger description of spectra in that two-variable extension.
working_summary: The spectrum of a first-order sentence is the set of positive sizes of its finite models. Asser’s problem asks whether the complement of every such set is again a first-order spectrum. The representing sentence may use a new vocabulary and must work at all sizes simultaneously, with no effective construction required. The general question is equivalent to closure of nondeterministic single-exponential time under complement for binary-encoded sizes. Two-variable counting spectra are understood, while reductions to three-variable graph inputs and later restricted-logic results leave the general question open.

title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational question connecting description logics, database queries and infinite-model reasoning, with sharply different outcomes for nearby restrictions.
formal:
Is Boolean conjunctive-query entailment for classical SROIQ decidable under semantics allowing both finite and infinite models? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(D\) such that for every finite legal SROIQ knowledge base \(K\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), in the syntax and semantics below, \(D(K,q)\) halts with a bit satisfying
\[D(K,q)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\models q?\]
Both \(K\) and \(q\) are input. Query atoms may use non-simple roles, including roles made transitive or affected by legal role chains. There is no bound on the size of models and no finite-model, named-witness, Horn or simple-query-role restriction. No running-time bound is requested beyond termination on every legal pair.
question_excerpt: The selected problem is Boolean CQ entailment for classical SROIQ under all-model semantics, using the normalized 2006 syntax, no datatypes and no unique-name assumption. Original universal-role uses in concepts and ABox assertions are retained. Non-simple roles are allowed in query atoms. Neither finite-model semantics nor OWL2-specific syntax restrictions are silently substituted.
definitions:
Names and role expressions. Use disjoint countable sets of ordinary concept names \(A\), nominal concept names \(o\), individual names \(a\), ordinary role names \(r\), and query variables \(x\), each effectively indexed by natural numbers. There is also a distinguished universal role \(U\). A role expression is \(r\), \(r^{-}\), or \(U\). The operation \(\operatorname{Inv}\) swaps \(r\) and \(r^{-}\) and fixes \(U\). Only finitely many names occur in an input. Nominal concepts and individual names are different syntactic sorts; a nominal will denote a singleton, while an individual denotes an element. They can be linked by an assertion \(o(a)\). There are no datatypes, datatype predicates or additional rule language.

Role hierarchies and regularity. The knowledge base includes a finite role hierarchy \(\mathcal H\) of inclusions \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\sqsubseteq r\), with \(\ell\ge1\), every \(R_i\ne U\), and \(r\) an ordinary role name. We use the normalized syntax of classical SROIQ: an inverse on the right can be removed by inverting both sides and reversing the left-hand string. Trivial self-inclusions are omitted; aliases connected by cycles of ordinary role equivalences can first be identified consistently throughout the knowledge base and query. The formal input domain here consists of the normalized inclusions satisfying the following finite regularity test.

There must exist an irreflexive transitive relation \(\prec\) on the occurring non-universal role expressions and their inverses such that \(S\prec R\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Inv}(S)\prec R\). Every inclusion \(w\sqsubseteq r\) must have one of the forms
\[w=rr,\qquad w=r^{-},\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=rS_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t r,\]
where, in the last three cases, \(t\ge1\) and \(S_i\prec r\) for every \(i\). The same order must work for the whole hierarchy. It need not be supplied with the input. This excludes arbitrary mutually recursive role-chain rules. Transitivity and symmetry of a role name can be written as \(rr\sqsubseteq r\) and \(r^{-}\sqsubseteq r\), respectively.

Simple roles and role assertions. Declare a role non-simple if it belongs to the least set \(\mathcal N\) satisfying these closure rules: the right-hand role of every inclusion whose left side has length at least two lies in \(\mathcal N\); \(R\in\mathcal N\) implies \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\in\mathcal N\); and an ordinary single-role inclusion \(R\sqsubseteq S\) propagates membership from \(R\) to \(S\). For the last rule also include the inverse inclusion \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\sqsubseteq\operatorname{Inv}(S)\) for each single-role inclusion. Every other role is simple. In the selected 2006 syntax, \(U\) is absent from role hierarchies and is simple; number restrictions on \(U\) are allowed and count all elements of the qualified concept. This makes the original universal-role convention explicit, rather than substituting the separate OWL2 syntax restrictions.

Besides \(\mathcal H\), the role box may contain \(\operatorname{Ref}(R)\), \(\operatorname{Irr}(S)\), \(\operatorname{Asy}(S)\), and \(\operatorname{Dis}(S,T)\). Here \(R,S,T\ne U\), and \(S,T\) must be simple, while the reflexive role \(R\) need not be simple. Asymmetry is strict: an edge forbids its reverse, even on the diagonal.

Concepts and the rest of the knowledge base. Concepts are the finite expressions generated by
\[C::=A\mid o\mid\top\mid\bot\mid\neg C\mid(C\sqcap C)\mid(C\sqcup C)\mid\exists R.C\mid\forall R.C\mid(\ge h\,S.C)\mid(\le h\,S.C)\mid\exists S.\mathsf{Self}.\]
The role \(R\) is arbitrary, \(S\) must be simple, and \(h\) is any nonnegative integer written in binary. A finite knowledge base \(K\) consists of the legal role box, a finite TBox of inclusions \(C\sqsubseteq E\), and a finite ABox of assertions \(C(a)\), \(R(a,b)\), \(\neg R(a,b)\), or \(a\ne b\). Positive and negative role assertions may use non-simple roles. In particular, number restrictions, self restrictions and role-property assertions have the simplicity restrictions just stated, but ordinary ABox role assertions do not acquire an extra simplicity restriction.

Interpretations. An interpretation \(\mathcal I\) has a nonempty set \(\Delta^{\mathcal I}\), finite or infinite. Each ordinary concept denotes a subset, each nominal denotes a singleton subset, each individual name denotes an element, and each ordinary role denotes a binary relation on this domain. Different names need not denote different elements or sets. Set \(U^{\mathcal I}=\Delta^{\mathcal I}\times\Delta^{\mathcal I}\) and \((r^{-})^{\mathcal I}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in r^{\mathcal I}\}\). The relation for a string \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\) contains \((d_0,d_\ell)\) exactly when there exist intermediate elements \(d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}\) with \((d_{i-1},d_i)\in R_i^{\mathcal I}\) for all \(i\).

Interpret \(\top\) as the whole domain, \(\bot\) as the empty set, negation as complement in the domain, and \(\sqcap,\sqcup\) as intersection and union. An element belongs to \((\exists R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if it has an \(R\)-successor in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\forall R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if all its \(R\)-successors are in \(C^{\mathcal I}\). It belongs to \((\ge h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if at least \(h\) distinct \(S\)-successors lie in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\le h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if there are no \(h+1\) distinct such successors. These definitions also apply to infinite successor sets. Finally \((\exists S.\mathsf{Self})^{\mathcal I}=\{d:(d,d)\in S^{\mathcal I}\}\).

A hierarchy inclusion requires inclusion of the corresponding binary relations. Reflexivity means that every \((d,d)\) belongs to the role relation; irreflexivity means that no such pair belongs; asymmetry means that \((d,e)\) in the relation excludes \((e,d)\); disjointness means the two role relations have empty intersection. A TBox inclusion requires \(C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq E^{\mathcal I}\). An ABox concept assertion requires membership of \(a^{\mathcal I}\), a positive or negative role assertion requires membership or nonmembership of \((a^{\mathcal I},b^{\mathcal I})\), and inequality requires \(a^{\mathcal I}\ne b^{\mathcal I}\). A model of \(K\) satisfies every one of its axioms and assertions.

Queries and entailment. A Boolean conjunctive query is a finite formula
\[q=\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_t\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{b}\alpha_j,\qquad t,b\ge0,\]
whose terms are the displayed variables or individual names. Each atom is \(A(v)\), \(o(v)\), or \(r(v,w)\), allowing also the role name \(U\). All variables occurring in atoms are bound. Ordinary query role names may be simple or non-simple. Query symbols need not occur in \(K\); their interpretation still obeys the name conventions above. No query negation, inequality, equality atom, disjunction, counting, self operator or regular-path operator is included. Repeated terms are allowed, so \(r(x,x)\) is allowed without being the concept constructor \(\exists r.\mathsf{Self}\). Query assignments map variables to arbitrary domain elements, may identify different variables and may use unnamed elements. The same assignment must make every atom true; individual terms keep their interpretations. The empty conjunction is true. Write \(\mathcal I\models q\) when such an assignment exists, and \(K\models q\) when every model of \(K\) satisfies it. If \(K\) has no models, it entails every query.

Effective decision problem. Encode the finite sets of axioms and query as fully parenthesized prefix expressions, with fixed distinct tags for the constructors and name sorts, binary indices for names, and binary counts for number restrictions, separated by delimiters. Lists of expressions are delimited as finite lists. This is a finite-string representation with effective parsing; replacing it by another computably equivalent explicit encoding does not change decidability. The finite syntax, simplicity and regularity conditions are part of legal input, and can be checked effectively. The requested machine has one finite program, no oracle or nonuniform advice, and must halt with the correct bit on every legal pair. No bound on its time, space or intermediate objects is prescribed; behavior on malformed pairs is irrelevant.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that one such total decision procedure exists, or a proof of its logical negation. For a positive answer, establish soundness, completeness and termination on every finite legal pair in the full language, including arbitrary non-simple query predicates and knowledge bases whose only models are infinite. For a negative answer, establish that every deterministic Turing machine fails on some legal pair by not halting with a bit or by returning the wrong entailment answer. Undecidability only for finite-model semantics or for a stronger query or axiom language does not settle this target. Likewise, a terminating method only for Horn knowledge bases, simple-role queries, satisfiable instances with a finite model bound, or other proper restrictions is insufficient. Empirical termination of a reasoner is not a universal termination proof.
context:
A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let the knowledge base assert \(\mathsf{Person}(a)\) and \(\mathsf{Person}\sqsubseteq\exists\mathsf{knows}.\mathsf{Person}\). Every model then satisfies \(\exists x\exists y\,(\mathsf{Person}(x)\land\mathsf{knows}(x,y)\land\mathsf{Person}(y))\). No named witness for \(y\) is required. The same domain element may serve as both variables if the model permits it. A query that reuses variables across several atoms requires one common assignment satisfying all those atoms.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

The finite-model distinction already appears with one simple role \(r\). Require \(\top\sqsubseteq(\ge1\,r.\top)\sqcap(\le1\,r.\top)\), \(\top\sqsubseteq(\le1\,r^{-}.\top)\), and \((\le0\,r^{-}.\top)(a)\). These axioms describe an injective total successor function with a named element outside its image. They have the natural-number successor chain as a model but have no finite model, since an injective function on a finite set is surjective. A fresh ordinary concept \(A\) can be empty on that infinite model, so \(\exists x\,A(x)\) is not entailed under the chosen semantics. It is vacuously entailed if only finite models are considered.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.
why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.
status_note: Checked through16 September2026. No general decision procedure or all-model undecidability proof for the specified Boolean-CQ problem was found in the bounded primary-source review. The May2026 theorem concerns S; the other checked results concern simple query roles, Horn knowledge bases, finite-model semantics or conditional termination of a practical reasoner. The distinction from the selected full classical SROIQ target is explicit.
progress: 2006: Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler define SROIQ and prove decidability of its standard consistency reasoning tasks. | 2010: Rudolph–Glimm establish query decidability with nominals, inverses and counting, including SROIQ queries restricted to simple roles. | 2011: Ortiz–Rudolph–Šimkus establish decidable path-query answering for Horn-SROIQ. | 2016: Rudolph proves finite-model conjunctive-query entailment undecidable in a SROIQ fragment; this uses finite semantics. | 2019: Steigmiller–Glimm present absorption-based checking, while explicitly retaining the full decidability question and a termination condition involving new nominals. | 2026-05-08: The revised full version of the AAAI 2026 paper proves 2ExpTime-completeness for S, including Boolean-query hardness with two transitive roles.
working_summary: A SROIQ knowledge base describes incomplete information using concepts, individuals, relations, inverse relations, counting and restricted role chains. A Boolean conjunctive query asks whether one finite relational pattern must occur in every model, including infinite models and witnesses that have no individual name. The question is whether one ordinary algorithm can always decide that entailment for the complete specified language, with no running-time bound. A complete Lean proof must establish a sound, complete and universally terminating decision procedure or prove that no such procedure exists. The checked finite-model undecidability, simple-role and Horn decision procedures, practical reasoner and2026 S-fragment theorem do not settle this all-model SROIQ target.

title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every pair \((q_1,q_2)\) of finite conjunctive queries with the same output arity and correctly decides whether
\[
 \forall\text{ finite bag databases }D\quad
 \forall a\in U_D^r:\qquad q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a),
\]
with the unrestricted syntax and natural-number sum-product semantics defined below? Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
question_excerpt: The maintained question list asks whether conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics is decidable and what its complexity is. This card selects decidability alone, fixing bag input and output multiplicities over the nonnegative integers as in the seminar problem and the ICDT semantics.
definitions:
A relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified nonnegative integer arity. It is part of the query input, with no fixed bound on the number of symbols or their arities. Both queries use a common signature; unused relation symbols have no effect. They also use a finite set \(C\) of named constants. A finite bag database \(D\) consists of a finite domain \(U_D\), an injective interpretation \(\iota_D:C\to U_D\) of the constant names, and a function
\[
 D_R:U_D^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\to\mathbb N
 \quad\text{for every }R\in\tau,
\]
where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The value is the tuple's multiplicity; zero means absence. All natural multiplicities and all finite domain sizes are allowed, without a bound determined in advance. No key, dependency or other integrity constraint is imposed. The domain may be empty when there are no constants. A nullary relation has one possible tuple, the empty tuple.

A conjunctive query has syntax
\[
 q(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\;:\!-\;A_1,\ldots,A_m,
\]
where each \(A_j\) is a positive relational atom \(R_j(t_{j,1},\ldots,t_{j,a_j})\), \(a_j\) is the arity of \(R_j\), and each term is a variable or a named constant. Every variable occurs in at least one body atom. The head \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\) is a list of variables from the body; variables may repeat in the head. Body variables not in the head are existentially quantified. Distinct variable names may be assigned the same domain element, and a variable may be assigned the value of a constant. Different named constants denote distinct elements. The body is a list of atom occurrences: relation names, variables and entire atoms may repeat. There is no disjunction, negation, inequality, built-in comparison, aggregation syntax, recursion or duplicate-elimination operation. Identifying variables can enforce equality, but no additional predicate is interpreted specially.

Write \(\operatorname{Var}(q)\) for the finite set of variables in \(q\). For an assignment \(h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\), extend \(h\) to constants by \(h(c)=\iota_D(c)\), and write \(D(A_j[h])\) for \(D_{R_j}\) evaluated at the instantiated tuple. For every output tuple \(a\in U_D^r\), define
\[
 q(D)(a)=
 \sum_{\substack{h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\\
                  (h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_r))=a}}
       \prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h]).
\]
The arithmetic is ordinary exact addition and multiplication of nonnegative integers. The sum is finite; an empty sum is zero and an empty product is one. Each repeated occurrence contributes its own factor. For example, the bodies \(R(x)\) and \(R(x),R(x)\) give multiplicities \(D_R(a)\) and \(D_R(a)^2\), respectively. Output tuples that violate equalities forced by repeated head variables receive zero.

A Boolean query has \(r=0\) and returns a natural multiplicity at the unique empty tuple; it does not merely report whether a witness exists. An empty body is permitted only with no variables, hence has empty head and returns one. These conventions also define evaluation on empty domains.

Input queries, signatures, variable names and constant names have finite, effectively parseable binary encodings, for example length-prefixed symbol lists and atom lists. The machine receives only these two queries and their signature, not a database or a database-size bound. It must accept exactly when the displayed inequality holds for every database and every output tuple and reject otherwise. It can reject ill-formed encodings immediately. There is no required bound on its running time beyond halting on every input, and there is no noncomputable advice or external oracle. The inequality is exact and one-sided, with no input scale factor or additive slack.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total decision algorithm exists, with an implementation and proofs of termination and correctness on every input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists.

Enumerating finite counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment and does not establish decidability. A decision procedure for equivalence, set semantics, or a proper query subclass is insufficient on its own. A theorem about bag-set inputs may be used only together with a proved effective reduction covering the bag-valued input model here. Undecidability after adding unions, inequalities, integrity constraints or a numerical transformation of the query count must likewise be reduced to this exact plain-CQ problem. No approximation tolerance or complexity-class upper bound is requested.
context:
With duplicates, a join multiplies tuple multiplicities and projection adds contributions of different assignments. Queries returning the same set of answers can therefore produce different numbers of copies.

Every proposed counterexample is a finite database with exactly computable counts. Exhaustively searching databases will eventually discover a counterexample when one exists, but gives no stopping rule for true containment.

The join-on-free theorem allows existential variables but forbids joins between body atoms through those variables in the contained query. Its decidability result therefore covers more than projection-free queries, while keeping a restriction absent from this target.

The literature relates bag-bag and bag-set containment by transformations of the query input. This does not justify silently treating the same original relations as sets; repeated atoms can affect the original bag comparison.

Nearby undecidability results add unions, comparisons or a transformation of the count. The June 2025 CQ-versus-UCQ paper still leaves the ordinary two-CQ inequality open.

The August 2026 discussion continues to identify general CQ bag containment as unresolved.

The September 2026 finite-witness result addresses equivalence in a mixed set/bag framework. Equality of two query functions and a one-sided inequality are distinct decision predicates; that abstract does not provide a general containment decision algorithm.
why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.
status_note: The August 2026 primary discussion, 2025 seminar problem and maintained question list retain general CQ bag-containment decidability as open. The September equivalence preprint addresses a different predicate and semantics. Bounded primary-source checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the exact bag-bag problem here; cited proofs were not independently certified.
progress: 1993: Chaudhuri and Vardi pose the bag-containment decidability question, as recorded in the seminar history. | 2024: Undecidability is established for nearby extensions involving a supplied transformation of a query count. | 2025-03-21: Join-on-free containment into a general CQ is proved decidable. | 2025-06-01: The revised CQ-versus-UCQ paper retains ordinary two-CQ containment as open. | 2026-08: The SQL semantics discussion still lists general CQ bag-containment decidability as unknown. | 2026-09-09: Finite witness bounds are proposed for equivalence under combined semantics, a different target.
working_summary: A conjunctive database query produces answer multiplicities by summing products of input multiplicities. Containment means that the first query never produces more copies of any answer than the second on any finite bag database. The question asks whether one total algorithm can decide this property from the two unrestricted queries alone. Restricted joins are decidable and nearby extensions are undecidable, while new equivalence results do not settle this one-sided comparison. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove a terminating exact decision procedure or unconditional undecidability.

title: A logic capturing logarithmic space
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A broad descriptive-complexity existence question for a central resource class, with consequences for the expressive limits of order-independent database queries. It is distinct from improving one proposed recursion operator.
formal: Does there exist one effective logic \(\mathcal L\), in the precise sense below, whose sentences define exactly all deterministic logarithmic-space Boolean properties of finite unordered relational structures, for every finite relational vocabulary?
definitions:
A vocabulary \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A \(\tau\)-structure \(A\) has a finite nonempty domain and, for each \(r\)-ary symbol, an \(r\)-ary relation on that domain. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving and reflecting every relation. A Boolean property of \(\tau\)-structures is a class closed under isomorphism. The mathematical input supplies no distinguished ordering of its elements.

For computation, label the domain by \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by all relation truth tables in the vocabulary order and lexicographic tuple order, using one bit per tuple. Write \(N\) for the full encoding length. All labelings of a structure are valid encodings. A property is in deterministic logarithmic space, denoted \(\mathrm L\), if a fixed deterministic Turing machine halts and decides it correctly on every such encoding using at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells for some fixed positive integer \(C\). Machines have a read-only two-way input tape, a finite control, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Work space counts all cells visited on the work tapes; the input tape is not writable. They have no oracle, advice, auxiliary input, or random bits. A machine may use the encoding order internally, but its answer must be the same on all isomorphic inputs.

The proposed logic has a decidable set of finite binary encodings of pairs \((\tau,\varphi)\), where \(\varphi\) is a sentence over \(\tau\). Each valid sentence has a Boolean satisfaction relation \(A\models\varphi\) on all finite nonempty \(\tau\)-structures, invariant under isomorphism. There must be one total computable compiler that, on a valid pair, outputs a deterministic Turing machine \(M_\varphi\) and a positive integer \(C_\varphi\). For every valid encoding of every \(\tau\)-structure, \(M_\varphi\) must halt, return its satisfaction value, and use at most \(C_\varphi\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work cells. On invalid sentence encodings the compiler may return a fixed error symbol. Syntax checking and compilation are not required to run in logarithmic space or polynomial time.

Expressive completeness requires that for every finite \(\tau\) and every isomorphism-invariant \(\mathrm L\) property \(Q\) of its structures, there is one fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) such that \[ \forall A:\quad A\models\varphi\iff A\in Q.\] The sentence and its space constant may depend on \(Q\) and \(\tau\), but not on \(A\). The same syntax and compiler work across all vocabularies. No computable translation from arbitrary invariant machines to sentences is required. There is no uniform logarithmic-space requirement when the sentence is part of the evaluation input. A relational query with a fixed tuple of distinguished elements can be represented as a Boolean property in a vocabulary expanded by singleton unary relations marking those elements; the target uses the Boolean convention throughout.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a logic exists, including decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective evaluation with certified per-sentence space constants, and expressive completeness; or prove that no logic meets all those conditions. The formalism and its semantics must be specified, rather than merely assigning an uninterpreted name to each logarithmic-space property. A result for one candidate logic or for a restricted family of input structures does not settle this general existence question.
context:
The source motivation is computation on large relational inputs with very little working memory. A representation necessarily labels the elements, but a query about the abstract structure must not change when those labels are permuted. Capturing asks for both expressive completeness and an effective resource-bounded evaluation of every sentence.

The 2019 paper constructs CLogspace as a logic for computations that preserve input symmetries. Its objects are finite sets built from input elements and further finite sets, equipped with size annotations and restricted recursion. Theorem 27 proves that this particular logic is strictly weaker than logarithmic space. That negative result concerns a candidate, not the existence of any capturing logic.

The saved passage asks whether ideas from CLogspace can yield a stronger logic. It specifies no formal class of permitted extensions. This card makes explicit the general logic-existence objective discussed in the same paper’s introduction and Section 5; it does not require a particular extension grammar or claim that CLogspace itself captures the class. The effective-syntax and compiler requirements follow the standard capturing convention, with the space bound stated separately here.

An externally supplied order changes the descriptive problem. The 2019 source recalls that deterministic transitive-closure logic captures logarithmic space on ordered structures. More recently, Bell, Day and Freydenberger obtain LOGSPACE-capturing fragments for string queries; the June 2026 abstract concerns strings, not arbitrary unordered relational inputs.
why: This asks whether all order-independent queries evaluable with logarithmic working memory have an effective logical language with exactly that expressive power. It would connect a central low-space computation model to a complete account of queries on finite relational data, beyond the familiar setting where an input order is supplied.
status_note: The general objective and the failure of CLogspace were checked in the 2019 full text. The standard effective capturing convention was checked in the 2015 author survey. The June 2026 FC-Datalog abstract and history were checked for domain and date; its full proofs were not independently reviewed. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching general existence or impossibility result. This is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
progress: 2019-08-20: CLogspace is introduced and proved to be a strict fragment of logarithmic space; the broader search for a capturing logic remains in the discussion. | 2026-06-21: The revised FC-Datalog manuscript states LOGSPACE-capturing results for fragments on strings. Its domain restriction prevents these results from settling the present target.
working_summary: The input is a finite relational structure with no distinguished ordering of its elements. The question asks for an effective logic expressing exactly all isomorphism-invariant Boolean queries decidable in deterministic logarithmic space. Each sentence must compile to a halting evaluation algorithm with a certified logarithmic workspace bound. The proposed CLogspace logic is known to miss some such queries, while ordered structures and strings admit stronger capturing results. A solution would settle a broad descriptive-complexity question linking small-memory computation to the expressive power of logical queries.

title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: Computability of entropic query-size bounds tests whether the strongest information-theoretic join estimates are algorithmically accessible.
formal:
Is the logarithmic entropic query-size bound uniformly computable? More precisely, does a single deterministic Turing machine, given any finite set of degree constraints \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) on \([n]\) with nonnegative rational logarithmic budgets, and any \(m\in\mathbb N\), halt and output either \(+\infty\) when \(E(\mathcal D)=+\infty\), or a rational \(q\) satisfying \(|q-E(\mathcal D)|\leq 2^{-m}\) when
\[E(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\overline{\Gamma_n^*},\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\ (1\leq i\leq k)\}<+\infty?\]
Here \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) is the closure of the discrete entropy region defined below; \(n\) is part of the input.
question_excerpt: Does an algorithm compute the entropic bound on query output size from the supplied constraints?
definitions:
Let \(n\geq1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. Given jointly distributed discrete random variables \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), each with a finite alphabet, their entropy vector is the real set function
\[h(S)=H(Z_S)=-\sum_z\Pr[Z_S=z]\log_2\Pr[Z_S=z],\qquad h(\varnothing)=0,\]
where \(Z_S\) is the tuple with indices in \(S\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). Alphabets and real joint probabilities are unrestricted. The set of all such vectors is \(\Gamma_n^*\). Its closure \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space of subset coordinates consists of all limits of sequences of entropy vectors and is the almost-entropic cone. Neither alphabet sizes nor convergence rates are input bounds. Continuous differential entropy is not used.

A degree constraint is a triple \((X,Y,b)\), where \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\). It bounds the conditional entropy \(h(Y)-h(X)\). The case \(X=\varnothing\) gives a cardinality-type constraint, and \(b=0\) gives a functional dependency. Equal sets, repeated triples and an empty list are permitted. The all-zero entropy vector is always feasible, so the supremum is in \([0,+\infty]\). The optimization is over the closed almost-entropic cone, not just the nonclosed set of entropy vectors satisfying the constraints exactly; this distinction matters on faces defined by zero budgets.

For a database interpretation, a full conjunctive query returns the natural join of finite relations: an output tuple assigns all variables and its projection onto each relation's columns is present in that relation. There are no duplicate output tuples and no existentially projected variables. A bound of \(N\) on the number of extensions from columns \(X\) to columns \(Y\) gives the entropy budget \(b=\log_2 N\). Drawing a join tuple uniformly makes its full entropy the logarithm of the join size. The quantity \(2^{E(\mathcal D)}\) is the information-theoretic upper bound; the question asks to compute its logarithm, rather than to enumerate joins or compute the exact maximum size of a finite database instance.

The finite encoding used here writes \(n\) and the list length in unary, every subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and each rational budget as a nonnegative binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, with delimiters. The precision \(m\) is given in unary. This is an explicit rational logarithmic-budget version of the source's numerical problem, with no real-number oracle. At the level of computability it also covers positive integer degree bounds supplied as \(N\): cone homogeneity handles rational budgets by scaling them to integer logarithms, while positive values \(\log_2 N\) can be bracketed multiplicatively by rational numbers, keeping zero budgets exactly zero. This equivalence concerns computability, not polynomial-time equivalence of the two encodings.

Unbounded inputs are included. They can be recognized by starting with \(S=\varnothing\) and repeatedly adjoining \(Y_i\) whenever \(X_i\subseteq S\). The optimum is finite exactly when the resulting closure is \([n]\). In that case conditional-entropy inequalities and subadditivity supply an explicit finite upper bound. If some variables remain outside, let them all share an arbitrarily high-entropy random variable and make the other variables constant; every constraint is satisfied while the objective is unbounded. Thus recognizing infinity is not the unknown part of the problem.

The machine must halt on every valid input, with a finite binary rational output in the bounded case; malformed strings may be rejected. There is no time or space bound, no advice, oracle, fixed dimension or randomness. Accuracy is absolute in base-two entropy units. In particular the machine must achieve error at most \(1/100\), by taking \(m=7\), and also every finer requested accuracy. A one-sided sequence of estimates without a computable error guarantee does not suffice.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the displayed uniform machine exists, or that it does not. An affirmative proof must provide an effective procedure and prove termination and the requested two-sided absolute error for every finite dimension, rational degree-constraint list and precision, including zero budgets and the stated infinity convention. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this particular functional, not merely undecidability of a different entropy-region membership or information-inequality problem. An exact symbolic formula is unnecessary, while a computable value for each separately fixed input without one uniform procedure is insufficient. There are no unproved complexity assumptions in the target.
context:
The seminar groups several algorithmic questions about information-theoretic database bounds. Question 7.1 asks for computability of the entropic bound; Question 7.2 separately asks about the complexity of its polymatroid relaxation. The first issue is whether any terminating numerical algorithm exists, before asking whether one is efficient.

Entropy inequalities constrain correlations among columns in a join. Using every valid inequality gives a potentially sharper bound than the familiar Shannon inequalities alone. Suciu formulates the entropic upper bound by such inequalities and identifies its value with optimization over the closed almost-entropic cone. This closure specifies which limiting entropy vectors belong to the target.

Replacing the almost-entropic cone by normalized monotone submodular set functions gives a finite linear program, with exponentially many subset coordinates. This yields a computable upper relaxation, but a gap between that relaxation and the entropic optimum prevents it from settling the question. Restricting alphabet sizes also changes the feasible region unless a sufficient effective approximation theorem is proved.

For simple degree constraints, where every conditioning set has size at most one, the entropic and polymatroid bounds coincide and a polynomial-size linear program is available. This tractable subclass does not cover arbitrary conditioning sets or all zero-budget functional dependencies.

Mengel and Romashchenko still describe general computability as unresolved in August 2026. Their new work examines acyclic dependencies and shows that allowing projected variables can create gaps between entropy and polymatroid bounds. That result concerns the comparison of bounds in a richer query setting, not an algorithm or impossibility proof for the full general numerical target here.

A computability theorem would make this extremal use of arbitrary discrete distributions accessible to uniform algorithms; a noncomputability theorem would identify a fundamental limit on exact information-theoretic database estimation, even with unlimited running time.
