working_summary: Entropy bounds limit the number of tuples returned by a database join from constraints on conditional degrees. The entropic bound optimizes total entropy over the closure of all finite discrete entropy vectors. The question asks for one terminating algorithm that computes this value to every requested absolute accuracy in arbitrary dimension. Simple constraints admit effective special cases, while the general polymatroid relaxation can overestimate the desired value. Resolving computability would determine whether the strongest information-theoretic estimate is accessible to algorithms at all.

title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.
formal:
Does there exist a universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(p\ge0\), integer \(n\ge1\), commutative \(p\)-stable semiring \(S\), and polynomial map \(F:S^n\to S^n\) with coefficients in \(S\), the synchronous sequence
\[
x^{(0)}=(0,\ldots,0),\qquad x^{(t+1)}=F(x^{(t)})
\]
satisfies \(x^{(t+1)}=x^{(t)}\) for some integer \(0\le t\le C(p+1)n\)? The constant must be independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials and polynomial degrees. Only the number of rounds is measured.
question_excerpt: The seminar proposes a convergence bound O((p+1)n), matching the scale of the stated lower bound, for iterative evaluation over p-stable semirings. This card expresses that proposal for grounded commutative-semiring polynomial systems.
definitions:
A commutative semiring is a set \(S\) with binary operations \(\oplus,\otimes\) and elements \(0,1\) such that \((S,\oplus,0)\) and \((S,\otimes,1)\) are commutative monoids, multiplication distributes over addition, and \(0\otimes a=a\otimes0=0\). No additive inverses, additive idempotence, order, finiteness or effective encoding is assumed. The trivial semiring is allowed. All equalities are equalities of semiring elements.

For \(a\in S\), set \(a^0=1\) and \(a^{j+1}=a^j\otimes a\). The semiring is \(p\)-stable when
\[
\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p}a^j=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p+1}a^j\qquad\text{for every }a\in S.
\]
The same integer \(p\) must work for every element, not merely for the coefficients appearing in one system. It need not be the smallest possible stability index. The case \(p=0\) means \(1\oplus a=1\) for all \(a\).

Each coordinate of \(F\) is given by a finite polynomial expression, equivalently
\[
F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\bigoplus_{j\in J_i}\left(a_{ij}\otimes\bigotimes_{r=1}^{n}x_r^{e_{ijr}}\right),
\]
where \(J_i\) is a finite index set, \(a_{ij}\in S\) and \(e_{ijr}\in\mathbb N\). An empty sum is 0 and an empty product is 1. Repeated monomials, arbitrary finite exponents and constant terms are allowed. There is no bound on the degrees or the number of terms, and no requirement of linearity. The coefficients remain fixed during iteration.

One round evaluates every \(F_i\) from the entire previous vector \(x^{(t)}\). Partially updated coordinates cannot be reused within that round. The rule is precisely \(F\), not a replacement such as \(x\mapsto x\oplus F(x)\), unless their iteration behavior is proved to agree for the system under consideration. The initial vector is always zero. Once two successive vectors are equal, all later vectors equal them because the map is fixed.

The dimension \(n\) counts all coordinates, including those that stay zero. In a grounded Datalog system they represent potential derived facts, each carrying a semiring annotation. The statement counts applications of the polynomial map, irrespective of the arithmetic work, representation size or equality-testing cost within a round. It therefore asks for an algebraic convergence theorem, not a fast implementation of one database operation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal bound or its logical negation. A positive proof must use one constant valid simultaneously for every \(p,n,S,F\) in the definitions, including \(p=0\) and nonlinear systems of unbounded finite degree.

A negative proof must establish that, for every proposed constant \(C\), some allowed system has no fixed-point equality at any integer \(t\le C(p+1)n\). Equivalently, the first fixed-point times divided by \((p+1)n\) are unbounded, treating nonconvergence as infinite time. One example requiring more than \(n\) rounds does not refute an unspecified universal constant. A bound with an additional growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients or dimension, or a faster method using a different update rule, does not prove this exact synchronous-round target. A title announcing optimal convergence is not a substitute for a theorem with the required hypotheses and quantifiers.
context:
A Boolean derived fact changes from absent to present at most once. A semiring annotation can change repeatedly, so counting facts alone no longer immediately bounds the number of rounds.

Stability controls a truncated geometric sum for each individual semiring element. The target asks whether interactions among many nonlinear equations multiply this delay by only a linear factor in the number of coordinates.

The inspected polynomial-convergence theorem has dependencies on the number \(\sigma\) of referenced coefficients and the maximum product length \(\lambda\), in addition to \(p\) and \(n\). Its separate 0-stable discussion gives linear convergence, but the general theorem does not give the universal bound stated here.

The authors now list a paper entitled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo. The inspected listings provide no theorem text for that entry, and their venue-year labels disagree. The catalogue therefore preserves uncertain current status while keeping the historical mathematical target precise.
why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.
status_note: Uncertain current status. The universal linear bound is open in the 2025 seminar, but a directly relevant Optimal Convergence paper is announced by its authors. On 17 September 2026, Ngo and Zhao label it PODS 2027 and Moseley labels it PODS 2025; no accessible theorem text for the entry was obtained. Its exact semiring assumptions, iteration rule and parameter bounds are therefore not verified here, and the card is not labeled confirmed open or resolved.
progress: 2024-02-21: The revised preprint gives polynomial convergence with explicit coefficient-count and product-length dependencies, and separately recalls linear convergence for the 0-stable case. | 2025: The seminar proposes a universal linear-in-(p+1)n bound. | 2026-09-17: The new Optimal Convergence title remains listed by its authors, but the inspected pages did not provide a theorem sufficient to verify the selected target.
working_summary: The system consists of finitely many polynomial recurrences over a commutative semiring. Every round updates all coordinates from the previous vector, starting from zero. The question asks whether p-stability forces a fixed point within a universal constant times (p+1)n rounds. An announced optimal-convergence paper makes the current status uncertain because its precise theorem was not available in the inspected sources. The requested answer remains a complete Lean-checked universal convergence proof or refutation for the specified synchronous rule.

title: Complexity of polymatroid query-size bounds
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: The complexity of polymatroid query bounds affects the feasibility of a general framework for controlling join output size.
formal:
Is computing the general polymatroid query-size bound NP-hard? Use the following exact comparison formulation and deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Given \(n\geq1\), a finite list \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) of rational logarithmic degree constraints and a rational threshold \(t\), let
\[P(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\Gamma_n,\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\},\]
where \(\Gamma_n\) is the cone of normalized monotone submodular set functions on \([n]\). Is the language
\[\mathrm{POLYBOUND}=\{\langle n,\mathcal D,t\rangle:P(\mathcal D)\geq t\}\]
NP-hard under the reduction convention below, when dimension and all constraints are part of the input?
question_excerpt: Determine the complexity of computing the polymatroid bound; in particular, is the general computation NP-hard?
definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a polymatroid function is a real-valued function \(h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[h(\varnothing)=0,\qquad h(S)\leq h(T)\quad(S\subseteq T),\]
\[h(S)+h(T)\geq h(S\cup T)+h(S\cap T)\quad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\]
These conditions imply \(h(S)\geq0\). Their cone is \(\Gamma_n\). Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers; functions need not be integer-valued matroid ranks or entropy vectors. A constraint \((X,Y,b)\) has \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\), and means \(h(Y)-h(X)\leq b\). An empty list, zero budgets, equal sets and repeated constraints are allowed. The zero function is feasible. Set \(P(\mathcal D)=+\infty\) for an unbounded objective; in that case every finite threshold is accepted. Otherwise the finite rational linear program attains a rational optimum, and equality with the threshold counts as yes.

The input explicitly lists the constraints, not the \(2^n\) values of a candidate function. Write \(n\) and the list length in unary, each subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and every rational as a binary integer numerator and a positive binary denominator with delimiters; the threshold numerator may be negative. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits. Invalid strings are rejected. This card fixes the usual rational logarithmic-budget bit model for the source's optimization question: numbers \(b_i\), rather than potentially enormous degree counts \(2^{b_i}\), are supplied. It does not assume unit-cost exact arithmetic on arbitrary real inputs. Comparison is exact, with no numerical tolerance, promise gap, fixed dimension or fixed constraint arity.

The database meaning is as follows. A full conjunctive query joins finite relations by matching common columns and returns all variable columns, with set semantics. A degree bound \(N\) limits how many distinct \(Y\)-tuples extend each fixed \(X\)-tuple. For a uniform random output tuple, conditional entropy is at most \(\log_2 N\), while the entropy of the complete tuple is the logarithm of the result size. Every entropy vector satisfies the displayed polymatroid inequalities, so maximizing over polymatroids yields a valid logarithmic upper estimate. The source's linear-program framework is formalized here with rational logarithmic budgets. No database instance is an input to POLYBOUND, and maximizing the actual finite join size is a different optimization problem.

A language lies in NP when yes instances have binary certificates of polynomially bounded length verified by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. NP-hardness here means that every such language can be decided by a deterministic oracle Turing machine with access to exact POLYBOUND membership and worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\), for some constants depending only on the reduced language. An oracle query returns one membership bit; writing the query and all other bit operations count toward the time bound. Equivalently, it suffices to give such a reduction from satisfiability of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause. Clauses are disjunctions of variables or their negations, and the formula is the conjunction of its clauses. This explicitly chosen Turing-reduction convention avoids changing hardness when the complementary threshold convention is used. No randomized reduction, advice or entropy oracle is allowed.

The full optimization has \(2^n\) subset variables and exponentially many monotonicity and submodularity inequalities, so explicit rational linear programming gives a terminating algorithm taking time at most exponential in a polynomial of \(L\). That upper bound does not establish NP-hardness. The issue is the cost in the compact input length; with \(n\) fixed the linear program has fixed dimension.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that POLYBOUND is NP-hard under the stated deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, or a proof of the logical negation of that assertion. A positive proof must preserve the general polymatroid feasible cone and the finite input encoding, and establish correctness for every source instance. Hardness of a restriction on the admissible functions, such as the cone of normal functions, does not imply this claim unless a valid reduction to POLYBOUND is proved. A polynomial-time algorithm would settle the principal algorithmic side of the source's broader complexity question, but by itself proves the negation of NP-hardness only together with a proved separation of P from NP; an unproved separation must be stated as a conditional result. Neither an exponential-size LP formulation nor difficulty computing a different entropic bound is a negative algorithmic result for this problem.
context:
The source asks both for the complexity of the polymatroid bound and, explicitly, whether it is NP-hard. The displayed yes/no target is this stated hardness question for the entire degree-constraint class. The companion entropic question concerns existence of any computation procedure; the polymatroid bound is already computable by finite linear programming.

Unlike minimizing one supplied submodular function, this problem optimizes over the values of an unknown submodular function. The constraint list is compact but a direct feasible function has exponentially many subset coordinates. Standard polynomial-time solvability of explicit linear programs therefore leaves the desired compact-input complexity unresolved.

A degree constraint is simple when its conditioning set has at most one variable. For this class, Im and coauthors give a linear program with O(k n²) variables and O(k n) constraints, and an efficiently obtainable derivation of the bound using Shannon inequalities. The 2022 preprint already reports the tractability breakthrough; the 2025 paper supplies the formulation and theorem locators used here.

Theorem 1.3 of the 2025 paper reduces the general problem to several apparently restricted degree languages, including constraints with conditioning sets of size at most two and total sets of size at most three. Its statement that these cases are as hard as the general case is a reduction result, not a proof that any of them is NP-hard.

The same paper does prove NP-hardness after restricting feasible polymatroids to normal functions. Such functions have the form h(S)=Σ_T w_T·1[S∩T≠∅], with nonnegative weights indexed by nonempty variable subsets T. This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.
why: A general polynomial-time procedure would make a broad information-theoretic relaxation available for query planning without enumerating exponentially many subset entropies. A hardness theorem would explain why the known algorithms require special dependency structure. Determining which conclusion is justified separates a useful compact optimization method from a bound whose direct formulation is mainly an existential certificate.
status_note: The 2022 source explicitly asks whether computing the general polymatroid bound is NP-hard. Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs, 3 April 2025, still describe general polynomial-time computability as open and distinguish their normal-function hardness theorem from the unrestricted cone. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution; the exact rational-threshold and Turing-reduction conventions are stated editorial choices, and absence of a located resolution is not a proof of openness.
progress: 2022: The seminar records Hung Ngo’s question about the general complexity and possible NP-hardness of the polymatroid bound. | 2022-11-15: The Optimizing Polymatroid Functions preprint reports polynomial-time optimization for simple constraints and NP-hardness for the distinct normal-function optimization. | 2025-04-03: Theorem 1.1 supplies a polynomial-size LP for simple constraints; Theorem 1.3 gives general-to-restricted reductions, and Theorem 1.4 proves hardness only for normal functions. The introduction and conclusion still leave general polynomial-time computability open.
working_summary: Polymatroid query bounds maximize a normalized monotone submodular function subject to supplied degree constraints. The obvious linear program has exponentially many coordinates even when its input constraint list is short. The source explicitly asks whether computing this general bound is NP-hard, formalized here through exact rational threshold comparisons. Simple constraints admit polynomial-time algorithms, while hardness for the smaller cone of normal functions leaves the general question unresolved. An answer would clarify whether this broad database estimation framework can be computed efficiently from compact dependency descriptions.

title: BDD/FC conjecture
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: Finite controllability from bounded derivation would connect logical semantics with query reasoning over finite databases.
formal: Is every finite set \(R\) of existential tuple-generating dependencies with bounded derivation depth finitely controllable? Use the precise query-rewriting definition of bounded derivation depth below. The required conclusion is that for every finite database \(I\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), \[(I,R)\models q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I,R)\models_{\mathrm{fin}}q.\] The left side quantifies over all models extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\); the right side quantifies only over finite such models. The conjecture quantifies over every finite relational signature of arbitrary finite arities, and permits conjunctions of several atoms in rule heads.
definitions: A relational signature is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a fixed nonnegative integer arity. An atom has the form \(P(t_1,\ldots,t_a)\), with repeated arguments allowed. In rules and queries the arguments are variables; there are no function symbols, built-in equality or inequality, negation, or interpreted order. A rule is the sentence \(\forall\bar x\,\forall\bar y\,(B(\bar x,\bar y)\to\exists\bar z\,H(\bar y,\bar z))\), where \(B,H\) are finite nonempty conjunctions of atoms, each universal variable occurs in \(B\), and the only universal variables in \(H\) come from \(\bar y\). The tuples of universal and existential variables are disjoint. The existential tuple may be empty, so ordinary positive Datalog rules are included. A rule set is finite, and rule heads may contain several atoms. A database \(I\) is a finite set of relational facts on finitely many named distinct elements; its active domain is the set of elements appearing in these facts. Empty active domains and nullary facts are allowed. A model extending \(I\) has a nonempty domain containing its named elements and includes every fact of \(I\); it may add elements and facts, including new facts on old elements. It satisfies \(R\) with ordinary first-order semantics, and must preserve the identities of the named database elements. “Finite model” means a finite domain, with no prescribed cardinality bound. A conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)=\exists\bar v\,A(\bar u,\bar v)\) uses a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms, with every displayed free variable occurring in an atom. A Boolean query has no free variables. A union of conjunctive queries is a finite disjunction of such queries with the same free variables; the empty disjunction denotes false. Query evaluation on a database means a variable assignment into its active domain satisfying all required facts, and for a union means satisfaction of at least one disjunct. For an answer tuple \(\bar a\) from the active domain, \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) means that every model extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\) satisfies this instantiated query. Define \(R\) to have bounded derivation depth if for every conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)\) there is a finite union of conjunctive queries \(Q(\bar u)\) over the same signature such that, for every finite database \(I\) and every compatible answer tuple \(\bar a\), \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) if and only if \(I\models Q(\bar a)\). The rewriting \(Q\) may depend on \(R,q\) but not on the database or answer tuple. This is the source’s equivalent positive query-rewriting formulation of bounded derivation depth; it does not require one depth bound for all queries. Finite controllability is the displayed unrestricted-versus-finite equivalence for every \(I,q\). There is no syntactic guardedness, stickiness, binary-arity or single-head restriction on \(R\), and no time bound for constructing a rewriting or countermodel.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every finite signature and rule set, or refute it. A positive answer must show that whenever a Boolean conjunctive query fails in some possibly infinite model of \(I,R\), it also fails in some finite model of the same database and rules, assuming only the stated bounded derivation depth property. A negative answer must provide one finite signature and rule set \(R\), prove its rewriting property for every conjunctive query, and provide a finite database \(I\) and Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) such that every finite model of \(I,R\) satisfies \(q\) but some infinite model does not. Showing bounded behavior for a single query does not establish the premise on \(R\). A counterexample whose rules lack bounded derivation depth, or a theorem for binary single-head rules alone, does not settle this target.
context:
Amarilli’s source page states the implication using positive query rewriting and finite-model entailment. The named BDD/FC conjecture originates in Gogacz and Marcinkowski’s work, which supplies the formal definitions behind that summary.

Gogacz and Marcinkowski prove the implication for binary signatures under their convention that tuple-generating dependencies have single-atom heads. Their Section 5.3 explicitly discusses the multi-head issue. Thus the source page’s shorter “binary signature” summary must be read with the head restriction; arbitrary multi-head binary rules are not covered by that theorem.

Larroque, Ostropolski-Nalewaja and Thomazo’s 2025 paper uses general existential rules and records the equivalence between bounded derivation depth and UCQ rewritability as Proposition 4. Its introduction explicitly leaves the unrestricted BDD/FC conjecture open.

Their Theorem 1 establishes a structural implication about arbitrarily large directed cliques and a self-loop query for BDD rule sets. The authors expressly distinguish this partial result from the full finite-controllability conjecture. The March 2026 arXiv posting is a posting of this PODS 2025 work, not a newly claimed complete proof.
why: Bounded derivation depth permits queries under existential rules to be answered through finite positive rewritings on the original database. Finite controllability asks whether considering only finite possible worlds changes those answers. Connecting the two would clarify when this useful query-processing property also supports finite-model semantics, across arbitrary relational arities.
status_note: The general conjecture is explicitly open in the checked PODS 2025 paper, which was posted to arXiv in March 2026. Its structural theorem does not imply full finite controllability, and the original binary-signature theorem assumes single-head rules. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the review is not an exhaustive proof or literature certification.
progress: 2013: Gogacz and Marcinkowski pose the BDD/FC conjecture and establish their binary-signature, single-head result at PODS. The saved arXiv version was posted in August 2014. | 2025-05: Larroque, Ostropolski-Nalewaja and Thomazo publish a structural property of BDD rule sets in Proc. ACM Management of Data 3(2), article 101, for PODS 2025; the general conjecture remains open in their introduction. | 2026-03-10: The PODS 2025 paper is posted to arXiv. Its abstract describes the theorem as a step toward the conjecture, and its full introduction explicitly says it does not establish the conjecture.
working_summary: The BDD/FC conjecture asks whether every finite existential rule set with bounded derivation depth is finitely controllable. Bounded derivation depth is expressed by a finite positive rewriting for each conjunctive query that works on every database. Finite controllability means that a query failing in some unrestricted model also fails in a finite model. The question allows arbitrary finite relational arities and several atoms in a rule head. The known binary theorem requires single-head rules, and the checked PODS 2025 result posted in 2026 leaves the general conjecture open.

title: Uniform reliability of homomorphism-closed queries
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A decidability or tractability question for a specified logical or probabilistic database model.
formal: Is the following dichotomy true? For every finite relational signature \(\sigma\) of arbitrary fixed finite arities and every homomorphism-closed Boolean query \(Q\) on finite \(\sigma\)-instances, at least one of the following holds: (i) \(Q\) is equivalent on all finite instances to a finite union of conjunctive queries \(U\) for which exact tuple-independent probabilistic query evaluation \(\mathrm{PQE}(U)\) is computable in deterministic polynomial time; (ii) the function \(\mathrm{UR}_Q(I)=|\{J\subseteq I:Q(J)=1\}|\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. This is the semantic formulation below of the source's proposed safe-UCQ versus hardness dichotomy; it retains arbitrary homomorphism-closed \(Q\), not only queries expressed by a UCQ.
definitions: A signature is a finite set of relation symbols, each with a nonnegative integer arity; no function symbols, distinguished constants or built-in relations are supplied. An instance \(I\) is a finite set of facts \(R(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\), with \(r\) the arity of \(R\) and elements \(a_i\) drawn from \(\mathbb N\). Facts have set semantics, with no multiplicities. The active domain \(\operatorname{dom}(I)\) consists of elements occurring in its facts; for arity zero a fact has an empty tuple. Empty instances are allowed. A homomorphism \(h:I\to K\) is a function \(\operatorname{dom}(I)\to\operatorname{dom}(K)\) mapping every fact of \(I\) to a fact of \(K\) with the same relation symbol. The function \(Q\) is homomorphism-closed if \(Q(I)=1\) and \(h:I\to K\) imply \(Q(K)=1\). No finite syntactic representation, decidability or polynomial-time evaluation of \(Q\) is assumed. A subinstance \(J\subseteq I\) is an arbitrary subset of facts, with its own active domain; it is not an induced substructure. A finite Boolean UCQ can be specified by finitely many finite pattern instances \(A_1,\ldots,A_t\): it holds on \(I\) exactly when some \(A_i\) has a homomorphism to \(I\). The empty list expresses false, and an empty pattern expresses true. Repeated relation symbols are allowed. Equivalence means agreement on every finite instance. For a fixed query \(U\), \(\mathrm{PQE}(U)\) takes an instance \(I\) and a rational probability \(p_F\in[0,1]\) for each fact \(F\in I\), and returns the exact rational number \[\sum_{J\subseteq I,\ U(J)=1}\ \prod_{F\in J}p_F\prod_{F\in I\setminus J}(1-p_F).\] Facts are sampled independently. Probabilities are input as binary integer numerators and positive denominators; the output is a reduced binary numerator/denominator pair. For \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\), only \(I\) is input and the output is the exact count in binary. It equals \(2^{|I|}\) times the probability when every fact has probability exactly \(1/2\); there are no mandatory facts. Encode an instance by its list of distinct facts, with binary element names and fixed relation identifiers. Polynomial time refers to the total bit length on a deterministic Turing machine, including rational encodings for \(\mathrm{PQE}\); the fixed query, signature, algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on one another. No uniform procedure taking \(Q\) as an additional input is required. The class \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of functions counting accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machines. Turing hardness means that every such function can be computed by a deterministic polynomial-time oracle machine with access to exact values of \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) on encoded instances; polynomially many adaptive oracle calls are permitted. No membership of \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) in \(\#\mathrm P\) is asserted for arbitrary \(Q\).
answer_criterion: Give a mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated universal dichotomy, or a Lean-checked refutation: a finite signature \(\sigma\) and homomorphism-closed Boolean query \(Q\) for which there is no equivalent finite UCQ with polynomial-time exact \(\mathrm{PQE}\), and \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) is not \(\#\mathrm P\)-hard under the specified reductions. The target covers every fixed finite arity and permits queries of unrestricted evaluation complexity. A result only for maximum arity two, only for UCQs, or only for approximation does not settle the full statement. The alternatives are not required to be disjoint, and no assumption separating \(\mathrm{FP}\) from \(\#\mathrm P\) is imposed.
context:
The original question asks which fixed homomorphism-closed queries allow polynomial-time counting of satisfying subdatabases, and whether the remaining cases are hard. Its linked paper states the proposed boundary explicitly: queries equivalent to a safe finite UCQ are tractable, and all others should be #P-hard. The present card uses the equivalent semantic formulation through tractability of weighted PQE on finite UCQs; it does not require an algorithm deciding a query's side from a query description.

Dalvi and Suciu establish the dichotomy for arbitrary rational fact probabilities on finite UCQs. This supplies the known tractable boundary used in the semantic formulation. Restricting every fact to probability one half prevents simply importing all weighted hardness results.

For conjunctive queries without repeated relation symbols, uniform reliability is in polynomial time when every two variables occur in nested or disjoint sets of atoms, and is #P-complete otherwise. The full question also allows repeated symbols, finite unions and queries beyond finite UCQs.

The 2023 theorem proves hardness for every homomorphism-closed query on a signature of maximum arity two that is not equivalent to any finite UCQ. Its conclusion explicitly leaves arbitrary-arity unbounded queries and the general finite-UCQ case as the remaining parts of the conjecture. It allows even undecidable queries, which is why the full target asserts hardness rather than completeness in #P.

The 2024 Shapley-value paper distinguishes ordinary model counting from generalized counting, where some facts must be present. Its cited full graph-query dichotomy concerns that generalized model.

The 2025 work on probabilistic graphs studies approximation guarantees and does not provide an exact-counting resolution of the statement here.

It would connect finite logical descriptions and recursive query behavior to the complexity of counting possible databases, extending the established weighted-query theory to a basic unweighted model.

working_summary: Fix a Boolean query that remains true whenever its input database maps homomorphically to another database. Uniform reliability counts exactly how many subsets of an input database's facts satisfy that fixed query. Equivalently, each fact is retained independently with probability one half, and the resulting probability is rescaled to an integer count. Known results cover several query classes, including all unbounded queries of maximum arity two, while the full arbitrary-arity dichotomy remains unverified by this bounded review.

title: Cai–Fürer–Immerman definability in choiceless polynomial time
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A foundational benchmark for descriptive complexity and the expressive power of symmetry-preserving polynomial computation. Existing score retained.
formal: Is the parity query for Cai–Fürer–Immerman graphs over arbitrary connected unordered base graphs definable in Choiceless Polynomial Time with counting? In the source’s construction below, is there one CPT program \(P\) that, for every finite connected base graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every \(T\subseteq V\), accepts the unordered input graph \(G^{T}\) exactly when \(|T|\) is odd?
question_excerpt: However, there are some properties for which we do not know whether they can be expressed in CPT, and which might witness a separation from […]
definitions:
The base graph is finite, nonempty, simple and undirected. Write \(E(v)\) for the edges incident with \(v\). Use the vertex-parity construction of Section 3 of the primary source. For each base edge \(e\), introduce two distinct vertices \(e_{0},e_{1}\). For each base vertex \(v\), introduce a vertex \(v^{X}\) for every subset \(X\subseteq E(v)\) satisfying
\[|X|\equiv\mathbf1_{v\in T}\pmod2.\]
For each such \(v^{X}\) and each \(e\in E(v)\), join \(v^{X}\) to \(e_{1}\) if \(e\in X\), and to \(e_{0}\) otherwise. These are all the edges in this primary-source convention. Thus an even gadget uses even subsets, and an odd gadget uses odd subsets.

The constructed names describe the mathematical construction; they are not readable labels in the input. The program receives only an unordered graph isomorphic to \(G^{T}\), through its adjacency relation. It receives no order of base vertices, no designation of which edge-gadget vertex is 0 or 1, no set \(T\), and no list of the subsets \(X\). There is no auxiliary coloring, padding or supplied circuit. The source’s parity query distinguishes the two CFI types over each connected base graph. Inputs outside the promised CFI family need not be recognized.

The resource parameter is \(N=|V(G^{T})|\), the size of the explicit expanded input, not \(|V(G)|\). A high-degree base vertex can generate exponentially many gadget vertices. The program and its polynomial resource bound must work uniformly over all base graphs and all twists \(T\).

CPT here includes counting. Its data domain consists of the input vertices as indivisible atoms and hereditarily finite sets built from these atoms: finite sets whose members are atoms or further such finite sets, with finite nesting depth. The available constants include the empty set and the set of all atoms. Operations are unordered pairing \(\{x,y\}\), union, extracting the unique member of a singleton (returning the empty set otherwise), and cardinality. Cardinalities are encoded as von Neumann ordinals, where \(0=\varnothing\) and \(m+1=m\cup\{m\}\). Counting an atom returns the empty set.

Terms are built from variables, these constants and operations, and bounded set comprehensions
\[\{s(\bar x,y):y\in r(\bar x)\text{ and }\varphi(\bar x,y)\}.\]
Tests use equality, membership and input adjacency, combined by Boolean connectives. Comprehensions range over an already constructed finite set; there is no primitive that arbitrarily chooses a member of a non-singleton set or provides an order on the atoms.

A program is fixed finite syntax for a state-update term and two tests, for halting and acceptance. Beginning with empty state, it repeatedly applies the update and checks the tests. There is a fixed polynomial bound in \(N+1\) on the number of iterations and on the number of distinct objects in the transitive closures of the states. A transitive closure includes all recursively nested members, so a huge set cannot be hidden inside a small outer container. Exceeding a bound aborts and rejects. Equivalent standard encodings of the CPT formalism give the same definability question.

All permitted operations respect permutations of the input atoms that preserve adjacency. Numerical ordinals can be ordered, but this does not authorize an arbitrary order of graph vertices. The question permits unbounded finite nesting depth subject to the polynomial size bound; it is not limited to fixed-rank sets or tuples.
answer_criterion: Give one CPT program with counting and prove its polynomial resource bound and correct parity decision on every promised unordered CFI input, or prove no such program exists. A negative result for a restricted family of CPT programs, or failure to construct a particular auxiliary order, does not establish nondefinability in full CPT.
context:
The source presents the parity query as a polynomial-time problem whose status in full choiceless computation is unknown. Merely giving an ordinary algorithm that uses arbitrary vertex choices would not answer the definability question.

The primary paper gives CPT procedures when the base graph has a supplied preorder with logarithmically sized color classes, and when its maximum degree is linear in its size. In the latter case the expanded CFI graph is exponentially larger than the base graph. Neither theorem covers arbitrary unordered bounded-degree bases.

The primary paper proves limitations for computation without set-like objects. Pago’s CSL 2021 paper shows that sufficiently fine preorders cannot be constructed on all hypercubes; this blocks a particular strategy rather than deciding the parity query’s expressibility. The 2023 XOR-circuit result imposes additional conditions on CPT programs and explicitly retains a gap in its circuit lower-bound argument.

The 2025 paper connects CPT with symmetric algebraic proofs and gives polynomial-size symmetric IPS proofs for CFI-related equations. An existence or simulation theorem for those proofs does not supply a uniform CPT parity algorithm. The paper continues to treat full CPT with counting as a candidate for capturing polynomial time.
why: CFI parity is a central test of whether computation that preserves all input symmetries can match ordinary polynomial time. A negative answer would separate CPT with counting from polynomial time; a positive answer would remove an important candidate obstruction without by itself proving that CPT captures every polynomial-time property.
status_note: Read the full primary CPT definition and exact CFI construction, the later hypercube nondefinability statement and restricted XOR-circuit theorem, and the 2025 symmetric-IPS model comparison. Searched through 12 September 2026 without finding a full resolution. The 2024 arXiv hypercube upload is a copy of a 2021 conference paper. The original 1999 separation for a version without counting is not a separation for this counting model. The 2023 paper’s extra edge-gadget pairing is not silently inserted into the primary-source construction.
progress: 2016: The source extends positive results to additional base-graph classes and retains the arbitrary unordered case. | 2021: A lower bound for constructing fine preorders on hypercubes limits one known approach. | 2023: Symmetric XOR-circuits provide partial lower-bound connections, with additional hypotheses and a remaining gap. | 2025: Symmetric algebraic proof results further connect these models without settling full CPT parity definability.
working_summary: CFI graphs hide an even-or-odd parity in symmetric gadgets built over a base graph. The input provides adjacency but no arbitrary order or labels revealing the hidden parity. The question asks for one choiceless polynomial-time program with counting that recovers parity for every base graph. The model may construct nested sets, but its total resources are polynomial in the expanded input size. Known positive cases and restricted lower bounds do not settle the full unordered question.

title: \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) conjecture
importance_reason: Would provide a universally informative comparison for sorting with partial-order information; retained as a computationally motivated combinatorial exception.
focus_reason: Would provide a universally informative comparison for sorting with partial-order information; retained as a computationally motivated combinatorial exception.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every partial order \(\mathrm{P}=([n],\le _{\mathrm{P}})\) that is not a total order, do there exist incomparable elements \(x,y\in [n]\) such that \(e(\mathrm{P})/3\le e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y)\le 2e(\mathrm{P})/3\)?
definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite non-total partial order has an incomparable pair with \(e(P)/3\le e_P(x,y)\le2e(P)/3\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair violates that closed interval. All extension counts and probabilities must use the full set of linear extensions defined here.
context:
A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.
why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Aires–Kahn state the general conjecture separately from their large-width theorems; Gupta reports a finite census through fourteen elements. No unrestricted resolution was located in the bounded later-work check. Census computations and source proofs were not rerun independently.
progress: 1995: Brightwell–Felsner–Trotter establish the general balance bound \((5- \sqrt{5})/10\). | 2023 onward: Chan–Pak survey distinguishes the open universal conjecture from established structural cases. | 2025: Aires–Kahn prove stronger balance under width and other size hypotheses. | 2026-07: Gupta reports exhaustive verification of Gold Partition through fourteen elements, implying the target in that finite range.
working_summary: A partial order records known comparisons, and its linear extensions are all compatible complete rankings. The conjecture asks whether every finite non-total order has an incomparable pair that appears in either relative order in at least one third of all extensions. The extensions are weighted uniformly, and both endpoints of the interval are allowed. A three-element order with only one comparison shows that the constant one third cannot be improved universally. A resolution would identify the sharp balance guarantee for a comparison in sorting with partial information.

title: Seese’s conjecture
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.
focus_reason: Seese directly connects decidability of monadic second-order satisfiability with bounded clique-width; retain this major computability/structure boundary question as a cross-disciplinary exception.
formal:
For every isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, does
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\ \text{decidable}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists k\ge1\ \forall G\in\mathcal C,\quad\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k
\]
hold?

The language \(\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\) contains exactly the encoded vertex-set monadic second-order sentences satisfied by at least one graph in \(\mathcal C\). The bound \(k\) may depend on the whole class but must hold for every graph in it.
question_excerpt: The inherited paper states that Seese’s conjecture says the MSO theory of every graph class of unbounded clique-width is undecidable. It places this as a consequence of its stronger Conjecture 40. The card retains Seese’s original plain-MSO implication, equivalently phrased using satisfiability.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, multiple edges, labels or additional relations in the logical vocabulary. The empty graph is allowed. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) contains only such graphs and is closed under isomorphism: renaming vertices does not change membership. It may be empty, finite or infinite, and no hereditary, degree, minor or forbidden-subgraph restriction is imposed. Equivalently, classes can be viewed as arbitrary collections of finite graph isomorphism types.

The logic \(\mathrm{MSO}_1\) has individual variables \(x,y,\ldots\) and vertex-set variables \(X,Y,\ldots\). Its atomic formulas are \(x=y\), \(E(x,y)\) and \(x\in X\). Formulas are finite expressions built from these atoms using Boolean connectives and existential or universal quantification over either sort. Set equality, when used, is shorthand for equality of membership at every vertex. A sentence has no free variables. On a finite graph, individual quantifiers range over \(V\) and set quantifiers over all subsets of \(V\), with the ordinary truth conditions. There is no vertex order, arithmetic relation, edge-set quantifier, cardinality predicate or modular counting extension.

Fix an effective, uniquely parsed finite-string encoding of this syntax, with binary variable indices and symbols for the finitely many logical operations. Define
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)
=\{\operatorname{enc}(\varphi):
\varphi\text{ is an }\mathrm{MSO}_1\text{ sentence and }
\exists G\in\mathcal C\ (G\models\varphi)\}.
\]
Decidable means that some deterministic Turing machine halts on every string, rejects malformed encodings and answers membership in this language correctly. That machine may depend on \(\mathcal C\); its only input is the sentence encoding. The class is not supplied as another input or as an oracle, and no running-time bound is imposed. No effective presentation of the class is assumed separately from this decidability premise. By negation of sentences, the premise is equivalent to decidability of the theory consisting of sentences true in every graph of \(\mathcal C\). It is not the model-checking problem in which a particular finite graph is also supplied.

For a positive integer \(k\), a \(k\)-expression is a finite term constructing a graph with temporary vertex labels in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its permitted operations are creation of a single vertex with any one label; disjoint union of two previously constructed labelled graphs; relabelling every vertex with label \(i\) to label \(j\); and, for distinct labels \(i,j\), adding every missing edge between a vertex labelled \(i\) and a vertex labelled \(j\). Vertices and existing edges are never deleted. Repeated edge additions have no further effect. The labels are forgotten in the final graph and are not extra relations available to the logic.

For a nonempty graph \(G\), the clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the minimum positive \(k\) for which a \(k\)-expression yields a graph isomorphic to \(G\). Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing)=0\). Every finite graph has finite clique-width, but bounded clique-width of a class requires a single \(k\) independent of its members and their orders. For the empty class the conclusion is vacuous.

The quantifier order is: for every class, if some class-specific sentence decider exists, then some class-specific finite width bound exists. The proposition does not demand one decider for all classes, a method to extract \(k\) from machine code, or an algorithm producing clique-width expressions. It is an exact universal implication, not a request for a numerical estimate of a width.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every stated graph class. Alternatively, specify one isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\), a total sentence-deciding machine, and complete Lean-checked proofs of its correctness and of
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists G\in\mathcal C,\qquad\operatorname{cw}(G)>k.
\]
A single finite graph cannot refute a class-wide boundedness claim. Decidability for a restricted set of sentences, model checking on a given graph, a theorem with parity or edge-set quantification in the premise, or a result for only specially restricted graph classes does not establish the full target.
context:
A finite graph can be checked against any one MSO sentence by exhaustive evaluation. The difficult premise here concerns a whole class: the algorithm must decide whether any member, of any size, satisfies the input sentence.

Clique-width measures how many temporary vertex labels suffice to build a graph with repeated disjoint unions, complete joins between labels and relabellings. The conjectured bound concerns every member of a class together; individual finiteness of clique-width is automatic.

Courcelle and Oum prove the implication when the language additionally tests whether a vertex set has even cardinality. Deciding that larger language is a stronger premise than deciding ordinary MSO, so the theorem does not prove the card’s assertion.

The inherited ICALP paper concerns shrub-depth and expressiveness and ends with a stronger conjecture about MSO dependence. Its discussion explicitly presents Seese’s conjecture as an unresolved consequence, rather than a theorem established in that paper.

Dawar and Sankaran establish results for specified hereditary families and analyze a stronger grid-interpretation conjecture. Their title does not mean that all hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width have already been covered.

The July 2026 theorem gives bounded clique-width for hereditary classes that are 2-WQO: after arbitrary two-colour vertex labellings, every infinite sequence contains an earlier graph embedded as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. That hypothesis is different from a decision procedure for the plain MSO theory.
why: The conjecture asks whether decidability of an expressive graph language forces a uniform structural restriction. It connects computability of theories to finite graph construction with a bounded number of labels, without assuming an efficient decision procedure or a restricted graph class.
status_note: The checked literature retains the plain-MSO Seese implication as open. The inherited 2025 source conjectures a stronger characterization, the classical proved variant adds a parity predicate, and the July 2026 theorem assumes hereditary 2-WQO. No resolution of the stated implication was found in the bounded later-work search.
progress: 1991: Seese formulates the decidability question, as recalled in Courcelle–Oum §5.4. | 2006–2007: The parity-extended satisfiability premise is proved to force bounded clique-width. | 2023–2025: Work on hereditary classes supplies partial results and a decomposition of the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture. | 2025-06-30: The inherited ICALP source states a stronger open conjecture and explicitly identifies its implication for Seese. | 2026-07-26: The revised hereditary 2-WQO paper proves bounded clique-width under a distinct labelled-ordering hypothesis.
working_summary: Seese’s conjecture concerns arbitrary classes of finite simple undirected graphs. Its premise is an algorithm deciding whether some graph in the class satisfies any input monadic second-order sentence over vertices and vertex sets. Its conclusion is one finite clique-width bound holding for all graphs in that class. The algorithm and bound may depend on the class, and parity predicates or edge-set quantifiers are excluded from the premise. A complete Lean-checked solution must prove the universal implication or verify a class with decidable satisfiability and unbounded clique-width.

title: Extremal size of sunflower-free set families
importance_reason: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
formal: For each fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), determine, up to constant factors as \(k\to \infty , S_{r}(k)\): the largest number of distinct k-element sets in a family containing no r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, where the finite ground set is unrestricted.
definitions: The r members in a sunflower must be distinct. Their common pairwise intersection is the core, and deleting it leaves pairwise disjoint petals. For each integer \(k\ge 1\), take the maximum cardinality over all sunflower-free families on arbitrary finite universes. The classical sunflower bound makes these cardinalities bounded by an integer depending only on k,r, so the maximum exists despite the unrestricted universe. No algorithm or encoding bound is imposed. The parameter r is fixed before k grows; asymptotic constants may depend on r.
answer_criterion: Give functions \(f_{r}(k)\) and, for every fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), constants \(0<c_{r}\le C_{r}<\infty\) with \(c_{r} f_{r}(k)\le S_{r}(k)\le C_{r} f_{r}(k)\) for every \(k\ge 1\), absorbing finitely many small k into the constants if needed. Prove both a universal upper bound and existence of matching sunflower-free families in Lean. An exponential upper bound by itself does not determine the growth within constant factors.
context:
The target is the extremal function itself. The sunflower conjecture states that \(S_{r}(k)\) has at most exponential growth in k for each fixed r, a weaker qualitative question than matching its full asymptotic order.

Sunflowers capture a simple repeated pattern inside a large family of small sets. Bounds on their forced occurrence are basic tools in circuit complexity, pseudorandomness and kernelization.

The breakthrough bound of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang replaces a much larger dependence by roughly \((\log  k)^{O(k)}\) for fixed r. The conjecture asks for a constant base to the k-th power. This is admitted as a computationally motivated exception to the exclusion of general combinatorics, not to fill a combinatorics category.
why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2020: The source proves substantially improved bounds while leaving \(C_{r}^{k}\) open.
working_summary: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets with one common pairwise intersection. For fixed r, the target is the maximum size of a family of k-element sets containing no r-member sunflower. Determine its growth as k increases within constant factors that may depend on r. The ground set is any finite universe and the question imposes no algorithmic restrictions. The sunflower conjecture predicts at most exponential growth, a weaker claim than determining the full extremal order.
